It was "available" for a secular political project: the movement needed a Jewish symbol, but one that did not tie its politics to rabbinic authority, and the star fit where the Temple's lampstand would not have. [cite:scholem_star_david] The more cautious reading starts from the movement's make-up. By the 1890s the Magen David had become the closest thing to a widely recognized, non-sectarian Jewish emblem, and the Zionist movement drew members from many religious and secular backgrounds. Unlike ritual objects tied closely to synagogue practice, the star worked as a legible, adaptable political sign. On this reading, practical legibility, more than any documented theological reasoning, is what the record actually supports as the reason for its selection. Both readings agree on the outcome: a symbol with modern movement associations, rather than one anchored to the Temple cult, became the movement's flag.

The state was declared on 14 May 1948. [cite:declaration_israel_1948] In the weeks that followed, the Provisional Council of State had to adopt a flag as a matter of administrative necessity. The Basel banner, by then fifty-one years old and already the recognized symbol of the Zionist movement worldwide, was the obvious default. The flag was formally confirmed on 28 October 1948. [cite:wiki_flag_of_israel]

That outcome was not reached without argument, and the argument is the most revealing part of the record. Before simply taking over the movement's flag, the Provisional Council tried to create a distinct state flag. Its stated reason was a concern about Jews abroad: Diaspora communities already flew the Zionist flag at their own events, and officials worried that once the same banner became a foreign state's official flag, those communities would face accusations of dual loyalty. A government-preferred alternative, a seven-stars design by Otto Wassisch, was considered and rejected. In July 1948 the Foreign Minister, Moshe Sharett, cabled Jewish leaders across the Diaspora to ask their view. The answer came back overwhelmingly in favor of keeping the existing Zionist flag rather than adopting a new one. [cite:crwflags_israel_flag_1948] [cite:wjc_flag_unveiled_1948] So the flag was the low-friction choice in one sense, because it required no new design. In another sense it was a considered one: the objection was raised by the decision-makers themselves, an alternative was tested, and the people the objection was meant to protect were asked, and chose continuity.

The menorah did not disappear. It became the state's emblem, placed on the state seal by the Provisional Council of State in 1949, a year after the flag decision. [cite:wiki_menorah] That process was longer and more contested than the flag's. The selection committee rejected outright a first round of 450 proposals from 164 applicants. A second public competition followed. The winning design, by the Shamir brothers, was sent back for revision twice: once to add the word "Israel," and once to replace their own modern rendering of the menorah with the specific historical version carved on the Arch of Titus. [cite:nli_emblem_israel_blog] The emblem was made, in the end, to copy the lampstand as Rome had recorded it in 81 CE.

Nearly 1,300 years separate the menorah's oldest surviving image and the star's first documented Jewish use, and the newer symbol took the flag. None of this makes either symbol less real. Both are genuine Jewish symbols with genuine histories, and a symbol can become deeply meaningful regardless of its age. Nor was anything hidden: the Zionist movement never concealed that the state flag was its own 1897 banner, and the flag's history is public and uncontested. What the record settles is narrower. The common claim that the star is the ancient symbol, on the flag as it always was, overstates its age. The flag's lineage runs through a nineteenth-century political movement, not through the Temple period.

An interpretation, not a finding. What follows is a reading of the documented sequence above, and it should be weighed as one. One reading holds that the choice encodes the state's sense of its own origin. A state that understood itself as continuing a religious tradition might have led with that tradition's oldest symbol. This one put the political movement's 1897 emblem on its flag, the face it shows the world, and placed the Temple's lampstand on its seal, the stamp of administration. On this reading the flag signals that the state understands itself to continue the political project of Herzl and the Basel Congress, rather than the ancient Temple cult, which is consistent with a founding that was political, secular and modern. [cite:basel_program] An analogy sometimes used is a company with a founding logo and a later campaign design: the newer design can be entirely legitimate, but calling it "the company's timeless symbol" would be inaccurate.

The same reading goes a step further. Displayed in synagogues, schools and community centers, a flag that joins the movement's emblem to Jewish religious life may reinforce, through repetition rather than argument, the idea that the political project of 1897 and a religious tradition of millennia are one thing. That is the distinction between Zionism and Judaism examined in [scene:s00c|the next chapter's section on the movement and the religion], made here through an image instead of a claim. It is a plausible mechanism, not a measured effect. Most people who display the flag do so out of a real connection to Israel or to Jewish identity, not as part of any messaging effort, and this reading assumes nothing about any individual's intent. Many Israelis and Jews abroad experience the flag as holding both the political founding and the older tradition at once, which is an equally defensible way to read it. And the 1948 record itself cuts both ways: the very worry about conflation that this reading describes was raised by the state's own founders, who tested an alternative, consulted the communities most affected, and kept the movement's flag at their request.

What the documents do not settle is motive. They show which symbol is older, which one the movement chose, and the dated sequence by which the state confirmed it. They do not show that the choice was made to diminish the menorah or the Temple tradition. Scholem's argument about the star's secular availability and the narrower argument from practical legibility both remain on the table, and the record available here does not decide between them.

sections.h: The Word as a Shield
sections.html:
The starting point should be stated plainly. Hatred of Jewish people is antisemitism, and nothing in this book says otherwise. A question about what a government does is a question about a government, whether the government is Canada's, Mexico's or Israel's. The difficulty is that a widely repeated claim, that questioning Israel is itself antisemitic, merges these two things. The meaning of the word has not changed: antisemitism means hatred of Jews. What has changed is where the charge is aimed, and what it now costs the person it is aimed at. This section sets out the definitions in competition, the definition's own drafter's warning, the path by which a guideline became law, and what is also true on the other side: antisemitism is real, and in the United States it stands at a record level.

The most widely cited definition is the working definition of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), adopted in 2016. Beyond its core sentence, it attaches eleven examples, and seven of them concern Israel. [cite:reformjudaism_five_definitions] [cite:peacenow_ihra_faq] Among them are "denying the Jewish people their right to self-determination, e.g., by claiming that the existence of a State of Israel is a racist endeavor," applying double standards to Israel, and comparing Israeli policy to that of the Nazis. The first of these is listed as a potential example of antisemitism. [cite:reformjudaism_five_definitions] The definition was adopted by the United States government and, as of August 2024, by 35 states and the District of Columbia. [cite:peacenow_ihra_faq]

The definition also contains a safeguard that is rarely quoted. Its own text says that criticism of Israel similar to that leveled against any other country cannot be regarded as antisemitic. [cite:ihra_text_safeguard] That is the standard the definition sets for itself: the questions a person may ask of Canada or Mexico may be asked of Israel. What is disputed is the territory the attached examples cover, the point at which criticism of Israel crosses into hostility to Jews. The history of how the word came to be pointed at that territory is told in [scene:s00b|the section on "Semitic"].

The strongest case for IHRA, in its supporters' terms, runs as follows. Some hostility to Jews does express itself through talk about Israel: holding Jews collectively responsible for a state, singling Israel out by standards applied to no other country, or comparing Jews to their Nazi persecutors. A definition that ignored those forms would miss antisemitism where it actually appears. The examples are framed as potential cases, judged against a text that explicitly protects ordinary criticism. [cite:ihra_text_safeguard] The definition was written, according to its lead drafter, to help governments collect data on antisemitism, which requires a common yardstick. [cite:stern_guardian_2019] And on this view the main alternative goes too far the other way: Britain's Community Security Trust argues that the Jerusalem Declaration legitimizes calls for Israel's elimination. [cite:cst_jda_critique]

That alternative, the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism, was presented in March 2021 by scholars working with the Van Leer Jerusalem Institute and signed by more than 200 scholars of Jewish history and the Holocaust. [cite:jwa_jda] Its signatories and drafters are specialists in antisemitism, in Holocaust and genocide studies, and in Jewish history. By its own framing they are not activists opposed to fighting antisemitism, but scholars who judged that IHRA's examples conflate two distinct things: hatred of Jews, and disagreement with a state's policies or the ideology behind it. [cite:jda_text] Its definition of antisemitism, discrimination, prejudice, hostility or violence against Jews as Jews, or against Jewish institutions as Jewish, is close in spirit to IHRA's core sentence. [cite:jda_text] The divergence lies entirely in the guidelines that follow. Guideline 5 states that opposing Zionism as a form of nationalism, or arguing for constitutional arrangements other than a Jewish-majority state for everyone between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean (a binational state, a unitary democratic state, a federal state or a confederation), is not, on the face of it, antisemitic. [cite:jda_text] The Declaration treats Zionism as one variety of national ideology, and holds that criticizing or opposing it does not on its own constitute antisemitism. But it also lists examples of speech about Israel that are antisemitic. [cite:jwa_jda]

The Declaration has its own critics, who argue that it understates the antisemitism present in some anti-Zionist discourse. Further named critics are set out in the section on "Semitic." Between the two documents sits a third, the Nexus Document, produced by a task force linked to the University of Southern California and Bard College, which takes an intermediate position. [cite:thirdnarrative_three_defs] The question "is anti-Zionism antisemitism?" therefore has no single answer, because the three definitions give three different answers. Each is held by credentialed people, in print.

The sharpest criticism of how IHRA is used comes from the man who led its drafting. Kenneth Stern was the American Jewish Committee's expert on antisemitism and the definition's lead drafter. He has testified that it "was not drafted, and was never intended, as a tool to target or chill speech on a college campus"; it was written to help governments collect data. [cite:politifact_aaa_2024] In December 2019 he published an op-ed in the Guardian under the headline "I drafted the definition of antisemitism. Rightwing Jews are weaponizing it," calling the executive order that applied the definition to campuses an attack on academic freedom that would harm pro-Palestinian advocates and Jewish students alike. [cite:stern_guardian_2019] In 2024 he told NPR that weaponizing the definition makes students less safe. [cite:npr_stern_2024] Americans for Peace Now makes a parallel argument: that IHRA chills speech by treating anti-Zionist views as antisemitic. [cite:peacenow_ihra_faq]

The executive order Stern objected to marked the definition's move from guideline into law. In December 2019 it directed federal agencies, including the Education Department's civil rights office, to consider the definition when enforcing Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. [cite:politifact_aaa_2024] By August 2024, 35 states and the District of Columbia had adopted the definition in some form. On 1 May 2024 the House of Representatives passed the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which would write the definition into federal civil rights enforcement, by 320 votes to 91, with members of both parties voting no. The American Civil Liberties Union urged a no vote, warning that the bill would likely chill student speech by wrongly equating criticism of the Israeli government with antisemitism. [cite:politifact_aaa_2024] Status as of October 2026: the bill is not law, and its Senate version, S.558, stalled in committee in 2025. [cite:legiscan_s558]

The same logic reached private platforms. In July 2024, after an advocacy campaign, Meta began treating the word "Zionist" as a stand-in for Jews in narrowly defined hate-speech cases. The policy does not cite IHRA by name. The argument against it is that the mechanism it applies, treating the name of a political ideology as a proxy for a protected ethnic or religious identity, is exactly the conflation the Jerusalem Declaration had been written three years earlier to name and reject. The stated objective of Cotler-Wunsh, one of those who pressed for the change, was protected-characteristic status for Zionism: the precise claim the Declaration's Guideline 5 runs against. [cite:jda_text] Whatever one concludes about the policy, a platform that adopted one side of a live dispute among credentialed scholars was not simply following expert consensus, because no consensus existed. The full record of the Meta decision, including who pressed for it and who objected, is in [scene:s00a2|the section on the platforms].

A label works by raising the price of a question, and the price has been documented. In 2025 Columbia University lost $400 million in federal funding within four days of a notice from a federal task force, and about 60 more universities received warning letters. Five days after that notice Mahmoud Khalil, a recent Columbia graduate who had negotiated on behalf of the campus protesters, was detained for deportation. Each case has its own record, and that record includes real failures at Columbia: federal investigators found that the university had no reporting system until the summer of 2024, and that swastika vandalism had gone uninvestigated. Taken together, the cases show why many people choose not to ask.

This is the chilling effect that the ACLU and the definition's own drafter warned about. [cite:politifact_aaa_2024] [cite:stern_guardian_2019] Being called antisemitic is a serious charge because antisemitism is a serious hatred, and that seriousness is exactly what gives the label its force when it is aimed at a question about a government. The person asking risks a job, a place at a university, a visa or an online account. Many stop asking, and the version of events they learned in school goes unexamined. The effect is documented as an institutional one, working through rules and penalties. The record does not measure what happens in any individual's mind, and this book makes no claim about that.

What is also true is that antisemitism is real and rising. The Anti-Defamation League counted 9,354 antisemitic incidents in the United States in 2024, the most since it began counting in 1979, with incidents on campuses up 84 percent. [cite:algemeiner_adl_2024] Some speech that calls itself anti-Zionist does cross into hatred of Jews, and even the Jerusalem Declaration, written to defend criticism of Israel, lists examples of it. [cite:jwa_jda] The long history of that hatred, older than the word itself, is told in [scene:ch01_hatred|the section on the hatred]. At the same time, many of the strongest critics of Israeli policy are themselves Jewish. Misusing the charge and ignoring real antisemitism both do damage, to Jews and to everyone asking honest questions.

A common test case is the slogan "Free Palestine," which is often described in public comment as simply code for antisemitism. That claim is an opinion, not a fact about the phrase, and the record of who uses the slogan contradicts it. Jewish organizations such as Jewish Voice for Peace campaign for Palestinian rights; [cite:w_jvp] Orthodox anti-Zionist traditions predate the state; and Israeli human-rights groups such as B'Tselem document the occupation. Some people who use the slogan do express antisemitism, and that is documented too; many do not. The record supports judging speech by its content, not by its slogan.

That leads to the test. Two questions sort almost every case. The first: is the speech aimed at Jewish people, or at what a government does? The second is the definition's own standard: would the criticism be fair if it were aimed at any other country? [cite:ihra_text_safeguard] If it concerns a government's actions, and the same would be said of Canada or Mexico, it is a political question, and asking it is not hatred. If it concerns Jews as a people, holds them responsible for a state, or recycles old tropes, it is antisemitism, whatever it calls itself.

Several things remain unsettled. The record does not decide which of the three definitions is correct; that is a live dispute among credentialed scholars, and the answer to "is anti-Zionism antisemitic?" depends on which one is adopted. It does not measure how many people have stayed silent, or why. Whether the Antisemitism Awareness Act, or a successor, will become law is open as of October 2026. And the sources used here do not record how Mahmoud Khalil's case was resolved.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: Peoples and Traditions
chapters.intro:
The two peoples at the center of this history are not uniform blocs, and the land has never held only two. This chapter describes the communities themselves before the political story begins: their lineages, a long shared history in the Muslim world, the minorities who fit neither side of the usual shorthand, the difference between a religion and a political movement, and the arguments each tradition has had with itself. It comes here because the history that follows is full of statements about "the Jews," "the Arabs" or "the Christians," and the record speaks instead of named institutions, movements and individuals.

It begins with the Jewish lineages, Mizrahi, Sephardi and Ashkenazi, and the genetic record: a 2010 study that compared 14 Jewish communities with 69 other populations, the 2013 test of the Khazar claim, and the recognition of Ethiopia's Beta Israel in 1973 and 1975.[cite:behar_2010_nature] [cite:behar_2013_khazar] [cite:w_ethiopian_jews_israel] A map follows of some two dozen communities, then a grid that sorts them twice, by ancestry and by language, to show why "Semitic" names languages and not lineages.[cite:an_behar2010_pubmed] A section on coexistence runs from the Babylonian exile of 586 BCE through al-Andalus and the expulsion from Spain in 1492 to the Ottoman millet, weighing the "golden age" and "persecution" readings against each other.[cite:huc_farhud] [cite:stillman_jews_arab_lands] The land's other communities follow: the Druze, the Negev Bedouin, the Circassians, the Samaritans and Palestinian Christians. Then comes the distinction between Judaism and Zionism, a movement founded at Basel in August 1897, with the Jewish positions set against it, from Reform's Pittsburgh Platform of 1885 to Satmar's VaYoel Moshe of 1958.[cite:basel_program] [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] [cite:wiki_satmar] A section on dissent shows that opposition to Zionism, and critique of the state, came from every Jewish lineage, and sets a 2025 poll of American Jews beside it.[cite:wapo_jews_poll] The chapter ends with Christians and one verse, Genesis 12:3, read in opposite ways, and with the Vatican, which withheld recognition of Israel until 1993.[cite:wiki_fundamental_agreement]

The strongest case for each position is given in its own terms. What the chapter shows throughout is how much variety the collective words conceal.

sections.h: The Jewish Lineages: Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi
sections.html:
No one seriously disputes that Ashkenazi Jews are Jewish. What is disputed, often loudly and usually online, is where they come from. Two opposite errors circulate. The first holds that Ashkenazi Jews descend from Central Asian Khazar converts and carry no real Middle Eastern ancestry, and therefore no ancestral connection to the land. The second, less often stated but just as often assumed, treats all Jewish communities as genetically and historically identical, as if two thousand years spent in different countries had left no trace. The genetic record supports neither. What it shows is a set of distinct communities, each with its own documented history, sharing a detectable common origin and each carrying the marks of the places where it lived.

The word "Semitic" already names a family larger than any one people. The genealogy of Genesis 10, 11 and 25 runs from Shem through many generations to Abraham, and then divides: Ishmael, traditionally associated with Arab peoples, and, through Isaac, both Esau, traditionally associated with Edom, and Jacob, later renamed Israel.[cite:genesis_10_11_bible] [cite:genesis_25_esau_ishmael] By the text's own family tree, Jacob's line is one branch of Shem's descendants, not the whole of it, a point taken up with the history of the word itself in [scene:s00b|the section on "Semitic"]. The text establishes scope, not rank: it presents all three lines as branches of the same root. The same structure, a shared category holding real internal variety, applies to the Jewish communities themselves.

Three broad lineages make up most of world Jewry. Mizrahi Jews, the Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Egypt, Iran, Syria and elsewhere, never left the Middle East. Their presence there goes back millennia; in Iraq it is traced to the Babylonian Exile of 586 BCE, and as late as 1945 Baghdad alone held roughly 140,000 Jews, about a third of the city. The Jews of Iran, one of the oldest of these communities, are treated in their own chapter of this library, [scene:ira_src_s16|the Jews of Iran]. Sephardi Jews trace to Iberia, Spain and Portugal, where their roots predate the Muslim conquest. Ferdinand and Isabella expelled them in 1492, and most resettled across the Ottoman Empire and North Africa, regions that already held related Middle Eastern Jewish populations; Salonika became a majority-Sephardic city for centuries under Ottoman rule. Ashkenazi communities formed in the Rhineland, in Central Europe, in the early medieval period, and later moved east into Poland, Lithuania, Russia and Ukraine. By the nineteenth century Ashkenazi Jews were the demographic majority of world Jewry, and they produced most of the Jewish immigration to the United States.

These are histories, documented in the ordinary way. The question of what each community carries in its genes is a separate one, and it was answered most thoroughly by a study published in Nature in 2010. Behar, Yunusbayev, Metspalu and eighteen co-authors compared genome-wide data from 14 Jewish communities spanning Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia against 69 non-Jewish populations.[cite:behar_2010_nature] This was a large genome-wide analysis, not a study of a single marker or a handful of anecdotes. Its core finding was that most of the Jewish populations examined, Ashkenazi, Sephardi and North African among them, cluster together genetically and share their closest non-Jewish relationships with Middle Eastern populations, more so than with the European or other populations among whom they lived. The authors' own framing was that the data support common origins in the Middle East, followed by migrations into the diaspora.[cite:behar_2010_nature]

The same study found real structure inside that shared origin. The Jewish samples divided into three groups: an Ashkenazi, North African and Sephardi cluster; a Caucasus and Middle Eastern cluster; and a distinct Yemenite cluster.[cite:behar_2010_nature] The result is therefore not that every Jewish community is genetically identical. It is that every community examined carries a detectable shared ancestral signal, with real regional differences layered on top. The study does not by itself settle the size or the timing of particular episodes of admixture, and genetic work of this kind is continually refined by newer data. It is cited here because it remains the most comprehensive genome-wide study of its kind and because its core finding has held up under later attempts to replicate it, not because any single study is beyond revision.

The Khazar hypothesis is a different claim, and it deserves to be stated precisely before it is tested. The Khazars were a Turkic people of the Caucasus and southern Russia whose ruling elite, according to the historical record, converted to Judaism around the eighth or ninth century CE. As a fact about one medieval kingdom's ruling class, that conversion is a real and separately documented event. The hypothesis takes it much further: it proposes that the Ashkenazi population as a whole descends substantially from the Khazars rather than from the ancient Levant. In its modern scientific form the claim was argued in a 2012 paper by the geneticist Eran Elhaik in Genome Biology and Evolution, which proposed a Khazar component in European Jewish ancestry.[cite:adl_khazar] [cite:aap_khazar_factcheck] Critics faulted the paper for its method: Elhaik used modern Armenians and Georgians as proxies for the Khazars.[cite:aap_khazar_factcheck]

The test came in 2013. Behar and colleagues, more than twenty co-authors in all, published a study in Human Biology that analyzed 1,774 samples from 106 Jewish and non-Jewish populations, including populations native to the region of the former Khazar Khaganate.[cite:nli_behar_khazar] [cite:behar_2013_khazar] They found no particular similarity between Ashkenazi Jews and the populations of the Caucasus, and in their own words "no indication" of a Khazar genetic contribution. Ashkenazi ancestry, they concluded, derives primarily from the Middle East and Europe.[cite:behar_2013_khazar] [cite:aap_khazar_factcheck] Genome-wide and ancient-DNA studies since then have modeled Ashkenazi Jews as a mixture of Levantine and European ancestry. How large each share is remains open; one researcher, cited in a published fact-check, puts the Middle Eastern share at between 15 and 50 percent.[cite:nli_behar_khazar] [cite:aap_khazar_factcheck]

What is European in Ashkenazi ancestry is real, documented and partial. The European contribution is substantial, and it shows most clearly on the maternal line, reflecting some two thousand years of intermarriage and conversion within European societies. The same studies document a shared ancient Levantine origin on the paternal line, and the two findings sit side by side: the European layer is part of the history, not a replacement for the older one. There is no contradiction between them, only a contradiction between the data and either of the two errors with which this section began.

The Khazar theory is addressed directly here because of what it has been used to do. Since the nineteenth century it has served antisemitic arguments that portray Jews as alien impostors with no genuine connection to the Land of Israel, and so as not "really" Jewish or Semitic at all.[cite:jewishpress_khazar] [cite:aap_khazar_factcheck] Viral claims built on it continue to appear and continue to fail. One widely shared post asserted that a study had proved 97.5 percent of Israeli Jews have no ties to the land; fact-checkers rated it false, noting that the study in question included no Israeli Jews.[cite:aap_khazar_factcheck] The finding that the Ashkenazi population as a whole is not primarily of Khazar descent does not deny that the Khazar elite converted, and it does not settle every question about European admixture. What it settles is the specific claim, which does not hold when tested.

That claim returned to a large audience in February 2026. On 19 and 20 February, Tucker Carlson interviewed the United States Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, and asked: "Why don't we do genetic testing on everybody in the land and find out who Abram's descendants are? It's really simple. We've cracked the human genome. We can do that." He went on to single out Netanyahu, citing his family's Polish origin.[cite:jta_carlson_khazar_2026] [cite:toi_carlson_khazar_2026] Huckabee, a committed Christian Zionist rather than a reflexive critic, pushed back in the room, calling the idea a "dangerous conspiracy theory" from "some of the darkest realms of the internet." Reporters at JTA, the Times of Israel, the Jerusalem Post and the Forward identified the underlying claim as the Khazar theory: the premise that Eastern European ancestry among some Israeli Jews would undo their connection to the land.[cite:jta_carlson_khazar_2026] [cite:toi_carlson_khazar_2026] That identification was the reporters' own, made independently across outlets.

The exchange also raised a separate and more general question, which should be kept apart from the discredited one. What share of ancestry would make any identity claim, or any claim to land, "legitimate"? No geneticist, historian, court or international convention has ever defined such a threshold, for this question or for any other claim based on ancestry anywhere in the world. That is not a gap in the research. Ancestry percentages have never been the legal or historical basis on which such claims rest: treaties, borders and citizenship laws do not run on DNA, for Israel or for any other state. Collapsing the open philosophical question into the tested genetic claim is one of the ways the discredited version gets carried back into argument.

An analogy, offered as an analogy and not as a genetic argument, may help with the teaching gap underneath all this. Many people are taught that "Jewish" and "Semitic" are simple synonyms, and few are taught that Jewish identity itself contains several lineages with different histories. A Salvadoran, a Mexican and a Peruvian are all Latino, while each carries a different mix of Indigenous American, Spanish colonial and other ancestry, varying by country and family. No one is less Latino for having a different mix. In the same structural sense, Mizrahi Jews carry concentrated, continuous Levantine ancestry, and Ashkenazi Jews carry that same documented root together with substantial European admixture. The comparison borrows one idea, that a shared category can hold real internal variety, and nothing more; Jewish and Latino identities have entirely different histories, religious and genetic.

The Beta Israel of Ethiopia show that the question of who counts as a Jew has also been settled, in practice, by institutions rather than by genes. The Beta Israel, the "House of Israel," lived for centuries in the Gondar and Tigray regions of northern Ethiopia and practiced a Judaism distinct from rabbinic tradition.[cite:w_beta_israel] The familiar account holds that Israel always welcomed them as Jews. The record is slower and more conditional. Their status was disputed by Israel's religious authorities until 1973, when the Sephardi Chief Rabbi, Ovadia Yosef, ruled that they were Jews. The government applied the Law of Return to them in 1975, which made them eligible to immigrate.[cite:w_ethiopian_jews_israel] Even then, in 1985, the chief rabbinate required a symbolic conversion ritual before it accepted them fully.[cite:moment_failing] By the end of 2019 about 155,300 Ethiopian Jews lived in Israel.[cite:w_beta_israel]

The sequence shows where the power to decide lay. A religious ruling by one chief rabbi opened the door; a government decision under the Law of Return turned that ruling into a right to immigrate; and the chief rabbinate still imposed a further condition of its own twelve years after the ruling. The terms of the Law of Return itself are set out in [scene:ch01_citizenship|the section on citizenship]. The record available here does not explain why recognition took until 1973, or how the 1985 requirement was received within the community and how long it lasted; those questions remain open in this account.

Two points of discipline follow from all of this, and they apply in every direction. Genetics does not determine anyone's political rights, Jewish, Palestinian or any other. And the case against any state policy examined in this library never depends on the ancestry of the people who carry it out. A documented argument about policy stands on documents. Claims about the ancestry of Jews or of Palestinians add nothing to it, and in the Khazar case they are also false.

What the record leaves unsettled is real but narrow. The size and timing of particular admixture events in Ashkenazi ancestry are still being refined, and estimates of the Middle Eastern share vary widely. The genetic studies measure ancestry; they do not decide identity, which in the case of the Beta Israel was decided by a rabbinic ruling and a government decision. What is settled is that the Jewish lineages share a detectable Middle Eastern origin, that each also carries its own regional history, and that the claim of wholesale Khazar descent was tested and did not hold.

sections.h: Where the Lineages Lived: A Map of Jewish Communities
sections.html:
The previous section followed three broad Jewish lineages, Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Mizrahi, through the genetic record. This section puts them on the map, together with the smaller communities that fit none of the three. It shows where each community lived, the language it spoke, the event that changed it most, and where most of its descendants live now. The picture that results is not one diaspora moving in one direction, but some two dozen communities, each with its own documented history, spread across three continents for more than two thousand years.

The names need a word first. Ashkenaz is a name in Genesis, and medieval rabbis used it for Germany; Sepharad appears in the book of Obadiah, and by the ninth century it meant the Iberian Peninsula. [cite:jl_jvl_ashkenazim] [cite:jl_wiki_sepharad] Both words also name prayer rites, so a Jew of Iraqi or Moroccan family may be counted as Sephardi in synagogue. "Mizrahi," meaning "Eastern," is a modern umbrella term for Jews from Arab and Muslim lands. Sources date it to the 1940s or the 1950s; writers including Ella Shohat have criticised it as a construction, many people prefer to name their own community, and grouping North African Jews, historically called "Westerners," under "Eastern" is itself contested. [cite:jl_mjl_mizrahim] [cite:jl_wiki_mizrahi] This book uses the terms because the sources do, with those caveats.

Ashkenazi. By the tenth century there were centres of rabbinic learning at Mainz and Worms on the Rhine, and the name Ashkenaz came to mean the Jews of that region. [cite:jl_jvl_ashkenazim] After the Crusades of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries they moved east into Slavic lands. [cite:jl_brit_ashkenazi] Royal charters in Poland, from 1264 and 1334, opened the way to real settlement in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; by the early sixteenth century the centre of Ashkenazi life had shifted to Poland, Lithuania, Bohemia and Moravia, and a tax inquiry of 1764 found that about seven percent of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth was Jewish. [cite:jl_ego_ashkenazi] [cite:jl_jvl_ashkenazim] Their common language was Yiddish. [cite:jl_jvl_ashkenazim] Estimates of their share of world Jewry vary: the Jewish Virtual Library puts it at 90 percent before the Second World War, and Britannica at more than 80 percent today. [cite:jl_jvl_ashkenazim] [cite:jl_brit_ashkenazi] According to the Jewish Virtual Library, the United States later became the main Ashkenazi centre. [cite:jl_jvl_ashkenazim]

Sephardi. The Jewish Virtual Library dates a Jewish "Golden Age" in Spain from the Muslim conquest of 711. In 1492 Spain gave Jews who refused baptism four months to leave; about 100,000 went, by that source's estimate, and in 1497 Portugal forced almost all of its Jews to convert. [cite:jl_jvl_sephardim] Large numbers of exiles settled across the Ottoman Empire and in North Africa, and Sephardi communities also formed in Venice, Livorno, Bordeaux, Hamburg and London. [cite:jl_jvl_sephardim] Salonica, today's Thessaloniki, became their great city, with about 35,000 Jews in the sixteenth century and about 80,000 around 1900. [cite:jl_uw_salonica] In 1943 the Germans deported more than 45,000 of its Jews to Auschwitz-Birkenau. [cite:jl_ushmm_salonika] Their language, Judeo-Spanish, also called Judezmo or Ladino, flourished in the Ottoman lands. [cite:jl_jlp_judezmo] A second branch, the Western Sephardim, grew from Portuguese "New Christians" who returned to Judaism in Amsterdam from the late sixteenth century, and in London where a petition to Oliver Cromwell in 1656 led to open Jewish life in England for the first time since the expulsion of 1290. [cite:jl_posen_western] [cite:jl_jcruk_bevis]

The map above shows the communities of Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Each number is a community, coloured by family; the dotted arrows are documented migrations; and the diamonds mark places the communities moved to rather than came from. The key under the map gives each community's language, its dates and where most of its descendants live today.

Mizrahi and North African. Iraq's community traces its start to the Babylonian exile of about 586 BCE, and the Babylonian Talmud was compiled there. [cite:jl_wiki_iraq] [cite:jl_jvl_ezra] By 1900 Baghdad's roughly 50,000 Jews were more than a quarter of the city. [cite:jl_wiki_iraq] After the Farhud riots of 1941 and an Iraqi law of March 1950 that let Jews leave if they gave up their citizenship, Operation Ezra and Nehemiah flew more than 120,000 of them to Israel. [cite:jl_wiki_iraq] [cite:jl_jvl_ezra] Iran's community traces its roots to the sixth century BCE and wrote in Judeo-Persian; about 80,000 Jews lived there in 1978 by unofficial statistics, and a community of several thousand remains, with a reserved seat in parliament. [cite:jl_jvl_iran] [cite:jl_jlp_judeo_persian] Jews are recorded in Yemen from the third century CE; Operation Magic Carpet airlifted about 49,000 Jews, most of them from Yemen, in 1949 and 1950. [cite:jl_jvl_yemen] [cite:jl_cojs_magic_carpet] Syria's community, in Aleppo and Damascus, dates its presence to the Seleucid period; after the government allowed emigration in 1992, thousands left, mainly for Brooklyn and New Jersey; others settled in Israel and Mexico. [cite:jl_jvl_syria] In Egypt, Jews probably settled in Old Cairo soon after its founding in 641, and the famous Cairo Genizah was found in its Ben Ezra Synagogue; the community numbered about 75,000 at its peak; about 25,000 were expelled or forced out after the Suez war of 1956, and nearly all had left by the early 1970s. [cite:jl_jvl_cairo] [cite:jl_jvl_egypt]

Further east and north, the Jews of Kurdistan spoke a Neo-Aramaic language; the Bukharan Jews of Central Asia spoke Bukhori, a language close to Tajik, and now live mostly in Israel and in Queens, New York; the Mountain Jews of the eastern Caucasus spoke Juhuri; and the Jews of Georgia, by a tradition not confirmed by contemporary records, arrived after 586 BCE. [cite:jl_ej_kurdistan] [cite:jl_ela_bukhori] [cite:jl_ela_juhuri] [cite:jl_jlp_judeo_georgian] In North Africa, sources distinguished the toshavim, the Jews already living there, from the megorashim, the Iberian exiles who arrived after 1391 and 1492. [cite:jl_wiki_toshavim] Morocco's community is documented from the second century CE; more than 90,000 left for Israel in Operation Yakhin between 1961 and 1964, and many others settled in France and Canada. [cite:jl_jvl_morocco] France made Algeria's Jews French citizens in 1870, and almost 130,000 moved to France after Algerian independence in 1962. [cite:jl_jvl_algeria] Tunisia had about 105,000 Jews in 1946, including the old community of the island of Djerba. [cite:jl_jvl_djerba] How these communities left in the twentieth century is told in [scene:s00e2|The Exodus of 1941–1972].

Other communities. Several communities belong to none of the three families. The Romaniotes of Greece, in Ioannina, Arta and Chalkida, are documented from the Byzantine period and spoke Yevanic, a Jewish Greek; the language declined as Romaniotes merged into the Sephardi communities of Greece, and the Holocaust nearly destroyed it. [cite:jl_wiki_yevanic] Rome's community, which the Jewish Virtual Library dates to 161 BCE and calls the oldest in Europe, kept its own Italian rite; it was confined to a ghetto by papal order in 1555, and on 16 October 1943 the Nazis rounded up Jews in Rome and deported them to Auschwitz; by the Jewish Virtual Library's count, only a dozen of those deported survived. [cite:jl_jvl_rome] [cite:jl_jlp_judeo_italian] The Karaites, a movement that accepts the Hebrew Bible but not the Talmud as binding, grew from the followers of Anan ben David in Babylonia about 760 CE, with later centres in Cairo, Crimea and Lithuania. [cite:jl_nwe_karaites] [cite:jl_je_anan]

The Beta Israel of Ethiopia prayed in Ge'ez and spoke Amharic or Tigrinya. Their origins are disputed: the historian Steven Kaplan argues that they formed as a group in Ethiopia between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, while other accounts place their arrival in the first to sixth centuries. [cite:jl_jvl_ethiopian] [cite:jl_kaplan_beta_israel] [cite:jl_mjl_ethiopian] Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi ruled them Jews in 1973; Operations Moses in 1984–85 and Solomon in 1991 brought about 7,700 and 14,400 of them to Israel, by one historian's count. [cite:jl_jvl_ethiopian] [cite:jl_ency_ethiopian] India had three communities: the Bene Israel of the Konkan coast, who spoke Marathi; the Cochin Jews of Kerala, documented by copper plates of about 1000 CE, who spoke Jewish Malayalam; and the Baghdadi Jews, Arabic-speaking merchants who came in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. [cite:jl_ej_bene_israel] [cite:jl_mjl_cochin] [cite:jl_mjl_baghdadi] In Kaifeng, China, a community that most scholars think came from Persia in the twelfth century kept a synagogue until the nineteenth century; between 500 and 1,000 people there are estimated to claim descent today. [cite:jl_iranica_kaifeng] [cite:jl_wiki_kaifeng]

Three further groups appear on these maps with a different status. The Abayudaya of Uganda began practising Judaism in 1919 as a religious movement, and do not claim continuous descent from ancient Israel in the sources consulted. [cite:jl_ijn_abayudaya] The Bnei Menashe of northeastern India say they descend from the tribe of Manasseh; a Chief Rabbi recognised that claim in 2005, but formal conversion was still required, and no peer-reviewed genetic study has confirmed it. [cite:jl_aljazeera_bnei_menashe] [cite:jl_eastmojo_bnei_menashe] The Lemba of South Africa and Zimbabwe have an oral tradition of origin in a place called "Sena"; early genetic studies were read as support, but a 2014 reassessment found the markers used to be unreliable predictors of Jewish ancestry. [cite:jl_ency_lemba] [cite:jl_tofanelli_2014] On the map the Bnei Menashe and the Lemba are marked as claims of descent, not settled facts, and the Abayudaya as a twentieth-century movement.

What the record shows, and what it does not. The record shows Jewish communities spread from the Atlantic to China and from the Baltic to southern Africa, each with its own documented history, language and turning points, and most of them reshaped in the twentieth century by genocide in Europe or by mass emigration from the Middle East and North Africa, much of it to Israel. It shows that the three familiar labels are partly modern conveniences: they overlap with prayer rites, and "Mizrahi" in particular is a term whose dating and fairness are debated. The record does not settle the origins of every community: the dates for the Beta Israel, the Kaifeng Jews and the Georgian Jews are disputed, and the descent claims of the Bnei Menashe and the Lemba are not established. The places on the map are approximate centres, and most population figures are estimates from the sources named. None of it decides anyone's rights, a point made in [scene:s00b2|the section on the lineages].

sections.h: Language and Ancestry: Two Different Questions
sections.html:
People sometimes ask which Jews are "Semitic Jews" and which are not. The question runs two separate things together. "Semitic" is the name of a family of languages, as [scene:s00b|the section on the word] sets out. Where a community's ancestors came from is a question for history and genetics. The answers to the two questions do not line up, and neither answers a third question: who is Jewish. Jewish law answers that one. A Jew is someone born to a Jewish mother or someone who has converted, and the movements differ on the details. [cite:fw_mjl_whoisjew] This section takes the first two questions in turn, then places every community from the map in the previous section on a single grid.

Start with language. Hebrew was the language of prayer and study, and for many centuries almost no Jewish community spoke it at home; everyday speech followed the region. [scene:ch01_four_words|Four words] Some of those everyday languages were Semitic. The Jews of Baghdad spoke Judeo-Arabic, Yemen's Jews spoke Judeo-Yemeni Arabic, Kurdish Jews spoke a Neo-Aramaic language, and Morocco's older Jewish communities spoke Judeo-Arabic or Judeo-Berber. [cite:jl_wiki_iraq] [cite:jl_wiki_judeo_yemeni] [cite:jl_ej_kurdistan] [cite:jl_wiki_toshavim] The Beta Israel of Ethiopia mostly spoke Amharic, or Tigrinya in Tigray, both of them Semitic languages, and they prayed in Ge'ez, another. [cite:jl_jvl_ethiopian] Many more of the languages were not Semitic. Ashkenazi Jews spoke Yiddish, a Germanic language, and Sephardi Jews spoke Judeo-Spanish, a Romance one. [cite:jl_jvl_ashkenazim] [cite:jl_jlp_judezmo] The Jews of Iran, Bukhara and the eastern Caucasus spoke Iranian languages: Judeo-Persian, Bukhori and Juhuri. [cite:jl_jlp_judeo_persian] [cite:jl_ela_bukhori] [cite:jl_ela_juhuri] Georgia's Jews spoke a Jewish form of Georgian and Greece's Romaniote Jews a Jewish Greek. [cite:jl_jlp_judeo_georgian] [cite:jl_wiki_yevanic] The Bene Israel spoke Marathi and the Jews of Kerala spoke Jewish Malayalam. [cite:jl_ej_bene_israel] [cite:jl_jlp_malayalam]

Ancestry is a separate question, and the most complete answer comes from a genome-wide study published in Nature in 2010 by Doron Behar and colleagues. They genotyped 121 people from 14 Jewish communities. [cite:an_behar2010_pdf] Most of the Jewish samples formed a tight cluster lying over the Druze and Cypriot samples, and the authors traced the origins of most diaspora communities to the Levant. [cite:an_behar2010_pubmed] Within that cluster they found two subgroups. One held the Ashkenazi, Moroccan and Sephardi Jews. The other held the Middle Eastern communities, Iranian and Iraqi Jews, and the Caucasus communities of Georgia and Azerbaijan. Yemenite Jews formed a compact cluster of their own, closest to Bedouin and Saudi samples. The ancestry component typical of Europeans was larger in Ashkenazi, Moroccan and Sephardi Jews than in the Middle Eastern communities. The paper gives no percentages for it. [cite:an_behar2010_pdf]

Two groups did not fit that pattern. The Beta Israel of Ethiopia and the Jews of India, both the Bene Israel and the Cochin Jews, clustered with the non-Jewish populations living around them, although the Bene Israel showed a clear link to the Levant on the male line. [cite:an_behar2010_pubmed] A 2016 study of the Bene Israel alone found both substantial Jewish and substantial Indian ancestry. The mixing happened within the last thousand years, the Jewish side came mostly through men, and the local side mostly through women. [cite:an_waldman2016]

Put side by side, the two answers show why the word "Semitic" cannot sort Jews by descent. The Beta Israel spoke Semitic languages, yet their genomes sit closest to their Ethiopian neighbours. More precisely, they sit closest to the Semitic-speaking Ethiopians rather than the Cushitic-speaking ones. [cite:an_behar2010_pdf] Ashkenazi Jews spoke a Germanic language, yet they carry Middle Eastern ancestry. The grid below places each community twice: down the side, by what the record shows about its ancestry; across the top, by whether its everyday language was Semitic.

The bottom three rows hold communities that the genetic studies cited here did not cover, or covered without settling anything. The Jews of Kaifeng in China most likely descend from Persian Jews who arrived in the twelfth century, and Israel requires their descendants to convert formally. [cite:jl_iranica_kaifeng] [cite:jl_wiki_kaifeng] The Abayudaya of Uganda began practising Judaism in 1919 as a religious movement; they do not claim descent from ancient Israel, and since 2002 their conversions have been overseen by the Conservative movement. [cite:jl_ijn_abayudaya] The Bnei Menashe of northeast India and the Lemba of southern Africa claim descent from ancient Israel. For the Bnei Menashe the claim is not established: one test was never published, and a second was not peer-reviewed. [cite:jl_eastmojo_bnei_menashe] Studies of the Lemba from 1996 and 2000 reported Middle Eastern markers on the male line. A 2014 reassessment found that such markers do not reliably predict Jewish ancestry, and most Lemba today are Christian. [cite:jl_ency_lemba] [cite:jl_tofanelli_2014]

The grid has limits, and they are marked on it. Communities drawn with an outline (Syrian, Kurdish, Bukharan, Italian and Romaniote Jews among them) are placed by their documented history alone, because no genome study of them was consulted for this book. The 2010 study is one study, though a large one, and work of this kind keeps being refined. The origins of the Beta Israel are still argued among historians: one view holds that they emerged as a group in Ethiopia between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, another that they arrived far earlier. [cite:jl_kaplan_beta_israel] [cite:jl_mjl_ethiopian]

What the grid does not say matters as much as what it does. It does not rank Jewish communities, and it does not make any of them more or less Jewish. Every community on it includes converts and their descendants, and under Jewish law a convert is fully Jewish. [cite:fw_mjl_whoisjew] Israel's own institutions recognised the Beta Israel as Jews in 1973 and 1975, and declared the Bene Israel "Jews in every respect" in 1964. [cite:jl_jvl_ethiopian] [cite:jl_ej_bene_israel] Nor does ancestry decide a modern political question. The same genetic research finds that Palestinians and Jews of the Levant share substantial common ancestry, a point taken up in [scene:s00b|the section on "Semitic"]. Whether people speak a Semitic language, where a community's ancestors came from, and who is Jewish are three separate questions, and each has its own answer.

sections.h: Jews in the Muslim World: Coexistence Without Utopia
sections.html:
For more than a thousand years, Jewish communities lived across the Muslim-majority Middle East and North Africa: in Baghdad, Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo, Sana'a, Fez, Tunis and Casablanca. In some of these cities they formed a plurality or even a majority. A common claim holds that Jews and Arabs never lived together in peace, and that an ancient, irreconcilable hatred is the natural and permanent state between them. The documented record does not fit that frame. Neither does the opposite picture of an unbroken harmony. What the record shows is a long, uneven coexistence: real violence, and real legal inequality, alongside intellectual, commercial and civic collaboration on a scale that, in the judgment of the historians cited below, Christian Europe of the same period did not match. How that coexistence ended, between 1941 and 1972, is a separate and grave story, told in [scene:s00e2|the section on the exodus from the Arab world].

The oldest of these communities is older than Islam, older than Arab rule in the region and older than either modern state that now claims part of its story. In 586 BCE Babylon destroyed the First Temple in Jerusalem, conquered Judah and deported its population to Mesopotamia, the land that is now Iraq.[cite:huc_farhud] The exiles took root and stayed. Over the following centuries the community became one of the great centers of Jewish religious and intellectual life, and between roughly the third and sixth centuries CE its scholars compiled the Babylonian Talmud, a foundational work of Jewish law that is still the primary text of rabbinic study, nearly 1,500 years after it was compiled in what is now Iraq.[cite:huc_farhud] [cite:ushmm_farhud] One of the two foundational texts of rabbinic Judaism was produced there, not in the land of Israel. Popular accounts often begin this relationship in 1948, as if it started with modern statehood. Historical and religious sources agree, without dispute, on continuous Jewish presence in Mesopotamia from the sixth century BCE, more than a thousand years before the Muslim conquest of the region, and long before the Iraqi state of 1932 or the Israeli state of 1948.[cite:huc_farhud] [cite:ushmm_farhud]

That community was still large in the twentieth century. Sasson Somekh, born a Jew in Baghdad and later a professor of Arabic literature at Tel Aviv University, documents its scale in his memoir Baghdad, Yesterday (2007).[cite:somekh_baghdad_yesterday] The figures vary by year and by source. One account gives 140,000 Jews in 1917, about 40 percent of Baghdad's civilian population; another gives roughly 140,000 in 1945, about a third of the city; a more cautious reckoning puts the mid-century community at 90,000 to 140,000, depending on the year and the source, in that reckoning close to a third of the city. Jews formed much of the commercial, banking and professional life of modern Iraq. Trading families such as the Sassoons, the Kadoories and the Basris built networks that reached across the region, into British India and across the British Empire. Iraq's first finance minister, Sassoon Heskel, was Jewish, and the community's chief rabbis served as advisers to the government. In 1917 the community welcomed the arriving British forces.[cite:somekh_baghdad_yesterday] This was not a marginal sect. It was a city community as old as Jewish life in Europe, integrated into the economy and the state. Its place in the new kingdom under Faisal is told in [scene:irq_e02|Faisal's Iraq].

The best-known chapter of this history is al-Andalus, Muslim Iberia, home to what is called the Jewish Golden Age of the tenth to twelfth centuries. Its figures include Maimonides (born in Córdoba, 1135–1204), Judah Halevi (of Toledo and Córdoba), Solomon ibn Gabirol and Samuel HaNagid. Jewish scholars wrote philosophy in Arabic, held the office of vizier and produced foundational works of rabbinic literature.[cite:menocal_ornament] The term usually attached to this period, convivencia, "living together," is contested precisely because the period was not utopian. In 1066 a pogrom struck the Jews of Granada. The historians on whom this account relies, María Rosa Menocal, David Nirenberg and Mark Cohen, do not deny such violence. Their work nonetheless documents a substantial period of Jewish and Muslim intellectual and civic collaboration that, they argue, had no parallel in Christian Europe of the same period.[cite:menocal_ornament]

The Iberian story ended in Christian hands. In 1492 the Catholic monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, ordered Spain's Jews to convert or leave; historians estimate that at least 200,000 people were affected. The Ottoman sultan, Bayezid II, opened his territories to receive the exiles, and Salonika became a majority-Sephardic city for centuries.[cite:stillman_jews_arab_lands] The expulsion's long afterlife reached into the present. Spain established diplomatic relations with Israel only on 17 January 1986, the last Western European state to do so, as a condition of joining the European Community, while pledging continued "friendship and solidarity" with the Arab world; in 1948, according to reports, Franco had sought relations and Ben-Gurion had refused because of Franco's ties to Nazi Germany.[cite:israeled_spain_1986] Spain hosted the Madrid peace conference of 1991. In 2015 the Spanish parliament passed a law offering citizenship to descendants of the expelled Sephardim, to repair what it called a "historical mistake." By the 2019 deadline 132,226 people had applied, most of them from Latin America: about 20,000 from Mexico, the largest single group, followed by applicants from Venezuela and Colombia.[cite:euronews_sephardic] [cite:yahoo_sephardic_close] Less than a decade later, on 28 May 2024, Spain, with Ireland and Norway, recognized the State of Palestine on the pre-1967 lines with East Jerusalem as its capital. Israel recalled its ambassador, and its foreign minister said the three states were rewarding Hamas.[cite:catalannews_spain_recognition] [cite:wiki_palestine_spain] Pro-Israel commentators read Spain's position as hostility with historical echoes; the Spanish government presents it as support for a two-state solution and for international law. Both acts, the atonement of 2015 and the recognition of 2024, are documented, and reading either as canceling the other misses the record.

The Ottoman Empire, which lasted from 1299 to 1922, a span of 623 years, gave this coexistence its most durable legal form. It organized its non-Muslim subjects through the millet system, under which each religious community governed itself under its own leaders in matters of law, education and religion. The Chief Rabbi of Istanbul was responsible for all Ottoman Jews. Jewish communities lived under this arrangement in Istanbul, İzmir, Salonika, Damascus, Aleppo, Baghdad, Cairo and Jerusalem. The system was not one of equality: Jews held the status of dhimmi, protected non-Muslims, paid the jizya tax and lived under legal restrictions that did not apply to Muslims. It was also not the persecution of the Nazi regime or of imperial Russia. For four centuries after 1492 it framed daily civic life, and it produced Sephardi and Mizrahi literature and the mystical school of Safed, the Kabbalah associated with Isaac Luria and Joseph Caro. Norman Stillman's The Jews of Arab Lands is the standard documentary sourcebook for this history.[cite:stillman_jews_arab_lands]

The mechanism matters for reading this history fairly. Under the millet, a Jewish community could run its own courts, schools and religious life; it could not stand as an equal of Muslims before the state, and it paid for its protection through a special tax. That is why the same arrangement can be described, accurately, as both tolerant and unequal.

Historians divide over how to weigh this record, and both readings rest on evidence. The first, sometimes called the "golden age" reading, stresses the length and depth of the collaboration: Jewish philosophers writing in Arabic, Jewish viziers in Muslim courts, the Talmud compiled in Mesopotamia, the Ottoman welcome of 1492, and Baghdad's community still a third of the city in the twentieth century. In its strongest form it argues, with Menocal, Nirenberg and Cohen, that nothing comparable existed in Christian Europe at the same time, and that a hatred described as ancient and permanent cannot explain a millennium of shared life. The second reading stresses the limits and the ruptures: dhimmi status as a permanent legal subordination, the jizya, the restrictions, and violence such as the Granada pogrom of 1066. In its strongest form it warns that the golden-age image can idealize what was, in law, a hierarchy. The record supports both sets of facts. It does not support either extreme: not "harmonious coexistence, full stop," and not a story of unbroken persecution.

The twentieth century shows both forces at work in a single community. In Baghdad in June 1941, seven years before Israel's founding, a pogrom known as the Farhud killed 150 to 180 Jews by the count of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and more by some other estimates. Nazi-inspired, it came during the political turmoil of a short-lived pro-Axis coup, during the Anglo-Iraqi War, and was encouraged by pro-Axis Iraqi elements.[cite:ushmm_farhud] [cite:huc_farhud] After 1948 came further legal restrictions, confiscations of property and violence; at the same time, the Israeli state and the Jewish Agency actively encouraged and organized emigration. Both forces are documented, and neither explains the exodus without the other. The same holds across the region, where roughly 850,000 Jews left Arab and Muslim countries between 1948 and 1972, for several reasons operating at once. In Iraq the mass departure came in 1950–51, and within a decade a presence of some twenty-five centuries had all but ended. The full account, including its disputed episodes and its sequel in Israel, belongs to the section on the exodus. One point should be recorded here: the scholar Ella Shohat has documented the second-class treatment of Iraqi Jews after their arrival, a displacement upon a displacement.[cite:shohat_sephardim_israel]

Several things remain unsettled. The figures for Baghdad's Jewish population differ by source and by year, and the record here cannot reconcile 40 percent of the city in 1917 with a third in 1945 beyond noting that the counts and their bases differ. The toll of the Granada pogrom of 1066 is not given in the sources used here. The comparison with Christian Europe is a judgment by named historians, well supported, but a judgment all the same. And the balance between persecution and recruitment in the Iraqi exodus remains a matter of genuine dispute. What the record does establish is narrower and firmer: Jewish life in the Muslim world was long, large and productive; it was never free of inequality or violence; and the frame of an ancient, irreconcilable hatred does not describe it. The hostility of the twentieth century had dates and causes, and it is in those dates and causes, not in a supposed permanent enmity, that the history of the break has to be sought.

sections.h: The Land's Other Communities
sections.html:
A common shorthand presents the conflict as Jews against Muslims, and Palestinians as uniformly Muslim. The land's population has never fitted that frame. Alongside its Jewish and Muslim Arab majorities it holds Druze, whose faith took shape in the Middle Ages and accepts no converts; Bedouin, whose relationship with the state turns on land; Circassians, Muslims from the Caucasus who serve in Israel's army; Samaritans, a community of a few hundred who trace their descent to ancient Israel; and Palestinian Christians, members of some of the oldest Christian communities on earth. Each stands in a different relationship to the State of Israel, and those differences are documented in law, in census figures and in the record of demolitions and conscription. The legal situations of Palestinians in general, and the numbers of Arab citizens of Israel as a whole, are set out earlier in this volume [scene:pr_s02|who the Palestinians are in law].

The Druze. The Druze faith took shape in the Middle Ages and has accepted no converts since the eleventh century [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_druze]. According to Minority Rights Group, about 150,000 Druze live in Israel proper, in eighteen villages, and about 24,000 to 25,000 more in the Golan Heights [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_druze]. Central Bureau of Statistics figures reported in April 2024 give a slightly higher total for Israel, about 152,000, against 14,500 in 1949; the largest Druze localities at the end of 2022 were Daliyat al-Karmel and Yarka, each with more than 17,000 people [cite:rs_ch01_tps_druze].

The Druze relationship with the state was set early. Druze in Galilee and on Mount Carmel fought alongside the Jewish forces in 1948. In 1956 Druze men were included in military conscription, and in 1961 separate Druze religious courts were established [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_druze] [cite:rs_ch01_tps_druze]. The Golan Druze followed a different course. After Israel captured the Golan Heights in 1967 it offered citizenship to the Druze living there, and, according to the same April 2024 report, most refused [cite:rs_ch01_tps_druze]. The sources used here do not say how many have since accepted, or whether Golan Druze who did not take citizenship are subject to the draft.

The Circassians. Israel's Circassians are Muslims whose origins lie in the Caucasus. They live mainly in two Galilee villages: Kfar Kama, with about 2,000 people of the Shapsug group, and Rehaniya, with about 1,000 of the Abadzakh group. According to a community-sourced account, they were settled there at the Ottoman Sultan's request in the late nineteenth century, and Circassian men serve in the army and the police [cite:rs_ch01_mjl_circassians]. That account rests on a single source drawn from a Circassian foundation, and it does not settle when and why the families left the Caucasus; this book does not go beyond what it states.

The Negev Bedouin. The largest of these communities, and the one whose position is most contested, is the Bedouin of the Negev. About 92,000 Bedouin lived in the Negev before 1948. After the war about 11,000 remained inside Israel, from 19 of the original 95 tribes, according to Minority Rights Group and the Israeli-Arab legal center Adalah [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin] [cite:rs_ch01_almonitor_bedouin]. Those who stayed were concentrated in an area known as the siyag, Arabic for "fence," of about 1.5 million dunams, against some 13 million dunams they had used before [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin].

The legal mechanism that followed ran through two statutes. The Land Acquisition Law of 1953 and the Planning and Building Law of 1965 registered much of the Bedouin's land as state land [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. From the 1960s the state built seven planned townships, beginning with Tel Sheva, Rahat and Kseifa [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. Villages outside the townships and outside the state's plans were left "unrecognized": without legal standing as settlements, and with their buildings treated in official policy as illegal construction on state land. Israel does not recognize the Bedouin as an indigenous people [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. Just over 300,000 Bedouin live in Israel today, about 3% of the population [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin].

Recognition has moved slowly. The Association for Civil Rights in Israel counted 46 unrecognized Bedouin villages in the Negev, of which the state had recognized 11 by about 2011, leaving 35. The same organization recorded 275 buildings demolished in 2010 and 1,000 in 2011 [cite:rs_ch01_acri_bedouin]. The demolitions have continued. In May 2024 Israeli authorities demolished about 47 to 50 homes in the unrecognized village of Wadi al-Khalil; National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called the buildings illegal constructions and the demolition "an important step" [cite:rs_ch01_almonitor_bedouin] [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin].

Even the number of people affected is disputed. Minority Rights Group puts the population of the unrecognized villages at about 100,000 people in roughly 35 villages [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. Adalah, as reported by Al-Monitor in May 2024, puts it at about half of some 300,000 Negev Bedouin, which is about 150,000 [cite:rs_ch01_almonitor_bedouin]. An ACRI fact sheet from about 2011 gave about 70,000 [cite:rs_ch01_acri_bedouin]. The figures come from different years and partly from advocacy organizations, and the sources do not explain the gap between them. Note also that Adalah's base of some 300,000 refers to the Negev Bedouin, while Minority Rights Group's figure of just over 300,000 refers to the Bedouin of Israel as a whole.

Behind the numbers lies a deeper disagreement over what the villages are. The state and its ministers treat construction in unrecognized villages as illegal building on state land, which is the basis on which demolition orders are issued and on which Ben-Gvir defended Wadi al-Khalil [cite:rs_ch01_almonitor_bedouin] [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. On that view, the law is the 1953 and 1965 statutes, and the land is registered to the state. Bedouin and rights groups answer that the villages either predate the state or were placed where they stand by the state itself, and that 35 of them meet every Central Bureau of Statistics test for a settlement except the minister's declaration [cite:rs_ch01_acri_bedouin] [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. On that view, the Bedouin are a dispossessed indigenous people rather than squatters. One reading of the dispute is that the two sides differ less over what the statutes say than over whether the allocation of land they made was just.

The Samaritans. The smallest of these communities has the longest claimed history. The Samaritans hold that they descend from Israelites who escaped the Assyrian deportation after 722/721 BCE. They keep their own version of the Pentateuch and hold Mount Gerizim sacred; their temple there was destroyed by John Hyrcanus in 128 BCE [cite:rs_ch01_ency_samaritans]. By 1917 the community had fallen to a low of 146 people. In January 2003 it numbered 654: 349 in Holon, inside Israel, and 305 at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim near Nablus [cite:rs_ch01_ency_samaritans]. The Oslo arrangements placed the Nablus community under Palestinian administration, so that a single community of a few hundred people now lives on both sides of the lines described at the start of this volume [cite:rs_ch01_ency_samaritans].

Palestinian Christians. Palestinians include one of the world's oldest Christian communities. In the early twentieth century Christians were about 12% of Palestine's population. According to the 2017 census, fewer than 50,000 live in the West Bank and East Jerusalem today, between 47,000 and 50,000, or about 1% of the population; most are concentrated in Bethlehem, Ramallah and East Jerusalem [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025] [cite:noonpost_christians]. Gaza's Christians fell from about 3,000 in the early 2000s to about 1,000 before October 2023, and to a few hundred since [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025] [cite:noonpost_christians]. The decline is attributed to war, displacement and economic hardship [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025].

The war since October 2023 reached them directly. On 17 July 2025 Israeli fire struck the compound of the Holy Family Church, Gaza's only Catholic parish, where about 600 Christians and Muslims had taken shelter. Three people were killed and the parish priest was wounded [cite:persecution_holyfamily]. Pope Leo XIV said he was deeply saddened and called for a ceasefire. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel "deeply regrets" that "stray ammunition" had hit the church, and that the incident was being investigated [cite:persecution_holyfamily] [cite:lorient_pope_holyfamily]. The same month, in the West Bank, arsonists targeted the area of the ancient church of St George in Taybeh, the last all-Christian town there, in what the reporting describes as settler arson [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025]. Munther Isaac, the Lutheran pastor in Bethlehem, has warned that Palestinian Christians risk disappearing from the Holy Land [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025]. Palestinian Christians live under the same occupation and the same war as their Muslim neighbors, and their presence alone is enough to show that "Jews against Muslims" does not describe the conflict. Their fuller story belongs to a later volume [scene:pc_s03|Palestinian Christians, 1900s–2025].

What the record does not settle. Several questions remain open on the sources used here. How many people live in the Negev's unrecognized villages is disputed, with estimates from about 70,000 to about 150,000, and no source explains the gap. Whether those villages are illegal construction on state land or the homes of a dispossessed indigenous people is a question of how the land was allocated after 1948, on which the state and the Bedouin and their advocates disagree. The Druze figures differ slightly between Minority Rights Group's 150,000 and the Central Bureau of Statistics' 152,000. The Circassian account rests on one community-derived source and does not establish when or why the families left the Caucasus. The fate of the Golan Druze offer of citizenship after the first refusals is not covered here. And the figures for Palestinian Christians are drawn from news reporting that cites the 2017 census rather than from the census itself.

sections.h: Zionism and Judaism: A Movement and a Religion
sections.html:
Judaism is a religion and a set of ethnic and cultural lineages thousands of years old. Zionism is a political movement. Its ideas were argued from the 1840s, but as an organized movement it has a place and a date of birth: Basel, Switzerland, in August 1897, convened by Theodor Herzl, a secular journalist from Vienna [cite:basel_program]. The two are often spoken of as one thing, so that opposing the movement is taken to mean opposing a people. The documents of the period do not support that equation. The line between the religion and the movement was drawn by Jews themselves: by the movement's founder in his own diary, by the largest American Jewish denomination twelve years before the movement existed, by a mass Jewish labor party founded the same year, by a cultural Zionist who warned against the political version, and by the largest Hasidic dynasty in the world, which still teaches its position today.

That the line exists does not settle every argument built on top of it. Many Jews, religious and secular, have understood and still understand their support for Zionism as part of their Jewish identity, and nothing in this record shows them wrong to do so. What the record settles is narrower: the distinction between the religion and the political project was not invented by outside critics. It was argued inside Jewish life from the start.

Herzl's founding. Herzl was not a rabbi or a religious scholar. He was an assimilated Viennese Jew, secular in outlook, a correspondent for the Neue Freie Presse, whose turn to politics was a response to the antisemitism he witnessed while covering the Dreyfus Affair. He set out his program in Der Judenstaat in 1896 and convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel from 29 to 31 August 1897 [cite:herzl_judenstaat] [cite:herzl_diaries]. Afterward he wrote in his diary: "At Basel I founded the Jewish State." The verb was his, written privately rather than for public consumption, and on this reading it describes a beginning: a political project that had not existed as such before Basel [cite:herzl_diaries].

The same diary shows that the territory was not fixed in advance. Herzl gave serious consideration to Argentina and to Uganda as candidate territories before Palestine was settled on [cite:herzl_diaries]. At its founding, political Zionism treated location as an open, practical question rather than a foregone theological conclusion. Two limits apply to this evidence. It documents the founder's own outlook and process, not the outlook of everyone who joined him; the movement drew religious and secular support alike from very early on. And it does not mean that Palestine was arbitrary to the movement's members, only that its founder weighed alternatives in writing. The rabbinic argument over whether Jews may return to the land by political means at all is a separate and older debate, told elsewhere in this library [scene:oaths_s01|the Three Oaths debate], and the Congress itself has its own section [scene:s04|the Basel Congress of 1897].

Reform Judaism, 1885. Twelve years before Basel, in November 1885, American Reform Judaism adopted the Pittsburgh Platform. Its words are explicit:

We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine, nor a sacrificial worship under the sons of Aaron, nor the restoration of any of the laws concerning the Jewish state.

This was not a reply to Zionism, which did not yet exist as an organized movement. It was an independent religious position, adopted publicly as the founding statement of what was then the largest Jewish denomination in America, that already disagreed with what would be proposed more than a decade later [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885]. It is difficult to reconcile with the simpler story in which Judaism naturally wanted a return to Zion and Zionism merely organized that existing desire. The platform remained mainstream American Reform's position for over half a century, until the Columbus Platform of 1937 softened it, and substantial Reform opposition to political Zionism continued after that. On this evidence, American Jewish institutional support for the political Zionist state is a development of the period after the Holocaust, not an ancient religious commitment [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885]. The platform documents the position of 1885. Reform Judaism's institutional stance shifted considerably over the twentieth century, and the 1885 text is no guide to its views today.

One reading finds a concession in the platform's wording. To declare that "we consider ourselves no longer a nation" is to acknowledge that the idea of Jewish nationhood had been there to set aside. On that reading, the question that divided the 1880s and 1890s was less whether Jews were a people than what that peoplehood required.

Ahad Ha'am, 1891. That question was argued most sharply from inside the Zionist camp. Asher Zvi Hirsch Ginsberg (1856–1927), who wrote as Ahad Ha'am, "One of the People," was a committed Zionist in the cultural sense: he wanted a Jewish spiritual and cultural center in Palestine [cite:wiki_ahad_haam]. In 1891, six years before Basel, he published "Truth from Eretz Israel," a firsthand report on the country. "We are used to believing abroad that Palestine is nowadays almost totally desolate," he wrote, "but in fact this is not the case. It is difficult to find in the land any tillable land which is not already tilled" [cite:wiki_ahad_haam]. He recorded the existing Arab population and warned that a political approach that did not account for it would produce conflict. His opposition was to the political, state-building version of Zionism that Herzl went on to champion, and to its handling of the people already there, not to Jewish attachment to the land.
