His essay establishes that the population, and the risk, were documented from within the movement's own intellectual circle before the political project took shape. It does not establish that his alternative, a cultural center rather than a state, would have been more workable in practice.

The Bund, October 1897. Two months after Basel, in Vilna, Jewish workers founded the Algemeyner Yidisher Arbeter Bund, the General Jewish Labor Bund in Lithuania, Poland and Russia [cite:wiki_bund]. It organized across the Russian Pale of Settlement on socialist and Yiddishist lines and rejected the Zionist proposal of national return to Palestine. Its watchword was doikayt, "hereness": Jewish cultural and political life was to be built where Jews already lived, with Yiddish as its vernacular and national-cultural autonomy inside the existing states as its goal. The Bund, too, spoke of Jews as a nation. It disagreed with the Zionists about where that nation's future lay.

The Bund was not a debating society. The historian Henry Tobias, in The Jewish Bund in Russia: From Its Origins to 1905, documents it as a genuine mass movement with real weight in the wider Russian and Polish socialist and labor movements; for a significant stretch of the early twentieth century, more organized Jewish political energy in Eastern Europe ran through the Bund than through the Zionist movement [cite:wiki_bund]. The sources differ on its size. One account gives a membership of more than 400,000 across the Russian Empire by 1917, larger than the Zionist movement in Eastern Europe and the largest Jewish political organization in the Empire in the decade before the Balfour Declaration; another describes it in the early twentieth century as having tens of thousands of members [cite:wiki_bund]. Either figure makes it a major current, not a fringe.

Its eclipse came from outside, not from losing an open argument with Zionism. Its membership and infrastructure were devastated by the Holocaust, and its remaining structures in the Soviet sphere were suppressed as Stalin moved against independent Jewish political organizations [cite:wiki_bund]. Most of its members, or their children, died in the Holocaust before the State of Israel was declared; their opposition to Zionism did not save them. The earlier fate of the Bund in Soviet Russia, dissolved by its Bolshevik allies, is told in the next section [scene:s00b3|Jewish dissent across every lineage]. What the Bund's existence settles is specific. It does not show that the Bund's position was the authentic Jewish position any more than Zionism's was; both were real, competing currents in Jewish political life. It does show that equating "Jewish" with "Zionist" was contested by Jews, at scale, from the movement's first year, and it means the record cannot support the statement that "the Jewish people wanted Israel" as a description of that era.

Satmar, 1958. The religious case against political Zionism received its most substantial modern statement ten years after the state was founded. In 1958 Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, published VaYoel Moshe, the central Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) theological argument against political Zionism [cite:wiki_satmar]. It rests on the Three Oaths of the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Ketubot 111a, a rabbinic tradition holding that the Jewish people swore not to reclaim the land by force or rebel against the nations before the messianic era. In this reading, a state established by human political and military effort is not the fulfillment of Jewish religious hope but a violation of a specific religious commitment. Its objection is to the means and the timing: sovereignty in the land by human political force before the arrival of the Messiah.

Satmar numbers roughly 130,000 people in the United States alone, concentrated in Williamsburg, Kiryas Joel and Monsey, with further communities in Israel, London, Antwerp and Montreal. It is the largest single Hasidic dynasty in the world, and it still teaches this position [cite:wiki_satmar]. That is the documented position of a specific, identifiable tradition. It is not the majority position of Orthodox or Haredi Judaism in general, and it should not be generalized into one.

The strongest case for the other side. Read fairly, these documents also contain the materials of the Zionist argument. Jewish peoplehood was not a Zionist invention: the Bund organized Jews as a nation seeking cultural autonomy, the Reform rabbis of 1885 had to declare that they were "no longer a nation," and Ahad Ha'am, whose quarrel was with Herzl's methods, still placed the Jewish cultural center in Palestine. Satmar's objection is to the timing and the means of a return. And Herzl's turn to politics was a response to antisemitism he witnessed at first hand. On this reading, Zionism was one answer among several to a question that Jews widely shared, and one that drew religious and secular support from its early years; in America, the institutional support it later won came after the Holocaust. Nothing in the record contradicts that reading. What the record contradicts is the stronger claim that Zionism and Judaism are the same thing, so that the one cannot be opposed without opposing the other.

Why the distinction carries weight. The line between a political movement founded in 1897 and a religion and set of lineages far older is one that the founders themselves recognized, that Reform recorded in 1885, that the Bund built a mass movement on in 1897, and that Satmar still teaches in 2026 [cite:basel_program] [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] [cite:wiki_bund] [cite:wiki_satmar]. It continues in contemporary Jewish life in Judith Butler's Parting Ways, in Peter Beinart's The Crisis of Zionism and in the organization Jewish Voice for Peace [cite:butler_parting_ways] [cite:beinart_crisis_zionism] [cite:jvp_org]. When the two are collapsed into one, criticism of a documented political project and the state it produced comes to read as an attack on a people and a religion. That conversion is the slide the section on the word "Semitic" first examines. The Jewish critique of Zionism is not an attack from outside; it is a Jewish tradition older than the state.

A test of the accusation. One argument this book offers takes Herzl's alternatives as a thought experiment. Had the state been built in Uganda or Argentina, could criticism of it plausibly have been called "antisemitic"? The historically dominant local languages of Uganda are Bantu languages, Luganda among them; Argentina's are Spanish and Indigenous American languages such as Quechua, Guaraní and Mapudungun. Neither population speaks a Semitic language. Palestine's population spoke Arabic, which is one [cite:wiki_bantu_languages] [cite:wiki_languages_argentina] [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology]. Since "Semitic" was coined in 1781 as a term for a language family that includes Hebrew, Arabic and Amharic together, and was never a synonym for "Jewish," the argument holds that the conflation is no more valid in Palestine than it would have been anywhere else; it simply found a surface hook there, through a coincidence of geography. The argument has firm limits. It explains a pattern in how a rhetorical move spread; it is not a claim that the move is correct anywhere. Nor does it address whether some criticism of Israeli policy is antisemitic in the settled sense of the word, which is hostility to Jews and which the following sections treat on its own terms.

The same argument names an inconsistency in how the word's root is used. The correct point that Palestinians speak a Semitic language, and share substantial ancestral overlap with Levantine Jewish populations according to the genetic studies of Nebel (2000) and Behar (2010), is often deployed to argue that criticism of Israeli policy cannot coherently be called antisemitic [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] [cite:nebel_pop_genetics_2000]. On the word's linguistic terms, that argument is accurate. But the same breadth of the word rarely appears when the subject is the displacement of some 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians in 1948, or the conditions in Gaza documented later in this library, including a formally confirmed famine. The argument does not propose that "antisemitism" be applied to harm done to Palestinians. Its position is that the word has always meant hatred of Jews specifically and never fit that harm in either direction. Its point is that Palestinian displacement and casualties are documented on their own terms and deserve the same seriousness, whichever way the "Semitic" argument is being pointed.

What the record does not settle. The documents establish a distinction and a debate; they do not decide the debate. They do not show that any one of these positions was the authentic Jewish one, or how Jews outside these organizations and platforms would have answered the national question. The sources differ on the Bund's size, and the record does not show how the Bund and the Zionist movement would have fared against each other had the Holocaust and Soviet repression not destroyed one of them. Reform's 1885 position shows where a major denomination stood in that year, not where it stands now. And the existence of a Jewish tradition of dissent does not show that Zionism's supporters are wrong to experience their support as Jewish. It shows that the distinction itself is real, documented, and older than the state.

sections.h: Dissent from Every Lineage
sections.html:
A common account of Jewish opinion about Zionism runs in one of two directions. In the first, Jewish opposition to the Zionist project is a small and marginal position, held by a handful of eccentrics. In the second, it belongs to one particular community, usually imagined as the Jews of the Middle East set against the Jews of Europe. The documented record supports neither version. Organized opposition to political Zionism, and organized critique of the state it produced, appears on the record in Ashkenazi religious tradition, in Ashkenazi secular socialism, in Ashkenazi-founded Reform theology, among the cultural Zionists who rejected partition, and in the scholarship of Mizrahi Jews living inside Israel itself. The earlier section on [scene:s00c|Zionism and Judaism] set out the distinction between a political movement founded at Basel in 1897 and a religion far older than it. This section follows the people who held that distinction, what each of them actually argued, and what became of them.

The sequence matters, because the traditions differ in kind as well as in origin. Some rejected the Zionist project outright. Some accepted a Jewish national life in Palestine but rejected a Jewish sovereign state and partition. One critiques the state's treatment of its own Jewish citizens. Folding all of these into a single category called "Jewish opposition to Zionism" would flatten a real spectrum, and the record is clearer when they are kept apart.

The first is the Bund, whose founding in Vilna in 1897 the previous section described. It organized Jewish workers across the Russian Empire's Pale of Settlement, the region of the 1880s pogroms and the mass emigration that followed them. It was an overwhelmingly Ashkenazi, Eastern European, socialist movement, and it explicitly rejected emigration to Palestine in favor of Jewish cultural and political autonomy where Jewish communities already lived [cite:wiki_bund]. Its position was not indifference to antisemitism: its members lived through the same pogroms that gave the Zionist movement its urgency. Its argument was strategic. The two movements were born in the same year, from the same communities, in response to the same crisis, and one said leave and build elsewhere while the other said stay and fight for the right to be who you are, where you are. The Bund was a serious, organized mass movement, not a fringe dissent.

Most accounts stop at the founding. What happened next is part of the record too. When the Bolsheviks took power in October 1917, the Bund split. A majority faction, believing it was joining a genuine ally on workers' rights, merged into the Communist Party. A minority led by Vladimir Medem rejected Bolshevik rule as undemocratic and hostile to Jewish national rights. Bundists disagreed among themselves over whether the Bolsheviks could be trusted, and decided the question differently. In 1921 the Bolsheviks formally dissolved the Bund, merger or no merger. Its remaining members were imprisoned or fled abroad, under a government now hostile to independent Jewish political organizing of any kind, socialist or not. Mark Liber, one of the Bund's leading figures and its representative on the Executive Committee of the Petrograd Soviet during the revolution itself, was executed during the Stalinist purges in 1937. He was killed by the state his movement had helped bring to power two decades earlier [cite:jewishcurrents_bund_rise_fall] [cite:britannica_bund].

The Polish Bund took a different path. It survived independently through the interwar years and into the Holocaust, and its members fought alongside Zionists and Communists in the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Survivors tried to regroup in Poland after the war and were suppressed again, this time by Poland's new Communist government. Within a single generation, the organization was dissolved twice, by two different governments, one of which its own members had helped install [cite:jewishcurrents_bund_rise_fall] [cite:britannica_bund]. That history shows what happened to the organization. It does not show that the Bund's argument against Zionism was refuted by it. A movement crushed by force has not thereby been proved wrong, and the record of its suppression is not a verdict on its ideas, in either direction.

Reform Judaism belongs on the same list for a different reason. Its Pittsburgh Platform of 1885, quoted in the previous section, defined Jewish identity as a religious community rather than a nation awaiting territorial restoration, and the movement that adopted it was founded and led by Ashkenazi Jewish immigrants and their American-born successors [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885]. Coming twelve years before Basel, it was not a reaction against Zionism but a Jewish religious position that existed first, on its own terms. It was also not permanent: Reform's institutional position shifted considerably over the twentieth century.

Neturei Karta is today the most publicly visible Haredi Jewish community that opposes Zionism, and it is Ashkenazi in origin and practice. Its ground is theological. Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, set out the argument in VaYoel Moshe in 1958. In this reading, Jewish tradition holds that the ingathering of the exiles and the restoration of sovereignty are to come through divine action in the Messianic era, not through human political and military effort beforehand. To establish a state ahead of that time is itself the transgression, and the central one rather than a side issue [cite:wiki_satmar]. The rabbinic sources behind it, the Three Oaths of the Talmud, have their own history in [scene:oaths_s01|the debate over the Three Oaths].

This is not a lukewarm position. It takes the scriptural promises of restoration seriously enough to conclude that a state built by human political action violates them, the opposite of what many outsiders assume religious Jews believe. Neturei Karta continues to hold it as a current practice and appears at public demonstrations [cite:wiki_satmar]. The record is equally clear about its scale: Neturei Karta is a specific and relatively small community, and most Haredi and Orthodox institutions today hold other positions. What is documented is that a serious, theologically grounded opposition from within Orthodox tradition exists and is active, not that it speaks for Orthodox Judaism as a whole.

The binationalists are the hardest case to classify, which is why they matter. Martin Buber and Judah Magnes, with colleagues including Gershom Scholem and Henrietta Szold, founded Brit Shalom in 1925. It advocated a binational state with full civic equality between Jews and Arabs, rather than a Jewish-majority sovereign state [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom] [cite:wiki_brit_shalom]. Brit Shalom was never a mass movement. It worked more as a small study circle of elite academics and intellectuals. It drew fierce, documented hostility from the dominant Labor and Revisionist Zionist currents, some of whose members called its members traitors. It also had notable public support: Albert Einstein backed it publicly, a fact seldom mentioned alongside his name. Brit Shalom dissolved around 1933, roughly eight years after its founding [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism].

Historians trace its failure to a specific sequence, not simply to unpopularity. The violence at Hebron in 1929 and the Arab Revolt of 1936–39 undermined Brit Shalom's founding premise, that the Arab political leadership would accept binational equality. And the movement never grew beyond its intellectual core into a mass constituency on either side [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism].

The idea outlived the organization. In 1942 Buber and Magnes founded Ihud as a direct response to the Biltmore Conference's demand for a Jewish Commonwealth, again advocating a binational state with full civic equality [cite:wiki_ihud]. In 1947 the two men testified in person against partition before the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP), to David Ben-Gurion's documented fury. Buber told the commission that it was "ethically and politically incumbent" on a regenerated Jewish people to live not merely alongside the Arabs but genuinely with them, developing the country for equal benefit. He called the treatment of the Arab population "the moral acid test of Zionism" [cite:britainpalestine_buber_magnes] [cite:wiki_ihud].

Hannah Arendt reached a related conclusion separately, from outside the Brit Shalom circle. Her 1944 essay "Zionism Reconsidered" warned that pursuing an exclusively Jewish sovereign state, rather than a binational arrangement, risked permanent regional conflict and long-term dependence on a great-power patron for security. She wrote it years before the state was founded [cite:researchgate_arendt_zionism_reconsidered].

The founding of Israel in May 1948 made binationalism moot, and Magnes's position changed with events. He began advocating a confederation between the new Jewish state and a future Palestinian Arab state, a documented development in his thinking cut short by his death that October. Ihud outlived the founding. The following year Buber wrote that "our cause has lost its footing, its face has been sullied, but it has not been overcome." Its publication, Ner, continued until 1964, sixteen years after the state it had argued against creating in that form already existed [cite:wiki_ihud] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism].

Precision about this group is a matter of accuracy. Buber and Magnes are best described as cultural and binational Zionists who rejected the model of sovereignty and partition, not as anti-Zionists in the sense of the Bund or Neturei Karta. Their dissent came from inside the movement's own intellectual core. It shows that the argument was never only between Zionists and their opponents, but also among Zionists over what form Jewish national life in Palestine should take.

The last kind of dissent is different again. The Bund, Reform Judaism and Neturei Karta argued, in their different ways, against the Zionist project itself, before the state existed or regardless of it. The Mizrahi critique comes from people who did move to Israel, live there and are its citizens. Scholars including Ella Shohat, Sami Shalom Chetrit and Yehouda Shenhav documented specific patterns in how the Ashkenazi-dominated Israeli establishment treated Mizrahi Jewish immigrants after 1948: placement in peripheral development towns, discrimination in employment, and the cultural marginalization of Middle Eastern Jewish identity in favor of an Ashkenazi-coded national culture [cite:chetrit_mizrahi_struggle]. The arrival itself, in the transit camps and the affairs that followed, is told in [scene:s00e2|the exodus from the Arab world].

This is a Middle Eastern-lineage critique of the state's conduct, running alongside the Ashkenazi traditions rather than standing in for them. Its limits are also documented. It is a scholarly tradition with named authors and named mechanisms of discrimination. It does not show that all Mizrahi Israelis share it, or that Mizrahi communities are anti-Zionist as a whole. Many Mizrahi Israelis identify strongly with the state.

Placed on one line, the traditions span more than 140 years. Reform's platform of 1885 and Teitelbaum's book of 1958 stand 73 years apart, and none of these currents waited for the others to reach the same conclusion.

The historical traditions say nothing about how many Jews hold any view today. For that, the evidence is polling, and the most detailed recent survey is of American Jews only. The Washington Post surveyed 815 American Jews between 2 and 9 September 2025, with a margin of error of 4.7 points. Sixty-one percent said Israel had committed war crimes against Palestinians [cite:wapo_jews_poll]. Thirty-nine percent said Israel had committed genocide and 51% said it had not; among respondents aged 18 to 34, half said genocide [cite:toi_jews_poll]. Forty-six percent approved of Israel's military conduct and 48% disapproved, and 68% disapproved of Benjamin Netanyahu. The same respondents held other views at the same time. Seventy-six percent said Israel's existence is vital to the Jewish future, 94% said Hamas had committed war crimes, and 91% blamed Hamas for prolonging the war [cite:jta_jews_poll]. For comparison, in February 2024 Pew had found that 62% of American Jews said Israel's conduct was acceptable.

A second set of figures separates attachment from the label. Jewish Federations data show that about 90% of American Jews support Israel's existence as a Jewish and democratic state, while only 37% call themselves "Zionist" [cite:forward_zionist]. Organized opinion spans a wide range: J Street, pro-Israel and pro-two-state; Jewish Voice for Peace, which is anti-Zionist; and Haredi groups such as Neturei Karta, which oppose a Jewish state on religious grounds [cite:forward_zionist]. The pattern in these numbers is a community and not a bloc. Most American Jews are attached to Israel and critical of the war at the same time.

Two fair readings can be drawn from this record. The first holds that dissent has mostly been held by minorities. Neturei Karta is a small community. Brit Shalom was a study circle that lasted about eight years, and Ihud never grew into a mass constituency. Reform Judaism moved away from its 1885 position over the following century. Many Mizrahi Israelis identify strongly with the state. In the 2025 poll, three in four American Jews called Israel vital to the Jewish future, and about nine in ten support its existence as a Jewish and democratic state. On this reading the dissenters were real, but the main current of Jewish life moved the other way.

The second reading holds that dissent has been a real and continuous current. The Bund was a mass movement, not a fringe, and it ended because two governments crushed it, not because its members changed their minds. The binationalists came from the intellectual center of Zionism itself and testified against partition before the United Nations in 1947. The theological case against a state is still taught and still practiced. And the gap between the roughly 90% who support Israel's existence and the 37% who call themselves Zionist suggests that the word and the attachment are not the same thing for many American Jews. Both readings rest on documented facts. They differ over weight, not over the record.

What the record shows plainly is that the dividing line in these debates has not been lineage. Some of the earliest, most organized and most theologically serious Jewish opposition to Zionism was Ashkenazi, and one of the most developed critiques of the Israeli state's conduct was Mizrahi. To frame opposition as something only Middle Eastern Jews do, while European Jews uniformly support Zionism, would invert the evidence. The line runs through every lineage, between those who hold the specific political position of Zionism and those who contest or reject it.

Several things the record here does not settle. It contains no current polling on what share of Ashkenazi, Sephardi or Mizrahi Jews support or oppose Zionism, and it cannot say how any lineage divides today. It documents no distinctly Sephardi tradition of dissent alongside the Ashkenazi and Mizrahi ones. The detailed polling is of American Jews alone, and it measures views of Israel's conduct in a war, which is not the same question as support for Zionism. And none of these traditions shows by itself which side of the argument was right. The record establishes something narrower and firmer: that support and opposition have both had serious, long-standing representation within Jewish life, across every lineage it documents.

sections.h: One Verse, Two Readings: Christians and the Promise to Abraham
sections.html:
Two opposite claims are often made about the Bible and the modern State of Israel. One holds that scripture requires Christians to support the state. The other holds that scripture has nothing to do with the question. Neither describes the actual situation, which is a long-running argument among Christians themselves over what one set of verses means and to whom they now apply. The verse at the center of it is Genesis 12:3, the text Christian Zionists cite most. It was spoken to Abram, later Abraham: "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you." The promise of land follows in the same narrative, at Genesis 12:7, 15:18 and 17:8.

The words themselves are not in dispute. The question is who the "you" of the promise is today. One answer identifies it with the Jewish people and, since 1948, with the State of Israel, a secular state. Another holds that the promise was fulfilled in Christ and the church and does not pass to any modern government. The two answers lead to opposite political conclusions from the same text.

The Christian Zionist reading treats the verse as a standing instruction. Groups such as the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem describe it as the biblical mandate for standing with Israel [cite:icej_cz] [cite:rmc_cz]. On this reading the blessing and the curse attach to how nations and individuals treat the Jewish people and their state now, and the land promise of Genesis 12:7, 15:18 and 17:8 remains in force. Many believers in dispensationalism, a system of reading biblical prophecy, go further and regard Israel's restoration as a precondition of Christ's return. That framework was popularized by the notes of the Scofield Reference Bible, whose history is told in [scene:s05|the Scofield Bible]. The older British and American Protestant campaign for a Jewish restoration to Palestine is told in [scene:bc_s05|the Protestant restoration lobby]. The strongest form of this reading rests on the text's plain wording: the blessing and the curse as spoken, and the land promised again at 12:7, 15:18 and 17:8.

The other reading belongs to covenant theology and to what theologians call "amillennial" theology. It holds that the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ and in the church, citing Paul's letter to the Galatians (3:16 and 3:29), and that it does not transfer to a modern government [cite:studylight_gen12] [cite:pctii_gen12]. Some scholars add a point about emphasis: the passage stresses blessing to all the nations of the earth more than it stresses land [cite:pctii_gen12]. The strongest form of this reading is that it takes its key from within the Christian scriptures themselves, in Paul's own reading of the promise, and gives full weight to the verse's last clause: "all peoples on earth will be blessed through you."

The argument is old, but in June 2025 it became public in a way that reached far beyond seminaries. Senator Ted Cruz cited Genesis 12:3 in an exchange with Tucker Carlson, and Carlson asked whether the political state led by Benjamin Netanyahu is the same "Israel" as the one in scripture [cite:think_gen12]. The question he put is the hinge of the whole dispute. Cruz's position rests on the identification of the biblical Israel with the modern state. Carlson's question rests on the distinction between them. Neither man settled it, and no verse can settle it on its own, because the disagreement is about how to read the verse, not about what it says.

The first reading is the theology behind the largest pro-Israel constituency in the United States. How an annotated Bible became a political force, from the dispensationalist pulpit to organized lobbying in Washington, is drawn in the map below. Its organizations, members and money are documented in later volumes of this library, where the figures carry their own sources.

A frequent question about the dispensationalist reading is why the Roman Catholic Church never campaigned against it. The premise is half right. Rome never ran a public campaign. But it did rule on the theology. In the 1940s the Holy Office, the Vatican's doctrinal authority and the predecessor of today's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, judged that premillennialism, the prophetic framework at the core of Scofield's system, "cannot safely be taught" [cite:catholic_answers_rapture_tract]. The rejection is still in force. Paragraph 676 of the Catechism of the Catholic Church rejects millenarianism as "the intrinsic perversity" of a falsely secularized understanding of the Kingdom of God [cite:catholicculture_five_myths_rapture]. The position is public and available to anyone. It is simply not widely known.

It stayed quiet for structural reasons. Catholic doctrinal statements are addressed to Catholics, through the Church's own teaching, not issued as public rebuttals of particular Protestant authors or their reference Bibles. Rulings against specific Protestant theological systems routinely remain inside Church documents and catechetical teaching rather than becoming public campaigns, and the Church generally does not campaign against the doctrines of Protestant denominations with which it is not in active dialogue. This was a general pattern, not a special case invented for dispensationalism [cite:worldfinance_vatican_bank_history]. Rome also had no authority over Protestant publishing in the first place. Its doctrinal jurisdiction runs over Catholic teaching, and the Reformation had ended any mechanism by which it could approve or block a Protestant publisher's Bible centuries before Scofield. What the ruling records is the Church's own position on the theology, not an attempt or an ability to control what Protestant publishers printed. Nor does the silence show indifference: the ruling, and its place in the current Catechism, record a sustained position, only not a public one. Whether individual Catholics or parishes ever hear of paragraph 676 is a different matter, and the record here does not measure it.

Rome's diplomatic record shows what a church that did not read the promise in dispensationalist terms actually did when Zionism came to it. In January 1904 Theodor Herzl sought an audience with Pope Pius X to ask for Vatican support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine. The Pope refused. His documented answer was that the Church could not support Jewish restoration to a land central to its own theology while denying Christ [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition]. That refusal held as Vatican policy for 89 years. In 1949, a year after Israel's founding, the Vatican worked behind the scenes at the United Nations to make Israel's admission conditional on two commitments: allowing the return of Palestinian refugees, and formal guarantees for Christian and Muslim holy sites, particularly in Jerusalem. Ben-Gurion said that year: "There is a major religion in the world, which has to settle with us a historical reckoning." The campaign failed. Israel was admitted to the United Nations in May 1949 without the guarantees the Holy See had sought.

What changed the Church's course was a change in its doctrine. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate of 1965 revised Catholic teaching on Judaism, stating that God "holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers." That shift was the precondition for what followed. On 30 December 1993 the Holy See and Israel signed the Fundamental Agreement in Jerusalem, establishing diplomatic relations, 45 years after Israel's founding, and ambassadors were exchanged in 1994. Even then, property rights, tax exemptions and the status of Jerusalem were left for continuing negotiation under the agreement's own terms [cite:wiki_fundamental_agreement]. The documented reasons for the long delay were three: the Church's theology of the Jewish people's role in salvation history, the unresolved status of Jerusalem's holy sites, and concern for the Palestinian Christian and Muslim communities under the new state [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition]. After the UN General Assembly's vote of November 2012, the Vatican formally recognized the State of Palestine, and in 2015 it signed an accord governing the Church's activity in Palestinian-controlled territory, which drew a formal Israeli protest [cite:gulfnews_vatican_palestine_accord]. The full story is told in [scene:vat_s01|the Vatican's 45 years].

Two further points complicate any picture of a simple religious alignment. Within Judaism, too, views of the state's religious meaning differ: early Zionism was largely secular, and some Haredi Jews oppose a Jewish state before the coming of the Messiah. And Palestinian Christians, about 1% of the population today, are part of this story too, as a community with its own history in the land and not only as a subject of other Christians' theology.

The record settles what the verse says, which traditions read it which way, what Rome ruled and when, and how long it took the Holy See to recognize Israel. It does not settle the theological question, which is not a historical one: whether a promise made to Abraham applies to a state founded in 1948 depends on a reader's prior commitments about how scripture is to be read. Nor does the material here say how many Christians hold each reading. What it does show is that "the Bible requires it" and "the Bible is irrelevant" are both wrong as descriptions. The verse matters a great deal to many Christians, and they draw opposite conclusions from it.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Two Displacements
chapters.intro:
In the middle of the twentieth century two large movements of people reshaped the region. In the war of 1947–1949 roughly 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians were displaced, the event Palestinians call the Nakba.[cite:wiki_nakba] Between 1948 and 1972 roughly 850,000 Jews left Arab and Muslim countries. The two are often told as one story, in which each cancels the other. This chapter tells them separately, each on its own record, and then tests the comparison.

It sits in the Baseline, ahead of the history of 1948, because the comparison is made constantly and usually without its evidence, and because the Jewish exodus belongs to many countries and runs through decades that the history of the Mandate does not reach. The Palestinian displacement is told in full in the next volume; here it appears as one side of the comparison.

The first section follows the exodus from Iraq, where the turning point came in Baghdad on 1–2 June 1941, seven years before Israel existed, with the pogrom known as the Farhud.[cite:ushmm_farhud] It traces Iraq's criminalization of "Zionism" in 1948, the law of March 1950 that made departure conditional on surrendering citizenship, the airlift called Operation Ezra and Nehemiah, the disputed Baghdad bombings and Israel's sabotage operation in Egypt in 1954, and then the arrival in Israel: the transit camps, the Yemenite Children Affair and the Ringworm Affair.[cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The second section goes country by country, through Libya, Egypt, Aleppo, Aden and Bahrain, Yemen, Morocco and Algeria, and sets out the arguments over the total and over the word "refugees."[cite:rs_ch01_beker_jpsr] [cite:rs_ch01_ahram_amayreh] The third compares the two displacements on mechanism, duration, the number of governments involved and citizenship afterwards, and shows why the claim of an even exchange is rejected from both directions.

Throughout, two readings of the Jewish departures are kept side by side: rescue from persecution, and active recruitment by the Israeli state and the Jewish Agency. The record documents both, in proportions that differed from country to country.

sections.h: The Exodus of 1941–1972 and Its Aftermath
sections.html:
Between 1948 and 1972, roughly 850,000 Jews left Arab and Muslim countries, from about two dozen states over some 24 years. The usual way of telling it is short: Jews were persecuted throughout Arab lands until Israel gave them refuge. That sentence contains real history, and it leaves out most of it. The documents show several causes working at once, each recorded on its own: violence and legal persecution by Arab governments, organized and named recruitment operations run by Israel and the Jewish Agency, and, in one specific and well-documented Egyptian case, sabotage carried out by Israeli military intelligence. They also show that arrival in Israel was not the end of the story. What happened to many of the newcomers in their first years is a second, separate story, in places a grave one, and Israel's own state commissions and independent researchers have investigated it without reaching full agreement.

This section follows that record in order: Iraq first, because its documentation is richest and its turning point came earliest; then the other airlifts and the Egyptian operation, briefly; then the transit camps, the disappearance of children from Yemenite and other Mizrahi families, and the mass irradiation of immigrant children for ringworm. The country-by-country figures, and the argument over the total, are set out in [scene:ch01_exodus_map|the next section].

Baghdad, June 1941. The turning point in Iraqi Jewish memory came seven years before Israel existed. Rashid Ali al-Gailani led a pro-Axis coup in Iraq. The British defeated it, and his government collapsed days before the violence began. Its fall left a vacuum in the capital and inflamed the nationalist and pro-Axis feeling it had stirred.[cite:wiki_farhud] On 1–2 June 1941, during the Jewish festival of Shavuot, crowds in Baghdad turned on the city's Jews. Iraqi soldiers and police who had backed the coup, together with the pro-Axis youth militias known as the Futuwwa, incited and led two days of killing, rape and looting. Civilian mobs and Bedouin from the city's outskirts joined them. British forces, victorious just outside the city, did not intervene.[cite:ushmm_farhud] [cite:wiki_farhud] The event is known as the Farhud. The vague word "riots" is sometimes still used for it. The record describes a targeted pogrom with members of the state's own security forces among the perpetrators.

The death toll is given differently in different sources, and the differences should be stated rather than smoothed over. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the most authoritative single source on the event, gives 150 to 180 Jews killed, 600 injured, an undetermined number of women raped, and roughly 1,500 stores and homes looted.[cite:ushmm_farhud] An official commission of inquiry appointed by the Iraqi government recorded 128 killed by its own count, with independent estimates running as high as 180; the same account gives more than 1,000 injured and roughly 900 Jewish homes and more than 1,500 businesses looted or destroyed.[cite:ushmm_farhud] Some other sources put the dead at 500 or more.[cite:wiki_farhud] On any of these counts, the event marked the point after which Iraq's ancient Jewish community began its decline toward near-total emigration within a decade.[cite:ushmm_farhud]

The date matters for the argument as much as the toll. The Farhud took place in June 1941. Israel was declared in May 1948. Whatever role the pogrom later played in hastening departures, it cannot have been a reaction to the 1948 war or to the Nakba, the Palestinian displacement of that war. It does not show, on the other hand, that every later departure from Iraq was driven by the same forces. The departures of 1950 and 1951 had their own, additional causes.

Iraq at war, 1947–1949. After the United Nations voted for partition in November 1947, anti-Jewish measures in Iraq escalated. Pogroms gave way to systematic confiscation of property and to prosecutions on what one account calls trumped-up charges.[cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] On 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared its independence, Iraq joined the Arab invasion. When the fighting ended, Iraq was the only Arab combatant that refused to sign an armistice with Israel, so that a formal state of war between the two has, technically, never ended.[cite:govil_aliyah] This is easy to lose inside the phrase "the 1948 war." For Iraq's Jews it meant that their state remained formally at war with the state that most of them would soon enter.

On 19 July 1948, Iraq made "Zionism" a crime punishable by up to seven years in prison. Because every Jew was presumed to be a Zionist, the law worked as a blanket criminalization of the whole community. The testimony of two Muslim witnesses was enough to convict, and there was little avenue for appeal.[cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] On 23 September 1948, Shafiq Ades, a prominent and well-connected Jewish businessman, was publicly hanged in Basra on charges of selling weapons to Israel and to the Iraqi Communist Party. His body was left hanging for hours as a public spectacle. The case is widely cited as the one that broke what remained of the community's sense of security: if a man of his standing was not safe, no one was.[cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:govil_aliyah]

The law of March 1950 and the airlift. On 2 March 1950, Iraq's parliament passed a law permitting Jews to leave on condition that they surrender their Iraqi citizenship.[cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] It was framed as permission. It worked, once people registered, as a mechanism for stripping them of nationality and then of property: a subsequent law required departing Jews to sell their property and liquidate their businesses before leaving, and the state denaturalized those who registered and stripped them of their assets.[cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] [cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] Economic loss was written into the exit itself.

Israel and the Jewish Agency organized the airlift that followed, Operation Ezra and Nehemiah. It was named for the biblical leaders of the return from the Babylonian exile, a deliberate echo of the community's own origins.[cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] Shlomo Hillel, an Iraqi-born agent of Mossad LeAliyah Bet, negotiated personally with the Iraqi authorities and helped organize the operation; he later described it from the inside in a memoir, Operation Babylon.[cite:wiki_shlomo_hillel] The aircraft were provided by the Near East Transport Company and El Al. One account gives the route as through Cyprus and Iran; another gives it as through Cyprus at first and later by direct flights from Baghdad to Lod.[cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] [cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] The cost was largely met by the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, at about $4 million.[cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] [cite:govil_aliyah]

The pace overwhelmed the planning. Israeli immigration authorities had prepared to receive about 300 people a day; at the peak, 1,400 arrived daily. By the end of 1951 more than 107,000 Iraqi Jews had been airlifted, and about 16,000 more had left by other routes.[cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] By early 1952, a community of some 2,800 years' standing had been reduced to about 6,000 people. Israeli government sources put its size before the airlift at about 135,000; another account gives roughly 130,000.[cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] Summary accounts give the number airlifted as about 120,000 to 130,000.[cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah]

These facts establish a real, organized, named Israeli operation and a real Iraqi legal mechanism that made departure conditional on giving up citizenship and property. They do not, by themselves, say why so many Iraqi Jews chose to go. The Farhud, the criminal law of 1948, the hanging in Basra, the conditions of the 1950 law and the airlift's own active recruitment are all documented as contributing causes. None of them is the single cause.

The Baghdad bombings, 1950–1951. One part of this story is disputed, and the dispute is real. Between April 1950 and June 1951, at least five bombing incidents struck Jewish institutions and gathering places in Baghdad, among them the Masuda Shemtov synagogue. At least four Jews were killed and others injured.[cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] The attacks fell in exactly the months when the March 1950 law was driving mass registration for emigration. Iraq tried men for the bombings, and two of them, Basri and Shalom, were hanged in January 1952.[cite:meforum_exodus]

Two accounts of who was responsible have stood against each other ever since. The Iraqi government of the time, and later some historians, attributed the bombings to Zionist underground agents seeking to panic the community into leaving faster. Israeli officials have consistently and firmly denied any involvement, and have called the accusation an antisemitic fabrication meant to shift blame for a persecution the Iraqi state had itself created through years of pogroms, denaturalization and criminalization.[cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] A review of newly released Israeli, British and American archives, published by the Middle East Forum, found insufficient evidence to confirm Israeli involvement, while not closing the question entirely. The executions do not settle it either: the fairness and evidentiary basis of the trials, held amid intense anti-Zionist feeling, are themselves disputed.[cite:meforum_exodus]

What the record shows is real bombings, real deaths, and a real Iraqi prosecution that ended in executions. What it does not show is proof of who was responsible. Both the contemporary Iraqi accusation and the Israeli denial are documented positions. The evidence now available does not decide between them, and this book does not pretend that it does in either direction.

Yemen, Morocco and Egypt. Iraq's was one of three major named operations, each in a different country on a different timetable. Operation Magic Carpet airlifted approximately 48,000 to 49,000 Yemenite Jews to Israel in 1949–50. Operation Yachin, conducted in secret from 1961 to 1964, brought Moroccan Jews, later than the other two because Morocco's political timeline was different. Both, like Ezra and Nehemiah, were organized operations of the Israeli state and the Jewish Agency, not spontaneous flight, though the hardships in the countries of origin were also real and documented.[cite:wiki_idf_operations_list] Conditions and causes were not the same in all three countries, and they are not treated here as one undifferentiated movement; Yemen's and Morocco's own circumstances, including the payments made for Moroccan departures, are set out country by country in the next section.

Egypt supplies the one documented case of sabotage, and it touches this story because of whom it used. In July 1954, Israeli military intelligence, known as Aman, activated Unit 131, a cell of Egyptian Jews it had recruited and trained for the purpose. The cell placed incendiary devices at a post office, at American information-agency libraries in Cairo and Alexandria, and at British-owned cinemas. The intention was that the attacks would be blamed on Egyptian nationalists or communists and would persuade Britain to keep its troops in the Suez Canal Zone.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] Another summary of the same operation gives the intended scapegoats as Egyptian nationalists or the Muslim Brotherhood, and the aim as damaging Western confidence in Nasser's government.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The plan unraveled when a device ignited prematurely in an operative's pocket in Alexandria, and the cell was arrested.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair]

The people who paid were the local operatives, not the planners. At the Egyptian trial Moshe Marzouk and Shmuel Azar were sentenced to death and executed in January 1955. Max Bennett, an Israeli officer, took his own life in prison. Others received long sentences. Israel did not acknowledge the operatives for decades, and publicly honored the survivors in 2005.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The operation, later called Operation Susannah, is the earliest documented case of the Israeli state attacking a close ally's facilities under a false attribution.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] That it took place is not in dispute. Who ordered it is. Defense Minister Pinhas Lavon denied giving the order; the head of military intelligence, Binyamin Gibli, claimed that he had. Lavon resigned in 1955; one account describes him as forced out. The question was reopened in 1960 amid evidence that documents had been forged, split the ruling Mapai party, and contributed to Ben-Gurion's resignation in 1963. Who gave the order was never formally resolved.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The full affair is told in [scene:lv_s01|the Lavon Affair]. The record documents this pattern for Egypt only; it does not establish it for any other country in this account.

Two readings. The rescue reading holds that these were communities in danger, and that Israel brought them out. Its evidence is strong and specific: a pogrom in 1941 with soldiers and police among the killers, a 1948 law that made every Jew in Iraq a presumed criminal, a public hanging meant to be seen, an exit law that took citizenship and property together. The recruitment-and-sabotage reading holds that the Israeli state did not only receive these communities but actively worked to bring them, and in one place used local Jews in an operation that endangered them. Its evidence is also specific: named operations, a named agent negotiating with the Iraqi government, organized airlifts at a pace the reception system could not absorb, and the documented operation in Egypt. The disputed Baghdad bombings sit between the two readings, and the record cannot assign them to either. Neither reading cancels the other. Persecution, recruitment and, in one documented case, sabotage all operated, in proportions that differed from country to country.

Arrival: the ma'abarot. Being airlifted out of danger and being welcomed into equal opportunity were two different things. New arrivals, disproportionately Mizrahi, were housed in crowded transit camps called ma'abarot, at first in tents and later in basic shacks. These were spartan, temporary conditions, not immediate settlement in established communities or housing.[cite:honestreporting_forgotten_refugees] Ashkenazi immigrants arriving in the same period tended to be better educated on arrival and more likely to assimilate into the existing, largely Ashkenazi-run secular establishment. They also qualified for German war-reparations payments, which Mizrahi immigrants, who had never lived under Nazi occupation, could not receive.[cite:honestreporting_forgotten_refugees] The difference in starting conditions was structural, tied to reparations eligibility and to who already ran the institutions, not to prejudice alone. Individual lives varied widely. The pattern itself is documented.

The Yemenite Children Affair. Between 1948 and 1954, hundreds of infants and small children of Yemenite and other Mizrahi immigrant families disappeared from Israeli state hospitals and transit camps. Families were frequently told that their children had died, often without receiving a body, a death certificate or any information about burial.[cite:nytimes_disappeared_children] That basic pattern, of disappearance and inadequate explanation, is not in dispute.

What lay behind it is. A state inquiry, the Cohen-Kedmi Commission, investigated for nearly seven years, from 1995 to 2001. Its official finding was unequivocal: claims that the children had been deliberately kidnapped in a government-organized plot were not substantiated. It also acknowledged that the fates of 42 children remained unaccounted for even after its work.[cite:wiki_kedmi_commission] Against that finding stands serious, evidence-based dissent, not a fringe theory. The researcher Shoshana Madmoni-Gerber and hundreds of collected family testimonies support the argument that the disappearances reflect a real, coordinated pattern rather than isolated administrative failures.[cite:nytimes_disappeared_children] The activist Uzi Meshulam campaigned prominently for a fuller inquiry and was imprisoned in connection with his campaign, which is itself a disputed chapter in how the authorities handled the issue.[cite:wiki_uzi_meshulam]

Both positions are documented, and the people who have studied the primary evidence most closely still disagree. This book does not hold the commission's finding to be definitively right, nor the dissenting researchers and families. What is not in dispute is that children disappeared, that their families were given inadequate answers, and that what happened, and why, remains contested. The state's later decisions on the affair belong to a later period; they are taken up in [scene:mz_s02|a later chapter].

The Ringworm Affair. A separate scandal touched the same communities, and the two should not be confused. Through the 1950s, Israeli medical authorities treated scalp ringworm, a common condition at the time, by irradiating immigrant children with X-rays. The children treated were disproportionately Mizrahi and North African. One frequently cited figure puts the total in this campaign at roughly 27,000 children; estimates of the affected population run from about 20,000 to more than 100,000, the higher figures including comparable campaigns elsewhere.[cite:wiki_ringworm_affair]

Part of the motive was practical and is documented. Ringworm was grounds for exclusion under the immigration rules of the United States and other countries, which put direct institutional pressure on the authorities to treat and clear affected children so that their resettlement could proceed.[cite:wiki_ringworm_affair] Irradiation was a recognized treatment for ringworm elsewhere in the world in the same period, including among children who were not Mizrahi, and the record does not show that each individual decision was taken in bad faith. What it does show is the scale, the disproportionate effect on Mizrahi and North African children, and the immigration-driven pressure behind it. A 2003 Israeli documentary, The Ringworm Children, presented the episode as a serious, state-linked medical scandal, and used language as strong as "holocaust" to describe it. That choice of word is itself a measure of how gravely the episode is remembered in the communities it affected.[cite:wiki_ringworm_affair]

What left, and what remained. The headline figure of 850,000 is large and real. It is not the same claim as the end of Jewish life in the Middle East. It was a minority of the total Jewish population that had lived across the Muslim-majority world for more than a thousand years, in cities where Jewish communities were sometimes a third of the population or more. The presence thinned, in some cities dramatically: one account describes Baghdad's community of 140,000 as functionally gone today. But it did not vanish everywhere, and it did not go all at once or for one reason. The flattened version, "they all left because they were persecuted," survives because it is a simpler sentence than "a partial departure with several causes took place over 24 years, with real differences from country to country." It undersells how long the shared life lasted, and it oversells how complete the departure was.

The record leaves three questions open. It does not establish who planted the bombs in Baghdad in 1950 and 1951. It does not establish who gave the order for the Egyptian operation of 1954. And it does not establish what became of the children of Yemenite and other Mizrahi families whose fates even the state's own commission could not account for. Nor can it weigh, family by family, how much each departure owed to fear and how much to recruitment. The exact total of those who left, and whether they should be called refugees, are themselves argued over, as the next section shows.

sections.h: Country by Country: How the Jews of the Arab World Left
sections.html:
The departure of the Jews of the Arab world is usually told as one event with one number attached. It was a series of departures, country by country, each with its own dates, its own laws and its own violence, and each recorded by different sources with different degrees of certainty. The previous section followed Iraq, the largest single case, and the arrival camps in Israel [scene:s00e2|the exodus and its aftermath]. This section takes the other communities in turn: what happened in each place, who decided it, and where the people went. It ends with the two arguments that still surround the whole movement: how many left, and whether they should be called refugees.

Two common shortcuts fail on the record. One says that Israel's ties to Yemen began with the Houthis and that its ties to Morocco began with the agreements of 2020. In both countries the first connection was a community of people who left decades earlier. The other shortcut makes every departure an expulsion, or every departure a voluntary emigration organized from Israel. The country record shows both, often in the same place.

Libya. Libya had about 21,000 Jews in 1911, about 4% of a population of 550,000, and 30,387 on the eve of the Second World War. Italy's racial laws of 1938 were enforced in Libya from 1940. By June 1942 some 2,584 Jews had been deported to the camp at Giado, where 562 of them died.[cite:rs_ch01_yv_libya] More violence came after the war, under British military administration. In November 1945 a three-day attack on the Jews of Tripoli killed 120 Jews and destroyed at least five synagogues. Riots in 1948 killed 12 more and destroyed 280 homes.[cite:rs_ch01_yv_libya] According to Yad Vashem, 30,972 Libyan Jews emigrated to Israel in the wake of the violence around 1948. Those who stayed were pushed to the margins by law: a 1961 law denied nearly all Jews proof of citizenship. After riots in 1967 about 6,000 were airlifted to Rome, and by 2004 no Jews remained in Libya.[cite:rs_ch01_yv_libya] In Libya, then, the sequence ran from a fascist camp to a postwar pogrom under a European administration, then a mass departure to Israel, and finally legal exclusion. The Tripoli killings of 1945 came before the partition vote and before Israel existed.

Egypt. Egypt's community numbered an estimated 75,000–80,000 at its height in 1948. That figure is an Israeli Foreign Ministry estimate, cited by the University of Washington's Stroum Center. Bombs in Cairo's Jewish quarter between June and November 1948 killed more than 70 Jews, according to the same essay.[cite:rs_ch01_uw_egypt1956] A second break came with the Suez war. From 29 October 1956 the Egyptian government treated Jews as enemies of the state. About 1,000 were arrested in Cairo and 450 Jewish-owned businesses were confiscated. From 15 November, Jews leaving the country had to sign forms renouncing their property and their Egyptian citizenship. These details rest on the historian Joel Beinin and on an American Jewish Committee factsheet of March 1957.[cite:rs_ch01_uw_egypt1956] According to figures cited by the Stroum Center, about 25,000 Jews left Egypt in 1956, leaving roughly 15,000 in the country in 1957.[cite:rs_ch01_uw_egypt1956] Egypt's departures therefore came in at least two waves, eight years apart, with different triggers: the violence of 1948, and state measures taken during the Suez war. A third episode belongs to Egypt's story, the 1954 Israeli sabotage operation in which Egyptian Jews were recruited; it is told in the previous section.

Aleppo, Aden and Bahrain: the partition vote. The United Nations voted to partition Palestine on 29 November 1947. Within a week, Jewish communities far from Palestine were attacked. According to the Center for Israel Education, rioters in Aleppo on 30 November damaged the Great Synagogue and the Aleppo Codex, a manuscript of the tenth century. They destroyed some 150 Jewish homes, 50 shops, five schools and 18 synagogues.[cite:rs_ch01_cie_nov1947] In Aden, then under British rule, rioting from 2 December 1947 killed 82 Jews and wounded 76. In Manama, Bahrain, on 5 December, the synagogue was destroyed and one Jewish woman was killed, according to the same source.[cite:rs_ch01_cie_nov1947] These three accounts rest on one outlet, and the figures are given here as it reports them. The sources available for this book do not record how many Jews left each of these places afterwards, or where they went.

Yemen. Yemen's Jews were among the oldest Jewish communities in the world and had lived there for well over a thousand years. Between June 1949 and September 1950 Operation Magic Carpet, also called "On Wings of Eagles", airlifted about 49,000 of them to Israel. It was organized with the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee and flown by Alaska Airlines and other carriers. Many of the emigrants first walked for weeks to reach the British colony of Aden, where the flights began.[cite:w_magic_carpet] Some accounts round the total to nearly 50,000. In Israel many were placed in transit camps, where hundreds of children were reported dead or missing. This became the Yemenite Children Affair, for which Israel expressed "regret" and paid compensation in 2021 [scene:mz_s02|the Yemenite Children Affair]. So Israel's first tie to Yemen was a people moved by airlift, some seventy years before the missiles.

Morocco. Morocco's Jewish community had been rooted there for two millennia and was among the largest in the Arab world, numbering in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s. Most emigrated after 1948, the majority to Israel. Between 1961 and 1964 a secret operation, Operation Yachin, brought about 97,000 Moroccan Jews to Israel with the Moroccan government's quiet consent. Historians record that Israel, together with American Jewish organizations, made payments to the Moroccan government to allow the departures.[cite:w_yachin] The money chain here ran in the opposite direction from Egypt's confiscations. A foreign state and diaspora organizations paid a sovereign government, and that government allowed its citizens to leave. The records available here do not give the amount. Israelis of Moroccan descent became one of Israel's largest communities. The two states' official ties came much later and did not last at first: Morocco and Israel opened low-level liaison offices in 1994, after the Oslo agreements, and closed them in 2000 during the second intifada.[cite:w_isr_morocco] The relationship formalized in 2020 rested on people and quiet arrangements that were decades older.

Algeria. Algeria shows how much the map depended on which empire held a country. The Crémieux Decree of 24 October 1870 made Algeria's Jews French citizens. The Vichy regime withdrew that citizenship on 7 October 1940, and it was restored on 20 October 1943. Rioting in Constantine in 1934 killed 25 Jews.[cite:rs_ch01_jvl_algeria] According to the Jewish Virtual Library, Algeria had about 140,000 Jews in the mid-1950s, and almost 130,000 of them moved to France when Algeria became independent in 1962. Over the whole period from 1948, 25,681 Algerian Jews immigrated to Israel.[cite:rs_ch01_jvl_algeria] Most of Algeria's Jews went to the country whose citizens they already were, at independence, more than a decade after 1948.

Read together, the cases show three separate mechanisms, often working at once. The first was violence by crowds, sometimes in places under British rule, as in Tripoli in 1945 and Aden in 1947. The second was the action of states: Egypt's renunciation forms in 1956, Libya's citizenship law of 1961 and, in Iraq, the denaturalization law told in the previous section. The third was organized emigration arranged from outside: airlifts by Israel and Jewish organizations in Yemen, and a paid, secret agreement in Morocco. Who could act also differed from place to place. In Morocco and Iraq governments negotiated the terms of exit. In Egypt in 1956 the government set them alone. In Algeria the decisive fact was a French citizenship that dated from 1870.

How many? The total is disputed, and the figures come from sources with different purposes. The account of the exodus in this book uses roughly 850,000 Jews leaving Arab and Muslim countries between 1948 and 1972. A survey of the regional aftermath gives estimates "commonly in the range of 800,000–900,000" for Arab countries and Iran from 1948 to the 1970s.[cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] Avi Beker, writing in the Jewish Political Studies Review, gives about 900,000 Jews "forced out" of Arab countries, of whom about 650,000 went to Israel.[cite:rs_ch01_beker_jpsr] Beker writes as an advocate of one side of the argument that follows, and his figure is a position in that argument, not a settled count. The figures also differ in scope: one includes Iran, their end years differ, and Beker's counts those he describes as forced out.

Refugees? The sharper dispute is over the word itself. One position holds that these Jews were refugees in the same sense as the Palestinians of 1948. Beker sets out this "dual refugee problem" case, which the United States House of Representatives took up in H. Con. Res. 311 in October 2003. In this view about 900,000 Jews were forced out of Arab countries, and their case has been forgotten through international indifference and Israel's own reluctance to call it expulsion.[cite:rs_ch01_beker_jpsr] The strongest form of the case rests on records like those above: the Giado camp, Tripoli, the partition-vote riots, the Egyptian renunciation forms, and laws that stripped people of citizenship and property.

The opposing position holds that the comparison does not fit. The Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav argued in Haaretz in 2006 that Palestinians did not leave of their own volition, while Arab Jews moved to Israel under initiatives by the state and Jewish organizations, some willingly and some not. The Palestinian writer Khalid Amayreh, in an opinion piece in Ahram Online in 2012 that quotes Shenhav, called the equation propaganda meant to offset the Nakba.[cite:rs_ch01_ahram_amayreh] The strongest form of this case also rests on the record: the organized airlift from Yemen, the payments to Morocco, and the recruitment operations described in the previous section.

A middle line accepts parts of both. The Stroum Center essay treats the Egyptian departures of 1956 as an expulsion. It also warns, citing the historian Eyal Bizawe, against using Mizrahi history to cast Arab societies as permanent enemies, and asks that the history of coexistence be taught alongside the history of the expulsions.[cite:rs_ch01_uw_egypt1956] This book's reading of the country record is close to that line. Some communities were expelled or driven out by violence and law, some left through organized operations, many left under both pressures at once, and the balance differed by country and by year. Whether the Jewish departures and the Palestinian displacement of 1948 can be set side by side as an "exchange" is a separate question, taken up in [scene:s00e3|the next section].

Much remains unsettled. The overall total is a range, and different authors set its ends for their own reasons. For Aleppo, Aden and Bahrain this book has the violence but not the departures that followed. For Egypt it has neither the destinations nor a full count of the 1948 wave. The amount paid to Morocco under Operation Yachin is not given. The sources also leave open the question each family faced: how far a given departure was flight, how far it was choice, and how far it was the result of someone else's negotiation. The record shows only that all three happened.

sections.h: "An Even Population Exchange"? Two Displacements Compared
sections.html:
Two great displacements followed the end of British rule in Palestine. In the war of 1947–1949 roughly 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians were displaced, the event Palestinians call the Nakba. Over the next quarter-century most of the Jewish communities of the Arab world left the countries where they lived. A familiar way of settling the account sets one against the other. In this telling the two were a clean and roughly equal population exchange: Jews out of Arab countries, Arabs out of Palestine, the one canceling the other. Both displacements are real and documented, and both were grievous for the people who lived through them. What does not hold up is the claim that they were one matched exchange. Set side by side, they differ in mechanism, in duration, in the number of governments involved and in what happened to the displaced afterwards.

Start with the Palestinian displacement. Its scale and timing are documented as concentrated: roughly 700,000 to 750,000 people displaced within a single war of about eighteen months, from 1947 to 1949. Direct military and paramilitary action substantially drove it, including massacres at named places, Deir Yassin, Lydda, Ramla and al-Dawayima. It was carried out by an identifiable set of forces: the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi, and after independence the Israel Defense Forces.[cite:wiki_nakba] [cite:tandfonline_nakba_education] The displaced were not allowed to return. The causes, the individual episodes and the historians' arguments over them are told in their own place [scene:s10|the Nakba] and [scene:np_s01|the historiography of 1948]. For the comparison here, the shape is what matters: one war, one set of forces, a compressed timeline.

The dashboard panel above gives the round number most often used, about 700,000 Palestinians displaced in 1948, beside a United Nations estimate of about 711,000. Both fall at the low end of the 700,000–750,000 range used in this section. Precision matters less here than order of magnitude and speed: a population of that size left or was driven from its towns and villages within roughly eighteen months.

The Jewish departures had a different shape. They unfolded from roughly 1948 to 1972, nearly a quarter of a century, across many countries under separate governments, each with its own triggers. Iraq's community left largely in an airlift of 1950–51. Egypt's Jews left in two waves, in 1948 and again after the Suez Crisis of 1956. Algeria's exodus came during that country's war of independence in the early 1960s, more than a decade after 1948.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] [cite:hxstem_long_shadow_nakba] The causes ranged from persecution and violence, including the Farhud in Baghdad in 1941 and the riots that followed the partition vote, to organized emigration operations run by Israel and Jewish organizations. Even the total is disputed. Estimates run from roughly 650,000 to 900,000, depending on method and on the end year chosen.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] [cite:hxstem_long_shadow_nakba] A survey of the regional aftermath puts the figure for Arab countries and Iran, from 1948 into the 1970s, "commonly in the range of 800,000–900,000".[cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] The country-by-country record, with each figure's source, is set out in [scene:ch01_exodus_map|the previous section]. None of this lessens what individual communities suffered. It describes a process of a different kind.

The two processes also sat inside the same regional upheaval. The 1947–49 war ended with about 700,000 Palestinians displaced. In the following years the large Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt, Syria and North Africa shrank sharply through emigration, pressure, expulsion and state persecution, in proportions that varied by country.[cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] The defeat discredited the Arab governments that had fought the war. Armies and publics blamed their rulers. Syria's government fell to a military coup in March 1949,[cite:w_1949_syria_coup] Egypt's monarchy in 1952[cite:w_1952_egypt] and Iraq's in 1958.[cite:w_1958_iraq] Three governments fell within a decade. Neither of the easy readings survives this record. 1948 changed a great deal, so "nothing changed after 1948" is wrong. But the revolts of the 1920s and 1930s show that the region's instability was already there, so "every problem comes from 1948" is wrong too. What 1948 added was a permanent refugee question, a state of war, and a powerful political cause. The departure of Arab Jews belongs to that upheaval, but it was spread across years and governments that the war of 1948 did not itself control.

A second difference lies in what came after. Israel's government granted citizenship to the Jewish arrivals and absorbed roughly 600,000 immigrants over four years, doubling the country's Jewish population.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] Most Arab host states did not extend citizenship to Palestinian refugees or their descendants, even after more than seven decades. The continuing work of UNRWA, a refugee agency dedicated to Palestinians alone, reflects that difference.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] Different sides cite this asymmetry for opposite arguments, but the fact itself is documented either way. It does not explain each host state's reasons, which differed by country and period.

The common question "why don't Arab countries just take the refugees?" has a different answer in each country. Jordan is the main exception. Under its nationality law of 1954 it gave citizenship to most of the Palestinians who arrived after 1948. It hosts more than 2 million registered Palestinian refugees, most of them citizens, although Human Rights Watch has documented arbitrary revocations of that citizenship.[cite:jns_arab_citizenship] [cite:adl_refugees] Lebanon hosts about 400,000 registered refugees, roughly 10% of its population. Palestinians there were barred from dozens of professions outside the camps and, under a property law of 2001, from owning real estate. Lebanon justified these measures as preventing tawteen, permanent settlement, and they are linked to the country's sectarian balance.[cite:fmr_lebanon] [cite:aj_lebanon_property] Egypt and the Gulf states offered residency without a path to citizenship.

The two sides explain the policy differently. The Arab states' stated reason is that the Arab League instructed its members not to grant citizenship, "to avoid dissolution of their identity and protect their right of return". The League's Casablanca Protocol of 1965 promised refugees rights to work and travel, but it was applied unevenly.[cite:fmr_lebanon] Critics, including Israeli and pro-Israel analysts, argue that the policy kept refugees in limbo as a political tool. Both readings describe the same outcome: Jordan absorbed refugees, while other states restricted them in order to keep a claim of return alive. The question returned, outside this volume's period, after 7 October 2023. Egypt's President el-Sisi and Jordan's King Abdullah refused to take in people from Gaza. Analysts noted that Palestinians forced to leave had historically not been allowed to return, and Egypt warned of militants in Sinai. The position was summed up in reporting as "no refugees in Jordan, no refugees in Egypt": a fear that any exit would be a one-way door.[cite:pbs_egypt_refugees] Later chapters take this up in its own period.

The "even exchange" framing is rejected from both directions, which is unusual in this debate. Sources sympathetic to the Palestinian narrative call the comparison "profoundly unfounded", given the different mechanisms involved.[cite:palestineremembered_arab_jews_expelled] Some sources sympathetic to the Israeli narrative reject it for the opposite reason. They argue that the Jewish displacement, sometimes cited as the larger in raw numbers, has been ignored in international discourse.[cite:israelfactcheck_jewish_refugees] The two camps agree on nothing beyond this point, and their own preferred framings differ sharply. They do agree, for opposite reasons, that treating the two processes as one symmetrical event flattens real differences. The strongest version of the Palestinian objection is that a war-driven displacement by one set of forces, with return then barred, cannot be offset by departures from other countries that unfolded over decades, often through organized emigration. The strongest version of the opposing objection is that hundreds of thousands of Jews lost homes, property and citizenship and have received little recognition, while Palestinian refugees have a dedicated international agency of their own.

The record leaves several things open. The Jewish total remains a range, and the Palestinian figure is itself a range of estimates. This section does not rank the two displacements or judge which caused greater suffering. Its point is narrower. Two real events had different shapes, and the word "exchange" fits neither of them. The sources here also do not give each Arab host state's full reasons for withholding citizenship, beyond the Arab League's stated rationale and Lebanon's stated fear of permanent settlement. Recognizing that the two histories differ does not make either group's loss count for less. It means each has to be told on its own record.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: How the Story Is Told
chapters.intro:
The Baseline ends with the channels through which most people meet this history: the classroom, the historians, organized state messaging, and the platforms on which the argument is now conducted. The chapter comes last because the reader can now set those channels against the record laid out in the chapters before it, and because the contest over how the story is told is itself part of the documented history.
