The first section follows the story as American students meet it: the textbooks of four publishers, a federal law that bars the Department of Education from directing curriculum, publishers who certify their own accuracy, and the day schools and Birthright trips that reinforce the story for some Jewish students.[cite:usc_20_1232a] [cite:wiki_birthright_israel] It holds the Palestinian Authority's textbooks to the same test, through a study commissioned by the European Union and published in 2021.[cite:gei_faq] The second section maps how historians argue about 1948: the older Israeli account, the "new historians" who worked in archives opened in the 1980s, their critics, and the dispute between the settler-colonial and national-liberation frames.[cite:wiki_deir_yassin] [cite:massad_settler_colonial] The third sets out coordination on the record: a pollster's language guide of 2009, a covert campaign that Israeli officials tied to a ministry which denies it, and paid influencer contracts disclosed under American foreign-agent law, alongside an Iran-linked network aimed at Israelis.[cite:luntz_pdf] [cite:toi_stoic] [cite:jta_esther_project_fara] [cite:calcalist_iran_social_media_network] The last examines content moderation: a Human Rights Watch report of 1,050 cases, Meta's own commissioned review, the takedown requests of Israel's Cyber Unit, and antisemitic content that evaded moderation in the same years.[cite:hrw_meta_broken_promises] [cite:hrw_meta_promises] [cite:adl_tiktok_antisemitism_loopholes]

The record in this chapter runs in more than one direction, and the sections say so. What it supports is narrower than either familiar story: not purely organic opinion and not a single directing hand, but named institutions, documented sums and stated limits.

sections.h: How the Story Is Taught
sections.html:
Most Americans meet this history long before they meet its documents. It reaches them in a sequence: a textbook, then a teacher, then a museum, a film and the evening news. Each pass reinforces the one before it. The version that results is usually remembered as the story itself, the true account of an ancient people returning home. What it actually is, on inspection, is one framing of a documented modern political project, and the framing and the project are not the same thing. This section is an inventory rather than an accusation. It sets out where the story is taught, who pays for which parts of the teaching, what the teaching leaves out, and how the same test applies to the textbooks on the other side.

The first stage is the classroom. Four publishers, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Pearson, McGraw-Hill and Holt McDougal, reach the great majority of American world-history students in grades 6 through 12. How their books cover Israel and Palestine has been studied in the peer-reviewed literature: Sean Yom examined the framing of American world-history textbooks in 2013, and Nurit Peled-Elhanan published a mirror study of Israeli school textbooks in 2012. [cite:peled_elhanan_textbooks] The pattern these studies describe is not falsehood. It is emphasis. Some events are named: the Holocaust, the 1948 declaration, the 1967 war. Others are compressed: the Nakba, the 1953 CIA coup in Iran that reshaped the region, the Sabra and Shatila massacre of 1982. Some words are used, such as "conflict," "war" and "unrest." Others tend to be avoided. One is "occupation," a status that, as this book counts it, international law has applied for 59 years. Another is "apartheid," the subject of published reports since 2021 by B'Tselem, [cite:btselem_apartheid_2021] Human Rights Watch [cite:hrw_israel_apartheid] and Amnesty International. [cite:amnesty_israel_apartheid] The effect, on this account, is that a student can reach adulthood with a vocabulary and a set of reflexes but without the record itself.

"Emphasis, not lies" can sound like a small distinction. A concrete case shows how large it can be. A textbook can say, accurately and in one clean sentence, that Jewish settlers purchased land in Palestine. A fuller account would add what this library had to assemble from scratch, because the survey textbooks did not supply it. The Ottoman government passed a Palestine-specific law in 1881–82 barring land purchase by foreign Jews. In 1892 it required imperial approval even for purchases by Ottoman Jewish citizens. Buyers worked around these rules through Ottoman-citizen intermediaries and through the consular protections known as the "capitulations," and in the 1890s the United States State Department found itself in a dispute over Russian Jewish emigrants who had naturalized as Americans in order to claim consular protection for land purchases in Palestine. Entire villages of tenant farmers were evicted as a result of such sales. None of this is obscure. It appears in Wikipedia's article on Jewish land purchase in Palestine and in the United States government's own published diplomatic archive. It does not appear in the four publishers' coverage. Both versions "cover the topic." Only the second describes the laws, the loopholes and the institutions through which the process actually ran, and a reader who knows only the first has no way to ask the next question, because nothing signals that there is one.

That example has limits, and they should be stated. It shows one significant mechanism missing from mainstream coverage. It does not show that every omission is this consequential, and it does not show that the omission was deliberate rather than the ordinary product of space limits in a survey course. What it does show is that emphasis alone, without one false sentence, can remove a documented mechanism from what a reader is able to know.

Compression works on people as well as events. Jews are not one lineage. The documented traditions include the Ashkenazi of Central and Eastern Europe, the Sephardi of Iberia and the diaspora after 1492, the Mizrahi of the Middle East and North Africa (including Iraq, Yemen, Morocco, Iran, Syria and Egypt), the Beta Israel of Ethiopia, the Bene Israel of India, the Jews of Kaifeng in China, the Bukharan Jews of Central Asia, and Georgian, Yemenite and Karaite communities. No one disputes that any of these are Jewish. The point is that they exist, and that American K-12 material typically folds the whole tradition into a single narrative centered on Ashkenazi experience, with Mizrahi and Sephardi Jews appearing briefly or not at all. Ella Shohat's 1988 essay documented the same asymmetry inside Israel. [cite:shohat_sephardim_israel] The compression has a consequence. Political Zionism, organized in 1897, emerged in specifically European Jewish settings, and an education that leaves out the non-European traditions makes it easier to treat "Zionism" and "all Jews" as one thing, a conflation the record does not support. The lineages themselves are treated at length elsewhere in this volume.

Why the textbook chain carries no correction is a question of structure, and each link in it is a matter of law or record. Federal law, at 20 U.S.C. § 1232a, bars the Department of Education from exercising any "direction, supervision, or control" over school curriculum. [cite:usc_20_1232a] That is a legal prohibition, not an oversight gap. Approval of textbooks falls to the states, and even there the review process places responsibility for accuracy on the publishers, who certify their own books. Virginia's textbook review documentation says so directly. [cite:va_textbook_review] In 2015, after a widely publicized error, Texas considered adding independent university historians to check textbooks for factual accuracy, and the state board voted the proposal down. [cite:tx_board_rejects_factcheck] The third link is ownership. A major textbook publisher is a private company in a market with no ownership screening related to accuracy, so anyone may acquire one, for any reason and with any history.

Once an unchecked claim enters a textbook, it can also compound. Students and later writers meet it in good faith and cite it; others cite them; and each new citation looks like independent confirmation when it is the same uncorrected origin repeated. The cartoonist Randall Munroe coined a name for this sequence, "citogenesis." [cite:xkcd_978_citogenesis] A tracked case shows it at work: a false claim about the history of health economics began on Wikipedia with no real source behind it, was repeated across several apparently independent articles, and was finally cited as settled fact by a newspaper columnist who had no way of knowing that the whole trail led back to one unverified starting point. [cite:cornell_citogenesis_blog] No one in that chain acted in bad faith. Each assumed that someone earlier had done the checking.

The mechanism is general. Any well-funded owner of a major textbook or reference publisher inherits the same structural gap, on any subject, not because of a conspiracy but because no layer of the system performs an accuracy check. Each link is legal and, taken alone, unremarkable. Chained together, they describe a system in which the absence of a check is a matter of design rather than neglect.

The ownership link has a documented example. The story travels through the press, and the ownership of the press is a matter of record. Robert Maxwell was born Jan Ludvik Hoch in Czechoslovakia in 1923. He survived the Holocaust, which killed most of his family, served in the British Army and anglicized his name after the war. Between 1984 and 1991 he assembled Mirror Group Newspapers, publisher of the Daily Mirror, one of Britain's highest-circulation tabloids, which reached millions of readers a day; the academic publisher Pergamon Press; the language-education company Berlitz; and Macmillan Publishing, one of the largest textbook and reference publishers used in American schools, which he acquired in 1988 for $2.6 billion. His relationship with Israeli intelligence is described in Seymour Hersh's The Samson Option, [cite:hersh_samson] in the work of Tom Bower, whose biography Maxwell: The Outsider appeared in 1988, [cite:bower_maxwell] and in Gordon Thomas and Martin Dillon's Robert Maxwell, Israel's Superspy of 2002; the name Bergman also appears among the sources on the point. The biographies, working from different sources, describe a relationship with Mossad that reportedly included helping to sell software from Israeli technology firms to intelligence services around the world. The exact mechanism is contested in its specifics. The broader pattern, a well-connected publisher with intelligence relationships on several sides, including British ties and alleged Soviet-era contacts through Pergamon's dealings with Eastern Bloc academic publishing, appears in more than one of these books rather than resting on any single one.

Maxwell died on 5 November 1991, found floating near his yacht, the Lady Ghislaine, off the Canary Islands. The official Spanish autopsy and a later Israeli examination both concluded that he fell overboard, with drowning the probable cause. Whether that was an accident, a suicide amid mounting financial exposure or something else was never settled to the satisfaction of every investigator, and this book leaves the uncertainty as uncertainty. He received an Israeli state funeral on the Mount of Olives, with six intelligence chiefs in attendance. Days after his death it emerged that he had taken hundreds of millions of pounds from his companies' pension funds to cover debt. His daughter Ghislaine was convicted in 2021 of sex trafficking with Jeffrey Epstein, a later turn the record captures but does not explain. His full story is told in [scene:s16|Robert Maxwell and the press empire].

What the Maxwell case shows must be stated as carefully as what it does not. It shows that a man who owned major British media and a major American textbook publisher is described, in independently researched biographies, as having ties to Israeli intelligence. It does not show that any Daily Mirror story about Israel or Zionism was ordered by an intelligence service, and it does not show that Maxwell altered any Macmillan textbook. No primary source located for this book makes either claim, and this book does not make them. The point is structural. Ownership is a documented fact; editorial influence is a separate and much harder claim that would need its own evidence, case by case. What the case establishes is that the opportunity existed in a chain designed with no one checking the checker.

Beyond the drift of editorial emphasis there is a second, different thing: a formal, state-funded operation built to shape this same narrative. Its name is hasbara, Hebrew for "explanation." It was formalized as Zionist institutional policy before the Second World War, a step credited to Nahum Sokolow, and it has served continuously since as Israel's own name for its public diplomacy and propaganda. It is not a term invented by critics; it is the word the apparatus uses for itself. According to reporting on the 2026 budget, Israel quadrupled its public-diplomacy budget to $730 million, and the foreign minister described the matter as an "existential issue." [cite:nuclearnews_730m_budget] Israel's Institute for National Security Studies mapped, in a single research pass after October 2023, more than 120 civilian "war rooms," 40 organizations building hasbara technology and 100 databases, which is the apparatus documenting its own scale rather than an outside estimate. One documented influencer contract has been calculated at roughly $7,000 per pro-Israel social-media post. Many still-circulating talking points have been traced to a named source, Frank Luntz's 2009 "Global Language Dictionary," commissioned by The Israel Project. [cite:medium_luntz_kryptonite_hasbara] The contracts, filings and budgets of this operation are examined in [scene:s00a3|coordination on the record].

The difference between the two mechanisms matters. Textbook emphasis is closer to organic drift: many editors, trained alike, reaching for the same framing without coordination. Hasbara has a name, a budget and a stated goal. Neither explains all pro-Israel opinion. Many people hold pro-Israel views independent of any funded campaign, just as many hold critical views independent of any funded campaign. What is documented is the existence and the scale of the organized effort, not a claim that it accounts for every view.

For a subset of Jewish students, the story is reinforced twice more, through two separate programs at two different ages. The two should not be merged into one organization, which would overstate what is documented. The first is the day school. Jewish day schools set their own curricula, and disclosed philanthropic funding, from the Jim Joseph Foundation among others, specifically supports Israel-centered educational content, including elementary-level pilot programs. Comparable day-school systems exist in other countries. The schools are expensive. According to SAPIR journal's 2025 reporting, average annual tuition nationally is about $24,000, and runs from $25,000 to $50,000 a year in cities such as New York; according to reporting in JNS and the Cleveland Jewish News, a full K-12 day-school education for one child can cost about half a million dollars before college. In 2026 the Israeli government approved a NIS 100 million ($33.4 million) budget, matched by philanthropic donations through the Jewish Federations of North America, to raise day-school enrollment in the United States and Canada, a combined $66.7 million. A further NIS 200 million plan, about $67 million, was approved unanimously by the Israeli cabinet in 2026 with a focus on enrolling more American Jewish children in day schools, a direct government line for Diaspora education. The sources describe these as separate plans; whether they overlap is not established in the material behind this book. Behind both stands the broader base of the Jewish Federations of North America, whose combined endowments are described as holding "tens of billions" in assets and whose annual campaigns raise "hundreds of millions."

The second program is Birthright Israel, also known as Taglit. Founded in 1999, it offers a free ten-day trip to Israel to young adults aged 18 to 26. Benjamin Netanyahu made the first Israeli government funding guarantee in 1998, during his first term. More than 800,000 young adults have taken the trip. [cite:wiki_birthright_israel] Roughly 27 percent of the funding comes directly from the Israeli government; about 67 percent comes from individual donors, among them Sheldon Adelson, who gave more than $400 million before his death in 2021; the remainder comes from the Claims Conference and other sources, including Jewish Federations. More than $2 billion has been spent over the program's history. The Birthright Israel Foundation's own figures put current annual worldwide programming at $172 million to $175 million, up from a reported $92.9 million budget in 2023. Security has historically been its single most expensive line, at $72 million. An Ernst & Young study found that in its first 13 years the program brought more than $825 million into the Israeli economy through tourism, hotels and meals, separate from its own budget.

The program is international. Participants come from roughly 68 to 70 countries, and the foundation itself presents the trip as "part of a global movement," naming Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, France, the United Kingdom, South Africa and India among them. About 80 percent of participants come from the United States and Canada; the remaining fifth is spread across dozens of countries. [cite:birthright_global_movement] Birthright has also served as a model that heritage-trip programs in Hungary, Greece and Macedonia were built to copy.

Its effect has been measured by its own commissioned research. A 2025 Brandeis University study, funded by Birthright, found that the year's participants came back "much more connected to Israel, and much more likely to identify with the political right," and more likely to "provide a counterargument to claims that Israel is committing genocide." [cite:intercept_birthright_2025] This is the program's own research describing its own effect, not an outside accusation. It measured an average across a cohort, not a uniform outcome for every participant, and it describes only the subset of students who attend day school and later take the trip, not Jewish education as a whole.

The cumulative product of textbook, press, museum, film, news and, for some, school and trip is described here as a reflex rather than a conclusion. A person who has passed through the sequence reaches adulthood with associations already in place: Israel with democracy, Palestinians with terrorism, criticism with antisemitism, the conflict with antiquity. These are associations, not findings the record supports. This section draws on Daniel Kahneman's work on fast, intuitive "System 1" thinking, in which emotional associations bypass analytical review. The practical test is simple. When the reflex fires against something the documents show, the sequence is doing its work, and noticing that is where examination begins. How the same associations were first put before the American public, through the themes of refuge, the Bible and democracy, is the subject of [scene:sell_s01|how Israel was sold to Americans in 1948].

A standard applied to one side's schoolbooks must be applied to the other's. The familiar claim runs in two forms: that Palestinian children are taught to hate, or that their textbooks are fine. A study commissioned by the European Union tested the question. The Georg Eckert Institute for International Textbook Research analyzed about 200 Palestinian Authority textbooks and teachers' guides released in 2020, and published its findings in 2021. It concluded that the books "adhere to UNESCO standards" on human-rights education while expressing "a narrative of resistance" and "antagonism toward Israel." It found some content with "escalatory potential," including in science, technology and mathematics subjects, and some antisemitic depictions. It found no direct calls for violence against Israelis. [cite:gei_faq] The Institute's director later told the European Parliament that books containing antisemitism or incitement do not comply with UNESCO standards. [cite:hansard_textbooks]

Each side reads the same study as proof of its case. IMPACT-se, a monitoring group whose reports the European Parliament has cited, says the study confirms systemic incitement. [cite:impactse_gei] That reading draws its strength from the study's documented findings of antagonism, escalatory content and antisemitic depictions, and from the director's statement that such material falls short of UNESCO standards. Others, including European analysts, say the study largely disproved exaggerated claims, and they note that it did not examine Israeli textbooks, which other researchers have also criticized. [cite:eumep_textbooks] That reading draws its strength from the study's finding of UNESCO-standard human-rights content and its finding of no direct calls for violence. Peled-Elhanan's work on Israeli schoolbooks, mentioned above, is one such criticism. Read as a whole, the study supports neither headline. Problem content exists and is documented; a curriculum of incitement to violence is not what the study found.

Several things remain unsettled. The record set out here establishes what the four American publishers emphasize and omit, but not why: whether through deliberate choice or the ordinary compression of a survey course. It establishes Maxwell's ownership and the biographies' account of his intelligence ties, but not that he used either to shape a single story or textbook, and it does not resolve how he died. It measures Birthright's effect on one cohort through a study the program paid for, and has no independent study to set beside it. It reports the hasbara budget and the influencer payments through secondary reporting, not the budget documents themselves. And the European study covered one side's textbooks only. The lesson that follows from all of this applies to any account: name the source, say who made it and who paid for it, separate what a document shows from what it is said to show, and apply the same test to both sides.

sections.h: How Historians Argue About 1948
sections.html:
A common assumption holds that historians agree on what happened in 1948, and that only politicians and activists dispute it. They do not agree. The scholars whose work is cited throughout this library divide in two separate ways. The first division is over events and intent: what happened to the Palestinian Arabs who left or were driven from their homes, and how far it was planned. The second is over framing: what kind of movement Zionism was in the first place. Knowing where each scholar stands does not settle either question, but it allows a reader to see, when a later chapter cites a historian, whose interpretation is being offered and what the other camp would say in reply. This section maps the camps. It is a guide to the interpreters, not a verdict on them.

The first debate has a history of its own, and it turns on access to documents. Until the 1980s the dominant Israeli account held that the Palestinians had largely left on their own, or at the urging of Arab leaders. In the 1980s Israel began to declassify its state and military archives, and a group of scholars who came to be called the "new historians," Benny Morris and Ilan Pappé among them, went into those files. What they documented was expulsions, massacres and the deliberate prevention of Palestinian return. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The older account had denied these things; the archives recorded them.

The new historians did not reach one conclusion. Morris and Pappé, working with the same newly opened material, came to sharply different judgments about how far the expulsions were planned. That disagreement matters because the documents of the period can be read in more than one way: an order or a pattern of operations can be read as evidence of a design, or not. The arguments over one such document are traced in [scene:pd_s01|Plan Dalet and the argument about what it was]. The historian Walid Khalidi, writing on Deir Yassin, argued that the Haganah, a Jewish armed force of the period, was involved there at every stage. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] These are claims about intent and responsibility, and some of the archival material bearing on them remains classified.

The new historians have their own critics. Historians such as Efraim Karsh reject the expulsion-centered account altogether. In their reading, the decisive facts of 1948 are the choices of Arab leaders and the Arab rejection of partition; the departure of the Palestinian population follows from those choices rather than from a design on the Jewish side. [cite:dailyalert_194_karsh] The strongest form of this case is that a war launched against partition carries responsibility for its consequences, and that an account which begins with expulsions has already chosen where the story starts. The strongest form of the new historians' case is that the expulsions, massacres and the barring of return are recorded in Israel's own state and military files, and that no account of the war's causes removes what those files show was done. The two camps are not arguing about whether the archives exist. They are arguing about what the archives show regarding intent, and where responsibility lies.

A second debate concerns framing rather than events, and it runs alongside the first. Scholars such as Joseph Massad describe Zionism as a settler-colonial project. Their evidence is, in part, the movement's own vocabulary: Zionist leaders used the word "colonization" of their own work, including Vladimir Jabotinsky in his 1923 essay "The Iron Wall." [cite:massad_settler_colonial] On this reading, the events of 1948 are one phase of a longer process of settlement and displacement. Others describe Zionism as a national liberation movement, and as a refugee movement: the effort of a people with ancient roots in the land to find safety after centuries of persecution. On that reading, the same events belong to the founding of a refuge and to a war over partition. Each frame can point to documents. Neither is settled by them, because the dispute is over which category best describes a set of facts that both sides can read.

How the older account came to be told, and how it changed as the files opened, is the subject of [scene:np_s01|how the Nakba was told]. For further reading across these positions, the works include Shlaim's The Iron Wall, [cite:shlaim_iron_wall] Masalha's Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History [cite:masalha_four_thousand] and Said's work on the question of Palestine. [cite:said_question_palestine]

Part of the record is still closed. Material in Israeli military archives on some events, including Deir Yassin, remains classified. That means some of the questions above cannot be answered by any historian on the documents now available: claims about planning and about responsibility for particular events rest, in part, on files that no one outside the archive has read. The framing dispute will not be resolved by new files at all, because it is a disagreement over interpretation rather than over evidence.

The working rule that follows is to read the document first and the interpreter second. Facts drawn from the archives, such as an order, a report or a dated record of what was done in a given village, are shared ground, and historians on every side work from them. Judgments about intent, and the choice of frame, are where scholars divide. The chapters that follow cite the documents and say whose interpretation is whose, so that a reader can keep the two apart and reach a judgment of their own.

sections.h: Who Coordinates What Gets Posted
sections.html:
A common assumption holds that pro-Israel content on social media is organic grassroots enthusiasm, and that any suggestion of coordination is conspiracy thinking. The opposite assumption, that every pro-Israel post is centrally directed, is just as common in other circles. The record for the years from 2009 to 2025 supports neither. It names a pollster and the organization that hired him, government ministries and the sums they spent, consulting firms and the contracts they registered with the United States Justice Department, the instructions sent to paid influencers, and a meeting attended by a head of government. It also documents an Israel-aligned campus organization caught running fake pages, and influence networks aimed against Israel. What follows sets out each piece in turn, with the weight each piece of evidence can bear.

A point of method comes first. Knowing where a talking point came from is one step; checking it against the record is another. A talking point that was written, tested and paid for is not false for that reason. Many are sincerely held by people who were never paid to repeat them, and some are accurate. The origin of a claim is not a verdict on it. That is why the coordination documented here sits beside, rather than replaces, the graded catalog of claims elsewhere in this library. The contracts tell the reader who chose a message and paid to spread it. They do not tell the reader whether the message is true.

Where the talking points come from. In 2009 The Israel Project commissioned the pollster Frank Luntz to test which language would win Americans' support.[cite:wiki_tip] The result, the Global Language Dictionary, was an internal document marked not for distribution. It was leaked to Newsweek.[cite:archive_luntz] Its rules read as a manual of persuasion rather than a statement of belief. Advocates were told not to pretend that Israel was without fault, and to concede a point before making their own. They were told to repeat the phrase "Iran-backed Hamas." They were told that "no matter what you're asked," they should "bridge to a productive pro-Israel message," and that Israel should be framed in "the language of America: democracy, freedom, security, and peace."[cite:luntz_pdf] The guide's own polling found that settlements were unpopular with the American public, even among Israel's supporters, and so it advised advocates to turn conversations toward peace.[cite:luntz_pdf]

The guide matters for two reasons. First, it shows that phrases a reader may meet as spontaneous opinion were, in at least this documented case, selected by survey for their effect on an American audience. Second, its own findings undercut the idea that support for Israel in the United States meant support for every Israeli policy: the polling located a weak point, settlements, and the advice was to steer around it rather than defend it. An earlier section traces how some of the guide's phrases still circulate [scene:s00a|how the story is taught]. The guide itself does not show that any given statement online came from it.

STOIC: a ministry, a firm, and fake accounts. The most concrete case of covert activity concerns STOIC, a political consulting and marketing firm based in Tel Aviv. According to the New York Times, which cited four Israeli officials and documents, Israel's Ministry of Diaspora Affairs allocated about $2 million in October 2023 and hired STOIC to run the campaign.[cite:toi_stoic] The Times reported that the operation ran fake accounts and three fake news sites aimed at members of the United States Congress, especially Black Democrats such as Hakeem Jeffries and Raphael Warnock, urging them to keep funding Israel's military.[cite:toi_stoic] [cite:opb_stoic] Hundreds of the accounts posed as Americans.[cite:opb_stoic] NPR's account of the same operation describes AI-generated content aimed at younger, progressive Americans, carrying pro-Israel messaging on the Gaza war.[cite:npr_stoic_ai_influence]

The operation was first identified by FakeReporter, an Israeli watchdog group that tracks misinformation. It was an Israeli organization, not a foreign critic, that found it, and it tied five websites to the operation.[cite:npr_stoic_ai_influence] The New York Times confirmed the reporting independently. The platforms then acted. Meta removed 510 Facebook accounts and 32 Instagram accounts that had posed as Jewish students, Black Americans and "concerned citizens."[cite:cyberscoop_stoic] OpenAI called STOIC a "for-hire Israeli threat actor."[cite:cyberscoop_stoic] Meta stated that it had deleted the accounts before they gained traction with real users, and both companies said the campaign won little engagement.[cite:npr_stoic_ai_influence] [cite:cyberscoop_stoic]

The reports do not agree in every detail, and the differences are worth setting out rather than smoothing over.

The central fact is disputed by the party named in it. The Ministry of Diaspora Affairs denied involvement.[cite:toi_stoic] Against that denial stands the Times's sourcing to four Israeli officials and documents, the watchdog's findings, and the two platforms' own enforcement actions. Criticism also came from an Israeli former diplomat: Michael Oren, a former ambassador, called the campaign damaging interference.[cite:toi_stoic] STOIC did not respond to interview requests.[cite:npr_stoic_ai_influence] The record therefore shows a covert operation with a named firm, a specific sum and a ministry identified by officials as its funder, caught by a watchdog and removed by the platforms. It does not show that the operation was the only one of its kind, or the largest, and the companies' own statements indicate it failed to reach many real people.

The budget behind the open campaign. STOIC was covert. The larger effort that followed was conducted largely in the open, under American disclosure law. In December 2024, during coalition negotiations, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar secured an allocation of $150 million for global public diplomacy, hasbara in Hebrew. According to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, that was about twenty times previous hasbara budgets, and the ministry received the funds from May 2025.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] An earlier section records a separate figure for 2026, a public-diplomacy budget of $730 million, and the history of the word hasbara.[cite:nuclearnews_730m_budget] The two figures belong to different years and come from different sources; this book does not have a basis for breaking either down line by line.

The paper trail: the foreign-agent filings. The details of how that money was spent in the United States became public through filings with the Justice Department under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, known as FARA. Every figure in the paragraphs that follow exists because that law compelled its disclosure.

The first track was run by Bridges Partners LLC, a Washington-based firm. It worked for Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs through an intermediary, Havas Media Group Germany.[cite:honestreporting_bridges_partners_fara] Its filings show it was hired to manage an influencer network code-named the "Esther Project," from June to November 2025, under a contract of up to $900,000.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] [cite:wiki_esther_project_israel] The contract was itemized: $60,000 upfront for recruitment; $140,000 as five or six influencers began posting; up to $250,000 a month for influencer fees and production; and $50,000 for wrap-up.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] HonestReporting's reading of the same filings found roughly $900,000 invoiced for an "Influencer Campaign," of which roughly $552,946 remained for payments to the influencers themselves once administrative and production costs were taken out.[cite:honestreporting_bridges_partners_fara] The campaign expected 75 to 90 posts. Dividing the money by the posts, analysts arrived at roughly $6,100 to $7,400 per post.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] [cite:wiki_esther_project_israel] That calculation is the source of the figure of about $7,000 per post that circulates widely.[cite:globeistan_7000_per_post] [cite:honestreporting_bridges_partners_fara]

The second track was larger. Brad Parscale, formerly Donald Trump's campaign manager, registered his firm, Clock Tower X LLC, as a foreign agent for Israel under a reported $6 million contract for "strategic communications." It promised 100 ads or pieces of content a month, plus 5,000 variations, an output the Jewish Telegraphic Agency notes would likely require automated tools.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] [cite:globeistan_7000_per_post] A related trip in 2025 was partly funded by a foreign-ministry contract worth $86,000.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara]

The money can be followed from its source to its effects, as far as the filings and the complaint they prompted allow.

What coordination looked like from the inside. A payment shows that someone was hired. It does not show what they were told to say. That second layer was documented by an investigation in Time magazine, which found private group chats in which influencers taking part in a pro-Israel campaign were guided on the specific language to use in posts on X, Instagram and TikTok, and were paid up to $4,250 per post.[cite:meo_israel_influencer_backfire] A separate case shows the mechanism from the side of someone who said no. A Jewish influencer reported receiving a confidential brief from a different campaign, offering $1,500 to promote specific talking points under a non-disclosure agreement. He declined to sign it.[cite:meo_israel_influencer_backfire] Refusal is part of the record too: the offer was made, and it was not universally accepted.

The effort reached the top of the Israeli government. In September 2025, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met several American social media influencers in New York, specifically to enlist them in amplifying pro-Israel messaging in the United States.[cite:meo_israel_influencer_backfire] This was not a campaign run by a communications office several steps removed from political leadership; the head of government took part himself. The meeting's occurrence is documented. What was said in it, and whether every influencer present agreed to take part, is not in the public record these sources draw on.

The several payment figures in these reports, $1,500, up to $4,250, and roughly $6,100 to $7,400 per post, come from different campaigns and different documents. They should not be read as one price list, and the sources do not say whether the chats Time examined belonged to the Bridges Partners campaign.

The complaint and the open question. The firms registered. The influencers, Public Citizen alleges, did not. Public Citizen filed a formal complaint with the Justice Department's FARA Unit. It alleged that approximately 14 to 18 US-based influencers paid through the Bridges Partners contract were acting as unregistered agents of Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and it asked the department to require disclosure of their names and contracts.[cite:citizen_fara_complaint] The sources available to this book do not record a ruling on the complaint. Whether individual influencers paid through a registered firm must register themselves is the legal question it raises, and it remains open. There is also a naming question. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency noted that it is unclear whether the "Esther Project" has any link to the Heritage Foundation's similarly named Project Esther, which a later volume of this library examines.[cite:wiki_esther_project_israel] [cite:citizen_fara_complaint]

The disclosure itself says something about how the law works. The same statute that a later volume of this library shows going unapplied to AIPAC did apply to these contracts, which is the only reason the campaign is documented in such detail. Openly registered persuasion and covert fake accounts are different things, and the record contains both.

A campus organization and a takedown. The record also contains a case where a platform acted against an Israel-aligned group on its own authority. The Israel on Campus Coalition (ICC) is the main convening organization of pro-Israel campus groups. Two claims about it carry different weight and should be kept apart. The first is reported, and less independently verified: that ICC gathered information on pro-Palestinian students through informants inside Jewish and pro-Israel student organizations, and passed it to Israel's Ministry of Strategic Affairs.[cite:wiki_israel_campus_coalition] The second is more concretely documented. ICC secretly ran misleading Facebook pages and advertisements aimed at the Palestinian-American poet Remi Kanazi, and in 2018 Facebook itself removed the pages, citing its own policies against misrepresentation.[cite:wiki_israel_campus_coalition] That is a platform's enforcement action, not only an outside accusation. Neither claim shows that such tactics are unique to ICC among advocacy organizations, or that every campus group affiliated with it engaged in them; what is documented is attributed to its national organization.

The other direction. An account that documented only one side's influence operations would not be a fair account. Operations aimed against Israel are documented in the same record. An Iran-linked network ran fake profiles, bots and groups across WhatsApp, X, Telegram, Facebook, TikTok and Instagram. It spread disinformation, impersonated journalists and rabbis, and worked specifically to stoke tensions among Israelis themselves, including content aimed at Israel's LGBTQ+ community and at ultra-Orthodox Jews.[cite:calcalist_iran_social_media_network] A 2025 report by an independent research organization, titled "Conflict Amplified: Disinformation and Hate in the Israel-Hamas War," documented disinformation and coordinated hate campaigns from several sides of the conflict, not from one alone.[cite:isd_conflict_amplified_2025] These sources establish that both kinds of operation exist. They give no basis for saying that the Iran-linked operations and the Israeli-funded ones were of comparable size or reach, in either direction. How the platforms themselves policed this content is the subject of the next section [scene:s00a2|the platforms].

What the record shows, and what it leaves open. Taken together, the documents establish a funded and coordinated messaging apparatus. Its parts can be named: a pollster's tested vocabulary; a ministry's covert contract, which the ministry denies; a foreign ministry's budget and the registered firms it paid; private instructions to paid influencers; and a prime minister's personal recruitment. That is the familiar claim of pure organic enthusiasm answered by the record. The same record does not support the opposite claim, that every pro-Israel or pro-Palestinian post is centrally directed. Unpaid supporters exist alongside the paid campaigns, one influencer turned the offer down, and influence operations run against Israel as well.

Several questions remain unsettled. The Ministry of Diaspora Affairs' denial of the STOIC campaign stands against the New York Times's sources, and the published accounts differ on its target and its number of websites. The breakdown of the $150 million beyond the single Bridges Partners contract is not public in these sources, nor is the outcome of Public Citizen's complaint. What was said in the September 2025 meeting is unknown. The informant claim against ICC is reported but less independently verified. No source here measures the relative scale of the Israeli-funded and Iran-linked operations, or how many people any of them persuaded. The firms' names, the sums and the dates are documented. How much effect the money had is not.

sections.h: The Platforms: Moderation as Contested Ground
sections.html:
The paid campaigns of the previous section, like the [scene:s00a|classroom and the textbook] before them, reach people through channels someone else controls. The newest of those channels is entirely contemporary: what happens to Palestinian and pro-Palestinian content on Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and X, and what those platforms remove, suppress or leave up. Two simple stories dominate that argument. One holds that moderation is neutral, a matter of each company applying its own rules. The other holds that it is a secret, coordinated campaign to silence one side, and which side depends on who is telling it. The record for 2021 to 2026 is made up of formal human rights investigations, reviews the platforms commissioned themselves, a government office's own request figures, leaked internal data, the platforms' written policies and their denials, and watchdog findings that cut the other way. Read in full, it supports neither story.

The heaviest finding rests on two inquiries, begun by different parties two years apart. The first was Meta's own. In 2021 the company commissioned an independent investigation from Business for Social Responsibility (BSR) into its handling of content during the escalation of May 2021. The review, published in September 2022, concluded that Meta's moderation "appear[s] to have had an adverse human rights impact on the rights of Palestinian users." [cite:hrw_meta_broken_promises] The same review did not identify intentional bias. [cite:ibt_echoicide] The second inquiry came from outside. In December 2023 Human Rights Watch published a 51-page report, Meta's Broken Promises: Systemic Censorship of Palestine Content on Instagram and Facebook, which documented 1,050 cases of content being removed or suppressed, from more than 60 countries. [cite:hrw_meta_broken_promises] After its publication, Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to Meta's chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, demanding accountability. [cite:hrw_meta_broken_promises] An outside critic's conclusion is one kind of evidence. A conclusion reached by reviewers the company itself hired and paid is a stronger kind, and here the two point the same way on harm, while differing in emphasis on intent.

The number most often repeated from the Human Rights Watch report is "1,049 to 1." The cases were gathered from October and November 2023. Of the 1,050 the organization reviewed, 1,049 involved peaceful pro-Palestinian content and one involved content supporting Israel. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] [cite:bhrrc_hrw_meta] The report named the causes it found: flawed Meta policies, opaque enforcement, heavy reliance on automated systems, and deference to government requests, among them those of Israel's Cyber Unit. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] What the number can and cannot show matters as much as the number. Human Rights Watch described its cases as a collected dataset, not a representative global sample and not a comparison of censorship across platforms. The cases were reported by users who chose to send them in. [cite:ibt_echoicide] A set built that way can establish that a pattern of suppression occurred and what it looked like. It cannot, by its construction, measure the ratio of all pro-Palestinian to all pro-Israel content removed on Meta's services. Meta, for its part, disputes that it deliberately or systemically suppresses any voice. [cite:ibt_echoicide]

A methodological critique of the report also exists, and it belongs beside the report rather than after it. Calcalist, an Israeli technology publication, examined the Human Rights Watch study and identified potential biases in its sampling and in its choice of platforms, which could have affected its findings. [cite:calcalist_hrw_methodology_critique] The critique and the organization's own statement of its limits overlap: both turn on how the cases were collected.

The most precise reading of these sources together is narrower than either popular story. The record documents lopsided harm to pro-Palestinian speech on Meta's platforms. It does not document a deliberate plan. What it does document, in the BSR review and in the causes Human Rights Watch listed, is a design: policies, automated enforcement at scale, and a channel through which a government's requests reach the moderators. That finding is harder to dismiss than an accusation of intent, because it does not depend on proving what anyone wanted.

That channel has a name and its own published figures. Israel's Cyber Unit sits inside the State Attorney's Office. It sends what it calls "voluntary" requests to platforms asking them to remove content it considers incitement or support for terrorism. The requests carry no public legal process. [cite:eff_cyber_unit] The platform decides whether to act, and it almost always has. Since the office began reporting, the compliance rate has never fallen below 77 percent. In 2018 the Unit sent more than 14,000 requests to Google and Facebook, with compliance of about 90 to 92 percent. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] [cite:cjr_cyber_unit] In 2021 it sent 5,990 requests with 82 percent compliance, about 90 percent of them to Facebook and Instagram during the May escalation, the same weeks the BSR review examined. [cite:cjr_cyber_unit]

After 7 October 2023 the volume rose sharply. Between 7 October and 14 November 2023, a little under six weeks, the Unit sent 9,500 takedown requests, 60 percent of them to Meta. According to an Israeli official, the compliance rate was 94 percent. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] Leaked internal data reported by Drop Site News in 2025 indicates that Meta removed more than 90,000 posts at Israel's request, often within seconds and without human review. [cite:dropsite_meta_leak] Drop Site also reported that Meta expanded its automated removals after 7 October, affecting an estimated 38.8 million additional posts. These are reported figures from leaked material and are attributed here as such. [cite:dropsite_meta_leak]

The gap in this part of the record is one of accountability. Meta's Oversight Board recommended that the company formalize and publish how it handles government requests. Human Rights Watch asked the Cyber Unit which policies the removed posts had violated, and received no response. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] Israel describes the Unit's work as countering incitement and terrorism, which is a legitimate aim, and no source here disputes that some of what it flags is exactly that. The dispute is over scope, over transparency, and over who ends up silenced when a state office routinely asks platforms to remove speech and nearly always gets its way, with little public accounting of what was removed or why.

Human Rights Watch concentrated on Meta and noted that it received fewer reports about TikTok. [cite:sada_social_digital_rights_index_2024] A more granular, platform-by-platform count comes from Sada Social, a tracking organization, whose Digital Rights Index 2024 documented more than 25,000 violations against Palestinian digital content across the major platforms. It broke them down as Instagram 31 percent, TikTok 27 percent, Facebook 24 percent and X 12 percent. [cite:sada_social_digital_rights_index_2024] The breakdown is real and should be read precisely. A larger share for one platform can reflect more suppression on that platform. It can equally reflect a larger user base, easier complaint mechanisms, or the reach of Sada Social's own monitoring. The difference in reporting volume between Meta and TikTok is documented. What it says about each platform's actual moderation rate is not settled by these figures.

TikTok's ownership changed in the period. After the Oracle-led acquisition of TikTok's US operations in 2025–26, a Palestinian journalist and influencer known as Owda was banned from the platform. The new ownership has not publicly addressed the case. [cite:meo_us_tiktok_ownership_bans] Larry Ellison, central to the Oracle side of that deal, has an extensively documented history of major personal donations to Israeli military-support causes, traced elsewhere in this library. Those two facts, the ownership history and the ban, stand side by side in the record. The causal link between them has been discussed by observers. It has not been documented, and one named, dated case after a change of owner is not, on its own, proof of a new policy.

The rules themselves are another layer, and here the companies' own texts are the best evidence. Meta's Transparency Center states that the term "Zionist" "often refers to supporters of a political movement, which is not itself a protected characteristic under our policies, but in some cases may be used as a proxy to refer to Jewish or Israeli people, which are protected characteristics." [cite:meta_transparency_zionist_update] The distinction between a political movement and a people, which [scene:s00c|an earlier section of this volume] draws at length, is therefore written into the platform's own policy. Under its longstanding approach, Meta treated "Zionist" as a proxy for a protected group in two narrow circumstances: comparisons to rats, a documented antisemitic trope, and clear contextual substitution for "Jew" or "Israeli." Following a Policy Forum in March 2024, it expanded that proxy treatment further. [cite:meta_transparency_zionist_update] The policy text sets out the framework. It does not record the individual enforcement decisions made under it.

Meta's own press materials say it consulted roughly 145 stakeholders on the 2024 expansion, among them more than 10 pro-Palestinian, Muslim and Arab organizations, and Jewish Voice for Peace, an anti-Zionist Jewish organization. Jewish Voice for Peace was inside the consultation, then, and it remained among the policy's critics. An academic co-signer of the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism publicly criticized the resulting policy as ambiguous. Existing frameworks, including that declaration, already give clearer guidance on separating anti-Zionism from antisemitism, the critic argued, and under the new wording a call for equality within a single state could be misread as an antisemitic "denial of existence." [cite:novara_meta_zionist_ban] How much weight any one participant's input carried in the final text is not on the public record.

The case for the policy also rests on documented evidence. The American Jewish Committee, which advocated for it, cited its own 2023 survey, which found that 80 percent of American Jews say caring about Israel is an important part of being Jewish. On that basis it argued that "Zionist" is a meaningful proxy for Jewish identity in moderation decisions. [cite:ajc_meta_policy_welcome] The figure is real, and it carries weight: for a large majority of American Jews surveyed, caring about Israel is, by their own account, part of Jewish identity. By the same survey's arithmetic, roughly one in five American Jews do not say this. The survey figures do not describe what that fifth believe, only that a rule built on the proxy does not straightforwardly fit them.

TikTok moved separately to treat "Zionist" as hate speech in circumstances comparable to Meta's. [cite:chrisbennett_tiktok_zionist_label] As of July 2025, its Public Policy Manager for Hate Speech, who joined in 2025, was Erica Mindel, an American-Israeli former soldier in the Israel Defense Forces, described in press coverage including the Jerusalem Post and Jewish Insider as a "proud Zionist." [cite:wiki_erica_mindel] That is a fact about who holds the role that shapes the platform's rules on this exact question. It is stated here as such. No source here documents any specific biased decision by her, and none is implied.

Meta's rules then moved again. In January 2025, after a reported six-week internal review led by Zuckerberg and a small group of confidants, the company rolled back broader hate-speech enforcement and permitted content it had previously banned. The Anti-Defamation League's chief executive, Jonathan Greenblatt, publicly criticized the reversal. Meta did not immediately clarify whether the "Zionist" proxy rule survived it. [cite:jta_meta_reversal] Separately, a formal letter from Senator Warren's office set out that Meta had applied uneven moderation standards to Palestinian-related content compared with other comparable material. [cite:warren_senate_meta_letter]

The record also runs in the other direction, and it is just as documented. In November 2023 the Anti-Defamation League published a study finding specific loopholes in TikTok's own moderation that were being used to spread antisemitic content. It named two: slideshows made in TikTok's Photo Mode, and hashtag manipulation, both of which slipped past automated detection. [cite:adl_tiktok_antisemitism_loopholes] In January 2025 CyberWell, a watchdog organization, praised TikTok for improved removal of Holocaust-denial content relative to other platforms. And TikTok has formally denied the bias accusations made against it: Reuters reported the company calling claims from Malaysia that it suppressed pro-Palestinian content "unfounded." These findings do not cancel the earlier ones. Moderation failures that harm Palestinian users and moderation failures that let antisemitic content through are not mutually exclusive, and on this record both occurred, on the same platforms, in the same years.

Users, for their part, adapted. Palestinian and pro-Palestinian users developed documented ways around automated filters, the most visible being the watermelon. Its red, green, black and white match the colors of the Palestinian flag, and users turned to it because keyword- and image-based filters that flagged the flag did not flag the fruit. It is now recognized worldwide as shorthand for solidarity with Palestine, and it became that because of its origin as a way around moderation. [cite:wagingnonviolence_watermelon_algorithms] The workaround is evidence that the moderation of flag-related content was experienced widely enough to prompt one. It does not, by itself, measure how widespread or systematic the underlying pattern was. That measurement is what the other sources in this section attempt, each with its own limits.

Held together, the record looks like this. A formal human rights investigation and a review Meta commissioned and paid for both found an adverse pattern affecting Palestinian users, and the review found no intentional bias. A government office's own figures show it asking platforms to remove speech at scale, through a channel without public legal process, with compliance above 90 percent in its busiest period. A platform's written policy distinguishes a political movement from a protected people and then defines when it treats one as the other, a rule opposed by an anti-Zionist Jewish organization it consulted and defended with survey evidence by a Jewish organization that advocated it. A separate watchdog found antisemitic content evading moderation on TikTok, and another credited TikTok with improvement. TikTok denies systemic bias, and a named methodological critique of the most prominent report exists. The "neutral platforms" story does not survive the Cyber Unit's own numbers or Meta's own review. The "coordinated conspiracy" story does not survive the absence of documented intent, the antisemitic content that got through, or the limits the investigators stated themselves.

What the record does not settle should be stated plainly. No source here measures the overall rate at which pro-Palestinian and pro-Israel content was removed across any platform, and the best-known dataset was not built to. No source documents intent behind Meta's pattern, and Meta's own reviewers found none. Whether the "Zionist" proxy rule survived Meta's January 2025 overhaul was left unclear. Whether the ban that followed TikTok's change of ownership reflects a new policy is unknown. And the Cyber Unit did not tell Human Rights Watch which rules the posts it asked to remove had broken. How the same years were covered by the major newspapers, where the record shows a different kind of asymmetry, is examined in [scene:gx_s07|the study of how press coverage differed].

sections.h: "Never Again" and the Classroom
sections.html:
A sentence many readers have heard runs roughly as follows: Israel was the world's answer to the Holocaust, the place created so that it could never happen again. It is one of the founding stories many people learned as fact, and it is worth checking in two halves, because the record shows two things at once: the plan came first, and the Holocaust then shaped what followed. This section takes the order of events first, then what American schools actually teach about the Holocaust and who supplies the material, and finally the history of the phrase "Never Again" itself, which has carried two different meanings for most of its life.

The first half concerns timing. The political program for a Jewish state was in print long before the Holocaust. Theodor Herzl's Der Judenstaat of 1896 weighed Palestine against Argentina as the territory for a political answer to European antisemitism, thirty-seven years before Hitler took power in Germany. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] The Sixth Zionist Congress voted in 1903 to investigate British East Africa, and the Seventh formally rejected it in 1905, so Palestine was confirmed by the movement's own choice against a real alternative. [cite:wiki_seventh_zionist_congress] In November 1917 Britain committed in writing to "the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people." [cite:balfour_letter] At San Remo in 1920 the Allied powers assigned Britain the Mandate for Palestine and carried the Balfour language into an international agreement. [cite:san_remo_wiki] The League of Nations approved the Mandate in July 1922, and it took legal force in September 1923; its Article 6 bound Britain to facilitate Jewish immigration and "close settlement by Jews on the land." [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] By 1933, then, the movement had a written program, a settled territorial choice, a great-power pledge, its international ratification and a binding legal mandate. The program, the pledge and the Mandate predate Hitler's rise by between eleven and thirty-seven years. [scene:s07a|Five dates that predate the Holocaust] sets out each date in full.

The second half is just as documented. The Holocaust changed the pace and the public demand. The Biltmore Program of May 1942 called openly for a "Jewish Commonwealth," the movement's first explicit, public statehood demand; it is best read as the culmination of the forty-six years of institution-building before it, not as their origin. [cite:biltmore_wiki] [cite:biltmore_medoff] Reading it that way does not minimize the Holocaust's effect, which was real: the catastrophe reshaped the world's willingness to act. "Never again" describes why the powers finally moved. It does not describe when the planning began.

The scale of what had happened is itself the best-documented fact in this story, and it bears on the classroom questions below. The historian Raul Hilberg's demographic breakdown produced an estimate of 5.1 million Jewish deaths; Lucy Dawidowicz's 1975 research in the birth and death records of prewar European cities produced 5,933,900. [cite:wiki_destruction_european_jews] Yad Vashem's Book of Names project, still under way, has identified about 4.8 million victims individually through testimony and archives. [cite:wiki_book_of_names] Independent methods, using different material, converge on the same range. Auschwitz alone, operating from May 1940 to January 1945, received at least 1.3 million people, of whom at least 1.1 million were murdered there, the largest toll at any single site among more than 44,000 camps and places of incarceration. [cite:wiki_auschwitz_camp] [cite:ushmm_evidence_documentation] Soviet troops liberated it on 27 January 1945, after the SS had driven most of the remaining prisoners onto death marches; the date has been marked since 2005 as International Holocaust Remembrance Day. [cite:wiki_auschwitz_liberation] The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum describes the Holocaust as the best-documented genocide in history, and it lists the core claims of denial: that the six million deaths never occurred, that Nazi Germany had no official extermination policy, and that the gas chambers of Auschwitz-Birkenau never existed. [cite:ushmm_evidence_documentation] The documentation is told in full in [scene:hol_s05|six million, and how that number is known].

The years 1945 to 1948 are where the Holocaust and Palestine actually met, and they met through the survivors. In 1945 Earl G. Harrison's team visited 30 displaced-persons camps in Germany and Austria. They found Jewish survivors held under armed guard behind barbed wire. Harrison wrote:

"we appear to be treating the Jews as the Nazis treated them, except that we do not exterminate them."

He delivered the report to President Truman on 24 August 1945, and the White House released it on 29 September. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_harrison] Harrison reported that most Jewish displaced persons wanted to go to Palestine, and he cited the Jewish Agency's petition for 100,000 additional immigration certificates. Truman asked Prime Minister Clement Attlee to admit 100,000. Attlee refused. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_harrison] The decision over entry to Palestine sat with Britain as the Mandatory power, and Truman's request was refused. Truman's own lever was American immigration law. His directive of 22 December 1945 gave displaced persons preference within the existing quotas, and about 22,950 entered the United States over two years, roughly two-thirds of them Jewish. [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_harrison] The directive worked inside the existing quotas, so the 100,000 Truman asked Britain to admit stood against some 22,950 admitted by his own country over two years.

That refuge argument became the core of how support for the new state was presented to Americans. In 1948 the case rested on humanitarian grounds, with some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons in Europe, on Christian restorationist belief, and on the new state's presentation as a democracy. The national-security establishment argued the reverse: the State Department, the Joint Chiefs, the Defense Secretary and the CIA warned that American backing would harm American interests. Hostile framing of Arabs in pro-Zionist publicity drew heavily on the Grand Mufti's documented wartime collaboration with Hitler, a real episode used as a broad brush; the organized, well-funded anti-Islam network in the United States is documented mainly from the 2000s. [cite:cap_fear_inc] The "strategic asset" argument came later, growing after 1967 and formalized under President Reagan in 1981. That story belongs to [scene:sell_s01|how Israel was sold to Americans]. Among the founding narratives this library checks, "born of the Holocaust" fails in the same way: the Holocaust accelerated support; it did not create the program.

Turn now to the American classroom. The federal instrument is the Never Again Education Act, H.R. 943, signed on Friday, 29 May 2020. It requires the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum to develop and disseminate resources that improve awareness and understanding of the Holocaust, and it authorizes Holocaust education programs for prospective and current teachers and educational leaders. [cite:rs_ch01_wh_naea] The museum received $2 million under the Act in fiscal year 2025. [cite:rs_ch01_gao_holed]

The fullest account of what the states do is a report by the Government Accountability Office, delivered on 7 July 2026 to the House and Senate appropriations subcommittees for Labor, Health and Human Services and Education: GAO-26-108023, K–12 Education: How States and the U.S. Holocaust Museum Support Holocaust Education, prepared under a provision in Senate Report 118-84. [cite:rs_ch01_gao_holed] GAO counted 51 jurisdictions, the District of Columbia among them. Forty-three have academic standards that explicitly mention the Holocaust or laws that require it to be taught: 35 include it in their standards and 25 require it by law. Eight have neither: Kansas, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, Vermont, Washington and Wyoming. [cite:rs_ch01_gao_holed]

The requirements vary widely. Arizona's law requires at least three class periods, or the equivalent, on at least two occasions between the seventh and twelfth grades. Florida's standards run from fifth through twelfth grade. New Hampshire's mention the Holocaust in a single world-history standard. Michigan's law covers grades 8 to 12 and names both the Holocaust and the Armenian Genocide. GAO gives no typical number of hours; state officials told it that teachers "had to choose which parts of the Holocaust to cover." [cite:rs_ch01_gao_holed] The history of these mandates is mostly recent. According to Echoes & Reflections, which tracks them, the earliest were California's in 1985, for grades 7 to 12; Illinois in 1990, expanded in 2005; New Jersey in March 1994; and New York in 1996, amended in 2022. Most of the others date from 2016 onward. [cite:rs_ch01_er_map]

Who supplies the material matters as much as who mandates it. Per GAO, 35 states use materials from local or state Holocaust museums and centers, 34 from the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and 20 from state Holocaust commissions. Ten of the 48 states that responded write their own materials, and none of them requires schools to use them. Of 70 teachers who acquired materials, 56 found them on their own. [cite:rs_ch01_gao_holed] The main gap GAO found was teacher preparation. Only 3 of 48 states require Holocaust-specific teacher training. Forty-one of 48 called teacher preparedness very or somewhat challenging; 39 cited insufficient time, 37 funding and 34 misinformation. [cite:rs_ch01_gao_holed] The mandate has spread widely; the training, and the choice of materials, rest largely with teachers.

A survey of young adults followed in early 2020. The Claims Conference commissioned it, and Schoen Cooperman Research compiled it, from 1,350 Americans aged 18 to 39. According to J. Weekly's account of it, 63% did not know that six million Jews were murdered: 37% chose six million and 15% chose two million. Thirty-six percent could not name a camp, 12% said the number who died had been "greatly exaggerated," 90% said the Holocaust happened, and 49% had seen Holocaust denial online. The Berkeley sociologist Samuel Lucas cautioned that "not sure" answers and the wording of questions are hard to interpret, and that social-desirability bias could make denial look smaller than it really is. [cite:rs_ch01_jw_claims] His caution runs both ways: some answers are hard to read, and the denial figure may understate denial.

One curriculum GAO names is Echoes & Reflections, which it identifies as a partnership of the Anti-Defamation League, the USC Shoah Foundation and Yad Vashem. [cite:rs_ch01_gao_holed] According to J. Weekly's report of its launch in 2005, it was announced by the ADL, the Shoah Visual History Foundation and Yad Vashem, which the paper described as "Israel's Holocaust Remembrance Authority." It offered ten lessons with maps, photographs, timelines and primary sources, and 51 video testimonies drawn from the Shoah Foundation's 52,000 interviews. Yad Vashem supplied the historical expertise; the ADL handled outreach to schools and state officials. [cite:rs_ch01_jw_er2005] Yad Vashem's own status is set by law. It had operated privately since 1946. The Yad Vashem Law was brought to the Knesset on 18 May 1953 and passed on 19 August 1953, making it a body of the State of Israel. Its mandate includes representing the State at national and international commemorations, and the Knesset limited it to the Holocaust and the destroyed communities, not the rebuilding of the homeland. [cite:rs_ch01_yv_law] A body of the Israeli state is therefore one of three partners in an American curriculum, and its legal remit is the Holocaust and the destroyed communities, not the rebuilding of the homeland.

The program's lesson "Antisemitism after the Holocaust," for middle and high school, lists this learning objective: "Identify current features of antisemitism including Holocaust denial and distortion, and demonization of Israel." [cite:rs_ch01_adl_lesson] Whether that belongs in Holocaust education became an open fight in 2025. On 5 July delegates at the National Education Association's Representative Assembly narrowly adopted a new business item, NBI 39, saying the union would not use, endorse or publicize ADL materials or programs. Because it called for a boycott, it went to the union's executive committee, which rejected it on 18 July 2025. [cite:rs_ch01_njea_nbi39] [cite:rs_ch01_edweek_nea] The two positions deserve to be stated at their strongest. The ADL lesson treats demonization of Israel as one current feature of antisemitism, alongside denial and distortion, and the NEA's leadership kept the ADL as a partner; its president, Becky Pringle, said the boycott "would not further NEA's commitment to academic freedom, our membership, or our goals." [cite:rs_ch01_adl_lesson] [cite:rs_ch01_edweek_nea] The item's sponsor, Judy Greenspan, and the teachers behind it argued that the ADL's definition of antisemitism folds criticism of Israel into antisemitism and has made real antisemitism harder to track and fight. [cite:rs_ch01_edweek_nea] The union's delegates and its executive committee came down on opposite sides within two weeks, which is a fair measure of how unsettled the question is.

The phrase at the center of all this has its own history. According to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, its first use is murky. JTA traced it most likely to postwar Israel: it appeared in secular kibbutzim in the late 1940s and in a Swedish Holocaust documentary in 1961. Some trace it further back, to Isaac Lamdan's 1926 Hebrew poem "Masada," with its line "Never shall Masada fall again!" [cite:rs_ch01_jta_never]

Its English currency, by JTA's account, came from Meir Kahane, who founded the Jewish Defense League in 1968 and titled his 1972 manifesto Never Again. For Kahane it meant "that if it happens again, it won't happen in the same way," and he used it to justify acts of terror against antisemitism. After his assassination in November 1990, Sholom Comay, president of the American Jewish Committee, said Kahane "must always be remembered for the slogan Never Again." [cite:rs_ch01_jta_never] The phrase later took on a universal meaning. Barack Obama said in 2011 that it should be "not just a phrase but a principled cause." The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum made it the theme of its 2013 Days of Remembrance. Elie Wiesel wrote in 2012 that it "becomes more than a slogan: It's a prayer, a promise, a vow." [cite:rs_ch01_jta_never] In 2010 Benjamin Netanyahu used both senses. At Auschwitz he said, "never again will we allow the hand of evil to sever the life of our people"; in the guestbook of the Rwanda genocide memorial he wrote, simply, "Never again." [cite:rs_ch01_jta_never]

That is the second dispute, and again both sides have a case. On the particular reading, set out by the scholar Shaul Magid, Kahane's "Never Again" was a call to militancy as the only act of prevention, and leaders have used the phrase to mean the protection of the Jewish people specifically. On the universal reading, Holocaust museums, Wiesel and others use it as a vow against genocide anywhere, and it has been taken up for refugees, for Japanese-American internment and for other causes; the historian Hasia Diner argues that objecting to such uses is not, by itself, reasonable. [cite:rs_ch01_jta_never] Neither reading owns the phrase. Netanyahu's two uses in one year show that the same speaker can mean both.

The record leaves real gaps. GAO's report, the most complete federal account of Holocaust education, does not mention Israel at all. [cite:rs_ch01_gao_holed] No national study measures how classrooms connect the Holocaust to Israel, whether through the Echoes & Reflections lesson objective or otherwise, so any claim that American schools teach the Holocaust as the reason for Israel, or that they do not, goes beyond what is documented. The survey of young adults measured knowledge of the Holocaust, not beliefs about Israel, and its own critic questioned how far even its knowledge figures can be read. The origin of the phrase itself remains unsettled. What the record does settle is the order of events: the plan came decades before the Holocaust, and the Holocaust, through the survivors in the camps, then shaped the years from 1945 to 1948.

sections.h: The Holocaust in the World's Classrooms
sections.html:
The previous section asked what American schools teach about the Holocaust, who supplies the material and what young Americans actually know. [scene:ch01_never_again|"Never Again" and the Classroom] The same questions can be put to every other country, in the same way: what the curriculum requires, who wrote it, how the event is framed, and what the public knows. A familiar assumption holds that the Holocaust is a fixed lesson taught alike wherever history is taught. The documents show a mandatory topic in some systems, a line about human rights in others, and nothing at all in some.

The fullest global picture is a mapping for UNESCO by the Georg Eckert Institute, published in 2015. It analysed 272 curricula valid in 2013–2014 from 135 of a possible 195 countries, and 89 textbooks from 26 countries published since 2000. [cite:rs_ch01_unesco_sum] [cite:rs_ch01_ucl_unesco] Its summary reports that the Holocaust appears in the history curricula of approximately half of the countries investigated, and that about a quarter of all curricula do not name the Holocaust but refer to its context, such as the Second World War or National Socialism. [cite:rs_ch01_unesco_sum] A report on the study in The Conversation gave the count differently: 57 curricula directly stipulate the Holocaust with words such as "Holocaust" or "Shoah," eight countries address it only partially, and 46 provide only the context of the war or National Socialism. [cite:rs_ch01_conv_unesco] Both summaries mix units, counting countries in some figures and curricula in others, so their numbers cannot be lined up directly; they are two summaries of one study, not two measurements.

Most curricula, the summary found, do not specify which victim groups to cover; where groups are named, Jews are usually the only ones explicitly listed. [cite:rs_ch01_unesco_sum] Which curricula leave the Holocaust out entirely is one point on which the two summaries diverge. The UNESCO summary gives Brunei Darussalam, Iceland and Thailand as examples of curricula with no reference to it; the Conversation report on the same study names Egypt, Palestine, Iraq, New Zealand and Thailand. [cite:rs_ch01_unesco_sum] [cite:rs_ch01_conv_unesco] Only Thailand appears on both; the full list that would reconcile them has not been published in these summaries. The summary also lists Argentina, Belize, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico and Slovenia as countries whose curricula refer to the Holocaust only partially, framing it as a violation of human rights; in Mexico it appears as one aspect among others of human-rights education. [cite:rs_ch01_unesco_sum] [cite:rs_ch01_conv_unesco]

Framing varied as much as coverage. In the textbooks the study examined, the Holocaust was generally located in "Europe" and "Germany," while Russian and Indian textbooks cast it in transcontinental terms, setting Europe against Asia. [cite:rs_ch01_unesco_sum] Rwandan textbooks apply Holocaust vocabulary to the genocide of 1994. Chinese textbooks use the terms "genocide" (datusha) and "kinds of crimes" (zhongzhong zuixing) rather than "Holocaust" or "Shoah," and apply such language to the Nanjing massacres of 1937.
