The states that define the region's later conflicts, Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel, did not exist. Iran stood apart: it was never Ottoman, and it had its own dynasty, its own language and a Shia majority. Almost every border that matters in today's conflicts was drawn later, in a six-year window between 1916 and 1922, by two European powers, Britain and France.

Inside the empire, religion rather than territory organized much of law. Under the millet system, recognized religious communities (Muslims, Christians of several churches, and Jews) administered their own religious law, courts and schooling, and governed marriage, inheritance and education under their own leaders. [cite:w_ottoman_millet] The arrangement was not a golden age, and nothing in the record presents it as one. Its costs were real: heavy taxation, conscription, periodic violence, and a second-class status for non-Muslims, who paid special taxes and held lesser standing. Revolts were suppressed. The point the record makes is narrower than nostalgia. The order was imperfect, but it was not the patchwork of rival states the twentieth century created.

Palestine sat inside this order as a set of administrative units rather than as a country with its own frontier. Apart from a period of Egyptian rule from 1831 to 1840, it was administered as Ottoman provinces, chiefly the district of Jerusalem and parts of the provinces of Beirut and Damascus, with no border separating it from what are now Syria, Lebanon or Jordan. The precise word for that rule is imperial. Governors, garrisons and tax collectors ruled over a population that remained largely Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, with long-established Jewish communities in Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias. Rule came through administration and taxation, not through replacing the population. It ended when British forces captured Jerusalem in December 1917, and the Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923, formally renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces in the Treaty of Lausanne that year. [cite:w_lausanne] Modern Turkey is the empire's successor state, not a claimant to the land. Lausanne belongs to a later volume. It is mentioned here only to mark where the Ottoman story ends.

Two maps drawn for this library begin at this point. In the first, the Ottoman order of 1516 to 1917, with no internal borders, is the root from which the later layers of the region grow, beginning with the Anglo-French carve-up of 1916 to 1922. In the second, Ottoman rule is the first station in the long relationship between Turkey and Israel, and the next is the 1923 renunciation at Lausanne. Only their first box belongs to this chapter. Every later station is told in later volumes.

The period from 1799 to 1840 shows how this imperial order behaved under pressure from outside. Within a single generation, a French army, an Egyptian army, a peasant revolt and a coalition of European fleets all fought over the coast and hills of Palestine. On this section's reading, the decisive choices were made each time in Paris, Cairo, Istanbul or London.

The first pressure came from France. During his Egyptian and Syrian campaign, Napoleon Bonaparte besieged Acre in 1799, and the campaign was defeated by combined British and Ottoman forces. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] He never reached Jerusalem. The Jewish Virtual Library's account dates his retreat from Acre to 22 May 1799. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_jvl] That is also the date given for a French newspaper report about him. A reference summary of the scholarship records that the Gazette nationale of 3 Prairial, Year VII (22 May 1799) printed a short report that Bonaparte had invited the Jews of Asia and Africa to gather under his flag. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] Whether one source has run the two events onto one date has not been settled in this book's research.

That newspaper item stands beside one of the most contested documents in the prehistory of Zionism. A much fuller text, a "Letter to the Jewish Nation," headed "General Headquarters, Jerusalem, 1st Floréal [Year VII], April 20th, 1799" and addressed to the "rightful heirs of Palestine," was first published only in 1940, when Franz Kobler announced a German translation in The New Judaea. No original has ever been found. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_jvl] [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_akadem] The letter is dated and placed in Jerusalem, a city its supposed author never reached.

Historians have divided sharply over what, if anything, Napoleon proclaimed. The case for forgery is made by four of the scholars the sources name. Simon Schwarzfuchs (1979), Henry Laurens, Ronald Schechter and Jeremy Popkin regard the German text as forged. Schechter goes further and reads even the 1799 newspaper report as a rumor. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] A French Jewish educational site calls the forgery "almost certainly established" and attributes it to Frankist circles. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_akadem] The strongest form of this case rests on the document's history: it surfaces only in 1940, in translation, with no original, and its heading places Napoleon where he never was.

The other side does not dismiss the episode. Mordechai Gichon argues that Napoleon did conceive of a Jewish national home in the Land of Israel. Nathan Schur reads the 1799 report as propaganda aimed at local Jews. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] The Jewish Virtual Library prints the letter and says only that its authenticity "has been debated ever since." [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_jvl] The strongest form of this side's case is that a contemporary French newspaper did print a report of an appeal to Jews in May 1799, so that something was said or rumoured at the time, whatever became of the text. What the record does not settle is whether Bonaparte himself issued any appeal, what it said, and who composed the letter that appeared in 1940.

The second pressure came from Egypt, whose ruler, Muhammad Ali, fielded his own army against the Sultan. Ibrahim Pasha, son of Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali, invaded Ottoman Syria on 31 October 1831 and made Haifa his main base from December 1831. According to a reference summary, Palestine remained under Egyptian rule until 1840. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki] Ibrahim's conscription order of 25 April 1834 required one Muslim man in five, beginning with 200 from Jerusalem, and conscripts were to serve for life. He also disarmed Nablus and the Hebron district and imposed new taxes, including one on the Muslim administrative class. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834] [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki]

The result was a revolt. Judith Mendelsohn Rood reconstructed it from the records of Jerusalem's Islamic court. In her account, the revolt was led from Nablus by Qasim al-Ahmad, with 'Isa Amar leading the Hebron district, while the mufti of Jerusalem, Tahir Afandi al-Husayni, acted as mediator and was later exiled. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834] He should not be assumed to be the Muhammad Tahir al-Husayni who appears later in the [scene:rd0_limits|campaign against land sales in the 1890s]; the sources name the two muftis separately and do not connect them.

On 19 and 20 May 1834, about 36 rebels entered Jerusalem through an abandoned sewer near the Dung Gate and opened the gate to the rest. The first day's fighting killed 50 peasants, 16 townspeople and five soldiers. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834] [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki] Rood reports that Ibrahim lost 1,500 of his 9,000 soldiers in rebel ambushes. The violence did not run along a single line: 33 Christian men and women of Bayt Jala were killed on suspicion of looting. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834]

The sources differ on Hebron, and both versions are given here. In Rood's account, Hebron was besieged on 24 July, and 630 young men were afterwards sent to Egypt for the army. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834] A reference summary instead dates Hebron's defeat to 4 August and gives about 500 killed and 750 men conscripted. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki] Rood's study rests on the Jerusalem court records, but neither figure can be confirmed against the other with the material in hand. Qasim al-Ahmad was captured in Transjordan in August 1834 and beheaded in Damascus. His sons were beheaded in Acre. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834]

The wider cost is known only from the reference summary, and it is reported here as that source's figure. It states that some 10,000 peasants were deported to Egypt, and that deportation, conscription and flight together reduced Palestine's male population by about one-fifth. The same source records the rebels' stated aim: to expel the Egyptians and restore Ottoman rule. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki]

That stated aim lies at the center of a real argument among historians. The question is whether 1834 was an early moment of Palestinian national identity. Baruch Kimmerling and Joel Migdal, in The Palestinian People (2003), treat the revolt as formative, because it joined disparate groups against a common enemy, and those groups later re-emerged as the Palestinian people. The strongest form of their case, as this section reads it, rests on the shape of the revolt itself: peasants and townspeople from Nablus, Jerusalem and the Hebron hills, with the city's religious leadership as intermediary, acting together against one ruler. Benny Morris argues the opposite. The rebels demanded no independence, they likely saw themselves as Ottoman subjects, Arabs or Syrians, and they left no lasting national tradition. The reference summary that reports his view adds that the revolt is largely absent from Palestinian collective memory, and that its declared purpose was to restore the Ottomans, not to replace them. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki]

Two further readings complicate both positions. Shimon Shamir sees the Egyptian period as the first application of the territorial state in Palestine. Adel Manna argues that the way twentieth-century writers felt about the Ottomans and about Muhammad Ali shaped how the revolt was later written about. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki] On Manna's point, the debate over 1834 is partly a debate about the twentieth century carried back into the nineteenth. What the sources do not settle is what the rebels thought they were: the sources preserve their acts and their stated aim, but not a statement of identity in their own words.

The third pressure came from Europe, and it ended the Egyptian interlude. On 15 July 1840, in the Convention of London, Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia backed Sultan Abdülmecid I against Muhammad Ali. They offered him hereditary rule of Egypt if he withdrew from Syria. [cite:rs_rd0_oriental1840_wiki] [cite:rs_rd0_oriental1840_ellison] British and allied ships then shelled Beirut and Sidon on 11 September 1840 and bombarded Acre on 3 November 1840. On 27 November 1840 Muhammad Ali accepted terms. He withdrew from Syria and the Holy Land in return for hereditary rule of Egypt and Sudan. [cite:rs_rd0_oriental1840_wiki] Acre, where a French campaign had been defeated in 1799, was bombarded by European ships in 1840.

Britain's reason for acting was stated plainly, and it was not about Palestine as such. In William Erich Ellison's 2024 analysis of the crisis, Britain sought to "preserve Turkey" as a route to India and as a bulwark against Russian expansion. [cite:rs_rd0_oriental1840_ellison] The same years saw a separate, religious current in British policy toward Jerusalem, which is told in [scene:bc_s05|the section on Protestant restorationism]. The two converged in 1840 without being the same thing. The interest that moved the fleets was imperial and strategic. In the same years, Istanbul began its own program of reform, the subject of [scene:rd0_tanzimat|the next part of the Ottoman story].

Seen as a mechanism, the four decades follow a single pattern. The power to decide who ruled Palestine lay with the Sultan in Istanbul, with the ruler of Egypt in Cairo, who could raise his own army, and, by 1840, with a concert of European powers that could settle the question by treaty and enforce it with ships. The people of the land had one instrument of their own, revolt, and in 1834 they used it against conscription, disarmament and new taxes. They could make Egyptian rule costly, at the price of deportations, executions and a lost fifth of the male population, if the reference figure is right. They could not decide the outcome. That was settled in London in July 1840 and enforced off Acre in November, and the settlement returned the land to the empire that the rebels of 1834 had said they wanted back.

Several things remain open. No original of Napoleon's supposed letter has been found, and the scholars who have studied it disagree about whether even the 1799 report reflects anything he said. The Hebron figures differ between the court-record study and the reference summary. The deportation total and the one-fifth estimate rest on a reference summary rather than on a study of the records. And whether the revolt of 1834 was the first stirring of a Palestinian national identity, a provincial rising for the old order, or both at once remains a matter of interpretation on which the historians named here continue to disagree.

sections.h: N M Rothschild & Sons: The London House and Its Legend
sections.html:
The British state whose fleets returned Palestine to the Sultan in 1840 borrowed through the City of London, and one of its lenders was the house Nathan Mayer Rothschild had founded there. The best-known story about that house is a single episode. Nathan Rothschild, it says, watched the Battle of Waterloo, raced the news to London, and made the family fortune by buying up British bonds before anyone else knew the result. The story is still repeated. The documented record of the London house is a different kind of history, slower and more ordinary: a merchant bank that lent to a foreign state on new terms, supplied the Bank of England in a panic, sent the first Jewish member to the House of Commons, and found the money for Britain's Suez Canal shares while Parliament was not sitting. The legend can be traced to a pamphlet published in 1846, ten years after Nathan's death, and written to stir hostility toward Jews.

The house began as one part of a family design. Mayer Amschel Rothschild of Frankfurt placed five sons in five European financial centers: Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples. The result was a cross-border house that could move capital and information between capitals faster than most governments could. That structure, rather than any single trade, is the documented source of the family's position in the nineteenth century. [cite:wiki_nathan_mayer_rothschild] The father's rise, and the dispersal of the five brothers, are told in [scene:s01|an earlier section].

The London house was founded by Nathan Mayer Rothschild, who lived from 1777 to 1836. Its founding date is given two ways in this book's sources. One account dates N M Rothschild & Sons to 1809, and places Nathan in London from that year. [cite:wiki_nathan_mayer_rothschild] Another gives 1811. [cite:schama_two_rothschilds] The sources do not explain the difference, and both dates are recorded here. This Nathan, the founder, should not be confused with a later namesake, Nathan Mayer Rothschild, 1st Baron, the father of the Walter Rothschild to whom the Balfour Declaration was addressed in 1917.

The house's first great contribution to state finance came in 1818. It arranged a £5 million loan for Prussia, denominated in sterling, with interest payable in London. Until then, the currency risk of foreign bonds had kept British investors out of them. A loan written in sterling and paid in London removed that risk. The Rothschild Archive describes the Prussian loan as "the true precursor of the public borrowing which transformed the international capital market in the nineteenth century." [cite:jwatte_rothschild_myths_record] That description is quoted from the family's own institutional record, and it should be read as such: the archive's judgment of the loan's importance, not an independent one. In this book's sources it reaches the reader through a personal website that reproduces the archive's words, since the archive's own page could not be checked directly.

In 1825, during a banking panic, the house supplied the Bank of England with specie, that is, hard coin. The institution that had been chartered in 1694 to lend to the Crown [scene:rd0_bank1694|as the chapter has shown] now drew on a private house in a crisis. On this book's reading, the two were not rivals but parts of the same London system of state credit.

The London house's political ties to the state came through Nathan's son, Lionel de Rothschild. Lionel was elected to the House of Commons repeatedly from 1847, but he could not take his seat, because members were required to swear an oath as Christians. When the Jews Relief Act ended that requirement, he took his seat in 1858 as the first Jewish member of the House of Commons. [cite:wiki_lionel_de_rothschild]

Lionel was also head of the house when it carried out its most famous transaction with the British state. The Suez Canal had opened in 1869. It was owned by French financiers and by the Khedive of Egypt, but by 1874 four-fifths of its trade was British. [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023] On 15 November 1875, Benjamin Disraeli learned that the Khedive meant to sell his shares. Ten days later, on 25 November 1875, the purchase was concluded: Britain acquired 44% of the company's shares for £4,000,000. [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023]

The speed is what made the house necessary. Parliament was not sitting, so the government could not vote the money. N M Rothschild & Sons, under Lionel de Rothschild, advanced it. The Rothschild Archive calls it a "technically unsecured loan" and says it was repaid within five months. [cite:rs_rd0_rotharchive_suez] [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023] The mechanism matters more than the drama of the story. An executive that wanted to act before the legislature could meet borrowed from a private house in the City, and asked Parliament to approve the act after it was done.

The purchase did not pass without objection. William Gladstone attacked it for its "lack of reference or consent from Parliament." The purchase also left France as the majority shareholder. [cite:rs_rd0_rotharchive_suez] Disraeli answered his critics in the House of Commons on 14 and 21 February 1876, and his own words, preserved in Hansard, state the government's reason without ambiguity. He defended the purchase "as a political transaction, and one which I believe is calculated to strengthen the Empire," and said it "secures to us a highway to our Indian Empire." He did not recommend it, he said, "as a financial investment." [cite:rs_rd0_disraeli_1876] He also described what the advance had to meet: after the first £1,000,000, he told the House, a further £2,000,000 "might be demanded in gold the next day." [cite:rs_rd0_disraeli_1876] Parliament approved the purchase on 21 February 1876. [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023]

What the house earned is the one point in the Suez story that the sources leave open. Critics in Parliament said the Rothschild commission amounted to 15 percent interest. Disraeli rejected that reading, and denied that the commission had "anything to do with the interest on the advance." [cite:rs_rd0_disraeli_1876] The critics' case, as Disraeli's speech reports it, was that the commission amounted to 15 percent interest; Disraeli's was that the commission was not interest at all. None of the sources consulted states the actual commission rate. [cite:rs_rd0_rotharchive_suez] Who was right cannot be settled from them. Disraeli's stated aim, the route to India, belongs to the story of why Britain wanted the region at all, which is taken up in [scene:or_s01|a later volume].

Set against that record, the Waterloo story belongs to a different category. It first appears in 1846, in a pamphlet by Georges Dairnvaell, published under the name "Satan." Dairnvaell wrote it after a railway accident on a line the Rothschilds had financed, and he wrote it explicitly to inflame hostility toward Jews. [cite:wiki_dairnvaell_satan_pamphlet] Nathan had died in 1836. He could not answer it. The story's origin is antisemitic. The sources describe that aim as explicit, not as something read into the pamphlet afterwards.

The family's archive rejects the story on the evidence. According to the Rothschild Archive, nothing in the record suggests that Nathan was the first in London to know of the victory. Niall Ferguson, author of the family's authorized history, estimates that any quick profit Nathan could have made on British bonds after the battle could not have exceeded about £7,000. The archive's verdict, as quoted in this book's sources, is short: "The legend of Nathan Rothschild and Waterloo is just that: a legend." [cite:jwatte_rothschild_myths_record] [cite:leonardo_english_rothschild_waterloo] These words reach this book through the same personal website noted above, and are given here as the archive's position as reported there.

Not every account in this book's research tells the story the same way. A summary of the Frankfurt dynasty's history, drawing on volume 1 of Ferguson's The House of Rothschild (1998), credits him with a different verdict: that the tale is partly documented and partly embellished, that Nathan's information advantage was real, that the market timing was more complex than the mythology, and that the version in which Nathan "cornered the market" was a nineteenth-century antisemitic caricature by Édouard Drumont, later amplified. That version and the one given here agree that the legend's popular form is an antisemitic invention. They differ on its origin, Dairnvaell in 1846 or Drumont, and on whether Nathan had any advantage in news at all. Both accounts invoke Ferguson, and this section cannot settle between them: the archive's statement and the £7,000 ceiling point toward the narrower reading, but the archive's words reach this book secondhand, and neither summary could be checked here against Ferguson's own text.

The legend also fed a larger claim. The claim that the family secretly directed governments rests on the line that runs from the 1846 pamphlet and on later elaborations. The family's own archive, Ferguson's authorized history and the journalist Mike Rothschild's 2023 study each take those claims apart. [cite:publishersweekly_jewish_space_lasers] The Waterloo legend is antisemitic in origin, and naming it as such is part of the record.

The documented house, in short, was a creditor and contractor to states, not a puppeteer of them. Its relationships with the British government were contracts: sovereign loans, a central bank supplied in a panic, the Suez advance, and a seat in Parliament won by election and delayed by an oath. All of them operated inside the City of London that the chapter began with. The documents also show who held the power to decide. The Suez purchase was Disraeli's to make, Parliament's to approve and Gladstone's to attack. Disraeli's own justification for it was the empire, not the bank.

Some things remain open. The founding year of the London house is recorded two ways. The size of the Suez commission, and so the real cost of the advance to the Treasury, is not stated in any source consulted. The Rothschild Archive's verdict on Waterloo is known here only secondhand, and published summaries of Ferguson describe his findings differently. None of these gaps changes the central finding. The record of the London house is a record of public, contractual business with states, and the legend that replaced it in popular memory was made, from its first printing, as an attack on Jews.

sections.h: The Pope's Bankers: Torlonia, the Rothschilds and the Papal Loans, 1794–1870
sections.html:
London was not the only sovereign borrower the Rothschild houses served. A common assumption holds that the papacy has always managed its money through its own institutions, apart from any private banking family. For the nineteenth century the record points the other way. Before 1870 the Pope was also the ruler of a territorial state, the Papal States, and like other rulers of his time he borrowed. One lender was a Roman banker whom the papacy ennobled. Then came the Rothschild houses. The arrangement between them, and the hostility it drew, are a small but revealing part of the European board on which Palestine's future would later be decided.

This section rests on a narrower base of evidence than most in the chapter, and the reader should know that from the start. Almost every detail of the papal loans below reaches this book through a single reference article on the Rothschild loans to the Holy See, which in turn relies on Niall Ferguson's history of the house of Rothschild. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] The specific terms of the 1831 arrangement, its reported exclusivity clause, the 1834 episode and the 1906 encyclopedia phrase have not been independently confirmed. The accounts also contradict one another at several points. Those contradictions are set out below rather than resolved.

The story begins with Giovanni Torlonia, who lived from 1754 to 1829. According to the account summarized here, he was born to modest circumstances in the Auvergne region of France and built one of the largest banking fortunes in Rome through cloth trading, money-lending and papal patronage. He opened his banking house in Rome in 1780. By the 1790s he had become the Holy See's principal banker, providing loans, managing financial transactions and handling the papacy's increasingly complex needs during the Napoleonic period. Pope Pius VI made him a noble in 1794, on 9 March according to the date the account gives from the Archivio di Stato, as Don Giovanni Torlonia, 1st Prince of Civitella Cesi. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see]

The mechanism here is plain. The banker supplied the papacy with financial services, and the papacy supplied the banker with aristocratic standing. The account describes the exchange as mutually reinforcing: the Torlonia house became the papacy's main financial institution and gained the social legitimacy of papal nobility at the same time. The French Revolutionary period enlarged its role. When French forces occupied Rome in 1798 and 1799 and papal finances were thrown into disorder, the account says, Torlonia's house managed the transfer of papal funds and lent the money that kept the papacy's operations going through the occupation and the restoration that followed. By Napoleon's final defeat in 1814, the family was established as the papacy's principal financial manager. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see]

The papacy also stood at the center of an older Roman aristocracy. The Orsini and the Colonna, two of its oldest families, had held the ceremonial office of Prince Assistant to the Papal Throne in alternation since 1735. The Orsini had produced three popes: Celestine III in 1191, Nicholas III in 1277 and Benedict XIII in 1724. None came in the modern era. [cite:wiki_black_nobility] [cite:wiki_orsini_family]

In 1823 the new banking family married into this old one, when Giovanni's son Alessandro Torlonia married an Orsini. The bride's name is itself recorded two ways in the same account: once as Maria Luisa Orsini, and once as Teresa Orsini. The account cites the evidence of the marriage as Rome diocesan records, the Orsini family genealogies held in the Archivio Segreto Vaticano and in private family archives, and Pompeo Litta's Famiglie celebri d'Italia (1819–83), a record of the great Italian noble lineages. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] It goes on to interpret the match: Alessandro needed the legitimacy that only centuries-old noble blood could provide, while the Orsini needed to keep their finances afloat after the disruptions of the Napoleonic years, and the marriage was arranged, as such marriages were, with both families' positions in mind. In this telling, the timing of the Rothschild connection eight years later was "not accidental." That is the account's own interpretation. No document quoted in it shows the marriage being made with the later banking arrangement in view.

The Rothschilds entered Roman finance in 1831. The reference account explains why. After the Napoleonic wars and the Restoration, the Papal States were in fiscal distress. The Torlonia house lacked the capital to meet the papacy's needs at the scale now required. And the Rothschild houses were, by 1830, the dominant private banking operation in Europe. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] On 30 November 1831, according to the account, Alessandro Torlonia co-signed a contract in Rome with James Mayer de Rothschild of the Paris house. The account's short summary describes the contract as giving the Rothschilds an exclusive right of first refusal on all papal sovereign debt, by a clause kept secret. Its more detailed description, drawn from Ferguson, describes the terms differently, as exclusive management of papal loan issues and key papal financial operations through the London house of Nathan Mayer Rothschild and the Paris house of James Mayer de Rothschild, with the Torlonia house as local intermediary. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] A right of first refusal and the exclusive management of loans are not the same thing. The record available here does not settle which description fits the contract, because the contract itself is not quoted.

The loan that followed is the part the account itself calls documented. In 1832 the Rothschilds lent £400,000 to Pope Gregory XVI. The loan was negotiated through Carl Mayer von Rothschild, with James acting as the official papal banker. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] According to the account, a letter from Gregory XVI dated 15 January 1832 acknowledges the Rothschilds' help in terms that confirm the relationship. Who repaid the loan, over what term and at what rate are not stated in the sources available. Nor do they say from what revenues of the Papal States it was serviced.

The episode of 1834 is where the sources diverge most sharply, and the two versions cannot both be true as told. In one, the 1834 affair was the enforcement of the secret clause. A cardinal named Tosti tried to refinance the papal debt with six other banks, and Carl Mayer de Rothschild traveled to Rome, produced the original contract and blocked him. In the other, Antonio Tosti was not a cardinal refinancing the debt but the papal treasurer (elsewhere, the papal envoy), and he had embezzled papal funds. The Rothschild houses' records of their dealings with the papacy could be compared against the papacy's own accounts, the discrepancies revealed the embezzlement, and the Rothschild correspondence, as Ferguson describes it, refers to the affair and to the banking relationship's role in uncovering it. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] The second version comes with an interpretation: that the papacy's own financial management could not detect fraud by its own treasurer, that the external auditor, however informal, was the Rothschild house, and that the papacy's finances before any internal institution existed, before the Vatican bank, the IOR, was founded in 1942, depended on this outside relationship. That reading depends on which version of 1834 is right, and the record available here does not decide it.

The question of which Rothschild house was the counterparty is itself unsettled. The account's summary names James Mayer de Rothschild of the Paris house as the signatory in 1831. Its detailed description names the London and Paris houses together. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] A separate explanatory treatment in this book's research names the Paris house and the Naples house of the Rothschilds as the lenders, and in another version names the London house, N M Rothschild & Sons. What the account does show is that Carl Mayer and James both appear in the record of the 1832 loan.

The same explanatory treatment offers an analogy for the relationship, given here as an analogy, not a finding. Imagine a family that takes out one loan from one lender in a crisis. From then on, whenever money is needed, everyone simply calls the same number. Nobody decides it each time. It was decided once, long ago, and the number stays taped to the wall. The analogy's authors insist that this is not a conspiracy but the way long-lived institutions prefer to work: a relationship that is expensive to set up and hard to replace, so that the first lender becomes the default for every later need. As a description of institutional habit it is useful. As history it claims more than the sources show, because it assumes a continuity of lending that the record of this period does not document beyond the loans of the 1830s.

The relationship was public knowledge by the early twentieth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia, published by Funk & Wagnalls between 1901 and 1906, and compiled, according to the account, by about 400 Jewish and non-Jewish scholars, describes the Rothschilds in its "Rothschild" entry as "guardians of the papal treasure." [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] The account reads the phrase in strong terms: as proof that the connection was publicly known by 1906, was not treated as secret by the parties, and was understood as a custodial relationship in which the Rothschilds managed papal assets rather than simply lending. The phrase itself has not been confirmed against the encyclopedia. Even if it is exact, a single phrase in a reference work describes a reputation. It does not show what assets, if any, were held, or on what terms.

The loans drew hostility from Catholic critics, and the record is clear about its character. Catholic criticism at the time, as a remark by Alfred de Vigny shows, centered on the Rothschilds' Jewishness. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] Objection to the terms of a loan, or to a sovereign's debts, is a political argument. Objection to a lender because he is a Jew is antisemitism, and this book names it as such. The documented business was a set of loans to an indebted state. The trope built on top of it is a different thing.

The territorial state that did the borrowing ended in 1870, with the fall of the Papal States. The Roman families who stayed loyal to the Pope afterwards, the Black Nobility, including the Orsini and the Colonna, distanced themselves from the new Italian monarchy in a specific act of protest: they kept the doors of their palaces closed in mourning. [cite:wiki_black_nobility] From this point the papacy was a church without a state, and it remained so until 1929. The settlement that later compensated it for the lost territory, and what it did to the Black Nobility's court positions, belong to 1929 and are told in [scene:vat_s00d|a later volume].

The same account draws a line from these loans to the present. It runs from the 1831 arrangement through the Torlonia family's rental of their Roman villa to Mussolini (from 1923 in one account and from 1925 in another, until 1943) to the appointment in 2026 of François Pauly, a former chief executive of the Edmond de Rothschild group, as president of the supervisory board of the Vatican bank, dated 25 March 2026 in one account and 28 April 2026 in another. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] Those events lie far outside this chapter and are told in [scene:bc_s08|a later volume]. The discipline that applies to them applies here too: each is separately documented, nothing in the record shows that they form one continuous project, and the 2026 appointment is an institutional adjacency, a former executive of a bank that bears the Rothschild name, not a family tie.

The documented core is modest and real: the 1832 loan of £400,000 to Gregory XVI, and the religious hostility it drew. What the record available here does not establish is the exact text of the 1831 contract, whether it contained an exclusive clause and of what kind, which house signed it, what happened in 1834, and whether "guardians of the papal treasure" meant more than a reputation. Each of those rests, for now, on a single reference account and its reading of one historian, and each awaits a check against the documents themselves.

sections.h: A Fortune Kept Private: How the House of Rothschild Held Its Wealth
sections.html:
Start in the present, where the rules are written down. In February 2023 the Rothschild family's holding company, Rothschild & Co Concordia, offered to buy every share of the Paris-listed bank that it did not already own. The offer was €48 a share, and Reuters put the bank's value at about €3.6 billion. Before the offer the wider family already held close to 55% of the shares and 69% of the voting rights, by Reuters' count (the company's own figures are 54.5% and 66.8%). Other wealthy families joined the shareholder pact, among them the Wertheimer brothers, who own Chanel, and the Peugeot and Dassault families. [cite:wb_reuters_rco_feb6] [cite:wb_rco_presentation] [cite:wb_reuters_rco_feb13] On 11 October 2023 the last outside shares were bought out and the bank left the Paris stock exchange. [cite:wb_amf_squeezeout] From that day there has been no market price for the business. The bank still publishes its yearly accounts, but no one can watch its value change from day to day. Nothing about this was hidden. It was a takeover offer, filed with the market regulator. But its result is that the daily public number is gone.

The same gap opens in other ways. In June 2021 ProPublica reported, from leaked tax records, that the twenty-five richest Americans saw their wealth grow by a combined $401 billion between 2014 and 2018, while they paid $13.6 billion in federal income tax. ProPublica called the ratio, 3.4%, a "true tax rate." The comparison is with growth in wealth, not with income, and that is the point: under American law a gain that has not been sold is not income, and is not taxed. [cite:wb_propublica_2021] The reporters described a pattern known as "buy, borrow, die," a phrase they credit to the tax law professor Edward McCaffery. Hold assets that rise in value; borrow against them, since a loan is not income; and at death pass them on. The heir takes the assets at their value on the day of death, so the gain built up over a lifetime is never taxed as a gain at all. [cite:wb_propublica_2021] [cite:wb_openjurist_1014] [cite:wb_wiki_stepup] For 2026, the first $15 million of each estate passes free of federal estate tax, an exemption Congress has now made permanent and tied to inflation. [cite:wb_kpmg_rp2025_32] [cite:wb_morganlewis_2026]

A public figure can also be whatever a contract declares. On the Albanian coast, in a protected wetland known for its flamingos, land at Zvërnec was agreed for sale in November 2025 at an estimated €5.5 million and completed in April 2026 at a declared €122 million (AFP; Reuters gives about €110 million), for a resort project in which Jared Kushner is a confirmed investor. Both prices came after a February 2024 change in the law on protected areas that opened certain protected zones to luxury hotels. [cite:wb_afp_timeline] [cite:wb_reuters_shehu] Albania's anti-corruption prosecutor has since frozen the sale money. Its case files, as Reuters reported in July 2026, accuse the seller's network of buying the land with drug money and forged deeds, which the seller denies. The files make no allegation against Kushner or the other investors. As of August 2026, the latest reporting found, the money remained frozen, the seller faced charges he denies, the investors said they were not under investigation, and the government said the project would go ahead. [cite:wb_reuters_shehu] [cite:wb_occrp_freeze] [cite:wb_deepdive_aug] [cite:wb_protothema_aug]

None of these rules existed in 1810. The principle behind them did: a fortune seen from outside is only the part that its owners choose, or are made, to show. The economist Thomas Piketty's argument that the return on capital tends to outrun the growth of the economy as a whole explains why that hidden part matters over time, and the section returns to it below. [cite:wc_ted_piketty]

The earlier sections of this chapter follow what the Rothschild houses did in public in the nineteenth century: the loans to Prussia and to Britain, the Suez advance, the money lent to the Pope. This section turns to the structure underneath those transactions, which was private by design. It asks four questions in order. How was the business held, and who could see inside it? How did the partners talk to one another? How large did the fortune become, and in what forms was it kept? And did it simply grow, as compound interest says money should, or did something pull it apart? Each answer rests on documents that are now open, most of them in the family's own archive, and each comes with the points that the record still leaves unsettled.

A partnership closed to outsiders. The business began as a written partnership, not a company with shareholders. On 27 September 1810 Mayer Amschel Rothschild and three of his sons, Amschel, Salomon and Carl, signed the first agreement, under the name Mayer Amschel Rothschild & Sons. James, still under age, was to join when he came of age. Nathan, already established in London, was not a party to it. The agreement ran for ten years and could be renewed, and five signed and sealed copies were made. [cite:wa_ra_partnership1810] [cite:wa_ra_mars] The capital was set out in gulden: 370,000 from the father, 185,000 each from Amschel and Salomon, and 30,000 each from Carl and James, James's share held without interest until he came of age. Profits were divided in fifty parts, twenty-five to Mayer Amschel and twelve each to Amschel and Salomon. [cite:wa_ra_partnership1810]

The terms that mattered most were the ones that kept the business closed. The heirs of a partner who died could not demand to see the books. They had to accept the last balance sheet, and they were paid their share in company stock, not in cash. Balance sheets themselves were to be drawn up, in the Archive's summary, only as soon as business allowed. No partner could trade on the Stock Exchange without the others knowing first. Disputes did not go to a court: they went to Mayer Amschel as arbitrator, and after his death to two arbitrators and a chairman, with a penalty of 20,000 thalers for any breach, payable within twenty-four hours. [cite:wa_ra_partnership1810] The family's own archive states the reason for one further rule. Partners were male family members only. Women advised and used their social connections, but they could not formally join, so that a son-in-law could never claim a controlling interest. [cite:wa_ra_partnership1810]

Mayer Amschel died on 19 September 1812. His will, as History Today summarizes it, laid down that only his sons should own the business; his daughters, their husbands and their children were excluded. [cite:wa_ht_founder] A 2022 review of Natalie Livingstone's history of the family's women says the will explicitly barred female descendants, daughters and the wives of male descendants alike, from holding shares or having a say. [cite:wa_hadassah] Reviewing Niall Ferguson's authorized history, Robert Skidelsky called the founder's insistence on a family partnership "law for a century," and noted Ferguson's count that of twenty-one marriages involving his descendants between 1824 and 1877, fifteen were between direct descendants. [cite:wa_skidelsky] [cite:wa_pw_vol1] Several further provisions are often attributed to the will: that it forbade any public inventory of the estate, barred lawsuits, and named the eldest son of the eldest son as head of the family. None of the sources consulted states them, and they are set aside here as unverified until they can be checked against Ferguson's first volume or Amos Elon's biography of the founder. [cite:wa_ht_founder] [cite:wa_ra_mars]

Later partnership agreements exist, but their terms were not found in the sources consulted. The Archive's own list of acquisitions records "Family partnership agreements, 1815-1862" and balance sheets from 1828 to 1910, and its history of the London house says that Lionel de Rothschild modified the partnership agreement in 1838 to keep the London house's relative autonomy. [cite:wa_ra_acq2002] [cite:wa_ra_nmr_london] Nathan's own will, drawn up in his last days in July 1836, told his four sons to work with their mother, Hannah, and not to undertake "any transactions of moment" without first asking her advice. [cite:wa_ra_nmr_person] The Foreign Affairs review of Ferguson describes the result: a transnational partnership that held together for five generations through family loyalty, written agreements and intermarriage. [cite:wa_fa_cooper]

The partnership was not a temporary arrangement. The London house remained one for a century and a half. In 1941 it formed a corporate partner, Rothschilds Continuation Ltd, to ensure continuity in wartime. It admitted its first partner from outside the family in 1960. It ceased to be a partnership and became a limited company, N M Rothschild & Sons Limited, only on 30 September 1970. [cite:wa_ra_nmr_london] [cite:wa_ra_timeline] The Paris house became a limited company at about the same time, on dates the Archive and a reference summary give as 1967 and 1 January 1968. [cite:wa_ra_paris] [cite:wa_wiki_banque] One review of Ferguson states that "the partnership system ended in 1905"; what it refers to is unclear, and it conflicts with the Archive's date for London, so it is noted and not relied on. [cite:wa_skidelsky]

A private channel. The houses ran on information, and the information travelled in a form outsiders could not easily read. The brothers wrote to one another in Judendeutsch, which the Archive defines as German written in Hebrew characters. The Archive is careful to add that this was "not in itself a code," but it was hard to decipher, and so it protected the letters from prying eyes. [cite:wa_ra_judendeutsch1816] [cite:wa_ra_breakseal] The letters went almost daily, to keep up the cooperation the partnership agreements required, and the family's couriers delivered news faster than almost anyone else in Europe could. The Archive's account also mentions private code names. It gives no example of one, and no other source consulted does either. [cite:wa_ra_breakseal]

That correspondence survives in the Rothschild Archive in London: about 20,000 letters between the brothers, from 1811 to 1868, in some 142 boxes, though the Archive says no precise count has been made. James, the last surviving brother from 1861, went on writing to his London nephews in Judendeutsch until his death in 1868. Transcription began in 1989, mainly by Mordechai Zucker, and by about 2000 some 2,500 letters had been fully translated. [cite:wa_ra_breakseal] [cite:wa_ra_jewishstudies] The Archive itself was founded in 1978 by Victor, 3rd Lord Rothschild, and passed to a trust in 1999. Ferguson had free access to all of it except the most recent thirty years, without censorship, according to Jonathan Steinberg's review in the London Review of Books. [cite:wa_ra_about] [cite:wa_steinberg_lrb] The Archive describes the letters as more revealing of their writers than comparable correspondence of the period. [cite:wa_ra_breakseal]

There is a hole in the record. "There is a break in the letters from 1818 to 1825 for reasons which are not clear," the Archive writes, and it offers accidental destruction as the likeliest explanation. [cite:wa_ra_breakseal] Nothing in the sources shows anything more deliberate, and nothing rules it out. A second family archive had a stranger history. Founded by Salomon in Frankfurt in 1844 and moved to Vienna in 1927, it was seized after the German annexation of Austria, inventoried on 2 April 1938, sent to a Gestapo store in Berlin, taken by the Red Army to a special archive in Moscow in 1945, opened there in 1990, and returned to the Viennese branch's descendants in 2001. [cite:wa_provenienz] [cite:wa_trentmann] The letters were private for a century because the family kept them so. Their opening, when it came, came from the family's own decision in London and from war and its aftermath in Vienna.

How large it became. Because the houses published no accounts, their size has to be reconstructed from their own balance sheets, and the most complete reconstruction is Ferguson's. On his figures, as his reviewers report them, the combined capital of the houses grew from £10,000 in 1797 to £1.77 million in 1818. [cite:wa_skidelsky] By 1825 it was about nine times the capital of Baring Brothers, the leading London rival. [cite:wa_wiki_nmr] [cite:wa_steinberg_lrb] It reached £7.78 million in 1844, ten times the Barings'; £9.5 million in 1852; £22 million in 1862; and £34 million in 1874. [cite:wa_skidelsky] [cite:wa_wiki_nmr] By 1899 it stood at £41 million, more than the five largest German joint-stock banks combined. [cite:wa_wiki_nmr] For most of the nineteenth century, Steinberg writes, the Rothschilds were "the biggest bank in the world by a wide margin." [cite:wa_steinberg_lrb]

Two further numbers from the same history give the scale of individual fortunes. Ferguson puts Nathan's net worth at his death in 1836 at 0.62 percent of British national income, and James's at his death in 1868 at just over 4 percent of French national output. [cite:wa_wiki_nmr] [cite:wa_skidelsky] No probate figure for Nathan's estate, or for that of his grandson Natty, the first Lord Rothschild, who died in 1915, has been found. [cite:wa_ra_nmr_person] [cite:wa_wiki_natty]

A capital figure is a number on a balance sheet. Much of the family's wealth took forms that never appear as one. Nathaniel de Rothschild bought the Bordeaux estate of Brane-Mouton in 1853 and renamed it Château Mouton Rothschild, for 1,175,000 francs according to a reference summary. [cite:wa_ra_timeline] [cite:wa_wiki_nathaniel] Agents of James de Rothschild bought Château Lafite at auction in Paris on 8 August 1868 for 4,140,000 francs, with a further 300,000 francs for the neighbouring Carruades estate; James died on 15 November 1868, the Archive notes, "never having set foot on the property." [cite:wa_ra_lafite] Ferdinand de Rothschild bought the Waddesdon estate in Buckinghamshire, about 2,700 acres, from the Duke of Marlborough in 1874 for about £200,000, and built the house between 1874 and 1885, with a wing added in 1889. [cite:wa_waddesdon] James began the Château de Ferrières in 1853, and Joseph Paxton designed Mentmore for Mayer de Rothschild. [cite:wa_ra_timeline]

Assets of this kind have no daily price. A vineyard, a country house or a collection of paintings has a value only when someone sells it, and until then any figure is an estimate. Family spending also drew on the houses' profits. Skidelsky, summarizing Ferguson, attributes part of the halt in capital growth after 1874 to profits withdrawn for family spending. [cite:wa_skidelsky] Some of what was bought later passed to the public. James de Rothschild bequeathed Waddesdon, its main collections and its grounds to the National Trust in 1957, and it opened to visitors in 1959; Ferdinand's Renaissance collection had already gone to the British Museum as the Waddesdon Bequest. [cite:wa_waddesdon] Guy and Marie-Hélène de Rothschild gave Ferrières to the University of Paris in 1975. [cite:wa_ra_timeline] The Archive's chronology credits James's widow, Dorothy, with the Waddesdon gift; Waddesdon's own history says James bequeathed it and Dorothy chaired its management committee until 1988. [cite:wa_ra_timeline] [cite:wa_waddesdon]

Lending to governments: power in both directions. The houses' largest business was lending to states, and those loans were an exchange that ran both ways. The clearest documented case is in London. In November 1875 N M Rothschild & Sons advanced the British government £4,000,000 to buy 44 percent of the Suez Canal Company's shares while Parliament was not sitting. The Archive calls it a technically unsecured loan, and it was repaid within five months. [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023] [cite:rs_rd0_rotharchive_suez] The government gained a strategic asset its prime minister defended as a highway to India; the house earned a commission that critics in Parliament said amounted to 15 percent interest, a claim Disraeli rejected. [cite:rs_rd0_disraeli_1876] The full story is told in [scene:bc_s02|the section on the London house].

The papal loans show the same exchange in Rome. The Archive records that the papal administration sought the Naples house's services and that five loans were issued between 1831 and 1850, without describing their terms. [cite:wa_ra_naples] A reference summary gives the first as a £400,000 loan in 1832 on a 5 percent contract signed by Rothschild and Torlonia. [cite:wa_wiki_papal] The economic historian Daniela Felisini describes that first loan as made in partnership with James de Rothschild of Paris, and as one of the most controversial operations of its period, both for its financial conditions and because the lender was a Jewish banker; the reference summary names Carl of Naples instead. [cite:wa_felisini] [cite:wa_wiki_papal] The most striking term attributed to the loan, a clause requiring the Holy See to tell the Rothschilds before approaching any other lender and to give them preference on equal terms, is footnoted in that summary to a popular book of 1913, Ignatius Balla's The Romance of the Rothschilds, and to no other source this book could find. Until it is confirmed from the contract or from Ferguson, it should be treated as unconfirmed. The papal loans are told in full in [scene:bc_s03|the section on the Pope's bankers].

Compounding, and what pulled against it. A fortune that is never sold is never priced, but it is not standing still. Money that earns a return and is left to earn again grows on itself. The economist Thomas Piketty, in Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014), argues that the return on capital has usually run ahead of the growth of the economy as a whole, and that as the gap widens, wealth concentrates faster; on the figures summarized from his book, the return on capital held at roughly 4 to 5 percent for most of history and rose above 5 percent during the Industrial Revolution. [cite:wc_ted_piketty] The arithmetic is simple to state. A pound that compounds at 5 percent a year for two hundred years becomes about £17,000; at 3 percent, about £370. That is an illustration of the mechanism, not a measurement of any family's fortune.

The Rothschild record shows the mechanism at work and the forces that worked against it, side by side. On one side stood everything this section has described: the family-only partnership, books closed to heirs, intermarriage that kept the capital inside the family, and a correspondence outsiders could not easily read. On the other stood division among heirs, spending, revolution, war and the state. The capital stopped growing after 1874, by Skidelsky's account of Ferguson partly because profits were drawn off for family spending, and the London house's return on capital fell from 9.8 percent in the 1870s to 3.9 percent in the 1900s, while Barings earned 27.1 percent in the later decade. [cite:wa_skidelsky]

The houses closed one after another. In Naples, the house Carl had founded in 1821 stopped trading in 1863, after Garibaldi took the city in September 1860; Adolphe Carl would not work with the new regime and left the partnership, and the other houses would not back the deposed king. [cite:wa_ra_naples] [cite:wa_ra_naples_soulie] In Frankfurt, after the death of the last partner, Wilhelm Carl, in 1901, the family voluntarily liquidated the founding house, with no male heir and no family member willing to move there; its remaining business went to the Disconto-Gesellschaft of Berlin, and the Naples records were destroyed in the liquidation. [cite:wa_ra_mars] [cite:wa_ra_naples_soulie]

In Vienna the end came by force. The Archive says the house closed in March 1938. Louis von Rothschild was arrested after the annexation, held first in prison and then in the Hotel Metropole, and released, by the Archive's account, in July 1939, after family negotiations and a payment it gives as $21,000,000; his assets were put under a German commissioner. [cite:wa_ra_timeline] [cite:wa_ra_louis] The sources differ on the date of his release: the Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported on 14 May 1939 that he had already reached Switzerland. [cite:wa_jta1939] Austria's commission for provenance research recorded in 2013 that the Nazi authorities moved to expropriate the Viennese branch immediately after the annexation. [cite:wa_provenienz] In Paris, Banque Rothschild was one of thirty-nine banks nationalized by the Mitterrand government, in 1982 by the Archive's dating; the family started again as P.O. Gestion in 1983 and regained the use of its name in October 1986. [cite:wa_ra_timeline] [cite:wa_ra_paris] [cite:wa_wiki_banque]

What the record shows, and what it does not. The documented finding is narrow and firm. The Rothschild houses kept their affairs private by design: through a written partnership that barred outsiders, closed the books to heirs and sent disputes to private arbitration; through a correspondence in a script few outsiders could read, carried by the family's own couriers; and through wealth held in forms that are never priced until they are sold. The partnership form lasted, in London, until 1970, and the company stayed private after it. It was not unusual in kind. Private partnerships among bankers were common in the period, and other banking families worked on similar lines, as an earlier section of this chapter sets out. What set this one apart was its scale and how long it lasted.

The record does not show what a long tradition of hostile writing has claimed: a hidden family hand directing the affairs of states. The houses' great loans are known because governments had to raise, vote and repay them in public. The privacy covered the family's own books, not the policy of the states it lent to. The record also leaves real gaps. The terms of the partnership agreements after 1810 were not found in the sources consulted. The papal exclusivity clause rests on a single popular source. The letters of 1818 to 1825 are missing. No probate figure was found for the estates of Nathan in 1836 or Natty in 1915. And no one outside the family can price the land, houses and art that were never sold. A careful reader can hold both conclusions at once: the fortune was larger and more deliberately private than its public figures suggest, and the documents that are open describe a family business, not a secret government.

sections.h: Restoration Before Zionism: The Protestant Lobby, 1839–1891
sections.html:
Catholic Rome borrowed from Jewish bankers, and its critics attacked the lenders for their religion. In Protestant Britain, in the same decade, Jews entered politics by another door, as the subject of a prophecy. A common assumption holds that Christian political support for a Jewish state was a product of the twentieth century: a response to the Holocaust and to the founding of Israel in 1948. The documents place its political beginnings more than a century earlier, and in a different place. Before any Jewish political movement for a state existed, a Protestant current in Britain and the United States had already put the idea of a Jewish "restoration" to Palestine before a Foreign Secretary and a President. Restorationism, the belief that a Jewish return to Palestine would fulfil biblical prophecy, was an organized political current decades before Theodor Herzl. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism]

The British story begins inside a family. Anthony Ashley-Cooper, Lord Shaftesbury, was an evangelical peer and reformer. He was also Palmerston's stepson-in-law: the Foreign Secretary, Lord Palmerston, was his wife's stepfather. In 1839 Shaftesbury pressed Palmerston to sponsor Jewish settlement in Palestine under British protection. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] [cite:wiki_shaftesbury] On this section's reading, the access mattered. Shaftesbury's request needed a government to carry it, and the Ottoman sultan, who ruled Palestine, answered to no British minister. What Shaftesbury had was the ear of the Foreign Secretary, whose instructions reached Constantinople.

Palmerston acted. In 1840 he instructed his ambassador at Constantinople to urge the Ottoman sultan to encourage Jewish settlement, and Britain's new consulate in Jerusalem was given a brief to protect Jews. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] [cite:wiki_shaftesbury] Those were the two instruments Britain used: diplomatic pressure on the sultan's government, and a consul on the ground who could take named people under his protection. Neither could settle anyone. The decision to admit or encourage settlers lay with the Porte, and the instruction asked the sultan to use a power that only he held.

The sources are frank that the motive was double. Restorationism was theological and imperial at once. Shaftesbury and Palmerston saw a protected Jewish presence as a British foothold in Ottoman Syria; American evangelicals read the same prospect as prophecy. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] A minister could pursue it as policy and an evangelical as faith, and the two readings did not have to agree for the request to be made. What neither reading drew on was Jewish opinion. Most Jewish communal bodies of the period opposed restorationism or ignored it. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] The idea was advanced on behalf of Jews, by Christians, for reasons of prophecy and empire.

The restorationist current also produced the most quoted slogan in the later conflict, and its history is not the one usually told. The earliest published version of "a land without a people for a people without a land" appeared in an 1843 book by Alexander Keith, a Church of Scotland clergyman and an advocate of Jewish "restoration" who had traveled to Palestine in 1839. Shaftesbury used similar wording in 1853. [cite:meq_land_without_people] [cite:aijac_slogan_origin] His own phrase for Palestine was a country without a nation for a nation without a country. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] [cite:wiki_shaftesbury] The first use by a Zionist came only in 1901, when Israel Zangwill wrote that Palestine was "a country without a people." [cite:meq_land_without_people] [cite:aijac_slogan_origin] The phrase was first published by a Christian restorationist more than half a century before the first recorded Zionist use.

What it meant is debated. One reading takes it literally: the land was described as empty. The other holds that it meant a land "without a nation." Shaftesbury's own wording, "without a nation," is consistent with the second reading. Against the first, the counts are plain: every Ottoman and British census shows a populated country. Keith, the man who first published the phrase, had visited Palestine and knew it was populated. [cite:meq_land_without_people] [cite:aijac_slogan_origin] Whichever reading is preferred, the phrase described a country that had people in it. The same set of checks examines two other claims that are often paired with this one, that Arab leaders "rejected every offer" and that the conflict is a religious war two thousand years old; both concern later periods and are taken up in [scene:sq_s05|three slogans checked against the record].

The American counterpart came half a century after Shaftesbury. In March 1891 the Chicago evangelist William E. Blackstone presented President Benjamin Harrison with a petition urging American support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine. The Blackstone Memorial, as it became known, was signed by more than four hundred prominent Americans, among them John D. Rockefeller, J. P. Morgan and the Chief Justice. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] It preceded Herzl's Der Judenstaat by five years and the first Zionist Congress at Basel by six. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] The instrument was different from Palmerston's. Shaftesbury had worked through a minister who could instruct an ambassador; Blackstone worked through public petition, using the names of men of finance and law to press a head of state. The President, like the Foreign Secretary before him, could only ask; the land was still the sultan's.

Set side by side, the two currents show the sequence that most accounts reverse. The familiar order runs from a Jewish political movement to Christian sympathy for it. The documents run the other way: Christian political support for a Jewish return came first, and Jewish political Zionism came second. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] By the time the Zionist movement had an organization, a Christian political base for a Jewish state already existed in Britain and the United States, at a time when most Jewish communal bodies still opposed or ignored the idea. That ordering helps explain why the Balfour Declaration of 1917 found a ready constituency in Britain's governing class. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism]

The constituency did not stand still after 1891. In 1909 the Scofield Reference Bible gave it a theology: its dispensationalist reading made support for a Jewish state a mass Protestant doctrine. Balfour, whose name the 1917 declaration bears, was himself a Christian restorationist. Later still, Christians United for Israel in the Hagee era stands at the twentieth-century end of a lineage that begins in 1839, not in 1948. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] The Scofield Bible and its public belong to the next part of this book, in [scene:s05|the Scofield Reference Bible, 1909].

The finding should be kept at its proper size. Before the Zionist Congress, and before Rothschild money built colonies in Palestine, Protestant restorationism had already made a Jewish return a live question in British and American politics, for reasons of prophecy and empire that had little to do with Jewish opinion. That constituency, not any single family, was the pre-existing structure into which the Zionist project would later connect. It does not follow that restorationists created Zionism, which had its own Jewish sources in prayer, persecution and nationalism, nor that they could deliver Palestine: in 1840 and in 1891 the land was the sultan's, and neither a Foreign Secretary nor a President could do more than ask.

Much is left open by the record as it stands here. The text of Palmerston's 1840 instruction is not quoted in these sources, and neither the sultan's response nor any settlement it produced is recorded. The consulate's brief to protect Jews is documented; what the consuls did with it in these decades is not described here. The record does not say how Harrison answered Blackstone, or whether the memorial changed anything in American policy. And the statement that most Jewish communal bodies opposed or ignored restorationism is made in general terms, without naming the bodies or their statements. Those are the limits of what can be said about this current before 1896.

sections.h: Reform from Istanbul: Edicts, a Constitution and Jerusalem's Deputy, 1839–1878
sections.html:
Palmerston's instruction of 1840 reached a sultan who had, the year before, begun to reform his empire from the center. A claim met earlier in this chapter, in the sketch of the Ottoman Empire on the board of 1789–1815, holds that the Ottoman parliamentary reforms of 1876 gave Palestine representation and that "Palestinian delegates sat in the Ottoman parliament." [cite:wiki_ottoman_palestine] The claim is right in substance and loose in its detail. The record supports one named deputy for the district of Jerusalem in the parliament of 1877, a man who used his seat to oppose the sultan and lost it within a year. To see what that seat was, and what it was not, the story has to begin almost four decades earlier, with a series of promises issued from Istanbul to all the sultan's subjects.

The reform era the Ottomans called the Tanzimat opened on 3 November 1839. On that day Sultan Abdülmecid I proclaimed the Edict of Gülhane, at the urging of his Grand Vizier, Mustafa Reşid Pasha. According to a reference account, which draws on Cleveland and Bunton and on Liebesny, the edict promised three things: security of life, honor and property; a regular system of taxation in place of tax farming; and regular conscription. [cite:rs_rd0_gulhane_wiki] Its concessions were said to extend "to all our subjects, whatever religion or sect they may belong to." [cite:rs_rd0_gulhane_wiki] The same account is careful about its force. The edict changed no laws by itself and was never fully implemented. [cite:rs_rd0_gulhane_wiki] It was a declaration of the state's intentions, and its force depended on the legislation and enforcement that followed.

The mechanism matters for Palestine. On this section's reading, the two practical promises of Gülhane, regular taxation and regular conscription, required the state to know who its subjects were and what they held. That need is the thread that runs from this edict to the registration of land under the Land Code of 1858, the subject of the next section, where many cultivators avoided the register precisely because it brought taxes and conscription with it. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] Read this way, the promise of security of property and the demand for a regular revenue were the same reform seen from two sides.

The second great instrument came at the end of a war. The Reform Edict of 18 February 1856 was issued as the Crimean War ended. According to the reference account, it promised equality in education, government appointments and justice regardless of creed, freedom of worship, and mixed tribunals for cases between Muslims and non-Muslims. Among its provisions was military service for non-Muslims, which proved unpopular. [cite:rs_rd0_reform1856_wiki] Where Gülhane had extended its concessions to all subjects in general words, the 1856 edict spelled out equality in particular fields of public life. Both remained edicts: promises made from the center, whose effect in a given province depended on how far they were enforced there.

The third step went further than any edict. On 23 December 1876 an Ottoman constitution was promulgated, and on 19 March 1877 the first Ottoman parliament opened at Dolmabahçe Palace. Its deputies were not elected directly by the population. They were chosen indirectly, through the provincial councils. [cite:rs_rd0_firstconst_wiki] That detail shapes what "representation" meant. A deputy was the choice of a provincial council, not of a popular vote.

The sources disagree on the size of the chamber. The Institute for Palestine Studies' PalQuest counts 120 deputies, fourteen of them Arab. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] The reference account of the First Constitutional Era gives 115 members, and for the second elections a split of 69 Muslim and 46 non-Muslim deputies. [cite:rs_rd0_firstconst_wiki] The sources do not reconcile the two figures, and neither is adopted here as settled.

Jerusalem's deputy in that chamber was Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi. Born in Jerusalem in 1842, he was educated well beyond the city's own schools. He studied at the al-Fakhriyya school, at the British Diocesan Boys' School in Jerusalem, at a Protestant college in Malta, and in Istanbul. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] In 1875, two years before he took his seat, The Jewish Chronicle published two of his letters on the Jews of Palestine. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] He had also served as head of Jerusalem's municipality, though the sources date that service differently. PalQuest gives his mayoralty as 1870–1874, with two later terms. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] Jerusalem Story says he was appointed in September 1865, at the age of 23, and headed the municipality for nine years. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] Both agree that he governed the city before he represented it.

In 1877 al-Khalidi was elected as the sole deputy for the Jerusalem mutasarrifate, and by PalQuest's count he was one of fourteen Arab deputies among 120. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] He did not sit quietly. Both biographical sources describe him as a prominent opponent of Sultan Abdul Hamid II in the chamber. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] How that district was constituted, and how many people lived in it, is set out in [scene:s00h|the Baseline account of Ottoman Palestine].

The parliament was short-lived. Abdul Hamid II suspended both the parliament and the constitution in February 1878, on 14 February in one account and on 13 February in another. [cite:rs_rd0_firstconst_wiki] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] When the chamber was dissolved, al-Khalidi was one of ten opposition deputies ordered out of Istanbul. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] The chain of power is visible in that sequence. The constitution had created a chamber, but it had not created a body the sultan could not dismiss. The man who had promulgated it could suspend it, and the deputies who had opposed him could be sent away from the capital. Jerusalem's representation in the imperial parliament had lasted less than a year.

Measured against this record, the earlier claim can now be stated exactly. It is documented that the 1876 constitution produced a parliament in which the Jerusalem district had an elected deputy, and that this deputy, al-Khalidi, was a native of Jerusalem, a former head of the city's municipality and an outspoken member of the opposition. That is a real fact of formal political representation, and it answers any account in which the people of the country had no part in the empire's politics. What the record assembled here does not support is the plural. It names one deputy for Jerusalem. Fourteen Arab deputies sat by PalQuest's count, but the sources used here do not say which, if any, of the others sat for districts that lay in what would later be Palestine. "Palestinian delegates" should therefore read, on present evidence, "Jerusalem's deputy."

In the same year the parliament closed, religious equality in the Ottoman lands was written into an international treaty. Article 62 of the Treaty of Berlin of 1878 declared that "in no part of the Ottoman Empire shall difference of religion be alleged against any person." [cite:rs_rd0_fo1893_berlin62] Where the edicts had been the sultan's own promises to his subjects, Article 62 stood in a treaty, and foreign diplomats could invoke it. British diplomats later did exactly that, citing the article against Ottoman restrictions on Jews. [cite:rs_rd0_fo1893_berlin62] How those restrictions arose, and how Britain and the United States contested them, is told in [scene:rd0_limits|the Ottoman limits of 1882–1896].

These decades also saw the first departures in the other direction. From the 1870s Palestinian emigration to the Americas began, mostly of Christian families from Bethlehem, Beit Jala and Beit Sahour who traveled on Ottoman papers and were therefore long called "Turcos." [cite:palquest_sv] Where they settled and what became of their communities is told in [scene:dsp_s01|the account of the Palestinian diaspora].

Al-Khalidi's part in this book does not end in 1878. On 1 March 1899, through Zadok Kahn, Chief Rabbi of France, he wrote to Theodor Herzl urging that Palestine be left in peace, and on 19 March Herzl replied that Jewish immigration would benefit the country. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] That exchange belongs to the next part of this book.

Several questions remain open on this record. The reference accounts of the two edicts say what was promised and that Gülhane was never fully implemented, but they do not measure how far either edict was carried out in the district of Jerusalem, or how the people of Palestine received them. The size of the 1877 chamber stands at 115 or 120, depending on the source. Al-Khalidi's years as head of the municipality are dated from 1865 in one biography and from 1870 in the other. The day of the suspension is given as 13 or 14 February 1878. And the sources consulted here are silent on what the people who chose al-Khalidi through the provincial councils expected of him, beyond the fact that he went to Istanbul and opposed the sultan.

sections.h: The Land Code of 1858: How the Deeds Became Sellable
sections.html:
The Tanzimat's promise of secure property and a regular revenue took its most lasting form in land law. A familiar account of the early Zionist land purchases holds that Jewish buyers acquired empty or unused land in Palestine from willing local owners. That account begins at the moment of sale. The legal history begins earlier, in a set of Ottoman laws of 1856 to 1867 that decided who could hold a deed, whose name went on it, and who could buy it. Those laws did not concern Zionism, which did not yet exist. They concerned revenue, conscription and the control of foreign purchasers. But they produced the documents through which land in Palestine would later change hands, and they explain how a sale could be perfectly lawful between owner and buyer and still pass over the heads of the people who farmed the land.

The starting point is a prohibition. According to a reference summary drawing on work by Ruth Kark published in 1984, foreigners were officially barred from buying land in Palestine from 1856, and the ban held in practice until 1867. [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki] For a decade, then, the question of who could own land was settled against outsiders, whatever the paper said about who owned it inside the country.

Inside the country the paper itself was about to change. In 1858, as part of the reforms known as the Tanzimat, the Ottoman state issued a Land Code, the Arazi Kanunnamesi. It classified land into categories and required titles to be registered individually. The purpose was fiscal and military: registration would secure tax revenue and the conscription rolls. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] The same year brought the Tabu law, the law of title deeds. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] The two can be read as giving practical form to promises made in the Edict of Gülhane of 1839, which had pledged security of property, a regular tax system and regular conscription, as the [scene:rd0_tanzimat|previous section] describes. A state that wished to tax and conscript its subjects needed a register of what they held.

In Palestine the register opened a gap between who owned land on paper and who worked it. Many cultivators did not register the land they farmed. A reference summary, citing Nasser Abufarha, gives the reason: registration brought taxes and conscription, and cultivators resisted it for that reason. [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki] Title was frequently recorded instead in other names: village heads, urban merchants or notables, and absentee families living in Beirut and Damascus. The fellahin, the peasant cultivators, went on working the same fields, in practice as tenants. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] Nothing on the ground had to change for this to happen. The village continued to plough and harvest. What changed was the document, and the document now named someone else.

Historians have described the result in strong terms. The same reference summary quotes Yehoshua Porath, writing in 1977, that the 1858 code "brought about the appropriation by the influential and rich families of Beirut, Damascus" and other cities of vast tracts. [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki] Kark, in a study published in 2017, finds that land came to be concentrated in "families of urban effendis (absentee landlords)" who lived in cities in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Palestine.
