In August 1903, months afterwards, Herzl twice met the Interior Minister, Vyacheslav von Plehve, a man widely regarded as responsible for the atmosphere that had produced the pogrom. He did so without consulting Russia's own Zionists. The meetings produced a letter in which the Tsar's government agreed to press the Sultan for a charter and to allow Zionist societies to operate in Russia.[cite:wiki_sixth_zionist_congress] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_herzl]

Russian Zionists criticized the meetings sharply.[cite:wiki_sixth_zionist_congress] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_herzl] The two sides of that quarrel can be stated from the record. On one side stood what the meetings produced: a written commitment to press the Sultan, and legal room for Zionist societies inside Russia. On the other stood the manner of them: the movement's leader had met the minister widely held responsible for the climate of Kishinev, without consulting Russia's Zionists. The record shows the letter and the anger; it does not show that the letter ever moved the Sultan. Weeks later Britain's offer of territory in East Africa split the Sixth Zionist Congress.[cite:wiki_sixth_zionist_congress]

The last of these approaches went to Rome. On 26 January 1904 Herzl had a private audience with Pope Pius X, Giuseppe Sarto, to ask for the Vatican's support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine. The refusal was direct and on the record.[cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] Herzl's diary records the Pope's words: "We cannot give this movement our blessing... We cannot prevent the Jews from going to Jerusalem — but we could never sanction it. The ground of Jerusalem, if it were not always sacred, has been sanctified by the life of Jesus Christ. As the head of the Church, I cannot tell you anything different." Herzl also met the Vatican Secretary of State, Cardinal Rafael Merry del Val, who is described as similarly unreceptive.

Two readings of the Pope's grounds appear in the sources, and they are not identical. One stresses doctrine: the Church could not support Jewish restoration to a land central to its own theology while the Jews denied Christ, a position later accounts call supersessionist.[cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] The other stresses place: the Vatican's specific concern was Jerusalem and the status of the holy sites, which would be complicated by a non-Christian sovereign, rather than Jewish settlement as such. The Pope's own words, as Herzl recorded them, contain both: he would not prevent Jews going to Jerusalem, but he would not sanction the movement, and he grounded that in the sanctity of the city. Either way, the founder of the movement went to Rome and was refused. The Vatican did not recognize the State of Israel until 30 December 1993, forty-five years after its independence; that longer story is told in [scene:vat_s01|the Vatican's long refusal].[cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition]

Set side by side, the approaches show a pattern. Herzl did not carry one proposal from capital to capital. He shaped each offer to its listener: finance for an indebted empire, a strategic buffer for a Britain anxious about Suez, and, in the Russian case, a movement that would draw Jews out of the empire. Germany, the Ottoman Empire, Britain and Russia were all approached within five years. On this reading, Britain's sponsorship in 1917 was the strategy finally succeeding with one power after failing with the others, not its point of departure.

On their own terms these approaches produced almost nothing. The Kaiser lost interest, the Sultan granted nothing, Cairo vetoed El-Arish, the Russian letter yielded no charter and sharp criticism from Russian Zionists, and the Pope said no. Herzl died in 1904. What outlasted him was the method itself, the search for a sovereign's signature, and an organization able to keep searching.

The record leaves several questions open. It does not say what, if anything, Herzl offered the Kaiser in return for his intercession, nor exactly what the Kaiser asked of the Sultan. The Sultan's refusal of land is known through Herzl's own diary, as a message relayed to him; the sources here do not give its date or its intermediary, or an Ottoman record of it. The precise terms of the debt offer, how much and from whom, are not documented in this material. Plehve's responsibility for Kishinev is a matter of how he was widely regarded, not a finding of a court. And while the Pope's words survive in Herzl's account, the weight Pius X himself gave to doctrine and to the holy sites cannot be separated from that one record.

sections.h: The People Already There: Herzl, al-Khalidi and the Arab Question, 1895–1905
sections.html:
A common belief holds that the founders of political Zionism imagined Palestine as empty, and that the existence of its Arab population came as a later surprise. The record of the movement's first decade does not support that belief. Herzl, his correspondents and his allies wrote about the people living in the land, sometimes privately and sometimes in print, from the movement's earliest days. What they disagreed about, and what historians still argue over, is what they intended to do about them.

The question had been put to the movement before Herzl came to it. In 1891 Asher Ginsberg, writing as Ahad Ha'am, published an account of his visit to Ottoman Palestine reporting that the land was farmed and lived on by a substantial Arab population, who would not simply acquiesce to displacement; his warning, and his wider quarrel with Herzl, are told in [scene:s04|the Basel section].[cite:wiki_ahad_haam] The historian Steven Beller, reviewing Derek Penslar's biography of Herzl, writes that Herzl, in Beller's words, "lacked a realistic view about the antagonistic effect" a Jewish settlement would have on the local Arab population, a point Ahad Ha'am raised at the time.[cite:rs_rd1_beller_arab]

The phrase most often attached to this period has an older and non-Zionist origin. The earliest published version of "a land without a people for a people without a land" appeared in an 1843 book by Alexander Keith, a Church of Scotland clergyman and an advocate of Jewish "restoration," who had himself traveled to Palestine in 1839 and knew it was populated. Lord Shaftesbury used similar wording in 1853. The first use by a Zionist came in 1901, when Israel Zangwill wrote that Palestine was "a country without a people."[cite:meq_land_without_people] [cite:aijac_slogan_origin] Historians debate whether the phrase meant a land literally empty or a land "without a nation." Whatever its authors meant, the Ottoman counts of the period, set out in [scene:rd1_ottoman|the opening section], show a populated country. The slogan's later career, and the other talking points that grew up beside it, are examined in [scene:sq_s05|three claims checked].

Herzl's own first recorded thoughts on the matter came before the movement existed. In June 1895 he wrote a passage in his diary that is still argued over. As the Israeli researcher Shaul Arieli quotes it, by way of Edward Said, it reads: "We shall try to spirit the penniless population across the border by procuring employment for it in the transit countries, while denying it any employment in our country."[cite:rs_rd1_arieli_transfer]

Two serious readings of that passage stand against each other, and each has its evidence. Arieli, in a 2025 survey, places it at the head of a chronicle: in his account the idea of moving the Arab population out was a long-standing strand of Zionist strategic thinking, and this 1895 entry is where it begins.[cite:rs_rd1_arieli_transfer] Beller, drawing on Penslar, accepts that Herzl was "quite prepared to remove any local population," but adds two qualifications that matter. Herzl preferred to do it peacefully. And "the context in which he was discussing this was not Palestine": the passage concerned South America.[cite:rs_rd1_beller_arab] The strongest form of Arieli's case is continuity: whatever territory Herzl had in mind, the passage shows that the founder of the movement treated a resident population as something to be moved, and later Zionist thinkers returned to the same idea. The strongest form of Beller's case is context: a private note about an unchosen territory, preferring economic pressure to coercion, is not the same thing as a plan for Palestine. Both scholars quote the same sentence. Neither the exact day of the entry nor its full surrounding text is given in the sources used here, so this book does not go beyond Arieli's quotation.

Four years later the question arrived at Herzl's desk from Jerusalem itself. The writer was Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi. According to the reference account of his career, he served as mayor of Jerusalem in 1870–76, 1878–79 and 1899–1906, sat for Jerusalem in the first Ottoman parliament, and had taught at the Oriental Academy in Vienna.[cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_wiki] On 1 March 1899 he wrote to Zadoc Kahn, the chief rabbi of France, asking that the letter be passed to Herzl. Al-Khalidi called the Zionist idea in itself "natural, beautiful and just." But he set two facts against it: Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire, and it was inhabited by others. And he wrote: "in the name of God, let Palestine be left alone."[cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_wiki] [cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_intercept]

Herzl answered on 19 March 1899. His reply, as quoted, did not deny that the land was inhabited. His argument was that Jewish immigration would benefit the people already there: "It is their well-being, their individual wealth, which we will increase by bringing in our own." And he asked: "who would think of sending them away?"[cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_intercept] [cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_wiki]

How to read that reply is itself disputed. Taken on its own terms, it is a statement of good intent and a prediction: Jewish capital and labor would enrich the country, and no one proposed expulsion. The historian Rashid Khalidi, a descendant of al-Khalidi's family, reads it otherwise. He calls the reply condescending and argues that it did not answer al-Khalidi's central objection, that the people of Palestine would not accept being displaced.[cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_intercept] One reading of the exchange, between the founder of political Zionism and a senior Jerusalem notable, is that the two men were writing past each other: one about sovereignty and consent, the other about prosperity.

Herzl returned to the argument in fiction. His novel Altneuland, published in German in 1902, imagines Palestine in 1923, run by a cooperative "New Society" in which land is publicly owned. The book has one Arab character, Reschid Bey. According to the standard summary of the novel, Reschid Bey says that Arabs had no reason to oppose Jewish immigration, because the newcomers "developed the country and raised everybody's standard of living."[cite:rs_rd1_altneuland_wiki] The character speaks almost the same argument Herzl had put to al-Khalidi three years earlier. A reader sympathetic to Herzl can see in the novel a sincere vision of a shared, prosperous country without expulsion. A reader persuaded by Rashid Khalidi can see the same objection unanswered: the only Arab voice in the book is one that agrees.

A blunter statement came from Zangwill, the writer who had first given the "country without a people" phrase a Zionist voice. In 1905, as Arieli quotes him, Zangwill wrote that "Palestine itself is already occupied," and that Zionists must be prepared either "to drive out by the sword the tribes in possession as our forefathers did" or "to grapple with the problem of a large alien population, mostly Mohammedan and accustomed to despise us."[cite:rs_rd1_arieli_transfer] The quotation reaches this book through Arieli's survey; its original place of publication is not confirmed in the sources used here. That same year Zangwill broke with the Zionist Organization over the East Africa question and went looking for a territory elsewhere.

Read in order, these documents settle the first question a reader is likely to ask. The founders knew Palestine was inhabited. Keith had seen it in 1839; Ahad Ha'am reported it in 1891; al-Khalidi told Herzl in writing in 1899, and Herzl answered him without denying it; Zangwill, the first Zionist to use the slogan, wrote in 1905 that the land was "already occupied." What they said about it ranged widely: from Herzl's assurance that no one would send the inhabitants away, through Altneuland's picture of shared prosperity, to Zangwill's choice between the sword and the "problem" of a large population. These are the words of individuals, in a diary, a letter, a novel and Zangwill's own statement, not resolutions of a Zionist Congress.

What the record does not settle is the question historians still divide on: what Herzl himself intended for the Arabs of Palestine. The sources here give the passages on which Arieli, Beller and Rashid Khalidi build their readings, not Herzl's full diary entry or his letter in its entirety, and a reader should weigh those readings with that limit in mind. What can be said plainly is that the warning al-Khalidi put to Herzl, that the people of Palestine would not accept displacement, was on paper in March 1899, and that the movement's founder answered it, in the passages quoted, with an economic argument.

sections.h: The Jewish Colonial Trust: A Bank Owned a Pound at a Time
sections.html:
The Basel Program of 1897 named its means but not its money. A movement that hoped to obtain a charter from a great power, and then to settle people on land under it, needed capital of its own, and it needed an institution that could hold that capital, lend it and answer for it in law. The Second Zionist Congress, meeting in 1898, decided to create one. On 20 March 1899, the Jewish Colonial Trust, in Hebrew Otẓar Hityashvuth Hayehudim, was incorporated in London under the English Companies Acts. Its stated aim was to acquire the capital, and the "charter," that would make large-scale settlement in Palestine possible. Its authorized capital was £2,000,000, divided into shares of £1 each.[cite:jct_wiki]

The legal form mattered. Incorporated under English company law, the Trust was not a charity collecting gifts. It was a company selling shares, and the people who bought them became owners of a bank whose purpose was political. It was political Zionism's first financial institution.

A familiar account of Zionist finance holds that the movement was paid for by a few great patrons, with the name Rothschild usually standing in for all of them. The design of the Trust points the other way. Its shares were priced deliberately low, at a single pound, and could be paid for in installments, with plans running to as many as 55 to 80 payments.[cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] [cite:bia_jewish_colonial_trust] The purpose was to let working-class Jews across Europe, and not only the wealthy, become shareholders in the national project. A buyer who could not spare a pound at once could pay it off in small sums over time. The logic is the one a modern crowdfunding campaign uses, applied in 1899: many small commitments in place of a few large ones. Herzl set the example by buying the first 1,000 shares himself.[cite:jct_wiki]

The Trust's founders each brought something different. Herzl supplied the political leadership and the public name. David Wolffsohn, a German-Jewish timber merchant and one of Herzl's closest associates, co-founded the Trust and would hold a remarkable run of offices: he chaired the Anglo-Palestine Company from its founding in 1902 and succeeded Herzl as president of the Zionist Organization in 1905.[cite:wiki_flag_of_israel] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] Wolffsohn is also documented as the designer of the two-stripes-and-star flag adopted at Basel in 1897, the design that later became the state flag of Israel.[cite:wiki_flag_of_israel] The third co-founder, Jacobus Kahn, was a Dutch-Jewish banker. His contribution was technical rather than political: he supplied the banking expertise the new institution needed in order to function as a financial body and not merely as a symbol.[cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] The record does not give Kahn a role in the wider movement comparable to Herzl's or Wolffsohn's, and none of the three acted alone; each institution they helped found had other named colleagues.

Measured against its own target, the Trust fell far short. The plan called for 2 million shares. Roughly 250,000 were sold worldwide, raising about £250,000, which is 12.5 percent of the authorized £2,000,000.[cite:jct_wiki] The sources document the shortfall but do not explain it in full. The installment design shows what the founders intended, not why the target was missed, and no account in this book's sources weighs the competing explanations. What the sources do support is that the gap did not make the Trust a failed institution. It continued for decades, and in time became a major shareholder of Bank Leumi, the bank that grew out of its Palestine subsidiary.[cite:jct_wiki]

The sum raised was not the real innovation. The Trust showed that a political movement could be financed by tens of thousands of ordinary owners, each holding a small stake, rather than by the goodwill of a handful of magnates. That model would carry the movement for the next fifty years. The Jewish National Fund, founded two years later, turned it into a physical object, the blue collection box, and after 1920 Keren Hayesod made small-donor fundraising permanent.[cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] [cite:bia_jewish_colonial_trust] The pound share is the direct ancestor of both.

Wide ownership, however, was not the same thing as wide control. By 1899 more than 100,000 people had subscribed for shares, yet lasting control of the Trust sat with a small founding bloc, through a block of "founders' shares" that carried super-voting rights.[cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust] How that mechanism worked, and how long it lasted, is traced in [scene:s04j|the land-purchase pipeline]. The point here is the shape it gave the institution from the start: the cost of the project was spread across a mass of small shareholders, while its direction stayed with the founding leadership of the Zionist Organization.

A bank incorporated in London still had to reach Palestine. On 27 February 1902, the Trust founded the Anglo-Palestine Company as its Palestine-facing banking subsidiary.[cite:encyclopedia_jewish_colonial_trust] This was the point at which fundraising turned into settlement: the subsidiary would finance land purchases directly, run a network of credit cooperatives offering long-term agricultural loans to settlers, and in 1909 lend to the association that built the first neighborhood of Tel Aviv. Its founding, its managers and its branches are the subject of [scene:s04e|the next section]. The parent company in London raised the capital; the subsidiary in Jaffa put it to work.

The library's funding ledger places the Trust at the head of every documented stream of money behind the pre-state architecture. Its row for the Trust records it as £2,000,000 authorized and about £250,000 raised in £1 shares, the money that bought "the movement's own bank."[cite:jct_wiki]

A second ledger, which sets each stream beside its value in today's money, gives the same £250,000 for 1899–1901 and converts it to about $47 million in 2025 dollars.

That conversion needs to be read with its method in view. The ledger multiplies each amount by the ratio of the 2025 consumer price index to the index of the year in question, the method of the United States government's own inflation calculator, converting pounds into dollars at the period exchange rate first. For years before 1913 it relies on estimates from the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, and it labels those conversions approximate. The ledger also warns against adding its rows together: pounds of 1899 and dollars of 1948 are different units, and the streams partly overlap. The $47 million figure is therefore a rough measure of scale, not a precise sum. By that measure the Trust's raise was modest beside what came later. The ledger's own rows put Keren Hayesod's worldwide income for 1921–1929 at $20.1 million, about $370 million today, and the United Jewish Appeal's 1948 campaign at $150 million, about $2 billion. The Trust's importance did not lie in its size.

The full map of the money behind the state, from the Trust through the land fund, Keren Hayesod and the wartime campaigns, shows where the Trust sits: first in time, and the base on which the later institutions were built. The Trust began the pattern of organized, small-donor finance in 1899, and it began it with a registered company, a stated capital, and shares sold in the open.

The record leaves several questions about the Trust unanswered. The sources give no full breakdown of who bought the 250,000 shares, by country or by size of holding, and no account of how many installment buyers completed their payments. They do not explain why the £2,000,000 target was missed. And while they document that ownership was wide and control narrow, they do not record whether small shareholders objected to that arrangement at the time.

sections.h: The Jewish National Fund: Land Bought and Never Resold
sections.html:
A bank could lend money, but it could not by itself hold land for a nation. The idea of a fund that would do exactly that was older than the Jewish Colonial Trust. Hermann Schapira proposed a national land fund at the very first Zionist Congress, in Basel in 1897. He died in 1898 without seeing it established.[cite:jnf_wiki] For four years the proposal sat on the Congress agenda, debated and deferred, Congress after Congress.

It came to a head at the Fifth Zionist Congress in Basel in December 1901. With the delegates ready to disperse once more without a decision, Herzl stood before them and pushed the matter to a vote: "After striving for so many years to set up the fund, we do not want to disperse again without having done anything." The motion passed, and the Jewish National Fund was founded on 29 December 1901.[cite:jnf_wiki] Within a month it had its first director, Johann (Yona) Kremenetzky, who ran it from Vienna.[cite:jnf_wiki]

The delay might be read as resistance to the fund's purpose. The record does not show that. The sources describe repeated deferral, and the deferral appears to reflect ordinary institutional delay and competing priorities on a crowded Congress agenda, not organized opposition to a land fund as such. What the sequence does show is that the fund was not an automatic creation of the movement. It existed because its first proponent pressed for it and its leader forced a vote four years later.

The founding resolution was brief and absolute. As the sources give it: "The JNF shall be the eternal possession of the Jewish people. Its funds shall not be used except for the purchase of lands in Palestine and Syria."[cite:jnf_wiki] Two rules followed from it. The fund's money was restricted to a single purpose, the purchase of land, within a defined region. And whatever it bought became, in the resolution's language, the eternal possession of the Jewish people. The resolution as quoted applies that phrase to the fund itself; the sources' own summaries apply it to the land, and the practice that followed treated the land that way.

That practice was a deliberate structural choice, not an incidental one. Ordinary land changes hands again and again; a farmer buys it, his heirs sell it, a later buyer sells it on. The JNF built a rule to prevent that. From the start its land was removed from the market permanently. It was leased to settlers on long terms, not sold, so that no later transaction could reverse an acquisition once made.[cite:jnf_wiki] Land came into the fund and, by design, did not leave. That single rule is why the fund's totals, tracked across nearly half a century, only ever rose. The sources are careful on one point: the arrangement was not unique in kind. Permanent, inalienable land trusts exist in other places and other contexts. What is documented here is this particular, explicit rule, written into this fund's founding terms.

The money that paid for the land came, as with the Trust, from many small givers. The fund's best-known instrument was not designed at its headquarters. Haim Kleinman, a bank clerk in Nadvorna, in Galicia, put a blue box labeled "Keren Le'umit" in his own office and wrote to the movement's newspaper, Die Welt, proposing that the idea be taken up more widely. Kremenetzky adopted the suggestion, and the first mass-produced boxes were distributed in 1904.[cite:wiki_blue_box_jnf] By the interwar years roughly one million blue-and-white collection boxes sat in Jewish homes around the world.[cite:wiki_blue_box_jnf] The box made physical what the Trust's pound share had begun: a national project paid for in coins, household by household.

Kleinman himself was one of them. He visited Mandate Palestine in the 1930s and planned to settle there, but he perished in the Holocaust before he could do so.[cite:wiki_blue_box_jnf] The man whose idea paid for land across the diaspora never lived on it.

Who the box's donors were, and what each of them understood their coins to be for, is a different question. The mass adoption of the box is documented. The intentions of a million households are not, and the record cannot say whether every donor knew of, or would have endorsed, each later use to which the fund's money was put.

The fund's first land was not bought at all. In 1903 Isaac Leib Goldberg of Vilnius, a Russian Zionist leader, gave it 200 dunams east of Hadera, a parcel that later became an olive grove.[cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg] From that gift the totals can be followed almost to the eve of statehood. By 1920 the fund held 22,363 dunams. By 1935 its holdings were about 89,500 acres, some 362 square kilometers, with 108 communities on them. By 1940 they reached 516,000 dunams, and by 1947–48 approximately 936,000 dunams.[cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg] [cite:jnf_wiki]

The units in that series shift: the 1935 figure is reported in acres and square kilometers, the others in dunams. A dunam is about 1,000 square meters, so 362 square kilometers is roughly 362,000 dunams, which is how the library's land chart plots it. Read in a single unit, the series grows from 200 dunams to about 22,000, then to about 362,000, then 516,000, then about 936,000.

The chart makes the shape of the record plain. Growth was slow for two decades, then steep. The fund's first twenty years added about 22,000 dunams; the five years from 1935 to 1940 added well over 150,000. The record also places the fund within Jewish landholding as a whole. At the moment of statehood, total Jewish holdings in Palestine came to roughly 2 million dunams, about 7 percent of Mandate Palestine's roughly 26 million dunams, and the sources describe the JNF's share as more than half of that total.[cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg] Taken at face value, the two rounded figures do not quite agree: 936,000 out of 2 million is a little under half. The fund's exact share depends on the precise total, which these sources give only as an approximation.

A common account holds that Zionist land buying before 1948 was sporadic and small. The record shows something different: a single institution, operating continuously for forty-seven years, under one rule, with its holdings rising in every period for which a figure exists. At the same time, the figure needs its context. Even at the end, all Jewish-owned land together amounted to about 7 percent of the country. The land fund was large within Jewish landholding and small within Palestine as a whole. Both facts are true, and a reader who hears only one of them will be misled.

These totals do not show that every dunam was acquired in the same way. The legal framework of the purchases, the sellers, and the tenants who lived on land that changed hands are treated in [scene:s04j|the land-purchase mechanism], which carries this section's numbers into the Ottoman and Mandate land system. The same JNF series appears again, with later figures beside it, in [scene:pm_s01|the ledger of the land's outcomes].

Several matters remain open. The record traces the fund's land but not, in these sources, its full annual income: how much the blue boxes collected in any given year is not documented here, and the library's funding ledger lists the JNF's income series among the totals still unavailable. The 1935 figure is given in a different unit from the rest, which makes the series harder to compare than it should be. And the precise share of Jewish-held land the fund owned in 1947–48 depends on a total that is reported only as roughly 2 million dunams.

sections.h: A Bank for Palestine, and an Offer for East Africa
sections.html:
In the eighteen months from early 1902 to the summer of 1903 the Zionist movement ran on two tracks at once. On one, it built a bank inside Palestine. On the other, under the pressure of a massacre in the Russian Empire, its own Congress voted to look seriously at land in East Africa. The two tracks pulled in opposite directions, and the conflict between them nearly broke the organization apart.

The first track began in London. On 27 February 1902, the Jewish Colonial Trust founded a subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Company, with initial capital of about £50,000.[cite:apc_wiki] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] Its chairman was David Wolffsohn, the Trust's co-founder and later Herzl's successor. Its manager was Zalman David Levontin, one of the founders of Rishon LeZion in 1882, whom Herzl had recruited personally.[cite:apc_wiki] The parent company in London raised capital from small shareholders; the subsidiary was the arm that would put the capital to work on the ground, as [scene:s04c|the Trust's own history] describes.

The company opened its first branch in Jaffa in 1903. From there it financed land purchase and agriculture and supported the credit cooperatives through which settlers borrowed. By 1914 it had branches in Jerusalem, Beirut, Hebron, Haifa, Safed, Tiberias and Gaza.[cite:apc_wiki] Its name later changed twice: it became the Anglo-Palestine Bank around 1930, and Bank Leumi in 1950–51.[cite:apc_wiki] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] The line runs unbroken from a £50,000 subsidiary of 1902 to one of the major banks of the State of Israel, though the bank's later operations are a different story from its founding years, and are not told here.

What "settlement financing" meant in practice can be seen in a single loan. The Anglo-Palestine Company lent to the Ahuzat Bayit association, which used the money to build the first neighborhood of what became Tel Aviv in 1909, six years after the Jaffa branch opened.[cite:apc_wiki] One bank, one association, one neighborhood: the record documents the financial link directly. The founding of the neighborhood itself, its lots and its first families, belongs to the story of the Second Aliyah and is told there.

The second track began with a massacre. At Easter, on 6–7 April 1903, a pogrom broke out in the town of Kishinev. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, 49 Jews were killed and more than 500 injured; 700 houses were looted and destroyed and 600 businesses and shops looted; about 2,000 families were left homeless; and the losses were put at 2,500,000 gold rubles.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev] Incitement had come first, in print. P. Krushevan's newspaper Bessarabets had incited the population with a steady stream of articles, among them a blood libel.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev]

The same encyclopedia goes further, and its words should be read as its own judgment. Local and central officials, it states, prepared the pogrom, "evidently with the backing of the minister of the interior, V. Plehve," and the town's garrison of 5,000 soldiers did not intervene.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev] The word "evidently" marks an inference from the evidence, not a document of instruction, and the role of Plehve rests in this book's sources on this one reference work. Herzl's own meetings with Plehve that August are told with [scene:hz_s01|his search for a charter].

The world responded. Protest meetings were held in London, Paris and New York. In the United States a protest petition was handed to President Theodore Roosevelt for transmission to the tsar, and the tsar refused it. The poet Bialik answered the pogrom with his poem "In the Town of Death."[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev] Kishinev was not the end. A second riot in the town in October 1905 killed 19 Jews and injured 56, and some Jewish youth formed self-defense units.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev]

The pogrom fell inside a movement of people far larger than Zionism. Between 1881 and 1914, according to the historian Shmuel Ettinger, more than 2.5 million Jews left Eastern Europe, about 80,000 a year. About 2 million went to the United States, about 350,000 to Western Europe, and about 300,000 to other overseas countries, Palestine among them.[cite:rs_rd1_ettinger] The proportions matter for everything that follows. The great majority of Jews leaving Eastern Europe in this period chose America. Palestine was one destination within a category of about 300,000. The question in 1903 was urgent and practical: where could people in danger go now?

That question produced the offer. After the Kishinev pogrom, Joseph Chamberlain, Britain's Colonial Secretary, offered Herzl the Guas Ngishu plateau in British East Africa for Jewish settlement.[cite:uganda_scheme_wiki] [cite:wiki_kishinev_pogrom] The territory lay in what is now Kenya, not Uganda, but the plan has been remembered ever since, inaccurately, as "the Uganda Scheme." The documented record ties the offer's timing to the pogrom. It does not establish what longer-term purposes, if any, Chamberlain or the British government had in making it; the record documents the offer and its trigger, not Britain's wider calculations, which belong to the later story of British policy.

The Sixth Zionist Congress opened in Basel on 23 August 1903, with about 600 delegates, the largest Congress to that date. It was the last Herzl would chair.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] He put the offer before it with careful limits. In his opening address he said of East Africa that "Zion this certainly is not and can never become," and described it as only an auxiliary colonizing measure.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] He also called it a Nachtasyl, a night shelter: a temporary refuge from immediate danger, not a replacement for the Land of Israel.[cite:uganda_scheme_wiki]

The question before the delegates was narrow. They were not asked to accept East Africa as the national home. They were asked whether to send a commission to examine it. The Congress voted 295 in favor and 178 against, with 98 abstentions.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_c] [cite:uganda_scheme_wiki] Another source used in this book gives the vote as 295–177.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] The difference is a single vote and does not change the outcome, but it is a disagreement between sources, and the more widely given figure, 295–178, is the one used here.

The numbers describe a divided body. With 98 abstaining, the 295 in favor were only just over half of the 571 delegates who voted or abstained. Then members of the Russian delegation walked out, arguing that the plan violated the Basel Program.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_c] The sources differ slightly on who left: one describes the Russian Zionist delegation walking out, another speaks of members of the delegation.[cite:uganda_scheme_wiki] [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] Either way it was a stronger act than a recorded vote against.

Both sides had a serious case. Herzl's, as his own framing of a night shelter implies, was a case about time. People were being killed now; a great power was offering land; and a refuge, explicitly temporary and explicitly not Zion, could save lives while the political work for Palestine went on. His opponents' case was about the program the movement had adopted six years earlier. The Basel Program named Palestine. To send a commission elsewhere, in their view, was to break the founding commitment of the organization they belonged to. The record does not show, however, that every Russian Zionist shared the walkout, nor that the rift was never repaired. The movement went on functioning after 1903, and the question was settled two years later.

The familiar account has it that Palestine was always the only place Zionists were seriously prepared to build. The record of 1903 does not support that. Six years after Basel, the movement's own Congress voted to examine a territory in East Africa, as a considered answer to escalating violence and not as a gesture, and the vote split its delegates badly enough that one delegation left the hall. It was the nearest the movement came, after 1897, to turning away from Palestine. At the same time the record limits the point: what passed was an inquiry, framed by its own sponsor as a shelter for the night. Whether the 1903 vote would have led anywhere had Herzl lived is a question no document can answer. How the matter ended, at the Seventh Congress of 1905, is told in [scene:s04f|the next section].

The sources leave some things unsettled. They do not give the exact date of Chamberlain's offer, beyond placing it after the pogrom. They rest the role of Plehve on a single reference work's inference. They do not say how many of the 98 abstainers sympathized with either side, or what each delegate's reasons were.

sections.h: East Africa Rejected: Palestine Chosen by Elimination
sections.html:
The East Africa question did not end with the walkout of 1903. It ended two years later, by a second Congress vote, and it ended at a price: a permanent split in the movement and the founding of a rival organization that spent twenty years looking for a homeland anywhere but Palestine.

The man who led that rival organization had already led one side of the 1903 debate. Israel Zangwill, a British-Jewish writer and Zionist leader, led the "Territorialist Faction" at the Sixth Congress. His argument was not that East Africa should replace Palestine. It was that the British offer should be used as leverage in later negotiations with the Ottomans over Palestine.[cite:jewishaction_uganda_truth] He was not alone among the movement's prominent figures. Otto Warburg, a German botanist (1859–1938) from a wealthy Hamburg banking family, also supported the East Africa plan at the Sixth Congress.[cite:wiki_otto_warburg_botanist] [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] He is a different man from the better-known twentieth-century biochemist of the same name, and his later career, traced below, shows that support for East Africa in 1903 did not rule out leading the movement's work in Palestine.

Between the two Congresses the movement lost its founder. Herzl died in 1904.[cite:wiki_seventh_zionist_congress]

The Seventh Zionist Congress met in Basel from 27 July to 2 August 1905. It did two things. It formally rejected the East Africa offer, closing the question the Sixth Congress had opened, and Britain withdrew the offer. And it elected David Wolffsohn, co-founder of the Jewish Colonial Trust and designer of the movement's flag, as president of the Zionist Organization in Herzl's place.[cite:wiki_seventh_zionist_congress] One reference work states the decision in broader terms: the Seventh Congress rejected a national home outside Palestine and its vicinity.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_c] The two decisions came at the same meeting, but the record does not link them as cause and effect. The succession followed from Herzl's death and would have come whatever the Congress decided about Africa.

For Zangwill the rejection was final. When the Congress turned the offer down outright, he led 28 delegates out of the hall and founded the Jewish Territorial Organization, the ITO, dedicated to finding land for Jewish settlement anywhere, no longer bound to Palestine.[cite:jewishaction_uganda_truth] He did not go alone or without means. The ITO had support at the time from two members of the Rothschild family, the brothers Leopold and Baron Nathan Mayer Rothschild, not to be confused with Baron Edmond de Rothschild.[cite:jewishaction_uganda_truth]

The ITO's search was wide. It sent exploratory expeditions to Canada, Australia, Mesopotamia (today's Iraq), Cyrenaica (in today's Libya) and Angola.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism] It also ran the Galveston Movement, which directed Jewish immigrants to the United States through the port of Galveston, Texas, instead of New York.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism] Zangwill himself, looking back, said that "there was not a land on earth that we did not think about." The search also went to court. Zangwill fought a case in the English courts against the Jewish Colonial Trust; as the sources describe it, the suit sought to restrain the Trust from colonizing anywhere outside Palestine, Syria, Asiatic Turkey, Sinai and Cyprus.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism] The sources do not explain the reasoning behind the suit or record its outcome, so its purpose has to be left as they state it. What it shows is that the boundaries of the movement's territory were contested in law as well as in Congress.

None of the expeditions produced lasting settlement. The sources characterize the result in slightly different terms. One calls the Galveston effort a failed attempt to settle Jewish refugees in Texas and says the ITO's search met with little success; another speaks of a single modest, temporary success without naming it. They agree on the larger outcome: the ITO achieved little lasting settlement anywhere.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism] [cite:wiki_jewish_territorial_organization] Zangwill rejoined the mainstream Zionist movement before his death in 1921. The ITO officially disbanded around 1925, four years later.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism]

Otto Warburg's path ran the other way. Having backed East Africa in 1903, he became the Zionist Organization's third president, serving from 1911 to 1921, and with Arthur Ruppin founded the Palestine Land Development Company, which he named and led until his death, bringing the Jewish National Fund in as a shareholder.[cite:wiki_otto_warburg_botanist] [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] The company's work is told in [scene:s04g|the section on the Palestine Office]. His career shows how fluid positions on the territorial question could be.

A common view treats East Africa as a footnote and holds that no real alternative to Palestine ever existed. The record does not bear that out. The alternative was put to two Congresses. It cost the movement a walkout in 1903 and a permanent split in 1905. And after the split, an organized faction with prominent backers and a court case of its own spent two decades looking for other land and did not find it. That is a different finding from "no alternative existed." Alternatives existed, were pursued, and failed.

It is in that sense that Palestine was confirmed by elimination. Its place as the movement's target survived two organized internal challenges: the 1903 vote to examine East Africa, and the ITO's departure in 1905 to search elsewhere.[cite:wiki_jewish_territorial_organization] The phrase needs care, though, in both directions. It does not mean the 1903 Congress chose East Africa: it voted to examine the offer, under a sponsor who said plainly it was not Zion. Nor does it mean Palestine won only because everything else failed. The Seventh Congress rejected East Africa in 1905, while the ITO's search had barely begun; the decision came first, and the failures came after.

What "confirmed by elimination" cannot show is why. The record documents the votes, the walkouts, the split and the search. It does not record a single rationale shared by the delegates who chose Palestine. Some, like the Russian delegates of 1903, argued from the Basel Program, which named Palestine. Others, like Warburg, backed East Africa in 1903 and later led the organization's work in Palestine. A reading that ties the outcome to the Jewish masses' religious and historical attachment to the land is offered in [scene:s04fa|the section on the Uganda counterfactual], and it is a reading, not a documented finding.

The gaps are real. The sources here say nothing about what the East Africa commission reported, or when exactly Britain withdrew its offer. They do not give the vote at the Seventh Congress, only its result. They do not name the 28 delegates who left with Zangwill, explain his suit against the Trust, or identify the "modest success" one of them mentions.

sections.h: The Uganda Test: Could the Project Have Moved?
sections.html:
This section runs a thought experiment, and it should be read as one. Suppose the Sixth Zionist Congress had gone the other way in 1903, and a Jewish state had been built in British East Africa or in Argentina. What would it have been called, and would the structures later built on the name "Israel" still have worked? No document can answer a question about a history that never happened. What the documents can do is test one assumption that is often made without testing: that geography was incidental, and that the name and the theology later gathered around the state could have attached themselves to whatever territory the movement settled. The argument offered here is that, put to the record, that assumption does not hold up well. The record cannot settle the counterfactual, but it can be used to ask which parts of the project depended on one particular place and which did not.

The test is therefore built from documented pieces: what Theodor Herzl wrote in 1896, what the Congress did in 1903 and 1905, what Genesis 15:18 says, and what Cyrus Scofield's prophetic notes require. The argument assembled from them is an argument, offered as such.

In Der Judenstaat Herzl put the choice of territory as an open question: "Shall we choose Palestine or Argentine? We shall take what is given us, and what is selected by Jewish public opinion." He noted that Argentina's government would "gladly provide" Jews with land.[cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896] His framework was, in the first instance, a political answer to European antisemitism, and Herzl himself was a secular Jew. One account of the text holds that he considered Argentina first and Palestine second, and that when he did prefer Palestine, it was because it would give "the Jewish problem" a solution "not only just, but brilliant," a practical and political reason (Palestine would mobilize Jewish public opinion) rather than a religious one. The Israeli peace activist and writer Uri Avnery went further, judging that Herzl "had obviously thought very little about Palestine as a concrete entity" and had inserted it into his original blueprint as an afterthought.[cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896]

The same pamphlet also sets the two territories side by side in different terms. Argentina offered practical advantages, fertile land and a sparse population. Palestine was "our ever-memorable historic home... a force of marvelous potency."[cite:herzl_judenstaat] Read this way, Herzl named, seven years before anyone offered him East Africa, the very difference the Uganda dispute would turn on: one territory had only practical merits, the other carried a weight no practical merit could replace. Both readings rest on the same 1896 text. They differ on emphasis: whether Palestine's pull, for Herzl, was mainly its power to rally Jewish opinion or its historic charge. Neither reading claims that every later leader or delegate shared Herzl's reasons. His words are evidence of his own stated view, not of a consensus.

The Congress's own record bears on the same difference. Herzl laid the British offer before the Sixth Congress in August 1903 as a temporary refuge for Jews fleeing persecution; the vote to send a commission and the walkout that followed are told in [scene:s04e|the section on 1903]. One account used here gives the vote as 295 to 177, one fewer against than the 295–178 followed elsewhere in this book.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] That account describes the minority as mainly Russian and Eastern European delegates who had lived through the worst of the pogroms, and reads their walkout as a statement that they were not looking for any land; they were returning to Zion.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] Herzl died in 1904, and the Seventh Zionist Congress formally rejected the scheme in 1905.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903]

Zionist historical scholarship describes two broad strands that the dispute brought into the open. "Territorial Zionism," sometimes called Ugandism, held that any safe territory would serve: the purpose was refuge from persecution, and location came second to safety. "Zion Zionism" held that only Palestine, the biblical Land of Israel, Eretz Yisrael, would serve, because the purpose was not refuge alone but national restoration to an ancestral homeland. The debate of 1903–1905 settled the question in favor of Zion.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] The conclusion this account draws is that even secular political Zionism could not override the religious and historical attachment of the Jewish masses to that land; for most supporters, location was not interchangeable.

The land-promise on which the later theology rests is specific. Genesis 15:18, in one translation, reads:

"On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, 'To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates.'" [cite:genesis_15_18]

Another rendering has "I have given this land" and "the Euphrates river."[cite:genesis_1518_text] Other texts add detail. Deuteronomy 11:24 reads: "Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours; your territory shall be from the wilderness, from Lebanon, from the river, the Euphrates river, to the western sea." Numbers 34 describes specific borders. Together these passages describe a territory in the Levant bounded by the Euphrates to the northeast, the Nile (or Wadi el-Arish) to the southwest, Lebanon to the north and the Mediterranean to the west.[cite:genesis_1518_text] A promise naming a bounded river-to-river territory is a different kind of promise from a blessing on wherever a people comes to live, and that specificity is what makes the test possible at all. It does not settle how the verse ought to be read. Non-literal, allegorical reading of scripture is an ancient and formally recognized tradition, not a modern alternative to the literal one.[cite:genesis_15_18] The test concerns only the literal reading, because that is the reading on which Scofield's framework rests.

Scofield's dispensationalism, set out in the notes of his annotated Bible (told in [scene:s05|the section on the Scofield Bible]), arranges prophecy into an ordered sequence. Every step after the second depends on the regathering happening at the place the earlier covenant named, Zion and Jerusalem.[cite:wiki_scofield_bible]

A state in East Africa calling itself Israel would not satisfy "Israel regathered" in the sense the sequence's own logic requires. It would not be a variant of the same prophecy but a different claim, one Scofield's notes never made. On this argument, the 30 to 40 million Christian Zionists who later grew out of his framework exist because the state that formed stood where their theology pointed; move it, and there is a serious case that this constituency, and the sustained American political support it supplied, would never have formed.[cite:wiki_scofield_bible] The argument concerns what the theology's own text requires. It is not a claim about what every believer has consciously reasoned through.

A second line of argument, made elsewhere in this library, pushes the same logic further. It holds that the idea of Greater Israel, Eretz Yisrael HaShlema, the "Complete Land of Israel," is a biblical concept that can exist only because the state was established in the biblical Land of Israel. In Argentina or East Africa, it reasons, five things would have been missing: the biblical land-promise framework, since Genesis 15:18 has no Argentine equivalent; the narrative of return to an ancestral homeland, since Jews had no historical claim to Argentina or East Africa; the concept of the Complete Land of Israel itself; the Revisionist Zionist claim to "both banks of the Jordan"; and the religious-nationalist settler ideology that draws explicitly on biblical texts about Levantine territory.[cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896] [cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] The argument's central step is that the same attachment to the land that made Argentina or Uganda unacceptable in 1903–1905 is the attachment that later generates territorial maximalism, so that the founding choice of Palestine already posed the question of the land's "completeness." As the argument itself puts it, "you cannot have the one without the other."[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] Those later claims belong to later periods and are followed in [scene:gia_src_s01|the Greater Israel question].

The opening of this library sets out one symbolic interpretation of the name, reading "Israel" as IS-RA-EL: a state of consciousness a person arrives at, rather than a bloodline or a border. That is an interpretation, not a documented finding, and it is labeled as such wherever it appears. Put to the same counterfactual, even this reading draws its resonance from places named in the text: Jerusalem, the Temple, and Peniel, where Jacob wrestled. A state in East Africa that borrowed the word would not carry that resonance by borrowing it.[cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] The literalist theology and the symbolic reading disagree about almost everything. On this one narrow point they converge: the place mattered, not only the word. The convergence goes no further, and it does not mean the symbolic reading endorses any of the literalist theology's other claims.

Fairness requires saying what a move would not have destroyed. The movement's financial and political institutions, among them the Jewish Colonial Trust and the Jewish National Fund, and later bodies such as AZEC, were built to fund and organize settlement, and nothing in their design tied them to one territory. Before Herzl, real settlement infrastructure had in fact been built in Argentina under the JCA. That machinery could have unloaded anywhere. What could not have traveled was the theological and symbolic layer.

If the test holds, it changes how the outcome of 1905 should be understood. Palestine was not merely the sentimental favorite among roughly equal choices. For at least one major source of the movement's eventual support, it was close to a structural requirement: the only site compatible with the theological and symbolic machinery that later supplied decades of American political and financial backing.

There is a strong case against reading too much into this. The familiar account holds that Zionism was first of all a response to European antisemitism, a movement for Jewish self-determination and safety; that the choice of Palestine was contested inside the movement, with some leaders open to other places; and that the eventual choice reflected the deep historical and religious attachment of most Jews to the biblical Land of Israel. Much of that account is borne out by the same record. The East Africa offer was a real offer of refuge, debated and voted on; on the account cited above, those who walked out in 1903 were delegates from the communities that had suffered the worst pogroms, and what moved them was attachment to Zion, not a program of borders. The same source that builds the Greater Israel argument says plainly that the internal debate "was resolved by religious and historical attachment to the specific land, not by territorial maximalism."[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] That the later maximalist claims draw on the same attachment to the land is supported by the texts they cite. That the attachment by itself produced those claims is the argument's own inference, and it needs the later history, not the events of 1903–1905, to bear it out. The Scofield test, likewise, bears on the support the state later received from Christians; it does not explain the choice the Zionist delegates themselves made.

No one knows what the founders would actually have named a state in East Africa, or how a Christian constituency would have responded to it, because those things never happened and cannot be documented. The movement did seriously consider East Africa; that is on record. What is offered here is a structural test applied to documented facts, and its answer is narrow: the theological apparatus examined in this book depended on the place, not only on the name. Whether Herzl's own preference was chiefly political or chiefly historic remains a matter of reading the same pages two ways.

sections.h: For and Against: Jewish Currents, 1885–1914
sections.html:
The years between the Basel Congress and the First World War are easy to tell as the story of one movement gathering a people behind it. The record shows something less tidy. Jewish opinion on Zionism in this period was plural, organized and argued in public, and several of its currents were founded expressly to oppose the movement or to contest what it should be. The first wave of opposition, in 1897, came from the German rabbis of the Protestrabbiner declaration, from the Bund and from Ahad Ha'am, and is told in [scene:s04|the section on Basel]. This section follows the currents that took shape around it, from a rabbinical platform in Pittsburgh in 1885 to a declaration in the Berliner Tageblatt in 1914. Some stood outside Zionism and rejected it on principle. Others stood inside the Zionist Organization and fought over its program. A third group opposed both the movement and its religious wing.

The earliest of these positions predates Herzl. In 1885 the Reform movement in the United States adopted the Pittsburgh Platform, which declared: "We consider ourselves no longer a nation but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine" nor the restoration of the laws of a Jewish state.[cite:rs_rd1_reform_wiki] The position was put again in the year of the First Congress. In 1897 the Central Conference of American Rabbis resolved: "We reaffirm that the object of Judaism is not political nor national, but spiritual." Isaac Mayer Wise described Judaism as "not tied down to a piece of land here or there."[cite:rs_rd1_reform_wiki] These words come to this book through a reference work quoting N. W. Cohen's study of the subject; the original text of the 1897 resolution has not been checked. The substance is clear enough. For these rabbis the Jews were a religious community whose object was spiritual, and a national program, in Palestine or anywhere, contradicted that self-definition. Their objection was not to a particular piece of land. It was to the idea that Jews were a nation needing one.

Within the Zionist Organization the argument was over what Zionism should do besides diplomacy. At the Fifth Congress in Basel in 1901, the Congress that also founded the Jewish National Fund, a group known as the Democratic Faction, among them Leo Motzkin, Martin Buber and Chaim Weizmann, pressed for Hebrew culture and for more democracy inside the organization.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] That December the Congress declared cultural work an essential part of Zionism.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] Whether a national movement should take charge of Jewish culture at all was a question on which Zionists themselves divided, and the division soon had an organization of its own.

Three months later, on 4–5 March 1902, a convention in Vilna called by Rabbi Isaac Jacob Reines founded Mizrachi, the religious-Zionist faction within the Zionist Organization.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_mizrachi] Tobias Grill counts 72 delegates at Vilna, 24 of them rabbis.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] The faction grew fast. In its first year it built 210 branches in the Russian Empire, and its first world conference, held at Pressburg on 21–23 August 1904, drew about 100 delegates. Its motto set out the synthesis it stood for: "The Land of Israel for the people of Israel according to the Torah of Israel."[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_mizrachi] Mizrachi worked inside the Zionist Organization, and its motto put the Torah at the center of the national program.

The arrangement held for nine years and then broke at the point where it had started. When the Tenth Zionist Congress, meeting in Basel in 1911, added cultural work to the organization's formal program, all the Mizrachi delegates walked out. A later Mizrachi conference decided not to leave the Zionist Organization; some leaders who disagreed with that decision broke away.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_mizrachi] Mizrachi as a body chose to stay.

Religious Zionism had religious opponents from its first year. In 1902–03 Orthodox leaders of the Free Association, based in Frankfurt, declared Mizrachi's principles incompatible with traditional Judaism. A pamphlet by Raphael Breuer published in 1903 carried the title Nationaljudenthum ein Wahnjudenthum![cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] Here the objection ran opposite to Reform's. Reform rejected Jewish nationhood in the name of a spiritual religious community; the Frankfurt Orthodox opposed it from within traditional religious observance, declaring Mizrachi's attempt to join Torah and nationalism incompatible with traditional Judaism.

Orthodox opposition acquired an international organization a decade later. Agudat Israel was founded at Kattowitz in late May 1912 as a worldwide association of Torah-observant Jews. Grill describes it as founded largely as a countermeasure to Mizrachi.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] Another account in this library puts the emphasis more broadly: Agudat Israel was founded to strengthen Torah-observant Judaism as a separation from the emerging secular Jewish nationalist movement, which its founders regarded as a danger to Torah-observant Jewish life.[cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history] [cite:wiki_neturei_karta] The two descriptions do not exclude each other; one names the religious-Zionist faction as the immediate rival, the other names the secular nationalism that faction had joined. Either way, organized Orthodox opposition to political Zionism on religious grounds existed thirty-six years before the State of Israel did. It was not a reaction to the state, which did not yet exist, but a theological position taken toward a movement that did not yet control any state. The organization's later history, and the more uncompromising current that split from it, are followed in [scene:df_s13|a later volume].

In the same year liberal German Jews organized against Zionism on political grounds. In October 1912 they founded a league to combat Zionism, soon renamed the Antizionistisches Komitee. Its first pamphlet, issued early in 1913, reached about 45,000 copies by July of that year. An appeal of 1913 carried about 300 signatures, and the committee's declaration appeared in the Berliner Tageblatt on 5 February 1914. Before the war it reportedly had more than 1,000 members.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] Its instruments were those of a liberal civic organization: pamphlets, signed appeals and a declaration in a major daily newspaper.

The argument outlasted the outbreak of war. About twelve days after the Balfour Declaration, in November 1917, anti-Zionist British Jews formed the League of British Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] The Declaration itself belongs to the next stage; see [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration].

Set side by side, these currents answer a common assumption: that Zionism in its first two decades spoke for the Jews of the world, and that its Jewish critics were a fringe. The record shows at least four distinct positions, each organized and each documented in its own words. American Reform rejected Jewish nationhood as such. Liberal German Jews organized a committee against it. Frankfurt Orthodoxy and then Agudat Israel rejected it as a departure from the faith. And within the movement, secular nationalists and Mizrachi fought over whether culture or Torah would define it. The strongest case on the Zionist side is also in the record. Mizrachi's 210 branches in a single year show that religious Jews in the Russian Empire could be organized for the movement in large numbers, and the decision after 1911 to stay inside the Zionist Organization shows that the movement could absorb deep disagreement without losing the faction as a whole, though some of its leaders broke away. The strongest case on the other side is that its opponents were not marginal cranks but the established rabbinical bodies of American Reform, leading Orthodox circles in Germany and an international Orthodox association, each stating a principled objection in public.

The record has its limits. The sources give the founding dates, the counts of delegates, branches, pamphlets and signatures, and the key texts. They do not measure what share of the world's Jews held each position. The figures that exist count organizers and printed copies, not adherents, and they cannot be added up into a census of opinion. Nor does the material here say how these organizations were funded. The 1885 and 1897 Reform texts are quoted through a secondary source, and the Komitee's membership figure is reported rather than established.

sections.h: The Second Aliyah, 1904–1914
sections.html:
While the Zionist Organization argued in Basel and Hamburg, a second wave of immigrants was arriving in Jaffa. The Second Aliyah, the immigration of 1904 to the outbreak of war in 1914, was small beside the more than 2.5 million Jews who left Eastern Europe between 1881 and 1914, about 2 million of them for the United States.[cite:rs_rd1_ettinger] And about half of those who came to Palestine did not stay.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] But the years of the wave produced the first collective farm, the first Jewish guards' commune, the first Hebrew high school, and the neighborhood that became Tel Aviv. They also built, in the same years and through the same institutions, a principle of "Hebrew labor" that set Jewish and Arab workers apart. How historians weigh those two achievements against each other is one of the central disputes of the period.

The sources do not agree on the size of the wave. The National Library of Israel puts it at about 35,000 immigrants, mostly from Eastern Europe, with a minority from Yemen; the Jewish Virtual Library gives 40,000.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_second] Both agree that departures were heavy. At least half, by the National Library's estimate, and nearly half, by the Jewish Virtual Library's, left within a few years because of economic hardship. By the end of the period the Jewish community numbered about 80,000.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_second] That end-of-period total is itself one of several competing counts of the Jewish population in 1914, which range from under 40,000 Ottoman subjects to over 90,000; the reasons the counts differ are set out in [scene:rd1_ottoman|the opening section].

The newcomers did not arrive in empty institutional space. The farming colonies of the First Aliyah, financed by Edmond de Rothschild, were by then under new management. The Jewish Colonization Association, founded by Baron de Hirsch in September 1891 with a capital of £2,000,000, had taken over the administration of Rothschild's Palestine colonies. The 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia dates that arrangement "since 1899."[cite:rs_rd1_je_ica] The year-by-year ledger compiled for this library places it in 1900; the sources differ by a year. On Gershon Shafir's account, discussed below, the First Aliyah colonies relied on cheap Arab labor.[cite:rs_rd1_beinin_shafir]

The best-known immigrant of the wave shows its pattern. David Ben-Gurion, born David Green in Płońsk on 16 October 1886, landed at Jaffa on 9 September 1906, according to Ben-Gurion House, and went that same evening to work in Petah Tikva. Another educational source, the Center for Israel Education, gives his arrival as 7 September 1907; the two dates cannot both be right, and this book does not choose between them. He joined the leadership of Poalei Zion; from 1912 he studied law in Istanbul with Yitzhak Ben-Zvi; and in 1915 the Ottoman authorities expelled him, and he went to Alexandria and then to New York.[cite:rs_rd1_bghouse] [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_bg]

The immigrants of the Second Aliyah came with an ideal of "Hebrew labor." The National Library of Israel notes that the ideal met friction in practice, because many Jewish farmers went on employing Arab workers.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] What the workers built next, guards and farms of their own, can be read as an answer to that friction; how far it was an answer, and how far the expression of an ideal held in advance, is the dispute taken up below.

The first answer was armed. In 1907 Bar-Giora was founded at Yitzhak Ben-Zvi's home in Neve Tzedek and set up the first Jewish guards' commune at Sejera. In 1909 Hashomer grew out of it under the leadership of Yisrael Shohat. It existed until 1920.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_defense] Hashomer took over the guarding of Jewish settlements from Arab night watchmen, whom the Jewish Virtual Library's account describes as colluding with thieves; that characterization is the account's own, and the material here contains no Arab account of the same events. Hashomer also made it a condition of guarding a settlement that only Jewish laborers be employed there.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_defense] One reading takes that condition as the mechanism in miniature: a security service the settlements needed was tied to the labor policy the workers wanted, so that guarding became a lever for Hebrew labor.

The second answer was settlement on national land. Kinneret Farm, set up in 1908, was the first Zionist instructional farm.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] At Umm Juni, on land owned by the Jewish National Fund, the first collective took root, though the sources date its founding differently. According to the Center for Israel Education, Degania, counted as the first kibbutz, was founded on 28 October 1910, when the "Hadera Commune," ten men and two women, leased the land from the Jewish National Fund; an earlier group that Ruppin had placed there in 1909 had dispersed. The Jewish Virtual Library dates Degania to 1909.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_degania] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_second] The difference appears to be not only one of dates: it may turn on whether the dispersed group of 1909 or the commune of 1910 counts as the founding. Ruppin's role came through the Zionist Organization's Palestine Office, whose work is told in [scene:s04g|the section on the Palestine Office]. Two other experiments followed in 1911: the Merhavia cooperative, which disbanded in 1918, and a women's training farm, which trained about 70 young women before it closed in 1917.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] The arrangement at Degania shows the money's path: the land belonged to the Jewish National Fund and was leased to the workers who farmed it rather than sold to them.

The same years produced the first Hebrew urban institutions. The Hebrew Gymnasium, the first Hebrew high school, was founded in Jaffa in 1905; it later became the Herzliya Gymnasium. The idea of a new neighborhood, Ahuzat Bayit, arose in summer 1906. Its building plots were raffled at Passover 1909 among 60 founding families, and the neighborhood took the name Tel Aviv by majority vote.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] The loan that helped finance it came from the Anglo-Palestine Company, as told in [scene:s04e|the section on the Anglo-Palestine Company].

The Second Aliyah is usually told as a story of young Eastern European socialists. A significant part of it came from Yemen, and that migration had begun long before. From 1881 to 1882 a few hundred Jews left Sanaa and nearby settlements for Palestine, and migration from Yemen continued almost without interruption until 1914; in that period about 10% of Yemen's Jews left, according to a reference account.[cite:rs_rd1_yemen_wiki] In 1884 Yemenite families settled in a new neighborhood, Kfar Hashiloach, in Silwan, outside the walls of Jerusalem.[cite:rs_rd1_yemen_wiki] These early arrivals came independently of the Zionist Organization, which did not yet exist.

In 1911 the organization took a hand. Shmuel Yavne'eli went to Yemen, at his own request, on behalf of the Palestine Office of the Zionist Organization, to encourage immigration; his journey lasted more than a year.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_yavneeli] He returned in April 1912. About 1,000 Jews left central and southern Yemen as a result of his efforts, and several hundred more arrived before 1914, according to the 2003 study by Simon, Laskier and Reguer as summarized in the same reference account.[cite:rs_rd1_yemen_wiki] The National Library of Israel calls the Yemenite immigration of 1911–12 "the first planned immigration operation in the history of Zionism," and counts about 2,000 Yemenite immigrants in the Second Aliyah as a whole, about half of them sent to farming settlements.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_yemen] Yavne'eli's own report, written in 1913, gives the scale from the inside: over the past year, he wrote, "some two hundred and fifty to three hundred Yemenite families have settled in the colonies."[cite:rs_rd1_posen_yavneeli]

Why the colonies wanted them is where the dispute begins. On Gershon Shafir's reading, as summarized by Joel Beinin, the planters brought in Yemenite Jews "who were to be paid Arab wages": Jewish workers who would satisfy the national ideal of Hebrew labor at the price of Arab labor.[cite:rs_rd1_beinin_shafir] One group's later story rests on a single source. Yemenite families from Sharab reached the Kinneret area in spring 1912 and cleared and farmed land there. According to the Yemenite heritage site Wysinfo, which reproduces the group's letters, their disputes with the neighboring Kvutzat Kinneret over land ended in 1930 with the Yemenites' removal to Marmorek, near Rehovot.[cite:rs_rd1_wysinfo] That ending falls well beyond this period and rests on a single heritage source; a later volume returns to it.

Two readings of the Second Aliyah stand against each other, and each has real evidence behind it. Gershon Shafir's study of 1989, as summarized by Joel Beinin, argues that the First Aliyah colonies relied on cheap Arab labor; that the Second Aliyah workers' "conquest of labor" failed to exclude Arab workers but did split the labor market in two; that the planters imported Yemenite Jews to be paid Arab wages; and that the kibbutz and Hashomer were forged in conflict over land and labor rather than mainly by prior ideology.[cite:rs_rd1_beinin_shafir] On this reading the institutions grew chiefly out of competition over land and labor on a settler frontier, not mainly out of prior ideology. The record above gives this case its strongest evidence: the farmers' continued hiring of Arab workers, Hashomer's condition that only Jewish laborers be employed, and Yavne'eli's families settled in the colonies.

Against such readings, Anita Shapira argues, as summarized by Rebecca Stein, that the early socialist settlers became conquerors reluctantly, out of "good will and purity of faith."[cite:rs_rd1_stein_merip] On this reading the motive force was a socialist-national ideal, and the settlers became conquerors reluctantly rather than by design. This case rests on the settlers' own convictions, and the material gathered here records what they did, not what moved them, so it cannot by itself decide between the readings. The two readings agree on what happened. They disagree on why, and on whether intention or structure should carry the weight.

Much stays uncertain. The size of the wave is known only within a range of 35,000 to 40,000, and the share who left only as "about half." Degania's founding date depends on which group counts as the founders, and Ben-Gurion's arrival is dated to two different years by two reputable sources. The characterization of the Arab watchmen Hashomer replaced comes from one account, the Jewish Virtual Library's; the material gathered here holds no account from the watchmen, the Arab workers displaced by Hebrew labor, or the villages near the new settlements. The Yemenite figures come partly from reference summaries, and the Kinneret group's later removal from a heritage site. And the central question, whether the Second Aliyah's institutions were driven chiefly by ideals or by the competition for land and work, remains a matter of interpretation on which serious historians differ.

sections.h: The Palestine Office: Settlement Gets a Bureaucracy
sections.html:
Behind the farms and guards of the Second Aliyah stood an office. A familiar picture of Zionist settlement before the First World War shows lone pioneers improvising on the land, with no real organization behind them. The record shows otherwise. By 1908 the movement had built an office, a land company and a small group of named purchasing agents, and it had set them up to work together.

The decision came from the top of the Zionist Organization. In 1907 its president, David Wolffsohn, sent Arthur Ruppin to Palestine. In 1908 Ruppin opened the Palestine Office in Jaffa. It became the organization's central operating agency in the country for buying land and coordinating settlement, and it worked directly with the funds of the Jewish National Fund. [cite:ruppin_wiki] Ruppin, a German-trained lawyer and economist, had first come on a pilot study of the prospects for colonization. His fuller record, including the documented evidence that he believed Zionism required Jewish "racial purity," is set out in [scene:s04j|the section on how the land was bought]. [cite:haaretz_ruppin_retrospective] [cite:tandfonline_ruppin_weltanschauung] Here the subject is narrower: the institution he founded.

The Palestine Office had three jobs. It coordinated land purchase with the Jewish National Fund, it assisted immigration, and it helped settle the people who arrived. [cite:wiki_palestine_office] The office mattered because of the order in which the movement's tools appeared. The Zionist Organization had founded a bank, the Jewish Colonial Trust, in 1899 and a land fund, the Jewish National Fund, in 1901. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:jnf_wiki] The Palestine Office, added in 1908, was the body in the country itself through which money raised abroad was turned into specific purchases and specific settlements. That is why a modest field office in Jaffa holds a central place in the institutional history.

The Palestine Land Development Company was founded beside the office. Ruppin set it up with Otto Warburg, and the sources date its founding to 1908 or 1909. One account gives 1908 and calls the company the office's operational purchasing arm. The company bought land and prepared it physically for ownership by the Jewish National Fund and for use by settlers. By the outbreak of the First World War it had handled approximately 50,000 dunams. [cite:wiki_otto_warburg_botanist] [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] This division of labor defined the structure. The Jewish National Fund was the owner, in whose name land was held. The company was the buyer and preparer, which negotiated, purchased and readied the ground. The office coordinated the two and placed people on the land.
