Warburg, the German botanist who became the Zionist Organization's third president in 1911, had backed the East Africa offer in 1903; his path from that vote to Palestine is traced in [scene:s04f|the section on the territorialist split]. He chose the company's name himself, led it until his death in 1938, and brought the Jewish National Fund in as a shareholder. [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] [cite:wiki_otto_warburg_botanist]

The shareholding is the main financial fact the record gives about the company. Through its stake, the land fund that owned land had a share in the company that bought it. The record does not give the company's capital, its other shareholders or its accounts. Nor does it give the Palestine Office's budget or staff. What can be said is where the money came from at the start of the chain. It was raised by the Zionist Organization's own instruments, the Jewish Colonial Trust's shares and the Jewish National Fund's collections, which are described in their own sections. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:jnf_wiki]

Named people stood behind the land totals. In these prewar years Yehoshua Hankin, Arthur Ruppin and Jacob Thon negotiated and carried out land purchases. [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin] [cite:wiki_arthur_ruppin] Hankin was also the chief negotiator of the Sursock purchases, which are told in the section on how land was bought. Thon is recorded as the company's sole manager from 1907 until his death in 1950. The sources do not fully agree here. A manager from 1907 would predate a company founded in 1908 or 1909. Warburg is said to have led the company until 1938, and the section on land purchase has Hankin becoming its head in 1932. The material does not say how these roles divided. The question stays open. Naming these men turns a dunam total into a historical process with identifiable actors. They did not work alone, however. They worked inside the funding, legal and organizational framework that the neighboring sections describe.

The relationship to later institutions is direct. The Palestine Office is the institutional ancestor of the Jewish Agency, established in 1929. [cite:wiki_palestine_office] The Jewish Agency became the institutional engine of state-building in Mandate Palestine. [cite:wiki_wzo] The line of descent is documented. It does not follow that every later Jewish Agency practice goes back directly to the methods of 1908. Organizations change, and what runs from Jaffa to 1929 is an institutional line, not an unbroken set of procedures.

The money chain for the whole pre-state period is set out as seven steps in the dashboard panel below. It begins with building a bank in 1899–1902 and buying land through the Jewish National Fund from 1901. It moves through the permanent fundraising of the 1920s and the enlarged Jewish Agency to the war financing of 1948 and the step of 1948–49 that turned donors into state policy. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_palestine_office] The Palestine Office does not have a step of its own in the panel. In this period it was the operating office through which the first two steps reached the ground. The panel's own note is a useful discipline for this section too. It does not claim that any government secretly funded the movement, or that money bought every decision. The record documents private, organized finance, and one specific money-for-policy episode in 1948.

Two qualifications keep the picture accurate. First, the system did not always run in order. The section on land purchase records that agents such as Hankin sometimes bought land first, at their own financial risk, and were reimbursed by the Jewish National Fund or the Jewish Agency only afterward. The infrastructure existed, but the financing was not always planned centrally in advance. [cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust] Second, the record here describes the structure, not its scale in money. It gives no budget for the office and no figure for what the company paid for its approximately 50,000 dunams. It does not say from whom that land was bought, or what happened to the people living on it. Those questions belong to the section on how land was bought, and the material here does not answer them.

sections.h: The Scofield Reference Bible, 1909
sections.html:
In 1909 Oxford University Press published a King James Bible with one man's notes printed beneath the text on every page. A common view holds that Christian support for Israel comes straight from ancient scripture, read plainly. The verses involved are ancient. The framework that links them to a modern political return of Jews to Palestine, and that made such a return a matter of prophecy for millions of American Protestants, has a more recent and more traceable origin. Its main vehicle was this annotated Bible. One line of scholarship argues that before Scofield the framework was "substantially absent" from American Protestant tradition, and that afterward it became a mainstream evangelical framework. Over the following century, on this argument, it produced a political constituency of roughly 30 to 40 million Christian Zionists, which supported the Zionist project in America before American Jewish support consolidated. [cite:wiki_dispensation_theology] That is a strong claim. The record supports parts of it more firmly than others, and this section sets out which parts are which.

The ideas did not begin with Scofield. The earlier volume of this library traces [scene:bc_s05|the Christian restorationists] who came before him. The more immediate source was John Nelson Darby (1800–1882), an Anglo-Irish minister who founded the Plymouth Brethren and developed dispensationalist premillennialism in the 1830s. Darby made at least five journeys to North America between 1862 and 1877 and spread the framework among American Protestants decades before Scofield's Bible existed. [cite:ts3_wiki_darby] That qualifies the claim of absence, and the record goes further: the framework was not absent from America before 1909. In 1878 the Niagara Bible Conference's creed looked for Christ's personal return "when Israel shall be restored to their own land", the first of a series of national prophetic conferences met in New York the same year, and the Bible institutes founded from the 1880s taught the new premillennialism almost without exception. [cite:ts3_ak_niagara] [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] What it lacked was a place in the mainstream. According to the research, standard nineteenth-century American Protestantism was largely amillennialist or postmillennialist, and did not treat the Church as a separate dispensation from Israel; the premillennial Bible-conference movement was a growing minority within it. Nor did Darby himself make a Jewish return a precondition of Christ's return: his rapture could come at any moment, and the restoration of Israel belonged to the events that followed it. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] [cite:ts3_darby_hopes10]

The man who carried Darby's framework into the American mainstream had an unusual biography for the purpose. Cyrus Scofield was born in Michigan in 1843 and was staying with relatives in Tennessee when the Civil War began. He enlisted in the Confederate Army in 1861 and was discharged in September 1862 as a Michigan-born alien; ordered back to camp, he crossed to Union lines and took the federal oath. In 1873 President Ulysses S. Grant appointed him United States Attorney for Kansas. He held the post for about six months and, in the Justice Department's words, "was forced to resign" over "questionable financial transactions". In October 1878 he was jailed in St. Louis on forgery charges and held awaiting trial for much of a year; on 6 November 1879 the prosecution dropped the charges by nolle prosequi, and he was never convicted or sentenced. In these years he abandoned his first wife and their daughters, and she divorced him for desertion in 1883; it was his only divorce. He began pastoral work in Dallas in 1882 and was ordained a Congregationalist minister in October 1883, without formal seminary training. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_doj_ks] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] He was not a scholar of Hebrew or Greek. Between 1901 and 1907 he wrote the annotations. He died in 1921, and the book stayed in print after him. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] [cite:wiki_dispensation_theology] The full record, and the rumours that have grown around it, are in [scene:ts4_record|The Theology Shield: Scofield's record].

The most cited critical biography is Joseph M. Canfield's The Incredible Scofield and His Book (1988), a hostile account; the legal record above rests on later work with court and newspaper sources, which shows no conviction. [cite:ts4_rushing] Canfield is also the origin of a widely repeated claim: that Samuel Untermyer, a New York lawyer who later became a prominent Zionist, stood behind Scofield. It is not a documented association. Scofield and Untermyer were both members of New York's Lotos Club, but Scofield's proposers were other men, no record shows the two ever met, and Canfield introduced Untermyer with the words "we assume". [cite:ts4_sfiles] The backers Scofield's contemporaries named were businessmen, among them Alwyn Ball Jr. and John T. Pirie, and a 2025 fact-check rated the later claim that the Rothschilds funded the Bible false. [cite:ts4_cyf] The story's shape, Jewish money steering Christian belief, is an old antisemitic one, and it is examined, with its chain of sources, in [scene:ts4_rumours|The Theology Shield: the rumours tested]. Even the documented backers are no evidence of who caused the book's success or wrote its theology. The theology came largely from Darby, and Scofield's work would have found some readers in any case. The research's own account of what produced the book's scale points elsewhere: Oxford's distribution, and what it calls the funding architecture that put the Bible "into every seminary, Sunday school, and pulpit in the American South and Midwest." The material does not say how much the backers gave or how their support was arranged. The biographical record is also no argument against the theology. Scofield's personal history and the framework's later influence are separate facts, each to be checked on its own terms.

The book's form did as much work as its content. Each page carried the King James Version, the standard English Protestant translation of 1611, at the top. Scofield's notes filled a substantial part of the bottom. A reader did not open a Bible and then consult a separate commentary. The commentary was already in place on the page, printed under Oxford's imprint and bound in the same covers as the text. According to the research, the notes did three things. First, they divided biblical history into seven "dispensations," periods in which God deals with humanity in different ways. Second, they introduced a pre-tribulation rapture, the belief that the faithful will be taken up before a time of catastrophe. The research calls this a modern doctrine that is not found in the biblical text. It dates its origin once to the eighteenth century and elsewhere to Darby in the 1830s. Third, on the research's account, they presented the political return of Jews to Palestine as a prerequisite for the Second Coming of Christ. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] The notes themselves do not put it that way. Scofield's note on Deuteronomy 30:3 sets out Israel's future in order, and "The return of the Lord" comes before "Restoration to the land" and "National conversion". [cite:ts5_sac_deut30] What the notes did was write a future national restoration to the land into the prophetic scheme that ordinary readers met on the page. Scofield had systematized Darby's framework and put it into the vocabulary of American Protestants. The decisive step was placing it in the margins of the Bible ordinary readers already used.

The research describes the effect of that placement as cumulative. Over years of daily reading, text and note merged in the reader's memory, until Scofield's reading became simply "what the Bible says." A claim is hard to examine if the reader never registers it as a separate claim. The label on the book stayed the same, the Bible, while what the reader received under that label now included one man's interpretation. The Reference Bible sold millions of copies through the twentieth century. On the research's account, a mid-century American evangelical who studied the Bible seriously was likely to meet Scofield's notes as the frame for reading it. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] A revised edition followed in 1917. It is often said to have added references to the Balfour Declaration, issued that November, but no source for this has been found, and the 1917 notes checked for this library contain no such reference; they still describe Israel as "now in the third dispersion". [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] [cite:ts1_sac_gen15]

Oxford's part is the step most easily misread. Oxford University Press is one of the two oldest and most prestigious academic publishers in the English-speaking world; Cambridge University Press is the other. [cite:wiki_oxford_university_press] Its name gave a marginal framework an authority it could not have earned on its content alone. A self-published set of the same notes would probably have reached a small readership. Under Oxford's imprint, bound into the scriptural text, it reached millions. The research calls this a transfer of legitimacy, not a conspiracy, and the Press's governance supports that reading. Oxford University Press has never been privately owned. It is a department of the University of Oxford. Since the seventeenth century it has been governed by the Delegates of the Press, 15 sitting academics appointed by the university's Vice-Chancellor, who met fortnightly to approve every title. There was no owner or publishing family whose interests could explain the decision, and no single person positioned to ask why a new theological framework should be bound into scripture. The book went through the same committee process as any other title. Because the underlying text was technically just the King James Version with added footnotes, no special theological review was triggered. [cite:wiki_oxford_university_press] The record shows a gap in review. It does not show that anyone used that gap deliberately, and it does not show any promotional strategy by the Press. The Press did not set out to shape American policy in the Middle East, but its imprint gave the notes an authority its editors had not intended to confer. The Press has never withdrawn the book. Later editions, the New Scofield of 1967 and the Scofield Study Bible III of 2002, were revised but kept the core dispensationalist framework. The research counts 117 years of continuous publication.

The research then sets out what the doctrines meant politically, as later Christian Zionist teaching drew them out. Two of the verses are ancient. Genesis 12:3 reads "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse," and Genesis 15:18 gives the land promise. The research's argument concerns how Scofield's framework applied them to a modern state.

On the research's reading, none of these doctrines had been part of mainstream American Protestant theology before Scofield placed them there. The research summarizes the change this way: the framework was standard by 1950 and taken for granted by 2000. It also argues that the framework leaves no theological role for the people already living in Palestine. Palestinian Christians, members of a community older than most European churches, become an anomaly. Palestinian Muslims become obstacles to the fulfillment of prophecy. These are arguments about the logic of a doctrine, and they should be read as arguments. They are not a census of what each believer holds.

The research also makes a theological critique, and it is presented here as one side of a dispute. Evangelical Protestantism teaches salvation through Christ alone. Scofield's scheme runs a separate track for national Israel, in which an ethnic nation and a literal grant of land carry weight of their own in the history of salvation, alongside the work of Christ. The sequence the research reads in the notes runs as follows. Israel is dispersed. Israel is regathered, in unbelief. The regathered nation passes through the Tribulation. Only then does Israel turn to Christ. The Second Coming follows, Christ establishes a millennial kingdom, and Israel stands at its center. Scofield's own summary at Deuteronomy 30:3 orders the end differently, placing the Lord's return before the restoration to the land and the national conversion. [cite:ts5_sac_deut30] The critique fixes on the fourth step. In a tradition of salvation by grace, it asks, why must a people be regathered in unbelief and pass through catastrophe before conversion? On this reading, the notes never reconcile the two tracks; they simply print them on the same page. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] [scene:s04fa|The Uganda counterfactual] tests the same sequence against a different geography. The material does not give the replies of dispensationalist theologians to this critique. A reader should treat it as a contested theological argument, not a settled finding.

A separate passage is not history at all, and is labeled here as interpretation. One symbolic reading, put forward in this library's opening volume, holds that the confusion dissolves if "Israel" is read not as land but as IS-RA-EL, a "consciousness architecture." In that reading IS stands for Isis, the receptive or lunar principle, RA for the solar or radiant principle, and EL for the unifying divine force. Of the three, only EL is real Hebrew etymology. On this reading "Israel" names a spiritual condition rather than a nation, and Scofield's notes performed a literalizing move, turning a symbol into a flag, a border and an ethnic deed. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] This is offered as a key for thinking, not a documented claim. The documentary case stands without it.

What followed belongs to later volumes and is summarized here only in outline. Dallas Theological Seminary, founded in 1924, became an institutional home for training pastors in the framework. Between the 1920s and the 1960s, according to the research, Scofield's theology became standard in Southern Baptist and other evangelical denominations and in Bible colleges of the South and Midwest. Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), the best-selling nonfiction book of the 1970s, carried it to a mass readership. In 1979 Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority. Tim LaHaye and Jerry Jenkins's Left Behind novels, published from 1995 to 2007, had sold over 50 million copies by one count and some 80 million by another at LaHaye's death in 2016. [cite:ts7_cp_lahaye] [cite:ts7_sa_lahaye] In 2006 John Hagee, pastor of Cornerstone Church in San Antonio, published Jerusalem Countdown and founded Christians United for Israel (CUFI). [cite:hagee_jerusalem_countdown] CUFI claims more than 10 million members, a self-reported figure. It holds an annual Washington Summit. [cite:cufi_org] Membership claims of this kind cover a wide range of engagement and do not mean that every member holds the same views. The alliance between these organizations and Israeli leaders is told in [scene:bwm_src_s15|the Christian Zionist network].

The size of the constituency rests on survey figures, and they should be stated exactly. The research cites "Pew 2019" figures (42 percent of white evangelicals against 27 percent of American Jews, and 75 to 80 percent of white evangelicals backing Israel as a biblical requirement) for which no 2019 survey has been traced; they are not used here. The documented figures are these. In a Pew Research Center survey published on 3 October 2013, 82 percent of white evangelical Protestants said God gave the land of Israel to the Jewish people, against 40 percent of American Jews. [cite:ts1_pew_2013] In a LifeWay Research poll of 2,002 Americans with evangelical beliefs in September 2017, 80 percent said Israel's founding in 1948 fulfilled biblical prophecy, but only 23 percent favoured a treaty giving the Palestinians a state, 31 percent opposed one and 46 percent were unsure. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] In Pew's survey of May 2026, white evangelical Protestants were the only religious group in which a majority, 57 percent, held a favourable view of the Israeli government. [cite:ts11_pew_2026] The figure of 30 to 40 million Christian Zionist voters is a commonly cited estimate, not derived from any of these surveys. [cite:wiki_dispensation_theology] It is not a count, and the range is wide.

Two limits keep the account honest. First, nothing in it was hidden. Scofield published openly, Oxford's decisions were public, and Christian Zionist organizations argue their positions in public. To read the chain as a conspiracy would be a category error. Scofield published in 1909, the Balfour Declaration came in 1917, and the state was declared in 1948. He was one factor among many, and nothing here claims that he or Oxford brought the State of Israel about. The research does use the word "manufactured" for the constituency. What the documents support is narrower: a publishing event put a specific framework into wide circulation, and institutions carried it forward for decades.

Second, this is a dispute within Christianity, not a case against Christianity. Mainline Protestant denominations, including the United Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian (PC-USA), Evangelical Lutheran and United Church of Christ churches, largely do not embrace Christian Zionism. Roman Catholic tradition does not endorse it. The research describes Orthodox tradition as rejecting it explicitly in one passage, and speaks of "most Orthodox tradition" in another. In 2006 the heads of four Jerusalem churches signed the Jerusalem Declaration on Christian Zionism, which calls it a "false teaching that corrupts the biblical message of love, justice, and reconciliation", and in 2009 Palestinian Christian leaders from across denominations issued the Kairos Palestine document. [cite:ts1_wiki_jerdecl] The research names the Palestinian Christian Sami Awad, the mainline Protestant scholar Gary Burge and the evangelical Shane Claiborne as public figures whose positions show that the framework can be contested inside the tradition. They show that holding it is not required of Christians. The Christians who reject Scofield's framework do so on grounds within their own traditions.

The record establishes the book, its publisher, its author's history, its notes and their place on the page, and the later institutions that carried the framework. It leaves open how far the Reference Bible itself, as distinct from Darby's earlier preaching, the Bible colleges and later popular writers, caused American Christian support for Zionism. It does not show the size or terms of the money behind the annotations. It also does not show what Oxford's Delegates discussed when they approved the book. The constituency figures are survey estimates. The research's account of later American policy, which it partly traces to this constituency, is examined in later volumes against the full record of who decided what.

sections.h: Who Bought the Land, From Whom, and at What Cost
sections.html:
The Palestine Office and its land company existed to buy land, and that land had owners and occupants. A common account holds that the British government sold Palestinian land to outside Zionist buyers, and that it did so with little scrutiny and little resistance. Almost every part of that sentence fails against the documents. The land was bought in private transactions, overwhelmingly from absentee landowners who had acquired large estates under Ottoman rule. The British, when they came, regulated the process rather than selling into it. And resistance was there from the first large purchase: an Ottoman governor tried to block it in 1910, and two decades later tenants fought an eviction through the courts for years. The mechanism that did the work was assembled before 1917, and its first test came in the Jezreel Valley.

The chain of ownership began before Zionism existed as an organized movement. In 1872 the Ottoman government itself sold the Jezreel Valley, Marj ibn Amir, to the Sursock family of Beirut, wealthy Greek Orthodox Christians.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] From that moment the valley was no longer, in any sense, land the government held; it was the private estate of a family that lived in another city. Between 1901 and 1925, and mainly in the 1920s, the family sold roughly 60,000 to 75,000 dunams to Zionist purchasing organizations, for a fraction of the land's later value. The Sursock Purchases alone represent approximately 22 percent of all Jewish land acquired in Palestine through 1948, and 58 percent of all land bought specifically from absentee landlords.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:sursockhouse_rothschild_purchases] The chain ran through three parties and contained no government sale to Zionist buyers: the Ottoman state sold to a Beirut family, and the family later sold to Zionist purchasers.

That last step is the hinge of the whole mechanism. Ottoman property law recognized two main categories of land. Mulk was true private freehold. Miri was state land held on a kind of lease, but treated in practice as owned by whoever held the registered rights to it. Most of the agricultural land that tenant farmers worked fell into the miri category, and the registered rights belonged to the landlord, even when the landlord had never once worked the land himself. Families who had cultivated the same fields for generations under hereditary arrangements, paying tithes to absentee owners like the Sursocks, typically held no registered title at all. When the landlord sold, the tenant had no ownership claim to assert.[cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine] [cite:israelfactcheck_ottoman_land_laws] [cite:wiki_jewish_land_purchase_full] The sale was lawful, and so was the eviction that followed; under the law of the time they were the same transaction. Nothing about this was a hidden device. It was a documented feature of Ottoman land tenure that predated Zionist land purchase entirely, and the record does not show that it was created for that purpose. What the record shows is that it was used, extensively, once purchase began on a large scale.

It would be wrong, though, to say that no law stood in the way. Starting in 1881–82 the Ottoman government issued a restriction specific to Palestine: foreign Jews could settle anywhere else in the empire, but not there. By March 1883 only Ottoman Jewish citizens could buy land in Palestine at all; foreign citizens were barred outright. In 1892 Sultan Abdul Hamid II went further, requiring imperial approval even for Ottoman Jewish citizens to buy.[cite:israelfactcheck_ottoman_land_laws] [cite:wiki_jewish_land_purchase_full] [cite:state_gov_1892_naturalization]

The Ottoman authorities explained their reasoning to foreign diplomats, and the explanation survives in American correspondence from the 1890s. American diplomats reported the Ottoman position that individual visitors of any background were welcome, but that the government "does not regard it to its interest to have too large a number of any race or nationality established there." What it opposed was organized, large-scale colonization aimed at a concentrated territorial presence.[cite:state_gov_1892_naturalization] That distinction, between individual presence, which was tolerated, and organized mass settlement toward territorial concentration, which was resisted, was the government's own. It was also an exact description of what Herzl's movement had been organized to achieve.

The restrictions were evaded by three documented routes. First, Ottoman Jewish citizens, who were still permitted to buy, purchased land and later transferred it to Zionist organizations. Second, Jews holding British, French or German passports could sometimes invoke the capitulations, the extraterritorial privileges that European powers had negotiated with the Ottoman Empire, and claim consular protection that Ottoman domestic law could not easily override. Third, and most directly documented, United States State Department correspondence from the 1890s records Russian Jewish emigrants who traveled to America, completed naturalization, and returned to Palestine as American citizens in order to claim American consular protection for residence and land purchase. One named case, that of Simon Ben Nachman Lowenstein, was argued over directly between American and Ottoman diplomats.[cite:state_gov_1892_naturalization] [cite:wiki_jewish_land_purchase_full]

Scholars who have examined the period agree that the restrictions "created real obstacles without constituting an absolute prohibition," and the totals bear that out. After roughly four decades of organized purchasing against these laws, Jewish-held land in Palestine in 1918 came to approximately 418,000 dunams, around 2 percent of the territory.[cite:israelfactcheck_ottoman_land_laws] [cite:wiki_jewish_land_purchase_full] The law did not stop the process. It slowed it considerably.

Three named organizations did the buying and holding, each with its own task. The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, was the holding body: land went in and, by design, never came back out, held as inalienable Jewish national property. The negotiating was done for the Palestine Land Development Company by Yehoshua Hankin, who personally negotiated the Sursock deal and most of the major Jezreel Valley acquisitions. The third, the Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, or PICA, was founded in 1924 by Baron Edmond de Rothschild, a man who had opposed Herzl personally; it ran a separate, parallel operation on Rothschild money and became the single largest Jewish landowner in Palestine.[cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]

Hankin was not an anonymous institutional process but a named individual at the center of the whole mechanism. His working relationship with the Sursock family dated to 1891, and in 1932 he became head of the land development company.[cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin] The point of naming him and the companies is not to allege illegality, since the purchases were lawful under the property law of the time, but to document who did the buying and how.

The answer to a reader's obvious question, how the buyers knew where to buy, is bureaucratic. In 1907 the Zionist Organization sent Arthur Ruppin, a German-trained lawyer and economist, to make a pilot study of colonization in Palestine. In 1908 he opened the Palestine Office in Jaffa, and the same year, by this account, founded with Otto Warburg the Palestine Land Development Company as its operational purchasing arm; other sources date the company to 1909, a discrepancy taken up with the office's founding in [scene:s04g|the Palestine Office and its land company]. Ruppin identified the strategic importance of the Jezreel Valley as early as 1907, years before the large Sursock sales closed.[cite:wiki_arthur_ruppin] His office coordinated directly with the Jewish National Fund, negotiated with Ottoman and later British authorities on behalf of Jewish immigrants, and, through the land company, handled the surveying, valuing and acquisition of land before settlers arrived. It turned land purchase from an individual pursuit into a coordinated institutional program, and Ruppin became known as "the father of Jewish settlement in Palestine."[cite:wiki_arthur_ruppin]

The same documented record contains a second fact about Ruppin, and it has to be stated with equal precision. His Wikipedia biography says that early in his career he "accepted the crude racial views of his age, including the idea that Jews were an inferior race," and that he later "believed that realization of Zionism required 'racial purity' of Jews and was influenced by works of antisemitic thinkers, including some Nazis." A peer-reviewed article in History of European Ideas examines these views at length. Haaretz, in its own retrospective, states plainly: "Arthur Ruppin believed that the realization of Zionism demanded 'racial purity' among the Jews." He is also documented as holding Ashkenazi Jews to be racially superior to Sephardi and Yemenite Jews, a view that, according to the same record, shaped in practice whom his office prioritized for settlement.[cite:wiki_arthur_ruppin] [cite:haaretz_ruppin_retrospective] [cite:tandfonline_ruppin_weltanschauung] Three independent kinds of source, an encyclopedia entry, peer-reviewed scholarship and the mainstream Israeli press, agree on this. The finding is about one individual who held real operational authority over settlement and land selection. It does not show that everyone involved in Zionist settlement shared his views, or that the purchase program as a whole was organized around them. Both facts about Ruppin, the institutional achievement and the racial ideology, are part of the accurate account; neither cancels the other.

The first large purchase in the valley shows the mechanism working, and shows that it was contested from the start. Ruppin recalled, in a memoir written in May 1929, that in February 1910 Hankin concluded an agreement for 9,500 dunams at Fule, al-Ful, the site that became Merhavia. The Jewish National Fund took over 3,500 dunams and the land company the rest.[cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] The seller was Elias Sursock, of the same Beirut family; one account describes the land as about 2,500 acres.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] Disputes over evicted tenant farmers followed this first significant acquisition, though the sources used here give no count of the tenants concerned.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases]

Ruppin's own account records the opposition. The Turkish government, he wrote, refused to authorize the sale, and "the Governor in Nazareth, a rabid anti-Zionist," declared that he would fight it. Permission was finally obtained through Hankin's friends in Constantinople.[cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] The governor, according to the biographical record, was Shukri al-Asali, district governor (qaimaqam) of Nazareth from 1910, who tried and failed to stop the sale.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] He did not drop the matter. In 1911 he resigned to win a by-election to the Ottoman parliament for Damascus, and there he argued that Jewish settlers held Ottoman citizenship alongside foreign citizenship and were taking control of rural villages. He sat until April 1912.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] His argument about dual citizenship can be read as describing, from the other side, the evasion routes the American consuls had been documenting since the 1890s. On 6 May 1916, by order of Jamal Pasha, al-Asali was hanged in Marjeh Square in Damascus with a group of Arab nationalists, a wartime story told with [scene:rd1_wwi|Palestine at war], where the dating of those executions is also discussed.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki]

Ruppin's memoir also gives the long arc of prices and quantities, and the figures show how the valley moved from a single deal to a program. Hankin, he wrote, had first reached agreement as early as 1891 for 160,000 dunams at 15 francs a dunam. In 1920 about 70,000 dunams were bought at £3 a dunam for unirrigated land and £6.5 for partly irrigated land, about £300,000 in all. By 1929 about 290,000 dunams had been bought in the Emek and the Acre plain since 1910, for £970,000.[cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] Elsewhere the record gives a broader benchmark: land sold by absentee landlords to Jewish buyers went for roughly six Palestine pounds a dunam by the early Mandate period.[cite:emory_zionist_land_acquisition] That figure sits at the upper end of Ruppin's 1920 prices, and either way the scale explains why a dedicated financial system existed.

Settlers were not, in the main, buying the land out of their own savings. Individual circumstances varied, and some settlers may have used personal savings alongside institutional support, but the purchases at this scale ran through a purpose-built banking and philanthropic system. The Jewish Colonial Trust, founded in 1899, was the Zionist Organization's overall financial instrument. Its subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Company (later the Anglo-Palestine Bank), established in 1902 with Jaffa as its base, did the work on the ground: financing land purchases directly and running a network of credit unions that gave long-term agricultural loans to Jewish colonists. Herzl put the principle in one line: "Settlers in the Land of Israel need credit rather than charity." On the philanthropic side, from 1920, Keren Hayesod raised donations specifically for settlement infrastructure.[cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust] [cite:palquest_wzo_funding] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust]

Ownership of this system and control of it were deliberately separated. The Trust was not the property of one family or a small circle of bankers: over 100,000 people had subscribed for shares by 1899, so many that London's Somerset House needed special accommodation for the shareholder register. But the first 100 shares were designated founders' shares, carrying voting rights equal to all the other shares combined at any general meeting. However widely the rest were held, the founding Zionist leadership kept permanent control.[cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] [cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust] The preparatory committee that launched the Trust was David Wolffsohn, the designer of what became the Israeli flag, Bodenheimer of Cologne, and Rudolf Schauer of Mainz. Zalman David Levontin, whom Herzl personally summoned to a director's seat in 1901 and who had sold his own earlier land holdings to Edmond de Rothschild in 1883, ran the Jaffa branch from 1903.[cite:encyclopedia_levontin] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] The pattern lasted for decades. As late as 1969 the Trust controlled 88.3 percent of the voting ordinary shares of Bank Leumi, the bank's descendant, while holding only 23.5 percent of its total share capital, a structure that lasted until the late 1980s, when it was sold to private investors.[cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust]

The system was not always planned from the center. Purchasing agents like Hankin sometimes bought land first, at personal financial risk, and secured reimbursement from the Jewish Agency or the Jewish National Fund only afterward.[cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust] [cite:emory_zionist_land_acquisition]

How the sales looked depends heavily on who is describing them, and the two surviving accounts of al-Fula should be read side by side. Ruppin's 1929 memoir presents willing sales by owners who wanted cash, through a buyer they trusted: Hankin, he wrote, "enjoyed the confidence of the Arabs." His account does not mention the tenants on the land at all.[cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] Al-Asali's record describes a sale that the Ottoman district governor tried to block and later raised in parliament as a danger to rural villages.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] Both can be true at once: the owners in Beirut may well have wanted cash and trusted Hankin, while the official responsible for the district saw the transaction as a threat to rural villages. Ruppin's case, at its strongest, is that this was ordinary commerce, lawful and voluntary on both sides of the contract. The opposing reading is that the contract had only two sides because the law left the cultivators off it.

Sellers, too, felt the pressure of their own society. Selling land to Jewish purchasers was regarded by some in the Arab community as a serious betrayal, and in at least one documented case negotiations stalled for years because the selling landowners did not want to be seen to take responsibility for evacuating the tenants.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]

No documented consultation preceded any of this. There is no documented record of a formal negotiation in which Zionist organizations sought the consent of the existing Arab political leadership, or of the Old Yishuv's leadership, before organized purchase began. Within the movement the warning had been given early: Ahad Ha'am, a committed cultural Zionist, wrote in 1891, in "Truth from the Land of Israel," that the Arab population was being treated as effectively invisible in Zionist planning, years before political Zionism was formally organized (his critique is set out with [scene:s04|the founding Congress and its critics]). What took place was land acquisition and settlement building toward a territorial and political fact, not a negotiated agreement, which is precisely why the Ottoman restrictions existed.

The Jewish communities that had lived in Palestine before organized Zionist immigration were neither uniform supporters of the purchases nor absent from them. The clearest documented window is Avraham Albert Antébi, a Sephardi Jew active in Jerusalem from 1897 to 1916. He ran the Caisse de Prêts, a low-interest loan fund that served both the Old Yishuv, the Sephardi and Ashkenazi communities already in the country, and the settlers of the New Yishuv. That role gave him working relationships with affluent Arab landowners and Ottoman officials as well as with the Zionist institutions. Research on his surviving correspondence, published in Shofar: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Jewish Studies, examines Sephardi reaction to Zionist land purchases and the Arab-Jewish tension that followed, and finds a community financially and socially entangled with every side of the transaction.[cite:shofar_antebi_sephardim] Antébi does not speak for every Old Yishuv resident; views varied by person, community and moment. What his record establishes is that some of the Jews already in Palestine watched the displacement from inside the deals themselves.

The human cost of the Sursock purchases is documented in specific figures. In the largest single group of Sursock-related purchases, 1,746 Arab farming families, 8,730 people, were evicted. Under the tenure system described above they were owed no compensation, since they held no registered title to compensate; they were paid roughly $17 a person as a voluntary goodwill settlement. Across the full span of Sursock-linked purchases, an estimated 20 to 25 villages were depopulated.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin] These are the figures for the best-documented single group, not an estimate for every transaction of the period, which varied case by case; nor does the record show that every evicted family received exactly that amount.

Most of that cost fell after 1917, and the later history is told in later volumes, but its outline belongs here because the mechanism built before the war carried it. The main Sursock sales came in 1920–25, negotiated directly with Hankin.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] Britain, as the Mandate power, enacted five separate laws between 1920 and 1940 meant to protect tenant cultivators from eviction after a sale. Analysis of the period concludes that they "failed to provide the protection that Palestinian Arabs demanded, often due to loopholes, which allowed individuals and agencies to circumvent the legislation."[cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine]

Wadi al-Hawarith became the case that tested the system. In 1929 the Jewish National Fund bought 30,800 dunams there at auction from absentee landlords, which the historian Weldon Matthews counts as the third-largest single acquisition of the Fund in the whole Mandate period. The Bedouin Palestinian tenants who lived on the land refused to leave, and the Fund began formal eviction proceedings. Awni Abd al-Hadi, a significant Palestinian national political figure, represented the residents through a multi-year court battle. The final eviction order was issued on 15 June 1933, and the response was immediate: the Istiqlal Party, the Palestine Communist Party and the Congress of Youth called strikes and issued public declarations of protest.[cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith] The case does not show that every sale met organized opposition; many proceeded with less. It shows that resistance existed, was organized, and reached formal legal representation and cross-party protest when the stakes were high enough.

In 1938 the Mandate authorities moved in the opposite direction from their tenant laws. They granted Zionist officials direct permission to copy land-registration and taxation records documenting Arab land ownership, explicitly to facilitate further Zionist acquisition.[cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine] [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] Britain was neither seller nor bystander: it first attempted regulation that failed, then took a specific, dated step of facilitation. That does not mean Britain orchestrated the purchase program from the start, or that 1938 was the whole of its policy; its immigration restrictions in the same years, the 1939 White Paper among them, cut sharply the other way. The Mandate's record on land was inconsistent rather than a single coherent policy.

The end point of the land series puts the whole mechanism in proportion. By 1947–48 total Jewish holdings came to roughly 2 million dunams, about 7 percent of Mandate Palestine's roughly 26 million dunams, of which the Jewish National Fund held approximately 936,000.[cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg] The panel below sets the 7 percent against the rest of the land; its second chart, the 1947 partition plan, belongs to a later volume. The Sursock land, around a fifth of everything acquired, was the single largest component of that total; and the restrictions, the evasions, the bank and the office that produced it were all in place before 1917.

What the record does not settle is substantial. Ruppin's memoir does not count the tenants at al-Fula, and the sources used here give no figure for them or for the price paid in 1910. The documented eviction figures, 1,746 families at about $17 a person, describe one large group of purchases, not the period as a whole, and there is no comparable count for the 418,000 dunams held by 1918. How the owners in Beirut weighed cash against the objections of officials like al-Asali survives only in the buyer's account. And how far Ruppin's racial views shaped individual settlement decisions, beyond the documented fact that they shaped his office's priorities, is not set out case by case in the record this book has.

sections.h: A Newspaper Called Palestine: The Arab Public Sphere Before 1914
sections.html:
The governor who tried to stop the al-Fula sale was not a lone voice. It is often said that "Palestinian" was an identity invented after 1948, or even after 1967. The newspapers, parliamentary records and political programs of the years before the First World War answer that claim directly. By 1914 the country had Arabic newspapers arguing about Zionism in print, elected deputies who had raised it in the Ottoman parliament, a governor who had tried to block a land sale, and a paper in Jaffa whose masthead carried the name Filastin, "Palestine." What these sources show, and what they do not, needs to be stated precisely, because the record is richer than the claim allows and more complicated than a simple reversal of it.

One early statement came from outside Palestine, in French. In 1905 Negib Azouri published Le Réveil de la nation arabe, and in it he set the Arab national awakening beside the Jewish one and wrote of the two movements: "Both these movements are destined to fight each other continually until one of them wins."[cite:rs_rd1_azouri] It was a prediction, not a program, written eight years after the Basel Congress and before any large Zionist purchase in the Jezreel Valley; but it framed the encounter as a contest between two national movements six years after Herzl had answered a Jerusalem notable's warning by writing that the existing population would be enriched by Jewish settlement (that exchange is told in [scene:rd1_arabquestion|Herzl and the Arab question]).

The same year Najib Nassar began the most sustained campaign. From 1905 he wrote against Zionism in two Arabic papers, al-Muqattam in Cairo and Lisan al-Hal in Beirut. In 1908 he founded his own paper, al-Karmil, in Haifa, appearing twice a week.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_nassar] It was the year of the Young Turk revolution. The authorities' tolerance of the new paper had limits: they closed al-Karmil for two months in June 1909. In 1910 the Ministry of Justice ordered Nassar tried on a complaint from the Jewish community alleging incitement, and the court acquitted him.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_nassar] The episode cuts in more than one direction. It shows an Arab journalist prosecuted for his writing on Zionism; it shows a complaint brought in the name of the Jewish community through the Ottoman courts; and it shows those courts declining to convict.

Nassar did not stop. In October 1911 he collected his articles as a book, Zionism: Its History, Objectives and Importance. In 1913 he called for a non-Zionist national society based in Nablus. In the summer of 1914 he urged Palestinian youth to press Arab landowners not to sell land to Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_nassar] That last appeal addressed the sellers in the mechanism described in [scene:s04j|the land purchases]: Arab landowners, many of them absentee, under a law that gave the tenants on their land no registered title.

The 1908 revolution also gave Palestine elected deputies in the Ottoman parliament. Ruhi al-Khalidi was one of three deputies elected for Jerusalem that year. In 1911, with his fellow Jerusalem deputy Sa'id al-Husayni, he raised Zionism in the Ottoman parliament, and he stressed that what he opposed was Jewish immigration, not the residence of Palestine's own Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_ruhi_wiki] The distinction closely tracked the line the Ottoman government's own restrictions had drawn since the 1880s: between Jews who were already subjects of the empire and organized settlement from abroad. In the same parliament Shukri al-Asali, now a deputy for Damascus, pressed the argument about dual citizenship and rural villages described in the previous section.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] Ruhi al-Khalidi went further than speeches. He left an unpublished manuscript, "Zionism and the Zionist Question," and died of typhoid in Istanbul in 1913, while serving as deputy to the head of parliament.[cite:rs_rd1_ruhi_wiki] The texts of the 1911 speeches, and the month in which they were given, are not established in the sources used here.

Into this setting came Filastin. It was founded in Jaffa on 15 January 1911 by Issa El-Issa and his cousin Yousef El-Issa, Arab Orthodox Christians educated in Beirut.[cite:wiki_falastin] [cite:nli_filastin_archive] It began as a twice-weekly paper, and its first cause was not Zionism at all but the dispute between the Arab Orthodox community and the Greek-led hierarchy of its church.[cite:wiki_falastin] Between 1911 and 1914 its coverage of Zionism shifted. A scholarly study of the paper documents its reporting on land purchases, immigration, violent incidents and the Zionist Congresses moving from cautious ambivalence to open hostility before the war.[cite:academia_filastin_zionism] The editors sent a copy of each issue to every village in the Jaffa district, so that the paper reached the countryside, not only readers in the town.[cite:academia_filastin_zionism] [cite:wiki_falastin]

The record also contains an event that complicates any account in which Arab politics before 1914 revolved around Zionism. The Arab Congress met in Paris on 18–23 June 1913 with 25 official delegates. It adopted ten resolutions, on Arab participation in the central government of the empire, on Arabic as an official language, and on administrative decentralization. Its resolutions did not address Zionism. Two Zionist representatives, Victor Jacobson and Sami Hochberg, attended unofficially.[cite:rs_rd1_arabcongress_wiki] The Congress's agenda was reform within the Ottoman Empire, framed in Arab rather than specifically Palestinian terms, and its silence on Zionism suggests that the subject that dominated al-Karmil and, by 1914, Filastin was not yet the first item for the wider Arab reform movement. Why the Congress left it out, and what Jacobson and Hochberg sought there, the sources used here do not say.

Filastin outlived the empire in which it was founded. Under the British Mandate it became one of the most influential Arabic dailies, known for its network of correspondents, and in 1927 Issa El-Issa helped found the Palestine Free Party. The paper appeared in Jaffa until 7 April 1948, shortly before the city fell, and later moved to Jerusalem.[cite:wiki_falastin] [cite:palquest_issa_el_issa] The National Library of Israel's Jrayed archive holds 6,692 issues, from 1911 to 1948.[cite:nli_filastin_archive]

Set against the claim that the identity was invented later, the record is plain on its central point. A paper named "Palestine," carrying a public argument about land and immigration, was printed in Jaffa from 1911, sent to the villages of its district, and preserved in Israel's own national library.[cite:nli_filastin_archive] That documents a Palestinian name in print and a Palestinian public sphere decades before 1948. The fair statement of the other side is that this public sphere operated inside larger frames: its deputies sat in the Ottoman parliament and drew the Ottoman government's own line between subjects and immigrants, and its most ambitious political gathering, in Paris, spoke as Arabs seeking reform within the empire. What the record does not settle is how widely, outside the press and the elected deputies, a distinctly Palestinian political identity was held before the war, how many people read these papers, and what weight the villagers who received Filastin gave it. The sources used here give no circulation figures. They establish the name, the argument and the people making it; they do not measure its reach.

sections.h: The American Machine: Hadassah, Brandeis and the ZOA, 1912–1918
sections.html:
While Filastin was finding readers in the villages of the Jaffa district, a different public was being organized in the United States. A familiar assumption holds that American support for Zionism became organized and significant only after 1948, or at the earliest after the Holocaust. The institutional record places its foundations three decades earlier. By 1918 the movement in the United States had a national women's organization raising money for medical work in Palestine, a Justice of the Supreme Court as its most influential advocate with direct access to the President, and a merged national political organization reporting more than 147,000 members.[cite:zoa_wiki] [cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] None of this was built in Palestine. It was domestic American institution-building, carried out years before there was a British Mandate to build under.

The first piece was built by women. On 24 February 1912 Henrietta Szold founded Hadassah in New York. Sources give the number of founding members variously, from 38 to 122; on any count it was a meeting of fewer than 130 people.[cite:ushmm_youth_aliyah] The organization moved quickly from meeting to practice. In 1913 it sent the movement's first two nurses to Palestine, to provide maternity care and to treat trachoma.[cite:ushmm_youth_aliyah]

Hadassah's significance for the architecture of the movement lies in the channel it created as much as in the clinics it funded. Most of the financial and political machinery traced elsewhere in this stage, the Jewish Colonial Trust, the Jewish National Fund and, from 1918, the ZOA's own fundraising, was built and run by men. Hadassah was a distinct American fundraising channel, financed specifically by American Jewish women and directed to medical and settlement infrastructure in Palestine. It ran alongside the male-led institutions rather than through them.[cite:hadassah_wiki] It did not operate in isolation, however: in 1918 Hadassah became one of the founding member organizations of the Zionist Organization of America, so the two channels were joined institutionally while remaining distinct in organization and purpose.[cite:zoa_wiki] [cite:hadassah_wiki]

Szold's own arc reached far beyond this period. She later directed Youth Aliyah, founded in 1933, which the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum credits with bringing more than 14,000 unaccompanied children to Palestine and Britain between 1933 and 1945.[cite:ushmm_youth_aliyah] That work belongs to a later volume. It is recorded here because it shows the scale an organization founded at a small New York meeting in 1912 would eventually reach, and with the caution that a child-rescue and resettlement operation of that size involved real hardships for the children, a fuller story than a founding-to-scale summary can tell.

The second piece was a single convert. In 1914 Louis Brandeis, who would join the United States Supreme Court in 1916, moved into active Zionist leadership after a meeting with Jacob de Haas, who had been Herzl's secretary.[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] The line from Herzl to Brandeis ran through one of Herzl's own staff. From 1914 Brandeis led the American movement, and he remained its leader until 1921.

What Brandeis brought was access. He worked with the Reverend William Blackstone on the Blackstone Memorial of 1916 to influence President Wilson. In 1917 he met Balfour, and during the drafting of the Balfour Declaration he worked as a conduit between the British government and the President.[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] His direct line to Wilson in those months is documented by multiple historians; the channel itself is not in dispute.[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] How the Declaration was drafted, and what Brandeis's part in it was, is told with [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration].

How much that access mattered is a separate question, and the answer offered most often is an assessment rather than a finding. Nahum Goldmann later argued that without Brandeis "the Balfour Declaration would probably never have been issued."[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] That is one historian's judgment about a counterfactual. It may be right, but no document can prove what Britain would have done without him, and it should be read as an argument, not as settled fact.

Why Brandeis made the turn is a third question, and it remains open. His personal motives for converting to Zionist leadership are contested among historians. Some argue that the conversion was partly career-strategic, a reading that outlets such as Mondoweiss have cited in critical treatments of his role.[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] No primary source in the record this book has definitively settles his motivation. The distinction matters for how the American story is told: that a Supreme Court Justice had direct access to a sitting President is a documented, checkable fact about influence; why he chose to spend that access on this cause is a matter of interpretation on which historians can reasonably differ.

The third piece was consolidation. In 1918 the Federation of American Zionists, Young Judaea, Hadassah and other bodies merged into the Zionist Organization of America. Brandeis became honorary president and Julian W. Mack president. The new organization reported 147,551 members in 1918.[cite:zoa_wiki]

The size of the merged organization is the figure that the summary of the movement's whole build carries for these years: in the step-by-step account of how the state was built, 1912–18 is "the American machine," made up of Hadassah, Justice Brandeis and the ZOA at 147,000.[cite:zoa_wiki] That compressed row follows directly from the documents above, and it sits between the bank and land fund of 1899–1902 and the promise and endorsement of 1917–22. Its placement makes a point the familiar account misses. The American institutions were not a response to the Balfour Declaration; they were built before it, and one of their leaders was working the channel to the President while it was drafted.

The unity of 1918 did not last. Brandeis and his adherents favored private economic investment over the Zionist Organization's model of national fundraising, and at the Cleveland convention of 1921 they split away. Louis Lipsky then became president of the ZOA.[cite:zoa_wiki] The movement's most famous American member thus lost the argument over what kind of institution it should be within three years of its founding; the dispute and its consequences belong to the next stage.

Several things remain unsettled. The number of Hadassah's founders depends on which source is counted, from 38 to 122. Brandeis's motives remain contested, and Goldmann's claim that the Declaration would probably not have been issued without him cannot be tested. The record establishes that the 1921 split concerned private investment against national fundraising, but not every argument made on either side.

sections.h: The Federal Reserve, 1913: Structure, Need and a Coincidence of Dates
sections.html:
On 23 December 1913 the Federal Reserve Act was signed into law, creating the central banking system of the United States.[cite:federalreservehistory_fed_act] The date sits in this chapter for one reason. It falls sixteen years after the First Zionist Congress at Basel and seven years before the Keren Hayesod fund existed, and an often-repeated claim holds that the two stories are one: that the Federal Reserve was founded by, or to serve, the same financial network that was funding Zionism. A history of the movement's money that said nothing about the claim would leave a silence open to misreading. This section therefore does two things. It sets out what the Federal Reserve actually was and why Congress created it, in the same plain terms this book uses for every other institution. Then it sets out what the record shows about the supposed link, and where the claim comes from.

Most Americans learn the institution's name without learning its structure, and two simple accounts compete to fill the gap. In one, the Federal Reserve is an ordinary federal agency like any other. In the other, it is a purely private bank secretly running the country. Neither matches the documents. The system created in 1913 was a deliberate hybrid. It consisted of twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks. Each was owned by the commercial banks that were its members, and those member banks were required to hold stock in their district's Reserve Bank. Each regional bank historically financed itself from its own earnings rather than from appropriations voted by Congress. Above the regional banks sat a public body, the Board, known at first as the Federal Reserve Board and later as the Board of Governors, whose members are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.[cite:eh_net_federal_reserve_system] Part of the system is owned by banks, and part of it is a presidentially appointed public authority; the two were designed to work together.

The private ownership of the regional banks and their self-financing are unusual facts, and they are stated here as plainly as the sources state them. They do not mean the system escaped public control. Presidential nomination and Senate confirmation of the Board are real mechanisms of democratic oversight. They exist alongside the private regional ownership, not instead of it.[cite:eh_net_federal_reserve_system]

Why Congress accepted so unusual a design begins with the decades before it. Between 1865 and 1913 the United States suffered at least five major financial crises. The Federal Reserve's own historical research states the pattern directly: nationwide banking panics came on average every fifteen years, each forcing financial institutions to suspend operations and each followed by a long, deep recession.[cite:federalreservehistory_jekyll_island] The underlying structural problem was an "inelastic" currency. The money supply had no mechanism to expand when demand for money rose, so severe shortages of currency arrived exactly when the economy most needed cash.[cite:history_com_fed_origins] This was a recurring failure in the system's design rather than one bad year. The five crises did not share an identical cause or identical severity, and the sources single out one of them.

The Panic of 1907 is documented as among the most severe financial crises of the era before the Federal Reserve, and as the direct, immediate trigger for its creation. With no central bank able to intervene, the nearest thing the country had to a backstop was the financier J.P. Morgan. He organized a rescue using his own money, his reputation and his private authority, and it stopped the panic from spreading further.[cite:libertystreet_panic_1907_fed] [cite:history_com_fed_origins] The question of what would happen without a central bank therefore has a documented answer: in 1907 a private citizen's fortune stood in for an institution the country did not have. The sources record that the rescue worked as a stopgap. They do not settle Morgan's motives, and this book makes no claim about them.

The plan that answered 1907 was drafted by bankers. In November 1910 Senator Nelson Aldrich gathered a party at the Jekyll Island Club, off the Georgia coast. They traveled by private rail car and used only first names to keep the meeting secret. The Federal Reserve's historians describe the party as five bankers and a former Treasury official, and they give the reason for the secrecy plainly: "the plan was written in secrecy, as the public would never approve of a banking reform bill written by bankers, much less...a central bank." The resulting Aldrich Plan gave private banks substantial control.[cite:federalreservehistory_jekyll_island]

The people at the table are named in the record, along with the institution each belonged to. Aldrich chaired the National Monetary Commission, the body whose work produced the meeting. Henry Davison was a senior partner at J.P. Morgan & Co.[cite:wiki_henry_davison] Frank Vanderlip was president of National City Bank, documented as the flagship institution of the Rockefeller banking interests.[cite:wiki_frank_vanderlip] Paul Warburg was a partner at Kuhn, Loeb & Co. Between them, these three men brought the era's three dominant banking houses to the table, each tied to his house directly by partnership or office. A. Piatt Andrew, Assistant Treasury Secretary, is described as a technical bridge, on good terms with both the Morgan and the Rockefeller spheres but employed by neither.[cite:wiki_a_piatt_andrew] Arthur Shelton was Aldrich's personal secretary, tied to Aldrich himself and with no banking connection of his own. Aldrich's own link to the Rockefeller interests went beyond politics. His daughter Abby married John D. Rockefeller Jr., which made Aldrich the younger Rockefeller's father-in-law; his grandson Nelson Rockefeller was named for him.[cite:wiki_nelson_aldrich] (The named list does not quite match the historians' summary: it holds three bankers from the great houses, a serving Treasury official and a secretary, besides Aldrich himself.)

Bankers drafting the plan for the institution that would regulate banks, at a meeting kept secret, is a genuinely unusual fact. It is not a hidden one. The Federal Reserve's own historical researchers record it and explain it. Nor was the Aldrich Plan simply handed to Congress and passed. Public reaction to it was hostile, and historians are specific about why: "what people were really upset about was the political structure of Aldrich's plan."[cite:richmondfed_jekyll_island] The objection was to how much control the plan gave private bankers.

Congress and President Wilson's administration rewrote that structure before anything became law. In the Federal Reserve Act, private banks received considerably less control than Aldrich had designed. A combination of regional independence and federal oversight replaced a more centralized model. All nationally chartered banks were required to join the system, rather than each bank choosing how far to take part.[cite:richmondfed_jekyll_island] [cite:minneapolisfed_born_of_panic] Congress accepted the final structure because it had first forced the reduction of private banking control that the public and many legislators objected to. The result did not satisfy everyone. Many private banks opposed the provisions that reduced their influence, so the Act was a genuine compromise and not a full victory for either side.[cite:minneapolisfed_born_of_panic]

That leaves the claim this section began with. It usually rests on one man. Paul Warburg, the Kuhn, Loeb partner, was really present at Jekyll Island in 1910 and served on the first Federal Reserve Board, from 1914 to 1918.[cite:wiki_paul_warburg] That is the full documented core of his role. It is a significant role in one institution's founding, and it should be stated without inflating or shrinking it. The record shows no part for him in Zionist fundraising or planning. A person can have one well-documented role in one major institution and no documented role in an entirely different one, and both facts can be stated plainly.

The record also points the other way. Paul Warburg's brother, Felix Warburg, and his father-in-law, Jacob Schiff, were prominent non-Zionists and opponents of Zionism in exactly this period. Schiff put his position on record: "I cannot for a moment concede that one can be at the same time a true American and an honest adherent of the Zionist movement." Felix Warburg held a similar, documented non-Zionist position at the same time.[cite:schiff_zionism_wiki] If the claim is that a single family network was quietly coordinating American central banking and Zionist fundraising, a public, quoted rejection of Zionism by that family's most prominent members contradicts it about as directly as the historical record can. This goes beyond the absence of a connection: it is an opposite position held inside the same family. The quotation documents the position in this period only. Views on Zionism shifted over the following decades across the wider Warburg and Schiff families, and the sources here do not claim that every member held the same view for life. Other named Jewish leaders and bodies also opposed Zionism in these years, set out in [scene:rd1_currents|Jewish positions for and against].

The institutional record was checked as well. The Federal Reserve Act created a central banking system sixteen years after Basel, and there is no documented institutional or financial link between it and the Zionist Organization or its funds: neither the Jewish Colonial Trust, nor the Jewish National Fund, nor the Keren Hayesod, which did not yet exist.[cite:federalreservehistory_fed_act] A search of the founding documents of the Trust, the Fund and the Federal Reserve shows no connection between them. The absence is itself a finding. It is the result of a search that was carried out, not a gap left by one that was not. It does not mean that no individual moved in both worlds; Paul Warburg's case shows exactly how far such overlap went in a small early-twentieth-century financial world. Two events sixteen years apart, in different countries, sharing a few individuals is not the same as the two events being connected.

The claim has a traceable origin. The specific assertion of a connection between the Federal Reserve and Zionism goes back to Eustace Mullins's tract The Federal Reserve Conspiracy, promoted from the 1950s and recycled since by extremist groups and figures. Mainstream fact-checking and civil-rights research organizations classify "Jewish control of the Federal Reserve" as a documented antisemitic myth, not a contested historical question.[cite:adl_fed_myth] Naming the source explains where the claim came from as well as answering it. It does not mean that everyone who repeats some version of the claim knows or endorses its origin; myths travel independently of their sources. Tested against the documents, the claim fails on each point. The timing is a coincidence. The one documented individual link runs to a man whose own family publicly opposed Zionism. The institutional records show no tie.

A few limits remain. The sources document that Morgan's 1907 rescue happened and worked; they do not establish his motives. They document the Warburg and Schiff positions in this period, not across the families' whole later history. And this section cannot dispose of every version of the claim that circulates. What it offers is the specific, checkable facts about the Federal Reserve's founding and the specific origin of the myth, so that any other version can be tested against the same documents.[cite:federalreservehistory_fed_act]

sections.h: Palestine at War, 1914–1917
sections.html:
The war reached Palestine before it reached its battlefields. When the Ottoman Empire entered the First World War, the country was still a set of Ottoman districts, centered on the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem.[cite:rs_rd1_jerusalemstory] Its people were Ottoman subjects, but not all of them. A large share of the Jewish community held foreign nationality. The Ottoman register of 1914–15 recorded 38,754 Jews, apparently counting only Ottoman subjects, while other estimates run as high as 94,000; the counting dispute is set out in the opening section of this stage. In wartime, foreign nationality turned from a bureaucratic detail into a matter of who could stay. Over the next three years Palestine's people, Arab and Jewish, lived through expulsion, a plague of locusts, famine in the wider region, the hanging of Arab nationalists and the emptying of Jaffa. This section tells that story to the end of 1917.

The first blow fell on the Jews of Jaffa who held Russian citizenship. In December 1914 up to 6,000 Russian citizens, all of them Jewish, were expelled from the city, according to a reference account of the period.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] Many went to Egypt. Contemporary reports in the New York Times, cited in a 2021 opinion column, put some 7,000 Jewish refugees from Palestine in British-held Alexandria by the end of January 1915.[cite:rs_rd1_bulut] Those figures come to us through a newspaper column rather than an archive, and they are given here as reported.

In 1915 the Ottoman authorities went further. Non-citizens, Jews included, were required to take Ottoman citizenship or leave.[cite:rs_rd1_yishuv_wwi] The order forced a choice on every immigrant who had kept a foreign nationality. Some of those who left became soldiers. In the same year the British Army formed the Zion Mule Corps from Jews exiled to Egypt, and it served at Gallipoli; that story, and the wider record of Jewish service to Britain, is told in [scene:ww_s01|Services rendered to Britain].[cite:rs_rd1_yishuv_wwi] [cite:algemeiner_jewish_legion]

Then came the locusts. From March to October 1915 swarms covered Palestine, Mount Lebanon and Syria. The historian Zachary Foster estimates that they cut the 1915 winter harvest of wheat and barley by 10 to 15 percent, and destroyed between 60 and 100 percent of the summer and autumn fruit and vegetables.[cite:rs_rd1_locust_wiki] The Ottoman response was a labor quota. Every male aged 15 to 60 in the cities had to collect 20 kilograms of locust eggs or pay a fine of £4.40. By 21 November 1915, the New York Times reported, 800 people had paid the fine rather than collect the eggs.[cite:rs_rd1_locust_wiki]

The locusts struck a region already under strain, and in Greater Syria, the wider territory of which Palestine was a part, the result was famine. The American University of Beirut's documentary exhibit names four causes acting together. The Allies blockaded the eastern Mediterranean in 1915. There was drought. There were the locusts. And the exhibit names Ottoman paper money as a fourth cause.[cite:rs_rd1_aub_famine] The mortality figures given are for Mount Lebanon, and they are disputed. The AUB exhibit says Mount Lebanon lost 20 to 30 percent of its population.[cite:rs_rd1_aub_famine] A higher figure, nearly half of the inhabitants of the Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate, appears in the reference account of the locust plague, but without a source.[cite:rs_rd1_locust_wiki] The sourced range is the one to rely on. For Palestine itself the record used in this book gives no reliable death toll from the famine, and none is offered here.

The war also brought the state's hand down on Arab nationalists. On Jamal Pasha's orders a group of them was hanged in Marjeh Square in Damascus. One was Shukri al-Asali, the former governor of Nazareth who had tried to stop the al-Fula land sale of 1910 and had then argued against Zionist settlement in the Ottoman parliament; his part in that sale is told with [scene:s04j|the land mechanism].[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] The sources on his life date his execution to 6 May 1916.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] The American University of Beirut's exhibit, however, dates the hangings in Damascus and Beirut to 1915.[cite:rs_rd1_aub_famine] The two accounts differ by a year, and the evidence gathered does not resolve the difference. Either way, an Ottoman official who had opposed a Zionist land purchase in public was put to death by the same Ottoman state, as one of a group of Arab nationalists.

In the spring of 1917 the war emptied Jaffa. On 28 March 1917 Jamal Pasha ordered the evacuation of Jaffa. The deportation took place on 6 April 1917.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] How many people were driven out is disputed, and three figures circulate. One estimate puts those displaced at about 10,000, of whom 8,000 were Jews. Another puts the number evacuated from Tel Aviv, the new Jewish neighborhood beside Jaffa, at up to 16,000.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] A United States consular report of 1917 gave 8,000 Jews evicted.[cite:rs_rd1_bulut] The figures measure different things: the whole city or only its Jewish residents, Jaffa or Tel Aviv. The lower Jewish figures agree with each other, and the highest figure applies only to Tel Aviv.

The deportation did not fall equally. The order covered the city, but Jaffa's Muslim residents were able to return soon afterwards, while the Jewish deportees could not return until the summer of 1918.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] About 1,500 people are thought to have died as a result of the deportation, though the deaths were not properly recorded.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] Reports reached the outside world within weeks. A US consular report, published in the New York Times on 3 June 1917, described looting and killings of deportees; the report survives in that newspaper and is cited in the 2021 column.[cite:rs_rd1_bulut] The evidence here is a contemporary diplomatic report as carried by the press, not a court record, and no primary text of Jamal Pasha's orders is among the sources used here.

By the end of the war the Jewish community of Palestine was smaller than in 1914. How much smaller is a real dispute between serious sources. The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question holds that about a third of the Jewish population left Palestine during 1914–18.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_chron] The demographer Justin McCarthy, as summarized by Roger Owen, argues that the fall was much less than the commonly cited quarter, because many of those who fled to Alexandria came back.[cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen] Both sides have evidence. The expulsions of 1914–15 and the deportation of 1917 were real and large. Return was also real: the Jaffa deportees were allowed back in the summer of 1918, and McCarthy's case rests on returns from Alexandria.
