The "Jordan is Palestine" argument treats the same separation as a settlement already made: the Arabs of the Mandate received the larger share in 1921–23, so the Palestinian question was answered then. The historian Bernard Wasserstein has documented that, in later ideological use, the separation came to be called "the myth of Palestine's first partition." [cite:wiki_borders_of_israel] His phrase does not deny the administrative fact, which is documented. It flags the gap between that fact and the political conclusion later drawn from it.

The strongest form of the case for the claim rests on the documents of 1921–23: the national-home provisions were written for the whole Mandate, Article 25 withdrew them east of the river, and Arab rule was established there. The strongest form of the opposing case rests on the documents of 1988 and after: whatever weight the 1921 separation carries, a state's sovereign status is not conferred by outside argument, and Jordan's own government has formally, explicitly and repeatedly rejected the role of Palestinian state since 1988, most recently in its king's words. That Jordanian monarchs once made the claim themselves complicates any reading of it as a one-sided talking point. That Jordan then withdrew it, formally, is the documented end point of that history.

What the record leaves open. The material here does not say why Britain chose 1921 for the Article 25 formula, or record the reactions of Transjordan's own population to the memorandum. It does not set out the full reasoning behind Jordan's 1988 timing. The administrative history of 1921–23 is settled; its political meaning has been asserted and rejected by different parties at different times for different reasons, and it remains contested.

sections.h: The Churchill White Paper of 1922: The First Narrowing
sections.html:
The policy paper that marked the second stage of that separation said a good deal more. On 3 June 1922 the Colonial Secretary, Winston Churchill, published a command paper titled "Palestine: Correspondence with the Palestine Arab Delegation and the Zionist Organisation." Historians call it the Churchill White Paper. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] It was made up of nine documents, with Churchill's own memorandum as an enclosure, and it was an official British clarification of what the Balfour Declaration meant, put on the record five years after the declaration itself. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] It appeared seven weeks before the League Council's conditional approval of the Mandate text in July 1922.

Why 1922. The paper was drafted partly in response to the Jaffa riots of May 1921, in which dozens were killed on both sides. [cite:wiki_jaffa_riots_1921] Those riots pushed Britain toward its first restatement of policy; their course and Britain's inquiry into them are told in [scene:ri_s01|the first riots and the first inquiries]. [cite:wiki_jaffa_riots_1921] A major narrowing of policy thus came within roughly a year of serious violence. The record does not show that the riots were the only cause, and Britain's wider strategic and administrative concerns were almost certainly in play as well.

What the paper said. The White Paper reaffirmed the Balfour Declaration. In the same breath it set limits on what the declaration meant. Palestine, it insisted, was not intended to become "as Jewish as England is English." [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] That sentence did not withdraw the promise of a national home. It narrowed what the promise could be taken to mean, and it did so in Britain's own official words.

The second limit concerned immigration. The White Paper laid down the principle that Jewish immigration should be limited by the country's economic capacity to absorb new arrivals. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] This was the first formal mechanism under the Mandate for limiting immigration, seventeen years before the 1939 White Paper imposed a harder, fixed numerical ceiling. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] The 1922 rule was a standard rather than a number. It tied the flow of immigrants to an economic judgment about what the country could take. How the rule had been foreshadowed in Herbert Samuel's statements of 1921, and how immigration actually moved under it in the early 1920s, belongs to the story of the Third Aliyah.

The third limit was territorial. The White Paper is associated with the separation of Transjordan, the land east of the Jordan River and roughly three-quarters of the Mandate's total area, from the part of the Mandate open to Jewish settlement. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] It was one stage of that separation, not the whole of it. Abdullah had been installed in Transjordan in March 1921; the League approved the memorandum that formally excluded the national-home provisions on 16 September 1922; and the separation was complete by 1923. [cite:w_cairo1921] [cite:rs_md_transjordan] [cite:wiki_borders_of_israel] Those stages, and the arguments later built on them, are traced in [scene:s06a2|the separation of Transjordan]. The separation was the largest territorial reduction in the whole pre-1948 history, and it came by administrative decision, not by war and not through negotiation with the Zionist leadership. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922]

How it was received. The paper's own title shows that it was framed as an answer to two parties at once, the Palestine Arab Delegation and the Zionist Organization. The Arab Delegation, then in London, had demanded a "national independent Government" and refused the Balfour Declaration as a basis for discussion; the White Paper gave it neither, and its exchanges with the Colonial Office are set out in the account of the Palestinian national movement. [cite:rs_mca_cmd1700] The Zionist leadership accepted the paper without treating it as a triumph, and Chaim Weizmann and others believed the absorptive-capacity principle could still allow a Jewish majority to be built; that acceptance, and the Arab refusal of the 1922 constitution, are treated in [scene:rd2_council|the Legislative Council]. [cite:rs_lc_cojs_whitepaper] Acceptance did not mean agreement. The record of the Mandate years shows continuing tension between the Zionist Organization and Britain over exactly this kind of step-by-step retreat, and real Zionist objection to the territorial decision, even though it was never reversed. The sharpest objection came from Jabotinsky, who built the Revisionist movement in part on rejecting the separation of Transjordan. [cite:sunnafiles_jordan]

What happened to immigration anyway. The policy limited growth; it did not stop it. By the figures given in one account of the White Paper, the Jewish population of Palestine grew under the absorptive-capacity rule from about 80,000 in 1922 to roughly 380,000 by 1936, nearly a fivefold increase in fourteen years. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] The 80,000 is a round estimate; the British census of October 1922 counted 83,794 Jews. [cite:rs_ta_report1922] The same pattern of a formal restriction followed by continued growth recurs with the harder cap of 1939.

Reversal or narrowing. The familiar account holds that the Balfour promise stood unchanged from 1917 until Britain suddenly reversed it in 1939. The documents tell a different story. Within five years of making the promise, Britain narrowed its meaning, attached an economic test to immigration, and set in motion the removal of roughly three-quarters of the territory from the area open to Jewish settlement, seventeen years before the better-known reversal. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] Whether 1922 should be called the first reversal or only a narrowing is a matter of judgment, and the record supports both readings in part. The case for "reversal" rests on scale: the territorial reduction was larger than any later one before 1948, and the immigration rule was the first formal mechanism for limiting immigration. The case for "narrowing" rests on the paper's own words: it reaffirmed the declaration, kept immigration open, and left the national home in force west of the Jordan, where the Jewish population then grew almost fivefold. On either reading, the 1939 White Paper was not the first time Britain redefined its promise. It was the second.

What the record leaves open. The growth figures show that the absorptive-capacity rule did not prevent large-scale immigration. They cannot show what immigration would have been without it: growth might have been faster with no cap at all, and the record here makes no counterfactual claim. Nor does it show that "economic absorptive capacity" was applied consistently or predictably in the years that followed. The weight of the Jaffa riots against Britain's other motives in drafting the paper is likewise unsettled; the riots are documented as a direct contributing factor, not as the sole cause.

sections.h: The Mandate for Palestine: The Text and the Polity It Created
sections.html:
The document that wrote a British wartime letter into a League of Nations instrument ends with a place and a date: "Done at London the twenty-fourth day of July, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two." [cite:rs_md_avalon] Behind that line lay two years of diplomacy. At the San Remo Conference in April 1920 the victorious Allies assigned Palestine to Britain, and in July 1922 the Council of the League of Nations approved the text under which Britain would hold it. [cite:san_remo_wiki] [cite:mandate_text] How a letter of policy became an instrument of the League, and the argument over whether that instrument honored the League's own Covenant, is told in [scene:blg_s01|By What Right?]. This section reads the instrument itself: what its articles said, when it actually took effect, what kind of state apparatus it brought into being, and what it gave and withheld.

The League of Nations, founded in 1920 under the Treaty of Versailles, was the authority in whose name the arrangement was made. [cite:san_remo_wiki] The mandate system was Woodrow Wilson's attempt to separate a temporary trusteeship, meant to lead toward self-government, from outright colonial annexation. In practice, mandates were administered essentially as colonies. [cite:san_remo_wiki] [cite:mandate_text] That judgment concerns Palestine; the record summarized here does not show that every mandate across the world was run the same way. The League itself did not survive the Second World War, and its successor, the United Nations, inherited its records. [cite:san_remo_wiki]

What the articles said. Article 1 gave the Mandatory, Britain, "full powers of legislation and of administration." [cite:rs_md_un_origins] Everything else in the text operated inside that grant.

Article 2 set out the Mandatory's core obligations, and it set out three of them in one sentence. Britain was responsible for conditions that would secure the Jewish national home; for the development of self-governing institutions; and for "safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all the inhabitants of Palestine." [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_md_un_origins] The national home and the protection of rights were both binding. The text did not say how they were to be weighed against each other if they collided.

Article 4 provided that "an appropriate Jewish agency shall be recognized as a public body" to advise the Administration, and it recognized the Zionist Organization as that agency for as long as its constitution was deemed appropriate. [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_md_un_origins] The League later recorded that in 1929 the Zionist Organization was replaced in this role by the "Jewish Agency for Palestine." [cite:rs_md_lon1945] The articles summarized here name no equivalent public body for the Arab majority. Britain's later offer of an "Arab Agency" analogous to the Jewish Agency, with members chosen by the High Commissioner, and its rejection in October 1923, belong to the story of the Legislative Council of 1922–23. [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_arabagency]

Article 6 turned the national home from a principle into a working instruction. The Administration was to "facilitate Jewish immigration under suitable conditions" and to encourage close settlement by Jews on the land, while ensuring that other sections of the population are not prejudiced. [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_md_lon1945] Read closely, in the article that governs immigration and settlement the majority of the country's people appear in that form: as other sections of the population, protected against prejudice but not named.

Article 7 provided the basis for a Palestinian citizenship, and part of it concerned the acquisition of Palestinian citizenship by Jews. [cite:rs_md_transjordan] Three years later, that article became the legal ground of the Palestinian Citizenship Order, discussed below.

Article 11 dealt with the country's wealth. It allowed the Administration to place natural resources and public works under public ownership or control, and to make arrangements with the Jewish agency for such works, with the profits that could be distributed capped. [cite:rs_md_avalon] The clause named the Jewish agency as a body that could be brought in to develop public resources, and it limited the profits that could be taken out of them.

Article 22 made English, Arabic and Hebrew the official languages of Palestine, and required that any Arabic inscription on stamps or money be repeated in Hebrew, and any Hebrew inscription in Arabic. [cite:rs_md_avalon] The rule is small, but it fixed in law that the coins and stamps of the new polity would speak to both communities at once.

Article 25 concerned the lands east of the river. It let the Mandatory, with the consent of the League Council, postpone or withhold the application of provisions of the Mandate in the territories between the Jordan and Palestine's eastern boundary, so long as nothing was done that conflicted with Articles 15, 16 and 18. [cite:rs_md_avalon] Britain used that power within two months of the text's approval. The memorandum of September 1922 that removed the national-home provisions from Transjordan, one stage in a separation completed by 1923, is the subject of its own section, with the long political afterlife of that separation.

Set beside the letter it absorbed, the Mandate shows what changed in five years. The 1917 declaration expressed a government's favor and promised its best efforts. The 1922 text made the national home a legal responsibility of the governing power, added an immigration duty and a recognized Jewish public body, and widened the protected group from "existing non-Jewish communities" to "all the inhabitants." It also added a promise the letter had not contained: self-governing institutions, with no date and no form specified.

When the Mandate took effect, and the dispute over it. The approval of July 1922 was conditional. The League Council approved the terms of the Palestine and Syria mandates together, pending an agreement between France and Italy over Syria. [cite:rs_md_lon1923] At its meeting in Geneva on 29 September 1923, the Council took note that the France–Italy agreement had been reported and that the two mandates had "automatically and simultaneously entered into force." [cite:rs_md_lon1923] The United Nations later used that date. [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj]

That date has been challenged. John Quigley, writing in July 2026, argues that the Council only noted, in the future tense, that the mandates would enter into force, and that the Secretary-General, Drummond, changed the tense in the circular that reported the meeting. [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj] Quigley adds a second argument: Britain lacked title to the territory at that point, because the Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923, entered into force only on 6 August 1924. [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj] The case for the conventional date rests on the League's own record, circular C.L.101.1923.VI, which states that the mandates had "automatically and simultaneously entered into force," and on the United Nations' later reliance on it. [cite:rs_md_lon1923] [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj] The case against rests on the minutes' wording and on the sequence of the Ottoman peace treaty. The dispute is about the legal moment the Mandate began, not about whether Britain governed: British administration of Palestine was already in place, under a High Commissioner, from 1920.

The government the text created. Britain administered Palestine under the Mandate until 1948. It issued passports, minted the currency, printed the stamps, ran the police and the courts, operated the railways and the ports, and staffed a civil service that employed Arabs and Jews alike, all under a High Commissioner headquartered in Jerusalem. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] Beneath him sat a postal system and a customs and taxation apparatus that functioned for the whole of the Mandate's span. The Mandate had a legal text, published borders and recognized standing in international law. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki]

The first High Commissioner, appointed in 1920 by the Cabinet that had issued the Balfour Declaration, was Sir Herbert Samuel, a British Jew and a committed Zionist. [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel_hc] [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] One reading holds that his appointment embedded the declaration's contradiction in the administration itself: a single government was charged at once with fostering a Jewish national home and safeguarding the rights of an existing Arab majority, two obligations that, on this reading, could not both be honored. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] His tenure and those of the six men who followed him are traced in [scene:s07a2|the High Commissioners].

Citizens, passports, money. The Palestinian Citizenship Order of 1925, which came into force on 1 August 1925, gave legal form to a Palestinian citizenship under Article 7. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] Under it, about 70,000 brown passports were issued over the years of the Mandate, each stamped "BRITISH PASSPORT / PALESTINE." [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] The word "British" on the cover is what later led casual observers to misremember them. The holders were citizens of Palestine, Arab and Jewish. They used the documents to cross borders, conduct trade, study abroad and perform the hajj. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] The Palestine pound was minted from 1927 and circulated as legal tender; Palestine issued its own postage stamps, ran its own courts, and registered its own births, deaths, marriages and land titles. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki]

The historian Lauren Banko's study The Invention of Palestinian Citizenship, 1918–1947 traces how this status was built. It was not an informal identity but a specific legal status created by British administrative order, with its own bureaucratic history, population records, and legal disputes over who qualified. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] Many of the passports survive. They are held today by the descendants of Palestinian families in Ramallah and Haifa, in the refugee camps of Lebanon and Jordan, and across the diaspora, as evidence that their grandparents were citizens of a recognized polity. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship]

The people of the polity. By one general account of the Mandate, its population at the start was roughly 90 percent Arab and 10 percent Jewish, about 600,000 Arabs and 60,000 Jews. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] An account of the 1922 White Paper puts the Jewish population at about 80,000 in 1922. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] Both are round estimates. The one count from these years is the British census of October 1922, which recorded 757,182 people: 590,890 Muslims, 83,794 Jews and 73,024 Christians. [cite:rs_ta_report1922] Its figures are set out with [scene:rd2_aliyah|the Third Aliyah]. The census total is well above the first estimate, and its Jewish count is close to the second. By 1947, the last full year of the Mandate, the figures had moved to roughly 1.3 million Arabs and 600,000 Jews. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] Jewish growth came substantially through waves of immigration from Europe between the wars, heaviest in the 1930s as antisemitism in Europe intensified. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] The start and end points are documented here; the year-by-year course of that change, and the immigration and land machinery that drove it, belong to later chapters.

Land ownership moved more slowly than population. The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, and the other Zionist institutions had acquired about 9.8 percent of Mandate Palestine by purchase by 1948. [cite:jnf_wiki] The same source's further point is that most of the territory of the state that emerged in 1948 came not through purchase but through the war and displacement of that year. [cite:jnf_wiki] The two measures are taken against different wholes, Mandate Palestine in one case and the territory of the new state in the other, so they should not be read as a single sum. What the comparison does establish is that fifty years of organized, funded purchase left Jewish institutions owning under a tenth of the country's land on the eve of statehood.

The claim and the record. A familiar line holds that Palestine was an empty desert until Jewish pioneers made it bloom. The administrative record of the Mandate answers the first half of that sentence directly. The territory Britain governed had a High Commissioner, a treasury, a passport office, courts, a postal service, a registry of births and land titles, a currency, and a population numbering in the hundreds of thousands. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] [cite:san_remo_1920] The Mandate text itself legislated for "all the inhabitants of Palestine" and for "other sections of the population" whose rights were not to be prejudiced, wording that presupposes people already living there. [cite:rs_md_avalon] None of this asserts a modern nation-state before 1948, or settles any present political claim. It establishes something narrower: that a functioning civic polity called Palestine, with a documented citizenry, existed for a quarter-century before 1948. That matters for what followed. If the land was empty, no one was displaced; if it had citizens, the events of 1948 require a different accounting.

The record also supports the strongest form of the Zionist reading of the same document. The Mandate was not a British favor that could be quietly withdrawn. It was an instrument approved by the Council of the League of Nations that wrote the national home into binding articles: Britain was responsible for securing it, was obliged to facilitate Jewish immigration and close settlement, and was required to work with a recognized Jewish public body. [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_md_un_origins] For the Zionist movement, that was international legitimacy in the most formal sense then available. The Arab leadership's reading pointed to what the framework did not give: in February 1922 the Palestine Arab Delegation demanded a "national independent Government" and said the Balfour Declaration could not be a basis for discussion, and the Colonial Office replied that "the creation at this stage of a national Government would preclude the fulfilment of the pledge." [cite:rs_mca_cmd1700] Both readings rest on the same articles. On one reading, the disagreement is over which of Article 2's obligations governed when they could not all be met at once.

What the record leaves open. The passport count is an approximation, and the record does not give the number that survive today. It does not resolve present arguments about citizenship, return or statehood; it shows only that a formal, legal Palestinian citizenship existed under British administration decades before 1948. The two estimates of the Jewish population at the Mandate's start, 60,000 and about 80,000, are not reconciled with each other or with the census count of 83,794. Whether the Mandate entered into force on 29 September 1923 remains, as of the scholarship cited, contested. And the text never answered its own central question. It bound Britain to a national home, to self-governing institutions and to the rights of all inhabitants, and it named no rule for choosing among them. The documents of 1922 that tried to supply such a rule, the Churchill White Paper and the Transjordan memorandum, are where the next sections turn.

sections.h: The First American Campaigns: Weizmann, Einstein and the Fight Over the Money
sections.html:
The Mandate's text was settled in London and Geneva, but much of the money and some of the political backing for the national home were being sought in the United States. American support for a Jewish homeland is usually dated to the years after the Second World War, as a response to the Holocaust. The organized American campaign began a generation earlier. By the spring of 1921 the Zionist movement was running national fundraising tours across the United States, and by January 1922 one of its leaders was sitting with the President. It was also, in those same months, fighting an internal battle over who would control the money it raised. American Jewish opinion was not yet its own: much of the established community still kept its distance.

The United States had figured in Zionist and British calculations from the start. Among the motives the British War Cabinet weighed in 1917, when it approved the Balfour Declaration, was the hope of winning sympathy in Russian and American Jewish communities, to help keep Russia in the war and bring America into it. [cite:cohen_palestine_great_powers] What changed after the war was that the movement now needed money on a new scale. At a London conference on 24 December 1920 the Zionist Organization founded the Keren Hayesod, the Palestine Foundation Fund, as its central and permanent fundraising arm, open to non-Zionist donors as well, with an original five-year target of £25,000,000. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki] The fund's structure and what it went on to finance are told in [scene:s04i|the account of the Keren Hayesod]. America was where a large part of that money would have to come from.

In March 1921 Chaim Weizmann invited Albert Einstein to accompany him to the United States. The two toured the country for two months that spring, raising money for the new Keren Hayesod and for the Hebrew University. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_intro] [cite:hnn_isaacson_einstein] The movement was sending the world's most famous scientist on a national fundraising tour. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc252]

The tour also brought into the open a struggle over control. The Einstein Papers document it. Weizmann wanted the Keren Hayesod centralized under the Zionist Executive. The American faction led by Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis and Judge Julian Mack wanted American control of the money and businesslike management of how it was spent. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc168] [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_intro] At stake was who would decide how American donations were spent: the world movement's executive, or the American organization that raised them. The sources record each side's position; they do not set out the full arguments each made for it.

The dispute came to a head at the 1921 convention of the Zionist Organization of America in Cleveland. Weizmann's side won, and the Brandeis group withdrew from the leadership of American Zionism. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc168] [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_intro] Weizmann's centralized model for the fund had prevailed.

The campaign did not stop with the split. In November 1921 a second delegation arrived for a Keren Hayesod tour: Nahum Sokolow, who with Weizmann had drafted the Balfour Declaration, Otto Warburg and Jabotinsky. [cite:balfour_letter] Their tour raised nearly $5 million. On 13 January 1922 Sokolow met President Warren Harding for nearly an hour. [cite:israeled_sokolow_harding] Within months, Congress would take up a resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration, the subject of [scene:us_s02|the next section].

None of this meant that American Jewry as a whole had embraced Zionism. Much of the established community remained non-Zionist. Paul Warburg avoided the cause, and when Einstein invited about fifty non-Zionist notables to take part, few responded. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc252] The campaign of 1921 and 1922 was the work of an organized movement within American Jewish life, not the voice of that community entire, and the distance kept by many of its leading figures is as much a part of the record as the money raised.

So the common account needs correcting on two counts. American support for a Jewish national home did not begin after 1945: by 1921, twenty-seven years before statehood, the movement had a national fundraising operation in the United States, a public figure of Einstein's standing on tour, a fight over control of the proceeds, and an audience with the President. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc252] But that support was not yet broad, even among American Jews.

The record here leaves several things open. It does not say what Sokolow and Harding discussed, or whether the meeting bore on the congressional resolution that followed. It does not break down the nearly $5 million by source or show how it was spent, nor does it give the sums raised by the spring tour itself. And it records the outcome of the Cleveland convention, not the vote or the arguments made on its floor.

sections.h: Congress Endorses Balfour: The Lodge–Fish Resolution of 1922
sections.html:
Official American support for a Jewish homeland is usually dated to 1948 and President Truman's recognition of the new state. The first formal endorsement by the United States government came twenty-six years earlier. On 21 September 1922 President Warren Harding signed a joint resolution of Congress favouring a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. It had been requested by American Zionist leaders, opposed by the State Department, and passed by the House and, by unanimous consent, the Senate.

The initiative came from the American Zionist movement, then in the middle of the fundraising campaigns described in [scene:us_s01|the previous section]. American Zionist leaders approached two Republicans, Senator Henry Cabot Lodge of Massachusetts and Representative Hamilton Fish III of New York, and asked them to introduce a resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration of 1917. The Jewish Virtual Library credits a significant lobbying effort by the American Zionist community, and in particular the work of Rabbi Simon Glazer. [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:israeled_sokolow_harding] Nahum Sokolow had met Harding for nearly an hour on 13 January 1922, during the Keren Hayesod tour that raised nearly $5 million. [cite:israeled_sokolow_harding] The record used here does not say whether that meeting touched on the resolution.

The resolution met objection from two quarters. The State Department opposed it, and so did the New York Times. [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:wjc_lodge_fish] It passed regardless. The House approved it on 30 June 1922, and the Senate followed by unanimous consent on 13 July. [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:wjc_lodge_fish] The Senate's passage came eleven days before the Mandate for Palestine, which wrote the Balfour Declaration into an instrument of the League of Nations, was done at London on 24 July 1922. [cite:rs_md_avalon] The Mandate itself is examined in [scene:s07|the section on the Mandate text].

Harding signed the measure on 21 September 1922 as Public Resolution 67-73. Its text favoured "the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people," repeating the phrase the Balfour Declaration had used in 1917. [cite:wiki_lodge_fish] [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:balfour_letter] It also carried a condition: that nothing should be done which might prejudice "the civil and religious rights of Christian and all other non-Jewish communities in Palestine." [cite:wiki_lodge_fish] [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] The condition belongs in any account of the resolution as fully as the endorsement does. Congress, like the British government before it, favoured a national home for one people and stated in the same text that the rights of the communities already living in the country were not to be prejudiced.

Inside American Jewish life the resolution mattered too. The World Jewish Congress notes that it helped legitimize Zionism within American Jewry by giving it a "stamp of approval" from the non-Jewish world. [cite:wjc_lodge_fish] That carries weight against the background of the previous year, when much of the established American Jewish community still kept its distance from the cause, and when Einstein's invitation to about fifty non-Zionist notables drew few replies. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc252]

The episode shows how this resolution was made. The initiative did not come from the State Department, the arm of government responsible for foreign policy, which opposed it. It came from an organized domestic movement that approached members of Congress directly and won passage in both houses, after which the President signed. The resolution was lobbied for and passed over the objection of the foreign-policy bureaucracy. [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:wjc_lodge_fish]

What it committed the United States to is a narrower question than its importance might suggest, and the record used here answers it only in part. The text says what Congress favoured and on what condition. The sources do not show that it obliged the government to take any particular action, and they do not describe any action taken under it. Nor do they give the grounds on which the State Department and the New York Times objected, or the House vote count. What is documented is the sequence, the words of the text with their condition, and the fact that the first official American endorsement of a Jewish national home came in 1922, not 1948.

sections.h: The Council That Never Sat: The Legislative Council of 1922–1923
sections.html:
The Mandate obliged Britain to do two things that pulled against each other. Article 2 made the Mandatory responsible for conditions that would secure the Jewish national home and for the development of self-governing institutions, while also "safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all the inhabitants of Palestine." [cite:rs_md_avalon] The first test of how those duties would be reconciled came in 1922, when London offered Palestine a constitution with a partly elected legislature. Within a year the offer had failed. The record of that failure is more specific than either side's later shorthand: a share in government was offered, on terms that the Arab leadership refused and the Zionist leadership accepted, and its rejection left the High Commissioner ruling without any elected legislature for the rest of the Mandate.

The negotiation began before the text was final. Through the first half of 1922 the Palestine Arab Delegation in London, the body sent by the Fourth Palestine Arab Congress, corresponded with the Colonial Office about the draft constitution [cite:rs_mca_jvl_congress]; its rejection of the draft in February and the Colonial Office's replies are told in [scene:pp_s01|the account of the Palestinian national movement]. Two of the delegation's specific objections bore directly on the council. An earlier draft had included two nominated members, and the Colonial Office agreed to drop them. The delegation went further: it demanded that every member be elected, and it objected to a quorum of ten. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] By the arithmetic of the final text, the ten official members would by themselves have made a quorum of ten.

The Zionist side answered the same correspondence differently. On 18 June 1922 the Executive of the Zionist Organization assured the government that its activities "will be conducted in conformity with the policy therein set forth," meaning the policy of the statement now known as the Churchill White Paper. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] According to the historian Shira Klein, the Zionist leadership did not treat the White Paper as a triumph. Weizmann and others accepted it because they believed its principle of "economic absorptive capacity" could still allow a Jewish majority to be built over time. [cite:rs_lc_cojs_whitepaper] The White Paper itself, and the immigration rule at its center, are examined in [scene:s06a|the section on the Churchill White Paper].

The constitution was issued in London as the Palestine Order in Council on 10 August 1922, and Herbert Samuel, as High Commissioner, proclaimed it in force on 1 September 1922. [cite:rs_lc_order1922] Article 19 set out the Legislative Council: twenty-two members plus the High Commissioner, of whom ten were to be official members and twelve unofficial, elected members. Article 30 set the quorum at ten. [cite:rs_lc_order1922] The two nominated seats were gone, as the Colonial Office had conceded. The quorum of ten, to which the delegation had objected, remained.

The twelve elected seats were divided by community: eight Muslim, two Christian and two Jewish. The historian Philip Mattar has set that allocation against the population. Palestinian Arabs, by his reckoning, were allotted 43 percent of the seats while forming 88 percent of the population. [cite:rs_lc_mattar] The figure explains the shape of the dispute that followed. Even if every Muslim and Christian seat had been filled, the ten Arab members would have held ten places in a chamber of twenty-three.

The two sides' reasons for accepting and refusing are the heart of the matter, and each deserves its strongest form. The Arab leadership's case was that the council was built on the Mandate and on the Balfour Declaration, which the delegation said could not be a basis for discussion; that it gave the Arabs a minority of the seats although they were the large majority of the people; and that it fell short of what they had asked for, a national government with control over immigration. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] [cite:rs_lc_mattar] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_whitepaper] In February 1922 the delegation had already demanded a "national independent Government," and the Colonial Office had replied on 1 March that "the creation at this stage of a national Government would preclude the fulfilment of the pledge" to the Jewish people. [cite:rs_mca_cmd1700] To take part in the council, on this reading, was to accept the frame that made the Arab majority a minority in its own legislature. The Zionist leadership's case was that the framework, whatever its limits, kept the national-home commitment intact and tied immigration to the country's economic capacity rather than to Arab consent. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_whitepaper] Both readings rest on the same documents. They differ on what those documents were for.

The Arab answer came at the Fifth Palestine Arab Congress, meeting in Nablus in August 1922, which resolved to boycott the elections to the Legislative Council. [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] [cite:rs_lc_albright] According to the Jewish Virtual Library's account, the congress opened on 22 August and also resolved to reject the new constitution. [cite:rs_mca_jvl_congress]

The boycott was tested in the primary elections of late February 1923. Voting was in two stages, and the primaries chose secondary electors. Of 809 secondary electors expected, no more than 213 were chosen. The Muslim districts, expected to yield 663, produced only 107. [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] The 1947 Yale study of the Mandate by Albright and others records the pattern by community. Jews and Druze took part fully. Muslims filled about one-sixth of their allotment and Christians about one-third. The polling was extended on 7 March 1923, and even then the result was too unrepresentative for a council to be formed. [cite:rs_lc_albright]

Britain then tried twice more within the year. It first proposed a nominated Advisory Council in place of the elected one. The Arab nominees refused their seats, and the idea collapsed. [cite:rs_lc_albright] It next offered an "Arab Agency," a body meant to parallel the Jewish agency recognized under Article 4 of the Mandate, but with its members chosen by the High Commissioner. [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_arabagency] That offer was rejected in October 1923. The president of the Arab Executive, Musa Kazim al-Husseini, wrote that the Arabs' "sole object is independence." [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_arabagency] [cite:rs_mca_palquest_musakazim] One difference between the two agencies is plain in the documents: the Zionist Organization had been named in the Mandate itself as the Jewish agency, while the Arab body would have been the High Commissioner's own selection. Britain reported the episode to the League. Its report on the administration for 1923 lists a White Paper of November 1923 on the "Proposed Formation of an Arab Agency" and "Papers relating to the Elections for the Palestine Legislative Council." [cite:rs_lc_report1923]

By the end of 1923 Britain was governing with an advisory council made up of British officials only. The High Commissioner ruled without an elected legislature for the rest of the Mandate. [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] One asymmetry follows from the documents: with no legislature, the Arab leadership held no elected place in government, while the Zionist Organization kept the advisory standing that Article 4 of the Mandate gave it as the recognized Jewish agency. [cite:rs_md_avalon]

The idea did not die at once. A council was proposed again in 1930, under Passfield, and again in 1935, when Britain offered a council of twenty-eight members: fourteen Muslims and Christians, eight Jews, five officials and one commercial member. That proposal was suspended amid Jewish opposition and Arab division, and the idea died with the revolt of 1936–39. [cite:rs_lc_mattar] The terms had shifted since 1922. The 1935 council would have given Muslims and Christians fourteen seats to the Jews' eight, and this time the opposition recorded on the Jewish side was part of the setting in which the proposal was suspended.

Several things the record here does not settle. The sources give the turnout by community, not the reasons of individual voters who stayed away. It does not establish whether a council of this shape, had it sat, could have changed policy on immigration or land, since no such council ever met. The formal instrument by which the 1923 elections were set aside, and the exact membership of the Advisory Council Britain then proposed, are not established in the sources used here and are left out rather than guessed at. Nor do the sources detail the 1930 proposal beyond its date. What the record does show is the sequence: a constitution offered on terms one side accepted and the other refused, three British attempts in a single year to find some form of Arab participation, and, from the end of 1923, a High Commissioner who governed with officials alone.

sections.h: Who Ran Palestine: The High Commissioner and the Seven Who Held the Office
sections.html:
The council's failure left one office at the center of Palestine's government. The Mandate is often written about as though "the British government" ran Palestine as a single, faceless machine. The documents show something more particular. From 1920 to 1948 the country was governed day to day by a sequence of seven appointed High Commissioners, with acting commissioners filling the gaps between them, and each of them made decisions that can be dated and traced. [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine] Herbert Samuel opened the office in 1920. His successors, Plumer, Chancellor, Wauchope, MacMichael, Gort and Cunningham, presided in turn over the riots of 1929, the Arab Revolt, the years of the 1939 White Paper, the Jewish armed campaign against British rule, and the withdrawal of 1948. What follows describes the office itself, the first man to hold it, whose decisions fall inside these years, and, more briefly, the six who came after.

The office drew its power from the Mandate itself. Article 1 gave the Mandatory "full powers of legislation and of administration." [cite:rs_md_un_origins] Britain exercised those powers through a High Commissioner based in Jerusalem, at the head of a civil government that ran everything from passports and currency to police, courts and railways, and that employed Arabs and Jews alike. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] Above him stood London and, more distantly, the League of Nations. The Colonial Office conducted the negotiations over Palestine's constitution in 1922, and the Mandatory reported to the League on its administration. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] [cite:rs_lc_report1923] Beside the administration, Article 4 of the Mandate recognized the Zionist Organization as the "appropriate Jewish agency," a public body to advise it. [cite:rs_md_avalon]

What the office lacked tells as much as what it held. The constitution of 1922 placed the High Commissioner at the head of a Legislative Council of twenty-two members, ten of them officials and twelve elected. [cite:rs_lc_order1922] That council never sat. After the boycott of the 1923 elections, Britain governed with an advisory council of British officials only, and the High Commissioner ruled without an elected legislature for the rest of the Mandate. [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] How that happened is told in [scene:rd2_council|the account of the Legislative Council]. Its effect on the office was lasting: for the rest of the Mandate, the "full powers of legislation and of administration" that Article 1 gave the Mandatory were exercised in Palestine through the High Commissioner without any elected body beside him.

The first man to hold this office had a direct link to the Balfour Declaration. Herbert Samuel was a British Cabinet minister and an advocate of Zionism, and a memorandum he wrote in 1915 influenced the Balfour Declaration itself. [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel] He was appointed in 1920 by the same British Cabinet that had issued the declaration, and by many accounts he was the first Jewish governor of the land since Roman times. [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel_hc] [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] The appointment was itself a point of contemporary debate. It sharpened Arab suspicion that the Mandate was built to deliver the Balfour promise, and it placed inside a single administration the double charge of fostering a Jewish national home while safeguarding the rights of the Arab majority. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] He served until 1925, and the administrative and legal foundations he laid framed the work of every administration after him. [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel] [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine]

Samuel's record in office does not fit either of the simple portraits drawn of him. According to J. B. Schechtman's account in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, one of his first acts, in July 1920, was an amnesty for those imprisoned over the Jerusalem riots of that April, Jews and Arabs alike. [cite:rs_hg_ej_jabotinsky] He also pardoned Amin al-Husseini, whom a British military tribunal had convicted in his absence after the same violence. [cite:rs_mu_ushmm] [cite:rs_mu_jvl] What became of Jabotinsky's sentence under the amnesty is disputed, as told with [scene:ri_s01|the riots of 1920 and 1921]. Samuel lent his name, as Honorary President, to the Pro-Jerusalem Society of Ronald Storrs, Jerusalem's military governor until 1920 and its civil governor from that year. [cite:rs_al_ashbee1921] [cite:rs_al_openjerusalem] In 1921 he made Amin al-Husseini Mufti of Jerusalem, after recording Amin's pledge to keep the city calm and after Storrs, at his request, secured a rival candidate's withdrawal. [cite:rs_mu_cojs_samuel_note] [cite:rs_mu_cojs_klein] On 20 December 1921 the Supreme Moslem Sharia Council Order created the council over which Amin would preside. [cite:rs_mu_smc_order] Whether the Mufti's appointment was a manipulation of an election or a judgment about public order is set out in [scene:rd2_mufti|the account of the Mufti's appointment].

The violence of 1921 tested the office early. After the Jaffa riots, on 15 May 1921, Samuel temporarily prohibited Jewish immigration, and on 3 June he tied future immigration to the country's economic capacity, the principle the 1922 White Paper would write down. [cite:rs_ta_cojs_whitepaper] He created a mixed Arab-Jewish militia, which the last 400 Palestinian Legionnaires of the Jewish Legion joined. [cite:rs_hg_jvl_legion] On 1 September 1922 he proclaimed the Palestine Order in Council in force, the constitution under which the Mandate was to be governed. [cite:rs_lc_order1922] When the Legislative Council it created failed in 1923, the office he handed on governed with officials alone. [cite:rs_lc_albright]

Taken together, these acts resist a simple portrait. A Zionist by conviction, chosen by the Cabinet that issued the Balfour Declaration, Samuel suspended Jewish immigration after Jaffa and backed as Mufti a man he had pardoned. The documents support neither the portrait of a governor who simply served the national home nor its opposite.

The six who followed him inherited the office he had shaped and held it through crises that belong to later chapters of this book. They are told here only as the record gives them, to show how the office ran in practice.

Field Marshal Herbert Plumer, who came to the post from command of the British Expeditionary Force's Second Army, served from 1925 to 1928. He was named without consultation with the World Zionist Organization, yet he was regarded as committed to fairness toward Zionist aspirations. When he died in 1932, a Jewish Telegraphic Agency obituary described his tenure as "the only period when complete tranquility existed in Palestine." [cite:jta_plumer_obituary] [cite:toi_diaries_1929_officials] That is a contemporary judgment of comparative calm, set against what came before and after, not a claim that those three years were free of tension.

Sir John Chancellor served from December 1928 to September 1931, a period of what has been described as "tremendous tension." It began with a dispute at the Western Wall on Yom Kippur 1928 and culminated in the Hebron Massacre of 24 August 1929. Chancellor was not in the country when the massacre happened. He was on home leave in England through the critical period of July and August 1929. Harry Luke served as acting High Commissioner throughout, and Chancellor returned to Jerusalem only on 29 August 1929, five days after the killings. [cite:toi_diaries_1929_officials] [cite:encyclopedia_hc_palestine] Two facts stand side by side here, and both are real: his absence during the acute crisis, and his responsibility as head of the administration whose wider policies formed its setting. The episode also shows how the office worked when its holder was away. Authority did not lapse; it passed to an acting commissioner, who carried it through the massacre itself.

Arthur Wauchope held the office from 1931 to 1938, through years of rising Jewish immigration and the outbreak of the Arab Revolt of 1936–39. Historians generally regard him as more sympathetic to Zionist settlement than his successors, and his approach has been called relatively conciliatory. He resigned as the revolt intensified. [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine] The record used here gives his general reputation and the crisis that ended his term, not an itemised account of his decisions.

Harold MacMichael, from 1938 to 1944, administered Palestine as the 1939 White Paper was put into effect and through the early years of Jewish paramilitary resistance. In 1944 Lehi, also known as the Stern Gang, attempted to assassinate him in an ambush on his motorcade. He survived, wounded; his wife was seriously injured. [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine]

The shortest tenure, and the one most often left out of popular accounts, belonged to Field Marshal John Vereker, 6th Viscount Gort. He served from November 1944 to November 1945 and retired because of ill health after barely a year. He died the following year, 1946. [cite:wiki_john_vereker_gort] His brevity is itself the notable fact. The record does not attribute major policy shifts to him, and this book does not claim any.

The last was Alan Cunningham, from 1945 to 1948. He presided over the most violent period of Jewish paramilitary resistance, including the bombing of the King David Hotel, and over the chaotic British withdrawal from Palestine in May 1948. [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine]

Naming all seven matters because twenty-eight years of rule did not run on a single setting. Each administration made its own choices within the broader policy framework: how firmly to enforce limits on immigration, how to respond to violence coming from more than one direction, and even whether to be present or on leave when a crisis broke. [cite:encyclopedia_hc_palestine] Treating the period as one undifferentiated British policy erases a calm three years under one man, an absence during a massacre under another, and an assassination survived under a third. The opposite error is just as real. No one High Commissioner's character explains the Mandate's outcome. Each worked inside a much larger structure: a Mandate held by Britain under the League, directed from London, and from 1923 governed without an elected chamber in Palestine.

Some of what a reader would want to know is not in the record used here. It does not name every acting commissioner who filled the gaps between tenures, beyond Harry Luke in 1929. It does not show, for any of the seven, how much of what he did was his own decision and how much followed instructions from the Colonial Office. It does not give the content of Samuel's 1915 memorandum, only that it influenced the Balfour Declaration. And for Wauchope, MacMichael, Gort and Cunningham it gives a reputation and a few dated events rather than a full account of their administrations; those belong to the later chapters in which their crises fall.

chapters.label: Stage Three
chapters.title: Build
chapters.intro:
At the end of 1922 the promise of 1917 had become an instrument of the League of Nations, but not yet a settled one. The League Council had approved the Mandate for Palestine on 24 July 1922 on a condition that still had to be met, and the Ottoman Empire's successor had not yet given up its claim to the land. [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force] [cite:w_lausanne] Britain's first census that year counted 757,182 people, 83,794 of them Jews, about 11 percent. [cite:jvl_census_1931] The institutions of the Jewish community were small. The Histadrut, the labor federation founded in Haifa in December 1920 and open only to Jews, had about 8,400 members in 1922; the Haganah, placed under its control, counted "a few hundred" volunteers. [cite:wiki_histadrut] [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] The Palestinian Arab congresses had an Executive under Musa Kazim al-Husseini, which Britain never recognized. [cite:palquest_musa_kazim]

This stage asks what was built in the fourteen years that followed, by whom, on what terms, and what was left unbuilt. The answer lies less in declarations than in institutions: a labor federation with its own bank and building firm, a land fund that never resold, a Jewish Agency widened to take in non-Zionist money, an electricity monopoly, a currency board in London. It asks with equal weight what Palestinian Arabs built in the same years, what Britain tried to change after the violence of 1929, and why it reversed itself within four months. [cite:w_passfield]

The cast is wide. On the British side stood the High Commissioners in Jerusalem, down to Sir Arthur Wauchope; Lord Passfield at the Colonial Office; Ramsay MacDonald in Downing Street; and the inquiries of the Shaw Commission, Sir John Hope Simpson and the Murison Commission. [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d] [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal] [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest] The Zionist movement worked through Chaim Weizmann; through David Ben-Gurion, the Histadrut's secretary from the end of 1921; through Pinhas Rutenberg's power company and Yehoshua Hankin's land purchases; and, from 1929, through the American non-Zionists Louis Marshall and Felix Warburg. [cite:wiki_histadrut] [cite:wiki_israel_electric] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin] [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14] Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionists contested the leadership from within, and Jewish dissent reached further: Jacob de Haan spoke for the Orthodox old Yishuv until he was shot in 1924, and Brit Shalom argued for a binational country. [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists] [cite:w_dehaan] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom] On the Palestinian side were the Mufti, Hajj Amin al-Husseini; his rival Raghib al-Nashashibi; Jamal al-Husseini; the founders of the Istiqlal party; the women of the 1929 congress; and, outside every party, Shaykh 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam. [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi] [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_jamal] [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_hajibrahim] [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_womens] [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam] Beyond Palestine, Turkey signed at Lausanne, and in Berlin a democracy fell to a regime that soon signed a transfer agreement with Zionist bodies. [cite:rs_rd3_lausanne_fcdo] [cite:history_weimar_republic] [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]

The sections follow that building roughly in time. They begin with the Histadrut and "Hebrew labour", Rutenberg's concession and the grid it produced, and the country as the census counted it. Then come the legal steps of 1923–1925, from Lausanne to the Citizenship Order. They follow the Revisionist line from Betar and the "Iron Wall" to secession, the killing of de Haan, the immigration of the Fourth and Fifth Aliyot, the enlarged Jewish Agency, the Hebrew University and Brit Shalom, and the money and currency of the Mandate economy. August 1929 at the Wall, in Hebron and in Safed is the hinge. After it come Palestinian politics from the last congress to the parties of 1935; Weimar's collapse; the inquiries, the Passfield White Paper and MacDonald's letter; land and labor; and the armed line from the Haganah to the Irgun. The American Palestine Committee and the Jews of Baghdad and Constantine widen the view. So do [scene:hv_s01|the Haavara Agreement], the murder of Chaim Arlosoroff and the Nuremberg Laws. The stage ends with al-Qassam's death in the hills near Ya'bad and with [scene:rd3_council_1935|Wauchope's offer of a legislative council], rejected by the Zionist leadership and dividing Arab leaders as the country moved toward [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt].
chapters.outro:
By the end of 1935 the Mandate had been in operation for twelve years, and the frame of 1922 had been filled in. Some of what filled it was law, much of it institutions and money, and the two communities had filled it very unequally.

The legal layer was settled in practice and contested in principle. Turkey renounced the Arab provinces at Lausanne, in a treaty signed on 24 July 1923 and in force from 6 August 1924; as John Quigley stresses, it renounced them in no one's favor. [cite:rs_rd3_lausanne_fcdo] [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026] The League Council's minutes record the Mandate in force from 29 September 1923, and Britain, the League Secretariat and, in 1947, the United Nations treated it as the date. Quigley's challenge holds that the wording came from the Secretary-General's circular, not from a Council resolution. [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force] [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026] The Citizenship Order of 1925 tied citizenship to residence on 1 August 1925. It left out Arab emigrants abroad and opened naturalization to newcomers; by 1946, on one study's figures, about 130,000 people had been naturalized, 99 percent of them Jews. [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil] [cite:rs_rd3_banko_podcast] Article 11 carried Rutenberg's 70-year monopoly. [cite:zaoerv_mandate_article11] [cite:wiki_israel_electric] In 1930 a League commission ruled the Western Wall Muslim property and sacred to both parties, with Jewish access on Ottoman-era terms. [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_wall_1930]

The administrative layer stayed in British hands alone. A Currency Board appointed by the Colonial Secretary issued the Palestine pound from 1 November 1927, at par with sterling. [cite:wiki_palestine_pound] On the Jewish Agency's figures, revenue rose from LP 2,371,000 in 1922–23 to LP 5,452,000 in 1934–35. [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937] Britain paid £1.5 million for the garrison in 1923–24, but in August 1929 about 150 British and 1,500 local police served the whole country. [cite:league_report_garrison] [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots] The administration governed by inquiry and ordinance. Shaw found the tenant-protection laws had failed. Hope Simpson counted 29.4 percent of families landless in 104 villages. [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_e] [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal] The Passfield White Paper built on both, and MacDonald's letter of 13 February 1931 reinterpreted it away. [cite:w_passfield] [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal] Britain's one direct lever on immigration was the labor schedule, set at 8,000 for April–September 1935 and cut to 3,250 for the half-year that followed. [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531]

The institutional and financial layer is where the stage's building happened. The Histadrut ran Solel Boneh, Bank Hapoalim and Kupat Holim. [cite:wiki_histadrut] The Anglo-Palestine Bank carried the movement's money. [cite:wiki_palestine_pound] The Keren Hayesod raised $20.1 million from April 1921 to December 1929, $11.0 million of it in the United States. [cite:jta_kh_decade] At Zurich in 1929 the Jewish Agency became half non-Zionist, with the Keren Hayesod as its financial instrument. [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14] The Jewish National Fund grew from 22,363 dunams in 1920 to roughly 362,000 in 1935, leased on terms that, in its draft lease, bound lessees to cultivate "only with Jewish labour". [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal] Recorded Jewish immigration reached 61,854 in 1935, and the Haavara transfer moved about 105 million Reichsmarks of German goods by the outbreak of war. [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828] [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] The armed bodies divided as they grew. The Haganah came under a parity command in 1931, the Irgun broke away the same year, and the Revisionists left for the New Zionist Organization in 1935. [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]

The Palestinian Arab layer was a national movement without a channel into government. The Arab Executive, never recognized, dissolved in 1934 after Musa Kazim al-Husseini's death. [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] What replaced it was more varied and more divided. There was a women's congress in 1929, Istiqlal in 1932, and parties built around the Nashashibi and Husseini camps in 1934–35, which formed a short-lived united front at the end of 1935. [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_womens] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_istiqlal] [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi] [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_jamal] [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512] Its instruments were delegations, boycotts, the courts at Wadi al-Hawarith and demonstrations. In October 1933, by Murison's count, 26 members of the public and one policeman were killed. [cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith] [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest] Al-Qassam's band, which, by one account, the Mufti declined to back, shows the other road some took. [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]

The regional layer tied Palestine to its neighbors by oil and by politics. The Iraq Petroleum Company's line brought its first oil to Haifa on 16 October 1934. [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline] In December 1931 a General Islamic Congress gathered 130 delegates from 22 countries in Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd3_mee_congress_1931] Outside Palestine, Jewish communities met state measures in Iraq from 1934, as one source reports, and killing at Constantine. [cite:rs_rd3_sephardivoices_iraq] [cite:rs_rd3_cole_constantine] Germany became a party to Palestine's economy through Haavara two years before the Nuremberg Laws. [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_laws] The American layer was money and method more than policy. American donors supplied more than half of the Keren Hayesod's first decade, the American quota act of 1924, by one account, turned emigrants toward Palestine, and in 1932 Emanuel Neumann founded a committee of prominent, mainly non-Jewish Americans. [cite:jta_kh_decade] [cite:rs_rd3_cie_1924_act] [cite:aja_neumann_bio]

What was settled, then, was the chain of authority and the institutions the Jewish community built beneath it. What was contested ran through every layer, and each side's case had documents behind it. For the Zionist leadership, the MacDonald letter corrected a breach of a Mandate owed "to the Jewish people", and the Passfield White Paper had been the breach. For Arab leaders it was the "Black Letter", and in 1936, 137 Arab officials still cited it as a cause of their lost faith in official pledges. [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal] [cite:w_passfield] [cite:rs_rd3_officials_memo_1936] The Agency argued that Arabs gained from Jewish investment through revenue, wages and land prices; Hope Simpson found families displaced and not resettled. [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937] [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal] Haavara was a rescue and a breach of the boycott at once. [cite:jvl_haavara] What the record leaves open is no smaller. It does not say who killed Arlosoroff, or who, if anyone, stood above Tehomi in 1924. [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1985_panel] [cite:w_dehaan] It does not settle how many Jews died in August 1929, 133 or 113, how many immigrants came in any year, or whether the Mandate ever validly entered into force. [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_buraq] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table] [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026] The structure that met 1936 was lopsided: one community held an apparatus without sovereignty, and the other held a majority without an institution.

sections.h: The Histadrut and "Hebrew Labour"
sections.html:
In December 1920, in Haifa, the two labor Zionist parties of the day, Ahdut HaAvoda and Hapoel Hatzair, joined forces to found the General Federation of Hebrew Workers in the Land of Israel, known by its Hebrew short name, the Histadrut [cite:wiki_histadrut]. It began small, and it began closed. Membership stood at about 4,400 in 1920 and about 8,400 in 1922, in a country where, by a Zionist historian's estimate, there were roughly 50,000 Arab workers [cite:wiki_histadrut] [cite:marxists_histadrut_union_boss]. Those workers were outside the federation by rule, not by accident: from its founding, membership was restricted to Jews [cite:wiki_histadrut].

Labour Zionism is often remembered as a socialist workers' movement, committed to class solidarity across national lines. The Histadrut, however, was not a union of the country's workers. It was a union of one community's workers, and much of its work in the 1920s and 1930s was to build that community's separate economy. How a trade union became, in practice, a government-in-waiting is the story of these years.

The decisive figure was David Ben-Gurion, elected secretary of the federation at the end of 1921 [cite:wiki_histadrut]. In the account of the historian Zeev Sternhell, Ben-Gurion turned the Histadrut into a national instrument for realizing Zionism rather than a conventional class union [cite:wiki_histadrut]. Its campaign in the labor market went by the name "Hebrew labour," avoda ivrit. The Histadrut pressed Jewish employers, especially citrus growers and builders, to hire only Jewish workers [cite:wiki_histadrut]. The demand was made of Jewish employers; the workers it was meant to exclude were Arab. This was separation in the labor market long before there was any separation in law.

The federation did not stop at organizing workers. From December 1920 it also took responsibility for defense, and the Haganah was placed under its direct control; through the 1920s the Haganah had only "a few hundred" volunteer members [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. How that militia grew after 1929, and how part of it broke away, is told in [scene:s07e2|the armed line].

The Histadrut also owned the places where its members worked. It built the construction and public-works company Solel Boneh. In association with the World Zionist Organization it founded the Workers' Bank, Bank Hapoalim. It ran the Kupat Holim health fund, on which many Israelis later depended for their health insurance, and it gathered industrial holdings that later became Koor Industries [cite:wiki_histadrut]. Read one way, a union that ran a bank, a building contractor, a health system and its own militia was a parallel economy with its own means of protection. The scale it eventually reached shows what this structure made possible: by 1989 the Histadrut employed about 280,000 workers [cite:marxists_histadrut_union_boss].

Land was the other half of the same design. The Jewish National Fund held land that could not be resold to non-Jews and leased it on terms requiring Jewish labor; that clause is set out in [scene:rd3_land|the land section]. Taken together, the land fund and the labor federation meant that the Yishuv had separate economic institutions decades before 1948: land that stayed in Jewish hands, a labor market organized for Jewish workers, its own bank and its own health system.

How to read this is disputed, and both readings deserve their strongest form. The movement described itself as socialist. Pinhas Lavon, the Histadrut's secretary-general in 1960, described its founders as young people seeking work in a country "which rejected its inhabitants." On this reading the Histadrut was what young immigrants built in order to find work at all, and its enterprises were a means of employing them.

The critical reading starts from the same facts. On Sternhell's account, under Ben-Gurion the Histadrut became a national instrument for realizing Zionism rather than a conventional union; its socialism served the national project, not the other way round [cite:wiki_histadrut]. Critics including the BDS movement go further, describing the pre-state Histadrut as a national-exclusivist rather than a socialist body, and "Hebrew labour" as national exclusivism in place of worker solidarity [cite:bds_histadrut_critique]. That is their characterization; it is not a finding of this book. What is not in dispute is the membership rule. A labor federation that excluded the majority of the country's workers from the day of its founding cannot be described, on the record, as practicing class solidarity across national lines, whatever its members believed about themselves.

The Histadrut was also a school for government. Ben-Gurion went on to chair the Jewish Agency from 1935 and became prime minister in 1948. He was followed by two Histadrut veterans, Levi Eshkol and Golda Meir [cite:wiki_histadrut] [cite:marxists_histadrut_union_boss]. The membership rule outlasted independence. Arab workers were admitted to full membership only in 1959, eleven years after the state was founded. By 1983 about 170,000 of the federation's 1.6 million members were Arab [cite:wiki_histadrut] [cite:marxists_histadrut_union_boss].

The record leaves some questions open. The sources give no year-by-year membership series between 1922 and the 1950s, so the federation's growth through the period of this chapter cannot be traced here. Nor do they measure how far "Hebrew labour" actually succeeded: how many Jewish employers complied, how many Arab workers lost work in Jewish-owned groves and building sites, or what the policy cost employers in wages. The campaign is documented; its economic effect, in numbers, is not.

sections.h: The Electricity Concession and the Grid
sections.html:
Land, labor and arms are the usual measures of how the Yishuv was built. Electricity belongs beside them. On 12 September 1921 the Mandate government signed the Auja (Yarkon) Concession. It granted the Jaffa Electric Company of Pinhas Rutenberg the exclusive right, for 70 years, to generate, distribute and sell electricity in the Jaffa district, using hydroelectric turbines on the Auja [cite:wiki_israel_electric]. It was a monopoly over a whole district, granted by the governing power to a single company.

The common view of the Mandate's public works is that they were neutral economic modernization, of benefit to everyone in the country. The concession tests that view. Its terms, the politics of its approval and, above all, the shape of the network it produced show something more particular: infrastructure that followed Jewish settlement and helped bind it together.

The concession had a legal footing in the Mandate itself. Article 11 allowed the administration to arrange with the Jewish Agency to construct or operate public works [cite:zaoerv_mandate_article11]. Rutenberg also had backing at the top. The High Commissioner, Herbert Samuel, and the Colonial Secretary, Winston Churchill, both supported him [cite:jc_turnberg_rutenberg]. The point of the arrangement, in mechanical terms, was that the British administration did not have to build or run a power system itself; it could grant the right to a concessionaire, and the Mandate named the body with which such arrangements could be made.

The grant did not pass unopposed. In 1922 the House of Lords passed an amendment to stop the concession. The House of Commons then overturned the Lords by a large majority, in a vote led by Churchill [cite:jc_turnberg_rutenberg]. The Lords had tried to stop the monopoly; the elected chamber chose to keep it. A challenge came from abroad as well. Euripides Mavromatis, a rival Greek concessionaire, contested the monopoly before the Permanent Court of International Justice. The sources used here record the challenge but not its outcome, so this book does not state one.

What was built did not match what was promised. The hydroelectric plant on the Auja was never built. When the grid switched on in 1923, it ran on diesel, in Tel Aviv [cite:jstor_electrifying_conflict] [cite:military_wiki_rutenberg]. The concession had also brought Rutenberg irrigation rights in the Auja valley, and those rights ended up benefiting only Jewish settlers [cite:jstor_electrifying_conflict] [cite:military_wiki_rutenberg]. A concession framed around hydroelectric power from the Auja produced a diesel network in the Jewish city and water for Jewish farms.

In 1923 Rutenberg founded the Palestine Electric Corporation. It built the country's only hydroelectric plant, not on the Auja but at Naharayim, on the Jordan. In 1961 the corporation was renamed the Israel Electric Corporation [cite:wiki_israel_electric]. The company founded under the Mandate thus carried on, under a new name, in the state.

The money in this arrangement moved through rights rather than cash. The Mandate government granted a monopoly over a whole district's electricity for 70 years; the concessionaire gained a protected market and, with it, the irrigation rights in the valley. The sources do not give the sums invested, the tariffs charged or the company's revenue, so the financial size of the monopoly cannot be stated here. What they do show is who gained the water and where the power went.

The fullest study of where the power went is the historian Fredrik Meiton's prize-winning work on electrification in Palestine. Meiton finds that the centralized grid knit Jewish settlements together while marginalizing and bypassing most Palestinian Arab communities [cite:mesa_meiton_award] [cite:wiki_israel_electric]. Another historian writes that the Yishuv's economic separatism "was given a tremendous push" by the 1921 monopoly. On this reading, electricity was statecraft: a network laid along the lines of Jewish settlement drew a map of a future state in copper and diesel, decades before any partition line was proposed.

The other reading deserves its strongest statement. The familiar account holds that the Mandate's development of Palestine was neutral economic modernization that benefited everyone, carried out by the means the Mandate text itself provided, a concession under Article 11. The Commons approved the concession by a large majority. Nothing in the sources shows that Arab communities were barred from connection by rule. The findings of Meiton and the second historian concern the shape and effect of the network, not a written policy of exclusion.

That is also where the record runs out. The sources here do not say how many Arab towns or villages were connected by 1936, or on what terms; whether the bypassing Meiton describes was planned or followed from where the company chose to build; or how the Mavromatis case ended.

sections.h: Counting the Country
sections.html:
Rutenberg's grid followed the map of Jewish settlement; the census showed how small that map still was. Every later argument about Palestine, about immigration, land and partition, rests on numbers, and the most important of them were gathered by the British administration in these years. Two slogans have grown up around those numbers, one on each side. The first says Palestine was "a land without a people." The second says Palestinian Arabs owned 94 percent of the land. Neither survives the Mandate's own statistics.

Britain's first census of Palestine, taken in 1922, counted 757,182 people. Of these, 83,794 were Jews, about 11 percent of the population [cite:jvl_census_1931]. The second census, in 1931, found Jews at 17 percent of the population, Muslims at 73 percent and Christians at 9 percent [cite:jvl_census_1931]. In nine years the Jewish population had doubled. Yet the growth of the non-Jewish population over the same years was larger than the entire Jewish population [cite:jvl_census_1931]. The 1931 census also asked where people were born: 42 percent of Jews had been born in Palestine and 58 percent abroad [cite:jvl_census_1931]. The Yishuv of 1931 was, by a clear majority, a community of immigrants, though a substantial share was native-born.

The line above traces the Jewish share of the population across three counts: about 11 percent in 1922, 17 percent in 1931 and about 33 percent at the end of 1946 [cite:jvl_census_1931] [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]. The first two points are British census results. The third is an estimate, made by the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP). UNSCOP put the population at the end of 1946 at about 1,846,000: roughly 1,203,000 Arabs (65 percent) and 608,000 Jews (33 percent) [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]. Over almost the same span, British records count 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946 [cite:ssrn_mandate_immigration]. How those arrivals were distributed year by year, and why two published series for the same years disagree, is taken up in [scene:rd3_aliyot|the immigration section].

These three figures frame the period. The 757,182 people of 1922 are the country as Britain found it when the Mandate began; the 376,415 recorded Jewish immigrants of 1920–1946 are the arrivals that changed its composition; and the roughly 1.85 million of late 1946 are the country UNSCOP had in front of it when it made its recommendation [cite:jvl_census_1931] [cite:ssrn_mandate_immigration] [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]. Even at the end of 1946, after a quarter-century of immigration, about two in three of the inhabitants were Arabs.

A second count from these years does not match the census. The Jewish Agency's economic case to the Peel Commission in 1937 put the Jewish population of 1922 at 84,000, or 13 percent, on a non-Jewish base of only 565,000 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. That paper was advocacy, and its figures are examined in [scene:us_s06|the economy section]; this book uses the census figure of about 11 percent.
