His forecast was that the Labour government would not try to implement it, and would instead "modify or repeal the White Paper policy of 1939," above all on immigration, since the remaining quota would soon be exhausted. He also expected the government to consult the Soviet and American governments before deciding Palestine's future status. [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale]

The distance between the two columns is the mechanism this section turns on. A party conference could adopt a resolution; only a government could change the policy of the mandatory power, and a government answered to considerations a conference did not have to weigh. Yale's reading was that the Labour government would act on the part of its record that was narrow and legal, its objection to the White Paper's immigration limits, and would leave aside the part that called for moving a population and redrawing borders. He also read the decision as one Britain would no longer take alone: the future status of Palestine, in his forecast, would be settled only after consulting the Soviet and American governments.

The memorandum is a forecast, not an outcome. Whether the Labour government modified the White Paper, how it handled immigration once the quota ran out, and how its relations with Washington over Palestine developed belong to the postwar period and are told in the next stage of this history. What this record establishes is the starting point: a party pledged by its own words in 1939 and 1944 against the White Paper, and an American diplomat predicting in July 1945 that it would keep the first pledge in a modified form and not the second.

Much of the British side of these years is not documented in the sources used here. They do not name the Colonial Secretaries who served during the war, the High Commissioners who governed Palestine on Britain's behalf, or the deliberations of the wartime cabinet on Palestine's future, and they do not cover the appointment of the Labour government's Foreign Secretary. Who governed Palestine for Britain during the war, and how that government's thinking moved between 1939 and 1945, is therefore a question this chapter cannot yet answer.

chapters.label: Stage Five
chapters.title: Execute
chapters.intro:
In the summer of 1945 the war in Europe was over, and the full scale of the Holocaust was becoming documented and public. [cite:sonneborn_toi] Palestine was still a British Mandate, and Britain had a new government: Clement Attlee formed his Labour cabinet on 26 July 1945, with Ernest Bevin as Foreign Secretary. [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] In Washington, Harry Truman had been President since 12 April, when Franklin Roosevelt died one week after putting in writing his assurance to Ibn Saud that nothing would be done hostile to the Arabs without consultation. Truman had been Vice President for eighty-two days and arrived with no foreign-policy experience. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The Arab League, founded that March, stood for a "unitary and independent Palestinian state." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] The Arab Higher Committee, the Palestinian Arabs' leading body, had not functioned for years and would be re-established only in 1946, by a decision of the Arab League; the man who would chair it, Hajj Amin al-Husayni, was being held by France. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] In New York, David Ben-Gurion had already reached a judgment of his own: that the Arab states would go to war, and that the Haganah had neither the weapons nor the money to survive it. [cite:sonneborn_toi]

Three years later the Mandate was gone, a Jewish state had been proclaimed and recognized, and some 700,000 Palestinian Arabs had become refugees. This stage asks how that happened in so short a time: who decided each step, through what instrument, with whose money and whose arms, and who objected. It asks with equal weight what the Palestinian Arab leadership and the Arab states chose to do, and what they were unable to do. The answer is not one decision but a chain of them, taken in London, Washington, Lake Success, Cairo, Amman, Prague and Tel Aviv, and it ends in a war that produced, in the same months, a state for one people and what the other calls the Nakba, the "catastrophe."

The cast is the widest of any stage. In London stood Bevin, Attlee and the Colonial Secretary Arthur Creech Jones. In Washington the President's political advisers, Clark Clifford and David Niles, and his old business partner Eddie Jacobson, faced the Secretary of State George Marshall, the State Department's Loy Henderson and Robert Lovett, the Defense Secretary James Forrestal, the Joint Chiefs and a newly created CIA. The Jewish Agency worked through Ben-Gurion, Chaim Weizmann, Moshe Shertok and Golda Meyerson, and through American supporters such as Rudolf Sonneborn, Henry Montor and Abba Hillel Silver; the Irgun under Menachem Begin, and Lehi, fought on their own account. On the Arab side were the Arab Higher Committee under the Mufti and Jamal Husseini, the commanders Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni and Fawzi al-Qawuqji, the Arab League, and King Abdullah of Transjordan with his British-officered Arab Legion. Andrei Gromyko spoke for Moscow. Dissenters, among them the American Council for Judaism, Judah Magnes and Hannah Arendt, objected throughout and were outweighed.

The sections follow the chain roughly in the order it was forged. They begin with the change of president and the men around him, Truman's own recorded words, and the July 1945 meeting in [scene:s07d|Sonneborn's apartment] that founded an arms network on American soil. Bevin's policy, the Anglo-American Committee and the Jewish armed campaign of 1945–46 lead to Operation Agatha and the King David Hotel. The Jewish Agency's early turn to partition, the White House's inner channels and Britain's decision to hand Palestine to the United Nations set the stage for the Soviet turn, the UN special committee, the written warnings of State, the Pentagon and the CIA, and the dissenters at home. Resolution 181 is followed by the Arab League's control of Palestinian decision-making, the civil war that began on 1 December 1947, the violence against Jews in Arab cities, and the money and arms of early 1948. Plan Dalet, Washington's retreat to trusteeship, Deir Yassin, the fall of the mixed towns and Abdullah's double course lead to independence and the Nakba, recognition, the Arab states' war and [scene:s10b|the actual military balance]. The stage closes with the making of one army and with [scene:rd5_refugees|the refugees], whose return the new government had refused by June 1948.
chapters.outro:
By the end of 1948 the structure that had governed Palestine since 1922 was gone, and what replaced it had been built in three years by different hands, each holding something the others did not.

The legal layer was thinner than it looked. Resolution 181, adopted on 29 November 1947 by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstaining, recommended two states, an economic union and an international Jerusalem, on a timetable that ran to 1 October 1948; Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen said they regarded it as a recommendation and would not be bound by it. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] Britain, which had abstained, declined in September 1947 to impose any policy "by force of arms," so the plan's handover had no one to carry it out. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_creechjones] The Declaration of 14 May 1948 rested the state on "natural and historic right" and on three international instruments, promised equal rights "irrespective of religion, race or sex," stated no borders, and set a constitution deadline of 1 October 1948 that passed without one. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] Recognition came by executive act: American de facto recognition eleven minutes after the proclamation, Soviet de jure recognition on 17 May, American de jure recognition on 31 January 1949, Britain's in January 1949. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit] Resolution 194 of December 1948 affirmed a right of return that, as of 2026, has not been implemented. [cite:morris_1948]

The administrative layer was the most complete, because most of it already existed. The Jewish Agency's institutions became a government's. The order of 26 May 1948 made the Israel Defense Forces the only lawful armed force; the shelling of the Altalena on 22 June and the arrests after Lehi killed Count Bernadotte on 17 September enforced it, and an amnesty in February 1949 released those arrested. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination]

The financial layer was private and transnational. The Sonneborn network bought and smuggled material from 1945, some 800 shipments and about 2,400 tons, while, by one account, the Justice Department declined FBI recommendations to prosecute key figures; nine men were tried only in 1950. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] [cite:forward_oss] [cite:schwimmer_wiki] Golda Meyerson's tour was reported to have raised $50 million in about two months, spent largely on weapons. [cite:jwa_golda_50m] The library's funding ledger puts the 1948 United Jewish Appeal at a record $150 million, of which $74.7 million went to the Palestine share. Czechoslovakia sold arms with Soviet consent for almost $14.5 million by its own foreign minister's figure, though estimates run to about $90 million. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] Against this stood an American embargo and, by the same ledger, a British bill of about £100 million for its forces in 1945–47.

The Palestinian Arab layer was the weakest, and the record shows both choices and constraints. The Arab Higher Committee was re-established in 1946 "by a decision of the Arab League," its chairman the Mufti, who had spent the war allied with the Axis and led from Cairo. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] It boycotted UNSCOP, rejected partition, and promised a "line of fire and blood." [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:wiki_un_partition_plan] In February 1948 the League refused it a government-in-exile and a loan; its Army of the Holy War and the League's Arab Liberation Army did not cooperate. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] [cite:rs_rd5_lodz_2019] By the end of the year two bodies claimed to speak for Palestinians, a government in Gaza and a congress at Jericho, and on the UN's technical estimate about 711,000 had become refugees. [cite:rs_rd5_unccp_1949] As early as June 1948 Israel's cabinet had reached a consensus against their return. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref]

The regional layer was a coalition of states with different ends. The League's cablegram of 15 May spoke of restoring "law and order" and of a "United State of Palestine"; Lebanon chose war deliberately, Saudi Arabia sent a contingent under Egyptian command, and the Arab Legion, on the Office of the Historian's account, entered only areas assigned to the Arab state or Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] [cite:lebanon_1948_war] [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] The armistices of 1949 left Egypt in Gaza and Jordan on the West Bank, with about 78 percent of Mandate Palestine under Israeli control. [cite:morris_1948] In Arab cities the vote set off riots against Jews, and the governments of Egypt and Iraq followed with arrests, sequestrations and, in Iraq, a law against Zionism. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities] [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951]

The American layer was a government divided against itself. Henderson, the Joint Chiefs, Forrestal and the CIA warned in writing; the President's political advisers prevailed; the delegation retreated to trusteeship on 19 March and was still arguing for it when the President recognized the state. [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994] [cite:cia_ore55] [cite:rs_rd5_avalon_austin] [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition]

What was settled was the existence of the state, its army and the lines its army held. What was contested was nearly everything about how. Zionist leaders could point to a UN plan they accepted, a rejection announced as a "line of fire and blood," and a Declaration that offered Arab citizens equality; Palestinian leaders and their historians to a plan that gave a majority of the land to a community owning under a tenth of it, to statehood for a largely immigrant minority while the majority was denied self-determination, and, in Khalidi's reading, to a displacement written into Plan Dalet's village clause. Whether that plan was a design for removal or a military plan whose expulsions were decided locally remains argued between Morris and Khalidi. So are Truman's motive, Abdullah's understanding with the Agency, and how far the insurgency drove Britain out. The record also leaves things open: a refugee count that runs from about 520,000 to 957,000 depending on who counted and how, Arab war dead not compiled in these sources, and Deir Yassin's archives still partly closed. [cite:rs_rd5_prrn_1996] [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] Above all it leaves the refugees themselves, outside the lines and refused return, the question [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194] inherited.

sections.h: FDR Dies, Truman Chooses
sections.html:
The American decision on Israel was made by a president whom almost no one, three years earlier, had expected to be making it. The story of that decision therefore begins not in 1948, and not even in 1945, but at the Democratic convention in Chicago in 1944.

Henry Wallace had served as Franklin Roosevelt's Vice President since 1941. He was a progressive in the full sense of the word in his time: pro-labor, anti-imperialist and anti-colonial, an early and forceful advocate of civil rights well ahead of the American political mainstream, and a supporter of accommodation rather than confrontation with the Soviet Union. To the Democratic Party's conservative and machine wings he was unacceptable. At the 1944 convention, with an ailing Roosevelt unlikely to survive another term, the party bosses maneuvered Wallace off the ticket and replaced him with a compromise choice, the little-known senator from Missouri, Harry Truman. [cite:wiki_choosing_truman] [cite:trumanlibrary_missouri_compromise] Wallace went on to run for president on the Progressive Party ticket in 1948, lost badly, and died in 1965. [cite:wiki_choosing_truman] The fuller account of his removal, including the reasons behind it and Wallace's own Zionist sympathies, belongs to an earlier part of this book; what matters here is the single substitution and its timing.

Roosevelt himself had one more Middle Eastern act left. In February 1945, aboard the USS Quincy in the Suez Canal, he met King Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia and gave assurances that no action would be taken hostile to the Arab people without consultation. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] A letter of 5 April put the assurance in writing. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] One week later, on 12 April 1945, Roosevelt, born in 1882, died at Warm Springs, Georgia, less than three months into his new term and before any of the postwar decisions on Palestine had to be made. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] That meeting and that letter are told in full in [scene:s07ca|FDR and Ibn Saud]. Their place in this chapter is only their timing: the president who had given the assurance did not live to be tested by it.

What Roosevelt would have done had he lived cannot be known, and this book does not pretend to know it. The record shows the promise and the date of the death, side by side, and nothing more. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud]

One interpretive reading, and it is a reading rather than a documented finding, draws a larger lesson from the 1944 convention. On this reading, but for the convention maneuver, Henry Wallace and not Harry Truman would have become president in April 1945, and the 1948 recognition of Israel, along with the opening of the Cold War, might have unfolded very differently. The reading uses Wallace to mark the contingency of the whole story: an American commitment to Israel that is often narrated as destiny turned, at its origin, on a party back-room and a single substitution, so that "FDR dies, Truman chooses" became the operative sequence only because the machine had already chosen Truman over Wallace four years before recognition. The reading's own limit should be stated as plainly as its claim. Wallace's dated removal is documented; what Wallace would have decided about recognition had he been president is not, and no record can supply it. The counterfactual is untestable, and it is offered here as a way of seeing the period, not as a conclusion about it. [cite:wiki_choosing_truman]

Truman, born in 1884, a Missouri Democrat and a former haberdasher turned senator, had been Vice President for eighty-two days when Roosevelt died. He arrived in the presidency with no prior foreign-policy experience and minimal briefing on the major foreign questions then pending. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] Over the next three years he would make the single decision on which this chapter's American story turns, and he would make it with a recurring cast around him. That cast is set out here, because its members reappear, in one combination or another, at each American turning point between 1945 and 1948.

The first is Clark Clifford (1906–1998), White House Special Counsel. In November 1947 Clifford sent Truman a memo arguing that the Jewish-American vote was likely decisive in several key swing states, New York, Pennsylvania and Illinois, for Truman's uncertain reelection prospects in 1948, and framing early and unambiguous recognition of a Jewish state as electorally advantageous. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] This is not a reconstruction by later historians from indirect evidence. Clifford's own memoir, Counsel to the President, published in 1991, openly describes this domestic-political framework as part of the advice he actually gave Truman, and acknowledges both Marshall's opposition and the argument between the two men. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] It is a rare case of a key adviser putting his own strategic reasoning on the record, after the fact, in his own words, and it is the strongest single document behind the reading that electoral politics drove the timing of recognition. A related document appears in another source: a November 1947 memo to Truman titled "The Politics of 1948 and the Jews," which analyzed the Jewish vote for the coming election. [cite:jvl_truman_index] The sources used here do not say whether that title and Clifford's memo are one document or two.

The second figure is the man who objected to Clifford most strongly. George Marshall, Secretary of State, architect of the strategy that won the war in Europe and of the Marshall Plan, was one of the most prestigious figures in postwar American public life. He told Truman directly: "If you follow Clifford's advice and if I were to vote in the election, I would vote against you." [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] He threatened to resign. Because his standing was so uniquely high, his opposition was politically dangerous to the President. Truman recognized Israel anyway, and Marshall did not resign. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] Marshall's decision not to carry out the threat is itself part of the documented record; it does not show that his broader relationship with Truman was permanently damaged.

Behind Marshall stood the third element of the cast, the professional State Department. Loy Henderson, director of Near Eastern Affairs, Under Secretary Robert Lovett and Marshall himself opposed early recognition. Their argument was cold strategic realism: recognizing a Jewish state would damage American relations with the Arab world, jeopardize access to Middle Eastern oil at the opening of the Cold War, and possibly require American troops to enforce partition. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] The written warnings they and others filed in the autumn of 1947 belong to a later section of this chapter. The pattern they form is the point here, and it is a pattern this book meets again: the permanent foreign-service establishment judged support for the Zionist program to be against American strategic interest, and the elected political leadership overruled it. Not every career diplomat held an identical view; what is on record is the opposition of these named senior officials.

The fourth figure entered by a door that no organization chart shows. Eddie Jacobson, an American Jew from Kansas City, was Truman's old army comrade and his former partner in a men's clothing store, Truman & Jacobson, which went bankrupt in the early 1920s; Jacobson had been best man at Truman's wedding and remained one of his most trusted friends. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] By March 1948 Truman, worn down by Zionist lobbying, had refused to see Chaim Weizmann through official channels. Jacobson went to the Oval Office and, invoking their friendship and Truman's admiration for the aging Zionist leader, persuaded the President to receive Weizmann privately. That meeting, on 18 March 1948, is documented in multiple biographies and in Truman's own recollections, and historians widely credit it with securing Truman's commitment to recognition. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] Jacobson's documented contribution is that one meeting; the record does not give him a broader coordinating role in the recognition decision.

The meeting with Weizmann had an immediate and awkward sequel. The very next day the American delegation at the United Nations announced a retreat from partition toward a temporary trusteeship, and the collision between what the President had told Weizmann in private and what his diplomats said in public is the subject of [scene:rd5_trusteeship|Washington's retreat in March 1948].

The end of this American arc can be stated briefly here. On 14 May 1948, at 6:11 p.m. Washington time, eleven minutes after David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel in Tel Aviv, the United States extended de facto recognition, with Clifford arranging the timing and Marshall's professionals, and the American delegation still arguing for trusteeship at the United Nations, left uninformed. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] De jure recognition followed in January 1949, after Truman's election victory; the Soviet Union had extended full de jure recognition first, in May 1948. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The constitutional basis of the President's power to act alone, and the comparison with other governments, are taken up in [scene:rec_s01|who recognizes a nation].

Why did Truman do it? One account in the sources gives a pointed answer. On its reading, the recognition was primarily a domestic political calculation for the 1948 election, orchestrated by Clifford: Marshall threatened to resign, the State Department opposed, and the President's personal channel to Zionist leadership ran through his former business partner. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] Eleven minutes, on this reading, is not the interval of a deliberative foreign-policy consensus; it is the interval of a decision executed for maximum effect by a president facing a hard election. Truman's own memoir later presented the recognition as principled, and Clifford's memoir and Marshall's documented opposition tell a different story. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] The case is strengthened by Clifford's own admission, which is first-person evidence and not inference.

The familiar account holds the opposite: that Truman recognized Israel out of moral conviction. That account has evidence too, and the strongest form of it rests on Truman's own words. As a senator in 1943, years before any recognition question or any campaign money, he spoke at a mass rally for Europe's Jews, as the next section shows. In February 1947 he publicly called the impression that partisan and local politics motivated American policy on Palestine "most unfortunate and misleading," and said his position had been consistent since 1945. [cite:jvl_truman_feb1947] The same documents that show Clifford's arithmetic also show that Truman was pressed by Zionist lobbying to the point of refusing to see Weizmann, and that it took a friend's personal appeal, not a political operative's, to change his mind about that meeting. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel]

The evidence on both sides does not resolve into a single cause, and the sources say as much themselves. Clifford's memo documents one real and significant thread in the decision; it does not show that electoral calculation was the only factor, or that humanitarian and strategic considerations played no part. Multiple motives existing together is the more accurate picture than any single-cause explanation. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] What the record does show, specifically, is a president with little foreign-policy grounding moving faster than his own government's formal machinery, guided partly through a personal relationship outside normal channels, against the explicit, documented objection of his Secretary of State. That was not a uniquely corrupt way for foreign policy to be made; personal relationships and domestic pressure shape presidential decisions in many administrations and on many issues. It was, however, plainly not the product of careful interagency deliberation reaching a clean consensus. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition]

The cast also answers a different and more corrosive question, one the record settles more firmly than the question of motive. Accounts of 1948 as a hidden-hand operation, in which an organized interest secretly controlled American policy, cannot accommodate the documents. A plot that controls a government does not have that government's Secretary of State, its Near Eastern division and its oil-strategic establishment fighting it openly in signed memoranda, as Marshall and Henderson did. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] Nor was Jacobson a secret agent; he was the opposite. His role shows the actual texture of the decision: friendship, fatigue, sentiment and access, one old friend reaching a tired president while the professional foreign service advised the other way. To readers inclined to conspiracy he looks like proof of hidden influence; on the record he is proof of something more ordinary, that a haberdasher's personal loyalty could move a president when the State Department could not, and that the channel was a friendship documented in biographies, not a secret. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] What 1948 shows, in this reading of the evidence, is convergence and contingency: a president's political judgment prevailing over his own experts, not coordinated control.

What remains open is the weight of each motive in Truman's own mind. The record establishes the sequence: the 1944 substitution, the April 1945 death, the November 1947 memo, Marshall's threat, the 18 March meeting, the eleven minutes. It establishes who argued what. It does not establish which argument decided the President, and no document yet found does. Nor can it say what Roosevelt, or Wallace, would have done in Truman's place; those questions are counterfactuals, and they stay open by their nature.

sections.h: Truman in His Own Words, 1943–1948
sections.html:
If no document settles which argument decided the President, his own words are the nearest evidence there is. Harry Truman is often remembered as a lifelong and uncomplicated champion of a Jewish state. The record of what he himself said and did between 1943 and May 1948, before any campaign money of the 1948 election entered the story, does not support so simple a picture, and it does not support the opposite picture either. It shows a public conviction, a frank awareness of voters, and a private irritation at the pressure he was under, all in the same man and in the same years. This section sets out those words in order, and identifies each for what it is: a public speech, an official record, a single witness's later account, a private diary.

The first item comes from Truman's years in the Senate. In April 1943, before he was Vice President and long before any decision about Palestine was his to make, Senator Truman spoke at a mass rally in Chicago Stadium urging help for Europe's Jews. According to David McCullough's biography, he said that under "mad Hitler" they were being "herded like animals" into camps. [cite:csm_truman_diary_2003] Whatever weight one gives later political motives, this was said by a senator with no Palestine policy of his own to defend, and it is the earliest documented evidence for the humanitarian side of his outlook.

The second item is the most often quoted, and it needs the most careful handling. On 10 November 1945, seven months into his presidency, Truman met his chiefs of mission from the Arab world. The meeting itself is in the State Department's official record. [cite:frus_1945_chiefs_mission] The words most often attributed to him there are not. They come from William Eddy, the American minister to Saudi Arabia, who attended and who wrote, in a pamphlet published in 1954, that Truman had told the diplomats: "I'm sorry, gentlemen, but I have to answer to hundreds of thousands who are anxious for the success of Zionism; I do not have hundreds of thousands of Arabs among my constituents." The historian John Judis has quoted Eddy's account. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_globe] Three cautions apply to it, and all three should be kept in view. It rests on a single witness. It was written down nine years after the meeting. And Eddy was himself a State Department opponent of Zionism, so his account comes from a witness with a settled view of the policy under discussion. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_globe] None of that proves the quotation false; Eddy was in the room. It does mean that the remark, however vivid, cannot carry the weight of an official record, and a careful reader should treat it as one participant's recollection of what was said.

The third item is public and dated. On 4 October 1946, the eve of Yom Kippur and a month before the midterm elections, Truman issued a statement urging immediate large-scale immigration to Palestine and saying the United States could support a viable Jewish state "in an adequate area of Palestine." [cite:avalon_yomkippur_1946] The statement, the advisers around it and the argument over its timing are the subject of [scene:wh_s01|inside the White House]; here it marks the point at which a president's stated sympathy and an election calendar first visibly coincided.

The fourth item was never meant to be read by anyone else. On 21 July 1947, after Henry Morgenthau telephoned him about the refugees aboard the ship Exodus, Truman wrote in his private diary: "The Jews, I find are very, very selfish." He added that once underdogs gain power, "neither Hitler nor Stalin has anything on them for cruelty." [cite:jvl_truman_diary_1947] [cite:aljazeera_truman_diary] The diary was found at the Truman Library and released by the National Archives in 2003. [cite:cbs_truman_diary] [cite:csm_truman_diary_2003] The entry should be named for what it is. It is a sweeping judgment about Jews as a people, written by a sitting president in anger at a particular telephone call, and it is antisemitic in the plain sense of the word. It is also private, written by the same man who had spoken at the Chicago rally four years earlier and who would recognize Israel ten months later. The entry is evidence of how the pressure felt to him; it is not, by itself, evidence of what his policy would be, and ten months later he recognized the Jewish state.

The fifth group of items brings the record to the decision itself. In November 1947 a memo to Truman titled "The Politics of 1948 and the Jews" analyzed the Jewish vote for the coming election. [cite:jvl_truman_index] In March 1948, after refusing to see Zionist leaders, he met Chaim Weizmann at the urging of his old business partner Eddie Jacobson. [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] [cite:jvl_truman_index] On 14 May 1948 he granted de facto recognition to Israel eleven minutes after its proclamation, against the opposition of Secretary of State George Marshall. [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] [cite:jvl_truman_index] Four days later, on 18 May 1948, he described American Jews as "very emotional." The people around those decisions, Clifford, Marshall and Jacobson among them, are introduced in [scene:s08|the preceding section].

Read together, these items resist every single-motive story. Those who see Truman as a man of principle can point to the 1943 rally, given years before any Palestine decision was his, and to a recognition decision he took against the most respected member of his own cabinet. Those who see electoral calculation can point to Eddy's account, to the Yom Kippur timing and to the November 1947 memo on the Jewish vote. Those who see reluctance can point to the diary, to his refusal to see Zionist leaders until a friend intervened, and to the "very emotional" remark days after recognition. Each reading is built from real documents. None of them accounts for all of the documents.

The fairest summary of the record is that humanitarian conviction, open awareness of voters and private resentment of the pressure all appear in it, in the same man and in the same years, before any 1948 campaign money had changed hands. The record shows that all three were present. It does not show which of them decided the outcome, and this book does not claim to know. The remark attributed to him in November 1945, which would bear most directly on that question, is the one item that rests on a single witness who opposed the policy it describes.

sections.h: The Meeting in Sonneborn's Apartment, July 1945
sections.html:
A common account of Israel's founding war holds that its weapons arrived only after May 1948, once the state existed and could ask the world for help. The documents place the start of the supply effort almost three years earlier, in a private apartment in Manhattan, in the summer that the war in Europe ended.

By July 1945 the fighting in Europe was over, and the full scale of the Holocaust was becoming documented and public. David Ben-Gurion, chairman of the Jewish Agency Executive and the de facto head of the Yishuv, the Jewish community of Palestine, had traveled from Palestine to New York with a specific purpose. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] His assessment, made three years before independence and not in response to any declared war, was that the Arab states would go to war against the Jews of Palestine, and that the Haganah, the Yishuv's underground defense force, had neither the weapons nor the money to survive such a war. [cite:sonneborn_toi] He needed a supply and financing pipeline in America, and it was a task he could not ask the Jewish Agency to carry out openly. [cite:mexico_arms_1948]

The meeting took place in the Manhattan apartment of Rudolf Sonneborn, a wealthy New York industrialist and scion of an oil-and-chemical business, who had traveled to Palestine himself and formed a friendship with Ben-Gurion. [cite:sonneborn_toi] [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The sources differ slightly on who called it. One account has Ben-Gurion convening the meeting; another has Sonneborn convening it at Ben-Gurion's request. [cite:sonneborn_toi] [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The two are compatible: the request was Ben-Gurion's, the room Sonneborn's. The man who gathered the guests was Henry Montor, who by 1948 was executive vice-chairman of the United Jewish Appeal, a connection that would matter again in 1948 when the same Montor arranged Golda Meyerson's appeal to the American federations, told in [scene:us_s07|Golda Meyerson's American tour]. [cite:jta_golda_1948]

The sources also differ on the date and the number present, in small but real ways. One account dates the meeting to 1 July 1945; another says only that it took place on a July afternoon. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] [cite:sonneborn_toi] Accounts describe roughly seventeen prominent Jewish businessmen in the room. [cite:sonneborn_toi] One account gives seventeen American businessmen in one place and seventeen Americans and one Canadian in another. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] Ben-Gurion warned them of the coming war and of the Haganah's poverty, and the men in the room, moved, by later accounts, by the warning together with the recent revelation of the Holocaust's scale, agreed that same afternoon to build what became a Jewish-American arms underground. [cite:sonneborn_toi]

How much weight that last detail can bear needs saying. Firsthand descriptions of the meeting, including Leonard Slater's 1970 book The Pledge, were written decades afterwards, sympathetically, by an author who interviewed participants long after the fact. [cite:sonneborn_toi] The meeting itself, its date, its convener and the organization that came out of it are well documented. Any single participant's stated motives, recorded a quarter-century later, deserve the caution owed to any retrospective account. The record also does not show that every donor or participant fully understood, at the time, that the network would be operating illegally. [cite:sonneborn_toi]

What emerged from the meeting was the Sonneborn Institute, a network that became the financial and logistical backbone of the Haganah's transatlantic supply effort. [cite:sonneborn_jps] [cite:ampalestine_haganah] It was not a fundraising drive in the ordinary sense. It was the operating base of an armed procurement effort that ran for three years outside any registered or public channel, and by one account continuously until 1949. [cite:sonneborn_toi] Ben-Gurion directed its formation; the day-to-day American procurement work was run by Sonneborn and a small operational circle. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] Sonneborn received no formal recognition for his part beyond a private letter of thanks from Ben-Gurion after Israel was founded. [cite:sdjw_winters]

The network worked through a front company, and here the sources disagree on its name. One historical account calls it Materials for Palestine; another calls it Materials for Israel. [cite:sonneborn_jps] [cite:mexico_arms_1948] They also describe its cover somewhat differently. In one account it operated under the guise of an ordinary commercial and charitable enterprise, providing cover for buying and shipping machinery, tools and industrial materials, legally purchasable surplus, destined for Ta'as, the Yishuv's clandestine arms-production effort. [cite:sonneborn_jps] In the other, the network operated under the legal cover of a charity for European Jewish relief, raising funds and moving industrial equipment, machine tools and eventually munitions toward Haganah forces in Palestine. [cite:ampalestine_haganah] [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The two descriptions are not contradictory so much as describing different stages: the first stresses the legal machinery bought for production inside Palestine, the second the move toward finished munitions as the war drew closer.

The methods are documented end to end. Donors gave money for which no receipts were issued. The front company bought under its commercial or charitable cover. Shipments moved under falsified manifests and disguised invoices, routed through Panama, Mexico, Czechoslovakia, Canada and France to evade American export controls, and arrived with Haganah forces in Palestine. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] By the time the United States formally tightened arms-export enforcement under the Neutrality Act in December 1947, the network already had two years of working tradecraft in place. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The scale it reached, about 2,400 tons in some 800 consignments by one count, and the routes, aircraft and trials of its working years are told in [scene:s07e|the arms network in operation]. [cite:mexico_arms_1948]

The structure was designed around one legal fact. What the network did was, under American law, illegal arms export, and the people who built it arranged matters so that the official Jewish Agency would not be directly exposed. Historians who have documented the network note that it was kept deliberately separate from the Agency, and that this compartmentalization was a choice, not an accident of organization. [cite:sonneborn_jps] They also note that the separation was not total. Abba Hillel Silver, chairman of the Jewish Agency's American section, served as a liaison between the two. [cite:sonneborn_jps] The record therefore shows both things at once: a structure built to insulate the Agency, and a named senior figure connecting it to the Agency anyway. It does not show that the Agency was unaware of what the network did, nor does it give an account of what each Agency official individually knew.

Where the money came from, and how much there was, is less well recorded than how it moved. Donors were issued no receipts. The sources give no total for what the Sonneborn circle raised or spent, and no ledger of individual shipments or transactions. [cite:sonneborn_jps] The panel below places the network in the longer sequence of channels that paid for the Yishuv's defense, from the Jewish Agency's own budget and a community levy of the 1930s to the American appeals of 1948.

That sequence matters because the Sonneborn network sat in the middle of it, and because the same people moved along it. Montor's role in both the 1945 meeting and the 1948 appeal shows that the arms network and the open federation-and-appeal fundraising overlapped directly through named individuals. [cite:jta_golda_1948] Among the network's key financiers was Abraham Feinberg, who met repeatedly with Sonneborn and later founded Americans for Haganah. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] In 1952 the United States government would order him to register as a foreign agent, a later chapter of his story told in [scene:s07f2|Abraham Feinberg]. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file]

The procurement network had an intelligence counterpart. The first Jewish intelligence organization in Palestine had been established under the Haganah in 1929, and the Shai (Sherut Yediot, the Information Service) was set up in 1940 as the Haganah's intelligence and counter-espionage arm. [cite:shai_wiki] By 1948, according to one account, the Shai had 68 staff, 60 British and Jewish agents and 80 Arab agents, and spent nearly $700,000 a year. Its stated objectives were to promote an independent Israeli state, to infiltrate British Mandate offices, to collect intelligence for propaganda, to penetrate Arab factions, and to secure the Rekhesh arms-smuggling operations. It had American branches, Zionist networks in New York and Detroit that served as procurement and intelligence points, and these were not registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. [cite:shai_wiki] [cite:ips_espionage] After 1948 the Shai became the seed from which Israeli military intelligence grew, and its American networks formed the early North American foundation of the Mossad. [cite:shai_wiki]

Rekhesh, Hebrew for "acquisitions," was the Haganah's arms and munitions procurement branch in the United States in the mid-1940s. It built an extensive illegal procurement network despite the arms embargo on the Palestine region. Its operations were funded by American Jewish donors and involved buying surplus military equipment from demobilized United States Army stocks and from black-market dealers, then smuggling it out through covert shipping routes, often with the help of organized crime to get around export controls. [cite:ips_espionage] [cite:medium_zionist] One account describes the networks as violating both American export law and the British arms embargo. [cite:forward_oss]

The federal government knew. The FBI documented these operations and repeatedly recommended that key figures be prosecuted or required to register as foreign agents; the Justice Department declined each time. [cite:forward_oss] [cite:medium_zionist] One case shows the pattern in detail. The attorney William Bernstein, according to the FBI, trained Mossad agents, incorporated companies that smuggled arms for Zionist groups, and conducted surveillance of Arab delegates at the United Nations; the Bureau linked him to sophisticated technical surveillance of Arab officials and to break-ins at consular offices. The Justice Department declined every FBI recommendation that Bernstein be prosecuted or made to register. [cite:ips_espionage] [cite:medium_zionist] The enforcement record, set side by side, is uneven rather than empty. Federal agencies, the FBI and Customs among them, were aware of the network while it operated. No prosecution of its top organizers, Sonneborn or Feinberg, is documented. At least one participant, Charlie Winters, was convicted and sentenced to eighteen months; one account adds a $5,000 fine, a detail on which the sources differ, as the account of the network's trials shows. And the operation was not shut down before the 1948 war ended; it continued through the conflict. [cite:mexico_arms_1948]

A second government agency was watching from a different angle. During the war the Office of Strategic Services, the predecessor of the CIA, ran a Palestinian Desk in its Foreign Nationalities Branch that tracked Zionist activity in the United States. [cite:forward_oss_palestine_desk] A 2016 review of declassified documents by the Forward found that much of its information came from Jewish officials, some highly placed in Jewish organizations, who volunteered it as a wartime patriotic duty and not under coercion. [cite:forward_oss] [cite:forward_oss_palestine_desk] Its target list reportedly included Moshe Shertok, later Moshe Sharett, Israel's second prime minister. [cite:forward_oss_palestine_desk] The desk built a picture of which American Jewish leaders were aligned with which Zionist factions; it took no action against the Rekhesh procurement networks. [cite:forward_oss] The two agencies should not be merged into a single "intelligence community." The OSS's wartime foreign-intelligence interest and the FBI's domestic-security interest had separate rationales and separate reporting chains, and they are documented independently. [cite:forward_oss_palestine_desk]

Why the Justice Department declined is the question on which the sources divide. One account, built on FBI records reported by the Forward and on later analysis, argues that the non-enforcement was deliberate and political: the Truman administration was moving toward support for Jewish statehood, and prosecuting the future state's arms networks, or requiring its American political organizations to register as foreign agents, would have been incompatible with that course. On this reading the decision not to enforce was a foreign-policy decision in the form of prosecutorial discretion, and it set a precedent, never reversed, that later shaped pro-Israel lobbying in the United States; the same account traces it to 1963, when Isaiah Kenen, himself formerly registered as a foreign agent, moved the lobbying function from the American Zionist Council to the newly created AIPAC. [cite:forward_oss] [cite:medium_zionist] [cite:ips_espionage] The same sources, in their own accounting, mark the central link as contested. That the FBI recommended prosecution or registration, that the Justice Department declined, and that the procurement operations broke American law are, in their judgment, documented. Whether the Justice Department acted on explicit direction from the Truman White House, or exercised its own discretion, is not established. [cite:forward_oss] The reading of a fixed political will also has to account for the rest of the record of these years: the same administration's State Department opposed early recognition of a Jewish state, as the opening section of this chapter shows, so "the government" did not speak with one voice on Palestine.

The case for the network, as its founders and sympathetic historians put it, also deserves its strongest form. In July 1945 Ben-Gurion expected a war that he believed the Haganah could not survive without weapons it did not have, and a British arms embargo stood between it and the means to get them. On that view the procurement effort was the preparation of a community's defense, organized by American donors who had just learned the full scale of the Holocaust. [cite:sonneborn_toi] [cite:forward_oss] The case against it, as stated in the sources critical of it, is that it was a foreign-directed intelligence and arms operation on American soil that broke American law and was allowed to continue because of whom it served. [cite:forward_oss] [cite:medium_zionist] Both cases rest on the same documented facts: the meeting, the front company, the deliberate separation from the Agency, the false paperwork, and the decisions not to prosecute.

What the record leaves unsettled is substantial. It does not give the total sums raised or spent, or a ledger of shipments. It does not establish what each donor understood about the law when he gave. It records the name of the front company two different ways. It does not show whether the Justice Department's restraint came from the White House or from its own discretion. And by the sources' own account, the full extent of Zionist intelligence operations on American soil in the 1940s is only partly documented, with part of the record still classified. [cite:forward_oss] What it does establish is the starting point: a working, financed, deliberately compartmented supply network on American soil from 1945, three years before the state it was built to arm.

sections.h: Ernest Bevin and the Palestine Question, 1945–1946
sections.html:
In the same month that the network took shape in New York, the power that actually governed Palestine changed hands. Clement Attlee formed his Labour government on 26 July 1945 and chose Ernest Bevin as Foreign Secretary. Bevin had been born on 9 March 1881; he would die on 14 April 1951. [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] Over the next eighteen months his statements set the terms of British policy on Palestine, and his name became attached to it, by the Zionist leaders who fought him, by the Americans who pressed him, and by the historians who have tried to explain him.

His reputation in this story is unusually divided. To Chaim Weizmann and to Christopher Mayhew, who dealt with him, he was a man who disliked Jews. To the historian Alan Bullock, to Ben-Gurion and to Attlee, he was an opponent of a Jewish state, not an enemy of Jews. To a third school, his policy followed from what the Foreign Office took to be Britain's interests in the Middle East, and his personal feelings mattered little. All three readings rest on documents. Before weighing them, it helps to set out what Bevin actually said and did in his first eighteen months.

The general reference works are sparing. Britannica's entry on Bevin offers only one judgment on Palestine: that his plans of 1947–48 "for a federal Jewish-Arab nation or other partition of Palestine collapsed" in the face of the Arab-Israeli conflict. [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] The detail lies in his own statements, in American diplomatic reports, and in the scholarship that has tried to explain him.

The statement of 13 November 1945. Bevin's first major act on Palestine came on 13 November 1945. He announced a "joint Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, under a rotating chairmanship." Until it reported, he said, there would be "no interruption of Jewish immigration at the present monthly rate." The text did not state what that rate was. Looking further ahead, he spoke of a trusteeship agreement that would "supersede the existing mandate." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] The statement also set out the terms in which London saw the problem. Bevin referred to the Palestinian Arabs' "90,000,000 co-religionists in India," and he said that Palestine "does not by itself provide sufficient opportunity" for solving the Jewish problem. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] Read together, the two phrases framed Palestine as one part of an answer for Europe's Jews, not the whole of it, and placed the Arabs of Palestine within a far larger population whose opinion London had to weigh.

The committee itself, its twelve members, its hearings and its report are the subject of [scene:aac_s01|the next section]. What matters here is that the inquiry was Bevin's chosen instrument. It brought Washington into the question, and in the interim it left immigration where it stood.

The same day, Bevin spoke privately to the American ambassador in London, John Winant. Winant's telegram, received in Washington on 14 November 1945, reported that Bevin said he would be willing to "stake his political future on finding solution for Palestine problem," and that he "made a plea against approaching this subject in spirit of racial antagonism." [cite:rs_rd5_frus_winant_1945] The telegram is a primary American record, not Bevin's own text, but it shows how he wished to be understood by the government he most needed to persuade: as a minister who had staked his career on a settlement and who wanted the question kept out of racial politics.

His public words that day did not always match that wish. According to the historian Raphael Langham, Bevin told the House of Commons on 13 November, "We cannot accept the view that the Jews should be driven out of Europe." At a press conference the same day, he warned that if Jews "want to get too much at the head of the queue" there was a danger of an antisemitic reaction. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The first sentence stated a principle: the survivors had a future in Europe and should not be treated as people to be removed from it. The second, read plainly, made the survivors' claims the cause of the hostility they might meet. Langham calls the remark "unfortunate." [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012]

"Too many Jews in New York." The pressure Bevin resisted came above all from the United States, where President Truman was pressing for the admission of Jewish refugees to Palestine. At the Labour Party conference in June 1946, Bevin said of that pressure that "They did not want too many Jews in New York." Langham calls it "a gratuitous sneer." It angered Truman and provoked protests in the United States. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The remark was an antisemitic jibe from a sitting Foreign Secretary. It suggested that American support for Jewish immigration to Palestine was a way of keeping Jews out of America, and it was made at a party conference, in public. Whatever conclusion one reaches about Bevin's policy, the sentence itself needs no softening.

The London conference and the American visit. In September 1946 Britain convened a conference at Lancaster House in London. According to Langham, Bevin told the Arab delegation there that no solution could ignore Jewish claims. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] This sits awkwardly beside the remarks above, and that is part of what makes him hard to read: the same minister who sneered at American motives told the Arab states that Jewish claims had to be part of any settlement. Two months later he traveled to the United States, in November and December 1946. During that visit, Langham writes, Bevin reportedly came to the view that Britain would have to give up the Mandate. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The decision itself, taken in February 1947, belongs to [scene:rd5_britain_exits|Britain's exit], the subject of a later section.

The mechanism. In these months Bevin held the levers that mattered for Palestine: the rate of Jewish immigration, the choice of forum, and the timing of any settlement. The November 1945 statement used each one. It kept immigration at the existing rate rather than opening the gates or closing them, it moved the question into a joint inquiry with the United States, and it pointed toward trusteeship rather than either a Jewish or an Arab state. The parties most affected could not set any of these terms. The Jewish Agency and the Arab representatives could put their cases to the inquiry but could not decide; and Washington, though it pressed hard on immigration, did not govern Palestine. What Bevin could not control was the American response, and his June 1946 remark shows how much that pressure grated.

The dispute over his motives. Why did Bevin oppose a Jewish state? Historians have given three answers, and Langham sets them out side by side. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012]

The first answer is personal hostility. Two contemporaries who dealt with him said so plainly. Christopher Mayhew said that "Ernest detests Jews," and Chaim Weizmann said Bevin was "blinded by his hatred of the Jews." The historian Peter Weiler takes a more careful line: he finds that Bevin "held antisemitic views" but sees "no evidence that they shaped his policy." [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The strength of this case is the remarks themselves, which are on the record and were made in public. Its weakness, as Weiler's own wording shows, is the step from a man's prejudices to the reasons for his decisions.

The second answer is that Bevin was an anti-Zionist, not an antisemite. The historian Alan Bullock wrote that he "was not moved by hatred of the Jews." David Ben-Gurion, who had every reason to think the worst of him, said, "I prefer to consider Bevin simply as an anti-Zionist." Attlee defended him in the same terms in the House of Commons in 1949. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The strength of this case is that it comes in part from Bevin's opponents, Ben-Gurion above all, and that it fits his statement to the Arab delegation in September 1946. Its weakness is that the remarks of November 1945 and June 1946 are hard to describe as political opposition to Zionism alone.

The third answer is strategic interest. A Foreign Office briefing attributed to Harold Beeley stressed Middle East oil, communications and the Suez route as Britain's interests in the region, and Langham cites the historian W. Roger Louis on Britain's Middle East position. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] On this reading, Bevin's policy was the Foreign Office's policy: Britain needed the goodwill of the Arab states and of Muslim opinion, the "90,000,000 co-religionists in India" whom Bevin himself had invoked, and a Jewish state imposed against that opinion would put those interests at risk. The strength of this case is that it explains the policy without needing to explain the man, and that it rests on the Foreign Office's own statement of British interests. Its weakness is that it says little about why the remarks were made.

Langham's own conclusion leans toward the third answer. Bevin, he writes, was probably not motivated by antisemitism when he made policy, and "genuinely thought it was in the best interests of Britain." But his opposition hardened over time into anti-Zionism, and Langham leaves open whether, in that later stage, Bevin crossed into antisemitism. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] That conclusion keeps two things apart that are often run together: what a man said about Jews, which in Bevin's case included antisemitic remarks stated in public, and why his government did what it did, which Langham ties to what Bevin judged to be Britain's interests.

What the record does not settle. The sources used here do not show what "the present monthly rate" of immigration was in November 1945, since Bevin's text gave no figure. They do not show what Bevin said to American officials during his visit in late 1946, only Langham's report that he came to think the Mandate would have to be given up. Nor can any document settle what Bevin felt, as against what he said and did. The remarks are a matter of record; the motive behind the policy remains a matter of judgment, and the historians who have studied him most closely still disagree.

sections.h: The Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, 1945–1946
sections.html:
It is sometimes said that no international body heard the Arab case, or the case for a shared state, before the United Nations voted to partition Palestine in November 1947. The record shows otherwise. More than a year and a half before the vote, a joint British and American committee heard the Jewish Agency, Arab spokesmen, Jewish advocates of a binational state, Christian and Jewish organizations, and the refugees themselves. It then produced a unanimous report that rejected both a Jewish state and an Arab state. What happened next is the more important part of the story. Washington took the one recommendation it wanted and left the rest; London attached a condition to even that one; and the follow-up plan pleased no one.

Twelve members, two governments. The committee was announced in November 1945 by the Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, as a "joint Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, under a rotating chairmanship" (the announcement and its context are told in [scene:rd5_bevin|the section on Bevin]). [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] It was created as Washington pressed London to admit Jewish displaced persons to Palestine, and it was built to share the question between the two governments. It had six American and six British members. The Americans included Bartley Crum and James McDonald; the British included Richard Crossman. [cite:w_aac]

Hearings on three continents. Between January and March 1946 the committee held hearings in Washington, London, the displaced-persons camps of Europe, Cairo and Jerusalem. [cite:w_aac] It took evidence from governments, the Jewish Agency, Arab states and the Arab Office, Christian and Jewish organizations, and refugees in the camps. It was, in the judgment of one account, the most complete hearing of competing cases before 1947. [cite:w_aac]

Three of the cases put to it deserve naming. The Jewish Agency's leaders presented the Zionist case. Arab representatives presented theirs, among them the Arab Office, where the historian Albert Hourani gave testimony that the record describes as notable. [cite:w_aac] The sources used here do not give the substance of what Hourani said, so this book does not paraphrase it. The third case came from Jews who opposed a Jewish state. Judah Magnes, president of the Hebrew University, and the Ihud association argued that Arabs and Jews should share one state with political parity. [cite:w_aac] Their testimony shows that a Jewish alternative to partition was argued, in person, before an official body. It was not a position invented afterward by critics of the state that emerged.

The April 1946 report. The committee reported unanimously in April 1946. It recommended four things. First, the immediate issue of 100,000 immigration certificates for Jewish refugees. Second, the repeal of the 1940 land regulations, which restricted land transfers. Third, the continuation of the Mandate toward a United Nations trusteeship. And fourth, as a principle of the future constitution, that Palestine should be neither a Jewish state nor an Arab state, with neither people dominating the other. [cite:avalon_aac]

The report was a package. The 100,000 certificates answered the plight of the survivors in Europe; the repeal of the 1940 land regulations lifted restrictions on land transfers; trusteeship and the "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle expressed the report's principle that neither people should dominate the other. Unanimity mattered: the six Americans and six Britons had agreed on all of it together.

What Washington kept, and what London required. President Truman publicly endorsed the 100,000 and was silent on the rest. [cite:w_aac] The admission of refugees was popular with American voters. The constitutional recommendation against a Jewish state was not something he endorsed. Prime Minister Attlee answered by tying any admissions to the disarmament of the Jewish and Arab armed groups in Palestine. [cite:w_aac] The British condition was not abstract. At the time, the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi were acting together against British rule, as told in [scene:rd5_revolt|the Jewish Resistance Movement]. By making the 100,000 depend on disarmament, London made the one recommendation Washington wanted depend, in part, on the surrender of arms by Jewish groups then in open revolt against British rule.

Morrison–Grady. The two governments tried once more. In July 1946 a follow-up Anglo-American plan, known as Morrison–Grady, proposed provincial autonomy for Palestine. Zionist and Arab leaders both rejected it, and Truman declined to back it. [cite:w_morrisongrady] With that, the joint Anglo-American attempt to settle Palestine was finished. The question went to the United Nations the following year. [cite:w_morrisongrady]

The mechanism. The episode shows how the decision was structured in 1946. The committee could hear anyone and recommend anything, but it could decide nothing. The two governments could decide, but each took from the report what served its own position. Washington, which did not govern Palestine, could press on the one point that cost it nothing at home and had public support. London, which governed Palestine, could attach conditions. The people heard by the committee, whether the Jewish Agency, the Arab Office, Magnes and Ihud, or the refugees in the camps, had a hearing but no hand in what followed. The binational option that Magnes argued, and that the report's "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle partly echoed, had no government willing to carry it.

The two readings. One reading of this record is that the hearing was real and the outcome was a failure of politics: the committee did its work, and the governments that commissioned it then ignored most of it. Another reading puts it more sharply: what survived into American policy was the part with domestic political value. Both readings start from the same facts. They differ on how much weight to give Truman's own reasons, a question taken up in [scene:wh_s01|the section on the White House]. What neither reading supports is the claim that the Arab and binationalist cases went unheard before 1947. They were heard; they were not adopted.

What the record does not settle. The sources used here name only three of the twelve members, and do not record the committee's internal debates or how it reached unanimity. They do not give the content of Hourani's testimony or of the Jewish Agency's. They do not say what, if anything, London said about the land regulations, trusteeship or the "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle once the report was published, beyond its disarmament condition on the 100,000. And they do not show whether any of the 100,000 certificates were issued as a result of the report.

sections.h: The Jewish Resistance Movement, 1945–1946
sections.html:
For fourteen months after the Second World War, the three Jewish armed organizations in Palestine fought the British together. The Haganah and the two other organizations, the Irgun and Lehi, whose origins are told in [scene:s07e2|the section on the Irgun and Lehi], had been separate commands. In the autumn of 1945 they joined forces for a time. The arrangement they made has a name, the Jewish Resistance Movement, and a beginning and an end that can be dated. What it cost in lives cannot, at least from the source available here.

That source needs to be named before anything else is said. The account of the movement used in this section comes from the Lehi heritage association, which keeps the memory of one of the three organizations. It is written from Lehi's own perspective, and it gives no casualty totals for the movement's operations. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] Every operational detail below is therefore Lehi's account of events, reported as such. British records, Haganah records and independent scholarship on these operations are not part of the material available here for this period.

The agreement. In early September 1945, according to the heritage account, four men agreed to form a united Jewish Resistance Movement: Moshe Sneh and Yisrael Galili for the Haganah, Natan Yellin-Mor for Lehi, and Menachem Begin for the Irgun. The Haganah took part through its Palmach. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] The structure matters. Three separate commands kept their own organizations and their own leaders; what they agreed was to act against the British in concert. As the ending of the movement would show, the Haganah's part in it could be switched off by the Jewish Agency and the Zionist Congress; the Irgun's and Lehi's could not.

The timing also matters. The agreement came in the weeks after a new Labour government took office in London on 26 July 1945. [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] Its Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, did not set out his policy on Palestine until 13 November 1945, when he announced a joint Anglo-American inquiry and said that Jewish immigration would continue only "at the present monthly rate" in the meantime. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] The first coordinated operations came almost two weeks before that statement.

The Night of the Trains, 1 November 1945. Operations began on the night of 1 November 1945, remembered as the "Night of the Trains." At the railway station at Lydda, Lehi and Irgun fighters destroyed three engines and damaged a train and a signal box; some police and railway workers were killed or injured. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] The heritage account does not give their number or their names. The same night, a Lehi bomb at the Haifa refinery went off early and killed the operation's commander, Moshe Bar-Giora. The heritage account itself calls that operation a failure. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance]

The targets of that first night were infrastructure: the railway and the oil refinery. The source that records the deaths and injuries of police and railway workers at Lydda does not count them. That silence is the first of the gaps in this record.

The Night of the Bridges, 17 June 1946. Between the two nights, the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry heard evidence and reported, in April 1946, and the British Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, tied the admission of the 100,000 refugees it recommended to the disarmament of the Jewish and Arab armed groups (see [scene:aac_s01|the Anglo-American Committee]). [cite:w_aac] The resistance movement's answer, in the sense that it was the next major operation the heritage account records, came on 17 June 1946, the "Night of the Bridges." The Palmach attacked eleven bridges across Palestine. The heritage account gives no casualty figure. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] Where the first night had been carried out by Lehi and the Irgun, this one was the Haganah's own operation, through the Palmach.

Britain's answer and the summer of 1946. Twelve days later, on 29 June 1946, Britain launched Operation Agatha, a raid by roughly 17,000 troops and police that arrested more than 2,700 people, including senior Jewish Agency officials, and seized documents from the Agency's Jerusalem headquarters. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] On 22 July 1946 the Irgun, commanded by Begin, bombed the King David Hotel in Jerusalem, killing 91 people. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] Both events are told in the two sections that follow.

The halt. In early August 1946 the Jewish Agency's leadership met in Paris, and there, according to the heritage account, the decision was taken to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met. The Congress, meeting in Basel, decided on 9 December 1946 to halt the armed struggle. After that, in the Lehi account's words, the fight "fell to Lehi and IZL", that is, to Lehi and the Irgun. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance]

The mechanism of the ending is the clearest thing in the record. The movement had been an alliance of three commands, but only one of them, the Haganah, answered to the Jewish Agency and the Zionist Congress. When those bodies decided to stop, the fight, in the Lehi account, passed to Lehi and the Irgun; their decisions were not the Congress's to make. The decision in Paris was a political one, taken by the leadership that also had a diplomatic course to pursue that same August (see [scene:s07h|the Agency's partition proposal]). The decision in Basel confirmed it. The united movement thus ended by a political decision on the Jewish side, not by British arms, and the armed campaign against Britain went on without the Haganah.

Two ways of reading it. The movement is remembered in two registers. In the Lehi account, it was a "united armed offensive against the British," and the decisions in Paris and Basel left the fighting to Lehi and the Irgun. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] Read from the British side and from the side of those killed or injured at Lydda, the same operations were attacks on railways, a refinery and bridges in which police and workers died. The two readings do not disagree about what happened on the nights the source records. They disagree about what to call it, and the source available here belongs to one side of that disagreement.

What the record does not settle. Much remains open. The heritage account gives no casualty totals for the movement's operations, no number for the police and railway workers killed or injured at Lydda, and no casualty figure for the Night of the Bridges. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] It does not say whether the King David Hotel bombing was carried out under the united movement's coordination or by the Irgun alone, and the available material does not settle that question. It does not record the reasons given in Paris for the halt, or whether the bombing of 22 July weighed in that decision; the sequence is plain, with the bombing coming about two weeks before the Paris meeting, but the source draws no causal line, and neither does this book. A full account of the movement would need British military and police records and the Haganah's own papers, set against the Lehi account. Until that work is done, the dates and the targets are as firm as this record gets.

sections.h: Black Sabbath: Operation Agatha, 29 June 1946
sections.html:
Relations between Britain and the Jewish community of Palestine are often described as having worn down slowly after the war, with no single moment at which they broke. The slow wearing-down is real: from September 1945 the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi had acted together against British targets, from the railways at Lydda in November 1945 to eleven bridges on the night of 17 June 1946 (see [scene:rd5_revolt|the Jewish Resistance Movement]). [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] But the record also holds a dated break, with a codename, a troop count and an arrest total. Twelve days after the Night of the Bridges, on Saturday 29 June 1946, Britain launched Operation Agatha.

The operation. Roughly 17,000 British troops and police searched Jewish settlements, kibbutzim and offices across Mandate Palestine at the same time. More than 2,700 people were arrested. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] The operation was a direct response to the escalating operations of the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi against British installations. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] What set it apart was whom it reached. Those arrested included senior officials of the Jewish Agency. Agatha was not a narrow sweep for known fighters of the two underground groups. It struck the mainstream political leadership's own institutions. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha]

One reading of that choice of target ties it to what the united resistance had become. The Night of the Bridges had been carried out not by Lehi or the Irgun but by the Haganah, acting through its Palmach. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] The campaign Britain was answering was no longer only the work of the two underground groups, and the raid reached past them to the political leadership.

The sources do not give a site-by-site inventory of what was searched, and they do not name the individuals arrested. What they establish is the scale, the simultaneity and the reach of the operation into the Agency's leadership. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha]

The documents. The arrests were only part of it. British forces also seized a substantial cache of documents from the Jewish Agency's headquarters in Jerusalem. The material was believed to include evidence linking the Agency's leadership to Haganah operations. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] That belief is what gave the seizure its weight. The Jewish Agency had kept a deliberate legal and organizational separation between the political leadership and armed resistance. Documents tying the one to the other threatened that separation directly. The sources describe what the documents were believed to contain; they do not set out the actual contents or the full extent of what was taken. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha]

Two names. The operation carries two names, and each records something. "Agatha" was the official British codename. "Black Sabbath" was the name given by the Jewish community whose institutions were raided, because the raid fell on a Saturday, the Jewish Sabbath. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] The second name is itself evidence of how the operation was experienced and remembered by those it targeted. There is no evidence that the British name carried any hidden meaning; codenames of the period were, as a rule, assigned without symbolic intent. The community's own name is the more telling of the two for understanding what the raid meant to those on the receiving end.

Why the King David Hotel. The documents did not stay at the Agency. They were taken to be processed and stored in the Secretariat wing of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The building needs describing. Its southern wing housed the Mandate Secretariat, the central administrative offices of the Mandate government, and served as the regional British military headquarters. Hotel business went on in the rest of the building at the same time. It was not a hotel that happened to contain a few government offices; it was, in effect, the center of British administration in Palestine. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

That double character is what made it a target. In the Irgun's planning, the hotel was at once a symbol of British authority and the physical place where the evidence against the Jewish Agency's leadership was held. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] Irgun intelligence assessed that the documents seized in Agatha, including the material believed to implicate the Agency's leadership in coordinating with the Haganah, were being processed and stored in the Secretariat wing specifically. The bombing's documented objective was to destroy that evidence and to strike the administrative apparatus that had just carried out the mass raid and the arrests. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

Twenty-three days. The Irgun's planning for what became the King David Hotel bombing began in direct response to Black Sabbath. Its motive, as documented, was specific, retaliation and the destruction of evidence, rather than a general rise in tension. The bombing took place on 22 July 1946, twenty-three days after the raid. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The line from one event to the other is short and traceable: raid, seizure, intelligence assessment, choice of target, attack.

Two cautions belong beside that line. The first is that it does not establish that retaliation for Black Sabbath was the bombing's only motive; the bombing's planning and its stated objectives are taken up in [scene:s07e4|the next section]. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The second is that tracing a cause is not the same as weighing a deed. The bombing killed 91 people, many of whom had no connection to the administrative work the Irgun meant to strike. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] Setting out the chain from Agatha explains how the hotel came to be chosen. It does not excuse or justify the deaths that followed, and it is not offered here as doing so.
