The claim and the record. The familiar account of steadily worsening relations is not wrong so much as incomplete. The armed campaign of 1945–46 and the British response to it built up over months. Within that build-up, Agatha stands out as a single dated operation of a different order, with a troop count, an arrest total, a seizure of the Agency's own papers and a direct line to the deadliest single attack on the British of the whole Mandate period. A gradual decline and a sharp turning point are both in the record.

What the record does not settle. The sources do not name those arrested or say how long they were held. They do not give the contents of the seized documents, so the belief that they tied the Agency's leadership to the Haganah cannot be tested here. They do not record what the British government said, at the time, to justify the decision to arrest the Agency's senior officials. And they do not show how the raid bore on the decisions the Agency's leadership took a few weeks later, in early August 1946, to halt armed action. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] Those questions need the British and Jewish Agency archives, which are not part of the material verified.

sections.h: The King David Hotel Bombing, 22 July 1946
sections.html:
The bombing of the King David Hotel is sometimes passed over as an incident in a British office building, one act of violence among many in the last years of the Mandate. The numbers alone tell against that view. On 22 July 1946 an explosion in the hotel's southern wing in Jerusalem killed 91 people, British, Arab and Jewish. It was the deadliest single attack against the British in the whole Mandate period. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] It was carried out by an organization whose commander would later lead the government of Israel, it drew a public condemnation from the Jewish Agency, and it hardened British opinion toward leaving Palestine. Each of these points is on the record, and each is taken in turn below.

From Agatha to the hotel. The attack came twenty-three days after Operation Agatha. On 29 June 1946 British forces had arrested more than 2,700 people, including senior Jewish Agency officials, and seized documents from the Agency's Jerusalem headquarters; the documents were believed to link the Agency's leadership to Haganah operations, and they were taken to the Secretariat wing of the King David Hotel to be processed and stored (see [scene:s07e3|Operation Agatha]). [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] The hotel's southern wing housed the Mandate Secretariat, the central administrative offices of the Mandate government, and the British military command; hotel business carried on in the rest of the building. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The Irgun, assessing that the seized papers were held there, planned the attack in direct response to the raid, with the documented aims of destroying that evidence and striking the administration that had carried out the arrests. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

The attack. The Irgun was commanded at the time by Menachem Begin. [cite:wiki_menachem_begin] Its fighters placed explosives, reportedly concealed in milk churns, in the basement of the southern wing, beneath the Secretariat and the military command, and detonated them. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The explosion killed 91 people. They were a mix of British, Arab and Jewish civilians and administrative personnel. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The sources give the total and the fact that the dead came from all three communities; they do not itemize who each person was or what work each did. Many had no connection to the administrative functions the Irgun meant to strike. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

The warning calls. Whether those inside were warned is one of the oldest disputes about the attack, and it has not been resolved. The Irgun's own account holds that warning calls were placed about 25 minutes before the detonation to three places: the hotel switchboard, the French consulate and the office of the Palestine Post newspaper, each urging evacuation. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] British investigators, and later historians, have disputed whether any warning actually reached the hotel's management in time to act on it, or whether a call that did arrive was dismissed as a hoax. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

Each side has a case. The Irgun's account is specific: it names the time, the three recipients and the purpose of the calls, and, taken on its own terms, it presents an intention to empty the building rather than to kill those in it. The British case rests on the outcome and on the investigation: 91 people did not leave, and the investigators doubted that any usable warning had reached the people who could have ordered an evacuation. Even on the Irgun's own account, the question of whether a warning of about 25 minutes, sent partly to outside offices, was adequate remains open. The record does not settle which account is right, and this book does not pretend that it does.

The Jewish Agency's condemnation. The Jewish Agency publicly condemned the bombing. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The condemnation carried an edge that is easy to miss. It was the Agency's own documents, seized in Agatha, that the attack was meant to destroy. And the Haganah, whose ties to the Agency's leadership the seized documents were believed to show, had itself been part of the united Jewish Resistance Movement with the Irgun and Lehi since September 1945, carrying out the Night of the Bridges only five weeks earlier through its Palmach. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] The condemnation is therefore a real instance, in the open, of the tension between the mainstream political leadership and the paramilitary groups, played out around the most consequential single attack of the period. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The sources record the public condemnation; they do not record the internal debate behind its wording or the private views of individual Agency officials.

Did it end the united resistance? A reader will want to know whether the bombing broke the alliance. The sequence is suggestive: about two weeks later, in early August 1946, the Jewish Agency's leadership, meeting in Paris, decided to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met, and the Congress confirmed the halt in December. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] But the only source for those decisions, the Lehi heritage association, does not say that the bombing caused them, and no other source verified does either (see [scene:rd5_revolt|the Jewish Resistance Movement]). The order of events is clear; the link between them is not established.

What it changed in London. The bombing is documented as having significantly hardened British public and parliamentary opinion toward disengaging from Palestine altogether. It contributed directly to Britain's decision, the next year, to hand the whole question to the United Nations. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] It was one factor among several. The same record that ties the bombing to Britain's change of mind does not claim that the attack alone caused the referral of 1947; other pressures were at work, and how much weight the armed campaign carried in Britain's withdrawal is itself disputed, as the section on [scene:rd5_britain_exits|Britain's exit] sets out.

Begin, then and later. Menachem Begin personally commanded the Irgun at the time of the bombing. He later served as Israel's sixth Prime Minister, from 1977 to 1983. [cite:wiki_menachem_begin] The line from the command of 1946 to the premiership three decades later is direct and documented. What the sources used here do not provide is Begin's own account: his justification for the attack and what he said about it in later years are not part of this material, and they are not supplied here.

The claim and the record. The view of the bombing as a minor, passing incident does not survive the facts. Ninety-one people from three communities were killed in a single attack, the largest such toll against the British in the Mandate. Its commander went on to lead the government of Israel. It drew a public condemnation from the Jewish Agency, and it moved British opinion toward leaving. On its own documented merits it was among the most consequential single events of the Mandate period. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

What the record does not settle. Three questions stay open. The first is the warning: whether the calls the Irgun describes were made as it says, whether any reached someone able to order an evacuation, and whether they were treated as a hoax. The second is the full list of the dead, by name, nationality and role, which the sources here do not give. The third is cause and effect after the attack: how far the bombing drove the Jewish Agency's August decision to halt armed action, and how far it, rather than the other pressures on Britain, drove the decision to go to the United Nations. On all three, the documents available here establish the sequence and leave the weighing to further evidence.

sections.h: The Jewish Agency Prepares: Partition as Policy, 1946
sections.html:
In the weeks after the King David Hotel bombing, the Jewish Agency was also at work on a map. The partition plan voted on in November 1947 is usually described as the product of the United Nations' own process: an eleven-member committee that investigated the problem from scratch and reached its recommendation independently. That committee was real, and its conclusions were its own. But one of the parties before it had arrived at partition long before the committee existed. The Jewish Agency had prepared its own partition proposal more than a year before the committee reported, and by then had made partition its declared aim.

Two separate diplomatic tracks lay ahead: recognition by the United States, and a decision at the United Nations. The Agency worked both, and the groundwork for the second was laid early. In August 1946 it submitted its own detailed partition proposal, with boundaries drawn for a Palestinian rump state [cite:jewishagency_1946plan]. Those boundaries bear a documented resemblance to the area that became the West Bank after 1948 [cite:jewishagency_1946plan]. The resemblance is real, and easy to overstate. The source records a likeness between two maps, not a line of descent: it does not show that the United Nations committee, or anyone after it, adopted the Agency's exact lines.

The proposal did not stand alone. Historical accounts of the United Nations process note that by 1946 partition had become the Jewish Agency's avowed, public policy [cite:unscop_testimony]. That is a different thing from a position adopted because an international body demanded one. The Agency did not arrive at partition in reaction to the United Nations. It came to the United Nations with partition already as its stated goal, and with a prepared case for it. The details of what it later presented were not necessarily identical to its 1946 position, and the sources here do not claim they were; what was fixed by 1946 was the commitment itself.

August 1946 was also a turning point in the Agency's other policy, the armed one. According to the heritage association of Lehi, one of the underground groups then allied with the Haganah, the Agency's meeting in Paris in early August 1946 decided to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met, and the Congress, in Basel, confirmed the halt on 9 December 1946 [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance]. That account, written from Lehi's own perspective, is the only source here for the Paris decision. The sources do not say whether the partition proposal was discussed or adopted at the same Paris meeting, and this book does not join the two. What can be said is that in the same month the record shows the Agency submitting a partition plan, the Lehi account has it standing down from armed struggle until its Congress could meet. The story of that resistance movement is told in [scene:rd5_revolt|the Jewish Resistance Movement].

The timeline makes the central point plain. The Agency's proposal came roughly nine months before the United Nations created its committee, and more than a year before that committee's report. When the committee did hear the Agency in 1947, its head, David Ben-Gurion, told it that an independent Jewish state was the only acceptable outcome, and the Agency presented a prepared map and a large body of supporting material [cite:unscop_testimony]. That hearing, and the Arab Higher Committee's decision to boycott it, are the subject of [scene:s07i|UNSCOP and the empty chair].

None of this makes the committee's recommendation a copy of the Agency's plan, and the evidence here does not support saying so. It does correct the impression that the United Nations faced a blank page. One party came to it with a position fixed and a proposal already drafted, the product of a diplomatic campaign that had begun before the international process did. Whether that preparation shaped the committee's final lines, and by how much, is not something the sources used here can measure. Nor do they say to whom, exactly, the August 1946 proposal was submitted, or set out its boundaries line by line. Those questions remain open; the date and the policy do not.

sections.h: Inside the White House, 1945–1948
sections.html:
The Agency's other diplomatic track ran to Washington, and there it met a peculiarity of the Truman presidency. American policy on Palestine is often described as a State Department product, made on the merits by career diplomats. In the Truman years that description leaves out the building where the decisions were finally taken. Inside the White House a small number of aides and friends gave the President views and visitors that the State Department did not, and at least one of his most consequential statements was issued a month before a national election. Who had access, and when the President spoke, are both on the record. Why he spoke as he did is still argued.

The longest-serving of those aides was David K. Niles. He served in the White House from 1942 to 1951, first under Franklin Roosevelt and then under Harry Truman, and he was one of only two Roosevelt aides whom Truman kept on [cite:wiki_david_niles] [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. His brief was minority affairs. Niles was a committed Zionist, and he became an important channel through which American Zionists reached the White House [cite:wiki_david_niles] [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. That is a documented role, not an accusation: he had been entrusted with minority affairs, and his own commitment was to the Zionist cause.

Around Niles stood others. Max Lowenthal advised the President's special counsel, Clark Clifford, on Palestine [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. And outside the staff altogether there was Eddie Jacobson, Truman's personal friend and former business partner, who provided a separate, private channel to the President; his role, including the March 1948 meeting he arranged, is told in [scene:s08|Truman and the men around him]. What they offered was proximity: being in the room, or being able to get someone else into it.

The clearest test of that influence came in the autumn of 1946, after a conference on Palestine in London had adjourned; the conference and Britain's part in it are set out in [scene:rd5_bevin|Bevin and Palestine, 1945–1946]. On 4 October 1946, the eve of Yom Kippur and a month before the congressional midterm elections, Truman issued a statement on Palestine [cite:avalon_yomkippur_1946] [cite:nuremberg_yomkippur]. He regretted the adjournment of the London conference. He urged immediate, large-scale Jewish immigration into Palestine. And he said that the United States could support a solution along the lines of a viable Jewish state "in an adequate area of Palestine" [cite:avalon_yomkippur_1946] [cite:nuremberg_yomkippur].

The statement landed hard in London. The British Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, was furious, and Truman wrote to him that he "very much" regretted any embarrassment it had caused [cite:frus_truman_attlee_1946]. The apology concerned the embarrassment; the documents cited here do not record any change in the position itself.

The timing invited an explanation, and the New York Times printed one within three days. On 7 October 1946 James Reston wrote in that paper that the President "went against his advisers' foreign policy and chose to follow the promptings of those who were primarily interested in retaining Democratic majorities in Congress" [cite:palestinestudies_christison_truman]. On Reston's reading, the statement was electoral, and its date, a month before the midterms, was part of the evidence.

Truman rejected that reading publicly. In February 1947 he issued a statement calling the impression that partisan and local politics motivated American policy on Palestine "most unfortunate and misleading", and insisting that his position had been consistent since 1945 [cite:jvl_truman_feb1947]. On his own account, the statement of October 1946 restated a view he had held since his first months in office, not a new position adopted for an election.

Each side has real evidence. Reston's case rests on the calendar, which no one disputes, and on his reporting that the statement went against the foreign-policy advice the President had received. Truman's case rests on consistency: the October statement's call for immediate, large-scale immigration was, on his account, the position he had held since 1945, and a statement that restates an existing position is not by itself proof of a new electoral calculation. His own earlier words on the subject are gathered in [scene:tr_s01|Truman in his own words].

The two readings are not mutually exclusive, and the documents do not force a choice between them. Who had the President's ear, and when he chose to speak, are on the record. Whether electoral politics or conviction drove him is argued by named sources on both sides, and the answer can be both: a man may hold a view sincerely and still choose the most politically useful day on which to announce it.

The White House channel was the last link in a longer chain, told in the previous stage of this book. Two American Zionist campaigns of the 1940s, a rival and aggressive one led by the Irgun's delegation in the United States and a disciplined mainstream lobby, moved American opinion through advertising, local committees and Christian supporters into Congress and both parties' platforms. From there the pressure reached the White House, where Niles provided access and the Yom Kippur statement of 1946 put the President on record, and finally the United Nations, where the United States lobbied for the partition vote of November 1947. That chain shows how the pieces connected; it does not show that any one of them decided the outcome.

What the record does not settle is the weight of each influence. The sources here document Niles's access but not the content of his advice on any given day, nor whether he drafted or proposed the October statement. They record Lowenthal's role as an adviser to Clifford without detailing what he advised. And no document in this section records Truman saying, in private, that the midterms were or were not on his mind when he spoke on 4 October 1946. The accounts of motive therefore remain what they are: Reston's reporting on one side, the President's own public denial on the other.

sections.h: Britain Lets Go, February–September 1947
sections.html:
While Washington argued over the President's motives, London was deciding to give the problem up. In the space of eight months in 1947, Britain went from governing Palestine to announcing that it would leave. The steps were formal and dated: a Cabinet decision in February, a letter to the United Nations in April, and a statement to the General Assembly's Ad Hoc Committee in September. Between them came hangings, kidnappings, riots in British cities and a refugee ship turned back to Europe. The question historians still argue over is how these events related to one another, and in particular how far the Jewish armed campaign drove Britain out.

By the start of 1947 the policy that Ernest Bevin had staked his name on in November 1945 had run out of road; that earlier course, from the Anglo-American Committee to the London conference, is traced in [scene:rd5_bevin|Bevin and Palestine, 1945–1946]. On 14 February 1947 Bevin told the Arab delegates in London that the Cabinet had agreed the question should go to the United Nations without British recommendations, "inasmuch as plan offered by British Delegation had met with no acceptance from either Arabs or Jews". Britain, he said, would present the matter "as impartially as possible" [cite:rs_rd5_frus_gallman_1947]. The words survive in a telegram from the American embassy in London to the Secretary of State.

Four days later, on 18 February 1947, Bevin explained the decision in the House of Commons. In the text reproduced by the Center for Online Judaic Studies, which gives no archival citation, he described "an irreconcilable conflict of principles". For the Jews, the essential principle was a sovereign Jewish state. For the Arabs, it was to resist Jewish sovereignty anywhere in Palestine. He called the Mandate "unworkable in practice", and he put the country's population at about 1,200,000 Arabs and 600,000 Jews [cite:rs_rd5_cojs_bevin_1947]. Because that text could not be checked against Hansard, its wording should be read as reported rather than verified. The historian Raphael Langham adds that in the Commons Bevin blamed the Jews and the United States for the failure [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit].

The formal handover followed. On 2 April 1947 Sir Alexander Cadogan, for the United Kingdom, asked the United Nations to "place the question of Palestine on the Agenda of the General Assembly at its next regular Annual Session", and to "summon, as soon as possible, a special Session" to constitute a special committee [cite:rs_rd5_un_a286]. The letter was circulated as document A/286, dated 3 April 1947. The mechanism matters. Britain did not surrender the Mandate in April. It asked the Assembly to take up the question and to set up a committee, while it went on governing. The committee that resulted, UNSCOP, spent the summer in Palestine and the region; its work is told in [scene:s07i|UNSCOP and the empty chair].

Inside Palestine the violence that ran alongside the diplomacy moved in a cycle of death sentences and reprisals. The dates below come from a single encyclopedia entry and are given here as reported, without the casualty and riot figures that the same source carries but which could not be confirmed. On 16 April 1947 Britain executed four members of the Irgun: Dov Gruner, Yehiel Dresner, Mordechai Alkahi and Eliezer Kashani. On 4 May the Irgun broke into Acre prison. Three of the attackers who were captured, Avshalom Haviv, Yaakov Weiss and Meir Nakar, were sentenced to death and hanged on 29 July 1947 [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_sergeants].

By then the Irgun held two British hostages. On the night of 11 to 12 July 1947 it kidnapped two Intelligence Corps sergeants, Clifford Martin and Mervyn Paice, in Netanya. On 30 July, the day after the Acre men were hanged, it hanged the sergeants, and booby-trapped their bodies [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_sergeants]. The killings provoked a reaction in Britain itself. From 1 August 1947 anti-Jewish rioting broke out, beginning in Liverpool and spreading to other cities [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_sergeants]. It should be named for what it was: antisemitic violence in British cities, aimed at Jews in Britain in response to killings carried out by the Irgun in Palestine.

The same month brought an episode that, in the Holocaust Memorial Museum's account, helped shift diplomatic sympathy. In July 1947 a ship formerly called the President Warfield, renamed Exodus 1947, sailed from Sète in France with more than 4,500 Jewish passengers, most of them displaced persons and Holocaust survivors [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus] [cite:rs_rd5_yv_july1947]. It was one vessel in the clandestine immigration fleet whose wider history is told in [scene:ab_s01|Aliyah Bet]. When the Royal Navy boarded it, three Jews were killed, one crew member and two passengers according to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and dozens were wounded [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus] [cite:rs_rd5_yv_july1947].

The two institutions that record the boarding do not agree on its date. Yad Vashem states that the ship was attacked on 17 July in international waters, that three people were killed, and that it reached Haifa on 18 July [cite:rs_rd5_yv_july1947]. The Holocaust Memorial Museum dates the clash to 18 July 1947 and specifies one crew member and two passengers among the dead [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus]. Neither source explains the difference, and it is left standing here.

What Britain did next made the ship a symbol. The passengers were moved onto three navy transports and taken back to Port-de-Bouc in France. France declined to remove them by force. After a hunger strike of 24 days and about three weeks in the summer heat, they were carried to Hamburg and interned in camps in the British zone of Germany [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus]. Langham records that Bevin insisted the passengers be returned to their port of embarkation, and suggests that prejudice may have played a part [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit]. That is Langham's suggestion, and he frames it as a possibility rather than a finding. Yad Vashem states that the voyage was meant to draw the attention of the UNSCOP members then working in the country; the Holocaust Memorial Museum says the "public embarrassment for Britain" helped shift diplomatic sympathy [cite:rs_rd5_yv_july1947] [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus].

The decision to leave outright, rather than to hand over a question for advice, was announced at the United Nations. On 26 September 1947 Arthur Creech Jones, the Colonial Secretary, told the Ad Hoc Committee that "in the absence of a settlement" Britain had to plan for "an early withdrawal of British forces and of the British administration". Britain, he said, "was not prepared to undertake the task of imposing a policy in Palestine by force of arms" [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_creechjones]. That sentence is the hinge of the whole year. The Assembly could recommend what it liked; Britain would not enforce it. When the Assembly voted on partition on 29 November 1947, Britain abstained [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit].

There was also a bill. The funding ledger compiled for this library puts the cost of the forces in Palestine in 1945–47 at about £100 million, with some 100,000 troops deployed and about 750 British killed over the period; in today's money the cost is roughly $6.7 billion. The ledger's sources are listed with the panel below, and the full account of Britain's bill appears in the next stage of this book. The panel below sets it beside the other large sums of the pre-state years, for scale rather than as a total. Britain's military bill for 1945–47 is the second-largest item on it, behind only the Jewish capital invested in Palestine between 1921 and 1937, and well above the United Jewish Appeal's wartime giving of 1939–45. The sources used here do not say how much weight the Cabinet gave to that cost when it decided to leave; they show only that the cost was being paid.

How much did the Jewish insurgency, and the sergeants affair in particular, cause the withdrawal? Two positions have serious support. On one view the armed campaign was decisive or close to it. The historian J. Bowyer Bell called the sergeants affair the "straw that broke the Mandate's back", and Creech Jones himself, writing in 1961, listed the sergeants affair as one of four major factors behind the Cabinet's September 1947 decision to evacuate [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_sergeants]. The strength of this case is the testimony of the minister who announced the withdrawal, and the timing: the sergeants were hanged on 30 July, riots broke out in Britain on 1 August, and the withdrawal was announced eight weeks later.

On the other view the insurgency was one factor among several. Britain's own stated reason, in February, was the irreconcilable Arab and Jewish positions and the failure of its own plan; the Cabinet had agreed to hand the question to the United Nations before the executions, the Acre break-in, the kidnapping or the Exodus [cite:rs_rd5_frus_gallman_1947]. Langham points to strategic considerations and Britain's relations with the Arab states [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit]. The strength of this case is the sequence of documents: the decision to give up the problem predates the events of the summer. The two readings are not wholly opposed. February's decision referred the question; September's decision ended the Mandate; the events between may explain why the second followed the first so fast, even if they did not cause the first.

Britain's departure did not end Bevin's part in the story. In May 1948 he told the Commons, "there are, after all, no Arabs in the House", and Britain recognized Israel only in January 1949, with Bevin's acceptance, in Langham's word, "grudging" [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit].

Several things remain unsettled on this record. The Commons text of 18 February 1947 is known here only through a reproduction without archival citation. The Cabinet's own minutes for February and September 1947 are not among the sources used, so the weight the ministers themselves gave to cost, to the insurgency, to American pressure or to Arab opinion cannot be measured from them. Creech Jones's four factors are known from a later account, written in 1961, and only one of the four is named in the source. The exact date of the Exodus boarding differs between two reputable institutions. And whether prejudice shaped Bevin's handling of the Exodus is, in the one historian's account that raises it, a possibility and not a demonstrated fact. What the documents do show is the order of events: Britain referred the question because its plan had failed with both sides, endured a summer of executions, reprisals and a refugee ship that embarrassed it before the world, and then announced that it would not stay to enforce whatever the world decided.

sections.h: Moscow Said Yes First
sections.html:
The popular memory of 1948 has two superpowers in fixed places: the United States as Israel's sponsor, and the Soviet bloc hostile from the start. For the years in which the state was actually made, the record runs the other way on the second point. Between May 1947 and May 1948 the Soviet Union backed a Jewish state earlier, and held to it more steadily, than Washington did. Its satellites voted for partition, it stood firm at the Security Council when the Americans retreated, it was the first government in the world to recognize Israel in law, and arms from a Soviet-bloc country reached the new state while an American embargo was in force. In December 1948 the bloc voted against the UN resolution on refugee return, and only in the 1950s did Moscow turn toward the Arab states.

The first move came at the special session of the General Assembly that Britain had requested. On 14 May 1947, the day before the Assembly created the Special Committee on Palestine [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop], the Soviet representative Andrei Gromyko addressed the session. He said the Soviet Union preferred a single Arab–Jewish state in which both peoples would have equal rights. But if that proved impossible to achieve, he said, partition into two states was a justifiable alternative [cite:israeled_gromyko_speech] [cite:israeled_gromyko_timeline]. Coming from Moscow, that was a reversal. For decades the Soviet state had opposed Zionism [cite:israeled_gromyko_speech]. Gromyko's speech did not endorse partition outright; it ranked it second. But it put the Soviet Union on record, before Washington had committed, as willing to accept a Jewish state.

Why Moscow changed course is not stated in any Soviet document among the sources used here. Analysts at the time and since have read the motive as a wish to remove British influence from the region [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel]. It remains an interpretation of Soviet interest, drawn from what Moscow did, rather than a finding from Moscow's own records. What it does explain is why the Soviet Union and the Zionist movement could find themselves on the same side without sharing any larger aim. This was convergence of interest, not alliance.

When the Assembly voted in November 1947, the Soviet Union and its satellites voted for partition [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel]. The test came four months later. In March 1948 the United States moved to retreat from partition toward a temporary United Nations trusteeship, a shift told in [scene:rd5_trusteeship|Washington's retreat, March 1948]. The Soviet Union did not follow. At the Security Council it stood behind partition, and Gromyko told the Council that the rapid creation of two states was the only way to reduce the bloodshed [cite:yated_stalin_israel] [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel].

On 14 May 1948 Israel declared its independence, and Truman's recognition followed the same day, but it was de facto recognition. On 17 May 1948, three days after independence, the Soviet Union became the first state to grant Israel full legal, or de jure, recognition [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel]. The Soviet recognition was thus the fuller of the two. The wider story of who recognized Israel, when and on what legal basis, is told in this chapter's section on recognition.

Recognition was not the only support that came from the Soviet side. Arms reached the new state from Czechoslovakia, a Soviet-bloc country, at a time when an American embargo was in force [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel]. The contracts, the airlift and their price are documented in [scene:cz_s01|the Czechoslovak pipeline]; the point here is that the first great power to recognize Israel in law and the government behind its Czechoslovak arms both stood on the same side of the Cold War line.

The first sign that the alignment had limits came seven months after independence. In December 1948 the Soviet bloc voted against United Nations Resolution 194, the resolution on the return of refugees [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli]. The sources used here do not explain the bloc's reasons for that vote, and they should not be supplied by guesswork. The resolution itself, and what followed from it, belong to the next stage of this book and are told in [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194]. From the 1950s, Moscow turned toward the Arab states [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli].

That later turn largely erased the earlier record from popular memory. The common account holds that Israel was created by American support while the Soviet bloc was hostile from the start. The documents support only half of it. American support mattered, but it wavered in March 1948. Soviet support came first, held through that wavering, and produced the first full recognition. In 1947 and 1948 both superpowers backed the new state, for different reasons, Moscow earlier and more firmly, apparently to push Britain out.

What the record does not settle is the question of motive. Gromyko's speech, the votes, the Security Council statement and the recognition are all documented acts. The reasoning behind them inside the Soviet leadership is not documented in the sources used here; the "remove Britain" explanation is the reading analysts have drawn from those acts. Nor do these sources show how far Soviet diplomacy and the Czechoslovak arms sales were coordinated as a single policy, rather than running in parallel. The first-to-recognize fact, by contrast, is not in doubt.

sections.h: UNSCOP and the Empty Chair
sections.html:
The plan that the General Assembly voted on in November 1947 began as the report of an eleven-nation committee that spent the summer of 1947 between Lake Success, Jerusalem, Beirut, Amman, Geneva and the displaced-persons camps of Munich, Salzburg, Vienna, Berlin, Hamburg and Hanover. The United Nations Special Committee on Palestine, known as UNSCOP, is usually remembered as a neutral fact-finding body that heard both sides equally and reached its own conclusion. Its own report tells a more specific story. The committee was genuinely international, and it did reach its conclusions by its own votes. But it did not weigh two prepared Palestinian cases against each other. One party, the Jewish Agency, came with a map, witnesses and a proposed itinerary. The other, the Arab Higher Committee, chose to stay away. The Arab case was put to the committee instead by the governments of six Arab states, in Beirut, and members also called on Transjordan's king in Amman.

The committee was Britain's doing. On 2 April 1947 Sir Alexander Cadogan, for the United Kingdom, asked the United Nations to put Palestine on the agenda of the next regular Assembly and to summon a special session as soon as possible to constitute a special committee [cite:rs_rd5_un_a286]. (How London reached that point is told in [scene:rd5_britain_exits|Britain hands Palestine to the United Nations].) The special session convened at Flushing Meadow on 28 April 1947. On 15 May it adopted Resolution 106 (S-1), which created the Special Committee on Palestine with "the widest powers to ascertain and record facts" and told it to report by 1 September 1947 [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop] [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report].

Who would sit on it was itself contested. Australia proposed eleven members, none of them permanent members of the Security Council. The Assembly adopted that proposal by 13 votes to 11, with 29 abstentions [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. The members chosen were Australia, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, India, Iran, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden, Uruguay and Yugoslavia [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:unscop_ecf]. On its face this was a multi-continent body, not a proxy for Washington or London. It held its first meeting at Lake Success on 26 May 1947, and on 2 June elected Justice Emil Sandström of Sweden as chairman and Alberto Ulloa of Peru as vice-chairman [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]. Its members arrived in Palestine on 14 and 15 June and first met in Jerusalem on 16 June [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report].

The day before the members landed, the Arab Higher Committee had informed the Secretary-General that it would abstain from cooperating with the committee. On 10 July 1947 its vice-chairman, Jamal Husseini, wrote again to say that it would not reverse that decision [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. The boycott was a deliberate political choice with stated reasons. The Arab Higher Committee regarded the whole framework as illegitimate: in its view any United Nations body that set out to decide Palestine's future without first affirming the self-determination rights of the country's existing majority was biased before it began [cite:unscop_ecf]. The Jewish Agency took the opposite course. It engaged fully and supplied detailed logistical help, including its own proposed itinerary for the committee's visits around the country [cite:unscop_ecf].

The consequence inside Palestine was a hearing room in which only one of the two Palestinian communities' organized leaderships made a formal case. For the Jewish Agency the committee heard Moshe Shertok and David Horowitz, and it heard Chaim Weizmann in a personal capacity [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. David Ben-Gurion, testifying as head of the Jewish Agency, told the committee plainly that an independent Jewish state was the only acceptable outcome. The map presented on the Zionist side was substantially the Peel Commission's map of 1937, with the Galilee, the Negev and West Jerusalem added [cite:unscop_testimony]. One historical account describes the Agency's presentation as forthright and exhaustive, overwhelming the committee "with data, logic, and cogent analyses of every central and tangential issue" [cite:unscop_testimony]. That account is a judgment about the presentation's weight, and it should be read with care. The imbalance it describes did not come from the Arab argument being weak. It came from the Arab Higher Committee's argument never being formally put before the committee in Palestine at all. Nor was the Agency improvising. By 1946 partition had already become its avowed policy, and in August 1946 it had drawn up its own partition proposal, more than a year before UNSCOP existed [cite:unscop_testimony] [cite:jewishagency_1946plan]. That earlier preparation is the subject of [scene:s07h|the Jewish Agency's 1946 proposal].

It is here that the familiar charge against UNSCOP, and the committee's own record, have to be read side by side. The charge, as it is often put, is that the committee heard testimony "almost exclusively" from the Zionist side [cite:unscop_ecf]. The committee's report shows something narrower and more exact. No Palestinian Arab body testified, because the Arab Higher Committee boycotted the proceedings [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. But the Arab states did put their case. After an informal visit to Damascus on 21 July 1947, the committee heard the governments of Egypt, Iraq, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Yemen in Beirut on 22 July, with the Lebanese Foreign Minister, Hamid Frangié, among them. Transjordan declined to send a representative outside the country, so on 25 July the chairman and seven members went to Amman to see King Abdullah [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]. The committee also traveled through the region and could observe conditions directly; it did not hear literally nothing of Arab objections [cite:unscop_ecf].

Both readings therefore hold, each within its limits. "One side only" is accurate for the Palestinian parties: the Jewish Agency was heard at length and the Arab Higher Committee by its own decision not at all. It is not accurate for the Arab case as a whole, which six governments presented in Beirut; members also met Transjordan's king in Amman. What the record establishes is that no prepared Palestinian Arab case, with its own witnesses and its own maps, stood in the committee's record beside the Agency's. That is a more specific claim than "the process was rigged", and a more defensible one.

The committee also looked beyond Palestine. After a vote of six to four, with one abstention, a subcommittee visited displaced-persons camps in Munich, Salzburg, Vienna, Berlin, Hamburg and Hanover between 8 and 14 August 1947 [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]. The vote on whether to go at all was close, and the record used here does not say which members voted which way or why.

The drafting began in Geneva on 28 July. On 29 August the committee approved eleven recommendations unanimously and a twelfth with two dissents, and it signed its report on 31 August 1947; the report's cover carries the date 3 September 1947 [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]. On the central question, the committee split. A majority of seven, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden and Uruguay, recommended partition into a Jewish state and an Arab state joined in an economic union, with an international regime for Jerusalem. A minority of three, India, Iran and Yugoslavia, recommended a single federal state with Jerusalem as its capital. Australia abstained on both votes, which were recorded as 7 to 3 and 3 to 7 [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop] [cite:unscop_wiki].

The precise count matters, because it is sometimes given wrongly. The Center for Israel Education states that eight of the eleven members endorsed partition, and that the Jewish Agency accepted the plan while the Arab Higher Committee rejected it [cite:rs_rd5_cie_unscop]. The committee's own report records seven, with Australia abstaining [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. The report is the primary document, and on this point the summary is in error. The split also corrects a second simplification: the recommendation behind the partition vote was not a unanimous international finding but a majority view, with three members preferring a single federal state.

The majority plan became the working text. The Assembly's Ad Hoc Committee revised it in the autumn, and the revised plan went to the General Assembly vote of 29 November 1947 [cite:unscop_wiki]. That vote, its lobbying and its tally are told in [scene:s09|Resolution 181].

Several questions remain open on this record. The documents used here do not say what the Arab governments argued in Beirut, beyond the fact that they were heard, nor what King Abdullah told the members in Amman. They do not record how individual members weighed the Jewish Agency's testimony against the Arab governments' statements, or whether the Arab Higher Committee's absence changed any member's vote; the account of the Agency "overwhelming" the committee is one historian's characterization, not a record of members' private responses. And while the boycott is documented as a choice, with its reasons, whether a Palestinian presence would have altered the outcome is a counterfactual that no document can settle. What the record does show is how the recommendation was built: by a committee chosen in a close vote, that heard one Palestinian party in full, heard the Arab case only through Arab governments, visited the displaced-persons camps after a divided vote, and ended seven to three.

sections.h: The Warnings of 1947: State, the Pentagon and Oil
sections.html:
On 22 September 1947 the State Department's senior official for the Middle East put a blunt judgment on paper: the partition of Palestine was "not workable." Eighteen days later the Joint Chiefs of Staff said much the same in a memorandum of their own, and the Secretary of Defense made the argument in public, before a committee of Congress. The oil company that held America's concession in Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, was lobbying the White House directly. A familiar explanation of American policy holds that the strategic costs of backing partition were not understood until much later, and that the gap was one of limited information or the slow communications of the era. The documents do not support that explanation. Each warning was written down, each was dated, and the most important of them was read aloud to the President. The question the record raises is not whether Washington knew, but why what it knew did not decide the outcome.

The answer is not a hidden hand. It is a government divided against itself: career diplomats, the military command and the Defense Secretary on one side, the President's political advisers on the other, with an oil company pressing from outside and a President who had to choose. This section follows the warnings in the order they were made, then the decision that set them aside.

The State Department's regional expert. Loy Henderson directed the State Department's Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs, the office whose job was to understand the practical consequences of American policy in the region. He was not a desk theorist. He had served as American ambassador to Iraq in the mid-1940s and had watched at first hand how Arab governments were reacting as the Palestine question took shape. [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994]

On 22 September 1947 Henderson sent Secretary of State George Marshall a memorandum warning that partition was "not workable" and would lead to "untold troubles" in the future. He did not present this as a private opinion. His views, he wrote, were shared by "nearly every member of the Foreign Service or of the department who has worked to any appreciable extent on Near Eastern problems." [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994] On Henderson's own account, then, the memo stated the shared view of the government's regional specialists, not one official's dissent. Later historians have described the memo as one of the most perceptive warnings in the documentary record of the period, and it came from inside the government rather than from a critic outside it.

It was not filed and forgotten. Under Secretary of State Robert Lovett was impressed enough by its substance to read it aloud to President Truman himself. [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994] That is a documented escalation: the warning reached the President in the Under Secretary's own voice. What the record does not show is that every one of Henderson's predictions proved right in every detail. Historians continue to debate how much of the violence that followed was inevitable and how much depended on other factors. What is not in dispute is that the warning existed, in writing, before the vote, and that it came from the department's own experts.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff. The military reached the same conclusion through its own channel. On 10 October 1947 the Joint Chiefs of Staff filed a memorandum titled "The Problem of Palestine." It warned that dividing Palestine into Jewish and Arab states would open the way for the Soviet Union to displace American and British influence in the region, and that it would endanger American access to Middle East oil. [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] These were the two concerns, regional alignment and access to resources, that drove American policy in the Middle East generally in these years. The memo did not come from diplomats worried about relationships or from oil executives worried about profits. It came from the country's senior military command, whose task was to assess strategic and resource risk.

The timing is what makes the document stand out. On 11 October 1947, one day after the Joint Chiefs filed it, the United States announced its support for the UN partition plan. [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] There are few cases in the period with so narrow a gap between a formal military warning and a policy decision that ran against it. The surviving record documents both the warning and the announcement. It does not contain a stated internal explanation of why this warning, arriving when it did, did not change the timetable. The connection between the two has to be inferred; it is not written down.

The Secretary of Defense, in public. James Forrestal had been Secretary of the Navy and became the first Secretary of Defense, overseeing the consolidation of the armed forces under the new Department of Defense created by the National Security Act of 1947, the same year as his warning. He was the Cabinet official most directly responsible for whether the American military could function. Testifying before a House committee, he said that oil was "the life blood of a war machine," and warned that the Arab world's response to partition would threaten the pipelines carrying oil out of the Persian Gulf, the physical infrastructure on which American forces and the American economy relied. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] The sources available here do not give the date of the testimony or the name of the committee.

Forrestal's testimony and the Joint Chiefs' memorandum made the same argument through two different routes, one public and political, the other internal and military. The record does not show that his warning decided any particular administration decision. It shows it as one voice in a chorus of institutional warning, alongside Henderson and the Joint Chiefs, that was set aside together. Forrestal's diary entries decrying the "bullying" that preceded the final vote belong to the story of the vote itself, told in [scene:s09|the partition resolution].

The oil company. The oil industry did not wait on the government. A 1947 memorandum submitted to President Truman was published under the title "Oil and the State Department policy on Palestine: the documentary evidence of how ARAMCO attempts to destroy the partition resolution of the United Nations." [cite:loc_aramco_oil_pamphlet] Its title states its thesis: that it presents documentary evidence of an active lobbying campaign by the Arabian American Oil Company against partition. ARAMCO held the core American oil concession in Saudi Arabia, the same relationship that lay behind Franklin Roosevelt's meeting with King Ibn Saud two years earlier. A Middle East turned against the United States by partition threatened that concession's value and its security.

Here the money and the policy can be seen side by side. ARAMCO's interest was commercial; the Joint Chiefs' was strategic; Henderson's was diplomatic. All three pointed in the same direction at the same time. The sources treat them as separate and independent warnings, not as one coordinated effort. Nor does the published memorandum reproduce ARAMCO's internal communications or give a full account of its methods. What the record establishes is that a documented lobbying campaign existed and that it failed: the company with the most money at stake in Arab goodwill did not move the decision.

The decision. None of this changed the outcome. Truman had heard Henderson's memo directly. According to several historical accounts, he was worried about his prospects in the 1948 election, and his adviser Clark Clifford urged him to endorse partition in order to secure Jewish-American votes in key swing states. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] Clifford's memorandum to Truman of November 1947 made the electoral case, naming New York, Pennsylvania and Illinois, and his later memoirs acknowledged both the political framework and Marshall's opposition to it. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The President's own account of his motives, and the case that conviction rather than calculation moved him, are examined in [scene:s08|Truman's succession and his advisers]; the sources used here present the decision as a political calculation weighed against strategic warnings, not as a failure of information.

The chronology needs one correction. One of the sources says the United States voted for partition at the General Assembly "five days" after Henderson's memo. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] The dates in the record do not fit that interval. The memo is dated 22 September; the American announcement of support came on 11 October; the General Assembly vote came on 29 November 1947. [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] [cite:unscop_wiki] Whatever the "five days" originally referred to, it cannot be the interval between the memo and the vote, and this book follows the dated documents.

What followed was what the warnings had described. In the months after the vote, Palestine descended into serious violence. By 24 February 1948 George Kennan, the State Department's Director of Policy Planning, was warning that only the introduction of foreign troops could now stop it, an escalation of exactly the "untold troubles" Henderson had forecast five months earlier. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] A month later Washington itself would retreat from partition at the United Nations, a reversal told in [scene:rd5_trusteeship|the trusteeship proposal].

The map of the decision. The figure below draws the whole structure at once. Its first node is the Anglo-American Committee, whose unanimous report of April 1946 recommended that Palestine be neither a Jewish nor an Arab state; Washington kept only one of its recommendations, the immediate admission of 100,000 Jewish refugees. [cite:avalon_aac] [cite:w_aac] The next three nodes are the warnings of September and October 1947: Henderson at State, the Joint Chiefs, and Forrestal at Defense. A fifth, the Central Intelligence Agency's estimate ORE-55 of 28 November 1947, came the day before the vote and is the subject of the next section. All five lines run into Truman; the four warnings are marked as overruled, and the committee's line as one recommendation kept. On the other side of the scale sit Clifford and David Niles, who made the domestic political case, and Eddie Jacobson, Truman's former business partner, whose personal channel brought Chaim Weizmann to the President on 18 March 1948. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] The final node is the outcome: American support for Resolution 181 in November 1947, and recognition of Israel in May 1948.

Read as a whole, the map shows a structure rather than a plot. Every warning came through an established institution doing the work it existed to do: the regional desk assessing the region, the military assessing strategic risk, the Defense Secretary speaking for readiness, the oil company protecting its concession. The counterweight came through the White House's own political staff and through a personal friendship. The President stood where those lines met, and he had the authority to decide. Neither the warnings nor the political advice were secret. Both were on paper.

What the record does not settle. Two limits apply. First, the record cannot show that a different decision would have produced a better outcome by every measure; that counterfactual cannot be tested. Second, the surviving documents show the warnings and the decision but do not contain a written internal rationale connecting the two, so the weight Truman gave to the 1948 election, against his own stated convictions, rests on the accounts of his advisers and on historians' readings rather than on a single decisive document. What the record does settle is the question the familiar account gets wrong. This was not a blind spot or a failure of communication. The State Department's regional director, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense reached the same conclusion independently, in writing, within a few weeks of each other, and the President heard it. The decision to back partition was taken in full knowledge of the strategic risk, by a government in which those who warned and those who prevailed both had a documented voice.

sections.h: The New CIA's First Warning: ORE-55
sections.html:
When the State Department and the Joint Chiefs of Staff warned against partition in September and October 1947, the Central Intelligence Agency was only weeks old. Ten weeks after it came into being, it delivered a formal estimate of its own, dated the day before the General Assembly vote. It predicted war if partition passed, and it warned that American backing for partition was already costing the United States prestige and would endanger its interests. A common assumption holds that American intelligence either never assessed partition or supported it. The declassified record shows the opposite: the intelligence service assessed it, in writing, and advised against what the government was about to do.

Who ran American intelligence. Before 1947, American foreign intelligence ran through the wartime Office of Strategic Services, which operated from 1942 and led by William J. Donovan, whom Roosevelt appointed. The OSS was dissolved in October 1945, and its analysts and operatives fed the agencies that followed. In 1946 an interim body, the Central Intelligence Group, carried the work forward. [cite:w_oss] The OSS also had a Palestine desk during the war; that history, and the Zionist intelligence service that operated on American soil in the same years, are told with the July 1945 Sonneborn meeting in [scene:s07d|the network founded in 1945].

The National Security Act of 1947 put the system on a permanent footing. It created the Central Intelligence Agency, the National Security Council, and the structure that became the Department of Defense; the CIA came into existence on 18 September 1947. [cite:w_nsa1947] Its first Director of Central Intelligence was Rear Admiral Roscoe Hillenkoetter, appointed by Truman. [cite:w_hillenkoetter] James Forrestal, the first Secretary of Defense, oversaw the department that grew from the same Act, so his warning on oil and the agency's estimate on partition came from two parts of one newly built national-security structure. The CIA was born four days before Loy Henderson sent his "not workable" memorandum to Secretary of State Marshall.

What ORE-55 said. The agency's Office of Reports and Estimates issued ORE-55, titled "The Consequences of the Partition of Palestine," dated 28 November 1947, one day before the General Assembly voted on partition. The declassified document is held in the CIA's own reading room. [cite:cia_ore55] Its summary makes five points. Armed hostilities between Jews and Arabs would break out if the General Assembly adopted partition. The United Nations would be morally bound to enforce its decision. Jewish forces would at first prevail, because of superior organization and equipment. The United States, by backing partition, had already lost much of its prestige in the Arab world. And imposed partition would place American commercial and strategic interests in serious danger. [cite:cia_ore55]

The first prediction was borne out quickly: sustained fighting began as a two-sided civil war inside Palestine within days of the 29 November vote, five and a half months before the armies of neighbouring Arab states crossed any border. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] The prediction of early Jewish advantage through organization and equipment belongs to the long argument over the balance of forces taken up later in this chapter. The estimate's concern for American standing in the Arab world restated, in the language of intelligence, what Henderson had put to Marshall and the Joint Chiefs had put in "The Problem of Palestine." Its summary, as recorded here, does not propose an alternative policy.

A chorus of four. Within ten weeks, four separate parts of the American government warned in writing against American sponsorship of partition: the State Department's Near East office, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of Defense, and the new CIA. Each of the first three is set out in [scene:s07j|the warnings of 1947]. They did not form one coordinated campaign. Each institution reached its conclusion through its own work, and the agreement among them is the finding.

Overruled. The President's domestic political advisers, led by Clark Clifford and David Niles, argued the opposite case, and their view prevailed, first in the partition vote and then in the recognition of Israel eleven minutes after its independence was proclaimed on 14 May 1948. The record shows that the warnings were made and read. It does not show them shaping the outcome. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman]

A later chapter of this library carries the story into 1948 and beyond, and adds claims that should be read with care. It states that declassified CIA and State Department documents from 1947 and 1948 warned consistently against recognizing Israel on strategic grounds; that CIA assessments noted Zionist arms-procurement networks operating across Europe and the United States and predicted that recognition would at once produce armed conflict with Arab states; that the State Department under Marshall opposed recognition on the same grounds; and that Truman's recognition came at 6:11 p.m. on 14 May 1948, eleven minutes after the declaration, the fastest diplomatic recognition in American history, so fast that his own State Department was caught unprepared. That account cites no specific document for these points, and they are given here as its claims. It goes on to describe the intelligence relationship with Israel that grew out of 1948, a later story told in [scene:cia_s02|1948: the CIA opposes].

One claim in that account does not match the document examined here. It states that a CIA report predicted that an arms embargo would lead to "peaceful coexistence." No such prediction appears in ORE-55's summary as recorded in this book, which predicts the reverse: armed hostilities if partition passed. If such a report exists, it is a different document, and it has not been identified.

What the record shows, and what it leaves open. The answer to "didn't they know?" is that they did. American intelligence assessed partition, did so in writing, and predicted war and damage to American interests; the decision was taken anyway. [cite:cia_ore55] What the record does not establish is how much weight the President gave the estimate, which arrived on the eve of a vote whose American position had been announced seven weeks earlier. A document dated 28 November could inform the vote on 29 November only if the decision were still open, and the 11 October announcement suggests it was not. Nor does the summary say what Hillenkoetter or Truman did with it once it was delivered. The estimate stands as a record of what the government's new intelligence service believed, not as evidence of what it changed.

sections.h: Who Objected at the Time
sections.html:
It is sometimes said that no one in the United States questioned the campaign for a Jewish state, or the money raised for it, until much later. The record of the 1940s says otherwise. Objections were raised while the decisions were being made, by an anti-Zionist Jewish organization, by a mainstream Jewish body, by a future intelligence officer and a former college dean, by a foreign parliament, and in 1948 by Hannah Arendt, Albert Einstein and others who signed their names to public protest. They were made in public and published. They were also outweighed. This section sets out who objected, what each said, and how large or small each voice was.

The American Council for Judaism. The most direct objection came from Jews who rejected Zionism on religious grounds. The American Council for Judaism was founded in 1942 and led by Lessing Rosenwald, with Rabbi Elmer Berger. It argued that Judaism was a religion, not a nationality, and it opposed partition. [cite:djn_1948_acj] [cite:jvl_acj_truman] In 1948 it went further and objected to funds raised by the United Jewish Appeal being used "for political and foreign governmental purposes." [cite:djn_1948_acj] The complaint touched the same charitable campaigns whose 1948 proceeds are traced in this chapter's account of Golda Meyerson's American tour: in the Council's view, charity was being put to political ends abroad.

How representative was it? On this the sources agree more than they differ. The Council's own historian documents it as a small minority that the mainstream Jewish organizations opposed, and Zionist sources describe it as a fringe group. [cite:kolsky_acj] [cite:jvl_acj_truman] Its argument mattered less for its numbers than for its content: it showed that the claim to speak for American Jews as a whole on Palestine was contested from inside the community.

The American Jewish Committee. A larger and more established body took a different path. At the congressional hearings of 1944, the American Jewish Committee, a mainstream organization, proposed an international trusteeship for Palestine instead of a Jewish commonwealth. [cite:djn_1944_hearings] This was not anti-Zionism of the Council's kind. It was an alternative arrangement offered by a leading Jewish organization, and it shows that support for a Jewish state was not yet a settled position among American Jewish institutions in the middle of the war. The same 1944 congressional resolutions drew protest abroad: Iraq's parliament formally objected to them. [cite:djn_1944_marshall]

Judah Magnes, president of the Hebrew University, had argued before the Anglo-American Committee in 1946 for a single binational state shared by Arabs and Jews, an argument told in [scene:aac_s01|the Anglo-American Committee]. He did not stop there. In May 1948, the month of independence, Magnes met Truman to press for a federation under trusteeship. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026]

Kermit Roosevelt and the Gildersleeve committee. In 1948 Kermit Roosevelt Jr. published a 24-page pamphlet, "The Partition of Palestine: A Lesson in Pressure Politics." [cite:ptsem_kr_pamphlet] Its title states its argument: that the partition decision had been produced by political pressure. Roosevelt was later the CIA's field commander in Iran's 1953 coup. [cite:w_kermit_jr] With Virginia Gildersleeve, the former dean of Barnard College, he formed the Committee for Justice and Peace in the Holy Land, which warned that "extreme Zionist pressure" risked disrupting national unity. [cite:mosaic_cia_zionism] [cite:w_kermit_jr] These objections echoed, from outside government, the warnings that the State Department, the Joint Chiefs and the Defense Secretary had made from inside it the year before.

Arendt: "There Is Still Time." The fullest argument came in May 1948. Hannah Arendt's essay "To Save the Jewish Homeland: There Is Still Time" appeared in Commentary that month, on pages 398 to 406. [cite:rs_rd5_arendt_commentary] In the historian Robert Manne's account, Arendt argued that Jewish near-unanimity for a state, reached before any settlement with the Arabs, would bring war, and that even a victorious Jewish state would remain small, surrounded by hostile neighbors and absorbed in its own defense. She proposed instead a gradual binational federation, built on mixed Jewish-Arab local councils under United Nations trusteeship with American and British support, and wrote that "It is still not too late." She condemned the Irgun's attacks, including Deir Yassin. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026]

Arendt worked closely with Magnes, and their proposals ran in parallel: a federation, under trusteeship, in place of partition. In 1952 she called Magnes "the conscience of the Jewish people." Manne also reports that she later estimated the Arab "evacuation" of 1948 at 500,000, a figure that sits among the many estimates of the refugee exodus discussed elsewhere in this chapter. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026] Her essay is arguably the fullest statement of the dissenting case at the time. As her title said, her aim was to save the Jewish homeland; her case was that a state won by war against its neighbors would leave it small, besieged and absorbed in self-defense.

The Einstein–Arendt letter. The last objection of the year was aimed not at partition, which had happened, but at what one wing of the new state's politics had become. A letter dated 2 December 1948 and published in the New York Times on 4 December, signed by 28 people including Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and Sidney Hook, protested Menachem Begin's visit to the United States. It described his Tnuat Haherut, the Freedom Party, which had grown out of the Irgun, as bearing "the unmistakable stamp of a Fascist party." [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt] The Irgun's own path from underground army to political party, after the Altalena and the absorption of the militias into one army, is told in [scene:mil_s01|from three militias to one army].

The letter named Deir Yassin directly. It said that on 9 April "terrorist bands" had attacked a "peaceful village, which was not a military objective," and "killed most of its inhabitants (240 men, women, and children)." [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt] The figure of 240 is the one in circulation in 1948. Later research has revised the count of the dead at Deir Yassin, and the current state of that evidence is set out in [scene:ma_s01|Deir Yassin, the Hadassah convoy and Tantura]. The letter is evidence of what its signers believed and said in December 1948, not a settled casualty figure.

Raised, published, outweighed. These objections differed in their grounds. The Council for Judaism objected in principle to Jewish nationhood; the American Jewish Committee to the form a solution should take; Roosevelt and Gildersleeve to the political pressure behind the decision; Arendt and Magnes to partition by war rather than federation by agreement; and the signers of December 1948 to a specific party and its record. None of them prevailed. Partition was voted, the state was proclaimed and recognized, and the fundraising the Council objected to continued. Formal action on foreign-agent questions came only much later, with the 1962 order under the Foreign Agents Registration Act and the Fulbright hearings of 1963, told in a later volume.

What the record does not settle is how much support these positions had beyond their authors. The sources measure the Council for Judaism only in words, a small minority in its own historian's account and a fringe in Zionist accounts, and give no membership figures. They say nothing about how many Americans read Roosevelt's pamphlet or Arendt's essay. What they do establish is that the objections existed, in print, in the years the decisions were made, and that several of the most pointed came from Jewish organizations and Jewish writers.

sections.h: Resolution 181: The Vote, the Pause and the Numbers
sections.html:
By the autumn of 1947 the question of Palestine had passed from Britain to the United Nations. A special committee had visited the country and recommended partition (its work is told in [scene:s07i|UNSCOP]). It now fell to the General Assembly, the body that had replaced the League of Nations as the forum of the world's states, to decide what to do with that recommendation. [cite:un_unispal_186560] The Assembly did so in two stages: first in an Ad Hoc Committee on Palestine, where the plan was debated and alternatives were voted down, and then in plenary session, where a two-thirds majority was required. [cite:avalon_res181] [cite:britannica_res181]

The familiar account compresses all of this into one image: the nations of the world, gathered peacefully, created Israel by democratic consensus. The documents do not support that picture, and they do not support its mirror image either. What they show is a recorded international act with real weight, adopted after a contested count, a pause, and pressure applied by one great power to small states, while the other great power voted the same way for reasons of its own, and while the majority population of the country in question had no seat in the room.

The first count came in the Ad Hoc Committee on 25 November 1947. There the partition plan was adopted by 25 votes to 13, with 17 abstentions. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] On the same occasion the committee rejected the alternative: a draft for a single, unitary state, known as Draft Resolution III, failed by 29 votes to 12, with 14 abstentions. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] A Pakistani amendment that would have capped land ownership at 10% for each community was also rejected, by 22 votes to 8. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] So by 25 November the Assembly had, in committee, turned down both a unitary state and a limit on land holding, and had approved partition. What it had not yet shown was that partition could clear two-thirds in plenary. Published accounts describe the initial tally of 25 in favor as short of that threshold, and record that the Assembly's president, Aranha, arranged a three-day postponement before the decisive vote. [cite:un_181_records] [cite:un_181_text] The Yearbook excerpt dates the committee vote to 25 November and the plenary vote to 29 November; the material does not record the exact day on which the postponement was called.

The three days are the hinge of the story. A resolution that lacked the votes and then passed after a pause had a specific window in which something changed. The record of that window is uneven. It does not explain every delegation's reasoning, and it was never meant to; what it does document is several of the forces at work inside it, and the plainest of them was the government of the United States. [cite:un_unispal_186560]

The Truman administration's executive branch pushed for a yes vote. Its own foreign-policy and military establishment pushed the other way: the State Department and the Pentagon opposed the push, citing Arab anger and the Cold War stakes of Middle Eastern oil. [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] The most senior internal objection on record came from James Forrestal. Forrestal had been a Wall Street financier before entering government, had served as Secretary of the Navy, and had become the first Secretary of Defense. He approached Palestine through strategy and petroleum, and believed that alienating the Arab world would endanger American access to Middle Eastern oil and hand an advantage to the Soviet Union. [cite:un_unispal_186560] His diaries, published after his death as The Forrestal Diaries (1951), record his distaste for what he called the "bullying" and "coercion" of small, dependent states to secure their votes, and his conviction that American policy in the Middle East was being driven by domestic political calculation rather than national interest. [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] [cite:un_unispal_186560]

The weight of that evidence comes from its form. A diary written for oneself, and not for an audience, is a first-person and contemporaneous source, stronger than a later recollection or a historian's characterization. It records a sitting cabinet officer objecting to the pressure campaign his own government was running. Its limits are just as clear. Forrestal's diary records his characterization and his objection; it is not an operational record of which tactics were used on which country by which official. His warnings were overruled. He left office early in 1949 and, weeks later, died in a fall from a high window at Bethesda Naval Hospital, where he was being treated for depression and exhaustion. The death was ruled a suicide; a minority of historians have noted contested details, and it remains one of the unsettled anomalies of the period. [cite:un_unispal_186560] His opposition is documented. Nothing in the record ties the manner of his death to it, and this book builds no theory on the coincidence of timing.

The pressure Forrestal deplored had named targets. Three states moved from a no vote or an abstention to a yes during the postponement: Haiti, Liberia and the Philippines. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] The historian Michael Cohen, in Palestine and the Great Powers (1982), documents the shift and connects it to a broader pattern of pressure on smaller, economically dependent states in exactly this window. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition]

Liberia is the best-documented case, because its dependency was so large and so visible. The Firestone Tire and Rubber Company held a rubber concession in Liberia that the sources put at about 1.1 million acres; the company was the country's dominant employer, its largest source of foreign exchange, and, in effect, its economy. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] One account in the sources used here dates the concession from 1926 and describes it as roughly one million acres on a 99-year lease. The sources also attribute the Firestone material to two works by Cohen: Palestine and the Great Powers (1982) in most places, and Truman and Israel (University of California Press, 1990) in one. Liberia's own ambassador complained that the American delegation had threatened aid cuts to several countries in the same period. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] Firestone had no stake in Palestine. The point of the case is the transmission mechanism: a great power's commercial hold over a small client could be turned into that client's vote on a question a hemisphere away. The economic relationship is well documented; the precise way the leverage was exercised is less fully documented than the relationship itself. The corporate pressure and the diplomatic pressure the ambassador described were two separate channels converging on one small state, not one orchestrated scheme.

The Philippines, a recent American possession bound to Washington by aid and security ties, came under American pressure through those economic ties.
