The letter to the New York Times of 4 December 1948, signed by Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and 26 others against Menachem Begin's visit, said the attackers had "killed most of its inhabitants (240 men, women, and children)." [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt] Arendt had already condemned the Irgun's attacks, Deir Yassin among them, in May 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026] The 240 is a figure given in 1948, not the one scholars now give; the letter itself is told in [scene:rf_s01|the section on dissent].

The killings had effects well beyond the village. Benny Morris wrote that Deir Yassin was followed by mass Arab flight. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] An account drawn from Israeli historians adds two details: that the attackers announced the killings by radio to nearby villages, which the official Haganah history by Yehuda Slutsky records, and that Ben-Gurion later noted in his diary that Deir Yassin "had a decisive effect" on Arab flight. That account gives the toll as about 107 civilians, at the low end of the current range. [cite:morris_1948] Material on Deir Yassin in Israeli military archives remains classified. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] [cite:aljazeera_deir_yassin_75]

Four days later the violence ran the other way. On 13 April 1948 Arab forces attacked a convoy travelling to Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus and killed 78 Jews, most of them doctors and nurses. The attack was a reprisal for Deir Yassin. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The victims were medical staff on their way to a hospital, and their deaths belong in the same record, with the same weight, as the villagers killed four days before.

The Hadassah convoy was not the only such killing of Jews in these weeks. Before the Mandate ended, the Arab Legion attacked the Gush Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements; its defenders surrendered, and some of them were massacred, according to Avi Shlaim's account. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_cw] During Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni's command, the Army of the Holy War's explosives unit blew up the Jewish Agency building in Jerusalem; the source does not give the date or the toll. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_abdelqader] These belong to the civil war that had begun on 1 December 1947, in which attacks ran in both directions. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition]

Tantura shows most clearly how the record has grown. It was a coastal village captured by the Alexandroni Brigade on 22–23 May 1948, about a week after the state was proclaimed. A master's thesis by Theodore Katz later recorded testimony that villagers had been killed after the village surrendered. Veterans of the brigade sued him for libel, and he retracted. [cite:npr_tantura] [cite:jewishindependent_tantura]

The question did not end with the retraction. In the 2022 Israeli documentary Tantura, veterans then in their nineties described on camera killings and a mass grave near what is now Dor Beach, a popular resort. A document shown in the film acknowledges that soldiers dug a mass grave. Other veterans deny that any massacre took place, and the number killed cannot be established. [cite:npr_tantura] [cite:jewishindependent_tantura]

The Deir Yassin numbers show how a toll can move in both directions. The figure of 254 was repeated for decades; contemporaries in December 1948 wrote 240; scholarship now gives about 110. The Red Cross representative's 150 bodies is a count of what one witness saw in one place, not a total. None of these figures is a final count, and each should be read with its source.

The way these events entered the record is itself part of the history. Much of what is known came from Israelis: historians working in Israeli archives, a student who gathered veterans' testimony, and veterans who decided late in life to speak. [cite:npr_tantura] Atrocities against Jews in the same weeks, at the Hadassah convoy and at Gush Etzion, are equally part of the record. The later expulsions at Lydda and Ramla in July 1948, with their own disputed tolls, are told with the Arab states' war in [scene:rd5_invasion|the invasion and the war].

Much remains unsettled. Israeli military archives on Deir Yassin are still partly closed, so the exact toll and the full chain of command cannot yet be documented. The number killed at Tantura cannot be established, and the veterans who were there disagree about what happened. The sources used here give no date for Katz's thesis or for the libel case, and no toll for the bombing of the Jewish Agency building. For Gush Etzion it says that some defenders were massacred but gives no number. What the record does establish is that killings of civilians and prisoners took place on both sides in these weeks, and that the documentary record of them is still growing.

sections.h: The Fall of the Mixed Towns, April–May 1948
sections.html:
For four months after the partition vote, the fighting in Palestine was a civil war, with attacks in both directions. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] In April 1948 it changed character. The Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi writes that the Zionist forces "did not begin to seize and hold on to Arab territory" until the offensive that began on 1 April 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] That offensive opened under Plan Dalet, issued three weeks earlier ([scene:pd_s01|Plan Dalet]). Within six weeks the towns in which Arabs and Jews had lived side by side, and the Arab towns near them, had changed hands one after another.

Khalidi's phrasing is precise, and it should be read beside his own correction elsewhere: a footnote in his study of Plan Dalet records that at least ten Arab villages had been captured by 1 March 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The two statements can stand together. Villages were taken before April; the systematic seizing and holding of Arab territory, in his account, began with the April offensive.

Tiberias was the first town to fall, on 18 April 1948. Its Arab population, about 4,500 to 5,000 people and swollen by refugees from nearby villages, was evacuated. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa]

Haifa followed within the week, and its fall is the best documented and the most argued over. Early on 21 April 1948 the Haganah's Carmeli Brigade, under Moshe Carmel, attacked as British forces withdrew from their dividing positions in the city. That same day Major-General Hugh Stockwell, the British commander, had told Arab representatives that his forces would redeploy. The city fell on 22 April. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa]

The cost is known from British figures, which Khalidi cites: about 100 Arabs killed and 200 wounded, and about 20 Jews killed and 40 wounded. On 22 April about 50,000 Arabs were crowded into the Old Town. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa]

On 22 April the Arab delegates met Stockwell at the Town Hall over the terms of a truce; Haifa's Jewish mayor was there too, according to one account. What was said there, and what it meant, is the heart of the dispute over why Haifa's Arabs left. Khalidi's account, which draws on an account by Koussa, runs as follows. Stockwell warned the Arab delegates that if they did not sign the truce he would not be responsible if "three or four hundred more" were killed. The delegates had asked Damascus for instructions and had no reply. Their request for transport out of the city, according to Koussa's account, was made "on the spur of the moment," not under orders from the Arab states. Khalidi concludes: "Within a week, some 50,000 Arab inhabitants had been expelled." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa]

Khalidi goes further on the British role. He argues that the Haganah had advance knowledge of the British redeployment, and he calls Stockwell "an accomplice in the fall of Haifa." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] The strongest form of his case is that the timing of the attack, the redeployment and the ultimatum at the Town Hall fit together too closely to be chance, and that the evacuation request was the improvised act of men without instructions under military pressure, not a plan from outside.

A sharply different account appears in an opinion article in the Jewish Chronicle by Florit Shoihet, published on 12 August 2026. According to that article, Haifa's Jewish mayor, Shabtai Levy, pleaded with the Arab delegates at the same meeting: "Stay in the city and be equal citizens." Stockwell, it reports, told the delegates, "You have made a foolish decision." The Haganah, it says, broadcast assurances of safety and civil rights, and about 60,000 Arabs left. [cite:rs_rd5_jc_haifa] The strongest form of this case is that Haifa's Arabs were offered terms of equal citizenship by the Jewish mayor and urged to stay by the British commander, and that their own delegation chose to leave. The article is an opinion piece and cites no specific archive for these details, and it should be weighed as such.

The third position is the historian Benny Morris's, as Khalidi reports it, and it has shifted. Morris first acknowledged, in 1987, that there were no Arab evacuation orders. He later argued that such orders were issued after the fighting. Khalidi disputes the later position. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] The broader question of evacuation orders, and the June 1948 Israeli intelligence estimate that attributed no more than 5 percent of departures to them, is set out in [scene:rd5_refugees|the refugee section]. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref]

The two departure figures, 50,000 and about 60,000, come from opposite sides of the argument and are not far apart. The dispute is less about how many left than about why.

Even the Haifa operation's name is unsettled: Khalidi's Haifa study says the operation planned as Misparayim was renamed Chametz, while his list of Plan D operations keeps the two apart, a discrepancy set out with the Plan Dalet record. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988]

After Haifa the other towns followed in the last three weeks of the Mandate. Khalidi's operation list gives the frame: Chametz against the villages around Jaffa from 27 April; Yiftach in eastern Galilee from 28 April; Matateh in the Tiberias area from 3 May; Gideon at Beisan from 11 May; and Ben Ami at Acre on 14 May, the day the state was proclaimed. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Jaffa and Safed fell in these weeks. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] During the war an estimated 100,000 to 110,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were displaced into Lebanon, the large majority from northern Palestine, including the Acre area. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy]

The available record is uneven across these towns. Tiberias and Haifa are documented in detail; Jaffa, Safed, Beisan and Acre appear here only through Khalidi's list of operations, and the exact dates on which Jaffa, Safed and Acre fell are not established in the sources used here. For Haifa, the British casualty figures and the timing of the redeployment are documented. Whether the Haganah knew of the redeployment in advance rests on Khalidi's argument. What was said at the Town Hall rests on two accounts that cannot both be complete: Khalidi's, from the Arab side, and an opinion article that cites no archive. And Morris's own changing view shows that the question of evacuation orders in Haifa has not been settled even by a historian whose archival work documented the expulsions in detail.

sections.h: Abdullah Between the Jewish Agency, Britain and the Arab League, 1947–1948
sections.html:
Of the Arab rulers who sent armies into Palestine in May 1948, one had been talking to the Jewish Agency for months beforehand. King Abdullah of Transjordan commanded the Arab Legion, a force trained and commanded by British officers, and he had territorial aims of his own. [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] A familiar account holds that Jordan went to war in 1948 solely to destroy the new Jewish state alongside its allies, with no separate interest of its own. The record of his meetings, and of what his army actually did, tells a more complicated story. Whether it amounts to "collusion" is one of the longest-running arguments in the history of the war.

Abdullah's separate position was visible before the partition vote. When the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine toured the region in the summer of 1947, Transjordan declined to send a representative to testify outside the country. Instead the committee's chairman and seven of its members visited the king in Amman on 25 July 1947. [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]

In early November 1947, at Naharayim on the Jordan, Abdullah met Golda Meyerson, later Golda Meir, of the Jewish Agency. According to the Center for Israel Education's account, he told her that he intended to annex the Arab areas of Palestine, and she replied that the Zionist leaders would not oppose this if there were no clashes between Jewish and Transjordanian forces. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_golda] The historian Avi Shlaim calls the understanding reached that November a "tacit agreement." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab] The sources record no written text. What existed, on this account, was a shared expectation: the king would take the Arab part of Palestine, and the Jewish state would not fight him for it.

The British side of the triangle came into view in February 1948. That month Britain's Foreign Secretary, an office Ernest Bevin had held since July 1945 [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin], met the prime minister of Transjordan and John Glubb, the British officer who commanded the Arab Legion. After that meeting, according to Graham Jevon's study of Glubb and the Legion (Cambridge University Press, 2017), Glubb "actively sought to thwart the efforts of the Arab irregular forces" in Palestine and sought a military accord with the Zionists. Jevon writes that his findings corroborate Shlaim's disputed claim that Britain gave Abdullah a "green light" to occupy the areas allotted to the Arab state. He also concludes that Glubb was not the architect of this Greater Transjordan scheme but the man who carried it out. [cite:rs_rd5_jevon_2017] The abstract of Jevon's chapter, which is what this book has drawn on, does not give the date of the meeting or record what was said.

Shlaim states the British policy plainly. Britain, he writes, "was resigned to the emergence of a Jewish state but supported her client, King Abdullah," and in doing so "helped to abort the birth of a Palestinian state." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_ab]

The Arab League pulled Abdullah the other way. The League's anti-Hashemite members suspected him of collaborating with the Zionists. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab] He, for his part, opposed every move toward Palestinian independence and refused to deal with Hajj Amin al-Husayni, the Mufti, who led the Arab Higher Committee. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] The quarrel over who would speak for the Palestinians is told in [scene:rd5_arab_leadership|the section on Arab leadership]. On 30 April 1948 the League's Political Committee decided that "all the Arab states must prepare their armies for the invasion of Palestine on 15 May." Under pressure from Transjordan and Iraq, Abdullah was named commander-in-chief. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab] The man suspected of a private arrangement with the Jewish Agency was now the nominal head of the Arab war against it.

On 10 May 1948, four days before the end of the Mandate, Meyerson crossed to Amman with Ezra Danin. The two traveled disguised as an Arab couple. According to the Center for Israel Education, Abdullah told her that he was now "one of five" and asked: "why don't you wait a few years? Drop your demands for free immigration." [cite:rs_rd5_cie_golda] Meyerson's own report at the time, as summarized in Shlaim's notes, records that the king did not deny their earlier understanding, said he had no choice but to join the invasion, and that they did not part as enemies. On 13 May Yaacov Shimoni of the Jewish Agency weighed it up: the king "has not entirely betrayed the agreement, nor is he entirely loyal to it." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab]

On 15 May, as the armies moved, Syria's president, Shukri al-Quwwatli, urged a halt to the advance. Abdullah refused. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab]

What the Arab Legion then did can be set against those meetings. Even before the Mandate ended, the Legion attacked the Gush Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements; its defenders surrendered and some were massacred, according to Shlaim's notes. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_cw] Once the war between states began, the State Department's Office of the Historian records, Transjordanian forces intervened only in areas designated for the Arab state or for the Jerusalem corpus separatum, the separate Jerusalem zone of the partition plan. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] Within those limits the Legion fought hard. In the first round, according to Shlaim's notes, the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem surrendered on 28 May, and three frontal Israeli attacks on Latrun, on 25 and 30 May and 9 June, were repelled by the Arab Legion. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] After the second truce began on 18 July, the Legion continued shelling West Jerusalem through October and on 12 August demolished the Latrun pumping station, which the United Nations held, according to an Israeli army account. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce2] The Legion's commander was also the source of many of the most-quoted figures on the balance of forces, which historians treat with caution because he commanded one of the sides. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance]

By the end of the war the Legion held East Jerusalem's Old City and the West Bank. It was Jordan's most consequential military action of the war, and the territory remained under its administration for the next nineteen years. [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] Under the armistice agreements of 1949, Jordan kept the West Bank. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] Abdullah opposed the Arab League's All-Palestine Government in Gaza and answered it, on 1 December 1948, with the Jericho congress that proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan under his crown, as told in the section on Arab leadership. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni]

The formal annexation came later and is told in full in [scene:ijr_src_s05|Jordan's war, armistice and annexation]. In brief: on 24 April 1950 Jordan's parliament annexed the West Bank, declaring support for "complete unity between the two sides of the Jordan and their union into one State." [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] Only Britain, Iraq and Pakistan recognized it, and Britain's recognition excluded Jerusalem. The strongest regional opposition came from Jordan's fellow Arab League states, whose Political Committee ruled in Cairo that the annexation violated the League's earlier resolution and considered expelling Jordan. [cite:sixdaywar_jerusalem] During the nineteen years of Jordanian rule that followed, Jewish access to the Western Wall and other religious sites in the Old City was denied, contrary to the 1949 armistice terms, and dozens of historic synagogues were damaged or destroyed. One reading notes that the 1950 resolution's "two banks" language mirrors the Revisionist Zionist claim, associated with Jabotinsky, that both banks of the Jordan belong together, used here in the opposite direction; it is a structural parallel, and the record does not show that either side was answering the other.

Was there collusion across the Jordan? The case that there was, in substance, is Shlaim's, and on the British side Jevon's study says its findings corroborate it. On this view there was a tacit understanding between Abdullah and the Jewish Agency to divide the territory the United Nations had allotted to an Arab state, Britain gave the king a green light to take his share, and Glubb restrained the Arab irregulars and sought an accord with the Zionists. The Legion's conduct fits: it stayed out of the territory allotted to the Jewish state, and the Palestinian state that the partition plan foresaw was never born. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_ab] [cite:rs_rd5_jevon_2017] [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b]

The case that the arrangement was partial at best rests on the same meetings. In Amman on 10 May Abdullah called himself "one of five," asked the Jews to defer statehood and drop their demand for free immigration, and joined the invasion. The Jewish Agency's own Shimoni judged him neither loyal to the understanding nor in full breach of it. And the Legion fought Israeli forces hard where their aims met, in Jerusalem and at Latrun. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_golda] [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab] [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war]

The two cases are not as far apart as the word "collusion" suggests. Both accept that Abdullah and the Jewish Agency talked, that he wanted the Arab part of Palestine, and that he went to war as part of the Arab coalition. They differ on how firm the understanding was and how much it shaped the fighting. Several things remain unsettled by the record gathered here. The Naharayim and Amman exchanges come largely through the Center for Israel Education's account and Meyerson's own report, not through a Jordanian record. The February 1948 meeting is known from the abstract of Jevon's study, without its date or the words spoken. And the Legion's restraint toward the Jewish state's territory can be read as the keeping of an understanding or as the pursuit of the king's own aims, which happened to coincide with it.

sections.h: Independence and the Nakba, 1948
sections.html:
On Friday 14 May 1948, at four in the afternoon, David Ben-Gurion stood in a hall of the Tel Aviv Museum and read out the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel. The British Mandate was due to expire at midnight, a few hours later. [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal] [cite:morasha_czech_arms] The document itself notes the day: it was signed "on this Sabbath eve." Its dating is not quite consistent. The signing line reads "5th day of Iyar, 5708 – 14th May 1948," while the body of the text, referring to the end of the Mandate, gives "6th Iyar, 5708 (15th May, 1948)." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] The discrepancy stands in the text as it is reproduced.

Ben-Gurion, born in 1886 and dead in 1973, was a Polish-born organizer of the labor Zionist movement. He became the new state's first Prime Minister and the most consequential single figure in its creation. [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal] Palestinians call what followed the Nakba, Arabic for "catastrophe." [cite:morris_1948] The founding of the state and the displacement of much of the Arab population from the territory it came to hold took place in the same months, and this section follows both. Along the way it tests two claims that have long been taught about 1948. The first is that the Palestinians left of their own accord, on instructions broadcast by Arab radio. The second is that America created and armed Israel. Both claims rest on something real, and the record contradicts both.

The Declaration began with its grounds. It based the state on "our natural and historic right," on the Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917, on the Mandate of the League of Nations, and on the General Assembly resolution of 29 November 1947. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] The order matters. The first ground was a claim of right that did not depend on any outside power. The other three were international instruments: a British pledge, a League mandate and a United Nations vote. Taken together, the text claimed the state both as an inheritance and as an act of international law.

The document also made promises. It pledged equality of social and political rights to all inhabitants "irrespective of religion, race or sex." It appealed to the Arab inhabitants of the state "to preserve peace" and to take part in building it on the basis of "full and equal citizenship." To the neighbouring states it extended "an offer of peace and good neighbourliness." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] These clauses are the strongest written form of the founders' case. They promised a state for the Jewish people in which its Arab citizens would be full citizens, and they offered peace to its neighbors. Whether and how the first promise was kept is a question for the later volumes of this library, because the record of the Arabs who stayed inside Israel begins after 1948. The answer to the second came within hours: armies from Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Egypt invaded, and Transjordanian forces entered the areas designated for the Arab state and Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] That war is the subject of a later section of this chapter.

Two further features of the text are often missed. The Declaration stated no borders. It referred to Eretz-Israel, the Land of Israel, and it pledged steps toward "the economic union of the whole of Eretz-Israel." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] Economic union between the two states was what the UNSCOP majority had recommended in 1947. [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] And it set a deadline for its own replacement. The People's Council became the Provisional Council of State, and a constitution was to be adopted by an elected Constituent Assembly "not later than the 1st October 1948." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration]

That deadline passed. When the First Knesset met, it deadlocked over what a constitution should contain, above all over the place of religion in public life. Instead it resolved to enact Basic Laws one at a time. [cite:gov_legalclarity] The first came in 1958. There are now fourteen, covering the Knesset, the government, the military, the judiciary and civil rights, and the Supreme Court treats them as having constitutional weight, though a simple Knesset majority can amend them. [cite:basiclaw_britannica] The constitution promised in May 1948 has never been adopted. The consequences of that gap belong to a later period and are traced in [scene:ilgov_s01|No Constitution, Only Basic Laws].

The structures of the new state appeared quickly, because most of them already existed. The institutions the Jewish Agency had built under the Mandate became, almost overnight, the institutions of a sovereign government. The Haganah, the pre-state militia, became the Israel Defense Forces; a state intelligence service, the Mossad, was established in 1949. The United States extended de facto recognition within eleven minutes, a timing arranged by Clark Clifford over the State Department's objection. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] Recognition is examined in the next section. What matters here is a distinction the familiar account often blurs. Recognition was a political act. Weapons were another matter.

The United States imposed an arms embargo on all parties to the 1948 war. The Truman administration recognized Israel within minutes, but it did not lift the embargo. [cite:morasha_czech_arms] The weapons that reached the new army in the decisive months came instead from communist Czechoslovakia, flown in by C-54 transports from Žatec airfield in an airlift code-named Operation Balak. One account describes them as former German arms: Mauser rifles, Messerschmitt Bf 109G fighters and ZK 383 submachine guns. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_shipments] The fuller record of [scene:cz_s01|the Czechoslovak pipeline] is more precise about the fighters, Avia S-199s, a Czech-built derivative of the Bf 109, about 25 of them, and adds some 35,000 Karabiner 98k rifles sent by sea and a 1952 Czechoslovak figure of almost $14.5 million in receipts. [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] Israeli military historians have documented the operation, and so has Zeev Sternhell in his work on the founding. Ben-Gurion's verdict survives in two forms: "Czech arms saved the State of Israel," in his memoir, [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal] and, in 1968, "Czechoslovak arms saved the State of Israel, really and absolutely." [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel]

The embargo, too, is described two ways. The shorter statement has the United States, Britain and the United Nations all embargoing; the pipeline record has Britain supplying aircraft and training to the Arab air forces. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] Both versions are given here. Nor was Czechoslovakia the only source: the clandestine American procurement network, and the money Golda Meyerson raised in the United States early in 1948, are described in earlier sections of this chapter.

Czechoslovakia did not act alone. It lay inside the Soviet sphere, and the sales went ahead with Moscow's permission. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] The motive usually given is the same one read into the Soviet vote for partition in November 1947: anything that hastened the end of the British Mandate weakened Britain's position in the eastern Mediterranean. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] On that reading, Soviet interest and the new state's survival ran in the same direction for a few years and then parted. Two conclusions are sometimes drawn from this episode, and both go too far. The first is that the state later regarded as America's closest ally was armed at birth by the Soviet bloc while Washington held back. That is accurate for 1948, but it was a dated episode, and Soviet-Israeli relations changed markedly in the years that followed. The second is that Israel was a Western implant. The arms record is the strongest evidence against that view: at the decisive moment, the Western power most often credited with Israel's birth was withholding weapons from it.

The same months produced the Nakba. The figures given in the main account in this book's sources are between 700,000 and 750,000 Palestinians displaced, with about 500 villages depopulated or destroyed. [cite:morris_1948] [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] Benny Morris estimates 700,000. Walid Khalidi gives 750,000, and Rashid Khalidi accepts the higher figure. Walid Khalidi's All That Remains (1992) documents the villages one by one. [cite:walid_khalidi_all_that_remains] Much of the sustained documentation comes from Israeli historians writing from inside the country's own archives: Morris's 1948: A History of the First Arab-Israeli War, Ilan Pappé's The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine, Tom Segev's 1949: The First Israelis and Avi Shlaim's The Iron Wall. [cite:morris_1948] [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing]

One account in this library calls the 750,000 figure undisputed by any credible historian. The wider record does not bear that out. The UN Conciliation Commission's technical estimate of 1949 was about 711,000; a later summary gives the same commission's figure as 726,000. Other figures run from a past Israeli government estimate "as low as 520,000" up to 850,000 from Palestinian researchers. UNRWA's rolls of 1950 held 957,000, but the commission had already warned that relief rolls were inflated by duplicate ration cards and by people who were not refugees. [cite:rs_rd5_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd5_prrn_1996] Counts of depopulated villages also vary with method, from 369 in Morris's 1987 count to 418 in Khalidi's and 531 localities in the Palestine Land Society's list, which includes towns and tribal lands. [cite:rs_rd5_plands_villages] There is no dispute that the displacement happened, or about its rough scale. The exact numbers are disputed, and [scene:rd5_refugees|the section on the refugees] sets out each estimate and its method.

The territorial figures show what the war decided. By 1948, land in Jewish ownership, bought parcel by parcel over decades, amounted to roughly seven percent of Mandate Palestine. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The same account elsewhere puts legally purchased land at 9.8 percent, so the sources disagree on the exact figure, but both are under a tenth. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] Resolution 181 had allotted about 55 percent of the country to the Jewish state (56 percent in other sources used in this chapter). By the 1949 armistice, about 78 percent of Mandate Palestine was under Israeli control. [cite:morris_1948] Purchase accounts for the first figure. The difference between it and the last was made, in this account, by the war and by the displacement this section describes. The familiar phrase about making the desert bloom on land that was bought and settled describes the first figure. The rest has a different history.

How the departure happened is the core of the dispute, and Plan Dalet is the central document in it. The Haganah finalized it on 10 March 1948; according to the account in the sources used here it was released from the Israeli archives in the 1980s, and Walid Khalidi published its text as an appendix to his article "Plan Dalet: Master Plan for the Conquest of Palestine," republished in 1988. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Its text, its village clause and the operations carried out under it are set out in the section on Plan Dalet. One account in this book's sources summarizes the plan as authorizing three things: securing the areas assigned to the Jewish state by expelling villages that resisted; taking Arab-majority cities in those areas; and a stated vocabulary of destruction (haricha) and expulsion (gerush). [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing]

What the plan meant is where historians divide. Walid Khalidi argues that it created "the military fait accompli upon which the state of Israel was to be based," and that the exodus was its product. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Pappé argues in The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine (2006) that Plan Dalet meets the UN definition of ethnic cleansing. [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] Morris, who stands politically to Pappé's right and does not use that term, documents many of the same operations but reads the plan differently: as a military plan whose village provisions gave local commanders discretion, used in some places and not others, rather than a central order to expel. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] His wider conclusions on the causes of flight, and Avi Shlaim's reply, are set out with the refugees at the end of this chapter.

One summary in this book's sources holds that "the debate is over the term, not the facts," and that the Haganah carried out a plan to secure and expel which produced the outcome of 750,000 displaced. [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] That is one reading. The fuller record shows the disagreement reaching further, into the facts of intent. Was there a central decision to remove the Arab population, or a military plan whose village clause left expulsion to local commanders and the course of battle? The documents cited on each side are real. The disagreement is over what they show.

The record names particular episodes. On 9 April 1948, Irgun and Lehi forces, the two right-wing militias later folded into the Israel Defense Forces, attacked the village of Deir Yassin west of Jerusalem, with Haganah and Palmach support. [cite:morris_1948] [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] Current scholarship puts the toll at about 110, generally between 107 and 120, against the 254 cited for decades and the 240 of the letter signed by Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and others in December 1948; one account in this book's sources gives about 107. [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt] [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The figures and their sources are weighed in the section on the massacres of 1948, and Israeli military archives on the attack remain partly classified. [cite:aljazeera_deir_yassin_75] According to Yehuda Slutsky's official history of the Haganah, the attackers announced the killings by radio to nearby villages in order to spread panic, and in the following weeks many families in those villages fled. Ben-Gurion later wrote in his diary that Deir Yassin "had a decisive effect" on Arab flight. [cite:morris_1948] The account in this book's sources argues that the panic was the purpose, not a by-product: terror used as an instrument of removal. That is an inference from Slutsky's record and from the flight that followed, and it is presented here as such. Four days after Deir Yassin, on 13 April, Arab forces attacked a convoy to the Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus and killed 78 Jews, most of them doctors and nurses, in reprisal. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The two killings belong in the same account.

The same account argues that the mechanism did not depend on any one militia, and points to Lydda and Ramla in July 1948. There, it says, about 50,000 civilians were expelled by the Haganah on written orders signed by Yitzhak Rabin, with no Irgun or Lehi involvement. [cite:morris_1948] By July, however, the Haganah had been merged into the Israel Defense Forces under the provisional government's order of 26 May. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] The two main accounts of the episode give wider numbers: 50,000 to 70,000 inhabitants and 250 to 400 Palestinian civilians killed in Lockman's summary of Morris; about 70,000 driven out and close to 1,000 dead, counting the march that followed, in the Palestinian encyclopedia Palquest. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war] [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] Citing Morris, both report that on 12 July Ben-Gurion answered a question about the inhabitants with the words "Expel them," and that Rabin then signed the expulsion order. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war] The operation is told in full in the section on the Arab states' war.

Ben-Gurion appears on both sides of this record. He led a community that included Holocaust survivors and refugees from the Middle East to statehood against invading armies. He also held executive authority over a founding that included the documented expulsions. The account in this book's sources calls him the architect of the new state's territorial and demographic policy, and treats his own diaries and directives as part of the evidence for the expulsions. [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal] That account also admits that it does not trace every decision he made about them. Whether his authority amounted to a general policy of expulsion is the point on which Morris and his critics differ. Neither the heroic version of his career nor the purely damning one can be kept without leaving out half of what the record shows.

The first of the two taught claims was put to a direct test in 1961. For years after the war, it was widely said that Arab governments had broadcast instructions telling Palestinians to leave their homes for a short time, with the promise that they could return once the Arab armies had won. If true, the claim placed the cause of the refugee problem with Arab leaders, not with events on the ground. The Irish journalist Erskine Childers went to the monitoring records. The BBC Monitoring Service had recorded and transcribed Middle Eastern radio throughout the period for British intelligence, and American monitors had done the same. These records were made at the time, independently of any later political narrative. Childers searched them for the evacuation orders and published his findings in The Spectator: [cite:spectator_childers_1961]

There was not a single order, or appeal, or suggestion about evacuation from Palestine from any Arab radio station, inside or outside Palestine, in 1948. There is a repeated monitored record of Arab appeals, even flat orders, to the civilians of Palestine to stay put.

He challenged anyone to produce the broadcasts, and no one did. [cite:decolonizepalestine_childers] Walid Khalidi, citing the BBC monitoring and its American counterpart, the FBIS, called the evacuation-order claim "a piece of mythmaking." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] One summary in this book's sources says that Morris, working in the archives in the 1980s, found no evidence of the broadcasts in Israeli, Arab or British records either. [cite:decolonizepalestine_childers]

The Israeli archival record Morris used points the same way. An IDF intelligence report of June 1948, in Lockman's summary, attributed about 70 percent of the flight up to that date to direct Jewish military operations and no more than 5 percent to evacuation orders from Arab leaders; its full breakdown is given with the refugees. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] So some local evacuation orders were given; the Israeli army's own estimate at the time counted them as a small cause, and they were not the blanket radio campaign of the later story. Lockman also writes that Yosef Weitz's report of October 1948 falsely blamed Arab leaders for organizing the flight. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] Childers's finding is narrow, and its narrowness is its strength. It does not explain every departure, village by village; the record shows many different circumstances of flight and expulsion. What it settles is that a single blanket explanation, repeated for years, was not in the broadcast record when someone checked.

The account of 1948 in this book's sources closes with a moral argument, stated here as its authors' own. Jewish need for safety after the Holocaust was real. The Zionist claim that Europe's Jews needed a place of refuge after 1945 was not false. That need was met in a land whose Arab inhabitants bore no responsibility for the crimes committed in Europe, and the cost of meeting it fell on them. On this view, the founding was at once the rescue of one people and the dispossession of another. Neither half cancels the other, and an account that drops either one is incomplete.

The same sources set a second contrast beside this one, again as an interpretation, not a finding. Jewish communities had lived among Arab populations across the Muslim world for more than a millennium: in Andalusia's Golden Age, under the Ottoman millet system, in Baghdad, with a community of 140,000, and in Damascus, Cairo, Sana'a and Fez. That life was not a utopia, and pogroms occurred. [cite:morris_righteous_victims] The claim that this coexistence was "substantial" and of a kind "Europe never matched" is a reading of a long and varied history, and is offered as one. The exodus of roughly 850,000 Jews from Arab lands between 1948 and 1972 had several documented causes, including active recruitment by Israeli and Jewish Agency operations. [cite:morris_righteous_victims] The violence against Jews in Arab cities after the partition vote, which was among those causes, is set out in its own section of this chapter.

A smaller decision closed the founding year. On 28 October 1948 the Provisional Council adopted the state flag. It chose the design of the First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897, a Magen David between blue stripes, and placed the ancient Menorah on the state seal. [cite:wiki_flag_of_israel] [cite:wjc_flag_unveiled_1948] The date and the choice are documented. One symbolic reading holds that the choice shows which lineage the new state saw itself as continuing: the political project of 1897 rather than the ancient Temple. That is an interpretation, not a finding. Placing the Menorah on the seal did not mean it was disregarded. It shows only the order of precedence the Council set between two available symbols.

The refugee question did not end in 1948. On 11 December 1948 the General Assembly's Resolution 194 affirmed a right of return for the refugees. It has not been implemented as of 2026. Israel has refused it on the ground that a return would end the Jewish majority in the state. [cite:morris_1948] According to the same account, the Palestinians registered with UNRWA as descendants of the displaced numbered some 6 million as of 2026, most of them stateless. Resolution 194 and the negotiations that followed it belong to the next stage of this volume.

The account of the Nakba in this book's sources goes further, and its argument should be stated in full and labelled for what it is. It holds that the Nakba was not a single event but a structure that has continued for 78 years. It lists, as of 2026, what it treats as later expressions of that structure. Among them are the occupation of the West Bank since 1967 and the blockade of Gaza since 2007, with some 2 million people in 365 square kilometres. West Bank settlers numbered 110,000 in 1993 and more than 500,000 in 2025, plus 250,000 in East Jerusalem, according to Peace Now and Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics. The list includes the war in Gaza since October 2023, South Africa's genocide case at the International Court of Justice, filed on 29 December 2023, and the International Criminal Court's arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant, issued on 21 November 2024. It also cites the conclusions of Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and B'Tselem that the two legal systems in the West Bank meet the international-law definition of apartheid, and Israel's unilateral annexation of East Jerusalem in 1980 under Basic Law: Jerusalem. Those conclusions are the organizations' own legal judgments and are attributed to them here. The account then traces the effects across the region. In Jordan, more than 2 million Palestinians hold citizenship, about 40 percent of the population. Lebanon hosts about 500,000 refugees in 12 UNRWA camps, barred from most professions and from owning property. Syria hosts about 500,000, many displaced again since 2011. Egypt administered Gaza from 1948 to 1967. In Egypt's 1979 treaty, Jordan's of 1994 and the Abraham Accords of 2020 with the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan, Arab states normalized relations with Israel without resolving the Palestinian question. The book's sources do not attach citations to these present-day figures. They are reported here as that account gives them, with the date, and they are examined in the volumes that cover those years. The opposite reading treats each of these episodes as a separate event with its own causes. This volume does not settle between the two. It records that the refugee problem created in 1948 was not resolved in 1948, and that every later chapter of this history inherits it.

The year-by-year ledger for this stage sets 1948 beside the two years before it. In 1946 and 1947 the entries are the Anglo-American Committee, the King David Hotel bombing, UNSCOP, the CIA's estimate ORE-55 and Resolution 181, a sequence of pressure, inquiry and warnings overruled. The entry for 1948 lists Deir Yassin, Plan Dalet, independence, the eleven-minute recognition, the Czech arms and the Nakba under a single heading: execution. Its money column holds two sums. The first is about $50 million reported raised on Golda Meyerson's American tour, spent largely on weapons. The second is almost $14.5 million in Czechoslovak arms receipts. [cite:jwa_golda_50m] [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] The objectors' column for the year names the letter of December 1948, signed by 28 people including Albert Einstein and Hannah Arendt, which protested Menachem Begin's visit to the United States and described his new party, which had grown out of the Irgun, as bearing "the unmistakable stamp of a Fascist party." [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt] The two sums show the connection the ledger draws. Money raised in America paid in part for weapons sold by the Soviet bloc, under an American embargo.

Much remains unsettled. The number of refugees is known only within a range, and the count of villages depends on what is counted. Whether the expulsions followed a central decision or accumulated from local orders under a plan that allowed them is still the main point of disagreement between Morris and his critics, and the documents do not close it. The death toll at Deir Yassin is now put at about 110, but part of the Israeli military record remains classified. The tolls at Lydda and Ramla vary by source. This book has not yet compiled the Arab military and civilian dead of the war. The radio claim is settled in its broad form and not in every local detail: the Israeli army's own estimate allowed a small share for Arab evacuation orders. On the arms, the scale of Czechoslovak supply is clear, but the sources differ on the aircraft, on Britain's role and on whether any other supplier mattered. What is not in doubt is the pairing at the center of this section: in the same months, one people gained a state and hundreds of thousands of another were displaced from their towns and villages. Both facts are documented, and much of the documentation is Israeli.

sections.h: Who Recognizes a Nation?
sections.html:
The United States recognized Israel on the day it was declared. The decision is sometimes remembered as an act of Congress, as if the House and Senate had voted the new state into American favor. They did not. Recognition came in a short press release from the White House, issued on the authority of one office, and Congress had no vote on it. How that power came to rest with one office, how Truman used it, and how other governments answered the same question in 1948 and 1949 together show what recognition did and did not decide.

The constitutional basis is a single clause. Article II, Section 3 provides that the President "shall receive Ambassadors and other public Ministers." [cite:const_art2s3] In Zivotofsky v. Kerry (2015) the Supreme Court held that the clause gives the President the exclusive power to recognize foreign sovereigns. [cite:scotus_zivotofsky] The ruling came sixty-seven years after 1948, so it does not describe a rule that anyone cited at the time. It states the law as it now stands, and it confirms that the power Truman used was his alone.

He used it on 14 May 1948. Eleven minutes after Israel's proclamation, he announced de facto recognition in a short press release. [cite:truman_recognition] De facto recognition accepted the new government as the authority actually in control. Full legal recognition, de jure, followed on 31 January 1949. [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] In one account in this library, the second step came only after Truman's election victory. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] Two accounts in this library give the time of the first announcement as 6:11 p.m. Washington time. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The Declaration had been read in Tel Aviv at four in the afternoon, and the Mandate expired at midnight. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] The sources do not say whether the eleven minutes are counted from the reading or from the moment the state came into being at the Mandate's end. The figure is exact; its starting point is not stated.

The speed was arranged. Clark Clifford, the President's counsel, managed the timing against the objection of the State Department, which was not told in advance. The American delegation at the United Nations was caught out too: at that moment it was still pressing the trusteeship proposal that Washington had put forward in March as an alternative to partition. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The decision came after Eddie Jacobson, Truman's old business partner, had brought Chaim Weizmann to see him, and after a November 1947 memorandum had analyzed "The Politics of 1948 and the Jews." [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] [cite:jvl_truman_index] Recognition went against the written advice of the Secretary of State, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of Defense and the CIA. The CIA's estimate ORE-55, dated 28 November 1947, the day before the partition vote, had predicted armed hostilities if partition passed and warned that American commercial and strategic interests would be put in danger. [cite:cia_ore55] One account in this library goes further. It describes declassified CIA assessments predicting that recognition would immediately produce war with the Arab states, and calls the eleven minutes the fastest diplomatic recognition in American history. Those claims are that account's own and are not repeated in ORE-55's summary. The warnings and the advisers who overrode them are traced in [scene:ore_s01|the CIA's estimate].

Why Truman acted as he did is argued in the opening sections of this chapter. One reading stresses the domestic calculation that Clifford's memorandum set out. Another stresses Truman's own repeated statements of humanitarian conviction. The record holds evidence for both. The constitutional point holds whatever his motive. Because the power to recognize was the President's alone, the months of argument over partition, trusteeship, oil and strategy ended in one decision by one man. The State Department, the Pentagon and the new intelligence agency could advise. Advocates could press. Only the President could decide.

Congress's part was real but indirect. It could pass resolutions of support, it controlled appropriations, and the Senate confirmed ambassadors, including the first American ambassador to Israel. None of these powers decided whether the United States would recognize Israel. They shaped what recognition would mean in practice afterwards.

Other governments answered the question differently, and on different grounds. The Soviet Union went further than Washington, and almost as fast. On 17 May 1948, three days after independence, it became the first state to recognize Israel de jure, while the American recognition was still de facto. [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] It was the same course Moscow had followed since Andrei Gromyko's speech at the United Nations in May 1947, and analysts at the time and since have read its motive as removing British influence from the region. That is their reading, not a stated Soviet aim. [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel] The convergence had limits. In December 1948 the Soviet bloc voted against Resolution 194 on the return of refugees. [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] The fuller Soviet story is told in [scene:so_s01|Moscow said yes first].

Britain, the outgoing Mandatory power, came slowly. It had abstained in the partition vote of 29 November 1947. In May 1948 Ernest Bevin told the House of Commons that "there are, after all, no Arabs in the House." Britain recognized Israel in January 1949; the historian Raphael Langham describes Bevin's acceptance as "grudging." [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit] The government that had issued the Balfour Declaration and held the Mandate accepted the state that emerged from it only after eight months.

Some governments declined altogether. In 1947, according to secondary reports, Ben-Gurion sent a secret telegram or telephone message to Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, proposing that Pakistan recognize the Jewish state when it was established. Jinnah's reply was reportedly negative. [cite:timesofisrael_blog_secret_diplomacy] [cite:infogalactic_israel_pakistan_relations] The account rests on secondary reporting, not on a surviving primary document, and should be read with that limit. According to the sources used here, Pakistan has never recognized Israel and has no diplomatic relations with it. The later record of unacknowledged contacts between the two belongs to a later volume.

The Holy See withheld recognition for longer than almost any other major power. Its documented reasons were three: Catholic doctrine on the place of the Jewish people in salvation history, the unresolved status of the holy sites of Jerusalem, and concern for the Christian and Muslim communities of Palestine under the new state. [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] Its opposition was active. In 1949 the Vatican pressed at the United Nations to make Israel's admission conditional on two commitments: a return of Palestinian refugees and formal guarantees for the Christian and Muslim holy sites, above all in Jerusalem. Ben-Gurion is recorded as saying that year: "There is a major religion in the world, which has to settle with us a historical reckoning." The campaign failed. Israel was admitted to the United Nations in May 1949 without the guarantees the Vatican had sought. The Holy See did not establish diplomatic relations until the Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993, forty-five years after independence. [cite:wiki_fundamental_agreement] How that change came about is told in [scene:vat_s01|the Vatican's long refusal].

Set side by side, these answers show what recognition was in 1948. It was a decision each government took alone, through whatever office its own constitution named, and for its own reasons. In Washington that office was the presidency, and the reasons were contested inside the government itself. In Moscow, on the analysts' reading, the reason was Britain. In London it was reluctant acceptance of a settled fact, and in Rome theology and the holy places. None of these decisions created the state, which existed by its own proclamation. What recognition decided was who would deal with it, and on what terms.

Some questions remain open. The press release and the date of de jure recognition are documented. The exact moment from which the eleven minutes are counted is not stated in the sources used here. The approach to Jinnah is known only from secondary accounts. The details of the Vatican's 1949 campaign at the United Nations, beyond its two demands and its failure, are not documented in this book's sources. How much any single adviser or argument weighed with Truman remains, as the earlier sections show, a matter of interpretation.

sections.h: The Arab States' War, May 1948 – 1949
sections.html:
The British Mandate ended at midnight on 14 May 1948. Within hours the fighting already under way inside Palestine became a war between the new State of Israel and the armies of its neighbors. The fighting that followed lasted, with two long truces, into the winter. It ended not in peace treaties but in a set of separate armistice agreements signed in 1949, whose lines became the borders of the next two decades.

The familiar account of this war has two versions, and each tells only part of the story. In one, five Arab armies set out to destroy a newborn state on the day of its birth. In the other, the Arab states sent their armies to protect the Palestinian Arabs from a Jewish force already on the offensive. The documents show that both sides had grounds for their account. They also show that the armies did not come as one, did not come in the strength their own planners had called for, and did not all come for the same purpose.

The League's own words. On 15 May 1948 the Secretary-General of the Arab League sent a cablegram to the Secretary-General of the United Nations, registered as document S/745. It is the Arab states' own statement of why they were going to war, and it deserves to be read as such. The Mandate, it said, had ended "leaving no legally constituted authority behind," and the Arab states were therefore intervening "to restore law and order and to prevent disturbances prevailing in Palestine from spreading" into their own territories. [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] The cablegram made two further claims. It stated that "approximately over a quarter of a million of the Arab population have been compelled to leave their homes," and it declared support for "the creation of United State of Palestine based upon the democratic principles." [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] The first was a statement about displacement that had already taken place before the invasion; the second was a political aim, a single state in place of the partition the General Assembly had voted for six months earlier. The document thus carries both readings of the war within it. It framed the intervention as an act of order and pointed to a displacement already under way; it also set out, in its own words, to replace the partition plan with a single state.

Who came, and how. The US State Department's Office of the Historian records that the war began with an Arab air attack on Tel Aviv on the eve of 14 May. Armies from Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Egypt invaded; a Saudi formation fought under Egyptian command; and Transjordanian forces intervened only in the areas designated for the Arab state or for the Jerusalem corpus separatum, the international zone the partition plan had drawn around the city. Through all of it the United States kept an arms embargo on all belligerents. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] Other accounts in this library describe the entry differently. The record on Lebanon says that on 15 May Lebanon "joined Egypt, Syria, Jordan, and Iraq in declaring war and invading the new state," and the record on Egypt likewise counts Jordan among the invaders. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] The difference matters. Whether Transjordan's Arab Legion invaded Israel or entered the parts of Palestine the United Nations had assigned to the Arabs is the heart of a long argument about King Abdullah's intentions, told in the section on his dealings with the Jewish Agency.

Each state made its own decision. Lebanon's is often passed over. It fielded the smallest of the five Arab armies, and its choice to fight was its own. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] According to Makram Rabah, a history lecturer at the American University of Beirut, the country's founding leaders, Riad al-Solh and Bechara el-Khoury, who had led Lebanon to independence from France in 1943, had debated and rejected an alliance with the Zionist movement before 1948, concluding that they could not keep relations with the neighbouring Arab states while holding one. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] Lebanon's posture was thus a deliberated political choice, not simply a reaction imposed from outside. Egypt joined the invasion in May 1948 after the end of the Mandate. [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] Saudi Arabia did not launch an invasion of its own. Its part was a small contingent of troops placed under Egyptian command. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] Accounts of the kingdom's role explain the modest scale by its greater distance from Palestine. Its larger weapon was economic. The Arab League's boycott of Israel, formalized in 1948, barred member states from any direct economic relationship with the new state; a secondary boycott added in 1950 extended the bar to foreign companies doing business with Israel, and a tertiary boycott later reached companies dealing with those on the secondary list. According to the account of the kingdom's role, Saudi Arabia was among its most consistent enforcers and kept it in some form for over seven decades, and it has never established diplomatic relations with Israel.

How many men. The size of the armies is itself disputed. Avi Shlaim gives the forces on 15 May 1948 as 35,000 Israeli troops against 20,000–25,000 Arab troops, and argues that "illicit arms-imports decisively tipped the military balance in favour of Israel." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_war] His seminar notes add that the forces the Arab states actually sent were "well below the level demanded by the Military Committee of the Arab League," and that the Israeli army had more men but weaker firepower. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] A US assessment of July 1948, discussed in [scene:s10b|the next section], counted about 90,000 Israeli forces by then. The two figures describe different dates and should not be merged. The fuller argument over the balance, and over whose numbers the "outnumbered" story rests on, belongs to that section.

The first round, 15 May to 11 June. Shlaim's notes give the outline of the first four weeks. The Egyptian advance stalled at Ramat Rahel on 24 May and at Ashdod on 29 May. The Syrians were stopped at Degania but held Mishmar Hayarden. The Iraqis held the triangle of Jenin, Nablus and Tulkarem. In Jerusalem the Jewish Quarter surrendered on 28 May, and three frontal Israeli attacks on the Arab Legion's position at Latrun, on 25 and 30 May and on 9 June, were repelled. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] Syria's army fought on the northern front and ended the war holding small areas west of the international border. [cite:tf_zaim] Lebanon's invasion was repelled, and Israeli forces for a time occupied part of southern Lebanon. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] The first round thus ended with the Egyptian and Syrian advances stopped, the Iraqis holding their triangle, the Jewish Quarter lost and Latrun still in the Legion's hands. Shlaim calls the truce that followed "a turning-point." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war]

The first truce, 11 June to 9 July. The United Nations mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte, had been appointed on 21 May. The truce he supervised ran 28 days, from 11 June to 9 July 1948, with observers from Belgium, France, Sweden and the United States. According to the Israel Defense Forces' own account, published by the Jewish Virtual Library, materiel reached the Israeli army during the truce from Europe, "particularly Czechoslovakia." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce1] Bernadotte used the pause to propose a settlement: the Galilee to Israel, the Negev to the Arabs, and Jerusalem under the United Nations. Both sides rejected it. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce1] The arms that crossed during those four weeks are the subject of the section on the Czechoslovak pipeline; Bernadotte's own fate, at the hands of Lehi in September, is told in the section on the founding of the army.

Lydda and Ramla, July 1948. Fighting resumed on 9 July. Operation Dani was launched from Ben Shemen on the night of 9–10 July. The assault on Lydda began on 11 July, and by 12 July the town was under full Israeli control, without a formal surrender. According to Sana Hammoudi's account in the Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, between 80 and 176 people were killed at the Dahmash mosque and more than 400 in the town. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] Both that account and Zachary Lockman, each citing the Israeli historian Benny Morris, report that on 12 July David Ben-Gurion answered a question about the inhabitants with the words "Expel them." Yitzhak Rabin then signed an order to expel Lydda's inhabitants quickly. Israeli censors later made Rabin remove the episode from his memoir. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war]

The numbers are disputed, and the two sources should be read side by side. Lockman, summarizing Morris, puts the combined population of Lydda and Ramla at 50,000–70,000, about 15,000 of them refugees, with 250–400 Palestinian civilians and four Israeli soldiers killed. The Palestinian encyclopedia estimates that about 70,000 people were forced out on 13 July and that close to 1,000 died in the towns and on the march that followed. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war] [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] Neither figure is a count; both are estimates, and the higher one includes deaths on the march.

The second truce and Jerusalem. The second truce began at 19:00 on 18 July 1948. It did not bring quiet to Jerusalem. According to the IDF account, the Arab Legion continued to shell West Jerusalem through October and on 12 August demolished the pumping station at Latrun, then held by the United Nations. A "sincere cease-fire" in the city was agreed only on 30 November. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce2]

The armistices of 1949. The war ended in separate armistice agreements between Israel and Egypt, Lebanon, Transjordan and Syria; Egypt kept the Gaza Strip and Jordan the West Bank. The Office of the Historian dates them, collectively, to "February 1949." [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] The individual agreements in the record carry later dates for two of them. The agreements with Egypt were negotiated on the Greek island of Rhodes; they set a ceasefire line, not a peace, which served as the de facto border along the edge of the Gaza Strip for the next two decades. [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] From 1948 to 1967 Egypt governed Gaza directly as a military protectorate, and its officials maintained throughout that it had not annexed the territory. Why Cairo avoided annexation is not settled by the record: some accounts stress an Arab League consensus against it, others Egyptian strategic caution. Lebanon's armistice, signed on 23 March 1949, restored the internationally recognized border. [cite:lebanon_1948_war]

Syria's took longer, and the delay holds one of the war's least-known episodes. After Husni al-Za'im seized power in Damascus in March 1949, armistice talks opened on 5 April; Za'im offered a peace treaty and military cooperation, proposed meeting Ben-Gurion or Moshe Sharett, and offered to resettle 250,000–300,000 Palestinian refugees in Syria, with the border drawn through the middle of Lake Hula and the Sea of Galilee. [cite:tf_zaim] [cite:ecf_zaim] [cite:majalla_zaim] Ben-Gurion would not stake policy on him, partly from distrust of his ties to Washington. [cite:majalla_zaim] The armistice signed on 20 July 1949 turned the areas Syria evacuated into demilitarized zones, which became the fault line of the frontier; in August Za'im was deposed and executed in Syria's second coup of the year, and the offer died with him ([scene:sy_s01|Syria and Za'im's offer]). [cite:ecf_zaim]

The cost. More than 6,000 Israelis were killed in the war, about 1% of the roughly 650,000 Jews then in the country, according to a Reuters figure published by Ynet in 2005. [cite:rs_rd5_ynet_dead] The war's other costs fell on the Palestinian Arabs: the quarter of a million already displaced by 15 May on the League's own count, and many more after it, as told in [scene:rd5_refugees|the section on the refugees]. In Lebanon alone an estimated 100,000–110,000 arrived from northern Palestine. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy]

What the record does not settle. Several things remain open on the sources gathered. The number of Arab soldiers and civilians killed in the war has not been established here, and no figure is offered. The fighting of the autumn and winter of 1948–49, between the second truce and the armistices, is not covered by the sources used here beyond the Jerusalem front. The sources disagree on whether Transjordan invaded Israel or entered only the areas assigned to the Arab state, and on the date of the armistices. The tolls at Lydda and Ramla rest on estimates that differ by a factor of two or more. And the deepest question, whether the armies came to save the Palestinian Arabs, to prevent a Jewish state, or to take territory for themselves, has no single answer: the League's cablegram, Lebanon's deliberated choice, Saudi Arabia's distant contingent, the Legion's entry, on the Office of the Historian's account, only into the areas assigned to the Arab state or the international zone, and Egypt's nineteen-year administration of Gaza without annexation point in different directions, because the states that went to war in May 1948 were pursuing different ends.

sections.h: The Military Balance of 1948
sections.html:
Two stories about the military balance of 1948 have outlived the war. In the first, Israel was a tiny nation, vastly outnumbered, that defeated overwhelming Arab armies through will and endurance, a story often told as a near-miracle. In the second, Israel won not through real capability but because international sympathy, born of the Holocaust, tipped the scales. Each is repeated as if it described the whole war. The documents describe something neither story accounts for: a balance that changed, in stages, between the invasion of May 1948 and January 1949.

A report written during the war. The most valuable single document is a US government assessment dated 1 July 1948, written while the outcome was still unknown. It put Israeli forces at roughly 90,000 in total, with about 35,000 of them used in active operations. It also found that the Arab armies were, at that moment, stronger than Israel in artillery and tanks, while carrying a wide variety of small arms. [cite:frus1948_military_situation] Its value lies in its timing. Nobody writing it could shape the numbers around how the war ended, because nobody yet knew. Its limit lies in the same place: it is a snapshot of one moment, not an account of the war's course.

The sources disagree on what kind of report it was. One account calls it, in one place, a contemporaneous CIA assessment and, in another, a US State Department report. [cite:frus1948_military_situation] This book has not resolved which office produced it, and refers to it here simply as the July 1948 US assessment.

Two phases, not one picture. Historians describe the war as two distinct military phases. From the invasion of 15 May until the first truce in June 1948, accounts describe the Israeli forces as initially inferior in both numbers and armament. After the truce, new enlistments and arms deliveries, among them the Czechoslovak shipments traced in [scene:cz_s01|the section on the Czech arms], allowed Israel to seize the initiative. One historical anthology states that for most of the war, excluding that first period, "the Jews were superior in personnel, equipment, logistics and organization." [cite:jvl_israel_studies_1948] The early disadvantage was real; so was the reversal that followed it.

On one point within that first phase, the sources do not agree. Avi Shlaim gives the forces on 15 May 1948 as 35,000 Israeli troops against 20,000–25,000 Arab troops. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_war] His seminar notes put it more precisely: the Israeli army had more men but weaker firepower, and the forces the Arab states actually sent were "well below the level demanded by the Military Committee of the Arab League." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] On Shlaim's figures, then, Israel was not outnumbered even in May; it was outgunned. The anthology's "inferior in both numbers and armament" and Shlaim's "more men but weaker firepower" cannot both be right about numbers, though they agree about weapons. The reader should also keep the dates apart. Shlaim's 35,000 describes 15 May. The US assessment's 90,000 describes 1 July, and its own figure of about 35,000 refers to the troops in active operations at that later date, not to the army's size at the invasion. The coincidence of the two 35,000s is not a confirmation of either.

Shlaim calls the June truce "a turning-point," and he argues that "illicit arms-imports decisively tipped the military balance in favour of Israel." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_war] That judgment places the turn where the anthology places it: in the weeks of the first truce, when arms reached the Israeli army and the Arab states did not match them. The course of that fighting, from the first round to the armistices, is told in [scene:rd5_invasion|the section on the Arab states' war].

Whose numbers. Much of the popular "tiny, outnumbered Israel" arithmetic traces back to estimates by John Glubb, commander of Jordan's Arab Legion during the war. Historians who have worked on the order of battle note that, as the commander of one of the fighting armies, Glubb had a direct and plausible incentive to exaggerate Israeli numbers and play down Arab ones. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance] This is ordinary source criticism, and it cuts only so far. It does not show that Glubb falsified anything; it shows that a widely repeated figure comes from an interested party, a fact rarely mentioned when his numbers are cited as neutral.

The ending the story leaves out. By the later stages of the war, accounts state that Israel's army outnumbered the combined Arab armies by roughly two to one. The Arab states reinforced their forces over the course of the war, but they never matched the pace of Israeli growth in men and arms. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance] A story about beating impossible odds usually implies that the odds stayed impossible until the end. On this record they did not: the advantage had passed decisively to Israel well before the fighting stopped. That does not make the outcome inevitable or easy in hindsight. The difficulty of the first weeks, when the Arab armies held real advantages in heavy weapons, stands in the record beside the reversal.

Why neither story survives. The underdog story holds, at most, for the opening weeks, and even there it leans on one commander's disputed figures and on a count of men that Shlaim's figures contradict; what the record does support is an Arab advantage in firepower, in artillery and tanks, which the US assessment still found on 1 July. The sympathy story fares no better. To hold, it must pass over a dated military reversal, the arms that arrived during and after the first truce, and a final numerical advantage of about two to one that, in one account, owed nothing to international goodwill and a great deal to logistics, organization and weapons that arrived and were used. [cite:jvl_israel_studies_1948] [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance]

What remains open. The record gathered here does not settle the size of the Israeli force on 15 May: one account says it was inferior in numbers, Shlaim says it was larger. It does not say which office of the US government wrote the July 1948 assessment. It gives the final two-to-one ratio as an approximation without a precise date or count of either side. And it offers no independent figures for the Arab armies' strength after May against which Glubb's estimates could be checked. What it does establish is the shape of the war's balance: a real early disadvantage in firepower, a turn at the first truce, and a decisive Israeli superiority by the end.

sections.h: From Three Militias to One Army, May 1948 – February 1949
sections.html:
It is often assumed that Israel's army was a single national force from the day of independence. It was not. On 14 May 1948 three armed bodies claimed to fight for the new state: the Haganah; the Irgun, commanded by Menachem Begin; and Lehi, led by three men. Each had its own command and its own arms. Making them one army took four months, an order, a confrontation on a Tel Aviv beach in which Jews killed Jews, and an assassination that the new government itself called terrorism.

The order of 26 May 1948. Twelve days after the declaration of independence, the provisional government headed by David Ben-Gurion issued an order establishing the Israel Defense Forces. It outlawed any other armed force and required the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi to merge into the new army. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] The order was the instrument; the question was whether the undergrounds would obey it. The war with the Arab states, told in [scene:rd5_invasion|the section on the Arab states' war], was then in its second week, and the new army was being formed while it fought.

The Altalena, June 1948. The test came within a month. In June 1948 the Irgun brought an arms ship, the Altalena, to the coast, carrying weapons that it intended partly for its own units. Ben-Gurion refused to let the cargo bypass the army. The two positions could not both stand: an Irgun that kept its own weapons was an army beside the army, which the order of 26 May had outlawed. On 22 June IDF units under the command of Yitzhak Rabin shelled the ship off the Tel Aviv beach. Sixteen Irgun members and three IDF soldiers were killed, nineteen dead in all. The Irgun's separate units were then disbanded. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair]

The episode fell during the first truce of the war, which ran from 11 June to 9 July, when arms were reaching the Israeli army from Europe. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce1] The dispute over the Altalena was therefore not about whether weapons should come in, but about who would hold them once they arrived. The same commander, Rabin, would sign the order to expel the inhabitants of Lydda three weeks later. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda]

The killing of Bernadotte, September 1948. The second test came from Lehi. Count Folke Bernadotte had been appointed United Nations mediator on 21 May 1948; he had supervised the first truce and proposed a settlement giving the Galilee to Israel, the Negev to the Arabs and Jerusalem to the United Nations, which both sides rejected. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce1] On 17 September 1948 members of Lehi assassinated him in Jerusalem. The government declared Lehi a terrorist organization and arrested its members. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] The word matters: the government of the new state applied it, in its own name, to a Jewish underground.

The arrests did not last. In February 1949 the Lehi members were released under a general amnesty. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] The record gathered here does not say why the amnesty was granted, how many were held, or whether anyone was tried for the killing.
