[cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] Six months later, on 4 April 1967, the Prime Minister's adviser on Arab affairs, Shmuel Toledano, wrote to Levi Eshkol that "in practice, hardly any restrictions have been loosened," since closed areas and travel passes remained. [cite:rs_rd6_akevot_toledano] An official close to the policy thus recorded that the formal end of the regime had changed less than its abolition suggested.

Some accounts draw a further conclusion: that before Israel governed a single Palestinian in the West Bank or Gaza, it had already run an eighteen-year separate administration for Palestinian citizens inside its own borders, and that the occupation after 1967 inherited a model rather than inventing one. That is an argument about continuity, and it rests on the resemblance of the instruments: permits, closed areas and military courts. The later regime is the subject of a later volume.

The record leaves several things unsettled. The sources used here give conviction figures but not the number of permit applications refused, or how permits were allocated among villages and individuals. They date the regime's start two ways. They do not give a source-backed count of Israeli casualties from cross-border attacks in these years, a figure that would bear directly on the weight of the security case. And they do not settle the central dispute, whether security or control of movement and land was the regime's main purpose. What they do establish is the structure: a population with the vote, held for eighteen years under British emergency law, through a permit system that for its first eighteen months had no legal basis at all.

sections.h: The Absentees' Property Law: From Flight to State Title, 1948–1953
sections.html:
Military rule kept the internally displaced from their villages; a parallel set of laws decided who owned them. The war of 1948 left hundreds of Palestinian localities empty of their inhabitants. [cite:rs_rd6_plands_villages] Flight alone did not decide who would own the land and houses left behind. That was settled afterward, on paper, by a sequence of regulations and statutes passed between July 1948 and 1953. Together they moved the property of the refugees first into the custody of the state, then into its ownership and that of the Jewish National Fund, and finally into retroactive legal validation. The same chain reached people who had never left the country at all.

It is widely believed that the Palestinian Arabs who stayed inside Israel in 1948 kept their homes and land as full citizens. But tens of thousands who had moved from one village to another inside the lines Israel held were classed in law as "absentees," and their property was taken on the same terms as that of refugees across the border. They were registered as citizens and could vote, and still could not reclaim what they had owned.

The first link came during the fighting. A Custodian of Abandoned Property was appointed on 15 July 1948. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] The occupation of empty houses that followed, and the cabinet decision of June 1948 against return during the war, are told in [scene:rd6_return_barred|how return was barred]. In December 1948 the government issued Emergency Regulations on absentees' property, which transferred control to a new Custodian of Absentee Property. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] Even the date of this step is uncertain. The historian Michael Fischbach, working from Israeli sources, gives 2 December 1948; an American document he cites refers to an "Israeli ordinance of December 12, 1948." [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] The sources consulted here do not resolve which is correct.

The regulations were temporary in form. The international body charged with a settlement objected to them while they were still temporary. In April 1949 the United Nations Conciliation Commission for Palestine proposed, as a preliminary measure, "suspension of the application of the Absentee law until the final peace settlement." Arab delegations argued that the law treated nationals of Palestine as enemy aliens. Israel did not suspend it. [cite:un_ccp_absentee_1949] The talks in which that request was made are told in [scene:lau_s01|the Lausanne conference].

Instead the regime was made permanent. On 14 March 1950 the Knesset passed the Absentees' Property Law, an expanded version of the 1948 regulations, and it remained the main law governing refugee property for decades. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] The law, numbered 5710-1950, is plain in its terms. All absentees' property is vested in the Custodian. Every right an absentee had passes automatically to the Custodian. Anyone holding absentee property must hand it over. And the fact that an absentee's identity is unknown does not prevent property from being vested. [cite:un_absentees_property_law_text] [cite:wiki_present_absentee] Anyone found occupying such property, including its original owner, was in breach of the law.

Everything turned on the definition of an "absentee." The law reached anyone who, during the war, had left his usual place of residence for areas outside Israeli control, or for anywhere else. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] The second clause was the decisive one. It captured not only the refugees beyond the armistice lines but also Arabs who had moved between villages inside Israel and had then been registered as citizens, issued identity numbers, and allowed to vote and to stand for the Knesset. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] In law they were absent. In fact they were citizens living inside the state. They came to be called "present absentees."

Their numbers were large and remained so. By 2001 the present absentees were estimated at about 200,000 people, nearly 17 percent of Israel's Arab citizens, and half the populations of the two largest Arab towns in Israel are internally displaced. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] [cite:wiki_land_day] [cite:cornell_bilsky_absentee_law] The law did not act alone on them. Military rule over Arab citizens restricted their movement and, combined with the absentee laws, prevented the internally displaced from physically returning to reclaim their homes. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] [cite:wiki_land_day] That regime is described in [scene:rd6_military_government|the military government].

One interpretive reading, used elsewhere in this library, borrows a term from programming for what the law did: the word "absentee" kept its everyday meaning while its working definition was swapped to include people who were present. It is a reading of the mechanism, not a finding about anyone's intent.

Custody was not yet ownership. The next steps moved the land on. Fischbach records that in early 1949 Ben-Gurion wanted to sell a significant amount of refugee land to the Jewish National Fund, and that the Fund wanted legal title transferred to it. His book tabulates a sale in January 1949 and a further purchase in 1950 known as the "second million" dunams. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] The exact acreage and prices of these transactions are not reproduced here, because they could not be confirmed from the material consulted.

In 1950 a Development Authority was established. A 2016 study in the Journal of Israeli History describes it as both a major allocator of land and the body that set "the rules of the game." The same study finds that the ban on selling "national lands" was strictly kept in rural areas but not in urban ones. [cite:rs_rd6_jih_devauthority] According to an analysis published by the organization BADIL, the 1950 law allowed the Custodian to transfer absentee land to the Development Authority, which could in turn pass it to the Jewish National Fund. BADIL states that nearly 2.4 million dunams were transferred in this way, "more than trebling the JNF's holdings as of 1941," and that by 1951 the government, together with the Fund, held 92 percent of the land within the state. [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime]

The last link closed the chain. The Land Acquisition (Validation of Acts and Compensation) Law of 1953 retroactively validated land seizures made during and after the war on grounds of security and development. The Finance Minister said its purpose was to "instill legality in some acts undertaken during and following the war." [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime] Read plainly, the minister's words concede that some of the earlier seizures had needed legality supplied after the fact. Adalah, in its database of laws it classes as discriminatory, states that 1.2 to 1.3 million dunams were expropriated from Arab owners under the 1953 law, from 349 towns and villages, and that Arab ownership has fallen to 3 to 3.5 percent of the land, compared with 48 percent in 1948. [cite:rs_rd6_adalah_landacq] These are Adalah's figures. Over a longer span, Salman Abu-Sitta estimates that more than 1,000 square kilometres were expropriated from Arab citizens between 1948 and 2003. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] [cite:wiki_land_day]

Who gained and who bore the cost follows from the chain. The property of the refugees and the present absentees passed first to a state custodian, then to a development body, and from there to the state's own land holdings and to the Jewish National Fund. The owners, inside and outside the country, lost title. The law offered them no route back to it: occupying one's own former house was itself a breach.

The two sides of the argument were set out at the time. The Israeli government's stated grounds, written into the 1953 law, were security and development, and in its own account it was regularizing acts taken in war. Israel declined the Conciliation Commission's request to suspend the regime pending a peace settlement. [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime] [cite:un_ccp_absentee_1949] The Arab delegations' objection, made in 1949, was that the law treated nationals of Palestine as enemy aliens, and the Commission's own proposal implied that permanent measures should wait for a final settlement. [cite:un_ccp_absentee_1949] The present absentees are the hardest case for any reading of the law as a wartime measure against the enemy's side, because they never left the state's territory and became its citizens.

According to the sources used here, the Absentees' Property Law remains in force and has been applied in East Jerusalem. [cite:wiki_present_absentee]

The record does not settle the totals. The 2.4 million dunams and the 92 percent figure come from BADIL, and the 1.2 to 1.3 million dunams, the 349 localities and the fall from 48 percent to 3 to 3.5 percent come from Adalah. Both are advocacy organizations, and the scholarly sources consulted here, Fischbach and the 2016 study, describe the same legal chain without confirming those totals in the material available. The acreage of the Jewish National Fund's purchases of 1949 and 1950 is unconfirmed, and so is the exact date of the December 1948 regulations. What the record establishes beyond dispute is the mechanism: the text of the 1950 law, the Conciliation Commission's request to suspend it, the definition that turned residents into absentees, and the 1953 law that validated what had been taken.

sections.h: One Week in December 1948: The Rights Order and the Refugees
sections.html:
In the same month that Israel issued its first regulations on absentees' property, the United Nations General Assembly adopted, in the second week of December 1948 and on three successive days, the founding texts of the modern human-rights order and its first resolution on the return of the Palestinian refugees. In those same days the refugees themselves were being counted. It is sometimes assumed that the new international system examined the Palestinian displacement and passed judgment on it in 1948. The chronology tells a different story. The machinery that might have judged what happened did not yet exist, and the machinery that was built in the following three years set the Palestinian refugees apart from every other refugee population.

Before 1948 there was no worldwide system of human-rights treaties. The League of Nations' Permanent Mandates Commission reviewed Britain's administration of Palestine, but there was no treaty of individual rights and no court to which an individual could turn. The International Committee of the Red Cross worked under the laws of war, the Geneva Conventions of 1929. Its delegate Jacques de Reynier entered Deir Yassin on 11 April 1948 and reported what he found. That was a record of events, made under the laws of war. It was not a judgment, and no body existed to turn it into one.

Then, in a single week, the General Assembly adopted three instruments. On 9 December it adopted the Genocide Convention. [cite:w_genocideconv] On 10 December it adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, by 48 votes to 0 with 8 abstentions. Article 13(2) of the Declaration reads:

Everyone has the right to leave any country, including his own, and to return to his country. [cite:un_udhr]

On 11 December came Resolution 194, on the return of refugees and compensation for those choosing not to return. Its text, its vote and the two readings of it are set out in [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194 read as a whole]. The modern rights order was thus written in the same days that the Palestinian refugee population was being counted. [cite:w_genocideconv] [cite:un_udhr]

How many people that count covered was itself disputed from the start. Some 700,000 Palestinians were already refugees by that week, and the UN Conciliation Commission later estimated about 711,000. Israel's official figure was lower and Arab officials' figures higher, as [scene:rr_s01|the next section] shows. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] The dashboard panel below gives the round figure of about 700,000 displaced, with the Commission's estimate beside it.

Both are estimates, not registration counts; UNRWA's registration, at 726,000, produced a different total again. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix]

Article 13(2) and Resolution 194 became the two texts most often cited together. Palestinians cite the Declaration's article alongside the resolution as grounds for a right of return. Israel has argued that neither creates a binding right of return for descendants. The text of Article 13(2) itself is not disputed. [cite:un_udhr] What is disputed is its reach, including whether a right "to return to his country" is binding and passes to descendants. The sources used here record the positions; they do not settle the legal question.

The institution that was actually built for the refugees was an agency of relief, not of rights. The General Assembly created the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees, UNRWA, in December 1949, and it began work in May 1950. It provides schools, health care and relief to registered Palestine refugees. Its mandate is relief and works. It is not charged with resettlement, with legal protection, or with securing return. [cite:unrwa_who] Where the refugees lived and how host governments treated them in these years is told in [scene:dsp_s01|where the refugees went].

The decisive step came in 1951. The Refugee Convention adopted that year defined who was a refugee and what protection states owed. Its Article 1D excluded people already receiving protection or assistance from another United Nations agency. Because the Palestinian refugees had UNRWA, the clause left them outside the protection system that covers every other refugee population, and outside the durable-solutions mandate of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees. [cite:w_refconv]

In practice, this meant that through the 1950s the Palestinian refugees had an agency that gave them relief, schooling and health care, but no international body whose task was to protect their legal status or to find them a permanent solution, whether return, settlement where they were, or settlement elsewhere. The one body with a political mandate, the Conciliation Commission created by Resolution 194, was a commission of three member states, not a protection agency. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194]

There was also no court. No international criminal court existed to examine the events of 1948. The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court was adopted in 1998 and entered into force in July 2002, without retroactive reach. Palestine acceded in 2015, which is why the Court's jurisdiction in Palestinian matters begins in that era. [cite:w_romestatute] The displacement of 1948 was counted, relieved and debated, but it was never adjudicated by any international tribunal.

The common claim that the international human-rights system examined the Palestinian displacement and judged it in 1948 therefore runs ahead of the record. In 1948 the system consisted of declarations and a convention on genocide, with no enforcement body for individual rights. What followed was relief through UNRWA and a refugee convention that, by its own text, did not apply to the Palestinians.

The record leaves open why the drafters of the 1951 Convention wrote Article 1D as they did, and the sources used here do not give the debates. Nor do they settle the legal weight of Article 13(2) for the 1948 refugees and their descendants, which remains the subject of the opposing positions set out above. What is not in dispute is the sequence: rights declared in December 1948, relief organized in 1949 and 1950, protection withheld by the 1951 text, and no court until 2002.

sections.h: Resolution 194: What It Says, How Each Side Reads It, and How Many Refugees There Were
sections.html:
The last of that week's three texts, Resolution 194, is usually remembered for one paragraph, the eleventh, on the return of the refugees. It is a longer document than that: it also set up a conciliation commission, called for an international regime for Jerusalem and protection for the Holy Places, and urged a final settlement. Two popular versions dominate: that international law guarantees every refugee's descendant a return, or that the resolution means nothing. Neither matches the text, which is short enough to read as a whole.

The General Assembly adopted Resolution 194 (III) at its 186th plenary meeting on 11 December 1948, by 35 votes to 15, with 8 abstentions. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] [cite:rs_rd6_ecf_194] It followed the September 1948 report of the UN Mediator, told in [scene:rd6_bernadotte|Bernadotte's mission].

Paragraph 2 established a Conciliation Commission of three UN member states. France, Turkey and the United States were named to it. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] [cite:rs_rd6_ecf_194] Paragraph 5 urged the governments concerned to negotiate "the final settlement of all questions outstanding between them." Paragraph 7 called for the protection of, and free access to, the Holy Places, including Nazareth, under "effective United Nations supervision." [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] Paragraph 8 called for the Jerusalem area to be treated separately and placed under "effective United Nations control," asked the Security Council to ensure its demilitarization, and instructed the Commission to propose a permanent international regime for it. Paragraph 9 called for the "freest possible access to Jerusalem by road, rail or air." [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] What became of the Jerusalem paragraphs in 1949, when the Assembly returned to the city and Israel moved its parliament there, is told in [scene:rd6_un_admission|Israel's admission and the Jerusalem question].

Then came paragraph 11. It resolved:

that the refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date

and that compensation should be paid for the property of those choosing not to return. [cite:unispal_194_survey] [cite:wiki_res_194] The paragraph did not stop at return. It instructed the Conciliation Commission to facilitate the "repatriation, resettlement and economic and social rehabilitation" of the refugees and the payment of compensation, working with the Director of United Nations Relief for Palestine Refugees. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] Resettlement thus sat in the same sentence as repatriation. The resolution offered the Commission both tools and did not say how the choice between them was to be made, beyond the refugees' own wish to return.

The General Assembly has reaffirmed the resolution every year since 1949. [cite:unispal_194_survey] [cite:wiki_res_194] At the time of its adoption, however, the Arab states and Palestinian representatives rejected it, because it implied acceptance of Israel. Only later did Palestinians come to cite it as the foundation of the right of return. [cite:wiki_res_194]

Israel's reading was stated by Ben-Gurion to the UN conciliators. The words "live at peace with their neighbours," he argued, made return contingent on peace with the Arab states. [cite:unispal_194_survey] [cite:unwatch_194] Critics of the Palestinian reading add three further points. General Assembly resolutions are recommendations, not binding law. The text says refugees "should be permitted" to return, not that they have a right to. And the return of several million descendants would end Israel's Jewish majority. [cite:unwatch_194] In its strongest form, the Israeli case is that the resolution itself made return part of a peace, and that no peace was made.

The Palestinian reading treats return as a right, not a concession. Its supporters argue that the right is grounded in broader international law, not in this resolution alone, and they cite Article 13(2) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted the day before. They also point to the Assembly's annual reaffirmation, and to the terms on which Israel was admitted to the United Nations in May 1949, which they say came with a pledge to honor the resolution. [cite:wiki_res_194] The exact assurances given on Israel's behalf at that time are not confirmed in the UN records consulted, and they are not relied on here. In its strongest form, the Palestinian case is that the right does not depend on this resolution's wording at all, and that the Assembly's repetition of it every year since 1949 shows how the international community has understood it.

The two readings met at the conference the Conciliation Commission convened at Lausanne in 1949, and the talks broke down on this question; it remained unresolved at Camp David in 2000. [cite:wiki_res_194] The sequence of offers at Lausanne is told in [scene:lau_s01|the Lausanne conference].

Behind the dispute over the text lay a dispute over numbers, which began at once and has never been closed. Benny Morris's survey of the estimates gives the range. Israeli spokesmen publicly said "about 520,000," and Israel officially held to a figure of 520,000 to 530,000. Arab officials, from 1949, spoke of 900,000 or one million. The British estimated 810,000 in February 1949: 210,000 in Gaza, 320,000 in the West Bank, and 280,000 in Lebanon, Syria and the East Bank of the Jordan. The UN Economic Survey Mission and UNRWA counted 726,000. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] The UN Conciliation Commission's own estimate, given in the previous section, was about 711,000.

One private Israeli judgment stands out. According to Morris, in late 1950 Walter Eytan, director-general of Israel's Foreign Ministry, privately called UNRWA's registration of 726,000 "meticulous," but said that "the real number was close to 800,000." [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] The official public figure and the Foreign Ministry's private view thus differed by more than a quarter of a million people.

The question of compensation also produced a number. The Conciliation Commission's progress report of November 1951 put the value of abandoned Arab immovable property at about P£100 million, P£100,383,000 exactly, on 16,324 square kilometres of land, of which 4,574 were cultivable. For its calculations the Commission took the refugee population as approximately 900,000. [cite:rs_rd6_unccp_1951] That figure was a working approximation for the property estimate, not a count. How the property itself passed to the state is told in the section on the Absentees' Property Law.

The count of places emptied in the war differs as much as the count of people, and here the difference lies mostly in definitions. Benny Morris, in 1987, identified 369 villages. Walid Khalidi, in 1992, counted 418, excluding towns and sites without permanent structures. Earlier lists gave 399 (al-Arif), 443 (Nijm and Muammer) and 472 (Saleh). The Palestine Land Society, counting towns, tribal lands and police stations as well, gives 531 localities. [cite:rs_rd6_plands_villages] The lower figures count villages in a narrow sense. The highest counts every kind of inhabited place. Each total follows its own definition, and none can be compared with another without it.

Much here remains unsettled. The record does not establish a single agreed number of refugees: every estimate between 520,000 and one million had a named source behind it, and the private Israeli view, close to 800,000, lay nearer the UN and British figures than to Israel's public one. Whether paragraph 11 created a right or a recommendation is a question of law and interpretation, not of record, and both readings are documented. What the text itself settles is narrower and clearer: it tied return to the refugees' wish and to living at peace, it set compensation beside return, it named resettlement and rehabilitation as tasks for the Commission, and it called for Jerusalem to be placed under effective United Nations control. The refugee question it addressed was still unresolved at Camp David in 2000.

sections.h: The Rhodes Armistices, 1949: Lines That Were Not Borders
sections.html:
Resolution 194 urged a final settlement. What the parties actually signed in 1949 was something less: the war of 1948 did not end with a peace. It ended with four separate agreements, signed between February and July 1949, each of which declared in its own text that it settled nothing political. The lines they drew lasted until 1967 and became known as the Green Line. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] Because the lines lasted so long, they are often remembered as the borders the war produced. The documents themselves say the opposite, and they say it repeatedly.

The man who brought the parties to the table was Ralph Bunche, who had succeeded the assassinated UN mediator, Count Bernadotte. In January 1949 he brought Israeli and Egyptian delegations to negotiate on the island of Rhodes. [cite:rs_rd6_nobel_bunche] The mediation he inherited had already cost lives: in July 1949 he reported to the Security Council that ten members of the UN mission, the Mediator among them, had died over fourteen months, and that about twice as many had been wounded. [cite:rs_rd6_bunche_letter_1949] The plans Bernadotte had put forward, and the killing that ended his mission, are told in [scene:rd6_bernadotte|the mediator's mission]. Bunche's task was narrower than Bernadotte's had been. He was not drawing a settlement. He was stopping a war.

The first agreement, between Egypt and Israel, was signed at Rhodes on 24 February 1949. Mahmed Seif El Dine and M. K. El Raliniany signed for Egypt; Walter Eytan, Yigael Yadin and Elias Sasson signed for Israel. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] Its operative terms dealt with three places. Egyptian forces encircled in the Al Faluja pocket were to withdraw beyond the Egypt–Palestine frontier under UN supervision, a movement that Annex I set to begin at 0500 GMT on 26 February 1949. The village of El Auja and its surroundings were demilitarized under Article VIII. In the Gaza–Rafah area, Article VI froze Egyptian forces at the positions they held. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] The Gaza Strip, which Egypt held under the armistice, became the territory whose administration is described in the section on Arab Palestine after the war. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map]

The Egyptian text is also the clearest statement of what an armistice was meant to be. Article IV(3) says that its provisions are "dictated exclusively by military considerations" and are valid only for the period of the armistice. Article V says that the demarcation line "is not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary," and that it is drawn without prejudice to the rights of either party in the ultimate settlement. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] Supervision was given to a seven-member Mixed Armistice Commission: three members appointed by each party, with the Chief of Staff of the UN Truce Supervision Organization in the chair, and its headquarters at El Auja. The agreement was to remain in force "until a peaceful settlement between the Parties is achieved" (Article XII). [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text]

The structure explains who could act and who could not. Neither side could change the line by itself without breaking a signed agreement; neither side gave up its claims by signing; and the body set up to supervise the agreement was a commission on which the two parties had equal numbers and a UN officer held the chair. The agreement froze the military facts. It left every political question exactly where the war had left it.

Lebanon had entered the war by its own government's decision. On 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared independence, Lebanon joined Egypt, Syria, Jordan and Iraq in declaring war and invading the new state, fielding the smallest of the five Arab armies. Israeli forces repelled the invasion and temporarily occupied part of southern Lebanon. The armistice signed on 23 March 1949 restored the internationally recognized border between the two states. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] The decision to fight was not simply imposed on Lebanon from outside. According to Makram Rabah, a historian at the American University of Beirut, the country's founding leaders, chiefly Riad al-Solh and Bechara el-Khoury, who had led it to independence from France in 1943, had debated and rejected an alliance with the Zionist movement before 1948, concluding that they could not keep relations with the neighbouring Arab states if they made one. [cite:lebanon_1948_war]

The armistice returned the frontier to where it had been. It did not return the people who had crossed it. During the war an estimated 100,000–110,000 Palestinian Arabs, the large majority from northern Palestine, including the Acre area, fled or were displaced into Lebanon, a country of about 1.3 million people at the time. The International Committee of the Red Cross, and from 1950 UNRWA, ran the camps that received them. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy]

The agreement with the Hashemite Jordan Kingdom was signed at Rhodes on 3 April 1949. Colonel Ahmed Sudki El-Jundi and Lieutenant-Colonel Mohamed Maayte signed for Jordan; Reuven Shiloah and Lieutenant-Colonel Moshe Dayan signed for Israel. Article II(2) repeats the reservation of the Egyptian text: no provision shall prejudice the rights, claims and positions of either party in the final settlement. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text]

Two features set this agreement apart. The first was Jerusalem. Article VIII set up a Special Committee whose agreed agenda included free access to the Holy Places and cultural institutions, use of the cemetery on the Mount of Olives, the resumption of the institutions on Mount Scopus, and free movement on the Bethlehem road and the Latrun–Jerusalem road. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text] That agenda was written into the text. Whether it was carried out is another matter: according to Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education, Jews were denied access to their holy sites in the eastern part of the city that Jordan held after the war. [cite:rs_rd6_bpb_jerusalem] The fate of the city at the United Nations is taken up in the section on Israel's admission and Jerusalem.

The second feature was the Iraqi front. Iraq's army had fought in 1948 and held a sector of the line. Under Article VI, Jordanian forces replaced the Iraqi forces on that front, and the Wadi Ara area passed to Israel. The villagers there were to keep "full rights" of residence, property and freedom; those who chose to leave could take their movable property and were to be compensated for their land. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text] Here a transfer of inhabited territory came with written guarantees for the people living on it. How those guarantees fared under the regime later imposed on Arab citizens is a question for the section on military government.

The last agreement, with Syria, was signed on 20 July 1949 and completed the Rhodes armistice negotiations. [cite:rs_rd6_nobel_bunche] It was negotiated under a new regime: Syria's talks with Israel opened on 5 April 1949, days after Husni al-Za'im seized power in a coup, and the agreement turned the areas Syria evacuated into demilitarized zones that became the setting of two decades of clashes. [cite:tf_zaim] Both the negotiation and its aftermath are told in [scene:rd6_syria_1949|Syria in 1949].

The next day, 21 July 1949, Bunche wrote to the Security Council. He listed the four agreements by their UN document numbers: S/1264 (Egypt), S/1296 (Lebanon), S/1302 (Transjordan) and S/1353 (Syria). He called them "agreements voluntarily entered into by the parties," each of which incorporated "what amounts to a non-aggression pact." He noted that the Transjordan agreement also covered the Iraqi front, so that separate negotiations between Iraq and Israel were unnecessary. And he concluded that, with the armistices signed, "the mission of the Mediator has been fulfilled." [cite:rs_rd6_bunche_letter_1949] Bunche received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1950 and accepted it in Oslo on 10 December 1950. [cite:rs_rd6_nobel_bunche]

Set side by side, the four texts follow one pattern with local variations. Each froze a military position; each reserved the final settlement; each was built around the particular ground in dispute on that front.

Two Arab states that had taken part in the war signed nothing. Iraq never signed an armistice with Israel; its front was handed over to Jordan under the Jordanian agreement, which Bunche judged sufficient. [cite:rs_rd6_bunche_letter_1949] [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] Iraq's policies toward its own Jewish citizens in the same months, including the law of July 1948, are told in [scene:rd6_exodus|the section on the Jews of the Arab world].

Saudi Arabia never signed either. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] Its part in the fighting had been different in kind from its neighbors'. It did not launch a direct invasion in 1948; it sent a limited contingent of troops placed under Egyptian command, a modest commitment that the record attributes to its greater distance from Palestine. Saudi Arabia never established diplomatic relations with Israel, and for decades it barred entry to anyone holding an Israeli passport or a passport with an Israeli stamp. Instead of a military front, it took part in an economic one. The Arab League's boycott of Israel was formalized in 1948 and barred member states from any direct economic relationship with Israel. A secondary boycott, added in 1950, extended the ban to foreign companies doing business with Israel, and a tertiary boycott later targeted companies that did business with firms on the secondary list. Saudi Arabia was among the boycott's most consistent participants and maintained it in some form for over seven decades. The armistices ended the shooting on four fronts; the boycott carried the conflict into trade.

The new lines enclosed far more territory than the United Nations had proposed for the Jewish state. The 1947 partition plan had allotted that state 56% of the land, a figure set beside the founding narratives at the close of this volume. Israel's Foreign Ministry describes the territory inside the 1949 armistice demarcation lines as "about 78% of the Mandate area." [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map]

The same Foreign Ministry page states the limits of that territory as plainly as the treaties do. The agreements, it notes, were meant to be interim until replaced by peace treaties. The lines became known as the Green Line. Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt the Gaza Strip, and Iraq and Saudi Arabia never signed agreements with Israel. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] The difference between 56% and about 78% is the measure of what the fighting of 1948 changed on the ground. The texts of 1949 are the measure of what it did not change in law: by their own words, nothing in them settled where Israel's borders lay.

The year-by-year ledger of this period sets the armistices beside the other events of 1949: Israel's admission to the United Nations, the Lausanne conference and the creation of UNRWA. In the ledger's terms, 1949 was the year of consolidation, and the year the talks on return failed.

The common belief that the Green Line was Israel's agreed border in 1949 does not survive a reading of the texts. Article V of the Egyptian agreement and Article II(2) of the Jordanian one deny it in terms. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text] What the texts leave open is how much weight the line should carry afterwards, and here the two sides' readings diverge. At Lausanne a few months later, Israel held that the 1947 partition plan had been nullified by the Arab invasion; the Arab delegations, for their part, wanted the 1947 lines and demanded that Israel first accept the return of the refugees. The final frontiers remained, on both positions, open for the settlement the agreements anticipated. Bunche's own description is more modest than either: a set of voluntary agreements amounting to non-aggression pacts, nothing more and nothing less. [cite:rs_rd6_bunche_letter_1949]

What the record here does not settle is how the machinery the agreements created actually worked in the years that followed. The sources used here describe the Egyptian Mixed Armistice Commission in detail but not the commissions on the other fronts, and they do not give the commissions' rulings or the number of complaints they heard. Whether the Special Committee for Jerusalem ever met to any effect on its agenda is not documented here either; the only evidence on that point is the report that access to the holy sites in the eastern city was denied. The armistices were written as a bridge to peace treaties. None of those treaties came in the period this chapter covers, and the bridge became, for eighteen years, the only structure there was.

sections.h: The Constitution That Was Deferred, 1948–1950
sections.html:
The armistices left Israel's borders unsettled. Its first parliament left something else open as well. Most readers assume that Israel, like most democracies, has a written constitution. It does not, and it never has. The absence was not an oversight. It was the result of a decision taken in the state's first two years, by its first parliament, for reasons that were argued openly at the time and are documented. What was put in place instead, a promise to write the constitution chapter by chapter, is a compromise that, according to the sources used here, remains in effect.

The promise came first. The Declaration of Independence of May 1948 committed the new state to a constitution "adopted by the Elected Constituent Assembly not later than the 1st October 1948." [cite:rs_rd6_dickerman_2007] The date passed in the middle of the war. The assembly that was to write the constitution was elected in January 1949 and convened on 14 February 1949. Two days later it renamed itself the Knesset. [cite:rs_rd6_dickerman_2007] The body elected to draft the founding charter thus became the First Knesset, the state's ordinary legislature, and the constitution became one item on its agenda among many.

The man most responsible for what followed was David Ben-Gurion, the prime minister. He opposed a written constitution, and the account by Michael Dickerman gives two reasons. The first was that a constitution would place judicial limits on what the government could do. The second was a fear that a fight over religion, which a constitution would force into the open, would deepen the divide between religious and secular Israelis while the conflict with the Arab states was still unresolved. [cite:rs_rd6_dickerman_2007] The religious parties, for their part, had a demand that any constitution would have had to meet or defeat: they insisted that religious courts keep exclusive authority over matters of personal status. [cite:rs_rd6_dickerman_2007] On one reading, a constitution with guaranteed individual rights would have collided with that demand, and deferral avoided the collision.

The question was debated nine times. On 13 June 1950 the Knesset adopted a compromise moved by Yizhar Harari of the Progressive Party, known since as the Harari Resolution. It provided that the constitution "will be made up of chapters, each of which will constitute a separate basic law," and that "all the chapters together will constitute the constitution of the state." [cite:rs_rd6_dickerman_2007] As quoted, the resolution set no date for any chapter, and it did not say how a basic law would differ from any other law in the way it was passed or amended. The First Knesset, in the summary of a later account, deadlocked over what the constitution would contain, above all over the place of religion in public life, and chose to enact Basic Laws one at a time instead. [cite:gov_legalclarity]

The mechanism the state ran on in the meantime was a parliamentary one. Voters did not elect a head of government. They elected a parliament. All members of the Knesset are elected in a single nationwide district by proportional representation, so that the whole country forms one constituency and parties win seats in proportion to their share of the vote; under today's rules a party must clear a threshold of 3.25% to win any seats. No party has ever won an outright majority of 61 seats. [cite:knesset_idi] Every government has therefore been a coalition, in which the parties trade their votes for ministerial posts and policy concessions, and in which a small faction holding the balance can carry weight out of proportion to its size. [cite:gov_goodauthority] The religious parties' insistence on their demand in 1949 and 1950 fits that arithmetic, although the sources used here do not record the coalition bargaining of those years directly.

The head of state stood outside that bargaining. Israel's president is elected by the Knesset, not by the public, and under the present rules serves a single, non-renewable term of seven years. The office's formal powers are limited to granting pardons, tasking a member of the Knesset with forming a government, and representing the country abroad. The president has no part in day-to-day government, no veto over legislation and no command of the armed forces. [cite:president_time] Executive power rests with the prime minister and the cabinet. The procedure for forming a government, as it now stands, gives the member most likely to command 61 seats a mandate of 28 days, extendable by 14. If that member fails, the president may task another, or the Knesset can name a candidate with a 21-day window if 61 members support it; if every attempt fails, the country goes to new elections. [cite:pm_brookings]

The figure shows the structure as the sources describe it; several of the specific rules, such as the 3.25% threshold and the 28-day mandate, are documented as they stand today rather than as they stood in 1949, and this book does not have a source for their earlier form.

The Harari Resolution's effect became visible only slowly. The first Basic Law, on the Knesset itself and its elections, was not passed until 1958. Others followed: on the military and its subordination to civilian government in 1968, on Jerusalem as the united capital in 1980, on human dignity and liberty in 1992, a partial bill of rights that the Supreme Court later used to justify judicial review, and in 2018 on Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people, which enshrined Jewish self-determination as a national right without parallel language for Arab citizens. [cite:basiclaw_britannica] As the sources used here count them, there are 14 Basic Laws, covering the Knesset, the government, the military, the judiciary, land, Jerusalem and civil rights. The Supreme Court treats them as having constitutional weight, but most can be amended by a simple majority of the Knesset; only a few clauses are entrenched, Freedom of Occupation and the Knesset's electoral clause needing 61 of the 120 members and the Referendum law requiring 80 members or a referendum before territory under Israeli law is given up, unlike the United States Constitution, which needs two-thirds of Congress and three-quarters of the states, or Germany's Basic Law, some provisions of which cannot be amended at all. [cite:us2_wiki_basiclaws] The Nation-State Law passed by 62 votes to 55; the 2023 law on the "reasonableness" standard passed 64 to 0 because the opposition walked out. [cite:basiclaw_britannica] The tension between laws called constitutional and a parliament that can change most of them by an ordinary majority lay at the root of the judicial crisis of 2023, which is followed in [scene:ilgov_s01|the later history of the Basic Laws]. The coalition arithmetic described above produced five national elections between April 2019 and November 2022 [cite:gov_wiki], and in July 2023 the Biden administration invited President Isaac Herzog, rather than Prime Minister Netanyahu, to address a joint session of Congress and visit the White House, a choice TIME described as honouring "a largely ceremonial role with no executive authority" in place of "the man who runs the country." [cite:president_time]

Two judgments about 1950 remain open. The first concerns motive. Dickerman's account gives Ben-Gurion two reasons: fear of deepening the religious–secular divide in wartime, and reluctance to bind the government by courts. Read with the first in mind, deferral looks like a truce that kept a divided society together during a war; read with the second, it looks like a government keeping its own hands free. The record cited here documents both reasons and does not say which weighed more. The second judgment concerns consequences. Whether a formal constitution adopted in 1948 or 1950 would have prevented the crisis of 2023 is a question on which scholars disagree, and the record does not settle it. [cite:basiclaw_britannica] Nor does it settle how much of Israel's later instability belongs to the structure set up in these years and how much to the choices of individual leaders; political scientists contest that attribution, and this book treats the structure as a documented contributor, not a sole cause. [cite:pm_brookings]

What the record does settle is the sequence. A constitution was promised for a fixed date; the date passed; the body elected to write it became a parliament instead; and after nine debates that parliament resolved to write it in pieces, without a deadline. The pieces began to arrive eight years later, and the whole has never been completed.

sections.h: Syria in 1949: The Offer, the Coups and the Demilitarized Zones
sections.html:
The last of the four armistices was negotiated with a Syrian ruler who had seized power days before the talks opened. A familiar account holds that Syria rejected every chance at peace with Israel from 1948 onward. The record of 1949 complicates it. For a few months that year Syria's ruler offered Israel a peace treaty, a meeting at the highest level, and the resettlement of a large share of the Palestinian refugees inside Syria. Israel's prime minister declined, the ruler was overthrown and executed, and the armistice frontier the two states left behind, the border for the next 18 years, became the setting of two decades of clashes. Each part of that sequence is documented, and so is the conduct of both sides along the line.

Syria's army had entered the war in May 1948 and fought on the northern front. When the fighting stopped, Syrian forces held small areas west of the international border. On 30 March 1949 Syria's elected government was overthrown by an army officer, Husni al-Za'im, in the first of three coups that year. Declassified records and historians document contacts between US officials and Za'im before the coup; how far the United States directed it is debated. [cite:w_1949_syria_coup]

Armistice talks between Syria and Israel opened on 5 April 1949. In the course of them, Za'im offered a peace treaty and military cooperation, proposed a meeting with Ben-Gurion or with Moshe Sharett, and offered to resettle 250,000–300,000 Palestinian refugees in Syria. The border he proposed would have run through the middle of Lake Hula and the Sea of Galilee. [cite:tf_zaim] [cite:ecf_zaim] [cite:majalla_zaim] The offer is documented in Israeli archives and by historians. [cite:tf_zaim] [cite:ecf_zaim] Its scale is clearest against the numbers at Lausanne a few months later, where Israel offered to take back 100,000 refugees as part of a final peace: Za'im was offering to absorb two and a half to three times as many himself.

Ben-Gurion was unwilling to stake policy on him, in part from distrust of Za'im's ties to Washington. [cite:majalla_zaim] That is the reason the record gives. A wider argument for caution can be built from documented facts: Za'im had seized power by force less than a week before the talks opened, his contacts with American officials before the coup are on the record, and the border he asked for ran through the middle of both lakes. On that argument, a treaty with such a ruler might not outlast him; he was in fact overthrown within months. The argument on the other side also rests on documented facts. The offer included a treaty, a summit and a resettlement figure larger than anything Israel itself put forward on refugees that year, and it addressed, for a large number of refugees, the question on which the Lausanne conference failed. The record shows that the offer was made and that it was declined. It does not show whether it could have been carried out.

The question was soon closed. In August 1949 Za'im was deposed and executed in Syria's second coup of the year, and the offer died with him. [cite:ecf_zaim] The armistice had already been signed on 20 July 1949, the last of the four agreements negotiated under Ralph Bunche. [cite:rs_rd6_nobel_bunche] Under its terms, the areas Syria evacuated west of the international border became demilitarized zones. How the four agreements were made, and what they did and did not settle, is told in [scene:rd6_armistices|the Rhodes armistices].

The zones were small strips of land whose sovereignty the armistice left unsettled, and they became the fault line of the frontier. In a meeting in 1953–54, recorded by the State Department, Moshe Dayan told American officials that Israel claimed sovereignty over Jewish-owned lands inside the zones, that "someone must keep the area alive," and that Israel did not want Syria to have direct access to the Jordan River. [cite:frus_dayan_dmz] The conduct of both sides along the line is documented. Syrian forces fired from the heights on Israeli farmers and fishermen. Israel sent armoured tractors to cultivate disputed land in the zones and carried out reprisal raids.

The map traces the line from Za'im's offer forward. Two later developments belong to the following volumes and are given here only in outline. In the 1960s the dispute turned to water: Israel built its National Water Carrier, the Arab League backed a plan in 1964 to divert the headwaters of the Jordan, and Israeli strikes hit the diversion works between 1965 and 1967. And in an interview given in 1976 and published in 1997, Dayan said that at least 80 percent of the clashes had been provoked by Israel, which sent tractors into the zones until the Syrians fired. [cite:w_dayan] That account is his own, given long after the events; others contest it, and it does not cancel the documented Syrian fire on farmers and fishermen. It does show that the familiar picture of clashes caused entirely by shelling from the Golan is incomplete. The fuller story of the frontier to 1967 is in [scene:sy_s02|the demilitarized zones and the water war].

Syria's three coups of 1949 opened a decade in which the region's old order gave way. Egypt's Free Officers, the movement Nasser led, overthrew King Farouk in July 1952. [cite:w_1952_egypt] In August 1953 the CIA and MI6 removed Iran's elected prime minister. [cite:w_1953_coup] After Egypt nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956, Britain, France and Israel invaded, and US and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw. [cite:w_suez] Iraq's monarchy was overthrown on 14 July 1958. [cite:w_1958_iraq] By the end of the decade, military or royal autocrats, Cold War alignments and outside intervention had become the pattern of the region's politics. The record ties that pattern to the coups of named officers and, in Iran, to the CIA and MI6, not to local culture or religion alone. Za'im's coup was the first of the decade.

Three things remain unsettled. The first is the degree of American involvement in Za'im's coup, which the declassified record documents as contacts and historians still debate as direction. [cite:w_1949_syria_coup] The second is whether his offer was a serious basis for peace or the gesture of a ruler whose hold on power proved brief; the record establishes the terms but cannot establish what would have followed acceptance. The third is responsibility for the clashes in the demilitarized zones. Dayan's statements of 1953–54 and 1976 are on the record, and so is Syrian fire on civilians; the dispute over which side bore more responsibility continues. [cite:w_dayan]

sections.h: Lausanne, 1949: Two Sequences That Never Met
sections.html:
Za'im's offer was made in the same months as the conference that was meant to settle the refugee question for all the parties at once. Two opposite accounts of that conference, at Lausanne, are still repeated. One says that Israel never offered anything on the refugees. The other says that the Arab states refused every offer. The United Nations' own report on the talks supports neither. It records an Israeli offer, a number, and the conditions attached to it; it records an Arab position with conditions of its own; and it shows that each side's conditions came in an order the other would not accept. That is why the conference failed, and why the refugee question it was meant to settle outlived it.

The forum was the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine, created by Resolution 194 of December 1948. That resolution named France, Turkey and the United States to the Commission [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194]; its full text, and the competing readings of its refugee paragraph, are set out in [scene:rr_s01|the section on Resolution 194]. The Commission convened talks at Lausanne from 27 April to 12 September 1949. The Arab delegations refused to negotiate directly with Israel, so the Commission shuttled between the parties. [cite:wiki_lausanne_1949] [cite:pij_lausanne]

The Commission had begun to press on the refugee question before the conference opened. In April 1949 it asked Israel to suspend its absentee regulations until the final peace settlement, and Israel declined. [cite:un_ccp_absentee_1949] That request, and the law of 1950 that made the regime permanent, are told in [scene:ap_s01|the section on absentee property].

On 12 May 1949 the parties signed the Lausanne Protocol, which took the 1947 partition map as a basis for discussion. [cite:wiki_lausanne_1949] [cite:pij_lausanne] The two sides read it differently from the start. The Arab states wanted the 1947 partition lines, and demanded that Israel first accept the return of the refugees under Resolution 194. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report] [cite:jvl_israel_studies_peace] Israel held that the partition plan had been nullified by the Arab invasion, and that the refugees could be dealt with only within a final peace. Israel first floated a proposal to annex the Gaza Strip together with its refugee population. Egypt refused.

Washington intervened while the talks were under way. On 28 May 1949 Truman's secret note to Ben-Gurion warned that if Israel kept rejecting the December 1948 resolution, "a revision of its attitude toward Israel has become unavoidable." Israel rejected the demands in June, and the revision never came. [cite:jvl_truman_note_may1949] [cite:djn_1977_truman_note] The note is set in the sequence of Truman's decisions in [scene:tr_s02|the section on Truman after recognition].

Israel's offer came on 3 August. According to the Commission's own progress report, Israel offered to accept the return of 100,000 refugees, which would have brought its Arab population to a maximum of 250,000. The offer was made "only as an integral part of a general and final peace settlement." [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report] [cite:jvl_ccp_fourth_report] The Arab delegations called it contrary to Resolution 194 and to the Protocol. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report] [cite:jvl_israel_studies_peace] Israel later withdrew it. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report] [cite:jvl_ccp_fourth_report] The same report records that Israel blocked a committee on orange groves owned by refugees. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report] The conference ended on 12 September without agreement, and the United States warned Israel that it might revise its relations over the impasse.

The positions on Jerusalem at Lausanne are not recorded in the sources used here, which is why the comparison leaves them out.

Each side's case had force in its own terms. Israel's rested on three points: the partition plan the Arab delegations now invoked had, in its view, been nullified by the Arab invasion; Resolution 194 itself spoke of refugees who wished to return "and live at peace with their neighbours," which Ben-Gurion read as making return contingent on peace with the Arab states [cite:unispal_194_survey] [cite:unwatch_194]; and an offer of 100,000 within a final peace was a concrete figure, not a refusal. The Arab case rested on three points as well: paragraph 11 of the resolution said that refugees wishing to return "should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date" [cite:unispal_194_survey] [cite:wiki_res_194], which on their reading made return something owed rather than something to be traded for peace; the Protocol Israel had signed took the 1947 map as its basis; and an offer conditional on a final peace, later withdrawn altogether, returned no one. Both cases rest on documents.

The shape of the failure explains why it lasted. Israel would discuss return only after peace. The Arab states would discuss peace only after return. With neither moving, some 700,000 refugees remained refugees, and the question has outlived every negotiation since. The offer of 100,000 shows that Israel was prepared to put a number on the table; the conditions attached to it, and the Arab rejection of those conditions, show why the number never became policy. In the same months Israel was declining Husni al-Za'im's offer to resettle 250,000–300,000 refugees in Syria as part of a peace, an episode told in the section on Syria in 1949. [cite:tf_zaim]

What the record does not settle is whether either sequence could have been moved. The Commission's report shows the positions as stated; it does not show what either side would have accepted under sustained pressure, and the one external power that threatened such pressure, the United States, did not apply it. Whether a larger Israeli offer, or Arab acceptance of the 100,000 as a first step, would have led to a settlement is a matter of judgment, not of documents. What the documents do show is the moment at which the refugee problem stopped being a consequence of the war and became one of the conflict's permanent features.

sections.h: Admission to the United Nations and the Question of Jerusalem, 1949–1950
sections.html:
The General Assembly voted on Israel's membership while the Lausanne talks were still in session. In the year after the war Israel sought two kinds of acceptance: recognition by other states, and membership of the United Nations. It won both within a few months. The terms on which it won the second, and the argument over Jerusalem that followed within the year, show how much of the 1947 plan the new state's admission left formally in place, and how little of it was carried out.

Recognition came from an unexpected direction in March 1949, when Turkey established diplomatic relations with Israel, the first Muslim-majority state to do so. [cite:w_isr_tur] The relationship that grew from it, including a secret intelligence pact with Israel and Iran in 1958 and military-cooperation agreements in 1996, belongs to later volumes and is followed in [scene:tk_s03|Turkey's alliance years]. In 1949 its significance was simpler: a Muslim-majority state had recognized Israel.

Membership was a harder question, because the United Nations had already set out terms for the territory in two resolutions. Before voting, the General Assembly's Ad Hoc Political Committee met on 6 May 1949 to take up Israel's attitude to Resolution 181 of November 1947 and Resolution 194 of December 1948. It named three issues: the internationalization of Jerusalem, the repatriation of the refugees, and the investigation of the assassination of Count Bernadotte and Colonel Sérot, the UN mediator and the French officer serving as a UN observer who was killed with him in September 1948. Egypt had opposed inviting Israel's representative to explain. [cite:rs_rd6_ahpc_47]

The committee was not the only pressure. Alongside it, the Holy See ran a diplomatic campaign at the United Nations to make Israel's admission conditional on two commitments: allowing the return of the Palestinian refugees, and formal guarantees protecting Christian and Muslim holy sites, particularly in Jerusalem. These were specific negotiating positions, pressed through diplomatic channels. In that context Ben-Gurion is documented as saying in 1949: "There is a major religion in the world, which has to settle with us a historical reckoning." The Vatican's position had a long history. In January 1904 Theodor Herzl had sought Pope Pius X's support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine and been refused, on the ground that the Church could not support the restoration of the Jews to a land central to its own theology while they denied Christ. That refusal held as official Vatican policy for 89 years. [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] The campaign of 1949 was not silence or indifference at the founding of the state. It was active opposition to unconditional admission.

It did not succeed. On 11 May 1949 the General Assembly adopted Resolution 273 (III), admitting Israel to membership of the United Nations, by 37 votes to 12, with 9 abstentions. [cite:rs_rd6_ecf_273] The resolution's text records the conditions it did attach, which were declaratory. It noted Israel's declaration that it "unreservedly accepts the obligations of the United Nations Charter." It recalled the resolutions of 29 November 1947 and 11 December 1948, the partition resolution and Resolution 194. And it took note of "the declarations and explanations made by the representative of the Government of Israel" before the Ad Hoc Political Committee. [cite:rs_rd6_unga273_text] Israel was admitted without the guarantees the Vatican had sought, a documented diplomatic defeat for the Holy See at that moment.

What those "declarations and explanations" were matters to a later argument. Palestinians and their supporters, who treat Resolution 194 as establishing a right of return, note that Israel's admission came with a pledge to honor it; one reference account names Israel's representative, Abba Eban, as giving an assurance that Israel would honor Resolutions 181 and 194. [cite:wiki_res_194] The committee's summary record consulted documents the agenda of 6 May, not the content of Israel's answers, and the resolution itself only "takes note" of them. [cite:rs_rd6_ahpc_47] [cite:rs_rd6_unga273_text] The wording of any assurance, and how binding it was meant to be, cannot be stated here from the primary record; the competing readings of Resolution 194 are set out in [scene:rr_s01|the section on Resolution 194].

Jerusalem was the issue on which the gap between the resolutions and the ground was widest. Resolution 181 had made Jerusalem and Bethlehem a corpus separatum, a separate entity under UN administration. After the war, according to Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education, Israel held West Jerusalem and Jordan held East Jerusalem, including the Old City, the Temple Mount and the Western Wall, and Jews were denied access to their holy sites there. [cite:rs_rd6_bpb_jerusalem] The armistice with Jordan had put free access to the holy places on the agenda of a special committee. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text]

On 9 December 1949 the General Assembly, in Resolution 303, again called for international status for Jerusalem. The response came in four weeks. Ben-Gurion spoke against the resolution in the Knesset on 13 December. On 26 December the Knesset moved from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. On 23 January 1950 it declared Jerusalem the capital of Israel by 60 votes to 2; the two votes against were cast by Communists who supported international status. [cite:rs_rd6_bpb_jerusalem] The same source reports that the declaration was not internationally recognized, and that no state opened an embassy in West Jerusalem until 1967. [cite:rs_rd6_bpb_jerusalem]

The sequence can be read two ways. On one reading, Israel joined an organization whose resolutions on refugees and Jerusalem it then declined to carry out, and moved its parliament into the city the same organization had just asked to be placed under international control. On the other, the internationalization of Jerusalem had already been overtaken by a war that left the eastern city, and the holy sites in it, under Jordanian rule with Jewish access denied, and Israel's admission resolution had recorded the UN's resolutions without making membership conditional on carrying them out. Both readings rest on the same dated record.

The Vatican's own reckoning took decades. It maintained non-recognition for 45 years after Israel's founding. The precondition for change was doctrinal: the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate of 1965 revised Catholic teaching on Judaism, stating that God "holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers." The Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993, signed in Jerusalem, established diplomatic relations, and ambassadors were exchanged in 1994; property rights, tax exemptions and the status of Jerusalem were left for continuing negotiation. [cite:wiki_fundamental_agreement] After the General Assembly's vote of November 2012, the Vatican recognized the State of Palestine in 2013 and in 2015 signed an accord governing the Church's activity in Palestinian-controlled territory, which drew a formal Israeli protest. [cite:gulfnews_vatican_palestine_accord] That history is told in [scene:vat_s01|the Vatican's long non-recognition].

The record leaves two matters open. The first is the content of Israel's statements to the Ad Hoc Political Committee, which this book has not been able to read in the primary record. The second is the Vatican campaign's reach: the sources used here document the campaign and its aims, but not which governments, if any, it moved among the twelve that voted against admission.

sections.h: Where the Refugees Went, and the Diaspora That Came Before Them
sections.html:
While their return was argued over at Lausanne and at the United Nations, the refugees themselves were living in the states around Israel. Their flight, too, has been confused with something else: two Palestinian migrations are often run together, and the confusion costs both of them their history. The first began under the Ottoman Empire, some seventy years before the state of Israel existed, and carried families from a handful of towns around Bethlehem to the Americas. The second was the flight and expulsion of 1948, which carried some 700,000 people across the new armistice lines into the neighbouring Arab states and into the parts of Palestine that Israel did not hold. A common assumption holds that the Palestinian communities of Latin America are made up of 1948 refugees who found open doors there. The record shows an older population, a different legal status, and, in El Salvador at least, doors that were not open.

Palestinian emigration to the Americas began in the 1870s. Most of the early migrants were Christian families from Bethlehem, Beit Jala and Beit Sahour. They traveled on Ottoman papers, and so in their new countries they were long called "Turcos", Turks. [cite:palquest_sv] The movement continued into the 1930s. Its scale, relative to the towns that sent it, was large: El Salvador's population of Bethlehem descent is described today as several times larger than Bethlehem's own. [cite:palquest_sv]

Chile became the largest center. Its Palestinian-descended population is the largest anywhere outside the Arab world, with estimates commonly running into the hundreds of thousands. In 1920, nearly three decades before the Nakba, the Santiago football club Club Deportivo Palestino was founded; it plays in Chile's national first division. [cite:w_palchile] [cite:w_palestino]

El Salvador shows how little the doors were open. Its Palestinian community, estimated at roughly 70,000 to 100,000 people and overwhelmingly of Bethlehem origin, is described as the third-largest in Latin America after Chile and Honduras. In 1921 the Salvadoran state declared Arabs and Chinese to be "pernicious" races, a documented act of exclusion written into policy. Salvadoran elites looked down on the "Turcos" as peddlers. The community built its standing in commerce despite that discrimination, and in time rose to economic and political prominence. [cite:palquest_sv]

The rise reached the presidency twice. Antonio Saca won the presidency in 2004, and his opponent, Schafik Handal, was also of Palestinian descent. Nayib Bukele was elected in 2019; his paternal grandparents had emigrated from Jerusalem and Bethlehem in the early twentieth century, and his father became a well-known imam. [cite:palquest_sv] [cite:jweekly_bukele] Bukele's own politics on Israel are pro-Israel, a reminder that descent does not decide a person's position. [cite:jweekly_bukele]

The refugees of 1948 were a different population, uprooted at a different date, and held a different legal status. The 1948 war resulted in approximately 700,000 Palestinians fleeing or being expelled from their homes, the event Palestinians call the Nakba, "catastrophe". They settled in Gaza, which was under Egyptian administration; in the West Bank, under Jordanian administration; and in Lebanon, Syria and Jordan itself. [cite:npr_hamashistory] From 1950 the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, UNRWA, registered them as refugees. Treating the earlier emigrants as Nakba refugees erases both histories: that of the Ottoman-era families who built communities under discrimination, and that of the 1948 refugees, whose displacement remains unresolved.

Where the 1948 refugees stood depended on which state they had reached. Jordan was the exception. Under its 1954 nationality law, it gave citizenship to most of the Palestinians who had come after 1948. [cite:jns_arab_citizenship] [cite:adl_refugees] According to the sources cited here, it hosts more than 2 million registered Palestinian refugees, most of them citizens, although Human Rights Watch has documented arbitrary revocations of that citizenship. [cite:jns_arab_citizenship] [cite:adl_refugees]

Lebanon took the opposite course, and the choice was made in Beirut. Palestinian refugees in Lebanon have never been eligible for Lebanese citizenship as a class, lack political rights, and have had no access to most state-provided health and education services, a policy that has persisted from 1948 to the present according to European Union Agency for Asylum assessments current through 2025. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy] The application was not uniform in the early years. Middle- and upper-class Palestinians, and Christian Palestinians in particular, could obtain Lebanese citizenship, and some did, so that religion and class shaped individual outcomes inside a restrictive framework. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy]

The reasoning was stated openly. Lebanon's political system allocates parliamentary seats, the presidency and the premiership by religious sect, under the power-sharing formula of the 1943 National Pact, later revised by the Taif Agreement of 1989. Lebanese officials and analysts across several decades have named the central concern: that naturalizing a refugee population that was overwhelmingly Sunni Muslim would upset that sectarian balance. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy] The restrictions that followed are only partly dated in these sources. Palestinians were barred from dozens of professions outside the camps, and a property law of 2001 barred them from owning real estate. These measures were justified as preventing tawteen, permanent settlement. [cite:fmr_lebanon] [cite:aj_lebanon_property] According to the sources cited here, Lebanon counts about 400,000 registered refugees, roughly 10 percent of its population. [cite:fmr_lebanon] The same sources record twelve official camps run by UNRWA and more than 150 informal ones, on land that, in Amnesty International's description, has "barely changed" in seven decades despite the growth of the population living on it. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy] The longer story is told in [scene:ilb_s03|Lebanon's refugee policy].

Egypt and the Gulf states offered residency without a path to citizenship. Behind these different national policies sat a common line. The Arab League instructed its members not to grant citizenship to the refugees, "to avoid dissolution of their identity and protect their right of return". Its Casablanca Protocol of 1965 later promised refugees the right to work and to travel, but it was unevenly applied. [cite:fmr_lebanon]

Two readings of these policies run side by side, and each has a real case. The Arab League's own stated reason was protective: to give the refugees citizenship elsewhere would dissolve their identity and give up the claim that they should go home. [cite:fmr_lebanon] Critics, including Israeli and pro-Israel analysts, argue that the same policy kept the refugees in limbo as a political tool. The record shows that the states did not act as one. Jordan absorbed refugees as citizens; Lebanon restricted them, and gave as its reason its own sectarian balance as well as the politics of return; Egypt and the Gulf offered residence only. The argument has continued to the present. After 7 October 2023, Egypt's President el-Sisi and Jordan's King Abdullah refused to take in people from Gaza; analysts noted that, historically, Palestinians forced to leave have not been allowed to return, and Egypt warned of militants in Sinai. [cite:pbs_egypt_refugees] The full treatment is in [scene:sq_s20|the question of why Arab states did not absorb the refugees].

The camps also became a political base. The displacement of 1948 is the foundational fact around which every later Palestinian political movement organized. [cite:npr_hamashistory] The Palestine Liberation Organization was founded in 1964, and Fatah, Yasser Arafat's secular nationalist movement, became its dominant faction by 1969. [cite:npr_hamashistory] That history, and what came after it, belongs to a later volume and is traced in [scene:hma_src_s02|Palestinian political origins].

What the record here does not settle is the weight of motive. The documented policies are clear, and so are the reasons each government gave. Whether the League line served the refugees' own interest, or chiefly the interests of the states that adopted it, is a judgment the sources cited here do not make. Nor do these sources give a count, for the 1950s, of how many refugees reached each host state.

sections.h: The Jews of the Arab World After 1948
sections.html:
The war of 1948 produced refugees in two directions. About 700,000 Palestinians were displaced and not allowed to return. In the years that followed, the large Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt, Syria and North Africa shrank dramatically, through emigration, pressure, expulsion and state persecution in proportions that varied from country to country. [cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] Estimates of the total who left Arab countries and Iran between 1948 and the 1970s commonly fall in the range of 800,000 to 900,000 people. [cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] The historian Philip Mendes counts nearly one million Jews, Mizrahim, who left Arab countries in the decade or so after 1947–48, most of them for Israel. [cite:rs_rd6_mendes_2010] The two figures cover different spans and different sets of countries.

A familiar framing treats 1948 either as a moment after which nothing in the region changed, or as the source of every problem that followed. The record supports neither. The revolts of the 1920s and 1930s show that instability was already there; 1948 deepened and redirected it. What 1948 added was a permanent refugee question, a state of war, and a powerful political cause. The governments that lost the war were discredited, as armies and publics blamed their rulers: Syria's government fell to a military coup in March 1949, Egypt's monarchy in 1952, and Iraq's in 1958. [cite:w_1949_syria_coup] [cite:w_1952_egypt] [cite:w_1958_iraq] For the Jewish communities living under those governments, the years after 1948 were the years in which a long presence came to an end. What follows takes the countries one at a time, because the causes were not the same in each.

Iraq. Iraq's Jewish community was a community of some 2,800 years' standing. [cite:govil_aliyah] After the United Nations voted for partition in November 1947, anti-Jewish measures in Iraq escalated, and pogroms gave way to systematic confiscation of property and trumped-up prosecutions. On 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared independence, Iraq joined the invasion. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:govil_aliyah] When the fighting ended, Iraq refused to sign an armistice with Israel; Israeli government sources describe it as the only Arab combatant to refuse, leaving a formal state of war that, by their account, has technically never ended. [cite:govil_aliyah] Saudi Arabia, whose limited contingent had fought under Egyptian command, signed no armistice either. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] The armistice talks themselves are told in [scene:rd6_armistices|the Rhodes armistices].

On 19 July 1948 Iraq made "Zionism" a crime punishable by up to seven years in prison. Since every Jew was presumed to be a Zionist, the law worked as a criminalization of the whole community. The testimony of two Muslim witnesses was enough to convict, and there was little avenue for appeal. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] Two months later the law found its most public victim. On 23 September 1948 Shafiq Ades, a prominent and well-connected Jewish businessman, was hanged in public in Basra on charges of selling weapons to Israel and to the Iraqi Communist Party. His body was left hanging for hours as a spectacle. The case is widely cited as the one that broke the community's remaining sense of security, convincing many that no one, however powerful, was safe. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:govil_aliyah]

In March 1950 Iraq passed a law allowing Jews to emigrate if they renounced their citizenship. It was framed as permission to leave.
