In practice it worked as a mechanism to strip Jewish citizens of nationality and then of property once they had registered: those who signed up were denaturalized and their assets taken. [cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] Israel and the Near East Transport Company flew the community out, first by way of Cyprus and later on direct flights from Baghdad to Lod. The airlift, named Operation Ezra and Nehemiah after the biblical leaders of the return from Babylonian exile, was largely funded by the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, at a cost of about $4 million. [cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] [cite:govil_aliyah] By 1952, according to Israeli government sources, a community of roughly 135,000 had been reduced to about 6,000. [cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] Other sources count differently: the Jewish Agency gives 121,512 of Iraq's 130,000 Jews as arriving in Israel, and a table drawn from the Israel State Archives gives 124,226 immigrants from Iraq between 1948 and the end of 1952. [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852]

Between April 1950 and June 1951, during exactly the months when the denaturalization law was driving mass registration, at least five bombing incidents struck Jewish institutions and gathering points in Baghdad, including the Masuda Shemtov synagogue. At least four Jews were killed and others were injured. [cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] Who set the bombs is a genuinely unresolved question, and it is presented here as one. The Iraqi government of the time, and later some historians, attributed them to Zionist underground agents trying to panic the community into leaving faster. Israeli officials have consistently and firmly denied any involvement, calling the accusation an antisemitic fabrication meant to shift the blame for a persecution the Iraqi state had itself created through pogroms, denaturalization and criminalization. [cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] [cite:meforum_exodus] Iraq tried and executed men for the bombings: two, Basri and Shalom, were hanged in January 1952. The fairness of those trials, held amid intense anti-Zionist fervour, and the evidence on which they rested are themselves disputed. Independent historical work, drawing on newly released Israeli, British and American archives as reviewed by the Middle East Forum, finds insufficient evidence to confirm Israeli involvement, without fully closing the question. [cite:meforum_exodus]

The bombings were real, the deaths were real, and so were the prosecutions and executions. What the available record does not show is definitive proof of who was responsible. Both the Iraqi government's accusation and Israel's denial are documented positions, and the evidence does not decide between them. What is not in dispute is the legal sequence that preceded them: the 1948 law that made the community presumptively criminal, the hanging of Ades, and the 1950 law that turned emigration into the loss of citizenship and property.

Yemen. The Jews of Yemen had lived there for well over a thousand years, one of the oldest Jewish communities in the world. [cite:w_magic_carpet] Between June 1949 and September 1950, Operation Magic Carpet, also called "On Wings of Eagles", airlifted about 49,000 of them to Israel. It was organized with the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee and flown by Alaska Airlines and other carriers. Many reached the airlift only after walking for weeks to the British colony of Aden. [cite:w_magic_carpet] The counts differ here too. The Jewish Agency says that nearly all of Yemen's 45,000 Jews came, and the State Archives table gives 48,375 immigrants from Yemen and Aden together between 1948 and 1952. [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852] In Israel many of the newcomers were placed in transit camps, where hundreds of children were reported dead or vanished, the subject of [scene:mz_s02|the Yemenite Children Affair]. [cite:w_magic_carpet]

Morocco. Morocco's Jewish community was rooted over two millennia and numbered in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s, one of the largest in the Arab world. [cite:w_yachin] On 7 and 8 June 1948, three weeks after Israel's founding, riots against Jews broke out in Oujda and Jérada, killing 5 Jews in Oujda and 38 people in Jérada, with more than a hundred wounded. According to the record compiled by JewishGen, the riots are linked to young Jews crossing the border near Oujda on their way to France and Israel. [cite:rs_rd6_jewishgen_oujda] Most of the community emigrated after 1948, mostly to Israel. The largest single movement came later and lies outside this chapter: between 1961 and 1964 the secret Operation Yachin brought about 97,000 Moroccan Jews to Israel with the Moroccan government's quiet consent, and historians record that Israel, together with American Jewish organizations, made payments to that government to allow the departures. [cite:w_yachin] Israelis of Moroccan descent became one of Israel's largest communities, and a human link between the two countries long before Morocco and Israel opened liaison offices in 1994, after Oslo, and closed them in 2000 during the second intifada. [cite:w_yachin] [cite:w_isr_morocco]

Egypt. Egypt's Jewish population was about 75,000 in 1948. Between June and November of that year, bombs set off in the Jewish quarter of Cairo killed more than 70 Jews and wounded nearly 200, according to the historian Howard Sachar as cited by the Jewish Virtual Library. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_egypt] The State Archives table counts 17,114 immigrants from Egypt to Israel between 1948 and 1952, a much smaller share of the community than left Iraq or Yemen in those years. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852] Mendes notes that many Egyptian Jews appear to have left for economic reasons rather than because of specific persecution. [cite:rs_rd6_mendes_2010] The decisive rupture came after this chapter's period. After the Sinai campaign of 1956 the Egyptian government expelled almost 25,000 Jews and confiscated their property, and about 1,000 more were detained. A proclamation read in mosques on 23 November 1956 declared that "all Jews are Zionists and enemies of the state", according to contemporary reports by the Associated Press and the New York World-Telegram cited by the Jewish Virtual Library. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_egypt] That war is the subject of a later volume.

Libya. The sources here are thin on causes and give only numbers. The Jewish Agency records that 30,500 of Libya's 35,000 Jews came to Israel in the first years of the state; the State Archives table gives 32,129 immigrants from Libya between 1948 and 1952. [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852]

Why did they leave? Three answers have been given, and Mendes describes the first two as partisan narratives. One, which he associates with Zionist and Israeli accounts, attributes the exodus almost solely to Arab violence or the threat of it. The other, which he associates with Arab and anti-Zionist accounts, attributes it to Zionist activity and agitation, in its strongest form "a malicious Zionist conspiracy". [cite:rs_rd6_mendes_2010] Each has evidence it can point to. The first can cite the Iraqi law of July 1948, the hanging of Ades, the denaturalization and confiscation of 1950, the dead of Oujda, Jérada and the Cairo Jewish quarter, and the Egyptian expulsions and mosque proclamation of 1956. The second can cite the Iraqi government's accusation over the Baghdad bombings, which independent historians have not been able to confirm but have not fully closed either. Mendes's own conclusion is the third answer: the exodus is best explained as "a complex combination of push and pull factors", with harassment, discrimination and, in Iraq, expulsion on one side, and the pull of Zionism and of life in Israel on the other. [cite:rs_rd6_mendes_2010] The country-by-country record bears out the variation. In Iraq the state criminalized and then denaturalized a community; in Yemen people walked for weeks to reach an airlift; in Egypt, before 1956, many appear to have left for economic reasons.

The antisemitism in this record is named here because it is documented: a law that presumed every Jew a criminal, a public hanging staged as a warning, bombs in a Jewish quarter, a state proclamation that all Jews were enemies. These were the acts of named governments, courts and rioters in particular places and years. They do not describe Arabs or Muslims as peoples, and the same record shows Jewish communities that had lived among their neighbors for one, two and nearly three thousand years.

Several things remain unsettled. The bombers of Baghdad have not been identified beyond dispute. The totals differ from source to source, for Iraq (about 135,000 reduced to about 6,000; 121,512 of 130,000; 124,226), for Yemen (about 49,000; nearly all of 45,000; 48,375 with Aden) and for the region as a whole (800,000 to 900,000 across three decades including Iran; nearly one million in about a decade), and no one figure can be preferred on the evidence given here. How the newcomers were received in Israel is the subject of [scene:rd6_ingathering|the mass immigration of 1948–1952].

sections.h: The Ingathering: Mass Immigration, 1948–1952
sections.html:
Most of the Jews who left Iraq, Yemen and Libya came to Israel, and they arrived in a state already absorbing survivors from Europe. In its first three and a half years the new state took in more Jewish immigrants than its entire Jewish population at independence. According to the Jewish Agency, 203,000 Jews from 42 countries arrived in Israel's first year alone, and 684,201 immigrants arrived between May 1948 and the end of 1951, "more than the entire Jewish population when independence was declared". [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] This section sets out who came, in what order, how they were housed and fed, and when the flow slowed.

According to the Jewish Agency, the first to come were the former illegal immigrants whom the British had held in detention camps on Cyprus, and Holocaust survivors from the displaced-persons camps in Germany, Austria and Italy. Then whole communities followed. The Jewish Agency records 121,512 of Iraq's 130,000 Jews, more than 37,000 of Bulgaria's 45,000, 30,500 of Libya's 35,000, and nearly all of Yemen's 45,000. [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] Why the communities of the Arab world left when they did is told in [scene:rd6_exodus|the Jews of the Arab world after 1948].

A table drawn from the Israel State Archives gives a fuller count, through the end of 1952. It records 738,891 immigrants from 1948 to the end of that year. Of these, 377,251 came from Muslim countries and 307,082 from Communist states. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852] Of the countries it names, the largest were Iraq, with 124,226, and Romania, with 121,537, followed by Poland, with 106,751. From the Muslim countries the table lists Iraq; Yemen and Aden, 48,375; Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria together, 52,584; Turkey, 35,025; Syria and Lebanon, 34,608; Libya, 32,129; Iran, 25,593; and Egypt, 17,114. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852] The two blocs together account for 684,333 of the total; the remaining 54,558, by subtraction, came from elsewhere, and the figures given here do not break that remainder down.

The counts do not agree across sources, and the gaps are not trivial. For Iraq, the Jewish Agency's 121,512 sits beside the State Archives' 124,226, and Israeli government sources describe the community as reduced from about 135,000 to roughly 6,000 by 1952. For Yemen, the Jewish Agency's "nearly all of Yemen's 45,000" sits beside the archive figure of 48,375 for Yemen and Aden together, and the commonly cited count of about 49,000 flown out in Operation Magic Carpet. [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852] [cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:w_magic_carpet] Part of the difference is in the categories (Yemen alone, or Yemen with Aden; arrivals counted by year of immigration, or by community before and after), and part cannot be explained from the sources given here.

Housing could not keep pace. By May 1950, of the 393,197 people who had arrived since May 1948, 112,015 were still living in immigrant camps and temporary housing. [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] In 1950 the state introduced a second kind of settlement, the ma'abara, or transitional camp, where newcomers could work while they waited for permanent homes. The ma'abarot multiplied fast. By May 1952 there were 113 of them, housing 250,000 people. [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] Jews arriving from Arab and Muslim countries were often placed in these camps and, according to the Times of Israel, largely sidelined by the European-born leadership of the ruling Labor party. [cite:toi_yemenite_2021] The gravest charge to come out of the camps is the subject of [scene:mz_s02|the Yemenite Children Affair], which sets out what the families allege and what the inquiries found.

Feeding the population took a regime of its own. Under the austerity program known as tzena, food was rationed by coupon: oil, sugar, margarine and rice, with meat about once a week and fish about twice a month. Furniture and clothing were rationed too. [cite:rs_rd6_nli_tzena] The system bred its own resistance. A black market grew, and merchants went on strike in the summer of 1950. In the Knesset election of 1951, the General Zionists, who campaigned against rationing, won 20 seats. A New Economic Policy began to ease the controls in 1952, and rationing was officially abolished in 1959. [cite:rs_rd6_nli_tzena]

Then the flow fell away. Immigration peaked in 1951; in the three years from 1952 to 1954 only 51,463 immigrants arrived. [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] Who paid for the absorption and the state around it, through American aid, the sale of bonds and German reparations, is told in [scene:rd6_financing|how the new state was paid for].

The same numbers correct two easy assumptions. One is that the immigration of these years came mainly from Europe. Survivors from the displaced-persons camps came first, but by the end of 1952 more immigrants had come from Muslim countries, 377,251, than from the Communist states, 307,082. The other is that the newcomers were absorbed smoothly into a prepared country. In May 1952 a quarter of a million people were living in transitional camps, under a rationing regime that began to ease only in 1952 and was not abolished until 1959. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852] [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption] [cite:rs_rd6_nli_tzena]

What these sources do not settle is how the burdens of absorption were shared among the newcomers: who was sent to the ma'abarot and who to permanent housing, for how long, and on what criteria. The figures show the scale of the camps; they do not show who lived in them by origin. That question, and whether selection followed origin, is where the record of discrimination begins, and it is not answered by the numbers given here.

sections.h: The Yemenite Children Affair
sections.html:
Of the charges that came out of the immigrant camps, the gravest concerns infants. The founding generation of Israel is often remembered as having received every Jewish immigrant on equal terms. For many of the Jews who came from Arab and Muslim countries after 1948, the record is different, and its most painful chapter is the disappearance of children from the camps. The affair runs from the first years of the state to a cabinet decision of 2021, and its central question has still not been answered to the satisfaction of the families who raised it.

The setting was the transit camps, the ma'abarot described in [scene:rd6_ingathering|the mass immigration of 1948–1952]. Among those placed there were the Yemeni Jews flown in by Operation Magic Carpet between June 1949 and September 1950, about 49,000 people, many of whom had walked for weeks to reach the airlift at Aden; their journey is told in [scene:rd6_exodus|the Jews of the Arab world after 1948]. [cite:w_magic_carpet] In those camps hundreds of children were reported dead or vanished. [cite:w_magic_carpet]

The families' account is this. Between 1948 and 1954, they say, their infants were taken from the camps and from clinics and hospitals. Doctors told the parents that the children had died, but refused to give them the bodies or death certificates. [cite:arabnews_stolen_babies] Most of the families were Yemenite, but others came from the Balkans, North Africa and elsewhere. They allege that the babies were given to Ashkenazi families, in Israel and abroad. [cite:arabnews_stolen_babies] The children who disappeared are counted in the hundreds. [cite:arabnews_stolen_babies] [cite:w_magic_carpet]

The state's own answer came through inquiries. Three official inquiries, the first of them in 1967, concluded that most of the children had died of disease. [cite:arabnews_stolen_babies] That finding did not end the matter. The newspaper Israel Hayom later published documents that, it said, indicated the possible organized involvement of state bodies. [cite:israelhayom_yemenite] The sources cited here do not give the dates of the second and third inquiries or of the newspaper's publication.

In February 2021 the Israeli cabinet approved NIS 162 million, about $50 million, in compensation for the families. About 1,050 families were eligible. The government stated that it "regrets" the events and recognizes the suffering of the families. [cite:tps_yemenite_2021] [cite:toi_yemenite_2021] Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called the affair one of the most painful in the state's history and asked that it be taught in schools. [cite:toi_yemenite_2021] The decision expressed regret but did not accept responsibility. The family organizations said that it lacked the essential element: an official apology and an acceptance of responsibility by the state. [cite:toi_yemenite_2021]

The affair matters to the history of the founding years for a reason beyond its own facts. It can be read as evidence of discrimination among Jews inside the Jewish state. According to the Times of Israel, the immigrants from Arab and Muslim countries housed in the ma'abarot, which it describes as shantytowns, were largely sidelined by the European-born leadership of the ruling Labor party. [cite:toi_yemenite_2021] It is part of the record that many readers raised in Israel come to late.

What the record does not settle is the central question. The inquiries' finding, that most of the children died of disease, and the families' allegation, that children were taken and given away, are both on the record. The documents Israel Hayom published point toward possible state involvement without, on the evidence cited here, establishing its extent. The 2021 decision paid compensation and expressed regret without resolving which account is true, and without the admission of responsibility that the families asked for. How many children died, how many, if any, were given to other families, and who decided are questions this record leaves open.

sections.h: Who Belongs: The Law of Return and the Nationality Law
sections.html:
While the camps filled, the Knesset wrote down who had the right to come. Two statutes, passed two years apart, answered the question of who belonged to the new state. The Law of Return of 1950 said who had the right to come. The Nationality Law of 1952 said who became a national, and how. Read together, they set up two routes into citizenship, one for Jews from anywhere and one for the Arabs who had lived in Palestine and remained, and the conditions on the two routes were not the same. Both laws were short, and the clearest way to understand them is through their own texts.

The Law of Return opens with a single sentence. Section 1 states: "Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh", that is, as an immigrant who comes to settle. [cite:rs_rd6_mjl_lawofreturn] Section 2 makes the right operational. Every Jew who wishes to settle in Israel receives an oleh's visa, unless the minister finds that the applicant is acting against the Jewish people, or is likely to endanger public health or the security of the state. Section 4 closes the circle backward: Jews already in the country, and Jews born there, are deemed to have come as olim. [cite:rs_rd6_mjl_lawofreturn] The law was signed by Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion, by the Minister of Immigration, Moshe Shapira, and by Yosef Sprinzak as Acting President and Chairman of the Knesset. [cite:rs_rd6_mjl_lawofreturn] [cite:rs_rd6_adalah_lawofreturn]

Even its date is disputed in the sources. The law itself is dated 20 Tammuz 5710, which is 5 July 1950, and the Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East gives the same day; the Palestinian jurist Anis Kassim says the bills were submitted on 3 July and the law adopted on 5 July. [cite:rs_rd6_mjl_lawofreturn] [cite:rs_rd6_adalah_lawofreturn] [cite:rs_rd6_ej_lawofreturn] [cite:rs_rd6_kassim_aardi] The Encyclopaedia Judaica gives 3 July 1950, the anniversary of Herzl's death. [cite:rs_rd6_ej_lawofreturn] On this reading, the law's own dating is the firmer evidence for when it was enacted. Kassim's account, in which the bills were submitted on 3 July, would explain how the earlier date arose, but none of the sources says so directly, and the discrepancy stands.

Ben-Gurion's case for the law was stated in its own terms when he presented the bill. The right it recognized, he said, "is inherent in every Jew by virtue of his being a Jew", and "This right preceded the State of Israel". [cite:rs_rd6_ej_lawofreturn] On this reading the law granted nothing new. It declared a right that already existed. The Encyclopaedia Judaica places it in a line of documents running back half a century: the Basel Program of 1897, Article 6 of the Mandate of 1922, and the Declaration of Independence. [cite:rs_rd6_ej_lawofreturn] The law was passed in the middle of the mass immigration, in which 684,201 people arrived between May 1948 and the end of 1951, described in [scene:rd6_ingathering|the mass immigration of 1948–1952]. [cite:rs_rd6_ja_absorption]

The exclusions were widened once in the period. An amendment of 23 August 1954 added a further ground for refusal: a person "with a criminal past, likely to endanger public welfare". [cite:rs_rd6_adalah_lawofreturn] A definition of who was a Jew entered the law only twenty years later, when an amendment in 1970 extended the law's rights to a Jew's child and grandchild and to their spouses, and defined a Jew as one "born of a Jewish mother or has become converted to Judaism and who is not a member of another religion". [cite:rs_rd6_adalah_lawofreturn] That amendment, and the long dispute over "who is a Jew" that produced it, belong to a later volume.

The Nationality Law took effect on 14 July 1952 and turned the right to come into the status of a national. It provided two main routes. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_nationality] The first was nationality "by return": every oleh under the Law of Return became an Israeli national by that fact alone. The second was nationality "by residence", for former Palestinian citizens. They could become nationals only if they met three conditions together: that they had been registered as inhabitants on 1 March 1952; that they were inhabitants on the day the law took effect; and that they had been in Israel continuously from the establishment of the state, or had entered it legally in the meantime. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_nationality] The same law repealed the Palestinian Citizenship Orders retroactively to the day the state was established. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_nationality]

The mechanism matters because of what had happened in 1948. A Jew came into nationality by coming; the only bars were the minister's grounds for refusal. A former Palestinian citizen came into it only by passing a test of registration and continuous presence. Anyone who was not on the register of 1 March 1952, or who had been outside the state after its establishment without entering legally, failed the test. And because the Mandate's citizenship had been repealed retroactively, those who failed it were left, in Kassim's argument, without a nationality at all. How the Arabs who remained were governed in the same years is told in [scene:rd6_military_government|the military government].

The case against the law is made here by Kassim. In his reading, the Law of Return amounts to "legally-authorized racial discrimination": it grants Jews from anywhere what it denies to Palestinians who lived on the land, so that "an indigenous Palestinian has no such inherent right even if he used to live on the land". He argues that the Palestinians who stayed were left stateless for about thirty years. [cite:rs_rd6_kassim_aardi] The two positions face each other directly. To Ben-Gurion and the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the law was one of return, recognizing a right older than the state. To Kassim it was one of discrimination, granting to Jews from anywhere what it denied to Palestinians who had lived there. [cite:rs_rd6_ej_lawofreturn] [cite:rs_rd6_kassim_aardi] The word "return" itself carries the dispute, because the same word stands at the center of the United Nations' resolution on the Palestinian refugees, read in [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194 and the refugee count].

The debate was not only between Jews and Palestinians. Within Jewish life the law drew argument from several directions. According to the Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East, some Orthodox leaders wanted the definition of "Jew" narrowed; the Reform and Conservative movements opposed that; and some non-Zionists called for the law's repeal as discriminatory. [cite:rs_rd6_ej_lawofreturn] Those arguments, about the boundaries of the people the law was written for, ran alongside the argument about the people it left out.

Several things the record here does not settle. It does not give the number of Arab inhabitants who met the residence test in 1952, or the number who failed it. Kassim's figure of about thirty years of statelessness is his own, and the sources cited here do not show how many people it describes or how their status was later resolved. And the date on which the Knesset passed the Law of Return, 3 or 5 July 1950, remains in conflict between the law's own text and the Encyclopaedia Judaica.

sections.h: From AZEC to AIPAC: The American Organization After Statehood
sections.html:
The stage now turns from the new state to its accounts, beginning in Washington, where the movement's wartime organization outlived the founding. A common account holds that the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, AIPAC, appeared suddenly in the 1950s as a new and independent lobbying group with no institutional past. The record shows something less abrupt and more interesting. The wartime body that had organized American Zionist political work did not dissolve when Israel was founded. It changed its name, spun off a separate lobbying committee, came under a federal foreign-agent order, and saw its lobbying work reorganized. Each of those steps is dated, and each concerned a specific organization. Keeping them apart is the only way to read the story accurately, because the most serious episode in it, the Justice Department's foreign-agent order of 1962, was aimed at one successor body at one time, not at the whole line of descent.

The starting point is the American Zionist Emergency Council, AZEC, which Abba Hillel Silver had built in 1943. In 1949, a year after statehood, it was renamed the American Zionist Council, the AZC, and registered as a tax-exempt nonprofit. [cite:azec_powerbase] This was a continuation, not a new founding: the same body under a new name and a new tax status. What the record cited here does not give is a full account of who led the Council after the change or how its internal structure shifted; it documents the continuity itself, not every change that came with it.

Where the Council's money came from is the question behind the next step. In 1953–54 Isaiah "Si" Kenen founded a new body, the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs, AZCPA. It was a separate entity, not tax-exempt, and not the same organization as the American Zionist Council, which had existed since 1949 under different leadership. [cite:cjh_kenen_papers] [cite:wiki_american_zionist_council] According to these sources, Kenen created it because word had spread in Washington that the Eisenhower administration suspected Israel of funding the AZC and might force the Council to register as a foreign agent. [cite:cjh_kenen_papers] [cite:wiki_american_zionist_council] Kenen had earlier worked in Israel's own foreign ministry and brought that experience of government relations to the new committee. [cite:cjh_kenen_papers] [cite:britannica_aipac] In 1959 the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs was renamed the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. [cite:britannica_aipac] The fear that prompted its creation, a foreign-agent finding against the Council, was the same fear that came true against the Council itself nine years later.

The same years saw the first such order against an individual in this network. In 1952 the hosiery manufacturer and Truman donor Abraham Feinberg was ordered to register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act for publishing a bimonthly, Israel Speaks; he closed the publication rather than comply. That case is told with Feinberg's career in [scene:s07f2|the section on Abraham Feinberg]. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file]

The order against the Council came on 21 November 1962. The Internal Security Section of the Justice Department, under Attorney General Robert Kennedy, ordered the American Zionist Council to register as an agent of a foreign principal under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. The department alleged that the Council had received more than $5 million from the Jewish Agency over the preceding eight years. [cite:azc_fara_doj] The mechanism was the one Kenen had feared: the department's position was that money flowing from the Jewish Agency made the Council an agent of that foreign principal.

Two points of precision matter here. First, the order was directed at the 1949 successor, the American Zionist Council, seventeen years after AZEC's founding in 1943. It is not a finding about AZEC's activities from 1943 to 1949 under its original name, and it should not be read back across the whole lineage as one continuous violation. [cite:azc_fara_doj] Second, it was an allegation contained in an order, not a court judgment. The eight years it covered ran back to roughly the time Kenen had set up his separate committee, which is consistent with the account of why he did so, though the sources do not draw that connection themselves.

The Justice Department later withdrew its demand that the Council register. In 1963 the Council's lobbying functions were separated from it and placed in a restructured American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which operated solely on private American donations and on that basis asserted that it was not a foreign agent. [cite:aipac_wiki] The restructuring was deliberate and had a stated purpose: a funding structure that could support a claim of non-foreign-agency status from then on. [cite:aipac_wiki]

The sources describe AIPAC's beginning in two ways, and the difference is worth stating rather than smoothing over. One account dates AIPAC's emergence to 1963, when the Council's lobbying functions were spun off into it after the foreign-agent order. [cite:aipac_wiki] The other dates its founding to 1953–54, when Kenen created the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs, and its present name to 1959. [cite:cjh_kenen_papers] [cite:britannica_aipac] Read closely, the two accounts refer to different things. The earlier date marks the creation of a distinct committee and the later name change; the 1963 date marks the moment the American Zionist Council's own lobbying work was moved into that committee and the committee was restructured to rest on American donations alone. Both are true of their own subject. What neither account in the material supplies is a full picture of how the Council and Kenen's committee related to each other between 1954 and 1963: who directed which lobbying, and how money moved between them, if it did.

Either way, the claim that AIPAC had no earlier institutional history does not survive the record. Its lineage runs through Kenen's 1953–54 committee and, from 1963, through the lobbying work of the Council that descended from the wartime AZEC. The 1953 founding date also coincides with the Anglo-American coup in Iran; the two are paired in [scene:s11|another chapter], which states plainly that no operational link between them is documented.

The gaps should be stated as plainly as the findings. The material does not say why the Justice Department withdrew its 1962 demand, or exactly when. It does not establish whether the $5 million allegation was ever tested, and it does not assess whether the 1963 restructuring fully answered the questions the order had raised; it documents what changed and the reason given for the change, not a legal judgment of its adequacy. Nor does it trace AZEC's place in the wider American network beyond these institutional steps; that network, including the 1962 finding as it concerned the Council rather than AZEC, is mapped in [scene:nw_s02|the network of the American build-up].

sections.h: Paying for the New State, 1949–1953
sections.html:
While the American organization was reorganizing itself, the state it supported had bills to pay. The state that emerged from the war of 1948 had to house and feed a mass immigration, a story told in [scene:rd6_ingathering|the mass immigration of 1948–1952]. The money for that effort came from three outside channels that opened in quick succession: loans and grants from the United States government, bonds sold to buyers abroad, and reparations from West Germany. Each worked differently, each was paid for by different people, and one of them divided Israel's own public. A common assumption is that American military support flowed to Israel from the beginning. The documents of the period show something else: American help in these years was economic, modest and uneven, and the largest single agreement of the early 1950s was made with West Germany.

The first channel was the American government. After Truman's re-election an Export-Import Bank loan of $100 million was earmarked for Israel, a decision placed in its political sequence in [scene:tr_s02|Truman's decisions after the election]. The Congressional Research Service's table of US aid to Israel, compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, records the year-by-year sums in millions of dollars: 100.0 in 1949, from the Export-Import Bank and other sources; nothing in 1950; 35.1 in 1951; 86.4 in 1952; 73.6 in 1953; 74.7 in 1954; 52.7 in 1955; 50.8 in 1956; 40.9 in 1957; 85.4 in 1958; and 53.3 in 1959, the last including a first military loan of 0.4. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] Added together, the table's eleven years come to $652.9 million, an average of under $60 million a year, with the largest single figure in the first year.

The character of that aid mattered as much as its size. From Israel's founding through the early 1960s, US assistance was economic aid and loans only. According to one study of the aid relationship, Washington avoided direct arms sales because it did not want to alienate the Arab oil-producing states. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990]

Among the American-dollar flows in the record from 1921 to 1949, the $100 million loan of 1949 is the largest single sum, double the $50 million of Golda Meyerson's 1948 American tour and a thousand times the $100,000 that Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann provided for Truman's whistle-stop campaign, as the chart in the section on Truman shows. The largest flow was not the most politically disputed: it was a government credit, open to view and recorded in the official tables.

When American military aid began is a point on which the sources differ, and both versions should be stated. The CRS table shows a military loan of $0.4 million in 1959. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] The study of the aid relationship cited above dates the first US military aid, itself in the form of loans rather than grants, to 1962. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] The sources do not explain the difference; a reader can say only that a very small military loan appears in the official table three years before the date that study gives for the start of military aid.

The later shape of the relationship belongs to later chapters and can be summarized in a few dates. Congress first designated a dedicated earmark for Israel in 1971. [cite:everycrsreport_israel_foreign_assistance] The 1973 war was the turning point: President Nixon ordered an emergency military airlift and requested $2.2 billion in emergency aid, a rise of roughly 800 percent over prior annual levels. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] [cite:legalclarity_when_did_us_start_funding] Economic aid became all grants in 1981, and military aid in 1985, the year of a separate $1.5 billion supplemental economic package, the largest aid package for a single country since the Vietnam War era. [cite:legalclarity_when_did_us_start_funding] [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] The often-quoted cumulative total of $300 billion is the Council on Foreign Relations' inflation-adjusted estimate; the Congressional Research Service, in its most recent tally, using the same appropriations data without adjusting for inflation, places cumulative bilateral assistance and missile defense funding at about $174 billion. [cite:cfr_aid_four_charts] [cite:legalclarity_how_much_money_given] Those totals were built almost entirely after the period of this chapter, as told in [scene:iaa_s01|how the aid relationship grew].

The second channel was private, but organized by the state. According to the Jewish Virtual Library's history of the program, David Ben-Gurion conceived an overseas bond issue in 1950, amid economic crisis and mass immigration. In September 1950 he convened American Jewish leaders at the King David Hotel in Jerusalem, and sales were launched in the United States the following spring with a rally at Madison Square Garden. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_bonds] The 1951 Independence Issue paid 3.5 percent, and first-year sales topped $52 million. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_bonds] Within six years, the same source reports, bond sales accounted for 35% of Israel's special development budget, financing the National Water Carrier, the Dead Sea Works, power plants, ports and immigrant towns. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_bonds]

The mechanism differed from the charitable campaigns of the pre-state years. The 1951 issue paid its buyers interest rather than asking for a gift, it was sold in the United States, and its proceeds went to the state's special development budget and the projects named above. The record cited here does not give the month of the first sales, saying only that they began the following spring.

The third channel was the most contested. On 12 March 1951 Moshe Sharett presented a claim of $1.5 billion against Germany. It was calculated as the cost of absorbing 500,000 victims of the Nazis at $3,000 each. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations] The method framed the claim as compensation for a concrete burden on the new state: the cost of resettling survivors. On 9 January 1952 the Knesset voted 61–50 to negotiate directly with West Germany, while thousands demonstrated outside and police used tear gas. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations]

The opposition was led by Menachem Begin, who spoke at mass demonstrations in the spring of 1952. Opponents called the payments "blood money" from the "land of the murderers." [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] The dispute was not between Israel and its adversaries but within Israel. The case for the agreement, in the government's own terms, was that the new state was bearing the cost of absorbing hundreds of thousands of the Nazis' victims and that Germany should meet it. The case against, in the opponents' own words, was that money from the "land of the murderers" was "blood money" and should not be taken. The narrow vote, 61 to 50, shows how evenly the Knesset was divided.

The agreement was signed in Luxembourg on 10 September 1952 by Sharett, Nahum Goldmann and Konrad Adenauer, and took effect on 21 March 1953. [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations] Payments ran in annual instalments from 1 April 1953 to 31 March 1966. They came not as cash transfers but in kind: 30% for crude oil bought in Britain and 70% for German goods. Over the decade they made up 12–14% of Israel's annual imports. [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations]

How much the agreement was worth is itself disputed between the two sources. The Jewish Virtual Library, citing Israeli Foreign Ministry documents of 1953 and the Encyclopaedia Judaica, gives a total of $845 million, of which $100 million went to the Claims Conference, paid over 14 years from 1953 to 1966. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations] The National Library of Israel gives goods and services valued at 3.5 billion marks over 12 years, plus 450 million marks more. [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] The two figures are expressed in different currencies and over periods described differently; the sources do not reconcile them, and this book does not either.

Taken together, the three channels answer the question of who paid for the new state in its first years only in part. The American government lent and granted modest sums, without arms, for reasons tied to its relations with Arab oil producers. Private buyers abroad lent money through bonds that built the state's water, power and ports. West Germany paid in oil and goods, over the objections of a large part of Israel's own public. What the record cited here does not settle is the whole: it gives no single account of the state's budget in these years, no measure of how much of the cost of absorption fell on Israel's own taxpayers and on the immigrants themselves, and no agreed figure for the largest of the three transfers. The month the first bonds were sold, and the reason the two sources date the first American military loan three years apart, also remain open.

sections.h: How the Flight Was Explained, 1948–1988
sections.html:
Money was one account the founding left to be settled; the explanation of the refugees' flight was another. Once the war ended, the question of why so many Palestinian Arabs had left their homes became a political argument as much as a historical one, because the answer seemed to settle who was responsible for the refugees. For more than a decade the account that prevailed in the West was that they had left voluntarily, on the orders of Arab leaders, and that this had been established at the time. The record shows a slower and more complicated history: some of the war's events were reported within days, the explanation for the mass flight that took hold was not the one the documents supported, and the correction came in stages, the last and weightiest of them from Israel's own archives forty years later.

Parts of what happened were known almost at once. The killings at Deir Yassin in April 1948 were reported in Western newspapers within days, and they were documented by the delegate of the Red Cross who entered the village. [cite:w_morris_birth] News of the massacre spread through Arab Palestine. The Israeli historian Benny Morris, writing four decades later, records it as a major accelerant of flight. [cite:w_morris_birth] The Red Cross's place in that moment, before any international human-rights treaty existed, is part of [scene:ud_s01|the week of December 1948].

Objection in the West was public, and some of it came from prominent Jews. On 4 December 1948 a group that included Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and Sidney Hook published a letter in The New York Times warning against Menachem Begin's new Herut party. The letter described Deir Yassin and called the party fascist in its methods. [cite:w_arendt_letter] It is a documented Jewish objection, made at the time and printed in America's paper of record. It also shows that the facts of Deir Yassin were not hidden in 1948; what remained in contest was the larger question of why the flight as a whole had happened.

On that larger question an explanation took hold that ran the other way. Arab leaders, it held, had broadcast orders by radio telling civilians to leave. In the 1950s this became the standard explanation in Western and Israeli official accounts. Its political effect was clear: it placed responsibility for the refugee problem on the Arab states. The strongest form of the account rested on a real point that later research would confirm in part, that some evacuations were ordered by Arab commanders. Its weakness was that the general claim, a broadcast order to an entire population, was a claim about a record that existed and could be checked.

The broadcasts had been monitored. In 1959 the Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi argued from Arab sources that no such general order had been given. [cite:w_childers] In May 1961 the Irish writer Erskine Childers published "The Other Exodus" in The Spectator. He reported that he had examined the British and American monitoring records of Arab broadcasts in 1948, described in another summary as the BBC's and American records, and had found no evacuation orders; what he found were appeals to stay. [cite:w_childers] The article set off a long published dispute, with claims and counterclaims running for weeks in the magazine's letters pages. [cite:w_childers] Childers's test was of one kind of evidence, the broadcasts; it could not by itself show what had driven people from particular towns and villages.

That evidence lay in Israeli military and state files. In 1988 Benny Morris published The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem, drawn from those newly opened archives. He concluded that the main causes of flight were military attack, expulsion and fear. In some places local Arab commanders had ordered the evacuation of women and children, but there was no general Arab order to leave. [cite:w_morris_birth] Later editions of the book found more expulsion orders. [cite:w_morris_birth]

The three tests did not cover the same ground, and the order in which they came matters. Khalidi and Childers answered the specific claim about broadcasts. Morris answered the larger question of causes, and he did so from the files of the Israeli state. The documents that corrected the early account were therefore not an adversary's claims but Israel's own.

Where this leaves each side's case can be stated fairly. The account that the refugees left on orders is no longer defended by mainstream scholarship in its general form. [cite:w_morris_birth] What survives of it is real but limited: Morris's own research found local evacuation orders by Arab commanders in some places, and he named fear, alongside attack and expulsion, among the main causes. The account that people were driven out by attack and expulsion is supported by what Morris found in the Israeli archives, and later editions of Morris's work added to the record of expulsion orders. [cite:w_morris_birth]

What the record does not settle is intent. Historians still disagree about intent and planning, an argument that turns on the military plan discussed in [scene:pd_s01|Plan Dalet]. The material here establishes the causes of flight that the archives show; it does not resolve the question of design. It also does not explain, beyond the sequence of dates, why the early account held for so long. What it does show is the length of the gap: the explanation that took hold in the 1950s was checked against the broadcasts only in 1959 and 1961, and against Israel's own archives only in 1988.

sections.h: How the Case Was Made to Americans: Refuge, Bible and Democracy
sections.html:
The flight was explained to Western readers; so, from the start, was the case for the state itself. A familiar explanation for American support of Israel runs backward from the present. Because the two countries later became close strategic partners, it is assumed that Americans backed the new state in 1948 for the same reason: that Israel was already a proven ally whose value to Washington was plain. The record of 1948 does not bear this out. The case put to the American public in the founding years rested on three different arguments, none of them strategic, and the men responsible for American strategy in that period made the opposite case in writing.

The first and central argument of 1945–48 was refuge. In Europe after the war some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons were still waiting in camps, and the destruction of European Jewry in the Holocaust was recent. The argument was humanitarian before it was political: the survivors needed somewhere to go. America's own door was part of the same argument: Truman signed the Displaced Persons Act of June 1948 while condemning it as discriminatory against Jewish displaced persons, a story told in [scene:tr_s02|Truman's decisions after recognition]. [cite:truman_institute_dpact]

The second argument was religious. Christian restorationist belief, the conviction that the Jews would be restored to the land of the Bible, had a history going back to 1839. For Christian supporters the new state could be read as a biblical fulfillment. The third argument was political in the plainest sense: the new state was presented to Americans as a democracy.

Against all three stood the American national-security establishment. The State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of Defense and the Central Intelligence Agency each warned that American backing for a Jewish state would harm American interests. The warnings were consistent and on paper. Declassified CIA documents from 1948 predicted that recognition would produce armed conflict and damage American access to oil. Far from calling the future state a strategic asset, the government's own strategists treated it as a strategic liability. Truman overruled them. He recognized Israel eleven minutes after its declaration of independence on 14 May 1948, so quickly that his own State Department was caught unaware. The White House aides who argued the domestic political case, Clark Clifford and David Niles among them, and the personal channel that reached him through his friend Eddie Jacobson, carried the day. [cite:wiki_david_niles]

Whatever moved American policy in 1948, it was not a consensus inside the government that Israel served American strategy. The government's strategic voices said the reverse and lost.

The publicity of the period also had a hostile side, aimed at the Arab opponents of partition. Here the record requires care in both directions. Pro-Zionist publicity drew heavily on the wartime collaboration of the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem with Hitler. That collaboration was real and is documented; it was not invented for propaganda. What the publicity did with it was another matter. A single leader's alliance with the Axis was used as a broad brush to color Arab opposition as a whole, which the documented episode does not support. The episode should be stated plainly, as fact, and the generalization drawn from it should be named for what it was.

It is tempting to read later developments back into this period, and two of them in particular. The first is the organized anti-Islam network in the United States. The organized, well-funded anti-Islam network is documented mainly from the 2000s, building on currents that formed after 1967 and after 1979. [cite:cap_fear_inc] It was not part of the 1948 argument. The anti-Arab framing of 1948 leaned on a specific wartime episode, not on an industry.

The second is the argument most often assumed to have been there from the beginning. The claim that Israel was a strategic asset to the United States grew after Israel's victory in 1967, a generation after the founding, and was formalized under President Reagan, who called Israel a strategic asset and signed a strategic-cooperation agreement with it in 1981. Until then American aid was cautious: from 1948 into the early 1960s it consisted of economic aid and loans, with Washington avoiding direct arms sales for fear of alienating Arab oil-producing states, a pattern taken up in [scene:rd6_financing|how the new state was paid for]. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990]

Set side by side, the sequence corrects the familiar account. In 1948 Americans were asked to support Israel as a refuge for survivors, as the fulfillment of a promise that some Christians read in scripture, and as a new democracy. The strategic argument was then being made by the other side of the debate, inside the American government, and it pointed against support. The alliance framing came later and was built on later events.

What the record does not settle is how much each argument weighed with the public at the time. The documents establish which arguments were made and which officials opposed the policy; they do not measure how many Americans were moved by the survivors, how many by scripture and how many by the language of democracy, or how far the hostile portrait of Arab opposition shaped opinion. No survey or source in this chapter's research answers that, and this book does not guess at it. Nor does the record here trace the precise path by which the 1967 argument became the 1981 doctrine; that belongs to a later volume.

sections.h: Did Money Buy the Politicians? What the Record Can Show, and Where It Goes Dark
sections.html:
Behind the arguments put to the public lies a harder question: what money did to American policy on Palestine before and during 1948. It is usually answered in one of two ways. In one version, Zionist money bought Congress and the White House. In the other, money played no role at all. Both answers share a flaw: they treat a bundle of separate claims as a single claim, and so they deliver one verdict where the evidence supports several different ones. Pulled apart, the question becomes four claims. They stand on very different footing, and one of them cannot be settled in either direction with the records that exist.

The first claim is that there was organized political pressure. This is documented in detail, much of it in the movement's own files. The American Zionist Emergency Council, the movement's national lobbying body in the 1940s, built local committees across the country and ran letter and telegram campaigns aimed at members of Congress. It compiled legislators' statements of support into a book, America and Palestine, and used it to press for more. The same files document the campaign around both parties' 1944 platforms and the Wagner–Taft resolution in Congress. [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] Nothing about this was hidden. It was lobbying, organized openly and on a national scale, and the way it worked is traced tie by tie in [scene:nw_s02|the network of the American build-up].

The second claim is that money changed a specific decision. This is documented once. The historian John Judis records that in mid-1948 Truman wanted Israel to stop taking territory beyond the United Nations partition lines and was disturbed by its refugee policy, but backed away from pressing either objection, in part because his nearly broke campaign needed $100,000 from Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann for a whistle-stop tour. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] That account, and the man behind it, are set out in [scene:s07f2|the section on Abraham Feinberg]. It is one historian's account of one decision. It is specific, dated and sourced, and it is also the only instance of its kind in the record.

Among the dollar flows the record documents between 1921 and 1949, the Feinberg–Kaufmann money is the smallest, about a tenth of a million dollars beside a $100 million Export-Import Bank loan of 1949 and tens of millions raised for arms. [cite:jvl_truman_marshall_dejure] [cite:israelaffairs_italy] Yet it is the only sum tied in the historical literature to a particular policy decision. The size of a payment and its documented effect are different measures, and here they point in opposite directions.

The third claim is that members of Congress were paid, systematically, before 1948. This cannot be established either way, and the reason is legal rather than historical. Until the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971, the governing law was the Federal Corrupt Practices Act of 1925. It required disclosure mainly from party committees operating in more than one state rather than from candidates. It carried few penalties. It left enforcement to Congress itself, and it was rarely enforced. It was riddled with loopholes, and the donors to individual candidates were largely undisclosed until 1971. [cite:wiki_fcpa_1925] [cite:sage_fec_history] [cite:crs_campaign_finance] The records that would answer the question were never required to exist. In the absence of disclosure, any claim that particular legislators were paid is unsupported. So is any claim that they were not. Silence of this kind is not evidence of innocence and not evidence of guilt; it is a gap produced by the law of the time, and it should be reported as a gap.

The fourth claim is the one most often left out by those who argue that money explains the outcome: other documented forces pushed in the same direction without money. The moral urgency of the Holocaust years was real and widely felt. Jewish voters were concentrated in electorally important states such as New York. Christian restorationist conviction, the belief that the Jews would be restored to their ancient land, was sincere and had a history going back to 1839. Henry Wallace held Zionist views of his own. And the 1922 Lodge–Fish resolution, by which Congress endorsed the Balfour Declaration, is credited to lobbying with no payment documented. Each of these points the same way as the money, and none of them needs it.

The opposing record belongs in the same account. The State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense opposed the policy in writing, and they were overruled. The documented forces that beat them were political: organization, votes, conviction and access. A financial force is documented only in the single case above.

Set out this way, the two familiar answers both fail. "Money bought Congress and the White House" stretches one documented episode, involving one decision and one campaign, into a general claim about legislators for whom no payment record exists. "Money played no role at all" contradicts the one case that is documented. The defensible position sits between them and is narrower than either: an organized, well-funded political movement with direct access to decision-makers, plus one documented case in which money shifted a decision.

The note above, from the dashboard that follows the money of these years, states the same limit in its own terms. The record documents private, organized finance and one specific episode of money bearing on policy in 1948. It does not show that any government secretly funded the movement, and it does not show that money decided every outcome. The money itself, how much there was and where it went, is the subject of [scene:gf_s01|the next section].

What remains open is exactly what the law of the time left open. Whether any member of Congress received money in connection with a vote on Palestine before 1948 cannot be known from the records that exist, and this book does not supply an answer the documents cannot. Nor does the Judis account, by itself, measure how much weight the campaign's need carried against the other pressures on Truman in the summer of 1948; it records the need as one reason among others, and that is how it is reported here.

sections.h: Who Paid for It All? The Ledger, 1899–1949
sections.html:
Two explanations of how the pre-state movement was financed have long circulated, and they point in opposite directions. One holds that it ran on a handful of wealthy patrons, the Rothschilds or a few Jewish bankers. The other holds that it ran on secret government money. The documented record supports neither. What it shows is organized private giving on a mass scale, conducted openly through permanent institutions, raised from donors in many countries and, by the 1940s, overwhelmingly from the United States. It was not cheap, and it was not secret. The slogan version of the patron myth is taken apart, alongside the founding slogans, in [scene:pn_s01|the closing account of the founding narratives]; this section sets out the ledger itself.

The panel above carries the headline sums, each shown as it was then and in today's dollars. The largest single figure is the United Jewish Appeal's campaign of 1948: $150 million, about $2.0 billion today, raised from more than a million contributors in 4,950 American communities. [cite:jta_uja_1948] [cite:bls_cpi] At the time it was described as the largest non-government humanitarian campaign in American history. [cite:cambridge_solidarity] Behind it lay the wartime appeals of 1939–45, more than $124 million, and before those the worldwide giving of the 1920s. [cite:raphael_uja] The panel also lists the transfer of German Jewish capital in the 1930s, whose terms and sums are told in their own place earlier in this volume.

The story begins with a permanent fund. Keren Hayesod, created as the Zionist movement's standing fundraising arm, raised $20.1 million worldwide between April 1921 and December 1929, roughly $370 million in today's money. More than half of it, $11.0 million, came from the United States. The rest came in descending order from South Africa ($1.5 million), Germany ($0.98 million), Romania ($0.88 million), Britain ($0.88 million), Poland ($0.82 million) and Canada ($0.74 million). [cite:jta_kh_decade] Measured over the fund's first twelve years in sterling, the United States gave about half of the £4.82 million raised. [cite:jta_kh_12yr] Before 1948 the fund's mandate covered immigration, settlement, defense, water development and public works. [cite:jvl_kh]

The country breakdown shows how early the balance had shifted. In the 1920s the American share was already larger than every other country's combined. The gap only widened. In the late 1930s American Jewish organizations set up their own joint campaign, the United Jewish Appeal, formed in 1939. It raised more than $124 million during the war years of 1939–45 and $100 million in 1946. [cite:raphael_uja] In 1947 it raised about $110 million. [cite:cambridge_solidarity] In 1948 it reached the record $150 million. [cite:jta_uja_1948] Over those last three years alone, 1946 to 1948, the campaigns raised some $360 million, about $5.2 billion in today's dollars. A single American year in 1948 brought in more than seven times what the entire world had given Keren Hayesod in its first decade.

The scale makes one distinction essential, and it is the one most often lost. The United Jewish Appeal did not raise money for Palestine alone. It split its proceeds three ways. Of the $150 million raised in 1948, $74.7 million went to the United Palestine Appeal, the Palestine and Israel arm; $64.9 million went to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe; and $10.4 million went to the United Service for New Americans, which resettled refugees in the United States. [cite:jta_uja_1948] Roughly half of the dollar went to Palestine, some 43 percent to Europe and about 7 percent to resettlement at home.

Much of the 1948 total fed and housed Holocaust survivors in Europe. Counting all of it as "funding Israel" would roughly double the true Palestine figure. The Palestine share alone, $74.7 million, comes to about $1.0 billion in today's dollars. [cite:bls_cpi] That share paid for what Keren Hayesod's own history lists as its prewar purposes: immigration and absorption, settlement, defense, water and public works. [cite:jvl_kh]

The chain of giving can be followed from donor to purpose. Contributors gave through local federations; the federations passed their campaign totals to the national appeal; the appeal divided them among its three beneficiary agencies; and each agency spent on its own mandate.

War money is harder to count. Arms for the 1948 war were bought through front companies, and the record yields ranges rather than a total. Estimates of what was paid for Czechoslovak arms run from about $14.5 million to roughly six times that figure. Golda Meyerson's American fundraising tour in early 1948 raised about $50 million, which went largely to weapons. The government of Somoza's Nicaragua extended $3 million in letters of credit for arms buying. [cite:israelaffairs_italy]

The arms table shows why no single number can be given. Its Czechoslovak line spans a six-fold range, and Golda Meyerson's money flowed in part through the same community federations as the United Jewish Appeal, so that adding her $50 million to the appeal's $150 million would count some dollars twice. For that reason the ledger keeps every stream separate and never adds them into one sum.

Every "today's dollars" figure in this section follows one method, the method of the United States government's own inflation calculator: the amount is multiplied by the ratio of the consumer price index for 2025, which stands at 321.943, to the index for the year in question. Sums in pounds are first converted to dollars at the exchange rate of the period, and values from before 1913 are approximate. [cite:bls_cpi] The conversions are a guide to scale, not a claim that a 1948 dollar bought exactly what its modern equivalent buys.

The answer to the question this section asks is therefore plain in outline and incomplete in detail. The money came overwhelmingly from organized private giving: decades of worldwide contributions through a permanent fund, then American federated campaigns on a scale without precedent, joined in 1948 by arms purchases financed partly by the same donors and, in one documented case, by a foreign government's credit. What the record does not provide is a grand total. No audited sum for the whole pre-state operation has been published, the arms figures are ranges, and several streams overlap. The honest ledger is a set of documented streams side by side, not a single figure, and that is how it is given here. What the money for the army looked like inside these budgets, and what Britain spent on the other side of the ledger, is the subject of [scene:gf_s02|the operating budgets and Britain's bill].

sections.h: Charity for an Army: The Operating Budgets and Britain's Bill
sections.html:
Two assumptions often sit beneath accounts of the Mandate's last decades. The first is that the Jewish community's underground army was paid for secretly, by means no one can now trace. The second is that Britain held Palestine cheaply. Neither survives the documents. The defense money moved through budgets, a community levy and, by 1948, an openly advertised charity channel, all of which left a paper trail. Britain's own accounts, meanwhile, record a bill that by the end ran to about £100 million in three years. What the record does not contain is a single audited total for the army itself, and that gap is stated at the end of this section.

The clearest early view of the operating budget comes from an American diplomat. After the Zionist Congress of 1939, the United States consul in Jerusalem reported that the Jewish Agency's budget had been set at £720,000, about $74 million in today's money. Of that, £100,000 was earmarked for refugee settlement and £80,000 for what the budget itself called "the Jewish security service (defense)." [cite:frus_1939_ja_budget] The line is small, about one-ninth of the whole, but it is explicit: defense sat inside the Agency's budget, under its own heading, nine years before the state.

The budgets grew quickly during and after the Second World War. In 1944 the Jewish National Fund spent $10.8 million and the Jewish Agency and Keren Hayesod together $14.9 million of money raised in the United States, some $25.7 million in all. The United Palestine Appeal's budget for 1945 was $35.3 million. [cite:djn_1945_upa] In 1946 the Agency reported that it had received $12 million from the United States the previous year and asked for a budget of $56 million, about $0.93 billion in today's dollars. [cite:djn_1946_budget] In seven years the ask had moved from hundreds of thousands of pounds to tens of millions of dollars.

The table above sets these budgets beside Britain's spending, each in the money of its year and in today's dollars. It also shows the private capital that immigrants themselves brought into the country, which was mostly not donated money and belongs to a different account from the campaigns; the rows are placed side by side for scale and are not meant to be added together.

Inside Palestine, the community taxed itself for defense. In 1938 the Jewish National Council created Kofer HaYishuv, a levy on cigarettes, restaurant bills and luxuries, to fund central security and expand the Haganah. [cite:w_kofer] It was run by the community's own council, not by the Mandate government, and it gave the Haganah a revenue stream raised inside the country alongside the money that came from abroad.

By 1948, on this evidence, charity abroad and defense at home ran through the same channel. In June 1948 a community campaign in Detroit ran an advertisement telling donors that "the United Jewish Appeal is the official American agency for aid to Haganah," and that the only channel for aid to the Haganah was the local Allied Jewish Campaign. The advertisement warned that collecting money for the dissident militias was fraud. [cite:djn_1948_haganah] The same campaign that fed survivors in Europe and resettled refugees in America was, in its own words, the official channel for the Haganah. Charity and defense ran through the same pipe, and the advertisement said so in print.

The warning about dissident militias matters as well. It shows the mainstream campaign separating the Haganah from the armed groups outside it in what it told American donors, and naming one channel as the only legitimate one.

The flow above follows the defense money from the £80,000 budget line of 1939 through the 1938 levy to the American arms network of 1945–48, Golda Meyerson's tour of 1948, which raised about $50 million largely for weapons, and the advertisement naming the United Jewish Appeal as the channel for Haganah aid. [cite:frus_1939_ja_budget] [cite:w_kofer] [cite:israelaffairs_italy] [cite:djn_1948_haganah] Each step is documented separately, and each left a record: the levy was public, the budget line was reported to a foreign consul, and the charity channel was advertised.

The other side of the ledger is Britain's. The cost of governing Palestine rose steadily under the Mandate. Civil government spending grew from £P1.9 million in 1922–23 to £P3.2 million in 1934–35, a rise of about two-thirds in twelve years; the Palestine pound was then at par with sterling. [cite:horowitz_1937] The garrison was a separate charge, paid by Britain: £1.5 million in 1923–24. [cite:league_report_garrison] In today's dollars those figures are roughly $161 million and $388 million for the civil budget and $129 million for the garrison.

The bill rose sharply at the end. By the British government's own account in its statement on the termination of the Mandate, the military forces in Palestine cost the British taxpayer about £100 million in 1945–47, roughly $6.7 billion today. [cite:hmg_termination_1948] Parliament debated keeping 80,000 to 100,000 soldiers in the country, and some 100,000 troops were deployed. [cite:hansard_1947_08] The human cost was about 750 British military and police killed over the period. [cite:nam_palestine] Measured in today's dollars, Britain's three-year military bill was larger than any single year of American giving, and larger than the whole of the wartime appeals of 1939–45.

Put together, the two sides of this ledger correct both assumptions. The Jewish community's defense was financed through documented channels: a budget line, a community levy, an arms network funded by American donors and, at the end, a national charity that called itself the Haganah's official American agency. The figures are partial, but the mechanism is on paper. Britain, for its part, did not hold Palestine cheaply. Its civil and garrison costs grew through the interwar years, and its last three years cost it about £100 million and some 750 lives.

The gap is the army's own total. No audited figure for the Haganah's budget is publicly available, and the documents gathered here do not allow one to be reconstructed: they show individual streams, not the sum of them, and some of those streams overlap with the campaigns described in [scene:gf_s01|the ledger of who paid]. The Jewish National Fund's full annual income series is likewise not available as an audited total.

The note above records the same limit. The Agency budgets of 1939 and 1944–46, the Mandate's civil spending, Britain's military cost and the defense channels are all documented. The Haganah's own budget is not, and this book gives no figure for it.

sections.h: The Network of the American Build-Up, 1897–1948
sections.html:
The money in those ledgers moved through people and organizations, and the ties between them can be mapped. A common picture of American support for Zionism before 1948 is of a loose and scattered sympathy: individuals of goodwill, a few friendly senators, some generous donors, acting each on their own. The documented record shows something more organized than that. Its pieces were connected, and the connections can be named: who founded which body, who chaired which committee, who sponsored which resolution, who raised which money and who carried which message to the President. Laid out by distance from the center, they form a network with a clear structure and two loops that fed themselves.

A word first on what such a map shows. Every tie below is a documented relationship of a specific kind: an organizational founding, a chairmanship, a sponsorship, an appointment, a transaction. None is inferred from shared identity, religion or background. A senator appears because he chaired a named committee or sponsored a named resolution; a donor appears because he raised a named sum. Where the record does not establish a tie, the map does not draw one.

At the apex stood the Jewish Agency and the World Zionist Organization, led in these years by Weizmann and Ben-Gurion. They set the movement's program and goals. [cite:aja_azec_local_1945] One later document defines the financial side of the relationship more sharply than anything from the 1940s. In November 1962 the Justice Department ordered the American Zionist Council to register as a foreign agent, alleging that it had received more than $5 million from the Jewish Agency over the preceding eight years. [cite:azc_fara_doj] The precision matters. The 1962 finding concerned the American Zionist Council, the body into which the wartime emergency council was renamed in 1949, and the years it covered; it was not a finding about the emergency council of the 1940s, and the record here does not document Agency funding of that earlier body. The later case is traced in [scene:s07g|the organization after statehood].

At the first degree, bound to the apex by direct organizational ties, stood three American bodies. The American Zionist Emergency Council, co-chaired by Abba Hillel Silver and Stephen Wise, ran the national political campaign of the 1940s. The Zionist Organization of America was the mass-membership body; it had reached 147,000 members by 1918. [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] Hadassah completed the first ring.

At the second degree were bodies created or coordinated by those first-degree organizations. The American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine presented themselves as independent voices of American and Christian opinion. Both were organized by the Zionist executive Emanuel Neumann, and one historian has described them as "hardly autonomous." [cite:hnn_clark_truman] The United Jewish Appeal, under its executive Henry Montor, was the fundraising engine described in [scene:gf_s01|the ledger of who paid]. The Sonneborn Institute and its front company, Materials for Palestine, were set up at Ben-Gurion's 1945 meeting with American donors, to buy arms. Abraham Feinberg, who appears again at the third degree, was one of the original seventeen members of the Sonneborn Institute. [cite:emory_feinberg_thesis]

At the third degree were the political and financial endpoints, the people through whom the network reached decisions. In Congress, Senator Robert Wagner chaired the American Palestine Committee, and Senator Robert Taft co-sponsored the 1944 Palestine resolution. Senator Henry Cabot Lodge and Representative Hamilton Fish III gave their names to the 1922 resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration. Sol Bloom, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, was a target of the telegram campaigns. [cite:aja_azec_silver_resignation] In the White House, the aides David Niles, Clark Clifford and Max Lowenthal, and Truman's friend Eddie Jacobson, carried the Zionist case to the President. [cite:wiki_david_niles] Among donors, Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann raised the $100,000 that Truman's 1948 campaign needed, and Golda Meyerson's tour of 1948 raised about $50 million through Montor's network, largely for arms. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] [cite:israelaffairs_italy]

The diagram simplifies in one respect. The White House channel, Niles, Clifford, Lowenthal and Jacobson, sat at the third degree but did not hang beneath any one second-degree body; it connected to the legislators on one side and, through the 1948 campaign money, to the donors on the other. It is left out of the tree for legibility and shown in the network drawn with this section.

Two parts of the structure were circular, and on this map's reading the loops, with the structure itself, are the finding. The first was a commitment loop. The emergency council collected statements of support from legislators; printed them in its book America and Palestine; mailed the book to every member of Congress; used it to press for votes and platform planks; and so gathered new statements, which went into the next round. Each public commitment became leverage for the next one.

The second was the Montor loop, and it ran through one fundraiser. Henry Montor gathered the donors for the 1945 Sonneborn meeting; that meeting produced the arms network; Montor then secured Golda Meyerson's platform before American audiences in 1948; and her tour raised about $50 million, largely for arms, which returned the money to the purpose the 1945 meeting had set. [cite:israelaffairs_italy] One man's network ran from the founding of the arms channel to its largest single injection of money. Feinberg's place inside it is documented further: the FBI file released decades later documents his ongoing meetings with Sonneborn, and in 1952 he was ordered to register as a foreign agent over a publication he ran, a story told in [scene:s07f2|the section on Abraham Feinberg]. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file]

The headline figures above give the scale of what this network sat on top of. Two of them belong to it directly: the Zionist Organization of America's 147,000 members by 1918, the mass base of the first degree, and the roughly $50 million of Golda Meyerson's 1948 tour, the largest single return of the Montor loop.
