That summer the crisis turned inward. In the summer of 1952 Mossadeq demanded the right to name the minister of war, and the Shah refused. Mossadeq resigned. Three days of pro-Mossadeq rioting followed, and the Shah reappointed him. In August 1952 the Majlis granted him full powers for six months, a grant later extended. [cite:rs_cw1_loc_iran_study] The episode showed where power lay in mid-1952: the crowd and the parliament could restore a prime minister the monarch had let go, and the parliament could then hand him powers beyond the ordinary. It also showed the cost of that route. A government that ruled by full powers, renewed, was a different thing from the parliament that had voted nationalization in March 1951.

Washington's position moved during the same months, and the State Department's own papers show how. A United States aide-mémoire of 31 July 1952 proposed "an immediate grant of $10 million to the Iranian Government," together with British purchases of stored oil and arbitration on compensation. On 30 August 1952 Truman and Churchill sent Mossadeq a joint message, which he first called "flatly unacceptable." [cite:rs_cw1_frus_iran_byroade] The joint message mattered as a signal as much as for its terms: the two governments now addressed Tehran together.

Inside the State Department, however, Assistant Secretary Byroade argued for a different course. In September 1952 he judged that "a nationalist government will neither bring in the communists nor fall victim to a communist revolt before next March." He recommended telling Britain that keeping Iran out of the communist world outweighed legal considerations, consulting American oil companies about buying 100,000 to 150,000 barrels a day, and telling Mossadeq plainly that "the United States Government is not in the oil business." [cite:rs_cw1_frus_iran_byroade] Byroade's memorandum is a useful corrective in two directions. It shows that in the autumn of 1952 a senior American official did not regard Mossadeq's government as a Communist danger in the short term. And it shows that the American interest, as he framed it, was strategic, keeping Iran out of the Soviet camp, rather than the defence of a British company's legal claim, which he was prepared to subordinate. Whether that view prevailed is taken up in the account of the coup at the close of this chapter.

In October 1952 Mossadeq cut diplomatic relations with Britain, according to diplomats' oral histories collected by the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training. [cite:rs_cw1_adst_iran] It ended the formal diplomatic channel between the two governments at the height of their dispute.

One image of Mossadeq from these months needs correcting. He is often remembered as Time's "Man of the Year" for 1951, and the title is sometimes cited as proof of the world's esteem. Time did name him Man of the Year, in its issue of 7 January 1952. But the magazine's own text described him as "an appalling caricature of a statesman" and "the strange old wizard." [cite:rs_cw1_time_1952] The title marked his importance in the year's news, not approval; the magazine's words were openly hostile. That hostility is itself part of the record of how Western opinion saw the crisis while it was under way.

The longer arc, from the empire and the first democracy through the oil concessions, the installed rulers and the coups, is shown as a single sequence of layers in the map below. Iran's second parliamentary period sits near its centre, between 1948 and the coup decade.

What followed is told at the close of this chapter. In August 1953 Mossadeq dissolved the parliament by a plebiscite that his opponents called rigged, and on 19 August 1953 a coup organized by the CIA and MI6 removed him. [cite:loc_mossadeq] [cite:w_1953_coup] The Shah then ruled as an autocrat for 26 years. [cite:w_1953_coup] The planning, the approval, the money and the long concealment of that operation are told in [scene:s11|the coup of August 1953].

The record of 1941 to 1952 answers the familiar claim plainly. Iran in these years had an elected parliament that chose its own course on oil and a prime minister who held office on that parliament's strength; it also had political violence, including the assassination of a sitting prime minister, and a government that came to rule by delegated full powers. Both halves are documented, and neither cancels the other. What these sources do not settle is just as important. They do not give the company's profits, the revenue Iran lost year by year, or the terms of the 1933 concession beyond the Court's description of it; they do not show how the full powers were used between August 1952 and the end of the year; and they do not establish what the British and American governments were already planning when relations were broken in October 1952. On that last question the documents begin in 1953, and they are taken up with the coup itself.

sections.h: The Huleh Crisis, 1951: Drainage, a Demilitarized Zone and Resolution 93
sections.html:
In the same spring that Iran's parliament voted to nationalize its oil, the armistice on Israel's northern border produced its first crisis at the Security Council. The armistice with Syria, signed in July 1949, had turned the ground Syria evacuated west of the international border into demilitarized zones; how that came about, under a ruler who seized power days before the talks opened, is told in [scene:rd6_syria_1949|Syria in 1949]. The agreement said who could keep troops where. It did not say who owned the zones, who could work their land, or who could decide what was built in them. Those questions came to the Council over a drainage project in the Huleh area. The crisis is worth following closely, because arguments that recurred along the Syrian front until 1967 were made on the record between March and September 1951.

The work itself had begun earlier. By Israel's account, drainage had been going on since October 1950, with the knowledge of both Syria and the United Nations. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] The contractor named in the Council's later decision was the Palestine Land Development Company. [cite:rs_cw1_unispal_res93] Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Abba Eban, described the aim of the project in terms of land: it would reclaim, he said, "10,000 acres from desolation and 25,000 acres from disease." [cite:rs_cw1_jvl_eban_huleh] Part of the work ran through the demilitarized zone, and that is where the dispute began.

Between 29 March and 6 April 1951 Syria lodged three complaints with the Security Council (S/2061, S/2065 and S/2074). It charged that Israel was violating the armistice of July 1949 in five ways: by draining and deepening the bed of the Jordan, by occupying the demilitarized zone, by firing on Syrian posts, by forcibly evacuating the zone's Arab inhabitants and demolishing their villages, and by bombing El Hamma and Syrian outposts. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] Syria's reasons went beyond the incidents. Drainage, it argued, would give Israel a military advantage, would create more refugees, would require Syria to build new outposts, and would impair irrigation. Because most of the zone had been under Syrian occupation, Syria said, it should have been consulted before any work began. And it presented the Arab landowners in the zone not as bystanders but as people protecting their land from expropriation. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951]

Israel answered in its own complaint (S/2072). The work, it said, had been under way since October 1950 in plain view of Syria and the United Nations; it was lawful; and it needed no Syrian consent, because Israel held sovereignty over the zone. Israel also put forward an incident of its own. On 4 April 1951, it reported, Syrian forces entered El Hamma and attacked an Israeli police patrol, killing seven policemen and seriously wounding three. Israel's air action of 5 April was, in its account, a response to that attack. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951]

The two cases did not meet, because they began from different premises about the zone itself. If the zone was Israeli territory under special military restrictions, as Israel held, then a civilian drainage project inside it was Israel's business, and Syria's objections were interference. If the zone's status had been left open by the armistice, as Syria held, then work that changed the land and moved its inhabitants changed the facts the armistice had frozen, and Syria had a right to be consulted. Each government's complaint was consistent with its premise. The Council's task was to decide what the armistice permitted, and it did so without settling whose premise was correct.

A second front opened while the Council was deliberating. On 7 May 1951 Israel complained (S/2126) of an attack by Syrian irregulars on Tel el Mutilla, inside Israel. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] Syria denied that its army had been involved (S/2360). The question of who had fought there was left to a later UN report, taken up below.

On 18 May 1951 the Security Council adopted Resolution 93 at its 547th meeting, by 10 votes to none, with the Soviet Union abstaining. [cite:rs_cw1_unispal_res93] The resolution did three things. It found that "Aerial action taken by the forces of the Government of Israel on 5 April 1951" was a violation of the cease-fire ordered by Resolution 54 of 1948. It endorsed the requests that the Palestine Land Development Company be told "to cease all operations in the demilitarized zone" until agreement was reached. And it decided that Arab civilians who had been removed from the zone "should be permitted to return forthwith to their homes," under the supervision of the Mixed Armistice Commission. [cite:rs_cw1_unispal_res93] The resolution censured one act by name, stopped the work pending agreement, and ordered the people who had been moved to be let back.

Eban addressed the Council the same day, and his statement is the strongest form of Israel's case. He argued that the draft "does confer a veto power upon the very interests which are implacably opposed" to drainage: by requiring agreement before work could resume, the Council had handed the decision to the party that wanted the work stopped. He set the project's purpose against that outcome, the reclamation of "10,000 acres from desolation and 25,000 acres from disease." He objected that Israel's action of 5 April was censured while Syrian attacks were not. And he put the strategic stake plainly: whoever holds the Huleh area, he said, "clutches Israel at its throat." [cite:rs_cw1_jvl_eban_huleh] On Eban's reading, Israel was being asked to suspend a lawful civilian project on what it held to be its own territory, while the attacks on its police went uncensured.

Syria's case, stated with equal care, was that the project was not simply civilian and the territory not simply Israel's. Drainage changed the military balance along a line the armistice was meant to hold still; it would create more refugees; and it was carried out without consulting the state whose forces had held most of the zone before it was demilitarized. On that reading, which goes beyond the words of Syria's complaints, the Council had not given Syria a veto but had required that changes in the zone be agreed, not imposed. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] Both cases drew on the same agreement, and both governments read the same silence in it differently.

The question the resolution left open was sovereignty, and the UN's own officer answered it soon afterwards. In a memorandum of June 1951 the UN Chief of Staff concluded that neither Israel nor Syria held sovereignty in the demilitarized zone, and that the work should stop until the two governments agreed. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] That finding rejected Israel's claim of sovereignty outright. It did not accept Syria's either: Syria had not claimed sovereignty in the summary of its case, but a right to be consulted, and the Chief of Staff's conclusion that the work needed agreement was closer to Syria's position than to Israel's on the practical question, while denying both a sovereign title. The same memorandum reported a fact that complicated any compromise. The Arab landowners in the zone, he wrote, rejected every proposal to rent, sell or exchange their land. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] Whatever the governments decided, the people who held the land had already said no to every arrangement that would have removed them from it.

Those people are the part of the story most easily lost behind the diplomacy. On 8 July 1951 the Chief of Staff reported that 785 civilians had been evacuated from the zone. The chairman of the Mixed Armistice Commission interviewed 632 of them, and about 260 chose to return. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] The sources describe them as the zone's Arab civilians and inhabitants; they do not record their citizenship, or what became of those who did not go back. The Council had ordered that they be permitted to return. The figures show that fewer than half of those interviewed took up that right, and the record cited here does not say why the others chose as they did.

The Tel el Mutilla complaint was settled on the evidence in September. A UN report of 23 September 1951 (S/2359) stated that the allegation of Syrian army participation in the fighting "could now be considered as having been proved." The proof it cited was Syrian: medal awards published in the Syrian Official Gazette. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] Syria had denied army involvement, and its denial stands in the record beside the finding. Here a UN body reached a firm conclusion against a party's own account, and it ran against Syria, just as the resolution of May had run against Israel on the air action of 5 April.

One reading of the mechanism the crisis exposed runs as follows. The Mixed Armistice Commission supervised the zone; the Security Council could censure and order; and the record of 1951 cited here shows neither enforcing its decisions on the ground. Israel carried out work on the ground and argued its legality afterwards. Syria complained to the Council, and Israel charged Syrian forces and irregulars with attacks of their own. The UN found against each in 1951, Israel on the air action and Syria at Tel el Mutilla, but the record does not show what those findings changed on the ground. The Arab inhabitants of the zone, who held the land and refused to part with it, had no seat in any of these bodies. They appear in the record as complainants through Syria, as a figure in a report and as the subject of an order.

What the record cited here does not settle should be stated plainly. It gives no casualty figure for the Israeli air action of 5 April, and no independent account of the El Hamma clash beyond Israel's own report. It does not show whether the drainage resumed, on what terms, or when. It does not record the citizenship of the evacuated civilians, or why most of those interviewed chose not to return. And it leaves the sovereignty question where the Chief of Staff placed it: Israel continued to assert sovereignty, Syria continued to insist on its say, and the UN's own officer held that neither owned the zone. The eighteen-year struggle that grew out of that unresolved question, over farming and building in the zones, over water and the Jordan's headwaters, is told for 1953–67 in [scene:sy_s02|the demilitarized zones and the water war].

sections.h: The First Grant: How Washington Came to Give Israel Money, 1951–1952
sections.html:
In the month that Syria lodged its first complaint over the Huleh, Israel's diplomats were asking Washington for money. Until then the United States had extended Israel credit; the sources cited here record no outright grant before then. How the new state met its first bills, through American government credit, bonds sold abroad and the opening of the German reparations claim, is told in Volume II, in [scene:rd6_financing|how the new state was paid for]. This section takes up the next step: the fifteen months, from March 1951 to June 1952, in which Israel asked for a grant, the Administration offered far less, Congress raised the figure, and the money arrived in a form that was economic, regional and argued over at every stage. The familiar picture of American support for Israel holds that Washington gave massive, unconditional military backing as an unbroken policy from 1948. The documents of 1951 and 1952 show something narrower and more contested. The first grant was for the relief of immigrants, not for arms. The State Department resisted its size. It was set beside a matching programme for Arab refugees and the Arab states. And the case that carried it through Congress was made partly in the language of the Cold War, by senators from both parties.

The request was made in March 1951. Abba Eban, Israel's ambassador, and David Horowitz of Israel's Finance Ministry handed Acheson a note asking for a grant-in-aid of $150 million for the period from 1 July 1951 to 1 June 1952. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_eban_request] The note gave three grounds. The first was population: 510,000 people had arrived since statehood, and 600,000 more were expected over the next three years. The second was the cost of defence. The third was Israel's commitments to the reintegration fund of UNRWA, the new UN agency for Palestine refugees. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_eban_request] In the same conversation the two men asked for American support for a separate claim of $1.5 billion in reparations from Germany, the claim whose negotiation and divisive passage through the Knesset Volume II follows. Acheson's answer on another matter was a refusal: an official invitation for Ben-Gurion to visit, he said, was impossible that year. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_eban_request]

The request was new in kind. Israel's earlier American money had come as credit; a memorandum written that summer inside the State Department lists $135 million in earlier Export-Import Bank credit to Israel. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_feinberg_memo] A grant would not be repaid, and it would have to be voted by Congress. The editors of the State Department's documentary series record that the request for a fiscal year 1952 grant of $150 million "had generated a great deal of discussion within the United States Government." [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mcghee_note] The department's answer was to turn a request from one state into a programme for a region. On 17 April 1951 McGhee wrote a memorandum proposing a programme of economic aid to the Near East as a whole. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mcghee_note] The record cited here gives the memorandum's date and its proposal, not its full reasoning.

Congress had already moved. On about 3 April 1951, according to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency's report at the time, Senators Paul Douglas, a Democrat from Illinois, and Robert Taft, a Republican from Ohio, introduced a bill for $150 million in aid to Israel, the full sum of the Israeli note, and the House Majority Leader, John McCormack, introduced a companion bill. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_douglas_taft_1951] The senators described Israel as "a bulwark in that area of world democracy" against Communist threats, "particularly in Iran", and McCormack called it "a dependable ally of the United States." [cite:rs_cw1_jta_douglas_taft_1951] The phrase about Iran was written in the weeks after Iran's parliament voted to nationalize its oil, the crisis told in this chapter's section on Iran. The Israeli note had made its case on immigrants, defence and refugees. The sponsors in Congress made theirs, at least in part, on the Soviet threat to the region. The two cases sat side by side from the start.

The Administration's own figure came on 24 May 1951. Its recommendation to Congress was $23.5 million in economic aid for Israel, the same $23.5 million for the Arab states, $50 million for the Arab refugee programme, and authority for $41.5 million in direct military grants. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_feinberg_memo] The published summary of the memorandum does not say which states the military authority was meant for, and nothing in it assigns any of that sum to Israel. The shape of the proposal was parity: Israel and its Arab neighbours were offered equal sums, and the larger single line went to the refugees.

American advocates pressed for more, and the State Department's memoranda record how it answered them. McGhee declined a request from Jacob Blaustein for $75 million each. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_feinberg_memo] In July 1951 McGhee wrote to the Secretary of State about a visit from Abraham Feinberg, the memorandum's title noting that Feinberg came "at the Suggestion of the President". McGhee proposed telling Feinberg that the $50 million for Arab refugees could be seen as indirect aid to Israel. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_feinberg_memo] The memorandum, as summarized here, does not say why money for the refugees should count as help to Israel, and this book does not supply a reason. What the exchange does show is the structure of the argument. An advocate who came at the President's suggestion carried the case into the department, and the department defended its lower figure by pointing to money appropriated for someone else.

The mechanism of these months explains who could act. The Israeli government could ask, and did, through its ambassador. The Secretary of State and his officials shaped the Administration's recommendation, which set the figure Congress started from. Congress could raise or cut that figure, first by authorizing a sum and then by appropriating it. Between those points American advocates worked: Blaustein and Feinberg inside the department, and in the Senate the lobbyist I. L. Kenen, whose work and organization are told in [scene:cw1_lobby|the lobby in its Cold War frame].

The decisive moment came on the Senate floor in August 1951, and the best account of it is Kenen's own. In a letter from Washington to Abba Hillel Silver he described a Douglas amendment, backed by Taft, that raised the figure for Near East economic aid and, with it, Israel's total, to about $68.8 million. The scan of the letter is partly illegible, so that figure is approximate. The amendment passed on a close standing vote. [cite:rs_cw1_kenen_silver_letter] Kenen measured the gain as a share of the whole: about 1% of the Administration's bill had gone to Israel, against about 5.2% of the Senate's. And he warned his correspondent not to celebrate too soon: "all this is still an authorization." [cite:rs_cw1_kenen_silver_letter] An authorization permitted spending; it did not yet provide the money.

Truman signed the Mutual Security Act of 1951 on 10 October 1951. It provided $50 million for the UN refugee programme in fiscal 1952. [cite:rs_cw1_truman_unrpr_letter] How much it gave Israel is a point on which the sources differ, and both versions should be stated. Kenen's obituary in the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, published in 1988, says that the 1951 campaign sought $150 million and that, despite State Department opposition, Kenen won approval for $65 million. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_kenen_obit] Kenen's own letter of 1951 gives about $68.8 million, at the Senate authorization stage, and stresses that this was not yet money in hand. [cite:rs_cw1_kenen_silver_letter] The two figures need not contradict each other. One describes an authorization in August 1951; the other is a retrospective total written decades later, which may describe the sum finally approved after the Senate and House versions were reconciled. Neither source, as cited here, is the text of the appropriation itself, and the year-by-year official table summarized in Volume II counts American aid by a different method. This book gives both figures and does not choose between them.

A third account describes the design differently again. According to Israel Hayom's report of research by Kobby Barda, the refugee-aid plan provided $50 million each for Israel and the Arab states for the absorption of refugees, a further $53 million for the Arab states in technical cooperation, and $50 million for the Arab refugees, channelled through UNRWA. [cite:rs_cw1_israelhayom_barda] Those sums do not match the Administration's recommendation of May 1951, and the report, as cited here, does not say at which stage of the process they applied. The $50 million for the refugees through the UN agency agrees with the Mutual Security Act as Truman described it; the other figures are Barda's account and are not confirmed by the other sources.

The money for Arab refugees ran alongside Israel's throughout, and it was larger at the start. Truman's letter of 27 July 1951 to the chairmen of the congressional committees records an American contribution of $25,450,000 to the UN Palestine refugee programme in fiscal 1951, and a request for $50,000,000 in the Mutual Security Program for the following year. [cite:rs_cw1_truman_unrpr_letter] In the Administration's proposal of May 1951, the refugee line was more than twice Israel's. The refugees' own history in these years, the UN agency's first operations and the conference in Paris, is told in this chapter's section on the refugees.

The second round, for fiscal 1953, went differently, because this time the Administration began high. In March 1952 it asked Congress for $76 million for the relief and resettlement of Jewish immigrants in Israel and $65 million for the UN to resettle Arab refugees in Arab lands: together $141 million of a Near East request of $196 million. Acheson and W. Averell Harriman testified in support, according to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_76m_1952] The Administration's own figure for Israel was now more than three times the $23.5 million it had proposed ten months earlier. The language had changed too. The money for Israel was described as aid for immigrants, set beside the programme for Arab refugees.

Congress trimmed the Israeli figure only slightly. The House voted $76 million and the Senate $64,456,000. In June 1952 a conference of the two chambers split the difference, setting Israel's figure at $70,228,000 for the relief and rehabilitation of Jewish refugees, plus $2,772,000 in technical assistance: $73,000,000 in all. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_conference_1952] [cite:rs_cw1_jta_house_1952] The comparison the Jewish Telegraphic Agency drew at the time shows where the political weight now lay. Congress cut the Administration's overall aid by about 20%, but Israel's figure by less than 8%. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_conference_1952] [cite:rs_cw1_jta_house_1952] In 1951 the department had held the line and Congress had pushed past it. In 1952 the department proposed the larger figure itself, and Congress, cutting overall aid by about a fifth, left this one nearly whole.

None of this money was military, and that remained true for another decade. From Israel's founding through the early 1960s, American assistance to Israel was economic aid and loans only. According to one study of the aid relationship, Washington avoided direct arms sales because it did not want to alienate the Arab oil-producing states, and the first American military aid, itself in the form of loans rather than grants, came in 1962. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] The first step of the dashboard below sets out that period: economic aid and loans only, from 1948 to 1961, with arms withheld for fear of alienating Arab oil states. The grants of 1951 and 1952 belong entirely inside that step. The later steps, from the first military loan to the earmarks, the airlift of 1973 and the conversion of aid to grants, are told in [scene:iaa_s01|how the aid relationship grew].

The record allows the competing explanations of the first grant to be stated, each in its strongest form, without deciding between them. The case its sponsors made in public was strategic: Israel as a "bulwark" of democracy against Communist threats in the region, and "a dependable ally." [cite:rs_cw1_jta_douglas_taft_1951] The case Israel's government made was humanitarian and fiscal: hundreds of thousands of immigrants, the cost of defence, and its obligations to the refugee reintegration fund. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_eban_request] The State Department's position, as its own papers show it, was regional and balanced: a programme for the whole Near East, equal sums for Israel and the Arab states, the larger share for the Arab refugees, and resistance to the higher figures pressed on it by Israel's American supporters, including one who came at the President's suggestion. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mcghee_note] [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_feinberg_memo] Who gained is clear enough on paper: Israel's absorption budget, and in parallel the Arab states and the UN refugee programme. The cost fell on the American government's budget, and in 1951 it was carried over the objection of the department responsible for the region.

What the record does not settle should be said plainly. The sources cited here do not give the text of the fiscal 1952 appropriation, so the sum Israel finally received that year rests on two accounts, $65 million and about $68.8 million, that describe different stages. They do not reconcile Barda's figures with the Administration's. They do not say which states the $41.5 million in military grant authority of May 1951 was meant for, or why McGhee thought refugee money could be described to Feinberg as help for Israel. Nor do they show which argument moved the votes in Congress: the Cold War language of the sponsors, the immigrant arithmetic of the Israeli note, or the work of the advocates in the corridors. All three were present. The documents record that the grant passed, and how much it was, more clearly than they record why.

sections.h: The Lobby in Its Cold War Frame, 1950–1954
sections.html:
The Senate fight over Israel's first grant had an organizer behind it, and his path to Washington explains a good deal about the lobby he built. The institutional line of descent, from the wartime American Zionist Emergency Council through the American Zionist Council to the committee later called AIPAC, and the federal foreign-agent order of 1962, is told in Volume II, in [scene:s07g|From AZEC to AIPAC]. This section does not retell it. It follows the man who opened the Washington office, the argument he brought, the campaign in which he first used it, and the three different dates the sources give for what he founded. It also sets beside him two American Jewish positions that did not share his aims, because the lobby was born into a community that was arguing with itself about what it owed the new state.

I. L. Kenen came to Washington from inside the movement and, for a time, from inside the Israeli state. According to his obituary in the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, he directed the lobbying of the American Emergency Committee on Zionist Affairs from 1943; he was the Jewish Agency's information director at the United Nations in 1947–48; and in 1949 he was a member of Israel's first delegation to the UN. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_kenen_obit] Those were three different kinds of employer: an American Zionist organization, the Jewish Agency, and the government of Israel.

The move to Washington was, by one account, suggested from the Israeli side. According to Israel Hayom's report of research by Kobby Barda, it was Abba Eban, then Israel's ambassador to the UN, who suggested that Kenen go to Washington. [cite:rs_cw1_israelhayom_barda] Kenen brought an argument with him. In the same account, he held that the best route to American aid was to extend the approach of the Marshall Plan to the Middle East, inside a broader framework of aid for refugees. [cite:rs_cw1_israelhayom_barda] The logic was political. A grant for Israel alone would stand as a favour to one state; a grant for refugees, Jewish immigrants in Israel and Arab refugees in the Arab states alike, would stand as a regional programme on the Marshall Plan's model. Both the suggestion and the argument rest on a single reported account, and they should be read as that.

The aid that followed did take something like that shape. The fiscal 1953 request described Israel's money as aid for the relief and resettlement of Jewish immigrants and set it beside money for Arab refugees, as told in [scene:cw1_grant_aid|the first grant]. The record cited here does not show that Kenen's argument produced that design. The State Department had its own reasons for a regional programme, and its papers show it resisting the higher figures Israel's supporters pressed. What can be said is that the lobbyist's argument and the eventual form of the aid pointed the same way.

The first test was the Senate, in August 1951. Kenen's letter from Washington to Abba Hillel Silver, the leader who had built the wartime council, reports the floor work on the aid amendment and names those involved: Senators Douglas, Taft and Brewster, and the lobbyist Julius Klein. [cite:rs_cw1_kenen_silver_letter] The amendment raised Israel's figure, and Kenen reminded Silver that "all this is still an authorization." [cite:rs_cw1_kenen_silver_letter] The language in which the bill had been introduced that spring placed the effort in the Cold War. Its Senate sponsors, a Democrat and a Republican, called Israel "a bulwark in that area of world democracy" against Communist threats, "particularly in Iran." [cite:rs_cw1_jta_douglas_taft_1951] The lobby's first campaign thus ran on two arguments at once: a refugee argument about immigrants and absorption, and a strategic argument about the Soviet Union. The letter names Klein, but the record cited here does not describe what he did, or for whom.

When the lobby itself was founded, and under what name, is a question the sources answer in three ways. Kenen's JTA obituary says he moved to Washington in 1951 and set up the American Zionist Committee "to lobby Congress in support of Israel", and that the committee became AIPAC in 1954. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_kenen_obit] The Jewish Virtual Library dates AIPAC's beginnings to 1951, but inside the American Zionist Council. It says the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs was set up as a separate lobbying body in 1954, because the Council's non-profit status limited how much lobbying it could do, and it dates the name American Israel Public Affairs Committee to 1959. [cite:rs_cw1_jvl_aipac] Volume II, drawing on Kenen's papers and other references, dates the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs to 1953–54, describes it as a new body that was not tax-exempt, and also gives 1959 for the change of name. [cite:cjh_kenen_papers] [cite:wiki_american_zionist_council] [cite:britannica_aipac]

Read closely, the three accounts disagree less than they first appear to, because they date different things. All agree that Kenen's lobbying in Washington began in 1951. They differ on whether, in that year, it was his own committee (the obituary) or work carried on within the American Zionist Council (the Jewish Virtual Library). All three place the creation of a separate lobbying committee in 1953 or 1954. The real conflict is over the name: the obituary says the committee became AIPAC in 1954, the other two that it took that name in 1959. One reading, which is this book's and not a finding of the sources, is that the obituary applied the later name to the committee created in 1954. The sources also give two reasons for the separation, and these do not conflict either. The Jewish Virtual Library gives the limit that non-profit status placed on lobbying. Volume II's sources give a fear that the Eisenhower administration suspected Israel of funding the American Zionist Council and might force it to register as a foreign agent. [cite:rs_cw1_jvl_aipac] [cite:cjh_kenen_papers] [cite:wiki_american_zionist_council] Both reasons may have been at work. The record cited here does not say which weighed more.

The sources say little about the committee's size or budget. One detail of scale survives: the obituary records that in 1957 Kenen used a $700 speaking honorarium to start a weekly, the Near East Report. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_kenen_obit]

American Jewish opinion was not of one mind about any of this, and two positions from these years show the range. The first was a settlement of terms between Israel's government and an American Jewish organization that did not speak for it. On 23 August 1950, at a luncheon in Jerusalem, Ben-Gurion and Jacob Blaustein of the American Jewish Committee exchanged statements. Israel recognized that American Jews owed their allegiance to the United States, and each side undertook not to speak on behalf of the other. [cite:rs_cw1_jmm_blaustein] The statement drew a line through the middle of the question that a Washington lobby for Israel would always face: whose interest it represented. Blaustein himself was no bystander to the aid effort. The following year he asked the State Department for $75 million each, and McGhee declined. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_feinberg_memo] Support for aid to Israel and a public insistence that American Jews' allegiance lay with the United States were, for him, compatible positions.

The second position was opposition. The American Council for Judaism, whose first president was Lessing Rosenwald and whose chief spokesman was Elmer Berger, had opposed the establishment of Israel, and after 1948 it remained critical of what it called "the Israel-Zionist domination of American Jewish life." It claimed 20,000 members, and by the end of 1955 it had set up ten schools teaching the positions of classical Reform Judaism. [cite:rs_cw1_ej_acj] Its case, in its own terms, was that American Jewish life should not be organized around the state of Israel or the Zionist movement. It is a reminder that the lobby Kenen built spoke for a movement within American Jewry, not for American Jews as a whole, and that some of its critics in these years were themselves Jewish organizations.

One more date needs care. The committee's founding in 1953–54 falls in the same year as the Anglo-American coup in Iran, and elsewhere in this library the two are paired in one account, [scene:s11|the coup of 1953]. That account states its own limit plainly: the shared year is a coincidence of timing, and no documented operational connection links the founding of the lobby to the overthrow of Mossadeq. The sources cited in this section add nothing that would change that. The only Iranian thread in them is rhetorical: the Senate sponsors' phrase of 1951 about Communist threats "particularly in Iran." [cite:rs_cw1_jta_douglas_taft_1951]

The gaps are several, and they are worth stating because the founding of this lobby is so often told with more confidence than the sources allow. The record cited here does not give the founding document of either the 1951 operation or the separate committee. It does not say who paid Kenen's salary or the committee's costs between 1951 and 1954, which is the question the foreign-agent inquiry of 1962 would later put to the American Zionist Council. Eban's suggestion that Kenen go to Washington, and the refugee argument Kenen carried there, rest on one reported account of one scholar's research. Klein is named but not described. And the sources disagree on the year the name AIPAC was first used, a disagreement this book has set out rather than resolved.

sections.h: The First Ties with American Intelligence, 1951 and After
sections.html:
While the aid argument was being fought in public, a second relationship with Washington was beginning in private. It is one of the longest-lasting intelligence partnerships the United States has had, and it has been publicly acknowledged since the 1970s. Its beginning, however, is less well documented than its later history, and the accounts of how and when it started disagree. A common view holds that the CIA and Israel's services operated from the outset as a single, seamless apparatus. The record of the early 1950s shows something more hesitant: an American agency that first counted Israel on the wrong side of the Cold War, a prime minister who persuaded its director to try cooperation, and a formal arrangement whose date, terms and American manager are all in dispute. This section tells that beginning only. What the partnership became belongs to later stages.

The starting point was suspicion. According to the journalists Yossi Melman and Dan Raviv, the CIA in 1948 initially viewed the new state as part of the Soviet sphere of influence. [cite:rs_cw1_tablet_spies] How the agency's analysts had opposed recognition in 1948, and been overruled, is told in [scene:cia_s02|the CIA in 1948]. Israel's own services were then only months old. Their founding, from the dissolution of the Haganah's intelligence service in June 1948 to the creation of the coordinating institute under Reuven Shiloah that became the Mossad, is told in [scene:cw1_intelligence|the founding of Israel's intelligence community].

The turn, in Melman and Raviv's account, came in 1951. Ben-Gurion, touring the United States, met General Walter Bedell Smith, Truman's Director of Central Intelligence, and "convinced U.S. intelligence to give Israel a try." [cite:rs_cw1_tablet_spies] Their account describes no formal agreement and no terms. After the visit, they write, James Jesus Angleton "was put in charge of the U.S. side", with Amos Manor and Teddy Kollek as his Israeli counterparts. [cite:rs_cw1_tablet_spies] Manor later described the difficulty: "It wasn't easy to persuade the anti-communist Angleton that we could be friends." [cite:rs_cw1_tablet_spies] The remark fits the starting point. On one reading, the obstacle on the American side was a doubt about which side of the East–West line Israel stood on.

Shiloah, the head of the new coordinating institute, had his own Western channels. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says he developed contacts with the CIA and with other Western intelligence services. It gives no date. [cite:rs_cw1_ej_shiloah] Whether those contacts came before Ben-Gurion's meeting, prepared it or followed it, the record cited here does not say.

Another account gives the beginning a firmer shape. In it, formal liaison between the CIA and the Mossad began in 1951, when the two agencies agreed not to spy on each other, a "friends don't spy on friends" arrangement, and the CIA's counterintelligence chief, Angleton, personally managed the relationship from 1951 onward. [cite:wrmea_cia_mossad_tradeoffs] [cite:michaelcronin_cia_mossad_relationship] The same account credits Angleton with greater influence on American relations with Israel in his time than any Secretary of State except possibly Henry Kissinger, and describes the exchange that followed: American intelligence on the Arab states, in return for high-value material from Israel. [cite:wrmea_cia_mossad_tradeoffs] [cite:michaelcronin_cia_mossad_relationship] On two points, its date for Angleton's role and its date for the no-spying understanding, this account is contradicted by other sources, one of them the CIA's own historian.

The first correction comes from the CIA's own historian. David Robarge writes that Angleton became head of the new Counterintelligence Staff in 1954, not 1951. [cite:rs_cw1_robarge_angleton] He calls Angleton's control of Israel's account at the CIA "an administrative anomaly", and he counts it among the foundations of Angleton's influence inside the agency. Angleton, he writes, saw Israel as a bastion against the Soviet Union. [cite:rs_cw1_robarge_angleton] On this reading, Angleton could not have run the relationship as counterintelligence chief in 1951, because by Robarge's dating he did not head the Counterintelligence Staff, which Robarge describes as new, until 1954. And the account was his by an arrangement that was itself irregular, not by the ordinary working of the agency's structure.

The second correction concerns the understanding not to spy. Jeff McConnell, writing in 1986, said that Angleton had exercised formal authority over CIA liaison with Israel "since the early 1950s (how early is a matter of dispute)", and that the Israel desk sat under his counterintelligence staff. [cite:rs_cw1_merip_mcconnell] He placed the deliberate effort to end covert operations against each other in the mid-1950s, and cited the journalist Wolf Blitzer for a "discreet arrangement since the 1950s, banning covert operations against each other." [cite:rs_cw1_merip_mcconnell] That is a looser and later date than the 1951 agreement of the other account.

Each version has its strongest form. The case for 1951 rests on Ben-Gurion's meeting with Bedell Smith, which Melman and Raviv date to that year, and on the agreement of several accounts that something began then. [cite:rs_cw1_tablet_spies] The case for a later and more gradual start rests on the CIA's own historian, who dates Angleton's post to 1954, and on McConnell, who says plainly that the date is disputed and dates the no-spying effort to the mid-1950s. [cite:rs_cw1_robarge_angleton] [cite:rs_cw1_merip_mcconnell] The two can be partly reconciled. A first contact in 1951, at the level of a prime minister and a director, may well have preceded both a formal liaison channel and a mutual understanding by several years. Robarge's date and McConnell's caution weigh against the specific claim that Angleton ran the relationship as counterintelligence chief in 1951, and against a no-spying agreement in that year. They do not weigh against a beginning in 1951.

The mechanism, as far as the sources show it, was personal before it was institutional. On the American side the decision ran from the Director of Central Intelligence, persuaded by the Israeli prime minister in person, to a single officer who held the account by what the agency's own historian calls an anomaly. On the Israeli side the counterparts named are Manor and Kollek, with Shiloah's separate contacts in the background. The Israeli services themselves answered to the prime minister, as told in the section on their founding. Who is absent is as telling: the sources cited here do not show the State Department or Congress involved at all. Nor do they describe any money moving between the services.

A further piece of the structure was laid in 1952. According to the reference account cited here, Israel's signals intelligence corps, Unit 8200, was founded in 1952, subordinate to Aman, the Military Intelligence Directorate. [cite:unit8200_wiki] Military publications call it the Israeli SIGINT National Unit, ISNU, the designation later used in American documents, and it is widely described as Israel's rough equivalent of the American National Security Agency. [cite:unit8200_wiki] This book has not confirmed the founding date from a primary document, and it should be read as reported. The same source's estimate of 5,000–10,000 personnel is not a figure for 1952. [cite:unit8200_wiki] Its later cooperation with the NSA, and the friction recorded in an NSA officer's account of the 2006 war in Lebanon, belong to a much later chapter: [scene:nsa_s01|Unit 8200 and the NSA].

The relationship's later course can be marked here only in outline. Melman and Raviv call the handover to the CIA in 1956, through Israeli intelligence in Warsaw, of Khrushchev's secret speech "the great turning point" of the relationship, an episode that belongs to Stage Two. [cite:rs_cw1_tablet_spies] The partnership's own record also documents friction alongside cooperation, including the Jonathan Pollard espionage case, which belongs to a later volume. [cite:wiki_israeli_espionage_us]

One discipline from the account that dates the liaison to 1951 deserves to be carried forward, because it applies from the first year to the last. Two real relationships that share one partner do not, by themselves, prove a third relationship between the other two. That account applies the rule to a twenty-first-century case: the CIA's documented tie to Israel's services, and its separate venture investment, from around 2005, in the data company Palantir, do not establish any tie between Israel's services and Palantir, and none is documented. [cite:wiki_palantir_technologies] A shared hub is not a pipeline. The same rule governs the early 1950s. That the CIA dealt with Israeli intelligence, and also with other Western services, and that Shiloah had contacts with several of them, does not make them one network, and the record of these years shows no such thing.

What the record does not settle should be stated without hedging. No document cited here records the terms of any agreement made in 1951, and the fullest account of that year says plainly that it describes none. The date of Shiloah's Western contacts is not given. When Angleton first took responsibility for the Israeli account, and on whose authority, is disputed by the sources themselves, one of which is the CIA's own historian. The no-spying understanding has three dates in circulation: 1951, "since the 1950s", and the mid-1950s. And the founding date of Unit 8200 rests on a reference account rather than a primary record. The beginning of the partnership is real. Its precise shape in 1951 is not yet documented.

sections.h: The Canal Closed to Israel: Egypt's Restrictions and Resolution 95, 1951
sections.html:
In August 1951, while Israel's aid was before the Senate, the Security Council took up a quarrel over the Suez Canal. The armistice between Egypt and Israel stopped the fighting. It did not, in Egypt's view, end the war. The clearest test of that view came not on the armistice line but at the Suez Canal, where Egypt stopped and searched ships and seized goods bound for Israel. On 1 September 1951 the Council ruled on the practice. The resolution it adopted, Resolution 95, is short. The argument behind it, over whether a state could remain at war with a neighbour it had signed an armistice with, ran on for years.

Egypt's legal case deserves to be stated first and at full strength, because it was a legal case and not merely a refusal. Leo Gross, writing in the American Journal of International Law in 1957, reconstructed it from the record. [cite:rs_cw1_gross_ajil_1957] Its foundation was that a state of belligerency still existed between Egypt and Israel. In the words Gross quotes from the record, the measures were taken "in the state of belligerency which in our opinion still exists between Egypt and Israel." An armistice, on this reading, suspended hostilities; it was not peace. A belligerent at war keeps the rights of a belligerent, among them the right of visit, search and seizure of contraband, and Egypt's regulations of 1950 rested on that right. [cite:rs_cw1_gross_ajil_1957]

Three further arguments stood on that foundation. The first concerned the Constantinople Convention of 1888. Israel was not a signatory, and Egypt argued that the Convention did not bind it toward a state that had not signed. The second concerned the Security Council's competence: Egypt maintained that the Council lacked authority over the matter. The third was practical. The restrictions, Egypt said, guarded against sabotage in the Canal. [cite:rs_cw1_gross_ajil_1957] Taken together, the case was coherent. If the war continued, the searches were lawful acts of war; if Israel had no rights under the Convention, it could not complain of a breach of it; and if the Council had no authority, its view did not bind.

The case against Egypt was made in the Council debate. On 16 August 1951, at the 553rd meeting, the representative of Ecuador answered Egypt's foundation directly. "There are at present no real hostilities," he said. Self-defence could not be invoked without an actual armed attack, and the interference with shipping could not be reconciled with the Constantinople Convention. [cite:rs_cw1_spv553] Ecuador's argument turned Egypt's own terms around. Egypt claimed a war; Ecuador pointed to the absence of any fighting. Egypt claimed self-defence; Ecuador asked where the attack was.

The Council adopted its resolution on 1 September 1951, at its 558th meeting, by eight votes to none. The United States voted in favour. China, India and the Soviet Union abstained. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_res95] [cite:rs_cw1_spv558] The text proceeded in steps. It noted that the armistice regime had now lasted nearly two and a half years and was "of a permanent character," and that Egypt had not heeded the plea of the UN Chief of Staff to stop "interfering with the passage through the Suez Canal of goods destined for Israel." [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_res95] It then gave its findings. Egypt's practice was "an abuse of the exercise of the right of visit, search and seizure." It could not be justified as self-defence. It was an "unjustified interference with the rights of nations to navigate the seas and to trade freely with one another." And, the Council held, neither party could reasonably claim to be "actively a belligerent." [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_res95]

Its demand followed from those findings. The Council called on Egypt to terminate the restrictions on "the passage of international commercial shipping and goods" through the Canal, except for what was needed for the safety of shipping in the Canal itself. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_res95] The exception mattered. The Council did not deny Egypt all control over the Canal; it allowed whatever measures the safety of the waterway required, and ruled out only those aimed at Israel-bound trade.

The resolution answered Egypt's foundation without using Egypt's terms. Egypt had said that belligerency continued; the Council said the armistice was of a permanent character and that no party could be "actively a belligerent." It did not declare the war over, and it did not say the armistice was peace. It said that whatever the formal state of relations, a party to an armistice of two and a half years' standing could not exercise wartime rights against the other's trade. The abstentions are part of the record of what the Council decided. Three of its members declined to vote for that conclusion.

The final exchange at the 558th meeting shows how far apart the two sides remained once the vote was taken. Egypt's representative, Mahmoud Fawzi, told the Council that "Peace is acts and facts." He spoke of people driven from their homes, likened the Council's demand to an unconditional surrender, and reserved his government's rights. [cite:rs_cw1_spv558] The record cited here does not say further whom he meant; twelve days later the Conciliation Commission opened its conference in Paris on the future of the Palestinian refugees, as told in [scene:cw1_refugees|the refugee question after Lausanne]. Eban, for Israel, read the vote the other way. The Council, he said, had rejected "one-sided belligerency or unilateral blockade" and had affirmed the armistice as a path to permanent peace. [cite:rs_cw1_spv558] For Eban the armistice was a step toward peace that Egypt was refusing to take; for Fawzi a demand to behave as if at peace, while the conditions of peace were absent, was a demand for surrender.

The mechanism behind the dispute was simple, and that is why it was hard to move. Egypt held the Canal. Its regulations of 1950 gave its officials the instrument: the right to stop, search and seize. The only body that could pronounce on the practice was the Security Council, whose competence Egypt disputed, and the Council's resolution called on Egypt to act. It did not provide any means to make it act. Israel, whose trade bore the cost, could complain but could not open the Canal. The United States, which voted for the resolution, could press Egypt; in the same autumn it was also seeking, with Britain, Turkey and France, Egypt's partnership in a regional defence command, as told in [scene:cw1_mec|the Middle East Command]. The vote of 1 September and the invitation of 13 October were addressed to the same government six weeks apart.

The dispute itself should be left where the sources leave it. Egypt's position, that a state of belligerency survived the armistice, that the Constantinople Convention did not run in favour of a non-signatory, and that the Council lacked authority, was argued on legal grounds and is documented as Egypt's position. [cite:rs_cw1_gross_ajil_1957] The opposite position, that the armistice was permanent in character, that no party could claim to be actively a belligerent, and that the searches were an abuse of visit and search, was the position of the resolution and of Israel and Ecuador in the debate. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_res95] [cite:rs_cw1_spv558] [cite:rs_cw1_spv553] What the Council decided is a matter of record: by eight votes to none it adopted the second view. Whether that decision settled the legal question is a separate matter, and three abstaining members, along with Egypt's own reservation of its rights, show that it was not settled by agreement.

Several things the sources used here do not record. They do not give the number of ships stopped or the value of the cargoes seized under the 1950 regulations. They do not explain why China, India and the Soviet Union abstained. And they do not show what Egypt did after 1 September 1951 in response to the resolution beyond Fawzi's reservation of rights. The Canal's story after 1951, through the crisis of 1956, belongs to Stage Three.

sections.h: Outside the Command: Western Defence Plans and Israel, 1951–1953
sections.html:
The Canal vote of 1 September was one half of the West's dealings with Cairo in the autumn of 1951; the other was an invitation. By then Israel's government had moved toward the West, through the Korean vote and Ben-Gurion's offers of 1950, as told in [scene:cw1_korea|the Korean decision]. Moving toward the West did not make Israel part of the West's defence plans for the region. The plans Britain and the United States drew up in 1951 were built around a different country, Egypt, and they treated Israel in two ways that Ben-Gurion found equally unwelcome: first as a site for British bases, then as a state to be told about a command it had not been asked to found. This section follows those plans from the first British approach in February 1951 to the fading of the idea in 1953.

The British approach came first. Before General Sir Brian Robertson visited Israel on 19 February 1951, Sir William Strang had already floated two possibilities: a British base in Gaza with a corridor running through Israel, or British bases in Israel itself under a treaty. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] Ben-Gurion's answer, as Avi Shlaim records it, was that this was "an insulting proposal." What he asked for instead was a relationship of a different kind: that Israel be treated "as if they were Australia or New Zealand." [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] The comparison asked for the standing of a partner rather than the role of a host. Ben-Gurion was not refusing alignment with the West. He was refusing a form of it in which Israel supplied ground and Britain supplied the terms.

The British reply did not meet him. Herbert Morrison's answer of 23 April 1951 was, in Shlaim's description, lukewarm, and offered Israel only a back-door association with a regional defence body. Ben-Gurion insisted on full membership. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] The gap between the two positions was the whole of the question. Britain wanted Israel's territory, or at least its association, in a scheme whose centre lay elsewhere; Israel wanted a seat at the table on the same footing as the scheme's founders.

Where the centre lay became clear in October. On 13 October 1951 the United States, Britain and Turkey, joined by France, formally tendered to Egypt an invitation to join a Middle East Command "as a founding member." [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mec_note] The timing could hardly have been worse for the sponsors. By the day the invitation was delivered, Egypt had already abrogated its 1936 treaty with Britain and the 1899 agreements on the Sudan. On 15 October it rejected the invitation. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mec_note] The United States did not accept the abrogation. Acheson's note to Egypt, sent through the American embassy, called it "without validity" and a "serious retrograde step" for collective defence. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_egypt_note] Six weeks earlier the United States had voted to call on Egypt to end its restrictions on Israel-bound shipping; now it was asking the same government to be the founding regional member of its defence command and protesting when that government abrogated its treaty with Britain.

The rest of the region was to be handled differently. The State Department proposed that the four sponsoring powers inform the Arab states, Egypt excepted, and Israel that they "intend establish MEC," without exhorting them to join. Israel was to receive a separate approach in Tel Aviv, asking it to "give most serious consideration" to a question that "involves vitally" its security. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mec_circular] The wording sets out the hierarchy exactly. Egypt was invited to found the command. The other Arab states and Israel were informed that it would be established. Israel alone was told, separately, that the matter concerned it vitally, and was asked to consider it seriously. It was not asked to found anything.

One reading, offered here as interpretation, is that the structure reflects a convergence of interests rather than any single design. Three interests met in these documents, and none of them was secret. Britain's was a base: Strang's proposals of early 1951 were proposals for British bases and a corridor, and the Middle East Command was offered first to Egypt. Egypt's was sovereignty: the abrogation of the 1936 treaty and the Sudan agreements came before the invitation was delivered, and Egypt rejected the command two days after receiving it. Israel's was recognition as a partner: Ben-Gurion rejected the base proposal as insulting and asked for full membership on the model of Australia and New Zealand. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mec_note] The American documents show Washington trying to hold these together, protesting Egypt's abrogation while keeping the invitation open, and approaching Israel with care but without an offer of founding status. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_egypt_note] [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mec_circular] No one in the record cited here proposed a command in which all three interests could be satisfied at once.

The mechanism, on the same reading, also suggests who could act. The sponsoring powers decided who would be invited and on what terms. Egypt, as the invited founding member, held a veto in practice: without it, a command built around it had no centre, and Egypt used that position to refuse. The other Arab states and Israel could only respond to a decision already taken. Israel had the clearest wish to join and the least say in the design. Its willingness to join gave it little leverage while the sponsors were still seeking Egypt.

The scheme did not recover from Egypt's refusal. According to Shlaim, a British military delegation failed to break the deadlock in October 1952, and in 1953 the idea of a Middle East Command faded. Israel's hope of military integration with the West, he writes, faded with it. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] Egypt itself had changed in the meantime: its Free Officers overthrew King Farouk in July 1952, and the new regime's course belongs to Stage Two. [cite:w_1952_egypt] The new American administration's own reassessment of the region in 1953, and of Israel's place in it, is told in [scene:cw1_dulles_1953|Dulles's line].

The record cited here leaves several things open. It does not show how Israel answered the separate approach in Tel Aviv, or whether the four powers' intended notice to the Arab states was ever delivered in the form the State Department proposed. It does not record the Arab states' responses to the command. It gives Ben-Gurion's reaction to the British proposals through Shlaim's account, not through the British or Israeli documents themselves, and it does not give the text of Morrison's reply. What it does establish is the order of priority in 1951: in the West's plans for the region's defence, Egypt was the state to be won, and Israel, however willing, was a state to be informed.

sections.h: The Refugee Question After Lausanne: UNRWA, Paris and the Reintegration Fund, 1950–1953
sections.html:
Neither the Canal dispute nor the plans for a defence command touched the largest human question the war of 1948 had left behind. The Conciliation Commission's conference at Lausanne in 1949 had ended without a settlement of the refugee question; the positions that failed to meet there are told in [scene:lau_s01|Lausanne, 1949]. In the four years that followed, the question moved along two tracks at once. One was diplomatic: the Commission tried again, in Paris in the autumn of 1951, with a package of five specific proposals. The other was administrative: a new UN agency, UNRWA, took over relief for the refugees, and the General Assembly gave it money to do more than provide relief. The two tracks were meant to converge in a settlement. By 1953 they had not, and a new generation of Palestinian students had begun to organize politically.

UNRWA's first report covered the period from 1 May 1950 to 30 June 1951. It gave the agency's headquarters as Beirut and divided its work into five districts: Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Gaza and Israel. It employed 133 international staff and 5,840 local staff. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] Israel's appearance on the list is easily overlooked; in its first year the agency counted Israel among the districts where it worked, though the report as excerpted does not give the numbers it served there. The agency's first director, Howard Kennedy, was succeeded by John B. Blandford Jr., who arrived on 4 July 1951. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951]

The money that paid for this came overwhelmingly from one government. The report lists cash contributions for the period: the United States $27,450,000, Britain $6,200,000, France $2,285,714, Canada $894,313 and Israel $50,000. It lists separately the direct contributions made in the region by the host and neighbouring states: Egypt $1,961,300, Iraq $980,000, Lebanon $457,800 and Jordan $323,900. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] The two lists measure different things. The first is money paid to the agency; the second is support given directly in the region, by states several of which were also hosting refugees. Read together, they show who paid for the refugee system in its first year: the United States far more than any other government, Britain second, and Israel a small cash contribution. How the American share was voted in Congress, alongside the first US grant aid to Israel, is told in [scene:cw1_grant_aid|the first US grant aid].

From the start the money was meant to do two things. The General Assembly's Resolution 393 (V) had recommended $20 million for relief and $30 million for a reintegration fund for the year to 30 June 1952. [cite:rs_cw1_un_yearbook_1951] Reintegration, as the Assembly later put it, could come "either by repatriation or resettlement," and the choice between the two was the political question the agency could not answer for itself. [cite:rs_cw1_ga_res513]

In Washington the case for paying was made in the language of stability. On 27 July 1951 President Truman wrote to the congressional committee chairmen that the refugees' condition was "one of the principal causes of tension in the Near East." He added that the Arab League had endorsed a large resettlement program for Palestinian refugees in Arab states. [cite:rs_cw1_truman_unrpr_letter] That second statement is Truman's account of the League's position, and it should be read as such: the record cited here does not include the League's own resolution, and it sits uneasily beside what the Arab delegations said in Paris weeks later.

The Paris conference opened at the Hôtel de Crillon on 13 September 1951 and ran until 19 November. The Commission put five proposals to the Arab delegations on 17 September and to Israel on 21 September. The proposals were mutual cancellation of war-damage claims; repatriation by Israel of "a specified number of Arab refugees"; payment by Israel of a global sum in compensation; mutual release of blocked accounts; and revision of the armistice agreements. [cite:rs_cw1_unccp_a1985] Read as a whole, the package asked each side to give something on a point where the other most wanted movement: Israel on return and compensation, the Arab states on war damages and on revising the armistices. The record cited here does not say how the Commission itself described the logic of the package.

To make compensation discussable, the Commission needed a figure, and its Refugee Office supplied one. It valued the land the Arab refugees had abandoned at 100 million Palestine pounds, about $280 million at the rate then current, and their movable property at about £P20 million. The land covered 16,324 square kilometres, of which 4,574 square kilometres were cultivable. [cite:rs_cw1_unccp_a1985] The valuation gave the negotiation a figure to discuss. It did not settle who would pay it, to whom, or on what terms.

Israel's answers, as the Commission recorded them, were consistent and specific. It refused mutual cancellation of war damages, on the ground that the Arab states had been the aggressors and should bear war damages. It rejected repatriation, because "major considerations of security and of political and economic stability made the return of Arab refugees impossible." It offered compensation, but as a global sum that would end the refugee problem for Israel. And it attached a condition of its own: any settlement must unfreeze the Jewish accounts blocked in Iraq. [cite:rs_cw1_unccp_a1985] That last condition linked the Palestinian refugees' property to the property of Iraq's Jews, whose departure from Iraq in these years is told in [scene:rd6_exodus|the Jews of the Arab world]. In Israel's case the two losses were part of one account.

The strongest form of Israel's position followed from its premises. A state that held the Arab states responsible for the war, and that judged the return of the refugees a danger to its security and to its political and economic stability, could argue that it should not be required to take them back. A global payment would close the matter. And if property was to be compensated, the property Jews had left in an Arab state belonged in the same reckoning. Each of these points is stated in the Commission's report in Israel's own terms. [cite:rs_cw1_unccp_a1985]

The Arab delegations answered from the opposite premise. "There could be no limitations on the return of the refugees," they said. Compensation should be individual, paid in cash, and not tied to Israel's ability to pay. They accepted the release of blocked accounts. On the fifth proposal, Syria said that revising the armistices sought to "ratify a fait accompli." [cite:rs_cw1_unccp_a1985] The strongest form of this position, too, followed from its premises. Return, on the Arab reading of Resolution 194, was a right belonging to each refugee, not a concession to be measured out by number; compensation was owed to individuals for their own property, not to be negotiated down to a lump sum that ended a state's responsibility; and changing the armistice lines before a settlement would have turned the results of the war into borders. On one proposal, the release of blocked accounts, the Arab delegations said yes; Israel's recorded answer on that point was its Iraqi condition.

The Commission's verdict named both sides. Neither side, it found, showed "a willingness substantially to recede from its rigid position," and it ended the conference on 19 November 1951. Its report named the two refusals that had stopped it. Israel was not prepared to implement paragraph 11 of Resolution 194, the paragraph on return. The Arab governments were not prepared fully to implement paragraph 5, the paragraph calling for peace negotiations. Together, the Commission wrote, these positions had made it "impossible for the Commission to carry out its mandate." [cite:rs_cw1_unccp_a1985] That finding is the best answer the record gives to the question of who blocked a settlement at Paris. It does not assign the failure to one side. It names a refusal by each, on the paragraph of the same resolution that the other side most needed.

The General Assembly's response was to fund the administrative track on a larger scale while protecting the diplomatic one. Resolution 513 (VI), adopted on 26 January 1952, endorsed a programme of $50 million for relief and $200 million for reintegration over about three years from 1 July 1951. The reintegration was to come "either by repatriation or resettlement," and the whole programme was declared to be "without prejudice to the provisions of paragraph 11 of resolution 194 (III)." The budget for 1952–53 was set at $118 million: $100 million for reintegration and $18 million for relief. [cite:rs_cw1_ga_res513] The phrase "without prejudice" carried the weight of the resolution. It allowed the UN to pay for resettlement without conceding that resettlement replaced return. Whether the refugees would accept that distinction was another matter.

The clearest test came in Sinai. According to Jonathan Adler, writing in 2023 from the papers of Blandford and of Labouisse, UNRWA had begun working with Egypt on Sinai schemes as early as July 1950. In June 1953, Adler writes, the agency reserved $30 million of its $200 million reintegration fund for a siphon scheme to resettle 60,000 refugees from Gaza on nearly 52,000 acres. Palestinians objected to the scheme as a threat to the right of return. [cite:rs_cw1_newlines_sinai] The objection put into practice what the Arab delegations had said in Paris: resettlement funded "without prejudice" to return was, to the Palestinians who objected, a prejudice all the same. What became of the scheme and of the opposition to it belongs to Gaza in 1955, told in Stage Two.

The refugees' own politics were taking shape in these same years, among students. Yasir Arafat, studying engineering in Cairo, took part in founding the Palestinian Students League in 1951, was elected its president at the start of the 1952 academic year, and held the post until he graduated in 1956. [cite:rs_cw1_palquest_arafat] George Habash came to politics by a different road. His family was expelled from Lydda after the town fell on 11 July 1948. He had been general secretary of the student society al-'Urwa al-Wuthqa in 1949–50, graduated from the American University of Beirut in 1951, and in 1952 opened a free clinic for refugees and the poor in Amman with Wadi Haddad. [cite:rs_cw1_palquest_habash] In 1953 both were at the beginning: one led a students' league in Cairo, the other ran a clinic in Amman.

When Habash's own movement began is itself disputed. One account places the founding of the Arab Nationalist Movement at the beginning of the 1950s, at the American University of Beirut, by founders who included Habash and Hani al-Hindi. [cite:rs_cw1_encyc_anm] Another dates it to December 1956, when Habash announced the movement at a general congress in Amman under the slogan "Unity, Liberation, Revenge." [cite:rs_cw1_palquest_habash] The two dates may describe different things, a circle formed at the university and a movement publicly launched, but the sources do not say so, and the question is left open here.

What the record of 1950–1953 does not settle should be stated plainly. It shows the positions each side took at Paris, in their own words, and the Commission's finding that both refused to move; it does not show what either would have accepted under sustained pressure, and no power in the record cited here applied any. It gives Truman's statement that the Arab League had endorsed a large resettlement programme, but not the League's own text, and that statement does not square easily with the Arab delegations' insistence on unlimited return; the sources do not reconcile the two. It gives the Refugee Office's valuation, but no agreed figure was ever reached, and the record does not show how the valuation was calculated beyond its totals. It does not give the number of refugees UNRWA served in its Israel district. And the account of the Sinai scheme rests on one historian's reading of the agency's papers, reported in a single article. By the end of 1953 the UN had a large fund, an agency with 133 international and 5,840 local staff, and a valuation of the refugees' land. It had no agreement on whether they would go home, and, by the one account cited here, Palestinians had objected to the largest resettlement scheme yet proposed as a threat to their return.

sections.h: "Under God": The American Home Front, 1951–1953
sections.html:
While the United Nations argued over the refugees' future and Israel's government chose a side abroad, the country it was turning toward was arguing about how to describe itself at home. The words "under God" entered the American Pledge of Allegiance in June 1954, and the familiar account treats the change as a single act of Congress in a single anti-communist moment. The record shows a longer campaign with more than one origin. Its documented engine for most of 1951–1953 was a fraternal order, the Knights of Columbus, working through its own rituals, its state councils and finally the mail to every member of Congress. A second, earlier campaign, traced by the historian Kevin Kruse, ran through business-funded clergy and had a domestic target as much as a foreign one. This section tells the campaign to the end of 1953; the law itself, and the question the law left open, belong to Stage Two.

The first documented step was internal. On 22 April 1951, according to an account published by Gene T. Janikowski of the Knights of Columbus South Carolina State Council, the order's Board of Directors adopted a resolution adding "under God" to the Pledge as it was recited at the order's Fourth Degree assemblies. [cite:rs_cw1_kofc_janikowski] The change applied to the Knights' own meetings, not to the country. It was a fraternal order amending its own ritual, with no legal force outside the order. One reading of why the step mattered is that it gave the wording a body of members who already said it, before anyone asked Congress to adopt it.

In 1952 the order turned outward. Knights of Columbus state councils in Florida, South Dakota, New York and Michigan urged Congress to amend the Pledge, and on 21 August 1952 the order's Supreme Council urged that the change be made general. [cite:rs_cw1_crec_2002] [cite:rs_cw1_kofc_janikowski] Both of these steps rest on accounts written later, one in the Congressional Record of 2002 and one by the order's own state council; neither reproduces the resolutions themselves, and the dates should be read as those sources give them.

The same sources disagree on one date in the campaign. The National Fraternal Congress, meeting in Boston, adopted a resolution on 24 September. The Congressional Record account of 2002 places that resolution in 1952. [cite:rs_cw1_crec_2002] Janikowski places it in 1953, though his chronology is not consistent with itself elsewhere. [cite:rs_cw1_kofc_janikowski] Neither text supplied here reproduces the resolution, so the year cannot be settled from these sources. If 1952 is right, a wider body of fraternal societies endorsed the idea within weeks of the Knights' Supreme Council; if 1953, it followed the order's second, larger push.

That second push came on 20 August 1953. According to the Congressional Record account of 2002, the Supreme Council repeated its call and, this time, sent copies to the President, the Vice President, the Speaker of the House and every member of Congress.
