Seventeen House resolutions followed. [cite:rs_cw1_crec_2002] The mechanism is plain in the sequence: a ritual change inside one order, then resolutions from state councils, then a national resolution, then a mailing that put the proposal on the desk of every legislator.

Kevin Kruse's account does not begin with the Knights at all. He traces an earlier campaign by the Reverend James Fifield, whose organization, Spiritual Mobilization, was funded by business leaders including J. Howard Pew and Alfred Sloan. It had about 17,000 minister representatives and used the slogan "Freedom Under God". Among its events was a ceremony on 4 July 1951 organized by Cecil B. DeMille. [cite:rs_cw1_npr_kruse] The money in this second story is named: it came from business leaders, it moved through a clerical organization, and its product was a phrase, "under God", attached to a political idea of freedom. Kruse also judges the Knights' role more modestly than the order's own historians do. In his telling, their proposal at first "doesn't go anywhere", and it "catches fire" only after Eisenhower's own pastor endorsed it. [cite:rs_cw1_npr_kruse] That endorsement is told in Stage Two.

The two accounts are not simply rival chronologies. They are rival explanations of motive, and both have documentary support of different kinds. The first is the explanation Congress gave for itself. When the change passed in 1954, the House report (H.R. Rep. No. 1693) presented the words as rejecting the communist philosophy "with its attendant subservience of the individual", and the Senate report (S. Rep. No. 1287) said: "The spiritual bankruptcy of the Communists is one of our strongest weapons in the struggle for men's minds." [cite:rs_cw1_doj_newdow_brief] Those reports survive here as quoted by the United States Solicitor General in his 2003–04 brief in Elk Grove Unified School District v. Newdow, and they are the strongest evidence for the Cold War reading: they are the legislators' own stated reasons, written at the time.

The second explanation is Kruse's interpretation, and it should be read as one. He argues that the common story, in which "the Soviet Union discovered the bomb and the United States rediscovered God", papers over a domestic conflict, and that the architects of this language were most worried about the New Deal and Fair Deal administrations. [cite:rs_cw1_npr_kruse] The strongest form of his case is the timing and the money: a business-funded campaign using "Freedom Under God" was already running, with thousands of ministers attached, before the Knights' resolutions reached Congress. Its limit is that the source given here is an interview, not his full documentation, and that it does not show the Knights of Columbus themselves acting for Fifield's sponsors. The two readings can both be partly true: a domestic campaign could have supplied the phrase, and a Cold War consensus could have supplied the votes.

The outcome, briefly, because it is told in full in the next stage. The resolution of Representative Louis C. Rabaut of Michigan passed both houses, and President Eisenhower signed the change on Flag Day, 14 June 1954. On the House floor Rabaut said: "From their earliest childhood our children must know" what "under God" means. [cite:rs_cw1_crec_2002] [cite:rs_cw1_doj_newdow_brief] On 17 August 1954 Eisenhower wrote to the Supreme Knight, Luke Hart, that he was "particularly thankful to you for your part in the movement", and said the words would remind Americans "that despite our great physical strength we must remain humble." [cite:rs_cw1_crec_2002] The letter is the documented acknowledgement of the order's role, from the President who signed the law. Religious language entered the national coinage and motto in the same years: according to Kruse, "In God we trust" went onto a stamp in 1954, onto paper money by act of Congress in 1955, and became the national motto in 1956. [cite:rs_cw1_npr_kruse]

One question a reader of this volume will bring to the subject should be answered directly. Nothing in these sources connects the campaign to Israel, to any Zionist organization, or to the diplomacy told elsewhere in this stage. The 1954 committee reports, Rabaut's floor remark, Eisenhower's letter and Spiritual Mobilization's slogan, as documented here, speak of communism, of the individual, of children, of humility and of freedom; none mentions Israel. Any reading that ties the change to Israel would be interpretation, and it is not made here. What the campaign does show is the domestic side of the alignment this stage describes: in the same years that Washington was asking Middle Eastern states to choose between East and West, the language of American public life was being recast in religious terms, by a fraternal order and by business-funded clergy, terms that the 1954 committee reports would present as a contrast with communism.

Several things the record here does not settle. The year of the National Fraternal Congress resolution remains open between 1952 and 1953. The text of the Knights' 1951 and 1952 resolutions is not reproduced in these sources, so their stated reasons cannot be compared directly with the 1954 reports. Whether the Knights' campaign drew on Fifield's, or ran in parallel without contact, is not shown. And the weight of each motive, the Cold War contrast the legislators named and the domestic quarrel Kruse identifies, is a matter of interpretation that the documents can inform but not decide. What the law said, and how the President's own pastor came to endorse it, are taken up in [scene:cw2_pledge|Stage Two's account of the Pledge].

sections.h: From Patron to Rupture: Moscow and Israel, 1947–1953
sections.html:
While the American campaign was recasting public language against communism, the communist power that had helped found Israel was turning against it. A common account of Israel's early foreign policy runs in one line: the Soviet Union helped create the state, the state chose America, and Moscow turned hostile in return. The record supports each part of that sentence and complicates the order. Soviet support in 1947–48 was real. Soviet hostility from late 1951 was also real, and it took a form that cannot be described accurately without naming it: show trials and an announced conspiracy in which Jews, Zionism and Israel's own diplomats were cast as agents of Western intelligence. Between those two points lies a dispute that historians have not closed, over whether Moscow pushed Israel away or Israel's own turn to the West drew Soviet hostility on itself. This section follows the relationship from the partition vote to the restoration of diplomatic relations in July 1953.

The beginning was cooperation, and in Cold War terms an unusual one. In 1947 the United States and the Soviet Union both voted for the partition of Palestine, which the historian Avi Shlaim calls "one of rare occasions of agreement between them during the Cold War". The Soviet Union extended recognition to the new state, and in 1948 the Eastern bloc was Israel's main supplier of arms. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] Drawing on the work of Uri Bialer, Shlaim argues that the Czechoslovak arms sales "continued for longer than would have been necessary" merely to create a Jewish state. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] That is an interpretation, but it matters to everything that followed. If the arms were meant only to help create a Jewish state, they need not have run on as long as they did. If they ran on, then on this reading Moscow was investing in a relationship with the state itself, and what it expected in return becomes the question.

The first public sign of a cooler Soviet line came over Jerusalem. On 9 December 1949 Moscow voted at the United Nations for the internationalization of the city. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] According to Bialer, as Shlaim reports him, Soviet attitudes shifted further when Israel publicly backed the American position on Korea in 1950. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] How that decision was made, in the cabinet and in the Knesset, is told in [scene:cw1_korea|the section on the Korean decision]. For the Soviet side of the story its significance is simple: the government that had called its policy non-identification with either bloc had now taken a public position with one of them.

The next turn came not in Moscow but in Prague. Rudolf Slánský, the former general secretary of the Czechoslovak Communist Party, was arrested in November 1951. In November 1952 he and 13 others were put on trial, and 11 of them, Slánský among them, were sentenced to death. The charges included that he was a Zionist agent and a Western spy. Most of those condemned were Jews. Slánský was executed on 3 December 1952. [cite:rs_cw1_britannica_slansky] The Jewish Telegraphic Agency, reporting during the trial, gave the count as 12 of the 14 defendants Jewish. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_prague_trial] The two figures measure slightly different things, defendants in one case and the condemned in the other, and they do not conflict.

What made the trial an event in Israel's foreign relations, and not only in Czechoslovakia's internal purge, was the indictment's reach. According to the JTA, it named Ben-Gurion and Sharett. It described Ehud Avriel, Israel's former minister to Czechoslovakia, as "an American spy covered by the immunity of Israel diplomatic passports". And it used the alleged confessions of Mordecai Oren, a leader of Israel's left-wing Mapam party who was then under arrest in Czechoslovakia, to tie Israel to the case. [cite:rs_cw1_jta_prague_trial] Shlaim describes the show trial as denouncing Zionism and calling Israel an agent of American imperialism. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] The mechanism, as these sources describe it, was a court in a Soviet-bloc state using alleged confessions to present Zionism, and Israel's own officials, as instruments of Western espionage. The trial's verdicts were not the last word on Slánský himself. He was cleared of the criminal charges in 1963 and restored to party membership in 1968. [cite:rs_cw1_britannica_slansky]

Six weeks after Slánský's execution the same pattern appeared in Moscow. On 13 January 1953 Pravda and Izvestiya announced the arrest of nine doctors, at least six of them Jewish. They were accused of poisoning Andrei Zhdanov and Alexander Shcherbakov, of plotting against Soviet marshals, and of working for American and British intelligence and "the interests of international Jewry." [cite:rs_cw1_britannica_doctors_plot] An American intelligence analysis written that summer read the affair the same way. A working paper of the CIA's Office of Current Intelligence, dated 14 July 1953, records that the announcement tied the doctors to a "Jewish-bourgeois nationalist group" backed by American and British intelligence, and notes the affair's "clearly antiSemitic overtones". It also records that the Soviet journal New Times, on 21 January, called Zionists and Israeli officials the "executors of a US State Department spy ring in the USSR." [cite:rs_cw1_cia_doctors_plot_1953] The charge had moved from Soviet-bloc defendants accused of Zionism, in Prague, to Zionists and Israeli officials as such, in Moscow.

The antisemitism in both cases should be named plainly, as the sources name it. It was the policy of named states and named organs: a Czechoslovak court, the Soviet official press, a Soviet journal. In Prague the condemned were mostly Jews and the charge was Zionism; in Moscow the official announcement invoked "international Jewry", and the CIA's own analysts called the overtones "clearly antiSemitic." [cite:rs_cw1_britannica_slansky] [cite:rs_cw1_britannica_doctors_plot] [cite:rs_cw1_cia_doctors_plot_1953] Israel's foreign minister said so in public. On 19 January 1953 Sharett condemned Soviet antisemitic and anti-democratic practices in the Knesset. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west]

Three weeks later the crisis turned violent. On 9 February 1953 a bomb of about 70 pounds of explosives went off in the garden of the Soviet legation in Tel Aviv. It injured one Soviet diplomat and the wives of two others. The attack was blamed on a group known as the Tzrifin Underground, whose leader, Yaakov Heruti, denied involvement; according to the Center for Israel Education, the government lacked proof. [cite:rs_cw1_israeled_legation] Israel apologized officially. Moscow broke relations anyway. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] According to the Jewish Chronicle's account, the Soviet Foreign Minister, Vyshinsky, summoned Israel's minister in Moscow, Samuel Eliashiv, at 1 a.m. and handed him a note demanding that the legation's diplomats "leave Moscow without delay", citing the "terrorist act". The Chronicle dates the break to 11 February 1953, and Shlaim gives the same day. [cite:rs_cw1_jc_soviet_break] [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] The bombing gave Moscow its stated reason. Whether it was the cause, or the occasion for a break that the trials had already prepared, is part of the dispute below.

The rupture lasted five months, and it ended after a death in Moscow and a pledge from Jerusalem. Stalin died on 5 March 1953, before any trial of the doctors had been held. In April 1953 Pravda announced that the charges against them were false and that their confessions had been obtained by torture; the surviving doctors were exonerated. [cite:rs_cw1_britannica_doctors_plot] Relations were restored in July 1953, after Israel said it would not join any alliance against the Soviet Union. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] The Center for Israel Education gives the date of the announcement as 21 July 1953. [cite:rs_cw1_israeled_legation] Restoration followed a statement about alignment: Israel would not make its Western tilt into a military pact against Moscow. The pledge bore on a question Israel had pursued since 1951, its place in Western regional defence, told in [scene:cw1_mec|the section on the Middle East Command].

The dispute is about causation, and both positions are serious. The first was the view of the Israeli establishment at the time, and Sharett gave it a phrase: Soviet policy followed its own "developmental logic". On this reading, the Prague trial and the Doctors' Plot were products of Soviet internal politics in Stalin's last years, and Israel was swept into them by the identity of the accused and the needs of the prosecutors, not by anything it did. The strongest evidence for it is in the documents themselves: the doctors' confessions were later declared by Pravda itself to have been obtained by torture, Slánský was cleared of the criminal charges in 1963, and the doctors' case collapsed within weeks of Stalin's death, which points to the regime's internal dynamics rather than to Israeli conduct. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] [cite:rs_cw1_britannica_doctors_plot]

The second position, Bialer's, as Shlaim presents it, is that Soviet aid and goodwill had been tied to Israel's foreign-policy orientation more closely than Israeli leaders assumed, and that they cooled as Israel sided with the West, most visibly over Korea. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] Its strongest evidence is the sequence before the trials: arms that ran on longer than state-building required, a cooler line on Jerusalem in December 1949, and a further shift after the Korean vote in 1950, all before Slánský's arrest. And the terms of restoration in July 1953, a pledge about alliances, suggest that Moscow cared about Israel's alignment, not only about the bombing it had cited. The two readings are not mutually exclusive. The trials could have had their own Soviet-bloc logic and still have been aimed at Israel more readily because Israel had already chosen a side.

Shlaim's own judgment, which is interpretation, is that the rift was "probably beyond repair", and that by the end of 1953 non-identification had been "replaced by an explicit pro-Western position." [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] On his reading, the restoration of July 1953 repaired the formal relationship but not the alignment that had produced the break.

Several matters remain open on these sources. Who set off the bomb at the Soviet legation was not proved: the Tzrifin Underground was blamed, its leader denied it, and the government lacked proof. Whether Moscow would have broken relations without the bombing cannot be shown from the record cited here. The sources do not say what the Soviet government demanded in the talks that led to restoration beyond Israel's statement on alliances, nor what became of Mordecai Oren after the trial in which his confessions were used. And the weight to give each side of the causal dispute rests on interpretation of a Soviet decision-making process that these sources describe only from the outside.

sections.h: "Impartial": The Dulles Line, May–July 1953
sections.html:
Moscow's break with Israel was not the only change of course in 1953. In the spring the new Eisenhower administration's Secretary of State travelled through the Near East, and when John Foster Dulles came home he told the American public what he had found. A familiar account treats American policy toward Israel as a straight line rising from 1948. The documents of 1953 show a bend in it. Dulles's report spoke of Arab resentment of the United States "that has resulted from the creation of Israel", of Arab fear that America would back Israel "in aggressive expansion", and of a policy toward Israel and the Arab states that must be "impartial". Within two months Washington publicly regretted an Israeli decision about Jerusalem. Neither step cut the relationship, and both need to be read with care about what each source actually is.

The address itself is a documented fact. On 1 June 1953 Dulles reported on his Near East trip over radio and television, and the text is printed in the Department of State Bulletin of 15 June 1953, pages 831 to 835. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1953_dulles_report] The words quoted in this section, however, do not come from the Bulletin text. They come from a contemporary newspaper account of the address and of Dulles's testimony to Congress, published in the Detroit Jewish News on 5 June 1953. [cite:rs_cw1_djn_dulles_1953] They are reported quotations, close to the event, and they should be checked against the Bulletin's pages before they are treated as the official wording.

As that account reported it, Dulles said the United States "should seek to allay the deep resentment against it that has resulted from the creation of Israel." He said: "Today the Arab peoples are afraid that the United States will back the new state of Israel in aggressive expansion." He said that Israel "should become a part of the Near East community", and that the United States would stand by the Tripartite Declaration. Before the House Foreign Affairs Committee he said that policy toward Israel and the Arab states must be "impartial." [cite:rs_cw1_djn_dulles_1953] On the two most contested questions of the period he went further. He said that "the world religious community has claims in Jerusalem which take precedence over the political claims of any particular nation." And on the refugees he said that some "could be settled in the area presently controlled by Israel", while most could more readily be integrated into neighbouring Arab countries, depending on irrigation. [cite:rs_cw1_djn_dulles_1953]

Each of those sentences touched a specific instrument of American policy. The Tripartite Declaration of 25 May 1950, in which the United States, Britain and France declared their "unalterable opposition to the use of force or threat of force" between states in the area, was the existing guarantee of the armistice lines, and Dulles kept it. [cite:rs_cw1_avalon_tripartite] On refugees, his formula left a door open to some return to Israeli-held territory, while placing most of the solution in Arab countries and tying it to water; the stalled diplomacy behind that question is told in this stage's account of the refugees after Lausanne. On Jerusalem, his words gave priority to the claims of "the world religious community" over those of "any particular nation", a formula that on its face covered Israel's claims as well.

The Jerusalem sentence was not abstract. The city's status in 1949–50 is told in [scene:rd6_un_admission|Israel's admission and the Jerusalem question]. In 1952 Israel's Foreign Ministry, through which foreign governments dealt with Israel, was still in Tel Aviv, and Israel planned to move it. The United States had objected to the plan in July 1952, under Truman, and again in March 1953, under the new administration. [cite:rs_cw1_jvl_fm_jerusalem_1953] Israel went ahead. On 28 July 1953 the United States publicly regretted the move of Israel's Foreign Ministry from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. The statement said the move would embarrass the United Nations, which "has a primary responsibility for determining the future status of Jerusalem"; that it "will add to rather than to relax" tensions in the area; and that the United States would not move its embassy. [cite:rs_cw1_jvl_fm_jerusalem_1953]

The mechanism was simple and limited. Two American objections had not stopped the move. What Washington controlled was where its own embassy stood, and therefore where American diplomats would do their business with the Israeli state. The statement used exactly that lever, and only that one: the embassy stayed in Tel Aviv. It also placed the question back where American policy held that it belonged, with the United Nations. The objections of July 1952 and March 1953 show that this was a continuing position across two administrations, not a new departure by Dulles; what was new in 1953 was the public statement after the fact.

Set side by side, the statements show both continuity and change. The guarantee of the armistice lines and the objection to the Foreign Ministry's move carried straight over from the Truman years. So did the logic of the Middle East Command proposal of 1951, in which Egypt was invited to be a founding member and Israel received a separate approach asking it to "give most serious consideration" to a question that "involves vitally" its security. [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mec_note] [cite:rs_cw1_frus1951_mec_circular] That proposal had faded by 1953, and with it, in Avi Shlaim's account, Israel's hope of military integration with the West. [cite:rs_cw1_shlaim_east_west] What changed in 1953 was the public diagnosis. In the address as reported, a Secretary of State told an American audience that the creation of Israel had produced resentment against the United States, and that Arab peoples feared Israeli expansion with American backing. The prescription followed from the diagnosis: Israel was to become "a part of the Near East community", and policy toward Israel and the Arab states must be "impartial".

How each side read the word "impartial" can be told only as far as the sources go, and here they go only a short way. The word had an Arab history in this chapter. When Lebanon's minister Charles Malik asked the State Department about the Tripartite Declaration in June 1950, he called it potentially the three powers' most important contribution to peace if it was carried out with "honest and sustained impartiality." [cite:rs_cw1_frus1950_malik] For one Arab diplomat, on that evidence, impartiality was the test American policy would have to meet; the source does not record what he took it to require. Whether Arab governments heard Dulles's 1953 word as the answer to that request, and whether Israel's government heard it as a retreat from the relationship of the Truman years, these sources do not record. They contain no Israeli or Arab government response to the address. The Detroit Jewish News account reports what Dulles said; it is not, on the evidence here, a statement of how Israel received it.

Two episodes followed in the next months, outside this stage. In September 1953 Washington suspended aid to Israel, an episode told in [scene:cw2_banat_yaacov|the 1953 aid suspension]. Then came Qibya, told in [scene:cw2_unit101_qibya|Unit 101 and Qibya]. Whether Dulles's June address foreshadowed those decisions, or whether they arose from their own events, is a question for Stage Two.

The gaps are plain. The Bulletin text of the address is cited but not quoted here, so the reported wording cannot be confirmed against it in this book. The sources do not record why Dulles chose the word "impartial", what instructions, if any, followed from it inside the State Department, or what Israel and the Arab states said in reply. Nor do they record Israel's own stated reasons for moving the Foreign Ministry in July 1953 despite two American objections. What is documented is the sequence: an address that named Arab resentment as a problem for American policy, and a public statement, eight weeks later, that drew the line on Jerusalem at the American embassy's door.

sections.h: The Coup of August 1953: TPAJAX and Boot
sections.html:
By the autumn of 1952 the Anglo-Iranian dispute had run through a court case, two missions, an embargo and a diplomatic break, as told earlier in this chapter. In 1953 it was settled by other means. On 19 August 1953 Mohammad Mossadeq, the prime minister the Majlis had brought to office in 1951, was overthrown in a coup that the American Central Intelligence Agency and Britain's Secret Intelligence Service had planned under the names TPAJAX and Boot. The fact of the operation is no longer in dispute; the CIA's own history of it has been released. What remains argued is narrower and harder: exactly when it was approved, how much it cost and on what, how much of the result was the work of foreigners and how much of Iranians, and whether oil or fear of the Soviet Union drove it.

A common explanation of the long hostility between Iran and the United States holds that it springs from religious fanaticism and nothing else. The record of 1953 shows a documented foreign operation against a constitutional, nationalist government, a quarter-century before the Islamic Republic existed. It does not, on its own, prove that later hostility began there, or that the operation was undertaken only to protect oil. Both of those are arguments about the record, and historians make them in more than one direction. This section sets out what the documents establish and where the arguments begin.

The planning began in mid-May 1953. That is the date given by a CIA Directorate of Plans memorandum of March 1954, titled "Campaign to Install Pro-Western Government in Iran," which the State Department later printed in its documentary series. The memorandum sets out two objectives: to bring about the fall of the Mossadeq government "through legal or quasi-legal methods," and to replace it with a pro-Western government under the Shah, with General Fazlollah Zahedi as prime minister. [cite:rs_cw1_frus_iran_d363] The plan built on earlier British planning. [cite:greydynamics_tpajax_overview] [cite:globalsecurity_operation_ajax] For Britain the operation was Boot; for the CIA it was TPAJAX, also called Operation Ajax. [cite:greydynamics_tpajax_overview]

The British motive was the one the oil crisis had made plain. Mossadeq's government had nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, later BP, and Britain wanted the concession restored. [cite:wiki_1953_iranian_coup] According to one widely cited account, Britain first tried to bring Mossadeq down through blockade and boycott, and when that failed, its intelligence service planned a coup and brought it to the Americans; the British supplied the original networks and much of the apparatus on the ground, and the CIA the scale, the money and the political will once Washington had been persuaded to treat an oil dispute as a front of the Cold War. [cite:wiki_1953_iranian_coup] That is a summary reading, not a quotation from the British or American files; the files themselves are taken up below.

On the British side, the approval is dated. According to the historian Malcolm Byrne's reading of the State Department's 2017 volume, Donald Wilber's internal CIA history confirms that Winston Churchill approved the overthrow on 1 July 1953. [cite:rs_cw1_atlantic_byrne_2017] On the American side, the date is disputed, and the dispute itself tells something about how such decisions were recorded. Kermit Roosevelt, the CIA officer who ran the operation in Tehran, wrote in his memoir that high-level approval was given at a State Department meeting on 25 June 1953, but no official record of that meeting has been found. The Library of Congress country study likewise dates the Eisenhower administration's approval to June 1953. [cite:rs_cw1_frus_iran_d225] [cite:rs_cw1_loc_iran_study] The CIA's March 1954 memorandum gives a different date. It records that the project was approved by the President, the Secretary of State and the Director of Central Intelligence on 11 July 1953, under National Security Council paper NSC 136/1. [cite:rs_cw1_frus_iran_d363] A CIA chronology dates State Department and Foreign Office authorization to the same day, and a handwritten note says the Director obtained presidential approval that day. The State Department's editors add a sentence that has to stand beside every account of the decision: "No written authorization from the President has been found." [cite:rs_cw1_frus_iran_d225] The men behind the 11 July approval were President Eisenhower, Secretary of State John Foster Dulles and CIA Director Allen Dulles. [cite:greydynamics_tpajax_overview] [cite:globalsecurity_operation_ajax]

The two dates need not exclude each other. A meeting in late June may have settled the matter in principle and the formal sign-off may have followed on 11 July; the sources do not say so, and that reconciliation is no more than a possibility. What the record does establish is the form the approval took: on the American side, a decision attested by the CIA's own memorandum, a chronology and a handwritten note, without a presidential signature on any document yet found.

The approval came with conditions. According to the same memorandum, before approving, the President and the Secretary of State asked for assurances that the British would be flexible on oil and that adequate American interim economic aid would go to the successor government. [cite:rs_cw1_frus_iran_d363] The conditions show where the two governments' interests met and where they differed. Washington's conditions for joining were an assurance of British flexibility on oil and American interim aid for the government that would follow.

The money is the part of the story most often reduced to a single round number. A widely repeated summary puts the cost of the operation at about $5 million and calls it one of the cheapest covert operations in the CIA's history. [cite:wiki_1953_iranian_coup] [cite:globalsecurity_operation_ajax] The documents give a more exact and more interesting picture, because they show several different sums for several different purposes. Wilber's 1954 CIA history records that the Director approved, on 4 April 1953, a budget of $1,000,000 that the Tehran Station could use. [cite:rs_cw1_maryferrell_tpajax] The approval date is itself telling: the money was authorized more than a month before the inception date that the March 1954 memorandum gives for the project. The memorandum's own figure is a grand total of $5,330,000, spread across three phases: the operations up to Zahedi's installation, a follow-up phase to solidify the Shah and Zahedi, and emergency funds for the new government. The amount of each phase is still not declassified. [cite:rs_cw1_frus_iran_d363] So the "$5 million" figure, read against the documents, is not the price of the coup alone; much of the documented total may have gone to propping up the government that followed, but because the phases have not been released, no one can say from the public record how the total divides.

Two further figures come from reporting and scholarship rather than from released documents. James Risen, writing in the New York Times in 2000, reported that the CIA covertly funnelled $5 million to Zahedi's government two days after the coup. The historian Mark Gasiorowski found that Zahedi and his colleagues received at least $50,000 beforehand. [cite:rs_cw1_maryferrell_tpajax] Risen's $5 million and the memorandum's $5,330,000 may overlap, since the memorandum's third phase was emergency money for the new government; the sources do not say whether they are the same funds.

How the money was used is described in general terms. The operation used bribed newspaper editors to fill the press with material against Mossadeq, paid crowds to stage demonstrations, and coordinated with royalist officers in the Iranian army. [cite:wiki_1953_iranian_coup] [cite:globalsecurity_operation_ajax] Kermit Roosevelt Jr., a grandson of Theodore Roosevelt, ran it on the ground. [cite:wiki_1953_iranian_coup] He arrived in Tehran on 19 July 1953 as its field commander. [cite:roosevelt_nl_operation_ajax] [cite:npr_declassified_1953_coup] Not every American in Tehran shared the purpose with the same conviction. In oral histories recorded long afterwards, Lewis Hoffacker, third secretary at the embassy in 1951–53, said that "our goal was to support the Shah and to try to contain Mossadegh"; John Stutesman recalled Ambassador Loy Henderson's "deep reluctance to have a covert operation displace a chief of state," a recollection at second hand. [cite:rs_cw1_adst_iran]

The decisive weeks were August's. On 3 August 1953 Mossadeq held a plebiscite on dissolving the Majlis and then dissolved it. [cite:rs_cw1_loc_iran_study] His opponents called the plebiscite rigged. [cite:loc_mossadeq] This is part of the record and part of the case his critics made: a prime minister who had come to office through parliament ended that parliament by a popular vote whose fairness was disputed. On 13 August the Shah appointed Zahedi prime minister. Mossadeq refused to step down and arrested the Shah's emissary, and the Shah fled the country. [cite:rs_cw1_loc_iran_study] This was the first attempt, of 14–15 August, and it failed. [cite:rs_cw1_atlantic_byrne_2017]

What happened next depended, on these accounts, in part on one man's decision to stay. According to Byrne's reading of the 2017 volume, CIA headquarters advised Roosevelt to evacuate his team after the failure, but he stayed and, with Iranian collaborators, revived the operation. [cite:rs_cw1_atlantic_byrne_2017] Another account describes headquarters as directing that the operation stop, and Roosevelt as continuing regardless, organizing staged demonstrations and securing military backing. [cite:roosevelt_nl_operation_ajax] [cite:npr_declassified_1953_coup] The two descriptions differ in force, advice to evacuate in one and an order to stop in the other, and the difference matters for how much the outcome depended on Roosevelt personally; both agree that he did not leave. On 19 August pro-Shah army units and street crowds defeated Mossadeq's forces. [cite:rs_cw1_loc_iran_study] "Some 300 people died during fighting in Tehrān," in Britannica's words; Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty gives at least 300 dead in gun battles in the capital. [cite:rs_cw1_britannica_1953_coup] [cite:rs_cw1_rferl_1953]

The record of those last four days is thinner than for any other part of the operation, and for a specific reason. According to Byrne, most of the operational cables for 16 to 19 August no longer exist; CIA officers destroyed many records in the early 1960s. [cite:rs_cw1_atlantic_byrne_2017] The days on which the question of agency is most acute, who in the streets of Tehran was paid, organized or simply moved by events, are the days for which the American paper record is weakest.

The aftermath was a political purge. Mossadeq was sentenced to three years' imprisonment and then kept under house arrest until his death in 1967. His foreign minister, Hosain Fatemi, was executed. Hundreds of activists of the National Front, the Tudeh party and other groups were arrested. [cite:rs_cw1_loc_iran_study] Another account compresses this into a sentence of house arrest; the Library of Congress study separates the prison term from the house arrest that followed it. [cite:kathryn_palmer_1953_coup] [cite:rs_cw1_loc_iran_study] Mohammad Reza Pahlavi (1919–1980), the Shah, had his authority restored and centralized, and became the last Shah of Iran. [cite:kathryn_palmer_1953_coup] [cite:wiki_1953_iranian_coup] The founding bargain, as one account puts it, was a client arrangement: the Shah's rule in exchange for oil access and an anticommunist alignment on the Soviet Union's southern border. [cite:wiki_1953_iranian_coup] The commercial settlement that followed in 1954, and the secret police, SAVAK, created in 1957, belong to the next stage, in [scene:ira_s00b|the 1954 consortium and SAVAK]. One claim often attached to this story, that Israel's Mossad trained SAVAK from 1957, is not established for that year by the sources used here; the question of Israel's part, before and after the coup, is examined in the closing section of this chapter.

The man at the centre of these events is sometimes presented in terms the record does not support in either direction. Mossadeq, born in 1882, was a nationalist and constitutionalist, and in the account summarized here a liberal nationalist rather than a Communist. [cite:wiki_1953_iranian_coup] He came to office as the Majlis's choice, named by the Shah under parliamentary and popular pressure, not by a direct popular election. [cite:rs_cw1_loc_iran_study] Time named him its Man of the Year for 1951, but in words that were openly hostile, as told earlier in this chapter. [cite:rs_cw1_time_1952] He was the prime minister of a constitutional government that had come to rule by full powers and ended by dissolving its parliament through a disputed plebiscite; he was also removed by force, with foreign money and foreign planning, by men acting for two other governments. Both statements are documented.

The dispute over who carried out the coup, and why, runs through every serious account. On one side stands the CIA's own internal history, which, in the National Security Archive's description, "specifically states the agency planned and helped implement the coup." [cite:rs_cw1_nsarchive_2013] The strongest form of this case is that the operation was conceived in London and Washington, approved by named officials on both sides, paid for from a documented budget, directed by a CIA field commander who revived it when it failed, and carried out with bribed editors, paid crowds and officers coordinated from outside. On the other side, Byrne notes that whether Americans and Britons or Iranians ultimately carried the coup out remains heavily disputed. [cite:rs_cw1_atlantic_byrne_2017] The strongest form of that case is that the forces which prevailed on 19 August were Iranian: army units loyal to the Shah and street crowds, in a country already divided over the plebiscite, and that foreign money could exploit these divisions but did not create them. The released record cannot fully settle it, because the cables for the decisive days are gone.

The question of motive divides the same way. One reading, put strongly in some accounts, holds that the coup was at bottom an Anglo-American oil operation dressed in anticommunist language, the anticommunist case serving as the wrapper that made the repossession of an oil concession acceptable in 1953. [cite:wiki_1953_iranian_coup] The British motive, the restoration of the concession, is documented, and the American conditions for approval, British flexibility on oil, show that oil was part of the American calculation too. [cite:rs_cw1_frus_iran_d363] But the 2017 documents complicate the oil-only reading. Byrne writes that the Soviet threat dominates most of the volume's reports, and that American analysts saw Ayatollah Kashani as a source of trouble and feared an "unholy alliance" between him and Mossadeq. [cite:rs_cw1_atlantic_byrne_2017] The documents are read both ways, and historians continue to weigh British oil interests against Cold War fears in explaining why the United States joined. [cite:nsarchive_cia_confirms_role] [cite:explaininghistory_1953_coup] One reading is that the convergence is itself the finding: a British company's lost concession and an American fear of Soviet advance were distinct interests that met in one operation, and the condition Washington set, that Britain be flexible on oil, is where they can be seen meeting on paper.

The official record of the coup was withheld for decades, and the history of its concealment is part of the history of the event. Wilber's 200-page internal history was written in March 1954. In 1978, according to British Foreign Office papers, London sought to keep material out, and a State Department official warned that it contained "very embarrassing things about the British." The State Department's 1989 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States on the period did not mention the American role at all. The historian Bruce Kuniholm called it "a fraud," and Warren Cohen, chair of the department's Historical Advisory Committee, resigned in 1990. In 1991 Congress passed a statute requiring a "thorough, accurate, and reliable documentary record." In April 2000 Wilber's history was leaked to the New York Times. [cite:rs_cw1_nsarchive_2013]

The acknowledgement came on the coup's sixtieth anniversary. On 19 August 2013 the National Security Archive posted 21 CIA items, including the internal history "The Battle for Iran," with the TPAJAX name now restored; it is believed to be the CIA's first formal acknowledgement of its role. [cite:rs_cw1_nsarchive_2013] [cite:nsarchive_cia_confirms_role] The State Department's retrospective volume, more than 1,000 pages, followed in June 2017. According to Byrne, the Obama administration had held it back out of concern for the nuclear deal with Iran. [cite:rs_cw1_atlantic_byrne_2017] The documentary record of a 1953 decision was thus still being managed for reasons of policy, in London in 1978 and in Washington until 2017.

Whether Iran's later course would have differed without the coup is a question of another kind, because it asks what would have happened, not what did. Historians answer it in two broad ways, and both are interpretations. Those who stress the coup's weight argue that it foreclosed Iran's path toward a secular, nationalist, parliamentary government and replaced it with twenty-six years of increasingly repressive royal rule, whose abuses produced the particular revolutionary coalition, its Islamist wing included, that took power in 1979; on this view a Mossadeq-style government, developing however imperfectly, plausibly would not have produced that specific form of clerical rule. [cite:wiki_1953counterfactual] Those who stress structure point to Iran's religious establishment, the distortions of an oil economy, the pressure of the great powers and the wave of anti-colonial upheaval across the region, forces that would likely have produced some volatile turn against the West under more than one alternative history; on this view the coup shaped or hastened what followed but did not by itself cause it. [cite:cfr_coup_legacy] Neither position can be proved. Both rest on the same documented events. What neither disputes is that the coup happened, that the Shah's long rule followed it, and that the revolution of 1979 followed that. The question persists because it tests whether the hostility of later decades should be read as fixed and inevitable or as the outcome of a chain of documented choices that might have gone otherwise.

One other event is often set beside the coup. I. L. Kenen's American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs, in Washington, is dated to 1953 in some accounts, though the sources place its beginnings anywhere from 1951 to 1954; the name American Israel Public Affairs Committee is dated to 1959 in two accounts and to 1954 in a third. Its founding, and the uncertainty over its dates, are told in [scene:cw1_lobby|the lobby's founding] and, for its organizational line, in [scene:s07g|From AZEC to AIPAC]. [cite:cjh_kenen_papers] [cite:britannica_aipac] The two events may share a year and nothing else that the record documents: no source shows any operational connection between the coup in Tehran and the committee's founding in Washington. Their later histories, including the lobby's role in Congress in the 2020s, belong to later volumes.

The gaps in this record are specific. The amount of each of the three funding phases is still classified, so the share of the $5,330,000 spent before the coup, rather than on the government after it, cannot be stated. No written presidential authorization has been found, and the June and July approval dates have not been reconciled by any document. The operational cables for 16 to 19 August were largely destroyed, which leaves the decisive days, and with them the balance between foreign direction and Iranian action, the most poorly documented part of the operation. And the counterfactual that gives the coup much of its later weight, what Iran would have become without it, is by its nature beyond documentation.

sections.h: Israel and the Coup in Iran: Participant or Beneficiary, 1947–1953
sections.html:
The coup leaves one question that belongs to this volume in particular: where Israel stood in it. Two claims about Iran circulate together and are often answered together. The first holds that Iran has been a theocracy hostile to the West since time immemorial and never had a democratic government. The second holds that the coup of 1953 had nothing to do with Israel, or, in its mirror image, that Israel had a hand in it. The record answers the first claim directly and the second with a distinction. Before 1979 Iran was a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament, the Majlis. In 1951 the Majlis made Mohammad Mossadeq prime minister and voted to nationalize the British-controlled Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. [cite:explaininghistory_1953_coup] [cite:kathryn_palmer_1953_coup] In August 1953 an operation run by the CIA and Britain's MI6 removed him and restored the Shah's power, a role the CIA formally acknowledged in documents released in 2013. [cite:nsarchive_cia_confirms_role] [cite:npr_declassified_1953_coup] The theocracy came in 1979, twenty-six years after the elected government was removed. On Israel, the finding of this section is plain: no documented Israeli role in the coup exists. Whether Israel benefited from it, and from when, is a separate question with a separate answer.

The oil crisis and the coup themselves are told earlier in this chapter, the coup in [scene:s11|the account of August 1953]. This section follows a thread those accounts leave aside: what Iran's governments did about Israel from 1947 to 1953, and where the coup falls in that sequence.

Iran began on the other side. In 1947 it sat on the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine as one of three members that opposed partition and favoured a federal solution. On 29 November 1947 it voted against partition in the General Assembly. [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] In the war of 1948 it showed tacit solidarity with the Arab states but avoided combat and resisted Arab demands for direct military support. [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] The pattern of those first two years was a government that voted with the Arab states at the United Nations while keeping its own forces out of the fighting.

The first practical contact concerned Iran's own people. In March 1949 Iran sent an unofficial envoy, Abbas Sayqal, to handle the claims of Iranian residents of Palestine. In the same year it refused Israel's request to station a non-resident minister, based in Ankara, in Tehran. And on 11 May 1949 it voted against Israel's admission to the United Nations. [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] Iran was willing to deal with the new state over property and residents, but not to receive its diplomats or to vote it into the world body.

Then, in March 1950, it recognized Israel, in the most limited form available. On 6 March 1950, while the Majlis was in recess, the government recognized Israel de facto, without a formal announcement. The Foreign Minister, Entezam, informed Abba Eban the next day, 7 March, and on 26 March 1950 Reza Safinia presented credentials as a "special envoy". [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] One reading of the timing and the form is that recognition while parliament was not sitting avoided a Majlis debate, and recognition without announcement a public one; and de facto recognition stopped short of official, de jure recognition. According to Eitay Mack, Iran avoided official recognition because of domestic and Arab pressure. [cite:rs_cw1_972_mack]

The next step under Mossadeq went the other way. On 7 July 1951, shortly after he took office, his government closed Iran's consulate in Jerusalem, citing "financial difficulties". It did not revoke the de facto recognition. [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] [cite:mossadegh_org_israel_relations] The stated reason was financial, and the sources here give no other. Whether it was the whole reason, or a formula that let a nationalist government distance itself from Israel without breaking the recognition its predecessor had granted, the record cited here does not say. What it does show is the limit of the step: a consulate closed, a recognition left standing.

The first economic ties of 1953 complicate the simplest version of the "beneficiary" story. On 11 June 1953, before the coup and while Mossadeq was still prime minister, the national banks of the two countries signed an agreement opening a line of credit. In 1953 the Iranian–Israeli trading company IRIS was founded. [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] Some accounts place IRIS after Mossadeq's fall, as the first sign of a reversal. [cite:iranica_israel_iran] [cite:mossadegh_org_israel_relations] The encyclopaedia entry dates it only to 1953, and it dates the credit line explicitly before the coup. [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] On these sources, then, the first financial link between the two states was made under the government the coup removed, not under the one it installed.

Against that record the question of participation can be answered. No documented Israeli role in the coup exists. [cite:iranica_israel_iran] [cite:mossadegh_org_israel_relations] Israel was five years old in 1953; the operation was planned, paid for and run by the American and British services, as told in the account of the coup itself. Nothing in the sources gathered for this stage places an Israeli official, agency or payment in the planning or the events of August 1953. The claim that Israel took part is therefore not supported by these sources; it should not be confused with the separate, documented question of what Israel gained afterwards.

On that second question the evidence is real but later, and it needs dating. According to the encyclopaedia entry by David Menashri, Israel began buying Iranian oil in 1957, through foreign-flagged ships. [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] Menashri dates the first intelligence contact to September 1957, when General Teymur Bakhtiar, head of the newly established SAVAK, met Israel's ambassador Yaacov Zur in Paris and offered an exchange of intelligence, and he dates Ben-Gurion's periphery concept to the late 1950s. [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] Eitay Mack writes that Israel's Foreign Ministry files on relations with Iran, covering 1953 to 1979, have been declassified [cite:rs_cw1_972_mack], and the account behind this section reads those files as showing that Israel bought a significant portion, and in some years all, of its oil from the Shah's Iran. [cite:mag972_israel_shah]

The same account, and the account of the coup in this stage, go further: they state that the Mossad helped found and train the Shah's secret police, SAVAK, from 1957, and that the "Trident" intelligence pact began in 1958. [cite:globalsecurity_savak_cia_training] [cite:mag972_israel_shah] The sources assembled for this chapter do not establish that claim for 1957. What they document for that year is narrower: an offer to exchange intelligence, made by SAVAK's head to an Israeli ambassador in Paris in September. [cite:rs_cw1_iranica_israel] The fuller question of SAVAK, the periphery and the Trident belongs to the late 1950s and is examined, with its own sources, in [scene:cw4_iran|Stage Four's account of Iran and Israel].

The synthesis this section's source offers is that the coup served Washington and London directly and Israel indirectly: not a participant, but a beneficiary. On its account, the sequence ran from an elected government in 1951, through its removal by two foreign intelligence services in 1953, to a quarter century of the Shah's rule as an American ally and as Israel's main oil supplier and regional partner, and then to revolution in 1979. [cite:mag972_israel_shah] That is a judgment made with hindsight across twenty-six years, and its parts carry different weight. That the coup served American and British interests is the burden of the coup's own documented history. That Israel later gained from the Shah's Iran in oil and in partnership is supported by the dated evidence from 1957. That Israel's gains were a result of the coup, rather than of the Shah's own later choices and Israel's periphery policy, is an inference the sources here do not test. The record of 1950–53, with recognition granted before Mossadeq, a consulate closed under him, and a credit line signed in his last months in office, does not show a straight line from his fall to Israel's gain.

The record leaves several questions open. Why Mossadeq's government closed the consulate beyond the "financial difficulties" it cited is not documented here. Whether IRIS was founded before or after August 1953 is not given. How much of Iran's later oil trade with Israel is owed to the coup, as against the decisions of the late 1950s, cannot be settled from these sources, and the Mossad's role in SAVAK's founding is not established by them for 1957. Iran's own Jewish community, whose history runs beside this one, is the subject of [scene:ira_src_s16|a separate section on Iran's Jews].

chapters.label: Stage Two
chapters.title: Retaliate
chapters.intro:
In the late summer of 1953 Israel's borders were still the armistice lines of 1949, and none of them had become a peace. Egypt governed the Gaza Strip as a military protectorate that it never annexed. On the Syrian front, small demilitarized zones whose ownership the armistice had left open were already the subject of one Security Council crisis, told in Stage One. In Cairo, the Free Officers had dethroned King Farouk on 23 July 1952, with Colonel Gamal Abdel Nasser as their leader and Major General Muhammad Naguib as their figurehead. [cite:rs_cw2_ebsco_farouk] From Washington, Israel received $73.6 million in US assistance in 1953. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] In Israel, David Ben-Gurion, prime minister and defence minister, was granted a long leave on 7 July 1953. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_bg_portfolio] The next month the army appointed Ariel Sharon to establish and command Unit 101, created, in the words of Israel's Defense Ministry archive, "to carry out reprisal operations in enemy territory". [cite:rs_cw2_mod_sharon]

This stage asks what that policy produced, and what the governments outside the region did with a border that would not stay quiet. Its three years run from the founding of Unit 101 to 26 July 1956, when Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company. [cite:rs_cw2_state_suez] In that time the quarrel along the armistice lines became tied to the Cold War: to who would arm Egypt and who would arm Israel, to which camp each state in the region would join, and to the terms on which Washington would lend money, sell weapons or guarantee borders. The stage asks with equal weight what the governments and peoples of the region decided for themselves. Egypt chose its own suppliers. In Jordan, riots brought down a prime minister who had said he would join the Baghdad Pact, and the king dismissed Glubb. Palestinians in Gaza organized against the Egyptian administration that governed them.

The cast is wide, and most of it was divided against itself. In Israel, Ben-Gurion and his chief of staff, Moshe Dayan, led what the historian Avi Shlaim calls the "retaliation" school, and Moshe Sharett, prime minister from January 1954, led the "negotiation" school against them; Pinhas Lavon, Abba Eban and Shimon Peres each had a part. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] In Egypt, Nasser contended with Naguib and with the Muslim Brotherhood. In Jordan stood Prime Minister Hazza al-Majali, King Hussein and Glubb, the commander of the Arab Legion. [cite:rs_cw2_loc_jordan] In Gaza, communists and the Muslim Brotherhood formed a joint committee, and Egypt later raised Palestinian fida'i units under Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Hafez. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] In Washington, John Foster Dulles held the purse and the policy. Henry Byroade spoke for the State Department. Eric Johnston and Robert Anderson carried plans to the region as envoys, and James Angleton held the Israeli account at the CIA. In London there was Anthony Eden. At the United Nations there were General Vagn Bennike, General Burns and Dag Hammarskjöld. Nasser put the question of arms to the Soviet ambassador, D. S. Solod, in 1954; Egypt's arms came in the end through Czechoslovakia, and Israel's from France.

The sections follow that story roughly as it happened. They begin with [scene:cw2_free_officers|Egypt's revolution], because the power that shaped most of the stage sat in Cairo. Next come Unit 101 and Qibya, and in the same weeks the aid that Washington held back over a canal at Banat Yaacov, followed by Johnston's two-year effort to divide the Jordan. The oil settlement in Iran is followed by the contest between Sharett and Ben-Gurion, and then by the Pledge of Allegiance and the national motto, a domestic American thread whose links to Israel are examined and found undocumented. The year after Qibya brings the Scorpion Pass, Nahhalin, Byroade's speeches and the Bat Galim, and alongside it Operation Susannah, Israel's covert operation in Egypt. The Angleton channel and the Anglo-American plan called Alpha come next. Then the region chooses sides at Baghdad, Bandung and Amman. The Gaza raid of February 1955 and the fedayeen lead to the arms race, the Council's censures and Hammarskjöld's mission. The stage closes with [scene:cw2_aswan|the dam offer and the Canal] and a synthesis of the structure as it stood on that July day.
chapters.outro:
By the summer of 1956 the armistice system of 1949 still stood, but, on the argument of this stage, little rested on it any longer. On this reading, each layer of the structure had been rebuilt in these three years around a single fact: the lines could be condemned, negotiated over and financed, but no one outside the region could hold them.

The legal layer was dense and weak. The armistice agreements and the Security Council's resolutions defined what was forbidden, and the Council used them. It found reprisal raids to be violations three times, and in January 1956 it rejected outright Israel's plea that Syrian interference justified the raid at the lake. [cite:rs_cw2_un_res101] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res106] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res111] Its findings ran in both directions: the Commission had called the killings at Yehud "intolerable aggression", and Resolution 101 asked Jordan to stop the crossings. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_qibya] [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_res101] What the law lacked was a means of enforcement. On the Jordanian commission the chairman's vote decided, and Israel had cut its connection with that commission in March 1954. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3252] Hammarskjöld's assurances bound every government only while the others complied, and each reserved its right of self-defence. [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] At Suez, the Council said its resolution of 1951 kept "continuing validity", and Egypt offered to release the Bat Galim only if it sailed south, away from the Canal. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_batgalim] The one new instrument that changed facts on the ground was bilateral, not international. The base agreement of October 1954 recognized the Canal as "an integral part of Egypt", and on 26 July 1956 Nasser nationalized the Canal Company. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_suez_base] [cite:rs_cw2_state_suez]

The administrative layer is the story of how decisions were made, and in both Israel and Egypt power was drawn into one office. In Israel the record shows force used outside the ordinary chain. Sharett, as prime minister, was "kept out of the loop" on Operation Susannah, and who ordered it is disputed: Gibli said he had a verbal instruction from Lavon, who denied any knowledge. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] The raid at the lake was authorized by Ben-Gurion alone, in Shlaim's account, while his foreign minister sought arms in Washington. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_kinneret] By June 1956 the premiership and the defence ministry were in Ben-Gurion's hands and Sharett was gone. [cite:rs_cw2_kaller_bg] In Egypt the same three years ran from a ruling council to a sole candidate elected with 99.95 per cent, as HISTORY.com reports. [cite:rs_cw2_history_nasser] The Free Officers' rival claimants were removed along the way: Naguib from all his functions, the Brotherhood by ban and arrest. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_naguib] [cite:rs_cw2_origins_mb] Gaza was run by a military governor answerable to Cairo. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza]

The institutional and financial layer showed money following alignment only part of the way. American economic aid to Israel continued, falling from $73.6 million in 1953 to $50.8 million in 1956. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] It was held back once, over Banat Yaacov, and released the day after the Council's resolution, once Israel had undertaken to suspend the works. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_pr604] The large Western offers were attached to settlements that never came: two-thirds of the Jordan valley's development costs, and, as Parker Hart recalled it, a grant for the dam at Aswan with a conditional loan to follow. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_unified_plan] [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] Elsewhere, interests were settled in kind or in shares. Egypt bartered cotton and rice for Soviet-bloc arms. Iran's oil was divided among the Anglo-Iranian company, Royal Dutch Shell, five American firms and a French participant. Washington paid a sixth of the Baghdad Pact's budget without joining it. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_tel632] [cite:rs_cw2_fo_consortium] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_baghdad_us] One arrangement rested on no documented written agreement: the CIA's Israel account, held by Angleton as what the agency's historian calls "an administrative anomaly". [cite:rs_cw2_robarge]

The Palestinian Arab side appears in this stage chiefly as a subject of other governments' plans: 900,000 refugees in Dulles's address, 75,000 to be resettled in Israel under Alpha, 12,000 families to be settled in Sinai. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_dulles55] [cite:rs_cw2_ecf_alpha] [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] Its own voice is recorded in Gaza. In March 1955 a committee of communists and Brotherhood members demanded an end to the Sinai scheme, arms for the camps and civil freedoms. The governor's promise on the scheme was followed by mass arrests. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] In September 1955 Egypt formed fida'i units under its own command. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] At Bandung, twenty-nine states declared "support for the rights of the Arab people of Palestine". [cite:rs_cw2_enc_bandung] The raids also fell on civilians: the villagers of Qibya, the woman killed at Nahhalin on the Jordanian side of the line, and at Khan Yunis twenty-five refugees by Egypt's count. [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3251] [cite:rs_cw2_un_a3157]

The regional layer was reordered around Cairo. Egypt had secured the British evacuation, a Soviet-bloc supplier and, after Bandung, a leader with standing beyond the Arab world. Iraq had joined Turkey and Britain in the Pact. Jordan had moved toward it, and turned back. [cite:rs_cw2_enc_bandung] [cite:rs_cw2_loc_jordan] The American layer was defined by what Washington declined to do. It refused Israel arms, stayed out of the Pact, withdrew the dam offer and stood apart from Eden's formula. Each refusal left the decision to someone else: France on Israel's aircraft, Britain and Iraq on the Pact, and, as Fraser Wilkins later put it, the Russians on the dam. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_mystere] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eden_uk] [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] At home, the same government wrote God into the Pledge and the motto, as a stand against Communism; the sources record no link to Israel. [cite:rs_cw2_ucsb_pledge] [cite:rs_cw2_ffrf_kramnick]

What was settled, then, was the shape of the coming confrontation: Egypt armed from the East and sovereign over the Canal, Israel armed from France, and the United States committed to neither. What was contested was the meaning of retaliation itself. Israel's strongest case was that civilians were being killed across lines that no commission could close, and that the only guarantee offered required giving up the reply. The strongest case against it was made by the UN and inside Israel's own cabinet. UNTSO found "a striking disparity" between reply and provocation, and the Council held that provocation did not justify the raid. Sharett held that avoiding escalation was the way to prevent war. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_kinneret] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res111] What the record leaves open is whether any party could have chosen otherwise. Nasser had asked Moscow for arms before the Gaza raid and before the Pact. [cite:rs_cw2_wilson_solod] Dulles, by Shlaim's account, had decided to sell Israel defensive arms on the eve of the raid at the lake. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] Whether those were real alternatives or only moments is the question the crisis of the autumn, told in [scene:cw3_sevres|the next stage], would answer by force.

sections.h: Egypt's Revolution, 1952–1956: The Free Officers, the Base and the Presidency
sections.html:
The stage that this chapter calls "Retaliate" opens on the border between Israel and its neighbours, but the power that would shape most of its turns sat in Cairo. In the four years between July 1952 and June 1956, Egypt changed from a monarchy with a British army on its soil into a republic led by a colonel who had removed the king, outmanoeuvred his own figurehead, negotiated the British out of the Canal Zone, banned the Muslim Brotherhood and asked Moscow for weapons. Each of those steps was taken by Egyptians, for Egyptian reasons, and each later reached Israel: through the arms race, through the fedayeen, through the Canal. The Egyptian story comes first, because the rest of the stage cannot be read without it.

Egypt came to 1952 without a peace with Israel. It had joined Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq in invading the newly declared State of Israel in May 1948, and the war had ended not with a peace treaty but with the armistice negotiated at Rhodes in 1949, whose line functioned as the de facto Egypt–Israel border along the edge of the Gaza Strip. [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] Inside that line Egypt held the Gaza Strip, which it governed from 1948 to 1967 as a military protectorate: direct administration, but never annexation, a distinction Egyptian officials maintained throughout. Why Egypt chose not to annex is not settled by the sources used here. Some accounts stress an Arab League political consensus against formal annexation; others stress Egyptian strategic caution. Volume II tells how that administration began. A common belief holds that Egypt has never had any administrative role in Gaza and that the Strip was always a purely Palestinian territory apart from Egypt. The record is the reverse: for nineteen years Egypt was the governing power there, and in 1952 it had already been so for four. Gaza under Egyptian rule is the place where several of this stage's later crises began, from the raid of February 1955 to the fedayeen units, and both are told later in this chapter.

The coup of 23 July 1952. The Free Officers carried out their coup in Cairo on 23 July 1952. Their leader was Colonel Gamal Abdel Nasser; their figurehead was Major General Muhammad Naguib. King Farouk was dethroned and ordered to leave the country. [cite:rs_cw2_ebsco_farouk] [cite:w_1952_egypt] HISTORY.com puts the number who acted with Nasser at 89 other Free Officers; that count comes from a popular reference source and is given here as its figure. [cite:rs_cw2_history_nasser]

What the officers wanted can be read most reliably from what they did, because the sources do not set out the movement's programme in its own words. In the months after the coup the new regime decreed agricultural land reform. In the summer of 1953 the monarchy gave way to a republic. Naguib served as prime minister from 1952 to 1954 and as president from 1953 to 1954. [cite:rs_cw2_ebsco_farouk] The exact date on which the republic was proclaimed, and the date Farouk actually left, are not given in those sources. The pattern of the acts is plain enough: an end to the crown, a reform of land holding, and, as the next two years showed, an end to the British military presence that the monarchy had lived with.

The coup belongs to what can be called a decade of coups in the region, running from Syria's three in 1949 to the fall of Iraq's monarchy in 1958. Syria's are told in Volume II, Iran's of August 1953 in Stage One, and the others in later stages. [cite:w_1952_egypt] One common explanation for that decade holds that the region's dictatorships and wars grew only out of local culture and religion. Egypt's case, as these sources document it, fits neither that account nor its mirror image. The officers who took power were Egyptian and acted on their own decision; but every major question they then faced, from the British base to the source of their weapons, ran through London, Washington and Moscow. The regime's character was shaped by both.

Nasser against Naguib, 1954. The figurehead did not stay one. In early 1954 a power struggle split the ruling council. By April 1954 Nasser had majority support, and the "April Decrees" removed Naguib from effective power; Nasser became prime minister. [cite:rs_cw2_ebsco_farouk] [cite:rs_cw2_history_nasser] Naguib kept the title of president for some months more, but the decisions of the rest of 1954 were Nasser's.

Asking Moscow, June 1954. The first of those decisions to reach beyond Egypt's borders was taken quietly. On 15 June 1954 Nasser received the Soviet ambassador, D. S. Solod. According to the Soviet record of the conversation, he told Solod that Britain had stopped arms shipments to Egypt and had blocked supplies from other European states, that Egypt could not meet "a hundredth of its army's needs," and he formally asked what the Soviet position would be on selling arms to Egypt. [cite:rs_cw2_wilson_solod] That request, more than a year before the Czech arms deal was announced, matters for one of the stage's central disputes: whether Israel's raid on Gaza in February 1955 pushed Egypt toward Soviet weapons, or whether Nasser was already looking. The deal itself and that argument are told in [scene:cw2_czech_arms|the arms race]. Here it is enough to note Egypt's own stated case: a Western supplier had cut it off.

The same summer an Israeli military intelligence network of Egyptian Jews began a sabotage campaign inside Egypt meant to damage Egypt's ties with the West during the base negotiations; its course and its consequences are told in [scene:lv_s01|Operation Susannah and the Lavon affair].

The British leave the Canal Zone. The negotiation that operation was aimed at produced Egypt's largest gain of the period. The Anglo-Egyptian Heads of Agreement were initialled on 27 July 1954, and the final agreement was signed on 19 October 1954. It abrogated the treaty of 1936. British troops would leave the Canal Zone. The base would be kept in working order by 1,200 civilian technicians, of whom up to 800 could come from outside Egypt. Britain could return only in the event of an attack on Egypt, on any other Arab state, or on Turkey; an attack on Iran or on Israel would not count. The agreement ran for seven years. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_suez_base] In the same document Egypt pledged to uphold "the principles of the 1888 Convention of Constantinople concerning the free use of the Suez Canal," and the accord recognized the Canal as "an integral part of Egypt." [cite:rs_cw2_frus_suez_base]

The terms show who could act and who could not. Britain kept a right of return and a working base, but only on triggers it had agreed with Egypt and only for seven years. Egypt gained the departure of foreign troops and a written recognition that the Canal was part of its territory, in exchange for a pledge on free passage drawn from an 1888 convention. Israel was not a party, and the agreement's trigger clause excluded it: an attack on Israel was not among the events that would bring British forces back. Whether the pledge on free use extended to ships bound for Israel was not answered by the text. The Security Council had already ruled against Egypt's restrictions on Israel-bound shipping in 1951, as Stage One tells, and the question was being tested again even as the agreement was concluded: the seizure of the Israeli ship Bat Galim at the end of September 1954 is told later in this chapter.

Manshiya Square and the Brotherhood, October–November 1954. Not every Egyptian accepted the bargain, and the regime's opponents were not only foreign. On 26 October 1954, a week after the signing, Nasser was speaking about the new treaty in Manshiya Square in Alexandria when Mahmoud Abdel-Latif, a young member of the Muslim Brotherhood, fired at him. Nasser kept speaking. [cite:rs_cw2_origins_mb] Who ordered the attempt is not established. The historians who wrote the account used here, in the Origins series of Ohio State and Miami universities, say plainly that it is not clear; the gunman's membership is documented, but the chain of command behind him, if there was one, is not.

The consequences are documented. The Brotherhood was banned. More than 1,000 of its members were arrested, a small number were executed, and the movement went underground. [cite:rs_cw2_origins_mb] The ban removed the Brotherhood from legal political life, and the use the regime made of the shooting was not limited to the Brotherhood.

Naguib was next. In mid-November 1954 the Revolutionary Command Council removed him "from all his functions"; the announcement was planned for 15 November. The Council accused him of "conniving with Muslim Brotherhood extremists." The American ambassador in Cairo, Caffery, reporting the move to Washington, noted that Naguib had opposed the Suez agreement. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_naguib] Two charges sat side by side: the Council's, that the president had been in league with the men behind the attempt on Nasser, and the ambassador's observation that he had also been against the treaty Nasser had just signed. The telegram does not resolve which weighed more, and the sources here do not either. What it does show is that the contest of early 1954 ended, after the shooting, with Naguib's complete removal.

The presidency, June 1956. The consolidation was completed at the ballot box, on terms that left no room for a contest. On 23 June 1956 Nasser, the only candidate, was elected Egypt's first president with 99.95 per cent of the vote, in a referendum that also approved a new constitution by 99.8 per cent. [cite:rs_cw2_history_nasser] The figures come from HISTORY.com and are given as it reports them. The man who had been the hidden leader of a junta in 1952 was, four years later, the sole holder of the state's highest office.

What that rise meant beyond Egypt can be stated more broadly: Nasser's ascent after 1952 made Egypt the leading voice of pan-Arabism and of non-aligned Third World politics through the 1950s and 1960s, the Arab world's central power and its most vocal opponent of Israel's existence. That is a broad characterization, and the documents in this section show its foundations rather than its full extent: a leader who had removed his rivals at home, ended a foreign military presence, and opened a channel to the Soviet bloc. A month after the presidential vote Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company, and a few months after that Britain, France and Israel invaded; that war and the pressure that reversed it belong to Stage Three and are told in [scene:egi_src_s02|the first war and the Suez crisis]. [cite:wikipedia_suez_crisis]

The record leaves several things unsettled. It does not establish who, if anyone, ordered Mahmoud Abdel-Latif to fire in Manshiya Square, and it therefore cannot say whether the Brotherhood's leadership bore responsibility for an attempt that cost the whole movement its legal existence. It does not show whether Naguib's removal turned more on the Brotherhood charge or on his opposition to the Suez agreement. It does not give the Free Officers' programme in their own words, the scale of the land reform, or the precise date the republic was proclaimed. And it does not explain why Egypt kept Gaza as an administered territory rather than annexing it. What it does establish is the sequence: by the middle of 1956 one Egyptian government, under one man, held every lever that the rest of this stage would test.

sections.h: Unit 101 and Qibya, 1953: Retaliation Becomes Policy
sections.html:
While Egypt's officers were still settling their revolution, Israel's own border policy took a new form. Volume II followed the armistice lines through the years of crossings, killings and expulsions that followed 1949, in [scene:rd6_return_barred|how return was barred]. This section picks up the border in the late summer of 1953, when the Israeli army created a unit whose stated purpose was to strike across it, and when one of that unit's first large operations brought Israel a censure in the strongest language the Security Council used. The operation was Qibya. What happened there over one night in October 1953 is no longer seriously disputed. How it was described at the time, by whom, and with what knowledge is the more revealing story.

A unit for reprisals. According to the archives of Israel's Ministry of Defense, Ariel Sharon was appointed in August 1953 to establish and command Unit 101, created "to carry out reprisal operations in enemy territory." [cite:rs_cw2_mod_sharon] Walid Khalidi and Neil Caplan, who introduced and annotated the relevant excerpts of Moshe Sharett's diaries for the Journal of Palestine Studies in 2002, describe Sharon in 1953 as a 25-year-old major. [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] The unit was short-lived as a separate formation, but its purpose was written into its founding: it existed to answer attacks from across the line with attacks across the line.

It was in action within weeks. Khalidi and Caplan record that Sharon led an attack on the al-Burj refugee camp in Gaza in late August 1953 in which, according to the historian Benny Morris, twenty people were killed, among them seven women and five children, and twenty-two were wounded. [cite:rs_cw2_jps_qibya] The camp lay in the Strip that Egypt administered, and its inhabitants were refugees.

Yehud, 12–13 October 1953. The raid on Qibya followed a killing inside Israel. On the night of 12–13 October 1953 a grenade was thrown into a house at Yehud (the Jewish Virtual Library spells the place Tiryat Yehuda), killing Suzanne Kinyas and her two children.
