[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] According to the Defense Ministry archive, the unit was commanded by Major Motke Ben-Zur. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] The archive is explicit about the aim. The bombings were meant to sabotage Egypt's relations with the West while Egypt negotiated with Britain over evacuating the Canal area, and they were to be blamed on the Muslim Brotherhood, on Egyptian Communists, or on "local nationalists." The targets were Egyptian, American and British-owned cinemas, libraries and American educational centres, and the bombs were timed to go off hours after closing. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] An older summary of the affair adds the strategic object: the attacks were meant to persuade Britain to keep its forces in the Suez Canal Zone. [cite:wiki_lavon_affair]

The intended logic, as the sources describe it, was a chain of attributions: American and British property in Egypt would burn, Egyptians would be blamed, Egypt's relations with the West would suffer, and Britain might keep its troops at Suez. Each link depended on the one before it, and the whole depended on no one discovering who had actually lit the fires.

Reduced to its mechanism, the operation was a redirected message: an act designed so that it would appear to come from a different sender. That is a description of how it was meant to work, not a judgment of its place in any longer history. The operation is sometimes called the earliest documented Israeli false-flag operation; the sources used for this section do not establish that it was the first of its kind, and this book does not rest anything on the claim.

July 1954. The most detailed dated sequence comes from the Arab outlet Raseef22, which reconstructed it from Egyptian sources, and it should be read as that outlet's account. According to Raseef22, coded signals went out on Israeli radio on 16 June 1954. On 2 July devices were placed in mailboxes in Alexandria. On 14 July the American libraries in Cairo and Alexandria were set alight. For 23 July the cell planned devices at a Cairo station, at the Rivoli theatre, and at Alexandria's Metro and Rio cinemas. [cite:rs_cw2_raseef_lavon] An Israeli account broadly agrees on the first two dates. Writing in The Jewish Press in 2022, Saul Jay Singer dates the bombings to 2 July, at the Alexandria post office, and 14 July, at the USIA libraries in Alexandria and Cairo and a British-owned theatre. [cite:rs_cw2_jewishpress_susannah] The two accounts differ on detail: Singer places a British-owned theatre among the targets of 14 July, while Raseef22 places the cinemas among the devices planned for 23 July.

The night of 23 July ended the operation. Raseef22 reports that on that evening an Alexandria police officer put out the burning trousers of Philip Natanson outside the Rio cinema, and that his arrest led to the others. [cite:rs_cw2_raseef_lavon] Point of No Return, a blog on the Jewish refugees from Arab countries, describes a phosphorus device igniting in his pocket. [cite:rs_cw2_jr_hanged] The older summary gives the same essential fact: a device ignited prematurely in an operative's pocket in Alexandria, and the cell was arrested. [cite:wiki_lavon_affair]

Did anyone die? On this the sources conflict, and the conflict cannot be settled from the material available. Ynet, reporting in 2005, says the attacks caused no casualties. [cite:rs_cw2_ynet_2005] Singer, in 2022, also writes that the July operations "caused no injuries or deaths." [cite:rs_cw2_jewishpress_susannah] Raseef22's Egyptian-sourced account says that people died in the Alexandria fire of 2 July. [cite:rs_cw2_raseef_lavon] None of these sources cites a primary record of casualties. On one side stand two Israeli outlets; on the other, one account drawn from Egyptian sources. Neither side's version can be confirmed or ruled out on this evidence, and the question remains open. [cite:rs_cw2_jewishpress_susannah] [cite:rs_cw2_ynet_2005] [cite:rs_cw2_raseef_lavon]

The arrests and the trial. Eleven Egyptian Jews were arrested. Their trial ran from 11 December 1954 to 27 January 1955. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] [cite:rs_cw2_jr_hanged] Two defendants, Moshe Marzouk and Shmuel Azar, were sentenced to hang. Six received long prison terms: Victor Levi, Philip Natanson, Robert Dassa, Marcel Ninio, Meir Meyuhas and Meir Za'afran. Two were acquitted. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] [cite:rs_cw2_jr_hanged]

Appeals for mercy went to Egypt's leader, Gamal Abdel Nasser, who rejected them, and Marzouk and Azar were executed in Cairo on 31 January 1955. [cite:rs_cw2_jr_hanged] Two of those arrested died in custody. One of them was Max Bennett, an Israeli officer, also recorded as Meir Max Bineth. [cite:rs_cw2_jr_hanged] [cite:wiki_lavon_affair] According to Raseef22, he took his own life in detention before the trial session; the older summary says he took his own life in prison. [cite:rs_cw2_raseef_lavon] [cite:wiki_lavon_affair]

The cell's handler was not among the condemned. Avri Elad, the cell's handler, is identified in the sources as a double agent. He was later tried in secret in Israel and jailed for ten years. [cite:rs_cw2_jr_hanged] [cite:rs_cw2_ynet_2005] The sources used here say no more about what Elad passed to whom, or when.

The exposure had consequences inside Egypt's own state as well. Raseef22 writes that the affair accelerated the founding of Egypt's General Intelligence Directorate in 1955, under Zakaria Mohieddin. [cite:rs_cw2_raseef_lavon] That is the outlet's assessment and is reported here as such.

Who gave the order. In Israel the failure turned at once into a struggle over responsibility, and the struggle took its name from the minister at its centre. The question was disputed from the start, and three men gave three answers. Defence Minister Pinhas Lavon denied any knowledge of the operation. The head of military intelligence, Colonel Binyamin Gibli, said he had received a verbal instruction from Lavon. The Chief of Staff, Moshe Dayan, blamed the minister. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] The Prime Minister, Moshe Sharett, according to the Defense Ministry archive, "was kept out of the loop." [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] Sharett appointed a two-man commission to establish the facts; in the archive's words, it "did not expose the truth." [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon]

The structure helps explain why the question was not answered. The order, on Gibli's account, was verbal. The Prime Minister had not been told, and the inquiry he set up did not resolve it. A chain of command with no written order in the record left each man able to deny the decision.

Sharett's private diary records what the affair did to the government he led. On 14 January 1955, less than two weeks before the verdicts in Cairo, he wrote that he "would never have imagined that we could reach such a horrible state of poisoned relations." [cite:rs_cw2_rokach_lavon] Elsewhere he gave his own verdict on the minister, one that neither convicted nor acquitted him: even if Lavon "did not give the order, his role in preparing the ground for the Affair is undeniable." [cite:rs_cw2_rokach_lavon] These passages are quoted in the translation published by Livia Rokach in her 1980 study of the diaries. They are Sharett's contemporaneous words, and they show the Prime Minister himself unable to say who had issued the order.

The two cases can each be put at full strength. The case against Lavon rests on Gibli's statement that he had a verbal instruction, on the Chief of Staff's support for that account, and on Sharett's judgment that Lavon had, at the least, prepared the ground. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] [cite:rs_cw2_rokach_lavon] The case for Lavon rests on his own consistent denial, on the absence of any written order in the record used here, and on the fact that the only formal inquiry of the time, in the archive's words, "did not expose the truth." [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] Each side's evidence was testimony from an interested party, which helps explain why the affair outlived the operation.

The outcome in 1955. Lavon resigned in February 1955. Gibli and Ben-Zur were dismissed. On 21 February 1955 David Ben-Gurion returned to the government and replaced Lavon as defence minister. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] [cite:rs_cw2_israeled_lavon] The political consequences of Ben-Gurion's return, and the widening split between him and Sharett over the use of force on the borders, are told in [scene:cw2_sharett_ben_gurion|the section on Sharett and Ben-Gurion].

Who paid. The cost of the operation fell almost entirely on the people Aman had recruited to carry it out. The planners lost their offices; the operatives lost their lives or their liberty. Marzouk and Azar were hanged. Bennett died in custody. Six others served long sentences in Egyptian prisons. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] [cite:rs_cw2_jr_hanged] For decades the state that had sent them did not acknowledge them. Israel long denied involvement, including after the peace treaty with Egypt in 1979. [cite:rs_cw2_ynet_2005] [cite:wiki_lavon_affair]

The first official recognition came half a century later. On 30 March 2005 President Moshe Katsav presented certificates to the nine agents Aman had recruited; three survivors attended. Ynet reported the words of David Kimche, a former deputy chief of the Mossad, on the lesson the services drew: "We knew never to go down that road again." [cite:rs_cw2_ynet_2005] The ceremony was the state's first official recognition of the agents. It did not settle the question of which official had given the order.

The operatives came from Egypt's Jewish community, and the operation belongs to that community's history as well as to Israel's. The larger history, of the departures of Jews from Arab and Muslim countries between 1948 and 1972, is told in [scene:s00e2|the history of the Jews of the Arab world], where this affair is treated as one documented case among several causes, specific to Egypt.

What the record does not settle. Four questions remain open on the evidence used here. The first is the order: the testimony points in opposite directions, the order was verbal, and the inquiry of 1955 did not resolve it. The second is casualties: two Israeli accounts say no one was hurt, one Egyptian-sourced account says people died in Alexandria on 2 July, and no primary record has been found to decide between them. The third is the tally of the accused: the sources give eleven arrests and account for ten by verdict, two hanged, six imprisoned and two acquitted, while also saying that two of the arrested died in custody, and they do not name the second or fully reconcile the count; nor do they say whether Bennett, described as an Israeli officer, is counted among the eleven Egyptian Jews. The fourth is the operation's institutional home: the Defense Ministry archive places it in military intelligence, while Raseef22's headline calls it the Mossad's first operation in Egypt. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] [cite:rs_cw2_raseef_lavon] [cite:rs_cw2_jr_hanged] The double agent Elad's role is identified but not described.

The affair did not end in 1955. In 1960 it was reopened amid evidence that documents had been forged; the renewed dispute split the ruling Mapai party and contributed to Ben-Gurion's resignation in 1963, and the question of the order's origin remained formally unresolved. [cite:wiki_lavon_affair] That second round belongs to the years of Stage Four, where it is told in full.

sections.h: The Angleton Channel, 1954–1956
sections.html:
The intelligence relationship between the United States and Israel did not begin with a treaty, and its starting point is told in three different ways, set out in [scene:cw1_cia_liaison|the section on the liaison's origins]. What changed in 1954 was not the existence of a channel but the man who held it. In that year James Jesus Angleton became head of the Central Intelligence Agency's new Counterintelligence Staff, and he controlled the agency's Israel account. [cite:rs_cw2_robarge] For the next two years, the period this stage covers, the channel's best-documented product was a single document: the text of Nikita Khrushchev's secret speech of February 1956.

The familiar account of the relationship presents it as a valuable Cold War partnership, professionally managed, that served American interests in a dangerous period. Another account presents it as a case of one official's capture by a foreign service. The documents of 1954–56 support a narrower statement than either: one CIA officer held an unusual personal control over the Israel account, he regarded Israel as a strategic asset against the Soviet Union, and in 1956 the channel delivered something of real value to Washington. What it cost, and what it may have hidden, are questions for later years.

The administrative anomaly. The clearest description of Angleton's position comes from inside the CIA. David Robarge, the agency's chief historian, writing in the CIA's journal Studies in Intelligence, records that Angleton became head of the new Counterintelligence Staff in 1954, and that his "control of that country's account at CIA, an administrative anomaly, was one of the foundations of his influence." [cite:rs_cw2_robarge] The phrase invites two readings. The word "anomaly" can be read as the agency historian's own acknowledgement that the arrangement was irregular: the Israel account sat with the chief of counterintelligence rather than wherever the agency's normal structure would have put it. And the phrase "foundations of his influence" says that the account was not a side duty but one of the sources of Angleton's power inside the agency.

Robarge also states Angleton's view of the country. Angleton, he writes, "ardently supported Israel" and "saw Israel as a bastion against the Soviet Union." [cite:rs_cw2_robarge] That is the official historian's judgment of Angleton's motive, and it is a Cold War motive: Israel mattered to him as a front against Moscow. Read together, the two statements suggest a mechanism: the officer who held the Israel account was also the officer who valued Israel most and who drew influence from managing it.

A more critical account of Angleton adds a personal history: it states that he had met future Israeli intelligence leaders in wartime Rome. [cite:adst_pollard] [cite:cia_old_ally] [cite:ips_espionage] [cite:nsarchive_pollard] The same account goes further, charging that over his tenure he passed to the Mossad the identities of CIA sources in Arab countries, against the agency's counterintelligence protocols, and that his dual role made a genuine counterintelligence assessment of Israel impossible. [cite:adst_pollard] [cite:cia_old_ally] [cite:ips_espionage] [cite:nsarchive_pollard] Those charges are undated in the source and cover some twenty years. Nothing in the material used here ties any specific instance to 1954–56, and they are reported as that account's characterization, not as a finding for this period. Robarge's own words, "ardently supported," describe a disposition, not an act.

What kind of agreement. No formal written liaison agreement for 1954–1956 is documented in these sources. Neither the CIA historian nor the other accounts used here describes one. Shammai Siskind, writing in the Middle East Quarterly in 2020, says only that the United States had agreed "a few years earlier" to cooperate with Israel on intelligence. [cite:rs_cw2_robarge] [cite:rs_cw2_meq_siskind] The arrangement that governed the channel in these years, so far as the record shows, was an understanding between services, held together by the officials who ran it.

One description of its terms comes from much later. Samuel Lewis, the United States ambassador to Israel from 1977 to 1985, described in a diplomatic oral history a "gentleman's agreement" during Angleton's tenure: an informal understanding that neither the CIA nor the Mossad would recruit agents in the other's country. Lewis said it "may well have been honored during that period." He added: "By the time I got to Israel in 1977, Jim Angleton had long since retired and the relationship between the American and the Israeli services was less close." Lewis was speaking of a period before his own service, and his "may well have been" is a hedge, not a confirmation. His testimony establishes that such an understanding was believed to exist. It does not establish when it began, who agreed to it, or whether it held in 1954–56. Nor is it a treaty or a written institutional commitment of any kind; the critical account describes it as a personal arrangement that depended on Angleton.

The speech. In February 1956 Khrushchev delivered his "secret speech" to a closed session of the Twentieth Congress of the Soviet Communist Party. [cite:rs_cw2_meq_siskind] Its route to the West ran through Israel, and the fullest account of that route is Siskind's, which is reported here as his.

According to Siskind, Victor Grayevsky, a Polish Jewish journalist, borrowed a copy from the office of the Polish Communist Party where his girlfriend worked. He gave it to Yaakov Barmor, an agent of the Shin Bet, who photographed it. [cite:rs_cw2_meq_siskind] Ben-Gurion then sent a copy to Washington by courier, to Israel's liaison there, Izzy Dorot. On the American side, Siskind writes, only Angleton was to see it. The text reached Allen Dulles by mid-April 1956, and in early June 1956 the CIA gave it to The New York Times. [cite:rs_cw2_meq_siskind]

A second account, published when Grayevsky died, agrees on the essentials but leaves one point open. NEWSru.co.il, an Israeli Russian-language outlet, reported in October 2007 that Grayevsky immigrated to Israel in 1957, served for fourteen years as a double agent reporting his KGB contacts to the Shin Bet until 1971, and was honoured by the Shin Bet's chief, Avi Dichter, in August 2006. [cite:rs_cw2_newsru_grayevsky] Its headline says he passed the report to the Mossad; its text names both the Mossad and the Shin Bet as recipients of the speech, without resolving which. [cite:rs_cw2_newsru_grayevsky] Siskind names the Shin Bet. [cite:rs_cw2_meq_siskind] The difference matters for a history of the two institutions. The sources used here do not settle which service first held the document, or whether both did.

The speech shows what the channel was for, from each side. For Washington, Israel offered access the United States did not have on its own: a document out of a closed Communist Party session, obtained through a Jewish journalist in Warsaw and an Israeli agent, and in American hands within about two months. The critical account of the relationship places the speech among the high-value assets Israel provided in exchange for American intelligence on Arab states. [cite:wrmea_cia_mossad_tradeoffs] [cite:michaelcronin_cia_mossad_relationship] For Israel, the delivery demonstrated its worth to the one American officer who controlled its account, at a time, told in the other sections of this stage, when Washington was refusing it arms and courting Egypt. The sources used here do not record what, if anything, Israel received in return for this particular document.

The dispute. The two ways of reading the Angleton years can each be put at full strength. The case for the partnership, as the familiar account presents it, is that in the conditions of the early Cold War a small ally with sources inside the Soviet bloc was worth an unusual arrangement, and the secret speech is its best evidence: a document of world importance, delivered to the CIA and then to the public. The case against, as the critical account presents it, is that the same arrangement placed the judgment of a foreign service in the hands of the officer most committed to it, and that the cost appeared only later. [cite:rs_cw2_robarge] [cite:adst_pollard] [cite:cia_old_ally] For 1954–56 the record used here supports the first case's facts and the second case's structural point: Robarge's "administrative anomaly" is both. It does not supply evidence, for these years, of the harms the second case alleges.

The later history of the relationship, including the case of the nuclear material company NUMEC, the Israeli Science Liaison Bureau known as LAKAM, founded in 1960, and the Pollard affair of 1985, belongs to Stages Four to Six and to later volumes. The discipline that governs it is set out in [scene:df_s04|the account of the CIA–Mossad liaison]: two agencies that share an officer, a hub or a channel are not thereby shown to share everything that passes through either one.

What the record does not settle. The sources do not document a written agreement for 1954–56, and they do not show what the "gentleman's agreement" contained in these years or whether it held. They do not agree on which Israeli service first received the speech. They give no Israeli or American document for the speech's route; the sequence rests on Siskind's account and the 2007 obituary report. They do not date the conduct the critical account attributes to Angleton. And they disagree on when the liaison itself began: the critical account of the CIA–Mossad liaison dates a formal liaison to 1951 and has Angleton managing it from that year, while the CIA historian dates Angleton's counterintelligence command to 1954. [cite:rs_cw2_robarge] [cite:wrmea_cia_mossad_tradeoffs] Both may be true, if Angleton held the account before he held the staff; the sources used here do not say.

sections.h: Alpha: The Anglo-American Search for a Settlement, 1954–1956
sections.html:
While Israeli and Arab forces traded raids across the armistice lines, the governments in Washington and London were working, in secret, on a plan to end the conflict altogether. The effort had a public prelude in 1954, when Assistant Secretary Henry Byroade delivered the speeches that so angered Israel's government, told in [scene:cw2_border_1954|the year after Qibya]. It had a private start at the end of that year. "Alpha" was the State Department's code word for a secret American–British effort to devise an Arab–Israeli settlement, and on 20 December 1954 Secretary of State John Foster Dulles assigned Francis Russell to coordinate it with his British counterpart, Evelyn Shuckburgh. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_alpha]

The familiar account of these years treats the conflict as a contest between local parties, with the great powers looking on or taking sides. The record of Alpha, as the sources used here present it, shows something else: for fifteen months, two Western governments drafted the terms of a peace on the parties' behalf, set out its principles in a public speech, carried them to Cairo and Jerusalem by a secret envoy, and found that neither side would accept them. What follows is the record of that effort, and of the reasons each side gave for saying no.

The mechanism mattered from the start. Alpha was not a negotiation between Israel and Egypt. It was a planning exercise run by two foreign ministries, coordinated by two named officials, whose product would then be offered to the governments concerned. Neither Israel nor Egypt was bound by anything Washington and London agreed between themselves. What the two Western governments could offer was inducement: money, guarantees, and their own diplomatic weight. What they could not do was make either party sign.

The terms the two governments reached in 1955, according to the Jewish Virtual Library and the Economic Cooperation Foundation's database, had three main parts. Israel would cede parts of the Negev to Egypt and Jordan, creating a land link between the two Arab states. Israel would resettle 75,000 Palestinian refugees inside its territory. And the parties would agree to non-belligerence "in lieu of peace", a lesser state than a full treaty. [cite:rs_cw2_ecf_alpha] [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_alpha] Each term asked something specific of Israel: land in the south and the admission of a fixed number of refugees. What the Arab states would give in return was an end to the state of war, short of recognition in a peace treaty.

The public face of the plan came on 26 August 1955, when Dulles addressed the Council on Foreign Relations in New York under the title "American Policy Toward the Middle East". [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_dulles55] Read closely, the address is a careful document. Dulles named three problems. The first was "the tragic plight of the 900,000 refugees". The second was "the pall of fear that hangs over the Arab and Israel people alike". The third was the lack of fixed permanent boundaries between Israel and its neighbours. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_dulles55]

On the refugees, he proposed that they should be enabled to live in dignity "through resettlement and, to such an extent as may be feasible, repatriation". The order of the words carried the policy: resettlement came first and without qualification; return to their former homes came second, and only as far as it proved feasible. He then turned to money. "Compensation is due from Israel to the refugees," he said, and he suggested an international loan to help pay it, to which President Eisenhower would recommend "substantial participation by the United States". [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_dulles55] The money chain he sketched ran from an international lender, with American participation, through Israel, to the refugees: the obligation lay with Israel, but the means would be partly borrowed abroad, with Washington underwriting a share.

On borders and security he offered a guarantee. Eisenhower, he said, would recommend formal American treaty engagements "to prevent or thwart any effort by either side to alter by force" the boundaries the parties agreed. He did not treat the existing lines as final: the armistice lines, he said, were not "permanent frontiers in every respect". He backed a United Nations review of the status of Jerusalem, and shared use of the waters of the Jordan Valley rivers, the subject of the Johnston mission then under way. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_dulles55]

Set beside the secret terms, the speech is notable for what it left general. In the passages of the address quoted in the sources used here, Dulles named no figure for refugees to be admitted to Israel and named no territory to be ceded; he spoke of agreed boundaries and of armistice lines that were not permanent in every respect. Whether the full text was more specific, the excerpts available here do not show. The specifics of Alpha, on this evidence, stayed in the private channel. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_dulles55] [cite:rs_cw2_ecf_alpha]

The address had to be explained in Cairo almost at once. On 1 September 1955 the State Department sent Telegram 421 to its embassy in Egypt with instructions to reassure Nasser on three points. The speech did not exclude some refugees returning to Israel. The proposed guarantee treaties concerned only the borders between Israel and the Arab states, not the wider defence of the Middle East. And the proposals were "only a beginning". The same record reports that Fawzi, for Egypt, had said there was "no plan" to discuss the speech seriously. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_tel421] One reading of the second reassurance is that Washington expected Cairo might read a treaty guarantee as a step toward a Western regional defence system, the kind of system taking shape that year in [scene:cw2_baghdad_bandung|the Baghdad Pact].

On 27 September 1955 Nasser announced the arms deal with Czechoslovakia. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_czech] London made the next public move. On 9 November 1955 Prime Minister Eden addressed the subject in a speech that the American Embassy in London called his "Mansion House" speech; the Economic Cooperation Foundation's database calls it the Guildhall speech. The sources used here do not settle the venue's name; the date is not in doubt. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eden_uk] [cite:rs_cw2_ecf_eden]

Eden set out the two positions as he saw them. Israel preferred the status quo, the armistice lines as they stood. The Arab states demanded the 1947 partition plan and the other United Nations resolutions. The two sides, he said, "must make some compromise between these two positions". He also called the Soviet arming of Egypt "a new element of danger". [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eden_uk] [cite:rs_cw2_ecf_eden] In Jerusalem, as the Israeli replies below show, the formula was read as a territorial demand on Israel.

Washington kept its distance. Dulles, replying from Geneva on 12 November, said the "US is in no sense committed" to the speech. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eden_uk] The two governments that had built Alpha together were now speaking separately in public, and the American Secretary of State would not stand behind the British Prime Minister's formula.

Israel's response came at two levels. Eytan, Director-General of the Foreign Ministry, told the American Embassy that the speech "focused entirely on territorial question" and that the "armistice lines had to be starting point", while adding that Israel was "quite prepared to discuss it". Ben-Gurion went further, in public. On 15 November he told the Knesset that the proposals would "truncate Israel for benefit of neighbors". [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eden_il] The official's reply left a door open for talks on Israel's own terms; Ben-Gurion's closed it on Eden's.

Israel's own priorities by then lay elsewhere. In February 1955 Dulles had offered Israel a mutual defence pact on condition that Israel not expand its borders by force or carry out military retaliation; Ben-Gurion and Sharett accepted the first condition but not the second, an episode told in [scene:cw2_sharett_ben_gurion|the leadership split]. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_east_west] Avi Shlaim records that after the Gaza raid of 28 February 1955, Israeli diplomats shifted from seeking a defence pact to seeking arms. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_alpha] Alpha offered a guarantee of borders in return for concessions of land and refugees; on the record here, Israel wanted weapons rather than a guarantee paid for in territory. The arms requests, and the final American refusal of them in April 1956, are told in the section on the arms race that follows. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_alpha]

With the speeches failing, Eisenhower turned to a personal envoy. Facing opposition from both Egypt and Israel, he sent Robert Anderson, a Texas lawyer and a personal friend, on a secret mission supported by the CIA between January and March 1956. Anderson travelled between Ben-Gurion, Sharett and Nasser. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_alpha] On 27 February 1956 he approved letters to Ben-Gurion and to Nasser for Anderson to carry on his return trip; the record notes that "The President went over these drafts and approved them". [cite:rs_cw2_frus_anderson] The documentary record itself places the mission beside a second question: the State Department's published volume files the Anderson papers in one chapter with its "Continued U.S. Consideration of Funding the Aswan High Dam", the dam whose fate closes this chapter. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_anderson] The filing suggests that peace and the dam were being weighed in the same months, by the same officials, with the same Egyptian leader. Both sides, according to the Jewish Virtual Library, rejected the plan Anderson carried. [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_alpha]

Side by side, the American proposals and the parties' documented positions show how little common ground the record holds. On several of the questions Dulles raised, the sources record no position at all from one side or the other, and the table says so rather than filling the gap.

How each side received the effort can be stated from the record, and it should be stated in each side's own terms. Egypt's government, on the evidence of Telegram 421, declined to engage seriously with the public proposals at all; Washington's anxiety to reassure Nasser that the guarantees were not a back door into a Western defence pact suggests what Cairo feared. Ben-Gurion rejected the territorial proposals in plain words, and Israel's diplomats, by Shlaim's account, had shifted from seeking a pact to seeking arms. From Israel's side, a plan whose central terms were a slice of the Negev and the admission of 75,000 refugees asked it to give up tangible assets for an undertaking from a power that was, in the same months, declining to sell it weapons. From the Arab side, as Eden summarized it, the starting demand was the 1947 plan, and the Western proposals offered far less than that. [cite:rs_cw2_ecf_alpha] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eden_uk] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eden_il]

The strongest case for Alpha's designers is that they addressed every one of the questions left open by the armistices, refugees, borders, security, Jerusalem and water, and offered American money and American treaty commitments to make an agreement possible. The strongest case against it is that it was built without the parties, kept its most demanding terms secret, and asked each side to accept what its leaders had publicly ruled out. Both cases are consistent with the documents. Neither is proven by them.

What the record does not settle is the question every account of Alpha eventually reaches: whether either leader could have accepted it. The sources show refusals; they do not show the internal deliberations behind them, or what Nasser or Ben-Gurion might have accepted on different terms, at a different moment, or without the arms race that began in September 1955. The Anderson papers are cited here only for the President's approval of his letters; their contents, and the envoy's own reports of what each leader told him, are not in the record used for this section. Nor do these sources show what Shuckburgh and Russell argued between themselves, or how the 75,000 figure was reached. The plan failed. Why, beyond the reasons each government stated, remains open.

sections.h: Choosing Sides: Baghdad, Bandung and Amman, 1955–1956
sections.html:
In the twenty months between February 1955 and October 1956, the states of the Middle East were asked, in one forum after another, which side of the Cold War they stood on. Two answers took institutional form within two months of each other. In February 1955 Iraq and Turkey signed a defence pact open to Western membership. In April 1955 twenty-nine Asian and African states met at Bandung, without Israel. Between those poles stood Jordan, whose government tried to join the first camp in December 1955 and whose streets, army and voters pulled it toward the second over the following ten months. It is tempting to read this sequence as a single design. The documents show something less tidy: several governments, each pursuing its own interest, whose decisions converged and collided.

The Pact of Mutual Cooperation between Iraq and Turkey was signed at Baghdad on 24 February 1955. Its text is short and its commitments are general. Article 1 bound the two states to "co-operate for their security and defence". Article 5 opened accession to "any member of the Arab League" or to any other state actively concerned with the security of the region and recognized by both parties. The pact was to run for five years, renewable. [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_baghdad] The accession clause carried the political weight. A treaty between Iraq and Turkey alone was a bilateral arrangement. A treaty open to every member of the Arab League invited each Arab government to decide whether to join, and made the decision a public test.

The membership grew through 1955. Britain adhered on 5 April 1955, Pakistan on 23 September 1955, and Iran on 23 October 1955, the dates as given in the footnote to the Avalon Project's text. [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_baghdad] By the end of the year the pact joined one Arab state, Iraq, to Turkey, Iran, Pakistan and Britain. No other Arab government had acceded. Turkey's own path toward Israel ran on a separate track: it had recognized Israel in March 1949, [cite:w_isr_tur] and its secret intelligence arrangement with Israel belongs to Stage Four, told in [scene:tk_s03|Turkey and Israel].

The United States never signed. Its reasons are set out in a State Department position paper forwarded by Rountree to the Acting Secretary of State in November 1956. Joining, the paper concluded, "would not serve the U.S. national interest". It gave several reasons. Membership would revive Israeli demands for an American security guarantee, and that would complicate ratification in the Senate. It would entangle Washington in the rivalries among the Hashemite monarchies, Saudi Arabia and Egypt. And it would provoke the Soviet Union. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_baghdad_us] The first reason ties the pact directly to Israel's position. A treaty commitment to Iraq, on this logic, would have invited the question why Israel, too, should not have one, in the Senate that would have to ratify it.

Staying out did not mean staying away. Washington joined the pact's Economic and Counter-Subversion Committees in April 1956, set up a military liaison group in Baghdad on 1 November 1956, and paid a one-sixth share of the pact's administrative budget: $76,350 of $459,746. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_baghdad_us] The money was small. The United States took part in the pact's work and paid toward its upkeep while declining the treaty obligation that would have required the Senate's consent. One reading is that this gave Washington a place inside the pact without the commitments that membership would have created.

The alternative alignment assembled at Bandung on 18–24 April 1955. The Asian-African Conference brought together twenty-nine states. It was convened by the prime ministers of Pakistan, India, Burma, Ceylon and Indonesia. [cite:rs_cw2_enc_bandung] One of the convenors, Pakistan, would accede to the Baghdad Pact five months later; the two camps were not sealed off from each other. For the Middle East, one consequence, on Zachary Karabell's reading, was a person. In his words, Bandung "saw Nasser emerge as an international leader". [cite:rs_cw2_enc_bandung] Egypt, which stayed outside the pact, now had a leader with standing well beyond the Arab world.

Israel was not there. It was not invited, according to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, despite the insistence of Burma's U Nu. [cite:rs_cw2_jta_bandung] Middle East Eye adds that Nehru and U Nu both tried to have Israel invited, and that Indonesia "vehemently opposed" it. [cite:rs_cw2_mee_bandung] The two reports differ in emphasis rather than substance: one names a single advocate for Israel's inclusion, the other two, and names Indonesia as the opponent. Neither source explains the full reasoning of the governments involved.

Before the conference opened, the Arab delegations sought a resolution condemning Israel. Nehru was reported to be cool to the idea, and India's delegate, Arthur Lall, said it "remains to be seen" whether such a resolution would reach the floor. [cite:rs_cw2_jta_bandung] What emerged was not a condemnation. The final communiqué declared "support for the rights of the Arab people of Palestine" and called for the implementation of the United Nations resolutions on Palestine and for a peaceful settlement. [cite:rs_cw2_enc_bandung] [cite:rs_cw2_mee_bandung] The wording is worth reading closely. It named the Arab people of Palestine as holders of rights and tied the question to the United Nations resolutions; in the passages quoted in the sources here, it did not name Israel as an aggressor, and it asked for a peaceful settlement. Among the delegates was Haj Amin al-Husseini, who attended as part of Yemen's delegation. [cite:rs_cw2_enc_bandung] [cite:rs_cw2_mee_bandung]

The two gatherings offered two different answers to the same question. The pact's text presented it as cooperation for security and defence, open to any Arab League member that chose to join, and its membership included Britain. Bandung gathered twenty-nine Asian and African states, and, on Karabell's reading, gave Nasser his international stage. Neither text, as quoted in the sources here, states the other camp's objections, and this book does not supply them. Israel had no place in either: it was not invited to Bandung, and nothing in the sources here records any approach to it about the pact. [cite:rs_cw2_avalon_baghdad] [cite:rs_cw2_jta_bandung]

The test came in Jordan. In December 1955, after a British military delegation visited Amman, Prime Minister Hazza al-Majali said he would take Jordan into the Baghdad Pact. Three days of rioting followed. The Arab Legion restored order, and Majali's government resigned within a week. [cite:rs_cw2_loc_jordan] The sequence matters. The announcement came from Jordan's own prime minister; the record shows that it followed the British visit, not that the visit dictated it. And the decision was reversed not by a foreign government but by the reaction in Jordan's own streets.

The reckoning with Britain's place inside Jordan came three months later. In March 1956 King Hussein dismissed Glubb as commander of the Arab Legion. [cite:rs_cw2_loc_jordan] A report from Amman dated 11 March 1956 records how it was done and why. Glubb, it says, was given about 19 hours and left on 2 March. Among the triggers it lists his "open endorsement of Hazza' al-Majali and the supporters of the Baghdad Pact", and a radio station that attacked Egypt while defending Iraq. [cite:rs_cw2_wilson_glubb] The report thus ties Glubb's removal to the pact crisis of December: the commander of Jordan's army had been seen to take one side in a dispute that had brought crowds into the streets.

The army itself was then remade. The Arab Legion was renamed the Jordan Arab Army, its British officers were phased out, and Ali Abu Nuwar succeeded Glubb in command. [cite:rs_cw2_loc_jordan] The force that had restored order in December after the pact riots was, by the spring, under Jordanian command and Jordanian name.

The voters completed the turn. In Jordan's elections of 21 October 1956, the National Socialist Party won a plurality, and Hussein named its leader, Sulayman Nabulsi, an admirer of Nasser, as prime minister. [cite:rs_cw2_loc_jordan] Within a year, a government that had announced its intention to join the Western pact had been replaced by one led by a man who looked to Cairo.

Read together, these events show convergence rather than conspiracy. Iraq's Hashemite government chose a Western alignment. Britain joined it, and sent a military delegation to Amman. The United States paid toward the pact and worked inside its committees but stayed out of the treaty, for reasons its own officials wrote down, Israel's guarantee demand among them. Egypt stood outside, and its leader emerged from Bandung, in Karabell's phrase, as an international leader. Jordan's prime minister moved toward Baghdad; Jordan's crowds, its king and finally its voters moved the other way. Each decision has a named author and a stated or documented reason. None of the sources used here shows a single hand directing them.

What the record does not settle matters as much as what it does. It gives Washington's reasons for staying out only as they were set down in November 1956, after the events of this chapter; whether the same reasoning governed American decisions in 1955 is not shown. It does not give Egypt's own statements against the pact, so Cairo's case appears here only through others' records: the American paper's mention of rivalry, the radio station that the Amman report says attacked Egypt, Nabulsi's admiration for Nasser. It does not show whether the British delegation that visited Amman in December 1955 asked Majali to join, or whether he acted on his own. And on Bandung, the two reports of who argued for Israel's invitation, and why Indonesia opposed it, leave the governments' full reasoning undocumented. The alignments are clear. The private calculations behind several of them are not.

sections.h: The Gaza Raid and Its Aftermath, February–September 1955
sections.html:
On the night of 28 February 1955 Israeli forces crossed the armistice line into the Gaza Strip, then under Egyptian administration, and attacked an Egyptian army camp. Israel's Defense Ministry archive records the action as Operation Black Arrow. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_black_arrow] It set off three chains of consequence that this section follows in turn: a censure at the United Nations, a political uprising in Gaza against the Egyptian authorities themselves, and the creation by Egypt of Palestinian fida'i units that carried attacks into Israel. A fourth consequence, whether the raid drove Egypt to buy Soviet-bloc arms, is the subject of a dispute that the documents allow to be stated precisely but not closed.

Israel's case for the raid. The Defense Ministry archive places the operation at the end of a sequence. It followed a series of border incidents, the archive says, which ended with the infiltration of an Egyptian intelligence squad into Israel and the murder of an Israeli citizen. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_black_arrow] On this account the raid was an answer to attacks organized from Egyptian-held territory, aimed at the army that held it. The raid came one week after David Ben-Gurion returned to the government as defence minister, on 21 February 1955; [cite:rs_cw2_mod_lavon] the internal Israeli argument over this policy of reprisal is told in [scene:cw2_sharett_ben_gurion|the section on Sharett and Ben-Gurion].

The night of 28 February. Egypt's account went to the Security Council the next day. In a letter of 1 March 1955, Egypt's representative described a force of about two platoons that advanced some 3 kilometres into the Strip, blew up an army camp and a water-pump house, and ambushed a relief platoon of 35 men sent to help. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3365] The sources do not agree on the toll, and each count should be read with its source.

Israel's Defense Ministry archive records thirty-eight Egyptian soldiers and eight Israelis killed. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_black_arrow] Egypt's letter to the Council gave 37 members of the armed forces and 2 civilians killed, and 30 soldiers and 2 civilians injured, 32 in all. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3365] The historian Avi Shlaim gives 38 Egyptian soldiers killed and 31 wounded. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_gaza] PalQuest, the Institute for Palestine Studies' reference work, gives 38 dead and 33 injured. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] The sources converge on thirty-eight or thirty-nine Egyptian dead. Only Egypt's letter records civilians among them, and only the Israeli archive records the eight Israeli dead.

The armistice machinery and the Council. The Egyptian–Israeli Mixed Armistice Commission, the joint body that supervised the 1949 agreement, ruled on 6 March 1955. It found that a "planned attack ordered by Israel authorities" had been "committed by Israel regular army forces against the Egyptian regular army force." [cite:rs_cw2_un_res106] The finding mattered for its precision. It established that this was not an act by irregulars or settlers, but a state action by a regular army against another regular army.

The Security Council acted on 29 March 1955. Resolution 106, adopted unanimously at its 695th meeting, condemned the attack as a violation of the cease-fire and as "inconsistent with the obligations of the parties." [cite:rs_cw2_un_res106] No member voted against it or abstained. Its weight lay in the record it made: an armistice body and the Council itself had placed responsibility on the Israeli government.

The two readings of the raid can each be stated at full strength. Israel's case is that a state whose citizens were being killed by squads sent from across the line was entitled to strike the force that controlled that territory, and that Egypt, which administered Gaza, bore responsibility for what was launched from it. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_black_arrow] Egypt's case, which matches the Commission's finding and the Council's resolution, is that a planned attack by a regular army across an armistice line was a breach of the cease-fire, and that the toll fell on soldiers in their camp and on a relief platoon caught in an ambush. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3365] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res106] The resolution, as quoted in the sources here, does not address the incidents Israel cited; the archive does not address the Commission's finding.

Gaza's own response. One political consequence of the raid came not in Cairo but in Gaza, and it was directed against Egypt. On 1 March 1955, the day after the attack, a mass demonstration filled the streets of Gaza. According to PalQuest, the crowds chanted against relocation and against "US agents." Egyptian police opened fire and killed a textile worker, Hosni Belal. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza]

The protesters had a programme. They demanded the cancellation of the Sinai resettlement plan, a scheme agreed by Egypt in 1953 to settle 12,000 refugee families in Sinai; arms and military training for the residents of the camps; and civil freedoms. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] The demands joined two grievances: refugees who refused permanent settlement away from Palestine, and a population that wanted the means to defend itself.

The organization behind the protests was itself unusual. PalQuest records that they were organized jointly by communists and the Muslim Brotherhood, through a Supreme National Committee. Mu'in Bseiso of the Palestinian Communist Party and Fathi al-Balaawi of the Brotherhood negotiated with Egyptian officials. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] Gaza's military governor promised to end the relocation scheme. Then, on the night of 8–9 March 1955, he ordered mass arrests, and the detainees were held until July 1957. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] The episode shows Palestinians in Gaza acting as a political force of their own, with leaders, organizations and stated aims, pressing an Arab government that administered them and paying for it in a death and more than two years of detention.

Late summer: the escalation of August 1955. Within six months the Gaza line had broken into open fighting. General Burns reported to the Security Council at its 700th meeting on 8 September 1955. On his account, Israeli forces occupied an Egyptian post on 22 August, killing an Egyptian officer and two soldiers. Organized attacks by marauders inside Israel followed, killing eleven military and civilian personnel and injuring nine. [cite:rs_cw2_io_1955]

Israel put its own record before the Council. Its letter of 31 August 1955 listed attacks of 30–31 August that it attributed to Egypt, among them the killing of four civilians in a vehicle south of Kfar Menahem, a woman gravely wounded by grenades at Nahala, and three soldiers wounded. [cite:rs_cw2_un_s3427]

On the night of 31 August–1 September 1955 Israeli forces attacked Khan Yunis, in the south of the Strip. Two counts survive in the Council's annual report to the General Assembly. The UNTSO Chief of Staff's account gives "the killing of thirty-six Egyptians, and the wounding of thirteen." Egypt's letter of 6 September 1955 gives "ten Egyptian soldiers and twenty-five refugees" killed, 35 in all, and nineteen injured. [cite:rs_cw2_un_a3157] The difference is not only in the total. The UN observer's figure does not distinguish soldiers from civilians; Egypt's figure says that most of the dead were refugees.

The fedayeen. One of the protesters' demands, arms for Gaza's Palestinians, was answered by Egypt in its own way and on its own terms. The following month, in September 1955, Egypt formed Palestinian fida'i units, known as Battalion 141, under Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Hafez, based in Gaza. Their operations ran until Israeli intelligence assassinated Hafez in July 1956. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza] How the Egyptian government presented these units in public, and how they fit the longer history of crossings over the line since 1949, is told in Volume II's account of [scene:rd6_return_barred|the infiltration years].

The dispute: did the raid push Egypt to Moscow? The most consequential claim about the Gaza raid concerns its effect on Egypt's foreign policy, and here the evidence divides.

The case that it did is made most fully by Avi Shlaim. He writes that the raid "seriously destabilised" Nasser's regime, that Nasser sought arms in its wake, and that the search ended in the Czech arms deal. His conclusion: "by pressing its military advantage too far, Israel inadvertently helped to push Egypt into the arms of Moscow." [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_gaza] An American official at the time read the raid in a similar way. On 11 October 1955 George Allen, the Assistant Secretary of State, met Israel's ambassador Abba Eban; both treated the raid as a turning point. Allen said that Nasser had been "deeply impressed" by reports of Israeli superiority. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_allen]

The case that it did not, or not by itself, rests on two pieces of evidence. The first is Eban's own argument at the same meeting: it was the Turkish–Iraqi pact, not the raid, that changed Nasser's attitude. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_allen] The second is a Soviet document. A Soviet record of a conversation between Nasser and the Soviet ambassador, Solod, shows Nasser formally asking about Soviet arms on 15 June 1954, eight months before the raid. [cite:rs_cw2_solod_gaza]

The two cases are less opposed than they first appear. The Soviet record shows that Nasser was already exploring Soviet arms before the raid; it does not show that he would have bought them without it. Shlaim's argument concerns what turned exploration into a deal; Eban's points to a different cause for the same turn. The participants in October 1955 agreed that something changed in 1955, and disagreed about what. The October 1955 readings came from officials of interested governments, not from detached observers, and should be weighed as such. The arms deal itself, and Washington's handling of Israel's request for arms in response, are told in [scene:cw2_czech_arms|the section on the arms race].

What the record does not settle. The toll of the raid of 28 February varies by source between thirty-eight and thirty-nine Egyptian dead, with Israel's eight dead recorded only in its own archive and the number of wounded given as 31, 32 or 33. The Khan Yunis toll stands at thirty-six by the UN's count and thirty-five by Egypt's, with the two sources disagreeing on how many of the dead were civilians. A higher figure of 72 dead circulates in secondary works and has not been verified; it is not used here. The identity and the full record of the Egyptian squad whose infiltration preceded the raid are not given in the sources. Nor do the sources give the casualties caused by the fida'i units between September 1955 and July 1956, or establish who in Egypt decided to form them and why. Whether the raid caused the Czech deal remains, on this evidence, a question of weight rather than of fact: the documents establish the sequence, and historians and participants still disagree on its cause.

sections.h: The Arms Race: Prague, Washington and Paris, 1954–1956
sections.html:
The question of who would arm Egypt, and who would arm Israel, was settled in the twelve months after September 1955. Egypt found its weapons in the Soviet bloc. Israel asked Washington and was refused, and found its aircraft in France. The documents of those months show each government's reasons in its own officials' words, and they show that the outcome was produced by several decisions taken in several capitals, each for its own purposes.

Egypt's approach to Moscow began well before the deal became public. On 15 June 1954, more than a year earlier, Nasser had told the Soviet ambassador that Britain had stopped arms shipments and blocked supplies from other European states, that Egypt could not meet "a hundredth of its army's needs", and had formally asked the Soviet position on selling arms to Egypt. [cite:rs_cw2_wilson_solod] That conversation, and the revolution that brought Nasser to power, are told in [scene:cw2_free_officers|Egypt's revolution]. Its date matters for what follows, because it predates by eight months the Gaza raid that some accounts treat as the deal's cause.

On 27 September 1955 Nasser announced that Czechoslovakia would supply Egypt with Soviet heavy weapons: tanks, MiG-15 fighters and bombers. The Jewish Virtual Library values the deal at "more than $83 million"; no primary figure for its value appears in the sources used here. Nasser called the arrangement "unconditional". [cite:rs_cw2_jvl_czech] [cite:rs_cw2_adst_czech] The American embassy in Cairo had already grasped its form. Byroade reported on 29 September that the "actual agreement on arms was with Czechoslovakia": the weapons were Soviet, but the contracting party was Prague. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_tel632]

Around 1 October 1955, Assistant Secretary George Allen and Byroade met Nasser, and he told them how the deal would be paid for. Egypt had already sent one million Egyptian pounds to Prague "on account". Cotton and rice would be shipped "more or less parallel" with the arms. And the agreement, he said, was "without any conditions whatsoever". [cite:rs_cw2_frus_tel632] The payment mechanism was barter backed by a cash deposit. Egypt would pay largely in its own crops, and the deliveries of goods and weapons would move together.

Why had Egypt not bought from the United States instead? Allen gave his account to Ambassador Abba Eban on 11 October 1955. The deal, he said, "would go through", and it would not be "of token proportions". Nasser had first presented it to the Americans as trading "cotton which Egypt could not sell elsewhere for arms which Egypt could not obtain elsewhere". And the sticking point in the American arms talks with Egypt, Allen said, had been the American requirement that a military mission accompany any sale, not a demand for a non-aggression pledge. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_allen_czech] Allen and Eban also disagreed that day about what had turned Nasser toward Moscow, the Gaza raid or the Turkish–Iraqi pact; that dispute, with the evidence on each side, is set out in [scene:cw2_gaza_raid|the Gaza raid and what followed].

Israel's answer was to ask Washington for arms of its own. On 16 November 1955 Eban, with Shiloah and Salmon, met Hoover, Murphy and Allen and presented a confidential list of arms "solely for defensive purposes". The request, he said, "sprang directly" from the imbalance created by the Czech deal. He added that, despite press reports, Israel had not obtained any Mystères from France. Hoover replied that the United States had to consider the other signatories of the Tripartite Declaration. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_hoover] That reply named the constraint Washington would invoke: it did not act on arms to the region alone, but with regard to the other governments that had signed the declaration.

According to Avi Shlaim, Dulles had decided, on the eve of the raid at Lake Tiberias in December 1955, to sell Israel defensive arms. In Shlaim's account, the raid changed the decision. On 13 December 1955 Eban was told it had been postponed. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] The raid itself, Israel's attack on Syrian positions east of Lake Tiberias on the night of 11–12 December, and the Council's response to it, are told in [scene:cw2_border_un_1956|the border and the United Nations]. Its effect on the arms question was immediate. Sharett had been in Washington seeking those arms when, Shlaim writes, Ben-Gurion alone authorized the raid. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_kinneret] Sharett recorded his reaction in words Shlaim quotes: "My world became black, the matter of arms was murdered." [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms]

Sharett pressed again at the end of the month. In late December 1955 he stressed to the American Embassy Israel's "almost complete lack of defensive facilities" against Egyptian jets. Israel wanted twelve Mystère IVs that it had ordered from France, and the French had said their release rested "entirely with US Government". The first 15 MiGs had reached Egypt about two months earlier. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_tlv_jan56] The documents thus show a chain of dependence. Israel had ordered French aircraft; France would not release them without Washington's approval; and Washington had postponed its own decision on arms for Israel. The final American refusal of Israel's request came in April 1956. [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_alpha]

The policy behind these refusals had a longer history. The aid relationship as summarized in the panel below began with economic aid and loans only, from 1948 to 1961, and the panel gives the reason as Washington's wish to avoid selling arms for fear of alienating the Arab oil states; the first American military aid to Israel came in 1962, and then as loans.

The documents of 1955 and 1956 fill in that general rule with particular reasons, and they are not quite the same reason. Hoover cited the Tripartite partners. The postponement followed the Kinneret raid. Neither of those documented statements mentions oil. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_eban_hoover] [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] The panel's reason describes the policy across fourteen years; the records of these months show what officials said when they applied it to a specific request.

Refused in Washington, Israel turned to Paris. Shlaim presents the French orientation as the result of the American refusal. Peres, he writes, went directly to the French defence establishment. Shlaim's reading of the two Western governments' motives is sharply drawn: "France offered arms in the hope of inducing Israel to go to war against Egypt," while "America allowed its allies to supply arms to Israel on condition that Israel did not go to war." [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms] That is a historian's interpretation of motive, not a document's statement of it, and it should be read as such. The American records used here show Washington's role in the French channel as a veto rather than a sponsorship: the French said release of the first twelve Mystères depended on the United States, and in September 1956 Washington judged a further French sale undesirable. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_tlv_jan56] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_mystere]

By September 1956 Israel was believed to hold French jets. A State Department memorandum from Rountree to Hoover, dated 20 September 1956, said that Israel was believed to have 24 Mystères and that it "appears possible" it had 48. British sources reported "forty-eight Mystere IVs from France". Eighteen aircraft seen passing through Brindisi may have been heading to Israel. And France had proposed selling 24 more through the Near East Arms Coordinating Committee, a proposal Washington called undesirable. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_mystere] The memorandum's own uncertainty is part of the record: the State Department did not know, in September 1956, whether Israel had 24 French jets or twice as many.

Laid side by side, on the record used here, the governments' positions explain the outcome without any need for a hidden design. Cairo had asked Moscow for arms in June 1954, its leader saying that Britain had cut off supplies, and its talks with Washington had stalled, on Allen's account, over an American military mission; it paid in cotton and rice for weapons that came without conditions. Washington would not supply Israel directly, cited its Tripartite partners, postponed its decision after an Israeli raid, and refused in April 1956, while keeping a say over what its allies sold. Paris, on Shlaim's reading, had reasons of its own for arming Israel against Egypt. In Jerusalem, the leadership was divided: Sharett sought arms through Washington and saw his effort undone by a raid authorized while he was there, and Peres went to the French. Each capital acted on its own interest. The result was that by September 1956 Egypt held Soviet-bloc arms and Israel held French jets, and the United States had supplied neither.

Several things remain open in the sources used here. The value of the Czech deal rests on a secondary figure, "more than $83 million", with no primary confirmation. The number of Mystères in Israel by September 1956 was uncertain even to the State Department, at 24 or possibly 48. Allen's explanation of why the American talks with Egypt stalled is one official's account, given to Israel's ambassador, and no Egyptian record of those talks is before this book. Shlaim's account of Dulles's decision on the eve of the Kinneret raid, and his reading of French motives, are a historian's reconstruction rather than documents quoted here; whether the United States would have sold Israel arms had the raid not happened cannot be settled from these sources. What the record does establish is the sequence: an Egyptian request in 1954, a Soviet-bloc deal in 1955, an American refusal in 1956, and a French supply line open by the autumn of that year.

sections.h: The Lake, the Council and the Secretary-General, December 1955–October 1956
sections.html:
By the end of 1955 the pattern of the border had been set for two years: an attack across the line, an Israeli military reply on a larger scale, a complaint to the Mixed Armistice Commission and then to the Security Council, and a resolution of censure. The last year of this stage tested whether that pattern could be broken by the United Nations itself. It began with a raid on the Syrian front, brought a unanimous censure from the Council and a personal mission by the Secretary-General, and ended, in October 1956, with Israeli forces again crossing the line at night.

On the night of 11–12 December 1955 Israeli regular forces attacked Syrian army positions on the eastern side of Lake Tiberias. Syria complained to the Security Council on 13 December. [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_kinneret] The operation, which Avi Shlaim names Olive Leaves, was in his account authorized by Ben-Gurion alone. Ben-Gurion had returned as defence minister in February 1955 and as prime minister on 3 November 1955; Moshe Sharett, his predecessor as prime minister, was now foreign minister, and he was in Washington asking for arms. [cite:rs_cw2_mod_bg_portfolio] [cite:rs_cw2_pmo_govts] Shlaim quotes Sharett's jibe that "Ben-Gurion the defence minister consulted with Ben-Gurion the foreign minister," and Abba Eban's verdict that "the short-term objective had triumphed unduly over our long-term aims." [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_kinneret] The timing was the injury. As the section on the arms race tells, the answer Sharett had come to Washington for was put off in the days after the raid, and in the end refused ([scene:cw2_czech_arms|the arms race]). [cite:rs_cw2_shlaim_arms]

Israel's case was the lake itself. UNTSO's Chief of Staff reported to the Council on 15 and 30 December 1955 that Israel linked the attack to Syrian fire on Israeli fishing boats and on the police escorts that accompanied them. He did not dismiss the provocation. He weighed it, and found "a striking disparity between the scale of retaliation and the provocation." [cite:rs_cw2_frus_kinneret] The word retaliation was the UN's own here: the dispute was not over whether the raid answered something, but over whether the answer bore any proportion to it.

Inside Israel's government the reaction ran along the line that had divided it since 1953, told in [scene:cw2_sharett_ben_gurion|the leadership split]. The American Embassy in Tel Aviv reported, in a telegram received on 3 January 1956, that Sharett did not condemn the government's action but appeared to regard it "as a severe blunder." [cite:rs_cw2_frus_tlv_kinneret] On the Embassy's report, the foreign minister would not break with the cabinet in public, and did not defend the decision either.

The Council's answer came on 19 January 1956. Resolution 111 was adopted unanimously at the 715th meeting, on a draft put forward jointly by the United States, Britain and France. It condemned the attack as "a flagrant violation" of the cease-fire, of the Israel–Syria Armistice Agreement and of the Charter. It took up Israel's case directly and rejected it: Syrian interference with Israeli activities on the lake, the resolution held, "in no way justifies the Israel action." And it closed with a warning. If Israel did not comply, the Council would "have to consider what further measures under the Charter are required." [cite:rs_cw2_un_res111] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_kinneret]

That last sentence threatened more than it imposed: it named no measure and set no deadline. The resolution was the third Council censure of an Israeli raid in this stage, after Resolution 101 on Qibya in November 1953 and Resolution 106 on Gaza in March 1955, and it was the one that answered Israel's stated justification most directly. [cite:rs_cw2_un_res101] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res106] [cite:rs_cw2_un_res111]

Censure had not changed the pattern, and in the spring the Council tried a different instrument: the Secretary-General in person. On 4 April 1956 it asked Dag Hammarskjöld, unanimously, to survey how far the parties were complying with the armistice agreements. He travelled in the region from 10 April to 3 May 1956 and reported on 9 May. [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] What he brought back was a set of assurances. Each government undertook to observe the cease-fire "unconditionally", provided the other side complied, and each reserved its right of self-defence under Article 51 of the Charter. [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] On one reading, an unconditional pledge that was conditional on the other party's conduct, with self-defence reserved, left every government the judge of when it was released from it.

The Council adopted the Secretary-General's approach on 4 June 1956, again unanimously. It endorsed his view that full compliance with the armistice agreements "represents a stage which has to be passed" before progress could be made on the main issues, and it declared that the freedom of movement of UN observers "must be respected." [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] The first point set the order of things: no progress on the main issues until the armistice itself was kept.

The summer showed how much the assurances held. In mid-August 1956 mines and attacks near the Gaza Strip killed four Israeli citizens and wounded eight. The next day an Egyptian car carrying medical personnel was ambushed in territory under Egyptian control, and nine Egyptians were killed. [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] The two incidents sit side by side in the UN's own annual record, a day apart. The Gaza front by then had its own history of escalation, from the raid of February 1955 through the Egyptian-organized fida'i units, whose commander, Mustafa Hafez, had been killed by Israeli intelligence in July 1956. [cite:rs_cw2_palquest_gaza]

On the Jordanian line, the UN Yearbook lists incidents at Sheikh Abd el Aziz and Mount Scopus on 24–25 July 1956 and at Sharafi near Husan on 25–26 September. [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] Then, on the night of 10–11 October 1956, Israeli forces demolished the police post at Qalqilya, in Jordan, with explosives. The Yearbook says the attack inflicted "heavy casualties". It gives no figure. [cite:rs_cw2_unyb1956] This book gives none either, because no figure from the sources used here supports one.

The case for the Israeli government across these ten months rested on what it faced: fire on its fishermen on the lake, mines and attacks on the Gaza line that killed Israeli citizens. It had accepted the Secretary-General's cease-fire on the same reciprocal terms as its neighbours, and it held that each raid answered a breach. The case made by the Council was put in the Council's own words: that there was a "striking disparity" between the scale of retaliation and the provocation, as UNTSO reported of the lake, and that no interference by Syria could justify what was done there. Both cases were made at the time, by the governments and bodies charged with the line, and both stand in the record.

Several things the record used here does not settle. It gives no casualty figures for the Lake Tiberias raid or for Qalqilya. It does not say, for the August killings near Gaza, which incident each government regarded as the first breach. And it does not show that Resolution 111's warning of "further measures" was ever followed by any. Two weeks after Qalqilya the Jordanian elections of 21 October 1956 brought Sulayman Nabulsi, an admirer of Nasser, to the premiership. [cite:rs_cw2_loc_jordan] The killings at Kafr Qasim and the Sinai campaign that followed belong to Stage Three.

sections.h: From the Dam to the Canal, December 1955–26 July 1956
sections.html:
The stage ends with Washington's offer to Egypt withdrawn. For seven months the United States, Britain and the World Bank held out an offer to finance the High Dam at Aswan. On 19 July 1956 the United States withdrew it. A week later Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company. The familiar story runs these two events together as cause and consequence. The documents show the sequence clearly enough; what they do not show with one voice is why the offer was withdrawn, and the officials who took part gave different answers in their later recollections.

The offer dated from 16 December 1955. It was a joint undertaking of the United States, the United Kingdom and the World Bank. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_aswan_ike] Its terms are known in detail only from later recollection. Parker Hart, in an oral history recorded for the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training, recalled that the United States was prepared to make a grant of about $56 million at once, with roughly 85 per cent of the grant share coming from the United States and 15 per cent from Britain. The American loan that was to follow carried conditions: Egyptian fiscal reforms, and a prior agreement between Egypt and Sudan on the Nile waters. [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] Hart remembered Nasser's reaction to the conditions in one line: "This is a denigration of Egypt." [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] These are the figures of one participant's oral history, recorded long afterward. No primary text of the offer is in the record used here.

The objection can be read against the year before. In 1954 the same government had negotiated British troops out of the Canal Zone, in an agreement that recognized the Canal as "an integral part of Egypt"; on one reading, conditions on its fiscal policy and on its dealings with Sudan touched the same question of who decided Egypt's affairs. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_suez_base] The offer was nonetheless kept open, and by July 1956 Egypt's ambassador, Ahmed Hussein, was returning to Washington to announce that Egypt accepted it. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_aswan_ike]

The decision to withdraw was taken before he arrived. At 9:40 on the morning of 19 July 1956 Eisenhower met John Foster Dulles and Herbert Hoover Jr. at the White House. The meeting lasted twelve minutes. The President agreed with Dulles that "we should withdraw the U.S. offer upon the occasion of the Ambassador's visit." [cite:rs_cw2_frus_aswan_ike] The memorandum records four reasons: Egypt's economic conditions had changed since the offer was made; the dispute over the Nile waters was unresolved; the austerity the project would demand would make whoever built the dam unpopular in Egypt; and it had become harder to work with Nasser's government. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_aswan_ike]

That afternoon, from 4:10 to 5:07, Dulles received Hussein at the State Department. He told him it was "not feasible at present" to go ahead. He put the cost of the dam at $1.3 billion, of which $900 million would have to be found inside Egypt. He said that "no single project in the Mutual Security Program was as unpopular today," and that the dam should be "put on the shelf." Then he gave a reason that had not appeared in the morning's list in these words: the basic opposition, he said, came from a feeling that Egypt was working with those "hostile to us." [cite:rs_cw2_frus_dulles_hussein]

Hussein made Egypt's case in reply, and it deserves to be heard at the strength he gave it. The dam, he said, was "the only solution to the population problem." Moscow was making a "very generous" offer. And "there were strong pressures which Nasser might not be able to resist." Dulles answered that any Soviet offer would be made "for political purposes." [cite:rs_cw2_frus_dulles_hussein] The exchange set out the two positions: for Egypt's ambassador the dam was the answer to the population problem, and for Dulles the choice of financier was a political question.

Why the offer was withdrawn is the question this section cannot close, because those who took part answered it differently. The first answer is the one in the documents of the day: a policy judgment about Egypt itself. Its economy had changed, the Nile question was open, the austerity would turn Egyptians against the builder, and Nasser's government was drawing closer to the Soviet bloc. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_aswan_ike] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_dulles_hussein] The compilers of the oral histories add that the Czech arms deal of September 1955 ([scene:cw2_czech_arms|the arms race]) and Egypt's recognition of Communist China had angered Dulles. [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan]

The second answer is domestic politics. Robert Bowie recalled that Congress was turning hostile to the project and that the hostility came from several directions at once: cotton growers, supporters of Israel and the China lobby. Members threatened legislation that would forbid the use of aid funds for the dam. Fraser Wilkins called Congress the "real reason." [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] Read carefully, this account names three separate constituencies, cotton growers, supporters of Israel and the China lobby, converging in one Congress; it does not describe a single hand behind the decision, and Dulles's own remark to Hussein about the project's unpopularity is consistent with it without proving it. [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_dulles_hussein]

The third answer is personal. Parker Hart called Dulles's decision "impulsive." James Cortada, in the same oral-history collection, read it the other way round, as a trap that Nasser had set for Washington. [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] On one reading, the record of the morning meeting does not support the word impulsive in any simple sense, since the decision came with four stated reasons and was taken in advance of the ambassador's visit; nor does it rule out that the reasons were assembled for a conclusion already reached.

A week later, on 26 July 1956, Nasser announced the nationalization of the Suez Canal Company, and offered full compensation. The State Department's own historians note that the company had been jointly British and French owned and operated. [cite:rs_cw2_state_suez] Bowie recalled that the nationalization came "within a matter of ten days" of the withdrawal. [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] The interval was in fact seven days, from 19 to 26 July; the dates are those of the primary record. [cite:rs_cw2_frus_aswan_ike] [cite:rs_cw2_state_suez]

The money in this episode moved, or failed to move, along clear lines. On the offer as Hart recalled it, the United States would have carried most of the grant and Britain the rest, with the World Bank alongside. Dulles's own figures put the greater part of the cost on Egypt: $900 million of $1.3 billion was to be raised internally. [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] [cite:rs_cw2_frus_dulles_hussein] When the offer was withdrawn, by the oral histories' account, Egypt turned to the Soviet Union; Wilkins later described the dam as a "$600 million project under the Russians." [cite:rs_cw2_adst_aswan] That figure and Dulles's $1.3 billion are not reconciled in the sources used here, and they may not measure the same thing. The Canal Company passed from its British and French owners to Egypt, with full compensation offered to them. [cite:rs_cw2_state_suez]

Egypt's case, as far as the record used here gives it, rested on sovereignty and on need: the 1954 accord with Britain had recognized the Canal as "an integral part of Egypt", and the dam was, in its ambassador's words, the only answer to the country's population problem.
