Second, the Arab states would feel "profound dismay and frustration," and the United States would be among the main targets of their resentment. Third, they would turn to the Soviet Union. Fourth, Israel would seek American acceptance of its capability. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

Each judgment was a forecast of behaviour, not a finding of fact. Taken together they set out why the matter was an American problem and not only a regional one. On Kent's reading, an Israeli bomb would harden Israel's posture, turn Arab anger against Washington, open the region further to Moscow, and then present the United States with a request to accept the result. The memorandum treated Israeli acquisition as a real prospect with consequences that would land on American policy; it did not say that Israel had decided to acquire the weapon.

NSAM 231, 26 March 1963. The memorandum reached the President through McCone, the Director of Central Intelligence. On 26 March 1963, the day after Kennedy received Kent's estimate from McCone, McGeorge Bundy issued National Security Action Memorandum 231. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] It gave three instructions. It ordered "every feasible measure to improve our intelligence on the Israeli nuclear program." It ordered prompt arrangement of "the next informal inspection." And it asked for proposals to forestall nuclear programmes in the region. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

The memorandum also shows a small discrepancy in the record. The editors of the National Security Archive's collection describe it as addressed to the Departments of State and Defense and the CIA. The document itself is addressed to State, the Atomic Energy Commission and the Director of Central Intelligence. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] This book follows the document's own list, on which the Atomic Energy Commission was among those charged with acting. The day after NSAM 231, the State Department's telegram 658 instructed the ambassador in Tel Aviv to seek "semi-annual" visits to Dimona, the opening move of [scene:s11b|the battle of the letters]. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

SNIE 30-2-63, 8 May 1963. In May the intelligence community put dates on its judgment. Special National Intelligence Estimate 30-2-63, of 8 May 1963, judged that Israel "could detonate a domestically developed nuclear device by late 1965, but a more likely date would be sometime in 1966," and that a deliverable weapon would take "a year or two more (1967-68)." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The language is again conditional: "could," "more likely." It was a forecast of when a capability could exist, not a report that a decision had been taken. But it converted January's yield estimate into a timetable, and its deliverable-weapon date matched the "67-68" of Komer's warning.

Kennedy and Couve de Murville, 25 May 1963. Dimona had been built with substantial French assistance. [cite:wilsoncenter_kennedy_dimona_61_62] Kennedy raised it with the French foreign minister, Couve de Murville, on 25 May 1963. The conversation survives in two records, and they do not say the same thing. In the French record, Kennedy said that "we would be blamed equally, you for furnishing uranium, and we for the financial aid." In the American record, he said that Israel's position gave "a pretext to the Russians." Couve, for his part, said that Israel could make at most one or two bombs. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

The two versions reveal different concerns, and both may be accurate records of different parts of one conversation. The French note has Kennedy thinking about responsibility: American aid money and French uranium would be named together if Israel built a weapon. The American note has him thinking about the Soviet Union: an Israeli programme would hand Moscow an argument. Couve's "at most one or two" happened to match the January estimate's yearly figure.

Why Kennedy cared. The editors of the collection place Kennedy's concern within his general view of proliferation as "a major challenge to American power." He feared that an Israeli bomb would draw the Soviets into the region and lead others to "follow suit." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] That is the motive the editors' reading supports, and it is consistent with both versions of the Couve conversation and with Kent's third forecast. The documents present it as a matter of American strategy: a world with more nuclear states was one in which American power counted for less, and a nuclear Israel would invite Soviet involvement and imitation. They do not show a motive beyond that, and none should be read into them.

The two readings. The disagreement inside the American government in these months was real, and each side had documents. On one side stood the evidence of inspection and the embassy's judgment. American visits, the latest in September 1962, had found nothing inconsistent with peaceful use, and the State Department had said so to its posts in October. In February the embassy's science attaché judged that Israel was "not making a serious effort." [cite:rs_cw5_frus18_d87] [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The strongest form of this case was that the people closest to the reactor had looked and found no serious effort, and that capability is not intent.

On the other side stood the estimates. NIE 30-63 put potential output at one or two weapons a year at full power. SNIE 30-2-63 dated a first device to late 1965 or 1966. Kent's memorandum treated acquisition as a real prospect with consequences for American policy across the region. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The strongest form of this case was that a reactor of this size, whatever its operators said, would give Israel the means within a few years, and that a government ought to plan for a capability before it existed, not after.

The estimates themselves kept the distinction that the argument turned on. They spoke throughout of what Israel "could" do and when. None of them stated that Israel's government had decided to build a weapon, and none claimed knowledge of its intentions. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:wilsoncenter_kennedy_dimona_61_62] On the documents reached here, what moved Kennedy in the spring of 1963 was a forecast of capability joined to his own view of proliferation, not proof of a decision. By March that was enough to produce a presidential directive; by May it was enough to put a date on the problem.

The longer American effort to watch Dimona, and the arguments about what that effort later found and failed to find, run well beyond this period and are taken up in [scene:cia_s16|the Dimona surveillance loop].

The record leaves several questions open. The documents collected here do not show what information, if any, separated the embassy's February reading from the January estimate, or whether the two were ever reconciled on paper. They do not give the date of Komer's warning. They do not settle whether the French or the American record of the Couve conversation is the fuller account, or whether both are partial. And they do not show what Israel's government had decided by the spring of 1963. The estimates said what Israel could do; what it intended remained, for Washington, a question the next round of inspections was meant to answer.

sections.h: The Fulbright Inquiry: Thirteen Parts and the Foreign Agents Act, 1963–1964
sections.html:
The Justice Department's order to the American Zionist Council, told in [scene:s11a|the order of 21 November 1962], was issued while a Senate committee was preparing a wider question: how foreign governments and foreign interests were represented in Washington by people who were not diplomats, and whether the law that was supposed to make that representation visible was working. The published record shows a broader investigation, in which the Agency was the subject of one part out of thirteen. This section sets out the inquiry as a whole and the state of the Foreign Agents Registration Act at the time, so that the Agency's case can be read in its setting.

The mandate. The inquiry was authorized by Senate Resolution 362 of the 87th Congress, second session, and continued by Senate Resolution 26 of the 88th Congress, first session. Both rested on sections 134 and 136 of the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1946. [cite:rs_cw5_sres26] Resolution 26 directed the Committee on Foreign Relations to study the activities of nondiplomatic representatives of foreign principals "tending or intended to influence the foreign or domestic policies or interests of the United States", and to consider existing and proposed legislation and recommend changes. [cite:rs_cw5_sres26] The wording mattered. The committee was not charged with investigating a particular country or lobby; it was charged with examining a category of activity, influence on American policy exercised on behalf of foreign principals by people outside the diplomatic system, and with judging whether the law covering that activity was adequate.

The resolution ran from 1 March 1963 to 31 January 1964. It capped the committee's expenses at $48,600, drawn from the Senate's contingent fund, and required a report with recommendations to the Senate by 31 January 1964. It gave the committee power to hold hearings, issue subpoenas, take testimony and hire temporary staff. [cite:rs_cw5_sres26] The committee's chairman, J. William Fulbright, Democrat of Arkansas, presided over the sessions on the Jewish Agency. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630628]

The thirteen parts. The hearings were published as Activities of Nondiplomatic Representatives of Foreign Principals in the United States (88th Congress, 1st session). They run to thirteen parts and 1,998 pages, with hearing dates catalogued from 4 February to 14 May 1963. [cite:rs_cw5_ol_hearings] The subjects range across the world. Part 2 dealt with the Philippine sugar lobby and John A. O'Donnell. Part 3 examined payments by the Dominican Republic Information Center to the International News Service, and Parts 4 and 5 took up Dominican sugar lobbying. Part 6 concerned news agencies writing for foreign interests. Parts 7 and 10 followed the Hamilton Wright Organization's work for the Republic of China and for South Africa. Part 8 examined Selvage and Lee's work for Portuguese businessmen. Part 11 concerned I. Irving Davidson's work for Nicaragua's President Luis Somoza, and Part 13 the West German public relations of Julius Klein. [cite:rs_cw5_ol_hearings] Part 9 concerned the activities of the Jewish Agency for Israel and related lobbying organizations; the catalogue lists "Jewish Agency for Israel (U.S.)" among the subjects of the set. [cite:rs_cw5_ol_hearings]

The catalogue records reached for this book do not describe Parts 1 and 12. Two parts can be dated more closely. Part 8 records hearings on 12 April and 6 May 1963 and occupies pages 827 to 1209 of the series, close to a fifth of the whole. [cite:rs_cw5_unt_pt8] Part 13 prints a sworn letter of 21 October 1963 from Edwin Hartrich in Düsseldorf about a dispute with General Julius Klein (retired), which shows that the record was still being compiled in the autumn of 1963, months after the last catalogued hearing date. [cite:rs_cw5_sres26] The Jewish Agency's sessions also fell outside the catalogued range: the Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported closed sessions in June 1963, and Barda places the hearings on the Agency's funding in August. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630628] [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The catalogue's dates do not describe the whole of the committee's work.

The question the committee was asking. By June 1963, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported, the committee had for "several months" been studying the administration of the Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630628] That framing explains the Agency's place in it. The Jewish Agency–American Section was already a registrant under the Act in 1963, as the agent of the World Zionist Organization and of the Jewish Agency in Jerusalem. The committee's question was therefore not whether the Agency was registered, but how the law was being administered. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630628] On this book's reading, the same question ran through the other parts: sugar lobbying, payments to a news agency and public-relations contracts were each a form of influence on behalf of a foreign principal that the Act was meant to bring into view.

The law in practice. The Act's requirements, registration within ten days and penalties of up to five years in prison, are set out with the order of November 1962. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] How it was administered is visible in the Attorney General's annual report to Congress for 1964, published in April 1965, the nearest such report reached for this volume. The Attorney General counted 419 active registrations at the close of 1963 and 480 at the end of 1964. [cite:rs_cw5_doj_fara_1964] For 1964 he reported that "No prosecutive action for willful violations of the Act was required to be undertaken during the year." [cite:rs_cw5_doj_fara_1964] Enforcement, in that year at least, worked through disclosure rather than prosecution: after the Department asked registrants for fuller disclosure, more than 200 amended registration statements were filed in 1964. [cite:rs_cw5_doj_fara_1964]

The report shows where Israel-related activity sat within the registry. It lists the Jewish Agency for Israel, American Section, among registrants, and records that it distributed The Israel Digest, a biweekly news pamphlet, in 8,500 copies. It states that "Two registrants distributed the bulk of Israeli publicity in the United States", and it lists among Israel-related registrants the Israel Government Tourist Office, Israel Information Services and the Israel Philatelic Agency in America. [cite:rs_cw5_doj_fara_1964] It does not mention the American Zionist Council. [cite:rs_cw5_doj_fara_1964] The silence cuts both ways: the report records no registration by the Council, and it records no enforcement action against it either.

The report also shows the law itself in motion. It refers to proposed legislation that would allow the Attorney General to require registrants to "maintain separate books and records" for their foreign principal. [cite:rs_cw5_doj_fara_1964] And it discusses Rabinowitz and Boudin v. Attorney General (376 U.S. 605), decided on 30 March 1964, in which the Supreme Court held that the petitioners' work for Cuba fell within the Act's registration provisions. [cite:rs_cw5_doj_fara_1964] That pattern was not peculiar to 1964. The Act, enacted in 1938, was historically rarely invoked as a criminal statute, and after 1966 its enforcement generally shifted toward civil penalties. [cite:crustnews_aipac_history] That was a general pattern across the Act, and it is the context in which any one organization's non-registration has to be read. In the year after the inquiry, then, the Act was being tested in the courts, tightened on paper and enforced by requests for amendment, while no one was prosecuted under it.

One case among many, or a case of special weight? The two readings of the inquiry rest on different evidence and ask different questions. The first rests on the published record itself. The catalogue shows thirteen parts covering principals from the Philippines, the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua, Portugal, the Republic of China, South Africa and West Germany, of which the Jewish Agency was Part 9. [cite:rs_cw5_ol_hearings] On this reading the committee was doing what its resolution asked: surveying influence by nondiplomatic agents of many foreign principals, of which Israel-related organizations were one group among several, and the Agency an existing registrant whose disclosure was examined like others'.

The second reading concerns weight, not count. Grant F. Smith of IRmep, an advocate of registration, presents the Jewish Agency–American Zionist Council material as the inquiry's central finding: evidence of an Israeli funding conduit into American lobbying. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_antiwar_2013] The strongest form of his case is that Part 9 touched a body the Justice Department had separately ordered to register, and that the sums involved, on the figures in the order and the Senate record, ran into millions of dollars. Kobby Barda, writing in Modern Judaism in 2026, rejects that reading. He calls the arrangement an American lobby operating within the law, and treats the payments as purchases that ended before the hearings. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The strongest form of his case is that the inquiry's subject was the administration of the Act, that the Agency was already registered under it, and that the committee's chairman, by the account of the Agency's own chairman, said there had been no wrongdoing. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630816] Both readings, and the evidence each side brought, are set out in [scene:cw5_jewish_agency_hearing|the Jewish Agency before the committee].

The record answers part of the question and leaves the rest open. It settles the count: the Agency was one subject among many in a survey whose breadth is a matter of record. It does not settle the weight, which depends on what Part 9 showed and on figures for the Agency's payments that remain unreconciled. Nor do the sources reached for this volume show the committee's final report, whether it was delivered by its 31 January 1964 deadline, or what it recommended. What is documented is the inquiry's mandate, its budget, its thirteen parts, and the state of the law it examined: 480 registrants by the end of 1964, none prosecuted that year, and a proposal, not yet law, to make them keep their foreign principals' accounts apart.

sections.h: The German Scientists in Egypt and the Fall of Isser Harel, 1962–1963
sections.html:
In the same summer that Washington was weighing wheat for Cairo, Israel's government learned that Egypt was building rockets with the help of German engineers, some of whom had worked on the V1 and V2. What followed over the next nine months, a covert campaign against the scientists, a scandal in Switzerland, a crisis with Bonn and the resignation of the head of the Mossad, Isser Harel, is known in the literature as Operation Damocles. It is an episode in which much rests on secondary accounts, and in which several of the most dramatic events are told differently by different writers. This section sets out what each source says, and which details remain without a date or a firm attribution.

The rockets, July–August 1962. In July 1962 Egypt test-fired rockets and paraded two new types through the streets of Cairo. Nasser announced four successful tests. Israel learned that he had recruited German scientists who had worked on the V1 and V2. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_damocles] [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_damocles] In August 1962, according to accounts compiled from the secondary literature, the Mossad obtained a document written by Wolfgang Pilz about Egypt's Factory 333; it cited 900 rockets under construction. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_damocles] The figure is the document's, as these accounts report it. Neither the document itself nor an assessment of whether the number was a plan, a boast or a production record is in the sources reached for this book.

For Israel's leaders the difficulty lay in the combination. The programme was Nasser's; the men building it were veterans of the V1 and V2; and they were German citizens, so that any action against them touched Israel's relations with West Germany, which, as the record below shows, Ben-Gurion and Peres believed the campaign would rupture. How Israel answered would depend on which of those facts it put first.

Krug, September 1962. The first event in the accounts reached here is a disappearance. In September 1962 Heinz Krug, head of a Munich company that supplied the Egyptian programme, vanished. Who killed him is disputed between the writers who have told the story. Raviv and Melman name Otto Skorzeny as the killer; Ronen Bergman attributes the killing to a Mossad squad. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_damocles] [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_damocles] The two versions are incompatible, and neither rests on a document quoted in the sources reached for this book. The exact day of the disappearance is not given.

The parcel bombs, November 1962. On 27 November 1962 a parcel bomb exploded in Pilz's office in Cairo, injuring his secretary. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_damocles] The Jewish Virtual Library, drawing on Bergman, adds that a second parcel killed five Egyptian workers. [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_damocles] The second detail appears in one compilation and is not dated separately there; it is recorded here as that source's account. The accounts place the parcels within the campaign against the scientists; no Israeli document ordering them is quoted in the sources reached here.

Kleinwächter and Switzerland, February–March 1963. In February 1963 an ambush on Hans Kleinwächter failed. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_damocles] [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_damocles] Then came Switzerland. There, Joseph Ben-Gal and Otto Joklik were arrested for threatening the daughter of Paul Goerke. The arrests caused a public scandal. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_damocles] [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_damocles] The day of the ambush and the day of the arrests are not given in the sources reached here, and neither is the outcome of the case against the two men.

Harel against Ben-Gurion and Peres, March 1963. Isser Harel had headed the Shin Bet from 1948 and the Mossad from 1952. [cite:rs_cw5_enc_harel] The end of his tenure came from inside Israel's own government. In 2013 the Israel State Archives released 105 documents from the period. As reported by Israel Hayom, they show that the "fear campaign" was exposed in March 1963, and that Harel "had to resign" after clashing with Ben-Gurion and with Shimon Peres, who believed the campaign would rupture Israel's relations with West Germany. [cite:rs_cw5_israelhayom_2013] An encyclopedia entry on Harel states simply that he was "forced to resign in 1963." [cite:rs_cw5_enc_harel] The exact day of his resignation is not given in the sources reached for this book.

The mechanism of the crisis is visible in that account. Harel ran the services that carried out the campaign; Ben-Gurion, on the archives' account and on Begin's charge below, was the one who ended his tenure, and Peres stood with Ben-Gurion. On one reading of that account, the issue between them was not whether the rockets were a danger but what the campaign was costing: Ben-Gurion and Peres weighed the threat from Cairo against the relationship with Bonn. Harel, on that reading, put the first fact first; his superiors put the third.

The Knesset and Bonn, April 1963. The resignation became a political fight at home. In the Knesset debate reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency on 12 April 1963, Menachem Begin said that Ben-Gurion had "forced" the security chief's resignation. Ben-Gurion answered that "Our grave concern over the designs of the Egyptian dictator to destroy Israel" should not throw Israel off balance. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630412] The same report announced that an Israeli ministerial body would study what course to take on the German scientists working in Egypt's arms race. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630412] Ben-Gurion's sentence is a direct statement of his position: he did not deny the danger, and called it grave, but said it should not throw Israel off balance.

Bonn's answer was carefully limited. The Adenauer government said it had done all it could about the scientists. Carlo Schmid, Vice-President of the Bundestag, called their work unconstitutional. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630412] Israel formally asked Germany to end their involvement, and Germany denied that its citizens were developing non-conventional weapons in Cairo. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630412] [cite:rs_cw5_israelhayom_2013] On the German side, then, the government did not deny that the scientists were there, and a senior parliamentarian called their work unconstitutional, while the government denied the most serious charge and said it had done all it could. Israel's request was formal; whatever followed was not, on these sources, a German law or order.

How it ended. By the end of 1963, according to the accounts reached here, pressure and diplomacy had driven the scientists out of Egypt. Bergman writes that West Germany offered them jobs, and that "Nearly all the scientists accepted." [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_damocles] [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_damocles] The outcome Harel had pursued by threat was reached, on this account, by an offer of employment from Bonn. His successor, Meir Amit, later judged that Harel had overestimated the danger. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_damocles] [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_damocles] [cite:rs_cw5_enc_harel] That judgment is a successor's verdict, given after the fact, and the sources do not record when Amit gave it.

The two readings. The episode can be read in two ways, and the evidence supports elements of each. On Harel's side, the case is that Egypt was openly testing rockets, that a document from inside the programme spoke of 900 under construction, and that the engineers were veterans of the V1 and V2; a state threatened by such weapons acted to stop the men building them, and the scientists did in the end leave. On the other side, the case drawn from Ben-Gurion and Peres, as the archives report it, is that the campaign would rupture the relationship with West Germany; Amit later added that Harel had overestimated the danger; and on Bergman's account the scientists left because Bonn offered them work. The sources reached here do not allow this book to measure the rocket programme's real capacity, and so cannot decide which side judged the danger rightly.

What the record leaves open. Much of this story rests on Bergman and on compilations that draw on him and on Raviv, Melman, Black and Morris, and on Time magazine's reporting of 1963; the operations themselves are not documented here by an Israeli order. Krug's killer is disputed. The day of Krug's disappearance, the day of the Kleinwächter ambush, the day of the Swiss arrests, the verdict in the Ben-Gal and Joklik case and the day of Harel's resignation are all missing from the sources reached. The second parcel and its five dead come from one compilation. Whether this crisis weighed on Ben-Gurion's own decision to leave office in June 1963 is a separate question: the sources reached for this book do not make that link, and it is taken up, as a question, in [scene:cw5_bengurion_resigns|the resignation].

sections.h: Baghdad and Damascus, 1963: Two Coups and a Unity Charter
sections.html:
In the spring of 1963 Israel's Prime Minister answered an American request about the Dimona reactor with a letter about something else: a new Arab federation. To understand why, the reader needs the events of the preceding three months in Baghdad and Damascus. In February and March 1963 officers and party members of the Ba'ath Party seized power first in Iraq and then in Syria. In April the two new governments and Nasser's Egypt announced in Cairo that they would unite. By late July the union was dead, broken by a failed coup in Damascus and by Nasser's public denunciation of the Syrian regime. This section tells that sequence, naming the parties and officers concerned, and sets out the dispute over whether the United States had a hand in the first of the two coups.

Iraq, 8–9 February 1963. On 8 February 1963 the Iraqi Ba'ath Party overthrew the Prime Minister, Abd al-Karim Qasim, after about two days of fighting. Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr became prime minister and Abdul Salam Arif president, while the party's secretary-general, Ali Salih al-Sa'di, controlled the National Guard, the party's militia. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan] Qasim was executed on 9 February 1963 after a summary proceeding broadcast on Baghdad radio. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan] Qasim had been one of the six Arab heads of state to whom Kennedy wrote on 11 May 1961, in the letter told in [scene:cw5_nasser_outreach|Kennedy and Nasser]. [cite:rs_cw5_jvl_jfk_arab_letter]

How many people died in the coup and its aftermath is uncertain, and the estimates differ widely. Ariel Ahram estimates that about 80 Ba'athists and "between 300 and 5,000" communist sympathizers were killed in the fighting. Bryan Gibson cites 1,500 to 5,000 suspected communists killed by the Ba'ath militia. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan] [cite:rs_cw5_gibson_majalla] The two ranges overlap at their upper end but differ fivefold at their lower. They also count somewhat different things: Ahram the dead of the fighting, Gibson those killed by the militia. No single figure can be given. The militia in Gibson's count was the National Guard under al-Sa'di, which grew to 34,000 by August 1963. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan]

The Ba'ath did not keep Iraq long. About nine months later, in November 1963, Arif, the president it had installed, ended Ba'athist rule in a counter-coup. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan]

Was the United States behind the Iraqi coup? This is the most disputed question in the episode, and scholars who have worked on it reach opposite conclusions. Both cases deserve to be set out in their strongest form.

The case for an American role is made by several historians. Wolfe-Hunnicutt calls American involvement "an open secret." Jacobsen writes that there is "ample evidence" of it. Citino is more guarded: he concludes that the United States "at best ... condoned and at worst ... contributed" to the coup, and that the full extent of its role "cannot be fully established." [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan] Those who argue for a role also point to two statements by participants or neighbours. Al-Sa'di, the party secretary-general who commanded the National Guard, is reported to have said that the Ba'athists came to power on a "CIA train." And King Hussein of Jordan made a claim in 1963 about CIA lists. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan] On this reading, an American government whose intelligence service was working against Qasim helped bring him down, and figures in the region said as much.

The case against a direct role is made by other scholars, from the declassified American record. Gibson, writing in Al Majalla in 2012, concludes on "the preponderance of evidence" that the CIA, though it had been plotting against Qasim, "was not behind" the coup. Hahn finds that the declassified documents "offer no evidence" of direct American involvement, and Barrett and West reach the same view. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan] [cite:rs_cw5_gibson_majalla] Former CIA officials describe their role as watching the plotters, not supporting them. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_ramadan] On this reading, American officials knew a great deal about the plot, but knowing of a coup is not the same as organizing it, and the documents show only the first.

A single document sits at the centre of the dispute. Robert Komer wrote a memorandum to Kennedy about the coup; Wikipedia's citation dates it 8 February 1963, while Gibson describes it as written "the day after the coup." Gibson reads it as showing that the CIA had "excellent reporting on the plotting" without having arranged it. Other scholars cite the same memorandum as evidence of complicity. [cite:rs_cw5_gibson_majalla] The disagreement is therefore not only over what evidence exists but over what the same sentence means: whether excellent reporting on a plot is the mark of an agency with sources inside it, or of one that had helped to make it.

This book does not resolve the question, because the sources reached for it do not. Two points can be stated plainly. First, Gibson, who rejects a direct role, accepts that the CIA had been plotting against Qasim. Second, even the most cautious of those who argue for a role, Citino, says that its extent cannot be fully established. The open ground between those two positions is what remains in dispute.

Syria, 8 March 1963. A month after Baghdad, Damascus followed. On 8 March 1963 the Ba'athist Military Committee and allied officers seized power in Syria, with little violence, and declared a state of emergency. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_1963] That emergency was not lifted until 2011. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_1963] A National Council for the Revolutionary Command was formed to hold power, though the sources date it differently: Wikipedia's account gives 9 March, while the Library of Congress country study dates to 24 March the provisional constitution that confirmed the Council's power. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_1963] [cite:rs_cw5_countrystudy_syria] The two dates need not conflict, since one may date the Council's formation and the other the confirmation of its authority, but the sources reached here do not say so, and both are given.

The Cairo agreement, 17 April 1963. With Ba'athist governments in Baghdad and Damascus, the three states announced in Cairo on 17 April 1963 an agreement for a federal union of Egypt, Syria and Iraq. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_1963] [cite:rs_cw5_countrystudy_syria] The proclamation of that day called for a military union to bring about "the liberation of Palestine." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Ben-Gurion took it up. His letter to Kennedy of 26 April 1963 did not answer the American request on Dimona; it raised the Arab Federation instead, and proposed a joint US–Soviet guarantee of the territorial integrity of the states of the region. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] That exchange is told in [scene:s11b|the battle of the letters].

The union unravels, April–July 1963. The federation began to come apart within days of its announcement, and it came apart in Damascus. Between 28 April and 2 May the Syrian Military Committee purged more than 50 Nasserist officers, and Nasserist ministers resigned from the government. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_1963] [cite:rs_cw5_countrystudy_syria] The Ba'athist officers who held power in Syria were removing the officers loyal to the leader with whom they had just agreed to unite.

The Nasserists answered by force. On 18 July 1963 Colonel Jassem Alwan led a Nasserist coup attempt in Damascus. Amin al-Hafiz crushed it. Twenty-seven conspirators were executed. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_july1963] [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_1963] [cite:rs_cw5_countrystudy_syria] Estimates of the casualties range from 40–70 to "hundreds," and the sources reached here do not settle the number. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_july1963] [cite:rs_cw5_countrystudy_syria] Four days later, on 22 July 1963, Nasser announced that he was abandoning federation with Syria and called the Ba'athist regime "fascists." The Library of Congress study says that the union effort had "collapsed by July 22." [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_july1963] [cite:rs_cw5_countrystudy_syria]

What the sequence meant. The proclamation of 17 April and its collapse by 22 July frame the spring of 1963 from two sides. In Israel the proclamation was the document Ben-Gurion set before Kennedy. In Damascus the same union was undermined within days by the purge of Nasser's officers, and Nasser's own break in July ended it as a working project. Both facts are true at once: the union was proclaimed in terms that called for "the liberation of Palestine," and the three governments that proclaimed it could not hold it together for a hundred days. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Which of the two weighed more heavily on Israel's security that year is a judgment the sources reached here do not make.

What the record leaves open. The number of people killed in Iraq in February 1963 is known only as a range, from Ahram's 300 to Gibson's 5,000 among communists and suspected communists, besides about 80 Ba'athists. Whether the United States helped to bring about the Iraqi coup remains disputed among named scholars, and the declassified record reached here does not decide it. The date of the National Council for the Revolutionary Command differs between two sources. The casualties of the July coup attempt in Damascus run from 40–70 to "hundreds." The rule of the Ba'ath in Syria did not end with the failure of the union; what followed for the regime of Amin al-Hafiz and the officers around him is told in [scene:cw6_syria|Stage Six].

sections.h: The Battle of the Letters, March–June 1963
sections.html:
Between the end of March and the middle of June 1963, the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Israel conducted, in writing, what the editors of the declassified record call "the toughest American-Israeli confrontation over the Israeli nuclear program." Its subject was whether American scientists would be allowed to visit the reactor at Dimona on a regular schedule. The letters, telegrams and memoranda of that argument are now declassified and published, most of them by the National Security Archive. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:nsarchive_battle_letters_1963] [cite:avner_cohen_wsj_2009] They answer a common assumption directly. It is often said or supposed that American support for Israel's nuclear programme was unconditional and uncontested from the start. The documents show a sitting president spending much of 1963 in an escalating confrontation with Israel's government over exactly that programme, and writing, in his own letters, that American support could be put at risk by it.

The exchange also shows something the assumption misses on the other side. Ben-Gurion did not answer Kennedy's question. He answered a different one, about Egypt and the survival of Israel, and he did so at length and in the strongest terms. The argument was therefore never only about inspections. It was about what each government thought the other owed it.

The background. The reactor had been built with substantial French assistance after the Suez war of 1956, and Ben-Gurion had acknowledged its existence to the Knesset in December 1960 in terms that presented it as serving peaceful research and played down its weapons-relevant capacity. [cite:wilsoncenter_kennedy_dimona_61_62] How and when Washington first learned of the site, and Ben-Gurion's statement itself, are told with their disputed dates in [scene:cw4_dimona_discovery|how Washington found Dimona]; that section's dating governs here where the shorter accounts differ from it. The spring of 1963 opened with a new American estimate, NIE 30-63 of 23 January, which judged that the reactor at full power could produce plutonium for one or two weapons a year, and with National Security Action Memorandum 231 of 26 March, issued by McGeorge Bundy, ordering that "the next informal inspection" be arranged promptly. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Those documents, and the estimates that led to them, are told earlier in this stage. The letters began the next day.

Telegram 658 and the meeting of 2 April. On 27 March 1963 the State Department's telegram 658 instructed the ambassador in Tel Aviv, Barbour, to seek Israel's assent to "semi-annual" visits to Dimona. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Barbour raised the matter with Ben-Gurion on 2 April 1963, at the end of a meeting that had run two hours. Ben-Gurion asked to put the subject off until after Passover. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] That request for delay was the first of several. The American demand, from this point, was specific: not a single visit but a standing schedule, twice a year.

Peres at the White House, the same day. On the same 2 April, Shimon Peres was in Washington, where Myer Feldman had arranged for him to see Kennedy. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] What Peres promised exists in two records, and they differ in a way that matters.

The Israeli record has Peres saying: "we will not introduce nuclear weapons to the region, and certainly we will not be the first." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Feldman's American record of the same meeting has Peres giving "an unequivocal assurance" that Israel "would not do anything in this field" unless others in the area did. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The editors of the National Security Archive's collection draw the distinction plainly: "'Not do anything' has a different meaning than 'not introduce.'" [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] One reading of the difference: a promise not to "introduce" weapons leaves room to develop the capacity to make them; a promise not to "do anything in this field" does not. Which words Peres used, or whether each side heard what it wanted, the two records cannot settle. Each is a record made by one party to the meeting.

The démarche, 4 April. Two days later the pressure moved to Washington. On 4 April 1963 Assistant Secretary of State Phillips Talbot delivered a démarche to Ambassador Harman of Israel. On 19 April telegram 720 asked Barbour to press Ben-Gurion for "an affirmative reply." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] By then the region had changed under both governments' feet.

The Arab Federation, 17 April. On 17 April 1963 Egypt, Syria and Iraq, the latter two newly under Ba'athist rule after the coups of February and March told earlier in this stage, announced in Cairo an agreement for a federal union. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_syria_1963] The Arab Federation Proclamation of that day called for a military union to bring about "the liberation of Palestine." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] For Ben-Gurion the proclamation was the issue. Nine days later he wrote to Kennedy.

Ben-Gurion's letter of 26 April. The letter of 26 April 1963 did not answer the request about Dimona. It took up the Arab Federation, and it proposed that the United States and the Soviet Union jointly guarantee the territorial integrity of the states of the region. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The proposal reframed the problem. Washington had asked about a reactor; Ben-Gurion replied, in effect, that the danger was the declared aim of three Arab governments to form a military union for "the liberation of Palestine," and that the remedy was a great-power guarantee of borders.

Kennedy's reply, 4 May. Kennedy answered on 4 May 1963, in telegram 780; Ben-Gurion afterwards referred to it as the letter of 5 May. Kennedy said he was "much less worried about an 'early Arab attack'" than about the spread of advanced offensive weapons systems in the region. He was puzzled by the idea of a joint declaration with Moscow, because it would add to Soviet prestige. And he proposed that the two governments "consider carefully together how such a trend can be forestalled." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The reply turned Ben-Gurion's argument back toward the question Washington had asked. If the danger was an arms race, then Dimona was part of the arms race.

Ben-Gurion's letter of 12 May. Ben-Gurion's answer, dated 12 May 1963, ran to nine pages. It is the fullest statement in the exchange of Israel's case, and it should be read in its own terms. Ben-Gurion invoked "another Holocaust": "I have no doubt," he wrote, "that a similar thing might happen to Jews in Israel if Nasser succeeded in defeating our army." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] He asked for four things: a security agreement between the United States and Israel; parity in arms with Israel's neighbours; a demilitarized West Bank; and disarmament with inspection. The letter did not address Dimona. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

The case behind the letter was a coherent one. Three Arab governments had, the month before, proclaimed a military union for "the liberation of Palestine." Ben-Gurion's letter drew the line from the destruction of Europe's Jews to Israel's position in 1963; he read the proclamation as a statement of intent and asked the one power that might deter it to commit itself in writing. His proposals were not only requests for American protection; they included a demilitarized West Bank and disarmament under inspection, terms that would have bound Israel's neighbours and, in principle, Israel. In this reading, the reactor was not a separate subject from the Arab Federation; it was a reason for Israel to want a guarantee, and a guarantee was the price at which the reactor might be discussed.

Another reading of the same letter is different. On this view Ben-Gurion was redirecting the exchange toward conventional threats, which both he and later Eshkol described as their people's major anxiety, rather than refusing inspections outright. [cite:timesofisrael_kennedy_eshkol] [cite:jvl_dimona_inspections_memo_aug63] The historian Avner Cohen and the journalist Seymour Hersh, in The Samson Option (1991), both document this pattern of delay in detail. [cite:timesofisrael_kennedy_eshkol] [cite:jvl_dimona_inspections_memo_aug63] The two readings describe the same letter. What one side saw as a statement of Israel's real priorities, the other saw as a way of not answering.

The guarantee Washington would not give. Inside the administration, Ben-Gurion's requests were weighed seriously. On 16 May 1963 Robert Komer of the National Security Council staff called a State Department proposal a "good opening bid": security assurances to Israel tied to a standstill on nuclear weapons and missiles. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The idea was a trade, assurances for restraint. It did not become policy. Kennedy had already refused Ben-Gurion's April idea of a joint American–Soviet guarantee, an American official named Grant advised that a unilateral American guarantee "should not be considered," and through the summer of 1963 Kennedy remained "unwilling to make 'explicit' guarantees" of Israel's security. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The commitment he had given Golda Meir at Palm Beach in December 1962, to support Israel "in case of an invasion," stayed a spoken assurance. It was not turned into a document. Kennedy's own condition at Palm Beach, that the relationship could not damage American ties with the other states of the region, may point to one reason. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

Kennedy's letter of 17 May. Kennedy's next letter carries more than one date in the record. Telegram 835 dates it 17 May 1963; another document gives 19 May; some published summaries give 18 May. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:nsarchive_battle_letters_1963] Whatever its day, it changed the terms of the argument. It pressed for the visits "first put to you by Ambassador Barbour on April 2." [cite:nsarchive_battle_letters_1963] It separated Israel's existential security from Dimona. And it warned, for the first time, that American "commitment to and support of Israel could be seriously jeopardized" without "reliable information" on Dimona. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The editors note that this language "remained in all subsequent letters." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

That sentence is the core of the exchange. Kennedy did not say that aid would be cut, or name any sanction. He said that the American commitment itself "could be seriously jeopardized," and he tied that risk to the one thing he wanted: reliable information. The letter thus did what Ben-Gurion's letters had tried to prevent. It refused to treat a guarantee and an inspection as items in one bargain, and it made the inspection a condition of the relationship rather than a concession to be traded for one.

Ben-Gurion's reply of 27 May. Ben-Gurion answered on 27 May 1963. He asked for delay. There would be nothing to see at Dimona, he wrote, until the reactor started up in early 1964, and he did not take up the request for visits twice a year. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] One secondary account describes the same reply as proposing alternative, more limited inspection arrangements than Kennedy had asked for, and quotes the historian Sandler, as cited in several secondary sources, to the effect that Kennedy was "far from satisfied," "particularly his attempt to stall any inspection in Dimona." [cite:timesofisrael_kennedy_eshkol] The declassified text, as the National Security Archive's editors summarize it, is the firmer guide: a request for delay and silence on the schedule. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

The schedule, and the letter that was never delivered. Washington answered with a timetable. A State Department draft of 11 June 1963, prepared by Brubeck, proposed a visit in mid-summer 1963, another in June 1964, and visits at six-month intervals after that. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Kennedy's letter of 15 June 1963, sent as telegram 938, set out that schedule. It was never delivered to Ben-Gurion. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] His resignation, announced in the days that followed, is the subject of the next section, which also weighs the claim that the letters helped bring it about.

The exchange did not end with Ben-Gurion. On 4 July 1963 Kennedy sent the new Prime Minister, Levi Eshkol, a telegram repeating the undelivered text, including the sentence that had first appeared in May: "this government's commitment to and support of Israel could be seriously jeopardized if it should be thought that we were unable to obtain reliable information on a subject as vital to peace as Israel's effort in the nuclear field." [cite:nsarchive_battle_letters_1963] Eshkol's own reply of 19 August 1963 has been read as continuing his predecessor's approach, which would suggest an institutional policy rather than one leader's style. [cite:timesofisrael_kennedy_eshkol] [cite:jvl_dimona_inspections_memo_aug63] What Eshkol actually agreed, and whether it met Kennedy's demand, is told in [scene:cw5_eshkol_agreement|Eshkol's answer].

An ultimatum, or not? Historians and participants have disagreed over how to describe Kennedy's letters, and both sides have a case. The editors of the National Security Archive's collection call the exchange "the toughest American-Israeli confrontation over the Israeli nuclear program," with Kennedy writing "in a near ultimatum tone," "akin to an ultimatum." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Some Israelis at the time went further. Yuval Ne'eman (1925–2006) called the demands an "ultimatum," and some of Eshkol's advisers read the July letter the same way. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] On this view, a letter from the President telling a small state that his support "could be seriously jeopardized" unless it accepted inspections was an ultimatum in everything but name, and was understood as serious pressure by both governments. [cite:nsarchive_battle_letters_1963]

The case on the other side rests on the text. The letters named no sanction. They did not threaten to cut aid or to break off relations. They said that support "could be" jeopardized, not that it would be. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:nsarchive_battle_letters_1963] By that standard "near ultimatum," the editors' own phrase, is accurate, and "ultimatum" overstates the documented words. Kennedy was, in the same months, arming Israel and refusing it a guarantee; the letters linked support to inspection without spelling out what would happen if inspection were refused.

Did Kennedy threaten to cut aid? On the documents, no. He threatened the relationship in general terms and left the consequences unstated. What did Israel promise? In April, through Peres, either not to "introduce" nuclear weapons or not to "do anything in this field," depending on whose record one reads; in May, through Ben-Gurion, nothing on Dimona beyond delay. Why did Ben-Gurion answer about Nasser instead of Dimona? Because in his reading, stated at length in the letters, the Arab Federation was the threat to peace and a guarantee was the prior question. The other reading, Cohen's and Hersh's, was that this was a way of not answering. Both readings are on the record.

What came after. The first visit under the arrangement that came out of the letters took place in January 1964, after Kennedy's death. The Johnson administration kept insisting on the visits begun under Kennedy. [cite:rs_cw5_frus6468_summary] What those visits actually found, including a 2020 release of declassified records from 1964–65 that its editors titled "Duplicity and Self-Deception," is told in [scene:s11d|Johnson's inspections]. [cite:nsarchive_duplicity_1964_65]

The record leaves some questions open. The exact date of Kennedy's May letter is given three ways in the sources, as 17, 18 and 19 May. The two records of Peres's assurance cannot be reconciled from the documents, and nothing here shows which formula Kennedy himself took away from the meeting. The letters establish what each leader asked and refused; they do not establish what Israel's government had decided about the reactor's purpose in the spring of 1963, and none of Ben-Gurion's replies confirms or denies a weapons intention. Nor do they show what Kennedy would have done had Ben-Gurion refused outright, because he never did. He delayed, and then he resigned.

sections.h: 16 June 1963: Ben-Gurion Resigns
sections.html:
In the middle of June 1963 a letter from Kennedy to Ben-Gurion was waiting to be delivered. Sent as telegram 938 and dated 15 June, it set out the schedule of visits to Dimona that the State Department had drafted four days earlier: one in mid-summer 1963, another in June 1964, and visits every six months after that. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] It was never handed over. Ben-Gurion announced his resignation, and the letter had no addressee. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] That undelivered letter is the only point at which the documents connect the battle of the letters, told in [scene:s11b|the previous section], to the end of Ben-Gurion's premiership. Whether there was any connection beyond the timing is the question this section has to answer, and the honest answer is that the record does not show one.

The date. Even the day is given differently by different sources. The document reproduced in the National Security Archive's collection gives 16 June 1963 as the day Ben-Gurion stepped down. The editors' own introduction to the same collection gives 15 June. Wikipedia's infobox gives 26 June 1963 as the end of his term. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_bengurion] The three dates need not all describe the same act. The first two refer to the resignation itself, and this book follows the document's 16 June; the third is given as the end of his term. The date on which Levi Eshkol's government was sworn in has not been confirmed from a primary source, and 26 June is therefore given here as Wikipedia gives it, not as an established fact. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_bengurion]

What Ben-Gurion said. He gave "personal reasons," and he never explained them publicly. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_bengurion] The resignation was unexpected. According to Wikipedia's account, the cabinet asked him to reconsider, but, unlike in 1953, few serious efforts were made to dissuade him. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_bengurion] He chose his own successor, Levi Eshkol. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_bengurion]

Because Ben-Gurion said so little, every other explanation is someone else's. There are three, and they rest on evidence of very different kinds.

The first explanation: exhaustion and isolation. The historian Yechiam Weitz, as summarized in Wikipedia's account, attributes the resignation to Ben-Gurion's political isolation, his suspicion of colleagues and rivals, an inability to engage with the full range of reality, and a belief that his life's work was disintegrating. Weitz suggests that the decision may reflect Ben-Gurion's state of mind at the time. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_bengurion] This is a historian's interpretation, not a document; it is reached here through a secondary summary, not Weitz's own text. But it is consistent with the one thing Ben-Gurion said, "personal reasons," and with the cabinet's muted response.

The second explanation: Germany. The CIA believed at the time that Ben-Gurion's conciliatory policy toward West Germany was a cause of his resignation. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] This is a contemporary American intelligence judgment, recorded in the declassified documents; it shows what the agency believed, not what moved Ben-Gurion. Its context was real. In March 1963 Isser Harel, head of the Mossad, "had to resign" after clashing with Ben-Gurion and Shimon Peres, who believed his campaign against the German scientists in Egypt would rupture relations with West Germany. [cite:rs_cw5_israelhayom_2013] [cite:rs_cw5_enc_harel] In the Knesset, Menachem Begin said Ben-Gurion had "forced" the resignation. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630412] That crisis, told in [scene:cw5_damocles|the German scientists], set Ben-Gurion's German policy against his own intelligence chief and drew an attack from the opposition. It is background to the resignation. No source collected here states that it caused it.

The third explanation: Kennedy. Some Israeli leaders thought Kennedy's pressure over Dimona may have contributed. Pinhas Sapir and Israel Galili are named among them. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The historian Avner Cohen goes furthest, suggesting that the resignation "may have been triggered, in part, by Kennedy's pressure." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_findings] The wording is careful and should be kept as it is: "may have," "in part." Cohen offers it as a possibility, not a finding. The editors of the letters, of whom Cohen is one, do not claim that the pressure caused the resignation. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

What the record shows. No document collected for this stage shows that the letters caused the resignation. The strongest evidence for a connection is circumstantial. Kennedy's letter of 17 May had warned that American support "could be seriously jeopardized" without reliable information on Dimona; Ben-Gurion's reply of 27 May had asked for delay; a sharper letter with a fixed schedule was ready by 15 June; and Ben-Gurion resigned the next day. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Two of his senior colleagues and a historian who co-edited the letters have thought the pressure may have played a part. The strongest evidence against treating it as the cause is that Ben-Gurion never said so, that he did not receive the 15 June letter, that the CIA at the time looked to Germany instead, and that the one historian of his state of mind cited here looks to his isolation. The sequence of dates is real. A sequence is not a cause, and none of these sources presents documentary proof that one followed from the other.

The question a reader is most likely to ask, whether Kennedy's pressure made Ben-Gurion resign, therefore has a plain answer on the present record: it may have contributed, in the view of some who were close to the events, and no document shows that it did.

What followed for the letters is clear. Kennedy did not wait long for the new government. On 4 July 1963 he sent Eshkol the same text and schedule that Ben-Gurion had never received, and the argument resumed with a new prime minister, as told in [scene:cw5_eshkol_agreement|Eshkol's answer]. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

After the resignation. Ben-Gurion did not leave politics. A year later he insisted that the Lavon affair be investigated and Eshkol refused; in 1965 he failed to unseat Eshkol, broke with Mapai in June 1965 to found Rafi, and lost to the Alignment in the election of November 1965. [cite:rs_cw5_wiki_bengurion] That struggle belongs to Stage Six.

The record leaves the central question open. Ben-Gurion's "personal reasons" were never explained, and the sources reached here do not include any statement of his own that ties the resignation to Washington, to Germany or to anything else. The exact date on which his successor's government took office remains to be confirmed. What the documents establish is narrower: a letter was waiting, and the man it was addressed to resigned before it arrived.

sections.h: Part 9: The Jewish Agency Before the Senate Committee, May–August 1963
sections.html:
Of the thirteen parts of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee's inquiry into nondiplomatic agents of foreign principals, Part 9 concerned the Jewish Agency for Israel and the lobbying organizations connected with it. [cite:rs_cw5_ol_hearings] It was the part that touched the body the Justice Department had ordered, the previous November, to register as a foreign agent, as told in [scene:s11a|the order of 21 November 1962]. It was also the part conducted most fully behind closed doors, and the part whose meaning has been argued over most since. This section follows the hearing through the summer of 1963: who appeared, what the money bought, what the committee is recorded as concluding, and how the two sides have read the result.

The closed sessions. On 28 June 1963 the Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported that the committee had "continued a closed inquiry on the activities of the Jewish Agency", with Senator J. William Fulbright, Democrat of Arkansas, presiding. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630628] The witness named in that report was Gottlieb Hammer of New York, a former officer of the New York section of the Jewish Agency for Israel and, since April 1960, executive vice chairman of the Jewish Agency, Inc., a body the report described as not itself a subject of the inquiry. He was accompanied by the Agency's attorney, Maurice Boukstein. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630628] The report added that the committee had for "several months" been studying how the Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938 was administered. That was the frame: the Agency's American Section was already registered under the Act, and the question was how the law was working, not whether the Agency was registered. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630628]

Boukstein's role was to contest the premise. Fulbright treated the Agency's payments to the American Zionist Council as functionally equivalent to direct funding of an American lobby by the Israeli government. Boukstein challenged that characterization directly and sharply on the record, describing the Agency as "a completely independent body composed of representatives of Zionist organizations from all over the free world." [cite:jta_fulbright_jewish_agency_hearing] (One later account calls Boukstein the Council's counsel; the contemporary report of 28 June calls him the Agency's attorney.)

The funding inquiry. Kobby Barda, in a 2026 article in Modern Judaism, dates the opening of the committee's investigation of the Agency's American funding of the Council's publications to 2 August 1963, a date he takes from Isaiah L. Kenen's affidavit, and he places the hearings in August. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The central witness was Isidor (also spelled Isadore) Hamlin, director of the Agency's American branch. Barda quotes his answer on the core question of where the money went: "we did not pay Mr. Kenen directly, we paid for the subscriptions of the American Zionist Council." [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] From the exchange with Hamlin, Barda reports Agency payments of $38,000 for subscriptions to Kenen's newsletter, the Near East Report. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026]

Hamlin's distinction is the hinge of the whole dispute. A payment for subscriptions is a purchase from a publisher; a payment to Kenen would have been a payment to the head of a lobbying committee. On Hamlin's account the Agency had bought copies of a newsletter through the Council, not paid the lobbyist who wrote it. On the opposing account the distinction was one of form: money from a registered foreign agent reached the lobbyist's publication by way of an unregistered American body.

Kenen's affidavit. Kenen was not called as a witness. He submitted a written affidavit instead. In it he stated that the Council's purchases had never exceeded 23 per cent of the newsletter's distributed copies, even at their peak; that he had stopped his work for the Council in July 1960; and that the subscription purchases had ended in 1962. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] He gave his salary while working for the Council as $100 a week. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The affidavit's argument was proportion and time: the Council's purchases were a minority of the run, its link with Kenen had ended three years earlier, and the money had stopped before the hearing began.

The newsletter's origins. According to the Council's records as Barda reads them, its board decided on 25 January 1955 to launch the newsletter that became the Near East Report, with an initial run of 6,500 copies for the public-relations committee and a further 5,500 taken by the Council at 15 cents a copy. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] At that rate the Council's share of a single issue came to $825; the records reached here do not say how many issues it bought. By October 1957 the newsletter was building a paying readership. On 21 October 1957 Kenen reported to Rabbi Philip Bernstein that 1,100 subscriptions had been added that week and that 7,000 copies were being distributed, and he proposed cutting the price from $10 to $5. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] Kenen's own later account gives a different starting point. Speaking off the record on 13 September 1963, he said the Near East Report began in 1957 as a biweekly newsletter. [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963] The sources do not reconcile the two dates, and the difference is left as they give it.

The money in dispute. How much Agency money reached the Council is the first of the two disputes the hearing left behind. On one side stands a figure of about $5.1 million. The Justice Department's order had alleged "more than $5 million" over eight years, and the Senate record carries a figure of $5,100,001.02 for the period from 1 January 1955 to 31 December 1962, which Fulbright entered into the committee's record. [cite:azc_fara_doj] [cite:jta_fulbright_jewish_agency_hearing] On the other side stands Barda, who writes that the Council "received $1.5 million from the Jewish Agency" between 1955 and 1962. He presents that as a claim raised in the matter, gives no source for it, and does not mention the $5.1 million figure. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] He frames the payments he does document, the $38,000, as subscription purchases for a commercial newsletter. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] These figures do not measure the same thing. The $5.1 million is a total of Agency payments to the Council; the $38,000 is the part of them that Barda reports, from Hamlin's testimony, as spent on the Near East Report. The sources reached here do not say what the rest of the Council's receipts paid for, and they do not reconcile the $5.1 million with the $1.5 million.

What the hearing established. The second dispute concerns what Part 9 showed, and here the evidence on each side is of a different kind.

The first reading comes from the Agency itself and from Barda. In August 1963, Dr Emanuel Neumann, chairman of the Jewish Agency–American Section, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that Fulbright had praised the Agency's achievements and had said repeatedly that there was "no wrong doing". The only open question, Neumann said, was a technical one: whether the Agency's periodic reports were detailed enough. [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630816] He called the result a vindication: "a prolonged and meticulous examination has turned up absolutely nothing damaging to the status of the Jewish Agency." [cite:rs_cw5_djn_19630816] Barda, working from the hearing record and the Council's papers, concludes that the separation between the Agency and Kenen was "absolute". [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The strongest form of this case is that the Agency was a registered agent, its payments were for copies of a newsletter sold to the public, the purchases were a minority of the run and had ended, Kenen had left the Council's employ in 1960, and the committee's own chairman is reported to have found nothing wrong.

The second reading comes from Grant F. Smith of IRmep, an advocate of registration, and from the American Council for Judaism, whose dissent from Zionism is told later in this stage. Both read Part 9 as showing Agency money funding American lobbying and public relations, and both treat the closed sessions, and what they describe as White House involvement, as evidence that the full story was withheld. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast] [cite:rs_cw5_acj_1997] Barda records that Smith obtained the 1963 hearing records under the JFK Records Act and cites his books America's Defense Line (2008) and Foreign Agents (2009). [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026] The strongest form of this case is that the Justice Department's own lawyer, as Smith reports him, read the hearings as showing that the Council was receiving large transfers for publicity and lobbying, not distributing educational material, and that the sums on the order and in the Senate record run to millions, not thousands. [cite:rs_cw5_smith_podcast]

Some of the conduit reading's specific claims are unconfirmed and should be read as such. An unsigned article published by the American Council for Judaism on 1 September 1997 states that the Agency's executive director and his deputy testified in executive session "because the White House intervened"; that some witnesses asked to appear without oath, transcript or publicity and were refused; and that the closed transcript was withheld. These are the Council's account; the contemporary reports found for this book do not confirm them. [cite:rs_cw5_acj_1997] The same article attributes to Fulbright's biographer, Randall Bennett Woods, a claim that Agency representatives admitted paying expenses of Lyndon Johnson's entourage at the 1960 Democratic convention. That claim could not be checked against Woods's book or the hearing transcript, and it stands unverified. [cite:rs_cw5_acj_1997]

The two readings are not wholly incompatible. Neumann's report concerns the Agency's status as a registrant, which the committee is reported to have left intact. The conduit reading concerns the Council's status, which was the subject of the Justice Department's order, not of the Senate's finding. Both can be accurate about their own question. What divides them is whether a newsletter subscription bought by a registered agent through an American umbrella body was a sale or a subsidy, and that the record reached here does not decide.

Kenen's own words. About a month after the hearings, Kenen spoke to the Third Annual Young Leadership Conference of the United Jewish Appeal in New York, off the record, on 13 September 1963. He described his American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs as founded in 1953 and later renamed the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963] Of the inquiry he said: "We seem to have anticipated the issues raised in the Fulbright investigation by a dozen years", and that neither AIPAC nor the UJA "was seriously involved in the Senate Hearings." [cite:rs_cw5_kenen_uja_1963] The remark states his position precisely. On his account, the committee he ran had been built from the start to stand outside the arrangement the senators were examining. It is the account of an interested party, given in private to a sympathetic audience, and it sits beside an affidavit in which he acknowledged that the Council had bought copies of his newsletter until 1962 and had once paid his salary. [cite:rs_cw5_barda_2026]

The legal position that emerged. By the end of 1963 the lobby's legal footing rested on a structural argument that has defined it since. AIPAC's defence is that it is funded by American donors, not directly by the Israeli government, and that its activity is domestic political advocacy rather than action at a foreign principal's direction. [cite:factually_aipac_fara] That was a real distinction from the arrangement the 1962 order had named, in which an American body received money directly from the Agency, whatever one concludes about its persuasiveness. [cite:factually_aipac_fara] The question was raised again in a 1988 petition by the former Senator Fulbright and Victor Marchetti, a former senior CIA official, which the Justice Department rejected, and in a 2024 bill by Representative Thomas Massie; those episodes, and the Act's later shift toward civil enforcement, are told in [scene:fis_s07|why AIPAC is not registered]. [cite:crustnews_aipac_history] How the same distinction looks beside a European organization that, according to Mediapart (November 2025), was reimbursed by the Israeli government for a French Senate event is examined in [scene:s19g|the lobby beyond America].

The gaps in the record are larger than the findings. The full transcript of the closed sessions is not among the sources reached for this volume, and neither are the dates of any public sessions on the Agency. The committee's own conclusions are known here only through Neumann's account of what Fulbright said, which is the account of a party to the hearing. The total of the Agency's payments to the Council stands at two unreconciled figures, $5,100,001.02 in the Senate record and $1.5 million in Barda, and what most of that money paid for is not documented in the material reached here. What is documented is narrower: a registered foreign agent bought $38,000 of subscriptions to a lobbyist's newsletter through an American umbrella body; the lobbyist said those purchases never exceeded 23 per cent of his run and ended in 1962; and the committee's chairman, by the Agency's account, found no wrongdoing, while the Justice Department's order against the umbrella body had still not been complied with.

sections.h: Eshkol's Answer: The Dimona Agreement, July–September 1963
sections.html:
When David Ben-Gurion left office in June 1963, the last letter Kennedy had written him was still in the State Department's files. It had never been delivered. The exchange that produced it, from the first instruction to Ambassador Barbour in March to the undelivered text of 15 June, is told in [scene:s11b|the battle of the letters]. This section follows the same demand into the hands of Ben-Gurion's successor, Levi Eshkol, and through the seven weeks it took his government to answer. The result was an agreement that the record, read to its end, shows to have been something narrower than Kennedy's language of "basic agreement" suggested.

The letter that was waiting. On 4 July 1963 the State Department sent telegram 193, carrying Kennedy's letter to the new prime minister. It repeated the text and the schedule of the letter that Ben-Gurion never received, and Ambassador Barbour delivered it on 5 July. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] That schedule had been drafted in the State Department on 11 June: a visit to Dimona in mid-summer 1963, another in June 1964, and visits at six-month intervals after that. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The letter also carried the warning that Kennedy had first written into his letter of 17 May: that the American "commitment to and support of Israel could be seriously jeopardized" without "reliable information" on Dimona. The editors of the declassified correspondence, William Burr and Avner Cohen, note that this language "remained in all subsequent letters." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

The new prime minister therefore inherited, in his first weeks, both the request and the threat. Some of his advisers read the letter as "a real ultimatum, a crisis in the making." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Whether it was one is the dispute already met in Ben-Gurion's time: the editors' "near ultimatum" against a text that named no sanction and said only that support "could be" jeopardized. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The documents do not record Kennedy saying which he meant.

Asking for time, 17 July. Eshkol did not answer the substance at once. On 17 July 1963 he sent an interim reply asking for time, and raised the idea of an arrangement under which the two governments would "consult in advance." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The phrase moved the question a step away from the one Kennedy had asked. Kennedy's letters asked to see the reactor on a fixed schedule; on one reading, consultation in advance described a relationship between governments, in which Israel would tell Washington of its intentions rather than show American scientists its facilities.

Seven weeks in the cabinet. The answer took about seven weeks. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] In that time Eshkol told Barbour that Israel "would do what it had to do for its national security," and Barbour reported to Washington that Eshkol "has not had an easy time in obtaining agreement of his colleagues." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The two sentences together describe the structure on the Israeli side. The decision was the prime minister's to sign, but not his alone to make: he needed his colleagues' agreement, and some of them, by Barbour's report, were hard to persuade. Eshkol's own phrase stated Israel's case in its own terms, the case Ben-Gurion had pressed in May when he asked for a security agreement with the United States: that Israel would decide for itself what its security required. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Kennedy, through the summer, remained "unwilling to make 'explicit' guarantees" of Israel's security. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Washington was asking for access without offering the guarantee that Ben-Gurion had asked for in return. Barbour's cables do not name which of Eshkol's colleagues resisted, or on what grounds, in the documents the editors reproduce.

The reply of 19 August. Eshkol's answer came on 19 August 1963. He agreed in principle to regular visits. He agreed to a visit in late 1963, before the reactor went critical, and to a follow-up visit in mid-1964. He made no commitment to inspections twice a year. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] Set beside the schedule Kennedy had sent, the reply moved the first visit from mid-summer to late 1963, kept a second for mid-1964, accepted the principle of regularity, and declined the interval that would have given the principle its force. A visit every six months would have let American scientists watch a reactor as it came into operation. A visit before criticality and another mid-1964, with nothing fixed after that, left the frequency of later visits to be negotiated each time.

Kennedy's acceptance, 26 August. Kennedy chose to read the reply as a settlement. His letter of 26 August 1963 assumed "basic agreement on regular visits." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The word "basic" carried the weight. It allowed the President to treat the principle as conceded, while the interval, the one point Eshkol had declined, remained unagreed, as a State Department official noted in September.

The working arrangement, 16 September. The terms were filled in by officials. A memorandum of conversation dated 16 September 1963 recorded Israel's agreement to a "third visit prior to the activation of the reactor," to be "thorough" and to include the "plutonium separation plant." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The count reflected the visits already made: the editors call the improvised American visit of late September 1962 the second, and describe it as a "fiasco." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The memorandum's reference to a plutonium separation plant is the most specific item in the whole exchange. Rodger Davies, for the State Department, noted in the same memorandum that semi-annual visits had not been agreed. He also recorded the Israeli assurances of "peaceful purposes," which, he wrote, the United States was "inclined to believe." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The memorandum thus records three things at once: what had been gained, what had not, and the degree of trust on which the remainder rested.

The visit that came after the reactor. The visit before activation did not take place. According to the Israelis, the reactor went critical on 26 December 1963. The Hebrew-language website of the Israel Atomic Energy Commission gives July 1963 for the start of operations. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] The two dates cannot be reconciled from the sources reached here, and they may not measure the same event: one names criticality, the other the start of operations. What both show is that the visit Eshkol had promised for before criticality did not happen before it, on either date. The first visit under the new arrangement took place on 18 January 1964. The editors write that it "may have been delayed because of Kennedy's assassination." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] They offer that as a possibility and draw no other connection; what the record shows about the weeks around 22 November is set out in [scene:s11c|22 November 1963].

What the first team found. The January 1964 team's report, written by Harry S. Traynor and dated 30 January 1964, found no suspicion of weapons work.
