Citing Israel's own investigations, he now concluded that civilians had not been intentionally targeted as a matter of policy, while "the crimes allegedly committed by Hamas" were, he wrote, intentional. [cite:gz_jvl_goldstone] The mission's other three members, Hina Jilani, Christine Chinkin and Desmond Travers, replied on 14 April that "there is no justification for any demand or expectation for reconsideration of the report", since nothing of substance had appeared to change its findings. [cite:gz_aj_goldstone_coauthors] Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said Goldstone's reversal "must lead to the shelving of this report once and for all." [cite:gz_jvl_goldstone] The report was never withdrawn; its chief author's reconsideration and his colleagues' refusal stand side by side in the record.

sections.h: 2012, and the War of 2014
sections.html:
Pillar of Defense, November 2012. On 14 November 2012 an Israeli airstrike killed Ahmed Jabari, the head of Hamas's military wing in Gaza, and began an eight-day operation. Israel cited more than a hundred rockets fired in twenty-four hours and attacks on its soldiers near the fence, and said its aim was "to halt rocket attacks against civilian targets originating from the Gaza Strip"; Palestinian armed groups cited the blockade of Gaza and the occupation of the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights counted 174 Palestinians killed, 107 of them civilians; B'Tselem counted 167, of whom 62 had taken part in hostilities. Six Israelis were killed, four civilians and two soldiers. More than 1,456 rockets were fired into Israel, and Israel's new Iron Dome system intercepted about 421. [cite:gz_wiki_2012]

The Egyptian-brokered ceasefire of 21 November required Israel to stop "all hostilities in the Gaza Strip land, sea and air including incursions and targeting of individuals", required the Palestinian factions to stop all attacks including rockets, and provided for the opening of the crossings to be taken up within 24 hours. The fishing limit was raised to six nautical miles; in March 2013 it was cut back to three. [cite:gz_wiki_2012]

The road to 2014. On 12 June 2014 three Israeli teenagers, Naftali Fraenkel, Gilad Shaer and Eyal Yifrah, were abducted in the West Bank; they were found dead on 30 June. Israel blamed Hamas, though, the record notes, "no evidence of Hamas involvement was offered by Israeli authorities at the time"; the Hamas leader Khaled Meshaal later acknowledged that Hamas members were responsible. Israel's search operation in the West Bank killed about eleven Palestinians and arrested between 350 and 600, including nearly all of Hamas's West Bank leadership. After the teenagers' burial, a Palestinian teenager, Mohammed Abu Khdeir, was murdered in revenge. Rocket fire from Gaza resumed and Israel struck targets in Gaza between 4 and 6 July; on 7 July, after an explosion in a Khan Yunis tunnel killed seven Hamas militants (an Israeli strike, by Hamas's account; its own munitions, by the Israeli army's), Hamas claimed the rocket fire. [cite:gz_wiki_2014]

The war. Israel began its air campaign on 8 July with the stated aim of stopping the rocket fire, and sent in ground forces from 17 July to 5 August with the stated aim of destroying the tunnels dug from Gaza toward Israel. An open-ended ceasefire took effect on 26 August, ending what the UN inquiry called "the 51 day operation". [cite:gz_wiki_2014] [cite:gz_un_coi2015]

The dead. The UN's humanitarian office counted 2,220 Palestinians killed, 1,492 of them civilians; the UN Human Rights Council counted 2,251, with 1,462 civilians. Israel's Foreign Ministry counted 2,125 dead and classed about 36 percent as civilians. Sixty-seven Israeli soldiers were killed, and six civilians in Israel, one of them a Thai worker. More than 7,000 homes were razed and about 89,000 damaged, and at the height of the war the UN estimated that up to 520,000 people, about thirty percent of the population, might have been displaced. [cite:gz_wiki_2014]

The inquiry. A UN commission of inquiry chaired by the American judge Mary McGowan Davis reported in June 2015 that it had found "substantial information pointing to the possible commission of war crimes by both Israel and Palestinian armed groups." On Israel's side it recorded more than 6,000 airstrikes and about 50,000 tank and artillery shells, and 142 families who lost three or more members in attacks on homes, 742 deaths in all; it asked whether Israel's unchanged targeting practice reflected a policy "at least tacitly approved at the highest level of government." On the Palestinian side it recorded 4,881 rockets and 1,753 mortars, fired indiscriminately in a way that "appeared to have the intention of spreading terror among civilians", and the tunnels that traumatised Israeli communities near the fence. Israel did not respond to the commission's requests for access. [cite:gz_un_coi2015] A week before it reported, Israel published its own account of the war, which said its army had done "the utmost to avoid civilian casualties" and blamed Hamas for firing from residential areas; Netanyahu said that "whoever wants a baseless, automatic accusation against Israel can waste their time reading the UN report." [cite:gz_euronews_2015]

sections.h: The March at the Fence, and May 2021
sections.html:
The Great March of Return, 2018–2019. From 30 March 2018 Gazans gathered, week after week, at protest camps along the fence with Israel, in protests that took their name from the demand for refugees' return. A UN commission of inquiry examined the protests through 31 December 2018. It counted 189 Palestinians killed at the protest sites, 183 of them by live ammunition, including 35 children, two clearly marked journalists and three clearly marked paramedics, and 6,106 wounded by live fire. One Israeli soldier was killed on a protest day, outside the protest sites, and four were wounded at them. [cite:gz_un_coi2019]

The commission found that the demonstrations "were civilian in nature, with clearly stated political aims," and that there were reasonable grounds to believe Israeli snipers had shot journalists, health workers, children and people with disabilities "knowing they were clearly recognizable as such"; the violations, it said, "may constitute war crimes or crimes against humanity." It acknowledged "some acts of significant violence" by demonstrators and that some were members of armed groups, but found that those killed and injured had not been taking a direct part in hostilities or posing an imminent threat. It also found that Hamas, as the authority in Gaza, had "failed to prevent" the incendiary kites and balloons launched from the strip, which burned land and frightened civilians in southern Israel. [cite:gz_un_coi2019] Israel refused to take part in the inquiry. Its acting foreign minister, Yisrael Katz, said that "Israel totally rejects the report", called it "hostile, false and incorrect," and placed the responsibility on Hamas: "Whoever pushes the residents of Gaza to the fences, including women and children, is the Hamas organization." [cite:gz_cnn_katz2019]

May 2021. The last of these wars began in Jerusalem. Palestinians in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood had been protesting the expected eviction of six families, and on 7 and again on 10 May Israeli police raided the al-Aqsa compound; the second raid left about 300 Palestinians and 21 police officers injured; police said protesters had thrown stones and fireworks at them. Hamas demanded that Israel withdraw its police from the compound and from Sheikh Jarrah by six that evening, and when the deadline passed it and Islamic Jihad fired rockets at Israel. [cite:gz_wiki_2021] In eleven days of fighting, according to the UN, at least 256 Palestinians were killed in Gaza, 66 of them children, while Israel said it had killed 200 militants; at least 13 people were killed in Israel, two of them children. About 4,360 rockets were fired from Gaza, some 680 of which fell short inside the strip, and Israel's Iron Dome intercepted about 95 percent of those heading toward populated areas. On 15 May an Israeli strike destroyed the al-Jalaa tower, which housed the offices of Al Jazeera and the Associated Press; the army said Hamas military intelligence was based there, a claim the AP asked it to prove. An Egyptian-mediated ceasefire took effect on 21 May, and both sides claimed victory. [cite:gz_wiki_2021]

Between the wars the closure stayed in place, and after each one the reconstruction of what had been destroyed passed through the same crossings and permits that Part Four described; Part Eight follows that money. The war that began on 7 October 2023 was of a different order, and Parts Six and Seven are given to it.

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: October 7, 2023
chapters.intro: Part Six is about a single day. On 7 October 2023 armed groups led by Hamas broke through the fence around Gaza and attacked the communities, army posts and festivals beyond it, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. The part sets out what happened, as the human rights organizations and Israeli inquiries that examined it record; the warnings that preceded it and why they were dismissed; and the accounts of the day given by Hamas, by the UN and by Israel's own army, including the parts of those accounts that remain disputed.
chapters.outro: Part Six followed one day. Armed groups led by Hamas crossed the fence at more than sixty points and killed about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and took 251 hostages; 378 were killed at the Nova festival alone. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] [cite:gz_wiki_nova] [cite:gz_pbs_idfprobe] Israel had held the attackers' plan for more than a year and judged it beyond them, and its army has since said it underestimated Hamas; no state commission of inquiry has been set up. [cite:gz_nyt_jericho] [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026] Hamas calls the attack a necessary response and says any harm to civilians was accidental, admitting "some faults"; Human Rights Watch found the killing of civilians a central aim and a crime against humanity; the UN found reasonable grounds to believe rape occurred, and found some allegations unfounded. Israel's army was reported to have invoked the Hannibal procedure, and its own probes have found individual cases of Israelis killed by Israeli fire, without a published total. [cite:gz_aj_narrative] [cite:gz_aj_patten] [cite:gz_toi_hannibal] [cite:gz_idf_beeri_probe] Part Seven turns to the war in Gaza that followed.

sections.h: The Attack
sections.html:
The assault began on the morning of Saturday 7 October 2023. Gunmen from the Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades, Hamas's armed wing, and from at least four other Palestinian armed groups crossed the fence at many points at once. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] The Israeli army's later inquiry found that Hamas used more than sixty routes of attack, where Israel's plans had expected attackers at no more than eight points along the border. [cite:gz_pbs_idfprobe]

They attacked at least nineteen kibbutzim and five moshavim, the towns of Sderot and Ofakim, army bases and posts along the border, two music festivals and a beach party. Human Rights Watch, which investigated the day, cites the news agency AFP's cross-checking: 1,195 people killed, 815 of them civilians. The armed groups took 251 people, civilians and members of the security forces, back into Gaza as hostages. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7]

Nova. The largest single loss of life was at the Nova music festival near Re'im. Rockets were seen at about 6:30 a.m., and at 6:35 a police officer, Deputy Superintendent Nivi Ohana, decided to shut the event down, a decision credited with saving hundreds of lives. Gunmen reached the site soon after. The Israeli army's investigation, released in April 2025, counted 378 people killed there, 344 civilians and 34 members of the security forces, revising an earlier count of 364; 44 were taken hostage. [cite:gz_wiki_nova]

Be'eri. In Kibbutz Be'eri, a community of about a thousand people, 101 civilians and 31 members of the security forces were killed, and 30 residents and two other civilians were taken to Gaza. Large Israeli forces did not enter the kibbutz until about six in the evening; the army later said it had "failed in its mission to protect the residents of Kibbutz Be'eri." [cite:gz_idf_beeri_probe] In one house, that of Pessi Cohen, gunmen held fourteen Israelis; a brigadier general, Barak Hiram, ordered a tank to fire on the house, a gun battle followed, and thirteen of the fourteen were found dead. [cite:gz_toi_beeri] The army's investigation, presented in July 2024, concluded on the information it had examined that no one inside the house was hit by tank fire and that most of the hostages inside were killed by the gunmen, but that one hostage outside was "highly likely" killed by tank shrapnel; it judged the order to fire, given after negotiations were exhausted, "reasonable in view of the conditions." Be'eri residents said the probe "failed to answer critical questions" and called for a state inquiry. [cite:gz_idf_beeri_probe] [cite:gz_jc_beeri]

What the investigators found. Human Rights Watch concluded that killing civilians and taking hostages were "central aims of the planned attack", not an afterthought or isolated acts, and that "the planned murder of civilians and the hostage-taking were crimes against humanity." It documented war crimes including wilful killing, cruel treatment, the mutilation of bodies and crimes involving sexual and gender-based violence. Hamas's authorities told it that their fighters had been instructed not to target civilians; its investigation found evidence to the contrary in many cases. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7]

sections.h: The Warnings, and the Inquiries
sections.html:
"Jericho Wall." More than a year before the attack, according to documents, emails and interviews reported by the New York Times, Israeli officials had obtained a Hamas battle plan of about forty pages, which they code-named "Jericho Wall." It set out, step by step, an invasion to overwhelm the border defences, seize Israeli towns and storm military bases, with rocket barrages, drones to knock out the border cameras and machine guns, and gunmen crossing on paragliders, on motorcycles and on foot. The attack of 7 October followed it closely. Israeli military and intelligence officials judged the plan "aspirational", an attack on that scale being, in their view, beyond Hamas's capabilities. [cite:gz_nyt_jericho]

In July 2023 a veteran analyst in Unit 8200, Israel's signals intelligence unit, warned that Hamas had held a day-long training exercise resembling the plan. A colonel in the Gaza division called the exercise part of a "totally imaginative" scenario. "I utterly refute that the scenario is imaginary," she wrote. The colonel answered: "In short, let's wait patiently." [cite:gz_nyt_jericho]

The army's inquiry. In February 2025 the Israeli army published the findings of its own investigation. It concluded that Israel had "underestimated its capabilities" and had misread Hamas's aims, working from the belief that Hamas "was more interested in governing the territory than fighting Israel." The chief of staff, Herzi Halevi, said: "I was the commander of the military on October 7th, and I have my own responsibility," and he had announced his resignation the month before. [cite:gz_pbs_idfprobe]

The inquiry that has not been held. Israel's law provides for a state commission of inquiry, whose members are appointed by the president of the Supreme Court. Benjamin Netanyahu said in October 2023 that the failures would be investigated and that everyone, himself included, would have to answer, after the war. As of October 2026 no state commission has been established. In the summer of 2025 the government told the Supreme Court it did not intend to set one up at that stage; Netanyahu argues that a commission appointed under the existing law would lack public trust, and prefers one with equal representation for the coalition and the opposition. He rejected a compromise proposed by President Isaac Herzog. A bill for a different kind of commission passed a first reading in July 2026 but was not completed before the Knesset dissolved. The State Comptroller has conducted a separate examination. [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026] [cite:gz_pbs_idfprobe]

sections.h: The Accounts of the Day
sections.html:
Several accounts of 7 October now exist, given by the attackers, by UN and human rights investigators and by Israel's own army and press. They agree on the scale of the killing and on the hostages; they disagree, or remain incomplete, on intent, on sexual violence and on how some of the Israeli dead were killed. This section sets them side by side.

Hamas's account. In January 2024 Hamas published a sixteen-page document titled "Our Narrative." It called the attack, which it named Operation Al-Aqsa Flood, "a necessary step and a normal response to confront all Israeli conspiracies against the Palestinian people," and cited the Palestinians held in Israeli prisons, settlement construction and what it called the "Judaization" of the West Bank and Jerusalem. It said its fighters had targeted only soldiers and people carrying weapons, and that "maybe some faults happened" because of "the rapid collapse of the Israeli security and military system." It also said that many Israelis "were killed by the Israeli army and police due to their confusion." [cite:gz_aj_narrative] Human Rights Watch's investigation found that the killing of civilians was a central aim of the attack, not a fault. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7]

Sexual violence. A UN team led by Pramila Patten, the Secretary-General's special representative on sexual violence in conflict, visited Israel in early 2024 and reported on 4 March that there were "reasonable grounds to believe" that sexual violence, including rape and gang rape, had occurred during the attack, among other places on Road 232 by the festival and at Kibbutz Re'im, and "clear and convincing information" that some hostages in Gaza had been subjected to it. It also found at least two widely repeated allegations from Be'eri to be "unfounded", said it had been unable to meet any victims of sexual violence, despite efforts to encourage them to come forward, and said that a "fully-fledged investigation" would be needed to establish the scale. Hamas has denied the allegations. [cite:gz_aj_patten]

The Hannibal reports. In July 2024 the Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that army commands had, on 7 October, invoked the "Hannibal" procedure, a directive meant to prevent soldiers being taken captive even at risk to their lives, which had been officially repealed in 2016. It reported an order of "Hannibal at Erez" with an attack drone, similar orders at the Re'im base and the Nahal Oz post, and an instruction that "not a single vehicle could return to Gaza." A Southern Command source told it that no vehicle known to carry hostages was attacked, but that "you couldn't really know if there were any such people in a vehicle." [cite:gz_toi_hannibal] Israeli inquiries have found individual cases: an air force probe found that Efrat Katz of Nir Oz was likely killed by helicopter fire, and the army's Be'eri probe found that one hostage was highly likely killed by tank shrapnel. The army has said friendly-fire deaths that day were "not many" but has published no total, and no published inquiry has established an overall number. [cite:gz_toi_hannibal] [cite:gz_idf_beeri_probe] [cite:gz_pbs_idfprobe]

The first response. On 9 October Israel's defence minister, Yoav Gallant, announced: "We are putting a complete siege on Gaza … No electricity, no food, no water, no gas – it's all closed." [cite:gz_aj_siege] The war that followed is the subject of Part Seven.

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: The War Since: Deaths, Famine and the Courts
chapters.intro: Part Seven covers the war that followed October 7, from the siege announced two days later to the ceasefire of October 2025 and the year since. It sets out the course of the fighting and the two ceasefires; the dead, the destruction and the famine, and how each was measured and disputed; and the cases brought in the international courts and the findings of UN investigators, with Israel's response to each. Much of it is recent, and the figures here are dated to the sources that give them, as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: Part Seven followed the war from the siege of October 2023 to the year after the ceasefire of October 2025. A first truce in January 2025 collapsed in March; the second freed the last living hostages and some 1,900 Palestinian prisoners and detainees, but by October 2026 nearly 1,500 more Palestinians had been killed, aid moved at a third of the agreed rate and Israel held nearly two-thirds of the strip. [cite:gz_wiki_ceasefire2025] [cite:gz_kt_hostages] [cite:gz_aj_year2026] The health ministry counted 74,382 dead, a figure that Haaretz reported the Israeli army had accepted in its earlier form, which the army then said did not reflect official data and the Lancet found likely to be low; about 81 percent of the strip's buildings were damaged, and famine was confirmed in Gaza City in August 2025, which Israel denied. [cite:gz_aj_lancet] [cite:gz_yahoo_idf71k] [cite:gz_tna_idfdeny] [cite:gz_unosat2025] [cite:gz_aj_ipc] The World Court found South Africa's genocide claims plausible and ordered Israel to prevent genocide and halt the Rafah offensive; the International Criminal Court issued warrants for Israel's prime minister and defence minister and for Hamas's military commander; and a UN commission found that Israel had committed genocide. Israel rejected each. [cite:gz_oj_icj2024] [cite:gz_lawfare_rafah] [cite:gz_almon_icc] [cite:gz_un_coi2025] [cite:gz_ctv_coi2025] Part Eight follows the money.

sections.h: The Course of the War
sections.html:
The siege. Two days after the attack, on 9 October 2023, Israel's defence minister Yoav Gallant announced: "We are putting a complete siege on Gaza … No electricity, no food, no water, no gas – it's all closed." [cite:gz_aj_siege] Israel described its aims as a "defensive and just war to eliminate Hamas and to secure the release of our hostages," the 251 people taken into Gaza on October 7. [cite:gz_toi_rafah] [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] The air campaign was followed by a ground invasion, and the war went on until January 2025.

The first ceasefire, and its collapse. A ceasefire took effect on 19 January 2025, planned in three stages of forty-two days each. In the first stage Hamas released 33 hostages, and Israel agreed to free up to 1,904 Palestinian prisoners over the whole deal. When Hamas refused an Israeli proposal to extend the first stage instead of moving to the second, Israel stopped all aid from entering Gaza on 2 March. On 18 March it resumed its strikes, citing "Hamas's refusal to release hostages and its rejection of proposals to extend the cease-fire"; Hamas said the second stage should proceed as originally planned. Netanyahu declared that Israel had "resumed combat in full force." [cite:gz_wiki_ceasefire2025]

The second ceasefire. In October 2025 Israel and Hamas accepted the first stage of a plan put forward by the United States and mediated with Qatar, Egypt and Turkey, and a ceasefire took effect on 10 October. [cite:gz_wiki_timeline2025] [cite:gz_aj_year2026] On 13 October Hamas released all twenty remaining living hostages, and Israel freed more than 1,900 Palestinians: about 250 serving life sentences for attacks on Israelis, and about 1,700 taken from Gaza during the war and held without charge. [cite:gz_kt_hostages] The remains of the dead hostages were returned over the following months, some of them disputed, until the army announced that the last had been recovered. The UN Security Council endorsed the plan's "Board of Peace" and authorized an international stabilization force. Israel's forces held a line inside the strip, the "yellow line", and repeatedly fired on people who crossed or approached it, saying they threatened its forces; Gaza health officials reported civilians killed near the line. [cite:gz_wiki_timeline2025]

A year on. When the ceasefire marked its first anniversary, in October 2026, the Gaza health ministry counted 1,493 Palestinians killed and 5,299 wounded since it began. Aid trucks were entering at about a third of the agreed rate, no international stabilization force had deployed, and Israel controlled nearly two-thirds of the strip, against the roughly half it was to keep. [cite:gz_aj_year2026]

sections.h: The Dead, the Ruins and the Famine
sections.html:
The count. As of 12 October 2026, the Gaza health ministry counted 74,382 Palestinians killed since October 2023. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] Its figures do not distinguish civilians from fighters, and they leave out people missing under the rubble and those who died of starvation or disease. For more than two years Israel cast doubt on them. On 29 January 2026 Haaretz reported that the Israeli army had accepted the ministry's estimate of about 71,000 dead and was analysing how many were combatants; the next day an army spokesman said such reports "do not reflect official data." [cite:gz_yahoo_idf71k] [cite:gz_tna_idfdeny] A classified Israeli military database, reported in August 2025 by the Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call, listed 8,900 named Hamas and Islamic Jihad fighters as dead or probably dead by May 2025, when the ministry's count stood at about 53,000: about 17 percent, leaving roughly 83 percent who were not listed fighters. The army said the figures were "incorrect." [cite:gz_aj_83pct]

The ministry's count is also likely to be low. A study in The Lancet by researchers at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and Yale, using three independent sources of names, estimated 64,260 deaths from traumatic injury between October 2023 and the end of June 2024, when the ministry had counted 37,877: an undercount of about 41 percent. It found that 59 percent of the dead were women, children or people over sixty-five, and it did not estimate how many were fighters. Israel says it goes to great lengths to avoid civilian deaths, and accuses Hamas of using hospitals as cover, which Hamas denies. [cite:gz_aj_lancet]

The ruins. The UN's satellite centre, examining images taken on 11 October 2025, the day after the ceasefire began, identified, in a preliminary analysis, 123,464 structures destroyed, 17,116 severely damaged and 33,857 moderately damaged, and estimated that about 81 percent of all structures in the Gaza Strip had been damaged. [cite:gz_unosat2025]

Aid. From March 2025 Israel blocked aid, saying that Hamas was stealing what the UN delivered; it did not make public evidence for the claim. In late May, UN-led distribution was replaced in part by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, backed by Israel and the United States, which handed out food at its own distribution sites. The UN human rights office recorded more than 2,146 people killed near those sites and along aid convoy routes by early September. The foundation said it was the only operation that "reliably and safely" fed Gazans, and that it distributed more than three million boxes of food; it closed its sites in November 2025, after the ceasefire. [cite:gz_aj_ghf]

Famine. On 22 August 2025 the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, the UN-backed system that defines famine, found that "famine is now occurring in Gaza City and its surrounding area," with more than half a million people in catastrophic conditions, and projected that it would spread south by the end of September. It attributed it to conflict, displacement, restricted access and the collapse of the food system. [cite:gz_aj_ipc] Israel's foreign ministry said: "There is no famine in Gaza," called the findings "based on Hamas lies laundered through organisations with vested interests," and said that "a massive influx of aid has flooded the Strip with staple foods." [cite:gz_olj_ipc]

sections.h: The Courts and the Inquiries
sections.html:
The genocide case. South Africa brought a case against Israel at the International Court of Justice under the Genocide Convention, alleging that Israel had committed genocidal acts with genocidal intent, shown by its conduct and by the statements of its leaders. Israel answered that it was entitled to defend itself, that the statements cited were not government or military policy, and that it had no genocidal intent. [cite:gz_ch_icj] On 26 January 2024 the Court found that "at least some of the rights claimed by South Africa" were plausible, and ordered Israel to take all measures within its power to prevent acts within the scope of the Convention, to prevent and punish incitement to genocide, and to enable humanitarian aid. It did not order a ceasefire, and it did not decide whether genocide was being committed, a question for the merits, which will take years. [cite:gz_oj_icj2024] [cite:gz_ch_icj] On 24 May 2024, by thirteen votes to two, it ordered Israel to "halt its military offensive and any other action in the Rafah Governorate, which may inflict on the Palestinian group in Gaza conditions of life that could bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part," to keep the Rafah crossing open and to admit UN investigators. [cite:gz_lawfare_rafah] Israel's National Security Council and foreign ministry answered that Israel "has not and will not conduct military actions in the Rafah area which may inflict on the Palestinian civilian population in Gaza conditions of life that could bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part," and called the genocide charges "false, outrageous and morally repugnant." [cite:gz_toi_rafah]

The arrest warrants. On 21 November 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant, finding reasonable grounds to believe they bore responsibility for the war crime of starvation as a method of warfare, for intentionally directing attacks against civilians, and for the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution and other inhumane acts, from at least 8 October 2023 to at least 20 May 2024. It issued a warrant on the same day for Mohammed Deif, the commander of Hamas's armed wing, for murder, extermination, torture, rape and hostage-taking on and after 7 October; the court withdrew that warrant on 26 February 2025, after prosecutors reported that he had been killed in July 2024. [cite:gz_un_icc] [cite:gz_almon_icc] [cite:gz_ji_deif] Israel challenged the court's jurisdiction; as of October 2025 the challenge was still pending, and the court had found "no legal basis" to quash the warrants in the meantime. [cite:gz_toi_icc2025] Netanyahu called the warrants "anti-Semitic" and the accusations "absurd and false"; Hamas welcomed them; President Joe Biden called them "outrageous" and said there was "no equivalence" between Israel and Hamas. [cite:gz_almon_icc]

The UN commission's finding. On 16 September 2025 the UN's independent Commission of Inquiry, chaired by the South African judge Navi Pillay, concluded that "Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip," finding that four of the five acts defined in the 1948 Convention had been committed, and that President Isaac Herzog, Netanyahu and Gallant "have incited the commission of genocide." [cite:gz_un_coi2025] Israel's foreign ministry said it "categorically rejects this distorted and false report," called for the commission to be abolished, and said the report "relies entirely on Hamas falsehoods." [cite:gz_ctv_coi2025]

Aid and the occupying power. On 22 October 2025, in an advisory opinion requested by the UN General Assembly, the Court said that Israel, as occupying power, must "ensure the basic needs of the local population," and was "under an obligation to agree to and facilitate relief schemes provided by the United Nations and its entities," UNRWA among them; it found that Israel had not substantiated its allegations against UNRWA's staff. The opinion is not binding. Israel, which did not take part, "categorically rejects" it, its foreign ministry spokesman said. [cite:gz_ji_ao2025]

The genocide case is undecided. The International Court of Justice has issued orders but not a judgment on the merits; the arrest warrants have not been executed; and the UN commission's finding is the conclusion of investigators, not of a court. Israel has filed its counter-memorial, and the Court has set further written pleadings to run to May 2029, so a judgment is years away. [cite:gz_icj_timelimits] The record so far is of findings and orders on one side and Israel's rejection of them on the other.

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: The Money: Occupation, Aid and Reconstruction
chapters.intro: Part Eight follows the money that moved into and around Gaza: the Qatari cash that Israel allowed into the strip from 2018, the reconstruction money pledged after the war of 2014 and the system built to control it, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees and the fight over its funding after October 7, and the bill for the war that followed, both for the weapons and for rebuilding what they destroyed. The library's volume Follow the Money traces the American side of that ledger in detail; this part keeps to Gaza.
chapters.outro: Part Eight followed the money. From 2018 Israel let Qatari cash into Gaza, at first mainly for Hamas-government salaries and later, at times about $30 million a month, for needy families; Netanyahu called it a humanitarian step to keep the quiet, while reporting after October 7 described it as part of a policy of keeping Hamas strong, which he denies. [cite:gz_ds_qatar2018] [cite:gz_aj_qatar2021] [cite:gz_week_qatar] After 2014 donors pledged $5.4 billion and rebuilding passed through a mechanism that gave Israel the final say. [cite:gz_un_cairo2014] [cite:gz_aj_grm] After Israel's allegations against twelve UNRWA staff, donors cut funding; UN investigators found nine may have been involved, and the Knesset barred the agency from operating in Israel. [cite:gz_crs_unrwa] [cite:gz_unrwa_oios] [cite:gz_jp_knesset_unrwa] The United States spent $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel in the war's first two years; rebuilding Gaza is estimated to need $71.4 billion. [cite:gz_cow_aid] [cite:gz_rdna2026]

sections.h: The Qatari Cash
sections.html:
In November 2018 $15 million in Qatari money was brought into Gaza through Israel, the first of six monthly payments totalling $90 million. The money went mainly to pay the salaries of officials working for the Hamas-run government. The transfer was authorized by Israel, which Netanyahu said his security cabinet and security establishment supported, and appeared to be tied to talks in which Hamas would halt the border protests in return for an easing of the blockade. Benjamin Netanyahu called it "the right step," taken to restore quiet near the border and prevent a humanitarian crisis. Inside his own government, the education minister Naftali Bennett compared it to "protection money" paid to criminals, and the opposition leader Tzipi Livni called it "submission to Hamas." [cite:gz_ds_qatar2018]

The payments continued. By 2021 about $30 million in Qatari cash was being carried into the strip in suitcases each month, through a crossing Israel controlled. Israel halted them after the war of May 2021, insisting on safeguards that none of the money would reach Hamas, and in August 2021 agreed to a new arrangement under which the UN would pay part of the Qatari grant directly to families, with Israel overseeing the list of recipients. [cite:gz_aj_qatar2021]

The policy behind it. After October 7 the payments became evidence in an argument about what Israel's policy toward Hamas had been. The New York Times, drawing on interviews with more than two dozen officials in Israel, the United States, Qatar and elsewhere, reported in December 2023 that Netanyahu had "not only tolerated" the payments but "had encouraged them," that Israeli intelligence officers had escorted the Qatari official who carried the cash into Gaza, and that Netanyahu had spoken since at least 2012 of keeping Hamas strong as a counterweight to the Palestinian Authority. Politico, among others, cited a remark he was reported to have made to Likud lawmakers in 2019, that anyone who wanted to prevent a Palestinian state should support strengthening Hamas; the remark was first reported by the Jerusalem Post from an unnamed lawmaker's paraphrase, and the reporter has since written that it concerned letting money into Gaza and has been distorted in later retellings. [cite:gz_harkov_2019] Netanyahu said the payments had been made "to avoid a civilian humanitarian collapse" in Gaza, and called the claim that he had wanted to build up Hamas "a big lie." [cite:gz_week_qatar]

The record establishes the payments, their size, their route through Israel and the government's approval of them. What they were for is where the accounts divide: a humanitarian measure and a price for quiet, in Netanyahu's account, or, in his critics', part of a strategy of keeping Gaza and the West Bank under divided Palestinian rule. Part Three noted that the question of Israel's earlier dealings with the Islamist movement is older than this. [scene:gz3_uprising|The first intifada and the rise of Hamas]

sections.h: Rebuilding, and the Refugee Agency
sections.html:
After 2014. On 12 October 2014, seven weeks after the war of that summer ended, donors meeting in Cairo pledged about $5.4 billion, half of it for the reconstruction of Gaza. [cite:gz_un_cairo2014] Israel had barred cement, steel and other construction materials as "dual-use" goods that Hamas could use to build tunnels, and the money could only become buildings through a new arrangement, the Gaza Reconstruction Mechanism, overseen by a steering team of Israel, the Palestinians and the UN. It placed security personnel and video cameras at the points where materials were handed out, vetted suppliers and buyers, and kept a database of the materials entering Gaza that Israeli intelligence could see; it gave Israel's security concerns priority and the final say on large projects. Israel's foreign ministry said it would stop Hamas from diverting funds and materials "to violence." Critics said it relieved Israel of its responsibilities and entrenched Palestinian dependency; Oxfam called for the blockade to end and warned that at the rate materials were then entering, rebuilding could take more than fifty years. [cite:gz_aj_grm]

UNRWA. The UN Relief and Works Agency, created for the refugees of 1948 and described in Part One, received $1.47 billion in funding in 2023. In January 2024 Israel alleged that twelve UNRWA employees had taken part in the October 7 attacks; it also accused the agency of employing hundreds of staff in Gaza linked to armed groups, which UNRWA disputes. The United States paused its funding on 26 January 2024 and other major donors followed, though the European Union and Germany later resumed. In March 2024 Congress barred US funding to UNRWA until at least March 2025. An independent review led by the former French foreign minister Catherine Colonna reported in April 2024 that the agency had "many mechanisms in place" to keep its neutrality, along with gaps it recommended closing. [cite:gz_crs_unrwa]

The UN's internal investigators examined nineteen staff members in all. In one case they found no evidence, and in nine the evidence was insufficient; in the other nine, they found that the evidence, "if authenticated and corroborated," could indicate the staff "may have been involved," and UNRWA ended their contracts. [cite:gz_unrwa_oios] On 28 October 2024 the Knesset passed, by large majorities, two laws barring UNRWA from operating in Israel and barring Israeli officials from contact with it. [cite:gz_jp_knesset_unrwa] [scene:gz1_refugees|The refugees, and the agency created for them]

sections.h: The Bill
sections.html:
The weapons. According to a study by William Hartung for Brown University's Costs of War project, the US government spent at least $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel between October 2023 and September 2025, not counting the tens of billions of dollars in arms sales committed for later years. The same project estimated that the United States spent a further $9.65 billion to $12.07 billion on its own military operations in Yemen and the wider region in the same period. [cite:gz_cow_aid] The library's account of [scene:pm10_costs|what the architecture costs] sets this against the longer history of American aid.

The rebuilding. In April 2026 the World Bank, the United Nations and the European Union published a joint assessment of the damage done in Gaza between October 2023 and October 2025. It put the physical damage at $35.2 billion and the economic and social losses at $22.7 billion, counted 371,888 housing units destroyed or damaged, found that the economy had contracted by 84 percent, and estimated that recovery and reconstruction would need $71.4 billion over the next decade, $16.2 billion of it for housing alone. [cite:gz_rdna2026]

Who pays the second bill is not settled. After 2014 the pledges came from donor governments and the materials passed through a mechanism Israel controlled; the US plan announced in September 2025, under which the October ceasefire took hold, places a Palestinian technocratic committee under an international "Board of Peace." [cite:gz_gn_20points] Part Nine turns to who decides.

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: Who Decides
chapters.intro: Part Nine asks who has decided Gaza's fate since October 2023. Inside Israel, the decisions rest with a coalition government whose partners have pressed it, publicly, against the January 2025 ceasefire and for the emigration of Gaza's people. Inside Hamas, most of the leaders who planned October 7 have been killed. Outside, the United States has supplied the weapons, blocked or shaped the Security Council's resolutions, and in 2025 wrote the plan that now governs the ceasefire, with Qatar, Egypt and Turkey as mediators. The part sets out what each has said and done, on the record.
chapters.outro: Part Nine set out who decides. In Israel, coalition partners threatened to bring down the government over the January 2025 ceasefire and pressed for the emigration of Gaza's people, which Netanyahu embraced as part of the Trump plan in 2025; the government gave Hamas's refusals as its reason for resuming the war. [cite:gz_aj_bengvir] [cite:gz_jc_smotrich] [cite:gz_jweekly_may25] [cite:gz_wiki_ceasefire2025] Hamas's leaders of October 2023 have mostly been killed. [cite:gz_almon_hamasleaders] The United States vetoed six Security Council drafts between October 2023 and November 2024, one of them on Palestinian UN membership, and two more ceasefire drafts in June and September 2025, supplied $21.7 billion in military aid, proposed in February 2025 to take over Gaza and move its people, and in September 2025 wrote the plan under which the ceasefire holds, with a board chaired by its president. [cite:gz_aj_unsc] [cite:gz_axios_veto2025] [cite:gz_jurist_veto2025] [cite:gz_cow_aid] [cite:gz_whyy_riviera] [cite:gz_gn_20points] Part Ten turns to the plans that American and Israeli leaders have made for Gaza's future.

sections.h: Inside the Two Governments
sections.html:
The coalition. Israel's decisions on Gaza are taken by Benjamin Netanyahu's government, which depends for its majority on parties of the religious right. Their leaders have stated their positions openly. When the January 2025 ceasefire was put to the cabinet, the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, said: "If this irresponsible agreement is approved and implemented, the Jewish Power Party will not be part of the government and will leave it." He argued that aid and utilities to Gaza should be "completely stopped" to force the release of the hostages, and he called on the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, to quit with him. [cite:gz_aj_bengvir] Smotrich, who has long advocated what he calls the "voluntary emigration" of Gazans, told his party later that month that he was developing an "operational plan" to move them out of the territory, and threatened to leave the government if that policy was not carried out after the ceasefire's first phase. [cite:gz_jc_smotrich] Ben-Gvir said he did not intend to "overthrow" the government and would consider returning if the ceasefire failed. [cite:gz_aj_bengvir] He resigned on 21 January 2025, and his party rejoined the government on 18 March, hours after the truce collapsed. [cite:gz_jc_bengvir_return]

The government's own position. Emigration was not only the partners' demand. On 17 February 2025 Netanyahu said he was "committed to US President Trump's plan for the creation of a different Gaza," and the defence minister, Israel Katz, announced a body to oversee the "voluntary departure" of Gazans to third countries. [cite:gz_aj_netanyahu_feb25] On 21 May Netanyahu called the plan "so revolutionary," summed it up as "Residents of Gaza who want to leave can leave," and named its implementation among five conditions for ending the war, with the hostages' release, Hamas's surrender, the expulsion of its leaders and the strip's demilitarisation. [cite:gz_jweekly_may25] The ceasefire collapsed on 18 March 2025, as Part Seven describes. [scene:gz7_war|The course of the war]

The record here is of the ministers' public statements and threats. Whether those pressures, rather than the government's stated reasons, decided particular turns of the war is a question of motive the record does not settle; the government's stated reason for resuming the war in March 2025 was, in its words, Hamas's "refusal to release hostages and its rejection of proposals to extend the cease-fire"; Hamas said the second phase should proceed as agreed. [cite:gz_wiki_ceasefire2025]

Hamas's leadership. The men who led Hamas on October 7 have mostly been killed. Ismail Haniyeh, the head of its political bureau, was killed in Tehran in July 2024, an act Israel's defence minister acknowledged in December 2024. Yahya Sinwar, its leader in Gaza and then its overall leader, was killed by the Israeli army in Gaza in October 2024. Israel says it killed Mohammed Deif, the commander of the armed wing, in a strike near Khan Younis in July 2024, his deputy Marwan Issa in March 2024, and Yahya Sinwar's brother Mohammad, who succeeded to the military command, in May 2025. Khalil al-Hayya, based in Qatar and a member of a five-man leadership council, is seen as its most influential figure abroad. [cite:gz_almon_hamasleaders]

sections.h: Washington, and the Mediators
sections.html:
At the Security Council. Between October 2023 and November 2024 the UN Security Council voted fourteen times on drafts about Gaza. Four resolutions passed, the last of them, in June 2024, an American draft. The United States vetoed six others, on 18 and 25 October and 8 December 2023, 20 February, 18 April (on Palestinian membership of the UN) and 20 November 2024; Russia and China vetoed two American drafts. [cite:gz_aj_unsc] The United States again cast the only vote against ceasefire drafts on 4 June 2025, when its acting ambassador, Dorothy Shea, said the text did not condemn Hamas or call on it to disarm and "draws false equivalence" between Israel and Hamas, [cite:gz_axios_veto2025] and in September 2025, which JURIST counted as its sixth veto of a Gaza ceasefire draft; its deputy envoy, Morgan Ortagus, said the text did not condemn Hamas or recognize Israel's right to defend itself, and "seeks to return to a failed system." [cite:gz_jurist_veto2025]

The weapons. The United States spent $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel in the first two years of the war, as Part Eight records. [cite:gz_cow_aid] [scene:gz8_bill|The bill]

The "Riviera." On 4 February 2025, with Netanyahu beside him, President Donald Trump said that "the U.S. will take over the Gaza Strip," that "we'll own it," and that it could become "the Riviera of the Middle East," and he proposed that its people be moved to other countries. Hamas called the remarks irresponsible; the Palestinian president, Mahmoud Abbas, rejected them; and Saudi Arabia restated its rejection of any displacement of Palestinians. [cite:gz_whyy_riviera]

The plan. At the end of September 2025 the White House published a twenty-point plan that became the basis of the October ceasefire, mediated by the United States with Qatar, Egypt and Turkey. [cite:gz_wiki_timeline2025] It placed Gaza under a "Board of Peace" chaired by Trump and including the former British prime minister Tony Blair, with a temporary, apolitical Palestinian committee to run services. Hamas's tunnels and weapons were to be destroyed under independent monitoring, and members who gave up their weapons pardoned. Israel's troops were to withdraw in stages as an International Stabilisation Force took over. "No resident will be forced to leave," it said, and once the Palestinian Authority had reformed, "conditions may finally exist for Palestinian self-determination and statehood." Netanyahu endorsed the plan. [cite:gz_gn_20points] On 3 October Hamas announced its "approval of releasing all occupation prisoners — both living and remains" and its readiness "to hand over the administration of the Gaza Strip to a Palestinian body of independents (technocrats)," while seeking to negotiate the details; it did not say whether it would disarm. [cite:gz_almon_hamas_plan]

A year later, as Part Seven records, the first stage's exchange of hostages and prisoners had been completed, though aid entered at about a third of the agreed rate, and the rest had not: no stabilisation force had deployed, and Israel held nearly two-thirds of the strip. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] Who decides Gaza's future, under the plan, is a board chaired by an American president; who decided its past three years is set out above.

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: The Plans for Gaza
chapters.intro: Part Ten turns from what has happened in Gaza to what is planned for it. Since early 2024, American and Israeli leaders have said in public what they want the strip to become, and since late 2025 those statements have taken the form of a board, a budget and a master plan. This part sets out what each of them has said, in their words and with their dates; what the plans contain; what they leave out, above all the more than two million people who live there; and who sits on the bodies that will decide.
chapters.outro: Part Ten set out the plans. In 2024 Jared Kushner called Gaza's waterfront "very valuable" and proposed to "move the people out"; in 2025 President Trump said the United States would "take over" and "own" Gaza, that its people would have no right to return, and posted a video of a golden "Trump Gaza." [cite:gz_jc_kushner2024] [cite:gz_whyy_riviera] [cite:gz_pbs_noreturn] [cite:gz_fortune_aivideo] Israel's government embraced "voluntary departure," planned a "humanitarian city" its own former prime minister called a concentration camp, and its finance minister spoke of a "real estate bonanza." [cite:gz_aj_netanyahu_feb25] [cite:gz_aj_humcity] [cite:gz_toi_bonanza] A prospectus offered $5,000 to leave. [cite:gz_bg_great] The Board of Peace, chaired for life by Trump with Kushner, Blair and Witkoff among its members and no Palestinians, presented a master plan of coastal towers; a year after the ceasefire, reconstruction had not begun. [cite:gz_mada_bop] [cite:gz_gpb_newgaza] [cite:gz_hrw_anniv] Part Eleven turns to how all of this reached, or did not reach, American audiences.

sections.h: What They Said They Want
sections.html:
"Waterfront property." In February 2024, four months into the war, Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and former senior adviser, spoke at Harvard. "Gaza's waterfront property could be very valuable," he said, "if people would focus on building up livelihoods." From Israel's perspective, he would "move the people out and then clean it up"; for the civilians, "I would just bulldoze something in the Negev"; and, he added, "I am not sure there is much left of Gaza at this point." [cite:gz_jc_kushner2024]

"We'll own it." A year later, on 4 February 2025, with Benjamin Netanyahu beside him at the White House, President Trump said that "the U.S. will take over the Gaza Strip," that "we'll own it," that it could become "the Riviera of the Middle East," and that its people should go to other countries; the aim, he said, was ending "the death and destruction." [cite:gz_whyy_riviera] Asked days later whether Palestinians would have the right to return, he said: "No, they wouldn't." He would build "safe communities, a little bit away from where they are, where all of this danger is." His press secretary and secretary of state had said any relocation would be temporary. "Think of it," he said, "as a real estate development for the future." [cite:gz_pbs_noreturn] On 26 February he posted on his own social network an AI-generated video titled "Trump Gaza": a giant gold statue of himself, yachts off the beach, dollar bills falling from the sky, Elon Musk dipping bread in hummus and Netanyahu drinking by a pool. [cite:gz_fortune_aivideo]

Israel's government. On 17 February 2025 Netanyahu said he was "committed to US President Trump's plan for the creation of a different Gaza," and his defence minister, Israel Katz, set up a body to oversee the "voluntary departure" of Gazans. [cite:gz_aj_netanyahu_feb25] In May Netanyahu called the plan "so revolutionary," summed it up as "Residents of Gaza who want to leave can leave," and made it one of his conditions for ending the war, alongside the return of the hostages and Hamas's disarmament and removal. [cite:gz_jweekly_may25] In July the government's plan for a "humanitarian city" on the ruins of Rafah, to hold 600,000 people at first and eventually the whole population, drew the former prime minister Ehud Olmert's verdict: "It is a concentration camp. I am sorry." The opposition leader Yair Lapid called it "a bad idea from every possible perspective"; the government said any transfer would be "voluntary." [cite:gz_aj_humcity] On 7 August Netanyahu said Israel intended to take control of all of Gaza, but "we don't want to keep" it: "We want to have a security perimeter. We don't want to govern it," and would hand it to Arab forces that would give Gazans "a good life." [cite:gz_mm_netanyahu_aug25] In September his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, told a real estate conference in Tel Aviv that Gaza was a "bonanza" that "pays for itself," that "we have to see how we are dividing up the land in percentages," and that a "business plan" was "on President Trump's desk." Netanyahu has said he does not intend to re-establish settlements in Gaza. [cite:gz_toi_bonanza]

The prospectus. On 31 August 2025 the Washington Post published a 38-page prospectus circulating in Washington, titled the Gaza Reconstitution, Economic Acceleration and Transformation Trust, the "GREAT Trust." It proposed an American-run trusteeship of at least ten years. Gaza's people would leave "voluntarily" or move into "restricted, secured zones" while the strip was rebuilt. Each person who left would receive $5,000 in cash, four years of rent subsidy and a year of food. Landowners would receive digital tokens redeemable for apartments in "AI-powered, smart cities." Its financial model counted $23,000 saved for every person who left, and a nearly fourfold return on $100 billion in ten years. It was drawn up by Israelis who had helped create the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, with financial modelling by a team then working at Boston Consulting Group, which said the work had not been approved and dismissed two senior partners. [cite:gz_bg_great]

The alternative. In March 2025 Arab leaders meeting in Cairo adopted an Egyptian plan to rebuild Gaza in under six years for about $53 billion, under a committee of Palestinian technocrats, so that its people could "stay on their land without displacement." The White House rejected it, saying it did not "address the reality that Gaza is currently uninhabitable"; Israel's foreign ministry called relocation an "opportunity for the Gazans to have free choice based on their free will." [cite:gz_nbc_arabplan]

None of these statements is in dispute; each is on the record in the speaker's own words. What they show, side by side, is a consistent subject. The land is described in the language of property, development and return on investment. The people who live on it appear as a cost to be relocated, or as beneficiaries of a choice to leave. Their stated reasons were security, the defeat of Hamas and a better life for Gazans who chose to go. In September 2025 the plan that became the basis of the ceasefire said: "No one will be forced to leave Gaza, and those who wish to leave will be free to do so and free to return," and "Israel will not occupy or annex Gaza." [cite:gz_almon_plantext] The next section sets out what was built on that promise.

sections.h: From Vision to Structure
sections.html:
Project Sunrise. In December 2025 the Wall Street Journal reported a plan drafted in about 45 days by a team led by Kushner and Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff, called Project Sunrise. It would cost more than $112 billion over a decade and turn the strip into a coastal hub of luxury beach resorts, high-speed rail and AI-powered infrastructure. The United States would anchor it with nearly $60 billion in grants and loan guarantees, and the plan was contingent on Hamas disarming fully and dismantling its tunnels. [cite:gz_tnnd_sunrise]

The Board of Peace. Trump announced the board on 15 January 2026, and its charter was signed at the World Economic Forum in Davos on 22 January. The UN Security Council had welcomed it in November 2025. Trump is its chairman for life, with power to choose his successor and to invite its members; a permanent seat costs a payment of $1 billion. On 19 February the United States pledged $10 billion and nine other members $7 billion. France, Norway, Sweden and Slovenia declined to join; Britain did not join. The EU's foreign policy chief noted that, unlike the Security Council resolution, its charter made no provision for Palestinians to have a say. [cite:gz_wiki_bop]

The master plan. At Davos, after the signing, Kushner presented a "New Gaza." "In the beginning, we were toying with a free zone, and then a Hamas zone," he said. "And then we said, you know what? Let's just plan for catastrophic success." [cite:gz_almon_newgaza] The plan gives the entire Mediterranean coastline to "coastal tourism," with 180 mixed-use towers. A "New Rafah" would hold more than 100,000 housing units. Industrial zones, the plan says, would create more than half a million jobs, and an airport, rail hub and port would be built in the south. The northern towns of Beit Lahia and Jabalia would become farmland, data centres and advanced manufacturing. People would live in four housing districts, separated by parks and industrial zones and linked by a few roads, which together cover less ground than housing did before the war. Rebuilding would begin only where Hamas had been disarmed, or where areas had been emptied and were under Israeli military control. "We've already started removing the rubble and doing some of the demolition," Kushner said. [cite:gz_gpb_newgaza] On the day he presented it, Israeli fire killed five Palestinians in Gaza; Israel's military did not immediately comment. [cite:gz_almon_newgaza]

What the plans leave out. Reporting on the master plan found no provision for the deeds to the land, for how new homes would be allocated to the people of Gaza, for where families in buildings marked for demolition would live, or evidence that Palestinians had been consulted; the slides shown at Davos did not address property rights or compensation. [cite:gz_gpb_newgaza] [cite:gz_almon_newgaza]

Where it stands, October 2026. A year after the ceasefire, Human Rights Watch reported that reconstruction had not begun. The Board of Peace presented a six-month recovery programme on 23 September 2026, to start "the moment funding and access allow." Ninety-four percent of Gaza's people lacked adequate shelter. The area behind the Yellow Line covered about 64 percent of the strip, a line Israeli officials had begun to call a "new border." [cite:gz_hrw_anniv] In its report to the Security Council in May 2026 the board blamed the lack of progress on Hamas's refusal to disarm. [cite:gz_wiki_bop] In July Hamas dissolved the body that had governed Gaza and offered to hand power to the Palestinian committee, which had stayed outside the strip, reportedly because of Israeli objections. [cite:gz_aj_hamas_dissolve] In August the board's High Representative, Nickolay Mladenov, told the Security Council that Hamas had accepted a disarmament agreement covering every category of weapon, which Hamas's spokesman disputed, saying it covered heavy weapons only; Mladenov argued that Israeli strikes were delaying demilitarisation, while Israeli officials said Hamas kept violating the ceasefire. [cite:gz_ih_mladenov] The six-month programme presented on 23 September costs $2.45 billion across 66 projects, and Mladenov said its progress hinged on disarmament. [cite:gz_pbs_245]

The record does not show which of these visions will be carried out, and some have been superseded. What it shows is who has been drawing up Gaza's future, the terms in which they have described it, and that the people who live there, more than two million of them, have had no seat at the table: no Palestinian sits on either board, and the Palestinian committee that answers to them had not been allowed into Gaza by October 2026.

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: What Americans Were Shown
chapters.intro: Part Eleven asks how the war reached American audiences, and why so much of what earlier parts record was seen by so few of them. It starts with access: who was allowed into Gaza to report, under what rules, and how many of the journalists who were there were killed. It then follows the coverage inside American newsrooms, through their own internal rules, independent measurements of what they published, and the ownership of one network, and ends with what Americans came to think. Where the record documents a cause, the part names it; where the cause is a question of motive, it gives the evidence and the outlets' own answers.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven followed the war to American audiences. Israel barred foreign journalists from entering Gaza independently, a ban its Supreme Court upheld in January 2024 and that remained in force in October 2026, and embedded reporters had their footage reviewed by Israeli commanders. [cite:gz_tna_fpa] [cite:gz_wlrn_ban] Gaza's own journalists were killed in greater numbers than in any war Costs of War has measured. [cite:gz_wiki_journalists] Inside American newsrooms, CNN routed coverage through its Jerusalem bureau and cautioned against Hamas statements, and the New York Times restricted words such as "genocide" and "occupied territory"; in the first six weeks, emotive language was reserved almost entirely for Israeli victims. [cite:gz_intercept_cnn] [cite:gz_nl_nytmemo] [cite:gz_aa_intercept] CBS passed to new owners who named Bari Weiss, known for pro-Israel positions, editor-in-chief. [cite:gz_aj_weiss] Opinion moved regardless: by 2026, for the first time in Gallup's annual measurement since 2001, Americans no longer sympathized more with the Israelis than with the Palestinians. [cite:gz_gallup_2026] [cite:gz_ap_gallup2026] Part Twelve closes the volume.

sections.h: Who Could Report, and Who Was Killed
sections.html:
The ban. From October 2023 Israel did not allow foreign journalists to enter Gaza independently. In January 2024 its Supreme Court upheld the ban on security grounds, accepting the state's argument that independent reporters could give away the positions of Israeli troops; the Foreign Press Association, which had petitioned the court, said the ban, then 95 days old, was "unprecedented." Almost all foreign reporters who entered went in embedded with the Israeli army, on the condition that its commanders reviewed their material and footage before publication. [cite:gz_tna_fpa] A second petition was still undecided in October 2026 after repeated postponements; Israel says independent entry is too dangerous, and three years into the war, with a ceasefire in place, the ban remained. [cite:gz_wlrn_ban]

The censor. Inside Israel, foreign correspondents work under the military censor. To receive a press card they sign an undertaking to abide by its rules, and during the war the censor restricted reporting on subjects including security cabinet meetings and information about the hostages. [cite:gz_intercept_cnn]

The journalists who were there. That left Gaza's own journalists, and they were killed in numbers without precedent. As of 24 September 2026 the Committee to Protect Journalists counted 189 Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza, and two more in Israeli detention, after a review in June 2026 removed names it found had engaged in combat; the UN counted 242 by August 2025. [cite:gz_cpj_2026] Brown University's Costs of War project found that more journalists had been killed in Gaza since October 2023 than in the American Civil War, both world wars, Korea, Vietnam, the Yugoslav wars and the war in Afghanistan combined. On 10 August 2025 an Israeli strike targeting Al Jazeera's correspondent Anas al-Sharif killed him outside al-Shifa hospital; on 25 August a strike on Nasser Hospital killed twenty people, five of them journalists, including a Reuters cameraman. Israel denies targeting journalists, and has said that some of those killed, al-Sharif among them, belonged to Hamas, often, according to NPR, without providing evidence. [cite:gz_wiki_journalists] [cite:gz_wlrn_ban]

The consequence is structural, and it is documented: the war was reported to the world by local journalists who were being killed at a historic rate, and by foreign reporters who could see it only from Israel or from inside Israeli army units, under rules that Israel set. Much of what Parts Six to Ten record reached the outside world through UN agencies, human rights groups and Palestinian reporters rather than through the correspondents of American networks.

sections.h: Inside American Newsrooms
sections.html:
CNN. CNN requires all reporting on Israel and Palestine, wherever its journalists are based, to be reviewed by its Jerusalem bureau before publication; the network says the policy reflects "many unique and complex local nuances that warrant extra scrutiny," and that it does not share copy with the censor in advance. A November 2023 directive from its standards department, citing Hamas's "inflammatory rhetoric and propaganda," warned: "We should be careful not to give it a platform." [cite:gz_intercept_cnn] In February 2024 The Guardian reported, from six CNN staffers and more than a dozen internal memos, that staff believed the rules led the network to take Israeli government statements at face value; one called the coverage "journalistic malpractice." CNN answered that its reporting "has confronted Israel's response to the attacks, including some of our most detailed and high-profile investigations." [cite:gz_an_cnnstaff]

The New York Times. An internal memo first issued in November 2023, reported by The Intercept in April 2024, told Times journalists to restrict the terms "genocide" and "ethnic cleansing," to avoid "occupied territory," to use "Palestine" only in rare cases, and not to describe areas historically settled by displaced Palestinians as "refugee camps." [cite:gz_nl_nytmemo] A Times spokesman, Charlie Stadtlander, said: "Issuing guidance like this to ensure accuracy, consistency and nuance in how we cover the news is standard practice." [cite:gz_dawn_nyt]

What was published. The Intercept analysed more than 1,100 articles in the New York Times, the Washington Post and the Los Angeles Times from the first six weeks of the war. For every Israeli killed, Israelis were mentioned eight times, a rate sixteen times higher per death than for Palestinians. The words "slaughter," "massacre" and "horrific" were used almost only for Israelis killed by Palestinians, and only two headlines in the whole sample mentioned the children of Gaza. [cite:gz_aa_intercept]

Ownership. In August 2025 Skydance, controlled by David Ellison, son of the Oracle founder Larry Ellison, completed its takeover of Paramount, owner of CBS, after promising the federal government greater "viewpoint diversity" at the network, according to the chairman of the FCC. In October Paramount bought The Free Press and made its founder, Bari Weiss, known for her pro-Israel positions, editor-in-chief of CBS News, reporting directly to David Ellison. The Free Press had published an article titled "The Gaza Famine Myth." [cite:gz_aj_weiss] The library's [scene:ell_s02|account of the Ellison architecture] sets out the family's documented ties. What the record documents here is ownership and appointment; whether owners direct particular coverage is a question of motive that these sources do not settle.

What Americans came to think. Despite all of this, opinion moved. In February 2026, for the first time in Gallup's annual measurement since 2001, Americans' sympathies no longer lay more with the Israelis: 41 percent sympathized more with the Palestinians and 36 percent with the Israelis, a gap Gallup said was not statistically significant; three years earlier the figures had been 31 and 54. [cite:gz_gallup_2026] About two-thirds of Democrats and half of Americans aged 18 to 34 now sympathized more with the Palestinians, while about seven in ten Republicans still sympathized more with Israel. [cite:gz_ap_gallup2026]

The record shows the mechanisms: an access ban, a military censor, newsroom rules, a measured imbalance in language, and changes of ownership. It does not show a single directing hand, and the outlets named here deny bias and point to their own investigations, several of which this volume cites, among them the New York Times's reporting on the "Jericho Wall" plan in Part Six. The gap between what happened in Gaza and what most Americans were shown is documented in the mechanisms themselves.

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: Settled, Contested and Open
chapters.intro: Part Twelve closes the volume. It gathers what the preceding eleven parts established, separates what the record settles from what it leaves contested, and names what was still undecided in October 2026. Nothing new is introduced here; each statement points back to the sources cited where it was first set out.
chapters.outro: This closes Gaza, Documented. Its twelve parts followed the strip from the war that made it in 1948 to the ceasefire of October 2025 and the year after.

sections.h: What the Record Settles
sections.html:
The strip was made by war. The Gaza Strip was the remainder of a Mandate district, about 1.3 percent of Palestine, left in Egyptian hands by the fighting of 1948 and fixed by the armistice of 1949. Its population was transformed within a year: about 80,000 residents were joined by more than 200,000 refugees from the towns and villages Israel took, and the camps built for them still stand. [cite:gz_wiki_subdistrict] [cite:gz_palquest_refugees]

It has been governed from outside for most of its history. Egypt administered it without annexing it until 1967; [cite:gz_wiki_history] Israel occupied it from 1967, took a census, put down an insurgency, built settlements and controlled who could work in Israel. [cite:gz_jvl_census67] [cite:gz_wiki_insurgency] [cite:gz_wiki_occupation] [cite:gz_carnegie_labor] Oslo brought a Palestinian Authority in 1994, while Israel kept the settlements and the crossings; in 2005 Israel removed its settlers and soldiers but kept control of its airspace, territorial waters, population registry and six of its seven land crossings. [cite:gz_wiki_gazajericho] [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement]

The closure was a system, and its effects were measured. From 2007 Israel and Egypt restricted goods, exports, people, fishing and farming; Israel said the closure was to stop weapons smuggling and rocket fire after Hamas took control. The UN recorded an economy shrinking while the West Bank's grew, 96 percent of the groundwater unfit to drink, from over-extraction and contamination, and 1.2 million people needing aid. [cite:gz_un_hostile2007] [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] [cite:gz_un_gaza10]

October 7 was a planned attack on civilians. Armed groups led by Hamas killed about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and took 251 hostages, in an attack in which, Human Rights Watch found, killing civilians and taking hostages were central aims, and whose plan Israel had held for more than a year and judged beyond Hamas's reach. Hamas said its fighters targeted only soldiers and armed people. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] [cite:gz_nyt_jericho] [cite:gz_aj_narrative]

The war that followed was the most destructive in the strip's history. By October 2026 the health ministry counted 74,382 Palestinians killed; about 81 percent of the strip's structures had been damaged; the IPC found famine in Gaza City in August 2025, a finding Israel rejected. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:gz_unosat2025] [cite:gz_aj_ipc] [cite:gz_olj_ipc]

sections.h: What Remains Contested
sections.html:
On several questions the record holds two documented positions, each sourced, and the volume has set them side by side without deciding between them. They are gathered here.

Some disputes are of a different kind: not between two positions, but between counts. The dead of the wars since 2008 were counted differently by Palestinian, Israeli and UN bodies, above all on how many had been fighting; the volume has given each count with its source. [cite:gz_wiki_castlead] [cite:gz_wiki_2014] [cite:gz_aj_83pct] [cite:gz_aj_lancet] And some questions about October 7 itself, how many Israelis were killed by Israeli fire, what the state knew and when, remain without the state commission of inquiry that would answer them. [cite:gz_idf_beeri_probe] [cite:gz_toi_hannibal] [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026]

sections.h: What Is Still Open
sections.html:
As of October 2026, the following were undecided.

The ceasefire's second stage. Hamas's disarmament, the deployment of an international stabilisation force and the further withdrawal of Israeli troops, all set out in the plan of September 2025, had not happened; Israel held nearly two-thirds of the strip, and, by the health ministry's count, 1,493 Palestinians were killed in the ceasefire's first year. [cite:gz_gn_20points] [cite:gz_aj_year2026]

Who governs Gaza. The plan places a Palestinian technocratic committee under a board chaired by the American president, until the Palestinian Authority reforms, an arrangement the Security Council authorized. [cite:gz_gn_20points] [cite:gz_wiki_timeline2025]

Whose plan. Plans for Gaza's future, from the GREAT Trust prospectus to Project Sunrise and the Board of Peace's master plan, were drawn up by American and Israeli teams, with no Palestinian on either board and no published evidence that Palestinians were consulted. In February 2025 the American president said Gaza's people would have no right to return; his September 2025 plan says no one will be forced to leave and those who leave will be free to return. None had been carried out by October 2026. [cite:gz_bg_great] [cite:gz_gpb_newgaza] [cite:gz_mada_bop] [cite:gz_pbs_noreturn] [cite:gz_almon_plantext] [cite:gz_hrw_anniv]

Who pays. Rebuilding is estimated to need $71.4 billion over ten years. [cite:gz_rdna2026]

The courts. The ICJ genocide case runs to written pleadings due in 2029; the ICC warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant stand, with Israel's challenge to the court's jurisdiction pending as of late 2025. [cite:gz_icj_timelimits] [cite:gz_toi_icc2025]

Accountability in Israel. No state commission of inquiry into October 7 has been set up. [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026]

The volume ends where the record does. Gaza's history since 1948 has been decided mostly by others, from Cairo, Jerusalem and Washington, and by the armed movement that governed it from 2007; its people have lived inside the consequences. What the record documents, it has stated; where it divides, both sides are given; what is still to be decided is named above.

books.title: The West Bank, Documented
books.subtitle: Settlements, Separation and Expansion, 1947–2026
books.intro:
This volume follows the West Bank, the hill country west of the Jordan River, about 5,655 square kilometres, from the partition plan of 1947 to October 2026. It asks what happened to the land and to the people on it: who governed them, how the land passed from Palestinian to Israeli control acre by acre, how movement, law and surveillance were organized around that change, and what the law says about it and why it has not been enforced.

It begins with the plan that assigned this hill country to an Arab state that was never created, and with the war of 1948 that left it in Jordan's hands. It follows nineteen years of Jordanian rule; the occupation of 1967 and the first settlements; the settlement enterprise that grew from them; the map drawn at Oslo, which divided the territory into Areas A, B and C; the barrier, the roads and the checkpoints that divided the Palestinian towns from one another; the two legal systems and the surveillance that govern daily life; the demolitions, the evictions and the settler violence through which communities have been displaced; and the years since October 2023. Four parts then step back: to the law and the reasons it has not been enforced; to the split between Fatah's West Bank and Hamas's Gaza; to the money; and to what is settled, contested and open.

Israel's stated reasons, security above all, are given beside each policy, and where the record divides, both sides are given. It describes the acts of governments, armies, settler organizations and armed groups, not the character of peoples. Its companion is Gaza, Documented, and the two volumes are written to be read together.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Hill Country and the Partition
chapters.intro: Part One covers the two years in which the West Bank was made. It begins with the United Nations plan of November 1947, which assigned the hill country of Samaria and Judea to an Arab state, and sets out what each of the planned states was to receive, by land, by population and by kind of land. It follows the war that began the next day and ended with the hill country in Jordanian hands and much of the rest of the planned Arab state inside Israel, and it ends with the armistice line of 1949, the line now called the Green Line.
chapters.outro: Part One followed the making of the West Bank. The 1947 plan gave the proposed Arab state the hill country of Samaria and Judea and gave the Jewish state, about 56 percent of the land, most of the Negev desert, the Jezreel Valley and most of the coastal plain, when Jews owned about 6.6 percent of Palestine. [cite:wb_ej_partition] [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] [cite:wb_wiki_landpurchase] The war that followed left Israel holding about 78 percent of the Mandate, including towns such as Lydda and Ramle that the plan had assigned to the Arab state, whose people were driven east. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] Jordan's Arab Legion held the hills, as its king had told the Zionist leaders he would, and the armistice of April 1949 drew the Green Line around them.
