[cite:wb_ahram_unga2024] The twelve months ended in September 2025. Part Nine set out what happened in them: record settlement approvals and E1. [scene:wb9_annex|Since October 2023]

The International Criminal Court. Palestine joined the Court in 2015, and on 3 March 2021 the prosecutor opened an investigation into the situation in Palestine. Israel, which, like the United States, is not a party to the Court's statute, said it does not recognize the Court's authority. [cite:wb_aj_icc_timeline] In November 2024 the Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defense minister, Yoav Gallant, over the war in Gaza. [cite:gz_un_icc] In February 2025 President Trump declared a national emergency over the Court, saying neither the United States nor Israel is subject to it, and sanctioned its officials; four of its judges were sanctioned in June 2025, and in June 2026 three judges sued in the federal court in Manhattan; no ruling had been reported as of that month. [cite:wb_hrw_iccjudges] [cite:wb_jurist_iccsuit]

Why None of It Is Enforced

The record does not show inaction. It shows rulings and resolutions, each of which stopped at a specific point. The table sets out each one, what it asked, and where it stopped.

Three mechanisms run through the table. The World Court's opinions on this question were advisory opinions, not judgments in a case between states. [cite:wb_asil_icj2004] [cite:wb_livelaw_icj2024] The General Assembly's resolutions are not binding. [cite:wb_ahram_unga2024] And the bodies that can bind or punish, the Security Council and national governments, depend on the positions of states, above all the United States, whose positions have changed with each administration, as the timeline above shows. Israel's answer, consistently, has been that the territory is not occupied in law and that the settlements are lawful, and it has said so to each body that ruled otherwise. [cite:wb_wiki_levy] [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024]

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: The Split: Fatah's West Bank, Hamas's Gaza
chapters.intro: Part Eleven turns to the division of the Palestinian territories between two rival governments: the Palestinian Authority, led by Fatah, in the West Bank, and Hamas in Gaza. It sets out how the split happened, why it has never been healed, and why no Palestinian election has been held since 2006. It then takes up an argument made by many critics of Israeli policy: that the division served Israel, by keeping one territory at war and the other, where settlement advanced, under a weakened authority. This part sets out the statements and actions of Israeli leaders that support that argument, the counter-arguments and Israel's stated reasons, and the limits of what the record can show about intent.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven followed the split. Hamas won the 2006 election, took Gaza by force in 2007, and Fatah and Hamas have since signed and abandoned agreement after agreement; no Palestinian election has been held since 2006, and Abbas cancelled the one called for 2021. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] [cite:wb_medialine_agreements] [cite:wb_gpb_elections2021] The Palestinian Authority coordinates security with Israel in a West Bank that Israel also occupies. [cite:wb_fp_coordination] Israeli leaders have described the division as useful: Smotrich called Hamas "an asset" in 2015, Netanyahu let Qatari cash reach Gaza and refused to hand it to "Fatahstan," and the Authority's revenues were withheld. [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich] [cite:gz_week_qatar] [cite:wb_jns_fatahstan] [cite:wb_ynet_smotrich2024] Whether that was a strategy is argued from those statements; Netanyahu denies it. Part Twelve follows the money.

sections.h: How the Split Happened
sections.html:
In January 2006 Hamas won the Palestinian legislative election, judged free and fair by international observers, and formed a government in March. Donors imposed sanctions, Israel withheld the tax revenues it collects for the Palestinian Authority, and the Quartet stopped aid to a Hamas-led government. In February 2007 Fatah and Hamas signed the Mecca Agreement and formed a unity government; in June 2007 fighting between them ended with Hamas in control of Gaza, and President Mahmoud Abbas dissolved the government. From then on there were two Palestinian administrations: Fatah's in Ramallah, Hamas's in Gaza. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] Gaza, Documented sets out the takeover and the blockade that followed. [scene:gz4_takeover|The takeover]

The record assigns the failures to both factions. The Media Line, reviewing the agreements, describes the 2007 seizure of Gaza as a Hamas coup, and says the later agreements foundered on mutual accusations. [cite:wb_medialine_agreements]

No Elections Since 2006

The legislature elected in 2006 has not been renewed. Elections were finally called for May and July 2021. On 29 April 2021, two days before campaigning was to begin, Abbas postponed them indefinitely, saying "We will not move to hold elections without Jerusalem," because Israel would not commit to allowing Palestinians in East Jerusalem to vote. Critics, including Palestinian officials, said the real reason was that Fatah had split into rival lists and Hamas was likely to win the most seats. The United States and Israel, wary of Hamas's participation, did not press for the vote. [cite:wb_gpb_elections2021]

Security Coordination

Under the Oslo arrangements the Palestinian Authority's security forces share information with Israel and act to prevent attacks on Israelis, soldiers and civilians alike. Abbas has called the coordination "sacred." It is deeply unpopular among Palestinians, many of whom see it as collaboration with the occupation. After an Israeli raid on Jenin camp killed ten people in January 2023, Abbas announced its suspension, and then quietly assured US officials that intelligence-sharing would continue. [cite:wb_fp_coordination] The result, in the West Bank, is an authority that polices its own population in coordination with the army that occupies it, while holding no election and, as Part Twelve shows, depending on revenues that Israel collects and can withhold.

sections.h: "Hamas Is an Asset"
sections.html:
The argument that the split served Israel rests on statements by Israeli leaders and on documented policy. Four items carry most of the weight.

Smotrich, 2015. In a 2015 interview Bezalel Smotrich, later finance minister and the minister in charge of settlement administration, [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis] said: "The Palestinian Authority is a burden, and Hamas is an asset." He explained that the Authority harmed Israel in international forums, while Hamas, designated a terrorist organization, would never be recognized, given standing at the International Criminal Court, or able to table a Security Council resolution. [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich]

The Qatari money. From 2018 Israel allowed Qatar to bring cash into Gaza, much of it for the salaries of the Hamas government's officials. Netanyahu called it "the right step" to restore quiet and avert a humanitarian crisis; Naftali Bennett compared it to "protection money." [cite:gz_ds_qatar2018] The New York Times reported in December 2023, from more than two dozen officials, that Netanyahu had "not only tolerated" the payments but encouraged them. Netanyahu has said the payments were to avoid a humanitarian collapse and called the idea that he wanted to build up Hamas "a big lie." [cite:gz_week_qatar] Gaza, Documented sets out the money in full. [scene:gz8_cash|The Qatari cash]

The 2019 remark. A line widely attributed to Netanyahu, that anyone who wanted to prevent a Palestinian state should support strengthening Hamas, was first reported by the Jerusalem Post from an unnamed Knesset member paraphrasing his remarks to his party's lawmakers in March 2019. The reporter has said it concerned letting money and aid into Gaza and has been "rewritten and twisted" online. [cite:gz_week_qatar] [cite:gz_harkov_2019] It is a paraphrase, not a recorded quotation.

"Fatahstan." After 7 October 2023 Netanyahu rejected an American request that the Palestinian Authority take over Gaza, saying: "I will not replace Hamastan with Fatahstan." [cite:wb_jns_fatahstan] In 2024 Smotrich withheld the Authority's tax revenues, about 70 percent of its budget. Israeli security officials, speaking anonymously, warned that it was weakening the Authority and could lead to violence; Smotrich's office answered that the Authority "promotes terror, pays for terror and acts against Israel in the international arena." [cite:wb_ynet_smotrich2024] His 2017 "Decisive Plan" had proposed filling the West Bank with settlements and leaving Palestinians, in the journalist Ron Ben-Yishai's summary, "a life of subjugation under Israeli rule, emigration, or a shahid [martyr] death." [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich]

What the Record Shows, and What It Cannot

The record shows that the split was made by the two rival factions, Fatah and Hamas, in the fighting of June 2007 and in a decade and a half of failed reconciliation, and that President Abbas postponed the 2021 elections. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] [cite:wb_medialine_agreements] [cite:wb_gpb_elections2021] It also shows that, once it existed, senior Israeli figures described it as useful, that Israeli governments let money reach Hamas while withholding money from the Authority, and that settlement approvals reached records in 2023–2025, the years of the Gaza war. [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich] [cite:gz_week_qatar] [cite:wb_ynet_smotrich2024] [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis] Whether that amounted to a deliberate strategy of division is a question about intent. Some officials' own words support it; Netanyahu denies it, and the documents that would settle it, if they exist, have not been published. The volume leaves it there: the statements and the outcomes are documented; the strategy is argued.

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: The Money
chapters.intro: Part Twelve follows the money. Two flows run through the West Bank. The first is the Palestinian Authority's: most of its revenue is collected for it by Israel, under an economic agreement of 1994, and Israel can, and does, withhold it. The second is the settlements': state budgets, security money for outposts, roads, private donations from abroad and the businesses that supply them. This part sets out both, with Israel's stated reasons for its decisions and the dates on which the figures were counted.
chapters.outro: Part Twelve followed the money. Israel collects about two-thirds of the Palestinian Authority's revenue under the 1994 Paris Protocol, and has deducted from it the Authority's payments to prisoners' families, which it says encourage violence, and withheld it after political disputes; since June 2025 it has withheld all of it, and the Authority was paying half salaries in 2026. [cite:wb_shabaka_clearance] [cite:wb_aj_payslaw2018] [cite:wb_mas_jun2026] The World Bank estimated in 2013 that the restrictions on Area C cost the Palestinian economy $3.4 billion a year. [cite:wb_toi_wb_areac] Settlement, meanwhile, is funded by ministry budgets, security money for outposts, new roads, American tax-deductible donations and businesses that the UN lists by name. [cite:wb_pn_budget2026] [cite:wb_toi_220m] [cite:wb_un_database2025] Part Thirteen sets out what is settled, contested and open.

sections.h: Revenue Collected by Someone Else
sections.html:
The Paris Protocol. The economic agreement signed at Paris in 1994, as part of the Oslo arrangements, left the West Bank and Gaza inside Israel's customs system. Israel collects the tariffs, purchase taxes and import VAT on goods bound for the Palestinian territories and transfers them, minus deductions, to the Palestinian Authority. These "clearance revenues" make up about two-thirds of the Authority's public revenue. [cite:wb_shabaka_clearance] [cite:wb_mas_jun2026]

The withholdings. Israel has suspended the transfers before: after Hamas won the 2006 election, in December 2012 after Palestine gained upgraded status at the UN, and in 2015 after it joined the International Criminal Court. [cite:wb_shabaka_clearance] In July 2018 the Knesset voted, 87 to 15, to deduct from the transfers the amount the Authority pays to Palestinian prisoners and the families of those killed by Israeli forces, about $330 million that year, supporting some 35,000 families. Israel's case is that the payments reward and encourage violence; the Palestinian official Hanan Ashrawi called the deduction "highway robbery." [cite:wb_aj_payslaw2018] Those deductions came to 3.54 billion shekels between 2019 and mid-2024. [cite:wb_shabaka_clearance]

After 7 October 2023 the security cabinet withheld the part of the revenue the Authority spent in Gaza, to prevent payments reaching Hamas; Norway agreed to hold that share in an account of its own so that the rest could flow. Norway's prime minister said the money was "necessary to ensure that the Palestinian Authority does not collapse." [cite:wb_norway_2024] On 10 June 2025, hours after Britain, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Norway sanctioned him and Itamar Ben-Gvir for incitement, Smotrich moved to cut the Palestinian banks' links to Israeli banks, citing the Authority's "delegitimisation campaign against the State of Israel internationally." [cite:wb_aj_bankwaiver2025] From that month Israel withheld the transfers entirely. [cite:wb_mas_jun2026]

By the Palestine Economic Policy Research Institute's count, Israel withheld 11.7 billion shekels and deducted another 12.5 billion between January 2021 and March 2026, together 44 percent of the clearance revenue due. In June 2026 the Authority paid half of its public servants' February salaries. By March 2026 its arrears and public debt together reached about $12.4 billion, 72 percent of the 2025 economy. [cite:wb_mas_jun2026] Part Eleven set out the Israeli statements on both sides of the question of whether the Authority should survive. [scene:wb11_asset|"Hamas is an asset"]

The Cost of Area C

In 2013 the World Bank estimated that if Palestinians could use the land and resources of Area C, the Palestinian economy could gain $3.4 billion a year, about 35 percent of its 2011 output, and the Authority's deficit could be halved. Israel's Foreign Ministry answered that the issues belonged in negotiations, that Palestinian economic development was in Israel's strategic interest, and that Israel had approved more than 300 projects in Area C in the previous two years. [cite:wb_toi_wb_areac]

sections.h: Who Pays for Settlement
sections.html:
The state. Settlement is financed through several lines of Israel's budget. Peace Now's reading of the government's July 2026 budget requests found 335.4 million shekels for the Ministry of Settlements, 294.5 million of a defense emergency line earmarked for settlements, and 125 million for security roads, part of 550 million approved in January 2026 for 2026 and 2027; more than 220 kilometres of new roads had opened in 2024 and 2025. The farms and outposts described in Part Eight, which are unauthorized under Israeli law, received 103 million shekels from 2023 to 2025 for "security components" such as vehicles, drones, cameras, gates and fences; the legal basis given is that this is security equipment, not permanent construction. [cite:wb_pn_budget2026] [scene:wb8_settlers|The herding outposts]

American donors. A Haaretz investigation in 2015 found that about fifty American organizations had raised $281 million between 2009 and 2013 and sent $224 million of it to settlements through Israeli nonprofits, as tax-deductible gifts. The money paid for property and amenities, and some of it, through the group Honenu, supported the families of Jews convicted of terrorism, among them the family of Ami Popper, who killed seven Palestinian labourers in 1990. A White House official said the administration had "never defended or supported any activity associated with the settlements." [cite:wb_toi_220m]

Businesses. In September 2025 the UN Human Rights Office updated its database of businesses involved in settlement activities to 158 companies from eleven countries, most of them Israeli, others based in the United States, Britain, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Spain, Portugal, Luxembourg, Canada and China. The listed activities include supplying equipment and materials for settlement construction, demolishing Palestinian property, surveillance, and the use of natural resources. [cite:wb_un_database2025]

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: Settled, Contested and Open
chapters.intro: Part Thirteen closes the volume. It gathers what the preceding twelve parts established, separates what the record settles from what it leaves contested, and names what was still undecided in October 2026. Nothing new is introduced here; each statement points back to the sources cited where it was first set out.
chapters.outro: This closes The West Bank, Documented. Its thirteen parts followed the hill country from the partition plan of 1947 to October 2026.

sections.h: What the Record Settles
sections.html:
The West Bank was meant for an Arab state that was never created. The 1947 plan assigned the hill country to an Arab state; the war of 1948 left it in Jordan's hands, and the armistice of 1949 drew the Green Line around it. Jordan annexed it in 1950, recognized by almost no other state, and made its people Jordanian citizens. [cite:wb_ej_partition] [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text] [cite:wb_wiki_annex] [cite:wb_palquest_nationality]

Settlement was a decision of Israel's governments, begun in 1967 against the advice of the Foreign Ministry's own legal adviser. In 1967 Israel's Foreign Ministry legal adviser warned that civilian settlement would breach the Fourth Geneva Convention; the cabinet approved Kfar Etzion the same month, presented as a military outpost. [cite:wb_gorenberg_meron] Later governments declared hundreds of thousands of dunams state land, drew Oslo's map with 60 percent of the territory left under Israeli control, and, since 2022, moved civil powers in Area C from the army to a minister responsible for settlement. [cite:wb_wiki_stateland] [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas] [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis]

Two populations live under two systems. Settlers live under Israeli law and civilian courts; Palestinians under military orders and military courts, which convicted in 99.74 percent of cases in 2010. Israel's Justice Ministry did not dispute the description and defended it on security grounds. [cite:wb_acri_twosys] [cite:wb_972_conviction]

Palestinians build under a system that seldom lets them. As of 2021, less than one percent of Area C had been planned for Palestinian use, and in 2025 Israel demolished 1,657 Palestinian structures, 93 percent for lack of a permit. [cite:wb_ocha_areac] [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025]

Settler violence rose, and is seldom prosecuted. The UN counted 1,828 settler attacks causing casualties or damage in 2025; Yesh Din found 93.6 percent of the police files it followed closed without indictment; by Kerem Navot's count, 57 Palestinian communities were emptied or partly emptied between October 2023 and December 2024. Israel's leaders have condemned the attacks as the work of a minority. [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025] [cite:wb_yeshdin_2025] [cite:wb_972_villages] [cite:wb_toi_netanyahu2025]

The international bodies that have ruled found the settlements unlawful, and none of the rulings has been enforced. The Security Council in 2016, the International Court of Justice in 2004 and 2024, and the General Assembly in 2024; Israel rejects each, and each stopped at a documented point. [cite:wb_wiki_2334] [cite:wb_asil_icj2004] [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] [cite:wb_ahram_unga2024] [scene:wb10_rulings|The rulings, and where each stopped]

sections.h: What Remains Contested
sections.html:
On several questions the record holds two documented positions, each sourced, and the volume has set them side by side without deciding between them.

Some of these questions are legal and will be argued in courts; some are questions of intent, which the published record does not settle. The volume has given the documented statements on both sides and left the judgment to the reader.

sections.h: What Is Still Open
sections.html:
As of October 2026, the following were undecided.

Annexation. The Knesset voted for annexation in principle in July 2025, and a sovereignty bill passed a preliminary reading in October 2025; no law has been enacted, and the US President has said it "won't happen." [cite:wb_toi_71_13] [cite:wb_toi_trump_annex] Meanwhile the cabinet approved 34 more settlements in March 2026, and in February 2026 extended Israeli powers into Areas A and B. [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis]

E1. The 3,401 homes approved in August 2025 would divide the West Bank in two. [cite:wb_itv_e1]

The northern camps. More than 33,000 people displaced from Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams had not been allowed back as of July 2026. [cite:wb_jurist_ohchr2026]

Khan al-Ahmar and Sheikh Jarrah. On 20 May 2026 Smotrich said he would sign an evacuation order for Khan al-Ahmar, which would still need cabinet approval; the Diab family's eviction was frozen by the Supreme Court in November 2025 pending appeal. [cite:wb_newarab_khan2026] [cite:wb_amnesty_diab2025]

The Palestinian Authority. With all transfers withheld since June 2025 and half salaries being paid, whether the Authority can keep functioning is open. [cite:wb_mas_jun2026] No Palestinian election has been held since 2006. [cite:wb_gpb_elections2021]

The courts. The ICC's investigation continues under US sanctions on its officials, which its judges were challenging in a US court; no ruling had been reported as of June 2026. [cite:wb_aj_icc_timeline] [cite:wb_jurist_iccsuit]

Israel's account of the same architecture is that each element answers a security need or a legal right: the barrier and checkpoints against attacks, military courts in a territory it does not regard as occupied, building rules applied under the Oslo agreements, and settlement on land to which the Jewish people have a historical claim. [cite:wb_asil_icj2004] [cite:wb_cow_israelview] [cite:wb_cogat_2015] [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] The volume has set out both accounts, and the record beneath them.

books.title: PRESS
books.subtitle: The Dead of Gaza and the West Bank, and the Journalists Killed Counting Them
books.intro:
This book is about two kinds of people. The first are the dead of Gaza and the West Bank since October 2023: by the count of Gaza's health ministry, 74,382 people in Gaza alone by October 2026, with thousands more under the rubble and, by independent estimates, tens of thousands more who were never counted. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:pr_almon_survey2026] The second are the people who tried to count them and to tell the world: the journalists, most of them Palestinians from Gaza itself, who reported the war from inside it, because Israel did not allow foreign reporters in independently, saying it was too dangerous. [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] By the count of the International Federation of Journalists, at least 241 journalists and media workers were killed in Gaza by July 2026; the Committee to Protect Journalists, which removed from its list people its research found had taken part in combat, counted 189 Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza as of 24 September 2026. Israel denies deliberately targeting journalists and says some of those killed were members of armed groups. [cite:pr_wiki_killing] [cite:gz_cpj_2026] [cite:gz_wlrn_ban]

The book sets out the record of both. It begins with how the dead are counted and why the counts differ; then the children, the women and the unborn, and the hunger. It turns to the journalists: how many were killed and by whose count, who they were, what Israel said about each, and what investigations found; the gate that kept foreign reporters out; the press of the West Bank; the organizations that keep reporting with no power, no money and no protection; and what of all this reached American readers. Where Israel disputes a count or says a journalist was a combatant, its position and the evidence it gave are set beside the record. The numbers in this book are the record the journalists were trying to deliver.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Count
chapters.intro: Part One asks the first question of the book: how many people have been killed in Gaza, and how anyone knows. It sets out how Gaza's health ministry builds its count, name by name; how independent researchers have tested it; what Israel has said about it, including its own military's estimate; and the people the count does not include: the missing under the rubble, those who died of hunger and disease, and the deaths that independent surveys say were never recorded.
chapters.outro: Part One set out the count. Gaza's health ministry recorded 74,382 deaths by October 2026, most of them with names and ID numbers; an independent check of its early lists found them largely reliable, and in January 2026 an Israeli military official put the toll at about 70,000, before the army said that did not reflect official data. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:pr_airwars_lists] [cite:pr_toi_idf70k] [cite:pr_newarab_iddeny] Independent surveys found the count too low: about 75,200 violent deaths in the first fifteen months against about 49,000 recorded, and about 16,300 more from indirect causes; about 10,000 people remain under the rubble. [cite:pr_almon_survey2026] [cite:pr_aj_rubble2026] How many were fighters is disputed: 8,900 named in an Israeli database, or 22,000 by the army's estimate. [cite:pr_aj_83pct] [cite:pr_toi_idf70k] Part Two turns to the children.

sections.h: Name by Name
sections.html:
How the ministry counts. Gaza's health ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, records deaths reported by hospitals and health workers, and matches them where it can to the national ID numbers of the dead. In October 2023, after President Biden said he had "no confidence" in its figures, it began publishing the names of everyone it said had been killed. It does not record whether the dead were civilians or fighters. [cite:pr_walrus_counters] By January 2026, according to the Times of Israel, its records included names and ID numbers for more than 90 percent of the bodies. [cite:pr_toi_idf70k] As of 12 October 2026 its count stood at 74,382 killed since October 2023, 1,493 of them after the ceasefire of October 2025. [cite:gz_aj_year2026]

Testing the lists. Airwars, a British group that monitors civilian harm in war, checked the ministry's first list against its own open-source archive of the war's first seventeen days. Of 2,993 civilians it had identified by full name, 2,236, three in four, appeared on the ministry's list. It judged the early recording "largely reliable" for that period, and noted that later recording became harder as hospitals stopped functioning. [cite:pr_airwars_lists] The statistician Michael Spagat said the figures up to 26 October 2023 were much more reliable than those since, as hospitals were destroyed. [cite:pr_walrus_counters]

What Israel Says

Through most of the war Israel's government rejected the ministry's figures as the product of a Hamas-run body. In January 2026 a senior Israeli military official told reporters, anonymously, that the army believed about 70,000 Gazans had been killed, close to the ministry's count of 71,667 at the time, and that the share who were fighters was still under review. The army had said before the ceasefire that it had killed at least 22,000 combatants, and its officials had put the ratio at two to three civilians for each fighter. [cite:pr_toi_idf70k] [cite:pr_jw_idf71k] The next day the army's spokesman, Nadav Shoshani, said reports that the army had accepted the toll "do not reflect official data." [cite:pr_newarab_iddeny]

sections.h: The Uncounted
sections.html:
Under the rubble. In April 2026, six months into the ceasefire, about 10,000 people were missing in Gaza, believed buried under collapsed buildings. Authorities had recovered 759 bodies from the rubble; heavy machinery had not been let in, and the UN estimated more than 61 million tonnes of rubble. [cite:pr_aj_rubble2026] The missing are not in the ministry's count of the dead. [cite:pr_toi_idf70k]

The surveys. Two independent studies, published in The Lancet's journals, found the ministry's count too low, not too high. The first, using a statistical method that compares overlapping lists, estimated 64,260 deaths from traumatic injury by the end of June 2024, against the ministry's 37,877 at the time, an undercount of 41 percent. [cite:gz_aj_lancet] The second, led by Spagat and published in February 2026, was the first independent household survey of mortality in Gaza: interviewers visited 2,000 households from 30 December 2024. It estimated about 75,200 violent deaths in the war's first fifteen months, when the ministry had counted about 49,000, and about 16,300 more deaths from disease, untreated illness and other indirect causes. By January 2025, it found, three to four percent of Gaza's people had been killed by violence. [cite:pr_almon_survey2026] [cite:pr_ctv_survey2026]

According to Reuters, the study contradicts claims that the ministry inflates its figures and suggests its numbers are, if anything, conservative. [cite:pr_almon_survey2026]

Civilians and Fighters

The ministry's count does not say how many of the dead were fighters, and here the record holds two readings. In August 2025 the Guardian, with the Israeli outlets +972 Magazine and Local Call, reported that a classified Israeli military database listed 8,900 named Hamas and Islamic Jihad fighters as confirmed or "probably" dead by May 2025, when the ministry counted at least 53,000 dead, implying that about 83 percent of the dead were civilians. The army said the figures were "incorrect." [cite:pr_aj_83pct] Sharon Levy of HonestReporting, a pro-Israel media-monitoring group, answered that the database lists only fighters the army has confirmed by name, that unidentified fighters were counted as civilians, and that the army's estimate of 22,000 combatants killed, set against the ministry's then total of 62,000, gives about two civilians for each fighter. [cite:pr_alg_83critique]

Both readings put civilians at a majority of the dead. The ministry's count, the army's estimate and the household survey differ in size, but none of them is small. The rest of this book follows the people inside these numbers.

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: The Children
chapters.intro: Part Two turns to the children. It sets out how many were killed and injured in Gaza, by the UN's count, broken down by age down to infants under one year old; how that share compares with earlier wars; what the UN's commission of inquiry concluded and how Israel answered; the children of the West Bank and the Israeli children killed and taken on 7 October; and the children who survived: the amputees, the orphans, and those killed after the ceasefire.
chapters.outro: Part Two set out the children. The UN commission counted at least 20,179 children killed in Gaza in two years, 1,029 of them infants, and 44,143 injured; children were 30 percent of the dead. [cite:pr_nw_coi2026] It found grounds to conclude that children were targeted as part of a deliberate strategy, which Israel called a "libelous sham" that ignored Hamas's tactics. [cite:pr_un_coi2026] [cite:pr_nw_coi2026] Forty Israeli children were killed on 7 October, and children were taken hostage; 213 Palestinian children were killed in the West Bank in two years. [cite:pr_un_coi2026] [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] Thousands of children lost limbs, tens of thousands lost parents, and after the ceasefire children were still killed at about one a day. [cite:pr_newarab_amput] [cite:pr_aj_orphans2025] [cite:pr_unicefusa_2026] Part Three turns to women, mothers and the unborn.

sections.h: Twenty Thousand
sections.html:
In June 2026 the UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry reported that at least 20,179 children had been killed in Gaza between 7 October 2023 and 7 October 2025, and 44,143 injured. Of the dead, 5,031 were under five years old, and 1,029 were under one. Children were 30 percent of all those killed, against about 24 percent in the wars of 2008–2009 and 2014, and about two percent of all the children in Gaza had been killed. Save the Children estimated that another 5,160 children were buried under the rubble, not yet counted. [cite:pr_nw_coi2026]

The commission's finding. The commission concluded that there were "reasonable grounds" to find that these acts formed part of "a deliberate strategy to destroy the future of the Palestinians in Gaza by targeting their children." It listed the army units it believed responsible for specific killings, and said Israel had not answered any of its thirteen requests for information or access. [cite:pr_un_coi2026]

Israel's answer. Israel's mission in Geneva called the report a "libelous sham" that ignored "the brutal tactics of Hamas," and said it omitted Israel's part in vaccination campaigns and field hospitals; Israel's foreign ministry said the commission was "a fundamentally flawed mechanism" without "any credible verification mechanism for its claims." [cite:pr_nw_coi2026]

The Other Children

The same commission had found that 40 Israeli children were killed on 7 October 2023, hundreds were injured, and children were taken hostage, several of them alone; it attributed war crimes and crimes against humanity against them to Hamas and other armed groups. [cite:pr_un_coi2026] In the West Bank, the UN Human Rights Office counted 213 Palestinian children among the 1,001 Palestinians killed there by Israeli forces and settlers in the two years to 17 October 2025. [cite:wb_ohchr_1001]

sections.h: The Children Who Lived
sections.html:
Amputees. By the end of 2024 Gaza's hospitals had recorded 4,500 amputations, about 800 of them on children. [cite:pr_newarab_amput] The UN commission found in 2026 that Gaza "now has the highest concentration of child amputees in the world." [cite:pr_un_coi2026]

Orphans. In April 2025 the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics counted 39,384 children in Gaza who had lost one or both parents, about 17,000 of them both. [cite:pr_aj_orphans2025]

After the ceasefire. The ceasefire of October 2025 did not end the killing of children. UNICEF reported that at least 300 were killed in its first 300 days. "A ceasefire that leaves an average of one child dead each and every day is failing children," said its regional director, Edouard Beigbeder, in August 2026. [cite:pr_unicefusa_2026]

These were the stories Gaza's journalists filed day after day: the child pulled from the rubble, the ward of amputees, the family with no parents left. Part Three turns to the women.

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: Women, Mothers and the Unborn
chapters.intro: Part Three turns to the women of Gaza: those killed and maimed, the mothers who gave birth without hospitals, and the pregnancies lost. It sets out the counts kept by UN agencies and the health ministry, with their different definitions; what midwives and doctors described; and the UN commission's finding on the destruction of Gaza's fertility clinic, with Israel's answer.
chapters.outro: Part Three set out the women and the unborn. UN Women estimated that more than 38,000 women and girls were killed in Gaza by the end of 2025, and close to 11,000 left with lifelong injuries. [cite:pr_mm_women2026] Births continued in a health system with 15 facilities left for obstetric care in October 2025, and the ministry recorded about 4,000 pregnancies lost in the first half of 2026, with anaemia in most pregnant women. [cite:pr_unfpa_oct2025] [cite:pr_memo_starv2026] The UN commission found that Gaza's main fertility clinic was destroyed deliberately; Israel rejected its findings as unfounded. [cite:pr_aj_coi_repro] Part Four turns to hunger.

sections.h: Women and Girls
sections.html:
UN Women, the UN agency for women, estimated in April 2026 that more than 38,000 women and girls had been killed in Gaza between October 2023 and December 2025, about 47 a day, and warned that the true number was likely higher because the systems that record deaths had collapsed. Close to 11,000 women and girls were left with lifelong injuries. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, counting adult women alone, put the number killed at 12,400. The share of households headed by a woman rose from 9 to 14 percent, about 58,600 households. [cite:pr_mm_women2026]

The two counts are not added together: one includes girls and the other does not. How deaths are recorded in Gaza is set out in Part One. [scene:pr1_lists|How the dead are counted]

sections.h: Giving Birth in Gaza
sections.html:
Babies kept being born. In October 2025 UNFPA, the UN's reproductive health agency, reported about 130 births a day in Gaza, more than a quarter of them by Caesarean section, with only 15 facilities still able to provide obstetric and newborn care and an estimated 55,000 pregnant women cut off from medical help. About one newborn in five was premature, underweight or born with complications. Nasser hospital held 200 newborns in intensive care with capacity for 40, sometimes three to an incubator. A midwife told the agency she had cut a baby's umbilical cord with a knife "heated over a fire." [cite:pr_unfpa_oct2025]

The losses. The health ministry recorded about 3,958 miscarriages in the first half of 2026, a rate more than three times that of the previous six months, and anaemia in 61 percent of pregnant women. [cite:pr_mm_women2026] [cite:pr_memo_starv2026] These are ministry figures, kept by a health system the war had largely destroyed.

The Fertility Clinic

In March 2025 the UN commission of inquiry reported that Israeli forces had "intentionally attacked and destroyed" Al-Basma, Gaza's main in-vitro fertilisation centre, in December 2023, destroying about 4,000 embryos, and that it had found no credible evidence the building was used for military purposes. It called the destruction a measure intended to prevent births, one of the acts that define genocide, and found that forced public stripping, nudity and sexual harassment had become part of Israeli forces' "standard operating procedures" toward Palestinians. [cite:pr_aj_coi_repro]

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: Hunger
chapters.intro: Part Four turns to hunger. It follows the decisions that governed what food entered Gaza, from the siege announced on 9 October 2023 to the blockade of March 2025 and the aid sites that replaced the UN's distribution; the finding of famine in August 2025, Israel's rejection of it, and the arrest warrants that named starvation as a war crime; the deaths from starvation, about a third of them children; and the easing after the ceasefire, by the UN's account and by Israel's.
chapters.outro: Part Four set out the hunger. Israel announced a "complete siege" on 9 October 2023 and stopped all aid in March 2025; more than 2,146 people were killed near the aid sites that replaced the UN's distribution, and along aid convoy routes, by 4 September 2025. [cite:gz_aj_siege] [cite:gz_aj_ghf] The IPC found famine in Gaza City in August 2025; Israel said there was none. [cite:gz_aj_ipc] [cite:gz_olj_ipc] The health ministry recorded 466 starvation deaths, 157 of them children, by October 2026. [cite:pr_memo_starv2026] After the ceasefire famine eased, by the IPC's finding, while most of Gaza remained hungry. [cite:pr_un_ipc_dec2025] These were the stories Gaza's journalists were reporting. Part Five turns to them.

sections.h: The Siege, and the Blockade
sections.html:
On 9 October 2023, two days after the Hamas-led attack, Defence Minister Yoav Gallant announced: "We are putting a complete siege on Gaza … No electricity, no food, no water, no gas – it's all closed." [cite:gz_aj_siege] When the first phase of the January 2025 ceasefire ended without agreement on an extension, Israel stopped all aid from entering on 2 March 2025, saying Hamas was stealing it; it did not publish evidence for the claim. On 18 March it resumed strikes. [cite:pr_wiki_ceasefire2025] [cite:gz_aj_ghf]

The aid sites. From 27 May 2025 food was distributed by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, backed by Israel and the United States, at a handful of sites, replacing the UN's network. By 4 September 2025 the UN Human Rights Office had recorded more than 2,146 people killed near the foundation's sites and along aid convoy routes. The foundation said it was the only operation that delivered food reliably and safely, more than three million boxes, before it announced on 24 November 2025 that it was closing its sites. [cite:gz_aj_ghf]

Famine, and the Denial

On 22 August 2025 the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, the UN-backed system that declares famines, found that "famine is now occurring in Gaza City and its surrounding area," with more than half a million people in catastrophic conditions, and named "conflict, displacement, restricted access, and food system collapse" as its causes. [cite:gz_aj_ipc] Israel's foreign ministry answered: "There is no famine in Gaza." It called the findings "based on Hamas lies laundered through organisations with vested interests," and said "a massive influx of aid has flooded the Strip with staple foods." [cite:gz_olj_ipc]

The warrants. In November 2024 the International Criminal Court had already issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant for, among other crimes, "starvation as a method of warfare." Netanyahu's office said Israel "rejects with disgust the absurd and false actions" against it. [cite:gz_un_icc] [cite:pr_bc_icc2024]

sections.h: The Starved
sections.html:
By 16 October 2026 Gaza's health ministry had recorded 466 deaths from starvation and malnutrition since 2024, 157 of them children. It counted more than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition among children under five between 2024 and August 2026, about 18 percent of them severe, and projected that 74,200 children would need treatment through April 2027. [cite:pr_memo_starv2026] An Israeli military official, in January 2026, rejected the ministry's malnutrition deaths, saying they included people with serious underlying illness. [cite:pr_toi_idf70k]

After the Ceasefire

In December 2025 the IPC found that no part of Gaza was any longer in famine, after the October ceasefire and the reopening of crossings to aid and commercial goods. It still found at least 1.6 million people, 77 percent of the population, in high acute food insecurity, and projected that more than 100,000 children and 37,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women would suffer acute malnutrition by April 2026. "Gaza's children are no longer facing deadly famine, but they remain in grave danger," said UNICEF's Lucia Elmi. [cite:pr_un_ipc_dec2025] Israel's coordinator of activities in the territories said 600 to 800 aid trucks had entered a day since late October, nearly 30,000 of them carrying food, and called the IPC's December report "distorted, biased, and unfounded." [cite:pr_fdd_ipc_dec2025] By October 2026, aid trucks were entering at about a third of the rate the ceasefire agreement set. [cite:gz_aj_year2026]

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: The Journalists
chapters.intro: Part Five turns to the people who reported the war. Because Israel did not let foreign reporters into Gaza on their own, the war was told to the world almost entirely by Gaza's own journalists: staff of local and Arab outlets, and freelancers working for the international agencies. This part sets out how many of them were killed, by the counts of the main press-freedom organizations and why those counts differ; the record year of 2025; and what it meant to report while hungry, displaced and bereaved.
chapters.outro: Part Five set out who reported the war, and how many of them died. By the counts of the UN, the IFJ and the CPJ, the counts range from 189 (CPJ, September 2026, after removals) to 242 (UN, August 2025), the differences coming from what each counts and whom each removed after review. [cite:pr_wiki_killing] [cite:gz_cpj_2026] In 2025 Israel was responsible for about two-thirds of all journalists killed worldwide, in a record year. [cite:pr_cpj_2025report] They were Gazans reporting on their own people, hungry by July 2025 and in many cases bereaved. [cite:pr_aj_afp2025] [cite:pr_nbc_dahdouh] Part Six turns to the named cases.

sections.h: How Many
sections.html:
Three bodies count journalists killed in the war, and their counts differ because their rules differ. The UN counted 242 Palestinian journalists killed by Israel as of August 2025. The International Federation of Journalists, which also counts media workers, put the number at 241 by July 2026, after removing eight names and adding fourteen. The Committee to Protect Journalists counted 192 killed by Israel, at least 184 of them Palestinian, by 10 August 2025. It later removed people its research found had engaged in combat, eight in a review covering 2023 to April 2025 and 19 more in June 2026, and as of 24 September 2026 counted 189 Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza, plus two killed in Israeli detention. [cite:pr_wiki_killing] [cite:gz_cpj_2026]

The removals matter. They show that the counting bodies revised their lists when their own research found a person had taken part in combat. Israel denies deliberately targeting journalists and says some of those killed were members of armed groups; the cases in dispute are the subject of Parts Six and Seven. [scene:pr6_cases|The named]

The Record Year

In February 2026 the Committee to Protect Journalists reported that 129 journalists and media workers had been killed worldwide in 2025, the most since it began counting in 1992, and that Israel was responsible for about two-thirds of them, most of them Palestinians in Gaza. It classified 47 of the year's killings as murders, journalists deliberately killed for their work, the most in a decade, and documented 28 killings of journalists by Israeli drones in Gaza. "Journalists are being killed in record numbers at a time when access to information is more important than ever," said its chief executive, Jodie Ginsberg. [cite:pr_cpj_2025report]

A study by Brown University's Costs of War project concluded that the war had killed more journalists than the US Civil War, both world wars and several later wars combined; a European journalism-education group rated the comparison "mostly false," because the database it relies on was not designed as a complete historical record. [cite:pr_wiki_killing] The Committee to Protect Journalists' own records, which go back to 1992, show no deadlier year for journalists than 2025. [cite:pr_cpj_2025report]

sections.h: Who Reported Gaza
sections.html:
The journalists of Gaza were, for the most part, Gazans. With foreign reporters kept out, the international agencies relied on local freelancers and staff, and Arab networks such as Al Jazeera on their own Gaza bureaus. [cite:gz_wlrn_ban] [cite:pr_aj_afp2025] They reported from the same streets, shelters and hospitals as the people in their stories, and lived under the same bombardment and the same hunger.

Reporting hungry. In July 2025, as the IPC moved toward its finding of famine, Agence France-Presse asked Israel to let it evacuate its freelance journalists from Gaza, saying their situation had become "untenable." AFP's journalists' society wrote: "We fear learning of their deaths at any moment." One of its photographers, Bashar, wrote that his "body is thin" and that he no longer had the strength to work. [cite:pr_aj_afp2025]

Reporting bereaved. In October 2023 Wael Dahdouh, Al Jazeera's Gaza bureau chief, learned on air that an Israeli strike on Nuseirat camp had killed his wife, a son, a daughter and a grandson. In December he was wounded in a drone strike that killed his cameraman. On 7 January 2024 his eldest son, Hamza, also an Al Jazeera journalist, was killed with a colleague when their car was struck; the army said it had targeted a "terrorist" operating a drone that threatened troops, and Al Jazeera said they were not flying a drone. "We are going to proceed as long as we are alive and breathing," Dahdouh said. [cite:pr_nbc_dahdouh] [cite:pr_wiki_killing] Part Six follows Hamza Dahdouh's case and others, one by one.

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: The Named
chapters.intro: Part Six names some of them. A count can hide the people inside it; these four cases are documented closely enough to follow one by one. For each, the record gives what the journalists were doing, what the army said about them and when, the evidence it offered, and what independent investigations found. They are not the only cases; they are the ones the record lets us lay out in full.
chapters.outro: Part Six followed four cases. In each, the army said afterwards that the dead were fighters or that a legitimate target was present; in each, the evidence it published was thin or contradicted, and, in the Nasser case, no findings had been released a year later: a drone with no soldiers in its footage, a rank awarded to a ten-year-old, a dossier the Guardian called unconvincing, a hospital camera that, an Israeli soldier told AP, had no link found to Hamas. [cite:pr_bg_wapo_dahdouh] [cite:pr_wiki_ghoul] [cite:pr_wiki_sharif] [cite:pr_ap_nasser2026] Part Seven turns to the argument behind the army's accounts: that some journalists were combatants.

sections.h: Hamza Dahdouh and Mustafa Thuraya, 7 January 2024
sections.html:
Hamza Dahdouh, 27, Wael Dahdouh's eldest son, and Mustafa Thuraya, a videographer who flew a camera drone, were driving back from filming the aftermath of a strike near Khan Younis when an Israeli missile hit their car. Both were killed, with their driver; two freelancers were badly wounded. The next day the army said it had struck "a terrorist who operated an aircraft that posed a threat to IDF troops." Two days later it said Thuraya belonged to Hamas and Dahdouh to Palestinian Islamic Jihad. The Washington Post recovered the footage from Thuraya's drone: "No Israeli soldiers, aircraft, or other military equipment are visible in the footage taken that day." Fourteen witnesses and colleagues gave it "no indications" that either man was doing anything but journalism, and Dahdouh had recently been approved to leave Gaza. Asked for more, the army said it had "nothing further to add." The UN special rapporteur on free expression, Irene Khan, said: "It's not enough to say that we suspected them so we killed them." [cite:pr_bg_wapo_dahdouh]

Ismail al-Ghoul and Rami al-Rifi, 31 July 2024

Ismail al-Ghoul, an Al Jazeera correspondent, and his cameraman, Rami al-Rifi, were killed by an airstrike in al-Shati camp as they reported on the assassination of Hamas's leader, Ismail Haniyeh. The army called al-Ghoul a "Nukhba terrorist," citing a document from a Hamas computer that said he had received his rank in 2007. Al-Ghoul was born in 1997; in 2007 he would have been about ten. Al Jazeera pointed out that Israeli forces had arrested and released him in March 2024. Reporters Without Borders filed complaints with the International Criminal Court; asked for more, the army said it "did not have anything more to say on the topic." [cite:pr_wiki_ghoul]

Anas al-Sharif and Four Colleagues, 10 August 2025

Anas al-Sharif was Al Jazeera's best-known correspondent in northern Gaza. His father had been killed in a strike in December 2023. In July 2025 the Committee to Protect Journalists and the UN's Irene Khan warned that an Israeli campaign accusing him of being a Hamas fighter was putting his life at risk. On 10 August 2025 an Israeli strike on a press tent by the gate of al-Shifa hospital killed him, his Al Jazeera colleagues Mohammed Qreiqeh, Ibrahim Zaher, Mohammed Noufal and Moamen Aliwa, and others. The army said he had led a Hamas rocket cell, citing documents it had released in October 2024. The Guardian called them "an unconvincing dossier of unverified evidence"; the Committee to Protect Journalists said Israel had offered no "credible evidence"; the army gave no reason for killing the others. The UN Secretary-General called for an independent investigation. A message al-Sharif had written in advance was posted after his death: "If these words reach you, know that Israel has succeeded in killing me and silencing my voice." [cite:pr_wiki_sharif]

Nasser Hospital, 25 August 2025

At Nasser hospital in Khan Younis, Israel struck the hospital four times with tank shells; the first strike killed the Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri and one other person. As journalists and rescuers climbed an outside staircase to help, a second strike killed twenty more, among them Mariam Dagga, a visual journalist who worked for the Associated Press. In all 22 people were killed, five of them journalists. The army said the target was a suspected Hamas camera on the roof and that six of those killed were linked to Hamas, without giving evidence; Netanyahu's office said Israel "deeply regrets" the incident. A year later the army had published no findings; it said the incident was being examined and that findings would go to the Military Advocate General. An Israeli soldier told the Associated Press that the army had found no evidence linking the camera to Hamas, and that none of the six it named had been the target. [cite:pr_ap_nasser2026] [cite:pr_wiki_killing]

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: “Journalists Are Not Terrorists”
chapters.intro: Part Seven sets out the argument behind the cases in Part Six. Israel says it has never deliberately targeted journalists, and that some of the dead it calls journalists were members of Hamas or Islamic Jihad using press work as cover. Press-freedom groups answer that Israel labels journalists as fighters after killing them, without evidence. This part sets out what the laws of war say about journalists, Israel's argument in its own words, the cases in which the counting bodies accepted it, the reporting on an army unit tasked with finding such links, and the record of the same claims before this war.
chapters.outro: Part Seven set out the argument. Under the laws of war journalists are civilians, protected unless and while they take a direct part in hostilities. [cite:pr_icrc_journalists] Israel says it has never deliberately targeted journalists and that some of the dead were fighters using the press as cover, on intelligence it cannot disclose. [cite:pr_idf_cpj2025] The counting bodies accepted some of those claims and removed names; in the named cases they did not, and +972 reported an army unit tasked with finding links to justify strikes. [cite:pr_wiki_killing] [cite:pr_an_legitcell] The same accusations, without published evidence, run back through earlier wars. [cite:pr_cpj_smear2024] Part Eight turns to the gate that kept foreign reporters out.

sections.h: What the Law Says
sections.html:
Under the laws of war, a journalist is a civilian. Article 79 of the First Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions says journalists "are considered civilians and must be respected and protected," a rule the International Committee of the Red Cross treats as binding in every kind of armed conflict. A journalist loses that protection "only if, and for such time as, they directly participate in hostilities." Reporting, expressing opinions or spreading information does not make a journalist, or a newsroom, a lawful target, however hostile the reporting. [cite:pr_icrc_journalists]

Israel's Argument

Israel's position is that it does not target journalists. "The IDF has never, and will never, deliberately target journalists," the army wrote in February 2025, in reply to the Committee to Protect Journalists. It said it takes all feasible measures to reduce harm to civilians, including journalists, but that remaining in a combat zone carries risk, and that Hamas hides its command posts in civilian places. It named people it said were fighters presenting themselves as journalists: Mustafa Thuraya (spelled "Thuria" by the army), listed in a captured document as a Hamas squad deputy commander; Hamza Dahdouh, an Islamic Jihad operative "disguised" as an Al Jazeera cameraman; Ismail Abu Omar, who it said filmed himself in Kibbutz Nir Oz on 7 October; and Ismail al-Ghoul. It said it "cannot disclose the intelligence" proving these affiliations without exposing its sources. [cite:pr_idf_cpj2025] Three weeks into the war it had written to Reuters and AFP that "we cannot guarantee your employees' safety," because Hamas operated "in the vicinity of journalists and civilians." [cite:pr_cm_idfletter]

Where the Counters Agreed

Israel's claims were not all rejected. The Committee to Protect Journalists removed from its list people its research found had engaged in combat, eight in a review covering 2023 to April 2025 and 19 more in June 2026; the International Federation of Journalists removed eight names and added fourteen in July 2026, raising its count from 235 to 241. [cite:gz_cpj_2026] [cite:pr_wiki_killing] In the cases set out in Part Six, the army's evidence was disputed or contradicted by independent reporting. [scene:pr6_cases|The named]

The Legitimization Cell

In August 2025, after the killing of Anas al-Sharif, the Israeli magazine +972 reported, from three intelligence sources, that the army had set up a unit after 7 October, called the Legitimization Cell, to find intelligence that could be declassified to link Gaza journalists to armed groups. Its purpose, the sources said, was not security but to answer international criticism and protect support abroad, including American arms supplies. One source described "a push to find one journalist who might not be so innocent." Arab News's account of the report carries no army response. [cite:pr_an_legitcell]

Before This War

The Committee to Protect Journalists has documented the same pattern in earlier wars: Yaser Murtaja, killed in 2018, whom a defence minister called a Hamas officer without evidence, and whom the Washington Post found had been vetted for an American aid grant; Hussam Salama and Mahmoud al-Kumi, killed in 2012, whom Human Rights Watch found no proof were militants; Hamid Shihab, killed in 2014; and Mohamed Abu Halima, killed in 2004. "Smear campaigns endanger journalists and erode public trust in the media," its programme director said. [cite:pr_cpj_smear2024]

The organizations' answer is the title of this part, in the words of Reporters Without Borders: "Journalists are not terrorists and the mere publication of these documents doesn't constitute proof of their affiliation." [cite:pr_wiki_killing]

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: The Gate
chapters.intro: Part Eight turns to the gate. Since October 2023 Israel has not allowed foreign journalists into Gaza except on escorted visits with its army. This part follows the court cases the foreign press brought to open it, the state's reasons for keeping it shut, what reporters see on an embed, the rules of the military censor, and the law under which Israel closed Al Jazeera. It is the gate that left Gaza's own journalists to tell the story alone.
chapters.outro: Part Eight set out the gate. Israel has allowed foreign journalists into Gaza only with its army since October 2023, on grounds of security that its Supreme Court accepted in January 2024; a second petition was still undecided in October 2026, three years into the war. [cite:pr_mm_fpa2024] [cite:pr_yahoo_state_hcj] [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] Foreign reporters work under the military censor, and Israel closed Al Jazeera under a law it has since extended. [cite:gz_intercept_cnn] [cite:pr_aj_ajlaw] Part Nine turns to the press of the West Bank.

sections.h: No Independent Entry
sections.html:
From October 2023 Israel, which controls entry, allowed foreign journalists into Gaza only on visits escorted by its army. [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] The Foreign Press Association, which represents the international media in Israel, petitioned Israel's Supreme Court for independent access. The state argued that journalists moving on their own could endanger soldiers and reveal the positions of troops; on 8 January 2024 the court rejected the petition, allowing escorted access to continue. The association said the ban, by then 95 days old, was "unprecedented." [cite:pr_mm_fpa2024]

In September 2024 it petitioned again, with Israeli and international press-freedom groups. After the ceasefire, the state told the court that "there is no basis to allow the entry of journalists – Israeli or foreign – into the Gaza Strip without accompaniment," citing the danger to reporters, interference with military operations and the remains of a hostage still in Gaza. It counted about 25 escorted entries by Israeli journalists and five group visits by foreign journalists since late October 2025. [cite:pr_yahoo_state_hcj]

Three years on. As of October 2026 the court's decision on the second petition had been postponed "numerous times," and no foreign reporter had entered Gaza on their own. Embeds remained "tightly controlled": the army decides what reporters see and where they go, and they do not interview Palestinians. "We haven't really been able to get a straight answer as to why this ban continues," said Joe Federman, the AP's deputy director for the Middle East and a longtime member of the association. "This is a risk that most journalists are willing to take." The Committee to Protect Journalists' Jodie Ginsberg warned that "the longer this goes on, the more normalized that lack of access becomes"; foreign reporters, she said, could "corroborate what is being documented by their colleagues." NPR's producer in Gaza City, Anas Baba, said open access "would mean we are no longer carrying this burden alone." [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full]

The Censor

Foreign journalists working from Israel must agree to abide by the military censor to receive a press card, and the censor restricted subjects including security cabinet meetings and the hostages. [cite:gz_intercept_cnn] Part Eleven follows how this, and the policies of American newsrooms, shaped what reached readers. [scene:gz12_coverage|What Americans were shown]

The Al Jazeera Law

In April 2024 the Knesset passed a law allowing the prime minister and communications minister to shut down foreign networks judged harmful to state security. Netanyahu wrote that Al Jazeera had "harmed Israel's security, actively participated in the October 7 massacre, and incited against Israeli soldiers"; the network called these "slanderous accusations." Israel closed Al Jazeera's operations in the country in May 2024. In December 2025 the Knesset extended the law to 2027, allowing its use even outside a state of emergency and with amendments aimed at eliminating judicial oversight. [cite:pr_aj_ajlaw]

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: The West Bank Press
chapters.intro: Part Nine turns to the West Bank, where journalists are not kept out but are watched, arrested and, in one case that became known worldwide, killed. It begins with Shireen Abu Akleh, the Al Jazeera correspondent shot in Jenin in 2022, and the conclusions of the Israeli army and the United States; then the arrests of journalists since October 2023, most of them held without charge; and the raid that closed Al Jazeera's bureau in Ramallah.
chapters.outro: Part Nine set out the West Bank press. Shireen Abu Akleh was likely killed by an Israeli soldier in May 2022, by the army's own finding and the US State Department's, and no one was charged. [cite:pr_npr_abuakleh] Since October 2023 Israel has arrested journalists 112 times, holding most without charge, and the Palestinian Authority six times; two have died in Israeli custody. [cite:pr_cpj_arrests] Al Jazeera's bureau in Ramallah was closed by raid in September 2024. [cite:pr_newarab_ramallah] Part Ten turns to the people still reporting, and what it costs them.

sections.h: Shireen Abu Akleh
sections.html:
Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian American correspondent for Al Jazeera, was shot dead in May 2022 while covering an Israeli military operation near Jenin. The Israeli army concluded in September 2022 that there was a "high possibility" one of its soldiers had fired the fatal shot, believing, from a vehicle with minimal visibility during what the army said was very heavy gunfire, that he was shooting at "a terrorist." It found no reason to open a criminal investigation. A US-supervised test of the bullet could not match it to a gun, but the State Department concluded that Israel was likely responsible. Her family said Israel was trying "to avoid responsibility" and asked for an International Criminal Court investigation. NPR's correspondent said video from the minutes before the killing showed no gunshots at the scene. [cite:pr_npr_abuakleh]

Arrests

Since October 2023, the Committee to Protect Journalists has recorded 118 arrests of journalists and media workers in Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and Jerusalem: 112 by Israeli authorities and six by the Palestinian Authority. As of October 2026, 39 remained in custody. One journalist and one media worker died in Israeli custody. On 1 December 2025 Israel held 31 Palestinian journalists, most of them under administrative detention, without charge or trial. Of 58 journalists the Committee interviewed after their release, 48 had never been charged, and they described "physical assault, forced stress positions, sensory deprivation, sexual violence, and medical neglect." The army told the Committee it "does not arrest journalists simply for being journalists." [cite:pr_cpj_arrests] Part Seven of The West Bank, Documented sets out the system of administrative detention. [scene:wb7_courts|Two systems of law]

The Ramallah Bureau

On 22 September 2024, masked and armed Israeli soldiers entered Al Jazeera's bureau in Ramallah, while it was on air. "There is a court ruling for closing down Al Jazeera for 45 days," a soldier told the bureau chief, Walid al-Omari, on camera; the order, al-Omari said, accused the network of "incitement to and support of terrorism." A soldier ordered staff to take all the cameras and leave the office. [cite:pr_newarab_ramallah] Israel had already closed Al Jazeera's operations inside Israel that May, under the law described in Part Eight. [scene:pr8_gate|The gate]

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: Keeping the Lights On
chapters.intro: Part Ten turns to the people who are still reporting, and what it costs them to keep going. A journalist in Gaza needs electricity to charge a camera, an internet connection to file, fuel to reach a story, and a roof to work under; for most of the war they had little of any of it. This part sets out the conditions recorded by press-freedom groups, before and after the ceasefire; the money: the price of fuel and data, and the freelancers working without contracts; and what the organizations that support them have done, including taking Israel to court.
chapters.outro: Part Ten set out what it costs to keep reporting. Gaza's journalists worked from ruined newsrooms and tents, with internet at up to ten times its usual price and fuel ten times its 2023 cost, and lost work as the world's attention moved on; many are freelancers without contracts or protection. [cite:pr_rsf_feb2025] [cite:pr_rsf_feb2026] The organizations that support them have taken Israel to court for access, and were still waiting in October 2026. [cite:pr_cpj_motion2026] [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] Part Eleven turns to what of their work reached America.

sections.h: No Power, No Signal, No Office
sections.html:
A month into the first ceasefire, in February 2025, Reporters Without Borders described the press of Gaza working among ruins. The army had destroyed newsrooms and journalists' homes. Islam al-Zaanoun of Palestine TV said: "With no place to work, no internet or electricity, I was forced to stop working for several days." Fuel was scarce, travel slow and costly, and reporters queued for hours for water and food like everyone else. Journalists who had left Gaza could not return. "Reporters need multimedia and security equipment, internet and electricity," said the group's editorial director, Anne Bocandé. [cite:pr_rsf_feb2025]

A year later, four months after the October 2025 ceasefire, RSF's Middle East desk head, Jonathan Dagher, said they were "at breaking point." Electricity and internet were scarce, slow and expensive: internet access sometimes cost ten times the usual price. Cameras, tripods, batteries, phones and safety gear were short. Many reporters lived in tents or damaged flats. The price of fuel had risen from about 7 shekels in 2023 to nearly 75. About half the territory, east of the line held by the army, was closed to them. On 21 January 2026 an Israeli drone killed three freelancers working for Al Sharq TV and AFP; the army said it had struck "suspects who activated" a Hamas drone that threatened troops, and that the details were under review. [cite:pr_rsf_feb2026] [cite:pr_almon_drone2026]

Without Contracts

Many of those reporting Gaza to the world are freelancers, paid by the story. After the ceasefire, with the world's attention elsewhere, the assignments fell. "In 2026, we are no longer the main story," said Nour Swirki of Al Sharq TV, whose live reports had fallen from six or seven a day to one or two. NPR's Anas Baba said that reporting had become "a struggle for survival rather than just a journalism job," with freelancers "working without contracts, without stability and without protection." "We are all targets, vulnerable at any given moment, and no place is safe," said Swirki. Thaer al-Moustafa, who works with the Guardian, put it in three words: "We need protection." [cite:pr_rsf_feb2026] In July 2025, at the height of the hunger, AFP had asked Israel to let it evacuate its freelancers. [cite:pr_aj_afp2025]

The Organizations

The press-freedom groups have counted the dead, published the names, and gone to court. In April 2026 the Committee to Protect Journalists, with the Foreign Press Association, the Union of Journalists in Israel and Reporters Without Borders, filed an emergency motion asking Israel's Supreme Court to rule at last on independent access to Gaza. "There are no substantiated or specific threats against journalists, and journalists pose no threat to Israeli troops," the Committee said. [cite:pr_cpj_motion2026] The state has argued that unescorted entry endangers journalists and troops. [cite:pr_yahoo_state_hcj] As of October 2026 the court had not ruled. [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] The published record does not include totals of the money these groups have given Gaza's journalists; it records what the journalists say they lack: equipment, protection, contracts and a way out.

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: What Reached America
chapters.intro: Part Eleven asks what of all this reached American readers. Gaza's journalists filed their stories; the question is how American newsrooms carried the count of the dead and the deaths of the journalists themselves. This part sets out studies of the coverage from both directions: critics who found Israeli deaths given more weight and Israeli claims repeated in headlines, and critics who found the press relying too heavily on the Gaza health ministry; the internal policies of two major newsrooms; how fifteen outlets reported the killing of Anas al-Sharif; and how American opinion moved.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven set out what reached America. One study found Palestinian deaths given far less weight than Israeli deaths in three major US papers; another found the press relying on the Gaza health ministry without distinguishing fighters from civilians. [cite:gz_aa_intercept] [cite:pr_hjs_counting] Newsroom rules at the New York Times and CNN shaped the language used, and when Anas al-Sharif was killed, all fifteen outlets FAIR examined carried Israel's allegation against him, while few named Israel as the main killer of journalists. [cite:gz_nl_nytmemo] [cite:gz_an_cnnstaff] [cite:pr_fair_sharif] By 2026, Americans' sympathies had shifted. [cite:gz_gallup_2026] Part Twelve sets out what is settled, contested and open.

sections.h: How the Dead Were Reported
sections.html:
Studies of the coverage have reached opposite conclusions, and both are part of the record. The Intercept analysed more than 1,100 articles in the New York Times, the Washington Post and the Los Angeles Times from early in the war. It found Israelis mentioned eight times for every Israeli death, a rate sixteen times higher per death than for Palestinians; words such as "slaughter," "massacre" and "horrific" were reserved almost entirely for Israelis killed by Palestinians; and only two headlines mentioned the children of Gaza. [cite:gz_aa_intercept] The Henry Jackson Society, a British think tank, analysed 1,378 articles from February to May 2024 and reached the opposite worry: 98 percent cited the health ministry's figures, 84 percent did not distinguish fighters from civilians, and 19 percent gave the ministry's numbers without saying where they came from. It argued that the ministry, run by a party to the war, should be treated as a contested source, and noted that the army's figures for fighters killed received far less attention than the ministry's. [cite:pr_hjs_counting]

Part One set out what the later independent studies found about those figures: that the early lists were largely reliable and that the count, if anything, was too low. [scene:pr1_uncounted|The uncounted]

Newsroom Rules

An internal New York Times memo first issued in November 2023 told its journalists to restrict the words "genocide" and "ethnic cleansing," to avoid "occupied territory," to use "Palestine" only in rare cases, and not to call areas settled by refugees "refugee camps." The paper said such guidance was "standard practice" for "accuracy, consistency and nuance." [cite:gz_nl_nytmemo] [cite:gz_dawn_nyt] At CNN, according to the Guardian's reporting from six staff and internal memos, stories had to be cleared by the Jerusalem bureau, quoting Hamas was severely restricted, and, staff said, Israeli government statements were taken at face value; CNN said its reporting had "confronted Israel's response to the attacks." [cite:gz_an_cnnstaff] Every foreign reporter based in Israel works under the military censor. [cite:gz_intercept_cnn]

How the Journalists' Deaths Were Reported

The media watchdog FAIR examined how fifteen Western outlets reported the killing of Anas al-Sharif and his colleagues on 10 and 11 August 2025. All fifteen reported Israel's allegation that he was a Hamas member; four put it in a headline or subheading. Six left out his final message. Only two noted that the other journalists killed with him had not been accused of anything. Thirteen mentioned how many Palestinian journalists had been killed, but only four named Israel as the main cause. Reuters first headlined its story "Israel Kills Al Jazeera Journalist It Says Was Hamas Leader," and later changed it. [cite:pr_fair_sharif]

What Americans Came to Think

In February 2026 Gallup found that, "for the first time in Gallup's annual measurement since 2001, Americans' sympathies no longer lie more with the Israelis": 41 percent sympathized more with the Palestinians and 36 percent with the Israelis, a difference Gallup said was not statistically significant, against 31 and 54 percent three years earlier. [cite:gz_gallup_2026] [cite:gz_ap_gallup2026] The fuller account of the coverage, its owners and its rules is in Gaza, Documented. [scene:gz12_coverage|What Americans were shown]

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: Settled, Contested and Open
chapters.intro: Part Twelve closes the book. It gathers what the earlier parts established, separates what the record settles from what it leaves contested, names what was still open in October 2026, and ends with the names of the journalists whose cases this book has followed. Nothing new is introduced; each statement points back to its sources.
chapters.outro: This closes PRESS. Its twelve parts followed the dead of Gaza and the West Bank and the journalists who were killed counting them, from 2022 to October 2026.

sections.h: What the Record Settles
sections.html:
The dead are many, and most are named. Gaza's health ministry counted 74,382 dead by October 2026, with names and ID numbers for most of them; an independent check of its early lists found them largely reliable, and an Israeli military official put the toll at about 70,000 in January 2026. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:pr_airwars_lists] [cite:pr_toi_idf70k]

The count is more likely too low than too high. A household survey estimated about 75,200 violent deaths in the war's first fifteen months, when about 49,000 had been recorded, and about 16,300 non-violent deaths in the same period; Al Jazeera reported about 10,000 people missing under the rubble in April 2026. [cite:pr_almon_survey2026] [cite:pr_aj_rubble2026]

Children, women and the unborn bore much of it. The UN commission counted at least 20,179 children killed in two years; UN Women, more than 38,000 women and girls by the end of 2025; the ministry recorded about 4,000 pregnancies lost in the first half of 2026 and 466 deaths from malnutrition and starvation since 2024, 157 of them children, by 16 October 2026; an Israeli military official rejected the ministry's malnutrition-death figures. [cite:pr_nw_coi2026] [cite:pr_mm_women2026] [cite:pr_memo_starv2026] [cite:pr_jw_idf71k]

Journalists were killed in great numbers. The Committee to Protect Journalists counted 189 killed in Gaza as of 24 September 2026, after removing those it found had engaged in combat; the UN counted 242 Palestinian journalists by 11 August 2025. In 2025, the Committee's record year worldwide, it held Israel responsible for about two-thirds. Israel says it has never deliberately targeted journalists and that some of the dead were militants. [cite:gz_cpj_2026] [cite:pr_wiki_killing] [cite:pr_cpj_2025report] [cite:pr_idf_cpj2025]

The foreign press was kept out. Three years into the war, Israel had not allowed foreign journalists to enter Gaza independently; it permitted only escorted visits with its army. [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full]

sections.h: What Remains Contested
sections.html: The book has set the two positions side by side, and given the evidence each offers. Where a claim rests on intelligence that has not been published, it has said so.

sections.h: What Is Still Open
sections.html:
As of October 2026, the following were undecided.

The gate. Israel's Supreme Court had not ruled on the foreign press's second petition, filed in September 2024, despite an emergency motion in April 2026. [cite:pr_yahoo_state_hcj] [cite:pr_cpj_motion2026] [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full]

The investigations. A year after the strike on Nasser hospital, the army had published no findings, saying the incident was being examined and findings would go to the Military Advocate General; in Shireen Abu Akleh's case it had found no reason for a criminal investigation. [cite:pr_ap_nasser2026] [cite:pr_npr_abuakleh]

The count. Al Jazeera reported about 10,000 people still missing under the rubble in April 2026, and how many of the dead were fighters had not been established by any published list. [cite:pr_aj_rubble2026] [cite:pr_toi_idf70k]

The courts. The ICC's warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant, including for starvation as a method of warfare, had not been withdrawn; Netanyahu's office had rejected them "with disgust" as "absurd and false."
