Press-freedom groups had filed complaints with the court over the killing of journalists. [cite:gz_un_icc] [cite:pr_bc_icc2024] [cite:pr_wiki_ghoul]

The journalists still working. Gaza's reporters were still filing, mostly as freelancers without contracts, with little power, costly internet and half the territory closed to them. [cite:pr_rsf_feb2026]

The Named

This book has followed the cases of these journalists, among the hundreds killed: Shireen Abu Akleh, Jenin, May 2022; Hamza Dahdouh and Mustafa Thuraya, near Khan Younis, January 2024; Ismail al-Ghoul and Rami al-Rifi, al-Shati camp, July 2024; Anas al-Sharif, Mohammed Qreiqeh, Ibrahim Zaher, Mohammed Noufal and Moamen Aliwa, by al-Shifa hospital, August 2025; Hussam al-Masri and Mariam Dagga, among five journalists killed at Nasser hospital, August 2025. [cite:pr_npr_abuakleh] [cite:pr_bg_wapo_dahdouh] [cite:pr_wiki_ghoul] [cite:pr_wiki_sharif] [cite:pr_ap_nasser2026] [cite:pr_wiki_killing] The full lists kept by the Committee to Protect Journalists and the International Federation of Journalists name the rest. [cite:gz_cpj_2026] [cite:gz_wiki_journalists]

Anas al-Sharif wrote, in the message published after his death: "If these words reach you, know that Israel has succeeded in killing me and silencing my voice." [cite:pr_wiki_sharif] This book is an attempt to make sure the record he and the others were keeping still reaches its readers.

books.title: The Vatican Architecture
books.subtitle: Sovereignty, Money, Zionism and the Inner Traditions
books.intro:
This volume is about the Holy See, the sovereign at the head of the Catholic Church, and two questions about it. Book One asks whether its public refusal of Zionism, from Pius X's "Non possumus" to Theodor Herzl in January 1904 until the Fundamental Agreement with Israel of 30 December 1993, was what it appeared to be or a front for private support. The question was first put in this library by The Divine 3+1, which promised a volume on Rome; this is that volume. Answering it fairly means answering the questions underneath it, and the book takes them in turn. Why is there a Vatican at all, who designed the settlement of 1929, and who paid for it? Why is the Holy See still treated as a state, and who checks it? Who holds power inside it, and what of the Jesuits' "Black Pope", the Orsini, the Order of Malta and the "Grey Pope"? What does it own, what does its bank do, and what is the truth of its Rothschild loans? What did it do about the sexual abuse of children by clergy? How far does it reach through schools, universities and bishops? What do its texts and archives show? And what happened to Emanuela Orlandi, the Vatican citizen who disappeared in Rome in 1983?

The record answers the central question more firmly than most of the others. It shows Herzl recording Pius X's refusal in his own diary, Benedict XV speaking in 1919 against a "position of privilege and preponderance" in Palestine, and, in private letters of 1943 that the Holy See later published, its Secretary of State, his officials and his delegate in Washington opposing a Jewish home there, the delegate proposing "a more fitting territory than Palestine." [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] [cite:vt16_va_1919] [cite:vt16_jta1976] [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] It shows the Holy See's one material commitment of 1949 going to Palestinian refugees, forty-five years without recognition, and a treaty in 1993 that secured the Church's institutions and committed the Holy See to remain "a stranger to all merely temporal conflicts" over "disputed territories and unsettled borders." [cite:vt17_cnewa_pmp] [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] It finds no transfer of money or favours from the Holy See to the Zionist movement or to Israel, and no document behind the "unbroken chain" of Rothschild control said to run from the papal loans of 1831 to 2026. [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] [cite:vt11_iv_pauly] Its verdict is that the refusal was real policy toward a movement and a state, kept apart after 1965 from the Church's teaching on the Jewish people, and that the verdict could be reopened only by the Holy See's own files on Palestine after 1945, which are open to 1958 but have barely been studied, and closed after that. [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] [cite:vt17_berghahn_rioli] [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] Around that answer it finds a sovereign recognised by 184 states ruling a territory of 0.44 square kilometres, a bank holding 5.9 billion euros of clients' money in 2025, secrecy rules over abuse trials lifted only in 2019, and an Orlandi case that three inquiries opened in 2023 have not closed. [cite:vt4_vcs_geography] [cite:vt5_pv_relations2026] [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] [cite:vt12_vn_rescript2019] [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025]

Book One is in nineteen parts. Part One states the question and fixes five tests before the evidence is weighed. [scene:vt1_question|The question] Parts Two to Five build the sovereign: the papal state from 754 to 1929, the 1929 deal and what remains of it, how the city actually runs, and the recognition and outside checks on which its statehood rests. [scene:vt2_papal_states|Why there is a Vatican] [scene:vt3_what_each_got|The 1929 deal] [scene:vt4_holy_see_vs_city|How it runs] [scene:vt5_recognition|Sovereignty] Parts Six to Eight examine who holds power: the popes and the Curia, the Black Nobility and the Orsini, and the Jesuits, Opus Dei and the Order of Malta. [scene:vt6_curia_2022|Popes and Curia] [scene:vt7_black_nobility|The Black Nobility] [scene:vt8_jesuits|The orders] Parts Nine to Eleven follow the money, the scandals that reshaped it and the Rothschild claims. [scene:vt9_ior|The money] [scene:vt10_ambrosiano_calvi|Scandal and reform] [scene:vt11_papal_loans|Rome and the Rothschilds] Parts Twelve to Fifteen turn to abuse and its cover-up, the Church's reach, its texts and archives, and the Orlandi and Gregori case. [scene:vt12_the_rules|Abuse] [scene:vt13_schools|Reach] [scene:vt14_canon|Texts and archives] [scene:vt15_the_case|Orlandi and Gregori] Parts Sixteen to Eighteen set out the record on Zionism and Israel from Herzl's audience to the war in Gaza, and Part Nineteen scores the five tests and gives the verdict. [scene:vt16_herzl_1904|Herzl to the war] [scene:vt17_jerusalem_1947_49|Non-recognition to recognition] [scene:vt18_relations_since_1994|Israel, Palestine and Gaza] [scene:vt19_predictions_tested|The verdict]

Book Two, "The Church Before the State: What Rome Took, What It Buried, What Survived", asks the older question underneath the first. A sovereign church needed a church first, and Parts Twenty to Thirty-Six follow how it was made and what it excluded, from Yeshua and Paul through Constantine and the Council of Nicaea, which settled the creed in 325 but did not choose the Bible, to the lists and councils that did, from Athanasius's letter of 367 to Trent's vote of 1546. [scene:vt20_yeshua_record|Yeshua, Paul and the first followers] [scene:vt21_conversion|Constantine] [scene:vt22_the_room|Nicaea] [scene:vt23_lists_and_letters|How the Bible was made] [cite:vt22_canons] [cite:vt23_na_festal39] It tests one thesis, set out on the Sophia platform: that institutional religion built a mediated, taxed and obligatory system of priest, tithe, Sunday duty and commandments over teachings that offered direct knowledge of God, and then condemned, burned or absorbed those who kept them. It lays out the teachings of the excluded texts in full, the Gnostic teachers the platform calls the Evangelical Gnostics, the Nag Hammadi library codex by codex, the Gospels of Mary and Judas and the Pistis Sophia, and the 81-book Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church with Enoch and Jubilees. [scene:vt24_who_they_were|The Evangelical Gnostics] [scene:vt25_the_jar|Nag Hammadi] [scene:vt26_gospel_of_mary|Mary, Judas and Pistis Sophia] [scene:vt27_church_and_canon|The Ethiopian Bible] It follows what the institution did to the Cathars, the Templars and the mystics, to Bruno and Galileo, to Rosicrucians, Freemasons and the Bavarian Illuminati, to accused witches and the forbidden arts, and how the tithe and the Sunday obligation became law. [scene:vt28_cathars|Cathars and Inquisition] [scene:vt29_templars|Templars and mystics] [scene:vt30_rosicrucians_masons|Fraternities and witches] [scene:vt31_tithe|Tithe and Sunday] Four further parts widen the test to the world beyond: the mystery schools closed by emperors and bishops from 391, the inquisitions of the Spanish and Portuguese crowns and the books friars burned in the Americas, the sun cults of the Inca and the Mexica, and the mother goddesses carried into Marian devotion from Tepeyac to the Caribbean. [scene:vt33_the_schools|The mysteries closed] [scene:vt34_spain_portugal|The inquisitions beyond Rome] [scene:vt35_inti_and_the_andes|The suppressed suns] [scene:vt36_guadalupe_tonantzin|The suppressed feminine] [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] [cite:vt34_arch_mani] [cite:vt36_sahagun1576] Part Thirty-Six grades the thesis in the three registers Book One used. It finds documented that the excluded texts teach a kingdom within and that no tithe or Sunday duty is recorded for any Gnostic school, while the winning church built mediation, a compulsory tithe from 585 and, from 1231, a law that sent obstinate heretics to the stake; it finds the ancient Gnostic gospels excluded and their meetings banned but no surviving order to burn them, the canon not chosen at Nicaea and the Ethiopian Bible never Rome's to suppress; it finds the wider suppression documented but carried out by emperors, crowns, conquistadors, friars and bishops, and in two cases by governments with no tie to Rome; and it leaves the motive, fear of unmediated access, as a reading rather than a finding. [cite:vt24_gthom] [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] [cite:vt24_ce_tithes] [cite:vt28_herodote_1233] [cite:vt21_vc3_66] [cite:vt27_hessayon] [scene:vt32_verdict_two|Verdict II]

The myths of hidden control, the "Grey Pope" and the Rothschild chain among them, are named and traced to their sources, and the antisemitic history of the "Rothschilds control the Pope" trope is stated where it arises. [cite:vt11_wiki_francejuive] Two details often misstated are fixed by the record: Cardinal Becciu was convicted on 16 December 2023, and Cardinal Parolin's phrase "inhuman and indefensible" described the attack of 7 October 2023, not the war in Gaza. [cite:vt10_vn_verdict2023] [cite:vt18_vn_parolin2025] As of October 2026, the renewed proceedings against Cardinal Becciu, in which every defendant is presumed innocent, were due to resume on 29 October, and the Holy See's economic agreement with Israel, promised in 1993, was still unsigned. [cite:vt10_us_oct2026] [cite:vt18_press_2017] The volume credits the explainer channel Wendover Productions, whose video on how the Vatican's embassies work is weighed in Part Five. [scene:vt5_soft_power|Soft power] It is a companion to The Divine 3+1, The Theology Shield, Road to 1948 and Greater Israel.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Question: Refusal or Front?
chapters.intro: Part One states the question this volume exists to answer: whether the Holy See's public refusal of Zionism, from Pius X's "Non possumus" to Theodor Herzl in January 1904 until the Fundamental Agreement with Israel of 30 December 1993, was a real policy or a front for private support. It sets out the public record of that refusal and its end, turns the front hypothesis already framed in The Divine 3+1 into five tests that can be checked against the private record, the timing of the Holy See's changes of position, its treaties, the flow of money and favours, and the cost of its opposition, and fixes in advance what result would count for each side. It then explains the volume's vocabulary, separating the Holy See, Vatican City State and the Catholic Church, and Zionism, the State of Israel and Judaism; the few labelled places where interpretation is offered; and the route through the nineteen parts.
chapters.outro: Part One has fixed the question and the terms of the test. The public record is clear at both ends: Herzl's diary records Pius X's refusal in January 1904, Pius XII asked in 1949 for an internationally guaranteed Jerusalem, and the Holy See recognized Israel only by the Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993 and the protocol that opened relations on 15 June 1994, relations still in place as of October 2026. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] [cite:dv1_rnc_1949] [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] [cite:vt1_jvl_protocol1994] [cite:vt1_aleteia_lingua] Whether that refusal was a front will be decided by five tests written before the evidence is weighed: the private record, now open for Pius XII's pontificate to October 1958, the flow of money and favours, the timing of shifts, treaty behaviour, including the neutrality clauses of 1929 and 1993, and the cost of opposition. [cite:vt1_va_archive2019] [cite:vt1_va_lateran] The Holy See, Vatican City State and the Catholic Church are kept apart throughout, as are Zionism, Israel and Judaism, a separation the Holy See's own 1985 Notes drew. [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] The test begins with the sovereign itself, and with the question of why there is a Vatican at all: [scene:vt2_papal_states|Part Two] starts with the papal state of the eighth century.

sections.h: The Question
sections.html:
This volume asks one question and answers it as far as the documents allow. For almost ninety years the Holy See publicly refused Zionism. It refused the movement when Theodor Herzl asked a pope for support in January 1904, it argued for an international Jerusalem when the United Nations divided Palestine in 1947, and it declined to recognize the State of Israel from 1948 until it signed the Fundamental Agreement in Jerusalem on 30 December 1993. The question is whether that refusal was what it appeared to be, a real policy with real costs, or a front: a public position that covered private support. Everything else in the book, from the origins of the papal state to its bank, its courts and its archives, is here because it bears on that question or on the questions a reader has to settle before it can be answered fairly.

The refusal, in the Holy See's own record

The refusal begins with a conversation known from a single source. Herzl's diary entry dated 26 January 1904 opens "Yesterday I was with the Pope", and records Pius X's answer to his request: "We cannot prevent the Jews from going to Jerusalem—but we could never sanction it." The pope gave a theological reason: "The Jews have not recognized our Lord, therefore we cannot recognize the Jewish people." He closed with "Non possumus", the formula of papal refusal, and said that if Jews settled in Palestine the Church would have "churches and priests ready to baptize all of you." The audience had been arranged by Count Berthold Dominik Lippay, a papal portrait painter. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] The account of the audience rests on Herzl's diary alone, so the words are Herzl's account of what he heard; the volume treats them as documented evidence of what Herzl recorded, and as one party's report of what the pope said. [cite:dv1_ej_piusx]

That first refusal fused two different things. One was a political judgment about a movement and about who should hold Jerusalem. The other was a theological statement about the Jewish people. The distinction matters for everything that follows, because the Holy See itself later pulled the two apart. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate of 28 October 1965 said that "God holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers" and that the Passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today"; it said nothing about land or a state. [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] Twenty years later the Holy See's Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews wrote that the existence of the State of Israel and its political options "should be envisaged not in a perspective which is in itself religious, but in their reference to the common principles of international law." [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] From 1985 at the latest, then, the Holy See said in writing that its position on Israel was a matter of diplomacy and law, not doctrine. This volume keeps the two subjects apart in the same way: Zionism is a political movement, Israel is a state, and neither is Judaism.

The political refusal took its clearest form over Jerusalem. The United Nations General Assembly's resolution 181 of 29 November 1947 placed Jerusalem in a corpus separatum "under a special international regime" to be administered by the United Nations, and the Holy See supported that internationalization. [cite:vt1_wiki_corpus] When the war of 1948 divided the city instead, Pius XII's encyclical Redemptoris nostri cruciatus of 15 April 1949 asked that Jerusalem be "accorded and legally guaranteed an 'international' status" and urged Catholics to press their governments for it. [cite:dv1_rnc_1949] The State of Israel, proclaimed on 14 May 1948, was not recognized by the Holy See for the next forty-five years. [cite:vt17_jcpa_schvindlerman] [cite:vt1_va_fa1993]

The end of the refusal

The Fundamental Agreement was signed in Jerusalem on 30 December 1993 by Monsignor Claudio Celli for the Holy See and Yossi Beilin, Israel's deputy foreign minister. Its Article 14 provided for the exchange of special representatives at once and for full diplomatic relations, at the level of an apostolic nunciature and an embassy, once the agreement was in force. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] A joint protocol signed in Jerusalem on 14 June 1994 established those relations from 15 June. [cite:vt1_jvl_protocol1994] The same agreement also contained a clause that any test of the front hypothesis has to read closely. In Article 11 the Holy See, while keeping the right to teach on moral questions, declared itself "solemnly committed to remaining a stranger to all merely temporal conflicts", a principle that "applies specifically to disputed territories and unsettled borders." [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] That language echoes Article 24 of the Lateran Treaty of 1929, in which the Holy See declared that it would remain outside the temporal disputes of other states unless they jointly asked for its mediation. [cite:vt1_va_lateran]

Recognition did not end the Holy See's separate dealings with the Palestinians. On 26 June 2015 Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Holy See's Secretary for Relations with States, and Riad Malki, foreign minister of the State of Palestine, signed a Comprehensive Agreement at the Vatican on the life and activity of the Church in Palestine. [cite:vt1_rv_palestine2015] Israel's foreign ministry called the Holy See's recognition of Palestine one-sided. [cite:ts11_wiki_hspal]

As of 21 October 2026 the relations established in 1994 remained in place. On 4 September 2025 Pope Leo XIV, elected on 8 May 2025, received President Isaac Herzog; the Holy See's statement called for the release of all hostages, a permanent ceasefire in Gaza and humanitarian access, and repeated that "a two-state solution is the only way out of the current war." [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican] [cite:vt1_vn_herzog2025] On 22 January 2026 Leo XIV named Archbishop Giorgio Lingua apostolic nuncio to Israel and apostolic delegate in Jerusalem and Palestine. [cite:vt1_aleteia_lingua] Those contacts continued after Israeli fire struck the Holy Family church compound in Gaza City on 17 July 2025, killing three people; Netanyahu expressed regret over "stray ammunition", while the Latin Patriarch, Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa, said he believed a tank shell had hit the church directly, adding that he was not sure. [cite:ts11_ncr_holyfamily] [cite:vt1_audit_ncr_holyfamily] Part Eighteen sets out that record and asks why the Holy See has spoken so strongly and yet not suspended relations.

Why the other questions belong here

A reader cannot judge whether a sovereign's public position was a front without knowing what kind of sovereign it is, how it makes decisions, where its money comes from and goes, and what it keeps out of view. That is why the volume begins not in 1904 but with the papal state of the eighth century and the settlement of 1929 that created Vatican City, and why it spends whole parts on the Holy See's bank, its courts, its archives, its handling of abuse and the unsolved disappearance of Emanuela Orlandi. Each of those subjects is a place where the public face of the institution and its private conduct can be compared on the documents, and the comparison shows how far, and in which matters, the Holy See's public statements have been a reliable guide to what it did. The record on Zionism is then read against that background, in Parts Sixteen to Eighteen, and the verdict is given in Part Nineteen.

sections.h: What a Front Would Look Like
sections.html:
The front hypothesis has already been stated in this library in its strongest form: that the Holy See's refusal of Zionism was a public facade, that it was connected to the project from the start, and that it kept its support out of view so that no one would question it. [scene:dv1_three_functions|The Divine 3+1, Part One] sets that hypothesis out and names the three predictions that make it testable: the private record should contradict the public one, money or favours should flow from the Holy See to the movement or the state, and public opposition should never have cost the movement anything it needed. This section turns the three predictions into specific things a reader can look for in the documents, adds the two tests the Holy See's own record makes possible, the timing of its changes of position and its behaviour in treaties, and sets out in advance what result would count for each side.

A hypothesis about concealment is easy to keep alive by reading every fact as part of the cover; a test written before the evidence is weighed prevents that. Each test below names an observation that would favour the front reading and one that would favour the reading that the refusal was real policy, and each can also come back empty because the papers are closed or because both readings predict the same thing. All three results are reported in Part Nineteen.

Test one: the private record

If the refusal was a front, the Holy See's internal papers should show its diplomats encouraging in private what they opposed in public: instructions to nuncios to go easy on the Zionist case, assurances given to Zionist or Israeli envoys and kept from Catholic governments, or internal memoranda that treat the public line as presentation. If the refusal was real, the internal papers should match the public line or be harder than it, and private warmth should appear only where it also appears in public.

Two bodies of Holy See papers bear on this. The first is the eleven-volume edition of wartime documents, Actes et documents du Saint Siège relatifs à la Seconde Guerre mondiale, authorized by Paul VI in 1964 and published from 1965 to 1981 by four Jesuit historians; critics questioned whether it was selective, and its editor Pierre Blet replied that the editors "did not deliberately overlook any significant document." [cite:vt1_wiki_adss] The second is the archive of Pius XII's whole pontificate, which Pope Francis announced on 4 March 2019 would open to researchers on 2 March 2020, saying "The Church is not afraid of history." [cite:vt1_va_archive2019] Those files run to Pius XII's death on 9 October 1958. [cite:vt1_va_archive2019] The years from 1958 to 1993, which include Nostra Aetate and the negotiation of the Fundamental Agreement, lie beyond that line, and Part Fourteen sets out what researchers can and cannot see for them.

A third kind of private record is the account kept by the other side. Herzl's diary of 1904 is one; reports by later Zionist envoys of their audiences in Rome are others. These are real documents and some of them record more warmth than the Holy See's public line. They are also, by their nature, one party's account of a private conversation, written by envoys reporting to their own colleagues on the success of their missions. Such reports are evidence of what the envoy wrote; a claim resting on them alone remains disputed, and a second record is needed before they can be treated as evidence of what the pope intended.

Test two: money and favours

If the refusal was a front, something of value should have passed from the Holy See to the Zionist movement or to Israel: funds, loans, land, diplomatic cover at a decisive vote, or pressure on Catholic governments to support what the Holy See publicly opposed. If the refusal was real, no such transfer should appear, and the documented transfers should run the other way or not at all. The best-known financial link, the Rothschild loans to the Papal States from the 1830s, runs from a bank to a pope, more than sixty years before Herzl, and [scene:vt11_papal_loans|Part Eleven] examines what the loan documents show and what has been added to them without documents. A banker's later appointment to a Vatican board is a fact about a career, not a transfer of value to a state, and [scene:vt11_pauly_2026|the 2026 appointment] is tested on that basis.

Test three: the timing of shifts

The Holy See's public position did change, in 1965, in 1985 and in 1993. If the refusal was a front, the changes should track the movement's needs: softening when Zionism or Israel needed support and hardening only when it cost nothing. If the refusal was real policy, the changes should track the Holy See's own stated interests, which its documents name repeatedly: Jerusalem and the holy places, the legal security of Catholic institutions and communities, and its standing as a neutral party. The Fundamental Agreement itself records a negotiating agenda agreed in Jerusalem on 15 July 1992 and confirmed at the Vatican on 29 July 1992, so the timing of the final step can be read against what that agenda covered and what was happening in the region at the time. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] Parts Sixteen and Seventeen date every shift against both sets of interests.

Test four: treaty behaviour

Treaties are the best evidence of a sovereign's real commitments, because they bind it and they are published. If the refusal was a front, the Holy See's treaties with Israel should give Israel more than the public line would suggest, for instance on Jerusalem or on borders. If the refusal was real, the treaties should protect the interests the Holy See had named in public and should not concede what it had refused. Two clauses, sixty-four years apart, say the same thing. In Article 24 of the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929 the Holy See declared that it would remain outside the temporal disputes of other states unless they jointly appealed to it, while keeping its moral and spiritual authority. [cite:vt1_va_lateran] In Article 11 of the Fundamental Agreement of 1993 it committed itself to "remaining a stranger to all merely temporal conflicts", a principle that "applies specifically to disputed territories and unsettled borders." [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] Those clauses do not by themselves decide the question. They are what a genuinely neutral sovereign would sign, and also what a covert partner might sign to avoid taking a public side. What separates the readings is what else the treaties contain and how the Holy See behaved under them, including its separate agreement with the State of Palestine in 2015. [cite:vt1_rv_palestine2015]

Test five: the cost of opposition

The third of the predictions in the earlier volume is perhaps the sharpest. A front costs its holder little: it is words that leave the other side's interests untouched. A real policy spends something: influence used against the other side at a moment that mattered, complaints from that side's leaders, and traces in the files of governments that were lobbied. The test therefore asks what the Holy See's opposition actually cost the movement and Israel at each point, and what it cost the Holy See to keep it up.

A comparison helps keep the result in proportion. Non-recognition is not proof of hostility, and recognition is not proof of alliance. The United States and the Holy See did not establish full diplomatic relations until 10 January 1984, under Ronald Reagan and John Paul II, more than a century after its consular relations with the Papal States, and its minister in Rome, ended in 1870. [cite:vt1_state_holysee] The Holy See's long withholding of relations from Israel has to be read against its practice with other states, not in isolation.

What will not count

Some things often offered as evidence cannot distinguish the two readings. Convergence is not coordination: the fact that a pope and a Zionist leader wanted the same thing at the same moment, for different reasons, shows a shared interest, not a shared plan. Adjacency is not evidence: a banker who once worked for a Rothschild house, or a cardinal who dined with a Zionist envoy, is a fact about two careers until a document shows a transaction. The views of individual Catholics, Catholic politicians or Catholic commentators are not acts of the Holy See, in either direction. And the long antisemitic tradition of claiming that Jewish financiers control the papacy, which the library has met before, is a claim to be named and tested where it arises in Part Eleven, never a premise. A finding of "checked, nothing documented" is a result, and it is reported as one.

sections.h: How to Read This Volume
sections.html:
A book about the Vatican has to settle its words before it can settle anything else, because the same word is used in the press for three different things and many of the errors this volume corrects begin with that confusion. This section sets out the vocabulary, the few places where the volume offers an interpretation, and the route through its nineteen parts.

Three subjects, not one

The Holy See is the sovereign authority of the pope as head of the Catholic Church, and it is the subject of international law: it makes treaties, sends and receives ambassadors and has been a permanent observer at the United Nations since 6 April 1964. [cite:dv1_wiki_holysee_un] The Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929 recorded Italy's recognition of "the sovereignty of the Holy See in the international field" as an attribute inherent to its nature. [cite:vt1_va_lateran] As of January 2026 it had full diplomatic relations with 184 states, the European Union and the Sovereign Order of Malta. [cite:dv1_dfat_holysee] When this volume describes a recognition, a refusal or a treaty, the actor is the Holy See, and usually its Secretariat of State.

Vatican City State is the territory: the small enclave in Rome created by the same treaty, in which Italy recognized the Holy See's "full ownership and exclusive and absolute power and sovereign jurisdiction." [cite:vt1_va_lateran] It is an elective absolute monarchy in which the pope holds legislative, executive and judicial power, and it had 882 residents in 2024. [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican] Its government, courts, police, post office and museums belong to the City State. The Holy See existed for centuries before 1929 and does not depend on the City State for its legal personality; the City State exists to give the Holy See a territory it does not have to share with any other sovereign. [scene:dv1_sovereignty|The Divine 3+1] applies the standard tests of statehood to it, and [scene:vt4_holy_see_vs_city|Part Four] sets out how the two are run.

The Catholic Church is a worldwide communion of believers organized in dioceses, religious orders, parishes, schools, hospitals and charities, most of which are separate legal persons under the law of the countries where they stand. A diocese in Pennsylvania or an order's university in Spain is not the Holy See, and its property and its debts are not the Holy See's. This volume writes "the Church" only where the subject really is the whole Church, as in the acts of a council. Elsewhere it names the body that acted: the Secretariat of State, the Institute for the Works of Religion, a named nuncio, a named bishop, a named order. "The Vatican" is used only for the place, or where a quoted source uses it.

The same care applies to the other side of the central question. Zionism is a political movement; the State of Israel is a state; Judaism is a religion, and Jews are a people with every range of view on all three. The Holy See's own documents have come to separate them. Its 1985 Notes asked Catholics to understand the Jewish religious attachment to the land "without however making their own any particular religious interpretation of this relationship", and placed the State of Israel under "the common principles of international law." [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] This volume follows that separation. A pope's teaching about the Jewish people and the Holy See's policy toward a state are different subjects, and the volume never writes "the Jews" where a document speaks of the Zionist Organization, the State of Israel or a named person.

Myths, and where interpretation is allowed

Much of what is written about the Vatican online repeats claims that have no documentary basis: a "Grey Pope" said to rule both the pope and the head of the Jesuits, an unbroken chain of Rothschild control over papal finance from 1831 to the present, a single family descended from antiquity standing behind the throne. This volume does not ignore such claims. It names each one, dates its first appearance, follows the chain of sources it rests on and shows where the chain breaks, in [scene:vt6_grey_pope_myth|Part Six] and [scene:vt11_chain_tested|Part Eleven]. Where a claim belongs to an antisemitic tradition, as the claim that Jewish bankers control the papacy does, the volume says so.

A small number of interpretive readings appear because they are part of how the subject has been discussed, including on the Sophia platform: the wordplay that reads the bank's initials, IOR, backwards; the description of the Holy See as an operating system written in code; the line of imperial succession some writers draw from Babylon to Rome; the "loud silence" said to link papal reticence in different eras; and the philosophical argument that an institution offering a promise no one can verify must protect itself. Each appears under a subhead that begins "Interpretation, not finding" and is attributed to whoever holds it.

The route through the volume

The nineteen parts fall into six groups. Parts Two to Five explain what kind of sovereign the Holy See is: why there is a Vatican at all, from the papal state of 754 to the pacts of 1929 ([scene:vt2_papal_states|Part Two]); what each side gained in 1929 and what the deal still costs Italy ([scene:vt3_what_each_got|Part Three]); how the City State is actually governed ([scene:vt4_fundamental_law|Part Four]); and who recognizes and checks its sovereignty ([scene:vt5_recognition|Part Five]). Parts Six to Eight turn to people and orders: popes, the Roman Curia and the myths of hidden popes ([scene:vt6_curia_2022|Part Six]); the old Roman aristocracy and the Orsini ([scene:vt7_black_nobility|Part Seven]); and the Jesuits, Opus Dei and the Order of Malta ([scene:vt8_jesuits|Part Eight]).

Parts Nine to Eleven follow the money: the Institute for the Works of Religion, the property administration and Peter's Pence ([scene:vt9_ior|Part Nine]); the scandals from Banco Ambrosiano to the trial over the London property and the appeal court's order of 2026 to rehear it ([scene:vt10_ambrosiano_calvi|Part Ten]); and what the documents show about Rome and the Rothschilds ([scene:vt11_papal_loans|Part Eleven]). Parts Twelve to Fifteen test the Holy See where its public statements and its conduct have most often diverged: clergy sexual abuse and its cover-up ([scene:vt12_the_rules|Part Twelve]); its reach through schools, universities and the appointment of bishops ([scene:vt13_schools|Part Thirteen]); its texts and archives ([scene:vt14_apostolic_archive|Part Fourteen]); and the disappearances of Emanuela Orlandi and Mirella Gregori in 1983 ([scene:vt15_the_case|Part Fifteen]).

Parts Sixteen to Eighteen give the record on Zionism and Israel in order: from Herzl's audience to the end of the Second World War ([scene:vt16_herzl_1904|Part Sixteen]); from the Jerusalem campaign of 1947–49 to recognition in 1993 ([scene:vt17_jerusalem_1947_49|Part Seventeen]); and from 1994 to the Gaza war and the present ([scene:vt18_relations_since_1994|Part Eighteen]). [scene:vt19_predictions_tested|Part Nineteen] applies the five tests of the previous section to that record and gives the verdict, with what remains open.

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: Why There Is a Vatican: 754 to 1929
chapters.intro: Part Two answers the first set of questions this volume takes up: why there is a Vatican at all, who designed it, who paid for it, and who controlled it then and now. It begins with the grant of Italian territory by the Frankish king Pippin to Pope Stephen II in 754–756, the forged Donation of Constantine that later decorated that grant, and the eleven centuries in which the popes ruled a clerical state across central Italy. It follows the collapse of that state from the Roman Republic of 1849 to the Italian capture of Rome on 20 September 1870, the Law of Guarantees that Pius IX refused, and the fifty-nine years in which the popes would not leave the Vatican. It ends with the Lateran Pacts of 11 February 1929: the motives each side stated or was credited with, the men who drafted the texts, the money Italy paid, the Catholic party that had already been dissolved, and the line of control that runs from Pius XI to Leo XIV.
chapters.outro: Part Two established that the papal state began as a documented exchange, Pippin's grant of 756 in return for religious legitimacy, later dressed in a forged imperial title that Lorenzo Valla exposed in 1440. [cite:vt2_britannica_pippin] [cite:vt2_britannica_constantine] That state lasted only as long as Catholic armies defended it: Austria put down the revolts of 1830 and 1848, France restored Pius IX in 1849 and left Rome in 1870. [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates] [cite:vt2_wiki_romanrep1849] Pius IX refused Italy's unilateral Law of Guarantees and its endowment, and his successors stayed inside the Vatican for fifty-nine years. [cite:vt2_ce_guarantees] [cite:vt2_ewtn_ubinos] [cite:vt2_wiki_prisoner] The Lateran Pacts of 11 February 1929 were designed by named people, Pius XI, Cardinal Gasparri and the lawyer Francesco Pacelli, with Mussolini on the other side. Italy paid 750 million lire in cash and 1 billion lire in 5 per cent bonds, and recognised the Holy See's sovereignty in exchange for recognition of Rome as Italy's capital. [cite:vt2_lateran_text] [cite:vt2_vn_pacelli2019] The Catholic Partito Popolare had already been dissolved under the fascist laws of November 1926, and Article 43 of the Concordat kept Catholic Action out of party politics. [cite:vt2_wiki_ppi] [cite:vt2_museo_cronologia] Control of the money passed from Nogara's Special Administration to APSA, and sovereign power passed from Pius XI to Leo XIV under fundamental laws of 1929, 2000, 2023 and 2026. [cite:vt2_wiki_specialadmin] [cite:vt2_open_fundlaw2023] [cite:vt2_sussidiario_fundlaw2026] Part Three takes the 1929 deal clause by clause and follows each part of it, the Concordat, the clergy's funding and the tax exemptions, to the present. [scene:vt3_what_each_got|Part Three: the 1929 deal, then and now]

sections.h: A State Before the State: The Papal States, 754–1870
sections.html:
The Vatican City of today is 44 hectares created by a treaty in 1929. [scene:dv1_three_cities|Part One of The Divine 3+1: the three cities measured] The popes, however, had governed territory for more than eleven centuries before that treaty, and the 1929 settlement makes sense only as the end of that older story. Its own Financial Convention says so: the money Italy paid in 1929 was compensation for "the events of 1870," the year the last of the papal territory was taken. [cite:vt2_lateran_text] This section traces how a bishop of Rome came to rule a state in central Italy, how large that state was, how it was run, and why it was already failing well before Italian troops entered Rome.

The bargain with the Franks, 754–756

The usual starting point is a meeting between a pope and a king. In January 754 Pope Stephen II crossed the Alps and met the Frankish king Pippin (Pepin the Short) at the palace of Ponthion. The Lombard king Aistulf had seized Ravenna and was pressing on Rome, and the Byzantine emperor, nominally the lord of both, was not coming to help. At Quierzy in April 754 Pippin promised to restore to the pope the lands the Lombards had taken; no record of that promise survives. The same year Stephen anointed Pippin and his sons, Charlemagne and Carloman, as kings, giving the new Carolingian dynasty a sanction it needed after Pippin had deposed the last Merovingian king in 750. [cite:vt2_britannica_pippin]

Pippin kept his side. He invaded Italy in 755 and 756, defeated Aistulf and imposed a peace. In 756 the keys of the cities that had submitted, with a list of them, were laid on the altar of Old St Peter's. Papal accounts say the grant covered the former Byzantine exarchate, including Ravenna, and the duchy of Rome. Britannica notes that much of it was imperial territory "to which Pippin had no clear legal claim." Charlemagne and later Louis the Pious, in 817, confirmed the donation. [cite:vt2_britannica_pippin] Britannica dates the Papal States from 756 to 1870. [cite:vt2_britannica_pippin] (Some popular timelines give 752 for the donation; the documented dates are 754 for the promise and 756 for the grant.)

The answer to "why did a church get a state" is therefore a specific exchange, not a mystery. A Frankish dynasty wanted religious legitimacy; a papacy without an army wanted a protector against the Lombards and independence from Constantinople. Each gave the other what it lacked. [cite:vt2_britannica_pippin]

The forged title deed

A second, older-sounding title soon appeared beside the real one. The Donation of Constantine claims to record the emperor Constantine granting Pope Sylvester I primacy over the great sees of Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople and Jerusalem, together with the imperial palace in Rome and "the regions of the Western Empire." It was written by an unknown author in the eighth century, most likely in the 750s or 760s, the same decades as Pippin's grant; its earliest surviving manuscript is from the ninth century. Leo IX (1049–54) was the first pope to cite it in an official act, and later popes used it against emperors and kings. [cite:vt2_britannica_constantine]

Doubts were raised around the year 1000 in the circle of the emperor Otto III. In 1440 the humanist Lorenzo Valla proved the document a forgery by showing that its Latin was not the Latin of Constantine's century. [cite:vt2_britannica_constantine] The forgery matters to this volume for a narrow reason. The papacy's claim to temporal power rested in part, for several centuries, on a fabricated document, and the case against that document was made on evidence of language and date. The real foundation, Pippin's grant, stands on its own record; the forged one fell to a philologist.

Extent and government

The territory changed size often. At its fullest it covered most of modern Lazio, Umbria and the Marche and part of Emilia-Romagna, a band across the middle of Italy from the Tyrrhenian to the Adriatic. [cite:vt2_britannica_pippin] During most of the fourteenth century the popes lived at Avignon, and Avignon and the surrounding Comtat Venaissin were added to their holdings. In Italy, local lords and cities slipped out of papal control, and on 29 April 1357 Cardinal Gil Álvarez Carrillo de Albornoz, sent as legate with a mercenary force, issued the Constitutiones Aegidianae, a single civil code for the state that stayed in force until 1816. Alexander VI and Julius II, the "warrior pope," reasserted papal control over autonomous fiefs by war, and Parma and Piacenza were annexed in 1512. [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates]

The state was governed by clergy. The pope was an elective absolute monarch; the major provinces, the legations, were run by cardinal legates, and the central administration worked through congregations led by cardinals. [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates] Before 1859 the state covered about 44,000 square kilometres, a thousand times the size of today's Vatican City, and a census of 1853 counted 3,124,668 inhabitants. [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates]

Revolution and restoration, 1796–1850

The French Revolution broke the arrangement. Napoleon annexed the Marche to his Kingdom of Italy on 2 April 1808 and, on 17 May 1809, made Rome and the rest of the state into French departments. The Congress of Vienna restored the Italian territories in 1815 but not Avignon. The restored clerical government faced revolts in 1830 and 1848, aimed at what opponents saw as a corrupt administration run by priests, and Austrian troops put them down. [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates]

The crisis of 1848–49 showed how far papal rule now depended on foreign armies. On 15 November 1848 Pius IX's chief minister, Pellegrino Rossi, was assassinated; on the night of 24 November the pope fled to Gaeta in the Kingdom of Naples. A Constituent Assembly elected by universal male suffrage on 21 January 1849 proclaimed the Roman Republic on 9 February 1849, and from late March it was led by a triumvirate of Carlo Armellini, Giuseppe Mazzini and Aurelio Saffi. Its constitution abolished the death penalty and guaranteed freedom of religion while leaving the pope his spiritual government. Pius IX appealed to the Catholic powers. French troops under General Oudinot landed at Civitavecchia on 25 April 1849, and after a siege entered Rome on 3 July 1849. Pius IX returned in April 1850. [cite:vt2_wiki_romanrep1849] [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates]

From then on a French garrison held Rome for the pope. In 1860 the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia conquered the eastern two-thirds of the state, much of it already in revolt; by November 1860 Bologna, Ferrara, Umbria, the Marche, Benevento and Pontecorvo had been annexed. Only Rome and Lazio remained. In March 1861 the first Italian parliament declared Rome the capital of a kingdom that could not yet enter it, because French troops stood in the way. [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates] How that ended is the subject of the next section. [scene:vt2_roman_question|The Roman Question, 1870–1929]

The record so far answers the first of this volume's questions in plain terms. The papacy held a state because a Frankish king granted one in 756 in exchange for religious legitimacy, because a forged document later lent that state an imperial pedigree, and because, from 1815 onward, Catholic powers were willing to defend it with their armies. When Austria and then France stopped doing so, the state fell. [cite:vt2_britannica_pippin] [cite:vt2_britannica_constantine] [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates]

sections.h: The Roman Question: Porta Pia to the Prisoner Years, 1870–1929
sections.html:
For fifty-nine years after 1870 the bishop of Rome lived inside a city that belonged to a state he refused to recognise. Italians called the dispute the "Roman Question." The Lateran Treaty of 1929 named it in those words and declared it "definitively and irrevocably settled and therefore eliminated." [cite:vt2_lateran_text] This section sets out how the dispute began, what Italy offered in 1871, why Pius IX refused it, and how the refusal shaped papal conduct and Catholic politics until 1929.

20 September 1870

The French garrison was what had kept Rome papal after 1860. When the Franco-Prussian War broke out in July 1870, Napoleon III recalled it, and the French defeat at Sedan removed any prospect of its return. Italy offered to send troops into Rome on the pretext of protecting the pope; Pius IX refused. Italy declared war on 10 September 1870. Its army crossed the frontier the next day and reached the Aurelian Walls on 19 September. [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates_rq]

On 20 September Italian artillery opened a breach beside the Porta Pia, in a stretch of wall in poor repair, and the city was taken. Papal resistance was token. The stated reason was that Pius IX wanted the record to show that Italy had taken Rome by force and not with his consent. A plebiscite followed in October, and the annexation of Rome to the Kingdom of Italy is dated 9 October 1870. [cite:vt2_wiki_papalstates_rq] That choice, to lose visibly rather than to negotiate, set the pattern for the next half-century: the Holy See preserved its legal claim by refusing every arrangement that implied acceptance of the loss.

The Law of Guarantees, 13 May 1871

Italy needed to show Catholic governments abroad that the pope would remain free to govern the Church. It could have convened an international congress on the pope's status, but Catholic governments showed no interest, so the Italian parliament legislated on its own. The Law of Guarantees, passed on 13 May 1871, declared the pope's person "sacred and inviolable," granted him royal honours and guards, left him the use of the Vatican and Lateran palaces and the villa at Castel Gandolfo, guaranteed free communication with the Catholic world and the freedom of a conclave, and assigned him an annual endowment of 3,225,000 lire. [cite:vt2_ce_guarantees] The law did not recognise papal sovereignty over any territory: the palaces remained, in Italian law, Italian. [cite:vt2_ce_guarantees]

Pius IX rejected it. Two days after its passage, in the encyclical Ubi Nos of 15 May 1871, he wrote that he "never can and never shall allow or accept those 'guarantees' devised by the Piedmont Government." His argument was that only civil sovereignty could secure the Church's freedom: Providence had given the popes civil rule so that the pope "may never be subject to any ruler or civil power." [cite:vt2_ewtn_ubinos] A privilege granted by an Italian statute could be withdrawn by another Italian statute; that was the core of the objection, and the later popes repeated it. [cite:vt2_wiki_prisoner] Pius IX expressly refused the endowment on 13 November 1872. Neither he nor his two successors ever drew on it, and the Holy See lived instead on donations from Catholics abroad. [cite:vt2_ce_guarantees]

The prisoner years

The popes of the period described themselves as prisoners of the Italian state. In practice this meant a self-imposed confinement. Pius IX, Leo XIII, Pius X, Benedict XV and Pius XI, until 1929, did not set foot outside the Vatican. They did not appear on the loggia of St Peter's facing the square, which lay in Italian Rome; the blessing Urbi et Orbi was given from a balcony facing an inner courtyard or from inside the basilica, and papal coronations were held in the Sistine Chapel. Pius IX had excommunicated King Victor Emmanuel II. [cite:vt2_wiki_prisoner] No physical barrier held the popes in; the confinement was a legal statement made with the body of the pope, and it lasted fifty-nine years. [cite:vt2_wiki_prisoner]

The same refusal applied to Catholic voters. Under the non expedit ("it is not expedient"), adopted by the Holy See in 1868 and confirmed by Pius IX in 1874, Italian Catholics were not to take part in national politics, summed up as "neither elected nor electors." Pius X largely relaxed the ban in 1904–05 to improve relations with the government, and Benedict XV formally lifted it in 1919, when he approved the new Partito Popolare Italiano (PPI). [cite:vt2_britannica_nonexpedit] The PPI took 20.5 per cent of the vote and 100 seats in 1919 and 108 seats in 1921. [cite:vt2_wiki_ppi] For the first time since unification a mass Catholic party sat in parliament; within seven years it had been destroyed, and how that happened is part of the story of the 1929 deal. [scene:vt2_pacts_signed|The pacts signed, 1929]

What the dispute was and was not

Two misreadings of the period circulate in popular accounts. The first is that the Vatican has been "a sovereign enclave since the fourth century." The record does not support it. The papacy held a territorial state from 756 to 1870; from 1870 to 1929 it held no territory at all in its own understanding of the law, only palaces whose use an Italian statute granted and which the pope refused to accept on those terms. [cite:vt2_britannica_pippin] [cite:vt2_ce_guarantees] Whether the Holy See itself remained a subject of international law in those years is a separate question, examined in Part One of The Divine 3+1; the Lateran Treaty later described its sovereignty "in the international field" as "an attribute inherent to its nature," not a gift of Italy. [cite:vt2_lateran_text] [scene:dv1_sovereignty|The Divine 3+1: the tests of sovereignty]

The second misreading is that the popes were literally held captive. They were not. They chose not to leave so as not to appear to accept Italian rule over Rome, and the Italian state had offered them guarantees they declined. [cite:vt2_wiki_prisoner] [cite:vt2_ce_guarantees] The Holy See's stated position at the time was that any arrangement short of sovereignty would leave the head of a worldwide Church subject to one government; Italy's position was that its law gave the pope everything he needed except a state. The 1929 settlement split the difference: Italy conceded sovereignty, and the pope accepted that the sovereignty would be very small.

The end of the prisoner years was staged as deliberately as their beginning. On 25 July 1929, seven weeks after the treaty took effect, Pius XI led a eucharistic procession into St Peter's Square. The New York Times reported the next day that the pope had left the Vatican for the first time in 59 years, watched by 300,000 people. [cite:vt2_umich_procession1929] After the treaty the popes resumed visits to the Lateran basilica and summers at Castel Gandolfo. [cite:vt2_wiki_prisoner]

sections.h: The Pacts Signed: Who Designed the 1929 Deal, Who Paid, Who Controlled It
sections.html:
On 11 February 1929, in the Lateran Palace, Cardinal Pietro Gasparri, Secretary of State, signed for Pius XI and Benito Mussolini, "Prime Minister and Head of Government," signed for King Victor Emmanuel III. They signed three instruments: a Treaty of 27 articles that created the State of Vatican City and closed the Roman Question, a Concordat of 45 articles that governed the Church's position inside Italy, and a Financial Convention that settled the money. Ratifications were exchanged in the Apostolic Palace on 7 June 1929, and the new state existed from that day. [cite:vt2_lateran_text] [cite:vt2_vn_dallatorre2019] This section covers why both sides wanted the deal, who designed it, who paid, and who controlled the result then and now; Part Three follows the terms to the present. [scene:vt3_what_each_got|Part Three: what each side got]

Why the pope wanted it, in his own words

Pius XI explained the deal twice in the week it was signed. On 11 February, to the parish priests of Rome, he said the territory he had asked for was "very little, very very little, the least possible," and compared it to the minimum of body needed to keep a soul attached. Asking for little, he said, was meant to show that no earthly greed drove the request. He defended the money on the same ground: the Holy See "has the right to provide for its own economic independence." [cite:vt2_pius11_19290211]

Two days later, on 13 February 1929, he told professors and students of the Università Cattolica in Milan that the pacts had "given God back to Italy and Italy to God," and added a sentence about Mussolini that has followed the papacy since: "perhaps also a man was needed like the one Providence has caused us to meet." [cite:vt2_pius11_19290213] The phrase is usually shortened to "the man of Providence." In context it credits Mussolini with making the settlement possible; it is not, on its face, an endorsement of fascism as a doctrine. The historian David Kertzer reads it more broadly: in his account Pius XI came to see Mussolini as the leader who might reverse the Church's losses since 1870 and as "the best bet, perhaps, to prevent a socialist takeover of Italy." [cite:vt2_npr_kertzer2014]

Why Mussolini wanted it

Mussolini had been, in Kertzer's words, "a committed anti-cleric." Once in power from 1922 he came to see the value of the pope's support: fascist rallies opened with Mass, and religious instruction in schools was one of his early gestures toward the Church. In Kertzer's judgement the Church lent the regime "organizational strength and moral legitimacy." [cite:vt2_npr_kertzer2014] The treaty text records what the Italian state gained in law. The Holy See recognised "the Kingdom of Italy under the dynasty of the House of Savoy with Rome as capital of the Italian State," declared the Roman Question eliminated, and accepted the repeal of the 1871 Law of Guarantees (Art. 26). [cite:vt2_lateran_text]

Who designed it

The negotiation ran from 1926 to 1929 and was conducted for the Holy See by a layman. Francesco Pacelli, a lawyer and professor born in 1874, led the talks with the Italian government at Pius XI's wish from 1926. [cite:vt2_vn_pacelli2019] He reported to the pope in more than two hundred long audiences while the text passed through some twenty successive drafts. [cite:vt2_wiki_fpacelli] Gasparri directed the Holy See's side and signed. Francesco's brother, Eugenio Pacelli, then nuncio in Germany and later Secretary of State and Pius XII, was not a negotiator; Francesco kept up a private correspondence with him about the talks. Francesco's own account is his Diario della Conciliazione, published in 1959. [cite:vt2_vn_pacelli2019]

Pacelli also drafted the new state's internal law. With the jurist Federico Cammeo he prepared the first laws of Vatican City, issued on 7 June 1929. He was rewarded with a seat as general counsellor of the state and, by papal brief of 9 June 1929, the hereditary title of marquess. [cite:vt2_vn_pacelli2019] [cite:vt2_wiki_fpacelli] The design is documented to named people: Pius XI, Gasparri, Francesco Pacelli and, on the other side, Mussolini.

The party that was gone before the deal

A claim repeated in popular accounts says the deal included "the dissolution of the Catholic Centre Party." Both halves are wrong. Italy's Catholic party was the Partito Popolare Italiano, founded by the priest Luigi Sturzo in January 1919; the Centre Party (Zentrum) was German, and its fate belongs to the 1933 Reichskonkordat, a separate treaty. [cite:vt2_wiki_ppi] And the PPI was not dissolved by the Lateran Pacts. Sturzo resigned as its leader on 10 July 1923 after consulting the Holy See, following Mussolini's threats of reprisals against the clergy, and left for exile in London on 25 October 1924, an exit Gasparri arranged. [cite:vt2_wiki_sturzo] The party itself was dissolved on 5 November 1926 under the "most fascist laws," which made the National Fascist Party the only party, suppressed freedom of association and the press and created a special tribunal. [cite:vt2_wiki_ppi] [cite:vt2_museo_cronologia] That was twenty-seven months before the pacts were signed.

The Holy See's role in the PPI's decline is contested. The historian John Molony argued that the fascist state and the Vatican "worked hand in hand to help destroy the People's Party." Other accounts describe Pius XI's stance as ambiguous, and Sturzo as a priest already inclined to step aside. [cite:vt2_wiki_ppi] [cite:vt2_wiki_sturzo] What the documents establish is the sequence: the party's founder stepped down after consulting the Holy See and left Italy with Gasparri's help, the regime then dissolved the party, and the negotiations went ahead with no Catholic political party left in Italy.

The Concordat then wrote that outcome into law. Article 43 recognised the organisations of Azione Cattolica (Catholic Action) on condition that they act "outside any political party," and barred clergy and religious from joining or campaigning for any party. [cite:vt2_lateran_text] The clause did not end the friction. In 1931 the regime's police dissolved Catholic youth and university associations, and Pius XI answered with the encyclical Non abbiamo bisogno of 29 June 1931, accusing the regime of seeking to "monopolize completely the young," of "a real pagan worship of the State," and declaring the fascist oath, as it stood, "unlawful." [cite:vt2_pius11_nonabbiamo] The deal was a settlement between two powers, not a merger.

Who paid, and how much

The Italian state paid, from public funds. Article 1 of the Financial Convention obliged Italy to pay the Holy See 750,000,000 lire in cash on the exchange of ratifications and to hand over, at the same time, 5 per cent Italian state bonds of a nominal value of 1,000,000,000 lire. Article 2 records that the Holy See accepted this as the "definitive settlement" of its financial claims arising from "the events of 1870." The preamble adds that the pope had limited his request "to the strictly necessary," taking account of the state's finances and the economic condition of the Italian people after the war, and that the sum was far lower than what the state would have owed under the 1871 law. [cite:vt2_lateran_text]

Who controlled it then

In 1929 control was concentrated in one man. The pope was sovereign of the new state, and the money went into a body that answered only to him. On 7 June 1929 Pius XI created the Special Administration of the Holy See to manage the Financial Convention funds, reporting directly to the pope, and put Bernardino Nogara in charge; Nogara ran it until 1954. [cite:vt2_wiki_specialadmin] The historian John Pollard records that the endowment transformed papal finances at once, that losses followed within two years, which he attributes to ambitious spending, weak controls and the Wall Street crash. [cite:vt2_pollard1999] Paul VI merged the Special Administration into the new Administration of the Patrimony of the Apostolic See (APSA) in 1967. [cite:vt2_wiki_specialadmin] [scene:vt9_apsa_governorate|Part Nine: APSA and the Governorate]

Who controls it now

The Treaty still stands and was, in the words of Giuseppe Dalla Torre, then president of the Vatican City tribunal, "substantially unchanged" when the Concordat was revised in 1984. [cite:vt2_vn_dallatorre2019] [scene:vt3_concordat_1984|Part Three: the 1984 Concordat] The pope remains the sovereign. Pius XI's fundamental law of 1929 was replaced by John Paul II's in 2000 and by Francis's of 13 May 2023, in force from 7 June 2023, under which only the pope holds "powers" and the bodies of the state exercise "functions" on his behalf. [cite:vt2_open_fundlaw2023] Pope Leo XIV, elected on 8 May 2025, signed a further fundamental law dated 31 July 2026, under which he appoints the president of the Governorate, the members of the Pontifical Commission and the judges of the state's courts; as of October 2026 the Governorate is headed by Sister Raffaella Petrini. [cite:vt2_or_leo14] [cite:vt2_sussidiario_fundlaw2026] [scene:vt4_fundamental_law|Part Four: the Fundamental Law]

One clause signed in 1929 bears directly on this volume's central question. In Article 24 the Holy See declared that it "wishes to remain and will remain extraneous to temporal competitions between other States," and Vatican City is to be considered "always and in every case" neutral and inviolable territory. [cite:vt2_lateran_text] Any test of whether the Holy See's later refusal to back Zionism was a front, and of why it has never broken with Israel over Gaza, has to start from that written commitment, made nineteen years before the State of Israel existed. [scene:vt16_herzl_1904|Part Sixteen: Herzl and Pius X] [scene:vt18_why_no_sever|Part Eighteen: why no break]

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: The 1929 Deal, Then and Now
chapters.intro: Part Two ended with three signatures on 11 February 1929. This part reads what was signed, and then follows the bargain to the present. It sets out, article by article, what the Holy See and Mussolini's government each took from the Treaty, the Concordat and the Financial Convention, and how quickly the bargain was tested when the regime closed Catholic youth groups in 1931. It then turns to the Republic: the Constitution that kept the Pacts, the 1984 revision signed by Bettino Craxi and Cardinal Agostino Casaroli that ended Catholicism's status as the state religion, and the 1985 law that replaced state salaries for priests with the otto per mille, a share of income tax that taxpayers direct. The last section follows a property-tax exemption from Rome to the courts in Luxembourg and back to Italian tax offices in 2026. Together the four sections answer a plain question: who benefits from the 1929 settlement today, and what it costs Italy.
chapters.outro: Part Three has read the 1929 bargain and followed it to 2026. In 1929 the Holy See gained a sovereign territory, protected properties, 750 million lire in cash and a billion lire in bonds, a state religion, civil effect for its marriages and religious teaching in state schools; Mussolini's government gained recognition of Rome as Italy's capital, a Holy See pledged to stay out of disputes between states, a bishops' oath of loyalty and a clergy barred from parties. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] The 1931 clash over Catholic Action showed that the two sides bargained rather than merged. [cite:vt3_nab_1931] [cite:vt3_isacem_1931] The Villa Madama Agreement of 18 February 1984 ended the state religion and the oath, and Law 222 of 1985 replaced state pay for priests with the otto per mille, which in 2026 gave the Italian Bishops' Conference about 1.06 billion euros, allocated by the choices of about 27 per cent of taxpayers. [cite:vt3_l121_1985] [cite:vt3_l222_text] [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026] The property-tax exemption that the European Commission found unlawful for 2006 to 2011 was ordered recovered after the Court of Justice's judgment of 6 November 2018, and as of October 2026 Italy had yet to report collecting any of it. [cite:vt3_curia_pr2018] [cite:vt3_ff_sept2026] The Holy See, Vatican City and the Church in Italy have appeared here as three different beneficiaries of one settlement. Part Four separates them properly and shows how the smallest of the three, the City, actually runs, beginning with [scene:vt4_holy_see_vs_city|the Holy See and the City State].

sections.h: What Each Side Got in 1929
sections.html:
The Lateran Pacts were three documents, not one. The Treaty settled sovereignty and closed the dispute over Rome; the Concordat set the place of the Catholic Church inside Italy; the Financial Convention paid the Holy See for what it had lost in 1870. All three were signed on 11 February 1929 by Cardinal Pietro Gasparri for Pius XI and by Benito Mussolini as head of the Italian government, and all three are published together, in Italian, on the Holy See's own website. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] How the negotiation was conducted is told in [scene:vt2_pacts_signed|Part Two]. This section reads the texts for a narrower purpose: to list what each side received, article by article, before turning to the commentary that has grown around them.

What the Holy See received

The first gain was a state. Article 3 of the Treaty recognized the Holy See's "full ownership and exclusive and absolute power and sovereign jurisdiction" over the Vatican, which became Vatican City. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] What that sovereignty means in international law is set out in [scene:dv1_sovereignty|The Divine 3+1]; here the point is that Italy granted it by treaty, after nearly six decades of dispute over Rome ([scene:vt2_roman_question|the Roman Question]).

The second gain was a ring of protected property outside the walls. Article 13 left to the Holy See the patriarchal basilicas of St John Lateran, St Mary Major and St Paul Outside the Walls, with their annexed buildings; Article 14 added the papal palace and Villa Barberini at Castel Gandolfo; Articles 15 and 16 gave the seats of named curial offices the immunities of foreign embassies and exempted listed pontifical institutions, among them the Gregorian University and the Biblical Institute, from expropriation and from taxes. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] These properties are not Vatican territory; they are Italian land with special status, a distinction that matters again in [scene:vt4_holy_see_vs_city|Part Four].

The third gain was money. Article 1 of the Financial Convention obliged Italy to pay 750,000,000 lire in cash and to hand over 5 per cent consolidated state bonds with a nominal value of one billion lire, at the exchange of ratifications. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] Those are the treaty figures. Conversions into pounds or dollars that circulate in popular accounts (30 million pounds, 92.1 million dollars, "1.75 billion lire in cash") are not in the text, and any modern equivalent has to state its date and method. How the money was invested belongs to [scene:vt9_apsa_governorate|Part Nine].

The fourth gain, and the largest in daily life, was the Concordat's place for the Church in Italian law. The Treaty's first article reaffirmed the principle of the 1848 Statute that "the Catholic, apostolic and Roman religion is the only religion of the State." [cite:vt3_lateran_text] The Concordat then gave civil effect to the sacrament of marriage as governed by canon law (Article 34); declared that Italy considered "the teaching of Christian doctrine" the "foundation and crown of public education" and extended it from elementary to secondary schools (Article 36); committed the state to keep supplementing the incomes of poorly endowed benefices, the system of clergy pay known as the congrua (Article 30); and promised that the government would prevent in Rome anything contrary to "the sacred character of the Eternal City" (Article 1). [cite:vt3_lateran_text]

What Mussolini's government received

Italy's first gain was the end of the Roman Question on its own terms. In Article 26 the Holy See recognized "the Kingdom of Italy under the dynasty of the House of Savoy with Rome as capital of the Italian State" and declared the question "definitively and irrevocably" closed. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] Since 1870 the popes had refused to accept the loss of Rome; after 1929 no pope could claim it back.

The second gain was a Holy See that undertook to stay out of politics between states. In Article 24 the Holy See declared that it "wishes to remain and will remain extraneous to the temporal competitions between other States," and Vatican City was to be treated as neutral territory. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] That clause still stands, and its bearing on the Holy See's conduct over Israel and Gaza is examined in [scene:vt18_why_no_sever|Part Eighteen].

The third gain was a measure of control over the clergy inside Italy. Under Article 19 of the Concordat the Holy See chose bishops freely but communicated each name to the government in advance, "to make sure that it has no reasons of a political character to raise" against the appointment. Under Article 20 every bishop, before taking possession of his diocese, swore before the Head of State "fidelity to the Italian State." [cite:vt3_lateran_text] Article 43 recognized the organizations of Catholic Action and, in the same article, renewed for Italian clergy and members of religious orders "the prohibition on enrolling and being active in any political party." [cite:vt3_lateran_text] The Concordat's political clause binds the clergy; it does not mention any party by name.

The fourth gain was the least tangible: approval. Two days after the signing, Pius XI told professors and students of the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart in Milan that perhaps "also a man was needed like the one Providence has caused us to meet" to reach the settlement, and that with the Concordat he believed he had "given God back to Italy and Italy to God." [cite:vt3_pius_13feb1929] The passage does not name Mussolini, but its subject is plain from the context. Reviewing David Kertzer's history of the two men, the historian Saul Friedländer described the accords as "advantageous for both sides" and wrote that Mussolini could thereafter "rely on the Holy See's support of his regime and his policies," a benefit he called priceless "in a deeply Catholic country." [cite:vt3_tnr_kertzer] That is a historian's reading of the documents, not a clause in them, and it is given here as such.

The bargain tested: 1931

Within two years the clauses on Catholic Action were tested. After a press and police campaign that the Catholic Action historical institute dates from 19 March 1931, the regime dissolved all of Catholic Action's youth circles, male and female, on 30 May 1931. [cite:vt3_isacem_1931] Pius XI answered with the encyclical Non abbiamo bisogno, dated 29 June 1931. He protested the dissolution of the youth and university associations, accused the regime of seeking to "monopolize completely the young," and called its doctrine "a true, a real pagan worship of the State," which he named "Statolatry." [cite:vt3_nab_1931] He declared the oath demanded of party members "as it stands, is unlawful" and suggested that Catholics add a reservation for "the laws of God and of the Church." [cite:vt3_nab_1931]

The encyclical also drew a line. "We have not said that We wished to condemn the party as such," Pius XI wrote; what he condemned were the doctrines and practices he judged incompatible with Catholic teaching. [cite:vt3_nab_1931] An agreement signed on 2 September 1931 ended the crisis, and Catholic Action survived in reduced form; the same institute records that harassment of individual members continued until the regime fell in 1943. [cite:vt3_isacem_1931]

The episode is the best single test of how the 1929 settlement should be described. It was not a merger of Church and regime: within two years each side was defending its share of the bargain against the other, in public, over the one thing both wanted, the education of the young. Nor was it a rupture: the pope condemned an ideology while declining to condemn the party, and the dispute ended in a new agreement rather than a denunciation of the Concordat. The documents support a narrower description, the one Friedländer gives: a bargain between two authorities that needed each other and each expected to gain. [cite:vt3_tnr_kertzer] [cite:vt3_nab_1931] The Holy See's own stated aim, in Pius XI's words of 13 February 1929, was religious rather than political: to give "God back to Italy and Italy to God." [cite:vt3_pius_13feb1929]

sections.h: The Revision of 1984
sections.html:
The Pacts survived the regime that signed them. When the Italian Republic wrote its Constitution after the war, Article 7 declared that "the State and the Catholic Church are, each in its own order, independent and sovereign," that "their relations are regulated by the Lateran Pacts," and that "amendments to the Pacts accepted by both parties do not require a procedure of constitutional revision." [cite:vt3_cost_art7] The last clause shaped everything that followed. The Republic could change its relationship with the Church by negotiating with the Holy See and passing an ordinary law, without a two-thirds majority or a referendum; but it could not change the Pacts alone without touching the Constitution. The 1929 settlement therefore entered the republican order as a treaty to be renegotiated, not a statute to be repealed.

For more than three decades the Concordat stood largely as written, with its state religion, its bishops' oath and its religious teaching as the "foundation and crown" of public education. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] The revision came under a Socialist prime minister. Bettino Craxi took office on 4 August 1983 and put the file in the hands of his adviser Gennaro Acquaviva; on 28 January 1984 the Chamber of Deputies authorized him to conclude an agreement, by 338 votes to 67 with 30 abstentions. [cite:vt3_agi_1984]

Villa Madama, 18 February 1984

The agreement was signed in Rome on 18 February 1984, at Villa Madama, by Cardinal Agostino Casaroli, Secretary of State, for the Holy See and by Craxi for the Italian Republic, with an Additional Protocol. Parliament ratified it by Law 121 of 25 March 1985. [cite:vt3_l121_1985] [cite:vt3_agi_1984] It amended the Concordat, not the Treaty: Vatican City's sovereignty, the Financial Convention's settlement and the Treaty's Article 24 were not reopened.

The new text began where the Constitution did. Article 1 restated that State and Church are "each in its own order, independent and sovereign." [cite:vt3_l121_1985] The first point of the Additional Protocol then removed the principle on which the 1929 Concordat had rested: "The principle, originally referred to in the Lateran Pacts, of the Catholic religion as the sole religion of the Italian State is considered no longer in force." [cite:vt3_l121_1985] From 1984 Italy had no state religion.

The rest of the agreement followed from that change. Religious teaching stayed in state schools, but Article 9 gave every pupil, or every parent, "the right to choose whether or not to make use of" it; under the 1929 text it had been the "foundation and crown" of public education. [cite:vt3_l121_1985] [cite:vt3_lateran_text] Church marriages kept their civil effects under Article 8, on condition that banns were published and the marriage transcribed in the civil registers. [cite:vt3_l121_1985] Article 3 left the Church free to appoint its bishops and required only that the civil authorities be notified of appointments to diocesan sees; the text contains no oath, and the prior political check of 1929 disappeared. [cite:vt3_l121_1985] [cite:vt3_agi_1984] Rome kept a special mention, but the wording changed: Article 2 recognized "the particular significance that Rome, episcopal see of the Supreme Pontiff, has for Catholicism," in place of the state's 1929 duty to protect the city's "sacred character." [cite:vt3_l121_1985] [cite:vt3_lateran_text]

Two further changes concerned money. Activities of Church bodies other than religion and worship became subject to ordinary taxation, and Article 7 set up a joint commission of the two parties to draft the rules on Church bodies and property. [cite:vt3_l121_1985] [cite:vt3_agi_1984] The commission's work replaced the congrua, the state's direct supplement to clergy incomes under Article 30 of the 1929 Concordat. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] [cite:vt3_agi_1984]

Law 222 of 1985: Church bodies and clergy pay

The joint commission's rules became Law 222 of 20 May 1985, "Provisions on ecclesiastical bodies and property in Italy and on the support of the clergy." [cite:vt3_l222_text] It did three things. First, it set up a network of institutes for the support of the clergy: one in each diocese, and a central institute established by the Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI). Each institute was to provide "the adequate and dignified support of the clergy who serve the diocese," at a level set by the CEI rather than by the state. [cite:vt3_l222_text] Second, from 1989 it allowed individuals to deduct gifts to the central institute from taxable income, up to two million lire a year. [cite:vt3_l222_text] Third, from tax year 1990 it allocated "a share equal to eight per thousand of personal income tax" among the state and the Catholic Church according to taxpayers' choices: the otto per mille. [cite:vt3_l222_text] For the transition years 1987, 1988 and 1989 the state paid the old contributions, increased by 5 per cent a year, to the CEI, and the earlier legislation on clergy pay was repealed.
