[cite:vt3_l222_text] How the eight per thousand works, and how much it now produces, is the subject of [scene:vt3_otto_per_mille|the next section].

The effect, by design, was to move the Church's Italian income out of the state's budget lines and into a mechanism that taxpayers direct. The state stopped paying priests. Priests are now paid by the Church's own institutes, which draw on parish income, deductible gifts and, above all, the share of income tax allocated to the Church. In 2024 the system supported 31,053 priests; full-time priests received between 1,049.60 and 1,981.12 euros a month, twelve times a year, and bishops 2,204.16 euros. [cite:vt3_icsc_2024] Of the total, 389 million euros came from the eight per thousand and just under 8 million from deductible gifts. [cite:vt3_icsc_2024]

The revision is often summarized as the moment Italy stopped being a Catholic state, and on the legal question that is exact. It is less exact as a summary of the relationship. The Holy See kept its treaty, its territory and its treaty properties; the Church kept religious teaching in state schools, civil effect for its marriages and a public source of income that, as the next section shows, now exceeds a billion euros a year. What changed was the basis. In 1929 the state had paid the clergy and declared a religion; after 1985 it declared none, and taxpayers chose each year where a share of their income tax would go. The Holy See's own representative signed the change; the Republic's prime minister negotiated it with a parliamentary mandate. [cite:vt3_l121_1985] [cite:vt3_agi_1984]

sections.h: The Eight per Thousand
sections.html:
The otto per mille is the largest public money flow that the 1929 settlement, as revised in 1984, still produces. It is also the most misdescribed. It is not a church tax added to Italian income tax, and it is not a payment to the Holy See or to Vatican City. It is a share of the revenue Italy already collects from personal income tax (IRPEF), which the law divides among the state and a list of religious bodies; the Catholic share goes to the Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI), the body of the Church in Italy. [cite:vt3_l222_text] [cite:vt3_cei_ripart2026]

How the share is allocated

Article 47 of Law 222 of 1985 provides that, from tax year 1990, "a share equal to eight per thousand of personal income tax" is allocated according to the choices taxpayers make on their returns. [cite:vt3_l222_text] Each taxpayer may sign one box: the state, the Catholic Church, or one of the other confessions that have since signed agreements with the state. Signing costs nothing; the taxpayer's own tax bill is the same whichever box is chosen or if none is.

The point that decides the money is what happens to the shares of taxpayers who sign nothing. The law answers in one sentence: "In the case of choices not expressed by taxpayers, the allocation is determined in proportion to the choices expressed." [cite:vt3_l222_text] The whole 0.8 per cent of IRPEF is therefore divided according to the choices of the minority who sign. Those who do not choose have not chosen the state, or any other recipient; their share follows the decision of those who did.

The figures show how much this matters. For tax year 2022, the year on which the 2026 payments are based, about 42 million taxpayers filed and just over 16.8 million, about 40.1 per cent, made a valid choice, according to figures released by the Ministry of Economy and Finance in July 2026. [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026] Of those who chose, 11.35 million signed for the Catholic Church and 4.53 million for the state. [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026] The Church's signers were about 27 per cent of all taxpayers; through the proportional rule, the Church received between 67.3 and 67.8 per cent of the total, about 1.06 billion euros out of roughly 1.6 billion. The state received 426 million euros. [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026]

The Catholic share has been falling slowly. For tax year 2020 it was 71.00 per cent of the amount; for tax year 2021, 68.72 per cent, with 11,599,375 taxpayers choosing the Church out of 16,687,453 who made a choice and 41,497,318 who filed. [cite:vt3_open_8x2025] For tax year 2022 it fell below 68 per cent. [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026] The other recipients are much smaller: in 2026 the Waldensian Evangelical Church received 46.4 million euros, the Italian Buddhist Union 17.4 million, the Soka Gakkai Buddhist Institute 8.5 million, the Union of Italian Jewish Communities 4.5 million, the Orthodox Archdiocese 3.68 million, the Italian Hindu Union 2.41 million, the Seventh-day Adventists 1.86 million and the Assemblies of God 1.58 million. [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026]

What the CEI does with it

The law fixes the purposes in Article 48. The state's share is for extraordinary interventions against world hunger, natural disasters and similar public purposes; the Church's is for "the worship needs of the population, the support of the clergy" and charitable work in Italy and in developing countries. [cite:vt3_l222_text] Each year the CEI's General Assembly divides the money and publishes the result. The 82nd General Assembly, meeting in Rome from 25 to 28 May 2026, divided 1,086,752,778.01 euros: an advance of 1,063,069,466.83 euros for 2026 and an adjustment of 23,683,311.18 euros on the sums for 2023. [cite:vt3_cei_ripart2026]

Clergy support is the single largest use. In 2024, the latest year for which the clergy institute has published accounts, 389 million euros of the eight per thousand went to priests' pay, supporting 31,053 priests; most received an integration on top of their parish or other income, and 2,444 needed none. [cite:vt3_icsc_2024] A full-time priest's monthly pay ranged from 1,049.60 to 1,981.12 euros. [cite:vt3_icsc_2024] Charity took just over a quarter of the 2026 total, and worship and pastoral needs, including church building and the upkeep of historic churches, a little under two-fifths. [cite:vt3_cei_ripart2026] The allocation table has no line for the Holy See or for Vatican City; the money stays with the Church in Italy. [cite:vt3_cei_ripart2026]

The criticism and the reply

The proportional rule has been criticized from inside the Italian state. In 2015 the Corte dei conti, the national audit court, objected that the mechanism involves citizens "regardless of their own will": the minority who choose decide the destination of the whole sum. It also criticized the state's "scant interest" in promoting its own share and the churches' heavy spending on advertising. [cite:vt3_avv_cdc2015] The CEI's reply, sent to the court after hearings in October 2015, called the eight per thousand "a case of democracy in the direction of public spending," compared those who do not choose to citizens who do not vote, whose abstention does not stop seats being filled, and noted that it publishes its accounts every year. [cite:vt3_avv_cdc2015] The CEI's daily, Avvenire, reported the exchange under the headline that the court had gone "beyond measure." [cite:vt3_avv_cdc2015]

Both descriptions are accurate as far as they go. Those who do not sign have not "chosen" the Church, and it would be wrong to say they actively refused it; they made no choice, and the law assigns their share by the choices of others. [cite:vt3_l222_text] On the 2026 figures that rule roughly multiplied the effect of the Church's signers: about 27 per cent of taxpayers directed about two-thirds of the fund. [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026] The cost to the Italian budget is not the whole of the fund, since the law dedicates the 0.8 per cent to the listed recipients whatever the choices; it is the difference between what the state would receive if unexpressed shares came to it and what it receives under the proportional rule. Neither the ministry nor the CEI publishes that counterfactual figure, and this volume does not estimate it.

sections.h: The Property-Tax Case
sections.html:
The second money question that the 1929 settlement leaves in Italian public life is a tax not paid. It is often reported as "the Church's ICI," after the municipal property tax (imposta comunale sugli immobili) that Italy levied until 2011. The phrase is too narrow in one direction and too broad in another. The exemption at issue was not in the Lateran Pacts, whose tax exemptions cover only the basilicas, palaces and institutions listed in Articles 13 to 16 of the Treaty. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] It was in Italian tax law, and it covered all "non-commercial entities": not only parishes, dioceses and religious institutes, but bodies active in social assistance, health, education and sport, including amateur sports clubs. [cite:vt3_ec_ip2012] Church bodies were among those exempted, which is why the case has been reported as a Church case; the beneficiaries were a wider class.

The Commission's decision, 2012

The problem lay in a 2006 amendment. It extended the exemption to property where non-commercial entities carried on activities "not exclusively of a commercial nature," which opened it to buildings partly used for paying activities such as schools, clinics and accommodation. [cite:vt3_ec_ip2012] Competitors complained to the European Commission, which opened a formal investigation under the state-aid rules of the European Union treaties (case SA.20829). [cite:vt3_ec_dec2012]

The Commission decided on 19 December 2012. It found that the ICI exemption, as it applied from 2006 to 2011, was new state aid and "incompatible with the internal market." [cite:vt3_ec_dec2012] It found no aid in the replacement tax, the IMU, which from 1 January 2012 limited the exemption to premises where non-commercial entities carried on non-economic activities, nor in a separate income-tax provision that the Commission said "does not confer any selective advantage on ecclesiastical institutions or amateur sports clubs." [cite:vt3_ec_ip2012] [cite:vt3_ec_dec2012] Then it declined to order repayment. Italy had argued that it could not identify, years after the fact, which properties had been used for which activities, and the Commission accepted that recovery was "objectively impossible." [cite:vt3_ec_ip2012] The competition commissioner, Joaquín Almunia, stated the principle the decision rested on: non-profit bodies play an important social role, but when they compete with commercial operators they should not gain an undue advantage. [cite:vt3_ec_ip2012]

The courts, 2016 and 2018

Two of the competitors went to court: Scuola Elementare Maria Montessori, a private school, and Pietro Ferracci, who ran a bed and breakfast. On 15 September 2016 the EU General Court held their actions admissible but dismissed them (cases T-220/13 and T-219/13). [cite:vt3_curia_pr2018] The school, Ferracci and the Commission each appealed.

On 6 November 2018 the Court of Justice gave judgment in Joined Cases C-622/16 P to C-624/16 P. It agreed that competitors could bring the action. On recovery it reversed the lower court. Repayment, the Court held, is the logical consequence of a finding of unlawful aid, and it can be treated as "objectively and absolutely impossible" only if the Commission shows, after a scrupulous examination, both that the difficulties are real and that no alternative method of recovery exists, including partial recovery. [cite:vt3_curia_pr2018] The Commission had relied only on gaps in the land register and the tax databases. The Court annulled the part of the 2012 decision that declined to order recovery. [cite:vt3_curia_pr2018] It upheld the finding that the IMU exemption was not state aid. [cite:vt3_curia_pr2018] Commentators drew the rule out plainly: difficulties caused by a state's own poor records do not make recovery impossible. [cite:vt3_lexxion_2018]

The recovery, 2023 to October 2026

The Commission took a new decision on 3 March 2023. It ordered Italy to recover the unpaid ICI for 2006 to 2011 on property used for economic activities, case by case; property used for non-economic purposes was excluded. It accepted that the Italian authorities faced real difficulty in identifying beneficiaries but held that this did not rule out at least partial recovery. [cite:vt3_eunews_2023] [cite:vt3_dpcm_2025] It did not state an amount.

Italy legislated the procedure eighteen months later, in Article 16-bis of Decree-Law 131 of 16 September 2024, converted into law on 14 November 2024. [cite:vt3_dpcm_2025] The implementing decree of the prime minister's office, due by 14 January 2025, was late. [cite:vt3_avv_ici2025] It was signed on 23 December 2025. [cite:vt3_dpcm_2025] Its scope is narrow. It applies only to entities whose IMU and TASI returns for 2012 or 2013 showed liabilities above 50,000 euros a year; nothing is due where the aid stayed within the EU's limits for small amounts of aid or counts as compensation for services of general economic interest; where the effective local rate cannot be identified, an average rate of 5.5 per thousand applies; and compound interest runs from the date the aid was received. [cite:vt3_dpcm_2025] Activities of religion and worship are non-economic by definition, so no recovery applies to them. [cite:vt3_avv_ici2025]

The deadlines have moved twice. The declaration was first due by 31 March 2026. [cite:vt3_dpcm_2025] [cite:vt3_io_ici2026] A further decree of 26 March 2026, published on 31 March, extended it to 30 September 2026. [cite:vt3_ff_proroga] As of 21 September 2026 the declaration was due by 30 September and payment by 30 October 2026, with sums over 100,000 euros payable in four quarterly instalments. [cite:vt3_ff_sept2026] As of 21 October 2026, no figure for the number of declarations filed or the sums recovered had been published, and the payment deadline had not yet passed. [cite:vt3_io_ici2026] The only widely quoted estimate of the sums at stake is one attributed to ANCI, the association of Italian municipalities, of roughly 100,000 properties and 4 to 5 billion euros; it is not an official figure, and the threshold and exclusions in the 2025 decree mean the amount actually due may be well below it. [cite:vt3_money_anci] [cite:vt3_dpcm_2025]

Who benefits today, and what it costs

Set side by side, the four sections of this part allow a plain accounting. The Holy See still holds what it gained in 1929: a sovereign territory, protected properties in Rome and Castel Gandolfo, and the settlement of its claims, none of which the 1984 revision reopened. [cite:vt3_lateran_text] [cite:vt3_l121_1985] The Church in Italy, a different subject from the Holy See, receives the largest recurring flow: about 1.06 billion euros a year through the eight per thousand, distributed by its bishops' conference among clergy pay, worship and charity, on the strength of the choices of about 27 per cent of taxpayers. [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026] [cite:vt3_cei_ripart2026] Italy, for its part, no longer pays priests from its budget, no longer has a state religion, and in 2012 closed the property-tax exemption for economic activity from that year on. [cite:vt3_l121_1985] [cite:vt3_ec_ip2012]

What remains unpaid is the ICI for 2006 to 2011, owed by a class of non-commercial entities of which Church bodies are a part. Italy argued in 2012 that the sum could not be recovered, was told by the Court of Justice in 2018 that it could, and as of October 2026 was still waiting for the first payments under a procedure designed to collect only from the largest debtors. [cite:vt3_curia_pr2018] [cite:vt3_dpcm_2025] [cite:vt3_ff_sept2026] Italy's stated position throughout was that the records needed to identify the debtors did not exist; the Commission's stated position since 2023 is that partial recovery is possible all the same. [cite:vt3_ec_dec2012] [cite:vt3_eunews_2023]

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: How It Actually Runs
chapters.intro: Part Four sets aside the history and the money for a moment and answers a plainer question: who lives in the Vatican, and how is it governed from one day to the next. It begins by separating the two subjects that the word "Vatican" runs together, the Holy See, which signs treaties and sends ambassadors, and Vatican City State, the walled territory of 44 hectares that the Holy See has ruled since 1929. It then reads the state's constitution, the Fundamental Law, in its four versions from 1929 to the one Pope Leo XIV signed on 31 July 2026, and shows how a pope who holds every power of government delegates them to a commission and a Governorate. The third section explains how a person becomes a Vatican citizen and stops being one, what courts the state has, and why its convicts would serve their sentences in Italian prisons. The last section follows the ordinary machinery: the euro coins, the untaxed salaries and VAT-free shops, the water, trains, post and power that Italy supplies, the hospital the Holy See owns outside the walls, and the two small forces that keep order inside them.
chapters.outro: Part Four has separated the two subjects that "the Vatican" names. The Holy See, recognized by 184 states, signs the treaties and holds the diplomatic relations; Vatican City State is a territory of 0.44 square kilometres, with 673 citizens and 882 residents, that the Holy See has ruled since 1929. [cite:vt4_press_relations2026] [cite:vt4_vcs_geography] [cite:vt4_vcs_population] Its constitution, rewritten by Leo XIV on 31 July 2026, keeps every legislative, executive and judicial power in the Pope and delegates the daily work to a commission and a Governorate that, since November 2025, need not be led by a cardinal. [cite:vt4_vn_fl2026] [cite:vt4_wipo_fl2000] Citizenship comes with an office and ends with it; the state's courts, reformed in 2020, 2021 and 2023, try even cardinals, but the state has no prison and relies on Italy for punishment and fugitives under Article 22 of the Lateran Treaty. [cite:vt4_loc_citizenship] [cite:vt4_vn_cardinals2021] [cite:vt4_lateran_text] Its currency, tax position, water and rail links all rest on agreements with Italy and the European Union, the euro agreement binding it to EU rules against money laundering. [cite:vt4_vcs_monetary] What is settled is how the territory runs; what this part did not test is whether the outside checks on the Holy See work, which is the subject of Part Five, beginning with [scene:vt5_recognition|recognition and who grants it].

sections.h: Two Subjects Behind One Word
sections.html:
"The Vatican" is used in news reports, in popular books and even in official sources for at least three different things: the government of the Catholic Church, a small state in the middle of Rome, and the Catholic Church itself. Most errors about how the Vatican works begin with that slippage. In law there are two subjects, and the 1929 treaty that created the state keeps them apart in its first articles. The Holy See is the papal office and the government around it. Vatican City State is a territory of 0.44 square kilometres over which the Holy See is sovereign. Part One of the companion volume has already set out why the Holy See counts as a subject of international law under the usual tests, and that argument is not repeated here. [scene:dv1_sovereignty|The Divine 3+1: what makes a state] This section shows, as concretely as the documents allow, which of the two does what.

What the treaty says

The Lateran Treaty, signed on 11 February 1929, deals with the two subjects in two separate articles. In Article 2, Italy recognizes the sovereignty of the Holy See "in the international field" as something inherent in its nature, in keeping with its tradition and the needs of its mission in the world. That is a recognition of a sovereignty Italy did not create. In Article 3, Italy recognizes the Holy See's full ownership and "exclusive and absolute" sovereign power and jurisdiction over the Vatican, "constituted" for that purpose as Vatican City. [cite:vt4_lateran_text] The order matters. The Holy See comes first and already exists; the city is a territory handed to it so that its independence would rest on ground no other state controlled. Part Three described what each side gained from this bargain. [scene:vt3_what_each_got|Part Three: what each side got]

The same article of the treaty also shows how small the territory's independence is in practice. St Peter's Square belongs to Vatican City, but it stays normally open to the public and under the powers of the Italian police, whose officers stop at the foot of the basilica steps and go no further unless invited. When the Holy See closes the square for a ceremony, the Italian authorities withdraw behind the outer line of Bernini's colonnade. [cite:vt4_lateran_text] Inside the sovereign state, in other words, the largest open space is policed by the neighbouring country by treaty.

Which one signs

The Holy See conducts the diplomacy. As of 9 January 2026, 184 states maintained diplomatic relations with it, along with the European Union and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, and 93 of the embassies accredited to it had their chancelleries in Rome. [cite:vt4_press_relations2026] It is the Holy See, not the city, that holds observer status at the United Nations, since 6 April 1964. [cite:dv1_wiki_holysee_un] [cite:dv1_dfat_holysee] It is the Holy See that signed the Fundamental Agreement with Israel on 30 December 1993 and the Comprehensive Agreement with the State of Palestine in 2015, the two documents at the centre of this volume's question, which Parts Seventeen and Eighteen read in detail. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] [cite:vt1_rv_palestine2015] [scene:vt17_fundamental_agreement|Part Seventeen: the Fundamental Agreement] [scene:vt18_state_of_palestine|Part Eighteen: the State of Palestine]

Vatican City State signs very little in its own name, and when it does, the Holy See signs for it. The Secretariat of State publishes a list of the Holy See's agreements from the Lateran Pacts of 1929 to 2009; of about fifty-nine entries, only one carries the city's name in its title: the Monetary Agreement between the European Union and the Vatican City State of 17 December 2009. [cite:vt4_vatva_agreements_list] That agreement was signed in Brussels by Archbishop André Dupuy, the apostolic nuncio to the European Union, for the Holy See acting "as representative" of the city, and by Commissioner Joaquín Almunia for the Union. [cite:vt4_rv_monetary2009] The euro is a matter for the territory, which is why the city is the party; the Holy See is still the hand that signs. The Fundamental Law states the rule outright: representation of the state abroad and the making of treaties are reserved to the Pope, who exercises them through the Secretariat of State. [cite:vt4_wipo_fl2000]

How large, and who lives there

The Governorate, the city's own administration, gives the territory's area as 0.44 square kilometres, or 44 hectares, partly enclosed by walls. [cite:vt4_vcs_geography] A second figure, 49 hectares, is also in circulation and goes back to a 1930 atlas; the Governorate's own page uses 44. [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican] Forty-four hectares is about 109 acres. Some popular accounts give "44 acres", which confuses the unit and shrinks the state by more than half.

The population is small and unusual. On the Governorate's figures the state has 673 citizens, of whom 458 live inside the walls, 120 of them members of the Swiss Guard. Some 30 per cent of Vatican citizens do not live in the state at all; most of them are diplomats at their posts abroad. Sixty-six cardinals held Vatican citizenship at the end of 2024, and ten of them lived inside. Counting everyone who lived in the territory, citizen or not, there were 882 residents on 31 December 2024. [cite:vt4_vcs_population] The Governorate does not give a single date for all its figures, so the gap between 458 resident citizens and 882 residents, roughly four hundred people living in the city without its citizenship, is an approximation from its numbers, not a count it publishes. Section three explains why so many residents are not citizens and so many citizens are not residents: in the Vatican, citizenship follows the job.

The people who work there are far more numerous than those who live there. Il Post, reporting in May 2025, put the workforce at nearly 5,000, about 2,000 in the Curia, which serves the Holy See, and the rest employed by the state, including some 700 at the Vatican Museums. [cite:vt4_ilpost_workers] The two employers sit in the same buildings, but they are different: a curial official works for the Holy See, a museum guard for Vatican City State.

Outside the walls: the extraterritorial properties

The Holy See's property in Italy does not stop at the walls. Articles 13 to 16 of the Lateran Treaty created a second category of places that are not Vatican City but enjoy special status inside Italy. Italy recognized the Holy See's ownership of the three other patriarchal basilicas, St John Lateran, St Mary Major and St Paul Outside the Walls, of the papal palace at Castel Gandolfo with the Villa Barberini, and of buildings on the Janiculum hill facing the Vatican. Article 15 gives these, along with the palaces of the Datary, the Cancelleria, Propaganda Fide on Piazza di Spagna, the Holy Office and the Vicariate, the immunities that international law grants to the embassies of foreign states. Article 16 adds that they may not be expropriated without the Holy See's consent and are exempt from taxes, and extends those two protections to a list of pontifical universities and colleges. [cite:vt4_lateran_text] The Governorate calls the zones around such buildings "extraterritorial areas". [cite:vt4_vcs_geography]

The list has grown by later agreement. Santa Maria di Galeria, outside Rome, holds the shortwave transmitters of Vatican Radio and has extraterritorial status under agreements with Italy of 1951; on 31 July 2025 the two sides signed a further agreement for a solar plant there, which the Italian Senate approved for ratification on 7 January 2026. [cite:vt4_vcs_galeria] The Bambino Gesù children's hospital, owned by the Holy See since 1924, sits on extraterritorial ground on the Janiculum, and the plan to move it is discussed in section four. [cite:vt4_wiki_bambino] An embassy-like immunity is not sovereignty: these buildings remain in Italy, and the treaty itself provides for the handover of suspects who take refuge in them, as section three shows. [cite:vt4_lateran_text]

The distinction has a direct bearing on this volume's question. When the record says that "the Vatican" recognized a state, protested a strike in Gaza or signed an agreement, it was the Holy See acting, through the Pope and the Secretariat of State, on behalf of a church that spans every continent. The 44 hectares are what guarantee that the Holy See answers to no other government while it does so; they are not where its weight comes from. The next section reads the constitution by which the Pope governs the territory itself.

sections.h: The Fundamental Law: One Ruler, Delegated Powers
sections.html:
Vatican City State has a written constitution, called the Fundamental Law. It has had four versions in under a century, and the most recent was signed on 31 July 2026. Each version starts from the same principle, which makes the state unlike any other in Europe: every power of government belongs to one person, the Pope, and every other office exercises power because he has delegated it. The working machinery of the state, a commission that makes laws and an administration that carries them out, is real and has its own rules, but it rests on that delegation and can be overridden by it.

Four versions, 1929 to 2026

The first Fundamental Law was published on 7 June 1929, the day the Lateran Treaty came into force, under Pius XI. John Paul II replaced it with a new text promulgated on 26 November 2000, which took effect on 22 February 2001, the feast of the Chair of St Peter. Francis published a third version on 13 May 2023, in force from 7 June 2023. [cite:vt4_wiki_fl] Leo XIV signed a fourth on 31 July 2026, the memorial of St Ignatius of Loyola, with immediate effect, replacing the 2023 text. [cite:vt4_vn_fl2026] Catholic News Agency counted it as the fourth constitution since the state was created. [cite:vt4_cwr_fl2026]

The Pope's three powers

The 2000 text, whose structure later versions kept, opens by stating that the Pope, as sovereign of Vatican City State, holds "la pienezza dei poteri legislativo, esecutivo e giudiziario", the fullness of legislative, executive and judicial power. When the papacy is vacant these powers pass to the College of Cardinals, which may legislate only in urgent cases and only for the period of the vacancy. Representation of the state abroad and the making of treaties are reserved to the Pope and exercised through the Secretariat of State. Amnesties, pardons and remissions of sentence are reserved to him alone. [cite:vt4_wipo_fl2000] Francis's 2023 law confirmed the same "fullness of legislative, executive and judicial powers" in the Pope. [cite:vt4_vn_fl2023] [cite:vt4_ncr_fl2023]

In the vocabulary of political science this is an elective absolute monarchy: the ruler is chosen for life by the cardinals in conclave, and no other body can bind him. [cite:dv1_wiki_vatican] There is no parliament of residents, no separation of powers in the modern sense, and no court that can review the sovereign's acts. The judges themselves, under the 2020 judicial law, are "hierarchically dependent on the Supreme Pontiff", and the Pope may remove any case to a particular court at any stage. [cite:vt4_cwr_judicial2020] [cite:vt4_vcs_judicial] What the Fundamental Law does supply is a set of ordinary channels through which those powers are normally used.

The Commission and the Governorate

Under the 2000 law, legislative power was exercised by a Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State made up of cardinals, with a cardinal president, all appointed by the Pope for five years, except in matters the Pope chose to reserve to himself. Executive power belonged to the president of that commission, assisted by a Secretary General and a Vice Secretary General. [cite:vt4_wipo_fl2000] The executive offices together are called the Governorate, and its president is in effect the head of the state's administration: the state's directorates, among them those for security and for infrastructure and services, report to it. [cite:vt4_vcs_geography] The same person is president of both the Commission and the Governorate. [cite:vt4_vn_fl2023]

The 2023 law changed the composition. The Commission would consist of cardinals, including the president, and "other members", appointed by the Pope for five years, which allowed laymen and laywomen to sit on the state's legislative body. It also expanded the budget rules: the Commission must adopt annual budgets and a three-year financial plan, the plan to be approved directly by the Pope, and the budget must aim at balance and follow "principles of clarity, transparency and fairness". [cite:vt4_vn_fl2023] [cite:vt4_ncr_fl2023]

The presidency was still reserved to a cardinal. In 2025 Francis nonetheless appointed Sister Raffaella Petrini as President of both the Commission and the Governorate, the first woman and the first non-cardinal in the post. Catholic News Agency described the appointment as "legally irregular" until the law caught up. [cite:vt4_cwr_fl2026] On 19 November 2025 Leo XIV issued a motu proprio repealing the paragraph of the 2023 law, Article 8(1), that limited the presidency to cardinals. [cite:vt4_vn_fl2026] The episode illustrates the system: the sovereign appointed first and amended the constitution afterwards, and no body in the state could have objected.

What the 2026 law changed

Leo XIV's Fundamental Law of 31 July 2026 repeals the 2023 text in full and restates, in line with the Lateran Pacts, that the state exists to guarantee the independence and international sovereignty of the Holy See. [cite:vt4_infovat_fl2026] According to Vatican News, its Article 8 describes the Commission as "composed of Cardinals and other Members, including the President", all appointed by the Pope for five years, so that the presidency is no longer reserved to cardinals. The Governorate is described as directly accountable to the Pope. The law sets out more precisely how the President and the Secretary General divide their work, stresses that the Secretary General's post is an institutional office, and allows it to be entrusted to more than one person. Article 22(1) refers the organisation of the courts to the separate law on the judicial system. [cite:vt4_vn_fl2026] Catholic News Agency added that a General Councillor may attend the Commission's meetings in a consultative role. [cite:vt4_cwr_fl2026] When the law was promulgated, Sister Raffaella Petrini held both presidencies, and no change had been announced as of October 2026. [cite:vt4_vn_fl2026] [cite:vt4_cwr_fl2026] The reports consulted for this section summarize the 2026 law; they do not reproduce its full text, and this section claims nothing about articles they do not describe.

What the law does not cover

The Fundamental Law governs the 44 hectares. It does not govern the Curia, the body that serves the Holy See and the Church worldwide: that is ordered by a separate apostolic constitution, whose 2022 version Part Six describes. [scene:vt6_curia_2022|Part Six: the Curia since 2022] Nor does it govern the Holy See's finances as a whole. The Governorate has its own budget, from the museums and the state's commercial services among other things; the Holy See's investment arm, APSA, and the Institute for the Works of Religion are separate bodies whose accounts Part Nine reads. [scene:vt9_apsa_governorate|Part Nine: APSA and the Governorate] A reader trying to work out who runs "the Vatican" therefore has to ask which part: the territory is run by the Governorate under a commission, the Holy See by the Secretariat of State and the dicasteries, and both by the same Pope.

The design also explains a feature that outsiders sometimes take for secrecy. A state with a single sovereign and no electorate has no parliament to publish debates and no opposition to force disclosure. The 2023 law's language on "clarity, transparency and fairness" in the budget, and the judicial reforms described in the next section, were introduced by the sovereign himself; the record shows the rules changing by papal decision, not by any outside check. [cite:vt4_vn_fl2023] Part Five describes the outside checks that do exist, through treaties and international bodies. [scene:vt5_moneyval_euro|Part Five: MONEYVAL and the euro]

sections.h: Citizens by Office, Courts by Delegation, Prisons in Italy
sections.html:
Most states make citizens by birth or descent and keep them for life. Vatican City State makes citizens by appointment and lets them go when the appointment ends. It has a full set of courts but almost no criminal caseload, and it has never needed a prison of its own, because the Lateran Treaty lets it hand the work of punishment to Italy. This section sets out those three arrangements from the laws that create them and from the few cases that have tested them.

Who is a citizen

The Lateran Treaty laid down the base rule in 1929. Article 9 makes everyone with stable residence in Vatican City subject to the Holy See's sovereignty, and Article 21 adds that cardinals resident in Rome, even outside the city, are Vatican citizens for all purposes. [cite:vt4_lateran_text] The details were set by a citizenship law of 1929 and, since 22 February 2011, by Law No. CXXXI on citizenship, residence and access, issued by Benedict XVI. [cite:vt4_loc_citizenship]

The 2011 law creates two routes. Citizenship follows automatically, by right, for three groups: cardinals who live in Vatican City or Rome, the diplomats of the Holy See, and people who live in the state because of their office or service there, a group that includes the Swiss Guards. It may be granted by administrative decision to three further groups: residents authorised to live in the state because of their work, people the Pope personally authorises to reside there, and the spouses and children of citizens who are themselves authorised to live in the state. [cite:vt4_loc_citizenship] Nobody becomes a Vatican citizen by being born there.

Citizenship ends the same way it begins. Except for the Pope's, every grant is temporary. It lapses when the holder leaves the office that justified it, when he or she stops living in the state, or, for a cardinal, when he moves his residence outside Vatican City and Rome. Family members lose it at the same moment as the holder, and children lose it at eighteen unless they apply for permission to remain. A person who loses Vatican citizenship and has no other becomes an Italian citizen automatically, under Article 9 of the Lateran Treaty. [cite:vt4_wiki_citizenship] The rule prevents statelessness and explains why the Vatican can afford a citizenship that lasts only as long as a contract.

The result is the population described in section one: 673 citizens, of whom 458 live inside the walls, including 120 Swiss Guards, with about 30 per cent abroad, mostly as diplomats; and 882 residents of any citizenship at the end of 2024. [cite:vt4_vcs_population] Many residents, such as employees' relatives without a grant, members of religious communities or staff housed in the city, are not citizens, and many citizens, such as nuncios abroad and cardinals living elsewhere in Rome, are not residents. The Law Library of Congress, writing in 2012, gave a figure of about 800 people and 450 citizens, which shows how little the numbers move. [cite:vt4_loc_citizenship]

The courts

Judicial power in the state is exercised in the Pope's name by a single judge (the Giudice Unico) for minor matters, a Tribunal of first instance, a Court of Appeal and a Court of Cassation. Investigation and prosecution belong to the Office of the Promoter of Justice. The judges are appointed by the Pope and are, in the Governorate's words, subject only to the law; the Pope may nonetheless transfer any civil or criminal case to a particular court at any stage, and the power of clemency is his. [cite:vt4_vcs_judicial] These courts are civil and criminal courts of the state. They are not the Church's canon-law tribunals, which judge clergy under church law and are a separate system.

The present structure comes from a run of reforms under Francis. On 13 March 2020 he signed Law CCCLI on the judicial system, replacing John Paul II's law of 1987. It described the judges as "hierarchically dependent on the Supreme Pontiff", required them to be drawn from university professors or recognised jurists, barred curial officials from serving because of the conflict of interest, gave the judicial offices their own spending autonomy within the Governorate's budget, and placed the judicial police, a section of the Gendarmerie, under the Promoter of Justice. [cite:vt4_cwr_judicial2020] On 30 April 2021 he ended a privilege: until then cardinals and bishops accused of crimes could be tried only by the Court of Cassation, presided over by a cardinal; from then on they would be tried by the ordinary Tribunal, through the same three levels as anyone else, though "with the prior consent of the Supreme Pontiff". [cite:vt4_vn_cardinals2021] A motu proprio in force from 13 April 2023 defined the Promoter's powers more closely, allowed the Promoter to ask for a case to be dropped where the offence was minor or reparation had been made, removed the requirement that one judge of the Tribunal serve full-time, and provided for substitute judges on long trials. [cite:vt4_vn_judicial2023]

The 2021 change came shortly before the largest case the courts have heard: the trial over the Secretariat of State's investment in a London building, in which Cardinal Giovanni Angelo Becciu was convicted at first instance on 16 December 2023 and sentenced to five and a half years. [cite:vt10_ap_verdict2023] On 17 March 2026 the Court of Appeal found a "relative nullity" in the proceedings, ordered key hearings to be held again before the appeal court itself and directed the Promoter of Justice to file the complete record of the investigation. Vatican News and ANSA reported that the first-instance judgment kept legal effect for the time being; AP reported that the errors had nullified the original indictment. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] [cite:vt10_ansa_becciu2026] [cite:vt10_ap_mistrial2026] As of 19 September 2026, the appeal court had set a hearing for 29 October 2026, and Becciu's lawyer, Fabio Viglione, said the defence was confident of "the cardinal's complete innocence". [cite:vt4_unione_becciu] As of October 2026, therefore, Becciu's 2023 sentence is not final, the appeal court will decide the case afresh, and he is presumed innocent; he has denied wrongdoing throughout. [cite:vt10_ansa_becciu2026] The case and its money are the subject of Part Ten. [scene:vt10_london_trial|Part Ten: the London trial]

Before that trial, criminal cases were rare. In September 2012 Giovanni Giacobbe, the Promoter of Justice at the Court of Appeal, told reporters that Vatican criminal trials were "extremely" rare, and that the only recent comparison was a drug-possession case about ten years earlier. [cite:vt4_cns_tribunal2012] The case he was preparing for was that of Paolo Gabriele, the papal butler who leaked private documents. A three-judge panel convicted him of aggravated theft on 6 October 2012 and sentenced him to eighteen months. [cite:vt4_aj_gabriele]

No prison: the Italian arrangement

The Gabriele case also showed what the state lacks. At his conviction the Vatican said that a sentence would be served in an Italian prison, because it "does not have any long-term prison facilities". [cite:vt4_aj_gabriele] Giacobbe had already explained that this would mean invoking, for the first time, a long-standing agreement with Italy that had never been used. [cite:vt4_cns_tribunal2012] It was not used in the end. Gabriele was held in the Vatican police barracks, and on 22 December 2012 Benedict XVI visited him there, told him in person that he accepted his request for pardon, and commuted the sentence. [cite:vt4_spokesman_pardon]

The treaty basis is Article 22 of the Lateran Treaty. At the Holy See's request, or by a delegation it grants, Italy will punish in its own territory crimes committed in Vatican City; if the offender flees into Italy, Italian law applies directly. In the other direction, the Holy See will hand over people who take refuge in Vatican City after committing acts in Italy that are crimes under the laws of both states, and the same applies to suspects who shelter in the immune buildings listed in Article 15, unless the officials there prefer to invite Italian police in to make the arrest. [cite:vt4_lateran_text] The best-known use of Italian jurisdiction came after 13 May 1981, when Mehmet Ali Ağca shot John Paul II in St Peter's Square: he was handed to the Italian police and tried and convicted by an Italian court, not by the Vatican. [cite:vt4_cns_tribunal2012]

Put together, these arrangements answer a common question about the state's independence. Vatican City does have its own laws, judges and police, and in the London trial it showed that it can prosecute its own senior officials. [cite:vt4_vn_cardinals2021] [cite:vt4_unione_becciu] But the system was built on the assumption that serious crime would be rare and that Italy would do the heavy work of prisons and fugitives when it occurred. [cite:vt4_lateran_text] [cite:vt4_cns_tribunal2012] The Holy See's position, stated in each reform, is that the changes bring the courts closer to equality before the law; Francis described the 2021 change as answering "the overriding need" for the procedural system to ensure equality among the Church's members. [cite:vt4_vn_cardinals2021] The courts remain, in the end, the sovereign's courts, appointed by him and answerable to him, as the Fundamental Law provides. [cite:vt4_vcs_judicial]

sections.h: Euros, Untaxed Pay and Borrowed Utilities
sections.html:
Day-to-day life in Vatican City depends on two sets of arrangements. Treaties with Italy and the European Union supply the currency, the water, the railway link, customs-free goods and the tax treatment of salaries. Then there is what the state runs itself: shops, a pharmacy, a petrol station, a post office, a health fund, a police force and a guard. This section takes each in turn from the documents that set it up and from reporting on how it works now.

The euro, by agreement

Vatican City State does not have its own currency. It uses the euro under a Monetary Agreement with the European Union signed in Brussels on 17 December 2009, in force from 1 January 2010, which replaced an earlier agreement of 29 December 2000. [cite:vt4_vcs_monetary] [cite:vt4_rv_monetary2009] The agreement lets the state issue its own euro coins within a ceiling. Article 3 sets that ceiling in two parts: a fixed part, €2,300,000 in 2010 and revisable each year for Italian inflation and changes in the collector market, plus a variable part equal to Italy's average coin issuance per head in the previous year multiplied by the Vatican's population. In a year when the papacy is vacant, the state may also issue a commemorative coin and collector coins, with any excess charged against the ceiling of the year before or after. [cite:vt4_vcs_monetary] The European Commission's summary of the microstates' agreements still gives the Vatican's annual ceiling as €1 million; the text of the agreement, published by the Governorate, gives the fixed part from 2010 as €2.3 million plus the variable part, and this volume follows the text. [cite:vt4_eurlex_summary] [cite:vt4_vcs_monetary]

Vatican coins are prized by collectors, and the agreement addresses that directly: under Article 6(4) at least 51 per cent of the coins issued each year must be put into circulation at face value. [cite:vt4_vcs_monetary] The microstates may not issue banknotes. [cite:vt4_eurlex_summary] The agreement also binds the state to more than coinage. Article 8 obliges it to adopt, by direct transposition or equivalent measures, the European Union acts listed in an annex on euro notes and coins, money laundering, fraud and counterfeiting of cash and non-cash means of payment, and statistical reporting, by deadlines the annex sets; the Commission updates the annex each year. A Joint Committee of Vatican and Union representatives (the Commission, Italy and the European Central Bank) meets at least once a year and decides unanimously. [cite:vt4_vcs_monetary] This clause is one reason the claim, repeated in popular writing on the Vatican, that the Vatican stands outside European anti-money-laundering rules is wrong; Part Five describes how the obligation is checked. [scene:vt5_moneyval_euro|Part Five: MONEYVAL and the euro]

No income tax, no VAT

The tax position of Vatican pay rests on Article 17 of the Lateran Treaty. Salaries and other payments made by the Holy See, by the central bodies of the Church and by bodies the Holy See manages, to dignitaries, employees and staff, are exempt in Italian territory from any tax from 1 January 1929. [cite:vt4_lateran_text] The state itself levies no income tax on them. Il Post reported in May 2025 that Vatican salaries remain untaxed on the basis of the 1929 Pacts and are set broadly in line with Italian pay for comparable roles. [cite:vt4_ilpost_workers] The exemption is the treaty's, not a concession the state grants itself; Italy agreed to it in 1929, as part of the bargain Part Three described. [scene:vt3_what_each_got|Part Three: what each side got]

Goods are treated the same way. Article 20 of the treaty admits goods destined for Vatican City or Holy See institutions through any Italian border point or port, fully exempt from customs and local duties. [cite:vt4_lateran_text] No value-added tax applies to goods sold inside the state. [cite:vt4_ilpost_workers] That makes the state's shops cheaper than Italian ones, and access to them is controlled. When the Associated Press reported in November 2017 that the Vatican would stop selling cigarettes to employees at its duty-free shop and supermarket, it noted that shopping required a "commercial card" issued to employees, retirees, residents, accredited diplomats and members of religious congregations, and that purchases avoided Italy's 22 per cent VAT. The Holy See said it could not "contribute to an activity that clearly damages the health of people", giving up an estimated €10 million a year. An Ernst & Young audit in 2013 had found 41,000 cards in use against about 5,000 employees. [cite:vt4_cbs_cigarettes] The same report cited a 2015 book, Avarice, as saying that tax-free petrol was the largest source of such sales. [cite:vt4_cbs_cigarettes]

The perks have been under pressure. Il Post reported that the Annona supermarket, opened almost a century earlier for Holy See and Governorate staff, closed on 13 January 2025 for renovation and a five-year concession to an outside chain; that seniority increments were frozen from 2021 to 2023; that the staff contract had not been renewed since 2008; and that hiring was limited to one new employee for every three who retired. [cite:vt4_ilpost_workers] These measures followed budget cuts ordered as donations fell; Part Nine sets out the finances behind them. [scene:vt9_peters_pence|Part Nine: Peter's Pence]

Water, rail, post and power

The 1929 treaty made Italy responsible for the physical connections. Under Article 6, Italy undertook to secure an adequate supply of water owned by Vatican City, to build a railway station inside the city at a site marked on the treaty's map and let Vatican rolling stock run on Italian railways, and to link the city's telegraph, telephone, radio and postal services directly with other states, all at Italy's expense and within a year. [cite:vt4_lateran_text] The Vatican's post office is used today mainly by nunciatures sending parcels and vestments, and by visitors who buy its stamps. [cite:vt4_ilpost_workers]

Electricity is the one service the Holy See has set out to supply itself. On 21 June 2024 Francis issued the motu proprio Fratello Sole, setting the goal of "the complete energy self-sufficiency of the Vatican City State" through an agrivoltaic plant, solar panels raised above working farmland, at Santa Maria di Galeria, the extraterritorial site of Vatican Radio's transmitters. [cite:vt4_vcs_fratellosole] Italy and the Holy See signed an agreement for the plant on 31 July 2025, which the Italian Senate approved for ratification on 7 January 2026; it takes effect when both sides have completed ratification. [cite:vt4_vcs_galeria] On 1 June 2026 Leo XIV created the Fratello Sole Foundation to build and run the plant, led for its first three years by the President of the Governorate and the President of APSA. As of June 2026 the plant was still a plan. [cite:vt4_vcs_fratellosole]

Health and the hospital outside the walls

There is no hospital inside Vatican City. Employees are covered by a health fund, the Fondo assistenza sanitaria (FAS), paid for by monthly contributions from salaries; its clinics stand near the Annona, and serious cases are given priority access to the Bambino Gesù and Gemelli hospitals in Rome. Il Post reported that the fund had dropped physiotherapy and raised some charges amid the cuts. [cite:vt4_ilpost_workers] The Vatican pharmacy, with about fifty staff, sells medicines on prescription, some not available in Italy, without VAT. [cite:vt4_ilpost_workers]

The Bambino Gesù children's hospital is the Holy See's own. Founded in 1869 by Duchess Arabella Salviati and given to the Holy See in 1924, it stands on extraterritorial ground on the Janiculum, has been recognised as an Italian research hospital since 1985 and works within Rome's National Health Service. [cite:vt4_wiki_bambino] Its main site is too small. On 8 February 2024 Cardinal Pietro Parolin and Alfredo Mantovano, Under-Secretary to Italy's Council of Ministers, signed a non-binding declaration of intent to build a new hospital at the former Forlanini hospital in Rome: the Holy See would buy the site from the Lazio Region, INAIL, Italy's workplace-insurance institute, would build and lease the complex, and a further agreement would extend the immunities of Lateran Treaty Articles 15 and 16 to the new premises. [cite:vt4_press_bambino2024] On 3 December 2025 the budget committee of Italy's Chamber of Deputies approved an amendment providing the property exchange between the State and Lazio needed to free the Forlanini site for the Holy See. [cite:vt4_qs_forlanini] This volume did not find a report, as of October 2026, that the transfer or the immunities agreement had been completed.

Police and guard

Two bodies keep order. The Corps of Gendarmerie, founded by Pius VII in 1816, numbered 122 in 2022 and handles policing, border and traffic control and criminal investigation under the Governorate. [cite:dv1_wiki_gendarmerie] Its judicial police section works under the Promoter of Justice. [cite:vt4_cwr_judicial2020] The Pontifical Swiss Guard, founded in 1506, protects the Pope; it was enlarged from 110 to 135 members in 2019 and recruits unmarried Catholic Swiss men who have done Swiss military service. [cite:dv1_wiki_swissguard] The Governorate counts 120 Swiss Guards among the citizens living inside the walls. [cite:vt4_vcs_population] Outside the basilica steps, St Peter's Square is policed by Italy under Article 3 of the treaty, as section one described. [cite:vt4_lateran_text]

The picture that emerges is of a state that is sovereign in law and dependent in practice. Its currency is the European Union's, used under rules that oblige it to follow EU law on money laundering and fraud; its water, rail links and prisons were to be provided by Italy; its pay and goods are untaxed because Italy agreed in 1929 that they would be. [cite:vt4_vcs_monetary] [cite:vt4_lateran_text] What the state runs for itself is small: shops, a pharmacy, a post office, a health fund and two small forces, with the Governorate controlling the commercial activities. [cite:vt4_ilpost_workers] [cite:dv1_wiki_gendarmerie]

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: Sovereignty and Who Checks It
chapters.intro: Part Four showed how the Vatican governs itself. Part Five asks why the rest of the world treats the Holy See as a sovereign, and who, if anyone, examines how it uses that status. It follows three lines of outside contact: recognition by other states and the United Nations, including the campaign to remove its UN seat and the lawsuits in which its sovereign immunity was tested; the 2014 reviews by two UN treaty committees of its record on clerical sexual abuse, with the Holy See's replies; and the euro agreement with the European Union and the anti-money-laundering evaluations by the Council of Europe's MONEYVAL committee, which together answer the claim that the Vatican's bank sits outside European anti-money-laundering rules.
chapters.outro: Part Five established that the Holy See's standing as a state rests on recognition practice older than Vatican City itself: Article 2 of the Lateran Treaty recognised a sovereignty "inherent to its nature," it kept relations with 16 to 27 states while holding no territory, and by 9 January 2026 it had relations with 184 states, the European Union and the Order of Malta. [cite:vt1_va_lateran] [cite:vt5_wiki_forrel] [cite:vt5_pv_relations2026] Its UN seat was confirmed and widened by resolution 58/314 in 2004 despite the See Change campaign, and US and European courts have treated it as a foreign state, with abuse claims against it failing on where the acts occurred and on whether priests are its employees. [cite:vt5_hsm_58314] [cite:vt5_un_seechange2000] [cite:vt5_jurist_doe2012] [cite:vt5_eapil_jc2021] It is not unchecked. Two UN committees examined its abuse record in 2014 and rejected its view that its treaty obligations stop at the city's walls, and the Holy See rejected theirs. [cite:vt5_crc_co2014] [cite:vt5_cat_co2014] [cite:vt5_rv_cat_reply] On money, the 2009 Monetary Agreement binds Vatican City to EU anti-money-laundering acts, and MONEYVAL's reports of 2012, 2021 and 2024 record real reform alongside weak prosecution and confiscation, which corrects the claim that the IOR is exempt from those rules. [cite:vt5_va_monetary] [cite:vt5_mv_2021mer] [cite:vt5_fatf_fur2024] What the Holy See does with this standing is speak without a vote: its record on cloning, Cuba and abortion at UN conferences shows real influence through words and good offices and no means to enforce them. [cite:vt5_sp_un_news2005] [cite:vt5_sp_ncr_cuba2025] [cite:vt5_sp_ewtn_cairo1994] [scene:vt5_soft_power|A voice without a vote] Part Six turns from the Holy See's outside relations to the people who run it: the popes, the Curia as reorganised in 2022, and the myths of hidden popes. [scene:vt6_curia_2022|Part Six: the Curia]

sections.h: Why It Is Still Treated as a State
sections.html:
Part Four described the machinery inside the walls. This section asks a question from outside them: why other governments, the United Nations and foreign courts treat a papal office with a city of 44 hectares as a sovereign at all. The short answer is that they do not, strictly, treat the city as the sovereign. The subject of international law is the Holy See, the office of the pope and the central government of the Catholic Church, and Vatican City State is the territory over which it has ruled since 1929. [scene:vt4_holy_see_vs_city|Part Four: the Holy See and the city] [scene:dv1_sovereignty|The Divine 3+1: the sovereignty tests] The statehood tests applied to the city in The Divine 3+1 are not repeated here; this section follows how the Holy See is recognised, where that has been challenged, and what immunity it has claimed in court.

A claim older than the city

The Lateran Treaty did not create the Holy See's international standing; it acknowledged it. In Article 2 of the treaty signed on 11 February 1929, Italy recognised the sovereignty of the Holy See in the international field "as an attribute inherent to its nature," and only in Article 3 did it recognise the Holy See's sovereign power over the Vatican, creating the city. [cite:vt1_va_lateran] [scene:vt2_pacts_signed|Part Two: the Pacts signed] The order of the two articles mirrors the order of events. Between the fall of Rome to the Italian army in September 1870 and the treaty of 1929 the Holy See held no territory, yet it continued to send and receive diplomats: the number of states with which it had relations rose from 16 to 27, it concluded 29 concordats and other agreements, and it was asked to mediate 13 international disputes. [cite:vt5_wiki_forrel] Some jurists of the period doubted whether a sovereign without land could remain an independent actor in international law; in practice most governments kept dealing with it. [cite:vt5_wiki_forrel] [scene:vt2_roman_question|Part Two: the Roman Question]

That practice is the real basis of the Holy See's standing today. International law does not issue certificates of statehood; a subject exists to the extent that other subjects deal with it as one, by exchanging ambassadors, signing treaties and admitting it to conferences. On that measure the Holy See's position is strong. The Holy See Press Office's annual note of 9 January 2026 recorded diplomatic relations with 184 states, plus the European Union and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, and 93 embassy chancelleries accredited to the Holy See with their seats in Rome; the offices of the League of Arab States, the International Organization for Migration and the UN refugee agency accredited to it are also in Rome. [cite:vt5_pv_relations2026] It listed no new relations in 2025. [cite:vt5_pv_relations2026] Older figures in circulation, "183" or "about 180", are out of date.

Recognition and its gaps

The 184 are not the same set as the 193 members of the United Nations. They include 181 UN members, the State of Palestine, the Republic of China on Taiwan and the Cook Islands, and they leave out twelve UN members. [cite:vt5_wiki_forrel] Among those twelve are the People's Republic of China, Saudi Arabia, Vietnam, Afghanistan and North Korea. [cite:vt5_wiki_forrel] Several of the absences are themselves acts of recognition policy. The Holy See keeps its relations with Taipei, not Beijing, while dealing with Beijing through the Provisional Agreement on the appointment of bishops, signed on 22 September 2018, renewed for two years in 2020 and 2022 and extended for four years on 22 October 2024. [cite:vt5_vn_china2024] [cite:vt5_wiki_forrel] On 26 June 2015 it signed a Comprehensive Agreement with the State of Palestine, a step Part Eighteen examines. [cite:vt1_rv_palestine2015] [scene:vt18_state_of_palestine|Part Eighteen: the State of Palestine]

Recognition also came late from the two governments most often cast in popular accounts as the Holy See's partners. The United Kingdom established full relations on 16 January 1982 and the United States on 10 January 1984. [cite:vt5_wiki_forrel] Israel and the Holy See established full relations by a protocol signed on 14 June 1994, after the Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993 that is the subject of Part Seventeen. [cite:rs_cw2_holysee_israel_protocol] [scene:vt17_fundamental_agreement|Part Seventeen: the Fundamental Agreement] Oman, on 23 February 2023, was the most recent state to establish relations before the 2026 note. [cite:vt5_wiki_forrel] Recognition has been extended state by state, for each state's own reasons, and remains incomplete.

The United Nations seat

The Holy See became a Permanent Observer State at the United Nations on 6 April 1964 and has chosen not to seek membership. [cite:vt5_hsm_58314] [cite:dv1_wiki_holysee_un] [scene:dv1_three_cities|The Divine 3+1: the three cities] Its rights were set out forty years later in General Assembly resolution 58/314, "Participation of the Holy See in the work of the United Nations," adopted without a vote on 1 July 2004. [cite:vt5_hsm_58314] [cite:vt5_va_migliore2004] The annex gave the Holy See the right to take part in the Assembly's general debate, the right of reply, the right to raise points of order on matters that concern it (without the right to challenge the chair's ruling), and the right to co-sponsor draft resolutions that refer to it, which go to a vote only if a member state asks. It "shall not have the right to vote or to put forward candidates." [cite:vt5_hsm_58314] It is a voice without a vote.

The challenge: "See Change"

That voice was contested in the years before 58/314. On 14 March 2000, at a press conference at UN Headquarters, Frances Kissling, president of Catholics for a Free Choice, and four other speakers presented the "See Change" campaign, which asked Secretary-General Kofi Annan to open a review of the Holy See's status as a non-member state permanent observer and to give it instead the standing of a non-governmental organisation, as the World Council of Churches has. [cite:vt5_un_seechange2000] Kissling said almost 400 organisations had endorsed it. One speaker, Anika Rahman, argued that the Holy See met only one of the four criteria of statehood, the capacity to enter into relations with other states; the others criticised its positions on contraception, condoms and abortion at UN conferences since the 1995 Beijing conference on women. [cite:vt5_un_seechange2000] [cite:vt5_rns_seechange]

The response was organised and immediate. The United States bishops' conference said Catholics for a Free Choice merited "no recognition or support," a former US ambassador to the Holy See, Ray Flynn, defended its diplomatic role, and counter-campaigns gathered endorsements of their own. [cite:vt5_rns_seechange] No member state proposed a review. Four years later the General Assembly confirmed and widened the seat by consensus. [cite:vt5_va_migliore2004] The contest shows where the Holy See's standing is weakest: on the Montevideo test of a permanent population, which the city's small resident population meets only thinly. [scene:dv1_three_cities|The Divine 3+1: the city's residents] It also shows that the test did not decide the outcome. Recognition practice did.

Sovereign immunity in foreign courts

Statehood has a practical consequence that matters most to people who have sued the Holy See: a foreign state cannot ordinarily be sued in another state's courts. In the United States that rule is set by the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, and two abuse cases tested how far it protects the Holy See. In O'Bryan v. Holy See, brought in Kentucky, the Sixth Circuit held on 24 November 2008 that the Holy See is a foreign state under the Act, and that its role as head of a religious body "cannot be separated from its position as a foreign state." [cite:vt5_jurist_obryan2008] [cite:vt5_findlaw_obryan] The court let claims proceed on the conduct of bishops and Holy See personnel in the United States who supervised abusive clergy, under the Act's exception for torts committed in the country, but barred claims based on the abuse itself and on acts of the Holy See abroad. [cite:vt5_findlaw_obryan] In August 2010 the plaintiffs' lawyer, William McMurry, dropped the case, citing the high bar of sovereign immunity and the lack of further plaintiffs; the Holy See's US counsel, Jeffrey Lena, said the outcome confirmed "there has never been a Holy See policy requiring concealment of child sexual abuse." [cite:vt5_ncr_obryan2010]

Doe v. Holy See, brought in Oregon over abuse in about 1965 by a Servite priest, Andrew Ronan, went further. On 3 March 2009 the Ninth Circuit allowed the claim against the Holy See to proceed, on Oregon's definition of employment, and on 28 June 2010 the Supreme Court declined to review that ruling; Lena said the refusal was "not a comment on the merits." [cite:vt5_wiki_doe] [cite:vt5_am_doe2010] Back in the district court, Judge Michael Mosman held on 20 August 2012 that the facts did not establish that Ronan was an employee of the Holy See, and dismissed the claim. [cite:vt5_jurist_doe2012] Neither case found the Holy See beyond the reach of US courts; both turned on where the acts took place and whether a priest is the pope's employee. What became of the abuse claims outside these suits is followed in Part Twelve. [scene:vt12_accountability|Part Twelve: accountability]

In Europe the same question reached the European Court of Human Rights. Twenty-four people who said they had been abused as children by Catholic priests in Belgium sued the Holy See, among others; the Ghent court of first instance declined jurisdiction over it in 2013 and the Ghent Court of Appeal upheld its immunity in February 2016. [cite:vt5_eapil_jc2021] In J.C. and Others v. Belgium, decided on 12 October 2021, the Strasbourg court found no violation of the right of access to a court. It held that the Belgian courts had not acted arbitrarily in treating the Holy See as having the characteristics of a foreign state, and accepted their reasoning that the bishops' conduct could not be attributed to the Holy See and that the failures alleged against it had taken place in Rome, not Belgium. [cite:vt5_eapil_jc2021] Immunity covers the Holy See itself, not local dioceses and bishops, which are separate legal persons under national law.

The Holy See is treated as a state because, for more than a century and through a period when it held no land, other states have treated it as one, and courts follow that practice; challenges on the statehood criteria and on its conduct have not changed it. The next two sections turn to the two bodies of outside review it has accepted: UN treaty committees and the anti-money-laundering evaluators. [scene:vt5_treaty_bodies|Treaty bodies] [scene:vt5_moneyval_euro|MONEYVAL and the euro]

sections.h: The UN Treaty Bodies: the 2014 Reviews
sections.html:
A sovereign that signs human rights treaties accepts that committees of independent experts will examine it. The Holy See has signed fewer of them than most states. It ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child on 20 April 1990 and the Convention against Torture on 26 June 2002, and it is party to the convention against racial discrimination, the 1951 Refugee Convention and the Geneva Conventions; it has not signed the two International Covenants of 1966 or the convention on discrimination against women. [cite:vt5_umn_ratif] The two treaties it did accept produced, in 2014, the most searching outside examination of its record on clerical sexual abuse that any international body has made. This section sets out what the two committees found, what the Holy See replied, and the point on which the two sides never agreed: for whom the Holy See answers.

The Committee on the Rights of the Child, January 2014

The Holy See's first report to the Committee on the Rights of the Child was filed in 1994 and its second in 2011, years after it was due. [cite:vt5_tapsell2025] The committee examined the second report in a public session in Geneva on 16 January 2014. The Holy See's representative, Archbishop Silvano Tomasi, set out the distinction on which its whole defence rested: the Holy See as a subject of international law, Vatican City State as the territory with its own small population and its own criminal law, and the local Churches, which adopt guidelines within their own countries' laws. [cite:vt5_va_tomasi_crc] Serious cases of abuse, he said, "have rightly been adjudicated and punished by the competent civil authorities in the respective countries." [cite:vt5_va_tomasi_crc] He also pointed to Vatican City laws of 11 July 2013 that gave its courts jurisdiction over crimes committed abroad by its public officials, curial staff and diplomats among them. [cite:vt5_va_tomasi_crc]

The committee adopted its concluding observations on 31 January 2014 and issued them as document CRC/C/VAT/CO/2 on 25 February. [cite:vt5_crc_co2014] It rejected the distinction at the outset: by ratifying, it wrote, the Holy See had undertaken to implement the Convention "not only within the territory of Vatican City State, but also, as the supreme power of the Catholic Church, worldwide." [cite:vt5_crc_co2014] On abuse it found that known abusers had been "transferred from parish to parish or to other countries," that a "code of silence" had been imposed on clergy under penalty of excommunication, and that reporting to the police "has never been made compulsory." [cite:vt5_crc_co2014] It recommended that known and suspected abusers be removed and referred to law enforcement, that reporting be made mandatory, that archives be opened, and that canon law treat child abuse as a crime rather than a "delict against the moral." [cite:vt5_crc_co2014] It noted that a Commission for the Protection of Minors had been announced on 5 December 2013, and urged the Holy See to withdraw its reservations, which made the Convention's application depend on its compatibility with the law of Vatican City State. [cite:vt5_crc_co2014]

The observations went beyond abuse. The committee asked the Holy See to oppose all corporal punishment, to investigate the forced labour of girls in the Irish Magdalene laundries and compensate them, to "review its position on abortion" and amend canon 1398, to allow adolescents access to contraception, and to remove gender stereotyping from Catholic school textbooks. [cite:vt5_crc_co2014] Those recommendations went to the content of Catholic teaching, and they shaped the reply.

The Holy See's statement of 5 February 2014 said it "takes note" of the observations, which would "be submitted to a thorough study and examination," and it objected to "an attempt to interfere with Catholic Church teaching." [cite:vt5_ba_hs_crc_reply] [cite:vt5_am_crc2014] Tomasi said his first reaction was surprise, since the document's negative tone made it seem it was "prepared before" the January hearing, and called the abortion recommendation "a real contradiction" in a treaty on children; he stressed "a policy of transparency and zero tolerance for abuse." [cite:vt5_am_crc2014] The reply thus answered two different things at once: the abuse findings, which it did not contest in terms, and the recommendations on doctrine, which it rejected as outside the committee's remit.

The Committee against Torture, May 2014

Three months later the Holy See presented its initial report under the Convention against Torture. Its delegation told the committee that between 2004 and 2013 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith had confirmed 3,420 credible allegations of abuse of minors by priests, 848 priests had been dismissed from the priesthood and 2,572 had received lesser penalties. [cite:vt5_cat_co2014] These are counts of cases decided by one Vatican office over ten years, not an estimate of victims, and they are not to be added to any national figure. [scene:vt12_the_numbers|Part Twelve: the numbers]

The committee's observations, adopted on 21 and 22 May and issued as CAT/C/VAT/CO/1 on 17 June 2014, again took up jurisdiction. It noted the Holy See's interpretative declaration that the Convention applied only to Vatican City State, found that position inconsistent with the Convention and with the Holy See's own law, and said a state's obligations extend to its officials "wherever they exercise effective control over persons or territory." [cite:vt5_cat_co2014] It was concerned that church officials "resist the principle of mandatory reporting" to civil authorities, asked the Holy See to suspend accused clergy at once and stop transfers that frustrated investigation, asked for information on the Vatican investigation of Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, cited a 2013 refusal to share information with an Australian inquiry, and asked for follow-up information by 23 May 2015. [cite:vt5_cat_co2014]

The Holy See's communiqué of 23 May 2014 was warmer than its February statement. It said the observations "include many positive outcomes" and a "few points that require further clarification." [cite:vt5_rv_cat_reply] It repeated that the Convention "applies to Vatican City State," objected to the impression that priests worldwide were "indirectly legally dependent" on the Vatican, called an "implicit fundamental assumption" that sexual abuse amounts to torture "fundamentally flawed," and reminded the committee that its role was "to monitor and report, and not to adjudicate." [cite:vt5_rv_cat_reply]

What the reviews checked, and what they could not

The two reviews are the clearest answer to the claim, made in some popular writing, that the Holy See faces "zero external accountability." On abuse, it faced two committees in four months, gave figures in public, and was told in writing that its reading of its own obligations was wrong. The reviews also show the limits of that kind of check. A treaty committee has no power to enforce its observations; it can ask, record and publish. The Holy See accepted the jurisdiction of the committees under the two treaties it chose to ratify, and it held throughout that its treaty obligations stopped at the borders of Vatican City, so that the conduct of bishops and priests abroad fell under the laws of the states where they served and under canon law. [cite:vt5_rv_cat_reply] [cite:vt5_va_tomasi_crc] The committees held the opposite. Neither side moved.

The reporting cycle has also slowed. In December 2025 the Australian lawyer and writer Kieran Tapsell, a critic of the Holy See's handling of abuse, wrote that it had filed no report to the Committee on the Rights of the Child since 2011, although reports are due every five years, and that after the 2014 review it had described its obligation as running only to the children who live in Vatican City; he urged Pope Leo XIV to submit one. [cite:vt5_tapsell2025] The reporting status as of October 2026 rests on that December 2025 account. The legal changes that followed the reviews inside the Church, among them the 2019 abolition of the pontifical secret for abuse cases and the reporting duties of Vos estis lux mundi, belong to the history of the Holy See's own rules and are set out in Part Twelve. [scene:vt12_the_rules|Part Twelve: the rules] [scene:vt12_accountability|Part Twelve: accountability] The other outside check the Holy See accepted in the same years was financial, and it was built very differently: by agreement with the European Union and by membership of a Council of Europe evaluation body. [scene:vt5_moneyval_euro|MONEYVAL and the euro]

sections.h: Money Under Watch: the Euro Agreement and MONEYVAL
sections.html:
A claim runs through much popular writing on the Vatican: that its bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), sits outside European banking rules and is "exempt" from the European Union's anti-money-laundering law, with no outside audit until 2013. The documents show something different. Vatican City State uses the euro under a treaty with the European Union that obliges it to apply the Union's anti-money-laundering acts, and since 2011 the Holy See has submitted, as a member, to the Council of Europe's anti-money-laundering evaluators, MONEYVAL, who have published two full evaluations of it and a series of progress and follow-up reports. What is true in the claim is narrower: the IOR's supervisor is a Vatican authority, not an Italian or EU one. [scene:vt9_ior|Part Nine: the IOR] This section sets out the agreement, the supervisor and the evaluations, in that order.

The Monetary Agreement of 2009

Vatican City's use of the euro first rested on an agreement of 29 December 2000 concluded with the European Community, represented by Italy. [cite:vt5_va_monetary] That agreement was replaced by the Monetary Agreement between the European Union and the Vatican City State, signed at Brussels on 17 December 2009 by Commissioner Joaquín Almunia and, for the Vatican City State represented by the Holy See, Archbishop André Dupuy; it entered into force on 1 January 2010. [cite:vt5_va_monetary] [scene:vt4_euro_tax_utilities|Part Four: the euro, taxes and utilities] The agreement makes the euro the city's official currency, bars it from issuing its own notes, coins or substitutes without EU consent, and caps the face value of the coins it may issue each year, with a fixed part (2.3 million euros for 2010) and a part tied to its population. [cite:vt5_va_monetary]

Article 8 is the clause that answers the "exemption" claim. It obliges Vatican City to adopt measures implementing the EU acts listed in an annex on euro notes and coins, on preventing money laundering, on fraud and counterfeiting of cash and non-cash means of payment, on medals and tokens, and on statistical reporting. [cite:vt5_va_monetary] The European Commission updates the annex every year. Its decision of 15 May 2025, for example, listed the Union's 2024 anti-money-laundering package, the Regulation 2024/1624, the Directive 2024/1640 and the Regulation 2024/1620 creating the new EU anti-money-laundering authority, with a deadline of 31 December 2028, and the 2023 regulation on information accompanying transfers of funds with a deadline of 31 December 2026; it also carries a section on entities carrying out financial activities on a professional basis. [cite:vt5_eurlex_2025_898] The deadlines were agreed in a joint committee of the two sides between 2013 and 2024. [cite:vt5_eurlex_2025_898] The Vatican is not an EU member and EU law does not apply in it directly; it applies there because the Vatican undertook by treaty to transpose it.

A supervisor of its own

The first Vatican anti-money-laundering law followed.
