John Paul II gave it a form no other body has held. By the apostolic constitution Ut sit of 28 November 1982 he erected Opus Dei as a personal prelature. [cite:vt8_va_charisma] A diocese is defined by territory: its bishop has authority over the Catholics who live in it. A personal prelature is defined by persons: its prelate has authority over the priests incardinated in it and over the lay members for the purposes the prelature serves, wherever they live, while those lay members remain parishioners of their local dioceses. Opus Dei remained the only personal prelature. John Paul II beatified Escrivá in 1992 and canonised him in 2002, and Fernando Ocáriz has been the prelate since 23 January 2017. [cite:vt8_wiki_opus]

Who belongs

Opus Dei states that it has about 93,000 members, of whom about 2,095, or 2 per cent, are priests. About 70 per cent are supernumeraries, mostly married people living ordinary family lives. Numeraries are celibate and usually live in Opus Dei centres, available for the organisation's apostolic work and the formation of other members; associates are celibate but live with their families or where their work requires. [cite:vt8_od_members] Female "numerary assistants" do the domestic work of the centres; their testimony is at the centre of the criticism discussed below. [cite:vt8_wiki_opus] Opus Dei has no monks or nuns, despite its portrayal in The Da Vinci Code. [cite:vt8_wiki_opus]

Francis's reform, 2022 and 2023

On 14 July 2022 Francis issued the motu proprio Ad charisma tuendum ("to protect the charism"), which took effect on 4 August 2022. It moved Opus Dei from the Dicastery for Bishops to the Dicastery for the Clergy: "the Prelature depends on the Dicastery for the Clergy". It required the prelate to report to that dicastery every year. It ruled that "the Prelate shall not be honoured with the episcopal order", so the head of Opus Dei would no longer be made a bishop, and gave him instead the title of Supernumerary Apostolic Protonotary, a rank of monsignor. [cite:vt8_va_charisma] The change took the prelature out of the line of bodies treated like dioceses and placed it beside clergy associations.

A second motu proprio, in force from 8 August 2023, rewrote the two canons of the Code of Canon Law that govern personal prelatures. Canon 295 now says a personal prelature is "similar to public clerical associations of pontifical law with the ability to incardinate clerics", headed by a Moderator with the faculties of an Ordinary. Canon 296 now says that lay people "can dedicate themselves to the apostolic works of the personal prelature", language that describes them as cooperating in its works rather than as its members in the sense of a flock. [cite:vt8_vn_prelatures2023] Opus Dei was required to revise its statutes to fit. After an extraordinary internal congress in April 2023 it submitted revised statutes to the Dicastery for the Clergy on 11 June 2025; its prelate said the prelature "awaits the Holy See's response". [cite:vt8_exaudi_statutes]

The response had not been published as of October 2026. On 16 February 2026, according to a prelature statement, Leo XIV told Ocáriz that the updating of the statutes "continues in its study phase and that no publication date can yet be foreseen". [cite:vt8_ncr_leo_statutes] No later approval was found in the sources checked for this volume.

Influence: what is documented

The best-documented case of political influence is Spain. Several Opus Dei members served as ministers under Franco, among them Alberto Ullastres, and critics have cited their presence as evidence of the organisation's power inside the regime. The historians Paul Preston and Brian Crozier concluded that these ministers were chosen for their technical ability rather than their membership. [cite:vt8_wiki_opus] The finding the record supports is that individual members reached high office; the claim that Opus Dei as an organisation directed Spanish policy through them is contested and is not settled by the appointments themselves.

The same distinction applies to Rome. Opus Dei's rise in Church law under John Paul II, from secular institute to the only personal prelature, and the canonisation of its founder in 2002 are documented. So is its reduction under Francis. [cite:vt8_va_charisma] [cite:vt8_vn_prelatures2023] A body that controlled the papacy would not have been moved to a lower dicastery, lost the episcopal rank of its head and been made to rewrite its statutes, which as of October 2026 still awaited the pope's decision. [cite:vt8_ncr_leo_statutes]

The criticism and the response

Criticism of Opus Dei comes mostly from former members. María del Carmen Tapia, who held senior posts in the organisation, and Vladimir Felzmann, a former Opus Dei priest, published accounts describing strict control of members' lives, correspondence and reading. Critics also describe recruitment through friendships and social events and the practice of corporal mortification, including the cilice, a spiked band worn on the thigh. [cite:vt8_wiki_opus] In 2024 a joint investigation by the Financial Times and El País, based on testimony from former numerary assistants, reported that women had been "coerced into domestic servitude" through a system of psychological control; the same year Gareth Gore's book Opus described the organisation's finances and recruitment. Opus Dei denied the allegations, said that membership requires repeated, explicit personal consent over several years, and called Gore's book "a false picture of Opus Dei based on distorted facts, conspiracy theories and outright lies". Its spokespeople have also admitted mistakes in the treatment of some members. [cite:vt8_wiki_opus]

The most serious case is in Argentina. Forty-three women who were members between 1974 and 2015 complained; prosecutors described a system that targeted girls and alleged that they had been made to work without pay under false promises of education and employment. After a two-year investigation with the federal office for trafficking and exploitation, prosecutors named four former regional vicars, and on 11 June 2025 asked to question Mariano Fazio, the organisation's auxiliary vicar, who had led it in Argentina from 2010 to 2014. [cite:vt8_ncr_argentina2025] Opus Dei "categorically rejects the accusation of trafficking and exploitation" and says the complaint misrepresents a vocation the women freely chose. [cite:vt8_od_argentina] As of 11 September 2026 the judge in charge, Daniel Rafecas of Federal Court No. 3 in Buenos Aires, had not carried out any of the requested questionings, and a survivors' organisation, Ending Clergy Abuse, had asked him to move the case forward. [cite:vt8_lcmdp_2026] No one has been charged; the accused are entitled to the presumption of innocence.

The documented picture is of a lay organisation of modest size whose standing in Church law rose under one pope and fell under another, and whose treatment of some of its own members is the subject of an unresolved criminal investigation that it denies. That is a record of influence and of serious allegations. It is not a record of control over the Holy See.

sections.h: The Order of Malta: a Second Catholic Sovereign
sections.html:
Two Catholic bodies in Rome are treated by other states as sovereign. One is the Holy See. The other is the Sovereign Military Hospitaller Order of St John of Jerusalem, of Rhodes and of Malta, usually called the Order of Malta, which has no territory, about 13,500 members, and diplomatic relations with more than a hundred countries. Two questions are often asked about it: whether it is connected to the Vatican, and why it exists at all. The documents answer the first plainly: it is connected in two different ways at once, as a religious order that depends on the Holy See and as a sovereign body that exchanges ambassadors with it. The answer to the second lies in its history: a hospital that became a military order, ruled two islands, lost them, and kept the recognition that ruling them had brought.

A hospital in Jerusalem, recognised by a pope

The Order's own account begins in the second half of the eleventh century, when merchants from the Italian maritime republic of Amalfi obtained permission from the caliph of Egypt to build a church, convent and hospital dedicated to St John the Baptist in Jerusalem, to care for pilgrims. Under its first master, Blessed Gerard, the community became a lay religious order. Pope Paschal II's bull of 15 February 1113 recognised it, placed it under the protection of the Church and gave it the right to elect its superiors without outside interference. [cite:vt8_om_history] Popular accounts date the foundation to 1048 or to 1099; the hospital's exact start is not fixed by a single document, but the papal recognition of 1113 is. That bull is the first documented tie between the Order and the papacy, and it placed the Order under the Holy See and outside the control of local bishops. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom]

The Order took on armed defence of pilgrims and the sick in the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, and later the defence of the faith. [cite:vt8_om_history] After the crusader states fell it ruled Rhodes from 1310 until 1523, when it left the island under a negotiated surrender to Suleiman the Magnificent's besieging army. In 1530 the Emperor Charles V and his mother Joanna granted it Malta, with Pope Clement VII's approval, in return for a symbolic tribute of a falcon. It held Malta until June 1798, when Napoleon's forces took the island and Grand Master Ferdinand von Hompesch surrendered. After moving through Messina, Catania and Ferrara, the Order settled in Rome in 1834. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom]

Sovereignty without territory

The Order has been without land for more than two centuries. Italy recognises its two seats in Rome, the Palazzo Malta on Via Condotti and the Villa of the Priory on the Aventine Hill, as extraterritorial, and Italy's Supreme Court of Cassation held in 1974 that the Order should be treated in law as a foreign state. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom] Legal scholars disagree about what this amounts to. Some describe the Order as a subject of international law without territory; the British jurist Ian Brownlie argued that its legal capacities "must be limited" because it lacks the territory and population of a state. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom]

Its reach is nonetheless real. The Order states that it has diplomatic relations with 118 countries and with the European Union, cooperation agreements with more than 50 states, and accredited missions in more than 100 countries (its page as modified on 29 September 2026). [cite:vt8_om_diplomacy] An independently maintained list counts 114 members of the United Nations plus the Holy See, with Andorra, on 16 June 2025, the latest addition; the difference reflects how relations and recognitions are counted and should be stated with its source. The Order exchanges ambassadors with the State of Palestine and with the EU. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom_rel] On 24 August 1994 the UN General Assembly, by resolution 48/265 adopted without a vote, invited the Order to take part in its sessions as an observer. [cite:vt8_un_48_265] The Holy See itself, by comparison, had diplomatic relations with 184 states, the EU and the Order of Malta as of 9 January 2026. [cite:vt5_pv_relations2026]

The Order issues its own passports, coins and stamps. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom] The Grand Master, its head, is often described as a cardinal. He is not one: a royal Italian decree of 1929 gives him in Italy "the honors due to the Cardinals", which is a matter of precedence, not of rank in the Church. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom]

How it is tied to the Holy See

The tie runs through religious law, not through the Vatican City State. The Holy See said on 16 October 2012 that among orders of knighthood it "recognizes and protects only the Sovereign Military Order of Malta" and the Equestrian Order of the Holy Sepulchre, apart from its own pontifical orders. [cite:vt8_rv_equestrian2012] A Tribunal of Cardinals ruled in 1953 that the Order's sovereignty is "functional", serving its own purposes. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom] The two bodies have had formal diplomatic relations since February 1930. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom_rel] The Order is therefore at once a sovereign partner of the Holy See and a religious order under it. The limit of the first role was tested in 2016 and 2017.

In December 2016 Grand Master Matthew Festing removed the Grand Chancellor, Albrecht von Boeselager, after condoms had been distributed by other aid groups in a project in Myanmar run jointly with the Order's relief agency. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom] On 22 December 2016 the Holy See announced that Francis had set up a group to investigate the dismissal. On 10 January 2017 the Order called the dismissal "an internal act of governance" and said the papal inquiry was "legally irrelevant" given its sovereignty. On 24 January 2017 Francis received Festing and asked him to resign, and the resignation was accepted the next day. [cite:vt8_cna_festing] Boeselager was reinstated, and on 2 February 2017 Francis named Archbishop Giovanni Angelo Becciu as his special delegate to the Order. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom] (Becciu was convicted at first instance in a separate Vatican financial trial on 16 December 2023; on 17 March 2026 the Vatican Court of Appeal found a relative nullity and ordered the hearings renewed before the appeal court. Vatican News and ANSA reported that the first-instance judgment keeps effect for now, while AP reported that the indictment was nullified; the 2023 sentence is not final. As of October 2026 the next hearing was set for 29 October; Becciu denies wrongdoing and is presumed innocent. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] [cite:vt10_ap_mistrial2026] [cite:vt10_us_oct2026] [scene:vt10_london_trial|Part Ten: the London trial])

The reform that followed was imposed by papal decree. On 3 September 2022 Francis promulgated a new Constitutional Charter and Code for the Order with immediate effect, revoked its high offices, dissolved its Sovereign Council, appointed a provisional council and convened an extraordinary General Chapter for 25 January 2023. The decree quoted the 1953 judgment that the Order is "a religious Order, approved by the Holy See", and stated: "being a religious Order, it depends, in its various articulations, on the Holy See." [cite:vt8_va_smom2022] The Order announced the same day that the new texts had entered into force and that the provisional council had taken its oath. [cite:vt8_om_const2022] On 3 May 2023 the Chapter elected Fra' John Dunlap as Grand Master for a ten-year term, renewable once; he is the 81st head of the Order counted from Gerard. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom] [cite:vt8_om_history]

What it does: Malteser International

The Order's stated reason for its diplomatic network is humanitarian: it describes its relations with states as "humanitarian diplomacy" serving its medical and relief work. [cite:vt8_om_diplomacy] The largest part of that work abroad is Malteser International, its relief agency. In 2024 the agency reported 152 projects in 36 countries, 7.2 million people supported, 3.2 million of them with emergency relief, 1,202 staff, revenue of €105.8 million and programme spending of about €74.5 million. In the Middle East and North Africa it spent €30.7 million on 18 projects in six countries. It reported 200 tonnes of food delivered into Gaza, including six convoys to the north, preparation of a container clinic in Gaza with the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem, support for seven mobile medical units and eleven health centres in Lebanon, and named the Holy Family Hospital in Bethlehem as a focus of its work. [cite:vt8_mi_ar2024] The Order counts about 13,500 members and roughly 95,000 to 100,000 volunteers worldwide. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom]

The answer to the question

The Order of Malta is connected to the Vatican, but not as a hidden arm of it. The documents show two open ties: a religious tie, under which the Order "depends … on the Holy See" and a pope can remove its Grand Master and rewrite its constitution, as Francis did in 2017 and 2022; and a diplomatic tie, under which the two exchange ambassadors as sovereign equals. [cite:vt8_va_smom2022] [cite:vt8_cna_festing] [cite:vt8_wiki_smom_rel] It exists because a pilgrims' hospital of the eleventh century became a military order that governed two islands, and the recognition it gained as a ruler outlived the loss of its land; Italian courts, the UN General Assembly and more than a hundred states have continued to treat it as sovereign for the purposes of its medical and relief work. [cite:vt8_wiki_smom] [cite:vt8_un_48_265] [cite:vt8_om_diplomacy] When the Order claimed in January 2017 that its sovereignty put its internal acts beyond papal review, the claim did not hold. [cite:vt8_cna_festing] Its sovereignty is real in relation to states and limited in relation to the pope.

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: The Money: IOR, APSA, Peter's Pence
chapters.intro: Part Eight closed with the orders and the Order of Malta. This part follows the money. It separates the three bodies usually lumped together as "the Vatican's money": the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), a bank for Church clients founded by Pius XII in 1942; the Administration of the Patrimony of the Apostolic See (APSA), created in 1967 out of the office that managed Mussolini's 1929 payment and now the owner of the Holy See's buildings, securities and gold; and the Governorate, which runs Vatican City and its museums. It then reads Peter's Pence, the pope's annual collection, for what each year's report says the money paid for, and ends by sorting the Holy See's wealth into what is on published books, what is left off them, and what was never the Holy See's to count, tracing two famous totals to their sources. Every figure comes from the body's own report for a stated year, or from named reporting on it.
chapters.outro: Part Nine has set the Holy See's money out body by body. The IOR, founded on 27 June 1942, serves about 12,000 Church clients. In 2025 it held 5.9 billion euros of their money and 815.3 million euros of its own capital, earned 51 million euros and paid the pope a dividend of 24.3 million. [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] APSA, created in 1967 from the office that managed the 1929 payment and given the Secretariat of State's investments from 1 January 2021, reported net equity of 2,686 million euros in 2025 and paid 22.7 million euros to the Curia. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa_mandate] [cite:vt9_mp_2020] [cite:vt9_apsa_bil2025] The Holy See as a whole closed 2024 with a surplus of 1.6 million euros only after investment gains and asset sales covered an operating deficit of 44.4 million, and its pension fund has an imbalance the pope himself acknowledged. [cite:vt9_america_hs2024] [cite:vt9_ap_pension] Peter's Pence sent between about 12 and 22 per cent of its spending directly to charity in the years reported, and the rest to the Holy See's offices, as the Holy See says it intends. [cite:vt9_vn_pp2024] [cite:vt9_vn_pp2025] [cite:vt9_vn_guerrero2021] The famous totals, "73 billion dollars" and "177 million acres", describe Church property held by separate legal owners, or have no stated method, and are not Holy See figures. [cite:vt9_marketplace_2023] [cite:vt9_cic_1254] Today's figures are the product of reforms forced by earlier scandals. Part Ten tells that history, beginning with [scene:vt10_ambrosiano_calvi|the collapse of Banco Ambrosiano].

sections.h: The Institute for the Works of Religion
sections.html:
Three different bodies hold and move the money that is usually called "the Vatican's". The Institute for the Works of Religion (Istituto per le Opere di Religione, IOR), often called the Vatican Bank, takes deposits and manages assets for clients. The Administration of the Patrimony of the Apostolic See (APSA) owns and manages the Holy See's own property and investments. The Governorate of Vatican City State runs the territory and its museums. They publish separate reports, and the sums in one cannot simply be added to the sums in another. This section deals with the IOR. The next deals with APSA, the Governorate and the Holy See's consolidated accounts. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa_mandate] [cite:vt9_ior_ar2024]

From a charitable commission to an institute

The IOR's own statutes trace its origin to 1887, when Leo XIII created a Commission ad pias causas (for pious causes), which became the Administration for the Works of Religion. Pius XII approved that Administration's statutes on 17 March 1941. By a chirograph (a papal letter with the force of law) dated 27 June 1942, he founded the Institute for the Works of Religion, gave it legal personality and folded the Administration into it. A second chirograph of 24 January 1944 issued new rules, and John Paul II gave the Institute a new framework on 1 March 1990. [cite:vt9_ior_statutes2019] Summaries that credit Pius XI with the founding are wrong: the 1942 chirograph is Pius XII's. [cite:vt9_ior_statutes2019]

The present statutes come from Francis. He renewed them on a two-year trial basis by chirograph of 8 August 2019 and issued them in final form on 30 January 2023, saying that the aim was to define clearly what each organ is responsible for. [cite:vt9_ior_statutes2019] [cite:vt9_ior_statutes2023] Article 1 sets the purpose that both texts repeat: the IOR exists to provide for the custody and administration of movable and immovable goods that natural or legal persons transfer or entrust to it, intended for works of religion or charity. [cite:vt9_ior_statutes2023] It is not a bank licensed in Italy or the European Union. It describes itself as "the only institution authorized to provide financial services in the Vatican City State". [cite:vt9_ior_ar2024] Its supervision under Vatican anti-money-laundering law, and the Council of Europe's MONEYVAL evaluations of it, are covered in [scene:vt5_moneyval_euro|Part Five].

Who may hold an account

The IOR is not open to the public. After the scandals that [scene:vt10_ambrosiano_calvi|Part Ten] covers, it reviewed its client files and closed accounts that did not fit its purpose. When it published its 2014 results in May 2015, the Associated Press reported that it had closed about 4,600 accounts by the end of 2014, some dormant and some held by clients outside the categories it now accepted: religious communities, Catholic bodies, clergy, current and former Vatican employees, and embassies and diplomats accredited to the Holy See. It had 15,181 account holders left. By October 2015, when the review was completed, about 4,800 accounts had been closed in all ([scene:vt10_reform_aml|Part Ten]). [cite:vt9_ap_ior2015] [cite:vt10_ansa_aif2016] Its 2024 and 2025 reports describe "over 12,000 clients" in more than 110 countries, all belonging to or serving the Catholic Church, and the 2025 report singles out religious congregations as the group it worked hardest to serve. [cite:vt9_ior_ar2024] [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] [cite:vt9_vn_ior2025]

Who runs it

The statutes set up five organs, each above the next. A Commission of Cardinals, five cardinals named by the pope for five years and renewable once, checks that the Institute keeps to its statutes and approves the dividend. A Prelate, appointed by the Commission, acts as its secretary and attends the board. The Board of Superintendence, seven members appointed by the Commission for five years, manages the Institute and approves its accounts; its President is the IOR's legal representative. A Director General, appointed by the Board with the Commission's approval, runs daily operations. An external auditor, appointed by the Commission on the Board's proposal, serves three years and can be renewed once. [cite:vt9_ior_statutes2019] [cite:vt9_ior_statutes2023] The 2024 accounts were audited by Mazars Italia and the 2025 accounts by Deloitte & Touche; both gave clean opinions. [cite:vt9_ior_ar2024] [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025]

Jean-Baptiste de Franssu finished his term when the 2025 accounts were approved on 28 April 2026, and François Pauly took office as President. [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] Pauly's earlier career at Edmond de Rothschild and the claims made about it are examined in [scene:vt11_pauly_2026|Part Eleven]. No wrongdoing by him is documented in any source used in this volume.

What the 2024 and 2025 reports show

The 2025 report was the IOR's fourteenth annual report. Its press release on the 2024 report, dated 11 June 2025, gave a net profit of 32.8 million euros, up 7 per cent; net equity of 731.9 million euros; and a Tier 1 capital ratio of 69.43 per cent, which the release said placed the IOR among the most solidly capitalised institutions in the world. Client funds were 5.7 billion euros, up from 5.4 billion, covering "deposits, current accounts, asset management and securities under custody". [cite:vt9_ior_ar2024] The 2025 report, published on 11 May 2026, gave net income of 51 million euros, up 55.5 per cent and the highest in ten years. Net assets were 815.3 million euros, the Tier 1 ratio was 71.9 per cent, client assets were 5.9 billion euros, and the Institute had 115 employees. [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] [cite:vt9_vn_ior2025]

Two of these figures are often confused. Client assets of 5.9 billion euros are money the IOR holds or manages for its clients: congregations, dioceses, Holy See offices, clergy and staff. The IOR does not own that money. Net assets of 815.3 million euros are the Institute's own capital. Reports that call the 5.7 or 5.9 billion the IOR's "total assets" or its "wealth" mistake the clients' money for the bank's. [cite:vt9_ior_ar2024] [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025]

The dividend and what it pays for

The IOR has no shareholders. Each year the Commission of Cardinals decides how much of the profit to pass to the pope and how much to keep as capital. For 2024 it voted a dividend of 13.8 million euros. For 2025 it voted 24.3 million euros, up 76.1 per cent, having considered "the Institute's capitalization needs". [cite:vt9_ior_ar2024] [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] The releases say only that the dividend serves the Institute's "mission to support works of religion and charity"; they do not list what it is spent on. [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] The Holy See's own accounts show where the money goes. In 2015, the first year of consolidated accounts under the new rules, the Secretariat for the Economy listed a 50 million euro contribution from the IOR as one of the Holy See's main sources of income beside its investments, together with 24 million euros from dioceses. [cite:vt9_hs_2015] The IOR's dividend therefore helps cover the running costs of the Roman Curia. It is not a separate charity fund.

One bank for the Holy See, and then not only one

Before 2022, offices of the Holy See could keep money in foreign banks as well as at the IOR. On 23 August 2022 Francis issued a rescript (a papal ruling on how a law is to be read) interpreting Article 219 of his new constitution for the Curia, Praedicate Evangelium. It made the IOR's role as "asset manager and custodian of the movable patrimony of the Holy See" its "exclusive responsibility" and ordered funds held elsewhere moved to the IOR within thirty days of 1 September 2022. [cite:vt9_ewtn_rescript2022] Leo XIV reversed this in part. His rescript Coniuncta Cura, made public on 6 October 2025, repealed the exclusivity. APSA is to use the IOR as a rule but may use banks abroad if the competent bodies "deem it more efficient or convenient", provided it follows the policies of the investment committee chaired by Cardinal Kevin Farrell. [cite:vt9_cna_coniuncta] As of October 2026 that is the rule in force.

Interpretation, not finding: "IOR" read backwards

A reading held on the Sophia platform notes that "IOR" read backwards gives "ROI", the business abbreviation for return on investment. It calls this either a coincidence or an accidentally honest name for an institution that produces a return for the papacy every year. Read through this lens, the dividend figures above give the joke a point: in 2025 the Institute that exists for "works of religion" returned 24.3 million euros to the pope.

The reading proves nothing. The acronym comes from an Italian name chosen in 1942, Istituto per le Opere di Religione, and no document suggests that anyone at the time intended a second meaning. The figures above would be the same under any name. In this volume the wordplay is a way to remember the dividend, not evidence of what the IOR is for. What the IOR is for, by its own account, is stated in Article 1 of its statutes. [cite:vt9_ior_statutes2023]

sections.h: APSA, the Governorate and the Holy See's Accounts
sections.html:
If the IOR is the bank, APSA is the owner. The Administration of the Patrimony of the Apostolic See holds the Holy See's own buildings, land, securities and gold, and pays a share of the income to the Roman Curia. The Governorate of Vatican City State runs the territory: museums, post, shops, police and services. Above both sits the Holy See's consolidated financial statement, which the Secretariat for the Economy has published, with gaps, since the Francis reforms. This section takes each in turn and gives only figures the bodies themselves have published, each with its year. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa_mandate] [cite:vt9_hs_fs2024]

From the 1929 settlement to APSA

APSA's oldest component came from the Lateran settlement. In June 1929 Pius XI created a Special Administration to manage the money Italy paid the Holy See under the Financial Convention annexed to the Treaty of 11 February 1929. That money was 750 million lire in cash and one billion lire in state bonds, and [scene:vt3_what_each_got|Part Three] sets out the terms. On 15 August 1967 Paul VI's apostolic constitution Regimini Ecclesiae Universae created APSA to administer the Holy See's property and the goods other Holy See bodies entrusted to it, with the purpose of funding the Curia. The Special Administration became its Extraordinary Section. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa_mandate] Under Francis's constitution Praedicate Evangelium (2022), APSA is "the body entrusted with the administration and management of the movable and immovable patrimony of the Holy See". It also keeps the Curia's accounts and runs its purchasing, and it carries out its financial operations through the IOR. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa_mandate]

The Secretariat of State's money moves to APSA

Until 2020 the Secretariat of State, the pope's chief office, managed a large investment portfolio of its own, including the London building at 60 Sloane Avenue that led to the trial covered in [scene:vt10_london_trial|Part Ten]. Francis ended this by motu proprio (a decree issued on the pope's own initiative), Una migliore organizzazione, of 26 December 2020. From 1 January 2021, ownership of the Secretariat's funds, bank accounts, investments in property and securities, and company shareholdings passed to APSA. Cash balances, whether at the IOR or in foreign banks, had to be transferred by 4 February 2021. Where a change of owner was impossible, APSA's president received a general power of attorney. Peter's Pence became a sub-account of the "Papal Funds" that APSA administers, and the Secretariat for the Economy was given oversight of the whole. [cite:vt9_mp_2020] The decree gave its reason: the Secretariat of State should not perform economic functions already assigned to other offices. [cite:vt9_mp_2020] The change is often dated to 2022. That was the year Praedicate Evangelium wrote APSA's role into the Curia's constitution and the August rescript sent the Holy See's liquid funds to the IOR, as the previous section explains. The transfer of ownership itself took effect on 1 January 2021, and APSA's 2025 accounts still date it from the 2021 financial year. [cite:vt9_apsa_bil2025] [cite:vt9_ewtn_rescript2022]

What APSA owns and earns

APSA published its first budget in July 2021. It listed about 4,051 properties in Italy and about 1,120 abroad, not counting embassies. About 14 per cent of the Italian properties were let at market rents; most of the rest were let at reduced rents, many of them to Church employees. [cite:vt9_globe_apsa2020] The 2023 report put the units let at market rent at 19.2 per cent, at subsidised rent 10.4 per cent and at zero rent 70.4 per cent. Holdings outside Italy, in London, Paris, Geneva and Lausanne, are owned through companies. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa2023] The 2024 report named the foreign companies as British Grolux Investments in England, Sopridex in France and Profima in Switzerland. It counted 4,234 units in Italy, 2,866 owned by APSA (1,367 residential and 395 commercial among them) and 1,368 belonging to other Holy See bodies and managed by APSA. It also recorded that APSA paid Italy 6 million euros in municipal property tax (IMU) and 3.19 million in corporate income tax (IRES) that year. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa2024]

APSA's results have moved a good deal from year to year. In 2021 it reported a surplus of 8.11 million euros and gave the Curia 30 million. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa2021] In 2022 it broke even after contributing 32.27 million euros. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa2022] In 2023 it made 45.9 million euros and contributed 37.9 million. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa2023] In 2024 it made 62.2 million euros, its president, Archbishop Giordano Piccinotti, called it one of the best results of recent years, and it contributed 46.1 million: a fixed 30 million plus half of the remaining profit. That year the Curia's financial needs were 170.4 million euros. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa2024] In 2025 the operating result fell to 22.8 million euros, all of it, 22.7 million, paid to the Holy See. Piccinotti described 2024 as extraordinary and 2025 as "a return to ordinary operating conditions". He explained that about 16 million euros of 2025 investment gains had been booked directly to net worth under a new accounting rule, the Vatican Financial Management Policy, instead of passing through the income statement. [cite:vt9_vn_apsa2025] [cite:vt9_apsa_bil2025]

APSA's 2025 balance sheet is the most complete picture of what the Holy See itself owns. Net equity was 2,686 million euros, up 89 million in the year, mostly because gold, property and securities were revalued. Total assets were 3,337.5 million euros, of which investment property was valued at 2,211 million. APSA managed 4,281 units in Italy, 2,945 of its own and 1,336 belonging to other Holy See bodies, and about 1,200 more abroad through its companies. Physical gold made up 29 per cent of its own portfolio. Of the roughly 1.95 billion euros in securities and cash it managed, 65.5 per cent belonged to third parties and 22.8 per cent to APSA itself. [cite:vt9_apsa_bil2025] [cite:vt9_vn_apsa2025] Two features of the property figures matter for anyone using them. First, they are book values set by APSA's own accounting rules, not market appraisals. Second, most of the units earn little or nothing, because they house Holy See offices and staff.

The Governorate and the museums

The Governorate's main source of income is culture, above all the Vatican Museums. The last separate figure the Secretariat for the Economy released for it was for 2015: a surplus of 59.9 million euros, which it attributed mainly to cultural revenue, above all from the Museums. [cite:vt9_hs_2015] This volume found no published Governorate statement for later years. The Holy See's 2024 statements show the Governorate as a contributor of 20 million euros to the Holy See (15 million in 2023). [cite:vt9_hs_fs2024] The Museums publish their prices. Since 1 January 2024 a full ticket has cost 20 euros and a reduced ticket 8 euros, plus an optional 5 euro booking fee. [cite:vt9_mv_tariffe] Quotidiano Nazionale reported about 6.9 million visitors in 2025, the Jubilee year. [cite:vt9_qn_museums2025] Revenue figures for the Museums in circulation, such as "135 million euros in 2019" or "at least 120 million dollars a year", come from outside estimates, not accounts; Catholic World Report's 2020 figure of "at least" 120 million dollars a year from ordinary tickets was its own reporter's estimate. [cite:vt9_cwr_museums2020] Without published accounts, this volume reports none of them as fact.

The Holy See's consolidated statement and the pension fund

The consolidated statement for 2024, published on 26 November 2025, is the broadest official account. Including the hospitals the Holy See owns, operating income was 1,230.7 million euros and operating expenses 1,275.2 million: an operating deficit of 44.4 million euros, down from 83.5 million. Investment income, one-off asset sales and higher donations turned this into a surplus of 1.6 million, against a deficit of 51.2 million in 2023. Excluding the hospitals, revenue was 546.5 million euros and expenses 527.8 million. Total assets were 6,326.7 million euros and net equity 4,277.0 million. [cite:vt9_hs_fs2024] [cite:vt9_america_hs2024] Of 393.3 million euros spent on the "apostolic mission", 37 per cent went to local churches in difficulty, 14 per cent to worship and evangelisation, 12 per cent to communications and 10 per cent each to the nunciatures and to charity. [cite:vt9_vn_hs2024] The Prefect for the Economy, Maximino Caballero Ledo, said that "an operating deficit of 44.4 million euros remains". [cite:vt9_america_hs2024]

The statement does not include a separate account of the Vatican pension fund. On 21 November 2024 Francis wrote that an analysis showed "a serious prospective imbalance in the fund" and appointed Cardinal Kevin Farrell as its special administrator. The Association of Lay Vatican Employees asked for the fund's balance sheet to be published. [cite:vt9_ap_pension] The 2024 consolidated statements record actuarial losses on employee benefits of 22.5 million euros (34.4 million in 2023) but give no figure for the fund's shortfall. [cite:vt9_hs_fs2024] As of October 2026 this volume found no published balance sheet for the fund.

sections.h: Peter's Pence: What the Collection Pays For
sections.html:
Peter's Pence (the Obolo di San Pietro) is the annual collection that dioceses, foundations, religious institutes and private donors send to the pope. It is the one stream of Holy See money that ordinary churchgoers pay into directly, and so it is the one whose use donors have questioned most sharply. The answer is in the Holy See's own reports, which since 2021 have broken the fund's income and spending down each year. Most of the money supports the running of the Holy See, and a smaller part goes directly to charity. The Holy See says so itself. [cite:vt9_vn_guerrero2021] [cite:vt9_vn_pp2024]

What the Holy See says the fund is for

Fr Juan Antonio Guerrero Alves, then Prefect of the Secretariat for the Economy, set out the official account in an interview with Vatican News on 25 June 2021. Peter's Pence, he said, supports the pope's charity in two ways. Part of it goes directly to local churches, institutions, families and people in need. Part of it pays for offices of the Curia that serve the universal Church but earn little or no income: those responsible for doctrine, liturgy and the Church's courts, the papal communications offices, and the Vatican Library and Archives. "People have the right to know how we spend the money that is given to us," he said. [cite:vt9_vn_guerrero2021] Francis's decree of 26 December 2020 had already made the fund a sub-account of the Papal Funds administered by APSA. Under it, money is paid out at the Secretariat of State's request, within the approved budget, and spending outside the budget needs the Secretariat for the Economy's approval. [cite:vt9_mp_2020]

The disclosures began in a crisis of trust. Reuters reported in June 2022 that giving had fallen 23 per cent between 2015 and 2019 and a further 18 per cent in 2020. Many Catholics said they had stopped giving because of the Vatican's financial scandals, above all the London building purchase then at the centre of the trial covered in [scene:vt10_london_trial|Part Ten]. [cite:vt9_reuters_pp2021] Guerrero acknowledged that Peter's Pence investments had been mixed with other Secretariat of State funds, so that it was hard to tell which assets belonged to which. At the end of 2020 the fund held about 205 million euros, partly in illiquid investments that included the London building. [cite:vt9_vn_guerrero2021] His position was that the losses on the London building "did not weigh on" Peter's Pence but on other Secretariat of State funds. [cite:vt9_vn_guerrero2021] When the building was sold to Bain Capital for 186 million pounds, announced on 1 July 2022, the Holy See said the capital loss had been charged entirely to the Secretariat of State's reserve funds and that Peter's Pence "has not been touched". [cite:vt9_vn_sloane] These are the Holy See's own statements. The court record on the investment is the subject of Part Ten.

The numbers, year by year

In 2021, according to Reuters' reading of the first detailed report, contributions came to about 46.9 million euros and spending to about 65.3 million. About 55.5 million euros went to Vatican offices, nunciatures, communications and local churches, and about 10 million to 157 direct-aid projects. The deficit was covered from other Holy See income. [cite:vt9_reuters_pp2021] For 2023 the report gave income of 52 million euros: 48.4 million in donations and 3.6 million in financial income. Spending was 109.4 million euros, of which 90 million supported the apostolic mission through 68 Holy See bodies and 13 million went to 236 projects in 76 countries. The 2022 income figure, 107 million, was inflated by a one-off capital gain on the sale of property the fund owned. [cite:vt9_vn_pp2023]

For 2024 the fund collected 58 million euros: 54.3 million in donations and 3.7 million in financial and other income. It spent 75.4 million. Of that, 61.2 million went to the work of the dicasteries, about 17 per cent of the Holy See's 367.4 million euros of mission costs, and 13.3 million went to 239 projects in 66 countries. [cite:vt9_vn_pp2024] For 2025, the report published on 30 June 2026 gave revenue of 57.6 million euros, with donations of 54.5 million, and spending of 59.8 million: a deficit of 2.2 million, which it attributed to exchange rates. Of the spending, 41.2 million euros supported the Holy See's mission, about 10 per cent of the 404.5 million spent on that mission in 2025, and 13.3 million went to 252 projects in 74 countries. Africa received the largest regional share, 5.2 million euros for 73 projects. [cite:vt9_vn_pp2025]

The share that goes to charity

The share of spending that went directly to charity projects can be worked out from the reports themselves. It was about 15 per cent in 2021 (10 of 65.3 million), about 12 per cent in 2023 (13 of 109.4 million), about 18 per cent in 2024 (13.3 of 75.4 million) and about 22 per cent in 2025 (13.3 of 59.8 million). [cite:vt9_reuters_pp2021] [cite:vt9_vn_pp2023] [cite:vt9_vn_pp2024] [cite:vt9_vn_pp2025] These are this volume's own divisions. They depend on what is counted as spending: the 2023 report, for example, gives total disbursements of 103 million beside spending of 109.4 million. A widely repeated claim holds that only "roughly 10%" of the collection goes to charitable works. That figure matches neither the 2024 or 2025 reports nor the general pattern; it is closest to the 2021 and 2023 shares. In every year the cash projects took a minority of the money and the Holy See's offices took the majority.

Two points keep this in proportion. First, the Holy See does not hide the split. Its reports put the mission figure first, and Guerrero's account counts paying for the Curia's non-earning offices as part of the pope's service. A donor who expects the whole gift to reach the poor will not find that promise in the Holy See's own description of the fund. [cite:vt9_vn_guerrero2021] [cite:vt9_vn_pp2024] Second, "mission" spending is not all administration. In the consolidated accounts, 37 per cent of the 2024 mission budget supported local churches in difficulty and 10 per cent went to the service of charity. [cite:vt9_vn_hs2024] The reports do not say how much of Peter's Pence money ended up in each of those lines.

Who gives

Dioceses give most of the money. In 2023 they gave 31.2 million euros (64.4 per cent of donations) and foundations 13.9 million. By country, the United States led with 13.6 million euros (28.1 per cent), followed by Italy with 3.1 million and Brazil with 1.9 million. [cite:vt9_vn_pp2023] In 2024 donors in the United States gave 25.2 per cent, France 15 per cent, Italy 5.2 per cent, Brazil 3 per cent and Germany 2.8 per cent. [cite:vt9_vn_pp2024] In 2025 dioceses gave 34.7 million euros (63.6 per cent), foundations 13 million, private donors 5.4 million and religious institutes 1.4 million. The United States again gave the most, 14.2 million euros. [cite:vt9_vn_pp2025] Set beside the Holy See's budget, Peter's Pence is modest. Its 54.5 million euros in donations for 2025 were about a tenth of the Holy See's non-hospital revenue, which was 546.5 million euros in 2024, and about a twentieth of the 1.06 billion euros that the Italian Bishops' Conference received from the otto per mille in 2026, money that goes to the Church in Italy, not to the Holy See ([scene:vt3_otto_per_mille|Part Three]). [cite:vt9_hs_fs2024] [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026]

sections.h: True Wealth and Public Wealth: What Is on the Books
sections.html:
The wealth of "the Vatican" is usually given as a single large number. The documents allow a more exact answer. Some assets are on published books, with a year and an auditor or a responsible office attached. Some are deliberately left off or carried at a symbolic value. A third group, much the largest, belongs to other legal owners and was never the Holy See's to count. The popular totals mostly blur these three groups together. This section separates them and then traces two of the best-known totals to where they came from.

Who owns Church property: one Church, many legal owners

Canon law answers the ownership question directly. Canon 1256 provides that "under the supreme authority of the Roman Pontiff, ownership of goods belongs to that juridic person" that lawfully acquired them. A diocese, a parish, a religious order, a Catholic university or hospital foundation is each its own juridic person (a legal entity under Church law), and in almost every country it is also a separate legal person under national law. [cite:vt9_cic_1254] Canon 1273 makes the pope "the supreme administrator and steward of all ecclesiastical goods". That gives him authority over how Church goods are managed. It does not make the Holy See their owner, and it does not put a diocese's buildings on APSA's balance sheet. [cite:vt9_cic_1254] Money moves in the other direction by rule: canon 1271 asks bishops to help supply what the Apostolic See needs, in proportion to their dioceses' means. The Holy See's 2015 accounts recorded 24 million euros from that source. [cite:vt9_cic_1254] [cite:vt9_hs_2015]

The large national flows of Church money follow the same rule. The Italian otto per mille, more than a billion euros a year, goes to the Italian Bishops' Conference, not to the Holy See, and it does not pass into the Holy See's accounts except through contributions like those under canon 1271 and Peter's Pence. [scene:vt3_otto_per_mille|Part Three] follows the Italian money. [cite:vt3_teleborsa_8x2026]

What is on the published books

Four bodies now publish figures, each for itself. The IOR holds 5.9 billion euros of clients' money and 815.3 million euros of its own capital (2025). [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] APSA reported net equity of 2,686 million euros and total assets of 3,337.5 million (2025), including investment property at 2,211 million and a gold holding equal to 29 per cent of its own portfolio. [cite:vt9_apsa_bil2025] Peter's Pence took in 57.6 million euros in 2025. [cite:vt9_vn_pp2025] The Holy See's consolidated statement for 2024 gave total assets of 6,326.7 million euros and net equity of 4,277.0 million, hospitals included. [cite:vt9_hs_fs2024]

These figures cannot be added together. Since 2022 the Holy See's funds have been kept at the IOR as a rule (exclusively until Leo XIV's rescript of October 2025), and APSA, by its own description, carries out its financial operations through the IOR, so adding the two would count some of the same money twice. [cite:vt9_ewtn_rescript2022] [cite:vt9_cna_coniuncta] [cite:vt9_vn_apsa_mandate] The IOR's 5.9 billion also includes the savings of religious congregations and other Church bodies that are separate owners under canon 1256. [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] [cite:vt9_cic_1254] The consolidated statement is the nearest thing to a total for the Holy See, and even it does not say exactly which bodies it covers. [cite:vt9_hs_fs2024]

What is carried at a symbolic value

The largest gap between book value and any imaginable market value is the Holy See's art and its historic buildings. In 2005 the Associated Press reported that St Peter's Basilica and the Sistine Chapel were listed in the Holy See's accounts at a symbolic one euro each, the officials' reasoning being that such works are "a treasure for all humanity" and cannot be sold. Its other real estate was then valued at about 700 million euros. [cite:vt9_ap_2005_deficit] Marketplace in 2023 quoted a Vatican accountant from 2004 to the same effect. [cite:vt9_marketplace_2023] The 2024 consolidated statements give no valuation of the historic, artistic or cultural heritage at all. "Historic Patrimony" appears only as a cost, an expense line of 19.58 million euros for its upkeep under the apostolic mission. [cite:vt9_hs_fs2024] The accounts treat the heritage as a cost to maintain, not as an asset that could be sold. Whatever such works might fetch is therefore not part of any published Holy See figure, and an estimate of it, such as the "10–15 billion dollars" sometimes given for the art, is a guess about a sale the owner says will never happen. No document supports any such figure.

Two famous numbers, traced

"73 billion dollars." This figure circulates as a total for "Holy See assets". Its likely origin is a Marketplace explainer of 10 February 2023, which estimated the Catholic Church's assets at "at least $73 billion". Marketplace reached that total by adding a few unrelated published estimates: diocesan assets in Australia (extrapolated from the state of Victoria) and in Germany, Trinity Church's portfolio in New York, and the IOR's and Holy See's own figures. It said plainly that dioceses are separate and that the real figure could not be known. [cite:vt9_marketplace_2023] Most of the total was therefore not the Holy See's. One of its pieces, Trinity Church Wall Street's portfolio of about 6 billion dollars, is not even Catholic: Trinity is an Episcopal parish. [cite:vt9_npq_trinity] As a measure of "Holy See assets", the number fails on its own source's terms.

"177 million acres." This figure, often given with "larger than Texas" and "the world's second-largest landowner", is a claim about land held by all Catholic entities worldwide, not by the Holy See. It circulates through business and lifestyle journalism, among them Bisnow in 2015 (citing a 2011 Business Insider list of landowners) and Benzinga in 2022, and none of these gives a method. Bisnow itself called the true figure "virtually impossible to calculate". [cite:vt9_bisnow_2015] [cite:vt9_benzinga_land] Other writers give other numbers: David Owen, in a New Yorker profile in 2021, put Church holdings at about 200 million acres, and Gerald Posner, author of God's Bankers, at about 277,000 square miles, which is the same 177 million acres expressed differently. [cite:vt9_longreads_owen] [cite:vt9_marketplace_2023] The cartographer Molly Burhans, who was mapping Church land with Vatican permission, found that no comprehensive inventory existed. [cite:vt9_benzinga_land] With no inventory and no stated method, the figure is an estimate repeated from one article to the next, not a measurement. This volume does not use it.

The wider ranges that circulate, such as "a Catholic institutional network of 300 billion to 1 trillion dollars" or IOR assets of "2 to 8 billion dollars, never published", fail for the same reasons. They have no source, they mix separate owners, and in the IOR's case they are out of date: the IOR has published its figures every year since its first annual report.

What can be said

The defensible statement is narrow. On its own published books, the Holy See is an institution with net equity of about 4.3 billion euros (2024), a property and investment arm worth about 2.7 billion on its own valuation (2025), and a bank holding about 5.9 billion euros of other people's money (2025). It has an operating deficit and a pension fund that its own head has described as seriously imbalanced. [cite:vt9_hs_fs2024] [cite:vt9_apsa_bil2025] [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] [cite:vt9_ap_pension] Beyond those books lie art and buildings it says it will never sell, and a worldwide body of Church property that belongs, in law, to thousands of other owners. A larger single figure for "the Vatican's wealth" can be produced only by counting those things as the Holy See's, and the documents do not support doing so.

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: Scandal and Reform: Ambrosiano to the Becciu Retrial
chapters.intro: Part Nine described the Holy See's money as its own reports show it today. Part Ten tells how it came to be reported that way. It begins with the IOR's crisis years under Archbishop Paul Marcinkus: the collapse of Michele Sindona's banks in 1974, the failure of Banco Ambrosiano in 1982, the death of its chairman Roberto Calvi under Blackfriars Bridge in London, the settlement of 1984 by which the IOR paid the Ambrosiano's creditors while denying liability, and the ruling of 1987 that the Lateran Treaty kept IOR officials out of Italian courts. The second section follows the Secretariat of State's investment in a London building through the trial that ended on 16 December 2023 with the conviction of Cardinal Giovanni Angelo Becciu and eight others, and the appeal ruling of 17 March 2026 that ordered the hearings to be held again, with the case's status as of October 2026. The third section traces the reforms, from the first anti-money-laundering law of 2010 to the rule of 2022 that every Holy See body keep its money at the IOR, relaxed by Leo XIV in 2025, each of them written after a scandal had exposed a gap, and sets the outside evaluators' ratings beside them.
chapters.outro: Part Ten has shown that the Holy See's financial rules were written in the wake of its scandals. Under Paul Marcinkus the IOR did business with Michele Sindona and Roberto Calvi, issued letters that creditors read as backing for Calvi's offshore companies, and in 1984 paid those creditors about $240–250 million while denying any liability; in 1987 Italy's Court of Cassation held that the Lateran Treaty barred the prosecution of its officials, and no one has ever been convicted of Calvi's death. [cite:vt10_avv_anfossi] [cite:vt10_time_1984] [cite:vt10_cc_609_1988] [cite:vt10_wiki_calvi] The Secretariat of State's London investment, sold at a loss in 2022, led to the conviction of Cardinal Giovanni Angelo Becciu and eight others on 16 December 2023; on 17 March 2026 the Court of Appeal found the summons defective and ordered the hearings renewed, and as of October 2026 the next hearing was set for 29 October, with every defendant presumed innocent. [cite:vt10_vn_verdict2023] [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] [cite:vt10_us_oct2026] Each exposure brought a reform: the 2010 law and supervisor, the closure of about 4,800 IOR accounts, the Secretariat for the Economy, and the centralisation of the Holy See's money in APSA and the IOR, which MONEYVAL rated as substantially or moderately effective in 2021 while faulting prosecution and confiscation. [cite:vt5_va_aif_profile] [cite:vt10_ansa_aif2016] [cite:vt6_gc_spe] [cite:vt6_vn_apsa2020] [cite:vt10_ncreg_rescript2022] [cite:vt5_mv_2021mer] Popular accounts link these scandals to a centuries-long Rothschild hand in Vatican finance; Part Eleven tests that claim against the documents, beginning with [scene:vt11_papal_loans|the papal loans of the nineteenth century].

sections.h: God's Bankers: Sindona, Marcinkus and the Fall of Banco Ambrosiano
sections.html:
The Holy See's bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), is described in [scene:vt9_ior|Part Nine] as it runs today: a small institution with published accounts and a Church clientele. Its reputation was made in the 1970s and 1980s, when its president was an American archbishop, Paul Marcinkus, and two Italian bankers who did business with it, Michele Sindona and Roberto Calvi, ended their lives in a prison cell and under a London bridge. This section sets out what the court records and contemporary reporting establish about that period, what they leave unresolved, and what the Holy See said about it at the time. It names individuals because the record names them; none of them stands for the Church, and the Holy See's legal position, that it bore no liability, is given beside each finding.

Marcinkus and Sindona

Paul Marcinkus, a priest of the Archdiocese of Chicago, was made secretary of the IOR by Paul VI in 1968 and was its president from 1971 to 1989. [cite:vt10_wiki_marcinkus] [cite:vt10_wiki_ior] The Holy See had begun to use the Sicilian financier Michele Sindona as an adviser after it lost its Italian tax exemption on investment income in 1968, and his association with the IOR dates from 1969. [cite:vt10_wiki_ior] [cite:vt10_wiki_sindona] Sindona's banks failed in 1974. In the United States, Franklin National Bank, which his holding company had controlled since 1972, was declared insolvent on 8 October 1974; in Italy his Banca Privata Italiana went into liquidation, and its liquidator, the lawyer Giorgio Ambrosoli, was shot dead in Milan on 11 July 1979. [cite:vt10_wiki_sindona] A federal court in Manhattan convicted Sindona in 1980 on 65 counts, including fraud and perjury, and sentenced him to 25 years. Extradited to Italy on 25 September 1984, he was sentenced to 12 years for the fraudulent bankruptcy of Banca Privata Italiana on 16 March 1985 and to life imprisonment on 18 March 1986 as the instigator of Ambrosoli's murder. Two days later he drank coffee laced with cyanide in Voghera prison; he died on 22 March 1986. [cite:vt10_wiki_sindona] One estimate put the IOR's loss from the Sindona collapse at 35 billion lire. [cite:vt10_wiki_ior]

Calvi, the IOR and the Ambrosiano

Banco Ambrosiano was a Milan bank founded in 1896 by a Catholic lawyer, Giuseppe Tovini. Roberto Calvi became its general manager in 1971 and its chairman in 1975, and built a web of foreign subsidiaries in Luxembourg, the Bahamas and South America; Marcinkus sat on the board of one of them, Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau. [cite:vt10_wiki_ambrosiano] [cite:vt10_wiki_marcinkus] The IOR was a major shareholder in the bank. [cite:vt10_wiki_ambrosiano] [cite:vt10_wiki_ior] Calvi was a member of Licio Gelli's masonic lodge Propaganda Due (P2), and in 1981 he was given a four-year suspended sentence and a fine of $19.8 million for moving $27 million out of Italy in breach of currency law; he kept his post while he appealed. [cite:vt10_wiki_calvi]

Before the collapse the IOR gave Calvi letters of patronage, also called letters of comfort, concerning companies in his network; their creditors could read them as a sign that the Vatican bank stood behind those companies' debts. [cite:vt10_sage_ambrosiano] [cite:vt10_lat_marcinkus] In 1982 the Ambrosiano could not account for about $1.29 billion, most of it lent to Panamanian companies that were nominally owned by the IOR. [cite:vt10_wiki_ambrosiano] [cite:vt10_csm_1984] The Bank of Italy took control in June, and in August 1982 a new bank, Nuovo Banco Ambrosiano, under Giovanni Bazoli, took over the old one's business. [cite:vt10_wiki_ambrosiano] [cite:vt10_sage_ambrosiano] Marcinkus's own account was that the letters had been issued to limit further lending to the affiliated companies, that Calvi used them for other purposes, and that Calvi had released the IOR in writing from any liability under them. [cite:vt10_avv_anfossi] [cite:vt10_lat_marcinkus] In 1990 he said: "I have never done anything wrong." [cite:vt10_lat_marcinkus]

Blackfriars Bridge

Calvi left his Rome flat on 10 June 1982 on a false passport in the name "Gian Roberto Calvini." At 7.30 on the morning of Friday 18 June 1982 a postal clerk found his body hanging from scaffolding beneath Blackfriars Bridge in London, with five bricks and about $14,000 in three currencies in his pockets. [cite:vt10_wiki_calvi] A first London inquest, in July 1982, returned a verdict of suicide; a second, in July 1983, returned an open verdict, finding that the cause could not be determined. [cite:vt10_wiki_calvi] [cite:vt10_sage_ambrosiano] Calvi's family pressed the case for years. His body was exhumed in December 1998, a forensic report commissioned by an Italian court confirmed in October 2002 the findings of an earlier private report obtained by the family, and the City of London Police reopened the case as a murder inquiry in September 2003. [cite:vt10_wiki_calvi]

In Rome, five people went on trial for the murder on 5 October 2005: Giuseppe Calò, Flavio Carboni, Manuela Kleinszig, Ernesto Diotallevi and Silvano Vittor. On 6 June 2007 the court acquitted all five for insufficient evidence, while holding that Calvi had been murdered. The appeal court confirmed the acquittals of Calò, Carboni and Diotallevi on 7 May 2010, and the Court of Cassation confirmed them on 18 November 2011. [cite:vt10_wiki_calvi] No one has been convicted of killing Calvi. The record therefore supports two statements and no more: Italian courts treated the death as murder, and no court found who committed it. No document in that record ties the death to the Holy See or to the IOR, and the theories that do so remain theories.

The Geneva settlement

The Italian Treasury minister, Beniamino Andreatta, called the IOR a de facto partner of the Ambrosiano and demanded that the Vatican pay 1,159 million dollars. The Secretary of State, Cardinal Agostino Casaroli, set up a joint Italian–Vatican commission; it split in the autumn of 1983, two of the three Italian experts finding the IOR responsible and the three Vatican members taking the opposite view. [cite:vt10_avv_anfossi] On 17 August 1983 the Vatican members advised a negotiated settlement, and a meeting at Castel Gandolfo that month, attended by John Paul II, approved one, with Marcinkus the only dissenter, according to documents published in 2023 by Francesco Anfossi. [cite:vt10_avv_anfossi]

The agreement was signed in Geneva on 25 May 1984. The IOR undertook to pay the creditors of the old Ambrosiano about $240–250 million, described as a voluntary contribution, and admitted no liability. [cite:vt10_avv_anfossi] [cite:vt10_time_1984] TIME reported that the payment was made "solely because of moral considerations" and that the Holy See "has always insisted that it has no legal or financial responsibility." [cite:vt10_time_1984] Vatican officials said they had been the victims of a "hidden project" by Calvi. [cite:vt10_csm_1984] The sum is reported differently in different sources, as the figure below shows; none of the sources found gives the text of the agreement, so the exact figure should be read as a range.

The arrest warrant and the Lateran Treaty

The settlement did not end the criminal case. On 20 February 1987 the examining magistrate in Milan issued arrest warrants against Marcinkus and two IOR lay officials, Luigi Mennini and Pellegrino De Strobel, for complicity in the fraudulent bankruptcy of Banco Ambrosiano. [cite:vt10_cc_609_1988] Marcinkus stayed inside Vatican City. On 17 July 1987 the Court of Cassation annulled the order confirming the warrant and held that the Italian courts had no jurisdiction, because Article 11 of the Lateran Treaty exempts the "central entities" of the Catholic Church from interference by the Italian state; the Constitutional Court declared further challenges to Article 11 inadmissible on 6 June 1988. [cite:vt10_cc_609_1988] [scene:vt3_what_each_got|Part Three: what each side got in 1929] Others in the Ambrosiano affair were convicted in Milan: Gelli's 12-year sentence for the crash was confirmed by the Court of Cassation in April 1998. [cite:vt10_wiki_ambrosiano] Marcinkus resigned from Vatican service on 30 October 1990, served as a parish priest in Sun City, Arizona, and died there on 20 February 2006, aged 84, without having been tried. [cite:vt10_wiki_marcinkus] [cite:vt10_lat_marcinkus]

What the record settles

The documents establish that the IOR under Marcinkus did business with two bankers who were later convicted, that it issued letters which creditors could read as support for Calvi's offshore companies, that it paid roughly a quarter of a billion dollars to those creditors while denying liability, and that the Lateran Treaty, as read by Italy's highest court, kept its officials out of an Italian dock. [cite:vt10_cc_609_1988] [cite:vt10_time_1984] They do not establish who killed Calvi, and no source found supports claims that the Ambrosiano had ties to a "Rothschild banking network" or that Gelli organised postwar escape routes through the Vatican; neither rests on any document. The later cases, from 2010 onward, are taken up in [scene:vt10_reform_aml|the reform section] of this part.

sections.h: Sloane Avenue: the London Building, the Trial and the Retrial
sections.html:
The largest criminal case the Vatican's courts have heard concerned a former Harrods warehouse at 60 Sloane Avenue in Chelsea, bought in stages by the Secretariat of State, the pope's chief office, with money from its own reserves. [cite:vt10_rns_sale2022] The case produced the first criminal conviction of a cardinal by a Holy See court, on 16 December 2023, and then, on 17 March 2026, an appeal ruling that found the prosecution's founding acts defective and ordered the hearings to be held again. [cite:vt10_ap_verdict2023] [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] As of October 2026 the renewed proceedings had not concluded. Every defendant whose case is being reheard is presumed innocent, and each has maintained his or her innocence throughout. [cite:vt10_ap_mistrial2026] How the Vatican's courts are built, and why a 2021 change let them try cardinals, is set out in [scene:vt4_citizens_courts_prisons|Part Four].

The investment

In 2013 and 2014 the Secretariat of State paid about $200.5 million for shares in Athena Capital Commodities, a fund linked to the financier Raffaele Mincione; the Vatican tribunal later described the sum as about a third of the funds the Secretariat then had available. [cite:vt10_vn_verdict2023] The money went in part into the company that owned the London building and in part into other investments. [cite:vt10_vn_verdict2023] The investment was first made through accounts the Secretariat held at Swiss banks, including Credit Suisse. [cite:vt10_ncreg_rescript2022] Later the Secretariat sought to take the building over directly, using a second broker, Gianluigi Torzi; prosecutors alleged that the Holy See was then extorted into paying him 15 million euros to give up control, which his defence called the negotiated exit from a binding contract. [cite:vt10_ap_mistrial2026] [cite:vt10_ap_verdict2023] In all, the Secretariat put about 350 million euros into the building, plus fees and commissions. [cite:vt10_rns_sale2022]

The Vatican Gendarmerie searched offices of the Secretariat of State and of the Financial Information Authority on 1 October 2019. [cite:vt5_cwr_egmont2020] On 24 September 2020 the Holy See announced that the pope had accepted the resignation of Cardinal Giovanni Angelo Becciu, who had been the Secretariat's second-ranking official, the Substitute, from 2011 to 2018, as prefect of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints "and from the rights connected with the Cardinalate." [cite:vt10_vn_becciu2020] [cite:vt10_wiki_becciu] On 1 July 2022 the Vatican announced it had sold the building to Bain Capital for 186 million pounds (about 215 million euros). Prosecutors put total losses above 200 million euros; the Vatican said the losses had been absorbed by the Secretariat's reserves and did not touch Peter's Pence, the collection described in [scene:vt9_peters_pence|Part Nine]. [cite:vt10_rns_sale2022]

The first trial and the verdict of 16 December 2023

Becciu was indicted on 3 July 2021, with Pope Francis's approval, and the trial of ten people and four companies opened on 27 July 2021 before the Tribunal of Vatican City State, presided over by Giuseppe Pignatone, and ran to 86 hearings. [cite:vt10_wiki_becciu] [cite:vt10_vn_verdict2023] On 16 December 2023 the tribunal convicted Becciu on three counts of embezzlement and sentenced him to five years and six months, a fine of 8,000 euros and permanent disqualification from public office. The three counts were the Athena payment; payments of more than 570,000 euros to a company linked to Cecilia Marogna, made on grounds the court found untrue, that the money would help free a kidnapped nun; and 125,000 euros sent to the Caritas of the diocese of Ozieri in Sardinia but meant for a cooperative, SPES, chaired by Becciu's brother. The court acquitted him of the other charges, including the charge that the building had been overvalued. [cite:vt10_vn_verdict2023] Mincione received five years and six months, Torzi six years, the former financial manager Enrico Crasso and the Secretariat official Fabrizio Tirabassi seven years each, the lawyer Nicola Squillace a suspended term, and Marogna three years and nine months; the former heads of the Financial Information Authority, René Brülhart and Tommaso Di Ruzza, were fined for failing to report a suspicious transaction, and Becciu's former secretary, Mauro Carlino, was acquitted. [cite:vt10_vn_verdict2023] The tribunal ordered 166 million euros confiscated and 200 million euros paid in civil damages to Vatican offices; prosecutors had asked for more than 400 million. [cite:vt10_ap_verdict2023]

The positions on each side were stated on the day. The Promoter of Justice, Alessandro Diddi, said the result "showed we were correct." Becciu's lawyer, Fabio Viglione, said his client respected the sentence and would appeal. [cite:vt10_ap_verdict2023] Becciu said the 125,000 euros were for a bakery that employed young people at risk and had never left diocesan accounts, and he has maintained that Francis authorised payments to free the nun and called the case "a machination" against him; prosecutors produced letters in which Francis denied authorising the Marogna engagement or the London investment. [cite:vt10_ap_verdict2023] [cite:vt10_avv_nullita2026] [cite:vt10_wiki_becciu] Defence lawyers argued that the Vatican's old procedural rules had given prosecutors "enormous leeway to withhold evidence." [cite:vt10_ap_verdict2023]

The appeal and the ruling of 17 March 2026

The appeal opened on 22 September 2025 before the Vatican Court of Appeal, presided over by Archbishop Alejandro Arellano Cedillo, Dean of the Roman Rota. [cite:vt10_s24_appeal2025] The defence asked for messages exchanged among the public-relations consultant Francesca Chaouqui, Genoveffa Ciferri and Monsignor Alberto Perlasca, a former Secretariat official who became the prosecution's main witness; the messages had been withheld at first instance. [cite:vt10_s24_appeal2025] [cite:vt10_avv_nullita2026] In January 2026 the Court of Cassation upheld the dismissal of the prosecutor's own appeal for a procedural error, and Diddi stepped aside from the case. [cite:vt10_ap_mistrial2026]

On 17 March 2026 the Court of Appeal issued a 16-page ruling. It held that the prosecutors' failure to give the defence all of their evidence vitiated the summons to trial, and that one of four rescripts, decrees by which Pope Francis had widened the prosecutors' powers during the investigation, had not been published in time and so may have undermined some investigative acts. [cite:vt10_ap_mistrial2026] [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] The court affirmed that papal rescripts are a legitimate exercise of the pope's authority and rejected the defence's arguments based on the European Convention on Human Rights, which the Vatican has not incorporated. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] It declared a "relative nullity", declined to annul the whole first-instance trial, kept the acquittals of defendants against whom no valid appeal lay, and ordered key hearings, including witness evidence, to be held again before the appeal court itself. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] [cite:vt10_avv_nullita2026] It ordered the Promoter of Justice to deposit the complete investigative file by 30 April 2026. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026]

Reports differ on what the ruling did to the 2023 convictions. Vatican News, ANSA and EWTN reported that the first-instance judgment kept legal effect for the time being; AP reported that the errors "nullified the original indictment" and required a new trial. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] [cite:vt10_ansa_becciu2026] [cite:vt10_cwr_retrial2026] [cite:vt10_ap_mistrial2026] Read together, the sources show that the 2023 sentences cannot become final until the renewed hearings end and that the appeal court will decide afresh. Becciu said, through his lawyers, that "my complete innocence will be recognized soon"; Tirabassi's lawyers said it was the first time in Vatican history that a court had found a papal rescript invalid. [cite:vt10_ansa_becciu2026] [cite:vt10_ap_mistrial2026] The Holy See issued no comment beyond its news report of the ruling. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026]

Status as of October 2026

The defence said that the Promoter of Justice's office had not deposited the complete file by the 30 April deadline. [cite:vt10_adige_atti2026] The court had fixed 22 June 2026 for a hearing to set the calendar; by 19 September 2026 the court had fixed 21 September for defence briefs and 29 October 2026 for the next hearing, and Viglione said the defence was "at peace," confident of Becciu's innocence. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] [cite:vt10_us_oct2026] No later ruling was found as of 22 October 2026. Becciu and the other defendants in the renewed proceedings are presumed innocent until a final judgment. The case's lasting effect on how the Holy See holds its money is the subject of [scene:vt10_reform_aml|the next section].

sections.h: Reform by Scandal: From the 2010 Law to Central Control of the Funds
sections.html:
The Holy See's financial rules today were not drawn up on a clean sheet. Nearly every layer of them was added after a particular case exposed a gap: a seizure by Italian prosecutors in 2010, the arrest of a curial accountant in 2013, an embezzlement found inside the IOR's own property sales, and the London building examined in [scene:vt10_london_trial|the previous section]. This section follows those cases and the reforms that answered them, in order, and closes with the outside evaluators' verdict on the result. The external checks themselves, the euro agreement with the European Union and the Council of Europe's MONEYVAL committee, are described in full in [scene:vt5_moneyval_euro|Part Five] and are summarised here only where a reform responded to them.

The first law and the 2010 seizure

Vatican City's Monetary Agreement with the European Union, signed on 17 December 2009, obliged it to adopt the Union's anti-money-laundering rules. [cite:vt5_va_monetary] The Holy See's first anti-money-laundering law and a supervisory body to apply it, the Financial Information Authority (AIF), followed on 30 December 2010, by motu proprio of Benedict XVI. [cite:vt5_va_aif_profile] In between came the case that showed why. On 21 September 2010 Italian prosecutors seized about 23 million euros of the IOR's money held at a small Italian bank, Credito Artigiano, after two transfers were reported as suspicious, and placed the IOR's president, Ettore Gotti Tedeschi, and another senior official under investigation. The Holy See said it was "perplexed and astonished," expressed full confidence in Gotti Tedeschi, and said it was already working to bring its finances into line with international anti-money-laundering rules. [cite:vt10_bbc_seizure2010] The money was released in 2011. Gotti Tedeschi was ousted as president on 24 May 2012; the laundering case against him was dropped in 2013. [cite:vt10_wiki_ior] The Holy See joined MONEYVAL in 2011, and the committee's first report, in July 2012, found 9 of 16 key standards met and "strongly recommended" that the IOR be given a prudential supervisor. [cite:vt5_ncreg_aml2017] [cite:vt5_mv_2012es]

2013–2015: the IOR clears its books

In June 2013 Italian police arrested Monsignor Nunzio Scarano, for 22 years a senior accountant at the Administration of the Patrimony of the Apostolic See (APSA), on charges of plotting with a secret-service agent and a broker to bring 20 million euros into Italy from Switzerland; the IOR froze more than 2 million euros in his ten accounts there. In January 2016 a Rome court acquitted him of corruption and attempted smuggling and convicted him of making a false accusation; he said his money came from donations. [cite:vt10_rns_scarano2016] The same year the IOR hired the consultancy Promontory to review every client relationship, and from October 2013 it asked lay customers who were neither clergy nor Holy See employees to close their accounts. [cite:vt10_wiki_ior] By the end of 2014 it had closed 2,600 dormant accounts and 554 that did not fit its client profile, while 1,460 more ended normally, leaving 15,181 clients. [cite:vt10_ansa_ior2015] By October 2015 about 4,800 accounts had been closed as "no longer in compliance with the Vatican regulatory framework," on grounds of the holder's nationality, residence or use of the money. [cite:vt10_ansa_aif2016] The IOR's president, Jean-Baptiste de Franssu, said the institute had shown "great commitment in dealing with offenses that in past have affected the Institute." [cite:vt10_ansa_ior2015]

The clean-up also reached the IOR's past. Promontory's review of 2014 led to the prosecution of Angelo Caloia, IOR president from 1989 to 2009, and the lawyer Gabriele Liuzzo. On 21 January 2021 the Vatican tribunal found that 29 properties of the IOR and its subsidiary SGIR had been sold below value between 2002 and 2007 and that about 19 million euros had been taken; it sentenced Caloia and Liuzzo to eight years and eleven months, Liuzzo's son Lamberto to five years and two months, and ordered about 38 million euros confiscated and more than 20 million euros paid in damages. [cite:vt10_vn_caloia2021] The defendants maintained their innocence and had sought to call former secretaries of state and cardinals to show that the sales were approved. [cite:vt10_aj_caloia2021] The Holy See described the case as the first application of its December 2018 anti-laundering legislation. [cite:vt10_vn_caloia2021] An earlier case had ended less clearly: in February 2017 two former senior IOR managers, Cipriani and Tulliò, were convicted of reporting omissions and acquitted of laundering. [cite:vt10_wiki_ior]

2014–2022: new offices and one bank for the Holy See

Francis created the Secretariat for the Economy on 24 February 2014, with Cardinal George Pell as its first prefect. It supervises the administration of the curial offices and Peter's Pence and prepares the Holy See's budget and consolidated accounts, under a Council for the Economy.
