[cite:vt6_gc_spe] [cite:vt6_va_spe] The AIF received prudential supervision of the IOR in 2013 and was renamed the Supervisory and Financial Information Authority (ASIF) in December 2020. [cite:vt5_va_aif_profile] [cite:vt5_wiki_asif] The IOR received new statutes from Francis on 8 August 2019, on a two-year trial basis, made definitive on 30 January 2023. [cite:vt10_wiki_ior] [cite:vt9_ior_statutes2023]

The London case then changed who holds the money. By a motu proprio of 26 December 2020, in force from 1 January 2021, Francis took the management of the Secretariat of State's investments, property and funds, including the administration of Peter's Pence, away from the Secretariat and gave it to APSA under the oversight of the Secretariat for the Economy. [cite:vt6_vn_apsa2020] [scene:vt9_apsa_governorate|Part Nine: APSA] The 2022 constitution of the Curia, Praedicate Evangelium, provided that the Holy See's financial transactions run through the IOR, and a rescript of 23 August 2022 interpreted that as making the IOR "the exclusive" manager and custodian of the Holy See's movable assets: every Holy See body, the Secretariat of State included, had to move its money out of other banks into the IOR within 30 days of 1 September 2022. [cite:vt10_ncreg_rescript2022] The Secretariat had held accounts at Swiss banks, including Credit Suisse, through which the London investment was first made. [cite:vt10_ncreg_rescript2022] The exclusivity lasted three years. Leo XIV's rescript Coniuncta Cura, made public on 6 October 2025, repealed it: APSA is to use the IOR as a rule but may use banks abroad where the competent bodies judge it more efficient or convenient, under the policies of the investment committee chaired by Cardinal Kevin Farrell. [cite:vt9_cna_coniuncta]

The evaluators' verdict

MONEYVAL's second evaluation of the Holy See, adopted in April 2021, rated its system's effectiveness "substantial" in five areas and "moderate" in six, with none "low." It also found that insider risk at middle and senior levels was underrated, that the Promoter of Justice's office lacked staff for complex financial cases, and that far less money had been confiscated than had been frozen. [cite:vt5_mv_2021mer] The Holy See said it "welcomes the Moneyval Report" and would keep working towards full compliance. [cite:vt5_pv_moneyval2021] A follow-up report in May 2024 raised the rating on correspondent banking, the IOR's links to foreign banks, from non-compliant to compliant, and two others from partially to largely compliant. [cite:vt5_fatf_fur2024] [cite:vt5_pv_moneyval2024] No later MONEYVAL report on the Holy See was found as of October 2026.

What the record shows

The pattern across forty years is plain in the documents: reform followed exposure. The Ambrosiano losses produced a settlement but no supervisor; an Italian seizure produced the first law; an arrest and a consultancy review produced the account closures; a London investment produced the transfer of the Secretariat of State's money to APSA and the rule of 2022 that the IOR alone hold the Holy See's funds, which Leo XIV relaxed in 2025. [cite:vt10_avv_anfossi] [cite:vt10_bbc_seizure2010] [cite:vt10_ansa_aif2016] [cite:vt6_vn_apsa2020] [cite:vt10_ncreg_rescript2022] [cite:vt9_cna_coniuncta] The record does not show the opposite claims either: the IOR is not outside anti-money-laundering law, and its money is not yet fully transparent, by the evaluators' own findings. [cite:vt5_mv_2021mer] Whether the system that the London trial was meant to vindicate also respects the rights of the accused is the question that the Court of Appeal's ruling of 17 March 2026 has left open. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026]

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: Rome and the Rothschilds: What the Documents Show
chapters.intro: Part Eleven takes the claim that the Rothschild family has stood behind the papacy's money since the 1830s and tests it against the documents. It sets out what is on record: the papal bankers of the Torlonia family, the loans that the Rothschild houses made to the Papal States from 1831 to the 1850s, what those loans paid for and how they ended. It traces the alleged "exclusivity clause" of 1831 to its single source and explains how contemporary remarks about a Jewish banker and the pope grew into an antisemitic trope. It then follows the "unbroken chain" said to run from 1831 to 2026 link by link, through the 1929 money, Bernardino Nogara's Special Administration and the IOR, and shows where the documents stop. It ends with the one recent fact that gave the chain new life: the appointment in 2026 of François Pauly, a former Edmond de Rothschild executive, to chair the IOR's board, and a Paris inquiry of the same year that touched the bank but not the Vatican.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven has separated what is documented from what was added. The documented core is a series of loans: from 1831 the government of the Papal States, short of money after the revolts in the Legations, borrowed through Alessandro Torlonia and the Rothschild houses of Paris and Naples, which issued five papal loans between 1831 and 1850 and lent again in the 1850s, with the pope as debtor. [cite:vt11_felisini_ch4] [cite:wa_ra_naples] [cite:vt11_ehnet_pollard] The alleged exclusivity clause rests on a single popular book of 1913, and even there it is a preference on equal terms. [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] [cite:vt11_tamu_balla] Contemporary anger at a Jewish banker lending to the pope, voiced by Alfred de Vigny and others, was carried by the Union Générale crash and Drumont's La France juive into the antisemitic trope that "the Rothschilds control the Pope". [cite:vt11_wiki_carl] [cite:vt11_wiki_francejuive] [cite:vt7_pw_lasers] Tested link by link, the "unbroken chain" from 1831 to 2026 has two documented ends and nothing between them: no Rothschild role was found in the 1929 money, Nogara's Special Administration, the IOR's foundation, Sindona, Ambrosiano or Jean-Baptiste de Franssu's presidency. [cite:vt2_wiki_specialadmin] [cite:vt11_va_ior1990] [cite:vt11_wiki_franssu] François Pauly, IOR president since the spring of 2026, led the Edmond de Rothschild group from 2021 to 2023, a fact about one banker's career with no wrongdoing documented; the Paris prosecutor's inquiry of 2026, which targets Fabrice Aidan, who has not been charged and denies wrongdoing, does not mention the Vatican or the IOR. [cite:vt11_vn_ior2025] [cite:vt11_of_pauly2021] [cite:vt11_pnf_aidan] [cite:vt11_reuters_aidan] Part Twelve turns from money to the most serious charge against the institution: the sexual abuse of minors by clergy and its cover-up, beginning with the rules the Holy See wrote and rewrote. [scene:vt12_the_rules|Part Twelve: the rules]

sections.h: The Papal Loans, 1794–1870
sections.html:
The Rothschild family's dealings with Rome are documented, and the documents are about debt. Between 1831 and the 1850s the government of the Papal States, which the popes ruled as kings until 1870, borrowed through the Rothschild banking houses. The pope was the borrower: money ran from the bank to the papal treasury, and interest ran back. This section sets out what the record shows, what it does not, and how loan contracts became a story that "the Rothschilds control the Pope".

The pope's bankers before the Rothschilds

The Papal States already had a banking family of their own. Giovanni Torlonia, a Roman banker who administered finances for the Holy See, received papal titles at the turn of the nineteenth century: sources date his dukedom of Bracciano to a grant of 1794 or to the family's purchase of the title and castle in 1803 (Part Seven sets out the conflict), and Pius VII made him Prince of Civitella Cesi in 1803. [cite:vt7_wiki_torlonia] His son Alessandro Torlonia (1800–1886) took over the family bank and, in the words of the historian Daniela Felisini, "became the Pope's banker". [cite:vt11_felisini_ch4] Felisini's 2016 study, based in part on the Rothschild bank's Paris archives, is the main scholarly account of the papal debt in this period. [cite:vt11_tv_felisini] The Torlonia family's marriages and its place among the Roman nobility, including the 1823 marriage that joined a Torlonia daughter to the Orsini, are covered in [scene:vt7_orsini_record|Part Seven] and are not repeated here.

Why the pope borrowed in 1831

The first Rothschild loan followed a political crisis. In early 1831 revolts broke out in the northern provinces of the Papal States, the Legations around Bologna. Austrian troops put them down and withdrew on 15 July 1831; by December much of the territory was again in revolt, Cardinal Giuseppe Albani called the Austrians back, and they retook Bologna. France answered by seizing the port of Ancona, which it held until the Austrians left in 1838. [cite:vt11_ce_gregory16] Felisini's chapter on the period describes how the uprisings strained the papal budget and how Torlonia, in partnership with James de Rothschild of the Paris house, brought new methods to the management of the public debt. [cite:vt11_felisini_ch4]

The 1831–1832 loan

The agreement was negotiated by Alessandro Torlonia on behalf of the Holy See with James de Rothschild, signed on 30 November 1831 and put into effect in 1832, under Pope Gregory XVI. Wikipedia's account, drawing on Felisini and older works, gives the amount as £400,000 and refers to "the original 5% contract, signed by Rothschild and Torlonia". [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, whose article on the family includes a table of Rothschild loans, lists a loan to the "Papal States" in 1831 of 16,000,000 francs. [cite:vt11_je_rothschild] The two figures do not match, and neither comes from the contract itself, which this volume has not seen; the amount should be read as reported, not established. James's brother Carl von Rothschild, who ran the family's house in Naples, travelled to Rome and was received by Gregory XVI in January 1832, when he was given the insignia of the Constantinian Order of Saint George. [cite:vt11_wiki_carl] [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans]

The Rothschild Archive in London, the family's own historical archive, states that the Naples house served "the Papal administration in Rome, on whose behalf five loans were issued between 1831 and 1850". [cite:wa_ra_naples] It does not give their terms. Felisini names James in Paris as Torlonia's partner on the first loan; Wikipedia names Carl in Naples as the family's man in Rome. [cite:vt11_felisini_ch4] [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans]

The 1834 dispute and the loans that followed

The second episode on record shows competition, not control. In July 1834 Cardinal Antonio Tosti became papal treasurer and tried to refinance the debt on better terms. According to Wikipedia's summary of Felisini, the Rothschilds opposed an early refinancing, Tosti approached a group of rival Paris banks, and the two sides were eventually reconciled and shared the new loan. [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] The Jewish Encyclopedia tells a similar story from the Rothschild side: after a rival syndicate won a Sardinian loan in 1834, the Rothschilds used their usual tactic of driving down the rivals' bonds, "with the result that the next papal loan was financed by them". [cite:vt11_je_rothschild]

The Encyclopedia's table lists a further papal loan in 1845 of 2,160,000. [cite:vt11_je_rothschild] After the revolution of 1848, the short-lived Roman Republic of 1849 and the restoration of Pius IX by French troops, the papal government borrowed again from the same houses in the early 1850s. [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] The historian John Pollard, in his study of papal finance from 1850 to 1950, shows that the budget reforms of Cardinal Giacomo Antonelli, Pius IX's Secretary of State, depended on borrowing from the Rothschilds, a reliance that many contemporaries found unseemly. [cite:vt11_ehnet_pollard]

What the loans paid for is documented only in general terms. The 1831 loan met the deficit opened by the revolts and the cost of order in the Legations; the loans of the 1850s financed a restored government that depended on French troops. [cite:vt11_felisini_ch4] [cite:vt11_ehnet_pollard] The line-by-line uses of the money are in Felisini's archival work, which this volume has seen only in abstract, and are not stated here.

Two events ended the relationship. The Naples house ceased trading in 1863, after Garibaldi took Naples (the Jewish Encyclopedia dates its closure to 1861). [cite:wa_ra_naples] [cite:vt11_je_rothschild] Then, in 1870, the Kingdom of Italy took Rome, and the Papal States, the borrower of all five loans, ceased to exist. [cite:vt11_jvl_rome] How Rome fell and what the Holy See refused afterwards is explained in [scene:vt2_roman_question|Part Two].

The "exclusivity clause": one source, graded

A widely repeated claim holds that the 1831 contract contained a "secret clause" giving the Rothschilds an "exclusive right of first refusal on all Vatican sovereign debt", co-signed by Alessandro Torlonia and "enforced" in 1834. The claim can be traced. Wikipedia's article on the loans describes a narrower clause: the Holy See was to inform the Rothschilds before approaching another firm for a new loan and to give them preference if a rival offered equal terms. It footnotes this to Ignatius Balla, The Romance of the Rothschilds (London, 1913), pages 228–229, and places the clause after Carl von Rothschild's visit to Rome in the wake of the 1834 dispute. [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] Balla's book is a popular biography of the family, not a work of financial history. [cite:vt11_tamu_balla] No second source for the clause was found: it is not in the Rothschild Archive's account, the Jewish Encyclopedia's account of the papal loans or the published abstract of Felisini's archival study. [cite:wa_ra_naples] [cite:vt11_je_rothschild] [cite:vt11_felisini_ch4] This volume could not open Balla's text at the cited pages.

Graded: not established. Even in Balla's form, the clause was a preference on equal terms, not exclusivity. It could bind only the government of the Papal States, which ended in 1870. The documented events of 1834 also run against an exclusive right, since the papal treasurer was able to approach other banks at all. [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] "Right of first refusal on all Vatican sovereign debt" goes beyond the one source the claim rests on.

How a loan became a trope

The loans drew attacks from the start, and much of the anger was about the lender's religion. Felisini notes that the first loan was controversial for its financial terms and also because Rothschild was a Jewish banker. [cite:vt11_felisini_ch4] Reports that Carl von Rothschild had been allowed to kiss the pope's hand rather than his foot provoked complaints in Catholic circles that the pope was selling Rome to "a Jew". [cite:vt11_wiki_carl] The French poet Alfred de Vigny is quoted as writing that "a Jew now reigns over the Pope"; the German writer Ludwig Börne mocked the loan; the Roman dialect poet Giuseppe Gioachino Belli wrote a sonnet that blamed the pope as much as the bankers. [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] Vigny's remark is quoted here from that secondary account; this volume did not locate it in his own journal.

Two things happened later in the century that set the remark into a durable form. In January 1882 the Union Générale, a Paris bank founded to serve Catholic and conservative investors, collapsed; its founder blamed "Jewish-German banks and Freemasons", a conspiracy that historians do not accept. [cite:vt11_wiki_crash1882] In 1886 Édouard Drumont's La France juive, which went through 140 printings in two years, blamed the crash on the Rothschilds. [cite:vt11_wiki_francejuive] The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 closed its account of the episode with the remark that, by "a somewhat curious sequel", the Rothschilds were "at the present time … the guardians of the papal treasure". [cite:vt11_je_rothschild] The sentence gives no source, date or detail, and no Holy See document found for this volume describes any such custody; it is an aside in an encyclopaedia, not evidence of a role, and it is the source of the phrase later quoted in claims of a Rothschild chain.

The idea that "the Rothschilds control the Pope" belongs to a wider family of stories that present one Jewish banking family as the hidden power behind governments, a theme the historian Mike Rothschild, who is not related to the family, traces through two centuries of antisemitic conspiracy theory. [cite:vt7_pw_lasers] It should be named for what it is: an antisemitic trope built on a real but ordinary fact, that a government short of money borrowed from the largest bankers of its day. The record also shows the limits of the lenders' leverage. The Rothschilds pressed, through the Austrian chancellor Metternich, for relief for the Jews of the Papal States, including those of Ancona, from special taxes, property restrictions in the ghetto and bans on professions. [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] Rome's ghetto, where Jews had lived for almost three hundred years, was dismantled only in 1870, by the Italian state after the papal government had fallen. [cite:vt11_jvl_rome] Whether the documented ties ran on beyond 1870, as the "unbroken chain" claims, is the subject of [scene:vt11_chain_tested|the next section].

sections.h: The "Unbroken Chain", Tested Link by Link
sections.html:
Some writing on Rome and the Rothschilds goes further than the loans. It presents a chain running "1831 → 2026" with "no documented breaks": the 1831 contract, the Jewish Encyclopedia's phrase of 1906, the founding of the IOR in 1942, the banker Michele Sindona in 1969–1971 as "Rothschild-adjacent", Jean-Baptiste de Franssu as IOR president from 2014, and François Pauly as his successor in 2026. The only source cited for the chain is Wikipedia. The test applied here is simple. A chain of Rothschild involvement in the Holy See's money would need, at each link, a document showing a Rothschild house or family member in a role: a loan, a mandate, an ownership stake, a board seat or a contract. Proximity, a shared city or a later employer does not count.

Link 1: the loans, 1831 to the 1850s (documented)

The first link holds. The Rothschild Archive records five loans issued on behalf of the papal administration between 1831 and 1850, and the papal government borrowed from the same houses again in the early 1850s, as set out in [scene:vt11_papal_loans|the previous section]. [cite:wa_ra_naples] [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] [cite:vt11_ehnet_pollard] These were contracts between a borrowing state and lending banks.

Link 2: 1863–1906 (the documents stop)

The Naples house closed in 1863, and in 1870 the Papal States, the borrower, ceased to exist. [cite:wa_ra_naples] [cite:vt11_jvl_rome] For the next fifty-nine years the popes had no state and refused the endowment Italy offered them (see [scene:vt2_roman_question|Part Two]). [cite:vt2_ce_guarantees] No loan, mandate or contract between a Rothschild house and the Holy See in these years was found in any source used for this volume. The only item offered for this gap is the Jewish Encyclopedia's sentence of 1906 calling the Rothschilds "the guardians of the papal treasure". [cite:vt11_je_rothschild] It is a single unsourced aside, with no date, account, amount or office attached, and it cannot stand in for a document.

Link 3: the 1929 money and Nogara (no Rothschild role found)

The Lateran Pacts of 11 February 1929 ended the dispute with Italy. Under the Financial Convention, Italy paid the Holy See 750 million lire in cash and 1 billion lire in 5 per cent state bonds. [cite:vt2_lateran_text] On 7 June 1929 Pius XI created the Special Administration of the Holy See to manage that money, answering directly to him, and put Bernardino Nogara in charge; Nogara ran it until 1954. [cite:vt2_wiki_specialadmin] John Pollard, the historian of papal finance, calls Nogara the first non-Roman to control the Vatican's finances and credits him with inserting the Church "into the structures of international capitalism". [cite:vt11_ehnet_pollard] [cite:vt2_pollard1999] The terms and uses of the 1929 money are set out in [scene:vt3_what_each_got|Part Three]. No source consulted for this volume names a Rothschild bank as lender, adviser, manager or counterparty of the Special Administration. This is the point at which the chain would have to resume, and it does not.

Link 4: the IOR, 1942 (an internal papal body)

The IOR's own founding documents trace it to a commission ad pias causas set up by Leo XIII in 1887, then to an Administration for the Works of Religion given a statute on 17 March 1941; Pius XII's chirograph of 27 June 1942 created the Institute for the Works of Religion with legal personality and absorbed that administration. [cite:vt11_va_ior1990] Since John Paul II's chirograph of 1 March 1990 it has been governed by a commission of five cardinals, a prelate and a lay Board of Superintendence. [cite:vt11_va_ior1990] Its work today is described in [scene:vt9_ior|Part Nine]. Nothing in these instruments names an outside bank, and no source found for this volume connects a Rothschild house to the IOR's foundation. The year 1942 is in the chain because it is the IOR's founding date, not because any Rothschild document attaches to it.

Link 5: Sindona and Ambrosiano (no document)

Michele Sindona, a banker and friend of the future Paul VI, did business with the Vatican bank from 1969; his American bank failed in 1974, and he was convicted in the United States in 1980 and in Italy in 1985 and 1986, the last time as the instigator of the murder of the lawyer Giorgio Ambrosoli. [cite:vt11_wiki_sindona] The standard account of his career does not mention the Rothschilds. [cite:vt11_wiki_sindona] The label "Rothschild-adjacent" sometimes attached to him has no source. The same is true of the claim that Banco Ambrosiano had "documented ties" to "the Rothschild banking network"; [scene:vt10_ambrosiano_calvi|Part Ten] found no source for it.

Link 6: de Franssu, 2014 (no connection)

Jean-Baptiste de Franssu, appointed president of the IOR on 9 July 2014, came from fund management: the French public financial group Caisse des Dépôts from 1987, Invesco France from 1990, chief executive of Invesco Europe from 1997 to 2011 and president of the European Fund and Asset Management Association from 2009 to 2011. [cite:vt11_wiki_franssu] [cite:vt11_agi_franssu2014] In March 2014 Pope Francis had named him to the commission reviewing the Vatican's economic structures. [cite:vt11_wiki_franssu] No source links him to any Rothschild firm. His place in the chain rests only on the fact that he preceded Pauly.

Link 7: Pauly, 2026 (a CV, not a chain)

François Pauly, chair of the IOR's board since the spring of 2026, had led the Edmond de Rothschild private-banking group from June 2021 until March 2023. [cite:vt11_of_pauly2021] [cite:vt11_audit_pbi_pauly] [cite:vt11_iv_pauly] That is a documented fact about one banker's career. It joins the IOR to a former employer of its chairman; it does not join the Rothschild houses of 1831 to the Holy See, and the Edmond de Rothschild group is a separate firm from Rothschild & Co. [cite:vt11_iv_pauly] The appointment is examined in [scene:vt11_pauly_2026|the next section].

Where the documents stop

The documents support two separate facts more than 150 years apart: a series of loans to the Papal States that ended with the Naples house in 1863 and the Papal States in 1870, and the appointment in 2026 of an IOR chairman who had earlier run a Rothschild-named private bank. [cite:wa_ra_naples] [cite:vt11_vn_ior2025] Between them, through the 1929 settlement, Nogara, the IOR's foundation, Sindona, Ambrosiano and de Franssu, no source found for this volume shows a Rothschild house in any role in the Holy See's finances. A chain that has two dated ends and nothing in the middle is not a chain; it is two facts joined by an assumption. The assumption is the trope traced in [scene:vt11_papal_loans|the previous section], and this volume treats the "unbroken chain" as unsupported. The test of the front hypothesis set out in [scene:dv1_three_functions|The Divine 3+1] and [scene:vt1_front_test|Part One] asked whether money or favours flowed in a pattern that a public refusal of Zionism would hide; on this evidence the Rothschild line supplies no such pattern after 1870, a result carried into [scene:vt19_predictions_tested|Part Nineteen].

sections.h: François Pauly, the IOR and the Paris Inquiry, 2026
sections.html:
In 2026 two pieces of news put the word "Rothschild" back beside the Vatican. In March the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), the Holy See's financial institution, announced that a former chief executive of the Edmond de Rothschild group would chair its board. In the same month French prosecutors searched the Paris offices of a company of that group in an unrelated inquiry. Some commentary joined the two and read them as the latest link in the "unbroken chain" tested in [scene:vt11_chain_tested|the previous section]. This section sets out what each record says, as of October 2026, and what it does not say. No wrongdoing by François Pauly is documented in any source used for this volume.

The appointment

The IOR is governed under a structure set by John Paul II's chirograph of 1 March 1990: a commission of five cardinals oversees it, and a lay Board of Superintendence is responsible for its administration and management. [cite:vt11_va_ior1990] The chair of that board is commonly called the IOR's president. On 25 March 2026 the IOR announced that François Pauly would be the next president of the Board of Superintendence, succeeding Jean-Baptiste Douville de Franssu, who had held the post since 2014. It described the change as the result of a carefully planned succession process run over the previous twelve months by the Board and the Commission of Cardinals. [cite:vt11_teleborsa_pauly] According to the Luxembourg business paper Paperjam, the Board had proposed Pauly in December 2025 and the Commission of Cardinals approved him on 28 January 2026. [cite:vt11_paperjam_pauly] De Franssu stayed in office until the Board's meeting of 28 April 2026, which approved the IOR's accounts for 2025. [cite:vt11_teleborsa_pauly] When the IOR published its 2025 report on 11 May 2026, recording net profit of €51 million, a dividend of €24.3 million to the pope and client assets of €5.9 billion, Vatican News reported that de Franssu had concluded his term and that Pauly "has taken office". [cite:vt11_vn_ior2025] No later change in the post was found in this volume's check as of October 2026.

The Holy See's stated reasons are on record. Cardinal Giuseppe Petrocchi, president of the Commission of Cardinals, praised de Franssu's "essential contribution" and called Pauly's experience a factor of great importance for consolidating what had been achieved and strengthening relations with the financial sector; de Franssu described the years since 2014 as a "profound structural transformation". [cite:vt11_paperjam_pauly]

The career, as the record gives it

Pauly is a Luxembourg citizen whose career in finance spans some 35 years, mostly in private banking. [cite:vt11_ubp_pauly] [cite:vt11_teleborsa_pauly] The IOR's own announcement listed: banking from the late 1980s; deputy chief executive of Dexia Crediop in Italy (2002–2003); chief executive and chairman of Banque Internationale à Luxembourg (2011–2016); a seat on the board of the Vatican pension fund (2017–2021); chairman of the insurer La Luxembourgeoise; and membership of the Economic Affairs Commission of the Archdiocese of Luxembourg. [cite:vt11_teleborsa_pauly] That list, as reported, does not mention Edmond de Rothschild.

Other records fill the gap, and they describe the job in slightly different words. On 7 June 2021 the French financial weekly Option Finance reported his appointment as "CEO du Groupe" Edmond de Rothschild, noting that he had been a director of Edmond de Rothschild (Suisse) and of its Luxembourg subsidiary since 2016; the trade journal Private Banker International gave the same title, "group CEO", after the group board's meeting of 4 June 2021. [cite:vt11_of_pauly2021] [cite:vt11_audit_pbi_pauly] The Spanish Catholic site InfoVaticana describes him as chief executive and chair of the executive committee of Edmond de Rothschild (Suisse) from June 2021, after the death of Benjamin de Rothschild, with his departure formalized in March 2023. [cite:vt11_iv_pauly] Union Bancaire Privée, on whose board he has sat since 2024, says that "most recently" he was chief executive of Banque Edmond de Rothschild, and lists him at 31 December 2024 as a member of the IOR's Board of Superintendence. [cite:vt11_ubp_pauly] He was therefore already on the IOR board before he was chosen to chair it.

Two points about the employer matter. First, InfoVaticana, which framed the appointment critically under the headline "an ex-CEO of the Rothschild group", states in its own text that Edmond de Rothschild is distinct from Rothschild & Co, the other main firm bearing the family name; it does not claim that any Rothschild interest influences Vatican decisions. [cite:vt11_iv_pauly] Second, Pauly was a salaried executive of that group for under two years; no source describes him as a member of the Rothschild family or an owner of its bank. [cite:vt11_of_pauly2021] [cite:vt11_iv_pauly] The finding is one banker's CV. It is not evidence that a family or a firm controls the IOR.

His predecessor's career is a useful comparison. De Franssu came from the French public financial group Caisse des Dépôts and from Invesco, whose European business he ran from 1997 to 2011, and he presided over the European Fund and Asset Management Association from 2009 to 2011; Pope Francis named him to the commission reviewing the Vatican's economic structures in March 2014, and he became IOR president on 9 July 2014. [cite:vt11_wiki_franssu] [cite:vt11_agi_franssu2014] Its last two chairs both came from European banking and asset management; the Rothschild name appears in one of their CVs, not in the IOR's governance.

The Paris inquiry: what the release says

On 24 March 2026 the French national financial prosecutor, Pascal Prache, issued a press release. [cite:vt11_pnf_aidan] It states that searches took place on Friday 20 March 2026 at several places, including the Paris head office of Edmond de Rothschild (France) in the 8th arrondissement. It states that the national financial prosecutor's office had opened a preliminary inquiry on 17 February 2026 into "corruption passive d'agent public étranger et complicité de ce délit" (passive bribery of a foreign public official and complicity), entrusted to the central anti-corruption police office. It states that the inquiry followed a report sent on 16 February 2026 by the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, made after the revelations of the "Epstein Files" and the French press coverage that followed. And it states that the inquiry is directed "notamment" (in particular) at Fabrice Aidan. [cite:vt11_pnf_aidan]

The release does not describe Aidan's role or position. It does not say that he or anyone else has been charged, placed under formal investigation or taken into custody. Edmond de Rothschild appears in it only as a place searched. It does not mention the Vatican, the IOR or François Pauly. [cite:vt11_pnf_aidan] A preliminary inquiry in French law is an investigation by the prosecutor's office, not a charge. Fabrice Aidan is the target of a preliminary inquiry and has not been charged, according to the prosecutor's release, and he is presumed innocent. Reuters reported on the same day that he has denied wrongdoing, and that a source close to the bank said it was co-operating fully with the investigation. [cite:vt11_reuters_aidan] No later public step in the case was found for this volume as of October 2026.

Pauly had left Edmond de Rothschild in March 2023, almost three years before the inquiry opened, and no source connects him, the IOR or the Holy See to it. [cite:vt11_iv_pauly] [cite:vt11_pnf_aidan]

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: Abuse and Cover-up
chapters.intro: Part Eleven tested the documents on Rome's bankers. Part Twelve turns to the record that has done most to shape public trust in the Holy See since 2002: the sexual abuse of children by clergy and its concealment. It sets out, first, the rules written in Rome, from the secret procedure of 1922 to the abolition of the pontifical secret in December 2019 and the papal commission's reports of 2024 and 2025, separating what they required inside the Church from what they said about the police. It then gives each national report on its own terms, with its method, period and scope, without adding figures together; follows the named cases in which the Holy See itself decided, and the bill paid by American dioceses; and ends with inquiries into Anglican, Baptist and German Protestant churches, so that what is particular to the Catholic case can be told apart from what is not.
chapters.outro: Part Twelve established four things. The Holy See's own rules placed abuse trials under the secret of the Holy Office from 1922 and under the pontifical secret from 2001, said nothing to bishops about the police until the 2010 guide told them to follow civil law, and lifted the secret only on 17 December 2019, while still imposing no reporting duty where a state imposed none. [cite:vt12_va_crimen1962] [cite:vt12_va_ddg2001] [cite:vt12_va_cdfguide2010] [cite:vt12_vn_rescript2019] The national reports, each counted by its own method, found allegations against about 4 per cent of US priests (1950–2002), 4.4 per cent of German clerics in the files (1946–2014) and 7 per cent of Australian priests (1950–2010), while France's survey estimated 216,000 victims of clergy and religious since 1950, a figure that cannot be added to any other. [cite:vt12_am_johnjay2004] [cite:vt12_ba_mhg2018] [cite:vt12_tablet_rc7pct] [cite:vt12_cna_ciase2022] Rome disciplined Maciel in 2006 and McCarrick in 2019, published its own McCarrick report in 2020, and saw Francis retract his defence of a Chilean bishop in 2018, while compensation was paid by dioceses, 44 American Catholic bodies having sought bankruptcy protection by March 2026, and suits against the Holy See itself failed on immunity. [cite:vt12_zenit_maciel2006] [cite:vt12_ru_mccarrick2020] [cite:vt12_cc_chile2018] [cite:vt12_dick_bankruptcy2026] [cite:vt5_eapil_jc2021] And inquiries into Anglican, Baptist and German Protestant bodies found the same failures without the Holy See's structures. [cite:vt12_iicsa_anglican2020] [cite:vt12_ap_guidepost2022] [cite:vt12_it_forum2024] Part Thirteen turns from the Church's failures to its reach: the schools, universities and bishops through which Rome's influence travels. [scene:vt13_schools|Part Thirteen: schools]

sections.h: The Rules: From the Secret of the Holy Office to Vos estis
sections.html:
Every national inquiry discussed in the next section asked the files it read what the bishop did when a complaint arrived and what the Church's own law told him to do. That law was written in Rome. This section follows it from 1922 to 2026, document by document, and keeps two questions apart that public debate often merges: what the rules required inside the canonical system, and what they said, or did not say, about the police and the civil courts. The documents themselves are on the Holy See's website, and the Holy See has published a historical introduction to them; both are cited here alongside the readings of canon lawyers and critics. [cite:vt12_va_histintro]

Crimen sollicitationis, 1922 and 1962

In 1922 the Holy Office, the Roman congregation responsible for doctrine and for certain grave crimes, issued an instruction called Crimen sollicitationis. Its main subject was a priest who used confession to solicit a penitent for sex. It also set procedure for what it called the "worst crime", a sexual act between a cleric and a person of the same sex, and treated sexual acts with prepubescent children and with animals in the same way for penal purposes. [cite:vt12_va_histintro] [cite:vt12_wiki_crimen] In 1962, under John XXIII, the Holy Office reissued it with additions. Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani signed the new edition, dated 16 March 1962, and addressed it to all patriarchs, archbishops, bishops and other local ordinaries, to be kept in diocesan archives, not published and not commented upon. [cite:vt12_va_crimen1962] [cite:vt12_wiki_crimen] The Holy See's own account says copies were meant for bishops attending the Second Vatican Council, but "most of the copies were never distributed." [cite:vt12_va_histintro]

The secrecy clauses are the reason the document became notorious. Under section 11, proceedings were covered by the "secret of the Holy Office", during the trial and after the sentence; everyone attached to the tribunal was bound by it, and breach brought automatic excommunication that only the pope could lift. An accused priest who broke it was suspended. Accusers and witnesses could be put under an oath of secrecy, with excommunication as the sanction, under section 23. [cite:vt12_va_crimen1962] [cite:vt12_wiki_crimen] The Holy See describes this as "a strict code of confidentiality which was meant to protect all persons concerned from undue publicity" until a verdict. [cite:vt12_va_histintro]

The document says nothing about reporting to the police. That silence is read in two ways. When it reached the press in 2003, a headline in The Guardian called it a "Vatican order to conceal priests' sex abuse." [cite:vt12_wiki_crimen] Canon lawyers answered that nothing in it would have stopped a bishop, or anyone else, from going to the police, and that the secrecy bound people only inside a canonical trial. [cite:vt12_wiki_crimen] Thomas Doyle, a canon lawyer and long-standing advocate for survivors, called it in 2006 "an explicit written policy to cover up cases"; he later wrote that he did not believe it "to be proof of an explicit conspiracy." [cite:vt12_wiki_crimen] Both readings agree on the narrower finding: the instruction put canonical proceedings under the strictest secrecy the Church had, and it gave a bishop no instruction to tell the civil authorities. It stayed in force until 2001. [cite:vt12_wiki_crimen]

2001: reserved to the Congregation, and still secret

On 30 April 2001 John Paul II issued the motu proprio Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela, which replaced the 1922 instruction. [cite:vt12_va_histintro] On 18 May 2001 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (CDF), the successor of the Holy Office, sent all bishops the letter De delictis gravioribus, signed by its prefect, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, and its secretary, Archbishop Tarcisio Bertone. It listed the "graver delicts" now reserved to the Congregation, among them a cleric's sin against the Sixth Commandment with a minor under 18. It set a ten-year limitation period that began only when the victim turned 18, and it stated: "Cases of this kind are subject to the pontifical secret." [cite:vt12_va_ddg2001] Like its predecessor, the letter does not mention civil authorities. [cite:vt12_va_ddg2001]

The 2001 rules did two things at once. They centralised: a bishop could no longer close a credible case of child abuse locally, because the file had to go to Rome. And they kept the case under the pontifical secret, a formal confidentiality rule of the Holy See's own administration. Whether centralisation served victims or shielded clergy is the argument of the next two decades; the text of 2001 supports neither reading on its own. In 2014 the Holy See told the UN Committee against Torture that the CDF had confirmed 3,420 credible allegations between 2004 and 2013 and that 848 priests had been dismissed from the clerical state. [cite:vt5_cat_co2014] [scene:vt5_treaty_bodies|Part Five: the 2014 UN reviews]

2010: the civil law sentence

In April 2010, months after the Murphy report on Dublin described in the next section, the Holy See published a short guide to the CDF's procedures. Its first operative instruction read: "Civil law concerning reporting of crimes to the appropriate authorities should always be followed." [cite:vt12_va_cdfguide2010] Benedict XVI approved revised norms on 21 May 2010, which modified a limited number of points in the 2001 text. [cite:vt12_va_histintro] The civil-law sentence was guidance in a guide, not a canon of law; it told bishops to obey whatever reporting duty their own state imposed, and created none where the state imposed none.

2019: the secret lifted

The decisive change came under Francis. In May 2019 he issued Vos estis lux mundi, on a three-year trial basis. It made reporting obligatory for clerics and religious who learned of abuse or of its cover-up, required every diocese to have a public office to receive reports, set a procedure for investigating bishops through their metropolitan archbishop, extended protection to vulnerable adults, and forbade any "obligation of silence" on those who report. [cite:vt12_ewtn_vosestis2023] On 17 December 2019 a rescript signed by Cardinal Pietro Parolin abolished the pontifical secret for reports, trials and decisions on the crimes in Vos estis. Confidentiality remained, but the instruction stated that it does not prevent obligations under civil law, including any duty to report and enforceable requests from civil judges, and that victims and witnesses are under no obligation of silence. The same act raised the age in the child-pornography offence from 14 to 18. [cite:vt12_vn_rescript2019] The seal of confession was not affected.

Francis made Vos estis permanent on 25 March 2023, effective 30 April 2023, and extended it to lay leaders of international associations recognised by the Holy See. [cite:vt12_ewtn_vosestis2023] Separately, the penal book of the Code of Canon Law was rewritten. The apostolic constitution Pascite gregem Dei, signed on 23 May 2021 and in force from 8 December 2021, created a new canon 1398 punishing a cleric's sexual offence against a minor, including grooming and child pornography, with loss of office and other penalties up to dismissal from the clerical state. [cite:vt12_wiki_pascite] The victims' advocate Bart Smeets noted that the revised code still did not oblige Church members to report to secular authorities. [cite:vt12_wiki_pascite]

The Commission and its reports, 2024–2026

Francis created the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors in 2014, under Cardinal Seán O'Malley of Boston; several founding members later resigned, citing resistance inside the Vatican. [cite:vt12_ncr_pcpm2024] In 2022 he asked it for an annual report. The first, presented on 29 October 2024, looked at a dozen countries, two religious orders and two Vatican offices, and said plainly that it was not an audit of how much abuse had occurred. Its sharpest criticism was aimed at the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith: slow procedures and secrecy that retraumatised victims, and a refusal to publish statistics or its own case law that "continues to foment distrust." It called for victims' right to information about their cases, an ombudsman, and compensation, which it framed as "conversional justice." [cite:vt12_ncr_pcpm2024]

The second report, released on 16 October 2025 under the Commission's new president, Archbishop Thibault Verny, ran to about 200 pages and covered 18 bishops' conferences, mainly in Africa and Europe, and two religious institutes. Forty survivors helped shape it, answering the criticism that the first report had heard too few of them. One member, Maud de Boer-Buquicchio, described a "global data gap" on abuse figures, and the Commission acknowledged that it still lacked a mature reporting instrument. Its six recommendations on reparation covered listening, apology, therapy and money. [cite:vt12_vn_pcpm2025] [cite:vt12_ncreg_pcpm2025] Leo XIV told its plenary on 16 March 2026 that listening to victims "must find concrete expression in every ecclesial community and institution," and approved new statutes on 20 May 2026 that place the Commission alongside the Dicastery and make it report directly to the pope; it advises and does not govern. [cite:vt12_va_leo_pcpm2026] [cite:vt12_vn_pcpmstatutes2026] As of 21 October 2026 no third annual report had been located in this research.

The record of the rules, read in order, shows a canonical system that for most of the twentieth century treated abuse as a matter for secret internal trial and said nothing to bishops about the state; a centralisation in 2001 that kept the secret; a first instruction to follow civil law in 2010; and the removal of the secret, with an explicit carve-out for civil law, only in December 2019. What the rules did not do, at any stage, was oblige a bishop to report to the police where his country's law did not. [cite:vt12_va_crimen1962] [cite:vt12_va_ddg2001] [cite:vt12_va_cdfguide2010] [cite:vt12_vn_rescript2019] [cite:vt12_wiki_pascite]

sections.h: The Numbers: Nine Countries, Nine Methods
sections.html:
Claims about clerical abuse are often carried by a single total: "over 500,000 victims" and similar sums circulate widely. No report states that number. It is produced by adding a French survey estimate, which includes abuse by lay staff, to case counts from other countries that measure something different. This section does not add any figures together. It sets out each national report on its own terms: who commissioned it, how it counted, which years and which perpetrators it covered, and what its authors said its limits were. Three kinds of count recur and must be kept apart: allegations or claims found in Church files, which are a floor because many victims never come forward; findings by courts or grand juries, which are narrower still; and population surveys, which estimate the hidden total but carry a margin of error and have been contested.

The United States: John Jay, 2004, and Pennsylvania, 2018

The first national count was commissioned by the US bishops' National Review Board from John Jay College of Criminal Justice and published in February 2004. It counted allegations that had reached Church authorities. It found allegations against 4,392 priests, about 4 per cent of those who served between 1950 and 2002, made by 10,667 people who had come forward to the Church; two-thirds of the allegations had been made since 1993, and 149 priests with more than ten allegations each accounted for 27 per cent of the total. Dioceses had paid $472.5 million by then. [cite:vt12_am_johnjay2004] Later updates raised the count: by the end of 2005, more than 5,000 priests and almost 13,000 minors. [cite:vt12_am_johnjay2004] These are counts of allegations reported to the Church, not of proven offences and not of all victims.

A state grand jury in Pennsylvania worked differently. Its 884-page report, released on 14 August 2018 after an 18-month investigation, drew on internal diocesan documents, including written admissions, and on testimony before the grand jury. It covered six of the state's eight dioceses (Erie, Allentown, Greensburg, Harrisburg, Pittsburgh and Scranton) over about 70 years, found credible evidence against 301 priests, and identified more than 1,000 child victims, while stating its belief that the true number was higher. Only two priests could be charged; the limitation periods had run out for the rest. The grand jury described a "systematic" and "sophisticated" cover-up. Cardinal Donald Wuerl, formerly bishop of Pittsburgh, said he had "acted with diligence," and the Archdiocese of Washington disputed the report's account of his role. [cite:vt12_osv_pa2018]

Ireland: four reports, 2005–2011

Ireland produced the densest run of state inquiries, each with a different scope. The Ferns report of October 2005 examined complaints from 100 people against 21 priests in one diocese over about 40 years. [cite:vt12_ba_irishreports] The Ryan report of 20 May 2009 was not about parishes but about some 60 industrial and reformatory schools run by Catholic religious orders and supervised by the state's Department of Education, among 216 institutions examined; about 1,500 former residents came forward, and the commission found sexual abuse "endemic" in the boys' institutions. It named no abusers, after the Christian Brothers won a court challenge, and it found the state's inspection system fundamentally flawed. [cite:vt12_wiki_ryan] [cite:vt12_ba_irishreports]

The Murphy report of 26 November 2009 studied the Archdiocese of Dublin from January 1975 to April 2004, through a sample of 46 priests and 320 complainants. It found that the archdiocese had put "the maintenance of secrecy, the avoidance of scandal" ahead of children's welfare and that complaints were generally not passed to the Gardaí before 1996. The commission's letters to the Vatican asking for files were not acknowledged, according to a leaked US embassy cable; the Holy See's position was that such requests should come through diplomatic channels. [cite:vt12_wiki_murphy] The Cloyne report of 13 July 2011 led to the sharpest exchange between a state and the Holy See in the whole record. Taoiseach Enda Kenny told the Dáil on 20 July that it exposed "an attempt by the Holy See, to frustrate an Inquiry in a sovereign, democratic republic." The Holy See recalled its nuncio for consultation, and on 3 September 2011 replied that it had "in no way hampered or interfered in the Inquiry," that a 1997 letter from the nuncio was open to misreading out of context, and that it was "sorry and ashamed." [cite:vt12_ba_kenny2011] [cite:vt12_tj_nuncio2011] [cite:vt12_va_cloyne_reply] Ireland closed its embassy to the Holy See in November 2011, citing cost, and announced its reopening in January 2014. [cite:vt12_tablet_embassy2014]

Australia, 2017: the 7 per cent figure

Australia's Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse required Catholic Church authorities to complete a data survey. On 6 February 2017 counsel assisting reported that 7 per cent of Catholic priests who ministered between 1950 and 2010 were alleged perpetrators, and that 4,444 people had made claims of abuse to Catholic authorities between January 1980 and February 2015, waiting on average 33 years to come forward. [cite:vt12_tablet_rc7pct] The method matters. "Claims" included settled, discontinued and rejected matters as well as accepted complaints, so they are allegations, not findings; the proportions were weighted by each person's length of ministry; and the commission later revised its count to 4,445 claimants and 4,765 claims. In some orders the proportion was far higher: over 40 per cent of the St John of God Brothers were accused. [cite:vt12_tjhc_rcmethod] [cite:vt12_tablet_rc7pct] Francis Sullivan, who led the Church's own Truth, Justice and Healing Council, called the figures "shocking … tragic and … indefensible." [cite:vt12_tablet_rc7pct] The columnist Andrew Bolt argued that the denominator of total priests was never produced and that the 1,880 alleged perpetrators included 500 unknown, leaving a risk of double counting. [cite:vt12_ba_bolt2017]

Germany, 2018: the MHG study

The German Bishops' Conference commissioned researchers from Mannheim, Heidelberg and Giessen, who reported on 25 September 2018. They did not have direct access to archives; they read 38,156 personnel and case files supplied by all 27 dioceses for 1946 to 2014. They found allegations against 1,670 clerics, 4.4 per cent of those in the files, and 3,677 victims, and found that about a quarter of canonical proceedings ended without any sanction. Files had been destroyed or altered, and the authors called their figures lower estimates. [cite:vt12_ba_mhg2018]

France, 2021: the CIASE survey

The Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church (CIASE), chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé, published on 5 October 2021. It combined a public call for testimony that drew 6,500 contacts, 250 hearings, archives, and a general-population survey of 28,010 adults. From the survey it estimated that 216,000 people (plus or minus 50,000) had been abused as minors by clergy and religious between 1950 and 2020, and 330,000 (plus or minus 60,000) if lay people working in Church institutions such as schools and youth movements are included; it counted at least 2,900 to 3,200 abusers among clergy and religious. [cite:vt12_ji_ciase2021] [cite:vt12_cna_ciase2022] Sauvé spoke of "a profound, even cruel indifference" toward victims until the early 2000s, and François Devaux, a co-founder of a survivors' association, said: "The system is deviant." [cite:vt12_ji_ciase2021] Eight members of the Académie catholique de France challenged the survey method in November 2021; the commission published a rebuttal in February 2022, and its statistical experts concluded that significant bias could neither be ruled out nor shown to push the estimates far from reality. [cite:vt12_cna_ciase2022]

Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, 2023

In Portugal an independent commission set up by the bishops' conference and coordinated by Pedro Strecht reported on 13 February 2023. It validated 512 of 564 testimonies and gave a "minimum, very minimum" figure of 4,815 victims between 1950 and 2022, sending 25 cases to prosecutors. [cite:vt12_vn_portugal2023] In Spain the parliament, not the Church, ordered the inquiry. The Ombudsman, Ángel Gabilondo, presented his report on 27 October 2023: his office heard 487 cases, and a survey of 8,000 adults found that 1.13 per cent said they had been abused as children by priests or lay people connected to the Church, and 0.6 per cent by clergy. Media projected the first figure onto the adult population as about 440,000; Gabilondo did not convert the survey into a count. [cite:vt12_ncr_spain2023] The bishops' conference apologised and said of the projection: "This number does not correspond to the truth." [cite:vt12_vn_spainbishops2023] Miguel Hurtado of Ending Clergy Abuse called the report "disappointing." [cite:vt12_ncr_spain2023] In Switzerland historians at the University of Zurich, commissioned by the bishops and two Church bodies, published a pilot study on 12 September 2023: 1,002 cases, 510 accused and 921 victims in archives since the mid-twentieth century, "without a doubt only the tip of the iceberg," with evidence that files had been destroyed in two dioceses. [cite:vt12_uzh_swiss2023]

Read together, the reports establish a pattern without establishing a total. In every country that looked, the Church's own files held allegations against a few per cent of priests over the second half of the twentieth century (4 per cent in the United States, 4.4 per cent in Germany, 7 per cent in Australia by a different method), and every report that examined bishops' responses found transfers, unsanctioned cases or lost files. [cite:vt12_am_johnjay2004] [cite:vt12_ba_mhg2018] [cite:vt12_tablet_rc7pct] Only the French and Spanish surveys tried to estimate the hidden number, and they did so with stated margins of error and under public challenge. [cite:vt12_cna_ciase2022] [cite:vt12_ncr_spain2023] None of these reports was produced by the Holy See; the next section turns to what Rome itself examined and decided.

sections.h: Accountability: Cardinals, Founders, Bishops and the Bill
sections.html:
National reports count what happened in dioceses. The question for this volume is narrower: what the Holy See knew about particular men, what it decided, and what it later said about its own decisions. Five cases are documented well enough to answer that from Rome's own records or statements: Cardinal Bernard Law of Boston, Marcial Maciel of the Legionaries of Christ, Theodore McCarrick, the Chilean bishops in 2018, and Joseph Ratzinger's years in Munich. The section then turns to the money paid in the United States, where most of the bill has fallen, and to the limit set by the Holy See's sovereign immunity. Each person named here is an individual; none of them stands for the Church as a whole.

Boston: Cardinal Law, 2002

The Boston Globe's reporting from January 2002 showed that the Archdiocese of Boston had kept abusive priests in ministry for years. The best-known was John Geoghan, whom Law reassigned to a parish in 1984 despite a warning from an auxiliary bishop; Geoghan was removed in 1993, dismissed from the priesthood in 1998, and found to have abused more than 130 children in six parishes. [cite:vt12_wiki_law] John Paul II accepted Law's resignation as archbishop on 13 December 2002. Law wrote: "To all those who have suffered from my shortcomings and mistakes I both apologize and from them beg forgiveness." [cite:vt12_wiki_law] In May 2004 John Paul II appointed him archpriest of the Basilica of St Mary Major in Rome, a largely ceremonial post he held until November 2011; he died in Rome on 20 December 2017. [cite:vt12_wiki_law] The appointment in Rome is the fact critics cite; the often-repeated claim that he "fled" to Rome is an interpretation of a move that followed his resignation by more than a year.

The Legionaries: Marcial Maciel, 2006–2010

The CDF had received accusations against Maciel, the Mexican founder of the Legionaries of Christ, since 1998. On 19 May 2006 it announced that, in view of his age and health, it would not open a canonical trial and instead invited him to "a reserved life of prayer and penance," renouncing all public ministry; Benedict XVI approved the decision. The Legion said Maciel maintained his innocence and accepted the decision "with faith." [cite:vt12_zenit_maciel2006] Maciel died in 2008, so the decision came during his life, not after it, contrary to a claim sometimes made. [cite:vt12_wiki_maciel] The Legion admitted his "reprehensible actions" in March 2010, and a Vatican statement of 1 May 2010 called his acts "true crimes" and described a "mechanism of defense" built around him. In 2019 the Legion acknowledged 175 victims of 33 of its priests, 60 of them abused by Maciel. [cite:vt12_wiki_maciel]

McCarrick: the Holy See's own report, 2020

Theodore McCarrick, formerly cardinal archbishop of Washington, was dismissed from the clerical state in 2019 and continued to deny misconduct. [cite:vt12_ru_mccarrick2020] On 10 November 2020 the Holy See published a 449-page report on what it had known, drawing on more than 90 interviews. It is the most detailed account any part of the Holy See has published of its own handling of one abuser. It found that John Paul II named McCarrick to Washington in 2000 despite allegations made the year before, relying on "inaccurate and incomplete information" from three New Jersey bishops and on his own experience of false accusations used by Poland's communist government; that Benedict XVI chose to believe McCarrick and did not sanction him; and that Francis had not covered up reports but continued his predecessors' approach. On Archbishop Carlo Maria Viganò's claim that Benedict had imposed sanctions that Francis lifted, it said: "No records support Vigano's account." [cite:vt12_ru_mccarrick2020] The report is a self-examination; no external body tested it.

Chile, 2018: a pope's own error

Francis appointed Juan Barros bishop of Osorno in 2015 over objections from Chilean bishops and his own advisory commission. Victims of the priest Fernando Karadima said Barros had witnessed their abuse. During a visit to Chile in January 2018 Francis called their accusations "calumny" and asked for proof. [cite:vt12_cc_chile2018] He then sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna, who returned with a 2,300-page dossier from 64 witnesses, and in April 2018 Francis wrote that he had made "grave errors" of judgment and invited the victims he had discredited to Rome. [cite:vt12_cc_chile2018] All 34 Chilean bishops offered their resignations in May 2018; on 11 June Francis accepted those of Barros, Cristián Caro of Puerto Montt and Gonzalo Duarte of Valparaíso. [cite:vt12_aje_chile2018] It is the clearest case in which a sitting pope publicly retracted his own defence of a bishop.

Munich: Benedict XVI, 2022

On 20 January 2022 the law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising, reported on abuse there from 1945 to 2019 and found four cases in which Joseph Ratzinger, archbishop from 1977 to 1982, could be accused of misconduct. Ratzinger later acknowledged that he had attended a 1980 meeting about an abusive priest. [cite:vt12_ap_benedict2022] In a letter published on 8 February 2022 the retired pope asked forgiveness for any "grievous faults," without admitting specific wrongdoing; his lawyers issued a separate technical response to the report. [cite:vt12_ap_benedict2022]

The bill: settlements and bankruptcies in the United States

In the United States the cost has been carried by dioceses and religious orders, which are separate legal persons, not by the Holy See. By early 2004 dioceses had paid $472.5 million; by 2006 the total had reached $1.5 billion. [cite:vt12_am_johnjay2004] The bishops' 2025 annual audit report, published in June 2026, recorded about $390 million in diocesan abuse-related costs in fiscal 2025 alone (about $484 million with religious communities), up 61 per cent on the year before, and OSV News estimated that dioceses had paid roughly $5 billion from 2004 to June 2025, and likely more than $6 billion including recent settlements. The same report counted 1,070 new allegations from 973 survivors in the audit year, 24 of them involving people who were minors at the time. [cite:vt12_ev_usccb2026]

Bankruptcy has become the main legal route. The Archdiocese of Portland in Oregon filed first, on 6 July 2004. [cite:vt12_ncr_bankruptcy2018] Filings accelerated after states opened "lookback windows" that revived old claims: Minnesota from 2013 to 2016, New York from August 2019, California from 2020 to 2022. [cite:vt12_ncreg_bankruptcy2023] As of March 2026, the latest update of a tracker kept at Penn State Dickinson Law when it was checked in October 2026, 44 Catholic organisations in the United States had sought chapter 11 protection, 15 cases pending and 29 concluded. [cite:vt12_dick_bankruptcy2026]

Where the Holy See stands: immunity

Survivors have also sued the Holy See itself. Those suits, described in Part Five, have failed. In O'Bryan v. Holy See a federal appeals court held in 2008 that the Holy See is a foreign state under US law, and the plaintiffs withdrew in 2010 citing the high bar of immunity; in Doe v. Holy See a federal judge held in 2012 that the priest concerned was not the Holy See's employee; and in 2021 the European Court of Human Rights accepted Belgium's grant of immunity to the Holy See. [cite:vt5_ncr_obryan2010] [cite:vt5_jurist_doe2012] [cite:vt5_eapil_jc2021] [scene:vt5_recognition|Part Five: sovereignty and immunity] The Holy See's counsel, Jeffrey Lena, said the outcome of O'Bryan confirmed "there has never been a Holy See policy requiring concealment of child sexual abuse." [cite:vt5_ncr_obryan2010] The narrower finding is that no court has held the Holy See itself liable for an abuser's acts; claims that its bank, the IOR, "shields" abuse money have no source, since the IOR has not been a defendant in any case found. [scene:vt9_ior|Part Nine: the IOR]

The record thus divides along the line the Holy See itself draws. Rome has disciplined individuals, sometimes late (Maciel in 2006, McCarrick in 2019), has published one detailed self-examination (McCarrick, 2020), and has seen a pope retract his own judgment (Chile, 2018). [cite:vt12_zenit_maciel2006] [cite:vt12_ru_mccarrick2020] [cite:vt12_cc_chile2018] Compensation, by contrast, has been paid locally, by dioceses and orders under national law, while the Holy See has defended its immunity from the same claims. [cite:vt12_dick_bankruptcy2026] [cite:vt5_eapil_jc2021]

sections.h: Beyond the Catholic Church: The Same Questions Asked of Others
sections.html:
The abuse record is part of this volume because the Holy See's sovereignty, secrecy rules and central control of canonical trials make it a distinct case. It is not part of the volume because abuse or its concealment is peculiar to Catholicism. Inquiries that looked at other churches and institutions found the same failures: priority given to reputation, survivors disbelieved, offenders moved or left in place. This section sets out five of those inquiries from their own reports, so that the Catholic record can be read against them. As in the previous section, each has its own method and scope, and no figure is comparable with another.

England and Wales: the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse

The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA) was set up in 2015 and chaired, after its first chair resigned, by Professor Alexis Jay. Its fifteen investigations included the Anglican Church, the Roman Catholic Church and other religious organisations and settings. [cite:vt12_ct_iicsa2022] Its report on the Anglican Church, published on 6 October 2020, found that between the 1940s and 2018, 390 people who were clergy or held positions of trust in the Church of England had been convicted of sexual offences against children. It found that alleged abusers often received more support than victims, that record-keeping was poor, and that the Church had neglected "the well-being of children in favour of protecting its own reputation," creating "a culture where abusers were able to hide." Archbishop Justin Welby called the findings "profoundly and deeply shocking." [cite:vt12_iicsa_anglican2020]

The final report, published on 20 October 2022, drew on more than 7,300 victims and survivors. Its central recommendation was a legal duty on people in regulated activities to report known or suspected child sexual abuse; Jay said that "mandatory reporting should be an absolute obligation." It also recommended a national redress scheme and a Child Protection Authority. The Church of England said it would include mandatory reporting in its own work and that a working party was examining the seal of confession, which only its General Synod could change. [cite:vt12_ct_iicsa2022]

The Church of England: the Makin review and Welby's resignation, 2024

John Smyth QC abused boys and young men in England, in settings linked to the Iwerne holiday camps and Winchester College, and continued after moving to Africa in 1984; he died in Cape Town in 2018. The independent review by Keith Makin and Sarah Lawrence, published on 7 November 2024, put the number of his victims at between 115 and 130 and found an "active cover-up" after a report on him by the Reverend Mark Ruston in 1982. [cite:vt12_wiki_makin] Welby, who was told of the allegations in 2013 and was assured that the police had been informed, announced his resignation as Archbishop of Canterbury on 12 November 2024. He wrote that he had "believed wrongly that an appropriate resolution would follow" and accepted "personal and institutional responsibility." [cite:vt12_vn_welby2024] [cite:vt12_wiki_makin] The nearest Catholic parallel in this part is the Chilean bishops' collective offer to resign in 2018. [scene:vt12_accountability|Accountability: Chile, 2018]

The Southern Baptist Convention: the Guidepost report, 2022

The Southern Baptist Convention has no pope, no canon law and no central court; each congregation is autonomous. Delegates at its 2021 annual meeting voted for an outside investigation of the Convention's Executive Committee, which hired the firm Guidepost Solutions. Its report, released on 22 May 2022 after seven months, found that for about two decades a few senior Executive Committee leaders, working with outside lawyers, had "largely controlled" the response to abuse reports and were "singularly focused on avoiding liability." Survivors were ignored or disbelieved and some were told that congregational autonomy meant nothing could be done. A staff member had kept a private list of hundreds of accused ministers, and the investigators found no sign that anyone acted to keep them out of ministry. [cite:vt12_ap_guidepost2022] The finding matters for this volume because it shows the same conduct in a body with none of the Holy See's structures: no secrecy rule, no central tribunal, no sovereign immunity.

Australia: the Royal Commission across institutions

Australia's Royal Commission examined institutions of every kind, religious and secular. Its final report, published on 15 December 2017, drew on almost 8,000 private sessions. Of the survivors heard, 58.1 per cent had been abused in an institution run by a religious organisation; of those, 61.4 per cent were in Catholic institutions, 14.8 per cent in Anglican institutions and 7.2 per cent in Salvation Army institutions. [cite:vt12_guardian_rc2017] These are shares of the people who came to the Commission, not rates of abuse, and they do not account for how many children each body had in its care. The Commission's 189 new recommendations included two addressed to Catholic rules: that there be no exemption from mandatory reporting for abuse disclosed in confession, and that the Australian bishops ask the Holy See to consider voluntary celibacy for diocesan clergy. [cite:vt12_guardian_rc2017]

Germany: the Protestant ForuM study, 2024

The Evangelical Church in Germany (EKD), a federation of twenty regional Protestant churches, commissioned an independent research consortium that reported on 25 January 2024, four years and about €3 million later, on abuse in the churches and in their welfare organisation, Diakonie. In the files the researchers could examine they found 2,225 survivors and 1,259 alleged perpetrators, pastors being the largest group; extrapolating, they estimated about 9,300 survivors and 3,500 perpetrators since the war, and called the confirmed figures "the tip of the tip of the iceberg." Only one of the twenty churches cooperated fully, and the planned systematic review of personnel files did not take place. The EKD's president, Bishop Annette Kurschus, said the Church accepted the findings "in humility." [cite:vt12_it_forum2024] The comparison with the Catholic MHG study of 2018 is direct: both were commissioned by the churches themselves, both depended on files the churches chose to supply, and both described their figures as minimums. [cite:vt12_ba_mhg2018]

What the comparison shows, and what it does not

Placed side by side, the inquiries show that the core failures documented in Catholic dioceses (protecting the institution's reputation, disbelieving survivors, leaving offenders in post) also occurred in a national Anglican church, a decentralised Baptist convention and a federation of German Protestant churches. [cite:vt12_iicsa_anglican2020] [cite:vt12_ap_guidepost2022] [cite:vt12_it_forum2024] The comparison does not cancel what is particular to the Catholic case: a single legal system run from Rome that, until December 2019, placed abuse trials under the pontifical secret; a central office in Rome to which every credible case of child abuse had to be sent from 2001; and a sovereign at the top that can invoke immunity in foreign courts. [cite:vt12_va_ddg2001] [cite:vt12_vn_rescript2019] [scene:vt5_recognition|Part Five: immunity] It also does not settle relative rates: the Australian shares measure who came forward, not how often abuse occurred in each church. [cite:vt12_guardian_rc2017] What the comparison supports is a narrower reading: the failures documented in Catholic dioceses also appear in institutions without the Holy See's structures, and those structures bear on how cases were handled in the Catholic Church and who could be held to account, which is the subject of this part.

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: Reach: Schools, Universities, Bishops
chapters.intro: Part Twelve examined abuse and how it was handled. Part Thirteen turns to the question of reach: how far the institutions that carry the name Catholic extend, and which of them the Holy See actually directs. It counts the schools, universities, hospitals and charities reported in the Church's own statistics, by continent; it tests the competing figures for Jesuit universities, including the claim of 228, against the Jesuit networks' own count; it builds a ledger of 33 leading American universities by the body that founded them, with the University of Virginia, founded without a professor of divinity, as the contrast case; and it ends with the instrument through which Rome's reach is most direct and best documented, the appointment of bishops through nuncios, including the agreement with China, followed by the dialogues that link the Holy See to other churches without giving it authority over them.
chapters.outro: Part Thirteen established that the Church's own statistics count 229,090 Catholic schools with about 64.6 million pupils, 4.47 million university students and 103,951 charitable and health institutions at the end of 2023, with Africa holding most primary pupils, the Americas most university students and Europe most homes for the elderly; under canon law these are directed by bishops, parishes and orders, not owned by the Holy See. [cite:vt13_pv_dossier] [cite:vt13_fides_pdf] [cite:vt13_cic_803] The Jesuit networks count 177 universities, not 228, and 27 in the United States plus one in Belize; their American members have been held since the late 1960s and early 1970s by boards with lay members, under norms from Rome that give the local bishop a defined say over the teaching of theology. [cite:vt13_em_map2024] [cite:vt13_ajcu_home] [cite:vt13_bc_jesuithist] [cite:vt13_usccb_excorde] Of the 33 universities ranked highest by U.S. News in September 2026, three were founded by Catholics, thirteen by Protestant churches or ministers, ten by private nonsectarian founders and seven by legislatures, among them the University of Virginia, whose founders "proposed no professor of Divinity". [cite:vt13_pq_usnews2027b] [cite:vt13_wiki_colonial] [cite:vt13_fo_rockfish] Rome's most direct reach is the appointment of bishops through 128 nunciatures, shared by negotiation with China since 2018, while its ties to Lutheran, Orthodox and Anglican churches rest on signed agreements, not authority. [cite:vt13_cic_377] [cite:vt13_aleteia_dipl2026] [cite:vt5_vn_china2024] [cite:vt13_lwf_jddj] Part Fourteen turns to the texts and archives through which that authority is exercised and remembered, beginning with the canon of scripture. [scene:vt14_canon|Part Fourteen: the canon]

sections.h: Schools, Hospitals and Who Runs Them
sections.html:
Claims about the Vatican's reach usually begin with a number: so many schools, so many universities, so many hospitals, all said to answer to Rome. The numbers exist, and they are large. What they measure needs care. They come from the Church's own statistical yearbook, the Annuarium Statisticum Ecclesiae, which Agenzia Fides, the news agency of the Pontifical Mission Societies, summarises each October for World Mission Day. The edition released on 17 October 2025 gives Catholic population figures to 30 June 2023 and all other figures to 31 December 2023, and it describes the institutions as those the Church "runs". [cite:vt13_fides2025] This section sets out those figures, worldwide and by continent, and then asks what "Catholic" means in law for a school or university, because the answer decides whether these numbers describe a network the Holy See commands or something looser.

The worldwide count

At the end of 2023 the yearbook counted 74,550 Catholic kindergartens with 7,639,051 pupils, 102,455 primary schools with 36,199,844 pupils and 52,085 secondary schools with 20,724,361 pupils. [cite:vt13_pv_dossier] [cite:vt13_fides2025] Taken together that is 229,090 schools and about 64.6 million pupils. Beyond school age, the same summary counted 2,688,625 students in higher institutes and 4,468,875 students in Catholic universities. [cite:vt13_pv_dossier] [cite:vt13_cna_stats] The summary gives no count of universities themselves, only of their students, so any figure for the number of Catholic universities in the world has to come from elsewhere and will depend on the definition used.

The same yearbook counted 103,951 charitable and health institutions. Among them were 5,377 hospitals, 13,895 dispensaries, 504 leprosaria, 15,566 homes for the elderly, the chronically ill and the disabled, 8,593 orphanages, 10,858 creches, 10,827 marriage counselling centres, 3,147 centres for social education or rehabilitation and 35,184 institutions of other kinds. [cite:vt13_fides_pdf] [cite:vt13_fides2025] The figures do not travel cleanly between versions. The Holy See Press Office's Italian summary omits the orphanages, so its listed categories add up to 95,358 rather than the stated total, and the National Catholic Register's English report gives "other" institutions as 5,184 where Fides and the press office give 35,184. [cite:vt13_pv_dossier] [cite:vt13_cna_stats] The continental tables in the Fides dossier close the gap: with 8,593 orphanages the categories sum to 103,951. [cite:vt13_fides_pdf]

Where the institutions are

The continental breakdown changes the picture of a European or American network. Africa had 45,206 of the world's 102,455 Catholic primary schools and 21,125,043 of their 36,199,844 pupils, which is 58 per cent of all Catholic primary pupils; an average African Catholic primary school taught about 470 children against about 190 in Europe. [cite:vt13_fides_pdf] Africa also had the most Catholic secondary schools (18,392) and the most hospitals (1,634, or 30 per cent of the total). [cite:vt13_fides_pdf] University education points the other way: 2,543,486 of the 4,468,875 students in Catholic universities, 57 per cent, were in the Americas, and 1,032,715 in Europe. [cite:vt13_fides_pdf] Europe dominated one category of care: 8,515 of the 15,566 homes for the elderly, chronically ill and disabled, and 5,092 of the 10,827 marriage counselling centres. [cite:vt13_fides_pdf]

The distribution follows where Catholics live and where the state does or does not provide the service. Of the 1.405 billion Catholics counted at 30 June 2023, 671.9 million lived in the Americas, 286.3 million in Europe, 280.7 million in Africa, 155.2 million in Asia and 11.3 million in Oceania. [cite:vt13_fides_pdf] Asia is the clearest case of reach beyond the faithful: Catholics were 3.3 per cent of its population, yet the yearbook counted 16,273 Catholic primary schools with 5,687,465 pupils and 11,629 secondary schools with 5,974,049, more secondary pupils than in Europe. [cite:vt13_fides_pdf]

National counts are kept separately and on their own methods. In the United States the National Catholic Educational Association reported on 24 March 2026 that there were 5,829 Catholic schools in the 2025–26 school year, 4,644 elementary and middle schools and 1,185 secondary schools, with 1,674,907 pupils, of whom 22.2 per cent (372,244) were not Catholic. [cite:vt13_ncea2026] Its figures come from the education offices of 176 dioceses, which shows where the records, and the responsibility, sit. [cite:vt13_ncea2026]

What makes a school Catholic

The Code of Canon Law of 1983 defines the term. Under canon 803 a Catholic school is one that "a competent ecclesiastical authority or a public ecclesiastical juridic person directs", or one that ecclesiastical authority recognises as Catholic in a written document; no school may call itself Catholic without that authority's consent.
