[cite:vt13_cic_803] In practice the directing authority is a diocesan bishop, a parish or a religious institute: canon 806 gives the diocesan bishop the right "to watch over and visit the Catholic schools in his territory, even those which members of religious institutes have founded or direct." [cite:vt13_cic_803] For universities, canon 808 likewise reserves the title "Catholic university" to institutions with the consent of competent ecclesiastical authority, canon 810 makes the authority named in each university's statutes responsible for appointing teachers of sound doctrine, and canon 812 requires those who teach theological disciplines to hold a mandate from that authority. [cite:vt13_cic_803]

The Holy See's own role is narrower than the totals suggest. Canon 816 reserves to the Apostolic See the erection or approval of "ecclesiastical" universities and faculties, those that teach theology, canon law and related sacred disciplines, and gives it their "higher direction"; their statutes and plans of study must be approved in Rome. [cite:vt13_cic_803] Since the 2022 reform of the Curia that work belongs to the Dicastery for Culture and Education. [cite:vt6_va_pe] [scene:vt6_curia_2022|Part Six: the Curia since 2022] The tens of thousands of parish primary schools in Africa and Asia, the hospitals and the homes for the elderly are counted in the yearbook because dioceses and orders report them, not because the Holy See owns or manages them. Each is directed by its own bishop, parish or order under canon law and, in civil law, by whatever body the local state recognises. The figures therefore measure the reach of a church spread across many legal owners, bound by a common law and a common head, and should not be read as the property or payroll of the Vatican; what the Holy See itself owns is the subject of Part Nine. [scene:vt9_true_vs_public_wealth|Part Nine: true and public wealth]

Within that common law the Holy See's levers over a school are indirect but real: it appoints the bishop who may visit and supervise it, it sets the canons that define it, and through the bishop it controls the use of the name. [cite:vt13_cic_803] The last section of this part follows the most important of those levers, the appointment of bishops. [scene:vt13_appointments_nuncios|How bishops are appointed]

sections.h: Jesuit Universities: Counting Them and Asking Who Governs Them
sections.html:
The Society of Jesus is the religious order most often named in claims about Catholic influence over education, and the figure attached to it varies with the speaker. The order itself is described in Part Eight; this section deals only with its universities. [scene:vt8_jesuits|Part Eight: the Jesuits] Two questions run through it: how many Jesuit universities there are, which turns on definition, and who governs them, which turns on documents that changed in the late 1960s.

The count

The most recent count by the Jesuit networks themselves is the second edition of a printable map, "Jesuit World of Universities and Schools (2024)", produced by the International Association of Jesuit Universities (IAJU), the Jesuit Global Network of Schools (JGNS) and Educate Magis and published on 30 October 2024. It lists 177 universities in the IAJU, 937 schools in the JGNS, 2,127 schools of Fe y Alegría, a popular-education movement, and 388 schools of the Jesuit Refugee Service: 3,629 institutions in all. [cite:vt13_em_map2024] The map calls its figures a snapshot, noting that institutions join or leave the networks each year. [cite:vt13_em_map2024] The IAJU was founded in 2018 with the approval of the Superior General, Arturo Sosa, and is organised in six regional associations, from AUSJAL in Latin America to the Kircher Network in Europe and the Association of Jesuit Colleges and Universities (AJCU) in North America. [cite:vt13_javeriana_iaju]

Other figures circulate. Popular accounts give about 190, "over 200" or "250+" universities. Wikipedia's list of Jesuit educational institutions, which carries no date, gives a total of 189 colleges and universities. [cite:vt13_wiki_jesuitlist] The differences are mostly definitional. The IAJU counts members of its regional associations; a looser count may include institutions founded by Jesuits but no longer run by them, Jesuit faculties within other universities, or colleges that are not universities. Historical totals are larger still: the historian Paul Grendler, cited on the same list, counted over 700 Jesuit colleges and universities in Europe by 1749 and about a hundred elsewhere, before the order's suppression later that century. [cite:vt13_wiki_jesuitlist] For the present, the defensible figure is 177 IAJU members in 2024, stated with its definition. [cite:vt13_em_map2024]

The American figure has a similar history of error. Several sources say there are 28 Jesuit colleges and universities in the United States. The AJCU does have 28 members, but they are in 17 states, the District of Columbia and Belize: 27 are in the United States, and the 28th is St. John's College in Belize City, which joined in July 2020, the year after Wheeling Jesuit University ended its affiliation with the order. [cite:vt13_ajcu_home] [cite:vt13_ajcu_about] [cite:vt13_jesuits_stjohns] Three Canadian institutions are associate members. [cite:vt13_ajcu_home] As of October 2026 the association's own page gave the same count. [cite:vt13_ajcu_home]

Notable institutions

Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., describes itself as "the oldest Catholic and Jesuit institution of higher learning in the United States." It was established in 1789 by John Carroll, who obtained land for it that year. [cite:vt13_gu_history] Its presidents were Jesuits until 2001, when John J. DeGioia became its 48th president and its first lay one. [cite:vt13_gu_history] Boston College received its charter in 1863 and opened on 5 September 1864, at the request of Bishop John Bernard Fitzpatrick and after years of fund-raising by the Jesuit John McElroy; Jesuits ran it as presidents, teachers and administrators. [cite:vt13_bc_jesuithist]

The Jesuit institution with the closest tie to the papacy is in Rome. Ignatius of Loyola opened a school of grammar, humanities and Christian doctrine there in 1551; Gregory XIII built it a new seat, inaugurated in 1584, and the university calls him its "founder and protector"; in 1873, after the Italian state had expelled its faculties from the Collegio Romano, Pius IX gave it the name Pontifical Gregorian University. [cite:vt13_unigre_history] [scene:vt2_roman_question|Part Two: the Roman Question] As recently as 2006 Benedict XVI confirmed that the university is entrusted to the Society of Jesus. [cite:vt13_unigre_history] A pontifical university of this kind is one of the "ecclesiastical" universities whose statutes the Apostolic See approves under canon 816; most Jesuit universities elsewhere are not. [cite:vt13_cic_803]

Who governs them

The governance of the large American Catholic universities changed in a few years at the end of the 1960s. At Notre Dame, founded by the Congregation of Holy Cross rather than the Jesuits, the order's superior general approved in January 1967 a plan to transfer the university's property and governance to a two-tier board of lay and religious trustees and fellows, after Theodore Hesburgh had sought and received written permission from Rome. [cite:vt13_nd_hesburgh] The same year a meeting of Catholic university leaders sponsored by Notre Dame at Land O'Lakes, Wisconsin, issued a statement, drafted by Neil McCluskey at Hesburgh's request, that a Catholic university must have "true autonomy and academic freedom" in the face of authority, lay or clerical, from outside the academic community. [cite:vt13_wiki_landolakes] At Boston College a new board of Jesuit and lay trustees took legal responsibility for the university in 1972. [cite:vt13_bc_jesuithist]

Rome's answer came in 1990. John Paul II's apostolic constitution Ex corde Ecclesiae, issued on 15 August 1990, set general norms for Catholic universities and has been read as a repudiation of the Land O'Lakes position. [cite:vt13_usccb_excorde] [cite:vt13_wiki_landolakes] The American bishops approved an application of it for the United States on 17 November 1999; the Congregation for Bishops granted the required approval on 3 May 2000, and the norms took effect as particular law on 3 May 2001. [cite:vt13_usccb_excorde] They require Catholics who teach theology at a Catholic university to hold a mandatum from the diocesan bishop, ask that boards have a Catholic majority and faculties a majority committed to the faith "to the extent possible", and ask that the president be Catholic. [cite:vt13_usccb_excorde] The text also limits the instrument: the mandatum is "not an appointment" or approval of a professor's teaching, it is the professor's personal responsibility rather than the university's, and no fixed percentage of Catholic trustees or faculty is set. [cite:vt13_usccb_excorde]

The record therefore shows three distinct layers of authority over a Jesuit university, which claims of a single chain of command tend to merge. The Society of Jesus sponsors it and, in many cases, supplies some of its leaders; a board of trustees, usually mixed and often mostly lay, holds it in civil law; and the local bishop, under norms approved in Rome, has a defined say over the teaching of theology and the use of the name Catholic. [cite:vt13_bc_jesuithist] [cite:vt13_usccb_excorde] [cite:vt13_cic_803] No document found for this volume shows the Holy See or the Superior General directing the admissions, appointments or research of these universities outside those channels. Part Six treats the separate myth that the Superior General, the so-called Black Pope, commands the pope himself. [scene:vt6_black_pope|Part Six: the "Black Pope"]

sections.h: The Ledger: 33 American Universities by Founding Tradition
sections.html:
A recurring claim in material about Catholic influence holds that the leading universities of the United States, and of the West generally, are Catholic or Jesuit institutions, or are controlled by them. The way to test a claim of that kind is to take a fixed list chosen in advance by someone else, record for each institution who founded it and what its relationship to any church is now, and count. This section does that for 33 American universities, with the University of Virginia, founded in 1819 under a plan that deliberately left out a professor of divinity, as the contrast case.

The selection rule

The list is the top of the best-known American ranking, the U.S. News & World Report "Best National Universities" list in its 2027 edition, reported on 22 and 23 September 2026. Because of ties, exactly 33 institutions occupy ranks 1 to 31; the next institutions are tied at 34. [cite:vt13_pq_usnews2027a] [cite:vt13_pq_usnews2027b] [cite:vt13_boston_usnews] Using a ranking says nothing about whether the ranking is right; it only fixes the list before the founding records are examined, so that the selection cannot be tilted toward or away from church-founded institutions. The University of Virginia ranks 26th, so the contrast case is inside the list. [cite:vt13_pq_usnews2027b]

Each institution is placed in one of four groups by the body that founded it, according to the institution's own history or a standard reference: Catholic (founded by a diocese, a bishop or a religious order), Protestant (founded by a denomination, its ministers or a church body), private nonsectarian (founded by private persons with no church sponsor, or expressly as nonsectarian) and public (founded by a state or territorial legislature). The present-status column records only what the cited source states; where the source records no present church tie, the column says "private" or "public".

What the count shows

Of the 33, three were founded by Catholics: Notre Dame by the Congregation of Holy Cross in 1842, and Georgetown (1789) and Boston College (1863) in the Jesuit tradition. [cite:vt13_wiki_nd] [cite:vt13_gu_history] [cite:vt13_bc_jesuithist] None was founded by a diocese. Thirteen were founded by Protestant denominations or their ministers: Congregationalists (Harvard, Yale, Dartmouth), Presbyterians (Princeton), the Church of England (Columbia), Baptists (Brown, Chicago), Methodists (Duke, with Quakers; Northwestern; Vanderbilt; Emory; USC) and Universalists (Tufts). [cite:vt13_wiki_colonial] [cite:vt13_wiki_duke] [cite:vt13_wiki_nu] [cite:vt13_wiki_uchicago] [cite:vt13_vu_manual] [cite:vt13_emory_methodist] [cite:vt13_wiki_usc] [cite:vt13_wiki_tufts] Ten were private foundations with no church sponsor, several of them expressly nonsectarian, and seven were founded by state or territorial legislatures. [cite:vt13_wiki_cornell] [cite:vt13_washu_hist] [cite:vt13_wiki_nyu] [cite:vt13_wiki_uc]

Pennsylvania is the one hard call. The standard table of colonial colleges records its tradition as Church of England but "officially nonsectarian", and it is counted here as nonsectarian; moving it to the Protestant column would make the count 14 Protestant and 9 nonsectarian and change nothing else. [cite:vt13_wiki_colonial] Penn's founding date is also a choice: 1740 was adopted in 1899, while its charter dates from 1755. [cite:vt13_wiki_colonial]

Founding is not present governance, and the Protestant column shows it most clearly. Vanderbilt's Board of Trust severed the university's ties with the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, in June 1914; the University of Southern California severed its formal church ties in 1952; Northwestern later became non-sectarian; Tufts describes itself as nonsectarian. [cite:vt13_vu_manual] [cite:vt13_wiki_usc] [cite:vt13_wiki_nu] [cite:vt13_wiki_tufts] Only Duke and Emory still record a link to the United Methodist Church, described in Emory's case as a "historical affiliation". [cite:vt13_wiki_duke] [cite:vt13_emory_methodist] The three Catholic institutions keep their religious identity, but each is held by a board that includes lay members, a change made at Notre Dame in 1967 and at Boston College in 1972. [cite:vt13_nd_hesburgh] [cite:vt13_bc_jesuithist] [scene:vt13_jesuit_universities|Jesuit universities: who governs them]

The contrast case: Virginia

The University of Virginia was designed as an argument. On 4 August 1818 the commissioners who had met at Rockfish Gap signed a report, drafted by Thomas Jefferson, that sent the legislature a plan for the university. In it they wrote that, "in conformity with the principles of our constitution, which places all sects of religion on an equal footing," they had "proposed no professor of Divinity". [cite:vt13_fo_rockfish] [cite:vt13_fo_rockfish_draft] The same report did not remove religion from the curriculum: "the proofs of the being of a god" were assigned to "the province of the professor of ethics". [cite:vt13_fo_rockfish] The Virginia General Assembly established the university's charter on 25 January 1819; its Board of Visitors met for the first time that year with Jefferson as Rector, and it opened on 7 March 1825 with five professors present, all of them foreign-born. [cite:vt13_uva_charter] [cite:vt13_monticello_timeline] The colonial colleges on the list were all founded within a church tradition, even where, as at Princeton and Pennsylvania, they were officially nonsectarian; Virginia's founders put in writing why their university would have no professor of divinity. [cite:vt13_wiki_colonial] [cite:vt13_fo_rockfish]

The contrast should not be overdrawn. Virginia was not the only public foundation of its time: the University of North Carolina had been chartered by its legislature on 11 December 1789, and the University of Michigan was established by the territorial legislature on 26 August 1817 as the Catholepistemiad, with a Catholic priest, Father Gabriel Richard, and a Protestant minister, John Monteith, among its founders. [cite:vt13_ncdncr_unc] [cite:vt13_um_founding] Michigan is a useful corrective: a public university, created by a legislature, with a priest among its founders. [cite:vt13_um_founding] By mid-century private founders were also writing nonsectarian rules into their charters, as at Washington University in 1853 and Cornell in 1865. [cite:vt13_washu_hist] [cite:vt13_wiki_cornell]

What the ledger cannot show

The ledger records founders and present affiliation. It does not measure influence, and it cannot support a claim that any church, the Holy See or the Society of Jesus controls any of these universities today: no document found for this volume shows such control beyond the sponsorship and canonical links described in the previous section. [scene:vt13_jesuit_universities|Jesuit universities] On the evidence of the list itself, the claim that America's leading universities are Catholic or Jesuit institutions fails: three of 33 are Catholic, and the founding tradition most represented is Protestant, most of it long since detached from the churches that began it. [cite:vt13_pq_usnews2027b] [cite:vt13_wiki_colonial] [cite:vt13_vu_manual] [cite:vt13_wiki_usc] The ranking itself is a snapshot as of October 2026 and will change; the founding records will not. [cite:vt13_pq_usnews2027a]

sections.h: Bishops, Nuncios and Other Churches
sections.html:
The previous sections showed that most Catholic schools, hospitals and universities are run by dioceses, parishes, orders and boards, not by the Holy See. The instrument through which Rome's reach is most direct is a different one: it chooses the bishops who govern those dioceses and supervise those schools. This section sets out how that choice is made, the diplomatic network that carries it, the one major state that has negotiated a share in it, and, by contrast, the links between the Holy See and other churches, which rest on agreement rather than appointment.

The rule: the pope appoints

Canon 377 of the Code of Canon Law states the rule in one sentence: "The Supreme Pontiff freely appoints bishops or confirms those legitimately elected." [cite:vt13_cic_377] The second clause covers the cases where a body elects and Rome confirms. The procedure behind the rule is set out in the same canon. At least every three years the bishops of each province or conference compile, in secret, a list of priests they consider suitable and send it to the Apostolic See. When a diocese falls vacant, the pontifical legate, in most countries the apostolic nuncio, gathers the views of the metropolitan archbishop, the other bishops of the province and the president of the bishops' conference, hears some of the diocese's consultors and cathedral chapter and, if he judges it useful, consults other clergy and lay people individually and in secret; he then sends three names, the terna, to Rome "together with his own opinion". [cite:vt13_cic_377]

In Rome the file goes to the Dicastery for Bishops, which discusses it and votes; its prefect presents the result to the pope, usually at a Saturday audience; the pope decides, and the nuncio asks the candidate whether he accepts. The process often takes six to eight months. [cite:vt6_usccb_bishops] Part Six described this machinery in the Curia as reformed in 2022. [scene:vt6_curia_2022|Part Six: the Curia since 2022] Its importance for this volume is personal as well as structural: Robert Prevost was prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops from 30 January 2023 until his election as Leo XIV on 8 May 2025, and in September 2025 he named Archbishop Filippo Iannone to succeed him. [cite:vt6_vn_leobio] [cite:vt6_aleteia_appts] The pope who now signs the appointments spent two years running the office that prepares them.

Canon 377 also closes a door that earlier centuries had left open to princes. Its fifth paragraph provides that "in the future, no rights and privileges of election, nomination, presentation, or designation of bishops are granted to civil authorities." [cite:vt13_cic_377] The words "in the future" leave existing arrangements in concordats where they are, and each such arrangement has to be read in its own text; but the general rule since 1983 is that a government obtains no new say in choosing Catholic bishops.

The nuncios

The nuncio is therefore two things at once: the Holy See's ambassador to a state and the pope's investigator of the local church. The Holy See Press Office recorded on 9 January 2026 that 184 states had diplomatic relations with the Holy See, together with the European Union and the Order of Malta, and that 93 embassies accredited to it were based in Rome. [cite:vt5_pv_relations2026] I.Media, reporting the same note, counted 128 apostolic nunciatures and 12 states with no formal ties. [cite:vt13_aleteia_dipl2026] Because there are fewer nunciatures than partner states, a number of nuncios are accredited to more than one country. A figure of "approximately 180" nunciatures, which sometimes circulates, confuses the number of states with relations with the number of missions. [cite:vt13_aleteia_dipl2026] [scene:vt5_recognition|Part Five: recognition]

China: a negotiated share

The People's Republic of China, which has no diplomatic relations with the Holy See, is the clearest case of a state negotiating a role in the choice of bishops. The Holy See and China signed a Provisional Agreement on the appointment of bishops on 22 September 2018; it was renewed for two years in 2020 and again in 2022, and on 22 October 2024 it was extended for four years. [cite:vt5_vn_china2024] Its text has never been published; the Holy See describes appointments as made "in accordance with" an agreement whose terms remain secret. [cite:vt13_aleteia_datong]

The record shows both the agreement working and its limits. In April 2023 Bishop Joseph Shen Bin was installed as bishop of Shanghai without the Holy See's approval, a breach of the agreement; on 15 July 2023 Francis confirmed him in the post, and Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Secretary of State, said the pope wished "to remedy the canonical irregularity" and that his intention was "fundamentally pastoral". [cite:vt13_tablet_shenbin] Under Leo XIV appointments have continued. On 28 July 2026 he named Andrea Ding Yang archbishop of Chongqing "within the Provisional Agreement", and Ding was ordained on 8 September 2026. [cite:vt13_vn_chongqing] On 10 August 2026 he appointed Paul Liu Honggang bishop of Datong, a diocese vacant since 1947; Aleteia counted him as the 19th bishop appointed under the 2018 agreement and the seventh Chinese bishop approved by Leo XIV, and noted that the Catholic Patriotic Association, which Rome does not recognise, had announced his "election" on 28 April 2026. [cite:vt13_aleteia_datong] As of October 2026, then, the sequence in China runs from a local selection under state auspices to papal appointment, with the papal appointment as the final, formal step.

Other churches: agreement, not appointment

The appointing power stops at the Catholic Church's own bishops. Rome's ties with other Christian churches run through the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity and take the form of dialogues and signed texts between partners. [cite:vt6_va_pe] The most substantial is the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, signed at Augsburg in October 1999 by the Lutheran World Federation and the Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity, represented by Ishmael Noko and Walter Kasper, which the Federation describes as resolving one of the key theological conflicts of the Reformation. [cite:vt13_lwf_jddj] The World Methodist Council joined it in July 2006; the Anglican Consultative Council welcomed and affirmed its substance in April 2016; and the World Communion of Reformed Churches joined in July 2017 at Wittenberg. [cite:vt13_lwf_jddj]

With the Orthodox, the anchor is the joint declaration of Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras in 1965. On 29 November 2025, at the Phanar in Istanbul, Leo XIV and Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew I marked its sixtieth anniversary and the 1,700th of the Council of Nicaea in a joint declaration that committed them to keep seeking a common date for Easter, to support the joint theological commission, and stated: "we reject any use of religion and the name of God to justify violence." [cite:vt13_va_phanar2025] With the Anglicans, the limits are older and still standing: Leo XIII's bull Apostolicae curae of 13 September 1896 declared Anglican ordinations "absolutely null and utterly void", and a 1998 commentary of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith cited it as teaching to be held definitively. [cite:vt13_wiki_apcurae] Gestures have moved further than doctrine. On 23 October 2025 Leo XIV and King Charles III prayed together in the Sistine Chapel with the Archbishop of York, which Buckingham Palace called the first such joint prayer by a pope and a British monarch since the Reformation. [cite:vt13_ncr_charles]

The documents give a plain answer to the question of reach. Over its own church the Holy See's reach is strong and formal: a single legal rule gives the pope the choice of bishops, and a network of 128 nunciatures runs the inquiries that feed it. [cite:vt13_cic_377] [cite:vt13_aleteia_dipl2026] Where a state insists, as China does, the Holy See has accepted a negotiated procedure and has at least once regularised an appointment made without it. [cite:vt13_tablet_shenbin] Over other churches it has no appointing power at all, only the texts it has agreed with them. [cite:vt13_lwf_jddj] [cite:vt13_va_phanar2025] How the Holy See uses its standing in a particular conflict, including Israel and Palestine, is the subject of Parts Sixteen to Eighteen. [scene:vt18_relations_since_1994|Part Eighteen: relations since 1994]

chapters.label: Part Fourteen
chapters.title: Texts and Archives
chapters.intro: Part Fourteen deals with the two kinds of paper that critics of the Holy See most often say are hidden: the books of the Bible and the papers in the pope's archive. The first section follows how Christians came to agree on which books belong in their scripture, from second-century lists to the Council of Trent in 1546, and corrects three claims that recur in popular writing: that the Council of Nicaea chose the Bible, that it did so by a vote of "218 to 2", and that Athanasius ordered rival gospels burned. It sets the Nag Hammadi find of 1945 and the Index of Forbidden Books, which ran from 1559 to 1966, on their documented footing. The second section describes the Vatican Apostolic Archive, which was called the "Secret Archive" until 2019: what the old name meant, how large the archive is, who may use it, and how it opens one pontificate at a time. The third section reports what scholars have found since the papers of Pius XII's pontificate were opened on 2 March 2020, and where they still disagree about what he knew of the murder of Europe's Jews and what he did about it.
chapters.outro: Part Fourteen established three things. The Christian canon was not chosen at Nicaea: that council, attended by 250 to 300 bishops by contemporary reports (318 by later tradition), whose surviving signature lists hold 200 to 220 names, settled the Arian dispute and the date of Easter, while the list of 27 New Testament books first appears in Athanasius's letter of 367, was accepted at Hippo and Carthage, and was fixed for Catholics only at Trent on 8 April 1546 by 24 votes to 15. [cite:vt14_wiki_nicaea] [cite:vt14_ect_festal39] [cite:vt14_wiki_trentcanon] The pope's archive was "secret" in the sense of private, was renamed the Vatican Apostolic Archive on 22 October 2019, and opens by whole pontificates, now up to October 1958. [cite:vt14_va_mp2019] [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] The Pius XII files opened on 2 March 2020 show that detailed reports of mass murder reached the Secretariat of State and the pope's secretary in 1942, while scholars and the Holy See still read his public silence differently. [cite:vt14_toi_wolf2020] [cite:vt14_euronews_coco2023] [cite:vt14_lrb_evans] [cite:vt14_vn_napolitano2022] Part Fifteen turns to a case that has long turned on what Vatican files do or do not contain: the disappearance of Emanuela Orlandi in 1983. [scene:vt15_the_case|Part Fifteen: Emanuela Orlandi and Mirella Gregori]

sections.h: Who Chose the Bible: The Canon from the Second Century to Trent
sections.html:
A canon, from the Greek word for a measuring rod, is a closed list of books that a community treats as scripture. Christians did not receive one at a single moment. For about three hundred years after the books of the New Testament were written, churches in different cities read overlapping but not identical sets of texts, and bishops wrote lists that differed at the edges. The modern Catholic list was defined as binding only in 1546, and Protestant and Ethiopian churches today use lists of different lengths. This section sets out the documented steps, then tests three claims that circulate widely: that the Council of Nicaea chose the books, that it did so by a vote of "218 to 2", and that the losing books were ordered destroyed. [cite:vt14_wiki_ntcanon]

Lists before councils

The oldest surviving list of New Testament books is the Muratorian fragment, a Latin text. Most scholars date the list it preserves to the late second century, around 170 to 200; a minority place it in the fourth century. [cite:vt14_wiki_ntcanon] Either way, it shows a church already sorting books into those read in worship and those not, well before any council addressed the question.

The first list that matches the 27 books of today's New Testament exactly comes from Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, in his 39th Festal Letter of 367. Egyptian bishops wrote such a letter each year to announce the date of Easter, and Athanasius used this one to list the books "included in the Canon": the four Gospels, Acts, the seven general letters, fourteen letters of Paul (counting Hebrews) and Revelation. [cite:vt14_ect_festal39] [cite:vt14_wiki_easterletter] He then named a second group, including the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Teaching of the Apostles and the Shepherd, that were "not indeed included in the Canon" but "appointed by the Fathers to be read" by new converts. A third group he rejected outright: books "called apocryphal", which he described as "an invention of heretics". [cite:vt14_ect_festal39]

The letter warns readers away from those books. It does not order anyone to burn, bury or destroy them. [cite:vt14_ect_festal39] The often-repeated claim that Athanasius "ordered the destruction of non-canonical texts" is an overstatement of what the document says.

The Western councils

A council at Rome in 382 under Pope Damasus is often said to have issued the same list that Trent later adopted. That attribution depends on the so-called Gelasian Decree, a text that Ernst von Dobschütz and others regard as a private compilation of the early sixth century. Geoffrey Hahneman, Edmon Gallagher and Clare Rothschild argue that the list cannot be a decree of the 382 synod, chiefly because Jerome, who was probably present, never mentions one; William Jurgens holds that the canon section is genuinely from 382. The question is open, and a careful account should say so. [cite:vt14_wiki_rome382]

The firmer record is North African. The Council of Hippo in 393 is the first council known to have accepted the present New Testament canon, and a summary of its acts was read and accepted again at the councils of Carthage in 397 and 419. Augustine of Hippo, the leading figure at these meetings, treated the canon as closed. [cite:vt14_wiki_ntcanon] These were regional councils; their lists carried authority because other churches came to accept them, not because a central office imposed them.

The East, Florence and Trent

The Greek-speaking and Syriac-speaking churches were slower and less concerned to draw a sharp line. Revelation was accepted in most of the East only by the fifth century, the Armenian Bible did not include it until about 1200, and the Syriac Peshitta originally left out 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation. [cite:vt14_wiki_ntcanon]

For the Catholic Church the decisive step came in the dispute with the Reformers. The Council of Florence had approved a list in 1442. [cite:vt14_wiki_trentcanon] The Council of Trent, at its fourth session on 8 April 1546, issued a decree naming every book of both Testaments, including the books Protestants were questioning (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Baruch and the two books of Maccabees), and declared anathema anyone who did not accept them "in their entirety and with all their parts". The same decree made the Latin Vulgate the authentic text for public use. [cite:vt14_trent_s4] The decree was not unanimous: it passed by 24 votes to 15, with 16 abstentions. [cite:vt14_wiki_trentcanon] Trent, not Nicaea, is the council at which a vote fixed the Catholic list.

The Protestant and Ethiopian lists

Protestant Bibles have 66 books, 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. This did not come from a single decision by Martin Luther. His complete German Bible of 1534 kept the disputed Old Testament books, printing them in a separate section headed, in translation, "Apocrypha: These Books Are Not Held Equal to the Scriptures, but Are Useful and Good to Read". The English King James Version of 1611 also printed them between the Testaments. [cite:vt14_wiki_protbible] Exclusion was hardened later, in confessions such as the Westminster Confession of 1646, which states that the Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture", and in the British and Foreign Bible Society's decision of the 1820s to stop funding their printing. [cite:vt14_wcf_ch1] [cite:vt14_wiki_protbible]

At the other end of the range, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts 81 books, the largest canon in traditional Christianity. It includes 1 Enoch and Jubilees, which no other major church treats as scripture, and three books of Meqabyan unrelated to the Greek Maccabees. [cite:vt14_wiki_tewahedo] The church reaches 81 in two ways: its own count, from the commentary tradition on its law book, is 46 Old Testament and 35 New Testament books, the 35 including eight books of church order; a narrower reckoning, printed in the imperial Bibles, is 54 and 27. Both total 81. [cite:vt27_eotc_books] [cite:vt27_cowley1974] [scene:vt27_church_and_canon|How the Ethiopian church counts to 81]

What Nicaea did, and the "218 to 2" figure

The Council of Nicaea met in 325 at the summons of the emperor Constantine. At least 200 bishops attended; contemporary reports range from about 250 to 300, and the traditional figure of 318 became standard later. The surviving signature lists contain between 200 and 220 names. [cite:vt14_wiki_nicaea] Those lists were compiled and copied in different languages and are incomplete; they record who subscribed, not a tally of votes. [cite:vt14_wiki_nicaea_list] A figure such as "218 bishops signed, 2 refused" therefore takes a number from the range of names on surviving lists and presents it as the result of a ballot. What the record does show is that all but two bishops subscribed the creed: Theonas of Marmarica and Secundus of Ptolemais refused and were excommunicated and exiled with Arius to Illyria. [cite:vt14_wiki_nicaea]

The council's business was the teaching of the Alexandrian priest Arius about the Son's relation to the Father. It produced the first form of the Nicene Creed, with the term homoousios ("of one substance with the Father"); Eusebius of Caesarea ascribed the term to Constantine himself, while Hosius of Córdoba also backed that side. [cite:vt14_wiki_nicaea] It also fixed a common method for dating Easter, dealt with the Melitian schism in Egypt and issued about twenty disciplinary canons. There is no record that it discussed which books belong in the Bible. The story that the bishops placed books on an altar and kept those that did not fall off comes from the Synodicon Vetus, a text of about 887, and historians treat it as fiction. [cite:vt14_wiki_nicaea] The one documented order to burn books in the Nicene story concerned Arius's own writings, and it came from the emperor, not from a list of scripture. [cite:vt14_wiki_nicaea]

Nag Hammadi and the Index

In late 1945 an Egyptian farmer, Muhammad Ali al-Samman, dug up a cache of books near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt containing twelve leather-bound papyrus codices and part of a thirteenth: 52 treatises in Coptic, most of them Gnostic, including the only complete text of the Gospel of Thomas. The manuscripts date mainly from the fourth century and are kept in the Coptic Museum in Cairo; a full facsimile appeared between 1972 and 1977 and an English translation in 1977. [cite:vt14_wiki_naghammadi] Why they were buried is not known. James Robinson proposed that monks of a nearby Pachomian monastery hid them after Athanasius's letter of 367; others have argued for a private burial with a wealthy owner. The link to Athanasius is a hypothesis, not a finding, and no document records an order to bury these books. [cite:vt14_wiki_naghammadi]

The Index of Forbidden Books is a documented instrument of control, and it should be described as one without being inflated. Pope Paul IV issued the first Roman Index in 1559; a revised Index followed the Council of Trent in 1564, and a Congregation of the Index ran it from 1571 until 1917, when the Holy Office took it over. [cite:vt14_nwe_index] Over four centuries it listed works by Erasmus, Descartes, Hobbes, Hume, Kant, Voltaire, Zola and Sartre, among many others. [cite:vt14_brit_index] Its last edition, in 1948, listed about 4,000 titles. On 14 June 1966 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, in a notification signed by Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, ended its force as church law while saying it kept its "moral value". [cite:vt14_nwe_index] [cite:vt14_brit_index] The Index restricted what Catholics might read; it did not and could not remove the listed books from circulation, and almost all of them stayed in print throughout.

The canon was argued over by named bishops across three centuries, closed for Catholics by a contested vote in 1546, and still differs between churches; Rome also kept a list of forbidden books until 1966. Neither fact requires a hidden council. The Holy See's own papers, the subject of the next section, are where claims of hidden history can be checked. [scene:vt14_apostolic_archive|The Apostolic Archive]

sections.h: The Apostolic Archive: What "Secret" Meant and Who Gets In
sections.html:
For most of its history the pope's central archive was called the Archivum Secretum Vaticanum, the Vatican Secret Archive. The name has done more to shape popular ideas about the Holy See than almost anything kept inside the building. This section explains what the word meant, why it was dropped in 2019, how large the archive is, what it is known to hold, who may read in it, and the rule that decides which decades are open. It ends with the Vatican Library, a separate institution that is often confused with the archive.

Private, not hidden

The archive was created at the wish of Pope Paul V around 1610 to 1612, when papal records that had been kept with the Apostolic Chamber and the Apostolic Library were gathered in one place. The name Archivum Secretum is attested from about 1646. [cite:vt14_va_mp2019] In the Latin of the period, secretum meant separate or reserved: this was, in Pope Francis's words, "the Pope's private, separate, reserved archive", as distinct from the archives of curial offices. [cite:vt14_va_mp2019]

Francis changed the name by an apostolic letter issued motu proprio (on his own initiative) dated 22 October 2019 and published on 28 October 2019. He gave as the reason that the word "secret" had acquired "ambiguous, even negative nuances" in modern languages, a reading he called the opposite of the archive's purpose. The new name, Vatican Apostolic Archive, was meant to stress its tie to the Roman see, as the name of the Vatican Apostolic Library already did. The letter changed the name, not the archive's structure or its rules of access. [cite:vt14_va_mp2019] Claims that still speak of a "Secret Archive" in the present tense are describing an institution that no longer uses that name, and the old name never meant that its contents were concealed as a class.

Size and holdings

The archive holds about 85 linear kilometres of shelving, part of it in an underground store known as the Bunker, beneath the Cortile della Pigna of the Vatican Museums. Its more than 600 archival collections, or fonds, cover about twelve centuries, from the eighth to the twentieth. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] The papal registers, the copies of outgoing papal letters, survive in a continuous series from Innocent III (1198–1216), with a few earlier volumes. [cite:vt14_wiki_vaa]

Among the documents reference works list in the archive are Henry VIII's petition for the annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, a transcript of Galileo's trial, letters of Michelangelo about unpaid work on the Sistine Chapel, and the bull of 1521 excommunicating Martin Luther. [cite:vt14_wiki_vaa] These are famous items in a mass of routine administrative paper: appointments, dispensations, correspondence of nunciatures and the accounts of the papal government.

The Apostolic Archive is not the only Holy See archive. When the papers of Pius XII's pontificate were opened, they included, besides the Apostolic Archive, the historical archive of the Secretariat of State's section for relations with states, the archive of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, the historical archive of Propaganda Fide, the archive of the Congregation for the Eastern Churches and the archives of other offices and tribunals. [cite:vt14_cchq_brownfleming] Much of the most consulted diplomatic material for the twentieth century sits in the Secretariat of State's archive, not in the Apostolic Archive proper. [cite:vt14_cchq_brownfleming]

Who may read, and how

Leo XIII opened the archive to researchers of every country in 1881; the reading room opened on 1 January of that year. [cite:vt14_va_mp2019] [cite:vt14_wiki_vaa] Today, according to Vatican News, access is free of charge and open to scholars of all nationalities regardless of religion. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] In practice it is restricted to qualified researchers, usually from universities, who apply with a letter of introduction. Readers order a limited number of items at a time, the reading room admits a limited number of people a day, and ink pens and personal cameras are not allowed. [cite:vt14_wiki_vaa] These are reading-room rules of the kind most major archives apply to fragile originals; they limit who may come in and how, not which documents exist.

The real limit is chronological. The Holy See opens its archives by whole pontificates, and only a pope can authorise access to his predecessors' papers. [cite:vt14_vn_open2020] [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] The papers of Pius XI (1922–1939) were opened on 18 September 2006 by decision of Benedict XVI, after a partial release of the files on relations with Germany, at John Paul II's direction, on 15 February 2003. [cite:vt14_cna_piusxi2006] [cite:vt14_audit_rte2003] Those of Pius XII (March 1939 to October 1958) were opened on 2 March 2020 by decision of Francis, who had announced the date a year earlier with the words "The Church is not afraid of history; rather, she loves it." [cite:vt1_va_archive2019] As of August 2025 Vatican News gave the end of Pius XII's pontificate, October 1958, as the current limit. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] We found no announcement, as of October 2026, of a date for opening the papers of John XXIII (1958–1963), the next pontificate in line. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025]

That is the accurate content of the common claim that "everything after 1958 is classified". Papers after October 1958 are closed, but under a rolling rule that has applied to every earlier period too, and that has so far opened each pontificate six or more decades after its end (Pius XI's after 67 years, Pius XII's after 61). One claim, that the Pius XII papers were held back for eighty years "due to the beatification process", gives a motive for which no source has been found; the documented practice is that whole pontificates open together, by papal decision. [cite:vt14_vn_open2020] [cite:vt14_cna_piusxi2006] The rolling rule is a real restriction on what can be known about the Holy See after 1958, including its relations with Israel and the Palestinians, and the volume says so wherever it bears on a finding. It is not evidence that any particular document is being hidden.

The Library

The Vatican Apostolic Library is older and separate. It descends from the early papal library; Nicholas V (1447–1455) enlarged it greatly and opened its manuscripts to scholars, and Sixtus IV formally established it by the bull Ad decorem militantis Ecclesiae of 15 June 1475. [cite:vt14_brit_bav] [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] Under Paul V the Library and the Archive were separated as institutions. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] The Library holds more than 80,000 manuscripts, mostly Latin and Greek, more than 1.6 million printed volumes and some 8,600 incunabula (books printed before 1501), together with coins, medals, prints and drawings. [cite:vt14_brit_bav] About 6,000 scholars use it. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025]

The archive therefore answers the question of "hidden history" in a specific way: the papers up to October 1958 can be read and are being read, and what they show about the Second World War is the subject of the next section. [scene:vt14_pius_files|The Pius XII files]

sections.h: The Pius XII Files: What Six Years of Research Have Shown
sections.html:
No pope's record has been argued over more than that of Eugenio Pacelli, Pius XII, who reigned from March 1939 to October 1958. The question is what he knew about the murder of Europe's Jews, when he knew it, and why he did not condemn it by name. For decades the debate rested on the Holy See's own selection of wartime documents and on the archives of other governments. On 2 March 2020 the papers of his whole pontificate were opened. This section reports what has been found since, who found it, how the Holy See has answered, and what remains in dispute. The wartime narrative itself, and its bearing on the Holy See's attitude to Zionism, is told in Part Sixteen. [scene:vt16_war_and_pius_xii|Part Sixteen: the war and Pius XII]

What was opened

Before 2020 the main published source was the Holy See's eleven-volume edition Actes et documents du Saint Siège relatifs à la Seconde Guerre mondiale, prepared by Jesuit historians, whose first volume appeared in 1965. [cite:vt14_vn_napolitano2022] [cite:vt14_toi_wolf2020] Critics had long pointed out that it was a selection made by the institution under examination.

Pope Francis announced on 4 March 2019 that the full papers would open a year later. He said he trusted serious research to show that the pope's decisions, in "moments of serious difficulties, of tormented decisions", reflected "human and Christian prudence". [cite:vt1_va_archive2019] The opening on 2 March 2020 covered the Apostolic Archive and the archives of the Secretariat of State and other curial offices: about 120 series and some 20,000 archival units, much of it digitised, with room for about 120 researchers at a time. [cite:vt14_vn_open2020] [cite:vt14_cchq_brownfleming] The reading rooms closed again soon afterwards because of the coronavirus pandemic, so the first findings came from the few researchers who had got in during those first days. [cite:vt14_toi_wolf2020] [cite:vt14_brown_kertzer2022]

The first finding: a report the Vatican said it could not confirm

A team from the University of Münster led by the church historian Hubert Wolf reported in 2020 on the Holy See's answer to an American inquiry of September 1942. A US diplomat had passed the Vatican a Jewish Agency report on the mass killing of about 100,000 Jews in the Warsaw ghetto and about 50,000 in Lviv, and asked whether the Vatican could confirm it from its own sources. The Vatican replied that it could not. [cite:vt14_toi_wolf2020]

Wolf's team found that a note confirms Pius XII read the American report, and that the Secretariat of State already held two corroborating accounts: a letter from the Greek Catholic archbishop of Lviv, Andrey Sheptytsky, describing 200,000 Jews massacred in Ukraine, and the report of an Italian businessman who had described the "incredible butchery" of Jews in Warsaw to Monsignor Giovanni Battista Montini, the future Paul VI. [cite:vt14_toi_wolf2020] They also found a memo by Angelo Dell'Acqua, a Secretariat of State official, casting doubt on the Jewish report on the ground that Jews tended to exaggerate. Wolf said the memo was missing from the eleven-volume edition. [cite:vt14_toi_wolf2020] The memo is one official's view on file; it rests on a stereotype about Jews held in the office that drafted the reply, and it is not a policy statement of the pope.

Kertzer's The Pope at War and the replies

David Kertzer of Brown University was among the first scholars in the reading room. His book The Pope at War, published by Random House in June 2022, drew on more than 7,000 pages of Vatican and state documents. [cite:vt14_brown_kertzer2022] He argued that Pius XII's overriding aim was to protect the institutional Church in a Europe he expected Hitler and Mussolini to dominate, not admiration for Hitler, and that memos from his aides show antisemitism among his trusted advisers. [cite:vt14_brown_kertzer2022] [cite:vt14_cchq_cucchiara] He described secret contacts with Hitler in 1939 through Prince Philipp von Hessen, who met the pope on 11 May 1939, and the Vatican's response to the SS roundup of Rome's Jews in October 1943, when officials intervened for those who were baptised or married to Catholics and made no wider protest. [cite:vt14_lrb_evans]

The British historian Richard J. Evans, reviewing the book, concluded that the pope's "main concern was always to preserve the interests of the Church as an institution". [cite:vt14_lrb_evans] Martina Cucchiara called it "an unsparing and detailed narrative" but faulted it for thin engagement with research on the rescue of Jews in Roman convents and for overstating how far the Vatican's wartime role had been forgotten. [cite:vt14_cchq_cucchiara]

The Holy See's newspaper answered as the book appeared. Writing in L'Osservatore Romano on 21 June 2022, the historian Matteo Luigi Napolitano argued that the 1939 talks were already known from the first volume of the Actes et documents, that Hitler rather than the pope had sought a new arrangement, and that Pius XII set five conditions Hitler would not accept. He cited the warning Cardinal Maglione gave the German ambassador on 16 October 1943, disputed the date of an American audience on which part of Kertzer's case rests, and called the view that Pius cared only for baptised Jews "worn-out". [cite:vt14_vn_napolitano2022]

The König–Leiber letter

In September 2023 the Italian daily Corriere della Sera published a letter found by Giovanni Coco, an archivist at the Apostolic Archive. Dated 14 December 1942, it was written by the German Jesuit Lothar König, who was linked to the Catholic resistance to Hitler, to Robert Leiber, a fellow Jesuit who was Pius XII's secretary and long-time adviser. König reported that up to 6,000 people a day, especially Poles and Jews, were being killed in the "blast furnace" at Bełżec, with transports from Rava Ruska. [cite:vt14_euronews_coco2023] [cite:vt14_cns_coco2026] The letter had been registered in the archive in 2019 and the rest of the correspondence has not been found. [cite:vt14_cns_coco2026]

The letter shows that detailed information on an extermination camp reached the pope's closest aide. It does not prove that Pius read it, and the reports are careful to say so. [cite:vt14_euronews_coco2023] Ten days later, in his Christmas radio message of 24 December 1942, Pius XII spoke of people "marked down for death or gradual extinction" because of their nationality or race, without naming the Jews or Germany. [cite:vt14_cns_coco2026] The same weeks brought British and Polish diplomatic notes reporting up to a million Jews killed in Poland. [cite:vt14_euronews_coco2023]

The "Ebrei" series

The Holy See's own contribution has been to publish one archival series in full. In June 2022, at Francis's request, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher announced the online release of the Secretariat of State's "Ebrei" (Jews) series: 170 volumes, nearly 40,000 files and more than 2,700 cases of Jews, baptised and not, who asked the pope for help with visas, asylum, release from detention or news of deported relatives. [cite:vt14_vn_ebrei2022] The last part went online in February 2023 with an inventory of more than 2,500 people who made requests. [cite:vt14_aleteia_ebrei2023] For most requests, the outcome is not recorded in the file. [cite:vt14_vn_ebrei2022]

Johan Ickx, head of the historical archive that holds the series, presented it in his book Pius XII and the Jews (2021) as "the list of Pius XII", evidence of an effort aimed at "saving every single human being, regardless of colour or creed". [cite:vt14_vn_ickx2021] That is the Holy See archivist's reading; the series itself documents requests and the office's handling of them, and its incomplete record of outcomes limits what it can prove about how many were saved.

What is settled and what is not

Six years of research have narrowed the old argument without ending it. On knowledge, the files point one way: by the second half of 1942 the Secretariat of State held detailed reports of mass killing from several independent sources, Pius XII read at least one of them, and his office told the United States it could not confirm what it had on file. [cite:vt14_toi_wolf2020] [cite:vt14_euronews_coco2023] Wolf and Evans both conclude from the new material that the pope was well informed, which leaves little room for the older defence that reliable information was lacking. [cite:vt14_toi_wolf2020] [cite:vt14_lrb_evans]

On motive and on action the record is still read in two ways. Kertzer and Evans read the silence as institutional caution, the protection of the Church as an organisation. [cite:vt14_brown_kertzer2022] [cite:vt14_lrb_evans] The Holy See's stated position, given by Francis in 2019 and developed by Napolitano and Ickx, is that the pope's decisions were "tormented" acts of prudence meant to keep humanitarian help alive, and the "Ebrei" series documents that such requests were handled. [cite:vt1_va_archive2019] [cite:vt14_vn_napolitano2022] [cite:vt14_vn_ickx2021] Reviewers such as Cucchiara note that the scale of rescue in Rome's religious houses still needs to be integrated with the critical findings. [cite:vt14_cchq_cucchiara] Whether particular letters reached the pope's desk, and how far rescue was directed from the top, remain open questions that the files have not yet answered.

For this volume's central question, one gap matters most. The same opening made available the Secretariat of State's papers for 1945 to 1958, the years of partition, the founding of Israel and Pius XII's encyclicals on Jerusalem. Studies drawn from those papers are the private record against which the Holy See's public refusal of Zionism can be tested; they are taken up, so far as they have been published, in Part Seventeen. [scene:vt17_jerusalem_1947_49|Part Seventeen: Jerusalem, 1947–49]

chapters.label: Part Fifteen
chapters.title: Emanuela Orlandi and Mirella Gregori
chapters.intro: Part Fourteen closed with the texts and archives. This part turns to the most famous unsolved case connected with the Vatican: the disappearance in Rome of Emanuela Orlandi, a fifteen-year-old Vatican citizen, on 22 June 1983, and of Mirella Gregori, also fifteen, forty-six days earlier. It sets out what is known of both disappearances, the calls and letters that demanded the release of the pope's would-be assassin, and John Paul II's appeals. It then grades every major theory against the documents: the Ağca exchange, the Magliana gang and Enrico De Pedis's tomb, the Vatican bank and Archbishop Marcinkus, the sexual-abuse claims including the 2023 remarks about John Paul II, the disputed 2017 expense memo and the uncle. It ends with the investigations, from Rome's closures in 2015 and 2016 and the empty tombs of 2019 to the three inquiries opened in 2023, with their status as of October 2026. Theories are reported as theories. The families' statements are given as theirs, and every person named who has not been charged is presumed innocent.
chapters.outro: Part Fifteen has established a short record and a long list of claims. Emanuela Orlandi, a Vatican citizen, vanished in Rome on 22 June 1983, forty-six days after Mirella Gregori. Callers demanded Ağca's release and the Vatican opened a line to them, but no one ever proved they held her. [cite:vt15_cwr_senate] [cite:vt15_csm_1983] [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] De Pedis's tomb was opened in 2012 and the Teutonic Cemetery's tombs in 2019, and both searches found nothing of her. [cite:vt15_ap_2012] [cite:vt15_vn_2019] The Marcinkus, abuse and John Paul II claims rest on uncorroborated recollections, witness evidence a judge found insufficient, or an anonymous recording with no supporting evidence. The 2017 memo is unauthenticated and denied by the Holy See. [cite:vt15_fq_2015] [cite:vt15_vn_francis] [cite:vt15_crux_2017] Rome archived its second investigation in 2015. Three inquiries opened in 2023: the Vatican's, Rome's and Parliament's under Law 202. As of October 2026 none has charged anyone or issued a report. [cite:vt15_fp_cass2016] [cite:vt15_law_202] [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025] The case remains open, and the family still holds that the Vatican knows more than it has said. Part Sixteen returns to the volume's central question, beginning with [scene:vt16_herzl_1904|Herzl's audience with Pius X in January 1904].

sections.h: Two Girls, Forty-Six Days Apart
sections.html:
This part deals with two missing teenagers and with what was said about them for more than forty years. It is not a part about money or treaties, and it is not here because it proves anything about the Holy See. It is here because Emanuela Orlandi was a citizen of Vatican City State and the daughter of a Vatican employee, because the Holy See became a party to the case within days, and because the theories that grew around it have been used to make claims about popes, cardinals, the Vatican bank and organised crime. Throughout the part, what the record shows is kept apart from what has been alleged, and each allegation carries its grade. Both girls' families are still waiting for an answer. Neither girl has been found, alive or dead, as of October 2026. [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025]

Mirella Gregori, 7 May 1983

Mirella Gregori was fifteen and lived with her family in central Rome. On 7 May 1983, after school, she told her mother she was going out briefly to meet a friend named Alessandro. She was last seen near a bar below the family's apartment. She had no connection to the Vatican. [cite:vt15_cwr_senate] Her case was joined to Orlandi's only later, when callers and written communiqués in 1983 claimed to be holding both girls. [cite:vt15_cwr_senate] [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] The Gregori family's lawyer, Nicodemo Gentile, has argued that the two cases should not be merged and that Mirella's disappearance was a local matter. Investigative attention in her case has turned to the bar on Via Volturno, run by the parents of the friend who last saw her, and to memoranda that another lawyer and a criminologist sent to the parliamentary commission in December 2025 on a police sketch and on a pattern of minors who went missing in Rome in May and June 1983. [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025] None of those lines has produced a charge.

Emanuela Orlandi, 22 June 1983

Emanuela Orlandi was also fifteen. She lived with her family inside Vatican City. Her father, Ercole Orlandi, was a lay employee of the Prefecture of the Papal Household and a citizen of Vatican City State, as she was. [cite:vt15_cwr_senate] [cite:vt15_npr_reopen] On the afternoon of Wednesday 22 June 1983 she went to her flute lesson at the music school on Piazza Sant'Apollinare, in the centre of Rome. From a public telephone she called home to say that a man had offered her 375,000 lire to hand out publicity for a cosmetics firm at a fashion show. She was last seen at about 7.30 that evening at a bus stop on Corso del Rinascimento, in front of the Senate's seat at Palazzo Madama. Her father reported her missing. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] [cite:vt15_wiki_case]

The family put up about 3,000 posters across Rome on 1 July. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] Two men who called themselves "Pierluigi" and "Mario" telephoned the family in late June, describing a girl called Barbara who sold cosmetics; one of the calls was recorded. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] [cite:vt15_wiki_case]

The pope's appeal and the "Amerikano"

On Sunday 3 July 1983 John Paul II spoke about her at the Angelus. He prayed that Emanuela "possa presto tornare incolume", might soon come home unharmed, and appealed to those responsible. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] It was the first time a pope had spoken publicly of the case, and it changed its character: from then on it was treated in public as a kidnapping. [cite:vt15_wiki_case]

On 5 July a man with an English-speaking accent, whom the press called "l'Americano", telephoned the Vatican press office, claimed to be holding Emanuela, and asked for a direct line to the Vatican. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] The Vatican installed one. On 19 July 1983 it confirmed that it had set up a telephone line for contact with the presumed kidnappers. A tape on which a girl's voice could be heard was released, and a voice on it demanded the release of Mehmet Ali Ağca, the Turkish gunman serving a life sentence for shooting John Paul II in St Peter's Square on 13 May 1981. [cite:vt15_csm_1983] From August 1983 into 1984, written communiqués arrived in the names of a "Turkish Anti-Christian Liberation Front" calling itself Turkesh, of a group calling itself Phoenix, of a "new Muslim organisation" and of the Turkish nationalist Grey Wolves. They repeated the demand for Ağca's release. None of them ever supplied proof that its authors held Emanuela. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] Some of these messages claimed both girls, which is how Mirella Gregori's name entered the Orlandi file. [cite:vt15_wiki_case]

The President of the Republic, Sandro Pertini, appealed for the girls' release on 20 October 1983. On 24 December 1983 John Paul II visited the Orlandi family at home and described the disappearance as a case of international terrorism. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] [cite:vt15_wiki_case] That phrase was the pope's reading of the demands that had been made, not a finding by any investigator. No court has found who made the calls or whether they had anything to do with the girl's disappearance.

Why the case touches the Holy See

Three facts tie the Orlandi case to the Holy See, and none of them is a theory. Emanuela was a citizen of Vatican City State, so her disappearance concerned a sovereign whose territory begins at the edge of Rome ([scene:vt4_holy_see_vs_city|Part Four on the Holy See and the City]). The calls were made to the Vatican and the Vatican answered them, including by installing a line on request. And the pope himself took up the case in public, twice in its first six months. [cite:vt15_csm_1983] [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] Everything else that came to be said about the Vatican's part in the affair, from a mobster's tomb in a basilica to a disputed expense memo, is examined in the next section, where each claim is graded.

The case also lasted. A first Italian investigation was dismissed in 1997, a second ran from 2008 and was archived in 2015, and in 2023 three inquiries opened at once: one by the Vatican's Promoter of Justice, one by Rome's prosecutors and one by a commission of the Italian Parliament. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] [cite:vt15_fq_2015] [cite:vt15_npr_reopen] Those are covered in [scene:vt15_investigations_2023|the third section]. Ercole Orlandi died in 2004 without learning what happened to his daughter. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] Her brother Pietro has led the family's public campaign since, and the family's own statements are reported in this part as theirs.

sections.h: Every Theory, Graded
sections.html:
More than forty years of investigation, journalism and television have produced many explanations of what happened to Emanuela Orlandi. Each of them names people, some living and many dead, and none has been proved in a court. This section takes the major ones in turn and grades each against the documents, using four grades. Documented means a primary record or official statement shows it. Reported means named outlets or witnesses have stated it but it has not been confirmed by a court or an independent record. Speculation means it rests on inference, a single uncorroborated source, or a source a judge has found unreliable. Refuted means a physical search or a document has shown it to be false. A theory can carry two grades: the fact it starts from may be documented while the conclusion drawn from it is speculation. Beside each critical claim, the stated position of the Holy See or of the person concerned is given. No theory below is this volume's finding.

The Ağca exchange and the Grey Wolves

That callers and letter-writers demanded Mehmet Ali Ağca's release in exchange for Emanuela is documented: the Vatican installed a line for them and confirmed it on 19 July 1983, and the demand was repeated in communiqués signed "Turkesh", "Phoenix" and the Grey Wolves into 1984. [cite:vt15_csm_1983] [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] That any of these senders held her is not. None ever produced proof of custody. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] Ağca's own statements have shifted: he first attributed the kidnapping to Bulgarian agents and the Grey Wolves, and years later, in prison, said she was alive in a convent in central Europe. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] In November 2024 the parliamentary commission declined his request, made through his lawyer, to testify. [cite:vt15_crux_nov2024] The family's lawyer complained in 2016 that Rome's prosecutors had not pursued the international-terrorism line and had concentrated on the Magliana gang instead. [cite:vt15_fp_cass2016] Grade: the demand is documented; the claim that the senders held her is speculation.

The Magliana gang and Enrico De Pedis

Enrico De Pedis, known as "Renatino", was a leader of the Banda della Magliana, a Rome criminal organisation. He was shot dead in Campo de' Fiori on 2 February 1990. He was then buried in the crypt of the Basilica of Sant'Apollinare, beside the music school where Emanuela had studied, after the basilica's rector, Monsignor Piero Vergari, wrote that De Pedis had been a benefactor of the poor; Cardinal Ugo Poletti signed the authorisation. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] [cite:vt15_wiki_case] The burial of a gang leader in a basilica is documented and was a scandal in its own right.

The link to Orlandi came later. In 2005 an anonymous caller to a television programme said the answer to the case lay in De Pedis's tomb. [cite:vt15_ap_2012] In 2006 a former gang member said he recognised the voice of the caller "Mario" as one of De Pedis's men, and in 2008 Sabrina Minardi, De Pedis's former girlfriend, told prosecutors that De Pedis had carried out the abduction. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] [cite:vt15_ap_2012] Her account changed over time. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] In April 2012 the Vatican said it had no objection to opening the tomb, and on 14 May 2012 forensic police did so. The casket held one male body. Samples were taken, and about 200 boxes of bones in a nearby ossuary were removed for testing. No trace of Orlandi was found. [cite:vt15_ap_2012] [cite:vt15_aje_2012] [cite:vt15_wiki_case] In October 2015 the judge who archived the investigation, in which Vergari, Minardi and three men linked to De Pedis were among the suspects, found that the evidence had never become coherent enough to support a trial. [cite:vt15_fq_2015] Grade: the burial is documented; the claim that she lay in the tomb is refuted; De Pedis's part in an abduction is reported by witnesses and was found insufficient by a judge.

The Vatican bank and Archbishop Marcinkus

The financial theory holds that the abduction was meant to put pressure on the Vatican over money, in the years when the Vatican bank, the IOR, was entangled in the collapse of Banco Ambrosiano ([scene:vt10_ambrosiano_calvi|Part Ten]). Its specific form rests on witnesses from the same gang. Minardi said in 2008 that the order for the abduction came from Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, then head of the IOR; she did not say why. [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] [cite:vt15_ap_2012] Another former gang member said in 2011 that it was tied to money lost in Banco Ambrosiano. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] The Holy See said Minardi's claim had "extremely doubtful value", and its spokesman, Federico Lombardi, said defamatory accusations without foundation were being spread against a man who had died and could not reply. [cite:vt15_ap_2012] [cite:vt15_ilpost_2013] Marcinkus always denied wrongdoing in the banking scandal. [cite:vt15_ap_2012] Grade: speculation. The IOR's troubles in those years are documented; a connection between them and the girl rests on gang witnesses whose evidence a judge found insufficient for a trial.

Sexual-abuse theories

Several claims allege that Emanuela was a victim of sexual abuse by clergy. In May 2012 the exorcist Gabriele Amorth said she had been abducted for sexual exploitation by people inside the Vatican; he offered no evidence. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] In the Netflix series Vatican Girl (2022) a school friend said that Emanuela had told her, a week before she vanished, that a high-ranking cleric had made advances to her. [cite:vt15_npr_reopen] The friend's account is her own recollection; no investigator has corroborated it or identified the cleric. Grade: reported (the friend's statement) and speculation (any link to the disappearance).

The most serious of these claims touched John Paul II. On 11 April 2023 Pietro Orlandi spent about eight hours with the Vatican's Promoter of Justice, Alessandro Diddi. That evening, on the La7 programme DiMartedì, he played a recording in which a man described as a former mobster alleged that the late pope had gone out at night with monsignors in pursuit of girls. [cite:vt15_cwr_jp2] [cite:vt15_crux_jp2] No evidence or testimony supporting the allegation was offered. [cite:vt15_vn_francis] Andrea Tornielli, editorial director of the Holy See's media, wrote: "Evidence? None. Clues? Least of all." Cardinal Stanisław Dziwisz, John Paul II's secretary, called the claims false from beginning to end. [cite:vt15_crux_jp2] On 16 April 2023, after the Regina Caeli, Pope Francis said John Paul II had been the "object of offensive and unfounded inferences". [cite:vt15_vn_francis] Pietro Orlandi's lawyer, Laura Sgrò, then said he "did not intend to make accusations against any person." [cite:vt15_crux_jp2] Grade: speculation, from an anonymous recorded voice with no corroboration, rejected by the Holy See and not taken up by any prosecutor.

The 2017 expense memo

In September 2017 the journalist Emiliano Fittipaldi published, in La Repubblica and in a new book, a memo said to come from Cardinal Lorenzo Antonetti, then head of the Administration of the Patrimony of the Apostolic See (APSA), addressed to two senior officials of the Secretariat of State, Giovanni Battista Re and Jean-Louis Tauran. It listed about half a billion lire supposedly spent between 1983 and 1997 on Emanuela's upkeep, including a residence in London. The memo is unsigned, on plain paper, with no letterhead or protocol number, and misspells Tauran's first name. Fittipaldi said from the start that he could not verify it. [cite:vt15_crux_2017] The Holy See's spokesman, Greg Burke, called it "false and ridiculous"; Re said he had never seen it; the Secretariat of State said it "firmly denies" its authenticity. [cite:vt15_crux_2017] Grade: the existence of the paper is documented; its authenticity is unproven and denied; its contents are speculation. Descriptions of it as a "five-page dossier" circulate, but this volume found no source that confirms the page count.

The uncle

On 10 July 2023 the La7 news reported 1983 letters between Cardinal Agostino Casaroli, then Secretary of State, and the Orlandi family's Colombian confessor, asking whether Emanuela's elder sister Natalina had suffered unwanted advances from their uncle, Mario Meneguzzi, who has since died. [cite:vt15_crux_uncle] The Holy See said the correspondence showed no breach of the seal of confession. [cite:vt15_cwr_seal] Natalina Orlandi said the advances were verbal, happened in 1978 and ended when she rejected them. The family said Meneguzzi was on holiday outside Rome on 22 June 1983, and Pietro Orlandi said, "The Vatican wants to offload responsibility on my family." [cite:vt15_crux_uncle] [cite:vt15_cwr_seal] Rome's prosecutors have since examined the family among their lines, and searched the uncle's former home in 2024. [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025] Grade: the 1983 correspondence is reported; a link between the uncle and the disappearance is speculation, rejected by the family.

A Vatican cover-up

The broadest theory is that people inside the Vatican knew more than they said. It rests on statements, not on a document of concealment. The 1997 Italian dismissal cited a lack of Vatican cooperation; in April 2012 the prosecutor Giancarlo Capaldo said the Vatican knew the truth and later said two Vatican emissaries had spoken to him of Orlandi as dead; and in 2024 the former head of the Vatican gendarmes confirmed that he had compiled a file on the case in 2012, which he called a "historical reconstruction" with nothing new. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] [cite:vt15_crux_nov2024] The Holy See's position, stated by Lombardi in 2012, is that it "had done everything possible". [cite:vt15_ap_2012] Grade: reported and contested; no document of concealment has been produced.

Read together, the grades say something plain. The documented record of the case is short: two disappearances, the 1983 calls and letters, a pope's appeals, a gangster's burial, and a series of searches that found nothing. Every explanation of why the girls vanished lies beyond that record. That includes the theories that blame the Holy See and those that clear it. [cite:vt15_fq_2015] [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025]

sections.h: The Investigations, 1983 to 2026
sections.html:
Four kinds of inquiry have looked for Emanuela Orlandi and Mirella Gregori: Italian criminal investigations, physical searches of graves and bones, a Vatican investigation, and a commission of the Italian Parliament. This section sets out what each did and what it found, to October 2026. The order matters for the theme of this volume, because jurisdiction runs along the border described in [scene:vt4_holy_see_vs_city|Part Four]: Italian prosecutors could not search Vatican territory or compel Vatican officials, and the Vatican's own prosecutor could not act in Rome. Every search inside Vatican ground was made by Vatican authorities at the family's request.

Rome's prosecutors, 1983 to 2016

The first Italian investigation was dismissed in 1997; the dismissal cited, among other things, a lack of cooperation from the Vatican. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] A second opened in 2008 after Sabrina Minardi's testimony and led to the opening of Enrico De Pedis's tomb on 14 May 2012. [cite:vt15_ap_2012] In April 2012 the prosecutor who had led it, Giancarlo Capaldo, was replaced on the file by Rome's new chief prosecutor, Giuseppe Pignatone. [cite:vt15_wiki_case] Pignatone and two colleagues asked for the case to be archived. On 19 October 2015 the preliminary-investigations judge, Giovanni Giorgianni, agreed, for both Orlandi and Gregori. Six people had been under investigation for complicity in kidnapping and murder: Monsignor Piero Vergari, the former rector of Sant'Apollinare; De Pedis's driver Sergio Virtù; Angelo Cassani; Gianfranco Cerboni; Minardi; and Marco Accetti, a photographer who had claimed a part in the events. The judge found that the mass of material gathered had never become coherent, precise or consistent enough for a trial, that Minardi could not say where a body had been disposed of, and that Accetti was unreliable. [cite:vt15_fq_2015] None of the six was charged; each is entitled to the presumption of innocence. The family appealed. By 6 May 2016 the Court of Cassation had rejected the appeal, and Pietro Orlandi said that no power could stop the truth. [cite:vt15_fp_cass2016] Pignatone later became president of the Vatican City State tribunal. [cite:vt15_tablet_2023]

The bones, 2018 and 2019

In late October 2018 builders renovating Villa Giorgina, the seat of the Apostolic Nunciature to Italy in Rome, found human bones in the basement; the Holy See announced the find on 30 October. Rome's prosecutors had them tested. The remains were male, and carbon dating placed them before 1964; they were neither Orlandi's nor Gregori's. [cite:vt15_tablet_2018] [cite:vt15_lng_2018]

In March 2019 the family received a letter with a photograph of an angel on a tomb in the Teutonic Cemetery inside the Vatican, and the words "Look where the angel is pointing." [cite:vt15_cp_2019] On 27 June 2019 the Vatican's Promoter of Justice, Gian Piero Milano, ordered the two tombs opened, at the family's request. On 11 July 2019, in the presence of the family and its lawyers, workers opened the tombs of Princess Sophie von Hohenlohe, who died in 1836, and Duchess Charlotte Frederica of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, who died in 1840. Both were empty. The interim press director, Alessandro Gisotti, said that "no human remains or funerary urns were found." [cite:vt15_cp_2019] [cite:vt15_crux_2019] Two ossuaries found beneath the floor of the neighbouring Teutonic College were opened from 20 July. On 28 July the Holy See Press Office reported that they held several hundred partly intact skeletal structures and thousands of fragments, and that a morphological analysis led by Professor Giovanni Arcudi dated none of them later than the end of the nineteenth century. The family's lawyer asked for laboratory tests on about 70 fragments; Arcudi did not support the request, and the samples were kept by the Vatican Gendarmerie. [cite:vt15_vn_2019]

The Vatican's inquiry, January 2023

On 9 January 2023 the Holy See said that its Promoter of Justice, Alessandro Diddi, had opened a file on the case, based in part "on the requests made by the family in various places." [cite:vt15_npr_reopen] He and the Gendarmerie planned to re-examine the files and testimony from the day of the disappearance onward. [cite:vt15_tablet_2023] Pietro Orlandi called it a "positive step." [cite:vt15_npr_reopen] Diddi said Francis had given him "maximum freedom of action." [cite:vt15_cwr_jp2] He interviewed people who had worked in the Vatican in 1983 and, about six months later, sent his material to Rome's prosecutors. [cite:vt15_cwr_senate] In March 2024 Francis wrote that an inquiry had been opened at the Vatican "to shed light on the story and bring out the truth." [cite:vt15_crux_mar2024] By June 2024 Pietro Orlandi was calling it "a farce", saying that the witnesses he had suggested had not been called after more than a year. [cite:vt15_crux_jun2024] As of October 2026 this research found no announced result.

Rome's third investigation, from May 2023
