Rome's prosecutors reopened the case in May 2023 under prosecutor Stefano Luciani, with the Carabinieri's investigative unit. [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025] By the end of 2025 they were following three lines: the family, including a 2024 search of the uncle's former home; friends and schoolmates; and a blogger investigated in 2024 over a supposed eyewitness. The Orlandi family rejects the family line. [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025] In December 2025 a woman who had been a classmate at the music school, and who may have been one of the last people to see Emanuela, was registered as a suspect for allegedly giving false information to prosecutors. Registration is not a charge and does not imply involvement in the disappearance. [cite:vt15_ansa_dec2025] [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025] No one had been charged as of October 2026.

The parliamentary commission

On 23 March 2023 the Chamber of Deputies voted 245 to none for a bill to create a commission of inquiry. [cite:vt15_giornale_2023] At a Senate hearing in June 2023, Diddi said that a new commission would be "a pernicious intrusion" on the integrity of the investigations already under way, and a letter from the Secretary of State, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, objected to the way Diddi had been summoned. Diddi later said this was a request to wait, not an absolute no. [cite:vt15_domani_2023] The Senate approved the bill on 9 November 2023 with almost no votes against. [cite:vt15_cwr_senate] It became Law no. 202 of 4 December 2023, in force from 6 January 2024. The law sets up the commission under Article 82 of the Constitution, which gives it the powers and limits of the judicial authority. It runs for the rest of the legislature. Its tasks are to reconstruct both disappearances, to review judicial and journalistic material, to examine conduct that obstructed or delayed the truth, including by asking foreign states for documents, and to report to both chambers. [cite:vt15_law_202] It has 40 members from both chambers. On 14 March 2024 it elected Senator Andrea De Priamo of Fratelli d'Italia as president. [cite:vt15_fp_2024] [cite:vt15_crux_mar2024]

Pietro Orlandi said in April 2024 that the Vatican "didn't want the commission." [cite:vt15_crux_apr2024] The commission's president said in June 2024 that the Foreign Ministry was helping it obtain the 1983 diplomatic correspondence between Italy's ambassador and the Secretariat of State, and that these papers would help dispel portrayals of the Vatican as "absolute evil." [cite:vt15_qn_jun2024] On 21 November 2024 it heard Domenico Giani, head of the Vatican Gendarmerie from 2006 to 2019, who said he had compiled a file in 2012 that contained nothing new and that "I am not a witness to anything"; the family's lawyer replied that the file must have been the product of investigation. [cite:vt15_crux_nov2024] In early 2025 the commission found empty folders on the case in Italy's Central State Archive and asked the Interior Ministry to check where their contents had gone. [cite:vt15_eco_mar2025] Its hearings continued into 2026; at its 76th and 77th sittings, on 29 January and 5 February 2026, it heard a journalist, an author and a witness from 1984, and commissioners said that one witness's hypotheses had no objective confirmation. [cite:vt15_sen_jan2026] [cite:vt15_sen_feb2026] As of October 2026 this research found no final or interim report from the commission.

The family's position

The Orlandi family has never accepted any of the closures. Its stated view, through Pietro Orlandi and the lawyer Laura Sgrò, is that the truth is known inside the Vatican and that the Holy See has not given it the file compiled in 2012 or named the people who met Capaldo, despite requests since 2017. [cite:vt15_crux_nov2024] [cite:vt15_crux_apr2024] On 2 August 2025 Pietro Orlandi said that Pope Leo XIV had not mentioned Emanuela at the Angelus on 22 June, the anniversary, and that no meeting had been arranged; "a single word would have been enough," he said. [cite:vt15_qn_aug2025] The Holy See's stated position is that the search for the truth is "in the interest of the Holy See and the Orlandi family." [cite:vt15_vn_2019]

chapters.label: Part Sixteen
chapters.title: Rome and Zionism I: Herzl to the War, 1904–1945
chapters.intro: Part Sixteen lays out the documents for the first half of the volume's central question, from Theodor Herzl's audiences in Rome in January 1904 to the end of the Second World War. It sets the Holy See's interests in Ottoman and Mandate Palestine, the shrines, the Latin Patriarchate and the Custody, beside each document in turn: Herzl's diary of his meetings with Cardinal Merry del Val and Pius X; Nahum Sokolow's audience with Benedict XV in May 1917, known from Sokolow's own report; the Holy See's reaction to the Balfour Declaration, Benedict XV's allocutions of 1919 and 1921 and Cardinal Gasparri's notes to the League of Nations against the draft Mandate; the Latin Patriarch Barlassina and the 1920s and 1930s; the Secretariat of State's notes of 1943, including Archbishop Cicognani's letter to the United States government of 22 June 1943; and the note Pius XII is claimed to have written in 1944 in favour of a homeland. Each document is given with its date, author, content, where it is held or published, and how strong it is, and the part ends by setting the refusal record against the evidence offered for a front.
chapters.outro: Part Sixteen has set out the record from 1904 to 1945, and on the private-record test it runs one way. Herzl's own diary records Pius X's "Non possumus" and a refusal tied to Jerusalem and the shrines. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] The one exhibit for private warmth, Sokolow's audience of May 1917, rests on Sokolow's report, while Minerbi's archival account gives the pope's conditions as the protection of the holy places, to be settled "between the Church and the Great Powers." [cite:vt16_ej_minerbi] [cite:vt16_wiki_sokolow] From December 1917 the written record is opposition: Benedict XV's allocution of 10 March 1919 against a "position of privilege and preponderance" in Palestine, his allocution of 1921, and Gasparri's notes to the League in 1922, which failed when the Mandate was approved on 24 July 1922. [cite:vt16_va_1919] [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] [cite:vt16_un_mandate] The private papers of 1943, published by the Holy See itself, are harder than its public line: Maglione, Tardini and Cicognani's letter of 22 June 1943 all opposed a Jewish home in Palestine, while the same letter recorded the Holy See's help for interned Jewish children. [cite:vt16_jta1976] [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] The 1944 note said to favour a homeland remains unverified. [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit] The record of the war ends with Moshe Shertok leaving his audience of April 1945 without the support he sought; [scene:vt17_jerusalem_1947_49|Part Seventeen] takes up what the Holy See did when the United Nations divided Palestine in 1947 and Israel declared its independence.

sections.h: Herzl in Rome, January 1904
sections.html:
The record of the Holy See and Zionism begins with two conversations in Rome in January 1904, and both are known from one side only. Theodor Herzl, founder of the Zionist Organization, came to the Vatican to ask for support, or at least for the absence of opposition, at a time when the Holy See held no territory of its own and the popes had not left the Vatican since 1870. [scene:vt2_roman_question|Part Two] explains that position. [cite:vt2_wiki_prisoner] Palestine was an Ottoman province, and the interests the Holy See had there were old, specific and written down. This section sets out those interests, the two conversations as Herzl recorded them, and what the record can and cannot carry.

What Rome had in Palestine before Herzl

The Latin presence in Ottoman Palestine had three parts. The oldest was the Custody of the Holy Land, a Franciscan body founded in the fourteenth century that had long been the main Latin representative at the shrines. The second was the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem, re-established in 1847, in the historian Paolo Zanini's words, "to counter the influence of an Anglican-Lutheran diocese", which gave the Holy See a bishop in Jerusalem answering directly to Rome. The third was a foreign protector: "France had protected the Latin and Eastern Catholic communities since the sixteenth century." [cite:vt16_zanini_jq] The legal status of the Christian holy sites in Jerusalem was part of the wider Eastern Question that the European powers argued over throughout the nineteenth century. [cite:vt16_zanini_jq] The Ottoman background is set out in [scene:rd1_ottoman|Road to 1948].

Sergio Minerbi, whose English-language study was written from unpublished diplomatic archives, describes the Holy See before 1914 as balancing Ottoman rulers, rival Christian churches and the Catholic powers that claimed to protect the holy places. [cite:vt16_minerbi_book] Those were the interests in play when a Zionist leader asked for an audience: who held the shrines, who protected Catholic institutions, and who would govern Jerusalem.

The two conversations

Herzl's audience with Pius X was arranged by Count Berthold Dominik Lippay, an Austrian papal portrait painter whom Herzl had met in Venice. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] Before it, according to Minerbi, Herzl put his proposal to the Cardinal Secretary of State, Rafael Merry del Val, on 22 January 1904: the holy places would be given extraterritorial status. Merry del Val replied that the holy places could not be separated from the Holy Land. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] The audience with the pope followed on 25 January. [cite:dv1_ej_piusx] Herzl's diary entry dated 26 January 1904 opens "Yesterday I was with the Pope", and an editor's note gives the audience as about twenty-five minutes. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl]

In Herzl's account, he "recited my little piece about extraterritorialization, res sacrae extra commercium", the idea that sacred things should stand outside ordinary commerce and sovereignty. The pope's first answer was political: "We cannot give approval to this movement. We cannot prevent the Jews from going to Jerusalem—but we could never sanction it." When Herzl said "We are not asking for Jerusalem, but for Palestine—only the secular land", the pope answered "We cannot be in favor of it." [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] On the city itself Herzl recorded the pope as saying that "The soil of Jerusalem, if it was not always sacred, has been sanctified by the life of Jesus Christ", and that Jerusalem "must not get into the hands of the Jews." [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl]

The second answer was theological. Herzl recorded the pope as saying that "The Jewish religion was the foundation of our own; but it was superseded by the teachings of Christ", and that "The Jews have not recognized our Lord, therefore we cannot recognize the Jewish people." He closed with "Non possumus", the formula of papal refusal, and said that if settlers came to Palestine "we shall have churches and priests ready to baptize all of you." [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] Herzl also noted that Lippay knelt and kissed the pope's hand and had told him to do the same, and that he did not. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl]

Where the record is held, and how strong it is

The diary is Herzl's own, written the day after the audience and published in English in 1960 in Raphael Patai's English edition of the complete diaries, where the entry runs to pages 1601–1605. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] It is a primary document of what Herzl wrote. As evidence of what Pius X said, it is one party's account of a private conversation, and the reference works that report the audience say that it rests on Herzl's diaries. [cite:dv1_ej_piusx] The Merry del Val meeting is reported by Minerbi from his research; the volume has not seen a Holy See minute of either conversation. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] What strengthens the diary is that nothing in it flatters its author: Herzl recorded a refusal, not a success, and the refusal matches the line Merry del Val took three days earlier and the line the Holy See took in writing in the decades that followed (see [scene:vt16_benedict_mandate|the next section]).

Two refusals in one audience

The audience fused two different claims, and keeping them apart is the first discipline of this part. One was a political judgment about a movement and about who should govern Jerusalem and the shrines. The other was a theological statement about the Jewish people. The political judgment had a long life: it reappears in the Holy See's written diplomacy from 1917 to 1949, always tied to the holy places, the rights of Catholic institutions and the Catholic communities of Palestine. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] The theological statement did not last in that form. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate of 1965 and the Holy See's 1985 Notes separated the Church's teaching on the Jewish people from its position on a state, the latter saying that Israel's existence and political options were to be seen "not in a perspective which is in itself religious" but by "the common principles of international law." [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] [scene:vt17_nostra_aetate_notes|Part Seventeen] follows that change. This volume does not read the 1904 theology as the Holy See's teaching today, and it does not read the Holy See's later political position on Israel as a judgment about Jews.

Minerbi's reading of the period is blunter than the documents alone require. His publisher's summary says the Holy See preferred British rule to a Jewish state and that its opposition drew both on theological doctrines about Judaism and on Christian antisemitism of the time. [cite:vt16_minerbi_book] The second half of that reading is an interpretation of motive by a named historian; the first half is visible in the documents set out in the next two sections. Other studies used in this part are Andrej Kreutz's Vatican Policy on the Palestinian-Israeli Conflict (1990), Silvio Ferrari's study of the Vatican and Israel from the Second World War to the Gulf War (1991), and, for the Israeli side after 1948, Uri Bialer's Cross on the Star of David (2005), built on declassified Israeli files. [cite:vt16_kreutz] [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] [cite:vt16_bialer]

What 1904 contributes to the front test

Measured against the tests set out in [scene:vt1_front_test|Part One], the 1904 record is the first entry on the side of a real refusal. The private conversation, as recorded by the man who had every reason to report success, matched the public position; nothing passed from the Holy See to the movement; and the refusal cost Herzl the support he had come to ask for. It is also a thin record: one diary and one historian's archival summary. Its weight lies in how closely the later documents, written by different officials for different audiences over forty years, repeat its political half. Those documents begin with the next Zionist envoy to Rome, Nahum Sokolow, in the spring of 1917. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] [cite:vt16_ej_vatican]

sections.h: Benedict XV, Balfour and the Mandate, 1917–1939
sections.html:
Between 1917 and 1922 the future of Palestine was decided by the war, by British policy and by the League of Nations, and the Holy See tried to influence each stage. This is the period that supplies both the strongest exhibit for the view that the refusal was a front, a friendly papal audience given to a Zionist envoy in May 1917, and the densest run of written opposition: a cardinal's warnings after the Balfour Declaration, two papal allocutions, and notes to the League against the draft Mandate. Each document is set out below with its date, author, content, where it is held or published, and how strong it is.

Sokolow's audience, May 1917

Nahum Sokolow, a journalist and a leader of the World Zionist Organization, came to Rome in the spring of 1917 to win support for Zionist aims in Palestine. [cite:vt16_wiki_sokolow] According to Minerbi, he met Monsignor Eugenio Pacelli, the future Pius XII, on 29 April, Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Gasparri on 1 May, and Benedict XV on 4 May. [cite:vt16_ej_minerbi] Other accounts date the papal audience to 6 May and give it forty-five minutes; they describe Pacelli as receiving Sokolow "in a friendly mood" and offering to put his case to the pope. [cite:vt16_wiki_bxvj] The dates differ by two days, and this volume gives both.

What the pope said is known from the Zionist side. Sokolow wrote a report on his reception dated 12 May 1917; the Pave the Way Foundation, which published extracts in 2012, cites it from file A 18/25 of the Yad Vashem archive, and the accounts that describe Pacelli's warmth rest on Sokolow's report to the Zionist Executive. [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit] [cite:vt16_wiki_bxvj] In the version most often quoted, the pope called the return to Palestine "providential; God has willed it", and Sokolow reported an "expression of favour" to Chaim Weizmann. [cite:vt16_wiki_sokolow] Minerbi, working from the diplomatic archives, gives the pope's words differently: "The problem of the holy places is of extraordinary importance for us. The sacred rights must be protected", and "We will settle this between the Church and the Great Powers. You must respect those rights to their full extent." In Minerbi's account Gasparri had asked for a "reserved zone" covering Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Nazareth, Tiberias and Jericho. [cite:vt16_ej_minerbi]

The audience was real and it was cordial; both readings agree on that. What it meant is disputed. Weizmann told a Zionist conference in London on 20 May 1917 that the Church would "favor the establishment of a Jewish National Home in Palestine"; Minerbi calls that claim far from the truth. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] On the record available, the 1917 audience is one party's report of private warmth, and the Holy See's own conditions as Minerbi reports them were territorial: a protected zone for the shrines and a settlement made with the Great Powers rather than with the movement. Grade: documented that the audience took place; the warmth is reported by one party; the pope's words are disputed.

After the Balfour Declaration

Arthur Balfour's letter of 2 November 1917 to Lord Rothschild committed the British government to a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. [cite:wb_ra_balfour] [scene:rd2_addressee|Road to 1948] explains why the letter went to that address. The Holy See's response, as Minerbi reconstructs it from diplomatic reports, came within weeks. In December 1917 Gasparri told a Belgian diplomat that a Jewish state "would not only endanger the Holy Places and injure the feelings of all Christians". On 28 December Benedict XV told the British representative that he feared Palestine might be handed to "the Jews to the detriment of the Christian interests." [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] The Holy See was excluded from the Paris Peace Conference, and in 1919 Gasparri said that "The danger that we most fear is the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine." [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] Grade: reported by a named historian from foreign diplomats' records; the texts were not seen by this volume.

The allocutions of 1919 and 1921

The first public statement is a primary document published by the Holy See. On 10 March 1919 Benedict XV addressed the cardinals in a secret consistory in the allocution Antequam ordinem. He said that the Holy Land had returned to Christian hands, that he was anxious about what the Peace Conference would decide, and that it would be a grave sorrow to him and to all Christians "se gl'infedeli venissero a trovarsi in Palestina in una posizione di privilegio e di preponderanza" ("if unbelievers were to find themselves in Palestine in a position of privilege and preponderance"), all the more if the shrines were entrusted to non-Christians. [cite:vt16_va_1919] The text says "unbelievers", not Zionists or Jews; Minerbi reads it, in its context, as aimed at Jewish rule over the holy places. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican]

The second allocution, of 13 June 1921, followed the violence in Jaffa on 1 May 1921, which the Vatican newspaper L'Osservatore Romano blamed on Zionism and Bolshevism. In it, according to Minerbi, Benedict XV said that Jews had been given a "position of preponderance and privilege in Palestine." [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] The Holy See's own summary of that allocution, written in 1943, adds the other half: the pope "did not want to interfere with any rights of the Jewish people." [cite:vt16_cicognani1943b] That is the Holy See's stated position for the whole period: no objection to Jewish life in Palestine, and objection to a political order in which a Zionist body held privileges over the Catholic and other Christian communities. Grade: 1919 primary text; 1921 reported by Minerbi and summarized by the Holy See itself.

The Mandate, 1922

The draft Mandate for Palestine gave Britain responsibility for putting the Balfour Declaration into effect and provided that "An appropriate Jewish agency shall be recognised as a public body for the purpose of advising and co-operating" with the administration; the final text kept both provisions. [cite:vt16_un_mandate] The Holy See sent written objections to the League. Minerbi dates a note from Gasparri to 15 May 1922; it opposed "the Jews being given a privileged and preponderant position in Palestine vis-à-vis the Catholics" and opposed the recognition of the Jewish Agency. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] The Holy See's own later account names two documents with different dates: "a letter from Cardinal Gasparri under date of March 6, 1922" and "an 'Aide Memoire' to the Council of the League of Nations on June 4, 1922." [cite:vt16_cicognani1943b] The three dates may describe three documents or may reflect different datings of the same exchange; the texts themselves were not available to this volume, and the discrepancy is recorded as open.

The objections did not change the outcome. The League Council approved the Mandate on 24 July 1922; its Article 13 gave the Mandatory "All responsibility in connection with the Holy Places", and Article 14 provided for a special commission on "the rights and claims in connection with the Holy Places." [cite:vt16_un_mandate] Minerbi records that the Holy See then accepted the Mandate as the lesser evil. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] For the front test this is the clearest early case of opposition that spent influence: written notes to an international body against a text the Zionist Organization wanted, at the moment it was being drafted.

The Latin Patriarch and the 1920s–1930s

In Jerusalem the Latin Patriarch, Luigi Barlassina, went further than Rome. His pastoral letter of 20 July 1920 said: "Let Palestine be internationalized rather than someday be the servant of Zionism." [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] Zanini describes Barlassina and most of the patriarchal clergy as showing "radical opposition to Zionism and their open support for the Arab cause", and his relations with the British authorities as strained from the start. Urban Catholic elites helped promote the Muslim-Christian Associations of the early 1920s, which opposed a Jewish national home. [cite:vt16_zanini_jq] The first of those associations was founded in Jaffa on 8 May 1918; its statement of November 1918 declared that "Palestine was an Arab country." [cite:vt16_wiki_mca] Those are the acts of a patriarch and of local Arab Christian and Muslim notables, not of the Holy See.

Rome restrained its patriarch. A deputy acceptable to the British was appointed in 1924, and in February 1929 Valerio Valeri became Apostolic Delegate with instructions to act as the link to the British and to rein Barlassina in. Zanini notes that Valeri did not share antisemitic stereotypes but held that Catholic and Zionist aims were opposed; in the 1930s the Holy See kept away from Arab nationalist initiatives and worked to improve relations with the Mandate government. [cite:vt16_zanini_jq] Its public line stayed critical. After the violence of August 1929 L'Osservatore Romano blamed "the politics of Zionism"; on 6 August 1937 a Vatican verbal note objected to the Peel Commission's partition plan; in October 1938 the paper wrote that "only one of the two races" could live in Palestine; and it welcomed the British White Paper of May 1939. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] Zanini adds that the Holy See's answer to Peel was to try to keep as many sanctuaries as possible under the Mandate. [cite:vt16_zanini_jq]

Read against the front test, the period between the wars gives one exhibit for private warmth, the 1917 audience as Sokolow reported it, and a long run of written opposition that cost the Holy See something: it lobbied the League, lost, and accepted the result. The same years show that the Holy See and its own patriarch did not always want the same thing, a reminder that "Rome" is not a single voice even inside its own hierarchy. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] [cite:vt16_zanini_jq]

sections.h: The War Years: Pius XII and the 1943 Notes
sections.html:
The Second World War produced the fullest written statement of the Holy See's position on a Jewish homeland before 1948, and it was written in private, to governments, not in public. The documents were published by the Holy See itself thirty years later, and one of them circulates in full. They are the most important test of the front hypothesis for the period before Israel's independence, because they are exactly the kind of record the hypothesis predicts should contradict the public line. This section sets them out, then grades the one document offered for the opposite view: a note said to have been written by Pius XII in 1944.

What Pius XII knew of the destruction of European Jewry, what he said and did not say, and what the files opened on 2 March 2020 have added are treated in [scene:vt14_pius_files|Part Fourteen] and are not repeated here. This section keeps to a narrower question: what the Holy See said, in its own papers, about Zionism and a Jewish state in Palestine. The two questions must be kept apart. The same files that record the Holy See's opposition to a Jewish home in Palestine also record its interventions for persecuted Jews, and neither set settles the other.

Tardini and Maglione, spring 1943

The internal record of 1943 begins with Monsignor Domenico Tardini of the Secretariat of State, who wrote in March 1943 that the Holy See "has never approved the project of making Palestine a Jewish home." [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] In May 1943 Cardinal Luigi Maglione, Secretary of State, wrote to Archbishop Amleto Cicognani, the Apostolic Delegate in Washington, on the question. According to the extracts reported when the volume was published, Maglione wrote: "If Palestine fell under the rule of the Jews, it would give birth to new and grave international problems", and asked "how can you historically justify a criterion of bringing people back to those territories." [cite:vt16_jta1976] Minerbi adds that Maglione suggested other territories would better serve as a "Jewish Home" and wrote that Catholics "would be wounded in their religious sentiments" if Palestine became exclusively Jewish. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican]

The same line went to London. Maglione told Monsignor William Godfrey, the papal representative in Britain: "The Holy See has never approved the plan to make Palestine a Jewish homeland." [cite:vt16_jta1976] From Istanbul, the Apostolic Delegate to Turkey, Angelo Roncalli, later Pope John XXIII, wrote to Maglione that "the reconstruction of the Kingdom of Judah and of Israel is only a utopia." [cite:vt16_jta1976]

These letters are held in the Holy See's archives and were published in the multi-volume edition of wartime documents, Actes et documents du Saint Siège relatifs à la Seconde Guerre mondiale, prepared by four Jesuit historians under a mandate from Paul VI and issued between 1965 and 1981. [cite:vt1_wiki_adss] The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported the extracts on 26 January 1976, days after the volume on the Holy See and the victims of the war for January to December 1943 was made public. [cite:vt16_jta1976] Grade: primary documents, published by the Holy See; the selection was made by the Holy See's editors, whose completeness critics have questioned and whose editor said they "did not deliberately overlook any significant document." [cite:vt1_wiki_adss]

Cicognani to Myron Taylor, 22 June 1943

The document that put the position before a government survives in full. On 22 June 1943 Cicognani wrote to Myron C. Taylor, President Roosevelt's personal representative to Pius XII, as letter no. 219/43, following "our conversation of a few days back." The text now circulates through the Simon Wiesenthal Center. [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] It covers two subjects, and the order matters. It first records that "The aid of the Holy See has recently been enlisted" for "Jewish youths and infants interned in Slovackia" (the spelling of the transcription). [cite:vt16_cicognani1943b] It then turns to Palestine.

On Palestine the letter argues from religion, from history and from international order. "Catholics the world over are piously devoted to this country", it says, and "If the greater part of Palestine is given to the Jewish people, this would be a severe blow to the religious attachment of Catholics to this land." [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] [cite:vt16_cicognani1943b] It warns that "grave new, international problems would arise." [cite:vt16_cicognani1943b] It concedes that "at one time Palestine was inhabited by the Hebrew Race", but holds there is "no axiom in history to substantiate the necessity of a people returning to a country they left nineteen centuries before." [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] It proposes an alternative: "If a 'Hebrew Home' is desired, it would not be too difficult to find a more fitting territory than Palestine." [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] On the shrines it says that "Catholics rejoice in certain rights regarding these places" and that "Repeated formal assurances that these rights will be respected are ever necessary." [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] It traces this line back through the Holy See's own record: Benedict XV in 1919 and 1921, who "did not want to interfere with any rights of the Jewish people", Gasparri's letter of 6 March 1922 and the aide-mémoire to the League of 4 June 1922. [cite:vt16_cicognani1943b]

Three things about this letter bear on the front test. It was private, addressed to a government that could not be swayed by a public stance, and it is harder than anything the Holy See said in public in those years. It is continuous with the record of 1917 to 1922, which it cites as its own precedent. And it separates the two subjects that the 1904 audience had fused: help for persecuted Jews was one question, a Jewish political home in Palestine another, and the letter answers them differently. The Holy See's stated position in the letter is that its concern was the rights and religious attachment of Catholics in the Holy Land and the risk of new international conflict. Grade: primary.

Shertok's audience, April 1945

The last contact of the war years is again reported from the Zionist side. On 10 April 1945 Moshe Shertok of the Zionist leadership in Palestine was received by Pius XII and asked for the Church's "moral support" for the Jewish community in Palestine. Minerbi records that he received none, and that the Holy See's effort went instead toward an international status for Jerusalem. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] That effort, and the encyclicals of 1948 and 1949, are the subject of [scene:vt17_jerusalem_1947_49|Part Seventeen]. Grade: reported by a named historian.

The claimed 1944 note

The only document offered for private papal support of a Jewish homeland in this period is a note said to have been written by Pius XII in 1944. It was announced on 8 March 2012 by the Pave the Way Foundation, a New York organization led by Gary Krupp that has published tens of thousands of pages of research on Pius XII's record, through the Catholic news agency Zenit. In the Foundation's account, Tardini warned the pope against helping Jews establish a homeland and Pius XII replied in his own hand: "The Jews need a land of their own." [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit] The Foundation said the note was unpublished, held in "the closed section of the Vatican Library", and that it had "learned of the existence" of the document; it gave no image, no transcription and no archival reference. [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit]

The same release made other claims: that Pacelli asked the German government on 15 November 1917 to protect the Jewish community of Palestine "even with the use of arms"; that he met Sokolow again on 15 February 1925; that he urged Catholics in 1926 to join a German pro-Palestine committee; and that the Vatican encouraged Spain to recognize Israel in 1955. The release names no source for the 1926 and 1955 claims. [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit] The 1917 intervention, if documented, concerns the physical protection of a community in wartime and is not evidence of support for a state.

The 1944 note is graded here as unverified. The papers of Pius XII's pontificate have been open to researchers since 2 March 2020, and a search made in October 2026 found no publication, image or catalogue reference for such a note in the reporting since then. [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit] [cite:vt14_vn_open2020] Holy See papers of this kind would sit in the Apostolic Archive or the Secretariat of State's historical archive, not the Library, two institutions that [scene:vt14_apostolic_archive|Part Fourteen] distinguishes. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] If the note exists and says what the Foundation reports, it would show that Pius XII held a private view different from his Secretariat of State's in one year. It would still stand against the documented letters of 1943, written in his name by his Secretary of State and his delegate, and against the Holy See's policy from 1945 to 1949.

On the first of the five tests, the private record, the years from 1904 to 1945 come out against a front. The private documents that are primary and published match the public line, and in 1943 they are harder than it. The two items that point the other way are a Zionist envoy's report of a cordial audience in 1917, which the Holy See's own conditions as Minerbi reports them do not support, and an unpublished note known only from an advocacy foundation's announcement. Neither shows money, favours or diplomatic help passing from the Holy See to the movement. The final weighing is left to [scene:vt19_predictions_tested|Part Nineteen].

chapters.label: Part Seventeen
chapters.title: Rome and Zionism II: Non-Recognition to Recognition, 1945–1993
chapters.intro: Part Seventeen follows the Holy See's position on Zionism and Israel from the end of the Second World War to recognition in 1993. The first section covers the years of partition and war, when Pius XII asked in three encyclicals for an internationalised Jerusalem, founded a relief mission for Palestinian refugees and declined to recognise the new state, and reports what the private record, including the Pius XII files opened in 2020, has so far shown. The second follows two tracks that ran side by side for three decades: the Holy See's teaching on the Jewish people, transformed by Nostra Aetate in 1965 and the documents that followed, and its diplomacy toward the State of Israel, which named the state for the first time only in 1984 and declared in 1985 that it was to be judged by international law, not theology. The third reads the Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993 article by article and tests whether the timing of each change tracked Israeli pressure, Arab and Palestinian sensitivities, or the Holy See's own stated interests.
chapters.outro: Part Seventeen established that the Holy See's refusal to recognise Israel from 1948 to 1993 was stated in public, pursued at a cost to Israel's position and grounded in reasons the Holy See named: an international Jerusalem, sought in the encyclicals of 1948 and 1949 and replaced in 1967 by a call for an internationally guaranteed statute, the refugees, to whom its one material commitment of those years went, and the legal security of Catholic communities. [cite:vt17_va_imc1948] [cite:dv1_rnc_1949] [cite:vt17_cnewa_pmp] [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] The one private record available for 1948–49 shows the Holy See declining to turn that aim into a Catholic political project, and the first study of the Pius XII files on Palestine has yet to be weighed. [cite:vt17_ewtn_irishfiles] [cite:vt17_berghahn_rioli] Its teaching on the Jewish people changed on a separate track: Nostra Aetate rejected the deicide charge in 1965, and the 1985 Notes placed the state under "the common principles of international law." [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] Recognition came after Madrid and after the Israel–PLO recognition of September 1993, in a treaty that secured the Church's institutions and, in Article 11, kept the Holy See "a stranger to all merely temporal conflicts" over "disputed territories and unsettled borders." [cite:vt17_state_madrid] [cite:vt17_jcpa_schvindlerman] [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] Part Eighteen follows the relationship from 1994 through the recognition of the State of Palestine and the Gaza war to October 2026. [scene:vt18_relations_since_1994|Part Eighteen: Israel, Palestine and Gaza, 1994–2026]

sections.h: Jerusalem First: Partition, the Encyclicals and the Refugees, 1947–1958
sections.html:
When the United Nations took up the future of Palestine in 1947, the Holy See had no vote and no seat. It was not a member of the organisation and would not become a permanent observer until 6 April 1964. [cite:dv1_wiki_holysee_un] What it had was a stated interest older than the Zionist movement: the holy places of Christianity, above all in Jerusalem, and the Catholic communities and institutions around them. The record of the years from partition to the death of Pius XII in October 1958 shows that interest expressed in public, in three encyclicals and a relief mission, and, so far as the private papers have yet been read, pursued in private with more caution than force. This section sets out what the Holy See asked for, what it got, and what the private record has added.

Partition and the corpus separatum

The General Assembly adopted resolution 181 on 29 November 1947 by 33 votes to 13, with 10 abstentions. [cite:vt17_audit_wiki_partition] It recommended an Arab state and a Jewish state and, between them, a third unit: Jerusalem and its surroundings were to be a corpus separatum, a "separate body" under a special international regime administered by the United Nations. [cite:vt1_wiki_corpus] The Holy See supported internationalisation, and accounts of the period credit its diplomacy with helping to keep an international status for Jerusalem inside the partition plan. [cite:vt1_wiki_corpus] [cite:vt17_wiki_hsisrael] Israel's later ambassador to the Holy See, Zion Evrony, summarised the same record from the other side: the Holy See had objected to the partition resolution "on the basis of theological reasons and practical interests." [cite:vt17_evrony_menorah] The two readings are compatible. The Holy See did not want Jerusalem under either new state, and the corpus separatum was the part of the plan that met that aim.

Whether the Holy See went further and pressed Catholic-majority delegations to vote against partition has been asserted and denied, and the documents to settle it have not been published in a form this volume could check. The Latin American bloc was the largest group of Catholic-majority states at the Assembly; twelve or thirteen of them (depending on whether Haiti is counted) voted for partition, six abstained and Cuba voted against. [cite:vt17_tenembaum_sneh] One account, by Baruch Tenembaum of the International Raoul Wallenberg Foundation, says that Moshe Shertok of the Jewish Agency feared the Holy See would turn those delegations against partition, and that the Agency's Moshe Sneh was received on 3 October 1947 by Domenico Tardini, a senior official of the Secretariat of State, in a meeting arranged by the nuncio in Paris, Angelo Roncalli. Tardini, the account says, "did not make any promises." [cite:vt17_tenembaum_sneh] The account cites no archive and rests on later recollections, so it is reported here as disputed. What the vote itself shows is that most Catholic-majority delegations supported partition, which is not what a successful campaign against it would have produced. Whether there was an unsuccessful one, or none, remains open (GAPS: the nunciature papers for 1947 and the Foreign Relations of the United States volumes for that autumn are the places to look).

Three encyclicals

The war that followed partition brought the Holy See's position into public teaching. Pius XII's encyclical Auspicia quaedam of 1 May 1948, two weeks before Israel declared independence, asked for prayers for peace and expressed concern for the holy places. [cite:vt17_wiki_hsisrael] On the day of the declaration, 14 May 1948, the Holy See's newspaper L'Osservatore Romano wrote that "Modern Zionism is not the true heir of Biblical Israel", a line that treated the new state as a political fact rather than a religious one. [cite:vt17_jcpa_schvindlerman] That distinction between theology and politics would become the Holy See's formal position in 1985.

The second encyclical, In multiplicibus curis of 24 October 1948, was devoted to the war. Palestine, it said, "occupies a particular place on account of the war which harasses it"; "thousands of refugees, homeless and driven, wander from their fatherland in search of shelter and food." [cite:vt17_va_imc1948] It lamented damage to churches and charitable buildings around the holy places, and it asked those negotiating peace to give Jerusalem and its surroundings "an international character which, in the present circumstances, seems to offer a better guarantee" for the shrines, with free access to the holy places throughout Palestine assured "with international guarantees." [cite:vt17_va_imc1948] The text named no state. It spoke of the refugees without saying who had driven them out.

The third, Redemptoris nostri cruciatus of 15 April 1949, went further. It asked that Jerusalem and its vicinity be "accorded and legally guaranteed an 'international' status", urged Catholics to press their own governments by legitimate means for that juridical status, and asked that the other holy places in Palestine be protected by international guarantee, with the rights Catholics had acquired over the centuries preserved. [cite:dv1_rnc_1949] It is the only one of the three that told Catholics to act politically, and it is the clearest public statement of the Holy See's aim in these years: an internationalised Jerusalem, not a Christian or papal one, and the security of Catholic institutions under whichever authority emerged.

On 9 December 1949 the General Assembly adopted resolution 303, restating its intention that Jerusalem "be placed under a permanent international regime" as a corpus separatum, with the Trusteeship Council as the administering authority. [cite:vt17_frus_res303] The vote was 38 to 14 with 7 abstentions. The Arab and Muslim states voted for it, having opposed partition in 1947; so did the Soviet bloc, France, Belgium, Australia and several Latin American states; Israel, the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada voted against. [cite:vt17_wiki_res303] Israel declared Jerusalem its capital that month while holding only the western city; Jordan held the east, including the Old City. [cite:vt17_wiki_res303] The resolution was never implemented. [cite:vt1_wiki_corpus] Israel's foreign ministry says the Vatican "orchestrated" a further, unsuccessful attempt at internationalisation at the United Nations in 1950. [cite:vt17_mfa_relations]

The Pontifical Mission for Palestine

The refugees named in the 1948 encyclical became the object of the Holy See's one material commitment of these years. In April 1949 Pius XII summoned Monsignor Thomas J. McMahon, national secretary of the Catholic Near East Welfare Association, who had made a fact-finding journey to Palestine the year before, and named him president of a new Pontifical Mission for Palestine. [cite:vt17_cnewa_pmp] The mission, founded that June, was meant to unify the Church's relief among Palestinian refugees and was administered through the Association; it provided food, medical care, housing and training, and acted as the Holy See's liaison with the United Nations agencies. [cite:vt17_wiki_cnewa] [cite:vt17_cnewa_pmp] It was aid, not diplomacy; its beneficiaries were Palestinian Arab refugees, and the Association's own history says that, as "misery did not discriminate among its victims", neither did the mission. [cite:vt17_cnewa_pmp] No document in any source shows a comparable transfer from the Holy See to the new state or to the Zionist movement.

What the private record has shown

The papers of Pius XII's pontificate, opened on 2 March 2020, include the Secretariat of State's files for 1945 to 1958, the years of partition and the encyclicals. [cite:vt14_vn_open2020] The first published study devoted to them on this subject is Maria Chiara Rioli's chapter "Archives in War: The Pius XII Papers and the Israeli–Palestinian Conflict", in a volume edited by Simon Unger-Alvi and Nina Valbousquet and published by Berghahn in 2024. [cite:vt17_berghahn_rioli] Its findings could not be checked for this volume, and nothing is attributed to it here. Rioli's earlier book on the Latin diocese of Jerusalem from 1946 to 1956, based on the archives of the Latin Patriarchate, the Franciscan Custody and the Catholic Near East Welfare Association rather than the Vatican's own, describes a local church left without an active patriarch for about two years after 1947, a Holy See unsure how far to commit to its Palestinian faithful, and a church whose first task was refugees, at times arguing for their return. [cite:vt17_robson_rioli]

One private record from these years is available through another government's files. Irish diplomatic papers released in Dublin and reported in January 2004 show that in December 1948 Spain, citing a remark by Pius XII, proposed that Catholic states seek an international mandate for Jerusalem, and that in April 1949 the Irish, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese ambassadors met at the Vatican on the idea. [cite:vt17_ewtn_irishfiles] The plan was dropped. The Irish files attribute that to "the reluctance of the Vatican to disclose its hand" and to its fear of being "saddled with responsibility" for the city. [cite:vt17_ewtn_irishfiles] Here the private record does not contradict the public one; it shows the Holy See declining to turn its public aim into a Catholic political project.

In the same years the two sides had working contacts without recognition. An Israeli delegation went to the Vatican in September 1948 and reached what Israel's foreign ministry calls "various understandings"; Foreign Minister Moshe Sharett met Pius XII in 1952; and in May 1955 the Israel Philharmonic played for the pope at the Vatican, though the occasion was presented without naming Israel. [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] [cite:vt17_wiki_hsisrael] Contact without recognition was the pattern the next four pontificates kept.

The record of 1947 to 1958, read against the front hypothesis set out in [scene:vt1_front_test|Part One], points one way on the evidence so far published. The Holy See's public demand, an international Jerusalem, was opposed by Israel and lost; its one material commitment went to Arab refugees; and the one private record available shows it holding back rather than working against its public line. The Pius XII files may yet change that picture, and Part Nineteen keeps the question open until Rioli's and later studies can be weighed. [scene:vt19_what_stays_open|Part Nineteen: what stays open]

sections.h: Two Tracks: Nostra Aetate, the Notes and the State Left Unnamed, 1958–1990
sections.html:
Between the death of Pius XII in 1958 and the opening of negotiations with Israel in 1992, the Holy See changed its teaching on the Jewish people more than in any comparable period of its history, while its diplomatic position on the State of Israel moved only by small, dated steps. The two changes ran on separate tracks, and the Holy See said so in writing in 1985. Keeping them apart is the only way to read this period accurately. A reader who treats the end of the deicide charge as recognition of Israel, or the refusal of recognition as a judgment on Jews, mixes two subjects the documents themselves distinguish.

Paul VI in the Holy Land, January 1964

Paul VI was the first pope in modern times to travel to the Holy Land. He flew to Amman on 4 January 1964, where King Hussein received him, and spent most of the three days in the Jordanian-held Old City of Jerusalem and in Bethlehem; there he met the Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras. [cite:vt17_ebsco_paul1964] On 5 January he crossed into Israel at Megiddo, where President Zalman Shazar and Prime Minister Levi Eshkol greeted him, and visited sites in Galilee before returning through the Mandelbaum Gate. [cite:vt17_ebsco_paul1964] [cite:vt17_jta_nissim1963]

The visit to Israel lasted about eleven hours. According to Evrony, the pope did not use the name "Israel" during it, and his telegram of thanks afterwards was addressed to "President Shazar, Tel Aviv", naming neither Israel nor Jerusalem. [cite:vt17_evrony_menorah] Official Vatican statements spoke of "the Holy Land." [cite:vt17_wiki_hsisrael] Israel's foreign ministry later wrote that the visit made "patently, and painfully, clear that the Holy See did not recognise Israel de jure." [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] Israel's Chief Rabbi, Yitzhak Nissim, had declined to join the welcome at Megiddo, saying he could take part only "on the basis of reciprocity", meaning a papal call on the Chief Rabbinate. [cite:vt17_jta_nissim1963] The pope had come as a pilgrim; no Holy See document gives a reason for the wording, and the visit was not a diplomatic act.

Nostra Aetate, 28 October 1965

The road to the Second Vatican Council's declaration on the Jews began with a private audience. On 13 June 1960 John XXIII received the French Jewish historian Jules Isaac, whose work on the Christian "teaching of contempt" had moved him, and the task of drafting a text was given to Cardinal Augustin Bea's Secretariat for Christian Unity. [cite:vt17_va_fumagalli] [cite:vt17_rutishauser_scjr] The draft was a statement of Catholic theology written by the Council's own commission; the documented consultations with Jewish scholars and organisations are part of the ordinary history of the text, and the claim that the declaration was "written under Jewish influence" belongs to an antisemitic narrative of infiltration, not to the record.

The text was delayed by politics from outside. In 1962 the World Jewish Congress announced that Dr Chaim Wardi, an official of Israel's Ministry of Religious Affairs, would represent it at the Council. Arab governments protested, Wardi never attended, and the draft on the Jews was taken off the agenda of the first session. [cite:vt17_rutishauser_scjr] [cite:vt17_va_fumagalli] Representatives of Arab states described the draft as "a Zionist conspiracy" and asked that the Council also address Islam. [cite:vt17_rutishauser_scjr] The final text became a declaration on all non-Christian religions, with Judaism treated in its fourth paragraph. It was adopted on 28 October 1965 by 2,221 votes to 88. [cite:vt17_va_fumagalli] [cite:vt17_rutishauser_scjr]

Paragraph 4 said that "God holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers." [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] It addressed the oldest charge in the Christian repertoire against Jews, the claim that "the Jews" as a people were guilty of killing Christ, known as the deicide charge, and rejected it: what happened in the Passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today." [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] Jews were not to be presented "as rejected or accursed by God", and the Church decried "displays of anti-Semitism, directed against Jews at any time and by anyone." [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] The declaration repudiated the charge of collective and permanent responsibility for the death of Christ. [cite:vt17_va_fumagalli] It said nothing about the land, Zionism or the State of Israel. Pius X's reply to Herzl in 1904 had joined the two subjects ("The Jews have not recognized our Lord, therefore we cannot recognize the Jewish people"); Nostra Aetate changed the teaching on the people and left the state untouched. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] [scene:vt16_herzl_1904|Part Sixteen: Herzl and Pius X]

The diplomatic track moved after the Six-Day War. Once Israel held the whole of Jerusalem, Paul VI in December 1967 replaced the call for internationalisation with a call for a "special statute, internationally guaranteed" for the city and its holy places. [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] [cite:vt1_wiki_corpus] Contacts continued without recognition: Paul VI received Foreign Minister Abba Eban in 1969, Prime Minister Golda Meir on 15 January 1973, the first such audience for an Israeli prime minister, and Moshe Dayan on 12 January 1978. [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] [cite:vt17_wiki_hsisrael]

The Commission and the 1974 Guidelines

On 22 October 1974 Paul VI set up the Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, and placed it beside the Holy See's office for Christian unity (today the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, which still publishes its documents), not in the Secretariat of State that conducts diplomacy. [cite:vt17_va_guidelines1974] The placement matched the subject: relations with Jews were treated as a matter of religion, not of foreign policy. Its first document, the Guidelines and Suggestions for Implementing the Conciliar Declaration Nostra Aetate, dated 1 December 1974 and signed by Cardinal Johannes Willebrands, asked Christians to learn "by what essential traits the Jews define themselves in the light of their own religious experience" and condemned antisemitism as contrary to the spirit of Christianity. [cite:vt17_va_guidelines1974] The Guidelines did not discuss the land or the State of Israel. [cite:vt17_va_guidelines1974]

John Paul II: naming the state, keeping the line

John Paul II's first decade sent signals both ways. On 15 September 1982 he received the PLO chairman Yasser Arafat. Prime Minister Menachem Begin denounced the audience and accused the Vatican of inaction during the Holocaust; an Israeli official said the government was "very disturbed"; the Vatican "angrily rejected Israel's charges." [cite:vt17_csm_arafat1982]

Two years later the pope named the state for the first time in a signed papal document. In the apostolic letter Redemptionis anno of 20 April 1984 he wrote: "For the Jewish people who live in the State of Israel ... we must ask for the desired security and the due tranquility." [cite:vt17_ccjr_redemptionis] [cite:vt17_evrony_menorah] The same letter said the Palestinian people "have the natural right in justice to find once more a homeland", and asked for Jerusalem "a special statute internationally guaranteed so that no party could jeopardize it." [cite:vt17_ccjr_redemptionis] Israel's security and a Palestinian homeland were named in the same letter, and neither naming was a diplomatic act.

The decisive text came from the Commission. Its Notes on the Correct Way to Present the Jews and Judaism in Preaching and Catechesis, with a preface dated 24 June 1985, asked Christians to understand Jews' "religious attachment" to the land, "which finds its roots in biblical tradition", "without however making their own any particular religious interpretation of this relationship." [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] It then drew the line in one sentence: "The existence of the State of Israel and its political options should be envisaged not in a perspective which is in itself religious, but in their reference to the common principles of international law." [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] The Holy See had stated, in an official document, that its view of Israel was a matter of law and politics. That closed the theological route to a hostile reading of the state, and equally closed the route by which a Catholic might read the state as the fulfilment of prophecy, the reading Protestant Christian Zionism adopts. [scene:ts11_churches|The Theology Shield: the churches]

On 13 April 1986 John Paul II became the first pope on record to visit a synagogue, Rome's Great Synagogue, where Chief Rabbi Elio Toaff received him and he called the Jews "our dearly beloved brothers" and "our elder brothers." [cite:vt17_vn_synagogue1986] The next year showed the limits of the new climate. In June 1987 the pope received Austria's president, Kurt Waldheim, whom Jewish organisations accused of participation in Nazi war crimes during his service in the German army. [cite:vt17_csm_castel1987] Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir called it an "unfriendly act" and said that, without relations, Israel "can do nothing but express its unhappiness." [cite:vt17_djn_waldheim] The Vatican replied on 20 June that it received democratically elected heads of state at their request and that the reaction caused it "surprise and profound pain." [cite:vt17_criterion_waldheim] After a meeting with Jewish leaders on 1 September 1987, the Vatican agreed to prepare a document on the Holocaust and to give further consideration to relations with Israel. [cite:vt17_csm_castel1987] In Miami that month the pope spoke of the Jewish people's right to a homeland "as does any civil nation, according to international law." [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] Recognition did not follow for six years.

What the timing shows

The theological changes of 1965, 1974 and 1985 came from the Council and a commission with a religious mandate; none was tied to a diplomatic concession, and each left the state aside. The diplomatic steps followed events on the ground: the 1967 change adjusted the Jerusalem demand to Israel's capture of the eastern city, and the 1984 naming of the state came with a Palestinian right to a homeland. Public Israeli pressure, over Arafat in 1982 and Waldheim in 1987, did not change the Holy See's course. Arab-state pressure appears in the sources used here once, over the Wardi affair, and it delayed the conciliar text without changing its theology. Rabbi David Rosen, who later served on the bilateral commission, wrote that the Holy See had long said there was no theological barrier to relations and that its reluctance was "the consequence of secular political considerations." [cite:vt17_rosen_1994] What those considerations were, and how they were resolved in 1993, is the subject of the next section. [scene:vt17_fundamental_agreement|The Fundamental Agreement]

sections.h: The Fundamental Agreement: Recognition on Terms, 1991–1994
sections.html:
The Holy See recognised the State of Israel in a treaty signed in Jerusalem on 30 December 1993, forty-five years after Israel's independence. The document, the Fundamental Agreement between the Holy See and the State of Israel, is short, legal in tone and explicit about what each side wanted. Read with the dates around it, it is the best single test in this volume of what drove the Holy See's position: Israeli or Zionist pressure, Arab and Palestinian sensitivities, or the Holy See's own doctrine and interests. This section sets out how the negotiation began, what the treaty says, how it was received, and what its timing shows.

From Madrid to the working commission

The reasons the Holy See gave for withholding recognition were political and legal, and by the 1980s it said so openly. Rabbi David Rosen, who later served on the bilateral commission that drafted the treaty, wrote that the Holy See had for years said there was no theological barrier to relations, and that its reluctance was "the consequence of secular political considerations." [cite:vt17_rosen_1994] He listed them: the Catholic Church's communities, institutions and property in Arab and Muslim countries, which it feared would suffer a backlash; the weight of the Arab world in its work across the global South; and the position of the local church, most of whose members identified as Palestinian and whose leadership opposed any advance with Israel "until Palestinian political claims had been satisfied." [cite:vt17_rosen_1994] Israel's foreign ministry gives a similar list: Israel's sovereignty over Jerusalem, the absence of recognised borders, the holy places, the needs of local Catholics, the Palestinian refugees, and the fear of reprisals against Christian minorities in Arab states. [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] When the treaty was signed, the Associated Press summarised the Holy See's long-standing grounds as Israel's treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, church property and the status of Jerusalem. [cite:vt17_ap_fa1993]

The political setting changed after the Gulf War. The Madrid Conference opened on 30 October 1991, co-chaired by Presidents George H. W. Bush and Mikhail Gorbachev, and for the first time brought Israel face to face with Syria, Lebanon, Egypt and a joint Jordanian-Palestinian delegation. [cite:vt17_state_madrid] In April 1992, according to Israel's foreign ministry, John Paul II directed the Curia to open negotiations toward full relations, and Archbishop Tauran informed Ambassador Pazner of the decision about ten days later. [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] The Bilateral Permanent Working Commission agreed its agenda in Jerusalem on 15 July 1992 and confirmed it at the Vatican on 29 July. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] Rosen, from inside the process, described the Holy See's aim as turning into binding law what it already enjoyed in practice under Israeli rule: the legal status of its institutions, freedom of worship, schools, welfare work and tax treatment. [cite:vt17_rosen_1994] The Holy See's spokesman, Joaquín Navarro-Valls, put the change of setting more simply, as Rosen reports him: "The Palestinians are talking with Israelis, why shouldn't we?" [cite:vt17_rosen_1994]

The negotiation took about a year and a half. [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] In the middle of it, on 13 September 1993, Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization signed the Declaration of Principles in Washington, together with letters of mutual recognition. [cite:vt17_state_madrid] [cite:vt17_wiki_oslo1] Julian Schvindlerman of the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs, a pro-Israel institute, read the sequence directly: "Only after the PLO agreed to formally recognize Israel in September 1993 did the Holy See decide to do the same." [cite:vt17_jcpa_schvindlerman] That is his reading of the order of events; the negotiation itself had begun fifteen months before Oslo.

What the treaty says

The agreement was signed at Israel's Foreign Ministry in Jerusalem by Monsignor Claudio Maria Celli, the Holy See's under-secretary for relations with states, and Deputy Foreign Minister Yossi Beilin, in English and Hebrew texts of equal authority. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] [cite:vt17_ap_fa1993] Its preamble records the parties' awareness of "the unique nature of the relationship between the Catholic Church and the Jewish people." [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] Its fifteen articles fall into three groups.

The first group concerns the Church in Israel. Israel affirmed its commitment to freedom of religion and conscience (Article 1); recognised "the right of the Catholic Church to carry out its religious, moral, educational and charitable functions, and to have its own institutions" (Article 3); agreed to "maintain and respect the 'Status quo' in the Christian Holy Places" (Article 4); and the two sides reaffirmed the Church's right to property while listing "unclear, unsettled and disputed issues, concerning property, economic and fiscal matters" for further negotiation (Article 10). [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] These were the institutional interests the Holy See had named since 1948.

The second group concerns the Jewish people. In Article 2 both parties committed themselves to combat "all forms of antisemitism and all kinds of racism and of religious intolerance", and the Holy See reiterated its "condemnation of hatred, persecution and all other manifestations of antisemitism directed against the Jewish people" and deplored "attacks on Jews and desecration of Jewish synagogues and cemeteries." [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] This article carried the theology of Nostra Aetate into a treaty for the first time. [scene:vt17_nostra_aetate_notes|Nostra Aetate and the Notes]

The third group concerns the state and the region, and it is here that the Holy See set its terms. Article 11 reads, in its second paragraph:

"The Holy See, while maintaining in every case the right to exercise its moral and spiritual teaching-office, deems it opportune to recall that, owing to its own character, it is solemnly committed to remaining a stranger to all merely temporal conflicts, which principle applies specifically to disputed territories and unsettled borders." [cite:vt1_va_fa1993]

The clause echoes Article 24 of the Lateran Treaty of 1929, in which the Holy See declared that it would remain extraneous to temporal disputes between states. [cite:vt1_va_lateran] [scene:vt2_pacts_signed|Part Two: the pacts signed] In the 1993 setting it did two things at once. It reserved the Holy See's right to speak on moral grounds, and it stated that recognising Israel did not mean taking a position on the territories Israel had held since 1967 or on its borders. Article 13 added that the treaty did not prejudice either party's existing treaties with other states. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] Article 12 committed both sides to continue negotiating, and Article 14 provided for an exchange of special representatives on signature and full diplomatic relations at the level of nunciature and embassy after entry into force. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993]

The Holy See also issued a statement on the day of signing that it continued to seek an internationally guaranteed "special status" for Jerusalem, with freedom of worship and access to the holy places for all religions. [cite:vt17_ap_fa1993] The 1967 position on the city survived recognition intact.

Reception and the 1994 protocol

Beilin said the agreement opened a new era; President Ezer Weizman hoped for a papal visit. [cite:vt17_ap_fa1993] About eighty religious Israelis demonstrated outside the ministry with placards about the Inquisition, and the daily Haaretz wrote that the Church, for its persecution of Jews in the Middle Ages, "should not be forgiven." [cite:vt17_ap_fa1993] A Syrian Orthodox Christian interviewed in Jerusalem called it "against the Palestinian people"; the Latin Patriarch, Michel Sabbah, a Palestinian, placed it within a "general process of reconciliation in the whole area." [cite:vt17_ap_fa1993]

The nunciature in Israel and Israel's embassy to the Holy See opened on 19 January 1994; the agreement entered into force on 10 March 1994. [cite:vt17_wiki_hsisrael] A joint protocol signed in Jerusalem on 14 June 1994 established full diplomatic relations from 15 June, and Israel's first ambassador, Shmuel Hadas, presented his credentials on 29 September. [cite:vt1_jvl_protocol1994] [cite:vt17_wiki_hsisrael] A Legal Personality Agreement followed on 10 November 1997; neither it nor the Fundamental Agreement has been ratified by the Knesset. [cite:vt17_wiki_hsisrael] The agreement on property and fiscal matters foreseen in Article 10 is followed, with its status as of October 2026, in Part Eighteen. [scene:vt18_relations_since_1994|Part Eighteen: relations since 1994]

What the timing shows

Laid out by date, the shifts do not follow the needs of the Zionist movement or of Israel. The Holy See withheld recognition from 1948 onward, through the whole period before 1967 and for a quarter-century after, and held to its own Jerusalem demand against Israel's stated position throughout. Public Israeli pressure, in 1982 and 1987, did not move it. The steps it did take came in two forms: doctrinal changes about the Jewish people that were explicitly kept apart from the state, and diplomatic changes that followed the Palestinian track, opening talks after Palestinians sat at the Madrid table and signing after the PLO recognised Israel. The stated interests named in 1948 to 1949, the holy places and the legal security of Catholic institutions, are the ones written into Articles 3, 4 and 10 of the treaty, and the reservation on "disputed territories and unsettled borders" in Article 11 kept recognition from becoming a position on the territories Israel had held since 1967. This reading rests on the published record; the Holy See's own files for 1958 to 1993 are closed, and the Secretariat of State's negotiating papers cannot yet be checked against it. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] Part Nineteen applies this result to the front hypothesis as a whole. [scene:vt19_predictions_tested|Part Nineteen: the predictions tested]

chapters.label: Part Eighteen
chapters.title: Israel, Palestine and Gaza, 1994–2026
chapters.intro: Part Eighteen follows the Holy See's relations with Israel and with the Palestinians from the opening of full diplomatic relations in June 1994 to October 2026. It sets out the treaties signed after the Fundamental Agreement and the one still unsigned, the three papal visits, the nuncios and the quarrels; the Holy See's agreements with the PLO in 2000 and with the State of Palestine in 2015; what Francis, Leo XIV, Cardinal Parolin and the Latin Patriarch said about the war in Gaza from October 2023, with Israel's replies beside each statement; and why, despite those words, the Holy See has kept its relations with Israel intact. Every item from 2025 and 2026 carries its status as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: Part Eighteen has established that the relations opened in 1994 were kept, argued over and used for thirty-two years: the Legal Personality Agreement of 10 November 1997 is in force and was invoked by the Latin Patriarchate as late as 31 December 2025, while the economic and fiscal agreement promised in 1993 is still unsigned as of October 2026. [cite:vt18_jvl_lpa1997] [cite:vt18_caritasjr_2025] [cite:vt18_press_2017] The Holy See signed with the PLO on 15 February 2000 and with the State of Palestine on 26 June 2015, and in both texts and in its statements to September 2026 it held to two states and an internationally guaranteed Jerusalem. [cite:vt18_va_plo2000] [cite:vt18_va_bull2015] [cite:vt18_ncr_unga2026] On Gaza, Francis spoke of terrorism and cruelty and asked for an investigation of the genocide question, Parolin called the 7 October attack "inhuman and indefensible" and Israel's war "disastrous and inhuman" in its consequences, and Leo XIV called for an end to "the barbarity of the war", while Israel's government protested and the relationship held. [cite:vt18_ncr_terror2023] [cite:vt18_ncreg_genocide2024] [cite:vt18_vn_parolin2025] [cite:vt18_vn_angelus2025] The Holy See's own treaty commitments of 1929 and 1993, and its practice in Berlin, Damascus and Managua, account for that combination of loud words and unbroken relations without any hidden alignment, though critics on both sides contest the balance it struck. [cite:vt1_va_lateran] [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] [cite:vt18_vn_nicaragua2023] With the whole record from 1904 to 2026 now on the table, [scene:vt19_predictions_tested|Part Nineteen] tests the front hypothesis against it and gives the volume's verdict.

sections.h: Relations with Israel since 1994
sections.html:
When the Holy See and Israel exchanged ambassadors in 1994, the Fundamental Agreement signed in Jerusalem on 30 December 1993 had already set the work that was still to be done. Its Article 12 said negotiations would continue on the agenda agreed in July 1992, and its Article 10(2) committed both sides to negotiate in good faith "a comprehensive agreement" on the Catholic Church's unresolved property, economic and fiscal questions, to begin within three months of entry into force and to aim for a deal within two years. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] The agreement entered into force on 10 March 1994; the nunciature and the Israeli embassy to the Holy See opened, and the protocol of 15 June 1994 raised relations to full diplomatic level, with Israel's first ambassador, Shmuel Hadas, presenting credentials on 29 September 1994. [cite:vt18_wiki_hsisrael] [cite:vt1_jvl_protocol1994] Thirty-two years later, as of October 2026, those relations are intact, the second agreement promised in 1993 has been signed, and the third has not.

The 1997 Legal Personality Agreement

The first follow-up treaty dealt with a practical problem: under Israeli law it was not clear which Catholic bodies existed as legal persons able to own land, sign contracts or go to court. The Agreement signed in Jerusalem on 10 November 1997 settled it. Israel undertook to give "full effect" in Israeli law to the legal personality of the Catholic Church itself, with the Holy See recognised as its sovereign authority, and of the Eastern Catholic patriarchates, the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem, the dioceses, the Assembly of Catholic Ordinaries of the Holy Land, the Franciscan Custody of the Holy Land and the religious orders, which were listed in annexes. Ordinary transactions in Israel were to be governed by Israeli law, while questions of internal authority were left to canon law; the Church's entities were deemed to consent to be sued in the proper Israeli court; and the treaty was to enter into force on the later of the two parties' notifications of ratification. [cite:vt18_jvl_lpa1997] Neither the 1993 nor the 1997 agreement has been incorporated by a vote of the Knesset. [cite:vt18_wiki_hsisrael]

The 1997 agreement is not a dead letter. On 31 December 2025, when Israel's new registration rules for aid organisations took effect, the Latin Patriarchate said that Caritas Jerusalem was an "Ecclesiastical Legal Person" whose status Israel had recognised through the 1993 and 1997 agreements, that it had not applied for re-registration with the Israeli authorities, and that it would continue its work in Gaza, the West Bank and Jerusalem. [cite:vt18_caritasjr_2025]

The economic agreement that was never signed

The third treaty has not been concluded. Formal negotiations on property, taxes and economic matters opened on 11 March 1999, almost five years after the date by which the 1993 text had said they would begin. [cite:vt18_asianews_2009] The issues were reported consistently over the following years: formal recognition of the tax exemptions the Church had long enjoyed in practice; protection of Church property, especially the holy places; and restitution of property lost since 1948, such as a church at Caesarea expropriated and razed in the 1950s. [cite:vt18_asianews_2009] By one summary of the record, the plenary commission had met briefly in 1994 and then not again until 2004; talks broke down on 10 December 2009, when Israel's deputy foreign minister Danny Ayalon spoke of a crisis, with the room of the Last Supper on Mount Zion reported as a sticking point. [cite:vt18_wiki_hsisrael] In June 2012 the commission said the talks had reached a "final stage", but the Catholic bishops of the Holy Land said "a signing is not imminent"; the Holy See's negotiator, Msgr Ettore Balestrero, said the talks would not address East Jerusalem or the West Bank, after Palestinian officials objected that a reported draft could concede them. [cite:vt18_ncreg_2012]

The last joint communiqué found for this volume is dated 14 June 2017. It reported a plenary meeting in Vatican City the day before, led by Msgr Antoine Camilleri for the Holy See and Minister Tzachi Hanegbi for Israel, which hoped for a "rapid conclusion of ongoing negotiations". [cite:vt18_press_2017] No signed economic agreement, and no later plenary communiqué, was found in searches made in October 2026; the matter is therefore open as of October 2026.

Three papal visits

Three popes visited Israel after 1994. John Paul II's pilgrimage in March 2000 is remembered for the prayer he left in the Western Wall on 26 March. It said "we are deeply saddened by the behaviour of those who in the course of history have caused these children of yours to suffer", and committed the Church "to genuine brotherhood with the people of the Covenant". [cite:vt18_va_jp2wall2000] Benedict XVI's visit in May 2009 was cooler in its reception. At Yad Vashem on 11 May he said the victims "will never lose their names", but Rabbi Israel Meir Lau, chairman of the Yad Vashem Council, said something was missing: the pope had said "killed" rather than "murdered" and offered no apology. Benedict did not enter the museum hall whose caption then criticised Pius XII's wartime silence, and the visit came a few months after he had lifted the excommunication of a bishop who denied the Holocaust. [cite:vt18_csm_bxvi2009]

Francis's visit of 24–26 May 2014 gave both sides gestures. He entered the West Bank directly from Jordan, spoke of the "state of Palestine" in Bethlehem and prayed with his forehead against Israel's separation barrier on 25 May. The next day he became the first pope to lay a wreath at the grave of Theodor Herzl, stopped at Prime Minister Netanyahu's request at a memorial to victims of terrorism, and at Yad Vashem asked for "the grace to be ashamed". He invited Presidents Shimon Peres and Mahmoud Abbas to pray for peace at the Vatican the following month, and both accepted. [cite:vt18_jta_francis2014] A pope who had refused Herzl's movement in 1904 had now honoured its founder's grave; the meaning of that fact for this volume's question is weighed in [scene:vt19_predictions_tested|Part Nineteen].

Nuncios, ambassadors and friction

The Holy See has had seven nuncios in Israel since 1994. Andrea Cordero Lanza di Montezemolo, who had been apostolic delegate in Jerusalem since 1990, became the first; he was followed by Pietro Sambi (1998–2005), Antonio Franco (2006–2012), Giuseppe Lazzarotto (2012–2017), Leopoldo Girelli (2017–2021) and Adolfo Tito Yllana (2021–2026). [cite:vt18_wiki_nunciature] On 22 January 2026 Pope Leo XIV appointed Archbishop Giorgio Lingua, previously nuncio to Croatia, as nuncio to Israel and apostolic delegate in Jerusalem and Palestine, and he holds the post as of October 2026. [cite:vt1_aleteia_lingua] The nunciature is in Jaffa, in Tel Aviv, not in Jerusalem; the double title of nuncio to Israel and delegate in Jerusalem and Palestine keeps the Holy See's position that the city's status is still to be settled. [cite:vt18_wiki_nunciature]

The frictions are on record on both sides. Israel objected to the Holy See's 2015 treaty with the State of Palestine, discussed in the next section. [cite:ts11_wiki_hspal] It objected to papal and curial words on Gaza from November 2023, set out in [scene:vt18_gaza_words|the third section]. When Francis died on 21 April 2025, Netanyahu's office took three days to issue condolences and only Israel's ambassador to the Holy See attended the funeral; President Isaac Herzog attended Leo XIV's inauguration. [cite:vt6_wiki_conclave2025] [cite:vt18_efe_herzog2025] On Palm Sunday, 29 March 2026, during the US–Israeli war on Iran that had begun on 28 February, Israeli police stopped Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa, the Latin Patriarch, and the Custos of the Holy Land, Fr Francesco Ielpo, from reaching the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, citing the risks of a mass-casualty incident during the war; the Latin Patriarchate said its heads had been prevented from celebrating the Palm Sunday Mass there "for the first time in centuries".
