[cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar] [cite:vt18_rte_palmsunday2026] Italy's prime minister and France's president condemned it; the same night Netanyahu said Pizzaballa had "full and immediate access", and Herzog said the incident stemmed from security concerns over Iranian missile attacks. [cite:vt18_rte_palmsunday2026] [cite:vt18_cl_reversal2026] No separate Holy See statement on the incident was reported. [cite:vt18_cl_reversal2026]

Cooperation continued alongside. Leo XIV received Herzog on 4 September 2025, with Cardinal Parolin and Archbishop Gallagher, and the Holy See's statement asked for a return to negotiations, the release of all hostages, a permanent ceasefire and humanitarian access, and called a two-state solution "the only way out of the current war". [cite:vt1_vn_herzog2025] On Good Friday, 3 April 2026, Leo telephoned Herzog; the Holy See's readout said "the need to reopen all possible channels of diplomatic dialogue was reiterated", while Herzog's office said they had discussed Iran's missile threats and the safety of Christians in Lebanon. [cite:vt18_crux_herzog2026] The pattern from 1994 to 2026 is a relationship that both states kept, argued inside, and used.

sections.h: The Holy See and the State of Palestine
sections.html:
The Holy See's treaty with Israel was one half of a pattern. Within weeks of the 1994 protocol with Israel, it opened official, non-diplomatic relations with the Palestine Liberation Organization on 26 October 1994, and it went on to sign two treaties with the Palestinian side: a Basic Agreement with the PLO in 2000 and a Comprehensive Agreement with the State of Palestine in 2015. [cite:ts11_wiki_hspal] The texts matter for this volume because they show what the Holy See committed itself to in writing on Jerusalem, on borders and on Palestinian statehood, in the same years that it was building relations with Israel.

The Basic Agreement: 15 February, not 15 January, 2000

Secondary sources disagree on the date of the Basic Agreement. The text itself settles it. The version published by the Secretariat of State closes "Signed in the Vatican, the fifteenth of February, 2000", and its Latin note gives the same date; it was signed by Mgr Celestino Migliore for the Holy See and Dr Emile Jarjoui for the PLO, and Article 12 put it into force on signature. [cite:vt18_va_plo2000] The Holy See Press Office used the same date, 15 February 2000, when it announced the 2015 treaty, and the Holy See's statement of November 2012 on Palestine's status at the United Nations also cites "the Basic Agreement of 15 February 2000". [cite:vt18_va_bull2015] [cite:vt18_rv_un2012] No primary source consulted for this volume gives 15 January; that date should be treated as an error.

Most of the Basic Agreement concerns the Church: freedom of religion and conscience (Article 1), equal civil rights regardless of religion (Article 3), the Status Quo regime in the Christian holy places where it applies (Article 4), and the legal personality and the economic, legal and fiscal rights of the Church and its institutions under Palestinian law (Articles 5 to 7). [cite:vt18_va_plo2000] Its political weight is in the preamble. It calls for "a special statute for Jerusalem, internationally guaranteed", and declares that "unilateral decisions and actions altering the specific character and status of Jerusalem" are "morally and legally unacceptable". [cite:vt18_va_plo2000] This is the line Pius XII had drawn in 1949, restated in a treaty six years after the Holy See recognised Israel; see [scene:vt17_jerusalem_1947_49|Part Seventeen] for its origin. The Fundamental Agreement with Israel contains no comparable clause on Jerusalem, which is one of the asymmetries between the two sets of texts. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993]

From the 2012 vote to recognition in 2015

On 29 November 2012 the United Nations General Assembly made Palestine a non-member observer state. The next day the Holy See said it welcomed the decision "with favour", repeated its call for an internationally guaranteed special statute for Jerusalem, and quoted Benedict XVI's words of 2009 that the two-state solution should "become a reality, not remain a dream". [cite:vt18_rv_un2012] From then on, the Holy See's counterpart in its own documents was the State of Palestine.

On 26 June 2015, at the Apostolic Palace, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, Secretary for Relations with States, and Riad al-Malki, the Palestinian foreign minister, signed the Comprehensive Agreement between the Holy See and the State of Palestine: a preamble and 32 articles in eight chapters. [cite:vt18_va_bull2015] [cite:vt1_rv_palestine2015] Gallagher tied the change of signatory from the PLO to the State of Palestine directly to the General Assembly resolution of 29 November 2012 and said he hoped "the much desired two-State solution" would soon become a reality and that the agreement might be "a stimulus" towards ending the conflict. Al-Malki said the agreement included the Holy See's official recognition of Palestine as a state and tied it to two states on the 1967 borders. [cite:vt18_va_bull2015] The preamble refers to a State of Palestine consisting of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip. [cite:ts11_wiki_hspal] On 2 January 2016 the Holy See announced that the parties had notified each other under Article 30 and that the agreement "has come into full force". [cite:vt18_rv_force2016] [cite:vt18_press_bull2016] One news agency later dated the signing to 13 May 2015; that was the date the negotiating commission concluded the text, and the signing was on 26 June. [cite:vt18_ewtn_abbas2017] [cite:vt18_va_bull2015]

Israel's foreign ministry called the agreement one-sided. Its spokesman said it ignored the rights of the Jewish people in the "Land of Israel" and the places in Jerusalem holy to Judaism, and that recognising a Palestinian state harmed the peace process by strengthening Palestinian refusal to negotiate. [cite:ts11_wiki_hspal] The protest did not become a rupture: Israel's ambassador to the Holy See, Zion Evrony, who had presented credentials in 2012, stayed in post until 2016. [cite:vt18_wiki_hsisrael]

Abbas at the Vatican, and Leo XIV's position

Mahmoud Abbas became a regular visitor. He accepted Francis's invitation of May 2014 to pray for peace in the Vatican gardens with Shimon Peres. [cite:vt18_jta_francis2014] On 14 January 2017 he met Francis for about 23 minutes, then Parolin and Gallagher, and inaugurated the Palestinian embassy to the Holy See, which he called a "sign that the Pope loves the Palestinian people". [cite:vt18_ewtn_abbas2017] On 6 November 2025 Leo XIV received him to mark the tenth anniversary of the Comprehensive Agreement; the Holy See's statement recorded agreement on the "urgent need to provide assistance to the civilian population in Gaza" and discussion of a two-state solution. [cite:vt18_press_abbas2025] Israel's president had been received two months earlier. [cite:vt1_vn_herzog2025]

Leo XIV has kept the two-state position at the centre of his statements. On the flight from Istanbul to Beirut on 30 November 2025 he said the Holy See had long backed that solution and added: "We all know that at present, Israel still does not accept this solution." In the same answer he said: "We are also friends with Israel, and we are trying to act as a mediating voice for both parties." [cite:vt18_ewtn_flight2025] On 9 January 2026 he told the diplomatic corps accredited to the Holy See that the two-state solution "remains the institutional perspective" for the aspirations of both peoples. [cite:vt18_vn_twostates2026] At the United Nations General Assembly in September 2026 Cardinal Parolin called it "the only viable and equitable path", said the Holy See "continues to uphold the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people", and repeated the call for an internationally guaranteed special statute for Jerusalem. [cite:vt18_ncr_unga2026] As of October 2026 the Holy See recognises both Israel and the State of Palestine, keeps an embassy-level relationship with each, and holds the Jerusalem position it has held since 1949.

sections.h: Gaza, 2023–2026: What the Popes and Their Officials Said
sections.html:
From October 2023 the Holy See's relationship with Israel was tested by a war in which the Catholic parish of Gaza City sheltered hundreds of people, two of its parishioners were killed in December 2023 and three more in July 2025, and two popes and the Secretary of State spoke about the war in public again and again, in terms that Israel's government protested several times. This section sets out what was said, by whom and when, with the Israeli government's responses beside it. It does not decide whether the words were right; it records them precisely, because several of them are misquoted in circulation. As of 12 October 2026, the Gaza health ministry counted 74,382 people killed since October 2023, 1,493 of them after the ceasefire of 10 October 2025. [cite:gz_aj_year2026]

Francis: calls to a parish, "terrorism", "cruelty"

The most personal act was a telephone habit. Through the war Francis kept in constant contact with Fr Gabriel Romanelli and the Holy Family parish, where about 500 people were sheltering; his last call was on 19 April 2025, Holy Saturday, two days before he died. Romanelli said the pope "told us he was praying for us, blessed us, and thanked us for our prayers". [cite:vt18_cwr_lastcall2025]

His first public words to cause a diplomatic dispute came on 22 November 2023. That morning he met relatives of Israeli hostages and, separately, Palestinians with family in Gaza; at the general audience he said: "This isn't war anymore, this is terrorism." [cite:vt18_ncr_terror2023] Palestinian participants said he had also used the word "genocide" in their meeting; the Vatican spokesman, Matteo Bruni, said he had not. [cite:vt18_jta_clarify2023] Jewish bodies objected that the remark put the two sides on one level. Noemi Di Segni, president of the Union of Italian Jewish Communities, said she would have preferred a "clear condemnation of Oct. 7"; the council of the Assembly of Italian Rabbis said the pope was "publicly accusing both sides of terrorism"; the American Jewish Committee wrote that Hamas's killing and kidnapping of civilians was terrorism and "Israel's self-defense is not". Cardinal Matteo Zuppi answered that the pope's words did "not mean putting everyone on the same level". [cite:vt18_jta_clarify2023]

On 16 December 2023 the Latin Patriarchate said an Israeli army sniper had killed two parishioners, Nahida and her daughter Samar, inside the Holy Family compound, with no warning given. At the Angelus the next day Francis said that some called such acts terrorism and war: "Yes, it is war, it is terrorism." The Israeli army said no report of a hit on the church or of civilian casualties had been raised with it, that its operational findings supported this, and that it does not target civilians. [cite:vt18_almon_dec2023]

On 17 November 2024 an excerpt was released from a book of interviews with Francis by Hernán Reyes Alcaide, Hope Never Disappoints, published on 19 November. In it Francis said that "according to some experts" what was happening in Gaza "has the characteristics of a genocide", and that it should be carefully investigated to determine whether it fits the technical definition used by jurists and international bodies. [cite:vt18_ncreg_genocide2024] He did not say it was genocide; he said the question should be investigated. Israel's ambassador to the Holy See, Yaron Sideman, replied that Israel was defending itself after 7 October and that "any attempt to call it by any other name is singling out the Jewish state". [cite:vt18_ncreg_genocide2024]

Between those two remarks came an object rather than a statement. On 7 December 2024 Francis inaugurated a nativity scene in the Paul VI Hall made by Bethlehem artisans, in the presence of Palestinian embassy officials and representatives of President Mahmoud Abbas; the infant Jesus lay in a manger on a keffiyeh, the chequered scarf worn as a Palestinian national symbol. Speaking to the donors, Francis said: "Brothers and sisters, enough war, enough violence!" [cite:vt18_kf_ap_nativity2024] One of the artists, Faten Nastas Mitwasi, later said Palestinian officials had placed the keffiyeh on the manger shortly before the pope arrived, and that it was not first meant as a political statement. [cite:vt18_kf_rns_nativity2025] The American Jewish Committee said its members were "disappointed and troubled", and Genoa's chief rabbi, Giuseppe Momigliano, said the pope's behaviour "surely doesn't help" dialogue; the Israeli embassy declined to say whether it had complained. [cite:vt18_kf_rns_nativity2025] [cite:vt18_kf_ap_nativity2024] By 11 December the manger, the infant and the keffiyeh had been taken away; the Vatican pointed to the custom that the infant is placed in the crib only at Christmas. When the hall reopened on 4 January 2025 the infant was back, lying on hay, and the keffiyeh was not; neither the Vatican nor the artists explained why. [cite:vt18_kf_ap_nativity2024] [cite:vt18_kf_rns_nativity2025] The figure itself was not changed; what was removed, and not restored, was the scarf.

On 21 December 2024, speaking to members of the Holy See's government, Francis said: "Yesterday children were bombed. This is cruelty, this is not war." He added that the Latin Patriarch had not been let into Gaza as promised. An Israeli foreign ministry spokesman called the remarks "particularly disappointing" and said: "Enough with the double standards and the singling out of the Jewish state and its people"; the Israeli army said the strike had targeted militants and that the reported casualty figures did not match its information. [cite:vt18_almon_cruelty2024]

Parolin: "carnage", and what "inhuman and indefensible" referred to

Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Secretary of State, spoke for the Holy See's diplomacy rather than for the pope personally. On 13 February 2024 he said Israel's response could not be called proportionate "with 30,000 dead" and spoke of "carnage". Israel's embassy to the Holy See called the remarks "regrettable" and said he had not considered "the relevant facts"; its Italian version used "deplorevole", and the embassy said the next day that the English word was the original. [cite:vt18_ap_parolin2024]

Parolin's interview with Vatican Media on 6 October 2025, on the eve of the second anniversary of the Hamas attack, is the statement most often misquoted. He called "the terrorist attack carried out by Hamas and other militias" against Israelis and migrants "inhuman and indefensible", and "a shameful and, I repeat, inhuman massacre". He then said the war that followed had brought "disastrous and inhuman consequences", that it was "unacceptable and unjustifiable to reduce human beings to mere 'collateral damage'", and that the states able to influence events "have so far failed to act to stop the ongoing massacre". He said those attacked have a right to defend themselves but "even legitimate defence must respect the principle of proportionality", called on Hamas to release the hostages, and said: "Antisemitism is a cancer that must be fought and eradicated." [cite:vt18_vn_parolin2025] [cite:vt18_cns_parolin2025] The phrase "inhuman and indefensible" is often quoted as if it described the situation in Gaza; it described the 7 October attack, and the interview was given to Vatican Media.

Leo XIV: the church strike and after

Leo XIV was elected on 8 May 2025. [cite:vt2_or_leo14] On 17 July 2025 an Israeli strike hit the Holy Family compound, killing Najwa Abu Daoud, 69, Foumia Issa Latif Ayyad, 84, and Saad Issa Kostandi Salameh, 60, and wounding about ten people, including Fr Romanelli. Pizzaballa told Vatican News he believed a shell from an Israeli tank had hit the church directly, adding that "we are not sure about this"; the Israeli army said the incident was under investigation. Israel's foreign ministry expressed "deep sorrow" and said Israel "never targets churches or religious sites"; Netanyahu said "stray ammunition accidentally struck" the church and on 18 July telephoned the pope, the first public contact between them, in which Leo urged "a ceasefire and an end to the war". [cite:vt18_ncr_netcall2025] [cite:vt1_audit_ncr_holyfamily] At the Angelus at Castel Gandolfo on 20 July Leo called for "an immediate halt to the barbarity of the war" and reminded states of "the prohibition against collective punishment, indiscriminate use of force" and "forced displacement of the population". [cite:vt18_vn_angelus2025]

Leo has been more guarded than Francis on the word genocide. In excerpts of an interview with the journalist Elise Ann Allen released on 18 September 2025 he said: "Officially, the Holy See does not believe that we can make any declaration at this time about that", noting "a very technical definition". [cite:vt18_ansa_genocide2025] His later statements turned increasingly to the West Bank: on 9 January 2026 he told diplomats that violence against Palestinian civilians there had increased, and at the Angelus of 16 August 2026 he appealed for an end to "repeated acts of violence against the Palestinian population of the West Bank" and for progress "toward a two-state solution". [cite:vt18_ncr_westbank2026] [cite:vt18_vn_westbank2026] As of October 2026 no further statement of his on genocide was found.

Pizzaballa, the Patriarch on the ground

Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa, the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, is the Church's senior figure in the territory, not an official of the Holy See. On 16 October 2023, asked whether he would offer himself in exchange for child hostages held by Hamas, he said: "Anything, if that can lead to freedom and bring those children home, no problem." [cite:vt18_cwr_pizza2023] On 26 August 2025 the Latin and Greek Orthodox Patriarchates said their clergy and nuns would stay in the Gaza City compounds, where hundreds of civilians were sheltering, because fleeing south "would be nothing less than a death sentence"; the same statement asked for "the return of the missing people and the Israeli hostages". [cite:vt18_ncreg_patriarchs2025] On 15 August 2026 he visited Taybeh, a Christian village in the West Bank whose parish priest, Fr Bashar Fawadleh, called settler violence there a "deliberate strategy of harassment"; Israel said its army's presence was meant to protect the residents. [cite:vt18_ncr_westbank2026]

sections.h: Why the Holy See Speaks but Does Not Sever
sections.html:
Through three years of war in Gaza the Holy See said things about Israel's conduct that Israel's government called regrettable, disappointing and a double standard, and it did nothing institutional that Israel would have felt as a sanction. As of October 2026 no recall of the Holy See's nuncio, no downgrade or suspension of the relations opened in 1994 and no economic measure has been reported; on the contrary, Leo XIV appointed a new nuncio to Israel, Archbishop Giorgio Lingua, on 22 January 2026. [cite:vt1_aleteia_lingua] [cite:vt18_wiki_hsisrael] For readers of this volume the gap between the words and the acts is a live question, because the front hypothesis predicts that public opposition never costs the other side anything. Before that gap can be read as evidence of anything, the documented reasons for it have to be set out: what the Holy See's treaties say, how it has behaved towards other states in comparable conflicts, what its critics argue, and what it says itself.

What the treaties say

Two treaty clauses state the Holy See's posture in its own words. Article 24 of the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929 reads, in the official Italian text, that the Holy See "vuole rimanere e rimarrà estranea alle competizioni temporali fra gli altri Stati": it wishes to remain, and will remain, extraneous to the temporal competitions between other states and to international congresses called for that purpose, "a meno che le parti contendenti facciano concorde appello alla sua missione di pace", unless the contending parties together appeal to its mission of peace. It reserves "in ogni caso" the right "di far valere la sua potestà morale e spirituale", to assert its moral and spiritual power, and in consequence Vatican City is to be "sempre ed in ogni caso" neutral and inviolable territory. [cite:vt1_va_lateran] [cite:vt2_lateran_text]

The Fundamental Agreement with Israel repeats the principle and applies it to the Holy Land. In Article 11(1) both parties commit themselves to the peaceful resolution of conflicts, "excluding violence and terror from international life". In Article 11(2) the Holy See, "while maintaining in every case the right to exercise its moral and spiritual teaching-office", recalls that it is "solemnly committed to remaining a stranger to all merely temporal conflicts", a principle that "applies specifically to disputed territories and unsettled borders". [cite:vt1_va_fa1993]

Read together, the two clauses match the pattern seen in 2023–2026: a right to judge in moral terms, which both texts reserve explicitly, and a commitment not to become a party to the territorial conflict. Neither clause forbids the Holy See to recall a nuncio or to suspend relations; diplomatic relations are not a "temporal conflict". But a measure taken to press one side in a war over territory would sit uneasily with a treaty in which the Holy See promised Israel, by name, to stay out of "disputed territories and unsettled borders". That is a documented constraint, written in 1929 and 1993, not an inference about motive.

How the Holy See has behaved elsewhere

The Holy See's practice elsewhere points the same way. It kept its nuncio, Cesare Orsenigo, in Berlin from 1930 until the nunciature lost its official status after Germany's defeat in May 1945; he left the bombed nunciature for Eichstätt only in February 1945. [cite:vt18_wiki_orsenigo] Through the Syrian civil war "the Apostolic Nunciature in Damascus always remained open", and the nuncio, Mario Zenari, kept his residence in the capital; many other embassies reopened in Damascus only from 2019. [cite:vt18_fides_zenari2019] When the breach came in Nicaragua it came from the other side: the government expelled the nuncio, Archbishop Waldemar Sommertag, on 12 March 2022, and suspended relations in March 2023 after a bishop, Rolando Álvarez, had been sentenced to 26 years in prison. The Holy See answered with "great surprise and regret", and Francis said the Holy See always tries to save diplomatic relations through patience and dialogue. [cite:vt18_vn_nicaragua2023]

The exception in this volume's record shows where the line is. In July 2011, after Ireland's Taoiseach accused the Holy See in the Dáil of trying to frustrate an inquiry into clerical abuse, the Holy See recalled its nuncio to Rome for consultation; Ireland closed its embassy to the Holy See in November 2011, citing cost, and announced its reopening in January 2014. [cite:vt12_tj_nuncio2011] [cite:vt12_tablet_embassy2014] The one documented recall in this volume concerned an accusation against the Holy See itself, not a war between other parties; see [scene:vt12_accountability|Part Twelve]. On this record, "speak, do not sever" is the Holy See's normal practice, not a policy made for Israel.

What the critics argue

Critics have attacked the gap from two opposite sides, and both are named here as individuals and groups, not as "the Church" or "the Jews". Those who want more than words include an Association of Priests Against Genocide, about 3,000 clergy, most of them Italian parish priests, whose open letter asked Italy's bishops for "a word calling for an immediate and permanent ceasefire" and asked the Italian state to end its "military, economic, and diplomatic complicity" with Israeli policy. [cite:vt18_972_caridi2026] The journalist Paola Caridi, writing in +972 Magazine on 10 July 2026, argued that Leo XIV has called for peace and aid but has rarely named Israeli responsibility, and that pressure from clergy and Palestinian Christian leaders will decide whether he changes course. [cite:vt18_972_caridi2026] The Palestinian Christian ecumenical initiative Kairos Palestine, in its second document of November 2025, called the war a "genocide, ethnic cleansing and forced displacement" and asked churches worldwide for pressure, sanctions and boycotts, including support for the BDS movement. [cite:vt18_maryknoll_kairos2026]

From the other side, Israel's government and several Jewish organisations argued that the Holy See's words already went too far. Israel's foreign ministry spoke of "double standards and the singling out of the Jewish state"; its ambassador to the Holy See said calling the war by another name than self-defence was "singling out the Jewish state"; the Assembly of Italian Rabbis said Francis had accused "both sides of terrorism". [cite:vt18_almon_cruelty2024] [cite:vt18_ncreg_genocide2024] [cite:vt18_jta_clarify2023] For these critics the problem was not the absence of sanctions but the content of the speech.

What the Holy See says

The Holy See's own account is consistent with its treaties. Parolin, in October 2025: "The Holy See—sometimes misunderstood—continues to call for peace, to invite dialogue, to use the words 'negotiation' and 'discussion.'" [cite:vt18_vn_parolin2025] Leo XIV, on 30 November 2025: "We are also friends with Israel, and we are trying to act as a mediating voice for both parties." [cite:vt18_ewtn_flight2025] On 3 April 2026, in the middle of a regional war, the Holy See described the pope's call to Israel's president as a reminder of "the need to reopen all possible channels of diplomatic dialogue". [cite:vt18_crux_herzog2026] There is also a documented practical stake: the Church's institutions in Israel rest on the 1993 and 1997 treaties, as the Latin Patriarchate showed on 31 December 2025 when it relied on them to keep Caritas Jerusalem working in Gaza, the West Bank and Jerusalem. [cite:vt18_caritasjr_2025] That stake is a fact; whether it, the treaty clauses or a theory of mediation weighs most in any given decision is not stated in any document found, and this volume does not assign a motive.

Interpretation, not finding: the "loud silence" reading

A reading held on the Sophia platform calls this the "loud silence": a pattern in which the Holy See speaks forcefully but declines institutional action, set beside Pius XII's wartime reticence. Read through this lens, 2023–2026 repeats a habit of moral speech without cost. Its holders caution that the pattern does not prove any single motive, and the treaty clauses and the Nicaraguan, Syrian and German cases above offer a documented account of the same behaviour that requires no hidden alignment. The lens is reported here as a reading, not as a finding.

chapters.label: Part Nineteen
chapters.title: The Verdict on the Front Hypothesis
chapters.intro: Part Nineteen closes the volume. It takes the five tests fixed in Part One, the private record, money and favours, the timing of shifts, treaty behaviour and the cost of opposition, and scores each against what Parts Two to Eighteen documented, adding no new evidence. It then gives the volume's answer to its central question, whether the Holy See's public refusal of Zionism from 1904 to 1993 was a front, stated plainly and graded by strength into what is settled, what is probable and what is not established, while keeping the Holy See's position on a movement and a state separate from its teaching on the Jewish people. It sums up the answers to the volume's other questions, from the papal state's origins to the Orlandi case, sets out in one labelled passage the interpretive lenses the volume declined to treat as findings, and ends with the questions that stay open as of October 2026 and the dates on which some of them may move.
chapters.outro: Part Nineteen has scored the front hypothesis against the whole record and found that none of the five tests favours it. The private record published so far, from Herzl's diary of 1904 to the Holy See's letters of 1943, matches the public refusal or is harder than it; no transfer of money or favours from the Holy See to the Zionist movement or to Israel was found; the Holy See's shifts followed its own stated interests and the Palestinian track; its treaty with Israel conceded nothing on Jerusalem or the territories; and its opposition cost Israel recognition for forty-five years and drew complaints from its leaders, though it rarely changed outcomes. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] [cite:vt17_cnewa_pmp] [cite:vt17_rosen_1994] [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] [cite:vt17_djn_waldheim] The refusal was real policy toward a movement and a state, separate after 1965 from the Holy See's teaching on the Jewish people. [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] The verdict is settled on the published record, probable where it relies on inference from dates and on one set of foreign files, and open where the Holy See's own papers on Palestine after 1945 have yet to be studied or opened; the Becciu proceedings, the Orlandi inquiries, the ICI recovery and the economic agreement with Israel all remained unresolved as of October 2026. [cite:vt17_berghahn_rioli] [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] [cite:vt10_us_oct2026] [cite:vt18_press_2017] The library's companion volumes take up the other sides of the question: [scene:dv1_three_functions|The Divine 3+1] first framed the front hypothesis and tests the other cities said to have parented the State of Israel, [scene:ts14_record|The Theology Shield] follows the Protestant Christian Zionism that the Holy See's 1985 Notes declined to adopt, and [scene:gi13_record|Greater Israel] sets out the record on the claims to the territories that Article 11 of the 1993 treaty left to be settled by others.

sections.h: The Five Tests, Scored
sections.html:
Part One wrote down five tests before any evidence was weighed, so that the front hypothesis could not be kept alive by reading every fact as part of the cover. [scene:vt1_front_test|What a front would look like] Each test named an observation that would favour the reading that the Holy See's refusal of Zionism was a front for private support, an observation that would favour the reading that it was real policy, and the possibility that the test would come back empty because the papers are closed or because both readings predict the same thing. Parts Two to Eighteen have now set out the record from 1904 to October 2026. This section scores each test against what those parts documented, adding no new evidence, and states for each whether it favours one reading, the other, or neither. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] [cite:vt1_va_lateran]

Test one: the private record

The front reading predicted internal papers encouraging what public statements opposed. The record runs the other way wherever it can be read. The earliest private account is Herzl's own diary of January 1904, written by the man with every reason to report success, and it records a refusal: "We cannot give approval to this movement." [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] The densest private record is the Holy See's wartime correspondence of 1943, published in its own edition of documents: Tardini wrote that the Holy See "has never approved the project of making Palestine a Jewish home", Maglione warned of "new and grave international problems", Roncalli called the restoration of a Jewish kingdom "only a utopia", and Cicognani told President Roosevelt's envoy on 22 June 1943 that a "more fitting territory than Palestine" could be found. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] [cite:vt16_jta1976] [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] These letters were private, sent to governments, and harder than anything the Holy See said in public in those years. The one later private record available, Irish diplomatic files on the Catholic-mandate idea of 1948–49, shows the Holy See declining to "disclose its hand", holding back from its public aim rather than working against it. [cite:vt17_ewtn_irishfiles]

Two items point the other way, and Part One's rule for them was that one party's report of private warmth needs a second record before it counts. Nahum Sokolow's report of a cordial audience with Benedict XV in May 1917 is one party's account, and Sergio Minerbi's archival version gives the pope's terms as protection of the holy places, to be settled "between the Church and the Great Powers." [cite:vt16_ej_minerbi] The handwritten 1944 note in which Pius XII is said to have written that "The Jews need a land of their own" was announced by the Pave the Way Foundation in 2012 without an image, a transcription or an archival reference, and no publication of it was found after the Pius XII files opened. [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit] Neither item was confirmed by a Holy See paper. The test therefore favours real policy for 1904 to 1949, on the papers published. It is empty for 1958 to 1993, whose papers are closed, and incomplete for 1945 to 1958, whose papers are open but whose first study on Palestine, Maria Chiara Rioli's chapter of 2024, could not be checked for this volume. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025] [cite:vt17_berghahn_rioli]

Test two: money and favours

The front reading predicted something of value passing from the Holy See to the Zionist movement or to Israel. No such transfer was found in any part of this volume. The Holy See's one material commitment of the years of Israel's founding went to Palestinian Arab refugees, through the Pontifical Mission for Palestine set up by Pius XII in 1949 under Monsignor Thomas McMahon. [cite:vt17_cnewa_pmp] The best-known financial link between the papacy and a Jewish banking family runs the other way and ends early: the Rothschild houses lent to the government of the Papal States from 1831 into the 1850s, with the pope as debtor, and the borrower ceased to exist in 1870. [cite:wa_ra_naples] [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] Part Eleven tested the claimed "unbroken chain" from those loans to 2026 link by link and found two dated ends with nothing between them; the appointment of François Pauly, a former head of the Edmond de Rothschild group, to chair the IOR's board in 2026 is a fact about one banker's career, with no wrongdoing documented. [cite:vt11_iv_pauly] [scene:vt11_chain_tested|The chain tested]

The favours that would matter most, diplomatic help at a decisive moment, were looked for and not found. Whether the Holy See pressed Catholic delegations at the United Nations in 1947, for or against partition, is not settled by any document checked; the one account of a meeting between the Jewish Agency's Moshe Sneh and Domenico Tardini on 3 October 1947 says Tardini "did not make any promises" and cites no archive. [cite:vt17_tenembaum_sneh] Pave the Way's further claim that the Vatican encouraged Spain to recognise Israel in 1955 names no source. [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit] "Checked, nothing documented" is a result: the test favours real policy.

Test three: the timing of shifts

The front reading predicted softening when the movement or the state needed support. Part Seventeen dated every shift, and none fits that pattern. The theological changes of 1965, 1974 and 1985, from Nostra Aetate to the Notes, came from a council and a commission with a religious mandate and left the state aside; the Notes said the state was to be judged by "the common principles of international law." [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] The diplomatic changes followed events and the Palestinian track: the call for an internationalised Jerusalem became a call for an internationally guaranteed statute after Israel took the eastern city in 1967; the first naming of the State of Israel in a papal letter, in 1984, came with a Palestinian right to a homeland in the same text; negotiations opened in 1992 after Palestinians sat at the Madrid table; and recognition followed the Israel–PLO letters of September 1993. [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] [cite:vt17_state_madrid] [cite:vt17_jcpa_schvindlerman] Public Israeli pressure, over the Arafat audience of 1982 and the Waldheim audience of 1987, did not move the Holy See. [cite:vt17_csm_arafat1982] [cite:vt17_djn_waldheim] The reasons Rabbi David Rosen recorded from inside the negotiation, the Church's communities in Arab countries, the local church and the legal security of its institutions, are the Holy See's own stated interests. [cite:vt17_rosen_1994] The test favours real policy, with one caution: the Secretariat of State's negotiating papers for 1992–93 are closed, so the reading rests on dates and published texts.

Test four: treaty behaviour

Part One warned that the neutrality clauses alone could not decide this test, because a covert partner might also sign them; the answer lay in what else the treaties contain. The Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993 secures what the Holy See had named since 1948: the Church's right to its institutions (Article 3), the status quo in the holy places (Article 4) and negotiation of its property and fiscal questions (Article 10). Article 11 kept recognition from becoming a position on "disputed territories and unsettled borders", and the Holy See said on the day of signing that it still sought a special status for Jerusalem. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] [cite:vt17_ap_fa1993] Nothing in the treaty concedes the city or the territories. The political clauses the Holy See did sign are in its treaties with the Palestinian side: the Basic Agreement with the PLO of 15 February 2000 called unilateral changes to Jerusalem's character "morally and legally unacceptable", and the Comprehensive Agreement of 26 June 2015 was signed with a State of Palestine whose territory the preamble defines to include East Jerusalem. Israel's foreign ministry called the 2015 treaty one-sided. [cite:vt18_va_plo2000] [cite:vt18_va_bull2015] [cite:ts11_wiki_hspal] The economic agreement promised to Israel in 1993 remains unsigned as of October 2026. [cite:vt18_press_2017] The test favours real policy.

Test five: the cost of opposition

The front reading predicted opposition that cost the movement nothing it needed. The record shows opposition that was spent and complained of, though it rarely won. The Holy See sent written objections to the League of Nations against the draft Mandate in 1922 and lost when the Mandate was approved on 24 July. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] [cite:vt16_un_mandate] It objected to the Peel partition plan in 1937, gave Moshe Shertok no support in 1945, supported an international Jerusalem that Israel opposed in the vote on resolution 303 in 1949, and withheld recognition for forty-five years. [cite:vt16_ej_vatican] [cite:vt17_wiki_res303] Israeli leaders said what that cost them: Israel's foreign ministry wrote that Paul VI's visit of 1964 made "patently, and painfully, clear" that the Holy See did not recognise Israel, and Prime Minister Shamir said in 1987 that without relations Israel "can do nothing but express its unhappiness." [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] [cite:vt17_djn_waldheim] Those are the complaints and foreign-file traces the real-policy reading predicted. The opposition did not stop the Mandate, partition or Israel's hold on Jerusalem, and most Catholic-majority delegations voted for partition in 1947. [cite:vt17_tenembaum_sneh] The test favours real policy, but it also shows a policy of limited effect.

After recognition, Part One's table predicted that a front would tilt toward Israel once the cover was no longer needed. Part Eighteen found the same interests pursued with both sides: treaties with the PLO and the State of Palestine, Francis honouring Herzl's grave in May 2014 a day after praying at the separation barrier and speaking of the "state of Palestine", and, from 2023, words on Gaza that Israel's foreign ministry called "double standards", without any rupture of relations. [cite:vt18_jta_francis2014] [cite:vt18_almon_cruelty2024] The gesture at Herzl's grave was public, made after recognition, and balanced on the same journey; it is evidence of the relationship opened in 1994, not of an alignment hidden before it. The absence of rupture matches the treaty clauses and the Holy See's practice in Berlin to 1945, Damascus and Nicaragua. [cite:vt18_wiki_orsenigo] [cite:vt18_vn_nicaragua2023] [scene:vt18_why_no_sever|Why the Holy See does not sever]

No test came back in favour of the front reading. Four came back clearly for real policy, one of them with a closed archive behind it, and the fifth showed a real policy that cost Israel something without changing the decisive outcomes. What that adds up to, and how strong the answer is, is the subject of [scene:vt19_verdict|the next section].

sections.h: The Verdict
sections.html:
The question this volume set out to answer was whether the Holy See's public refusal of Zionism, from Pius X's "Non possumus" to Theodor Herzl in January 1904 until the Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993, was a front for private support. On the documents available as of October 2026, it was not. The refusal was a real policy: stated in public, held in private in the same terms or harder, defended at a cost the Holy See accepted and Israel's leaders complained of, and ended by a treaty on terms the Holy See had named for forty-five years. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] [cite:vt17_mfa_relations] [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] The answer is not equally strong at every point, and the strength of each part of it is set out below.

What is settled

The public record at both ends is settled: Herzl's diary of Pius X's refusal, the allocutions of 1919 and 1921 against a "position of privilege and preponderance" in Palestine, the encyclicals of 1948 and 1949 asking for an internationally guaranteed Jerusalem, forty-five years without recognition, and the treaty of 1993 with its reservation on "disputed territories and unsettled borders." [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] [cite:vt16_va_1919] [cite:vt17_va_imc1948] [cite:dv1_rnc_1949] [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] So is the private record of 1943, published by the Holy See itself, in which its Secretary of State, a senior official of his Secretariat and its apostolic delegates in Washington and Istanbul all opposed a Jewish home in Palestine in letters to governments and to one another. [cite:vt16_jta1976] [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] So is the negative finding on money and favours: no transfer of value from the Holy See to the Zionist movement or to Israel appears in any source used for this volume, and the documented Rothschild loans ran from banks to a pope and ended with the Papal States in 1870. [cite:vt17_cnewa_pmp] [cite:vt11_wiki_papalloans] And so are the terms of recognition: Church institutions secured, the holy places' status quo kept, nothing conceded on Jerusalem or the territories. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] [cite:vt17_ap_fa1993]

What is probable

Two parts of the answer rest on reasonable inference from published texts rather than on the Holy See's own internal files. The first is that the private record of 1945 to 1958 matches the public one. The only private source for those years checked here, Irish diplomatic files, shows the Holy See declining to "disclose its hand" over a Catholic mandate for Jerusalem, and the Vatican files opened in 2020 have produced one study on Palestine, which this volume could not read. [cite:vt17_ewtn_irishfiles] [cite:vt17_berghahn_rioli] The second is that recognition in 1993 followed the Palestinian track and the Holy See's institutional interests rather than Israel's needs. The dates and the reasons Rabbi David Rosen recorded from inside the talks support that reading; the Secretariat of State's negotiating papers are closed. [cite:vt17_rosen_1994] [cite:vt17_state_madrid] [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025]

What is not established

The weighting of motives is not established. The documents give several reasons side by side: the holy places, the legal security of Catholic institutions, the Catholic communities of the Arab world, and, in 1904 and 1943, theological claims about Jewish return. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] [cite:vt16_cicognani1943] [cite:vt17_rosen_1994] The historian Sergio Minerbi reads the Holy See's opposition before 1948 as drawing also on the Christian antisemitism of the period; that is a named historian's reading of motive, and the documents alone do not settle how much each reason weighed. [cite:vt16_ej_minerbi] Also not established: whether the Holy See lobbied Catholic delegations in 1947, whether the 1944 note exists, and what the papers of 1958 to 1993 contain. [cite:vt17_tenembaum_sneh] [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit] A document in those files showing the Holy See encouraging in private what it opposed in public would reopen the verdict. None has been produced.

What the verdict is about, and what it is not

The verdict concerns the Holy See's position on a political movement and a state. It is not a judgment about Jews or Judaism, and the Holy See's own documents draw the same line. In 1904 Pius X fused the two subjects, saying "we cannot recognize the Jewish people." Nostra Aetate rejected the deicide charge in 1965, and the 1985 Notes placed the State of Israel under "the common principles of international law"; after that, theology and diplomacy were separate subjects in the Holy See's own writing. [cite:vt1_ccjr_herzl] [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] The same file of 1943 that opposed a Jewish home in Palestine recorded the Holy See's help for interned Jewish children. [cite:vt16_cicognani1943b] Opposition to Zionism, as the Holy See practised it, is therefore not evidence of hostility to Jews; nor is recognition of Israel, under Article 11, an endorsement of any Israeli government's policies. [cite:vt1_va_fa1993]

The other questions, in brief

The volume also answered the questions around the central one. The table gives, for each, what the record settles and what remains contested, as of October 2026.

One pattern runs through the table. Where claims about the Holy See alleged a hidden controller, a Rothschild chain, a Grey Pope, an Orsini dynasty behind the throne, the documents did not support them; where they alleged real power and real failure, the bank's past, the abuse rules, the court that relies on Italy for its prisoners, the documents did, often in the Holy See's own publications. [cite:vt6_wiki_eminence] [cite:vt11_va_ior1990] [cite:vt12_vn_rescript2019] The stated positions of the Holy See and of the people named are given beside each finding in the parts themselves.

Interpretation, not finding: the lenses this volume set aside

Readings held on the Sophia platform view the Holy See through five lenses. The first is the wordplay that reads the IOR's initials backwards as "ROI", return on investment; read through this lens, the bank's annual dividend to the pope gives the joke a point. The second is the description of the Holy See as an operating system, "VaticanOS", with popes, offices and doctrines rendered as code; in this reading the Jesuit general becomes an implementation layer and recognition a lazily loaded property. The third is a chain of imperial succession from Babylon through Rome to later financial centres, in which the papacy inherits an ancient temple economy. The fourth is the "loud silence": a habit, in this reading, of speaking forcefully while declining institutional action, linking Pius XII's wartime reticence to the Holy See's conduct over Gaza. The fifth is the argument that an institution offering a promise no one can verify must build legal and financial protection around itself.

These are readings, not findings, for reasons the parts made concrete. None names a document, a transaction or a decision that could be checked; each describes a pattern that a reader can see or decline to see. Where a lens touched the documents, it either restated a documented fact in other words, as the dividend and the policy of speaking without severing relations are documented on their own terms, or it needed a link the record does not show: the Babylon chain has no documented line of transmission, and the "implementation layer" picture of the Jesuit general does not match an order bound to the pope by a vow of obedience. [cite:vt9_ior_ar2025] [cite:vt6_gc35_d4] The last of the five is a philosophical argument about faith and institutions, which no archive can confirm or refute. The lenses can help a reader remember a structure; in this volume none of them carries a claim.

The verdict on the central question therefore rests where Part One said it would, on the private record, money, timing, treaties and cost, and all five point the same way. What could still change it, and the other questions the record leaves open, are set out in [scene:vt19_what_stays_open|the final section].

sections.h: What Stays Open
sections.html:
A verdict built on documents is only as final as the documents. This section lists the questions the record left open as of October 2026, what each would take to settle, and where the answer is likely to come from. Some bear on the central question and could, in principle, change the verdict. Others concern the volume's surrounding questions and will change only the details. None is answered here in advance; each is stated with its status as of October 2026.

The private record after 1945

The single most important gap is the Holy See's own file on Palestine from 1945 to 1958. The papers of Pius XII's pontificate, opened on 2 March 2020, include the Secretariat of State's files for those years, the years of partition, Israel's independence and the encyclicals on Jerusalem. [cite:vt14_vn_open2020] The first study devoted to them on this subject, Maria Chiara Rioli's chapter "Archives in War: The Pius XII Papers and the Israeli–Palestinian Conflict" in a volume published by Berghahn in 2024, could not be checked for this book, and nothing has been attributed to it. [cite:vt17_berghahn_rioli] What would settle the question for those years is a body of published research from the Secretariat of State's files, by Rioli and others, showing whether instructions to nuncios and internal memoranda match the encyclicals. After October 1958 the archive is closed: no date had been announced, as of October 2026, for opening the papers of John XXIII, the next pontificate in line, and the papers that would show how Nostra Aetate and the Fundamental Agreement were negotiated lie further ahead still. [cite:vt14_vn_libarch2025]

The 1947 vote and the Sneh–Tardini meeting

Whether the Holy See pressed Catholic delegations at the United Nations in the autumn of 1947 remains open in both directions. The one account of a meeting between Moshe Sneh of the Jewish Agency and Domenico Tardini on 3 October 1947, arranged through the nuncio in Paris, Angelo Roncalli, rests on later recollections and cites no archive; it says Tardini "did not make any promises." [cite:vt17_tenembaum_sneh] What would settle it: the Paris nunciature's papers for 1947 and the Secretariat of State's files now open in Rome, the Jewish Agency's own records of the meeting, and the American diplomatic record of that autumn. Until then, the only firm fact is the vote itself, in which most Catholic-majority delegations supported partition.

The 1944 note

The handwritten note in which Pius XII is said to have written "The Jews need a land of their own" has been announced but not shown. The Pave the Way Foundation said in 2012 that it was held in "the closed section of the Vatican Library", and gave no image, transcription or reference. [cite:vt16_ptwf_zenit] What would settle it is publication of the document with its archival signature, most likely from the Apostolic Archive or the Secretariat of State's historical archive rather than the Library. If it exists and says what is claimed, it would show a private view of the pope in one year at odds with the letters his Secretariat sent in 1943; it would not by itself show money, favours or diplomatic help.

The Becciu proceedings

The conviction of Cardinal Giovanni Angelo Becciu and eight others on 16 December 2023 was set aside on 17 March 2026, when the Court of Appeal found the summons defective and ordered the hearings renewed. [cite:vt10_vn_mistrial2026] As of 22 October 2026 the court had received defence briefs on 21 September and fixed the next hearing for 29 October 2026. [cite:vt10_us_oct2026] Becciu and every other defendant in the renewed proceedings are presumed innocent. What would settle it is a judgment, and then the exhaustion of appeals; the case also tests the court reforms described in [scene:vt4_citizens_courts_prisons|Part Four].

The Orlandi and Gregori inquiries

Three inquiries opened in 2023 and none had reported as of October 2026. The parliamentary commission set up by Law no. 202 of 4 December 2023 runs for the rest of the legislature and must report to both chambers; it had held at least 77 sittings by February 2026. [cite:vt15_law_202] [cite:vt15_sen_feb2026] Rome's prosecutors were following three lines at the end of 2025, and the Vatican's Promoter of Justice had sent his material to them. [cite:vt15_agi_dec2025] [cite:vt15_cwr_senate] What would settle the case is evidence of what happened to Emanuela Orlandi and Mirella Gregori; what would settle the narrower question of the Vatican's role is the commission's report and the release of the papers the family has asked for since 2017. The family holds that the Vatican knows more than it has said; the Holy See's stated position is that the search for the truth is in its interest. [cite:vt15_qn_aug2025] [cite:vt15_vn_2019]

The ICI recovery

Italy's procedure for recovering the property tax not paid for 2006 to 2011 set 30 September 2026 for declarations and 30 October 2026 for payment, with sums over 100,000 euros payable in four quarterly instalments. [cite:vt3_ff_sept2026] As of 21 October 2026 no figure had been published for declarations filed or sums recovered. [cite:vt3_io_ici2026] The only widely quoted estimate, 4 to 5 billion euros attributed to Italy's association of municipalities, is not official, and the 2025 decree's threshold and exclusions mean the amount due may be far lower. [cite:vt3_money_anci] [cite:vt3_dpcm_2025] What would settle it is a published account by the Italian government or the European Commission of what was declared and paid, and by whom.

The economic agreement with Israel

The agreement on property, tax and economic matters promised in Article 10 of the 1993 treaty has been under negotiation since 11 March 1999. The last joint communiqué found is dated 14 June 2017 and hoped for a "rapid conclusion." [cite:vt18_press_2017] [cite:vt1_va_fa1993] What would settle it is a signature, or a published statement that the talks have ended. Israel votes on 27 October 2026, and any further round will be conducted with the government that election produces. [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve]

Leo XIV's next steps

As of October 2026 Leo XIV had kept relations with Israel, appointed a new nuncio, Archbishop Giorgio Lingua, on 22 January 2026, said in September 2025 that the Holy See could make no declaration on genocide "at this time", and, through Cardinal Parolin at the United Nations in September 2026, restated the two-state position and the call for an internationally guaranteed statute for Jerusalem. [cite:vt1_aleteia_lingua] [cite:vt18_ansa_genocide2025] [cite:vt18_ncr_unga2026] His published travel list for 2026 includes no visit to Israel or Palestine; his next announced journey, to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, runs from 6 to 17 November 2026. [cite:vt19_va_travels2026] What would change the picture is a diplomatic act the volume's record does not yet contain: a visit, a signed economic agreement, a change in the Holy See's language on the war, or a change in its relations with either state.

Of these, only the first three bear directly on the central question, and each could in principle change the verdict: a document showing the Holy See encouraging in private what it opposed in public, in 1944, 1947 or the years of the encyclicals, would reopen the test of the private record. The rest will change the volume's details rather than its answer.

chapters.label: Part Twenty
chapters.title: Yeshua, Paul and the First Followers
chapters.intro: Book One of this volume asked whether the Holy See's refusal of Zionism was a front, and answered it in [scene:vt19_verdict|Part Nineteen]. Book Two, "The Church Before the State: What Rome Took, What It Buried, What Survived", turns to the institution's foundations: how a movement around a Galilean teacher became an imperial church, which texts it kept and which it excluded, and how it treated the groups that taught direct, unmediated knowledge of God, from the second-century teachers of gnosis to the Cathars, Templars, mystics, fraternities, witches and the forbidden arts, ending with the excluded texts themselves laid out in full. Its working thesis, set out on the Sophia platform, is that institutional religion built a mediated and obligatory system of priests, tithes and Sunday duty on top of teachings about a kingdom within; the book lays the record against that thesis, saying plainly where it holds, where popular versions overstate it, and where the evidence runs out. Part Twenty starts at the beginning, before any bishop of Rome had special standing: what the earliest Jewish, Roman and Christian sources show about Yeshua and his teaching on the kingdom, what Paul, who never met him in life, says about his own revelation and his dealings with Peter and James, and how the first communities met, led themselves and shared money in the century and a half before Constantine.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty has set out what the earliest record shows. Yeshua was a Galilean Jew with a common name, born around 6 to 4 BCE and crucified under Pontius Pilate between about 30 and 36 CE, an execution confirmed by Tacitus and a family confirmed by Josephus's notice of "the brother of Jesus who was called Christ". [cite:vt20_wiki_chronology] [cite:vt20_tacitus_ann15] [cite:vt20_josephus_ant20] His message centred on a coming kingdom of God, and whether Luke has him place it "within" or "among" his hearers is a live translation dispute; the Gospel of Thomas, of disputed date, says plainly that it is "inside of you". [cite:vt20_esv_mark1] [cite:vt20_ramelli_luke17] [cite:vt20_thomas_lambdin] Paul, the earliest Christian writer, grounded his gospel in a revelation rather than acquaintance, yet spent fifteen days with Cephas, met James, and took part in the Jerusalem meeting of about 48 to 50 that opened the movement to Gentiles, the only council he is recorded as attending. [cite:vt20_nrsv_gal12] [cite:vt20_wiki_jerusalem] The first communities met in houses, named women in recognised roles, and gave voluntarily, "not as an exaction", with no tithe system; church tithe laws appear only in 567 and 585. [cite:vt20_esv_rom16] [cite:vt20_esv_2cor9] [cite:vt20_justin_67] [cite:vt20_cathen_tithes] Offices formed early all the same: the Didache had communities appoint bishops and deacons, and by Ignatius's time a single bishop controlled baptism and the common meal in some cities, years before any emperor favoured the church. [cite:vt20_na_didache] [cite:vt20_na_ignatius_smyrn] [scene:vt21_conversion|Part Twenty-One] follows what changed when one did: Constantine, his conversion, his titles and his patronage of the bishops.

sections.h: Yeshua in the Record: What the Earliest Sources Show
sections.html:
Book Two begins three centuries before an emperor convened a council and nineteen centuries before a Vatican City existed, with a Jewish teacher from Galilee who was executed by a Roman governor. This section sets out what can be said about him from the sources historians actually use, how early those sources are, and what the earliest layer of his teaching said about the "kingdom of God". It also explains a choice of names that runs through the rest of the book.

Two names for two subjects

The man's name in his own languages was Yeshua, a shortened form of Yehoshua (Joshua), meaning roughly "the Lord saves". It was an ordinary name in his time. The archaeologist Amos Kloner called it "one of the common names in the time of the Second Temple"; it appears on 71 burial finds from the period, and Tal Ilan's lexicon of Jewish names counts 85 bearers of the form Yeshua. Greek-speaking Jews wrote it Iesous, which passed through Latin into English as "Jesus". [cite:vt20_wiki_yeshua] This book uses "Yeshua" when it discusses the historical figure, a first-century Jew reconstructed by the ordinary methods of history, and "Jesus Christ" when it describes the figure defined in the creeds of the councils, beginning with Nicaea in 325 ([scene:vt22_what_it_decided|Part Twenty-Two]). The two names do not mark two different people. They mark two different kinds of claim: one about what the evidence of a life can show, the other about what churches came to teach about that life. This book keeps the two claims apart throughout.

Dates

No source gives an exact birth year. The gospels of Matthew and Luke both place the birth in the reign of Herod the Great, and most scholars, following Emil Schürer's calculation that Herod died in 4 BCE, place it between about 6 and 4 BCE. The crucifixion fell under Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judaea from 26 to 36 or 37 CE; scholars generally place it between 30 and 36, and astronomical work on the Passover calendar has narrowed the candidates to two Fridays, 7 April 30 and 3 April 33. [cite:vt20_wiki_chronology]

The non-Christian witnesses

Two writers outside the Christian movement mention Yeshua within a century of his death. The Jewish historian Josephus finished his Antiquities of the Jews around 93 to 94 CE. In Book Twenty he describes how the high priest Ananus, in the interval between two Roman governors, brought before the Sanhedrin "the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James" and had him stoned; citizens complained to King Agrippa and to the incoming governor Albinus, and Ananus was removed after three months. [cite:vt20_josephus_ant20] Scholars accept this passage almost without exception; Louis Feldman described its authenticity as "almost universally acknowledged". [cite:vt20_wiki_josephus]

Book Eighteen of the same work contains a longer paragraph about Jesus, known as the Testimonium Flavianum. In the form transmitted by Christian copyists it calls him the Christ, hedges whether it is "lawful to call him a man", and reports his resurrection, which no Jewish author who stayed outside the movement would plausibly have written. Most scholars now hold that Josephus wrote a shorter, neutral notice that Christian copyists later expanded; a tenth-century Arabic version preserved by the bishop Agapius, published by Shlomo Pines in 1971, reads that "Pilate condemned him to be crucified" without the confessional phrases. A minority, following Ken Olson, argue that the whole paragraph was composed by the fourth-century church historian Eusebius; Feldman adopted that view in 2012, while James Carleton Paget and Alice Whealey rejected it. [cite:vt20_wiki_josephus] The popular claim that "Eusebius forged it" is therefore one scholarly position, not the consensus.

The Roman historian Tacitus, describing the fire of Rome in July 64 [cite:vt20_audit_wiki_fire64], says Nero blamed it on a group "whom the crowd styled Christians", and explains the name: "Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilatus." [cite:vt20_tacitus_ann15] Tacitus wrote with contempt for the movement, which makes his notice the more useful as independent confirmation of the execution and of who ordered it. Crucifixion was a Roman penalty, imposed by a Roman official. The later Christian charge that "the Jews" as a people bore guilt for the death was rejected by the Catholic Church at the Second Vatican Council: Nostra Aetate, proclaimed on 28 October 1965, states that what happened in the passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today". [cite:vt20_va_nostra]

The earliest layer: the kingdom sayings

The four gospels were written decades after the events by authors who do not name themselves. Mark, the earliest, is dated around 70 CE, either just before or just after the Roman destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem; it was therefore written after Paul's letters, not before them. [cite:vt20_wiki_mark] Mark summarises Yeshua's message in one line: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel." [cite:vt20_esv_mark1] The "kingdom of God" in this sense is God's rule arriving in the world, and much of the sayings tradition is about its timing and its nature.

One saying in Luke has become central to the reading this platform brings to the subject. Asked by Pharisees when the kingdom would come, Yeshua answers that it does not come with signs to be observed, because "the kingdom of God is entos hymōn". [cite:vt20_audit_esv_luke17] The King James Version (1611), Luther's Bible and the Latin Vulgate (intra vos) render the phrase "within you"; the Revised Standard and New Revised Standard versions and most modern Catholic and Protestant translations render it "among you" or "in the midst of you". Ilaria Ramelli, in a 2009 study of the ancient Syriac versions, argues that "inside" is the correct translation: the Greek for "among" would normally be en mesō, which Luke uses elsewhere; the sense "among" is, she writes, "practically unattested" for entos; and Greek church writers such as Origen and Athanasius read the phrase as "inside you". She notes that most modern commentators follow "among" without explaining why. [cite:vt20_ramelli_luke17] Her reading is a scholarly argument with evidence behind it, not a consensus; the translation question is genuinely open, and the book records it as contested.

The Gospel of Thomas, a collection of sayings known complete only from a Coptic manuscript copied shortly before 350 and found near Nag Hammadi in Egypt, carries the same theme in plainer form. Its third saying says that "the kingdom is inside of you, and it is outside of you"; its last-but-one says that "the kingdom of the father is spread out upon the earth, and men do not see it". [cite:vt20_thomas_lambdin] When Thomas was composed is disputed. Greek fragments found at Oxyrhynchus date from shortly after 200 onward; scholars who think it independent of the canonical gospels, such as Stephen Patterson and Ron Cameron, place it in the late first century, while others place it in the second, and the overall range proposed runs from about 50 to 140 CE. [cite:vt20_ecw_thomas] If the early date holds, Thomas preserves sayings as old as the gospels; if the late date holds, it is an early reading of them. Part Twenty-Five returns to Thomas in full ([scene:vt25_sayings_gospels|The Sayings Gospels]).

The face: what is documented about the image

No gospel describes Yeshua's appearance. The historian Joan Taylor, in What Did Jesus Look Like? (2018), concludes from skeletal studies of Second Temple Judaean populations and from the texts that he was most likely of average height for his time, about 165 centimetres, with "olive-brown skin, brown-black hair and brown eyes", and probably short hair. She finds that the earliest images show him as a philosopher figure, and that the long-haired, bearded type became standard between the fourth and seventh centuries, when artists borrowed the hair and beard of gods such as Serapis and Zeus to signal divinity. [cite:vt20_toi_taylor] The specifically white, often fair-haired Jesus is later still. The historians Edward Blum and Paul Harvey, in The Color of Christ (2012), trace how a white Jesus became widespread in the United States in the early nineteenth century and grew more Nordic in look between the 1880s and 1910s, and note that the Native American writer William Apess was already calling Jesus "a man of color" in the 1830s. [cite:vt20_unc_colorofchrist] Warner Sallman's Head of Christ, painted in 1940, was reproduced more than 500 million times by the end of the twentieth century. [cite:vt20_wiki_headofchrist] The image most people carry is therefore a documented artistic and cultural construction, centuries after the man; that much is record, not interpretation.

sections.h: Paul: Revelation, Tradition and the Quarrel with Jerusalem
sections.html:
Paul of Tarsus wrote the oldest surviving Christian documents, and he never met Yeshua during Yeshua's lifetime. Both facts are in the record, and both matter to the platform's question of how a movement around a Galilean teacher became an institution. This section sets out who Paul was, which letters are his, what he says about the source of his message, whom he actually met, and the one "council" he did attend, a meeting in Jerusalem around 48 to 50 CE, nearly three centuries before Nicaea.

Who he was and what he wrote

Paul was born around the turn of the era in Tarsus in Cilicia, described himself as "a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee" [cite:vt20_audit_esv_phil3], and by his own account persecuted the early followers of Yeshua before joining them, a turn usually dated to about 31 to 36 CE. He "did not know Jesus during his lifetime", but he knew eyewitnesses, including Peter and James, from the mid-30s onward. Tradition holds that he was executed in Rome under Nero, probably between the fire of July 64 and 68; the Acts of the Apostles ends before his death, and no New Testament text describes it. [cite:vt20_wiki_paul] [cite:vt20_audit_wiki_fire64]

Thirteen letters in the New Testament carry Paul's name. Critical scholars accept seven as his own: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon, written around the middle of the first century. Most regard Ephesians and the three Pastoral letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) as written in his name by later followers, and are divided on Colossians and 2 Thessalonians. The Letter to the Hebrews, traditionally counted as Paul's fourteenth, does not name its author, and most modern scholars do not think Paul wrote it. [cite:vt20_wiki_pauline] The widely repeated figure "Paul wrote 14 of the 27 books" counts Hebrews; the defensible figures are thirteen letters claiming his name and seven accepted as his. The distinction matters for what follows, because the Pastoral letters are where the New Testament sets out qualifications for "the office of overseer" (in Greek episkopos, the word later rendered "bishop"), and they are among the letters least likely to be Paul's own. [cite:vt20_esv_1tim3]

Revelation, not acquaintance

Paul's own account of his message is in the opening chapters of Galatians. He insists that the gospel he preaches "is not of human origin": "I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ." After that revelation, he writes, he "did not confer with any human being" and did not go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before him, but went into Arabia and returned to Damascus. [cite:vt20_nrsv_gal12] In 1 Corinthians he lists those to whom the risen Christ appeared, Cephas (Peter), the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James, all the apostles, and last of all himself. [cite:vt20_esv_1cor15] Paul, in other words, grounds his authority in a vision, not in having followed Yeshua in Galilee.

The same letters also show him receiving and passing on what others taught. 1 Corinthians 15 opens: "I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received." [cite:vt20_esv_1cor15] His account of the Last Supper is introduced, "I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you." [cite:vt20_esv_1cor11] Paul rarely quotes sayings of Yeshua, and when he does he marks them: on divorce he gives a charge as "not I, but the Lord", and a few lines later adds his own ruling, "I, not the Lord". [cite:vt20_esv_1cor7] Scholars debate how to reconcile "not from any human being" in Galatians with "what I also received" in Corinthians. One common answer is that Paul distinguishes the core of his gospel, which he says came by revelation, from traditions about Yeshua's death, resurrection appearances and words, which he learned from others. The record allows that reading; it also leaves Paul as the clearest early example of a teacher whose authority rested on a claimed direct revelation, a point Part Twenty-Four returns to when the same kind of claim is made by teachers the churches later called heretics ([scene:vt24_who_they_were|The Evangelical Gnostics]).

Whom he met

Paul's independence did not mean isolation. "After three years", he writes, he went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and stayed with him fifteen days, and saw no other apostle except "James the Lord's brother". [cite:vt20_nrsv_gal12] This is one of the most important sentences in early Christian history: a first-hand statement, from the 50s, by a man who spent two weeks with Yeshua's leading disciple and met Yeshua's brother, the same James whom Josephus records being stoned in Jerusalem decades later ([scene:vt20_yeshua_record|the previous section]). The claim that Paul "never met anyone who knew Jesus" is therefore wrong. The accurate statement is narrower: Paul never met Yeshua before the crucifixion, and he says his gospel did not depend on those who had.

The Jerusalem meeting and the Antioch quarrel

Fourteen years later Paul returned to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, a Greek convert, to lay his gospel before the leaders. He reports that Titus was not compelled to be circumcised; that the leaders "contributed nothing to me"; and that James, Cephas and John, "acknowledged pillars", gave him and Barnabas "the right hand of fellowship", agreeing that Paul would go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. They asked only that he "remember the poor", which he was eager to do. [cite:vt20_nrsv_gal12] This meeting is generally dated around 48 to 50 CE, and most scholars identify it with the gathering of "apostles and elders" that Acts 15 describes. In Acts' version the meeting issues a decree that Gentile converts need not keep the law of Moses but should abstain from food offered to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals and from sexual immorality; scholars debate the decree's origin, and Paul's own account does not mention it. [cite:vt20_wiki_jerusalem]

When readers ask about "Paul and the council deciding what Christianity would be", this is the council Paul took part in. It decided a real and lasting question: that non-Jews could join the movement without becoming Jews. It did not set a creed, a canon or a priesthood, and it was a meeting of a small Jewish sect's leaders, not of bishops summoned by an emperor. Nicaea, the council usually meant by that phrase, met in 325, about two and a half centuries after Paul's death, and is the subject of [scene:vt22_the_room|Part Twenty-Two].

The agreement did not hold smoothly. Paul reports that at Antioch he opposed Cephas "to his face" because Cephas, who had been eating with Gentile believers, withdrew from them after "certain people came from James". Paul's argument there is the core of his theology: a person is justified "not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ". [cite:vt20_nrsv_gal12] The record therefore shows a movement with at least two centres of authority within twenty years of the crucifixion, Jerusalem under James and Paul's Gentile churches, disagreeing openly over who could eat with whom and what the law required. Only Paul's side of the Antioch quarrel survives in his own words.

What Paul did and did not found

Paul is often called the second founder of Christianity, and in one respect the label fits: his letters are the earliest Christian texts and his Gentile mission shaped who the movement's members would be. The record does not support the stronger claim that Paul invented a hierarchy or a system of obligatory payments. His letters address communities meeting in houses, name women and men as fellow workers, and describe his collection for Jerusalem as explicitly voluntary; those details belong to [scene:vt20_first_communities|the next section]. The structures later read back into his name, a single bishop over each city, appear first in other writers, beginning with Ignatius of Antioch, and in the Pastoral letters that most scholars think he did not write. [cite:vt20_wiki_pauline] [cite:vt20_wiki_ignatius]

sections.h: The First Communities: Houses, a Common Purse and Gifts Without a Tithe
sections.html:
The thesis Book Two tests is that institutional religion built a mediated, taxed and obligatory system on top of teachings that offered direct access to God. The fairest place to begin testing it is with the earliest communities themselves: how they met, who led them, and how money moved among them, in the century and a half before any emperor favoured the movement. The sources are few and mostly written by insiders. Read together, they show voluntary giving and no tithe system, and they also show leadership offices and rules forming early, well before Rome's bishop had any special standing.

Meeting in houses

The first followers in Jerusalem, as the Acts of the Apostles tells it, attended the Temple "day by day" and broke bread "in their homes". [cite:vt20_esv_acts2] Paul's letters, the earliest evidence, greet congregations by the houses they met in: Prisca and Aquila, his "fellow workers", and "the church in their house". [cite:vt20_esv_rom16] There were no church buildings in this period. The Christian meeting place excavated at Dura-Europos on the Euphrates, from the following century, was a private house built in 232 or 233, probably converted for Christian use around 240 and abandoned in 256. [cite:vt20_wiki_dura] For about two centuries, a "church" (in Greek ekklēsia, an assembly) meant the people who gathered, usually in a member's home.

A Roman governor's report gives an outsider's view. Pliny the Younger, governing Bithynia-Pontus in northern Asia Minor around 111, wrote to the emperor Trajan that the Christians he interrogated met "on a fixed day before dawn", sang a hymn to Christ "as to a god", bound themselves by oath not to commit fraud, theft or adultery, and later shared a meal of "ordinary and innocent food". He had two slave women whom the Christians called deaconesses tortured and found nothing but what he called excessive superstition. [cite:vt20_wiki_pliny]

Women named in the record

The same letter of Paul that greets the house church of Prisca and Aquila commends Phoebe, "a servant of the church at Cenchreae", where the Greek word is the one later used for deacons and several modern translations render it "deacon"; it also greets Andronicus and Junia, who are "well known to the apostles"; the ESV notes that "apostles" can also be rendered "messengers". [cite:vt20_esv_rom16] With Pliny's two deaconesses, these are documented women in recognised roles within the first eighty years. How far those roles extended is debated; their presence in the sources is the finding.

The common purse in Acts

Acts describes the Jerusalem community as holding property in common. Believers "had all things in common", sold possessions and distributed the proceeds "as any had need"; they were "of one heart and soul", and "there was not a needy person among them". Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet. [cite:vt20_esv_acts2] [cite:vt20_esv_acts4] This is the community's own account, written by the author of Luke's gospel, most likely between 80 and 90 CE, several decades after the events, and scholars read it as history written with theological aims.
