[cite:vt20_wiki_acts]

Acts' own next story shows that sharing was not, in its telling, a compulsory levy. When Ananias and Sapphira sell land and secretly keep part of the price, Peter says to Ananias: "While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?" The fault Peter names is lying about the gift, "not to man but to God", not keeping property, although the story treats that deception with great severity. [cite:vt20_esv_acts5]

Paul's collection: voluntary by his own insistence

At the Jerusalem meeting the leaders asked Paul to "remember the poor". [cite:vt20_nrsv_gal12] He did so by organising a collection among his Gentile churches for the believers in Jerusalem. To Corinth he wrote that on "the first day of every week" each should put something aside "as he may prosper", so that nothing would need collecting when he arrived, and that the gift would be carried to Jerusalem by people the church itself chose. [cite:vt20_esv_1cor16] In 2 Corinthians he insists that it be "a willing gift, not as an exaction": each should give "as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver". [cite:vt20_esv_2cor9] The money went to the poor of another community, not to a priesthood, and Paul did not set a rate.

The Didache: support for prophets, and a rule against charging

The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, is a short church manual most scholars date to around 100 CE, within a range of about 50 to 120. It was lost for centuries and published in 1883 by Philotheos Bryennios from a manuscript copied in 1056. [cite:vt20_ecw_didache] Its rules on money run in two directions. A travelling apostle may stay one day, or two if needed, and "if he ask money, he is a false prophet". A true prophet who settles in a community, however, is "worthy of his support": the community is to give the first-fruits of its winepress, threshing floor and flocks to the prophets, "for they are your high priests", and if it has no prophet, to the poor; first-fruits of money and clothing are to be given "as it may seem good to you". [cite:vt20_na_didache] This is the nearest thing in the early sources to a regular offering for religious leaders. It is a first-fruits gift, not a fixed tenth; its amount for money and goods is left to the giver; and it is matched by a rule that a teacher who asks for money is a fraud.

The Didache also shows structure. It tells communities to gather "every Lord's day" to break bread, and to "appoint for yourselves bishops and deacons worthy of the Lord", men who are meek, truthful and "not lovers of money". [cite:vt20_na_didache] Leaders here are chosen by the community and serve beside the prophets; the text does not place one bishop over a city.

Justin and Irenaeus: still voluntary in the second century

In a defence of the Christians addressed to the emperor between about 155 and 157, Justin Martyr described their Sunday gathering. [cite:vt20_audit_wiki_1apol] The "memoirs of the apostles" or the prophets were read, the "president" taught, bread and wine were shared, and then "they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit". The money was "deposited with the president", who used it for orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers. [cite:vt20_justin_67] Around 180, Irenaeus of Lyon drew the contrast with tithes directly: the Jews had "the tithes of their goods consecrated" to God, whereas Christians, having received liberty, "set aside all their possessions for the Lord's purposes". [cite:vt20_na_irenaeus_iv18] Irenaeus's point is that Christian giving should exceed a tenth, not that it was a tax; in his telling, it rested on the giver's freedom.

The Catholic Church's own 1913 encyclopedia agrees that support for clergy "in the beginning" came from "the spontaneous offerings of the faithful", and dates the earliest positive church legislation on tithes to a letter of bishops at Tours in 567 and the Council of Mâcon in 585, with the first civil enforcement under Charlemagne at the end of the eighth century. [cite:vt20_cathen_tithes] On the record, then, there was no tithe system in the first centuries of the movement. How the tithe became a church law and then a state-enforced tax for about a thousand years is the subject of [scene:vt31_tithe|Part Thirty-One].

From assembly to bishop

The record that supports the thesis on money complicates it on mediation. A generation after the Didache, Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote a series of letters on his way to execution in Rome, traditionally dated around 108 to 110, though some scholars place them in the 140s or later. He is the earliest known writer to insist on a single bishop in each city, assisted by presbyters and deacons, and the first known to call the church "catholic", meaning universal. [cite:vt20_wiki_ignatius] To the church at Smyrna he wrote: "See that you all follow the bishop"; "wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude also be"; and "it is not lawful without the bishop either to baptize or to celebrate a love-feast". [cite:vt20_na_ignatius_smyrn] That is the first clear statement in the sources that access to the community's central rites runs through an office. It came from Antioch, not Rome, and from a man about to be killed by the empire, not one backed by it.

Part Twenty-Four follows the teachers of gnosis who flourished inside and beside these communities in the same decades ([scene:vt24_who_they_were|The Evangelical Gnostics]), and Part Thirty-One sets the two economies side by side ([scene:vt31_two_economies|Two Economies of the Sacred]).

chapters.label: Part Twenty-One
chapters.title: Constantine: Emperor, Pontifex, Patron
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-One follows the eighty years in which the Christian churches of the Roman Empire passed from persecution to establishment. It begins with Diocletian's Great Persecution of 303, when the state itself burned Christian scriptures, and follows Constantine from his proclamation in 306 through the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312, comparing the two contemporary accounts of his conversion, to the Milan letter of 313 and his deathbed baptism in 337. The second section tests the popular claims that cluster around him: that he merged sun worship with Christianity, that his Sunday law of 321 created Christian Sunday worship, that Christmas and the Eucharist were taken from Sol Invictus and Mithras, and that the popes inherited his title of Pontifex Maximus. The third section sets out what imperial favour gave the bishops (immunities, courts, buildings and land), the first imperial edict against named Gnostic and other dissenting groups, and the laws of Theodosius that by 395 made Nicene Christianity the only lawful public religion, ending with a table of the documented state orders to burn religious books.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty-One established that the church's alliance with Roman power was built in documented steps. The state burned Christian scriptures in 303; ten years later the Milan letter of 313 granted liberty to "the Christians and all others" and returned church property. [cite:vt21_lact_dmp] [cite:vt21_lact_dmp48] The earliest account of Constantine's conversion is a dream reported around 315; the sky vision appears only in Eusebius's life of the emperor written after 337, and why Constantine converted remains a matter of interpretation. [cite:vt21_lact_dmp44] [cite:vt21_vc1] [cite:vt21_wiki_relpol] He kept Sol on his coins until about 325 and gave the church a civic day of rest in 321, but the popular claims of a Mithraic Christmas and a papal title inherited from him fail: emperors held the title Pontifex Maximus until Gratian gave it up after 379, and popes took it up as an honorific in the fifteenth century. [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] [cite:vt21_wiki_mithraism] [cite:vt21_cameron_jrs] [cite:vt21_wiki_pontmax] The bishops gained immunities, courts and imperial basilicas; Constantine's edict closed the meeting houses of Valentinians and four other groups and ordered their books sought, and Theodosius's edict of 27 February 380 made the faith of the bishops of Rome and Alexandria the legal standard. [cite:vt21_hist_x7] [cite:vt21_bateman] [cite:vt21_vc3_65] [cite:vt21_wiki_thessalonica] Part Twenty-Two enters the council Constantine called in 325 and tests what it did and did not decide. [scene:vt22_the_room|Part Twenty-Two: Nicaea, 325]

sections.h: From Persecuted to Patronised: Constantine's Conversion, 303–337
sections.html:
Within ten years the Christian churches of the Roman Empire went from being hunted by the state to being paid by it. Nothing else in this book explains as much about what followed. Before 312 the bishops of Rome, Alexandria, Antioch and Carthage led communities with no legal standing, no tax privileges and no claim on the emperor. By the time Constantine died in 337, those bishops had imperial money, imperial basilicas, legal immunities and a say in imperial law, and the emperor had a say in what they taught. This section sets out how that change happened, what the two contemporary witnesses report about Constantine's turn to Christianity, and what can and cannot be known about why he made it.

The Great Persecution as the starting point

The last and harshest state persecution of Christians began under Diocletian. On 23 February 303, the festival of the Terminalia, the praetorian guard levelled the church at Nicomedia, Diocletian's eastern capital. The Christian rhetorician Lactantius, who lived in the city, wrote that "the books of the Holy Scriptures were found, and they were committed to the flames." [cite:vt21_lact_dmp] The edict published the next day ordered the destruction of Christian scriptures, liturgical books and places of worship across the empire, banned Christian assembly and stripped Christians of legal rights. A second edict in the summer of 303 ordered bishops and priests arrested, and a fourth, in 304, required every inhabitant to sacrifice to the gods on pain of death. [cite:vt21_wiki_dioclpers]

This matters for Book Two for two reasons. First, the largest documented burning of Christian scriptures in antiquity was carried out by a pagan state against the church, not by the church against anyone. Second, the persecution left a wound inside the church: clergy who had handed over scriptures to the authorities were called traditores, "those who handed over", and the refusal of rigorists in North Africa to accept bishops ordained by them produced the Donatist schism, the first church dispute that Constantine would be asked to settle. [cite:vt21_wiki_dioclpers]

How many Christians were there? No census exists. The historian Keith Hopkins offered a tentative estimate of about six million by the year 300, roughly a tenth of the empire's population. [cite:vt21_wiki_dioclpers] The figure is an estimate, but it makes the point that Constantine joined a large minority, not a majority.

The persecution ended in stages. In 311 the dying emperor Galerius issued an edict that allowed Christians "again to be Christians" and to rebuild their meeting places, asking only that they pray to their God for the emperor and the state. [cite:vt21_lact_dmp]

Two accounts of one battle

Constantine was proclaimed emperor by his father's army at York after his father Constantius died there on 25 July 306. [cite:vt21_wiki_constantine] Six years of civil war followed among the rival claimants. On 28 October 312 he defeated his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome; Maxentius drowned in the Tiber. [cite:vt21_wiki_milvian]

There are two Christian accounts of what happened before the battle, and they do not match. Lactantius, writing around 315, says Constantine was told in a dream to mark "the heavenly sign" on his soldiers' shields, and describes the mark as the Greek letter Chi (X) with an upright line drawn through it: most read this as an early form of the Chi-Rho, the first two Greek letters of "Christ". He reports no vision in the sky. [cite:vt21_lact_dmp44] Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, gave no vision at all in his Ecclesiastical History. Only in his Life of Constantine, written after the emperor's death in 337, does he describe a cross of light above the sun around midday, carrying the words "Conquer by this", seen by Constantine "and his whole army", followed that night by a dream in which Christ told him to copy the sign. Eusebius says the emperor told him the story himself many years later "and confirmed his statement by an oath". He then describes the labarum, the battle standard topped with the Chi-Rho. [cite:vt21_vc1] [cite:vt21_wiki_milvian]

Historians weigh these differently. Some, such as John Julius Norwich, think the sky vision never occurred because no source mentions it until a quarter of a century later; others, following Peter Weiss, suggest Constantine saw a solar halo, a ring of light around the sun, which he first read in solar terms and later in Christian ones. [cite:vt21_wiki_milvian] What can be said firmly is that the earliest account is a dream, the fuller account is late and comes from the emperor through his admirer, and the two agree only that a sign associated with Christ was used in the campaign.

The public monuments are more cautious than either writer. The Arch of Constantine, dedicated by the Roman Senate on 25 July 315, credits the victory to the emperor acting "instinctu divinitatis", by the prompting of the divinity, without saying which divinity, and carries no Christian symbol. [cite:vt21_wiki_arch] His coins went on showing the sun god Sol for more than a decade, a point taken up in the next section. [cite:vt21_wiki_sol]

The Milan letter of 313

In early 313 Constantine met his eastern co-emperor Licinius at Milan. The policy they agreed survives as a letter Licinius issued in the East, dated by Lactantius to 13 June 313. It is usually called the Edict of Milan, though it was not an edict and was not issued at Milan. Its core sentence grants that "the Christians and all others should have liberty to follow that mode of religion which to each of them appeared best". Property taken from Christian congregations was to be returned "without money demanded or price claimed", with buyers compensated from the imperial treasury. [cite:vt21_lact_dmp48]

Two things in the text deserve attention. It is a grant of freedom to everyone, not an establishment of Christianity. And it treats the church as a corporate body able to own property, which later imperial gifts would build on. Christianity became the established faith of the empire only under Theodosius, in the 380s, as the third section of this part shows. [scene:vt21_church_and_empire|Church and empire]

A baptism at the end

Constantine was not baptised until he was dying. In the spring of 337, ill near Nicomedia, he asked for baptism; Eusebius's Life has him say he had hoped to be baptised in the river Jordan, records that he wore white and would not put on the imperial purple again, and says he died at Pentecost. [cite:vt21_vc4] Eusebius of Caesarea does not name the bishop who baptised him. Other sources identify him as Eusebius of Nicomedia, the bishop who had sided with Arius in the dispute settled against Arius at Nicaea twelve years earlier ([scene:vt22_the_room|Part Twenty-Two]). [cite:vt21_wiki_constantine] He died on 22 May 337. [cite:vt21_brit_constantine]

A late baptism was not unusual in the fourth century: many Christians delayed it because baptism was believed to wash away all earlier sins. It is still a fact that the emperor who convened Nicaea, built basilicas and legislated for bishops did so for 25 years unbaptised, and was finally baptised by a bishop of the party Nicaea had condemned. In 326 he had his eldest son Crispus executed and his wife Fausta was killed soon after; the reasons are not recorded in any reliable source. [cite:vt21_wiki_constantine]

Why he did it: what the record allows

A common view frames the conversion as a political calculation. That is one reading among several, and the record does not settle it. Jacob Burckhardt in the nineteenth century saw Constantine as essentially unreligious, using the church for power; Peter Brown called it "a very Roman conversion", a soldier's bargain with a god who gave victory; Peter Leithart argues he was "a sincere if a somewhat simple believer"; H. A. Drake holds that his personal views favoured Christianity while his public policy aimed at civic unity among Christians and pagans alike. [cite:vt21_wiki_relpol]

The documented acts point both ways. He gave the church money, buildings and legal privileges and took part in its councils. He also kept pagan forms in public: the unnamed divinity on the arch, Sol on the coinage until the mid-320s, the old title of chief priest of the Roman cults, and an early edict letting polytheists keep their rites. After he defeated Licinius in 324 he destroyed a few temples and stripped many more of their treasures to pay for his new capital, Constantinople. [cite:vt21_wiki_relpol] A careful reader can say that Constantine chose the Christian God as his patron and the Christian church as his partner, and that he did so as a Roman emperor who expected his god to deliver victory and unity. What he believed in private, the sources cannot show.

sections.h: Sun, Sunday and the Chief Priest's Title
sections.html:
A large body of popular writing holds that Constantine fused the worship of the sun with Christianity and handed the papacy the pagan high priest's title, and that Christmas, Sunday and much of Christian ritual were borrowed from the cults of Sol Invictus and Mithras. Some of this rests on solid evidence and some on nineteenth-century speculation repeated until it sounded like fact. This section takes the four strands one at a time (the sun on the coins, the Sunday law, 25 December, and the title Pontifex Maximus) and separates what the documents show from what has been added since.

Sol on the coins

The cult of Sol Invictus, the Unconquered Sun, was given new imperial standing by the emperor Aurelian in 274, who built a temple to Sol in Rome and created a new college of priests for him. [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] Constantine's family had a particular attachment to the sun god. From 310 Sol replaced Mars on his coinage, and Sol continued to appear on his official coins until 325 or 326, more than a decade after the Milvian Bridge; one older study puts the last issues in 323. [cite:vt21_wiki_constantine] [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] After that the labarum and other Christian signs took its place. [cite:vt21_wiki_relpol]

This is a real and well-documented overlap. It shows an emperor who presented himself under the sun god's protection while he was already funding Christian churches. What it does not show is a planned merger of the two religions: the coins are evidence of what Constantine's mints put out, not of a policy to make Christians worship the sun. A mosaic in the Tomb of the Julii beneath St Peter's, dated to around 300 and so before Constantine, shows a figure in a sun chariot that most scholars read as Christ pictured as the sun; Steven Hijmans has argued it may simply show Sol. [cite:vt21_wiki_sol]

The Sunday law of 7 March 321

On 7 March 321 Constantine ordered: "On the venerable day of the Sun let the magistrates and people residing in cities rest". People working the land were left free to carry on. [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] The law names the day by its planetary name, which pagan and Christian subjects alike used. Eusebius, describing the same policy, says he "enjoined on all the subjects of the Roman empire to observe the Lord's day, as a day of rest", and adds that soldiers were assembled on an open plain each Lord's day to pray. [cite:vt21_vc4]

Did this move Christian worship from Saturday to Sunday? No. Christians had gathered on Sunday for nearly two centuries. Justin Martyr, writing in Rome around 155, explained to the emperor that "on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place", because it was the first day of creation and the day of the resurrection. [cite:vt21_justin67] What the 321 law did was new in a different way: for the first time, the Roman state set a weekly day of rest that matched the Christian day of worship, and made rest on it a legal requirement for city dwellers. A day the church kept by its own choice became a day the state enforced. How later church law turned Sunday into a duty under pain of sin is traced in Part Thirty-One. [scene:vt31_sunday_and_law|Sunday and law]

December 25

The first Christian record that Christ was born on 25 December is a Roman almanac of the mid-fourth century, the Philocalian calendar, part of the Chronography of 354, which notes "Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea" under that date. The same almanac marks 25 December as a festival of the Unconquered (Natalis Invicti). [cite:vt21_bas_mcgowan] [cite:vt21_wiki_sol]

Scholars offer two explanations, and the evidence does not settle between them. The "history of religions" theory holds that Christians in Rome placed Christ's birthday on a sun festival to replace it. Its difficulty, as Andrew McGowan sets out, is that no early Christian writer describes choosing the date for that reason, and the first explicit claim that the feast was moved to match the sun festival is a marginal note in a twelfth-century Syriac manuscript. The "calculation" theory holds that Christians dated Christ's conception to 25 March, the date they gave his death (Tertullian around 200 already equated the crucifixion with 25 March), and counted nine months forward. McGowan concludes that "we cannot be entirely sure". [cite:vt21_bas_mcgowan] Even the older side of the comparison is less firm than it is often stated: Hijmans argues that the earliest certain evidence for a sun festival on 25 December comes from the reign of Julian (361–363), not from Aurelian. [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] Neither theory involves Constantine: no law or letter of his concerns the date of Christmas.

Mithras: what the sources show

The claim that Mithras was born of a virgin on 25 December, had twelve disciples and rose from the dead circulates widely. The surviving evidence for the Roman Mithras cult, which flourished among soldiers from the first to the fourth century and had disappeared by about 400, does not support it. Mithras is shown being born from a rock, already a youth, with a dagger and a torch. The idea that his birthday was 25 December is a modern scholarly proposal, made by Maarten Vermaseren and rejected by Roger Beck; Manfred Clauss treats the 25 December festival as a general feast of the sun rather than a Mithraic one. Twelve figures do appear around some Mithraic reliefs, but they are the signs of the zodiac. [cite:vt21_wiki_mithraism]

There is one genuine ancient comparison. Justin Martyr, writing around 150, said that "wicked devils have imitated" the Christian Eucharist in the Mithraic rites, in which bread and a cup of water were offered to initiates; Tertullian later called a Mithraic washing and a mark on the forehead a counterfeit of baptism. [cite:vt21_wiki_mithraism] Christian writers themselves noticed the likeness and explained it as demonic imitation. Whether either rite influenced the other, and in which direction, cannot be shown from the surviving sources.

Pontifex Maximus: whose title, and when

The pontifex maximus was the head of the college of priests who oversaw the public cults of Rome. Augustus took the office, and from then on every emperor held it as one of his titles. Constantine kept it, as did his Christian sons; the Christian emperors appear to have treated it as a formality of the imperial style. [cite:vt21_cameron_jrs] [cite:vt21_wiki_pontmax]

The emperor who gave it up was Gratian. The only ancient source for the event, the pagan historian Zosimus, says Gratian refused the priestly robe because he thought it improper for a Christian, and places this at the start of his reign. Alan Cameron showed that this early date cannot be right, since Gratian was still addressed as pontifex in January 379; the repudiation came later, probably in the early 380s, when Gratian also cut the public funding of the pagan priesthoods and removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house. [cite:vt21_cameron_jrs] [cite:vt21_wiki_paganpers] His eastern colleague Theodosius used a different style, pontifex inclytus. [cite:vt21_wiki_pontmax]

The claim that the title passed straight from the emperors to the bishop of Rome does not hold. Christian writers did call bishops pontifex and summus pontifex, but loosely and of bishops in general; Tertullian, around 220, used "pontifex maximus" sarcastically of a bishop he was attacking. [cite:vt21_wiki_pontmax] Popes began to use "Pontifex Maximus" as a regular honorific in the fifteenth century, during the Renaissance revival of classical Latin; Paul II (1464–1471) is an early example. [cite:vt21_sn_pontmax] It is still not one of the official titles listed in the Holy See's yearbook, the Annuario Pontificio, where the nearest is "Supreme Pontiff of the Universal Church". [cite:vt21_wiki_pontmax] The papacy did borrow a pagan Roman title, but more than a thousand years after Constantine and as a scholar's flourish, not as a legal inheritance.

The honest summary is narrower than the popular one, and still significant. Constantine ruled as a Christian patron while keeping the sun god on his money and the pagan high priesthood among his titles, and he gave the church a state-enforced weekly holiday. Those are documented facts about how imperial power and Christian practice met. The stronger claims (a deliberate fusion of sun cult and church, a Mithraic Christmas, a papal title inherited from Constantine) are not supported by the sources cited for them.

sections.h: Church and Empire: Privilege, Law and the First Heresy Edicts, 313–395
sections.html:
The Milan letter of 313 made the church legal. What Constantine and his successors did over the next eighty years made it something else: a privileged corporation inside the Roman state, funded and protected by the emperor, with its bishops sitting as judges, and with imperial law standing behind its definition of right belief. The same decades produced the first imperial laws that closed the meeting houses of Christian groups the bishops called heretical, ordered their books searched out, and, by the end of the century, banned the public and private worship of the old gods. This section sets those acts out in order. It is the institutional ground on which the later history of suppression in Book Two stands.

Money, immunity and courts

Constantine's first privileges came almost at once. In a letter of 313 to Anullinus, the governor of Africa, he ordered that the clergy of the catholic church be "entirely exempted from all public duties", the costly civic offices that wealthy Romans were obliged to carry, so that they would not be "drawn away from the service due to the Deity". The stated reason was that their worship benefited the state. [cite:vt21_hist_x7]

He also made bishops judges. Two enactments, in 318 and 333, allowed litigants to take civil cases to a bishop's court, a practice later called episcopalis audientia. Constantine had already used bishops as judges in the Donatist dispute in North Africa, and in 316 he himself sat with bishop-judges to hear the appeal. C. G. Bateman argues that he trusted bishops as honest judges at a time when he was legislating against corruption in the ordinary courts. [cite:vt21_bateman] Whatever the motive, by the 330s a bishop was not only a pastor but a public magistrate.

Then came property. From 312 Constantine built the Lateran basilica in Rome on the site of a demolished barracks of the imperial horse guard, then Old St Peter's over the shrine on the Vatican hill, and in Jerusalem the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. [cite:vt21_wiki_constantine] Eusebius describes the Jerusalem works in detail: a shrine of Venus over the site was torn down, the ground dug out, and a basilica raised at imperial expense, with further churches at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives dedicated by his mother Helena. [cite:vt21_vc3] After 320 the emperor endowed churches with land and other wealth. [cite:vt21_wiki_relpol] These are the first imperial endowments behind the church's later landed wealth. A later forgery, the "Donation of Constantine", claimed that he had handed Pope Sylvester primacy over the great sees and control of Rome and the western regions; it was composed in the eighth century, as Part Two of Book One sets out. [cite:vt2_britannica_constantine] What the church holds today is examined in [scene:vt9_true_vs_public_wealth|Part Nine].

The edict against the heretics

The last step in that list is the one most relevant to Book Two, and it is rarely mentioned in popular accounts. Eusebius's Life of Constantine preserves an undated edict addressed to "Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Paulians, ye who are called Cataphrygians": that is, rigorist Novatian Christians, followers of the Gnostic teacher Valentinus, followers of Marcion, followers of Paul of Samosata, and the Montanists of Phrygia. [cite:vt21_vc3_64] It ordered that "none of you henceforth presume to assemble yourselves together", in public or "in any private house or place whatsoever", and that their meeting houses "be made over without delay to the catholic Church", with other property confiscated to the state. [cite:vt21_vc3_65] Eusebius adds that the law "directed that search should be made for their books", and that many members, deprived of their meeting places, returned to the church. [cite:vt21_vc3_66]

This is the documented point at which imperial power first acted against a Gnostic group by name. It confiscated buildings, which shows that Valentinians and others had meeting houses of their own, and it ordered their books sought. Eusebius does not say that the books were burned, and no surviving text records what happened to them. How strictly it was enforced is not recorded. The same emperor, in a letter after Nicaea, ordered that any treatise by Arius be "consigned to the flames", with death for anyone caught concealing one, an order discussed in the next part. [cite:vt21_socrates19] [scene:vt22_what_it_decided|What Nicaea decided]

Constantine also ordered Christian books made. In a letter preserved by Eusebius he asked for fifty copies of the scriptures, written on prepared parchment in a portable form, for the churches of his new capital. [cite:vt21_vc4] The letter does not list which books they contained, and claims that surviving fourth-century codices are among them are speculation.

Reversal and restoration

The partnership did not move in a straight line. Constantine's son Constantius II banned sacrifice in Italy in 341 and in 356 made it a capital crime, though there is no evidence that anyone was executed under the law. His cousin Julian (361–363), the last pagan emperor, reopened temples, withdrew Christian privileges and in 362 effectively barred Christians from teaching the classics. [cite:vt21_wiki_paganpers] Julian died within two years, and his successors restored the church's position.

Theodosius: one faith by law

The decisive legal step came under Theodosius I. On 27 February 380, with his co-emperors Gratian and Valentinian II, he issued the edict known from its opening words as Cunctos populos. It required all peoples under their rule to follow the faith "delivered to the Romans by the divine Apostle Peter", as professed by Damasus, bishop of Rome, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria: belief in one deity in the Holy Trinity. Those who did not were "foolish madmen" and heretics, could not call their meeting places churches, and faced divine condemnation first and then imperial punishment. [cite:vt21_wiki_thessalonica] The edict was directed at Christian dissent, chiefly the non-Nicene parties; it named two bishops, of Rome and Alexandria, as the measure of orthodoxy. The Council of Constantinople in 381 then gave the Nicene creed its final, expanded form. [cite:vt21_wiki_thessalonica]

The laws against the old religion followed a decade later. Gratian had already, around 382, cut the public subsidies of the pagan priesthoods and the Vestal Virgins and removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house. [cite:vt21_wiki_paganpers] A law of 391 ordered that "no one is to go to the sanctuaries, walk through the temples, or raise his eyes to statues"; another closed temples; and a sweeping law of 392 banned all sacrifice and worship, down to honouring the household gods with fire, wine or incense in a private home. Historians including Malcolm Errington question how far these laws were enforced, and archaeologists Luke Lavan and Michael Mulryan note that only four of 43 temple destructions reported in written sources are confirmed on the ground. [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] [cite:vt21_wiki_paganpers] By Theodosius's death in 395, Christianity in its Nicene form was the only lawful public religion of the empire, at least on paper.

Burning books by law

Because Book Two returns often to the question of burned books, the documented orders are worth setting side by side. The Roman state burned books before and after it became Christian, and the targets were defined by whoever held power.

The table shows something the popular story misses in both directions. Christian emperors did order heretical books destroyed, under pain of death, and Constantine's edict reached a Gnostic group by name. But the surviving orders name Arians, Eunomians, Montanists and Nestorians far more than they name Gnostic gospels, and no surviving imperial or conciliar text orders the gospels of Thomas, Mary or Philip burned. [cite:vt21_fc_laws] [cite:vt21_vc3_66] How those texts were lost, and how some were found again, is the subject of Parts Twenty-Three to Twenty-Six. [scene:vt23_left_out|What was left out]

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Two
chapters.title: Nicaea, 325
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-Two goes into the room at Nicaea in the summer of 325, the council without which there would be no imperial Church and, in time, no Vatican. The first section reconstructs who called the council, who paid for the bishops' travel, who came from where and who was missing, and where the emperor Constantine sat. The second sets out what the council actually decided, from its own creed and canons and the letters of men who were present: a definition of the Son's relation to the Father built around the word homoousios, which one eyewitness says the emperor urged; the exile of those who refused to sign; the burning of Arius's books; a common rule for Easter, announced in language about Jews that the Catholic Church formally repudiated in 1965; and twenty canons, one of which first ranked the great sees. The third tests a common summary of the founding, "Constantine an emperor, Paul who never met Yeshua, and the council decided what Christianity was going to be", alongside the most repeated claims about Nicaea: that it chose the Bible, voted Jesus divine, burned rival gospels and removed reincarnation. In this Part "Yeshua" refers to the historical figure and "Jesus Christ" or "the Son" to the subject of the councils' doctrine.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty-Two established what the Council of Nicaea did and did not do. Summoned by Constantine, carried by the imperial post and attended by 250 to 300 mostly eastern bishops, with Rome represented by two presbyters and no Ethiopian bishop yet in existence, the council adopted a creed defining the Son as "of one substance" with the Father, a term that Eusebius of Caesarea says the emperor himself urged. [cite:vt22_vc3] [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea] [cite:vt22_socrates1] Arius and the two bishops who refused to sign were exiled, and Constantine ordered Arius's writings "consigned to the flames" on pain of death; the council also fixed a common Easter, contained the Melitian schism, and in canon 6 recognised the regional authority of Alexandria, Rome and Antioch. [cite:vt22_socrates1] [cite:vt22_canons] It did not choose the books of the Bible, a story that goes back to the Synodicon Vetus of about 887 to 920 and was popularised by Voltaire; it did not invent belief in Christ's divinity, attested by Pliny around 111 to 113; it ordered no gospel burned; and it said nothing about reincarnation, a matter confused with the anathemas against Origen of 553. [cite:vt22_wiki_synodicon] [cite:vt22_pliny] [cite:vt22_origen_anath] Its lasting finding is a method: belief defined in a written formula, adopted under an emperor and enforced by the state. The books Christians would read were settled more slowly, through letters and regional councils, and Part Twenty-Three follows that process. [scene:vt23_lists_and_letters|Part Twenty-Three: How the Bible Was Made]

sections.h: The Room: Who Summoned Nicaea, Who Came, Who Ran It
sections.html:
The Council of Nicaea is often described as the moment when the Church took shape. It happened in a specific place: the lakeside town of Nicaea in north-western Asia Minor, near the emperor's residence at Nicomedia. It ran from about May to the end of July 325. Socrates Scholasticus, writing about a century later, dates the opening to 20 May; some modern historians think business began in June. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea] This section reconstructs the room from the people who described it: why it was called, who paid for the journey, who came and who did not, and where the emperor sat. The next section sets out what the room decided. [scene:vt22_what_it_decided|What Nicaea decided]

A quarrel in Alexandria becomes an imperial problem

The dispute began in Egypt around 318. Arius, a priest in Alexandria born about 250 in Libya, taught that the Son of God had been created by the Father and was not eternal. His bishop, Alexander of Alexandria, condemned the teaching, and a synod at Alexandria denounced Arius around 321. Arius did not go quietly. About 323 he set out his views in the Thalia ("Banquet"), a work in verse, and his ideas spread through popular songs. [cite:vt22_brit_arius] [cite:vt22_wiki_arianism] Bishops outside Egypt took sides, and by the time Constantine became sole ruler of the empire in 324 the eastern churches were divided.

Constantine's first move was a letter to both men, preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea in his Life of Constantine. In it the emperor called the cause "of a truly insignificant character, and quite unworthy of such fierce contention", described the matter as "this truly idle question", and asked the two to resume "your mutual feelings of friendship". [cite:vt22_vc2] The letter shows Constantine's priority at the start: peace among the bishops, not a ruling on the Son's nature. The letter failed, and the emperor then did something no emperor had done before. He called bishops from across the empire to one assembly under his own eye.

Summoned and carried by the state

Eusebius, who attended, says Constantine sent letters summoning the bishops and that "he allowed some the use of the public means of conveyance", while others were given horses. [cite:vt22_vc3] The imperial post was a state service normally reserved for officials. Using it for bishops was a material sign that the meeting was the emperor's project. Eusebius also describes a banquet for the twentieth year of Constantine's reign, held near the end of the council, at which "not one of the bishops was wanting". [cite:vt22_vc3] Bishops who had lived through the persecution begun under Diocletian in 303 now travelled at the emperor's expense and dined at his table. Part Twenty-One sets out how that change came about. [scene:vt21_church_and_empire|Church and empire under Constantine]

How many came, and from where

No full register of the council survives, and the figures differ by source. Eusebius gives "exceeding two hundred and fifty" in the Life of Constantine; Socrates, quoting the same passage, gives the number as one that "exceeded three hundred", and himself speaks of 318. [cite:vt22_vc3] [cite:vt22_socrates1] The figure of 318, which became the traditional number in later writers, matches the 318 servants of Abraham in Genesis 14 and is not a count. Contemporary reports range from about 250 to 300, and the surviving lists of signatures, copied in several languages, hold between 200 and 220 names. If the priests and deacons who travelled with each bishop are included, modern estimates of everyone present run from about 1,200 to 1,900. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea] A widely repeated figure of "1,800 invited bishops" has no ancient source: no invitation list survives, and the 1,800 figure seems to be a modern estimate of the number of sees in the empire, not of letters sent.

The room was overwhelmingly eastern and Greek-speaking. Only five western bishops are known to have attended: Hosius of Corduba in Spain, Caecilianus of Carthage, Nicasius of Die in Gaul, Marcus of Calabria and Domnus of Pannonia. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea] Eusebius notes the reach at the edges: "A Persian bishop too was present", and "even a Scythian" from the Black Sea region. [cite:vt22_vc3] The bishop of Rome, Sylvester, did not come. Eusebius says the bishop of the imperial city was absent because of his age, "but his presbyters were present, and supplied his place"; later lists name these two priests as Victor (or Vitus) and Vincentius. [cite:vt22_vc3] [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea] Rome's see was represented and respected, but it did not run the meeting. Alexandria, Antioch and the bishops of Asia Minor carried the debate.

Two absences are often misread. There was no Ethiopian bishop at Nicaea because there was not yet an Ethiopian bishop. The first, Frumentius, was consecrated for the kingdom of Aksum by Athanasius of Alexandria, traditionally in 328 and on other reckonings between 340 and 346; the Ethiopian church that grew from his mission accepts Nicaea. [cite:vt22_wiki_frumentius] Part Twenty-Seven tells that church's story. [scene:vt27_church_and_canon|The Ethiopian church and its canon] Nor is there a record that the council kept out bishops of rival Christian groups. The one documented case runs the other way. Sozomen reports that Constantine called Acesius, bishop of the Novatians, a rigorist church that had broken with the majority over readmitting Christians who had lapsed under persecution. Acesius accepted the creed and the Easter ruling but would not rejoin, and the emperor told him: "take a ladder and ascend alone to heaven". [cite:vt22_sozomen122] There is equally no record that Valentinians, Sethians or other teachers of gnosis were invited or debated. Their quarrels with the bishops had been fought in books during the second and third centuries; Nicaea was about something else.

Where the emperor sat

Eusebius describes the opening scene as theatre. The bishops waited in the palace hall in rows; Constantine entered "clothed in raiment which glittered as it were with rays of light", and he sat only when the bishops signalled, on "a low chair of wrought gold". [cite:vt22_vc3] Popular retellings turn this into a golden throne. The source says a low chair, and the detail matters to Eusebius because it shows the emperor deferring to the bishops in form. In substance he was the most powerful person present. He spoke in Greek, and Eusebius says he heard each side and moved the most heated toward agreement by "occasionally assisting the argument of each party in turn". [cite:vt22_vc3]

Constantine was not a bishop and did not vote; he was baptised only on his deathbed in 337. Hosius of Corduba, a western bishop close to the court, most likely presided over the sessions as the emperor's representative. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea] [cite:vt22_wiki_eusnic] That arrangement, a bishop presiding and an emperor present, summoning, paying and later enforcing, is the core of what Nicaea changed. Before 325 bishops had met in regional synods on their own initiative. At Nicaea the question of how Christians should describe their God was settled in a hall of the imperial palace, by men brought there by the state, in a session the emperor opened.

The room was therefore neither a free assembly of all Christians nor a stage-managed vote. It was a gathering of several hundred mostly eastern bishops, summoned and supplied by an emperor who wanted unity, in which one priest's teaching was on trial. What they produced, and how the emperor's preferences shaped it, is the subject of the next section. [scene:vt22_what_it_decided|What Nicaea decided]

sections.h: What Nicaea Decided: A Creed Under an Emperor's Eye
sections.html:
The Council of Nicaea did not decide which books were in the Bible, and it did not invent belief in the divinity of Jesus Christ; the next section tests both claims. What it did decide is large enough on its own. In the summer of 325, with the emperor present, the assembled bishops adopted a single written definition of how the Son relates to the Father, wrote into it a philosophical term that appears nowhere in the scriptures, attached curses to the opposing view, and saw the emperor exile those who would not sign and order the losing side's books burned. It also fixed a common rule for Easter, settled a schism in Egypt and issued twenty canons on church order. This section sets out each decision from the council's own texts and the letters of the men who were there. [cite:vt22_canons] [cite:vt22_socrates1]

The question on trial

Arius's position, as his opponents recorded it and as the council condemned it, was that "there was a time when the Son was not": the Son was begotten by the Father before time, but he was not eternal alongside the Father and was a creature, however exalted. [cite:vt22_wiki_arianism] Arius did not deny that Christ was divine in some sense; his surviving fragments call the Son God, but a God who had a beginning. [cite:vt22_wiki_arianism] His opponents, led by Alexander of Alexandria, held that the Son was eternal and shared the Father's own being, and argued that a Christ who was less than fully God could not carry the gospel's promise of salvation. [cite:vt22_canons] [cite:vt22_america_hagen] The dispute was therefore not whether Christ was divine, but what kind of divine and on whose terms.

The creed and the word homoousios

The creed the council adopted begins "We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible", and says of the Son that he is "of one substance" with the Father, in Greek homoousion. It ends with anathemas against anyone who says "that there was a time when the Son of God was not", that he was created, changeable, or of another substance than the Father. [cite:vt22_canons] The Holy Spirit receives one line. The creed is short and polemical: it was written to exclude Arius, not to summarise all Christian belief.

The decisive word came, by the account of one bishop in the room, from the emperor. Eusebius of Caesarea, a moderate who had been sympathetic to Arius, wrote to his own church explaining why he had signed. He said he had offered a creed from his home church, and that "our most pious emperor himself was the first to admit that they were perfectly correct", urging all to subscribe "with the insertion, however, of that single word homoousios". The emperor then explained that the word did not imply anything bodily, and on that reading Eusebius accepted it, "having regard to peace". [cite:vt22_socrates1] Eusebius had reason to present his signature as the emperor's wish rather than his own surrender, and other accounts credit Hosius of Corduba and Alexander with promoting the word. What is not in doubt is that Constantine and Hosius backed it. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea]

The term was not new, and its earliest surviving uses come from the very teachers the bishops called heretics. The Alexandrian teacher Basilides, in the first half of the second century, and the Valentinian Ptolemy, in his Letter to Flora, both used homoousios for divine beings that share the nature of their source; Origen was the first writer in the later orthodox line to apply it to the Father and the Word. [cite:vt22_wiki_homoousion] A council at Antioch around 268 had condemned the word in the case of Paul of Samosata, and opponents at Nicaea objected that it was unscriptural. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea] [cite:vt22_wiki_homoousion] Part Twenty-Four returns to Basilides and Ptolemy. [scene:vt24_what_they_taught|What the Evangelical Gnostics taught] Its meaning was disputed for the next fifty years. That a contested philosophical word, absent from scripture, became the test of orthodoxy at an emperor's urging is the council's most consequential finding, and the record supports it directly.

Signatures, exile and the burning order

The council's own synodal letter, preserved by Socrates, reports that Theonas of Marmarica and Secundus of Ptolemais refused to sign and "suffered the same condemnation" as Arius. [cite:vt22_socrates1] Socrates himself names five bishops who objected to homoousios: Eusebius of Nicomedia, Theognis of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon, Theonas and Secundus. [cite:vt22_socrates1] The two accounts can be reconciled. Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis of Nicaea objected but in the end signed the creed, Eusebius after long resistance; both were exiled a few months after the council, Eusebius for his continued contacts with Arius's party, and Eusebius was restored about 329. [cite:vt22_wiki_eusnic] [cite:vt22_audit_wiki_theognis] Arius, Theonas and Secundus were excommunicated and sent into exile in Illyria. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea] The penalty for refusing a church definition was imposed by the state.

The emperor then wrote "to the bishops and people". He ordered that Arius and his followers be called "Porphyrians", after a pagan philosopher who had written against Christianity, and he commanded that "if any treatise composed by Arius should be discovered, let it be consigned to the flames"; anyone found hiding one faced death. [cite:vt22_socrates1] This is the one documented order to burn books in the Nicene story. It concerned Arius's own writings, not any gospel. Historians accept that burning took place to some degree, but no execution under the order is recorded. [cite:vt22_wiki_arius] Its effect on the record is visible: Arius's Thalia survives only in fragments quoted by his opponents, chiefly Athanasius. [cite:vt22_wiki_arius]

Easter, and the language used about Jews

The council's second task was the date of Easter. Some eastern churches calculated it from the Jewish reckoning of Passover; Rome and Alexandria did not. The synodal letter says those "who have heretofore kept this festival when the Jews did" would now conform to Rome and Alexandria. [cite:vt22_socrates1] The council set uniformity as the rule but, as far as the record shows, did not prescribe a method of calculation. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea]

Constantine's letter announcing the Easter ruling to the churches justified it in hostile terms. It speaks of "the detestable Jewish crowd" and of "that nation of parricides who slew their Lord". [cite:vt22_vc3] Those phrases are the emperor's, written to make a calendar decision into a mark of separation from Judaism, and they became part of a long tradition of Christian anti-Jewish polemic. The Catholic Church formally rejected the collective charge behind them at the Second Vatican Council. Nostra Aetate, proclaimed on 28 October 1965, states that Christ's passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive", nor against Jews today, and "decries hatred, persecutions, displays of anti-Semitism, directed against Jews at any time and by anyone". [cite:vt22_nostra]

The Melitians and the twenty canons

The synodal letter also dealt with Melitius of Lycopolis, an Egyptian bishop who had ordained clergy in rivalry with Alexandria. He was allowed to "remain in his own city but exercise no authority either to ordain or nominate for ordination". [cite:vt22_socrates1] The settlement did not hold, and the Melitians later allied with Arius's supporters against Athanasius. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea]

The twenty canons are rules of church order, and several had long consequences. Canon 6 confirmed that "the ancient customs in Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis prevail", giving the bishop of Alexandria authority over those provinces, "since the like is customary for the Bishop of Rome also", and kept Antioch's privileges. Canon 7 gave the bishop of Jerusalem, then called Aelia, a place of honour while preserving the rights of his metropolitan. [cite:vt22_canons] This is the first time a general council recognised that some bishops held authority over whole regions: the start of the system later called the patriarchates, in which Rome was one great see among several. Fifty-six years later the Council of Constantinople gave Constantinople "the prerogative of honour after the Bishop of Rome" because it was "New Rome". [cite:vt22_wiki_const381] Other canons set terms for receiving clergy of the Novatian church, whom the council called Cathari ("the pure"), unrelated to the medieval Cathars, and required followers of Paul of Samosata to be rebaptised. Canon 20 ordered that prayer on Sundays and at Pentecost be made standing. None of the twenty names a book of scripture. [cite:vt22_canons]

What happened next

Nicaea did not end the dispute. Constantine became more lenient toward the exiles within a few years. [cite:vt22_wiki_arianism] A synod at Jerusalem restored Arius to communion in 336, and he died in Constantinople that year before he could be received; Socrates presented the death as divine judgement, and some modern scholars suspect poison. [cite:vt22_wiki_arius] The bishop who baptised Constantine on his deathbed in May 337 was Eusebius of Nicomedia, the exile of 325. [cite:vt22_wiki_eusnic] Constantine's son Constantius II favoured Arius's heirs, and after the twin councils of Rimini and Seleucia in 359, Jerome wrote that the world "awoke with a groan to find itself Arian". [cite:vt22_wiki_arianism] The Nicene position was restored only when Theodosius I convened about 150 eastern bishops at Constantinople in 381, which reaffirmed and expanded the creed. [cite:vt22_wiki_const381]

The documented finding is therefore precise. Nicaea did not create Christianity, but it created a new way of deciding what Christianity was: a written test of belief, framed in disputed philosophical language, adopted in the emperor's presence, and enforced by exile and the burning of books. That method outlived Constantine and every one of the bishops in the room.

sections.h: Myths Tested: What Nicaea Did Not Do, and What It Did
sections.html:
A common summary of the founding of institutional Christianity runs like this: Constantine, an emperor; Paul, who never met Yeshua; and a council that decided what Christianity was going to be. Each of the three parts points at something real. Each also carries a popular overstatement that the record does not support. This section tests the summary piece by piece, and then tests the most widely repeated claims about Nicaea itself: that it chose the Bible, that it voted Jesus divine by a narrow margin, that it burned rival gospels, that it removed reincarnation from Christian teaching, that it shut out Ethiopian or Gnostic bishops, and that the creed said in churches today is the one written in 325. The aim is not to defend the council. The previous section showed that its central act, a definition of Christ's nature adopted under an emperor's eye and enforced by exile and book-burning, is a documented finding. [scene:vt22_what_it_decided|What Nicaea decided] The aim is to keep that finding from being buried under claims that fail.

Constantine: supported, with one correction

The emperor's part is the strongest element of the summary. Constantine summoned the bishops, moved them by the imperial post, opened the council in person, and, on the testimony of Eusebius of Caesarea, urged the insertion of the word homoousios into the creed. He then exiled the bishops who would not sign and ordered Arius's books burned. [cite:vt22_vc3] [cite:vt22_socrates1] The correction concerns motive and consistency. His own letter of about 324 called the dispute "this truly idle question", which suggests he wanted agreement more than any particular answer, and within a few years he recalled the exiles. The bishop who baptised him in 337 was Eusebius of Nicomedia, one of the men exiled after Nicaea. [cite:vt22_vc2] [cite:vt22_wiki_eusnic] Constantine shaped the outcome of 325, but he did not hold to it as a fixed doctrine of state; that came later, under Theodosius I. Part Twenty-One covers the emperor's conversion and titles. [scene:vt21_conversion|Constantine's conversion]

Paul: real, but not at Nicaea

Paul's own letters claim a revelation of the risen Christ rather than acquaintance with Yeshua in life, and they also record that he met Peter and James in Jerusalem; Part Twenty sets out that record. [scene:vt20_paul|Paul] Paul had no part in Nicaea. He wrote in the first century, and the council he describes attending was the meeting in Jerusalem of Galatians 2: "after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas". [cite:vt22_gal2] By 325 his letters had been read in churches for more than two centuries, and both Arius and his opponents argued from them. The point in the summary that holds is that Paul's letters, written by a man who knew the risen Christ only by his own account of revelation, were already the shared foundation of the debate at Nicaea. The council did not add them; it inherited them.

"The council decided what Christianity would be": partly supported

Nicaea decided one central question, the relation of the Son to the Father, for the churches in communion with the emperor, and set the method by which later councils would decide others. That is a large finding. It did not decide the scriptures, it did not create belief in Christ's divinity, and it did not settle even its own question: the Nicene party lost imperial favour within a generation and regained it only in 381. [cite:vt22_wiki_arianism] [cite:vt22_wiki_const381] Nor did it decide for all Christians. Communities outside the empire and groups already separated, such as the Novatians, kept their own life; the Novatian bishop Acesius accepted the creed and still refused to rejoin. [cite:vt22_sozomen122]

The canon and the altar

The most widespread claim is that Nicaea chose the books of the Bible. Its creed and twenty canons name no book of scripture, and no ancient account of its sessions mentions a list. [cite:vt22_canons] The first list matching the 27 books of the New Testament is Athanasius's letter of 367, more than forty years later; Part Fourteen sets out the steps from the second century to Trent in 1546, and Part Twenty-Three goes deeper. [scene:vt14_canon|Who chose the Bible] [scene:vt23_lists_and_letters|Lists and letters]

The claim has a traceable origin. The Synodicon Vetus, a Greek summary of church councils written between about 887 and 920, says the books were "placed down by the holy altar" and that the council prayed for the inspired works to be found on top and the spurious beneath. It is the earliest source to link the canon to Nicaea, and historians describe it as unreliable and full of errors. [cite:vt22_wiki_synodicon] It was first printed in 1601 by the theologian Johannes Pappus, from a copy supplied by Andreas Darmarios, a manuscript dealer with a poor reputation. [cite:vt22_wiki_synodicon] In the eighteenth century Voltaire retold the story in his Philosophical Dictionary, with the books to be rejected falling to the floor, and added drily: "It is a pity that this eloquent procedure has not survived". [cite:vt22_voltaire] Voltaire is the main channel through which the altar story, and the wider idea that Nicaea made the canon, reached modern readers. [cite:vt22_wiki_nicaea] [cite:vt22_wiki_synodicon]

"They voted Jesus divine"

Dan Brown's novel The Da Vinci Code (2003) told readers that Christ's divinity was passed at Nicaea by "a relatively close vote". [cite:vt22_america_hagen] Two parts of that are wrong. First, there was no close vote: all but two bishops signed. [cite:vt22_socrates1] Second, Christians called Christ divine long before 325. Around 111 to 113 the Roman governor Pliny reported to the emperor Trajan that Christians in Asia Minor met before dawn to sing "a hymn to Christ as to a god". [cite:vt22_pliny] Ignatius of Antioch, writing early in the second century, called him "our God, Jesus Christ". [cite:vt22_ignatius] Arius himself called the Son God. [cite:vt22_wiki_arianism] What Nicaea voted on, if subscription under the emperor's eye can be called a vote, was a definition of how the Son is divine: eternal and of the Father's own substance, against Arius's created Son. A fairer statement of the platform's point is that the council chose one disputed account of Christ's divinity and made it binding. The record supports that statement.

"They burned the other gospels"

The one documented burning order of the council's aftermath is Constantine's letter commanding that Arius's treatises be "consigned to the flames". [cite:vt22_socrates1] No order from Nicaea, or from Constantine in connection with it, concerns the Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Mary or any other gospel. The Nag Hammadi codices were buried in Egypt some decades later for reasons that are not documented; Part Twenty-Five sets out the hypotheses. [scene:vt25_the_jar|The jar] Constantine did act against a Gnostic group by name, in a separate edict that Eusebius preserves without a date. Addressed to "Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Paulians" and Montanists, it forbade them to "assemble yourselves together" in public or in "any private house", and ordered their houses of prayer "made over without delay to the catholic Church". [cite:vt22_vc3_64] [cite:vt22_vc3_65] Eusebius adds that the law ordered a search for their books, but he does not say the books were burned, and no surviving text records what was done with them. [cite:vt22_audit_vc3_66] That edict suppressed meetings, confiscated buildings and sought out books; it is not an order to burn gospels. Part Twenty-One places it in Constantine's wider church policy. [scene:vt21_church_and_empire|Church and empire] The documented suppression of books at Nicaea is real but narrow: it was aimed at the losing party in the council's own dispute.

"They removed reincarnation"

Nothing in the creed or canons of 325 concerns reincarnation or the fate of souls. [cite:vt22_canons] The claim usually confuses Nicaea with a council held 228 years later. In 553 the Second Council of Constantinople met under the emperor Justinian, chiefly to condemn writings known as the Three Chapters; a set of fifteen anathemas against the teachings of Origen and Evagrius, which most scholars think the bishops signed before the council formally opened, condemned "the fabulous pre-existence of souls" and the "restoration" of all things. [cite:vt22_wiki_const553] [cite:vt22_origen_anath] Pre-existence of the soul is not the same as reincarnation, and no book of the Bible was edited as a result. The documented act is a sixth-century condemnation of a speculative teaching associated with Origen, not a removal of reincarnation from scripture at Nicaea.

"Ethiopian and Gnostic bishops were shut out"

Ethiopia had no bishop until Athanasius consecrated Frumentius, traditionally in 328 and possibly in the 340s. [cite:vt22_wiki_frumentius] No record says that teachers of gnosis were invited or barred. The one rival bishop known to have been present, the Novatian Acesius, was called by the emperor himself. [cite:vt22_sozomen122] The council's canons also set terms for receiving Novatian and Paulianist clergy into communion, which shows the council dealing with other Christian groups by rules of admission rather than by exclusion from the room. [cite:vt22_canons]

"The creed said on Sunday is the creed of 325"

The creed recited in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and many Protestant services is the longer Niceno-Constantinopolitan form. Compared with 325, it adds clauses on the Holy Spirit, the Church, baptism and the resurrection, adds "whose kingdom shall have no end", and drops the anathemas. No surviving document quotes it before the Council of Chalcedon in 451, which accepted it as an authentic interpretation of Nicaea. [cite:vt22_wiki_creed] Latin churches later added that the Spirit proceeds from the Father "and the Son" (Filioque); Rome took the addition into its liturgy in 1014, and the Eastern Orthodox churches still reject it. [cite:vt22_wiki_creed] The words most Christians say are therefore the product of at least three councils and a later western addition, not of Nicaea alone.

Tested this way, the summary loses its two weakest parts and keeps its strongest. Paul was not in the room and the Bible was not on the table. An emperor was, and the council he convened established that the content of Christian belief could be defined in a written formula and enforced with exile and fire. Which books Christians would read was settled by a different and slower process, in letters and regional councils over the following two centuries, and Part Twenty-Three follows it. [scene:vt23_lists_and_letters|How the Bible was made]

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Three
chapters.title: How the Bible Was Made
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-Three tells how Christians came to agree, and still disagree, on which books are scripture. Part Fourteen gave the milestones and showed that the Council of Nicaea did not choose the Bible; this part goes into the documents themselves. The first section reads the lists and letters that did the sorting, from Irenaeus of Lyon around 180 through the Muratorian fragment, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius's Easter letter of 367, the African councils and Jerome, to the Council of Trent's binding vote of 8 April 1546. The second section names the books that were left out, who excluded each and in what document, and counts what was in circulation against what was kept, to test how much of the claim that the institution "suppressed most of the books" the record supports. The third sets the four Bibles in use today side by side: the Protestant 66, the Catholic 73, the Eastern Orthodox list of about 76 and the Ethiopian 81.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty-Three established that the Christian canon was sorted over three centuries by named bishops and scholars in Lyon, Alexandria, Antioch, Caesarea, Bethlehem and Carthage, with Rome asked to confirm Africa's list in 419 and doubting Hebrews in Eusebius's day, and was made binding for Catholics only at Trent on 8 April 1546, by 24 votes to 15. [cite:vt23_na_irenaeus_3_11] [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] [cite:vt23_na_carthage] [cite:vt14_wiki_trentcanon] Measured by gospels and revelations, most of the books named in the sources were left out: four of at least twenty-one gospels and one of five revelations were kept. Measured against the books bishops actually debated, most were kept: 27 of the 38 titles in Eusebius's catalogue. [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] [cite:vt23_tert_decretum] [cite:vt23_bt_origen_luke] The documents excluded books from public worship, warned against them and pronounced anathemas, but none examined here ordered a gospel destroyed; the documented burning order of the period was Constantine's against Arius's writings. [cite:vt23_na_festal39] [cite:vt23_na_socrates1] Today's Bibles still differ, from the Protestant 66 to the Ethiopian 81, which keeps Enoch and Jubilees. [cite:vt23_wiki_ot] [cite:vt14_wiki_tewahedo] Part Twenty-Four turns to the people who read many of the excluded books: the teachers of gnosis whom the Sophia platform calls the Evangelical Gnostics. [scene:vt24_who_they_were|Part Twenty-Four: The Evangelical Gnostics]

sections.h: Lists and Letters: How the Books Were Sorted, c.180 to 1546
sections.html:
Part Fourteen set out the milestones of the Christian canon and corrected the claim that the Council of Nicaea chose the Bible. [scene:vt14_canon|Who Chose the Bible] This section goes one layer down, into the documents themselves: who wrote each list, where, for what audience, and in what words. The pattern that emerges is that most of the sorting was done in letters, sermons and handbooks written by individual bishops and scholars in Lyon, Alexandria, Caesarea, Carthage and Bethlehem, and only at the end by councils. The see of Rome was one voice among several for most of this period, and at one point was itself the doubter. The first binding definition of the full list by the Roman Church came in 1546. [cite:vt14_wiki_ntcanon] [cite:vt14_wiki_trentcanon]

Why four gospels: Irenaeus, c.180

The earliest surviving argument that there must be exactly four gospels comes from Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon in Gaul, in his work Against Heresies, written around 180. He wrote that "it is not possible that the Gospels can be either more or fewer in number than they are", and supported the number by pointing to "four zones of the world" and "four principal winds", and to the four-faced cherubim. [cite:vt23_na_irenaeus_3_11] The argument is theological, not historical: it does not say how the four had been chosen, only that four was fitting. In the same passage Irenaeus rejected a book that the followers of Valentinus called "the Gospel of Truth", which he described as "comparatively recent" and "totally unlike" the gospels handed down from the apostles. [cite:vt23_na_irenaeus_3_11] A Coptic text known by that title was among the books found at Nag Hammadi in 1945. [cite:vt14_wiki_naghammadi] [scene:vt25_sayings_gospels|The Nag Hammadi gospels]

The Muratorian fragment

The oldest surviving list of New Testament books is a damaged Latin text named after the scholar Muratori, who discovered it. It survives in a single copy, in poor Latin, and was probably drawn up in Greek. Most scholars date the list to about 170 to 200, partly because it calls the Shepherd of Hermas recent; a minority date it to the fourth century. [cite:vt23_ecw_murat] Its contents show how open the edges still were. It accepts the Wisdom of Solomon, a book now in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, which it says was "written by the friends of Solomon in his honour". It accepts two revelations, John's and Peter's, adding that "some of us are not willing that the latter be read in church". It says the Shepherd was written "very recently, in our times" and "ought indeed to be read", but not publicly in church. [cite:vt23_ecw_murat_metzger]

The fragment also names what it rejects. Letters to the Laodiceans and the Alexandrians, "forged in Paul's name" to support the teaching of Marcion, are refused because "it is not fitting that gall be mixed with honey". The list ends by accepting "nothing whatever" of Arsinous, Valentinus or Miltiades, and rejecting Basilides. [cite:vt23_ecw_murat_metzger] Hebrews, James and the letters of Peter do not appear in the surviving text, though the beginning of the page is lost, so their absence is not proof of rejection. [cite:vt23_ecw_murat_metzger]

Origen and Eusebius: the scholars' shelves

Origen of Alexandria, the most prolific Christian scholar of the third century, called the four gospels "the only indisputable ones in the Church of God under heaven". He counted the Old Testament books "as the Hebrews have handed them down" at twenty-two, and openly recorded doubts: 2 Peter was "doubtful", not everyone accepted 2 and 3 John, and as for who wrote Hebrews, "God knows". [cite:vt23_na_eus_he6] Commenting on the opening of Luke, he contrasted the Church's four gospels with the several held by "heresy", naming gospels of the Egyptians, of the Twelve, of Basilides, of Thomas and of Matthias. [cite:vt23_bt_origen_luke]

A story preserved by Eusebius shows how local the decisions were. Serapion, bishop of Antioch around 200, first told the congregation at Rhossus in Syria that if a Gospel of Peter was the only thing dividing them, "let it be read". After reading the book himself and finding additions he judged unorthodox, he wrote against it as falsely ascribed to Peter. [cite:vt23_na_eus_he6] One bishop, one town and one book: this is the scale at which much of the early sorting happened.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine and the first historian of the Church, wrote around 325 the most systematic account. In Book III of his Church History he sorted the books into four shelves. Recognised: the four gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul, 1 John, 1 Peter and, "if it seem proper", Revelation. Disputed but "recognized by many": James, Jude, 2 Peter, and 2 and 3 John. Spurious: the Acts of Paul, the Shepherd, the Apocalypse of Peter, the Letter of Barnabas, the Teachings of the Apostles and the Gospel according to the Hebrews. And a fourth group "put forward by heretics": the Gospels of Peter, Thomas and Matthias and the Acts of Andrew and John, which he said should be "cast aside as absurd and impious". [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] Elsewhere he called Paul's fourteen letters "well known and undisputed", while noting that some rejected Hebrews, "saying that it is disputed by the church of Rome". [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] In the early fourth century, then, Rome was the church holding back on one of the books now in every Bible.

Athanasius, 367

Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, used his Easter letter of 367 to give his churches a list. It counts twenty-two Old Testament books, including Baruch and "the epistle" with Jeremiah but not Esther, then the twenty-seven books of today's New Testament. "These are fountains of salvation", he wrote. A second group, Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Teaching of the Apostles and the Shepherd, was not in the canon but appointed to be read by new converts. Books called apocryphal he dismissed as "an invention of heretics". [cite:vt23_na_festal39] The letter warns; it orders nothing burned, as Part Fourteen showed. [scene:vt14_canon|Part Fourteen on Athanasius]

Africa writes to Rome

The Council of Hippo in 393 is the first council known to have accepted the present New Testament list, and councils at Carthage repeated it in 397 and 419. [cite:vt14_wiki_ntcanon] The canon as preserved in the African code of 419 is headed "That nothing be read in church besides the Canonical Scripture", which shows what a canon was for: a rule about public reading in worship. Its Old Testament includes Tobit, Judith, two books of Maccabees and "five books of Solomon", and a separate canon allows the stories of martyrs to be read on their feast days. The bishops ordered the list sent to "our brother and fellow bishop, Boniface", the bishop of Rome, and to other bishops, so that they might confirm it. [cite:vt23_na_carthage] Rome was asked to agree with Africa, not to decide for it. The claim that a council at Rome under Pope Damasus had already issued the list in 382 rests on the Gelasian Decree, which Ernst von Dobschütz judged a pseudonymous compilation of 519 to 553; the attribution remains disputed. [cite:vt23_wiki_gelasian] [cite:vt14_wiki_rome382]

Jerome's doubts

Jerome, the scholar who made the Latin translation later called the Vulgate, worked from the Hebrew where he could, and the Hebrew Bible did not contain several books that Greek-speaking Christians read. In the preface known as the Prologus Galeatus (391–392) he put Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit and the Shepherd outside the canon, "among the apocrypha". [cite:vt23_wiki_galeatus] In his preface to the books of Solomon he wrote that the Church reads Judith, Tobit and Maccabees "but does not admit them among the canonical Scriptures", and reads Wisdom and Sirach "for the edification of the people, not to give authority to doctrines". [cite:vt23_ccel_jerome_solomon] He translated Judith anyway, and in its preface gave a reason that touches this book's earlier parts: the Council of Nicaea, he said, "is read" to have counted Judith among the scriptures. [cite:vt23_gallagher_htr2015] No canon of Nicaea records any such decision; it is a report, not a document. [cite:vt23_owiki_otcanon] [scene:vt22_myths_tested|Nicaea's myths tested]

From Florence to Trent

Jerome's doubts did not disappear. Cardinal Cajetan, before the Reformation hardened positions, and Cardinal Girolamo Seripando at Trent itself, are named among Catholic churchmen who followed Jerome in setting these books apart. [cite:vt23_wiki_deutero] The Council of Florence approved a full list on 4 February 1442. The Council of Trent, on 8 April 1546, made the list an article of faith under anathema, by 24 votes to 15 with 16 abstentions. [cite:vt14_wiki_trentcanon] [cite:vt14_trent_s4] Twenty years later, in 1566, the theologian Sixtus of Siena coined the word "deuterocanonical", meaning of second-stage recognition, for the books whose standing had been argued over. [cite:vt23_wiki_deutero]

The record therefore shows a long sorting carried out by named people in many cities, with the centre of the list stable early (four gospels and Paul's letters) and the edges argued over for centuries. Which books fell off those edges, and who pushed them, is the subject of the next section. [scene:vt23_left_out|What was left out]

sections.h: What Was Left Out, by Whom, and in What Document
sections.html:
The thesis this book tests holds that the institution "suppressed most of the books". That sentence contains two claims that can be checked separately. The first is about quantity: were most of the books in circulation left out? The second is about action: what did the people who left them out actually do? This section answers both from the documents, book by book, and counts where the documents allow counting. [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] [cite:vt23_tert_decretum]

The excluders, document by document

Irenaeus of Lyon, around 180, rejected the Valentinian "Gospel of Truth", accused the followers of Marcus of using "an unspeakable number of apocryphal and spurious writings, which they themselves have forged", and wrote that a group he called Cainites "produce a fictitious history of this kind, which they style the Gospel of Judas". [cite:vt23_na_irenaeus_3_11] [cite:vt23_na_irenaeus_1_20] [cite:vt23_na_irenaeus_1_31] That last line is the earliest known mention of the Gospel of Judas, whose Coptic text, found in the 1970s, was published on 6 April 2006. [cite:vt23_wiki_judas] [scene:vt26_gospel_of_judas|The Gospel of Judas] Irenaeus wrote as a bishop in Gaul with no power beyond persuasion; his books were polemic, and he is a hostile witness to what his opponents read. [scene:vt24_the_heresy_hunters|The heresy hunters]

The Muratorian fragment rejected letters to the Laodiceans and Alexandrians as forgeries for Marcion's cause and kept the Shepherd of Hermas out of public reading. [cite:vt23_ecw_murat_metzger] Origen set gospels of the Egyptians, the Twelve, Basilides, Thomas and Matthias on the side of "heresy". [cite:vt23_bt_origen_luke] Serapion of Antioch withdrew his permission for the Gospel of Peter. [cite:vt23_na_eus_he6] Eusebius put the Acts of Paul, the Shepherd, the Apocalypse of Peter, Barnabas, the Teachings of the Apostles and the Gospel of the Hebrews among the spurious, and the Gospels of Peter, Thomas and Matthias with the Acts of Andrew and John among the books of heretics. [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] Athanasius named no apocryphal titles in the surviving Greek of his letter but kept the Teaching of the Apostles and the Shepherd for new converts only. [cite:vt23_na_festal39] Jerome set Wisdom, Sirach, Judith and Tobit "among the apocrypha", though the African councils kept them. [cite:vt23_wiki_galeatus] [cite:vt23_na_carthage]
