The longest list of rejections is the fifth chapter of the Gelasian Decree, headed in the manuscripts as a decree of Pope Damasus or Pope Gelasius but judged by its modern editor, Ernst von Dobschütz, to be a pseudonymous private compilation of 519 to 553, probably by a writer from southern Gaul. [cite:vt23_wiki_gelasian] It says the Roman church "does not in any way receive" the writings that follow and that they "are to be avoided by catholics". The entries include gospels "in the name of" Matthias, Barnabas, James the younger, Peter and Bartholomew, "the Gospel in the name of Thomas which the Manichaeans use", Acts of Andrew, Thomas, Peter and Philip, revelations in the names of Paul, Thomas and Stephen, the Shepherd, the Assumption of Mary and the Testament of Job. [cite:vt23_tert_decretum] One entry, "Leptogeneseos", is Greek for "Little Genesis", a name used for the Book of Jubilees, which the Ethiopian church keeps in its Bible to this day. [cite:vt23_tert_decretum] [cite:vt23_wiki_jubilees] The entry on Thomas does not say which Thomas text it means.

The decree also shows that its list was not only about scripture. Among the 62 entries "not received" are the works of Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Lactantius, Cassian and Eusebius's own Church History, alongside amulets and a poem stitched together from Virgil's verses. [cite:vt23_tert_decretum] It was a reading guide for Catholics, as much a list of approved and disapproved authors as a list of rejected gospels. It closes by declaring the authors of heresies and their followers under anathema "forever". [cite:vt23_tert_decretum]

Trent, a council called by the papacy, listed what was in rather than what was out. Books it did not list, notably the Prayer of Manasseh and the books known in Latin as 3 and 4 Esdras, were printed in a separate apocrypha section at the back of the official Sixto-Clementine Vulgate. [cite:vt23_wiki_deutero] [cite:vt14_trent_s4]

The texts that resurfaced at Nag Hammadi and in Codex Tchacos are laid out in Parts Twenty-Five and Twenty-Six. [scene:vt25_the_whole_library|The whole Nag Hammadi library] [scene:vt26_gospel_of_judas|The Gospel of Judas]

Counting: what was in circulation and what was kept

No ancient catalogue lists every Christian book in circulation, so any count has to say what it is counting. Three counts are possible from the documents above. The first uses Eusebius's own catalogue of around 325. Counting Paul's letters as the fourteen he recognised, it names 38 titles. Twenty-seven of them, the recognised books, Revelation and all five disputed letters, are in today's 27-book New Testament; eleven are not. [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] By this measure, most of the books a fourth-century bishop treated as candidates were kept.

The second count looks only at gospels. Irenaeus, Origen, Eusebius and the Gelasian Decree between them name at least seventeen gospels outside the four, from the Gospel of Truth and the Gospel of Judas to gospels under the names of Thomas, Peter, Matthias, Barnabas, Bartholomew and Andrew and two infancy books. [cite:vt23_na_irenaeus_3_11] [cite:vt23_na_irenaeus_1_31] [cite:vt23_bt_origen_luke] [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] [cite:vt23_tert_decretum] Four of at least twenty-one gospels named in these sources were kept, fewer than one in five. Of the revelations named in the same sources, those of John, Peter, Paul, Thomas and Stephen, one was kept. Measured by gospels and revelations, most were left out.

The third count is of the Nag Hammadi library: 52 treatises in 13 codices, with several duplicates, which leaves about 46 distinct titles by the library's own table. [cite:vt14_wiki_naghammadi] Only a handful of those titles appear in any of the exclusion lists above. Most were never named and rejected by any surviving document; they belong to the much larger body of early Christian writing that was never a candidate on any bishop's list, as were the letters of bishops and martyr stories that Carthage itself allowed to be read on feast days. [cite:vt23_na_carthage]

What "left out" meant

The documents use three kinds of sanction. Most exclude a book from reading in church: that is what the Carthage canon governs, and what the Muratorian list means for the Shepherd. [cite:vt23_na_carthage] [cite:vt23_ecw_murat_metzger] Some warn readers away, as Athanasius did. [cite:vt23_na_festal39] Two pronounce anathema on people: the Gelasian Decree on authors and followers of heresies, Trent on anyone who rejects the books it listed. [cite:vt23_tert_decretum] [cite:vt14_trent_s4] None of the documents examined here orders any of the left-out books to be burned. The book-burning order of this period that is documented concerns Arius's own writings: Constantine wrote that any treatise of Arius found "let it be consigned to the flames", with death for anyone who hid one. [cite:vt23_na_socrates1] [scene:vt22_myths_tested|Nicaea's myths tested] Later imperial laws against heretical groups and their meetings are part of the next part's story. [scene:vt24_the_heresy_hunters|The heresy hunters]

The excluded books also kept being copied. Codex Sinaiticus, made in the mid-fourth century, after Eusebius had called both books spurious, includes the Letter of Barnabas and part of the Shepherd after the New Testament. [cite:vt23_wiki_sinaiticus] The Gelasian list itself was still being copied in the eighth century, a sign that the books it warned against were still around to be warned against. [cite:vt23_wiki_gelasian]

How much of the thesis holds

On quantity, the thesis holds for gospels and revelations: by the documents' own lists, most were left out. It does not hold for the New Testament as a whole measured against the books bishops actually debated, where 27 of the 38 titles in Eusebius's catalogue were kept. [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] On action, "suppressed" fits in the sense the documents support: named bishops excluded books from public worship, called them forgeries or heretical, and in the Gelasian Decree and at Trent attached anathemas. No document examined here orders the destruction of a gospel. On the actor, "the institution" needs to be named precisely: until Trent the people doing the excluding were bishops and scholars in Lyon, Alexandria, Antioch, Caesarea, Bethlehem and Carthage and an anonymous sixth-century compiler, with Rome asked to confirm Africa's list rather than issuing its own. [cite:vt23_na_carthage] [cite:vt23_wiki_gelasian] The four Bibles in use today, which the next section compares, still disagree about where the line falls. [scene:vt23_four_bibles|Four Bibles]

sections.h: Four Bibles: 66, 73, About 76 and 81 Books
sections.html:
Ask four Christians how many books are in the Bible and the answers can be 66, 73, around 76 or 81, depending on whether the person is Protestant, Catholic, Eastern Orthodox or a member of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. [cite:vt23_wiki_ot] [cite:vt14_wiki_tewahedo] The New Testament is almost the same in all four: 27 books, though the Ethiopian church's own count adds eight books of church order. Nearly all the difference sits in the Old Testament, and specifically in the books that the Greek-speaking churches read but the Hebrew Bible does not contain. This section sets the four lists side by side and names who fixed each, when, and with what authority. [cite:vt23_wiki_bibcanon]

Protestant: 66

The Protestant Old Testament has 39 books, the same contents as the Hebrew Bible arranged and counted differently, and the New Testament has 27. [cite:vt23_wiki_ot] The list did not come from one act. In his September Testament of 1522 Martin Luther placed Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation at the end as disputed books, and called James an "epistle of straw" with, in his view, no evangelical character. [cite:vt23_wiki_lutherscanon] His full Bible of 1534 printed Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, the Maccabees and the additions to Esther and Daniel in a separate section as "Apocrypha", books not equal to scripture but "useful and good to read". [cite:vt14_wiki_protbible] Luther was following Jerome's Hebrew-based list rather than inventing a new one. [cite:vt23_wiki_lutherscanon] [scene:vt23_lists_and_letters|Jerome's doubts]

The Church of England's Articles allowed the same books to be read "for example of life and instruction of manners" but not to establish doctrine. [cite:vt23_wiki_deutero] The Reformed Westminster Confession of 1646 went further: the Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture". [cite:vt14_wcf_ch1] The British and Foreign Bible Society's decision in the 1820s to stop funding Bibles that printed them is what made the slim 66-book Bible the common Protestant edition. [cite:vt14_wiki_protbible] Lutheran confessions never formally defined a canon at all. [cite:vt23_wiki_lutherscanon]

Catholic: 73

The Catholic Old Testament has 46 books and the New Testament 27. [cite:vt23_wiki_ot] The seven additional Old Testament books are Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1 and 2 Maccabees, together with longer forms of Esther and Daniel. These are the books the African councils of 393 to 419 had kept and Jerome had doubted. [cite:vt23_na_carthage] [cite:vt23_ccel_jerome_solomon] The Council of Florence listed them in 1442, and the Council of Trent made the list binding under anathema on 8 April 1546, by 24 votes to 15 with 16 abstentions. [cite:vt14_wiki_trentcanon] [cite:vt14_trent_s4] Three books that some Greek and Latin Bibles had carried, the Prayer of Manasseh and the books known in Latin as 3 and 4 Esdras, were not on Trent's list and went into an appendix of the official Latin Bible. [cite:vt23_wiki_deutero]

Eastern Orthodox: about 76, not fixed by any single council

The Eastern Orthodox churches read the Old Testament in the Greek Septuagint and keep the Catholic deuterocanon plus further books: 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, Psalm 151 and the Prayer of Manasseh, with 4 Maccabees often printed in an appendix. Russian Bibles also include the book Catholic Bibles relegate as 4 Esdras. [cite:vt23_wiki_bibcanon] The Old Testament therefore runs to as many as 49 books, about 76 in all with the New Testament, and the exact count depends on the edition and how books are divided. [cite:vt23_wiki_ot] [cite:vt23_owiki_otcanon]

No ecumenical council has defined the Orthodox canon. The Council in Trullo of 692 endorsed several earlier lists, including Athanasius's, Laodicea's and Carthage's, which "do not agree" with one another; Pope Sergius I refused to accept that council. [cite:vt23_wiki_bibcanon] The Synod of Jerusalem of 1672 issued a list close to Trent's, but it was a regional synod, not binding on all Orthodox churches, even though Greek Bibles follow it. [cite:vt23_owiki_otcanon] Orthodox practice is the clearest case in this part of a church that lives with a canon whose edges are settled by use rather than by definition.

Ethiopian Tewahedo: 81

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts 81 books, and it reaches that number in two ways. The church's own count, given on its website and taken from the traditional commentary on its law book, the Fetha Negest, is 46 Old Testament and 35 New Testament books: the 27 familiar New Testament books plus eight books of church order. [cite:vt27_eotc_books] [cite:vt27_cowley1974] A narrower reckoning, printed in the Ge'ez–Amharic and Amharic Bibles issued under Emperor Haile Selassie, is 54 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books, also 81. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] The narrower canon contains the whole Hebrew Bible, the Catholic deuterocanon except 1 and 2 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, 3 and 4 Ezra, and all 27 New Testament books, together with four works no other major church treats as scripture: 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the three books of Meqabyan, which share a name with the Maccabees but are different works, and the Paralipomena of Jeremiah, also called 4 Baruch. [cite:vt14_wiki_tewahedo] The broader canon, the church's own count, lists fewer Old Testament books by grouping some together, yet holds more distinct works: nine that the narrower list lacks, a medieval history called the Josippon and eight books of church order (the four books of the Sinodos, two books of the Covenant, an Ethiopic Clement and the Didascalia). It is a different arrangement of 81, not 81 plus nine. [cite:vt27_eotc_books] [cite:vt27_cowley1974] The number 81 is older than either list: the Fetha Negest's heading says the books are 81, though its list as written totals 73, and the commentary tradition filled the gap. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] The detail is in [scene:vt27_church_and_canon|Part Twenty-Seven].

The Ethiopian church was never under Rome's jurisdiction, and its canon was not shaped by the Latin lists in the previous section. Where the two meet, they disagree: the Gelasian Decree, read in the West, rejected "Little Genesis", the Book of Jubilees, which Ethiopia kept and which about fifteen scrolls found at Qumran show was widely used by the community there. [cite:vt23_tert_decretum] [cite:vt23_wiki_jubilees] How Enoch dropped out of Western use while Ethiopia preserved it is the subject of Part Twenty-Seven. [scene:vt27_church_and_canon|The Ethiopian church and its canon] [scene:vt27_how_the_west_lost_enoch|How the West lost Enoch]

The New Testament's quieter differences

The 27 books of the New Testament are in all four Bibles today, but even that core was not universal. The Syriac Peshitta, the Bible of the Syriac-speaking churches, has a New Testament of 22 books, without 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation. [cite:vt23_wiki_bibcanon] The Armenian church added Revelation only around 1200. [cite:vt14_wiki_ntcanon] These are the same books Origen and Eusebius had marked as doubtful in the third and fourth centuries, which shows how long the disputes they recorded lasted in churches outside the Latin and Greek mainstream. [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] [cite:vt23_na_eus_he6]

What the four lists show

The comparison bears on the thesis Book Two tests in two ways. First, there is no single "the Bible" that one body fixed for all Christians: the four largest traditions use different lists today, and only one of them, the Catholic, defined its list as dogma. [cite:vt14_wiki_trentcanon] [cite:vt23_owiki_otcanon] Second, the Roman list is not the shortest. Trent's 73 books are seven more than the Protestant Bible, and the books Protestants removed to an appendix and then dropped, Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and the Maccabees, are ones Rome kept. The books every one of the four leaves out, from the Gospel of Thomas to the Gospel of Judas, were set aside centuries earlier by the bishops and scholars named in the previous section. [cite:vt14_wiki_protbible] [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] [scene:vt23_left_out|What was left out] Who those books' readers were, and what they taught, begins in Part Twenty-Four. [scene:vt24_who_they_were|The Evangelical Gnostics]

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Four
chapters.title: The Evangelical Gnostics
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-Four turns from the councils to the Christians they excluded. The Sophia platform calls them the Evangelical Gnostics; the record knows them as Valentinians, Sethians, Basilideans, Carpocratians and the readers of the Gospel of Thomas, teachers of the second and third centuries who held that salvation comes from knowing one's own origin in God. The first section sets out who they were and how we know, mostly through their enemies. The second sets out what they taught, and answers three of the platform's questions directly: whether they taught the kingdom within, the ascent of the soul and alchemy. The third describes how they lived and answers the other three: whether they asked for a tithe, imposed commandments, or demanded Sunday and holy-day attendance, measured against the proto-orthodox church of the same centuries rather than the church of the Middle Ages. The fourth follows the bishops and the one pagan philosopher who wrote against them, and the emperor who turned the argument into law.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty-Four established that the teachers of gnosis were a family of Christian schools, not one church, and that most of what was known about them until 1945 came from opponents. [cite:vt24_wiki_gnosticism] [cite:vt24_ah1_23] Their own texts do teach the kingdom within and the ascent of the soul past ruling powers, though the canonical Luke 17:21 was also read as "within" by orthodox Fathers; alchemy enters only later, through Zosimos of Panopolis. [cite:vt24_gthom] [cite:vt24_ah1_21] [cite:vt24_ramelli] [cite:vt24_fraser2007] No tithe, code of commandments or Sunday obligation is documented for any of these groups; the Apocryphon of John curses anyone who sells its teaching, while Ptolemy kept the Ten Commandments and the proto-orthodox churches themselves relied on voluntary gifts until the tithe canons of 567 and 585. [cite:vt24_apjohn] [cite:vt24_ect_flora] [cite:vt24_justin67] [cite:vt24_ce_tithes] They were excluded first by argument and the doctrine of apostolic succession, then by Constantine's edict, which named the Valentinians, seized their meeting houses and ordered a search for their books; no ancient order to burn Gnostic gospels by name, and no execution of their teachers, is documented. [cite:vt24_ah3_03] [cite:vt24_vc365] [cite:vt24_vc366] Part Twenty-Five opens the jar in which some of those books survived. [scene:vt25_the_jar|Part Twenty-Five: The Nag Hammadi Library, Text by Text]

sections.h: Who They Were: Teachers of Gnosis in the Second and Third Centuries
sections.html:
The Sophia platform's Reignite pillar calls them the "Evangelical Gnostics": Christians of the second and third centuries who read the gospels as a call to gnosis, a direct, inner knowing of God, rather than to belief in a set of propositions handed down by bishops. The label is the platform's own. No ancient group used it, and it should not be confused with modern evangelical Protestantism. This Part uses it once, here, and from now on uses the names the record supports: Valentinians, Sethians, Basilideans, Carpocratians, Simonians and the readers of the Thomas literature. The distinction matters because these were not one church. They were teachers, schools and writings that shared a few convictions and disagreed about much else, and almost every claim about "the Gnostics" as a single body turns out, on inspection, to be true of one group and false of another.

A word coined in the seventeenth century

Gnosis is ordinary Greek for knowledge. Some second-century Christians did use the word for themselves: Irenaeus of Lyon, writing about 180, says of the followers of Carpocrates that "they style themselves Gnostics". [cite:vt24_ah1_25] But "Gnosticism", the noun that bundles all these groups into one movement, was first coined in the seventeenth century by the Cambridge Platonist Henry More. [cite:vt24_wiki_gnosticism] Modern scholars dispute whether the category is useful at all. Michael Williams, who writes the Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry, argued in 1996 for "dismantling a problematic category", and Karen King made a related case in 2003. [cite:vt24_brit_gnosticism] [cite:vt24_wiki_gnosticism] Most specialists now treat the movement as having arisen inside Christianity: David Brakke and Simone Pétrement describe it as an intra-Christian response to Jesus's death and reported resurrection, and James Robinson, editor of the Nag Hammadi library in English, wrote that pre-Christian Gnosticism "is hardly attested" in a way that settles the question. [cite:vt24_wiki_gnosticism] A minority holds that the Sethian myth began as a Jewish or pagan speculation that was later Christianised. [cite:vt24_wiki_sethianism]

Simon Magus: a founder built by his opponents

The heresy hunters needed a first heretic, and they found him in the Acts of the Apostles: Simon, a Samaritan magician who offered the apostles money for the power to give the Holy Spirit. Acts says nothing about any doctrine of his. Irenaeus, writing around 180, made him the source "from whom all sorts of heresies derive their origin", and attached to him a full myth: Simon, he wrote, took a woman named Helena from a brothel in Tyre, called her the first conception of his mind, the mother of all, fallen and trapped in body after body, and presented himself as the highest power come to free her. Irenaeus adds that Simon's "mystic priests" practised magic and that his followers worshipped images of Simon as Jupiter and Helena as Minerva. [cite:vt24_ah1_23] Whether any of this goes back to the first-century Simon, or describes a later sect that took his name, cannot be settled; the account comes only from an opponent building a family tree of error back to a disreputable founder. The fallen-Wisdom pattern in it is real and recurs in later texts, which is why Simon appears at the head of the story at all.

Basilides and Carpocrates

Basilides taught in Alexandria in the first half of the second century. Irenaeus credits him with a heaven of 365 levels whose ruler is Abraxas, the letters of whose name add up to 365; with the teaching that "salvation belongs to the soul alone"; and with the claim that Simon of Cyrene was crucified in Jesus's place while Jesus, wearing Simon's form, stood by and laughed. [cite:vt24_ah1_24] Carpocrates, also Alexandrian, is the teacher whose followers called themselves Gnostics. Irenaeus says a woman of the school, Marcellina, came to Rome when Anicetus was its bishop and drew many followers, and that the group crowned images of Christ and set them beside images of Pythagoras, Plato and Aristotle. [cite:vt24_ah1_25] Both portraits come from hostile pens; for Basilides, almost nothing survives in his own words.

Valentinus and his students

Valentinus is the best documented of these teachers and the one closest to the centre of the church. Probably educated in Alexandria, he taught in Rome in the middle decades of the second century. [cite:vt24_wiki_gnosticism] Tertullian of Carthage, writing about 206, says Valentinus "had expected to become a bishop" and broke with the church when "another obtained the dignity" through the claim that confessing the faith under persecution had given him. [cite:vt24_tert_adval] The passage does not name the city, and it is a hostile story told sixty years later, so the popular version, that Valentinus was nearly elected bishop of Rome, is a reading of Tertullian rather than a documented event. In another work Tertullian places Valentinus and Marcion as believers in the Roman church who were expelled, and says Marcion's gift of money to that church was handed back to him. [cite:vt24_tert_praescr]

Valentinus's students carried the school across the empire. Ptolemy and Heracleon led its western branch; Theodotus taught in the East, and parts of his teaching survive only because Clement of Alexandria copied them into his notebooks. Ptolemy's Letter to Flora, addressed to a Christian woman asking about the Law of Moses, survives complete because Epiphanius of Salamis quoted it in order to refute it, in book 33 of his Panarion; before 1945 it was one of the few authentic Gnostic writings scholars could read. [cite:vt24_wiki_flora] [cite:vt24_ect_flora] The Valentinians did not think of themselves as a separate religion. They called themselves Christians, read the same gospels, and, as the next sections show, many of them stayed inside the ordinary congregations.

Sethians and the Thomas literature

"Sethian" is a modern label, introduced by the German scholar Hans-Martin Schenke and others, for a family of texts that trace true knowledge through Seth, the third son of Adam and Eve. The family includes the Apocryphon of John, Zostrianos, Allogenes, the Three Steles of Seth, Marsanes, the Trimorphic Protennoia and the Holy Book of the Great Invisible Spirit. Its myth runs from an unknowable God through a first emanation, Barbelo, to the fall of Sophia, whose unauthorised act produces the creator Yaldabaoth and the rulers of the visible world. [cite:vt24_wiki_sethianism] No ancient writer describes a "Sethian church", and whether the texts reflect one community or a reading tradition shared among several is open. The same caution applies to the Gospel of Thomas and related writings: a "Thomas community" is a scholarly hypothesis, and it has nothing to do with the living Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala in India. The texts themselves are treated in [scene:vt25_sayings_gospels|Part Twenty-Five] and [scene:vt25_secret_cosmos|its section on the Sethian cosmos].

Who is not in this Part, and who is still here

Three groups often bundled with the Gnostics are kept apart in this book. Marcion of Sinope taught two gods but had no Sophia myth, no aeons and no secret knowledge, and his followers founded churches across the empire with their own scripture, a shortened Luke and ten letters of Paul; Adolf von Harnack and many scholars since have declined to call him a Gnostic, though some, like G. R. S. Mead, did. [cite:vt24_audit_wiki_marcionism] The Manichaeans, followers of the prophet Mani (216 to about 274–277), formed a separate world religion. [cite:vt24_wiki_manich] The medieval Cathars, who also taught that an evil power ruled the visible world, are separated from the ancient groups by some eight centuries with no documented chain of transmission, and appear in [scene:vt28_cathars|Part Twenty-Eight].

One tradition of this family is not history. The Mandaeans, whose central figure is John the Baptist and whose scripture is the Ginza Rabba, practise repeated baptism in flowing rivers and keep their own priesthood. Encyclopedic sources describe them as the last surviving Gnostic religion from antiquity, though their origins are disputed. They number an estimated 60,000 to 100,000 worldwide. In Iraq their community fell to about 5,000 by 2007 and perhaps 3,000 by 2019; about 90 per cent of Iraqi Mandaeans were killed or fled after the 2003 invasion, and the largest diaspora community is now in Sweden. [cite:vt24_wiki_mandaeans] Modern Gnostic churches are a separate, recent strand: the Église Gnostique founded in Paris in 1890 by the archivist Jules Doinel, after visions he dated to 1888–89, is the best-known starting point, and its founder's later career, which included a return to Catholicism and work with the anti-Masonic hoaxer Léo Taxil, shows how quickly such revivals mixed with other currents. [cite:vt24_wiki_doinel] These churches describe themselves as revivals; none can document an unbroken line from the second century.

sections.h: What They Taught: Gnosis, the Hidden God and the Way Back
sections.html:
The question about these teachers has a teaching half and a practice half. The teaching half asks whether they taught the ascension of consciousness, alchemy and the kingdom within. The answer differs for each: the kingdom within and the ascent of the soul are documented in their own texts, while alchemy is not, except through a later bridge figure. This section sets out the core teachings first, using the groups' own writings where they survive and the heresy hunters' summaries where they do not, and then answers the three questions one by one. The practice half (tithe, commandments, Sunday duty) is answered in [scene:vt24_how_they_lived|the next section].

Salvation as knowing, not as believing

The common thread is that salvation comes from knowledge of one's own origin in God, not from faith in a past event or obedience to a rule. The Gospel of Thomas, a collection of 114 sayings found at Nag Hammadi, opens by promising that whoever finds the interpretation of these sayings "will not experience death", and its saying 70 puts the mechanism plainly: what you have will save you "if you bring it forth from yourselves". [cite:vt24_gthom] Irenaeus records that some Valentinians went further and rejected outward rites altogether, holding that "the knowledge of the unspeakable Greatness is itself perfect redemption", since the human problem was ignorance and knowledge undid it. [cite:vt24_ah1_21] This is a different account of what saves a person from the one the bishops defended, in which faith in Christ's death and resurrection and the church's sacraments did the saving. Both accounts were live in the second century.

The hidden God and the ignorant maker

The most distinctive teaching, and the one that most offended opponents, concerns who made the world. In the Apocryphon of John, the central Sethian text, the highest God is beyond all names. From this God come a first thought, Barbelo, and a series of eternal beings called aeons, which together make up the Pleroma, the fullness. The last aeon, Sophia (Wisdom), acts without the consent of the Spirit or her partner, and "something came out of her which was imperfect"; she casts it away and names it Yaltabaoth (Yaldabaoth). This being makes the rulers and the visible world and announces, "I am a jealous God, and there is no other God beside me", a claim the text says "indicated to the angels who attended him that there exists another God". [cite:vt24_apjohn] The line borrows the words of the God of Israel from Exodus and Isaiah, and the myth is in effect a second-century Christian rereading of Genesis. It is a claim about a figure inside a myth. It is not a statement about Judaism or about the God Jewish communities worship, and later attempts, ancient and modern, to turn it into hostility toward Jews misuse it. [cite:vt24_wiki_sethianism]

Valentinian teachers told a gentler version in which Sophia's lower aspect, not Sophia herself, produces the maker, who is ignorant rather than wicked. Ptolemy's Letter to Flora says the giver of the Law was neither the perfect God nor the devil but the maker of this universe, "neither good nor evil or unjust, but can properly be called just". [cite:vt24_ect_flora] In both the Sethian and Valentinian versions, humans carry within them light or seed from the Pleroma; awakening it is the point of the whole story. [cite:vt24_wiki_sethianism] [cite:vt24_apjohn] The Valentinians, according to Irenaeus, divided people into three kinds, material, "animal" (psychic) and spiritual, and said the spiritual are saved "because they are spiritual by nature" while ordinary believers, whom they called "animal", needed faith and good works. [cite:vt24_ah1_06] Critics then and now have pointed to this as spiritual elitism, and it is part of the record alongside the more attractive teachings.

The resurrection as something you do now

The Valentinians reread the resurrection. The Gospel of Philip says "Those who say they will die first and then rise are in error", and warns that whoever does not receive the resurrection while alive will receive nothing after death. [cite:vt24_gphil] The Treatise on the Resurrection, a letter to a student called Rheginos, insists that resurrection "is no illusion, but it is truth", tells him "already you have the resurrection", and asks "why not consider yourself as risen". [cite:vt24_treatres] Philip uses the language of transformation: "You saw the Spirit, you became spirit. You saw Christ, you became Christ." It is also a sacramental text, naming five mysteries, "a baptism and a chrism and a eucharist and a redemption and a bridal chamber". [cite:vt24_gphil] The claim, repeated in some popular writing, that the Gnostics rejected sacraments as empty symbols is wrong for Philip; it treats them as real participation in the divine.

On the Law

Ptolemy's letter is the clearest surviving Gnostic statement on commandments, and it does not reject them wholesale. He divides the Law of Moses into what came from God, what Moses added, and what the elders added. God's part is itself threefold: the pure law of the Ten Commandments, "which the Savior came not to destroy but to complete"; laws mixed with injustice, such as an eye for an eye, which the Saviour set aside; and symbolic law (offerings, circumcision, the sabbath, fasting, Passover), whose "names remained the same but the content was changed" into a spiritual meaning. True fasting, he writes, is "abstinence from everything evil". He closes by promising Flora more teaching "when you are judged worthy of the apostolic tradition which we too have received by succession". [cite:vt24_ect_flora] A Valentinian teacher, then, claimed his own apostolic succession and kept the moral core of the Decalogue.

Three questions about teaching

The kingdom within: yes, and plainly. Thomas saying 3 has Jesus say "the kingdom is inside of you, and it is outside of you", and saying 113 that the kingdom "is spread out upon the earth, and men do not see it". [cite:vt24_gthom] In the Gospel of Mary, preserved in the Berlin Codex, the risen Saviour tells the disciples that "the Son of Humanity exists within you" (older translations: "Son of Man"). [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] [cite:vt26_wiki_berlincodex] The idea was not confined to them, however. Luke 17:21, in the canonical Bible, has Jesus say the kingdom of God is entos hymōn. Most modern translations render it "among you"; the classicist Ilaria Ramelli has argued that "among" is practically unattested for entos, that the Latin Vulgate and later Syriac versions say "inside", and that orthodox writers including Origen, Athanasius, Basil and Gregory of Nyssa read it as "within". [cite:vt24_ramelli] The inner kingdom stayed inside the canon and inside orthodox commentary; what divided the parties was whether that inner knowing made bishops and sacraments unnecessary.

The ascent of the soul: yes, extensively, though in the language of the period rather than of "consciousness". The Gospel of Mary describes the soul rising past a series of powers, the last with seven forms of wrath. [cite:vt24_mary_pbs] Irenaeus reports Valentinian groups that anointed the dying so they would be "incapable of being seized or seen by the principalities and powers" and gave them words to speak on the way up, beginning "I am a son from the Father". [cite:vt24_ah1_21] Origen, writing against the pagan critic Celsus about 248, describes an Ophite diagram of ten circles that he says he had seen himself, and the formulas the soul addressed to the rulers Ialdabaoth, Iao, Sabaoth and Astaphaeus as it passed their gates. [cite:vt24_origen_cc6] The Sethian treatises Zostrianos and Allogenes are visionary ascents, and were read in the circle of the philosopher Plotinus. [cite:vt24_bmcr_plotinus] The Pistis Sophia carries the same passwords-and-seals scheme further; see [scene:vt26_pistis_sophia|Part Twenty-Six].

Alchemy: not in their own texts. No alchemical treatise survives among the Nag Hammadi codices or in any Valentinian or Sethian writing; Philip's line "God is a dyer" uses the image of a dye-works, not of transmutation. [cite:vt24_gphil] The documented bridge is Zosimos of Panopolis, an Egyptian alchemist active about 300 whose books are the oldest known on alchemy and who treated the transformation of metals as a mirror of inner purification. [cite:vt24_wiki_zosimos] The historian Kyle Fraser argues that Zosimos was a practising Hermetist who drew on Sethian works, including the ascent literature, to describe the alchemical work as a baptism bringing gnosis. [cite:vt24_fraser2007] That makes Zosimos a reader of Gnostic texts who practised alchemy, not evidence that Valentinians or Sethians practised it. How alchemy was later treated by Rome is in [scene:vt30_forbidden_arts|Part Thirty].

Interpretation, not finding: the myth as a map of inner ascent

Read through an esoteric lens, the fall and return of Sophia is not cosmology but a map of the mind: a descent of awareness into matter and its climb back through layers of conditioning, the archons, to its source. The best-known modern reader in this vein is Carl Jung, who in 1916 privately published his own Seven Sermons to the Dead under the name of Basilides. [cite:vt24_wiki_septem] Later spiritual-alchemy writers, and the Sophia platform's own Reignite material, read solve et coagula and the ascent through the powers as the same process told in two vocabularies. In this reading the Gnostic texts and the alchemists describe one inner work. It is a modern reading, held by those writers; the ancient texts describe a cosmos and a soul's journey through it, and the link to alchemy runs through Zosimos, not through the second-century teachers themselves.

sections.h: How They Lived: Rites, Women, Money and Rules
sections.html:
The practice half of the question is whether these Christians asked for a tithe, imposed commandments, or demanded attendance on Sundays and holy days. The evidence here is thinner than for their teaching, and most of it is hostile: apart from a handful of their own texts, what we know about how Valentinians, Sethians or Basilideans actually lived comes from bishops writing to discredit them. Each answer below says which kind of evidence it rests on. The answers also need a fair comparison. The proto-orthodox churches of the second and third centuries did not have a compulsory tithe or a Sunday law either; those came later, and the measure of the Gnostic groups has to be taken against the church of their own time, not the church of the Middle Ages.

Rites

These were not groups without ritual. The Gospel of Philip, a Valentinian anthology, names five mysteries: "a baptism and a chrism and a eucharist and a redemption and a bridal chamber". [cite:vt24_gphil] The Apocryphon of John ends with the saviour sealing the awakened "in the light of the water with five seals", a phrase the scholar Birger Pearson reads as a rite of repeated immersion. [cite:vt24_apjohn] [cite:vt24_wiki_sethianism] Irenaeus describes Valentinian "redemption" rites that varied from group to group: a "spiritual marriage", baptism in water with invocations of the unknown Father, an anointing with oil and water and balsam, and a final anointing of the dying. In the same passage he reports that some rejected all such rites as unnecessary. [cite:vt24_ah1_21] The "bridal chamber" gave opponents material for accusations of sexual ritual; the text of Philip supports a sacramental reading at least as well as a literal one, and no independent evidence for such rituals exists.

Women

Women held roles in several of these groups that the bishops denied them. Marcellina led the Carpocratians in Rome. [cite:vt24_ah1_25] Irenaeus says the Valentinian teacher Marcus had women consecrate the eucharistic cup and urged them to prophesy, telling one, "Open your mouth, speak whatsoever occurs to you, and you shall prophesy". [cite:vt24_ah1_13] Tertullian complained that among heretics women were "bold enough to teach, to dispute, to enact exorcisms, to undertake cures—it may be even to baptize". [cite:vt24_praescr41] Both writers present this as proof of disorder; read against the grain, it is evidence that women taught and presided. The Gospel of Mary, with Mary Magdalene as the disciple who receives the Saviour's private teaching and Peter asking "Did He prefer her to us?", is the best-known text on the question and is treated in [scene:vt26_gospel_of_mary|Part Twenty-Six]. [cite:vt24_mary_pbs] The record is not uniform: the last saying of the Gospel of Thomas promises the kingdom to "every woman who will make herself male", a line read either as symbolic or as reflecting the low view of women common to the period. [cite:vt24_gthom]

Leadership

Tertullian's complaint about the heretics' order is itself informative. Among them, he wrote, "it is doubtful who is a catechumen, and who a believer"; "to-day one man is their bishop, to-morrow another"; "on laymen do they impose the functions of priesthood". [cite:vt24_praescr41] He meant it as ridicule. It describes groups with rotating, looser offices and little separation between clergy and laity. At the same time the Valentinians were often members of the ordinary congregations rather than a rival church. Irenaeus says they called ordinary church members "ecclesiastics", used "our phraseology", and asked why, "when they say the same things, and hold the same doctrine", the bishops called them heretics. [cite:vt24_ah3_15] Ptolemy claimed an apostolic tradition "received by succession" of his own. [cite:vt24_ect_flora] Constantine's undated edict against heretics, preserved by Eusebius, ordered Valentinians and others to stop meeting in their "houses of prayer" and to hand them over, which shows that some groups had regular assemblies and buildings by then. [cite:vt24_vc365]

Answer one: tithe and money

No tithe system is documented for any second- or third-century Gnostic group. That is an absence of evidence, not proof that money never changed hands, but there is one direct statement on the point in their own writings: the Apocryphon of John closes with "Cursed be everyone who will exchange these things for a gift or for food or for drink or for clothing". [cite:vt24_apjohn] The teaching was not to be sold. Against this stands a single hostile allegation: Irenaeus says Marcus targeted women "of great wealth", that they gave him their possessions, and that he "collected a very large fortune". [cite:vt24_ah1_13] It comes with accusations of seduction from a writer whose purpose was to discredit Marcus, and no independent source confirms it.

The comparison matters. The proto-orthodox churches did not collect a tithe either. Justin Martyr, describing a Christian assembly in Rome about 155, says that "they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit", and that the president uses it to support "the orphans and widows". [cite:vt24_justin67] The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1912 states that the clergy were at first supported by "the spontaneous offerings of the faithful", and that the earliest church legislation on tithes is a letter of bishops at Tours in 567 and the canons of the Council of Mâcon in 585, with civil enforcement first under Charlemagne in the late eighth century. [cite:vt24_ce_tithes] The compulsory tithe came about four centuries after these groups flourished; it belongs to [scene:vt31_tithe|Part Thirty-One]. The closest thing to a fixed religious economy in this family is the Manichaeans, a separate religion, whose lay Hearers supplied food to the Elect in return for their prayers. [cite:vt24_wiki_manich]

Answer two: commandments

No Gnostic group is documented as issuing a code of commandments of its own, and some texts reject the idea of one. In the Gospel of Mary the Saviour tells the disciples, "Don't lay down any rules beyond what I've given you, nor make a law like the lawgiver, lest you be bound by it." [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] When the disciples in Thomas ask whether to fast, pray and give alms, Jesus answers "Do not tell lies, and do not do what you hate", and in saying 14 warns, "If you fast, you will give rise to sin for yourselves". [cite:vt24_gthom2] But "no rules" overstates the record. Ptolemy kept the Ten Commandments as God's "pure law", fulfilled rather than abolished by the Saviour, and reinterpreted fasting as "abstinence from everything evil". [cite:vt24_ect_flora] Irenaeus says Valentinians taught that ordinary believers needed faith and good works, while the spiritual were exempt "because they are spiritual by nature", and he and Plotinus both accused some groups of moral indifference. [cite:vt24_ah1_06] [cite:vt24_bmcr_plotinus] The fair summary is that these teachers rejected external law as the means of salvation, not ethics as such, and that their ethics ranged from rigorous to (according to their enemies) lax.

Answer three: Sunday and holy-day duty

No document shows a Gnostic group requiring attendance on Sundays or feast days, and their texts treat the calendar spiritually. Thomas saying 27 says that if you do not keep the Sabbath as a Sabbath you will not see the Father, and Ptolemy counts the sabbath, fasting and Passover among the laws whose "names remained the same but the content was changed". [cite:vt24_gthom2] [cite:vt24_ect_flora] They did meet: Constantine's edict, and Sozomen's account of it, forbade Valentinians and others to hold church "in private houses, or in public places". [cite:vt24_vc365] [cite:vt24_sozomen232] Here too the comparison cuts both ways. Justin describes the proto-orthodox Christians gathering "on the day called Sunday" in the 150s, but as a custom, not a legal duty. [cite:vt24_justin67] Constantine's civil law of 7 March 321 making the "venerable day of the Sun" a day of rest came long after these groups formed, and church rules on Sunday attendance followed; both are covered in [scene:vt31_sunday_and_law|Part Thirty-One]. [cite:vt21_wiki_sol]

sections.h: The Heresy Hunters: How the Teachers of Gnosis Were Written Out
sections.html:
For about sixteen centuries, almost everything known about the Valentinians, Basilideans and Sethians came from the people who wrote to defeat them. That fact shapes every claim in this Part. It also makes the heresy hunters a subject in their own right, because the methods they developed to exclude these teachers (a list of bishops, a rule of faith, a closed set of books, and a legal argument about who owned the scriptures) became the frame of the institutional church. None of them were Roman officials, and for most of the period Rome was one church among several. The first state action came only in the fourth century, from an emperor.

Irenaeus of Lyon: the list of bishops

Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon in Gaul, wrote the five books now called Against Heresies about 180, to expose what he called knowledge "falsely so called", the phrase of 1 Timothy 6:20. [cite:vt24_ah1_pref] Book One summarises the Valentinian system and then traces a genealogy of error from Simon Magus through Basilides, Carpocrates and others. [cite:vt24_ah1_23] His decisive move came in Book Three. Instead of arguing only over doctrine, he argued from structure: the apostles had appointed bishops, and their successors could be traced "to our own times". He gave the Roman list, from Linus to Eleutherius, "in the twelfth place from the apostles", and wrote that "every Church should agree with this Church, on account of its preeminent authority". [cite:vt24_ah3_03] Whatever the merits of a given teaching, a teacher outside that line had no claim to speak for the apostles. Irenaeus also argued that there could be four gospels and only four; that argument and the formation of the list are in [scene:vt23_lists_and_letters|Part Twenty-Three].

Tertullian: a plea from Roman law

Tertullian of Carthage, writing about 200, took the argument further in The Prescription Against Heretics. A praescriptio in Roman civil procedure was a plea that ended a case before its merits were heard. Tertullian applied it to scripture: he opposed "admitting them to any discussion of the Scriptures", because the scriptures belonged to the churches founded by the apostles and the heretics had no standing to argue from them. "Our appeal, therefore, must not be made to the Scriptures." [cite:vt24_praescr] The same work's account of the heretics' loose offices and women teachers, quoted in [scene:vt24_how_they_lived|the previous section], is part of the case: disorder was itself presented as proof of illegitimacy. [cite:vt24_praescr41]

Hippolytus, Origen, Plotinus

The Refutation of All Heresies, written in the early third century and attributed to Hippolytus or to an unknown author scholars call Pseudo-Hippolytus, argued that each heresy was a disguised Greek philosophy: Simon and Valentinus were made pupils of Pythagoras. Books four to ten were lost until a manuscript was recovered from Mount Athos in 1842; it gives independent accounts of the Naassenes, Peratae, Sethians, Valentinus and Basilides. [cite:vt24_wiki_refutation] Origen of Alexandria, defending Christianity against the pagan critic Celsus about 248, described an Ophite diagram of the heavens he had seen himself and called its formulas absurd. [cite:vt24_origen_cc6] The attack did not come only from Christians. The pagan philosopher Plotinus wrote a treatise known as Against the Gnostics (Ennead II.9) objecting to their contempt for the cosmos and its maker, their multiplication of divine realities, a salvation that asked no moral effort, and their magic. Porphyry, his student, names Zostrianos and Allogenes among the texts circulating in the school. [cite:vt24_bmcr_plotinus]

Epiphanius: the medicine chest

Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, began his Panarion in 374 or 375. Its title means a medicine chest, a stock of remedies against the poisons of 80 heresies, each compared to a snake. Its value is that it quotes documents found nowhere else, including Ptolemy's Letter to Flora; its weakness is that the author's zeal sometimes kept him from examining what he condemned, and he admitted writing on one heresy from hearsay. [cite:vt24_wiki_panarion] [cite:vt24_wiki_flora]

The state steps in

The change from argument to law came with Constantine. An undated edict preserved by Eusebius addressed "ye Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Paulians, ye who are called Cataphrygians", forbade them to assemble "not in public merely, but in any private house or place whatsoever", and ordered their houses of prayer "made over without delay to the catholic Church". [cite:vt24_vc364] [cite:vt24_vc365] Eusebius adds that "search should be made for their books", and that afterwards many members of these groups sought admission to the catholic church, some sincerely and some, he says, by pretence; he does not say the books were burned. [cite:vt24_vc366] This is the earliest documented state order that names a Gnostic group, and it is covered in its imperial setting in [scene:vt21_church_and_empire|Part Twenty-One]. Theodosius I's law of 380 declared that the gatherings of heretics "shall not receive the name of churches", and the laws on heretics collected in book 16 of the Theodosian Code limited privileges to Catholics and fined heretics; one, against the Manichaeans, fined their leaders and had the houses where they taught seized. [cite:vt24_cth_ect] [cite:vt24_cth_osu] Athanasius of Alexandria's Easter letter of 367 warned his churches against apocryphal books as "an invention of heretics", without ordering them destroyed; [cite:vt23_na_festal39] [scene:vt23_lists_and_letters|Part Twenty-Three] sets out its text and [scene:vt25_the_jar|Part Twenty-Five] the hypothesis linking it to the burial of the Nag Hammadi codices.

What the record does not show

The record shows exclusion by argument, by episcopal discipline and, from Constantine onward, by imperial law, including a search for heretics' books. It does not show any Valentinian or Sethian teacher executed by order of a bishop, or any ancient church order to burn Gnostic gospels by name. Book-burning orders in this period are documented against Arius's writings after Nicaea and against the Manichaeans by Diocletian, a pagan emperor. [cite:vt23_na_socrates1] [cite:vt24_wiki_manich] The Gnostic texts mostly vanished in a quieter way: once excluded from public reading and denied buildings, they stopped being copied, and survived only where someone hid or kept them, as at Nag Hammadi, or where an opponent quoted them in order to refute them. A sixteen-century silence, broken in 1945, is the result.

Why the bishops' side prevailed: Pagels and her critics

The best-known scholarly explanation is Elaine Pagels's The Gnostic Gospels (1979), which won the National Book Award. She argued that orthodox doctrines did institutional work: the insistence on a bodily resurrection witnessed by named apostles "serves an essential political function" by grounding the authority of their successors, and the Gnostic claim to direct knowledge offered "the theological justification for refusing to obey the bishops and the priests". She also concluded that the orthodox churches' openness to all comers and their communal structure were real strengths, and that "ideas alone do not make a religion powerful". [cite:vt24_enc_pagels] Critics have pressed back. Henry Chadwick found her lacking in "full rigour", especially on women; Hyam Maccoby said she idealised the Gnostics and passed over their elitism and hostility to the body; Raymond Brown judged the book too sympathetic to them. [cite:vt24_enc_pagels] Both points stand on the record: the heresy hunters did build an authority structure that a doctrine of direct knowing could not easily coexist with, and the teachers of gnosis did divide humanity into the spiritual few and the rest. How that tension plays out across the next fifteen centuries, and the platform's broader reading of it, is weighed in [scene:vt31_two_economies|Part Thirty-One] and [scene:vt32_verdict_two|Part Thirty-Six].

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Five
chapters.title: The Nag Hammadi Library, Text by Text
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-Five opens the jar. In December 1945 a cache of thirteen leather-bound papyrus books was dug up at the foot of a cliff near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt. It held 52 writings in Coptic, among them gospels attributed to Thomas and Philip, secret books of John and James, and myths of Sophia and the ignorant creator that bishops had argued against since the second century. The first section separates what is documented about the find (its date, its custody, the 348 date in its bindings) from the discovery story as it is usually told. It also weighs the competing explanations of why the books were buried. The next two sections take the texts in groups. First come the sayings gospels, where the "kingdom within" teaching is plainest. Then come the secret cosmologies, set out stage by stage from the unknowable Monad to the spark's return. The last section is a complete catalogue of every tractate in all thirteen codices. Each entry carries a one-line teaching, a note on whether it conflicted with the bishops' doctrine, and the bishop or document, where one is recorded, that condemned the text or its school.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty-Five established four things. First, the Nag Hammadi codices were bound after 348, buried by unknown hands, found in December 1945 and kept in the Coptic Museum in Cairo. The burning of some leaves by the finder's mother rests on James Robinson's interviews of the 1970s, which Mark Goodacre has shown to be unstable, and the monastic and grave-goods explanations of the burial both remain hypotheses. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] [cite:vt25_goodacre2013] [cite:vt25_lj2015] [cite:vt25_lewisblount2014] Second, the texts do teach what the "kingdom within" reading says they teach, in places: Thomas puts the kingdom "inside of you" and rejects fasting and prayer, and the Apocalypse of Peter calls self-appointed bishops "dry canals". But the library is mixed. Philip and the Valentinian Exposition are sacramental, Thomas the Contender and the Testimony of Truth are rigorist, and Plato, Hermes and Sextus sit beside Sethian myth. [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin] [cite:vt25_wiki_gapocpeter] [cite:vt25_wiki_gphil] [cite:vt25_wiki_testtruth] Third, more than half the tractates conflicted with the creed of 325 or with Irenaeus's four-gospel rule. [cite:vt25_nicaea_creed] [cite:vt25_iren_311] Fourth, the recorded condemnations came from bishops and heresy writers from Lyon to Jerusalem, and in two cases from pagan philosophers, and took the form of warnings, exclusions and anathemas, not burning orders. [cite:vt25_iren_129] [cite:vt25_cyril_cat4] [cite:vt25_decretum] [cite:vt25_bmcr_plotinus] Part Twenty-Six goes outside the jar to three texts found in other manuscripts: the Gospel of Mary, the Gospel of Judas and the Pistis Sophia. [scene:vt26_gospel_of_mary|Part Twenty-Six: Outside the Jar]

sections.h: The Jar: How the Nag Hammadi Codices Were Found, Kept and Dated
sections.html:
In December 1945 men digging for fertile soil at the foot of the Jabal al-Tarif, a cliff on the east bank of the Nile across from the town of Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt, found a sealed earthenware jar. One of them, Muhammad Ali al-Samman, broke it open and found leather-bound books of papyrus inside. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] What came out of the ground that winter is the largest single collection of early Christian writings outside the Bible, and most of it had been unread for about sixteen centuries. Part Fourteen set the find on its basic footing and showed that no document links its burial to an order from any bishop. [scene:vt14_canon|Part Fourteen: Who Chose the Bible] This part goes into the books themselves, text by text. Before the texts, though, the find has its own told version and its own record, and the two are not the same.

What was in the jar

The find is usually counted as thirteen codices. Strictly, scholars count twelve bound books and a set of loose leaves that someone in antiquity had cut out of a thirteenth book and tucked inside the cover of the sixth; those leaves are called Codex XIII, and what became of the rest of that thirteenth book is not known. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] [cite:vt25_wiki_nhl] Together the codices hold 52 separate writings, which scholars call tractates. Because some works appear more than once (the Apocryphon of John three times, the Gospel of Truth, On the Origin of the World and the Holy Book of the Great Invisible Spirit twice each, Eugnostos twice), the number of distinct works is 46. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] [cite:vt14_wiki_naghammadi]

All of them are in Coptic, the last stage of the Egyptian language written in an alphabet adapted from Greek, mainly in the Sahidic and Subakhmimic dialects. All were translated from Greek originals, most of which are lost. As many as fourteen different scribes' hands can be told apart. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] The books themselves were made around 350 CE. That date comes from the cartonnage: scrap papyrus, including old letters and receipts, that bookbinders glued together to stiffen the leather covers. The latest dated scrap is from 348 CE, so the covers were made after that year. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] The copies are fourth-century; the works copied into them are older, many of them composed in Greek in the second or third century. [cite:vt25_wiki_nhl]

The story of the discovery, and how much of it holds

The version most readers know comes from the American scholar James M. Robinson, who led the team that published the codices. In his telling, Muhammad Ali and his brothers were digging for sabakh, a nitrate-rich soil used as fertiliser; Muhammad Ali feared the jar held a jinn, smashed it anyway, carried the books home, and his mother burned some of the pages in her bread oven. Weeks later the brothers killed the man they held responsible for their father's murder, and fear of the police investigation is said to be why the books were handed off quickly. [cite:vt25_goodacre2013] The detail of the mother and the oven is the part most often repeated. It does appear in standard reference accounts, which state that "his mother used some of the leaves as fuel for an oven". [cite:vt25_enc_nh] Its source, though, is Robinson's interviews with the villagers, not a document from 1945.

Robinson built the story from interviews that began in late 1974, nearly thirty years after the event, and published versions in 1977, 1979 and 1981 that differ on how many people were present and who actually unearthed the jar. In 2013 the New Testament scholar Mark Goodacre examined those versions. He noted that the Coptic specialists Rodolphe Kasser and Martin Krause had in 1984 called much of the detailed history "stories and fables"; that Robinson himself questioned Muhammad Ali's reliability; that Robinson paid informants on his visits; and that in a 1987 film Muhammad Ali said he had smashed the pot alone. The French scholar Jean Doresse, who visited the area between 1947 and 1950, recorded a much shorter and vaguer account with no brothers, no jinn, no oven and no blood feud, and Goodacre judged Doresse's earlier testimony the more reliable of the two. [cite:vt25_goodacre2013] The burning of some pages by the finder's family is therefore a reported detail from one investigator's late interviews, not an established fact; it is also a domestic accident, not an act of suppression by any church.

The record from the books' arrival in Cairo onward is firmer. Most of the codices passed to a Cypriot antiques dealer in Cairo, Phokion Tanos. The Egyptian Department of Antiquities held them back for fear they would be sold abroad, and after the revolution of 1952 they were declared national property and placed in the Coptic Museum in Old Cairo, where they remain. [cite:vt25_wiki_nhl] [cite:vt25_enc_nh] One codex, the first, left Egypt: it was sold to a Belgian dealer and bought for the C. G. Jung Institute in Zurich through the Dutch scholar Gilles Quispel, which is why it is called the Jung Codex. After a dispute over ownership its pages returned to Cairo only in 1975. [cite:vt25_wiki_nhl] A photographic facsimile of all the codices came out over the 1970s, and the first complete English translation, edited by Robinson, was published in 1977, with a revised edition in 1988. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] [cite:vt25_wiki_nhl]

Who buried the books, and why

Nothing found with the jar says who owned the books or why they were buried. Three main answers have been proposed, and all three remain hypotheses.

The first, Robinson's, is monastic. The cliff lies near the site of ancient Pbow, the headquarters of the Pachomian monasteries, the first large communal monastic federation in Egypt, and some cartonnage scraps refer to places near the burial site. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] In 367 Athanasius of Alexandria sent his 39th Festal Letter to the Egyptian churches, listing the 27 books of the New Testament and warning against books "called apocryphal", which he called "an invention of heretics". [cite:vt14_ect_festal39] In Robinson's reading, monks who owned such books hid them after that letter. The letter warns readers; it contains no order to burn or bury anything, and no source records monks acting on it in this way. [cite:vt14_ect_festal39] The fullest modern version of the monastic case is Hugo Lundhaug and Lance Jenott's The Monastic Origins of the Nag Hammadi Codices (2015), which argues from the cartonnage, the scribes' notes and colophons, and comparison with other Egyptian manuscripts that the books were "produced and read by Christian monks, most likely Pachomians". On their reading the codices are not a Gnostic library at all but books "completely at home in the monastic manuscript culture" of the period. [cite:vt25_lj2015]

The second answer is a private owner. In 2014 Nicola Denzey Lewis and Justine Ariel Blount argued that the papyrologists who studied the cartonnage found no single Pachomian source for it, and that the scrap looked more like a town rubbish heap. They added, following David Brakke, that Athanasius's letter was aimed at Arian and Melitian opponents rather than at Gnostic books. [cite:vt25_lewisblount2014] Their alternative is the third answer, a burial with the dead. The Jabal al-Tarif was a cemetery used for centuries, and other codices of this period were found in graves: Codex Tchacos, which holds the Gospel of Judas, came from a family tomb, and the Codex Panopolitanus from a grave at Akhmim. On this view a wealthy Greek-speaking Egyptian with esoteric interests commissioned the books and was buried with them, much as earlier Egyptians were buried with the Book of the Dead. [cite:vt25_lewisblount2014]

Each explanation answers a different question. The monastic case answers who read these books: on the best available evidence, fourth-century Egyptian Christians, quite possibly monks, read Valentinian and Sethian treatises side by side with Plato, Hermetic prayers and orthodox wisdom sayings. The grave-goods case answers why a library might end up in a jar at a cemetery. Neither one records an order to destroy them. What can be stated without hypothesis is narrower: the books were made after 348, they were buried, they survived, and the Coptic Museum has kept them since the 1950s. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] [cite:vt25_wiki_nhl]

What kind of collection it is

Popular accounts call the find "the Gnostic Bible". The contents do not support that label. The jar held a short extract from Plato's Republic (588a–589b) in a loose Coptic version; three Hermetic texts in which the Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus teaches his disciples; the Sentences of Sextus, a collection of moral maxims that circulated widely among orthodox Christians in Latin; and the Teachings of Silvanus, which most scholars read as non-Gnostic Christian wisdom. [cite:vt25_wiki_nhl] [cite:vt25_wiki_sextus] [cite:vt25_wiki_silvanus] Alongside these are Valentinian works from the school of the second-century Roman teacher Valentinus and Sethian works from the circle of mythmakers who traced humanity's spiritual lineage to Adam's son Seth. The previous part described both schools. [scene:vt24_what_they_taught|Part Twenty-Four: What the Evangelical Gnostics Taught] Nothing in the codices sets out a canon, a list of approved books or a rule of faith, and some tractates argue against others: the Testimony of Truth attacks the Valentinians by name. [cite:vt25_wiki_testtruth] A scribe's note after the Prayer of Thanksgiving in Codex VI says the text was chosen from a larger collection, so whoever assembled these books was selecting from a wider library. [cite:vt25_wiki_prayerthanks]

The next three sections take the contents in three groups. First come the sayings gospels and the gospels that teach in Jesus's voice, where the "kingdom within" theme is strongest. Second are the secret cosmologies, the myths of Sophia, the ignorant creator and the spark of light trapped in humanity. Last is a full catalogue of every tractate in all thirteen codices.

sections.h: The Sayings Gospels: Thomas, Truth, Philip and the Secret Dialogues
sections.html:
Several Nag Hammadi texts call themselves gospels or present Jesus teaching his disciples in private. They are the texts most often cited for the claim that early Christians were taught to find the kingdom within themselves rather than through a church. This section takes each in turn. It gives what the text is, what it says in order, its core teachings in plain words, a few short quotations from the standard English translations, what bishops and heresy writers said about it, and where scholars disagree. The quotations are short because the modern translations are under copyright. [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin]

The Gospel of Thomas (Codex II, tractate 2)

What it is. The Gospel of Thomas is a list of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus, most introduced only by "Jesus said". There is no birth story, no miracles, no trial, no crucifixion and no resurrection narrative. It opens: "These are the secret sayings which the living Jesus spoke and which Didymos Judas Thomas wrote down." [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin] The only complete copy is the Coptic one in Codex II, written shortly before 350. Parts of the same work in Greek had already been found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt by Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt between 1897 and 1904, without anyone knowing which work they belonged to. Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 1, now in the Bodleian Library in Oxford, dates from shortly after 200, and Papyri 654 and 655 from the mid-third century. [cite:vt25_ecw_thomas]

Outline. The sayings are not arranged by plot. They are grouped loosely by catchword and theme. The prologue and saying 1 promise that whoever finds the interpretation of the sayings "will not experience death". Sayings 2 to 5 deal with seeking, finding and the kingdom. Sayings 6 and 14 take up fasting, prayer and alms. There follow parables (the sower, the mustard seed, the net, the pearl, the leaven, the lost sheep), many with close parallels in Matthew, Mark and Luke, and sayings about the light within, the world as a corpse, becoming "a single one", and Jesus's identity. The collection closes with saying 114, an exchange about Mary. [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin]

Core teachings. Salvation in Thomas comes through understanding, not through belief in a saving death. The reader is to seek, be troubled, marvel and finally "rule over the All" (saying 2). The kingdom is not a future place in the sky. Saying 3 mocks leaders who say the kingdom is in the sky, since then "the birds of the sky will precede you", and continues: "the Kingdom is inside of you, and it is outside of you." Saying 113 adds that it "will not come by waiting for it" and that the kingdom "is spread out upon the earth, and men do not see it". [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin] The emphasis on what lies within also appears in saying 70: "If you bring forth what is within you, what you bring forth will save you." In saying 108 the speaker promises that whoever drinks from his mouth "will become like Me". [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin] On religious practice the text is pointed. Asked whether the disciples should fast, pray and give alms, Jesus answers in saying 14: "If you fast, you will give rise to sin for yourselves; and if you pray, you will be condemned". [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin] No church office, sacrament or payment appears anywhere in the 114 sayings.

The text does not support a simple egalitarian reading. In saying 114 Peter says "Let Mary leave us, for women are not worthy of Life", and Jesus answers that he will "make her male" so that she too may become a living spirit. [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin] Scholars read this as metaphor for transcending the body and its divisions, but the saying assumes that the female has to be transformed.

What the institution said. The earliest writer who quotes Thomas by name is Hippolytus of Rome, writing between 222 and 235. He says the Naassenes, a group he classed as heretics, quoted a saying "according to Thomas" about finding the kingdom in a child of seven. He calls them "impious" and attributes the saying to the physician Hippocrates rather than to Christ. [cite:vt25_hipp_ref5] [cite:vt25_ecw_thomas] Around 350 Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, told candidates for baptism that only four gospels were authentic and that "The Manichæans also wrote a Gospel according to Thomas" that "corrupts the souls of the simple sort". He added that books not read in church should not be read privately either. [cite:vt25_cyril_cat4] Cyril's attribution cannot be right as stated: the Greek fragments of Thomas date from about 200, before Mani was born in 216. The Decretum Gelasianum, a sixth-century list issued under the names of Popes Damasus and Gelasius, classes "the Gospel in the name of Thomas which the Manichaeans use" among apocryphal books, under a closing anathema. [cite:vt25_decretum] [cite:vt25_ecw_thomas] These are warnings and lists of books not to read. None of them orders copies destroyed.

What scholars dispute. The date of Thomas and its relationship to the other gospels are the main disputes. Stephen Patterson has argued for composition around 70 to 80 CE, and Ron Cameron for the late first century. On their view Thomas preserves an independent stream of Jesus tradition, perhaps as early as some material in the canonical gospels. [cite:vt25_ecw_thomas] Mark Goodacre and Simon Gathercole argue that Thomas knew and reworded Matthew, Mark and Luke. Goodacre points to word-for-word agreements and dates the final form to around 135. Critics reply that oral tradition explains such agreements as well. [cite:vt25_goodacre_thomas] Most scholars now accept that the collection grew in layers, which leaves open how early its earliest sayings are.

The Gospel of Truth (Codex I, tractate 3; Codex XII, tractate 2)

What it is. Despite its title, the Gospel of Truth is a meditative sermon, not an account of Jesus's life. It survives almost complete in the Jung Codex and in fragments in Codex XII. The Greek original is usually dated between 140 and 180. Several scholars have proposed Valentinus himself as the author; others assign it to his followers. [cite:vt25_wiki_gtruth]

Outline and teachings. The sermon opens with joy at knowing the Father, then tells how ignorance of the Father produced anguish and terror. Error took shape like a fog and built its own substitute world. Jesus came as a teacher who exposed that error, and Error persecuted him and nailed him to a tree. When he taught, "the living book of the living" appeared in the hearts of those who listened. The sermon closes with the return of those who know to the Father and their rest in him. [cite:vt25_wiki_gtruth] Its central teaching is that life without knowledge of God is like a nightmare, and knowing God is like waking up. Salvation is the end of ignorance, and the believer's goal is rest. [cite:vt25_wiki_gtruth]

What the institution said. Irenaeus of Lyon, writing around 180, complained that the Valentinians had "arrived at such a pitch of audacity, as to entitle their comparatively recent writing the Gospel of Truth", which "agrees in nothing with the Gospels of the Apostles". [cite:vt25_iren_311] The same chapter makes his case that there can be exactly four gospels, neither more nor fewer. [cite:vt25_iren_311] Whether the Nag Hammadi sermon is the work Irenaeus meant is probable but not proven, since he does not quote it.

The Gospel of Philip (Codex II, tractate 3)

What it is. The Gospel of Philip is a collection of short teachings, sayings and comments, composed in Greek and preserved only in Coptic. Bentley Layton described it as a Valentinian anthology, and scholars generally place it in the school of Valentinus. Most date it to the third century. [cite:vt25_wiki_gphil] [cite:vt25_nasscal_gphil]

Teachings. Philip is a sacramental text. It is often described as hostile to ritual, and it is not. "The Lord did everything in a mystery," it says: "a baptism and a chrism and a eucharist and a redemption and a bridal chamber." [cite:vt25_wiki_gphil] The bridal chamber, the highest of the five, is a rite that joins male and female to each other and to the divine. Scholars dispute whether it was a performed ritual, and whether it had any sexual element. [cite:vt25_nasscal_gphil] On resurrection, Philip teaches that it must be received in this life: "Those who say they will die first and then rise are in error." [cite:vt25_wiki_gphil] Philip also calls Mary Magdalene Jesus's koinōnos, a Greek loanword that can mean companion, partner or spouse. The often-cited passage saying that Jesus "used to kiss her" breaks off at the decisive word because the papyrus is damaged. One translator restored "mouth"; the critical edition leaves the gap open, and the text cannot settle the question. [cite:vt25_wiki_gphil]

What the institution said. No surviving ancient condemnation names this Gospel of Philip. Its school, the Valentinians, was the main target of Irenaeus's Against Heresies and later heresy writers, as Part Twenty-Four sets out. [scene:vt24_the_heresy_hunters|Part Twenty-Four: The Heresy Hunters]

The dialogue gospels: James, Thomas the Contender and the Saviour

Three further texts present the risen Jesus teaching chosen disciples in private. The Apocryphon (Secret Book) of James (Codex I, 2), probably written in Egypt in the second century, is framed as a letter from James the Just about a revelation given to him and Peter. Jesus tells them to "be filled" with the spirit and not to fear suffering, and warns them not to let "the kingdom of heaven become a desert within them". [cite:vt25_wiki_apjas] The Book of Thomas the Contender (Codex II, 7) is the most ascetic text in this group. It teaches that whoever knows himself comes to know the depth of all things, and calls for renouncing visible, bodily pleasures and the burning fire of desire. [cite:vt25_wiki_thomcont] The Dialogue of the Saviour (Codex III, 5), probably complete by about 150, has Judas, Matthew and Mary questioning Jesus about rest, the place of life, and the dissolution of "the works of womanhood" at the end of bodily existence. Unusually for this library, it treats the Father as the good creator rather than blaming a lower god. [cite:vt25_wiki_dialsav]

A Valentinian letter belongs with these texts for its subject. The Treatise on the Resurrection (Codex I, 4), addressed to a student named Rheginos, holds that the resurrection is real, not a metaphor, but that believers should already count themselves risen in spirit. Most scholars date it to the second half of the second century. [cite:vt25_wiki_treatres]

What this group shows

These texts give the clearest documentary support for the "kingdom within" theme of this book. Thomas places the kingdom inside and outside the hearer and rejects the outward practices of fasting, prayer and alms. Truth makes knowledge itself the means of salvation. James warns against letting the kingdom become a desert within. [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin] [cite:vt25_wiki_gtruth] [cite:vt25_wiki_apjas] They do not support the claim that every Gnostic text rejected ritual and teachers. Philip prizes five sacraments, Thomas the Contender is rigorously ascetic, and the Valentinian authors wrote as teachers instructing pupils. [cite:vt25_wiki_gphil] [cite:vt25_wiki_thomcont] The record of what bishops said about these books is consistent. From Irenaeus in about 180 to the Decretum in the sixth century, they warned against them, excluded them from church reading and anathematised the books and their authors. No surviving document orders the books burned. [cite:vt25_iren_311] [cite:vt25_cyril_cat4] [cite:vt25_decretum] The next section turns to the second group: texts that do not teach in short sayings but tell a whole hidden history of the cosmos.

sections.h: The Secret Cosmos: Sophia, the Blind Creator and the Way Back
sections.html:
Most of the Nag Hammadi texts teach through myth rather than sayings. They tell where the true God is, how a divine power fell, how a lower and ignorant ruler made the visible world, how a spark of the higher light came to be trapped in human beings, and how that spark is to be awakened and brought home. Scholars group most of these myths under two schools described in Part Twenty-Four: the Sethians, named for their claim to descend spiritually from Adam's son Seth, and the Valentinians. [scene:vt24_what_they_taught|Part Twenty-Four: What They Taught] This section goes through the central myth text by text, then the texts that describe the soul's ascent, then those that turn the myth against the bishops of their day.

The Apocryphon of John (Codex II, 1; III, 1; IV, 1)

What it is. The Apocryphon (Secret Book) of John is the fullest statement of the Sethian myth and the most heavily copied text in the find. Three copies were in the jar, and a fourth is in the Berlin Codex, a separate manuscript bought in Cairo in 1896 that also holds the Gospel of Mary. The copies come in two recensions: a long one in Codices II and IV, and a short one in Codex III and the Berlin Codex. All four are fourth-century Coptic translations of a Greek work written in the second century, before about 180. [cite:vt25_wiki_apjohn] The Gospel of Mary is treated in the next part. [scene:vt26_gospel_of_mary|Part Twenty-Six: The Gospel of Mary]

Outline. After the crucifixion the apostle John is grieving. The Saviour appears to him in shifting forms, calms his fear and begins a revelation of how the world came to be and how it will end. [cite:vt25_wiki_apjohn] The revelation runs in a fixed order, set out in the figure below. It begins with the unknowable first principle, the Monad, of which the text says: "The Monad is a monarchy with nothing above it." [cite:vt25_ecw_apjohn] From the Monad's thought comes Barbelo, the first emanation, and from her a series of aeons, eternal beings that together make up the divine fullness, the Pleroma. The last of these aeons, Sophia (Wisdom), wants to bring forth a likeness of herself without the consent of the Spirit and without her partner.
