The result is a misshapen being with a lion's face and a serpent's body, whom she hides in a cloud and names Yaldabaoth. [cite:vt25_wiki_apjohn] Yaldabaoth has stolen some of his mother's power. He makes rulers, the archons, and a world of his own, and then he boasts: "I am a jealous God, and there is no other God beside me." [cite:vt25_ecw_apjohn]

The rest of the myth is the recovery of that stolen light. Sophia repents. A voice and an image of the true Human shine down on the waters, and the archons try to copy the image, which produces Adam, who lies motionless. The higher powers trick Yaldabaoth into breathing his mother's power into Adam, and the light passes out of the creator into the human being. [cite:vt25_wiki_apjohn] The archons then imprison Adam in a body and a false paradise. The Saviour says he himself caused Adam to eat from the tree of knowledge, which the archons had hidden. Eve is drawn from Adam, and through her Adam recognises his own nature. Yaldabaoth binds humanity with a "counterfeit spirit" that keeps people ignorant. Salvation comes when Christ, speaking as Pronoia (Providence), descends into this prison. "I am the remembrance of the pleroma," he says, and he wakes those who sleep and seals them in light with five seals. [cite:vt25_ecw_apjohn] [cite:vt25_wiki_apjohn] The text ends with a curse on anyone who would "exchange these things for a gift or for food or for drink". [cite:vt25_ecw_apjohn] The teaching may be given away, but it must not be sold.

What the institution said. Irenaeus does not name the Apocryphon of John. But in Against Heresies I.29, written around 180, he summarises a myth that closely matches its first half, which he attributes to "Barbeliotes". It has Barbelo, Ennoia, the Self-Begotten, Sophia "also called Prunicus", and a first ruler who says, "I am a jealous God, and besides me there is no one." Irenaeus answers from Exodus 20:5 and Isaiah 45 and calls the teaching a falsehood. [cite:vt25_iren_129] This is the strongest evidence that a version of the myth was in circulation before 180, and the text was still being copied in Egypt in the fourth century and again in the fifth (the Berlin Codex). [cite:vt25_wiki_apjohn]

What scholars dispute, and a caution. The creator's boast echoes Isaiah 45:5 and Exodus 20:5, so the myth is a reading of the Hebrew Bible's God as an ignorant lower power. [cite:vt25_iren_129] That reading belongs to second-century Christian writers who were reinterpreting scripture they shared with Jews; it is a claim made inside a Christian argument, and this book does not repeat it as a claim about Judaism or about Jews. Modern antisemitic uses of the "demiurge" idea exist, and they have no basis in the history recorded here. The long recension also inserts an excerpt from a Sethian book attributed to Zoroaster, a sign that the text was edited over time. [cite:vt25_wiki_apjohn]

Retellings of Genesis: the Hypostasis of the Archons and On the Origin of the World

The Hypostasis (Reality) of the Archons (Codex II, 4) is a Sethian retelling of Genesis 1 to 6, usually dated to the late second or third century. A spiritual woman gives Adam life and escapes the rulers, leaving only her shadow, the fleshly Eve; the serpent becomes the instructor, and eating from the tree of knowledge is a gain rather than a fall. Norea, Seth's sister, burns Noah's ark when she is refused passage, and the angel Eleleth rescues her from the rulers and foretells a "true Man" who will overthrow them. [cite:vt25_wiki_hyparch] Its neighbour in the codex, On the Origin of the World (Codex II, 5; opening lines also in XIII, 2), covers much of the same ground. It denies that chaos came first and ends with the defeat of darkness; both texts tell of the creator's son Sabaoth, who repents and is enthroned in the seventh heaven. [cite:vt25_wiki_origin] [cite:vt25_wiki_hyparch]

The voice of the divine feminine: Trimorphic Protennoia and Thunder, Perfect Mind

The Trimorphic Protennoia (Codex XIII, 1), a Sethian text, is spoken in the first person by Barbelo, the divine First Thought. She descends three times: first as Voice, then as Speech, then as Word, which takes human form. [cite:vt25_wiki_protennoia] The Thunder, Perfect Mind (Codex VI, 2) is a poem in a female divine voice made of paradoxes: "For I am the first and the last"; "I am the whore and the holy one"; "I am the wife and the virgin." [cite:vt25_pbs_thunder] It names no Sophia, no archons and no Christ, and scholars such as George MacRae and Hal Taussig have argued that it should not be classed as Gnostic at all. [cite:vt25_wiki_thunder]

Sethian scripture and the ascent texts

Several texts describe the Sethians' sacred history or an inner ascent through the heavens. The Holy Book of the Great Invisible Spirit, also called the Coptic Gospel of the Egyptians (Codex III, 2; IV, 2), traces Father, Mother and Son out of the invisible Spirit and makes Seth the father of an incorruptible race that is saved through baptism. [cite:vt25_wiki_holybook] In the Apocalypse of Adam (Codex V, 5), Adam tells Seth how knowledge was lost and how an Illuminator will come, while thirteen kingdoms give false accounts of where the Illuminator came from. It contains no clear Christian content, which leads some scholars to place it before or outside Christianity. [cite:vt25_wiki_apocadam]

Four treatises describe a visionary ascent. In Zostrianos (Codex VIII, 1), the longest tractate in the find, the seer leaves his body on a luminous cloud and rises through the aeons, receiving a baptism at each stage. [cite:vt25_wiki_zost] Allogenes (Codex XI, 3) describes contemplation rising through Barbelo toward an Unknowable God beyond being and mind, who can be approached only through a learned ignorance. [cite:vt25_wiki_allogenes] Marsanes (Codex X) ranks thirteen "seals" and links the soul's shape to the vowels and consonants, and the Three Steles of Seth (Codex VII, 5) is a liturgy of hymns to Barbelo for ascent and descent. [cite:vt25_wiki_marsanes] [cite:vt25_wiki_3steles] The Apocalypse of Paul (Codex V, 2) and the First Apocalypse of James (Codex V, 3) describe the soul's passage past toll collectors in the heavens. [cite:vt25_wiki_apocpaul] [cite:vt25_wiki_1apjas]

What the institution, and a philosopher, said. These ascent texts drew criticism from outside the church as well as inside it. The pagan philosopher Porphyry records that Christians in his teacher Plotinus's circle in Rome in the 260s circulated revelations under the names of Zoroaster, Zostrianos, Nicotheus, Allogenes and Messos. Plotinus wrote a treatise against them, now Ennead II.9, "Against the Gnostics", arguing that those who claimed sole possession of truth were the ones ignorant of it. [cite:vt25_bmcr_plotinus] [cite:vt25_ecw_allogenes] [cite:vt25_wiki_allogenes] Around 375 the bishop Epiphanius of Salamis reported in his Panarion that the Sethians and the Archontics "make use of books called 'Allogenes'". [cite:vt25_ecw_allogenes] So the first recorded attacks on the Sethian ascent books came from a pagan Platonist school and from a Christian heresy writer.

The Valentinian system: the Tripartite Tractate

The Tripartite Tractate (Codex I, 5) is the most systematic Valentinian work in the find, dated to the third or fourth century in its present form. In place of Sophia, the Logos is the power whose overreach causes the fall. Humanity is divided into three kinds: spiritual people, who will be saved completely; material people, who will perish; and "psychic" people in between, who can be saved if they choose the good. [cite:vt25_wiki_tripartite] This middle class matters for the history in this book. It gave Valentinian teachers a place for ordinary church members as people who could be saved, which helps explain why many Valentinians stayed inside the churches rather than founding separate ones; Irenaeus reports that they called church members "animal" (psychic) people. [cite:vt24_ah1_06] [scene:vt24_how_they_lived|Part Twenty-Four: How They Lived]

Texts that answer the bishops

Some of the texts in the jar argue back against the church that was condemning their schools. In the Apocalypse of Peter (Codex VII, 3), written around 200, Peter sees the living Jesus "glad and laughing" above the cross while only his fleshly body is nailed. The Saviour warns that some who call themselves "bishop" and "deacons", as if their authority came from God, are "dry canals". [cite:vt25_wiki_gapocpeter] The Second Treatise of the Great Seth (Codex VII, 2) also has Jesus die only in appearance. It calls the patriarchs, prophets and Moses a "laughingstock" of the lower rulers and mocks those who preach "the doctrine of a dead man". [cite:vt25_wiki_2seth] The Testimony of Truth (Codex IX, 3) turns in several directions at once. It rejects the Law, martyrdom, water baptism, marriage and childbearing, and it also condemns the Valentinians, the followers of Basilides and the Simonians as heretics. [cite:vt25_wiki_testtruth] Condemnation ran in both directions: these authors were rival Christians claiming authority of their own.

Interpretation, not finding: Sophia's fall and return as a map of ascent

The Sophia platform (Observe The System) reads this myth as a map of consciousness rather than a cosmology: Sophia's grasping as the mind acting apart from its source, Yaldabaoth as the self-made ego, the archons as the compulsions that keep awareness asleep, and the seals as stages of awakening. The platform's reading is set out in full in Part Twenty-Six, for the Pistis Sophia, the text it takes its name from. [scene:vt26_pistis_sophia|Part Twenty-Six: Pistis Sophia] It is a modern reading, close to Carl Jung's psychological treatment of Gnostic myth. The ancient sources show Sethian and Valentinian readers treating the myths as accounts of real divine powers and a real ascent, sometimes enacted in baptism and ritual, not as a coded psychology. The next section gives the whole library in a single table.

sections.h: The Whole Library: Every Codex, Every Tractate
sections.html:
This section lists the full contents of the Nag Hammadi find in codex order, from the Jung Codex to the loose leaves called Codex XIII. Each tractate gets a one-line summary of its teaching and two further judgements. The first is whether that teaching conflicted with what the bishops' church taught. The second is whether a bishop, a church writer or a church document is recorded as condemning the text by name or condemning the school it belongs to. The order and numbering follow the standard edition. [cite:vt25_wiki_nhl]

How the two judgement columns are made

"Institutional teaching" here means the doctrine the bishops' church set down in writing in the period these books were copied. The creed of the Council of Nicaea in 325 opens with belief in "one God, the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible", and says that the Son "was incarnate and was made man. He suffered and the third day he rose again." [cite:vt25_nicaea_creed] Irenaeus of Lyon, around 180, held that there could be only four gospels. [cite:vt25_iren_311] The same church baptised with water, expected the bodily resurrection and was governed by bishops and deacons. A tractate is marked as conflicting when its teaching contradicts one of these points. Most often the conflict is a lower creator separate from the true God, a Christ who only seemed to suffer, a resurrection already completed in spirit, a rejection of water baptism, or an attack on church offices. A text that teaches in the familiar language of Christian or philosophical morality is marked "no".

The condemnation column names only recorded acts. One general condemnation covers all of these books and is not repeated in every row. In 367 Athanasius of Alexandria warned the churches of Egypt against books "called apocryphal", which he called "an invention of heretics". [cite:vt14_ect_festal39] A row says "none by name" when no surviving bishop or church document names that particular text, even if the school it belongs to was attacked. For school-level condemnations, the reference is Irenaeus's Against Heresies (c.180), written to expose what he called "knowledge falsely so called" and aimed first at the Valentinians, and Tertullian's Against the Valentinians (early third century). [cite:vt24_ah1_pref] [cite:vt24_tert_adval] The Decretum Gelasianum, a sixth-century list later issued under papal names, names Valentinus and Basilides among heretics and closes with an anathema on all the books it lists. [cite:vt25_decretum]

What the catalogue shows

Counted by tractate, the conflict is real. More than half of the tractates teach something the creed of 325 or Irenaeus's rule excluded. Most of the rest conflict in part. The most common points are a creator who is not the highest God, a divine Mother or Sophia whose error produced the world, a Christ who did not truly suffer, or a resurrection already completed in spirit. [cite:vt25_nicaea_creed] [cite:vt25_wiki_apjohn] [cite:vt25_wiki_2seth] [cite:vt25_wiki_treatres] Several texts openly reject what the bishops' church practised: water baptism in the Paraphrase of Shem and the Testimony of Truth, the authority of bishops and deacons in the Apocalypse of Peter, and fasting, prayer and alms in Thomas. [cite:vt25_wiki_shem] [cite:vt25_wiki_testtruth] [cite:vt25_wiki_gapocpeter] [cite:vt25_thomas_lambdin] These are the passages most consistent with the reading that these texts offered direct access to God without the church as intermediary, and Part Thirty-One sets them against the institution's own rules. [scene:vt31_two_economies|Part Thirty-One: Two Economies of the Sacred]

The catalogue also complicates that reading in three ways. First, the library is not one teaching. It holds Plato, Hermes, the moral maxims of Sextus and the orthodox-sounding Teachings of Silvanus beside Sethian myth. Melchizedek insists that Jesus truly suffered, and the Testimony of Truth condemns other Gnostic schools as harshly as any bishop did. [cite:vt25_wiki_nhl] [cite:vt25_wiki_melch] [cite:vt25_wiki_testtruth] Second, the Valentinian texts carry their own rites (anointing, baptism, eucharist, bridal chamber), so these were not religions without ritual. [cite:vt25_wiki_valexp] [cite:vt25_wiki_gphil] Third, only a minority of the tractates were ever condemned by name. The Gospel of Truth was condemned by Irenaeus, if it is the work he names. Thomas was named by Hippolytus, Cyril and the Decretum, and the "Proverbs" of Sixtus by the Decretum. The Allogenes and Zostrianos revelations were attacked by the pagan Plotinus and his pupils and by the bishop Epiphanius. [cite:vt25_iren_311] [cite:vt25_hipp_ref5] [cite:vt25_cyril_cat4] [cite:vt25_decretum] [cite:vt25_ecw_allogenes] [cite:vt25_bmcr_plotinus] Most of the others were condemned only as part of a school, or not at all, and the earliest attacks on two of them came from a pagan philosophical school rather than from a church.

The condemnations that are recorded follow the same pattern as in the previous sections. Bishops and heresy writers from Lyon, Rome, Jerusalem, Alexandria and Salamis, writing between about 180 and the sixth century, warned against these books, excluded them from church reading and anathematised them. [cite:vt25_iren_311] [cite:vt25_cyril_cat4] [cite:vt14_ect_festal39] [cite:vt25_decretum] Most of these writers were not bishops of Rome, and the one document issued under papal names, the Decretum, is a later compilation. None of the sources gathered here contains an order to burn the Nag Hammadi books. The copies survived because someone in fourth-century Egypt valued them enough to bind them in leather, collect them and put them in the ground. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] Part Twenty-Six turns to three texts that were not in the jar but tell the same story from other manuscripts: the Gospel of Mary, the Gospel of Judas and the Pistis Sophia. [scene:vt26_gospel_of_mary|Part Twenty-Six: Outside the Jar]

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Six
chapters.title: Outside the Jar: Mary, Judas and Pistis Sophia
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-Six leaves the Nag Hammadi jar for three texts that are often wrongly placed in it. The Gospel of Mary came to Berlin in 1896 in a codex bought in Cairo; the Gospel of Judas surfaced in Middle Egypt in the 1970s and was published only in 2006; Pistis Sophia has sat in a London library since 1785. Each is laid out in the same way: the manuscript and its date, the text's outline in order, its teaching in plain words with a few short quotations, the points where it cuts against the emerging church (a woman teaching the apostles and Peter rebuked for doubting her; the twelve portrayed as priests sacrificing their own followers; Wisdom's fall and return, with Mary again out-speaking Peter), and what bishops, popes and councils actually said or did about it, with dates. The record that results is uneven, and the part says so: one of the three texts was named and condemned by a bishop around 180, the other two by no surviving authority at all, and the institution's most consequential act concerned not a text but the reputation of Mary Magdalene.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty-Six established three things. The Gospel of Mary, known from the Berlin Codex bought in Cairo in 1896 and two third-century Greek fragments, teaches that the Son of Humanity is within, warns against laying down rules beyond the Saviour's, and ends with Levi rebuking Peter for rejecting a woman's teaching; no ancient authority named it, but Gregory I's homily of about 591 fused Mary Magdalene with a sinful woman, a reading the Roman calendar dropped in 1969 before her memorial was raised to a feast on 3 June 2016, while ordination remains reserved to men. [cite:vt26_wiki_berlincodex] [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] [cite:vt26_pearse_greg33] [cite:vt26_va_feast2016] [cite:vt26_va_ordsac1994] The Gospel of Judas was condemned by Irenaeus around 180 and survived in a single codex copied between about 220 and 340, published on 6 April 2006; its scorn for the twelve and their sacrifice is clear, while whether its Judas is hero or demon remains disputed. [cite:vt26_na_iren131] [cite:vt26_natgeo_journey] [cite:vt26_getrel_deconick] Pistis Sophia, in London since 1785, tells Wisdom's fall and repentance, gives Mary the leading voice against Peter's objections, and lays down a long moral code of its own; nothing in the record shows it was ever condemned. [cite:vt26_wiki_askew] [cite:vt26_mead_ch72] [cite:vt26_mead_ch102] Part Twenty-Seven turns to a Bible that Rome never governed: the 81-book canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and the Book of Enoch it kept. [scene:vt27_church_and_canon|Part Twenty-Seven: The Ethiopian Bible]

sections.h: The Gospel of Mary: A Woman Teaches the Apostles
sections.html:
The Gospel of Mary is often described as one of the Nag Hammadi texts. It is not. It reached modern scholars half a century before the jar was opened, in a different codex. What survives is less than half of the original, but the surviving pages contain one of the sharpest scenes in early Christian literature about who had the right to teach after Yeshua was gone: Peter and Andrew refuse to believe a woman, and another disciple tells Peter he is wrong. This section sets out what the text is, what it says in order, what it teaches, and what the institution said and did about Mary Magdalene, the woman most scholars take it to be about. [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary] [cite:vt26_nasscal_gmary]

What it is

The main copy is in the Berlin Codex, catalogued as Papyrus Berolinensis 8502 and also called the Akhmim Codex. The German scholar Carl Reinhardt bought it in Cairo in January 1896. The dealer's account was that it had been found wrapped in feathers in a niche in a wall at a Christian burial site near Akhmim in Upper Egypt. It is a single-quire papyrus book in Sahidic Coptic, copied in the early fifth century or possibly the late fourth. The Gospel of Mary is its first text; the others are the Apocryphon of John, the Sophia of Jesus Christ and a short Act of Peter. Carl Schmidt presented the codex to the Prussian Academy of Sciences on 16 July 1896, but the full edition of its Gnostic texts did not appear until Walter Till's of 1955. It is held today in the Berlin papyrus collection. [cite:vt26_wiki_berlincodex]

Two small Greek fragments show that the text was copied in its original language a century or more earlier: Papyrus Rylands 463, published in 1938, and Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 3525, published in 1983, both from the third century. They add little to the Coptic text, but they fix a latest possible date. Karen King places the composition in the early second century, noting that the author seems to know the Gospel of John and perhaps Paul's letters; Christopher Tuckett places it in the first half of the second century; others prefer the second half. [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary] [cite:vt26_nasscal_gmary]

The loss is severe. Pages 1 to 6 and 11 to 14 of the Coptic codex are missing, so the text opens in the middle of a conversation and breaks off again in the middle of Mary's vision. King's The Gospel of Mary of Magdala (2003), Esther de Boer's study (2004) and Tuckett's Oxford edition (2007) are the standard works. [cite:vt26_nasscal_gmary] Quotations below follow Mark M. Mattison's translation, which he has placed in the public domain, cited by codex page. [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary]

Outline

The surviving text falls into five parts. First, the lost opening, which most scholars reconstruct as an appearance of the risen Saviour. Second, his final teaching (pages 7 to 9): the disciples ask about matter and sin; he answers, gives them parting instructions and leaves. Third, the disciples' grief (page 9): they weep and fear that they will be killed as he was, and Mary comforts them and turns their hearts "toward the Good". Fourth, Mary's account of her vision (pages 10 to 17), which includes a teaching on how a vision is seen and, after the four-page gap, the ascent of a soul past hostile powers. Fifth, the dispute (pages 17 to 19): Andrew and Peter reject her account, Mary weeps and answers, Levi rebukes Peter, and the disciples go out to preach. [cite:vt26_nasscal_gmary] [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary]

What it teaches

On matter, the Saviour teaches that every created thing will return to its own root. On sin, he gives the text's most quoted answer: "Sin doesn't exist, but you're the ones who make sin" when they act in accordance with what he calls the nature of adultery. Sin here is not a debt recorded against a person and cancelled by a priest; it is a confusion that a person produces and can stop producing. [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] De Boer reads these ideas against Stoic and Jewish parallels rather than a developed Gnostic myth; the NASSCAL entry likewise notes Stoic ideas on the dissolution of matter. [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary] [cite:vt26_nasscal_gmary]

His parting words carry three instructions. He warns them against anyone who says the Saviour is "here" or "there", "because the Son of Humanity exists within you" (other translations render it "Son of Man"). He tells them to go and preach the gospel. And he adds a limit: "Don't lay down any rules beyond what I've given you, nor make a law like the lawgiver, lest you be bound by it." [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] The first instruction stands close to the canonical saying on the kingdom "within" or "among" you, whose translation is discussed in [scene:vt20_yeshua_record|Part Twenty]. The third is the passage most often cited for the view that some early Christians resisted the growth of church law; it is one text's instruction, and how far its readers lived by it is not recorded. Part Thirty-One sets it beside the institution's precepts. [scene:vt31_sunday_and_law|Sunday and the law]

Mary's vision turns on a teaching about perception. She asks whether a person sees a vision through the soul or the spirit; the Saviour answers that it is seen through the mind, which lies between them, and earlier tells her that "where the mind is, there is the treasure". [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary] After the gap, the soul climbs past a series of powers that try to hold it: Desire, then Ignorance, then a fourth power that takes seven forms, named Darkness, Desire, Ignorance, Zeal for Death, the Kingdom of the Flesh, the Foolish "Wisdom" of Flesh and the "Wisdom" of Anger. The soul answers each and goes free, declaring that "what binds me has been killed" and that "ignorance has died". [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] The ascent is reached by the soul's own understanding; no rite, office or intermediary appears in it.

The dispute: where the text cuts against authority

The scene that follows is why the text matters to this book. Peter had opened the exchange by asking Mary to speak: "Sister, we know the Savior loved you more than all other women", so tell us what you remember that we have not heard. When she finishes, Andrew says: "I myself don't believe that the Savior said these things", because the teachings "seem like different ideas". Peter goes further and asks whether the Saviour would really have spoken with a woman privately, without their knowledge, and adds: "Will we turn around and all listen to her? Did he prefer her to us?" Mary weeps and asks whether he thinks she invented it or is lying about the Saviour. [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary]

Levi answers for her. "Peter, you've always been angry," he says, and now he is treating the woman as an adversary; "if the Savior made her worthy, who are you then to reject her?" The Saviour, Levi adds, knew her well and loved her more than them. He tells them to be ashamed, to put on the perfect human and to preach as they were told, without laying down rules beyond what the Saviour gave. The text ends: "they started to go out to teach and to preach." [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary]

Two challenges sit in this scene. One is about revelation: Mary's authority rests on a private vision, not on public commissioning, and Andrew rejects it because it is unfamiliar. The other is about gender: Peter objects that she is a woman. Karen King reads Peter and Andrew as voicing second-century positions that rejected both esoteric revelation and women's teaching authority, and the text as taking Mary's side against them. Tuckett also reads Mary as a model who fulfils the Saviour's role. [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary] Peter is the apostle from whom the bishops of Rome later traced their succession, and the text gives the last word against him to another disciple. The same conflict between Peter and Mary recurs in the Gospel of Thomas and Pistis Sophia, which Esther de Boer cites as evidence that the Mary of these texts is the Magdalene. [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary]

The identification is not unanimous. Most scholars, including King, take the Mary of this gospel to be Mary Magdalene. Stephen Shoemaker and F. Stanley Jones have argued for Mary the mother of Yeshua, and one writer has proposed a sister of Yeshua named Mary. Richard Valantasis, who accepts the Magdalene reading, adds that it does not confirm an earthly marriage. [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary]

What the institution said about the text

The record here is thin, and it should be stated precisely. No surviving church council, papal letter or heresy catalogue names the Gospel of Mary. The sixth-century Decretum Gelasianum, which lists dozens of rejected books and consigns their authors and followers to anathema, names gospels of Thomas, Peter, Matthias, Barnabas, Bartholomew and Andrew, but not one of Mary. [cite:vt26_tert_decretum] [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary] The nearest ancient reference is hostile and probably concerns a different book: Epiphanius of Salamis, in the 370s, described a "Greater Questions of Mary" used by a group he called the Borborites, a name meaning "the filthy", and attributed obscene content to it. That text does not survive, and its contents are known only from his attack. [cite:vt26_nasscal_qmary] [cite:vt26_wiki_panarion] The Gospel of Mary fell out of copying for reasons the record does not show; it was not, on present evidence, condemned by name.

What the institution said about Mary Magdalene

The canonical record of Mary Magdalene is substantial. Luke lists her among women who supported Yeshua from their own means and says seven demons had gone out of her. Mark, Matthew and John name her at the crucifixion. All four gospels name her at the empty tomb, and in John she is the first to see the risen Yeshua and is sent to tell the others. [cite:vt26_wiki_magdalene] That is the basis on which later writers called her "apostle of the apostles".

In a homily given in Rome in about 591, Pope Gregory I joined three women into one: the unnamed sinner of Luke 7 who anointed Yeshua's feet, Mary of Bethany, and Mary Magdalene. He read the seven demons as a figure for every vice: "what are these seven demons, if not the universality of all vices?" [cite:vt26_pearse_greg33] [cite:vt26_wiki_magdalene] The homily calls her a sinner in the city; it does not use the word prostitute, but it ties her sins to the flesh, and the image of the penitent prostitute that dominated Western art grew from this reading. [cite:vt26_pearse_greg33] [cite:vt26_wiki_magdalene] The Eastern churches did not make the conflation and honour her as a myrrh-bearer "Equal to the Apostles". [cite:vt26_wiki_magdalene]

The Roman calendar revised in 1969 separated the three women: the 22 July memorial now refers to Mary Magdalene alone, and Mary of Bethany is commemorated with Martha on 29 July. [cite:vt26_wiki_magdalene] A popular claim holds that the Church "declared her a prostitute in 591" and reversed itself in 1969 because of the Nag Hammadi find. The homily was a sermon, not a declaration; the Gospel of Mary was published from the Berlin Codex in 1955, not from Nag Hammadi; and no document links the 1969 change to either text.

On 3 June 2016 the Congregation for Divine Worship issued a decree, at the "express wish" of Pope Francis, raising her memorial to a feast, the same rank as the apostles. Its secretary, Archbishop Arthur Roche, explained it with the title "apostolorum apostola", citing Rabanus Maurus and Thomas Aquinas, and acknowledged that Western tradition after Gregory had identified her with the anointing woman and the sister of Lazarus. [cite:vt26_va_feast2016]

The question the Gospel of Mary raises, whether a woman may hold teaching authority among the apostles, has a present-day answer from Rome that does not refer to the text. John Paul II's apostolic letter Ordinatio Sacerdotalis of 22 May 1994 declared that "the Church has no authority whatsoever to confer priestly ordination on women" and that this judgment "is to be definitively held", resting the case on Christ's choice of "the twelve men" as the foundation of the Church. [cite:vt26_va_ordsac1994] A commission chaired by Cardinal Giuseppe Petrocchi, whose report Pope Leo XIV had made public on 4 December 2025, ruled out women deacons as a grade of holy orders by seven votes to one, while stating that the question did not yet allow a definitive judgment "as is the case with priestly ordination". [cite:vt26_vn_petrocchi2025] As of October 2026 that remains the position. The institution has thus raised Mary Magdalene's liturgical rank to the apostles' while keeping ordained authority male; the Gospel of Mary, in which Peter doubts a woman's teaching and is rebuked for it, is the ancient text that bears most directly on that choice, though none of these documents cites it.

sections.h: The Gospel of Judas: The Text a Bishop Named, Lost for 1,800 Years
sections.html:
The Gospel of Judas is the one text in this part that the institution's own writers named and condemned in antiquity. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, mentioned it in about 180, and for eighteen centuries his hostile sentence was all that was known of it. A Coptic copy surfaced in Egypt in the 1970s, passed through dealers, a theft, a bank vault and a freezer, and was published by the National Geographic Society on 6 April 2006 as the story of a Judas who obeyed Yeshua rather than betrayed him. Within a year other specialists argued that the published translation had made Judas a hero by mistranslating a text that makes him a demon. This section gives the text's history, its outline and teaching, both readings, and the institution's responses in 180, the 370s and 2006. [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas] [cite:vt26_natgeo_journey]

What the bishops said first

Irenaeus described a group that honoured the figures the Hebrew Bible condemns: Cain, Esau, Korah and the men of Sodom. Of Judas they taught that he "alone, knowing the truth as no others did, accomplished the mystery of the betrayal". "They produce a fictitious history of this kind," he wrote, "which they style the Gospel of Judas." [cite:vt26_na_iren131] Later heresiologists gave this group the label "Cainites". Epiphanius of Salamis attacked the same group and its gospel in his Panarion, begun in 374 or 375. [cite:vt26_arys_epiphanius] [cite:vt26_wiki_panarion] Whether the text Irenaeus knew is the one recovered in the twentieth century cannot be proved; the recovered text does not mention Cain or Korah, but it matches his central claim, that Judas alone understood. [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas]

Irenaeus's condemnation is the institution's documented act against this book. It was a bishop's polemic, not a council's decree, written in Gaul about a century and a half before Constantine, and it ordered nothing to be done to the text. No later council names it, and it is absent from the rejected books of the sixth-century Decretum Gelasianum. [cite:vt26_tert_decretum] On the survival of the Judas text, as on the Nag Hammadi books, the record shows condemnation by writing, not a documented order to destroy. The wider pattern is set out in [scene:vt24_the_heresy_hunters|the heresy hunters].

How the codex reached print

The modern history is a case study in what the antiquities trade does to a manuscript. In the 1970s an Egyptian farmer reportedly found a limestone box in a tomb near Maghagha in Middle Egypt, in the El Minya area. In 1978 he sold the codex to a Cairo dealer known as Hanna. In about 1980 it was stolen with other objects and taken to Geneva; Hanna recovered it in 1982. In May 1983 Stephen Emmel and two other scholars examined it in a Geneva hotel room; Hanna asked $3 million and no sale followed. In 1984 it was offered in New York, found no buyer and was placed in a safe-deposit box in Hicksville, New York, where it stayed for about sixteen years. [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas] [cite:vt26_natgeo_journey]

The Zurich dealer Frieda Nussberger-Tchacos bought it in April 2000, and the codex now bears her name. Yale declined to buy it over its provenance. She passed it to the American dealer Bruce Ferrini, who stored it in a freezer, which accelerated its decay; after a dispute over payment she recovered it and in February 2001 transferred it to the Maecenas Foundation for Ancient Art in Basel. Rodolphe Kasser announced its existence in July 2004. By then the papyrus had broken into nearly a thousand pieces, some blackened past reading; restorers recovered roughly 90 to 95 per cent of what had survived. A University of Arizona laboratory dated papyrus and leather samples to between 220 and 340 CE. The National Geographic Society unveiled the English translation in Washington on 6 April 2006, and a critical edition by Kasser, Marvin Meyer, Gregor Wurst and François Gaudard followed in 2007. National Geographic reported that the pages are to be returned to the Coptic Museum in Cairo; whether that has happened has not been publicly confirmed. [cite:vt26_natgeo_journey] [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas] [cite:vt26_wiki_tchacos] Further fragments held by Ferrini surfaced later; Meyer and Wurst presented a preliminary translation of photographs of them in November 2009. [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas]

What the codex contains

Codex Tchacos holds four texts in Coptic: the Letter of Peter to Philip, a version of the First Apocalypse of James (both also known from Nag Hammadi), the Gospel of Judas, and a fragment of a book featuring Allogenes that differs from the Nag Hammadi Allogenes. About a dozen original pages are missing. [cite:vt26_wiki_tchacos] The Gospel of Judas is a Coptic translation of a Greek work that most scholars date before about 180, in line with Irenaeus's report. [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas] Quotations below follow the 2006 National Geographic translation by Kasser, Meyer and Wurst, which is copyrighted and quoted in short phrases only.

Outline

The text names itself at the start as "the secret account of the revelation that Jesus spoke in conversation with Judas Iscariot". It then runs in five movements. First, Jesus finds the disciples giving thanks over bread and laughs at them, saying they do this because "it is through this that your god [will be] praised"; they grow angry, and only Judas can stand before him, telling him: "You are from the immortal realm of Barbelo." Second, Jesus takes Judas aside and tells him the mysteries of the kingdom. Third, the disciples report a vision of the great Temple, with priests offering sacrifices at the altar; Jesus interprets it for them: "Those you have seen receiving the offerings at the altar—that is who you are," and "the cattle you have seen brought for sacrifice are the many people you lead astray". Fourth, Judas reports his own vision, and Jesus gives him a long revelation of the cosmos: a great invisible Spirit and a "luminous cloud", the self-generated Adamas, and the rulers of the lower world, Nebro, also called Yaldabaoth, and Saklas, who made humanity. Fifth, Jesus tells Judas that he "will become the thirteenth", will be cursed by the other generations and will come to rule over them, and that he will surpass the others: "you will sacrifice the man that clothes me"; Judas looks up, sees the luminous cloud and enters it; the text ends with Judas taking money and handing Jesus over. [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas]

The cosmology belongs to the family of texts scholars call Sethian: Barbelo, Saklas and Yaldabaoth are the same names that appear in the Apocryphon of John, where the maker of this world is an ignorant lower power. That is set out in [scene:vt25_secret_cosmos|the secret cosmos of Nag Hammadi]. The text reinterprets the creator of Genesis inside a Christian argument; it is not a statement about Jews or Judaism, and should not be read as one.

What it teaches, and where it cuts against the apostles

Whatever Judas's role, the gospel's attack on the other eleven is not in dispute. Their thanksgiving meal, the rite that became the church's central sacrament, is mocked as worship of a lesser god. Their own vision turns them into the priests at the altar, and the animals they sacrifice into the people they lead astray. Elaine Pagels and Karen King, in Reading Judas (2007), read the text as "a kind of protest literature" aimed at church leaders of the author's day who, in a time of persecution, encouraged believers to die as martyrs; in Pagels's account the author was not against martyrdom as such but against the claim that God wants it, and questioned whether God requires a son's death at all. [cite:vt26_salon_pagels2007] On that reading, a Christian group in the second century used the figure most hated in the apostolic tradition to accuse that tradition's leaders of offering human sacrifice. That is the text's direct challenge to the institution: not a secret teaching outside the church, but a charge that the apostles' successors had misunderstood the god they served.

Hero or demon: two readings

National Geographic's 2006 presentation, with commentary by Bart Ehrman, read Judas as the one disciple who understood Yeshua and who, by handing him over, freed the divine being from "the man that clothes" it: obedience, not betrayal. Pagels argued that the Greek word behind "betray" means "hand over". [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas] [cite:vt26_salon_pagels2007]

April DeConick of Rice University, in The Thirteenth Apostle (2007) and a New York Times op-ed of 1 December 2007, argued that the published translation made three decisive errors. Jesus calls Judas a daimon, which the team rendered "spirit"; in these texts, she argued, a daimon is always a demon. Judas is set apart "from" the holy generation, not "for" it. And in one passage the team had dropped a negative, so that Judas will not ascend to the holy generation. In her reading Judas is a demon who truly betrays Jesus, and the "sacrifice" line condemns him rather than praising him. [cite:vt26_getrel_deconick] [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas] National Geographic replied that "virtually all" the issues she raised were addressed in the edition's footnotes. Others joined the dispute: André Gagné argued that a key word should be translated "denial"; Géza Vermes called the text typical Greek-Christian speculation of no historical value for Judas. [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas]

Both readings agree on what matters most for this book: the text's quarrel is with the twelve and with the sacrificial meaning the emerging church gave to Yeshua's death. They disagree on whether Judas is the exception to that error or its instrument. Neither reading claims the text tells us anything reliable about the historical Judas. [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas]

What the institution said in 2006

In January 2006, before publication, the Times of London reported that Vatican scholars intended to give Judas a "makeover", quoting Monsignor Walter Brandmüller as saying the manuscript could help reconstruct how early Christians saw Christ's teaching. [cite:vt26_ct_times2006] No Vatican document followed. On Holy Thursday, 13 April 2006, a week after the National Geographic launch, Pope Benedict XVI preached at St John Lateran on the "obscure mystery of rejection" in Judas, who "evaluated Jesus in accordance with the criteria of power and success" and for whom money mattered more than communion with Jesus. He did not name the new text. [cite:vt26_va_benedict2006] On 18 October 2006 he devoted a general audience to Judas, attributing the betrayal to Satan's influence and Judas's own responsibility, while adding that "it is not up to us to judge his gesture". [cite:vt26_va_aud2006] Rowan Williams, Archbishop of Canterbury, used his Easter sermon that year to call it "a demonstrably late text". [cite:vt26_wiki_gjudas] The documented response of 2006 was restatement of the canonical Judas, not condemnation of the codex; the condemnation on record is still the one Irenaeus wrote around 180.

sections.h: Pistis Sophia: Wisdom's Fall, Her Repentance, and Mary's Questions
sections.html:
Pistis Sophia is the longest of the texts in this part and the least read. It survives in a single parchment book that has been in London since 1785, so it was never lost in the way the Nag Hammadi books were; it was simply ignored by almost everyone except specialists and, from the 1890s, Theosophists. Its name joins two Greek words, pistis (faith) and sophia (wisdom), and its central figure is a divine being of that name who falls, cries out in a series of repentances and is restored. Its human protagonist is Mary Magdalene, who asks most of the questions, and its recurring complaint comes from Peter, who says she will not let the men speak. This section sets out the manuscript, the outline, the teaching, the Peter–Mary conflict, and the companion Books of Jeu, then gives one labelled esoteric reading. [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis] [cite:vt26_bge_pistis]

What it is

The text is preserved in the Askew Codex, now British Library Additional MS 5114. Anthony Askew bought it from a bookseller in 1772, and the British Museum bought it from his heirs in 1785. Where it was found and how it reached England are unknown; Egypt is most probable. It is a parchment book of 178 leaves (356 pages), with two leaves missing, written by two scribes of the same period. [cite:vt26_wiki_askew] Some scholars date the manuscript to the late fourth century, and the work itself to the third or fourth; it is a Coptic translation of a Greek original. [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis] [cite:vt26_bge_pistis] Moritz Gotthilf Schwartze's Coptic text and Latin translation was published after his death by J. H. Petermann in 1851, under a title that assigned it to Valentinus. Carl Schmidt's German translation followed in 1905, and G. R. S. Mead's English translation in 1896, revised in 1921. [cite:vt26_wiki_askew] [cite:vt26_wiki_mead] Mead's 1921 translation is in the public domain and is quoted here by chapter. Before 1945, the Askew, Bruce and Berlin codices were the only three manuscripts holding complete Gnostic works in Coptic. [cite:vt26_wiki_askew]

The ascription to Valentinus has not held. Carl Schmidt and Adolf von Harnack assigned the text to the Ophites; the Encyclopedia of the Bible notes possible Valentinian influence but calls it uncertain, and the text names no sect. [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis] [cite:vt26_bge_pistis] It is safest described as a late Gnostic revelation dialogue whose group cannot be identified.

Outline

The codex holds four books, though how many works they represent is debated. Book One (chapters 1 to 62) opens: "when Jesus had risen from the dead, ... he passed eleven years discoursing with his disciples", teaching them only the outer mysteries. [cite:vt26_mead_ch1] (One encyclopedia summary gives twelve years. [cite:vt26_bge_pistis]) Jesus then ascends in light through the aeons, defeats their rulers, returns and begins to tell the story of Pistis Sophia. Book Two (chapters 63 to 101) completes her fall and restoration and turns to long cosmological explanation. Book Three (chapters 102 to 135) gives an ethical code, rules for handing on the mysteries, teaching on repentance and on the make-up of the human being. Book Four, after a gap, is probably a separate and older work on the fate of souls, the punishment of sinners, the zodiac and a baptism called "the first offering". Books Two and Three refer the reader to "the two Books of Jeu" for mysteries necessary to all. [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis] [cite:vt26_bge_pistis] The crucifixion is not narrated. [cite:vt26_bge_pistis]

What it teaches: Sophia's fall and return

Pistis Sophia dwells in the thirteenth aeon, above the twelve aeons ruled by hostile powers. She sees a light-power below her and takes it for the true Light; she does not know it belongs to "the triple-powered Self-willed", a ruler resentful that she has turned toward the light. She leaves "the thirteenth æon", goes down through the twelve and into the chaos, where a lion-faced power "devoured all the light-powers in Sophia". [cite:vt26_mead_ch31] [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis] From the depths she sings repentances to the Light. After each, Jesus invites a disciple to interpret it, and the disciple matches it to a Psalm of David or an Ode of Solomon: Peter reads the second through Psalm 70; Martha reads the thirteenth through Psalm 50. [cite:vt26_mead_ch36] [cite:vt26_mead_ch57] [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis] She is rescued and brought back, but only to the thirteenth aeon, not to the highest realm. [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis]

The text's purpose is less the myth than the mysteries. Book Three, which sets the rules for handing them on, opens with a demanding moral standard. Jesus tells the disciples to say: "Renounce the whole world and the whole matter therein and all its care and all its sins", and then lists more than thirty things to renounce, among them false witness, avarice, wrath, cursing, theft, adultery, murder, magic potions and "the doctrines of error". [cite:vt26_mead_ch102] This matters for the popular picture of the Gnostic Christians as people without commandments. Some texts, like the Gospel of Mary, warn against adding rules; Pistis Sophia lays down a long code and attaches the mysteries of salvation to it. The difference between it and the institution is not that one had rules and the other did not, but who held the mysteries and on what terms. Part Thirty-One compares the two systems row by row. [scene:vt31_two_economies|Two economies of the sacred]

Mary and Peter

Mary Magdalene is the most prominent disciple in Pistis Sophia, asking many of the questions and giving many of the interpretations; John is second. [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis] Other women speak too: it is Martha who interprets Sophia's thirteenth repentance and is praised for it. [cite:vt26_mead_ch57]

Peter objects twice. In chapter 36, after Mary has interpreted at length, he breaks in: "My Lord, we will not endure this woman, for she taketh the opportunity from us", and she has let none of them speak. Jesus answers by inviting whoever is moved by the spirit to speak, and gives Peter his turn. [cite:vt26_mead_ch36] In chapter 72 Mary says she is ready to interpret but hesitates: "I am afraid of Peter, because he threatened me and hateth our sex." The reply is that anyone "filled with the spirit of light to come forward" may speak, and "no one shall be able to prevent him". [cite:vt26_mead_ch72] The pattern is the same as in the Gospel of Mary and in the last saying of the Gospel of Thomas: Peter resists a woman's spiritual authority, and the text sides with her. Esther de Boer uses this recurrence to argue that the Mary of the Gospel of Mary is the Magdalene. [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary] The Gospel of Thomas is treated in [scene:vt25_sayings_gospels|the sayings gospels].

The Books of Jeu and James Bruce

The two Books of Jeu that Pistis Sophia cites are probably the texts of that name in the Bruce Codex, now Bodleian Library MS Bruce 96. The Scottish traveller James Bruce bought it in about 1769 in Upper Egypt, near Medinet Habu, on the journey that also took him to Ethiopia; the Bodleian has held it since 1848. It contains the Books of Jeu and an untitled text, both in very poor condition from mildew and fading. Carl Schmidt edited it in 1892 and Violet MacDermot translated it into English in 1978. [cite:vt26_wiki_bruce] [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis] In them Jeu is the figure who orders the cosmos, and the books are tied to astrology. [cite:vt26_wiki_pistis] Bruce's journey reappears in [scene:vt27_how_the_west_lost_enoch|the next part], because the same traveller brought the Book of Enoch to Europe.

What the institution said

No ancient council, pope, or heresy catalogue names Pistis Sophia. It is absent from the Decretum Gelasianum's list of rejected books. [cite:vt26_tert_decretum] Epiphanius in the 370s attacked a lost "Greater Questions of Mary", which the NASSCAL catalogue lists alongside Pistis Sophia as related literature, but no source shows they are the same text. [cite:vt26_nasscal_qmary] The record shows a text that dropped out of use and was preserved in one copy; it does not show a condemnation. Its modern history ran through the British Museum, Schwartze's posthumous Latin edition and Mead, who had joined the Theosophical Society in 1884, served as Helena Blavatsky's private secretary from 1889 and in 1909 founded the Quest Society for the comparative study of religion. Mead helped make "gnosis" a central idea in the modern understanding of Gnosticism, and Gilles Quispel proposed that he influenced Carl Jung. [cite:vt26_wiki_mead] [cite:vt26_wiki_askew]

Interpretation, not finding: Sophia's fall as a map of ascent

The esoteric lens of the Sophia platform (Observe The System), which takes its name from this figure, reads the Pistis Sophia myth as a map of the soul rather than a story about the cosmos. In this reading, Sophia is the human soul: she mistakes a reflected light for the true one, descends into matter, loses her light to the powers of appetite and self-will, and returns only through repentance and knowledge, stage by stage, through the same aeons she fell through. The disciples' interpretations of her repentances through the Psalms are read, in this lens, as instruction in how a person turns from the false light to the true. Read through this lens, the text describes an ascent like that of the soul passing the powers in the Gospel of Mary; unlike that gospel, though, it ties the ascent to mysteries that Jesus holds and hands to his disciples, which is itself a form of mediation. This is the platform's reading, not a finding; the text itself presents the myth as an account of the heavens, and its third-century readers' own understanding is not documented.

What the canon kept

The canonical gospels did not keep any of these texts, but they kept Mary Magdalene at the centre of the resurrection. All four name her at the empty tomb, and in John she is the first to see the risen Yeshua and is sent to tell the others. [cite:vt26_wiki_magdalene] The texts outside the canon took that role and made it a teaching office: in the Gospel of Mary she instructs the apostles, in Pistis Sophia she out-questions them. In both, Peter objects, and in both he is answered. The institution that traced its authority to Peter kept her as witness and, in 2016, raised her feast to the apostles' rank; it did not keep the texts in which she teaches. [cite:vt26_va_feast2016]

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Seven
chapters.title: The Ethiopian Bible
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-Seven turns to the one ancient church whose Bible keeps books the rest of Christianity set aside: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The first section tells how Christianity reached the kingdom of Aksum through Frumentius and King Ezana in the fourth century, how the church relates to Nicaea and to Rome, and how it counts its canon of 81 books, which it reaches in more than one way; it gives the full list. The next two sections summarise the books found in no other major church's Bible: 1 Enoch, with its fallen Watchers, its Son of Man and its 364-day year, then Jubilees, the three books of Meqabyan, 4 Baruch and the books of church order. The last section follows how Enoch fell out of use in the West and came back with James Bruce in 1773, and sets that beside what Rome actually did in Ethiopia in the seventeenth century.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty-Seven established that the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, founded through Frumentius, whom Athanasius consecrated, holds the Nicene faith and counts 81 books of scripture, reached either as 54 plus 27 (the narrower canon of the imperial Bibles) or as 46 plus 35 (the broader canon of the commentary tradition and of the church's own website), with the Fetha Negest's heading of 81 standing over a list of 73. [cite:vt27_wiki_frumentius] [cite:vt27_eotc_chalcedon] [cite:vt27_cowley1974] [cite:vt27_eotc_books] Its unique books are old and new: 1 Enoch and Jubilees from Judea before the Christian era, quoted in Jude and copied at Qumran, and the Meqabyan books written in Ethiopia in the Middle Ages. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] [cite:vt27_wiki_meqabyan] Enoch left Western use through the judgments of Jerome and Augustine, not by any papal order found here, and returned through James Bruce's copies in 1773 and Laurence's translation in 1821; Rome's documented intervention in Ethiopia, the Latin patriarchate of 1625–1634, targeted the church's rite and Sabbath and was reversed in 1632. [cite:vt27_na_jerome_vir] [cite:vt27_logos_augustine] [cite:vt27_sc_enoch2] [cite:vt27_wiki_mendes] Part Twenty-Eight moves from texts to people: the Cathars of southern France, and the crusade and inquisition that ended them. [scene:vt28_cathars|Part Twenty-Eight: The Cathars]

sections.h: The Church of Aksum and Its 81 Books
sections.html:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church keeps the largest Bible in traditional Christianity, and it keeps it without ever having been under Rome. That makes it the natural place to end Book Two's survey of excluded texts: two books that the Latin and Greek churches let fall out of use, 1 Enoch and Jubilees, are read in Ethiopia as scripture today. This section tells how the church began, how it relates to the councils described in earlier parts, and how it counts its canon, which turns out to be more interesting than the single number 81 suggests. The church's canon is its own, not a museum piece, and it is described here in the church's own terms first. [cite:vt27_eotc_books]

Aksum, Frumentius and Ezana

The account of how Christianity reached the kingdom of Aksum, in what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, comes from the Latin church historian Rufinus, who said he heard it from one of the people involved. Around 316 two young brothers from Tyre, Frumentius and Edesius, were travelling with their uncle Meropius when their ship put in at a Red Sea harbour. Local people killed the crew and took the boys to the royal court at Aksum. Frumentius became the king's secretary and treasurer, and after the king's death the widowed queen asked both brothers to help educate the young heir, Ezana. Frumentius encouraged Christian merchants to worship openly. When Ezana came of age, Frumentius went to Alexandria and asked its bishop, Athanasius, to send a bishop to Aksum. Athanasius consecrated Frumentius himself, traditionally in 328, though some historians prefer a date between 340 and 346. [cite:vt27_wiki_frumentius] Ethiopians remember him as Abba Salama, "Father of Peace", and Kesate Birhan, "Revealer of Light". [cite:vt27_wiki_frumentius]

Ezana, who reigned from about 320 to about 350, became a Christian. His coins show it: the crescent and disk of the older South Arabian religion were removed and replaced with a cross. [cite:vt27_met_aksum] Around 356 the Roman emperor Constantius II, who favoured the Arian party that Athanasius opposed, wrote to Ezana and his brother asking them to replace Frumentius with an Arian bishop, Theophilos; the request was refused. [cite:vt27_wiki_frumentius] For about two centuries Christianity remained mainly the faith of the court; it spread more widely in the later fifth century, when monks from the eastern Roman provinces, remembered in Ethiopia as the Nine Saints, arrived after the Council of Chalcedon of 451. [cite:vt27_met_aksum] [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc]

The Old Testament was translated into Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia, from the Greek Septuagint, and later revisions show the influence of Hebrew, Syriac and Arabic texts. [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc] The two Garima Gospel books, kept at the monastery of Abba Garima, have been radiocarbon dated to about 390–570 and 530–660, which may make the older of them earlier than the Rabbula Gospels of 586, often cited as the oldest dated illustrated gospel book; one scholar, Curt Niccum, argues that most of the New Testament was in Ge'ez before the end of the fourth century. [cite:vt27_wiki_garima]

A church of the first three councils

"Tewahedo" is a Ge'ez word meaning "made one". It names the church's teaching that in Christ divinity and humanity are united in one nature, the position usually called miaphysite. [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc] The church belongs to the Oriental Orthodox communion with the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Eritrean and Malankara churches, which, in the church's own words, "followed the teachings of the first three Ecumenical councils", Nicaea in 325, Constantinople in 381 and Ephesus in 431, and rejected Chalcedon. [cite:vt27_eotc_chalcedon] The popular claim that the Ethiopian church was "never subject to Nicaea" is therefore wrong: it holds the Nicene faith. Its independence is from Rome and from Chalcedon, not from the councils discussed in [scene:vt22_what_it_decided|Part Twenty-Two].

Until the mid-twentieth century the head of the church, the Abuna, was always a cleric of the Coptic Church, sent from the patriarchate of Alexandria. [cite:vt27_wiki_basilios] After an agreement of 13 July 1948, Basilios became the first Ethiopian to lead the church in 1951, and on 28 June 1959 the Coptic pope Kirillos VI installed him in Cairo as the first Patriarch of Ethiopia: the church became autocephalous, self-governing. [cite:vt27_wiki_basilios] [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc] The Eritrean church received its own autocephaly on 28 September 1993. The present patriarch, Abune Mathias, the sixth, has led the church since February 2013. The World Council of Churches gives the church about 60 million members worldwide; the Pew Research Center counted about 38 million in Ethiopia in 2017. [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc]

How the church counts to 81

The church's own English website states the number plainly: "The Ethiopian Orthodox Church has 46 books of the Old Testament and 35 books of the New Testament that will bring the total of canonized books of the Bible to 81." [cite:vt27_eotc_books] Its New Testament of 35 is the familiar 27 books plus eight more: the four parts of the Sinodos (named on the site Sirate Tsion, Tizaz, Gitsew and Abtilis), the two books of the Covenant (called Dominos), the Ethiopic Clement and the Didascalia. Its Old Testament of 46 includes Jubilees, Enoch and the books of Meqabyan, and ends with "The Book of Josephas the Son of Bengorion", the Josippon, a medieval history of the Jews. It reaches 46 by grouping some books, such as 1 and 2 Samuel or Ezra and Nehemiah, under a single number; it lists Proverbs, Tegsats and "the books of wisdom" as three entries, and does not name Lamentations, Baruch, the Letter of Jeremiah or 4 Baruch separately. [cite:vt27_eotc_books]

That is not the only Ethiopian count. In 1974 the scholar R. W. Cowley set out to find the list that the church's most respected authorities treated as normative, and published the result in the journal Ostkirchliche Studien. He found that the corpus is "generally called 'the 81 books'" but that the number is reached in two different ways. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] The broader canon, taken from the traditional Amharic commentary on the Fetha Negest, the church's book of law, counts 46 Old Testament and 35 New Testament books, as the website does. The narrower canon, used in the church's book of prayers and in the large Ge'ez–Amharic and Amharic Bibles printed by order of Emperor Haile Selassie, counts 54 Old Testament books and the 27 of the New Testament. It gets to 54 by counting the 39 books of the Hebrew Bible as 40, with Proverbs split into two books, Messale (chapters 1–24) and Tagsas (chapters 25–31), and adding fourteen more. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] A third arrangement, in a work called Kwakweha haymanot, counts 49 and 32. All three come to 81. [cite:vt27_cowley1974]

So 81 is the number that stays the same, and the books that make it up change with how they are counted. Cowley's conclusions are precise. The books in the narrower canon are "undisputed" in the church. The extra works of the broader canon are, from a traditional point of view, "equally canonical", but in practice they may be treated more as commentary, with authority derived from scripture. And claims by some European writers that the Ascension of Isaiah and the Shepherd of Hermas are canonical in Ethiopia "may have been true in the past", but he did not find them so in the present. [cite:vt27_cowley1974]

The number is older than either list. The Fetha Negest was compiled in Arabic around 1240 by an Egyptian Coptic jurist, Abu'l-Fada'il ibn al-Assal, and translated into Ge'ez in the fifteenth century; it remained Ethiopia's supreme law until 1931. [cite:vt27_wiki_fetha] Its chapter on scripture, which draws on the Sinodos, has a heading saying the books are 81. Cowley noted that "the list does not total 81": read as written, it gives 46 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books, 73 in all, and whether some entries count as one book or two is unclear. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] The commentary tradition that grew up around the Fetha Negest is what filled the gap, and it is that tradition's count, 46 plus 35, that the church's website gives today. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] [cite:vt27_eotc_books]

Stated precisely, then: 81 is the church's count of its canon under either reckoning; the narrower canon is 54 plus 27, and the broader canon is not "81 plus nine" but a different 81, 46 plus 35, which contains more distinct works because it groups some Old Testament books and adds the Josippon and eight books of church order. The figure of nine extra works describes the difference between the two lists, not a separate total of 90. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] [cite:vt14_wiki_tewahedo] [cite:vt27_eotc_books] Part Twenty-Three's comparison of four Bibles gives both reckonings. [scene:vt23_four_bibles|Four Bibles]

The 81 books of the narrower canon

The table below gives the narrower canon in the order and division used in the church's 1995 description of its faith, as summarised in reference works. [cite:vt14_wiki_tewahedo] Cowley's 1974 count reaches the same 54 Old Testament books slightly differently: he counts Susanna and the other additions to Daniel as separate items and the Meqabyan books as two, where the church's 1995 list counts three Meqabyan books and keeps 4 Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah as separate books. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] [cite:vt14_wiki_tewahedo] The Prayer of Manasseh is read inside 2 Chronicles, not as a book of its own. [cite:vt27_cowley1974]

The rest of this part takes the books that are Ethiopian alone. Enoch comes first, because it is the one the New Testament quotes. [scene:vt27_enoch|1 Enoch] Jubilees, Meqabyan and 4 Baruch follow. [scene:vt27_jubilees_meqabyan|Jubilees, Meqabyan and 4 Baruch]

sections.h: 1 Enoch: The Book the New Testament Quotes
sections.html:
In Genesis, Enoch is a single paragraph: the seventh man in the line from Adam, who "walked with God" and then "was not, for God took him". Out of that gap grew one of the largest bodies of Jewish writing from the centuries before Yeshua, and its best-preserved form is the book Ethiopian Christians call Mashafa Henok and scholars call 1 Enoch. It is scripture for the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches and for the Beta Israel, the Jews of Ethiopia, and for no other living church or Jewish community. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] This section sets out what the book is, how it survived, what each of its five parts teaches and where scholars disagree.

What it is and how it survived

1 Enoch is not one book but five, written by different authors over about three centuries and later joined together. The oldest parts, the Book of the Watchers and the Astronomical Book, date to the third century BCE; the youngest, the Parables, is usually placed between the late first century BCE and the first century CE. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] It was written in Aramaic. Fragments of eleven Aramaic manuscripts were found in Cave 4 at Qumran from 1948 onward and published by Józef Milik in 1976; they cover every part of the book except the Parables. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] A Greek translation existed in antiquity, and a sixth-century Greek manuscript of chapters 1–32, the Codex Panopolitanus from Akhmim (ancient Panopolis) in Egypt, was published in 1892. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch]

The only complete text is the Ge'ez translation, made from the Greek in Aksumite times. Scholars sort its manuscripts into two families, one of six manuscripts from the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries and one of eleven mostly from the eighteenth; R. H. Charles used 23 Ge'ez manuscripts for his edition of 1906. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] Without Ethiopia, most of 1 Enoch would be known only from fragments. The English quotations below are from Charles's translation, published in 1912–1913 and now in the public domain. [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch1]

Book one: the Watchers

The book opens with a blessing and a vision of God coming to judge the earth, and its ninth verse is the one the New Testament quotes: "And behold! He cometh with ten thousands of His holy ones", to execute judgment and convict the ungodly. [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch1] Then comes the story that gives the book its name, an expansion of the six obscure verses of Genesis 6 about "the sons of God" and "the daughters of men". The Watchers, angels of heaven, see the "beautiful and comely daughters" of humankind and desire them. Led by Shemihazah, "they were in all two hundred; who descended in the days of Jared on the summit of Mount Hermon", and bound themselves by an oath. [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch1] [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch]

The Watchers take wives and father giants, who consume the work of human hands and then humans themselves. They also teach. "Azazel taught men to make swords", and the other angels teach metalwork, adornment, spells, root-cutting and the reading of the stars: in this book, knowledge that should not have been given comes down from fallen heaven. [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch1] [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] The cry of the earth reaches God; the archangels are sent; Azazel is bound in the desert, and God declares of the corruption his teaching caused, "to him ascribe all sin". [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch1] The giants destroy one another and the Flood cleanses the earth.

Enoch's role is that of a scribe between worlds. The fallen Watchers ask him to carry their petition for forgiveness to heaven; in a vision he is taken up through walls of crystal and fire into a house where "the Great Glory sat thereon", and returns with the answer that they will have no peace. [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch1] Angels then guide him through the cosmos: to the places where the stars are kept, the prison of the fallen angels, the mountain of the dead where souls wait for judgment, and the tree of life. [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch1] [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] This is among the oldest known Jewish accounts of a human being taken up to see the throne of God, and it shaped later Jewish and Christian writing on heavenly ascent.

Book two: the Parables and the Son of Man

The Parables return to judgment, now in three long "similitudes". Enoch sees "One who had a head of days", and with him "another being whose countenance had the appearance of a man"; the angel explains: "This is the son of Man who hath righteousness". [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch2] This figure was "named before the Lord of Spirits" before the sun and the stars were made, "For from the beginning the Son of Man was hidden", and he will sit on the throne of glory to judge the kings and the mighty who oppressed the righteous. [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch2] In the closing chapter the title is applied to Enoch himself: "This is the Son of Man who is born unto righteousness". [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch2]

Because the gospels use "Son of Man" as Jesus's way of speaking of himself, the Parables are at the centre of a long scholarly argument. Two points are settled. The phrase's main biblical source is Daniel 7, where "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days, and the Parables are themselves an expansion of that vision. And no fragment of the Parables was found at Qumran, while every other part of 1 Enoch was. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] What is not settled is their date. Milik proposed the third century CE, which would make them later than the gospels; most scholars reject that and place them around the turn of the era, which makes them a near contemporary of the gospel tradition. Whether the gospel writers knew them, or both drew on a shared Jewish expectation, is open. The claim that the Christian title "comes from Enoch" goes beyond the evidence; the claim that it has nothing to do with Enoch does too. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch]

Book three: the Astronomical Book

The third book, possibly the oldest of all, is a manual of heaven's order given by the angel Uriel. Sun, moon and stars move through gates in the sky by fixed laws, and the year has 364 days, four seasons of 91 days, so that each feast falls on the same weekday every year. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] The calendar was not academic. A 364-day year set its users against the lunar calendar of the Temple authorities, and the same calendar runs through Jubilees and the Dead Sea Scrolls. [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] The book's teaching is that the cosmos keeps God's law exactly and that sinners are those who fail to keep time with it.

Book four: the Dream Visions

Two dreams make up the fourth book. In the first Enoch foresees the Flood. The second, called the Animal Apocalypse, retells history from Adam to the Maccabean revolt in which people appear as animals and angels as men: the patriarchs are bulls, Israel are sheep, the nations wild beasts and birds of prey, and the sheep's careless shepherds are angels who let too many be destroyed. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] The vision ends with a ram with a great horn leading a revolt, the judgment of the shepherds and the fallen stars, and a new house in which all the animals become white bulls again. It was written during or just after the revolt of 167–160 BCE, and its scholars date it by the point at which its "prophecy" stops matching events, around 163 to 142 BCE. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch]

Book five: the Epistle of Enoch

The last book is Enoch's teaching to his children. It contains the Apocalypse of Weeks, which divides all history into ten "weeks" ending in the judgment and a new heaven. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] Its moral voice is sharp and social. Series of woes condemn those who build houses with others' toil, deal in deceit and oppress the poor: "Woe to you, you rich, for you have trusted in your riches", a line often set beside the Letter of James's "Come now, you rich!". [cite:vt27_itb_enoch94] The book ends with an account of the miraculous birth of Noah, whose shining appearance makes his father Lamech fear he is the child of a Watcher. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch]

Enoch in the New Testament and the early church

The Letter of Jude, one of the 27 New Testament books, cites Enoch by name: "Enoch, in the seventh generation from Adam, prophesied", and what follows is the verse quoted above, 1 Enoch 1:9, the Lord coming with his holy ones "to execute judgment upon all". [cite:vt27_biblia_jude] [cite:vt27_ccel_enoch1] The letter treats it as genuine prophecy. Other New Testament passages, such as the references in 1 and 2 Peter to imprisoned spirits and to angels held in chains until the judgment, are widely read as echoes of the Watchers story. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] The Epistle of Barnabas, an early second-century Christian writing, quotes Enoch as scripture, and Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Athenagoras, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Origen and Cyprian all knew it, some approvingly and some not. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] For the first three Christian centuries, in other words, Enoch was read across the church, not on its margins. How it fell out of use everywhere except Ethiopia is told in the last section of this part. [scene:vt27_how_the_west_lost_enoch|How the West lost Enoch]

What scholars dispute

Beyond the date of the Parables, three questions remain open. First, the book's relation to Genesis: some scholars read the Watchers story as an expansion of Genesis 6, others argue that an older Enochic tradition lies behind the terse Genesis text. Second, whether there was an "Enochic Judaism", in Gabriele Boccaccini's phrase, a distinct priestly or scribal movement for which these books were central and which fed the community at Qumran; the idea has strong advocates and sceptics. Third, how far the Ethiopic text, translated from Greek, preserves the Aramaic original; where the Qumran fragments survive, they show both agreement and real differences. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] None of these disputes concerns whether the book was read and valued by early Jews and Christians; that is documented. They concern who wrote it, for whom, and how the parts came together.

sections.h: Jubilees, Meqabyan, 4 Baruch and the Books of Order
sections.html:
Enoch is the most famous of Ethiopia's own books, but it is not alone. Three more works in the narrower canon appear in no other major church's Bible: Jubilees, a retelling of Genesis and Exodus given to Moses by an angel; the three books of Meqabyan, which share a name with the Maccabees but tell different stories; and 4 Baruch, a tale of the Babylonian exile. [cite:vt14_wiki_tewahedo] [cite:vt27_cowley1974] The broader canon adds books of church order. This section summarises each, with the same questions as the rest of Book Two: what the text is, what it teaches, who set it aside elsewhere and what scholars dispute.

Jubilees: what it is

Jubilees calls itself "the history of the division of the days of the law and of the testimony", and it presents everything that follows as revealed on Mount Sinai during Moses's forty days on the mountain. [cite:vt27_ccel_jub1] [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] God tells "the angel of the presence" to "Write for Moses from the beginning of creation", and the angel dictates a history from the first day to the giving of the law. [cite:vt27_ccel_jub1] It was written in Hebrew, probably around 160–150 BCE. About fifteen copies were found in five caves at Qumran, which shows how widely the community there read it. [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] No complete Hebrew, Greek or Latin text survives; a Latin translation covers about a quarter of the book, and only the Ge'ez version is complete, a translation that agrees closely with the Hebrew fragments from the Dead Sea. [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] It has 50 chapters and is canonical for the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches and for the Beta Israel. [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees]

Jubilees: the outline

Jubilees: what it teaches

Time is the book's first subject. History runs in jubilees of 49 years, fifty of them from creation to Sinai, 2,410 years in all, so that Israel's entry into its land completes a perfect cycle. [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] The year has 364 days in four quarters of thirteen weeks, the same calendar as Enoch's Astronomical Book, and the author rejects the lunar calendar "in the strongest terms", because a moon-based year lets feasts drift and so profanes them. [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] [cite:vt27_je_jubilees]

The second subject is a law older than Moses. Jubilees teaches that every event and statute is "written down on the tablets of heaven", and that the patriarchs already kept laws that Exodus and Leviticus later give: the Feast of Weeks was celebrated in heaven from creation and first kept on earth by Noah, then by Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. [cite:vt27_je_jubilees] The highest angels were created circumcised and keep the Sabbath in heaven, and Israel shares both with them. [cite:vt27_je_jubilees] The third subject is evil. The Watchers' story is told again, and after the Flood a tenth of the giants' spirits are allowed to remain under their chief, Mastema, to test humankind; in the Passover account Mastema stands where Exodus has God himself, as the power behind the killing of Egypt's firstborn. [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] [cite:vt27_je_jubilees] The book also insists on separation from the nations, forbidding intermarriage and eating with gentiles, and condemns public nakedness. [cite:vt27_je_jubilees]

Elsewhere Jubilees fell away. The Gelasian Decree, the sixth-century Latin list of books not to be received, named "Little Genesis", one of Jubilees' ancient titles, among the apocrypha. [cite:vt23_tert_decretum] [cite:vt23_wiki_jubilees] Eastern Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant churches classify it as pseudepigrapha; no Jewish community except the Beta Israel treats it as scripture. [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] Scholars dispute its exact date (estimates have ranged from the 160s BCE to the reign of John Hyrcanus later in the century), its relationship to the group at Qumran, and whether its calendar was ever actually used in the Temple. [cite:vt27_wiki_jubilees] [cite:vt27_je_jubilees]

Meqabyan: not the Maccabees

The three books of Meqabyan are the clearest case of a book that is easy to mislabel. The Greek books of the Maccabees, which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles contain, tell of the Hasmonean revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV in the 160s BCE. The Ethiopian canon does not include them.
