Its Meqabyan are "entirely different in their scope, content and subject": they do not tell the Hasmonean story, the martyrdom of the seven brothers and their mother, or the rededication of the Temple. [cite:vt27_wiki_meqabyan] Cowley noted that they "are not the same as any of the 4 LXX books of Maccabees". [cite:vt27_cowley1974] They were written in Ge'ez, probably in the high medieval period, since the Ethiopian church seems not to have known the Greek Maccabees until well into the fourteenth century. [cite:vt27_wiki_meqabyan] Little scholarly work has been done on them; a full English translation of all three appeared only in 2008 (Feqade Selassie), and an annotated translation of the first two by D. P. Curtin and Tesfaye in 2018 and 2023. [cite:vt27_wiki_meqabyan] One popular version describes them as the story of "three Ethiopian brothers" martyred in Ethiopia; they are not set in Ethiopia. [cite:vt27_wiki_meqabyan]

Scholars have suggested that the king's name, Tseerutsaydan, may preserve a folk memory of Antiochus IV, whose coins bore the names of Tyre and Sidon, and that Akrandis may echo Alexander Balas, a later Seleucid ruler; others note that the second and third books may draw on the Josippon. These are proposals, not findings. [cite:vt27_wiki_meqabyan] Meqabyan was never in any Western list to be excluded: it was written in Ethiopia, centuries after the Western canon lists were made.

4 Baruch: the sleeper and the eagle

4 Baruch is known in Greek manuscripts as the Paralipomena of Jeremiah, "things left out of Jeremiah", and in Ge'ez as the Rest of the Words of Baruch. [cite:vt27_wiki_4baruch] God tells Jeremiah that Jerusalem will fall; Jeremiah and Baruch see angels open the gates to the Babylonians; Jeremiah hides the Temple vessels in the earth and goes into exile with the people, while Baruch stays behind. Abimelech, the Ethiopian servant who rescued Jeremiah in the Book of Jeremiah (Ebed-melech), falls asleep under a tree and sleeps for 66 years, waking to find the figs in his basket still fresh. An eagle carries Baruch's letter and some of the figs to Jeremiah in Babylon, lands on a corpse at a funeral and brings it back to life, a sign that the exile is ending. The people return, but only those without foreign spouses may cross the Jordan. [cite:vt27_wiki_4baruch]

The book teaches that God keeps what is his through catastrophe, that the righteous are preserved as the figs were, and that the return from exile is a kind of resurrection. Its 66 years point scholars to about 136 CE, sixty-six years after the destruction of the Second Temple, which makes it a Jewish response to that loss; its last chapter, with Christian content, appears to be an addition made in the Christian era. [cite:vt27_wiki_4baruch] Only the Ethiopian church counts it as scripture. [cite:vt27_wiki_4baruch]

The books of order in the broader canon

The eight New Testament additions of the broader canon are not narratives or prophecies but rule books for the church. The Sinodos is a collection of canons attributed to the apostles and to early councils, and it is the source the Fetha Negest cites for its own canon of scripture. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] The Didascalia, or Didesqelya, is a church order in 43 chapters, close to the first seven books of the Greek Apostolic Constitutions, a fourth-century compilation of church law; the Ethiopic Clement is a letter presented as Peter's teaching sent to Clement of Rome; and the Book of the Covenant is a church-order work in two parts. [cite:vt14_wiki_tewahedo] [cite:vt27_eotc_books] These books govern fasting, ordination, worship and discipline. Cowley found that in practice they function more as authoritative commentary than as scripture read alongside the gospels. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] Their presence in the canon shows something the Western division between "Bible" and "church law" hides: in Ethiopia the rules of the community were counted among its holy books.

sections.h: How the West Lost Enoch, and What Rome Did in Ethiopia
sections.html:
A common version of this story says that the Vatican suppressed the Book of Enoch and that Ethiopia, beyond Rome's reach, kept the "uncensored" Bible. The record supports half of that. Ethiopia did keep Enoch while the Latin and Greek churches let it go, and Rome did try, once, to bring the Ethiopian church under its authority. But Enoch dropped out of Western use through the judgments of individual scholars and bishops in the fourth and fifth centuries, long before any papal act concerned it, and the Roman mission to Ethiopia in the seventeenth century fought over rite, Sabbath and doctrine, not over Enoch. No document found for this part shows a Roman order against the book. [cite:vt27_hessayon] [cite:vt27_wiki_mendes] This section sets out both stories in order.

Read, then doubted: c.100–420

Enoch's early Christian readership was wide. The Letter of Jude quotes it as prophecy, the Epistle of Barnabas cites it as scripture, and a long list of second- and third-century writers, from Justin Martyr and Irenaeus to Clement of Alexandria, Origen and Cyprian, knew it. [cite:vt27_biblia_jude] [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] The doubts were present from the start, and they came from the Jewish canon. Around 200 the North African writer Tertullian answered people who rejected the book because it "is not admitted into the Jewish canon either". His defence was that Noah, Enoch's great-grandson, could have preserved it through the Flood or renewed it by the Spirit, and that it "possesses a testimony in the Apostle Jude". [cite:vt27_na_tert_cultu]

The decisive judgments in the Latin West came from two of its most influential scholars. Jerome, the translator of the Latin Bible, wrote in 392 that the Letter of Jude was itself doubted, "because in it he quotes from the apocryphal Book of Enoch it is rejected by many". [cite:vt27_na_jerome_vir] Enoch was a liability that nearly cost Jude its own place. Augustine, in Book Fifteen of The City of God, written around 420, took a middle position that became the Western one. He accepted that "Enoch, the seventh from Adam, left some divine writings", because Jude says so, and that "there is some truth in these apocryphal writings". But "their antiquity brought them under suspicion", and they were not in the canon "preserved in the temple of the Hebrew people by the diligence of successive priests"; they contained so much that was false that they have "no canonical authority". [cite:vt27_logos_augustine] Augustine's test was the Jewish canon kept by the Temple priesthood, the same test Tertullian had argued against two centuries earlier.

Two points matter for Book Two's question. First, the objection was scholarly and textual: the book was not in the Hebrew Bible, it claimed to come from before the Flood, and parts of it seemed fabulous. Second, it came from individual writers in Bethlehem and Hippo, not from Rome, and it was an opinion about canon, not an order to destroy anything. In the Greek East the same doubt spread; rabbis of the second century and Church Fathers such as Athanasius likewise rejected the Enochic books, after which they "largely vanished from view". [cite:vt27_hessayon] None of the canon lists examined in Part Twenty-Three includes Enoch, and none needed to name it to leave it out. [scene:vt23_left_out|What was left out]

Fragments and rumours: c.800–1700

In the Greek world Enoch survived as quotation. Around 800 the Byzantine chronicler George Syncellus copied long excerpts from the Book of the Watchers into his world chronicle, and when the scholar Joseph Scaliger printed them in 1606 they started a European search for the whole book. [cite:vt27_hessayon] Reports that Ethiopia had a complete Enoch circulated. In the seventeenth century the French collector Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc obtained an Ethiopic manuscript said to be Enoch, but the German Ethiopic scholar Hiob Ludolf examined it and dismissed it as a different, worthless work, which for a time made Europeans doubt that an Ethiopic Enoch existed at all. [cite:vt27_sc_enoch2]

Bruce, Laurence and the return of the text: 1773–1912

The Scottish traveller James Bruce spent years in Ethiopia in search of the source of the Nile and returned in 1773 with three copies of the Ge'ez Enoch. He gave one to the Royal Library in Paris, one to the Bodleian Library in Oxford, and kept one at his family house, Kinnaird. [cite:vt27_sc_enoch2] [cite:vt27_hessayon] For nearly thirty years little was published. In 1800 the French orientalist Silvestre de Sacy translated the first chapters of the Paris copy into Latin. In 1821 Richard Laurence published the first English translation, from the Bodleian copy, and argued that it was the same work the Church Fathers had known in Greek. [cite:vt27_sc_enoch2] [cite:vt27_hessayon] August Dillmann published the first edition of the Ge'ez text in 1851, and R. H. Charles a critical edition in 1906 and his English translation in 1912. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] The Aramaic fragments from Qumran, published in 1976, then showed that the book Ethiopia had kept was a faithful descendant of texts read in Judea before the Christian era. [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch]

What Rome did in Ethiopia

Rome's direct dealings with the Ethiopian church are documented, and they were not gentle. In 1439, during the Council of Florence, Pope Eugene IV sent a message proposing union to the Ethiopian emperor Zara Yaqob; nothing came of it. [cite:vt27_wiki_ethcatholic] In the early seventeenth century Portuguese Jesuits worked at the Ethiopian royal court. From 1622 the emperor Susenyos moved toward Rome, and the pope named a Portuguese Jesuit, Afonso Mendes, Latin Patriarch of Ethiopia. Mendes reached the country in June 1625, and on 11 February 1626 Susenyos and Mendes publicly acknowledged the primacy of the Roman see and made Catholicism the state religion. [cite:vt27_wiki_mendes] [cite:vt27_wiki_ethcatholic]

What Mendes then did is the core of the record. He condemned the Ethiopian observance of the Saturday Sabbath, which the church had officially accepted alongside Sunday in the fifteenth century, and the church's frequent fasts. He ordained Catholic priests, had Latin texts including the Mass translated into the local language, and told Ethiopian women that their children were in hell because they had been baptised in the Orthodox church. Many people were forced to convert by threats, imprisonment and battle. [cite:vt27_wiki_mendes] [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc] Rebellion followed. After a battle on 7 June 1632 in which the emperor's soldiers killed large numbers of his own people, Susenyos rescinded his edict on 14 June 1632, declaring that Catholics might keep their faith but no one would be forced; he abdicated the same year. His son Fasilides restored the Orthodox church and in 1634 exiled Mendes and most of the missionaries; other accounts date the Jesuits' expulsion to 1633, the year Mendes began his journey out, and in 1665 Jesuit books were ordered burned. [cite:vt27_wiki_mendes] [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc]

The Latinisation campaign targeted the church's rite, its Sabbath, its fasts, its baptisms and its christology, and the attempt was coercive. The available record of it, however, says nothing about the canon, Enoch or Jubilees. [cite:vt27_wiki_mendes] The documented book-burning of the episode was done by the Ethiopian side, against Jesuit books, after the mission failed. [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc]

Rome and Ethiopia since

Catholic missions returned in the nineteenth century, when the Italian Lazarist Justin de Jacobis became the first prefect apostolic of Abyssinia in 1839. [cite:vt27_wiki_ethcatholic] In 1919 Pope Benedict XV founded the Pontifical Ethiopian College in the Vatican. [cite:vt27_wiki_ethcatholic] The Ethiopian Catholic Church today is a self-governing Eastern Catholic church in full communion with Rome, using the Ge'ez rite, with Addis Ababa as its metropolitan see since 20 February 1961; it counted about 70,800 members in 2017, against tens of millions in the Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Its Eritrean dioceses became a separate church in January 2015. [cite:vt27_wiki_ethcatholic] [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc]

The Ethiopian Bible matters for Book Two's argument not because Rome failed to cut it, but because it shows what a Christian canon looks like when it grows in a different place under different authorities: larger, with porous edges, holding the books the West doubted alongside its own laws and stories. The excluded texts of the earlier parts, from Thomas to Pistis Sophia, have no such home church; Enoch and Jubilees do. [cite:vt27_cowley1974] [cite:vt27_eotc_books]

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Eight
chapters.title: Cathars, Crusade and Inquisition
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-Eight moves from the ancient texts to the medieval movement in which Rome first met organised dualist Christianity, and to the institutions it built in response. The first section sets out what the Good Men, whom their enemies named Cathars, taught and practised, as far as their own surviving ritual and their prosecutors' records agree: two principles, souls trapped in matter, one sacrament given by the laying on of hands, a clergy of men and women who swore no oaths and, by a modern account, took no tithes, and a sharp critique of the Roman clergy and its sacraments. The second follows the Albigensian Crusade from the murder of a papal legate in 1208 through the sack of Béziers in 1209 to the burning at Montségur in 1244, testing the famous quotations and death tolls against their sources. The third traces how popes, councils and kings built a standing procedure against heresy between 1184 and 1252, including the authorisation of torture, and what its registers show of the last Good Men, who were gone by the 1320s.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty-Eight established that the Good Men of Languedoc and Lombardy were a medieval dualist church with bishops, a single sacrament given by the laying on of hands, and men and women perfect who promised not to lie, swear or kill, who by a modern account exacted no tithe from their believers, and whose teachers called the Roman clergy "Pharisees and false prophets". [cite:vt28_lyons_traditio] [cite:vt28_ency_cathars] [cite:vt28_gui_fordham] Innocent III answered with a crusade carrying Holy Land indulgences; at Béziers on 22 July 1209 the legate himself claimed "almost 20,000" dead, a figure historians doubt, and the war's total is unknown, with the popular 200,000 to 1,000,000 range resting on no contemporary count. [cite:vt28_fordham_lat4c3] [cite:vt28_wiki_beziers] [cite:vt28_nwe_crusade] About 210 to 215 people were burned at Montségur on 16 March 1244 after refusing to recant. [cite:vt28_wiki_montsegur] Between 1184 and 1252 the papacy, with councils and lay rulers, built a standing procedure that searched for heretics, barred lay people in Languedoc from owning the Bible, licensed torture and paid its officers from confiscations; its registers show how the last Good Men were found and burned by 1321. [cite:vt28_wiki_adabolendam] [cite:vt28_wiki_toulouse] [cite:vt28_wiki_adextirpanda] [cite:vt28_wiki_fournier] Part Twenty-Nine follows the same machinery as it turned on a military order of the Church itself, the Templars, and on mystics who claimed direct knowledge of God. [scene:vt29_templars|Part Twenty-Nine: Templars, Mystics and the Stake]

sections.h: The Good Men: What the Cathars Taught
sections.html:
Eight centuries separate the last ancient Gnostic texts from the people the medieval Church called Cathars. No manuscript, named teacher or community record bridges that gap, and this part treats them for what the record shows: a medieval Christian dualist movement in northern Italy and southern France, first clearly identifiable around 1143, when the cleric Eberwin of Steinfeld reported a group with these beliefs at Cologne, and largely gone by about 1350. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] They are in this book because their teaching shared a structure with the ancient texts of Parts Twenty-Four to Twenty-Six (a good God beyond the world, a lesser power that made matter, a soul that must find its way back), and because what the papacy built to destroy them became the Inquisition. [scene:vt24_what_they_taught|What the Gnostics taught]

Names and origins

"Cathar" comes from the Greek katharoi, "the pure ones". It was a label used by Catholic theologians and later by inquisitors; the people questioned never used it of themselves. They called themselves Good Christians, Good Men and Good Women (bons hommes, bonnes femmes), and their opponents also called them Albigensians, after the town of Albi. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] The same Greek word had been used nine centuries earlier for the rigorist Novatian Christians, whom the Council of Nicaea called Cathari; the two groups are unrelated. [scene:vt22_what_it_decided|What Nicaea decided]

The movement's eastern roots lie in the Balkans. In tenth-century Bulgaria a priest named Bogomil led a dualist movement, known from a treatise written against it by the priest Cosmas around 970. [cite:vt28_ency_cathars] Its ideas probably reached the West from Byzantium and the Balkans along trade routes, and the historian Malcolm Lambert judged that "a substantial transmission of ritual and ideas from Bogomilism to Catharism is beyond reasonable doubt". [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] One Bogomil text, the Interrogatio Iohannis (the "Secret Supper", a dialogue in which Christ answers John's questions about creation and the devil), was brought from Bulgaria to Italy around 1190 by Nazarius, Cathar bishop of Concorezzo. [cite:vt28_ency_cathars]

By the 1160s the Good Men of Languedoc had bishops. A bishopric existed at Albi around 1165; a council at Saint-Félix in the Lauragais, dated 1167 (the surviving charter's date and authenticity are debated), was attended by Nicetas, a Bogomil leader (papa), and was followed by bishoprics at Toulouse, Carcassonne and Agen, with Razès added around 1225. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] [cite:vt28_ency_cathars] Britannica counts eleven Cathar bishoprics across France and Italy by 1200. [cite:vt28_brit_cathari] Each bishop was assisted by an "elder son", who usually succeeded him, a "younger son" and deacons. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] The popular picture of a church with no hierarchy does not fit this record.

What they believed

Cathar teaching began from two principles. A good God made the spiritual realm: souls, light, what is eternal. A second power, which Cathar texts and their opponents call Satan or the "king of the world" (rex mundi), made the visible, material world. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] Cathars disagreed among themselves on how far this went. "Mitigated" dualists held that there was only one God and that Satan was a fallen creature; "absolute" dualists, whose position is set out in the Italian Book of the Two Principles (attributed to John of Lugio, mid-thirteenth century), held that good and evil were two eternal principles. [cite:vt28_ency_cathars] Many identified the maker of the material world with the God of the Old Testament and rejected most of the Old Testament. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] This was a medieval Christian reading of Christian scripture; it was not a teaching about Jews, and it should not be read as one.

Human souls, in this teaching, were angels who had fallen and been trapped in bodies. They passed from body to body, man to woman and back, until they were released. Christ was a spirit sent by the good God; his body, suffering and death only appeared real (the view called docetism), so the cross was not a sign of salvation but an instrument of torture, and Cathars refused to venerate it. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] [cite:vt28_brit_cathari] Because sexual reproduction kept souls in the cycle of bodies, the fully committed renounced sex and every food they believed came from it: meat, eggs, cheese and milk. Killing animals was abhorrent, since they might carry souls. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism]

Two grades: believers and the Good Men

Most people attached to the movement were credentes, believers, who married, worked, ate meat and lived ordinary lives while honouring the Good Men. A small elite, whom modern writers call the perfect (perfecti, women perfectae), had received the one Cathar sacrament and lived under its rules. [cite:vt28_brit_cathari] Believers greeted a Good Man with a ritual bow and blessing, the melioramentum, and many made the convenenza, an agreement to be given the sacrament when they were dying. [cite:vt28_wiki_perfect] [cite:vt28_lyons_traditio] The perfect travelled in pairs of the same sex, after Christ's instruction to the apostles, preached and cared for the sick, and many worked for their keep, often as weavers. [cite:vt28_wiki_perfect] [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism]

That sacrament was the consolamentum, the "consoling". It was a spiritual baptism by the laying on of hands, and it served at once as baptism, ordination and the forgiveness of sins. No bread or wine was used. [cite:vt28_ency_cathars] [cite:vt28_wiki_consolamentum] The Occitan ritual preserved in a manuscript at Lyon describes the preparation: an elder taught the candidate the Lord's Prayer phrase by phrase, and the candidate promised never to eat or drink without saying it; the elder asked, "Do you give yourself to God and the Gospel?", and the candidate promised "that you will not lie, that you will not swear, that you will not kill", along with the rules on food and chastity; then the Good Men laid their hands on the candidate. [cite:vt28_lyons_traditio] Some rites placed the Gospel of John or the New Testament on the candidate's head. [cite:vt28_wiki_consolamentum]

Because the rules were hard to keep and a lapse undid the sacrament, most believers received the consolamentum only on their deathbed. [cite:vt28_brit_cathari] A few dying people who had received it then refused food until death, a practice called the endura. It is known from a small number of cases late in the movement's history; Catholic writers' claims that Cathars smothered people who recovered have little supporting evidence, and how common the endura was is disputed. [cite:vt28_wiki_consolamentum] [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism]

Women

Women could be believers and Good Women. The encyclopedia entries on the movement describe women perfectae who "performed evangelical, pastoral, and sacramental functions", including giving the consolamentum, and who ran communal houses where girls and widows were taught the faith. [cite:vt28_ency_cathars] [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] Esclarmonde of Foix became a Good Woman after raising eight children. [cite:vt28_wiki_perfect] The record is not uniformly egalitarian: some later French Cathars taught that a woman's soul must be reborn as a man to be saved, and women perfect became rarer in Languedoc toward the end, though not in Italy. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism]

The Roman clergy, the sacraments, tithes and oaths

The best single account of Cathar criticism of the Church comes from their prosecutor. Bernard Gui, inquisitor at Toulouse, wrote in his manual that they called themselves "good Christians, who do not swear, or lie, or speak evil of others", said "that they do not kill any man or animal", and called Catholic prelates, clerks and monks "Pharisees and false prophets, who say, but do not". He recorded that they denied the consecrated host could be Christ's body, called baptismal water a corruptible creation of the evil power and accused the clergy of selling it, said confession to sinful priests was useless, compared the cross to a gallows, and read the Gospels and Epistles in the vernacular. [cite:vt28_gui_fordham] Gui was hostile, but his list matches the Cathars' own ritual on the central points. [cite:vt28_lyons_traditio]

Oaths are well attested: the ritual has the candidate promise not to swear, Gui records the refusal, and Gordon Leff's encyclopedia entry lists "the swearing of oaths" among the things the perfect rejected. [cite:vt28_lyons_traditio] [cite:vt28_gui_fordham] [cite:vt28_ency_cathars] Tithes are thinner. The historian Beverly Mayne Kienzle writes that Catharism "exacted no tithes" and placed no economic restrictions on believers, but no Cathar text located for this part, and nothing in Gui's excerpt, addresses tithes directly, so the point rests on her secondary account. [cite:vt28_ency_cathars] If it holds, the refusals reached beyond doctrine: a church that took no tithe offered an alternative to the clergy's main income, and a clergy that would not swear stood outside the oaths on which courts and feudal loyalty rested. That is an inference from the documents, not a statement any Cathar text makes. [cite:vt28_ency_cathars] [cite:vt28_gui_fordham] How the Church's tithe became a compulsory tax is the subject of Part Thirty-One. [scene:vt31_tithe|Tithe]

Whose voice survives

Most Cathar books were destroyed, and most of what is known comes from their opponents: polemical treatises, sermons, and above all inquisitors' interrogation records. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] A few of their own texts survive: the Book of the Two Principles, the Occitan ritual at Lyon, a Latin ritual, and the Bogomil Interrogatio Iohannis they used. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] [cite:vt28_ency_cathars]

That imbalance is the basis of a live dispute among historians. R. I. Moore, in The War on Heresy, argues that an organised "Cathar church" was largely "contrived from the resources of well-stocked imaginations" of churchmen, laid over local anticlericalism and a broader religious revival; Mark Pegg goes further on the crusade's character. Others, including Claire Taylor, Rebecca Rist and Lucy Sackville, accept that the Church exaggerated the threat but hold that a real heresy with an organised theology existed, pointing to the Cathars' own texts. The 2016 volume Cathars in Question, edited by Antonio Sennis, gathers both sides. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] This section has used the term "Cathar" because the record needs a name; it describes the Good Men's beliefs from their own surviving ritual wherever possible, and from their prosecutors only where the two agree.

The modern memory adds its own layer. The Aude department markets the region as "Pays cathare"; Otto Rahn, later an SS officer, tied Montségur to the Holy Grail in the 1930s; The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail linked the Cathars to the Templars. None of these links has documentary support. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism]

sections.h: The Crusade: Béziers to Montségur, 1208–1244
sections.html:
Innocent III became pope in 1198 resolved to deal with the heresy in Languedoc. He tried persuasion first: Cistercian legates and preachers, among them Dominic, founder of the Dominican order, debated the Good Men in the towns, and by the account of the movement's historians converted few. [cite:vt28_nwe_crusade] [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] The legates also pressed the local lords to act, above all Raymond VI, count of Toulouse, whom they excommunicated in 1207 for failing to move against the heretics. [cite:vt28_nwe_crusade]

The trigger and the call

In January 1208 the papal legate Pierre de Castelnau met Raymond VI; the meeting ended in anger, and on the following morning, 14 January, Castelnau was murdered. [cite:vt28_audit_wiki_crusade] [cite:vt28_audit_cathen_albigenses] Innocent answered with a call to crusade against Languedoc, offering the lands of heretics and their protectors to those who took them. [cite:vt28_nwe_crusade] [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] It is often called the first crusade against Christians, which is loose, since Christian armies had fought each other for centuries. What was new was a crusade aimed at heretics inside Latin Christendom, with the same spiritual rewards as an expedition to the Holy Land. Six years later the Fourth Lateran Council wrote that equivalence into law: those who "take up the cross" against heretics were to receive "the indulgences and privileges granted to those who go in defense of the Holy Land". [cite:vt28_fordham_lat4c3]

Béziers, 22 July 1209

The crusading army, led by the papal legate Arnaud Amalric, abbot of Cîteaux, reached Béziers on 21 July 1209. The town's bishop, Renaud de Montpeyroux, had drawn up a list of 222 people, mostly Cathars and some Waldensians, probably their perfect and leaders; the list survives. Handing them over proved impossible, because the town protected them, and Catholic residents overwhelmingly refused the offer to leave and save themselves. [cite:vt28_wiki_beziers] On the morning of 22 July a sortie from the town ended in a brawl, the army's mercenaries (routiers) followed the retreating townspeople through an open gate, and the leaders sent the whole army in. People who had fled into the churches were killed inside them; the town was plundered and burned, and the cathedral with it. [cite:vt28_wiki_beziers]

The numbers come from the attackers. Arnaud Amalric wrote to the pope in August that his men had put "almost 20,000" people to the sword, a report that admits no one was spared, while describing the attack as begun by low-ranking men without orders. [cite:vt28_wiki_beziers] [cite:vt28_nwe_crusade] The crusade's chronicler Peter of Les Vaux-de-Cernay put the dead in the church of Mary Magdalene alone at 7,000. [cite:vt28_wiki_beziers] Modern historians treat both figures as inflated: Christopher Tyerman writes that the true figure was "almost certainly far less", and Laurence Marvin concludes that most of the town's population and buildings survived. [cite:vt28_wiki_beziers] No count of the dead exists.

The most quoted sentence of the crusade, "Kill them all; God will know his own" (Caedite eos. Novit enim Dominus qui sunt eius), appears in only one source: the Dialogue on Miracles of the German Cistercian Caesarius of Heisterbach, written between 1219 and 1223, a decade after the event and far from it. Historians doubt that the abbot said it, and Marvin calls it apocryphal; the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1907 already stated that the words were "never pronounced"; it is better treated as a story told within the abbot's own order than as a record of his words. [cite:vt28_wiki_beziers] [cite:vt28_audit_cathen_albigenses] Amalric's own letter, which boasts of the slaughter, is the firmer document.

The war of sieges

Carcassonne surrendered on 15 August 1209; its inhabitants were expelled, not killed. The northern French baron Simon de Montfort took command and was granted the conquered lands. [cite:vt28_audit_wiki_crusade] [cite:vt28_audit_cathen_albigenses] Minerve surrendered on 22 July 1210 after a summer siege. Catholics, soldiers and believers were allowed to leave; the perfect were offered their lives if they recanted, and very few did. The crusade's chronicler Peter of Les Vaux-de-Cernay gives the number burned as 140. [cite:vt28_audit_wiki_minerve] [cite:vt28_audit_wiki_crusade] Lavaur fell on 3 May 1211 "amid dreadful carnage", in the Catholic Encyclopedia's words. Montfort had its lord, Aimery of Montréal, hanged with his knights, about eighty of them, and when the gallows gave way the rest were killed with the sword; modern historians put the Cathars burned there at up to 400, and here no offer to recant is recorded. [cite:vt28_audit_cathen_albigenses] [cite:vt28_audit_wiki_lavaur] The war then widened into a conflict for the lordship of the south. Peter II of Aragon came to the aid of Toulouse and was killed at Muret on 12 September 1213; Montfort was killed by a stone while besieging Toulouse in June 1218 (sources give the 25th or the 29th); the French crown took over the war in 1226 under Louis VIII, who died that November. [cite:vt28_audit_wiki_crusade] [cite:vt28_audit_cathen_albigenses] It ended with the Treaty of Paris, agreed at Meaux and sealed on 12 April 1229: Raymond VII kept Toulouse for his lifetime but ceded lands to the crown, promised his daughter in marriage to the king's brother Alphonse, undertook to hunt down heretics and pledged to pull down the walls of Toulouse; the same day he did public penance in Notre-Dame in Paris and was absolved. [cite:vt28_audit_wiki_crusade] [cite:vt28_audit_cathen_raymond7]

Montségur, 1243–1244

After 1229 the Good Men went underground, and the hilltop castle of Montségur in the Pyrenean foothills became the seat of their bishop and a refuge. Royal forces under the seneschal Hugues des Arcis besieged it from May 1243; its commander, Pierre-Roger de Mirepoix, surrendered in early March 1244. The terms let everyone leave, including men who had taken part in killing inquisitors, on condition that they renounce Catharism. A two-week truce followed. During it, some defenders asked for the consolamentum and joined the perfect. [cite:vt28_wiki_montsegur]

On 16 March 1244 about 210 to 215 people, about 190 of them perfect, the rest believers who would not recant or who had been consoled during the truce, were burned on a pyre at the foot of the mountain. Their bishop, Bertrand Marty, led them down. [cite:vt28_wiki_montsegur] The often repeated statement that they walked into the fire of their own accord is not established by a cited source; what the terms show is that they could have lived by recanting and did not. A claim that three or four perfect escaped with the community's money appears in later accounts and is unverified; the Holy Grail "treasure" of modern books is a twentieth-century invention. [cite:vt28_wiki_montsegur] [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism]

How many died

Popular accounts give the crusade's total dead as anything from 200,000 to 1,000,000. One reference work gives one million, citing a news-magazine article. [cite:vt28_nwe_crusade] Neither end of that range rests on a contemporary count or on a published demographic study. The only figures from the time are a handful of battlefield and siege claims, made by the crusade's own leaders and chroniclers, and the best documented of them, Béziers, is the one historians most doubt. [cite:vt28_wiki_beziers] The honest statement is that the war killed many thousands, through massacre, siege, battle and burning, and that there is no reliable overall figure.

Whether the crusade should be called a genocide is also disputed. Mark Pegg argues that it "ushered genocide into the West by linking divine salvation to mass murder"; Robert Lerner disputes the classification. The record adds one fact both sides must weigh: at Minerve and Montségur people could save their lives by recanting, and some did, though at Lavaur no such offer is recorded. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] [cite:vt28_audit_wiki_minerve] [cite:vt28_audit_wiki_lavaur] The war did not end the movement. That took a different instrument, built in the same years, and the next section turns to it. [scene:vt28_inquisition|The Inquisition]

sections.h: Building the Inquisition, 1184–1330
sections.html:
The Albigensian Crusade conquered the south but did not end the Good Men; they survived in households, villages and mountain refuges for almost a century more. What ended them was a legal procedure, assembled step by step by popes, councils and kings between 1184 and 1252, and run by named friars with notaries and registers. It is usually called "the Inquisition", but in this period it was not one office. It was a set of commissions given by the pope to individual judges, mostly Dominican and Franciscan friars, working with bishops and relying on lay rulers to carry out the gravest sentences. [cite:vt28_wiki_greg9] [cite:vt28_herodote_1233] It is a different institution from the Spanish Inquisition of 1478 and from the Roman Inquisition founded in 1542, which passed through later names to today's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith.

It was not the first time a Christian ruler had acted against a dissenting group by law. Constantine's edict against the Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites and others, preserved by Eusebius, had banned their meetings, given their buildings to the catholic church and ordered their books sought out, nine centuries earlier. [cite:vt22_vc3_64] [scene:vt21_church_and_empire|Part Twenty-One] What was new in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries was a standing procedure that searched for dissent rather than waiting for it to be reported.

From the bishop's visit to the papal judge

The first step was Ad abolendam, issued by Pope Lucius III at Verona on 4 November 1184, after a meeting with the emperor Frederick I. It condemned by name the Cathars, the Humiliati, the Poor of Lyon (Waldensians), the Arnoldists and others. It told every bishop to visit his diocese once or twice a year, put residents on oath to say what they knew of heretics, and treat anyone who broke that oath as a heretic. Those who could not clear themselves, would not recant or relapsed were to be handed to the lay power for "due punishment" (animadversio debita); their protectors lost public office, the right to go to law and the right to make a will. [cite:vt28_wiki_adabolendam] In 1199 Innocent III's Vergentis in senium classed heresy with treason, a crime against majesty punishable by death. [cite:vt28_wiki_adextirpanda]

The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 made the arrangement general. Its third canon ordered that condemned heretics be "handed over to the secular rulers" for punishment, that the property of lay heretics be confiscated, and that rulers "publicly take an oath" to exterminate the heretics in their lands. [cite:vt28_fordham_lat4c3] In 1229, as the war ended, a council at Toulouse ordered a search of every parish for heretics, the destruction of houses where they were found, and a ban on lay people owning the books of the Old and New Testaments; only a psalter, breviary or Book of Hours was allowed, and "we most strictly forbid their having any translation of these books". [cite:vt28_wiki_toulouse] The Good Men had read the Gospels aloud in Occitan; the council took vernacular scripture out of lay hands in the region where they had done so. [cite:vt28_gui_fordham]

Gregory IX's inquisitors

Gregory IX turned the bishops' duty into a papal commission. His constitution Excommunicamus of 1231 set the penalties: death by burning for heretics who persisted, prison or canonical penances such as fasting and pilgrimage for those who repented, and excommunication for Catholics who helped heretics. [cite:vt28_herodote_1233] The same year he began naming papal "inquisitors of heretical depravity", mostly Dominican and Franciscan friars, for France, Italy and parts of Germany, and on 20 April 1233 he set up the tribunal for the kingdom of France. Its judges opened cases on their own initiative and sought out suspects themselves, without waiting for an accuser. [cite:vt28_wiki_greg9] [cite:vt28_herodote_1233] The Church did not itself execute anyone; it handed the condemned to the secular arm, which was obliged to burn them. [cite:vt28_herodote_1233] [cite:vt28_fordham_lat4c3] Historians still weigh the design differently: Thomas Madden reads it as an attempt to bring due process and investigation to a field ruled by mobs and lords, while Walter Ullmann called the procedure "the denial of justice or a hideous caricature of it". [cite:vt28_wiki_greg9]

The new machinery reached beyond Christian dissenters. In 1239 Gregory ordered all copies of the Talmud confiscated, and in Paris in June 1242 a mass burning of Jewish manuscripts followed. [cite:vt28_wiki_greg9] That was an act of the papacy and the French crown against Jewish books, not a "Jewish" anything; it belongs to the same years and the same logic of seizing texts, and Part Thirty returns to the Church's control of books. [scene:vt30_forbidden_arts|The forbidden arts]

Torture by papal authority

On 6 April 1252 Cathar sympathisers murdered Peter of Verona, papal inquisitor in Lombardy. On 15 May 1252 Innocent IV issued Ad extirpanda to the rulers and cities of Lombardy, Romagna and the March of Treviso. It authorised the use of torture to extract confessions, provided it did not cause loss of life or limb, and required the city authorities to carry out the inquisitors' sentences on pain of excommunication and interdict: the convicted were to be delivered in chains within five days. Heretics' houses were to be razed and their confiscated property split in three, a third to the city, a third to the officials who handled the cases, and a third to the bishop and inquisitors to "promote the faith and extirpate heretics". [cite:vt28_wiki_adextirpanda] Judicial torture was already in use in secular courts; the bull's significance is that a pope authorised it for heresy trials and tied the inquisitors' finances to the property of the condemned. [cite:vt28_wiki_adextirpanda]

The registers

The inquisitors wrote everything down, and their registers are now the main source for the people they prosecuted. The mass burnings came early: on 13 May 1239 some 183 people were burned in Champagne. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] The later work was slower and more bureaucratic. Bernard Gui (1261–1331), inquisitor at Toulouse and author of the best known inquisitors' manual, left a book of sentences that the historian Julien Théry has analysed: 916 decisions concerning 636 people or communities. About 45 people, roughly 6 per cent of the decisions and mostly relapsed heretics, were burned; nearly 30 per cent ended in release or dismissal; more than half imposed prison or penance, often the yellow crosses that marked a repentant heretic. [cite:vt28_mednet_gui] The record is grim, and it is also not the film version of The Name of the Rose: Gui burned far fewer people than his reputation in fiction suggests, and far more than none.

The last Good Men of Languedoc were tracked through the mountains. A revival led by the brothers Pierre and Jacques Autier ended with Pierre Autier's execution at Toulouse in April 1310. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] Jacques Fournier, bishop of Pamiers from 1317, ran his own inquisition from 1318 to 1325; by Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie's count he conducted 578 interrogations over 370 working days, and five people were burned. His register, taken to Rome when he became Pope Benedict XII in 1334, is in the Vatican Library, and it is the source of Le Roy Ladurie's Montaillou (1975), the portrait of a Pyrenean village drawn from its inhabitants' own words under questioning. [cite:vt28_wiki_fournier] Guillaume Bélibaste, a pupil of the Autiers, was betrayed by Arnaud Sicre, a spy working for the inquisition, and burned at Villerouge-Termenès in 1321. He is remembered as the last Cathar perfect of Languedoc, though that is tradition rather than a demonstrable fact. [cite:vt28_wiki_belibaste]

What the Holy See says now

The Holy See has not repudiated the individual bulls, but it has repented of their method in general terms. At the Day of Pardon in St Peter's on 12 March 2000, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, prefect of the congregation that descends from the Roman Inquisition, confessed that "even men of the church, in the name of faith and morals, have sometimes used methods not in keeping with the Gospel". [cite:vt28_america_2000] In a letter of 15 June 2004 presenting the proceedings of a 1998 Vatican symposium on the Inquisition, John Paul II repeated the Church's repentance for "intolerance and even the use of violence" in the service of truth, and insisted that such judgements must follow "exact knowledge of the facts" established by historians. [cite:vt28_va_jp2_2004] Neither text names the Cathars, Béziers or Montségur.

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Nine
chapters.title: Templars, Mystics and the Stake
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-Nine follows the stake and the heresy trial from 1307 to 1633, through three kinds of target that popular accounts often fold into one story. It begins with the Knights Templar, a papal order arrested by the king of France, absolved in private at Chinon and dissolved at Vienne without a heresy verdict, and sets the record beside the legends that have gathered around them, from the origin of Friday the 13th to a parchment said to prove their innocence. It then turns to the mystics inside the Latin Church who taught that God is found within, Marguerite Porete, Meister Eckhart, the alumbrados of Castile and Miguel de Molinos, and sets what each taught beside the document that condemned it. It ends with Giordano Bruno, burned in 1600, and Galileo Galilei, made to abjure in 1633, and with what the Holy See has and has not said about them since.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty-Nine established three things. The Templars were arrested by Philip IV on 13 October 1307, tortured into confessions and, in fifty-four cases in May 1310, burned for retracting them; the Chinon parchment of August 1308 records the leaders' absolution after confession, not a finding of innocence, and Vox in excelso of 22 March 1312 suppressed the order "by apostolic provision", not by a heresy sentence, while the Friday-the-13th origin story is a twentieth-century invention. [cite:vt29_barber_cup2] [cite:vt29_barber_cup1] [cite:vt29_wiki_chinon] [cite:vt29_ewtn_vienne] [cite:vt29_natgeo_fri13] Teachers of the inner way inside the Church were condemned in named documents: Porete burned on 1 June 1310, Eckhart's propositions condemned on 27 March 1329, the alumbrados' forty-eight propositions listed in 1525, and Molinos's sixty-eight in Coelestis Pastor on 20 November 1687, while others who taught union with God under obedience were warned, cleared or published. [cite:vt29_wiki_porete] [cite:vt29_mckay_inagro] [cite:vt29_wiki_alumbrados] [cite:vt29_wiki_molinos] Bruno was burned on 17 February 1600 for theological heresies with cosmology and magic among the charges, and Galileo abjured on 22 June 1633 and lived under house arrest, with the 1992 papal address stopping short of annulling the sentence. [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] [cite:vt29_wiki_galileo] [cite:vt29_coyne_galileo] Part Thirty turns from individuals to the fraternities, the witch trials and the arts the Church called forbidden. [scene:vt30_rosicrucians_masons|Part Thirty: Fraternities, Witches and the Forbidden Arts]

sections.h: The Templars: Bankers, Heretics or Victims of a King?
sections.html:
The Knights Templar sit awkwardly in a book about inner traditions. They were not mystics, they had no secret gospel, and they were created and protected by the papacy for almost two centuries. They belong here for a different reason: their destruction between 1307 and 1314 is the clearest medieval case of heresy procedure being turned against a body of Catholic religious, and it has gathered more popular legend than almost any other episode of the period. This section sets the record beside those legends. [cite:vt29_barber_cup2] [cite:vt29_wiki_chinon]

From pilgrim guards to a papal order

The order began in 1119, when two French knights, Hugh of Payns and Godfrey of Saint-Omer, undertook to guard pilgrims on the road from Jaffa to Jerusalem. King Baldwin II and Patriarch Warmund gave them quarters on the Temple platform, in the building the Latins called the "Temple of Solomon", the al-Aqsa mosque; from it they took their name. Church approval probably came at a council at Nablus in January 1120. In January 1129 a council at Troyes, encouraged by Bernard of Clairvaux, gave them a Latin Rule of 71 clauses, and Bernard wrote a treatise in praise of this "new knighthood" of monks who fought. [cite:vt29_barber_cup1]

On 29 March 1139 Pope Innocent II issued Omne datum optimum. The bull called the Templars defenders of the Catholic Church, placed their possessions under papal protection and granted them privileges that freed them from much local church authority. This is the document behind the common statement that the Templars "answered only to the pope". It is accurate as a description of their legal standing, and it explains a later fact: the only authority that could lawfully dissolve them was the pope. [cite:vt29_barber_cup1]

Gifts of land across Europe, and the need to move money from estates in the West to castles in the East, made the order a financial institution as well as a military one. Pilgrims deposited valuables with one house and drew on them at another by letters of credit; kings and nobles borrowed from the order and stored treasure with it. [cite:vt29_nwe_templar] In France the Paris Temple became, in the words of a 2016 Madrid doctoral study of its accounts, "banker to kings", and the French royal treasury's accounts were kept there through much of the thirteenth century, the study covering 1221 to 1295. [cite:vt29_ucm_temple] Popular accounts call this "Europe's first international banking network". The safer description is one of the earliest cross-border deposit and transfer systems in Latin Europe; Italian banking houses developed alongside it, not out of it.

Friday 13 October 1307

In the early hours of Friday 13 October 1307, officials of King Philip IV of France arrested the Templars throughout his kingdom and seized their property, acting formally on behalf of the papal inquisitors in France. The charges were that at secret receptions new brothers were made to deny Christ and spit on the crucifix, that they exchanged indecent kisses, that sodomy was permitted and that they worshipped an idol. In October and November almost all the prisoners, including the Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, confessed. Malcolm Barber, the leading historian of the trial, writes that on many of the prisoners "torture was freely used". [cite:vt29_barber_cup2]

Pope Clement V had not authorised the arrests and at first treated them as an affront to his own authority over an exempt order. On 22 November 1307 he changed course and issued Pastoralis praeeminentiae, ordering every Christian ruler to arrest the Templars in his lands. [cite:vt29_barber_cup2] Why Philip acted is a question of motive, and the documents do not give a single answer. He was short of money for his war with England and owed the order large sums, and the arrests freed him from those debts and gave him control of its treasuries. [cite:vt29_nwe_templar]

No reliable count of those arrested across France survives. The best-documented number is a different one: by early May 1310 almost six hundred Templars in Paris had come forward to defend the order before the papal commission. The king's answer was swift. On 12 May 1310 fifty-four of them were burned outside Paris as relapsed heretics, men who had confessed, then withdrawn their confessions. [cite:vt29_barber_cup1]

Chinon, August 1308: what the parchment says

Between 17 and 20 August 1308, three cardinals sent by Clement V, Bérenger Frédol, Étienne de Suisy and Landolfo Brancacci, questioned Molay and four other leaders held in the castle of Chinon. The record of that inquiry is the Chinon parchment. The Vatican Apostolic Archive holds the original (Archivum Arcis, Armarium D 217) and an authentic copy (D 218). The Italian palaeographer Barbara Frale found it in September 2001, misfiled, and published it in the Journal of Medieval History in 2004; in 2007 the archive issued a facsimile edition, Processus contra Templarios, in 799 numbered copies. [cite:vt29_wiki_chinon] The Archive itself is described in [scene:vt14_apostolic_archive|Part Fourteen].

The parchment records that the leaders confessed to some of the charges, chiefly the denial of Christ and spitting at reception, which several described as done "in words only, not in spirit", denied others, asked for pardon, and were absolved from excommunication and restored to the sacraments. It does not declare the order innocent. Frale reads it as evidence that Clement thought the order was not heretical and could be reformed, and that he tried and failed to keep it out of Philip's hands. Other historians, such as Anne Gilmour-Bryson, warn that testimony given after torture cannot be read at face value in either direction. [cite:vt29_wiki_chinon]

Popular versions go further than this, saying that Clement found the Templars innocent and that the parchment proves a frame-up. An absolution is granted to people who have confessed and repented; it is the opposite of an acquittal. Some accounts also say the document was hidden for 700 years and then released in a costly edition to keep it from the public. The parchment was misfiled rather than locked away, a related Chinon document addressed to Philip IV, also recording absolution of confessing Templars, had been in print since Étienne Baluze published it in 1693, and Frale's article reached print three years before the facsimile. [cite:vt29_wiki_chinon]

Suppression by provision, 1312

At the Council of Vienne, on 22 March 1312, Clement issued Vox in excelso, approved in session on 3 April. Its wording matters. The pope suppressed the order "not by definitive sentence, but by apostolic provision or ordinance": the council had not convicted it of heresy, and the bull says that a definitive sentence would not have been lawful on the evidence. The reason given was scandal: the order had lost its good name, recruits would stop and its property would be lost, and the scandal was "impossible to allay as long as the order continues to exist". Anyone who joined it or wore its habit afterwards was excommunicated automatically. [cite:vt29_ewtn_vienne]

On 2 May 1312 Ad providam gave the order's houses, lands and revenues to the Knights Hospitaller, except in Castile, Aragon, Portugal and Majorca, where the pope reserved the property to himself. [cite:vt29_ewtn_vienne] In practice much Templar property in France stayed under the crown's control for years, and in Portugal King Dinis refounded the Templar houses as the Order of Christ. [cite:vt29_nwe_templar]

Molay and Geoffroi de Charney were held for almost two more years. They were sentenced on 18 March 1314, publicly withdrew their confessions, and were burned that evening on the Île des Javiaux in the Seine. [cite:vt29_barber_cup1] [cite:vt29_nwe_templar]

Friday the 13th and the afterlife of the order

The widely repeated claim that the arrests of Friday 13 October 1307 are the origin of the Friday-the-13th superstition has no documentary basis. Friday and the number thirteen were each thought unlucky before the twentieth century, but the combined date as a fixed superstition is hard to find before then; a 1907 novel titled Friday, the Thirteenth is one early landmark. The Templar link was spread by the 1980s bestseller Holy Blood, Holy Grail and popularised by Dan Brown's The Da Vinci Code in 2003. [cite:vt29_natgeo_fri13]

The claim that the Templars survived in secret and passed their knowledge to the Freemasons is a separate and contested question, treated with the other fraternities in [scene:vt30_rosicrucians_masons|Part Thirty].

What the record does support is narrower and still serious. A religious order under papal protection was arrested by a king, its members were tortured into confessions, men who defended it were burned, and the pope, who had privately absolved its leaders, dissolved it without a verdict because the scandal could not be undone. Read on its own terms, the Templar case shows the papacy losing a contest with the French crown rather than hunting an inner tradition. [cite:vt29_barber_cup2] [cite:vt29_ewtn_vienne]

sections.h: The Mystics: The Kingdom Within, on Trial
sections.html:
The thread that runs through this platform's reading of the Gnostic texts, from the Gospel of Thomas to the Gospel of Mary, is the "kingdom within": the claim that God can be known directly, inside the person, without a priest standing in between. [scene:vt25_sayings_gospels|Part Twenty-Five] and [scene:vt26_gospel_of_mary|Part Twenty-Six] showed where that idea appears in the ancient texts. This section follows it inside the Latin Church, where it returned through laywomen, friars and priests. For each, the record shows what they taught, what the institution condemned, and in which document. [cite:vt29_wiki_porete] [cite:vt29_mckay_inagro] [cite:vt29_wiki_alumbrados] [cite:vt29_wiki_molinos]

Beguines and Marguerite Porete

Beguines were laywomen who lived, alone or in groups, a life of prayer, work and charity without taking the vows of a nun. That freedom was the problem in the eyes of their critics. The Council of Vienne's decree on them, later known by its opening words Cum de quibusdam, complained that they "promise obedience to no one", renounce no property and follow no approved rule, and that some of them "argue and preach on the holy Trinity and the divine essence". It forbade their way of life under automatic excommunication, while exempting devout women living penitent lives in hospices. [cite:vt29_ewtn_vienne]

Marguerite Porete, born around 1258 probably in Hainaut, was a Beguine who wrote in Old French, probably in the 1290s, The Mirror of Simple Souls. It is a dialogue between Love, Reason, the Virtues and the Soul in the language of courtly romance. Its subject is the "annihilated soul": a soul that has given up everything except God, including its own will, through love. The book has Love say "I am God, says Love, for Love is God and God is Love". [cite:vt29_wiki_porete]

The bishop of Cambrai, Gui de Collemedio, condemned the book and had it burned in her presence at Valenciennes sometime between 1296 and 1306. She kept circulating it. Arrested around 1308, she was handed to the Dominican inquisitor William of Paris and refused to take the oath or answer any of his questions. In 1310 a commission of twenty-one theologians of Paris judged fifteen propositions drawn from the book heretical. As a relapsed heretic, one who had returned to an error already condemned, she was handed to the secular authorities and burned on the Place de Grève in Paris on 1 June 1310. The chronicler Guillaume de Nangis, no friend of hers, recorded that the crowd was moved to tears by her calm. [cite:vt29_wiki_porete]

The book outlived her. Extracts from it appear among the errors condemned in the Council of Vienne's decree Ad nostrum, aimed at the so-called Free Spirit. It went on circulating without her name, in Latin, Italian and Middle English, and was at one time thought to be the work of the Flemish mystic John of Ruusbroec. Only in 1946 did the Italian scholar Romana Guarnieri identify Porete as the author. [cite:vt29_wiki_porete]

Meister Eckhart: the ground of the soul

Eckhart, born around 1260, was not a marginal figure. He was a Dominican friar, a master of theology at Paris, and held senior posts in his order before teaching in Strasbourg and Cologne. In his sermons he taught that there is a "ground" in the soul where God and the soul are one; that God the Father gives birth to the Son, the Word, in that ground, in the person who has let go of everything; that this letting go, "detachment", is the way; and that beyond God as named and described lies the Godhead, which no name reaches. His best-known line runs: "The Eye with which I see God is the same Eye with which God sees me". [cite:vt29_wiki_eckhart]

In 1326 Archbishop Henry of Virneburg of Cologne opened an inquisitorial trial against him. Eckhart protested his orthodoxy, said he would retract anything shown to be in error, and appealed to Pope John XXII at Avignon. He died there, probably on 28 January 1328, before the case ended. On 27 March 1329 the pope issued the bull In agro dominico. It lists twenty-eight articles from his works: seventeen judged heretical and eleven judged "evil-sounding" and "very rash" but capable of a Catholic sense with explanation. The bull records that before his death Eckhart "absolutely and totally revoked" them and submitted his writings to the pope's judgment. [cite:vt29_mckay_inagro] [cite:vt29_wiki_eckhart]

Eckhart's readers Johannes Tauler and Henry Suso carried his teaching on within the Church, and in the 1990s the Dominican order sought his rehabilitation. A Vatican letter of 1992, made public in 2010, stated that he had never been condemned by name, only certain propositions attributed to him. [cite:vt29_wiki_eckhart]

The alumbrados: yielding to God

In Castile in the 1510s and 1520s, circles around Isabel de la Cruz, a woman from Guadalajara, and Pedro Ruiz de Alcaraz practised what they called dejamiento: yielding oneself to God's love, making no effort at methodical prayer, letting thoughts pass and doing whatever God moves one to do. Alcaraz put it in one sentence: "El amor de Dios en un hombre es Dios", the love of God in a man is God. It differed from the recogimiento, the disciplined, step-by-step prayer of recollection taught by the Franciscan Francisco de Osuna, which the Church accepted. [cite:vt29_hughes_cazalla] Critics called the dejados alumbrados, "the enlightened". In the Inquisition's summary they held that the soul could reach a perfection in which it saw God in this life, that outward worship and sacraments were superfluous, and that sin was impossible for a soul in union with God. [cite:vt29_wiki_alumbrados]

In 1525 the Inquisitor General, Alonso Manrique, issued an edict listing forty-eight propositions drawn from the trials of Isabel de la Cruz and Alcaraz. [cite:vt29_wiki_alumbrados] One of them, number eleven, condemned the view that once a person has left everything to God, nothing more is needed to save the soul, and that fasting and works of mercy are unnecessary. [cite:vt29_hughes_cazalla] Convicted alumbrados were generally not executed; in 1529 a group at Toledo was flogged and imprisoned. The suspicion spread wide. Ignatius of Loyola, the future founder of the Jesuits, was examined at Salamanca in 1527 for alumbrado sympathies and let off with a warning. [cite:vt29_wiki_alumbrados] María de Cazalla, a follower, was arrested on 22 April 1532 and after two years of questioning and torture abjured lightly suspected heresy and was fined 100 ducats; one study compares her teaching directly with Porete's Mirror. [cite:vt29_hughes_cazalla]

Spain's great mystics of the next generation wrote under the same shadow. The Augustinian Luis de León was held in the Inquisition's prison at Valladolid from March 1572 to December 1576, chiefly for translating the Song of Songs into Spanish, and was cleared; in 1588 he published the first collected edition of the works of Teresa of Ávila. [cite:vt29_wiki_luisdeleon]

Molinos and Quietism

Miguel de Molinos, a Spanish priest in Rome, published his Spiritual Guide in Italian in 1675 with the approval of several church censors. It went through about twenty editions in twelve years. It taught that after a time of meditation the soul could be drawn into a simple "prayer of quiet", resting in God, and that the way to perfection was "interior annihilation": people must, in Britannica's summary, "banish their individual wills" so that God's will could act in them. [cite:vt29_cathen_molinos] [cite:vt29_brit_molinos] [cite:vt29_wiki_molinos] Jesuits such as Paolo Segneri answered that this would lead people to abandon meditation, the sacraments and moral effort. [cite:vt29_wiki_molinos]

He was arrested on 18 July 1685. Some twelve thousand letters from people who had sought his direction were reportedly seized. On 3 September 1687, in the Dominican church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, he was declared a "dogmatic heretic", abjured and was sentenced to life imprisonment; on 20 November 1687 Innocent XI's bull Coelestis Pastor condemned sixty-eight propositions attributed to him, among them the annihilation of the soul's powers, the ceasing of acts of devotion and indifference to one's own salvation. He died in the prison of the Holy Office in December 1696. [cite:vt29_cathen_molinos] [cite:vt29_wiki_molinos] [cite:vt29_audit_denz_molinos] The trial also turned on charges of sexual misconduct with penitents, which, by the Catholic Encyclopedia's account, Molinos excused as acts in which his free will had no part; Britannica notes that the condemned doctrines do not appear in the Guide itself. [cite:vt29_cathen_molinos] [cite:vt29_brit_molinos]

What the four cases show

The record supports part of the thesis plainly. Each of these teachers said that God could be found in the depth of the person, and each was condemned in documents that object, among other things, to the idea that the soul in union with God no longer needs outward works, set prayers or the ordinary disciplines of the Church. [cite:vt29_wiki_porete] [cite:vt29_hughes_cazalla] [cite:vt29_wiki_molinos] The record also limits the thesis. The same Church kept reading and printing mystics who described union with God in comparable terms, and the line it drew ran at least as much through obedience as through the inner experience itself: Eckhart submitted and was not condemned by name; Porete refused to answer and was burned; the alumbrado-suspect Ignatius was warned and went on to found the Jesuits; Teresa of Ávila's works were printed by a friar the Inquisition had itself cleared. [cite:vt29_mckay_inagro] [cite:vt29_wiki_luisdeleon]

Interpretation, not finding: the kingdom within as a threat to mediation

In the Sophia platform's reading, these trials are one pattern repeated: whenever someone taught that the kingdom of God is within and needs no intermediary, the institution answered with a condemnation, because unmediated access makes the mediator unnecessary. Read through this lens, Porete's annihilated soul, Eckhart's birth of God in the ground, the alumbrados' yielding and Molinos's quiet are the Gospel of Thomas's saying about the kingdom spread out inside you, surfacing again in Latin Christendom. The counter-reading, set out in the cases above, is that the institution tolerated the inner way under obedience and condemned it when it was joined to claims that sin was impossible, that works and sacraments were superfluous, or that the teacher answered to no one. Both readings fit the documents; the documents alone do not decide between them. The fuller argument is weighed in [scene:vt31_two_economies|Part Thirty-One].

sections.h: Bruno and Galileo: The Stake and the Abjuration
sections.html:
Two trials of the Roman Inquisition, thirty-three years apart, became the standard proof that the Church fought science: Giordano Bruno burned in 1600 and Galileo Galilei forced to abjure in 1633. In esoteric writing they also appear as proof of something else, the suppression of inner and Hermetic knowledge; some popular accounts say Bruno was burned for advocating inner spiritual work over institutional religion. The record of each trial is now largely available. It shows two different cases, and neither fits either slogan cleanly. [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] [cite:vt29_wiki_galileo]

Giordano Bruno: the charges

Bruno was born at Nola, near Naples, in 1548, entered the Dominican order at seventeen and was ordained in 1572. He left Naples when an indictment was being prepared against him and spent the next years wandering through Europe, writing on memory, magic and cosmology. He argued that the universe is infinite and has no centre, that the stars are suns with planets of their own, and that those worlds may be inhabited. [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno]

On 22 May 1592, after the Venetian patrician Giovanni Mocenigo, who had brought him to Venice as a tutor, denounced him, the Venetian Inquisition arrested him, and in January 1593 he was sent to Rome. He was held for about seven years. The Roman trial volumes are lost; what survives is a summary of the case, the Sommario, found in the papers of the Holy Office on 15 November 1940 by Angelo Mercati, prefect of the Vatican Archives, after some fifteen years of searching, and published in 1942. [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] [cite:vt29_linder_bruno]

The charges recorded against him were mostly theological. He was accused of denying the Trinity, the divinity of Christ and the Incarnation, of denying the virginity of Mary and transubstantiation, and of teaching the transmigration of souls, the existence of many worlds, and magic and divination. Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, the leading theologian on the case, demanded a full retraction; Bruno refused. His cosmology was part of the case: in a late interrogation, probably in April 1599, the judges questioned him on his books about the infinite universe, and he defended them. [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] [cite:vt29_linder_bruno]

On 20 January 1600 Pope Clement VIII ruled that he was an obstinate heretic and should be handed to the secular authorities. When the sentence was read, Bruno is reported by a witness, Kaspar Schoppe, to have told his judges: "Perhaps you pronounce this sentence against me with greater fear than I receive it". On 17 February 1600 he was burned alive in the Campo de' Fiori in Rome, his tongue held in a gag, and denied the usual mercy of strangulation; his ashes were thrown into the Tiber. In 1603 all his works were put on the Index of Prohibited Books. [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] [cite:vt29_ht_bruno]

Martyr of science, Hermetic magus, or heretic

Each later age has read Bruno as its own. On 9 June 1889 the city of Rome set up his statue on the spot where he was burned. [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] In 1964 the historian Frances Yates argued in Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition that he was above all a Hermetic magus, who read Copernicus through the Hermetic texts and whose real cause was a magical religion. The thesis has been sharply contested: Hilary Gatti, among others, argued that Yates overstated the magic and understated Bruno's contribution to natural philosophy, and other scholars stress that cosmology was only one strand of a case built mainly on theology. [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] [cite:vt29_ht_bruno]

The record allows a narrower statement than any of these. Bruno was condemned by a church tribunal, and executed by the city authorities to which it handed him, for a long list of theological heresies that he refused to retract, with his cosmology and his magic among the charges. Nothing in the Sommario describes the case as one about "inner spiritual work", and the claim that he was burned for alchemy has no basis in the charges. [cite:vt29_linder_bruno] [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] The Holy See has not withdrawn the condemnation. In 2000, the fourth centenary, Cardinal Angelo Sodano called his death a "sad episode" while defending the judges' intentions, and Pope John Paul II's general request for pardon that year included the use of violence "in the service of truth". [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno]

Galileo: 1616

By the 1610s Galileo was the most famous defender of the sun-centred system of Copernicus. In a letter to his pupil Benedetto Castelli, expanded in 1615 into a letter to the Grand Duchess Christina, he argued that passages of Scripture about nature should not be read as settling questions that observation could decide. Dominican critics sent a copy of the Castelli letter to the Inquisition in February 1615. [cite:vt29_wiki_galileo]

On 24 February 1616 the Holy Office's theological consultants declared unanimously that the proposition that the sun stands still at the centre of the world was "foolish and absurd in philosophy, and formally heretical". On 26 February Cardinal Bellarmine instructed Galileo to abandon the opinion; whether he was also forbidden to teach or discuss it in any way is disputed, and that disputed wording later decided the trial. On 5 March 1616 the Congregation of the Index suspended Copernicus's book "until corrected" and banned a letter by Paolo Antonio Foscarini defending Copernicus. [cite:vt29_wiki_galileo]

1633: the trial

In 1632 Galileo published his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, which cost him the patronage of Pope Urban VIII. He was summoned to Rome. On 22 June 1633 the tribunal found him "vehemently suspect of heresy", required him to abjure, banned the Dialogue and sentenced him to formal imprisonment, commuted the next day to house arrest. He lived the rest of his life confined, first in Siena and then at his villa at Arcetri near Florence. [cite:vt29_wiki_galileo] Accounts that have him imprisoned from 1633 until his death in 1642 overstate the sentence as carried out: it was house arrest. The trial papers are among the holdings of the Vatican Apostolic Archive, described in [scene:vt14_apostolic_archive|Part Fourteen].

The slow reversal, 1758–1992

The Church dropped its general ban on heliocentric books from the Index in 1758 but did not touch the 1633 sentence. In 1820 a papal censor refused permission for a textbook by Canon Giuseppe Settele that taught the earth's motion as fact; the refusal was overturned on appeal. In the 1835 Index, Copernicus's book and Galileo's Dialogue were left out. [cite:vt29_wiki_galileo] [cite:vt29_coyne_galileo] The Index itself, from 1559 to its suppression in 1966, is treated in [scene:vt30_forbidden_arts|Part Thirty].

On 10 November 1979 John Paul II asked scholars to study the case afresh, and on 3 July 1981 a commission was set up. On 31 October 1992 Cardinal Paul Poupard presented its conclusions to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, and the pope spoke. He called the affair a "tragic mutual incomprehension" and said the theologians of the time had erred in treating the literal sense of Scripture as an account of the physical world. [cite:vt29_coyne_galileo] [cite:vt29_ap_galileo1992] News reports called it an admission that the Church had erred, and the physicist Giorgio Salvini, president of the Lincei Academy, welcomed it as "a recognition of errors and of guilt". [cite:vt29_ap_galileo1992]

The Jesuit astronomer George Coyne, writing for the Vatican Observatory, read the same texts more critically. He noted that the 1992 address attributed the "hasty and unhappy" decision to "certain persons" rather than to the popes or the congregations that issued it, that neither the 1616 decree nor the 1633 sentence was ever explicitly reformed, and that the conclusions were not submitted to the commission's own members for approval. [cite:vt29_coyne_galileo] The 1992 statement was a real change of tone; it was not a formal annulment.

Set side by side, the two trials show an institution that claimed the right to judge both doctrine and the reading of nature, and used the stake and the abjuration to enforce it. They do not show a campaign against inner religion: Bruno's case was about his theology, and Galileo's was about astronomy and the authority to interpret Scripture. Where they connect to the thread of this book is in the instrument: the same Inquisition procedure, born against the Cathars in [scene:vt28_inquisition|Part Twenty-Eight], was by 1600 the means by which Rome decided which knowledge could be held. [cite:vt29_wiki_galileo] [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno]

chapters.label: Part Thirty
chapters.title: Fraternities, Witches and the Forbidden Arts
chapters.intro: Part Thirty follows the institution's record from the medieval heresy trials into the modern world, where its targets were no longer mainly rival churches but fraternities, accused witches and the arts it called forbidden. It takes four subjects in turn. The Rosicrucian manifestos of 1614 to 1616 and the Freemasons, condemned by a papal bull of 1738 and still, in a Vatican note of November 2023, declared incompatible with the faith. The Bavarian Illuminati, a short-lived Enlightenment society banned by its own state in the 1780s, and the conspiracy myth that grew around it and was grafted onto antisemitism. The witch trials of about 1450 to 1750, with what a papal bull and an inquisitor's handbook did, what secular and prince-bishops' courts did, and how many people actually died. And the forbidden arts themselves: alchemy, astrology, divination, tarot and the books placed on the Index. For each the part sets out what the group or practice actually taught, what the Church's documents said about it and when, what states did separately, and where the popular story parts company with the record.
chapters.outro: Part Thirty established four things. The Rosicrucian manifestos of 1614 to 1616 were openly anti-papal Lutheran texts for which no order is documented before the eighteenth century, and drew one galley sentence from a Habsburg prince and a Paris panic rather than any papal condemnation found here; Freemasonry, by contrast, has been banned by Rome from In eminenti of 28 April 1738 to the Dicastery's note of 13 November 2023, which still holds membership incompatible with the faith as of October 2026. [cite:vt30_waite_confessio] [cite:vt30_wiki_haslmayr] [cite:vt30_wiki_ineminenti] [cite:vt30_va_cdf1983] [cite:vt30_vn_ddf2023] The Bavarian Illuminati were an Enlightenment society suppressed by the Elector of Bavaria in 1784 to 1787, and the myth of their survival, born with Barruel and Robison in 1797 and grafted onto antisemitism by the fabricated Simonini letter of 1806 and the Protocols, has no documentary basis. [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati] [cite:vt30_wiki_simonini] [cite:vt30_wiki_judeomasonic] The witch trials killed some 40,000 to 60,000 people, not nine million, mostly through secular and prince-bishops' courts, after Innocent VIII's bull of 1484 empowered the inquisitor who wrote the Malleus, while the Roman and Spanish Inquisitions were among the first tribunals to demand proof and stop the burning. [cite:vt30_wiki_witchtrials] [cite:vt30_fordham_summis] [cite:vt30_wiki_malleus] [cite:vt30_wiki_basque] [cite:vt30_luebke_ninemillion] And the forbidden arts were condemned on mixed grounds: alchemy as fraud in about 1317, divination and judicial astrology as usurping what is owed to God from Trent's rules of 1564 to the Catechism today, with the Index enforcing the ban on their books until 1966. [cite:vt30_wiki_spondent] [cite:vt30_fordham_rule9] [cite:vt30_va_ccc2116] [cite:vt14_nwe_index] Part Thirty-One turns from what the institution forbade to what it required: the tithe, the Sunday obligation and the commandments of the Church. [scene:vt31_tithe|Part Thirty-One: Tithe, Sabbath and Obedience]

sections.h: Rosicrucians and Freemasons: Two Fraternities and Rome
sections.html:
The Rosicrucians and the Freemasons belong side by side for a plain reason: both were brotherhoods that met, or claimed to meet, outside the parish and the confessional, and both bound their members by promises the Church did not administer. Their records with Rome are very different. The Rosicrucian manifestos drew polemic, one documented galley sentence imposed by a Catholic prince and a Paris panic, but no papal condemnation of them is recorded. Freemasonry drew a papal bull in 1738 and a line of condemnations that has never been withdrawn; the most recent is a note approved by Pope Francis in November 2023. This section sets out what each taught, what was done about it and by whom, and where the popular story of a "suppressed" fraternity holds or fails. [cite:vt30_wiki_rosic] [cite:vt30_wiki_ineminenti] [cite:vt30_vn_ddf2023]

The Rosicrucian manifestos

The Fama Fraternitatis circulated in manuscript from about 1610 and was printed at Kassel in 1614. The Confessio Fraternitatis followed in 1615 and the Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreuz in 1616. All three came out of a Lutheran milieu in south-west Germany; scholars connect them with a circle at Tübingen that included Tobias Hess, Christoph Besold and the young theologian Johann Valentin Andreae. Andreae later claimed the Chymical Wedding as his own and called the whole affair a ludibrium, a jest or play. [cite:vt30_wiki_rosic] [cite:ts13_wiki_rosicruc]

The Fama tells the story of a "Father C.R." who travels to the east, is taught by sages at Damcar in Arabia, passes through Egypt and Fez, and returns to Germany to found a brotherhood. Its members agree to heal the sick free of charge, to wear no special habit, to meet once a year at a "House of the Holy Spirit", to keep the fraternity secret for a hundred years and each to choose a successor.
