The manifestos promised a "universal reformation" of learning through a Christian natural philosophy that drew on alchemy and medicine. [cite:vt30_wiki_fama] [cite:vt30_wiki_rosic] They were not neutral about Rome. The Confessio of 1615, in its seventeenth-century English translation, declares that the brothers "condemn the East and the West (meaning the Pope and Mahomet)", calls the Pope Antichrist and says they "execrate the pope". [cite:vt30_waite_confessio] A movement that announced itself in those words was a Protestant one, and Catholic authorities treated it as part of the confessional conflict rather than as a hidden wisdom.

The documented consequences were limited and local. Adam Haslmayr, a German writer who had read the Fama in manuscript in 1610, published an enthusiastic reply in 1612; shortly afterwards Archduke Maximilian III of Austria, the Habsburg ruler of Tyrol, sent him to the galleys at Genoa, from which he was released four or five years later. [cite:vt30_wiki_haslmayr] The surviving account gives no formal charge; Rosicrucian histories often treat the sentence as a punishment for his Rosicrucian sympathies, a reading consistent with the timing but not stated in the record. In 1623 posters appeared in Paris, some on the walls of the Louvre, inviting readers to join the fraternity and promising invisibility and the making of gold. They caused alarm, and the Catholic librarian Gabriel Naudé answered with an Instruction à la France (1623) that mocked popular credulity. [cite:vt30_queyroux_naude] No order of the brotherhood has been found to have existed in the 1610s at all: the historian Roland Edighoffer states there is no proof that it ever did, and organised Rosicrucian bodies appear only in the eighteenth century. [cite:ts13_wiki_rosicruc] The told version, that a Rosicrucian order was hunted underground by the Church, has no document behind it; the record is one of print polemic, one galley sentence by a Catholic prince, and a Paris scare.

Freemasonry: what it was

Speculative Freemasonry took its organised form on 24 June 1717, when four London lodges met at the Goose and Gridiron ale-house and constituted themselves a Grand Lodge. James Anderson's Constitutions of 1723 gathered a legendary history of the craft, its "charges" and its regulations, and by the 1720s lodges had spread beyond London and to the continent. [cite:vt30_wiki_pgle] The lodges used the tools and building lore of the medieval stonemasons' guilds as an allegory of moral self-improvement, worked their members through graded rituals, required secrecy about those rituals, and admitted men of different Christian confessions to the same table. The descent of speculative Masonry from the operative guilds is documented; a Gnostic transmission behind it is not supported. [scene:ts13_mysteries|The Theology Shield: the mysteries and their modern heirs]

What Rome said, 1738 to 2023

Clement XII issued In eminenti apostolatus specula on 28 April 1738. It forbade Catholics to join or support the lodges under pain of excommunication and directed bishops and inquisitors to proceed against them, calling on the secular arm if needed. Its stated grounds were the members' oath of secrecy, the private rules that bound them outside civil or canon law, and the suspicion of heresy that the secrecy itself created; it reasoned that "if they were not doing evil they would not have so great a hatred of the light." [cite:vt30_wiki_ineminenti] The bull also noted that several states had already moved against the lodges as a threat to public order: the States General of the Dutch Republic had banned Masonic meetings in 1735, three years before Rome acted. [cite:vt30_wiki_ineminenti]

Benedict XIV confirmed the ban in Providas Romanorum of 18 March 1751, quoting his predecessor in full and adding reasons: the mixing of men of all religions, the oaths, the secrecy and the danger to church and state. [cite:vt30_wiki_providas] Leo XIII's encyclical Humanum genus of 20 April 1884 gave the condemnation its sharpest form. It described the human race as divided between "the kingdom of God on earth" and "the kingdom of Satan", and placed on the second side "that strongly organized and widespread association called the Freemasons", whose aim it said was "the utter overthrow" of the religious and political order. Leo listed and ratified the decrees of seven earlier popes from Clement XII to Pius IX. [cite:vt30_va_humanum]

The 1917 Code of Canon Law turned the bulls into a standing rule: canon 2335 imposed an excommunication, reserved to the Holy See, on those who joined "a Masonic sect" or similar societies. The 1983 Code dropped the name. Its canon 1374 punishes with "a just penalty" a person who joins "an association which plots against the Church". [cite:vt30_wiki_declmasonic] Because the new Code was silent about Masonry, the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith issued a declaration on 26 November 1983, signed by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger and approved by John Paul II: the Church's "negative judgment" on Masonic associations "remains unchanged", and "the faithful who enrol in Masonic associations are in a state of grave sin and may not receive Holy Communion." [cite:vt30_va_cdf1983] The declaration does not cite the old canon 2335 or name a penalty of excommunication, and its standing as an interpretation of the new Code has been disputed. [cite:vt30_wiki_declmasonic]

The latest act came in reply to Bishop Julito Cortes of Dumaguete in the Philippines, who reported rising Masonic membership in his diocese. A note of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith dated 13 November 2023, signed by its prefect, Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, and approved by Pope Francis, restated that "active membership in Freemasonry by a member of the faithful is prohibited" because of "the irreconcilability between Catholic doctrine and Freemasonry", applied the same to clergy, and asked the Philippine bishops for a doctrinal and pastoral strategy, including parish catechesis on the reasons. [cite:vt30_vn_ddf2023] No later revision was found as of October 2026. The Holy See's stated position across these documents is consistent: the objection is to secret oaths, to a religious relativism it sees in the lodges' admission of all faiths, and to political hostility to the Church, not to any secret doctrine said to be hidden inside them.

P2: the lodge in the Vatican banking scandal

One lodge became part of the Holy See's own financial history. Propaganda Due, founded in Turin in 1877 as Propaganda Massonica under the Grand Orient of Italy, was taken over by the businessman Licio Gelli, who became its master in 1975. The Grand Orient suspended the lodge in 1976, and a Masonic tribunal ruled in 1981 that it had legally ceased to exist after a 1974 vote, so that Gelli ran it as an irregular lodge. On 17 March 1981 police searching Gelli's villa found a list of 962 members, among them ministers, officers, journalists and the banker Roberto Calvi; its publication on 21 May 1981 brought down the Forlani government, and Law 17 of 25 January 1982 dissolved the lodge. The parliamentary commission chaired by Tina Anselmi concluded in its 1984 majority report that P2 was a secret organisation aimed at undermining Italian democracy; later court rulings took a narrower view of its power. [cite:vt30_wiki_p2] Calvi's dealings with the Institute for the Works of Religion are set out in [scene:vt10_ambrosiano_calvi|Part Ten: Ambrosiano and Calvi]. P2 is a documented case of a criminal network using a Masonic lodge as its shell; it is not evidence about Freemasonry in general, whose own Grand Orient had disowned it, and it is not evidence that the Holy See's ban on Masonry was either vindicated or hypocritical.

sections.h: The Bavarian Illuminati: The Order and the Myth
sections.html:
Two different things share the name Illuminati. One is a society founded in Bavaria in 1776, with named members, grades, correspondence and a short, documented life that ended under its own government's bans within a decade. The other is a conspiracy story, begun in the 1790s, that credits that society with surviving in secret and steering revolutions, wars and governments ever since, and that was grafted, early in the nineteenth century, onto the older hatred of Jews. The documented organisation and the myth attached to it are two different objects and must be kept apart. Popular esoteric writing also lists the order among suppressed inner traditions, which the record does not support: the Illuminati were Enlightenment rationalists, and the power that suppressed them was a Catholic state, not a church tribunal. [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati] [cite:vt30_natgeo_weishaupt]

What the order was

Adam Weishaupt was professor of natural and canon law at the University of Ingolstadt. On the night of 1 May 1776 he and four students founded a society first called the Bund der Perfektibilisten, the League of the Perfectible, renamed the Order of the Illuminati in April 1778. [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati] [cite:vt30_natgeo_weishaupt] Its stated aims were to oppose superstition and obscurantism, to reduce the influence of religion over public life, and to check abuses of power by rulers; Weishaupt said he wanted freedom from "religious prejudices" and "a state of liberty and moral equality". He had become strongly anticlerical after years of conflict with the Jesuits at his university. [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati] [cite:vt30_natgeo_weishaupt]

The order borrowed its structure from the Masonic lodges, which Weishaupt joined and found expensive and closed to his ideas. Members passed through grades, at first novice, Minerval and illuminated Minerval, after the Roman goddess of wisdom, and later through a thirteen-degree system designed by Baron Adolph von Knigge, who joined in 1780 and recruited heavily inside existing lodges. Members took classical code names: Weishaupt was "Spartacus", Knigge "Philo". Goethe was among those who joined. [cite:vt30_natgeo_weishaupt] [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati] Estimates of its size vary widely: about 650 members can be verified by the end of 1784, Weishaupt and a fellow leader claimed 2,500, historians have estimated about 1,300, and National Geographic's profile gives 2,000 to 3,000. [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati] [cite:vt30_natgeo_weishaupt] What it taught was not a secret gnosis but the reading programme of the German Enlightenment, applied through a hierarchy that asked members to report on their own moral progress to their superiors.

What the state did

The suppression was the work of the Elector of Bavaria, Charles Theodore, not of Rome. An edict of June 1784 banned all societies formed without government authorisation; one of March 1785, later called the order's death blow, banned the Illuminati by name; and a third in August 1787 confirmed the ban and made recruiting punishable by death. Further edicts followed into 1790. [cite:vt30_natgeo_weishaupt] [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati] The Bavarian authorities seized the order's papers in 1786 and 1787 and published them in 1787, which is why so much of its internal correspondence is known. Weishaupt lost his chair, was banished and lived the rest of his life in Gotha; Knigge had already left in July 1784 after quarrels with him. By the government's own account the order was dismantled. [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati] [cite:vt30_natgeo_weishaupt] Present-day groups that claim descent from it have no documented continuity. [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati]

Rome's direct part in the story is small. The order recruited through Masonic lodges that the popes had already condemned in 1738 and 1751, and its anticlericalism was aimed in the first place at the Jesuits who dominated Bavarian education. The ban that ended it was a state ban, issued by a Catholic prince for reasons of public order. [cite:vt30_wiki_ineminenti] [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati]

How the myth was made

The order would be a footnote but for the French Revolution. In 1797 and 1798 two writers, working separately, argued that the Revolution had been planned. The French Jesuit Augustin Barruel, writing in exile in London, published his Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire du Jacobinisme, which traced the Revolution to a decades-long conspiracy of the philosophes, the Freemasons and the Illuminati, carried out by the Jacobin clubs. The Scottish natural philosopher John Robison published Proofs of a Conspiracy with a similar thesis. Both books sold widely and were translated; Edmund Burke praised Barruel. Contemporaries including Jean-Joseph Mounier and Joseph de Maistre rejected the conspiracy claims, and historians reject the master-conspiracy view, while treating Barruel as the father of the modern conspiracy theory. [cite:vt30_wiki_barruel_memoirs] The story crossed the Atlantic at once: a Fast Day sermon by the Massachusetts minister Jedidiah Morse on 9 May 1798 was among the first printed American accounts of the Illuminati. [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati]

Barruel's Mémoires did not blame Jews; the historian Danny Keren is cited for that point. [cite:vt30_wiki_judeomasonic] The Jewish element entered through a letter. Dated 1 August 1806 and received by Barruel in Paris on 20 August, it came from a man signing himself Jean-Baptiste Simonini of Florence, who claimed to have posed as a baptised Jew in Piedmont and to have been told that Jews had founded both the Freemasons and the Illuminati and meant to take over Europe. Barruel could not trace the writer. He decided not to publish the letter, fearing it would provoke violence against Jews, but he circulated it in influential circles in France; the letter is thought to have been fabricated, probably by police opposed to Napoleon's liberal policy towards Jews. It was first printed in 1878, in the magazine Le Contemporain. [cite:vt30_wiki_simonini] [cite:vt30_wiki_judeomasonic] It is among the earliest texts of the "Judeo-Masonic" conspiracy theory, and its contents are believed to have fed the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, the forgery first serialised in St Petersburg in 1903 and exposed by historians and courts. [cite:vt30_wiki_simonini] [cite:hm_ushmm_protocols]

The graft spread through Catholic as well as secular channels, and the record should say so. Leo XIII's Humanum genus of 1884 did not mention Jews, but a French writer, Léo Taxil, staged a conversion to Catholicism the same year and then sold Catholic readers a fabricated exposé of a Luciferian "Palladist" rite at the top of Freemasonry; some bishops vouched for his invented witness, Diana Vaughan, until Taxil announced the hoax at the Société de Géographie in Paris on 19 April 1897. [cite:vt30_wiki_taxil] In 1902 the Catholic weekly Le Pèlerin printed a drawing captioned "Catholic France driven by Jews and Freemasons"; in the 1930s a Catholic priest, Juan Tusquets, translated the Protocols and built a "Judeo-Masonic-Communist" conspiracy theory that served as a justification for the Francoist regime; and in 1935 Nazi propaganda described Freemasonry as an organisation "beholden to Jewry". [cite:vt30_wiki_judeomasonic] In the United States the evangelist Pat Robertson's The New World Order (1991) linked the Illuminati and Freemasons to an alleged one-world plot by central bankers; reviewers in The Christian Century and The New York Review of Books showed that it drew on the antisemitic writers Nesta Webster and Eustace Mullins. Robertson said in 1995 that he had intended no antisemitism and regretted that his references to "European bankers" were read as meaning Jews. [cite:vt30_wiki_robertson_nwo] Contemporary "New World Order" and Bilderberg theories reuse the same tropes, often naming the Rothschilds or "international bankers". [cite:vt30_wiki_judeomasonic]

Every link in that chain fails on the documents. The Bavarian order's papers were seized and printed by its own government in 1787, and historians reject the claim built on them that it planned the Revolution; the order was dismantled between 1785 and 1787, before the French Revolution began; the Jewish element rests on a letter its own recipient would not vouch for and that historians treat as a fabrication; and the later forms rest on the Protocols, a proven forgery, or on Taxil, a confessed hoaxer. The claim that Jews direct the Freemasons or the Illuminati is an antisemitic conspiracy theory, not a contested historical question, and this book does not repeat it as anything else. The same applies to the "Rothschild" variant, whose documented core, papal loans arranged through the Rothschild bank from 1832, is examined and separated from the myth in [scene:vt11_papal_loans|Part Eleven: the papal loans]. [cite:vt30_wiki_barruel_memoirs] [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati]

sections.h: The Witch Trials: Bull, Handbook and Courts
sections.html:
Between about 1450 and 1750 European courts tried roughly 100,000 people for witchcraft and executed somewhere between 40,000 and 60,000 of them, most of them women. The trials are documented judicial history rather than folklore. The Malleus Maleficarum is often called their procedural template, and the popular version of the story goes further: that the Church burned nine million women, most of them healers and midwives, on the authority of a papal handbook. The record supports some of that and refutes the rest. A pope did authorise two inquisitors to hunt witches in 1484, and one of them wrote the most notorious witch-hunting manual of the age. But most of the killing was done by secular and territorial courts, Catholic and Protestant; the Roman and Spanish Inquisitions were, by the standards of the time, among the more sceptical tribunals in Europe; and the nine-million figure is an eighteenth-century miscalculation. [cite:vt30_wiki_witchtrials] [cite:vt30_wiki_malleus]

What the accused were said to do

The charge combined two older ideas. One was maleficium, harm done by magic: a neighbour's cow sickened, a child died, a harvest failed. The other was the diabolical pact: the claim, developed by theologians and inquisitors in the fifteenth century, that witches had renounced their baptism, worshipped the devil and met at night in sabbaths. Earlier church law had been sceptical of the second idea. The tenth-century Canon Episcopi treated night flight as an illusion rather than a real event, the Paris theology faculty's decree of 1398 still appeared to support it, and neither a majority of bishops nor the Council of Trent ever repudiated it; the Malleus opened by arguing against it. [cite:vt30_wiki_witchtrials] The descriptions of sabbaths that fill the trial records came from confessions taken by courts that, following manuals like the Malleus, used torture and leading questions. [cite:vt30_wiki_malleus]

The bull and the handbook

On 5 December 1484 Innocent VIII issued Summis desiderantes affectibus. It named two Dominican inquisitors, Henricus Institoris (Heinrich Kramer) and Jacobus Sprenger, and confirmed their authority in the provinces and dioceses of Mainz, Cologne, Trier, Salzburg and Bremen, where local clergy and laity had denied that their jurisdiction reached. The bull described people who "hinder men from begetting and women from conceiving" and blighted crops and vineyards, and it empowered the inquisitors to proceed to "the correction, imprisonment, and punishment" of those accused. [cite:vt30_fordham_summis] It is the clearest papal endorsement of witch-hunting on record, and it is real.

The Malleus Maleficarum was printed at Speyer in 1486 or 1487. Its author was Kramer; Sprenger's name was added as co-author only from 1519, long after his death, and his part is disputed. Kramer printed the 1484 bull at the front, which gave readers the impression of papal approval, but the bull authorised his prosecutions and said nothing about a book not yet written. The book also carried an approbation from the Cologne theology faculty that many historians consider forged in part; two of the named theologians later denied approving it, though Christopher Mackay, its modern translator, disputes the forgery case. [cite:vt30_wiki_malleus] Kramer's own record undercut his authority. His prosecutions at Innsbruck in the Tyrol in the mid-1480s collapsed, and the local bishop dismissed him as "senile and crazy". In 1490 clergy at Cologne condemned the book, and according to the historian Wolfgang Behringer the Inquisition "denied any authority to the Malleus". [cite:vt30_wiki_malleus]

The book taught that women were more prone to the devil's temptation than men, recommended torture, leading questions and deception to obtain confessions, accepted denunciations as evidence, and held death to be the only sure remedy. It ran to about 28 editions between 1486 and 1600. It became a reference for secular courts rather than for the inquisitions, and historians differ on how much of the later persecution it caused; Diarmaid MacCulloch counts it as one factor among several. The worst prosecutions came between about 1560 and 1630, two generations after it appeared. [cite:vt30_wiki_malleus]

Who did the killing

The courts that sent most victims to the stake were those of territorial rulers, towns and kingdoms. About half of all prosecutions fell in the Holy Roman Empire, with its hundreds of small jurisdictions; Poland, the French-speaking lands and Switzerland also saw heavy trials. Protestant Scotland hunted witches hard, while the Protestant Netherlands had among the fewest trials. In south-western Germany between 1561 and 1670, 2,527 of 3,229 recorded executions took place in Catholic territories, against 702 in Protestant ones. Historians still debate what drove such regional differences: one 2017 economic study links the most intense trials to areas where Catholic and Protestant churches competed for adherents, while studies of France tie the decline of accusations to stronger central government. [cite:vt30_wiki_witchtrials]

"Secular courts" does not always mean "not the Church". Several of the worst hunts took place in ecclesiastical principalities, where a bishop was also the territorial prince. In the prince-bishopric of Würzburg under Philipp Adolf von Ehrenberg (bishop 1623–1631), a commission using torture beyond the limits of the imperial criminal code executed an estimated 900 people across the territory between 1626 and 1631, among them between 19 and 43 priests, the bishop's own nephew and at least 49 children under twelve. Complaints by victims' relatives reached the pope and the emperor; the emperor condemned the trials in 1630, and they ended when Swedish troops occupied the city in 1631 and the bishop died. [cite:vt30_wiki_wurzburg] These were state courts, but the state was a Catholic bishop's.

The inquisitions behaved differently. The Roman Inquisition, the papacy's own central tribunal, founded in 1542, restrained Italian courts from liberal use of torture and execution; its Venetian tribunal never convicted anyone of maleficium, and in 1635 the Roman congregation admitted it had "found scarcely one trial conducted legally". Its instruction on procedure in witchcraft cases, the Instructio, warned against hasty convictions and careless executions. [cite:vt30_wiki_witchtrials] In Spain, whose Inquisition answered to the Crown rather than directly to Rome, after an auto de fe at Logroño burned six people alive and five in effigy on 1 November 1610, the inquisitor Alonso de Salazar Frías toured the Basque country in 1611 with an edict of grace. He collected nearly 2,000 confessions, 1,384 of them from children, most of which were retracted; he found no objective proof of any witchcraft and argued that judges should not sentence anyone "unless the case can be proven with external and objective evidence". In August 1614 the Council of the Inquisition dismissed the pending cases and issued stricter rules of evidence, which brought witch-burning in Spain to an end. [cite:vt30_wiki_basque] [cite:vt30_audit_spanishinq] [scene:vt28_inquisition|Part Twenty-Eight: the medieval Inquisition]

The numbers and the myths

Named estimates of executions are 40,000 (Scarre and Callow), 45,000 (Brian Levack), 40,000 to 50,000 (Ronald Hutton) and 50,000 to 60,000 (Wolfgang Behringer and Lyndal Roper). About 80 per cent of those convicted were women, most of them over forty. [cite:vt30_wiki_witchtrials] The figure of nine million comes from Gottfried Christian Voigt, a Quedlinburg lawyer who in 1784 took about thirty local witch trials, assumed the same rate for every town in Europe over many centuries, and multiplied. The historian David Luebke calls the method "a colossal error of misguided statistical extrapolation"; Behringer named it the "Nine Million Theory" and traced how it became an influential myth in twentieth-century feminist and neopagan writing. [cite:vt30_luebke_ninemillion] [cite:vt30_wiki_voigt] The real toll is large enough to need no inflation, and the inflated one erases the documented victims, whose names survive in trial records, behind a number that never described them.

The belief that the victims were mostly healers and midwives, whose deaths are said to have destroyed a body of empirical knowledge held mostly by women, has also been tested. David Harley's study "Historians as Demonologists: The Myth of the Midwife-Witch" (1990) found that midwives were not prominent among the accused, and a later study of Maltese inquisition records concludes it is "wrong to assume that midwives were accused en masse". The idea goes back to the Malleus itself, which portrayed midwives as stealers of infants for magic. [cite:vt30_harley_midwife] [cite:vt30_um_midwife] Village charmers and healers, the cunning folk, were sometimes among the accused, but the studies cited here do not support the claim that healers as a class were the trials' main target. The Catholic Church still forbids the practices they offered, as the next section shows, but the trials were not, on the record, a campaign against women's medicine.

The trials ended unevenly. Scotland executed its last witch, Janet Horne, in 1727; Britain's Witchcraft Act of 1735 removed witchcraft as a crime; the last capital trial in Salzburg was in 1750, Austria abolished witch-burning and torture in 1768, and Anna Göldi, executed in 1782, was formally condemned for poisoning. [cite:vt30_wiki_witchtrials] The finding that holds against the Church is specific: a pope gave a named inquisitor the authority he asked for, that inquisitor wrote the period's most influential witch-hunting book, and Catholic prince-bishops ran some of the deadliest hunts. The finding that does not hold is the general one, that the trials were the Church's inquisition at work, because the papacy's Roman Inquisition, and the Crown-controlled Spanish Inquisition beside it, were among the first tribunals in Europe to demand evidence and stop the burning.

sections.h: The Forbidden Arts: Alchemy, the Stars, the Cards and the Index
sections.html:
The Sophia platform's Forbidden Arts catalogue gathers alchemy, astrology, scrying, tarot, theurgy and their neighbours under one heading and gives one reason for their fate: each "offers information or experience obtained without institutional mediation", and the condemnations, it says, "rarely argue the practices don't work; they argue they are illegitimate." That is a claim about documents, and it can be checked against them. This section takes the main arts in turn, sets out what practitioners actually did, and names each document in which popes, councils and the Holy Office dealt with them, ending with the Index of Forbidden Books, which from 1559 to 1966 was the main instrument for controlling what Catholics could read about all of them. Where the catalogue's reason fits the record, the section says so; where the record shows a different reason, it says that too.

Alchemy: a fraud law, not a heresy

Alchemy was the art of transforming matter, above all of turning base metals into gold or silver, carried on in workshops with furnaces, stills and a symbolic language of marriages, deaths and rebirths of substances. Read by its practitioners, it was both laboratory work and, for some, a discipline of the operator's own transformation. The best-known papal act against it is a decretal of John XXII issued around 1317, named from its opening words Spondent quas non exhibent, "they promise what they do not deliver". It targeted alchemists who sold false gold and silver, and those who struck coin from it, at a time when counterfeit money was a real problem at the papal court in Avignon. The penalty was a fine equal to the weight of real gold or silver claimed, other punishment for those who could not pay, and permanent loss of benefices for clerics. It did not declare alchemy heretical; its grounds were fraud and harm to the poor. [cite:vt30_wiki_spondent] Popular accounts often say alchemy was suppressed as heresy; the documented papal act concerns fraud only. The art continued in the open among physicians and natural philosophers: Isaac Newton's alchemical manuscripts run to about a million words and are being edited by Indiana University's Chymistry of Isaac Newton project. [cite:vt30_shi_newton]

Astrology and divination: Trent, Sixtus V and Urban VIII

Astrology is the reading of human affairs from the positions of the planets. Catholic theology in the line of Thomas Aquinas did not reject it outright: Aquinas had allowed conjectural predictions, and the line the Church drew ran against claims to know free human acts and fortunes with certainty. [cite:vt30_ox_coeli] The Council of Trent's rules for the Index, published in 1564, fixed that line in law. Rule IX "absolutely repudiated" all books of geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, pyromancy, oneiromancy, chiromancy (palm reading), necromancy, sortilege, augury, sorcery and the magic arts, and told bishops to keep out of circulation books of astrology that claimed to determine destiny or affirm future human acts as certain, while expressly allowing astronomical observations written for navigation, agriculture and medicine. [cite:vt30_fordham_rule9]

Sixtus V's bull Coeli et terrae of 1586 went further than Thomas Aquinas had, banning even "uncertain predictions about future human actions"; Robert Bellarmine later wrote on how it should be applied. [cite:vt30_ox_coeli] The most severe act was political. In 1629 the Roman astrologer Orazio Morandi circulated a prediction that Urban VIII would die after a solar eclipse in June 1630; Morandi was jailed and died in prison in 1630. In 1631 Urban decreed death for anyone who predicted "the life or death of the sitting Roman Pontiff" or of his relatives to the third degree. [cite:vt30_torch_popes] The ground in that case was the destabilising force of prophecy in a papal election, not the illegitimacy of unmediated knowledge.

The modern position is set out in the Catechism of the Catholic Church. Paragraph 2116 says "All forms of divination are to be rejected", naming horoscopes, astrology, palm reading, the interpretation of omens and lots, clairvoyance and recourse to mediums, because they "conceal a desire for power over time, history, and, in the last analysis, other human beings" and "contradict the honor, respect, and loving fear that we owe to God alone." Paragraph 2117 calls magic and sorcery "gravely contrary to the virtue of religion", even when used to restore health, calls the wearing of charms reprehensible and warns against spiritism. [cite:vt30_va_ccc2116] Here the catalogue's reading fits the text closely: the Catechism does not argue that divination fails, it argues that seeking it is a wrong owed to God.

Tarot: a card game that became an oracle

The tarot's history is mostly documented, and the documented version is less ancient than the popular one. Decks with an added suit of picture trumps, trionfi, appear in Milan and Ferrara around 1440 to 1450 as cards for a trick-taking game played by the nobility. A Dominican sermon of about 1450 to 1470 condemned dice, playing cards and "triumphs" together, as gambling. [cite:vt30_wiki_taromancy] No divinatory use is documented for more than three centuries. In 1781 the French scholar Antoine Court de Gébelin, in volume eight of Le Monde primitif, claimed that the trumps preserved the wisdom of ancient Egypt, an etymology Egyptologists found no support for; an essay in the same volume by the Comte de Mellet first linked the cards to fortune-telling. Jean-Baptiste Alliette, who wrote as Etteilla, published a divination method in 1783, a treatise in 1785 and founded a society of tarot cartomancers in 1788. Éliphas Lévi tied the trumps to the Hebrew alphabet and the Kabbalah in 1861, the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, founded in 1888, built them into its system, and the Rider–Waite–Smith deck of 1909, designed by Arthur Edward Waite and painted by Pamela Colman Smith, gave the modern cards their images. [cite:vt30_wiki_taromancy] No papal document specifically condemning tarot was found for this section. The Church's objection today falls under the Catechism's general rejection of divination, which does not name the cards. [cite:vt30_va_ccc2116] [scene:ts13_mysteries|The Theology Shield: the mysteries and their modern heirs]

The Index of Forbidden Books, 1559–1966

The instrument that reached all these arts at once was the Index Librorum Prohibitorum. Paul IV issued the first Roman Index in 1557 and 1559; the Council of Trent's Index of 1564, with its ten rules, became the basis of every later edition; a Congregation of the Index was set up in 1571 and, when it was abolished in 1917, its work passed to the Holy Office. [cite:vt14_nwe_index] [cite:vt14_brit_index] The 1564 rules extended the ban beyond named titles to whole classes of "heretical and superstitious writings", with excommunication for possessing them, and Rule IX's ban on books of divination and magic was one such class. [cite:vt14_brit_index] [cite:vt30_fordham_rule9] The 1559 Index already banned astrological "divinations" of future events. [cite:vt30_torch_popes] Giordano Bruno's works were listed, along with Galileo, Descartes, Voltaire, Hume and Sartre, among many others; the last regular edition, of 1948, held about 4,000 titles. [cite:vt14_nwe_index] [cite:vt14_brit_index] [scene:vt29_bruno_galileo|Part Twenty-Nine: Bruno and Galileo]

The Index ended without a repudiation. A notification of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith dated 14 June 1966, signed by Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, stopped its publication and removed its force as church law, while stating that it kept its "moral value" as a guide to the faithful. [cite:vt14_nwe_index] [cite:vt14_brit_index] What it meant for the forbidden arts is plain from the rules: for four centuries a Catholic who owned a book of geomancy or judicial astrology without permission was, in canon law, liable to excommunication. [cite:vt30_fordham_rule9] [cite:vt14_brit_index] [scene:vt14_canon|Part Fourteen: the canon and the Index]

Interpretation, not finding: unmediated knowledge and the institution

Read through the lens of the Sophia platform's "Why These Were Forbidden" entry, the documents above share a structure: each art promises knowledge of the future, of hidden powers or of the self that is reached without a priest, a sacrament or a licence, and the Church answers not that the knowledge is false but that seeking it is owed to God and his ministers alone. In this reading the Catechism's phrase about honour owed "to God alone" is the clearest statement of the principle, and the Index was its enforcement arm. The reading is strongest for divination and judicial astrology, where the texts say almost exactly what it predicts. [cite:vt30_va_ccc2116] [cite:vt30_fordham_rule9]

The counter-reading is also on the record. The one papal act against alchemy is a law against counterfeiting; Urban VIII's decree protected a reigning pope from destabilising prophecy; the sermon against tarot was a sermon against gambling; and Thomist theology had itself allowed conjectural astrological prediction until Sixtus V narrowed it. [cite:vt30_wiki_spondent] [cite:vt30_torch_popes] [cite:vt30_wiki_taromancy] [cite:vt30_ox_coeli] A reader who holds the mediation thesis can fairly cite the divination texts in its support; a reader who doubts it can fairly cite the alchemy and astrology record against its claim to explain every case. Part Thirty-One sets this argument out at full length. [scene:vt31_two_economies|Part Thirty-One: two economies of the sacred]

chapters.label: Part Thirty-One
chapters.title: Tithe, Sabbath and Obedience: Two Economies of the Sacred
chapters.intro: Part Thirty-One follows the money and the rules. The thesis Book Two tests holds that institutional religion taxed and obligated believers where the inner traditions asked for nothing, and this is the part of the thesis that the institution's own documents can test most directly, because every step left a canon, a capitulary, a bull or a statute behind it. The first section traces the tithe from a voluntary gift to a church law in sixth-century Gaul, a royal tax under Charlemagne and a thousand-year revenue, with the papacy's own streams beside it: annates, indulgences and Peter's Pence. It ends with what is asked today, from the Code of Canon Law to Germany's church tax. The second traces Sunday from a custom to a duty under pain of "grave sin", the yearly confession and Easter communion fixed in 1215, and the penalties for leaving, and sets beside them the Gnostic texts that tell their readers to lay down no rule, including the passages that complicate that picture. The third puts the two economies side by side across eight questions, names the exceptions on both sides, and closes with the Sophia platform's reading of the contrast, labelled as interpretation, and the strongest arguments against it.
chapters.outro: Part Thirty-One established that the tithe was not a custom of early Christianity. It became church law at Mâcon in 585, with excommunication for refusal, and a royal obligation at Herstal in 779, and it was abolished in France in 1789 and ended in England only in 1977; Germany's Catholic dioceses still received €6.751 billion in church tax in 2025. [cite:vt31_shuler2012] [cite:vt31_wiki_tithe] [cite:vt31_wiki_herstal] [cite:vt31_wiki_august] [cite:vt31_pillar_tax2025] Beside the tithe ran annates, Peter's Pence and indulgences, whose sale the papacy itself abolished in 1567, fifty years after Albrecht of Brandenburg's Fugger-financed indulgence provoked Luther. [cite:vt31_wiki_annates] [cite:vt31_wiki_albrecht] [cite:vt31_brit_indulgence] Attendance moved from custom to the brief exclusion of Elvira's canon 21, the yearly confession and Easter communion imposed under excommunication in 1215, and the "grave sin" of the present Catechism. In Germany since 2012, leaving the church-tax roll costs a Catholic the sacraments. [cite:vt31_elvira21] [cite:vt31_lateran4] [cite:vt31_ccc2181] [cite:vt31_nss_2012] Against this, the Gospel of Mary forbids rules beyond the Saviour's, and no tithe or attendance law is recorded among the groups that read such texts. Thomas, Ptolemy, Pistis Sophia and the Cathars' own bishops and vows show that the inner traditions were not free of discipline or office. [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] [cite:vt24_gthom2] [cite:vt24_ect_flora] [cite:vt31_wiki_stfelix] Before the verdict, four parts widen the view beyond Europe and back before the councils, beginning with the mystery schools of the ancient world and how they were closed. [scene:vt33_the_schools|Part Thirty-Two: The Mysteries Closed]

sections.h: The Tithe: From Gift to Law to Tax
sections.html:
The thesis Book Two tests holds that institutional religion built a taxed system on top of teachings that asked for nothing. On money, the first half of that claim can be checked date by date, because the change from gift to obligation left a paper trail of council canons, royal capitularies, papal claims and modern statutes. Part Twenty showed that the earliest communities gave voluntarily and kept no tithe system ([scene:vt20_first_communities|The First Communities]). This section picks up where that record ends: how a tenth of the harvest became a church law in sixth-century Gaul, a state-enforced tax under Charlemagne, a revenue that kings and popes fought over for a thousand years, and, in Germany today, a surcharge on income tax whose non-payment carries church penalties.

The tithe before the church

The tenth was not a Christian invention. In the Hebrew Bible the tithe of the land's produce went to the Levites, the tribe set apart for the Temple service, who passed a share to the priests; a second tithe was spent on a sacred feast, and every third year a tithe went to the poor. [cite:vt31_ce_tithes] It belonged to a temple economy in which one tribe held no land and lived from the others' harvests. The first Christian writers knew this system and did not adopt it. Irenaeus, around 180, contrasted the Jewish tithe consecrated under the Law with Christians who, being free, were to set aside all they had for the Lord's purposes. [cite:vt20_na_irenaeus_iv18] The voluntary Sunday collection Justin describes, and the 1912 Catholic Encyclopedia's account of clergy supported by free offerings, are set out for the second and third centuries in [scene:vt24_how_they_lived|How They Lived]. Modern scholarship agrees: Eric Shuler, writing in the journal Traditio in 2012, sums up five decades of research with the finding that "mandatory tithing to the church was not a custom of early Christianity". [cite:vt31_shuler2012]

Sixth-century Gaul: the tithe becomes a duty

The first clear theory of the Christian tithe as an obligation comes from Caesarius, bishop of Arles (c.469–542), who taught that anyone earning income from farming or trade owed a tenth, and tied the payment to almsgiving. [cite:vt31_shuler2012] The first church legislation followed within decades. A letter of the bishops gathered at Tours in 567 urged the faithful to pay tithes, and the canons of the Council of Mâcon in 585 made payment a church law. [cite:vt31_ce_tithes] Mâcon attached the institution's strongest spiritual sanction: those who refused to pay were to be excommunicated. [cite:vt31_wiki_tithe] At this stage the obligation was enforced by the church alone. Its weight depended on whether a believer feared exclusion from the sacraments.

Charlemagne: the state collects

In March 779 Charlemagne's assembly at Herstal, meeting during a famine and a run of military and political crises, issued a capitulary that made the payment of tithes obligatory throughout the Frankish kingdom, with part reserved for relief of the poor. [cite:vt31_wiki_herstal] Shuler calls this "secular enforcement in 779" the decisive moment in the tithe's history. [cite:vt31_shuler2012] Under Charlemagne the tithe was divided into four parts: the upkeep of church buildings, the poor, the bishop and the parish clergy. [cite:vt31_wiki_tithe] From then on a tenth of the harvest was owed to the church by law, and royal officials could compel it. The Catholic Encyclopedia dates the earliest civil enforcement of the church tithe to these capitularies. [cite:vt31_ce_tithes]

The tithe spread with Latin Christendom. English law recognised it under Athelstan, Edgar and Canute before the Norman Conquest. [cite:vt31_ce_tithes] By the high Middle Ages the revenue was large enough to be fought over. Lords and princes acquired tithe rights, sometimes as hereditary property, and the Third Lateran Council of 1179 ruled that no tithe could pass to a layman without the pope's consent. In the late 1180s, under Pope Gregory VIII, a "Saladin tithe" was levied on those who did not themselves go on crusade. [cite:vt31_ce_tithes] The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 ordered that tithes be paid before any other tax or expense, and allowed church censure to compel payment. [cite:vt31_lateran4]

The other streams: indulgences, annates, Peter's Pence

The tithe supported local churches and bishops. The papacy built separate revenues of its own. Annates were payments owed by a cleric on receiving a benefice, eventually set at half or all of its first year's income. Clement V claimed the first-year revenues of all vacant benefices in England in 1305, and John XXII those of all Christendom falling vacant over two years in 1319; bishops and abbots paid a parallel fee, the servitia communia, on appointment. The Council of Basel tried to abolish these payments in the 1430s and failed. [cite:vt31_wiki_annates] Peter's Pence began in Anglo-Saxon England as a payment to Rome; Canute's letter of 1031 set it at a penny per hearth, with poorer households exempt. [cite:vt31_wiki_peterspence]

Indulgences, remissions of the punishment due for sin, began as rewards for crusading and became, by the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the object of constant complaints about their "sale" by pardoners; secular governments often took as much as two-thirds of the yield. [cite:vt31_brit_indulgence] The case that broke the system shows how the streams were joined. Albrecht of Brandenburg, already archbishop of Magdeburg, became archbishop of Mainz in 1514 in breach of the ban on holding several sees, and borrowed 20,000 guilders from the banker Jacob Fugger to pay the confirmation fee owed to the Roman Curia. He then proposed an indulgence whose proceeds would go half to the new St Peter's Basilica in Rome and half to his own treasury; Leo X's bull was issued on 31 March 1515. [cite:vt31_wiki_albrecht] In January 1517 Albrecht made the Dominican Johann Tetzel his indulgence commissioner. The Catholic historian Ludwig von Pastor judged that Tetzel's preaching on indulgences for the dead went beyond official teaching. [cite:vt31_wiki_tetzel] On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther sent his Ninety-five Theses to Albrecht. [cite:vt31_wiki_albrecht]

The institution reformed these practices, under pressure. The Council of Trent condemned "all base gain" from indulgences in 1563, and Pius V abolished their sale in 1567. [cite:vt31_brit_indulgence] Kings did the rest. Henry VIII stopped annates to Rome around 1532 and turned them over to the Crown in 1534, and an act of the same year ended Peter's Pence in England. [cite:vt31_wiki_annates] [cite:vt31_wiki_peterspence] In France the decrees of August 1789 abolished "any kind of tithes", on condition that another way be found to pay for worship. The historian D. M. G. Sutherland argues that peasants ended up paying twice, because landlords raised rents by the amount of the old tithe. [cite:vt31_wiki_august] The servitia paid to Rome ended by the same decree. [cite:vt31_wiki_annates] England commuted its tithes into rentcharges in 1836. The Tithe Act of 1936 turned these into annuities paid to the state, and the last payments ended in 1977. [cite:vt31_wiki_tithe]

What the institution asks today

Modern Catholic law contains no tenth. Canon 222 of the 1983 Code says the faithful "are obliged to assist with the needs of the Church" so that it has what it needs for worship, the apostolate, charity and "the decent support of ministers". [cite:vt31_cic222] Canon 1260 claims for the Church "an innate right to require" what it needs, while canon 1261 says the faithful "are free to give"; a bishop may impose a moderate tax on parishes and other church bodies, and an extraordinary levy on individuals only in grave necessity. [cite:vt31_cic1260] The Catechism lists the duty as part of the Church's precepts: the faithful must provide "for the material needs of the Church, each according to his abilities". [cite:vt31_ccc2043] The obligation remains, but the rate is left to the giver, much as Paul and the Didache left it.

How the obligation is met depends on each state's settlement with the Church. Peter's Pence, revived by Pius IX's encyclical Saepe venerabilis of 5 August 1871, is a voluntary collection taken around 29 June. [cite:vt31_wiki_peterspence] Its figures and uses are in [scene:vt9_peters_pence|Part Nine]. Italy's otto per mille lets taxpayers direct 0.8 per cent of income tax to a church or to the state, with undeclared shares divided in proportion to declared choices ([scene:vt3_otto_per_mille|Part Three]). [cite:vt31_wiki_tithe] Germany's Kirchensteuer, grounded today in Article 140 of the Basic Law, which takes over Article 137 of the Weimar Constitution, adds roughly 8 to 9 per cent to the income tax of registered members. [cite:vt31_wiki_tithe] German Catholic dioceses received €6.751 billion from it in 2025, up from €6.628 billion in 2024, even as about 307,000 people formally left the Church that year. [cite:vt31_pillar_tax2025] [cite:vt31_cwr_de2025] How that tax connects to church discipline, so that leaving the tax roll means losing the sacraments, belongs with the law of obligation in [scene:vt31_sunday_and_law|the next section]. For the overall scale of Church wealth, see [scene:vt9_true_vs_public_wealth|True Wealth and Public Wealth].

The money record therefore supports the thesis on one point and qualifies it on two. The change from voluntary gift to compulsory tithe is documented. It took about five centuries, began in sixth-century Gaul, and reached full force only when a king enforced it. The qualifications are these. The compulsion was often driven by kings as much as by popes, who quarrelled over the proceeds. And the institution itself later abolished the sale of indulgences and dropped the fixed tenth, leaving in law today a duty to support the Church with no rate attached.

sections.h: Sunday, Precept and the Law of Obligation
sections.html:
The second half of the thesis concerns obligation: that the institution made attendance, confession and obedience compulsory, under spiritual penalty, where the inner-tradition texts told their readers to lay down no rule. As with the tithe, the institutional side can be traced in its own documents, from a Spanish council around 300 to the Catechism of 1992 and a German bishops' decree of 2012. The other side is harder to state, because the Gnostic texts are not one body of law. Some reject rules outright, some reinterpret them, and at least one sets out a demanding code of its own. This section lays out both records and does not smooth either.

From gathering to duty

Christians met on Sunday long before any law required it: the Didache and Justin describe the weekly gathering as a custom, not a command ([scene:vt20_first_communities|Part Twenty]; [scene:vt24_how_they_lived|How They Lived]). [cite:vt21_justin67] [cite:vt20_na_didache] The first penalty for staying away appears in Spain. Canon 21 of the Council of Elvira, held around 300–309, rules that anyone living in a city who fails to come to church for three Sundays (tres dominicas ad ecclesiam non accesserit) is to be kept from communion for a short time, "so that he may be seen to be corrected". [cite:vt31_elvira21] The Catholic Encyclopedia reads the canon as a brief excommunication meant to correct, not expel. [cite:vt31_ce_sunday] It is a local council's rule for city-dwellers, and its penalty is mild, but the logic is set: attendance is owed, and absence is punished by exclusion.

The state then added its own weight. On 7 March 321 Constantine ordered magistrates, city people and workshops to rest on "the venerable day of the Sun", leaving farm work free, as Part Twenty-One sets out ([scene:vt21_sun_and_title|Sun, Sunday and the Chief Priest's Title]). [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] The Council of Laodicea in the later fourth century told the faithful to abstain from work on the Lord's day "as far as possible", and the Apostolic Constitutions of the same period prescribed both hearing Mass and resting, attributing the rule to the apostles. [cite:vt31_ce_sunday] In Gaul, the Council of Agde of 506, presided over by Caesarius of Arles (the same bishop who first theorised the tithe), required lay people to receive communion at Christmas, Easter and Pentecost. [cite:vt31_ce_agde] [cite:vt31_schaff_agde] Caesarius also insisted that the faithful stay for the whole Mass rather than leave after the readings. [cite:vt31_ce_sunday] From the eighth century, local councils forbade servile work, markets, lawsuits and public oaths on Sunday, and Sunday law took roughly its modern shape. Not every step pointed toward strictness: the Council of Orléans in 538 rejected attempts to apply the Jewish Sabbath code to Sunday. [cite:vt31_ce_sunday]

Lateran IV: the minimum fixed, the penalty named

The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 set the rule that still underlies Catholic practice. Every adult was to confess all sins to his or her own parish priest "at least once a year" and to receive the Eucharist at least at Easter. Anyone who failed was to be "cut off from the Church" while alive and "deprived of Christian burial" at death. [cite:vt31_lateran4] The same council also ordered tithes paid before secular taxes. [cite:vt31_lateran4] In medieval terms this joined three things into one system of membership: a priest one had to confess to, a payment one had to make, and a sanction (exclusion in life and in burial) for those who did not.

The law today

The 1983 Code of Canon Law calls Sunday "the primordial holy day of obligation" and states that on Sundays and holy days "the faithful are obliged to participate in the Mass" and to avoid work that hinders worship and rest. [cite:vt31_cic1246] The Catechism repeats the obligation and attaches its weight: "Those who deliberately fail in this obligation commit a grave sin", unless excused for a serious reason such as illness or the care of infants, or dispensed by their pastor. [cite:vt31_ccc2181] It lists five precepts of the Church, which it describes as a necessary minimum of prayer and moral effort: Mass on Sundays and holy days, confession at least once a year, communion at least at Easter, keeping the holy days, and the days of fasting and abstinence. Beside them stands the duty to provide for the Church's material needs. [cite:vt31_ccc2043] The Catechism also asks the state to help: public authorities should guarantee time for rest and worship, and Christians "should seek recognition of Sundays and the Church's holy days as legal holidays". [cite:vt31_ccc2181]

The practice of German Catholics shows how far law and life have parted. In 2025 about 6.8 per cent of the country's 19.2 million registered Catholics attended Sunday Mass. [cite:vt31_cwr_de2025] Few of the rest are disciplined for missing Mass. The penalties that are enforced in practice concern membership and money.

Leaving, and what it costs

Under the 1983 Code, "an apostate from the faith, a heretic or a schismatic incurs a latae sententiae excommunication", an exclusion that takes effect automatically, without a trial. [cite:vt31_intratext_1364] The late Roman state once backed such lines with civil penalties. Theodosius I legislated harshly against Christians who abandoned the faith, and Manichaeans lost the right to make or benefit from wills. [cite:vt31_wiki_theod_apost] Today the sharpest case is German. In September 2012 the German bishops issued a decree, approved by the Holy See after three years of talks, on Catholics who formally leave the Church at a state registry, which is the act that ends church-tax liability. Such a person may not receive the sacraments except a blessing before death, may not work for church institutions such as schools and hospitals, may not serve as a godparent, and may be refused a church funeral if there is no sign of repentance. The decree says that "one cannot partly leave the Church". [cite:vt31_nss_2012] [cite:vt31_npr_2012] On 26 September 2012 the Federal Administrative Court in Leipzig ruled against the canon lawyer Hartmut Zapp, who had sought to stop paying the tax while remaining a Catholic. [cite:vt31_nss_2012] The bishops' stated position, given by their president Robert Zollitsch, was that the church is a community of faith that co-exists alongside the legal order and the two "cannot be separated". The reform group We Are Church replied that the decree worked like an excommunication though it was not formally one. [cite:vt31_npr_2012] The tithe and the precept, separated in the Code, meet again here: in Germany, leaving the tax roll is treated as leaving the Church.

What the other texts say about rules

Against this law of obligation the thesis sets a handful of sayings, set out in full for the second and third centuries in [scene:vt24_how_they_lived|How They Lived]. In the Gospel of Mary the departing Saviour tells the disciples to lay down no rules beyond his own and to make no law "like the lawgiver" ([scene:vt26_gospel_of_mary|Part Twenty-Six]); Thomas 14 rejects fasting, prayer and alms as outward duties. [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] [cite:vt24_gthom2] The Gospel of Philip ties freedom to knowledge: "He who has knowledge of the truth is a free man", and "Ignorance is a slave. Knowledge is freedom." [cite:vt31_gphil_free]

The same texts also complicate the thesis. Thomas 27 asks its readers to keep the Sabbath "as a Sabbath", and Ptolemy's Letter to Flora keeps the Ten Commandments, reinterpreting fasting and the Sabbath rather than abolishing them; both are discussed in Part Twenty-Four. [cite:vt24_gthom2] [cite:vt24_ect_flora] Pistis Sophia, a later text, ends with a long code of renunciation, listing sins its hearers must give up. [cite:vt26_mead_ch102] What these texts reject is a law imposed from outside and enforced by an office. They do not reject discipline as such.

Two things should be kept apart when the two records are set side by side. One is a body of law that can be dated, enforced and appealed. The other is a set of sayings whose communities left no rulebook, so there is no way to show they never made rules of their own. On the documents alone, the institution built a law of obligation step by step, and several inner-tradition texts tell their readers not to. Whether those readers lived without rules is the question the next section takes up.

sections.h: Two Economies of the Sacred
sections.html:
The two previous sections traced the institution's side. The tithe moved from a gift to a church law in 585 and to a royal tax in 779. Attendance moved from custom to a canon of around 300, to the excommunication of 1215, and to the "grave sin" of today's Catechism. Part Twenty-Four set out the other side for the second and third centuries: no documented tithe among the Gnostic groups, no new code of commandments, no attendance rule, and a hostile record that nonetheless shows women teaching and laymen performing priestly functions ([scene:vt24_how_they_lived|How They Lived]). This section puts the two side by side across the whole period the book covers, from the second century to the Cathars, names the exceptions on both sides, and then gives the platform's reading of what the contrast means, labelled as a reading, followed by the strongest arguments against it.

The comparison, row by row

The table below uses "institution" for the bishops, councils, popes and canon law described in this book, not for Christians at large, and "inner tradition" for the second- and third-century Valentinian, Sethian and Thomasine texts and teachers (the groups the Sophia platform calls the Evangelical Gnostics) and, where marked, the medieval Cathars, who were a separate dualist movement with no documented line of descent from them. Where a cell says "none recorded", the documents cited in this part and in Parts Twenty to Twenty-Six say nothing on the point.

The exceptions, stated plainly

The table supports the thesis Book Two tests on payment, obligation, women and the sanction for leaving. It is weaker on intermediaries and authority, and the exceptions run in both directions. On the inner side, the second- and third-century exceptions are set out in [scene:vt24_how_they_lived|How They Lived]: Valentinians who sat inside the ordinary congregations, a hostile charge that the teacher Marcus collected "a very large fortune" from wealthy women, and the Manichaeans, a separate religion, whose lay Hearers fed the Elect. [cite:vt24_ah3_15] [cite:vt24_ah1_13] [cite:vt24_wiki_manich] Tertullian adds that Marcion was a member of the Roman church before his expulsion, and that his gift of money was handed back to him. [cite:vt24_tert_praescr] The later case is the Cathars of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. They rejected the Catholic Church's land and wealth, and their perfecti lived in poverty, but the believers supported them and competed to house them. [cite:vt31_wh_cathars] [cite:vt31_wiki_credentes] They also had bishops, apparently organised at a council at Saint-Félix in 1167 whose surviving record is disputed, and a two-tier membership. Perfecti kept lifelong vows of chastity and abstinence from meat, and believers competed to house them. [cite:vt31_wiki_stfelix] [cite:vt31_wiki_credentes] Their story belongs to [scene:vt28_cathars|Part Twenty-Eight].

On the institutional side, the early church also asked for no tithe, and the money it did collect was used largely for the poor. Justin's president used the Sunday gifts for orphans, widows and prisoners; even the Herstal capitulary reserved part of the tithe for poor relief, and Charlemagne's division gave the poor one of four shares. [cite:vt20_justin_67] [cite:vt31_wiki_herstal] [cite:vt31_wiki_tithe] The obligation to attend and to pay grew over centuries, often pushed by kings, and the institution itself later abolished the sale of indulgences and dropped the fixed tenth. [cite:vt31_brit_indulgence] [cite:vt31_cic1260]

The scholarly version: office and access

Two scholarly arguments give the contrast a mechanism. The sociologist Max Weber held that authority born of a charismatic founder is unstable and must be "routinised" if a movement is to survive, by rules that decide who holds power. One result is "office charisma": a sacred office such as holy orders conveys sanctity to its holder's acts whatever his personal character. [cite:vt31_swatos_routin] Read through Weber, a sacrament valid because of the office rather than the person, a succession list, and a regular revenue to support the office are the normal form a lasting religious body takes, not an aberration. Elaine Pagels, in The Gnostic Gospels (1979), made the sharper historical argument: doctrines such as bodily resurrection served "an essential political function" by grounding the authority of the bishops who claimed succession from the witnesses, while gnosis offered "the theological justification for refusing to obey the bishops". [cite:vt24_enc_pagels] Both are attributed arguments, and both have critics, noted below.

Interpretation, not finding: appropriation, suppression, occultation, recovery

The Sophia platform reads the two economies as one story in four movements. In this reading, the earliest teaching offered direct access, the kingdom within and knowledge that frees, and asked nothing in return. An institution then formed around that teaching and appropriated it: it kept the sayings that could be read as supporting its own offices, such as the kingdom "among you", and placed a priest, a sacrament and a payment between the believer and what the sayings had offered freely. Next came suppression. Teachers who said the office was unnecessary were named heretics from Irenaeus onward, their meetings were banned by imperial law, and later movements that revived the claim, the Cathars above all, were destroyed by crusade and inquisition. Occultation followed: what could not be destroyed survived hidden, in a jar at Nag Hammadi, a codex bought in Cairo, the Ethiopian canon, and orders that taught in secret. Recovery is the modern phase, in which the buried texts return and readers can again compare the two economies for themselves.

The core of this reading is an argument about incentives. In this view, what threatens a mediated institution most is not a rival doctrine but the claim that the institution is unnecessary, because a believer who can reach God directly owes no tithe, needs no confessor and fears no exclusion. Read this way, the sequence in the record (a voluntary community, then the obligatory tithe, the yearly confession to one's own priest and the penalty for leaving) is the shape such an institution would be expected to take, and the hostility to gnosis is the expected response to a teaching that made that shape optional. The reading is a lens on the record. It does not add facts to it, and the documents in this part neither prove nor require it.

The strongest counter-readings

The first counter-reading concerns the canon. Bruce Metzger, in his 1987 study of the New Testament canon, asked whether the canon is "a collection of authoritative books" or "an authoritative collection of books", and argued for the first: the church recognised books that communities were already reading as authoritative, over a long and gradual process, rather than conferring authority by decree. [cite:vt31_audit_metzger1987] On that view the exclusion of the Gnostic gospels reflects which texts the majority of congregations already used, not a decision by an office protecting its revenue; Part Twenty-Three shows that the lists were still disputed centuries later ([scene:vt23_lists_and_letters|Lists and Letters]).

The second concerns elitism. The Valentinians, by Irenaeus's account, divided humanity into the material, the "animal" and the spiritual, held that the spiritual were saved "because they are spiritual by nature", and called ordinary church members "animal". [cite:vt24_ah1_06] An inner tradition open only to a spiritual few is not obviously more democratic than a church open to anyone baptised. Critics of Pagels, among them Henry Chadwick and Hyam Maccoby, argued that her account idealised the Gnostics and passed over this elitism. [cite:vt24_enc_pagels]

The third concerns motive. Irenaeus stated his purpose as exposing "knowledge falsely so called" for the sake of believers he thought were being misled. [cite:vt24_ah1_pref] The heresy hunters wrote, in their own terms, as pastors protecting their congregations from what they believed to be falsehood, and they did so as a minority with no state power until the fourth century. A pastoral motive and an institutional interest can coexist. The record shows both at different times, and it does not show that the second was the cause of the first.

The fourth is structural. Every group in the table that lasted more than a generation built offices: the Valentinians claimed succession, the Manichaeans had an Elect, and the Cathars had bishops and lifelong vows. [cite:vt24_ect_flora] [cite:vt24_wiki_manich] [cite:vt31_wiki_stfelix] On this view the difference between the two economies is one of degree and of power, not of kind. The inner traditions did not avoid mediation. They lost before their own offices could become an establishment.

What the documents settle is narrower than either reading. The compulsory tithe, the obligatory Mass, the yearly confession, the anathema on the canon and the penalty for leaving are all the institution's own law, and none of them existed in the first two Christian centuries. The inner-tradition texts that survive tell their readers to lay down no rule, to find the kingdom within and not to sell the teaching, and no tithe or attendance law is recorded among the groups that read them. Whether that contrast was the reason those groups were condemned is the question [scene:vt32_verdict_two|Verdict II] answers in three registers.

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Two
chapters.title: The Mysteries Closed
chapters.intro: Part Thirty-Two asks whether the Christian empire closed the ancient mystery schools and erased what they taught about the soul, and answers by naming who acted, when, and in what document. The first section sets out what the mystery cults and the philosophical schools actually taught about the soul's descent and ascent: the higher grade of "seeing" at Eleusis, the open initiations of Samothrace, the Orphic gold tablets placed in graves, Pythagoras's doctrine of the soul's rebirth, the seven planetary grades of Mithras, the Isis initiation, and the Neoplatonists from Plotinus to Proclus. The second follows the closings from Theodosius's laws of 391–392 through the destruction of the Serapeum, the end of Eleusis, the killing of Hypatia, the conversion of temples into churches, Justinian's decree against teaching philosophy at Athens and the closing of the Isis temple at Philae, and grades the popular story of the burning of the Library of Alexandria. The third weighs what was lost against what survived, following the doctrine of ascent into Christian mystical theology, into Arabic philosophy and back to Renaissance Florence, and ends with the Sophia platform's reading of the pattern and the strongest objections to it.
chapters.outro: Part Thirty-Two established that the mystery cults and the philosophical schools shared a documented idea, that the soul could be prepared by rite or discipline to rise toward the divine, expressed in forms as different as the Orphic grave tablets, the seven planetary grades of a mithraeum at Ostia and Porphyry's report of Plotinus's four unions with God. [cite:vt33_getty_goldtablets] [cite:vt33_ostia_felicissimus] [cite:vt33_voegelin_plotinus] It established that the closings were carried out by named actors: Theodosius's laws of 391–392, Bishop Theophilus acting under imperial order at the Serapeum in 391, Alaric's Goths at Eleusis in 396, a crowd led by the church reader Peter who killed Hypatia in 415, Justinian's decree to Athens around 529 and his general Narses at Philae around 535–537. [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] [cite:vt33_socrates_516] [cite:vt33_wiki_telesterion] [cite:vt33_socrates_715] [cite:vt33_hannam_academy] [cite:vt33_procopius_philae] Cyril's part in Hypatia's death, the reach of Justinian's decree and the extent of enforcement remain disputed, Samothrace faded without a recorded closure, and the Library of Alexandria was not destroyed in one fire. [cite:vt33_romana_hypatia] [cite:vt33_watts_jrs] [cite:vt33_archaeology_samothrace] [cite:vt33_ou_library] The rites were lost and Porphyry's attack on Christianity was burned by imperial order, but the written doctrine of ascent survived through the Pseudo-Dionysian writings, Arabic versions of Plotinus and Proclus, and Ficino's translations of 1463 onward. [cite:vt33_wiki_againstchristians] [cite:vt33_sep_dionysius] [cite:vt33_wiki_theologyaristotle] [cite:vt33_brandeis_pimander] Part Thirty-Three follows the tribunals that came later, the Spanish and Portuguese Inquisitions run under their crowns and the Roman Inquisition, and their reach to Goa and the Americas. [scene:vt34_spain_portugal|Part Thirty-Three: The Inquisitions Beyond Rome]

sections.h: The Schools: What the Mysteries and the Philosophers Taught About the Soul
sections.html:
A widely repeated claim holds that the ancient world possessed "mystery schools" which taught, under oath of secrecy, a science of the soul: how it descends into a body, how it can be purified, and how it can rise again toward the divine, and that this knowledge was deliberately closed down when the Roman Empire became Christian. Before the closings can be weighed, the schools themselves have to be described from the record. That record is uneven. Some of these institutions kept their secret so well that almost nothing of their inner teaching survives; others, the philosophical schools, wrote a great deal down. This section sets out what can be documented about each, using their own texts where they exist and their critics' texts where they do not. The Eleusinian rites, the Isis initiation in Apuleius, the Hermetica and the general pattern of ascent across traditions are treated in an earlier volume and are not repeated here. [scene:ts13_mysteries|The Mysteries and the Ascent]

Two kinds of school

The word "school" covers two different things, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. The mystery cults (Eleusis, Samothrace, Isis, Mithras and others) were rites. A person was initiated, usually once, sometimes in stages, and was bound not to reveal what was shown. They had priesthoods and sanctuaries but no doctrinal books that have come down to us. The philosophical schools (Pythagorean, Platonic and later Neoplatonic) were teaching institutions. They had heads, pupils, lectures and libraries, and their doctrine of the soul's ascent was argued in writing. When the Christian empire acted against "the mysteries", it acted against both, but in different ways and with different results: the rites ended, while much of the philosophy passed into the hands of the people who had closed the temples. [cite:vt33_sep_pythagoreanism] [cite:vt33_sep_proclus]

Eleusis: the grade of seeing

At Eleusis, initiation had more than one level. Among those who attended the Greater Mysteries were first-time initiates and those who had returned and attained the epopteia, the state of the epoptai, "those who have seen", described as having learned the secrets of the greatest mysteries of Demeter. [cite:vt33_nwe_eleusis] What they saw is not recorded. What the initiates said they gained is. Cicero, himself an initiate, wrote that the mysteries had shown Romans how to live joyfully and had taught them "how to die with a better hope". [cite:vt33_wh_eleusis] That phrase, a better hope at death, is the most secure statement of what Eleusis offered: not a doctrine, but a changed relation to mortality, conferred by an experience.

Samothrace: open to all who came

The Sanctuary of the Great Gods on the island of Samothrace ran the second most famous Greek mystery cult. Its distinguishing feature, in the record, is who it admitted. Anyone who could reach the island and was free of blood guilt could be initiated, "whether enslaved, free, Greek, non-Greek, male, or female". Most ancient sources say the gods offered protection at sea; the historian Diodorus Siculus claimed initiates became "more pious and more just and better in all ways". Philip II of Macedon and Olympias, the parents of Alexander, were initiated there; Plutarch says they were initiated at the same time and that Philip fell in love with her and was betrothed to her. [cite:vt33_archaeology_samothrace] [cite:vt33_audit_plutarch_alex2] What the island did not experience, on the present evidence, is a dramatic closure. The last securely dated list of initiates belongs to the later second century CE, activity may have continued into the third or fourth, and the excavator Bonna Wescoat's view is that the cult "gradually died out". [cite:vt33_archaeology_samothrace] Samothrace is the first reminder in this part that not every mystery ended by force.

Orphic tablets and Pythagorean souls

The most direct surviving instructions for the soul's journey after death are not in a book at all. About forty thin gold tablets, most from the fourth to the first centuries BCE, were placed in graves in southern Italy, Sicily, Greece and Crete, on the chest, mouth or hand of the dead. They tell the deceased to avoid one spring and to drink instead from the cold water of the Lake of Memory, and they give a password to say to the guardians: "I am the son of Earth and Starry Heaven. But my race is heavenly." The label "Orphic" is a modern one; none of the tablets names Orpheus, though they reflect initiations associated with Orpheus and probably Dionysus. [cite:vt33_getty_goldtablets] The teaching they carry is clear enough: the soul has a heavenly origin, forgetting is the danger, and the initiate who remembers can claim a better lot.

Pythagoras, in the sixth century BCE, taught a related doctrine in a philosophical community. He held that the soul is immortal and passes into new bodies, human or animal (metempsychosis). Some Pythagorean teaching was secret, and a letter attributed to Lysis urged that the master's doctrines not be presented in public to the uninitiated, but much was openly taught. Late sources describe a division between the akousmatikoi, who followed oral rules for living, and the mathematikoi, who studied mathematics; some scholars think that split is a later invention. The connection between Orphic writings and Pythagoreans is real but, in the Stanford Encyclopedia's word, "elusive". [cite:vt33_sep_pythagoreanism]

Mithras: a ladder of seven gates

The Roman cult of Mithras, which flourished from the first to the fourth century CE among soldiers, officials and traders, left hundreds of underground sanctuaries and almost no texts. [cite:vt21_wiki_mithraism] Two pieces of evidence describe its inner structure. The first is a hostile literary witness at two removes. The second-century philosopher Celsus, as quoted by the Christian writer Origen in his reply, described a Mithraic "ladder with seven gates and, at the top, an eighth gate", each gate made of a metal and assigned to a planet: lead to Saturn, tin to Venus, copper to Jupiter, iron to Mercury, a mixed alloy to Mars, silver to the Moon and gold to the Sun. Celsus presented it as a symbol of the soul's passage through the heavens. Origen dismissed it. [cite:vt33_harland_celsus]

The second is archaeological. In the Mithraeum of Felicissimus at Ostia, Rome's port, installed probably in the second half of the third century, a floor mosaic runs from the entrance toward the altar in seven panels. Each pairs a grade of initiation with a planet and its symbols: Raven with Mercury, Bridegroom with Venus, Soldier with Mars, Lion with Jupiter, Persian with the Moon, Sun-Runner with the Sun, and Father with Saturn. An inscription names the donor, Felicissimus, who made it in fulfilment of a vow. [cite:vt33_ostia_felicissimus] The two orders do not match; Celsus's ladder and the Ostia floor rank the planets differently, which is itself evidence that the cult was not uniform. Both, however, document the same idea: a member advanced through seven ranks tied to the seven planets, and the walk from door to altar was a walk upward through the sky.

Isis

The cult of Isis spread from Egypt across the Roman world and is the one mystery whose initiation has a first-person literary account, the eleventh book of Apuleius's novel the Metamorphoses. Its narrator says he approached the boundary of death, passed through the elements, saw the sun shining at midnight and returned. [cite:ts13_cam_apuleius] Its great temples, including the one at Philae on the Nile, outlived most others; how the last of them closed is set out in the next section.

The philosophers of ascent

The fullest written doctrine of ascent belongs to the Neoplatonists. Plotinus, who taught in Rome in the third century, described the soul's return to the One through purification, the awakening of intellect and, finally, a union that cannot be forced. [cite:ts13_mac_plotinus] His pupil and editor Porphyry reported that during the six years he spent in the school, Plotinus four times attained union with the God "who has neither shape nor form". [cite:vt33_voegelin_plotinus] This is the closest the ancient sources come to a documented claim of repeated mystical experience by a named teacher.

The next generation divided over method. Porphyry wrote critically about ritual; Iamblichus, in the work known as On the Mysteries, answered that the soul is raised not by thought alone but by theurgy, rites that bring the soul into contact with the gods. [cite:ts13_wiki_iamblichus] Theurgy became the practice of the later schools.
