Proclus, who headed the Platonic school at Athens as its diadochos, Plato's "successor", for almost fifty years until his death in 485, practised it according to his pupil Marinus, wrote hymns to the gods and composed the Elements of Theology, a chain of more than two hundred propositions deriving all reality from the One. [cite:vt33_sep_proclus] In Proclus the two kinds of school met: a philosopher who argued the ascent in writing and also performed the rites that were meant to accomplish it.

The table shows why "the mystery schools" is a modern umbrella rather than an ancient institution. There was no single network, no shared hierarchy and no common text. There was a widely shared idea, documented in very different forms: that the soul is not at home in the body, that it can be prepared, and that a rite or a discipline can change what happens to it. That idea is what the next section follows into the decades when the temples were closed, and the final section follows into the institutions that, in the end, kept much of it.

sections.h: The Closings: Who Shut the Temples and the Schools, 391–c.537
sections.html:
The end of the ancient mysteries is often told as a single act: "the Church" closed the mystery schools and burned their knowledge. The record shows a sequence of separate acts over a century and a half, carried out by different people with different powers. Emperors issued laws. A bishop of Alexandria used those laws to lead the destruction of a temple. A Gothic army, not acting for any church, wrecked Eleusis. A mob led by a church reader killed a philosopher. Popes and bishops turned temples into churches. A sixth-century emperor ended philosophical teaching at Athens and sent a general to shut the last Isis temple on the Nile. Each act is set out below with the actor who carried it out and the document that records it. The laws of Theodosius themselves, Cunctos populos of 380 and the bans on sacrifice of 391 and 392, are set out in Part Twenty-One and summarised here only as the frame. [scene:vt21_church_and_empire|Church and Empire]

The legal frame, 391–392

A law of 391 in the Theodosian Code (16.10.10) ordered that no one go to the sanctuaries or walk through the temples; another (16.10.11) closed the temples; a third, in 392 (16.10.12), banned all sacrifice and worship of the old gods, down to burning incense to the household gods in a private house. Historians including Malcolm Errington question how far these laws were enforced, and the archaeologists Luke Lavan and Michael Mulryan found only four of 43 temple destructions reported in written sources confirmed on the ground. [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] [cite:vt21_wiki_paganpers] The laws made the mysteries illegal. They did not by themselves end them. What ended particular sanctuaries was local action, and local action is where the actors can be named.

The Serapeum, Alexandria, 391

The church historian Socrates Scholasticus, writing in Constantinople before 450, records the sequence in Alexandria. "At the solicitation of Theophilus bishop of Alexandria the emperor issued an order" for the demolition of the city's temples, and put Theophilus in charge of it. Theophilus cleared out the Mithraeum and put its mysteries on public display to ridicule them, then destroyed the Serapeum, the great temple of the god Serapis. Pagans, led by philosophers, fought back; there were deaths on both sides. The images of the gods were melted down into vessels for the church, which Socrates says were for the relief of the poor; one statue was kept on display so that, in Theophilus's words, pagans could not later deny that they had worshipped such gods. [cite:vt33_socrates_516] Rufinus, writing about 402 and possibly a witness, describes a soldier, at the bishop's urging, striking the colossal statue of Serapis on the jaw with an axe; it was broken up and burned. The site became a martyr's shrine and a church. [cite:vt33_romana_serapeum]

The actors are documented on the Christian side by Christian writers, which is unusual: they recorded it as a triumph. The bishop asked; the emperor ordered; the bishop directed; soldiers and crowds carried it out. What the Serapeum did not contain, on the evidence, was the Great Library, a point taken up at the end of this section. [cite:vt33_socrates_516] [cite:vt33_ou_library]

Eleusis, 392–396

The Eleusinian Mysteries were ended in two stages, by two different actors. Theodosius's laws of 391–392 forbade the cult; the sanctuary may nevertheless have continued to operate for some years. [cite:vt33_livius_eleusis] Then, in 395–396, the Visigothic king Alaric invaded Greece and his forces ravaged Attica, "destroying the Telesterion", the hall of initiation, "which was never to be rebuilt". [cite:vt33_wiki_telesterion] Alaric's Goths were Christians of the non-Nicene, "Arian" kind, and no source says they acted on any bishop's instruction. [cite:vt33_wh_eleusis]

The only near-contemporary account of the end comes from the pagan writer Eunapius, who had himself been initiated at Eleusis by the last legitimate hierophant, whose name, he says, it was not lawful to tell. Eunapius reports that this hierophant prophesied the ruin of the temples, and that afterwards a man from Thespiae, who held the rank of "pater in the ritual of Mithras", took the office. Alaric then passed through Thermopylae "as easily as though he were traversing an open stadium". Eunapius blamed the "impiety" of "men clad in black" cloaks, who entered Greece with Alaric, for opening the way. He does not name them in that passage. Earlier in the same book, describing the destruction of the Serapeum, he complains that monks had been brought into the sacred places and that any man "who wore a black robe" could act as a tyrant, which is why the Alaric phrase is commonly taken to mean monks. [cite:vt33_eunapius_hierophant] [cite:vt33_audit_eunapius_monks] What is disputed is how much of the destruction is owed to the laws and how much to the invasion; what Eunapius's account adds is that by the 390s the line of hierophants had already been broken and a Mithraic "Father" was presiding at Eleusis, a sign of how far the old cults had drawn together under pressure.

Hypatia, Alexandria, March 415

Hypatia, a mathematician and philosopher who taught in what Socrates calls "the school of Plato and Plotinus", was killed in Alexandria in March 415, during Lent, in the fourth year of Cyril's episcopate. Socrates gives the cause as politics: a rumour spread among the Christian population that she was preventing the prefect Orestes from being reconciled with the bishop. A crowd led by "a reader named Peter", a minor church officer, dragged her from her carriage to the church called the Caesareum, stripped her and killed her with tiles, then burned her remains. Socrates judged that the affair "brought not the least opprobrium, not only upon Cyril, but also upon the whole Alexandrian church". [cite:vt33_socrates_715]

Whether Cyril ordered it is disputed, and the sources divide along lines of loyalty. Socrates, a Christian, blames the crowd's zeal and the bishop's reputation but does not say Cyril gave an order. Damascius, a pagan philosopher of the next century, says Cyril envied her and plotted her death. John of Nikiu, a seventh-century Egyptian bishop, is hostile to her, repeats the charge that she practised magic and praises Cyril. [cite:vt33_romana_hypatia] The leader of the crowd is named in the record; whether anyone instigated it is not settled by it. The popular claim that Hypatia was the last librarian of Alexandria has no ancient source. [cite:vt33_romana_hypatia]

Temples into churches

Many sanctuaries ended not by demolition but by conversion. In Athens, the Parthenon was rebuilt inside as a three-aisled church of the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos, around the middle of the sixth century, and later served as the city's cathedral. [cite:vt33_byzleg_parthenon] In Rome, on 13 May 609, Pope Boniface IV, with the permission of the emperor Phocas, dedicated the Pantheon to Mary and all the martyrs, bringing in twenty-eight carriages of martyrs' bones from the city's cemeteries. [cite:vt33_chi_pantheon] Beneath the basilica of San Clemente in Rome lies a Mithraic sanctuary of about 200 CE, built in the courtyard of an apartment block; by the late fourth century the lower levels had been filled in and a church built over them, existing by 392, when Jerome mentions it. The mithraeum was found again in the 1860s by the Irish Dominican prior Joseph Mullooly. [cite:vt33_wiki_sanclemente]

Justinian: Athens, about 529

The end of the Platonic school at Athens rests on one sentence. The chronicler John Malalas, writing in the sixth century, recorded that the emperor Justinian sent a decree to Athens "ordering that no one should teach philosophy nor astrology". The decree itself is undated and was probably issued between 527 and 529. A law in Justinian's Code allowed only those of the orthodox faith to teach and draw a public salary, and it was aimed at Jews and heretics as well as pagans; it names no school. [cite:vt33_hannam_academy] The historian Agathias, writing about a generation later, tells how seven philosophers, among them the last head of the school, Damascius, and Simplicius, went to the Persian court and returned after a clause in the peace treaty of 532 protected them. That story rests on Agathias alone. [cite:vt33_hannam_academy]

How much the decree did is debated. Edward Watts argues that Malalas's notice is the only direct ancient statement on the subject, that the measure is best explained by local politics in Athens, and that contemporaries did not treat the closing as remarkable. [cite:vt33_watts_jrs] Alan Cameron argued that Justinian may only have cut public funding. No formal decision to suppress the philosophical schools of Alexandria is recorded, and Alexandria remained a leading centre of philosophy until the Arab conquest of Egypt in the seventh century. [cite:vt33_hannam_academy] What is documented is that an emperor forbade pagans to teach and that the Athenian succession from Plato, which Proclus had headed, ends in the record at this point.

Philae, about 535–537

The temple of Isis on the island of Philae, at Egypt's southern frontier, outlived the others; Procopius says peoples from beyond the frontier, whom he calls barbarians, had kept its sanctuaries up to his own time. Procopius also records its end: Justinian decided to tear the sanctuaries down, and his commander Narses "tore down the sanctuaries at the emperor's order", put the priests under guard and "sent the statues to Byzantium". [cite:vt33_procopius_philae] The buildings were not in fact pulled down. An inscription in the inner sanctuary records that it became a church of St Stephen under Bishop Theodore, and the last dated pagan graffiti on the island are from about 457. [cite:vt33_lemans_philae_church] Jitse Dijkstra's study of Philae argues that the old cult there was already dying of its own accord, its festival gone by the mid-sixth century, so that Justinian's order closed a temple whose priests were already few. [cite:vt33_gozzoli_dijkstra]

The Library of Alexandria: a myth graded

No account of the closings escapes the Library of Alexandria, and the popular version, that a single fire (lit by Caesar, by Christians or by Arabs) destroyed the wisdom of the ancient world, does not survive the record. Plutarch says the library burned in the fire Caesar started in 48 BCE, but another ancient account may refer only to warehouses. The papyrologist Roger Bagnall considers the war under the emperor Aurelian in the 270s the most probable occasion of large-scale damage, though no contemporary source mentions the library. Edward Gibbon in the eighteenth century blamed the Christian sack of the Serapeum in 391. The story that Arab conquerors in 641 used the books to heat the city's baths first appears six centuries later and is widely regarded as fiction. Bagnall's own conclusion is that "gradual processes of neglect and decay" did as much harm as any single act. [cite:vt33_ou_library] The Serapeum's destruction in 391 is documented; that it destroyed the Library is not.

sections.h: What Was Lost, and How the Ascent Survived
sections.html:
The closings of 391 to about 537 ended institutions. Whether they also erased knowledge depends on which knowledge is meant. The rites of the mysteries were transmitted by performance and oath, not by books, and when the performances stopped, the rites were lost. The written philosophy of ascent was a different matter. Much of it was copied, adapted and taught by Christians and Muslims for the next thousand years, often under false names, and returned to the Latin West in full in the fifteenth century. This section sets out both outcomes: what the record shows was destroyed or is now missing, and the routes by which the doctrine of the soul's ascent came through.

What is gone

The inner content of the mystery rites is gone, and in most cases it was never written down to be lost. No text of the Eleusinian ceremony survives, only the initiates' testimony that it gave them a better hope at death. [cite:vt33_wh_eleusis] The cult of Mithras, which left hundreds of sanctuaries and had ceased to exist by the end of the fourth century, left no scripture; its structure is known from mosaics, inscriptions and a summary by its critic Celsus preserved by its other critic Origen. [cite:vt21_wiki_mithraism] [cite:vt33_harland_celsus] The Samothracian cult left lists of initiates and no doctrine. [cite:vt33_archaeology_samothrace] For these, the loss was the end of the practice itself. The laws of Theodosius and the acts of bishops and emperors described in the previous section stopped the practice where the old cults were still alive; at Samothrace and, on Dijkstra's reading, at Philae, the practice was already fading. [cite:vt33_gozzoli_dijkstra]

Some losses were ordered in writing. The most explicit concerns not a mystery text but a philosopher's attack on Christianity. Porphyry, the pupil of Plotinus, wrote a work known as Against the Christians. Constantine banned it, and the emperor Theodosius II ordered every copy burned in 435 and again in 448. No copy survives; its arguments are known only from the roughly thirty Christian writers, among them Eusebius and Jerome, who quoted it in order to refute it. [cite:vt33_wiki_againstchristians] This is the clearest documented case in late antiquity of the Christian state destroying a pagan philosopher's book by name, and it belongs beside the orders against Arian, Montanist and Nestorian books set out in Part Twenty-One. [scene:vt21_church_and_empire|Church and Empire]

The schools lost their institutional line. After Justinian's decree, the succession of heads of the Platonic school at Athens, from Plato through Proclus to Damascius, ends in the record. Many of Proclus's own works survive only in fragments, preserved by the later Neoplatonists Damascius, Olympiodorus, Simplicius and the Christian John Philoponus, who quoted them. [cite:vt33_sep_proclus] [cite:vt33_hannam_academy] What is missing here is less a body of secret knowledge than the continuous teaching community that had carried it and the many commentaries that community would have produced.

The first route: inside Christianity

The most important survival route ran through the church itself. In the late fifth or early sixth century, an author writing under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian whom Paul converted in Acts 17, produced four treatises, On the Divine Names, On the Celestial Hierarchy, On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy and the Mystical Theology, with ten letters. The first clear citation of them is by Severus of Antioch between 518 and 528. They describe the soul's path in the triad of purification, illumination and perfection; they call theurgy "the consummation of theology"; and the Mystical Theology describes Moses' entry into the darkness of the unknowable God as the model of union. [cite:vt33_sep_dionysius] Modern scholarship places their author in Proclus's time and finds him drawing heavily on Proclus, so much that the classicist E. R. Dodds described Proclus as "conquering Europe in the guise of an early Christian". [cite:vt33_sep_proclus]

Because the church took the Areopagite to be Paul's disciple, his writings carried near-apostolic authority. John Scottus Eriugena translated them into Latin in 862 for Charles the Bald, and they shaped the Rhineland mystics Meister Eckhart, Johannes Tauler and Jan van Ruusbroec, as well as Nicholas of Cusa and the English Cloud of Unknowing. Doubts about the attribution were raised in the sixth century and by Lorenzo Valla in 1457, and Erasmus publicised them from 1504. [cite:vt33_sep_dionysius] The doctrine of ascent that Theodosius's laws had forced out of the temples therefore re-entered Christian monasteries under a borrowed name. The institution that kept it also, in time, policed it: Eckhart, one of its heirs, had propositions condemned by Pope John XXII in 1329, a story told in Part Twenty-Nine. [scene:vt29_mystics|Mystics and the stake]

The second route: through Arabic

The second route ran through the Islamic world. In the ninth century a paraphrase of parts of Plotinus's Enneads was made in Arabic by Ibn Na'ima al-Himsi, a Christian, and edited by the philosopher al-Kindi. It circulated as the Theology of Aristotle, an attribution modern scholars regard as certainly false, and it shaped how al-Kindi and later Avicenna, who wrote a commentary on it, understood the relation of the soul to the One. [cite:vt33_wiki_theologyaristotle] A second Arabic adaptation, of Proclus's Elements of Theology, became the Latin Liber de causis, also read in the medieval universities as Aristotle's until Thomas Aquinas identified its source in Proclus. [cite:vt33_sep_proclus] The Neoplatonic doctrine of emanation and return thus reached Paris and Oxford partly through Baghdad, under the name of a philosopher who had not written it.

The third route: Florence, 1463

The third route was the return of the Greek texts themselves. In Florence, Marsilio Ficino finished a Latin translation of the Hermetic treatise known as the Pimander in 1463, from a Greek manuscript brought from Macedonia for Cosimo de' Medici; eight printed editions appeared before 1500. Ficino went on to translate Plato and the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite. [cite:vt33_brandeis_pimander] He had interrupted his work on Plato to translate the Hermetica first, because they were believed to be older; in 1614 Isaac Casaubon showed from their Greek that they belonged to the Roman period. [cite:ts13_wiki_hermetica] The revival of Hermetic and Platonic ascent in Renaissance Europe, and the Church's later handling of it in the trials of Bruno and in the Index of Forbidden Books, are set out in Parts Twenty-Nine and Thirty. [scene:vt29_bruno_galileo|Bruno and Galileo] [scene:vt30_forbidden_arts|The forbidden arts]

Interpretation, not finding: closing the rite, keeping the map

The Sophia platform reads this sequence as a pattern rather than a set of separate events. In this reading, what the Christian empire closed was the independent practice of ascent: the rite a person could undergo at Eleusis or in a mithraeum, or the philosophical school where a teacher could claim, as Plotinus did, direct union with God. What it kept was the map of ascent, rewritten as a hierarchy of angels, sacraments and clergy under the name of an apostle's disciple. The platform holds that the knowledge was not so much destroyed as relocated, from free-standing schools into an institution that alone could administer it, a reading that connects this part to the "two economies" argument of Part Thirty-One. [scene:vt31_two_economies|Two economies of the sacred]

The strongest counter-readings come from the same record. First, not every ending was an act of suppression: Samothrace faded without a recorded closure, and at Philae the cult was, on Dijkstra's evidence, already dying when Justinian's general arrived. [cite:vt33_archaeology_samothrace] [cite:vt33_gozzoli_dijkstra] Second, not every actor was the church: Eleusis was wrecked by a Gothic army, and the decisive laws were imperial. [cite:vt33_wiki_telesterion] Third, much of the survival was the work of Christians and Muslims who valued the philosophy, not of pagans hiding it; the Pseudo-Dionysian writings were embraced by the hierarchy, not smuggled past it. [cite:vt33_sep_dionysius] Fourth, enforcement of the anti-pagan laws was uneven, as the archaeology of temple destruction shows. [cite:vt21_wiki_paganpers] What the record supports without interpretation is narrower than either reading: emperors outlawed the rites, bishops and soldiers destroyed specific sanctuaries, a named philosopher was killed and a named book burned, and the doctrine of ascent survived because people inside the victorious religions chose to keep it.

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Three
chapters.title: The Inquisitions Beyond Rome
chapters.intro: Part Thirty-Three follows the inquisitions that grew up outside the medieval papal commissions of Part Twenty-Eight, and outside Europe altogether. The first section sets out the three early modern tribunals: the Spanish Inquisition of 1478, a court licensed by the pope but staffed and steered by the crown, which pursued converted Jews and Muslims, Protestants, mystics and books until 1834; the Portuguese Inquisition of 1536; and the Roman Inquisition of 1542, the one that survives today as the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, with every death toll given as a range with the historian who made it. The second goes to Goa, where the Portuguese crown destroyed Hindu temples, banned Hindu rites and the Konkani language, and a tribunal sat from 1560 to 1812, and where an archbishop's synod in 1599 condemned the Syriac books of India's oldest Christians. The third crosses to the Americas, separating the Holy Office's tribunals, which the crown kept away from Indigenous people, from the friars and bishops who burned Maya codices at Maní in 1562 and ran Peru's campaigns against "idolatry", and setting beside them the books Mexica rulers burned before the conquest and the knowledge friars and Indigenous scholars preserved.
chapters.outro: Part Thirty-Three established that the early modern inquisitions were three institutions, not one. The Spanish tribunal was licensed by Sixtus IV in 1478 but named and steered by the crown, over a pope's protest in 1482; it pursued converted Jews and Muslims after royal decrees forced them to choose baptism or exile, and killed, by the estimates of named historians, from under 3,000 to about 7,300 people before its final abolition on 15 July 1834. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq] [cite:vt34_wiki_alhambra] [cite:vt34_eretico_victims] [cite:vt34_wiki_abolition] Portugal's, founded in 1536 at John III's request, executed about 1,180 people in person by 1794; Rome's, founded in 1542, sentenced about 1,250 to death in Italy by Del Col's estimate and continues as the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith. [cite:vt34_wiki_portinq] [cite:vt34_va_cdf_profile] [cite:vt34_wiki_rominq] In Goa the Portuguese crown, its viceroys and the religious orders razed hundreds of temples, outlawed Hindu rites and the Konkani language, while the tribunal burned 57 people in person and punished converts for their families' customs; an archbishop's synod condemned the Syriac books of Kerala's Christians in 1599. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] [cite:vt34_gedsh_diamper] In the Americas the crown kept Indigenous people out of the Holy Office's reach from 1571, and the destruction of their books, shrines and ancestors was the work of friars and bishops: Landa's Maní campaign of 1562, which burned 27 codices and left at least 157 dead, the Lima council's order against religious quipus, and Peru's extirpation campaigns to 1670; Mexica rulers had burned books before them, and Sahagún and his Nahua collaborators preserved what the Florentine Codex holds. [cite:vt34_wiki_ometochtzin] [cite:vt34_arch_mani] [cite:vt34_wiki_lima3] [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] [cite:vt34_wiki_itzcoatl] [cite:vt34_whe_florentine] Part Thirty-Four turns from courts to cults, and asks what happened to the sun gods of the Andes, Mexico and the wider world. [scene:vt35_inti_and_the_andes|Part Thirty-Four: The Suppressed Suns]

sections.h: Three Inquisitions: Spain, Portugal and Rome, 1478–1834
sections.html:
The medieval inquisition of Part Twenty-Eight was a set of papal commissions handed to friars. [scene:vt28_inquisition|Part Twenty-Eight] The early modern world produced something different: three standing tribunals with their own councils, archives, prisons and budgets. Two of them, in Spain and Portugal, were created at the request of kings, staffed by men the kings chose, and used for the kings' purposes as well as the Church's. The third, in Rome, was the pope's own, and it is the one that survives today under another name. Who acted matters to the question this part of the book asks, because the popular phrase "the Inquisition" folds crowns, bishops and popes into a single actor that the documents do not show.

Spain: a papal licence for a royal court

On 1 November 1478 Pope Sixtus IV issued the bull Exigit sincerae devotionis affectus, which allowed Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile to appoint inquisitors in their kingdoms. The first two, the Dominicans Miguel de Morillo and Juan de San Martín, were named on 27 September 1480, and at the first auto de fe, in Seville on 6 February 1481, six people were burned alive. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq] In 1483 a Council of the Supreme and General Inquisition, the Suprema, was created, and on 17 October 1483 Tomás de Torquemada became Inquisitor General for all the Spanish kingdoms. Both the Inquisitor General and the members of the Suprema were named by the crown; historians describe the tribunal as an institution at the service of the monarchy. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq]

The papacy did not simply bless what followed. On 18 April 1482 Sixtus IV issued a bull condemning abuses by the inquisitors in Aragon, which the nineteenth-century historian Henry Charles Lea called "the most extraordinary bull in the history of the Inquisition". Ferdinand answered on 13 May 1482 by professing to doubt that it was genuine, and the pope suspended it; the next year he issued the bull naming Torquemada. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq] The record shows a pope who protested and then gave way to a king, not a pope directing a king.

Who it was aimed at

Its first target was the conversos, Jews who had been baptised and their descendants, accused of practising Judaism in secret. On 31 March 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella issued the Alhambra Decree, ordering every Jew in their kingdoms to be baptised or leave by 31 July. Estimates of those expelled run from about 40,000 to 100,000; the decree was revoked, symbolically, only on 16 December 1968. [cite:vt34_wiki_alhambra] The decree was a royal act; its effect was to turn every Jew who stayed into a Christian under the tribunal's jurisdiction.

Muslims followed. A decree of 1502 ordered the Muslims of Castile to convert or leave, and the converts, the Moriscos, became the tribunal's second great category. After the Alpujarras revolt of 1568–1571 they were dispersed across Castile, and in 1609 Philip III ordered their expulsion; about 300,000 people left. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq] Books went with the people. In 1499 Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, archbishop of Toledo and Isabella's confessor, had the library of the Granada madrasa carried into the Bib-Rambla square and burned in a public bonfire. [cite:vt34_wiki_madrasa] How many volumes burned is not reliably known, and some Nasrid royal manuscripts long assumed lost in that fire survive, because the last sultan took the palace library with him into exile in North Africa. [cite:vt34_cuni_nasrid]

The tribunal's later targets reached the Christian mainstream. Between 1558 and 1562, under Philip II, it broke up small Protestant circles in Valladolid and Seville, about 120 people, and its autos de fe of those years sent about 100 to their deaths. Across the tribunal's history most of those it labelled "Lutheran" were not Protestants at all, but people charged for anticlerical remarks, drunken mockery or irreverence. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq] It tried the alumbrados, the "enlightened" contemplatives of Castile who taught that the soul could give itself directly to God, and sentenced them to long imprisonment, though no alumbrado was executed. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq] [scene:vt29_mystics|Part Twenty-Nine: the mystics] And it controlled print: Spain issued its own indexes of forbidden books in 1551, 1559, 1583 and later, alongside Rome's. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq] [scene:vt30_forbidden_arts|Part Thirty: the Index]

How many died

The numbers have been fought over for two centuries, and the honest answer is a range with names attached. Juan Antonio Llorente, the tribunal's former secretary, claimed in 1817 that 31,912 people had been burned. Modern counts begin with the summaries of cases (relaciones de causas) that regional tribunals sent to the Suprema: from those, Jaime Contreras and Gustav Henningsen counted 44,674 trials between 1540 and 1700, with 826 people executed in person and 778 burned in effigy. [cite:vt34_eretico_victims] Henry Kamen puts total executions at no more than about 3,000, some 2,000 of them in the first forty years; Joseph Pérez gives about 125,000 trials and fewer than 10,000 deaths; William Monter estimated 2,750. A recent synthesis by the reference work Ereticopedia, adjusting for the gaps in the surviving summaries, arrives at roughly 7,300 executions in person between 1480 and 1820, of which about 4,500 are confirmed, most of them before 1540. [cite:vt34_eretico_victims]

A Vatican-sponsored symposium has entered the argument too. When the proceedings of a 1998 Vatican symposium on the Inquisition were presented in June 2004, their editor, Agostino Borromeo of Rome's Sapienza University, said the Spanish tribunal had held about 125,000 trials and that about 1 per cent of defendants were executed, and that in Portugal 5.7 per cent of more than 13,000 people tried in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries were condemned to death. [cite:vt34_icn_borromeo] John Paul II's letter for the same volume repeated the Church's repentance for "intolerance and even the use of violence" in the service of truth. [cite:vt28_va_jp2_2004] The lower figures in this debate are not only the Church's: Kamen and Monter are secular historians working from the same archives. What no serious estimate supports is Llorente's thirty thousand, or the still larger numbers that circulate online.

Portugal: the same model, a later start

Portugal's Jews had been baptised by force. On 5 December 1496 King Manuel I, negotiating a marriage with the daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, ordered them to convert or leave; in 1497 he stopped them leaving and had them baptised. [cite:vt34_wiki_manuel] Their descendants, the New Christians, were the main target when, after years of royal lobbying by John III, Pope Paul III issued the bull Cum ad nihil magis on 23 May 1536. The grand inquisitor was named by the pope but chosen by the king, usually from the royal family. The first Portuguese auto da fé was held in 1540; tribunals sat in Lisbon, Évora and Coimbra, and from 1560 in Goa. [cite:vt34_wiki_portinq] Fortunato de Almeida counted 31,457 sentences between 1536 and 1794, with 1,183 people executed in person and 663 in effigy; Lea's count is almost the same. [cite:vt34_wiki_portinq] The Marquis of Pombal abolished the purity-of-blood laws against New Christians in 1773–1774 and wrote the tribunal's last procedural rules, and the Constituent Cortes abolished it on 31 March 1821. [cite:vt34_wiki_portinq]

Rome: the pope's own tribunal, still in office

Rome's tribunal had a different founder and a longer life. On 21 July 1542 Paul III's bull Licet ab initio set up a commission of six cardinals, led by Gian Pietro Carafa, later Pope Paul IV, as the Sacred Roman and Universal Inquisition. [cite:vt34_eretico_rominq] [cite:vt34_va_cdf_profile] The Holy See's own history of the office says it was "initially a tribunal exclusively for cases of heresy and schism". [cite:vt34_va_cdf_profile] Its courts worked mainly in central and northern Italy; Sicily and Sardinia belonged to the Spanish Inquisition. [cite:vt34_eretico_rominq] Andrea Del Col estimates about 1,250 death sentences among the 51,000 to 75,000 cases judged in Italy after 1542; Giordano Bruno in 1600 and Galileo's trial in 1633 are its best-known cases. [cite:vt34_wiki_rominq] [scene:vt29_bruno_galileo|Part Twenty-Nine: Bruno and Galileo]

Pius X renamed it the Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office on 29 June 1908, and Paul VI renamed it the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith on 7 December 1965, with the stated aim of moving from punishing error to promoting the faith. [cite:vt34_va_cdf_profile] Since Francis's constitution Praedicate evangelium entered into force on 5 June 2022 it has been the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith. [cite:vt34_wiki_rominq] [cite:vt6_vn_pe] The tribunal that judged Bruno is, institutionally, the office that ruled on Freemasonry in 2023. [scene:vt30_rosicrucians_masons|Part Thirty]

The end in Spain

The Spanish tribunal was abolished four times. Napoleon suppressed it in French-held Spain on 4 December 1808; the Cortes of Cádiz abolished it on 22 February 1813; Ferdinand VII restored it in 1814 and abolished it again on 9 March 1820 under a liberal revolt; after 1823 he did not revive it, and bishops set up local Boards of Faith instead. [cite:vt34_wiki_abolition] One of these, at Valencia, condemned the Catalan schoolmaster Cayetano Ripoll for teaching deism to his pupils; he was hanged on 26 July 1826, the last person executed in Spain for heresy. The protest that followed helped end the boards. [cite:vt34_wiki_ripoll] The final abolition came by a decree of 15 July 1834 from the moderate liberal government of Francisco Martínez de la Rosa, signed by the regent María Cristina. [cite:vt34_wiki_abolition] By then the Spanish and Portuguese tribunals had been carried overseas for almost three centuries, and the next two sections follow them there.

sections.h: Goa: The Inquisition in Asia, 1560–1812
sections.html:
Portugal's tribunal in Goa was the only inquisition to work for any length of time in a society where most people were neither Christian, Jewish nor Muslim. It sat for two and a half centuries in the capital of the Portuguese Estado da Índia, and its main business, by the end, was the religious life of Hindus who had become Catholics, or whose parents had. It is also the tribunal whose history is hardest to tell from the record, because most of that record was burned. This section sets out who asked for it, what the crown and the Church did to Hindu worship in the territory before and alongside it, what the surviving numbers show, and where historians disagree.

Before the tribunal: the crown against the temples

Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa for Portugal in 1510. The destruction of Hindu worship there began as royal and colonial policy, two decades before the Inquisition arrived. An order of 30 June 1541 directed that the temples be destroyed and their property handed to the missionaries, and a royal order of 8 March 1546 from John III forbade Hindu worship, ordered temples destroyed and banned Hindu festivals in Portuguese territory. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] By 1566 about 160 temples had been razed on the island of Goa itself; a Franciscan campaign destroyed about 300 more in Bardez in 1566–1567, and Portuguese officials and missionaries are reported to have destroyed a similar number in Salcete, though the evidence for that figure conflicts. A royal letter of 1569 stated that all the Hindu temples in the colony had been burned and razed. No exact count exists. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] The acts were ordered by the king and carried out by viceroys, captains and members of religious orders, Franciscans and Jesuits; the Inquisition was one part of a wider system, not its author.

The communities did not simply lose their gods. In 1560, according to the government of Goa's own account of the shrine, devotees of Shri Mangesh carried the linga by night from Kushasthali, the present Cortalim in Salcete, across the border to Priol, then ruled by the Adil Shahi sultans of Bijapur, to save it from destruction. [cite:vt34_goagov_mangueshi] The Mangueshi temple at Priol is today one of the best known in Goa. Other village deities made the same journey into the hinterland of Ponda, beyond Portuguese rule, which is why so many of Goa's great temples stand there rather than where they were founded.

Who asked for the tribunal

Francis Xavier, the Jesuit missionary later canonised (12 March 1622), wrote to John III asking, in the words quoted by the historian Stephen Neill, that "your highness should institute the holy Inquisition" in India. [cite:vt34_wiki_xavier] Sources date the letter to 1545 or 1546, and historians disagree about what he meant: some read it as a request for the tribunal that followed; others read it as a plea for an official to promote and protect the mission. He died in 1552, eight years before the tribunal opened. [cite:vt34_wiki_xavier] [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] Goa's vicar general, Miguel Vaz, also appealed for it. The tribunal was established in 1560; its first inquisitor, Aleixo Dias Falcão, was sent by Cardinal Henrique, head of the Portuguese Inquisition. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq]

Whom it tried

The first target was the same as in Lisbon: New Christians of Jewish descent and Old Christians suspected of Protestant ideas. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] Over time the largest category became converts and their descendants accused of keeping Hindu customs, which the records call gentilismo, though the tribunal also often prosecuted local people who had never been baptised, which the historian Célia Tavares calls "quite disconcerting at first sight" for a court built to judge Christian heresy. [cite:vt34_alzulaij_tavares] Antonio José Saraiva put the share charged with crypto-Hinduism at about 74 per cent; Ulrich Lehner finds that more than three-quarters of the cases concerned public Hindu worship. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq]

The laws behind those cases were made by the colonial state and church councils together. Laws of 1567 restricted Hindu life in Portuguese territory, among other things forbidding Hindu priests to officiate at weddings. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] Language came under the same regime. On 27 June 1684 the viceroy, at the urging of Franciscan friars, decreed that within three years the people of Goa should give up Konkani for Portuguese, on pain of imprisonment; the king confirmed the order on 17 March 1687, and it was renewed in 1745 and 1812. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] Konkani survived it as the everyday language of Goa's Hindus and Catholics alike.

What the surviving numbers show

Most of the tribunal's archive was burned by Portuguese officials after it was abolished in 1812. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] Every count is therefore a reconstruction. Lauren Benton gives 3,800 cases between 1561 and 1623; a widely repeated figure of about 16,000 people tried between 1561 and 1774 has no clear source. Seventy-one autos da fé are recorded. The most cited count of executions, drawn from Portuguese archival summaries by Saraiva and others, is 57 people burned in person and 64 in effigy, the effigies standing for people who had fled or died in custody. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] Agostino Borromeo, presenting the Vatican's 2004 symposium volume, gave a rate of 5.7 per cent condemned to death among more than 13,000 people tried by the Portuguese tribunals in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, a figure that does not isolate Goa. [cite:vt34_icn_borromeo] For converts convicted of Hindu practice the ultimate penalty was to be handed to the secular arm and burned; far more often, Tavares finds, the sentence was whipping, compulsory attendance at Sunday Mass and other corporal penalties, or four or five years in the galleys, a sentence that often ended in death, each imposed in public at an auto da fé. People convicted of sodomy received some of the harshest sentences. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] [cite:vt34_alzulaij_tavares]

The last auto da fé was held on 7 February 1773. The Marquis of Pombal's government suspended the tribunal in 1774; it was restored in 1778, kept prosecuting, and was abolished for good in 1812. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq]

The other Christians: Diamper, 1599

The same Portuguese church that ran the Goa tribunal also acted against an ancient Christian community. The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, whose liturgy was in Syriac and whose bishops came from the Church of the East in Mesopotamia, were not under Rome. In June 1599 Aleixo de Menezes, archbishop of Goa, convened a synod at Diamper (Udayamperur), attended by 153 local priests and 660 lay representatives, which passed more than 200 decrees to bring them into line with post-Tridentine Rome and cut their tie to their own patriarch. [cite:vt34_gedsh_diamper] One decree forbade anyone to keep, translate or read Syriac books "written by Nestorian heretics", under pain of excommunication, and a list of banned works followed, including an infancy gospel and the law code of the fourteenth-century metropolitan Abdisho bar Brika. [cite:vt34_hmml_diamper] During Menezes's tour of the churches afterwards, books judged heretical were burned. How many is unknown: Hidemi Takahashi concludes that a large share of Kerala's Syriac manuscripts was probably lost, while the Hill Museum and Manuscript Library has catalogued banned works that survived, including a copy of Abdisho's law code made in 1291. [cite:vt34_gedsh_diamper] [cite:vt34_hmml_diamper] This was not the Inquisition's work but the archbishop's and his synod's; it belongs here because it was the same colonial church acting on the same principle of control over books.

How the story is told, and argued

The modern account in India rests heavily on A. K. Priolkar's The Goa Inquisition (1961), published as Goa joined the Indian Union. C. R. Boxer, the leading historian of the Portuguese empire, called it a "dispassionate and objective account"; Délio de Mendonça and Dale Luis Menezes have criticised its reliance on Claudius Buchanan, a nineteenth-century Protestant polemicist, and on the French physician Charles Dellon, whose memoir of his own imprisonment shaped the tribunal's European reputation. [cite:vt34_wiki_priolkar] [cite:vt34_alzulaij_tavares] The Brazilian historian Célia Tavares argues that the tribunal's power has been overstated but its violence was real, that it heard far more cases than the tribunals in Portugal itself with similar conviction rates, that no Jesuit ever served as an inquisitor in Goa, and that Brahmin converts were punished more harshly than lower-caste ones. [cite:vt34_alzulaij_tavares] The argument has present-day weight: on 21 December 2021 Goa's chief minister, Pramod Sawant, said the temples destroyed by the Portuguese should be rebuilt. [cite:vt34_dh_sawant]

The documented core is not in dispute. A Catholic crown, its viceroys and religious orders destroyed the public temples of the territory it ruled, outlawed Hindu rites and tried to suppress the local language, and a tribunal licensed by the pope and staffed by the crown punished converts for continuing the practices of their families. What is disputed is scale, which the burned archive makes uncertain, and whether the tribunal or the wider colonial order did most of the damage. The Hindu worship of Goa survived in the temples carried over the border, and in households. Part Thirty-Four returns to Goa's temples in its survey of suppressed solar cults. [scene:vt35_suns_elsewhere|Part Thirty-Four] The next section crosses the Atlantic, where the Spanish crown carried its tribunal to Lima, Mexico City and Cartagena, and then kept it away from the people it had conquered.

sections.h: The Americas: Tribunals, Bishops and the Burning of Books
sections.html:
When people say "the Inquisition burned the Maya books", they compress three different things into one. The Spanish crown did set up tribunals of the Holy Office in its American kingdoms, at Lima, Mexico City and Cartagena. But from the 1570s those tribunals had no jurisdiction over the Indigenous peoples, who made up most of the population. The campaigns that destroyed Indigenous books, images, shrines and ancestral remains were run by friars and bishops, under their own authority, and sometimes against the wishes of other churchmen and of the crown. This section separates the actors, sets out what was destroyed and what was kept, and records the counter-record: that Mesoamerican rulers had burned books before the Spanish came, and that friars and Indigenous scholars together preserved much of what survives.

A burning in Texcoco, 1539, and the exemption that followed

Before any tribunal existed in Mexico, the first bishop, the Franciscan Juan de Zumárraga, held inquisitorial powers himself. In 1539 he tried Don Carlos Ometochtzin, a noble of Texcoco and grandson of the poet-king Nezahualcoyotl, for returning to the old gods and for sexual offences; Don Carlos admitted the sexual charges and denied the religious ones, and he was burned at the stake on 30 November 1539. [cite:vt34_wiki_ometochtzin] Recent scholarship reads the case as much a family and political quarrel as a religious one. Spanish authorities disapproved, Zumárraga was reprimanded, and the case led to inquisitorial jurisdiction over Indigenous people being withdrawn, on the reasoning that they were too recently converted to be judged as Old Christians were. [cite:vt34_wiki_ometochtzin] [cite:vt34_wiki_mexinq]

When Philip II created the American tribunals, he made that exemption law. The Lima tribunal was established on 9 January 1570 and the Mexico City tribunal on 4 November 1571, under Pedro Moya de Contreras; in 1571 Philip II excluded the Indians from the Inquisition's jurisdiction, leaving them, in the Mexican tribunal's case, within its reach only through printed matter in their languages. [cite:vt34_wiki_peruinq] [cite:vt34_wiki_mexinq] [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] The tribunals' work fell instead on Spaniards, people of mixed descent and Africans. In Mexico the historian Luis González Obregón counted 51 executions over the tribunal's life; crypto-Jews of Portuguese origin were its most frequent capital victims, among them nine members of the Carvajal family burned on 8 December 1596. [cite:vt34_wiki_mexinq] The Lima tribunal's best-known act was the Auto General de Fe of 1639 against Portuguese New Christians accused of a "great complicity". [cite:vt34_muse_lima] The Cartagena tribunal, established in 1610 for New Granada and the Caribbean, tried 56 people for witchcraft in its first fifty years, 52 of them of African descent; one of them, Paula de Eguiluz, born enslaved in Santo Domingo, was sentenced on 30 November 1624 to 200 lashes and two years' penance in a hospital, and later to perpetual imprisonment. [cite:vt34_utex_cartagena] The Mexican and Peruvian tribunals were abolished by the Cortes in 1813, briefly revived, and gone by 1820. [cite:vt34_wiki_mexinq] [cite:vt34_wiki_peruinq]

Maní, 1562

The most famous burning in the Americas was not an act of the Holy Office. In May 1562 idols and human bones were found in a cave near Maní, in Yucatán. Diego de Landa, head of the Franciscans in the newly created province, began an investigation that, according to Spanish legal records summarised in Archaeology magazine, questioned 6,300 Maya by July, many under torture; more than 4,500 people were punished, at least 157 died, 32 were permanently maimed and dozens took their own lives. [cite:vt34_arch_mani] At the auto de fe on Sunday 12 July 1562, 27 codices were burned, along with 64 effigies and 114 sets of exhumed human remains. [cite:vt34_arch_mani] Landa wrote that the books held "nothing in which there were not to be seen superstition and lies of the devil", and "we burned them all, which they regretted to an amazing degree". [cite:vt34_popar_mani] An excavation in 2015 in front of Maní's town hall found thousands of deliberately smashed incense burners, many made at Mayapán, the first physical evidence of the event. [cite:vt34_arch_mani]

Other churchmen stopped him. Francisco de Toral, the first bishop of Yucatán, arrived that year, and ended the campaign in October 1562. [cite:vt34_arch_mani] Landa was sent back to Spain to answer for running an inquisition he had no right to hold; the Council of the Indies condemned his actions, but a commission absolved him in 1569, and after Toral's death he returned as bishop. [cite:vt34_wiki_landa] In Spain, around 1566, he wrote the Relación de las cosas de Yucatán, which records the Maya calendar, festivals and a key to their script. Its "alphabet" was wrong in its premise, but in the 1950s Yuri Knorozov used it to show that Maya writing was largely syllabic, the breakthrough that opened the inscriptions. [cite:vt34_wiki_landa] The man who burned the books also left the tool that let the stones be read.

More than a hundred codices are thought to have been destroyed across the colonial period, and at most four Maya books survive. [cite:vt34_arch_mani] Three are in Dresden, Madrid and Paris. [cite:vt34_bas_codices] The fourth, long called the Grolier Codex, was declared authentic by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History in 2018, dated to between 1021 and 1154 and renamed the Maya Codex of Mexico; it is an almanac of the movements of Venus. [cite:vt34_wiki_cmm] What survives, then, is astronomy, divination and ritual calendar, the same matters of writing, calendar and religion that Landa himself recorded in his Relación; that is the kind of knowledge the fires consumed. [cite:vt34_arch_mani]

Mexico: what Zumárraga did, and what Itzcoatl did

Zumárraga is often credited with a great bonfire of Aztec books at Texcoco. The evidence is thin. In 1881 the Mexican historian Joaquín García Icazbalceta argued that most destruction came before Zumárraga arrived, that no Spanish chronicler mentions his burning books, and that the one burning described by the Texcocan historian Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl was carried out by Tlaxcalan allies of the Spanish in 1520. [cite:vt34_wiki_icazbalceta] Icazbalceta wrote as a defender; the charge remains unproven rather than refuted, and the destruction of temple archives during and after the conquest is not in doubt.

The Mexica themselves had destroyed books. Sahagún's Nahua informants recorded that Itzcoatl, ruler of Tenochtitlan from 1427 to 1440, had the historical paintings burned, saying it was "not wise that all the people should know the paintings", so that a new history centred on Huitzilopochtli could replace them. [cite:vt34_wiki_itzcoatl] Control of the record was a practice of Mesoamerican states before it was a Spanish one.

The largest single preservation also came from a friar. From 1559 the Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún gathered testimony from elders at Tepepulco and Tlatelolco, working with Nahua scholars, Antonio Valeriano, Martín Jacobita, Alonso Vegerano, Pedro de San Buenaventura and others; the result, completed between 1575 and 1577, is the twelve-book General History of the Things of New Spain, the Florentine Codex: 2,446 pages and 2,472 illustrations, in Nahuatl and Spanish, covering the gods, the calendar, divination, omens, rhetoric, the heavens, medicine, plants and the conquest from the Mexica side. [cite:vt34_whe_florentine] In 1577 Philip II ordered such manuscripts on Indigenous religion and history confiscated; the codex reached Florence, and is in the Laurentian Library. [cite:vt34_whe_florentine] The crown that wanted the knowledge collected also wanted it out of circulation.

Peru: the extirpation of idolatries

In the Andes the knowledge was kept in knotted cords, the quipus, and in sacred places and ancestors. The Third Council of Lima (1582–1583), under Archbishop Toribio de Mogrovejo, ordered bishops to destroy completely the quipus that recorded non-Christian rites, calling them "pernicious instruments", while encouraging Christians to use quipus for confession and memorising doctrine. [cite:vt34_wiki_lima3] The council also issued a catechism in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara. [cite:vt34_wiki_lima3] The order targeted religious content, not the quipu as such, and what the destroyed cords recorded is not known.

From 1609 the archdiocese of Lima ran formal campaigns, the "extirpation of idolatries", in three waves, 1609–1621, 1625–1626 and 1646–1670, with occasional cases into the mid-1700s. [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] They began with the priest Francisco de Ávila's trials in Huarochirí; the Jesuit Pablo José de Arriaga's manual, La extirpación de la idolatría del Pirú, was printed at Lima in 1621 [cite:vt34_wiki_arriaga]; Archbishop Pedro de Villagómez directed the last and largest wave. Visitors questioned villages, punished native priests with whipping, exile and, in some cases, death, and burned the huacas and the mummified ancestors, the mallquis, that families kept and honoured. [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] The historian Kenneth Mills called it "perhaps the most sustained religious persecution" of Indigenous people in colonial Spanish America; Nicholas Griffiths, noting how irregularly the campaigns came, reads them as "aberrations, not a commonplace phenomenon" of colonial rule. [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] The same campaign produced its own record: the Huarochirí Manuscript, compiled under Ávila and used in his prosecutions, preserves the beliefs it was meant to help suppress, and Arriaga's manual is itself an eyewitness description of the rites it set out to end. [cite:vt34_wiki_arriaga] [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] The suppression of the Andean sun cult, the Coricancha and the Taki Onqoy movement belongs to the next part. [scene:vt35_inti_and_the_andes|Part Thirty-Four: Inti and the Andes]

What the record shows

The documented findings are these. Friars and bishops, not the Holy Office, destroyed Indigenous books, images and shrines in New Spain and Peru, by their own authority, often with torture, and church councils ordered religious quipus destroyed. The crown kept the Inquisition away from Indigenous people after 1571 and also confiscated the ethnographies its friars produced. Other churchmen, Toral above all, resisted the worst of it. And Indigenous people kept their practices alive, in hidden shrines, in households and inside Catholic forms; Mills's work shows Andean religion adapting rather than disappearing. [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] Part Thirty-Five follows that adaptation in the cult of Guadalupe. [scene:vt36_guadalupe_tonantzin|Part Thirty-Five]

Interpretation, not finding: inner knowledge in the burned books

The Sophia platform reads the codices, quipus and ancestor shrines as carriers of an inner knowledge as well as an outer one: calendars that tuned human life to the sky, divinatory counts that were also disciplines of attention, and rites of ascent and return comparable to the mystery schools of [scene:vt33_what_was_lost|Part Thirty-Two]. In this reading, the friars' bonfires removed a technology of consciousness, not only a body of records. The surviving books support the first half: they are astronomical and ritual. They do not by themselves show a doctrine of consciousness, and the surviving Nahua and Maya testimony comes to us filtered through the friars who collected it. The strongest counter-reading is that of the communities themselves, many of whom kept, adapted and still practise these calendars and rites, so that what was lost was a library, not the knowledge's last carriers.

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Four
chapters.title: The Suppressed Suns
chapters.intro: Part Thirty-Four asks whether the powers allied with institutional Christianity suppressed the sun gods of the peoples they conquered, and answers place by place, naming who acted each time. The first section follows Inti, the sun of the Inca: the gold stripped from his temple in Cusco in 1533, the Dominican convent built on its walls, the festival of Inti Raymi suppressed under Spanish rule and rebuilt in 1944, the seizure of the sacred sun image in 1572, the suppression of the Taki Onqoy movement, and the sun that Andean Catholics still greet at Qoyllurit'i. The second turns to Mexico and the Maya: the Mexica sun religion and the sacrifice it demanded, the razing of the Templo Mayor and the cathedral raised from its stones, the Sun Stone buried by an archbishop and later displayed on the cathedral, the Maya astronomical books burned and the four that survive, and the communities that joined the sun to Christ. The third tests the claim worldwide, in Rome, Egypt, Portuguese Goa, the American Plains and Japan, where the actors included emperors, crowns, the United States government and a shogunate that suppressed Christians, and grades the claim that every saviour is a sun god.
chapters.outro: Part Thirty-Four established that the sun religions of the Americas were dismantled by named actors for different reasons. In Peru, conquistadors took the Coricancha's gold for Atahualpa's ransom in 1533, the Dominicans built their convent on its walls, Viceroy Toledo's government, credited with banning the Inca-cult ceremonies, seized the Punchao when it took Vilcabamba, and clerical visitors punished the Taki Onqoy movement, whose scale historians dispute. [cite:vt35_wiki_coricancha] [cite:vt35_infobae_inti] [cite:vt35_wiki_tupacamaru] [cite:vt35_guibovich_taki] In Mexico the Spanish razed the Templo Mayor in 1521 and built a church from its stones, Archbishop Montúfar had the Sun Stone buried, and priests, Landa among them, burned the Maya books, of which four survive; yet the colonial cathedral displayed the Sun Stone from 1791 and the Vatican Library has held the Codex Borgia since 1902. [cite:vt35_wiki_templomayor] [cite:vt35_wiki_cathedral] [cite:vt35_wiki_sunstone] [cite:vt35_wiki_mayacodices] [cite:vt35_wiki_borgia] The Mexica sun cult that ended was also a cult of human sacrifice. [cite:vt35_smith_tzompantli] Elsewhere the actors were Roman emperors, the Portuguese crown in Goa, and, for the Sun Dance, the United States Department of the Interior, whose 1883 ban was relaxed in 1934 and formally lifted only in 1978; in Japan the sun goddess was never suppressed and the Christians were. [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] [cite:vt35_wiki_goainq] [cite:vt35_narf_civ] [cite:vt35_ebsco_japan] Andean, Maya and Totonac communities carried the sun into their Catholic practice, and the claim that Christ is only a sun myth does not survive the sources. [cite:vt35_unesco_qoyllur] [cite:vt35_everyculture_chamula] [cite:vt35_wiki_zeitgeist] Part Thirty-Five turns from the suns to the mothers, beginning on the hill of Tepeyac. [scene:vt36_guadalupe_tonantzin|Part Thirty-Five: The Suppressed Feminine]

sections.h: Inti and the Andes
sections.html:
The Inca state was organised around the sun. Inti, the sun, was the most important deity of its official religion, and the empire's highest priest, the Willaq Umu, was a priest of the sun, usually a brother of the ruler and probably the second most powerful person in the empire. [cite:vt35_wiki_willaqumu] When the Spanish took Cusco, the sun was therefore not one god among many to them: it was the religion of the state they were replacing. This section sets out what happened to that religion's temple, its festival, its sacred image and its priests, who did each thing, and what survived. The campaigns of the bishops against Andean religion generally, the "extirpation of idolatries" of the seventeenth century, are told in the previous part. [scene:vt34_the_americas|The Inquisitions in the Americas]

The Coricancha: gold for a ransom, a convent on the walls

The Coricancha in Cusco was the temple of Inti. Its walls were covered in sheets of gold and its courtyard held golden statues. [cite:vt35_wiki_coricancha] The first act against it was not religious at all. In 1533, when Francisco Pizarro's company held the ruler Atahualpa prisoner at Cajamarca and demanded a ransom in gold for his life, most of the gold was collected from the Coricancha and melted down. [cite:vt35_wiki_coricancha] Atahualpa was killed anyway. The actor here was a band of conquistadors after treasure, and what they took was metal; that the metal was a temple's was, to them, beside the point.

The second act was religious. Spanish colonists, and then the Dominican friars who still hold it, built the church and convent of Santo Domingo directly on the Inca walls. Construction took most of a century, and the building that stands now went up after an earthquake in 1650 destroyed the first convent. [cite:vt35_wiki_coricancha] The choice of site followed a pattern the conquerors used across the Americas and the Romans had used before them: put the new sanctuary on the old one. Four rooms of the Inca temple still stand inside the convent, because their fitted stonework outlasted the earthquakes that brought down the Spanish building above. The Dominican order still manages the complex today, jointly with Peru's Ministry of Culture. [cite:vt35_wiki_coricancha]

Inti Raymi: banned, then rebuilt

Inti Raymi, "the festival of the sun", was the Inca new year at the June solstice, credited to the ruler Pachacuti and described in the early seventeenth century by the mestizo chronicler Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, son of a conquistador and an Inca noblewoman. [cite:vt35_wiki_intiraymi] [cite:vt35_infobae_inti] The last Inti Raymi held in the presence of an Inca ruler is commonly dated to 1535. [cite:vt35_wiki_intiraymi] Its prohibition is usually credited to Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, the crown's governor of Peru, who is said to have banned ceremonies tied to the Inca cult, Inti Raymi among them, in 1572 as part of a programme of evangelisation; other accounts name "the Spanish colonists and their Catholic priests" more generally. [cite:vt35_infobae_inti] [cite:vt35_wiki_intiraymi] No decree naming the festival has been identified, so the firm statement is narrower: the state festival ended with the Inca state, and its open celebration ceased under Spanish rule, the clergy opposing it, until the twentieth century.

The festival people attend in Cusco today is a reconstruction. In 1944 Humberto Vidal Unda and Faustino Espinoza Navarro staged a theatrical Inti Raymi with Indigenous actors, drawing largely on Garcilaso's description, and it has been performed at the fortress of Sacsayhuamán every 24 June since. [cite:vt35_infobae_inti] [cite:vt35_wiki_intiraymi] What was suppressed was a state rite; what returned, four centuries later, was a civic and Indigenous-heritage performance built from a colonial chronicle.

Corpus Christi on the solstice

The Church's answer to the sun festival was a festival of its own. Corpus Christi, the feast of the body of Christ in the Eucharist, falls in late May or June and so lands near the solstice; in Cusco it became the great public festival of the colonial city, held at the season of the Inca solstice celebration of Inti Raymi. [cite:vt35_smarthistory_corpus] The art historian Carolyn Dean, in the standard study of the Cusco festival, describes it as staging "the triumph of Christian orthodoxy over the imperial Inka patron (the Sun)". [cite:vt35_dean_muse] In the procession the host was carried in a monstrance, a vessel of gold rays round a white disc, through the streets of the former Inca capital.

Dean's study is also the main evidence that Andean people were not only spectators of this replacement. In the surviving colonial series of Corpus Christi canvases from Cusco (eighteen were made, sixteen survive), Inca nobles march in the procession wearing their own regalia, including a garment with a sun face on its front, marking them as Andean nobility within the Christian city. [cite:vt35_smarthistory_corpus] [cite:vt35_dean_muse] The festival was a symbol of conquest; it was also the stage on which the descendants of the Inca kept their rank visible.

The Punchao and the last Inca

The holiest image of the Inca sun cult was the Punchao, a gold figure that held the remains of the hearts of dead Inca kings. The Inca rulers who held out in the Vilcabamba region after the conquest kept it with them. In 1572 Viceroy Toledo sent an expedition into Vilcabamba; it captured the last ruler, Túpac Amaru, and seized the Punchao along with the mummified bodies of two earlier rulers. Túpac Amaru was executed in Cusco on 24 September 1572. [cite:vt35_wiki_tupacamaru] The execution was not a clerical act: numerous Catholic clergy, convinced of his innocence, knelt to plead that he be sent to Spain for trial, and Philip II is reported to have disapproved of it afterwards. [cite:vt35_wiki_tupacamaru]

The Punchao's fate is disputed. Some accounts say the seized sacred objects were destroyed. [cite:vt35_wiki_tupacamaru] The historian Catherine Julien traced a different trail: Toledo took the image to Spain when he returned in 1581; after his death in 1582 the Council of the Indies seized items from his estate; and a gold idol appears in the inventory made after Philip II's death in 1598, possibly kept in the royal treasure house in Madrid into the early 1600s. [cite:vt35_julien_punchao] If Julien is right, the sun of the Inca ended in a king's treasury, as a trophy, rather than in a bonfire.

Taki Onqoy: the huacas' rebellion, 1560s

The best-documented religious resistance of the period was not a sun cult. Taki Onqoy, "the dancing sickness", arose in the 1560s around Huamanga (modern Ayacucho). Its leaders taught that the huacas, the sacred places and beings of the Andes, had revived in order to defeat "the God of the Christians" and would send disease on the Spaniards; followers were to reject Spanish food, clothing and religion. [cite:vt35_guibovich_taki] [cite:vt35_wiki_taki] The priest Luis de Olvera later claimed to have been the first to detect and "correct" it, in 1564, and to have destroyed some 700 huacas and more than 8,000 idols. [cite:vt35_guibovich_taki]

The suppression was led by the cleric Cristóbal de Albornoz, acting as an official visitor with authority to investigate and punish. Penalties included public shaming, shaving of the head, whipping, forced labour and exile; leaders were taken to Cusco to renounce their beliefs in public, women participants were confined in convents and local lords were fined. [cite:vt35_guibovich_taki] [cite:vt35_wiki_taki] Historians disagree about the movement's size. The historian Pedro Guibovich, following Rafael Varón, argues that Albornoz, who built his career on the campaign, exaggerated its spread in his own record of services, and that it was a local phenomenon confined to parts of present-day Ayacucho, Huancavelica and Apurímac. [cite:vt35_guibovich_taki]

The sun inside Andean Christianity

Andean religion was not simply erased and replaced. Much of it continued inside Catholic forms that Andean communities made their own. The clearest living example is the pilgrimage to the sanctuary of the Lord of Qoyllurit'i in the Cusco region, inscribed by UNESCO in 2011. In UNESCO's description it "combines elements from Catholicism and worship of pre-Hispanic nature deities"; it begins fifty-eight days after Easter, involves about a hundred distinct dances, and ends with a procession that carries the sacred images to the village of Tayancani "to greet the first rays of sunlight". [cite:vt35_unesco_qoyllur] The pilgrims are Catholic; the mountains, the snow and the rising sun are honoured as well.

The record therefore shows three things at once. Crown officials and conquistadors stripped the sun's temple, seized its image and killed its last royal patron; clergy built on its walls, set a Christian feast on its festival and punished those who called the old powers back; and Andean people carried the sun into the new religion and, in the twentieth century, brought its festival back into public. Who "suppressed the sun" in Peru was, in turn, a band of soldiers, a viceroy, a religious order and a set of clerical visitors, each acting for their own reasons. The next section follows the sun in Mexico, where the conquest fell on the Mexica sun and war god and the Maya kept their sky in books. [scene:vt35_mexico_and_the_maya|Mexico and the Maya]

sections.h: Mexico and the Maya
sections.html:
In central Mexico the sun had two faces. Tonatiuh was the sun of the daytime sky, called the Fifth Sun because the Mexica held that four earlier worlds, each with its own sun, had been destroyed before this one. [cite:vt35_wiki_tonatiuh] Huitzilopochtli was the patron god of the Mexica and of their capital, Tenochtitlan, a god of the sun and of war. [cite:vt35_wiki_huitz] Among the Maya, the sun god known in Yucatec and Lacandon as Kinich Ahau (k'inich is usually read "sun-eyed") appears in the codices as the figure scholars call God G, and the word k'inich served as a royal title in the Classic period. [cite:vt35_wiki_mayasun] This section sets out what the Spanish did to the temples, images and books of these suns, who did it, what the record says about the religion they were destroying, and what survived. The book-burnings of the Franciscan Diego de Landa, later bishop of Yucatán, and the work of the friars Zumárraga and Sahagún are told in the previous part and are only summarised here. [scene:vt34_the_americas|The Inquisitions in the Americas]

A sun that had to be fed

The record has to start with what the Mexica sun religion asked of its worshippers, because the conquerors used it to justify everything that followed and because leaving it out would misdescribe the religion. In the Mexica account, the present sun was born when the god Nanahuatzin threw himself into a fire at Teotihuacan, and it needed to be kept moving across the sky, its daily journey sustained by human sacrifice. [cite:vt35_wiki_tonatiuh] The myth of Huitzilopochtli's birth at Coatepec, where he defeats his sister Coyolxauhqui and his four hundred brothers, was read as the sunrise defeating the moon and stars, and offerings to him were understood as "sustenance for the Sun". [cite:vt35_wiki_huitz]

The scale of sacrifice is disputed, but archaeology has confirmed its reality. Excavations by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) behind the cathedral had uncovered more than 600 skulls in the great skull rack, the huei tzompantli, by December 2020; it was built in stages between about 1486 and 1502. A reported figure of 20,000 prisoners sacrificed at the temple's rededication in 1487 is disputed, and archaeologists say they cannot tell how many of the dead were warriors. [cite:vt35_smith_tzompantli] The conquistador Andrés de Tapia described "tens of thousands of skulls"; that is a conqueror's estimate, not a count. [cite:vt35_smith_tzompantli]

The Templo Mayor and the cathedral

The Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan carried two shrines on its summit, one to Tlaloc, the rain god, and the red southern shrine to Huitzilopochtli; the pyramid was understood as a re-creation of the hill of Coatepec. [cite:vt35_wiki_templomayor] [cite:vt35_wiki_huitz] The friar Toribio de Motolinía recorded that a feast was held when the sun stood in the middle of Huitzilopochtli's temple, "at the equinox"; this is the only known text from the period linking a Mesoamerican temple to an astronomical observation, and archaeoastronomers still debate what exactly it describes. [cite:vt35_wiki_templomayor]

The temple was almost totally destroyed by the Spanish in 1521, during and after the siege of the city by Hernán Cortés's army and its Indigenous allies. [cite:vt35_wiki_templomayor] The conquistadors then decided to build a church on the site, using the stones of the destroyed temple of Huitzilopochtli; the present Metropolitan Cathedral was begun in 1573 around that first church and finished in 1813, on top of the former sacred precinct. [cite:vt35_wiki_cathedral] The temple itself vanished under the colonial city until 21 February 1978, when workers for the electricity company struck the great carved disc of Coyolxauhqui; the excavation that followed, directed by Eduardo Matos Moctezuma from 1978 to 1982, brought the temple's foundations back into view. [cite:vt35_wiki_templomayor]

The image of Huitzilopochtli itself had a stranger history. One account says a soldier was about to destroy it when an Indigenous man rescued it; it resurfaced in the 1530s during an investigation by Bishop Juan de Zumárraga and was then lost again. [cite:vt35_wiki_huitz] Zumárraga, who held the powers of an apostolic inquisitor from 1535, never set up a formal tribunal, but he tried Don Carlos Ometochtzin, a lord of Texcoco, for returning to the old religion and handed him to the secular authorities, who burned him in 1539; the case is told in the previous part. [cite:vt35_wiki_zumarraga] [cite:vt34_wiki_ometochtzin] [scene:vt34_the_americas|The Inquisitions in the Americas]

The Sun Stone: buried by an archbishop

The great carved disc now called the Sun Stone, or Aztec calendar stone, was carved between about 1502 and 1521. Many read its central face as Tonatiuh; other scholars identify it as the earth monster Tlaltecuhtli or a lord of the night, and the stone is not a working calendar but a ritual monument that uses calendar signs, possibly a platform for sacrificial combat. [cite:vt35_wiki_sunstone] Around the face are the four earlier suns, with the present era, Four Movement, at the centre.

After the conquest the stone lay exposed near the Templo Mayor. According to the Dominican chronicler Diego Durán, Archbishop Alonso de Montúfar, who led the archdiocese of Mexico from 1551, ordered it buried so that "the memory of the ancient sacrifice that was made there would be lost". [cite:vt35_wiki_sunstone] It stayed underground until 17 December 1790, when it was found during repair works at the cathedral. What followed cuts against a simple story of suppression: the scholar Antonio de León y Gama asked the cathedral's canon not to have it buried again, and on 2 July 1791 it was mounted on the west tower of the cathedral, where it stayed, on public view, until 1885. It has been in the National Museum of Anthropology since 1964. [cite:vt35_wiki_sunstone] The archdiocese whose archbishop buried it in the sixteenth century let it stand on its cathedral in the eighteenth.

The Maya sky in four books

The Maya kept their astronomy in books of bark paper. Most were destroyed by Catholic priests during the conquest of Yucatán; Landa ordered many destroyed in July 1562 and wrote that because they contained "superstition and lies of the devil" he "burned them all". [cite:vt35_wiki_mayacodices] Four Maya codices survive: those now in Dresden, Madrid and Paris, and the Maya Codex of Mexico, judged authentic by INAH in 2018. [cite:vt35_wiki_mayacodices] What one surviving book shows is the measure of what the others probably held. About 65 per cent of the Dresden Codex is astronomical tables tracking eclipses, equinoxes, solstices and the cycles of Venus and Mars; its eclipse tables predicted solar eclipses accurately for thirty-three years in the eighth century, and eclipses are drawn as serpents swallowing the sun. [cite:vt35_wiki_mayacodices] Landa's own account also preserves a piece of the sun cult he opposed: he recorded that Kinich Ahau was patron of one of the four kinds of year in the fifty-two-year cycle. [cite:vt35_wiki_mayasun]

Central Mexican books survived in the same accidental way. The Codex Borgia, a pre-conquest manuscript of the 260-day divinatory calendar (the tonalpohualli) from the Puebla–Tlaxcala region, reached Europe in the colonial period, passed into the collection of the eighteenth-century Cardinal Stefano Borgia, went from him to the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith and in 1902 to the Vatican Apostolic Library, which has digitised it and made it public. Its final calendar page shows Tonatiuh receiving offerings. [cite:vt35_wiki_borgia] One of the most important surviving books of the Mexican sun religion is thus held, and published, by the Vatican.

What lived on

The public cult of the Mexica sun ended with the Mexica state, and human sacrifice ended with it; no one now argues for its return. Other parts of the old relation to the sun continued under Christian forms. The Totonac ceremony of the voladores, in which four men tied to ropes descend in spirals from a tall pole, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2009 as a fertility rite expressing "respect for and harmony with the natural and spiritual worlds". [cite:vt35_unesco_voladores] Among the Tzotzil Maya of San Juan Chamula in Chiapas, Christ and the sun are joined in a single figure, Our Father Sun/Christ, and the Virgin, the moon and the earth in a single Our Mother; the oral cosmology recorded by the anthropologist Gary Gossen opens with a text called "Of Our Father Sun in Heaven". [cite:vt35_everyculture_chamula] [cite:vt35_gossen_famsi] Among the Lacandon Maya, Kinich Ahau survives in a narrative in which he will one day descend and end the world. [cite:vt35_wiki_mayasun]

A widely repeated claim holds that colonial churches were deliberately aligned to the sun on the old festival dates, so that the Indigenous sun cult carried on in the masonry. The evidence is thin and mixed. A study of forty-one Jesuit mission churches in north-western New Spain found no clear solar pattern at all, with "surprisingly few" facing the eastern sunrise range, and its authors could not say why the churches face as they do. [cite:vt35_arxiv_jesuit_orient] The claim should be treated as open, and as unsupported for the region that has been measured.

In Mexico, then, the actors were an army that razed the temple in war, conquistadors who built on it, an archbishop who buried a monument to erase a memory, friars and a bishop who burned books, and a later colonial city and cathedral that put the same monument on display. The religion they suppressed was a sun cult that required human sacrifice, and its astronomy, calendars and histories were lost with it, except where a few books and many living communities kept them. The next section turns to the suns of Rome, Egypt, India, the Great Plains and Japan, where the actor was not always Rome. [scene:vt35_suns_elsewhere|Suns Elsewhere]

sections.h: Suns Elsewhere
sections.html:
A widely repeated claim holds that Christianity suppressed the sun gods of the world wherever it went. The previous two sections showed that in Peru and Mexico the record supports a version of that claim, with named actors who were mostly agents of the Spanish crown and its Church. This section tests the claim in five more places: imperial Rome, Egypt, Portuguese India, the American Great Plains and Japan. In two of them the actor was not the Church or Rome at all, and in one the Christians were the suppressed party. It ends by grading the broadest form of the claim, that every saviour figure, Christ included, is a disguised sun god.

Rome: Sol Invictus and the temple laws

The Roman cult of Sol Invictus, the Unconquered Sun, was given new imperial standing by Aurelian in 274, and Constantine kept Sol on his coins until about 325, more than a decade after he began to favour the Christians. [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] Part Twenty-One tests the claims built on this, including the Sunday law of 321 and the origin of 25 December, and it is not repeated here.
