[scene:vt21_sun_and_title|Sun, Sunday and the Chief Priest's Title] What ended the sun cult as a public religion was imperial law. The laws of Theodosius issued in 391 and 392 forbade anyone to go to the sanctuaries or walk through the temples, closed the temples and banned all pagan sacrifice and worship. [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] These were laws of the emperor, applied by his officials and, in places, by bishops and monks acting under them; Part Thirty-Two follows how they were enforced. [scene:vt33_the_closings|The Closings]

Egypt: the last temple on the Nile

Egypt's ancient religion was in large part a religion of the sun, with Ra at its centre for much of its history. No surviving law singles out Ra; what the record shows is the end of the temple system as a whole. Its last stronghold was the island of Philae at the southern frontier, sacred to Isis rather than to the sun. The last known inscription in Egyptian hieroglyphs was carved there in 394, and the last known demotic one in 452; a treaty of 452 between a Roman commander and the Blemmyes and Nobades, peoples from beyond the frontier, guaranteed their access to the goddess's image. [cite:vt35_wiki_philae] According to Procopius the temple was closed on Justinian's order by the local commander Narses, an act dated to about 535–537, and five of the island's temples became churches, the Isis temple rededicated to St Stephen. [cite:vt35_wiki_philae] The historian Jitse Dijkstra argues that organised worship at Philae was already fading in the fifth century, the last evidence of an active priesthood dating from the 450s, so that the order closed a temple already near its end. [cite:vt35_wiki_philae] [scene:vt33_the_closings|The Closings] The actor was an emperor and his general, not a pope.

Goa: Hindu worship banned

Hindu devotion to the sun, Surya, is part of Hindu worship in general, and in Portuguese Goa it fell under bans on Hindu worship in general. A Portuguese order to destroy Hindu temples was issued on 30 June 1541; King John III's order of 8 March 1546 directed officials to forbid Hinduism, destroy the temples and prohibit public Hindu feasts; some 160 temples on the island of Goa had been razed by 1566, and laws of 1567 made public Hindu worship unlawful. [cite:vt35_wiki_goainq] The actor was the Portuguese crown and its viceroys, pressed by clergy; the Goa Inquisition (1560–1812) that followed is told in the previous part. [scene:vt34_goa|Goa] Hindu sun worship itself continued across India beyond Portuguese rule.

The Great Plains: a ban by the United States government

The Sun Dance, the great annual ceremony of many Plains peoples in which bands gather to renew their relation to the world and the powers above it, with participants offering their own bodily sacrifice as prayer for the community, was suppressed in the nineteenth century, but not by Rome. [cite:vt35_wiki_sundance] In his report for 1883 the US Secretary of the Interior, Henry M. Teller, called for an end to "the old heathenish dances, such as the sun-dance, scalp-dance, etc.", and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Hiram Price, issued rules for Courts of Indian Offenses on 30 March 1883 to enforce it, with punishments ranging from withheld food rations to imprisonment. [cite:vt35_tah_teller] [cite:vt35_narf_civ] No act of Congress authorised the code. [cite:vt35_narf_civ] Canada's Indian Act was amended in 1895 to outlaw dances involving wounding, a ban dropped in 1951. [cite:vt35_wiki_sundance]

Both countries' laws aimed at assimilation, including assimilation into Christianity; but the ban was a government's regulation, enforced by government agents. [cite:vt35_wiki_sundance] People kept the ceremony alive by holding it quietly, without the piercing, or with an agent's permission. [cite:vt35_wiki_sundance] In 1934 the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, John Collier, issued a circular on Indian religious freedom that challenged the bans on ceremonies and opened the way to their public revival. [cite:vt35_audit_nlm_collier] The prohibition itself was not formally removed until Congress passed the American Indian Religious Freedom Act in 1978. [cite:vt35_narf_civ] The Sun Dance is held every year in many communities today. [cite:vt35_wiki_sundance]

Japan: the sun goddess, and the Christians suppressed

Japan's sun goddess, Amaterasu, appears in the country's earliest texts, the Kojiki of about 712 and the Nihon Shoki of 720, as the ruler of the heavenly realm and the mythical ancestress of the imperial house; her chief shrine is at Ise. [cite:vt35_wiki_amaterasu] When Christianity reached Japan, with the Jesuit Francis Xavier's landing at Kagoshima in 1549, it was the newcomer that was suppressed. [cite:vt35_audit_brit_xavier] Twenty-six Christians were crucified at Nagasaki in 1597, after the ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered the arrest of foreign priests and brothers; a decree of the Tokugawa government of 27 January 1614 abolished Christianity across Japan; missionaries were imprisoned; and every Japanese household was eventually required to register at a Buddhist temple. [cite:vt35_wiki_xjapan] [cite:vt35_audit_jta_26martyrs] [cite:vt35_ebsco_japan] After the Shimabara rebellion of 1637–1638 an estimated 37,000 people, mostly Christians, were killed. [cite:vt35_wiki_xjapan] Hidden Christians kept their faith for more than two centuries behind Buddhist forms, praying to the Virgin as "Maria Kannon"; when the Meiji government lifted the legal ban on Christianity in 1873, about 30,000 came out of hiding. [cite:vt35_wiki_kakure] [cite:vt35_audit_spencer_kosatsu] The record in Japan runs the other way: a state that honoured a sun goddess as its ancestress suppressed a Christian minority, for reasons historians describe as mainly political. [cite:vt35_ebsco_japan]

"Every saviour is the sun": the claim graded

The broadest version of the solar thesis holds that Christ himself is a sun myth: that the gospel story is an astronomical allegory copied from Horus, Mithras and other solar saviours. Its best-known modern form is the first part of the film Zeitgeist (2007), which drew on the writer Acharya S (D. M. Murdock). [cite:vt35_wiki_zeitgeist] The ancient historian Chris Forbes of Macquarie University found that the film's first part had no basis in serious scholarship or ancient sources and that "it is extraordinary how many claims it makes which are simply not true"; the journalist Michelle Goldberg described the film as a whole as steeped in conspiracy theories that were covertly antisemitic, which is a reason for care with it beyond its errors of fact. [cite:vt35_wiki_zeitgeist] The specific parallels most often cited, a Mithras born on 25 December with twelve disciples, are tested in Part Twenty-One and fail. [scene:vt21_sun_and_title|Sun, Sunday and the Chief Priest's Title]

What stands is narrower. Early Christians did use solar language and images for Christ: Justin Martyr explained around 155 that Christians gathered on "the day called Sunday", and a mosaic in the Tomb of the Julii beneath St Peter's, from around 300, is generally read as Christ pictured as the sun in his chariot. [cite:vt21_justin67] [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] Borrowing an image is documented; inventing a saviour from a sun myth is not. The record supports the first and not the second.

Interpretation, not finding: the suppressed sun as inner light

The Sophia platform reads the suppressed suns as more than lost cults. In this reading, the sun in the mystery traditions stood for an inner light that could be known directly, the goal of the ascent the mystery schools taught, and the destruction of solar temples, calendars and books was also the removal of a path of direct knowing in favour of a light that could only be approached through the Church's sacraments, as the Corpus Christi monstrance replaced the Punchao in Cusco. This is a reading of symbols, not a documentary claim; the record does not show any of the named actors aiming at an inner practice. The strongest counter-readings are that the Mexica and Inca sun cults were state religions of empire and sacrifice rather than private paths of illumination; that the Plains Sun Dance was suppressed by a secular government; that Andean and Maya communities folded the sun into their Christianity rather than losing it; and that Christianity itself was the suppressed light in Japan.

The pattern across eight peoples is therefore not one actor but several: Roman emperors, a Spanish army, Spanish and Portuguese crowns and their churchmen, a United States department and a Japanese shogunate. Where the Church acted, it acted through bishops, friars and royal patronage, and the same Church later let the Sun Stone stand on its cathedral in Mexico City and keeps the Codex Borgia in the Vatican Library. The next part turns from the suns to the mothers: the goddesses whose places, images and titles were taken over or replaced, beginning with Tonantzin and Guadalupe. [scene:vt36_guadalupe_tonantzin|Part Thirty-Five: The Suppressed Feminine]

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Five
chapters.title: The Suppressed Feminine
chapters.intro: Part Thirty-Five asks whether the divine feminine was suppressed, and answers with three bodies of record. The first is the hill of Tepeyac outside Mexico City, where a Franciscan friar complained in 1576 that the Virgin of Guadalupe was being honoured under the name of a mother goddess, and where the first printed narratives of the 1531 apparition story appear only in 1648 and 1649. The second follows the mothers of other peoples, Pachamama in the Andes, Yemayá and Oshún in the Caribbean and Brazil, Brigid in Ireland, and the Black Madonnas of Europe, into the Virgins who carried them, and stops in Rome in October 2019, when female figures from the Amazon synod were thrown into the Tiber by Catholic critics and the pope apologised. The third tests the oldest claim of all, that Mary is Isis renamed, against the dated evidence for each borrowed image and title, sets out the feminine figures the institution did push down, Wisdom and Mary Magdalene, and weighs them against the Catholic Church's own elevation of Mary. It ends with a labelled interpretation and the strongest readings against it.
chapters.outro: Part Thirty-Five established a double record. Pressure on the divine feminine is documented: a Franciscan of 1576 wanted the Tepeyac pilgrimage corrected because it kept the name of Tonantzin, colonial Spain allowed only Catholicism in Cuba, Artemis's image at Ephesus was destroyed with a boast, and the Isis festival of the ships was suppressed in Egypt in the sixth century. [cite:vt36_sahagun1576] [cite:vt36_wiki_santeria] [cite:vt36_wiki_artemision] [cite:vt36_wiki_navigium] Persistence is documented as well: the Guadalupe devotion, first narrated in print in 1648–1649, was adopted by the archbishops and crowned by the canonization of Juan Diego on 31 July 2002; Pachamama, Oshún and Yemayá live on in Andean and Afro-Caribbean devotion paired with Virgins the popes honoured; and when female figures from the Amazon synod were thrown into the Tiber in October 2019, it was lay critics who threw them and the pope who apologised. [cite:vt36_wiki_huei] [cite:vt36_va_jd2002] [cite:vt36_wiki_yemoja] [cite:vt36_cwr_pacha2019] The claim that Mary is Isis renamed fails on the dated evidence for each image and title, while the demotion of Wisdom and of Mary Magdalene is documented, and the institution's own teaching raises Mary as high as it allows any creature and no higher. [cite:vt36_higgins_lactans] [cite:vt36_wiki_stellamaris] [cite:vt26_pearse_greg33] [cite:vt36_vn_mpf2025] The volume now closes with the full ledger of documented acts and the verdict on the whole of Book Two. [scene:vt32_suppression_ledger|Part Thirty-Six: Verdict II]

sections.h: Guadalupe and Tonantzin: The Mother on the Hill of Tepeyac
sections.html:
On the northern edge of Mexico City stands the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, the most visited Catholic shrine in the world; on 11 and 12 December 2009 alone, a record 6.1 million pilgrims passed through it. The hill behind it, Tepeyac, was a place of pilgrimage before the Spanish arrived, and a Franciscan friar who knew the Nahua world better than almost any European of his century wrote that the pilgrims were still coming to the same mother under a new name. Whether that friar was right, and what exactly happened on that hill, is one of the oldest open arguments in the history of the Americas. This section sets out the documents in the order they appeared, the debate about them, and the competing readings of the image itself, keeping the devotees' account and the critics' account side by side. [cite:vt36_wiki_olg]

The friar's complaint

The earliest and most direct statement linking Tepeyac to a pre-conquest mother goddess comes from Bernardino de Sahagún, the Franciscan who spent decades compiling, with Nahua collaborators, the encyclopedic work now known as the Florentine Codex. In an appendix to Book 11, written in 1576, he listed places where he believed the old worship continued under Christian cover. Of Tepeyac he wrote that the Nahua had there "a temple dedicated to the mother of the gods, whom they called Tonantzin, which means Our Mother," and that people came to its sacrifices from more than twenty leagues away. Now that a church of Our Lady of Guadalupe stood there, he complained, preachers were calling the Virgin "Tonantzin" too, when the proper Nahuatl title for the Mother of God was "Dios Inantzin." This, he wrote, "appears to be a satanic device to conceal idolatry," and he found the devotion "suspicious" because pilgrims walked past many other churches of Our Lady to reach this one. [cite:vt36_sahagun1576]

Two features of the complaint matter. First, it is the testimony of a hostile witness inside the Church: Sahagún wanted the pilgrimage corrected, not celebrated, and his account of the old temple is a written report; the modern belief that a goddess named Tonantzin had a temple there rests largely on it. Second, his objection is about a word. "Tonantzin" is built from to- ("our"), nān ("mother") and the honorific -tzin, and it was a title, used for several goddesses connected with earth, sustenance and maize, much as "Our Lady" is a title in Spanish. The theologian Rosemary Radford Ruether doubted that a single goddess called Tonantzin had a temple at Tepeyac at all, reading the word as the maternal title of any of several deities, which Nahua Christians could then carry over to Mary. Sahagún himself used the word in his own sermons as late as the 1560s before turning against it. [cite:vt36_wiki_tonantzin] [cite:vt36_wiki_olg]

The story and its paper trail

The apparition story, as the shrine and the Catholic Church tell it, runs as follows. Between 9 and 12 December 1531, by the Julian calendar then in use, a young woman appeared four times on Tepeyac to a Nahua man named Juan Diego and asked for a church to be built there. The bishop-elect of Mexico, Juan de Zumárraga, asked for a sign. Juan Diego gathered Castilian roses on the barren hill in his cloak, the tilma; when he opened it before the bishop the roses fell, and the image of the Virgin was found printed on the cloth. In the Nahuatl account she asks him whether she, his mother, is not there with him. [cite:vt36_wiki_olg]

The difficulty for historians is the order in which the documents appear. Zumárraga's surviving writings do not mention the event. The first clear record of a controversy comes in 1556. Archbishop Alonso de Montúfar, a Dominican, promoted the devotion at Tepeyac; on 8 September 1556, the Franciscan provincial Francisco de Bustamante preached against it, attacking the archbishop for encouraging a devotion to an image he said had been painted by an Indian named Marcos. The record of Montúfar's inquiry into the sermon was published only in 1888. The art historian Jeanette Favrot Peterson has argued that the painter was Marcos Cipac de Aquino; Stafford Poole and others have doubted that identification. Montúfar ended Franciscan custody of the shrine and authorised a larger church. [cite:vt36_wiki_olg] [cite:vt36_wiki_marcos]

The full narrative appears in print more than a century after the date it describes. In 1648 the priest Miguel Sánchez published Imagen de la Virgen María, the first printed account, which identified the Guadalupe image with the woman "clothed with the sun" of Revelation 12. In 1649 Luis Laso de la Vega, vicar of the Tepeyac chapel from 1647 to 1657, published the Huei tlamahuiçoltica, a 36-page tract mostly in Nahuatl. Its centrepiece is the Nican Mopohua ("Here is told"), the account of the apparitions, praised as a jewel of Nahuatl literature. [cite:vt36_wiki_huei]

Who wrote the Nican Mopohua is disputed. Laso claimed authorship in his preface, and Lisa Sousa, Stafford Poole and James Lockhart, in their 1998 edition, accepted him as its author, with possible collaborators, drawing on Sánchez's book. Mexican scholars, among them the Nahuatl specialist Miguel León-Portilla and the historian Edmundo O'Gorman, lean towards Antonio Valeriano, a Nahua scholar trained by the Franciscans, writing around 1556; the seventeenth-century savant Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora named Valeriano in a sworn statement, and the New York Public Library holds a partial copy that some date to about 1556. On this question the evidence does not close. [cite:vt36_wiki_huei]

Critics, defenders and a saint

Poole's 1995 history, Our Lady of Guadalupe: The Origins and Sources of a Mexican National Symbol, 1531–1797, read the silences in the sixteenth-century record as decisive; one reviewer summarised his conclusion as finding "no objective historical basis" for the apparition story. The book was widely praised by historians, while one reviewer doubted it would shake popular faith. The dispute reached the shrine itself: Guillermo Schulenburg, abbot of the basilica, resigned in 1996 after saying Juan Diego was a symbol rather than a historical person. Defenders pointed to other evidence, including the Codex Escalada, announced in 1995, a document dated 1548 said to bear the signatures of Valeriano and Sahagún; sceptics did not accept it as genuine. [cite:vt36_enc_poole] [cite:vt36_wiki_olg]

The institution's answer was given in its own register. John Paul II beatified Juan Diego on 6 May 1990 and canonized him at the basilica on 31 July 2002 as Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin, "the first indigenous saint of the American continent." His homily spoke of the Virgin's mestizo face and presented Guadalupe as a model of evangelization that entered Indigenous culture rather than erasing it. Earlier popes had built the devotion into the institution: Benedict XIV named her patroness of New Spain in 1754, when the Congregation of Rites approved a proper Mass and Office for her feast of 12 December, and Pius X issued the decree Gratia quae on her patronage on 16 June 1910, reported in some accounts as making her patroness of Mexico and in others of Latin America. [cite:vt36_va_jd2002] [cite:vt36_wiki_olg]

Reading the image

The image on the tilma shows a young woman with dark hair, eyes lowered and hands joined, in a rose-coloured dress with a dark sash and a blue-green mantle scattered with gold stars. She stands on a crescent moon held up by an angel, against a golden sunburst. Two families of readings exist, and both are serious. [cite:vt36_wiki_olg]

The first reads it as a European Marian image. The sunburst, the crescent underfoot, the stars and the joined hands are the elements of the woman of Revelation 12, "clothed with the sun," the type that Spanish and later Catholic art used for the Immaculate Conception; Sánchez made exactly this identification in 1648. [cite:vt36_ci_immac] [cite:vt36_wiki_olg]

The second reads it as a Nahua text in images. In this reading the blue-green of the mantle was the colour reserved for the divine couple Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl; the dark sash marks pregnancy; a small cross-shaped figure beneath the sash is the nahui ollin sign, the Nahua emblem of the cosmos; and the rays recall the spines of the maguey plant. Some writers go further: the historian María de los Ángeles López de Canseco reads the four-petalled flower as the four cardinal points and the four past ages awaiting a fifth, and says the stars on the mantle match the sky of 12 December 1531, a claim resting on planetarium software rather than a sixteenth-century source. Devotees and Church writers often hold that the Nahua reading was intended, a message addressed to Juan Diego's people in their own sign language; historians who trace the image to European models treat the Nahua reading as a later interpretation. [cite:vt36_wiki_olg] [cite:vt36_exp_signos]

What the record shows

Three findings stand. A Franciscan of the 1570s believed Tepeyac had been a shrine to a mother deity and that the Guadalupe pilgrimage continued that worship; he wanted it suppressed, and the archbishop's party, not the friars, won. The apparition narrative is first attested in print in 1648–1649, and whether an older Nahuatl original lies behind it is unsettled. And the institution did not erase the mother of Tepeyac; it took the devotion up, built it a basilica, made its visionary a saint and its image the patroness of a nation, while its own friar's complaint, that a goddess's name was being carried into the Virgin's, remains part of the record. Whether that is suppression, survival or both is the question the rest of this part follows, from the Andes and the Caribbean [scene:vt36_mothers_of_the_world|to the other mothers of the world] and back to the Mediterranean. [cite:vt36_sahagun1576] [cite:vt36_wiki_huei] [cite:vt36_va_jd2002]

sections.h: Mothers of the World: Pachamama, Yemayá, Brigid and the Dark Virgins
sections.html:
Tepeyac is not unique. Wherever Catholic missions met peoples who honoured a divine mother, of the earth, the mountain or the sea, a pattern followed that historians describe in two ways at once: the mother was pushed out of sight, and she came back inside a Virgin. This section follows four of those meetings, in the Andes, in Rome in 2019, in the Afro-Caribbean world shaped by slavery, and in Ireland, and closes with the Black Madonnas of Europe, about which more is claimed than documented. In each case it names who acted, including where the actor was not the Church. [cite:vt36_wiki_pachamama]

Pachamama and the Virgins of the Andes

Pachamama is the Andean mother of earth and time, worshipped across the Inca state alongside Inti, the sun, at sacred rocks and trees, with offerings of llamas and guinea pigs. After the Spanish conquest the Indigenous population was brought into the Catholic Church, and through the process scholars call syncretism many Andean people came to associate Pachamama with the Virgin Mary, especially with the Virgin of Candelaria. The campaigns waged against Andean religion in the colonial period, the bishops' "extirpation of idolatries" and its destruction of shrines and sacred objects, are set out in [scene:vt34_the_americas|Part Thirty-Three]; the devotion that survived them is the subject here. Her rites continue: the ch'alla, a libation poured to the earth before drinking, and the offerings made throughout August. John Paul II, in homilies in Peru in 1985 and Bolivia in 1988, spoke of homage to Pachamama as a way of recognising God's providence. [cite:vt36_wiki_pachamama]

The best-known Andean Virgin stands on a site the Inca held sacred. At Copacabana, on Lake Titicaca, near a site the Inca had held as a temple of the sun, the Indigenous sculptor Francisco Tito Yupanqui carved an image of the Virgin, which was brought to Copacabana and enthroned on 2 February 1583 (some accounts place the start of his work as early as about 1576); an adobe shrine was built for it around 1583; Augustinian friars took charge of it in 1589, and Pius XII made the church a minor basilica on 2 July 1940. The shrine remains a principal sacred place for Indigenous Andeans and Catholics alike. [cite:vt36_wiki_copacabana]

The most striking image of the fusion is a painting of 1720, the Virgin of the Mountain of Potosí, now in the Museo Nacional de Arte in La Paz. The Virgin's body is the Cerro Rico, the silver mountain that dominates the mining town; the Trinity crowns her from above, and the patrons who paid for the painting kneel below. Some scholars read the mountain-Virgin as Pachamama in Marian form, the earth goddess of the mountains visible inside the Mother of God. Others point out that Spain had its own mountain Virgins, Montserrat above all, so the image could draw on both worlds; the Smith College survey of colonial art concludes that it is transatlantic Catholic devotion made distinctly Andean in style and meaning. [cite:vt36_smith_cerro]

Rome, October 2019

Pachamama returned to the centre of Catholic controversy during the Synod of Bishops for the Pan-Amazon Region. On 4 October 2019 wooden female figures were part of a tree-planting ceremony in the Vatican Gardens attended by Pope Francis, and were later displayed in the Carmelite church of Santa Maria in Traspontina near St Peter's. On 21 October two men filmed themselves taking the figures from the church and throwing them from a bridge into the Tiber. The Italian Carabinieri recovered them undamaged. [cite:vt36_cwr_pacha2019]

On 25 October Francis told the synod that the figures had been in the church "without idolatrous intentions" and said: "I ask forgiveness from those who have been offended by this gesture." He called them "Pachamama"; Paolo Ruffini, prefect of the Vatican's Dicastery for Communication, had said that "fundamentally, it represents life". On 4 November an Austrian activist, Alexander Tschugguel, said in a video that he was one of the two men, and that the figures "do not belong in a Catholic church." [cite:vt36_cwr_pacha2019] [cite:vt36_cr_tschugguel]

The episode reverses the usual roles. The act of destruction was carried out by lay Catholic critics acting against their own pope; the pope apologised for it; and the Vatican's officials themselves did not settle what the figures represented, life, a mother, the earth or a goddess. The argument inside the Church about whether an Indigenous mother figure belongs in a Catholic church, in other words, is still live. [cite:vt36_cwr_pacha2019]

Yemayá, Oshún and the Virgins of the Caribbean

In Cuba and Brazil the meeting took place under slavery. A large share of the West Africans carried to Cuba between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries were Yoruba, and their religion, combined with Catholicism and later with Spiritism, became the religion known as Santería or Lucumí. The Spanish colonial government permitted only Catholicism. The orishas came to be paired with Catholic saints by shared attributes: Changó, who wears red, with Saint Barbara; Babalú Ayé with Saint Lazarus; Oshún with Our Lady of Charity of El Cobre, the patroness of Cuba. [cite:vt36_wiki_santeria]

Yemayá (Yemoja in Yoruba, Iemanjá in Brazil), the mother of waters, patron of the Ogun river in Nigeria and of the ocean in the Americas, is paired in Cuba with Our Lady of Regla, whose procession in Regla falls on 7 September, and in Brazil with Our Lady of the Navigators and of the Conception. Her largest festivals are Brazilian: offerings in the sea at Rio Vermelho in Salvador on 2 February and on beaches across the country on New Year's Eve. The Virgin of Charity, for her part, entered the Church's highest honours: Benedict XV declared her patroness of Cuba on 10 May 1916 at the request of veterans of the war of independence, and John Paul II crowned her image on 24 January 1998. [cite:vt36_wiki_yemoja] [cite:vt36_wiki_caridad]

Scholars disagree about what the pairing meant to the enslaved people who made it. One argument holds that they linked their deities to the saints to hide their worship from Spanish authorities, a mask over a continuing practice. Another holds that the linking also eased entry into colonial society by assimilating to Catholic norms. A third, from the ethnomusicologist María Teresa Vélez, sees the religion as something new, born from the encounter of diverse Yoruba peoples with one another, with other Africans and with Europeans. The pressure did not end with Spanish rule: after independence the Euro-Cuban Catholic establishment typically dismissed Santería as witchcraft, and in the United States the Supreme Court had to strike down a Florida city's ordinances aimed at its rites, in Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah (1993). [cite:vt36_wiki_santeria]

Brigid of Kildare

Ireland's case is the most uncertain. Saint Brigid is traditionally dated about 451 to 525 and said to have founded a monastery at Kildare around 480. A goddess Brigid appears in later Irish texts, including Cormac's Glossary, with the same name and the same domains of poetry, healing and smithcraft. In the late twelfth century Gerald of Wales described nineteen nuns at Kildare taking turns to tend a fire said to have burned since Brigid's time, inside a hedge no man could cross. Scholars divide: some see the saint as the goddess turned Christian, others as a real woman to whom the goddess's traits were later attached, and Dáithí Ó hÓgáin and others suggest she may have led a pagan sanctuary that became a monastery. Her earliest Lives are largely miracle stories and do not settle the question. What is documented is continuity, not a recorded suppression: since 2023 the Republic of Ireland has kept a public holiday in her name at her feast of 1 February. The losses that are recorded came later and from another actor: her relics at Down were desecrated and destroyed in 1538, in the Reformation, under the English lord deputy Lord Grey. [cite:vt36_wiki_brigid]

The Black Madonnas

Some 400 to 500 images of a dark-skinned Virgin survive in Europe, depending on how they are counted, with at least 180 in southern France alone; Montserrat in Catalonia and Częstochowa in Poland are the most famous. A widely repeated claim holds that they are Isis or an earth goddess in disguise. The record is thinner. In 1952 the anthropologist Leonard Moss sorted them into groups, and found that many were dark because of the wood used, or had darkened with age, candle smoke and the deterioration of lead-based pigments. Others may have been made dark deliberately, perhaps after the bride of the Song of Songs ("I am black, but comely"), and the writer Ean Begg argued for pagan origins; Monique Scheer argues the dark colour matters to worshippers because it signals age and authenticity. Research is limited and the origin theories remain debated. Some of the losses had nothing to do with the Church: the ebony Virgin that Louis IX gave to Le Puy in 1254 was destroyed during the French Revolution and replaced by a copy. [cite:vt36_wiki_blackmadonna]

Across these cases the record shows two forces working at once. Colonial states and Church officials did press against Indigenous and African mother figures, and some of that pressure was violent. Yet the figures most often survived by moving into Marian devotion, and the institution, from Pius XII at Copacabana to Benedict XV at El Cobre, honoured the Virgins in which they lived on. The oldest of these questions, whether Mary herself took the place of an older goddess, is the subject of the [scene:vt36_isis_and_mary|next section]. [cite:vt36_wiki_copacabana] [cite:vt36_wiki_caridad]

sections.h: Isis and Mary: The Old Queen of Heaven and the Approved Mother
sections.html:
The oldest form of the question this part asks is Mediterranean. Isis, an Egyptian goddess whose cult spread across the Roman world, was a mother holding her infant son, a queen of heaven and a protector of sailors, and her cult was among those the Christian emperors closed. Within a few centuries the Virgin Mary held a mother's place in Christian devotion, nursed her son in paintings, was hailed as Queen of Heaven and Star of the Sea. A widely repeated claim holds that the one simply became the other. This section tests that claim piece by piece, then turns to the feminine figures the institution did push down, Wisdom and Mary Magdalene, and to the counter-record: few Christian bodies, the Orthodox churches among them, have raised a woman as high as the Catholic Church raised Mary, and most have raised her far less. The mystery cults themselves, and how they ended, are in [scene:ts13_mysteries|the earlier account of the mysteries] and [scene:vt33_the_closings|Part Thirty-Two]. [cite:vt36_fordham_apuleius] [cite:vt36_wiki_navigium]

The nursing mother

Images of Isis suckling her son Horus (Harpocrates to the Greeks), the type called Isis lactans, circulated around the Mediterranean from about 700 BCE until the fourth century CE and were especially common in Ptolemaic Egypt. Images of Mary nursing Jesus, Maria lactans, look strikingly similar, and scholars since Tran Tam Tinh in 1973 have explored a possible link. The chronology is the difficulty. Sabrina Higgins, examining the Egyptian evidence, finds that Maria lactans appears there without dispute only from the seventh century, centuries after Isis images stopped being made, and concludes that the similarity is real but does not justify claiming a deliberate continuity of cult. In the Latin West the nursing Virgin was rare before the twelfth century, revived with Cistercian devotion, and was later discouraged in public settings after the Council of Trent on grounds of propriety. [cite:vt36_bham_isis] [cite:vt36_higgins_lactans] [cite:vt36_wiki_lactans]

Mother of God at Ephesus

In 431 the emperor Theodosius II convened a council at Ephesus, which met from 22 June to 31 July in the city's Church of Mary under Cyril of Alexandria. It condemned Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who preferred to call Mary Christotokos, "Christ-bearer," and affirmed the title Theotokos, "God-bearer," on the ground that the body she bore was united to the divine Word. [cite:vt36_wiki_ephesus] [cite:vt36_wiki_theotokos]

Ephesus had been the city of Artemis, whose temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world, and a widely repeated claim holds that the city's old devotion to its goddess carried over into the acclamation of Mary as Mother of God. The record does not support a direct transfer. The title was already in Christian use a century earlier, in Alexander of Alexandria around 321 and in Athanasius, so Ephesus confirmed rather than invented it. The temple of Artemis had been burned by Gothic raiders in 268 and was later closed in the anti-pagan measures of the late empire, a closure Christian authors place in the fifth century; a Christian named Demeas set up a cross there with an inscription boasting of "destroying the delusive image of the demon Artemis." Cyril himself credited John Chrysostom with the temple's destruction, a claim with little supporting evidence. What the record shows is a goddess removed and a Christian title, older than the council, enthroned in the same city; it does not show the council choosing the title because of her. One reference work notes that "mother of the god" was an Egyptian title of Isis, but no source shows the Alexandrian bishops borrowing it. [cite:vt36_wiki_theotokos] [cite:vt36_wiki_artemision]

Queen of Heaven and Star of the Sea

In Apuleius' novel the Metamorphoses, written in the second century, Isis appears to the narrator and names herself "Queen of heaven, the principal of the Gods celestial" and "the natural mother of all things," ruler of the winds of the sea, known to the Egyptians as "Queen Isis." Her spring festival, the Navigium Isidis of 5 March, carried a model ship to the sea for the safety of sailors; it outlived Theodosius' bans and was still celebrated in Italy in 416, and Christian authorities suppressed it in Egypt only in the sixth century. [cite:vt36_fordham_apuleius] [cite:vt36_wiki_navigium]

Mary's corresponding titles have their own documented paths. "Queen of Heaven" grew from the fourth-century Syriac poet Ephrem, who called her Lady and Queen; the title became common from the sixth century, the antiphon Regina Caeli dates from the twelfth, and Pius XII instituted a feast of her queenship on 11 October 1954. The Hebrew Bible itself condemns cakes baked for a "queen of heaven" (Jeremiah 7:18 and 44), a passage some critics of Marian devotion cite as a warning. "Star of the Sea," Stella Maris, comes from Jerome's book on Hebrew names, where Mary's name was probably glossed stilla maris, "a drop of the sea"; a copyist's stella for stilla produced the star, and from Isidore of Seville and the hymn Ave Maris Stella the title spread across medieval Europe. The resemblance to Isis is real; the documented route runs through scribes and hymns, not through a captured temple. [cite:vt36_wiki_queenheaven] [cite:vt36_wiki_stellamaris]

The policy of conversion

The continuity that is documented came from a stated policy rather than a hidden one. In 601 Pope Gregory I wrote to the missionary Mellitus, bound for England, that the temples of the gods should by no means be destroyed, only the idols in them; they were to be purified with holy water and given altars and relics, so that the people would "come to places familiar and dear to them," and their custom of sacrificing oxen should "receive some solemnity in exchange." The same reasoning, in later vocabulary, is what John Paul II called inculturation when he canonised Juan Diego in 2002. [cite:vt36_fordham_mellitus] [cite:vt36_va_jd2002]

The feminine the institution did push down

Two feminine figures did lose ground, and the record of each is clearer than the Isis story. The first is Wisdom. In the Greek Bible the Hebrew chokmah became Sophia, a female figure who "hath builded her house" in Proverbs. Paul called Christ "the wisdom of God," most Church Fathers followed him, and the great church Justinian inaugurated in Constantinople on 27 December 537, Hagia Sophia, was dedicated to Christ as Divine Wisdom. The Gnostic teachers had made Sophia a fallen and redeemed divine mother, the story laid out in [scene:vt26_pistis_sophia|Pistis Sophia]; orthodox theology gave her role to the Son. When Russian Orthodox thinkers revived Sophia as a near-feminine aspect of God, Sergei Bulgakov's sophiology was condemned by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1935. Eastern icons kept a trace: "Wisdom hath builded her house" shows the Theotokos as the house in which Wisdom dwelt. [cite:vt36_wiki_sophia]

The second is Mary Magdalene. All four gospels place her at the empty tomb, and in John she is the first to see the risen Jesus; around 591 Gregory I's Homily 33 merged her with the sinful woman of Luke and with Mary of Bethany, and the repentant sinner became her image in the Western Church until the twentieth century. The Roman calendar separated the figures in 1969, and a decree of 3 June 2016 raised her memorial to a feast as "apostle of the apostles," while ordination remains reserved to men. The full record, with the Gospel of Mary in which she teaches the apostles, is in [scene:vt26_gospel_of_mary|Part Twenty-Six]. [cite:vt26_pearse_greg33] [cite:vt26_wiki_magdalene] [cite:vt26_va_feast2016] [cite:vt26_va_ordsac1994]

The counter-record: the Mother raised

Against this stands one of the plainest facts in the history of Christian devotion: the Catholic Church, with the Orthodox churches, raised a woman higher than most Christian bodies ever have. The council of 431, which it counts as its own, named her Mother of God; popes defined her Immaculate Conception in 1854 and, on 1 November 1950, her Assumption, that she "was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory." It also fixed a limit. Its teaching holds that devotion to Mary "differs essentially from the cult of adoration" owed to God, and as recently as 4 November 2025 a doctrinal note approved by Pope Leo XIV judged it "always inappropriate" to call her Co-redemptrix, insisting that "Christ is the only Mediator." The institution has honoured the Mother at the highest level it allows a creature and refused, explicitly, to make her a goddess. [cite:vt36_va_munif1950] [cite:vt36_va_aud1997] [cite:vt36_vn_mpf2025]

Interpretation, not finding: the approved mother

The Sophia platform reads the material of this part as a single movement: an original divine mother, Isis in Egypt, Tonantzin on Tepeyac, Pachamama in the Andes, Yemayá on the African coast, Sophia among the Gnostics, was removed from her own temples and replaced by an authorised one, a Mother of God defined by councils, venerated within limits set by doctrine, and never permitted to be divine. In this reading the Virgin is the approved version: she keeps the people's devotion while the institution keeps the keys, and the suppression succeeds precisely because it does not look like suppression.

The strongest counter-readings deserve the same space. The first is Indigenous and African agency: the sculptor who carved the Copacabana Virgin, the painter of the mountain-Virgin of Potosí and the Afro-Cuban devotees who paired Oshún with the Virgin of Charity were not passive recipients but makers who chose what to carry forward, and some scholars see in Santería a new religion rather than a disguised old one. The second is the Church's own stated policy, from Gregory's letter of 601 to the inculturation John Paul II praised in 2002, which describes taking up local devotion openly as a method of mission, not concealing a theft. The third is the testimony of devotees themselves, millions of whom go to Tepeyac or El Cobre to meet the Mother of God, not a goddess in disguise, and do not experience their faith as a substitute. And the detailed record of Isis and Mary shows resemblance far more often than demonstrated transfer. Read through the first lens, the mother was replaced; read through the others, she was translated, by people who kept her. The documents establish both the pressure and the persistence; they do not decide which word fits. [cite:vt36_smith_cerro] [cite:vt36_wiki_santeria] [cite:vt36_fordham_mellitus] [cite:vt36_va_jd2002] [cite:vt36_higgins_lactans]

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Six
chapters.title: Verdict II: What Was Taken, Buried and Kept
chapters.intro: Part Thirty-Six closes Book Two and the volume. It adds almost no new evidence; it gathers what Parts Twenty to Thirty-Five found and weighs it. The first section sets out a ledger of every documented act against the people and books of the inner traditions, from Irenaeus's refutation of about 180 to the Holy See's 2023 note on Freemasonry, together with the acts of Parts Thirty-Two to Thirty-Five against the mystery schools, the books and sun cults of the Americas and the mother goddesses, from Theodosius's temple laws of 391 to the Tiber in 2019, naming in each case who acted, in what document, against whom and with what result, and sets the most common popular versions of that history beside the record. The second gives the verdict on the thesis Book Two tests, that institutional religion built a mediated, taxed and obligatory system over teachings of direct knowledge of God and then condemned, burned or absorbed those who kept them, in its narrower form and in the wider one the last four parts tested, split into its parts and graded, as Part Nineteen graded Book One's question, into what is documented, what is probable and what is not supported, with the platform's interpretive lenses set out in one labelled passage. The third follows what survived, buried, preserved by its enemies, kept alive or found again, from Nag Hammadi to the four Maya codices, the Florentine Codex and the revived Inti Raymi, names the questions that remain open, and ends the volume.
chapters.outro: Part Thirty-Six has laid the record of Book Two against the thesis Book Two tests and found it supported in substance and corrected in detail. The inner traditions taught what the thesis says: a kingdom inside, an ascent of the soul, no rule beyond the Saviour's, and no tithe documented for any school. [cite:vt24_gthom] [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] [cite:vt24_apjohn] The institution that prevailed did build mediation from the second century, a church tithe from 585, the inquisitorial search from 1184 and, from 1231, papal law that sent condemned heretics to the stake; under that system the Cathars of Montségur were burned, and Giordano Bruno was handed by a church tribunal to the city authorities who burned him, as Arius's books had been ordered burned by an emperor after 325. [cite:vt20_na_ignatius_smyrn] [cite:vt24_ce_tithes] [cite:vt28_wiki_adabolendam] [cite:vt28_herodote_1233] [cite:vt28_wiki_montsegur] [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] [cite:vt22_socrates1] But the ancient Gnostic schools were refuted, excluded and banned from assembling rather than burned, their gospels were never named in a surviving burning order, the canon was not chosen at Nicaea, and the Ethiopian Bible was never Rome's to suppress. [cite:vt21_vc3_66] [cite:vt22_canons] [cite:vt27_hessayon] In the wider form tested in Parts Thirty-Two to Thirty-Five the thesis is again supported in substance and corrected on its actors. Emperors and local bishops closed the mystery cults, from Theodosius's laws of 391–392 to Justinian's general at Philae; friars and bishops, outside the Inquisition's jurisdiction, burned the Maya codices at Maní in 1562 and the Andean shrines and religious quipus; Spanish conquistadors, a viceroy and an archbishop dismantled the sun cults of Cusco and Tenochtitlan; and the mother goddesses were pressed into Marian forms. [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] [cite:vt33_procopius_philae] [cite:vt34_arch_mani] [cite:vt34_wiki_lima3] [cite:vt35_wiki_coricancha] [cite:vt35_wiki_sunstone] [cite:vt36_sahagun1576] But the Inquisitions killed thousands, not millions; the United States, not Rome, banned the Sun Dance, and in Japan the Christians were the suppressed; Mary is not Isis renamed; and Indigenous and African devotees carried their sun and their mothers into Catholic practice, which the Church describes as inculturation and the platform reads as an "approved version". [cite:vt34_eretico_victims] [cite:vt35_narf_civ] [cite:vt35_ebsco_japan] [cite:vt36_higgins_lactans] [cite:vt36_wiki_santeria] [cite:vt36_va_jd2002] Whether fear of unmediated access was the motive is a reading, not a finding. What was excluded survived, buried, quoted by its enemies, kept by living churches and peoples from Ethiopia to the Andes, and found again, as Inti Raymi was in 1944, and the questions it leaves are named in [scene:vt32_what_survived|the final section]. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] [cite:vt24_wiki_flora] [cite:vt27_eotc_books] [cite:vt24_wiki_mandaeans] [cite:vt35_unesco_qoyllur] [cite:vt35_infobae_inti] This ends The Vatican Architecture. Its first verdict, on the Holy See and Zionism, is in [scene:vt19_verdict|Part Nineteen]; the companion volumes take up the other questions it touched: [scene:dv1_three_functions|The Divine 3+1] on the three cities said to have parented the State of Israel, and [scene:ts13_mysteries|The Theology Shield] on the mysteries and the ascent of the soul.

sections.h: The Suppression Ledger: Every Documented Act, c.180 to 2023
sections.html:
Book Two has followed one question through eighteen centuries: what the institutional church did to the people and books that taught a direct, unmediated knowledge of God. Parts Twenty to Thirty-One answered it one period at a time, and Parts Thirty-Two to Thirty-Five widened it: to the mystery cults and philosophical schools closed in late antiquity, to the inquisitions of the Spanish and Portuguese crowns and their reach to Goa and the Americas, and to the sun gods and mother goddesses of the peoples those crowns ruled. This section gathers their findings into a single ledger, so that the record can be read as a whole before the verdict in [scene:vt32_verdict_two|the next section] is given. The rule for entry is the same throughout: an act goes in only if a surviving document names who acted, when, against whom, and what followed. Acts that are told about but not documented are set out separately, in the second table, beside what the record shows instead.

Four kinds of act, and who did them

The documented acts fall into four kinds, and keeping them apart is the first finding. The first is argument and exclusion: a bishop writes a refutation, names a book or a teacher, and declares them outside the church. Irenaeus of Lyon did this about 180, naming the Valentinians, the "Gospel of Truth" and a "Gospel of Judas"; Tertullian of Carthage, about 200, argued that heretics had no standing even to dispute over scripture. [cite:vt24_ah1_pref] [cite:vt25_iren_311] [cite:vt23_na_irenaeus_1_31] [cite:vt24_praescr] The second is the restriction of reading: a list of approved books and a warning against the rest, as in Athanasius's Festal Letter of 367, which calls the apocrypha "an invention of heretics" but orders nothing destroyed. [cite:vt23_na_festal39] The third is the destruction of books by order. The fourth is force against people: confiscation, exile, imprisonment, torture and death. The third and fourth kinds required the power of a state, and for most of the period covered here that power belonged to emperors, kings and princes rather than to bishops. The ledger names the actor that acted, and notes where a church authority asked a ruler to act. In the later parts the list of actors grows longer still: emperors and their generals, a Gothic army, crowns and viceroys, conquistadors, friars and visiting clerics, the government of the United States and a Japanese shogunate all appear in it. So does a fifth kind of act beside the four, absorption, in which a sanctuary, a feast or a title was taken into Christian use rather than destroyed: Gregory I told a missionary in 601 to keep England's temples and give their feasts "some solemnity in exchange", the Pantheon was dedicated to Mary and the martyrs in 609, and in colonial Cusco the feast of Corpus Christi was set at the season of the Inca sun festival. [cite:vt36_fordham_mellitus] [cite:vt33_chi_pantheon] [cite:vt35_smarthistory_corpus] [cite:vt35_dean_muse]

The second finding is about Rome. Before the fifth century the bishop of Rome was one actor among several. The heresy hunters of the second to fourth centuries wrote from Lyon, Carthage, Alexandria and Cyprus; the first ranking of the great sees, Nicaea's canon 6, set Alexandria's authority beside Rome's customary one. [cite:vt24_wiki_panarion] [cite:vt22_canons] The papacy becomes the principal actor in the ledger only from the twelfth century, and the "Vatican", as a state, only in 1929.

What the first table shows

Four points stand out. The first state order in the table to burn religious books was a pagan emperor's, against the Manichaeans, and the second was the same government's against the Christian scriptures in 303. [cite:vt21_harland_mani] [cite:vt21_lact_dmp] The first Christian emperor used the same instrument against a Christian teacher: Constantine's letter ordered any treatise by Arius to be "consigned to the flames", on pain of death for concealment, and later laws did the same to Eunomian, Montanist and Nestorian books. [cite:vt22_socrates1] [cite:vt21_fc_laws] Second, the one imperial act that names a Gnostic group is Constantine's edict preserved by Eusebius. It names the Valentinians among five groups, forbids them to meet "in any private house", hands their houses of prayer to the catholic church and, Eusebius says, directed "that search should be made for their books". [cite:vt21_vc3_64] [cite:vt21_vc3_65] [cite:vt21_vc3_66] Eusebius does not say what was done with the books found, and no surviving order to burn a Gnostic gospel by name is known. [cite:vt24_vc366] Third, of all the texts laid out in Parts Twenty-Five and Twenty-Six, only the Gospel of Judas is condemned by name in an ancient source, by Irenaeus about 180 and Epiphanius in the 370s; the Gospel of Mary appears in no ancient condemnation, and the Gospel of Thomas enters the lists late, in Cyril of Jerusalem and the sixth-century Decretum, as a Manichaean book. [cite:vt26_na_iren131] [cite:vt26_arys_epiphanius] [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary] [cite:vt25_cyril_cat4] [cite:vt25_decretum]

Fourth, the mystery cults and the philosophical schools were closed by the same combination of imperial law and local action, not by a single act of "the Church". Theodosius's laws of 391–392 outlawed the rites; a bishop, Theophilus, used an imperial order to destroy the Serapeum; a Gothic army wrecked Eleusis; a crowd led by a church reader killed Hypatia; Justinian forbade pagans to teach at Athens and sent a general to close Philae. [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] [cite:vt33_socrates_516] [cite:vt33_wiki_telesterion] [cite:vt33_socrates_715] [cite:vt33_hannam_academy] [cite:vt33_procopius_philae] The one pagan book the Christian state is documented as burning by name is Porphyry's attack on Christianity, ordered burned in 435 and 448; no law ordering the burning of a mystery text is known, because the rites were not written down to be burned. [cite:vt33_wiki_againstchristians] [cite:vt33_wh_eleusis] Some endings had no actor at all: Samothrace faded without a recorded closure. [cite:vt33_archaeology_samothrace]

What the second table shows

The change between the two tables is the arrival of lethal force organised by the Church itself. From Ad abolendam in 1184, bishops and then papal inquisitors searched out heretics and handed the unrepentant to the secular power; the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 obliged rulers to swear to drive them out of their lands and gave crusaders against heretics the indulgence of the Holy Land; Ad extirpanda in 1252 authorised torture. [cite:vt28_wiki_adabolendam] [cite:vt28_fordham_lat4c3] [cite:vt28_wiki_adextirpanda] The fires were lit by lay officials, but under canons that required it. The scale is also documented within limits: Bernard Gui's own sentences, the best-counted series, record about 45 burned among 636 cases, and the Albigensian Crusade, often given a toll of a million, has no contemporary source for any total. [cite:vt28_mednet_gui] [cite:vt28_nwe_crusade] The Council of Toulouse in 1229 went further than any ancient authority against books: it forbade lay people to own the scriptures themselves, apart from the Psalter and prayer books. [cite:vt28_wiki_toulouse] And the pope who set up the inquisitors also ordered the Talmud confiscated in 1239, and in Paris in 1242 the papacy and the French crown had it burned, an act against Jews and Judaism that belongs in the same ledger. [cite:vt28_wiki_greg9]

After the sixteenth century the instruments change again: lists and declarations replace the stake. The Index of Forbidden Books ran from 1559 to 1966, and the ban on Freemasonry, first issued in 1738, still stands in the form of a note of 13 November 2023, approved by Pope Francis, that active membership "is prohibited". [cite:vt14_brit_index] [cite:vt30_wiki_ineminenti] [cite:vt30_vn_ddf2023] The later entries are of a different kind again, statements of regret: John Paul II's address on Galileo in 1992 and the Day of Pardon of 12 March 2000, when Cardinal Ratzinger said that "men of the church" had "sometimes used methods not in keeping with the Gospel". [cite:vt29_coyne_galileo] [cite:vt28_america_2000] That is the Holy See's stated position on the record set out above, and it is given here beside it.

Crowns, colonies and other states

The third table gathers the acts set out in Parts Thirty-Three to Thirty-Five, from the founding of the Spanish Inquisition to the Tiber in 2019. Most of them took place far from Rome, and in most of them the actor that held the power was a crown or its officers, with friars, bishops and tribunals acting under it; two of them have no church actor at all.

What the third table shows

Three points stand out here as well. First, the Spanish and Portuguese tribunals were licensed by popes but founded at kings' requests and staffed by kings' men; Sixtus IV protested at the Spanish inquisitors' abuses in 1482 and then gave way to Ferdinand. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq] [cite:vt34_wiki_portinq] Their death tolls are given by named historians as ranges in the low thousands, not the tens of thousands of Llorente's 1817 figure. [cite:vt34_eretico_victims] Second, the knowledge burned in the Americas, the books of calendar, history and ritual, the religious quipus, the shrines and the ancestors, was destroyed by friars and bishops acting under their own authority, outside the Holy Office, which from 1571 had no jurisdiction over Indigenous people. [cite:vt34_arch_mani] [cite:vt34_wiki_lima3] [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] Other churchmen resisted: Bishop Toral ended Landa's campaign within months. The destruction of records was not new to the region either: Itzcoatl, ruler of Tenochtitlan from 1427, had the historical paintings burned to rewrite his people's past. [cite:vt34_arch_mani] [cite:vt34_wiki_itzcoatl] Third, two entries have no church actor at all: the Sun Dance was banned by a department of the United States government, and in Japan a state that honoured a sun goddess as its ancestress suppressed the Christians for more than two and a half centuries. [cite:vt35_narf_civ] [cite:vt35_ebsco_japan] And the last entry reverses the usual roles: in 2019 it was lay critics who threw the Indigenous mother figures into the river and the pope who apologised. [cite:vt36_cwr_pacha2019]

Beside these acts stands the Holy See's stated position. John Paul II's letter of 2004 repeated the Church's repentance for "intolerance and even the use of violence" in the service of truth; the Church describes its taking up of local devotion, from Gregory's letter of 601 to the canonisation of Juan Diego in 2002, as a declared method of mission, which John Paul II called inculturation. [cite:vt28_va_jp2_2004] [cite:vt36_fordham_mellitus] [cite:vt36_va_jd2002]

Told and recorded

The fourth table sets the most common popular versions of this history against the record found in Parts Twenty to Thirty-Five. Each "told" claim is one that circulates widely; each correction is set out in the Part named. Rows marked in the record column are corrected by it; unmarked rows are partly right and partly corrected; the last row is broadly right.

The last row is marked differently because there the popular version is broadly right, and the record supports the thesis: no tithe was documented for any of the Gnostic schools, and the Apocryphon of John curses anyone who would exchange its teaching "for a gift". [cite:vt24_apjohn] What the record adds is that the proto-orthodox churches of the same centuries did not tithe either: Justin Martyr's Rome, about 155, collected what "each thinks fit", and Irenaeus contrasted the Jewish tithe with Christian giving of everything. [cite:vt20_justin_67] [cite:vt20_na_irenaeus_iv18] The compulsory tithe came with the church of the sixth century and the state of the eighth, as [scene:vt31_tithe|Part Thirty-One] sets out.

sections.h: Verdict II: Mediated Access and the Inner Traditions
sections.html:
Book Two set out to test a thesis that the platform put in one sentence: institutional religion built a mediated, taxed and obligatory system, of priest, tithe, Sunday duty and commandments, on top of teachings that offered direct and unmediated knowledge of God, and then condemned, burned or absorbed the groups who kept those teachings. Book One's verdict, in [scene:vt19_verdict|Part Nineteen], graded its answer in three registers: what is settled by documents, what is probable on reasonable inference, and what is not established. Parts Thirty-Two to Thirty-Five then put the thesis in its widest form, the one the Sophia platform asks in its own words: whether institutional Christianity, and the powers allied with it, suppressed the mystery schools, the solar gods and the divine feminine around the world, and erased knowledge the inner traditions guarded. This verdict grades both forms, in the same three registers. Because the thesis is a bundle of several claims, it is first split into its parts, and each part is graded on its own; a single verdict on the whole would hide where the record is strong and where it is silent.

The thesis, taken apart

Six separate claims are folded into the sentence. First, that the early teaching of Yeshua and his first followers included an unmediated "kingdom within". Second, that the Gnostic teachers of the second and third centuries, whom the Sophia platform calls the Evangelical Gnostics, kept that teaching and lived without tithe, commandments or obligatory Sunday service. Third, that the institutional church built a system of mediation and obligation. Fourth, that it condemned those teachers and their successors. Fifth, that it burned them or their books. Sixth, that it did so because unmediated access to God threatened an institution built on mediation. In the wider form, the fourth and fifth claims reach beyond the Gnostics to the mystery cults, the sun religions of the Americas and the mother goddesses, and the actors include the powers allied with the church as well as the church itself. The figure grades each, on the record of both.

What is documented

The record settles more of the thesis than its critics usually allow. The texts of the inner traditions do teach what the platform says they teach. The Gospel of Thomas places the kingdom "inside of you, and ... outside of you"; the Gospel of Mary says the Son of Humanity exists within and tells the disciples not to "lay down any rules" beyond the Saviour's, "nor make a law like the lawgiver"; the Gospel of Philip and the Treatise on the Resurrection teach that resurrection is to be realised now. [cite:vt24_gthom] [cite:vt26_mattison_gmary] [cite:vt24_gphil] [cite:vt24_treatres] No tithe, no fixed holy-day obligation and no church tax is documented for any Gnostic school, and the Apocryphon of John curses anyone who would trade its teaching for a gift or food. [cite:vt24_apjohn] [cite:vt24_ce_tithes]

It is equally documented that the institution which won built a system of mediation, obligation and enforcement. Ignatius of Antioch wrote early in the second century that it was not lawful "without the bishop" to baptise or hold the common meal; Irenaeus made the line of bishops the test of truth; Constantine's law of 321 made Sunday a civic day of rest; the bishops at Tours urged payment of the tithe in 567 and the Council of Mâcon made it a church law in 585, with excommunication for refusal; Charlemagne's capitulary of Herstal made it obligatory throughout the Frankish kingdom in 779; and the Church's law today binds Catholics to Sunday Mass, the Catechism stating that those who "deliberately fail in this obligation commit a grave sin". [cite:vt20_na_ignatius_smyrn] [cite:vt24_ah3_03] [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] [cite:vt24_ce_tithes] [cite:vt31_wiki_herstal] [cite:vt31_ccc2181] And, as the ledger in [scene:vt32_suppression_ledger|the previous section] shows, that institution condemned every group this book has followed. It had the state on its side against them from the fourth century, when emperors ordered heretical books burned (Arius's after 325, Eunomian and Montanist ones in 398, Nestorius's in 435), and from 1184 organised the search, trial and handing over of heretics to the secular power for punishment, which from 1231 meant the stake for the obstinate. [cite:vt22_socrates1] [cite:vt21_fc_laws] [cite:vt28_wiki_adabolendam] [cite:vt28_herodote_1233] [cite:vt28_fordham_lat4c3] The Cathars of Montségur who would not recant, Marguerite Porete and Giordano Bruno died by fire as heretics judged by church authorities; the Templar leaders Molay and Charney were burned on the evening they were sentenced in 1314, after withdrawing the confessions they had made. [cite:vt28_wiki_montsegur] [cite:vt29_wiki_porete] [cite:vt29_wiki_bruno] [cite:vt29_barber_cup1] [cite:vt29_nwe_templar]

The wider form of the thesis is documented in substance as well, once its actors are named. The mystery schools were closed, largely by emperors and by local bishops and monks: Theodosius's laws of 391–392 outlawed the rites, Bishop Theophilus used an imperial order to destroy the Serapeum, a crowd led by a church reader killed Hypatia in 415, Justinian forbade pagans to teach philosophy at Athens and had his general close the Isis temple at Philae, and Theodosius II ordered Porphyry's book against the Christians burned. [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] [cite:vt33_socrates_516] [cite:vt33_socrates_715] [cite:vt33_hannam_academy] [cite:vt33_procopius_philae] [cite:vt33_wiki_againstchristians] In the Americas, knowledge was burned: books of calendar, history and ritual, by friars and bishops acting outside the Inquisition's jurisdiction. Landa burned 27 Maya codices at Maní in 1562, writing that they held only "superstition and lies of the devil"; the Third Council of Lima ordered the quipus that recorded the old rites destroyed; Peru's visitors burned shrines and ancestor mummies until 1670; of the Maya books, four survive. [cite:vt34_arch_mani] [cite:vt34_popar_mani] [cite:vt34_wiki_lima3] [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] [cite:vt35_wiki_mayacodices] The sun cults of the Inca and the Mexica were dismantled by Spanish authorities: conquistadors stripped the Coricancha and razed the Templo Mayor, a viceroy seized the Punchao, an archbishop buried the Sun Stone, and clerical visitors punished the Taki Onqoy movement. [cite:vt35_wiki_coricancha] [cite:vt35_wiki_templomayor] [cite:vt35_wiki_tupacamaru] [cite:vt35_wiki_sunstone] [cite:vt35_guibovich_taki] In Goa the Portuguese crown razed the temples and outlawed Hindu rites. [cite:vt34_wiki_goainq] And the feminine figures were pressed into or replaced by Catholic forms: a Franciscan complained in 1576 that the Virgin of Tepeyac was honoured under a goddess's title, Pachamama came to be joined to the Virgin of Candelaria, and Oshún and Yemayá to the Virgins of El Cobre and Regla, under a colonial state that permitted only Catholicism. [cite:vt36_sahagun1576] [cite:vt36_wiki_pachamama] [cite:vt36_wiki_santeria]

What the record corrects

The same documents correct the thesis at five points, and a fair verdict has to carry the corrections with the findings. The first is timing. Mediation did not arrive with Constantine or Nicaea: the single bishop with presbyters and deacons is already demanded in Ignatius's letters, and Christians met on Sunday in Justin's Rome about 155, more than a century and a half before any Sunday law. [cite:vt20_na_ignatius_smyrn] [cite:vt20_justin_67] Nor was the early church taxed: no church law required a tithe until the sixth century, and it lived on offerings, as the Gnostic schools did, with imperial endowments added from Constantine. [cite:vt20_cathen_tithes] [cite:vt21_wiki_relpol] The contrast between a free inner tradition and a taxing institution is real, but it is a contrast with the church of the sixth century onward, not with the church of the second.

The second is the inner traditions themselves. They were not one movement and not all were free of rule. The Valentinians worshipped inside the catholic congregations and complained of being shut out; Ptolemy kept the Ten Commandments as the "pure law"; Sethian texts centre on a baptismal rite of five seals; Pistis Sophia lays down a long list of renunciations; and the Cathar perfecti of the twelfth century lived under bishops, vows and strict fasts. [cite:vt24_ah3_15] [cite:vt24_ect_flora] [cite:vt24_wiki_sethianism] [cite:vt26_mead_ch102] [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] Valentinian teachers also divided humanity into spiritual, animal and material people, an inner hierarchy of their own. [cite:vt24_ah1_06]

The third is the burning of the ancient Gnostics. For the second- to fourth-century schools, the documented means were refutation, exclusion and, from Constantine, a ban on assembly with confiscation of meeting houses and a search for books. [cite:vt24_vc365] [cite:vt24_vc366] No ancient order to burn a Gnostic gospel by name and no execution of a Gnostic teacher has been found. The Nag Hammadi books were buried, not documented as burned. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] Even the text most often called suppressed, the Gospel of Mary, appears in no ancient condemnation. [cite:vt26_wiki_gmary] The violence of the thesis belongs, on the record, to the medieval church and to the groups it pursued then.

The fourth is the actor. Before the twelfth century the bishop of Rome was seldom the actor in the ledger and most heresy hunters were not Roman; book-burning laws were imperial; the ban on the Illuminati was a Bavarian elector's; and the witch executions were mainly the work of secular courts, though in south-west Germany about four in five took place in Catholic territories, while the Roman and Spanish inquisitions were the more cautious tribunals. [cite:vt24_wiki_panarion] [cite:vt21_fc_laws] [cite:vt30_wiki_illuminati] [cite:vt30_wiki_witchtrials] [cite:vt30_wiki_basque] The papacy's own record, from 1184 to 1966, is heavy enough without carrying acts it did not perform. The new parts multiply the actors: the Spanish and Portuguese tribunals were founded at kings' request and staffed by kings' men; the burnings of the Americas were the work of friars and bishops, not the Holy Office, which the crown kept away from Indigenous people from 1571; Eleusis was wrecked by a Gothic army; the Sun Dance was banned by the United States government from 1883 until 1978; and in Japan, from 1614 to 1873, the Christians were the suppressed party. [cite:vt34_wiki_spaninq] [cite:vt34_wiki_portinq] [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] [cite:vt33_wiki_telesterion] [cite:vt35_narf_civ] [cite:vt35_ebsco_japan]

The fifth is the wider claim itself, which the record corrects on scale and on simplicity. Not every mystery ended by force: Samothrace faded, and at Philae the cult was dying when Justinian's general arrived. [cite:vt33_archaeology_samothrace] [cite:vt33_gozzoli_dijkstra] The Inquisitions killed thousands, not millions: Spanish executions are estimated by named historians at under 3,000 to about 7,300, Portugal's at about 1,180, Rome's at about 1,250. [cite:vt34_eretico_victims] [cite:vt34_wiki_portinq] [cite:vt34_wiki_rominq] The suppressed religions were not all paths of inner knowledge: the Mexica sun cult required human sacrifice, and the Mexica ruler Itzcoatl (1427–1440) had himself had his people's historical paintings burned. [cite:vt35_smith_tzompantli] [cite:vt34_wiki_itzcoatl] Much was kept by the same institution: Sahagún and his Nahua collaborators compiled the Florentine Codex, the Vatican Library holds and publishes the Codex Borgia, the cathedral of Mexico displayed the Sun Stone from 1791, and the doctrine of ascent passed into Christian mystical theology under the name of Dionysius. [cite:vt34_whe_florentine] [cite:vt35_wiki_borgia] [cite:vt35_wiki_sunstone] [cite:vt33_sep_dionysius] And the Marian forms of the mother goddesses were embraced, not only imposed: popes named the Virgins of Guadalupe and El Cobre patronesses, crowned the image of El Cobre and made Copacabana a basilica, and when Amazonian mother figures were thrown into the Tiber in 2019 it was lay critics who did it and the pope who apologised. [cite:vt36_wiki_olg] [cite:vt36_wiki_copacabana] [cite:vt36_wiki_caridad] [cite:vt36_cwr_pacha2019]

What is probable

Two parts of the thesis rest on reasonable inference rather than on a document that states them. The first is that the doctrine of apostolic succession served, among other things, to deny teachers of private revelation any authority. That is what Irenaeus's and Tertullian's arguments did in practice: Tertullian denied heretics the right even to argue from scripture, using a plea from Roman law. [cite:vt24_ah3_03] [cite:vt24_praescr] Elaine Pagels made the stronger version a scholarly thesis in 1979: that the doctrine of bodily resurrection "serves an essential political function" and that gnosis supplied a theological justification "for refusing to obey the bishops". [cite:vt24_enc_pagels] It is a named historian's argument, widely read and criticised by others: Henry Chadwick found it lacking in rigour, and Hyam Maccoby faulted it for idealising the Gnostics and passing over their elitism. [cite:vt24_enc_pagels] The second probable part is that institutional competition, not only doctrine, decided the outcome: the side with bishops, a closed list of books and, from 312, an emperor's patronage outlasted rivals that had none of these. The sequence of events supports that reading; no document states it as a plan.

A third probable point comes from the new parts: that much of what survived in the Andes, Mexico and the Caribbean survived by moving inside Catholic forms, and that some of that movement was deliberate concealment. The pilgrimage of Qoyllurit'i combines Catholic and pre-Hispanic worship and greets the rising sun; the Tzotzil Maya of Chamula pray to Our Father Sun/Christ; Kenneth Mills's work shows Andean religion adapting rather than disappearing. [cite:vt35_unesco_qoyllur] [cite:vt35_everyculture_chamula] [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] How much was concealment is argued: for Santería, one school reads the pairing of orishas and saints as a mask, another as accommodation to colonial society, and María Teresa Vélez as the birth of a new religion. [cite:vt36_wiki_santeria]

What is not supported

Three things are not supported by the record. That the motive for condemning the inner traditions was the threat of unmediated access, rather than the reasons the heresy hunters gave (doctrine, the unity of the church, the creator God of Genesis, the reality of Christ's body), is not shown by any document; it is an inference about intent that the sources neither confirm nor rule out. [cite:vt24_ah1_pref] [cite:vt25_iren_129] That the canon was chosen to remove these texts at a single moment is contradicted by the slow and uneven way the lists formed between Irenaeus and Trent. [cite:vt23_na_eus_he3] [cite:vt14_trent_s4] And that the ancient Gnostic texts were burned by church order is, as shown, unsupported. A document showing a church authority ordering Gnostic books destroyed in the fourth or fifth century would change that finding; none has been produced.

Of the wider claims, five popular versions are not supported. That the Library of Alexandria perished in one Christian fire in 391 is not shown; its decline ran over centuries. [cite:vt33_ou_library] That the Inquisition burned the Maya books, or killed millions, is contradicted by the jurisdiction of 1571 and by every modern count. [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] [cite:vt34_eretico_victims] That every saviour is a sun god, Christ included, fails on the sources: early Christians borrowed solar images, but no source shows the gospel built from a sun myth. [cite:vt35_wiki_zeitgeist] [cite:vt21_wiki_sol] That Mary is Isis renamed fails on the dated evidence for each image and title. [cite:vt36_higgins_lactans] [cite:vt36_wiki_theotokos] [cite:vt36_wiki_stellamaris] And that Guadalupe is simply Tonantzin renamed goes beyond the record: a friar's complaint that the name carried over is documented, but "Tonantzin" was a title used for several goddesses, the temple is attested chiefly by that friar, and the devotion's own documents are argued over to this day. [cite:vt36_sahagun1576] [cite:vt36_wiki_tonantzin] [cite:vt36_wiki_huei]

Beside these findings stands the Church's own stated position. Its councils and teachers held that they were guarding revealed truth; its modern leaders have said that "men of the church" sometimes "used methods not in keeping with the Gospel", and John Paul II in 2004 asked for "exact knowledge of the facts" about the Inquisition before judgment. [cite:vt28_america_2000] [cite:vt28_va_jp2_2004] On the religions of the peoples it met, the Church's stated policy has been to take up what it judged compatible rather than destroy it: Gregory I told a missionary in 601 to keep the temples and give their feasts a Christian form, and John Paul II, canonising Juan Diego in 2002, presented Guadalupe as a model of evangelisation that entered Indigenous culture rather than erasing it. [cite:vt36_fordham_mellitus] [cite:vt36_va_jd2002] This book has tried to supply that knowledge in both directions.

Interpretation, not finding: the lenses of Book Two

The Sophia platform reads this history through several lenses, set out here as readings, not findings. The first is the platform's four-stage pattern: appropriation, in which an institution takes over a teaching and its symbols; suppression, in which it condemns those who keep the original; occultation, in which the teaching survives hidden, buried in a jar, coded in ritual or carried by small orders; and recovery, in which it returns by accident and late, as at Nag Hammadi in 1945. Read through this lens, the ledger is not a list of separate events but one cycle repeated from the second century to the twentieth. The second is the argument that what threatens an institution most is the claim that it is unnecessary: a teaching that God is reached within makes priest, sacrament and tithe optional, and an institution built on them must answer it. The third reads the Gnostic myths as maps of inner transformation: Sophia's fall and return as the soul's descent and ascent, the alchemists' "solve et coagula" (dissolve and bind) as the same process in the language of the laboratory, and, in some modern esoteric teaching, a "sacred secretion" as its bodily form. These readings are held by the platform, and in different forms by Jung and by modern Gnostic and esoteric writers. [cite:vt24_wiki_septem]

They are readings because no document can confirm or refute them. The four-stage pattern fits some cases closely (the Cathars were suppressed and their rituals survived in inquisitors' registers) and others poorly (the Valentinians were refuted rather than hunted, and Enoch was dropped in the West by doubt, not by order). The "unnecessary institution" argument meets its strongest counter-evidence in the church's own mystics: John of the Cross taught the soul's way to union with God through the "dark night" from inside the church; he was jailed in Toledo in 1577, yet canonised in 1726 and made a Doctor of the Church in 1926, which suggests that the line the institution drew was submission to its authority rather than inner experience as such. [cite:ts13_brit_john] The alchemical link is attested from the alchemists' side and later than the texts: Zosimos of Panopolis, about 300, author of the oldest known books of alchemy, drew on Sethian and Hermetic writings and described the work as a baptism bringing gnosis, but the Nag Hammadi texts themselves are not alchemical treatises. [cite:vt24_wiki_zosimos] [cite:vt24_fraser2007] Orthodox scholars read the same history as communal consensus forming over centuries, and the heresy hunters as pastors defending what they believed true. The lenses can help a reader see a pattern; in this book none of them carries a claim.

The platform adds a further reading from Parts Thirty-Two to Thirty-Five, the "approved version". In this reading the institution did not so much erase the mysteries, the suns and the mothers as replace each with an authorised form: the ascent kept as a hierarchy of angels and sacraments under the name of an apostle's disciple, the sun's festival answered by the monstrance of Corpus Christi, and the original divine mother, Isis, Tonantzin, Pachamama, Yemayá or Sophia, replaced by a Mother of God defined by councils and never permitted to be divine.
