Read this way, the suppression succeeded because it did not look like suppression. The counter-readings are as strong. Indigenous and African devotees were makers, not recipients: an Indigenous sculptor carved the Virgin of Copacabana, and Afro-Cuban devotees chose what to carry into the Virgin of Charity. [cite:vt36_wiki_copacabana] [cite:vt36_wiki_santeria] The Church's taking-up of local devotion was a declared policy, from 601 to the inculturation praised in 2002, not a concealed theft. [cite:vt36_fordham_mellitus] [cite:vt36_va_jd2002] Millions of devotees at Tepeyac and El Cobre testify that they meet the Mother of God, not a goddess in disguise; the institution itself has set its limit openly, its 2025 doctrinal note holding that "Christ is the only Mediator"; and the record of Isis and Mary shows resemblance far more often than demonstrated transfer. [cite:vt36_vn_mpf2025] [cite:vt36_higgins_lactans] Read through the first lens the mother was replaced; read through the others she was translated by the people who kept her. The documents establish both the pressure and the persistence, and do not decide which word fits.

The verdict, then, is mixed in a precise way. The thesis is supported where it describes what the inner traditions taught and what the institution built and did from the sixth century, and above all from the twelfth. In its wider form it is supported where it describes the closing of the mystery cults, the burning of books, quipus and shrines in the Americas, the dismantling of the Inca and Mexica sun cults and the pressing of the mother goddesses into Marian forms. It is corrected on dates, on the variety of the inner traditions, on the burning of the ancient Gnostics, on scale and, above all, on the actors, who were emperors, crowns, viceroys, conquistadors, friars and bishops, and in two cases governments with no tie to Rome. It is not established on motive. What survived despite all of it is the subject of [scene:vt32_what_survived|the final section].

sections.h: What Survived, and What Stays Open
sections.html:
A ledger of suppression is also, read the other way, a record of survival. Almost every tradition this book has followed, from the Gnostic schools to the mysteries, the suns of the Americas and the mothers of the Andes and the Caribbean, reached the present, in some form, by one of four routes: buried in the ground, preserved in its enemies' books, kept alive by a community that never stopped using it, or revived by later readers who found it again. This section sets out what came through each route, then the questions the record still leaves open, and ends the volume.

Buried and found

The most famous survivals came out of the Egyptian ground. The thirteen Nag Hammadi codices, with 46 different works, were dug up at the foot of the Jabal al-Tarif in December 1945; they had been made about 350 and buried in the following decades, by whom and why is still argued. [cite:vt25_enc_nh] [cite:vt25_lj2015] [cite:vt25_lewisblount2014] The Berlin Codex, with the only extended text of the Gospel of Mary, was bought in Cairo in January 1896 and reportedly came from a burial site at Akhmim; Codex Tchacos, with the Gospel of Judas, was found near Maghagha in the 1970s and passed through dealers, a theft and a bank box on Long Island before its publication on 6 April 2006. [cite:vt26_wiki_berlincodex] [cite:vt26_natgeo_journey] The Greek fragments of the Gospel of Thomas came out of the ancient rubbish of Oxyrhynchus, and the Aramaic fragments of Enoch out of Qumran's Cave 4. [cite:vt20_ecw_thomas] [cite:vt27_wiki_enoch] Two codices left Egypt earlier, by purchase: the Askew Codex with Pistis Sophia, in the British Museum since 1785, and the Bruce Codex with the Books of Jeu, bought by James Bruce about 1769 and in the Bodleian since 1848. [cite:vt26_wiki_askew] [cite:vt26_wiki_bruce] None of these books was hidden from Rome, and none was found by Rome; most were found by chance, sold through the antiquities trade, and published decades later.

The Americas have their own buried survivors. Of the Maya books, more than a hundred of which are thought to have been destroyed in the colonial period, four survive: codices in Dresden, Madrid and Paris, and the Maya Codex of Mexico, an almanac of Venus declared authentic by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History in 2018 and dated to between 1021 and 1154. [cite:vt34_arch_mani] [cite:vt34_bas_codices] [cite:vt34_wiki_cmm] About 65 per cent of the Dresden Codex is astronomical tables, the kind of knowledge the fires consumed. [cite:vt35_wiki_mayacodices] Around 600 Andean quipus survive, most taken from graves; they have not been deciphered, and a database built by Gary Urton at Harvard is used to study their patterns of colour and knot. [cite:vt32_hyperallergic_khipu] The Sun Stone, buried on an archbishop's order, came up during repairs to the cathedral of Mexico on 17 December 1790, and the Templo Mayor beneath the colonial city was uncovered after workers struck the Coyolxauhqui disc on 21 February 1978. [cite:vt35_wiki_sunstone] [cite:vt35_wiki_templomayor]

Kept by their enemies

The second route is the strangest. Much of what survives of the condemned traditions survives because their opponents copied it in order to refute it. Ptolemy's Letter to Flora, one of the few complete Valentinian works known before 1945, exists only because Epiphanius quoted it whole in his catalogue of heresies. [cite:vt24_wiki_flora] Irenaeus's summary of the Barbelo myth was the main account of it until the Apocryphon of John came to light in the Berlin Codex and at Nag Hammadi, and the Refutation of All Heresies, recovered from a Mount Athos manuscript in 1842, preserves accounts of groups known from nowhere else. [cite:vt25_iren_129] [cite:vt26_wiki_berlincodex] [cite:vt24_wiki_refutation] The pattern repeats in the Middle Ages. The voices of the last Cathars of the Pyrenees survive in the register of Jacques Fournier, bishop of Pamiers and later Pope Benedict XII, whose 578 interrogations of 1318 to 1325 are kept in the Vatican Library and became the basis of Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie's Montaillou. [cite:vt28_wiki_fournier] The Chinon parchment of 1308, which records the Templar leaders' absolution, lay in the Vatican's archive until it was identified in 2001. [cite:vt29_wiki_chinon] The archive of the institution that condemned them is now one of the main witnesses to what they believed; the archives themselves are described in [scene:vt14_apostolic_archive|Part Fourteen].

The same is true of the ancient mysteries and of the Americas. The seven planetary gates of the Mithraic ladder are known from the critic Celsus, quoted by his own critic Origen, and Porphyry's burned book against the Christians from the roughly thirty Christian writers who quoted it to refute it. [cite:vt33_harland_celsus] [cite:vt33_wiki_againstchristians] In New Spain the Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún and his Nahua collaborators, Antonio Valeriano, Martín Jacobita, Alonso Vegerano, Pedro de San Buenaventura and others, compiled the twelve books of the Florentine Codex between 1559 and 1577: 2,446 pages and 2,472 illustrations on the gods, the calendar, the heavens, medicine and the conquest from the Mexica side, confiscated by the crown in 1577 and now in Florence's Laurentian Library. [cite:vt34_whe_florentine] Landa, who burned the Maya books, recorded their calendar and a key to their script in his Relación, which Yuri Knorozov used in the 1950s to show that Maya writing was largely syllabic. [cite:vt34_wiki_landa] The Huarochirí Manuscript, compiled in Quechua under the priest who prosecuted the practices it records, and Arriaga's manual of extirpation preserve Andean religion in its enemies' words. [cite:vt34_ency_extirp] [cite:vt34_wiki_arriaga] And the Codex Borgia, a pre-conquest book of the 260-day calendar showing Tonatiuh receiving offerings, has been in the Vatican Library since 1902, which has digitised it and made it public. [cite:vt35_wiki_borgia]

A few of the groups' own texts came through as well. The Cathar Book of Two Principles, the Occitan ritual of Lyon and the Bogomil Secret Supper, the Interrogatio Iohannis, all survive in manuscript. [cite:vt28_wiki_catharism] [cite:vt28_lyons_traditio]

Kept alive

The third route is continuous use, and here the survivors are living communities rather than manuscripts. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which has never been under Rome's jurisdiction, keeps a Bible its own website counts at 81 books, including 1 Enoch, Jubilees and the three books of Meqabyan; it became self-governing under its own patriarch in 1959 and counts its members in the tens of millions. [cite:vt27_eotc_books] [cite:vt27_wiki_basilios] [cite:vt27_wiki_eotc] Its canon is its own, not a museum of a lost Bible, and it accepts the Council of Nicaea. [cite:vt27_eotc_chalcedon] The Mandaeans, who honour John the Baptist as their greatest teacher and practise repeated baptism in running water, are the one living community that scholars commonly class among the Gnostic religions; they are not Christians, their origins are disputed, and the war in Iraq after 2003 killed or drove out about nine in ten of the Iraqi community, leaving 60,000 to 100,000 worldwide. [cite:vt24_wiki_mandaeans] In Ethiopia, Rome's one sustained attempt to change a church's practice, the Latinisation of 1622 to 1632, was reversed by the same emperor who had imposed it. [cite:vt27_wiki_mendes]

In the Americas continuous use took Catholic form. In the Andes, Pachamama is honoured with the ch'alla and the offerings of August and joined to the Virgin of Candelaria; the Virgin of Copacabana, carved by the Indigenous sculptor Francisco Tito Yupanqui and enthroned in 1583, stands near a site the Inca held sacred and draws Indigenous and Catholic pilgrims alike; and the pilgrimage of Qoyllurit'i, inscribed by UNESCO in 2011, combines Catholic and pre-Hispanic worship and greets the first rays of the sun. [cite:vt36_wiki_pachamama] [cite:vt36_wiki_copacabana] [cite:vt35_unesco_qoyllur] In Mexico the Tzotzil Maya of Chamula pray to Our Father Sun/Christ, and the Totonac voladores still descend from their pole. [cite:vt35_everyculture_chamula] [cite:vt35_unesco_voladores] In Cuba and Brazil the Yoruba orishas carried by enslaved Africans live on in Santería, Oshún beside Our Lady of Charity of El Cobre and Yemayá beside Our Lady of Regla, and Iemanjá is honoured on Brazil's beaches every 2 February and New Year's Eve. [cite:vt36_wiki_santeria] [cite:vt36_wiki_yemoja] The Plains nations kept the Sun Dance through the years of the ban, and hold it every year today. [cite:vt35_wiki_sundance] In Goa the devotees of Shri Mangesh carried their linga by night across the border in 1560, and the temples rebuilt beyond Portuguese rule still stand. [cite:vt34_goagov_mangueshi] And the counter-case also shows continuous use: Japan's hidden Christians kept their faith behind Buddhist forms for more than two centuries, and about 30,000 came out of hiding when the ban was lifted in 1873. [cite:vt35_wiki_kakure] [cite:vt35_audit_spencer_kosatsu]

Found again

The fourth route is revival, and for the philosophy of the mystery schools it began early. The doctrine of the soul's ascent passed into Christian mystical theology through the writings ascribed to Dionysius the Areopagite, which drew heavily on Proclus and were translated into Latin by Eriugena in 862; it passed into Arabic through the Theology of Aristotle, a ninth-century paraphrase of Plotinus that shaped al-Kindi and Avicenna, and through the Arabic Proclus that became the Latin Liber de causis. [cite:vt33_sep_dionysius] [cite:vt33_wiki_theologyaristotle] [cite:vt33_sep_proclus] Marsilio Ficino translated the Hermetic writings for Cosimo de' Medici in 1462 or 1463, and Renaissance readers took them for a wisdom older than Plato until Isaac Casaubon dated them to the Christian era in 1614. [cite:ts13_wiki_hermetica] The Rosicrucian manifestos of 1614 to 1616 announced a brotherhood for which there is no evidence; real Rosicrucian orders appeared only in the eighteenth century, and AMORC, among the best known today, was founded in the United States in 1915. [cite:ts13_wiki_rosicruc] [cite:ts13_wiki_amorc] Jules Doinel founded the Église Gnostique in Paris in 1890, the first of the modern Gnostic churches. [cite:vt24_wiki_doinel] G. R. S. Mead's English Pistis Sophia of 1896 and Jung's writing carried the word "Gnosis" into the twentieth century, and Elaine Pagels's The Gnostic Gospels of 1979 carried the Nag Hammadi texts to a general readership. [cite:vt26_wiki_mead] [cite:vt24_enc_pagels] Freemasonry, organised in its modern form by the Grand Lodge founded in London on 24 June 1717 and condemned by Rome since 1738, survives as a fraternity whose relations with the Church are set out in [scene:vt30_rosicrucians_masons|Part Thirty]. [cite:vt30_wiki_pgle] [cite:vt30_vn_ddf2023] In Cusco, Inti Raymi, the Inca sun festival whose open celebration ceased under Spanish rule, was restaged at Sacsayhuamán in 1944 by Humberto Vidal Unda and Faustino Espinoza Navarro from Garcilaso's description, and has been performed every 24 June since. [cite:vt35_infobae_inti] [cite:vt35_wiki_intiraymi] Each revival describes itself as the return of something old; the record usually shows a modern founding that drew on old texts, which is itself a kind of survival.

The institution has revived some of what it once set aside. Mary Magdalene, fused with a sinful woman by Gregory I about 591, was separated from her in the Roman calendar in 1969 and given a feast as "apostle of the apostles" on 3 June 2016. [cite:vt26_pearse_greg33] [cite:vt26_va_feast2016] Galileo's case was reopened by a papal commission and closed by John Paul II's address of 31 October 1992. [cite:vt29_coyne_galileo]

Parallels beyond Christianity

The tension between inner knowledge and religious authority is not only a Christian story. In Judaism, the Kabbalah developed a map of the divine in ten sefirot, aspects through which the divine is manifest, as an inner tradition within rabbinic Judaism rather than against it; the readings of Jacob's struggle as an ascent of the soul, from Philo to the Kabbalah, are set out in [scene:ts13_jacob|The Theology Shield]. [cite:ts13_wiki_tiferet] In Islam, the Sufi teacher al-Hallaj was executed in Baghdad in March 922 with the caliph's approval, charged in terms that presented him as a rebel against the Kaaba; one of his sayings put the true pilgrimage around "the Kaaba of one's heart". [cite:vt32_brit_hallaj] [cite:vt32_wiki_hallaj] The ancient mysteries and the ascent pattern they share with these traditions are traced in [scene:ts13_mysteries|The Theology Shield's chapter on the mysteries]. The parallels show a recurring pattern, not a single lineage: no documented line of transmission joins the Valentinians, the Sufis and the Kabbalists, and none is claimed here.

What stays open

Some questions this book could not settle, because the evidence that would settle them is lost, unpublished or still argued among specialists. The table names each and what would close it, as of October 2026.

The end of the record

Book One of this volume asked whether the Holy See's refusal of Zionism was a front, and found that it was not. Book Two asked what the institution took, buried and kept, and its answer is less tidy. The institution did build a mediated, obligatory and, from the sixth century, taxed system over teachings that had offered a direct path; it did condemn, exclude and, in the Middle Ages, burn the people who kept such teachings; and from the twelfth century it did so under its own canons; its own leaders acknowledged in 2000 that "men of the church" had sometimes used methods not in keeping with the Gospel. [cite:vt24_ce_tithes] [cite:vt28_fordham_lat4c3] [cite:vt28_america_2000] It did not choose its Bible at Nicaea, did not order the Gnostic gospels burned in any document yet found, did not suppress the Ethiopian Bible, and did not act alone. [cite:vt22_canons] [cite:vt27_hessayon] [cite:vt21_fc_laws] Beyond the Gnostics, emperors and bishops closed the mystery cults; crowns, conquistadors, friars and bishops dismantled the sun cults and burned the books and quipus of the Americas, outside the Inquisition's reach; and the mother goddesses were pressed into Marian forms that their own peoples then made theirs. [cite:vt21_wiki_theodpagan] [cite:vt34_arch_mani] [cite:vt34_wiki_lima3] [cite:vt36_sahagun1576] What it excluded did not disappear. It survived in a jar, in a bookseller's codex, in its enemies' refutations and its own inquisitors' registers, in a church in the Ethiopian highlands and a people baptising in the rivers of Iraq, in four Maya books, a friar's twelve volumes and a pope's library, in the pilgrims who greet the sun at Qoyllurit'i and the devotees of Oshún at El Cobre, and it is now printed, translated and read more widely than at any time since it was written. The record does not say whether that recovery was an accident or a pattern; it says what was done, and what was kept.

books.title: The Theology Shield
books.subtitle: Christian Zionism from the Puritans to CUFI, 1600s–2026
books.intro:
This volume is about Christian Zionism: the belief, held by some Protestants, that God's promises to Abraham still bind Christians to support the Jewish people's return to the land and, since 1948, the State of Israel. It was written to answer direct questions. Where did the belief come from, and is it true that Cyrus Scofield invented it? What did Darby's system and Scofield's notes actually teach about Israel, and who paid for the notes? How did a Protestant reading of prophecy become an organised political force, from Blackstone's petition of 1891 to Christians United for Israel, and what did Israeli governments and American politicians gain from it? How does what this volume calls the theology shield work, the move that turns a dispute about a state's policies into a dispute with God, and where has it failed? And what do the churches, Palestinian Christians and a younger generation of evangelicals say against it?

The record answers some of these questions and not others. It shows Christian belief in a Jewish return in print from 1609, a Foreign Secretary asking the sultan in 1840 to admit Jewish settlers as "a check" on Egypt's ruler, and a creed adopted at Niagara in 1878 that Israel "shall be restored to their own land," all before the Scofield Bible of 1909. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] [cite:ts2_cojs_palmerston1840] [cite:ts3_ak_niagara] It shows Scofield jailed on forgery charges in 1878 and released when they were dropped on 6 November 1879, his Bible funded by Brethren-linked businessmen, and no document behind the story that Samuel Untermyer or the Rothschilds paid for it. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts4_cyf] It shows the International Fellowship of Christians and Jews reporting $318 million in revenue for 2024, a vice president promising the embassy move at CUFI's summit in 2017, two Texas pastors praying at its opening on 14 May 2018, and a president saying in 2020 that it was "for the evangelicals." [cite:ts8_pp_ifcj] [cite:ts12_ncr_pence2017] [cite:ts12_cnn_pastors] [cite:ts9_almon_trump2020] It shows white evangelical Protestants in May 2026 the only American religious group with a majority favourable to the Israeli government, 57 per cent, down from 71 per cent in 2024, with Republicans aged 18 to 29 at 28 per cent. [cite:ts11_pew_2026] [cite:ts11_crosswalk_pew] It does not show that end-times belief caused any American decision on its own, that Scofield's notes called for a Jewish state, or that the millions who tell pollsters they support Israel reason the way the shield's most vocal users do. [cite:ts5_sac_deut30] [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway]

The book is in fourteen parts. The first twelve follow the belief from the Puritans to the officials of 2017 to 2026. [scene:ts1_defined|The shield defined] [scene:ts12_officials|The shield in office] Part Thirteen sets out, as a labelled interpretive lens beside what Hebrew philology and history document, the inner reading of the name Israel that this platform holds. [scene:ts13_israel_lens|The inner reading] Part Fourteen keeps a ledger of the claims made about Christian Zionism and sorts the volume's findings into what is settled, contested and open as of October 2026. [scene:ts14_myths|The ledger] [scene:ts14_record|What the record settles] Throughout, beliefs and acts are attributed to named churches, organisations and individuals, never to Christians, evangelicals, Jews or Israelis as a whole; survey figures carry their survey, date and population; myths are named as myths, with the evidence, including the antisemitic accusation behind the story of a Jewish financier steering Christian belief; and the stated position of each person or organisation is set beside the criticism of it. Several stories often told about the Scofield Bible, a forgery conviction, a second divorce, an Untermyer subsidy, a 1917 reference to the Balfour Declaration and a framework virtually absent before 1909, find no support in the record. [scene:ts4_rumours|Part Four: the rumours tested] The volume is a companion to The Greater Israel Architecture, Road to 1948 and The Divine 3+1.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Shield Defined
chapters.intro: Part One fixes the terms the rest of the volume uses. It defines Christian Zionism, distinguishes it from the things it is often confused with (restorationism, dispensationalism, evangelicalism as a whole, Catholic teaching and Jewish Zionism), and joins the two senses of the phrase "theology shield" into one working definition, stated as the volume's frame rather than its finding. It then takes the verse at the centre of the subject, Genesis 12:3, "I will bless them that bless thee", and sets out the two ways Christians read it: as a promise to Abraham's descendants that now applies to the Jewish people and the modern state, and as a promise fulfilled in Christ and the church. For each reading it names who holds it, from Scofield's 1917 note to a United States senator in 2025, and what it does and does not commit them to.
chapters.outro: Part One established that Christian Zionism is a belief carried by named organisations, not a church, and that it is older and wider than the end-times system most often tied to it: Britannica defines it by prophecy, while Goldman traces it from the Puritans through covenant, prophecy and cultural affinity. [cite:ts1_brit_cz] [cite:ts1_penn_goldman] Its premise is held by large shares of white evangelical respondents (82 per cent in Pew's 2013 survey said God gave the land to the Jewish people), but the premise does not fix a policy: in LifeWay's 2017 poll only 23 per cent backed a Palestinian state and 46 per cent were unsure. [cite:ts1_pew_2013] [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] The volume's working term, the theology shield, joins two senses (a promise substituted for an argument, and criticism recast as religious hostility), and is to be tested, not assumed; the case that illustrates the second, the removal of a commissioner in February 2026, carries both the chair's stated reason and the commissioner's own remarks. [cite:ts1_hill_boller] [cite:ts1_ji_boller] Genesis 12:3 is read in two ways: Scofield's 1917 note, CUFI and Senator Cruz apply the blessing clause to "the Jew" and later to the state, while Paul's reading in Galatians, the Catholic Church, the Jerusalem church heads of 2006, a Church of Scotland report of 2013 and the Presbyterian Church (USA) in 2024 locate its fulfilment in Christ and decline a religious warrant for the state. [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] [cite:ts1_cp_cruz] [cite:ts1_bg_gal316] [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] [cite:ts1_wiki_jerdecl] [cite:ts1_pcusa_2026] Part Two goes back before Darby, to the Puritans and British restorationists who first read a Jewish return into prophecy. [scene:ts2_puritans|Part Two: before Darby]

sections.h: What Christian Zionism Is, and What This Volume Means by a Theology Shield
sections.html:
Christian Zionism is support for the Jewish return to the land of Israel, and since 1948 for the State of Israel, on Christian theological grounds. Definitions differ on one point, which turns out to matter. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as "a religious and political Christian movement that supports the return of the Jewish Diaspora to a homeland in Palestine as a prerequisite for the end-time." [cite:ts1_brit_cz] That definition ties the movement to prophecy about the last days. The historian Samuel Goldman, in God's Country: Christian Zionism in America (2018), draws it more widely. His publisher describes the book as telling the story "from the Puritans to 9/11," and it names three sources of American Christian support for a Jewish state: covenant, prophecy and cultural affinity. [cite:ts1_penn_goldman] On the wider account, prophecy about the end of the world is one motive among three, not the definition of the thing.

This volume uses the wider definition and keeps the narrower one in view. Christian Zionism, as used here, means the belief, held by some Protestants, that God's promises to Abraham still apply to the Jewish people and to the land, that the modern state stands in some relation to those promises, and that Christians therefore have a duty to support it. The belief is older than the system of prophecy most often linked to it. It grew out of English Puritan "restorationism" in the seventeenth century and later out of John Nelson Darby's dispensationalism, and not every Christian Zionist is a dispensationalist. [cite:fw_wiki_christianzionism] Part Two follows the older line from the Puritans to Lord Shaftesbury, and Part Three follows Darby's. [scene:ts2_puritans|Part Two: before Darby] [scene:ts3_darby|Part Three: Darby]

What it is not

Christian Zionism is not a church. It has no creed of its own, no clergy and no membership roll. It lives inside denominations, seminaries, broadcasters and organisations that hold it in different forms and to different degrees. Its largest organised vehicle in the United States is Christians United for Israel (CUFI), founded by the San Antonio pastor John Hagee in 2006, which says it had more than seven million members by 2019 and more than ten million by 2023; those figures are CUFI's own. [cite:ts1_jvl_cufi] Hagee has stated the organisation's ground in one sentence: "We believe in the promise of Genesis 12:3 regarding the Jewish people and the nation of Israel," which he calls "an eternal covenant between God and the seed of Abraham." He has also said the support is not aimed at converting Jews and is owed as "a debt of gratitude to the Jewish people." [cite:ts1_jvl_cufi] Part Eight takes CUFI and its predecessors in turn. [scene:ts8_cufi|Part Eight: CUFI]

Nor is Christian Zionism the same thing as dispensationalism, though the two overlap heavily. Dispensationalism is a system for reading the whole Bible. The Reformed theologian Keith Mathison, a critic of the system, puts its centre plainly: "at its heart is the distinction between Israel and the church." It began with Darby in the nineteenth century and spread through the American Bible conferences and the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909. [cite:ts1_lig_dispens] A dispensationalist will usually be a Christian Zionist; a Christian Zionist need not be a dispensationalist.

It is not the position of American evangelicals as a whole, still less of American Christians. Belief that the land was a divine gift is widespread among white evangelical Protestants: in a Pew Research Center survey published in October 2013, 82 per cent of them said God gave the land of Israel to the Jewish people, against 40 per cent of American Jews. [cite:ts1_pew_2013] In a LifeWay Research poll of 2,002 Americans with evangelical beliefs in September 2017, 80 per cent said Israel's founding in 1948 fulfilled biblical prophecy, yet only 23 per cent said Israel should sign a treaty giving the Palestinians a state, and 46 per cent were unsure. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] A poll share describes the answers a sample gave to the questions it was asked. It does not describe every believer, and it does not show which policies respondents want. Part Eleven sets out the large body of evangelical, mainline, Catholic, Orthodox and Palestinian Christian opinion that rejects the belief. [scene:ts11_churches|Part Eleven: the churches]

It is not a Catholic doctrine. The Holy See's Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews asked Catholics in 1985 to understand the Jewish "religious attachment which finds its roots in biblical tradition" without adopting "any particular religious interpretation of this relationship," and said that "the existence of the State of Israel and its political options should be envisaged not in a perspective which is in itself religious," but by reference to "the common principles of international law." [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] Rome's earlier record, from Pius X's refusal to Herzl in 1904 to its rejection of millenarian teaching, is in the opening volume. [scene:gx_s05|One verse, two readings]

Finally, it is not Zionism among Jews, which has its own history, its own internal arguments and, in the religious Zionist current, its own reading of the land promise; that reading is treated in The Greater Israel Architecture. [scene:gi11_religious|The religious engine] Christian Zionism is a non-Jewish support for Jewish return, argued on Christian grounds. [cite:fw_wiki_christianzionism]

The theology shield: two meanings

The title of this volume uses a phrase that has two senses, and neither of them is simply another name for Christian Zionism. In the first, the theology shield is a substitute argument. Where the historical case for the founding of 1948 is contested, a biblical claim of divine promise and eternal covenant is offered instead, as a second line of argument meant to close discussion. In the second, the theology shield is a recasting: the treatment of political criticism of the Israeli state as if it were religious hostility to Judaism. The first sense is about what is said in defence of a state's claim. The second is about what is done to its critics.

An example from 2026 shows why the second sense needs care. At a hearing of the White House Religious Liberty Commission on antisemitism on 9 February 2026, the commissioner Carrie Prejean Boller told Rabbi Ari Berman of Yeshiva University: "I'm a Catholic and Catholics do not embrace Zionism. Just so you know." The commission's chair, the Texas lieutenant governor Dan Patrick, removed her two days later, writing that "No member of the Commission has the right to hijack a hearing for their own personal and political agenda on any issue." She refused to resign and wrote that she "will never bend the knee to the state of Israel." [cite:ts1_hill_boller] Jewish Insider reported that at the same hearing she pressed the Jewish witnesses on whether they would consider her antisemitic for believing that Jews killed Jesus, and that she had defended the commentator Candace Owens. [cite:ts1_ji_boller] One reading takes the removal as the shield at work against a religious position. Patrick's stated reason was her conduct of the hearing, and, by Jewish Insider's report, her own questions invoked the ancient charge that Jews killed Jesus. Both halves belong to the record, and Part Ten takes the case up in full. [scene:ts10_mechanism|Part Ten: how the shield works]

The definition used in this volume

The two senses describe one move seen from two sides, and this volume joins them. Here, the theology shield means the use of a scriptural claim, above all Genesis 12:3 read as applying to the modern state, to move a question about that state's policies off ground where it can be argued on evidence (history, law, the record of conduct) and onto ground where disagreement becomes a matter of faith. It works in two ways. It can substitute a promise for an argument, which is the first sense. It can recast an argument as an offence against God or against the Jewish people, which is the second.

Christian Zionism is the largest organised constituency that carries this move in American politics, but the two are not the same. Many Christian Zionists argue their case on strategic or moral grounds as well, and the shield is also used by people who are not Christian Zionists at all: religious Zionist Jewish arguments from the land promise belong to the first sense, and the charge that criticism of a state is hostility to a faith can be made by anyone. [scene:gi11_religious|The religious engine] The term is this volume's analytical frame, not a finding. A stronger claim, that the whole pro-Israel apparatus exists because without it the consensus would not hold, goes further, and this volume does not adopt it. Whether the shield has worked, where and on whom, and where it has failed are questions Parts Nine to Twelve test against the record. [scene:ts10_failures|Part Ten: where it fails]

Two cautions follow from the definition. First, it describes an argument, not a people. Statements are attributed in this volume to named organisations and named individuals, with their own stated positions beside any criticism, and survey results are given with their dates and populations. Second, it does not decide the theology. Whether God's promise to Abraham applies to a state founded in 1948 is a question about how scripture should be read, and the next section sets out the two main answers and who holds each. [scene:ts1_genesis|Genesis 12:3 read two ways]

sections.h: Genesis 12:3 Read Two Ways
sections.html:
One verse carries more of the weight of Christian Zionism than any other. In Genesis 12, God calls Abram, later Abraham, to leave his country for a land he will be shown, and promises: "And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed" (King James Version). The New International Version has "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you," and the English Standard Version renders the second clause "him who dishonors you I will curse." [cite:ts1_bg_gen123] The promise of land follows in the same narrative and is widened at Genesis 15:18 to run "from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates." [cite:gi1_bg_gen1518] Bruce Fisk, a senior research fellow of the Network of Evangelicals for the Middle East, writing in the journal Bibliotheca Sacra in 2023, opened his study of the verse with the observation that "Genesis 12:3 often serves as warrant for standing with Israel and blessing the Jewish people." [cite:ts1_fisk_bsac]

The words are not in dispute. The dispute is over who the "thee" of the promise is today. One reading identifies it with Abraham's physical descendants, the Jewish people, and, since 1948, with the State of Israel. The other holds that the promise reached its fulfilment in Christ and passes, through him, to all who share Abraham's faith, so that it is not a standing instruction about any modern government. The opening volume set out the two readings in brief; this section names who holds each and what each commits them to. [scene:gx_s05|One verse, two readings]

The first reading: a promise to Abraham's descendants

The reading did not begin with the Scofield Reference Bible, but Scofield gave it a widely printed form. His note summarising the covenant with Abraham, in the 1917 edition, now in the public domain, takes the promise clause by clause. On "curse him that curseth thee" it says: "Wonderfully fulfilled in the history of the dispersion. It has invariably fared ill with the people who have persecuted the Jew—well with those who have protected him. The future will still more remarkably prove this principle." [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] The same note calls the covenant "wholly gracious and unconditional" and says that the gift of the land "is modified by prophecies of three dispossessions and restorations", two of them past, with the Jewish people in the third dispersion until a restoration at Christ's return. [cite:ts1_sac_gen12] [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] Three details are often lost when the note is quoted. It speaks of "the Jew", a people, because no Jewish state existed when it was written. It reads the verse's last clause, the blessing of all families of the earth, as "the great evangelic promise fulfilled in Abraham's Seed, Christ." And it reads the "great nation" clause as fulfilled three ways at once: in Abraham's natural descendants, in a spiritual offspring of all who have faith, and through Ishmael. [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] Scofield held the two readings together; what was distinctive was his claim that the blessing-and-curse clause still governed how nations fared. The note itself is examined in Part Five. [scene:ts5_notes|Part Five: the notes]

Fisk traces the same use of the verse further back, to Lord Shaftesbury, who argued that God blesses the nations that bless Israel and judges those that do not, and to William Blackstone, who petitioned President Benjamin Harrison in 1891. [cite:ts1_fisk_bsac] [scene:ts2_shaftesbury|Part Two: Shaftesbury] The step from "the Jew" to the state came after 1948. John Hagee, who founded CUFI in 2006, has stated it directly, in a statement the Jewish Virtual Library quotes without a date: "We believe in the promise of Genesis 12:3 regarding the Jewish people and the nation of Israel." [cite:ts1_jvl_cufi] Replying to the Jerusalem church heads' declaration of 2006 (below), representatives of the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem, Bridges for Peace and Christian Friends of Israel grounded their support in the Bible, including God's gift of the land to the Jewish people. [cite:ts1_wiki_jerdecl]

The reading reached a national audience in June 2025. In an interview with the broadcaster Tucker Carlson posted on 18 June, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said: "As a Christian, growing up in Sunday school, I was taught from the Bible that those who bless Israel will be blessed," and "I want to be on the blessing side of things." Carlson asked: "Those who bless the government of Israel?" Cruz replied that the text "doesn't say the government of, it says the nation of Israel." David Friedman, a former US ambassador to Israel, wrote afterwards that "This is the same nation of Israel referred to in the Bible." [cite:ts1_cp_cruz] The hinge of the dispute is whether the Israel of the promise and the state of 2025 are the same Israel; Friedman said they are. How officials in office used the verse is the subject of Part Twelve. [scene:ts12_officials|Part Twelve: officials]

No major poll asks about Genesis 12:3 itself; the closest measures are questions about the land. Pew's 2013 finding that 82 per cent of white evangelical Protestants say God gave the land to the Jewish people, and LifeWay's 2017 finding that 80 per cent of Americans with evangelical beliefs see 1948 as fulfilled prophecy, show a large constituency for the premise. [cite:ts1_pew_2013] [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] The same LifeWay survey shows how far the premise is from a policy: under a quarter backed a Palestinian state and nearly half were unsure. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] Even Hagee separates the two. He has said that "Israelis – and they alone – have the right to make existential decisions about land and peace." [cite:gi11_jpost_hagee]

The second reading: fulfilled in Christ and the church

The second reading takes its key from Paul. In his letter to the Galatians he argues that the promise was made to Abraham's "seed" in the singular: "He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ." [cite:ts1_bg_gal316] Later in the same chapter (3:29) he tells his readers that if they belong to Christ they are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to the promise. Covenant theology, the system of the Reformed churches, builds on this. Mathison states its position as the affirmation "that there is one people of God", in which "Paul defines Abraham's seed in terms of Jesus Christ", so that Jewish and Gentile believers alike become Abraham's offspring through Christ. [cite:ts1_lig_dispens] On this reading the blessing of "all families of the earth" is the point of the verse, and it is not an instruction about any modern government.

The reading takes different forms in different churches. Modern Catholic teaching does not combine it with a claim that God has rejected the Jewish people: the Catechism states that the books of the Old Testament keep "a permanent value, for the Old Covenant has never been revoked." [cite:ts1_ccc_121] What the Catholic Church declines to do is read the modern state theologically. Its 1985 guidance, quoted in the previous section, says the state's political options are to be judged by "the common principles of international law." [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985]

Several churches have gone further and rejected the first reading by name. The Jerusalem Declaration on Christian Zionism of 22 August 2006, signed by the Latin Patriarch Michel Sabbah, the Syriac Orthodox Archbishop Swerios Malki Mourad, the Anglican Bishop Riah Abu El-Assal and the Lutheran Bishop Munib Younan, called Christian Zionism a "false teaching that corrupts the biblical message of love, justice, and reconciliation." [cite:ts1_wiki_jerdecl] A Church of Scotland report of 2013, "The Inheritance of Abraham?", called on the church to "refute claims that scripture offers any peoples a privileged claim for possession of a particular territory." Jewish bodies objected strongly: the Scottish Council of Jewish Communities called it "an outrage to everything that interfaith dialogue stands for," and Rabbi David Rosen of the American Jewish Committee called it "rather pathetic"; a revised version was issued on 17 May 2013, ahead of the General Assembly's debate. [cite:ts1_scojec_cos2013] In 2024 the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church (USA) adopted an overture "On Confessing our Complicity in Christian Zionism," which, in the words of a church official, called for "rejecting Christian Zionism in all its forms." [cite:ts1_pcusa_2026] Part Eleven sets out these and other statements, including Palestinian Christian ones, in full. [scene:ts11_palestinian|Part Eleven: Palestinian Christians]

The argument also runs inside evangelicalism. After Hagee's 2011 statement that Jerusalem should never be divided, Richard Mouw, president of Fuller Theological Seminary, argued that God's promise to bless Ishmael binds Christians too, and Joel Hunter of the National Association of Evangelicals' board said Hagee's view reflects "a limited portion of Christians who are millennial dispensationalists in their theology." [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] Fisk's 2023 article put the question directly to Christian Zionists, among four he posed: whether God promised to bless the modern state of Israel at all. [cite:ts1_fisk_bsac]

What the record settles

The record settles what the verse says, how Scofield annotated it, and which named churches, organisations and officials have taken which side, with dates. It shows that the first reading was in print long before the state existed and was applied to the state only after 1948, and that neither reading fixes a policy: a large share of those who hold the first are unsure about a Palestinian state, and churches that hold the second recognise Israel while declining to read it in scripture. [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] It does not settle the theology, which turns on prior commitments about how scripture is to be read; this volume does not adjudicate it. What it does test, from Part Two onward, is what happened when the first reading was turned into politics. [scene:ts2_puritans|Part Two: before Darby]

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: Before Darby: British Restorationism
chapters.intro: Part Two goes back before John Nelson Darby and Cyrus Scofield to the British and American Protestants who first read the Hebrew prophets as promising the Jewish people a return to their land. It follows that belief, which historians call restorationism, from Thomas Brightman's commentaries and Henry Finch's suppressed book of 1621, through Cromwell's readmission of the Jews and the Boston sermons of Increase Mather, to the London Society for Promoting Christianity amongst the Jews, founded in 1809 to convert them. It then shows how one evangelical peer, Lord Shaftesbury, brought the idea to his wife's stepfather, the Foreign Secretary Lord Palmerston, and what Palmerston did with it in 1840 for reasons of his own; how a Protestant bishopric was set up in Jerusalem in 1841; and how a restorationist chaplain, William Hechler, became Theodor Herzl's ally in 1896. A third section traces the phrase "a land without a people" from a Methodist sermon to Israel Zangwill and tests the claims made about it. Throughout, the prophetic motive and the imperial one are kept apart, and the aim most restorationists held, the conversion of the Jews, is stated plainly.
chapters.outro: Part Two established that Christian belief in a Jewish return to the land is three centuries older than the Scofield Bible: it ran from Brightman's commentaries, first printed in 1609, and Finch's book of 1621 through Increase Mather in Boston to the London Society of 1809, and in most of its forms it expected the Jews to convert. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] [cite:ts2_wiki_finch] It became policy only when it met a strategic interest. Shaftesbury helped secure a British consul in Jerusalem in 1838, and Palmerston's dispatch of 11 August 1840 asked the sultan to admit Jewish settlers as "a check" on Muhammad Ali, without a word of scripture; the sultan declined. [cite:ts2_wiki_young] [cite:ts2_cojs_palmerston1840] [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] The Anglo-Prussian bishopric of 1841 gave the mission a bishop, a convert from Judaism, and had little practical effect. [cite:ts2_wiki_bishopric] The phrase "a land without a people" was coined by Christian clergy before any Zionist used it; how widely Zionists later used it, and what it meant, remain contested among named historians. [cite:ts2_muir_meq] [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] By the 1890s a restorationist chaplain stood beside Herzl, and the centre of gravity had moved to the United States, where Blackstone presented his memorial in 1891. [cite:ts2_wiki_hechler] [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] What restorationism lacked was a system that told believers where they stood in a timetable of the end. Part Three turns to the man who supplied one, John Nelson Darby, and to the conferences that carried his system across the Atlantic. [scene:ts3_darby|Part Three: Darby and the system crossing the Atlantic]

sections.h: The Puritan Root, 1609–1815
sections.html:
The belief that the Jewish people would one day return to the land of Israel, and that Christians should welcome and even help that return, is older than every name usually attached to it. It is older than Cyrus Scofield's Bible of 1909, older than John Nelson Darby's system of the 1830s, and older than the Zionist movement itself. Historians call the earlier form "restorationism". Andrew Crome, writing in the Critical Dictionary of Apocalyptic and Millenarian Movements, defines it as "the pre-twentieth-century Christian belief that the Jewish people would return" to Palestine, and notes that it "is not synonymous with either premillennialism or dispensationalism" and "significantly predates Darby's innovations". [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] That is the first fact this part establishes, and it corrects a common claim: that Christian support for a Jewish return was a recent invention, scarcely present in Protestant thought before 1909. The 1909 Bible and its system are the subject of [scene:ts5_notes|Part Five] and Darby of [scene:ts3_darby|Part Three]. This section goes back three centuries further.

Reading the prophets literally

For most of Christian history the dominant reading of the Hebrew prophets held that their promises to Israel had passed to the Church. Restorationism began when a group of English Protestant scholars started to read some of those promises as applying to the Jewish people themselves, in a future that would include a return to the land. The earliest influential figure was Thomas Brightman (1562–1607), a Puritan commentator who leaned towards Presbyterian church government but remained a serving minister of the Church of England until his death. In commentaries on Daniel, Revelation and the Song of Songs, published after he died, he argued that prophecy concerned the Jews' earthly future: they would convert to Christianity and then rule the world from Palestine. His ideas first appeared in print in the United Provinces, the Dutch Republic, in 1609. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] Brightman and other commentators of the period suggested 1656 as the year of the Jews' restoration. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm]

The next step brought the idea into conflict with the Crown. In 1621 Henry Finch, a lawyer and Member of Parliament, published The World's Great Restauration, or Calling of the Jews, and with them of all Nations and Kingdoms of the Earth to the Faith of Christ. Finch appears to have predicted that the Jews would regain temporal dominion, and the book applied the prophets' sayings to the Jews themselves rather than to the Church in general. [cite:ts2_wiki_finch] James I treated it as a libel. Crome's account is that Finch had suggested kings would lay their crowns before the Jews in Jerusalem. Finch was arrested in April 1621 and released after he disavowed passages that could be read as derogatory to the sovereign and apologised for having written "unadvisedly"; William Laud attacked the book in a sermon in July 1621 and it was suppressed. [cite:ts2_wiki_finch] [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] The episode shows the limit of the early form. Finch's restoration was an act of God inside a Christian scheme, ending in conversion, and a king could read it as a claim against his own authority. It was not yet a policy anyone in government would carry.

Cromwell, Menasseh ben Israel and New England

The prophetic reading touched English law once in the seventeenth century, though not in Palestine. Jews had been expelled from England in 1290. Oliver Cromwell had hoped that the Barebones Parliament of 1653 might advance the Jews' return, and in December 1655 he called a conference at Whitehall on readmitting them. Menasseh ben Israel, a Sephardi rabbi from Amsterdam, made the case on two grounds at once: commercial benefit, and a prophetic argument that the Jews had first to be scattered to "the ends of the earth", England included, before their redemption. The conference ended without a resolution. In 1656 Cromwell quietly recognised a small Jewish community in London. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] The pairing of prophecy with commerce at Whitehall in 1655 recurs in every later episode in this part, down to Palmerston's dispatch of 1840 in [scene:ts2_shaftesbury|the next section].

The same reading crossed the Atlantic with the Puritans. Increase Mather, the Boston minister, argued in The Mystery of Israel's Salvation (1669) that God would use the Jews to overcome the Roman Church and the Ottoman Empire, and that they would gain earthly pre-eminence and return to Palestine before their conversion; he restated the view in a Dissertation of 1709. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] An American line of restorationist thought therefore existed more than two centuries before William Blackstone's petition of 1891, which is taken up in [scene:ts6_blackstone|Part Six].

Not a gap but a continuous strand

A common telling has restorationism flaring in the 1650s, going quiet for over a century, and reviving only with the French Revolution. Crome rejects that picture. He writes that restorationist thought "did not go into hibernation between the late 1650s and the French Revolution", and that it remained "an established part of Protestant discourse", carried in the commentaries of eighteenth-century churchmen such as Thomas Newton and the Baptist John Gill. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] The American and French Revolutions then increased prophetic speculation; in 1795 Richard Brothers, a former naval officer, claimed to be "king of the Hebrews" and promised a restoration by 1798. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] Brothers is a reminder that the strand had a fringe as well as a learned mainstream, and that both read the same verses.

The London Society, 1809

The strand acquired an institution in 1809. The London Society for Promoting Christianity amongst the Jews was founded that year, at first on a non-denominational basis, through the work of Joseph Frey, a German Jewish convert. It ran into large debts, and in 1815 it was reconstituted as an Anglican society, financed by Lewis Way, a wealthy lawyer. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] Its purpose is in its name: it was a mission to convert Jews. The Society itself denied any particular focus on prophecy, but Crome finds in its sermons, library and publications strong restorationist interests. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] The Society matters for the rest of this part because it supplied people and money. Its later president was Lord Shaftesbury, from 1848; its missionary and convert Michael Solomon Alexander became the first Protestant bishop in Jerusalem in 1841; and it helped fund that bishopric. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] [cite:ts2_wiki_bishopric]

What the restorationists wanted, and how Jews saw it

The documents support a precise statement of aim, which should not be read back into the stated aims of later Christian Zionist organisations; what those organisations say about conversion is set out in [scene:ts8_cufi|Part Eight]. Crome concludes that "the vast majority of restorationists attempted to effect the conversion of Jews to Christianity", and that this call to give up Jewish identity "was often seen by Jews themselves as a form of both personal and corporate attack". [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] Brightman's Jews convert and then rule; Finch's are called "to the Faith of Christ"; Mather's return before converting; the London Society existed to make converts. The restoration these writers expected was part of a Christian story whose ending was a Christian one.

The historian Donald M. Lewis, in The Origins of Christian Zionism (Cambridge University Press, 2010), offers a more generous frame. On the summary of his reviewer David Fox Sandmel, Lewis describes a Protestant "Teaching of Esteem", set against the older Catholic "Teaching of Contempt", in which Jews were honoured as God's chosen people; he ties it to Britain's view of itself as an elect nation and to evangelical anti-Catholicism. [cite:ts2_sandmel_lewis] Sandmel, writing in Studies in Christian-Jewish Relations in 2011, accepted that this philosemitism had been under-studied, but faulted the book on two counts that bear on this volume: Lewis does not explore the tension between esteem and the goal of conversion, and actual Jews, apart from converts and Moses Montefiore, are largely absent from his story. [cite:ts2_sandmel_lewis] Both readings can be held together. The restorationists of this period were, by their own lights, friends of the Jewish people, and the friendship they offered was conditional on a change of faith that most Jews refused.

The finding of this section is therefore narrower than either side of the modern argument usually allows. Christian belief in a Jewish return to the land did not begin with Darby or Scofield; it ran from Brightman's commentaries of 1609 through Finch, Mather and the eighteenth-century commentators to an organised missionary society in 1809. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] But it was a theology of conversion, not a programme for a Jewish state, and until the 1830s no government acted on it. How it reached a Foreign Secretary is the subject of [scene:ts2_shaftesbury|the next section]. The interpretive questions about Genesis 12:3 that underlie the whole tradition are in [scene:ts1_genesis|Part One].

sections.h: Shaftesbury, Palmerston and the Jerusalem Bishopric, 1838–1896
sections.html:
Restorationism became a matter of state through one man's family connections. Anthony Ashley-Cooper, known as Lord Ashley before he inherited the earldom, was an evangelical member of Parliament and a social reformer. On 10 June 1830 he married Lady Emily Cowper, the stepdaughter (and, his biographers' sources suggest, probably the natural daughter) of Lord Palmerston, the Foreign Secretary. [cite:ts2_wiki_shaftesbury] The outline is in [scene:bc_s05|Restoration before Zionism]. This section sets out the documents and the dates, and keeps two motives in view throughout: the prophetic hopes of Shaftesbury and the London Society, and the strategic calculations of the minister who acted on them.

A consul in Jerusalem, 1838–1839

The first concrete result was diplomatic. Shaftesbury helped persuade Palmerston to send a British consul to Jerusalem, and William Tanner Young, a protégé of Shaftesbury's, was appointed vice-consul in 1838 and arrived in 1839. [cite:ts2_wiki_shaftesbury] [cite:ts2_wiki_young] The timing was strategic as well as religious: since 1831 Syria, Palestine included, had been held by Muhammad Ali, the governor of Egypt, in rebellion against the Ottoman sultan, and Britain's position in the region was shifting. [cite:ts2_wiki_shaftesbury] From mid-1839 Young asked Palmerston for authority to extend British protection to Jews in the city. A modern study quoted in his biography suggests he tried to serve two masters, the London Society and the Foreign Office; the Scottish ministers Andrew Bonar and Robert Murray M'Cheyne, who met him, described him as moved by "a deep and enlightened attachment to the cause of God's ancient people". [cite:ts2_wiki_young] He was consul from 1841 to 1845.

In January 1839 Ashley carried the argument into print. Reviewing Lord Lindsay's travel letters in the Quarterly Review, he proposed that Jews be resettled in Palestine, the first such proposal by a major British politician, and he argued in economic terms that the land needed only "capital and skill". [cite:ts2_wiki_shaftesbury] Crome summarises the article as urging Britain to establish a Jewish homeland in Palestine. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm]

Palmerston's dispatch, 11 August 1840

The minister did not share the prophecy. In 1840, with the eastern crisis over Muhammad Ali at its height, Ashley pressed Palmerston to have Britain promote a Jewish presence in Palestine under Ottoman authority and British protection. Crome, drawing on Shaftesbury's diary, records that Ashley found himself "forced to argue from worldly reasons" because Palmerston had little interest in prophecy, and that Palmerston instructed his ambassador to raise the idea with the sultan without informing the cabinet. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm]

The instruction survives in the Foreign Office files (FO 78/390, No. 134), from Palmerston to Lord Ponsonby, the ambassador at Constantinople, dated 11 August 1840. It is written entirely in the language of interest. Palmerston reported that there existed among the Jews of Europe "a strong notion that the Time is approaching when their nation is to return to Palestine". He argued that if they returned "under the sanction and protection, and at the invitation of the Sultan", they would be "a check upon any future evil designs of Mehemet Ali or his Successor", and he added: "It is well known that the Jews of Europe possess great wealth." [cite:ts2_cojs_palmerston1840] The dispatch makes no appeal to scripture. It offers the sultan settlers and capital, and Britain a client population in a province contested with Egypt. The sultan did not view the proposal favourably, and nothing came of it. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm]

The Protestant bishop in Jerusalem, 1841

The second result was ecclesiastical. In 1841 King Frederick William IV of Prussia sent his envoy Christian Bunsen to London with a proposal for a joint Protestant bishopric in Jerusalem, which the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of London welcomed. The Act of Parliament that made it possible came into force on 5 October 1841. An endowment of £30,000 provided the bishop with £1,200 a year; Britain and Prussia were to nominate alternately, with a Canterbury veto over Prussian choices. [cite:ts2_wiki_bishopric] Crome credits Shaftesbury's work with Bunsen for the result, and records that the London Society partly funded it and that restorationists saw it as a means of preparing Jews for conversion. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm]

The choice of bishop made the purpose plain. Michael Solomon Alexander had been a rabbi in Plymouth before his conversion in 1825; he became a missionary of the London Society and professor of Hebrew and rabbinical literature at King's College London. He was consecrated on 7 November 1841, reached Jerusalem early in 1842, and died near Cairo on 23 November 1845. [cite:ts2_wiki_bishopric] Crome judges that the bishopric had little practical effect. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] It was contested at home from both sides: German Lutherans thought too much had been conceded, and the Tractarians of the Oxford Movement opposed it as a Protestant compromise; John Henry Newman counted it among the reasons for his move to Rome. Prussia ended the arrangement on 3 November 1886, after which the Church of England kept the see alone. [cite:ts2_wiki_bishopric] In Lewis's account, Shaftesbury's three aims, a consul, an Anglican church and a joint bishopric, had all been achieved by 1849. [cite:ts2_sandmel_lewis]

The long middle and the American handover

Shaftesbury became president of the London Society in 1848 and later helped found the Palestine Exploration Fund in 1865, but his influence in government waned from the mid-1850s. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] Lewis, who calls him the "leading Christian Zionist of the nineteenth century", traces a line from his advocacy to the British attitudes that helped produce the Balfour Declaration in 1917, more than thirty years after his death. [cite:ts2_sandmel_lewis] That line is an argument about a climate of opinion, not a documented chain of decisions, and it is tested where Balfour's own motives are examined, in [scene:ts6_balfour|Part Six] and [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration]. By the end of the century the centre of gravity was shifting to the United States. In March 1891 the Chicago evangelist William Blackstone presented a memorial to President Benjamin Harrison and Secretary of State James Blaine urging that Palestine be given back to the Jews. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] His petition, and the system of prophecy behind it, belong to the story told in [scene:ts3_darby|Part Three] and [scene:ts6_blackstone|Part Six].

Hechler and Herzl

The British strand had one more direct link to the Zionist movement, and it was personal. William Hechler, born in Benares in 1845, was chaplain to the British embassy in Vienna from 1885 to 1910. In 1884 he had published The Restoration of the Jews to Palestine, and from a reckoning of 1,260 years counted from a prophecy of the reign of the Caliph Umar (637–638) he expected a decisive event in 1897 or 1898. [cite:ts2_wiki_hechler] Theodor Herzl's Der Judenstaat appeared in 1896. Herzl recorded their first meeting, on 10 March 1896, and was not wholly persuaded by his visitor: "I take him for a naïve visionary with a collector's enthusiasm." [cite:ts2_wiki_hechler] Hechler was nonetheless useful. He had been tutor in the household of the Grand Duke of Baden and arranged Herzl's audience with the Grand Duke on 25 April 1896; he attended the First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897. [cite:ts2_wiki_hechler] The Jewish Telegraphic Agency's obituary in February 1931 said that he introduced Herzl to Wilhelm II and accompanied him when the Kaiser received him in Jerusalem, and that Herzl's diaries mention him more often than anyone else. [cite:ts2_jta_hechler1931] Hechler's own biography records a more indirect route to the Kaiser, through Philipp zu Eulenburg, after an early attempt failed. [cite:ts2_wiki_hechler] The Kaiser episode and what it achieved are told in [scene:hz_s01|Herzl's search for a charter], and Hechler's maps of a biblical Palestine in [scene:gi2_herzl|The Greater Israel Architecture].

Hechler differed from the restorationists of the earlier sections on one point that matters for the rest of this volume. His biography records that he did not hold Jewish conversion to be a precondition for the return or for the Second Coming, and quotes him: "It is the duty of every Christian to love the Jews." [cite:ts2_wiki_hechler] With him the strand passed from a theology of conversion towards practical support for a Jewish political movement on that movement's terms. What it did not have, in 1840, 1841 or 1898, was the power to deliver anything: Palestine was the sultan's, and each request failed at Constantinople. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] [cite:ts2_cojs_palmerston1840]

sections.h: "A Land without a People": The Phrase and Its Myths
sections.html:
The restorationist strand left one legacy that outlived every institution it built: a phrase. "A land without a people for a people without a land" is among the most quoted lines in the argument over Palestine, usually as a Zionist slogan that denied the existence of the Arab population. Its documented history is different on three counts. It was coined by Christians, not by Zionists; the clergyman who first published it had travelled in the country and knew it was inhabited, and the first Zionist to use it dropped it within a few years; and how widely Zionists later used it is a matter on which named historians disagree. Shorter accounts appear in [scene:bc_s05|Restoration before Zionism] and [scene:rd1_arabquestion|the Arab question]. This section sets out the chain in full.

The chain of wording

The earliest wording that the literature cites comes from Richard Watson, a Methodist minister who died in 1833, in a sermon: "There is a people without a country, and a country without a people." [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] Accounts that follow Diana Muir in the Middle East Quarterly (Spring 2008), name Alexander Keith as the first to publish the phrase. Keith remains the first well-documented printed use, but not the first use. [cite:ts2_muir_meq] [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout]

Keith was a Church of Scotland minister who travelled to Palestine in 1839 on behalf of his church. In The Land of Israel According to the Covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob (1843) he described the Jews as "a people without a country" and their land as, in great measure, "a country without a people". [cite:ts2_muir_meq] [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] The compressed form, "a land without a people and a people without a land", first appeared in an 1844 review of Keith's book in a Scottish Free Church magazine. [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] Muir points out that Keith knew the country was inhabited: he had travelled through it, and returned about five years later with his son, George Skene Keith. [cite:ts2_muir_meq]

Shaftesbury used a variant with a different noun. In a letter of July 1853 he described Greater Syria as "a country without a nation" that needed "a nation without a country", and he wrote the same idea in his diary. [cite:ts2_wiki_shaftesbury] [cite:ts2_muir_meq] The sources disagree about the recipient: Muir names Palmerston, though she gives him Aberdeen's family name, George Hamilton Gordon, while the encyclopaedic accounts name the Prime Minister, Lord Aberdeen. [cite:ts2_muir_meq] [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] The library's [scene:bc_s05|Restoration before Zionism] chapter is right to date the phrase to 1853; an account that places it within the 1839–40 episode is not. Shaftesbury returned to the image in 1875, at a meeting of the Palestine Exploration Fund, as "a country without a people". [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] His 1887 biography by Edwin Hodder carried the wording to a wide readership. [cite:ts2_muir_meq]

The first recorded use by a Zionist came from the writer Israel Zangwill, in the New Liberal Review of December 1901: "Palestine is a country without a people; the Jews are a people without a country." [cite:ts2_muir_meq] Zangwill did not hold the line. In a speech in New York around 1904 he said that "Palestine proper has already its inhabitants", and by 1917 he was writing that the country held 600,000 Arabs. [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout]

Three claims about the phrase, tested

Three claims circulate about the phrase, and they need to be separated because the evidence for each is different. The first is that it was a Zionist coinage. On the record it was not: every documented use before 1901 is by a Christian writer, and the earliest are by restorationist clergy. [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] [cite:ts2_muir_meq]

The second is that it was a widely propagated Zionist slogan. Here the historians divide. Muir, writing for a journal published by the Middle East Forum, searched seven major American newspapers up to 1948 and found "Jewish national home" more than 3,000 times and Zangwill's wording four times, all before 1906; she found no Zionist organisation or leader that adopted it, and notes that it does not appear in Herzl's books, letters or diary. She concluded that the "widely propagated" claim "should be retired" unless new evidence appears. [cite:ts2_muir_meq] Adam Garfinkle, in Jewcentricity (2009), wrote that early Zionists who validated the phrase did not do so "easily or for long". On the other side, the Israeli historian Anita Shapira describes it as common among Zionists of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and Boaz Neumann, citing among others a book by David Ben-Gurion and Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, finds pioneer writings full of descriptions of Palestine as empty and desolate. Rashid Khalidi calls it a "widely propagated Zionist slogan". [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] The newspaper count measures the phrase in the American press; it does not settle how often it was used in Hebrew or in the settlements, which is where Shapira and Neumann locate it. The claim is therefore contested, not settled in either direction.

The third is about meaning: whether the phrase claimed the land was empty. Muir and the historian Gertrude Himmelfarb read "people" in the nineteenth-century sense of a nation, so that the phrase denied the inhabitants national standing rather than existence; Shaftesbury's own noun, "nation", fits that reading. [cite:ts2_muir_meq] [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] Edward Said read it as a way to "cancel and transcend an actual reality", the Arab population. Nur Masalha argues that Zangwill and Chaim Weizmann did not mean it literally but treated the inhabitants as not "worth considering". Gudrun Krämer puts the middle position in one line: "Palestine contained people, but not a people." [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] The two readings differ less than the dispute suggests. On either one, the phrase described a country with inhabitants and declined to count them as the people whose claim mattered.

For this volume the significance is the direction of travel. The phrase began as a restorationist reading of prophecy and geography, made by Christian clergy, the best documented of whom had seen the country and its people, and passed to a Zionist writer half a century later, who abandoned it within a few years. Its later life as an emblem of the conflict, used by critics of Zionism and disowned or reinterpreted by its defenders, belongs to the politics of the twentieth century, and the volume's ledger of myths and settled points returns to it in [scene:ts14_myths|Part Fourteen].

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: Darby and the System Crossing the Atlantic
chapters.intro: Part Three follows the system that turned an old Protestant hope into a detailed map of the future. It begins with John Nelson Darby, the Anglo-Irish clergyman who left the Church of Ireland, helped found the Plymouth Brethren and set out, at the Powerscourt conferences of the early 1830s, a way of reading the Bible in which Israel and the church are two separate peoples with two separate destinies; it weighs the long-running claim that his doctrine of a secret rapture was borrowed from a young Scottish visionary, Margaret MacDonald. It then explains in plain terms what the system teaches about Israel and the church, and tests the common claim that Darby made a Jewish return to Palestine a condition of Christ's coming. Last, it follows the system across the Atlantic: Darby's own journeys, the St. Louis pastor James H. Brookes and the Niagara Bible Conferences with their 1878 creed, the evangelist Dwight L. Moody and his Bible institute, and Arno Gaebelein, who would supply the prophetic notes for the Scofield Reference Bible.
chapters.outro: Part Three established that the system later identified with the Scofield Bible was built in the British Isles in the 1820s and 1830s and was well rooted in America long before 1909. Darby, by his own account, separated the prophets' "kingdom" from the church in 1827 and taught at Geneva in 1840 that "The church is in relationship with the Father, and the Jews with Jehovah"; the claim that his rapture doctrine came from Margaret MacDonald's 1830 vision is unproven and, on her own text, unlikely. [cite:ts3_ice_darby] [cite:ts3_darby_hopes1] [cite:ts3_wiki_macdonald] [cite:ts3_strand_auss] His system did not make a Jewish return a precondition for Christ's coming: the rapture was "any-moment," and the restoration he described, in which "there will only be a remnant saved," belonged to the judgments that follow it; as late as 1905 Gaebelein called Zionism "a movement ... of unbelief." [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] [cite:ts3_darby_hopes10] [cite:ts3_wiki_gaebelein] Americans adopted the eschatology without the Brethren church order, and through Brookes's Niagara Creed of 1878, with its Israel "restored to their own land," the prophetic conferences from 1878, Moody and the Bible institutes, the system had institutions, a creed and a teaching network before any reference Bible existed. [cite:ts3_stunt_akenson] [cite:ts3_ak_niagara] [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] [cite:ts3_wiki_mbi] Part Four turns to the man who came out of that network and gave the system its most durable vehicle: Cyrus Ingerson Scofield, and what the record shows of his life. [scene:ts4_record|Part Four: Scofield the Man]

sections.h: John Nelson Darby and the Brethren
sections.html:
The British restorationists described in Part Two had read a Jewish return to Palestine into prophecy for two centuries before John Nelson Darby began to write. [scene:ts2_shaftesbury|Part Two: Shaftesbury and the restorationists] What Darby added was not the hope itself but a system: a way of dividing the whole Bible, and the whole of history, into separate stages with separate peoples, in which Israel and the church never merge. That system, later called dispensationalism, is the theology that most of the American organisations in later parts of this book grew out of. This section sets out who Darby was, how the movement he led began, and the long argument over where his most famous doctrine came from.

Lawyer, curate, separatist

Darby was born in Westminster on 18 November 1800, to an Anglo-Irish family, and was educated at Westminster School and Trinity College Dublin, where he graduated in 1819 as Classical Gold Medallist. He entered an inn of court to train for the law, then concluded that practising it conflicted with his religious beliefs. He was ordained a deacon of the Church of Ireland in 1825 and a priest in 1826, and served as curate of Delgany in County Wicklow. [cite:ts3_wiki_darby]

His break with the established church came in stages. He resigned his curacy in protest when William Magee, Archbishop of Dublin, required converts to swear allegiance to King George IV. Around 1827 and 1828 he joined a small interdenominational circle in Dublin, among them the missionary Anthony Norris Groves and John Gifford Bellett, that met to "break bread" without clergy or denominational rules. By 1832 the group regarded itself as a distinct assembly, and similar meetings at Plymouth in England gave the movement its common name, the Plymouth Brethren. He is believed to have left the Church of Ireland around 1831, though the year is uncertain. [cite:ts3_wiki_darby]

The movement divided in 1848 in a quarrel over whether one assembly's discipline bound the others, a dispute in which Darby's former ally Benjamin Wills Newton was a principal party. The result was two streams: the Open Brethren, whose congregations govern themselves, and the Exclusive Brethren, who followed Darby's view that assemblies must act together. [cite:ts3_wiki_darby] Darby spent the rest of his life travelling, writing and translating; he produced Bible translations in German (the Elberfeld Bible), French and English, the last finished after his death. He died at Bournemouth on 29 April 1882. [cite:ts3_wiki_darby]

Powerscourt, 1831 to 1833

The ideas took public form at the Powerscourt conferences, gatherings on prophecy held annually from 1831 to 1833 at the County Wicklow estate of Darby's friend Theodosia Wingfield, Lady Powerscourt, a wealthy widow. The Dictionary of Premillennial Theology records that Darby set out his views on the church and on the end times there, "including the pre-tribulation rapture." [cite:ts3_wiki_darby] That doctrine holds that true Christians will be taken up from the earth to meet Christ before a final period of tribulation, rather than living through it.

The conference record is thinner than the summary suggests. Notebooks from the 1831 meeting survive, and the historian James Fazio has argued from them that Darby was still resisting pre-tribulational ideas at that conference; others read the evidence differently. [cite:ts3_brarchive_powerscourt] Darby himself dated his turn earlier. Around 1827, while recovering from a riding accident, he came to believe that the "kingdom" promised in Isaiah and the other prophets was something entirely different from the Christian church. [cite:ts3_wiki_darby] In a letter of 1879 he wrote: "What set me free in 1827 is still the theme on which my soul dwells." [cite:ts3_ice_darby]

The Margaret MacDonald dispute

Where Darby's rapture doctrine came from has been argued over since the nineteenth century, and the argument still circulates. Its fullest form concerns Margaret MacDonald (1815–1840), a young woman of Port Glasgow in Scotland who, around 1830, during a wave of charismatic revival linked to the London preacher Edward Irving, gave a series of prophetic utterances about the coming of Christ. Her words were first published in 1840. [cite:ts3_wiki_macdonald]

Two critics built the case. The biblical scholar Samuel Prideaux Tregelles alleged that the idea of a secret rapture came from a charismatic "utterance" in Irving's church; in an account Thomas Ice summarises, Tregelles dated it "about the year 1832." [cite:ts3_wiki_macdonald] [cite:ts3_ice_darby] In the 1970s the American writer Dave MacPherson went further, arguing in The Unbelievable Pre-Trib Origin (1973) and later books that MacDonald's 1830 vision was the source, and that Darby had taken the doctrine from it during a visit to the MacDonalds in 1830. [cite:ts3_strand_auss] [cite:ts3_wiki_macdonald]

The case has not persuaded historians on either side of the theological argument.
