Darby and Newton, sent by the Brethren to investigate the 1830 manifestations, concluded that they were demonic, which makes borrowing from them unlikely; according to John Bray (1992), Darby had written down pre-tribulational views by January 1827, three years before the events in Scotland; and MacDonald's own text, read in full, places believers inside the "fiery trial," a posttribulational view, while the version printed in 1861 left out two passages that make this plain. [cite:ts3_wiki_macdonald] The sharpest assessment came from a reviewer outside Darby's tradition. Kenneth Strand, writing in the seminary journal of the Seventh-day Adventist Andrews University, found that MacPherson's chief witness attributed the idea to Irving, "not Margaret Macdonald," that "It is impossible to prove that Darby adopted" the view from her, and that "the case for the 'unbelievable pre-trib origin' falls apart." [cite:ts3_strand_auss]

Defenders of the doctrine add their own argument, which is stated here as theirs. Thomas Ice of the Pre-Trib Research Center holds that Darby reached his view by December 1826 or January 1827 from his reading of the church as distinct from Israel, and that MacDonald's text "does not come close to even teaching a pre-trib rapture." [cite:ts3_ice_darby] The fairest summary is that the MacDonald origin is unproven and, on the text, unlikely; that Darby's own account dates his central idea to 1827; and that whether he had fully worked out the rapture by the 1831 conference remains a matter on which specialists differ. The doctrine's novelty is not in dispute: Weber notes that earlier premillennialists placed the rapture at the end of the tribulation, and that the Princeton theologian A. A. Hodge called the new version "an unscriptural and unprofitable theory." [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999]

sections.h: What the System Teaches About Israel and the Church
sections.html:
Dispensationalism is often described by its most dramatic doctrine, the rapture, but its core is a rule for reading the Bible. This section sets that rule out in plain terms, using Darby's own lectures and the account of Timothy Weber, a historian of American premillennialism, and then tests two claims that circulate about it: that Darby taught the Jews must return to their land before Christ could come back, and that his system made its followers political Zionists from the start.

Two peoples, two plans

A "dispensation," in this usage, is a period in which God deals with humanity on particular terms. Dividing history into such periods was not new; the dispensationalist theologian Charles Ryrie argued that the scheme Scofield later printed followed the eighteenth-century hymn-writer Isaac Watts's division of the ages rather than Darby's. [cite:ts3_wiki_scofield] What was distinctive in Darby's system was the claim, in Weber's summary, that "God had two completely different plans operating in history": one for an earthly people, Israel, whose promises concern a land, a throne and a nation; and one for a heavenly people, the church, whose hope lies outside this world altogether. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999]

Darby stated the distinction directly in eleven lectures he gave in Geneva in 1840, published under the title The Hopes of the Church of God in connection with the destiny of the Jews and the nations as revealed in prophecy. "The church is in relationship with the Father, and the Jews with Jehovah," he said; the church's calling was "participation in a coming heavenly glory," and believers should learn to separate the prophecies about Israel "from those which refer to us Gentiles." [cite:ts3_darby_hopes1] In the tenth lecture he put the consequence for the reading of the Old Testament prophets plainly: "The gospel does not occupy itself with the earthly blessings of the Jews, which is the matter of these prophecies." [cite:ts3_darby_hopes10]

This cut against the older reading, discussed in Part One, in which the church inherited the promises made to Israel and the prophecies of a restored Israel were fulfilled spiritually in Christianity. [scene:ts1_defined|Part One: the shield defined] But it was not the first Protestant challenge to that reading. The English Puritans and their successors, described in Part Two, had already taught that the promises to the Jews would be fulfilled literally, including a return to the land. [scene:ts2_puritans|Part Two: the Puritan readers] Darby's contribution was to make the separation total and permanent: Israel's promises were not transferred to the church, and the church's hope was not Israel's.

The paused clock

The second element is a timetable. Dispensationalists read the "seventy weeks" of the Book of Daniel, chapter 9, as a prophetic calendar for Israel. In Weber's account of Darby's scheme, when the Jewish nation rejected Jesus, God "suspended the prophetic timetable at the end of Daniel's sixty-ninth week" and "began building a new and heavenly people—the church." The present age is therefore a gap in Israel's calendar, not a stage of it. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999]

The rapture closes the gap. Because the church belongs to heaven, it is removed from the earth in a "secret, any-moment, pre-tribulational Rapture," and only then does Israel's calendar resume. "Once the heavenly people of God have been raptured, Darby believed, the divine script can be played out to the end": the seventieth week of Daniel, a seven-year tribulation, the rise of the Antichrist, and finally the visible return of Christ to reign on earth for a thousand years. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999]

A Jewish return as precondition: what Darby taught

A widely repeated account holds that Darby taught that the Jews had to return to their land before Christ could come back, and that this turned a political programme into prophecy. The system as Darby set it out does not quite say that. Its central hope, the rapture, was "any-moment": nothing had to happen first. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] The restoration of Israel belonged to the events that follow the church's departure. In his 1840 lectures Darby described that restoration in grim terms. "Though the people of Israel will be restored in their land, there will only be a remnant saved," he said; "those who rejected the Christ will be subjected to the Antichrist," and "Two thirds of the inhabitants will be cut off in the country of Israel itself after their return." [cite:ts3_darby_hopes10]

Those lines are Darby's reading of the prophets in 1840, quoted so that the system is described in its founder's words rather than an opponent's. They are not a statement of what later dispensationalists, still less Christian Zionist organisations, teach or want; the stated positions of those organisations, including CUFI's, are set out with their own words in Parts Eight and Ten. [scene:ts10_mechanism|Part Ten: how the shield works] What the lines do show is that in Darby's own scheme a Jewish return to the land was not a reward, nor a precondition for Christ's return, but the opening of a time of judgment.

That had a practical consequence for how the first generation of American dispensationalists read the Zionist movement when it appeared in the 1890s. Premillennialists, Weber writes, read "signs of the times" in current events, and "the rise of Zionism" was among them. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] But a sign was not an endorsement. Arno Gaebelein, a dispensationalist teacher who had worked as a missionary among Jewish immigrants, told an audience in 1905 that "Zionism is not the divinely promised restoration of Israel," but "a political and philanthropic undertaking," and that "The great movement is one of unbelief." [cite:ts3_wiki_gaebelein] [cite:ts3_demy_gaebelein] His magazine was nonetheless sympathetic to Zionism's progress. [cite:ts3_demy_gaebelein] The move from reading Zionism as a sign to backing the state of Israel as a religious duty came later, and is the subject of Parts Six to Eight.

The finding for this part is therefore narrower than the familiar one. Darby did not invent the expectation of a Jewish return, and he did not make it a political cause. What he built was a framework in which Israel, as a people distinct from the church, kept its own future on earth, centred on its land, and in which world events could be read as the stage being set for that future. Later teachers, organisations and governments would draw political conclusions from that framework that Darby did not draw; how they did so is traced in the parts that follow.

sections.h: Crossing the Atlantic: Brookes, Niagara, Moody and Gaebelein
sections.html:
Darby's system reached the United States a generation before the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909, and it arrived through people and meetings, not a book. This section follows that route: Darby's own journeys, the Presbyterian pastor in St. Louis who became the system's chief American organiser, the summer Bible conferences that gave it a creed, the evangelist whose schools carried it to a mass audience, and the missionary who supplied the prophetic notes for Scofield's Bible. It ends with what the record shows about how far the system had spread by 1909, which corrects a common claim.

Darby in North America

Darby made at least five journeys to North America between 1862 and 1877, working mostly in New England, Ontario and the Great Lakes region; one extended trip took him on from Toronto across the Pacific. [cite:ts3_wiki_darby] Some accounts give the number as six; the index of his correspondence, on which the lower figure rests, supports "at least five."

What Americans took from him was selective. The Brethren way of church life, in which believers left the denominations to meet without clergy, found few takers among American Protestant pastors; Darby's reading of prophecy found many. The usual summary is that "America did not embrace Darby's ecclesiology as it did his eschatology." [cite:ts3_wiki_darby] The historian Timothy Stunt, reviewing Donald Akenson's 2018 study of Darby's American influence, Exporting the Rapture, describes dispensationalist eschatology as "the one aspect of his teaching that really caught on in North America." [cite:ts3_stunt_akenson] The Americans who took it up, such as the Presbyterian Brookes below, stayed inside their own denominations. In this book's reading, that is one reason the system spread as widely as it did: it asked nothing of a congregation's structure, only of its reading of the Bible.

James H. Brookes and the Niagara conferences

The most important of those carriers was James Hall Brookes (1830–1897), a Presbyterian minister from Tennessee who pastored the Walnut Street Presbyterian Church in St. Louis from 1864 and, after a move in 1879, the Washington and Compton Presbyterian Church until his death. He edited a periodical, The Truth, which with the journal Watchword served as an organ of the premillennial movement. [cite:ts3_wiki_brookes]

Brookes's lasting work was the Bible conference. Its origins are usually traced to an informal meeting in New York in 1868 of eight men linked to a premillennial periodical, Waymarks in the Wilderness; in 1875 a small group including Nathaniel West, Brookes, W. J. Erdman and H. M. Parsons met near Chicago, and in July 1876, at Swampscott, Massachusetts, the group named itself the "Believers' Meeting for Bible Study." From 1883 to 1897 it met at Niagara-on-the-Lake in Ontario, which gave it the name by which it is known. [cite:ts3_bt_niagara] Accounts differ on dates: Wikipedia gives 1875 as the founding and describes annual meetings from then to 1897, except 1884. [cite:ts3_wiki_niagara] According to Weber, the meeting ran for two weeks each summer, premillennialists quickly took over its leadership, and Brookes "presided for more than 20 years." [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999]

In 1878 Brookes drew up a fourteen-point statement of faith, which the conference formally adopted in 1890. [cite:ts3_bt_niagara] Its first article affirmed that "the Holy Ghost gave the very words of the sacred writings." [cite:ts3_bt_niagara] Its fourteenth set out the end-times view. As reproduced in reference sources, it holds that the world "will not be converted during the present dispensation" but "is fast ripening for judgment," amid "a fearful apostasy in the professing Christian body," and that Christ "will come in person to introduce the millennial age, when Israel shall be restored to their own land." [cite:ts3_ak_niagara] The creed does not set out Darby's full system or a pre-tribulation rapture, but it writes premillennial return and the restoration of Israel into a statement of faith adopted by a conference of American Protestant ministers. [cite:ts3_wiki_niagara]

The same year brought a public platform. "The First American Bible and Prophetic Conference was held in New York City in 1878," Weber records, and it was successful enough that six more followed. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] The premillennial movement was no longer a cluster of readers of British pamphlets; it had annual meetings, a creed and periodicals of its own.

Moody and the Bible institutes

Dwight L. Moody, the Chicago-based evangelist, was by the end of the century "Mr. Evangelical" to nearly everyone, in Weber's phrase, and he "was an early convert to premillennialism," though not a very doctrinaire dispensationalist. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] His best-known summary of his mission reflected the pessimism of that view about the present age: "I look upon this world as a wrecked vessel. God has given me a life boat and said to me, 'Moody, save all you can.'" [cite:ts3_en_moody] Weber notes that nearly every major revivalist from Moody's time to the First World War adopted his eschatology. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999]

Moody's lasting institution was a school. At a meeting in Chicago on 22 January 1886 he founded the Chicago Evangelization Society, to train Christian workers; it was renamed the Moody Bible Institute after his death in 1899, added a publishing arm and, in 1926, a radio station, WMBI. The institute has historically been identified as dispensational and as Zionist. [cite:ts3_wiki_mbi] It was one of many. "Almost without exception," Weber writes, "the scores of Bible institutes founded between 1880 and 1940 taught the new premillennialism," and their graduates, as pastors, missionaries and Bible teachers, carried it into congregations across the country. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] How those schools and their successors spread the system is traced in Part Seven. [scene:ts7_schools|Part Seven: the schools]

The road to Scofield

The man who would put the system into the margins of an Oxford Bible came out of exactly this network. Cyrus Scofield came under Brookes's mentorship in St. Louis; by late 1879 he was assisting Moody's evangelistic campaign in the city and became secretary of the St. Louis YMCA. He attended the Niagara conference in 1888, was called in 1895 to pastor Moody's church at East Northfield, Massachusetts, and presided at Moody's funeral in 1899. [cite:ts3_wiki_scofield] His earlier life, including his legal troubles in St. Louis, is set out in Part Four. [scene:ts4_record|Part Four: Scofield's record]

The last link was Arno C. Gaebelein (1861–1945), a German immigrant who became a Methodist minister in New York, began mission work among Jewish immigrants in 1887 and from 1893 published a monthly, Tiqweth Israel (The Hope of Israel), and from 1894 the magazine Our Hope, which he edited from 1896. [cite:ts3_demy_gaebelein] He left the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1899, objecting to theological liberalism. [cite:ts3_wiki_gaebelein] When Scofield prepared his reference Bible, he asked Gaebelein to supply its prophetic portions, writing that on prophecy he would "sit at your feet." [cite:ts3_demy_gaebelein] Gaebelein's own record on Jews is mixed and is stated as the scholarship states it: he wrote that Zionism was "a movement ... of unbelief," his journal reported on Nazi atrocities against Jews from 1937 to 1945, and historians have described some of his writing as anti-Jewish. [cite:ts3_wiki_gaebelein]

Before 1909: the common claim and the record

A common claim holds that before 1909 the dispensationalist framework was virtually absent from American Protestantism. The record above does not support that. By 1909 the system had a creed adopted by a long-running conference, a series of national prophetic conferences beginning in 1878, its own periodicals, a leading evangelist among its converts and a growing number of Bible institutes teaching it. [cite:ts3_bt_niagara] [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] Before 1909 the framework was known and held by some American Protestants; what it lacked was a place in the mainstream. [scene:s05|Road to 1948: the Scofield Reference Bible] Scofield's Bible, the subject of Part Five, did not create the system; it put it into the hands of readers who had never attended a conference. [scene:ts5_edition|Part Five: the edition]

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: Scofield the Man
chapters.intro: Part Four turns from the system to the man who put it in the margins of the Bible. Cyrus I. Scofield's life before his conversion has been told twice over: by an admiring biographer who left out his first family and his time in jail, and by critics who added a conviction, a prison term, a second divorce and, in the most widely shared version, a Jewish financier behind his work. The first section follows the paper record from his Confederate enlistment in 1861 through Kansas politics, a federal attorney's post he held for six months, much of a year in a St. Louis jail on forgery charges that were dropped, the wife and daughters he left, and his conversion, ordination and Dallas pastorate. The second takes the rumours one at a time and says which of them hold.
chapters.outro: Part Four established what is documented about Scofield and what is not. He enlisted in a Confederate regiment at seventeen, was discharged as an alien in September 1862 and crossed to Union lines; he sat in the Kansas legislature and held the post of US Attorney for about six months in 1873 before being, in the Justice Department's words, "forced to resign" over money. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_doj_ks] He was jailed in St. Louis from October 1878 on forgery charges that were dropped by nolle prosequi on 6 November 1879; he was never convicted. [cite:ts4_rushing] He deserted his wife and daughters, was divorced once, in 1883, was converted in 1879, ordained in October 1883 and built a Dallas congregation, and called himself a doctor of divinity without a degree. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] [cite:ts4_wiki_kellogg] [cite:ts4_dts] The story that Samuel Untermyer sponsored or financed him rests on shared membership of the Lotos Club and an author's stated assumption, and on no document. [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts4_cyf] None of this decides whether his notes read the Bible rightly. Part Five turns to the book itself: how Oxford came to publish it, what the notes say, and who actually paid for it. [scene:ts5_edition|Part Five: the Scofield Reference Bible]

sections.h: The Record: Soldier, Politician, Debtor, Convert, Pastor
sections.html:
Cyrus Ingerson Scofield, the man whose notes framed the most widely used reference Bible of American fundamentalism, left two accounts of his life. One is the authorised biography, The Life Story of C. I. Scofield, written by his admirer Charles G. Trumbull and published in 1920, the year before Scofield died. The other is the paper record: Confederate service files, Kansas legislative journals, Department of Justice lists, court dockets and newspapers, assembled most fully by the historian D. Jean Rushing in a thesis for East Tennessee State University in 2011. [cite:ts4_trumbull] [cite:ts4_rushing] This section follows the paper record, and notes where the authorised account departs from it. The record is unflattering in places. It is set out here as documented, with nothing added.

Michigan, Tennessee and the Confederate army

Scofield was born on 19 August 1843 in Lenawee County, Michigan, the youngest of seven children; his mother died three months after his birth. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] In February 1861, aged seventeen, he was staying with a married sister in Lebanon, Tennessee. When the war began he joined the local volunteers, who became Company H of the 7th Tennessee Infantry on 28 May 1861. [cite:ts4_rushing] On 8 April 1862 he was admitted to Chimborazo Hospital in Richmond for exposure. The next day the Confederate Conscription Act extended all enlistments by three years, and Scofield wrote to the Secretary of War, George Randolph, asking to be released: he was a native of Michigan, not a Confederate citizen, he had enlisted underage while visiting his sister, and he was worn down by exposure. [cite:ts4_rushing] The discharge came on 26 September 1862, on the ground that he was "an alien friend"; Rushing notes that only 373 such alienage exemptions were granted during the war. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield]

The discharge did not end his service. Confederate authorities soon ordered him to a camp of instruction at McMinnville. Instead he walked about 75 miles north to Union-held Bowling Green, Kentucky, took the oath of allegiance to the United States, and was paroled on 18 November 1862 at the age of nineteen. Rushing treats this as desertion. [cite:ts4_rushing] Four decades later, in 1903, the Dallas chapter of the United Daughters of the Confederacy awarded him the Southern Cross of Honor. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] Trumbull's version has him serving through the whole war, under fire in eighteen battles, and decorated "for bravery at Antietam". Rushing found nothing unusual in the Confederate records for Antietam, and the documented service ends in 1862. [cite:ts4_trumbull] [cite:ts4_rushing]

St. Louis, Kansas and the attorney's office

After the war Scofield went to St. Louis. On 27 September 1866 he married Leontine LeBeau Cerré, from a prominent French Catholic family of the city, in a civil ceremony; they had two daughters, Abigail and Marie Helene, and a son, Guy Sylvester, who died in December 1874. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] He read law in his brother-in-law's office and in late 1869 moved to Atchison, Kansas. In November 1871 he was elected to the Kansas House of Representatives as a Republican for Atchison County, chaired its Judiciary Committee, and the next year won a seat for Nemaha County. In 1873 he backed John J. Ingalls in the contest for the United States Senate. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield]

Ingalls, once seated, nominated him for federal office. President Ulysses S. Grant appointed Scofield United States Attorney for Kansas on 19 March 1873; he took the oath on 8 June and resigned on 20 December, about six months later. Five days before resigning he declined to prosecute the outgoing senator Samuel Pomeroy, on the day the Chicago Tribune reported affidavits in the Pomeroy bribery affair. [cite:ts4_rushing] The Department of Justice's own history of the Kansas office says he "was forced to resign from that position due to questionable financial transactions". [cite:ts4_doj_ks] A Kansas City Journal article of 28 December 1899, "A Preacher with a Past", said he had left owing thousands to Atchison Republicans, including money he had collected on Ingalls's behalf and kept. Biographers have also reported allegations of railway bribes and forged signatures on bank notes. None of the Kansas allegations was prosecuted, and they remain allegations. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] Trumbull gives a two-year term and says Scofield left because politics was interfering with his law practice. [cite:ts4_trumbull]

The forgery case, 1877–1879

The documented legal trouble came after Kansas, and it was a case that never reached trial. In June 1877 a man named Jeptha Simpson said Scofield had obtained money from him with a note bearing the forged signature of Scofield's sister Emeline; Simpson sued in August, Emeline denied any part in it, and Scofield avoided service. [cite:ts4_rushing] Between November and December 1877 he was arrested in Milwaukee under the name "Charles Ingerson" over unpaid hotel bills. In April 1878 a second, nearly identical forgery complaint was filed in St. Louis. In October 1878 he was found in Horicon, Wisconsin, under the name "Cyrus Ingerson"; the Milwaukee Daily Sentinel exposed him on 3 October, he was held for St. Louis, and he entered the St. Louis jail on 8 October 1878. He "remained jailed much of the year". [cite:ts4_rushing] The Department of Justice history records the same fact in plain terms: he was "jailed in St. Louis on forgery charges". [cite:ts4_doj_ks]

On 6 November 1879 the court entered a nolle prosequi: the prosecution dropped the charges because it had "failed to produce enough evidence". A Topeka newspaper later reported that his "wealthy sister came forward" and settled the forged notes. [cite:ts4_rushing] Scofield was therefore jailed for much of the year before the charges were dropped, awaiting a trial that never came, and was never convicted and never sentenced. Whether he committed the forgeries is a separate question; the court record does not answer it, and the settlement report suggests why the case lapsed.

The family he left

In these same years Scofield left his wife and daughters. Leontine took the girls back to Atchison and went to work to support them; she later became the town's librarian. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_wiki_kellogg] By his own later account he had become a heavy drinker. [cite:ts4_trumbull] Leontine divorced him on grounds of desertion in 1883. He married Hettie Hall von Wartz soon afterwards (1883 in the biographer David Lutzweiler's dating, 1884 in Trumbull's), and their son Noel was born in 1888. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] [cite:ts4_trumbull] Trumbull's 1920 biography does not mention the first marriage or the daughters at all, and Scofield's will left nothing to them; his estate, including the Oxford royalties, went to Hettie and Noel. [cite:ts4_trumbull] [cite:ts4_wiki_kellogg] There was one divorce, not two.

Conversion, ordination and Dallas

Scofield dated his conversion to 1879 in St. Louis. Trumbull names a lawyer, Thomas S. McPheeters, who read scripture to him until he said "I will", and quotes Scofield on his drinking: "Christ came in, and drink went out." [cite:ts4_trumbull] Rushing places a visit to a Washington Avenue mission after the charges were dropped in November 1879. [cite:ts4_rushing] By the autumn of 1879 he was helping in Dwight L. Moody's St. Louis campaign and serving as secretary of the city's YMCA, under the mentorship of the St. Louis minister James H. Brookes, whose place in the premillennial Bible-conference movement is told in [scene:ts3_niagara|Part Three]. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] Dallas Theological Seminary's archive records that he was licensed to preach in 1880. [cite:ts4_dts]

In 1882 he took charge of a small Congregational mission in Dallas with about fourteen members. [cite:ts4_trumbull] [cite:ts4_dts] He was ordained a Congregationalist minister in October 1883, while Leontine's divorce suit was pending. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] The church, later First Congregational and now Scofield Memorial Church, grew to more than five hundred members by 1895, when he left to lead Moody's church at East Northfield, Massachusetts; he returned to Dallas in 1902–03. [cite:ts4_dts] [cite:ts4_trumbull] He had no college or seminary training, a point Trumbull himself makes, and from the early 1890s he styled himself "Rev. C. I. Scofield, D.D." although no record shows any institution granting him the degree. [cite:ts4_trumbull] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] From 1902 he worked mainly on the reference Bible that Oxford published in 1909 ([scene:ts5_edition|Part Five]). He died in New York on 24 July 1921. [cite:ts4_dts]

The record answers what kind of man Scofield was before 1879 more fully than his admirers did: a deserter from one army who later accepted the other's honour, a federal prosecutor who left office under a financial cloud, a debtor jailed for much of a year on forgery charges that were dropped, and a husband who abandoned his family. It also shows a conversion that held, a pastorate that grew, and a working life after 1879 that drew no further charges. Neither half settles whether his reading of the Bible was right. A theology is tested against texts and arguments, not against its author's character, and the volume treats Scofield's notes that way in [scene:ts5_notes|Part Five].

sections.h: The Rumours, and Which of Them Hold
sections.html:
Scofield's life has been retold for a century by two camps with opposite needs. His admirers, starting with Trumbull in 1920, smoothed it into a story of a gallant soldier and lawyer redeemed by grace. [cite:ts4_trumbull] His critics, starting with Joseph M. Canfield's hostile The Incredible Scofield and His Book (1988), set out to show that the man behind the notes could not be trusted, and some later writers went further and made him the instrument of hidden financiers. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] [cite:ts4_sfiles] Both camps produced claims that the record does not support. This section takes the most repeated of them one by one and gives each a verdict: holds, partly holds, or fails. The test is the same in each case: what a document of the time shows, as against what a later writer asserted.

"A convicted forger who served a prison sentence"

This is the most common version online. It fails as stated. Scofield was the subject of two forgery complaints in 1877–78, was arrested in Wisconsin in October 1878 and held in the St. Louis jail for much of the following year, and on 6 November 1879 the prosecution entered a nolle prosequi, dropping the charges for lack of evidence. [cite:ts4_rushing] The Department of Justice history of the Kansas office confirms the jailing; it does not mention a conviction. [cite:ts4_doj_ks] There was no trial, no verdict and no sentence. The documented version is damaging enough: much of a year in jail on forgery charges, and a newspaper report that his sister paid off the notes. [cite:ts4_rushing] Even the research site Scofield-Files, which defends him against the funding stories, concludes that he "likely was guilty". [cite:ts4_sfiles] What fails is the word "convicted" and the prison term. Some reference works went the other way: Wikipedia's article still says there is "no extant evidence in the public records" of any jailing, which Rushing's newspaper and docket citations, and the Justice Department's own page, overtake. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_doj_ks] Verdict: jailed awaiting trial holds; convicted and imprisoned fails.

"He served time in a Canadian prison"

Canfield floated the possibility that Scofield had served a prison term in Canada. Scofield-Files reports that Canadian authorities have no record of it, and no document produced by Canfield or anyone since places Scofield in a Canadian prison. [cite:ts4_sfiles] Verdict: fails for want of any record.

"Twice divorced"

Some accounts call him "twice divorced". The record shows one divorce: Leontine Cerré Scofield divorced him for desertion in 1883. His second marriage, to Hettie Hall von Wartz, lasted until his death. [cite:ts4_wiki_kellogg] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] Verdict: fails. The underlying charge, that he abandoned a wife and two daughters and later wrote them out of his authorised life and his will, holds. [cite:ts4_wiki_kellogg] [cite:ts4_trumbull]

The war hero, and the deserter

Trumbull's claim that Scofield fought through the war in eighteen battles and won the Cross of Honor for bravery at Antietam fails against the Confederate records: he was discharged on 26 September 1862 after petitioning as an alien, and the Cross was awarded in 1903 by a Dallas veterans' society, not on the battlefield. [cite:ts4_trumbull] [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] The critics' counter-label, "deserter", partly holds: after his discharge he was ordered back to a Confederate camp, went instead to Union lines and took the federal oath. [cite:ts4_rushing] The same record places him there as a Michigan-born teenager who had asked to go home. Statements that he served "from 1861 to 1865" fail. Verdict: the heroic version fails; the desertion holds, with its context.

"Dr. Scofield"

From the early 1890s Scofield signed himself "Rev. C. I. Scofield, D.D.", and Trumbull calls him "Dr. Scofield" throughout while also stating that he had no formal academic education. No record shows any college granting him a doctorate, honorary or earned, and Wikipedia's article, citing the biographer John D. Hannah on his secrecy about his past, states that he almost certainly gave deliberately inaccurate information about himself to Who's Who and to Trumbull. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] [cite:ts4_trumbull] Verdict: the critics' point holds. It says something about his self-presentation; it says nothing about whether his notes read the texts correctly.

Kansas: bribes, embezzlement and forged notes

The Justice Department's own history states that he was "forced to resign ... due to questionable financial transactions", and the Kansas City Journal reported in 1899 that he left owing thousands to Atchison Republicans, including money collected for Ingalls. [cite:ts4_doj_ks] [cite:ts4_rushing] More specific charges, railway bribes and forged signatures on bank notes, appear in later biographies and remain allegations: none was prosecuted. [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] Verdict: a forced resignation over money holds; the specific crimes are unproven.

The Lotos Club and Samuel Untermyer

The most consequential story about Scofield is not about his past but about his patrons. It holds that Samuel Untermyer, a Jewish New York lawyer who became a prominent Zionist, sponsored Scofield's admission to New York's Lotos Club and lay behind the Reference Bible. Part of this is documented. Scofield did join New York's Lotos Club: its membership book enters him on 3 March 1900, proposed by Horatio Fraser and seconded by John Elderkin. Untermyer had been a member since 1894. [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] Nothing else in the story is documented. Untermyer's name is not among Scofield's proposers. Under the club's rules a candidate was elected unless two negative ballots were cast, so a single existing member had no power to admit anyone. No letter, diary or record shows that the two men ever met. [cite:ts4_sfiles]

The link begins with Canfield. According to Scofield-Files, which cites a scan of the pages, Canfield asked on pp. 173–74 why "a godly man" would "join such a godless club", wrote "we assume" and "There must have been anticipation", and then named Untermyer as the likely sponsor. [cite:ts4_sfiles] That wording has not been checked against a copy of the book for this volume, but no one has produced a document behind the inference. Untermyer's own Zionist prominence came later: his best-known Zionist office, the presidency of the Keren Hayesod fund, began in 1921, the year Scofield died, and the standard reference entry on his life does not mention Scofield at all. [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts4_wiki_untermyer] From Canfield's assumption the story grew through internet lists (1999), websites (2001–02), and Michael Collins Piper's The High Priests of War (2004), the first to say the Rothschilds paid for the Bible, and on into books and viral posts. [cite:ts4_sfiles] A fact-check by Check Your Fact in March 2025 rated the Rothschild claim false, and the writer Mike Rothschild, who studies conspiracy theories, found no primary source for it at all. [cite:ts4_cyf] [cite:ts4_mrothschild] The documented backers of the Bible were Brethren-linked businessmen and an oil executive, named in [scene:ts5_funding|Part Five]. [cite:ts4_goeman] [cite:ts4_cyf] [cite:ts4_sfiles]

The story fails for a second reason as well. Its shape, a Jewish financier secretly steering what Christians believe, is the shape of one of the oldest antisemitic accusations, and its Rothschild form leans on publications that the writers who traced it describe as antisemitic. [cite:ts4_mrothschild] [cite:ts4_goeman] That is not why it is rejected here: it is rejected because there is no evidence for it. It is named because a reader meets it constantly, and because its persistence is part of the history this volume records. Verdict: shared club membership holds; Untermyer's sponsorship, contact and money fail.

What the man's record can and cannot prove

Critics have used the record to argue that Scofield's Bible was a confidence trick, and admirers have answered that his conversion wiped the slate clean. Scofield's own stated account, through Trumbull, was that grace changed him in 1879, and the documented record after that year contains no further charges. [cite:ts4_trumbull] [cite:ts4_rushing] Neither argument reaches the question that matters for this volume. Whether a pre-tribulation rapture or a future national restoration of Israel is in the text of the Bible is a question for the text and its readers; it was argued before Scofield, by Darby and the restorationists ([scene:ts3_darby|Part Three], [scene:ts2_puritans|Part Two]), and it is argued on its merits today. The man's record explains how he presented himself, which is relevant to how the Reference Bible was sold as the work of a learned "Dr." It does not decide whether the notes are right, and it does not make him the author of a movement that was already in motion. The volume's own ledger of these and the wider myths is in [scene:ts14_myths|Part Fourteen].

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: The Scofield Reference Bible
chapters.intro: Part Five turns from the man to the book. The Scofield Reference Bible, published by Oxford University Press in 1909 and revised in 1917, put a full dispensational commentary on the same page as the King James text, and it stayed in print through a heavily revised "New Scofield" of 1967 and later editions. This part sets out how the edition was made and sold, and corrects two claims that are often repeated: the 1917 revision did not, on any source found, refer to the Balfour Declaration, and the citable sales figure is about two million copies by 1945, not "tens of millions". It then quotes what the 1917 notes actually say about Israel, the land and the nations, and what they do not say. The last section asks who paid for the work. The documented answer is a handful of Brethren-linked businessmen and an oil executive; the widely circulated story that a Jewish Wall Street lawyer, or the Rothschilds, paid for it is traced to its sources and shown to fail.
chapters.outro: Part Five established what the Scofield Reference Bible was, what it said and who paid for it. Oxford University Press published it in 1909, through Henry Frowde and the press's New York branch, with dispensational notes printed beside the King James text; Scofield revised it in 1917, adding Ussher's dates, and a committee of nine revised it again in 1967 while keeping its seven dispensations and its Israel/Church distinction. [cite:ts5_dunlap] [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] [cite:ts5_ct_1967] No source supports the claim that the 1917 edition referred to the Balfour Declaration, and the citable sales figure is about two million copies by 1945. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] The 1917 notes say that nations which persecuted "the Jew" fared ill, that Christians do not inherit "the distinctive Jewish promises", and that Russia was Ezekiel's Gog; they place Israel's restoration to the land after "The return of the Lord", not before it. [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] [cite:ts5_sac_rom11] [cite:ts5_sac_ezek38] [cite:ts5_sac_deut30] The work was paid for by Brethren-linked businessmen, Alwyn Ball, John Pirie, John Buss and Francis Fitch, with a reported gift from the oilman Lyman Stewart; the story that Samuel Untermyer or the Rothschilds paid for it rests on Canfield's "we assume" of 1988 and Piper's unsourced claim of 2004, and fails on the record. [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts4_cyf] [cite:ts5_wiki_piper] Part Six turns from the book to politics: William Blackstone's petition of 1891, the Christian restorationists around the Balfour Declaration and the Christian committees of the 1940s. [scene:ts6_blackstone|Part Six: Blackstone, Balfour and the 1940s Committees]

sections.h: The Edition: Oxford, 1909, 1917 and 1967
sections.html:
By 1909 the system described in Part Three already had its conferences, its creed and its Bible institutes ([scene:ts3_niagara|Part Three]). What it lacked was a single book that a reader could carry into church and open at any verse. The Scofield Reference Bible supplied that book. It first appeared in 1909 under the imprint of Oxford University Press, and Scofield revised it in 1917. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] Oxford published both, and a much-revised third edition in 1967. [cite:ts5_dunlap] This section sets out how the edition came to Oxford, what kind of object it was, and how widely it sold. It also tests two claims that are often repeated.

How the book came to Oxford

The route to Oxford ran through the same Brethren circles that paid for the work (see [scene:ts5_funding|who paid]). According to a history by David Dunlap, which draws on Arno Gaebelein's 1943 account and Trumbull's 1920 biography, Henry Frowde, the Oxford publisher, was himself in Brethren fellowship and advised Scofield that Oxford was the only house able to handle the work. [cite:ts5_dunlap] A passage quoted by the fact-checking site Check Your Fact adds that Frowde coordinated publication with John Armstrong in New York, head of Oxford's American branch. [cite:ts4_cyf] The Library of Congress copy of the 1917 edition carries the imprint "New York, Oxford University Press, American Branch; London, H. Milford". [cite:ts5_ia_1917] The book was therefore an Oxford product in the ordinary commercial sense: a university press publishing, printing and selling a study Bible prepared by an outside author. What Oxford's governing Delegates discussed about it, if anything, has not been found in any source used for this volume, and nothing in the record shows that the press reviewed or endorsed Scofield's theology.

Notes on the page

The book's power lay in its layout. Scofield's Bible carried a running commentary set on the same page as the King James text: headings, references linking one theme across both Testaments, and notes that told the reader what a passage meant and where it fitted in a scheme of seven dispensations. [cite:ts5_ia_1917] [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] A reader did not have to buy a separate commentary or attend a prophecy conference to meet the system. It was printed beside the verse, in the same binding, under the name of a university press. The scheme itself is examined in the next section ([scene:ts5_notes|what the notes say]).

The title page added a further mark of authority: a list of seven consulting editors, Henry G. Weston, James M. Gray, W. J. Erdman, A. T. Pierson, W. G. Moorehead, Elmore Harris and Arno C. Gaebelein, all known names in the premillennial conference movement. The historian Ernest Sandeen wrote in 1970 that their role "has been the subject of some debate" and that "Apparently Scofield only meant to acknowledge their assistance", though some suspected he wanted to win support from both wings of the millenarian movement. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] The notes were Scofield's.

The 1917 revision, and a claim that fails

Scofield revised the work in 1917. The changes most noted by historians concern chronology: the 1917 edition attempts to date the events of the Bible and printed dates derived from Archbishop Ussher, with creation at 4004 BC, alongside a note favouring the "gap theory" of Genesis 1, which set off a debate among fundamentalists. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] The 1917 notes are now in the public domain in the United States, and the 1917 edition has remained the best-selling Scofield edition in the United Kingdom and Ireland. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb]

Some accounts say the 1917 edition incorporated references to the just-issued Balfour Declaration. That claim has no source. The reference work cited for it does not mention Balfour or Zionism in connection with the revision. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] The 1917 notes examined for this part, on Genesis 12 and 15, Deuteronomy 30, Ezekiel 38 and Romans 11, make no reference to the declaration and still describe Israel as "now in the third dispersion", awaiting restoration at Christ's return. [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] The timing also tells against it: the declaration is dated 2 November 1917 and a revision prepared during that year would have had at most weeks to absorb it. The claim is dropped here as unsupported. The declaration itself, and the Christian restorationists around it, are the subject of [scene:ts6_balfour|Part Six].

How many copies

The book sold steadily. A reference account citing Gaebelein's history of 1943 puts sales above two million copies by the end of the Second World War (Gaebelein's book itself appeared in 1943, so his figure describes the war years), and Dunlap, citing the same source, gives Oxford's figure of 1,925,000 copies published within thirty years of first issue. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] [cite:ts5_dunlap] By 1967 Christianity Today reported that the original had "sold more copies than any other title issued by that press in the States" and spoke of "several million copies in print". [cite:ts5_ct_1967] Some accounts say Oxford published "tens of millions"; no source for that figure has been found, and it is not used here. The documented figure, about two million by 1945, is large for a study Bible with dense notes, and it sold through churches, Bible institutes and correspondence courses rather than general bookshops (see [scene:ts7_schools|Part Seven]).

The New Scofield, 1967

Fifty years after Scofield's revision, Oxford published a new edition prepared by a committee of nine: E. Schuyler English, Frank E. Gaebelein, William Culbertson, Charles L. Feinberg, Allan A. MacRae, Clarence E. Mason, Alva J. McClain, Wilbur M. Smith and John F. Walvoord. [cite:ts5_ct_1967] Christianity Today's review of 14 April 1967 listed the changes. Hundreds of archaic King James words were replaced and marked; Ussher's dates were dropped, so no dates appear before about 2000 BC; book introductions were rewritten. The seven dispensations were kept, with the sixth renamed from "Grace" to "Church"; the distinction between Israel and the Church was maintained; and the pre-tribulational, premillennial scheme was unchanged. A note that seemed to teach salvation by works in some dispensations was removed, and a new note rejected the "Anglo-Israel" theory that the British were the lost tribes. [cite:ts5_ct_1967] Other notes were softened: according to Campbell's 2010 study, as summarised in Wikipedia, the note on John 1:17 was rewritten so that it seemed to say the opposite of Scofield's original. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb]

Recent Oxford editions of the Scofield Study Bible have moved the 1967 changes to the King James text into the margin. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] The book has therefore existed in several forms. Statements about "what the Scofield Bible says" need a date: the passages quoted in the next section are from the 1917 text, the version most reprinted and the one now in the public domain.

sections.h: What the Notes Say about Israel and the Nations
sections.html:
Much is said about the Scofield notes and little is quoted from them. Popular accounts summarise them as teaching a seven-dispensation scheme, a pre-tribulation rapture and the political return of the Jews to Palestine as a prerequisite of the Second Coming. The first two hold. The third needs testing against the text. This section quotes the 1917 notes, now in the public domain, on five passages that bear on Israel, the land and the nations, and then sets out what they say and what they do not. The quotations are short; the full notes are longer and carry many cross-references.

The covenant with Abraham

Scofield's scheme divides history into seven "dispensations", periods in which God tests humanity under different terms. At Genesis 12:1 the note opens "The Fourth Dispensation: Promise", calls the covenant with Abraham "wholly gracious and unconditional", and says the dispensation "was exclusively Israelitish". [cite:ts1_sac_gen12] The summary of that covenant at Genesis 15:18 is the most quoted note in the book. On the clause "curse him that curseth thee" it says: "It has invariably fared ill with the people who have persecuted the Jew -- well with those who have protected him." [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] On the land it says that "The gift of the land is modified by prophecies of three dispossessions and restorations", two of them already past, and that "Israel is now in the third dispersion, from which she will be restored" at "the return of the Lord as King". [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] Part One examines this note and the verse behind it in detail ([scene:ts1_genesis|Part One]). Two points matter here. The note speaks of "the Jew", a people in dispersion, because in 1909 and 1917 there was no Jewish state. And it places the restoration of the land at Christ's return, not before it.

The "Palestinian Covenant"

The note at Deuteronomy 30:3 gives the clearest statement of the sequence. Scofield calls the passage "The Palestinian Covenant", which "gives the conditions under which Israel entered the land of promise", and lists seven parts in order: "Dispersion for disobedience"; "The future repentance of Israel while in the dispersion"; "The return of the Lord"; "Restoration to the land"; "National conversion"; "The judgment of Israel's oppressors"; and "National prosperity". [cite:ts5_sac_deut30] It adds that "the nation has never as yet taken the land under the unconditional Abrahamic Covenant, nor has it ever possessed the whole land". [cite:ts5_sac_deut30] In this list the Lord's return comes third and the restoration to the land fourth. On the 1917 text, then, a return of Jews to the land is something that follows the Second Coming. It is not a political precondition for it, and the notes examined here give no instruction to Christians to bring it about.

Israel and the Church

The notes on Romans 11 state the distinction on which the whole system turns. "That Israel has not been forever set aside is the theme of this chapter," the note at 11:1 begins; "That the Christian now inherits the distinctive Jewish promises is not taught in Scripture"; Israel "is yet to have its greatest exaltation as the earthly people of God." [cite:ts5_sac_rom11] The note on the remnant looks to the end: "During the great tribulation, a remnant out of all Israel will turn to Jesus as Messiah." At 11:26 Scofield writes that "Israel, regathered from all nations, restored to her own land and converted, is yet to have her greatest earthly exaltation and glory." [cite:ts5_sac_rom11] This is the core of the Scofield position. It rejects the older Christian teaching that the Church replaced Israel in God's promises, and it keeps a future for the Jewish people as a nation. It also expects that future to include a tribulation and a conversion to Christian faith. The 1967 revisers kept this Israel/Church distinction unchanged. [cite:ts5_ct_1967]

The nations: Gog, Magog and Russia

The notes also assigned roles to modern nations. At Ezekiel 38:2 the note says: "That the primary reference is to the northern (European) powers, headed up by Russia, all agree." It reads the names Meshech and Tubal as "Moscow and Tobolsk", calls "Russia and the northern powers" "the latest persecutors of dispersed Israel", and expects their destruction "at the climax of the last mad attempt to exterminate the remnant of Israel in Jerusalem", in the future "day of Jehovah" and the battle of Armageddon. [cite:ts5_sac_ezek38] The note joined a reading of prophecy to the politics of its own day, naming a contemporary power as the persecutor of Jews and as the enemy of the prophets. That habit of identifying a present-day state with a named enemy in Ezekiel or Daniel outlived Scofield; Part Seven follows the prophecy writers who carried it into the Cold War ([scene:ts7_media|Part Seven]).

From the note to the movement

The notes did not call for political action, yet they came to be credited with founding a political movement. The link runs through what happened after 1948. Once a Jewish state existed in the land, the notes' language about a regathered Israel and about nations that "fared ill" or well could be read as describing that state and the governments that dealt with it. Later teachers made the step explicitly. John Hagee, founder of Christians United for Israel, is quoted in the reference literature putting the Genesis principle in these terms: "The man or nation that lifts a voice or hand against Israel invites the wrath of God." [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] Scofield wrote of "the Jew" and of a restoration at Christ's return; Hagee speaks of "Israel" in the present. The difference is the history of the twentieth century, and Parts Eight and Ten follow it ([scene:ts8_cufi|Part Eight], [scene:ts10_mechanism|Part Ten]).

Two cautions follow from the text. First, the notes did not create the belief in a future for Israel. Restorationist writers had argued it since the seventeenth century, and Darby and the Niagara Creed of 1878 already held the Israel/Church distinction and a restored Israel ([scene:ts2_puritans|Part Two], [scene:ts3_niagara|Part Three]). What Scofield added was reach: the scheme printed beside the verse in a Bible that sold about two million copies by 1945. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] Second, the notes contain both of the features that later admirers and critics each emphasise. They deny that Christians inherit "the distinctive Jewish promises", and they keep a national future for the Jewish people; they also place that future after a "great tribulation" in which a "remnant" turns to Jesus as Messiah. [cite:ts5_sac_rom11] Which feature defines the system is argued between its teachers and its critics, and Part Ten sets out both sides with their named sources ([scene:ts10_failures|Part Ten]). This section quotes the text and leaves the theology to its readers.

Claims about further doctrines, such as a rebuilt Third Temple as a necessary precondition of Christ's return, are sometimes attributed to "the Scofield Bible" in general. They are not in the notes examined for this part, and where they appear in this volume they are attributed to the named teachers who made them.

sections.h: Who Paid for the Scofield Bible
sections.html:
Preparing the notes took Scofield several years, and friends paid so that he could give his time to the work. [cite:ts5_dunlap] Who did is a question with a documented answer and a widely circulated false one. The false answer, that a Jewish Wall Street lawyer or the Rothschild family financed the book in order to make American Protestants serve Zionism, is repeated in books, articles and viral videos. This section sets out the documented record first, then traces the false claim to its sources and shows why it fails.

The documented backers

The men who supported the work were named by people who knew Scofield. Arno C. Gaebelein, one of the book's consulting editors, named four in his History of the Scofield Reference Bible (1943), pp. 49–50: Alwyn Ball Jr., John T. Pirie, John B. Buss and Francis E. Fitch; Charles Trumbull's authorised biography of 1920 names Pirie as well. [cite:ts4_sfiles] David Dunlap, writing for a Brethren history site and drawing on Gaebelein and Trumbull, identifies three of them. Pirie was a partner in Carson, Pirie and Scott, the Chicago department store; Ball was a New York real-estate broker; Fitch ran a printing business and published Scofield's correspondence Bible course in its early years. All three, Dunlap writes, "fellowshipped at so-called 'Brethren assemblies'" around New York, the Plymouth Brethren congregations that had grown from Darby's movement. [cite:ts5_dunlap] Buss is listed as of St. Louis. [cite:ts4_goeman]

Scofield himself credited two of them. The historian D. Jean Rushing, in her 2011 thesis on his life, writes that while "others in the conference circuit" contributed, Scofield acknowledged that Ball and Pirie "made it possible" for him to prepare the work. [cite:ts4_cyf] A further gift is recorded by the historian Ernest Sandeen, whose The Roots of Fundamentalism (1970, p. 191) is cited for a $1,000 contribution in 1908 from Lyman Stewart; this figure is reported here from a site that reproduces Sandeen's page and was not checked against the book itself. [cite:ts4_sfiles] Stewart, a co-founder of the Union Oil Company of California, was a prominent lay funder of conservative Protestant causes: in 1908 he co-founded the Bible Institute of Los Angeles, and he and his brother Milton paid $300,000 for the publication of The Fundamentals. [cite:ts5_wiki_lstewart]

The rest of the money came from sales. Oxford University Press published, printed and sold the book as a commercial title. [cite:ts5_dunlap] [cite:ts5_ia_1917] None of the named backers was Jewish, and none had any documented connection to the Rothschilds or to the Zionist movement. [cite:ts4_cyf] [cite:ts4_goeman] They were evangelical businessmen paying for a Bible whose theology they shared.

The Untermyer claim and where it came from

The competing story names Samuel Untermyer, a prominent New York corporate lawyer. Its only documented element is that both men belonged to New York's Lotos Club: Untermyer from 1894, Scofield from 3 March 1900, proposed by Horatio Fraser and seconded by John Elderkin. Part Four sets out the membership record ([scene:ts4_rumours|Part Four]). [cite:ts4_sfiles] The link to Untermyer begins with Joseph M. Canfield's hostile biography, The Incredible Scofield and His Book (1988). According to a reproduction of the pages, Canfield asked why "a godly man" would join "such a godless club", and then named Untermyer as the likely sponsor with the words "we assume" and "There must have been anticipation". [cite:ts4_sfiles] That is an inference, and it concerns club membership, not money.

Later writers turned the inference into a statement of fact. David W. Lutz, in an essay in the 2005 collection Neo-Conned Again, wrote that Untermyer used Scofield "to inject Zionist ideas into American Protestantism" and that wealthy Zionists "promoted and funded" his career; in October 2015 the Washington Report on Middle East Affairs published an article by Maidhc Ó Cathail repeating this, citing Lutz and Canfield without page references. [cite:ts5_ocathail] That article dates Scofield's admission to 1901 and calls Untermyer a member of the admitting committee; the club's book records the entry in 1900 and names an election committee of William Henry White, John Elderkin and William Jay Ives. [cite:ts4_sfiles] Neither Lutz nor Ó Cathail, on the record of their own citations, produced a letter, payment, meeting or document of any kind. [cite:ts5_ocathail]

The Rothschild variant

The stronger claim, that the Rothschilds paid for the Bible, is younger still. The research site Scofield-Files traces it through an internet mailing list (1999) and websites (2001–02) to Michael Collins Piper's The High Priests of War (2004), the first known text to say the Rothschilds funded Scofield, and from there into later books and posts. [cite:ts4_sfiles] Piper wrote for The Spotlight and American Free Press, papers backed by Willis Carto that Wikipedia, summarising the press record, describes as noted for "antisemitic and White separatist" themes; the Anti-Defamation League, the Simon Wiesenthal Center and MEMRI described him as a promoter of antisemitic conspiracy theories and Holocaust denial. [cite:ts5_wiki_piper] The story revived in 2024 after the singer John Rich, on Tucker Carlson's programme, linked Darby to "the Rothschilds", in Mike Rothschild's paraphrase. [cite:ts4_mrothschild] [cite:ts4_goeman] The writer Mike Rothschild, who studies conspiracy theories, reported that he could not find "any primary source that connects the Scofield Bible, Scofield himself, or Darby to the family", and noted that Oxford University Press is owned by the University of Oxford. [cite:ts4_mrothschild] Check Your Fact rated the claim false on 12 March 2025. [cite:ts4_cyf]

Why the claim fails

The claim fails on four separate grounds. First, the documented backers are named by contemporaries, including Scofield himself, and none of them is Untermyer or a Rothschild. [cite:ts4_cyf] [cite:ts4_sfiles] Second, the only Untermyer link is shared membership of a large social club, and Untermyer was neither Scofield's proposer nor his seconder. [cite:ts4_sfiles] Third, the dates do not fit the motive alleged: Untermyer's leading Zionist office, the presidency of Keren Hayesod, began in 1921 according to Scofield-Files, twelve years after the Bible appeared, and in the 1900s Scofield's circle was not pro-Zionist in any political sense; Gaebelein, his consulting editor, called Zionism in 1905 "a movement ... of unbelief" ([scene:ts3_niagara|Part Three]). [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts3_wiki_gaebelein] Fourth, the theology needed no outside author: it is Darby's system, taught at Niagara from 1878, and the notes themselves place Israel's restoration after Christ's return rather than calling for a Zionist programme ([scene:ts5_notes|the notes]). [cite:ts5_sac_deut30]

The claim's shape also matters, and it should be named plainly. It says that Jewish financiers secretly paid to change what Christians believe in order to serve Jewish political ends. That is one of the oldest antisemitic accusations, and its strongest version here was first put into print by a writer whom the leading monitoring bodies describe as an antisemitic conspiracy theorist. [cite:ts5_wiki_piper] [cite:ts4_mrothschild] That is not the reason it is rejected in this volume: it is rejected because the record contradicts it. It is named because it travels faster than the record and because believing it hides the real history. The Scofield Bible was the work of an American evangelical network, paid for by its own businessmen and sold by a commercial publisher to a public that bought it in the millions. That network, not a hidden patron, is what later built the political alliances described in Parts Six and Eight ([scene:ts6_blackstone|Part Six], [scene:ts8_falwell|Part Eight]).

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: Blackstone, Balfour and the 1940s Committees
chapters.intro: Part Six follows the restorationist idea out of the prophecy conferences and into the offices of presidents and prime ministers, between 1891 and 1953. It begins with William E. Blackstone, a Chicago businessman turned evangelist, and the petition he carried to President Benjamin Harrison in March 1891, then follows the second petition he prepared at Louis Brandeis's request in 1916. It turns next to Britain: what can be shown about the Christian beliefs of Arthur Balfour and David Lloyd George, how much weight those beliefs carried beside the war aims their own cabinet recorded, and the career of Orde Wingate, a British officer whose Bible-reading Zionism shaped the Jewish night squads he led in 1938. Last, it examines the American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine of the 1940s, which the record shows were organised from the Zionist movement's political office and staffed largely by liberal Protestant clergy rather than end-times teachers, and Harry Truman's remark of 1953, "I am Cyrus." Throughout, the part separates what each person said and did from what historians argue about their motives.
chapters.outro: Part Six found that between 1891 and 1953 Christian support for a Jewish return reached the highest offices in Washington and London, but by routes that do not fit the story of a single end-times theology driving policy. William Blackstone, a dispensationalist who also hoped for the conversion of Jews, put the case to President Harrison on 5 March 1891 with 413 or 431 elite signatures, and at Brandeis's request prepared a second memorial whose presentation to Wilson the sources describe differently and which reached him, on Moorhead's account, after the Balfour Declaration. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial] [cite:ts6_wheaton_intro] In Britain, scholars such as Donald Lewis and Philip Alexander argue that Balfour's and Lloyd George's Christian formation made them receptive, while the cabinet's minutes and Lloyd George's own 1937 testimony give war aims and an exaggerated belief in Jewish power as the reasons; Orde Wingate, raised among the Plymouth Brethren, is the clearest case of the faith shaping conduct, and his superiors removed him for it. [cite:ts6_wiki_cz] [cite:ts6_wiki_balfourdecl] [cite:ts6_jn_lloydgeorge] [cite:ts6_wiki_wingate] In the 1940s the most visible Christian bodies, the American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine, were organised by Emanuel Neumann of the Zionist movement and led by liberal Protestants such as Henry Atkinson and Reinhold Niebuhr, and Truman's "I am Cyrus" of 1953 is read by Merkley as conviction and by Judis as a later self-portrait. [cite:aja_neumann_bio] [cite:ts6_aja_ccp_minutes] [cite:ts6_merkley_cyrus] [cite:rs_cw2_judis_truman_cyrus] The dispensationalist current that would carry the alliance after 1948 grew elsewhere, in the Bible institutes, seminaries, bestsellers and broadcasts that Part Seven follows. [scene:ts7_schools|Part Seven: Spreading the System]

sections.h: The Blackstone Memorials, 1891 and 1916
sections.html:
The first time the restorationist idea was put in writing before an American president, it came from a Chicago property developer. William E. Blackstone was born on 6 October 1841 in Adams, New York, was converted at a Methodist revival at the age of eleven, and settled in Oak Park, Illinois, in 1870, where he did well in building and property investment before giving most of his time to religious work. He died on 7 November 1935. [cite:ts6_wiki_blackstone] Earlier parts of this volume traced the British line of restorationist thought and the Bible-conference movement through which John Nelson Darby's system reached American Protestants. [scene:ts2_shaftesbury|Shaftesbury and the British restorationists] [scene:ts3_niagara|Niagara and the prophecy conferences] Blackstone belongs to that second current, and his case shows how a prophetic belief was turned into a political request.

The evangelist and his book

In 1878 Blackstone published Jesus Is Coming under his initials, W.E.B. It was translated into more than forty languages. [cite:ts6_wiki_blackstone] Jonathan Moorhead, writing in the journal of the Evangelical Theological Society in 2010, calls it "the most important early book on premillennialism" and its author "an ardent supporter of dispensational premillennialism." [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] The book predates the Scofield Reference Bible by thirty-one years, one of several dates that tell against the claim that Scofield invented Christian Zionism. [scene:ts14_myths|Myths, contested claims and what is settled]

Blackstone's interest in the Jewish people had a second side that later accounts often leave out. After a meeting in Chicago on 4 November 1887 he became the first superintendent of a committee for evangelistic work among Jews; renamed the Chicago Hebrew Mission two years later, it still operates as Life in Messiah. [cite:ts6_wiki_blackstone] [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] On 24 and 25 November 1890 he organised a Conference on the Past, Present, and Future of Israel at the First Methodist Episcopal Church in Chicago, attended by Orthodox Jewish and Protestant leaders but not by leaders of Reform Judaism, which called on the great powers, in the Wikipedia entry's words, to "give Palestine to the Zionists" and passed resolutions of sympathy for the Jews of the Russian Empire. [cite:ts6_wiki_blackstone] He first saw a Jewish return as a step toward the conversion of Jews to Christianity, which he hoped would hasten Christ's return; after the pogroms in Eastern Europe he came to argue that a homeland was needed because Europe and the United States would not admit enough Jewish refugees. [cite:ts6_wiki_blackstone] Both reasons stayed with him. As late as 27 January 1918, speaking to a Zionist meeting at Clune's Auditorium in Los Angeles, he told his audience that God's plan for the Jews was repentance and conversion to Christianity. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets]

The memorial of March 1891

On 5 March 1891 Secretary of State James G. Blaine introduced Blackstone to President Benjamin Harrison, and Blackstone handed over the petition that became known as the Blackstone Memorial. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] Its opening was a question about refugees: "What shall be done for the Russian Jews?" It went on: "Where shall 2,000,000 of such poor people go?", noting that "Europe is crowded and has no room for more peasant population." Its answer was a further question: "Why not give Palestine back to them again?" It described Palestine as the Jews' "inalienable possession from which they were expelled by force," and drew a parallel with the Treaty of Berlin of 1878, under which the powers had given "Bulgaria to the Bulgarians" and "Servia to the Servians." [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial] [cite:ts6_wiki_cz] The Wheaton College archive, which holds the Blackstone papers, quotes another line from it: "Let us restore them to the land of which they were so cruelly despoiled by our Roman ancestors." [cite:ts6_wheaton_intro]

The request itself was specific. The memorial asked the President and the Secretary of State to press the governments of Europe to hold "an International Conference to consider the condition of the Israelites, and their claims to Palestine." [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] It did not ask the United States to take Palestine or to send settlers; it asked for diplomacy among the powers that then decided the fate of Ottoman provinces.

Its signatories were the memorial's main political asset, and their number is not settled. Moorhead counts 413; the Wikipedia entry, drawing on Paul Merkley's history, gives 431. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial] The named signers are not in dispute: John D. Rockefeller, J. Pierpont Morgan, the Speaker of the House Thomas Reed, Cyrus McCormick, the evangelist D. L. Moody, Chief Justice Melville Fuller and the future President William McKinley were among them. [cite:ts6_wheaton_intro] [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial] The Wheaton archive describes the signers as religious leaders, Christian and Jewish, together with civic, business and political figures. [cite:ts6_wheaton_intro] The petition was therefore not a document of one denomination or one theology; it gathered men who signed for reasons of their own.

What the memorial achieved is modest on the record. Moorhead reports that Harrison "received the Memorial kindly and promised to give it his consideration," and that Blaine showed personal interest. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] The Wheaton archive states that there was no other official response, and suggests, without claiming more, that the memorial may have contributed to American protests to Russia, one factor in Russia's withdrawal of its expulsion decrees. [cite:ts6_wheaton_intro] Harrison's annual message to Congress in December 1891 did not mention Blackstone; one historian cited by Moorhead read it as a reaction to the appeal. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] No international conference was called.

The second memorial, 1916–1918

Blackstone's petition gained a second life a quarter of a century later, through the leader of American Zionism. In May 1916 Nathan Straus wrote to Blackstone that Louis Brandeis "agrees with me that you are the father of Zionism, as your work antedates Herzl." Moorhead dates the letter 8 May; the Wikipedia entry gives 16 May and quotes Straus describing Brandeis as "perfectly infatuated" with Blackstone's work. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial] Brandeis himself wrote on 28 May 1916 that the document "is destined to become of historical significance." [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] Brandeis asked Blackstone to prepare a new memorial for President Woodrow Wilson, and Zionist leaders worked with him on it. [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial] [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] Brandeis's own channel to Wilson in these months, and his part in the drafting of the Balfour Declaration, are set out in the Road to 1948 volume. [scene:s04h|Hadassah, Brandeis and the ZOA]

The second memorial carried a different kind of weight from the first. Instead of tycoons, it gathered churches. The General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. endorsed it, and Blackstone collected eighty-two individual endorsements from Chicago, Los Angeles, New York and Ithaca. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] The Wheaton archive holds addenda from the Los Angeles Methodists, the Los Angeles Baptists and the Chicago Methodists. [cite:ts6_wheaton_intro] The Wikipedia entry describes the endorsement as coming from most of mainstream American Protestantism, a wider claim than the named bodies support. [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial]

How, and whether, the memorial reached Wilson is disputed in the sources. The Wheaton archive says Blackstone presented it unofficially in May 1916; the Wikipedia entry says it was presented privately in May 1917 and never made public. [cite:ts6_wheaton_intro] [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial] Moorhead, working from the papers, says it was never formally presented, partly because the British disliked its international character, and that Wilson's approval of it reached Rabbi Stephen Wise only on 31 August 1918, after the Balfour Declaration and after British forces had taken Jerusalem. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] On that account the memorial was a document American Zionist leaders valued and used, not an instrument that moved Wilson before November 1917. The other accounts read it differently: the Wheaton archive suggests the 1916 presentation may have influenced Wilson's favourable response to the Declaration, and the Wikipedia entry says the memorial strongly influenced him. [cite:ts6_wheaton_intro] [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial]

What the record shows

Three things are documented. A dispensationalist evangelist put the case for a Jewish return to Palestine before an American president in 1891, five years before Herzl's Der Judenstaat; he did it with the signatures of the country's financial and political elite; and in 1916 the leader of American Zionism sought him out to do it again. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] [cite:ts6_wiki_memorial] [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] Blackstone also sent Herzl a Bible with the prophecies of return marked, but Moorhead notes that there is no proof Blackstone influenced Herzl. [cite:ts6_wiki_blackstone] [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] The title "father of Zionism" was a compliment from Straus and Brandeis, and Moorhead declines to argue for it. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets]

Two things are not shown. The record does not show that either memorial changed American policy; the first produced courtesy and the second arrived after the decision it was meant to support. And it does not show a single motive. Blackstone's own words joined humanitarian alarm at the fate of Russian Jews, a prophetic timetable, and an explicit hope for Jewish conversion. [cite:ts6_wiki_blackstone] [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] Brandeis's letters, as quoted, praise the petition's historical significance; nothing in the sources cited here shows that he shared its prophetic premises or its hope of conversion. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] The partnership was real, and on the evidence it rested on goals that were not the same.

sections.h: Balfour, Lloyd George and Wingate: Faith Among the Motives
sections.html:
On 2 November 1917 the Foreign Secretary, Arthur Balfour, signed a letter to Lord Rothschild stating that the British government viewed "with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people." [cite:wb_bl_addms41178] [cite:wb_ra_balfour] How the letter was drafted, why it went to Walter Rothschild, and what it promised the Arab majority are told in the Road to 1948 and Divine 3+1 volumes. [scene:s06|The Balfour Declaration] [scene:dv2_british_state|What the British state did] This section takes up a narrower question that belongs to the history of Christian Zionism: how much the religious beliefs of the two men most responsible, Balfour and the Prime Minister, David Lloyd George, weighed in the decision, and what the record allows a reader to say about it.

The case for a Christian formation

The religious reading has serious advocates. The scholar Philip Alexander has written that "a crucial ingredient in Balfour's Zionism" may have been "his Christian belief," and he names the historian Donald Lewis, author of The Origins of Christian Zionism (2010), as the most persuasive advocate of the thesis that British Christian formation prepared the ground for the Declaration. [cite:ts6_wiki_cz] On this view both Balfour and Lloyd George "were influenced by Christian Zionism," in the sense that they had grown up inside the restorationist reading of the Bible that Shaftesbury had carried into British politics in 1839–40. [cite:ts6_wiki_cz] [scene:ts2_shaftesbury|Shaftesbury and the British restorationists]

For Lloyd George there is specific testimony. Oren Kessler, writing on the Prime Minister's evidence to the Palestine Royal Commission, notes that his Baptist upbringing predisposed him toward Chaim Weizmann's vision and that he felt more at home with the place names of Palestine than with those of the Western Front. [cite:ts6_fathom_kessler] A sentence often quoted from a speech Lloyd George gave to the Jewish Historical Society, about being taught more Jewish history than the history of his own land, could not be traced to a dated primary text for this volume and is not used here.

The reasons the government recorded

The reasons the British government gave itself at the time were of another kind. The War Cabinet approved the Declaration for reasons ministers could name: the security of the approaches to the Suez Canal and the hope of keeping Russia in the war and drawing in American support [cite:cohen_palestine_great_powers]; the standing Weizmann had earned through his wartime work on acetone [cite:wb_ra_balfour]; and a belief in a unified and powerful "world Jewry" that could be won to the Allied side, which Schneer treats as stereotyped thinking about Jews. [cite:ts6_wiki_balfourdecl] The cabinet minutes of 31 October 1917 record Balfour's own argument that a declaration would allow "extremely useful propaganda both in Russia and America." [cite:ts6_wiki_balfourdecl] Lord Robert Cecil, a Foreign Office minister, wrote: "I do not think it is possible to exaggerate the international power of the Jews." [cite:ts6_wiki_balfourdecl] The historians Jonathan Schneer and James Renton both describe a foreign-policy elite that believed Jews held real power they could bring to bear on the war. [cite:ts6_wiki_balfourdecl]

Lloyd George's own later account points the same way. In secret evidence to the Peel Commission in 1937, released in 2017 and brought to light by Kessler, he explained the Declaration as a wartime measure: he said "the friendliness or hostility of the Jewish race might make a considerable difference," and called Jews "a dangerous people to quarrel with, but they are a very helpful people if you can get them on your side." [cite:ts6_jn_lloydgeorge] [cite:ts6_fathom_kessler] Kessler sums up the man as "Judeophobe and philo-Semite, militarist and appeaser, Zionist champion and Hitler enthusiast."
