[cite:ts6_fathom_kessler] The testimony was given twenty years after the event, when the Mandate was in crisis, and it is one man's justification; it is also the only account in his own words of why he acted.

The one Jewish member of the government, Edwin Montagu, opposed the policy in a memorandum of 23 August 1917 headed "Anti-Semitism in the Present Government," calling Zionism "a mischievous political creed." [cite:wb_tna_cab21_58_218] He was overruled.

Weighing the two

The two readings are not exclusive, and the strongest position the record allows combines them. Schneer calls the Declaration "the highly contingent product of a tortuous process," and his book concentrates so heavily on politics that one reviewer, Colin Chapman, faulted it for leaving out "the religious beliefs of key players like Lord Balfour and David Lloyd George." [cite:ts6_chapman_schneer] That criticism is fair as far as it goes: belief can explain why two men were receptive to Weizmann. It does not show that belief decided the matter. The documents that record the decision speak of empire, propaganda and an exaggerated notion of Jewish influence; the evidence for faith is about formation, not about the cabinet room. Accounts that present the Declaration as an act of Christian Zionism, or as a purely strategic act with no religious colour, both claim more than the record supports. [cite:ts6_wiki_balfourdecl] [cite:ts6_wiki_cz]

Orde Wingate: faith in the field

Where Christian Zionism can be seen directly shaping conduct in this period is in the career of one British officer. Orde Wingate's father, Colonel George Wingate, became a committed member of the Plymouth Brethren early in his army career, and the children memorised Scripture daily. [cite:ts6_wiki_wingate] The Brethren were the movement in which John Nelson Darby had developed his system, as Part Three describes, and Wingate grew into an ardent Christian Zionist who regarded a Jewish state as a religious duty. [cite:ts6_wiki_wingate] [scene:ts3_darby|Darby and the Brethren]

As an intelligence captain in Palestine during the Arab Revolt, he proposed joint units of British soldiers and Jewish supernumerary police drawn from the Haganah. General Haining approved the Special Night Squads in June 1938, and they operated from Kibbutz Ein Harod until October, with about seventy-five Haganah volunteers, among them Moshe Dayan and Yigal Allon. [cite:ts6_wiki_wingate] [cite:wiki_special_night_squads] [cite:nli_wingate_hebrew] [scene:br_s01|Wingate's Night Squads and the Palmach] Wingate returned often to Ein Harod, according to his biographers because of its association with the biblical judge Gideon. [cite:ts6_wiki_wingate] After rebels killed Ein Harod's leader, Chaim Sturman, with a mine in September 1938, Wingate led a reprisal on the Arab quarter of Beisan. [cite:ts6_wiki_wingate] The historian Tom Segev called him "quite mad, and perhaps a sadist, too"; Michael Oren disputed Segev's account. [cite:ts6_wiki_wingate] The Israeli writer Uri Avnery traced a line of retaliation-raid doctrine from Wingate to the Israel Defense Forces, a critic's argument rather than a settled finding. [cite:avnery_dayan_wingate]

His faith did not make him an agent of British policy; it put him at odds with it. He was transferred to Britain in May 1939: after he spoke publicly in favour of a Jewish state while on leave in Britain, his superiors in Palestine removed him from command, judging that he was "promoting his own agenda rather than that of the army or the government." [cite:ts6_wiki_wingate] The same administration that had sponsored the squads imprisoned Dayan in 1939 for training with arms outside British command. [cite:archiveshub_wingate] Wingate died on 24 March 1944 when the American B-25 carrying him crashed in the hills of Manipur. Israel's national sports institute, the Wingate Institute, the youth village of Yemin Orde and a square in Jerusalem bear his name. [cite:ts6_wiki_wingate]

The British record thus shows Christian Zionism at two levels. At the top, it was a predisposition in men whose recorded reasons were strategic, and whose strategic reasoning included a belief about Jewish power that historians such as Schneer describe as stereotyped. In the field, in Wingate, it was a personal conviction that shaped a military method and the careers of future Israeli commanders, and that the British army itself treated as a problem. Neither level fits the claim that the British state acted on prophecy.

sections.h: The 1940s Committees and Truman's Cyrus
sections.html:
In the decisive decade before 1948, the Christian voices most visible in American politics on Palestine did not come from the prophecy conferences. They came from two committees, the American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine, whose founding records survive in the American Jewish Archives. Those records show who started the committees, who sat on them and what they promised to do, and they complicate two familiar stories at once: that Christian support for a Jewish state in the 1940s arose on its own, and that it was the work of end-times believers. The Road to 1948 volume sets out the committees' place in the wider American campaign; this section looks at them as a chapter in the history of Christian Zionism. [scene:us_s04|The American Palestine Committee, 1932]

Two committees from one office

Emanuel Neumann, a member of the Zionist Executive, founded the American Palestine Committee in 1932 to organise prominent, mainly non-Jewish Americans in support of a Jewish homeland. In January 1941 he joined the Emergency Committee for Zionist Affairs as head of public relations and political action, and from that post revived the committee with Senator Robert Wagner of New York as its chairman. [cite:aja_neumann_bio] Carl Hermann Voss and David Rausch, writing in 1988, date the committee's founding to 1931 and record that Reinhold Niebuhr was a member from the early 1930s. [cite:ts6_voss_rausch]

The clergy's body was created at an all-day meeting on 14 December 1942 at the Pennsylvania Hotel in New York. Its minutes list thirty people present. Henry A. Atkinson chaired and W. Russell Bowie opened with prayer; the theologian Reinhold Niebuhr, Bishops Francis J. McConnell, James Cannon Jr. and Herbert Welch, and Carl H. Voss of Pittsburgh were among those present, and the archaeologist W. F. Albright sent a telegram regretting his absence through illness. Emanuel Neumann attended and explained the work of the American Palestine Committee; Rabbi Philip S. Bernstein of Rochester was also present. [cite:ts6_aja_ccp_minutes] The meeting elected Atkinson chairman, Howard B. Warren vice-chairman and Niebuhr treasurer. Its first policy point committed the new body "to the establishment of a Jewish commonwealth in Palestine" within a general post-war settlement. It named itself the Christian Council on Palestine, "an autonomous committee working in cooperation with the American Palestine Committee," to be funded by "popular subscription" in cooperation with that committee. [cite:ts6_aja_ccp_minutes] Neumann's own account in the Archives credits him with organising it. [cite:aja_neumann_bio] Two months later, in a statement filed with the minutes, he described it as a group of "hundreds of prominent Christian Clergymen." [cite:ts6_aja_ccp_minutes]

The committees grew quickly. By the end of the war the American Palestine Committee claimed some 6,500 members, among them senators, congressmen, cabinet members and governors, and the Christian Council about 3,000 clergy; these are the committees' own figures. [cite:wiki_american_palestine_committee] [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby] In 1946 they merged as the American Christian Palestine Committee, which, in the description of one reference work, became the leading American Christian lobby for a Jewish state and later coordinated opposition to United Nations plans to internationalise Jerusalem. [cite:ts6_wiki_cz2] Its end date is disputed. The common account says it disbanded after 1948; Voss and Rausch, writing as participants, say it carried on and wound down only in the late 1950s and early 1960s as its financial support shrank. [cite:wiki_american_palestine_committee] [cite:ts6_voss_rausch]

"Autonomous" or "hardly autonomous"

The founding minutes call the Council autonomous. The historian Peter Grose described the committees' operations as "hardly autonomous," and reporting drawn from his work states that Zionist funds reaching $150,000 by 1946 sustained them, a figure this volume has not seen in a primary account. [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby] The minutes themselves support part of each description. They record a Zionist executive explaining the political work the Council would join, and a funding arrangement made "in cooperation with" his committee; they also record named churchmen electing their own officers and adopting their own policy. [cite:ts6_aja_ccp_minutes] What the documents establish is specific: these bodies were organised by named officials of the Zionist movement, Neumann and the Emergency Committee, and staffed by Christians who lent their own names and, as far as any record shows, their own convictions. That is a finding about named organisations and named people, not about Jews or Christians in general.

Who the Christians were

The founding list is the clearest evidence of the decade's Christian Zionism, and it is not a list of end-times teachers. It names three bishops, several professors including the theologian Niebuhr, a rabbi, a Zionist official and pastors from New York, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and Connecticut; none of the sources consulted for this volume identifies any of them as a teacher of the dispensationalist system that earlier parts describe. [cite:ts6_aja_ccp_minutes] [cite:ts6_voss_rausch] Voss and Rausch describe the Council as "composed, as planned, almost entirely of Christian ministers," and the merged committee as mostly Protestant. [cite:ts6_voss_rausch] The historian Daniel Hummel, reviewing Samuel Goldman's God's Country (2018), notes that Goldman treats Niebuhr as the "most outspoken postwar Protestant supporter of Israel," who backed a Jewish state on moral and realist grounds rather than literal prophecy, and that Goldman traces a continuous Protestant tradition, back to the Puritan covenant theology of Increase Mather and Jonathan Edwards, that saw America as a Cyrus for the Jews. [cite:ts6_hummel_goldman]

Preachers outside these committees took up the cause in their own way. The pastor J. Frank Norris taught his followers that support for the Zionist cause was a Christian duty and wrote to President Truman in its favour in 1947 and 1948. [cite:ts6_wiki_cz2] The political organisation of Christian support in the 1940s, though, ran through liberal Protestant clergy recruited by the Zionist movement, not through the dispensationalist schools that Part Seven describes. [scene:ts7_schools|The schools] Stephen Spector's later study of evangelical support points in the same direction for a different era: he found Genesis 12:3, the promise to bless Abraham's descendants, to be the reason most often cited, reported that most Christian Zionists did not base their support on "a catastrophic end-times scenario," and estimated that only about five million American evangelicals were premillennial dispensationalists. [cite:ts6_tablet_spector] [scene:ts5_notes|Scofield's notes]

Christian opposition was organised as well. In 1948 Virginia Gildersleeve, the former dean of Barnard College, and Kermit Roosevelt Jr. formed the Committee for Justice and Peace in the Holy Land, which warned that "extreme Zionist pressure" risked disrupting national unity. [cite:mosaic_cia_zionism] [cite:w_kermit_jr] Partition was voted and the state recognised regardless. [scene:rf_s01|The objections of 1948] [scene:ts11_churches|The churches' counter-record]

"I am Cyrus"

The decade's most quoted Christian Zionist line came after it was over. In November 1953, at the Jewish Theological Seminary in New York, Truman's old friend and former business partner Eddie Jacobson introduced him as "the man who helped create the State of Israel." Truman is reported to have replied: "What do you mean 'helped to create'? I am Cyrus. I am Cyrus." [cite:ts6_merkley_cyrus] [cite:rs_cw2_judis_truman_cyrus] Cyrus was the Persian king who, in the biblical account, allowed the exiles of Judah to return. The remark is known from later accounts, not from a transcript, and the sources used here do not name the witness who recorded it.

Paul Merkley, the historian of Christian Zionism, reads the remark as the key to Truman. He notes that Truman joined a Baptist church in Kansas City at eighteen and stayed a member for life, writes that his Sunday School teachers had taught him that someone would one day be called to be a second Cyrus, and concludes, by his own description as an inference ("we must assume"), that although political calculation played its part, "personal commitment tipped the balance." [cite:ts6_merkley_cyrus] John Judis reads the same years the other way: the picture of Truman as an unwavering supporter is, he writes, "dead wrong," and the President was full of doubt and regret around the recognition of May 1948. [cite:rs_cw2_judis_truman_cyrus] Truman's own words from 1943 to 1948, which mix public conviction, open awareness of voters and private irritation at pressure, are set out in the Road to 1948 volume. [scene:tr_s01|Truman in his own words] On the evidence, "I am Cyrus" shows how Truman chose to describe his role five years later, before a Jewish audience; it does not by itself show why he acted in 1948.

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: Spreading the System
chapters.intro: Part Seven follows the end-times system from the study Bible into the institutions that taught it and the media that sold it. It begins with the Bible institutes and seminaries, Moody Bible Institute in Chicago and Dallas Theological Seminary above all, which trained pastors, missionaries and writers in a dispensational reading of prophecy. It then turns to the mass market: Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth in 1970, the Left Behind novels from 1995 to 2007, and the religious broadcasters, Pat Robertson's Christian Broadcasting Network among them, who carried prophecy and Israel to television audiences. The last section follows the system abroad, to the Protestant and Pentecostal churches of Latin America and Africa, and to the governments of Guatemala, Paraguay and Brazil when they had to decide where to put an embassy. Throughout, influence is measured only by what can be counted: enrolment, copies sold, census and survey shares, and dated decisions.
chapters.outro: Part Seven established how the end-times system spread and what can be counted of that spread. Bible institutes, more than 200 of them by 1961, and Dallas Theological Seminary, which opened in 1924 with 13 students and now counts more than 16,000 alumni, gave dispensationalism faculties, degrees, a press and, through Moody, a radio network reaching more than 700 outlets. [cite:ts7_ct_bibleinst] [cite:ts7_dts_story] [cite:ts7_wiki_moody] A Dallas graduate, Hal Lindsey, sold an estimated 28 to 35 million copies of The Late Great Planet Earth, and the Left Behind novels sold between 50 and 80 million by the reported counts; religious television gave preachers such as Pat Robertson a daily audience, though Israel's own government rebuked Robertson in January 2006 when he turned the land theology on an Israeli prime minister. [cite:ts7_wiki_lgpe] [cite:ts7_wrap_lindsey] [cite:ts7_cp_lahaye] [cite:ts7_sa_lahaye] [cite:ts7_cbs_robertson] Abroad, Protestants were 41 per cent of adults in Guatemala and Honduras in 2013–14 and evangelicals 26.9 per cent of Brazilians in 2022, and Guatemala and Paraguay moved embassies to Jerusalem, while Brazil, with 47.4 million evangelicals, opened only a trade office after its vice-president warned of $5 billion in halal exports. [cite:ts7_pew_latam2014] [cite:ts7_reuters_brcensus] [cite:ts7_abc_paraguay] [cite:ts7_ynet_brazil] Reach is documented; its effect on belief and on policy is not shown by sales or church growth alone. Part Eight follows the moment the system became an organised political force, from Jerry Falwell's Moral Majority to Christians United for Israel. [scene:ts8_falwell|Part Eight: Falwell and the political machine]

sections.h: The Schools: Bible Institutes and Dallas Theological Seminary
sections.html:
A theological system lasts when institutions teach it to people who will teach it to others. Darby's dispensationalism reached North America through travelling preachers and summer Bible conferences, and the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909 fixed it in the margins of a printed text; both stories are told earlier in this volume. [scene:ts3_niagara|Part Three: the Bible conferences] [scene:ts5_edition|Part Five: the 1909 edition] This section follows the next step, the schools. Two kinds mattered: the Bible institutes, which trained lay workers, missionaries and pastors in short practical courses, and one graduate seminary, Dallas Theological Seminary, which made dispensationalism the core of a full theological education.

The Bible institutes

The first Bible institutes were founded in the 1880s: Nyack, in New York, in 1882, and the school in Chicago that became Moody Bible Institute in 1886. Writing in Christianity Today in February 1961, the vice-president of one such school counted "more than 200 Bible institutes and colleges" then in existence, and listed "the imminent return of Jesus Christ" among the beliefs they proclaimed. [cite:ts7_ct_bibleinst] That phrase is the movement's own summary of its teaching, not a measure of how many students held a particular view of Israel; the article does not name dispensationalism, and the schools varied.

Moody Bible Institute is the clearest case of a school that built its own channels of distribution. The evangelist Dwight L. Moody founded it in 1886 as the Chicago Evangelization Society, and it took his name after his death in 1899. Its publishing arm began in 1894 as the Bible Institute Colportage Association, a book-distribution society, and became Moody Press in 1941. Its radio station, WMBI, went on the air in 1926 and is described as the first non-commercial Christian radio station in America; the Moody network now owns 36 stations and supplies programmes by satellite to more than 700 outlets. The institute reported 2,341 students in 2025 and is described as dispensational in theology. [cite:ts7_wiki_moody] A school with its own press and its own radio network did not depend on denominations or commercial publishers to reach people: that is the institutional fact that matters for this volume's question, more than any one teacher's lectures.

Dallas Theological Seminary

Dallas Theological Seminary opened in 1924 as the Evangelical Theological College. Its founders were Lewis Sperry Chafer, his brother Rollin T. Chafer, and the Anglican scholar W.H. Griffith Thomas, who was to teach theology but died before classes began. [cite:ts7_wiki_dts] The seminary's own history says it began with 13 students and graduated its first class in 1927. [cite:ts7_dts_story] Chafer's systematic theology took, in the seminary library's description, a "premillennial, dispensational interpretation of the Scriptures", and the seminary remains non-denominational and committed to premillennialism, dispensationalism and biblical inerrancy; it is known as the school that did most to popularize dispensationalism. [cite:ts7_wiki_dts]

The figures for its size depend on what is counted. The seminary reported 1,377 full-time-equivalent students in 2025, and more than 15,000 alumni serving in 97 countries in 2014. [cite:ts7_wiki_dts] Its own website speaks of "more than 16,000 DTS alumni" and about 2,600 current students, and offers programmes in Arabic, Chinese and Spanish. [cite:ts7_dts_story] The two student numbers are not in conflict: one counts full-time equivalents, the other people enrolled, many of them part time or online. Either way, a school that opened with 13 students now has alumni in most of the world's countries.

What the seminary teaches about Israel, in its own words

The point of the system for this volume is its distinction between Israel and the church. In a podcast published by the seminary's Hendricks Center on 8 October 2024, the theologian Craig Blaising of Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary, who earlier taught at Dallas, described dispensationalism as reading Scripture so that Israel and the church stay distinct, and said that "Israel stays in the plan of God all the way to the end"; the tradition, he and the Dallas professor Glenn Kreider explained, has "progressive" and "traditional" forms that differ on how separate the two peoples are. [cite:ts7_dts_hendricks] That is a statement about the people of Israel in God's plan, made in theological terms. It is not, on its own, a position on the borders of the modern state, on settlements or on American aid, and the seminary's published account does not take one.

The alumni list is not a political map

Dallas alumni include some of the best-known American preachers of the past half-century: Chuck Swindoll (1963), David Jeremiah (1967), Andy Stanley (1985) and Tony Evans; in a 2009 LifeWay Research study, three Dallas alumni were among the ten preachers Protestant pastors named as most influential. [cite:ts7_wiki_dts] Such names are sometimes listed as evidence of a Christian Zionist network. Having studied at Dallas is not evidence of any political activity on Israel. A pastor belongs in the record of Christian Zionism for what he has documentably said or done about Israel, and that record is taken name by name in later parts. [scene:ts8_cufi|Part Eight: CUFI] [scene:ts12_officials|Part Twelve: officials]

One Dallas graduate, however, changed the scale of the whole system. Hal Lindsey took a Master of Theology at the seminary in 1962 and worked with the student ministry Campus Crusade for Christ until 1969. [cite:ts7_wiki_lindsey] He held that "the establishment of the State of Israel in May 1948 is the fulfillment of this major prophecy", the regathering of the Jewish people. [cite:ts7_wiki_lindsey] The book he published the following year took the seminary's prophetic scheme out of the classroom to a mass readership. The next section measures how far it went. [scene:ts7_media|Part Seven: the mass market]

The finding is narrow and solid. Between the 1880s and the 1960s, Bible institutes and one seminary in Dallas gave dispensationalism something a reading of prophecy alone could not: degree programmes, faculty, a publishing house, a radio network and thousands of graduates. What these institutions taught about Israel was a theology of a people in a divine plan. The step from that theology to support for particular policies of a particular state was taken later, by named organisations and named people, and is documented, or not, in Parts Eight to Twelve. [cite:ts7_ct_bibleinst] [cite:ts7_wiki_moody] [cite:ts7_wiki_dts] [cite:ts7_dts_hendricks]

sections.h: The Mass Market: Prophecy Books and Religious Television
sections.html:
From 1970 the end-times system reached far more people through books and broadcasts than through any school. Three channels carried it: a prophecy bestseller by a Dallas graduate, a series of novels that turned the same scheme into fiction, and religious television, where Pat Robertson's Christian Broadcasting Network was the pioneer. This section measures each by what can be counted and records what its best-known figures said about Israel. Sales and audiences show reach. They do not show what readers and viewers came to believe, which only surveys can measure, and the one survey of the American public quoted here is given with its date.

The Late Great Planet Earth, 1970

Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth, written with Carole C. Carlson and published by Zondervan in 1970, applied the dispensational timetable to the news. The book appeared three years after the war of June 1967, and Lindsey read Israel's rebirth as the key to the prophetic clock. [cite:ts7_wrap_lindsey] He linked Jesus's saying in Matthew 24 that "this generation" would not pass away to the founding of Israel and treated a biblical generation as forty years, which some readers took to mean the end would come no later than 1988; the book was made into a film narrated by Orson Welles, released in January 1978. [cite:ts7_wiki_lgpe]

The sales figures vary with the source and the year. One history gives 28 million copies sold by 1990; Lindsey's obituary in TheWrap gave "an estimated 35 million copies by 1999." [cite:ts7_wiki_lgpe] [cite:ts7_wrap_lindsey] The book is regularly described as the bestselling nonfiction book of the 1970s, a judgment attributed to The New York Times; this volume found the attribution only in secondary works, not in the newspaper itself, and gives it as reported. [cite:ts7_wiki_lgpe] Lindsey's later prophecy books sold well but never matched the first. [cite:ts7_wrap_lindsey]

Lindsey moved to television. On the Trinity Broadcasting Network he hosted a programme called International Intelligence Briefing until the network pulled it for December 2005. Lindsey said that "some at the network apparently feel that [his] message is too pro- Israel and too anti- Muslim"; TBN's owner, Paul Crouch, disputed this and said the show had been pre-empted for Christmas programming. Lindsey resigned on 1 January 2006, broadcast on smaller networks, and returned to TBN in January 2007. He died on 25 November 2024, aged 95. [cite:ts7_wiki_lindsey] The episode shows that even inside religious broadcasting the weight given to Israel was argued over, and that the network's own account differed from his.

Left Behind, 1995–2007

The Left Behind novels, written by the pastor Tim LaHaye and the novelist Jerry B. Jenkins and published by Tyndale House, ran to 16 volumes between 1995 and 2007. [cite:ts7_sa_lahaye] They are thrillers "about Evangelical Christians living through an end-times apocalypse inspired by the Book of Revelation": the dispensational sequence of rapture, tribulation and return, told as a story. [cite:ts7_brit_leftbehind] The sales figures again conflict. The Christian Post reported at LaHaye's death in July 2016 that the series had sold "over 50 million copies", about 50 million of them by 2002; Shelf Awareness, a book-trade newsletter, gave "some 80 million copies" the same week. [cite:ts7_cp_lahaye] [cite:ts7_sa_lahaye] The difference probably reflects whether spin-off and children's editions are counted, but neither source says so. A circulating figure of "65 million" has no source and is not used here.

Pat Robertson and the Christian Broadcasting Network

Pat Robertson launched the Christian Broadcasting Network on 1 October 1961; CBN's own announcement of his death spoke of the network he founded in 1960. He hosted its flagship programme, The 700 Club, from 1966 to 2021, and died on 8 June 2023, aged 93. [cite:ts7_tvi_robertson] The historian Joseph Williams notes that Robertson played a crucial role in the Religious Right's rise in the 1980s and that he, like John Hagee, was closely identified with the pentecostal-charismatic movement. [cite:ts7_williams_pent] The political career that followed belongs to the next part. [scene:ts8_orgs|Part Eight: the organisations]

Robertson's best-documented statement on Israel shows both the theology and its limits as a shield. On 5 January 2006, the day after Prime Minister Ariel Sharon suffered a stroke, Robertson told The 700 Club audience that "God considers this land to be his" and suggested that a prime minister who gave up land would face God's opposition; Sharon had withdrawn Israel's settlers from Gaza the previous summer. [cite:ts7_cbs_robertson] [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] Israel's government did not welcome the theology. The tourism minister, Abraham Hirchson, said Robertson's help was no longer wanted for a planned Christian Heritage Center in the Galilee, for which Robertson was leading a group of evangelicals who had pledged to raise $50 million; a ministry official said the government remained "outraged". Robertson wrote to Sharon's son Omri: "I ask your forgiveness and the forgiveness of the people of Israel." [cite:ts7_cbs_robertson] A Christian broadcaster who claimed to speak for God about Israel's land had been rebuked by Israel's own ministers when the claim was turned on an Israeli leader.

Broadcasting beyond the United States

Williams's study in the journal Church History (2015) argues that pentecostal and charismatic ritual and media, more than formal end-times doctrine alone, helped forge Christian Zionism into a cohesive movement in the United States and abroad. A 1990s survey of evangelical leaders by James Guth and colleagues found that pentecostal and charismatic leaders gave Israel the highest political support, and that the strongest Christian Zionism went with premillennial eschatology. [cite:ts7_williams_pent] In 1994 CBN Conferences held an event in Virginia Beach, with Davidic worship and Jewish-style ceremonies, that drew on speakers from the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem; programmes broadcasting Israel-themed worship became "permanent fixtures on pentecostal-charismatic radio and television", and US-based evangelists and broadcast ministries spread this expression of Christian Zionism "well beyond North America", helping to "catalyze a transnational, global movement". [cite:ts7_williams_pent] The study gives no audience figures for those broadcasts, and none is offered here.

What the American public said

A survey shows how widely the core belief had spread by the early 2000s, though not what spread it. In a Pew survey of July 2003, 44 per cent of Americans said God gave the land that is now Israel to the Jewish people, and 36 per cent said Israel's existence fulfilled biblical prophecy about Jesus's second coming; white evangelical Protestants were the most likely to hold both views. [cite:ts7_pew_2003] The belief in the land as a divine gift was thus held by far more people than had bought a prophecy book, and by Americans of several traditions. Later surveys, including those that show younger evangelicals less attached to Israel, are taken up in Part Eleven. [scene:ts11_generations|Part Eleven: the generations]

The record supports a limited conclusion. Between 1970 and 2007 two publishing events put the dispensational timetable, with Israel at its centre, into tens of millions of copies, and religious television gave its preachers a daily platform. Those channels are documented by sales and by what their best-known figures said. The claim that they manufactured American support for Israel is a different claim; it would need surveys that tie exposure to belief, and none is cited in the sources this volume examined. [cite:ts7_wiki_lgpe] [cite:ts7_cp_lahaye] [cite:ts7_sa_lahaye] [cite:ts7_pew_2003]

sections.h: Abroad: Latin America and Africa
sections.html:
The system's fastest growth after 1970 was outside the United States, in the Protestant and Pentecostal churches of Latin America and Africa. That growth can be counted in censuses and surveys. Whether it carried a political attachment to Israel, and whether that attachment moved governments, is harder to show, and this section keeps the two apart. It sets out the church figures first, then the three Latin American governments whose decisions on an embassy in Jerusalem have been tied to their evangelical voters, then the thinner African record.

The Protestant shift in Latin America

In a survey of more than 30,000 people in 18 countries and Puerto Rico, conducted between October 2013 and February 2014, the Pew Research Center found that 19 per cent of Latin American adults identified as Protestant and 69 per cent as Catholic. The shares varied widely: Protestants were 41 per cent in Guatemala and in Honduras, 26 per cent in Brazil and 7 per cent in Paraguay. [cite:ts7_pew_latam2014] About two in three Protestants in the region identified as Pentecostal or attended a Pentecostal church. In Guatemala and Honduras most Protestants had been raised Protestant (only 23 and 26 per cent were former Catholics), while in Paraguay 68 per cent were converts. [cite:ts7_ct_pew2014] Pew reported that the region's Protestants were more likely than its Catholics to believe that Jesus would return in their lifetime, but it did not ask about Israel. [cite:ts7_pew_latam2014]

Brazil's census shows the trend continuing. In the 2022 count, released in June 2025, evangelicals were 26.9 per cent of the population, 47.4 million people, up from 21.6 per cent in 2010; Catholics fell from 65.1 to 56.7 per cent. [cite:ts7_reuters_brcensus] Williams's history notes that US-based broadcast ministries carried Israel-themed worship well beyond North America, and that one American preacher of the movement, Jonathan Cahn, held meetings in Honduras, Cuba, Haiti, India and Nigeria. [cite:ts7_williams_pent] What none of these sources gives is a measure of how many Latin American Protestants hold dispensational or Christian Zionist beliefs about the modern state. The church figures are a measure of the potential audience, not of the belief.

Guatemala, 2018

Guatemala opened its embassy in Jerusalem on 16 May 2018, two days after the United States. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Jimmy Morales, whom NPR described as "an evangelical", cut the ribbon. Morales called it "a step forward in favour of union and friendship." Guatemala's tie to Israel was older than its churches' growth: its UN ambassador, Jorge García Granados, had been "one of the architects" of the 1947 partition plan and lobbied Latin American governments to vote for it. [cite:ts7_npr_guatemala] Analysts cited by the University of Pittsburgh's Panoramas tied the 2018 move to three things together: the president's evangelical base, Guatemala's dependence on American aid and goodwill, and the history of Israeli arms, training and surveillance supplied to Guatemala's army in the 1980s after the United States cut military aid in 1977. [cite:pm_pitt_guatemala] Faith is one documented factor among several, and the Follow the Money volume treats the others. [scene:pm9_test|Follow the Money: what partner governments gain]

Paraguay, 2018–2024

Paraguay is the case that most complicates a religious explanation. Under President Horacio Cartes it moved its embassy to Jerusalem in May 2018, following Guatemala. [cite:ts7_npr_guatemala] Months later his successor, Mario Abdo Benítez, closed it, and Israel retaliated by temporarily closing its own embassy in Asunción. President Santiago Peña reopened the Jerusalem embassy on 12 December 2024, saying that "Israel is going to win, and the countries (that) are standing next to Israel, we are going to win." [cite:ts7_abc_paraguay] Paraguay was 89 per cent Catholic and 7 per cent Protestant in Pew's survey. [cite:ts7_pew_latam2014] A country with one of the smallest Protestant shares in the region moved its embassy twice, under two presidents, and reversed it once in between; the sequence follows changes of government, not changes in church membership. The Associated Press, reporting the reopening, noted that only the United States, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo and Papua New Guinea then had embassies in Jerusalem, and that Guatemala and Honduras had "similarly strong evangelical churches". [cite:ts7_abc_paraguay]

Brazil, 2019: the pledge and the meat exports

Brazil, with the largest evangelical population in the region, shows the system meeting a material interest. President Jair Bolsonaro suggested in January 2019 that Brazil would follow the United States in moving its embassy. When he visited Israel at the end of March 2019 he spoke of his Christian devotion to the Holy Land, and Netanyahu said Bolsonaro had called the move a matter of "when, not if". What Brazil announced on 31 March was an office in Jerusalem "to promote trade, investment, technology and innovation", attached to the embassy in Tel Aviv. Vice-President Hamilton Mourão had called an embassy move "a bad idea" because it would hurt exports to Arab countries, including an estimated $5 billion in halal food sales. [cite:ts7_ynet_brazil] The office opened on 15 December 2019 in the presence of the president's son, the lawmaker Eduardo Bolsonaro, who said his father was committed to moving the embassy; fears for meat exports to Arab markets were again reported. [cite:ts7_pti_brazil] Brazil's embassy did not move. In this case the documented commitment of a Christian president gave way to a documented export interest.

Africa: pilgrims and preachers

The African record in the sources examined is thinner and of a different kind. Nigeria has a government body, the Nigerian Christian Pilgrim Commission, which sends pilgrims to Israel as well as to Rome, Greece and Egypt. Christianity Today reported in December 2012 that about 30,000 Nigerians had travelled in the last three months of that year, up from 2,000 a decade earlier, and that the commission set a minimum age of 30 for Israel to stop pilgrims staying on illegally. [cite:ts7_ct_nigeria] State-organised pilgrimage is a measure of religious attachment to the Holy Land; it is not evidence of a political doctrine about the modern state, and Nigerian church leaders quoted in the same report disagreed about its spiritual value. [cite:ts7_ct_nigeria] The pentecostal broadcast and conference circuit that Williams traces reached Nigeria too. [cite:ts7_williams_pent] The parliamentary caucus network that the Israel Allies Foundation built on "faith-based diplomacy", which reached 50 countries by December 2020, is treated with Israel's own outreach in Part Nine. [cite:pm_ih_iaf50] [scene:ts9_israel|Part Nine: what Israel gained]

Abroad as at home, the counted facts are church growth and dated decisions. Protestants were 41 per cent of adults in Guatemala and Honduras in 2013–14, and evangelicals more than a quarter of Brazilians in 2022, and three of the six countries with embassies in Jerusalem at the end of 2024 (counting Paraguay's reopening) were in Latin America. The link between the two is a correlation that analysts explain by aid, arms, alliances with Washington and presidential faith together. Paraguay moved with few Protestants; Brazil, with many, did not move. The sources examined contain no survey that measures Christian Zionist belief in these countries, and that gap is recorded here as open. [cite:ts7_pew_latam2014] [cite:ts7_reuters_brcensus] [cite:ts7_abc_paraguay] [cite:pm_pitt_guatemala] [cite:ts7_ynet_brazil]

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: From Falwell to CUFI: the Political Machine
chapters.intro: Part Eight follows the end-times system into organised politics. It begins with Jerry Falwell's Moral Majority, founded in June 1979 for reasons that historians dispute but that did not centre on Israel, and with the Israeli prime minister Menachem Begin's choice of Falwell as his main American Christian partner. It then sets out three organisations built wholly around support for Israel: the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem, founded in 1980 when embassies left the city; Bridges for Peace; and the International Fellowship of Christians and Jews, a rabbi's fundraising body whose own tax returns show its scale. It ends with Christians United for Israel, founded by John Hagee in 2006: its self-reported membership, its summits and lobbying, its stated positions, the controversies around its founder, and what its finances do and do not disclose. Each organisation's own statements are set beside the record and its critics.
chapters.outro: Part Eight established that Christian Zionism became an organised political force through named people and bodies, not through a single machine. The Moral Majority, founded in June 1979 and disbanded in 1989, was not built on Israel, and Begin's partnership with Falwell, marked by the Jabotinsky medal of November 1980, was criticised by Jewish leaders at the time; Falwell told Peres in 1985 that he was "for Israel and not for the (Labor) Alignment or the Likud." [cite:ts8_balmer] [cite:ts8_wiki_mm] [cite:ts8_wiki_jabmedal] [cite:ts8_djn_tanenbaum] [cite:ts8_jta_peres1985] The ICEJ was founded in September 1980 because embassies left Jerusalem, and the IFCJ's revenue grew from $107 million in 2011 to $318 million in 2024, while senior Israeli rabbis opposed it. [cite:ts8_icej_about] [cite:ts8_pp_ifcj] [cite:ts8_jta_eckstein] CUFI's membership, from 400 pastors in 2006 to a claimed ten million in 2020, is its own uncounted figure; its summits drew vice-presidential speeches and remote addresses by Netanyahu, its Action Fund campaigned against Rand Paul in 2018 and Thomas Massie in 2026, and its stated land line is that Israel decides and Washington should not press it. [cite:ts8_wiki_cufi] [cite:ts8_hfl_10m] [cite:ts8_wh_pence2019] [cite:ts8a_inn_netanyahu2019] [cite:ts8_cufi_ky2018] [cite:ts8_ji_massie] [cite:gi11_jpost_hagee] Part Nine asks what the Israeli government and American politicians gained from the partnership. [scene:ts9_israel|Part Nine: What Was in It for Them]

sections.h: Falwell, Begin and the Moral Majority
sections.html:
By the late 1970s the end-times system traced in the earlier parts had schools, a press, radio and television behind it. [scene:ts7_media|Part Seven: the media] What it did not yet have was a national political organisation. That arrived in June 1979, when the Lynchburg, Virginia, pastor Jerry Falwell and the conservative strategist Paul Weyrich founded the Moral Majority. Weyrich coined the name. Three other New Right organisers, Richard Viguerie, Terry Dolan and Howard Phillips, had urged Falwell to lead such a body, and it was built on the mailing list of his broadcast, the Old Time Gospel Hour. At its height it claimed more than four million members and over two million donors. Falwell disbanded it in 1989 after money troubles, telling a meeting in Las Vegas that "Our goal has been achieved." [cite:ts8_wiki_mm]

What the movement was founded on

Israel was not the issue that brought the religious right into being, and the record of its founding should be stated before the record of its Israel policy. Historians disagree about the founding issue, and neither side names Israel. The historian Randall Balmer argued in 2014 that the movement began in the defence of private Christian schools against the Internal Revenue Service, which after the 1971 case Green v. Connally moved to withdraw tax exemptions from racially segregated schools, Bob Jones University among them. He quoted Weyrich's recollection, from a 1990 conference, of years spent trying to rally evangelicals on other issues: "I was trying to get these people interested in those issues and I utterly failed." [cite:ts8_balmer] Jonathan Whitehead, writing for The Gospel Coalition in 2022, disputed Balmer's emphasis. He placed the trigger in the IRS's proposed rules of 1978, which would have presumed church schools with few minority pupils to be discriminatory and drew about 150,000 letters of protest, and he treated opposition to abortion as one of several streams that came together under President Carter. [cite:ts8_tgc_whitehead] Either way, Israel came into the Moral Majority's programme as one item among several. It did not found it.

Begin's outreach

The Israeli side of the relationship began with Menachem Begin, whose Likud party won the election of 17 May 1977. [cite:gi5_djn_begin77] In 1979 Falwell joined a group of pastors, invited by the National Religious Broadcasters, on a tour of Israel, Jordan and Egypt, and met Begin, Anwar Sadat and King Hussein. Liberty University's own history counts about 15 visits by Falwell to Israel in his lifetime, including a group of 1,500 in January 1999 that it describes as the largest to visit Israel at once. [cite:ts8_lib_falwell] [cite:ts8a_lib_falwell] In November 1980 Begin presented the Jabotinsky Centennial Medal, named for the founder of his own political movement, to 100 Americans at a dinner in New York. The Jabotinsky Foundation of New York gave the medal, and Falwell was among the recipients; Senator Frank Church declined his in protest at its going also to Falwell. [cite:ts8_wiki_jabmedal] Liberty's account describes the award as an Israeli government honour; the encyclopaedic record names the foundation as the giver and Begin as the presenter, and that is the form used here. [cite:ts8_lib_falwell] [cite:ts8_wiki_jabmedal]

Begin's choice of partner drew criticism from Jewish leaders at the time. In September 1981 Rabbi Marc Tanenbaum wrote in a syndicated column that on his American visit Begin had "met only with Rev. Falwell" and had "in effect, ignored the presence in America of 50 million Roman Catholics." He called the "repeated singling out of Rev. Falwell as the only American Christian leader with whom to counsel" a mistake. Tanenbaum did not reject fundamentalist support, which he said Israel "badly needs"; his complaint was that a wider Christian friendship needed to be "cultivated and not alienated." [cite:ts8_djn_tanenbaum]

Two further stories about the Begin years recur in later accounts: that Israel gave Falwell a Learjet, and that Begin telephoned Falwell to explain the bombing of Iraq's Osirak reactor in June 1981. Neither was found in a contemporary report or a document checked for this volume, and neither is relied on here.

Across the Israeli party line

The relationship did not end with Likud. In March 1985 Prime Minister Shimon Peres of Labour received Falwell at his office, briefly and, by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency's account, reluctantly: his aides barred photographers. Falwell told Peres that Israel was "the most important democracy in the area" and preserved American influence in the face of "Soviet threats," and said: "We are for Israel and not for the (Labor) Alignment or the Likud." In the same visit he telephoned the retired Begin for about 15 minutes, met the Likud leaders Yitzhak Shamir and Ariel Sharon, and heard Moshe Arens address the 850 delegates of his "Friendship Journey to Israel–85". The agency recorded both sides of American Jewish opinion: many mainstream organisations objected strongly to the Moral Majority's positions on social questions, while others favoured the friendship because of its "consistent support for Israel." [cite:ts8_jta_peres1985] [cite:ts8a_jta_peres1985]

What this period established

The documented pattern of these years is a relationship between named people. An Israeli prime minister chose an American pastor with a national organisation as his main Christian interlocutor and honoured him publicly; the pastor declared his support for the state rather than for either of its main parties; and Jewish leaders in the United States argued openly about whether the partnership was wise. [cite:ts8_wiki_jabmedal] [cite:ts8_djn_tanenbaum] [cite:ts8_jta_peres1985] What the record does not show is that support for Israel was the reason the religious right organised, or that Falwell's organisation made Israel policy. Its founding issues lay elsewhere, and it dissolved in 1989. [cite:ts8_balmer] [cite:ts8_wiki_mm] The organisations that took up the Israel cause full time, beginning in Jerusalem in 1980, are the subject of the next section. [scene:ts8_orgs|The Jerusalem and fundraising organisations]

sections.h: The Embassy, the Bridges and the Fellowship
sections.html:
While the Moral Majority treated Israel as one cause among several, a set of smaller organisations made support for Israel their whole purpose. Three of them, founded or rooted in the 1960s to the 1980s, show the forms that work took: a Christian "embassy" in Jerusalem, a Jerusalem-based charity, and a Chicago fundraising body run by an Orthodox rabbi that became the largest channel of Christian money to Israel. Each is described here first in its own words, then by the documents and reporting about it.

The International Christian Embassy Jerusalem, 1980

The International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (ICEJ) dates itself to September 1980. In its own account, the Knesset had declared reunited Jerusalem the eternal and indivisible capital of the Jewish state, Arab oil states threatened an embargo against countries with embassies in the city, and the last 13 foreign embassies moved to Tel Aviv. A group of evangelicals then founded a "Christian Embassy" as an act of solidarity with what it called the Jewish people's "deep spiritual longing and attachment to this city." [cite:ts8_icej_about] [cite:ts8a_icej_about] The name and the location were chosen to make a point: unlike other international bodies, its members regarded Jerusalem as Israel's capital. [cite:ts8_wiki_icej]

The ICEJ describes its calling as a "ministry of comfort" to Israel and the Jewish people, based on Isaiah 40:1–2, and says it aspires "to develop pro-active expressions of Christian support for Israel in every nation on earth." [cite:ts8_icej_about] Its best-known event is an annual Christian celebration of the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem, which draws several thousand participants from almost 100 countries; its Israel and German branches are led by Jürgen Bühler. [cite:ts8_wiki_icej] The ICEJ was thus set up precisely because embassies left Jerusalem. Its stated position on the city is its own, not that of the governments whose citizens make up its branches. The embassy moves to Jerusalem from 2018 onward are taken up in [scene:ts12_embassy|Part Twelve].

Bridges for Peace

Bridges for Peace is a Jerusalem-based Christian charity that traces itself to Douglas Young, an American; a report of February 2015 described the organisation as marking its 50th year, and recalled that Young turned over his ministry's van for use as an ambulance as Israel prepared for war in May 1967. It describes its stance as "unconditional friendship to Israel and the Jewish community," and lists its work as serving Israel's needy, countering antisemitism and teaching Christians the history of Christian antisemitism. Through a US arm it has donated ambulances to Magen David Adom, Israel's emergency service; its international president in 2015 was Rebecca Brimmer. [cite:ts8_hfl_bfp] Other accounts give 1976 for the organisation's formal founding; no document establishing either date was found for this volume, so the year is left open. No audited figures for its scale were found.

The International Fellowship of Christians and Jews, 1983

The third model reversed the direction of the others. The International Fellowship of Christians and Jews (IFCJ) was founded in 1983 by Rabbi Yechiel Eckstein, an American Orthodox rabbi, to raise money from Christians for Jewish causes. By the time of his death at his home in Jerusalem in February 2019, aged 67, he had raised "hundreds of millions of dollars," mostly from Christians. [cite:ts8_jta_eckstein] Eckstein's own explanation, in a 2002 article quoted in the Jewish Telegraphic Agency's obituary, was that most evangelicals were pro-Israel "because it is part of their theology," and he said he could not accept "conditional love" from donors who expected a payback. [cite:ts8_jta_eckstein] [cite:ts8a_jta_eckstein]

The fellowship's sharpest critics were Israeli rabbis. In 2001 Chief Ashkenazi Rabbi Avraham Shapira published a letter condemning the use of Christian money to "expand Christian missionary propaganda," and Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv signed a letter forbidding cooperation with Eckstein, calling it "close to idolatry." The fellowship's funding of the Jewish Agency's immigration work stopped in 2014 amid a dispute over the agency's recognition of the fellowship, and Eckstein had long doubted the agency's efficiency; the IFCJ began its own immigration operation, offering each new immigrant a $1,000 grant on top of the Jewish Agency's benefits. [cite:ts8_jta_eckstein] [cite:ts8a_jta_eckstein] His daughter Yael Eckstein had become the fellowship's global executive vice-president before his death and is named as president and chief executive in its filings from 2020. [cite:ts8_jta_eckstein] [cite:ts8_pp_ifcj]

Because the IFCJ files a public Form 990 with the US tax authorities, its scale can be stated from its own returns rather than from claims. Its revenue was about $107 million in 2011 and stayed between $110 million and $133 million a year through 2019. It then rose steeply: $158 million in 2020, $220 million in 2021, $271 million in 2023 and $318 million in 2024, of which $307 million was contributions. In 2024 it reported expenses of $272 million and assets of $233 million. [cite:ts8_pp_ifcj] [cite:ts8a_pp_ifcj] The returns show how much was raised; they do not by themselves show what share came from evangelical donors, though the founder's obituary describes the donor base as mostly Christian. [cite:ts8_jta_eckstein]

Three models compared

Taken together, the three organisations show that "Christian support for Israel" was not one machine. The ICEJ made a political statement about Jerusalem its founding act; Bridges for Peace presented itself as a charity; the IFCJ was a Jewish-led fundraising body whose most determined opponents were senior rabbis in Israel, not critics of Israel. [cite:ts8_icej_about] [cite:ts8_hfl_bfp] [cite:ts8_jta_eckstein] None of them was set up as a lobby of the US Congress. That role, on a national scale, was taken in 2006 by a new organisation in San Antonio. [scene:ts8_cufi|Christians United for Israel]

sections.h: Christians United for Israel
sections.html:
The organisation that made Christian Zionism a standing lobby in Washington was founded by John Hagee, a pastor in San Antonio, Texas. Christians United for Israel (CUFI) had first been set up under that name in 1975 by David A. Lewis; Hagee relaunched it, and it was incorporated on 7 February 2006 with the backing of "over 400 pastors and ministry leaders." Its founding executive director was David Brog, who stepped down in April 2018; Diana Hagee and Shari Dollinger then became co-executive directors. [cite:ts8_wiki_cufi] Brog's book Standing with Israel (2006) and Hagee's In Defense of Israel (2007) set out the case for Christian readers, and a student wing, CUFI on Campus, followed. [cite:ts8_jvl_cufi]

Members: a figure it counts itself

CUFI's best-known number is its membership, and every version of it is the organisation's own. It has never published a definition of a member or an audited count, and the dated figures do not always agree with one another. It reported passing one million members in March 2012 and two million in January 2015. [cite:ts8_wiki_cufi] Vice President Mike Pence, addressing its summit on 17 July 2017, gave "more than 3.3 million believers." [cite:ts8_wh_pence2017] CUFI's own press release of 27 November 2018 gave "more than 4.5 million," while the encyclopaedic record puts "over 5.1 million" a month later. [cite:ts8_cufi_ky2018] [cite:ts8_wiki_cufi] On 8 July 2019 Pence said CUFI represented "6 million," then, after a call from the audience, "She said 7 million." [cite:ts8_wh_pence2019] CUFI announced on 22 December 2020 that it had passed 10 million, without saying how members are counted, and later accounts repeat "over ten million." [cite:ts8_hfl_10m] [cite:ts8_jvl_cufi] The growth from a few hundred pastors to millions of names is real as a claim and is unchecked as a count; on that basis this volume does not compare CUFI's size with that of other lobbies.

The summit and the lobbying day

CUFI's main instrument is an annual summit in Washington, followed by a day on which delegates visit congressional offices. In 2013 the eighth summit heard Netanyahu by satellite, and its eastern regional director, Victor Styrsky, reported, "We took Capitol Hill by storm today!" [cite:ts8_charisma_2013] [cite:ts8a_charisma_2013] In July 2014, during the Gaza war, the summit drew "some 4,800" delegates by one reporter's count; Netanyahu sent a taped message, Senator Lindsey Graham told Israel to "go as far as you need to go," and the next day members lobbied Congress to stop funding the Palestinian Authority. [cite:ts8_jp_summit2014] [cite:ts8a_jp_summit2014] Netanyahu had addressed the summit by video in 2010, and on 8 July 2019, the day Pence spoke, he addressed it again from Jerusalem. [cite:gi11_wiki_cufi] [cite:ts8a_inn_netanyahu2019]

The vice president's two speeches are the clearest record of what the summit meant to a sitting administration. In 2017 Pence said that "my passion for Israel springs from my Christian faith" and, on moving the embassy to Jerusalem, "It is not a question of if, it is only when." [cite:ts8_wh_pence2017] In 2019 he cited the embassy move and the recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights as done. [cite:ts8_wh_pence2019] The speeches show the administration presenting those decisions to CUFI as delivered; whether CUFI's lobbying caused them is a separate question, examined in [scene:ts12_embassy|Part Twelve].

Lobbying also reached individual members of Congress in their districts. In November 2018 CUFI and its legislative arm, the CUFI Action Fund, put $100,000 into two weeks of digital and cable advertising in Kentucky and bought full-page newspaper advertisements to press Senator Rand Paul to drop his hold on a bill codifying US security aid to Israel; Hagee said Paul was "way outside the mainstream on this." [cite:ts8_cufi_ky2018] Before the Republican primary of 19 May 2026 the Action Fund spent "six figures" on billboards in Representative Thomas Massie's district, reading "Tell Massie: Support Peace Through Strength" beside an image of Massie over the Iranian flag; Ari Morgenstern, a senior director of the Action Fund, said it was securing "every available billboard in the district." [cite:ts8_ji_massie] [cite:ts8a_ji_massie] Massie lost to the Trump-endorsed Ed Gallrein in a race that cost about $37 million in all, in which other pro-Israel committees spent about $8 million and the Associated Press judged Trump's opposition the key factor. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] [cite:pbs_massie_takeaways] The race is set out in [scene:pm5_massie|the Follow the Money volume].

What CUFI says it wants

CUFI's stated policy agenda, as summarised from its own materials, is support for US aid to Israel and its military edge, opposition to international pressure on Israel to make concessions, sanctions on Iran, adoption of the IHRA definition of antisemitism, opposition to the boycott movement through federal and state law, and support for recognising Israeli sovereignty over the Golan. [cite:ts8_jvl_cufi] On territory, Hagee's theology and his policy line are distinct. In a January 2011 webcast he said that Jerusalem "should never be divided for any reason." [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] He has also said that "Israelis – and they alone – have the right to make existential decisions about land and peace," and described CUFI's action as asking the White House not to press concessions Israel does not wish to make. [cite:gi11_jpost_hagee] The documented position is thus that Israel's government decides, and Washington should not push it; it is not a CUFI programme for territorial expansion. [scene:gi11_christian|Greater Israel volume, Part Eleven]

On conversion, CUFI states an official policy against proselytising Jews, and Hagee has said that Christian Zionists support Israel out of gratitude to the Jewish people, not to convert them. [cite:ts8_wiki_cufi] [cite:ts8_jvl_cufi] Jewish leaders and interfaith organisations have nonetheless raised concern, by the encyclopaedic record's account, that Hagee's teaching that salvation is through Christ alone may link the support to proselytising. [cite:ts8_wiki_cufi]

Controversy and disclosure

Hagee's preaching became a national issue in May 2008, when a 1990s sermon surfaced in which he said that God "sent a hunter" and that "Hitler was a hunter," reading the Holocaust as driving Jews towards their land. Senator John McCain, whom Hagee had endorsed for president, called the remarks "deeply offensive and indefensible" and repudiated them. Hagee called the charge that he condoned the Holocaust "the worst of lies" and withdrew his endorsement; earlier that month he had apologised for remarks critics considered anti-Catholic. [cite:ts8_cnn_hagee] [cite:ts8_ncr_hagee] He later apologised for saying Hitler had been fulfilling God's will. [cite:gi11a_wiki_cufi] The Middle East Council of Churches and Anglican and Catholic theologians have criticised CUFI's end-times theology. [cite:gi11a_wiki_cufi] Some accounts date the sermon to 2005; the 2008 reporting places it in the 1990s.

CUFI's finances are only partly public. The CUFI Action Fund, a 501(c)(4) in San Antonio, files returns: its revenue ranged from about $654,000 in 2015 to $1.8 million in 2017 and $1.7 million in 2021, and fell to $89,000 in 2024, when it spent $716,000; revenue in the intervening years was uneven, with $57,000 in 2019. [cite:ts8_pp_cufiaf] [cite:ts8a_pp_cufiaf] No return for the main CUFI organisation was found in the public database, and its budget and donors are not disclosed. A circulating claim that CUFI is registered with the IRS as a church could not be confirmed, nor could the claim that its returns show budgets in the tens of millions. The reference entry that lists CUFI as a 501(c)(4) gives the Action Fund's tax number. [cite:ts8_wiki_cufi] [cite:ts8_pp_cufiaf]

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: What Was in It for Them
chapters.intro: Part Nine asks what each side of the alliance gained from it. On Israel's side it follows the documented courtship of American Christian Zionist leaders by Israeli governments, from Menachem Begin's award to Jerry Falwell in 1980 and Benjamin Netanyahu's meeting with Falwell in 1998 to the Foreign Ministry's paid church campaigns of 2025, and it counts what came back in visitors, charitable money and parliamentary allies. On the American side it sets out what the polls show of the white evangelical vote, what a president said about the reason for one decision, what prophecy publishing earned, and which named donors funded the organisations in between. Motives are kept apart from money and votes: the reasons given by the people concerned and the readings of their critics are presented side by side as arguments, not as findings.
chapters.outro: Part Nine found an exchange that is documented in its transactions and argued in its motives. Israeli governments, most intensively under the Likud, cultivated named evangelical leaders: Begin presented Falwell's Jabotinsky medal in 1980, Netanyahu met Falwell and more than 1,000 supporters before meeting Clinton in January 1998, and in 2025 the Foreign Ministry paid for a $4.1 million church campaign and a $3.2 million contract to reach churchgoers. [cite:ts9_wiki_jabmedal] [cite:ts9_cc_wagner1998] [cite:pm_jta_730m] [cite:ts9_rs_showfaith] What came back can be counted in part: Christians were about 60 per cent of Israel's visitors in 2013, though Protestants, mostly evangelical, were only a fifth of Christian tourists, and the IFCJ raised more than $1.4 billion, mostly from evangelical donors, though a watchdog criticised its costs. [cite:ts9_mfa_tourism2013] [cite:ts9_ct_eckstein] [cite:ts9_mw_ifcj] In the United States about four in five white evangelical voters backed the Republican candidate in 2016, 2020 and 2024, Trump said the embassy move was "for the evangelicals," and Adelson's foundation funded CUFI and a campus group led by its former director. [cite:ts9_rns_exit2024] [cite:ts9_almon_trump2020] [cite:ts9_972_adelson] Whether the support springs from Christian nationalism, as Sarah Posner argues, or from the Genesis blessing and a sense of debt, as CUFI's leaders say, the record does not decide. [cite:ts9_dn_posner] [cite:ts9_jta_morgenstern2010] Part Ten puts these pieces together and asks how the shield works as a mechanism, and where it has failed. [scene:ts10_mechanism|Part Ten: How the Shield Works]

sections.h: Israel's Side: Courting a Constituency
sections.html:
An alliance has two ends. Earlier parts followed the end-times system from the Brethren assemblies to the Scofield Bible and into CUFI's summit halls; this section turns to the other end and asks what Israeli governments did to cultivate American Christian Zionists, and what flowed to Israel in return. The documented record here is of meetings, awards, ministry campaigns, tourism counts and charitable transfers. Why Israeli leaders pursued the relationship is a separate question; their own stated reasons and their critics' readings are given at the end, labelled as what they are. [scene:ts8_cufi|CUFI and its summit]

Begin and Falwell, 1980–81

The first sustained courtship came from the Likud. In November 1980, three years after Menachem Begin became prime minister, the Jabotinsky Foundation of New York awarded a Jabotinsky Centennial Medal to 100 Americans for service to Israel and the Jewish people, and Begin presented the awards at a dinner in New York. Jerry Falwell, whose Moral Majority had been founded the year before, was among the recipients; Senator Frank Church declined his own medal in protest at Falwell's. [cite:ts9_wiki_jabmedal] [cite:ts9_jta_falwell1999] On his visit to the United States in September 1981 Begin agreed to meet Falwell again. Rabbi Marc Tanenbaum, writing that month, called the "singling out of Rev. Falwell as the only American Christian leader" a mistake, and set against that choice an estimated 30 million "mainline" evangelicals, 50 million Roman Catholics and some 45 million liberal Protestants whom, in his view, Begin's singling out ignored. [cite:ts9_djn_tanenbaum] [cite:ts9a_djn_tanenbaum]

Tanenbaum's objection was not to Christian support but to its narrowness: in his reading, Begin's government had chosen one wing of American Christianity. That this wing was the one closest to the Likud's view of the land is this volume's observation, not his. The Anti-Defamation League's Leon Klenicki later made a related observation, that evangelicals received "a much warmer welcome" from Likud governments than from Labor ones. [cite:ts9_jta_falwell1999] That is a contemporary observer's judgement rather than a measured finding, but the pattern it describes, closer ties under the right, recurs in the record below.

Netanyahu's second channel

Benjamin Netanyahu made the channel a fixture. In January 1998, during his first term, he arrived in Washington for talks with President Bill Clinton on the Oslo process, and his first meeting in the capital was not with the president but with Falwell and more than 1,000 fundamentalist Christians, who hailed him as "the Ronald Reagan of Israel." Falwell pledged to contact more than 200,000 evangelical pastors and ask them to "tell President Clinton to refrain from putting pressure on Israel." [cite:ts9_cc_wagner1998] Netanyahu told the gathering, a Voices United for Israel conference that Falwell helped convene: "We have no greater friends and allies than the people sitting in this room." [cite:ts9_j_netanyahu2021] Falwell, by his own account, had "pledged to help him from our pulpits and our media ministries." [cite:ts9_jta_falwell1999]

The meeting had costs. Falwell was a vocal opponent of Clinton, and later reporting held that the association damaged Netanyahu's relationship with the president. [cite:ts9_j_netanyahu2021] It also divided Jewish opinion. Rabbi Yechiel Eckstein, himself the founder of an evangelical fundraising body, opposed Falwell's lobbying plan and said most evangelicals were "apolitical, contrary to public perception," and the Southern Baptist Convention said it did not intend to urge its pastors to lobby Congress. [cite:ts9_jta_falwell1999] Two decades on, the relationship was stated as doctrine by Netanyahu's closest adviser. Ron Dermer, his former ambassador in Washington, said in 2021 that "the backbone of Israel's support in the United States is the evangelical Christians," and CUFI's spokesman answered critics of the tie by saying that "Christian Zionists have had a relationship with every prime minister since Ben-Gurion." [cite:ts9_j_netanyahu2021] Netanyahu went on to address CUFI's summit by video in 2010 and, from Jerusalem, in 2019. [cite:gi11_wiki_cufi] [cite:ts9a_inn_netanyahu2019]

Pilgrims and tourists

The most measurable return is tourism. By Israel's own figures, Christians made up nearly 1.8 million of about 3 million visitors in 2008, and the number of American Christian visitors had risen by 40 per cent since 2000; Christians were about a third of American visitors, second only to American Jews. The Ministry of Tourism ran a campaign under the slogan "Visit Israel – You'll Never Be the Same," fronted by the Christian personalities Jack Hayford and Kay Arthur, and described its outreach to American church leaders, ministries and media. [cite:ts9_cp_tourism2009] In 2013, a record year of 3.54 million visitor entries, Christians were 53 per cent of overnight tourists and about 60 per cent of all visitors. Catholics were the largest Christian group at 49 per cent, the Orthodox 28 per cent and Protestants, "mostly Evangelical," 20 per cent; about four in ten Christian tourists called themselves pilgrims, and the United States was the largest source country. [cite:ts9_mfa_tourism2013]

Those shares matter for what this volume claims. Evangelical Protestants are a significant part of Christian tourism, but by the ministry's own breakdown they were a minority of it, well behind Catholic and Orthodox pilgrims. The state's interest in tourism therefore runs wider than Christian Zionism; the evangelical share is the part tied to an organised political network. The two met in the Galilee. Pat Robertson led evangelicals in pledging $50 million for a Christian Heritage Center there, and in January 2006, after Robertson suggested that Ariel Sharon's stroke was divine judgement for dividing the land, Israel's tourism minister Abraham Hirchson said Robertson's help was no longer welcome; Robertson wrote to Sharon's son asking forgiveness. [cite:ts7_cbs_robertson] The numbers rose to about 4.5 million tourists in 2019 and then fell with the war: foreign visitors in 2024 were down by about three-quarters, to 900,000, and Catholic pilgrim groups fell from about 16,000 in 2019 to fewer than 2,000. [cite:ts9_vn_pilgrims2024]

Money sent to Israel

The largest documented flow of evangelical money to Israel runs through a Jewish organisation. The International Fellowship of Christians and Jews, founded by Rabbi Yechiel Eckstein in 1983, raised more than $1.4 billion by 2019, mostly from evangelical donors, and in its own tax filings reported revenue of $132.8 million in 2015, rising to $318.2 million by 2024 (see Part Eight) [cite:ts8_pp_ifcj]; a decade before his death 98 per cent of its roughly 800,000 donors were Christian. It is credited with helping more than 730,000 Jews move to Israel. [cite:ts9_ct_eckstein] MinistryWatch, an evangelical donor watchdog, put its revenue at a peak of more than $135 million in 2015 (its tax return for that year shows $132.8 million) and $117 million in 2019, and criticised fundraising and management costs of just under 30 per cent of revenue, Eckstein's pay of more than $700,000 a year, and a Jerusalem outreach centre for which tens of millions were raised and which was then cancelled; it issued a donor alert from 2013. [cite:ts9_mw_ifcj] [cite:ts8_pp_ifcj] Eckstein's own account was that many Jews had viewed evangelical support as "utilitarian" and that his work was building friendship. [cite:ts9_ct_eckstein] John Hagee's ministries, separate from CUFI, have reportedly directed $100 million to Israeli charities, including right-wing and settlement groups. [cite:ts9_j_netanyahu2021]

The return also came as diplomacy. The Israel Allies Foundation, which grew from the Knesset Christian Allies Caucus founded in 2004, described its method as "faith-based diplomacy" and by December 2020 counted caucuses in 50 parliaments and about 1,200 parliamentarians, linking new caucuses to embassy moves by Honduras and Guatemala. [cite:pm_ih_iaf50] [cite:pm_wiki_iaf] [scene:pm9_test|Follow the Money: the caucus network]

The 2025 campaign

After 7 October 2023 the courtship became a budget line. In 2025 Israel's public-diplomacy spending included a $4.1 million campaign aimed at evangelical churches and about $40 million to host some 400 foreign delegations "of lawmakers, pastors, influencers and university presidents"; the 2026 budget set aside about $730 million for public diplomacy. [cite:pm_jta_730m] Among the contracts registered under the US Foreign Agents Registration Act was $3.2 million to a new firm, Show Faith by Works, working under the Foreign Ministry through Havas Media; its pitch proposed geofencing major churches in California, Arizona, Nevada and Colorado and all Christian colleges, to reach about 3.8 million churchgoers. Its principal, Chad Schnitger, said the plan was "an early planning document" with nothing "set in stone" and that "everything we do is vetted through teams of Christian pastors." [cite:ts9_rs_showfaith] [cite:pm_quincy_eighth] [scene:pm9_israel_direct|Follow the Money: Israel's direct spending]

Why: the stated reasons and the critics' readings

Israeli leaders have given their reasons on the record. Netanyahu called the gathering of 1998 Israel's greatest friends and allies, and Dermer called evangelicals the backbone of Israel's support in America. [cite:ts9_j_netanyahu2021] Critics within the Jewish community read the same facts as a strategic choice with a price. In 1981 Tanenbaum argued that tying Israel to one political wing of Christianity neglected the larger part of American Christian opinion; Klenicki noted the Likud's preference; Eckstein, while raising money from evangelicals himself, warned that most of them were not a political bloc. [cite:ts9_djn_tanenbaum] [cite:ts9_jta_falwell1999] What the record supports is narrower than either side's rhetoric: successive Israeli governments, most intensively under the Likud, cultivated named evangelical leaders and organisations, measured the return partly in visitors and donations, and in 2025 began paying contractors to reach churchgoers directly. Whether that investment changed American policy is the question of the next section and of Part Ten. [scene:ts9_us|The American side] [scene:ts10_mechanism|How the shield works]

sections.h: The American Side: Votes, Pulpits, Sales and Donors
sections.html:
On the American side the return is spread across several hands: a party that won a reliable bloc of voters, preachers and publishers whose ministries and books found a mass market, and donors who funded the organisations in between. This section takes each in turn, keeping three kinds of statement apart: what the polls and filings count, what named people said their reasons were, and what critics and defenders argue those reasons really are. [scene:ts9_israel|Israel's side]

The vote

White evangelical Protestants have been the most solidly Republican religious group in recent presidential elections, by every measure available. The national exit poll conducted for CNN found 80 per cent of white born-again or evangelical voters backing Donald Trump in 2016, 76 per cent in 2020 and 81 per cent in 2024. [cite:ts9_rns_exit2024] The Pew Research Center's panel, which re-interviews the same people, put the figure at 77 per cent in 2016 and 84 per cent in 2020, while the share of white adults calling themselves evangelical rose from 25 to 29 per cent. [cite:ts9_bng_pew2021] Pew's study of about 7,100 validated voters found white evangelical support in 2024 "no different" from 2020, and the political scientist Ryan Burge, using the Cooperative Election Study, put it at 83 per cent, the highest on record. [cite:ts9_rns_pew2025] [cite:ts9_ru_burge2025] The surveys define the group differently, and Burge warns that exit polls have structural flaws; the figures agree on the order of magnitude, roughly four in five, not on the decimal.

What the numbers do not show is why these voters chose as they did. None of the polls cited asks whether Israel decided a vote. The firmest evidence on belief is LifeWay's 2017 survey of Americans with evangelical beliefs, in which 80 per cent said Israel's founding in 1948 fulfilled prophecy but only 23 per cent backed a treaty for a Palestinian state, 31 per cent opposed it, and 46 per cent were unsure. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] What is documented is that at least one candidate drew the connection himself. At a rally in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, on 17 August 2020, Trump said of moving the US embassy to Jerusalem: "That's for the evangelicals," adding that "the evangelicals are more excited about that than Jewish people." [cite:ts9_almon_trump2020] That is a documented statement of his stated reason in a campaign setting. It is not proof that evangelical pressure caused the 2017 decision, a causal claim taken up in Part Twelve. [scene:ts12_embassy|The embassy move]

Pulpits and publishers

For preachers and publishers the return was a market. Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth sold an estimated 35 million copies by 1999 and has been described, in secondary sources, as the best-selling nonfiction book of the 1970s; Tim LaHaye and Jerry B. Jenkins's Left Behind novels, published by Tyndale House between 1995 and 2007, sold some 80 million copies by one count. [cite:ts7_wrap_lindsey] [cite:ts7_sa_lahaye] [scene:ts7_media|Spreading the system: books and broadcasting] Sales on that scale are revenue for authors and publishers and a sign of demand; they do not by themselves show that buyers adopted the books' politics.

The ministries that raise money for Israel also form an economy of their own. MinistryWatch found that the International Fellowship of Christians and Jews spent more than $19 million on fundraising in 2019, paid one direct-response agency, The Bigham Agency, nearly $8 million in 2018, and paid its founder more than $700,000 a year. [cite:ts9_mw_ifcj] [cite:ts9a_mw_ifcj] For the larger pastor-led ministries this volume found no audited, named-source revenue figure. John Hagee's ministries are reported to have given $100 million to Israeli charities, but their own income was not found in a filing or a named report consulted here, and CUFI's budget is treated in Part Eight. [cite:ts9_j_netanyahu2021] [scene:ts8_orgs|The organisations] Claims about pastors' personal fortunes that circulate on net-worth websites are not evidence and are not used.

Donors

The documented donor link runs mainly through one family. According to +972 Magazine's review of the Adelson Family Foundation's tax filings, Sheldon Adelson gave CUFI $4.6 million from 2012 and about $22.1 million to the Maccabee Task Force, a campus anti-boycott group he funded from its creation in 2015 and which is led by David Brog, CUFI's former executive director. [cite:ts9_972_adelson] Sheldon and Miriam Adelson spent $123 million on the 2018 midterm elections, nearly all of it benefiting Republicans, and in 2024 Miriam Adelson gave $5 million to the Republican Jewish Coalition's super PAC and was the largest individual donor to outside groups. [cite:pm_sludge_2019] [cite:pm_israelite_2024] These are funding relationships in the record. The figures for CUFI and Maccabee rest on one outlet's reading of the filings and were not re-checked against the returns for this volume.
