The +972 writer, Alex Kane, argued that Adelson's legacy was to fuse evangelical and Jewish right-wing politics; that is his interpretation, not a finding of the filings. [cite:ts9_972_adelson] [scene:pm3_donors_scale|Follow the Money: donors]

Motive: two arguments

Why American Christian Zionists back Israel is argued, not settled, and both sides are named here. The critical argument is put most sharply by the journalist Sarah Posner, in writing quoted to her on Democracy Now in November 2023: "At the heart of Christian Zionism is not a love for Israel but rather Christian nationalism." In her account Christian Zionists have merged support for Israel with being a good American Christian; Hagee's movement, she said, gives Israel's defenders a constituency with "the ear of the Republican Party," and treats Israel as "just a pawn" in a prophecy that ends with Jesus ruling the world, and he has "hoodwinked many Jews" into believing he supports Israel. [cite:ts9_dn_posner] [cite:ts9a_dn_posner] CUFI's answer is on the record too. Its spokesman Ari Morgenstern wrote in 2010 that most Christian Zionists back Israel because of the promise in Genesis that God will bless those who bless the Jewish people, and argued that end-times belief cannot be the motive because Hagee and other premillennialists read Matthew 24:36 as teaching that no human can hasten the end. [cite:ts9_jta_morgenstern2010] Its executive director David Brog told a San Francisco synagogue in 2017 that "Christians support Israel for the most noble of motives," that the support "starts with the Bible, but it does not end with the Bible," and that evangelicals rejected replacement theology and CUFI's members, knowing Jews better than other Christians did, were more sensitive to Jewish aversion to proselytising. [cite:ts9_j_brog2017] [cite:ts9a_j_brog2017]

Neither argument can be proved from the documents gathered here, and the volume does not adjudicate between them. Posner's describes an organisation and its leader, not the beliefs of every member; CUFI's describes the stated theology of its leaders, not the private reasons of every person it counts. What the record does establish is narrower. A large, reliably Republican voting group exists; one president said in public that a major Israel decision was made "for the evangelicals"; prophecy books sold in the tens of millions; and a small number of named donors and charities moved documented sums in both directions. [cite:ts9_rns_exit2024] [cite:ts9_almon_trump2020] [cite:ts7_sa_lahaye] [cite:ts9_972_adelson] How those pieces work together as a mechanism, and where the mechanism fails, is the subject of Part Ten. [scene:ts10_mechanism|How the shield works] [scene:ts10_failures|Where it fails]

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: How the Shield Works
chapters.intro: Part Ten takes the system described in the earlier parts and shows how it works in an argument, and where it stops working. The first section follows the mechanism step by step: a promise spoken to Abram in Genesis 12:3 is read as a promise about the Jewish people, then about the modern state, then about the policies of that state, so that opposing a policy can be described as opposing God. It traces each step through dated statements by named people: a senator, a Speaker of the House, an Israeli prime minister, a Dallas pastor and the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem, and it sets beside them the case of a Catholic commissioner removed from a White House commission in February 2026, where the argument ran in the other direction and was tangled with antisemitic statements. The second section records where the mechanism has failed: Christian theologians who reject the reading, an ambassador who withdrew a maximal statement, a Brazilian president who opened a trade office instead of an embassy, and a dispute on the American right that was argued openly after the killing of Charlie Kirk in September 2025.
chapters.outro: Part Ten established how the theology shield works and where it has been refused. Its mechanism runs in five steps that can be followed in dated statements: the ICEJ calls Genesis 12:3 the Christian Zionist "biblical mandate"; Senator Cruz, on 18 June 2025, read it as being about "the nation of Israel"; Speaker Johnson and Prime Minister Netanyahu applied it to nations in 2025; and Robert Jeffress, in 2017 and again in June 2025, said that those who oppose Israel are "on the wrong side of God". [cite:ts10_icej_hedding] [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] [cite:ts10_ww_kaylor] [cite:ts10_cbn_jeffress2017] [cite:ts10_cp_jeffress2025] The verse itself, spoken to Abram, does not name Israel, and the case of Carrie Prejean Boller, removed from the Religious Liberty Commission on 11 February 2026 after denying that Catholics embrace Zionism and repeating the deicide charge at the same hearing, shows the frame used in both directions. [cite:ts10_ww_kaylor] [cite:ts10_cam_prejean] [cite:ts10_ncr_prejean] The mechanism has also failed: theologians from Fuller to Catholic Answers rejected the reading, Cruz said he does not use his faith as the reason for his policy, Huckabee called his "take it all" answer hyperbolic within two days, Brazil opened a trade office instead of an embassy, and in December 2025 Tucker Carlson told Turning Point's conference that "God is not on any country's side". [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] [cite:ts10_ca_heschmeyer] [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] [cite:ts7_pti_brazil] [cite:ts10_aje_americafest] What the record shows is an argument made by named people, not the reasoning of every believer. Part Eleven turns to the Christians who have argued against the system from within the faith: the historic churches, Palestinian Christians, and a younger generation of evangelicals. [scene:ts11_churches|Part Eleven: the Christian counter-record]

sections.h: The Mechanism, Step by Step
sections.html:
The theology shield, as this volume defines it in [scene:ts1_defined|Part One], is not a doctrine that any church has adopted under that name. It is a way of arguing. A promise in the Hebrew Bible is read as applying to a modern state, and from there to that state's policies, so that a dispute about a policy can be presented as a dispute with God. Each step can be followed in dated statements by named people; beside each, this section sets what the text and its Christian critics say.

Step one: the verse

The text is Genesis 12:3, spoken to Abram before he is renamed Abraham; in the New International Version: "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you." Its place at the centre of the argument is stated by the organisations that use it. The International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (ICEJ) publishes an explainer by its executive director emeritus, Malcolm Hedding, which calls Genesis 12:3 the verse "most often referred to as their biblical mandate" by Christian Zionists. [cite:ts10_icej_hedding] Its definition of a Christian Zionist is modest: "a Christian who supports the Jewish people's right to return to their homeland". [cite:ts10_icej_hedding] The work is done in the steps that follow. The two Christian readings of the verse, the Christian Zionist and the covenantal, are set out in [scene:gx_s05|One verse, two readings] and in [scene:ts1_genesis|Part One].

Step two: "you" becomes the state

In the verse the "you" is one man. The Christian Zionist reading extends it to his descendants, the Jewish people, and from them to the State of Israel founded in 1948. The clearest recent instance came in an interview that Senator Ted Cruz of Texas gave to the broadcaster Tucker Carlson, released on 18 June 2025, while Israel was striking Iran's nuclear programme. Cruz said he had come to Congress intending to be "the leading defender of Israel in the United States Senate," and explained: "as a Christian, growing up in Sunday school, I was taught from the Bible" that "those who bless Israel will be blessed, and those who curse Israel will be cursed." Asked where that was, he said: "I don't have the Scripture off the tip of mind." Carlson pressed: "Those who bless the government of Israel?" Cruz replied that the verse "doesn't say 'the government of.' It says 'the nation of Israel,'" and added that "most people understand that line in Genesis to refer to the Jewish people." [cite:ts10_cl_cruz] [cite:ts10_cp_cruz]

Two corrections came from the reporting itself. Jewish Insider noted that the wording Cruz used is closer to Numbers 24:9, where the blessing is spoken over Israel as a people, than to Genesis 12:3, where it is spoken to Abram. [cite:ts10_ji_cruz] The Baptist editor Brian Kaylor made the point from the other side: Genesis 12:3 "does not actually mention Israel since Israel didn't yet exist at that point in the story." [cite:ts10_ww_kaylor] The step from Abram to the state is therefore an interpretation, made by named teachers, and not the text's own wording. Cruz's own account was also narrower than the exchange suggested. He called the verse his personal motivation and said: "Not everyone I represent is a Christian, so I don't use my faith as the reason we should support Israel." His main public case in the same interview was strategic: "Israel is doing a massive favor to America right now by trying to take out Iran's nuclear capacity." [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] [cite:ts10_ji_cruz]

Step three: the blessing becomes a test for nations

Once the "you" is the state, the blessing and the curse can be applied to other states. Word&Way reported two such uses in 2025. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, in July 2025, rendered the verse as "I'll bless the nation that blesses Israel and curse the nation that curses Israel", adding the word "Israel" to it; the outlet linked a video clip and did not name the venue. At a White House press conference with President Trump on 29 September 2025, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said: "It's also in the Bible. It says, 'Those who will bless you will be blessed, and those who will curse you will be cursed.'" [cite:ts10_ww_kaylor] Neither defined which acts count as blessing; both read a promise to one man as a standard for judging governments.

Step four: opposing a policy becomes opposing God

The decisive step is the one that turns a policy disagreement into a religious one. Robert Jeffress, senior pastor of First Baptist Church in Dallas, took it in plain words twice, eight years apart. After the Obama administration declined to veto a UN Security Council resolution condemning Israeli settlements in December 2016, he said on The Sean Hannity Show, as CBN News reported on 1 January 2017, that President Obama and Secretary of State John Kerry "are on the wrong side of God on this issue," and that "God will judge any nation that divides the land that God gave to Israel." [cite:ts10_cbn_jeffress2017] [cite:ts10a_cbn_jeffress2017] On 22 June 2025, in a sermon answering the Cruz–Carlson exchange, he said: "Unlike any other nation in the world, God created the nation of Israel," and: "Those who oppose Israel are always on the wrong side of history. And most importantly, they're on the wrong side of God." [cite:ts10_cp_jeffress2025]

John Hagee, the founder of Christians United for Israel, made the same move against his own government's diplomacy in a CUFI webcast on 6 January 2011: "God did not make a covenant with Washington, D.C. He made a covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] His stated policy line is narrower: "Israelis – and they alone – have the right to make existential decisions about land and peace," and CUFI asks the White House not to press Israel into concessions. [cite:gi11_jpost_hagee] [scene:gi11_christian|Christian Zionist land theology]

Step five: the argument closes

Step four moves a question about a resolution, a settlement or a weapons package from evidence to fidelity. The ICEJ states its own view of the critics: "Zionism" "has been turned into a negative word by Israel's enemies," and Christian Zionism is "under attack and often misrepresented". [cite:ts10_icej_hedding] The pattern recorded here is narrower: in each statement above, a named person answered a dispute over a specific policy by appeal to God's covenant rather than to the policy's effects. Whether any of them changed a decision is taken up for officials in office in [scene:ts12_officials|Part Twelve]; the statements show the argument being made, not its effect.

The mechanism in the other direction: the Prejean Boller case

The same machinery can be turned the other way, and one case from 2026 shows how quickly the result becomes tangled. At a hearing on antisemitism held by the White House Religious Liberty Commission on 9 February 2026, the commissioner Carrie Prejean Boller, a Catholic and former Miss California USA, told the Jewish witnesses: "Catholics do not embrace Zionism, just so you know. So are all Catholics antisemites?" She asked whether speaking about "what many Americans view as a genocide in Gaza" should be treated as antisemitic. [cite:ts10_cam_prejean] [cite:ts10_ji_prejean] At the same hearing she reiterated her belief that "Jews killed Jesus," the deicide charge, whose repudiation by the Catholic Church in 1965 is recorded in Part Eleven, and said that Candace Owens "just doesn't support Zionism" and should not be called an antisemite. [cite:ts10_cam_prejean]

On 11 February the commission's chair, Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick of Texas, announced her removal on X: "No member of the Commission has the right to hijack a hearing for their own personal and political agenda on any issue. … This was my decision." [cite:ts10_ncr_prejean] [cite:ts10_cam_prejean] Prejean Boller said members had asked her to resign months earlier; on X she called her stance "a matter of Catholic conscience" and said she would not surrender her "religious liberty" to "Zionist supremacy." [cite:ts10_ncr_prejean] [cite:ts10_cam_prejean] Both halves of the record belong together. Her question about Catholics and Zionism raised a real point of doctrine, set out in [scene:ts11_churches|Part Eleven]: the Catholic Church has never taught Christian Zionism. In the same session she repeated a charge against Jews that her own church has rejected. The case cannot be reduced either to a religious-liberty victim or to a simple instance of antisemitism; what it shows is that, once the argument is framed as fidelity to God, both sides can use the same frame.

The finding is about an argument, not about believers. A senator, a Speaker, a prime minister, a pastor and the founder of Christians United for Israel have, on dated occasions, cast opposition to a policy as opposition to God. The record does not show that the millions who tell pollsters they support Israel reason this way: in LifeWay's 2017 survey of Americans with evangelical beliefs, 23 per cent favoured a Palestinian-state treaty and 46 per cent were unsure, which is uncertainty, not a religious verdict. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway]

sections.h: Where the Shield Fails
sections.html:
An argument that turns policy into fidelity works only where the listener accepts the premise. The record shows several places where the premise was rejected, where a speaker withdrew from it, or where it met an interest it could not override. None of these cases shows that the shield has stopped working. Together they show that it is contested from inside Christianity, from inside the American right, and by governments that weigh other interests. This section takes the cases in four groups and keeps each attributed and dated.

Christians who reject the reading

The first failure is theological, and it is old. The covenantal reading of Genesis 12:3, which holds that the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ and extended to all who share Abraham's faith, is the reading of the Catholic Church and of many Protestant churches; the two readings are set out in [scene:gx_s05|One verse, two readings] and the churches' positions in [scene:ts11_churches|Part Eleven]. Within American evangelicalism there is dissent as well. In July 2007, 34 evangelical leaders signed a letter in The New York Times supporting a two-state solution. After Hagee's webcast of January 2011, Richard Mouw, president of Fuller Theological Seminary, argued that God's promise to bless Ishmael in Genesis 17:20 is one Christians have "an obligation today to honor" as well, and that Israel is done no favours if its leaders are not encouraged "to practice justice and righteousness"; Joel Hunter, a board member of the National Association of Evangelicals and the World Evangelical Alliance, said Hagee's view reflected "a limited portion of Christians who are millennial dispensationalists in their theology." [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] [cite:ts10a_cp_hagee2011]

The Cruz exchange of June 2025 drew the same answer from several traditions within a week. Joe Heschmeyer of Catholic Answers wrote on 25 June that the promises "apply to whoever shares the faith of Abraham, including the faithful Gentiles," citing Galatians 3, and called the reading that ties them to the modern state "disastrous theology, since it undermines the New Covenant itself." [cite:ts10_ca_heschmeyer] The Baptist editor Brian Kaylor pointed out that the verse "does not actually mention Israel." [cite:ts10_ww_kaylor] Cruz himself set a limit on the argument in the same interview: "Not everyone I represent is a Christian, so I don't use my faith as the reason we should support Israel." [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] The senator who made the most-quoted use of the verse in 2025 did not rest his public case on it.

An ambassador's maximal reading

The second failure came when the reading was stated at its widest by an official. In an interview with Tucker Carlson aired on 20 February 2026, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, an evangelical and a long-standing supporter of the settlement movement, was asked whether Israel had a right to the land promised in Genesis from the Nile to the Euphrates. He answered: "It would be fine if they took it all," and then, when Carlson listed the countries involved, "Not sure we'd go that far." [cite:gi11_abc_huckabee] Saudi Arabia called the remarks "extremist rhetoric"; Egypt, the Arab League, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation also condemned them. [cite:gi11_abc_huckabee] [cite:gi11a_abc_huckabee] Huckabee then called his answer "somewhat of a hyperbolic statement" and said Carlson's version "edited out my full response"; the State Department did not publicly address it, and neither government adopted the statement as policy. [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] [cite:gi11a_aje_huckabee] Once a theological reading was spoken by an ambassador, it was measured against the interests of the states it named, and its author withdrew it within two days. The episode and the ambassador's other duties are examined in [scene:ts12_officials|Part Twelve].

A president and his exporters

The third failure is the clearest case of the shield meeting a material interest. Brazil's president Jair Bolsonaro, who spoke of his Christian devotion to the Holy Land, suggested in January 2019 that Brazil would follow the United States in moving its embassy to Jerusalem; on his visit to Israel in March 2019 Netanyahu said Bolsonaro had told him the move was a matter of "when, not if". Vice-President Hamilton Mourão called the move "a bad idea" because of exports to Arab countries, including an estimated $5 billion in halal food. What Brazil announced on 31 March 2019 was an office to promote trade and investment, and when it opened on 15 December 2019 the embassy stayed in Tel Aviv. [cite:ts7_ynet_brazil] [cite:ts10a_ynet_brazil] [cite:ts7_pti_brazil] The case is set out in full in [scene:ts7_abroad|Part Seven].

A split on the American right

The fourth failure is political and recent. Charlie Kirk, the founder of Turning Point USA, had long presented himself as a defender of Israel and an opponent of antisemitism. In a letter to Netanyahu dated 2 May 2025, published after his death by the New York Post and reported by JTA, he wrote that he was "defending Israel in public more than your own government," that Israel "is losing the information war," and that "This should be a 5 alarm fire" because support was slipping even among conservatives. He wrote "from a place of deep love for Israel and the Jewish people," and complained that he was called "a paid apologist for Israel" when he defended it and antisemitic when he did not defend it enough. [cite:ts10_jta_kirk] Kirk was shot dead while speaking at Utah Valley University in Orem on 10 September 2025; Netanyahu later appeared to cite the letter in a pre-emptive denial of any Israeli involvement in his death. [cite:ts10_jta_kirk]

At Turning Point's AmericaFest in Phoenix, held from 18 to 21 December 2025, the dispute was argued from the stage. Tucker Carlson said: "God is not on any country's side," and, on Gaza: "If a man commits a crime, do we kill his kids? I don't care if it's in Minneapolis or Gaza City. No, we don't." Al Jazeera reported that he criticised Christian ministers he said had justified killing innocent people in Gaza. Ben Shapiro answered that Carlson's hosting of Nick Fuentes was "an act of moral imbecility" and that Candace Owens had been "vomiting all sorts of hideous and conspiratorial nonsense into the public square for years"; Steve Bannon called Shapiro and his allies the "Israel First" crowd. [cite:ts10_aje_americafest] Carlson's line is a direct denial of step three of the mechanism. That it was spoken at Turning Point's own conference, and answered there, shows the premise being argued over within the movement that had carried it.

What the failures show and do not show

The cases do not show that the shield has collapsed. The Brazilian decision turned on exports, not on theology; the Huckabee episode left US policy where it was; and Carlson and Owens are commentators, not church leaders, whose positions their opponents on the right have answered in strong terms. What the cases do show is that each step of the mechanism has been refused by someone with standing to refuse it: the reading of the verse by theologians, the transfer to policy by a senator who used it, the maximal map by the official who stated it, and the claim that God takes sides by a commentator speaking to the movement's young. The surveys point the same way. In LifeWay's 2017 poll, support for Israel among Americans with evangelical beliefs was 58 per cent at ages 18 to 34 and 77 per cent at 65 and over. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] The later polling, and the churches and Palestinian Christians who have argued against the system from within the faith, are the subject of [scene:ts11_generations|Part Eleven].

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: The Christian Counter-Record
chapters.intro: Part Eleven sets out the Christian record against Christian Zionism: the churches, theologians and believers who rejected the system from within the faith, in their own documents and in their own words. It begins with the historic churches, from Pius X's refusal to Herzl in 1904 through Nostra Aetate and the Catholic Catechism's rejection of millenarianism to the Holy See's agreements with Israel and Palestine, the statements of the Jerusalem church heads in 2006 and January 2026, and the divestment votes of the Presbyterian Church (USA) and the United Methodist Church. It then turns to Palestinian Christians, the community most directly affected and least heard: Naim Ateek and Sabeel, the Kairos Palestine document of 2009, the Christ at the Checkpoint conferences and Munther Isaac's preaching during the Gaza war, each with the criticism it drew. Last, it follows dissent among American evangelicals themselves and the dated surveys, from 2017 to May 2026, that show a generational shift. Every position is attributed to a named church, organisation or person, and every survey figure to its survey, date and population.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven established that the Christian counter-record is documented, old and specific. The Catholic Church refused Herzl in 1904, repudiated the deicide charge in 1965, rejects millenarianism in its Catechism, and recognises both Israel and Palestine without grounding either in prophecy. [cite:ts11_ccjr_herzl1904] [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] [cite:ts11_usccb_ccc676] [cite:rs_cw2_holysee_israel_protocol] [cite:ts11_wiki_hspal] Four Jerusalem church heads called Christian Zionist doctrines "false teaching" in 2006, and the Patriarchs and Heads of Churches of the Holy Land named Christian Zionism among "damaging ideologies" in January 2026, and the US ambassador answered that no church may speak for all Christians; the Presbyterian Church (USA) divested by 310 votes to 303 in 2014, and the United Methodist General Conference asked in 2024 that Israeli, Turkish and Moroccan government bonds not be bought. [cite:ts1_wiki_jerdecl] [cite:ts11_osv_heads2026] [cite:ts11_csm_pcusa2014] [cite:ts11_umnews_bonds2024] Palestinian Christians, about 1 per cent of the population of the West Bank and East Jerusalem, produced a theology that calls the occupation "a sin against God and humanity," and drew named critics who charge it with excusing violence. [cite:ts11_aje_christians2025] [cite:ts11_transcend_kairos] [cite:ts11_jcr_kairos] Among American evangelicals the shield still holds a majority, 57 per cent of white evangelicals favourable to the Israeli government in May 2026, but support has fallen since 2024 and is far weaker among the young. [cite:ts11_pew_2026] [cite:ts11_crosswalk_pew] [cite:ts11_tau_inbari] Part Twelve follows the shield into office, from the Jerusalem embassy to the officials of 2017–2026. [scene:ts12_embassy|Part Twelve: the shield in office]

sections.h: The Historic Churches: Rome, Jerusalem and the Mainline
sections.html:
Christian Zionism grew up inside one branch of Protestantism, and most of the world's Christians belong to churches that never adopted it. The largest of them, the Catholic Church, met political Zionism at its start with a refusal; it later revised its teaching about the Jewish people at its root, while still declining to read the modern state as the fulfilment of prophecy. The ancient churches of Jerusalem, Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant, have twice in twenty years named Christian Zionism directly as a teaching they reject. Several American mainline denominations have gone further and moved money. This section sets out what each body said and did, in its own documents, and gives the answers of those who disagreed.

Rome: from "non possumus" to Nostra Aetate

The first meeting between political Zionism and the papacy was short. In January 1904 Theodor Herzl was received by Pope Pius X in an audience arranged by the Austrian painter Count Berthold Dominik Lippay. Herzl's diary records the pope's answer to his request for support as "Non possumus" ("We cannot"), followed by: "The Jews have not recognized our Lord, therefore we cannot recognize the Jewish people." If Jews settled in Palestine, the pope added, "we shall have churches and priests ready to baptize all of you." [cite:ts11_ccjr_herzl1904] [cite:dv1_ej_piusx] The account is Herzl's own diary. The refusal was theological, not political: it rested on the old teaching that the covenant had passed to the Church, the view that Protestant restorationists, from the Puritans onward, had already broken with. [scene:ts2_puritans|Part Two: the Puritans]

After 1945 the Church's position changed in its foundations. In 1949 Pius XII asked that Jerusalem be given a legally guaranteed "international" status. [cite:dv1_rnc_1949] In 1965 the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate stated that "God holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers," that the Passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive," nor against Jews today, and that Jews "should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God." It decried "displays of anti-Semitism, directed against Jews at any time and by anyone." [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] The declaration says nothing about the land or the state. Twenty years later, in 1985, the Holy See's commission for relations with the Jews asked Catholics to understand the Jewish attachment to the land without adopting "any particular religious interpretation" of it, and to see the State of Israel's existence in terms of international law rather than of religion. [cite:ts1_crrj_notes1985] The Holy See signed a Fundamental Agreement with Israel on 30 December 1993 and opened full diplomatic relations in June 1994. [cite:rs_cw2_holysee_israel_protocol]

Catholic teaching also rejects the end-times system that underlies much Christian Zionism, though not by name. Paragraph 676 of the Catechism of the Catholic Church warns that the Antichrist's deception "already begins to take shape in the world" whenever it is claimed that the messianic hope can be realised within history, and states that the Church has rejected even modified forms of this falsification under the name of millenarianism, especially in the political form of a secular messianism. [cite:ts11_usccb_ccc676] The text addresses millenarian expectation in general, not dispensationalism or Scofield in particular; claims in earlier library material that Rome issued a ruling against "Scofield's entire prophetic system" go beyond what the documents checked for this book say. [scene:ts14_myths|Part Fourteen: myths and contested claims]

The Holy See has applied the same law-not-prophecy approach to Palestine. It signed a Basic Agreement with the PLO on 15 February 2000 and, on 26 June 2015, a Comprehensive Agreement with the "State of Palestine," which entered into force on 2 January 2016 and treated Palestine as a state. Israel's Foreign Ministry called the agreement one-sided, said it ignored Jewish rights and holy sites in Jerusalem, and argued that recognition "damages the peace process by strengthening Palestinian refusal to negotiate." [cite:ts11_wiki_hspal] The Church thus recognises both states and grounds neither in scripture.

Jerusalem: the patriarchs and heads of churches

The churches with the oldest presence in the land have spoken most directly. On 22 August 2006 the Latin Patriarch Michel Sabbah, the Syriac Orthodox Archbishop Swerios Malki Mourad, the Anglican Bishop Riah Abu El-Assal and the Lutheran Bishop Munib Younan issued the Jerusalem Declaration on Christian Zionism. It called the movement "detrimental to a just peace within Palestine and Israel" and stated: "We categorically reject Christian Zionist doctrines as false teaching." [cite:ts1_wiki_jerdecl] [cite:ts11_osv_heads2026] Representatives of the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem, Bridges for Peace and Christian Friends of Israel published a response that denied Christian Zionism is a heresy, grounded their position in the Bible, including God's gift of the land, and described it as "not a threat to anybody, but instead seeks to be a blessing." [cite:ts1_wiki_jerdecl] The declaration, not the later Kairos Palestine document, is the text that names Christian Zionism as false teaching; library material that attributes the word "heresy" to Kairos is not supported by the passages checked. [scene:ts11_palestinian|Palestinian Christians]

Twenty years later the Patriarchs and Heads of Churches of the Holy Land, as a body, returned to the subject. In a statement dated 17 January 2026 and published by the Patriarchate of Jerusalem the next day, the first day of the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, they named Christian Zionism among "damaging ideologies" whose recent activities "mislead the public, sow confusion, and harm the unity of our flock," described them as "interference in the internal life of the churches," and objected that their promoters had been "welcomed at official levels both locally and internationally." [cite:ts11_osv_heads2026] [cite:ts11_aje_heads2026] The statement followed a reported visit by about 1,000 evangelical pastors to Israel in early January, and a meeting on 31 December 2025 at which Prime Minister Netanyahu called evangelical Christians Israel's "closest allies." [cite:ts11_osv_heads2026]

The replies came from both an office of state and the academy. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, wrote on 20 January 2026 that he respected "the traditional, liturgical churches" but disagreed that "any sect of the Christian faith should claim exclusivity in speaking for Christians worldwide," and said the term "Christian Zionism" is used "in a pejorative manner to disparage free-church believers." [cite:ts11_osv_heads2026] Theologians published by the Middle East Forum, a pro-Israel think tank, answered on the merits: André Villeneuve of Sacred Heart Major Seminary argued that Zionism "is not the product of nineteenth-century Protestant dispensationalism"; Gavin D'Costa called the election of the Jewish people "the theological foundation of Catholic Zionism"; and A.J. Nolte of Regent University said Arab Christians are "expected to actively promote and support the Arab cause, or else." [cite:ts11_mef_theologians] Huckabee's own role is treated in Part Twelve. [scene:ts12_officials|Part Twelve: officials]

The American mainline: statements and money

The Presbyterian Church (USA) has gone furthest. On 20 June 2014 its General Assembly voted 310 to 303 to sell its holdings, about $21 million, in Caterpillar, Hewlett-Packard and Motorola Solutions, as a protest against the use of their products in the occupied territories; a similar proposal had failed by two votes in 2012. The measure reaffirmed Israel's right to exist, and supporters said it was not part of the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement; the moderator, Heath Rada, said it was "in no way" a reflection of "lack of love for our Jewish brothers and sisters." [cite:ts11_csm_pcusa2014] The Israeli Embassy in Washington called the resolution "shameful," the American Jewish Committee said the vote was "driven by hatred of Israel," and Rabbi Rick Jacobs of the Union for Reform Judaism said the church was no longer "a partner" for joint work on peace. [cite:ts11_csm_pcusa2014] In 2024 the same assembly adopted an overture "On Confessing our Complicity in Christian Zionism," and in August 2026 a church gathering in Louisville met under the title "Christianity without Christian Zionism." [cite:ts1_pcusa_2026]

The United Methodist Church has acted in smaller steps. In January 2016 Wespath, its pension agency, with more than $20 billion under management, excluded five Israeli banks, Hapoalim, Leumi, First International, Israel Discount and Mizrahi Tefahot, from its portfolios as part of a screen on "high-risk" countries. [cite:ts11_jta_wespath2016] On 30 April 2024, at the General Conference in Charlotte, delegates approved by consent calendar a resolution, written by the advocacy group United Methodists for Kairos Response, asking church institutions not to buy the government bonds of Israel, Turkey and Morocco because of their long-term occupations of Palestinian territory, northern Cyprus and Western Sahara. The resolution is advisory and does not bind Wespath, which said it "takes the call seriously"; at the end of 2023 it held about 0.12 per cent of its investments in those three governments' debt. [cite:ts11_umnews_bonds2024]

The documented pattern is that the churches outside the dispensational tradition have rejected its reading of prophecy in their own teaching documents, and that some have turned that rejection into votes on investment. What the record does not show is a single Christian position against Israel: the Catholic Church recognises Israel and condemns antisemitism in its highest teaching, the Presbyterian vote passed by seven votes out of 613, and Catholic and Anglican theologians publicly defend forms of Christian Zionism. [cite:rs_cw2_holysee_israel_protocol] [cite:ts11_va_nostra4] [cite:ts11_csm_pcusa2014] [cite:ts11_mef_theologians]

sections.h: Palestinian Christians: the Theology from the Other Side of the Wall
sections.html:
The Christians who live in the land the theology is about are almost absent from its literature. They are few and growing fewer. Christians made up about 12 per cent of the population of Palestine early in the twentieth century; by the Palestinian census of 2017 there were roughly 47,000 to 50,000 in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, about 1 per cent of the population, and about 1,000 in Gaza before the war that began in October 2023. [cite:ts11_aje_christians2025] Many belong to churches older than any European denomination, Greek Orthodox, Latin Catholic, Melkite, Armenian, Syriac, Anglican and Lutheran, and a small evangelical community. From the late 1980s some of their clergy and scholars built a theology that answers Christian Zionism directly. This section follows four of its landmarks: Naim Ateek and Sabeel, the Kairos Palestine document, the Christ at the Checkpoint conferences, and Munther Isaac's preaching during the Gaza war, each with the criticism it drew.

Naim Ateek and Sabeel

Naim Ateek was born in Beisan, now Beit She'an, in 1937; in 1948 his family was displaced to Nazareth, and he has said that Israeli forces destroyed the town. He became an Anglican priest in 1967 and later a canon of St George's Cathedral in Jerusalem. His book Justice, and Only Justice (1989), based on his doctoral dissertation, is described as the first statement of a Palestinian theology of liberation; it argues against Zionist readings of the Hebrew Bible. He founded the Sabeel Ecumenical Liberation Theology Center in Jerusalem (its own histories give 1991 and 1994) and wrote a 2006 paper calling for "morally responsible investment," which became a reference point for the church divestment campaigns described in the previous section. [cite:ts11_wiki_ateek] [scene:ts11_churches|The historic churches]

Ateek's language has been contested. His Easter message of 2001 described Palestine as "one huge golgotha," using the crucifixion as an image of Palestinian suffering. [cite:ts11_wiki_ateek] Critics have charged Sabeel with reviving older Christian teaching against the Jews of the kind Nostra Aetate repudiated: Dexter Van Zile's 2011 article in the Jewish Political Studies Review is titled "Updating the Ancient Infrastructure of Christian Contempt: Sabeel." The reference work consulted for this book lists the article without summarising its argument or recording a reply, so it is noted here as a criticism made, not a finding. [cite:ts11_wiki_ateek] [cite:ts11_va_nostra4]

Kairos Palestine, 2009

On 11 December 2009, in Bethlehem, a group of Palestinian Christians launched the Kairos Palestine document at an event chaired by the former Latin Patriarch Michel Sabbah. Its authors included Sabbah, Archbishop Atallah Hanna and the Lutheran Bishop Munib Younan, with Rifat Kassis as coordinator; according to the critic Malcolm Lowe, Younan later asked for his name to be removed. [cite:ts11_jcr_kairos] [cite:ts11_transcend_kairos] The document calls the Israeli occupation "a sin against God and humanity" and states that "any theology that legitimizes the occupation is far from Christian teachings." It asks churches abroad "to revisit theologies that justify crimes perpetrated against our people and the dispossession of the land," declares that "non-violent resistance to this injustice is a right and duty for all Palestinians including Christians," and calls for divestment and "an economic and commercial boycott of everything produced by the occupation." [cite:ts11_transcend_kairos] [cite:ts11_jcr_kairos] Sabeel endorsed it. [cite:ts11_wiki_ateek] In the passages checked, the document does not call Christian Zionism a "heresy," as some library material states; its target is "Biblical fundamentalism" and any theology used to justify the occupation. [cite:ts11_jcr_kairos]

The document's critics read it differently. Malcolm Lowe, a biblical scholar in Jerusalem, writing in 2010 in an analysis republished by the Jewish-Christian Relations site, argued that one of its aims was to neutralise Christian Zionist support for Israel, noted its call for economic sanctions against Israel, and quoted its section 4.3, which says that "the roots of 'terrorism' are in the human injustice committed and in the evil of the occupation." He argued that the scare quotes and the language of "resistance" served as euphemisms, and observed that the excerpts he examined contained no outright rejection of terrorism. [cite:ts11_jcr_kairos] The document's own text, as published at its launch, commits its authors to non-violent resistance. [cite:ts11_transcend_kairos] Both readings rest on the same text and are given here side by side.

Christ at the Checkpoint

The most direct challenge to Christian Zionism from within evangelicalism itself has come from Bethlehem Bible College, an evangelical school, which first held its Christ at the Checkpoint conference in 2010 and has held it every two years since. One of its stated objectives is to "create a platform for serious engagement with Christian Zionism"; its 2012 manifesto stated that "Any exclusive claim to land of the Bible in the name of God is not in line with the teaching of Scripture." [cite:ts11_bbc_catc] [cite:ts11_jta_catc2014] Its speakers have included American evangelical figures: Joel Hunter, a board member of the National Association of Evangelicals, in 2012, and Geoff Tunnicliffe, secretary-general of the World Evangelical Alliance, was announced among the 2014 speakers. Hunter said he "did not hear one word about Israel as an enemy" in 2012 and that the conference's aim was to "hear from Arab Christians." [cite:ts11_jta_catc2014]

Christian Zionist organisations answered in their own terms. The International Christian Embassy Jerusalem issued a briefing on 4 March 2012 describing the conference's message as "one-sided" and "based on a deeply flawed historical narrative," warning of "Cloaked versions of Replacement theology," and stating that some speakers had gone "into outright anti-Semitism." [cite:ts11_icej_catc] CUFI's David Brog said in 2014 that the "anti-Israel" message was "resonating" and that "This generation is in play." [cite:ts11_jta_catc2014] The exchange is a theological dispute between named evangelical institutions, each stating its own position.

Munther Isaac and the Gaza war

Munther Isaac, ordained in 2016 as a Lutheran pastor in Bethlehem and director of Christ at the Checkpoint from 2012, wrote From Land to Lands (2015), which challenges a Zionist reading of the Bible and argues that the land should be shared, and The Other Side of the Wall (2020), which criticises Christian Zionists for overlooking abuses against Palestinians. [cite:ts11_wiki_isaac] In Advent 2023 his Christmas Lutheran Church set its nativity scene in rubble, and on Christmas Eve he preached "Christ in the Rubble," which circulated widely; his book of that title followed in 2025. In April 2024 he told Tucker Carlson that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza [cite:ts11_wiki_isaac], a charge Israel's government rejects; it called the UN commission report that reached the same conclusion in September 2025 "distorted and false." [cite:gz_ctv_coi2025] One reviewer of The Other Side of the Wall wrote that he describes Palestinian suffering accurately but disregards Israeli security concerns. The Israeli government cancelled his travel permit, a step the reference work links to his activism. [cite:ts11_wiki_isaac]

The war reached the churches of Gaza themselves. On 19 October 2023 an Israeli airstrike destroyed a building in the compound of the Greek Orthodox Church of Saint Porphyrius, where displaced people were sheltering, killing 18 civilians; the Israeli military said it had struck a Hamas "command and control centre," and Amnesty International found no sign of a military objective and called the strike reckless, amounting to a war crime. [cite:ts11_amnesty_porph] On 17 July 2025 a tank shell struck the Holy Family Catholic Church in Gaza City, killing three people and wounding the parish priest, Gabriel Romanelli, among others. Israel's Foreign Ministry said that "Israel never targets churches," Prime Minister Netanyahu expressed regret that "stray ammunition" had hit the church, the Latin Patriarch Pierbattista Pizzaballa said "they hit the church directly," and the Vatican called the attack "unjustifiable." [cite:ts11_ncr_holyfamily] In the West Bank, arsonists targeted St George's Church in Taybeh in July 2025. [cite:ts11_aje_christians2025]

What the record shows is a body of Palestinian Christian theology, written by named clergy and institutions, that rejects Christian Zionism on scriptural grounds and calls on foreign churches to act. It also shows the counter-charges: that this theology echoes older anti-Jewish themes and is soft on violence, made by named critics and organisations. Neither side's case is settled by the other's assertion; the texts are cited so that each can be read.

sections.h: Evangelical Dissent and the Generational Shift
sections.html:
The strongest test of the theology shield is not what Catholics or Palestinian Christians think of it but whether it holds among American evangelicals, the constituency it was built on. Here the record shows two things at once. Evangelical scholars and leaders have argued against Christian Zionism from inside the movement for decades, and white evangelical Protestants remain, as of 2026, the American religious group most favourable to the Israeli government. Yet the surveys also show support falling, and falling fastest among the young. This section sets out the named dissenters first and then the dated polls, each with its population and method, because the shift is easily overstated in both directions.

Dissent from inside

The dissent is older than the polls. Gary Burge, who taught New Testament at Wheaton College for about 25 years and then at Calvin Theological Seminary from 2017 to 2023, published Whose Land? Whose Promise? in 2003 (revised in 2013) and Jesus and the Land: The New Testament Challenge to Holy Land Theology in 2010, which examines how the New Testament interprets the Old Testament promises of land. [cite:ts11_wiki_burge] In July 2007, 34 evangelical leaders signed a letter in The New York Times supporting a two-state solution. [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] After John Hagee's webcast of January 2011, Richard Mouw, president of Fuller Theological Seminary, argued that God's promise to bless Ishmael in Genesis 17:20 still binds Christians and that Israel's blessing depends partly on justice towards its neighbours, and Joel Hunter of the National Association of Evangelicals' board said Hagee's view reflects "a limited portion of Christians who are millennial dispensationalists in their theology." [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] Hunter later spoke at Christ at the Checkpoint in Bethlehem, and the World Evangelical Alliance's secretary-general, Geoff Tunnicliffe, was announced among its 2014 speakers. [cite:ts11_jta_catc2014] [scene:ts11_palestinian|Palestinian Christians]

The CUFI side has stated its position in the same debate. Hagee has said that "Israelis – and they alone – have the right to make existential decisions about land and peace," and CUFI describes its own aim as asking Washington not to press Israel into concessions. [cite:gi11_jpost_hagee] In 2014 CUFI's David Brog said he was "worried" that a generational shift might follow, and that "This generation is in play." [cite:ts11_jta_catc2014] The question the surveys answer is whether that worry was borne out.

What the surveys show

The first detailed baseline is LifeWay Research's survey of 2,002 Americans with evangelical beliefs, conducted from 20 to 28 September 2017 and sponsored by Chosen People Ministries and the author Joel C. Rosenberg. It found that 80 per cent said Israel's founding in 1948 fulfilled biblical prophecy, and that support for Israel stood at 58 per cent among those aged 18 to 34 and 77 per cent among those 65 and over. Only 23 per cent favoured a treaty creating a Palestinian state, 31 per cent opposed one and 46 per cent were unsure. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] The age gap was already there; so was a large share of undecided respondents, which is not the picture of a uniformly committed bloc.

The sharpest measured change comes from the political scientists Motti Inbari of the University of North Carolina at Pembroke and Kirill Bumin, whose surveys from 2018 to 2021 appear in their book Christian Zionism in the Twenty-First Century. Among evangelicals under 30, support for Israel fell from 68.9 per cent in 2018 to 33.6 per cent in 2021; support for the Palestinians rose from "a little over 5%" to 24.3 per cent; and those supporting neither side rose from 25 to 42.2 per cent. [cite:ts11_tau_inbari] The authors offered three explanations: an information environment shaped by social media in which Israel is portrayed as the "aggressor"; "a sort of youthful rebellion" against the evangelical establishment; and theology. Bumin reported that almost seven in ten young evangelicals surveyed in spring 2021 held postmillennial or amillennial views, which give Israel little role in end-times prophecy, and that the most pro-Israel, premillennial pastors were older. [cite:ts11_tau_inbari] Tel Aviv University's release of these findings does not give sample sizes, which limits how far a single drop over three years can be generalised.

The most recent large survey is the Pew Research Center's, fielded from 4 to 17 May 2026 among 12,574 American adults, with a margin of error of plus or minus 1.3 points. White evangelical Protestants were "the only religious group in which a majority (57%) have a favorable view of the Israeli government"; 74 per cent viewed the Israeli people favourably and 33 per cent the Palestinian people. Among Catholics the favourable share for the Israeli government was 34 per cent, among white non-evangelical Protestants 33, among Black Protestants 30 and among Jewish Americans 47. [cite:ts11_pew_2026] According to a report of the same data, white evangelicals' favourable view of the Israeli government had fallen from 71 per cent in 2024, and of the Israeli people from 84 per cent. [cite:ts11_crosswalk_pew] Pew's release does not break white evangelicals down by age; its age figures are for all adults and by party. Among Republicans and Republican-leaning adults, 28 per cent of those aged 18 to 29 viewed the Israeli government favourably, against 75 per cent of those 65 and over. [cite:ts11_pew_2026]

What the numbers do and do not show

Set side by side, the surveys measure different things. LifeWay counted people by belief, Inbari and Bumin asked young evangelicals which side they supported, and Pew measured favourable views of a government and a people among white evangelicals and among age groups by party. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] [cite:ts11_tau_inbari] [cite:ts11_pew_2026] The comparison below keeps those differences visible.

As of October 2026, then, the documented position is a split rather than a collapse. The constituency on which the shield was built still holds the most favourable view of the Israeli government of any American religious group, while within it, and within the Republican Party, younger cohorts hold markedly cooler views, and evangelical scholars and institutions have argued against the theology for two decades. [cite:ts11_pew_2026] [cite:ts11_tau_inbari] [cite:ts11_wiki_burge] How that split has played out in office, from the embassy move to the 2026 Huckabee episode, is the subject of Part Twelve. [scene:ts12_embassy|Part Twelve: the shield in office]

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: The Shield in Office
chapters.intro: Part Twelve follows the theology into government between 2017 and 2026. It sets out the decisions most often credited to Christian Zionist influence in the first Trump administration (the recognition of Jerusalem and the embassy's move, the recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, and the 2019 statement on West Bank settlements), the reasons the officials gave for them, and the governments abroad, in Latin America and the Pacific, that followed or declined to follow. It then takes the officials one by one, from Vice President Mike Pence and Secretary of State Mike Pompeo to Ambassador Mike Huckabee, Speaker Mike Johnson, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Senator Ted Cruz, and records what each said, in his own words, about faith and Israel. The question throughout is narrow: what did office-holders say and do, and what does that show, and not show, about the theology's effect on policy. Statements and statuses are given as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: Part Twelve found the theology present in office but not written into the decisions' own texts. Trump's recognition of Jerusalem rested on the 1995 Act and the failure of the waivers, Proclamation 9852 on security and Iran, and Pompeo's settlements statement on law and the stalled peace process; yet Pence promised the embassy at CUFI's summit, Jeffress and Hagee prayed at its opening on 14 May 2018, and Trump later said the move was "for the evangelicals," so its cause stays contested. [cite:ts12_toi_trump2017] [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852] [cite:ts12_toi_pompeo2019] [cite:ts12_ncr_pence2017] [cite:ts12_cnn_pastors] [cite:ts9_almon_trump2020] Officials stated religious grounds in their own words: Pompeo's Esther answer, Johnson's "promised" mountains of Judea and Samaria, Hegseth's Temple that "could happen," Cruz's Sunday-school Genesis, and Huckabee's "fine if they took it all," which he called hyperbolic within two days and which did not become policy. [cite:ts12_huff_pompeo] [cite:ts12_toi_johnson] [cite:ts12_mee_hegseth] [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] Abroad, Guatemala, Paraguay and Honduras moved for mixed reasons and Brazil did not move at all. [cite:ts7_abc_paraguay] [cite:ts12_ih_honduras] [cite:ts7_pti_brazil] Part Thirteen steps outside the documentary record to set out, as a labelled interpretive lens, the inner reading of the name Israel that the literal land theology sets aside. [scene:ts13_name|Part Thirteen: the name in the record]

sections.h: Jerusalem, the Golan and the Settlements, 2017–2019
sections.html:
Three decisions of the first Trump administration are the ones most often offered as proof that Christian Zionism had reached the levers of American policy: the recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital and the move of the embassy there, the recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, and the declaration that settlements in the West Bank were not in themselves contrary to international law. This section sets out what was decided, what reasons the officials gave at the time, where Christian Zionist figures appear in the record, and what the record does not show about cause.

The Jerusalem statement

On 6 December 2017 President Donald Trump announced that the United States recognised Jerusalem as the capital of Israel and would move its embassy there. His stated reasons were legal and diplomatic. Congress had passed the Jerusalem Embassy Act in 1995, and "for over 20 years, every previous American president has exercised the law's waiver" in the belief that delay would help peace; after those decades, he said, the parties were "no closer to a lasting peace agreement." He called the decision "nothing more, or less, than a recognition of reality," said the United States was "not taking a position on any final status issues," including boundaries, and asked all parties to "maintain the status quo at Jerusalem's holy sites." The one religious reference in the statement described Jerusalem as "the heart of three great religions." [cite:ts12_toi_trump2017] The statement did not mention evangelicals, prophecy or the Bible.

The promise had already been made before an evangelical audience. Addressing the Christians United for Israel summit in Washington on 17 July 2017, a month after the President had signed the usual waiver keeping the embassy in Tel Aviv, Vice President Mike Pence spoke of "the hand of heaven" in Israel's history and said of the move: "It is not a question of 'if.' It is only 'when.'" [cite:ts12_ncr_pence2017]

The opening, 14 May 2018

The embassy opened in Jerusalem on 14 May 2018, timed to the seventieth anniversary of Israel's founding, with Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner in the American delegation. [cite:ts12_pbs_gaza] Two Texas pastors bracketed the ceremony. Robert Jeffress, the Southern Baptist pastor of First Baptist Dallas, gave the opening prayer; John Hagee, founder of Christians United for Israel, gave the closing benediction. [cite:ts12_cnn_pastors] Jeffress thanked God "that you have given us a president who boldly stands on the right side of history." [cite:ts12_npr_religion]

The choice of speakers drew objections at the time. Mitt Romney wrote that Jeffress, who had called Mormonism a "cult" and Islam an "evil religion," was "a bigot" who should not be "giving the prayer" at the opening; Hagee's 1990s sermon describing Hitler as "a hunter" in a divine plan had led John McCain to reject his endorsement in 2008. [cite:ts12_cnn_pastors] A Republican congressman, Francis Rooney, said he would have chosen a more ecumenical group. [cite:ts12_npr_religion] Each pastor gave his own answer. Jeffress said that the Christian teaching that "salvation is through faith in Christ alone" was "neither bigoted nor newsworthy"; Hagee called the claim that he condoned the Holocaust "the biggest and ugliest of lies," and his spokesman said the sermon drew on the writings of Rabbi Yissachar Shlomo Teichtal. The White House said Jeffress had "a strong relationship with many people in the faith community" and its spokesman said he did not know who had selected him. [cite:ts12_cnn_pastors]

The same day, Palestinians protested at the Gaza border fence. The Gaza Health Ministry said at least 41 people, five of them minors, had been killed by mid-afternoon and at least 772 wounded; the Israeli military said its troops had come under fire and that protesters were trying to break through the fence. [cite:ts12_pbs_gaza]

Why the embassy moved: drivers set side by side

Earlier material in the library states that the move was made "in direct response" to evangelical pressure. That is a causal claim, and the record supports it only in part. The strongest evidence for it is Trump's own later remark, at a rally in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, on 17 August 2020: "That's for the evangelicals," adding that evangelicals were "more excited about that than Jewish people." [cite:ts9_almon_trump2020] That is a statement of his own account, made at a campaign rally three years later, and it is set out with the other drivers in Part Nine. [scene:ts9_us|Part Nine: what American actors gained] Against it stand his statement of the day, which grounded the decision in the 1995 Act and the failure of the waivers [cite:ts12_toi_trump2017]; a campaign promise his predecessors had also made and not kept; and the political giving of Sheldon and Miriam Adelson, who also gave CUFI $4.6 million from 2012, according to their foundation's filings. [cite:ts9_972_adelson] No document examined here allows the weight of each driver to be measured, and this book records the cause as contested.

The Golan and the settlements

On 25 March 2019, by Proclamation 9852, the United States recognised "that the Golan Heights are part of the State of Israel." The proclamation's reasons were security: Israel "took control of the Golan Heights in 1967 to safeguard its security from external threats," and faced "aggressive acts by Iran and terrorist groups, including Hizballah, in southern Syria." [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852] Syria called it a "blatant attack" on its sovereignty, the European Union and the Arab League rejected it, and the UN Secretary-General said the Golan's status had not changed; the recognition continued under President Biden. [cite:gi8_wiki_usrecog] [scene:gi8_golan|The Golan in the Greater Israel volume] A circulating claim that Trump framed the Golan as "fulfilling biblical prophecy" has no quotation behind it and is not carried here; the religious comparison of that week came from Secretary of State Pompeo, in an interview about Queen Esther discussed in the next section. [scene:ts12_officials|The officials and their stated reasons]

On 18 November 2019 Pompeo announced that the United States no longer regarded civilian settlements in the West Bank as "per se" inconsistent with international law, setting aside the State Department legal opinion of 1978. His stated reasons were practical and legal: President Reagan had "disagreed" with the 1978 conclusion; "calling the establishment of civilian settlements inconsistent with international law hasn't worked. It hasn't advanced the cause of peace"; Israeli courts reviewed settlement activity; and there "will never be a judicial resolution to the conflict." He said the United States expressed "no view on the legal status of any individual settlement" and was not "prejudging the ultimate status of the West Bank." [cite:ts12_toi_pompeo2019] [cite:wb_jvl_hansell] Secretary of State Antony Blinken reversed the position on 23 February 2024, calling settlements "inconsistent with international law." [cite:wb_axios_blinken] In his second term Trump said on 25 September 2025, "I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank," while not moving to curb settlement. [cite:gi6_ap_trump0925] [cite:gi6_reuters_reg2026] The record examined here shows no formal restoration of the 2019 position by October 2026.

Abroad: the governments that followed, and one that did not

Guatemala opened its embassy in Jerusalem on 16 May 2018, two days after the United States, under President Jimmy Morales, whom NPR described as an evangelical; Morales called it "a step forward in favour of union and friendship." [cite:ts7_npr_guatemala] Analysts tied the move to Guatemala's arms relationship with Israel in the 1980s, to its dependence on US aid and to the president's evangelical base together. [cite:pm_pitt_guatemala] Paraguay moved its embassy in 2018 under Horacio Cartes; his successor Mario Abdo Benítez reversed it months later, and President Santiago Peña reopened it on 12 December 2024. [cite:ts7_abc_paraguay] Honduras dedicated its embassy in Jerusalem on 24 June 2021 under President Juan Orlando Hernández. The reasons reported were diplomatic and personal, not religious: Hernández had attended an Israeli leadership course in 1991 and kept close contact with Netanyahu, who asked him to follow the United States and Guatemala, and Israel agreed in return to reopen its embassy in Honduras. [cite:ts12_ih_honduras] In August 2022 the foreign minister of Hernández's successor, Xiomara Castro, said a return to Tel Aviv "has already been discussed with President (Castro)," citing international law and "a balanced relationship with the other Arab countries and Israel." [cite:ts12_na_honduras] The embassy was still listed in Jerusalem in December 2024 and again in September 2025. [cite:ts7_abc_paraguay] [cite:ts12a_cp24_fiji] When Paraguay reopened in December 2024, AP counted embassies in Jerusalem for only the United States, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo and Papua New Guinea, besides Paraguay. [cite:ts7_abc_paraguay] Fiji added one on 17 September 2025, inaugurated by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, who cited "the special bond" between the two countries, bringing the count to seven. [cite:ts12a_cp24_fiji] Argentina's President Javier Milei announced a move for 2026; the plan was postponed in January 2026, and on his state visit in April he said the embassy would move "as soon as conditions are met." As of October 2026 no Argentine embassy had opened in Jerusalem in the record examined here. [cite:ts12a_wiki_milei2026]

Brazil was the counter-case. President Jair Bolsonaro, with a large evangelical constituency, suggested in January 2019 that Brazil would move its embassy; after warnings about some $5 billion in halal exports to Arab markets, Brazil opened a trade office in Jerusalem on 15 December 2019 instead, and the embassy stayed in Tel Aviv. [cite:ts7_ynet_brazil] [cite:ts7_pti_brazil] Part Seven sets out the church figures for all four countries. [scene:ts7_abroad|Part Seven: Latin America and Africa]

The documented finding is specific. Christian Zionist leaders were given a public place at the opening of the embassy, a vice president promised the move at their summit, and the President later called it a gift "for the evangelicals." The official texts of all three decisions gave legal, diplomatic and security reasons, not religious ones, and the record does not establish how much each driver weighed. Abroad, the governments that moved acted for mixed reasons, and Brazil, the Latin American country with the largest evangelical population among those considered here, did not move at all.

sections.h: The Officials and Their Stated Reasons
sections.html:
Between 2017 and 2026 a number of senior American office-holders spoke about Israel in religious terms. This section takes them one at a time and records what each said, where and when, in his own words. It does not infer a private motive from a public remark, and it does not treat a statement of faith as proof that the faith set a policy. Where an official gave a secular reason beside a religious one, both are given. Where a widely repeated claim about an official could not be found in a named source, it is listed at the end and not used.

Mike Pence, Vice President, 2017–2021

Pence put the case most directly in religious language. At the Christians United for Israel summit on 17 July 2017 he described "the hand of heaven" beneath Israel's history and promised the embassy move: "It is not a question of 'if.' It is only 'when.'" [cite:ts12_ncr_pence2017] He addressed the summit again in 2019, alongside Prime Minister Netanyahu. [cite:gi11_wiki_cufi] Earlier material calls Pence and Pompeo "documented, self-identified Christian Zionists"; no source was found in which either used that label of himself, and it is not used here. What is documented is Pence's own account of faith as a ground of his support.

Mike Pompeo, Secretary of State, 2018–2021

In an interview with the Christian Broadcasting Network published on 21 March 2019, during a Middle East trip, Pompeo was asked whether Trump might have been raised "for such a time as this," like Queen Esther in the Bible, to help save the Jewish people from "the Iranian menace." He answered: "As a Christian, I certainly believe that's possible," and added, "I am confident that the Lord is at work here." [cite:ts12_huff_pompeo] [cite:ts12_jn_pompeo] The Book of Esther is set in Persia, which made the comparison pointed. Eight months later, announcing the settlements decision, Pompeo gave no religious reason at all: his statement rested on Reagan's view, on the failure of the illegality finding to advance peace and on the role of Israeli courts. [cite:ts12_toi_pompeo2019] The two statements show the same official speaking in two registers, one for a Christian audience and one for the formal record.

David Friedman, Ambassador to Israel, 2017–2021

Friedman's best-known act was archaeological and political at once. On 30 June 2019, with the envoy Jason Greenblatt and in the presence of Sara Netanyahu, he swung a sledgehammer through a specially built wall to open the "Pilgrimage Road," an excavated ancient stairway at the City of David site in Silwan, East Jerusalem, described as a route by which Jews went up to the Temple Mount. He called it "a once-in-a-century discovery," said "No political message was intended," and said his view of Jerusalem "does not prejudge the outcome of future negotiations." The Palestinian Authority, several Israeli NGOs and Jordan, which warned of "Israeli efforts to Judaize the Holy City," condemned it. [cite:ts12_toi_friedman] After leaving office Friedman backed Cruz's reading of Genesis in June 2025: "This is the same nation of Israel referred to in the Bible." [cite:ts1_cp_cruz]

Mike Huckabee, Ambassador to Israel, 2025–

Huckabee, a former governor of Arkansas whom AP described as a well-known evangelical, was confirmed on 9 April 2025 by 53 votes to 46. He had long used "Judea and Samaria" for the West Bank, opposed a two-state solution and supported Israel's right to annex the territory, but said carrying it out would not be his "prerogative"; in 2024 he said he would not call Arab descendants of the Mandate's population "Palestinians." At his hearing he said he would "carry out the president's priorities, not mine." [cite:ts12_ap_huckabee] In June 2025 he told Bloomberg he did not think an independent Palestinian state remained a goal of US policy and told the BBC that "Muslim countries have 644 times the amount of land" Israel controls; the State Department said he "speaks for himself" and that the President sets policy. [cite:ts12_newser_huckabee]

The fullest meeting of theology and office came in February 2026. Asked by Tucker Carlson in an interview aired on 20 February whether Israel had a right to the land promised in Genesis from the Nile to the Euphrates, Huckabee said: "It would be fine if they took it all," then, "Not sure we'd go that far." Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, the Arab League and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned the remarks. [cite:gi11_abc_huckabee] Huckabee then called his answer "somewhat of a hyperbolic statement," said Carlson's version "edited out my full response," and said "Area C is Israel"; the State Department did not publicly address it. [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] [scene:gi11_christian|The Huckabee interview in the Greater Israel volume] In mid-2026 he was a public voice of the talks to replace military aid with a new memorandum, writing that it "ends aid & will be based on trade." [cite:gi16_wiki_nextmou] His February statement did not become US policy.

Mike Johnson, Speaker of the House, 2023–

Johnson has used the Genesis blessing in public. In July 2025 he said: "I'll bless the nation that blesses Israel and curse the nation that curses Israel." [cite:ts10_ww_kaylor] On 4 August 2025 he made what the Times of Israel called a landmark visit to the settlement of Ariel; according to the Ariel municipality's statement, he said the land is "an integral part of our faith," and he was reported, in accounts corroborated by the town's mayor and by Marc Zell of the Republican Party's Israel branch, to have said that "the mountains of Judea and Samaria were promised to the Jewish people" and "belong to them by right." The trip was organised by the US Israel Education Association and designated private. [cite:ts12_toi_johnson] Track AIPAC, an advocacy compiler whose broad definition counts all pro-Israel PACs, including J Street, their large donors and outside spending, credits Johnson with $1,134,227 in career pro-Israel money as of July 2026, fifth among House Republicans. [cite:trackaipac_congress] Donations are a disclosure record, not evidence that they caused his positions; his stated reason is scriptural.

Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defence, 2025–

Before he took office, Hegseth spoke at a conference in Jerusalem in 2018. He said there was "no reason why the miracle of re-establishing the temple on the Temple Mount isn't possible," and, "I don't know how it would happen, you don't know how it would happen, but I know that it could happen." He told the audience that Israel should act while there were "true believers" in Washington. [cite:ts12_mee_hegseth] [cite:ts12_cp_hegseth] No response from Hegseth to the 2024 reports of the speech was found. He still led the Pentagon in October 2026. [cite:gi15a_ibt_minab] The remark is a private citizen's hope voiced before an Israeli audience; no Defence Department policy on the Temple Mount has followed from it, and US policy as stated in 2017 supports the status quo at the holy sites. [cite:ts12_toi_trump2017] [scene:gi11_temple|The Temple Mount]

Ted Cruz, Senator from Texas

Cruz gave the clearest account of a religious motive and its limit. In an interview with Carlson released on 18 June 2025 he said he had come to Congress intending to be "the leading defender of Israel in the United States Senate," and that "as a Christian, growing up in Sunday school, I was taught from the Bible" that those who bless Israel will be blessed; pressed on whether that meant the government of Israel, he said the verse "doesn't say the government of" but "the nation of Israel." [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] [cite:ts10_cl_cruz] He also said, "Not everyone I represent is a Christian, so I don't use my faith as the reason we should support Israel," and his main argument in the interview was security: Israel was "doing a massive favor to America" against Iran's nuclear programme. [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] [cite:ts10_ji_cruz] Part Ten analyses the exchange as the mechanism at work and the point at which it was challenged. [scene:ts10_mechanism|Part Ten: how the shield works]

What the record shows, and what was dropped

The record shows that, from 2017 to 2026, a vice president, a secretary of state, an ambassador, a Speaker of the House, a defence secretary and a senator each stated, in public and in their own words, a Christian or biblical ground for supporting Israel, and that two of them, Huckabee and Johnson, applied it to the West Bank. It shows equally that the formal texts of the decisions most often credited to that theology rested on legal, diplomatic and security reasons, that Huckabee himself called his widest statement hyperbolic within two days, and that Cruz himself declined to make faith the public argument. Two widely repeated claims could not be found in a named source and are not used: that Huckabee said in 2008 "there's really no such thing as a Palestinian" (the sourced 2024 statement is given instead), and that Trump framed the Golan as prophecy. [cite:ts12_ap_huckabee] [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852]

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: The Inner Reading
chapters.intro: Part Thirteen turns from the politics of the name Israel to the name itself, and to an older way of reading it. It sets out first what the record documents: the name's earliest appearance, on an Egyptian victory stele of about 1208 BCE, the story of Jacob's night in Genesis 32, and what Hebrew philology says the name means. It then reports the readings that took Jacob's night as a story of the soul, from Philo of Alexandria and Origen to the Kabbalah and modern rabbinic commentary, and the later Christian image of the "dark night". A section headed as an interpretive lens lays out the IS-RA-EL reading this platform holds, beside the philology that does not support it and the little that can be traced of its origin. The part then separates what is documented about the ancient mysteries and the ascent of the soul from the modern claim of an Egyptian mystery-school lineage, and ends with a labelled argument about how the same name has been read as an inner map and as a land deed.
chapters.outro: Part Thirteen established that the name Israel first appears in the record as the name of a people, on Merneptah's stele of about 1208 BCE, and in Genesis as the name given to one man after a night of wrestling; that Hebrew philology reads it as a name about God striving, persisting or ruling, which Genesis explains as Jacob's striving with God. [cite:ts13_wiki_merneptah] [cite:ts13_esv_gen32] [cite:ts13_wiki_israelname] It showed that reading the name as a condition of the soul is old and documented: Philo's "man who sees God", Origen's Israel "according to the Spirit", the kabbalistic Jacob who stands at Tiferet between kindness and restraint, and Jonathan Sacks's Jacob who stops trying to be his brother. [cite:ts13_philo_mut] [cite:ts13_origen_dp] [cite:ts13_chabad_luria] [cite:ts13_sacks_be] The IS-RA-EL reading, by contrast, is modern, of unknown first author, documented no earlier than Heiser's 2008 critique of Jordan Maxwell, and unsupported by the Hebrew; this platform offers it as a labelled symbolic key. [cite:ts13_heiser_maxwell] The ancient mysteries and the ascent literature are documented in dated texts, while the claimed Egyptian lineage of modern lodges was built between the Rosicrucian manifestos of 1614 and AMORC's founding in 1915, much of it from a 1731 novel. [cite:ts13_wiki_rosicruc] [cite:ts13_wiki_terrasson] [cite:ts13_wiki_amorc] The part closed with an argument, labelled as one, that the institutional literalism documented in this volume read one level of the name as the whole of it, with the objections stated beside it. Part Fourteen sorts the myths, the contested claims and what is settled across the whole volume. [scene:ts14_myths|Part Fourteen: myths and what is settled]

sections.h: The Name in the Record
sections.html:
This part of the volume steps aside from the political history told in Parts One to Twelve to look at the word at the centre of it. Christian Zionism reads a promise made to "Israel" as a promise about a modern state and its land. Other readers, Jewish and Christian, have read the same name as describing something that happens inside a person. Before either reading can be weighed, the documented record of the name has to be set out on its own: where it first appears, what the Hebrew Bible says about it, and what scholars of Hebrew and the ancient Near East say it means. This section does that and nothing else. The interpretive readings follow in the sections after it, labelled as readings.

The earliest attestation: an Egyptian victory stele

The oldest securely dated mention of Israel is not in the Bible. It is on a black granite slab more than three metres high, carved in the fifth regnal year of the pharaoh Merneptah, about 1208 BCE, and found by the British archaeologist Flinders Petrie at Thebes in 1896. The text, 28 lines long, was cut into the back of an older stele of Amenhotep III and is now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo (JE 31408). [cite:ts13_wiki_merneptah] Britannica dates the campaign it celebrates, a victory over a Libyan invasion, to around 1209 BCE and describes the stele as containing "the earliest-known reference to Israel, which Merneptah counted among the peoples that he defeated." [cite:ts13_brit_stela]

The line reads, in the usual translation: "Israel is laid waste—its seed is no more." It is a stock boast that Egyptian kings made about defeated enemies. What makes it informative is the sign that follows the word. Egyptian scribes added a silent classifier, a determinative, to names. The Canaanite towns in the same passage, Ashkelon, Gezer and Yanoam, carry the sign for a city or foreign land. "Israel" carries the sign of a seated man and woman with a plural marker, the sign for a people. [cite:ts13_wiki_merneptah] Most Egyptologists read the word as Israel and place this group in the central hill country of Canaan. Minority readings exist, among them Othniel Margalith's "Jezreel" and Alessandra Nibbi's "wearers of the sidelock", which would refer to Libyans, and the Egyptologist John A. Wilson, while accepting the reading as a people, cautioned about "the notorious carelessness of Late-Egyptian scribes and several blunders of writing in this stela." [cite:ts13_wiki_merneptah] Read on the majority view, the first time "Israel" appears in any surviving document, it names a population, not a territory and not a state.

The name in Genesis

Within the Hebrew Bible the name begins with one man. Genesis 32:22–32 tells how Jacob, on his way back to meet the brother he had cheated, crossed his family over the ford of the Jabbok and stayed behind. "And Jacob was left alone.
