And a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day." The stranger, unable to win, struck Jacob's hip out of joint; Jacob would not let go: "I will not let you go unless you bless me." [cite:ts13_esv_gen32] The stranger then renamed him: "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed." Jacob called the place Peniel, "face of God", saying "I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered", and the passage closes on an image that later readers have returned to many times: "The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, limping because of his hip." [cite:ts13_esv_gen32] Genesis gives the renaming a second time, in a different setting, at 35:10. [cite:ts13_wiki_israelname]

The prophet Hosea, writing centuries later, recalled the same story and read it as a sign of character: "In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God." The next verse says that he strove with the angel and prevailed, and that he wept and sought his favour. [cite:ts13_esv_hos12] Two points follow from the texts themselves. The figure Jacob fought is called a man in Genesis, an angel in Hosea and God in Jacob's own words at Peniel, and the tradition never settled on one identity. The birth name and the new name are set against each other: Jacob, the one who held the heel, becomes Israel, the one who strove and prevailed. The account of the two names in [scene:s00f|the opening chapter] covers the same ground for the library's first volume.

What the philology says

The second element of Yisra'el is not in dispute. It is el, the common Northwest Semitic word for God, which was also the name of a Canaanite deity of importance in early Israelite religion. [cite:ts13_wiki_israelname] The first element is a verb, and here scholars give several options. One candidate root is sarah, glossed in the lexicons as to contend, have power, persist or persevere; another is sarar, to rule, be prince, prevail. [cite:ts13_wiki_israelname] Michael Heiser, a scholar of Hebrew and Semitic languages, lists a third, yashar, "upright" or "just", which some readers hear in the name. [cite:ts13_heiser_maxwell]

Grammar matters as much as the root. The name can be read with God as the subject of the verb, giving "God strives", "God persists" or "God rules", or with God as the object, which is how Genesis 32:28 explains it: Jacob is the one who strove with God. [cite:ts13_heiser_maxwell] [cite:ts13_esv_gen32] The two readings are not equivalent, and the scholarly proposals below lean to the first, which means the Genesis explanation is best treated as the story the text tells about the name, not as a settled account of its origin. John Day has argued that the name probably meant "El will rule", a reading he finds consistent with the Ugaritic texts, and Mark S. Smith argues that the name is built on El, not on Yahweh, and that "El was the original chief god of the group named Israel." [cite:ts13_wiki_israelname] Forms of the name are attested at Ebla and Ugarit in the Bronze Age, which suggests it was a personal or group name in use before the biblical narratives were written. [cite:ts13_wiki_israelname]

Layers of the one word

The record therefore shows a name with several layers, each added at a different time. In the surviving documents it first names a people in Canaan in about 1208 BCE. In Genesis it names one man after one night, and then the descendants of his twelve sons. Later biblical books use it for a kingdom and for the land. Much later it became the name of a modern state, proclaimed in May 1948. [cite:ts13_wiki_merneptah] [cite:ts13_esv_gen32] None of those layers cancels the others, and none of them is identical with another. The rest of this volume has shown what happens when one of them, the promise to a people about a land, is read by a Protestant prophetic system as a forecast about a modern government. The next section turns to the readers who took the story of Jacob's night in a different direction.

sections.h: Jacob's Night: The Documented Inner Readings
sections.html:
Reading the story of Jacob as a story about the soul is not a modern idea, and it is not confined to esoteric writers. It is one of the oldest ways the passage has been read, and the readers who developed it were among the central figures of Judaism and Christianity. This section sets out what four of those traditions documentably said: the Alexandrian Jewish philosopher Philo, the Christian theologian Origen, the Kabbalah, and modern rabbinic commentary. It then turns to a later Christian image, the "dark night of the soul", which some readers have brought to the story. Each reading is reported as its author wrote it. None is presented as what Genesis "really" means; the point is that the inward reading has a long and named history.

Philo: Israel as "the one who sees God"

Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher writing in Greek in the first century CE, read the books of Moses as an account of the soul's progress as well as a history. In his treatise On the Change of Names he explains the renaming directly: Jacob means "a supplanter", while Israel signifies "the man who sees God". The one who practises virtue, he writes, strives "acutely and clearly to behold the living God". [cite:ts13_philo_mut] The etymology is Philo's own; it does not match the Hebrew roots set out in the previous section, and it is best read as a teaching device, an interpretation dressed as a derivation.

The classicist Marta Alesso, in a study of every use of the name in Philo, calls this etymology new to biblical interpretation and notes that the Church Fathers later repeated it. In Philo, Israel is "the one who sees God", "the seeing race", or simply "the seer"; his praise of sight carries echoes of Plato. Alesso also shows that Philo widened the term: Israel was for him a nation (ethnos) and also a kind (genos), a philosophical category of those who see. [cite:ts13_alesso_philo] Two things are documented together here and should be kept together. Philo read Israel as a condition of the soul, and Philo also remained a Jew who wrote of Israel as a people bound by God's law. The inward reading was for him an added level, not a replacement for the people.

Origen: three senses of scripture

Origen of Alexandria, the third-century Christian theologian, inherited the allegorical method and made it a rule. In book four of On First Principles he wrote that "as man consists of body, and soul, and spirit, so in the same way does Scripture": the simple are edified by its "flesh", the obvious sense; those who have advanced, by its "soul"; and the perfect, by the "spiritual law". [cite:ts13_origen_dp] He applied the method to Israel itself. Quoting Paul's phrase "Israel after the flesh", he argued that there is also an Israel "according to the Spirit", a "race of Jews inwardly", and that Jerusalem should be read as the heavenly city. [cite:ts13_origen_dp]

Origen's reading has to be reported with its consequence. In it the bodily Israel becomes a "type" of a spiritual one, and that move can be used to argue that the church has taken Israel's place, the position its critics call replacement theology, which Christian Zionist organisations such as the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem warn against by name. [cite:ts11_icej_catc] The inward reading is therefore not innocent by default. Read within Philo it deepens a people's self-understanding; read within a Christian polemic it can be turned against that people. Part Five records how the Scofield Reference Bible and its dispensational successors set themselves against exactly this spiritualising, insisting that the Christian does not inherit "the distinctive Jewish promises". [cite:ts5_sac_rom11] [scene:ts5_notes|Scofield's notes] That dispute returns in the last section of this part.

Kabbalah: Jacob at the centre of the tree

Medieval Jewish mysticism built a different inner map. Kabbalah describes ten sefirot, aspects through which the divine is manifest, arranged as a tree. Two of them stand opposite each other: Chesed, loving-kindness, expansive giving, and Gevurah, strength or restraint. Between and below them sits Tiferet, "beauty, glory, adornment", the sefira of balance and integration, whose task is to hold the expansive and the restrictive together. In the astrological correspondences the tradition gives it, Tiferet is the sun. [cite:ts13_wiki_tiferet]

Kabbalah assigns the three to the three patriarchs. Abraham is Chesed, Isaac is Gevurah, and Jacob is Tiferet. In the teaching of Isaac Luria, known as the Ari, as translated by Moshe Yaakov Wisnefsky, Jacob corresponds to Tiferet because he reconciles the two before him: "Jacob reconciles the first two". [cite:ts13_chabad_luria] The writer Efraim Palvanov, setting out the same scheme, puts it plainly: "Jacob was Tiferet", and connects it to Micah 7:20, which pairs truth with Jacob and kindness with Abraham; he cites the Zohar's assignment of water to Chesed, fire to Gevurah and air, the balancing element, to Tiferet. [cite:ts13_palvanov] Read this way, the man who becomes Israel is the one who holds two opposed forces in balance. That is a documented teaching of Jewish mysticism, and it is the closest thing in the traditional sources to the "integration" the IS-RA-EL lens speaks of. It differs from that lens in one respect worth noting: the opposed pair in Kabbalah is kindness and restraint, while the feminine aspect of the divine is assigned to a different sefira, Malkhut, paired with the masculine cluster around Tiferet. [cite:ts13_wiki_tiferet]

Modern rabbinic commentary: the struggle with oneself

Reading the wrestle as an inner struggle is also current in mainstream Jewish teaching. Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, in his weekly commentary on the Torah reading, noted that the opponent's identity is disputed: the Torah calls him a man, Hosea an angel, the rabbinic sages identify him as Samael, Esau's guardian angel, and Jacob believed he had seen God. Sacks read the night through Jacob's whole life, in which he had repeatedly tried to be his brother. That night, he wrote, Jacob "throws off the image of Esau, the person he wants to be", and from then on "is content to be himself". His conclusion was a teaching about integration: "We have to be at peace with ourself before we can be at peace with the world." [cite:ts13_sacks_be] This reading keeps Israel as the name of a people; Sacks tied it to Jewish identity and leadership. But it locates the decisive event inside the man.

A later frame: the dark night of the soul

The phrase most often used for this kind of ordeal today is Christian and Spanish, and far younger than Genesis. John of the Cross (1542–1591), a cofounder of the Discalced Carmelites, was imprisoned by his own order in Toledo from the night of 3 December 1577 and escaped on 15 August 1578. [cite:ts13_brit_john] [cite:ts13_nwe_john] The spiritual term "dark night of the soul" takes its name from his poem "Noche oscura" and the prose commentary he wrote on it in the 1580s, in which the night stands for the hardships of detachment from the world on the way to union with God. He was canonised in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926. [cite:ts13_nwe_john] [cite:ts13_brit_john]

The sources consulted for this section do not show John applying the image to Jacob, and no early reader is documented doing so here. The pairing is a later reader's move, made among others in this platform's own reading, which describes Jacob's night as an ordeal in darkness completed at the coming of light. It is a fair description of the shape of Genesis 32, alone, at night, wounded, renamed at dawn, but it is a frame brought to the text, and it is labelled as such in this volume.

The pattern across these readings is consistent. Each takes the night at the Jabbok as a transformation, each places the change in the person before it places it in history, and none of them, except where Origen's method was turned into polemic, uses the inward reading to deny the people who bear the name. That is the documented ground on which the next section's lens stands, and from which it then departs.

sections.h: Interpretive Lens: IS-RA-EL
sections.html:
This section is an interpretive lens, not a finding. It sets out a symbolic reading of the name Israel that this platform holds and has offered since its first volume, and it is headed and phrased as a reading throughout. It does not claim that the name was built from the names of Egyptian gods, it does not replace the Hebrew philology set out in [scene:ts13_name|the first section of this part], and it generates no documentary claim anywhere in this volume. It is placed here, after the record and after the documented inner readings, so that a reader can see exactly where the record ends and the lens begins. The shorter version in the library's opening chapter is at [scene:s00g|IS-RA-EL: a symbolic reading].

The reading, stated in full

Read through this lens, the name divides into three syllables, and each is taken as a principle. IS is read as Isis, the great goddess of Egypt: in this reading, the divine feminine, the receptive, gathering, lunar principle. RA is read as the sun god of Egypt: the divine masculine, the radiant, generative, outward-moving principle. EL is the Most High, the Semitic word for God that stands above both. On this reading the name describes an architecture of consciousness in three tiers: two polarities, feminine and masculine, receptive and radiant, brought into union under the divine that contains them. "Israel", read this way, is not first a place or a lineage. It is a state a human being can arrive at, the condition of a person in whom the two sides have been integrated and turned toward the highest.

The lens then reads Genesis 32 as a picture of how that state is reached. Jacob is alone, at night, at a river crossing. He contends with a figure who is at once a man and divine, which in this reading is the meeting of the human self with the larger self it has avoided. He is wounded and does not let go. He asks for a blessing, not a victory. At dawn the sun rises on him and he receives a new name, and he names the place for what he saw: the face of God. In this reading the old name, the one who grasps at the heel of another, gives way to a name for the integrated person, who has stopped trying to be someone else, as Jonathan Sacks put it in his own terms, and stands upright. [cite:ts13_esv_gen32] [cite:ts13_sacks_be] The lens treats the story less as a record reserved for one line of descent than as a template open to anyone who undertakes the struggle.

Where the lens touches the documented traditions

The lens is the platform's own, but parts of it rest on documented teaching, and it is worth saying which. The idea that Israel names an inner condition is Philo's: for him Israel was "the man who sees God", and a kind of soul as well as a people. [cite:ts13_philo_mut] [cite:ts13_alesso_philo] The idea that Jacob is the one who holds opposed forces in balance is a teaching of Kabbalah, in which Jacob is Tiferet, the sefira that reconciles Chesed and Gevurah and whose planetary sign is the sun. [cite:ts13_chabad_luria] [cite:ts13_wiki_tiferet] The idea that the night was a struggle to become oneself is current in mainstream rabbinic commentary. [cite:ts13_sacks_be] What the lens adds is specific: the Egyptian names, the reading of the two poles as feminine and masculine, and the claim that this pattern is written into the syllables of the word. That addition is not found in Jewish or Christian commentary, and it is the part that philology does not support.

What philology says about the syllables

The objections are precise and should be stated in full. The name is Hebrew, Yisra'el, and its syllables do not divide as IS-RA-EL in the original script: the first element is a verb form built on a root such as sarah or sarar, and only the last element, El, is a divine name. [cite:ts13_wiki_israelname] The Hebrew scholar Michael Heiser, reviewing the reading in July 2008, set out three further problems. "Isis" is the Greek form of the goddess's name; the Egyptian was closer to "Awset". The middle syllable of the Hebrew name is written with the letters resh and aleph, while the Egyptian sun god's name, as it appears in Hebrew in the name of the pharaoh Hophra in Jeremiah 44:30, is written with ayin. And Hebrew and Egyptian belong to different branches of their language family, so their syllables do not line up. He conceded the third element: El is spelled with aleph and lamed, as the reading requires. [cite:ts13_heiser_pdf] [cite:ts13_heiser_maxwell] On the philology, then, IS and RA are a reading of the English spelling, and EL is the one element the reading shares with the etymology.

Who has proposed it

The origin of the IS-RA-EL reading could not be traced to a dated first source. The earliest proponent this volume could document is Jordan Maxwell, a lecturer who described himself as an "independent scholar in the field of occult / religious philosophy", dated his interest to 1959, was religion editor of Truth Seeker magazine for three and a half years and appeared on more than 600 radio programmes. [cite:ts13_sw_maxwell] Heiser's critique of July 2008 attributes the claim to him in these words: "Israel" derives from "three deity names: Isis-Ra-El". Heiser gives no title, lecture or year for Maxwell's statement, only his website, so the date of Maxwell's first use is not established. [cite:ts13_heiser_maxwell] [cite:ts13_heiser_pdf] A second current reads the syllables in a related but distinct way: the glossary of Glorian, a publisher of modern Gnostic teaching, reads IS as recalling "Isis and the Isiac Mysteries", RA as the solar Logos, and EL as "the inner, profound God within each one of us", and treats the people of Israel as the awakened parts of a person's inner being, with Egypt standing for enslavement to the ego. The entry is undated and unsigned. [cite:ts13_glorian] Beyond these, the reading circulates widely online in unsigned forms. No dated source earlier than Heiser's 2008 critique was found, and no ancient, rabbinic, patristic or medieval kabbalistic text that proposes it. The honest statement is that the reading is modern, that its first author is unknown, and that this platform has taken it up and labelled it.

Why the platform keeps it, and how

The platform's position is that a reader kept from the reading is not protected but left to meet it elsewhere without its limits. So it is given here with the philology beside it. What the lens offers is not an etymology but a symbolic key: a way of gathering into one memorable image the documented themes of the inner traditions, that the self must hold receptive and active together, and that the name of Israel, in the readings of Philo, the Kabbalah and modern rabbinic teaching, has long been understood to describe a transformation as well as a people. Read through this lens, the name holds together what many institutions separated. Read through philology, it is a Hebrew name about God's striving or ruling, explained in Genesis as Jacob's striving. A reader may hold the first as a meditation and the second as the record.

Two limits apply wherever the lens appears in this library. It never supplies evidence about any historical actor's intent, and nothing in this volume's account of Darby, Scofield, CUFI or any government depends on it. And it is never used to say that anyone has taken a name that belongs to someone else. The contrast the lens draws, examined in [scene:ts13_deed|the last section of this part], runs between an inward reading and a literal one, and both are found inside Judaism and inside Christianity.

sections.h: The Mysteries and the Ascent: What Is Documented
sections.html:
This platform's reading places the IS-RA-EL lens at the end of an account of the ancient "mystery schools" and holds that they taught, by ordeal and allegory, a single pattern: the ascent of the soul toward the divine. That pattern is a real subject of historical study, and much of it is documented. Some of what is said about it is not documented at all, and some is demonstrably a construction of the seventeenth to twentieth centuries. This section separates the two. It first sets out what the sources show about the Greek, Egyptian and Hellenistic mysteries; then the ascent pattern in Jewish, Greek and Indian traditions; then the later claims of an unbroken Egyptian "mystery school" lineage, and where they come from.

Eleusis: a secret that was kept

The Eleusinian Mysteries were, in Britannica's words, the "most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece". They were built on the myth told in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, in which the goddess searches for her daughter Kore, or Persephone, carried off by Hades. Candidates were purified at the Lesser Mysteries at Agrai in late winter and initiated at the Greater Mysteries at Eleusis in the autumn, after a ritual sea bath and three days of fasting. The central rites in the hall of initiation "were and remain a secret": there is "no sure evidence of what the rites actually were", and the initiate was "promised benefits of some kind in the afterlife". [cite:ts13_brit_eleusis] The documented fact is the secrecy itself, kept over centuries by large numbers of initiates. What was taught inside is not known, and any confident account of it is reconstruction.

Isis: Apuleius, Book Eleven

The fullest literary account of an initiation into the mysteries of Isis is in a Latin novel of the second century CE, the Metamorphoses of Apuleius, also called The Golden Ass. In its eleventh book the narrator, Lucius, restored from the shape of a donkey by the goddess, is initiated into her mysteries. He tells only what may be told to the uninitiated. He says he "reached the very gates of death" and, "treading Proserpine's threshold", passed through all the elements and returned; that he saw "the sun at midnight shining brightly"; and that he came before the gods below and the gods above. [cite:ts13_cam_apuleius] It is a novel, and a literary source, but it is the nearest thing to a first-person description of an ancient mystery initiation, and its shape, a symbolic death, a passage through darkness, light at midnight, a return, is the pattern the platform's reading draws on.

The Hermetica and Iamblichus

The Corpus Hermeticum is a collection of Greek treatises attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a figure who combines the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth. The treatises were written in about 100–300 CE and compiled by Byzantine editors; the best known is the Poimandres. When a manuscript reached Florence, Marsilio Ficino broke off his translation of Plato for Cosimo de' Medici to translate it first, because it was believed to be older than Plato. In 1614 the scholar Isaac Casaubon showed from its Greek that it belonged to the Roman period, and it "lost its claim to predate Plato". Some scholars since the Nag Hammadi finds of 1945, such as Jean-Pierre Mahé, have argued for a background in Hellenistic Egyptian texts. [cite:ts13_wiki_hermetica] The Hermetica are therefore genuinely Egyptian in setting and partly in inheritance, and genuinely late in composition: they are not a pharaonic text.

On the Mysteries, attributed to the Neoplatonist Iamblichus (an attribution first found in Proclus), is a reply, written under the name of an Egyptian priest, Abammon, to the critical Letter to Anebo of Iamblichus's teacher Porphyry. It is "primarily concerned with ritual and theurgy", the use of rites to bring the soul into contact with the gods, and its Greek text was printed in Venice by Aldus in 1497. [cite:ts13_wiki_iamblichus] It is the main surviving defence, from inside late pagan philosophy, of the view that ritual initiation, not argument alone, raises the soul.

The ascent pattern across traditions

The pattern of ascent appears in traditions that did not borrow from one another, and it is documented in their own texts. In Plato's Symposium, the priestess Diotima describes a lover whose attention rises from beautiful bodies to souls, then to institutions and knowledge, "until he catches a glimpse of Beauty itself". [cite:ts13_hooper_plato] Plotinus, the third-century Neoplatonist, taught an ascent that reverses the soul's descent from the One: purification, awakening of the intellect, and finally union with the One, which cannot be forced, on the principle that "like knows like". [cite:ts13_mac_plotinus]

Jewish mysticism had its own. Merkabah mysticism took its start from Ezekiel's vision of the throne-chariot. Its Hekhalot texts, redacted between the third and ninth centuries CE, describe rabbis such as Akiva and Ishmael ascending through seven heavens and seven palaces, past guardian angels, with purification, hymns and secret names. Its practitioners were called, paradoxically, yordei merkavah, "descenders to the chariot", and the Mishnah restricted the teaching of the chariot to the qualified few. [cite:ts13_wiki_merkavah] In India, the early Upanishads, dated by many scholars to about 800–500 BCE, teach that the individual self, atman, is one with Brahman, summed up in the Chandogya Upanishad's "tat tvam asi", "Thou art that", and that liberation comes through realising it. [cite:ts13_wh_upanishads]

The resemblance across these texts is documented; a single source behind them is not. The record shows similar maps drawn in Greece, Egypt, Judaea and India, some with clear lines of influence (Plato on Plotinus, Plotinus and the Hermetica on Iamblichus) and some with none that can be shown. To call them "one teaching under many names", as the platform's reading does, is an interpretation of that resemblance. It is a reasonable reading, but it is a reading, and this volume labels it so.

The "Egyptian mystery school" lineage: a later construction

A separate claim is often attached to this material: that an organised Egyptian mystery school passed its secrets in an unbroken chain to modern esoteric orders. That chain is not documented, and the record shows where much of it was made. In 1731 the Frenchman Jean Terrasson (1670–1750) published Sethos, a fantasy novel set in ancient Egypt that, in one reference work's words, "elided Masonic and ancient Egyptian ritual"; it inspired Mozart and Schikaneder's Magic Flute. [cite:ts13_wiki_terrasson] A Masonic encyclopedia notes that "under the form of fiction" it described Egyptian initiation and that later Masonic writers, Lenoir, Clavel and Oliver among them, drew on it freely for their accounts of ancient rites. [cite:ts13_umf_sethos] In 1779 the adventurer Cagliostro founded an Egyptian-themed lodge at Mitau, in today's Latvia; he claimed to have learned the secrets of Egypt and met Hermes Trismegistus, and a Masonic museum's account says he and an associate "invented the legend" of their Egyptian journey and calls the Egyptian rituals of the period "speculative and cosmetic in nature". [cite:ts13_mm_cagliostro]

The Rosicrucian story runs the same way. The manifestos that announced a secret Brotherhood of the Rose Cross were printed in Kassel in 1614, Frankfurt in 1615 and 1616; Johann Valentin Andreae, who claimed the third, later called the whole thing a "ludibrium", a jest; the historian Roland Edighoffer states that "there is no proof that the Brotherhood" ever existed; and actual Rosicrucian organisations appear only in the eighteenth century. [cite:ts13_wiki_rosicruc] The best known modern order, the Ancient Mystical Order Rosae Crucis (AMORC), was founded by Harvey Spencer Lewis in the United States in 1915, traces its origins to ancient Egypt and Egyptian pharaohs, and considers itself "a continuation of the ancient mystery schools". [cite:ts13_wiki_amorc] Those are the order's own stated claims; no document links it to Egypt.

The result is a clear division. The ancient mysteries, the Isis cult, the Hermetica, Iamblichus and the ascent literature of Greece, Judaea and India are documented, in texts that can be read and dated. The claim of an institutional Egyptian school surviving into modern lodges is a construction of the early modern period, much of it from a novel. The platform's argument that the mystery traditions preserved knowledge through allegory rests on the first body of evidence; it does not need, and this volume does not use, the second.

sections.h: From Inner Map to Land Deed
sections.html:
This section brings the two halves of the volume together. Parts One to Twelve documented how one Protestant system of reading prophecy became a political shield for a state's policies. The previous sections of this part documented an older way of reading the same name, as a description of what happens inside a person. The question here is how those two ways of reading relate. The section has two layers, kept apart. The first sets out, from the documents, how the literal reading and the inward reading each handle the name and the promise. The second, headed as an argument, gives the platform's reading of that contrast, with the strongest objections to it beside it.

Documented: the literal reading

Dispensationalism, the system that Darby built and Scofield's notes carried to millions of readers, is defined by its own exponents through one distinction. Keith Mathison of Ligonier Ministries, writing from the covenant-theology tradition that rejects it, summarises it: "at its heart is the distinction between Israel and the church". [cite:ts1_lig_dispens] The historian Timothy Weber describes the result as two plans running in history, one for an earthly people, Israel, and one for a heavenly people, the church. [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] In that scheme, the promises made to Israel are not read as allegories of the soul. Scofield's 1917 note on Genesis 12 calls the covenant with Abraham "wholly gracious and unconditional"; his note on Deuteronomy 30 sets out a "Palestinian Covenant" whose stages run from dispersion through repentance to "restoration to the land"; and his note on Romans 11 rules out the spiritualising move directly: "That the Christian now inherits the distinctive Jewish promises is not taught in Scripture." [cite:ts1_sac_gen12] [cite:ts5_sac_deut30] [cite:ts5_sac_rom11] Parts Three and Five trace this system at length ([scene:ts3_darby|Darby], [scene:ts5_notes|Scofield's notes]).

The same reading appears in the statements of the movement's largest organisation. In a CUFI webcast on 6 January 2011 John Hagee said that Jerusalem "is the property of the people of Israel" and that God "made a covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob"; Jacob, the man of Genesis 32, appears here as a party to a title. [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] Hagee's stated policy is narrower than the theology: Israelis "and they alone" decide on land and peace, and CUFI asks Washington not to press Israel for concessions. [cite:gi11_jpost_hagee] Among American evangelicals, the LifeWay survey of 2,002 people with evangelical beliefs, fielded 20–28 September 2017, found that 63 per cent supported Israel because "God gave the land of Israel to the Jewish people". [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] Not every Christian Zionist reasons from the end-times scheme: the scholar Stephen Spector found that "most Christian Zionists don't actually base their support for Israel on a catastrophic end-times scenario", and that Genesis 12:3 is the reason most often given. [cite:ts6_tablet_spector] But in the literal reading, wherever it is held, the promise is a promise about a territory and the name is the name of a people and a state.

Documented: the inward reading

The inward reading handles the same materials differently. For Philo, Israel is "the man who sees God", a kind of soul as well as a nation. [cite:ts13_philo_mut] [cite:ts13_alesso_philo] For Origen, scripture has a body, a soul and a spirit, and there is an Israel "according to the Spirit" beside Israel "after the flesh", with Jerusalem read as the heavenly city. [cite:ts13_origen_dp] In Kabbalah Jacob is Tiferet, the balance between expansive kindness and restraint. [cite:ts13_chabad_luria] In modern rabbinic teaching, the night at the Jabbok is the night a man stopped trying to be his brother. [cite:ts13_sacks_be] Both religions also built the levels into their method: Judaism's fourfold PaRDeS and the medieval Christian standard of literal and allegorical senses, described in [scene:s00g|the opening chapter], keep the plain sense and add the inner ones above it.

The record shows two things about this inward reading that matter for what follows. It is not the property of one religion: it appears in a Jewish philosopher, a Christian theologian, Jewish mystics and a modern rabbi. And it does not, in most of its forms, deny the plain sense. Philo's Israel remains a people, and so does Sacks's. The one documented form in which the inward reading has been used against the people who bear the name is the Christian move, possible from Origen's method, that treats bodily Israel as a mere "type" replaced by the church. Christian Zionist organisations attack that move by name: the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem warned in 2012 against "Cloaked versions of Replacement theology". [cite:ts13_origen_dp] [cite:ts11_icej_catc]

Argument: the platform's reading of the contrast

What follows is argument, labelled as such. Read through the IS-RA-EL lens, the history this volume has documented is the history of a map being read as a deed. In the inner traditions, the name describes a state a person can reach, the integration of opposed forces under the divine, completed after a night of struggle. In the institutional literalism that runs from Darby through Scofield to the organisations of Part Eight, the same name and the same promise are read as a title to territory and a timetable for history, and that reading has been turned, as Parts Nine to Twelve showed, into a political instrument: votes, lobbying, embassy moves and a shield against criticism of a government's policy. On this argument, the shield described in this volume did not require the inner reading to be refuted; it required only that one level of meaning be taken as the whole of it.

The argument has limits, and the platform states them. It is a reading of the contrast, not a claim about any person's motive; Part Nine's account of who benefited rests on documents, not on this lens. It is not an argument about Jews or Judaism. Literal and inward readings exist inside Judaism and inside Christianity alike, and the literalism this volume has examined is a specific Protestant system, named and dated. Nothing in the lens says that any people has taken a name not its own: the name Israel has named a people since the oldest document in which it appears, and the inward traditions that read it as a state of consciousness were, first of all, that people's own.

The objections, stated fairly

Three objections to the argument deserve to be stated in their strongest form. First, Christian Zionists hold that the literal reading is the faithful one, and that turning promises to Israel into allegories of the soul is the road to replacement theology, which in Christian history did real harm to Jews; on that view the "map" reading is not neutral but dangerous, and Scofield's insistence that the church does not inherit Israel's promises was a correction of it. [cite:ts5_sac_rom11] [cite:ts11_icej_catc] Second, the Jewish inward readings documented in this part did not set the inner meaning against the people or the land: Philo and Sacks both kept Israel a people. [cite:ts13_alesso_philo] [cite:ts13_sacks_be] An argument that treats literal attachment to the land as a loss of inner meaning can therefore be heard as an outsider's judgment on Jewish practice, which is not what the platform intends and which the lens must not become. Third, Spector's finding that most Christian Zionists reason from a blessing in Genesis 12:3 rather than from an end-times scheme suggests that the political shield rests less on a literal theory of prophecy than on a simpler conviction about loyalty, which the map-and-deed contrast does not fully capture. [cite:ts6_tablet_spector]

The platform's response is that the lens is offered as a key, not a verdict. It asks a reader to notice that the same name has been read in two registers for two thousand years, that the inward register belongs to Jewish and Christian tradition alike, and that the institutional politics documented in this volume chose one register and treated it as the only one. Whether that observation clarifies or distorts is a judgment the reader is entitled to make, with the record on one side and the reading on the other. The settled and unsettled claims of the whole volume are sorted in [scene:ts14_myths|Part Fourteen].

chapters.label: Part Fourteen
chapters.title: Myths, Contested Claims and What Is Settled
chapters.intro: The last part gathers what the volume found. It first keeps a ledger of the claims most often made about Christian Zionism, in print, in sermons and online, and judges each one on the evidence set out in Parts One to Thirteen: documented, contested between named sources, unsupported by any source found, or a myth that the record contradicts. The ledger includes the claims about Cyrus Scofield's life and patrons, among them the story that Samuel Untermyer or the Rothschilds paid for his Bible, which rests on an old antisemitic accusation and is named as such; the claims about what his notes said and how far they sold; the history of the phrase "a land without a people"; what Christian Zionist organisations say they want for Jews, beside what their critics say; and whether evangelicals set American policy. The second section sorts the volume's findings into what is settled, what is contested and what remains open as of 21 October 2026, answers the question the volume set out to test, and closes with the inner reading of Part Thirteen, kept as a labelled reading. No new evidence is introduced: every finding rests on documents already cited.
chapters.outro: This volume followed a Christian hope from a book suppressed in 1621 to a Pew survey of May 2026. It found that the hope of a Jewish return is three centuries older than the Scofield Bible, that it reached government first on strategic terms in Palmerston's dispatch of 1840, and that Darby's system, Scofield's notes and the prophecy bestsellers turned it into a timetable read by millions, while placing Israel's restoration after Christ's return rather than calling for a political programme. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] [cite:ts2_cojs_palmerston1840] [cite:ts5_sac_deut30] [cite:ts7_wrap_lindsey] It found Scofield jailed but never convicted, his Bible paid for by Brethren-linked businessmen, and the story of Untermyer's or the Rothschilds' money a myth built on an assumption of 1988 and a claim of 2004, resting on an old antisemitic accusation. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts4_cyf] It found the political machine built by named people and organisations, from the Zionist movement's Christian committees of the 1940s to Falwell, the ICEJ and CUFI, with money that can be read in filings and a membership that cannot be counted; the shield used in dated statements by a pastor, a senator, a Speaker and a prime minister; and its limits shown by an Israeli minister's rebuke in 2006, a Brazilian trade office, an ambassador's retraction and a younger generation, whose favourable view of the Israeli government stood at 28 per cent among Republicans aged 18 to 29 in May 2026. [cite:ts6_aja_ccp_minutes] [cite:ts8_pp_ifcj] [cite:ts8_hfl_10m] [cite:ts10_cp_jeffress2025] [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] [cite:ts10_ww_kaylor] [cite:ts7_cbs_robertson] [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] [cite:ts11_pew_2026] Whether the move of the embassy was made for evangelicals, as Trump later said, or for the reasons his statement of the day gave, remains contested, as do the motives that named critics and named leaders ascribe to the movement. [cite:ts9_almon_trump2020] [cite:ts12_toi_trump2017] [cite:ts9_dn_posner] [cite:ts9_jta_morgenstern2010] Parallel answers appear in The Greater Israel Architecture, whose section on Christian Zionist land theology this volume expands [scene:gi11_christian|The Greater Israel Architecture: Christian Zionist land theology] [scene:gi13_record|The Greater Israel Architecture: what the record settles], and in The Divine 3+1, which assigns Rome the function of theology and tests it against the documents. [scene:dv1_three_functions|The Divine 3+1: three functions, one test]

sections.h: The Ledger: Claims About Christian Zionism, Judged
sections.html:
This section gives a verdict on the claims about Christian Zionism a reader is most likely to meet. Documented means the record supports the claim. Contested means named sources stand on both sides and the record does not settle it. Unsupported means no source was found for it. Myth means the record contradicts it. Each verdict rests on documents cited in Parts One to Thirteen, with the stated position of those concerned beside each critical finding. [scene:ts4_rumours|Part Four: the rumours tested]

Origins

"Scofield created Christian Zionism." Myth. Christian belief in a Jewish return to the land was in print three centuries before his Bible: in Thomas Brightman's commentaries, first published in 1609, in Henry Finch's book of 1621, which James I treated as a libel, in Increase Mather's Boston sermons of 1669 and in the London Society, founded in 1809 to convert Jews. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] [cite:ts2_wiki_finch] Darby set out his system at Geneva in 1840, the Niagara Creed of 1878 declared that "Israel shall be restored to their own land," and Blackstone put the case to President Harrison on 5 March 1891. [cite:ts3_darby_hopes1] [cite:ts3_ak_niagara] [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] What Scofield added was reach: the system printed beside the verse, in about two million copies by 1945. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] Two related claims fail with it. The system was not "substantially non-existent" in America before 1909; it had a creed, conferences and Bible institutes. [cite:ts3_bt_niagara] [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] And neither Darby nor the 1917 notes made a political return of Jews a precondition of Christ's coming: Darby's rapture was "any-moment," and Scofield's sequence at Deuteronomy 30 puts "The return of the Lord" before "Restoration to the land." [cite:ts3_weber_ct1999] [cite:ts5_sac_deut30]

"A land without a people for a people without a land" as a Zionist coinage. Myth; its later use and meaning are contested. Every documented use before 1901 is by a Christian writer: the Methodist Richard Watson before 1833, Alexander Keith in 1843, a Free Church review in 1844 and Shaftesbury in 1853, who wrote of "a country without a nation." The first recorded Zionist use was Israel Zangwill's in 1901, and by about 1904 he was saying the country "has already its inhabitants." [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] [cite:ts2_muir_meq] How widely Zionists later used it divides historians (Diana Muir against Anita Shapira, Boaz Neumann and Rashid Khalidi), and so does whether it meant the land was empty or that its inhabitants did not count as a nation. [cite:ts2_muir_meq] [cite:ts2_wiki_landwithout] [scene:ts2_slogan|Part Two: the phrase]

The man and the book

"Scofield was a convicted forger who served a prison sentence." Myth; the jailing is documented. He was held in the St. Louis jail from 8 October 1878 on forgery charges, and on 6 November 1879 the prosecution entered a nolle prosequi, dropping them for lack of evidence; there was no trial, verdict or sentence. [cite:ts4_rushing] [cite:ts4_doj_ks] The rest of the unflattering record holds: the Justice Department says he was "forced to resign" as US Attorney in 1873 over "questionable financial transactions," he deserted his wife and daughters, and he styled himself a doctor of divinity with no degree on record. The embellishments fail: one divorce, not two; no Canadian prison term on any record; no medal for Antietam. [cite:ts4_doj_ks] [cite:ts4_wiki_kellogg] [cite:ts4_wiki_scofield] [cite:ts4_sfiles] His own account was that grace changed him in 1879; no later charge is recorded. [cite:ts4_trumbull]

"Samuel Untermyer, or the Rothschilds, paid for the Scofield Bible." Myth. The only documented link is that both men belonged to New York's Lotos Club: Untermyer from 1894, Scofield from 3 March 1900, proposed by Horatio Fraser and seconded by John Elderkin. No letter, meeting or payment is recorded. [cite:ts4_sfiles] The story begins with Joseph Canfield's hostile biography of 1988, which named Untermyer as a likely sponsor with the words "we assume"; David Lutz in 2005 and the Washington Report on Middle East Affairs in 2015 restated it as fact without citing a document; and Michael Collins Piper's The High Priests of War (2004) was the first text to say the Rothschilds paid. [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts5_ocathail] [cite:ts5_wiki_piper] Check Your Fact rated the Rothschild claim false on 12 March 2025, and the writer Mike Rothschild found no primary source for it. [cite:ts4_cyf] [cite:ts4_mrothschild] The documented backers were the Brethren-linked businessmen Alwyn Ball, John Pirie, John Buss and Francis Fitch, with a reported $1,000 from the oilman Lyman Stewart in 1908; Untermyer's leading Zionist office began in 1921, and in 1905 Scofield's own consulting editor called Zionism "a movement ... of unbelief." [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts5_dunlap] [cite:ts5_wiki_lstewart] [cite:ts3_wiki_gaebelein] The claim has the shape of one of the oldest antisemitic accusations, that Jewish financiers secretly steer what Christians believe. It is rejected because the record contradicts it, and named because it travels faster than the record. [scene:ts5_funding|Part Five: who paid]

"The 1917 edition referred to the Balfour Declaration." Unsupported. The reference work cited for the claim does not say so, and the 1917 notes examined for this volume still describe Israel as "now in the third dispersion." The declaration is dated 2 November 1917, which left a revision prepared during that year at most weeks to absorb it. [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] [cite:wb_bl_addms41178]

"Oxford sold tens of millions of Scofield Bibles." Unsupported. The citable figures are 1,925,000 copies in thirty years and more than two million by 1945. [cite:ts5_dunlap] [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] The tens of millions belong to two later books: Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth, an estimated 28 to 35 million, and the Left Behind novels, 50 to 80 million by the reported counts. The "65 million" for Left Behind in earlier library material has no source. [cite:ts7_wiki_lgpe] [cite:ts7_wrap_lindsey] [cite:ts7_cp_lahaye] [cite:ts7_sa_lahaye]

Aims and influence

"Christian Zionists want Jews to die, or to convert." Contested; as a statement of any organisation's stated aim, the first half is a myth. The theology's texts foresee a judgment and a conversion. Darby said in 1840 that after the return "there will only be a remnant saved" and that "Two thirds" would be cut off; Scofield's 1917 notes place a "remnant" turning to Jesus "During the great tribulation" and list "National conversion" after the restoration; most restorationists, and Blackstone as late as 1918, hoped for the conversion of Jews. [cite:ts3_darby_hopes10] [cite:ts5_sac_rom11] [cite:ts5_sac_deut30] [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] A forecast in a theology is not a stated wish, and the organisations state the opposite aim. CUFI has an official policy against proselytising Jews, Hagee says the support is "a debt of gratitude," David Brog says his members reject replacement theology, and CUFI's spokesman argues that no human can hasten the end. [cite:ts8_wiki_cufi] [cite:ts1_jvl_cufi] [cite:ts9_j_brog2017] [cite:ts9_jta_morgenstern2010] Critics answer with documents of their own: interfaith leaders question how that fits Hagee's teaching of salvation through Christ alone; his 1990s sermon calling Hitler "a hunter" led John McCain to repudiate his endorsement in 2008; Sarah Posner calls Israel "just a pawn" in the prophecy; and in 2001 Israel's Chief Ashkenazi Rabbi condemned Christian money used to "expand Christian missionary propaganda." [cite:ts8_wiki_cufi] [cite:ts8_cnn_hagee] [cite:ts9_dn_posner] [cite:ts8_jta_eckstein]

"Evangelicals set American policy on Israel." Contested. Their presence is documented: Pence promised the embassy move at CUFI's summit in July 2017, Jeffress and Hagee prayed at its opening on 14 May 2018, and Trump said in August 2020 that the move was "for the evangelicals." [cite:ts12_ncr_pence2017] [cite:ts12_cnn_pastors] [cite:ts9_almon_trump2020] The decisions' own texts gave other reasons: the 1995 Act and failed waivers for Jerusalem, security and Iran for the Golan, law and the stalled peace process for the settlements statement, which Blinken reversed in 2024. [cite:ts12_toi_trump2017] [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852] [cite:ts12_toi_pompeo2019] [cite:wb_axios_blinken] It also met limits: Huckabee called his "take it all" answer "hyperbolic," Trump said he would "not allow Israel to annex the West Bank," Brazil opened a trade office instead of an embassy, and in Thomas Massie's 2026 primary, where CUFI's Action Fund bought billboards, the Associated Press judged Trump's opposition the key factor. [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] [cite:gi6_ap_trump0925] [cite:ts7_pti_brazil] [cite:ts8_ji_massie] [cite:pbs_massie_takeaways] [scene:ts12_officials|Part Twelve: the officials]

Churches, members and stories

"Kairos Palestine calls Christian Zionism a heresy." Unsupported. The word is not in the passages checked; the document of 2009 rejects "any theology that legitimizes the occupation" and targets "Biblical fundamentalism." [cite:ts11_transcend_kairos] [cite:ts11_jcr_kairos] The condemnation belongs to the Jerusalem Declaration of 22 August 2006, which called Christian Zionist doctrines "false teaching"; in January 2026 the Heads of Churches named it among "damaging ideologies." [cite:ts1_wiki_jerdecl] [cite:ts11_osv_heads2026] Nor did Rome rule against "Scofield's entire prophetic system": paragraph 676 of the Catechism rejects millenarianism in general. [cite:ts11_usccb_ccc676]

"Israel gave Falwell a Learjet," and "Begin telephoned Falwell to explain the Osirak strike." Unsupported. Neither was found in a contemporary report or document. What is documented is Falwell's 1979 meeting with Begin, the Jabotinsky medal of November 1980 and Rabbi Marc Tanenbaum's criticism in 1981 of Begin's choice of Falwell. [cite:ts8_lib_falwell] [cite:ts8_wiki_jabmedal] [cite:ts8_djn_tanenbaum]

Four further claims. That Darby took the secret rapture from Margaret MacDonald's vision of 1830 is unsupported: he dated his idea to 1827, her text places believers inside the "fiery trial," and Kenneth Strand found the case "falls apart." [cite:ts3_wiki_macdonald] [cite:ts3_strand_auss] That the Balfour Declaration was an act of Christian Zionism is contested between Donald Lewis's argument from formation and the war aims in the cabinet's minutes. [cite:ts6_wiki_cz] [cite:ts6_wiki_balfourdecl] CUFI's ten million members, announced in December 2020, are its own uncounted figure. [cite:ts8_hfl_10m] Truman's "I am Cyrus" is known from later accounts, and Paul Merkley and John Judis read it in opposite ways. [cite:ts6_merkley_cyrus] [cite:rs_cw2_judis_truman_cyrus]

The claims that fail are those that give the movement one author, one patron or one secret aim; the documented record is less flattering to its founders than their admirers allowed and more ordinary than their critics supposed. What stays contested is motive and effect, taken up next. [scene:ts14_record|What the record settles]

sections.h: What the Record Settles, What Is Contested, What Is Open
sections.html:
Part One defined the theology shield as the use of a scriptural claim, above all Genesis 12:3 read as applying to the modern state, to move a question about that state's policies from evidence to faith, and promised to test it rather than assume it. [scene:ts1_defined|Part One: the definition] This section sorts the volume's findings into three groups: what the record settles, what named sources contest, and what remains open as of 21 October 2026. Nothing new is introduced.

Settled: the lineage

The belief is older than the system usually blamed for it. Restorationist commentary ran from Brightman's books, printed in 1609, to the London Society of 1809, and most of it expected the Jews to convert. [cite:ts2_crome_cdamm] It reached government once, on strategic terms: Palmerston's dispatch of 11 August 1840 offered the sultan Jewish settlers as "a check" on Muhammad Ali, without a word of scripture, and the sultan declined. [cite:ts2_cojs_palmerston1840] Darby supplied the system, separating Israel and the church at Geneva in 1840; Brookes's Niagara Creed of 1878, Moody's institute of 1886 and the Bible institutes carried it in America; Scofield's Bible, published by Oxford in 1909 and revised in 1917, printed it beside the verse; Dallas Theological Seminary from 1924, Lindsey's book of 1970 and the Left Behind novels took it to a mass public. [cite:ts3_darby_hopes1] [cite:ts3_ak_niagara] [cite:ts3_wiki_mbi] [cite:ts5_wiki_srb] [cite:ts7_wiki_dts] [cite:ts7_wrap_lindsey] [cite:ts7_sa_lahaye] The 1917 notes place Israel's restoration after "The return of the Lord" and did not call for a political programme. [cite:ts5_sac_deut30]

Settled: the machine and its money, as filed

The political machine was built by named people, and in stages. Blackstone's memorial of 1891 won elite signatures and no change of policy. [cite:ts6_moorhead_jets] The Christian committees of the 1940s were organised by Emanuel Neumann of the Zionist movement and led by liberal Protestants such as Reinhold Niebuhr, not by end-times teachers. [cite:ts6_aja_ccp_minutes] [cite:ts6_voss_rausch] The Moral Majority, founded in June 1979, was not built on Israel; Begin chose Falwell as his partner, and Jewish leaders objected at the time. [cite:ts8_balmer] [cite:ts8_wiki_jabmedal] [cite:ts8_djn_tanenbaum] The money that can be read from filings is specific: the International Fellowship of Christians and Jews reported $318 million in revenue for 2024; the CUFI Action Fund between $89,000 and $1.8 million a year from 2015 to 2024, while the main CUFI entity's budget is not public; $4.6 million from Sheldon Adelson to CUFI from 2012, on +972 Magazine's reading of his foundation's returns; and, from Israel's side, a $4.1 million church campaign and a $3.2 million contract registered under FARA in 2025. [cite:ts8_pp_ifcj] [cite:ts8_pp_cufiaf] [cite:ts9_972_adelson] [cite:pm_jta_730m] [cite:ts9_rs_showfaith] CUFI's membership, ten million by its own announcement of December 2020, is a claim, not a count. [cite:ts8_hfl_10m]

Settled: the shield in use, and where it failed

The mechanism is documented in dated statements by named people. Robert Jeffress said in 2017 and again in June 2025 that those who oppose Israel are "on the wrong side of God"; Senator Ted Cruz read Genesis 12:3 as about "the nation of Israel" on 18 June 2025; Speaker Mike Johnson told an audience at Ariel in August 2025 that Judea and Samaria were "promised" in Scripture. [cite:ts10_cbn_jeffress2017] [cite:ts10_cp_jeffress2025] [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] [cite:ts12_toi_johnson] Its failures are documented too. Israel's own tourism minister rebuked Pat Robertson in January 2006 when he turned the land theology on Ariel Sharon; Brazil opened a trade office instead of an embassy in 2019; Cruz said he does not use his faith as the reason for his policy; Ambassador Huckabee called his "take it all" answer "hyperbolic"; and at Turning Point's conference in December 2025 Tucker Carlson said that "God is not on any country's side." [cite:ts7_cbs_robertson] [cite:ts7_pti_brazil] [cite:ts10_cp_cruz] [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] [cite:ts10_aje_americafest] The churches outside the dispensational tradition rejected the reading in their own documents, from the Jerusalem Declaration of 2006 to the Heads of Churches in January 2026, and Palestinian Christians, about 1 per cent of the population, built a theology against it. [cite:ts1_wiki_jerdecl] [cite:ts11_osv_heads2026] [cite:ts11_aje_christians2025]

Settled: the generational split

The constituency still holds, and is dividing by age. In LifeWay's survey of September 2017, support for Israel among Americans with evangelical beliefs was 58 per cent at 18 to 34 and 77 per cent at 65 and over. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] Motti Inbari and Kirill Bumin found support among evangelicals under 30 falling from 68.9 per cent in 2018 to 33.6 per cent in 2021. [cite:ts11_tau_inbari] In Pew's survey of 4 to 17 May 2026, white evangelical Protestants were the only religious group with a majority, 57 per cent, favourable to the Israeli government, down from 71 per cent in 2024; among Republicans, 28 per cent of those aged 18 to 29 were favourable against 75 per cent of those 65 and over. [cite:ts11_pew_2026] [cite:ts11_crosswalk_pew]

Contested

Motive. Whether Balfour and Lloyd George acted from Christian formation or from the war aims their cabinet recorded, whether Truman's "I am Cyrus" explains 1948, and whether today's support springs from Christian nationalism, as Sarah Posner argues, or from the Genesis blessing and a debt to the Jewish people, as CUFI's leaders say: each rests on named sources on both sides, and the volume does not adjudicate. [cite:ts6_wiki_cz] [cite:ts6_jn_lloydgeorge] [cite:ts6_merkley_cyrus] [cite:rs_cw2_judis_truman_cyrus] [cite:ts9_dn_posner] [cite:ts9_jta_morgenstern2010] Influence on policy. Christian Zionist figures heard the embassy move promised and prayed at its opening, and Trump later called it "for the evangelicals"; the official texts of Jerusalem, the Golan and the settlements gave legal and security reasons, and no document allows the drivers to be weighed. [cite:ts12_ncr_pence2017] [cite:ts12_cnn_pastors] [cite:ts9_almon_trump2020] [cite:ts12_toi_trump2017] [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852] [cite:ts12_toi_pompeo2019] Whether Israeli governments were wise to tie the relationship to one wing of American Christianity has been argued since Tanenbaum in 1981. [cite:ts9_djn_tanenbaum]

Open as of 21 October 2026

Whether the generational shift continues is open, and Pew has not published an age breakdown of white evangelicals. [cite:ts11_pew_2026] CUFI's main budget, donors and membership count are undisclosed. [cite:ts8_pp_cufiaf] Canfield's exact wording and Sandeen's page on Lyman Stewart's gift are known only through a secondary site; the founding year of Bridges for Peace is unsettled; and no survey measures Christian Zionist belief in Latin America. [cite:ts4_sfiles] [cite:ts8_hfl_bfp] [cite:ts7_pew_latam2014] Honduras's embassy, whose return to Tel Aviv was discussed in 2022, was still listed in Jerusalem in December 2024. [cite:ts12_na_honduras] [cite:ts7_abc_paraguay] The 2019 settlements position has not been formally restored, and talks on a successor to the aid memorandum, which Huckabee said would be "based on trade," had not concluded. [cite:wb_axios_blinken] [cite:gi16_wiki_nextmou] The Israeli election of 27 October 2026 and the questions it leaves open are set out in the Greater Israel volume. [scene:gi13_open|The Greater Israel Architecture: what remains open]

The central question, answered

The volume asked how a Protestant end-times system became a political shield for a state's policies, who built and benefited from it, and where it holds and fails. On the record, the system did not become a shield by itself. A belief in Jewish restoration, three centuries old and mostly aimed at conversion, was given a timetable by Darby, a mass text by Scofield and a mass market by Lindsey; after 1948 named teachers moved the promise from "the Jew" to the state, and from 1977 Israeli governments, most intensively the Likud's, cultivated the teachers who did so. [cite:ts1_sac_gen15] [cite:ts1_jvl_cufi] [cite:ts9_wiki_jabmedal] [cite:ts9_j_netanyahu2021] The builders are named: Falwell, Hagee, the ICEJ, CUFI, and an Israeli Foreign Ministry that paid for church campaigns in 2025. [cite:pm_jta_730m] The documented beneficiaries are named too: organisations that raised money, a party that won a voting bloc, publishers who sold books, and Israeli governments that gained visitors, donations and allies. [cite:ts8_pp_ifcj] [cite:ts9_rns_exit2024] [cite:ts9_mfa_tourism2013] It holds best where it is least tested, as a premise in a constituency; it fails when stated as policy by an official, when it meets an export or an ally's interest, and among the young. It is a documented argument made by named people, not the belief of every Christian who supports Israel: in 2017 only 23 per cent of Americans with evangelical beliefs backed a Palestinian state and 46 per cent were unsure. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway]

A closing reading

What follows is a reading, not a finding. Part Thirteen set beside this record the inner reading of the name, from Philo's "man who sees God" to the kabbalistic Jacob at Tiferet and the platform's own IS-RA-EL lens, which Hebrew philology does not support and whose first author is unknown. [cite:ts13_philo_mut] [cite:ts13_chabad_luria] [cite:ts13_heiser_maxwell] Read through that lens, the history documented here is that of a map read as a deed: one level of an old name taken for the whole of it. The lens decides nothing in this volume's findings and supplies no evidence about anyone's intent. It sets an inner tradition against an institutional literalism found within Judaism and Christianity alike, and it does not say that any people has taken a name not its own; the name has named a people since the oldest document in which it appears. [cite:ts13_wiki_merneptah] [scene:ts13_deed|Part Thirteen: from inner map to land deed]

books.title: The Hamas Architecture
books.subtitle: Origins, Power and the War, 1928–2026
books.intro:
This volume is about Hamas: where it came from, what it has done, and how much power it actually holds. It was written to answer a set of direct questions. How and why was Hamas formed? Would it exist if Palestine had not been colonized and occupied? Would it be what it is if Israel had not cut Gaza off from the West Bank? Was it a response, and to what? And what is its true strength, in money, weapons and allies, against Israel's, with its economy, its own military budget and the billions in American aid behind it?

The record answers some of these questions and not others. It shows that the movement Hamas grew from, the Muslim Brotherhood, was founded in Egypt in 1928, two decades before Israel existed; that Israel licensed the Brotherhood's charity network in Gaza in 1979 and largely left it alone; and that Hamas itself was founded in December 1987, in the first weeks of an uprising against twenty years of occupation. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007] [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] It shows Hamas's charter, with its antisemitic articles, its suicide bombings and rockets aimed at civilians, its rule over Gaza and its attack of 7 October 2023, stated plainly. [cite:hm_avalon_charter] [cite:hm_wiki_suicide] [cite:hm_hrw_rockets2009] It shows Israel's separation of Gaza from the West Bank, the blockade, and the Qatari money Israel let into Gaza, with what Israeli leaders said about it and their denials, side by side. [cite:hm_aj_separation] [cite:hm_fdd_shinbet] [cite:hm_ynet_biglie] It tests the claim, often made, that Hamas has become the excuse for everything, against the record of the war. [scene:hm11_scale|Always Hamas] And it measures the gap between the two sides: before the war, Israel's economy was about 190 times the size of Gaza's. [cite:hm_fred_ilgdp] [cite:hm_aspi_gazagdp]

What would have happened otherwise cannot be documented, and the volume labels every such reading as an argument. It is a companion to Gaza, Documented, The West Bank, Documented and PRESS.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: Before Hamas
chapters.intro: Hamas was founded in December 1987, but the movement it grew out of is sixty years older. Part One follows that movement from its founding in Egypt in 1928 to the eve of the first intifada: its branches in Gaza, its suppression under Egyptian rule, its revival under Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, and the charity network that Israel licensed in 1979 and then largely left alone. It ends with what Israeli officials said about that choice afterwards, because they did not agree.
chapters.outro: Part One set out what came before Hamas. The Muslim Brotherhood was founded in Egypt in 1928 and opened branches in Gaza in the 1940s; under Egyptian rule it was suppressed; after 1967 Ahmed Yassin rebuilt it as a network of mosques and charities, which Israel licensed in 1979 and largely left alone while it fought the PLO. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007] [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] Some of the Israeli officials involved later called that a mistake and one called Hamas "Israel's creation"; others said Israel never funded or armed it. [cite:hm_intercept_2018] Part Two follows the founding of Hamas in December 1987.

sections.h: The Brotherhood, 1928–1967
sections.html:
The Society of the Muslim Brothers was founded in 1928 by Hassan al-Banna, a schoolteacher in Ismailiyah, Egypt. Its aim was to free Muslim lands from foreign rule and to build an Islamic state, and its method was gradual: reform the individual first, then the family, then society. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007] Twenty years before the State of Israel existed, then, the religious movement that Hamas would later call its parent was already organized. Hamas's own 1988 charter describes it as "one of the wings of Moslem Brotherhood in Palestine". [cite:hm_avalon_charter]

Branches opened in Gaza in the 1940s, and the Brotherhood inaugurated a central office in Jerusalem on 6 May 1946. In the war of 1948 it sent several hundred volunteers from Egypt and other countries to fight in Palestine. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007] The war left Gaza a narrow strip under Egyptian military administration, its population swollen by refugees from the towns and villages to the north; Gaza, Documented sets out how that happened. [scene:gz1_refugees|The refugees of 1948] Under Gamal Abdel Nasser, who crushed the Brotherhood in Egypt in the mid-1950s and again in the mid-1960s, its members in Gaza were arrested too, and many left the strip. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007]

Yassin and the Mujama, 1967–1987

Ahmed Yassin, a paraplegic cleric in Gaza, was detained by Egypt in 1965 for Brotherhood activity. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007] After Israel occupied Gaza in 1967, he rebuilt the movement there in the early 1970s, starting with religious education. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007] Its vehicle was the Mujama al-Islami, the Islamic Centre, which built mosques, schools and clinics and, after 1979, an Islamic university. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn]

What the Brotherhood did not do in these years matters for everything that follows. Through the 1970s and most of the 1980s it largely stayed out of armed resistance. Its position was that an Islamic society had to be built before any liberation could come, and it refused to join the secular, nationalist armed groups of the PLO. When Fatah offered in 1965 to absorb the Brotherhood, the Brotherhood asked Fatah to commit itself to Islamic ideology, and Fatah refused. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007] Its rivals in Gaza were those secular nationalists, and the two camps clashed. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn]

There were signs that this would change. In 1984 Israel found a cache of weapons linked to Yassin and sentenced him to prison; he said the arms were meant for use against rival Palestinians, not Israel, and he was freed about a year later in a prisoner exchange. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] Azzam Tamimi, a historian sympathetic to Hamas, writes that the decision to turn the movement into an armed one had been prepared for about a decade before it was taken in December 1987. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007]

sections.h: Licensed and Left Alone
sections.html:
In 1979 Israel's military government recognized the Mujama as a charity and then registered it as an association. It allowed the network to build schools, clinics and mosques and an Islamic university in Gaza. Israeli officials who served there at the time told The Wall Street Journal in 2009 that their main concern then was Fatah and the PLO, which were fighting Israel, and that they did not want to appear to be enemies of Islam; when the Islamists clashed with secular Palestinians, Israel often stayed out of it. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn]

Brigadier General Yitzhak Segev, the military governor of Gaza in the early 1980s, later described the arrangement in his own words: "The Israeli government gave me a budget, and the military government gives to the mosques." [cite:hm_intercept_2018] According to The Intercept, Segev told a New York Times reporter that he had helped fund the Islamist current as a "counterweight" to the secular and leftist factions of the PLO and Fatah. [cite:hm_intercept_2018] The funding he described went to mosques, at a time when the Brotherhood's network was not an armed movement.

What Israeli Officials Said Later

The officials who were there did not agree about what the choice amounted to. Avner Cohen, who worked on religious affairs in Gaza for more than twenty years, told the Journal: "Hamas, to my great regret, is Israel's creation." In the mid-1980s, he said, he had written to his superiors urging them to break up "this monster" before it was too late, and nothing was done. David Hacham, an Arab affairs adviser in Gaza in the late 1980s and early 1990s, said: "I think we made a mistake." [cite:hm_wsj_spawn]

Others disputed it. Shalom Harari, an intelligence officer in Gaza at the time, said Israel never financed or armed Hamas, and that its failure was one of neglect, not design. Arieh Spitzen, another officer, doubted that political Islam could have been stopped by acting sooner. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] [cite:hm_intercept_2018]

What the Record Supports

The record supports a narrow finding and not a broad one. It shows that Israel licensed and tolerated the Brotherhood's charity network in Gaza for most of a decade, at a time when it regarded the PLO as the threat, and that some of the officials responsible later called that a mistake. It does not show that Israel created, funded or armed Hamas as an armed movement: the Brotherhood came first by half a century, its turn to armed struggle in 1987 was its own decision, and the officials closest to the question disagree about what Israel's tolerance amounted to. Part Three takes up the counterfactual directly. [scene:hm3_question|Would Hamas exist?]

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: The Founding
chapters.intro: Part Two follows the founding of Hamas in December 1987, in the first weeks of the Palestinian uprising, and sets out the document in which it declared what it was: the charter of August 1988. The charter is quoted directly, including its antisemitic passages, because what an organization says about itself is evidence. Beside it stands the document Hamas issued in 2017, how it differs, and how Israel answered it.
chapters.outro: Part Two set out the founding. Hamas was founded in December 1987 by Ahmed Yassin and six others, in the first weeks of the uprising against the occupation, and carried out its first attack in 1989. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] Its 1988 charter claimed all of Palestine, rejected any solution but jihad, and repeated antisemitic conspiracy claims; its 2017 document spoke of a conflict with Zionism, not Jews, and accepted a 1967 state without recognizing Israel, which Israel dismissed as an attempt to fool the world. [cite:hm_avalon_charter] [cite:hm_jps_hroub2017] [cite:hm_cnn_2017doc] Part Three asks whether Hamas would exist at all.

sections.h: December 1987
sections.html: In December 1987, twenty years into Israel's occupation of Gaza and the West Bank, Palestinians in both territories rose up against it, in the uprising that became known as the first intifada. Gaza, Documented sets it out. [scene:gz3_uprising|The first intifada] In the same weeks, Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, the paraplegic cleric who led the Muslim Brotherhood's network in Gaza, and six others founded a new organization. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] They called it the Islamic Resistance Movement. [cite:hm_avalon_charter] The historian Tareq Baconi describes the moment as the point at which the Brotherhood's Islamic party in the territories "spun off" into Hamas, moving from social work to armed struggle. [cite:hm_pbs_baconi] Israel, which had licensed the Brotherhood's charity in 1979 and largely left it alone, did not move against the new group at first; Hamas carried out its first attack in 1989. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn]

sections.h: The Charter of 1988
sections.html:
On 18 August 1988 Hamas published its covenant. It describes the land of Palestine as an Islamic trust that cannot be given up, and rejects negotiated settlements: "There is no solution for the Palestinian question except through Jihad" (Article 13). It quotes a religious saying: "The Day of Judgement will not come about until Moslems fight the Jews" (Article 7). It blames Jews for the world's revolutions and wars, claiming they "were behind World War I, when they were able to destroy the Islamic Caliphate" (Article 22), and it cites as evidence of Zionist plans the "Protocols of the Elders of Zion" (Article 32), an antisemitic forgery first published in Russia in 1903. [cite:hm_avalon_charter] [cite:hm_ushmm_protocols]

The charter is not a document about the occupation of 1967 alone. It claims all of Palestine, and it speaks of Jews, not only of Israel or Zionism. These passages are why scholars such as Bruce Hoffman read Hamas as driven by ideology rather than by grievance. [cite:hm_atl_hoffman] [scene:hm3_question|Would Hamas exist?]

The Document of 2017

On 1 May 2017, in Doha, Hamas's political leader Khaled Mashaal presented a new "Document of General Principles and Policies." It said Hamas's conflict "is with the Zionist project, not with the Jews because of their religion"; accepted, as a "formula of national consensus," a Palestinian state on the lines of 4 June 1967, with Jerusalem as its capital and the return of refugees, without recognizing Israel; kept armed resistance as its "strategic choice"; and dropped its formal tie to the Muslim Brotherhood. The Palestinian scholar Khaled Hroub called it a significant change, while noting that the 1988 charter's antisemitic overtones had never before been fully renounced. [cite:hm_jps_hroub2017] [cite:hm_cnn_2017doc] A spokesman for Prime Minister Netanyahu answered that Hamas "is attempting to fool the world but it will not succeed." [cite:hm_cnn_2017doc]

Six years later, on 7 October 2023, Hamas led the attack described in Part Seven. Which of its two documents better describes it has been argued ever since.

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: Would Hamas Exist?
chapters.intro: Part Three asks the question beneath every argument about Hamas: would it exist if Israel had not taken the land, occupied Gaza and the West Bank, and divided them? No record can prove what would have happened in a history that did not occur. What the record can do is separate the question into parts that the documents speak to, and show where historians who have studied Hamas disagree. This part does that, in four questions, and ends with what can be said and what cannot.
chapters.outro: Part Three took the question apart. The Islamist movement that became Hamas predates the occupation and belongs to a region-wide movement; the armed Islamic Resistance Movement was founded in 1987 in the uprising against the occupation, and its first suicide bombing inside Israel was announced as revenge for the Hebron massacre. [cite:hm_pbs_baconi] [cite:hm_wiki_afula] Israel licensed and tolerated the Islamists as a rival to Fatah, and after 2007 Israeli governments let Qatari money reach Hamas's government, which Smotrich and a reported Netanyahu remark tied to keeping the Palestinians divided and Netanyahu denies. [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich] [cite:hm_ynet_biglie] [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich] Scholars read Hamas either as a national resistance movement or as an ideological one aiming at Israel's destruction, and its own charters supply evidence for both. [cite:hm_pbs_baconi] [cite:hm_atl_hoffman] [cite:hm_avalon_charter] Part Four follows its campaigns of bombs and its turn to the ballot.

sections.h: Four Questions
sections.html:
1. Would an Islamist movement exist in Gaza? Very likely, and this is the part least tied to Israel. Hamas grew out of the Muslim Brotherhood, a religious and political movement from Egypt whose Gaza branch was building a social network of charities, schools and mosques long before 1987. [cite:hm_pbs_baconi] [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] The religious and social network that became Hamas was not itself a product of the occupation.

2. Would that movement have taken up arms against Israel? Here the record points the other way. For most of the 1970s and 1980s the Brotherhood in Gaza built schools, clinics and mosques, under an Israeli licence granted in 1979, and fought the secular Palestinian nationalists of Fatah rather than Israel; when Ahmed Yassin was caught with a cache of weapons in 1984, he told his interrogators they were meant for his Palestinian rivals. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] It was in December 1987, in the first weeks of the uprising against twenty years of Israeli occupation, that the movement took the name the Islamic Resistance Movement, Hamas by its Arabic initials, and turned to armed struggle. [cite:hm_avalon_charter] The historian Tareq Baconi describes the change as a response to the uprising: the movement came to believe that "the only way that Israel can be compelled to end its occupation" was armed force. [cite:hm_pbs_baconi] Its first suicide bombing inside Israel, at Afula in April 1994, was announced as revenge for the massacre of 29 Muslim worshippers in Hebron by a settler six weeks before; an adviser to Israel's own Shin Bet said Hamas had refrained from attacking civilians inside Israel until then. [cite:hm_wiki_afula]

3. Would Hamas have grown as it did without Israel's early tolerance? Israeli officials who served in Gaza disagree among themselves. Avner Cohen, who handled religious affairs there, said: "Hamas, to my great regret, is Israel's creation." A former military governor, Yitzhak Segev, said the government gave him a budget and "the military government gives to the mosques." Others, such as Brigadier General Shalom Harari, said Israel's failures were neglect, not design, and that Israel never financed or armed Hamas; Arieh Spitzen doubted political Islam could have been checked sooner. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] [cite:hm_intercept_2018]

4. Would Hamas be what it is without the split and the separation? Israel restricted movement between Gaza and the West Bank from 1991, and kept restricting it after the Oslo agreement of 1993 called them "a single territorial unit"; more than 500,000 exits from Gaza were recorded in September 2000, against about 3,000 permits a month in 2013. [cite:hm_aj_separation] Hamas won the Palestinian election of 2006 across both territories before the split, and took Gaza by force in 2007. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] After that, Bezalel Smotrich, then a Knesset member, said in 2015 that "the Palestinian Authority is a burden, and Hamas is an asset", and Israeli governments let Qatari money reach Hamas's government while blockading Gaza.
