[cite:wb_wiki_smotrich] [cite:gz_week_qatar] Netanyahu denies the policy aimed to strengthen Hamas and says the money prevented a humanitarian collapse. [cite:hm_ynet_biglie] What Hamas would have become in a Gaza connected to the West Bank and open to the world cannot be known; what is documented is that its rule hardened inside a closed strip.

Two Readings

Scholars read this history in two ways, and the record holds both. One reading, Baconi's, sees Hamas as a Palestinian national movement with an Islamic identity, engaged in "armed resistance against a colonial force"; treating it only as a terrorist group, he argues, lets governments avoid the political question of Palestine. [cite:hm_pbs_baconi] The other, set out by the terrorism scholar Bruce Hoffman, holds that Hamas's aims come from its ideology, not the occupation: its 1988 charter, he writes, "spells out clearly Hamas's genocidal intentions," and its 2017 document changed the language without changing the goal. [cite:hm_atl_hoffman] The charter itself gives Hoffman's reading its evidence: it calls all of Palestine an Islamic trust, says "there is no solution for the Palestinian question except through Jihad," and repeats antisemitic conspiracy claims; Part Two quotes it. [cite:hm_avalon_charter] [scene:hm2_charter|The charter]

On the documents, the armed organization called Hamas was born of the uprising against the occupation, and its first attacks on civilians inside Israel followed a massacre of Palestinians; its ideology, written into its charter, reached beyond ending the occupation to the whole land. Both are true. The rest of this book follows what it did with both.

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: Bombs and Ballots
chapters.intro: Part Four covers the seventeen years in which Hamas became known to the world: first for bombs on buses and in restaurants, then for winning an election. It sets out when Hamas began killing civilians inside Israel and the reason it gave, the toll of the suicide-bombing campaigns, the Israeli attempts to kill its leaders, and the election of January 2006 and what followed it.
chapters.outro: Part Four set out how Hamas turned to killing civilians inside Israel, with the Afula bombing of April 1994 that it called revenge for the Hebron massacre, and how suicide attacks by Hamas and other groups killed 735 Israelis by 2005. [cite:hm_wiki_afula] [cite:hm_wiki_suicide] Israel tried to kill Khaled Mashaal in 1997 and killed Ahmed Yassin in 2004. [cite:hm_toi_mashaal] [cite:hm_wiki_yassin] In January 2006 Hamas won the Palestinian legislative election; the Quartet and Israel cut it off. [cite:hm_wiki_2006elect] Part Five follows the split that came next.

sections.h: Afula, 1994
sections.html:
Hamas carried out its first attack in 1989. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] The turn to killing civilians inside Israel came in April 1994. On 25 February 1994 Baruch Goldstein, an Israeli settler, opened fire on Muslim worshippers at the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron and killed 29 of them. On 6 April a Hamas suicide bomber blew up a car beside a bus in Afula, in northern Israel, and killed eight Israeli civilians. Hamas said it was revenge for Hebron. It was the first Palestinian suicide attack on civilians inside Israel; Matti Steinberg, an adviser to the Shin Bet, said that until then Hamas had refrained from attacking civilians inside Israel. [cite:hm_wiki_afula] The West Bank, Documented sets out the Hebron massacre and its aftermath. [scene:wb5_hebron|Hebron]

The bombings came in the years of the Oslo Accords, which Hamas opposed, and they continued, with pauses, for more than a decade. [scene:gz3_oslo|Oslo and Gaza] In October 1994 a Hamas bomber killed 22 people on a bus on Dizengoff Street in Tel Aviv. In the second intifada, from 2000, the campaign peaked: a Hamas bomber killed 21 people outside the Dolphinarium nightclub in Tel Aviv in June 2001, and another killed 16 at the Sbarro pizzeria in Jerusalem that August, in an attack claimed by both Hamas and Islamic Jihad. [cite:hm_wiki_suicidelist] On the first night of Passover in 2002, a Hamas bomber killed 30 people at the Park Hotel in Netanya; in March 2002 alone, Palestinian attacks killed 135 Israelis. [cite:hm_wiki_suicide]

In 2002 Human Rights Watch found that those who planned and carried out suicide bombings against civilians, naming Hamas, Islamic Jihad, the al-Aqsa Martyrs' Brigades and the PFLP, were guilty of crimes against humanity: "The people who carry out suicide bombings are not martyrs, they're war criminals," said its director, Kenneth Roth. [cite:hm_hrw_erased] Human Rights Watch later reached a similar finding on the rocket fire that replaced the bombings, which Part Six sets out. [scene:hm6_rockets|The rockets]

The Leaders Targeted

Israel's answer included killing Hamas's leaders. On 25 September 1997, two months after a Hamas suicide bombing in Jerusalem's Mahane Yehuda market, two Mossad agents tried to poison Khaled Mashaal, a Hamas leader living in Jordan, on a street in Amman; one sprayed him, and Jordanian police caught both. King Hussein demanded the antidote; Israel supplied it and Mashaal recovered. To recover its agents and repair relations with Jordan, Israel released Ahmed Yassin from prison, and he went back to Gaza to lead Hamas. [cite:hm_toi_mashaal]

On 22 March 2004 Israeli helicopters fired missiles at Yassin as he left dawn prayers in Gaza City, killing him and nine others nearby. Israel's UN ambassador, Dan Gillerman, said: "When you kill our citizens, you will not be spared." Britain's foreign secretary, Jack Straw, called the killing "unacceptable, unjustified". Yassin's successor in Gaza, Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi, was killed weeks later. [cite:hm_wiki_yassin]

sections.h: The Election of 2006
sections.html:
On 25 January 2006 Palestinians in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem voted for a new Legislative Council. Hamas, running as "Change and Reform", won 74 of the 132 seats with 44.45 percent of the national list vote; Fatah won 45 seats with 41.43 percent. The international observer mission of the National Democratic Institute and the Carter Center praised "a professional and impartial performance of election officials". [cite:hm_wiki_2006elect]

The Quartet of the United States, the European Union, Russia and the UN set three conditions for dealing with a Hamas government: recognize Israel, accept previous agreements and renounce violence. Hamas refused. Israel stopped transferring about $50 million a month in customs revenue it collected for the Palestinian Authority and barred Hamas legislators from travelling between Gaza and the West Bank. After militants from Gaza captured the soldier Gilad Shalit in June 2006, Israel arrested 8 Hamas ministers and 26 Hamas legislators in the West Bank on 29 June. [cite:hm_wiki_2006elect] Gaza, Documented follows the capture and the takeover that came a year later. [scene:gz4_takeover|An election, a capture, a takeover]

It was the last national election Palestinians held. Part Five follows what happened next: the split between Gaza and the West Bank, and the policies that kept it in place. [scene:hm5_split|The split]

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: The Split and the Separation
chapters.intro: The question for this part is direct: would Hamas be what it became if Israel had not split Gaza from the West Bank and cut the two apart? Part Five sets out the record that bears on it. It begins with how the split happened in 2006 and 2007, including the American plan to remove Hamas by force that was reported later. It then sets out Israel's separation of the two territories, which began long before Hamas took Gaza; the Qatari money that Israel let into Gaza from 2018; and what Israeli leaders said about all of it, including Prime Minister Netanyahu's denials. It ends with the two readings of what this means, labelled as arguments.
chapters.outro: Part Five set out the split and the separation. Israel restricted movement between Gaza and the West Bank from 1991; Hamas won the 2006 election, was cut off, and took Gaza by force in June 2007, and no national election has been held since. [cite:hm_aj_separation] [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] [cite:hm_aj_2021coup] From 2018 Israel let Qatari cash into Gaza; Smotrich and a reported Netanyahu remark tied the policy to keeping the Palestinians divided, Netanyahu denies it, and the Shin Bet says some of the money reached Hamas's military build-up. [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich] [cite:hm_toi_timefact] [cite:hm_fdd_shinbet] Part Six turns to Hamas as its own actor.

sections.h: From Election to Two Governments, 2006–2007
sections.html:
After Hamas won the election of January 2006, it formed a government in March. Israel withheld the tax revenue it collected for the Palestinian Authority, and the Quartet stopped aid to a Hamas-led government. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] [cite:hm_wiki_2006elect] Fatah and Hamas, fighting each other in the streets of Gaza, signed the Mecca Agreement in February 2007 and formed a unity government in March. In June the fighting resumed. Between 7 and 15 June 2007 Hamas forces took Fatah's security headquarters and bases in Gaza; on 14 June President Mahmoud Abbas dissolved the unity government, and by 15 June Hamas held the whole strip. The Palestinian Centre for Human Rights counted at least 161 people killed. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007]

What those days were is disputed. Fatah called it a Hamas coup. In April 2008 the journalist David Rose reported in Vanity Fair, from documents and on-record interviews with former Bush administration officials, that after the election the United States had worked on a plan for Abbas to dismiss the Hamas government and for Fatah forces to be armed, through Arab states, to handle the fighting that would follow; Rose's reading was that Hamas struck first. The State Department called the article "absurd". [cite:hm_dn_rose] [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] Gaza, Documented sets out the takeover in more detail. [scene:gz4_takeover|An election, a capture, a takeover]

Since then there have been two Palestinian governments: Hamas in Gaza and the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority in parts of the West Bank. In September 2007 Israel's security cabinet declared Gaza "hostile territory" and authorized cuts to fuel, electricity and goods. [cite:gz_un_hostile2007] No national Palestinian election has been held since 2006. Abbas called legislative elections for May 2021 and then postponed them, saying Israel would not allow voting in East Jerusalem; Israel's foreign ministry called the elections "an internal Palestinian issue". Hamas called the postponement "a coup against the path of national partnership and consensus". [cite:hm_aj_2021coup]

sections.h: The Separation Began First
sections.html:
Gaza and the West Bank were cut apart long before Hamas ruled Gaza, and the question has to start there. In 1991 Israel ended the general exit permit that had let Palestinians from Gaza move fairly freely into Israel and through it to the West Bank. The Oslo Accords of 1993 described the West Bank and Gaza as "a single territorial unit, whose integrity will be preserved during the interim period". From 2000 Israel barred students from Gaza from studying at West Bank universities and froze changes of address from Gaza to the West Bank; from 2007 Gazans living in the West Bank needed a "permit to remain". [cite:hm_aj_separation]

The effect can be measured. In September 2000 more than half a million exits from Gaza were recorded at the Erez crossing in a single month; by 2013 Israel was issuing about 3,000 permits a month. Sari Bashi of the Israeli rights group Gisha said of the policy: "Families are separated… It's not about security." Israeli officials such as Uzi Landau, then tourism minister, pointed to the attacks that followed Oslo; Israel's position is that the restrictions are a security measure. [cite:hm_aj_separation]

The separation has two sides in the record. Israel built it as a security policy, in years when bombers did come out of Gaza and the West Bank, as Part Four set out. [scene:hm4_bombs|The bombings] It also meant that by the time Hamas took Gaza in 2007, the strip's people had already been largely cut off from the West Bank for years, and the political split fell along a line that Israel's permit system had already drawn.

sections.h: The Qatari Money
sections.html:
From 2018 Israel let Qatar send cash into Hamas-run Gaza. In November 2018 the first $15 million arrived through Israel, the first of six monthly payments totalling $90 million, mainly for the salaries of officials of the Hamas government. Netanyahu called it "the right step" to restore quiet and prevent a humanitarian crisis; Naftali Bennett, then a minister, compared it to "protection money", and the opposition leader Tzipi Livni called it "submission to Hamas". [cite:gz_ds_qatar2018] Before May 2021 about $30 million in Qatari cash was carried into Gaza each month in suitcases through an Israeli-controlled crossing. After the war of May 2021 Israel stopped the cash, and a UN mechanism to pay families directly, with Israel approving the list, replaced it. [cite:gz_aj_qatar2021] The historian Adam Raz's account is that almost $30 million in cash entered every month from summer 2018 until October 2023; it does not match the 2021 record of the cash being stopped and replaced, and he gives no source for the figure. [cite:hm_972_raz]

Qatar's account is that the money was humanitarian and Israel controlled it. Majed al-Ansari, adviser to Qatar's prime minister, told Israel's public broadcaster in April 2024 that it moved under "complete Israeli oversight, complete Israeli vetting", "done for humanitarian reasons". [cite:hm_toi_ansari]

What Israeli Leaders Said

The strongest claim about the purpose comes from a remark Netanyahu is reported to have made to a Likud faction meeting in March 2019, and its wording matters. It was first reported by the Jerusalem Post's Lahav Harkov, from a Knesset member paraphrasing him: whoever is against a Palestinian state should support letting money into Gaza, because keeping the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank and Hamas in Gaza separate helps prevent a Palestinian state. Harkov has since written that the remark concerned money and aid into Gaza and has been "rewritten and twisted" online. [cite:gz_harkov_2019] Politico later reported it as: "Anyone who wants to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state needs to support strengthening Hamas." [cite:gz_week_qatar] It is a paraphrase from a closed meeting, not a recording; Asharq Al-Awsat, relaying the Jerusalem Post's source the next day, quoted him saying that "whoever is against a Palestinian state should be with" the transfers, and that with Israel supervising, "we know it's going to humanitarian causes." [cite:hm_aawsat_2019]

Other statements are on the record. Bezalel Smotrich, later finance minister, said in a 2015 interview: "The Palestinian Authority is a burden, and Hamas is an asset", reasoning that the Authority hurt Israel in international forums while Hamas never would. [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich] In December 2023 The New York Times, from interviews with more than two dozen officials, reported that Netanyahu "not only tolerated" the payments but "had encouraged them". [cite:gz_week_qatar] The Times of Israel's political correspondent wrote the day after October 7 that "most of the time, Israeli policy was to treat the Palestinian Authority as a burden and Hamas as an asset." [cite:hm_toi_schneider]

Netanyahu denies it. "It's a big lie that I wanted to build [up] Hamas. Ridiculous," he told Politico in November 2023; the money, he said, was to prevent a humanitarian collapse in Gaza. [cite:hm_ynet_biglie] Asked by Time in August 2024 about the 2019 remark, he said: "That's a false statement. I never said that," and that the policy was shared by governments before and after his: "It wasn't bankrolling Hamas." Time stood by the reporting and cited a remark by the former CIA analyst Chip Usher to The New York Times: "Anything that Hamas didn't have to use out of its own budget freed up money for other things." [cite:hm_toi_timefact] In September 2026 he told i24NEWS that the money had been for humanitarian aid, sent on the advice of the Mossad and the Shin Bet, and was "worth 2 percent – 2 percent of all the money that entered the Strip." [cite:hm_aj_i24_2026]

His own words after the war began. Two later statements are on the record. In January 2024 Israel's Channel 12 aired a leaked recording of Netanyahu at a meeting with hostage families, in which he called Qatar's role "problematic" and blamed Qatar for financing Hamas, money whose entry his own government had approved. [cite:hm_aj_tape2024] At a press conference in May 2025, by the Catalan newspaper Ara's account (an unverified translation), he asked, "Why did we want to keep Hamas and the Palestinian Authority divided?", said the policy had been recommended by the Shin Bet and the Mossad, and denied that Qatari money paid for 7 October, which he called a "low cost" attack. [cite:hm_ara_may2025]

What He Was Told

In September 2026 Yedioth Ahronoth, citing internal intelligence documents and testimony to the State Comptroller, reported that Netanyahu had been warned at least twice that the Qatari money was reaching Hamas's military wing: in 2019 by the Shin Bet chief, Nadav Argaman, and in 2020 by Military Intelligence; Egypt had warned in 2018. A Military Intelligence officer told the Comptroller that about $4 million a month was diverted to the Qassam Brigades between 2019 and 2021, roughly half the military wing's budget. Netanyahu's office called the report "a collection of recycled lies" and said security officials had supported the grants believing they went to humanitarian projects. [cite:hm_jc_warned2026]

What the Shin Bet Found

In March 2025 the Shin Bet published a summary of its own inquiry into October 7. Among the factors that let Hamas build its forces it listed the "atmosphere of quiet" Israel had sought and "the flow of Qatari funds and their transfer to the military wing and its force build-up", alongside money from Iran. [cite:hm_fdd_shinbet] Israel's Channel 12 reported that an unpublished annex, titled "The Path to October 7", said the policy had continued despite repeated Shin Bet warnings to the prime minister; the annex has not been published. [cite:hm_toi_annex]

sections.h: Would Hamas Be What It Is?
sections.html:
No document answers this question, and the volume does not pretend to. What follows are the two readings the record supports, each labelled as an argument.

The first reading: the split and the separation made Hamas what it became. On this reading, Israel had cut Gaza off from the West Bank for years before 2007; after Hamas won the only election it contested, Israel, the United States and Europe cut its government off, and a US-backed plan to remove it by force was reported; and from 2018 Israeli governments let Qatari cash into Gaza on the reasoning, stated by Smotrich and reported of Netanyahu, that a strong Hamas kept the Palestinian Authority weak and a Palestinian state off the table. A Hamas ruling a sealed strip, funded with Israel's consent and facing no election, was the product. The Shin Bet's own summary named the quiet and the Qatari money among the conditions for October 7. [cite:hm_aj_separation] [cite:hm_dn_rose] [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich] [cite:hm_fdd_shinbet]

The second reading: Hamas made its own choices. On this reading, Hamas took Gaza by force in 2007, refused the conditions that would have ended its isolation, chose rockets and tunnels over the economy of the strip, and planned October 7 itself; Israel's separation measures answered real attacks, and the Qatari money, which Israel says it let in to prevent a humanitarian collapse, did not decide what Hamas did with its own budget. Its charter, its ideology and its armed wing predate every one of these policies. [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] [cite:hm_ynet_biglie] [cite:hm_avalon_charter] Part Six sets out the record of Hamas as its own actor. [scene:hm6_rule|Hamas as its own actor]

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: Hamas as Its Own Actor
chapters.intro: Part Five set out the policies of others that shaped Hamas. Part Six sets out what Hamas did with the power it had: how it ruled the people of Gaza, how it fired rockets at Israeli towns, and how it dealt with the states that funded it. Hamas is not only a product of other people's choices, and the record of its own is set out here as plainly as Israel's is elsewhere in this library.
chapters.outro: Part Six set out Hamas's own record. It ruled Gaza with arbitrary detention and torture, and arrested more than 1,000 people when Gazans protested in 2019. [cite:hm_972_hrw2012] [cite:hm_hrw_2019] It fired thousands of rockets at Israeli towns that rights groups called war crimes, and its leaders called the 2014 kidnapping of three teenagers a "heroic operation". [cite:hm_hrw_rockets2009] [cite:hm_npr_arouri] Iran armed and funded it; Qatar hosted and paid. [cite:hm_state_iran] [cite:hm_fdd_shinbet] Part Seven sets out October 7.

sections.h: How Hamas Ruled Gaza
sections.html:
From 2007 Hamas governed Gaza as a one-party authority. In 2012 Human Rights Watch documented arbitrary detention, torture of detainees and executions carried out on the basis of confessions obtained under torture, with no one held to account. [cite:hm_972_hrw2012] In March 2019, when thousands of Gazans protested against the cost of living under the slogan "We Want to Live", Hamas's forces broke up the protests; the Independent Commission for Human Rights, the Palestinian rights ombudsman, said more than 1,000 people were arrested. Hamas's own figures showed it had arrested 4,235 people between January 2018 and March 2019. The Commission received 213 complaints of torture and mistreatment by Hamas forces in that period. [cite:hm_hrw_2019]

The Palestinian Authority did the same in the West Bank: the Commission received 242 complaints of torture and mistreatment by its forces over the same period. Eric Goldstein of Human Rights Watch said the two were "bitterly divided, but unified in a common approach to crushing dissent." [cite:hm_hrw_2019]

sections.h: The Rockets
sections.html:
After the suicide bombings came rockets. Human Rights Watch counted more than 4,000 rockets fired from Gaza at Israel between 2001 and 2008. "None of these rockets can be reliably aimed," it wrote; fired at populated areas, they were inherently indiscriminate and their use was a war crime. Hamas's spokesman Abu Obeida had promised, "We will double the number of Israelis under fire." Khaled Mashaal called the rockets "a method and not the goal". Human Rights Watch found no apparent action by Hamas to prosecute those responsible. [cite:hm_hrw_rockets2009]

The pattern held. In the war of May 2021, rockets from Gaza killed 12 civilians in Israel, and one that fell short killed seven Palestinians in Jabaliya; Human Rights Watch again called the indiscriminate fire a war crime. Hamas rejected the report and said it was developing the ability to "accurately target Israeli military headquarters". [cite:hm_almon_hrw2021] Gaza, Documented sets out the wars of 2008 to 2021 and Israel's conduct in them, which rights groups also found unlawful. [scene:gz5_castlead|Cast Lead] [scene:gz5_2012_2014|2012 and 2014]

2014: The Kidnapping and the War

On 12 June 2014 three Israeli teenagers, Eyal Yifrach, Gilad Shaer and Naftali Fraenkel, were abducted while hitchhiking in the West Bank; their bodies were found on 30 June. Israel blamed two Hamas members from Hebron and arrested hundreds of Hamas members in the West Bank. On 2 July a Palestinian teenager, Mohammed Abu Khdeir, was abducted and burned alive in Jerusalem in revenge, and Israeli suspects were arrested. [cite:hm_wiki_teens2014] Hamas at first denied involvement. In August Saleh al-Arouri, a senior Hamas leader, told a conference in Turkey that the kidnapping was a "heroic operation" by its armed wing, while saying Hamas "did not have the intention at this time to ignite a large battle". [cite:hm_npr_arouri] Rockets from Gaza and an Israeli air and ground war followed; by the UN's count 2,251 Palestinians were killed, 1,462 of them civilians; on the Israeli side 67 soldiers and six civilians in Israel were killed. Israel's foreign ministry counted 2,125 Palestinian dead, about 36 percent of them civilians. [cite:gz_wiki_2014]

sections.h: Patrons, Not Masters
sections.html:
Hamas has taken money from states with different aims, and has not always done what they wanted. Iran, a Shia state, has armed and funded this Sunni movement through its Revolutionary Guards: in 2018 the US State Department said Iran gave "up to $100 million annually in combined support" to Palestinian groups including Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the PFLP-General Command, with training and weapons. [cite:hm_state_iran] Qatar hosted Hamas's political leaders and, from 2018, sent cash into Gaza with Israel's consent, as Part Five set out. [scene:hm5_qatar|The Qatari money] Israel's Shin Bet attributed Hamas's strength before October 7 largely "to the strategic buttress provided by Iran and the use of the funds that came in from Iran and Qatar". [cite:hm_fdd_shinbet]

Hamas also changed its words when it suited it. In 2017 it published a document of principles that spoke of a conflict with the Zionist project, not with Jews, and accepted a Palestinian state on the 1967 lines as a "formula of national consensus", without recognizing Israel or giving up armed struggle; it did not revoke the 1988 charter. Israel called it an attempt to fool the world. [cite:hm_jps_hroub2017] [cite:hm_cnn_2017doc] Part Two sets out both texts. [scene:hm2_charter|The charter]

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: October 7
chapters.intro: Part Seven sets out what Hamas did on 7 October 2023. It covers the plan Israel had held and dismissed, the attack and its toll, the crimes that independent investigators found, the failures Israel's own inquiries admitted, and the account Hamas gave of itself. Gaza, Documented sets out the day in full; this part places it in Hamas's history.
chapters.outro: Part Seven set out 7 October. Hamas's Qassam Brigades led an attack that killed 1,195 people, 815 of them civilians, and took 251 hostages; Human Rights Watch found the murder of civilians and the hostage-taking to be crimes against humanity, and a UN mission found reasonable grounds to believe rape occurred. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] [cite:gz_aj_patten] Hamas called the attack a response to the occupation and claimed it targeted only soldiers; the evidence shows otherwise. [cite:gz_aj_narrative] Israel's army admitted it had underestimated Hamas, having held its plan for a year. [cite:gz_pbs_idfprobe] [cite:gz_nyt_jericho] Warnings reached Netanyahu in general form, from his intelligence chiefs and from Egypt; he said no warning had been given at any stage, retracted it, and has not set up a state commission; that he knew and chose to let the attack happen is not established. [cite:hm_ih_4letters] [cite:hm_aj_deletedpost] [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026] Part Eight measures the two sides.

sections.h: The Attack
sections.html:
More than a year before 7 October, Israeli officials obtained a Hamas plan of about forty pages, code-named "Jericho Wall," which called for rocket barrages, drones to disable border cameras and machine guns, and gunmen crossing on paragliders, motorcycles and foot; they dismissed it as "aspirational." [cite:gz_nyt_jericho] On the morning of 7 October 2023 Hamas's Qassam Brigades, with at least four other armed groups, carried it out. By AFP's count, cited by Human Rights Watch, 1,195 people were killed, 815 of them civilians, in at least nineteen kibbutzim, five moshavim, the towns of Sderot and Ofakim, two music festivals and a beach; 251 civilians and members of the security forces were taken to Gaza. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] At the Nova festival alone, the army's own count was 378 killed and 44 taken hostage. [cite:gz_wiki_nova]

What investigators found. Human Rights Watch concluded that "the planned murder of civilians and the hostage-taking were crimes against humanity," that killing civilians and taking hostages were "central aims of the planned attack," and documented war crimes including wilful killing, mutilation of bodies and sexual violence. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] A UN mission led by Pramila Patten found "reasonable grounds to believe" that rape and gang rape occurred, and "clear and convincing information" that some hostages were subjected to sexual violence. [cite:gz_aj_patten] The UN's commission of inquiry found that forty Israeli children were killed that day and children were taken hostage, some of them alone. [cite:pr_un_coi2026]

Hamas's Account, and Israel's Failures

In January 2024 Hamas published a sixteen-page account, "Our Narrative," calling the attack "a necessary step and a normal response to confront all Israeli conspiracies against the Palestinian people," citing prisoners, settlements and the "Judaization" of the West Bank and Jerusalem, and saying its fighters "only targeted Israeli soldiers and people carrying weapons" and that many Israelis "were killed by the Israeli army and police due to their confusion." [cite:gz_aj_narrative] The investigations above found the opposite of its first claim: civilians were a central target. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] Some Israelis were killed by Israeli fire: the army's inquiry into Be'eri found that a tank fired on a house where hostages were held, and the army said that friendly-fire incidents occurred but "there were not many." [cite:gz_idf_beeri_probe] [cite:gz_pbs_idfprobe]

Israel's own army found that it had "underestimated" Hamas's capabilities and wrongly believed Hamas "was more interested in governing the territory than fighting Israel"; its chief of staff resigned. [cite:gz_pbs_idfprobe] As of October 2026 no state commission of inquiry had been set up. [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026]

The power ledger in Part Eight explains how so small a force could do so much on one day: a plan prepared over years, a border defended by an army that did not believe it would come, and a decision to kill civilians. [scene:hm8_money|The power ledger] Gaza, Documented follows what came after. [scene:gz6_attack|The attack, in full]

sections.h: What Netanyahu Knew
sections.html:
The question this section answers is narrow and grave: what did Israel's prime minister know before 7 October, and what has he said about it since? The warnings are set out here as the record gives them, with Netanyahu's own account beside each.

What the state held. More than a year before the attack, Israeli intelligence held Hamas's battle plan, "Jericho Wall," and judged it "aspirational"; in July 2023 a Unit 8200 analyst warned that Hamas was training to carry it out and was told to "wait patiently." [cite:gz_nyt_jericho] Those warnings were dismissed inside the military and intelligence services. The record does not show that the plan itself was put before Netanyahu as a warning of imminent attack.

What reached Netanyahu. Several warnings did reach him, and they were general rather than specific:

Between March and July 2023, Military Intelligence sent him four letters on how Israel's enemies saw the damage to its national cohesion during the fight over the judicial overhaul; the army confirmed them in May 2024 after a freedom-of-information suit. [cite:hm_ih_4letters] In July 2023 the Shin Bet chief, Ronen Bar, told him he was delivering "a warning of war," without a date or a place. [cite:hm_ynet_bar_records] Egypt's intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, urged a return to talks with Hamas in June 2023 and warned in September that Gaza could explode; according to The Wall Street Journal, citing Arab officials, he called Netanyahu directly days before the attack, though none of the warnings specified timing or scale. Netanyahu's office had denied any contact with Kamel before 7 October and did not answer the Journal's questions. [cite:hm_ih_egypt2026] According to Haaretz, drawing on a 2026 book by Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval and on three senior foreign officials, the UAE's president, Mohammed bin Zayed, warned Netanyahu in a call in late September 2023 that Sinwar was planning a major operation, and Netanyahu answered that any Hamas action would likely come in the West Bank; his office called the report "a total lie" and said the two had not spoken in that period. [cite:hm_wlos_mbz] On 1 October 2023, by Channel 12's account of the Shin Bet's internal inquiry, Bar asked Netanyahu to approve killing Yahya Sinwar, and Netanyahu preferred "quiet in return for quiet"; Netanyahu's office called that "a complete lie" and said it was Bar who recommended civilian benefits for Hamas in return for calm. [cite:hm_toi_bar_sinwar]

The night. At 3:03 a.m. on 7 October the Shin Bet issued an alert on "unusual preparations and the possibility of offensive intentions by Hamas"; Israeli SIM cards were being activated in Gaza and Hamas commanders were entering tunnels. Bar says he ordered the prime minister's military secretary to be updated at 5:15; Netanyahu was first called at 6:29, as the attack began. Bar has called the night's misjudgement "a Shin Bet failure"; who was responsible for the gap before Netanyahu was called is not answered by the public record. [cite:hm_ynet_bar_records] [cite:hm_toi_bar_sinwar]

What Netanyahu has said. On 28 October 2023 he wrote: "At no time and no stage was a warning given to Prime Minister Netanyahu regarding war intentions of Hamas," and blamed the security chiefs, who he said had judged Hamas deterred; after an outcry he deleted the post and apologized. [cite:hm_aj_deletedpost] In February 2026 his office published a 55-page document that blames Bar for not alerting him on the night and says he received no warning of "a war in Gaza"; the full transcripts of the meetings it quotes have not been released, and Bar has said he will sue him for defamation. [cite:hm_ynet_bar_records] Three years on, Netanyahu has not established the state commission of inquiry that could settle these questions under oath. [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026]

Knew, and Chose Not to Act?

The claim that Netanyahu knew the attack was coming and chose to let it happen is the strongest form of the charge, and the record does not establish it: the warnings that reached him did not give a date, a place or a scale, and the plan that did was dismissed by the professionals below him.

What the record does establish is serious enough. A government that held its enemy's battle plan, received repeated strategic warnings that its enemies saw it as divided and weak, was told by its security chief that war was coming, and pursued a policy of "quiet" financed by Qatari cash that, by Yedioth's account, he had been warned was reaching Hamas's military wing, was caught unprepared by an attack that killed about 1,200 people. [cite:gz_nyt_jericho] [cite:hm_ih_4letters] [cite:hm_fdd_shinbet] [cite:hm_jc_warned2026] Its prime minister first said no warning had been given at any stage, retracted that, and has since blamed his security chiefs while declining the one inquiry that could test his account under oath. Whether those people had to die is the question a state commission exists to answer; it has not been allowed to.

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: The Power Ledger
chapters.intro: Part Eight measures the two sides. Hamas and Israel are often described as two parties to a war, and in law they are; in resources they are not comparable, and this part sets the numbers side by side. It compares the economies of Israel and Gaza; Israel's military spending and the aid that supports it, from the United States above all; Hamas's own money, from taxes, Iran, Qatar and investments; and the weapons and fighters on each side. It then puts the gap into everyday terms, and ends with what the gap does not mean.
chapters.outro: Part Eight set the two sides side by side. Israel's economy was about $513 billion in 2023 and its military budget $46.5 billion in 2024; the United States commits $3.8 billion a year and gave at least $21.7 billion more in two years of war. [cite:hm_fred_ilgdp] [cite:hm_globes_sipri] [cite:hm_dn_mou] [cite:hm_an_costsofwar] Gaza's whole economy was about $2.7 billion a year before the war, and Hamas's military budget an estimated $100–350 million. [cite:hm_aspi_gazagdp] [cite:hm_nbc_money] Israel has a modern air force, a navy and, by estimate, nuclear weapons; Hamas had rockets, tunnels and 20,000 to 25,000 fighters. [cite:hm_almon_idf] [cite:hm_inss_arsenal] The gap did not stop Hamas from killing about 1,200 people on 7 October; it measures the forces that met afterwards. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7]

sections.h: Two Economies
sections.html:
Israel. By the World Bank's figures, Israel's economy produced $513 billion in 2023, the year the war began, $542 billion in 2024 and $611 billion in 2025. [cite:hm_fred_ilgdp] In 2024 it spent $46.5 billion on its military, by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute's count: 8.8 percent of its economy, a rise of 65 percent in a year and the second-highest share in the world after Ukraine. [cite:hm_globes_sipri]

Gaza. In the three years before the war, Gaza's economy produced an average of about $670 million of value a quarter, by UNCTAD's estimate: roughly $2.7 billion a year, for about two million people. By the first quarter of 2024 its activity was 86 percent below that level. [cite:hm_aspi_gazagdp] By 2025, Palestinian official statistics put Gaza's real output at 84 percent below 2023, and its unemployment at 78 percent. [cite:hm_pcbs_2025]

UNCTAD's later figures make the gap concrete per person. In 2024 Gaza's economy shrank by 83 percent to $362 million, and its output per person fell to $161 for the year, less than 50 cents a day; UNCTAD put the cost of rebuilding at more than $70 billion and said recovery to pre-war conditions would take decades. [cite:hm_unctad_2025] Israel's economy that year was worth about $542 billion, and its arms industry alone exported a record $14.8 billion of weapons and systems, about forty times Gaza's whole economy. [cite:hm_fred_ilgdp] [cite:hm_globes_exports]

The Aid

From the United States. Under a memorandum signed in September 2016, the United States committed $38 billion in military aid to Israel for the ten years from 2019 to 2028: $3.3 billion a year in grants to buy weapons and $500 million a year for missile defence, $3.8 billion in all. [cite:hm_dn_mou] On top of that, Brown University's Costs of War project and the Quincy Institute counted at least $21.7 billion in American military aid to Israel in the two years after 7 October 2023, $17.9 billion of it in the first year, and between $9.65 and $12 billion more spent on American military operations in the region. [cite:hm_an_costsofwar]

From elsewhere. Between 2019 and 2023, by SIPRI's count, the United States supplied 69 percent of Israel's arms imports and Germany about 30 percent. [cite:hm_stripes_sipri] Israel is also a major exporter: its defence exports reached $14.8 billion in 2024, more than half of them to Europe and about half of them air-defence systems. [cite:hm_globes_exports]

Hamas's money. Hamas does not publish a budget, and the figures are estimates. Israeli and Palestinian sources cited by NBC News put its military spending at $100 million to $350 million a year. A former US Treasury official, Matthew Levitt, estimated its income from taxes, fees and smuggling in Gaza at $300 million to $450 million a year. The US State Department has put Iran's support at about $100 million a year. Qatar gave $1.49 billion in aid to Gaza between 2012 and 2021, for salaries, fuel and poor families, and denies funding Hamas. The US Treasury has described a Hamas investment portfolio of about $500 million in companies and property abroad. Hamas says it keeps its civil and military funds separate; Western governments and former Israeli officials say it does not. [cite:hm_nbc_money]

sections.h: Arms and Fighters
sections.html:
Israel. The International Institute for Strategic Studies counts 169,500 active personnel in Israel's forces and 465,000 reservists; in January 2024, 295,000 reservists had been called up. Israel's air force has 316 combat aircraft, 175 of them able to fly more than 1,000 kilometres; its navy has five submarines. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimates that Israel holds about 90 nuclear warheads. [cite:hm_almon_idf]

Hamas. Israel's Institute for National Security Studies estimated that at the start of the war Hamas had 18,000 to 30,000 rockets and inaccurate missiles, most of them short-range; 20,000 to 25,000 fighters organized in battalions; 500 to 700 kilometres of tunnels; anti-tank missiles; and an unknown number of drones. Unlike Israel, it has no air force and no navy. [cite:hm_inss_arsenal] [cite:hm_almon_idf]

The Gap, in Everyday Terms

The figures above are hard to hold in the mind; set against one another, they become simpler. (The comparisons below are this book's own arithmetic from the sources cited.)

What the Gap Does Not Mean

Asymmetry of resources is not the same as an inability to do harm. With its tunnels, rockets and fighters, Hamas carried out the attack of 7 October 2023, which killed about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and took 251 hostages; Part Seven sets it out. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] [scene:hm7_attack|October 7] Nor does the asymmetry settle the questions of law: the laws of war bind both sides regardless of strength. What the numbers do show is the scale of the two forces that met in Gaza after 7 October: a state ranked twelfth in the world for military spending in 2024, supplied by the United States and Germany, against an armed movement with no air force, ruling a territory whose whole economy was smaller than the American aid its enemy received each year. Part Nine follows what the war did to it.

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: After the War
chapters.intro: Part Nine follows Hamas after the war it started. It sets out the leaders Israel killed, the ceasefire of October 2025 and the plan behind it, the long negotiation over Hamas's weapons, and where things stood in October 2026: an agreement on disarmament that neither side had carried out, and an army holding most of Gaza.
chapters.outro: Part Nine followed Hamas after the war. Israel killed its leaders from Haniyeh to Sinwar; a ceasefire in October 2025 brought the hostages home and a plan for Hamas to disarm and give up power. [cite:gz_almon_hamasleaders] [cite:gz_gn_20points] By July 2026 Hamas had agreed to a disarmament roadmap and to step down from governing, on condition that Israel withdraw; Israel insisted on disarmament first, and by September said Hamas was retaking its weapons, while holding most of Gaza. [cite:hm_aj_disarm2026] [cite:hm_jp_noWithdraw] [cite:hm_jp_reclaim] Part Ten tests the claim that Hamas has been the reason for everything.

sections.h: The Leaders
sections.html:
Israel killed most of the men who led Hamas into the war. Its political leader, Ismail Haniyeh, was killed in Tehran in July 2024; Yahya Sinwar, its leader in Gaza, was killed by Israeli troops in Gaza in October 2024; Israel said it had killed the military commander Mohammed Deif in July 2024, his deputy Marwan Issa in March 2024, and Sinwar's brother Mohammad in May 2025. Khalil al-Hayya, based in Qatar, became the most prominent of those left. [cite:gz_almon_hamasleaders]

The Ceasefire and the Weapons

The ceasefire of October 2025 rested on a twenty-point American plan: Hamas's tunnels and weapons to be dismantled under independent monitoring, amnesty for members who gave up their arms, Gaza run by a Palestinian committee under a Board of Peace chaired by President Trump, and Israeli troops to withdraw in stages as an international force took their place. [cite:gz_gn_20points] Hamas agreed to release all the hostages and to hand Gaza's administration to independent technocrats, without saying whether it would disarm. [cite:gz_almon_hamas_plan] The last hostage's body was recovered in January 2026. A National Committee for the Administration of Gaza was formed that month; Hamas rejected a disarmament plan in April 2026 and announced in July that its civil administration would step down. [cite:hm_wiki_peaceplan]

On 30 July 2026 the Board of Peace announced an agreement on disarmament. Hamas's weapons were to be inventoried and held only by a Palestinian National Committee, never handed to Israel; heavy weapons, workshops, depots and tunnels were to go first; and Israeli troops were to withdraw stage by stage as each step was verified. Hamas's negotiator Ghazi Hamad said it would take no step if Israel did not withdraw. [cite:hm_aj_disarm2026] An Israeli diplomatic source said Israel required full disarmament before any withdrawal: "There will be no Israeli withdrawal from the Yellow Line." [cite:hm_jp_noWithdraw] In September the army said Hamas was taking weapons back out of its depots and struck several of them; Netanyahu said Israel held 60 percent of the Strip. [cite:hm_jp_reclaim]

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: Always Hamas
chapters.intro: Part Ten tests a question many people ask: how can a movement this small still be the reason for everything? For two years Israel named Hamas as the cause of strikes, closures and refusals, and as the obstacle to ending the war. This part sets the claim against the record. It compares the forces; counts the Hamas members killed, detained and charged, and the hostages rescued; asks how a state with Israel's surveillance failed to finish its enemy; checks the claims made in Hamas's name against what was later found, in both directions; and sets out the documented incentives Israel's prime minister had to keep the war going, beside the military explanations his own generals and American officials gave. Where the evidence ends and argument begins, the part says so.
chapters.outro: Part Ten tested the claim that Hamas has been the reason for everything. Israel's mobilized forces alone outnumbered Hamas's fighters about fourteen to eighteen to one, yet by its own leaked database, which the army disputes, named fighters were about 17 percent of the dead and about one in four detainees, and only eight hostages were rescued alive while some 160 came home through deals. [cite:hm_adn_360k] [cite:hm_aj_83pct] [cite:hm_guard_detainees] [cite:hm_ynet_rescued8] Several claims made in Hamas's name did not hold up when examined, while at least one claim against Israel also failed. [cite:hm_es_wapo_shifa] [cite:hm_un_oios] [cite:hm_mm_hrw_ahli] The documented incentives to keep the war going, a coalition that threatened to fall, a trial and no inquiry, sit beside the military explanation that Hamas was an idea and an underground force that could not simply be destroyed. [cite:hm_toi_nyt_prolonged] [cite:hm_ynet_hagari] Part Eleven follows one minister through the war's broken ceasefires.

sections.h: The Two Forces
sections.html:
Before the war, Israel's Institute for National Security Studies estimated Hamas's armed strength at 20,000 to 25,000 fighters, with 18,000 to 30,000 mostly short-range rockets and 500 to 700 kilometres of tunnels. [cite:hm_inss_arsenal] Israel had about 169,500 active troops and 465,000 reservists. [cite:hm_almon_idf] Within 48 hours of 7 October it called up 300,000 reservists, and about 360,000 in all, some 4 percent of its population; its army spokesman said it had "never mobilized so many reservists so quickly." [cite:hm_adn_360k] On the ground, then, Israel's mobilized reserve alone outnumbered Hamas's fighters by about fourteen to eighteen to one, before counting its air force, navy, armour and intelligence services. Part Eight sets out the money behind each side. [scene:hm8_money|The power ledger]

The Ledger

Killed. Israel's claims about how many Hamas fighters it killed were large and early. In May 2024 Netanyahu said: "Fourteen thousand have been killed, combatants, and probably around 16,000 civilians." [cite:hm_pa_netanyahu14k] A year later, Israel's own military intelligence database, leaked to The Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call, listed 8,900 Hamas and Islamic Jihad fighters as confirmed or probably dead by May 2025, against at least 53,000 Palestinians killed in the same period: named fighters were about 17 percent of the dead. The army said the figures in the reporting were "incorrect" without saying which. [cite:hm_aj_83pct] In January 2026 a senior Israeli military official, speaking unnamed to reporters, said the army estimated about 70,000 dead and at least 22,000 combatants killed; the army said the report did "not reflect official IDF data." [cite:pr_toi_idf70k] [cite:hm_jw_idf70k]

Replaced. In January 2025 Secretary of State Antony Blinken said Hamas had recruited almost as many new fighters as it had lost, and that it could not be defeated by "a military campaign alone." [cite:hm_aj_blinken2025]

Detained. Israel detained thousands of people from Gaza, most held without charge under its unlawful-combatants law. The same intelligence database, according to The Guardian, identified only about one in four of them as fighters. The army's spokesman called the report "based on numerous inaccuracies" and said most of those held were found after interrogation to be involved in terrorist activity, and the rest were released. [cite:hm_guard_detainees] [cite:hm_yh_idfrebut]

Rescued. Of the 251 hostages taken on 7 October, eight were rescued alive by military operations: one soldier in October 2023, two in Rafah in February 2024, four at Nuseirat in June 2024, and one from a tunnel in August 2024. [cite:hm_ynet_rescued8] The Nuseirat rescue killed at least 274 Palestinians, by the health ministry's count. [cite:hm_eun_nuseirat] Some 160 others came home alive because Hamas released them, almost all under negotiated deals: in November 2023, in early 2025 and in October 2025. [cite:hm_s24_hostages]

The ledger does not mean Hamas was weak where it mattered most: it killed about 1,200 people on 7 October, and its tunnels and its fighters' ability to vanish among two million civilians are the reasons Israel's commanders gave for the war's length. [scene:hm7_attack|October 7] It does mean that, by Israel's own internal count, the great majority of the people killed in Gaza were not named Hamas fighters, and that the hostages came home mainly through negotiation with Hamas, not through its defeat.

sections.h: The Surveillance Paradox
sections.html:
Israel's signals-intelligence service, Unit 8200, is counted among the most capable in the world, and the United States shares raw intercepts with it. [scene:ow4_memorandum|The One-Way Mirror: the NSA memorandum] In this war it used computerized target-generation systems. According to six Israeli intelligence officers interviewed by +972 Magazine and Local Call, a system called Lavender marked as many as 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants, with an error rate its operators put at about 10 percent; officers spent about 20 seconds checking each name, and a companion system, "Where's Daddy?", flagged when a target entered his family home. The army said such systems are "auxiliary tools" for its officers and denied much of the account. [cite:hm_972_lavender] Palantir signed a strategic partnership with Israel's Defense Ministry in January 2024, though it denies any role in Lavender, and Israeli reporting says Unit 8200 declined its services. [cite:ow9_globes_palantir] [cite:ow9_pal_unletter]

Against that capability stand three facts from the record. The first is October 7 itself: Israel held Hamas's attack plan more than a year before and judged it aspirational. [cite:gz_nyt_jericho] The second is how the war's most-wanted man was found. Yahya Sinwar was killed in October 2024 by troops on a routine patrol in Rafah who did not know he was there; Israel had known he was hiding in that district but not his exact location. [cite:hm_wiki_sinwar] The third is the hostages: in two years of war, military intelligence located and freed eight of them alive. [cite:hm_ynet_rescued8]

In Lebanon the same state showed what its intelligence could do against an enemy it had penetrated. Between the pager explosions of 17 September 2024 and the strike that killed Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September, Israel removed much of Hezbollah's chain of command in about ten days. [cite:hm_ns_hezbollah] Two years of war in Gaza did not do the same to Hamas: by September 2026 IDF sources said Hamas was taking weapons back out of its depots. [cite:hm_jp_reclaim]

The record allows more than one explanation. Israel's commanders pointed to Gaza's tunnels, 500 to 700 kilometres by the Institute for National Security Studies' estimate, and to an enemy fighting among two million civilians and holding hostages whose presence constrained every operation. [cite:hm_inss_arsenal] Critics read the same facts differently: a system built to generate targets quickly will produce many deaths and few decisive results against an enemy underground. Both explanations fit the evidence; neither is proved by it.

sections.h: Claims Made in Hamas's Name
sections.html:
Throughout the war, Israel justified strikes, raids and policies by naming Hamas: a hospital was a command centre, aid staff were members, the casualty count was Hamas propaganda. Some of these claims were later borne out in part, some were not, and in at least one major case the Hamas-run authorities' own claim proved wrong. The record is set out in both directions.

Al-Shifa hospital, November 2023. Israel said Hamas ran a command centre beneath Gaza's largest hospital, and the United States backed the assessment; Israel released video of a tunnel shaft and of hostages brought into the hospital on 7 October. A Washington Post analysis of the material Israel released found that it "falls short of showing that Hamas had been using the hospital as a command and control center": Israel exposed a tunnel, but none of the five buildings it named appeared connected to it, and the underground rooms showed no immediate sign of military use. [cite:hm_es_wapo_shifa]

UNRWA, January–August 2024. Israel accused 12, then 19, staff of the UN relief agency of taking part in 7 October, and several donor states suspended funding. The UN's internal investigators found that nine "may have been involved," that the evidence was insufficient for nine others and that there was none for one; they could not independently authenticate most of what Israel supplied. [cite:hm_un_oios]

The death toll. Israeli officials dismissed the count from Gaza's "Hamas-run" health ministry for most of the war; in January 2026 a senior military official, unnamed, said the army estimated about 70,000 dead, though the army said that did not reflect official data. [cite:pr_toi_idf70k] [cite:hm_jw_idf70k] PRESS sets out the counting. [scene:pr1_lists|The count]

Journalists. Israel said some journalists it killed were members of armed groups; PRESS sets out each case, the evidence offered and the press-freedom groups' findings, including their own removals of some names. [scene:pr7_law|PRESS: "Journalists are not terrorists"]

Al-Ahli hospital, October 2023: a claim against Israel that failed. Gaza's health ministry said an Israeli strike on the al-Ahli hospital killed 471 people. Human Rights Watch found the blast "resulted from an apparent rocket-propelled munition, such as those commonly used by Palestinian armed groups," and called the reported toll unusually high for the damage. [cite:hm_mm_hrw_ahli]

The pattern the table shows is not that every claim about Hamas was false. It is that the word "Hamas" was used to justify actions at a scale the evidence, when it came, often did not support, while the same scrutiny also caught false claims made against Israel.

sections.h: Why the War Lasted
sections.html:
Israel's government stated its war aims from the start: to destroy Hamas's military and governing capabilities and to bring every hostage home. [cite:hm_ynet_hagari] [cite:hm_gp_bengvir] The record also documents incentives its prime minister had to keep the war going that had little to do with Hamas.

The coalition. Netanyahu's government depended on parties that opposed ending the war. Itamar Ben-Gvir quit in January 2025 over the ceasefire and announced his return on 18 March 2025, the day Israel resumed its bombardment with strikes that killed more than 400 people, which strengthened the coalition before a budget vote it needed to survive; Netanyahu called the strikes "only the beginning." [cite:hm_gp_bengvir] In July 2025 a New York Times investigation, based on more than 110 officials and government records, reported that Netanyahu had shelved a truce that would have freed at least 30 hostages after Bezalel Smotrich threatened to bring down the government, and had derailed Saudi normalization, which required ending the war, in the face of Ben-Gvir's opposition. His office said the report "defames Israel"; the Times said the statement "does not refute the facts." [cite:hm_toi_nyt_prolonged]

The courts at home. Netanyahu has been on trial for bribery, fraud and breach of trust since 2020. His testimony was repeatedly delayed by his official duties, and in April 2026 he asked for another delay, citing classified security and diplomatic reasons; and in November 2025 he asked President Isaac Herzog for a pardon, citing the need for national unity after two years of war. [cite:hm_toi_trialdelay] [cite:hm_npr_pardon] Three years after 7 October, his government had not set up a state commission of inquiry into the failure; Netanyahu says he prefers a commission with equal numbers of coalition and opposition members. [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026]

The International Criminal Court. The court issued a warrant for Netanyahu in November 2024 and in October 2025 refused Israel leave to appeal, while Israel's challenge to its jurisdiction remained pending. Netanyahu's office said it "rejects with disgust the absurd and false actions." [cite:pr_bc_icc2024] [cite:gz_toi_icc2025] [cite:hm_jc_iccfreeze] A continuing war does not suspend that warrant, and Israel does not accept the court's jurisdiction. What the war does supply is the case Israel makes to the court and to the world: that its conduct is self-defence against Hamas, which hides among civilians. That argument depends on Hamas remaining the reason.

Two Readings

The first reading: Hamas became the permanent justification. On this reading, a government whose survival depended on continuing the war kept its aim, total victory over an enemy its own army spokesman said could not be destroyed (the army later said he meant Hamas as an ideology), deliberately out of reach; it shelved deals under coalition threat, resumed the war when its coalition needed it, and used Hamas's name to justify strikes and policies the evidence did not support, while its prime minister's trial waited and no inquiry into 7 October was held. [cite:hm_toi_nyt_prolonged] [cite:hm_ynet_hagari] [cite:hm_gp_bengvir] [cite:hm_aj_83pct]

The second reading: Hamas was the reason. On this reading, Hamas carried out an attack that killed about 1,200 people in a day, held hostages for two years, fought from tunnels beneath a dense civilian population, and replaced its losses, as American officials acknowledged; no army has quickly destroyed an armed movement in those conditions, and Israel's government denies that politics drove its decisions. [cite:hm_aj_blinken2025] [cite:hm_inss_arsenal] [cite:hm_toi_nyt_prolonged]

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: Ben-Gvir and the Broken Ceasefires
chapters.intro: Part Eleven follows one minister through the war's ceasefires. Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, opposed the deals that brought hostages home, in 2023 and 2025, said on the record that he had used his party's leverage to stop such deals "time and again," left the government when a ceasefire began and returned the day the bombing resumed. This part sets out who he is, how Benjamin Netanyahu brought him into government and came to depend on him, how each truce ended according to both sides, and how the language used about Hamas compares with the record of its strength and of the aid that reached Israel while the war went on.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven followed Ben-Gvir through the war. Netanyahu brought him into the Knesset in 2021 and gave him the police in 2022; he said in January 2025 that his party's strength had prevented a hostage deal "time and again"; he quit when the ceasefire began and returned the day the bombing resumed; and he voted against the deal that freed the last living hostages. [cite:hm_wiki_otzma] [cite:hm_jta_coalition2022] [cite:hm_ynet_bg_foiled] [cite:hm_gp_bengvir] [cite:hm_na_bg_oct2025] Each truce ended with Hamas named as the cause, while the force sent against it, and the American aid behind that force, were many times larger. [cite:hm_wiki_jan2025cf] [cite:hm_an_costsofwar] Part Twelve sets out what is settled, contested and open.

sections.h: Who Ben-Gvir Is
sections.html:
Itamar Ben-Gvir came out of the Kach movement of Rabbi Meir Kahane, which Israel outlawed and the United States listed as a terrorist organization from 1997 until 2022; [cite:hm_aj_kach2022] he was its youth coordinator. Weeks before Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin's assassination in 1995, he appeared on television holding an emblem taken from Rabin's car and said: "We got to his car, and we'll get to him too." He was later convicted of incitement to racism and of support for a terrorist organization, and for years kept on his wall a photograph of Baruch Goldstein, who murdered 29 Muslim worshippers in Hebron in 1994, removing it in January 2020 as he sought an electoral alliance with Naftali Bennett. [cite:hm_jvl_bengvir] [cite:hm_toi_goldstein2020] The West Bank volume sets out Hebron and its settlers. [scene:wb5_hebron|Hebron]

How Netanyahu Brought Him In

Ben-Gvir's road to power ran through Netanyahu. In February 2019 Netanyahu pressed for a joint list that included Ben-Gvir's party, Otzma Yehudit; AIPAC, the leading pro-Israel lobby in Washington, said it would not meet "members of this racist and reprehensible party." In February 2021 a joint list of Otzma and the Religious Zionist Party, "orchestrated by" Netanyahu, brought Ben-Gvir into the Knesset; in 2022 Netanyahu urged the far-right lists to run together again so their votes would not be lost. [cite:hm_wiki_otzma] In November 2022 the joint far-right list won 14 seats, the third-largest party. [cite:hm_jvl_bengvir] On 25 November 2022 Netanyahu's Likud signed a coalition deal giving Ben-Gvir an expanded Ministry of National Security with control of the police and of the Border Police in the West Bank. [cite:hm_jta_coalition2022]

The dependence ran both ways. Netanyahu, on trial since 2020, needed Ben-Gvir's seats for his majority; Ben-Gvir needed Netanyahu for the ministry and its powers. [cite:hm_toi_trialdelay] [cite:hm_gp_bengvir] Part Ten set out what the New York Times reported that dependence produced in the war: a truce shelved under coalition threat. [scene:hm11_incentives|Why the war lasted]

sections.h: Four Truces
sections.html:
November 2023. The first truce began on 24 November as a four-day pause and was extended twice. [cite:hm_aj_truce_ext1] [cite:hm_aj_truce_ext2] Ben-Gvir's ministers voted against the deal, and he urged others to do the same. [cite:hm_toi_bg_nov2023] It ended on 1 December when talks on a further extension failed: Hamas did not hand over a list of ten more hostages for another day of calm and fired rockets, and Israel resumed its campaign, saying it was "committed to achieving the goals of the war." About 137 hostages were still in Gaza. Hamas said it had offered to release more hostages, including older people, and called the resumption "a prior decision to resume the criminal aggression." [cite:hm_jw_truce2023] [cite:hm_salon_truce]

2024: the deals that did not happen. Through 2024 a hostage deal was repeatedly negotiated and not concluded. In September 2024 Israel recovered the bodies of six hostages, among them Hersh Goldberg-Polin, whom its army said Hamas had killed shortly before troops arrived. The Hostages Families Forum said that "were it not for the delays, sabotage, and excuses" they would likely still be alive; Netanyahu said: "whoever murders hostages doesn't want a deal." [cite:hm_katv_six] In January 2025 Ben-Gvir described his own role in that year, in a post on X: "In the past year, through our political strength, we succeeded in preventing such a deal from being made, time and again." The opposition leader, Yair Lapid, said this showed Netanyahu had blocked releases for political reasons; Netanyahu had denied rejecting deals for political reasons, and Secretary of State Blinken said Hamas had repeatedly failed to conclude deals it should have. [cite:hm_ynet_bg_foiled]

January–March 2025. The second ceasefire, in three phases, took effect on 19 January after a delay of about three hours, which Israel blamed on Hamas's failure to provide the hostages' names; Israeli strikes killed 19 people in those hours. Ben-Gvir quit the government in protest. On 1 March Hamas rejected an Israeli proposal to extend the first phase and demanded the second phase as agreed, which required Israel's withdrawal and a permanent calm; Israel then endorsed an American plan to extend the truce through Ramadan and Passover with half the remaining hostages released at once. On 2 March Israel stopped all aid entering Gaza, which Egypt, Qatar and the UN called a violation, and on 9 March it cut the electricity supply. On 18 March it resumed the war, citing Hamas's refusal to release hostages; by then reports submitted to the UN listed about 1,000 ceasefire violations attributed to Israel. [cite:hm_wiki_jan2025cf] Ben-Gvir announced his return the same day, strengthening the coalition before its budget vote. [cite:hm_gp_bengvir]

October 2025 onward. The third ceasefire, under President Trump's plan, brought the last 20 living hostages home on 13 October. Ben-Gvir voted against its first phase and threatened to quit if Hamas was not "dismantled politically and militarily," saying his party "will not be part of a national defeat and eternal disgrace." [cite:hm_na_bg_oct2025] The ceasefire held in name only: by February 2026 Gaza's health ministry counted more than 530 Palestinians killed since it began, and Israel's army four of its soldiers; Israel described its strikes as responses to Hamas violations. [cite:hm_npr_feb2026] Part Nine follows the disarmament deadlock that followed. [scene:hm9_after|After the war]

The record does not show that Ben-Gvir alone broke these ceasefires; Hamas's own conduct, the government as a whole and the prime minister bear on each. It does show, in his own words, that he counted the prevention of hostage deals as an achievement of his political strength, and that in 2025 he left the government when a ceasefire began and returned when the bombing resumed.

sections.h: The Language of Threat, and the Record
sections.html:
As the ground invasion began in late October 2023, Netanyahu told Israelis: "Remember what Amalek did to you," invoking the biblical enemy the Israelites were commanded to destroy. South Africa cited the phrase at the International Court of Justice as evidence of genocidal intent; Netanyahu's office called the charge "false and preposterous" and said it reflected "deep historical ignorance," and Israel's counsel at the court said the full quotation identified Amalek with Hamas. [cite:hm_na_amalek] [cite:hm_jta_amalek] Throughout the war, Hamas was presented as the reason for each strike and each refusal, as Part Ten set out. [scene:hm11_claims|Claims made in Hamas's name]

The record of capacity runs the other way. Hamas had an estimated 20,000 to 25,000 fighters before the war; Israel mobilized 360,000 reservists in days, on top of 169,500 active troops. [cite:hm_inss_arsenal] [cite:hm_adn_360k] [cite:hm_almon_idf] Israel spent $46.5 billion on its military in 2024, a wartime figure; Hamas's whole military budget was estimated at $100 million to $350 million a year. [cite:hm_globes_sipri] [cite:hm_nbc_money] And while the war went on, the aid did not stop: the United States provided at least $21.7 billion in military aid in the two years after 7 October, a total that includes funding under the $3.8-billion-a-year agreement of 2016. [cite:hm_an_costsofwar] [cite:hm_cow_hartung] [cite:hm_dn_mou] The One-Way Mirror sets out how that aid moves. [scene:ow8_pace|The One-Way Mirror: the pace since October 2023]

Two Readings

The first reading: the threat was inflated. On this reading, a movement that Israel outnumbered more than ten to one and outspent more than a hundred to one was presented in the language of an existential enemy because that language justified the scale of the war, the closures and the aid, and because a government that depended on ministers like Ben-Gvir had reasons to keep the war going; the gap between the rhetoric and the record is itself the finding. [cite:hm_na_amalek] [cite:hm_ynet_bg_foiled] [cite:hm_toi_nyt_prolonged]

The second reading: the threat was real. On this reading, Hamas killed about 1,200 people in a single day and took 251 hostages; the threat to Israelis is measured by what an enemy has done and intends, not by the size of its budget; and Israel's government denies that politics or Ben-Gvir's demands determined its decisions. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] [cite:hm_ynet_bg_foiled]

The record settles the asymmetry, the aid and Ben-Gvir's own words. Whether the language of threat was dishonest or sincere is a judgement about intent, which documents rarely prove; the reader has the evidence for both.

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: Settled, Contested and Open
chapters.intro: The last part takes the volume's findings in three groups: what the record settles, what it leaves in dispute between documented positions, and what is still open as of October 2026. It ends with the answers the record gives to the questions this volume set out to ask.
chapters.outro: This volume set out the record of Hamas from the founding of the Muslim Brotherhood in 1928 to the unfinished disarmament of 2026: a movement older than Israel that took up arms against the occupation in 1987, killed civilians by bomb and rocket, won an election, seized Gaza and ruled it harshly, and was shaped by Israeli policies of separation and, from 2018, by Qatari money Israel let in. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007] [cite:hm_avalon_charter] [cite:hm_fdd_shinbet] Its attack of 7 October 2023 began a war fought between two powers whose economies differed by a factor of about 190. [cite:hm_fred_ilgdp] [cite:hm_aspi_gazagdp]

sections.h: What the Record Settles
sections.html:
The Muslim Brotherhood, the movement Hamas calls its parent, was founded in Egypt in 1928 and had branches in Gaza in the 1940s, before the State of Israel existed. [cite:hm_tamimi_2007] Israel licensed the Brotherhood's charity network in Gaza in 1979 and largely left it alone while it fought the PLO; some of the officials responsible later called that a mistake. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] Hamas was founded in December 1987, in the first weeks of the uprising against twenty years of occupation, and its 1988 charter combined a claim to all of Palestine with antisemitic conspiracy theory. [cite:hm_avalon_charter]

From 1994 Hamas carried out suicide bombings against Israeli civilians, and from 2001 it fired thousands of rockets at Israeli towns; Human Rights Watch called the bombings crimes against humanity and the rockets war crimes. [cite:hm_wiki_afula] [cite:hm_hrw_erased] [cite:hm_hrw_rockets2009] It won the 2006 election, took Gaza by force in 2007, and ruled it with arbitrary detention and torture. [cite:hm_wiki_2006elect] [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007] [cite:hm_hrw_2019] Israel restricted movement between Gaza and the West Bank from 1991 and blockaded Gaza from 2007, and from 2018 let Qatari cash into the strip, some of which, by the Shin Bet's account, reached Hamas's military build-up. [cite:hm_aj_separation] [cite:gz_un_hostile2007] [cite:hm_fdd_shinbet]

On 7 October 2023 Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in Israel, most of them civilians, and took 251 hostages; the war that followed killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza by the health ministry's count. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [scene:hm7_attack|October 7] [scene:pr1_lists|The count] The two sides were never close to equal: Israel's economy was roughly 190 times the size of Gaza's before the war, and its military budget in 2024 was more than a hundred times Hamas's highest estimated military spending. [cite:hm_fred_ilgdp] [cite:hm_aspi_gazagdp] [cite:hm_globes_sipri] [cite:hm_nbc_money] [scene:hm8_money|The power ledger]

sections.h: What Is Contested
sections.html:
Whether Israel "created" Hamas. Israeli officials who served in Gaza disagree: one called Hamas "Israel's creation", another said Israel never financed or armed it. The record shows licensing and tolerance of a charity network, not the creation of an armed movement. [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] [cite:hm_intercept_2018]

Why the Qatari money flowed. Smotrich's 2015 statement and the reported 2019 Netanyahu remark tie it to keeping the Palestinians divided; Netanyahu calls that "a big lie" and says the money prevented a humanitarian collapse. [cite:wb_wiki_smotrich] [cite:gz_harkov_2019] [cite:hm_ynet_biglie]

What happened in June 2007. Fatah calls it a Hamas coup; Vanity Fair reported a US plan to remove Hamas by force, which the State Department called "absurd". [cite:hm_dn_rose] [cite:gz_wiki_battle2007]

Whether the 2017 document changed Hamas. Scholars such as Khaled Hroub read it as a real shift; Israel called it an attempt to fool the world, and the 1988 charter was never revoked. [cite:hm_jps_hroub2017] [cite:hm_cnn_2017doc]

What Is Still Open

As of October 2026, Hamas and the Board of Peace had agreed a disarmament plan that neither Hamas nor Israel had carried out; Israel held most of Gaza and said it would not withdraw until Hamas disarmed. [cite:hm_aj_disarm2026] [cite:hm_jp_noWithdraw] [cite:hm_jp_reclaim] Israel had held no state commission of inquiry into October 7. [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026] No Palestinian national election had been held for twenty years. [cite:hm_aj_2021coup]

The Questions This Volume Asked

books.title: The Iran Architecture
books.subtitle: Allies, Enemies and the Bomb That Never Came, 1948–2026
books.intro:
This volume is about Israel and Iran: how two states that were quiet allies for three decades became the region's central enmity, and how that enmity drew the United States into two wars. It was written to answer direct questions. How long has Benjamin Netanyahu been warning that Iran is about to have a bomb, and what happened each time? What did other Israeli leaders, and Israel's own intelligence chiefs, say? Does Iran want a war with the United States? What does Israel want from Iran, and why Iran? And how does a state that recognises its Jewish community in its constitution and reserves it a seat in parliament end up as the target of the Jewish state's longest campaign?

The record answers some of these questions and not others. It shows that Iran recognised Israel de facto in 1950, sold it oil through a pipeline the two built together, and bought Israeli arms, and that Israel kept selling arms to the Islamic Republic after 1979, including the missiles of the Iran-Contra affair. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel] [cite:ir1_wiki_eapc] [cite:ir2_walsh18] It shows Iran's constitution recognising its Jews, its census counting fewer than ten thousand of them, and the same state executing a Jewish leader in 1979 and hosting a conference that questioned the Holocaust. [cite:ir3_const_en] [cite:ir3_afp_census2012] It shows Iran enriching uranium to 60 percent while Israel holds an undeclared arsenal outside the treaty Iran signed. [cite:ir4_ap_may2025] [cite:ir4_fas_israel] It sets Netanyahu's dated warnings, from 1992 to 2026, beside what followed, including his own conditions and the US intelligence assessments that contradicted him. [cite:ir5_li_un2012] [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] And it states Iran's own record plainly: its leaders' calls for Israel's end, the armed groups it funds, its plots against Americans, and its repression at home. [cite:ir9_cnn_25yrs] [cite:ir9_doj_arbabsiar]

It ends with the wars of June 2025 and of 2026, the American bill, and a verdict on three claims tested across the volume: that the warnings were false alarms, that Iran does not want war with America, and that America was dragged in. [cite:ir10_bd_hammer] [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [scene:ir15_record|Settled, Contested and Open] Every motive the record does not document is labelled as argument. It is a companion to The Hamas Architecture, The Hezbollah Architecture and The One-Way Mirror.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Alliance
chapters.intro: Part One covers the three decades in which Israel and Iran were allies in all but name. It begins with Iran's vote against the partition of Palestine and its quiet recognition of Israel in 1950, and with the coup of 1953, which the CIA has since acknowledged directing and which restored a Shah who made the alliance possible. It follows the alliance through Israel's search for non-Arab friends on the region's edge, the intelligence partnership between Mossad and the Shah's security service, SAVAK, the route by which Iraqi Jews reached Israel through Iran, the trade, advisers and arms, and a secret missile project signed in 1977. It sets the Shah's public distance from Israel beside the private record, and corrects a widely repeated claim that Iran joined the 1973 oil embargo. It ends with the pipeline the two governments built together, whose ownership is still being argued over in Swiss arbitration nearly half a century after the alliance ended.
chapters.outro: Part One established that the alliance was real, sustained and deliberately hidden. Iran voted against partition in 1947 but recognised Israel de facto on 6 March 1950, never de jure; Mosaddegh's government closed the Jerusalem consulate in 1951 without withdrawing that recognition. [cite:ir1_wiki_embtehran] [cite:ir1_iranica_israel] The coup of August 1953, which the CIA's own history says was "carried out under CIA direction," restored the Shah, under whom the relationship grew; historians agree on the CIA's role and disagree on how decisive it was. [cite:ir1_afp_cia2013] [cite:ir1_iranica_coup] [cite:ir1_takeyh_fa] Through Ben-Gurion's periphery policy and the Trident arrangement, Israel's intelligence service worked with SAVAK from 1957, and historians report that Mossad helped found it; Iran was a route out of Iraq for its Jews; Israeli exports to Iran passed $100 million a year by 1977, and in that year the two governments signed oil-for-arms contracts including a missile project, Flower. [cite:ir1_alpher_fa] [cite:ir1_irb_savak] [cite:ir1_wiki_ezra] [cite:ir1_wiki_flower] Iran did not join the Arab oil embargo of 1973, though Egypt's blockade of the Red Sea cut the tanker route to Eilat during the war. [cite:ir1_wiki_1973oil] [cite:ir1_thompson_energy] The two governments built the Eilat–Ashkelon pipeline together in 1968; since the revolution Israel has kept it, kept it secret and, citing its law on trading with an enemy, has not paid an arbitral award of about $1.1 billion that a Swiss court upheld in 2016.
