[cite:ir1_calcalist_2017] [cite:ir1_ih_swiss2016] [cite:ir1_toi_2016] Part Two follows the alliance through the revolution that ended it, and the secret arms trade that continued afterwards. [scene:ir2_revolution|Revolution and the arms trade]

sections.h: Recognition and the Coup
sections.html:
The alliance between Israel and Iran began in a vote against Israel's creation. When the United Nations General Assembly voted on the partition of Palestine in November 1947, Iran, then ruled by the young Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, voted against it. [cite:ir1_wiki_embtehran] Two and a half years later the same government recognised the state it had voted against. On 6 March 1950, while the Majlis, Iran's parliament, was in recess, the government extended de facto recognition to Israel "without formal announcement," according to the Encyclopaedia Iranica entry on the two countries' relations by the historians David Menashri and Trita Parsi. The decision drew strong opposition inside Iran and in Arab capitals. Iran never extended de jure, or full legal, recognition, and that distinction shaped the whole relationship that followed: real but unannounced, with no ambassadors formally accredited. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel] Iran was the second Muslim-majority state, after Turkey, to recognise Israel, and Israel kept what amounted to an embassy in Tehran under the name of a political representation. [cite:ir1_wiki_embtehran]

The date matters because it is often given wrongly. Some accounts, including an earlier volume of this library, list Iran among the first states to recognise Israel in May 1948, immediately after the United States. The record does not support that. Iran voted against partition in 1947 and recognised Israel de facto in March 1950. [cite:ir1_wiki_embtehran] [cite:ir1_iranica_israel]

Mosaddegh and the oil

The recognition soon ran into Iranian politics. On 29 April 1951 Mohammad Mosaddegh, leader of the National Front, became prime minister, and two days later his government nationalised the oil industry, which until then had been run by the British-owned Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. Britain answered with economic sanctions, naval and military manoeuvres in the region and covert efforts to replace him. [cite:ir1_iranica_coup] On 7 July 1951, shortly after Mosaddegh took office, his government closed Iran's consulate in Jerusalem, citing "financial difficulties." It did not withdraw the de facto recognition. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel] The record examined for this book does not show Mosaddegh's government taking further steps against Israel; the consulate closure is the documented act, and its stated reason is the government's own.

The coup of August 1953

The British government failed twice to replace Mosaddegh with a prime minister of its choosing, in 1951 and 1952, and in October 1952 he broke diplomatic relations with Britain. President Truman declined to join a plan to remove him. The Eisenhower administration did not. On 3 February 1953 American and British officials agreed on a plan, code-named AJAX by the Americans, to be run by the CIA under Kermit Roosevelt with British support; it was given final approval at a State Department meeting on 25 June 1953. [cite:ir1_iranica_coup] The first attempt, around 15 August, failed: the officer carrying the Shah's decree dismissing Mosaddegh and naming General Fazlollah Zahedi in his place was arrested on arrival, and the Shah left the country for Baghdad and then Rome. On 19 August a crowd paid by the CIA, apparently raised through the clerics Ayatollah Abol-Ghasem Kashani and Mohammad Behbahani, marched on the bazaar and Radio Tehran; army and police units joined it, and tanks attacked Mosaddegh's house. He surrendered the next day. Zahedi became prime minister, the Shah returned, and Mosaddegh was convicted of treason and held under house arrest until his death in 1967. [cite:ir1_iranica_coup] The Shah was restored, not installed: he had been on the throne since 1941.

For decades the United States did not formally acknowledge its role. In August 2013 the National Security Archive at George Washington University published a CIA internal history, "The Battle for Iran," released under the Freedom of Information Act, which stated: "The military coup that overthrew Mossadegh and his National Front Cabinet was carried out under CIA direction." The same history gave the agency's reason: "The risk of leaving Iran open to Soviet aggression compelled the United States" to act. An earlier release of the document, in 1981, had blacked out the section on the coup. [cite:ir1_afp_cia2013] [cite:ir1_npr_cia2013]

How much the CIA decided: the historians' debate

That the CIA planned, paid for and directed the operation is documented in the agency's own history. How decisive it was is argued among historians. Mark Gasiorowski, author of the Iranica entry and the most detailed scholarly accounts, describes a joint British and American operation in which Iranian actors were central: Zahedi, the Rashidian brothers, whom he describes as British agents, and figures such as Kashani who wanted Mosaddegh gone for their own reasons, while Mosaddegh's support had been worn down within the National Front, the Majlis and the army. [cite:ir1_iranica_coup] The historian Ray Takeyh argued in Foreign Affairs in 2014 that after the first attempt failed Washington had largely given up, and that the second, successful attempt was "very much an Iranian initiative," because "Iranian royalists had more at stake and more to lose than the Americans." [cite:ir1_takeyh_fa] The historian Gregory Brew, reviewing the literature in 2019, groups the explanations for the American decision into those that stress the fear of communism (Gasiorowski), those that stress control of oil (Ervand Abrahamian), and revisionists who play down the foreign role (Darioush Bayandor, Takeyh); he notes Fakhreddin Azimi's detailed reply to the revisionists, and argues himself that Washington acted on a "collapse narrative," a belief that Iran was about to fall apart, without strong evidence of an imminent communist takeover. [cite:ir1_brew_tnsr]

The debate is about weight, not about the documented facts. No serious account disputes that the CIA and British intelligence organised the operation and that it removed an elected prime minister. What is argued is whether it would have succeeded without Iranian allies who wanted the same result, and why the United States chose it.

What the coup did for the alliance

The coup did not create the relationship with Israel, which predated Mosaddegh. What it did, on the documented sequence, was return power to a monarch who over the next decade concentrated it in his own hands, and it was under that monarch that the alliance grew. The Shah's new security service, SAVAK, was founded in 1957, and by the account of the historians Ervand Abrahamian and Mohsen Milani, Mossad helped found it alongside the CIA. [cite:ir1_irb_savak] Iran's crude sales to Israel accelerated from 1958, and on 24 July 1960 the Shah publicly reaffirmed Iran's recognition of Israel, a statement that led Egypt's President Gamal Abdel Nasser to break relations with Iran. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel] The next section describes that partnership. Whether a Mosaddegh government, had it survived, would have kept or ended the relationship cannot be known; the record shows only that his government closed the consulate and kept the recognition. The connection between the coup and Iran's later hostility toward Israel is an argument made by some writers; Part Two examines it. [scene:ir2_revolution|The revolution]

sections.h: The Periphery Alliance
sections.html:
Israel's first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion, looked for friends beyond the Arab states that surrounded Israel. In the late 1950s, in the Encyclopaedia Iranica's phrase, Israel sought the friendship of "the neighbors of the neighbors": non-Arab states on the region's edge that had their own reasons to fear Egypt's President Nasser and Soviet influence. This became known as the periphery policy, and its main partners were Iran, Turkey and Ethiopia. With Iran it produced an informal alliance that lasted until 1979. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel]

Trident and SAVAK

The intelligence side of the policy was organised through an arrangement known as Trident, which linked the intelligence services of Israel, Iran and Turkey. The Israeli analyst Yossi Alpher, who wrote its history, records that it was formed through separate meetings in Europe, Ankara and Tehran between 1956 and 1958, at which the heads of the three services set up joint ventures, some of them operations against Nasserist and Soviet influence. Ben-Gurion presented it to Washington as a Western asset. Alpher calls it "a lopsided intelligence alliance under a gloss of pompous protocol": Israel "provided far better information and more intelligence know-how than it received in return." [cite:ir1_alpher_fa]

Iran's partner in Trident was SAVAK, the security and intelligence organisation the Shah created in 1957. In September of that year SAVAK's first head, General Teymur Bakhtiar, offered Israel's ambassador in Paris an exchange of intelligence, and Israel accepted. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel] How far Israel helped build SAVAK itself is reported rather than documented in released files. The historian Ervand Abrahamian writes that Mossad, the CIA and the FBI helped the Shah's government establish it; the political scientist Mohsen Milani writes that Mossad and the CIA assisted its creation, as summarised by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada in 1991. [cite:ir1_irb_savak] SAVAK became the instrument of the Shah's political repression, as Amnesty International reported in a 1976 briefing. [cite:ir1_irb_savak] Israel's government has not published records of what training Mossad gave it, and the specific claims sometimes made, such as translated interrogation manuals, rest on secondary accounts and are not repeated here.

The route for Iraq's Jews

Iran was also a route out of Iraq. After 1948 Jews in Iraq faced persecution and restrictions on leaving. By 1949, according to historians of the community, the Zionist underground in Iraq was smuggling Jews into Iran at about 1,000 a month, from where they were flown to Israel; when Iraq allowed emigration in 1951–52, between 120,000 and 130,000 Iraqi Jews were airlifted to Israel via Iran and Cyprus. [cite:ir1_wiki_ezra] The Iranica entry records that Iran's role as a transit point for Iraqi Jews made contacts with Tehran more urgent for Israel in the years before the alliance took shape. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel]

Trade, advisers and arms

By the 1970s the relationship was substantial. Israeli official statistics, cited by Iranica, show Israeli exports to Iran rising from $22.3 million in 1970 to $92.4 million in 1975 and $103.2 million in 1977, almost doubling between 1973 and 1974; Israel's recorded non-oil imports from Iran were far smaller, $5.8 million in 1977. Oil, the largest flow, was handled separately and secretly. Israel helped develop Iran's armed forces and trained Iranian officers and students, and its presence was large enough to need an Israeli school in Tehran. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel] According to Israeli Foreign Ministry archives, more than 500 Israeli families lived in Iran before the revolution. [cite:ir1_wiki_embtehran]

The most ambitious project came last. In April 1977 Iran and Israel signed six contracts exchanging Iranian oil for Israeli arms. One, code-named Flower, was to develop a missile. On 18 July 1977 Iran's vice-minister of war, General Hassan Toufanian, met Foreign Minister Moshe Dayan and Defence Minister Ezer Weizman in Israel; the minutes of that meeting, from Israel's Foreign Ministry, are held by the National Security Archive. In 1978 Iran paid $280 million in oil as a down payment, and Iranian engineers began building an assembly plant near Sirjan and a test range near Rafsanjan. The project ended with the revolution in February 1979, and the Israeli engineers went home. [cite:ir1_wiki_flower] The deal became public in April 1986, when The New York Times reported on documents left behind by Israeli diplomats in Tehran; according to the report, "the Israelis told the Iranians that the missiles could be fitted with nuclear warheads," and Iranian and Israeli officials interviewed did not deny that the documents were authentic. [cite:ir1_djn_flower] The Israeli journalist Ronen Bergman later reported that Israel planned to supply Iran with technology that was already obsolete; that is his account, and the Shah's side did not live to test it. [cite:ir1_wiki_flower]

Public distance, private alliance

The Shah kept the relationship out of sight. Iran never granted de jure recognition, and distance from Israel, in Iranica's assessment, was one of his main tools for keeping relations with Arab states in order. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel] He acknowledged the ties when it suited him. In July 1960 he publicly reaffirmed Iran's recognition of Israel, and Nasser broke relations with Iran in response. [cite:ir1_iranica_israel] In a 1975 interview he openly acknowledged military and intelligence ties with Israel, justified them by Arab hostility in Nasser's time, and added that "the situation has changed," complaining of Israeli press attacks on Iran. [cite:ir1_alpher_fa] Golda Meir's visit to Tehran in July 1965, which began the pipeline negotiations described in the next section, was kept secret at Iran's insistence. [cite:ir1_granta_khalili]

The 1973 oil question

Two incompatible accounts of Iran in the October 1973 war circulate. One says the Shah "joined the Arab-led OPEC oil embargo," cutting off oil to Israel. The other says Iran stayed out and kept Israel supplied. Neither is quite what the sources show. The embargo was declared by the Organisation of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries, of which Iran, not an Arab state, was not a member. Standard histories of the crisis list Iran among the producers that did not join and record that it increased production during the embargo and sold at the higher prices; the Shah was the leading advocate of those higher prices. [cite:ir1_wiki_1973oil] Alpher, writing in 2015, nonetheless states that the Shah joined the embargo and cut shipments to Israel. [cite:ir1_alpher_fa] That account is contradicted by the embargo's own membership, and the claim of an Iranian embargo on Israel in 1973 does not appear in the other sources examined here.

The practical question, whether Iranian crude reached Israel during the three weeks of fighting, is harder. On 6 October 1973 Egypt's navy blockaded the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the mouth of the Red Sea, which, as the political economist Helen Thompson notes, cut Israel off from its main supplier, Iran, since tankers bound for Eilat had to pass through it; by then Israel also drew oil from the Sinai fields it had occupied in 1967. [cite:ir1_thompson_energy] The claim, sometimes made, that the Eilat–Ashkelon pipeline was Israel's "wartime lifeline" in 1973 therefore has its logic backwards. What the record supports is narrower: Iran did not join the embargo, and its oil sales to Israel continued before and after the war, until the last shipments in 1978, which are the subject of the arbitration described in the next section. [cite:ir1_wiki_1973oil] [cite:ir1_toi_2016] [cite:ir1_shomrim_2024] During the war itself the Shah sent a congratulatory telegram to Egypt's President Sadat and allowed six Soviet supply planes to cross Iran to Iraq, then revoked permission for a further thirty-two, according to the recollection of his deputy foreign minister. [cite:ir1_iranwire_1973]

The alliance ended with the Shah. How the revolution of 1979 treated it, and what the new government said about Israel, is the subject of Part Two. [scene:ir2_revolution|The revolution]

sections.h: The Pipeline
sections.html:
The most durable product of the alliance is a pipe in the Negev desert. It began with the Suez Canal. When Egypt closed the canal during the 1967 war, Iranian tankers bound for Europe had to sail around Africa, and Israel, which now controlled the Straits of Tiran, offered a shortcut. Golda Meir had proposed a joint venture during a secret visit to Tehran in July 1965: Iranian crude would be shipped to Israel's Red Sea port of Eilat and carried by pipeline to the Mediterranean. After the canal closed, Iran commissioned a feasibility study, and the two governments went ahead. [cite:ir1_granta_khalili] [cite:ir1_thompson_energy] The agreement was signed in February 1968, and oil began flowing within about eighteen months. [cite:ir1_shomrim_2024]

A company with hidden owners

The Eilat Ashkelon Pipeline Company, known as EAPC, was founded by the Israeli and Iranian governments as equal partners. [cite:ir1_calcalist_2017] Iran did not want to be seen trading with Israel, so its half was held by the National Iranian Oil Company through companies registered abroad: among them Trans-Asiatic Oil, registered in Panama, and APC Holdings, registered in Canada. The 254-kilometre, 42-inch line ran from Eilat to Ashkelon, where most of the oil was loaded onto tankers for Europe and a smaller share went to Israeli refineries. The franchise ran for 49 years. [cite:ir1_wiki_eapc] [cite:ir1_granta_khalili] [cite:ir1_ih_swiss2016] Throughput peaked at about 10 million tons in 1970, well below the planned capacity; Iranica notes that even that initial flow exceeded Israel's own annual consumption. [cite:ir1_wiki_eapc] [cite:ir1_iranica_israel]

Secrecy was written into Israeli law from the start. A decree of 17 July 1968 made information about the pipeline a state secret, and the company was exempted from ordinary disclosure rules. [cite:ir1_wiki_eapc] [cite:ir1_calcalist_2017] In December 2017, when the original franchise expired and the company was reorganised, the Knesset's Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee kept it under secrecy rules that made publishing classified information about it punishable by fifteen years to life in prison; after a petition by an environmental group, environmental and safety matters were exempted, but the company's oil sources and core business remained classified. Israel's stated reason has been national security. [cite:ir1_calcalist_2017] A 2024 amendment narrowed the order slightly, and in January 2025 Israel's State Comptroller reported significant failures in the company's financial and legal conduct and its maintenance record; environmental groups continue to press the Knesset to lift the secrecy. [cite:ir1_adamteva_2025]

After 1979

The revolution ended the partnership. Iran ended official oil sales to Israel and cut ties, and Israel ended the partnership and refused to compensate the new government. [cite:ir1_thompson_energy] [cite:ir1_calcalist_2017] The pipeline did not fall idle: in the years after 1979, Helen Thompson writes, Israel relied on spot markets and clandestine trade through it, organised by the commodities trader Marc Rich. [cite:ir1_thompson_energy] Laleh Khalili writes that the National Iranian Oil Company "continued to honour its deals with Marc Rich," much of that oil being routed to Eilat, and that over two decades Rich supplied up to 20 per cent of Israel's annual oil needs; that is her account, drawn from the trade's historians, not a disclosed Iranian or Israeli record. [cite:ir1_granta_khalili] In 2003 its flow was reversed so that oil from the Black Sea and the Caspian could be shipped east from Eilat. [cite:ir1_calcalist_2017] It remains a strategic asset, and since 2020 it has been part of plans to move Gulf oil to the Mediterranean. [cite:ir1_wiki_eapc]

The arbitration

The Islamic Republic did not give up its half. Iran's claim, filed in 1994, sought two things: payment for the last oil shipments delivered to Eilat before the revolution, which were never paid for, and Iran's share of the company's assets. Israel counterclaimed that Iran had broken its contract to supply oil. [cite:ir1_toi_2016] The cases went to arbitration, first in France and then in Switzerland. [cite:ir1_ih_swiss2016] In May 2015 an arbitral tribunal ordered Israel's side to pay Iran about $1.1 billion, plus interest, for roughly fifty shipments of crude delivered in 1978. [cite:ir1_asil_2015] [cite:ir1_shomrim_2024] Some accounts give the principal as $1.2 billion with $362 million in interest. [cite:ir1_wiki_eapc] Israel appealed to Switzerland's Federal Tribunal, which rejected the appeal in a ruling dated 27 June 2016 and ordered Israel to pay 450,000 Swiss francs in costs. [cite:ir1_ih_swiss2016] [cite:ir1_ogj_2016] A separate claim to Iran's share of the company's assets could, according to Global Arbitration Review, be worth up to $7 billion together with the first. [cite:ir1_toi_2016] [cite:ir1_shomrim_2024]

The two governments' positions are set out in the proceedings and in Israeli statements. Israel's Finance Ministry said in 2016: "Under the laws of trade we cannot transfer funds to an enemy country." Israel designated Iran an enemy state in 2011 and relies on its Trading with the Enemy Ordinance; it also argues that the company had no value in 1979 because it was making heavy losses, and that Iran broke the agreement first. [cite:ir1_toi_2016] [cite:ir1_shomrim_2024] [cite:ir1_asil_2015] Iran, which does not recognise Israel, has pursued the claim through the arbitration; its filings, as reported by Shomrim, argue that the National Iranian Oil Company is separate from the Iranian state, that the revolution was force majeure, and that it is owed a share of the benefits Israel drew from the pipeline. [cite:ir1_shomrim_2024]

Status as of October 2026

Israel has not paid. In December 2024 the Israeli investigative outlet Shomrim reported that in late 2017 and January 2018 the two sides' representatives had written to the tribunal that they were willing to negotiate a settlement; a hearing set for Geneva in 2019 was apparently postponed and never held. Israel's Finance Ministry and the Prime Minister's Office declined to answer Shomrim's questions. [cite:ir1_shomrim_2024] In April 2024, after Iran's missile and drone attack on Israel of 13 April, Yedioth Ahronoth reported that senior Israeli officials had discussed taking money from a fund, believed to hold more than $1 billion, into which the company sets aside half its annual profits, managed by the Finance Ministry and reportedly kept against the possibility of future relations with a different Iranian government, to offset the cost of the attack. [cite:ir1_newarab_2024] No decision on that was reported. The public record examined for this book, as of October 2026, shows no payment to Iran, no published settlement and no final ruling on the larger asset claim; reporting found for this book does not show whether the wars of 2025 and 2026 changed the arbitration. [cite:ir1_shomrim_2024] [cite:ir1_adamteva_2025]

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: Revolution and the Secret Arms Trade
chapters.intro: Part Two covers the decade in which Israel's ally became its declared enemy and, at the same time, one of its arms customers. It begins with the revolution of February 1979: how Israel's mission in Tehran was handed to the PLO, what Ayatollah Khomeini and the new constitution said about Israel and about exporting the revolution, and the declaration of Quds Day. It then follows Iraq's invasion of Iran in September 1980 and the Israeli tyres, spare parts and weapons that reached Iran during the war, with the competing estimates of their value, the contradictory statements of Ariel Sharon and other Israeli officials, the reasons Israeli officials gave, and the denials of Iran's leaders. It ends with the 1985 TOW and HAWK shipments that opened the Iran-Contra affair, itemised from the record of the American investigation, and with the question, still disputed, of whether Israel drew Washington in or the reverse.
chapters.outro: Part Two established that the revolution of 1979 ended the alliance in public within weeks: Israel's de facto mission was handed to the PLO on 19 February 1979, the new constitution committed Iran to exporting its revolution, and Khomeini named Israel as an enemy and declared Quds Day. [cite:ir2_wiki_embassy] [cite:hz1_iran_const] [cite:hz1_merip_khomeini] [cite:ir2_wiki_quds] It established, too, that the trade did not end. Israel sold Iran tyres in 1980 and arms from its own stocks in 1981, in amounts estimated at anywhere from tens of millions of dollars to far more, while Khomeini publicly called such reports "childish nonsense." [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] [cite:ir2_csm_relat86] Sharon confirmed small sales in 1982 and denied American equipment was involved; Israel's ambassador said American parts had gone with Washington's coordination. [cite:ir2_djn_sharon82] [cite:ir2_csm_relat86] In 1985 Israel shipped 504 TOW missiles and 18 HAWKs to Iran with American acquiescence, opening the channel that became Iran-Contra; the larger totals were American sales in 1986. [cite:ir2_walsh18] [cite:ir2_iranica_contra] Israeli officials explained the trade by the threat from Iraq, by intelligence contacts, by Iran's Jewish community and by the hope of a post-Khomeini Iran. [cite:ir2_csm_interests86] [cite:ir2_djn_fallguy86] That community, and the two facts about it that are often presented as a paradox, are the subject of Part Three. [scene:ir3_community|The Jews of Iran]

sections.h: The Break: February 1979
sections.html:
The alliance described in Part One ended within three weeks of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's return from exile at the start of February 1979. [scene:ir1_periphery|The periphery doctrine] Khomeini's hostility to the Shah's ties with Israel was not new. He had been arrested in 1963 after denouncing the Shah and Israel, and a manifesto he signed that year with eight other senior clerics accused the Shah of submission to the United States and Israel. [cite:ir2_wiki_1963] Within weeks of taking power, the new authorities cut the relationship he had attacked for sixteen years.

The mission and the keys

Israel never had a formally recognised embassy in Tehran. Iran's de facto recognition of Israel in March 1950 allowed a political representation that opened on 6 March 1950 and worked without the public standing of an embassy; its heads included Uri Lubrani in the 1970s and, from 1978, Yossef Harmelin, the last Israeli representative in Iran. [cite:ir2_wiki_embassy] Harmelin and his staff left the country on 18 February 1979. (One summary of the record gives the closing date as 17 February.) [cite:ir2_wiki_embassy]

Yasser Arafat, the chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization, arrived in Tehran on 17 February 1979, two weeks after Khomeini's return, as the first official visitor to the new government. Iran severed its ties with Israel during the visit. [cite:ir2_olj_arafat] [cite:hz1_aawsat_arafat] On 19 February his delegation was handed the keys of the former Israeli mission. The New York Times reported that day that "the sacked Israeli mission here has been donated to the Palestinian movement." The street outside, Kakh Street, was renamed Palestine Street, and the building became the Palestinian embassy, headed by the Fatah official Hani al-Hassan. [cite:ir2_wiki_embassy] [cite:ir2_olj_arafat]

The embrace did not last. One account, from a Palestinian militant close to Arafat's deputy Abu Jihad, holds that Khomeini told Arafat at their meeting that "there is no Palestinian cause; it is an Islamic cause"; the remark rests on that one recollection, given to L'Orient-Le Jour forty years later, and is reported here as such. [cite:ir2_olj_arafat] What is better documented is the rupture that followed: when Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980, Arafat sided with Iraq while trying to stay on terms with Tehran, and after the PLO left Lebanon in 1982 Iran built its own Lebanese ally in Hezbollah. [cite:ir2_olj_arafat] The Hezbollah volume tells that story. [scene:hz2_founding|The Hezbollah Architecture: the founding]

What Khomeini said

The new state wrote its foreign ambitions into its founding documents. The constitution adopted in late 1979 described itself as a basis for "the continuation of the Revolution at home and abroad," and gave the armed forces "the ideological mission of jihad in God's way." It recognises Iran's Jewish community, which Part Three examines, and does not mention Israel or Zionism. [cite:hz1_iran_const] [scene:ir3_community|The Jews of Iran] In his New Year message broadcast by Radio Tehran on 21 March 1980, Khomeini said "we should try hard to export our revolution to the world," named "America, Israel and Zionism" as enemies, and pledged support for "beloved Palestine and beloved Lebanon." [cite:hz1_merip_khomeini]

On 7 August 1979 Khomeini called on Muslims to "consecrate the last Friday of the holy month of Ramadan as Al-Quds Day," a day to show solidarity with the Palestinians against Israel. In Iran the government organises the day's marches; officials give speeches against Israel and the United States, and crowds chant "Death to Israel" and "Death to America." The day is also marked by Hezbollah in Lebanon, by Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and by smaller gatherings in Europe and North America, but in the BBC's assessment it never took root among Muslims at large and remained mainly an Iranian event. [cite:ir2_wiki_quds] Part Nine sets out what Iran's leaders said about Israel in the decades that followed. [scene:ir9_record|Iran's own record]

What happened to the alliance's assets

The break was costly for Israel in plain commercial terms. Trade between the two countries had run at about $200 million a year in the Shah's last years by a conservative estimate, and after Khomeini cut ties hundreds of workers were laid off in Israel's defence industries, which had sold heavily to the Shah. [cite:ir2_csm_plays86] The joint oil pipeline company, whose disputes would reach a Swiss arbitration decades later, is covered in Part One. [scene:ir1_pipeline|The pipeline and the oil] The Israeli journalist Ronen Bergman, who wrote the fullest account of Israel's dealings with Iran in these years, argues that the Shah's fall also stopped advanced Israeli weapons cooperation; he writes that had Khomeini come to power later, Iran might have had "long-range missiles capable of carrying nuclear warheads." That is his assessment of a programme that was never completed, not a documented capability. [cite:ir2_hnn_bergman]

What did not end was the interest both governments had in each other. Israel's defence industries had lost a major customer, and Iran's armed forces, built up under the Shah with American weapons, were cut off from American spare parts by a US arms embargo. Within a year, as the next section shows, Israeli spare parts were again reaching Iran, in the months when Iran was holding American diplomats hostage. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] [cite:ir2_csm_relat86] [cite:ir2_csm_interests86]

sections.h: Arming the Islamic Republic, 1980–1984
sections.html:
Iraq invaded Iran on 22 September 1980. The war lasted until a ceasefire on 20 August 1988 and killed, by most estimates, more than a million people, more of them Iranian than Iraqi. [cite:ir2_brit_war] [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] For the whole of that war Iranian officials denounced Israel as an illegitimate state; for much of it, Israeli weapons and spare parts reached the Iranian armed forces. This section sets out what the record shows about those sales before 1985, what Israeli officials said about them, and what Iran's leaders said. The section that follows covers the better-documented shipments of 1985 and 1986, which became part of the Iran-Contra affair. [scene:ir2_contra|Iran-Contra: the Israeli leg]

Tyres before the war

The first sales came before Iraq attacked. In early 1980, while Iran was holding American diplomats hostage in Tehran, Israel sold Iran tyres for its American-built F-4 Phantom jets; a shipment of 250 tyres was flown in on 24 October 1980, as The New York Times reported the following August. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] The Carter administration learned of the sales and pressed Israel to stop. Zbigniew Brzezinski, Carter's national security adviser, later wrote that "we learned, much to our dismay," that the Israelis had been secretly supplying spare parts. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] IranWire, the Iranian exile news outlet, reports that Prime Minister Menachem Begin confirmed the tyre shipment and that, in return for the military aid, Khomeini "permitted many Iranian Jews to emigrate to the United States or Israel." [cite:ir2_iranwire_oil] A direct exchange of arms for emigration is reported but not documented in any agreement this book found; a 1989 history of the war says only that the clandestine relationship "allowed thousands to emigrate." [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] Part Three examines the community's emigration on its own terms. [scene:ir3_facts|The Jews of Iran: the facts]

Operation Seashell and the scale of the trade

In 1981, according to Ronen Bergman's account, Israel sold Iran about $75 million worth of arms from its own stocks, including 150 M-40 anti-tank guns and 24,000 shells, in an operation code-named Seashell. The material was flown on aircraft chartered from an Argentine cargo airline until one of them crashed after colliding with a Soviet aircraft in July 1981; after that the shipments went by sea. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] [cite:ir2_hnn_bergman] Much of what Israel sold in these years, according to the historian Trita Parsi, was paid for with Iranian oil. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport]

How much Israel sold in total is not established. The estimates differ by more than a factor of twenty, and none rests on a published Israeli or Iranian government record. In March 1982 The New York Times reported that $100 million to $200 million in arms and ammunition had reached Iran from Western Europe over eighteen months, with Israel possibly involved in transferring nearly half. [cite:ir2_csm_1982] Israeli press reports cited in December 1986 put Israel's sales at $50 million to $100 million over several years. [cite:ir2_csm_relat86] Parsi gives an estimate from Tel Aviv University's Jaffee Center for Strategic Studies of about $500 million between 1981 and 1983; a 1987 book by Jonathan Marshall, Peter Dale Scott and Jane Hunter put it at more than $500 million a year; and in December 1991 Seymour Hersh reported in The New York Times that internal US government reports put Israel's sales close to $2 billion a year in the early 1980s. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] An Iranian arms dealer, Ahmad Haidari, told Parsi that about 80 percent of the weapons Tehran bought after the war began came from Israel. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] These are estimates by people with different access and different interests, and they are presented as a range.

Sharon's statements

Israel's government first acknowledged the trade in May 1982, when Defence Minister Ariel Sharon, on a visit to the United States, said he had "deliberately confirmed" reports of shipments in order to clear Israel of "the smear of being Iran's major arms supplier." He said that "no America-made equipment was involved and quantities shipped were very small," and that Israel had been telling American officials about the shipments for months. [cite:ir2_djn_sharon82] The same month, as quoted in a 1987 book, he told The Washington Post that "Iraq is Israel's enemy and we hope that diplomatic relations between us and Iran will be renewed as in the past." [cite:ir2_jc_sharon]

His later statements did not match the first. The same book quotes him at a press conference in Paris, four months after the Post interview, saying that "Israel has a vital interest in the continuing of the war in the Persian Gulf, and in Iran's victory." [cite:ir2_jc_sharon] Another account dates a Paris press conference at which Sharon said the sales had American consent to 28 September 1983, a year later; whether these are two events or one dated differently is not resolved in the sources this book could check. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] In 1982 Moshe Arens, then Israel's ambassador in Washington, told The Boston Globe that Israel had shipped American spare parts to Iran, coordinated with the US government "at almost the highest levels," which contradicted Sharon's assurance that no American equipment was involved. [cite:ir2_csm_relat86] The Washington Post later reported that Secretary of State Alexander Haig had secretly approved Israeli shipments of American arms in 1981; Haig denied it. [cite:ir2_csm_relat86] In December 1991 US officials told reporters that the Reagan administration had changed policy in 1981 to let Israel sell "several billion dollars' worth" of American-made arms to Iran; that account remains unconfirmed by any released US document this book found. [cite:ir2_tbt_1991]

Why Israel did it, in its officials' words

Israeli officials gave several reasons, at different times and mostly without their names. The reasons reported in 1986 were to keep Iraq, which Israel regarded as its most dangerous enemy, tied down in a long war; to keep intelligence contacts with Iranian officers and officials; and to earn foreign currency. [cite:ir2_csm_interests86] Officials quoted that November said the war "ties down Iraq" and kept Arab states distracted, and that Iran, "sitting astride the Persian Gulf," was too important to give up on after Khomeini. [cite:ir2_csm_plays86b] Senior officials quoted in December 1986 added the protection of Iran's Jewish community. [cite:ir2_djn_fallguy86] Bergman sums up three aims: to recover influence lost with the Shah, to prevent an Iraqi conquest of Iran, and to keep Israel's arms industry busy. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] These are the logic of the periphery doctrine described in Part One, applied to a government whose leader named Israel as an enemy of the revolution. [cite:hz1_merip_khomeini] [scene:ir1_periphery|The periphery doctrine]

The relationship also had a nuclear dimension. Iran's air force bombed Iraq's Osirak reactor in September 1980, damaging secondary buildings, and Israel destroyed it on 7 June 1981. A 2011 RAND study says Israel received Iranian intelligence for its strike; IranWire, reviewing the record in 2024, found "no credible evidence of direct collaboration." The claim is contested. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] [cite:ir2_iranwire_oil]

What Iran said

Iran's leaders denied the trade. In a speech on 24 August 1981 Khomeini called reports of Israeli arms deliveries false and the claims of cooperation "childish nonsense," according to Parsi. [cite:ir2_wiki_israelsupport] Later, Iranian officials acknowledged parts of the record: Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Speaker of parliament during the war and later president, described in an interview with the Tehran daily Hamshahri how Israeli HAWK missiles had arrived in 1985 and "had to be returned." [cite:ir2_iranwire_oil] The next section returns to that shipment.

The American tilt

Israeli and American policy diverged. In 1984 the government of Shimon Peres stopped arms supplies to Iran under American pressure. [cite:ir2_csm_plays86b] The United States moved closer to Iraq; by 1987 it was giving Iraq detailed intelligence on Iranian deployments, including satellite imagery, although it had firm evidence from 1983 onward that Iraq was using chemical weapons against Iranian troops. A retired US Air Force officer who served in Baghdad recalled President Reagan writing "An Iranian victory is unacceptable" in the margin of a memo. [cite:ir2_fp_saddam] For most of the war, then, Israel's stated interest was that Iraq should not win, and Washington's was that Iran should not.

sections.h: Iran-Contra: the Israeli Leg, 1985–1986
sections.html:
The best-documented Israeli arms deliveries to the Islamic Republic are those of 1985, because they became part of the largest American political scandal of the decade and were examined by an independent counsel, Lawrence Walsh, whose final report was published in 1993. [cite:ir2_walsh18] [cite:ir2_iranica_contra] Unlike the earlier sales, they are itemised by date and number in official records.

How it began

The channel opened through Israel. Prime Minister Shimon Peres first suggested contacts with Iran, and David Kimche, director general of Israel's Foreign Ministry, pressed the idea on the US national security adviser, Robert McFarlane, in mid-1985. [cite:ir2_iranica_contra] Michael Ledeen, a consultant to the US National Security Council, had met Peres on 3 May 1985 to discuss Iran and weapons transfers. [cite:ir2_wiki_contratl] Kimche met McFarlane in Washington on 3 July 1985 on behalf of Israelis who were talking with the Iranian businessman Manucher Ghorbanifar and the Saudi financier Adnan Khashoggi. [cite:ir2_brown_begin] According to a chronology published in 1987, Kimche said that arms sales "probably will be a condition" of any opening to Iranian "moderates." [cite:ir2_csm_chron87] The Israeli side of the operation was run by Peres's counter-terrorism adviser Amiram Nir, with Adolph Schwimmer, founder of Israel Aircraft Industries, and Yaakov Nimrodi, an arms dealer with long experience of Iran. [cite:ir2_iranica_contra]

The American aim was to free seven American hostages held in Lebanon by groups linked to Iran, among them the CIA's Beirut station chief, William Buckley. [cite:ir2_csm_interests86] [cite:ir2_jc_sharon] The emergence of Hezbollah in these years, and the 1983 bombings in Beirut, are described in the Hezbollah volume. [scene:hz2_1983|The Hezbollah Architecture: 1983] The plan agreed in August 1985 was that Israel would sell American-made TOW anti-tank missiles to Iran from its own stocks and the United States would replace them. McFarlane said President Reagan approved this orally; Reagan and Attorney General Edwin Meese later said the president had not known of the shipments before a written finding of January 1986. [cite:ir2_brown_begin] [cite:ir2_csm_interests86]

The 1985 shipments

On 20 August 1985 Israel delivered the first 96 TOW missiles. No hostage was released. A second shipment of 408 TOWs followed in September, and the Reverend Benjamin Weir was freed in mid-September (14 or 15 September in different accounts). [cite:ir2_brown_begin] [cite:ir2_csm_chron87] Walsh's final report records that "with U.S. acquiescence" Israel shipped 504 American-made TOWs to Iran in August and September 1985, and that Weir "was released as a result." [cite:ir2_walsh18] Earlier reporting gave the first shipment as "100" missiles, the approximate number Reagan approved; the itemised record is 96. [cite:ir2_jc_sharon] [cite:ir2_brown_begin]

In November 1985 Israel tried to send HAWK anti-aircraft missiles. An El Al 747 that was to carry 80 of them toward Iran by way of a European country turned back, and 18 were flown from Israel to Iran on a CIA-owned aircraft around 25 November. [cite:ir2_walsh18] They were not what Iran had asked for. Iranian officials test-fired one, found that the missiles lacked the high-altitude capability they had expected and bore Israeli markings, and sent the rest back. [cite:ir2_iranica_contra] [cite:ir2_csm_interests86] Rafsanjani later recalled that the Israeli HAWKs "remained at the airport for a long time and had to be returned." [cite:ir2_iranwire_oil] After this failure, American officials took over the operation themselves. [cite:ir2_csm_interests86]

From Israeli sales to American sales

On 4 December 1985 Oliver North, a National Security Council aide, proposed selling arms to Iran directly rather than through Israel, with part of the proceeds going to the Contra rebels in Nicaragua, whom Congress had barred the administration from funding; on 6 December he told Israeli defence officials that future profits would help the Contras. [cite:ir2_wiki_contratl] [cite:ir2_jc_sharon] On 17 January 1986 Reagan signed a secret finding authorising dealings with Iran, including arms sales, and instructed CIA Director William Casey to withhold the details from Congress. [cite:ir2_csm_chron87] From then on the sales were American. About 1,000 TOWs went in February 1986 under US direction; in May McFarlane, North and others, among them Amiram Nir, flew to Tehran with HAWK spare parts; Lawrence Jenco was released in July; more TOWs went in October, some of them through Israel, and David Jacobsen was freed on 2 November. [cite:ir2_iranica_contra] [cite:ir2_csm_chron87] [cite:ir2_wiki_contratl] Three more Americans were kidnapped in Lebanon in the same period. [cite:ir2_iranica_contra]

The money moved through a chain of intermediaries. By Encyclopaedia Iranica's account, Israeli middlemen paid Israel's defence ministry $6,000 per TOW, Ghorbanifar paid $10,000, and the Iranian government was charged $12,000; Iran later discovered it had been heavily overcharged. Residual funds from the February 1986 shipment were used partly for the Contras and for commissions to the businessmen Richard Secord and Albert Hakim. [cite:ir2_iranica_contra] Rafsanjani later said Iran paid $14 million of a $22 million deal and refused the rest because of the price. [cite:ir2_iranwire_oil]

On 3 November 1986 the Lebanese weekly Ash-Shiraa disclosed McFarlane's visit to Tehran. [cite:ir2_csm_chron87] The next day Rafsanjani, then Speaker of parliament, confirmed that the United States had shipped military equipment; his account to parliament did not satisfy some members, and when eight deputies summoned the foreign minister over the affair Khomeini rebuked them, saying their tone was "harsher than that of Israel, harsher than that of the US." [cite:ir2_iranwire_rafs]

How many weapons, and through whom

The totals are often misstated. Over seven shipments from August 1985 to November 1986, Iran received 2,004 TOWs, 18 HAWKs (which it returned) and more than 200 HAWK spare parts, and three hostages were freed. [cite:ir2_iranica_contra] Of these, Israel sold from its own stocks 504 TOWs and the 18 HAWKs, all in 1985; the rest were American sales under the January 1986 finding, although Israeli territory and personnel continued to be used in some deliveries. [cite:ir2_walsh18] [cite:ir2_iranica_contra] [cite:ir2_csm_chron87] Some accounts say that more than 2,000 TOWs and 235 HAWK parts kits went "via Israel." That figure traces to reporting of 20 November 1986, before the investigations, which attributed the whole programme to Israeli shipments with US approval; the itemised record of the Walsh investigation does not support it. [cite:ir2_csm_chron87] [cite:ir2_walsh18]

Who urged whom

Whether Israel drew the United States into the arms-for-hostages trade, or American officials drew Israel in, was disputed at the time and remains so. Israeli officials in November 1986 described Israel as a "willing helper" to Washington and did not deny reports that Israel had conceived the scheme; Peres, then foreign minister, repeatedly said Israel had acted only to help free American hostages. [cite:ir2_csm_plays86b] The record shows that a CIA draft of May 1985 had already proposed easing the arms embargo to reach Iranian "moderates," and that the NSC consultant's approach to Kimche followed it. [cite:ir2_csm_interests86] Zbigniew Brzezinski suggested that Kimche may have taken the first steps but that "there may have been a strong temptation on the US side to move in that direction as well." Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir rejected American suggestions that Israel had helped channel money to the Contras. [cite:ir2_csm_relat86] Both readings rest on documents; neither has been settled by them.

The Americans who ran the operation faced prosecution. Fourteen people were charged and eleven convicted. The convictions of Oliver North and John Poindexter were overturned on appeal; four of the others convicted or who pleaded guilty were later pardoned, and five, among them Richard Secord, Albert Hakim and Thomas Clines, were not, Clines serving sixteen months in prison. [cite:ir2a_walsh_summ] The claim, repeated in some accounts, that every conviction was overturned or pardoned is not correct. [cite:ir2_jc_sharon] On 24 December 1992 President George H. W. Bush pardoned six officials, among them former Defence Secretary Caspar Weinberger, who had not yet been tried, and McFarlane, saying he was doing what "honor, decency, and fairness require." [cite:ir2_procl6518] The public record this book examined does not show charges in the United States against any Israeli official.

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: The Jews of Iran
chapters.intro: Part Three turns to Iran's Jewish community, present in the country since the Persian empire and the subject of a question often put as a paradox: how Israel and the United States can be at war with a state whose constitution recognises its Jews and reserves them a seat in parliament. It sets out two records kept by the same state. The first is the community itself: its history, its numbers by census and by estimate, including the claim that it exceeds 20,000, its constitutional standing and representative, Khomeini's assurance of 1979 in the wordings that survive, and what its leaders said in public during the wars of 2025 and 2026, and under what constraints. The second is the record of execution, espionage trials, legal limits, state Holocaust denial and wartime questioning, together with the government's stated distinction between Jews and Zionists and the answers of its critics. It ends with what both records do and do not say about the war.
chapters.outro: Part Three established two facts that do not cancel each other. Iran's constitution names Jews as one of three recognised religious minorities and reserves them a seat in the Majlis, held since 2020 by Homayoun Sameh Najafabadi, and the community keeps synagogues and schools that are relatively free to worship within the law. [cite:ir3_const_en] [cite:ir3_wiki_sameh] [cite:ir3_fh_2026] Its size is smaller than often stated: censuses counted 8,756 Jews in 2011 and 9,826 in 2016, and no current source supports "over 20,000". [cite:ir3_afp_census2012] [cite:ir3_wiki_exodus] The same state shot Habib Elghanian for "friendship with Israel" in 1979, convicted ten Jews as Israeli spies in 2000, hosted Holocaust deniers in 2006, and questioned dozens of Jews about their relatives in Israel after the June 2025 war, while its leaders described their enmity as directed at Zionism, not at Jews. [cite:ir3_tablet_hakakian] [cite:ir3_ap_shiraz2000] [cite:ir3_wiki_conf2006] [cite:ir3_toi_summoned] [cite:ir3_toi_9point] The community's leaders condemned Israel in both wars, under documented pressure, and in April 2026 an Israeli strike on a commander next door destroyed a Tehran synagogue, which the Israeli military called collateral damage. [cite:ir3_ynet_2025] [cite:ir3_nw_assoc2026] [cite:ir3_wiki_rafinia] Part Four turns to the weapons at the centre of the conflict: Iran's nuclear programme and Israel's own undeclared arsenal. [scene:ir4_programme|The atom]

sections.h: Two Documented Facts
sections.html:
The question this part examines is often put as a paradox. Israel and the United States went to war in 2025 and again in 2026 against a state whose constitution recognises its Jewish community by name and reserves that community a seat in parliament. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [cite:ir3_const_en] The same state executed the community's best-known businessman in its first months, tried thirteen Jews as Israeli spies in 1999 and 2000, convened a conference of Holocaust deniers in 2006, and in the summer of 2025 summoned dozens of Jews for questioning about their relatives in Israel. [cite:ir3_tablet_hakakian] [cite:ir3_ap_shiraz2000] [cite:ir3_wiki_conf2006] [cite:ir3_fh_2026] They are better read as two documented facts than as a paradox: how a constitution treats a minority, and what a government's officials say and do, are separate questions with separate records. This part sets out both records in full. This section gives the first: the community, its numbers, its legal standing and its public voice. The next section gives the second. [scene:ir3_facts|The other fact]

Two thousand seven hundred years

Jewish life in what is now Iran is older than Islam, older than Persia's conversion to it, and older than most of the cities where Iranian Jews now live. Accounts that give "over 2,700 years" count from the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE, when, according to the Bible (2 Kings 18:11), some of the deported Israelites were settled in "the cities of the Medes", in what is now western Iran. [cite:ir3_wiki_history] The firmer historical marker is the Persian king Cyrus, who conquered Babylon in the sixth century BCE and allowed the exiled Jews to return to Judea; many stayed under Persian rule. [cite:ir3_wiki_history] The Book of Esther is set at the Persian court. In Hamadan, the ancient Ecbatana, a mausoleum believed to date from the 1600s is held by Iranian Jews and Christians to contain the tombs of Esther and her cousin Mordecai, and it is the most important Jewish pilgrimage site in the country. The tradition is not supported in the Talmud, and the archaeologist Ernst Herzfeld argued the tomb belonged to Shushandukht, the Jewish wife of the Sasanian king Yazdegerd I. [cite:ir3_wiki_tomb] On 14 March 2025 Iran's chief rabbi read the Book of Esther there for Purim; the site had been the target of an arson attempt in May 2020 and a firebomb in April 2024, both causing minor damage. [cite:ir3_wiki_tomb] The 2,700-year figure therefore rests on the biblical account; the continuous record from the Persian empire onward, about 2,500 years, is not in dispute.

How many: censuses and estimates

No figure for Iran's Jewish population is exact, and the sources that give them count differently. Iran's first national census, in 1956, counted 65,232 Jews. [cite:ir3_wiki_exodus] For the eve of the revolution, figures range from about 60,000, attributed to Iran's Statistical Centre, through about 80,000 to "over 100,000", the figure given by the Iranian-American writer Roya Hakakian. [cite:ir3_wiki_exodus] [cite:ir3_wiki_history] [cite:ir3_tablet_hakakian] The census figures since then are much lower. The 2011 census, released on 29 July 2012, counted 8,756 Jews, against 117,704 Christians and 25,271 Zoroastrians. [cite:ir3_afp_census2012] The 2016 census counted 9,826. [cite:ir3_wiki_exodus] The US State Department's 2014 religious freedom report gave both kinds of figure side by side: "fewer than 9,000 Jews" by Iran's census, "as many as 25,000" by media estimates. [cite:ir3_usip_irf2014]

The higher estimates come from earlier years or from individual community members. In December 2006 the then Jewish member of parliament, Maurice Motamed, spoke of about 25,000 Iranian Jews; in 2009 the State Department gave 20,000 to 25,000. [cite:ir3_wiki_conf2006] [cite:ir3_wiki_exodus] In 2014 Hakakian wrote that the government reported 25,000 and that she estimated no more than 10,000. [cite:ir3_tablet_hakakian] The Tehran Jewish Committee, as cited by the State Department, estimated about 9,000, while a community member visiting the United States in 2021 had given 20,000. [cite:ir3_iranwire_rallies] Reporting during the wars ranged from about 15,000 (Ynet, June 2025) to 8,000 to 10,000 (Times of Israel, June 2025) and 8,000 to 15,000 (Religion News Service, April 2026). [cite:ir3_ynet_2025] [cite:ir3_toi_summoned] [cite:ir3_rns_synagogue] The figure of "over 20,000" Iranian Jews today is therefore not supported by any census and matches only estimates made between 2006 and 2009 and one individual's claim in 2021. The census counts since 2011 put the community at under 10,000, and current estimates from outside Iran run from about 8,000 to 15,000. One study estimated that more than 80 percent of the Jews in Iran at the revolution had left by 2006. [cite:ir3_wiki_exodus] AFP describes the remaining community as the largest in the Middle East outside Israel, a ranking that depends on which estimate is used and whether Turkey is counted. [cite:ir3_olj_ghahremani]

What the constitution says

The constitution of the Islamic Republic, adopted in 1979 and amended in 1989, makes Twelver Shia Islam the official religion (Article 12). Article 13 states: "Zoroastrian, Jewish, and Christian Iranians are the only recognized religious minorities," free within the law to perform their rites and to follow their own rules in personal status and religious education. Article 14 requires the government and Muslims to treat non-Muslims with "Islamic justice and equity" and to respect their human rights, but only those who do not conspire against Islam or the Islamic Republic. [cite:ir3_const_en] [cite:ir3_const_es] Article 64 reserves seats in the parliament, the Majlis: "The Zoroastrians and Jews will each elect one representative," the Assyrian and Chaldean Christians share one, and Armenian Christians elect two. [cite:ir3_const_en] The text does not mention Zionism. Some earlier accounts, including the series this volume builds on, describe the constitution as distinguishing Jews from Zionists; that distinction is in Khomeini's reported words, discussed below, not in the constitutional text. [cite:ir3_const_es]

The Jewish seat has been held since 2020 by Homayoun Sameh Najafabadi, who in 2024 told Voice of America that state aid to the community's institutions had "increased greatly" in recent years. [cite:ir3_wiki_sameh] He was still the community's representative in April 2026. [cite:ir3_rns_synagogue] About 100 synagogues remained in Iran as of 2025, along with Jewish schools and Tehran's Jewish hospital, Dr Sapir. [cite:ir3_wiki_history] Freedom House records that the recognised minorities are "relatively free to worship." [cite:ir3_fh_2026] The schools run under limits: their heads are appointed by the state, and most have been Muslim; and until 4 February 2015 they were required to open on Saturdays. [cite:ir3_wiki_history]

Khomeini's assurance: three wordings

The founding statement of the Islamic Republic's position on its Jews is a remark Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini made to a Jewish delegation in Qom in May 1979, days after the execution of the community leader Habib Elghanian. [cite:ir3_tablet_hakakian] [cite:ir3_wiki_history] It survives in more than one wording, and no primary transcript was found for this book. Hakakian, drawing on the delegates' accounts, dates the visit to 10 May 1979 and gives his words as: "We recognize our Jews as separate from those godless, bloodsucking Zionists." She reports that by nightfall the sentence was painted on synagogue walls, Hebrew schools and kosher butcher shops. [cite:ir3_tablet_hakakian] The historian Trita Parsi quotes the same sentence. [cite:ir3_wiki_exodus] Another account places the meeting three days after the execution, with a delegation led by Yedidia Shofet, and reports that the newspaper Ettela'at headlined the next day: "We do not believe that all Jews are Zionists." [cite:ir3_wiki_history] A third, softer wording ("we make a distinction between the Jewish community and the Zionists") and a description of the remark as a formal fatwa circulate in later secondary material; this book did not find either traced to a primary record. What is consistent across the attested versions is the distinction itself: a protected Jewish community on one side, Zionism and Israel on the other.

The community's public voice in the wars

During Israel's strikes in June 2025, the community's leadership issued two statements condemning Israel. Sameh wrote that Israel "is committing war crimes — crimes against humanity," and the senior rabbi Younes Hamami Lalehzar published a similar letter. [cite:ir3_ynet_2025] The state news agency Mehr published photographs of Jews gathered at Tehran's Abrishami synagogue in support of the Supreme Leader and the armed forces. [cite:ir3_toi_summoned] After an Israeli strike destroyed a Tehran synagogue on 7 April 2026, the Iranian Jewish Association called the attack "heinous" and affirmed its "historic unity with the Leader, the Iranian nation, and the courageous defenders of our country." [cite:ir3_nw_assoc2026] The Leader in question was by then Mojtaba Khamenei, designated after his father was killed in the opening strikes of 28 February 2026. [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar]

These statements are the community's documented public position. They are not evidence of what its members privately think, and the record shows why they cannot be read that way. In 2023 the State Department said it had reports that Iranian authorities "coerced Iranian Jewish leaders and their communities" into anti-Israel rallies, and called this "abhorrent." [cite:ir3_iranwire_rallies] An Israeli radio host who knew of one 2025 gathering said it was meant to "avert any suspicion of spying or, heaven forbid, betrayal." [cite:ir3_toi_summoned] In December 2025 Sameh said he had been summoned by the security agencies over Jewish users' likes and comments on Israeli content, according to Iran International, a London-based opposition-leaning outlet. [cite:ir3_iranintl_summons] Ynet's anonymous sources described a community whose main fear in the war was vigilante violence. [cite:ir3_ynet_2025] A community that speaks under these conditions has a public voice; it does not have a free one.

sections.h: The Other Fact
sections.html:
The recognition described in the previous section sits beside a second record, kept by the same state. [scene:ir3_community|Two documented facts] It begins three months after the revolution. On 9 May 1979 a revolutionary court had Habib Elghanian, an industrialist and the most prominent figure in Iran's Jewish community, shot by firing squad. He was charged with "friendship with Israel, Zionists, and the enemies of God, and sowing corruption on earth." [cite:ir3_tablet_hakakian] Khomeini's assurance to the Jewish delegation in Qom came in the days that followed. [cite:ir3_wiki_history] Another Jewish businessman, Albert Danialpour, was executed on 5 June 1980. [cite:ir3_wiki_exodus] By one estimate about 30,000 Jews left within months of the revolution; another holds that more than 80 percent of those who remained in 1979 had left by 2006, most for Israel and the United States, many crossing illegally into Pakistan in the 1980s and 1990s. [cite:ir3_wiki_exodus] Israel's own officials later cited the protection of this community as one of their reasons for selling arms to Iran in the 1980s. [cite:ir2_djn_fallguy86] [scene:ir2_arms|The secret arms trade]

Recognised, not equal

The constitution that recognises Jews also sets limits. The president must be chosen from among "religious and political personalities" and must believe in the official Shia school of law, a requirement no Jew can meet; Article 14's protection extends only to non-Muslims who do not conspire against Islam or the Islamic Republic. [cite:ir3_const_en] Freedom House reports that non-Shia religious minorities are "rarely awarded senior government posts." [cite:ir3_fh_2026] The State Department's 2014 report found that the government "discriminated against all religious minority groups in employment, education, and housing." [cite:ir3_usip_irf2014] Rights activists note that Iranian law usually requires death when a non-Muslim kills a Muslim, while a Muslim who kills a non-Muslim usually owes financial compensation. [cite:ir3_wiki_ghahremani] The limits are not peculiar to Jews: Freedom House records that Bahá'ís, whose faith the constitution does not recognise, are "systematically persecuted," jailed and barred from higher education. [cite:ir3_fh_2026]

The Shiraz trial, 1999–2000

In January and March 1999 thirteen Jews, most of them from Shiraz, were detained and accused of spying for Israel. [cite:ir3_jta_freed2003] In July 2000 a revolutionary court in Shiraz convicted ten of them and two Muslim co-defendants and acquitted three Jews and two Muslims. The charges included "cooperating with a hostile government, membership in an illegal (spy) ring and recruitment of new agents"; the Jewish defendants received four to thirteen years. Eight defendants had confessed, and state television broadcast the confessions of two before their lawyers could consult them. [cite:ir3_ap_shiraz2000] Israel denied that any of the men had worked for it; Prime Minister Ehud Barak asked other governments to press for their release, and President Bill Clinton said he was "deeply disappointed" that Iran had again failed to act under the rule of law. Maurice Motamed, then the Jewish member of parliament, said the verdicts had "seriously affected the community." [cite:ir3_ap_shiraz2000] On 21 September 2000 an appeals court overturned the spy-ring and recruitment convictions, upheld the conviction for cooperating with Israel and cut the sentences to two to nine years; the provincial judiciary chief called them "the lowest possible sentences," reflecting "the ultimate of Islamic kindness and generosity." [cite:ir3_ap_appeal2000] The last five prisoners were freed in February 2003. [cite:ir3_jta_freed2003]

The execution of Arvin Ghahremani, 2024

On 4 November 2024 Iran hanged Arvin Ghahremani, a Jewish man, in Kermanshah prison. He had been convicted of murdering Amir Shokri, a Muslim man who owed him money, in a street fight in November 2022. [cite:ir3_olj_ghahremani] [cite:ir3_wiki_ghahremani] His family said Shokri attacked him with a knife and he acted in self-defence; the provincial prosecutor said the killing was intentional. Under Iran's law of retribution, the victim's family could have accepted blood money instead; the judiciary's news site said the family "refused to give consent." Iran Human Rights, a Norway-based group, said the case had "significant flaws" and that "institutionalized anti-Semitism in the Islamic republic undoubtedly played a crucial role" in the sentence being carried out; Iran's judiciary treated it as an ordinary murder case. [cite:ir3_olj_ghahremani] Israel's foreign ministry and the US antisemitism envoy condemned the execution, while some Iranian Jews told Voice of America it was an ordinary murder case. [cite:ir3_wiki_ghahremani] The case is contested: the record shows a homicide conviction, a disputed account of the killing and what one compilation describes as the first execution of an Iranian Jew since 1994 (AFP called it "unprecedented in recent years"); it does not establish that he was executed because he was Jewish.

Holocaust denial and the "anti-Zionist, not anti-Jewish" line

On 11 and 12 December 2006 the foreign ministry's Institute for Political and International Studies hosted a conference in Tehran on the "global vision of the Holocaust." Among its 67 listed attendees were David Duke, a former Ku Klux Klan leader, the convicted French Holocaust denier Robert Faurisson and six members of Neturei Karta, a small anti-Zionist Haredi group. Foreign Minister Manouchehr Mottaki said it was held "neither to deny nor prove" the Holocaust, while President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad told participants that the "Zionist regime will be wiped out soon the same way the Soviet Union was." [cite:ir3_wiki_conf2006] The UN secretary-general, Germany, Israel, the United States and the European Union condemned it. So did Motamed, who said it put pressure on Jews worldwide and upset Iran's Jews: a rare documented case of the community's representative publicly criticising a state initiative. [cite:ir3_wiki_conf2006] After Ahmadinejad left office, Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif wrote in September 2013 that "Iran never denied it"; on 20 March 2014 Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei called the Holocaust "an event whose reality is uncertain." [cite:ir3_brookings_2014] In 2025 the authorities again held an annual Holocaust cartoon competition, and the Friday prayer leader of Mashhad said "all the stories about the Holocaust are a complete lie." [cite:ir3_uscirf_2026]

The government's stated position is that its enmity is to Zionism and Israel, not to Jews. Khamenei set it out in November 2014: Israel "has no cure but to be annihilated," but that did not mean the "massacre of the Jewish people"; it meant a referendum of the "original people of Palestine including Muslims, Christians, and Jews," from which Jewish immigrants would be excluded. [cite:ir3_toi_9point] In May 2020 he called Israel "a cancerous tumor in the region." [cite:ir3_reuters_tumor2020] Critics answer that the line does not hold in practice. The State Department said in 2023 that Iranian officials "regularly" spread antisemitic views, and the US Commission on International Religious Freedom reported that after the June 2025 war the authorities "held Jews collectively responsible for Israeli actions." [cite:ir3_iranwire_rallies] [cite:ir3_uscirf_2026] Hakakian argues that the community serves the state as a "living political citation" against charges of antisemitism. [cite:ir3_tablet_hakakian]

Why this matters for the war

Israel's government framed both wars as a fight with Iran's government, not its people. On 13 June 2025 Benjamin Netanyahu told Iranians: "Our fight is against the murderous Islamic regime that oppresses and impoverishes you." [cite:ir3_toi_netanyahu2025] Iran's government, for its part, treated the community as a security question. From 23 June 2025 at least 35 Jews in Tehran and Shiraz were summoned and questioned, mainly about relatives in Israel, and warned not to contact them; the USCIRF reported "systematic" arrests in Isfahan, Yazd, Shiraz and Tehran. [cite:ir3_toi_summoned] [cite:ir3_uscirf_2026] In late July 2025 five Iranian Jews, one a US citizen, were reported still held on suspicion of collaborating with Israel. [cite:ir3_iranintl_five] The community's leaders, as the previous section showed, publicly sided with the state against Israel, under the conditions set out there.

The record examined for this book shows no reported damage to Jewish sites from the June 2025 strikes, although Hamadan, the site of Esther's tomb, was among the cities hit, and Ynet reported that prayers in synagogues had stopped during the fighting. [cite:ir3_ynet_2025] In the 2026 war, an Israeli strike during the night of 6 to 7 April destroyed the Rafi'-Nia synagogue in central Tehran, built in 1958. No deaths were reported; two people were pulled from the rubble. [cite:ir3_wiki_rafinia] Sameh said "our Torah scrolls were left under the rubble." [cite:ir3_rns_synagogue] An unnamed Israeli official first said "Israel doesn't target synagogues"; the military later said it had struck "a senior commander in Khatam al-Anbiya," Iran's emergency military command, in an adjacent building, called the synagogue's destruction "collateral damage" and expressed regret. [cite:ir3_nw_assoc2026] [cite:ir3_newser_idf] A former Jewish member of parliament, Siamak Moreh Sedgh, said there had been no military activity at the site. [cite:ir3_wiki_rafinia]

Set side by side, the two records answer the question in the part's title. The recognition is real: a named place in the constitution, a seat in parliament, open synagogues and a community continuous since antiquity. The restriction is also real: an execution for "friendship with Israel" in 1979, an espionage trial built on televised confessions, state-sponsored Holocaust denial, and questioning and arrests in wartime. Neither cancels the other, and neither answers whether the wars of 2025 and 2026 were justified. The community's existence does not show that Iran's government posed no threat, and its treatment does not show that the strikes on Iran were waged on its behalf; no Israeli or US statement examined here gave the protection of Iran's Jews as a war aim. What the record does show is that the community's public voice is exercised inside a state at war, and that its members bore costs from both directions: questioning and arrest by their own government, and the loss of a synagogue to an Israeli strike.

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: The Atom
chapters.intro: Part Four sets out the two nuclear programmes at the centre of this volume, side by side and in the same register. The first is Iran's: a programme that began with American help under the Shah, was revived after the revolution, was exposed in 2002 as larger than Iran had declared, was found by the International Atomic Energy Agency to have included coordinated work relevant to a weapon until the end of 2003, was capped by the 2015 nuclear deal, and by 2025 had produced a stockpile of uranium enriched to 60 percent that no other state without nuclear weapons possesses. The second is Israel's: a reactor built at Dimona with French help in the late 1950s, an arsenal that independent researchers estimate at about 90 warheads, a policy of neither confirming nor denying it, and a treaty Israel has never joined. The part records what each government has said about its own programme and about the other's, and what the inspectors and intelligence agencies found. It is the baseline against which the predictions examined in Parts Five and Six are tested.
chapters.outro: Part Four established two records. Iran's programme began with an American reactor and the Shah's ambitions, was revived in secret with centrifuge designs from the Khan network, and was exposed in 2002; the IAEA found that Iran had concealed activities and had run a coordinated effort relevant to a nuclear weapon until the end of 2003, with some studies to 2009, and US intelligence judged in 2007 that the weapons work had halted in 2003. [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] [cite:ir4_wnn_pmd2015] [cite:hz11_wh_nie2007] After the 2015 deal's limits were abandoned, Iran enriched to 60 percent and by May 2025 held 408.6 kg of it, and on 12 June 2025 the IAEA Board found it in breach of its safeguards obligations; yet neither the agency nor US intelligence reported, before the June 2025 war, that Iran had decided to build a weapon. [cite:ir4_ap_may2025] [cite:ir4_aje_bog2025] [cite:ir4_trib_grossi] [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard] Israel, outside the treaty, built a reactor with French help, accepted only limited American visits in the 1960s, adopted a policy of opacity under a 1969 understanding with Nixon, imprisoned the technician who exposed Dimona for 18 years, and is estimated to hold about 90 warheads; it says it will join the NPT only after a regional peace. [cite:ir4_fas_israel] [cite:ow11_aca_opacity] [cite:ir4_amn_vanunu] [cite:ir4_ynet_sipri] [cite:ir4_aca_gc2010] With that baseline set, Part Five turns to the man whose warnings about Iran's bomb span more than three decades, and tests each of them against this record. [scene:ir5_predictions|Always a year away]

sections.h: Iran's Programme: From Atoms for Peace to 60 Percent
sections.html:
Iran's nuclear programme began as an American project. On 8 December 1953 President Eisenhower offered nuclear technology for civilian use to the world in his "Atoms for Peace" speech at the United Nations, and in 1957 the United States and the Shah's government signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement under that programme. In 1967 the United States supplied a five-megawatt research reactor for Tehran, together with highly enriched uranium to fuel it. [cite:ir4_brook_afp] The Tehran Research Reactor went critical in November 1967; it ran at first on uranium enriched to about 93 percent, the level used in weapons, and was converted to 20 percent fuel in 1993. [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] Iran signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) in July 1968, its parliament ratified it in February 1970, and the treaty entered into force for Iran on 5 March 1970. [cite:ir4_wiki_timeline] [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] As a party without nuclear weapons, Iran gave up the right to build them and accepted IAEA inspection of its nuclear material, in exchange for the treaty's promise of access to civilian technology.

The Shah's plans

In 1974 the Shah founded the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) and announced plans for about 23,000 megawatts of nuclear power, with some 23 plants and "the development of a full nuclear fuel cycle." [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] In 1976 he raised the AEOI's budget from $31 million to $1 billion. [cite:ir4_brook_afp] In 1974 Iran had lent $1 billion to France's Eurodif enrichment consortium, and the West German firm Kraftwerk Union had begun building a power plant at Bushehr. [cite:ir4_wiki_timeline] A National Security Decision Memorandum signed by Henry Kissinger on 22 April 1975 set out conditions under which the United States would approve the reprocessing of American-supplied fuel in Iran, preferably in a multinational plant. In July 1975 the US embassy in Tehran judged the Shah's motives "Not Entirely Clear" and suggested his interest in plutonium might be a way of keeping a weapons option open. A cooperation agreement was initialed in 1978 but never signed; the revolution "effectively nullified" it. [cite:ir4_nsa_ebb268]

Halt, revival and the Khan network

The revolution of 1979 froze the programme, and the Bushehr contract was terminated. [cite:ir4_wiki_timeline] It did not stay frozen. In 1987 Iran acquired technical drawings for the P-1 gas centrifuge, the machine used to enrich uranium, from the network run by the Pakistani metallurgist Abdul Qadeer Khan. [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] In 1990 Iran opened talks with the Soviet Union on finishing Bushehr, and in January 1995 it signed an $800 million contract with Russia's atomic energy ministry to complete the plant under IAEA safeguards. [cite:ir4_wiki_timeline] Iran's centrifuge work, by contrast, was not declared to the IAEA. How the US and Israel later used a copy of the P-1 to test the Stuxnet computer worm is told in Part Eight. [scene:ir8_shadow|The shadow war]

Disclosure, 2002–2006

On 14 August 2002, at a press conference in Washington, Alireza Jafarzadeh of the National Council of Resistance of Iran, the political arm of the exiled opposition group the People's Mojahedin (MEK), described two undeclared sites: a facility near Natanz, built under cover of a desert-eradication project through a front company, and a heavy-water plant at Arak run through another. [cite:ir4_iw_ncri] [cite:ir4_carn_noncomp] The NCRI is an opposition group with its own aims, and its claims were at the time allegations; the two sites it named are the enrichment plant and the heavy-water reactor that the 2015 nuclear deal later regulated by name. [cite:ir4_aca_jcpoa]

In November 2003 the IAEA reported many breaches of Iran's safeguards agreement and a "policy of concealment," while finding "no evidence" that Iran was trying to build a bomb. [cite:ir4_wiki_timeline] In October 2003 Iran had agreed with the British, French and German foreign ministers to suspend enrichment. [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] On 24 September 2005 the IAEA Board found Iran in non-compliance with its safeguards agreement by 22 votes to one, with 12 abstentions; on 4 February 2006 it referred Iran to the UN Security Council, which passed binding resolutions demanding suspension and imposing sanctions between 2006 and 2010, from Resolution 1696 to Resolution 1929. [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] Iran maintained throughout that its programme was peaceful and that enrichment was its right under the NPT.

What the inspectors and the analysts found about a weapon

In December 2007 the US National Intelligence Estimate judged with "high confidence" that Iran had halted its covert nuclear weapons programme in the autumn of 2003, and with "moderate confidence" that it had not restarted it as of mid-2007; the White House said the risk of Iran acquiring a weapon remained "a very serious problem."
