[cite:hz11_wh_nie2007] [cite:hz11_npr_nie2007] On 8 November 2011 the IAEA published an annex to its report on the "possible military dimensions" of Iran's programme. It described information it judged "consistent in terms of technical content, individuals and organizations involved, and time frames": a structured programme, the AMAD plan under Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, mostly halted in late 2003; a containment chamber for high-explosive tests at the Parchin military complex; work on a neutron initiator; and studies of fitting a nuclear-sized payload to the Shahab-3 missile. For the first time the Director General said Iran "might be continuing to pursue some of the activities." Iran rejected the documents as "forgeries and fabrications." [cite:ir4_sipri_annex2011] [cite:ir4_wiki_timeline]

The agency's final assessment, presented to its Board on 15 December 2015, closed the file. It found that a range of activities relevant to developing a nuclear explosive device had been conducted before the end of 2003 as a coordinated effort, that some continued afterwards but "did not advance beyond feasibility and scientific studies," and that there were "no credible indications" of such activities after 2009 and none of nuclear material being diverted. [cite:ir4_wnn_pmd2015] [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] Both readings that later circulated are therefore incomplete: the IAEA did not find that Iran had never had weapons work, and it did not find that weapons work continued after 2009.

From 3.67 to 60 percent

Iran began producing uranium enriched to 20 percent in February 2010, saying it was fuel for the Tehran Research Reactor, and from January 2012 also enriched to that level at Fordow; the interim deal of November 2013 rolled the 20 percent stockpile back. [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] [cite:ir4_wiki_timeline] The 2015 deal, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), capped enrichment at 3.67 percent and the stockpile at 300 kg for 15 years, and limited Iran to 5,060 operating first-generation centrifuges for ten years. [cite:ir4_aca_jcpoa] Its making and its killing are told in Part Seven. [scene:ir7_deal|The deal] After the United States left the deal in May 2018, Iran exceeded the 300 kg limit on 1 July 2019 and enriched to about 4.5 percent a week later. [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] Having resumed 20 percent enrichment, it began enriching to 60 percent at Natanz on 16 April 2021, days after sabotage at the site that Iran presented as the reason. [cite:ir4_ap_60pct]

By 17 May 2025 the IAEA counted 408.6 kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent, up 133.8 kg in three months, and 9,247.6 kg of enriched uranium in all. About 42 kg of 60 percent material is, in theory, enough for one weapon if enriched further to 90 percent. The agency called Iran "the only non-nuclear-weapon state to produce such material," a matter of "serious concern." Iran's foreign ministry and AEOI, in a joint statement, expressed "disappointment" with the report; Netanyahu's office said it showed Iran was "totally determined to complete its nuclear weapons program." [cite:ir4_ap_may2025] On 12 June 2025 the IAEA Board found Iran in non-compliance with its safeguards obligations by 19 votes to three, with 11 abstentions, citing "many failures" since 2019 and unexplained uranium traces at undeclared sites; it was the first such finding in almost 20 years. Iran called the resolution without "technical and legal basis" and announced a new enrichment site. [cite:ir4_aje_bog2025] Israel struck Iran the next morning. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] [scene:ir10_strikes|The Twelve Days] In a CNN interview during that war, the IAEA's Director General, Rafael Grossi, said the agency "did not have any proof of a systematic effort to move into a nuclear weapon." [cite:ir4_trib_grossi] The US intelligence community had told Congress in March 2025 that Iran was "not building a nuclear weapon," while recording that its stockpile was at its highest level. [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard]

The fatwa and the treaty

Iran's government has cited a religious ruling by Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei as proof of peaceful intent. The ruling is reported to have been issued orally in October 2003; Iran cited it in an official statement at the IAEA in August 2005, saying that "the production, stockpiling and use of nuclear weapons" were forbidden under Islam, and in 2010 Khamenei called their use "haraam." [cite:ir4_wiki_fatwa] Its status is contested. No written text has been published; the research group MEMRI concluded in 2012 that "no such fatwa ever existed," a finding the historian Juan Cole disputed. [cite:ir4_hudson_fatwa] Senior Iranian figures have also signalled that the position could change: in 2021 an intelligence minister compared Iran to a "cornered cat," and in 2025 the adviser Ali Larijani said Iran would have "no choice" but to build a weapon if attacked. [cite:ir4_wiki_fatwa] After the war of 2026 began, a bill to leave the NPT was tabled in Iran's parliament on 28 March 2026; the foreign ministry said Iran "has never sought, and does not seek, nuclear weapons." [cite:ir4_aca_npt2026] As of October 2026 the latest reporting found for this book, of 29 September, showed the debate continuing, the Kremlin publicly urging Iran to stay and no formal notice of withdrawal under the treaty's Article X; Iran remained a party. [cite:ir4_k24_npt] [cite:ir4_aca_npt2026]

sections.h: Dimona: Israel's Undeclared Arsenal
sections.html:
Israel's nuclear programme is older than Iran's enrichment programme by more than three decades, and it is the only one in the Middle East that, by every independent estimate, has produced weapons. Israel's government has never confirmed that it has them. This section sets out what the documented record shows about that arsenal, how the United States came to accept it, and how Israel explains its position, so that the comparison with Iran running through the rest of this volume rests on both records and not one.

A reactor built with France

On 3 October 1957 France and Israel signed a revised agreement for a 24-megawatt reactor at Dimona in the Negev, with an unwritten protocol for a chemical plant to separate plutonium from spent fuel. Construction was secret and outside any IAEA inspection. [cite:ir4_fas_israel] How the deal was made at the time of the Suez war, and how Washington discovered the site in 1960, are told in earlier volumes. [scene:cw3_sevres|Sèvres] [scene:cw4_dimona_discovery|How Washington found Dimona] By January 1963 a US National Intelligence Estimate, NIE 30-63, judged that the reactor at full power could produce plutonium for one or two weapons a year. [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters]

Inspections that were not inspections

President Kennedy pressed Ben-Gurion and then Levi Eshkol for regular American visits to Dimona, in what the editors of the declassified letters call "the toughest American-Israeli confrontation over the Israeli nuclear program." [cite:rs_cw5_nsa_letters] [scene:s11b|The battle of the letters, 1963] The visits that followed were not IAEA inspections and not inspections in the treaty sense. US scientists visited Dimona seven times during the 1960s; Israel controlled the timing and agenda of each visit, and, according to later accounts summarised by the Federation of American Scientists, installed false control-room panels and bricked over lifts and corridors to hide parts of the plant. The visitors reported no weapons-related activity, such as a reprocessing plant. [cite:ir4_fas_israel] The Johnson administration ran the visits alongside the first sales of American combat aircraft to Israel. [scene:s11d|Skyhawks and Dimona, 1966] It is "widely reported," in the FAS summary, that Israel had two bombs by the June war of 1967. [cite:ir4_fas_israel] In November 1968, in the conditions attached to the sale of Phantom jets, Israel's ambassador Yitzhak Rabin repeated the formula Israel still uses: that it "will not be the first power in the Middle East to introduce nuclear weapons." [cite:ow1_jvl_phantomconds]

The 1969 understanding and the policy of opacity

The visits ended under President Nixon. At a White House meeting on 26 September 1969, according to the historian Avner Cohen's reconstruction, Nixon and Prime Minister Golda Meir reached an understanding: the United States would end its visits to Dimona and stop pressing Israel to sign the NPT, and Israel would not declare, publicise or test its arsenal. The written record of that understanding, reportedly kept by Kissinger and Rabin, has not been made public. [cite:ow11_aca_opacity] The Johnson administration's "protracted" efforts to bring Israel into the treaty had failed. [cite:ow11_aca_opacity] The Hebrew word for the resulting policy is amimut, opacity or ambiguity. Cohen describes it as a posture "credible enough to generate effects of deterrence" yet "opaque enough to maintain political distance": enough evidence to deter enemies and enough silence "to allow friends to look the other way." [cite:ow11_aca_opacity] What that silence means for American non-proliferation law, under which aid can be cut to states that traffic in enrichment technology outside safeguards, is examined in The One-Way Mirror. [scene:ow11_exceptions|Laws applied differently]

Vanunu

The fullest public evidence about Dimona came from a former technician there, Mordechai Vanunu. On 30 September 1986 agents of the Israeli government seized him in Italy and took him secretly to Israel; on 5 October the London Sunday Times published his account and photographs of the plant. [cite:ir4_amn_vanunu] His information indicated that Dimona was producing about 40 kg of plutonium a year, and analysts concluded from it that Israel had between 100 and 200 weapons; the FAS's own satellite-based analysis suggests a rate closer to 20 kg. [cite:ir4_fas_israel] [cite:ir4_aca_vanunu] He was tried behind closed doors, convicted of treason and aggravated espionage, and sentenced to 18 years. [cite:ir4_amn_vanunu] He served the full term, more than 11 years of it in solitary confinement; Amnesty International said in 1996 that holding him alone in a cell for ten years was "cruel, inhuman and degrading." [cite:ir4_aca_vanunu] [cite:ir4_amn_vanunu] On his release on 21 April 2004 he was barred from leaving Israel and his movements and foreign contacts were restricted. Israel's stated reason, given to Amnesty in 1996 and again in 2004, was that he might still reveal secrets; Vanunu said he had none left to reveal. [cite:ir4_amn_vanunu] [cite:ir4_aca_vanunu]

How many weapons

No official figure exists, so every number is an estimate. In the late 1990s the US intelligence community estimated 75 to 130 weapons; the FAS judges claims of up to 400 exaggerated and calculates that Israel's plutonium production would support at least 100 weapons but probably not many more than 200. [cite:ir4_fas_israel] The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimated in June 2024 that Israel holds about 90 warheads: about 30 for aircraft and up to 50 for Jericho ballistic missiles, with its German-built Dolphin submarines possibly giving it a sea-based option, which Germany denies. SIPRI also reported that Israel appeared to be upgrading the plutonium facility at Dimona. [cite:ir4_ynet_sipri] [cite:hm_almon_idf] Israel neither confirms nor denies any of it. [cite:ir4_ynet_sipri]

Outside the treaty, and the resolutions

Israel has never signed the NPT, so it has made none of the commitments Iran made in 1968, and its reactor at Dimona has never been under IAEA safeguards. [cite:ir4_fas_israel] [cite:ow11_aca_opacity] [cite:ir4_unp_res8067] The UN General Assembly has repeatedly called on it to join. Resolution 80/67, adopted on 1 December 2025 by 145 votes to six with 30 abstentions, called on Israel to accede to the treaty "without further delay," renounce nuclear weapons and place its unsafeguarded facilities under full-scope IAEA safeguards; Israel and the United States were among the six states voting against. [cite:ir4_unp_res8067] On 18 September 2009 the IAEA General Conference, by 49 votes to 45, adopted its first resolution in nearly two decades on "Israeli nuclear capabilities," calling on Israel to accede to the NPT and place all its facilities under safeguards; a similar resolution failed in 2010 by 51 votes to 46 after the United States lobbied against it. [cite:ir4_iaea_gc53] [cite:ir4_aca_gc2010]

Israel's stated position is that joining the treaty must follow, not precede, a comprehensive regional peace. Shaul Chorev, director-general of the Israel Atomic Energy Commission, told the IAEA in 2010 that singling Israel out diverted attention from Iran and Syria, "the real cases of dangerous proliferation and non-compliance." [cite:ir4_aca_gc2010] In 2018 Israel rejected the General Assembly's annual resolution "in its entirety," noting that four states of the region that had joined the NPT, Iran, Iraq, Syria and Libya, had "violated their NPT obligations." [cite:ir4_unidir_eov2018] The US position in 2010, in the words of its ambassador to the IAEA, was that defeating the resolution "preserved the opportunity for progress" toward a regional conference. [cite:ir4_aca_gc2010]

The asymmetry, stated plainly

The two records differ in kind. Iran signed the treaty, accepted inspection, was found by the IAEA to have concealed activities and to have conducted coordinated weapons-relevant work until 2003, and in June 2025 was found in breach of its safeguards obligations; by the agency's count it held more highly enriched uranium than any state without weapons, and it has no weapon. [scene:ir4_programme|Iran's programme] Israel never signed, has never opened Dimona to IAEA inspection, and by independent estimates holds about 90 weapons. Israel's governments argue that the comparison is false: a state that broke a treaty it signed, tests ballistic missiles able to carry nuclear warheads and backs armed groups presents a different danger from a state that never signed and has never tested or declared. [cite:ir4_aca_gc2010] [cite:ir4_unidir_eov2018] [scene:ir9_record|Iran's own record] Most UN member states, voting year after year, have held that both must be inside the same rules. [cite:ir4_unp_res8067] Which argument is stronger is a judgement for the reader; that the asymmetry exists is not in dispute. Why Israel has acted to keep a nuclear monopoly in the region, from Iraq in 1981 to Iran in 2025, is examined in Part Thirteen. [scene:ir13_why|Why Iran?]

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: Always a Year Away
chapters.intro: Part Five tests the claim at the centre of this volume: that Benjamin Netanyahu warned for more than three decades that Iran was weeks, months or a few years from a nuclear bomb, and that the bomb never came. It begins with his American years, from MIT and the Boston Consulting Group to the Jonathan Institute's terrorism conferences, the embassy in Washington and the United Nations, and asks what he warned about then. It sets out every dated statement on Iran's nuclear timeline that could be traced, from the reported Knesset remark of 1992 to the war statements of 2025 and 2026, each with its words, date and venue, and notes where versions differ or no source could be found. It then scores them against what followed, from the US intelligence estimates and IAEA findings to the testimony of 2025, and separates the estimates that carried a date from the warnings that were conditional, before setting Israel's argument that pressure and sabotage delayed the programme beside the critics' charge of crying wolf.
chapters.outro: Part Five found that Netanyahu's warnings about Iran began as warnings about terrorism, with Iran named as one state sponsor among several in 1986, and that his first dated estimate of an Iranian bomb is reported from 1992. [cite:ir5_nyrb_1986] [cite:hz11b_week_1992] Every estimate he gave with a date and no condition, in 1992, 1995 and 2009, passed without a bomb, though each was framed as capability rather than a weapon, and US intelligence had judged by 2007 that Iran's weapons work had stopped in 2003; the IAEA found none after 2009. [cite:hz11b_intercept_wolf] [cite:hz11_wh_nie2007] [cite:ir5_iaea_gov2015] His later warnings, at the UN in 2012 and on the first day of the 2025 war, were conditional, and the conditions changed before they could be tested; on Iran's growing stockpile the record bore him out, while on Iran's intent the US Director of National Intelligence and the IAEA's director general found no decision to build a weapon. [cite:ir5_li_un2012] [cite:ir5_dcnf_jun2025] [cite:ir4_ap_may2025] [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard] [cite:ir5_tbs_grossi] Whether pressure and sabotage delayed the bomb, as Israel argues, or the warnings outran the evidence, as its critics say, remains an argument both sides can support from the record. [cite:ir5_ap_dagan2011] [cite:ir5_ap_jun2026] Part Six turns to the Israeli officials, intelligence chiefs among them, who said otherwise at the time. [scene:ir6_officials|The other voices]

sections.h: The American Years
sections.html:
The warnings tested in this part came, for more than three decades, from one man. Benjamin Netanyahu built much of his early public career in the United States, and the subjects he first warned Americans about were terrorism, the states that sponsored it and the Soviet bloc behind them. Iran was on that list from the start, as a sponsor of terrorism. A dated warning that Iran was a set number of years from a nuclear bomb came later, in 1992. This section sets out what the record shows of the years before that, so that the predictions in the next section can be read against where they began. [cite:ir5_jvl_bio] [cite:ir5_nyrb_1986]

After his military service Netanyahu studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he took a bachelor's degree in architecture and a master's in management studies; reference works date the master's to 1976. He then worked as a consultant at the Boston Consulting Group, from 1976 to 1978 by one directory's account. [cite:ir5_jvl_bio] [cite:ir5_enc_bio] Accounts of the next step differ in their dates. He became executive director of the Jonathan Institute, a foundation named for his brother Yonatan, who was killed in 1976 commanding the rescue of hostages held at Entebbe after an airliner was hijacked; reference works give its founding as 1976, 1977 or 1980, and one lists him as its director from 1978 to 1980. Between 1980 and 1982 he was a manager at Rim, a furniture maker in Jerusalem. [cite:ir5_enc_bio] [cite:ir5_lobelog_ji]

The institute's work set the frame of his early career. In 1979 it held an international conference on terrorism in Jerusalem, and in 1984 a second one in Washington, D.C.; Netanyahu organised both. [cite:ir5_jvl_bio] The future President George H. W. Bush attended the Jerusalem conference, as did people from the American Enterprise Institute, the Center for Strategic and International Studies and Commentary magazine; the proceedings were published in 1981 as International Terrorism: Challenge and Response. The Washington meeting, by one later account, gave weight to "the relationship between Islam and terror." Netanyahu's own framing was broad: he wrote that the battle against terrorism was part of a larger struggle "between the forces of civilization and the forces of barbarism." [cite:ir5_lobelog_ji] [cite:ir5_enc_bio]

In 1982 Netanyahu joined Israel's embassy in Washington as deputy chief of mission, the second post in the embassy, serving under Ambassador Moshe Arens until 1984. He was then Israel's ambassador to the United Nations in New York for four years, from 1984 to 1988. [cite:ir5_jvl_bio] [cite:ir5_enc_bio] In 1988 he returned to Israel, was elected to the Knesset for the Likud on 1 November and became deputy foreign minister. [cite:ir5_enc_bio] [cite:ir5_jvl_bio]

What He Warned About Then

The fullest statement of his views from those years is Terrorism: How the West Can Win, a collection of papers from the 1984 conference that he edited, published in 1986. Reviewing it in The New York Review of Books in August 1986, the historian Shaul Bakhash summarised its case: international terrorism "poses a mortal danger to civilized society," it is aimed mainly at Western democracies, and it is sustained by an international network of groups backed by "terrorist states," "most notably Syria, Libya, Iran, and South Yemen," with the Soviet Union and its satellites as the presence behind them. The remedy it proposed was Western cooperation: shared intelligence, sanctions and, if necessary, force. [cite:ir5_nyrb_1986] The review does not mention nuclear weapons. Iran appears in the book as one state sponsor among four, beside Libya, Syria and South Yemen. [cite:ir5_nyrb_1986] The Palestine Liberation Organization appears as a group that, by one contributor's account cited in the review, trained fighters from about a dozen countries. [cite:ir5_nyrb_1986]

One remark from those years does join Iran's leadership to the bomb. An undated video excerpt, published by the media-clip service Grabien under a headline dating it to 1986, shows Netanyahu arguing that if such regimes came to believe they could act freely, "you may very well find yourself in a world in a few years from now with a Gaddafi or Khomeini with nuclear weapons." [cite:ir5_grabien_khomeini] Ruhollah Khomeini died in June 1989, so the remark must be earlier than that, but its exact date and venue are not given and this book could not establish them. It is also a different kind of statement from those that followed. It names no programme and no date; it is a conditional warning about what might happen if terrorism went unpunished, with Iran's leader named beside Libya's.

The record examined for this book therefore supports a plain statement. Before 1992 Netanyahu treated Iran as a sponsor of terrorism, one of several, and at least once raised the general danger of its leader gaining nuclear weapons; no estimate from him of how many years Iran was from a bomb has been found before his reported remark in the Knesset in 1992. The 1992 remark itself rests on retrospectives, not on a Knesset record found by this book, and the next section begins there. [cite:hz11b_week_1992] [cite:hz11b_intercept_wolf] [cite:hz11b_aje_rhetoric] [scene:ir5_predictions|The dated predictions]

sections.h: Thirty-Four Years of Dates
sections.html:
Part Eleven of the Hezbollah volume set five of Netanyahu's warnings beside the intelligence of their day. [scene:hz11_pattern|The Hezbollah Architecture: the thesis and the test] This section gives the fuller list, from 1992 to 2026, each in his own words where a text exists, with the date, the venue and what kind of claim it was. A warning that Iran "could" have a bomb if nothing changed is not the same claim as a statement that it "will" have one by a given year, and the test in the next section depends on keeping the two apart. Where only later retellings exist, or where versions differ, that is said.

1992 to 2002: Years, a Deadline and Iraq

The first dated estimate is reported from 1992, when Netanyahu was a member of the Knesset: Iran was three to five years from being able to produce a nuclear weapon, and the threat had to be "uprooted by an international front headed by the U.S." The remark is repeated in retrospectives by The Intercept, The Week and Al Jazeera; The Week traces it to a Christian Science Monitor timeline, and none of them cites a Knesset record, which this book did not find. [cite:hz11b_intercept_wolf] [cite:hz11b_week_1992] [cite:hz11b_aje_rhetoric] His 1995 book Fighting Terrorism gave a similar estimate, but its wording is disputed. Mondoweiss quotes page 121 as saying that "the best estimates at this time place Iran between three and five years away from possessing the prerequisites required"; The Week renders it as "five to seven years at most." [cite:hz11b_mw_book] [cite:hz11b_week_1992] On the first reading the claim concerned the prerequisites for a bomb, not a bomb.

On 10 July 1996, now prime minister, Netanyahu told a joint meeting of Congress that Iran was "the most dangerous" of the region's regimes and that its or Iraq's acquiring nuclear weapons "could presage catastrophic consequences." The sentence later quoted as a prediction, "the deadline for attaining this goal is getting extremely close," referred to the goal he had just set out: preventing the nuclear arming of such states, under American leadership. [cite:hz11b_jvl_1996] It set no date for an Iranian bomb. Versions in circulation that have him telling Congress Iran would have weapons "within a decade," or in "8–10 years," do not appear in the text. On 12 September 2002, out of office, he told a House committee that Saddam Hussein "is seeking and is working and is advancing toward the development of nuclear weapons" and that removing him "will have enormous positive reverberations on the region"; on Iran he said, "I don't know that Iran has nuclear weapons." [cite:hz11b_gpo_2002] That testimony was about Iraq. Two years later the Iraq Survey Group reported that Saddam had ended Iraq's nuclear programme after the 1991 Gulf War. [cite:hz11b_cnn_duelfer]

2009 to 2015: One or Two Years, a Red Line, a Bad Deal

In February 2009, weeks before he returned to office, Netanyahu told a visiting congressional delegation that Iran was "probably one or two years away," according to a US embassy cable (09TELAVIV457) later published by WikiLeaks; The Intercept, which quotes the cable only in that phrase, gives the end point as "weapons capability," and Al Jazeera as "nuclear capability," not a finished bomb. [cite:hz11b_intercept_wolf] [cite:ir5a_intercept] [cite:ir5a_aje_gallery] A second cable, from December 2009, as The Intercept reported it, records him telling another delegation that "Iran has the capability now to make one bomb," a statement about material on hand rather than a date. [cite:ir5a_intercept] In 2012, by The Intercept's account of a Ynet report, he said in closed talks that Iran was "a few months away" from nuclear capability. [cite:ir5a_intercept] On NBC's Meet the Press on 16 September 2012 he said Iran was "six month away from being about 90 percent of having the enriched uranium for an atom bomb." [cite:ir5_npr_mtp2012]

On 27 September 2012 he made the argument at the UN General Assembly with a drawing of a bomb. Iran had completed the first stage of enrichment, he said, and was "70% of the way there"; "by next spring, at most by next summer, at current enrichment rates," it would finish medium enrichment and move to the final stage, and "from there it's only a few months, possibly a few weeks," before it had enough enriched uranium for a first bomb. "A red line should be drawn right here," he said, marking the line before the final stage. [cite:ir5_li_un2012] Ynet's report of the speech as delivered gives the conditional the same way, "by next summer, at current enrichment rates," and his argument: "Red lines don't lead to war, red lines prevent war." [cite:ir5_ynet_un2012] The UN's own summary of the speech records the second stage as complete "by next summer at the latest." [cite:hz11b_un_2012] The claim was explicitly conditional on the rate of enrichment, and its subject was a quantity of uranium, not a finished weapon.

On 3 March 2015 he addressed a joint meeting of Congress again, to oppose the nuclear agreement then being negotiated; the White House made its displeasure plain. "It doesn't block Iran's path to the bomb; it paves Iran's path to the bomb," he said, and warned that the deal would "all but guarantee" that Iran obtained nuclear weapons. More than four dozen Democrats in the House and Senate had said beforehand that they would not attend, and Vice President Biden was abroad; President Obama, by The Washington Times's account, read the text afterwards and found nothing new in it. [cite:ir5_wt_2015] [cite:ir5_ap_2015] [cite:ir5a_wt_obama] This was a warning about the deal's design and its expiry dates, not a forecast with a date. Part Seven sets out the deal and its fate. [scene:ir7_deal|The deal]

2018 to 2026: An Archive, Two Wars and No Date

On 30 April 2018 Netanyahu presented in Tel Aviv what he said were about 55,000 pages and 183 discs from Iran's secret "Project Amad," taken by Israeli intelligence from a warehouse in Tehran, and said they proved Iran had lied about seeking weapons. The documents appeared to date from the early 2000s; Iran denied seeking nuclear weapons, and its foreign minister, Mohammad Javad Zarif, called Netanyahu "the boy who can't stop crying wolf." [cite:hz11b_cbs_archive] The presentation was a claim about the past, not a timeline. Accounts that place it at the UN are mistaken.

On 13 June 2025, as Israel's air force struck Iran in the operation it called Rising Lion, Netanyahu said in a recorded statement that Iran had produced "enough highly enriched uranium for nine atom bombs" and had taken "steps to weaponize" it. "If not stopped, Iran could produce a nuclear weapon in a very short time," he said. "It could be a year. It could be within a few months, less than a year." [cite:ir5_dcnf_jun2025] [cite:ir5_ani_jun2025] The day before, the IAEA's Board of Governors had found Iran in breach of its safeguards obligations for the first time in almost two decades. [cite:ir5_aj_iaea2025] On 24 June he declared victory: "For decades, I have promised you that Iran would not have nuclear weapons." [cite:ir5_pmo_jun2025]

For the second war no comparable date has been found. Meeting President Trump at Mar-a-Lago on 29 December 2025, Netanyahu raised a possible second round of strikes and reviewed Iran's nuclear status, but Israel's warnings by then centred on its missiles; Axios reported no timeline for a bomb. [cite:ir5_axios_dec2025] His statement announcing the joint US–Israeli strikes of 28 February 2026 spoke of removing "the existential threat" and said Iran "must never be allowed to arm itself with nuclear weapons," but gave no estimate of when it might. [cite:ir5_jvl_feb2026] A circulating version in which he said "months, or even weeks" before the 2026 war could not be traced to any dated source and is not used here. On 21 June 2026, at the JNS International Policy Summit, he looked back: "Had we not acted in Operation Rising Lion and then in Operation Roaring Lion, Iran would have had atomic bombs. And let me tell you something, they would have used them." [cite:ir5_ap_jun2026] [cite:ir5a_ap_jns]

sections.h: The Fair Test
sections.html:
The thesis tested in this part is that the warnings were false alarms: that Netanyahu said for more than thirty years that Iran was close to a bomb and it never came. A fair test sorts the statements in the previous section into three kinds before scoring them. Some were dated estimates with no condition attached: Iran was three to five years away in 1992 and 1995, "probably one or two years away" in 2009. None of these was a date for a finished bomb: as reported, they measured the time to the ability to produce a weapon, to its "prerequisites" or to "weapons capability," terms none of them defined. Some were conditional thresholds: Iran would reach a stated point "at current enrichment rates," or "if not stopped." The rest were warnings with no date at all: the 1996 deadline for action, the 2015 case against the deal, the 2018 archive and the 2026 war statement. Each kind can be tested only on its own terms. [scene:ir5_predictions|The dated predictions]

The dated estimates passed without an Iranian bomb. No Iranian weapon existed by 1997, by 2000 or by 2011. Because they were framed as capability rather than a bomb, scoring them strictly on their own terms depends on what capability meant; what the record does show is that the weapons work they implied was halted, not advancing. The US intelligence community judged in its National Intelligence Estimate of December 2007, "with high confidence," that Iran had halted its covert weapons programme in the autumn of 2003, and with moderate confidence that it had not restarted it by mid-2007. [cite:hz11_wh_nie2007] The IAEA's final assessment of December 2015 found that Iran had carried out a range of activities relevant to a nuclear explosive device "prior to the end of 2003 as a coordinated effort," that some continued after 2003 but "did not advance beyond feasibility and scientific studies," and that there were no credible indications of such work after 2009. [cite:ir5_iaea_gov2015] Those findings show that the weapons work was real, which Iran denies, and that it stopped years before the 2009 estimate was given. The 2002 claim about Iraq failed outright: the Iraq Survey Group found that Saddam had ended his nuclear programme after 1991. [cite:hz11b_cnn_duelfer] Part Four sets out the programme's own history. [scene:ir4_programme|The programme]

The conditional warnings cannot be scored the same way, because the conditions changed. When Netanyahu spoke at the UN in September 2012, Iran had been enriching to 20 per cent at Fordow since January. The interim agreement of November 2013 rolled that stockpile back, and from 20 January 2014 the IAEA confirmed that Iran had stopped enriching to 20 per cent. [cite:ir4_wiki_timeline] [cite:ir4_aca_timeline] [cite:ir7_aca_jpoa] Iran did not cross his red line in 2013, but whether it would have done so at the 2012 rates cannot be known. A Mossad assessment of October 2012, leaked in 2015, said Iran "is not performing the activity necessary to produce weapons"; The Times of Israel argued that the two documents differed over speed, not direction. [cite:hz11_rferl_spycables] [cite:hz11_toi_spycables] The 2025 warning is harder still to test, because the strikes it announced followed at once. Its premise about material was accurate: the IAEA reported 408.6 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 per cent in May 2025, and estimated 440.9 kilograms by 13 June; on 12 June its Board found Iran in breach of its safeguards obligations. [cite:ir4_ap_may2025] [cite:ir5_ynet_sep2026] [cite:ir5_aj_iaea2025] Its premise about intent was not supported by the agencies that watched the programme. In March 2025 the US Director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, said the intelligence community "continues to assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon." After President Trump said on 20 June that she was wrong, she wrote that her testimony had been taken out of context and that Iran could produce a weapon "within weeks to months, if they decide to finalize the assembly," a statement about capacity that left the question of a decision where her testimony had put it. On 19 June the IAEA's director general, Rafael Grossi, said, "We did not find in Iran elements to indicate that there is an active, systematic plan to build a nuclear weapon." [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard] [cite:ir6_ap_gabbard2025] [cite:ir5_tbs_grossi] A senior Israeli official later told Ynet, anonymously and in an account Ynet could not verify, that Iran's "weaponization group was very far from developing a nuclear weapon." [cite:ir5_ynet_sep2026] Iran maintained throughout that its programme was peaceful, and its diplomats cite a fatwa by Ali Khamenei against nuclear weapons. [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] [cite:ir5a_ap_jns]

The warnings without dates are tests of argument, not of timing. The 2015 claim that the deal "paves Iran's path to the bomb" was never run to its end: the United States left the agreement in 2018, and Part Seven traces what Iran did after that. [scene:ir7_withdrawal|The withdrawal] Before the 2026 war President Trump said Iran was rebuilding its programme; the IAEA said it had no evidence that Iran had resumed enrichment. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] Netanyahu's own statement that day gave no date. [cite:ir5_jvl_feb2026]

Two Readings of the Same Record

Israel's government reads the record as a series of dangers that were real and were stopped. The argument has documentary support. The 2007 estimate itself judged that Iran's halt had been "directed primarily in response to increasing international scrutiny and pressure." [cite:ir5_wh_nie2007] In January 2011 the departing head of the Mossad, Meir Dagan, was reported as saying that Iran would not be able to build a bomb before 2015 because its programme had been delayed by unspecified "measures." [cite:ir5_ap_dagan2011] The Stuxnet cyberattack, a US operation begun in 2006 to which Israel's Unit 8200 contributed, put out of action nearly a thousand of Iran's five thousand centrifuges in its last attack, by the account of the New York Times. [cite:ow3_sw_sanger] In June 2026 Netanyahu put the argument in its strongest form: without the two wars, "Iran would have had atomic bombs." [cite:ir5_ap_jun2026] On this reading the warnings did not fail; they were the reason the bomb never arrived.

The critics read the same record as a warning repeated beyond its evidence. The Intercept's Murtaza Hussain titled his 2015 survey of the statements "Benjamin Netanyahu's Long History of Crying Wolf About Iran's Nuclear Weapons." [cite:hz11b_intercept_wolf] Iran's foreign minister used the same image in 2018. [cite:hz11b_cbs_archive] Jon Hoffman of the Cato Institute argued in 2024 that Netanyahu had pressed for decades for American military action against Iran and had domestic political reasons to widen conflict; that is an argument about motive, and Part Thirteen weighs it. [cite:hz12_cato_hoffman] [scene:ir13_why|Why Iran] In June 2026 the Associated Press set his claim of averted bombs against the public evidence: Iran had been "months or years away" from a usable weapon before either war, and there was no evidence it had decided to build one. [cite:ir5_ap_jun2026] Dagan himself, the source of the delay argument, also said Israel "should not hurry to attack." [cite:ir5_ap_dagan2011]

Both readings have a weak point. Israel's cannot be disproved: any warning that is followed by no bomb can be credited to the pressure that followed it, and the halt the US agencies identified came in 2003, before Stuxnet, the assassinations of Iran's scientists and the strikes of 2025. The critics' reading cannot account for everything either: the weapons work of the years before 2004 was real, the 60 per cent stockpile was, in the IAEA's words of May 2025, unique among states without nuclear weapons, and the agencies that rejected the dates also recorded the capacity. [cite:ir4_ap_may2025] [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard] What the record shows as a pattern is narrower than either. Every dated estimate that Netanyahu gave without conditions passed without an Iranian bomb, though each was framed as capability rather than a finished weapon. His later warnings moved from dates to thresholds and to capacity, and on capacity the record largely bore him out. On intent, which the 2025 war was fought over, the American and international agencies of the time did not.

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: The Other Voices
chapters.intro: Part Six asks whether the warnings tested in Part Five were one man's or a state's. It sets out the dated statements of other Israeli leaders, generals and intelligence services on how close Iran was to a bomb and whether Israel should strike, from Shimon Peres in 1992 to the army's case for war in June 2025, and the American officials who echoed them. It then gives the other side of the same establishment: Mossad and Shin Bet chiefs and army commanders who disputed the timelines or warned against an attack, the orders to prepare strikes in 2010 and 2011 that some of them resisted, the leaked Mossad paper of 2012, and the US intelligence record from the 2007 estimate to the hearings of 2025 and 2026. Forecasts, claims about capability and arguments about policy are kept apart throughout.
chapters.outro: Part Six found that Netanyahu's short timelines were not his alone: Peres forecast Iranian warheads by 1999, an Israeli estimate reportedly put a weapon by March 2011, Barak's window for stopping Iran and the Mossad's estimate of capability ran to 2010 and 2011, and Ya'alon's three years ran out as Iran accepted the interim deal, none of them followed by a bomb. [cite:ir6_csm_peres1992] [cite:ir6_csm_yaalon2010] [cite:ir6_jta_samore2010] Later warnings, from Gantz's ten weeks in 2021 to the army's "point of no return" in 2025, concerned capability and rested on enrichment that was real, though the intelligence behind the 2025 claim was not published. [cite:ir6_toi_gantz2021] [cite:ir6_afp_idf2025] The same establishment produced the sharpest dissent: Dagan, Pardo, Diskin, Ashkenazi, Ayalon and Halevy disputed the timelines, the "existential" language or the case for a strike, and two orders to prepare an attack, in 2010 and 2011, were questioned by the chiefs who received them: Ashkenazi and Dagan resisted the first by their associates' account, and Pardo checked the second's legality. [cite:ir6_arabnews_dagan2011] [cite:ir6_ahram_pardo2011] [cite:ir6_fox_diskin2012] [cite:ir6_cbs_uvda2012] [cite:ir6_bg_pardo2018] US intelligence judged from 2007 to 2025 that Iran had not decided to build a weapon, while recording its growing stockpile, and Obama's defence chiefs argued in public against a strike. [cite:hz11_wh_nie2007] [cite:ir6_aca_clapper2012] [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard] [cite:ir6_usip_panetta2011] [cite:ir6_csm_dempsey2012] Part Seven turns to the one policy most of these dissenters came to support: the 2015 nuclear deal, and how it was killed. [scene:ir7_deal|The deal and its killing]

sections.h: The Chorus: Other Israeli Officials on the Timeline
sections.html:
Part Five set Benjamin Netanyahu's dated warnings against what followed. [scene:ir5_predictions|Always a year away] He was not the only Israeli leader to put a date on Iran's bomb, and the same test has to be applied to the others. This section collects the dated statements of other Israeli leaders, generals and intelligence services on how close Iran was to a weapon and whether Israel should strike. Each is given with its date and venue, and with whether it was framed as a condition ("if it decides") or as a flat forecast, because a conditional warning that did not come true is not the same failure as a dated prediction that did not.

Shimon Peres: The First Date and the Last Word

The earliest dated Israeli forecast found for this volume came from Shimon Peres, then foreign minister in Yitzhak Rabin's government. In 1992 he told French television, as The Christian Science Monitor's timeline of the warnings records it, that Iran was set to have nuclear warheads by 1999. He called Iran "the greatest threat and greatest problem in the Middle East" because it "seeks the nuclear option while holding a highly dangerous stance of extreme religious militancy." [cite:ir6_csm_peres1992] The same year Netanyahu, then an opposition member of the Knesset, was reported to put Iran three to five years away. [scene:ir5_predictions|Netanyahu's 1992 forecast] 1999 passed with no Iranian warhead; the United States intelligence community later judged that Iran had worked on weapons design until 2003 and then halted it. [cite:hz11_wh_nie2007]

Peres kept up the warning for fifteen years. As president, in a written statement on 18 October 2007, he compared the moment to the failure to stop Stalin and Hitler: "We are nearing a similar turn of events with Ahmadinejad. The world must open its eyes before it is too late." [cite:ir6_ynet_peres2007] Yet when the question became whether Israel should strike alone, Peres was among the first senior figures to say publicly that it should not. On 17 August 2012, at the height of the debate over an Israeli attack, he told Channel 2: "We can delay the Iranian nuclear plan, but it is clear to us that we need to go with the United States," adding that President Obama was determined to stop Iran "and Israel cannot do it." Members of Netanyahu's coalition answered him directly; the minister Gilad Erdan called the remarks "an unabashed and explicit attack on the official policy of the government of the State of Israel." [cite:ir6_jta_peres2012] Peres shows in one career what this part finds across the establishment: agreement that the programme was a danger, disagreement over what to do.

Ehud Barak: Windows, and the "Zone of Immunity"

Ehud Barak, defence minister from 2007 to 2013, was Netanyahu's partner in the planning of a strike, and his statements show both a date and a doubt. According to US diplomatic cables published by WikiLeaks and summarised by AFP in December 2010, Barak told American congressional delegations in June 2009 that there was a window of six to eighteen months in which stopping Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons "might still be viable"; at the same meeting the Mossad estimated Iran would have "the technological capability to build a nuclear weapon" by 2010 or 2011. [cite:ir6_csm_yaalon2010] [cite:ir6a_csm_barak] In August 2010 US officials said they had persuaded their Israeli counterparts that Iran was at least a year from a bomb; Gary Samore of the National Security Council told The New York Times that Iran's technical problems gave it at least a year of "dash" time, and Israel was reported to have previously believed Iran could have a weapon by the following March. [cite:ir6_jta_samore2010] No weapon followed. Of these, only the reported Israeli estimate of a weapon by March 2011 was a forecast of a bomb; Barak's window was a judgment about when prevention might stop being viable, and the Mossad's was an estimate of capability.

Barak did not, however, describe Iran as a threat to Israel's existence. In an interview with Yedioth Ahronoth in September 2009 he said: "I am not among those who believe Iran is an existential issue for Israel." [cite:ir6_jta_barak2009] His argument for acting was about time rather than survival. By early 2012 he had given it a name. Speaking in Tokyo on 18 February 2012, he urged tighter sanctions "before the Iranians fully enter this immunity zone," meaning the point at which so much of the programme was buried deep enough, at sites such as Fordow, that an Israeli attack could no longer reach it. [cite:ir6_ahram_barak2012] The zone of immunity was a claim about Israel's military reach, not about Iran's intent, and it could be true even if Iran never decided to build a weapon. The US defence secretary, Leon Panetta, said the same week that Israel had "indicated they're considering" a strike and that Washington had "indicated our concerns." [cite:ir6_ahram_barak2012]

Moshe Ya'alon: A Date Pushed Back

Moshe Ya'alon, a former chief of staff who was strategic affairs minister in 2010 and defence minister from 2013 to 2016, gave the clearest example of an Israeli estimate being revised in public. On 29 December 2010 he told Israeli public radio that Iran "does not have the ability to create nuclear weapons by itself at the moment," that "technological challenges and difficulties" had "postponed the timetable," and that a weapon was "likely to happen in the next three years, if it is successful." [cite:ir6_csm_yaalon2010] He did not name the difficulties; the report noted that the Stuxnet computer worm had struck the enrichment plant at Natanz the year before (see Part Eight). [scene:ir8_shadow|The shadow war] His three years ran out at the end of 2013, the month after Iran signed the interim agreement that froze much of its programme (see Part Seven). [scene:ir7_deal|The deal]

Gantz, Bennett and Lapid: The Threshold Years

Benny Gantz, chief of staff from 2011 to 2015, gave Haaretz in April 2012 the most reassuring assessment any serving Israeli commander offered in those years. "The Iranian leadership is composed of very rational people," he said, and of Ali Khamenei: "I don't think he will want to go the extra mile." Barak answered within days that Iran's leaders were not "rational in the Western sense of the word," and an aide to Gantz said his words had been "taken out of context" and that "they both view Iran in the same way." [cite:ir6_csm_gantz2012] [cite:ir6a_csm_gantz] Nine years later, as defence minister, Gantz used a timeline of his own. On 4 August 2021, after the United States had left the 2015 deal and Iran had expanded enrichment, he told ambassadors from the UN Security Council that Iran was "only around 10 weeks away from acquiring weapons-grade materials necessary for a nuclear weapon," and called for "diplomatic, economic and even military deeds." [cite:ir6_toi_gantz2021] His claim was about fissile material, not an assembled bomb, and it rested on enrichment the IAEA itself was recording (see Part Four). [scene:ir4_programme|The programme]

The prime ministers who followed Netanyahu in 2021 and 2022 kept the same line in the same venue. Naftali Bennett told the UN General Assembly on 27 September 2021 that "Iran's nuclear weapon program is at a critical point. All red lines have been crossed," and that "words do not stop centrifuges from spinning"; he gave no date. [cite:ir6_un_bennett2021] Yair Lapid told the Assembly on 22 September 2022 that "the only way to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is to put a credible military threat on the table." [cite:ir6_mm_lapid2022] Neither made a timeline prediction that can be tested; both made the argument for force.

The Military's Case in June 2025

When Israel struck Iran on 13 June 2025, its military gave an intelligence basis. It said information gathered "in recent months" showed Iran "approaching the point of no return," and its spokesman, Brigadier General Effie Defrin, said Iran was "rushing toward a nuclear bomb" and that Israel had uncovered a secret programme in which scientists worked on weapon components, which he called "unequivocal proof." [cite:ir6_afp_idf2025] Israel did not publish the intelligence. The IAEA's director general said six days later that the agency had not found "an active, systematic plan to build a nuclear weapon." [cite:ir5_tbs_grossi] In September 2026 Ynet quoted an unnamed senior Israeli official as saying the weaponization group had been "very far from developing a nuclear weapon"; that account cannot be checked independently. [cite:ir5_ynet_sep2026] Part Ten sets out the war itself. [scene:ir10_strikes|The twelve days]

Americans Who Echoed the Timeline

Some American officials gave short timelines too, usually framed as a condition. Leon Panetta said in an interview with 60 Minutes recorded on 17 December 2011 that if Iran's leaders decided to proceed at full speed they could have a weapon in about a year, sooner if they had a hidden enrichment site; "That's a red line for us," he said. [cite:ir6_afps_panetta2011] Hillary Clinton, by then the Democratic nominee, told Israel's Channel 2 on 8 September 2016 that Iran had been "weeks away from breakout" before the 2015 deal, and that the deal "has made Israel safer." [cite:ir6_toi_clinton2016] In June 2025 President Trump said Iran was "very close" to a bomb. [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] Panetta's and Clinton's claims, like Gantz's, concerned breakout, the time to make enough fissile material, not a finished weapon.

The flat dated forecasts of a weapon (Peres's 1999 and the reported Israeli estimate of March 2011) did not come true, as Netanyahu's did not; the Mossad's estimate of capability by 2010–11 is harder to score, because capability was not defined. Most later statements were claims about capability or about Israel's ability to strike, which Iran's expanded enrichment after 2019 partly bore out. What the record does not show is a single Israeli view: the same years produced Israeli voices that rejected both the timelines and the case for war, the subject of the next section.

sections.h: Israel's Own Dissenters
sections.html:
The strongest challenge to the warnings did not come from Iran, which had every reason to deny them, or from critics abroad. It came from men who had run Israel's intelligence services and army. Some disputed how close Iran was to a bomb; others accepted the danger but argued that an attack would make it worse. None said Iran's programme was harmless. Each is quoted with date and venue, beside the government's response where one was given.

Meir Dagan: "We Know How It Starts"

Meir Dagan led the Mossad from 2002 to the end of 2010 and oversaw the covert campaign against Iran's programme. In closed conversations in his last week in office, reported by Yedioth Ahronoth and the Associated Press on 7 January 2011, he assessed that Iran would not have a nuclear weapon before 2015, and credited unspecified "measures" with the delay. [cite:ir6_arabnews_dagan2011] [cite:ir5_ap_dagan2011] Four months later he went public. In a lecture at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem on 6 May 2011 he called a strike on Iran's nuclear facilities, in one English rendering, "a dumb idea that has no benefits." Barak said: "I am not sure, however, that his remark, as reported in the media, is correct." [cite:ir6_jta_dagan2011] By June 2011, as The Christian Science Monitor reported, Dagan had called an Israeli strike "the stupidest thing I have ever heard," said it would breach international law and predicted "war with Iran. It is the kind of thing where we know how it starts, but not how it will end"; a strike, he said, "will give the Iranians the best excuse to pursue the nuclear race." [cite:ir6_csm_dagan2011] On CBS's 60 Minutes in March 2012 he said "the regime in Iran is a very rational one" and that "an attack on Iran before you are exploring all other approaches is not the right way." He did not rule out force; he added that if someone had to act, "I always prefer that Americans will do it." [cite:ir6_cbs_dagan2012] [cite:ir6a_cbs_dagan]

The Order of 2010 and the Order of 2011

Dagan also objected to how the decision was being made. On 5 November 2012 the Channel 2 programme Uvda reported that at a meeting in 2010 Netanyahu and Barak ordered the chief of staff, Gabi Ashkenazi, and Dagan to put Israel's forces on "P Plus", a pre-attack status for a strike on Iran. Ashkenazi, by associates' account, warned that Israel's enemies would notice and that the step could itself start a war; Dagan, also through associates, said that without the security cabinet's approval the two leaders were making an illegal decision and trying to "steal" a decision to go to war. Barak told the programme that Ashkenazi had said the army lacked the capability, that the alert was part of preparation and that no final decision was made; Ashkenazi denied Barak's account, saying through associates that the army was ready but the mission would be a strategic mistake. Netanyahu said only that he was ready to act "if necessary." [cite:ir6_cbs_uvda2012] The account rests on competing versions; no record of the meeting has been published.

Dagan's successor told the same programme six years later of a second order. Tamir Pardo, Mossad director from 2011 to 2016, said in an Uvda interview broadcast on 31 May 2018 that in 2011 Netanyahu instructed him to start the countdown to a strike, not "for the sake of a drill": "When he tells you to start the countdown process, you know that he isn't playing games with you." Pardo said he checked with legal advisers so that he would not find himself having "carried out an illegal operation"; the report does not say that he refused the order. Netanyahu's office did not comment. [cite:ir6_bg_pardo2018] [cite:ir6a_bg_pardo] Pardo had already set out his view of the threat while in office. Speaking to Israeli ambassadors on 27 December 2011, as Haaretz reported, he said: "Does Iran pose a threat to Israel? Absolutely," but "the term 'existential threat' is used too freely." [cite:ir6_ahram_pardo2011]

Diskin, Ayalon, Halevy and Yadlin

Yuval Diskin, who headed the Shin Bet internal security service until 2011, made the sharpest personal attack. At a public meeting on 27 April 2012 he said: "I don't have faith in the current leadership of Israel to lead us to an event of this magnitude, of war with Iran," accused Netanyahu and Barak of making decisions "based on Messianic feelings," and warned that a strike could bring "a dramatic acceleration of the Iran program." Spokesmen for both men declined to comment. [cite:ir6_fox_diskin2012] When the 2015 nuclear deal was signed, two more former chiefs backed it against their own government's position: Ami Ayalon, former head of the Shin Bet, said "when it comes to Iran's nuclear capability, this is the best option," and Efraim Halevy, a former Mossad director, wrote that "in the Middle East, a decade is eternity," arguing for a real debate on whether no agreement was better than one. [cite:ir6_lobelog_2015] [cite:ir6_db_alter2015] After the United States left the deal, Ya'alon, Pardo and the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot called the withdrawal a mistake (Part Seven), and Amos Yadlin, a former head of military intelligence, said in November 2021 that "the Iranian issue was privatized to one person." Netanyahu's former national security adviser, Yaakov Amidror, answered on the same panel that the withdrawal was "correct, smart, and appropriate." [cite:ir6_toi_yadlin2021] [scene:ir7_withdrawal|The withdrawal]

The Mossad Paper of 2012

The most cited piece of dissent is not a speech but a document. Among intelligence files leaked to Al Jazeera and published with The Guardian on 23 February 2015, the "Spy Cables", was a Mossad assessment dated October 2012 and shared with South Africa's intelligence service. It said Iran "is not performing the activity necessary to produce weapons" and "does not appear to be ready to enrich" to higher levels. Netanyahu had told the UN a few weeks earlier that Iran could reach his red line by the following summer. [cite:hz11_rferl_spycables] [cite:hz11_wiki_spycables] The document has two readings. In one, the Mossad's analysts contradicted the prime minister. In the other, argued by The Times of Israel, the two were "hardly contradictory": the full passage described an Iran closing gaps toward a weapon, and Netanyahu's line concerned enriched material, not a finished bomb. [cite:hz11_toi_spycables] No public evidence shows whether Netanyahu read the paper before speaking. The Hezbollah volume sets the same documents beside the 2012 speech. [scene:hz11_pattern|The bomb that was about a year away]

The American Intelligence Record

US intelligence assessments ran on their own track throughout. The National Intelligence Estimate of December 2007 judged "with high confidence" that Iran halted its covert weapons programme in the autumn of 2003, and with moderate confidence that it had not restarted by mid-2007; the White House said the risk "remains a very serious problem." [cite:hz11_wh_nie2007] [cite:hz11_npr_nie2007] An update, reportedly finished in February 2011, did not overturn that judgment, and the Director of National Intelligence, James Clapper, told the Senate on 31 January 2012: "We continue to assess Iran is keeping open the option to develop nuclear weapons," but "we do not know, however, if Iran will eventually decide to build nuclear weapons." [cite:ir6_cfr_nie2011] [cite:ir6_aca_clapper2012] On 26 March 2025 Tulsi Gabbard, as Director of National Intelligence, testified that the intelligence community "continues to assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon" and that Khamenei "has not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003," while noting a stockpile "unprecedented for a state without nuclear weapons." [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard] [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] When President Trump said on 20 June 2025, "She's wrong," Gabbard wrote that her testimony had been taken out of context and that Iran could produce a weapon "within weeks to months, if they decide to finalize the assembly." [cite:ir6_ap_gabbard2025] At the annual threats hearing on 18 March 2026, three weeks into the second war, she declined to say whether the agencies had assessed an imminent nuclear threat: "the only person who can determine what is and is not an imminent threat is the president." The day before, Joe Kent, the administration's top counterterrorism official, had resigned, saying Iran posed no imminent threat. [cite:ir6_abc_gabbard2026] Gabbard herself, having defended the decision to go to war, resigned in May 2026, citing her husband's illness rather than the war (Part Fourteen). [cite:ir14_aje_gabbard] [scene:ir14_who|Who pushed]

Americans Who Resisted a Strike

In 2011 and 2012 the Obama administration argued against an Israeli attack in public. Panetta said on 2 December 2011 that a strike "at best... might postpone it maybe one, possibly two years," and that "of greater concern to me are the unintended consequences," including Iranian retaliation against American ships and bases. [cite:ir6_usip_panetta2011] President Obama told AIPAC on 4 March 2012 that he would use force if necessary but that "already, there is too much loose talk of war." [cite:ir6_wbur_obama2012] General Martin Dempsey, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, said in London on 30 August 2012 that an Israeli strike would "clearly delay but probably not destroy Iran's nuclear program" and that "I don't want to be complicit if they choose to do it"; Ya'alon replied that such remarks led Iran to believe it faced no real risk. [cite:ir6_csm_dempsey2012] Robert Gates, defence secretary until 2011, said on 4 October 2012 that a strike could "prove catastrophic, haunting us for generations" and "would make a nuclear-armed Iran inevitable." [cite:ir6_ynet_gates2012]

The dissent does not by itself prove the warnings false. Most dissenters agreed Iran was building the capacity to make a weapon, and the agencies that said it was not building one recorded its growing stockpile. It does show that the short timelines were contested inside Israel's own security establishment, often by those closest to the intelligence, and that Israeli and American officials alike argued against a strike years before the wars of 2025 and 2026 tested the question.

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: The Deal and Its Killing
chapters.intro: Part Seven covers the six years in which the dispute over Iran's nuclear programme came closest to a settlement and then came apart. It begins with the interim agreement of November 2013 and the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action of July 2015: what the deal actually limited, for how long, and how its limits were checked. It follows Benjamin Netanyahu's campaign against the deal, including his address to Congress in March 2015, and the lobbying effort in Washington that failed to stop it. It then sets out what the International Atomic Energy Agency reported about Iran's compliance, the archive Netanyahu presented in April 2018, the American withdrawal a week later, the "maximum pressure" sanctions that followed, and Iran's step-by-step breaches of the deal's limits from May 2019. It closes with what Israeli and American officials later said about the withdrawal, on both sides of the question, and with a comparison of the deal's limits against what the IAEA recorded in Iran in 2025.
chapters.outro: Part Seven established that the JCPOA imposed dated, verifiable limits on Iran's programme, 3.67 per cent enrichment, a 300-kilogram stockpile and 5,060 centrifuges among them, and that the IAEA found Iran within those limits from January 2016 until July 2019. [cite:ir7_aca_jcpoa] [cite:ir7_iaea_impday] [cite:ir7_ap_may19] Netanyahu fought the deal before Congress and AIPAC spent heavily against it, but the Senate fell two votes short of blocking it. [cite:ir7_fox_speech] [cite:ir7_972_clifton] [cite:ir7_npr_vote] The archive Netanyahu presented in April 2018 documented past weapons work that the IAEA had already assessed, not a breach of the deal. Eight days later the United States withdrew and restored sanctions. [cite:ir7_pmo_archive] [cite:ir7_rferl_archive] [cite:ir7_toi_trump] Iran answered from May 2019 with step-by-step breaches that it said were a lawful response to relief it never received. By May 2025 those breaches had left it with 408.6 kilograms of 60 per cent uranium and no Additional Protocol inspections. [cite:ir7_snsc_may19] [cite:ir7_aca_jan20] [cite:ir7_isis_may25] Israel's own former military and intelligence chiefs later called the withdrawal a mistake, while those who took the decision defended it. [cite:ir7_toi_eisenkot] [cite:ir7_nl_zilber] Part Eight follows the covert war that ran beside the diplomacy: sabotage, cyberattacks and the killing of scientists. [scene:ir8_shadow|The shadow war]

sections.h: The Deal
sections.html:
The agreement that came closest to settling the dispute over Iran's nuclear programme began as a stopgap. On 24 November 2013 Iran and six powers (the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Russia and China) agreed a Joint Plan of Action. Iran agreed to cap enrichment at 5 per cent, freeze the number of its centrifuges, dilute or convert its stock of uranium enriched to 20 per cent, and halt work on the heavy-water reactor at Arak. In return, the United States and the European Union suspended some sanctions on petrochemicals and gold, and the United States also eased sanctions on cars and allowed spare parts for civilian aircraft. When the plan took effect on 20 January 2014, the International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed that Iran had stopped producing 20 per cent uranium. Its monthly reports over the following year recorded Iran carrying out the plan. The one concern it flagged, the testing of a single advanced centrifuge in November 2014, ended when Iran agreed to stop. When the talks were extended that month, Secretary of State John Kerry said Iran had complied with all its obligations. [cite:ir7_aca_jpoa] [cite:ir7a_aca_jpoa]

What the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action Limited

The final agreement, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), was concluded in Vienna on 14 July 2015. Its core limits were concrete and dated. For fifteen years Iran could enrich uranium only up to 3.67 per cent, well below the roughly 90 per cent used in weapons, and could hold no more than 300 kilograms of enriched uranium. For ten years enrichment was confined to 5,060 first-generation IR-1 centrifuges at Natanz. Before the deal Iran had more than 19,000 centrifuges installed, about 10,200 of them enriching; the surplus went into storage under IAEA seal. The underground site at Fordow could enrich nothing for fifteen years. The Arak reactor was to be redesigned to produce about one kilogram of plutonium a year instead of more than seven, and its original core was to be made unusable, with its channels filled with cement. Iran was to apply the IAEA's Additional Protocol, which allows inspections at short notice, and to seek its ratification within eight years. For a disputed request to see an undeclared site, the deal set a procedure lasting up to 24 days: 14 for Iran to answer, 7 for a joint commission to rule, and 3 to comply. [cite:ir7_aca_jcpoa]

The deal's critics fixed on its end dates as much as its limits. The UN arms embargo was to lift after five years and the missile restrictions after eight. The ban on making IR-1 centrifuges was to end after ten years, the enrichment and stockpile caps after fifteen, and monitoring of centrifuge production after twenty. Monitoring of uranium mines and mills would continue for twenty-five years. Its supporters pointed to the arithmetic of "breakout," the time needed to make enough weapons-grade uranium for one bomb. The Arms Control Association put that time at two to three months under the interim deal and more than twelve months under the JCPOA, for over a decade. [cite:ir7_aca_jcpoa] At the end of December 2015 Iran shipped about 25,000 pounds of low-enriched material to Russia. Kerry called it "one of the most significant steps Iran has taken toward fulfilling its commitment." [cite:ir7_cnbc_russia]

On 20 July 2015 the UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2231, which endorsed the deal for ten years and set out a "snapback" procedure for restoring earlier UN sanctions if Iran broke its terms. The US ambassador, Samantha Power, said implementation would be "the only proper measure of this deal." Iran's Foreign Ministry said in return that if sanctions were restored, Iran would treat that as grounds to stop carrying out its own commitments. [cite:ir7_usip_2231] Snapback was used ten years later, in 2025; by then Iran had already stopped observing the deal's limits, for the reasons set out in the next section. [cite:ir7_crs_snapback]

The Campaign Against It

The Israeli government opposed the deal in public, at length and in the United States itself. In January 2015 the Republican Speaker of the House, John Boehner, invited Netanyahu to address a joint meeting of Congress without consulting the White House. The president's spokesman, Josh Earnest, called the invitation a "departure from protocol." The White House said President Barack Obama would not meet Netanyahu, citing the closeness of Israel's election, due on 17 March. [cite:ir7_aje_invite] On 3 March 2015 Netanyahu told Congress, "this is a bad deal." He said that "It doesn't block Iran's path to the bomb; it paves Iran's path to the bomb," and that the agreement "would be a farewell to arms control." He argued that a better deal would keep restrictions in place "until Iran's aggression ends," linking the nuclear limits to Iran's conduct in the region. [cite:ir7_fox_speech] The speech, and the place of its warnings in his three decades of predictions, are examined in Part Five. [scene:ir5_predictions|Always a year away] When the deal was concluded in July he called it "an historic mistake for the world" and said Israel's commitment to preventing an Iranian bomb "still stands." [cite:ir7_toi_historic]

The campaign also had a covert side, as one newspaper reported it. In March 2015 the Wall Street Journal reported that American intelligence had intercepted Israeli communications containing details of the confidential negotiations, and that Israel had passed such details to members of Congress to build opposition to the deal. A senior US official quoted in the report said, "It is one thing for the U.S. and Israel to spy on each other." Israeli officials denied spying on the talks and said the details had come from French officials. [cite:ir7_npr_spied] The account rests on the Journal's anonymous sources and is disputed by Israel; it is recorded here as reported, not as established.

In Washington the main organised opposition came from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). In July 2015 AIPAC backed a new group, Citizens for a Nuclear Free Iran, which ran a national television and digital advertising campaign. Its advisory board included the former senators Evan Bayh, Mark Begich, Mary Landrieu and Joe Lieberman. Its spokesman, Patrick Dorton, argued that the deal raised the risk of war and would set off a nuclear arms race. [cite:ir7_ap_cnfi] Politico reported a planned $20 million advertising buy in 30 to 40 states. [cite:ir7_wiki_cnfi] The totals actually spent are not fully public. The journalist Eli Clifton reported, citing earlier press reporting, that AIPAC had committed $20 to $40 million to television advertising, and that a review of FCC broadcast filings at the end of September 2015 showed at least $14.5 million spent. He also cited the JTA reporter Ron Kampeas's figure that the new group raised nearly $30 million. AIPAC did not respond to his request for comment. [cite:ir7_972_clifton] [cite:ir7a_972] These are reported figures from filings and journalists, not audited totals. The other side campaigned too. J Street, a liberal pro-Israel group, ran a full-page advertisement in the New York Times on 23 July 2015 urging Congress not to "sabotage" the deal, as part of what it described as a "multimillion dollar campaign." [cite:ir7_toi_jstreet]

The campaign failed. On 10 September 2015 the Senate's resolution of disapproval failed by 58 votes to 42, two short of the 60 needed to end a Democratic filibuster, and the deal went ahead. [cite:ir7_npr_vote] The record shows a foreign head of government lobbying the US Congress directly and a domestic lobby spending heavily against a president's signature agreement. Whether that lobbying changed any senator's vote is a separate question, and the record examined here does not answer it. The money is documented; its effect is a matter of argument.

What the Inspectors Found

On 16 January 2016, "Implementation Day," the IAEA reported that its inspectors had "verified that Iran has carried out all measures required under the JCPOA." Iran began applying the Additional Protocol on a provisional basis, which the agency said increased its ability to verify that Iran's nuclear activities were peaceful. [cite:ir7_iaea_impday] Over the next three years the agency's quarterly reports kept finding Iran within the deal's limits. The day after the American withdrawal, on 9 May 2018, the agency's director general, Yukiya Amano, said, "the IAEA can confirm that the nuclear-related commitments are being implemented by Iran." He described Iran as subject to "the world's most robust nuclear verification regime." [cite:ir7_iaea_may18] As late as 31 May 2019 the agency reported that Iran "continues to stay within the limitations" and that its inspectors had been able to visit all the sites they needed to, though Iran's stocks of low-enriched uranium and heavy water were rising. [cite:ir7_ap_may19]

The verification record answers a narrow question: whether Iran kept the deal's limits while the deal was in force. It did, on the IAEA's findings, from January 2016 until July 2019. It does not answer the deal's critics' wider objections. Those concerned what would happen when the limits expired, the 24-day delay for disputed sites, the missile programme the deal did not cover, and Iran's armed allies across the region, which Netanyahu had asked to be included. Those objections were about the deal's design, not about Iran's compliance, and they are given here as the Israeli government stated them. What happened when the United States acted on them is the subject of the next section. [scene:ir7_withdrawal|The withdrawal]

sections.h: The Archive
sections.html:
On the evening of 30 April 2018, at the Defence Ministry in Tel Aviv, Netanyahu gave a televised presentation. "Tonight, I'm here to tell you one thing: Iran lied. Big time," he said. He described "Fifty-five thousand pages. Another 55,000 files on 183 CDs," material he said Israel had obtained "a few weeks ago" from vaults in Tehran, and said they documented Project Amad, a secret Iranian weapons programme meant to produce the equivalent of "five Hiroshima bombs to be put on ballistic missiles." He said Iran had "lied again in 2015, when it didn't come clean to the IAEA," that "the Iran deal ... is based on lies," and that "in a few days' time, President Trump will decide" what to do with it. [cite:ir7_pmo_archive]

The US Secretary of State, Mike Pompeo, said the documents showed "that Iran had a secret nuclear-weapons program for years." The British government said it had "never been naive about Iran," and a German spokesman said Iran's past work was the very reason the deal had been signed. The IAEA said that its 2015 report had already found "no credible indications of activities in Iran relevant to the development of a nuclear explosive device after 2009," and that its Board had closed the matter. Iran's foreign minister, Mohammad Javad Zarif, called the presentation "a rehash of old allegations" and noted its "coordinated timing." [cite:ir7_rferl_archive] The archive was genuine intelligence about a weapons effort that the IAEA and US intelligence already believed had existed. Part Four sets out that history. [scene:ir4_programme|The atom] What the presentation did not show was any breach of the JCPOA's limits, which the IAEA was reporting Iran had kept. [cite:ir7_iaea_may18]

The Withdrawal and Maximum Pressure

Eight days later, on 8 May 2018, President Donald Trump announced "that the United States will withdraw from the Iran nuclear deal." He said that "we cannot prevent an Iranian nuclear bomb under the decaying and rotten structure of the current agreement," that "At the heart of the Iran deal was a giant fiction," and that its sunset clauses were "totally unacceptable." He also said that it "fails to address" Iran's ballistic missiles. He cited the documents Israel had just published and promised "the highest level of economic sanction." [cite:ir7_toi_trump] Netanyahu called the decision "correct, wise and courageous." [cite:ir7_ynet_praise] None of his stated reasons was a finding that Iran had broken the deal's limits.

On 21 May 2018, at the Heritage Foundation, Pompeo set out twelve demands. Iran was to stop all enrichment, give the IAEA "unqualified access to all sites throughout the country," and end its support for Hezbollah, Hamas and the Houthis. He promised that "These will be the strongest sanctions in history by the time we are done." President Hassan Rouhani replied, "Who are you to decide for Iran and the world?" [cite:ir7_voa_pompeo] The sanctions came back in two waves. The first, in August 2018, covered dollar purchases, gold, metals and the car industry. The second, on 5 November 2018, covered oil, the National Iranian Oil Company, shipping, insurance and foreign banks dealing with Iran's central bank. [cite:ir7_ac_waves] On 22 April 2019 Pompeo announced that the waivers allowing eight countries to keep buying Iranian oil would end on 2 May. "Our goal has been to get countries to cease importing Iranian oil entirely," he said. [cite:ir7_ap_waivers]

Iran's Breaches, Step by Step

For a year after the withdrawal Iran stayed within the limits, as the IAEA reported. [cite:ir7_ap_may19] On 8 May 2019, the anniversary of the withdrawal, Iran's Supreme National Security Council announced that it would no longer observe the caps on its stocks of enriched uranium and heavy water. It cited paragraphs 26 and 36 of the JCPOA, the clauses on reimposed sanctions and dispute resolution, and gave the remaining parties "sixty days to fulfil their obligations, especially in banking and oil fields." [cite:ir7_snsc_may19] On 1 July 2019 Zarif said Iran had "crossed the 300-kilogramme limit," and the IAEA confirmed it. Zarif said Iran was responding to the American withdrawal and would reverse the step once the European parties met their obligations. The White House answered that "maximum pressure" would continue and called for "no enrichment for Iran." Netanyahu called the step a "significant step toward making a nuclear weapon." [cite:ir7_aje_300kg]

Iran then began enriching to 4.5 per cent in July 2019 and restarted enrichment at Fordow in November. On 5 January 2020 it said it would observe no limit on the number of its centrifuges. Zarif described every step as "reversible upon effective implementation of reciprocal obligations." Iran's demand throughout was that the remaining parties find a way for it to sell oil and use the banking system. [cite:ir7_aca_jan20] In February 2021 Iran stopped applying the Additional Protocol and the deal's extra monitoring. [cite:ir7_crs_snapback] On 16 April 2021, days after an act of sabotage at Natanz that Tehran blamed on Israel and that Israel did not claim, Iran began enriching to 60 per cent, its highest level ever, and said the purpose was medical. [cite:ir7_aje_60pc] Talks in Vienna to restore the deal began that same month. They produced a European "final" text on 8 August 2022, to which Iran responded with demands for guarantees on sanctions and on the IAEA's open safeguards questions. [cite:ir7_afp_vienna] The deal was never restored. On 28 August 2025 Britain, France and Germany triggered the snapback, and UN sanctions were reimposed on 27 September 2025.
