Iran, Russia and China rejected the step as invalid, in a joint letter of 18 October 2025. [cite:ir7_crs_snapback] [cite:ir7a_crs]

Iran's stated reason for the breaches is a matter of record: it said the other parties had not delivered the sanctions relief the deal promised once the United States reimposed sanctions. The deal's own text gave each side a remedy if the other failed to perform, and that is the remedy Iran claimed to be using. The breaches were also real, and they went well beyond the first step, to 60 per cent enrichment, a level for which the European Union saw no civilian need. [cite:ir7_aje_60pc] Both facts stand.

By May 2025, a month before Israel's strikes, the IAEA counted 408.6 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 per cent and a total enriched stockpile of 9,247.6 kilograms. Some 21,900 centrifuges were installed, about 14,689 of them advanced models, and Fordow had been producing 60 per cent uranium since November 2022. The agency said it had lost continuity of knowledge over Iran's production of centrifuges and other items, and that this could not be restored. [cite:ir7_isis_may25] After the June 2025 strikes its inspectors withdrew, and as of September 2026 the agency had still had no access to the facilities hit in June 2025, as its director general told its Board on 7 September (Part Eleven). [cite:ir7_crs_snapback] [cite:ir11_iaea_sep7] [scene:ir11_now|Where things stand]

Was It a Mistake? What Officials Said Later

Within a few years several of Israel's own former security chiefs said in public that the withdrawal had harmed Israel. Gadi Eisenkot, chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces from 2015 to 2019, told Maariv in an interview reported on 28 January 2022 that the withdrawal was "a strategic mistake." He said "No one spoke with the security establishment," and that only Netanyahu, the Mossad director Yossi Cohen and the ambassador Ron Dermer had handled the question. He said he knew the Mossad was pushing the Americans to leave, and that the deal, though flawed, had slowed Iran's programme. [cite:ir7_toi_eisenkot] [cite:ir7_jpost_eisenkot] Moshe Ya'alon, defence minister when the deal was signed, told Haaretz in November 2021 that "the main mistake was the withdrawal from the agreement." [cite:ir7_rs_yaalon] Neri Zilber reported in New Lines that the former Mossad director Tamir Pardo called the 2018 decision a "disaster." He also reported that Amos Yadlin, a former head of military intelligence, said on Channel 12 in August 2021 that "The path that Netanyahu led got Iran extremely close to a bomb." [cite:ir7_nl_zilber] In the United States, Joe Biden, as a candidate, called Trump's policy "a dangerous failure" in a CNN article of 13 September 2020 and pledged to rejoin the deal if Iran returned to its terms. [cite:ir7_iranintl_biden] As president he did not rejoin it; the deal was never restored. [cite:ir7_crs_snapback]

The other side of the argument was made by the officials who took the decision. Trump said the deal's sunsets were unacceptable and that it could not prevent an Iranian bomb, and Pompeo set out sanctions and demands meant to force a broader settlement. [cite:ir7_toi_trump] [cite:ir7_voa_pompeo] Netanyahu hailed the exit in May 2018 as a "historic move." [cite:ir7_nl_zilber] Naftali Bennett, prime minister from June 2021, publicly thanked Trump for leaving. [cite:ir7_nl_zilber] The thesis this volume tests, that Israel pushed the United States into a choice that left Iran closer to a bomb, can be split into parts. That Netanyahu campaigned for the exit and that the Mossad pressed for it are documented, the second on Eisenkot's account. That Iran's stockpile and enrichment level grew far past the deal's limits after the exit is documented by the IAEA. That the exit caused the growth, rather than Iran's own choices or the Europeans' failure to deliver relief, is an argument. Iran's government chose each breach and said so. Israeli officials who once opposed the deal made that argument themselves, and those who took the decision rejected it. The next part turns to the covert campaign that ran alongside the diplomacy throughout. [scene:ir8_shadow|The shadow war]

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: The Shadow War
chapters.intro: Part Eight follows the covert war between Israel and Iran from the late 2000s to the open exchanges of 2024. It begins with the campaign against Iran's nuclear programme, which was reported to involve Israel acting alone or together with the United States: the Stuxnet worm, the killing of nuclear scientists in Tehran, the theft of Iran's nuclear archive, the explosions and blackout at Natanz, and the killing of Mohsen Fakhrizadeh by a remote-operated gun. It then turns to Iran's side of the war: the 2012 bomb plots against Israeli diplomats, the attacks on shipping, cyberattacks and the detention of foreigners. It ends with 2024, the year both governments began striking each other's territory openly. Throughout, the part separates what courts and governments have confirmed from what rests on anonymous officials, and it gives each government's own account beside the charges against it.
chapters.outro: Part Eight established that the covert campaign against Iran's programme was real and well reported, though almost never acknowledged. Stuxnet destroyed nearly 1,000 centrifuges and was estimated to have cost Iran 18 months to two years. Four scientists were killed and one wounded between 2010 and 2012, and Fakhrizadeh was killed in 2020. Natanz was sabotaged in 2020 and 2021, and after the second attack Iran began enriching to 60 per cent. [cite:ow3_sw_sanger] [cite:ow3_npr_sanger] [cite:ir8_mee_scientists] [cite:ir8_newarab_fakh] [cite:ir8_ap_natanz] [cite:ir7_aje_60pc] Iran's side of the war is documented by a Thai court verdict, Indian arrest warrants and an Argentine ruling on the 1990s bombings. Its role in the ship and cyber attacks rests, like Israel's, on the word of governments and unnamed officials, and Iran denied it. [cite:ir8_afp_bangkok] [cite:ir8_brec_delhi] [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] [cite:ir8_ap_mercer] [cite:ir8_aj_port2020] In 2024 the exchange became open. Israel struck the Damascus consulate and killed Haniyeh in Tehran. Iran fired two barrages at Israel, which American forces helped to defeat, and Israel struck Iran twice. Each step was explained by its author as a response to the one before. [cite:ir8_ap_consulate] [cite:ir8_gs_tp1] [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] [cite:ir8_usip_oct1] [cite:ir8_lwj_oct26] Part Nine turns to Iran's own record: at home, toward its neighbours and toward the people it holds. [scene:ir9_record|Iran's own record]

sections.h: Sabotage, Code and Killings: The Campaign Against the Programme
sections.html:
From the second half of the 2000s Israel, at times together with the United States, ran a covert campaign against Iran's nuclear programme. It used computer code, bombs, gunmen, a robotic machine gun, a burglary and drones. Almost none of it has been officially acknowledged. What follows rests on named reporting, chiefly by the New York Times and the Washington Post, on the statements of the governments involved, and on what Iran itself reported. Where the only source is anonymous officials, the text says so.

The best-documented operation is the computer worm later called Stuxnet. David Sanger of the New York Times reported on 1 June 2012 that it was the product of a programme code-named Olympic Games, begun under President George W. Bush in 2006 and continued by President Barack Obama, and that Israel's signals intelligence unit, Unit 8200, supplied technical expertise and intelligence on the enrichment plant at Natanz. It escaped onto the internet through a programming error and was discovered in 2010. Obama, briefed with Vice President Joe Biden and CIA Director Leon Panetta, decided to continue. According to Sanger's sources, the last attack took out nearly 1,000 of the roughly 5,000 centrifuges then running. [cite:ow3_sw_sanger] Sanger later said that a first piece of code had mapped the plant and "phoned home, back to the National Security Agency and the Unit 8200," and that Bush's motive was that he "didn't want to see the Israelis bomb the Iran facilities": in Sanger's words, "the Israelis needed to be convinced that there was an alternative to a military attack." The official estimate he reported was a delay of 18 months to two years. [cite:ow3_npr_sanger] Neither government has confirmed the operation. A related spy program, Flame, was reported by the Washington Post in June 2012 to have been developed jointly by the NSA, the CIA and Israel to map Iran's computer networks. The same report said Israel had, on its own, directed a disruptive attack on Iran's oil-industry computers that caught its American partners off guard. [cite:ir8_wapo_flame]

In the same years a series of Iranian nuclear scientists were attacked in Tehran, most of them by men on motorcycles. Masoud Alimohammadi was killed in January 2010 by a bomb on a motorcycle that appeared to be detonated remotely. In November 2010 Majid Shahriari was killed when a motorcyclist attached a bomb to his car; his wife and driver were wounded. Fereydoon Abbasi survived a similar attack the same morning. Darioush Rezaeinejad was shot dead by two gunmen in July 2011; Israeli reports linked him to nuclear work, which Iran rejected. Mostafa Ahmadi Roshan was killed with his driver by a magnetic bomb in January 2012. [cite:ir8_mee_scientists] The United States and Israel denied involvement in the Shahriari killing, and Washington condemned the Roshan killing and denied a role. Iran's president, Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, blamed "the hand of the Zionist regime" and Western governments for the Shahriari killing. After the Roshan killing Israel's military spokesman, Brigadier General Yoav Mordechai, wrote: "I don't know who took revenge on the Iranian scientist, but I am definitely not shedding a tear." [cite:ir8_mee_scientists] No court has ruled on who carried out these attacks, and no Israeli official has claimed them. The attribution to Israel is the consistent view of named reporting and of the Iranian government. It is a strong inference, not a documented finding.

The campaign also had a conventional military side. From 2017 Israel struck Iranian infrastructure in Syria. In January 2019 the departing chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot, said Israel had dropped about 2,000 bombs on Iranian targets in 2018 alone and had carried out "thousands of attacks without taking responsibility." [cite:hz10s_toi_eisenkot] Netanyahu told his cabinet on 13 January 2019 that the military had "attacked hundreds of times Iranian and Hezbollah targets." [cite:hz10s_jc_netanyahu] The Hezbollah volume covers that campaign. [scene:hz10_syria|The Syria campaign]

The archive operation is the one Israel itself made public. On 30 April 2018 Netanyahu displayed what he said were Iran's nuclear files; Part Seven describes the presentation and the IAEA's response. [scene:ir7_withdrawal|The archive] Israeli officials later told the New York Times how the files had been taken. A Mossad team entered a warehouse in Tehran at 10:30 p.m. on 31 January 2018, cut into most of 32 Iranian-made safes, and left before 5 a.m. with about 50,000 pages and 163 compact discs. Iran called the material fabricated. American and British officials said it was genuine. [cite:ir8_alarabiya_archive]

The most consequential killing came on 27 November 2020. Mohsen Fakhrizadeh had been named in the IAEA's 2011 annex as the head of the AMAD plan, Iran's pre-2003 weapons-related effort. [cite:ir4_sipri_annex2011] He was shot while driving with his wife near Absard, east of Tehran. On 18 September 2021 the New York Times reported, from interviews with American, Israeli and Iranian officials, that the weapon was a Belgian-made FN MAG machine gun on a robotic mount assisted by artificial intelligence. The device weighed about a ton, had been smuggled into Iran in parts and reassembled, and was fired by an operator "thousands of miles away." It fired 15 rounds in under a minute, and a truck carrying explosives was blown up afterwards. The paper reported that Israel had tracked Fakhrizadeh since at least 2007 and had begun preparing the operation in late 2019 and early 2020. On motive it reported that, in Netanyahu's "best-case scenario," the killing "would derail any chance of resurrecting the nuclear agreement even if Mr. Biden won." [cite:ir8_newarab_fakh] That last point is the newspaper's account of his reasoning from unnamed sources. Netanyahu has not stated it, and Israel has not acknowledged the killing. Iran blamed Israel at once and vowed revenge. [cite:ir8_newarab_fakh]

Natanz itself was hit twice more. In July 2020 an explosion tore through its advanced centrifuge assembly plant, which Iranian authorities later called sabotage. On 11 April 2021 the plant lost power. Iran's nuclear spokesman, Behrouz Kamalvandi, first said there was no casualty or damage, and Iran then called the incident "nuclear terrorism." Israeli broadcasters reported a cyberattack and said Israel was probably responsible, without citing sources. Israel did not claim either attack. The army chief, Aviv Kochavi, said only that Israel's operations "are not hidden from the eyes of the enemy." [cite:ir8_ap_natanz] [cite:ir8_ap_nucterror] Five days later Iran began enriching uranium to 60 per cent at Natanz, the highest level in its history. [cite:ir7_aje_60pc] On 29 January 2023 three drones struck a defence ministry workshop near Isfahan. Iran reported "minor damage" and called the attack "cowardly." The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that Israel was behind it, and other US officials said Washington had no part in it. [cite:ir8_aj_isfahan23]

What the campaign achieved can be measured only in part. Sanger's sources estimated that Stuxnet cost Iran 18 months to two years. [cite:ow3_npr_sanger] In January 2011 the departing Mossad chief, Meir Dagan, said Iran could not build a bomb before 2015, in part because of unspecified "measures." [cite:ir5_ap_dagan2011] Delay is therefore documented. Prevention is a different matter. Each blow was followed by reconstruction, and the April 2021 sabotage was followed by Iran's step to 60 per cent. Part Five tests Israel's dated predictions against this record. [scene:ir5_predictions|The predictions]

sections.h: Iran's Side: Plots Abroad, Ships, Water and Detainees
sections.html:
The shadow war was fought by both sides. Iran's government and the bodies it directs, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its Quds Force above all, were accused of attacks on Israeli diplomats and travellers abroad, of attacks on ships linked to Israeli owners, of a cyberattack on Israel's water system and of holding foreign and dual nationals as bargaining chips. The evidence for these accusations varies in strength. A few rest on court judgments. Others rest on the accusing government's word, and some on anonymous officials quoted in newspapers. Iran denied almost all of them. This section sets the evidence out case by case.

The clearest cluster came in February 2012, a month after Mostafa Ahmadi Roshan was killed in Tehran. On 13 February a motorcyclist attached a magnetic bomb to an Israeli embassy car in New Delhi. The explosion wounded the diplomat inside, her driver and two passers-by. The same day police in Tbilisi defused a bomb fixed to another Israeli embassy car. Netanyahu called Iran "the biggest exporter of terror in the world." Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Ramin Mehmanparast, replied: "It seems that these suspicious incidents are designed by the Zionist regime." [cite:ir8_aj_delhi2012] In March 2012 Indian police named three Iranian men, who had entered India on tourist visas and left after the bombing, as the main suspects and issued warrants for them. They also arrested an Indian journalist who had worked part-time for Iran's state news agency. [cite:ir8_brec_delhi]

The day after the Delhi bombing, on 14 February, explosives went off by accident in a rented house in Bangkok. One of the occupants, Saeid Moradi, threw a bomb at police and lost his legs when it went off beside him. An expert witness told the court that five C-4 charges had been hidden in radios inside the house. On 22 August 2013 a Thai court sentenced Moradi to life imprisonment and a second Iranian, Mohammad Khazaei, to 15 years. Both had denied the charges. Two other suspects were believed to have returned to Iran. Israel's ambassador, Simon Roded, said the sentence proved "once again that Iran is engaged and in proliferation of terror all around the world." [cite:ir8_afp_bangkok] The Bangkok judgment is a court finding against two Iranian nationals for an explosives plot. The verdict as reported did not establish the intended target, and it did not make a finding about who in Iran directed the plot. On 18 July 2012 a bus carrying Israeli tourists was bombed at Burgas in Bulgaria, killing five Israelis and the Bulgarian driver. A Bulgarian court later convicted two men in absentia for helping the bomber. That attack was attributed to Hezbollah, which denied it, and the Hezbollah volume covers it. [cite:hz4_aje_burgas] [scene:hz4_abroad|Attacks abroad] The highest court finding on Iran's own role in attacks abroad is the ruling of Argentina's Federal Criminal Cassation Court of 11 April 2024, which held that Iran ordered the 1992 Israeli embassy and 1994 AMIA bombings in Buenos Aires. [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] Part Nine returns to Iran's record abroad. [scene:ir9_record|Iran's record]

From 2019 the fight moved to the sea, and here the accusations ran both ways. On 11 March 2021 the Wall Street Journal reported that since late 2019 Israel had attacked at least 12 vessels bound for Syria, most of them carrying Iranian oil to the Syrian government in breach of US sanctions, using water mines and limpet mines. According to the report, some of the attacks hit weapons cargoes. No ship was sunk and no casualties were reported. Israeli and Iranian officials declined to comment. [cite:ir8_twz_tankers] [cite:ir8_almon_wsj] On 25 February 2021 the Israeli-owned car carrier Helios Ray was holed by an explosion in the Gulf of Oman. Israeli officials blamed the IRGC. Iran denied involvement and called the incident a "false flag." On 10 March Iran's state shipping line said one of its container ships, the Shahr-e Kord, had been hit by a "terrorist" attack in the Mediterranean. [cite:ir8_twz_tankers] The campaign turned lethal on 29 July 2021. Drones struck the tanker Mercer Street off Oman, killing a British and a Romanian crew member. The ship was managed by Zodiac Maritime, part of the Israeli businessman Eyal Ofer's group. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said the United States was "confident" that Iran had carried out the attack. The British foreign secretary said it was "highly likely," and Prime Minister Naftali Bennett said "Iran is the one who carried out the attack." Iran's foreign ministry called the accusation "baseless." None of the three governments publicly produced physical evidence. [cite:ir8_ap_mercer]

The water attack was reported in the same way, through officials speaking anonymously. On 24 April 2020, according to the Washington Post, hackers tried to break into the computers that run rural water systems in Israel. The attempt failed and caused no damage. Officials attributed it to Iran, and Iran denied it. On 9 May computer systems at the Shahid Rajaee port terminal near Bandar Abbas, on the Strait of Hormuz, failed, leaving trucks queued for kilometres and ships waiting offshore. Officials told the Post that Israel had carried out the attack in retaliation. One of them called it "highly accurate." Iran's port authority said the hackers "failed to penetrate" its systems. Israel did not comment. [cite:ir8_aj_port2020]

The detention of foreigners is documented more directly, because the releases were negotiated in public. On 18 September 2023 five Americans whom the US government described as "unjustly detained" in Iran, among them Siamak Namazi, Emad Shargi and Morad Tahbaz, were flown out. In return the United States released five Iranians and allowed $6 billion of frozen Iranian funds to be moved from South Korea to Qatar, for use only on humanitarian purchases. US officials warned that Iran might go on using detained Americans as "bargaining chips." The same day Washington imposed sanctions on Iran's intelligence ministry over the 2007 disappearance in Iran of Robert Levinson. [cite:ir8_voa_swap] Part Nine sets out the wider record of detentions of dual nationals. [scene:ir9_record|Iran's record]

The comparison shows a pattern that runs through the whole record. Most acts on both sides were neither confirmed nor denied by the state responsible, and most attributions rest on unnamed officials. The two kinds of evidence point in different directions. Court findings exist almost only against Iranian nationals and Iranian-directed operations abroad, because those acts took place in countries with open courts. The killings inside Iran were never tried anywhere outside Iran. Each government described the other's operations as terrorism. Netanyahu called Iran "the biggest exporter of terror in the world," and Iran called the Natanz blackout "nuclear terrorism." [cite:ir8_aj_delhi2012] [cite:ir8_ap_nucterror] In 2024 both sides moved into the open, as the next section shows. [scene:ir8_open|The shadow war in the open]

sections.h: 2024: The Shadow War Comes Into the Open
sections.html:
For more than a decade, neither government had attacked the other's territory openly and said so. That changed in 2024, during the Gaza war, in a sequence of strikes and counter-strikes that lasted seven months. Each step was announced, or soon became known, and each side gave its reasons in public.

On 1 April 2024 an air strike destroyed Iran's consulate building in Damascus. Seven Iranian officers were killed, among them Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Zahedi, who had commanded the IRGC's Quds Force in Lebanon and Syria until 2016, and his deputy, Mohammad Hadi Hajriahimi. A member of Hezbollah also died. Israel did not confirm the strike and said it had no comment. The US National Security Council said the United States had played no part and had not known about the strike in advance. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei said Iran would make the attackers "regretful." [cite:ir8_ap_consulate]

On the night of 13–14 April Iran attacked Israel directly from its own territory, in an operation it called True Promise. The IDF spokesman, Daniel Hagari, said Iran had launched 170 drones, more than 30 cruise missiles and more than 120 ballistic missiles. Israeli officials said 99 per cent had been intercepted; Hagari said none of the drones or cruise missiles had entered Israeli territory, and that the ballistic missiles that got through caused "minor damage only" to a base that stayed operational. [cite:ir8a_ap_apr14] [cite:ir8a_ynet_hagari] The Israeli military credited the United States, Britain and France with help, and Jordan shot down projectiles crossing its airspace. A seven-year-old girl was badly wounded by fragments. [cite:ir8_gs_tp1] The Pentagon said US forces, among them the destroyers USS Arleigh Burke and USS Carney, had destroyed more than 80 one-way attack drones and at least six ballistic missiles. [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] The IRGC called the attack a response to "the crime of the Zionist regime in the attack on the consular section." Iran's UN mission cited the right of self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter and declared that "The matter can be deemed concluded," while warning of a "considerably more severe" response to any further Israeli "mistake." [cite:ir8_gs_tp1]

Israel answered on 19 April with a deliberately small strike. A US official told ABC News that Israeli jets had fired three missiles at a radar site in Isfahan province linked to the air defences around Natanz. Satellite images later showed damage to an S-300 radar at an air base there, and the IAEA said Iran's nuclear sites were undamaged. Iran's foreign minister, Hossein Amir-Abdollahian, said that downed "mini-drones" had caused no damage. In Israel the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, posted a single word, "Weak." Blinken said the United States had not been involved in any offensive operation. President Biden had reportedly told Netanyahu after the April attack to "Take the win." [cite:ir8_usip_apr19]

The next blow fell in Tehran itself. At about 2 a.m. on 31 July 2024 Ismail Haniyeh, the head of Hamas's political bureau, was killed with his bodyguard in Neshat, an IRGC guesthouse compound in the north of the city. He was in Tehran for the swearing-in of the new president, Masoud Pezeshkian. A few hours earlier Israel had killed the Hezbollah commander Fuad Shukr in Beirut. [cite:hz7_aj_shukr] The New York Times reported, from five Middle Eastern officials, that a bomb hidden in the room about two months earlier had been detonated remotely. Three Iranian officials told the paper the killing was a "tremendous embarrassment" for the IRGC, which ran the guesthouse. [cite:ir8_toi_haniyeh] The IRGC's own account, issued on 3 August, was that a "short-range projectile" carrying about seven kilograms of explosives had been fired from outside the building with American support. The United States said it "was not aware of or involved in" the killing. [cite:ir8_aj_haniyeh] Israel said nothing until 23 December 2024, when the defence minister, Israel Katz, told an audience of ministry staff that Israel would behead the Houthis' leaders "just as we did to Haniyeh, Sinwar and Nasrallah in Tehran, Gaza and Lebanon." [cite:ir8_newarab_katz]

Iran's promised retaliation was delayed for two months. During that time Israel detonated thousands of pagers and radios carried by Hezbollah members in Lebanon and, on 27 September, killed Hassan Nasrallah in Beirut. The same strike killed an IRGC general, Abbas Nilforoushan. [cite:hz7_toi_netanyahu_pagers] [cite:ir8_usip_oct1] [scene:hz7_pagers|The pagers] [scene:hz7_war|The autumn war] On 1 October Iran fired at least 180 ballistic missiles at Israel in two waves, in an operation it called True Promise 2. It named the killings of Haniyeh, Nasrallah and Nilforoushan as the reasons, and its UN mission called the attack a "legal, rational, and legitimate response." Air bases at Nevatim and Tel Nof were among the targets. No one in Israel was killed. A Palestinian man in Jericho died, and two Israelis were lightly hurt. The IRGC claimed 90 per cent of its missiles had hit their targets. Biden said the attack "appears to have been defeated and ineffective," and Netanyahu said Iran had "made a big mistake – and it will pay for it." [cite:ir8_usip_oct1] The US destroyers USS Bulkeley and USS Cole fired about a dozen interceptors. [cite:ow7_usni_oct2024] On 13 October the Pentagon announced that it was sending a THAAD missile-defence battery to Israel, with US soldiers to operate it. [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024]

Israel struck back on 26 October in an operation it called Days of Repentance. Aircraft attacked in three waves. The first hit radars and air defences, and the later waves hit missile and drone production sites, including at Parchin, east of Tehran. The IDF said it had struck 20 sites, and Hagari described "precise and targeted strikes." [cite:ir8_lwj_oct26] Israel warned that Iran would "pay a heavy price" if it responded. A US National Security Council spokesman called the strikes "an exercise in self-defence," and Iran reported "limited damage." [cite:ir8_afp_oct26] Iran's army at first reported two air-defence soldiers killed, then four. [cite:ir8_iw_oct26] A senior US official said the strikes "should be the end of this direct exchange of fire." [cite:ir8_lwj_oct26] As of October 2026 that hope had not held: in June 2025 Israel and then the United States struck Iran's nuclear sites. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] Part Ten takes up the war of June 2025. [scene:ir10_strikes|The Twelve-Day War]

The 2024 record allows some findings that the covert years did not. The order of events is documented. Each side said publicly what it was responding to, and each kept its stated reply limited: Iran declared the April matter "concluded," and Israel struck a radar site on 19 April. [cite:ir8_gs_tp1] [cite:ir8_usip_apr19] The United States was not a bystander. Its forces shot down Iranian drones and missiles in April and October and then sent soldiers to Israel to operate THAAD, while it said it had no part in Israel's offensive strikes. [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024] [cite:ir8_usip_apr19] Whether this amounts to the United States being drawn into the conflict is a question of interpretation, not of record, and Part Twelve weighs it. [scene:ir12_question|Does Iran want war with the US?] What the record does show is that it was Israel's strikes on the Damascus consulate and in Tehran, neither acknowledged at the time, that set off Iran's two direct attacks, on Iran's own stated account. [cite:ir8_gs_tp1] [cite:ir8_usip_oct1] Israel's stated position, as Katz put it in December 2024, was that it would strike the leaders of the groups at war with it wherever they were. [cite:ir8_newarab_katz]

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: Iran's Own Record
chapters.intro: The Hamas and Hezbollah volumes each set out the record of the movement concerned in its own terms; this part does the same for the government of the Islamic Republic. It sets out what Iran's supreme leaders and one of its presidents have said about Israel, quoted with dates and with the dispute over the most famous of those remarks; the money and weapons Iran's institutions have supplied to allied armed groups; plots to kill people on American soil that US prosecutors have charged and courts have tried; the holding of foreigners as bargaining chips; and the killing, imprisonment and execution of Iran's own citizens from 1988 to 2026. These are the acts of named offices and institutions, chiefly the Office of the Supreme Leader, the Revolutionary Guards and the intelligence ministry, and the government's stated position is given beside each finding.
chapters.outro: Part Nine established that Iran's leaders called for the end of Israel as a state for four decades: Khamenei called it a "cancerous tumor" in 2000, 2009, 2018 and 2020, said in 2000 and 2018 that it should be removed, and said in 2015 it would not exist in 25 years, while proposing a referendum and denying any threat to Jews; Ahmadinejad's 2005 words are disputed in translation but not in hostility, and his government hosted Holocaust deniers in 2006. [cite:ir9_tnr_khamenei] [cite:ir9_cnn_25yrs] [cite:ir9_toi_tumor2018] [cite:ir9_farda_2018] [cite:ir9_rferl_tumor2020] [cite:ir9_atl_translation] [cite:ir3_wiki_conf2006] It established that Iran funded and armed Hezbollah, Palestinian groups, the Houthis and Iraqi militias, that US courts convicted men for IRGC-directed plots against a Saudi ambassador and an Iranian-American journalist, and that prosecutors charged plots against John Bolton and Donald Trump, which Iran denies. [cite:hz6_icg_crt2018] [cite:hm_state_iran] [cite:hz10_un_poe2024] [cite:ir9_mt_603] [cite:ir9_doj_arbabsiar] [cite:ir9_doj_alinejad] [cite:ir9_nbc_bolton] [cite:ir9_usip_shakeri] At home, the same state killed thousands of prisoners in 1988, hundreds or more of protesters in 2019 and 2022 and thousands in January 2026, and executed at least 1,639 people in 2025, by the most cautious count. [cite:ir9_amnesty_1988] [cite:ir9_rferl_2019] [cite:ir9_un_ffm2024] [cite:ir9_gn_jan2026] [cite:ir9_almon_ihr2025] None of this record, on its own, answers the question this book is testing: whether Iran's government was about to build a bomb, and whether that justified war. Part Ten turns to the first of the two wars, the twelve days of June 2025. [scene:ir10_strikes|The Twelve Days]

sections.h: What the Leaders Said
sections.html:
The earlier parts of this book set out what Israel and the United States did to Iran and with Iran. This part sets out, in the same register, what the government of the Islamic Republic has said and done. This section covers the statements of its two supreme leaders and of one president about Israel, and the state's sponsorship of Holocaust denial; the next covers its funding and arming of armed groups, plots on American soil and the detention of foreign and dual nationals [scene:ir9_reach|Money, weapons, plots and hostages]; the third covers repression at home. These are acts of a government and its institutions, chiefly the Office of the Supreme Leader, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its Quds Force, and the Ministry of Intelligence. They are not attributed here to Iranians at large, many of whom, as the third section shows, have been the first victims of the same institutions.

Khomeini and Khamenei

The founder of the Islamic Republic set the line. In his New Year message of 21 March 1980, Ruhollah Khomeini said "we should try hard to export our revolution to the world" and named "America, Israel and Zionism" as enemies; the year before, he had declared the last Friday of Ramadan as Quds Day, a state-organised day of rallies against Israel held every year since. [cite:hz1_merip_khomeini] [cite:ir2_wiki_quds] [cite:ir9_rferl_tumor2020] Part Two traces how this rhetoric sat beside the secret purchase of Israeli arms. [scene:ir2_revolution|The break, February 1979]

His successor, Ali Khamenei, supreme leader until he was killed in the US–Israeli strikes of 28 February 2026, returned to the same image for a quarter of a century. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] He called Israel a "cancerous growth" in 1998 and in 2000 said "this cancerous tumor of a state should be removed from the region," as quoted by The New Republic. [cite:ir9_tnr_khamenei] At a Tehran conference in support of the Palestinians on 4 March 2009 he again called Israel a "cancerous tumor" and proposed a referendum among those with a legitimate claim to Palestine to decide its government. [cite:ir9_cbs_2009] On 3 June 2018 his official account posted that Israel "is a malignant cancerous tumor in the West Asian region that has to be removed and eradicated: it is possible and it will happen." [cite:ir9_toi_tumor2018] A week later, in comments on his website, he denied threatening Israel and repeated the referendum proposal. [cite:ir9_farda_2018] On Quds Day, 22 May 2020, he said "The Zionist regime is a cancerous tumor in the region," and in the same speech praised Iran's supply of arms to Palestinian fighters, his first public confirmation that Iran was arming them. [cite:ir9_rferl_tumor2020] His office had circulated a poster headed "the final solution" in the days before; it was deleted from his Twitter account though it remained on the Persian version of his website, and he said his opposition to Israel was not antisemitic. [cite:ir9_ynet_2020]

The most quoted forecast came on 9 September 2015, two months after the nuclear deal was concluded. At the Imam Khomeini Mosque in Tehran Khamenei said: "God willing, there will be no such thing as a Zionist regime in 25 years." Netanyahu, in London for talks with the British prime minister, referred to "the tyrant in Tehran" and said: "Israel is a strong country and it will become even stronger." [cite:ir9_cnn_25yrs] Khamenei's own gloss, in a November 2014 post, was that the "elimination" of Israel did not mean a "massacre of the Jewish people" but a referendum of the land's "original" inhabitants, a position Part Three examines alongside his statement in March 2014 that the Holocaust was "an event whose reality is uncertain." [cite:ir3_toi_9point] [cite:ir3_brookings_2014] [scene:ir3_facts|The other fact]

"Wiped off the map": what Ahmadinejad said

On 26 October 2005 President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad addressed students at a Tehran conference titled "The World Without Zionism." He was widely reported as calling for Israel to be "wiped off the map." [cite:ir9_rferl_2005] The translation has been argued over ever since, and both sides of the argument rest on the same sentence, which Ahmadinejad attributed to Khomeini. Transliterated, it reads "een rezhim-i eshghalgar-i Qods bayad az safheh-i ruzgar mahv shavad." [cite:ir9_atl_translation]

The historian Juan Cole and the Guardian's Jonathan Steele rendered it as "the regime occupying Jerusalem must vanish from the page of time," and argued that it expressed a wish for the end of a regime, in the way Ahmadinejad in the same speech recalled the fall of the Shah, not a threat of war. [cite:ir9_steele_2006] [cite:ir9_atl_translation] The Middle East Media Research Institute (MEMRI), often cited by critics of Iran, translated it as "must be eliminated from the pages of history," and BBC Monitoring, after first writing "eliminated from the map of the world," said on review that "page of history" was closer. [cite:ir9_steele_2006] On the other side, the New York Times, whose correspondent Nazila Fathi first used "wiped off the map," defended its rendering; translators it consulted argued that the Persian verb is active and transitive, so that "wiped off" or "wiped away" is more accurate than "vanish." Official Iranian outlets, among them the state broadcaster IRIB, later ran the same English translation. [cite:ir9_atl_translation] [cite:ir9_steele_2006] Both readings agree that the president of Iran called for the end of what he called the regime occupying Jerusalem; they differ on whether the words carried a threat of Iranian military action. The dispute is about tense and agency, not about whether the hostility was real.

The record of Holocaust denial under Ahmadinejad is not disputed. On 11 and 12 December 2006 the foreign ministry's Institute for Political and International Studies hosted a conference to "review" the Holocaust, attended by the former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke, the convicted French denier Robert Faurisson and six members of the anti-Zionist Neturei Karta sect. Foreign Minister Manouchehr Mottaki said it was held "neither to deny nor prove" the Holocaust; Ban Ki-moon, Angela Merkel, the US State Department and Ehud Olmert condemned it. [cite:ir3_wiki_conf2006]

sections.h: Money, Weapons, Plots and Hostages
sections.html:
Iran's leaders did not confine their hostility to speeches. The institutions they commanded financed and armed allied groups across the region, planned killings on American soil, and held foreigners as leverage. Each strand below rests on court records, official estimates or the groups' own statements, with Iran's stated position given beside it.

Words were matched with money. The US State Department estimated in 2018 that Iran gave Hezbollah about $700 million a year, "the overwhelming majority" of its budget, and up to $100 million a year to Palestinian groups including Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ). [cite:hz6_icg_crt2018] [cite:hm_state_iran] Hezbollah's leader Hassan Nasrallah said on 24 June 2016 that its budget, salaries, weapons and rockets "come from the Islamic Republic of Iran." [cite:hz6_alarabiya_2016] The US lists PIJ as receiving "financial assistance and training primarily from Iran." [cite:hz10s_state_pij] The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported in 2024 that 53 weapons items it examined had strong similarities to Iranian materiel, and concluded that without foreign support the movement could not build such complex weapons; Iran's UN envoy rejected US and British claims that it supplied them. [cite:hz10_un_poe2024] [cite:ir9_iranintl_houthis] In Iraq, the Pentagon attributed at least 603 US deaths between 2003 and 2011 to Iran-backed militias, about 17 per cent of the total, many from explosively formed penetrators that it said Iran supplied; Iraqi militias under the "Islamic Resistance in Iraq" umbrella, which includes Kata'ib Hezbollah, mounted more than 160 attacks on US forces after 7 October 2023, including the drone strike that killed three US soldiers at Tower 22 in Jordan on 28 January 2024, which the United States blamed on Kata'ib Hezbollah; Iran denies ordering the attacks and says the factions act independently. [cite:ir9_mt_603] [cite:hz10_at_farida] [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] The Hezbollah volume follows each of these flows in detail, including the view of analysts such as the former CIA officer Norman Roule that Iran sought the product of these groups' actions rather than control of them. [cite:hz10_npr_roule] [scene:hz6_money|Who pays Hezbollah] [scene:hz10_houthis|The Houthis] [scene:hz10_iraq|Iraq's militias]

Iran's stated position is that it supports "resistance" to occupation and does not command it. On 10 October 2023 Khamenei said Iran was not behind the Hamas attack of three days earlier, while saying "we kiss the hands of those who planned the attack." [cite:ir9_reuters_kiss2023] The direct missile attacks of April and October 2024, Iran's first from its own territory on Israel, are set out in Part Eight. [scene:ir8_open|The shadow war in the open]

Plots on American soil

US federal courts have recorded several IRGC plots inside the United States. In 2011 Manssor Arbabsiar, a US citizen, arranged with a man he believed to be a Mexican cartel member, in fact a DEA informant, to kill the Saudi ambassador in Washington for $1.5 million, wiring a $100,000 down payment. He pleaded guilty, admitting he acted for senior Quds Force officials, and was sentenced to 25 years on 30 May 2013. [cite:ir9_doj_arbabsiar] On 10 August 2022 the Justice Department charged an IRGC member, Shahram Poursafi, with offering $300,000 for the murder of the former national security adviser John Bolton, which prosecutors said was "likely in retaliation" for the US killing of Qassem Soleimani. [cite:ir9_nbc_bolton] [cite:ir9_iranintl_bolton] Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Nasser Kanani, called the charge "ridiculous" and "politically motivated." [cite:ir9a_almon_bolton] On 8 November 2024 it charged Farhad Shakeri, described as an IRGC asset in Tehran, alleging he had been tasked on 7 October 2024 with planning the killing of Donald Trump; Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called it a fabricated "scenario." [cite:ir9_usip_shakeri] The Iranian-American journalist Masih Alinejad was the target of an intelligence ministry kidnapping plot in 2020–21 and then of an IRGC murder-for-hire plot; two men were convicted in March 2025 and sentenced to 25 years on 29 October 2025. [cite:ir9_doj_alinejad] When the kidnapping charges were announced in July 2021, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Saeed Khatibzadeh, called them "baseless and ridiculous." [cite:ir9a_ap_alinejad] Plots in other countries are covered in Part Eight. [scene:ir8_iranside|Iran's side of the shadow war]

Hostage diplomacy

The use of detainees as leverage began on 4 November 1979, when students seized the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans for 444 days. [cite:ir9_usip_hostages] It has continued with dual nationals. On 18 September 2023 five Americans, among them the businessman Siamak Namazi, held since 2015 on espionage charges his family rejects, were freed as $6 billion of Iranian funds frozen in South Korea were moved to Qatari banks and five Iranians in the US received clemency; Washington said the money was restricted to humanitarian purchases and was not a ransom, while Iran's foreign ministry said it expected "total access" to the funds and denied any spending restrictions. [cite:ir9_newarab_swap] [cite:ir8_voa_swap] In March 2022 the British-Iranian aid worker Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe was released after six years as Britain paid a £393.8 million debt dating from a cancelled pre-1979 tank contract; neither government said the two were linked. [cite:ir9_forces_nazanin] In both cases the detainees had been held on charges brought by Iran's courts, and in both cases their release coincided with the transfer of money that Iran said was its own.

sections.h: Repression at Home, 1988–2026
sections.html:
The same institutions that armed allies abroad have used lethal force against Iran's own citizens. The pattern is documented in five episodes: the prison killings of 1988, the crackdown after the 2009 election, the November 2019 fuel protests, the 2022 protests after the death of Mahsa Amini and the crackdown of January 2026. Each produced death tolls that differ widely by source, because the authorities have rarely published figures and have cut the internet while killing was under way. The figures below are given with their source and, where known, how they were counted. The government's own account is given beside each.

1988: the prison killings

In July 1988, weeks before the war with Iraq ended on 20 August, Khomeini issued a written order that imprisoned members of the opposition People's Mojahedin who remained loyal to it be executed as "waging war on God"; a second order reportedly covered leftist prisoners. [cite:ir9_usip_raisi] [cite:ir2_brit_war] Panels of judicial, prosecution, intelligence and prison officials, which came to be called "death commissions," sat in 32 cities and held summary proceedings with no appeal. Amnesty International put the number killed between late July and early September 1988 at no fewer than 5,000, most of them Mojahedin supporters and hundreds from leftist and Kurdish groups; the authorities have never told families how or why their relatives died or returned the bodies. [cite:ir9_amnesty_1988] Other estimates run from 2,800–3,800, the figure given at the time by Khomeini's designated heir Hossein-Ali Montazeri, to the 4,481 names published by Iranian activists. Montazeri protested in writing on 15 August 1988 and told the Tehran panel it was the biggest crime in the Islamic Republic's history; he resigned as heir under pressure in March 1989. [cite:ir9_usip_raisi]

One member of the Tehran panel was Ebrahim Raisi, then the 27-year-old deputy prosecutor of Tehran and later president of Iran. In 2018 he said he had not headed the court; at his first press conference as president-elect, on 21 June 2021, he said that a prosecutor who "defended the security of the people" should "be praised." [cite:ir9_usip_raisi] [cite:ir9_amnesty_1988] The government has never acknowledged the scale of the killings; officials have described the victims as a "few terrorists" and those responsible as deserving honour. [cite:ir9_amnesty_1988] In July 2024 the UN Special Rapporteur on Iran, Javaid Rehman, concluded that the killings of 1981–82 and 1988 amounted to crimes against humanity, and to genocide against people targeted for their beliefs, and called for an international accountability mechanism. Tehran rejects the findings. [cite:ir9_jurist_rehman]

2009, 2019, 2022

After the presidential election of 12 June 2009, which returned Ahmadinejad and which the defeated candidates said was rigged, mass protests were met by the security forces. A senior Revolutionary Guards commander put the death toll at 36, including three detainees who died in Kahrizak prison, which was then closed; the opposition counted 72. [cite:ir9_ht_2009] The killing of Neda Agha-Soltan on a Tehran street on 20 June 2009 was filmed and seen around the world; officials blamed foreign media and intelligence services, and state television later claimed she had staged her death. [cite:ir9_wiki_neda]

In November 2019 petrol rationing and a price rise set off protests that turned into calls for the clerical leadership to go, and the authorities shut down the internet for days. Reuters reported on 23 December 2019, citing three interior ministry officials, that about 1,500 people were killed in less than two weeks, and that Khamenei had told officials on 17 November: "Do whatever it takes to end it." Amnesty International confirmed at least 304 deaths; Iran Human Rights at least 324. The Supreme National Security Council called the Reuters report "false propaganda," and officials acknowledged only that "some rioters were killed." [cite:ir9_rferl_2019] [cite:ir9_farda_2019] A member of parliament said security officials had told a parliamentary committee the toll was 170; no official figure was published. [cite:ir9_farda_2019]

On 13 September 2022 the morality police arrested Mahsa Amini in Tehran for "inappropriate attire"; she died in custody three days later. [cite:ir9_aj_coroner] The protests under the slogan "Woman, Life, Freedom" spread to most of the country. A UN fact-finding mission reported in March 2024 that her death was "unlawful and caused by physical violence" for which the state was responsible, that credible figures put the number of protesters killed at 551, including 49 women and 68 children, that 104 people were killed in a single day in Zahedan on 30 September 2022, and that the crackdown included crimes against humanity. [cite:ir9_un_ffm2024] [cite:ir9_aj_ffm2024] At least nine young men were executed in connection with the protests between December 2022 and January 2024 after proceedings the mission found arbitrary. [cite:ir9_aj_ffm2024] The government's coroner said on 7 October 2022 that Amini died of cerebral hypoxia linked to "underlying diseases," not blows; her family disputed this. Khamenei blamed the United States and Israel for the unrest, the government said 54 security personnel were killed, and Iran refused to cooperate with the UN mission. [cite:ir9_aj_coroner] [cite:ir9_un_ffm2024]

January 2026

Protests that began in late December 2025 over the collapse of the currency and living costs turned into calls for the end of clerical rule. The authorities deployed the police, the Basij and the IRGC and imposed severe internet and phone restrictions. In a speech broadcast on state television in mid-January 2026, Khamenei acknowledged that "thousands" had been killed, some in an "inhuman, savage manner"; NPR reported that he blamed President Trump. [cite:ir9_npr_jan2026] The government's only published toll, on 21 January, was 3,117. Iran Human Rights counted more than 3,400 by mid-January; the US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), which AP noted relies on a network of activists inside the country to verify deaths and has been accurate in previous rounds of unrest, reached at least 7,002 by 12 February, with many more cases unconfirmed. AP said it could not verify any figure because of the communications blackout. [cite:ir9_gn_jan2026] [cite:ir9_npr_jan2026] Higher estimates circulated in some media; they are not used here because their method could not be checked. The government said it would not carry out mass executions of detainees, and at the UN it accused the US and Israel of interfering in its internal affairs. [cite:ir9_npr_jan2026] By April 2026, Iran Human Rights reported, seven people linked to the January protests had been hanged and at least 26 more sentenced to death. [cite:ir9_almon_ihr2025] Six weeks after the crackdown, on 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel went to war with Iran, the subject of Part Eleven. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] [scene:ir11_war|The 2026 war]

The gallows and the minorities

Executions rose steeply after 2022. The UN recorded 834 in 2023. [cite:ir9_un_ffm2024] For 2024 Amnesty counted at least 972, 64 per cent of all known executions worldwide, and Iran Human Rights 975. [cite:ir9_iranintl_amnesty2024] [cite:ir9_almon_ihr2025] For 2025 Iran Human Rights and its French partner ECPM counted at least 1,639, the most since 1989, almost half for drug offences, with 48 women among them; Amnesty, using its own sources, counted 2,159, about four-fifths of all executions it recorded worldwide outside China. [cite:ir9_almon_ihr2025] [cite:ir9_newarab_amnesty2025] Official sources announce only a small share: in 2024, 95 of the executions Iran Human Rights recorded. The same organisation found ethnic minorities overrepresented; nine of the 31 people executed on security charges that year were Kurdish political prisoners. [cite:ir9_usip_minorities2024]

The Bahá'í faith is not among the religions the constitution recognises, which are Zoroastrianism, Judaism and Christianity. [cite:ir3_const_en] More than 200 Bahá'ís were killed or executed after 1979; a 1991 government memorandum cited by Bahá'í organisations set out a policy of preventing the community's development, and Bahá'ís have since been barred from universities and much public employment. UN experts said in July 2026 that about 57 Bahá'ís were in detention, some reportedly subjected to mock executions to extract confessions that were then broadcast on state media. [cite:ir9_jurist_bahai2026] The government's position is that the faith is a banned sect: on 1 August 2022 the intelligence ministry announced arrests of what it called "the Bahai spy party," linked to "the Zionist centre," a reference to the faith's world centre in Haifa. [cite:ir9_almon_bahai2022] The treatment of Iran's recognised Jewish minority is examined in Part Three. [scene:ir3_facts|The Jews of Iran: the other fact]

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: The Twelve Days
chapters.intro: On 13 June 2025, two days before the United States and Iran were due to hold a sixth round of nuclear talks in Muscat, Israel began bombing Iran. Over the next twelve days Iran fired hundreds of ballistic missiles at Israeli cities, the United States dropped its heaviest bunker-busting bombs on Iran's enrichment plants, and Iran struck back at an American base in Qatar after warning first. The war ended in a ceasefire announced by President Trump. This part sets out, day by day and from named sources, the diplomacy that the strikes cut across, what each government said it was doing and why, the dead on both sides as each source counted them, and the dispute that followed over how much damage was done and where Iran's near-weapons-grade uranium went.
chapters.outro: Part Ten established that Israel opened the war during active, Oman-mediated US–Iran talks and the day after the IAEA Board found Iran in breach of its safeguards obligations, while the US intelligence community's last public position was that Iran was not building a weapon. [cite:ir10_an_round6] [cite:ir5_aj_iaea2025] [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] The twelve days killed 28 people in Israel and between about 1,060 and 1,190 in Iran, by the counts of the Iranian government and HRANA. [cite:ir10_toi_numbers] [cite:ir10_ap_toll] The United States, having said it was not involved, bombed Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, and its president called the sites "obliterated"; its own first intelligence assessment said months, later officials said years, and the IAEA said enrichment could resume within months. [cite:ir10_gov_address] [cite:ir10_ng_cia] [cite:ir10_ss_parnell] Iran answered the United States with a warned, casualty-free strike and then shut the inspectors out, and a year later the IAEA still could not say where its last estimated stock of 440.9 kilograms of 60 per cent uranium was. [cite:ir10_ax_udeid] [cite:ir10_aj_iaealaw] [cite:ir10_isis_jun26] The ceasefire held until 28 February 2026, when the United States and Israel went to war with Iran together; Part Eleven follows that war. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [scene:ir11_war|The 2026 war]

sections.h: Talks, a Resolution and Rising Lion
sections.html:
In the spring of 2025 the United States and Iran were negotiating. The talks were mediated by Oman. Iran described them as indirect, with the Omani foreign minister carrying messages between the delegations. The American envoy was Steve Witkoff and the Iranian negotiator was the foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi. A first round was held in Muscat in mid-April, and a second in Rome on 19 April 2025. [cite:ir10_gn_round2] A third round took place in Oman on 26 April and a fourth in Muscat on 11 May. [cite:ir10_ap_round4] On 21 May Oman announced a fifth round, to be held in Rome that Friday, 23 May. [cite:ir10_ap_round5] On 12 June the Omani foreign minister, Badr al-Busaidi, wrote: "I am pleased to confirm the 6th round of Iran US talks will be held in Muscat this Sunday the 15th." [cite:ir10_an_round6]

Enrichment was the point the talks turned on. Witkoff first suggested that Iran might be allowed to enrich to 3.67 per cent, the JCPOA ceiling, and then said that "An enrichment program can never exist in the state of Iran ever again." Araghchi answered that enrichment "should definitely continue and there is no room for compromise on that." He added that Iran might accept limits on its "dimensions, amount and level for trust building." [cite:ir10_ap_round4] In May he said enrichment "will continue — with or without an agreement." The Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, said: "I don't think nuclear talks with the U.S. will bring results. I don't know." [cite:ir10_ap_round5] At this point Iran held 408.6 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 per cent, and inspectors had worked without the Additional Protocol since 2021. Part Seven describes how that position was reached. [cite:ir7_isis_may25] [scene:ir7_withdrawal|The withdrawal]

Two other facts form the background. In March 2025 the Director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, told Congress that the US intelligence community "continues to assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon" and that Khamenei "has not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003". She also said that Iran's stockpile of enriched uranium was at its highest level, unprecedented for a state without nuclear weapons. [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] Then, on 12 June 2025, the IAEA Board of Governors voted 19 to 3, with 11 abstentions, that Iran was not complying with its safeguards obligations. The resolution cited failures since 2019 and uranium traces at undeclared sites. It was the Board's first such finding in nearly two decades. Iran said the resolution had "no technical and legal basis" and announced a new enrichment facility. [cite:ir5_aj_iaea2025]

Thirteen June

In the early hours of 13 June 2025, the day after the Board vote and two days before the scheduled sixth round, Israel attacked Iran. It called the operation Rising Lion. The strikes hit the Natanz enrichment site and military targets, and killed senior commanders and scientists. Among those killed were the chief of the armed forces general staff, Mohammad Bagheri; the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Hossein Salami; Gholamali Rashid, commander of the Khatam al-Anbiya central headquarters; and Amir Ali Hajizadeh, commander of the IRGC's aerospace force. Several nuclear scientists were also killed. They included Fereydoun Abbasi-Davani, a former head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran; Mohammad Mahdi Tehranchi; Abdolhamid Minouchehr, head of nuclear engineering at Shahid Beheshti University; Ahmad Reza Zolfaghari; and Amir Hossein Faghihi, a deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organization. [cite:ir10_na_killed] Counts of the scientists killed differ. Early reports named six. [cite:ir10_na_killed] By the end of the war Israel said it had killed at least 15 senior scientists and about 30 senior commanders. These are Israeli claims. [cite:ir10_toi_numbers] On 14 June Oman said the Muscat round would not take place; its foreign minister added that "diplomacy and dialogue remain the only pathway to lasting peace." [cite:ir10_ii_off]

Netanyahu gave Israel's reason in a video statement that day. He said Iran had "enough highly enriched uranium for nine atom bombs" and had taken "steps to weaponize." He continued: "if not stopped, Iran could produce a nuclear weapon in a very short time. It could be a year. It could be within a few months, less than a year." [cite:ir5_dcnf_jun2025] The warning was conditional, and it was not a claim that a bomb existed. Part Five tests it against his earlier predictions. [scene:ir5_predictions|The predictions] On 14 June the military spokesman said the aim was "eliminating the existential Iranian threat to the State of Israel—the nuclear and missile threat." He said Iran had built infrastructure for "reconverting enriched uranium for clear military purposes." [cite:ir10_idf_jun14] The public record does not include the intelligence behind that last claim. The US intelligence position given to Congress in March had not been publicly revised. When Gabbard's testimony was raised, Trump said: "I don't care what she said," and said Iran was "very close" to a weapon. Iran said its programme was peaceful. [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] [cite:hz11_pbs_gabbard] On 19 June the IAEA Director General, Rafael Grossi, said: "We did not find in Iran elements to indicate that there is an active, systematic plan to build a nuclear weapon." [cite:ir5_tbs_grossi]

What Washington knew is documented in three parts. The first is the public US statement. On the night of the attack, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "Tonight, Israel took unilateral action against Iran. We are not involved in strikes against Iran." He added that Israel had told the United States the action was necessary for its self-defence. [cite:ir10_wh_rubio] The second is what Trump himself said. On 12 June he said of an Israeli strike: "I don't want them going in because, I mean, that would blow it." [cite:ir10_olj_trump] On 13 June he told ABC that the attack had been "excellent" and that "there's more to come. A lot more." [cite:ir10_ih_trump] He also posted that he had given Iran "a 60-day ultimatum" two months earlier: "Today is day 61... Now they have, perhaps, a second chance!" [cite:ir10_olj_trump] The third is reporting. Fox News reported that the administration "knew about the Israeli plans in advance" and that "There were no surprises." The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had asked Netanyahu on 9 June not to strike. [cite:ir10_med_fox] Together these show that the US government knew the attack was coming and publicly said it was not taking part. Whether Trump privately approved it is not shown by the public record. His own words that week point both ways.

True Promise 3

Iran fired back from the night of 13 June. The IRGC called its attacks "Operation True Promise 3" and described them as "in direct retaliation against Israeli aggression." It said it was hitting military and fuel infrastructure. [cite:ir10_irna_tp3] By Israeli military count, Iran fired about 550 ballistic missiles and about 1,000 drones over twelve days. About 90 per cent of the missiles were intercepted, and at least 31 struck populated areas or critical infrastructure. [cite:ir10_toi_numbers] American THAAD batteries and warships helped intercept them, as set out in [scene:ow7_iran|Defending Israel, fighting Iran]; Part Fourteen counts the cost. [scene:ir14_bill|The American bill]

The worst single strike was in Bat Yam on 15 June, where a missile killed nine people and injured about 200. The same night four women from one family were killed in Tamra. The Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot was hit, and on 16 June a strike shut down the Bazan refinery in Haifa. [cite:ir10_aj_map] On 19 June a missile hit Soroka Medical Centre in Beersheba, the largest hospital in southern Israel. Iran's state news agency said the targets were Israeli military intelligence sites at the nearby Gav-Yam technology park. Netanyahu said Iran's "terrorist tyrants" had fired at a hospital and promised to "exact the full price." [cite:ir10_en_soroka] Israel's Health Ministry recorded 3,238 people taken to hospital. Twenty-eight people were killed in Israel, all but one of them civilians, and more than 9,000 were displaced. [cite:ir10_toi_numbers]

Iran's toll was much higher, and the counts differ. By 24 June Iran's Health Ministry gave at least 610 dead. [cite:ir10_toi_numbers] On 7 July the head of Iran's Foundation of Martyrs and Veterans Affairs, Saeed Ohadi, said at least 1,060 had been killed and the figure might reach 1,100. The Washington-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) counted 1,190 dead, including 436 civilians and 435 members of the security forces, and 4,475 wounded. [cite:ir10_ap_toll] The two counts use different methods. The government figure is an official total of the dead that does not separate civilians from combatants. HRANA's figure comes from case-by-case reports and includes deaths it could not classify. Neither can be checked independently. This book gives the range: about 1,060 to 1,190 killed in Iran, and 28 killed in Israel.

sections.h: Midnight Hammer
sections.html:
On 21 June 2025 the United States joined the war. Seven B-2 bombers took off from Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri around midnight and flew east for about eighteen hours with almost no radio contact. They dropped fourteen GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrators, bombs built to reach deeply buried targets, on the enrichment plants at Fordow and Natanz. A submarine fired more than two dozen Tomahawk cruise missiles at the nuclear site at Isfahan. In all, more than 125 American aircraft took part. The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, General Dan Caine, said initial assessments showed "extremely severe damage and destruction" at all three sites, but that "final battle damage will take some time." The Defense Secretary, Pete Hegseth, said the mission "was not, has not, been about regime change." [cite:ir10_bd_hammer]

Trump spoke from the White House at 10:02 that evening. He said: "Our objective was the destruction of Iran's nuclear enrichment capacity." He said that "Iran's key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated." He thanked and congratulated Netanyahu, and warned: "There will be either peace or there will be tragedy for Iran... Remember, there are many targets left." [cite:ir10_gov_address] Congress had not authorised the strike. On 27 June the Senate voted 47 to 53, rejecting a resolution by Senator Tim Kaine that would have required congressional approval for further hostilities against Iran. [cite:hz12b_ap_jun2025] Costs of War at Brown University later estimated the cost of the June operations at $2.04 to $2.25 billion. Most of that, $1.8 to $1.95 billion, was THAAD interceptors fired in Israel's defence. The bombers, the GBU-57s and the Tomahawks cost far less. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] Part Fourteen sets out the wider bill. [scene:ir14_bill|The American bill]

Iran replied on 23 June with missiles fired at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, where US forces are based. It warned in advance. According to Axios, Qatar and the Trump administration were both told beforehand. Qatari air defences intercepted the missiles, and one struck near the base without causing casualties. Iran's Supreme National Security Council said the number of missiles matched the number of bombs the United States had dropped. Axios read this as a signal that Iran wanted to de-escalate. Qatar condemned the attack and called for a return to negotiations. [cite:ir10_ax_udeid] Trump said that "NO Americans were harmed, and hardly any damage was done." [cite:ir10_gov_udeid] He thanked Iran for the "early notice." [cite:ir10_ax_udeid] Iran's choices that day are documented: it struck a US base, it warned beforehand, and it fired a matching, symbolic number. They bear directly on whether Iran wanted war with the United States, which Part Twelve examines. [scene:ir12_question|Does Iran want war?]

The Ceasefire

That evening Trump announced a "complete and total" ceasefire. It took effect early on 24 June. A White House official said Vice President JD Vance, Rubio and Witkoff had talked to Iran "through direct and indirect channels." Qatar played what the report called "an important role," and Trump thanked its emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani. [cite:ir10_en_ceasefire] Some accounts credit Oman with brokering the ceasefire. This book did not find a primary source for that, so it states only the announcement and Qatar's role. Netanyahu said that Israel "will respond forcefully to any violation." Strikes continued up to the deadline: local authorities reported five killed in Beersheba, and nine were reported killed in Iran. [cite:ir10_en_ceasefire] That morning Trump said Iran had violated the truce "but Israel violated it too." He wrote: "ISRAEL. DO NOT DROP THOSE BOMBS." [cite:ir10_kt_violations] The same day Netanyahu declared a "historic victory" and said: "For decades, I have promised you that Iran would not have nuclear weapons." [cite:ir5_pmo_jun2025] The ceasefire held for eight months. On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel attacked Iran together, and the Supreme Leader was killed. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] Part Eleven covers that war. [scene:ir11_war|The 2026 war]

Obliterated, or Set Back?

How much damage the strikes did became a dispute within days. On 24 June CNN and other outlets reported a preliminary Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) assessment that the programme had been set back by only months. The assessment was of low confidence and was made soon after the strikes. Fuller analyses could reach different conclusions. On 25 June the CIA Director, John Ratcliffe, said that "a body of credible intelligence indicates Iran's Nuclear Program has been severely damaged." He said several key facilities "would have to be rebuilt over the course of years." The CIA did not release its evidence. Gabbard said the facilities had been "destroyed." The Financial Times, citing European officials, reported that Iran's highly enriched uranium was largely intact. At the NATO summit Trump described the DIA report himself: "They said it could be limited or it could be very severe." [cite:ir10_ng_cia] On 2 July the Pentagon spokesman, Sean Parnell, said the programme had been degraded by "probably closer to two years." He did not explain how that estimate was reached. Grossi said Iran could resume enrichment within "a matter of months," calling the damage "severe" but "not total." [cite:ir10_ss_parnell]

In August 2025 Hegseth removed the DIA's director, Lieutenant General Jeffrey Kruse. Anonymous sources gave the reason as "loss of confidence." The Pentagon did not comment. Reporting placed the firing after the leaked assessment, but no official linked the two. [cite:ir10_adn_kruse] The connection is a sequence of events, not a documented cause.

Later evidence supports serious damage while leaving the most important material unaccounted for. An analysis of the IAEA's June 2026 reports by the Institute for Science and International Security, a Washington research group, concluded that "Iran has no identifiable route to produce weapon-grade uranium" in its centrifuge plants. This was the Institute's own assessment, not an IAEA finding. [cite:ir10_isis_jun26] In June 2026 AP reported that, before the wars, Iran had been "months or years away" from a usable weapon, with no evidence it had decided to build one. Netanyahu said that without the two operations Iran "would have had atomic bombs." [cite:ir5_ap_jun2026]

The Inspectors and the Missing Uranium

Iran then cut back the IAEA's access. On 25 June the Majlis voted 221 to 0, with one abstention, to suspend cooperation with the agency. The speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the IAEA had "put its international credibility up for auction." [cite:ir10_dp_majlis] On 2 July Iranian state television reported that President Masoud Pezeshkian had signed the law. It requires approval from the Supreme National Security Council before inspectors can visit nuclear sites. Iranian officials described the Board's 12 June resolution as one of the "excuses" for the attacks. The US State Department called the suspension "unacceptable," and Germany called it a "disastrous signal." [cite:ir10_aj_iaealaw] Iran and the IAEA reached the Cairo agreement on 9 September 2025 to resume inspections. Later that month UN sanctions were reimposed under the snapback mechanism that Britain, France and Germany had triggered in August, and on 20 November Iran ended the agreement. [cite:ir7_crs_snapback] [cite:ir10_isis_jun26] By November the agency had inspected only undamaged sites such as Bushehr. Iran said that "any cooperation with the Agency is conditional on the decision" of the Supreme National Security Council. [cite:ir10_ap_nov25]

The question that mattered most was what had happened to the uranium. The IAEA's last estimate, for 13 June 2025, the day the attacks began, was 440.9 kilograms enriched up to 60 per cent; earlier figures had been verified, this one was not. [cite:ir10_isis_jun26] Grossi said it could be enough for as many as ten bombs if Iran chose to build them, but that this did not mean Iran had a weapon. [cite:ir10_ap_nov25] Soon after the strikes he said: "We do not have information of the whereabouts of this material." [cite:ir10_fox_grossi] A year later the position had not changed. In its June 2026 report the IAEA said it "cannot provide any information on the current size, composition or whereabouts of the stockpile." It reported regular vehicle activity around the entrance to the tunnel complex at Isfahan, where some of the material had been stored, in February 2026, and asked Iran for access. The agency had stopped verification in Iran after 28 February 2026. [cite:ir10_isis_jun26] As of October 2026 the public record does not show the stockpile accounted for.

The twelve days can be summarised in three parts. The documented facts are these. Israel struck during active US–Iran talks and the day after an IAEA non-compliance finding. The United States knew the attack was coming, publicly stood aside, and then bombed the three main nuclear sites. Iran's retaliation against the United States was warned in advance and caused no casualties. [cite:ir10_wh_rubio] [cite:ir10_bd_hammer] [cite:ir10_ax_udeid] The pattern that can be shown is that each government's claims ran ahead of its evidence. The "obliterated" claim was not supported by the first intelligence assessment. Israel's claim that Iran was moving to weaponise was not matched by any public US or IAEA finding. Iran's insistence that its programme was peaceful sat beside a 60 per cent stockpile it would not let anyone verify. [cite:ir10_ng_cia] [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] [cite:ir10_ap_nov25] The question of motive remains an argument. On one reading, Israel's attack drew the United States into a war it had been trying to avoid by negotiation. On the other, Trump chose to bomb on his own stated aim of ending Iran's enrichment, a demand his envoy had already made at the table. [cite:ir10_ap_round4] Part Thirteen weighs both readings. [scene:ir13_why|Why Iran?]

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: The 2026 War
chapters.intro: Part Eleven covers the war that began on 28 February 2026, when the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran and killed its Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, on the first day. The first section covers the run-up: the January crackdown on protests inside Iran, the American and Israeli statements that followed, and the talks mediated by Oman that were still going on when the bombs fell. It then sets out the stated aims of each government, the succession in Tehran, Iran's missile and drone attacks on Israel, American bases and the Gulf states, its closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the tolls and how each was counted, and the response at the United Nations. The second section follows the war from the April ceasefire through the Islamabad Memorandum, its collapse in July and the American blockade, to where things stood in October 2026, with each side's stated position on each turn. The American bill in money and lives is told in full in Part Fourteen, and the Lebanese front in the Hezbollah volume; this part links to both and does not repeat them.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven established that the United States and Israel opened the 2026 war on 28 February, two days after a Geneva round that Oman, the mediator, said had made "significant progress", and that both governments stated aims reaching beyond the nuclear programme to Iran's missiles and its government. [cite:ir11_omanfm_geneva] [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026] The first strikes killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and the Assembly of Experts named his son Mojtaba as his successor on 8 March. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] [cite:ir11_reu_mojtaba] Iran answered with missiles and drones on Israel, American bases and the Gulf states and moved to close the Strait of Hormuz, and the Security Council demanded that Iran stop its attacks on the Gulf while passing nothing on the strikes that preceded them. [cite:ir11_airwars] [cite:ir11_week_2817] In the forty days to the April ceasefire Iran's government counted 3,468 dead and HRANA at least 3,636, of whom 1,701 were civilians, among them the children killed at a school in Minab by what Amnesty International found were American missiles, a strike the Pentagon was still investigating; Iranian missiles killed between 24 and 28 people in Israel and at least 23 in the other Gulf states. [cite:ir11_afp_tolls] [cite:ir11_amnesty_minab] [cite:ir11a_almon_minab] [cite:ir11_wiki_strikesisrael] [cite:ir11_amnesty_beitshemesh] The Islamabad Memorandum of 17 June promised a final settlement within sixty days and collapsed on 8 July, and as of October 2026 an American blockade had cut Iran's oil exports to almost nothing, the strait was still constrained, the IAEA had not been able to verify Iran's enriched uranium for more than a year, Iran remained a party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty, and Trump had said he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections of 3 November. [cite:ir11_sole_mou] [cite:ir11_aj_jul8] [cite:ir11_oilprice_exports] [cite:ir11_iaea_sep7] [cite:ir4_k24_npt] [cite:ir11_ap_midterms] Part Twelve asks the question this record raises: whether Iran wanted a war with the United States. [scene:ir12_question|Does Iran want war with America?]

sections.h: The War of 28 February 2026
sections.html:
Eight months after the Twelve-Day War, the United States and Israel went to war with Iran together. This section covers the run-up, the first strikes and their stated aims, the killing of the Supreme Leader and the succession, and Iran's response across the region; the tolls and the world's response follow in the next section. [scene:ir11_toll|The toll and the world's response] The account of June 2025 is in Part Ten. [scene:ir10_strikes|The Twelve Days]

The run-up: protests, threats and talks

Protests began in Iran in the last days of December 2025, when shopkeepers took to the streets over the collapse of the rial, which had fallen to about 1.4 million to the dollar, and the cost of living. Within a week they had become the largest anti-government demonstrations since the protests of 2022. On 2 January President Donald Trump warned that if Iran "violently kills peaceful protesters" the United States "will come to their rescue," adding, "We are locked and loaded and ready to go." Iranian officials answered at once. Ali Larijani, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, said Israel and the United States were stoking the protests, without offering evidence, and the parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, said American bases and forces would be "legitimate targets." [cite:ir11_ap_lockedloaded] On 11 January Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told his cabinet that "Israel is closely monitoring developments in Iran" and that he hoped Iranians would "soon be freed from the yoke of tyranny." [cite:ir11_olj_bibijan]

The crackdown that followed killed thousands. On 21 January the state Martyrs Foundation gave the first official toll, 3,117 dead, and the authorities described the unrest as "terrorist" riots fuelled by the United States.
