The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), a US-based group that verifies deaths through a network inside Iran, counted 4,519 killed at that point, 4,251 of them protesters and 197 security personnel, with 9,049 more deaths under review; Amnesty International documented security forces firing rifles and shotguns loaded with metal pellets at people's heads and torsos. [cite:ir11_aj_toll3117] Two days later HRANA's count passed 5,000. AP could not verify either figure because Iran had cut internet access for more than two weeks. [cite:ir11_gn_hrana5000] The crackdown is set out as part of Iran's own record in Part Nine. [scene:ir9_home|Iran's record at home]

Diplomacy ran alongside the threats. On 6 February American and Iranian delegations held indirect talks in Muscat: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi for Iran, the envoy Steve Witkoff with Jared Kushner for the United States, with Oman's foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, carrying messages between them. Iran wanted to discuss only its nuclear programme; Washington wanted missiles and Iran's support for armed groups on the table too. By then the United States had moved an aircraft carrier group into the region, and Iran had said it would strike American bases if attacked. [cite:ir11_gn_muscat] A round in Geneva on 26 February ended, in Albusaidi's words, with "significant progress", and technical talks were set for Vienna the following week. [cite:ir11_omanfm_geneva] Trump said that day, "My preference is to solve this problem through diplomacy," while Iranian state television said Iran would keep enriching uranium. [cite:ir11_fox_geneva] On 27 February Trump said he was "not happy with the fact that they're not willing to give us what we have to have" and that he did not want Iran enriching any uranium at all; Albusaidi said a deal was within reach and that Iran was willing to give up its enriched uranium and accept comprehensive inspections. The same day the American embassy in Jerusalem told non-essential staff they could leave, and a second carrier was on its way. [cite:ir11_ap_nothappy]

28 February: the strikes and their stated aims

The strikes began on 28 February, two days after the Geneva round and before the Vienna talks could meet. The Pentagon called its operation Epic Fury and Israel called its own Roaring Lion. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] Reuters reported, from three people briefed on the call, that Netanyahu had telephoned Trump less than 48 hours earlier to argue that there might never be a better chance to kill Khamenei; Reuters said its reporting did not suggest that Netanyahu forced Trump to go to war, and Trump has said the decision was his alone. That reporting, and the question of who drew whom in, is weighed in Parts Twelve and Fourteen. [cite:hz12b_reuters_call] [cite:ir11a_reu_call] [scene:ir14_bill|Dragged in: the American bill]

Each government stated its aims. Trump said the purpose was to eliminate "imminent threats from the Iranian regime," claimed Iran was rebuilding its nuclear programme, and told Iranians, "When we are finished, take over your government." Netanyahu said the aim was to "remove the existential threat posed by the terrorist regime in Iran." [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] Israel described its strikes as pre-emptive and said 200 of its aircraft had hit more than 500 targets on the first day. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] The House of Commons Library, the British Parliament's research service, summarized the stated aims as regime change and the destruction of Iran's nuclear and ballistic-missile programmes, with the United States claiming self-defence. [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026] Against the nuclear claim stood the International Atomic Energy Agency, which said it had no evidence that Iran had resumed enrichment, though it also said it could not confirm Iran's claim to have stopped, because it had not been allowed back into the bombed sites. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [cite:ir11_ap_nothappy] How this fits Netanyahu's long record of warnings is tested in Part Five. [scene:ir5_test|The fair test]

Khamenei was killed in the first strikes, at his compound in Tehran, where, according to Reuters's sources, intelligence indicated he would meet his key lieutenants. [cite:ir11a_reu_call] Iranian state television confirmed his death early on 1 March, after Trump had announced it. Iranian media reported that his daughter, son-in-law and granddaughter were also killed, and the judiciary said the commander of the Revolutionary Guards, Mohammad Pakpour, and the senior adviser Ali Shamkhani, who had written days before that Araghchi had "sufficient support and authority" to reach a final agreement, were among the dead. [cite:ir11a_almon_feb28] [cite:ir11a_fox_shamkhani]

The succession

Under Article 111 of Iran's constitution, a temporary council took over the Supreme Leader's functions on 1 March: President Masoud Pezeshkian, the chief justice Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei, and Ayatollah Alireza Arafi of the Guardian Council. Pezeshkian called avenging Khamenei a "legitimate duty and right." [cite:ir11_aj_council] On 8 March the Assembly of Experts named Khamenei's son, Mojtaba Khamenei, as Supreme Leader. Reuters described him as "a mid-ranking cleric with close ties to the powerful Revolutionary Guards" and noted that the Islamic Republic's ruling ideology "frowns on the principle of hereditary succession." [cite:ir11_reu_mojtaba] The war aimed in part, by the American and Israeli governments' own statements, at a change of government; in its first weeks it produced instead a succession from father to son.

Iran's response

Iran struck back on the first day. Its missiles and drones hit Israel, where the emergency service Magen David Adom said a woman was killed in the Tel Aviv area, and the Revolutionary Guards said they had targeted the US Fifth Fleet in Bahrain and other American bases in the Gulf. The United Arab Emirates said 137 missiles and 209 drones were fired at it on 28 February alone, killing two people in Abu Dhabi; explosions were reported in Dubai, Riyadh, Doha and Manama. The Revolutionary Guards moved to close the Strait of Hormuz. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] [cite:ir11a_almon_feb28] Shipping through the strait, which before the war carried about 130 vessels a day, almost stopped. [cite:ir11_aj_blockade] [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026] Hezbollah opened fire on Israel on 2 March, and Israel's war in Lebanon is told in the Hezbollah volume; the Houthis joined on 28 March. [cite:hz8_am_mar2] [cite:hz10_na_houthis2026] [scene:hz8_war2026|The 2026 war in Lebanon] American service members were killed from the first week, among them six soldiers killed by an Iranian drone at a port in Kuwait. [cite:hz12_ktar_deaths]

By 22 March the Israeli military said Iran had fired more than 400 ballistic missiles at Israel and that about 92 per cent had been intercepted. [cite:ir11_olj_400] The monitoring group Airwars estimated about 650 ballistic missiles and thousands of drones fired at Israel, and about 6,400 missiles and drones at the Gulf states, over the forty days to the April ceasefire; on the American and Israeli side, the two governments declared more than 17,000 targets struck in Iran. [cite:ir11_airwars]

sections.h: The Toll and the World's Response
sections.html:
Every count of the dead in the 2026 war comes from a party with a stake in it or from monitors working without access to the sites. This section sets the counts side by side, says how each was made, and then sets out how the United Nations, the Gulf states, the great powers and the International Criminal Court responded in the war's first weeks. It covers the forty days from 28 February to the ceasefire of 8 April; later deaths are covered in the next section and, for American forces, in Part Fourteen. [scene:ir14_bill|Dragged in: the American bill]

The counts, and how they were made

In Iran, two kinds of count exist and they do not measure the same thing. Iran's government gives totals without separating civilians from soldiers: the head of the state Foundation of Martyrs, Ahmad Mousavi, put the dead at 3,468 on 18 April, after a figure of 3,375 from the Legal Medicine Organisation on 12 April. HRANA, counting incident by incident from field reports, medical sources and open sources and using the lowest figure where a report says "more than", counted at least 3,636 dead by 7 April: 1,701 civilians, including at least 254 children, 1,221 military personnel and 714 people it could not classify. AFP could not verify either. [cite:ir11_afp_tolls] [cite:ir11_hrana_day22] The two totals are close; the division between civilians and combatants is where they cannot be compared, because only one of them makes it.

The strike on civilians in Iran documented in most detail hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab on 28 February. Iran's judiciary first put the toll at 108 and blamed Israel. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] Amnesty International later found that American Tomahawk missiles had hit the school, killing more than 150 people, 120 of them children, and that the US military "did not take all feasible precautions" to avoid civilian harm. The White House said on 10 March that the Pentagon was investigating and would publish a full report; Trump said the strike was not "on purpose." [cite:ir11_amnesty_minab] Reuters had reported on 5 March that an initial internal inquiry found American forces likely responsible, apparently because targeters used out-of-date intelligence; the head of Central Command, Admiral Brad Cooper, told Congress in May that the school sat on an active Iranian cruise-missile base, and Trump said on 24 June, "I don't think it was us." Iranian officials put the dead at more than 175 children and teachers. On 13 July, answering a demand from more than two dozen senators, the Pentagon said the investigation was ongoing, and the public record reviewed for this book shows no findings released as of October 2026. [cite:ir11a_almon_minab]

In Israel the deadliest Iranian strike reported came on 1 March, when an Iranian ballistic missile hit a shelter in the Ramat Lehi neighbourhood of Beit Shemesh, killing nine civilians, four of them teenagers. Amnesty International said the strike "must be investigated as a war crime." [cite:ir11_amnesty_beitshemesh] Israeli reporting put the dead from Iranian strikes at 24 over the forty days, a figure that may include four Palestinians killed in the West Bank, with more than 7,000 injured; later counts rose to between 26 and 28. These figures are compiled from Israeli outlets and are given here as a range. [cite:ir11_wiki_strikesisrael] Amnesty counted at least 23 people killed in the other Gulf states by 27 March. [cite:ir11_amnesty_beitshemesh] Iran's government said it was striking Israeli and American assets, and its ambassador to the United Nations accused the United States and Israel of possibly committing a "war crime" by attacking civilians in Iran. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] [cite:ir11a_almon_feb28]

The war's other fronts and later phases added their own dead, counted separately. In Lebanon the health ministry counted 4,387 people killed between 2 March and 11 October 2026; the Hezbollah volume sets out that front and its figures. [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] [scene:hz8_war2026|The 2026 war in Lebanon] The Pentagon's casualty database listed 21 American service members dead and 865 wounded in operations against Iran by 9 October, a count that rose through the summer and that The Washington Post and The Intercept reported as incomplete. [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] [cite:hz12_intercept_cas] No consolidated count of Iranian dead after the July collapse of the ceasefire was found in the sources reviewed for this book.

The international response

The Secretary-General, António Guterres, warned on the first day that military action "carries the risk of igniting a chain of events that no one can control." Russia called the strikes a "dangerous adventure"; the European Union called the situation "perilous"; Oman's foreign minister, the mediator, said he was "dismayed"; and the Gulf states jointly condemned Iran's "cowardly" attacks on them. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] [cite:ir11a_almon_feb28] Britain did not join the strikes. [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026]

The Security Council acted against Iran's attacks, not against the strikes that preceded them. On 11 March it adopted Resolution 2817, put forward by Bahrain for the Gulf Cooperation Council and Jordan, by 13 votes to none, with Russia and China abstaining. It demanded that Iran immediately stop attacking the Gulf states. Iran's ambassador, Amir-Saeid Iravani, called it "a deeply regrettable day" that left "a lasting stain" on the Council's record; the American ambassador, Mike Waltz, said, "This is exactly what the United Nations should be about." A Russian draft calling for an end to hostilities without assigning blame failed, with four votes in favour (Russia, China, Pakistan and Somalia), the United States and Latvia against, and nine abstentions. [cite:ir11_week_2817] [cite:ir11a_week_2817] Iran is not a party to the Rome Statute, so the International Criminal Court has no jurisdiction over acts on its territory unless Iran lodges a declaration accepting it or the Security Council refers the situation; the advocacy group DAWN urged it to do so, and the public record reviewed for this book does not show that Iran did, or any ICC action on the war. [cite:ir11_dawn_icc]

sections.h: From Ceasefire to Blockade, April–October 2026
sections.html:
The war did not end; it changed shape. After forty days of bombing came a ceasefire, a failed round of talks and an American naval blockade; then a signed memorandum that promised a final settlement within sixty days; then the memorandum's collapse in July and a second blockade that, by October, had cut Iran's oil exports to almost nothing. This section follows those turns, gives each government's stated position at each one, and sets the stated aims of February against what had happened by October 2026. Because the war was not formally over when this was written, every status below is given as of the date stated.

The April ceasefire and the first blockade

A two-week ceasefire mediated by Pakistan began on 7–8 April and was later extended. [cite:ow7_wiki_ceasefire2026] [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026] Talks between American and Iranian officials over the following weekend broke down, and on 12 April Trump announced that the US Navy would block all ships entering or leaving the Strait of Hormuz; Central Command narrowed the order to vessels travelling to and from Iranian ports, effective 13 April. Iran was by then letting only a limited number of vetted ships through: 17 crossed on 11 April, against about 130 a day before the war. Brent crude, which had topped $119 a barrel in March, went back above $103. [cite:ir11_aj_blockade] [cite:ir11a_aj_blockade] The truce held between the United States and Iran, but Israel said it did not cover Lebanon, where its war against Hezbollah went on until a separate ten-day truce from 16 April. [cite:hz8b_reu_apr8] [cite:hz8b_aj_yellow] [scene:hz8_war2026|The 2026 war in Lebanon]

The nuclear material that had been the war's first stated target was still unaccounted for. On 29 April the IAEA's director general, Rafael Grossi, said Iran's near weapons-grade uranium, thought to be buried at sites the United States had bombed, "is accessible if there's a wish to go there"; his inspectors had not been to those sites in ten months. [cite:ir11_bbg_grossi]

The Islamabad Memorandum

On 17 June the American authorities released the text of a memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran, negotiated through Pakistan. It declared an "immediate and permanent" end to military operations on all fronts, Lebanon included. The United States would begin lifting its blockade at once and end it within thirty days; Iran would restore commercial shipping through Hormuz within thirty days, allowing time to clear mines. Iran reaffirmed that it would not acquire nuclear weapons; its enriched stockpile would be diluted on site under IAEA supervision; enrichment itself was left to later talks. The United States would grant waivers for Iranian oil exports on signing, free frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions on a timetable to be set later, and join regional partners in a reconstruction plan of at least $300 billion. A final agreement was due within sixty days, to be ratified by a binding Security Council resolution. [cite:ir11_sole_mou] A ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah followed on 19 June, brokered, a US official said, with Iran's help under the interim deal. [cite:hz8b_olj_jun19]

The memorandum's nuclear clauses were read differently in each capital. Grossi said on 24 June that his inspectors would visit the enrichment sites: "This is going to happen." Iran's deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, said such issues would be decided "only within the framework of a final agreement," after sanctions ended. Iran said it was not enriching uranium, and the IAEA said the same, but without access to the bombed sites the agency could not verify the stockpile. [cite:ir11_ap_grossi]

The collapse, 7–8 July

The memorandum lasted three weeks. Iran told ships to use its own "safe route" close to its coast, marking part of Omani waters as a restricted zone. On 7 July three tankers were hit by projectiles off the Omani coast; Central Command blamed Iran, and local television reported that the ships had ignored warnings from Iranian forces to change course. The US Treasury reimposed oil sanctions that day. Early on 8 July American forces struck more than 80 targets in Iran, including air defences, coastal radars, anti-ship missiles and more than 60 Revolutionary Guard boats, and the Guards fired back at targets in Bahrain and Kuwait. Trump, at a NATO summit in Ankara, said the memorandum was "over." [cite:ir11_aj_jul8] [cite:ir11a_aj_jul8]

Each side said the other broke it first. The American account was that Iran had attacked commercial shipping. Iran's foreign ministry called the American strikes a "flagrant violation of Paragraph 1" of the memorandum, and the parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, Iran's negotiator, cited the reimposed oil sanctions and what he called the violation of "Iranian adjustments in the Strait." [cite:ir11_aj_jul8] The memorandum required Iran to ensure "unimpeded" transit and the United States to grant oil waivers; the record shows each government acting against one of those clauses within days of the other, and it does not settle which act came first in intent. [cite:ir11_sole_mou]

The second blockade and the war at sea

The American blockade of Iran's ports was reinstated on 14 July. [cite:hz12a_cbs_oct] Its effect on Iran's oil trade was close to total. The tanker-tracking firm Kpler counted Iranian loadings of about 740,000 barrels a day in July and about 260,000 in August, against 1.7 million in August 2025; TankerTrackers.com put the fall at 100 per cent against January and February. Mohsen Rezaei, the new secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, warned that "economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone." [cite:ir11_oilprice_exports] By 13 October Central Command said four vessels had been disabled and 135 turned back since the blockade took effect, while Iran was attacking ships in the strait; no direct exchange of fire between American and Iranian forces was reported in early October. [cite:hz12a_cbs_oct]

The bomb question after two wars

Two wars fought in the name of stopping an Iranian bomb left the world knowing less about Iran's nuclear material than before them. On 7 September Grossi told the IAEA Board that the agency had had no access to the facilities hit in June 2025 and had "lost continuity of knowledge in relation to the previously declared inventories" of enriched uranium, and he urged Iran to meet its obligations under its safeguards agreement. [cite:ir11_iaea_sep7] He called it a proliferation concern that "needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency"; Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, blamed the American and Israeli attacks for the lack of access. [cite:ir11_aj_iaea_sep8] On 9 September the Board voted 23 to 3, with eight abstentions, to report Iran to the Security Council for "continued non-compliance," the first such referral in twenty years; Russia, China and Niger voted against, and Iran's representative, Reza Najafi, called it "completely counterproductive." [cite:ir11_am_referral] Iran's parliament had debated leaving the Non-Proliferation Treaty since March, but as of the end of September no formal notice of withdrawal had been reported, and searches for this book found none by mid-October. [cite:ir4_aca_npt2026] [cite:ir4_k24_npt] Iran remained, as of October 2026, a party to the treaty that Israel has never joined. [scene:ir4_dimona|Israel's undeclared arsenal]

Oil and prices

The closure of Hormuz, through which much of the world's oil and gas passes, was the war's widest economic effect. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] The 32 members of the International Energy Agency released 400 million barrels from reserves. [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026] In its October outlook the US Energy Information Administration assumed that Middle East oil flows would stay constrained through the end of 2026, forecast Brent at $105 a barrel in the fourth quarter, and reported that American gasoline had averaged $4.35 a gallon in September, against about $3 before 28 February. [cite:ir11_eia_oct] [cite:hz12_almon_ipsos]

Where it stands, October 2026

In late September Iran offered to reopen the strait within a week if the United States lifted its blockade, released frozen Iranian assets and waived sanctions on Iranian oil. Trump rejected it, saying Iran wanted a deal because it was "losing so badly." Iran received an American counter-proposal at the start of October, and President Pezeshkian said, "We will make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition." [cite:ir11_egt_proposal] On 8 October Trump wrote that the United States "will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections" of 3 November, and that his team was "having productive discussions" with Iran; Araghchi said a formal reply would follow within days. [cite:ir11_ap_midterms] Trump had said in September that the conflict "is going to end immediately after the elections" and had told Time that more bombing after the vote was "possible"; Al Jazeera reported that a new deployment brought American forces in the region to about 20,000, with at least three carrier groups, a lower figure than the more than 50,000 the New York Times had reported in March. [cite:ir11_aj_midterms] [cite:ir13_nyt_50k] Central Command put the American cost at $43.6 billion as of 3 September. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] As of 19 October 2026 no agreement had ended the war, the American blockade and Iran's restrictions on shipping through the strait remained in place, and the latest reporting reviewed showed no direct exchange of fire between American and Iranian forces. [cite:hz12a_cbs_oct] [cite:ir11_eia_oct]

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: Does Iran Want War With America?
chapters.intro: Part Twelve tests the first half of one of the three theses this volume examines: that Iran's government does not want a war with the United States. It sets out the evidence for that claim, which includes negotiations stretching from a disputed Swiss fax in 2003 to talks in Geneva two days before the war of 2026, retaliatory strikes on American bases announced in advance, and its leaders' own statements. It then sets out the evidence against: Americans killed by forces Iran armed and directed, from Beirut in 1983 to Tower 22 in 2024, hostage-taking, assassination plots on American soil, attacks on shipping and oil, and the lethal strikes of 2026. It ends by separating what the record shows from what remains an argument about motive.
chapters.outro: Part Twelve found the thesis supported in its narrow form and not in its broad one. Iran's government negotiated with Washington in 2013–2015, 2021–2022, 2025 and 2026, with talks under way when Israel struck in June 2025 and when the United States and Israel struck in February 2026, and before 2026 it gave advance warning of its direct strikes on American bases, in which no American died. [cite:ir7_usip_2231] [cite:ir12_too_sixth] [cite:ir12_euronews_feb26] [cite:ir12_aj_iraqwarn] [cite:ir12_ahram_udeid] Yet forces it armed killed Americans in Beirut, Iraq and Jordan, by the findings of American courts and the assessments of the American government, which Iran denies or disputes, it held Americans as bargaining assets, its officers were charged with plotting killings in the United States, and in 2026 its strikes killed American soldiers. [cite:hz12_dcd_anderson] [cite:ir12_mt_603] [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] [cite:ir12_almon_swap] [cite:ir12_doj_arbabsiar] [cite:hz12_ktar_deaths] Iran avoided all-out war with the United States and harmed Americans repeatedly; whether that pattern is defence or expansion is an argument the documents do not settle. Part Thirteen asks why Israel has made Iran its principal target.

sections.h: The Case That Iran Has Avoided War
sections.html:
One thesis this volume tests is that Iran does not want a war with the United States, and that the United States has nonetheless been drawn into one. This part tests the first half of that claim; Part Fourteen tests the second. The question is about intent, and intent cannot be read directly from any document. What can be examined is conduct and words: whether Iran's government has negotiated with Washington, how it has answered American attacks, what its leaders have said on the record, and how analysts who study its military doctrine read the pattern. This section sets out the evidence for the thesis. The next sets out the evidence against it, and then weighs the two. Where a reading of the evidence is an argument rather than a fact, it is labelled as one.

Negotiation

The first offer is the most disputed. In May 2003, weeks after the American invasion of Iraq, the Swiss ambassador in Tehran, Tim Guldimann, faxed the State Department a one-page outline with a cover memo dated 4 May. According to documents later released and reported by Gareth Porter of Inter Press Service, it was drafted by Iran's ambassador in Paris, Sadeq Kharrazi, in consultation with Guldimann, and set out a possible agenda for comprehensive talks in which Iran would consider compromises on its nuclear programme, on its support for Hezbollah and Hamas, and on "acceptance of the two-states-approach" for Israel and the Palestinians. Kharrazi reportedly said that the Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, President Mohammad Khatami and the foreign minister had agreed to "85%-90%" of the text, though by the same account Khamenei had "some reservations as for some points." Flynt Leverett, a former National Security Council official, said it reached the administration; Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice later testified that she never saw it. [cite:ir12_ips_bargain] [cite:ir12a_ips_bargain] The document's authority is contested. State Department officials argued that Guldimann had acted on his own, and the analyst Michael Rubin, a former Pentagon official writing in National Review, calls the "grand bargain" story false, citing the deputy secretary of state Richard Armitage's reported view that the paper was "perhaps more the product of Guldimann" and an email in which, Rubin says, Mohammad Javad Zarif, then Iran's ambassador to the UN, denied that it originated in Tehran. [cite:ir12_nr_rubin] [cite:ir12a_nr_rubin] The public record shows that the paper existed and that Washington did not answer it; it does not settle whether Iran's leadership stood behind every line.

The second negotiation is not in dispute. Talks between Iran and six powers, which began in 2013, produced the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action in July 2015, endorsed unanimously by the UN Security Council in Resolution 2231. [cite:ir7_usip_2231] On 16 January 2016 the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported that Iran "has carried out all measures required" to begin implementation. [cite:ir7_iaea_impday] Part Seven tells how the deal was made and how the United States left it in 2018 ([scene:ir7_deal|the deal]; [scene:ir7_withdrawal|the withdrawal]). After the American withdrawal Iran negotiated again: talks in Vienna to revive the agreement began in April 2021 and ran until the European Union tabled a "final" text on 8 August 2022, which Iran answered with demands for guarantees on sanctions and the IAEA's open investigations. [cite:ir7_afp_vienna] That round failed, and both governments blamed the other.

The third round of talks was direct in substance if not in form. On 12 April 2025, in Muscat, an Iranian delegation under Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and an American one under the envoy Steve Witkoff sat in separate rooms while Oman's foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, carried messages between them; at the end the two men spoke for several minutes, and Iran called the meeting "constructive". [cite:ir12_aj_muscat2025] A second round followed in Rome on 19 April, with Oman stating the aim as a deal that would keep Iran free of nuclear weapons and of sanctions. [cite:ir12_om_rome2025] After a fifth round in Rome on 23 May, which Albusaidi said made "some but not conclusive progress", Oman announced on 12 June that a sixth would be held in Muscat on Sunday 15 June. [cite:ir12_too_sixth] Israel began striking Iran on 13 June, and the sixth round never took place. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] [cite:ir12_euronews_feb26]

The pattern repeated in 2026. Iran and the United States reopened talks in Muscat on 6 February, moving to Geneva the following week. [cite:ir12_olj_feb2026] After a round in Geneva on 26 February, the Omani mediators reported "significant progress" and Araghchi said the talks had "entered into the elements of an agreement very seriously", with another round expected in "perhaps less than a week". The gap remained wide: Washington wanted an end to enrichment, limits on long-range missiles and an end to support for armed groups, while Iran said it would discuss only the nuclear file, and President Trump had given Tehran 15 days. [cite:ir12_euronews_feb26] [cite:ir12a_euronews_feb26] Two days later, on 28 February, the United States and Israel opened their joint campaign against Iran. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar] Iran negotiated during that war too: a ceasefire from 8 April led to the Islamabad Memorandum of 17 June, which collapsed on 8 July [cite:ow7_wiki_ceasefire2026]; as of mid-October 2026 an Iranian ceasefire proposal of late September had been publicly rejected by Trump while contacts continued through mediators. [cite:hz12a_cbs_oct]

Calibrated retaliation

Before 2026, Iran twice struck American forces directly in answer to an American attack, and both times the strike was announced in advance. On 3 January 2020 a US drone killed Major General Qassem Soleimani, commander of the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, at Baghdad airport; the Pentagon called it "decisive defensive action" and Khamenei promised "harsh retaliation". [cite:hz10_rudaw_soleimani] [cite:hz10_fox_pentagon2020] Shortly after midnight on 8 January, the office of Iraq's prime minister, Adil Abdul-Mahdi, received what it called a "verbal message" from Iran that its response had begun or was about to begin and would hit only places where American forces were present. Iraq's military counted 22 missiles, 17 at Ain al-Asad air base and five at Erbil; the American count, as reported, was 15 missiles at two bases, ten of them at Ain al-Asad. [cite:ir12_aj_iraqwarn] [cite:ir12a_fn_tbi] Within hours Zarif, by then foreign minister, wrote that Iran had "took & concluded proportionate measures in self-defense" and that "We do not seek escalation or war, but will defend ourselves against any aggression." [cite:ir12_spg_zarif] No one was killed. The attack was not harmless: President Trump first said that no Americans had been harmed, but the Pentagon's count of service members diagnosed with traumatic brain injuries, all classed as mild, reached 109 on 10 February 2020 and 110 on 21 February. [cite:ir12_rferl_tbi] [cite:ir12a_fn_tbi]

The second case followed the American bombing of Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan on 21–22 June 2025. On 23 June Iran fired at the American base at Al Udeid in Qatar, after notifying the United States. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] Trump said 14 missiles were fired and 13 shot down, and added: "I want to thank Iran for giving us early notice, which made it possible for no lives to be lost, and nobody to be injured." [cite:ir12_ahram_udeid] Ali Vaez, Iran project director at the International Crisis Group, said that day that Iran "opted for a symbolic response to a US attack because they don't want further US involvement". [cite:ir12_c4_vaez]

What Iran's leaders said

Iran's leaders have repeatedly said, in public, that they do not seek a war with the United States, while refusing the talks Washington wanted. On 14 May 2019, at the height of the "maximum pressure" campaign, Khamenei told officials in Tehran: "There will be no war," and "Neither us, nor them are after a war"; in the same speech, answering American suggestions of talks on Iran's missiles, he called such negotiation a mistake because "the Americans will not stand by their promises." [cite:ir12_rf_nowar] Zarif's statement of 8 January 2020, quoted above, said the same in the moment of retaliation. These are statements of position. They show what the government chose to say; they do not by themselves prove what it intended.

How analysts read the doctrine

The argument that Iran avoids direct war rests on a reading of its military doctrine. The Iranian scholar Kayhan Barzegar describes what Iranian officials call "forward defence" as "preempting the penetration of symmetric and asymmetric threats inside Iran's borders": fighting through allied forces abroad so as not to fight at home. A New America study of the Revolutionary Guards found Iran's military strategy still "cautious". The same study records the opposite reading: the analyst Patrick Clawson described Iran as both "the fireman and the arsonist" in Iraq and Syria, and Iran's regional rivals see the doctrine as ideological expansion rather than defence. [cite:ir12_na_forward] Vaez, who read the 2025 strike as symbolic, warned in February 2026 that Iran's leaders had concluded that only inflicting casualties would deter American and Israeli strikes, that the government was "cornered and could act in a reckless way", and that it regarded conflict as less dangerous than accepting Washington's terms. [cite:ir12_npr_vaez2026] That is the strongest form of the thesis: by the analysts' account, Iran's government has tried to avoid war with the United States, but not at any price.

sections.h: The Case Against, and What the Record Supports
sections.html:
Avoiding all-out war is not the same as peaceful intent. The evidence against the thesis does not show an Iranian government seeking a full war with the United States. It shows something narrower and better documented: for more than four decades, Iran's government and forces it armed and directed have killed and held Americans, plotted killings on American soil, attacked shipping and oil in ways Washington attributed to it, and declared hostility in ritual form. Each item below is given with its source and with Iran's stated response.

Americans killed by Iran's allies

On 23 October 1983 a truck bomb destroyed the US Marine barracks in Beirut, killing 241 American servicemen. In Peterson v. Islamic Republic of Iran (30 May 2003), Judge Royce Lamberth of the US District Court in Washington found that Hezbollah carried out the attack with "massive material and technical support" from Iran, and a later ruling in the same line of cases found that Iran and its Ministry of Intelligence played "crucial and necessary roles in planning and ordering" it. Iran did not defend the suit; Hezbollah, Iran and Syria have denied involvement. [cite:hz12_dcd_anderson] [cite:hz2_anderson] Part Two of the Hezbollah volume examines the evidence in detail ([scene:hz2_1983|the 1983 bombings]). These are civil judgments in undefended cases, and their findings rest on the evidence the plaintiffs presented; they are the strongest legal findings that exist on the question.

In Iraq after 2003, militias trained and supplied by the Quds Force fought American troops. In April 2019 a Pentagon spokesman said that "at least 603 U.S. personnel deaths in Iraq were the result of Iran-backed militants" during the war, about 17 per cent of all American personnel deaths there from 2003 to 2011, up from about 500 in earlier official estimates. The causes listed included explosively formed penetrators, armour-piercing roadside bombs which the United States says Iran made and supplied. This is a US government figure: the Pentagon did not release the underlying study, and Military Times could not assess it independently. [cite:ir12_mt_603] The pattern continued after the war. A rocket attack in late December 2019 killed an American contractor; the United States blamed Kata'ib Hezbollah, an Iraqi militia, and American air strikes on the militia, its supporters' assault on the US embassy in Baghdad and the killing of Soleimani followed. [cite:hz10_fox_pentagon2020] On 28 January 2024 a drone struck Tower 22, a US outpost in north-eastern Jordan, killing Sergeant William Jerome Rivers, Specialist Kennedy Ladon Sanders and Specialist Breonna Alexsondria Moffett; President Biden blamed Iran-backed militias. [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] Washington named Kata'ib Hezbollah, which then said it was "halting" operations under pressure from Iran and Iraq; Iran denied ordering the attack. [cite:hz10_at_farida] The Hezbollah volume's account of the Iraqi militias is at [scene:hz10_iraq|Iraq's militias].

Hostages and plots

The relationship between the Islamic Republic and the United States began with hostage-taking. On 4 November 1979 students seized the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans for 444 days. [cite:ir12_usip_hostage] Khomeini took control of the hostages and rejected appeals to free them; they were released on 20 January 1981, minutes after Ronald Reagan's inauguration. [cite:ir12_histuk_release] The detention of Americans continued as a practice. On 18 September 2023 five Americans, among them Siamak Namazi, held since 2015, were freed in exchange for clemency for five Iranians and access to $6 billion of Iran's frozen oil revenue, moved to Qatar; the Biden administration said the money could be used only for humanitarian purchases, and President Ebrahim Raisi said it "belongs to the people" of Iran. [cite:ir12_almon_swap] Part Nine sets out Iran's record of detentions ([scene:ir9_record|Iran's own record]).

Three plots on American soil have been documented in court filings. Manssor Arbabsiar pleaded guilty on 17 October 2012 to conspiring with Quds Force members in Iran to kill Saudi Arabia's ambassador to the United States by bombing a restaurant he used; he wired about $100,000 as a down payment on a $1.5 million fee to an account that turned out to belong to the FBI, told agents that senior Quds Force officials had recruited, funded and directed him, and was sentenced to 25 years. [cite:ir12_doj_arbabsiar] On 10 August 2022 the Justice Department charged Shahram Poursafi, a member of the Revolutionary Guards, with offering $300,000 for the murder of the former national security adviser John Bolton, likely, the department said, in retaliation for Soleimani's killing; no attack was carried out. [cite:ir12_npr_bolton] On 8 November 2024 it charged Farhad Shakeri, believed to be in Iran, alleging that the Revolutionary Guards had tasked him on 7 October 2024 with planning the killing of Donald Trump; two New York men were charged over a related plot against an Iranian-American journalist, apparently Masih Alinejad. Iran's foreign ministry called the accusations "totally unfounded". The Poursafi and Shakeri cases are charges, not convictions. [cite:ir12_toi_shakeri]

Shipping, oil and the 2026 war

In 2019, during the maximum-pressure campaign, Washington attributed several attacks to Iran. After two tankers were struck in the Gulf of Oman on 13 June 2019, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said "Iran is responsible", and US Central Command released video it said showed a Revolutionary Guards boat removing an unexploded limpet mine from one of them; the ship's Japanese owner said it had been hit by projectiles, and Iran denied involvement. [cite:ir12_usni_tankers] On 14 September 2019 drones and cruise missiles struck the Saudi Aramco plants at Abqaiq and Khurais, shutting more than 5 per cent of world oil supply. The Houthis claimed the attack; the United States, European governments and Saudi Arabia blamed Iran, which denied it; a UN sanctions panel concluded that "the Houthi forces did not launch the attacks", without naming who did, and the UN Secretary-General said the UN was "unable to independently corroborate" that the weapons were of Iranian origin. [cite:ir12_aj_abqaiq] [cite:ir12a_aj_abqaiq] Part Eight covers the wider shipping war ([scene:ir8_shadow|the shadow war]).

In 2026 Iran's strikes on American forces were lethal; they came after the United States and Israel had attacked it. AP itemised the dead in July: six soldiers killed by an Iranian drone at a port in Kuwait shortly after 28 February, one at Prince Sultan Air Base after an Iranian attack on 1 March, and two in Jordan on 18 July while defending against Iranian missiles and drones, alongside deaths in accidents. [cite:hz12_ktar_deaths] As of October 2026 the Pentagon's casualty system counted 21 American service members dead and 865 wounded in operations against Iran. [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] Part Eleven tells that war ([scene:ir11_war|the 2026 war]).

Words

Hostility is also declared. At the Quds Day marches the Iranian government has organised since 1979, crowds chant "Death to America" alongside "Death to Israel". [cite:ir2_wiki_quds] Khamenei explained the slogan on 8 February 2019: "It means death to America's rulers … we have nothing against the American people." [cite:ir12_aj_dta] His explanation limits the target; it does not withdraw the hostility.

What the record supports

The record supports one part of the thesis. On every occasion examined here when Iran's government struck American forces directly in reply to an American attack, before 2026, it gave warning and no American was killed; it negotiated with Washington in 2003 (by the disputed fax), 2013–2015, 2021–2022, 2025 and 2026, and in two of those cases talks were still running, when Israel struck in June 2025 and when the United States and Israel struck in February 2026. [cite:ir12_aj_iraqwarn] [cite:ir12_ahram_udeid] [cite:ir12_too_sixth] [cite:ir12_euronews_feb26] Its leaders said they did not want war, and analysts who study its doctrine, from Vaez to Barzegar, read its use of allied forces abroad as a way of fighting without inviting a direct war at home. [cite:ir12_c4_vaez] [cite:ir12_na_forward]

The record does not support the stronger reading that Iran's government is not hostile to the United States or has not harmed Americans. Through Hezbollah in 1983, the Iraqi militias after 2003 and again in 2024, by hostage-taking from 1979 to 2023, by assassination plots on American soil in 2011, 2022 and 2024, and directly in 2026, the Iranian state or forces it armed have killed, held or sought to kill Americans. [cite:hz12_dcd_anderson] [cite:ir12_mt_603] [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] [cite:ir12_doj_arbabsiar] [cite:hz12_ktar_deaths] The fair statement of the evidence is therefore two-sided: Iran's government has repeatedly chosen to avoid a full war with the United States, and it has repeatedly harmed Americans while doing so. The analysts cited here largely agree on the method, calibrated pressure through allies with deniability, and disagree on whether that method is defence or expansion. [cite:ir12_na_forward] [cite:ir12_npr_vaez2026] That is an argument about motive, and the documents do not settle it.

One further point bears on the second half of the thesis. Trump's statement of 28 February 2026 justified the war partly by Iran's record, citing attacks on American citizens and soldiers and the 1979 hostage crisis. [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar] The record above shows that those grievances were real. Whether they, or Iran's nuclear programme, or Israel's urging, decided the American choice of war is a separate question. Part Fourteen takes it up ([scene:ir14_bill|Dragged In: the American bill]).

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: Why Iran?
chapters.intro: Part Thirteen asks why Israel has made Iran its principal target, and keeps two kinds of answer apart. The first is what Israel's governments have said they want: no nuclear weapon in a hostile state's hands, the doctrine Menachem Begin declared after bombing Iraq's reactor in 1981; an end to Iran's arming of Hezbollah, Hamas and the Houthis; and, by 2026, conditions for Iranians to overthrow their government. The second is why, which is a matter of argument: military supremacy, ideology, the collapse of the old alliance, domestic politics and American strategy are each set out with the case against them. The part then reads the two documents most often cited as proof of a long-laid plan, the 1996 paper "A Clean Break" and Oded Yinon's 1982 essay, for what they actually say about Iran, considers what oil and the Strait of Hormuz put at stake, and draws up a ledger of the two states' populations, economies, budgets, forces, missiles and bombs, with the American aid and forces on Israel's side.
chapters.outro: Part Thirteen established that Israel's stated aims toward Iran are documented and have widened over time. They began with the Begin doctrine, declared after the Osirak strike of 1981 and applied to Syria in 2007 and to Iran in 2025 and 2026. By 28 February 2026 Netanyahu was saying openly that the war would "create conditions" for Iranians "to cast off the yoke" of their government. [cite:ir13_wiki_begindoc] [cite:ir13_ap_kibar2018] [cite:ir13_axios_regime2025] [cite:ir13_pbs_bibi2026] Why Iran became the principal target remains an argument. Some explanations put the cause in Tehran's ideology, others in geopolitics after 1991, Israel's military edge or Netanyahu's politics, and each has named critics. [cite:ir13_ceip_sadjadpour] [cite:ir13_ips_parsi] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:ir13_aje_breathing] The documents often offered as proof of a long-laid plan say little about Iran. "A Clean Break" mentions it in four sentences, always alongside Syria, Hezbollah or Lebanon's Shia, and proposes nothing against it; in the text of Yinon's essay reviewed here it appears only as Iraq's enemy in war. [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak] [cite:ir13a_km_cleanbreak] [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] The ledger shows a state with nine times Israel's population, about one-sixth of its budgeted military spending, an aging air force and no nuclear weapon. That state was facing Israel with an estimated 90 warheads and American aid and forces beside it. Iran's strength lies in missiles, allied groups and the Strait of Hormuz. [cite:ir13_fred_irpc] [cite:ir13_sipri_2025] [cite:ir13_nst_irmil] [cite:ir4_ynet_sipri] [cite:ir13_eia_hormuz] Part Fourteen turns to what the conflict has cost the United States, and to who decided that it should pay. [scene:ir14_bill|Part Fourteen: the American bill]

sections.h: What Israel Says It Wants
sections.html:
Two kinds of answer are kept apart here. What Israel's governments have said they want from Iran is a matter of record. Why Iran, among the states that oppose Israel, became its principal target is a question of motive, and the answers to it are arguments, given below with the case against each.

No hostile bomb: the Begin doctrine

The oldest stated aim predates the Islamic Republic's nuclear programme. On 7 June 1981 Israeli aircraft destroyed Iraq's Osirak reactor near Baghdad. Prime Minister Menachem Begin's government declared: "On no account shall we permit an enemy to develop weapons of mass destruction against the people of Israel." Begin said the strike "will be a precedent for every future government in Israel." [cite:ir13_wiki_begindoc] On 19 June the UN Security Council, unanimously and with American support, "strongly condemns the military attack by Israel in clear violation of the Charter of the United Nations" and called on Israel "urgently to place its nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards." [cite:ir13_un_res487] Dimona, the reactor at the heart of Israel's own undeclared programme, has remained outside them. [cite:ir4_fas_israel] [scene:ir4_dimona|Part Four: Dimona] On 6 September 2007 Israeli jets destroyed a reactor under construction at Deir ez-Zor in Syria. Israel acknowledged the strike only on 21 March 2018, when its chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot, said: "This was the message in 1981, this is the message in 2007." The Associated Press noted that the disclosure could be read as a warning to Iran. [cite:ir13_ap_kibar2018] Writing the same day, Amos Yadlin, a former head of Israeli military intelligence, warned that the doctrine might not be "eternally viable" against Iran, whose centrifuges "can be dispersed, concealed, and protected more effectively" than a reactor, and that "the attack itself might accelerate the effort." [cite:ir13_inss_yadlin] The doctrine was applied to Iran in June 2025 and again from 28 February 2026. [cite:ir13_wiki_begindoc] [scene:ir10_strikes|Part Ten: the June 2025 strikes] [scene:ir11_war|Part Eleven: the 2026 war]

Stopping an Iranian bomb

The aim Israel stated most often was narrower: that the Islamic Republic must not obtain a nuclear weapon. On 13 June 2025 Netanyahu said Iran had enough highly enriched uranium "for nine atom bombs" and that, "if not stopped," it "could produce a nuclear weapon in a very short time." [cite:ir5_dcnf_jun2025] The record he spoke into was mixed, and Part Five tests his predictions against it. [scene:ir5_test|Part Five: the test] The day before, the IAEA Board of Governors had found Iran in breach of its safeguards obligations for the first time in nearly two decades; Iran rejected the finding. [cite:ir5_aj_iaea2025] In March 2025 the US Director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, had testified that Iran was "not building a nuclear weapon." A week after the strikes the IAEA's director general, Rafael Grossi, said his inspectors had not found "an active, systematic plan to build a nuclear weapon." [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] [cite:ir5_tbs_grossi] Iran's government has always said its programme is peaceful. [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard]

Ending Iran's network

The third stated aim concerns the armed groups Iran funds and arms. Netanyahu's statement of 28 February 2026 said that "for 47 years, the evil regime in Iran has called for death to Israel, death to America," and that if Israel did not act it would face "an Iran with tens of thousands of ballistic missiles." [cite:ir13_pbs_bibi2026] Washington had made the same demand before: in May 2018 Secretary of State Mike Pompeo's twelve conditions for Iran included an end to its support for Hezbollah, Hamas and the Houthis. Iran's President Hassan Rouhani replied: "Who are you to decide for Iran and the world?" [cite:ir7_voa_pompeo] Part Nine documents that support and Iran's leaders' own statements about Israel, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's 2020 description of it as "a cancerous tumor." [cite:ir3_reuters_tumor2020] [scene:ir9_reach|Part Nine: Iran's reach]

Regime change

The fourth aim moved from hint to statement in eight months. In June 2025 Israel's declared war aims were the destruction of Iran's nuclear and ballistic-missile capabilities, and Israeli officials told Axios that regime change was not among the objectives the security cabinet had approved. Netanyahu nonetheless suggested on Fox News on 15 June that the war could bring a change of government. On 16 June he told ABC that killing Khamenei was "not going to escalate the conflict, it's going to end the conflict," and told Israeli reporters "we could see many changes in Iran." [cite:ir13_axios_regime2025] On 28 February 2026 he recalled being asked in 2025 whether regime change was the goal: "I replied that this was not the goal, but it could certainly be the outcome." The new operation, he said, would "create conditions that will allow the brave Iranian people to cast off the yoke of this murderous regime," and he added: "You are not our enemies and we are not your enemies." [cite:ir13_pbs_bibi2026] President Trump told Iranians the same day, "When we are finished, take over your government." [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] The UK House of Commons Library summarised the two governments' stated aims as regime change and the destruction of Iran's nuclear and missile programmes; the United States called its action self-defence, and Iran said it would close the Strait of Hormuz. [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026]

Why Iran: Five Arguments

The explanations that follow are arguments made by named analysts and officials. None is established by a document of the kind that establishes the aims above.

Military supremacy. One argument is that the Begin doctrine is, in effect, a policy of nuclear monopoly. Israel is estimated to hold about 90 warheads, which it neither confirms nor denies, outside the Non-Proliferation Treaty, and it acts to keep any regional rival from acquiring one. [cite:ir4_ynet_sipri] American law reinforces the edge: the Naval Vessel Transfer Act of 2008 wrote a definition of Israel's "qualitative military edge" into American law, required the edge to be assessed every four years, and provided that arms sales to other states in the region may not adversely affect it. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] On this reading, Iran is targeted because it is the regional power with the population, the industry and the enriched uranium to end that edge. Israeli governments reply that the doctrine targets states whose leaders call for Israel's destruction, not rivals as such, though some of their own security chiefs questioned the scale of the threat: in 2009 Defence Minister Ehud Barak said he was "not among those who believe Iran is an existential issue for Israel." In 2011 the Mossad director, Tamir Pardo, said the term "existential threat is used too freely." [cite:ir6_jta_barak2009] [cite:ir6_ahram_pardo2011]

Ideology. A second argument says the hostility comes from Tehran. Iran is not the only state in the region that refuses to recognise Israel; in November 2023 Iraq, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Yemen did not recognise it either. [cite:ir13_vc_recog] What distinguishes Iran's government is that its supreme leader has predicted Israel's end and armed groups at war with it. Karim Sadjadpour of the Carnegie Endowment calls opposition to Israel "the most enduring pillar of Iranian revolutionary ideology," a hostility that, he argues, serves no national interest, and he quotes Khamenei's 2012 call for "a true cancer tumor" to be "cut off." [cite:ir13_ceip_sadjadpour] Trita Parsi, in Treacherous Alliance (2007), argues the reverse: the rivalry is "neither about ideology nor religion" but geopolitics, and the revolutionary rhetoric covers aims little changed from the Shah's. [cite:ir13_ips_parsi]

The periphery reversed. Parsi's account also dates the turn. Until 1979 Israel treated Iran as a partner on the region's edge against the Arab states, as Part One describes. [scene:ir1_periphery|Part One: the periphery alliance] After Iraq's defeat in 1991, in the reviewer's summary of Parsi, "Israeli politicians began describing Iran as the primary threat"; Brent Scowcroft, President George H. W. Bush's national security adviser, is quoted as saying that "the pro-Israeli community turned strongly against Iran." [cite:ir13_ips_parsi] Israel has since cultivated a new periphery around Iran: from 2016 to 2020 it supplied 69 per cent of the major arms imported by Azerbaijan, which borders Iran. [cite:ir13_sipri_azer] Critics of Parsi answer that what changed after 1979 was Iran's government and its alliances, documented in Part Nine, not Israel's view of the map. [cite:ir13_ceip_sadjadpour]

Domestic politics. A third argument concerns Netanyahu himself. Some of his own former security chiefs made the charge. In 2012 Yuval Diskin, the former head of the Shin Bet, said he had no faith in "the current leadership of Israel to lead us to an event of this magnitude"; Netanyahu's spokesman declined to comment. In 2021 Yadlin said that "the Iranian issue was privatized to one person." [cite:ir6_fox_diskin2012] [cite:ir6_toi_yadlin2021] The June 2025 war began while Netanyahu faced a coalition crisis, pressure for an inquiry into his government's failure to prevent the attack of 7 October 2023, and his corruption trial, and it gave him what Al Jazeera called political breathing room. The case against reading the war as a personal manoeuvre is that his opponents backed it. The opposition leader Yair Lapid supported the strikes, and former prime minister Naftali Bennett said, "There is no right, no left, no opposition and no coalition." [cite:ir13_aje_breathing] [cite:ir13a_aje_breathing]

American strategy. The last argument holds that Israel's Iran policy and Washington's converged: Pompeo's 2018 demands and Trump's 2026 aims matched Israel's own. [cite:ir7_voa_pompeo] [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] Whether Israel drew the United States in, or the United States pursued aims of its own, is tested in Parts Twelve and Fourteen. [scene:ir12_question|Part Twelve: does Iran want war?] [scene:ir14_who|Part Fourteen: who decided]

sections.h: The Documents People Cite
sections.html:
Two documents are often cited as evidence that the campaign against Iran was planned long in advance: a 1996 policy paper written for Netanyahu, and a 1982 essay by an Israeli journalist. Both are real, and both can be read. In both, Iran is a minor subject.

"A Clean Break", 1996

A Clean Break: A New Strategy for Securing the Realm was published on 1 June 1996 by the Institute for Advanced Strategic and Political Studies (IASPS), a think tank, for Netanyahu's incoming government. It came from the institute's "Study Group on a New Israeli Strategy Toward 2000," led by Richard Perle. The other members were James Colbert, Charles Fairbanks Jr., Douglas Feith, Jonathan Torop, David Wurmser, Meyrav Wurmser and the institute's president, Robert Loewenberg. [cite:ir13_wiki_cleanbreak] [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak]

The paper's targets were the Oslo process, Syria and Iraq. It urged Israel to "make a clean break" from the peace process of the preceding years. It proposed that Israel, with Turkey and Jordan, shape its region "by weakening, containing, and even rolling back Syria", an effort that could focus on "removing Saddam Hussein from power in Iraq." It recommended "striking Syrian military targets in Lebanon" and, should that prove insufficient, targets in Syria itself. It also urged Israel to free itself from American economic aid and loan guarantees. [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak]

Iran appears in four sentences, always in connection with Syria, Hezbollah or Lebanon's Shia, and always in the context of Lebanon or Iraq. Israel could seize the initiative on its northern border "by engaging Hizballah, Syria, and Iran, as the principal agents of aggression in Lebanon." Syria "and Iran might prefer a weak, but barely surviving Saddam." The Shia of southern Lebanon, the paper says, had long been tied to "the Shia leadership in Najf, Iraq rather than Iran," and so a Hashemite government in Iraq could help Israel "wean the south Lebanese Shia away from Hizballah, Iran, and Syria." [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak] [cite:ir13a_km_cleanbreak] The paper proposes no strike on Iran, no regime change in Tehran and no action against Iran's nuclear programme. Some later accounts describe it as a plan to roll back Iran along with Syria and Lebanon, but its own text applies "rolling back" to Syria. [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak]

Its significance lies in who wrote it. By 2002, as The Guardian's Brian Whitaker noted, several of its authors held key posts in Washington, in the administration of George W. Bush that went on to invade Iraq in 2003. Some critics drew a line from one to the other: Patrick Buchanan said the plan had been "imposed" on the United States, and the scholars John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt said it called on Israel to reorder the Middle East. Others found no evidence of influence. CBS's defence correspondent David Martin said in 2005 that he "never saw any evidence that Richard Perle had any determining effect on US policy", and Netanyahu himself did not adopt several of the paper's proposals. [cite:ir13_wiki_cleanbreak] Feith says he "neither wrote it nor signed it" and doubts that he saw it before publication. He describes David Wurmser as its principal author and says that he and a few others were consulted as Wurmser researched it, his own contribution being the idea that Israel "graduate" from American economic aid. [cite:ir13_feith_cleanbreak] [cite:ir13a_feith] The record supports a narrower statement than is often made: in 1996 a group of American policy advocates urged an Israeli government to topple Saddam Hussein and confront Syria, and several of them later served a US government that did invade Iraq. It does not show a 1996 plan for war with Iran.

The Yinon essay, 1982

In February 1982 Kivunim ("Directions"), a Hebrew quarterly published by the World Zionist Organization's information department, printed "A Strategy for Israel in the 1980s" by Oded Yinon, reputedly a journalist and a former Foreign Ministry official. Israel Shahak, an Israeli critic of Zionism, translated it into English; by the translation's own note it was disseminated on 13 June 1982, a week after Israel invaded Lebanon. It circulated as "The Zionist Plan for the Middle East." [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] [cite:ir13a_mb_yinon]

Yinon argued that the Arab states were fragile mosaics and that Israel should aim at their dissolution into ethnic and religious units. Iraq would split into Shiite, Sunni and Kurdish states; Syria would "fall apart" into several; he called Egypt a "corpse" and argued for Jordan's "liquidation." [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] Iran was not among the states whose break-up he proposed. In the text of the translation reviewed for this book, which lacks the essay's closing sections, Iran appears in two sentences, both about the Iran–Iraq war, which Yinon expected to weaken Iraq: "An Iraqi-Iranian war will tear Iraq apart." [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] [cite:ir13a_mb_yinon]

Its status is contested. The scholar Nisan said the views were Yinon's own and not government policy, and Noam Chomsky called them "ideological and geopolitical fantasies" outside mainstream Zionism. Peleg, by contrast, treated the essay as "an authentic mirror of the thinking mode of the Israeli Right" under Begin, and Becker and Polkinghorn (2017) argue that its ideas were refined in "A Clean Break." [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] The public record contains no evidence that any Israeli government adopted it. It does show the essay's later misuse: it has been offered as proof that Israel planned the 2003 invasion of Iraq, the Syrian civil war and the rise of the Islamic State. [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] Neither document is evidence about Iran.

Oil and Hormuz

Oil runs through the Iran question in a different way. About 20 million barrels a day, roughly a fifth of world consumption, passed through the Strait of Hormuz in 2024, together with about a fifth of the world's trade in liquefied natural gas; 84 per cent of that crude went to Asia. The pipelines of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates could carry only about 2.6 million barrels a day around the strait. [cite:ir13_eia_hormuz] That geography is Iran's strongest card. In March 2026 shipping through the strait almost stopped, and the United States answered with a blockade of Iran's ports. As of mid-October 2026 that blockade was still in force and Iran was attacking ships in the strait. [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026] [cite:hz12a_cbs_oct] [scene:ir11_now|Part Eleven: where things stand] Israel's statements of its aims do not mention oil. The stake the record shows is global supply, which is a reason other governments had to weigh a war with Iran, not one Israel gave for it.

sections.h: The Power Ledger
sections.html:
Iran is usually described as Israel's most dangerous enemy. A ledger of what each state has shows a less even contest than that description suggests. It also shows where Iran's real strength lies. The figures below come from the World Bank, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) and the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS). Where they are estimates, or where sources differ, the text says so.

People and money

Iran has about nine times as many people as Israel: about 92 million against about 10.1 million, as implied by the World Bank's figures for total and per-head GDP in 2025. [cite:ir13_fred_irpc] [cite:ir13_fred_ilpc] [cite:hm_fred_ilgdp] Israel's economy is nonetheless the larger of the two. In 2025 Israel's GDP was $610.8 billion and Iran's $362.7 billion, down from $475.3 billion in 2024; the fall reflects the collapse of the rial as well as a real contraction the World Bank estimates at 2.7 per cent. [cite:hm_fred_ilgdp] [cite:ir13_fred_irgdp] [cite:ir13_wb_iran] Per head the gap is wider still: about $60,300 in Israel against about $3,900 in Iran, roughly fifteen to one. [cite:ir13_fred_ilpc] [cite:ir13_fred_irpc]

The military budgets differ even more. SIPRI puts Israel's 2025 military spending at $48.3 billion, 7.8 per cent of GDP and the eleventh-largest in the world. Iran's is $7.4 billion, thirty-eighth. [cite:ir13_sipri_2025] [cite:hz9_sipri_2025] Iran's figure fell 5.6 per cent in real terms in 2025, mostly because of inflation of about 42 per cent, though allocations to its missile and drone makers rose by 44 and 50 per cent. SIPRI warns that Iran's budget "probably represent[s] only a relatively small proportion" of its procurement; parts of the drone and missile programmes are funded off-budget, often from oil revenue, and a SIPRI researcher, Zubaida Karim, put off-budget spending at about 40 per cent of the total. [cite:ir13_na_sipri] [cite:ir13a_na_karim] [cite:ir13a_sipri_fs] Even allowing for that, on this book's arithmetic from those figures, Israel spends roughly four times what Iran does, and on SIPRI's published figures more than six times. The $3.8 billion in American military aid Israel received in 2025 alone was equal to about half of Iran's entire budgeted military spending. [cite:ir13_na_sipri] [cite:hm_dn_mou] Saudi Arabia, Iran's Gulf rival, spent $83.2 billion. [cite:ir13_sipri_2025]

Forces and air power

Iran has more soldiers. The IISS counts about 610,000 active personnel, including about 190,000 in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, against the Israel Defense Forces' 169,500 active troops and 465,000 reservists. [cite:ir13_nst_irmil] [cite:hm_almon_idf] Numbers of soldiers count for little, though, between two states that share no border; what decides a war between them is air power and missiles. Iran has about 250 combat-capable aircraft, many bought before 1979, among them American-built F-4s and F-5s and a few F-14s. [cite:ir13_nst_irmil] Israel has 316 combat aircraft. Since 2010 it has bought the American F-35, of which it had ordered 50 by 2016, paid for with American aid and fitted with Israeli electronics. [cite:hm_almon_idf] [cite:ow7_wiki_f35i] In June 2025, and again from 28 February 2026, when some 200 Israeli jets struck more than 500 targets on the first day, Israeli aircraft operated over Iran. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] Part Ten tells the first of those wars. [scene:ir10_strikes|Part Ten: the strikes]

Missiles: Iran's main weapon

Iran's answer to that imbalance has been ballistic missiles and drones, and the estimates of how many it has are contested. Before June 2025, unnamed estimates put its stock at 2,500 to 3,000 ballistic missiles. [cite:ir13_nst_irmil] In the twelve days of June 2025 it fired about 525 to 550 ballistic missiles and more than 1,000 drones at Israel. By Israeli counts about 86 to 90 per cent of the missiles were intercepted, 28 people were killed in Israel and the Health Ministry counted 3,238 taken to hospital. [cite:ir13_alma_rl] [cite:ir10_toi_numbers] At the start of the 2026 war the Israeli military estimated that Iran had about 2,500 missiles able to reach Israel. In the forty days to 8 April it fired about 650 ballistic missiles and thousands of drones at Israel, and about 6,400 missiles and drones at the Gulf states. [cite:ir13_fdd_missiles] [cite:ir11_airwars] What survived is disputed. An Israeli Air Force official said in April 2026 that just over 1,000 missiles remained. A classified US assessment reported by the New York Times on 12 May put the surviving share at roughly 70 per cent, apparently counting cruise missiles too. The head of US Central Command, Admiral Brad Cooper, called such reports "not accurate" and said more than 85 per cent of Iran's missile, drone and naval industrial base had been damaged or destroyed. [cite:ir13_fdd_missiles] Iran has refused to put its missiles on the negotiating table; in February 2026 it would discuss only its nuclear programme. [cite:ir12_euronews_feb26]

The bomb

On the nuclear line of the ledger the count is not close. Iran has no nuclear weapon. Its stock of uranium enriched to 60 per cent stood at an estimated 440.9 kilograms on 13 June 2025, by the IAEA's last estimate, and by June 2026 the IAEA said it could "not provide any information on the current size, composition or whereabouts" of it. [cite:ir10_isis_jun26] [cite:ir11_iaea_sep7] Israel is estimated by SIPRI to hold about 90 warheads, deliverable by aircraft, by Jericho missiles and possibly by submarine; it neither confirms nor denies them. [cite:ir4_ynet_sipri] [scene:ir4_dimona|Part Four: Dimona]

The American column

The largest entry on Israel's side of the ledger is American. Under the 2016 memorandum of understanding the United States provides $38 billion over 2019–2028, $3.3 billion a year in military financing and $500 million for missile defence. [cite:hm_dn_mou] From October 2023 to September 2025 it gave at least $21.7 billion in military aid, and its own operations in the region cost a further $9.65 to $12.07 billion. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] In June 2025 American THAAD batteries fired about 150 interceptors in Israel's defence, about a quarter of the stock. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] Between 40,000 and 50,000 American troops were based in the region in mid-2025, at least 19 sites including Al Udeid in Qatar and the Fifth Fleet's base in Bahrain. By the end of March 2026 there were more than 50,000. [cite:ir13_aje_usbases] [cite:ir13_nyt_50k] Central Command put the cost of the 2026 war to the United States at $43.6 billion by 3 September 2026. That is nearly six times Iran's budgeted military spending for 2025. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:ir13_sipri_2025] Part Fourteen examines that bill. [scene:ir14_bill|Part Fourteen: the American bill]

On every conventional measure except headcount, the ledger favours Israel, and with the United States beside it the gap is very wide. Iran's power lies in other columns: missiles numerous enough to saturate defences for a time, armed allies across the region documented in Part Nine, and a coastline on the strait that carries a fifth of the world's oil. [scene:ir9_reach|Part Nine: Iran's reach] [cite:ir13_eia_hormuz] Israeli governments say the ledger understates the danger, because a single nuclear weapon would make the conventional balance meaningless; that is the reason they give for the Begin doctrine. [cite:ir13_pbs_bibi2026] Iran's government says it does not seek one. [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] Whether the gap in the ledger made Iran a threat to be removed, or a weaker state that Israel and the United States could strike at an acceptable cost, is an argument the figures cannot settle.

chapters.label: Part Fourteen
chapters.title: Dragged In: the American Bill
chapters.intro: Part Fourteen counts what the long conflict with Iran has cost the United States and asks how it came to pay it. The Hezbollah volume and The One-Way Mirror have already set out the deaths caused by Iran's allies in Lebanon and Iraq, the defence of Israel in 2024 and 2025, and the two wars of 2025 and 2026; this part does not repeat them. It adds the direct American–Iranian record they leave out, from the embassy hostages of 1979 to the tanker war of 1987–88 and the airliner shot down by an American cruiser, the Iraq war and the killing of Qassem Soleimani, and the price of the 2026 war at American petrol pumps. It then separates three questions the phrase "dragged in" runs together: who argued for war with Iran, who decided on it, and what Congress and the public did, and it tests the thesis against what the record shows about who began each American action.
chapters.outro: Part Fourteen established the American bill and who ran it up. Forces Iran's government commanded or, by the Pentagon's unpublished assessment, armed have killed and injured Americans: at least 603 in Iraq by that assessment, and 110 brain injuries at Ain al-Asad in 2020 after an attack Iran announced in advance. American forces killed 290 people aboard Iran Air 655 in 1988, for which the United States paid $61.8 million to families without admitting liability. [cite:ir14_mt_603] [cite:ir14_stripes_tbi] [cite:ir14a_rferl_tbi] [cite:ir14_na_warning] [cite:ir14_wiki_ia655] The heaviest costs followed decisions taken in Washington, and every American operation was ordered by a president: $43.6 billion and 21 American lives in the 2026 war by October, and, on this book's arithmetic from the EIA's October forecast, an average petrol price 81 cents a gallon higher than in 2025. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] [cite:ir14_eia_steo] [cite:ir14a_eia_steo] Israeli leaders pressed for strikes for nearly two decades, and in 2025 and 2026 Israeli action and Netanyahu's advocacy helped set the timing, by Rubio's own words and Reuters's anonymously sourced reporting. On the other side, Trump said he may have "forced Israel's hand" and that the decision was his, Netanyahu called the charge "fake news", and presidents had earlier refused Israeli requests. Majorities in the polls opposed the wars, and Congress's attempts to end them, including a concurrent resolution adopted in June 2026, did not stop them. [cite:hz12_cato_hoffman] [cite:ir14_aje_rubio] [cite:hz12b_reuters_call] [cite:ir14_sn_forced] [cite:hz12b_mediaite_bibi] [cite:ir14_rc_override] [cite:hz12_clerk_hcr86] [cite:ir14_cnn_poll2025] On the record tested here, "dragged in" overstates compulsion; the Israeli influence it points to is documented, while how much it weighed against Washington's own reasons remains disputed. Part Fifteen sets out what across this volume is settled, what is contested and what remains open. [scene:ir15_record|Settled, contested and open]

sections.h: The American Bill, 1979–2026
sections.html:
Two earlier accounts in this library already count much of what the United States has paid in the Middle East since 1983. The Hezbollah volume sets out the Beirut embassy and Marine barracks bombings of 1983, the kidnappings of the 1980s, the militia attacks of 2023–24 and the money spent from October 2023; The One-Way Mirror sets out the American interceptors fired in Israel's defence in 2024 and 2025. [scene:hz12_costs|The American bill, 1983–2026] [scene:ow7_iran|Defending Israel, fighting Iran] This section adds the direct record between the United States and Iran, keeping apart three things that are easily blurred: Americans killed by Iran's forces or by forces the United States says Iran armed; people killed by American forces in the same conflict; and costs the United States took on by its own decisions.

The hostages and Desert One, 1979–1981

The conflict began with Americans held captive, not killed. Fifty-two staff of the American embassy in Tehran, seized on 4 November 1979, were held for 444 days. President Carter called the hostage-taking "blackmail". On 24–25 April 1980 he sent a rescue force, Operation Eagle Claw; it was aborted at a desert staging site, and during the withdrawal a helicopter struck a transport aircraft, killing eight American servicemen, five airmen and three Marines. No Iranian fire was involved. The hostages were released on 20 January 1981, minutes after Carter left office. [cite:ir14_wiki_eagleclaw] Iran's government's handling of the crisis is told in Part Nine. [scene:ir9_record|Iran's own record]

The tanker war, 1987–1988

The first American combat with Iran came in the last years of the Iran–Iraq war, and it began with a request from Kuwait. In December 1986 Kuwait asked the Reagan administration to protect its oil tankers from Iranian attack; on 7 March 1987 the administration agreed, and Kuwaiti tankers were re-registered under the American flag. The Navy's escort operation, Earnest Will, ran from July 1987 to 26 September 1988. On its first convoy, on 24 July 1987, the reflagged tanker Bridgeton struck an Iranian mine; no one was hurt, and Iran's prime minister, Mir Hossein Mousavi, called it an "irreparable blow to America's political and military prestige." [cite:ir14_wiki_earnestwill]

The heaviest American loss of the tanker war came from Iraq, not Iran. On 17 May 1987 an Iraqi jet fired two Exocet missiles into the frigate USS Stark, killing 37 sailors and injuring 21; Iraqi officials said the targeting was accidental. [cite:ir14_wiki_earnestwill] It belongs in the ledger because it shows what the deployment cost, but it is not an Iranian death toll and should not be counted as one.

On 14 April 1988 the frigate USS Samuel B. Roberts struck a mine, and ten sailors were severely injured. Four days later the United States answered with Operation Praying Mantis: it destroyed the Sassan and Sirri platforms, which the Revolutionary Guard used for surveillance, sank the fast-attack craft Joshan and the frigate Sahand, and disabled the frigate Sabalan. [cite:ir14_nhhc_mantis] [cite:ir14_usni_mantis] Two Marine aviators, Captains Stephen C. Leslie and Kenneth W. Hill, died when their AH-1T Sea Cobra crashed at night south-west of Abu Musa; Navy officials reported no evidence of hostile fire, though the helicopter may have gone down while evading Iranian fire. [cite:ir14_pas_mantiskia]

Iran Air 655, 3 July 1988

The largest single loss of life in the whole American–Iranian conflict before 2026 was caused by the United States. On 3 July 1988 the cruiser USS Vincennes fired two missiles at Iran Air Flight 655, an Iranian Airbus, over the Strait of Hormuz, and killed all 290 people on board: 274 passengers and 16 crew, among them 254 Iranians and 65 children. The United States said the crew had mistaken the airliner for an attacking Iranian F-14; Iran's government said the shooting was deliberate and unlawful, and at the least negligent. President Reagan expressed regret, but the United States never formally apologised or admitted wrongdoing, and the ship's captain later received the Legion of Merit, in a citation that did not mention the downing. [cite:ir14_wiki_ia655]

Iran took the United States to the International Court of Justice in 1989.
