[cite:gi2_wiki_irgun] What Herut and Likud later said about the land, including the 1977 Likud platform's claim to sovereignty "between the Sea and the Jordan", which dropped the east bank, is examined in [scene:gi5_likud|Part Five]. [cite:gi1_jvl_likud1977]

Two other records bear on the claim. The first is that the Hashemite rulers of Transjordan made their own "one country" argument, joining the West Bank to their kingdom in 1950; that history, and the later Israeli slogan "Jordan is Palestine", are told in [scene:s06a2|the separation of Transjordan] and [scene:gi8_jordan|Part Eight]. The second is that the claim to the east bank, which was the Revisionists' defining demand, was given up by their heirs: Israel and Jordan signed a peace treaty in 1994, and in March 2023 Israel's Foreign Ministry restated its commitment to it and its recognition of "the territorial integrity of the Hashemite Kingdom." [cite:gi8_ynet_mfajordan] Jordan's position is that, in King Abdullah II's words of January 2004, "Jordan will never be an alternative homeland to anybody." [cite:gi8_king_althomeland] Both are covered in [scene:gi8_jordan|Part Eight] and [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve].

The finding for this section is precise. "Both banks of the Jordan" was the stated programme of a named movement, the Revisionist Zionists, from 1925, sung by its youth movement and drawn on its army's emblem. It was opposed within the Zionist movement, was never adopted by the Zionist Organization, and did not become the policy of the State of Israel. What did pass from the Revisionists into Israeli politics was a party lineage, through Herut to the Likud, and the habit of treating the land west of the Jordan as one undivided unit, which later chapters follow. [cite:gi2_ej_revisionists] [cite:gi2_ej_partition]

sections.h: Peel, 1937: A Partition Map and a Letter to Amos
sections.html:
In July 1937 a British royal commission produced the first official map dividing Palestine. The Palestine Royal Commission, chaired by Lord Peel, proposed to end the Mandate and create two states. The Jewish state would consist of Galilee, the Jezreel Valley and most of the Beth-Shean valley, and the coastal plain from near the Lebanese border south to Be'er Tuvia: about 17 percent of the country. The Arab state, about three-quarters of it, would take in the hill country of Samaria and Judea and the Negev, and would be united with Transjordan. Britain would keep a mandate zone of about 8 percent, covering Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Nazareth and a corridor from Jerusalem to the sea at Jaffa. [cite:gi2_jvl_peel] [cite:gi2_ej_partition] The commission also proposed an "exchange of population", compulsory in the last resort, which would have moved far more Arabs than Jews; that recommendation, and the record of how the Zionist leadership received it, are set out in [scene:pl_s01|Peel's "exchange of population"] and are not repeated here. The commission's work and the revolt that prompted it are in [scene:s07a6|the Peel Commission].

For the question of territorial aims, the Peel map is a test. It offered a Jewish state on less than a fifth of western Palestine and none of the east bank. How each party answered it is a direct record of what each would accept. [cite:gi2_jvl_peel]

Three answers

The Twentieth Zionist Congress met in Zurich from 3 to 16 August 1937. It called the Peel scheme "unacceptable", principally because the proposed state was too small, but it authorised the Zionist Executive to negotiate with the British government over a Jewish state, with any resulting arrangement to be submitted to a newly elected Congress. [cite:gi2_ej_partition] [cite:gi2_israeled_20th] Most of the Yishuv and the movement thus accepted partition in principle after a vigorous controversy, while rejecting this partition. [cite:gi2_ej_partition] The Revisionists' New Zionist Organization, outside the Congress since 1935, "opposed and combated" partition outright, because it gave up the claim to the whole land. [cite:gi2_ej_revisionists] The Arab Higher Committee rejected the plan, warning that "partition would create in Palestine two neighboring hostile states." [cite:gi2_jvl_peel]

The plan did not survive. A technical commission under Sir John Woodhead found it unworkable, and in November 1938 the British government told Parliament that its Partition Commission had advised "unanimously against the adoption of the scheme of partition outlined by the Royal Commission" and that partition was impracticable. [cite:gi2_unispal_cmd5893] That episode is in [scene:rd4_woodhead|Woodhead and St James's Palace].

The letter

The single document most often quoted on what the mainstream leadership intended is private. On 5 October 1937 David Ben-Gurion, chairman of the Jewish Agency Executive, wrote to his son Amos. The handwritten original is held in the IDF Archive; the English translation most cited was obtained from the Ben-Gurion Archives and published by the Institute for Palestine Studies. [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter]

Much of the letter is not in dispute. Ben-Gurion argued for accepting partition as a stage, not a settlement: a Jewish state was "not the end but the beginning." "The establishment of a state, even if only on a portion of the land," he wrote, would be "a powerful boost to our historical endeavors to liberate the entire country." [cite:gi1_wiki_greaterisrael] [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter] He wanted the Negev, which Peel had given to the Arab state, arguing that the Arabs "already have an abundance of deserts but not of manpower, financial resources, or creative initiative", and he wrote that force might be needed to secure Jewish settlement there. [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter] On this reading the letter is evidence that the leader of the movement's majority accepted a small state while intending, in time, to enlarge it. It is not evidence of a border he named, and "the entire country" here meant the land of the Mandate, not the biblical frontiers.

One sentence is disputed, and the dispute concerns what the manuscript says. In the original, several words in the middle of a sentence are crossed out. Read without them, the sentence says "We must expel the Arabs"; restored, it says the opposite. [cite:gi2_comm_morris] [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter]

The first reading came from Shabtai Teveth's English version of 1985, which Benny Morris quoted in 1988: "We must expel Arabs and take their places." [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter] [cite:gi2_comm_morris] Efraim Karsh argued in 2000 that the quotation left out the crossed-out words and that restoring them reversed the meaning; writing in 2008, he gave the original as "We do not wish and do not need to expel Arabs and take their place," and said it "unequivocally settled the matter." [cite:gi2_hnn_karsh] [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter] Morris, in an exchange in Commentary in 2011, said he had consulted the original, that the crossing-out was in it, and that Ben-Gurion "rarely made corrections," while others had suggested the deletion was made later by another hand. He said he had since either dropped the quotation or used the version the restoration allows, and called the focus on it "nothing more than (an essentially mendacious) red herring," because, he argued, Ben-Gurion endorsed transfer elsewhere, "either 'voluntarily' or by compulsion." [cite:gi2_comm_morris] [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter]

This book does not decide between the readings. It records that the undisputed text supports partition as a stage toward "the entire country"; that the disputed sentence cannot carry any finding on its own; and that the wider question it is used for, Ben-Gurion's views on transfer in 1937–38, rests on other documents, discussed in [scene:pl_s01|Peel's "exchange of population"]. A separate quotation sometimes confused with this one, "The Arabs will have to go, but one needs an opportune moment for making it happen, such as a war", comes from Ilan Pappé's writing of 2006, not from the letter. The Journal of Palestine Studies, which had published it, acknowledged in 2012 that its punctuation presented a paraphrase as a quotation, while rejecting the charge that it misrepresented Ben-Gurion's position of the late 1930s. [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter]

"Expand to the whole Land of Israel"

The same view, partition as a stage, appears in remarks Ben-Gurion is reported to have made to the Jewish Agency Executive in June 1938: that after building a strong force "we will abolish the partition of the country and we will expand to the whole Land of Israel." The wording comes from the historians Nur Masalha (1992) and Tom Segev (2000), citing the Executive's minutes; this book has not checked the minutes. [cite:gi1_wiki_greaterisrael] It is consistent with the undisputed passages of the Amos letter and should be read with the same limits: it is a statement of long-range aim by the leader of the mainstream, made privately, about the territory of the Mandate.

What Peel settles

Three points can be stated as findings. The mainstream Zionist movement accepted the principle of partition in 1937 and negotiated on a state far smaller than its 1919 claim. [cite:gi2_ej_partition] [cite:gi2_israeled_20th] The Revisionists refused it because they held to both banks. [cite:gi2_ej_revisionists] And the leader of the mainstream wrote privately that a partial state would be a beginning, not an end. [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter] Whether that last view was a programme of expansion or a negotiating posture is an argument, with both cases resting on documents. The argument for a programme points to the letter, the 1938 remarks and the later expansion of 1948. The argument against points to what the same leadership did when it held power and the choice was real: it accepted the 1947 partition plan, signed the 1949 armistice lines, and in 1957, under American pressure, withdrew from Sinai and Gaza, as [scene:gi3_borders|Part Three] shows.

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: Armistice Lines and the Sinai Test
chapters.intro: Part Three covers the years when Israel's borders were armistice lines, from the agreements of 1949 to the eve of the June 1967 war. It reads what the four armistice agreements said about borders, what Israel's governments said they wanted, and which named party, Herut, kept the claim to both banks of the Jordan alive in opposition. It then takes the one occasion in those years when Israel held a large area beyond the lines, the Sinai campaign of 1956, as a test. It sets out what Ben-Gurion proposed at Sèvres, checks where the words "Third Kingdom of Israel" were actually said, and follows the government from victory to its acceptance of withdrawal and, under American pressure, to its departure from Gaza and Sinai in March 1957.
chapters.outro: Part Three established that the armistice agreements of 1949 each denied that their lines were borders, and that Israel's governments nonetheless sought to make them permanent frontiers, with Israel giving back 13 Lebanese villages under the Lebanon agreement. [cite:gi3_un_syrarm] [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] [cite:gi3_wiki_armistice] The claim to both banks of the Jordan was the programme of Herut, an opposition party with 14 of 120 seats in 1949, and not of any government; on the Syrian front the documented pattern was pressure on the demilitarized zones, not a campaign to move the line. [cite:gi3_jvl_herut] [cite:gi3_wiki_herut] [cite:gi3_frus_dayan1953] The Sinai campaign of 1956 showed wider aims stated at the top: the Sèvres eighth point on eastern Sinai, Ben-Gurion's "fantastic" plan reaching to the Litani, a letter to the troops that, as reported, placed Tiran in a "Third Kingdom of Israel," and a government decision to hold Gaza. None of these was kept. The phrase is not in the Knesset speech of 7 November, Ben-Gurion wrote on 8 November that Israel had "never planned to annex the Sinai desert," and under United Nations and American pressure Israel left Gaza on 8 March 1957 and Sinai the same month. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] [cite:rs_cw3_walla_third_kingdom] [cite:gi3_jvl_bg7nov] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_ike_bg] [cite:rs_cw3_app_20feb57] [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Part Four turns to the war of June 1967, which put the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan in Israel's hands, and to the movement founded that summer to keep them. [scene:gi4_conquest|Part Four: 1967 and the Land of Israel Movement]

sections.h: The Lines of 1949
sections.html:
From 1949 to June 1967 Israel had no agreed borders, only armistice lines. Those eighteen years are the first test of the question this volume asks: once there was a state, did its governments claim land beyond the lines it held, and who did? The record of the period has three parts. The agreements themselves said the lines were not borders. Israel's governments treated them as borders in practice and proposed them, with small changes, as permanent frontiers. And the claim to the whole Land of Israel, including both banks of the Jordan, was carried in the Knesset by one named opposition party, Herut. How the Green Line was drawn on the Jordanian front is told in [scene:wb1_line|The West Bank, Documented: the Green Line], and the Gaza line in [scene:gz1_war|Gaza, Documented: the war and the line]. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] [cite:gi3_jvl_herut]

Four agreements, one formula

The United Nations mediator Ralph Bunche negotiated four armistice agreements in 1949. Egypt signed first, at Rhodes on 24 February. Its Article V says the demarcation line "is not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary." [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] Lebanon signed at Ras en Naqoura on 23 March. Its line "shall follow the international boundary between the Lebanon and Palestine," and forces were to withdraw to it within ten days. [cite:gi3_avalon_lebarm] Israel withdrew from 13 villages in Lebanese territory that it had occupied during the war. [cite:gi3_wiki_armistice] Jordan signed at Rhodes on 3 April. Its Article II states that no provision would prejudice the rights, claims and positions of either side in a final settlement. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text]

Syria signed last, on 20 July, near Mahanayim. Syria withdrew from most of the ground it held west of the old international border, and those strips became demilitarized zones. [cite:gi3_wiki_armistice] The agreement says the line and the zones "are not to be interpreted as having any relation whatsoever to ultimate territorial arrangements." The armed forces of both sides were to be "totally excluded" from the zones, and the agreement looked to "the gradual restoration of normal civilian life" there. [cite:gi3_un_syrarm] Each agreement, in other words, froze a military position and left sovereignty open. Israel's Foreign Ministry describes the territory inside the lines as "about 78% of the Mandate area" and the agreements as interim, meant to last until peace treaties replaced them. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map]

What Israel's government said

Israel's government of the time wanted the lines confirmed, not moved outward. Foreign Minister Moshe Sharett called them "provisional boundaries," and at the Lausanne conference of 1949 Israel proposed them, with minor changes, as the basis for permanent frontiers. [cite:gi3_wiki_armistice] Fifty-seven years later, at a memorial ceremony for Ben-Gurion on 27 November 2006, Prime Minister Ehud Olmert quoted a line he attributed to Ben-Gurion's speech in the 1949 Knesset debate on the armistice agreements: faced with a choice between "the entire land of Israel without a Jewish State" and a Jewish state without it, "we chose a Jewish State without the entire land of Israel." [cite:gi3_jvl_olmert2006] That wording comes through Olmert; the Knesset record of 1949 was not read. The historian Benny Morris, as quoted by Martin Kramer, gives a two-sided summary: Ben-Gurion in 1948–49 wanted borders wider than the 1947 partition lines, but he "also refrained from supporting the conquest of the whole Land of Israel." [cite:gi3_kramer_bgborders]

The Syrian channel shows the same thing from another side. In 1949 Syria's new military ruler, Husni al-Za'im, proposed a summit with Ben-Gurion, a peace agreement and the resettlement of 300,000 Palestinian refugees in north-eastern Syria in return for American aid. Privately he told the American minister, James Keeley, that he would share Lake Tiberias and give Israel its western half. Ben-Gurion refused to meet him until Syria pulled its forces back to their pre-war positions: "There will be no discussions on peace or cooperation until those borders are adjusted." [cite:gi3_majalla_zaim] The refusal cost a chance at talks that might have led somewhere, and historians still argue about how real that chance was. What Ben-Gurion demanded was a Syrian withdrawal to the old Mandate frontier. He made no claim on Syrian territory.

Who claimed more

The party that did claim more was Herut, founded by Menachem Begin in June 1948 as the political heir of the Irgun. Until it merged into the Gahal bloc in 1965, according to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Herut "maintained that the State of Israel should contain both banks of the River Jordan." [cite:gi3_jvl_herut] Its slogan was "Two banks of the Jordan River." It opposed the armistice agreements with the Arab states and refused to recognize the Kingdom of Jordan. [cite:gi3_wiki_herut] In the first Knesset election, in January 1949, it won 14 of 120 seats with 11.5 per cent of the vote, and it came fourth. [cite:gi3_wiki_herut] [cite:gi3_jvl_herut] The claim was the Revisionist one described in [scene:gi2_bothbanks|Part Two: both banks of the Jordan]. Between 1949 and 1967 it was the stated programme of an opposition party, not the policy of any government.

Jordan's parliament used the same language for the opposite claim. On 24 April 1950 it voted for "complete unity between the two banks of the Jordan, the eastern and western, and their union in one single state," annexing the West Bank. [cite:rs_rd6_kramer_annexation] According to a Library of Congress study, only Britain and Pakistan recognized the union, and it was condemned within the Arab League as serving Hashemite ambitions. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] Egypt held the Gaza Strip without annexing it and never gave its inhabitants Egyptian citizenship. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] The annexation and its reception are covered in [scene:wb2_annex|The West Bank, Documented: the annexation].

Pressure at the edges

The lines were not quiet. On the Syrian front the dispute was over the demilitarized zones, which the agreement had left without a sovereign. On 18 November 1953 Moshe Dayan, then deputy chief of staff, told the State Department's Henry Byroade that "Israel claims sovereignty only over Jewish lands in the Demilitarized Zone." He said that "someone must keep the area alive" and that Syria wanted the border "on the east water line of the Jordan River," while Israel did not want Syria to have direct access to the river. Byroade replied that the United States "cannot stand idly by and watch the United Nations machinery fall apart." [cite:gi3_frus_dayan1953] Israel's cultivation and water works in the zones led to repeated clashes and to Security Council condemnation, as in Resolution 171 of April 1962, told in [scene:cw2_banat_yaacov|the Banat Ya'qub canal dispute] and [scene:cw4_borders|the armistice lines 1960–1962]. [cite:rs_cw4_unsc171]

On the Jordanian and Egyptian fronts the conflict was over people crossing. Morris, as reported by Avi Shlaim, estimated that 90 per cent or more of the crossings of 1949–56 were motivated by economic and social concerns, such as returning to homes, fields, property or relatives, rather than by political aims, and that between 2,700 and 5,000 infiltrators were killed, the great majority of them unarmed. Israel's reprisal raids included Qibya in October 1953, where 69 Jordanian villagers were killed. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] These were fights over the lines. They were not campaigns to move them, with one exception, Sinai in 1956, which is the subject of [scene:gi3_sinai56|the next section].

What the period shows

The documented facts are these. The agreements denied that the lines were borders. Israel's governments sought to make them borders, at Lausanne and after. The claim to both banks of the Jordan was stated by Herut, which won 11.5 per cent of the vote in 1949, and not by any government. [cite:gi3_wiki_armistice] [cite:gi3_jvl_herut] The pattern that can be shown over time is pressure at the margins, in the Syrian demilitarized zones above all, where Israel claimed the Jewish-owned land and worked it against Syrian and UN objection. [cite:gi3_frus_dayan1953] Whether Labor's acceptance of the lines was a settled choice or a pause is a matter of argument. Olmert's Ben-Gurion quotation supports the first reading. Morris's wider-borders observation, Herut's programme and the Sinai campaign that followed support the second. [cite:gi3_jvl_olmert2006] [cite:gi3_kramer_bgborders]

sections.h: The Sinai Test, 1956–1957
sections.html:
Only once between 1949 and 1967 did Israel hold a large area beyond the armistice lines. Its forces took the Gaza Strip and the whole Sinai peninsula in the first days of November 1956 and stayed until March 1957. The full history of the war, including the collusion with Britain and France, the killings in Gaza and the diplomacy, is told in the Cold War volume, starting from [scene:cw3_sevres|the Protocol of Sèvres]. This section asks a narrower question. What did Israel's leaders say they wanted to keep, and what did they keep? The answer matters for this volume because the war produced the phrase most often quoted as proof of a territorial programme, Ben-Gurion's "Third Kingdom of Israel." Where it was actually said needs checking.

The aims at Sèvres

At the secret conference at Sèvres, outside Paris, on 22 October 1956, Ben-Gurion set out a reorganization of the region that he himself called "fantastic," according to the historian Avi Shlaim. Jordan would be divided, Israel extended to the Litani, the Suez Canal internationalized and Nasser removed. At his request an eighth point was added to the draft, seeking "permanent annexation of the entire area east of the El Arish-Abu Ageila, Nakhl-Sharm el-Sheikh" line. Britain and France never backed it, and it is not in the signed protocol. On 24 October he named the interest he did secure: "The Straits of Tiran are the State of Israel's Suez Canal." [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] According to the Gush Katif Heritage Center's history, which draws on the journalist Hagai Huberman, the cabinet meeting that approved the operation listed control of the Gaza Strip among its aims; Ben-Gurion had proposed retaking Gaza in March 1955, and the government rejected it. [cite:rs_cw3_katif_gaza]

"Third Kingdom": where the words were said

The phrase "Third Kingdom of Israel" is often attributed to Ben-Gurion's Knesset speech of 7 November 1956. The English text published by Israel's Foreign Ministry, reproduced by the Jewish Virtual Library, does not contain the words "Third Kingdom," "kingdom" or "Yotvat." It mentions Tiran only as an island that "for centuries" had been "desolate" until Egypt garrisoned it "for the purpose of interfering with Israeli shipping in the Gulf." [cite:gi3_jvl_bg7nov] Its strongest lines were about the armistice: "The armistice agreement with Egypt is dead and buried and cannot be restored to life," and the armistice lines "have no more validity." It said Israeli forces had orders not to cross the Canal "or to attack Egyptian territory proper, and remain entirely within the limits of the Sinai Peninsula," a phrase that set Sinai apart from Egypt proper without saying what Sinai was. It offered Egypt peace "under conditions of direct negotiations." It did not say whether Israel would keep the peninsula or leave it. [cite:gi3_jvl_bg7nov]

The phrase belongs to an earlier text. At a ceremony at Sharm el-Sheikh around 6 November, Moshe Dayan read the troops a letter from Ben-Gurion. According to a 2023 report by the Israeli news site Walla, which quotes the Hebrew, the letter said that Yotvat, the ancient name it gave Tiran, "will return to be part of the Third Kingdom of Israel." [cite:rs_cw3_walla_third_kingdom] Uri Avnery, a journalist and opponent of Ben-Gurion, later recalled the "victory announcement … proclaiming the 'Third Kingdom of Israel'," followed within about a day by a speech announcing that he had agreed to withdraw. [cite:rs_cw3_avnery] No archival copy of the letter was found. The wording is therefore reported, by two sources, and attributed to a letter to soldiers, not to the Knesset speech. It should be quoted that way.

Within a day

Eisenhower wrote to Ben-Gurion on 7 November. He warned that refusing to withdraw "could not but bring about the condemnation of Israel as a violator" and could "impair the friendly cooperation between our two countries." [cite:rs_cw3_app_ike_7nov] Ben-Gurion replied on 8 November that Israel would "willingly withdraw our forces" once satisfactory arrangements had been made with the UN for an international force, and he wrote: "We have never planned to annex the Sinai desert." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_ike_bg] The government announced the same day that "it was finally agreed to accept the United Nations Resolution and withdraw Israel's forces." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_cabinet_8nov] The opposition leader did not accept the turn. On 16 November Begin praised the government's refusal to leave Sinai before Egypt made peace and, in the Begin Center's summary of a press report, said parts of the Land of Israel still needed to be liberated. [cite:rs_cw3_begin_center] The hour-by-hour record is in [scene:cw3_third_kingdom|the Third Kingdom and the retreat].

Gaza: the attempt to stay

The government's acceptance of withdrawal in principle did not settle Gaza. According to Benny Morris, Ben-Gurion told the Knesset on 19 December 1956 that Israel would never let Egypt resume control of the Strip, and argued on 23 January 1957 that "This Strip was never Egyptian." [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] The Gush Katif Heritage Center records a government resolution of 13 January 1957 that "Israel will hold the Gaza Strip" and Knesset approval on 23 January of the decision not to withdraw. [cite:rs_cw3_katif_gaza] Of everything taken in 1956, Gaza, which had been part of Mandate Palestine, was the area Israel's government tried hardest to keep. Sinai, which had not been, it had already agreed in principle to leave. The occupation is told in [scene:cw3_gaza_occupation|Israel's first occupation of Gaza].

Eisenhower's pressure and the withdrawal

On 2 February 1957 the General Assembly adopted Resolution 1124 by 74 votes to 2. It "Deplores the non-compliance of Israel to complete its withdrawal behind the armistice demarcation line." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_1124] On 11 February Washington gave Israel an aide-mémoire. It said withdrawal from Gaza "should be prompt and unconditional," that the Gulf of Aqaba "comprehends international waters," and that the United States was "prepared to exercise the right of free and innocent passage." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_aidememoire] On 20 February Dulles named German reparations, the sale of Israel Bonds and US aid to congressional leaders as possible levers, and several of the leaders were reluctant. [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d120] That evening Eisenhower asked on radio and television: "Should a nation which attacks and occupies foreign territory in the face of United Nations disapproval be allowed to impose conditions on its own withdrawal?" [cite:rs_cw3_app_20feb57]

On 1 March Golda Meir announced at the UN that "Israel will withdraw from the Gaza Strip and Sharm el-Sheikh." She stated Israel's assumptions, among them that only the UN Emergency Force would take over, and warned that interference with Israeli shipping would be treated as an attack. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] Israel left Gaza on 8 March and Sinai the same month. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] UNEF stayed on Egyptian soil until Nasser ordered it out in May 1967. [cite:rs_cw3_origins_hahn] Ben-Gurion told the Knesset on 5 March that Israel had gained free passage through Tiran and UN forces at Sharm el-Sheikh and in Gaza. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] The historian Uri Bar-Joseph's view is that Israel left without formal security gains, under "brutal" American pressure. [cite:rs_cw3_barjoseph_hdiplo] Both readings are set out in [scene:cw3_withdrawal|the withdrawal fight].

What the test shows

The documented facts point both ways. On one side are the Sèvres eighth point, the "fantastic" plan reaching to the Litani and a divided Jordan, the "Third Kingdom" letter as reported, the Knesset speech's dismissal of the armistice lines, and four months of effort to keep Gaza. [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] [cite:rs_cw3_walla_third_kingdom] [cite:gi3_jvl_bg7nov] [cite:rs_cw3_katif_gaza] On the other are the written disavowal of 8 November, the government's war aims of security and navigation, and a full withdrawal by March 1957. It is the first withdrawal in this volume's counter-record, a quarter-century before Israel left Sinai again in 1982. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_ike_bg] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_cabinet_8nov] [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza]

Two readings follow, and both are arguments. On the first, the leader of a Mapai-led government held territorial aims beyond the armistice lines, in Sinai, Gaza and on paper as far as the Litani, and gave them up only under American, Soviet and UN pressure. On the second, the aims that decided the war were Tiran and the fedayeen bases, the letter was victory rhetoric for soldiers, and the speed of the concession shows that annexation was not a programme. [cite:rs_cw3_barjoseph_hdiplo] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_cabinet_8nov] The test supports a narrower finding than either reading. In 1956 Israel's leaders stated wider claims in private and in victory, and the government did not legislate or keep any of them. The claim to both banks of the Jordan stayed with Herut, which opposed the withdrawal. [cite:rs_cw3_begin_center] The memory of 1957 weighed on Israel's cabinet in June 1967, according to Bar-Joseph. [cite:rs_cw3_barjoseph_hdiplo] What came after that war is the subject of [scene:gi4_conquest|Part Four], and the 1957 withdrawal returns as the first entry in [scene:gi12_withdrawals|the counter-record].

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: 1967 and the Land of Israel Movement
chapters.intro: Part Four covers the decade in which "the whole Land of Israel" stopped being a question about maps on a wall and became a question about land Israel actually held. In six days of June 1967 Israel took Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. Within weeks its government had offered to give most of it back for peace, while a new movement of writers, Labor veterans, Revisionists and one prominent rabbi declared that no government had the right to give any of it up. The part sets out what was taken, what the government first decided, what is and is not available of that movement's 1967 manifesto, the Allon Plan with which Labor governments answered it, and the religious settlement movement, Gush Emunim, that took its cause over from 1974.
chapters.outro: Part Four established that the conquests of June 1967 did not produce a single Israeli answer. On 19 June the government voted, ten to nine and then unanimously, to offer Egypt and Syria peace on the basis of the international border. It deferred any decision on the West Bank, leaned toward annexing Gaza and kept East Jerusalem. [cite:gi4_cie_june19] [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] The whole-land programme was stated outright by one named body, the Movement for the Whole Land of Israel. Its manifesto, published on 22 September 1967 over 57 signatures from Labor activists, writers, Revisionists and Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook, declared that "no government in Israel is entitled to give up this wholeness". The full text is held in the Posen Library and in the movement's own 1977 history; only its opening sentences and that conclusion could be read online. [cite:gi4_972_twoads] [cite:gi4_posen_manifesto] [cite:gi4_inss_einav] On the same day the socialist group Matzpen published the opposite demand. [cite:gi4_972_twoads] The movement won no seat in 1969, joined Likud in 1973 and was absorbed by Gush Emunim, the religious settlement movement founded in 1974, whose stated aim was the permanent incorporation of the whole land. [cite:gi4_wiki_mgi] [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] The Labor governments' own design, the Allon Plan, was never adopted. It would have kept about a third of the West Bank and returned the populated hills to Jordan, and Hussein turned it down in 1968. [cite:gi4_wiki_allon] [cite:gi4_frus_d186] [cite:gi4_jcfa_gold] Part Five follows the whole-land programme into government, from Menachem Begin's victory in 1977. [scene:gi5_begin|Part Five: the ideology in government]

sections.h: Six Days, and What to Do With Them
sections.html:
The war itself is told elsewhere in this library. The crisis that led to it, from the closing of the Straits of Tiran to the eve of 5 June, ends the Cold War volume in [scene:cw6_tiran_june4|the Tiran crisis]; the war in the West Bank and the second Palestinian exodus are in [scene:wb3_war|the West Bank volume]; the occupation of Gaza and its first census are in [scene:gz2_1967|the Gaza volume]. This section takes up a narrower question, the one that matters for the phrase "Greater Israel": what Israel held when the fighting stopped, and what its government first said it would do with it.

What was taken

Between 5 and 10 June 1967 Israel took the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria. A ceasefire arranged by the United Nations took effect on 10 June. The territory under Israel's control roughly tripled. By a later estimate, some 20,000 Arabs and about 800 Israelis were killed. [cite:gi4_history_sixday] In June Israel set up a military government for the civilian population of all four areas. [cite:gz_wiki_occupation]

The land did not come empty, and on the Golan the population largely disappeared. Israeli Military Intelligence estimated about 90,000 Syrian residents on the plateau, some 20,000 of them in the town of Quneitra, three days after its capture; the census Israel took on 10 August 1967 counted 3,936 in its final figures, most of them Druze in the villages of the north. Israel's position was that the residents had left; Colonel Shlomo Gazit, in Akevot's account of his meeting with the Red Cross, said their departure should not be seen as an expulsion. The International Committee of the Red Cross concluded that most had been "expelled either violently upon arrival of the armed forces, or under duress at a later stage," and in 1968 the Israeli diplomat Michael Comay wrote of "the expulsion of Arabs from Quneitra, which has been going on for several months." These accounts, all drawn from Israeli and Red Cross archives by the Israeli research institute Akevot, are set side by side here because they disagree. [cite:gi4_akevot_golan] Quneitra's later history and the Golan Heights Law of 1981 belong to [scene:gi8_golan|Part Eight].

The decision of 19 June 1967

Nine days after the ceasefire the government met to decide what it would offer. Its minutes, released by the Israel State Archives, record three different answers for three fronts. For Egypt and Syria, the morning session voted ten to nine to propose "peace treaties with Egypt and Syria, that include security arrangements, based on the international borders"; nine ministers backed a rival text that leaned toward keeping territory. In the afternoon a formula for peace with Egypt, and with Syria, "on the basis of the international border" was approved unanimously. [cite:gi4_cie_june19] In other words, on the day the question was first put, a bare majority of Israel's cabinet was prepared to return Sinai and the Golan in exchange for peace and security arrangements.

The other two fronts were treated differently. On Jordan and the West Bank the government could not agree and decided, for the time being, not to decide. On Gaza, the drafting committee, with one dissent, that of Moshe Kol, agreed that the strip should be annexed to Israel. [cite:gi4_cie_june19] East Jerusalem was not on offer at all: on 27 and 28 June Israel applied its law to about 70 square kilometres of East Jerusalem and the surrounding villages, a step the Security Council rejected, as [scene:wb3_jerusalem|the West Bank volume] sets out. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex]

What happened to the 19 June offer is itself a matter on which accounts differ. The decision was passed to the United States in secret; Egypt and Syria gave no positive answer. [cite:gi4_aijac_1967] Both accounts of the 2012 archive release reviewed here say only that Israel "did not receive positive responses from Egypt and Syria"; AIJAC adds that the answer "would only come later in the year", at Khartoum. [cite:gi4_cie_june19] [cite:gi4_aijac_1967] Whether Washington ever conveyed the terms to Cairo and Damascus in a form those governments recognised as an offer is not established by the sources reviewed, and the question is left open here.

The Arab states' own stated position followed in September. The Arab summit at Khartoum adopted the formula remembered as the "three noes": "no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with it." [cite:gi4_aijac_1967] On 22 November 1967 the Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 242, which emphasized "the inadmissibility of the acquisition of territory by war" and called for "withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict," alongside the right of every state in the area to live within "secure and recognized boundaries." Israel and the Arab states read the absence of "the" before "territories" differently, a dispute the West Bank volume explains. [cite:wb_wiki_242]

Holding without deciding

The government's legal adviser on these questions warned early. In September 1967 the Foreign Ministry's legal counsel, Theodor Meron, advised that "civilian settlement in the administered territories contravenes the explicit provisions of the Fourth Geneva Convention"; days later the cabinet approved a settlement at Kfar Etzion, presented as an army outpost. [cite:wb_gorenberg_meron] Israel's governments came to argue that the Convention did not apply to the West Bank as a matter of law, since Jordan's annexation of it had not been recognized, while undertaking to observe its humanitarian provisions; critics answered that the Convention protects people rather than sovereign claims. [cite:wb_cow_israelview] The first decade of settlement was small: by Peace Now's count, 1,500 settlers lived in the West Bank outside East Jerusalem in 1972 and 4,400 in 1977. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop]

Three things can be stated as documented facts about mid-1967. First, Israel held, for the first time, almost all the land west of the Jordan that the Revisionist and maximal programmes described in [scene:gi1_versions|Part One] had claimed, together with Sinai and the Golan, which almost none of them had. Second, the government's first recorded answer was not "keep it all": it offered two of the five areas back on the basis of the international border, deferred the West Bank and kept East Jerusalem. Third, that answer was divided, ten votes to nine on the first ballot, so the question of how much to keep was open inside the government from its first week. The rest of this part follows the two answers that formed outside and inside the government: a movement that said none of it could be given up, and a Labor minister's plan to keep some of it and return the populated rest.

sections.h: The Movement for the Whole Land of Israel
sections.html:
The phrase "Greater Israel" entered English largely as the translation of one organization's name. HaTnu'a LeMa'an Eretz Yisrael HaShlema, "the Movement for the Whole Land of Israel," usually rendered the Movement for Greater Israel or the Land of Israel Movement, was formed in the summer of 1967 to keep the territories Israel had just taken and to settle them. [cite:gi4_wiki_mgi] Unlike the biblical border texts and the founders' maps discussed in Parts One and Two, this is a case where a named body stated the programme in so many words, so it can be documented directly. This section sets out what of its founding statement can be read today, who signed it, what became of the movement, and who answered it at the time.

When it was founded

The sources give three dates, and they describe different events. Wikipedia, citing the political scientists Myron Aronoff and Ehud Sprinzak, dates the founding to July 1967. [cite:gi4_wiki_mgi] The political scientist Ian Lustick places it "two months after the Six Day War", that is, in August. [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] The manifesto itself appeared as a newspaper advertisement in Yedioth Ahronoth on 22 September 1967, signed by 57 cultural figures. [cite:gi4_972_twoads] The essays that prepared the ground, collected that year by Aharon Ben-Ami under the title HaKol: Gvulot HaShalom shel Eretz Yisrael ("Everything: The Peace Borders of the Land of Israel"), had already run in Maariv, Haaretz, Davar and Lamerhav within about two months of the war. [cite:gi4_inss_einav] The most economical reading is that the circle formed in July or August and went public in September.

What the manifesto said

Few sources reproduce the manifesto, and only part of it is publicly available. The full Hebrew text is held in the Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization, whose public page reproduces the opening, and in Ben-Ami's 1977 history of the movement. [cite:gi4_posen_manifesto] [cite:gi4_inss_einav] The rest of the Posen text is available only to registered readers. What is publicly available online is the following.

The manifesto opened by declaring that the army's victory "placed the nation and the state in a new and fateful period." Its central sentence, in the Posen Library's translation, reads: "Now the whole Land of Israel is in the hands of the Jewish people, and just as we have no right to give up the State of Israel, so too we are commanded to maintain what we have received from its hands: the Land of Israel." [cite:gi4_posen_manifesto] The historian Omer Einav, writing for Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), quotes the same sentence from Ben-Ami's book and notes that the word metzuvim, "commanded," gives a secular document a religious tone. [cite:gi4_inss_einav] Lustick, writing in 1988, renders the opening clause as "The whole of Eretz Yisrael is now in the hands of the Jewish people." [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] Its operative conclusion, in the translation the Israeli journalist Noam Sheizaf took from the historian Nitza Erel, was that "no government in Israel is entitled to give up this wholeness." [cite:gi4_972_twoads]

So the document stated a programme in plain terms: the territory between the Jordan and the sea, and by implication the other areas taken in June, was not to be bargained away by any government. Beyond these sentences the public record available online does not show the full text. This book does not reconstruct it, and does not attribute to the manifesto wording that cannot be checked. A dealer's catalogue of the movement's papers from 1967 to 1969 confirms that a handwritten platform, a council list, protocols with Nathan Alterman's participation and a petition against withdrawal from the territories survive in private hands. [cite:gi4_kedem_archive]

Who signed

The signatories matter because they do not fit the usual picture. Einav names Labor-movement figures (the kibbutz leader Yitzhak Tabenkin, the novelist Moshe Shamir, a Palmach veteran and former member of the left-wing Mapam, and the poet Zerubavel Gilad); writers and intellectuals including the poet Nathan Alterman, Haim Gouri, Hayim Hazaz, S.Y. Agnon, Yaakov Orland and Rachel Yanait Ben-Zvi; the secular intellectual Aharon Amir; Shmuel Tamir of the Free Center; and Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook of the Merkaz HaRav yeshiva. About half the signatories were writers or academics. [cite:gi4_inss_einav] Wikipedia's list adds Revisionists, among them Shmuel Katz and Israel Eldad, together with the poet Uri Zvi Greenberg, Isser Harel, Yitzhak Zuckerman, Zivia Lubetkin and Avraham Yoffe, who became its leader. [cite:gi4_wiki_mgi] The historians Amir Goldstein and Elchanan Shilo describe its founders as "activist Labour movement members." [cite:gi4_biu_goldstein]

The finding, then, is that the post-1967 whole-land programme was not born in one camp. It joined the Revisionist claim described in [scene:gi1_versions|Part One] to a strand of the Labor movement's own activist wing and to the religious current around Kook, whose lineage [scene:gi11_religious|Part Eleven] follows. It was the programme of these named people and this named movement. It was not the position of the government, which was then led by Labor and had just voted to offer Sinai and the Golan back ([scene:gi4_conquest|above]).

What became of it

As a party the movement failed. Running in the 1969 Knesset election as the "List for the Land of Israel," it won 7,561 votes, 0.6 per cent, below the threshold, and took no seat. Before the 1973 election it joined the new Likud alliance of Herut, the Liberals, the Free Center and the National List; Yoffe sat as its one member from 1973 to 1976, when it merged into the La'am faction, which remained in Likud until it merged into Herut in 1984. [cite:gi4_wiki_mgi] As a cause it did better. Lustick describes it as an elite body of writers, intellectuals and generals that aspired to be "a respected pressure group", and which Gush Emunim eclipsed after 1973, absorbing many of its participants, so that by 1977 it had "virtually ceased to exist." [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] Goldstein and Shilo's study is built on the same handover: Gush Emunim, they write, "effectively took the lead" in the movement during the 1970s. [cite:gi4_biu_goldstein] How a cause carried by Labor-movement poets passed to religious settlers is the subject of the next section, and the party line that runs through La'am into Likud is taken up in [scene:gi5_likud|Part Five].

The answer the same day

The opposition to keeping the territories was published on the same date. On 22 September 1967 the small socialist group Matzpen, founded in 1962 by four former members of the Communist Party, placed a 52-word advertisement in Haaretz: "Occupation leads to foreign rule," it said; holding the territories "will make us a nation of murderers and victims"; "Let's leave the occupied territories now." [cite:gi4_972_twoads] That month also saw the first publication of Siach Lochamim (published in English as The Seventh Day), conversations with kibbutz soldiers edited by Avraham Shapira. Its invitation, drafted by Amos Oz, promised "not a victory album, nor a collection of heroic deeds." [cite:gi4_inss_einav]

Einav sets the two currents side by side as the start of a split. The movement spoke in a collective "we" and offered policy; the soldiers' book spoke in the first person and offered doubt. Before the war, he argues, disagreements over the state's borders had been "largely theoretical"; afterwards they divided most of the Zionist camp along a single line, with far-reaching changes inside both the Labor movement and religious Zionism. [cite:gi4_inss_einav] [cite:gi4_inss_einav_abs] That is an interpretation, and it is offered as one. What the documents establish is narrower: in September 1967 a named group of Israelis demanded that the whole land be kept, and other named Israelis demanded the opposite, in the same newspapers, on the same day.

sections.h: The Allon Plan and the Bloc of the Faithful
sections.html:
Between 1967 and 1977 Israel was governed by the Labor movement, and the government's answer to the whole-land demand was a plan to keep part of the land. It carries the name of Yigal Allon, who was then minister of labour and later foreign minister. It was never formally adopted, but it guided where the government settled for a decade. From 1974 a religious movement, Gush Emunim, set out to break those lines, and it inherited the cause of the movement described in the [scene:gi4_movement|previous section]. The West Bank volume gives the settlement story itself in [scene:wb3_first|its first decade] and [scene:wb4_movement|after 1977]; this section reads both programmes for what they said about borders.

The plan, 1967–1968

Allon put his first version to the cabinet on 27 July 1967. It proposed Palestinian autonomy in two large enclaves of the West Bank, and on 30 July most ministers rejected it. In early 1968 he revised it, dropping the Palestinian option in favour of a Jordanian one. Israel would keep the Jordan Valley, from the river up to the eastern slopes of the hill ridge, together with East Jerusalem, the Etzion bloc and, in the 1968 version, part of the Hebron hills. The densely populated hill country would go back to Jordan, joined to it by a corridor through Jericho. [cite:gi4_wiki_allon] [cite:wb_wiki_allon] Sinai was mostly to return to Egypt. For the Golan, Allon floated the idea of a Druze state on the Syrian side. Gaza he first wanted annexed and later placed in a Jordanian-Palestinian state. [cite:gi4_wiki_allon]

The plan's logic was the reverse of the manifesto's. It was built, in one summary of it, "to include as few Arabs as possible in the areas claimed for Israel": territory for depth and security where few Palestinians lived, and none of the towns where most did. Israeli leaders of the period, by the same account, ruled out absorbing the West Bank's population into a greater Israel because doing so would change the state's Jewish majority. [cite:gi4_wiki_allon] It did not start from a renunciation, though. The Israeli journalist Reuven Pedatzur reported that in June 1967, before drafting it, Allon had said that "the last thing we must do is to return one inch of the West Bank." [cite:gi4_wiki_allon] Both readings belong in the record. The plan kept roughly a third of the West Bank, and it was also the first official Israeli design to give most of it back.

The plan put to Hussein

The plan was put to King Hussein of Jordan, in secret. The United States followed the talks from May to November 1968. According to the State Department's own documentary history, "In November the Israelis proposed an agreement based upon the 'Allon plan,' which posited Israeli control over the West Bank, while returning political control of some two-thirds of a demilitarized West Bank to Jordan." Hussein grew sceptical that Israel would offer terms he could accept, and he eventually broke off the talks. [cite:gi4_frus_d186] Jordan's stated position was Resolution 242's principle that territory cannot be acquired by war. Under the plan Jordan would have recovered the towns while Israel kept a 10–15 kilometre strip along the river, most of the Judean Desert and East Jerusalem, which the cabinet had resolved in 1967 would not be returned. [cite:gi4_wiki_allon] [cite:gi4_aijac_1967]

No Israeli cabinet ever formally adopted the plan, but in the first decade of occupation settlement largely followed its map. Settlements went into the Jordan Valley as lookouts on the strip to be kept, and around Jerusalem, away from the Palestinian towns; Kiryat Arba, approved in 1970 beside Hebron, marked its western edge. [cite:gi4_wiki_allon] [cite:wb_wiki_allon] Allon held to the plan in office. As foreign minister he told President Ford on 11 October 1976 that "we need some changes in the Green Line," and that within Israel "the debate is about giving less, not more." [cite:gi4_ford_allon1976] In Foreign Affairs that October he set out the strategic zone he wanted, which the former Israeli ambassador Dore Gold later put at about 700 of the West Bank's 2,100 square miles. Gold notes that Allon's thinking shaped later plans of both Labor and Likud, and that in 1997 Netanyahu called his own map "Allon-Plus." [cite:gi4_jcfa_gold]

Gush Emunim, 1974

The challenge to Allon's lines came after the October 1973 war, and from a different quarter. Gush Emunim, the "Bloc of the Faithful," was founded in the spring of 1974; the name was coined in February at the home of Rabbi Haim Druckman. Its founders were rabbis, religious veterans of the war and activists of the National Religious Party's Young Guard, most of them influenced by Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook, the same rabbi who had signed the 1967 manifesto. Hanan Porat and Moshe Levinger led it with Druckman, and it called itself "nonpartisan, extra-parliamentary." [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:wb_ej_gush] Its stated aim, in Lustick's account, was the permanent incorporation of the whole Land of Israel into the state, together with a transformation of Israeli society. It opposed Palestinian autonomy and saw settlement as a way to block it. [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] The religious teaching behind it is the subject of [scene:gi11_religious|Part Eleven].

Its first campaign was against withdrawal. When the government negotiated the 1974 disengagement with Syria, the Gush backed a hunger strike against a withdrawal from Quneitra. [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] It then went to the hills the Allon Plan had left for Jordan. It made eight attempts to settle near Nablus in 1974 and 1975, and the army removed seven of them. At Hanukkah 1975 about 2,000 supporters gathered at the old railway station at Sebastia. After a long confrontation with Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin's government and the defence minister, Shimon Peres, the settlers were allowed to stay in the nearby army camp at Kadum. A march of some 20,000 people in May 1976 showed the size of its following. [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:wb_ej_gush] A Labor government had set the Allon lines; a Labor government also let the first settlement outside them stand.

The handover, 1977

By the time the Likud won the election of 1977, Gush Emunim had absorbed the activists of the older movement, which Lustick says had "virtually ceased to exist." [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:gi4_biu_goldstein] The new government gave official status to several Gush settlements. In September 1977 Ariel Sharon, the agriculture minister, put forward a plan for more than a million Jews in the West Bank within twenty years. Lustick counts about $400 million spent in the West Bank and Gaza between 1977 and mid-1981 and the settler population, excluding the Jordan Valley and East Jerusalem, rising from roughly 3,500 to 18,500; Peace Now's series, which excludes only East Jerusalem, puts the 1977 starting point at 4,400. [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:wb_ej_gush] [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] The alliance had limits. In 1979 the Gush attacked Begin's government for giving up Sinai and for its autonomy plan. [cite:gi4_lustick_gush]

The decade sorts into three kinds of material. The documented facts are a manifesto that stated a whole-land programme; a government plan, never adopted, that set out to keep about a third of the West Bank and hand back the populated rest; and a religious movement whose stated aim was the whole land. The pattern that can be shown over time is that unauthorized settlements, starting with the Hebron hotel in 1968 and Sebastia in 1975, ended in compromises that left the settlers in place. [cite:wb_wiki_hebron] [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] Whether that pattern reflected a hidden consent inside the Labor governments, or a weak government's failure to enforce its own map, is an argument that the documents cited here do not settle. The record above shows that the government's stated policy, through 1977, was partition along the Allon lines and not the whole land.

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: The Ideology in Government
chapters.intro: Part Five follows the idea of the whole Land of Israel from a movement into government, from 1977 to the end of 2022. It begins with Menachem Begin, the first Likud prime minister: the language he brought into office, the settlement plans his government adopted, the autonomy plan in which he claimed sovereignty over the West Bank and Gaza and then proposed to leave it open, the laws on East Jerusalem (1980) and the Golan Heights (1981), and the return of Sinai. It then reads the 1977 Likud platform, the source of the line "between the Sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty", for what it says and does not say, and sets the later votes of Likud's Central Committee beside what Likud prime ministers did in office. The part ends with two texts that carry the claim beyond a party: the Nation-State Law of 2018, which made Jewish settlement a "national value", and the guidelines and coalition agreements of the government formed in December 2022.
chapters.outro: Part Five established that the claim to the land west of the Jordan entered Israeli government with the Likud in 1977, in documents that can be quoted. The 1977 platform declared that "between the Sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty"; Begin called Judea and Samaria a land that "cannot be given up in any part", and his government made settlement in the hill country state policy. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [cite:gi5_djn_begin77] [cite:wb_ej_gush] It also established the limits of that record. Begin's autonomy plan kept the sovereignty claim but proposed to leave it "open"; the 1980 Jerusalem Law entrenched Israeli law in East Jerusalem and the 1981 Golan Heights Law applied it to the Golan, both declared null and void by the Security Council; and Sinai was returned in 1982. [cite:gi5_ecf_selfrule] [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] Likud's Central Committee voted in 2002 against any Palestinian state west of the Jordan and in 2017 for sovereignty over the settlements, while Likud prime ministers removed the Gaza settlements in 2005 and, in 2009, accepted a demilitarised Palestinian state on conditions. [cite:gi5_ap_likud2002] [cite:gi5_toi_likud2017] [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] [cite:gi5_aje_barilan] By December 2022 a Basic Law named Jewish settlement a national value without defining where, the government's guidelines claimed "an exclusive and inalienable right to all parts of the Land of Israel", and the coalition agreement committed the prime minister to a sovereignty policy at a time of his choosing. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] [cite:gi5_adalah_hcj] [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] [cite:gi5_cgtn_sov] None of these texts claims land east of the Jordan. Part Six follows what the government did with those commitments between 2019 and October 2026, from the annexation pledges and their suspension to the land-registration decision and the Knesset votes. [scene:gi6_plans|Part Six: the annexation track]

sections.h: Begin and "Judea and Samaria", 1977–1982
sections.html:
In May 1977 the Likud, led by Menachem Begin, won an Israeli general election for the first time, ending the Labor movement's hold on government since 1948. Begin came from the Revisionist current described in Part Two, and he brought into office a vocabulary as well as a programme. Within days of the vote he set out his position in public. As reported in the Detroit Jewish News of 27 May 1977, he said that Judea and Samaria, the biblical names he used for the West Bank, "cannot be given up in any part". He also said that their Arab residents "can have complete cultural autonomy" and that "it is not an occupied country". [cite:gi5_djn_begin77] Soon after the election he visited the Elon Moreh group of Gush Emunim, which the previous government had allowed to stay at the Kadum army camp after the stand-off at Sebastia, and told the settlers: "Soon, there will be many Elon Morehs." [cite:gi5_akevot_tzipori] [cite:wb_ej_gush] [scene:gi4_movement|Part Four: the Land of Israel Movement and Gush Emunim]

The words mattered because they changed the frame. Labor governments after 1967 had spoken of the West Bank as territory held pending a settlement. They had built settlements, mostly in the Jordan Valley and around Jerusalem along the lines of the Allon Plan, which offered the populated hills back to Jordan. [cite:wb_wiki_allon] Begin rejected the word "occupied" and spoke of the land as the Jewish people's by right. That was the language of the platform on which he had been elected, examined in the next section. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [scene:gi5_likud|The platform and the party]

Settlement as government policy

The new government turned the movement's demand into state planning. Gush Emunim presented an "emergency" settlement plan. Its blueprint of October 1978 resembled the plans drawn up by Matityahu Drobles of the Jewish Agency's settlement department and by Ariel Sharon, Begin's agriculture minister. Unlike the Allon Plan, these placed settlements in the hill country itself, among the Palestinian towns. [cite:wb_ej_gush] [cite:wb_wiki_allon] The settler population outside East Jerusalem, about 4,400 when Begin took office, reached 23,700 by 1983, by Peace Now's count. The West Bank volume tells that story in detail. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] [scene:wb4_movement|The West Bank, Documented: the movement and the government]

The United States objected from the start, and Begin answered on the record. In a message handed to Secretary of State Cyrus Vance and cabled to the embassy in Israel on 9 January 1978, Begin reported that his cabinet had decided "to establish four additional settlements, all of them in military camps". He relayed Foreign Minister Moshe Dayan's account of a meeting with President Carter, in which Carter spoke of "the illegality of the settlements and their being an obstacle to peace" and Dayan replied that "there cannot be a government in Israel that will not establish settlements." [cite:gi5_frus_begin78] Begin's own position in the same message was that his government kept "scrupulously" to every promise it had made. The American position, as Dayan reported it, was that the settlements were illegal. Both are recorded in the US government's own documentary history. [cite:gi5_frus_begin78]

The courts set a limit. In the Elon Moreh case of 1979 Israel's Supreme Court held that taking private Palestinian land for a settlement was unlawful when the motive was political and ideological rather than military. After that ruling the authorities turned to declaring "state land" under the Ottoman Land Code, a mechanism explained in the West Bank volume. [cite:wb_dweikat] [cite:wb_wiki_stateland] [scene:wb4_land|The West Bank, Documented: how the land was taken]

The autonomy plan: sovereignty claimed, then left open

Begin's formal proposal for the territories did not annex them. On 28 December 1977 his government put forward a 26-point "Self-Rule Plan" for the Arab residents of Judea, Samaria and Gaza. It offered administrative autonomy under an elected council. Security and public order would remain "the responsibility of the Israeli authorities", and residents would have "free choice of either Israeli or Jordanian citizenship". [cite:gi5_ecf_selfrule] It also stated that "residents of Israel will be entitled to acquire land and settle" in the territories. On the central question it made a claim and then set it aside. Israel, the plan said, stood by its claim of sovereignty over the areas but, knowing that other claims existed, proposed for the sake of peace that "the question of sovereignty in these areas be left open". The principles were to be reviewed after five years. [cite:gi5_ecf_selfrule]

That formula carried into the Camp David Framework of 17 September 1978, which provided for "transitional arrangements for the West Bank and Gaza for a period not exceeding five years" and "full autonomy to the inhabitants" under an elected self-governing authority. [cite:gz_campdavid] [scene:gz2_economy|Gaza, Documented: Camp David and the territories] The autonomy talks that followed produced no agreement. The pattern of Begin's years is that sovereignty was asserted in speeches and the platform and was not legislated for the West Bank and Gaza, while settlement there expanded under government plans. [cite:gi1_wiki_greaterisrael] [cite:wb_peacenow_pop]

Two laws and one withdrawal

In Begin's years the Knesset did legislate on two other territories. In 1980 it passed the Jerusalem Law, a Basic Law on the capital that entrenched the application of Israeli law to an enlarged East Jerusalem in June 1967; Security Council Resolution 478 declared it null and void. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] [scene:wb3_jerusalem|The West Bank, Documented: East Jerusalem] On 14 December 1981 the Knesset passed the Golan Heights Law by 63 votes to 21. Its operative sentence applied "the Law, jurisdiction and administration of the State" to the Golan. [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] The law does not use the word annexation. The Security Council answered three days later with Resolution 497, adopted unanimously, which declared the law "null and void and without international legal effect". The United States suspended the strategic cooperation memorandum it had signed with Israel two weeks earlier. [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] [cite:ow1_wiki_1981isr] The Golan front, including the American recognition of 2019, is covered in Part Eight. [scene:gi8_golan|Part Eight: the Golan]

In the same years Begin's government gave back far more land than it annexed. Under the peace treaty with Egypt it withdrew from the whole of Sinai, completing the handover on 25 April 1982. The settlement town of Yamit was evacuated and levelled, and Sharon, by then defence minister, said: "In Sinai, in Yamit, we have reached the red line of our concessions." [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve: the withdrawals] The record of Begin's government does not show the land-claim language of 1977 applied everywhere Israel held territory. It shows that language applied to the land west of the Jordan, the land of the platform. There the government settled, claimed sovereignty and left the claim formally open. Sinai, outside that claim, was traded for peace.

sections.h: The Platform and the Party, 1977–2017
sections.html:
The sentence most often quoted to show that Likud holds a Greater Israel programme comes from its 1977 election platform. It sits in a section headed "The Right of the Jewish People to the Land of Israel". The section opens: "The right of the Jewish people to the land of Israel is eternal and indisputable". It goes on to say that this right is linked to the right to security and peace, and that "therefore, Judea and Samaria will not be handed to any foreign administration; between the Sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty." [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] The quotation is accurate. The text is reproduced by the Jewish Virtual Library from the Likud's own website and from Laqueur and Rubin's documentary collection The Israel-Arab Reader. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977]

What the 1977 text says, and what it does not

Read whole, the section makes three claims. It makes a right claim: the land belongs to the Jewish people by a right described as eternal. It makes a sovereignty claim: between the Mediterranean and the Jordan only Israel will rule. And it makes a political argument: any plan that "relinquishes parts of western Eretz Israel" undermines that right and "unavoidably leads to the establishment of a 'Palestinian State'". [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] The section on settlement calls settlement "in all parts of the Land of Israel" "the focal point of the Zionist effort to redeem the country". It says the government will call on young people in Israel and abroad to settle, "while taking care not to dispossess anyone". [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] The peace section promised direct negotiations with Israel's neighbours "without pre-conditions on either side" and attendance at the Geneva conference. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977]

The boundaries of the claim are stated in the text itself. The phrase "western Eretz Israel" and the line "between the Sea and the Jordan" place the eastern limit at the river. The Revisionist claim to the east bank of the Jordan, the land that became the Kingdom of Jordan, is not in the platform. Nor are Sinai, southern Lebanon, Syria beyond the Golan, or anything like the "Nile to the Euphrates" of later polemics. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [scene:gi1_versions|Part One: the three versions] [scene:gi10_myths|Part Ten: the myths] On the platform's own terms, then, the documented Likud programme of 1977 was a claim to the West Bank and Gaza, held together with Israel inside its 1949 lines. Within that area the claim was categorical.

One common description of the text goes beyond the record. Several accounts say that the Likud charter "still says" these words and that this has been the party's position "since its founding". The text that can be sourced is the 1977 platform. Likud's current constitution and its platforms for later elections could not be found in a verifiable form. This book therefore does not claim that the 1977 sentence is current party text. It sets out instead what the party's governing bodies voted for later, which is on the record. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [cite:gi1_wiki_greaterisrael]

The party bodies: 2002 and 2017

On 12 May 2002, during the second intifada, Likud's Central Committee, the party's main policy body, voted on rival resolutions. Benjamin Netanyahu, then out of office and preparing to challenge Prime Minister Ariel Sharon for the leadership, backed a resolution stating: "No Palestinian state will be created west of the Jordan". Sharon's alternative, endorsing his government's diplomatic and security efforts, lost a secret ballot by 59 to 41 per cent, and Netanyahu's text then passed by a show of hands. [cite:gi5_ap_likud2002] Sharon had tried to block the vote. He had said he could accept a Palestinian state under strict conditions and had once called one "inevitable", and after the defeat he said he would keep leading "according to the same ideas". The Palestinian minister Saeb Erekat called the vote "a real slap in the face" for President George W. Bush, who had backed a Palestinian state. [cite:gi5_ap_likud2002]

On 31 December 2017 the Central Committee went further. It voted unanimously to call on the party's elected leaders "to extend Israeli law and sovereignty in all the areas of liberated settlement in Judea and Samaria" and to allow unhindered construction there. [cite:gi5_toi_likud2017] The resolution did not bind Likud's members of the Knesset. It carried weight because candidates depend on the committee's roughly 3,000 members in party primaries. Netanyahu, by then prime minister, did not attend; the Times of Israel noted that he had long opposed ideological declarations by party bodies. The Knesset speaker Yuli Edelstein, the Jerusalem mayor Nir Barkat and several ministers backed it, and the keynote speaker, Gideon Sa'ar, said annexation could come "in just a few years". [cite:gi5_toi_likud2017] Hamas called the decision "the continued harming of Palestinian rights" and said it would lead to "more resistance". [cite:gi5_toi_likud2017]

Unlike the 1977 platform's "between the Sea and the Jordan", the 2017 text applied sovereignty to "the areas of liberated settlement", the settlements and the land around them. It made no claim to every part of the West Bank. That narrowing reappears in the annexation proposals of 2019 to 2026 described in Part Six. [cite:gi5_toi_likud2017] [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [scene:gi6_plans|Part Six: the annexation plans]

The leaders in office

Likud's prime ministers have often acted differently from the party's platform and its committee. Begin, elected on the 1977 platform, applied Israeli law to the Golan and entrenched it in East Jerusalem. In the West Bank and Gaza he kept the sovereignty claim but proposed leaving it "open", and he returned Sinai. [cite:gi5_ecf_selfrule] [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] [scene:gi5_begin|Begin and "Judea and Samaria"] Sharon, who had planned settlement under Begin, removed every settlement in Gaza in 2005. Likud's members had rejected his disengagement plan in a party referendum on 2 May 2004, by about 65 per cent, and he carried it through the cabinet and the Knesset regardless. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] [scene:gz3_withdrawal|Gaza, Documented: the withdrawal]

Netanyahu has stated both positions. At Bar-Ilan University on 14 June 2009 he called the West Bank "the land of our forefathers", but said Israel would accept "a demilitarised Palestinian state" alongside the Jewish state if Palestinians recognised Israel as the Jewish state and security guarantees were met. He added that "we have no intention of building new settlements or of expropriating additional land for existing settlements", and that Jerusalem "must remain the united capital of Israel". [cite:gi5_aje_barilan] In 2002 he had sponsored the resolution against any Palestinian state west of the Jordan, and his later statements rejecting a Palestinian state, through to September 2025, are set out in Part Six. [cite:gi5_ap_likud2002] [scene:gi6_votes|Part Six: the votes]

The documented pattern is a party whose founding platform and governing body claimed the land west of the Jordan in categorical terms. Its prime ministers in office sometimes held the claim in reserve, sometimes narrowed it and in two cases (Sinai in 1982 and Gaza in 2005) gave up land. Whether those reversals show that the claim was rhetoric, or that it was pursued where possible and yielded where not, is a matter of interpretation; Part Eighteen weighs both readings. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [cite:gi5_toi_likud2017] [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] [scene:gi13_record|Part Eighteen: settled, contested and open]

sections.h: A Basic Law and a Coalition, 2018–2022
sections.html:
Platforms and party resolutions bind no one outside the party. Two later texts carried more weight: a Basic Law, part of the set of laws that serve as Israel's constitution, and the written guidelines and coalition agreements of a government. Both name the Land of Israel and Jewish settlement. Neither defines borders. That gap is itself a finding of this section. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines]

The Nation-State Law, 19 July 2018

Early on 19 July 2018 the Knesset passed "Basic Law: Israel as the Nation-State of the Jewish People" by 62 votes to 55, with two abstentions. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] Its first clause states that "the land of Israel is the historical homeland of the Jewish people, in which the State of Israel was established", and that "the right to exercise national self-determination in the State of Israel is unique to the Jewish people." It names "Jerusalem, complete and united" as the capital, makes Hebrew the state language and gives Arabic "a special status". [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] Clause 7, headed "Jewish settlement", reads: "The state views the development of Jewish settlement as a national value", and commits the state to encourage and promote its establishment and consolidation. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] [cite:gi5_adalah_nsl]

Prime Minister Netanyahu called the vote "a defining moment in the annals of Zionism and the history of the state of Israel." Arab members of the Knesset tore up copies of the bill and called it the "death of democracy"; one called it an "apartheid" law. [cite:gi5_voa_nsl] Its supporters argued that it wrote down the state's existing Jewish character. [cite:gi5_aje_hcj2021]

The settlement clause does not say where it applies. Clause 1 uses "the land of Israel" for the historical homeland and "the State of Israel" for the state, and clause 7 speaks of "Jewish settlement" without a territorial definition. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] The Arab rights group Adalah read clause 7 together with clause 1 to mean that the law covers the whole Land of Israel, including the West Bank and East Jerusalem. On that reading it gives constitutional backing to settlement there. Adalah also argued that inside the Green Line the clause could support Jewish-only towns in the Galilee and the Negev, and noted that the law contains no guarantee of equality. [cite:gi5_adalah_nsl] That is the reading of the law's leading opponent. It is not a finding of any court, and the law does not mention Judea, Samaria or the occupied territories by name. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw]

When the law was challenged, the state took a narrower position. In Hassoun v. The Knesset (HCJ 5555/18), decided on 8 July 2021, an eleven-justice panel of the Supreme Court upheld the law by ten votes to one. [cite:gi5_aje_hcj2021] The majority, according to the summary of the judgment translated by Adalah, held that the value of Jewish settlement can be realised alongside equality, and that clause 7 is not meant to legalise discrimination or to exclude non-Jews from state land. The state's lawyers had told the court the same. The justices said equality remains a basic principle of Israeli law, and most of them said it would have been better to write it into the law. [cite:gi5_adalah_hcj] Justice George Karra, the court's only Palestinian Arab justice, dissented. He held that the clause was meant to create a constitutional norm that would in practice negate the Supreme Court's earlier Qa'adan ruling and weaken equality in the allocation of land and housing. [cite:gi5_adalah_hcj] [cite:gi5_aje_hcj2021] The ruling, as summarised, did not decide whether clause 7 reaches beyond the Green Line. [cite:gi5_adalah_hcj] The Justice Minister, Gideon Sa'ar, welcomed it as anchoring "the essence and character of Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people". [cite:gi5_aje_hcj2021]

The record therefore supports three statements and no more. Since 2018, Jewish settlement has been a "national value" in a Basic Law. The law leaves its territorial reach undefined; its leading opponent, Adalah, reads it as reaching the West Bank, and no court has decided the point. [cite:gi5_adalah_nsl] [cite:gi5_adalah_hcj] And the Supreme Court has held that the clause cannot justify discrimination in land allocation, but has not ruled on where it applies. A claim that the Nation-State Law "annexed" the West Bank, or that it made Israel "the state of a religion", goes beyond its text, which speaks of "the nation-state of the Jewish people". [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw]

The 37th government's guidelines, 28 December 2022

After the election of November 2022 Netanyahu formed a coalition that included Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism and Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit, whose leader received an expanded national security ministry. [cite:hm_jta_coalition2022] On 28 December 2022 the new government published its basic guidelines. The first sentence reads: "The Jewish people has an exclusive and inalienable right to all parts of the Land of Israel." The guidelines continue: "The government will promote and develop the settlement of all parts of the Land of Israel – in the Galilee, the Negev, the Golan Heights and Judea and Samaria." [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] [cite:gi1_jns_guidelines] They also commit the government to "preserve the Jewish character of the state" and to respect "the practices and traditions of members of all religions in the country". [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines]

This is the guidelines' exact wording, and it differs from a common paraphrase. Some accounts have it as an "exclusive right on all the land between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River". The text says "all parts of the Land of Israel" and then lists four regions. Like the 2018 law, it does not define the Land of Israel.
