The list places Judea and Samaria, the West Bank, beside the Galilee and the Negev inside Israel and the Golan, which Israel annexed in 1981. [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw]

The coalition agreements went further than the guidelines. The agreement between Likud and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism, signed on 1 December 2022, states, as reported, that "the prime minister will lead the formulation and advancement of policies within the framework of applying sovereignty in Judea and Samaria, while choosing the timing and weighing all of the State of Israel's national and international interests." [cite:gi5_cgtn_sov] [cite:gi5_wiki_37gov] The clause commits the prime minister to a policy of sovereignty, leaves the timing to him, and names international interests as a reason to wait. The same agreement gave Religious Zionism a ministerial post inside the Defense Ministry with responsibility for the Civil Administration and the liaison offices in the West Bank. The minister was to act "with the coordination and agreement of the prime minister", and the party also took over the World Zionist Organization's Settlement Division. Smotrich said the government would "regulate and develop the settlement enterprise." [cite:gi5_ih_rzdeal] Defence Minister Yoav Gallant signed the transfer of those powers to Smotrich on 23 February 2023. [cite:gi5_wiki_37gov] What the government did with them is the subject of Part Six and of the West Bank volume. [scene:gi6_plans|Part Six: the annexation track] [scene:wb9_annex|The West Bank, Documented: since October 2023]

By the end of 2022 the land claim of the 1977 platform had moved from a party platform into a government's guidelines. It sat in the coalition agreement as a sovereignty policy whose timing was left to the prime minister, and a Basic Law named Jewish settlement a national value without saying where. These are documented facts. That the government intended formal annexation of the whole West Bank does not follow from them. The texts commit to settlement "in all parts" and to sovereignty at a chosen time; the formal steps that followed, the Knesset votes and the pressures that stopped or slowed them, are set out in Part Six. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] [cite:gi5_cgtn_sov] [scene:gi6_votes|Part Six: the votes]

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: The Annexation Track
chapters.intro: Part Six follows the years, 2019 to 2026, in which formal annexation of West Bank land moved from a principle in party documents to a pledge with a date, a map and a bill. It begins with Netanyahu's election promise of September 2019 to annex the Jordan Valley, the Trump plan of January 2020 that endorsed Israeli sovereignty over about 30 per cent of the West Bank, and the suspension of that step in August 2020 as the price of normalization with the United Arab Emirates. It then traces how the coalition formed in 2022 moved West Bank civil government into the hands of Bezalel Smotrich, how he set a "year of sovereignty" and drew a map to annex 82 per cent of the territory, and how the Knesset voted on the principle and on two bills in 2025 while Washington and Abu Dhabi said annexation would not happen. It ends with the measures of 2026, land registration and the E1 tender, that changed the administration of the land without declaring sovereignty over it, and with where each stood a week before the election of 27 October 2026. The settlement record beneath these decisions is documented in The West Bank, Documented, to which this part links rather than repeats.
chapters.outro: Part Six established that West Bank annexation has been, since 2019, a documented programme of named actors rather than a rumour. Netanyahu pledged sovereignty over the Jordan Valley in 2019; an American plan endorsed it over about 30 per cent of the territory in 2020; and the joint statement of 13 August 2020 suspended it, in a word each side read differently. [cite:gi6_ap_jv2019] [cite:gi6_crs_plan2020] [cite:gi6_dcpd_uae2020] [cite:gi6_jta_table2020] The 2022 coalition committed itself to sovereignty in principle and moved civil powers to Smotrich, who described the change as one that would not look like annexation and in 2025 proposed annexing 82 per cent of the West Bank. [cite:gi6_wiki_37gov] [cite:gi6_bg_nyt_smotrich] [cite:gi6_toi_82pct] The Knesset voted 71 to 13 for the principle and advanced two bills, 25 to 24 and 32 to 9, which Likud refused to carry and which neither became law; the United States said it would not allow annexation and the UAE called it a red line. [cite:wb_toi_71_13] [cite:gi6_toi_readings] [cite:gi6_ap_trump0925] [cite:gi6_axios_uae2025] In 2026 the government registered land in Area C and tendered homes in E1 without declaring sovereignty, until the Attorney General's Office pushed the tender past the election of 27 October 2026, which will decide who holds the ministries concerned. [cite:gi6_fmep_feb2026] [cite:gi6_ih_e1postpone] [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve] Part Seven turns from the West Bank to the maps Netanyahu held up at the United Nations and to his remark about a "vision" of Greater Israel. [scene:gi7_maps|Part Seven: the maps at the UN]

sections.h: Pledges, a Plan and a Pause, 2019–2024
sections.html:
Until 2019, formal annexation of West Bank land was a position held by parties and ministers on the right of Israel's governments, not a policy any prime minister had promised to carry out by a date. The Likud platform of 1977 and the coalition guidelines of 2022, read in Part Five, spoke of rights and sovereignty in principle. [scene:gi5_likud|Part Five: the Likud platform] This part follows the years in which the idea became a timetable: who pledged what, when, on what terms, and what stopped it. The settlement record underneath these years, the approvals, outposts and budgets, is set out in The West Bank, Documented and is not repeated here. [scene:wb9_annex|The West Bank, Part Nine: the fastest years of settlement]

The Jordan Valley pledge, September 2019

On 10 September 2019, a week before a closely fought general election on 17 September, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stood before a map and pledged that, if re-elected, he would extend Israeli sovereignty over the Jordan Valley soon after forming a government, and later over the settlements. He called it "a one-time opportunity, to extend Israeli sovereignty on our settlements in Judea and Samaria," and tied the timing to the peace plan President Donald Trump was expected to release after the vote. The Jordan Valley makes up nearly a quarter of the West Bank; annexing it would have left the Palestinian areas surrounded by Israeli territory. [cite:gi6_ap_jv2019] [cite:gi6_npr_jv2019]

The responses were immediate. The Palestinian president, Mahmoud Abbas, said all agreements with Israel would be cancelled if Netanyahu went ahead. Jordan's foreign minister, Ayman Safadi, called the pledge "a serious escalation that undermines all peace efforts," and the United Nations called it "devastating" to the prospects of two states. Inside Israel, the opposition politician Yair Lapid called it "an election stunt." American officials said they had been briefed in advance and raised no objection. [cite:gi6_ap_jv2019]

The Trump plan, January 2020

The plan arrived on 28 January 2020. Referred to in later official documents as the President's "Vision for Peace", it allotted Israel sovereignty over about 30 per cent of the West Bank, including the settlements and most of the Jordan Valley. The Palestinians were offered a demilitarized state in the remaining areas, which would be non-contiguous and joined by roads, bridges and tunnels, with a capital in Abu Dis or elsewhere on the edge of East Jerusalem. Statehood was conditional: among the criteria were the disarming of Hamas and recognition of Israel as "the nation state of the Jewish people," with four years to meet them. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said the United States would support annexation consistent with the plan's maps, and Netanyahu said his government would begin considering measures that, in the Congressional Research Service's words, would "effectively unilaterally annex" the settlements and the Jordan Valley. [cite:gi6_crs_plan2020]

Earlier Israeli schemes for keeping part of the West Bank, beginning with the Allon Plan of 1967, are read in Part Four, and the offers that went the other way in Part Twelve. [scene:gi4_allon|Part Four: the Allon Plan] [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve: the withdrawals] What was new in 2020 was an American president's map, and a secretary of state's statement that Washington would support Israel applying its law to the land the map assigned it, before any agreement with the Palestinians. [cite:gi6_crs_plan2020]

The Israeli coalition formed in April 2020 wrote the step into its founding agreement. Clause 29 of the Netanyahu–Gantz agreement, signed on 20 April, allowed Netanyahu to bring "the agreement reached with the US on the application of sovereignty" to the cabinet or the Knesset "starting July 1, 2020," in full agreement with the United States, including on maps, and while "maintaining regional stability" and existing peace agreements. Settler leaders welcomed it. The Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said: "Annexation means the end of any possibility for a negotiated solution." [cite:gi6_toi_unity2020] The date passed without a vote. Jordan's response, and its treaty of 1994, are followed in Part Eight. [scene:gi8_jordan|Part Eight: Jordan]

The pause, August 2020

What stopped the step was a trade. On 13 August 2020 the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates issued a joint statement announcing full normalization between Israel and the UAE. Its operative sentence on the West Bank read: "Israel will suspend declaring sovereignty over areas outlined in the President's Vision for Peace." [cite:gi6_dcpd_uae2020] The parties read the word differently from the first day. Netanyahu said annexation "remains on the table" and that there was "no change" in his plan to apply sovereignty in coordination with Washington. Trump said: "It's off the table," adding that he could not speak about the future. The American ambassador, David Friedman, said "suspend" had been "chosen carefully" and meant a "temporary halt": off the table now, "but it's not off the table permanently." [cite:gi6_jta_table2020] Emirati officials later described Israel's ruling out of annexation as the condition on which they had signed. [cite:gi6_axios_uae2025] The suspension, not a renunciation, is the line every later stage of this part pushes against.

Sovereignty in the coalition agreement, 2022

The government formed after the November 2022 election put the commitment in writing again, in different form. The coalition agreement of 1 December 2022 between Likud and Religious Zionism stated, as reported, that "the prime minister will lead the formulation and advancement of policies within the framework of applying sovereignty in Judea and Samaria, while choosing the timing and weighing all of the State of Israel's national and international interests." Judea and Samaria are the Hebrew biblical names the government uses for the West Bank; a shorter English rendering of the same clause, cited from the Times of Israel, has the prime minister "work towards the formulation and promotion of a policy whereby sovereignty is applied". [cite:gi5_cgtn_sov] [cite:gi6_wiki_37gov] The same agreement gave Bezalel Smotrich, the Religious Zionism leader and finance minister, a second ministerial post inside the Defense Ministry, overseeing civil matters in the West Bank. [cite:gi6_wiki_37gov] The government's general guidelines, which asserted the Jewish people's "exclusive and inalienable right to all parts of the Land of Israel," are read in Part Five. [scene:gi5_nationstate|Part Five: the Nation-State Law and the 2022 guidelines]

The civil powers, 2023

The administrative transfer followed. On 23 February 2023 Defense Minister Yoav Gallant signed an agreement assigning governmental powers in the West Bank to a body headed by Smotrich. [cite:gi6_wiki_37gov] In June 2023 the cabinet moved the approval of settlement planning to him, and civil powers in Area C that the army had held passed to a civilian deputy reporting to his Settlements Administration; in March 2023 the Knesset had already repealed the part of the 2005 disengagement law that barred Israelis from the evacuated sites in the northern West Bank. [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis] The West Bank volume documents how those powers have since been used. [scene:wb9_annex|The West Bank, Part Nine: who runs it]

What the transfer meant was described by Smotrich himself. On 9 June 2024, at a gathering of settlers in the West Bank, he was recorded saying, of moving authority from the army to civilians under him: "We created a separate civilian system." He called the change "mega-dramatic" and said: "Such changes change a system's DNA." The Defense Ministry had been kept formally involved, he explained, because "it will be easier to swallow in the international and legal context," "so that they won't say that we are doing annexation here." He said Netanyahu knew the details and was "with us full on." Smotrich's spokesman confirmed the speech. The prime minister's office replied that the West Bank's final status "will be determined by the parties in direct negotiations" and that "this policy has not changed." [cite:gi6_bg_nyt_smotrich]

Two things are established at this point, and one is not. It is documented that a sitting prime minister promised sovereignty over a defined area in 2019; that the United States endorsed it on a map in 2020; that it was suspended, in words both sides read as temporary, as the price of normalization with the UAE; and that the coalition of 2022 committed itself again in principle and moved West Bank civil government into a minister's hands. It is documented, in his own recorded words, that the minister who received those powers described their purpose as a change that would not look like annexation. Whether the prime minister shared that purpose is not settled by the recording: his office's stated position was that nothing had changed. [cite:gi6_ap_jv2019] [cite:gi6_crs_plan2020] [cite:gi6_dcpd_uae2020] [cite:gi6_wiki_37gov] [cite:gi6_bg_nyt_smotrich] The next section follows how the question returned to the cabinet table and the Knesset floor.

sections.h: Sovereignty on the Agenda, 2024–2025
sections.html:
After Donald Trump won the American election of November 2024, the annexation track moved from administration back to declaration. Over the following twelve months a minister set a year for it, drew a map for it and asked the cabinet to adopt it; the Knesset voted for it in principle and then advanced two bills; and the two governments whose agreement had suspended it in 2020, the United States and the United Arab Emirates, said publicly that it would not happen. This section sets those statements and votes side by side, each with the position of the government or party concerned.

"The year of sovereignty"

On 11 November 2024, at a meeting of his Knesset faction, Bezalel Smotrich declared "2025: the year of sovereignty in Judea and Samaria." He said he had instructed the Defense Ministry's Settlement Directorate and the Civil Administration, both now under his authority, to begin groundwork: "I have directed the start of professional work to prepare the necessary infrastructure." He said he had "no doubt" that Trump would support the move, and that "the only way to remove this danger from the agenda," meaning a Palestinian state, "is to apply Israeli sovereignty." The foreign minister, Gideon Saar, answered for the government: "A decision has not yet been made on the issue." The spokesman for the Palestinian president said the remarks confirmed Israel's intent to annex. [cite:gi6_aje_2025year]

The Knesset's motion, July 2025

On 23 July 2025 the Knesset voted 71 to 13 for a non-binding motion that declared the West Bank "an inseparable part of the Land of Israel" and called on the government to apply Israeli sovereignty to Judea, Samaria and the Jordan Valley. [cite:wb_toi_71_13] A motion of this kind creates no law and binds no minister; its weight is as a recorded count of members willing to vote for the principle. The West Bank volume gives the vote in its sequence. [scene:wb9_annex|The West Bank, Part Nine: the annexation votes]

The 82 per cent map, September 2025

On 3 September 2025 Smotrich presented the most specific proposal of the period: a map under which Israel would annex 82 per cent of the West Bank. The statement issued with it gave the principle as "maximum territory and minimum Arab population." Six Palestinian population centres, Ramallah, Nablus, Jenin, Tulkarem, Jericho and Hebron, would be left as islands inside the annexed area. Smotrich called on Netanyahu "to convene the government to approve applying sovereignty." The statement said that "preventing a Palestinian state is an Israeli consensus" and that "sovereignty takes the idea off of the global agenda." Asked about the Palestinian Authority's opposition, Smotrich said "we will destroy them just as we do Hamas." [cite:gi6_toi_82pct] The plan was a minister's proposal, not a government decision; no cabinet vote on it has been reported.

The same day the UAE answered. A senior Emirati official told Axios that annexation would be a "red line" for the UAE and "a death knell for the two-State solution," and that "the choice before Israel right now is annexation or integration." Lana Nusseibeh, an adviser to the Emirati foreign minister, said: "We trust that President Trump will not allow the Abraham Accords tenet of his legacy to be tarnished." The Emiratis had made Israel's ruling out of annexation a condition of signing in 2020. Israeli officials, speaking without attribution, replied that the 2020 commitment had been time-bound and had expired, and that no decision had been taken. [cite:gi6_axios_uae2025] The Times of Israel attributed the "red line" phrase to Nusseibeh herself. [cite:gi6_toi_82pct]

"No Palestinian state", September 2025

Netanyahu did not adopt Smotrich's map. On 11 September 2025, at Ma'ale Adumim, he signed a framework agreement to advance construction in E1, the land between that settlement and Jerusalem, and said: "We are going to fulfill our promise that there will be no Palestinian state; this place belongs to us." Smotrich, speaking at the same ceremony, said Israel would soon celebrate the application of sovereignty. [cite:gi6_toi_e1sign] The statement is a documented refusal of Palestinian statehood; it is not, in its words, a decision to annex. Part Seven reads Netanyahu's remark of August 2025 about a "vision" of Greater Israel, which belongs to the same weeks. [scene:gi7_interview|Part Seven: the "very much" interview]

Two weeks later, on 25 September 2025, as Britain, France, Australia and other states recognized a Palestinian state at the United Nations and some Israeli ministers proposed annexation in response, Trump said in the Oval Office: "I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank. I will not allow it. It's not going to happen." He said he had spoken to Netanyahu: "It's been enough. It's time to stop now." [cite:gi6_ap_trump0925]

The preliminary readings, October 2025

On 22 October 2025, while Vice President JD Vance was visiting Israel, the Knesset gave preliminary approval to two bills. The first, sponsored by Avi Maoz of the Noam party, would require Israel to "apply its laws and sovereignty to the areas of settlement in Judea and Samaria," that is, to all the settlements. It passed by 25 votes to 24, with the backing of Otzma Yehudit, Religious Zionism and part of United Torah Judaism. The deciding vote was cast by Yuli Edelstein of Likud, who broke his party's boycott, saying "Israeli sovereignty in all parts of our homeland is the order of the day"; Likud removed him from the Knesset's Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee. The second bill, sponsored by the opposition leader Avigdor Liberman of Yisrael Beytenu, would apply sovereignty to Ma'ale Adumim alone. It passed by 32 votes to 9, and the opposition leaders Yair Lapid and Benny Gantz voted for it. [cite:gi6_toi_readings]

Likud boycotted both votes and called them opposition "trolling … aimed at damaging our relations with the US," adding that "true sovereignty will be achieved not with a show-off law for the protocol," and said it was working to create the political conditions for it. Each bill needed three further readings to become law. [cite:gi6_toi_readings] Vance called the vote "a very stupid political stunt." Trump, asked about it, said: "It won't happen," because "I gave my word to the Arab countries," and that Israel "would lose all of its support from the United States" if it annexed. [cite:wb_toi_trump_annex]

Who held which position

The record of these months does not show a single programme held by "Israel". It shows named actors in different places. Smotrich and Religious Zionism, Otzma Yehudit and Noam asked for sovereignty over the settlements or over 82 per cent of the land, now. Netanyahu stated that there would be no Palestinian state; Likud said it was working to create the political conditions for sovereignty, and refused the bills put to the Knesset in October. A part of the centre-right opposition, Liberman, Lapid and Gantz, voted for sovereignty over Ma'ale Adumim, the large settlement east of Jerusalem, while Lapid's party opposed the wider bill. [cite:gi6_toi_readings] The United States and the UAE, whose 2020 statement had paused the step, said it would not happen. Palestinian and Israeli opponents of annexation, including Peace Now, are given in Part Twelve. [scene:gi12_opposition|Part Twelve: Israeli opposition]

What the votes established is narrower than the headlines of either side. As a fact, a Knesset majority voted for the principle of sovereignty over the West Bank, and a bare majority of members present advanced a bill to annex every settlement. As a pattern, each formal step met the same check: the two governments whose agreement had suspended annexation in 2020 restated their objection, and the prime minister's party declined to carry the bills forward. [cite:gi6_axios_uae2025] [cite:gi6_ap_trump0925] [cite:gi6_toi_readings] Whether that check stops annexation or only changes its form is an argument, and the next section sets out the measures that answer it in practice.

sections.h: Annexation Without a Declaration, 2026
sections.html:
By the start of 2026 the formal route was blocked by Washington's stated veto and by Likud's refusal to carry the Knesset bills. The government's measures in the West Bank that year did not declare sovereignty. They changed who records land, who may buy it and where building is tendered. This section sets out three of them, the land-registration decision of 15 February 2026, the related decisions of the same month, and the E1 tender of August 2026, with the government's stated reasons, the objections, and where each stood as of 21 October 2026, six days before Israel's general election.

The February 2026 decisions

On 8 February 2026 the cabinet transferred some demolition powers in Areas A and B, the zones the Oslo agreements left to the Palestinian Authority, to Israeli authorities, and changed the rules on Israelis buying land in the West Bank. [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis] One week later, on 15 February, it approved the registration of land in Area C, the zone under full Israeli control, for the first time since 1967. Area C covered 72–74 per cent of the West Bank when the Oslo II agreement drew the zones in 1995; after the later redeployments it was about 63 per cent by a 2013 count. [cite:gi6_reuters_reg2026] [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas] [scene:wb5_map|The West Bank, Part Five: Oslo's map]

The decision allocated NIS 244.1 million, about $78 million, over four years and up to 35 staff, placed the process in the Justice Ministry rather than the military government, and set a target of completing registration for 15 per cent of Area C within five years. [cite:gi6_fmep_feb2026] Only about a third of the West Bank's land had been registered and titled when Israel took it in 1967, after which Israel froze registration; the rest has remained without a completed title record. [cite:gi6_fmep_feb2026] The mechanism by which Israel has declared unregistered land "state land" since 1979 is described in the West Bank volume. [scene:wb4_land|The West Bank, Part Four: how the land was taken]

The government gave two reasons. A joint statement by the defence minister, Israel Katz, the justice minister, Yariv Levin, and Smotrich said the decision meant "the registration of extensive areas in Judea and Samaria that belong to the state," and Levin called it "a real revolution in Judea and Samaria." [cite:gi6_fmep_feb2026] Katz called registration "a vital security measure designed to ensure control, enforcement, and full freedom of action," and the cabinet described it as an "appropriate response to illegal land registration processes promoted by the Palestinian Authority" that would end disputes. Smotrich said: "We are continuing the revolution of settlement and strengthening our hold across all parts of our land." [cite:gi6_reuters_reg2026]

The objections were as direct. The Palestinian Authority's presidency called the decision "a de-facto annexation of occupied Palestinian territory and a declaration of the commencement of annexation plans." [cite:gi6_reuters_reg2026] Peace Now, the Israeli settlement monitor, called it "a mega land grab of Palestinian property," arguing that most of Area C would pass to the state. A land lawyer for the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, Shlomo Zacharia, said that because unclaimed plots pass automatically to the state and possession weighs heavily, the process favours whoever holds the land in practice, chiefly the Civil Administration and settlers. Arab governments, including some that had normalized relations with Israel, and the UN criticized the month's measures. [cite:gi6_fmep_feb2026] Reuters noted that Trump had ruled out annexation but had not moved to curb settlement. [cite:gi6_reuters_reg2026]

E1: the tender before the election

E1, the land between East Jerusalem and the settlement of Ma'ale Adumim, received final planning approval for 3,401 homes in August 2025, after two decades in which successive Israeli governments had held it back under international pressure; Smotrich said then that it would "permanently bury the idea of a Palestinian state." [cite:wb_itv_e1] [scene:wb9_annex|The West Bank, Part Nine: E1] On 18 August 2026 the Housing Ministry published a tender for 1,234 of those homes, about a third, with bids closing on 19 October, eight days before the election. Peace Now called it "a last-minute maneuver" and said the aim was to sign contracts that a new government would find harder to cancel. [cite:gi6_pn_e1tender]

The tender then met two Israeli institutions. Residents and three Israeli organizations, Ir Amim, Bimkom and Peace Now, had petitioned the Jerusalem District Court against the E1 plans, alleging a defective and discriminatory approval process; the state and the Ma'ale Adumim municipality rejected the claims. On 15 June 2026 the court refused the state's motion to dismiss. [cite:gi6_pn_e1tender] On 8 September Judge Nimrod Flax declined to freeze the tender, finding no irreversible harm while construction was distant, without ruling on the legality of the plans, which remained before the court. [cite:gi6_jpost_e1court] On 26 September the Attorney General's Office ordered the bid deadline postponed by a month, past the election, citing the area's diplomatic sensitivity and the aim of "reducing the concern that the tender could be used for prohibited election propaganda"; it did not cancel the tender. Ma'ale Adumim's mayor, Guy Yifrach, said the town would petition against the delay: "We will not give up and will not allow E1 to be turned into a hostage." [cite:gi6_ih_e1postpone]

Where the track stood, 21 October 2026

The Knesset dissolved on 17 July 2026 and set the general election for 27 October. A Channel 12 poll at the time projected neither Netanyahu's bloc nor his opponents reaching the 61 seats needed to govern. [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve] This volume found no report of a further reading of the 2025 sovereignty bills before the dissolution; neither had become law. The International Court of Justice's advisory opinion of July 2024, which found Israel's continued presence in the territory unlawful and called for an end to new settlement, stood unchanged, and Netanyahu's answer to it, "The Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land," remained his government's stated position. [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] [scene:wb10_rulings|The West Bank, Part Ten: the rulings]

Two readings of the same record

What the record establishes as fact is the set of decisions above, each dated and sourced, and the statements of the ministers who made them. Smotrich has described the purpose in his own words, in 2024 a change of the system's "DNA" that would not look like annexation, and in 2026 "strengthening our hold across all parts of our land." [cite:gi6_bg_nyt_smotrich] [cite:gi6_reuters_reg2026] Read with his 82 per cent map, those statements make annexation of most of the West Bank a documented programme of a named minister and party, the Religious Zionism party, which held the civil powers needed to advance it. [cite:gi6_toi_82pct]

Whether it is also the government's programme is an argument with two sides. The Palestinian Authority and Peace Now argue that the cumulative measures amount to annexation in fact, and the International Court of Justice found in 2024 that Israel's continued presence in the territory was itself unlawful. [cite:gi6_reuters_reg2026] [cite:gi6_fmep_feb2026] [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] The government's stated position is different: its prime minister has refused the bills, its statements present registration as order and security, and its official line in 2024 was that the territory's final status would be settled in negotiations. [cite:gi6_toi_readings] [cite:gi6_reuters_reg2026] [cite:gi6_bg_nyt_smotrich] Between them stands a documented pattern that both readings accept: formal sovereignty has been declared over no part of the West Bank since 1967 outside East Jerusalem, [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] and the administrative changes of 2023–2026 have moved in the direction the sovereignty motions asked for. The election of 27 October 2026 will decide who holds the ministries that made them.

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: The Maps at the UN and the "Very Much" Interview
chapters.intro: Part Seven examines the two moments, between 2023 and 2025, that put the phrase "Greater Israel" back into world headlines through the words and props of Israel's prime minister rather than through law. The first is a run of maps: the "New Middle East" map Benjamin Netanyahu held up at the UN General Assembly in September 2023, on which no Palestinian territory was marked; the map behind him at a Gaza press conference in September 2024; and the "Blessing" and "Curse" maps he showed at the UN later that month. The second is a television interview broadcast in August 2025, in which he was handed a map of the "Promised Land" and asked whether he felt connected to the vision of Greater Israel. For each the part sets out what was shown or said, as exactly as the record allows; what Netanyahu gave as his purpose; how Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the Arab League and others answered; whether Israel's government clarified; and what the episodes establish and what they do not.
chapters.outro: Part Seven established that in September 2023 and September 2024 Netanyahu displayed maps on which the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem appeared inside Israel and no Palestinian territory was marked, that Germany called the 2023 map "of no help" to a two-state solution, and that no Israeli government clarification of any of the maps was found. [cite:gi7_toi_un2023] [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023] [cite:gi7_ynet_germany] [cite:gi7_aje_phil2024] His stated purpose in 2023 was normalisation with Saudi Arabia without a Palestinian "veto," and none of the maps extended Israel into a neighbouring state. [cite:gi7_toi_un2023] In August 2025, handed a pendant whose outline takes in Jordan and parts of Egypt, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq, he affirmed on i24NEWS that he felt connected to the vision of Greater Israel, in words reported variously as "very much" and "absolutely." [cite:gi7_tml_i24] [cite:gi7_afp_i24] [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] Thirty-one states and the Arab League, OIC and GCC called the remark "a direct threat to Arab national security"; Israel's only reported reply, through diplomatic channels, was that he had not used the words himself. [cite:gi7_oman_joint] [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] The remark is documented attachment, not a documented policy: no law or government decision claims territory in a neighbouring state, and the formal annexation track concerns the West Bank. Part Eight turns from words to ground, front by front, from the Golan to Sinai, Jordan and Lebanon. [scene:gi8_golan|Part Eight: the fronts]

sections.h: The Maps at the UN
sections.html:
The phrase "Greater Israel" is usually argued over in words. Between September 2023 and September 2024 it was argued over in pictures, because Benjamin Netanyahu, as prime minister, held up maps of the region at the United Nations and at a televised press conference, and on several of them no Palestinian territory was marked. [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023] [cite:gi7_aje_phil2024] This section sets out what those maps showed, what Netanyahu said they meant, and how governments and critics answered. It keeps three things apart: what the maps documentably showed, what he stated as their purpose, and what others argued they revealed.

22 September 2023: "a new Middle East"

Netanyahu addressed the 78th session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Friday 22 September 2023, two weeks before the Hamas attack of 7 October. His subject was a possible peace with Saudi Arabia. He first showed what he called "a map of the Middle East in 1948, the year Israel was established," saying: "Here is Israel in 1948. It's a tiny country, isolated, surrounded by a hostile Arab world." He then took a red marker "to show a great blessing. The blessing of a new Middle East," and promised "a new corridor of peace and prosperity that connects Asia through the UAE" onward across the region. "Peace between Israel and Saudi Arabia," he said, "will truly create a new Middle East." [cite:gi7_toi_un2023]

The verbatim text settles one point on which accounts disagree: the first map was presented as the region in 1948, not "before the Abraham Accords." According to the Jerusalem Post, the 1948 map showed Israel alone in green, and the second, headed "The New Middle East," showed seven countries in green, Israel and Saudi Arabia among them, to illustrate the normalisation agreements signed since 2020 and the one he hoped for. On the map he held up, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem appeared inside Israel's colour, with no boundary and no Palestinian territory marked. [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023] Whether the 1948 map also coloured the West Bank and Gaza as Israel, which would be a factual error (Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt held Gaza from 1948 to 1967), could not be settled from the written reports found; the video record of the session is the primary source for it.

Netanyahu's stated purpose is on the record in the same speech. He said he believed "we must not give the Palestinians a veto over new peace treaties with Arab states," and also that peace with Saudi Arabia "will enhance the prospects of peace with the Palestinians" and that "a real path towards a genuine peace with our Palestinian neighbors can finally be achieved." [cite:gi7_toi_un2023] On his own account, then, the map was about normalisation without a Palestinian veto, not about borders. Critics read the map itself as the message. Laith Arafeh, the Palestinian Authority's representative in Germany, called it an insult to "every foundational principle of the UN"; Hadar Susskind of Americans for Peace Now wrote that "His map of Greater Israel is perhaps the only honest part of his speech today." [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023]

Two Western governments answered. In the days that followed, Germany's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Sebastian Fischer, said that showing a map "that does not depict territories that are occupied or annexed" was "of no help" to efforts toward a negotiated two-state solution. The US State Department spokesman, Matthew Miller, declined to "get into any discussion about the map that the prime minister chose to use" and restated American support for two states. Ynet asked Netanyahu's office to respond and had no answer when it published. [cite:gi7_ynet_germany] No Israeli government statement explaining or withdrawing the map was found.

2 September 2024: the Philadelphi press conference

Eleven months later, in the Gaza war, Netanyahu gave a televised press conference on 2 September 2024 to explain why Israel would keep forces on the Philadelphi Corridor along Gaza's border with Egypt. He used a pointer on a large map of Gaza captioned, in Hebrew, "Gaza after the disengagement, oxygen pipe of Hamas," and a separate map on which the West Bank appeared as part of Israel. [cite:gi7_aje_phil2024] The stated subject was security: the caption called the border Hamas's lifeline, and he framed control of the corridor as essential to Israel's security and to the war's aims. Critics again took the map as the finding. Mairav Zonszein of the International Crisis Group wrote that the speech would "go down in history as Netanyahu's open admission" that Israel meant to stay between the river and the sea; the Palestinian ambassador in London, Husam Zomlot, said it showed an aim "to erase the Palestinian people and take the rest of our land"; the UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese also criticised it; and the Israeli group Peace Now called the government "messianic." The opposition leader, Yair Lapid, called the speech "political spin." No clarification from the Israeli government about the map was reported. [cite:gi7_na_phil2024] [cite:gi7_aje_phil2024]

27 September 2024: "The Blessing" and "The Curse"

At the 79th General Assembly on 27 September 2024 Netanyahu held two maps. One, labelled "The Blessing," showed a corridor of normalisation through the Gulf linking Asia to Europe with, in his words, rail lines and fibre-optic cables; the other, "The Curse," showed Iran and its allies, which he called "Iran's arc of terror." "The line separating the blessing and the curse," he said, "could not be more clear." Many delegates left the hall as he began. [cite:gi7_ji_un2024] [cite:gi7_gzero_un2024] Middle East Monitor, citing Turkey's Anadolu Agency, reported that the maps "did not identify the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, but showed all the territory as part of Israel." [cite:gi7_memo_un2024] The Western reports of the speech found describe the two maps without addressing that point, so it rests on Turkish and advocacy reporting and on the video. [cite:gi7_ji_un2024] [cite:gi7_gzero_un2024] The speech's stated theme was a choice of alliances, not borders. The same blessing-and-curse language had already appeared in the 2023 speech. [cite:gi7_toi_un2023]

What the maps do and do not show

The documented fact is narrow and firm: on at least two occasions, in September 2023 at the UN and in September 2024 at a press conference, a sitting Israeli prime minister displayed maps on which the territories occupied in 1967 were shown inside Israel and no Palestinian territory appeared. [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023] [cite:gi7_aje_phil2024] A third case, the 2024 UN maps, is reported but less firmly sourced. [cite:gi7_memo_un2024] The pattern that can be shown is repetition without correction: in none of the cases was a government clarification found, and in 2023 Netanyahu's office did not answer a request for comment. [cite:gi7_ynet_germany] [cite:gi7_na_phil2024]

What the maps mean is an argument, and it has two sides. Critics, from Americans for Peace Now in 2023 to Israel's Peace Now in 2024, read them as a statement that the West Bank and Gaza are Israel's, and Germany's Foreign Ministry called the omission of occupied territory "of no help"; on that reading the maps are consistent with the 2022 coalition guidelines and the annexation steps described in Part Six. [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023] [cite:gi7_ynet_germany] [cite:gi7_na_phil2024] [scene:gi6_plans|Part Six: the annexation plans] [scene:wb9_annex|The West Bank, Documented: annexation] Netanyahu's own words at the time point the other way in one respect: none of the maps extended Israel's colour into Jordan, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria or Iraq, and the 2023 map placed Saudi Arabia and other Arab states on Israel's side of a peace, not inside its borders. [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023] [cite:gi7_toi_un2023] The maps are therefore evidence about the West Bank and Gaza, the territory the Likud platform of 1977 already claimed, not about the Nile-to-Euphrates map of the popular image. [scene:gi5_likud|Part Five: the Likud platform] [scene:gi10_myths|Part Ten: the myths] It was a television interview in August 2025, not a map, that brought the wider phrase back into a prime minister's mouth.

sections.h: The "Very Much" Interview
sections.html:
On the evening of Tuesday 12 August 2025 the Israeli channel i24NEWS broadcast an interview with Netanyahu conducted by the presenter Sharon Gal. The exchange that made headlines lasted seconds. Within four days the governments of more than thirty Arab and Muslim-majority states had condemned it in a joint statement. [cite:gi7_na_i24] [cite:gi7_afp_i24] [cite:gi7_oman_joint] This section sets out what was asked and answered, as far as the published reports allow; what the states concerned said; what Israel's government said in reply; and what the remark does and does not establish.

The question and the answer

Gal handed Netanyahu a piece of jewellery, which he said was for Sara Netanyahu, and described it as a "map of the Promised Land." The object was not clearly visible on air. Haaretz reported that Gal's company sells pendants shaped like "Greater Israel," with an outline that takes in parts of Egypt, all of Jordan, Lebanon and parts of Syria and Iraq. [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] [cite:gi7_lbc_i24] Gal then asked whether Netanyahu felt connected to that vision.

The exact words of the exchange are reported differently, and no Hebrew transcript or official English rendering was found. The Media Line, Lebanon's LBCI and The New Arab report the answer as "Very much"; L'Orient Today as "Very much so." [cite:gi7_tml_i24] [cite:gi7_lbc_i24] [cite:gi7_na_i24] [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] A second New Arab report says he felt "very attached" to the vision and described himself as on a "historic and spiritual mission." [cite:gi7_na_outrage] Agence France-Presse and Al Jazeera report a further question, whether he subscribed to a vision of Greater Israel, answered "absolutely"; AFP adds that he said "If you ask me what I think, we're there," then turned to Israel's founding and its "great mission" of ensuring its continued existence. [cite:gi7_afp_i24] [cite:gi7_aje_joint] The common ground is narrow but clear: asked about the vision of Greater Israel after being handed a map of it, Netanyahu affirmed a personal attachment to it and framed his role as a generational mission. In the same interview, speaking of Gaza, he said: "We are not pushing them out, but we are allowing them to leave." [cite:gi7_aje_joint] [cite:gi7_afp_i24]

The neighbours answer

Jordan, whose whole territory lay inside the pendant's outline, was among the first to answer, on 13 August. Its Foreign Ministry called the remarks "a dangerous and provocative escalation, a threat to the sovereignty of states," and its spokesman rejected what he called "delusional claims." [cite:gi7_na_outrage] [cite:gi7_afp_i24] [cite:gi7_tml_i24] Egypt's Foreign Ministry said it had "requested clarification on this matter," that the remarks reflected a rejection of peace, and that "there is no way to achieve peace except through a return to negotiations," restating its call for a Palestinian state on the lines of 4 June 1967 with East Jerusalem as its capital. [cite:gi7_ahram_egypt] [cite:gi7_afp_i24] [cite:gi7_na_outrage] Saudi Arabia, the state whose normalisation Netanyahu had made the centrepiece of his 2023 UN speech, expressed its "complete rejection of the settlement and expansionist ideas and projects adopted by the Israeli occupation authorities." [cite:gi7_ahram_egypt] The Arab League called the remarks "a blatant violation of the sovereignty of Arab states" and "a serious threat to collective Arab national security"; Qatar called them "an extension of the (Israeli) occupation's approach based on arrogance"; Iraq's Foreign Ministry said they revealed "expansionist ambitions"; and the Palestinian Authority called them "a disregard of the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people." [cite:gi7_ahram_egypt] [cite:gi7_na_outrage] [cite:gi7_afp_i24]

The collective answer followed. A joint statement dated 16 August 2025 and published by Oman's Foreign Ministry carried the names of the foreign ministers of 31 states (Oman, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Algeria, Morocco, Palestine, Iraq, Jordan, Egypt, Syria, Lebanon, Libya, Yemen, Mauritania, Sudan, Somalia, Türkiye, Bangladesh, Chad, Comoros, Djibouti, Gambia, Indonesia, the Maldives, Nigeria, Pakistan, Senegal and Sierra Leone) and of the secretaries-general of the Arab League, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the Gulf Cooperation Council. They "strongly condemn" Netanyahu's remarks "on the so-called 'Greater Israel'," calling them "a blatant violation of international law and a direct threat to Arab national security," and warned against the Israeli government's "expansionist approach in the West Bank." [cite:gi7_oman_joint] Al Jazeera reported the statement as released on Friday 15 August. [cite:gi7_aje_joint] The signatories included the UAE, Bahrain and Morocco, which normalised relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords in 2020, and Egypt and Jordan, at peace with Israel by treaty since 1979 and 1994. [cite:gi7_oman_joint] [scene:gi8_jordan|Part Eight: Jordan] [scene:gi8_sinai|Part Eight: Sinai and Egypt] France, according to diplomatic sources quoted by Haaretz, reaffirmed its commitment to Jordan's recognised borders. [cite:gi7_olj_pendant]

The remarks came in the same days as a West Bank decision. On 14 August 2025 the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, announced the advance of more than 3,000 housing units in the E1 area between Jerusalem and Ma'ale Adumim, saying it would bury the idea of a Palestinian state. [cite:gi7_tml_i24] [cite:wb_itv_e1] Several Arab statements treated the two together, which is why the joint statement's warning concerned the West Bank as much as the pendant's wider outline. [cite:gi7_oman_joint] [scene:gi6_plans|Part Six: the annexation track]

What Israel said

No public, on-record statement from the Prime Minister's Office clarifying or withdrawing the remark was found. According to Haaretz, as reported by L'Orient Today, the Prime Minister's Office and the Foreign Ministry told Jordan and Egypt, which had asked for clarification, that Netanyahu had not used the words "Greater Israel" and was not responsible for the headlines written after the interview. Haaretz described the replies as an attempt to sweep the matter under the rug. [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] [cite:gi7_afp_i24] The reply is accurate as far as it goes: in every account the phrase was the interviewer's, and Netanyahu answered a question about it. It does not deny the answer.

What the remark establishes

Three claims need to be kept apart. The first is documented: on 12 August 2025 the prime minister of Israel, shown a map described as the Promised Land and asked about the vision of Greater Israel, affirmed his attachment to it on television, and his government did not publicly retract the answer. [cite:gi7_tml_i24] [cite:gi7_afp_i24] [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] The second is also documented: the governments whose territory lay inside the outline took the remark as a threat to their sovereignty and said so, jointly and separately. [cite:gi7_oman_joint] [cite:gi7_na_outrage] The third is an inference: that the remark reveals a policy to take territory from Jordan, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria or Iraq. Netanyahu stated a personal and spiritual attachment, not a policy, and named no border. No law, cabinet decision or coalition guideline found claims territory in any of those states; Israel's peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan set agreed international boundaries, as Part Eight describes, and the formal annexation track documented in Part Six concerns the West Bank. [scene:gi6_votes|Part Six: the Knesset votes] [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve: the withdrawals] Critics, among them the joint statement's signatories, answer that a sitting prime minister's endorsement of the phrase, in the same week as E1, cannot be separated from the government's "expansionist approach in the West Bank"; whether the ground Israeli forces have held in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria since 2024 fits a wider pattern is weighed in Parts Nine and Thirteen. [cite:gi7_oman_joint] [scene:gi9_syria|Part Nine: the buffer belt] [scene:gi13_record|Part Eighteen: settled, contested and open] The remark is evidence of how Netanyahu chose to describe his mission; it is not, by itself, evidence of a plan.

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: The Fronts
chapters.intro: Part Eight goes front by front through the territories and neighbours named in arguments about Greater Israel, from the war of 1967 to the eve of 7 October 2023, and asks of each the same question: what did Israel's governments claim, legislate or do there, and what did they give up. It begins with the Golan Heights, the one front where a claim beyond the 1949 lines was written into law, and follows the Security Council's unanimous answer, the offers to withdraw, and the American and Colombian recognitions. It turns to Sinai, the largest territory Israel has returned, and to the treaty that left Gaza aside; to Jordan, where a ratified treaty sits beside the "Jordan is Palestine" current of the Israeli right; and to Lebanon, invaded in 1978 and 1982 and partly occupied until 2000. It ends by testing the claims made about Iraq, Iran and Saudi Arabia, three countries that appear in Greater-Israel writing but not, on the record reviewed here, in any Israeli government's territorial claim. The years since 2024 are the subject of Part Nine.
chapters.outro: Part Eight established that, between 1967 and 2023, the claim to land beyond the 1949 lines was written into Israeli law on one front only. The Golan Heights Law of 14 December 1981 applied Israeli law to the plateau; the Security Council declared it "null and void" unanimously, with the United States voting in favour; Netanyahu called the Golan Israel's "forever" in 2016; and the United States recognised it as Israeli in 2019, followed by Colombia in August 2026. Even there, Rabin and Barak negotiated over withdrawal between 1994 and 2000. [cite:gi8_wiki_golanlaw] [cite:gi8_rw_res497] [cite:gi8_mfa_cab2016] [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852] [cite:gi8_aje_colombia] [cite:gi8_enc_syrtalks] Elsewhere the record runs the other way. A Likud government returned all of Sinai by 25 April 1982, and Israel accepted arbitration over Taba in 1986 and handed it over in 1989 after losing the case, while the treaty left Gaza aside. [cite:gi8_avalon_egtreaty] [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] [cite:gi8_enc_taba] The 1994 treaty recognised Jordan's territorial integrity, and Israel's Foreign Ministry reaffirmed it in March 2023 after a minister spoke from behind a map that included Jordan; the "Jordan is Palestine" idea is documented as the argument of named Likud figures, not as policy. [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] [cite:gi8_ynet_mfajordan] [cite:gi8_pipes_jordanpal] In Lebanon Israel invaded twice and held a security zone for fifteen years, then withdrew in May 2000 with UN certification; the 1919 Litani wording was a water arrangement, not a frontier. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] [cite:gi8_bu_zo1919] For Iraq, Iran and Saudi Arabia no Israeli government claim to territory was found. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak] [cite:gi8_cnbc_mbs] Part Nine turns to the years since 2024, when Israeli forces took up positions in south Lebanon, southern Syria and around Gaza, and asks whether that pattern has changed. [scene:gi9_lebanon|Part Nine: the buffer belt]

sections.h: The Golan: the One Front Annexed by Law
sections.html:
Of the territories Israel took from its neighbours in June 1967, the Golan Heights is the only one outside the area of the former British Mandate that an Israeli government has placed under Israeli law. That makes it the clearest test case for this part. On the Golan, a territorial claim beyond the 1949 lines is not a matter of reading a map held up at a podium or a minister's speech: it is written in a statute, voted by the Knesset and repeated by later prime ministers. The section sets out that record, the reasons Israel's governments gave for it, the answer of the Security Council and of Syria, and the negotiations in which Israeli prime ministers offered to give much of the plateau back. The United States proclamation of 2019 records the basic sequence in its own words: Israel "took control of the Golan Heights in 1967 to safeguard its security from external threats." [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852]

The law of 14 December 1981

The Golan Heights Law passed the Knesset on 14 December 1981 by 63 votes to 21. Its operative clause is one sentence: "The Law, jurisdiction and administration of the State will take effect in the Golan Heights, as described in the Schedule." Prime Minister Menachem Begin told the Knesset that Israel could not wait indefinitely for a sign from Syria that it was willing to negotiate peace, and he gave historical, security and what he called "moral-political" reasons. Contemporary reporting in Time attributed the timing to pressure from the religious parties in his coalition, to the Likud's 1981 election manifesto, to the failure of the American envoy Philip Habib to get Syrian forces out of Lebanon's Beqaa Valley, and to Syria's rejection of the Saudi peace plan put forward by Crown Prince Fahd. [cite:gi8_wiki_golanlaw] The ideological setting of the law, in Begin's government and the Likud platform, is examined in Part Five. [scene:gi5_likud|Part Five: Likud in government]

Washington was not consulted. The State Department said so, President Ronald Reagan said the law "increased the difficulty of seeking peace", and the United States suspended the strategic cooperation memorandum it had signed with Israel on 30 November, only two weeks earlier; it was not reinstated until May 1983. [cite:gi8_wiki_golanlaw] [cite:ow1_wiki_1981isr] Among the people most directly affected, the response was refusal. The Druze of the Golan began a three-day general strike on 17 December, and their leaders wrote to Begin that they were first of all Syrian Arabs and would resist forced Israeli citizenship. A general strike in 1982 lasted about five months and was met with an Israeli blockade of the Druze towns. [cite:gi8_wiki_golanlaw]

Resolution 497: unanimous

Three days after the vote, on 17 December 1981, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 497 unanimously, fifteen votes to none, with the United States voting in favour. It decided that Israel's decision "to impose its laws, jurisdiction and administration in the occupied Syrian Golan Heights is null and void and without international legal effect", demanded that Israel, "the occupying Power", rescind it, and determined that the Fourth Geneva Convention continued to apply. [cite:gi8_rw_res497] [cite:gi8_wiki_res497] Where the United States did use its veto was on the follow-up: on 20 January 1982 it vetoed a draft that would have called for international measures against Israel under Chapter VII of the Charter. On 5 February 1982 the General Assembly, in emergency session, voted 86 to 21 for a resolution calling for a boycott of Israel; the United States and many Western states voted against. [cite:gi8_wiki_res497] Israel did not rescind the law. Syria has never accepted it, and the United Nations continues to treat the Golan as occupied Syrian territory. [cite:gi8_aje_colombia]

Offers to withdraw, 1994–2000

The statute did not end negotiation over the plateau, and the counter-record here is substantial. In 1994 Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin opened secret contacts with Damascus and proposed a phased partial withdrawal over about three years, within a comprehensive peace and subject to a referendum of Israeli voters; Syria insisted on complete withdrawal as the precondition. Under Ehud Barak the two sides met at Shepherdstown, West Virginia, from 3 to 11 January 2000 without agreement. On 26 March 2000 in Geneva President Bill Clinton presented Barak's latest proposal to Hafez al-Asad, who rejected it because it would have left Israel sovereign over a strip of land north of Lake Tiberias. That meeting was, in one reference account's words, "effectively the end of the negotiations." [cite:gi8_enc_syrtalks] Two Israeli governments, then, were prepared to give up much of the Golan for peace, and the last round failed over a strip of shoreline rather than over an Israeli claim to the whole plateau. Part Twelve sets these offers beside the other withdrawals. [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve: the withdrawals]

"Forever": the claim restated

After the Syrian civil war began, Israeli statements hardened. On 17 April 2016 Benjamin Netanyahu held the first official cabinet meeting on the Golan in the 49 years of Israeli rule and said: "The Golan Heights will forever remain in Israel's hands. Israel will never come down from the Golan Heights." [cite:gi8_mfa_cab2016] On 25 March 2019 President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 9852: "the United States recognizes that the Golan Heights are part of the State of Israel." The proclamation cited "aggressive acts by Iran and terrorist groups, including Hizballah, in southern Syria." [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852] Syria called it a "blatant attack" on its sovereignty; the European Union and its larger members and the Arab League rejected it; UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Golan's status had not changed. Israel named a planned community "Trump Heights" in June 2019, and the recognition stood under President Joe Biden. [cite:gi8_wiki_usrecog]

A change of Israeli government in 2021 did not change the policy. On 26 December 2021 the cabinet of Naftali Bennett, the coalition that had replaced Netanyahu's, met on the Golan and unanimously approved a plan of about one billion shekels, roughly $320 million, with two new communities, Asif and Matar. "Our goal today is to double the population of the Golan Heights," Bennett said. The Golan's population was then about 53,000, split almost evenly between Israeli settlers and Syrian Druze. Syria's Foreign Ministry said it rejected "the annexation decision and the policy of seizing lands by force." [cite:gi8_cnn_golan2021]

Who else recognises it

For seven years the United States stood alone, and much writing on the subject describes it as "the only country". That is no longer accurate. On 10 August 2026, three days after President Abelardo de la Espriella took office, Colombia's Foreign Ministry announced that it "recognises Israeli sovereignty over this territory", making it the second state to do so. Israel's foreign minister, Gideon Saar, called it "historic", and Netanyahu thanked Colombia. Syria lodged a complaint with the UN Secretary-General and the Security Council on 12 August, and Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Egypt, Jordan, Oman and Turkey condemned the decision. [cite:gi8_aje_colombia] [cite:gi8_alm_colombia] No third state was found in the reporting reviewed as of October 2026.

What the record shows

On the Golan, the claim is documented at the highest level an Israeli government can give it: a statute in 1981, restated as permanent by Netanyahu in 2016 and backed by a Bennett-led coalition's settlement plan in 2021. The reasons governments gave were security and Syria's refusal to make peace, with history named alongside them by Begin. It is a claim to one specific territory, not to Syria beyond it, and between 1994 and 2000 two prime ministers offered to trade most of it for a treaty. Whether the claim belongs in a "Greater Israel" programme or in a security doctrine is an argument; the statute and the statements themselves are facts. Since December 2024 Israeli forces have also held positions beyond the Golan, on the Syrian summit of Mount Hermon and in the 1974 buffer zone, which the defence minister said in January 2025 they would hold indefinitely; that is the subject of Part Nine. [cite:hz10s_cnn_480] [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] [scene:gi9_syria|Part Nine: Syria and Mount Hermon]

sections.h: Sinai and Egypt: the Largest Return
sections.html:
Egypt sits at the edge of the "Greater Israel" debate for two reasons. One is a single phrase: the "river of Egypt" of Genesis 15:18, which maximalist readings take to be the Nile. The other is that Israel has twice held the whole Sinai Peninsula and twice given it back. The first time, in 1956–57, is covered in Part Three. [scene:gi3_sinai56|Part Three: the Sinai test] This section covers the second: the fifteen years of Israeli rule after 1967, the 1979 peace treaty, the completion of the withdrawal in April 1982, and the arbitration over Taba that followed. It is the counter-record at its largest, and it also leaves one territory, Gaza, explicitly outside its terms. [cite:gi8_avalon_egtreaty] [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982]

The verse and the border

Genesis 15:18 promises Abram's descendants the land "from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates"; some modern translations render the first river as the "Wadi of Egypt". [cite:gi1_bg_gen1518] The historian Daniel Pipes, examining the claim that Israel aims at a Nile-to-Euphrates state, argued in 1994 that the river of Egypt most likely means the Wadi al-Arish in northern Sinai, following the medieval commentator Rashi, and that the narrower boundaries in Numbers 34 and Ezekiel 47 govern the general Genesis wording. He called the Nile-to-Euphrates idea a "groundless fantasy", while reporting that it had become conventional wisdom in Arab countries and Iran. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] Part One sets out the textual debate. [scene:gi1_phrase|Part One: the phrase] For this section the point is narrower: no Israeli government document reviewed claims Egyptian territory west of the international border, and the one Egyptian territory Israel held for any length of time it returned under a treaty.

From occupation to treaty, 1967–1979

Israel captured Sinai in June 1967 and held it under a military governorate together with Gaza, the West Bank and the Golan. [cite:gz_wiki_occupation] Israeli settlements followed in Sinai, among them the town of Yamit. [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] After the 1973 war two disengagement agreements pulled Israeli forces back from the Suez Canal; the second, in September 1975, came with a US–Israel memorandum guaranteeing Israel's oil supply for five years. [cite:ow1_jvl_moa1975]

The Camp David framework of 17 September 1978 had two parts. One concerned the West Bank and Gaza, providing for "transitional arrangements" of no more than five years and "full autonomy to the inhabitants" under an elected self-governing authority. [cite:gz_campdavid] The other led to the Treaty of Peace signed on 26 March 1979, witnessed by President Jimmy Carter. Its first article ended the state of war and stated: "Israel will withdraw all its armed forces and civilians from the Sinai." Article II fixed the permanent boundary as the recognised line between Egypt and the former mandated territory of Palestine, "without prejudice to the issue of the status of the Gaza Strip", and the parties recognised it "as inviolable". Annex I set an interim withdrawal within nine months of ratification and a final withdrawal "not later than three years" after it. [cite:gi8_avalon_egtreaty]

April 1982: the settlements removed

The handover ended on 25 April 1982. Yamit was evacuated and levelled before Egypt took it over. The defence minister who carried out the evacuation, Ariel Sharon, drew a line under it: "In Sinai, in Yamit, we have reached the red line of our concessions." [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] The sentence matters for what came after. A Likud government gave up the whole peninsula and removed civilian settlements from it; and the minister who did so said in the same breath that Israel's concessions stopped there; read in its context, the remaining territory at issue was the land west of the Jordan, though Sharon did not name it in the words reported. Part Five follows the Likud platform, and Part Twelve sets the Sinai withdrawal beside the others. [scene:gi5_likud|Part Five: Likud in government] [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve: the withdrawals]

Taba: the last 250 acres

One patch of coast remained in dispute. In January 1982, finalising the return, Israeli negotiators argued that Taba, about 250 acres on the Gulf of Aqaba some twelve miles south of Eilat, should stay in Israel, citing ambiguities in the 1906 description of the old Egyptian–Ottoman border; Israel built two hotels there. Under Article 7 of the treaty, which provides for mediation or arbitration if direct talks fail, Israel's cabinet accepted arbitration in principle on 13 January 1986. A three-member panel ruled for Egypt on 29 September 1988, and Israel evacuated Taba on 15 March 1989, with Israelis still allowed to enter without an Egyptian visa. [cite:gi8_enc_taba] The Taba case is small, but it is the plainest instance in this volume of an Israeli territorial claim beyond a treaty line being decided against Israel by an outside body and carried out.

Gaza and Sinai: the part the treaty left out

The treaty separated Gaza from Sinai, and that separation is where Egypt re-enters the Greater-Israel argument. Israel kept Gaza. Ideas of moving Gazans into Sinai have a documented Israeli history before the treaty. The Egyptian outlet Mada Masr, drawing on the economist Sara Roy, writes that the original Allon Plan envisaged moving large numbers of Palestinians from Gaza to Sinai and the West Bank, that some 12,000 relatives of suspected guerrillas were held in detention camps in Sinai, and that families displaced in 1972 were moved to "Canada Camp" on the Egyptian side of the Rafah line, where some waited about twenty years to return. [cite:gz_mada_sinai] Those were measures of an occupation that then included Sinai; they do not amount to a claim to Egyptian territory. The Gaza Strip's own history under Israeli rule, and the 2005 withdrawal of its settlements, are told in Gaza, Documented. [scene:gz2_egypt|Gaza, Documented: Egypt and Gaza]

What the record shows

The Sinai record cuts against a reading of Greater Israel as a fixed programme pursued by every Israeli government: a Likud government signed away the largest territory Israel has ever held, removed its settlers, and later accepted an arbitration that cost it Taba. It does not settle the question for the land west of the Jordan, which the same government treated as outside the bargain, as Sharon's "red line" remark of 1982 indicates, and the treaty itself left Gaza aside. Egypt's position from 1979 has been that the treaty border is final. When Netanyahu's August 2025 remark about the "Greater Israel" vision was reported, Egypt's Foreign Ministry asked for clarification and said there was no route to peace "except through a return to negotiations"; that exchange is in Part Seven. [cite:gi7_ahram_egypt] [scene:gi7_interview|Part Seven: the "very much" interview]

sections.h: Jordan: a Treaty Border and the "Jordan is Palestine" Current
sections.html:
Jordan is the neighbour most often named in Greater-Israel maps, because the Revisionist Zionist movement of the 1920s and 1930s claimed both banks of the Jordan River, east as well as west. [cite:gi1_wiki_greaterisrael] That history is told in Part Two. [scene:gi2_bothbanks|Part Two: both banks of the Jordan] After 1967 the claim to the East Bank faded from Israeli party programmes, and a different idea took its place on the Israeli right: that Jordan already was the Palestinian state, so that none was needed west of the river. This section traces that idea to the named officials who held it, sets it beside the 1994 peace treaty, which fixed the border and recognised Jordan's territorial integrity, and ends with the March 2023 episode in which a minister's podium map and his government's Foreign Ministry pointed in opposite directions.

"Jordan is Palestine": who said it

The slogan was used on both sides of the river, which is part of its history. King Hussein of Jordan said in 1981 that "Jordan is Palestine and Palestine is Jordan". On 31 July 1988 he said the opposite: "Jordan is not Palestine." Pipes and Garfinkle read the reversal as tactical. [cite:gi8_pipes_jordanpal] On the Israeli side, the clearest statement in the sources comes from Yitzhak Shamir, writing in 1982 that the Palestinian Arabs' homeland "is Trans-Jordan, or Eastern Palestine." The historians Daniel Pipes and Adam Garfinkle, who quote the passage in their 1988 Commentary article "Is Jordan Palestine?", wrote that the argument, though "closely associated with Ariel Sharon", "has long underlain the policy of the Likud bloc as a whole"; they gave no direct quotation from Sharon, and themselves judged it "historically wrong" and its implementation "extremely dangerous." [cite:gi8_pipes_jordanpal] The original of Shamir's article was not retrieved; the wording is as Pipes and Garfinkle give it.

Sharon is the figure most associated with the idea. The political scientist Marc Lynch, writing for the Middle East Research and Information Project in June 2004, described the view of Sharon and the Likud right that a Palestinian state already existed in Jordan as the Sharon vision that "Jordan is Palestine", reported that Sharon had at one time favoured the overthrow of King Hussein so that a Palestinian state could be set up on the East Bank, and noted that Sharon abstained in the Knesset vote on the 1994 treaty. [cite:gi8_merip_nojordan] These are attributions by analysts, not Sharon's own texts; no statement by Sharon in his own words was retrieved, and the attribution should be read with that limit. The idea, as documented, was a political argument about where a Palestinian state should be, not a claim to annex Jordanian territory to Israel, but Jordanian officials have consistently read it as a threat to the kingdom's existence.

The 1994 treaty

On 26 October 1994 Yitzhak Rabin and Jordan's prime minister, Abdelsalam al-Majali, signed a peace treaty at the Arava crossing north of Eilat, with President Bill Clinton present. The Knesset had approved it the day before, on 25 October, by 105 votes to 3 with 6 abstentions, according to the Knesset's own summary of the session; some reference works give 92 to 3. [cite:gi8a_jvl_k13] [cite:gi8_wiki_jotreaty] In Article 2 the two states "recognise and will respect each other's sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence." Article 3 delimits the border "with reference to the boundary definition under the Mandate" and makes it "the permanent, secure and recognised international boundary", adding that this is "without prejudice to the status of any territories that came under Israeli military government control in 1967", that is, the West Bank. Article 9 records Israel's respect for "the present special role of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in Muslim Holy shrines in Jerusalem." [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] The treaty also settled water: Israel would supply Jordan with 50 million cubic metres a year. [cite:gi8_wiki_jotreaty]

Two small areas show the treaty working in Jordan's favour. At Naharayim (Baqura), land Israel had held since 1950, and Tzofar (al-Ghamr), taken in 1967, Israel recognised Jordanian sovereignty while Israeli farmers kept the use of the land under 25-year arrangements that Jordan could decline to renew on a year's notice. [cite:gi8_wiki_jotreaty] [cite:gi8_ap_baqura] Jordan gave notice in October 2018. On 10 November 2019 King Abdullah II told parliament of "the expiration of the Peace Treaty annexes on Ghamr and al-Baqura" and the restoration of "full sovereignty". Israel's Foreign Ministry said Israel "regrets Jordan's decision to terminate the annexes", and complied. [cite:gi8_ap_baqura] Land Israel had used for decades thus passed fully to Jordan under the treaty's own terms, without dispute over the outcome.

Jordan's answer: "never an alternative homeland"

Jordan's monarchy has answered the "Jordan is Palestine" idea in the same words for two decades. On 7 January 2004, addressing officers from fourteen Arab countries in Amman, King Abdullah said the question of a substitute country "is being raised from time to time by different parties" and that "Jordan will never be an alternative homeland to anybody." [cite:gi8_king_althomeland] According to Lynch, in March 2004 the king also warned Sharon in person not to encourage talk of a "Jordan option", and repeated the concern to President George W. Bush that June. [cite:gi8_merip_nojordan]

March 2023: the podium map and the Foreign Ministry

The current resurfaced in March 2023. Bezalel Smotrich, finance minister and leader of the Religious Zionism party, spoke in Paris on Sunday 19 March 2023, at a memorial ceremony for a former far-right political activist, from a podium bearing a map of "Greater Israel" that included Jordan as well as the West Bank. He said the Palestinian people were "an invention" of the past century and that "there is no such thing as a Palestinian people." Jordan's Foreign Ministry summoned Israel's ambassador, accused Smotrich of breaching the peace treaty with his speech and the map, and condemned "racist, inciting and extremist statements." [cite:gi8_axios_smotrich] The speech did not mention Jordan by name in the passages reported; the claim on Jordan was in the map. Who designed the map, and what Smotrich meant by displaying it, is not documented in the reporting reviewed.

Israel's government answered on Monday 20 March. Its Foreign Ministry stated: "Israel is committed to the 1994 peace agreement with Jordan. There has been no change in the position of the State of Israel, which recognizes the territorial integrity of the Hashemite Kingdom." The national security adviser, Tzachi Hanegbi, gave the same assurance to Jordan's foreign minister, Ayman Safadi. Smotrich himself did not comment on Jordan's accusation. [cite:gi8_ynet_mfajordan] [cite:gi8_axios_smotrich] The government did not disown him or remove him; it restated the treaty. Part Seven follows the maps that came after, and Part Eleven the religious current behind Smotrich's party. [scene:gi7_maps|Part Seven: the maps at the UN] [scene:gi11_religious|Part Eleven: the religious engine]

What the record shows

Against Jordan, the binding record runs one way: a ratified treaty recognising Jordan's territorial integrity, two leased areas returned on request, and a 2023 Foreign Ministry reaffirmation issued within a day of a minister's provocation. [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] [cite:gi8_ap_baqura] [cite:gi8_ynet_mfajordan] The counter-current is also documented, but at a different level: a 1982 statement by Shamir, the Likud right's "Jordan is Palestine" argument attributed to Sharon by analysts, and Smotrich's 2023 map. Those are statements and displays by named politicians, and none has become law or government policy. Their significance lies in the reaction they draw from Amman, which reads them as a threat to the kingdom, and in the fact that the 2023 government answered its own minister with a restatement of the treaty rather than a rebuke. What Netanyahu's own August 2025 remark added, and how Jordan answered it, is in Part Seven. [scene:gi7_interview|Part Seven: the "very much" interview]

sections.h: Lebanon, 1978–2000: Invasion, Security Zone, Withdrawal
sections.html:
Lebanon enters the Greater-Israel argument through a river and a long occupation. The river is the Litani, which some accounts describe as the historic Revisionist Zionist claim line in the north. The occupation is the south Lebanon "security zone" Israel held from 1985 to 2000. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] The Hezbollah volume of this library tells the military and political history of those years in detail; this section does not retell it. It asks a narrower question of that record: what Israel's governments said they wanted in Lebanon, whether any of them claimed Lebanese territory, and how the occupation ended. The period after 2000, including the positions Israel has held since 2024, belongs to Part Nine. [scene:gi9_lebanon|Part Nine: south Lebanon since 2024]

The Litani in 1919: water, not a frontier

The documented origin of the Litani in Zionist planning is the Zionist Organization's statement to the Paris Peace Conference of 3 February 1919, a document of the mainstream movement rather than of the Revisionists. Its proposed northern boundary started "at a point on the Mediterranean Sea in the vicinity south of Sidon" and ran inland along the watersheds of the Lebanon foothills and the slopes of Mount Hermon. On the river itself it asked that "some international arrangement must be made" to protect the riparian rights of the people living south of the Litani, and it called the Hermon "Palestine's real 'Father of Waters'", which "cannot be severed from it." [cite:gi8_bu_zo1919] The request, in other words, was a northern line drawn with water in mind and an arrangement for the Litani's waters, made to the peace conference that drew the Mandate borders. The statement and its map are examined in Part Two; the description of a "traditional Revisionist" claim to the Litani is not supported by the sources reviewed and should not be repeated. [scene:gi2_map1919|Part Two: the 1919 map]

1978: Operation Litani

On 11 March 1978 gunmen who had come from Lebanon by sea attacked Israel's coastal road; 38 civilians, 13 of them children, were killed, and Fatah claimed the attack. [cite:hz1_wiki_coastal] On the night of 14–15 March some 25,000 Israeli troops crossed into Lebanon and within days held the south up to the Litani, except Tyre. Lebanon told the Security Council it had no connection with the attack, and on 19 March the Council adopted Resolutions 425 and 426, calling on Israel to withdraw and creating the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL). [cite:hz1_unifil_bg] Estimates of the Lebanese and Palestinian dead run from about 1,100 to about 2,000. When Israel withdrew it handed its positions not to UNIFIL but to the militia of Major Saad Haddad, which it armed and paid. [cite:hz1_wiki_litani] [cite:hz1_csm_haddad] The full account is in the Hezbollah volume. [scene:hz1_1978|The Hezbollah Architecture: 1978]

1982: the forty-kilometre aim and Beirut

After the shooting of Israel's ambassador in London, Shlomo Argov, on 3 June 1982, Israel launched Operation Peace for Galilee on 6 June.
