The IDF's own account gives the objective as pushing the PLO "40 km to the north"; the Menachem Begin Heritage Center says the operation was designed to make "the forty miles surrounding the border" free of armed groups, and that the IDF "was forced to continue north all the way to Beirut." [cite:hz2_idf_lw1] [cite:hz2_begin_pfg] Lebanese police counted 19,085 killed between 4 June and 31 August 1982, a figure that cannot be independently verified; the Israeli army gave 446 soldiers killed by mid-November. [cite:hz2b_csm_dec82] In September Lebanese Phalangist militiamen killed hundreds of civilians, by some counts thousands, in the Sabra and Shatila camps, which Israeli troops had surrounded. Israel's state commission of inquiry, chaired by Supreme Court President Yitzhak Kahan (a commission, not a ruling of the Supreme Court), found Israel indirectly responsible and Defence Minister Ariel Sharon personally responsible for "ignoring the danger of bloodshed and revenge." [cite:hz2b_jvl_kahan] [scene:hz2_invasion|The Hezbollah Architecture: the 1982 invasion]

What Israel sought from Lebanon at the end of the war was set down in a document. The agreement of 17 May 1983 between Israel and Lebanon declared the state of war "terminated", described the border as inviolable, and provided for Israeli withdrawal within eight to twelve weeks, a "Security Region" in the south, and a liaison committee with American participation. Syria's president rejected it, and Lebanon repudiated it on 5 March 1984. [cite:hz2b_jvl_may17] [cite:hz2b_wiki_may17] [cite:hz2b_majalla_may17] The terms Israel signed concerned security arrangements inside Lebanon, not a change of the border.

1985–2000: the security zone

On 14 January 1985 Israel's cabinet voted to withdraw in three phases, the last along the border, leaving a zone in which Haddad's successor force, the South Lebanon Army (SLA), would operate with Israeli backing. [cite:hz2b_jvl_jan85] Sidon was handed to the Lebanese army in February and Tyre in April, and by 10 June 1985 most Israeli troops had left, with a smaller force staying in the zone. [cite:hz2b_wiki_slc] Human Rights Watch put the zone at about 850 square kilometres, roughly a tenth of Lebanon, with about 150,000 people in 162 villages and towns. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] The Congressional Research Service described it as about nine miles deep, which places it south of the Litani, not along or beyond the river as some accounts have it. Israel funded and equipped the SLA, paid its members about $500 to $800 a month, and lost roughly 250 soldiers there between 1985 and April 2000. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] The zone's prison at Khiam, run by the SLA with Israeli security-service involvement, is documented in the Hezbollah volume. [scene:hz4_zone|The Hezbollah Architecture: the security zone]

The stated purpose of the zone was protection of northern Israel, and Israeli officials said early on that the occupation might produce the opposite. Yitzhak Rabin, as defence minister in February 1985, warned that if Israel replaced PLO terrorism with Shiite terrorism "we have done the worst" in its struggle against terrorism. [cite:hz3_djn_rabin85] The sources reviewed record no Israeli civilian settlement in the zone and no application of Israeli law to it, the two steps taken on the Golan.

May 2000: withdrawal to the Blue Line

Domestic pressure ended the occupation. The Four Mothers movement, formed in 1997 after 73 soldiers died in a helicopter collision on their way to Lebanon, campaigned for withdrawal, and Ehud Barak promised to "bring the boys home" by July 2000. [cite:hz4_csm_mothers] He ordered the pullout on 23 May, and the last soldier left early on 24 May, weeks ahead of schedule; the SLA collapsed, and about 1,500 of its members fled to Israel. [cite:hz4_merip_2000] [cite:hz4_crs_sla] The UN Secretary-General confirmed on 16 June 2000 that Israel had complied with Resolution 425. The one disputed patch, the roughly 25 square kilometres of the Shebaa Farms, the UN placed in the Syrian Golan rather than in Lebanon, so that its status falls under the Golan resolutions, not under 425; Hezbollah's leader, Hassan Nasrallah, said the withdrawal would not be complete until the farms were liberated. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] [cite:hz4_merip_2000] [scene:hz4_withdrawal|The Hezbollah Architecture: the 2000 withdrawal]

What the record shows

In Lebanon between 1978 and 2000, Israel invaded twice, reached Beirut, and held a tenth of the country for fifteen years through an allied militia it paid. Each step was justified in the government's own words as security for northern Israel, and the 1983 agreement Israel signed treated the international border as inviolable. No law, platform or government statement reviewed claims Lebanese territory for Israel; the 1919 Litani wording was a water arrangement put to the peace conference, and the zone was evacuated in 2000 and certified as such by the UN. [cite:hz2b_jvl_may17] [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] The argument that the invasions and the zone expressed territorial designs on south Lebanon is an inference; on this period the documents point the other way. Whether the positions held since 2024 change that picture is the question Part Nine takes up. [scene:gi9_lebanon|Part Nine: south Lebanon since 2024]

sections.h: Iraq, Iran and Saudi Arabia: the Claims Tested
sections.html:
Three more countries are regularly named in writing about Greater Israel: Iraq, because the Euphrates is the far river of Genesis 15:18; Iran, because it is Israel's principal adversary; and Saudi Arabia, because some maps circulated online extend the promised land into northern Arabia. Unlike the Golan, Sinai, Jordan and Lebanon, none of the three borders Israel, and Israel has never held territory in any of them. [cite:gi1_bg_gen1518] This section tests briefly what the record contains for each: what text or map puts the country into a Greater-Israel claim, whether any Israeli government has adopted that claim, and what Israel's relations with the country have actually turned on. It applies the volume's rule that "Greater Israel" is a finding only where a named actor states or legislates it.

Iraq: a river, a diary note and two papers

Iraq's place in the argument begins with scripture. Genesis 15:18 promises land "unto the great river, the river Euphrates", and Deuteronomy 11:24 repeats the river. [cite:gi1_bg_gen1518] [cite:gi1_bg_deut1124] The founder-era trace is Theodor Herzl's diary note of 1898, recording a plan to ask the Ottoman sultan for a territory from the Egyptian frontier to the Euphrates. The note is authentic; Daniel Pipes, who examined it, stresses that Herzl "did not in fact request" the territory from anyone and that it never became Zionist policy. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] Part Ten treats the note and the myths that grew around it, such as the claimed Knesset inscription. [scene:gi10_authentic|Part Ten: the authentic documents] [scene:gi10_myths|Part Ten: the myths]

Two later documents are cited as evidence of designs on Iraq, and both concern Iraq's government rather than its land. Oded Yinon's essay "A Strategy for Israel in the 1980s", published in February 1982 in Kivunim, a Hebrew quarterly of the World Zionist Organization's information department, argued that Arab states would and should fragment along ethnic and sectarian lines, with Iraq dividing into Shiite, Sunni and Kurdish centres. [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] Scholars disagree about its weight: Mordechai Nisan said the views were Yinon's own and not policy, while Ilan Peleg called the essay "an authentic mirror of the thinking mode of the Israeli Right" and Noam Chomsky called its views "ideological and geopolitical fantasies" rather than mainstream thinking. [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] "A Clean Break", published on 1 June 1996 by a study group of the Institute for Advanced Strategic and Political Studies led by Richard Perle and written for Netanyahu's incoming government, recommended "removing Saddam Hussein from power in Iraq". [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak] [cite:ir13_wiki_cleanbreak] Neither document proposes that Israel take Iraqi territory, and neither was adopted as government policy; how they have been read and misread is set out in the Iran volume and in Part Ten. [scene:ir13_papers|The Iran Architecture: the papers] [scene:gi10_misread|Part Ten: documents misread]

What Israel did do in Iraq was military and concerned weapons, not borders. On 7 June 1981 Israeli aircraft destroyed the Osirak reactor near Baghdad, and the government declared that it would not permit "an enemy to develop weapons of mass destruction against the people of Israel"; the Security Council condemned the strike unanimously. [cite:ir13_wiki_begindoc] [cite:ir13_un_res487] Iraq has never recognised Israel. [cite:ir13_vc_recog] Israel's more recent strikes on Iranian-aligned armed groups in Iraq are covered in the Hezbollah volume. [scene:hz10_iraq|The Hezbollah Architecture: Iraq] No Israeli law, platform, coalition agreement or government statement reviewed claims Iraqi territory. The one modern artefact that draws an outline into Iraq is commercial: the "Greater Israel" pendant sold by the company of the interviewer who gave one to Netanyahu in August 2025, which Haaretz reported as taking in parts of Egypt, all of Jordan, Lebanon, and parts of Syria and Iraq. [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] Part Seven examines that interview. [scene:gi7_interview|Part Seven: the "very much" interview]

Iran: an adversary, not a map

Iran appears in no Greater-Israel map or text examined, ancient or modern. Its conflict with Israel is documented on other grounds: Iran's nuclear programme, its arming of Hezbollah, Hamas and the Houthis, its leaders' calls for Israel's elimination, and Israel's strikes on Iran in June 2025 and from 28 February 2026. Iran, which had maintained de facto relations with Israel under the Shah, through a mission in Tehran that was never a formally recognised embassy, ended them after the 1979 revolution. [cite:ir13_vc_recog] [cite:ir2_wiki_embassy] Why Israel made Iran its principal target, set against what Israel's governments have said they want from it, is the subject of the Iran volume, which keeps the stated aims apart from the competing explanations. [cite:ir13_pbs_bibi2026] [scene:ir13_why|The Iran Architecture: why Iran] Treating that war as part of a territorial programme would join two separate records without a document to connect them; the territorial concept and the Iran security threat are analytically distinct.

Saudi Arabia: a partner on the map

Saudi Arabia's appearance in Greater-Israel claims rests on assertions that the maps extend into the Hejaz or ancient Midian. No source for that was found. The claim that the pendant given to Netanyahu in 2025 includes Saudi territory is not supported: Haaretz's description of it, as reported, does not include it. [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] The documented Israeli record on Saudi Arabia from 2020 to 2023 concerns diplomatic normalisation, not land. When Netanyahu addressed the UN General Assembly on 22 September 2023, his map of "the new Middle East" coloured Saudi Arabia green, as a partner in peace; the same map showed the West Bank and Gaza inside Israel with no Palestinian territory marked, which drew criticism and is examined in Part Seven. [cite:gi7_toi_un2023] [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023] [scene:gi7_maps|Part Seven: the maps at the UN]

The Saudi position in those months was stated by the crown prince. In a Fox News interview aired on 20 September 2023, Mohammed bin Salman said of normalisation: "Every day we get closer." He added: "For us, the Palestinian issue is very important, we need to solve that part", and said he hoped a deal would "ease the life of the Palestinians"; he set no explicit condition of statehood. [cite:gi8_cnbc_mbs] After the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023 the condition hardened. On 7 February 2024, outside this part's period but closing the episode, the Saudi foreign ministry said it had told Washington "there will be no diplomatic relations with Israel" unless "an independent Palestinian state is recognised on the 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital." [cite:gi8_reu_saudi2024] Saudi Arabia has never recognised Israel. [cite:ir13_vc_recog] The argument that normalisation without a Palestinian state is Greater Israel's diplomatic expression is an interpretation: it reads a diplomatic sequence as a territorial aim, and no Israeli document reviewed here states that aim with respect to Saudi Arabia.

What the test shows

For all three countries the Greater-Israel claim, where it exists at all, rests on scripture, on a diary note never acted upon, on papers by individuals that were not adopted as policy, or on a piece of jewellery; none rests on an Israeli law, platform, coalition agreement or official map. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] Israel's actual dealings with the three, a strike on a reactor, a war with Iran and its allies, and a pursuit of diplomatic ties, have documented causes of their own. That does not show that no Israeli politician holds a wider vision: Part Seven sets out what Netanyahu said in August 2025, and Part Eleven the religious currents in which the broader biblical borders still circulate. It shows that, for Iraq, Iran and Saudi Arabia, the record reviewed here contains no programme to test. [scene:gi11_religious|Part Eleven: the religious engine]

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: The Buffer Belt
chapters.intro: Part Nine moves from the fronts of the past to the ground Israel's forces held in October 2026. Between the end of 2024 and the autumn of 2026 Israeli troops came to hold three belts of land beyond the lines they had held on 7 October 2023: a strip of south Lebanon behind what Israel calls its Forward Defense Line, the United Nations buffer zone in Syria together with the Syrian summit of Mount Hermon, and a growing share of the Gaza Strip behind the "Yellow Line." This part sets out each one in turn: when and how it was taken, how large it is according to each source that has measured it, what Israel's government and military have said it is for, and what the neighbouring government, the armed groups concerned and the United Nations have said about it. Then it asks the question this volume puts to every front. Is this the expansion the phrase "Greater Israel" describes, or a security belt of the kind Israel has held and given up before? Every status is given as of October 2026, a week before Israel's election of 27 October.
chapters.outro: Part Nine established that by October 2026 Israeli forces held three belts of land beyond the lines of October 2023. In south Lebanon they held a zone behind the Forward Defense Line, five to ten kilometres deep on the army's own April map and about 6 per cent of the country by NPR's estimate, which Netanyahu said Israel would keep until Hezbollah is disarmed and from which the UN force that has watched the border since 1978 will begin to leave after 31 December 2026. [cite:gi9_alarabiya_map] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] [cite:gi9_un_2790] In Syria they held the UN buffer zone and the Hermon summit "for an indefinite period," demanded a demilitarised south and resumed the Sufa 53 fortifications, which Syria, the UAE, Jordan and Kuwait condemned with reference to the 1974 agreement and Qatar as "a flagrant breach of international principles." [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] [cite:gi9_fdd_demil] [cite:gi9_an_sufa] [cite:gi9_uae_sufa] In Gaza the share behind the Yellow Line rose from about 53 per cent at the ceasefire to between 64 and 70 per cent by the sources' various measures, with Netanyahu ordering the army toward 70 and the chief of staff calling the line "a new border line." [cite:gi9_aj_maps] [cite:gi9_reu_orange] [cite:gi9_olj_net70] [cite:gi9_unsco_jun26] [cite:gi9_olj_zamir] Each zone was explained as security against a named armed enemy; none had been claimed as sovereign territory by any government decision or law; and Lebanon, Syria, Hamas and the UN each objected: Lebanon and Syria as occupation of their territory, Hamas as a ceasefire violation, the UN as breaches of resolution 1701 and the 1974 agreement and as a squeeze on Gaza's civilians. [cite:gi9_nahar_saar] [cite:gi9_pbs_plan] [cite:hz10s_un_guterres] [cite:gi9_aa_hamas] [cite:gi9_unsco_jun26] [cite:hz5_un_1701] Whether the belt is a security perimeter or the first stage of a frontier is the argument of the moment, and the record will answer it only after the election of 27 October 2026. Part Ten turns from ground to paper: the documents and maps cited as proof of a Greater Israel plan, which of them are authentic, which are misread and which are myths. [scene:gi10_authentic|The documents and the myths]

sections.h: South Lebanon: From Five Hilltops to the Forward Defense Line
sections.html:
Israel's previous occupation of south Lebanon, the "security zone" it held from 1985 until May 2000, ended in a withdrawal that the UN Secretary-General certified on 16 June 2000 as compliance with resolution 425, leaving only the disputed Shebaa Farms. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] [cite:hz4_crs_sla] That history is told in Part Eight and in the Hezbollah volume. [scene:gi8_lebanon|The Lebanon front, 1978–2000] [scene:hz4_zone|The security zone] This section follows the second occupation, which began in the war of 2024 and grew in the war of 2026. The full military and diplomatic story is in the Hezbollah volume; [scene:hz8_war2026|The 2026 war] [scene:hz8_now|Where things stand] here the question is narrower: how much Lebanese ground Israel held, what it said the ground was for, and what Lebanon and the United Nations said.

Five positions, 2024–2026

The cessation of hostilities that took effect on 27 November 2024 provided for a phased Israeli withdrawal over a period that "should not exceed 60 days," with only Lebanese state forces to be armed south of the Litani River. [cite:hz8_toi_text] The deadline was extended to 18 February 2025, and on that date Israel announced it would stay at five hilltop posts inside Lebanon. Its military spokesman said, "We need to remain at those points at the moment to defend Israeli citizens"; President Joseph Aoun insisted on full withdrawal, and Hezbollah's leader, Naim Qassem, said Israel "must fully withdraw" and had "no excuse." [cite:hz8_nbc_jan26] [cite:hz8_national_five] UNIFIL, reporting on the first year of the truce, recorded the Israeli army at five locations plus two buffer areas north of the Blue Line, more than 2,500 Israeli ground activities north of the line and almost 7,800 air violations. [cite:hz8_un_unifil_year] By January 2026 the Lebanese army said it had operational control south of the Litani except at the five Israeli positions. [cite:hz8_cnn_phase1]

The 2026 war and the new line

The second war began on 2 March 2026, when Hezbollah fired on Israel after the joint US–Israeli strikes on Iran of 28 February. [cite:hz8_am_mar2] Israeli ground operations began on 16 March; Defence Minister Israel Katz said the displaced would not return south of the Litani until the safety of northern Israel's residents was guaranteed. [cite:hz8b_afp_ground] A ten-day truce began on the night of 16 April. Al Jazeera described the line Israel then held as up to about ten kilometres deep, with residents barred from 55 villages; Netanyahu said, "we are not leaving." [cite:hz8b_aj_yellow] On 19 April the Israeli military published its first public map of what it called the "Forward Defense Line," running roughly five to ten kilometres from the border and placing dozens of villages south of it. "Five divisions, alongside Israeli Navy forces, are operating simultaneously south of the forward defense line," the military said; their purpose was to dismantle Hezbollah's infrastructure and "prevent direct threats to communities in northern Israel." Katz said border houses that Hezbollah used would be demolished. [cite:gi9_alarabiya_map] Lebanese and international reporting came to call it the Yellow Line, the same name used in Gaza.

The line did not mark the furthest point of the advance. On 31 May Israeli troops crossed the Litani and took Beaufort castle, the deepest Israeli incursion into Lebanon in more than 25 years, and declared the area between the Litani and the Zahrani a combat zone. [cite:hz8b_ap_beaufort] A ceasefire took effect on 19 June under the US–Iran interim deal, and on 26 June Israel and Lebanon signed a framework in Washington for the Lebanese army to take over the south as Hezbollah was disarmed; Qassem called it "a surrender of sovereignty," and Katz ordered the army to prepare for an "extended stay." [cite:hz8b_olj_jun19] [cite:hz8b_almon_framework] [cite:hz8b_aj_reject] In July the two sides agreed on "pilot zones" to be handed to the Lebanese army, with no timetable for a wider withdrawal; Israel left the first village, Zawtar al-Gharbieh, at the end of July. [cite:hz8b_afp_pilot] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines]

By September, NPR reported, the zone behind the Yellow Line covered about 6 per cent of Lebanon and was about five miles (eight kilometres) wide in places, within the five-to-ten-kilometre range of the army's April map, with dozens of villages emptied or destroyed and their residents barred; Lebanon's government counted more than 1.2 million people displaced in the war, and Israel 39 soldiers, a contractor and two civilians killed by Hezbollah. [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] The depth is therefore best given as a range, about five to ten kilometres by the army's map, Al Jazeera's and NPR's accounts. The 6 per cent figure is NPR's; the Israeli military's April map gave a depth but no area, and no Israeli or Lebanese official figure for the zone's area was found.

What each side says the zone is

Israel's stated position is that the zone is a security measure tied to Hezbollah's weapons. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said on 28 April 2026: "Israel has no territorial ambitions in Lebanon," adding that the presence by the northern border "serves one purpose: protecting our citizens." [cite:gi9_nahar_saar] Netanyahu has tied the duration to disarmament rather than to a date: "as long as it is not disarmed, we will remain in this zone," he said in October, adding that he did not trust Lebanon's government to disarm Hezbollah. [cite:hz8b_national_tampa]

Lebanon's government treats the zone as an occupation of its territory and demands full withdrawal. Going into military talks in Tampa, Florida, on 20 October 2026, the presidency said its delegation would press for an "end to Israeli attacks in Lebanon"; it rejected direct coordination between the two armies and demanded third-party verification, while the pilot-zone process had stalled for months. [cite:gi9_toi_tampa] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said in September that dozens of villages remained under Israeli occupation. [cite:hz8b_olj_salam] Hezbollah's position, as Qassem put it on 6 October, is that it is "ready to cooperate" on the state's monopoly of arms but not under "American diktats," and that "Israel cannot remain in southern Lebanon indefinitely." [cite:hz8b_olj_qassem]

The United Nations position rests on resolution 1701 of 2006, which called for Israel's withdrawal and an area between the Blue Line and the Litani free of armed personnel other than the Lebanese army and UNIFIL. [cite:hz5_un_1701] The force charged with monitoring it is leaving. On 28 August 2025 the Security Council unanimously adopted resolution 2790, extending UNIFIL for a final time to 31 December 2026, followed by a year of "orderly and safe drawdown and withdrawal"; the United States said Lebanese forces should take on the responsibility, and France warned that a premature departure could weaken the Lebanese government's efforts in the south. [cite:gi9_un_2790] Aoun has said he would prefer an extension and otherwise another international force; as of late September none had been agreed. [cite:hz8b_olj_unifil] [cite:hz8b_olj_salam]

What this does and does not show

The documented facts are an occupied zone deeper than at any time since 2000, held without a date of departure, with villages destroyed inside it, and the departure of the UN force that has watched the border since 1978. [cite:hz8b_ap_beaufort] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] [cite:gi9_un_2790] Analysts at the Carnegie Middle East Center described the south as "a wasteland that has functioned as a de facto buffer zone," and noted that hard-line Israeli voices had floated the Awali River, north of the Litani, as the line for a Hezbollah-free zone. [cite:gi9_carnegie_ring] What the record reviewed does not contain is any Israeli government decision, Knesset bill or coalition document claiming sovereignty over Lebanese land, or any official statement that the zone is permanent; the government's stated position is the opposite. The one programme document that drew a line into Lebanon, the Zionist Organization's 1919 proposal, ran its border south of Sidon and asked for the Litani's waters by international arrangement, and the record reviewed here contains no Israeli government claim based on it. [scene:gi2_map1919|The 1919 map] Whether the 2026 zone follows the 1985 pattern, ending in withdrawal, or becomes a standing frontier is an open question as of October 2026; Part Twelve sets out the earlier withdrawals. [scene:gi12_withdrawals|The withdrawals]

sections.h: Syria: The Buffer Zone, Mount Hermon and Sufa 53
sections.html:
Since the disengagement agreement of 31 May 1974, Israeli and Syrian forces on the Golan have been separated by a strip of land patrolled by the UN Disengagement Observer Force, UNDOF, with zones of limited forces on either side. [cite:gi12_jvl_syrdis] Israel had held the western Golan since 1967 and extended its law there in 1981, a step the Security Council unanimously declared "null and void"; that history is in Part Eight. [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] [cite:gi8_rw_res497] [scene:gi8_golan|The Golan] For fifty years the buffer strip itself stayed outside Israeli control. That changed on the day Bashar al-Assad's government fell. The Hezbollah volume follows the air campaign and the post-Assad talks; [scene:hz10_syria|Syria: the corridor, the campaign and the buffer zone] this section sets out the ground Israel took, what it said that ground was for, and the response of Syria, its neighbours and the UN.

8 December 2024: "temporarily"

On 8 December 2024 Netanyahu declared that the 1974 agreement "has collapsed, the Syrian soldiers have abandoned their positions," and said he had ordered the army to seize the buffer zone "and the commanding positions nearby." [cite:hz10s_newarab_collapse] He gave the reason in one sentence: "We will not allow any hostile force to establish itself on our border." [cite:gi9_wiki_syriainv] Israeli forces took the Syrian summit of Mount Hermon, the highest ground in the area, and over the next two days, by the military's count, carried out about 480 strikes on Syrian military stockpiles and naval facilities. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said the aim was to keep the weapons from falling "into the hands of extremists," and Israel told the Security Council it had "deployed temporarily in few points." [cite:hz10s_cnn_480] The Biden administration called the incursion "a temporary action." [cite:gi9_wiki_syriainv]

The temporary framing did not last. On 17 December Netanyahu visited the Hermon summit and said the army would stay "until another solution ensuring Israel's security is found"; on 15 December his government had approved a plan to double the population of the Israeli-held Golan, a new plan distinct from, and following, the Bennett government's similar plan of 26 December 2021 described in Part Eight. [cite:gi9_wiki_syriainv] [cite:gi8_cnn_golan2021] On 28 January 2025 Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Hermon that the army would remain there and in the security zone "for an indefinite period," adding, "We will not return to the reality of October 7." [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] In January 2025 Israeli officials were reported to describe a 15-kilometre "zone of control" inside Syria and a 60-kilometre "sphere of influence" beyond it; these terms come from press reports of officials' briefings, not from a published order. [cite:gi9_wiki_syriainv]

The demand for a demilitarised south

On 23 February 2025, at an officers' graduation ceremony, Netanyahu set out a demand that went beyond the buffer zone: "we demand the full demilitarization of southern Syria, in the Quneitra, Daraa, and As Suwayda provinces," and Israel would not allow the forces of Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, the group that had taken Damascus, or the new Syrian army, into the area south of the capital. By then the army had at least nine posts in Syria, two on Hermon and seven in the buffer zone. Demonstrations against the statement followed in Quneitra, Daraa and Suwayda, and Syria's National Dialogue Conference warned against the partition or "surrender" of any part of the country. [cite:gi9_fdd_demil] In July 2025, during fighting between government forces and Druze militias in Suwayda, Israel bombed the defence ministry in Damascus; Netanyahu said Israel was "acting to save our Druze brothers" and was committed to keeping the south-west demilitarised. [cite:hz10s_npr_sweida]

Sufa 53

The most permanent-looking work is a fortified line inside the buffer zone in Quneitra province known as Sufa 53. Begun in mid-2022, under Assad, near the village of Hadr, it consists of a military road about eight metres wide, earth berms about five metres high, trenches and observation posts; according to Syria's state news agency it runs from near Hadr through Jubata al-Khashab and al-Hamidiya to al-Asha and the southern tri-border point. [cite:hz10s_eb_sufa] [cite:hz10s_aa_sufa] [cite:gi9_an_sufa] Israel resumed work on it on 4 October 2026. Israel says the line is "designed to prevent possible attacks by Iran-backed armed groups." [cite:hz10s_aa_sufa]

The response came the next day. Syria's foreign ministry said completing the project breached the 1974 agreement and UN resolutions. Qatar called it a "flagrant breach of international principles"; Jordan said the Israeli measures "violated the UN Charter and Israel's obligations under the 1974 agreement" and called for an end to the occupation of Syrian territory; Kuwait called the incursions "a dangerous escalation" and urged enforcement of the 1974 agreement. [cite:gi9_an_sufa] [cite:gi9a_an_sufa] The United Arab Emirates, which normalised relations with Israel in 2020, condemned the "resumption of excavation and bulldozing operations" on the "Sufa 53 line" and the construction of fortifications, and reaffirmed its "categorical rejection of any violation of Syria's sovereignty." [cite:gi9_uae_sufa]

The positions of Syria and the UN

The UN's position from the first week was that the 1974 agreement stood. UNDOF said Israel was in "violation of the 1974 disengagement agreement"; Secretary-General António Guterres said he was "deeply concerned by the recent and extensive violations of Syria's sovereignty," insisted the agreement "remains in force" and called for withdrawal. [cite:hz10s_almon_katz] [cite:hz10s_un_guterres] The UN envoy Geir Pedersen said in February 2025 that "the Israelis need to withdraw," and in July 2025 Guterres called the violations of Syria's sovereignty "unacceptable." [cite:gi9_wiki_syriainv] Syria's position under President Ahmed al-Sharaa has been to seek a security arrangement, not war. In Paris on 6 January 2026 the two sides agreed to a US-supervised de-escalation cell; [cite:hz10s_almon_paris] Syria's foreign minister met an Israeli delegation in Jordan on 23 August 2026, and Damascus said its priority was an Israeli return to the lines of 8 December 2024 and that the Golan's final status was not yet on the table. [cite:hz10s_eb_amman] On 23 September al-Sharaa said the talks had reached "almost 90%" agreement before Israel added conditions; that is his account, and no Israeli response to it was reported. [cite:hz10s_jpost_sharaa90] Katz was quoted in June 2026 as saying, "we will not withdraw from the security zone in Syria." [cite:hz10s_jpost_slim]

As of October 2026 there is no signed agreement; Israeli forces hold the buffer zone and the Hermon summit, and the Sufa 53 works have resumed. [cite:hz10s_eb_sufa] The documented facts are the seizure, the stated indefinite duration, the demand for a demilitarised south and the fortifications. The stated purpose, in every Israeli statement found, is security: keeping hostile forces from the Golan frontier. No Israeli government decision or bill has claimed sovereignty over the ground taken in 2024, and the Carnegie Middle East Center, describing a "ring of buffer zones," treated it as a security order "at the expense of the sovereign rights" of Syria rather than an annexation. [cite:gi9_carnegie_ring] The precedent cuts both ways: Israel returned the town of Quneitra to Syrian civil control under the 1974 agreement, after destroying much of it according to a UN-commissioned report, [cite:gi12_wiki_quneitra] [scene:gi12_withdrawals|The withdrawals] and it extended its law to the rest of the Golan seven years later. [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] [scene:gi8_golan|The Golan]

sections.h: Gaza: The Yellow Line, 53 Per Cent and Rising
sections.html:
Israel withdrew its army and removed its settlers from the Gaza Strip in 2005, a decision told in the Gaza volume and in Part Twelve. [scene:gz3_withdrawal|The withdrawal] [scene:gi12_withdrawals|The withdrawals] Even before the war of 2023 it enforced a restricted zone inside the Strip along the fence; the UN's humanitarian office, OCHA, estimated in 2010 that the restricted area covered 17 per cent of Gaza's land and 35 per cent of its farmland. [cite:gi9_aj_maps] This section follows the line Israel's army has held since the ceasefire of October 2025, the share of the Strip behind it as each source has measured it, and what Israel, the Palestinians and the UN have said it is. The war itself and the plans for Gaza's future are in the Gaza volume. [scene:gz7_war|The war] [scene:gz11_visions|The plans for Gaza]

The line in the plan

The ceasefire rested on the 20-point plan the White House released on 29 September 2025. Its third point said that "Israeli forces will withdraw to the agreed upon line to prepare for a hostage release," with "battle lines" to "remain frozen until conditions are met for the complete staged withdrawal." Its sixteenth point said: "Israel will not occupy or annex Gaza." As an international stabilisation force took control, the army would "progressively hand over the Gaza territory it occupies," "save for a security perimeter presence that will remain until Gaza is properly secure from any resurgent terror threat." The plan did not define either the line or the perimeter. [cite:gi9_pbs_plan] Netanyahu had described the aim in similar terms two months earlier: "We want to have a security perimeter. We don't want to govern it." [cite:gz_mm_netanyahu_aug25]

The line, marked on the ground by yellow-painted concrete blocks and later by earth berms, came to be called the Yellow Line. When the ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025 it left about 53 per cent of the Strip on the Israeli side, mostly farmland and the eastern border areas. [cite:gi9_aj_maps] [cite:gi9_wiki_yellow] Netanyahu himself later put the figure at 50 per cent. [cite:gi9_olj_net70]

How the share grew

The line moved. BBC Verify found blocks in the Tuffah district of Gaza City moved about 295 metres deeper into the Strip between 27 November and 25 December 2025. [cite:gi9_wiki_yellow] The research group Forensic Architecture estimated that Israel controlled 58 per cent of Gaza by December; Al Jazeera, reading Israeli military maps in January 2026, gave roughly the same figure. [cite:gi9_aj_maps] [cite:gi9_aj_jan26] On 7 December 2025 the chief of staff, Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir, told reservists in Gaza: "We have operational control over extensive parts of the Gaza Strip, and we will remain on those defense lines. The Yellow Line is a new border line, serving as a forward defensive line for our communities." [cite:gi9_olj_zamir]

In mid-March 2026 the army sent aid agencies maps of a second boundary, an "orange line," marking a restricted area beyond the Yellow Line that covers about 11 per cent of Gaza and inside which humanitarian movement must be coordinated with the army. Reuters reported the maps in April; Jad Isaac of the Applied Research Institute–Jerusalem put Israeli control at no less than 64 per cent. The army's coordinating body, COGAT, said the boundaries are "determined and updated in accordance with the operational situational assessment" and that the zone exists to allow coordinated aid, not to affect civilians; the military called the area beside the Yellow Line "a sensitive and dangerous operational environment." At least three Palestinians working with UN agencies had been killed by Israeli fire between the lines. [cite:gi9_reu_orange]

In May Netanyahu stated both the share and the aim. At a conference in the West Bank on 28 May, in remarks broadcast by Channel 12, he said: "Right now, we have Hamas by the throat. We control 60% of the territory of the Strip," and "my directive is to go to 70." [cite:gi9_olj_net70] (Anadolu dates a first such acknowledgement to 15 May.) [cite:gi9_aa_hamas] On 29 June the UN's deputy special coordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, told the Security Council: "Israel has said that it currently controls approximately 70% of the Gaza Strip." [cite:gi9_unsco_jun26] In July the Associated Press, from satellite imagery, reported berms more than 23 kilometres long separating the Israeli-held part of the Strip from the rest, and the army confirmed it was building the barrier. [cite:gi9_wiki_yellow] By October OCHA reported that access restrictions covered 65 per cent of Gaza, and Human Rights Watch put the area behind the Yellow Line at about 64 per cent, noting that Israeli officials called it a "new border." [cite:gi9_aj_maps] [cite:gz_hrw_anniv] On 11 October Israeli forces moved the blocks several metres west in Shujaiya, in eastern Gaza City. [cite:gi9_aj_shujayea]

The figures measure different things and should not be read as one series. The 53, 58 and 64 per cent figures estimate land behind the lines; Netanyahu's and Israel's 60 and 70 per cent are the government's own statements of control; OCHA's 65 per cent counts land where Palestinian movement is restricted. What they share is a direction. By Al Jazeera's arithmetic, about 2.1 million people were left on roughly 35 per cent of the Strip, some 128 square kilometres. [cite:gi9_aj_maps]

What each side says

Israel's stated position has two parts that sit in tension. The military describes the line as a defensive one: a "forward defensive line for our communities," in Zamir's words, and a restricted area whose limits follow the operational situation, in COGAT's. [cite:gi9_olj_zamir] [cite:gi9_reu_orange] The political leadership has tied it to Hamas: Netanyahu's "by the throat," and, in July 2026, an Israeli diplomatic source's statement that there would be "no Israeli withdrawal from the Yellow Line" before Hamas disarmed. [cite:gi9_olj_net70] [cite:hm_jp_noWithdraw] Against both stands the plan Israel accepted, which says Israel "will not occupy or annex Gaza." [cite:gi9_pbs_plan] Hamas's spokesman Hazem Qassem said in June 2026 that moving the line was "a blatant violation of the ceasefire agreement" meant to "blow up the negotiation track." [cite:gi9_aa_hamas] The UN's account, given to the Security Council, is that Israel's expanding control was reducing the space left to civilians. [cite:gi9_unsco_jun26] Armed groups opposed to Hamas operate from the Israeli side of the line, a story told in the Hezbollah volume. [cite:hz11_acled_gaza] [scene:hz11_proxies|Armed by Israel]

Three Zones: What the Record Shows

Set side by side, the three zones share a vocabulary and a sequence. Reuters noted that Israel describes the territory it holds in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon alike as buffer zones against militant attacks. [cite:gi9_reu_orange] In each, the first statement was temporary or conditional, and the later ones were not: "deployed temporarily" in Syria became "for an indefinite period"; five posts "at the moment" in Lebanon became a zone held until Hezbollah disarms; a line "frozen" pending withdrawal in Gaza became, to the chief of staff, "a new border line." [cite:hz10s_cnn_480] [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] [cite:hz8_national_five] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] [cite:gi9_pbs_plan] [cite:gi9_olj_zamir] In each, the line has been fortified, by berms in Gaza and Sufa 53 in Syria, or emptied of residents, as in south Lebanon. [cite:gi9_wiki_yellow] [cite:hz10s_eb_sufa] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] The Carnegie Middle East Center's term for the result is "a ring of buffer zones," an order "defined by reinforced boundaries and expanded buffer zones encircling Israel." [cite:gi9_carnegie_ring]

What the record does not show, as of October 2026, is the step that would make any of the three a finding about "Greater Israel" in this volume's sense: a government decision, law or coalition clause claiming the land. No such step was found for south Lebanon, the Syrian buffer zone or Gaza, and Israel's foreign minister has denied territorial ambitions in Lebanon. [cite:gi9_nahar_saar] The case for reading the belt as expansion rests on the pattern above, on the absence of any departure date, and on statements by named officials: Zamir's "new border line," and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's description of Gaza in September 2025 as a real-estate "bonanza," with the remark, "We have to see how we are dividing up the land in percentages"; Netanyahu, for his part, has said he does not intend to re-establish settlements in Gaza. [cite:gi9_olj_zamir] [cite:gz_toi_bonanza] [scene:gz11_visions|The plans for Gaza] The case against rests on the stated security purpose, on each zone's link to a named armed enemy, and on the precedents of 1957, 2000 and 2005, when Israel left ground it had held as a buffer. [scene:gi12_withdrawals|The withdrawals] Which reading the record will bear depends on what happens after the election of 27 October 2026 and the end of UNIFIL on 31 December; both are open.

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: The Documents and the Myths
chapters.intro: Part Ten sorts the evidence people cite for a "Greater Israel" plan into three classes, and says plainly which is which. Some items are authentic but narrower than their use: the verse in Genesis, a note in Herzl's diary from 1898 that he never acted on, the boundary the Zionist Organization asked for at Paris in 1919, and a rabbi's answer to a United Nations committee in 1947. Some are real documents or objects that are misread: Oded Yinon's essay of 1982, the 1996 paper "A Clean Break" and Israel's 10-agora coin. Two are myths: the inscription said to hang over the Knesset and the claim that the flag's blue stripes stand for the Nile and the Euphrates. The part corrects an error carried in earlier volumes of this library, which called the Herzl note a fabrication, and ends with a ledger of all nine items.
chapters.outro: Part Ten established that the most quoted proofs of a Nile-to-Euphrates programme fall apart on inspection, and that some of them are real. Genesis 15:18 names the Euphrates, Herzl noted in 1898 a plan, never carried out, to ask the sultan for land from Egypt's frontier to that river, and a Mizrachi rabbi gave the biblical promise as "From Egypt to the Euphrates" when a UN delegate asked him in 1947; but the one formal claim the movement made before 1948, at Paris in 1919, stopped south of Sidon and at the Hejaz Railway. [cite:gi1_bg_gen1518] [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:gi10_djn_fishman] [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] Yinon's essay forecast the break-up of Arab states and named only Sinai as an Israeli aim; "A Clean Break" urged Israel to keep the Golan and refuse land for peace, and Netanyahu's government signed the Wye memorandum two years later; the 10-agora coin copies a coin of Mattathias Antigonus. [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak] [cite:gi10_crs_wye] [cite:gi10_boi_coins] No one has produced the Knesset inscription, which a newspaper withdrew as an error in 1980, and the flag's stripes come from the prayer shawl. [cite:gi10_csm_1980] [cite:gi10_mfa_flag] The territorial language that carries weight in Israeli politics is in platforms, laws and coalition guidelines, and some of it is argued on religious grounds. Part Eleven turns to that religious engine: the Kook lineage, the Temple Mount movements and Christian Zionist land theology. [scene:gi11_religious|Part Eleven: the religious engine]

sections.h: Authentic and Narrow
sections.html:
Much of what circulates as proof of a "Greater Israel" plan falls into three classes, and this part takes them in turn. Some items are authentic: the text exists, the words were written or spoken, and the date and venue can be checked. Some are real documents that are misread, so that a forecast, a proposal or a coin design is made to carry a claim it does not contain. Some are myths: the object said to exist has never been shown to exist, or its origin is documented and is something else. This section deals with the first class. Each authentic item is real, and each is narrower than the use made of it. The finding has to be stated in both directions, because denying an authentic text in order to answer its misuse is an error that has been made about Herzl.

The verse

The phrase "from the Nile to the Euphrates" is built on Genesis 15:18, in which God makes a covenant with Abram: "Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates" (King James Version). The New International Version translates the same words "from the Wadi of Egypt". [cite:gi1_bg_gen1518] The text is authentic in the plainest sense: it is in every edition of the Hebrew Bible. What it is not is a map. The verse uses nahar, "river", and one standard reference work, the Encyclopedia of The Bible, reads "the river of Egypt" as the Nile; the boundary passages in Numbers 34 and Ezekiel 47 use a different term, the "brook of Egypt", which the same work takes to be "highly probably" the Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai. [cite:gi1_ebg_riveregypt] [cite:gi1_ebg_brookegypt] Those boundary passages describe a land much narrower than the Genesis promise, lying west of the Jordan. [cite:gi1_wiki_greaterisrael] Daniel Pipes, writing in 1994, argued that the specific boundaries govern the general promise, and that a covenant made with all of Abram's offspring, who in the narrative include Ishmael, cannot be read as a deed for a modern state. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] The readings, and the religious currents that take the broader verse literally, are set out in [scene:gi1_phrase|Part One] and [scene:gi11_religious|Part Eleven]. For this part the point is narrower. A verse is evidence of what a scripture says. It becomes evidence of a state's programme only when a named government, party or official adopts it as one, and that is the test Parts Five to Nine apply to each actor.

Herzl's note of 1898

Theodor Herzl's diary contains a note, from 1898, of a plan to ask the Ottoman sultan for a territory running from the frontier of Egypt to the Euphrates. The source for that statement is the scholar most often cited for having debunked it. Pipes wrote in the Middle East Quarterly in 1994: "In 1898, Herzl planned to ask the Ottoman sultan for a territory stretching from the Egyptian frontier to the Euphrates", citing the German critical edition of the diaries, volume 2, page 650. His verdict was confined to what followed: "Herzl did not in fact request the Nile-to-Euphrates region from the Ottoman king or anyone else." [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny]

That is the Pipes correction. Some rebuttals call the Herzl item a fabrication, or say that it is not in his writings and began as a 1994 misattribution; they rely, directly or indirectly, on the article that confirms the note. On the record, the note is authentic. What is false is the claim that Herzl put it to the sultan, or that it became the programme of the Zionist Organization. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] The exact English wording most often quoted ("From the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates") has not been checked against the printed English edition and is not quoted here as Herzl's words. The entry, the Hechler maps that preceded it and the requests Herzl actually made are examined in [scene:gi2_herzl|Part Two].

The map at Paris, 1919

The first boundary the Zionist movement formally put before the world's governments is also documented, and it is the clearest answer to the claim that the movement asked for the Nile and the Euphrates. The Zionist Organization's "Statement on Palestine" to the Paris Peace Conference, dated 3 February 1919, drew the northern line from "a point on the Mediterranean Sea in the vicinity south of Sidon", along the Lebanon foothills and the slopes of Mount Hermon; the eastern line ran "close to and west of the Hedjaz Railway terminating in the Gulf of Akaba"; in the south it asked for "a frontier to be agreed upon with the Egyptian Government." [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] That line takes in the Golan, the slopes of Hermon, a strip of southern Lebanon and a band east of the Jordan as far as the railway. It does not reach the Nile, Sinai, Damascus or the Euphrates. Its stated grounds were water and access: it called Hermon "Palestine's real 'Father of Waters'" and asked for Litani water rights by international arrangement, not for the river. [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] The map is authentic and it was a real claim to more land than any later border gave; it is also far narrower than the slogan. The powers rejected it, as [scene:gi2_map1919|Part Two] shows.

A rabbi's answer to UNSCOP, 1947

A fourth item is less often quoted and is also authentic. In July 1947 the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine heard Rabbi Judah L. Fishman, a leader of the religious Zionist Mizrachi movement, in Jerusalem. According to a Jewish Telegraphic Agency dispatch printed in the Detroit Jewish News on 18 July 1947, the Indian delegate Sir Abdur Rahman questioned him on theology and asked: "What were the boundaries of the land promised by God to the Jews?" Fishman replied: "From Egypt to the Euphrates." He added that "God promised it to Abraham 4,000 years ago", and that the promise ran to Isaac's descendants: "He gave Ishmael another land." [cite:gi10_djn_fishman] Pressed by the delegate, he then answered "No" when asked whether that included Egypt, Syria and Lebanon, Iraq or Transjordan. [cite:gi10a_djn_fishman] The exchange is sometimes cited as a "Rabbi Fischmann" testimony and marked unverified. The contemporary report confirms it. It also shows its scope. A rabbi answered a delegate's question about the extent of a biblical promise, and in the JTA's account he did not mention the Nile and, when asked, denied that the promise included Egypt, Syria, Lebanon, Iraq or Transjordan. That shows how one religious leader read Genesis in 1947. It is not evidence of what the Jewish Agency asked the committee to recommend, and the record of the borders the movement actually sought and accepted between 1937 and 1949 is in [scene:gi2_peel|Part Two] and [scene:gi3_borders|Part Three]. [cite:gi10_djn_fishman]

The pattern across the four is consistent. The broad formula appears in scripture, in a founder's private note and in a rabbi's answer about scripture. In the one formal territorial claim the movement made to the powers before 1948, it does not appear. The documents that carry territorial language into the policy of the State of Israel come later and are of a different kind: the 1977 Likud platform, the Golan Heights Law of 1981, the 2018 Nation-State Law and the 2022 coalition guidelines, examined in [scene:gi5_likud|Part Five] and [scene:gi6_plans|Part Six]. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] Those are better evidence than anything in this section, and they concern the land between the Jordan and the sea and the Golan, not the Nile.

sections.h: Real Documents, Misread
sections.html:
The second class is made of things that exist and are misdescribed. An essay in a Hebrew quarterly, a think-tank paper and a coin are all real, and each can be read or held in the hand. Each has been presented as evidence of a plan to rule from the Nile to the Euphrates. In each case the text or the object says something else. Two of them, Oded Yinon's essay and "A Clean Break", have already been read in [scene:ir13_papers|the Iran volume] for what they say about Iran; this section reads them for what they say about territory, and keeps to the same facts.

The Yinon essay, 1982

"A Strategy for Israel in the 1980s" was published in February 1982 in Kivunim ("Directions"), issue 14, a Hebrew quarterly on Judaism and Zionism issued from 1978 to 1987 by the World Zionist Organization's Department of Information. Its author, Oded Yinon, was reputedly a journalist and a former Foreign Ministry official, and by some accounts had advised Ariel Sharon. Israel Shahak, an Israeli critic of Zionism, translated it into English; his version was disseminated on 13 June 1982, a week after Israel invaded Lebanon, and circulated as "The Zionist Plan for the Middle East". [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] The title by which most readers know it was given in translation; the essay's own title describes a strategy, and its author held no office that could make it policy.

What the essay argued was that the Arab states were fragile mosaics of sects and peoples, and that Israel should aim at, and expect, their dissolution. "Syria will fall apart, in accordance with its ethnic and religious structure," it says, and "Lebanon's total dissolution into five provinces serves as a precendent for the entire Arab world." Iraq would divide into Shiite, Sunni and Kurdish parts. [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] Its programme is fragmentation of neighbours, not the annexation of their land. The only territory it names as an Israeli aim is Sinai, which Israel was then returning to Egypt under the 1979 treaty: "(Regaining) the Sinai peninsula with its present and potential resources is therefore a political priority," Yinon wrote, a priority "obstructed by the Camp David and the peace agreements". In the same passage he added that "Israel will not unilaterally break the treaty". [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] He also called for the "liquidation" of Jordan as a Hashemite state, with Palestinians moved from the West Bank to the east bank. [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] The English text available online is incomplete and lacks the essay's section on Jordan and its notes, so that passage is reported here from the secondary literature. [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon]

None of this is a Nile-to-Euphrates claim. The essay proposes no Israeli border on either river and no rule over Cairo, Damascus or Baghdad. It is real evidence of something narrower: one writer's view, published under the WZO's imprint, that Israel would gain from the break-up of the states around it. Scholars disagree about how representative that view was. Mordechai Nisan treated it as Yinon's alone and not government policy; Yehoshafat Harkabi found its analysis of Arab weakness largely correct but asked why, if fragmentation was inevitable, Israel would need to interfere; Ilan Peleg called it "an authentic mirror of the thinking mode of the Israeli Right" under Begin; Noam Chomsky placed it outside the Zionist mainstream, nearer the ultranationalist Tehiya party. Yinon himself replied in 1983 that he was not a supporter of Sharon or Begin. [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon]

What it became is a separate matter. From Roger Garaudy's use of it in 1983 to a column in Arab News in 2005 announcing that the plan was "in large part taking shape", the essay has been offered as the script for the 2003 invasion of Iraq, the Syrian civil war and the rise of the Islamic State, most of which happened decades later and none of which Israel's governments set in motion on the documented record. [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon] The record contains no Israeli government decision adopting it. The one aim it stated for Israel's own territory did not happen: Israel completed the return of Sinai on 25 April 1982 and did not go back (see [scene:gi8_sinai|Part Eight]). [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] Its call to dissolve Jordan was answered twelve years later by a treaty in which Israel undertook to respect Jordan's "sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence." [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] Becker and Polkinghorn (2017) argue that the essay's ideas were refined in "A Clean Break"; that is an argument about intellectual lineage, and the next document can be checked against it. [cite:ir13_wiki_yinon]

"A Clean Break", 1996

A Clean Break: A New Strategy for Securing the Realm came from a study group of the Institute for Advanced Strategic and Political Studies led by Richard Perle, with James Colbert, Charles Fairbanks Jr., Douglas Feith, Jonathan Torop, David Wurmser, Meyrav Wurmser and the institute's president, Robert Loewenberg, and was addressed to Netanyahu's incoming government in 1996. [cite:ir13_wiki_cleanbreak] Feith says he "neither wrote it nor signed it" and names David Wurmser as its principal author. [cite:ir13_feith_cleanbreak] Its authors were American policy advocates, not Israeli officials.

Its territorial content is real but limited. It urged Israel to drop "land for peace" in favour of "peace for peace", on the basis of "the unconditional acceptance by Arabs of our rights, especially in their territorial dimension"; it recommended "rejecting 'land for peace' deals on the Golan Heights"; and in a draft passage offered for the new prime minister to deliver, it said: "Our claim to the land - to which we have clung for hope for 2000 years - is legitimate and noble." [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak] That is a programme of keeping the territory Israel then held, the Golan in particular, and refusing to trade it. The text reviewed does not mention the West Bank by name, Judea and Samaria or settlements, and it claims no territory beyond the lines Israel held in 1996. Its phrase about "a redrawing of the map of the Middle East" describes what Syria might fear from the regional changes the paper proposed, not an Israeli border. [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak] Its strategic proposals concerned Syria and Iraq: weakening and "rolling back" Syria and removing Saddam Hussein, with Turkey and Jordan. [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak]

The paper is often cited as a Greater Israel blueprint and as the plan behind the Iraq war. The first reading does not survive its text, which is about refusing withdrawal, not about expansion. The second is the argument already weighed in [scene:ir13_papers|the Iran volume]: several of its authors held posts in Washington by 2002, and critics such as John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt saw a line from the paper to the war, while others, including CBS's David Martin, found no evidence of decisive influence. [cite:ir13_wiki_cleanbreak] Netanyahu did not adopt the paper as a document. His first government signed the Hebron Protocol of 17 January 1997 and redeployed from most of Hebron, and on 23 October 1998 he signed the Wye River Memorandum, which committed Israel to transfer a further 13 per cent of the West Bank from Area C to Palestinian control: land in exchange for Palestinian security commitments, the kind of trade the paper had urged him to refuse. [cite:gi10_crs_wye] [cite:ir13_wiki_cleanbreak] Israel carried out only about 2 percentage points of that transfer before implementation stalled. [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas]

The 10-agora coin

The third misread item is an object. At a specially convened session of the UN Security Council in Geneva on 25 May 1990, Yasser Arafat said of Israel's 10-agora coin: "This document is a 'map of Greater Israel' which is inscribed on this Israeli coin". Earlier that spring, at an Arab League committee meeting on 9 April 1990 and in the days after it, he had said the map was stamped "directly under" the menorah. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:gi10a_pipes] [cite:gi10_wiki_agorot] He relied on a 1989 article in the journal GeoJournal by the British geographer Gwyn Rowley, who wrote that the coin's background shape "seemingly" outlined an area reaching Amman, Beirut, Baghdad and Damascus and framed it as speculation. [cite:gi10_wiki_agorot]

The coin is real and its design is documented. The Bank of Israel describes its face as a "replica of a coin issued by Mattathias Antigonus (37 - 40 B.C.E.) with the seven-branched candelabrum", the last Hasmonean king, whose coin was struck around the Roman siege of Jerusalem in 37 BCE. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] The modern coin was issued on 4 September 1985 and its face was designed by Nathan Karp. [cite:gi10_boi_coins] The same design had appeared on the 100-sheqel coin in 1984. [cite:gi10_wiki_agorot] The irregular outline that Rowley and Arafat read as a map is, on the designer's account as Pipes reports it, the general outline of the ancient coin, reproduced with its design. Ya'akov Meshorer of the Israel Museum told the Jerusalem Post in June 1990 that "Karp was astounded" that anyone could see a coastline in it. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] A Hebrew University scholar, S. M. Berkowicz, answered Rowley in the same journal in 1991, calling the claim undocumented and without foundation; Rowley replied that the coin may have been chosen for its map-like shape. [cite:gi10a_wiki_agorot] The Bank of Israel's stated position is that the design was chosen for its historical value. [cite:gi10a_wiki_agorot] The verdict is misreading: a real coin carrying an ancient design, not a map.

sections.h: Two Myths: The Inscription and the Stripes
sections.html:
The third class is made of claims for which there is no supporting evidence, or for which the documented origin is something else. Two have travelled furthest: that the Knesset bears an inscription promising Israel the land from the Nile to the Euphrates, and that the two blue stripes on Israel's flag stand for those rivers. Both have been repeated by heads of state, and the Nile-to-Euphrates charge they are used to illustrate appears in the founding charter of an armed movement. Both are myths. This section sets out who made each claim, when, and what the record shows.

The Knesset inscription

The earliest dated version found is a newspaper error that was corrected. On 21 January 1980 the Christian Science Monitor ran a story, "Egyptians dispute Sadat bid to give Nile water to Israel," which attributed the slogan "From the Nile to the Euphrates" to the Israeli parliament building. A week later the paper printed a correction: "No such inscription is on the building." [cite:gi10_csm_1980]

The claim did not stop there. Daniel Pipes, in his 1994 survey of the Nile-to-Euphrates charge, recorded that Syria's president Hafiz al-Asad, his defence minister Mustafa Tlas and Iran's president had all said that the words "The Land of Israel from the Euphrates to the Nile" were carved over the Knesset's entrance, citing a report in Al-Jazira of 17 January 1982. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] Yasser Arafat added a twist at a meeting of the Arab League's Jerusalem Committee on 9 April 1990: the sign, he said, "remained for ten years" and had since been restored. Days later he changed his account, saying the plaque had been removed and the map engraved on the 10-agora coin instead. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:gi10a_pipes] Pipes observed that no one had ever seen it, and that a visitor who toured the building without finding it was told "it was removed in anticipation of his visit." [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny]

Pipes was himself a participant in the debate he surveyed, and a finding that rests on him alone would be weak. This one does not. The 1980 correction came from a newspaper with no stake in the dispute, which checked its own story and withdrew the claim. [cite:gi10_csm_1980] The Knesset's own description of its ceremonial Chagall State Hall lists three tapestries, twelve floor mosaics and a wall mosaic, on themes from the Bible, Jerusalem and the return of exiles, with no map and no border inscription. [cite:gi10_jvl_chagall] No photograph of the inscription and no date of its supposed removal or replacement appear in any source found. The claim that it was removed before each visit is the kind that cannot be tested, because it explains away every failure to find it. The verdict is myth: there is no evidence that the inscription exists or ever existed.

The flag's stripes

In an interview with Playboy published in September 1988, Arafat said that the two horizontal blue lines on Israel's flag represent the Nile and the Euphrates, "and in between is Israel." [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] The same year, the Covenant of the Islamic Resistance Movement, Hamas, issued on 18 August 1988, stated in Article 32: "After Palestine, the Zionists aspire to expand from the Nile to the Euphrates." [cite:hm_avalon_charter] The covenant does not mention the flag; it is quoted here as Hamas's own stated position, and its treatment of the "Zionists" as a single actor is the collective attribution this volume does not make. The flag reading has since been repeated in many places. [cite:gi10_wiki_flag]

The flag's history is documented, and it predates the State of Israel by half a century. Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs states that "the blue stripes on the Zionist flag were inspired by the stripes on the tallit (prayer shawl)," the shawl worn in Jewish prayer, and that Zionist tradition credits the design to David Wolffsohn, with the flag adopted by the Zionist movement at Basel. [cite:gi10_mfa_flag] Wolffsohn's own account reads: "The talith (prayer shawl) with which we wrap ourselves when we pray: that is our symbol." [cite:gi10_wiki_flag] Blue and white had been proposed as Jewish colours in Ludwig August Frankl's poem "Juda's Farben" in 1864, and the settlement of Rishon LeZion carried a blue-and-white flag with a Star of David in 1885. [cite:gi10_wiki_flag] The Provisional Council of State voted unanimously on 28 October 1948 to adopt the Zionist flag as the flag of the state. [cite:gi10_mfa_flag] Its proclamation specified two dark sky-blue stripes 25 cm wide on a white field and a Star of David between them; it said nothing about rivers. [cite:gi10_wiki_flag]

The design therefore came from a prayer garment, decades before there was a state with borders to claim. The verdict is myth. Arab writers have also rejected the wider belief: Saqr Abu Fakhr, in Al-Hayat in November 1997, listed the Nile-to-Euphrates belief among popular misconceptions about Jews that the evidence refutes. [cite:gi10_wiki_flag]

Why the distinction matters

The myths share a structure. Each takes an object that every visitor to Israel can see, a parliament, a flag or a coin, and attaches to it a territorial meaning that no Israeli law, platform or official statement gives it. Each was repeated by leaders of states and movements then at war or in conflict with Israel, and each claims to have found a secret plan written into the state's public symbols. None survives a check of the object itself. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:gi10_csm_1980] [cite:gi10_mfa_flag] [cite:gi10_boi_coins]

They also do damage to the question this volume asks. The documented evidence for territorial maximalism in Israeli politics is substantial, and it lies elsewhere: in the 1977 Likud platform's statement that between the sea and the Jordan "there will only be Israeli sovereignty", in the 2022 coalition guidelines' claim of an "exclusive and inalienable right to all parts of the Land of Israel", in the annexation motions of 2025 and the maps a prime minister showed at the United Nations ([scene:gi5_likud|Part Five], [scene:gi6_votes|Part Six], [scene:gi7_maps|Part Seven]). [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] [cite:wb_toi_71_13] That evidence concerns the West Bank, Gaza and the Golan, not the Nile. An argument built on an inscription no one has seen can be dismissed in a sentence, and the documented record dismissed with it. Keeping the three classes apart is what lets the real documents be weighed on their own terms.

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: The Religious Engine
chapters.intro: Part Eleven follows the religious currents that gave the claim to the whole land its most uncompromising form, and the religious voices that rejected it. It traces the line from Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook and his Mercaz HaRav yeshiva to his son Zvi Yehuda Kook, whose teaching that no government may give up any part of the land inspired Gush Emunim, and from there to the Religious Zionism party and Otzma Yehudit in Netanyahu's government, with their standing on the eve of the October 2026 election. It then turns to the Temple Mount: the arrangement Israel and Jordan have maintained there since 1967, the movements that seek a Third Temple, and the changes in practice between 2023 and 2026. Last, and briefly, it sets out what American Christian Zionist organisations and one US ambassador have said about the land. Throughout, the claims are attributed to named rabbis, movements, parties and officials, and set beside the many religious Jews and Christians, and their institutions, who held otherwise.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven found a documented religious version of the whole-land claim, held by named people rather than by a faith. Zvi Yehuda Kook taught that "no prime minister has the authority to renounce any part of the country," his students founded Gush Emunim, and their political heirs in the Religious Zionism party wrote sovereignty in the West Bank into the coalition agreement of 2022; one of them, Smotrich, was quoted saying that "the future of Jerusalem is to expand to Damascus," a statement no plan or law has followed. [cite:gi11_wiki_zvikook] [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:gi5_cgtn_sov] [cite:gi6_wiki_37gov] [cite:gi11_newarab_damascus] Against it stood Meimad, Netivot Shalom, Ovadia Yosef's 1979 ruling that land may be returned to save life, and the Satmar rejection of the state's rule itself; Israel's own institutions banned Kach. [cite:gi11_mjl_moderate] [cite:gi11_toi_ovadia] [cite:gi11_wiki_satmar] [cite:gi11_wiki_kach] On the Temple Mount, the government's stated policy as of October 2026 was that the status quo stood, while a minister led Jewish prayer there, the prime minister said such prayer did not breach the arrangement, and Jordan condemned each step. [cite:gi11_toi_tishabav25] [cite:gi11_na_netanyahu2026] [cite:gi11_reuters_tishabav26] In the United States, CUFI opposed American pressure for concessions, and the US ambassador's "It would be fine if they took it all" was condemned across the Arab world and called hyperbolic by Huckabee himself, without becoming policy. [cite:gi11_jpost_hagee] [cite:gi11_abc_huckabee] [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] Part Twelve sets out the counter-record in full: the withdrawals, the treaties and the Israelis who opposed expansion. [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve: The Counter-Record]

sections.h: The Kook Lineage and Religious Zionism
sections.html:
"Religious Zionism" names two different things, and the difference matters for this book. It is the name of a broad current within Orthodox Judaism that treats the modern state as religiously significant, and it is also the name of a specific political party led by Bezalel Smotrich. Neither is a synonym for religious Jews. Many observant Jews and several of their best-known authorities rejected the territorial theology traced here, and this section sets their record beside it. The political scientist Nadav Shelef, who followed how religious nationalist groups defined the homeland from 1925 to 2005, found that their claims changed over time: a minority backed a Nile-to-Euphrates homeland in 1925, the mainstream later narrowed its claim to Israel, the Golan, Gaza and the West Bank, and a hardline wing later revived the larger claim. [cite:gi1_wiki_greaterisrael] The lineage below is the one through which the post-1967 claim to the whole land acquired its religious form. [scene:gi1_versions|Part One: the versions]

Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook and Mercaz HaRav, 1904–1935

Abraham Isaac Kook (1865–1935) came from the Russian Empire to serve as rabbi of Jaffa in 1904–05, became the first Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Mandatory Palestine in 1921 and founded the Mercaz HaRav yeshiva in Jerusalem in 1924. Unlike most Orthodox authorities of his day, he respected the secular Zionist pioneers, worked with them and, in theological terms, hailed them as playing a role in "hastening the messianic deliverance." He supported the settlement of the land and held that the Western Wall and the Temple Mount were holy sites belonging to the Jewish people. [cite:gi11_wiki_aikook] [cite:gi11a_wiki_aikook] The same rabbi also ruled that Jews must not enter the Temple Mount because the purity laws could not be observed, a ruling the Chief Rabbinate still cited in 2013 against the activists who now go up to the site. [cite:gi11_toi_rabbis2013] His legacy therefore pointed in more than one direction, and the next section returns to that ruling. [scene:gi11_temple|The Temple Mount]

The son's theology of the whole land, 1967–1982

His son, Zvi Yehuda Kook (1891–1982), ran Mercaz HaRav from 1952 until his death. [cite:gi11_wiki_zvikook] At the yeshiva's celebration of Israel's nineteenth Independence Day in May 1967, about three weeks before the war, he spoke last and, in the account of one student, Yitzhak Shilat, "with a rage and fury that I had never heard before": "Where is our Hebron? Are we forgetting it?" He repeated the verse "My land was divided." After the June war, in which Israel took Hebron, Nablus (Shechem) and the rest of the West Bank, his students treated the speech as prophecy and distributed tens of thousands of copies. [cite:gi11_ynet_hebron] [cite:gi11a_ynet_hebron] He hailed the victory as a sign of divine leadership and signed the September 1967 manifesto of the Movement for the Whole Land of Israel. [cite:gi11_wiki_zvikook] [cite:gi4_inss_einav] [scene:gi4_movement|Part Four: the Movement]

After the 1973 war he opposed every proposal to give up territory. In a 1974 lecture he warned that yielding the Golan and the West Bank would mean a war fought "over our bodies and limbs," and he stated the principle in one line: "No one, no prime minister, has the authority to renounce any part of the country." He opposed Menachem Begin's negotiations with Egypt because, he said, Sinai "formed part of Biblical Israel." [cite:gi11_wiki_zvikook] [cite:gi11a_wiki_zvikook] His students, together with religious war veterans and activists from the youth wing of the National Religious Party, founded Gush Emunim, the "Bloc of the Faithful," in early 1974; its campaign to settle the hills of Samaria, removed by the army seven times before the government compromised at Sebastia in 1975, is told in the West Bank volume. [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:wb_ej_gush] [scene:wb4_movement|The West Bank: the settler movement] He died on 9 March 1982, about six weeks before the last of Sinai was handed back to Egypt. [cite:gi11_ynet_hebron]

This is the documented core of the religious version of the whole-land claim: a named rabbi, a named yeshiva and a named movement, which held that the land was not the government's to give. It was not the position of the Israeli governments of the day, which signed the Sinai withdrawal over his objection.

From movement to party

The current reached government through parties. The Religious Zionism party, led by Smotrich, ran in 2022 on a joint list with Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit that won 14 seats, and its coalition agreement with Likud of 1 December 2022 stated that "the prime minister will lead the formulation and advancement of policies within the framework of applying sovereignty in Judea and Samaria, while choosing the timing and weighing all of the State of Israel's national and international interests", and gave Smotrich civil powers there. [cite:gi11_reuters_rzp2026] [cite:gi5_cgtn_sov] [cite:gi6_wiki_37gov] [cite:gi5_ih_rzdeal] In a March 2025 profile, NPR quoted Smotrich: "My long-term desire is for the state of Israel to be governed according to the Torah." He objects to the word annexation, which, he said, "implies taking something that isn't yours," and says the West Bank, which he calls Judea and Samaria, "belongs to us." [cite:gi11_npr_smotrich] [cite:gi11a_npr_smotrich] His September 2025 proposal to apply sovereignty to 82 per cent of the West Bank is examined in Part Six. [cite:gi6_toi_82pct] [scene:gi6_votes|Part Six: the votes]

One statement goes beyond the West Bank. In the ARTE documentary Israel: Extremists in Power, reported in October 2024, Smotrich was quoted as saying: "It is written that the future of Jerusalem is to expand to Damascus." The outlet that reported it added a list of countries into which, it said, he wanted the state to extend; that list is the outlet's paraphrase, not his words, and this book found no clarification from Smotrich or the government. [cite:gi11_newarab_damascus] It is a documented statement by a named minister about scripture. It is not a government decision, and no plan, map or law to that effect was found.

Kahanism is a separate current, and the mainstream of the religious camp itself treated it as such. Rabbi Meir Kahane's Kach party called for the "immediate annexation of every part of Israel that is in our hands" and for every Arab in Israel to be offered "the right of residence as a non-citizen", with compensation for property for those who left. Israel's own institutions excluded it: the Central Elections Committee disqualified it in 1988 as "manifestly racist," and the cabinet outlawed it in 1994 after its supporters praised Baruch Goldstein's massacre of 29 Palestinian worshippers in Hebron. [cite:gi11_wiki_kach] [cite:gi11a_wiki_kach] Ben-Gvir was a Kach youth coordinator, was convicted of incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organisation, and kept Goldstein's portrait on his wall until about 2020; his party entered the Knesset in 2021 on a joint list arranged with Netanyahu's backing. [cite:hm_jvl_bengvir] [cite:hm_wiki_otzma] [scene:hm12_bengvir|The Hamas Architecture: Ben-Gvir]

As of October 2026, before the election of 27 October, the two parties were running separately. Religious Zionism held seven of the Knesset's 120 seats and, in polls reported between June and August, hovered around the 3.25 per cent electoral threshold (some reports give 3.5), below it in a June poll and just above it, at about five seats, in August; Smotrich rejected a renewed joint list in August, and Ben-Gvir had said in June that the two must run apart. The June poll gave Otzma Yehudit eight seats. [cite:gi11_reuters_rzp2026] [cite:gi11_jpost_rzp2026] [cite:gi11_toi_bg2026] Some former supporters told Reuters that Smotrich "no longer represents the values of Religious Zionism," over his handling of the ultra-Orthodox draft. [cite:gi11_reuters_rzp2026]

The religious counter-record

Within Religious Zionism itself, Oz VeShalom, founded about a year after Gush Emunim, and its successor Netivot Shalom argued that some in the movement had made the state an end in itself, above "justice, peace, and life itself," and in the 1990s supported the peace process including a Palestinian state.
