Rabbi Yehuda Amital, head of the Har Etzion yeshiva in a West Bank settlement bloc, founded Meimad in 1988; it held that putting the Land of Israel above all other values contradicts the Torah and was open to territorial compromise. On 9 May 2003, 170 religious Zionists published a manifesto urging the movement to give up control of the territories. [cite:gi11_mjl_moderate] [cite:gi11a_mjl_moderate] Meimad held a Knesset seat on Labor's list from 1999 until 2009. [cite:gi11_wiki_meimad]

The leading Sephardi authority of his generation, Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, spiritual leader of the Shas party, ruled in 1979, as peace with Egypt was debated, that "nothing is more important than the saving of life" and that it was permitted to return territory to achieve lasting peace; Shas's abstention helped the Oslo Accords pass in 1993, though he opposed the 2005 Gaza withdrawal. [cite:gi11_toi_ovadia] A letter published in 2013, undated and of unstated provenance, has him declaring land for peace void during the Second Intifada; it rests on one source and is treated here as unverified. [cite:gi11_jp_ovadia] Further from the state, the Satmar Hasidic movement, the largest Hasidic group, followed Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum in calling Zionism "a severe heresy"; after 1967 he held that the war was no miracle and forbade prayer at the Western Wall and the other captured holy sites, so as not to legitimise Israeli rule. [cite:gi11_wiki_satmar] The older argument from the Three Oaths is set out in the Road to 1948 volume. [scene:oaths_s01|Does scripture forbid a Jewish state?]

sections.h: The Temple Mount: The Status Quo and the Third Temple Movements
sections.html:
The walled platform in Jerusalem's Old City is the holiest site in Judaism, where the two ancient temples stood, and, as the Haram al-Sharif with the al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock, the third holiest site in Islam. [cite:gi11_reuters_tishabav26] It is not a border question in the way the Golan or the Jordan Valley are, but it belongs in this part for two documented reasons: the movements that seek a Third Temple on the site draw on the same religious nationalism traced in the previous section, and a serving minister has called for Israeli "sovereignty and governance" over it. [cite:gi11_toi_tishabav25] This section sets out the arrangement that governs the site, who has sought to change it, what changed between 2023 and 2026, and what Israel's government, Jordan and others have said.

The arrangement of 1967

When Israel took the Old City in June 1967 it took control of the site but left its administration with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, a religious trust run from Jordan; it barred the Israeli flag from flying over it and did not extend several of its laws on holy places there. The Chief Rabbinate declared that Jews were forbidden to enter, because the ritual purity required to approach the former Temple's grounds could not be attained. [cite:gi11_wiki_entry] The result, known as the status quo, is usually summarised as: Muslims pray, others may visit. It was never written into Israeli legislation. [cite:gi11_jp_aug2024] [cite:gi11_cnn_tishabav25]

Jordan's role has a treaty basis. In Article 9 of the 1994 peace treaty, Israel undertook to respect "the present special role of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in Muslim Holy shrines in Jerusalem." [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] In 2013 King Abdullah II and the Palestinian president, Mahmoud Abbas, signed an agreement recognising the king's custodianship of the Jerusalem holy sites, though neither Jordan nor the Palestinian Authority controls them in practice. After violence in October 2015, the US secretary of state, John Kerry, announced that Israel had accepted King Abdullah's proposal for round-the-clock monitoring, and Netanyahu reaffirmed Israel's "commitment to upholding unchanged the status quo of the Temple Mount, in word and in practise." [cite:gi11_aje_2015] The site has repeatedly been the point at which wider violence began: the Second Intifada followed Ariel Sharon's visit on 28 September 2000, and the Gaza war of May 2021 followed police raids on the compound. [cite:gz_wiki_intifada2] [cite:gz_wiki_2021] [scene:gz3_oslo|Gaza, Documented: Oslo to the intifada]

The Third Temple movements

The best documented of the groups that seek to rebuild the Temple is the Temple Institute, founded in Jerusalem in 1987 by Rabbi Yisrael Ariel with the stated aim of establishing the Third Temple and restoring its rites. It has made many of the more than ninety ritual objects it says the Temple requires, among them the high priest's breastplate and golden crown. Israel's education and culture ministries were reported to have given it between NIS 300,000 and NIS 700,000 over a decade, a sum its directors have described as neither reliable nor significant. [cite:gi11_wiki_templeinst] In September 2022 five red heifers were flown in from Texas, donated by an evangelical farmer, for the purification ritual that some hold must precede the Temple's rebuilding; the Temple Institute and an evangelical group, Boneh Israel, were involved, and the director general of Israel's Ministry of Jerusalem Affairs and Heritage spoke at the airport when they arrived. Hamas's military spokesman cited the heifers in a January 2024 speech as evidence of a plan against al-Aqsa. [cite:gi11_aje_heifers]

These groups are a minority position within Judaism, not its consensus. Orthodox opinion broadly expects the Temple to be rebuilt but divides over whether by human hands or by divine act, and the Temple Institute's reading of Maimonides has, in one reference account's words, "aroused substantial opposition." [cite:gi11_wiki_templeinst] The Chief Rabbis of Israel, Ashkenazi and Sephardi, reaffirmed the ban on Jews entering the site in December 2013, citing Abraham Isaac Kook's ruling and stating that the decision had "absolutely nothing to do with the political situation"; at the time, mainly national-religious groups encouraged visits, partly to assert a Jewish claim. [cite:gi11_toi_rabbis2013] Haredi authorities generally prohibit entry; some Religious Zionist rabbis permit it under purity rules or treat it as a commandment. [cite:gi11_wiki_entry]

What changed, 2023–2026

The change came through practice and through a minister. Ben-Gvir, as national security minister responsible for the police, said on 26 August 2024 that "the policies on the Temple Mount allow prayer, period." [cite:gi11_jp_aug2024] The Prime Minister's Office answered the same day that "there is no change to the status quo" and that "it is the government and the prime minister who determine policy on the Temple Mount"; the defence minister, Yoav Gallant, called his ascent "dangerous, unnecessary and irresponsible." [cite:gi11_jp_aug2024] On 3 August 2025, the fast of Tisha B'Av, Ben-Gvir openly led prayers on the Mount, reported as the first time a minister had done so, and demanded that Israel enforce "sovereignty and governance" there. Netanyahu's office replied that the policy of maintaining the status quo "has not changed and will not change." Jordan called the visit "an unacceptable provocation" and said Israel had "no sovereignty over the blessed Al-Aqsa Mosque"; Saudi Arabia said such acts "fuel conflict in the region." The Times of Israel reported that police enforcement against Jewish prayer had grown more lenient over the previous three years. [cite:gi11_toi_tishabav25] [cite:gi11_cnn_tishabav25]

In January 2026 Netanyahu said that allowing Jewish prayer "does not breach" the status quo and that policy there was coordinated with him; police had by then allowed Jewish prayer in the compound's eastern sector for about two years, and the deputy attorney general, Gil Limon, warned that Ben-Gvir was altering the status quo unilaterally. [cite:gi11_na_netanyahu2026] On 23 July 2026, Tisha B'Av again, Ben-Gvir filmed himself at the site praising Jewish visitors who had prayed: "Jews praying, feeling like they're the owners of the place." He added: "This has never happened before." Jordan's foreign ministry called it "a desecration of the sanctity of the mosque, an escalation, a barbaric act, and unacceptable provocation"; Netanyahu's office did not immediately comment. [cite:gi11_reuters_tishabav26] [cite:gi11_olj_tishabav26] [cite:gi11a_olj_tishabav26]

The consequences are documented in one of Israel's own reports. In March 2025 the Shin Bet listed, among three factors in Hamas's timing of the attack of 7 October 2023, Israel's handling of far-right Jewish religious activity at the al-Aqsa compound, alongside harsher treatment of prisoners and the perception that Israel's social cohesion had weakened during the protests over the judicial overhaul. [cite:gi11_npr_shinbet] That is the security service's assessment of Hamas's reasoning, not a finding that the policy caused the attack, and Hamas's own statements are examined in the Hamas volume. [scene:hm7_knew|The Hamas Architecture: what was known]

As of October 2026, then, the documented position is this. The Israeli government's stated policy is that the status quo stands; no law or written cabinet decision changing it was found. In practice Jewish prayer has been tolerated in part of the compound, a serving minister has led it, and the prime minister has said that this does not breach the arrangement. Jordan, which holds a treaty-recognised role at the site, has called each step a violation. The Third Temple movements remain small and rabbinically contested, with modest documented state support. What links them to the Greater Israel question, on this book's reading, is not a map but a line of argument: Zvi Yehuda Kook held that no government could give up any part of the land, and Ben-Gvir has demanded Israeli "sovereignty and governance" on the Mount.

sections.h: Christian Zionist Land Theology in the United States
sections.html:
The third religious current behind the whole-land claim is not Jewish. Christian Zionism, the belief among some Protestants that the modern state of Israel fulfils biblical prophecy and that Christians are bound to support it, has its own history, from John Nelson Darby's dispensationalism in the 1830s to the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909, which the Road to 1948 volume sets out. [scene:s05|The Scofield Reference Bible] The verse most often cited, Genesis 12:3 ("I will bless those who bless you"), and the two Christian readings of it are discussed in the opening chapter. [scene:gx_s05|One verse, two readings] A later volume, The Theology Shield, treats the subject in depth. This section confines itself to one question: what named American Christian Zionist organisations and officials have said about the land, and what the record shows of their effect.

CUFI and John Hagee

The largest organisation is Christians United for Israel, which the San Antonio pastor John Hagee incorporated on 7 February 2006, reviving the name of a group founded in 1975. Its membership figures are its own: one million in 2012, two million in 2015, 5.1 million in 2018, and "over 10 million" in an undated claim. Its annual Washington summit sends delegates to lobby members of Congress, and Netanyahu has addressed it, by video in 2010 and again remotely, from Jerusalem, at the 2019 summit where Vice President Mike Pence spoke. [cite:ts8a_inn_netanyahu2019] [cite:gi11_wiki_cufi]

Hagee has stated the land theology directly. In a CUFI webcast on 6 January 2011 he said: "Jerusalem should never be divided for any reason. It is the property of the people of Israel." Citing Genesis 13, 15 and 17, he said that "God did not make a covenant with Washington, D.C. He made a covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob," and that "that covenant stands." [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] His stated policy position is narrower than the theology. The Christian Post corrected its first report to say that Hagee was sceptical of land-for-peace agreements but held that Israel's government should make its own decisions; elsewhere he said that "Israelis – and they alone – have the right to make existential decisions about land and peace," and described CUFI's action as "asking the White House not to pressure Israel into making territorial concessions that she does not wish to make." [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] [cite:gi11_jpost_hagee] He also said that he and other Christian Zionists had grown sceptical of withdrawals after south Lebanon and Gaza. [cite:gi11_jpost_hagee] In policy terms, then, the documented CUFI position is opposition to American pressure for territorial concessions, not a programme of expansion beyond the lines Israel holds.

What American evangelicals told pollsters

The most detailed survey of the belief behind this is LifeWay Research's poll of 2,002 Americans with evangelical beliefs, conducted from 20 to 28 September 2017 and sponsored by Chosen People Ministries and the author Joel C. Rosenberg. Eighty per cent agreed that Israel's founding in 1948 fulfilled biblical prophecy, and 63 per cent said they supported Israel because "God gave the land of Israel to the Jewish people." Yet only 23 per cent said Israel should sign a treaty giving the Palestinians a state in the West Bank and Gaza, 31 per cent disagreed, and 46 per cent were unsure. Support for Israel was 58 per cent among those aged 18 to 34 and 77 per cent among those 65 and over. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] The survey measures belief about the land; it does not show that respondents favoured Israeli rule beyond its present lines.

An ambassador and the Genesis map

The clearest point at which the theology met an office of state came in 2026. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, an evangelical Christian and long-standing supporter of the settlement movement, was asked by the commentator Tucker Carlson, in an interview aired on 20 February 2026, whether Israel had a right to the land promised to Abraham's descendants in Genesis, from the Nile to the Euphrates. He answered: "It would be fine if they took it all." He added that Israel was not seeking to expand, and when Carlson listed Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and large parts of Saudi Arabia and Iraq, replied: "Not sure we'd go that far. I mean, it would be a big piece of land." [cite:gi11_abc_huckabee]

The response was immediate. Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry called the remarks "extremist rhetoric" and "unacceptable" and asked the State Department to clarify its position; Egypt called them a "blatant violation" of international law and said that "Israel has no sovereignty over the occupied Palestinian territory or other Arab lands"; the Arab League called them "extremist and lacking any sound basis"; Jordan, Kuwait, Oman and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation also condemned them. [cite:gi11_abc_huckabee] [cite:gi11a_abc_huckabee] Huckabee then called his answer "somewhat of a hyperbolic statement," said of Israel that "they're not asking to take it over," and complained that the version Carlson posted "edited out my full response"; in the same exchange he said "Area C is Israel," which Al Jazeera noted appears to contradict the official US position opposing annexation. The State Department did not publicly address the remarks. [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] [cite:gi11a_aje_huckabee] Neither the US government nor Israel's adopted the statement as policy. The territorial claim in Genesis is discussed in Part One and the 2025 interview in which Netanyahu was asked about a "Greater Israel" in Part Seven. [scene:gi1_phrase|Part One: the phrase] [scene:gi7_interview|Part Seven: the interview]

A smaller link runs through the Temple Mount. The red heifers flown to Israel in 2022 for the purification rite that some Third Temple activists consider a precondition for rebuilding were donated by an evangelical farmer in Texas, and an evangelical group, Boneh Israel, was involved in raising them. [cite:gi11_aje_heifers] [scene:gi11_temple|The Temple Mount]

The Christian counter-record

Christian Zionism is not the position of American Christianity, nor of all evangelicals. In July 2007, 34 evangelical leaders signed a letter in The New York Times supporting a two-state solution. After Hagee's 2011 webcast, Richard Mouw, president of Fuller Theological Seminary, argued that God's promise to bless Ishmael in Genesis 17:20 also binds Christians today and that Israel's blessing depends partly on justice towards its neighbours, and Joel Hunter, a board member of the National Association of Evangelicals, said Hagee's view reflects "a limited portion of Christians who are millennial dispensationalists in their theology." [cite:gi11_cp_hagee2011] The Middle East Council of Churches and theologians in the Anglican and Catholic churches have criticised CUFI's Christian Zionist and end-times theology, and Hagee apologised after claiming that Hitler had been fulfilling God's will by helping to return Jews to Israel. [cite:gi11_wiki_cufi] [cite:gi11a_wiki_cufi] The 2017 survey's age gap points the same way: younger evangelicals were markedly less supportive than older ones. [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway]

The finding is limited and documented. Named organisations and a named US official have stated a theology in which the land promised in Genesis belongs to the Jewish people, and CUFI has lobbied Washington against pressing Israel to give territory up. The record examined here does not show that this theology set US policy on borders, and the one official who voiced its widest version, the ambassador, called it hyperbolic within two days while his government stayed silent. Whether the lobby's influence shaped specific decisions, such as the US embassy's move to Jerusalem or the recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan, is a question for The Theology Shield; this book records it as open.

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: The Counter-Record
chapters.intro: Part Twelve sets out the record that runs against the expansion thesis, with the same care given to the record that supports it. It begins with the withdrawals: Sinai and Gaza in 1957, the disengagements of 1974 and 1975 on the Suez and Golan fronts, the return of all of Sinai and the evacuation of Yamit in 1982, south Lebanon in 2000, and Gaza with four northern West Bank settlements in 2005. Alongside them are the peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan, the Oslo agreements and two large offers that were never concluded. It then gives the critics' reply, which holds that most of these withdrawals were forced or traded and that some have been reversed. The second section turns to the Israelis who have opposed expansion: the reserve officers who founded Peace Now, the monitors and petitioners, former security chiefs, politicians and the polls. It also sets out what Israel's governments have said when accused of seeking a Greater Israel, and what those denials leave open. The third section reads the Supreme Court's rulings, from Elon Moreh in 1979 to the striking down of the settlement Regulation Law in 2020, and the limits of what the court has been willing to decide.
chapters.outro: Part Twelve established that the counter-record is substantial and documented. Israel withdrew from captured territory in 1957, 1974, 1975, 1982, 1989, 2000 and 2005, and a Likud government returned all of Sinai and levelled Yamit. [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] [cite:gi12_jvl_syrdis] [cite:gi12_ied_sinai2] [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] [cite:gi8_enc_taba] [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] The treaties with Egypt and Jordan have held, and in 2023 the Foreign Ministry restated Israel's recognition of Jordan's territorial integrity. [cite:gi8_avalon_egtreaty] [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] [cite:gi8_ynet_mfajordan] Israelis have opposed expansion in organised and costly ways, from the Officers' Letter of 1978 to the letter of 25 former security chiefs in 2019. In July 2026, 59 percent of Israelis polled opposed annexation into one state with limited Palestinian rights, and the High Court struck down the law legalising settlement homes on private Palestinian land in June 2020. [cite:gi12_pn_officers] [cite:gi12_jn_25chiefs] [cite:gi12_jvl_polls] [cite:gi12_toi_reglaw2020] The same record has a second side. Most withdrawals came under pressure or in exchange for something. Sharon's adviser described the Gaza disengagement as "formaldehyde" for the peace process, and the northern West Bank evacuation was partly reversed in 2023. [cite:rs_cw3_barjoseph_hdiplo] [cite:gi12_un_weisglass] [cite:gi12_toi_repeal2023] The court has limited how land is taken, not whether settlement continues, and most of the opposition's leaders reject annexation and a Palestinian state alike. [cite:wb_wiki_stateland] [cite:gi12_aje_contenders] The official denials rule out claims on Sinai and Jordan but leave the West Bank open, and on Syria they shifted from "temporary" to "indefinitely" within weeks. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_ike_bg] [cite:gi12_olj_saar] [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] Part Thirteen turns from maps and laws to what the operations of 2023–2026 did to the people and places in their path, beginning with Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon. [scene:gi14_gaza|Part Thirteen: the ledger]

sections.h: The Withdrawals and the Treaties
sections.html:
A territorial programme pursued by every Israeli government would leave a record of land taken and kept. The record contains that, and it also contains the opposite: eight withdrawals from captured territory, in seven different years between 1957 and 2005, three peace agreements, and two offers of large withdrawals that were never concluded. This section sets them out in order, and then gives the critics' reply, which is that almost every withdrawal came under pressure and several were meant to secure what was kept. Both are part of the record. The fullest single account, the return of Sinai, is in Part Eight. [scene:gi8_sinai|Part Eight: Sinai and Egypt]

From Sinai 1957 to the Suez Canal 1975

The first withdrawal followed the Suez war. Israel took Gaza and all of Sinai in November 1956, and on 8 November Ben-Gurion wrote to Eisenhower: "We have never planned to annex the Sinai desert." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_ike_bg] The government nonetheless tried for four months to keep Gaza, and left only after a UN resolution, an American aide-mémoire and Eisenhower's public demand. Israel left Gaza on 8 March 1957 and Sinai the same month. [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_1124] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_bg_mar57] [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] Part Three sets out the episode and its two readings. [scene:gi3_sinai56|Part Three: the Sinai test]

The 1973 war produced three more. In January 1974 Israel pulled its forces back from the western bank of the Suez Canal. [cite:gi12_ied_sinai2] The Israel–Syria agreement signed in Geneva on 31 May 1974 put all territory east of "Line A" under Syrian administration, let Syrian civilians return, and placed a UN force of about 1,200 between the armies; Israeli forces stopped at a separate line around Kuneitra. [cite:gi12_jvl_syrdis] The town of Quneitra returned to Syrian civil control when the agreement took effect on 6 June. It came back largely demolished. A report commissioned by the UN concluded that Israeli forces had destroyed it deliberately before leaving, and the General Assembly condemned the destruction on 29 November 1974 by 93 votes to 8. Israel's position was that most of the damage came from the 1967 and 1973 wars and the shelling between them. [cite:gi12_wiki_quneitra] In the second Sinai agreement, signed on 4 September 1975, Israel gave up the Mitla and Gidi passes and the Abu Rudeis oil fields. [cite:gi12_ied_sinai2] A US–Israel memorandum signed with it guaranteed Israel's oil supply for five years. [cite:ow1_jvl_moa1975]

Sinai 1982, Lebanon 2000, Gaza 2005

The Egypt–Israel treaty of 26 March 1979 required Israel to "withdraw all its armed forces and civilians from the Sinai." [cite:gi8_avalon_egtreaty] A Likud government did so. The handover ended on 25 April 1982, and the town of Yamit was evacuated and levelled. [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] When an arbitration panel ruled in 1988 that the 250-acre strip at Taba was Egyptian, Israel left it on 15 March 1989. [cite:gi8_enc_taba]

In southern Lebanon Ehud Barak had pledged to bring the soldiers home by July 2000, after a campaign led by the Four Mothers movement, which began when 73 soldiers died in a helicopter accident in 1997. [cite:hz4_csm_mothers] He ordered the withdrawal on 23 May 2000 and the last soldier left the next day. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz4_merip_2000] On 16 June 2000 the UN Secretary-General confirmed that Israel had complied with Security Council Resolution 425. Lebanon, backed by Syria, still claimed the Shebaa Farms, which the UN placed in the Syrian Golan. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] The Hezbollah volume tells the story. [scene:hz4_withdrawal|The Hezbollah Architecture: the withdrawal of 2000]

In Gaza, the withdrawal was carried out by Ariel Sharon, whom the analyst Marc Lynch describes as having held, with the Likud right, that a Palestinian state already existed in Jordan; he removed every settlement from Gaza. [cite:gi8_merip_nojordan] Likud members voted against his plan in a party referendum on 2 May 2004; the cabinet approved an amended version 14 to 7, and the Knesset passed the implementation law 59 to 40 on 16 February 2005. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] All 21 Gaza settlements were evacuated between 15 and 22 August 2005, with about 8,000 settlers removed, and the last soldier left on 12 September. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] [cite:gz_wiki_gushkatif] Four settlements in the northern West Bank, Homesh, Ganim, Kadim and Sa-Nur, were evacuated at the same time. They were the only West Bank settlements cleared. [cite:gi12_toi_repeal2023] Gaza, Documented covers the disengagement in full. [scene:gz3_withdrawal|Gaza, Documented: the withdrawal]

The treaties, and two offers not concluded

The Egyptian and Jordanian treaties have both held. The Jordanian treaty of 26 October 1994 committed both states to "respect each other's sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence" and fixed the border by the Mandate line. [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] On 20 March 2023, after Smotrich spoke at a podium bearing a map that included Jordan, Israel's Foreign Ministry stated that Israel "recognizes the territorial integrity of the Hashemite Kingdom." [cite:gi8_ynet_mfajordan] In the Oslo process Israel recognised the PLO "as the representative of the Palestinian people" on 9 September 1993, and the PLO recognised Israel's "right ... to exist in peace and security." [cite:gi12_jvl_letters1993] The interim agreement of 1995 handed parts of the West Bank to the Palestinian Authority, though Israel kept full control of Area C, 72 to 74 percent of the territory under Oslo II in 1995 and about 63 percent by a 2013 count. [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas]

Oslo's limits were stated by the prime minister who signed it. Presenting the 1995 agreement to the Knesset on 5 October, Yitzhak Rabin described a Palestinian "entity which is less than a state," said Israel's borders would be "beyond the lines which existed before the Six-Day War," set its security border in the Jordan Valley "in the broadest meaning of that term," and promised "not to uproot a single settlement" in the interim period. [cite:gi12_jvl_rabin1995] Later offers went further. In talks with Syria in 1994–2000 Rabin and then Barak discussed withdrawal from most or all of the Golan; the talks failed in March 2000 over a strip by Lake Tiberias. [cite:gi8_enc_syrtalks] In 2008 Ehud Olmert, by his own account, offered to keep 6.3 percent of the West Bank in exchange for Israeli land equal to 5.8 percent, and to place Jerusalem's Old City under international control. Mahmoud Abbas did not accept, saying Olmert had shown him a map but not given it to him. [cite:gi12_toi_olmert2008]

The critics' reply

Critics of the withdrawal record make three arguments. The first is that the withdrawals were forced. In 1957 the Eisenhower administration weighed cutting reparations, bond sales and aid; the historian Uri Bar-Joseph calls the pressure "brutal." [cite:rs_cw3_frus17_d120] [cite:rs_cw3_barjoseph_hdiplo] In 1975 Kissinger and Ford suspended arms deliveries to win the second Sinai agreement. [cite:gi12_ied_sinai2] Lebanon in 2000 followed fifteen years of attrition by Hezbollah, whose leader declared the withdrawal incomplete until the Shebaa Farms were "liberated." [cite:hz4_merip_2000]

The second argument is that land was given up to keep other land. Begin's autonomy plan of December 1977 gave residents of the West Bank and Gaza self-rule, entitled Israelis "to acquire land and settle" there, and left sovereignty "open." [cite:gi5_ecf_selfrule] In the decade in which Sinai was returned, the settler population of the West Bank, excluding East Jerusalem, grew from 4,400 in 1977 to 60,300 in 1987, by Peace Now's count. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] In Sinai itself, Sharon said "we have reached the red line of our concessions." [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] Gaza in 2005 is the case most cited. In an interview published by Haaretz on 6 October 2004, Sharon's adviser Dov Weisglass said that disengagement "supplies the amount of formaldehyde that is necessary so there will not be a political process with the Palestinians." He said a Palestinian state had been "removed indefinitely from our agenda," and that 190,000 of 240,000 settlers "will not be moved." [cite:gi12_un_weisglass] [cite:gi12_da_weisglass] Sharon's office said he remained committed to the road map. Weisglass told Israel Radio that Haaretz had cut part of one of his remarks, and that under existing conditions "there is not and will not be peace negotiations." [cite:gi12_ap_weisglass] [cite:gi12a_ap_weisglass] Six months earlier, President Bush had written to Sharon that, given "already existing major Israeli populations centers," a "full and complete return to the armistice lines of 1949" was unrealistic. [cite:gi12_ucsb_bush2004]

The third argument is that some withdrawals have been reversed. On 21 March 2023 the Knesset repealed, by 31 votes to 18, the clauses barring Israelis from the four northern West Bank sites. Labor's Gilad Kariv called it a "pre-annexation bill." [cite:gi12_toi_repeal2023] As of October 2026 Israel again holds ground it had left: positions in southern Lebanon, the Syrian buffer zone around Quneitra and Mount Hermon, and, by Human Rights Watch's estimate, about 64 percent of Gaza behind the Yellow Line, which Israeli officials have called a "new border" (Part Nine sets out the competing measures). [cite:hz8_un_unifil_year] [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] [cite:hz10s_eb_sufa] [cite:gz_hrw_anniv] Israel's stated reason in each case is security, not title. Part Nine examines those claims. [scene:gi9_lebanon|Part Nine: the buffer belt]

Read together, the record does not fit either strong claim. The withdrawals show that a single expansion plan was not carried out by every government: one Likud government gave up all of Sinai, and another took the settlers out of Gaza. The critics' evidence shows that most withdrawals came under pressure or as part of an exchange, while east Jerusalem and much of the West Bank, the land successive governments called central, were kept. That pattern is documented. Whether it amounts to a strategy is an argument, and Part Eighteen weighs it. [scene:gi13_record|Part Eighteen: settled, contested and open]

sections.h: Israelis Against Expansion, and the Official Denials
sections.html:
The ideology traced in this volume belongs to named movements, parties and officials. Other Israelis, also named, have opposed it from the start. In 1967, while the Movement for Greater Israel was calling on the government to keep all the captured land, Labor minister Yigal Allon drew up a narrower plan, designed to include as few Arabs as possible in the areas Israel would claim; successive cabinets never formally adopted it. [cite:gi4_wiki_mgi] [cite:gi4_wiki_allon] This section sets out the organised opposition, the security officials and politicians who have argued against annexation, what polling shows, and what Israel's governments have said when accused of seeking a Greater Israel. The opposition is real, but on several points it is narrower than its supporters abroad often assume.

Movements and monitors

Peace Now began with a letter. On 7 March 1978, while Begin was negotiating with Egypt, 348 reserve officers and soldiers wrote to him criticising a government that "prefers settlements beyond the Green Line to terminating the historic conflict." They warned that ruling about a million Arabs would endanger Israel's Jewish and democratic character, and said that "real security can be achieved only when we achieve peace." [cite:gi12_pn_officers] [cite:gi12_ecf_officers] After the Sabra and Shatila massacre in 1982 the movement says it helped bring 400,000 people into the streets to demand an inquiry. [cite:gi12_pn_officers] On 10 February 1983 a grenade thrown at a Peace Now rally outside the prime minister's office in Jerusalem killed one of its activists, Emil Grunzweig; the man who threw it, Yona Avrushmi, was convicted of murder in 1985. [cite:hz2b_wiki_grunzweig]

Since 1990 Peace Now's Settlement Watch has counted settlements, outposts and housing approvals, and much of the data in this volume comes from it. [cite:gi12_pn_officers] [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis] Other Israeli groups track the same ground and go to court. Yesh Din monitors police files on settler violence; Ir Amim, Bimkom and Peace Now are petitioners against the E1 plan east of Jerusalem. [cite:wb_yeshdin_2025] [cite:gi6_pn_e1tender] The recording of a June 2024 settlers' gathering at which Smotrich described "a separate civilian system" for the West Bank was supplied to the New York Times by a Peace Now researcher. [cite:gi6_bg_nyt_smotrich] Israeli monitors produced the core of the evidence against the policy they oppose. The West Bank volume covers this work in detail. [scene:wb7_watchers|The West Bank, Documented: the watchers]

Security chiefs and prime ministers

Some of the sharpest opposition has come from inside the security establishment. On 27 August 2019, twenty-five former senior security officials, among them former heads of the Mossad and the Shin Bet and three former advisers to Netanyahu, wrote to the four sponsors of a resolution in the US House of Representatives. Any unilateral annexation, they said, "will put Israel's security and safety" at risk, and they backed a negotiated two-state outcome. [cite:gi12_jn_25chiefs] [cite:gi12a_jn_25chiefs] Two prime ministers rejected the idea in plain words. In November 2006 Ehud Olmert recalled Ben-Gurion's choice of 1949: "we chose a Jewish State without the entire land of Israel." [cite:gi3_jvl_olmert2006] At a cabinet meeting in September 2008 he said "the notion of Greater Israel no longer exists, and anyone who still believes in it is deluding themselves." [cite:gi1_ynet_olmert]

Parties and votes

Several Knesset votes on settlement and annexation measures have been close. The 2017 law to legalise settlement homes on private Palestinian land passed 60 to 52. [cite:gi12_ynet_reglaw2018] When the Knesset reopened four northern West Bank sites in March 2023, Benny Gantz said it was "wrong to return to northern Samaria" and Labor called it a "pre-annexation bill." Two of Gantz's own colleagues, Gideon Sa'ar and Ze'ev Elkin, voted for it. [cite:gi12_toi_repeal2023] On 22 October 2025 a bill to apply sovereignty to the settlements passed its preliminary reading 25 to 24. Likud boycotted the vote. Yair Lapid and Gantz voted for a second bill, on Ma'ale Adumim alone, which passed 32 to 9. [cite:gi6_toi_readings] The record of the mainstream opposition is therefore mixed. Its leaders opposed the broad sovereignty bill, and Gantz backed the 2020 court ruling against the settlement law, but Lapid and Gantz voted to annex the largest settlement near Jerusalem. [cite:gi12_toi_reglaw2020] On the eve of the 27 October 2026 election, Al Jazeera reported that neither Naftali Bennett nor Lapid has supported a Palestinian state, and described Gadi Eisenkot as "notoriously ambiguous" on foreign policy. Of the leading contenders, only Yair Golan's Democrats treat a Palestinian state as a goal, and then "a distant, unspecified" one. [cite:gi12_aje_contenders] [cite:gi12a_aje_contenders] [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve]

What polling shows

Israeli polling separates two questions that are often merged abroad. Annexation does not command a majority. In the Tel Aviv University Peace Index of late July 2026, 59 percent of Israelis opposed annexing the territories to form a single state with limited Palestinian rights, and 28 percent supported it; among Jewish respondents support was 33 percent, down from 38 percent in March. [cite:gi12a_tau2026] In December 2024 the Institute for National Security Studies found 34 percent opposed to any annexation, with 21 percent for annexing the whole West Bank and 21 percent for the settlement areas only. [cite:gi12_jvl_polls] But a Palestinian state commands even less support. In the same 2026 poll 59 percent opposed one, and in September 2025 the Israel Democracy Institute found 70 percent calling a Palestinian state "undesirable" for Israel at that time. Asked to choose between the two, Jewish respondents preferred annexation by 42 percent to 26. [cite:gi12_jvl_polls] In April 2020, when annexation was on the cabinet's agenda, 45 percent supported it and 32 percent opposed. [cite:gi12_tml_idi2020]

The official denials

Israel's governments have repeatedly denied territorial aims beyond what they claim as security needs, and the denials vary in what they cover. On 8 November 1956 Ben-Gurion wrote that Israel had "never planned to annex the Sinai desert." [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_ike_bg] In June 2009 Netanyahu called the West Bank "the land of our forefathers" but accepted "a demilitarised Palestinian state" on conditions and said Israel had "no intention of building new settlements." [cite:gi5_aje_barilan] After Smotrich's Paris speech in March 2023 the Foreign Ministry restated Israel's recognition of Jordan's territorial integrity. [cite:gi8_ynet_mfajordan] When Netanyahu affirmed on i24NEWS in August 2025 that he felt connected to the vision of Greater Israel, in words reported variously as "very much" and "absolutely", his office and the Foreign Ministry, according to Haaretz, stressed that he had not used the words "Greater Israel" and was not responsible for the headlines. No on-record clarification by his office was found. [cite:gi7_olj_pendant] [scene:gi7_interview|Part Seven: the interview]

The denials over Syria have changed over time. On 9 December 2024 Foreign Minister Sa'ar called the move into the Syrian buffer zone "a limited and temporary step we took for security reasons." [cite:gi12_olj_saar] On 28 January 2025 Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army would stay on Mount Hermon and in the security zone indefinitely. [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] On the West Bank the governing party's line has been a denial of timing, not of aim. Boycotting the October 2025 readings, Likud said "true sovereignty" would not come from "a show-off law for the protocol." [cite:gi6_toi_readings]

The Israeli opposition record establishes that expansion has never been a national consensus. Officers, former security chiefs, a former prime minister, human rights groups and, in the latest poll cited, a majority of respondents (asked about one state with limited Palestinian rights) have rejected annexation, sometimes at personal risk. It also shows that rejecting annexation and supporting Palestinian statehood are different positions, and that by 2026 most of Israel's leading opposition figures held the first without the second. [cite:gi12_jvl_polls] [cite:gi12_aje_contenders]

sections.h: The Courts
sections.html:
Israel's Supreme Court, sitting as the High Court of Justice, hears petitions from Palestinians in the West Bank as well as from Israelis, and it has repeatedly been the place where the settlement enterprise met a legal limit. It has also approved much of that enterprise and left its foundations untouched. This section takes the rulings most often cited on each side. The West Bank volume covers the court's wider record on the territory. [scene:wb7_courts|The West Bank, Documented: the courts]

Elon Moreh, 1979: private land and military need

In the first decade of occupation the army requisitioned private Palestinian land for settlements on grounds of "military needs." In 1979 the landowners of Rujeib, near Nablus, challenged the seizure of their land for the Gush Emunim settlement of Elon Moreh, which Begin had welcomed after his election two years earlier. [cite:gi5_akevot_tzipori] The court ruled that the requisition was unlawful under Article 52 of the Hague Regulations. Political and ideological considerations, including the movement's pressure, had outweighed military need, and a military administration could not create facts meant to outlast military rule. [cite:wb_dweikat] The ruling closed one route to settlement and the government took another. Between 1979 and 1992 the authorities declared about 908,000 dunams "state land" under a strict reading of the Ottoman Land Code of 1858, about 16 percent of the West Bank by B'Tselem's count. Israel holds that such land is public land that it may administer in trust. [cite:wb_wiki_stateland] Part Five and the West Bank volume follow that mechanism. [scene:wb4_land|The West Bank, Documented: the land]

Amona, 2014–2017

Amona, an outpost near the settlement of Ofra, was built on land owned in part by Palestinians from the village of Silwad, who went to court. A High Court ruling in 2014 held that part of the land was privately owned, and the court later ordered the outpost removed by 25 December 2016. When the government tried to move the residents to a neighbouring hilltop, the court blocked the move after the legal aid group Yesh Din showed that that land was also privately owned by Palestinians. [cite:gi12a_toi_amona] Security forces evacuated 42 families in early February 2017, and dismantling began on 6 February. [cite:gi12_toi_amona] The government's response is part of the record. Netanyahu ordered a new settlement to replace Amona, described as the first new official settlement in the West Bank in about 25 years. [cite:gi12_toi_amona]

The Regulation Law, 2017–2020

The Knesset's answer to Amona was the Regulation Law, passed in February 2017 by 60 votes to 52. It would retroactively legalise about 2,000 homes built on privately owned Palestinian land. Use of the land would pass to the state's Commissioner of Government Property, and the owners would receive compensation above market value or another plot. [cite:gi12_ynet_reglaw2018] The government's own chief legal adviser would not defend it. Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit called it "a harmful law which would not stand up to the test of proportionality," and his representative told the court in June 2018 that "the Regulation Law is null and void." The government hired a private lawyer to argue for it. [cite:gi12_ynet_reglaw2018]

On 9 June 2020 the High Court of Justice ruled by eight justices to one that the law was unconstitutional and void. Experts cited by the Times of Israel put the number of settler homes on private Palestinian land at about 4,000. [cite:gi12_toi_reglaw2020] Reactions divided along the lines this volume has traced. Likud called the ruling "unfortunate" and promised a new law, and Knesset Speaker Yariv Levin said the judges had "trampled on Israeli democracy." The settlements minister, Tzipi Hotovely, called it "a declaration of war on the rights of Jews to settle the Land of Israel," and Naftali Bennett urged the government to answer with annexation. Benny Gantz, then defence minister, said the law should never have passed and that the ruling would be respected. Peace Now, one of the petitioners, welcomed the decision. B'Tselem said it did little to stop the settlement project. [cite:gi12_toi_reglaw2020]

The limits of the legal check

The court's rulings against the government have been about private Palestinian land and the means of taking it, not about settlement as such. It has not ruled the settlements themselves unlawful. In July 2021 it upheld the Nation-State Law by ten votes to one, including the clause declaring Jewish settlement a national value. The majority held that the clause was not meant to permit discrimination or the exclusion of non-Jews from state land, as the state had also clarified, and Justice George Karra dissented. [cite:gi5_adalah_hcj] [scene:gi5_nationstate|Part Five: the Nation-State Law] In May 2022 the Supreme Court rejected the petitions of the residents of Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron. It accepted the state's case that they had not proved permanent residence before the area was declared a firing zone, and treated the ban on forcible transfer as a treaty norm that Israeli courts do not enforce. [cite:wb_sabrang_masafer] It approved the demolition of Khan al-Ahmar in 2018, a demolition successive governments then postponed under international pressure. [cite:wb_toi_khan]

The E1 plan east of Jerusalem shows both sides of the check as of October 2026. The Jerusalem District Court refused on 8 September 2026 to freeze the tender for the first homes, without ruling on the legality of the plans, and three petitions remain pending. [cite:gi6_jpost_e1court] On 26 September the Attorney General's Office ordered the bid deadline moved past the 27 October election, citing diplomatic sensitivity and the risk that the tender could be used as election propaganda. [cite:gi6_ih_e1postpone] Part Six follows the case. [scene:gi6_ground|Part Six: on the ground]

The legal record supports a narrower finding than either side tends to draw from it. The court and the attorney general have stopped specific measures: seizure of private land on ideological grounds, an outpost on privately owned land, and a law to legalise such building across the territory. The cases were brought by Palestinian landowners and Israeli groups, the attorney general declined to defend the 2017 law, and some ministers answered the rulings by calling for annexation. The court has not blocked settlement on land the state declares its own, and it has left the larger question, whether Israel may keep the territory, to the government and the Knesset. [cite:wb_dweikat] [cite:gi12_toi_reglaw2020] [cite:wb_wiki_stateland]

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: The Ledger: Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon
chapters.intro: Part Thirteen begins a ledger that the rest of the book has so far kept apart from its subject: what Israel's wars and operations since October 2023 have done to the places nearest it. It takes Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon in turn. For each it sets out the operations, with the earlier rounds of 1982, 2006, 2008–09, 2014 and 2021 in brief; the dead and injured, with the body that counted them and how, and with women and children only where that body gives them; the people driven from their homes and the homes, hospitals, schools and water systems destroyed; and what the fighting did to the governments and economies left behind. Beside each it puts Israel's stated reasons and the attacks on Israel that preceded or accompanied its operations: the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, killings of Israelis in the West Bank, and Hezbollah's fire on the north and the Israelis it displaced. Figures from different sources and periods are given side by side, never added together, and the status of each front is stated as of October 2026. The question whether these operations served territorial expansion is treated as an argument, with the evidence on both sides, because this book found documented expansion programmes only for the West Bank and the Golan.
chapters.outro: Part Thirteen found the human cost of the wars since October 2023 to be documented in detail, though no single count is complete. In Gaza, after the attack of 7 October 2023 that killed 1,195 people in Israel, the health ministry counted 74,382 Palestinians killed by 12 October 2026. A peer-reviewed estimate suggests that count runs low, and of the dead identified by the end of 2025, 21,283 were children. About three-quarters of housing units were destroyed or damaged, and 94 per cent of the population needed shelter. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:gz_aj_lancet] [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] [cite:gz_rdna2026] In the West Bank more Palestinians were killed in three years than in the seventeen before them, with 59 Israelis killed by West Bank Palestinians in the first two years of the war. Some 42,000 Palestinians were displaced, most of them from refugee camps the army still held in October 2026. [cite:gi14_oxfam_wb] [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] [cite:gi14_ocha_wbsnap] In Lebanon the health ministry counted 8,954 people killed from 8 October 2023 to October 2026, across two wars that Hezbollah opened and the truce between them. On Israel's side, the record shows 128 deaths in the first round by Alma's count and 42 in the second by Israel's own, along with 60,000 Israelis displaced from the north. By October 2026 Israel held about 6 per cent of the country. [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] [cite:hz7_alma_summary] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] [cite:hz7_afp_north_return] In each place Israel's stated reason was security against an armed enemy whose own attacks are on the record. Whether the operations also served expansion is documented as a programme only in the West Bank, and elsewhere remains an argument. Part Fourteen continues the ledger in Syria, Iran, Iraq and Yemen. [scene:gi15_syria|Part Fourteen: Syria]

sections.h: Gaza
sections.html:
This ledger begins in Gaza because the war that began on 7 October 2023 began there. That morning the Qassam Brigades, Hamas's armed wing, led at least four other armed groups through the fence into southern Israel. They attacked at least 19 kibbutzim, five moshavim, the towns of Sderot and Ofakim and two music festivals. By AFP's cross-referenced count, cited by Human Rights Watch, 1,195 people were killed, 815 of them civilians, and 251 civilians and members of the security forces were taken into Gaza as hostages. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] The Hamas volume tells the day in detail. [scene:gz6_attack|Gaza, Documented: the attack] Israel's government called what followed, in a statement of May 2024, a "defensive and just war to eliminate Hamas and to secure the release of our hostages." [cite:gz_toi_rafah] What follows sets out what that war did to Gaza, by source and counting method, with Israel's stated reasons alongside.

The earlier rounds

The war of 2023 was the fifth large Israeli operation in Gaza since Hamas took control of the Strip in 2007. In Operation Cast Lead, from December 2008 to January 2009, Palestinian deaths were counted at between 1,391 (B'Tselem) and 1,440 (the Gaza health ministry); the Israeli army's own count was 1,166. Thirteen Israelis were killed, ten of them soldiers, four of those by friendly fire. [cite:gz_wiki_castlead] In the war of July and August 2014, OCHA counted 2,220 Palestinians killed, 1,492 of them civilians; Israel's foreign ministry counted 2,125, about 36 per cent of them civilians. Sixty-seven Israeli soldiers and six civilians in Israel were killed, more than 7,000 homes were razed, and up to 520,000 people were displaced at the peak. [cite:gz_wiki_2014] In May 2021 at least 256 Palestinians were killed in Gaza, 66 of them children by the UN's count, and at least 13 people in Israel; about 4,360 rockets were fired from Gaza. [cite:gz_wiki_2021] Part Five of the Gaza volume compares these wars. [scene:gz5_castlead|Gaza, Documented: Cast Lead] [scene:gz5_2012_2014|2012 and 2014] [scene:gz5_march_2021|2018 to 2021] The 2023 war killed many times more people than all of them together.

The dead and the wounded

The figures below come from three sources, which count in different ways, and they are not combined. The first is the Gaza health ministry, which counts deaths registered through hospitals, morgues and family reports and does not separate fighters from civilians. On 30 September 2026 the UN's humanitarian office (OCHA), citing the ministry, gave 74,032 Palestinians killed and 175,142 injured since 7 October 2023. [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] By 12 October the ministry's count had reached 74,382, of whom 1,493 had been killed since the ceasefire of 10 October 2025. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] The total kept rising for two reasons: people were still being killed, and bodies recovered from the rubble were added to the register: between 12 August and 12 October the count of those killed since the truce rose by 234, and the overall total by about a thousand. [cite:gi14_olj_toll_aug26] [cite:gz_aj_year2026] Israel cast doubt on the ministry's figures for more than two years. In late January 2026 Haaretz reported that the army had accepted its estimate of about 71,000 dead; on 30 January the army spokesman Nadav Shoshani said such reports did not reflect official data. [cite:gz_yahoo_idf71k] [cite:gi14a_na_idfdeny]

The ministry gives a breakdown only for the dead it has identified by name. Of 71,444 identified by 31 December 2025, 21,283 were children, 10,983 women, 5,100 elderly people and 34,078 men. [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] The UN Commission of Inquiry, working from the same records to 7 October 2025, put the number of children killed at no fewer than 20,179 and the number injured at 44,143. It found that children were 30 per cent of the dead, against about 24 per cent in the wars of 2008–09 and 2014. [cite:pr_nw_coi2026]

The second source is a peer-reviewed estimate. A study in The Lancet used three independent sources of names and estimated 64,260 deaths from traumatic injury up to the end of June 2024. The ministry had counted 37,877 by then, an undercount of about 41 per cent. [cite:gz_aj_lancet] The third is Israel's own data. A classified Israeli military database, reported in August 2025, listed 8,900 named fighters of Hamas and Islamic Jihad as dead or probably dead by May 2025, when the ministry's count was about 53,000. That is about 17 per cent. The army called the figures "incorrect." [cite:gz_aj_83pct] On Israel's side, OCHA, citing the Israeli military's website, gives 474 soldiers killed in the Gaza ground operation. Israeli media citing official sources put Israel's total dead, including 7 October and its immediate aftermath, at over 1,200. [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap]

Some of the people who died were there to help others or to report. OCHA counts 597 aid workers killed, among them 394 staff of UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, 55 Palestine Red Crescent workers and four of the International Committee of the Red Cross. The health ministry counted more than 1,700 health workers killed to October 2025, and Gaza's civil defence lost 145 staff on duty. [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] The Committee to Protect Journalists counted 189 Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza by 24 September 2026. The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate, which counts media workers more widely, gave 262 to 30 June 2026. [cite:gz_cpj_2026] [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] Foreign journalists were still barred from entering independently in October 2026. [scene:gz12_access|Gaza, Documented: why the record is thin]

Displacement and destruction

The damage was surveyed from satellite imagery and on the ground. Images taken by the UN's satellite centre on 11 October 2025, the day after the ceasefire, showed about 81 per cent of all structures in the Strip damaged or destroyed. [cite:gz_unosat2025] The World Bank, UN and EU damage assessment counted 371,888 of Gaza's 485,361 housing units destroyed or damaged, 76.6 per cent, and found that the economy had contracted by 84 per cent. It put recovery needs at $71.4 billion over a decade. [cite:gz_rdna2026] [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] By the Education Cluster's count, 526 of 564 school buildings needed full reconstruction or major repair. Eighty-eight per cent of above-ground water and sanitation assets and 76 per cent of underground networks were damaged. Only 3 per cent of cropland was undamaged and accessible. Of Gaza's 670 health facilities, 355 were not functioning at the end of September 2026, 273 were functioning only in part and 42 fully. [cite:gi14a_ocha_gazasnap]

Almost the whole population was displaced at some point. In mid-2026, 1.98 million people, 94 per cent, needed shelter assistance and 65 per cent of households surveyed lived in tents or makeshift shelters. In August 2026, 57 per cent of households surveyed had less than the six litres of drinking water a person needs each day. [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] On 22 August 2025 the IPC, the UN-backed system that classifies hunger, found that "famine is now occurring in Gaza City and its surrounding area." Israel's foreign ministry answered: "There is no famine in Gaza." [cite:gz_aj_ipc] [cite:gz_olj_ipc] After the ceasefire the IPC found no area in famine, but at least 1.6 million people still faced high levels of acute food insecurity. [cite:pr_un_ipc_dec2025] Part Seven of the Gaza volume sets out the siege, the aid blockade and the dispute over the counts. [scene:gz7_toll|Gaza, Documented: the dead, the ruins and the famine]

Israel's stated reasons

Israel's government has given two answers to the charge that it fought without regard for civilians. It accused Hamas of operating from hospitals and civilian buildings, which Hamas denies; and it said it went to great lengths to avoid civilian deaths. [cite:gz_aj_lancet] It also said in May 2024 that it "has not and will not" create conditions of life that could bring about the population's physical destruction. [cite:gz_toi_rafah] The rulings of the International Court of Justice, the warrants of the International Criminal Court and Israel's answers to them belong to Part Sixteen and the Gaza volume. [scene:gz7_courts|Gaza, Documented: the courts] [scene:gi17_courts|Part Sixteen: the courts] Hamas held living hostages until 13 October 2025, when it released the last twenty in exchange for more than 1,900 Palestinian prisoners and detainees; the remains of 28 dead hostages were still in Gaza that day and were returned in stages. [cite:gz_kt_hostages] [cite:gz_wiki_timeline2025]

Destabilisation, and where things stand

The ceasefire left Gaza without a functioning government, economy or security force of its own. A year on, aid entered at about a third of the agreed rate and no international stabilisation force had deployed. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] ACLED documented, as of April 2026, at least five anti-Hamas armed groups operating from Israeli-held areas, and assessed that Israel supplies them with weapons, logistics, intelligence and training; they had been involved in more than 40 violent events and nearly 80 deaths since the ceasefire. [cite:hz11_acled_gaza] Netanyahu had confirmed in June 2025 that Israel had "activated clans in Gaza who oppose Hamas," saying it saved soldiers' lives. [cite:hz11_ynet_clans] As of October 2026, OCHA reported restrictions on 65 per cent of the Strip, and Israel had told the UN in June that it controlled about 70 per cent. About 2.1 million people were left in roughly 35 per cent of the territory. [cite:gi9_aj_maps] Part Nine traces that line. [scene:gi9_gaza|Part Nine: the Gaza perimeter]

Whether the war served territorial expansion is an argument, and both sides of it rest on statements. On one side, Netanyahu said in May 2026 that his "directive is to go to 70" per cent of the Strip, and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said in January 2025 that he was developing an "operational plan" for what he calls the "voluntary emigration" of Gazans. [cite:gi9_olj_net70] [cite:gz_jc_smotrich] On the other, the US plan Israel accepted states that "Israel will not occupy or annex Gaza," and Netanyahu said in August 2025: "We don't want to govern it." [cite:gz_almon_plantext] [cite:gz_mm_netanyahu_aug25] No Israeli law or government decision claims Gaza as sovereign territory. This book's finding of documented expansion programmes is limited to the West Bank and the Golan. [scene:gi13_record|Part Eighteen: the record]

sections.h: The West Bank
sections.html:
In the West Bank, unlike Gaza or Lebanon, a documented programme of territorial expansion stands beside the military operations. That programme is a matter of law and record: settlement written into the Nation-State Law as a national value, Smotrich's civil powers, the votes in the Knesset and the land-registration decision of 15 February 2026. [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis] [scene:gi5_nationstate|Part Five: the Nation-State Law] Part Six of this book and The West Bank, Documented set it out. [scene:gi6_plans|Part Six: the annexation track] [scene:wb9_annex|The West Bank, Documented: record approvals] This section keeps to the other side of the ledger: who was killed, who was driven from their homes, and what was destroyed, with each figure tied to the body that counted it.

Before October 2023

The West Bank had no war of its own in 2006, 2008–09, 2014 or 2021, but violence there never stopped. In the second intifada, from September 2000 to February 2005, B'Tselem counted (to April 2008, across the West Bank and Gaza together) 4,745 Palestinians killed by Israeli security forces and 44 by Israeli civilians. About 1,053 Israelis were killed by Palestinians. [cite:gz_wiki_intifada2] From 2006 to the end of 2022, by Oxfam's analysis of UN data, Israeli forces and settlers killed 1,036 Palestinians in the West Bank, 225 of them children, and Palestinians killed 86 Israeli settlers. [cite:gi14_oxfam_wb] Those numbers serve as a baseline. What happened after 2023 should be measured against them.

The dead since 2023

Three counts cover the years since. They use different periods and are not added together. The UN Human Rights Office counted 1,001 Palestinians killed in the West Bank and East Jerusalem from 7 October 2023 to 17 October 2025, 213 of them children. Israeli forces killed 968 of them, and settlers, alone or with soldiers, killed 33. In the same two years 59 Israelis, 22 of them members of the security forces, were killed by West Bank Palestinians in the West Bank and in Israel. [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] Oxfam's count, which covers whole calendar years from January 2023 and so includes nine months before the war, gives 1,244 Palestinians killed by the end of 2025, 268 of them children. That is more in three years than in the previous seventeen combined. Over the same three years 43 Israeli settlers, ten of them children, were killed. [cite:gi14_oxfam_wb] OCHA's monthly data give 240 Palestinians and 17 Israelis killed in the West Bank in 2025. From January 2025 to the end of August 2026 the totals are 322 Palestinians killed, 74 of them children (284 by forces, 25 by settlers, 13 by one or the other), and 20 Israelis, eight of them members of the security forces. [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025] [cite:gi14_ocha_wbsnap]

The UN office found that 449 of those killed by Israeli forces in the first two years were unarmed and not involved in violence when they were shot. It said force was being used "as a tool to control and repress," and noted that Israel announced investigations only rarely. The army described many of those its airstrikes killed as "terrorists." [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] For the first time since the second intifada, Israel used aircraft in the West Bank on a regular basis: the UN counted 108 airstrikes in the two years, mostly on refugee camps. [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] The West Bank volume gives the names and cases. [scene:wb9_war|The West Bank, Documented: since 7 October 2023]

Displacement: the camps and the hills

Two kinds of displacement ran side by side. The first was military. On 21 January 2025 the army launched Operation Iron Wall in the Jenin refugee camp and extended it to Tulkarm and Nur Shams. Its stated aim was to degrade the armed groups' infrastructure and remove imminent threats. In February tanks entered Jenin, the first in the West Bank since 2002. [cite:wb_wiki_ironwall] UNRWA's count, as of August 2026, was 12,557 people displaced from Jenin camp (a figure that includes people displaced during the Palestinian Authority's own operation there), 12,412 from Tulkarm and 9,207 from Nur Shams, 34,176 from the operations in all. Most had been out of their homes for nineteen months. [cite:gi14_ocha_wbsnap] [cite:gi14a_ocha_wbsnap] By October 2025, 52 per cent of the structures in Jenin camp had been destroyed or damaged. In September 2026 the UN Human Rights Office said the displacement may amount to forcible transfer, a crime against humanity; Israel describes the operation as counter-terrorism. [cite:wb_jurist_ohchr2026]

The second was in the hills of Area C, by settler attack and by demolition. OCHA counted about 1,492 settler attacks in the first year of the war alone (7 October 2023 to 14 October 2024), and 3,459 attacks causing casualties or damage from January 2025 to August 2026. [cite:gi14_ocha_wb230] [cite:gi14_ocha_wbsnap] The Israeli group Kerem Navot counted 57 Palestinian communities displaced between October 2023 and December 2024, 50 of them entirely, while at least 41 new outposts and herding farms were set up. [cite:wb_972_villages] Israeli authorities demolished 2,702 Palestinian structures between January 2025 and August 2026, 94 per cent of them for lack of building permits. [cite:gi14_ocha_wbsnap] [scene:wb5_areac|The West Bank, Documented: living in Area C] In all, UNRWA counted 41,951 Palestinians displaced, about 15,882 of them children, as of August 2026. Oxfam counted nearly 46,000 displaced in three years, against just over 13,000 in the fourteen before. [cite:gi14_ocha_wbsnap] [cite:gi14_oxfam_wb] In the first three months of 2026 Oxfam recorded more than 540 settler attacks and more than 60 water and sanitation structures vandalised. [cite:gi14_oxfam_wb] The West Bank volume documents the attacks and prosecution rates. [scene:wb8_settlers|The West Bank, Documented: settler violence]

Israel's stated reasons, and the attacks beside them

Israel's government gives two reasons for its operations: armed groups in the northern camps, which the Palestinian Authority's own forces had been fighting in Jenin since December 2024, and attacks on Israelis. [cite:wb_wiki_ironwall] The attacks are part of the record. The 59 Israelis killed by West Bank Palestinians in the first two years, and the 20 killed in the West Bank from January 2025 to August 2026, were killed in shootings, stabbings and car-rammings in the West Bank and in Israel. [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] [cite:gi14_ocha_wbsnap] On settler violence, the record is one of rare prosecutions, which the West Bank volume sets out with the answers Israel's leaders gave. [scene:wb8_settlers|The West Bank, Documented: settler violence]

Destabilisation, as of October 2026

The Palestinian Authority, which Israel and the United States rely on for security coordination, was close to collapse. Israel withheld all clearance revenues, the taxes it collects on the Authority's behalf, from June 2025. By March 2026 it had withheld NIS 11.7 billion and deducted NIS 12.5 billion since 2021. The Authority paid half of February's salaries in June, and its debts and arrears reached about 72 per cent of GDP. [cite:wb_mas_jun2026] [scene:wb12_revenue|The West Bank, Documented: the money] In the same years the settlement enterprise grew at a record pace: 27,941 housing units were advanced in 2025, and the cabinet approved 102 new settlements between December 2022 and March 2026. [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis] As of October 2026 the northern camps were still under army control. [cite:wb_wiki_ironwall] Whether the violence and the settlement drive are connected is not left to inference here. The connection is made in documents, in the stated programme of named officials, which Part Six sets out. [scene:gi6_ground|Part Six: on the ground] Whether Iron Wall was a counter-terrorism operation, as Israel says, or part of that programme, is an argument. The UN office's forcible-transfer finding and Israel's rejection of it stand on opposite sides of it.

sections.h: Lebanon
sections.html:
The war with Lebanon after October 2023 began with Hezbollah's fire, not Israel's. On 8 October 2023, the day after the Hamas attack, Hezbollah fired on three Israeli positions in the Shebaa Farms "in solidarity with the victorious Palestinian resistance," and Israel answered with artillery and a drone strike. [cite:hz7_aj_8oct] This was far from the first round. Israel invaded in 1978 and 1982 and held a zone in the south until 2000. The Hezbollah volume and Part Eight of this book cover that history. [scene:gi8_lebanon|Part Eight: Lebanon, 1978–2000] [scene:hz4_zone|The Hezbollah Architecture: the security zone] The earlier tolls are counted there too: by the Lebanese police's count, 19,085 people were killed between 4 June and 31 August 1982, a figure that includes fighters; and in the 2006 war Human Rights Watch documented at least 1,109 Lebanese killed, "the vast majority of whom were civilians," while 121 Israeli soldiers and 44 Israeli civilians died. [cite:hz2b_csm_dec82] [cite:hz5_rw_why] [cite:hz5_wiki_war] [scene:hz5_toll|The Hezbollah Architecture: the toll of 2006]

The support front, 2023–2024

For almost a year the fighting stayed close to the border, and both sides shot at it. ACLED counted at least 13,608 cross-border attacks between 7 October 2023 and 18 October 2024. About 83 per cent were Israel's, and they killed at least 2,318 people in Lebanon; Hezbollah and allied groups carried out 2,370, which killed at least 41 Israelis. [cite:hz7_aj_acled_year] On 27 July 2024 a rocket killed twelve Druze children and teenagers on a football pitch in Majdal Shams, in the Israeli-held Golan. Israel and the United States attributed it to Hezbollah. Human Rights Watch found the damage consistent with a Hezbollah Falaq-type rocket. Hezbollah denied any connection. [cite:hz7_wiki_majdal] [cite:hz7_aj_majdal] About 60,000 residents of northern Israel were displaced by official count. About half had still not gone home by March 2025. [cite:hz7_afp_north_return]

In September 2024 Israel turned the border war into a campaign across Lebanon: the pager detonations, an air campaign that killed Hassan Nasrallah, and a ground invasion on 1 October. [scene:hz7_war|The Hezbollah Architecture: the autumn 2024 war] When the ceasefire of 27 November 2024 took effect, the Lebanese health minister counted at least 4,047 killed and 16,593 wounded since 8 October 2023, including 790 women and 316 children. The ministry did not separate civilians from fighters. [cite:hz7_olj_abiad_4047] Alma, an Israeli research centre, counted 45 Israeli civilians and 83 soldiers killed on the northern front over the same period. [cite:hz7_alma_summary] The World Bank put Lebanon's losses to 20 December 2024 at $14 billion, $6.8 billion of it physical damage, and recovery needs at $11 billion; the economy shrank 7.1 per cent in 2024. [cite:hz9_wb_rdna]

The truce that was not quiet, and the 2026 war

The truce largely stopped fire from Lebanon but not Israel's; the last reported rocket launches towards Israel before 2026 were in March 2025. [cite:hz8_scr_nov25] The UN Human Rights Office counted at least 127 civilians killed by Israeli forces in its first year. The health ministry counted 331 dead of all kinds by 24 November 2025. Israel said its strikes targeted Hezbollah's attempts to rearm. [cite:hz8_ohchr_nov25] [cite:hz8_aa_tabatabai] [scene:hz8_violations|The Hezbollah Architecture: the truce in numbers] On 2 March 2026, after the joint American and Israeli strikes on Iran that killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Hezbollah fired missiles and drones at Israel. It cited his killing and fifteen months of Israeli strikes. That afternoon the Lebanese cabinet banned all of Hezbollah's military activity. [cite:hz8_am_mar2] [cite:hz8_olj_ban] On 7 March Hezbollah told the residents of Kiryat Shmona to "evacuate immediately. Head south." Defence Minister Israel Katz urged northern residents to stay. [cite:gi14_almon_kiryat] Israel's stated aim was to remove Hezbollah's ability to threaten the north. On 16 March its forces entered the south, and Katz said displaced Lebanese would not return "south of the Litani" until northern Israel was safe. [cite:hz8b_afp_ground] [scene:hz8_war2026|The Hezbollah Architecture: the 2026 war]

A ten-day truce from the night of 16 April did not stop Israeli strikes and demolitions or Hezbollah's fire. [cite:hz8b_aj_yellow] [cite:hz8_an_jun8] Lebanon's health ministry counted 3,912 killed by 19 June 2026, when a further ceasefire took effect under the American–Iranian interim deal. By 11 October the total was 4,387 killed and 12,424 injured since 2 March. [cite:hz8b_olj_jun19] [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] The ministry's figure from 8 October 2023 onward was 8,954 killed and 30,660 injured, a total that spans both wars and the truce between them. [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] Over the 2026 war the ministry counted at least 100 health and rescue workers killed by mid-April. [cite:hz8_olj_toll] More than 1.2 million people were displaced at the peak, by the government's count. Israel put its losses to Hezbollah since March 2026 at 39 soldiers, a contractor and two civilians, and UNIFIL lost seven peacekeepers during the year. [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] Netanyahu claimed by 31 May that 3,000 Hezbollah fighters had been killed. The figure is Israel's alone; Hezbollah published none. [cite:hz8b_ap_beaufort]

The destruction was concentrated in the south. A rapid survey by the UN Development Programme and Lebanon's National Council for Scientific Research compared satellite images from late April 2026 with October 2025. It found 11,095 buildings completely destroyed, containing 17,891 housing units, and more than 11,500 damaged. It valued direct building damage at $1.38 billion, and it did not cover the weeks of fighting that followed. [cite:gi14_an_undp] In the border village of Yaroun the mayor told NPR that 180 of about 200 houses had been destroyed since March. Israel said it was targeting Hezbollah infrastructure, and in March Katz had said Israel meant to depopulate the border villages to create a "buffer zone." [cite:gi14_npr_yaroun] Lebanon's finance minister put the cost of the 2026 war at about $20 billion. [cite:hz8b_olj_salam]

Destabilisation, and where things stand

The war tested a Lebanese state that had been in economic collapse since 2019. Its economy had lost close to 40 per cent of its output since then. [cite:hz9_wb_rdna] [scene:hz9_economies|The Hezbollah Architecture: the economies] The state now faced two armed forces on its soil that it did not control. Hezbollah went to war in defiance of a cabinet decision. Israel held a strip behind the Yellow Line covering about 6 per cent of the country, kept up strikes and demolitions after the June ceasefire, and barred residents from dozens of villages. [cite:hz8_olj_ban] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] About 40 per cent of the displaced had returned by late June. [cite:hz8b_olj_salam] UNIFIL's mandate ends on 31 December 2026. [cite:hz8_scr_nov25] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] On 20 October 2026 military delegations met in Tampa, with the United States in the middle. Lebanon said it would demand "an end to Israeli attacks in Lebanon"; Israel says the targets it strikes violate the agreement. [cite:gi14_toi_tampa] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] Part Nine follows the Yellow Line. [scene:gi9_lebanon|Part Nine: south Lebanon] [scene:hz8_now|The Hezbollah Architecture: where things stand]

Whether this campaign served expansion is an argument, and the record cuts both ways. Netanyahu said that "as long as it is not disarmed, we will remain in this zone." Katz spoke of depopulating border villages, and the army crossed the Litani to take Beaufort castle, which Israel had held from 1982 to 2000. [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] [cite:gi14_npr_yaroun] [cite:hz8b_ap_beaufort] Against that reading, Israel signed a framework in June 2026 under which it may withdraw to its frontiers once the danger to its citizens ends. It withdrew from the first pilot village in July. It left Lebanon entirely in 2000 and has made no claim to Lebanese territory in any law or government decision. [cite:hz8b_almon_framework] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve: the withdrawals]

chapters.label: Part Fourteen
chapters.title: The Ledger: Syria, Iran, Iraq, Yemen and the Neighbours
chapters.intro: Part Fourteen continues the ledger begun in Part Thirteen, beyond Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon. It counts what Israel's operations since 2013 have cost in Syria, from the long air campaign against Iranian and Hezbollah targets to the buffer zone and the Sweida strikes of 2025; in Iran, across the wars of June 2025 and 2026; and in Iraq and Yemen, where Israeli aircraft struck militia depots in 2019 and Houthi ports, power plants and leaders from 2024. Each toll is given with the body that counted it and the method it used, beside Israel's stated reason and the other side's. The part then turns to the two neighbours at peace with Israel, Egypt and Jordan, which were not attacked but bore the Rafah closure, proposals to move Gaza's people onto their soil, and losses to trade and tourism. It closes with one table drawing together all nine countries and territories as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: Part Fourteen established that Israel's operations beyond Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon have been air, missile and raiding campaigns with stated reasons about weapons, armed groups and attacks on Israel, and that their tolls can be counted only through sources with limits that must be stated. In Syria, Airwars' provisional count of civilians alleged killed by Israeli strikes since 2013 is 60 to 108, and the deadliest week in the south, at Sweida in July 2025, was mostly Syrians killing Syrians, by SOHR's count. [cite:gi15_airwars_syria] [cite:gi15_olj_sweida] In Iran the counts for 2026 range from 3,468 dead (the government) to at least 3,636 (HRANA), with about 3.2 million people relocated by Iran's own figure. [cite:ir11_afp_tolls] [cite:ir11_hrana_day22] [cite:gi15_ocha_iran3] In Iraq the record shows depot strikes in 2019 and none found since; in Yemen, Israeli strikes that killed at least 86 people on the lowest Houthi figures, among them 31 journalists and media workers in a single raid. [cite:gi15_aje_iraq2019] [cite:gi15_gv_ap46] [cite:gi15_cpj_31] Egypt and Jordan were not attacked; their treaties held through a closed crossing, a gas dispute and missiles overhead. [cite:gi15_almon_rafah] [cite:gi15_aje_gas] [cite:gi15_mei_jordan] None of this adds to the documented expansion programmes, which remain the West Bank and the Golan; whether the security zones in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza become permanent stays an open argument. [cite:gi9_carnegie_ring] Part Fifteen turns to the bill: what American aid pays for, and whether it frees Israeli money for these operations. [scene:gi16_aid|Part Fifteen: the aid]

sections.h: Syria: Strikes, Sweida and the Southern Zone
sections.html:
Israel's only documented territorial programme in Syria concerns the Golan Heights, annexed in law in 1981 and treated in Part Eight. [scene:gi8_golan|The Golan] Everything else Israel has done in Syria since 2013 has been military: an air campaign against Iranian and Hezbollah targets during the civil war, a second and heavier campaign after Bashar al-Assad fell on 8 December 2024, and occupation of the UN buffer zone and the Syrian side of Mount Hermon. Part Nine sets out the ground taken, Israel's statements that it will stay, and the fortified line known as Sufa 53.
