[scene:gi9_syria|Part Nine: the Syrian buffer zone] This section counts what those operations cost in lives and says who did the counting. It also separates the deaths Israel caused from the far larger number caused by Syrians fighting one another, which are often run together. [cite:hz10s_cnn_480] [cite:gi15_olj_sweida]

The campaign between the wars, 2013–2024

For years Israel neither confirmed nor denied its strikes in Syria. The scale became public in January 2019. Netanyahu told his cabinet on 13 January that the army had "attacked hundreds of times Iranian and Hezbollah targets". The outgoing chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot, said about 2,000 bombs had been dropped on Iranian targets in 2018 alone, and that "we carried out thousands of attacks without taking responsibility". [cite:hz10s_jc_netanyahu] [cite:hz10s_toi_eisenkot] The stated aim was to stop Iran building a military presence in Syria and moving arms to Hezbollah. Iran's position was that its forces were in Syria at the Syrian government's invitation. [cite:hz10s_rferl_advisers] The Hezbollah volume tells that campaign in full, including Israel's medical aid to Syrian civilians and its arming of rebel groups on the Golan frontier. [scene:hz10_syria|The Hezbollah Architecture: Syria]

The best-known single strike attributed to Israel killed Iranian officers, not Syrians. On 1 April 2024 a strike that Iran blamed on Israel destroyed Iran's consulate building in Damascus and killed General Mohammad Reza Zahedi, his deputy and five other Iranian officers. Israel did not confirm or comment, and Iran answered on 13–14 April with its first direct attack on Israel. [cite:ir8_ap_consulate] [cite:ir14_cbs_damascus] [cite:ir8_gs_tp1] Strikes of this kind killed Syrian soldiers, Iranian personnel, Hezbollah fighters and, in some cases, civilians. No consolidated public count of all those killed by Israeli strikes in Syria between 2013 and 2024 was found. The monitoring group Airwars, which grades each allegation of civilian harm against the number and quality of local reports, tracks Israeli strikes in Syria from January 2013. Its tracker gives a headline estimate of 60 to 108 civilians alleged killed. It has graded only a small number of incidents so far, so the figure should be read as provisional. Airwars records the Israeli military's own assessment as zero civilian deaths, for the one incident it addressed. [cite:gi15_airwars_syria] [cite:gi15a_airwars] On every count available, the campaign's reported civilian toll was small beside the deaths of the civil war around it; what sets it apart is its length and the years in which Israel would not acknowledge it.

After Assad, December 2024 to 2025

When Assad fell, Israel struck on a far larger scale. Over 9 and 10 December 2024, by its own count, the military carried out about 480 strikes, hitting most of Syria's strategic weapons stockpiles, and its navy struck two naval facilities where 15 vessels were docked. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said the aim was to keep the weapons from falling "into the hands of extremists". [cite:hz10s_cnn_480] Those strikes hit depots, airfields and ships rather than towns, and no civilian toll for them was reported in the sources reviewed. The ground operations that followed were counted by the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR), a British-based monitor with sources inside Syria. In its review of 2025 it recorded 460 Israeli ground violations in southern Syria, mainly in the Quneitra and Daraa provinces, and more than 90 ground operations in November alone. It did not attribute a death toll to them. [cite:gi15_shafaq_sohr2025] Israel's stated reason for the presence was security: "We will not allow any hostile force to establish itself on our border," Netanyahu said on the first day. Syria's government and the UN called the presence a violation of the 1974 disengagement agreement. [cite:gi9_wiki_syriainv] [cite:hz10s_un_guterres]

Sweida, July 2025

The deadliest violence in southern Syria in 2025 was not, for the most part, Israel's doing. In mid-July 2025 fighting in Sweida province drew in Druze militias, Sunni Bedouin fighters and government forces. By SOHR's count, released on 22 July after a ceasefire, 1,311 people had been killed. They were 833 Druze (533 fighters and 300 civilians, 196 of the civilians "summarily executed" by members of the defence and interior ministries), 423 members of the government forces and 35 Sunni Bedouin, including three civilians executed by Druze fighters. [cite:gi15_olj_sweida] Israel intervened from the air. On 16 July it bombed the defence ministry in Damascus and an area near the presidential palace, and struck government positions in Sweida. Netanyahu said Israel was "acting to save our Druze brothers" and was committed to keeping south-western Syria demilitarised. Syria's foreign ministry condemned the strikes "in the harshest terms". [cite:hz10s_npr_sweida] SOHR also reported 15 government soldiers killed in Israeli strikes; it gives no separate total for all deaths caused by Israel that week. [cite:gi15_olj_sweida]

The figures show the order of responsibility. On SOHR's count for the whole of 2025, 990 civilians died in Sweida province. The same monitor documented by name 2,691 civilians killed in 63 massacres across Syria between March and November 2025, and attributed the field executions among them to factions affiliated with the transitional government's forces, not to Israel. [cite:gi15_shafaq_sohr2025] Israel's stated reason for striking was protection of the Druze. Syria's government saw an attack on its sovereignty and its capital. Both statements are on the record. The record also shows that the strikes on Damascus came five months after Netanyahu's demand, on 23 February 2025, that the three southern provinces be demilitarised. [cite:gi9_fdd_demil] Whether the protection of the Druze served a wider aim of a weak, divided south is an argument. Supporters of the strikes point to the documented executions of Druze civilians. Critics point to the demilitarisation demand and the continued presence of Israeli troops in the buffer zone. [cite:gi15_olj_sweida] [cite:gi9_carnegie_ring]

Displacement and status, October 2026

No figure for Syrians displaced by Israeli operations in the south was found in the sources reviewed. That is a gap in the record, not a finding that no one moved. The Sufa 53 works resumed on 4 October 2026, and Israeli forces still held the buffer zone and the Hermon summit as of October 2026. Syria's demand was a return to the lines of 8 December 2024, and talks through a US-supervised channel continued without a signed agreement. [cite:hz10s_eb_sufa] [cite:hz10s_eb_amman] [cite:hz10s_jpost_sharaa90] The documented record in Syria outside the Golan is a record of strikes, raids and a buffer zone that Israel's leaders have said they will hold until another arrangement ensures Israel's security. [cite:gi9_wiki_syriainv] No Israeli law, platform or coalition agreement found claims sovereignty over it. [scene:gi9_syria|Part Nine: the Syrian buffer zone] Whether the zone becomes a second Golan is a question the record leaves open.

sections.h: Iran: Two Wars and Their Tolls
sections.html:
Iran appears in no Greater-Israel map or text examined, and Israel has never claimed Iranian territory; Part Eight sets out that test. [scene:gi8_claims|Part Eight: the claims tested] Israel's wars with Iran in June 2025 and from 28 February 2026 had other stated grounds: Iran's nuclear and missile programmes, its arming of allied groups, and, by 2026, the aim of creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their government. [cite:ir10_idf_jun14] [cite:ir13_pbs_bibi2026] The Iran volume tells both wars and weighs those reasons. [scene:ir10_strikes|The Iran Architecture: the June 2025 strikes] [scene:ir11_war|The Iran Architecture: the 2026 war] This section brings together their human and physical cost: the dead and wounded on both sides by each counting body, the damage to civilian infrastructure, and the people who fled. In 2026 the war was waged jointly by Israel and the United States, and where a death or strike is attributed to one of them, the text says which.

June 2025: twelve days

Israel opened the war on 13 June 2025. Its military said the objective was "eliminating the existential Iranian threat", meaning the nuclear and missile threat. The strikes hit Natanz and other military and nuclear sites and killed the chief of the general staff, the commander of the Revolutionary Guards and several nuclear scientists. [cite:ir10_idf_jun14] [cite:ir10_na_killed] Iran called its missile and drone barrages "Operation True Promise 3", "in direct retaliation against Israeli aggression", and said it was hitting military and fuel infrastructure. [cite:ir10_irna_tp3] Israel also struck targets that were not military. On 23 June its aircraft hit Tehran's Evin prison, where the Iranian government said 79 people were killed, among them prisoners' visiting relatives, staff, conscript guards, a child and local residents. Israeli officials called the strike "symbolic". Human Rights Watch found it "unlawfully indiscriminate" and an apparent war crime. [cite:gi15_wiki_evin]

The counts of the dead in Iran differ by method. Iran's Health Ministry gave at least 610 dead by 24 June. On 7 July the head of Iran's Foundation of Martyrs said at least 1,060 had been killed. The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), counting case by case, recorded 1,190 dead, 436 of them civilians and 435 security forces, and 4,475 wounded. [cite:ir10_toi_numbers] [cite:ir10_ap_toll] In Israel, Iranian missiles killed 28 people, all but one of them civilians. The Health Ministry recorded 3,238 people taken to hospital, and more than 9,000 Israelis were displaced from damaged homes. [cite:ir10_toi_numbers] The worst single strike killed nine people in Bat Yam on 15 June; others hit the Weizmann Institute, the Bazan refinery in Haifa, which was shut, and Soroka Medical Centre in Beersheba. [cite:ir10_aj_map] [cite:ir10_en_soroka]

The 2026 war

The second war began on 28 February 2026 with joint American and Israeli strikes that killed Iran's Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] Three counts of the dead in Iran over the first forty days exist, and they measure different things. Iran's government gave totals without dividing civilians from soldiers: 3,468 dead by 18 April, according to the Foundation of Martyrs. [cite:ir11_afp_tolls] Iran's Health Ministry, as reported by the UN, counted at least 2,362 civilians killed and more than 32,314 injured between 28 February and 7 April. [cite:gi15_ocha_iran3] HRANA counted at least 3,636 dead by 7 April: 1,701 civilians, among them at least 254 children, 1,221 military personnel and 714 it could not classify. [cite:ir11_hrana_day22] [cite:ir11_afp_tolls] The two civilian figures, 2,362 and 1,701, cannot be reconciled from the published data. The first is a government ministry's count; the second is a monitor's count that leaves hundreds of deaths unclassified.

The single strike on civilians documented in most detail was American. On 28 February missiles hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab. Amnesty International found that US Tomahawks had struck it, killing more than 150 people, 120 of them children, and that the attack "clearly did not take all feasible precautions"; a UN fact-finding mission found in September 2026 reasonable grounds to believe the United States was responsible. President Trump said the strike was not done "on purpose," and a US admiral testified in May that the school sat on an active Iranian cruise missile base. As of 16 October 2026 the Pentagon said its investigation was ongoing and had published no findings. [cite:ir11_amnesty_minab] [cite:ir11a_almon_minab] [cite:gi15a_ibt_minab] In Israel, Iranian missiles killed between 24 and 28 people over the forty days by Israeli media counts (the lower figure may include four Palestinians in the West Bank), with more than 7,000 injured. The deadliest strike killed nine civilians in a shelter in Beit Shemesh on 1 March, which Amnesty said "must be investigated as a war crime". Amnesty counted at least 23 people killed in the Gulf states by 27 March. [cite:ir11_wiki_strikesisrael] [cite:ir11_amnesty_beitshemesh] No consolidated count of Iranian dead after the ceasefire collapsed in July 2026 was found. [cite:ir11_aj_jul8]

Infrastructure and displacement

The 2026 war damaged civilian infrastructure across Iran, on figures the UN compiled from Iranian institutions. By mid-April the Iranian Red Crescent reported about 125,600 civilian units damaged, about 100,000 of them homes. The Ministry of Energy reported more than 1,000 electricity distribution points with major damage, over 470 of them in Tehran province, and the Red Crescent reported 15 bridges, railway sites and five fuel storage tanks damaged. [cite:gi15_ocha_iran3] Iran's government said about 3.2 million people, some 800,000 households, had relocated inside the country, about 60 per cent of them women and children. The UN refugee agency counted about 118,300 Iranians crossing into Turkey and Pakistan by 16 April. Most of those movements, it said, appeared routine, family-related or precautionary rather than large-scale flight. [cite:gi15_ocha_iran3] These are Iranian official figures relayed by the UN, not independent surveys, and the UN gives them as such. The American and Israeli governments said they were striking military, nuclear and missile targets; Airwars recorded more than 17,000 targets declared struck by the two. [cite:ir11_airwars]

Status, October 2026

As of October 2026 the war with Iran has not formally ended. The Islamabad Memorandum of 17 June collapsed on 7 and 8 July, an American naval blockade of Iran's ports has been in force since 14 July, and Iran's oil loadings fell to about 260,000 barrels a day in August, by Kpler's estimate, against 1.7 million a year earlier. [cite:ir11_aj_jul8] [cite:hz12a_cbs_oct] [cite:ir11_oilprice_exports] On 8 October President Trump wrote that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterm elections of 3 November. [cite:ir11_ap_midterms] The IAEA has not had access to the sites bombed in June 2025 and has lost continuity of knowledge over Iran's declared enriched uranium, the material at the centre of both wars' stated aims. [cite:ir11_iaea_sep7] [scene:ir11_now|The Iran Architecture: from ceasefire to blockade] The documented record shows two wars with stated aims about weapons and, by 2026, about Iran's government. It contains no claim to Iranian land. Treating these wars as part of a territorial programme would join two separate records without a document to connect them, the same conclusion Part Eight reached. [scene:gi8_claims|Part Eight: the claims tested]

sections.h: Iraq and Yemen: Strikes at a Distance
sections.html:
Neither Iraq nor Yemen borders Israel, and no Israeli government has claimed land in either. [scene:gi8_claims|Part Eight: the claims tested] Both have nonetheless been struck by Israeli aircraft: Iraq in a series of raids on militia bases in 2019, Yemen from July 2024 in a war with the Houthi movement that began with Houthi missiles and drones fired at Israel. This section sets out each campaign with Israel's stated reason, the other side's stated reason, and the tolls as they were reported and by whom. It does not repeat the history of the Iraqi militias or of the Houthis, which the Hezbollah volume covers, along with the American wars against both. [scene:hz10_iraq|The Hezbollah Architecture: the Iraqi militias] [scene:hz10_houthis|The Hezbollah Architecture: Ansar Allah] [scene:hz10_redsea|The Hezbollah Architecture: the Red Sea war]

Iraq: the depot strikes of 2019

Between July and September 2019 a series of explosions hit bases and weapons depots of Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces, the umbrella of mainly Shia armed groups, several of them aligned with Iran. The first was on 19 July near Amerli, at a base that a senior militia official said housed Iranian and Lebanese advisers. Others followed: Camp Ashraf on 27 July; southern Baghdad on 12 August, where one civilian was killed and 29 injured; near Balad Air Base on 20 August; and a convoy near al-Qaim on the Syrian border on 25 August, where the militias said six were killed. [cite:gi15_wiki_iraq2019] No one claimed the attacks. On 23 August two American officials told the Associated Press that Israel had carried out at least the Amerli strike, which hit an Iranian weapons depot and, they said, killed two Iranian commanders. [cite:gi15_aje_iraq2019] [cite:gi15a_aje_iraq2019]

Israel's position was stated in hints and then plainly. Netanyahu said, "I don't give Iran immunity anywhere," and that he had given the security forces "a free hand". On 22 August he said, "We are working against Iranian consolidation — in Iraq as well." [cite:gi15_aje_iraq2019] [cite:gi15_wiki_iraq2019] Iraq's government closed its airspace to unauthorised flights on 13 August and ordered munitions depots moved out of cities. A deputy head of the militias blamed Israeli drones but, in the end, held Washington responsible and threatened retaliation. [cite:gi15_aje_iraq2019] [cite:gi15_wiki_iraq2019] The dead were mostly militia members and Iranian personnel. No consolidated count was published, and some tolls given for individual strikes rest on single, partisan sources.

After 2019 the record reviewed shows no further acknowledged or credibly attributed Israeli strike inside Iraq through October 2026. Some accounts say Israel struck Iranian-aligned militia positions in Iraq after 2023; no source documenting such strikes was found, and the claim is not adopted here. The Iraqi militias' war in those years was mainly with the United States, including the drone that killed three American soldiers at Tower 22 in Jordan on 28 January 2024. [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] [cite:hz10_at_farida] The statement sometimes made, that Israel has had no direct military engagement with Iraq since 1991, is therefore wrong for 2019; for the years since, the record found bears it out.

Yemen: the Houthi front

The exchange between Israel and the Houthis began from Yemen. From late 2023 the Houthis fired missiles and drones at Israel, and attacked shipping in the Red Sea, which they said was support for Gaza that would stop when the war on Gaza stopped. [cite:hz10_crs_if12587] [cite:hz10_aje_truce] On 19 July 2024 a Houthi drone killed one person in central Tel Aviv. Israel struck the port of Hodeidah the next day, its first strike on Yemen; an Israeli official called the port the main entry point for Iranian weapons. The Houthi-run health ministry first reported 80 wounded and later at least three killed and 87 injured. Defence Minister Yoav Gallant said the Houthis had attacked Israel more than 200 times. [cite:hz10_nbc_hodeidah2024] [cite:gi15a_aj_hodeidah]

The strikes grew heavier from December 2024. On 19 December Israeli aircraft hit the ports of Hodeidah, Ras Isa and Salif and two power stations near Sanaa, killing at least nine people, according to Houthi sources. On 26 December they struck Sanaa International Airport, ports and power stations while the head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, was at the airport; a member of his plane's crew was injured. Reported tolls for that day ran from three or four dead, the figure given by the Houthi channel al-Masirah, to six dead and about 40 wounded, reported by CNN. [cite:gi15_wiki_yemendec24] Israel said it was answering Houthi missile and drone fire and hitting port and energy infrastructure used for military purposes. [cite:gi15_wiki_yemendec24]

In 2025 the pace rose again. After a Houthi missile struck near Ben Gurion Airport on 4 May, Israel hit Hodeidah and a cement factory on 5 May and disabled Sanaa airport on 6 May; Houthi-linked media reported four and three dead. Later strikes destroyed Yemenia's last airliner at Sanaa on 28 May and hit ports and power plants through the summer. On 24 August strikes on Sanaa killed 10 people and wounded 102, according to the Houthi health ministry, and on 28 August a strike killed the Houthi prime minister, Ahmed al-Rahawi, and several ministers. [cite:gi15_wiki_yemen2025] [cite:hz10_aje_rahawi] On 10 September Israeli strikes on Sanaa and al-Jawf killed 46 people and wounded 165, by the Houthi health ministry's count. Netanyahu linked them to a Houthi drone that had hit the arrivals hall at Ramon Airport. [cite:gi15_gv_ap46] [cite:gi15_gcap_35] Among the dead were 31 journalists and media workers at the offices of the 26 September and al-Yemen newspapers, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. The IDF said it had struck the Houthis' "Public Relations Department". CPJ, which had confirmed at least nine of the dead as journalists and was investigating the rest, classed the killings as murders and called it the deadliest attack on the press anywhere in sixteen years. [cite:gi15_cpj_31] [cite:gi15a_cpj_31] A Houthi drone injured 22 people in Eilat in late September, and Israeli strikes on Sanaa around 25 September killed eight and injured 142, according to the BBC's report. [cite:gi15_wiki_yemen2025]

Counting the toll, and where it stands

No consolidated count of the people killed by Israeli strikes in Yemen exists in the sources reviewed. Almost every figure comes from the Houthi-run health ministry or Houthi media and could not be independently checked; a running total on one reference page, "61+ killed" for 2025, falls below the sum of its own per-strike entries and should be read as a floor. [cite:gi15_wiki_yemen2025] [cite:gi15_gv_ap46] [cite:gi15a_aj_hodeidah] Adding the lowest per-strike figures above gives at least 86 people killed by Israeli strikes in Yemen between July 2024 and September 2025, before counting the Houthi prime minister and ministers killed on 28 August and the unnumbered dead of other raids. The Houthi attacks on Israel in the same period killed one person in Tel Aviv and injured at least 22 in Eilat; by the count of Israel's defence minister the Houthis had attacked it more than 200 times by July 2024 alone, and most of their missiles and drones were intercepted. [cite:hz10_nbc_hodeidah2024] [cite:gi15_wiki_yemen2025] Israel's strikes were a small part of Yemen's dead. The UN Development Programme projected that the war since 2015 had caused about 377,000 deaths by the end of 2021, from all parties' violence, hunger and disease. In seven weeks of 2025 alone, Airwars counted at least 224 civilians allegedly killed by American strikes. [cite:hz10_aje_undp377k] [cite:hz10_airwars_rr]

The Houthis suspended attacks on Israel after the Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, as their stated condition implied. They resumed on 28 March 2026, a month into the Iran war, paused after that war's April ceasefire and fired briefly again in June. [cite:hz10_usni_crs2026] [cite:hz10_na_houthis2026] [cite:hz10_wiki_houthi2026] No Israeli strike on Yemen in 2026 was found in the sources reviewed. As of October 2026 Yemen's own war has reignited, with the Houthis fighting Saudi Arabia and Saudi-backed government forces. That war does not involve Israel. [cite:hz10_ahram_taiz] [cite:hz10_lwj_saudi2026] The documented Israeli record in Yemen is one of retaliatory and pre-emptive strikes on ports, power plants, an airport and the Houthi leadership, with a stated reason tied to Houthi fire on Israel. The Houthis' stated reason was the war on Gaza. Neither side's record contains a territorial claim.

sections.h: Egypt, Jordan and the Whole Ledger
sections.html:
Egypt and Jordan are the two neighbours at peace with Israel, under the treaties of 26 March 1979 and 26 October 1994, and neither has been attacked by Israel in the wars of 2023–2026, though on 27 May 2024 an Egyptian member of the security personnel near Rafah was killed in an exchange of fire with Israeli troops, which both militaries said they were investigating. [cite:gi15a_aj_egysoldier] [cite:gi8_avalon_egtreaty] [scene:gi8_sinai|Part Eight: Sinai and Egypt] [scene:gi8_jordan|Part Eight: Jordan] They have still borne costs: a closed border crossing, proposals to move Gaza's people onto their soil, lost revenue, missiles crossing their airspace, and treaties strained but not broken. This section sets out those effects with each government's stated position. It ends with a single table that draws together the ledger of Parts Thirteen and Fourteen, country by country.

Egypt: the crossing and the red line

Gaza's only crossing not on Israel's border is at Rafah, on the Egyptian frontier. Israeli forces seized it in May 2024, seven months into the war, and it stayed largely shut for most of the next two years. [cite:gi15_almon_rafah] On 24 May 2024 the International Court of Justice ordered Israel, by thirteen votes to two, to halt its offensive in the Rafah governorate where it might inflict conditions of life that could bring about the physical destruction of the Palestinian group in Gaza. [cite:gz_lawfare_rafah] [scene:gz7_courts|Gaza, Documented: the courts] Reopening the crossing was part of the first phase of the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel made it conditional on recovering the last hostage's body, and the crossing reopened for people in early February 2026. Returns from Egypt were limited to Gazans who had left during the war, "only after prior security clearance by Israel". [cite:gi15_almon_rafah] It closed again when the war on Iran began and, according to Israeli authorities, reopened on 18 March 2026 for "limited movement of people". No later change in its status was confirmed in the sources reviewed. [cite:gi15_libna_rafah]

The deeper strain was over where Gaza's people would go. On 25 January 2025 President Trump spoke of wanting to "clean out" Gaza, and on 4 February he proposed that the United States "take over" the Strip and that its people be relocated to other countries. [cite:gi15_toi_sisi] [cite:gz_whyy_riviera] President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi had already answered on 29 January. Displacing Gazans, he said, was an "injustice that we cannot take part in" that "can never be tolerated or allowed because of its impact on Egyptian national security". [cite:gi15_toi_sisi] Egypt put forward its own plan instead, adopted by an Arab summit in Cairo in March 2025, to rebuild Gaza for about $53 billion while Palestinians stayed "on their land without displacement". Israel's foreign ministry had called relocation an "opportunity for the Gazans to have free choice based on their free will," and the White House said the Arab plan did not address the reality that Gaza was uninhabitable. [cite:gz_nbc_arabplan] Israeli ministers' statements in favour of Palestinian emigration from Gaza are set out in Part Thirteen. [scene:gi14_gaza|Part Thirteen: Gaza] No official count of Gazans who entered Egypt during the war was found.

The economic cost to Egypt came mostly through the Red Sea, not from Israel directly. Sisi said in April 2025 that tension in the Red Sea had cost the Suez Canal about $7 billion in revenue in 2024, as Houthi attacks diverted shipping around Africa. That is his government's figure, not independently verified. [cite:gi15_toi_suez] [cite:hz10_crs_if12587] The treaty itself was strained over Sinai. In September 2025 Netanyahu ordered that a gas export deal not proceed without his approval, after Israeli allegations that Egypt's military deployments in Sinai violated the peace treaty; Egypt denied any violation. On 17 December 2025 he approved the deal, worth about $35 billion, as "the largest gas deal in Israel's history". Egypt's State Information Service called it "a purely commercial transaction" with "no political dimensions or understandings of any kind". [cite:gi15_aje_gas] The treaty has held, and Egypt was among the mediators of the October 2025 Gaza truce. [cite:gz_wiki_timeline2025]

Jordan: airspace, tourism and the "alternative homeland"

Jordan, too, was asked to take Gazans. King Abdullah II's answer in January 2025 was the one his government has given for decades: Palestinians must stay on their land, in line with a two-state solution. [cite:gi15_toi_sisi] In 2004 he had put it in the words Jordan uses against the "Jordan is Palestine" argument advanced by some Israeli politicians: "Jordan will never be an alternative homeland to anybody." [cite:gi8_king_althomeland] [scene:gi8_jordan|Part Eight: Jordan]

The wars reached Jordan through its sky. In April 2024 Jordan shot down some of the Iranian drones crossing its airspace towards Israel. [cite:ir8_gs_tp1] In 2026 Iran launched more than 250 missiles and drones at Jordan itself, aimed mainly at the American military presence and the port of Aqaba. Most were intercepted, the physical damage was slight, and no Jordanian casualties were reported. [cite:gi15_mei_jordan] Earlier, on 28 January 2024, a drone launched by an Iraqi militia had killed three American soldiers at Tower 22, a base in north-eastern Jordan. [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] The economic toll was larger. In February 2024 the IMF cut its growth forecast for Jordan to about 2.6 per cent, noting that hotel occupancy had fallen by about a third in the first week of December 2023. [cite:gi15_jn_imf] In 2026 gas imports from Israel were suspended at the start of the Iran war, raising the cost of generating power by about $140 million a month. Visitors fell to 3.1 million in the first half of the year, in a country where tourism makes up 14 to 16 per cent of GDP. [cite:gi15_mei_jordan] Jordan's government has protested Israeli acts beyond its own borders: in October 2026 it said the Sufa 53 works in Syria violated the UN Charter and Israel's obligations under the 1974 agreement. [cite:gi9_an_sufa] Part Seven records its response to Netanyahu's "Greater Israel" remark of August 2025. [scene:gi7_interview|Part Seven: the "very much" interview]

The whole ledger

The table below brings together the countries covered in Parts Thirteen and Fourteen. Each toll is given with the body that counted it and the date; counts made by different methods are not added together. Israel's stated reason stands in its own column. The status column describes the position as of October 2026, a week before Israel's election of 27 October. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] [cite:ir11_hrana_day22]

The table shows three things that the record supports and one that it does not. It shows that the heaviest tolls by far fell in Gaza and Lebanon, where Israel's wars were fought on the ground. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] It shows that in Syria, Iran, Iraq and Yemen the operations were air and missile campaigns whose stated reasons concerned weapons, armed groups and attacks on Israel, and that each was met by the other side's own stated reason. [cite:gi15_aje_iraq2019] [cite:gi15_gv_ap46] [cite:ir10_idf_jun14] It shows that, as of October 2026, Israeli forces hold ground taken in these wars in three places: in Gaza, in south Lebanon and in south-west Syria. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] [cite:hz10s_eb_sufa] It does not show that these operations are steps in a programme of territorial expansion. This volume found such a programme documented, in laws, platforms and named officials' statements, for the West Bank and the Golan only. [scene:gi13_record|The verdict] Whether the zones in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza become permanent is argued both ways. One view reads indefinite "security zones" as expansion by another name. The other points to the stated security purpose, the absence of any sovereignty claim, and the withdrawals of 1957, 1982, 2000 and 2005. [cite:gi9_carnegie_ring] [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve: the withdrawals] Part Fifteen turns from the toll to the bill: what American aid pays for, and whether it frees Israeli money for these operations. [scene:gi16_aid|Part Fifteen: the aid]

chapters.label: Part Fifteen
chapters.title: The Bill and America's Role
chapters.intro: Part Fifteen turns from the region to Washington. It asks what the $3.8 billion a year in American military aid actually is, how it is paid and spent, what share of Israel's defence budget and economy it represents now compared with fifteen years ago, and whether it frees Israeli money for wars and settlements, testing that argument against the numbers on both sides. It then sets out what the wars since October 2023 have cost each treasury, Israel's by its central bank and Finance Ministry and America's by Central Command and Brown University's Costs of War project. Finally it lists, by date, place and branch, every American service member killed in these theatres, and the American civilians killed in Israel, Gaza and the West Bank, with responsibility stated as the record states it, before weighing the argument that the United States was dragged into these wars.
chapters.outro: Part Fifteen established that the $3.8 billion a year is a fixed ten-year grant, $3.3 billion in military financing and $500 million for missile defence, paid early and by 2028 to be spent entirely on American weapons, and that at least $21.7 billion in military aid followed from October 2023 to September 2025. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gz_cow_aid] Its weight has fallen, from about a quarter of Israel's security spending and 1.5 per cent of GDP in 2011 to about 15 per cent and half a per cent now, while Israel's own war bill reached about NIS 350 billion for 2023–2026 by the Bank of Israel's count. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] [cite:gi16_boi_2025] The fungibility argument holds in principle, and Congress once acted on it for loan guarantees, but on the numbers the regular grant is a modest part of the cost of the wars, and Israel's prime minister now proposes ending it. [cite:gi16_jvl_loans] [cite:gi16_ji_netanyahu] For the United States the 2026 war was the largest cost, $43.6 billion by September, and the deadliest: 21 of the 28 service members killed in these theatres since October 2023 died in it. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] At least 33 Americans were killed on 7 October 2023, and five American citizens were killed in the West Bank by July 2025 in cases where Israeli accounts and those of families and rights groups often conflict; by one compilation, no killing of an American by Israelis since 2022 had led to criminal charges by March 2026. [cite:gi16_kshb_oct7] [cite:gi16_abc_musallet] [cite:gi16_wiki_abdeljabbar] The record shows Israeli action shaping when the United States fought, and American presidents deciding that it would. [cite:ir14_aje_rubio] [cite:ir14_sn_forced] Part Sixteen turns to what the United Nations, the courts and other states have said and done. [scene:gi17_un|Part Sixteen: the United Nations]

sections.h: The Aid: What $3.8 Billion a Year Is
sections.html:
The figure most often quoted in arguments about Israel and the United States is $3.8 billion a year. It comes from a single document. On 14 September 2016 the two governments signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) covering the American fiscal years 2019 to 2028: $38 billion in all, made up of $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing (FMF) grants and $5 billion for missile defence, or $3.3 billion and $500 million a year. Both sides undertook "not to seek changes to the FMF levels for the duration of this understanding", and the agreement runs to 30 September 2028. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:hm_dn_mou] It was the third such agreement: the 1999 MOU had promised $21.3 billion in military aid over ten years and the 2007 MOU $30 billion. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] Counting every kind of aid since 1946, the Congressional Research Service (CRS) puts the total at about $174 billion in current dollars, or about $298 billion in 2024 dollars. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025]

How the money moves

Three features of the arrangement matter for what follows. First, the money arrives early. Since 1991 Congress has required Israel's FMF to be paid as a lump sum within the first month of the fiscal year, into an interest-bearing account at the Federal Reserve Bank. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] Second, most of it has always had to be spent on American-made weapons. Israel was long allowed to spend part of its grant at home, a practice called offshore procurement: up to 26.3 per cent under the 2007 MOU. The 2016 agreement phases this out, slowly until 2024 and then more sharply, "ending entirely in FY2028". [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] Researchers at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) concluded in February 2026 that the aid is therefore now channelled "almost exclusively" to procurement in the United States. [cite:gi16_inss_aid] Third, the missile-defence money pays for systems built partly in Israel and partly in America, among them Iron Dome, David's Sling and Arrow; The One-Way Mirror follows that pipeline. [scene:ow8_coproduction|Co-production]

Since October 2023

The war that began on 7 October 2023 added emergency money on top of the MOU. On 24 October 2023 the United States transferred two of its own Iron Dome batteries to Israel. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow7_twz_irondome] The Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, signed in April 2024, totalled $26.38 billion. Its lines for Israel included $4 billion for Iron Dome and David's Sling, $1.2 billion for the Iron Beam laser, $3.5 billion in extra FMF and $1 billion for artillery and munitions production; another $4.4 billion was to replace American stocks sent to Israel, and $2.4 billion paid for American operations in the region. [cite:hz12b_hac_onepager] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] Arms sales followed. In August 2024 sales worth more than $20 billion were notified to Congress, including F-15IA aircraft at $18.82 billion. In January 2025 President Trump released a hold his predecessor had placed on 1,800 MK-84 bombs, and on 28 February 2025 Secretary of State Marco Rubio used an emergency declaration to approve nearly $4 billion in sales, saying it "reverse[d] the Biden Administration's partial arms embargo". By May 2025 Israel's Defence Ministry reported more than 90,000 tons of armaments delivered on 800 aircraft and 140 ships. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025]

The fullest independent count is by William Hartung for Brown University's Costs of War project: at least $21.7 billion in American military aid to Israel from October 2023 to September 2025, $17.9 billion in the first year and $3.8 billion in the second, not counting arms sales committed for later years. [cite:gz_cow_aid] [cite:hm_an_costsofwar] The total includes the MOU's own payments for those years, so it is not all additional money. [cite:hm_cow_hartung] The Gaza volume sets this against the cost of rebuilding Gaza. [scene:gz8_bill|Gaza, Documented: the bill]

A shrinking share

What the aid amounts to depends on what it is measured against, and on that the record shows a clear trend. In 2011 estimates by the analyst Gazit, cited by Doug Bandow of the Cato Institute, put American aid at 1.5 per cent of Israel's GDP and 24 per cent of its security spending. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] By 2025–26 the CRS put FMF at "approximately 14%" of Israel's defence budget, and INSS at "roughly 15%" of the budget and "about half a percent" of GDP. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] Israel's own spending meanwhile rose steeply. The Bank of Israel records defence spending at 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2022, 8.4 per cent in 2024 and 7.8 per cent in 2025. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] The 2026 budget, passed by the Knesset 62–55 on 30 March 2026, allotted about $44.8 billion to defence, about $9.5 billion more than the year before. [cite:gi16_bd_budget2026] Set against that figure, the $3.8 billion is about 8.5 per cent; that is this book's arithmetic, and the gap from the CRS and INSS figures reflects different years and budget definitions.

Testing the fungibility argument

A common argument holds that American aid, whatever it is spent on, frees Israeli money for other uses, among them military operations and settlements. It rests on the economist's point that money is fungible: a shekel Israel need not spend on an American jet is a shekel it can spend elsewhere. Bandow made the general case in 2012, applying it to aid to Egypt and Jordan. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] An article in The National Interest in June 2016 applied it to settlements directly. It argued that offshore procurement, then $815 million or just over 26 per cent of the package, let Israel "divert funds from its defense-technology accounts" to settlement projects it estimated at no less than $250 million a year, a figure it called uncertain. [cite:gi16_ni_osp] The United States government once acted on the same logic itself. Loan guarantees given to Israel in 1992 and 2003 could be cut by an amount equal to Israel's settlement spending in the territories, and were: by a net $773.8 million in 1994–97, and by $289.5 million in 2003 and $795.8 million in 2005, according to CRS data. [cite:gi16_jvl_loans] The settlement budgets themselves are documented in The West Bank, Documented. [scene:wb12_settlement|The settlement budget]

The counter-arguments rest on numbers too. The offshore channel that the 2016 article targeted closes entirely in 2028, after which every FMF dollar must buy American equipment. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] The aid's share of Israel's defence spending fell from about a quarter to about a seventh. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] Against the war, the sums are small. The Bank of Israel puts the gross budgetary cost of the war at about NIS 352 billion for 2023–2026, and the special American grant in its accounts at NIS 25 billion for 2023–2025, about 7 per cent of that cost by this book's arithmetic. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] Gazit argued that the requirement to buy in America itself cost Israel about $600 million a year, "a fifth of the nominal" aid, a view the United States government has not endorsed. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] And Israel's own prime minister now proposes ending the grants. In a CNBC interview in June 2026 Benjamin Netanyahu said, "I want it to start now," until the aid reaches "coming to zero"; formal talks on a new agreement began that month. A joint statement by Israel's Defence Ministry and Rubio set the aim to "gradually transition from aid to a completely reciprocal partnership", and the American ambassador, Mike Huckabee, wrote that the new MOU "ends aid & will be based on trade". [cite:gi16_ji_netanyahu] [cite:gi16_wiki_nextmou] No signing of a new agreement had been reported as of July 2026, the latest reporting this book found.

The test supports a narrower conclusion than either side usually draws. In principle the argument holds: the United States paid for interceptors and munitions used in the wars of 2023–2026, money Israel would otherwise have had to find, and Washington itself once treated settlement spending as offsetting aid. That wartime money is direct support for operations rather than an indirect release of funds. [cite:hz12b_hac_onepager] [cite:gi16_jvl_loans] In scale, though, the regular grant is now a modest and shrinking part of a defence budget that Israel's own taxpayers and borrowing have roughly doubled since 2022, and nothing in the record ties the MOU's dollars to any particular operation or settlement. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] Whether the aid's real weight lies in the money or in the diplomatic backing and access to American weapons that come with it is an argument. INSS, an Israeli institute, stresses the access to American systems and the symbol of the alliance, and also the leverage the aid gives Washington over Israeli policy. [cite:gi16_inss_aid]

sections.h: What the Wars Cost
sections.html:
The wars fought since 7 October 2023 have been paid for in two treasuries, Israel's and America's, and each has published its own estimates. This section sets those figures side by side. The human toll in each theatre is counted in Parts Thirteen and Fourteen and is not repeated here. [scene:gi14_gaza|Part Thirteen: Gaza] The figures below are budget costs as each government or research group defines them; they are not added together, because they count different things over different periods.

Israel's bill

The most complete Israeli account is the Bank of Israel's. In its annual report for 2025 the central bank put the gross budgetary cost of the war at NIS 34 billion in 2023, NIS 133 billion in 2024 and NIS 116 billion in 2025, with a further NIS 69 billion projected for 2026: about NIS 350 billion in all. That total leaves out decisions taken after the Iran war began in late February 2026. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] The twelve-day war with Iran in June 2025 was not costed separately; the bank records about NIS 4 billion, later about NIS 6 billion, in compensation for property damage from Iranian missiles, and a NIS 31 billion addition to the 2025 budget that paid for that war and the fighting in Gaza. [cite:gi16_boi_2025b] For the 2026 war, Israel's Finance Ministry gave a "preliminary estimate" on 12 April 2026 of NIS 35 billion ($11.5 billion) in budgetary costs, NIS 22 billion of it for defence, and said the sum had already been added to the 2026 budget. [cite:gi16_aa_iranwar]

The bill shows in Israel's public finances. Defence spending, 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2022, reached 8.4 per cent in 2024 and 7.8 per cent in 2025; the bank assumes about 5.5 per cent a year for 2026–2030. The central government deficit was 6.7 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 4.7 per cent in 2025, and gross public debt rose from 61.3 per cent of GDP in 2023 to 68.5 per cent in 2025. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] SIPRI's figures, measured differently, put Israel's military spending at $46.5 billion in 2024 and $48.3 billion in 2025. [cite:hm_globes_sipri] [cite:hz9_sipri_2025] The Knesset passed the 2026 budget on 30 March 2026, with about $44.8 billion for defence. [cite:gi16_bd_budget2026] Against all of this, the Bank of Israel's accounts show a special American grant of NIS 13 billion in 2023 and NIS 6 billion in each of 2024 and 2025, NIS 25 billion in all. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] The previous section weighs what that grant means. [scene:gi16_aid|The aid]

America's bill: the Red Sea and the region

The United States paid twice: in aid to Israel, and for its own forces. The Costs of War project at Brown University, which publishes its methods, estimated American regional operations in the 2024 fiscal year at $4.86 billion. That included $2.4 billion from the April 2024 supplemental for operations, force protection and deterrence, and $2.4 billion for additional carrier groups and strikes on the Houthis; a carrier strike group cost about $8.7 million a day, and by June 2024 the Navy had fired about $1 billion of munitions in the Red Sea. [cite:hz12_cow_2024] The American air campaign against the Houthis began on 11 January 2024, after attacks on shipping that the Houthis said were in support of Gaza. [cite:hz10_crs_if12587] [cite:hz10_aje_truce] Operation Rough Rider, from 15 March to 6 May 2025, cost more than $1 billion by NBC's reporting and between $2.76 billion and $4.95 billion for the 2025 fiscal year's Yemen operations by Costs of War's estimate, which includes carrier time and three F/A-18 fighters lost at sea, worth about $210 million. [cite:hz10_nbc_rrcost] [cite:hz12_cow_2025] Airwars recorded at least 224 civilians allegedly killed by American strikes in Yemen in those seven weeks; Central Command made no public determinations. [cite:hz10_airwars_rr] The Red Sea campaign is told in the Hezbollah volume. [scene:hz10_redsea|The Red Sea]

From October 2023 to September 2025, Costs of War put the cost of American operations in the wider Middle East at $9.65 billion to $12.07 billion, and at $31.35 billion to $33.77 billion when the $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel is added. [cite:hz12_cow_2025]

America's bill: interceptors and two Iran wars

The most direct American contribution to Israel's defence has been interceptors. On 13–14 April 2024 American forces, including the destroyers Arleigh Burke and Carney, destroyed more than 80 drones and at least six ballistic missiles aimed at Israel; on 1 October 2024 two destroyers fired about a dozen interceptors at Iran's second barrage, and the United States then sent a THAAD battery and its crew to Israel. [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] [cite:ow7_usni_oct2024] [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024] In June 2025 American THAAD batteries fired more than 100 and possibly 150 interceptors, about a quarter of the stock, by CNN's reporting; Costs of War, assuming about 150, put their cost at $1.8 billion to $1.95 billion. With Operation Midnight Hammer, the strikes on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, the June 2025 war cost the United States $2.04 billion to $2.25 billion. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025] The defence of Israel is set out in The One-Way Mirror. [scene:ow7_iran|Defending Israel, fighting Iran]

The 2026 war dwarfed these sums. Central Command estimated its cost at $43.6 billion as of 3 September 2026, more than half of it in munitions, with Patriot and THAAD interceptors in greatest demand; the Congressional Budget Office estimated $38 billion through 1 August. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] The war also raised petrol prices: the Energy Information Administration forecast an average of $3.91 a gallon in 2026 against $3.10 in 2025, which Part Fourteen of the Iran volume sets out with its caveats. [cite:ir14_eia_steo] [scene:ir14_bill|The American bill, 1979–2026]

What the two bills show

Two points stand out. The first is scale. The 2026 war alone cost the United States more by September 2026, on Central Command's estimate, than all its military aid to Israel and its regional operations in the two years after October 2023 combined, on Costs of War's. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:hz12_cow_2025] The second is who carried the cost. Israel bore the larger share of its own wars: the Bank of Israel's NIS 352 billion, with debt rising by about seven points of GDP. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] The United States bore most of the cost of the war with Iran it chose to join and lead in 2026, and of the Red Sea campaign against the Houthis, whose attacks on shipping the Houthis themselves tied to Gaza. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:hz10_aje_truce] How far those costs followed from Israel's wars, and how far from decisions of American presidents, is the question the next section takes up. [scene:gi16_americans|The Americans killed]

sections.h: The Americans Killed, and the "Dragged In" Argument
sections.html:
This section lists every American service member whose death the record ties to the theatres of the wars since 7 October 2023, from Gaza and the Red Sea to the militia attacks and the war with Iran. It then lists American civilians killed in Israel, Gaza and the West Bank, with responsibility stated as the record states it, and closes with the argument that the United States was dragged into these wars by Israel, setting out both sides. Earlier American losses to Iran and its allies, from the Beirut barracks in 1983 to Ain al-Asad in 2020, are counted in the Hezbollah and Iran volumes. [scene:hz12_costs|The American bill, 1983–2026] [scene:ir14_bill|The American bill, 1979–2026]

Service members, October 2023 to October 2026

The first deaths came at sea. On 11 January 2024, off Somalia, two Navy SEALs, Special Warfare Operators Christopher J. Chambers and Nathan G. Ingram, went into rough water while boarding a dhow that Central Command said was carrying Iranian weapons, including missile parts bound for the Houthis; one was knocked off by waves and the other went in after him. They were declared dead on 21 January. [cite:gi16_mt_seals] [cite:hz12_cow_2024] On 28 January 2024 a drone struck Tower 22, a small American outpost in north-eastern Jordan, killing three Army soldiers, Sergeant William Jerome Rivers and Specialists Kennedy Ladon Sanders and Breonna Alexsondria Moffett. President Biden blamed Iran-backed militia groups; the United States named Kata'ib Hezbollah, which then said it was halting operations under pressure from Iran and Iraq, and Iran denied ordering attacks. [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] [cite:hz10_at_farida] [scene:hz10_iraq|The Iraqi militias] On 20 March 2024 Aviation Machinist's Mate 2nd Class Oriola Michael Aregbesola, of a helicopter squadron aboard the destroyer USS Mason, which was then responding to Houthi attacks on shipping, died in the Red Sea region; the Pentagon called it a non-combat incident and opened an investigation. [cite:gi16a_tp_aregbesola] In May 2024 Army Sergeant Quandarius Stanley, 23, was critically injured when high winds and heavy seas damaged the temporary pier the United States had built to bring aid into Gaza; officials said the injury was not combat-related, and he died in late 2024. [cite:gi16_bdn_stanley] Not counted here: five Army special operations aviators killed on 10 November 2023 when their helicopter crashed in the eastern Mediterranean "during an air refueling mission as part of military training", which the reporting set in the build-up after 7 October but did not tie to the fighting. [cite:gi16a_nbc_med]

No American was reported killed in the June 2025 war with Iran. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] The war that began on 28 February 2026 was the deadliest for American forces. By the Pentagon's Defense Casualty Analysis System, 21 service members had died and 865 had been wounded by 9 October 2026, most of the wounded after 7 July. [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] [cite:gi16_tp_21] Eleven of the deaths were by hostile fire, by the official count The Intercept reported on 28 September, when it stood at 19; the two deaths added on 9 October were non-hostile. The Intercept calls the tally an undercount, and The Washington Post reported four more deaths than it showed. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called the Post's report "DISGUSTING and FAKE", and an official said the additional deaths it reported "were not directly related to the war with Iran". [cite:hz12_intercept_cas] [cite:gi16_tp_21] From AP, Army, Navy, Newsweek and Task & Purpose reporting, the 21 were these. On 1 March an Iranian drone struck a tactical operations centre at Port Shuaiba, a civilian port in Kuwait, killing six Army Reserve soldiers of the 103rd Sustainment Command: Chief Warrant Officer 3 Robert M. Marzan, Major Jeffrey R. O'Brien, Captain Cody A. Khork, Master Sergeant Nicole M. Amor, Sergeant 1st Class Noah L. Tietjens and Sergeant Declan J. Coady. Sergeant Benjamin N. Pennington, wounded in an Iranian attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia the same day, died on 8 March. [cite:gi16a_tp_kuwait] [cite:hz12_ktar_deaths] Major Sorffly Davius of the New York Army National Guard died of a medical emergency at Camp Buehring, Kuwait, on 6 March; he was added to the war count only on 9 October. [cite:gi16_tp_21] [cite:gi16a_inq_dcas] Six airmen, three of them from the Ohio Air National Guard, died when a KC-135 tanker crashed in western Iraq on 12 March; Central Command said the crash "was not due to hostile fire or friendly fire". [cite:gi16a_tp_kc135] Commander Gabriel Edwards, commanding officer of a Navy helicopter squadron, died when his MH-60S ditched in the Arabian Sea on 1 July; initial findings did not suggest hostile action. [cite:gi16a_usni_edwards] When fighting resumed in July, three soldiers were killed in an Iranian missile and drone attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan: Private Isabella Gonzales on 17 July, Sergeant Angel S. Rampersad, first listed as missing and believed to have died on 17 July, and First Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan on 18 July. [cite:gi16a_at_jordan] [cite:gi16_nw_19th] Army Sergeant Michael Emmanuel Swinton was killed in action at Erbil Air Base in Iraq on 19 July "during a controlled detonation of a downed One-Way Unmanned Aerial System", in the Army's words. [cite:gi16a_army_swinton] Captain Bianca C. Wilkerson of US Army Central died in a "non-combat related incident" in Qatar on 18 September, and a Navy sailor died in September of a cause listed as pending; both deaths were non-hostile. [cite:gi16_nw_19th] [cite:gi16_tp_21] One further death is outside the 21: Sergeant Devin A. Seibel, 26, died in a training accident in Iraq in May, which the military said was not tied to operations against Iran; it is recorded under Operation Inherent Resolve, the campaign against ISIS. [cite:gi16a_inq_dcas] The war itself is told in Part Eleven of the Iran volume. [scene:ir11_war|The 2026 war]

On those counts, 28 American service members died in these theatres between October 2023 and 9 October 2026: two SEALs at sea and a sailor in the Red Sea in 2024, three at Tower 22, one from the Gaza pier and 21 in the 2026 war. That total is this book's addition of the figures above, and it leaves out the Mediterranean training crash of November 2023 and the training death in Iraq in May 2026; 14 of the 28 deaths were hostile, and 21 of the 28 came in the war with Iran.

American civilians

The largest single loss of American civilian life came on 7 October 2023. On 24 October Secretary of State Antony Blinken told the United Nations that 33 Americans had been killed in the Hamas-led attack, and a State Department official said ten more were unaccounted for and might be held hostage. [cite:gi16_kshb_oct7] Hostages killed in captivity are described in the Hamas volume. [scene:hm12_ceasefires|The ceasefires and the hostages]

In the West Bank, ABC News counted five American citizens killed between 7 October 2023 and July 2025. [cite:gi16_abc_musallet] Tawfic Abdel Jabbar, 17, of Gretna, Louisiana, was shot dead on Highway 60 on 19 January 2024; Israeli police said an off-duty officer, a soldier and a settler had fired at the car, and police and the army said he had been throwing stones, which a passenger, his father and the Israeli rights group B'Tselem disputed. No findings or charges had been published by July 2025. [cite:gi16_wiki_abdeljabbar] Mohammad Alkhdour, 17, was killed on 10 February 2024; the reporting checked here does not set out who fired. [cite:gi16_abc_musallet] Aysenur Eygi, 26, an American and Turkish citizen, was shot in the head at a protest in Beita on 6 September 2024. The army found it "highly likely" she had been hit "indirectly and unintentionally" by fire aimed at a protest leader; President Biden called for "full accountability", and Blinken called the killing "unprovoked and unjustified". [cite:gi16_axios_eygi] Amer Rabee, 14, of Saddle Brook, New Jersey, was killed near Turmus Ayya in April 2025; the army said it had fired at "three terrorists who hurled rocks toward the highway", and the State Department said Israel was investigating. [cite:gi16_abc_rabee] Sayfollah Musallet, 20, of Tampa, Florida, was killed in Sinjil on 11 July 2025; his family and the Palestinian Health Ministry said settlers beat him to death and blocked an ambulance, and the army said a clash had followed stone-throwing at settlers and that the security service and police were examining it. [cite:gi16_abc_musallet] According to a compilation of the reporting, as of March 2026 no criminal charges had been brought in any killing of an American by Israelis since January 2022. [cite:gi16_wiki_abdeljabbar] Settler violence in this period is documented in The West Bank, Documented. [scene:wb8_settlers|Settler violence]

In Gaza, Jacob Flickinger, an American-Canadian, was one of seven World Central Kitchen workers killed by Israeli strikes on their convoy on 1 April 2024. The army's own inquiry called it "a grave mistake" caused by misidentification and breaches of its rules of engagement, and dismissed two officers and reprimanded three. [cite:gi16_dfat_wck] Two earlier cases frame these. Rachel Corrie, 23, was crushed by an Israeli military bulldozer in Rafah on 16 March 2003 while trying to stop a house demolition; the driver said he did not see her, and in February 2015 Israel's Supreme Court upheld a ruling that the state was not liable because the act was "wartime activity", a decision Human Rights Watch said implied "immunity even for deaths caused by alleged negligence". [cite:gi16_hrw_corrie] Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian-American Al Jazeera journalist, was killed near Jenin in May 2022; the army said there was a "high possibility" a soldier had shot her, and no criminal investigation followed. [cite:pr_npr_abuakleh]

"Dragged in": the argument on both sides

The claim that Israel dragged the United States into these wars is an argument about cause, not a finding of fact, and the Iran volume tests it in detail. [scene:ir14_who|Who pushed, who decided] [scene:ir12_question|Iran and war with America] The case for it rests on documented links. The Houthis described their attacks on shipping as support for Gaza, and the Iraqi militias attacked American forces more than 160 times between 7 October 2023 and early February 2024. [cite:hz10_aje_truce] [cite:hz10_at_farida] In 2026 Secretary of State Rubio said, "We knew that there was going to be an Israeli action," and that it would bring attacks on American forces; Reuters reported, from anonymous sources, that Netanyahu urged President Trump by phone less than 48 hours before the strikes. [cite:ir14_aje_rubio] [cite:hz12b_reuters_call] Joe Kent, director of the National Counterterrorism Center, resigned on 17 March 2026, writing that the war began "due to pressure from Israel and its powerful American lobby". [cite:ir14_fox_kent]

The case against rests on documents too. Every American operation was ordered by an American president: Trump said, "I might have forced Israel's hand," and Under Secretary of Defense Elbridge Colby said, "The president made our decision." [cite:ir14_sn_forced] President Bush refused an Israeli request to strike Iran in 2008, and by Netanyahu's own memoir President Obama declined one in 2013, and by one analyst's account Israel called off strikes in June 2025 when Trump asked it to; the same analyst cites Rubio's later statement that the war "had to happen no matter what". [cite:hz12_cato_hoffman] [cite:ir14_fdd_goren] Trump called Kent "very weak on security"; Senator Mitch McConnell said his letter was tainted by "virulent anti-Semitism", and J Street's Ilan Goldenberg said the claim played on "the worst antisemitic tropes" and that responsibility lay with Trump. [cite:ir14_npr_kent] [cite:ir14_fox_kent] Iran and forces the United States says it armed had also attacked Americans long before 2023, by the Pentagon's own unpublished count killing at least 603 in Iraq. [cite:ir14_mt_603] [scene:hz12_costs|The American bill, 1983–2026] Netanyahu called the claim that he dragged the United States in "fake news". [cite:hz12b_mediaite_bibi]

The deaths listed above fit neither side cleanly. The 2024 deaths came in theatres the Gaza war activated, but in operations that American commanders chose: interdicting Iranian arms at sea, patrolling the Red Sea, holding an outpost in Jordan, and building a pier for aid to Gaza. [cite:gi16_mt_seals] [cite:gi16a_tp_aregbesola] [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] [cite:gi16_bdn_stanley] Most of the dead, 21 of 28, fell in the 2026 war, which an American president ordered on a timetable his Secretary of State tied to a planned Israeli action. [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] [cite:ir14_aje_rubio] [scene:hz12_wars|Congress and the 2026 war] What the record supports is that Israeli action and advocacy shaped when the United States fought; no document shows that an American president was compelled to decide that it would.

chapters.label: Part Sixteen
chapters.title: The World's Response
chapters.intro: Part Sixteen sets out what the rest of the world has said and done since October 2023, and why the support Israel receives has largely held. It begins at the United Nations: the Security Council's votes and the American vetoes, the General Assembly's resolutions, the laws that barred the UN's refugee agency, the findings of the UN's own commission and the end of the peacekeeping mission in Lebanon. It then turns to the courts: the genocide case at the International Court of Justice, the Court's advisory opinions on the occupation and on aid, the arrest warrants of the International Criminal Court and the American sanctions on that court, and the cases brought in British and Dutch courts over parts for the F-35. The third section follows what states did on their own account, from recognising Palestine and restricting arms to sanctioning ministers and settlers, cutting trade or, in the other direction, joining the Abraham Accords and recognising Israel's claim to the Golan. The last section sets out the documented reasons support persists, in law, money, industry, intelligence and politics, and the evidence that it has begun to erode, and keeps the arguments about motive apart from the record.
chapters.outro: Part Sixteen established that the world's response since October 2023 has been broad in what it said and narrow in what it enforced. In the Security Council the United States vetoed six Gaza ceasefire drafts and Palestine's full membership, until the Council endorsed the American plan in Resolution 2803 in November 2025; the General Assembly voted by majorities of 124 to 149 states for an end to the occupation, a ceasefire and a two-state declaration, and the UN's commission of inquiry found genocide, which Israel called "distorted and false." [cite:gz_aj_unsc] [cite:ow11_afp_veto2025] [cite:gi17_wiki_res2803] [cite:wb_ahram_unga2024] [cite:gi17_un_unga2025] [cite:gz_un_coi2025] [cite:gz_ctv_coi2025] The World Court ordered aid "at scale" and a halt to the Rafah offensive, found the occupation unlawful and the settlements due to be evacuated, and will not rule on genocide before 2029; the criminal court's warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant stand unexecuted while the United States sanctions the court's judges. [cite:gi17_icj_order0328] [cite:gz_lawfare_rafah] [cite:wb_livelaw_icj2024] [cite:gz_icj_timelimits] [cite:ow11_wiki_eo14203] States recognised Palestine (157 of 193 by September 2025), sanctioned Ben-Gvir, Smotrich and settler groups, and Turkey cut trade, but Britain kept supplying F-35 parts, Germany lifted its curbs and the EU could not agree to suspend trade; no Arab treaty or Accords state broke with Israel, though the UAE named annexation a "red line." [cite:gi17_aje_recog2025] [cite:gi17_aje_sanctions2025] [cite:gi17_mp_eusettlers] [cite:gi17_tn_turkey] [cite:gi17_aje_f35uk] [cite:gi17_aje_germany] [cite:gi17_an_eutrade] [cite:gi6_axios_uae2025] Support has persisted on documented foundations: the 2016 memorandum and the law on Israel's military edge, arms industries on both sides, intelligence sharing, lobbying money and a shared war with Iran, while American sympathy has shifted toward the Palestinians and 27 Democratic senators voted to block arms sales in July 2025. Why it persists remains an argument. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:hm_globes_exports] [cite:ow_aj_nsamou] [cite:pm_israelite_2024] [cite:ow_inss_centcom] [cite:gz_gallup_2026] [cite:gi17_bg_senate2025] Part Seventeen asks the prior question: what the claim to the land rests on, and what would remain of a programme of "Greater Israel" had the Zionist movement settled in Argentina or Uganda, or had no state been founded. [scene:gi18_dependency|Part Seventeen]

sections.h: The United Nations
sections.html:
This volume found documented programmes of territorial expansion for the West Bank and the Golan Heights, and the UN's record on those two territories is older than the present war. [scene:gi13_record|Part Eighteen: the record] The Security Council declared Israel's Golan law "null and void and without international legal effect" in December 1981, unanimously and with American support, and in December 2016 it found that the settlements have "no legal validity." [cite:gi8_wiki_res497] [cite:wb_wiki_2334] [scene:gi8_golan|Part Eight: the Golan] [scene:wb10_rulings|The West Bank, Documented: the rulings] What follows concerns the period since 7 October 2023, when Gaza dominated the UN's business. Most of these votes were about the war, not about borders; they are set out here because they are the bulk of what the world's main forum said and did, and because they show where its power to act stopped.

The Security Council and the veto

Between October 2023 and November 2024 the Security Council held fourteen votes on Gaza. Four resolutions passed, on 15 November 2023, 22 December 2023, 25 March 2024 and 10 June 2024; the last was an American draft. The United States vetoed drafts on 18 October 2023, 8 December 2023, 20 February 2024 and 20 November 2024, and on 18 April 2024 it vetoed a draft that would have admitted Palestine as a full UN member. Russia and China vetoed American drafts on 25 October 2023 and 22 March 2024. [cite:gz_aj_unsc] In June 2025 the United States vetoed a draft, backed by the other fourteen members, demanding an "immediate, unconditional and permanent" ceasefire and unrestricted aid. Washington cited Hamas's "failure to disarm" and said the text did not address Israel's security or the release of hostages. [cite:gi17_air_veto2025] On 18 September 2025 it was again the only member to vote against a ceasefire demand, 14 to 1. Its deputy envoy, Morgan Ortagus, said the draft did not condemn Hamas or recognise Israel's right to self-defence and "seeks to return to a failed system." AFP and JURIST each counted it as the sixth American veto of a Gaza ceasefire draft. [cite:ow11_afp_veto2025] [cite:gz_jurist_veto2025]

Counts differ with method. Al Jazeera's tally of November 2024 also lists as vetoed by the United States and Britain a Russian draft of 25 October 2023, the same day on which Russia and China vetoed an American draft; AFP's "sixth" leaves it out. [cite:gz_aj_unsc] [cite:gi17a_aj_unsc] [cite:ow11_afp_veto2025] The long series is larger: AFP counted 46 American vetoes on the Palestinian territories as of September 2025, and Al Jazeera, in 2021, at least 53 vetoes of resolutions critical of Israel since the first in 1972. Part Eleven of The One-Way Mirror explains the different counting rules. [cite:ow11_afp_veto2025] [cite:ow11_aj_vetoes2021] [scene:ow11_exceptions|The One-Way Mirror: the veto record]

After the October 2025 ceasefire the Council changed course. On 17 November 2025 it adopted Resolution 2803, an American text endorsing the Gaza plan Israel and Hamas had agreed in October. It welcomed a "Board of Peace" for reconstruction and authorised an International Stabilization Force. The vote was 13 to none, with China and Russia abstaining; Russia's ambassador said the text gave "complete control over the Gaza strip to the Board of Peace." Netanyahu welcomed it, saying "we believe that President Trump's plan will lead to peace and prosperity." The Palestinian Authority welcomed it; Hamas denounced it. [cite:gi17_wiki_res2803] No further American veto on Gaza appeared in the reporting checked through October 2026. Part Nine of Gaza, Documented sets the vetoes beside the American plan. [scene:gz9_us|Gaza, Documented: the United States]

The General Assembly

The General Assembly, where no state has a veto and resolutions do not bind, voted by growing margins. On 18 September 2024, acting on the World Court's advisory opinion described in the next section, it demanded by 124 votes to 14, with 43 abstentions, that Israel end its presence in the occupied territory within twelve months. The United States called the text "inflammatory"; Israel's ambassador, Danny Danon, said it backed the Palestinian Authority's "diplomatic terrorism." [cite:wb_ahram_unga2024] In June 2025 the Assembly demanded an "immediate, unconditional and permanent ceasefire," the release of all hostages and the resumption of aid, by 149 to 12 with 19 abstentions; Israel and the United States voted against. [cite:gi17_un_unga2025] On 12 September 2025 it endorsed the "New York Declaration," a French and Saudi text on a two-state settlement, by 142 to 10 with 12 abstentions. The declaration condemned "the attacks committed by Hamas against civilians on the 7th of October" and demanded that Hamas free all hostages, end its rule in Gaza and hand its weapons to the Palestinian Authority. [cite:gi17_ewn_nydecl] Israel's foreign ministry said Israel "utterly rejects" it and called the Assembly "a political circus detached from reality"; the day before, Netanyahu had said: "We are going to fulfill our promise that there will be no Palestinian state." [cite:gi17_mm_nydecl] [cite:gi17_ewn_nydecl] The twelve-month deadline passed in September 2025, a month after the E1 settlement plan received final approval. [cite:wb_itv_e1] [scene:gi6_votes|Part Six: the votes]

UNRWA

The UN's agency for Palestine refugees, created by the Assembly in 1949, became a target in its own right. [cite:gz_un_res302] In January 2024 Israel alleged that twelve UNRWA employees had taken part in the attack of 7 October; the United States paused its funding on 26 January 2024, other donors paused and some later resumed, and American law then barred UNRWA funding until March 2025. [cite:gz_crs_unrwa] The UN's internal oversight office examined nineteen staff members named by Israel and reported in August 2024 that nine may have been involved, that the evidence was insufficient for nine and that there was none for one; it said it could not independently authenticate most of the information Israel supplied. [cite:hm_un_oios] On 28 October 2024 the Knesset voted 92 to 10 for two laws that barred UNRWA from operating in Israel and Israeli officials from contact with it. [cite:gz_jp_knesset_unrwa] Israel's position was that the agency had been penetrated by Hamas; the World Court, in October 2025, found that Israel had not substantiated its allegations against UNRWA's staff. [cite:gz_ji_ao2025] [scene:gz8_aid|Gaza, Documented: aid]

The UN's own findings

On 16 September 2025 the Commission of Inquiry appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, chaired by the South African judge Navi Pillay, concluded that "Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip," that four of the five acts defined in the 1948 Convention had been committed, and that President Isaac Herzog, Netanyahu and Gallant "have incited the commission of genocide." [cite:gz_un_coi2025] Israel's foreign ministry said it "categorically rejects this distorted and false report," which it said "relies entirely on Hamas falsehoods," and called for the commission to be abolished. [cite:gz_ctv_coi2025] The finding is that of investigators appointed by a UN body, not of a court; the genocide question before the World Court is undecided. [scene:gz7_courts|Gaza, Documented: the courts]

Lebanon: the end of UNIFIL

The UN peacekeeping force in south Lebanon is ending. On 28 August 2025 the Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2790, extending UNIFIL's mandate a final time to 31 December 2026, to be followed by a one-year "orderly and safe drawdown and withdrawal." The United States said Lebanese forces should take on more responsibility; France warned that premature withdrawal could weaken the Lebanese government's efforts. [cite:gi9_un_2790] [cite:hz8_scr_nov25] Part Nine describes the zone Israel held in south Lebanon as of October 2026, with Israel's stated security reasons beside it. [scene:gi9_lebanon|Part Nine: south Lebanon]

The pattern across these bodies is consistent. The Assembly and the UN's own investigators reached far-reaching positions by large majorities; the Council, the only body whose decisions bind, acted only when the United States agreed, and its peacekeeping force in south Lebanon is being withdrawn. Israel rejected each critical finding as biased, and the United States opposed most of them, on the stated ground that they failed to condemn Hamas or to recognise Israel's right to defend itself. [cite:ow11_afp_veto2025] [cite:gi17_mm_nydecl] [cite:gz_ctv_coi2025]

sections.h: The Courts
sections.html:
Three kinds of court have ruled on Israel's conduct since 2024: the International Court of Justice, which settles disputes between states and gives advisory opinions; the International Criminal Court, which tries individuals; and national courts, which decide whether their own governments may keep supplying arms. The record of each is set out below with Israel's answer beside it. The fuller accounts are in Gaza, Documented and The West Bank, Documented, and this section links to them rather than retelling them. [scene:gz7_courts|Gaza, Documented: the courts] [scene:wb10_rulings|The West Bank, Documented: the rulings]

South Africa v. Israel

South Africa brought its case under the Genocide Convention at the end of 2023, alleging genocidal acts committed with genocidal intent. Israel answered that it was defending itself, that the statements of officials South Africa cited were not policy, and that it had no genocidal intent. [cite:gz_ch_icj] The Court has ruled three times on provisional measures, which are orders made while a case proceeds and do not decide it. On 26 January 2024 it found "at least some of the rights claimed by South Africa" plausible and ordered Israel to prevent acts within the Convention, to prevent and punish incitement, and to enable humanitarian aid; it did not order a ceasefire. [cite:gz_oj_icj2024] On 28 March 2024, citing "the spread of famine and starvation," it ordered Israel unanimously to ensure the "unhindered provision at scale" of food, water, electricity, fuel, shelter and medical care, including by opening more land crossings, and, by 15 votes to 1, to ensure that its army did not violate Palestinians' rights under the Convention, including by blocking aid. [cite:gi17_icj_order0328] On 24 May 2024, by 13 votes to 2, it ordered Israel to "halt its military offensive and any other action in the Rafah Governorate" that might inflict conditions of life that could bring about the group's physical destruction. [cite:gz_lawfare_rafah] Israel said it "has not and will not" conduct such actions in Rafah and called the genocide charge "false, outrageous and morally repugnant." [cite:gz_toi_rafah]

The case is now in its written stage. Israel filed its counter-memorial, and on 21 May 2026 the Court set 22 November 2027 for South Africa's reply and 22 May 2029 for Israel's rejoinder. As of October 2026 no judgment on whether genocide was committed exists, and none is expected for years. [cite:gz_icj_timelimits]

The advisory opinions

The Court's most direct ruling on the territories this volume concerns came in an advisory opinion requested by the General Assembly. On 19 July 2024 it found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful and said Israel must end it "as rapidly as possible," cease all new settlement activity, evacuate all settlers and make reparation. It found that Israel's policies amounted to "systemic discrimination," and that all states must neither recognise the situation as lawful nor help maintain it. The judges divided on its findings: 11 to 4 on the unlawfulness of Israel's continued presence, 14 to 1 on settlements and 12 to 3 on other states' duty of non-recognition; the vice-president, Julia Sebutinde, dissented on all of them. [cite:gi18_idi_icj2024] [cite:wb_livelaw_icj2024] [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] Netanyahu replied: "The Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land, including in our eternal capital Jerusalem, nor in Judea and Samaria, our historical homeland." [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] The Assembly turned the opinion into a twelve-month deadline that expired in September 2025, as described in the previous section. [cite:wb_ahram_unga2024] [scene:gi17_un|The United Nations]

A second opinion, of 22 October 2025, concerned aid.
