The Court said that Israel, as occupying power, must "ensure the basic needs of the local population" and was "under an obligation to agree to and facilitate relief schemes provided by the United Nations and its entities," UNRWA among them, and it found that Israel had not substantiated its allegations against UNRWA's staff. Israel, which did not take part in the proceedings, said it "categorically rejects" the opinion. [cite:gz_ji_ao2025] Advisory opinions state the law as the Court finds it; they are not judgments in a case and carry no enforcement mechanism of their own. [cite:wb_livelaw_icj2024]

The arrest warrants

On 21 November 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, finding reasonable grounds to believe that they bore responsibility for the war crime of starvation as a method of warfare, for intentionally directing attacks against civilians, and for the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution and other inhumane acts. It issued a warrant the same day for Mohammed Deif, commander of Hamas's armed wing, for murder, extermination, torture, rape and hostage-taking. [cite:gz_un_icc] [cite:gz_almon_icc] The court ended proceedings against Deif on 26 February 2025 after prosecutors reported that he had been killed in July 2024. [cite:gz_ji_deif] Netanyahu called the warrants "anti-Semitic"; President Joe Biden called them "outrageous." [cite:gz_almon_icc] Israel, which like the United States is not a party to the court's statute, challenged its jurisdiction; in October 2025 the challenge was still pending and the court had found "no legal basis" to withdraw the warrants in the meantime, and no ruling on the challenge was found in the reporting checked through October 2026. [cite:gz_toi_icc2025] [cite:wb_aj_icc_timeline]

The United States answered with sanctions on the court itself. Executive Order 14203 of 6 February 2025 cited what it called "illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel," and the Treasury and State Department then listed the prosecutor, judges, both deputy prosecutors, the UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and three Palestinian human rights organisations. The court said it "stands firmly by its personnel." [cite:ow11_eo14203] [cite:ow11_wiki_eo14203] [cite:ow11_state_aug2025] [cite:ow11_icc_stmt2025] Three of its judges sued in New York in June 2026, and in October 2026 a federal court in Maine refused to dismiss a First Amendment challenge to the sanctions programme. [cite:ow11_jurist_judges2026] [cite:ow11_gs_maine2026] Part Eleven of The One-Way Mirror follows each designation. [scene:ow11_icc|The One-Way Mirror: sanctioning a court] As of October 2026 neither warrant against an Israeli official had been executed.

National courts and the F-35

The most concrete litigation concerned parts for the F-35 fighter, which Israel's air force flies and which is assembled from components made in several countries. In Britain, Foreign Secretary David Lammy suspended about 30 of 350 export licences for Israel in September 2024 after reviewing its compliance with humanitarian law, but the suspension did not cover F-35 parts. The Palestinian group Al-Haq, joined by Oxfam, challenged that exception. On 30 June 2025 the High Court rejected the challenge, saying the "acutely sensitive and political issue is a matter for the executive." The government had argued that suspending the parts would affect the "whole F-35 programme" and have a "profound impact on international peace and security." [cite:gi17_aje_f35uk]

The Dutch case went the other way and then back. In February 2024 an appeals court in The Hague ordered the government to stop exporting F-35 parts to Israel, citing a clear risk of violations of international law, and the government complied while appealing. On 3 October 2025 the Supreme Court held that the appeals court "was not entitled to make its own assessment" of that risk, but ordered the minister to reassess the licence within six weeks, with the halt remaining in force. The government had argued that foreign policy belongs to government and that the United States would supply the parts anyway. [cite:gi17_es_dutch] On 14 November 2025 the cabinet said it would keep the shipments halted pending a final decision within six months; since April 2025 Dutch permits for Israel have been assessed case by case. [cite:gi17_nlt_dutch2025] A later decision was not found in the reporting checked.

The table's last column is the finding of this section. International courts have issued orders and opinions of unusual breadth against a state that rejects their authority or their conclusions; the binding orders have no enforcement arm except states, and the national courts, which do have that arm, have deferred to their governments in one case and only partly in the other. Israel's position throughout has been that the courts are biased or lack jurisdiction, that it is fighting a war of self-defence, and that it has no intent to destroy anyone. [cite:gz_toi_rafah] [cite:gz_almon_icc] [cite:wb_aj_icc_timeline]

sections.h: What States Did
sections.html:
Governments acted on their own account in five ways after October 2023: they recognised a Palestinian state, restricted arms, sanctioned Israeli ministers and settlers, cut or threatened trade, and set conditions on normal relations. A smaller number moved the other way. Each measure is given with the reason the government stated and Israel's response.

Recognising Palestine

On 22 May 2024 Ireland, Spain and Norway announced that they would recognise a Palestinian state; Norway's recognition took effect on 28 May, on the lines that existed before 4 June 1967. Spain's prime minister cited "peace, justice and democracy," Ireland's the "appalling" conditions in Gaza, and Norway's the Palestinians' "fundamental, independent right to self-determination." Israel recalled its envoys from Dublin and Oslo, and its foreign minister said Israel "will not back down against those who undermine its sovereignty and endanger its security." [cite:gi17_na_recog2024]

The larger wave came in September 2025, around the UN General Assembly. Britain announced its recognition on 21 September; Canada, Australia and Portugal followed, and France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco and Andorra recognised Palestine at the Assembly. By Al Jazeera's count this brought the total to 157 of the 193 UN member states, with eleven new recognitions in 2025 and twenty since October 2023. [cite:gi17_aje_recog2025] Netanyahu called Britain's step a "prize" for Hamas and said a Palestinian state "will not happen"; Israel's ambassador to the UN called the statehood summit a "circus." [cite:gi17_aje_recog2025] In August 2025, after Britain, France and Canada had announced those plans, Smotrich presented final approval of the E1 settlement plan as an answer to them, saying it would "permanently bury the idea of a Palestinian state." [cite:wb_itv_e1] [scene:wb9_annex|The West Bank, Documented: since October 2023] Recognition creates no state on the ground; what it changes is the diplomatic standing of the territory Israel's annexation track would absorb. [scene:gi6_votes|Part Six: the annexation track]

Arms, and their limits

The arms measures were narrower than the recognitions. Britain suspended about 30 of 350 export licences in September 2024 but kept supplying F-35 parts, and its courts upheld the exception. The Netherlands stopped F-35 parts only under a court order. [cite:gi17_aje_f35uk] [cite:gi17_es_dutch] [scene:gi17_courts|The courts] Germany, which supplied 30 percent of Israel's major arms imports from 2019 to 2023 by SIPRI's count, restricted exports of weapons that could be used in Gaza in August 2025, after Israel's cabinet decided to seize Gaza City. It lifted the restriction from 24 November 2025; the chancellor's spokesman said that "since October 10, we have had a ceasefire in Gaza and it has fundamentally stabilised." Israel had said in August that such moves "reward terrorism"; in November its foreign minister, Gideon Saar, called on "other governments to adopt similar decisions, following Germany." [cite:gi17_aje_germany] The supplier that matters most, the United States, moved in the opposite direction: in March 2025 Secretary of State Marco Rubio used emergency authority to speed some $4 billion in military assistance, calling his predecessor's conditions a "partial arms embargo." [cite:ow1_state_rubio2025] [scene:ow8_pace|The One-Way Mirror: the pace of deliveries]

Sanctions on ministers and settlers

On 10 June 2025 Britain, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Norway froze the assets of, and barred entry to, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, two serving cabinet ministers whose parties lead the settlement and annexation agenda described in Parts Five and Six. Their joint statement said the two "have incited extremist violence and serious abuses of Palestinian human rights." Saar called the decision "outrageous"; the US State Department called it "extremely unhelpful"; Smotrich, at the inauguration of a new settlement in Hebron, expressed "contempt" for Britain and said Israel would keep building. [cite:gi17_aje_sanctions2025] Hours later he ordered the cancellation of the indemnity that lets Israeli banks deal with Palestinian ones, citing the Palestinian Authority's "delegitimisation campaign." [cite:wb_aj_bankwaiver2025] [scene:wb12_revenue|The West Bank, Documented: the revenue]

The American sanctions on violent settlers imposed in 2024 were revoked in January 2025. [cite:wb_ofac_20250124] The European Union, which needs unanimity for sanctions, was repeatedly blocked by Hungary. After Viktor Orbán lost Hungary's April 2026 election, EU foreign ministers agreed in principle on 11 May 2026 to sanction Hamas leaders and Israeli settler figures; Haaretz reported that the draft list named the organisations Amana, Nachala, Hashomer Yosh and Regavim and the Nachala leader Daniella Weiss, though no minister. The EU's foreign-policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said it was "high time we move from deadlock to delivery." Saar called the sanctions "arbitrary and political"; Weiss called them "ridiculous." [cite:gi17_mp_eusettlers]

Trade

The European Union's trade concessions to Israel run through its Association Agreement. In September 2025 the European Commission proposed suspending the agreement's trade provisions, which would affect about €5.8 billion of Israeli exports; suspension needs a qualified majority of member states, full suspension unanimity. In April 2026 Spain, Ireland and Belgium were pressing for action, while Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands were reluctant, and no majority existed. Israel called the proposal "morally and politically distorted." [cite:gi17_an_eutrade] In May 2026 ministers again failed to agree on suspending the agreement or banning settlement goods. [cite:gi17_mp_eusettlers] Turkey went furthest. It announced in May 2024 that it would stop all trade with Israel until aid flowed freely into Gaza, and on 29 August 2025 its foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, told parliament that Turkey had severed all economic and commercial ties, barred its ships from Israeli ports and was closing its airspace to Israeli aircraft, though the scope of the airspace ban was unclear and flight trackers showed Israeli airliners still crossing it that day. Bilateral trade had been nearly $6.8 billion in 2023. [cite:gi17_tn_turkey]

The Arab states and the Abraham Accords

In the reporting checked, none of the Arab states with a peace treaty or normalisation agreement with Israel broke it. The positions they took were conditions. Saudi Arabia told Washington in February 2024 that "there will be no diplomatic relations with Israel" unless an independent Palestinian state is recognised on the 1967 lines with East Jerusalem as its capital. [cite:gi8_reu_saudi2024] The United Arab Emirates, the Accords' principal Arab signatory, said in September 2025 that West Bank annexation would be a "red line," and that "the choice before Israel right now is annexation or integration." [cite:gi6_axios_uae2025] When Netanyahu said in August 2025 that he was attached to the vision of a "Greater Israel," the foreign ministers of 31 states, with the Arab League, the OIC and the Gulf Cooperation Council, called his remarks "a direct threat to Arab national security," and Jordan called them "a dangerous and provocative escalation." [cite:gi7a_oman] [cite:gi7_na_outrage] [scene:gi7_interview|Part Seven: the interview] On 25 September 2025 President Trump said: "I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank." [cite:gi6_ap_trump0925]

The Accords themselves held. The UAE and the other signatories kept their trade and security ties with Israel, and on 6 November 2025 Kazakhstan, which has had relations with Israel since 1992, said it would join them. [cite:gi17_aje_kazakh] One state moved toward Israel on the territorial question itself: on 10 August 2026 Colombia's new government recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, the second country after the United States to do so. [cite:gi8_aje_colombia] [scene:gi8_golan|Part Eight: the Golan]

The pattern is that symbolic and diplomatic measures spread widely while material ones stayed narrow or were reversed. The governments that acted named the war in Gaza, settler violence and annexation as their reasons; Israel's government answered that each measure rewarded Hamas or was biased. [cite:gi17_na_recog2024] [cite:gi17_aje_sanctions2025] [cite:gi17_aje_recog2025] Why the material support held is the subject of the next section.

sections.h: Why Support Persists
sections.html:
The previous sections showed wide condemnation and narrow consequence. This section sets out the documented reasons the material support, above all American support, has held: the law, the money, the industry, the intelligence, the politics and the strategy. It then sets out the evidence that support is eroding. What the record establishes is kept apart from arguments about motive, which are labelled as such and given with the case against them.

The documented drivers

Law and the memorandum. American support is written into statute and into a ten-year agreement. The memorandum of understanding signed on 14 September 2016 commits $38 billion for fiscal years 2019 to 2028, $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing and $5 billion for missile defence, and Congress has since written a floor of not less than $3.3 billion a year in military financing through 2028 into the defence authorisation act for 2021. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The Naval Vessel Transfer Act of 2008 defined Israel's "qualitative military edge" in law, required it to be assessed every four years and provided that arms sales to other states in the region may not adversely affect it. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] After 7 October Congress added a supplemental appropriation in April 2024 of $3.5 billion in military financing, $4 billion for missile defence and $1.2 billion for the Iron Beam laser. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] In March 2025 the State Department used emergency authority to expedite some $4 billion, with nearly $12 billion in arms sales approved since January. [cite:ow1_state_rubio2025] A government that wished to stop this flow would have to override law as well as policy. The amounts, and the test of whether they free Israeli money for operations, are set out in Part Fifteen. [scene:gi16_aid|Part Fifteen: the aid] [scene:ow1_partnership|The One-Way Mirror: the partnership]

Industry. Arms run both ways. Israel's defence exports reached a record $14.8 billion in 2024, 54 percent of them to Europe and about 48 percent in air defence. [cite:hm_globes_exports] Germany supplied 30 percent of Israel's major arms imports from 2019 to 2023. [cite:gi17_aje_germany] In court, two European governments defended continued supply by pointing to industrial ties rather than to Israel: Britain argued that suspending F-35 parts would affect the "whole F-35 programme," and the Netherlands, which hosts a regional warehouse for American-owned F-35 parts, argued that the United States would supply them anyway. [cite:gi17_aje_f35uk] [cite:gi17_es_dutch] Co-production of Iron Dome, David's Sling and Arrow with American firms is described in The One-Way Mirror. [scene:ow8_coproduction|The One-Way Mirror: co-production]

Intelligence. Under a memorandum agreed in principle in March 2009, published by the Guardian in 2013, the National Security Agency shares raw intercepts with Israel's signals intelligence unit, including communications of Americans; a 2013 NSA document describes "a far-reaching technical and analytic relationship" with a dedicated line for "the exchange of raw material." [cite:ow_aj_nsamou] [cite:ow_int_cash2014] [scene:ow4_memorandum|The One-Way Mirror: the memorandum]

Politics and lobbying. AIPAC and its super PAC, the United Democracy Project, spent $95.1 million combined in the 2024 cycle, up from $44 million in 2022, and the super PAC had raised about $104 million for the 2026 cycle by June. [cite:pm_israelite_2024] [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] It spent more than $30.6 million in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary of 4 August 2026, its largest outlay on one race; its opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, won. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:pm_itt_elsayed] The volume on that lobby sets out the money cycle by cycle. [scene:pm2_turn|The Pro-Israel Money Architecture: the turn] [scene:pm10_costs|The Pro-Israel Money Architecture: what it costs] These figures are disclosures. That money was spent is documented; that it caused any member's vote is a separate claim, which the disclosures alone do not establish.

Strategy against Iran. In January 2021 the Pentagon moved Israel from European Command to Central Command, saying "the Abraham Accords paved the way," which placed Israel's forces in the same command as America's Gulf partners. [cite:ow_inss_centcom] The United States joined Israel's war with Iran in June 2025 and again from 28 February 2026, when President Trump told Iranians, "When we are finished, take over your government." [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [scene:ir13_why|The Iran Architecture: why Iran] The cost of that alignment in American money and lives is in Part Fifteen. [scene:gi16_americans|Part Fifteen: the Americans]

Three readings

Three explanations of why the drivers above hold are commonly argued, and none is settled by the documents. The first is that Israel is a strategic asset: a military partner in a region where the United States fights Iran, whose aid largely returns to American factories. The case against it is that the alliance's costs, set out in Part Fifteen, are also documented, and that officials such as those quoted in The Iran Architecture have questioned whether the threats were as great as claimed. [scene:gi16_costs|Part Fifteen: the costs] [scene:ir13_why|The Iran Architecture: why Iran] The second is that domestic politics and lobbying keep support in place. The case for it is the scale of the spending and the defeat of incumbents it targeted, such as Jamaal Bowman and Cori Bush in 2024; the case against is that its candidates also lost, as in Michigan in 2026, and that public sympathy, not money, long ran in Israel's favour. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] [cite:pm_itt_elsayed] [cite:gz_gallup_2026] The third is that religious belief, above all among American evangelicals, sustains it: in a 2017 survey 63 percent of Americans with evangelical beliefs said they supported Israel because "God gave the land of Israel to the Jewish people." [cite:gi11_ct_lifeway] [scene:gi11_christian|Part Eleven: Christian Zionism] The case against is that the survey measures attitude, not policy, and that support in Congress and the executive has been bipartisan, as the recorded votes in The One-Way Mirror show. [scene:ow2_votes|The One-Way Mirror: the votes] Whether American support serves the expansion programmes this volume documented is a further argument: the support is given for Israel's security, and the American president who did most to accelerate it also said, in September 2025, "I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank." [cite:gi6_ap_trump0925] [scene:gi6_votes|Part Six: the annexation track]

Erosion

The clearest change is in American opinion. In February 2026, for the first time in Gallup's annual measurement since 2001, more Americans said they sympathised with the Palestinians (41 percent) than with the Israelis (36 percent), against 31 and 54 percent three years earlier; Gallup noted that the five-point gap was not statistically significant. About two-thirds of Democrats and half of those aged 18 to 34 sympathised more with the Palestinians, and about seven in ten Republicans with the Israelis. [cite:gz_gallup_2026] [cite:gz_ap_gallup2026] In July 2025 Gallup found that 8 percent of Democrats approved of Israel's military action in Gaza, down from 36 percent in November 2023. [cite:pm_gazette_reject] [scene:gz12_coverage|Gaza, Documented: coverage and opinion]

Congress followed more slowly. A measure by Senator Bernie Sanders on Israel's conduct drew 11 votes in January 2024; his resolution against about $8.8 billion in arms sales drew 15 in April 2025. [cite:ow2_jta_sanders2025] On 30 July 2025, 27 Democrats, a majority of the party's senators, voted to block a sale of 20,000 assault rifles and 24 to block a $675 million sale of bombs; every Republican voted against, and both resolutions failed. The previous high had been 18 Democratic votes in November 2024, or 19 by another count. [cite:gi17_bg_senate2025] [cite:ow2_jta_sanders2025] Sanders said Democrats were responding to "an Israeli government which is currently starving children to death"; the Foreign Relations chairman, Jim Risch, said Hamas uses Gaza's people "as human shields." [cite:gi17_bg_senate2025] [scene:ow2_votes|The One-Way Mirror: the votes] Abroad, erosion took the forms set out in the previous section: recognitions, sanctions on two ministers and on settlers, and Germany's temporary arms curbs. [scene:gi17_states|What states did]

The record therefore shows support that is anchored in law, contracts, industry, intelligence and a shared war, and opinion that has moved against it, most among Democrats and the young. As of October 2026 the opinion had changed faster than the law: the memorandum still runs to 2028 and no arms-blocking resolution had passed either chamber. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi17_bg_senate2025] [scene:ow1_partnership|The One-Way Mirror: the partnership]

chapters.label: Part Seventeen
chapters.title: Without 1948: The Uganda Test and the Question of Legitimacy
chapters.intro: Part Seventeen tests an argument rather than a document: that Greater Israel, as a state programme, presupposes the founding of 1948, and that without it there would be no programme to record. It first asks whether every programme found in this volume ran through the institutions of a state, whether the idea of a larger land was older than the state, and how close the founding came to not happening, from the two-thirds vote of November 1947 to the war of 1948. It then revisits the "Uganda Test": the documented alternatives of Argentina, East Africa, the territorialists and Birobidzhan, and what justifications and what kind of "Greater" claim could have survived a move away from the biblical land. Counterfactuals are labelled as arguments throughout. Last, it sets the arguments about legitimacy side by side, each attributed to the state, body or court that makes it, and separates two questions often run together: the legitimacy of the state within its pre-1967 lines, and the holding of land beyond them.
chapters.outro: Part Seventeen established that the argument it tested holds in part. Every Greater Israel programme documented in this volume was carried by a state's cabinet, Knesset, army or ministries, from the cabinet decisions of June 1967 to the 71 to 13 sovereignty motion and the 82 per cent map of 2025. [cite:gi4_cie_june19] [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] [cite:wb_toi_71_13] [cite:gi6_toi_82pct] The idea was older than the state, in the Zionist Organization's map of 1919 and the Revisionists' "both sides of the Jordan", and no government adopted it before 1967, so the programme presupposes both 1948 and 1967. [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] [cite:gi2_ej_revisionists] [cite:gi3_jvl_herut] The founding was contingent: partition passed 33 to 13 under a two-thirds rule that three switched votes would have defeated, and a proposal to ask the ICJ about partition without the inhabitants' consent failed by one vote, though whether a state would have been declared and fought for anyway remains argument. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] [cite:gi18_shindler_1947] [cite:gi18_un_gapal85] [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_trusteeship] The documented alternatives show that refuge and legal grant could have travelled to East Africa or Argentina, that a designated territory without a Jewish majority, Birobidzhan, did not work, and, as argument, that only the whole-land claim needed the biblical land, while buffer-zone expansion could arise anywhere. [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] [cite:gi1_jvl_territorialism] [cite:gi18_ency_birobidzhan] [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] On legitimacy, the state within its pre-1967 lines was admitted to the UN in 1949, is recognised by most states, and was accepted on conditions by the PLO in 1993 and the Arab League in 2002, while the holding of land beyond those lines has been rejected by the Security Council, the General Assembly and, in an advisory opinion of 19 July 2024, the International Court, a view Israel's government rejects. [cite:rs_rd6_ecf_273] [cite:ir13_vc_recog] [cite:gi12_jvl_letters1993] [cite:gi18_albab_api] [cite:gi18_icj_pr2024] [cite:gi18_idi_icj2024] [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] Part Eighteen draws the volume's verdict: what is documented programme, what is pattern, what is argument and what is myth. [scene:gi13_record|Part Eighteen: settled, contested and open]

sections.h: The Programme and the State
sections.html:
This part tests an argument put to the volume by its commissioning editor: that "Greater Israel" as a state programme presupposes 1948, and that had the state not been founded as it was, there would be no programme to document. The argument is about cause, and no document can prove a cause in a history that did not happen. What the record can do is test its parts. Three are taken in turn here: whether the programmes documented in Parts Four to Six were in fact carried by the institutions of a state; whether the idea of a larger land existed before the state, and so cannot have been produced by it; and how far the founding of 1948 itself was settled in advance or turned on votes and battles that could have gone otherwise. The first two are matters of record. The third mixes record with argument, and the argument is labelled where it begins.

Every documented programme ran through the state

The territorial programmes this volume has documented were each enacted, adopted or carried out by a state body. The conquest of June 1967, which put the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan in Israel's hands, was the work of its army, and the government's first decisions on what to do with them were cabinet votes: on 19 June 1967 the government chose, by ten votes to nine in the morning over an annexation-minded version and then unanimously in the afternoon, to offer Egypt and Syria peace on the international border with security arrangements, and decided not to decide for the time being on Jordan and the West Bank. [cite:gi4_cie_june19] The Movement for the Whole Land of Israel, which published its manifesto on 22 September 1967, was a private body, but its premise was a fact the state had made: "The whole of Eretz Yisrael is now in the hands of the Jewish people." [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:gi4_972_twoads] Gush Emunim, founded in 1974, was extra-parliamentary by design, yet the permanent incorporation it sought could be granted only by a government, and from 1977 it was one, Menachem Begin's, that made settlement in the hill country policy. [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [scene:gi5_begin|Part Five: Begin and "Judea and Samaria"]

The later steps are all acts of the Knesset, the cabinet or a minister. The Golan Heights Law of 14 December 1981 passed the Knesset 63 to 21. [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] The Nation-State Law of 19 July 2018, which named Jewish settlement a national value, passed 62 to 55. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] The guidelines of the government sworn in on 29 December 2022 claimed "an exclusive and inalienable right to all parts of the Land of Israel." [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] On 23 July 2025 the Knesset voted 71 to 13 for a non-binding motion to apply sovereignty to the West Bank, and on 3 September 2025 Bezalel Smotrich, as finance minister and minister in the Defence Ministry, presented a map for annexing 82 per cent of it. [cite:wb_toi_71_13] [cite:gi6_toi_82pct] [scene:gi6_plans|Part Six: the annexation track] On this first test the argument holds without qualification: there is no documented Greater Israel programme in this volume that was not carried by a state's legislature, army or ministries, because only a state has those instruments.

The idea came first

The second test cuts the other way. The idea of a land larger than any partition existed long before 1948. On 3 February 1919 the Zionist Organization, the movement's mainstream body, asked the Paris Peace Conference for a territory running from south of Sidon over Mount Hermon to a line west of the Hejaz Railway, east of the Jordan, justified chiefly by water. [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] [scene:gi2_map1919|Part Two: the 1919 map] In 1925 Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionists made a Jewish majority "on both sides of the Jordan" their programme. [cite:gi2_ej_revisionists] [scene:gi2_bothbanks|Part Two: both banks] The idea outlived the founding unchanged: Herut, the Revisionists' party, held until 1965 that the state "should contain both banks of the River Jordan", and won 14 of 120 seats in the first Knesset. [cite:gi3_jvl_herut] The record therefore separates two things the argument joins. The idea did not depend on the state; it was older. What depended on the state was the programme, meaning a claim with an army, a budget and a legislature behind it.

Even the state was not enough by itself. Between 1949 and 1967 no Israeli government adopted the claim to both banks or to the West Bank; it remained an opposition party's platform. The one large exception was in the south: after conquering Sinai in 1956 Ben-Gurion told the Knesset that the armistice lines with Egypt had "no more validity," yet Israel withdrew under American pressure and left Gaza on 8 March 1957. [cite:gi3_jvl_herut] [cite:gi3_jvl_bg7nov] [cite:gi3a_walla] [scene:gi3_borders|Part Three: the armistice lines] [scene:gi3_sinai56|Part Three: the Sinai test] The documented whole-land programme begins after the conquest of 1967. A precise form of the argument would therefore say that the programme presupposes 1948 and also 1967: a state, and then a war that put the land in that state's hands.

How contingent 1948 was

The founding rested on a recommendation of the UN General Assembly, and that recommendation needed a two-thirds majority of the states voting yes or no; abstentions and absentees did not count. [cite:gi18_shindler_1947] In the Assembly's Ad Hoc Committee on 25 November 1947 the partition plan passed 25 to 13 with 17 abstentions, a majority short of two-thirds. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] [cite:gi18_shindler_1947] The plenary vote was put off by three days, which the plan's supporters used to lobby the abstainers, and on 29 November it passed 33 to 13 with 10 abstentions. [cite:gi18_shindler_1947] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] On those figures, two-thirds of the 46 states voting was 31 votes; had three of the 33 voted no instead, the result would have been 30 to 16, short of two-thirds, and the plan would have failed. Had they abstained instead, it would still have passed. Both superpowers voted in favour, the United States and the Soviet Union alike, and the Soviet bloc's votes were among the 33. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] [scene:so_s01|Moscow said yes first] On 24 November, the day before the committee's vote on the plan, a proposal to ask the International Court of Justice whether the UN could enforce or recommend a partition adopted without the consent of Palestine's inhabitants had failed in committee by a single vote, 20 to 21, with 13 abstentions. [cite:gi18_un_gapal85] [cite:gi18_wiki_adhoc] The historian Colin Shindler called the result "a close-run thing." [cite:gi18_shindler_1947]

The vote did not settle the matter. On 19 March 1948 the United States told the Security Council that partition "cannot now be implemented by peaceful means" and proposed a temporary trusteeship instead. [cite:rs_rd5_avalon_austin] [scene:rd5_trusteeship|Washington retreats, March 1948] The state was declared on 14 May 1948, and on 15 May the Arab League told the UN that its members were intervening in Palestine; the armies of Egypt, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq invaded, and Transjordan's forces entered the areas allotted to the Arab state and Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] The borders Israel held after the armistices of 1949 were set by that war, not by the resolution. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] [scene:rd6_armistices|The armistices of 1949]

From here the reasoning is argument, and there are two readings. On the first, the closeness of the vote, the American retreat and the uncertainty of the war show that the state, and with it any later programme, could easily not have existed; nothing in the 1919 map or the Revisionist platform could have become law without it. On the second, the vote mattered less than it seems. The Jewish Agency's leadership had already refused trusteeship outright: on 20 March 1948 Ben-Gurion said "We shall not agree to any kind of trusteeship, whether permanent or temporary." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_trusteeship] On that reading a state would probably have been declared and fought for whatever the Assembly did, and its borders would still have been set by war. Neither reading can be proved. What both accept is the narrower finding of this section: the idea of a larger land predates the state, and the programme does not. The next section asks what would have been left of either had the movement settled somewhere else. [scene:gi18_uganda|The Uganda Test, revisited]

sections.h: The Uganda Test, Revisited
sections.html:
The Road to 1948 volume ran a thought experiment it called the Uganda Test: suppose the movement had settled in East Africa or Argentina, and ask which parts of the later structure would have survived the move. Its answer was that the movement's financial and political institutions could have worked anywhere, while the theological layer, the land promise of Genesis and the prophetic reading built on it, could not. [scene:s04fa|The Uganda Test] This section runs the same test on a narrower question, this volume's own: what justifications for a Jewish state would have remained without the biblical claim, and which "Greater" claim could have existed at all. Everything below that goes beyond the documented alternatives is argument, and is marked as such. The documented alternatives come first.

The alternatives on record

The first was in the founding text. In Der Judenstaat, published in February 1896, Theodor Herzl left the territory open: "Shall we choose Palestine or Argentine?" he asked, and answered, "We shall take what is given us." [cite:gi18_pbs_herzl] [cite:fw_gutenberg_judenstaat] His pamphlet insisted on legal sanction from the ruling power rather than gradual settlement without it. [cite:fw_gutenberg_judenstaat] Over the next eight years he sought a charter from the Ottoman sultan, proposed El-Arish in Sinai to the British, and in 1903 received from the Colonial Secretary, Joseph Chamberlain, an offer of land in British East Africa, in what is now Kenya. [cite:gi2_wiki_uganda] [scene:gi2_herzl|Part Two: Herzl's diaries]

The offer came four months after the Kishinev pogrom of 6 and 7 April 1903, in which 49 Jews were killed and more than 500 injured. [cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev] Herzl put it to the Sixth Zionist Congress in Basel in August 1903 as a measure of refuge, telling the delegates that "Zion this certainly is not and can never become." The Congress voted 295 to 178, with 98 abstentions, to send a commission to look at the land, and members of the Russian delegation walked out, arguing that the plan broke the Basel Program's commitment to Palestine. [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_c] [scene:s04e|The offer for East Africa] Herzl died in 1904. The Seventh Congress, in 1905, rejected any national home outside Palestine and its vicinity, and the British offer lapsed. [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_c] [cite:fw_jvl_uganda]

The minority that wanted any safe land did not disappear. Israel Zangwill founded the Jewish Territorial Organization in Basel in July 1905, and it looked for land in Africa, Asia and Australia for twenty years before dissolving in 1925 without founding a lasting settlement. [cite:gi1_jvl_territorialism] [scene:s04f|East Africa rejected] A fourth alternative came from outside the movement altogether. In March 1928 the Soviet government designated Birobidzhan, in the Russian Far East, for Jewish settlement, and on 7 May 1934 made it the Jewish Autonomous Region, with Yiddish as an official language. [cite:gi18_ency_birobidzhan] It never acquired a Jewish majority. In 1939 Jews numbered either 13,291, 18.6 per cent of the population, or "just less than 18,000" of about 109,000, depending on the source; the peak, about 20,000, came at the end of 1948, and by the early 1990s only several thousand remained among more than 200,000 inhabitants. Nikita Khrushchev called the settlement "a failure" in 1958. [cite:gi18_ency_birobidzhan] A fifth alternative was no Jewish state at all: Brit Shalom from 1925, and in 1948 Hannah Arendt and Judah Magnes, argued for a binational arrangement, Arendt for a federation under UN trusteeship. [scene:rd3_brit_shalom|Brit Shalom] [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026]

Two points of attribution follow from this record. The rejection of East Africa was the act of a named body, the Zionist Congress, led by a named delegation, the Russian Zionists, after a vote in which a majority had first agreed to look; it is not evidence of what Jews as a whole wanted, and a reading that rests it on "the Jewish masses" goes further than the vote does. [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] [scene:s04fa|The Uganda Test] And the alternatives show that the movement's own leaders treated the territory as a choice for a decade before they closed it.

What would remain without the biblical claim (argument)

Israel's founding declaration of 14 May 1948 grounded the state on four things: "our natural and historic right," the Balfour Declaration, the League of Nations Mandate, and the General Assembly's resolution of 29 November 1947. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] Three later lines of justification are also on record: refuge from persecution, national self-determination, and legal grant by an international authority. The argument that follows sorts them by whether they would have survived a move to East Africa or Argentina.

Refuge would have travelled intact. It was the stated ground of the East Africa offer, made after Kishinev, and in 1945 the Harrison report found most of the Jewish displaced persons in Europe's camps wanting to go to Palestine. [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_harrison] Nothing in the case for refuge names a place. A legal grant would also have travelled: the East Africa offer was a grant by the imperial power, as the Mandate of 1922 was. [cite:gi2_wiki_uganda] [cite:rs_md_avalon] So, on this argument, would its weakness. The League's Covenant said that for the former Ottoman lands "the wishes of these communities must be a principal consideration", and Palestinian Arab representatives rejected the Mandate as incompatible with self-determination. [cite:rs_a22_lon1945] [cite:rs_a22_deblois] Any territory offered by an empire in 1903 had inhabitants who had not been asked, and the consent question argued over in the next section would have followed the grant to Africa. Self-determination travels as a principle but not as a fact. It presupposes a people present in sufficient number to determine anything, and Birobidzhan, a territory designated for Jews that never held a Jewish majority, is the documented case of designation without that presence. [cite:gi18_ency_birobidzhan] The historic and religious claim alone would not have travelled. Herzl said as much of East Africa in 1903: "Zion this certainly is not." [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth]

Which "Greater" claim could have existed (argument)

The whole-land claim, as its own documents state it, is a claim to a named land. The 1977 Likud platform spoke of "the right of the Jewish people to the land of Israel" and of Judea and Samaria; the 2022 guidelines listed the Galilee, the Negev, the Golan and Judea and Samaria. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] A state in British East Africa or in Argentina would have had no such texts to cite, and on this argument a programme of the West Bank kind, a claim to a heartland by right, could not have arisen there.

A second kind of expansion could have. The Zionist Organization's map of 1919 asked for Mount Hermon because "The Hermon is Palestine's real 'Father of Waters'", a reason of water, not scripture. [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] The zones Israel has held in Syria and Lebanon since 2024 are justified by its government as security measures: in December 2024 Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar called the move into the Syrian buffer zone "a limited and temporary step we took for security reasons", and in April 2026 he said "Israel has no territorial ambitions in Lebanon." [cite:gi12_olj_saar] [cite:gi9_nahar_saar] [scene:gi9_syria|Part Nine: the Syrian buffer zone] Claims of that kind need no sacred map, and any state at war with its neighbours can make them. Critics answer that a security rationale can outlast its occasion and become a claim in practice; the Israeli government answers that the zones are temporary and tied to threats. Part Nine sets out both. [scene:gi9_lebanon|Part Nine: south Lebanon] The narrow conclusion of the test is that without the biblical claim there would be no whole-land programme, while buffer-zone expansion would remain possible anywhere. The commissioning argument holds for the first kind of "Greater" claim and not for the second.

sections.h: Two Questions of Legitimacy
sections.html:
This section sets out the arguments about the legitimacy of the state, and of the land it has held since 1967, as the governments, courts and bodies concerned make them. No people's right is affirmed or denied here as a collective matter; each position is attributed to a named state, body, court or document. Two questions that public argument often runs together are kept apart: whether Israel is legitimate within the lines it held before June 1967, and whether it may hold, settle or annex land beyond them. The record answers them very differently.

Israel's case

The declaration of 14 May 1948 rested the state on "our natural and historic right," on the Balfour Declaration of 1917, on the League of Nations Mandate and on the General Assembly's resolution of 29 November 1947, and promised equal rights "irrespective of religion, race or sex." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] Each step it names is documented. The Mandate of 24 July 1922 made Britain responsible for securing the Jewish national home, while "safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all the inhabitants of Palestine"; the League's own study of 1945 called it a mandate "of a very special character" because it carried out the Balfour Declaration. [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_a22_lon1945] The legal scholar Matthijs de Blois argues that it was unique in naming the Jewish people, wherever they lived, as its beneficiaries. [cite:rs_a22_deblois] The partition resolution passed 33 to 13. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] The United States recognised the provisional government de facto on 14 May 1948 and de jure on 31 January 1949; Britain followed de facto on 29 January 1949 and de jure on 27 April 1950. [cite:ow1_nara_recog] [cite:dv2_fathom_aridan] On 11 May 1949 the General Assembly admitted Israel to the United Nations by 37 votes to 12, with 9 abstentions, noting its declaration that it "unreservedly accepts the obligations of the United Nations Charter." [cite:rs_rd6_ecf_273] [cite:rs_rd6_unga273_text] [scene:rd6_un_admission|Admission to the UN]

Two further arguments complete the case. The first is self-determination, which Israel's Basic Law of 2018 states as "unique to the Jewish people" in the State of Israel. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] The second is defence. On 15 May 1948 the Arab League informed the UN that its members were intervening in Palestine, and the armies of Egypt, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq crossed into it. On Israel's side of the argument, the lines of 1949 were the outcome of a war that its neighbours entered by declared decision, not a seizure planned in advance. [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b]

The Palestinian and Arab case, and the critics'

The opposing case begins with consent. The League Covenant had said of the former Ottoman lands that "the wishes of these communities must be a principal consideration," and Palestinian Arab representatives rejected the Mandate as incompatible with self-determination. [cite:rs_a22_lon1945] [cite:rs_a22_deblois] In 1947 the Arab Higher Committee refused to cooperate with the UN Special Committee on Palestine, and at the Assembly Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen denounced partition as contrary to the Charter and said they would not be bound by it. [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] Their objection was concrete: by the Palestinian historian Muhsin Yusuf's figures the proposed Jewish state held about 498,000 Jews and about 494,000 Arabs. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] The proposal to ask the International Court whether partition could be enforced without the inhabitants' consent failed by one vote. [cite:gi18_un_gapal85]

The second ground is the Nakba, the flight and expulsion of 1948. The UN Conciliation Commission's technical committee put the refugees from Israeli-held territory at about 711,000 in 1949; Israel officially held to 520,000 to 530,000, and Arab officials spoke of 900,000 or a million. [cite:rs_rd5_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] [scene:rd5_refugees|The refugees of 1948] Resolution 194 of 11 December 1948 resolved that refugees "wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date." [cite:gi18_jvl_res194] Palestinian bodies read it as establishing a right of return; Ben-Gurion told the UN's conciliators that the condition of living at peace made return depend on a peace, and no peace was made. The two readings are set out in the Road to 1948 volume. [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194 and its two readings] In July 1968 the Palestinian National Charter declared partition and the establishment of Israel "entirely illegal," "contrary to the will of the Palestinian people" and to "the right to self-determination." [cite:gi18_avalon_plocov]

The question narrows to the 1967 lines

From 1988 the main Palestinian and Arab bodies moved the argument from the existence of the state to its borders. The Palestinian declaration of independence of 15 November 1988 called partition a "historical injustice" yet held that Resolution 181 "continues to attach conditions to international legitimacy" that guarantee Palestinian sovereignty. [cite:gi18_mx_pdoi1988] On 9 September 1993 Yasser Arafat wrote that "The PLO recognizes the right of the State of Israel to exist in peace and security." [cite:gi12_jvl_letters1993] Egypt in 1979 and Jordan in 1994 signed treaties recognising Israel's sovereignty and borders. [cite:gi8_avalon_egtreaty] [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] In March 2002 the Arab League's Beirut summit offered to "consider the Arab-Israeli conflict ended" and "establish normal relations with Israel" in return for "full Israeli withdrawal from all the territories occupied since 1967," a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital and a refugee solution based on Resolution 194. [cite:gi18_albab_api] As of November 2023, 30 of the 193 UN member states did not recognise Israel, among them Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Syria. [cite:ir13_vc_recog] As of 23 September 2025, 157 recognised the State of Palestine, which has been a non-member observer state at the UN since 2012. [cite:gi18_aje_recog2025] The legitimacy of Israel within its pre-1967 lines is, on this record, the position of most states and of the main Palestinian and Arab bodies; Iran's government, which withdrew recognition, rejects it, and Hamas's 2017 document accepted a state on the 1967 lines without recognising Israel. [cite:ir13_vc_recog] [cite:hm_cnn_2017doc]

Beyond the lines

The second question has drawn a consistent answer from the UN's organs. Resolution 242 of 22 November 1967 stressed "the inadmissibility of the acquisition of territory by war" and called for withdrawal "from territories occupied in the recent conflict," a phrase whose English text lacks the definite article that its French text has, a difference at the centre of the argument over how much land it requires. [cite:wb_wiki_242] The Security Council declared the Golan law "null and void" unanimously in 1981 and said in 2016 that settlements have "no legal validity." [cite:gi8_rw_res497] [cite:wb_wiki_2334] On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice advised that Israel's "assertion of sovereignty and its annexation of certain parts of the territory" "constitute a violation of the prohibition of the acquisition of territory by force," that Israel "is not entitled to sovereignty over" any part of the territory occupied in 1967, that its "security concerns" cannot override that prohibition, and that the Palestinian people "has been deprived of its right to self-determination over a long period." [cite:gi18_icj_pr2024] The judges divided 11 to 4 on the unlawfulness of the continued presence, 14 to 1 on settlements and 12 to 3 on states' duty of non-recognition; the opinion is advisory and not binding. [cite:gi18_idi_icj2024] The General Assembly then demanded, 124 to 14 with 43 abstentions, that Israel end its presence within twelve months. [cite:wb_ahram_unga2024] [scene:wb10_rulings|The West Bank, Documented: the rulings] [scene:gi17_courts|Part Sixteen: the courts]

Israel's government rejects that answer. Netanyahu responded to the opinion: "The Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land, including in our eternal capital Jerusalem, nor in Judea and Samaria, our historical homeland." [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] The 2022 guidelines claim "an exclusive and inalienable right to all parts of the Land of Israel." [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] Israel had asked the Court not to give an opinion; analysts at the Israel Democracy Institute faulted it for giving Israel's security concerns little weight, as some judges did. [cite:gi18_idi_icj2024] The United States recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Golan in March 2019, and Colombia's government followed in August 2026; on the West Bank President Trump said on 25 September 2025, "I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank." [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852] [cite:gi8_aje_colombia] [cite:gi6_ap_trump0925]

The two questions therefore have documented answers of different strength. The legitimacy of the state within its pre-1967 lines rests on a vote, an admission, treaties and recognition by most of the world, and the main bodies that once denied it, the PLO and the Arab League, moved by 1993 and 2002 to accepting it on conditions. The holding of land beyond those lines has been rejected by the Security Council, the General Assembly and, in advisory form, the International Court, and accepted as sovereign only in the Golan by two states. This is the line along which the volume has found its documented programmes: the West Bank and the Golan. [scene:gi13_record|Part Eighteen: settled, contested and open]

chapters.label: Part Eighteen
chapters.title: Settled, Contested and Open
chapters.intro: The last part takes the volume's findings in the groups used for the Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran volumes. It first sets out what the record settles about "Greater Israel" from Herzl's diary of 1898 to October 2026, sorted into four kinds of statement: programmes that named movements, parties and governments stated or legislated; patterns that can be shown by setting events side by side over time; arguments about intent, with the case on each side; and the myths and misreadings that Part Ten named. To these it adds what Parts Thirteen to Seventeen established: the human toll of the wars since October 2023, each figure with the body that counted it and its date; the bill, and the American service members killed; what the United Nations, the courts and other states found and did; and the test of whether the programme depends on the founding of 1948. It then lists what is still open a week before Israel's election of 27 October 2026, from the annexation track and E1 to the zones held in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza, the successor to the American aid agreement, the court cases still pending and the end of the UN force in Lebanon. It ends by answering the question the volume set out to test, whether there is a programme of territorial expansion beyond the 1967 lines and who holds it, territory by territory and actor by actor, with the counter-record set beside the verdict.
chapters.outro: This volume followed a phrase from a verse in Genesis to a Knesset vote. It found that the widest version of "Greater Israel," from the Nile to the Euphrates, rests on one reading of one verse, a diary note Herzl never acted on and a minority religious current, and that the inscription, the flag's rivers and the coin map offered as proof of it are myths or misreadings. [cite:gi1_bg_gen1518] [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:gi10_csm_1980] [cite:gi10_mfa_flag] [cite:gi10_boi_coins] It found a narrower claim fully documented: the Revisionists' "both banks" until Herut gave it up, then the land between the Jordan and the sea in the 1967 manifesto, the 1977 Likud platform and the 2022 government guidelines, the Golan placed under Israeli law in 1981, and a West Bank annexation track pursued by named ministers and parties through 2025 and 2026. [cite:gi2_ej_revisionists] [cite:gi4_972_twoads] [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] [cite:gi6_toi_82pct] [cite:gi6_fmep_feb2026] It found an equally documented counter-record of withdrawals, treaties, court rulings and Israelis who opposed expansion, and a critics' reply that most withdrawals were forced or traded. [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] [cite:gi12_toi_reglaw2020] [cite:gi12_jvl_polls] [cite:gi12_un_weisglass] And it found, in October 2026, three zones held in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza for security, with no sovereignty claimed and no date of departure. [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] [cite:gi9_unsco_jun26] The ledgers of Parts Thirteen to Seventeen set beside that finding what the wars since October 2023 cost: 74,382 Palestinians killed in Gaza by the health ministry's count to 12 October 2026 and 8,954 people in Lebanon by Lebanon's to 11 October, after an attack that killed 1,195 people in Israel; at least $21.7 billion in American military aid in two years and 28 American service members killed, 21 of them in the 2026 war with Iran; court orders and an advisory opinion that Israel rejects, and warrants not executed; and a programme that depends on the state of 1948 and the conquest of 1967, built on an idea older than both. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] [cite:gz_cow_aid] [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] [cite:gz_toi_icc2025] [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] None of that record turns the wars outside the West Bank and the Golan into a documented programme of expansion; whether they serve one remains argument. The election of 27 October 2026 will decide who holds the ministries that carry the West Bank programme, and who negotiates what follows the aid agreement of 2016; the record to that date is what this volume sets down. The same method reached parallel answers in The West Bank, Documented [scene:wb13_settled|The West Bank, Documented: what is settled], Gaza, Documented [scene:gz10_settled|Gaza, Documented: what is settled], The Hezbollah Architecture [scene:hz13_record|The Hezbollah Architecture: what the record settles] and The Iran Architecture [scene:ir15_record|The Iran Architecture: what the record settles].

sections.h: What the Record Settles
sections.html:
The last part sorts the volume's findings into the four kinds of statement Part One promised to keep apart: programmes that named actors stated or legislated, patterns that can be shown over time, arguments about intent, and myths or misreadings. [scene:gi1_phrase|Part One: how this volume reads the record] Each finding below rests on the documents already cited in Parts One to Seventeen; nothing new is introduced here.

Documented programmes

Both banks of the Jordan, 1925–1965. The Revisionist Union's founding programme of 1925 called for a Jewish majority "on both sides of the Jordan," sung by Betar and drawn on the Irgun's emblem, and Herut carried the claim in opposition until it merged into Gahal in 1965. [cite:gi2_ej_revisionists] [cite:gi1_wiki_eastbank] [cite:gi3_jvl_herut] It was the programme of a named minority, never of the Zionist Organization or of an Israeli government, and Likud's 1977 platform dropped the east bank. [scene:gi2_bothbanks|Part Two: both banks]

The whole land, 1967–1977. The Movement for the Whole Land of Israel declared on 22 September 1967 that "no government in Israel is entitled to give up this wholeness"; it won 0.6 per cent in 1969 and passed into Likud. [cite:gi4_972_twoads] [cite:gi4_posen_manifesto] [cite:gi4_wiki_mgi] Gush Emunim, founded in 1974, stated as its aim the permanent incorporation of the whole land, and its teacher, Zvi Yehuda Kook, held that "no prime minister has the authority to renounce any part of the country." [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:gi11_wiki_zvikook] [scene:gi4_movement|Part Four: the Movement]

Party and state, 1977–2022. The 1977 Likud platform stated that "between the Sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty." [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] The Knesset applied Israeli law to East Jerusalem in 1967 and entrenched it in 1980, and on 14 December 1981 applied "the Law, jurisdiction and administration of the State" to the Golan by 63 votes to 21. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] Likud's Central Committee voted unanimously in 2017 to extend sovereignty to "the areas of liberated settlement." [cite:gi5_toi_likud2017] Clause 7 of the Nation-State Law of 2018 made "Jewish settlement" a "national value" without saying where. [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] The guidelines of the 37th government opened with "an exclusive and inalienable right to all parts of the Land of Israel," and the Likud–Religious Zionism agreement of 1 December 2022 committed the prime minister to a sovereignty policy in Judea and Samaria at a time of his choosing. [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] [cite:gi5_cgtn_sov] [scene:gi5_nationstate|Part Five: the Basic Law and the coalition]

The annexation track, 2019–2025. Netanyahu pledged sovereignty over the Jordan Valley on 10 September 2019; the Trump plan of January 2020 assigned Israel about 30 per cent of the West Bank. [cite:gi6_ap_jv2019] [cite:gi6_crs_plan2020] Smotrich declared 2025 "the year of sovereignty," described his civil powers as a change to the system's "DNA" that would not look like annexation, and on 3 September 2025 proposed annexing 82 per cent of the West Bank on the principle of "maximum territory and minimum Arab population." [cite:gi6_aje_2025year] [cite:gi6_bg_nyt_smotrich] [cite:gi6_toi_82pct] The Knesset backed the principle by 71 to 13 and advanced a bill on all settlements by 25 to 24. [cite:wb_toi_71_13] [cite:gi6_toi_readings] [scene:gi6_votes|Part Six: the votes]

Every one of these texts names the land west of the Jordan, Gaza in the 1977 version, or the Golan. None claims territory in Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Iraq or Syria beyond the Golan. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines]

Patterns over time

Holding and settling where the claim applied. Settlers in the West Bank outside East Jerusalem numbered 1,500 in 1972, 4,400 in 1977, 23,700 in 1983 and 60,300 in 1987. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] When the court closed the seizure of private land in the Elon Moreh case of 1979, about 908,000 dunams were declared state land by 1992; when sovereignty was suspended in 2020, civil powers moved to a minister in 2023 and Area C land registration began in February 2026. [cite:wb_dweikat] [cite:wb_wiki_stateland] [cite:gi6_dcpd_uae2020] [cite:gi6_fmep_feb2026] Formal sovereignty has been declared over no part of the West Bank outside East Jerusalem. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex]

Withdrawing under pressure or by treaty elsewhere. Israel left Gaza and Sinai in March 1957 after Eisenhower's public demand; pulled back on the Suez and Golan fronts in 1974–75; completed the return of Sinai on 25 April 1982 and of Taba in 1989; left south Lebanon on 24 May 2000; and removed every Gaza settlement in 2005. [cite:rs_cw3_app_20feb57] [cite:rs_cw3_morris_gaza] [cite:gi12_jvl_syrdis] [cite:gi12_ied_sinai2] [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] [cite:gi8_enc_taba] [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] Most of those steps came under pressure or as part of an exchange; Sharon called Yamit "the red line of our concessions," and his adviser called the Gaza disengagement "formaldehyde" for the peace process. [cite:gi1_csm_sinai1982] [cite:gi12_un_weisglass] [scene:gi12_withdrawals|Part Twelve: the withdrawals]

The buffer belt, 2024–2026. In Syria, Lebanon and Gaza, the first statement was temporary and later ones were not: "deployed temporarily" became "for an indefinite period"; five posts held "at the moment" became a zone kept until Hezbollah disarms; a line "frozen" pending withdrawal became, to the chief of staff, "a new border line," with the share of Gaza behind it rising from about 53 per cent to between 64 and 70 per cent. [cite:hz10s_cnn_480] [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] [cite:hz8_national_five] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] [cite:gi9_olj_zamir] [cite:gi9_aj_maps] [cite:gi9_unsco_jun26] No government decision has claimed sovereignty over any of the three. [cite:gi9_nahar_saar] [scene:gi9_gaza|Part Nine: the three zones]

Maps without correction. In September 2023 and September 2024 the prime minister displayed maps on which the West Bank and Gaza appeared inside Israel; no government clarification was found. [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023] [cite:gi7_aje_phil2024] [cite:gi7_ynet_germany]

The ledger, the bill and the world's response

Parts Thirteen to Seventeen recorded what the wars since October 2023 cost, who paid, and how the world answered. What they settle is a record of acts and their consequences, not a further programme: the rule the ledger kept, and this part keeps, is that operations outside the West Bank and the Golan are reported with Israel's stated reason beside them, and are not counted as progress toward a "Greater Israel" that no document claims for those places. [scene:gi14_gaza|Part Thirteen: the ledger] The figures below are given with the body that counted them and the date, and counts made by different methods are never added together.

Gaza. The attack of 7 October 2023 killed 1,195 people in Israel, 815 of them civilians, by AFP's count cited by Human Rights Watch, and 251 people were taken into Gaza as hostages. [cite:gz_hrw_oct7] The Gaza health ministry, which does not separate fighters from civilians, counted 74,382 Palestinians killed by 12 October 2026, 1,493 of them since the ceasefire of 10 October 2025, and OCHA, citing it, gave 175,142 injured to 30 September 2026. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] Of the 71,444 dead the ministry had identified by name by 31 December 2025, 21,283 were children. [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] A peer-reviewed estimate in The Lancet put deaths from traumatic injury at 64,260 to the end of June 2024, when the ministry's count stood at 37,877. [cite:gz_aj_lancet] Israel's military gives 474 soldiers killed in the ground operation. [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap] The World Bank, UN and EU assessment counted 76.6 per cent of housing units destroyed or damaged. [cite:gz_rdna2026] [scene:gi14_gaza|Part Thirteen: Gaza]

The West Bank and Lebanon. The UN Human Rights Office counted 1,001 Palestinians killed in the West Bank and East Jerusalem from 7 October 2023 to 17 October 2025, 213 of them children, and 59 Israelis killed by West Bank Palestinians in the same two years; Oxfam, counting calendar years from January 2023, gave 1,244 Palestinians killed by the end of 2025, against 1,036 in the seventeen years from 2006 to 2022. [cite:wb_ohchr_1001] [cite:gi14_oxfam_wb] UNRWA counted 41,951 Palestinians displaced as of August 2026, 34,176 of them from the northern camps. [cite:gi14_ocha_wbsnap] In Lebanon the health ministry, which does not separate civilians from fighters, counted 4,047 killed from 8 October 2023 to 27 November 2024, among them 790 women and 316 children, and 4,387 killed from 2 March to 11 October 2026, 8,954 in all since October 2023. [cite:hz7_olj_abiad_4047] [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] On Israel's side, the research centre Alma counted 45 civilians and 83 soldiers killed on the northern front in the first round, Israel gave 39 soldiers, a contractor and two civilians killed in 2026, and about 60,000 Israelis were displaced from the north. [cite:hz7_alma_summary] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] [cite:hz7_afp_north_return] [scene:gi14_lebanon|Part Thirteen: Lebanon]

Syria, Iran, Iraq and Yemen. Airwars' provisional count of civilians alleged killed by Israeli strikes in Syria since 2013 is 60 to 108; most of the 1,311 killed at Sweida in July 2025, by the Syrian Observatory's count, were killed by Syrians. [cite:gi15_airwars_syria] [cite:gi15_olj_sweida] In Iran, the June 2025 war killed 1,060 or more by the Foundation of Martyrs' count and 1,190 by HRANA's, and Iranian missiles killed 28 people in Israel. [cite:ir10_ap_toll] [cite:ir10_toi_numbers] For the 2026 war, the counts in Iran run from 3,468 dead (the Foundation of Martyrs, to 18 April) to at least 3,636 (HRANA, to 7 April, 1,701 of them civilians), with the Health Ministry, as reported by the UN, giving at least 2,362 civilians to 7 April; between 24 and 28 people were killed in Israel. [cite:ir11_afp_tolls] [cite:ir11_hrana_day22] [cite:gi15_ocha_iran3] [cite:ir11_wiki_strikesisrael] In Iraq the record shows depot strikes in 2019 and none found since; in Yemen, Israeli strikes killed at least 86 people on the lowest Houthi per-strike figures, 31 journalists and media workers among them by CPJ's count. [cite:gi15_aje_iraq2019] [cite:gi15_gv_ap46] [cite:gi15_cpj_31] Egypt and Jordan were not attacked, and their treaties held. [cite:gi15_aje_gas] [cite:gi15_mei_jordan] [scene:gi15_neighbours|Part Fourteen: the whole ledger]

The bill. The $3.8 billion a year is a ten-year grant under the memorandum of 14 September 2016, $3.3 billion in military financing and $500 million for missile defence, running to 30 September 2028, and the share Israel may spend at home falls to nothing in 2028. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] At least $21.7 billion in American military aid followed from October 2023 to September 2025. [cite:gz_cow_aid] The grant's weight has fallen, from about 24 per cent of Israel's security spending and 1.5 per cent of its GDP in 2011 to about 15 per cent and half a per cent in 2025–26, while the Bank of Israel put the gross budgetary cost of the war at about NIS 352 billion for 2023–2026 and the special American grant at NIS 25 billion. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] [cite:gi16_boi_2025] The United States' own largest cost was the 2026 war with Iran, $43.6 billion by 3 September 2026 on Central Command's estimate. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [scene:gi16_costs|Part Fifteen: the costs]

American lives. Twenty-eight American service members died in these theatres between October 2023 and 9 October 2026 on the Pentagon's counts as reported, a total that is this book's addition; 21 of them died in the 2026 war with Iran, by the Defense Casualty Analysis System's figure of 9 October, and 14 of the 28 deaths were hostile. [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] [cite:gi16_tp_21] [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] At least 33 Americans were killed on 7 October 2023, and ABC News counted five American citizens killed in the West Bank by July 2025, in cases where Israeli accounts and those of families and rights groups often conflict. [cite:gi16_kshb_oct7] [cite:gi16_abc_musallet] [scene:gi16_americans|Part Fifteen: the Americans killed]

The courts, the UN and the states. The International Court of Justice ordered Israel in 2024 to prevent genocidal acts, to let aid in "at scale" and to halt its Rafah offensive; it will not rule on whether genocide was committed before Israel's rejoinder, due on 22 May 2029. [cite:gz_oj_icj2024] [cite:gi17_icj_order0328] [cite:gz_lawfare_rafah] [cite:gz_icj_timelimits] In its advisory opinion of 19 July 2024 it found Israel's continued presence in the occupied territory unlawful and said settlement must cease and settlers be evacuated; Netanyahu answered that "the Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land." [cite:wb_livelaw_icj2024] [cite:wb_jurist_icj2024] The International Criminal Court's warrants of 21 November 2024 for Netanyahu and Gallant stand unexecuted, and the United States sanctions the court's officials. [cite:gz_un_icc] [cite:ow11_wiki_eo14203] The United States vetoed six Gaza ceasefire drafts and Palestine's full membership before the Security Council endorsed the American plan in Resolution 2803; the General Assembly demanded an end to the occupation by 124 votes to 14; the UN's Commission of Inquiry found genocide, which Israel called "distorted and false"; and UNIFIL's mandate ends on 31 December 2026. [cite:ow11_afp_veto2025] [cite:gi17_wiki_res2803] [cite:wb_ahram_unga2024] [cite:gz_un_coi2025] [cite:gz_ctv_coi2025] [cite:gi9_un_2790] By September 2025, 157 of 193 UN members recognised Palestine, and five governments sanctioned Ben-Gvir and Smotrich; no Arab treaty or Accords state broke with Israel. [cite:gi17_aje_recog2025] [cite:gi17_aje_sanctions2025] [scene:gi17_un|Part Sixteen: the world's response]

The programme and 1948. Every programme documented in this volume was carried by a state's cabinet, Knesset, army or ministries; the idea of a larger land was older than the state, in the Zionist Organization's map of 1919 and the Revisionists' "both sides of the Jordan," and no government adopted the whole-land claim between 1949 and 1967. [cite:gi4_cie_june19] [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] [cite:gi2_ej_revisionists] [cite:gi3_jvl_herut] The programme therefore presupposes 1948 and 1967 together; the idea preceded both. [scene:gi18_dependency|Part Seventeen: the programme and the state] The state within its pre-1967 lines was admitted to the UN in 1949 and is recognised by most states, while the holding of land beyond them has been rejected by the Security Council, the General Assembly and, in advisory form, the International Court, a view Israel's government rejects. [cite:rs_rd6_ecf_273] [cite:gi18_icj_pr2024] [cite:gi18_idi_icj2024] [scene:gi18_legitimacy|Part Seventeen: two questions of legitimacy]

What is argument

Intent beyond the stated aims. Whether Ben-Gurion's partition as "the beginning" in 1937 and his eighth point at Sèvres in 1956 were a programme or a posture; whether Labor's tolerance of the Sebastia settlers showed consent or weakness; whether Netanyahu shares the purpose Smotrich described; whether the buffer zones are perimeters or frontiers: each rests on documents on both sides, and this volume has given both. [cite:gi2_wiki_bgletter] [cite:rs_cw3_shlaim_sevres] [cite:rs_cw3_jvl_ike_bg] [cite:gi4_lustick_gush] [cite:gi6_bg_nyt_smotrich] [cite:gi9_carnegie_ring] The disputed sentence in the Amos letter carries no finding on its own. [cite:gi2_comm_morris] [cite:gi2_hnn_karsh] Netanyahu's "very much" of August 2025 documents attachment to a vision he did not define; that it reveals a policy toward Jordan, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria or Iraq is an inference. [cite:gi7_afp_i24] [cite:gi7_olj_pendant]

"From the Nile to the Euphrates" as a programme. The phrase rests on one reading of Genesis 15:18. [cite:gi1_bg_gen1518] [cite:gi1_ebg_brookegypt] Its documented carriers are a 1898 diary note never acted on, a minority of religious nationalist groups, a rabbi's answer to a UN committee in 1947 (which he narrowed, when pressed, to exclude Egypt, Syria, Lebanon, Iraq and Transjordan), a minister's remark about Jerusalem expanding "to Damascus" and an ambassador's "It would be fine if they took it all," which he called hyperbolic. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:gi1_wiki_greaterisrael] [cite:gi10_djn_fishman] [cite:gi11_newarab_damascus] [cite:gi11_aje_huckabee] Hamas's covenant asserts it as Zionist aim. [cite:hm_avalon_charter] No law, platform, coalition agreement or government map found adopts it.

Whether the wars served expansion. Outside the West Bank this is an argument, and both sides rest on statements. For it: Netanyahu said in May 2026 that his "directive is to go to 70" per cent of Gaza; Smotrich spoke of an "operational plan" for the "voluntary emigration" of Gazans; Katz spoke of depopulating Lebanese border villages to create a "buffer zone"; and Netanyahu said Israel would remain in south Lebanon "as long as it is not disarmed." [cite:gi9_olj_net70] [cite:gz_jc_smotrich] [cite:gi14_npr_yaroun] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] Against it: the plan Israel accepted says it "will not occupy or annex Gaza," Netanyahu said "we don't want to govern it," Israel signed a framework in June 2026 for withdrawing from Lebanon, and no law or government decision claims any of the three zones. [cite:gz_almon_plantext] [cite:gz_mm_netanyahu_aug25] [cite:hz8b_almon_framework] [cite:gi9_nahar_saar] In Iran, Iraq and Yemen the stated aims concerned weapons, armed groups, attacks on Israel and, in 2026, Iran's government; no document in either side's record joins those wars to a territorial claim. [cite:ir10_idf_jun14] [cite:ir13_pbs_bibi2026] [cite:gi15_aje_iraq2019] [scene:gi15_iran|Part Fourteen: Iran]

The money and the "dragged in" claim. That American aid frees Israeli money for operations and settlements holds in principle, and Congress once deducted settlement spending from loan guarantees; on the numbers, the regular grant is a modest and shrinking part of a war bill Israel has mostly paid itself, and Netanyahu now proposes phasing it out. [cite:gi16_jvl_loans] [cite:gi16_boi_2025] [cite:gi16_ji_netanyahu] [scene:gi16_aid|Part Fifteen: the fungibility test] That Israel dragged the United States into war is likewise argued: the record shows Israeli action shaping when the United States fought in 2026, and American presidents deciding that it would. [cite:ir14_aje_rubio] [cite:ir14_sn_forced] Why support persists has documented drivers in law, industry, intelligence, lobbying money and a shared war with Iran; which of them decides policy is argument, and disclosure of lobbying money is not proof that it caused any vote. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:pm_israelite_2024] [scene:gi17_support|Part Sixteen: why support persists]

Without 1948. Whether a state would have been declared and fought for whatever the Assembly voted, and what would have remained had the movement settled in East Africa or Argentina, cannot be proved. The labelled argument of Part Seventeen is that refuge and legal grant could have travelled, that the whole-land claim could not, and that buffer-zone expansion for security could arise anywhere. [cite:gi18_shindler_1947] [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] [cite:gi18_ency_birobidzhan] [scene:gi18_uganda|Part Seventeen: the Uganda Test]

What is myth or misread

Part Ten's ledger stands: no one has produced the Knesset inscription, which the Christian Science Monitor withdrew in 1980; the flag's stripes come from the prayer shawl; the 10-agora coin copies a coin of Mattathias Antigonus; Yinon's essay forecast fragmentation and named only Sinai as an Israeli aim; "A Clean Break" urged keeping the Golan, not taking more. [cite:gi10_csm_1980] [cite:gi10_mfa_flag] [cite:gi10_boi_coins] [cite:ir13_mb_yinon] [cite:ir13_km_cleanbreak] [scene:gi10_myths|Part Ten: the ledger] The record also corrects claims that circulate widely: the Herzl note is authentic, not fabricated; "Third Kingdom" is not in the Knesset speech of 7 November 1956; the United States voted for Resolution 497; the Litani clause of 1919 was the mainstream's water request, not a Revisionist frontier; and Colombia joined the United States in recognising the Golan annexation in August 2026. [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:gi3_jvl_bg7nov] [cite:gi8_rw_res497] [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] [cite:gi8_aje_colombia]

sections.h: What Remains Open
sections.html:
The election and the annexation track. The Knesset dissolved on 17 July 2026, and a poll at the time projected neither bloc reaching 61 seats. [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve] As of 21 October 2026 neither sovereignty bill of October 2025 had become law, while land registration in Area C, begun in February, continued under the Justice Ministry. [cite:gi6_toi_readings] [cite:gi6_fmep_feb2026] The parties that drove the track were running apart: Religious Zionism polled near the 3.25 per cent threshold, and Otzma Yehudit separately. [cite:gi11_reuters_rzp2026] [cite:gi11_jpost_rzp2026] Of the leading contenders against Netanyahu, Al Jazeera found that only Yair Golan's Democrats treat a Palestinian state as a goal. [cite:gi12_aje_contenders] The public was split two ways at once: in July 2026, 59 per cent opposed annexation into one state with limited Palestinian rights, and 59 per cent opposed a Palestinian state. [cite:gi12_jvl_polls] Who holds the West Bank ministries after 27 October will decide whether the track is resumed, slowed or left as it stands. [scene:gi6_ground|Part Six: where the track stood]

E1. The tender for 1,234 homes published on 18 August 2026 had its bid deadline pushed past the election by the Attorney General's Office; the Jerusalem District Court declined on 8 September to freeze it, without ruling on the plans, whose legality remains before it. [cite:gi6_pn_e1tender] [cite:gi6_jpost_e1court] [cite:gi6_ih_e1postpone]

South Lebanon. Netanyahu said Israel would remain "as long as it is not disarmed"; Lebanon demands withdrawal with third-party verification; military talks in Tampa opened on 20 October with both unresolved. [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] [cite:gi9_toi_tampa] UNIFIL's mandate ends on 31 December 2026 under Resolution 2790, and no successor force had been agreed by late September. [cite:gi9_un_2790] [cite:hz8b_olj_salam]

Syria. No agreement has been signed. Israeli forces hold the buffer zone and the Hermon summit, work on Sufa 53 resumed on 4 October 2026, and Damascus says its priority is a return to the lines of 8 December 2024. [cite:hz10s_eb_sufa] [cite:gi9_an_sufa] [cite:hz10s_eb_amman]
