Gaza. The plan Israel accepted says it "will not occupy or annex Gaza"; an Israeli source said there would be no withdrawal from the Yellow Line before Hamas disarms, and on 11 October the blocks moved again in Shujaiya. [cite:gi9_pbs_plan] [cite:hm_jp_noWithdraw] [cite:gi9_aj_shujayea]

The Temple Mount. The stated policy is that the status quo stands; the practice since 2024 has included Jewish prayer that the prime minister says "does not breach" it and that Jordan calls a violation. [cite:gi11_toi_tishabav25] [cite:gi11_na_netanyahu2026] [cite:gi11_reuters_tishabav26]

The Golan. Two states recognise Israeli sovereignty, the United States since 2019 and Colombia since 10 August 2026; no third was found. [cite:gi8_ucsb_procl9852] [cite:gi8_aje_colombia]

The aid memorandum. The 2016 memorandum runs to 30 September 2028. Netanyahu said in June 2026 that he wanted American grants to start falling "now" until they reach zero, formal talks on a new agreement began that month, and the American ambassador wrote that it would be "based on trade"; no signing had been reported in the latest reporting found, of July 2026. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_ji_netanyahu] [cite:gi16_wiki_nextmou] [scene:gi16_aid|Part Fifteen: the aid]

Rafah. The crossing reopened for people in February 2026, closed when the Iran war began and, according to Israeli authorities, reopened on 18 March for "limited movement of people"; no later change was confirmed. [cite:gi15_almon_rafah] [cite:gi15_libna_rafah]

The courts. Israel's challenge to the International Criminal Court's jurisdiction was pending in October 2025, and no ruling on it was found through October 2026; neither warrant against an Israeli official has been executed, and the American sanctions on the court are being contested in two federal courts. [cite:gz_toi_icc2025] [cite:wb_aj_icc_timeline] [cite:ow11_jurist_judges2026] [cite:ow11_gs_maine2026] At the International Court of Justice, South Africa's reply is due on 22 November 2027 and Israel's rejoinder on 22 May 2029; no judgment on genocide will come before then. [cite:gz_icj_timelimits] The Dutch cabinet said on 14 November 2025 that F-35 parts would stay halted pending a final decision within six months; no later decision was found. [cite:gi17_nlt_dutch2025] [scene:gi17_courts|Part Sixteen: the courts]

States. By September 2025, 157 of the 193 UN members recognised Palestine; whether others follow, and whether the European Union turns its agreement in principle of May 2026 on settler sanctions into a list, or finds a majority to suspend trade, is open. [cite:gi17_aje_recog2025] [cite:gi17_mp_eusettlers] [cite:gi17_an_eutrade]

Pentagon reports. As of 16 October 2026 the Pentagon said its investigation of the strike on the Minab school was ongoing and had published no findings. [cite:gi15a_ibt_minab] Its casualty count for the 2026 war, 21 dead on 9 October, is disputed: The Intercept calls it an undercount and The Washington Post reported four more deaths, which an official said were not directly related to the war. [cite:gi16_tp_21] [cite:hz12_intercept_cas] The war with Iran has not formally ended; on 8 October President Trump wrote that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterm elections of 3 November. [cite:ir11_ap_midterms]

The election. Every one of these questions, from the annexation track to the aid talks and the zones in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza, passes on 27 October 2026 to whichever government follows. [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve]

What this volume could not check. The full text of the 1967 manifesto, the English wording of Herzl's 1898 note, the Hebrew of the August 2025 interview, the colouring of the 1948 map shown at the UN in 2023, and Shamir's 1982 article in the original were not available; each is reported with that limit. [cite:gi4_posen_manifesto] [cite:gi1_pipes_calumny] [cite:gi7_tml_i24] [cite:gi7_jpost_map2023] [cite:gi8_pipes_jordanpal] Nor were a consolidated count of Iranian dead after the ceasefire collapsed in July 2026, a figure for Syrians displaced by Israeli operations, an official count of Gazans who entered Egypt, or a consolidated count of the dead in Yemen; the Gaza count was still rising as bodies were recovered. [cite:ir11_aj_jul8] [cite:gi15_shafaq_sohr2025] [cite:gi15_almon_rafah] [cite:gi15_wiki_yemen2025] [cite:gz_aj_year2026]

The Central Question, Answered

The volume asked whether there is a programme of territorial expansion beyond the 1967 lines, and who holds it. The answer differs by territory, and the record gives it by named actor.

The West Bank, including East Jerusalem: yes, a documented programme of named parties and governments. East Jerusalem was placed under Israeli law in 1967. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] For the rest, the claim is stated in Likud's 1977 platform and its Central Committee's 2017 resolution, in the 2022 government guidelines and coalition agreement, in Smotrich's 82 per cent plan, and in the votes of the Religious Zionism party, Otzma Yehudit, Noam and part of Likud. [cite:gi5_jvl_likud1977] [cite:gi5_toi_likud2017] [cite:gi5_jl_guidelines] [cite:gi5_cgtn_sov] [cite:gi6_toi_82pct] [cite:gi6_toi_readings] Netanyahu has stated "there will be no Palestinian state" and that "this place belongs to us," while his party refused the 2025 bills and his office says final status is for negotiation. [cite:gi6_toi_e1sign] [cite:gi6_bg_nyt_smotrich] What separates the programme from its completion is documented: the US veto, the UAE's red line and Likud's choice of timing. [cite:gi6_ap_trump0925] [cite:gi6_axios_uae2025]

The Golan: yes, legislated. The Begin government and the Knesset annexed it in 1981, and Netanyahu in 2016 and Bennett's coalition in 2021 restated it; Rabin and Barak negotiated over most of it between 1994 and 2000. [cite:gi5_wiki_golanlaw] [cite:gi8_mfa_cab2016] [cite:gi8_cnn_golan2021] [cite:gi8_enc_syrtalks]

Gaza, south Lebanon and south-west Syria: documented holdings with security rationales; intent contested. Each zone is held without a departure date and against the neighbour's and the UN's objection, and none is claimed by law or government decision; Sa'ar denied territorial ambitions in Lebanon. [cite:gi9_nahar_saar] [cite:hz10s_un_guterres] The case for expansion rests on the pattern, on Zamir's "new border line" and on Smotrich's Gaza "bonanza"; the case against rests on the stated purposes and on 1957, 2000 and 2005. [cite:gi9_olj_zamir] [cite:gz_toi_bonanza] [scene:gi9_lebanon|Part Nine: the buffer belt] The wars that produced these zones carried the heaviest tolls in the ledger, counted in Parts Thirteen and Fourteen; the size of a toll is a finding about the war, not evidence of a territorial aim. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] [scene:gi14_gaza|Part Thirteen: the ledger]

Iran, Iraq and Yemen: wars and strikes, no territorial claim. Israel fought two wars with Iran, the second jointly with the United States, struck militia depots in Iraq in 2019 and struck ports, power plants, an airport and leaders in Yemen from 2024, each with a stated reason about weapons, armed groups or attacks on Israel, and each met by the other side's own stated reason. No Israeli map, law or platform claims land in any of the three. [cite:ir10_idf_jun14] [cite:gi15_aje_iraq2019] [cite:gi15_gv_ap46] [scene:gi15_iran|Part Fourteen: Iran]

Sinai and the east bank of the Jordan: no current programme. Sinai was returned under a treaty, and Taba after arbitration. [cite:gi8_avalon_egtreaty] [cite:gi8_enc_taba] The Revisionist claim to the east bank ended with Herut; the 1994 treaty recognised Jordan's territorial integrity, which the Foreign Ministry restated in 2023 after Smotrich spoke before a map that included Jordan. "Jordan is Palestine" was an argument by named Likud figures about where a Palestinian state should be, not a claim to Jordanian land. [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] [cite:gi8_ynet_mfajordan] [cite:gi8_pipes_jordanpal]

From the Nile to the Euphrates: no government programme found. What exists is a minority religious current and a set of rhetorical statements by named individuals, surrounded by myths. Iraq, Iran and Saudi Arabia appear in no Israeli government's territorial claim reviewed here. [cite:gi1_wiki_greaterisrael] [cite:gi11_newarab_damascus] [cite:gi7_afp_i24] [scene:gi8_claims|Part Eight: the claims tested]

The counter-record, and the verdict

The counter-record is as documented as the programme. Israeli governments withdrew from captured land in 1957, 1974, 1975, 1982, 1989, 2000 and 2005, signed treaties with Egypt and Jordan that have held, and offered most of the Golan and, in 2008, all but about 6 per cent of the West Bank against land swaps. [cite:gi12_ied_sinai2] [cite:gi8_incore_jotreaty] [cite:gi8_enc_syrtalks] [cite:gi12_toi_olmert2008] Israelis opposed expansion from the Officers' Letter of 1978 to the 25 former security chiefs of 2019, Olmert declared Greater Israel finished in 2008, and the High Court struck down the Regulation Law in 2020. [cite:gi12_pn_officers] [cite:gi12_jn_25chiefs] [cite:gi1_ynet_olmert] [cite:gi12_toi_reglaw2020] The critics' reply is documented too: most withdrawals came under pressure or in exchange, the court has limited how land is taken rather than whether settlement continues, and part of the 2005 evacuation was repealed in 2023. [cite:rs_cw3_barjoseph_hdiplo] [cite:wb_wiki_stateland] [cite:gi12_toi_repeal2023]

The verdict is precise. There is a programme of expansion beyond the 1967 lines on the record, held by named parties, ministers and governments and stated in platforms, guidelines, a coalition agreement and Knesset votes; it covers the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and the Golan, has been legislated for East Jerusalem and the Golan, and stops at the Jordan. It is not held by Israelis as a people, a majority of whom told pollsters in 2026 that they opposed annexation. [cite:gi12_jvl_polls] Beyond those lines the record shows holdings explained as security, whose future the election of 27 October 2026 and the end of UNIFIL will test, and beyond those a slogan with no government behind it. The wars of 2023 to 2026 are documented in their own right, with tolls counted by named bodies, bills carried by Israel's treasury and America's, and 28 American service members killed; on the documents they are not steps in that programme, though whether the zones they left become one is argued on both sides. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:gi16_boi_2025] [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] The programme presupposes the state founded in 1948 and the conquest of 1967 together, while the idea of a larger land is older than both; and the line the programme crosses, the 1967 line, is the line along which the UN's organs and the International Court separate the state they accept from the holding of land they reject. [cite:gi2_bu_zo1919] [cite:gi4_cie_june19] [cite:gi18_icj_pr2024] [scene:gi18_legitimacy|Part Seventeen: two questions of legitimacy] Part One took as a hypothesis that the record would prove worse than the rumour. It proves narrower and more concrete: the rumour fails, and the documented claim to the land between the Jordan and the sea stands. [scene:gi1_phrase|Part One: the hypothesis]

books.title: US System vs Israel System
books.subtitle: Government, Rights, Money and the Cost of Living, Compared Over Time
books.intro:
This volume compares how two states serve, and fail, the people under their authority: the United States and Israel. It was written to answer a question now asked in Congress as well as at kitchen tables: why does the United States send money to Israel when Americans lack things that Israelis have? To answer it, the book first asks what the aid actually is and what it frees up, and then asks the questions underneath. How is each state built, and how far do its courts check its government? How free and fair are its elections, its press and its protests? Whom does each police, imprison and detain without trial, and who is killed by violence and by guns? Who may become a citizen, and who is governed without citizenship at all? How does each treat religion, and its own minorities, women and disabled citizens? And on the measures households feel, wages, prices, housing, health care, schools, family benefits, pensions and the burden of military service, how has each system done since 1980?

The record answers most of these questions, measure by measure, and does not reduce to one verdict. It shows the aid as $3.8 billion a year of military money under the 2016 agreement, spent mostly with American contractors, which has fallen from about 12.7 per cent of Israel's GDP in 1985 to about 0.6 per cent in 2025 and is about 0.05 per cent of American federal outlays; it does not pay for Israel's health funds. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] [cite:us1_crfb_fy2025] [cite:us1_cmwf_israel] It shows Israel covering every citizen and resident's health care by law since 1995 and moving from level life expectancy with the United States in 1980 to about four years ahead, while 26.7 million Americans were uninsured in 2025. [cite:us16_wiki_ilhealth] [cite:us16_wb_le] [cite:us16_census_2025] It shows the United States paying higher average wages, imprisoning about two and a half times as many people per head, and recording its lowest homicide rate on record in 2025 as killings in Israel's Arab communities reached a record 252. [cite:us14_oecd_avwage] [cite:us4_wpb_us] [cite:us4_wpb_il] [cite:us5_fox_fbi2025] [cite:us5_yahoo_herzog] And it shows that Israel's national figures leave out the 5.56 million Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza, roughly a third of the people under its control, who hold no Israeli citizenship. [cite:us9_pcbs_2025] [cite:us1_fh_israel2026]

The book is in twenty-two parts. Part One states the aid precisely and sets the rules; Parts Two to Ten compare the state, democracy, justice, public safety, citizenship, religion, equality, the people governed without citizenship and surveillance; Parts Eleven to Eighteen compare the economy, industries, labour, the cost of living, housing and infrastructure, health, education and the safety net; Parts Nineteen and Twenty turn to the military and to the money that flows in both directions; Part Twenty-One sets every measure in one ledger and gives its answer measure by measure; and Part Twenty-Two grades both systems on 43 measures, including a family-budget area, publishing every goalpost and weight, and gives a final score. [scene:us22_method|The scorecard] [scene:us1_aid|The aid, stated precisely] [scene:us21_ledger|The ledger] It shows both countries' gaps, and it compares systems, laws and governments, never peoples. Every status is stated as of October 2026, days before Israel votes on 27 October and the United States on 3 November; governments, coalitions, budgets and court cases described as current may change within weeks, and the talks on what replaces the aid agreement after 2028 will be conducted by whoever those elections choose. [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve] [cite:us1_wjla_midterms] [cite:ow1_mod_mou2026]

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Question
chapters.intro: Part One sets out the question this volume answers and the terms on which it answers it. It first states precisely what American aid to Israel is: a fixed ten-year grant of military money, paid early and spent mostly with American contractors, whose weight in Israel's economy has fallen from about an eighth of GDP in 1985 to just over half a per cent today, and what that money does and does not free up in Israel's budget. It then asks why Americans compare the two countries at all, sets the aid against the size of the American budget, tests the common claim that American taxpayers pay for Israeli health care, and lays down the rules by which the rest of the book compares the two systems: systems rather than peoples, the same sources for both countries, figures over time rather than snapshots, and a plain statement of whom each figure covers.
chapters.outro: Part One established that the $3.8 billion a year under the 2016 agreement is military money, $3.3 billion in Foreign Military Financing and $500 million for missile defence, paid as a lump sum and, from 2028, to be spent entirely on American weapons. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] Measured against Israel's economy it has shrunk from about 12.7 per cent of GDP in 1985, when economic grants helped carry the 1985 stabilisation plan, to about 0.6 per cent in 2025, and from about a quarter of Israel's security spending in 2011 to about a seventh. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] [cite:us1_jvl_melnick] [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] What it frees in Israel's budget is at most the grant itself, and in the American budget it is about 0.05 per cent of federal outlays. [cite:us1_crfb_fy2025] It does not pay for Israel's health funds, which rest on a 1995 law and a dedicated health tax, while 26.7 million people in the United States were uninsured in 2025. [cite:us1_cmwf_israel] [cite:us1_census_uninsured] The differences between the two systems are therefore the work of each country's own laws and budgets, measured here over time and with each figure's coverage stated, including the West Bank and Gaza that Israel's headline scores leave out. [cite:us1_fh_israel2026] [cite:ir13_fred_ilpc] [cite:us1_fred_uspc] Part Two begins with how each state is built. [scene:us2_founding|Part Two: how the state is built]

sections.h: The Aid: What It Is, What It Weighs and What It Frees Up
sections.html:
Any comparison of the American and Israeli systems runs into the aid sooner or later, so this book states it precisely at the start. Under a memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed on 14 September 2016, the United States committed $38 billion over its fiscal years 2019 to 2028: $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing (FMF) grants and $5 billion for missile defence, or $3.3 billion and $500 million a year. The agreement runs to 30 September 2028. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] Counting every kind of aid since 1946, the Congressional Research Service (CRS) puts the total at about $174 billion in current dollars, or about $298 billion in 2024 dollars. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] Part Fifteen of the Greater Israel volume sets out the mechanics and the emergency money that followed October 2023 in full; this section keeps to what a comparison of the two systems needs. [scene:gi16_aid|The aid in detail]

Military money, spent mostly in America

Three facts govern what the aid can and cannot do. It is military money. The economic grants that Israel received for decades, about $1.2 billion a year through the 1990s, fell to $482 million in 2005 and $44 million in 2008, according to CRS data; none are listed from 2020. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] It is paid early: since 1991 Congress has required Israel's FMF to be disbursed as a lump sum in the first month of the fiscal year, into an interest-bearing account at the Federal Reserve. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] And it is spent mostly in the United States. Under the 2007 MOU Israel could spend up to 26.3 per cent of its grant on equipment made in Israel, a practice called offshore procurement; the 2016 agreement phases this out, "ending entirely in FY2028". [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] The White House said at signing that ending offshore procurement and fuel purchases would move up to $1.2 billion a year more into American-made goods. [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] Researchers at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) concluded in February 2026 that the aid now goes almost entirely to procurement in the United States. [cite:gi16_inss_aid] The missile-defence money pays for systems built partly in each country. [scene:ow8_coproduction|Co-production]

Forty years of a shrinking weight

The aid's dollar amount has changed less than its weight. CRS figures put total American aid to Israel at about $3.7 billion in 1985, $3.5 billion in 1990, $4.0 billion in 2000, $3.1 billion in 2010 and $3.8 billion in 2025, in the dollars of each year; the exception was 2024, when the wartime supplemental lifted the total to about $12.5 billion. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] Over the same years Israel's economy grew more than twentyfold in dollar terms, from $28.9 billion in 1985 to $610.8 billion in 2025, by the World Bank's count. [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] Set side by side, the two series give the ratio this book uses throughout. On the book's own arithmetic, US aid in a given American fiscal year equalled 12.7 per cent of Israel's GDP in 1985, 5.6 per cent in 1990, 2.9 per cent in 2000, 1.3 per cent in 2010, 1.0 per cent in 2019 and 0.6 per cent in 2025. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] The calculation divides fiscal-year aid by calendar-year GDP, both in current dollars, so each figure is approximate; it agrees with INSS's estimate of "about half a percent" for 2026 and with the 1.5 per cent that the Israeli analyst Gazit gave for 2011. [cite:gi16_inss_aid] [cite:gi16_cato_bandow]

Israel's own defence burden has moved on a different path, and the measures are not identical across the years, which the table below marks. By the economists Rafi Melnick and Yosef Mealem's account, defence spending fell from "more than 20% of GDP in the mid-1980s" to under 10 per cent by the late 2000s. [cite:us1_jvl_melnick] Shmuel Even of INSS, using the total cost of defence including costs outside the budget, put it at 10 per cent of GDP in 1993, 8.2 per cent in 2000 and 7.8 per cent in 2005. [cite:us1_inss_even2010] The Bank of Israel records 4.2 per cent in 2022, then 8.4 per cent in 2024 and 7.8 per cent in 2025 as the wars that began in October 2023 drove spending up. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] Measured against that spending, the aid's share has also fallen: about 24 per cent of security outlays in 2011 by Gazit's estimate, "approximately 14%" of the defence budget by the CRS in 2025 and "roughly 15%" by INSS in 2026. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] Against the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute's figure of $48.3 billion for Israel's military spending in 2025, the $3.8 billion is about 8 per cent, by this book's arithmetic; the gap from the CRS and INSS figures comes from different years and definitions of the budget. [cite:ir13_sipri_2025]

1985: when the aid did support the civilian economy

The over-time view changes the answer to the question of what the aid frees up. In 1985 the argument was at its strongest, because the aid was then partly civilian and large against a small economy. Israel had inflation "of over 400%" before its Economic Stabilization Plan of July 1985, and Melnick and Mealem write that the plan's success "was supported by the U.S. grant in the amount of $1.5 billion (over a two-year period)", while American loans for defence purchases were converted into grants. [cite:us1_jvl_melnick] CRS data show economic aid of $1.95 billion that year beside $1.7 billion in military grants. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] Part Eleven sets that plan beside the American economic turn of the same years. [scene:us11_turn|Part Eleven: the turn]

What the aid frees up now, stated precisely

Today the aid is military money that Israel does not have to raise itself, and that is the whole of the mechanism. Each dollar of FMF buys an American weapon that Israel would otherwise have had to buy with its own shekels, delay or do without; to the extent Israel would have bought it anyway, the grant leaves that much of its own budget free for other uses, military or civilian. Economists call this fungibility, and Washington once acted on it: loan guarantees approved in 1992 and 2003 were reduced by amounts equal to Israel's settlement spending, by a net $773.8 million in 1994–97 and by $289.5 million in 2003 and $795.8 million in 2005, according to CRS data. [cite:gi16_jvl_loans] Israel's budget counts the grant as income: of the 2026 defence budget of about $44.8 billion, passed on 30 March 2026, about ₪22 billion is "expenditure contingent on income, including the U.S. aid grant", according to Boaz Bismuth, who chairs the Knesset's Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee. [cite:gi16_bd_budget2026] [cite:us1a_bd_budget2026]

Three limits apply to that statement. The money freed is at most the amount of the grant, now about 0.6 per cent of Israel's GDP, and nothing in the record ties it to any particular Israeli programme, civilian or military. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] The requirement to buy in America has a cost of its own, which the Israeli economist Gazit put at about $600 million a year in 2011, a single analyst's estimate. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] And the dollars are spent mainly with American contractors, so the aid is at once a transfer to Israel's defence budget and a purchase from American industry. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] INSS describes the aid as more than a funding source: part of a security-technological relationship that shapes the army's force build-up and a "symbolic anchor of the alliance", which also "grants the United States a lever of influence over Israeli policy". [cite:us1a_inss_aid]

Status as of October 2026

The arrangement may not outlast 2028. Israel's Defence Ministry announced on 5 June 2026 that talks had begun on a framework to replace the MOU, with the aim to "gradually transition from aid to a completely reciprocal partnership". [cite:ow1_mod_mou2026] Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a CNBC interview that month that he wanted the wind-down to "start now", until the aid reaches "coming to zero". [cite:gi16_ji_netanyahu] As of October 2026 no new agreement had been reported concluded in the reporting this book found, and the talks will continue past Israel's general election of 27 October 2026. [cite:ow1_wiki_nextmou] [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve] Critics argue that folding support into defence procurement would leave "no line item to block". [cite:ow1_nation_susskind] Part Twenty follows the money in both directions. [scene:us20_aid|Part Twenty: the aid and the money flow]

sections.h: Why People Compare, and How This Book Does It
sections.html:
The question this volume takes up is usually put in a single sentence: why the United States sends money to Israel when people in the United States lack services that Israel's system provides. It is now asked in Congress as well as at kitchen tables. In the Senate, a resolution by Bernie Sanders to block arms sales to Israel failed 72–11 in January 2024; similar measures drew 19 Democratic votes in November 2024; one failed 82–15 on 3 April 2025; and on 30 July 2025, 27 Democrats backed a resolution to block a sale of 20,000 assault rifles and 24 a resolution on a $675 million bomb sale, though both failed and every Republican voted against. [cite:ow2_jta_sanders2025] [cite:gi17_bg_senate2025] In the House in July 2025, Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene's amendment to remove about $500 million a year in missile-defence funding for Israel, which she called "money we don't have", failed 422–6; the six in favour were two Republicans and four Democrats. [cite:us1_ji_greene] Public opinion moved in the same period. In February 2026 Gallup found, for the first time since it began asking in 2001, that Americans' sympathies did not lie more with the Israelis: 41 per cent sided more with the Palestinians and 36 per cent with the Israelis, a difference Gallup called not statistically significant. [cite:gz_gallup_2026] In a Pew survey in May 2026, 32 per cent of American adults viewed the Israeli government favourably, against 47 per cent in 2022. [cite:ts11_pew_2026]

The scale of the money in America's budget

The regular aid is small beside the American budget. Federal outlays in fiscal year 2025 were $7.0 trillion, with a deficit of $1.8 trillion, by the Congressional Budget Office's count. [cite:us1_crfb_fy2025] [cite:us1_cbo_fy2025] The $3.8 billion a year under the 2016 agreement is about 0.05 per cent of those outlays, or about $11 for each of the 341.8 million people the Census Bureau counted in July 2025, by this book's arithmetic. [cite:us1_wa_uspop] [cite:us1_iowa_uspop] The wartime money since October 2023 is larger, at least $21.7 billion in military aid in two years by Brown University's Costs of War project, and America's own operations in the region have cost more again. [cite:gz_cow_aid] [scene:gi16_costs|The costs of the wars] On these figures, no plausible accounting makes the aid the reason the United States lacks any programme that Israel has, or the reason Israel has it. The differences between the two systems are the product of each country's laws, budgets and taxes, and those are what this book compares.

The claim and the record: who pays for Israel's health care

The clearest case is health care. A claim that American taxpayers pay for Israelis' health care circulates among American commentators on both left and right; a January 2026 opinion column in London's Jewish News documented it while arguing it was false. [cite:us1_jn_claim] The record is plain. Israel's National Health Insurance Law of 1995 "introduced universal health care for all citizens and permanent residents", delivered through four nonprofit health funds, Clalit, Maccabi, Meuhedet and Leumit. It is financed by a dedicated health tax, 3.2 per cent of income up to 60 per cent of the average wage and 5.2 per cent above it, collected by the National Insurance Institute, plus money from the state budget. Government sources paid 65 per cent of Israel's health spending in 2024, and households paid 19.9 per cent out of pocket. Asylum seekers, undocumented migrants and foreign workers are excluded from the law. [cite:us1_cmwf_israel] The United States has no law guaranteeing coverage to every resident; 26.7 million people, 7.9 per cent of the population, were uninsured for the whole of 2025, a level not statistically different from 2024. [cite:us1_census_uninsured]

Today's aid does not pay for Israel's health funds: it is military money, spent mostly with American contractors. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] The record does carry one qualification. When the health law was passed in 1995, Israel still received $1.2 billion a year in American economic aid, money not tied to weapons, which was about 1.1 per cent of its GDP by this book's arithmetic; that aid dwindled after 2000 and is no longer given. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1a_fred_ilgdp] Whatever the aid frees in Israel's budget now is limited to its military grant, about 0.6 per cent of GDP. [scene:us1_aid|The aid, stated precisely] Part Sixteen compares the two health systems in full. [scene:us16_systems|Part Sixteen: health systems]

How this book compares

The book holds to five rules. First, it compares systems, laws and governments, never peoples: a gap in outcomes between groups is reported as a measure of how a system treats them, with the mechanism named, and never as a trait of the group. Second, wherever possible it uses one source for both countries, such as the World Bank or the OECD, and states each figure's year and definition, for example whether dollars are converted at market exchange rates or at purchasing-power parity, which allows for the different cost of living in each country. Third, it measures over time, from 1980 where series exist, and labels a figure as a snapshot when only a snapshot exists. Fourth, it shows both countries' gaps and gives no overall verdict that does not disclose its measures: the total that Part Twenty-Two gives publishes every measure, goalpost and weight. Fifth, it states whom each figure covers.

The fifth rule matters most for Israel. Freedom House scores Israel at 73 out of 100 and states that the score does "not reflect the actions of the Israeli military or Jewish Israeli settlers in the Gaza Strip or the West Bank", which it rates separately at 22 and 2. [cite:us1_fh_israel2026] Israel's national statistics likewise count its citizens and residents, about 10.3 million people in September 2026 by the Central Bureau of Statistics' provisional figure, including 2.17 million Arabs. [cite:us1_jpost_ilpop] A comparison of how each state serves "its people" therefore covers different populations unless it says otherwise. This book treats the Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza, who live under Israeli control without Israeli citizenship, in a part of their own. [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: people under control without citizenship] The United States also has people under its authority without citizenship, and that part sets out the two cases side by side while stating plainly how unequal the comparison is in scale.

Over time, not as a snapshot

Measuring over time changes the picture as much as measuring who is covered. At market exchange rates, Israel's GDP per person, by World Bank data, was 37 per cent of the American level in 1985, 56 per cent in 1990, 60 per cent in 2000, 65 per cent in 2010 and 68 per cent in 2019; it stood at 67 per cent in 2025, after two years of war. [cite:ir13_fred_ilpc] [cite:us1_fred_uspc] Over the same forty years the aid's weight in Israel's economy fell from about an eighth of GDP to just over half a per cent. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] The two systems compared in this book are thus a much richer Israel and a far smaller aid relationship than the ones that existed in 1985. Part Eleven examines the economies in detail, including what the exchange-rate figures leave out. [scene:us11_growth|Part Eleven: growth over time]

Every status in this book is dated as of October 2026. Both countries are about to vote: Israel holds a general election on 27 October 2026, after the Knesset dissolved on 17 July, and the United States elects all 435 members of the House and 35 senators on 3 November 2026. [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve] [cite:us1_wjla_midterms] Governments, coalitions and budgets described here as current belong to Prime Minister Netanyahu's government in Israel and President Trump's second administration in the United States, and may change within weeks of publication. [cite:gi16_ji_netanyahu]

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: How the State Is Built
chapters.intro: Part Two sets out how each state is put together before the rest of the book measures what it delivers. It compares America's single written constitution, amendable only with three-quarters of the states, with Israel's Basic Laws, written chapter by chapter since 1950 and mostly changeable by a Knesset majority; a president elected apart from Congress with a prime minister who governs only through a coalition; and fifty states with reserved powers with a centralised system of local authorities. It then follows the courts in both countries, from Israel's judicial overhaul of 2023 to 2026 to the American Supreme Court's tariff ruling of February 2026, and how far the public trusts them. It traces emergency powers, Israel's single state of emergency declared in 1948 and renewed ever since beside America's 51 standing national emergencies, and ends with the civil service and the corruption measures that track both states from 2012 to 2025.
chapters.outro: Part Two established that the two states are built on opposite principles. The United States has one constitution that Congress cannot change alone, 27 amendments in more than two centuries and fifty states with reserved powers; Israel has fourteen Basic Laws as of October 2026, the latest passed on 13 July 2026 by 63 to 52, most of them amendable by a simple Knesset majority, and a unitary system in which local budgets need the Interior Ministry's approval. [cite:us2_annenberg_art5] [cite:us2_toi_torahlaw] [cite:us2_sngwofi_israel] In both, the highest court has been the main check of this decade: Israel's annulled a Basic Law amendment for the first time on 1 January 2024 and the dismissal of the attorney general in December 2025, and America's held on 20 February 2026 that emergency powers do not extend to tariffs, while public trust in both courts fell. [cite:us2_toi_reasonableness] [cite:us2_toi_agfiring] [cite:us2_wiki_learning] [cite:us2_axios_gallup2026] Israel has been in a declared state of emergency since May 1948, renewed every year, alongside Mandate-era regulations that need no declaration; the United States had 51 national emergencies in force on 19 October 2026, the oldest from 1979. [cite:us2_acri_emergency2012] [cite:us2_adalah_emergency2003] [cite:us2_brennan_nea] On Transparency International's corruption index both scores fell in 2025, America's to 64, its lowest on the current scale and down from 73 in 2012, and Israel's to 62, narrowing a 13-point gap to two. [cite:us2_wiki_cpi] Both elections, Israel's on 27 October and America's on 3 November 2026, may change these institutions again. [cite:gi11_reuters_rzp2026] Part Three turns to democracy itself: elections, money and speech. [scene:us3_elections|Part Three: elections]

sections.h: Two Founding Plans: A Written Constitution and the Basic Laws
sections.html:
The two states rest on different kinds of founding law. The United States has a single written constitution, drafted in 1787, with a fixed and deliberately difficult method of change. Under Article V an amendment must be proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or by a convention called at the request of two-thirds of the state legislatures, and then ratified by three-quarters of the states. In more than two centuries that bar has been cleared 27 times, most recently in 1992. [cite:us2_annenberg_art5] Israel has no single document of this kind. Its Declaration of Independence of May 1948 promised a constitution adopted by an elected assembly "not later than the 1st October 1948". The date passed in wartime, the assembly elected in January 1949 renamed itself the Knesset, and on 13 June 1950, after nine debates, the Knesset adopted the Harari Resolution: the constitution would be written in chapters, each a separate Basic Law, with no deadline. [cite:rs_rd6_dickerman_2007] The Road to 1948 volume tells that story in full. [scene:rd6_constitution|The Road to 1948: the constitution that was deferred]

What the Basic Laws are, and how hard they are to change

The chapters arrived slowly. The first, on the Knesset, came in 1958; others followed on Israel Lands (1960), the President (1964), the Government (1968, replaced in 1992 and restored in 2001), the State Economy (1975), the Military (1976), Jerusalem (1980), the Judiciary (1984), the State Comptroller (1988), Human Dignity and Liberty (1992), Freedom of Occupation (1994), Referendum (2014) and Israel as the Nation-State of the Jewish People (2018). [cite:us2_wiki_basiclaws] On 13 July 2026 the Knesset added a fourteenth, Basic Law: Torah Study, by 63 votes to 52. It declares Torah study a "foundational value" of the Jewish people and the state; Haredi parties pressed for it as a shield for their members' broad exemption from military service, and the Movement for Quality Government petitioned the High Court to strike it down the same day. [cite:us2_toi_torahlaw] Sources written before July 2026 therefore count thirteen Basic Laws, and some count differently still; the count used here, fourteen as of October 2026, includes the 2026 law. Part Nineteen returns to the draft. [scene:us19_service|Part Nineteen: who serves]

A common description holds that any Basic Law can be changed by a simple majority of the Knesset. That is true of most, and it is the decisive difference from the American document, but it is not true of all. Basic Law: Freedom of Occupation says it "shall not be varied except by a Basic Law passed by a majority of the members of the Knesset", that is, 61 of 120 regardless of how many are present, and its override clause lets a conflicting ordinary law stand only if passed by that same absolute majority, stated expressly, and only for four years at a time. [cite:us2_jvl_occupation] The electoral-system clause of Basic Law: The Knesset is likewise amendable only by 61 members, and the Referendum law requires a treaty approved by 80 members or a referendum before territory under Israeli law is given up. [cite:us2_wiki_basiclaws] [cite:us2a_wiki_basiclaws] Even so, the strongest of these locks is a majority of a single chamber. The 2018 Nation-State Law passed by 62 to 55 and the 2023 reasonableness amendment by 64 to 0 after the opposition walked out. [cite:basiclaw_britannica] Nothing in the Basic Laws resembles the American requirement that three-quarters of the states agree.

The Basic Laws acquired their force over ordinary law from the courts, not from a single founding act. After the two rights laws of 1992, both passed in thin chambers, the Supreme Court held in the Bank Mizrahi case of 1995 that an ordinary law violating their limitation clauses is void, and that the Knesset acts as a constituent body when it passes Basic Laws, relying on the Harari Resolution. [cite:us2_wiki_basiclaws] That judgment is the root of the dispute over the courts that the next section follows. [scene:us2_courts|The courts and the overhaul]

Executive and legislature: separation against fusion

The two systems also join or divide power differently. The American president is elected separately from Congress for a fixed term, and Congress, in two chambers, can neither dismiss a president for policy reasons nor be dissolved by one; the founding design sets the branches against each other. Israel's is a parliamentary system in which the government needs the Knesset's confidence. Voters elect only the Knesset, in a single nationwide district by proportional representation with a 3.25 per cent threshold, and no party has ever won the 61 seats needed to govern alone. [cite:knesset_idi] Every government has therefore been a coalition. The president, elected by the Knesset for a single seven-year term, tasks the member most likely to command a majority with forming one, with 28 days and a possible 14 more; if every attempt fails the country votes again. [cite:president_time] [cite:pm_brookings] That arithmetic produced five elections between April 2019 and November 2022, and it gives small parties weight beyond their size, as the Torah Study law shows. [cite:pm_brookings] Israel votes next on 27 October 2026, a week before the American midterm elections of 3 November. [cite:gi11_reuters_rzp2026] Part Three compares the two electoral systems. [scene:us3_elections|Part Three: elections]

Federal against central

The third difference is where power sits geographically. The American constitution lists the federal government's powers and, in the Tenth Amendment of 1791, leaves the rest to others: "The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." [cite:us2_annenberg_10th] Fifty states therefore run their own courts, criminal law, schools, elections and much of health and welfare policy, which is why many later parts of this book report American figures that vary widely by state. Israel is a unitary state with a single tier of local government: 258 local authorities in 2021, made up of 76 municipalities, 126 local councils and 56 regional councils. In 2020 they accounted for 12.8 per cent of public spending and 5.9 per cent of GDP, and 54 per cent of their revenue came from grants rather than their own taxes. Councils' bylaws and budgets require the approval of the Interior Ministry, which also approves their borrowing with the Finance Ministry. [cite:us2_sngwofi_israel] Their main own tax, the arnona, is levied on the floor area of property rather than its value, and an OECD review recommended moving over time to a tax based on property value. [cite:us2_oecd_localfin] What that means for Arab towns' budgets and planning is a matter for Parts Eight and Fifteen. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: equality among Israel's citizens] [scene:us15_land|Part Fifteen: land]

The structural comparison is a snapshot: the documents and rules are what they are as of October 2026, and no comparable series measures them over time. What can be measured over time is how each structure has handled the conflicts it was built to contain, which the remaining sections take up through the courts, emergency powers and the integrity of the public service.

sections.h: The Courts and the Overhaul
sections.html:
In both countries the highest court can set aside acts of the elected branches, and in both that power has been the centre of political conflict in this decade. The difference lies in what stands behind it. An American court that strikes down a law relies on a written constitution that Congress alone cannot change. Israel's Supreme Court, sitting as the High Court of Justice, built its power of review on the Basic Laws of 1992 and the Bank Mizrahi judgment of 1995, and on standards of administrative law it developed itself; the Knesset that the court reviews can change the Basic Laws themselves, usually by a simple majority. [cite:us2_wiki_basiclaws] One of those judge-made standards was "reasonableness", which allowed courts to invalidate decisions by ministers or officials that were "extremely unreasonable". [cite:us2_loc_reasonableness]

Israel, 2023–2026

The government sworn in at the end of 2022 set out to curb that power. The only part of its programme to pass in 2023 was an amendment to Basic Law: The Judiciary, adopted on 24 July 2023, which barred every court, including the High Court, from assessing the reasonableness of decisions by the government, the prime minister or any minister, including appointments and decisions not to act. [cite:us2_loc_reasonableness] It passed by 64 votes to none after the opposition left the chamber. [cite:basiclaw_britannica] On 1 January 2024 the court struck it down by eight justices to seven, the first time in Israel's history that it annulled a Basic Law or an amendment to one. Writing for the majority, the outgoing president, Esther Hayut, said the amendment "does the most severe harm possible to the principle of the separation of powers and the principle of the rule of law"; Justice David Mintz, dissenting, called the doctrine she applied "something out of nothing". A larger majority held that the court may review Basic Laws in exceptional cases: 13 of the 15 justices by the Times of Israel's count, 12 by other accounts, the difference turning on how concurring opinions are read. [cite:us2_toi_reasonableness] [cite:us2_wiki_basiclaws]

The coalition then changed how judges are chosen. On 27 March 2025, after the opposition filed 71,023 objections and then boycotted the vote, the Knesset passed a law removing the two Israel Bar Association representatives from the nine-member Judicial Selection Committee, adding one lawyer chosen by the coalition and one by the opposition, and giving the coalition and the opposition each a veto over Supreme Court appointments in place of the three sitting judges' influence. It takes effect only with the next Knesset, the one elected on 27 October 2026. [cite:us2_toi_selection2025] The government also moved against the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, head of the government's legal advisers; critics argued she was targeted for repeatedly pointing out that the government was breaking the law. The cabinet voted to dismiss her in August 2025 under a procedure it had just changed. On 14 December 2025 a panel of seven justices, four of them counted as conservatives, unanimously annulled the dismissal because the new procedure had been adopted "hastily" and without an appropriate factual or legal basis; she remained in office. Justice Minister Yariv Levin called the ruling "unlawful intervention", and Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi urged the government to dismiss her in practice regardless. [cite:us2_toi_agfiring] [cite:us2a_toi_agfiring]

The United States: a court that checks, and is checked by, opinion

The American Supreme Court's power to review legislation is not written in the Constitution either; it rests on the court's own early judgments. But its decisions bind against a document that elected majorities cannot rewrite, and in this decade it has ruled both for and against presidents. The largest recent check came on 20 February 2026 in Learning Resources v. Trump, decided with Trump v. V.O.S. Selections. By six votes to three the court held that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, under which President Trump had imposed sweeping tariffs by declaring national emergencies, does not authorise tariffs at all; Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that the statute "contains no reference to tariffs or duties". Customs officials identified about $166 billion collected from more than 330,000 importers, and refunds with interest were ordered in March 2026. The administration replaced the tariffs within days under a different statute, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which caps such tariffs at 15 per cent for 150 days; challenges to those continued through mid-2026. [cite:us2_wiki_learning] The emergency basis of the original tariffs is part of the next section. [scene:us2_emergency|Emergency powers]

Trust in the courts over time

Public confidence in both courts has fallen, and the fall is measured. Gallup has asked Americans about trust in the judicial branch since 1972; it never fell below 50 per cent until September 2022, three months after the court overturned Roe v. Wade. By September 2026, 54 per cent said they had little or no trust in the judicial branch, and 61 per cent disapproved of the Supreme Court's work, tying the record, against 34 per cent who approved. Among Democrats trust fell from 58 per cent in 2020 to 23 per cent. [cite:us2_axios_gallup2026] Israel's annual Democracy Index, run by the Israel Democracy Institute since 2003, found in its 2025 edition that trust in almost every institution was below its multi-year average. Among Arab citizens the Supreme Court was the most trusted institution, "albeit only at 41%". [cite:us2_idi_di2025] [cite:us2_idi_di2025sf] The two surveys ask different questions of different populations, so they show the direction of change in each country, not a ranking between them.

Leaders before the courts

The courts' record on the powerful themselves is part of the comparison. Israel has imprisoned a former president and a former prime minister. Moshe Katsav was serving a seven-year sentence for rape when Ehud Olmert began a 19-month term in February 2016 for taking about $130,000 in bribes over a Jerusalem housing project during his time as mayor; Olmert, who denied the charge, said he accepted the sentence because "no one is above the law". [cite:us2_voa_olmert] Benjamin Netanyahu is the first sitting prime minister to be tried. Charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which he denies, he has been on trial since 2020. In November 2025 he asked President Isaac Herzog for a pardon, which has no precedent in mid-trial; on 26 April 2026 Herzog said efforts "should first be exhausted to reach an agreement between the parties", and President Trump had repeatedly urged a pardon. [cite:us2_almonitor_pardon] [cite:hm_toi_trialdelay] The attorney general's office agreed in May 2026 to plea talks; Netanyahu finished his testimony on 24 June 2026 after 98 hearings. [cite:us2_ynet_trial] As of October 2026 no verdict, plea agreement or pardon had been reported in the sources checked for this book, and the status should be re-checked after the 27 October election. This volume does not compare American prosecutions of officeholders, a gap left open here.

sections.h: Emergency Powers: Israel Since 1948, America Since 1976
sections.html:
Both states let the executive act with fewer constraints in an emergency, and in both the emergency has become a lasting condition rather than an interruption. The difference is one of scale and form. Israel has lived under a single declared state of emergency, renewed without a break, since its first week. The United States has accumulated dozens of separate emergencies, each declared by a president for a stated purpose, many of which have never been ended. [cite:us2_acri_emergency2012] [cite:us2_brennan_nea]

Israel: one emergency, renewed every year

On 19 May 1948 the Provisional State Council adopted the Law and Administration Ordinance, whose section 9 let the government declare a state of emergency and issue emergency regulations with the force of law. The declaration made that month has never lapsed. [cite:us2_wiki_ilemergency] [cite:us2_adalah_emergency2003] For decades it continued without parliamentary review. Basic Law: The Government of 1992 limited each declaration to one year but allowed unlimited renewals, and the power now sits in section 38 of the version re-enacted in 2001. Every government since has renewed it. [cite:us2_acri_emergency2012] [cite:us2_wiki_ilemergency] When Israel ratified the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights it told the United Nations, on 3 October 1991, that the emergency declared in 1948 "has remained in force ever since" and that it was derogating from the treaty's guarantee against arbitrary detention to the extent its measures required. [cite:us2_adalah_emergency2003]

The declaration matters because other laws hang on it. By Adalah's reading in 2003, regulations issued under section 9, the Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance of 1948 and the Prevention of Infiltration Law of 1954 are valid only while the emergency lasts, and the Control of Products and Services Law of 1957 gives ministers wide powers "during a state of emergency". [cite:us2_adalah_emergency2003] Governments have used the power for ordinary economic business: 204 emergency regulations on labour disputes and economic questions were issued between 1974 and 1982 alone. [cite:us2_wiki_ilemergency] A separate body of emergency law does not depend on the declaration at all. The British Mandate's Defence (Emergency) Regulations of 1945 were absorbed into Israeli law by the same 1948 ordinance, and Adalah notes that they "remain in force today" whether or not an emergency is declared. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] [cite:us2_adalah_emergency2003]

Those regulations were the legal frame of the military government imposed on most of Israel's Arab citizens from October 1948. Regulation 125 let a commander declare any area closed, and between 1948 and 1967 about a third of all convictions of Arab citizens were for breaches of the Defence Regulations, most of them for lacking a permit. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] When the military government ended on 1 December 1966 the regulations stayed. Enforcement passed to the police and in some cases the Shin Bet, and the powers kept included closed areas (Regulation 125), restriction orders (109), police supervision (110), administrative detention (111, replaced in 1979 by a statute) and deportation (112). [cite:rs_cw6_akevot_gl17005] [cite:rs_cw6_palquest_mg_e] Earlier volumes follow that history. [scene:rd6_military_government|The Road to 1948: military government] [scene:cw6_military_rule_end|The end of military rule] Part Four takes up administrative detention as it is used today. [scene:us4_detention|Part Four: detention without trial]

The only sustained legal challenge to the emergency itself failed slowly. The Association for Civil Rights in Israel petitioned the High Court in 1999. The court required the government to report on its progress in moving emergency rules into ordinary law, and on 8 May 2012 dismissed the petition, finding that it "has exhausted itself, although the work has not been finished"; some of the most contested emergency measures remained in force. [cite:us2_acri_emergency2012] [cite:us2_wiki_ilemergency]

The United States: many emergencies, rarely ended

The American framework dates from the National Emergencies Act of 1976. It requires a president to declare an emergency formally to use the special powers in other statutes, and lets Congress end one. In practice Congress has seldom done so, and the count has risen steadily. By the Brennan Center's count, 75 emergencies had been declared under the Act by May 2022, 68 of them chiefly to impose sanctions under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and 41 were still in force. The oldest, declared by President Carter in 1979 during the Iran hostage crisis, was still active. [cite:us2_brennan_2022] By 19 October 2026 the number in effect had reached 51. [cite:us2_brennan_nea] Since January 2025 President Trump has declared a national energy emergency and used IEEPA emergencies over synthetic opioids, migration and trade deficits as the basis for tariffs. [cite:us2_cato_nea50] On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, one of the few times a court has set limits on what a declared emergency can do. [cite:us2_wiki_learning] [scene:us2_courts|The courts and the overhaul]

The two records cut in different directions. Israel's single emergency is broader in principle, since it underpins whole statutes and sits beside colonial-era regulations that need no declaration at all, and its use against Arab citizens before 1966 shows whom such powers fell on hardest. The American emergencies are narrower one by one but have multiplied, and since 2025 they have been used as the basis for trade policy. Neither system has ended its emergencies through the legislature; in each the most consequential limit of recent years came from a court, and in Israel's case the court declined to impose one. This book did not find a current, itemised official list of which Israeli laws still depend on the declaration; Adalah's 2003 account is the latest such list found, and it should be read as of that date. [cite:us2_adalah_emergency2003] [cite:us2_acri_emergency2012] [cite:us2_wiki_learning]

sections.h: The Civil Service and Measures of Corruption
sections.html:
A state is built not only of constitutions and courts but of the officials who carry out its decisions and of the rules that keep those officials working for the public rather than for whoever appoints them. In both countries those rules were contested between 2023 and 2026, and in both the main international measure of perceived public-sector corruption fell in 2025. [cite:us2_wiki_cpi]

The United States: cutting and reclassifying the federal workforce

The federal civil service changed faster in 2025 than in any recent year. By the account of the director of the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), Scott Kupor, about 317,000 federal employees left during 2025: some 144,000 accepted a deferred-resignation offer, about 24,000 were separated involuntarily (17,000 through reductions in force and 7,000 on probation), about 21,000 took early retirement or buyouts, and about 129,000 left through ordinary attrition. About 68,000 were hired by the end of August, mostly for priorities such as immigration and border enforcement. [cite:us2_bloomberg_317k] Government data released in March 2026 showed the civilian workforce 12 per cent smaller in January 2026 than in September 2024. The cuts fell unevenly: the Treasury lost 24 per cent of its staff and Health and Human Services 20 per cent, while the Department of Homeland Security grew by under 1 per cent. [cite:us2_reuters_workforce]

The administration also changed the terms of employment for senior career staff. In February 2026 OPM issued a final rule creating "Schedule Policy/Career", a category for career positions judged to influence policy. Holders keep merit hiring and veterans' preference but lose the standard procedures that protect career employees from removal for poor performance or misconduct; the rule forbids patronage, loyalty tests and use of the category for mass layoffs, and lets the president place positions in it by executive order. [cite:us2_opm_schedpc] It took effect on 8 March 2026. Officials estimated that as many as 50,000 employees could be covered. Kupor said it was "not about political appointments or terminations"; Max Stier of the Partnership for Public Service said it "can be used to remove expert career federal employees", and the largest federal union promised a court challenge. [cite:us2_govexec_schedf] Whether the rule is used as its text promises or as its critics fear is a question of practice that the record does not yet settle as of October 2026.

Israel: the legal advisers and political appointments

Israel's equivalent conflict ran through the government's legal advisers rather than its headcount. The attorney general heads the government's system of legal advisers, and critics argued that Gali Baharav-Miara was targeted for repeatedly telling ministers their actions were unlawful; the cabinet's attempt to dismiss her in 2025 was annulled by the High Court in December of that year. [cite:us2_toi_agfiring] [scene:us2_courts|The courts and the overhaul] Researchers at the Israel Democracy Institute wrote in February 2026 that challenges by government and political figures to the independence of the police, the attorney general's legal advisory system and the judiciary, together with an expansion of political appointments in government companies, had blurred the line between public and partisan interests. In the institute's own survey about 74 per cent of respondents said corruption was more widespread than in the past, and roughly 80 per cent agreed fully or partly that the police were not doing enough to investigate it. [cite:us2_idi_cpi] [cite:us2a_idi_cpi]

Corruption perceptions, 2012–2025

The longest comparable measure for both countries is Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI), which scores perceived public-sector corruption from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (very clean) by combining expert and business surveys. The current scale dates from 2012, when the method changed, so earlier scores are not comparable and are not used here. [cite:us2_axios_cpi2024] The United States scored 73 in 2012, peaked at 76 in 2015 and has fallen since, with brief small recoveries, to 69 in 2019, 65 in 2024 and 64 in 2025, its lowest score on the current scale; it has not been among the 20 cleanest-rated countries since 2017. [cite:us2_wiki_cpi] [cite:us2_axios_cpi2024] For 2025 Transparency International pointed to "actions targeting independent voices and undermining judicial independence" and to the freeze on enforcing the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. [cite:us2_cnn_cpi2025] Israel's score has moved within a narrow band: 60 in 2012 and 2019, a high of 64 in 2016 and 2024, and 62 in 2025, when it ranked 35th of 182 against America's 29th. [cite:us2_wiki_cpi] [cite:us2_idi_cpi] The IDI authors described the 2025 drop as "moderate as of now" but "a concerning trend". [cite:us2a_idi_cpi]

The index measures perception among experts and business people, not the number of corrupt acts, and a country whose institutions expose more corruption can score worse for it. Read with that limit, the series shows a convergence. In 2012 the United States stood 13 points above Israel; by 2025 the gap was two points, almost all of the change on the American side. Israel's score was stable across a decade that included the prosecution of a sitting prime minister, while America's fell across four presidencies from 2016 onward, including four-point drops in 2018 and 2024. [cite:us2_wiki_cpi] The causes the CPI's own authors and the IDI give for the latest declines are similar in kind in both countries, centring on pressure on the independence of prosecutors, police and courts, and the record supports that description for the period from 2023 to 2026 in both. [cite:us2_cnn_cpi2025] [cite:us2_idi_cpi]

Two gaps remain. This book found no Israeli series on the size and political appointment of the civil service comparable to the American figures above, so the Israeli side of this section rests on the legal-adviser dispute and the IDI's survey rather than on headcounts. And neither the CPI nor the workforce figures say anything about the people living under Israeli authority without Israeli citizenship, whose dealings with the state run largely through the military administration covered in Part Nine. [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank]

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: Democracy
chapters.intro: Part Three compares how the two systems let people choose and criticise their governments. It begins with elections: Israel's nationwide party lists and rising threshold beside America's state-run contests and redrawn districts, turnout in each country over time, and the rules on who may stand, tested again weeks before Israel's vote on 27 October 2026 and the American midterms on 3 November. It sets the main democracy ratings, Freedom House, V-Dem, Reporters Without Borders and the Israel Democracy Institute's own survey, against each other over the years they cover, and states what each leaves out. It then follows the money: Israel's publicly funded parties and America's private campaigns, super PACs and lobbying, including the pro-Israel spending that features in American arguments about the two countries. Finally it covers the press, boycott and campus speech, protest, and the laws each state uses on civil-society groups and their foreign funding.
chapters.outro: Part Three established that both systems hold competitive elections but count and finance them very differently: Israel elects national lists behind a threshold raised to 3.25 per cent, which in 2022 left 8.8 per cent of the vote unrepresented, and its turnout has fallen from 86.9 per cent in 1949 to about 70 per cent, while American turnout among citizens ranged from 52.2 per cent in a midterm to 66.8 per cent in a presidential year. [cite:us3_taub_threshold] [cite:us3_jvl_turnout] [cite:us3_jvl_cec] [cite:us3_npr_2022] [cite:us3_usafacts_turnout] Israel's election committee barred the main Arab lists in September 2026 and the Supreme Court reinstated them on 2 October. [cite:us3_aje_cec2026] The ratings moved down in both: V-Dem demoted Israel to an electoral democracy in 2023 and the United States in 2025, and Freedom House's American score fell from 94 in 2010 to 81, while Israel's stood at 73, a score that excludes the occupied territories. [cite:us3_vdem2026] [cite:us3_fh_fiw2021] [cite:us3_fh_us2026] [cite:us3_fh_il2026] Israel funds its parties publicly and caps private gifts; American campaigns cost about $16 billion in 2024 and lobbying about $5 billion in 2025, with pro-Israel groups one interest among many that spend without limit through super PACs. [cite:us3_fh_il2025] [cite:us3_os_lobby2025] [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] On speech, Israel restricts by statute, through a military censor, a foreign-broadcaster law, a boycott tort and NGO disclosure rules, while American restrictions in 2025 came mainly by executive action that courts partly blocked; both fell in the 2026 press-freedom index. [cite:us3_rsf_il] [cite:us3_versa_avneri] [cite:us3_fh_us2026] [cite:us3_wboc_rsf] Part Four turns to what happens when the state arrests, tries and imprisons people. [scene:us4_policing|Part Four: Criminal Justice]

sections.h: Elections, Turnout and the Ratings Over Time
sections.html:
Both countries choose their governments in competitive elections, and Freedom House rates both "Free", with Israel's electoral process given full marks and the 2024 American results described as widely accepted. [cite:us3_fh_il2026] [cite:us3a_fh_us2026] The way they vote is very different, and so is the way their democratic ratings have moved since 2010. This section sets out the electoral rules, the turnout record and the main indices, with each figure tied to its definition and to the population it covers. Both countries go to the polls within a week of each other in 2026: Israel on 27 October and the United States, for its midterms, on 3 November. [cite:us3_aje_cec2026]

How each system votes

Israel elects its 120-member Knesset by nationwide proportional representation for four-year terms; voters choose a party list, not a local candidate. [cite:us3_fh_il2025] A list needs a minimum share of the valid vote to win any seat, and that threshold has been raised step by step: 1 per cent from 1951 to 1992, 1.5 per cent to 2003, 2 per cent to 2013 and 3.25 per cent since then. [cite:us3_taub_threshold] The last rise came in the Governance Law the Knesset passed on 18 March 2014, which the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) warned at the time could cost the small Arab parties their representation unless they merged. [cite:us3_inss_threshold2014] The threshold has a measurable cost in votes. In November 2022 almost 420,000 ballots, 8.8 per cent of the valid vote and about ten seats' worth, went to lists that fell below it; the threshold that year was 154,854 votes. [cite:us3_taub_threshold] Because no party has ever won a majority alone, every government is a coalition; Part Two explains how coalitions are formed. [scene:us2_founding|Part Two: how the state is built]

The United States has no single national election system. Federal elections are run by the states, each with its own registration and identification rules, and House members are elected in single-member districts whose boundaries state legislatures usually draw. Freedom House's 2026 report recorded that several states had tightened registration and identification rules; that Texas, Missouri and North Carolina had redrawn their maps in 2025 to favour Republicans and California to add Democratic seats; that a March 2025 executive order requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register had been permanently blocked by a federal court in October, with appeals pending; and that the Federal Election Commission (FEC) had been left with two members, too few to do much of its work. [cite:us3_fh_us2026] The Supreme Court decided Louisiana v. Callais on 29 April 2026: by six votes to three it held that Louisiana's second majority-Black congressional district was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander, and it made claims under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act harder to win without striking the section down. [cite:us3a_wiki_callais]

Turnout over time

Israel's turnout, measured as votes cast against the registered electorate, has fallen over the long run. It was 86.9 per cent in the first election in 1949, above 80 per cent through the 1960s, 78.5 per cent in 1981, 77.4 per cent in 1992 and 78.7 per cent in 1999. It then dropped to 68.9 per cent in 2003, 64.7 per cent in 2009 and 63.9 per cent in 2013, before recovering to 72.3 per cent in 2015. [cite:us3_jvl_turnout] The Taub Center describes three phases: above 80 per cent until the late 1960s, the high 70s from the 1970s to the 1990s, and the mid-60s to low 70s since the second intifada. [cite:us3_taub_threshold] In the five elections of 2019 to 2022, turnout was 68.5, 69.4, 71.3, 67.4 and 70.6 per cent; in 2022, 6,788,804 people were eligible. [cite:us3_jvl_cec] [cite:us3_i21c_2022]

Turnout among Arab and Druze voters has been lower and has swung more widely: 49.2 per cent in April 2019, 59.2 per cent in September 2019, 64.8 per cent in 2020, 44.6 per cent in 2021 and 53.2 per cent in 2022. [cite:us3_jvl_cec] [cite:us3_inss_arab2022] INSS had warned in 2014 that the higher threshold would push small Arab parties to merge or risk winning nothing. [cite:us3_inss_threshold2014] One source, INSS in 2014, put 2013 turnout at "some 56 percent"; the Knesset-based series gives 63.9 per cent, and this book uses the latter. [cite:us3_inss_threshold2014] [cite:us3_jvl_turnout]

The American figures come from a different measure: the Census Bureau's survey of the share of voting-age citizens who say they voted. On that measure 65.3 per cent voted in 2024, 1.5 points fewer than in 2020 (about 66.8 per cent); in the 2022 midterms the figure was 52.2 per cent, the second-highest midterm turnout since 2000. [cite:us3_usafacts_turnout] [cite:us3_npr_2022] This book did not pull the Census series for the years before 2020, so it gives no American figure for 1980 or 2000. The two countries' numbers are not directly comparable: Israel's is an official count against the voter roll, the American one a survey estimate against the citizen population, and American midterms, unlike Knesset elections, do not choose the head of government.

Who may run

Israeli election law allows parties and candidates to be barred if they deny Israel's Jewish character, oppose democracy, incite racism or support terrorism. The rules have been used against far-right Jewish lists and against Arab lists and candidates, and the Supreme Court has overturned several of the Central Elections Committee's initial disqualifications. [cite:us3_fh_il2025] The pattern held in 2026. In September the committee voted to bar the two main Arab lists, the Joint List (Hadash, Ta'al and Balad) and Ra'am, and two candidates, Ofer Cassif of Hadash and Sami Abu Shehadeh, Balad's leader. On 2 October 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously reinstated both lists and, by 7–2, Cassif. A majority signalled it would uphold the bar on Abu Shehadeh, the push against whom Al Jazeera attributed to National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and he withdrew, calling the episode "a historical catastrophe for democracy". [cite:us3_aje_cec2026] The United States has no equivalent ideological bar on candidates; disputes over ballot access there turn on state filing rules and the courts.

The ratings over time

Freedom House scores countries out of 100. The United States scored 94 in 2010 and 83 in 2020, an 11-point fall that Freedom House attributed to corruption and conflicts of interest, weak transparency and punitive immigration and asylum policies. [cite:us3_fh_fiw2021] It stood at 84 in the 2025 edition and fell to 81 in the 2026 edition, covering 2025, its lowest since the series began; Freedom House cited "legislative dysfunction and executive dominance", pressure on free expression and the weakening of anticorruption safeguards. [cite:us3_afp_fh2026] [cite:us3_fh_us2026] Israel scored 73 in both the 2025 and 2026 editions, with full marks for its electoral process but 2 of 4 for the political rights of minority groups. [cite:us3_fh_il2025] [cite:us3_fh_il2026] Israel's score explicitly excludes what its army and settlers do in Gaza and the West Bank, which Freedom House rates separately at 2 and 22, both "Not Free"; Part Nine deals with the people living there. [cite:us3_fh_il2026] [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank]

The Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) project, which classifies regimes on hundreds of expert-coded indicators, moved both countries down a category within three years. Israel lost its status as a liberal democracy in 2023, the year of the judicial overhaul, and is now classed as an electoral democracy, still the only one in the Middle East and North Africa; it is not listed among the countries currently autocratising. The United States lost its liberal-democracy status in 2025, "for the first time in over 50 years", and joined the list of autocratisers, with an episode dated from 2023. V-Dem found that legislative constraints on the American executive lost about a third of their value in 2025, reaching their lowest point in over a century. [cite:us3_vdem2026] Inside Israel, the Israel Democracy Institute's annual survey recorded in 2025 that only 24 to 27 per cent of Jewish respondents and 12 per cent of Arab respondents rated Israeli democracy good or excellent, and that 65.5 per cent expected the coming election to be free and fair. [cite:us3_idi_2025]

The ratings measure different things and should not be added into one verdict. Freedom House and V-Dem rate the institutions governing a country's citizens; neither score for Israel covers the Palestinians in the occupied territories, and neither American score covers the effect of American policy abroad. What they share is direction: V-Dem moved Israel down a category in 2023 and the United States in 2025, and Freedom House's American score fell 13 points between 2010 and 2026. [cite:us3_fh_fiw2021] [cite:us3_fh_us2026] [cite:us3_vdem2026] Status as of October 2026; both elections may change it.

sections.h: Money in Politics: Campaign Finance and Lobbying
sections.html:
The two systems pay for politics in opposite ways. Israel's parties are financed mainly by the state, and private giving to them is tightly capped. American candidates raise their own money, and since 2010 outside groups have been able to raise and spend without limit. [cite:us3_fh_il2025] [cite:pm_wiki_superpac] This section sets out how each system works, what the American totals show over time, and where pro-Israel money fits within them. It measures that money by dollars spent and by the documented record of what it bought, not by who the donors are.

Israel: public money, small private gifts

Freedom House summarises the Israeli system in two lines: parties "rely mostly on public funding", allocated according to their electoral performance, and private donations "are strictly limited". [cite:us3_fh_il2025] The weak point has been money that reaches politics around the parties rather than through them. In 2017 the Knesset passed what became known as the "V15 law", to stop wealthy donors using nominally separate political organisations to get around the election-finance rules. [cite:us3_toi_ngotax] This book did not verify the current per-seat funding amount, the donation caps in shekels or the State Comptroller's recent audit findings on party finance; these are gaps in the record presented here, not findings that nothing is there. Measures of corruption and the rules on the civil service are covered in Part Two. [scene:us2_integrity|Part Two: the civil service and corruption]

The United States: limits on candidates, none on outside spending

In the 2025–26 cycle an American candidate may accept $3,500 per election from an individual and $5,000 per election from a multicandidate political action committee (PAC). [cite:pm_fec_limits] Those limits apply to money given to a candidate. Since the Supreme Court's Citizens United ruling (January 2010) and the appeals court's SpeechNow.org decision (March 2010), groups that spend independently of candidates, known as super PACs, may raise and spend unlimited sums. They report their donors, but monthly or quarterly filing can delay disclosure until after a vote, and a "pop-up" super PAC formed within 20 days of an election can file its first report after it. [cite:pm_wiki_superpac] Freedom House put the cost of the 2024 cycle at an estimated $16 billion, the most expensive yet, and named Elon Musk as its top individual spender. [cite:us3_fh_us2026] The agency that enforces these rules was weakened at the same time: in 2025 the FEC was left with two members, which Freedom House said limited its ability to carry out its duties. [cite:us3_fh_us2026]

Lobbying, the other main channel, has also grown. Federal lobbying spending reached a record of about $5 billion in 2025, 14 per cent more than in 2024 and the largest one-year rise since 2008, in nominal dollars. [cite:us3_os_lobby2025] The biggest spenders are business and professional groups. In 2018, for example, the National Association of Realtors reported $72.8 million in lobbying, Boeing $15.1 million and Amazon $14.4 million. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying]

Pro-Israel money in American elections

The spending most often cited in arguments about the two countries is that of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and its super PAC, the United Democracy Project (UDP). Measured as lobbying it is modest. AIPAC reported about $3.5 million in federal lobbying in 2018, around 147th among all spenders, and about $3.3 million in 2024 and nearly $3.8 million in 2025.
