[cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] [cite:pm_cjn_lobby2025] Measured as election spending it is large. Until 2021 AIPAC did not give to candidates. [cite:opensecrets_aipac_2019] By the end of July 2024 its new PAC had spent $44.8 million, mostly earmarked individual donations passed to candidates, and UDP about $55.4 million, about $100.2 million combined. [cite:pm_sludge_2024] By early August 2026 the two had again passed $100 million for the cycle, $104.3 million by Sludge's count from FEC filings. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] The Library volume Follow the Money sets out the channels and the race-by-race record. [scene:pm1_channels|Follow the Money: the legal channels] [scene:pm5_2026|Follow the Money: the 2026 cycle]

What the money bought is less clear than its size. In 2024 UDP spent almost $9.9 million against Jamaal Bowman in New York's 16th district, and its preferred candidate won. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] In August 2026 it spent more than $30.6 million, its largest sum on a single race, in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary against Abdul El-Sayed, and he won. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:pm_itt_elsayed] A Guardian analysis found that members of Congress who received more pro-Israel money were more likely to back military aid to Israel, but that party affiliation best predicted their statements on civilian casualties, and that the data could not show money had changed anyone's position. [cite:guardian_gaza_donors] An analysis of 788 AIPAC-backed candidates in 2022–24 found that about 86 per cent were incumbents and that its success rate in close races, about 79 per cent, was close to those of the NRA, Planned Parenthood and the Sierra Club. [cite:ow2_bahar_forward] The record supports a narrower claim than either side usually makes: the American system lets any organised interest, this one included, spend almost without limit to shape primaries, and that spending sometimes wins and sometimes does not.

Foreign money and its limits

American law bars foreign nationals, including foreign governments, from contributing or spending in any federal, state or local election. [cite:fec_foreign_nationals] Foreign governments may lobby and run public-relations campaigns if their agents register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), but the Justice Department's inspector general found in 2016 that 62 per cent of new registrants had filed late and called compliance "unacceptable". [cite:ow2_pogo_oig2016] Israel's government spends in this registered space: its 2026 budget set aside about $730 million for public diplomacy, more than four times the 2025 figure, and the Quincy Institute estimated more than $100 million in FARA-registered spending since October 2023. [cite:pm_jta_730m] [cite:pm_quincy_eighth] Enforcement can bite: former Senator Robert Menendez was sentenced in January 2025 to 11 years in prison for secretly working on behalf of the Egyptian and Qatari governments in exchange for bribes. [cite:us3a_fh_us2026] Israel regulates the opposite flow, foreign-government money reaching its own civil society, through disclosure laws and a proposed 80 per cent tax; the next section covers those. [scene:us3_speech|Speech, press, protest and civil society]

The safeguards around the American money changed in the same year. Freedom House reported that the Justice Department's public corruption unit was cut from 36 career lawyers to two and that 18 inspectors general were removed, and it lowered the American anticorruption score from 3 to 2 out of 4. [cite:us3_fh_us2026] The comparison is lopsided in the evidence as well as in the systems: the American record is detailed and public, through FEC filings and lobbying disclosures, while this book's Israeli record rests on summaries. Both are stated as of October 2026.

sections.h: Speech, Press, Protest and Civil Society
sections.html:
Elections show who governs. Whether people can find out what the government is doing, say what they think of it and organise against it depends on another set of laws: on the press, on boycotts, on protest and on the groups that make up civil society. Both systems narrowed some of these freedoms between 2023 and 2026, by different means. Israel did so mainly through legislation and wartime controls; the United States mainly through executive action, which courts partly reversed.

The press

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) ranks 180 countries each year; its method changed in 2022, so only recent years are compared here. In the 2026 index Israel fell from 112th to 116th, its score dropping from 51.06 to 46.46, and the United States fell seven places to 64th, with a score of 62.61. [cite:us3_rsf_il] [cite:us3_wboc_rsf] RSF described the United States as "slipping due to growing political pressure". [cite:us3_rsf_regions] Freedom House gave Israel 3 of 4 for free media and recorded the arrest of a journalist, Israel Frey, over a social-media post. [cite:us3_fh_il2026]

Israel's media rules have three features the American system lacks. First, a military censor: reporting on a range of security subjects needs prior approval. [cite:us3_rsf_il] Second, a law passed in April 2024 that lets the government shut foreign broadcasters it deems a threat to state security; Al Jazeera's local operations were closed in May 2024, and in December 2025 the law was extended to 2027, usable outside wartime and with less judicial oversight. [cite:us3_fh_il2025] [cite:pr_aj_ajlaw] Third, foreign journalists have been barred from entering Gaza independently since October 2023, a ban the Supreme Court upheld in January 2024 and that was still in force in October 2026. [cite:pr_mm_fpa2024] [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] RSF counted more than 220 Palestinian journalists killed by the Israeli army in Gaza since 7 October 2023, at least 70 of them because of their work; the Committee to Protect Journalists counted 189 Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza as of 24 September 2026. Israel says that some of those killed were Hamas members; NPR reported that it often provides no evidence for this. [cite:us3_rsf_regions] [cite:gz_cpj_2026] [cite:gz_wlrn_ban] The Gaza volume covers the access ban and the journalists killed. [scene:gz12_access|Gaza, Documented: access]

Ownership and government pressure affect both. RSF found most Israeli outlets owned by "large corporations or magnates who are difficult to investigate", noted that the right-wing Channel 14 had become the second most watched channel by 2023, and reported that politicians have significant influence over appointments to the broadcast regulators. In 2024 the communications minister proposed privatising or even closing the public radio service and called for a boycott of the daily Haaretz; in November 2024 the government halted state advertising in it. [cite:us3_rsf_il] [cite:us3_fh_il2025] In the United States, Freedom House recorded in 2025 that the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission threatened the licences of broadcasters he objected to, that some media companies settled lawsuits brought by the president or made concessions, that the Associated Press was barred from presidential events for refusing the administration's renaming of the Gulf of Mexico, that Congress defunded the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which then closed, and that physical assaults on journalists rose to 188. [cite:us3_fh_us2026] After Skydance's merger with Paramount, approved with commitments on "viewpoint diversity" at CBS, Paramount bought The Free Press in October 2025 and made Bari Weiss editor-in-chief of CBS News. [cite:gz_aj_weiss] [scene:gz12_coverage|Gaza, Documented: coverage in the US]

Boycotts and campus speech

Both countries legislate against boycotts of Israel, in different ways. Israel's Boycott Law of 2011 makes it a civil wrong to call publicly for an economic, cultural or academic boycott of Israel, its institutions or "an area in its control", which includes the settlements, and allows the state to deny boycott supporters tenders and benefits. On 15 April 2015 a nine-justice panel of the Supreme Court upheld the core of the law by 5 to 4, struck down unanimously the clause allowing damages without proof of harm, and held that such calls "do not fall under the classic purposes of free speech". [cite:us3_versa_avneri] A 2017 law bars entry to foreigners who publicly support a boycott of Israel or the settlements. [cite:us3_fh_il2025]

American federal law since 1977 bars American companies from complying with boycotts imposed by foreign governments, a measure aimed at the Arab League boycott of Israel; it regulates commercial compliance, not individuals' speech. [cite:ow11_bis_oac] Thirty-eight states had by 2024 adopted laws or orders against boycotts of Israel, some requiring state contractors to certify they do not boycott, others requiring public funds to divest from companies that do. Courts split: federal judges blocked the laws in Kansas and Arizona, which were then amended, and found Texas's unconstitutional in 2019, while the Eighth Circuit upheld Arkansas's law in 2022 and the Supreme Court declined to hear the case. No federal anti-boycott law against individuals has passed. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip] [scene:pm8_laws|Follow the Money: state anti-boycott laws]

On campuses, a 2019 executive order directed agencies enforcing civil-rights law to consider the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's definition of antisemitism, while saying they "shall not diminish or infringe upon" First Amendment rights; a January 2025 order added steps toward monitoring and removing foreign students and staff. [cite:ow11_eo13899] [cite:ow11_eo14188] Freedom House reported that the government revoked hundreds of visas after social-media vetting, some over nonviolent speech about the Israel–Hamas war, and that a federal court ruled in September 2025 that the administration had unfairly targeted non-citizens for their speech; the government said it would appeal. [cite:us3_fh_us2026] [scene:ow11_boycott|The One-Way Mirror: boycott and speech] In Israel, Freedom House recorded the arrest, twice, of a Tel Aviv University lecturer over posts calling for "rebellion" against the government. [cite:us3_fh_il2026] The Israel Democracy Institute found in 2025 that 53 per cent of Jewish and 70 per cent of Arab respondents preferred to keep their political views to themselves among strangers, a share that has risen since 2016–17. [cite:us3_idi_2025]

Protest

Protest is common and mostly peaceful in both countries. In Israel, Freedom House found demonstrations widely permitted and detained protesters generally released by the courts, but recorded that police sometimes used excessive force and that the authorities disallowed some protests, mostly by Arab citizens calling for a ceasefire. [cite:us3_fh_il2025] In the United States, the "No Kings" demonstrations drew an estimated five million people in June 2025; there were clashes with police and federal agents at protests against immigration raids; the National Guard was deployed in Los Angeles without the governor's consent, the federalised deployments in Los Angeles, Chicago and Portland ended on 31 December 2025 after the Supreme Court refused to allow the Illinois deployment, and the Guard deployment in Washington, D.C., which does not need a governor's consent, was extended in July 2026 to 2029; [cite:us3_audit_lawdork_il] [cite:us3_audit_dc_guard] some states added restrictions on protest. [cite:us3_fh_us2026] [cite:us3a_fh_us2026] Policing is covered in Part Four. [scene:us4_policing|Part Four: policing]

NGOs and foreign funding

Israel has legislated specifically on foreign-government money to its non-governmental organisations (NGOs). A 2012 law requires NGOs to report foreign-government support every quarter, and a 2016 law requires NGOs that receive most of their funding from foreign governments to say so publicly; Freedom House notes it falls mainly on left-leaning groups critical of policy toward Palestinians. [cite:us3_fh_il2025] A further bill, sponsored by Likud MK Ariel Kallner, would tax foreign-government donations to NGOs that receive no Israeli state funding at 80 per cent and let courts disregard petitions from groups "primarily financed by a foreign political entity". The ministerial committee backed it on 16 February 2025; the Association for Civil Rights in Israel called it "a direct assault on Israel's democracy" and argued that it targets funding from allied governments while leaving untouched right-wing groups that rely on private donations, and Kallner said it would "block improper foreign interference". [cite:us3_toi_ngotax] [cite:us3_tml_ngotax] In May 2025 it was still in committee. [cite:us3_jpost_ngotax] This book could not confirm whether it advanced further before the October 2026 election. Freedom House gives Israel 2 of 4 for NGO freedom. [cite:us3_fh_il2026]

The United States has no comparable law on foreign funding of domestic NGOs; FARA covers agents of foreign principals, not charities that receive grants. [cite:ow2_doj_faq] Pressure on American NGOs in 2025 came through the executive: federal funding freezes and grant terminations forced many groups to suspend work, an order designating "antifa" a domestic terrorist organisation was followed by instructions to investigate NGOs with foreign ties, and officials signalled interest in investigating the Open Society Foundations and the Ford Foundation. [cite:us3_fh_us2026]

The comparison does not resolve into a single ranking. Israel's restrictions are written into statute and apply even when courts trim them; America's in 2025 came mainly by executive action, against a constitutional text that courts used to block some of it. Both fell in RSF's 2026 index, and V-Dem rates both lower than before 2023. [cite:us3_rsf_il] [cite:us3_wboc_rsf] [cite:us3_vdem2026]

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: Criminal Justice
chapters.intro: Part Four compares how the two states police, prosecute, imprison and detain. It sets the decentralised American police system, with more than 17,000 agencies, beside Israel's single national force, and asks what each records about the people its police kill and how often officers answer for it. It then follows incarceration rates in both countries from 1980 (Israel from 1972) to the latest data, explains why Israel's series breaks in 2006 and again after 7 October 2023, and looks at how cases end, overwhelmingly in plea bargains in both systems. It compares the American death penalty, executions by year since the 1999 peak, with Israel's last execution, in 1962, and its 2026 law for military-court convictions. Finally it turns to detention without trial: Israel's administrative detention and military courts, the treatment of children, and the American cases of Guantanamo and immigration detention.
chapters.outro: Part Four established that the United States imprisons about two and a half times as many people per head as Israel, 542 against 217 per 100,000 at the end of 2023, after a rise from 220 in 1980 to a peak of 755 in 2008, and that Israel's own figure has, since the army's prisons passed to the Prison Service in 2006, mixed citizens convicted of crimes with Palestinians held as security prisoners, whose numbers rose sharply after October 2023. [cite:us4_wpb_us] [cite:us4_wpb_il] [cite:us4_wiki_ofer] In both systems most convictions come by plea, 89.5 per cent of federal defendants in 2022 and more than 85 per cent of Israeli cases in the 2012 study. [cite:us4_pew_plea2023] [cite:us4_ynet_plea2012] American police killed 1,314 people in 2025 by a non-government count, with charges in a few per cent of cases, while Israel publishes no such count and its best-documented killings, the 13 of October 2000 and Eyad al-Hallaq in 2020, ended without convictions. [cite:us4_mpv_2025] [cite:us4_adalah_accused] [cite:us4_aje_hallaq] The United States carried out 47 executions in 2025; Israel, which last executed anyone in 1962, passed a death-penalty law in March 2026 aimed at military-court convictions of Palestinians, whose application was before its High Court as of the latest reporting. [cite:us4_dpic_2025] [cite:us4_ap_deathlaw] [cite:us4_wiki_deathlaw] Israel held 3,101 administrative detainees and 1,419 "unlawful combatants" in October 2026, and the United States 15 men at Guantanamo and, at the February 2026 peak, 68,289 people in immigration detention. [cite:us4_hamoked_charts] [cite:us4_amnesty_gtmo] [cite:us4_trac_ice] These figures are as of October 2026, before Israel votes on 27 October and the United States on 3 November. Part Five turns from courts and prisons to the violence they are meant to answer: homicide, guns and the record killings in Israel's Arab community. [scene:us5_homicide|Part Five: homicide]

sections.h: Policing: Who Polices, and Who Is Held to Account
sections.html:
The two countries organise policing in opposite ways. The United States has no national police force for ordinary crime. In June 2018 the Bureau of Justice Statistics counted 17,541 state and local agencies performing law-enforcement functions, employing about 1.2 million sworn officers and civilian staff between them: city police departments, county sheriffs, state highway patrols and a long tail of small-town forces, each with its own rules on the use of force, its own training and its own complaint system. [cite:us4_bjs_agencies] Israel has one national police force, the Israel Police, with the Border Police as its gendarmerie arm, answering to a single minister. Under the coalition agreement of 25 November 2022 that minister became Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose expanded National Security Ministry took control of the police and of the Border Police in the West Bank. [cite:hm_jta_coalition2022] One country spreads the power to police, and therefore the responsibility for abuses, across thousands of local governments; the other concentrates it in one office, so that a change of minister changes policing for the whole state at once.

Deaths at the hands of police: the American count

The United States government does not publish a complete annual count of people killed by police, so the standard series comes from outside government. Mapping Police Violence, a database run by the research group Campaign Zero, counted 1,383 people killed by police in 2024, the highest since its records began in 2013, and 1,314 in 2025, a preliminary figure that may rise. The 2025 fall of about 5 per cent was the first year-on-year decline since 2019. Measured against population, the rate hovered around 0.345 per 100,000 from 2013 to 2020 and rose after 2021. [cite:us4_mpv_2025] [cite:us4_cz_2025] The series is short, about thirteen years, so it cannot show what policing looked like in 1980 or 1990; that is a limit of the record, not a sign that nothing happened earlier.

The same report breaks the 2025 figure down. Black Americans were killed by police at 0.75 per 100,000 (300 of about 40 million) and white Americans at 0.29 (560 of about 193 million), a ratio of 2.6. About 22 per cent of those killed in 2025 were unarmed. [cite:us4_mpv_2025] These are measures of how the system's encounters end, not of anything about the people involved; the report itself finds that most killings follow a call for service, which is where the mechanism lies. [cite:us4_cz_2025] Prosecution is rare. Officers were charged in 15 of the 2025 incidents by the time of the report, about 1 per cent, a number that usually rises as cases proceed; between 2019 and 2023 the share of killings that led to charges rose from about 2 per cent to closer to 4 per cent. [cite:us4_mpv_2025]

Israel: no public series, and the cases that defined the record

Israel has no published annual series of people killed by police comparable to the American databases; that is a gap in this book's data, stated here rather than filled with an estimate. What the record does hold are a small number of cases that were fully investigated, and what they show is the accountability system at work. In October 2000, at the start of the second intifada, police killed 13 protesters, twelve of them Arab citizens of Israel and one a Palestinian from Gaza, during a week of demonstrations centred on the Galilee. A state commission of inquiry led by a three-member Supreme Court panel, known as the Or Commission, reported on 1 September 2003. Its 860-page report found that police commanders had made "errors of judgment", that police had used live rounds, rubber bullets and tear gas against stone-throwing demonstrators, that they had shown "prior hostility" towards them, and that some of their actions stemmed from prejudice against Arabs. It recommended dismissing several officers and barring the former internal security minister, Shlomo Ben Ami, from any future public security post, and it criticised Prime Minister Ehud Barak for giving the police a "green light"; its findings were not legally binding. [cite:us4_aje_orr] The criminal follow-up ended two years later. In September 2005 the Justice Ministry's Police Investigation Department (known by its Hebrew acronym Mahash) decided not to issue an indictment in any of the 13 killings. [cite:us4_adalah_accused]

A second case shows the same pattern in a courtroom. On 30 May 2020 a Border Police officer shot dead Eyad al-Hallaq, a 32-year-old autistic Palestinian man from East Jerusalem, near the Lions' Gate of the Old City, as he walked to a special-needs institution. The Justice Ministry said in October 2020 that al-Hallaq "posed no danger to police or civilians" and charged the officer with reckless manslaughter in June 2021. On 6 July 2023 the Jerusalem District Court acquitted him, calling the shooting a "tragic mistake" made in self-defence and good faith; the police investigations unit said after the verdict that he had defied instructions to stop shooting. [cite:us4_aje_hallaq] In the West Bank, where the Israel Police is responsible for Israeli civilians, the monitoring group Yesh Din followed police files on settler violence from 2005 to 2025: 93.6 per cent were closed without an indictment, and about 3 per cent led to a full or partial conviction. [cite:wb_yeshdin_2025] The West Bank volume sets out that record in detail. [scene:wb8_settlers|The West Bank: settlers and enforcement]

The exchange programmes

The two police systems are linked. Since the 1990s and early 2000s the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA), the Anti-Defamation League and Georgia State University's GILEE programme have taken more than 1,000 American law-enforcement officials, most of them senior, to Israel for seminars, and the New York Police Department has kept a liaison office at Israel Police headquarters in Kfar Saba since 2012. [cite:ow6_jpost_adl] [cite:ow6_toi_nypd2012] Critics, among them Amnesty International USA in 2016 and Jewish Voice for Peace's "Deadly Exchange" campaign from 2017, argued that the trips expose American police to methods used in an occupation. [cite:ow6_amnesty_2016] [cite:ow6_reason_cops] A review by Reason magazine found little evidence that the trips cause excessive force by American officers, and no evidence for the claim that American officers learn chokeholds in Israel; the organisers deny it, and GILEE's founder says Israeli rules on the use of force are "much more restrictive". [cite:ow6_reason_cops] The claim of a causal link is therefore unsupported on the present record, while the programmes themselves are documented. The One-Way Mirror sets out who pays for them and who takes part. [scene:ow6_exchanges|The One-Way Mirror: police exchanges]

The comparison so far is uneven in a way that matters. The American record has a yearly count and a measured racial gap but a weak prosecution record spread across thousands of jurisdictions. The Israeli record has formal commissions and a central investigations unit but no public count, and its best-documented cases, involving Arab citizens and Palestinians in Jerusalem and the West Bank, ended without convictions. Who the Israeli police serve and who they fail is taken further in the parts on public safety and on equality among citizens. [scene:us5_homicide|Part Five: homicide] [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: equality among Israel's citizens]

sections.h: Prisons, Pleas and the Death Penalty
sections.html:
The fairest way to compare how many people two states lock up is to use one compiler for both. The World Prison Brief, kept by the Institute for Crime and Justice Policy Research at Birkbeck, University of London, counts everyone held in prisons and jails, including people awaiting trial, and divides by the national population. On that basis the United States held 1,833,700 people at the end of 2023, 542 per 100,000 residents, and Israel held 19,756 people on 31 December 2023, 217 per 100,000 on an estimated population of 9.12 million. [cite:us4_wpb_us] [cite:us4_wpb_il] The American rate was about two and a half times Israel's. That single comparison, often cited, hides two very different histories, and the Israeli figure means something different from the American one.

The American rise and partial fall

In 1980 the United States held 503,586 people, 220 per 100,000, roughly where it had been for four decades (201 in 1940, 161 in 1970). The number then rose every year for nearly three decades: 457 per 100,000 in 1990, 683 in 2000 and a peak of 755 in 2008, when 2.3 million people were behind bars. It has fallen since, to 642 in 2018, sharply to 505 in 2020, the first pandemic year, and back up to 541 in 2022 and 542 in 2023. [cite:us4_wpb_us] [cite:us4a_wpb_us] The present rate is still about two and a half times that of 1980. About a quarter of those held (25.5 per cent in 2023) had not been convicted and were awaiting trial. [cite:us4_wpb_us]

Israel: a series with two breaks

Israel's series begins at 138 per 100,000 in 1972 and stayed in a band of about 140–190 for three decades: 189 in 1990, 146 in 1995, 158 in 2000. It then jumped, to 208 in 2004 and 302 in 2006, and stayed near 300 until 2008. [cite:us4_wpb_il] [cite:us4a_wpb_il] The jump reflects a change in who counted as an Israel Prison Service inmate rather than a crime wave. Palestinians held for security offences had been kept in army-run camps; under a national policy of "relieving the army of all its prisons", the military handed facilities such as Ketziot and Megiddo to the Prison Service, and Ofer, the last of them, was transferred on 3 October 2006. [cite:us4_jpost_ketziot] [cite:us4_wiki_ofer] From then on Israel's total combines two populations held under different law: Israeli citizens and residents convicted or accused of ordinary crimes, and Palestinians from the occupied territories held as "security" prisoners. The total fell back to 153 per 100,000 in 2021 and rose again to 217 by the end of 2023, after the arrests that followed the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023. [cite:us4_wpb_il] By December 2023 the Prison Service told the Knesset that it held about 19,372 people against a legal maximum of 14,500, that about 3,000 slept on mattresses on the floor, and that it was "very close to using up all the places for prisoners". [cite:us4_toi_jails2023] The World Prison Brief puts occupancy at 136 per cent. [cite:us4_wpb_il]

Because of this mix, Israel's headline rate cannot be read as a measure of how often Israel imprisons its own citizens. The Prison Service has not published a criminal-only series, so no rate for ordinary crime alone can be given. What can be said is that by October 2026, according to HaMoked's monthly figures from the Prison Service, 9,265 Palestinians were held in the "security" category, including those held as "unlawful combatants", a figure equal to almost half of the whole prison population at the end of 2023. [cite:us4_hamoked_charts]

How cases end: the plea bargain

In both countries the trial is the exception. Pew Research Center's analysis of federal data found that of 71,954 defendants in American federal criminal cases in fiscal year 2022, 89.5 per cent pleaded guilty, 8.2 per cent had their cases dismissed, 1.9 per cent were convicted at trial and 290, or 0.4 per cent, were acquitted. [cite:us4_pew_plea2023] Federal cases are a small share of American prosecutions, most of which are in state courts, and no national state-court series was found for this book. In Israel a study by the Supreme Court's research centre and Haifa University, reported in May 2012, found that more than 85 per cent of criminal cases filed in the courts ended in a plea bargain (76.5 per cent in the magistrates' courts and 85.7 per cent in the district courts) and that 0.3 per cent ended in full acquittal. [cite:us4_ynet_plea2012] The Hebrew University sociologist Josh Guetzkow, studying 2,012 Israeli cases decided in 2010–2011, concluded that plea bargaining in that period "was marked by the miscarriage of justice": defendants who pleaded guilty were, on his estimate, less likely to have been convicted at trial than similar defendants who went to trial. [cite:us4_osu_guetzkow] Both figures are snapshots; neither country publishes a long, comparable series on how cases end. Military courts in the West Bank, where the conviction rate in 2010 was 99.74 per cent, are a separate system, taken up in the next section. [cite:wb_972_conviction]

The death penalty

The two systems differ most sharply on execution. The United States resumed executions in 1977 after the Supreme Court allowed new death-penalty laws. Executions peaked at 98 in 1999, then fell to 85 in 2000, 46 in 2010 and 17 in 2020, before rising again to 25 in 2024 and 47 in 2025, the highest in fifteen years, in 11 states; Florida alone carried out 19. [cite:us4_dpic_facts] [cite:us4_dpic_2025] By 14 May 2026 there had been 12 more. New death sentences, which peaked at 325 in 1986, numbered 23 in 2025. On 1 October 2025, 2,024 people were on death row. Twenty-seven states have the death penalty and 23 do not; four of the 27 (California, Ohio, Oregon and Pennsylvania) have moratoriums on executions. Since 1973, 202 people sentenced to death have been exonerated. [cite:us4_dpic_facts] Public support, measured by Gallup, stood at 52 per cent in 2025, the lowest in fifty years. [cite:us4_dpic_2025]

Israel kept the death penalty on its books for genocide, wartime espionage and certain terror offences and has not executed anyone since it hanged Adolf Eichmann in 1962. [cite:us4_ap_deathlaw] [cite:us4a_ap_deathlaw] On 30 March 2026 the Knesset voted 62–48 for a law, pressed by National Security Minister Ben-Gvir and supported in person by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, that makes hanging the default sentence for West Bank Palestinians convicted in military courts of killings defined as rejecting Israel's existence; military judges may impose life imprisonment only in "special circumstances". In civilian courts, which try Israeli citizens, judges may choose between death and life, and legal experts quoted by the Associated Press said this effectively excludes Jewish citizens. The law requires no unanimous verdict, allows no clemency and does not apply to people already in prison. Ben-Gvir said "whoever takes a life, the State of Israel will take their life". The Association for Civil Rights in Israel petitioned the High Court, calling the law "discriminatory by design", and the foreign ministers of Australia, Britain, France, Germany and Italy called it "de facto discriminatory". [cite:us4_ap_deathlaw] The court asked the government on 31 March 2026 to respond to requests for an interim order; the commander of Central Command signed an order applying the law in the West Bank on 17 May 2026, and the law requires a sentence to be carried out within 90 days. As of the latest reporting checked for this book, no ruling on the petitions and no death sentence under the law had been reported; this should be rechecked after Israel's election on 27 October 2026. [cite:us4_wiki_deathlaw]

Conditions inside

Since October 2023 the record on conditions in Israeli custody has been dominated by deaths of Palestinian detainees. Physicians for Human Rights Israel counted at least 94 Palestinians who died in Israeli custody between 7 October 2023 and August 2025, 68 from Gaza and 26 from the West Bank, 29 of them at the army's Sde Teiman camp, against fewer than 30 in the previous ten years; post-mortems it reviewed showed bruising consistent with beatings, broken ribs and untreated infections. The Prison Service said it operates "in accordance with the law and under the supervision of official oversight bodies", and the army said detainees receive three meals a day and a medical check on arrival. [cite:us4_cbs_custody] Ben-Gvir had said he had cut prison conditions to the legal minimum and that prisons would no longer be "summer camps"; in September 2025 the Supreme Court ordered the state to provide more and better food to Palestinian inmates. [cite:us4_cbs_custody] The American record on conditions, from solitary confinement to deaths in local jails, is large and is not measured here with a national series; that is a gap in this part. What the two series in this section do show is that the United States imprisons a far larger share of its own population than it did in 1980 and executes again at a rising pace, while Israel's prisons have, since 2006 and above all since 2023, come to hold a large population of people from territory it controls whose residents are not its citizens, many of them under military rather than civilian law.

sections.h: Detention Without Trial, Military Courts and Children in Custody
sections.html:
Both states hold people without convicting them of a crime. The forms differ, and so does the scale relative to the population each governs. This section sets out Israel's administrative detention and military-court system, the American cases of Guantanamo and immigration detention, and how each system treats children. The comparison is unequal in one respect that should be stated at the start: most of the people Israel holds without trial are Palestinians from territory under its military rule who are not its citizens, while most of the people the United States holds without a criminal conviction are non-citizens held under immigration law. Neither group votes for the government that holds them.

How administrative detention works in Israel

Israel has two administrative-detention regimes. Inside Israel, the Emergency Powers (Detention) Law of 1979 lets the defence minister order a person detained for up to six months when there are "reasonable grounds to presume that the security of the state or public security require the detention". The detainee must be brought before the president of a district court within 48 hours, and the detention is reviewed every three months, with appeal to the Supreme Court. The law draws on Mandate-era emergency statutes and applies only during a declared state of emergency, which has been in force continuously since 1948. [cite:us4_acri_admin] Part Two sets out that standing emergency. [scene:us2_emergency|Part Two: emergency powers] In the West Bank, Military Order 1651 lets a military commander detain a person for up to six months at a time, renewable in six-month periods with no maximum total; at the time of the Association for Civil Rights in Israel's review, a military judge had to review the order within eight days. In both regimes most of the evidence is classified and not shown to the detainee or the lawyer, and the High Court may hear petitions with only the state present. [cite:us4_acri_admin] A third category, people classed as "unlawful combatants" under a separate law, is also held outside the criminal process and counted separately. [cite:us4_hamoked_charts]

The numbers show how far use of these powers has changed. HaMoked, an Israeli rights group that publishes monthly figures obtained from the Israel Prison Service, recorded 356 administrative detainees in June 2020. By August 2023 the number had reached 1,201, the most since its monthly data began in 2001. [cite:us4_hamoked_charts] [cite:wb_tna_hamoked2023] After the October 2023 attack and the war that followed, it rose much higher: on 1 September 2025 HaMoked counted 11,040 Palestinian prisoners in Prison Service custody, of whom 3,577 were administrative detainees and 2,662 were held as "unlawful combatants". [cite:wb_mem_hamoked2025] In October 2026 it counted 3,101 administrative detainees and 1,419 unlawful combatants among 9,265 Palestinians held in the "security" category; only 1,509 of them were serving a sentence after conviction, and another 3,236 were held on remand awaiting trial. [cite:us4_hamoked_charts] These figures cover the Prison Service only; people held in army facilities such as Sde Teiman are not included.

Two systems of courts on one territory

Administrative detention sits inside a wider arrangement. In the West Bank, Israeli citizens are tried under Israeli law in Israeli civilian courts, while Palestinians are governed by military orders issued since 1967 and earlier Jordanian law and tried in military courts for offences from traffic violations to theft. In the Association for Civil Rights in Israel's 2014 comparison, an Israeli suspect had to be brought before a judge within 24 hours and a Palestinian within 96. [cite:wb_acri_twosys] An internal army document reported by Haaretz showed that in 2010, 99.74 per cent of military-court trials of Palestinians ended in conviction: 25 acquittals in 9,542 cases. [cite:wb_972_conviction] The West Bank volume and Part Nine set out this dual system in full. [scene:wb7_courts|The West Bank: the courts] [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank]

Children

Military Order 1651 sets the minimum age of criminal responsibility in the West Bank military courts at 12. Children of 12 and 13 can receive up to six months in custody; those of 16 and over are sentenced as adults. A juvenile military court was set up in September 2009, and in 2012 Military Order 1685 cut the time a child could be held before a judge reviewed the case from eight days to four. [cite:us4_wiki_minors] UNICEF reported in March 2013 that about 700 Palestinian children aged 12 to 17 were arrested, interrogated and detained each year, and called their ill-treatment "widespread, systematic and institutionalized". [cite:wb_un_unicef2013] In June 2025, by B'Tselem's count from Prison Service data, 359 Palestinian minors were held. [cite:us4_wiki_minors]

The American juvenile system moved the other way over the same decades. The number of young people held in juvenile residential placement fell 65 per cent between 1997 and 2019, to 36,479; by 2022 the count was 75 per cent below 2000, though it had risen about 10 per cent since 2020. [cite:us4_ojp_juv2022] [cite:us4_nij_juv2024] The decline did not close the racial gap in who is held: Black youth made up 41 per cent of those in placement in 2019. [cite:us4_ojp_juv2022] The World Prison Brief records minors as 0.1 per cent of the American prison and jail population in 2023 and 2.3 per cent of Israel's in 2017, the latest Israeli figure it holds. [cite:us4a_wpb_us] [cite:us4a_wpb_il]

The American record: Guantanamo and immigration detention

The closest American counterpart to detention without trial on security grounds is the military prison at Guantanamo Bay in Cuba. Nearly 800 men have been held there as "law of war" detainees since January 2002. By 1 July 2026, 15 remained, according to Amnesty International; six of them had never been charged or tried, three of whom had been approved for transfer, some after more than two decades in custody. [cite:us4_amnesty_gtmo] The scale today is small, but the legal principle, indefinite detention without criminal trial on the executive's security assessment, is the same one that critics of Israel's administrative detention object to.

Immigration detention is far larger. It is civil, not criminal, detention: people are held pending a decision on whether they may stay, not as punishment. TRAC, a research centre at Syracuse University that tracks federal data, recorded a peak of 68,289 people in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention in early February 2026, 73.6 per cent of whom had no criminal conviction; on 4 April 2026 the figure was 60,311, of whom 70.8 per cent had none. [cite:us4_trac_ice] Part Six takes up the law and politics of that system. [scene:us6_asylum|Part Six: asylum and detention]

Put side by side, the two records show the same tool used at very different scales. In 2026 Israel held about 4,500 people without charge in security detention, nearly all of them Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza; the United States held 15 at Guantanamo. The United States, for its part, held tens of thousands of non-citizens in civil immigration detention, most with no criminal record. In both systems most of the people held have no vote in the government that holds them, and in both the executive, not a criminal court, decides how long security detainees stay.

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: Public Safety and Guns
chapters.intro: Part Five turns to the most basic thing a state owes the people under its authority: protection from being killed. It traces homicide in both countries over time, from the American peak of 1980 to the record low of 2025, and Israel's low national rate to its break in 2023. It then follows the killings in Israel's Arab communities, which reached a record 252 dead in 2025, and sets out what the police solved and what successive governments did and cut. Finally it compares the two gun regimes, an American constitutional right and an Israeli discretionary licence, including the loosening of Israel's licensing after 7 October 2023, and what each country's figures on gun deaths and mass shootings do and do not show.
chapters.outro: Part Five established that the American homicide rate fell from 10.2 per 100,000 in 1980 to 4.1 in 2025, a record low that continued into 2026, while firearms remained the weapon in more than seven of ten killings and Black Americans were killed at about eight times the rate of white Americans. [cite:us5_ccj_trends] [cite:us5_fox_fbi2025] Israel's national rate, about 1.5 for years, doubled to 3.04 in 2023, driven by killings in Arab communities, where the rate rose from 4.90 in 2019 to 11.11 in 2023 against 0.85 among Jewish Israelis. [cite:us5_taub_homicide] The Abraham Initiatives counted a record 252 Arab citizens killed in 2025 and 184 by 13 October 2026. Police solved about one Arab-community killing in ten, and the government's answer in July 2026 was a Shin Bet role paid for from the 2021 development plan. [cite:us5_yahoo_herzog] [cite:us5_toi_oct2026] [cite:us5_toi_shinbet] On guns, the United States protects ownership as a constitutional right and recorded 44,447 gun deaths in 2024, 62 per cent of them suicides. Israel licenses at the state's discretion and, after October 2023, roughly doubled its licences in a year, with more than a thousand under investigation as possible breaches of its own criteria. [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths] [cite:us5_duke_reznik] [cite:us5_jpost_gunreform] Part Six turns to who can become a citizen of each state, and who cannot. [scene:us6_citizenship|Part Six: citizenship]

sections.h: Homicide Over Time
sections.html:
Homicide is the most reliably counted crime in either country, because a body is hard to leave out of the record. Even so, the two countries count it differently. In the United States the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) compiles police reports and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) compiles death certificates, and both series run back for decades. In Israel the police publish counts of murder victims, the Central Bureau of Statistics records causes of death, and since the mid-2010s a civil-society group, the Abraham Initiatives, has kept a running count of Arab citizens killed in violence and crime. Their totals for the same year differ by a few per cent because of definitions: whether police killings are included, whether East Jerusalem residents are counted, and when a death is recorded. This section names the counter each time. [cite:us5_aawsat_police] [cite:us5_maariv_2025]

The United States: a fall, a spike and a record low

The American homicide rate stood at 10.2 per 100,000 people in 1980, the highest figure in the series compiled by the Council on Criminal Justice (CCJ). It fell through the 1990s and reached 4.4 in 2014. It then rose to 6.6 in 2020, the highest since 1997, when the number of homicides jumped by about 30 per cent in a single year, the largest one-year rise the FBI has recorded. [cite:us5_ccj_trends] [cite:us5_fox_fbi2025] The rate reached 6.8 in 2021 by The Crime Index's figures, and then fell. [cite:us5_npr_lowmurder] According to FBI data released in August 2026, it was 4.1 in 2025, after an 18.1 per cent fall in murders from 2024. That ties 1955 and 1956 as the lowest rate on record and is 60 per cent below 1980. [cite:us5_fox_fbi2025] [cite:us5_ccj_trends] The decline continued into 2026. Murders were down 18.7 per cent in the first four months of 2026 compared with the same months of 2025, and the FBI reported further falls for the first half of the year. [cite:us5_npr_lowmurder] [cite:us5_fox_fbi2025] Analysts do not agree on why. "What's driving it is about as clear as a glass of milk," said Adam Gelb of the CCJ, noting falls in cities with very different policing strategies. President Trump credited his administration: "We ended the war on police, and we declared a very strong war on crime." [cite:us5_fox_fbi2025] Even at its record low, the American rate was about double Canada's 1.9. [cite:us5_npr_lowmurder]

Guns account for most American homicides. Firearms were used in at least 59 per cent of homicides every year from 1976 to 2025, in 77 per cent in 2021 and in at least 71 per cent every year since 2015. [cite:us5_ccj_trends] The burden is also unequal. From 1976 to 2025 the homicide victimisation rate for Black Americans averaged about eight times the rate for white Americans, and about ten times in 2020. [cite:us5_ccj_trends] That gap is measured where American policing, housing segregation and the concentration of gun violence in particular neighbourhoods overlap. Part Four covers the policing side. [scene:us4_policing|Part Four: policing]

Israel: low overall, then a break in 2023

Israel's national homicide rate has long been among the lower rates in the OECD. Israel Police counted 135 murders in 2009 and 103 homicide victims in 2018, a rate of about 1.1 per 100,000. [cite:us5_wiki_crime] A Taub Center study of February 2024 gives a crude rate of 1.56 in 2019, which placed Israel 10th of 33 OECD countries; the United States, at 5.40 that year, was 4th. [cite:us5_taub_homicide] The study's series then shows 1.59 in 2020, 1.84 in 2021 and 1.50 in 2022, followed by a sudden doubling to 3.04 in 2023. [cite:us5_taub_homicide] Over these years the national figure averaged two very different rates. Among Arab citizens the rate was 4.90 in 2019 and 11.11 in 2023. Among Jewish and other Israelis it was 0.67 in 2019 and 0.85 in 2023. Taub's authors put the ratio between the two at about four to one until around 2015, about ten to one in 2020–2022 and thirteen to one in 2023. They called the rise "a sign of institutional failure". [cite:us5_taub_homicide] Israel Police data released to the Association for Freedom of Information show the same split in absolute numbers. From 1 January 2018 to 7 October 2023, 981 people were killed: 712 Arab citizens, 214 Jewish Israelis, 50 foreign citizens and 5 of unknown origin. Arab citizens, about a fifth of the population, made up 73 per cent of the victims. [cite:us5_aawsat_police]

No comparable Israeli series back to 1980 was found for this book. The figures above begin in 2009 for police counts and 2019 for Taub's rates, so the long American series stands beside a short Israeli one. The World Health Organization and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime hold longer ICD-coded series that would close this gap.

The next section follows the Arab-community killings that drove Israel's 2023 break, and the state's response. [scene:us5_arab|The killings in Israel's Arab communities]

sections.h: The Killings in Israel's Arab Communities
sections.html:
Israel's national homicide figures since 2019 are, in the main, a record of killings in its Arab communities: Arab citizens, about a fifth of the population, were 73 per cent of homicide victims from 2018 to October 2023. [cite:us5_aawsat_police] This section follows that record year by year, and then what the state did about it. [scene:us5_homicide|Homicide over time]

Year by year

The police count of Arab victims rose from 73 in 2018 to 94 in 2019, 110 in 2020 and 126 in 2021, fell to 109 in 2022 and reached 222 in 2023. [cite:us5_aawsat_police] The Abraham Initiatives' counts match or run slightly higher: 126 in 2021, then a record, and 244 in 2023, more than double 2022. In 2023 about 88 per cent were shot, nearly half the victims were men aged 18 to 30, and 16 were women. [cite:us5_toi_2021] [cite:us5_toi_2023toll] The group counted 230 in 2024. In 2025 it counted 252 Arab citizens killed in 218 incidents, the deadliest year on its record; 88 per cent were shot, and more than 72 per cent were aged 18 to 40. [cite:us5_yahoo_herzog] Twenty-three of them were women, also a record, and 12 were killed in police operations. Israel Police disputed the total, saying it counted offenders whom officers had killed while they were on their way to carry out a killing. [cite:us5_maariv_2025] With about 2.1 million Arab citizens, 252 deaths is about 12 per 100,000 by this book's arithmetic. That is above the highest American national rate in the CCJ series, 10.2 in 1980, and about three times the American rate of 2025. [cite:us5_taub_homicide] [cite:us5_ccj_trends]

President Isaac Herzog called the 2025 figures "shocking numbers - an unacceptable situation". [cite:us5_yahoo_herzog] Police Commissioner Daniel Levi declared "a state of national emergency" early in 2026. [cite:us5_cnn_killingaday] The killing continued at a high rate. The Abraham Initiatives counted 83 deaths by 6 April 2026, 30 per cent more than in the same period of 2025, and 149 by 2 July. By 13 October 2026 the count was 184, 156 of them shot, against 200 at the same point in 2025. As of October 2026, then, the year was running somewhat below 2025 but far above any year before 2023. [cite:us5_toi_oct2026]

What the record says about the state's part

The crisis is documented as a failure of policing and public services. The figures describe what the state did and failed to do, and say nothing about the character of the communities where the killings happened. The clearest measure is the share of killings the police solve. By the Abraham Initiatives' count the clearance rate for Arab-community homicides was 19 per cent in 2021, 21 per cent in 2022, 10.5 per cent in 2023 and about 10 per cent in 2025. [cite:us5_toi_2023toll] [cite:us5_toi_shinbet] Knesset and Eilaf data cited by CNN put it at about 15 per cent, compared with 65 per cent for killings of Jewish Israelis. [cite:us5_cnn_killingaday] State Comptroller Matanyahu Englman called the rise "a resounding failure of Israeli governments". [cite:us5_toi_2023toll]

Policy changed with each government. In 2021 the Bennett–Lapid government launched a five-year NIS 30 billion plan to close gaps between Arab and Jewish localities, along with NIS 2.4 billion for policing in Arab towns. The count fell in 2022. [cite:us5_toi_2023toll] [cite:us5_aawsat_police] Under the coalition agreement of 25 November 2022, Itamar Ben-Gvir received an expanded National Security Ministry with authority over the police. [cite:hm_jta_coalition2022] The Abraham Initiatives' report for 2023 said both plans had been "hollowed out", and it blamed the minister. Ben-Gvir had urged that the development plan be cancelled. [cite:us5_toi_2023toll] Funding for the "Stop the Bleeding" programme was cut after he took office, and in the following year the officer in charge of fighting crime in Arab communities was removed and replaced by a lower-ranking official. [cite:us5_cnn_killingaday] One finding points to police presence as a lever: in the two months after 7 October 2023, when more police were deployed in Arab towns, homicides fell by half compared with the two months before. [cite:us5_toi_2023toll] Ben-Gvir's own defence pointed elsewhere: "There is 20% less murder in the Jewish sector." [cite:us5_cnn_killingaday]

In December 2025 the Prime Minister's Office planned to move about $70 million from an Arab economic development programme to the police. [cite:us5_cnn_killingaday] On 15 July 2026 the government approved a role for the Shin Bet, the domestic security service, against the smuggling and trade of illegal weapons in Arab communities. The money, NIS 497 million, came out of the 2021 development plan: NIS 345 million for the Shin Bet and NIS 132.4 million for a new police unit. The proposal came from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Social Equality Minister May Golan and Ben-Gvir. The Abraham Initiatives objected that "Crime is not terror". The Association for Civil Rights in Israel said crime among Jewish Israelis is handled by the police, and the Mossawa Center said the money was being taken from youth, training, transport and housing programmes. [cite:us5_toi_shinbet]

Neither country's national average describes the risk any given resident faces. America's record-low rate in 2025 sits on top of a racial gap of roughly eight to one. Israel's low national rate before 2023 hid a gap that grew from four to one to thirteen to one. In 2025, a homicide rate inside Israel's Arab communities above any American national rate on record was matched by a police force that solved about one Arab-community killing in ten. [cite:us5_ccj_trends] [cite:us5_taub_homicide] [cite:us5_toi_shinbet] Both governments face elections with these figures before them: Israel votes on 27 October and the United States on 3 November 2026.

sections.h: Gun Laws, Gun Deaths and Mass Shootings
sections.html:
The two countries start from opposite legal premises. In the United States the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms, and the Supreme Court has said so in District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) and later cases. [cite:us5_duke_bsca] Israel has no such right. Its Firearms Law of 1949 says that "no person shall possess a firearm, except under license". Section 12 gives the licensing authority discretion to issue, condition, refuse or revoke a licence, and the courts treat licensing as an administrative matter rather than the exercise of a right. [cite:us5_duke_reznik] This section keeps crime, suicide and attacks classed as terrorism apart.

How the law works

To hold a private licence in Israel, an applicant has to clear threshold conditions set in regulation and also meet at least one criterion from a further list that is not fully public. As of 2023 the threshold was age 21 with two years of national or military service (one year for women), age 27 for a citizen without service, or age 45 for a permanent resident. Applicants must be physically and mentally fit, and a protective order, for example in a domestic-violence case, should bar a licence unless a court rules otherwise. The police also control which types of firearm civilians may hold. [cite:us5_duke_reznik] Licensing was widened in steps. Measures to increase private ownership began in 2015; where formerly only combat officers met the service requirement, from 2018 regular service in significant combat positions sufficed, and from 2023 any combat service counted. [cite:us5_duke_reznik] [cite:us5a_duke_reznik]

In the United States, federal law sets a floor and the states build on it. In New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, decided on 23 June 2022, the Supreme Court struck down New York's requirement that people applying to carry a concealed handgun show "proper cause". It also set a test under which a gun law must fit the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation. [cite:us5_duke_bsca] Two days later, on 25 June 2022, President Biden signed the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, the first major federal gun law in decades. It expanded background checks for buyers under 21, provided $750 million over five years for state crisis-intervention programmes including "red flag" laws, extended the domestic-violence ban to some dating partners, created federal crimes of straw purchasing and gun trafficking, and required people who sell guns predominantly for profit to be licensed dealers. [cite:us5_duke_bsca] Policy then reversed direction. On 7 February 2025 President Trump ordered Attorney General Pam Bondi to review federal rules, enforcement and court positions for "ongoing infringements" of the Second Amendment, including the reports of the White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention. [cite:us5_bloomberg_eo]

How many guns

The Small Arms Survey estimated about 857 million civilian-held firearms in the world at the end of 2017. About 393 million of them, or 120.5 per 100 residents, were in the United States. [cite:us5_sas_2018] The same survey put Israel at about 557,000 civilian firearms, or 6.7 per 100. [cite:us5_wiki_gunownership] The 2017 survey is a snapshot, and for Israel it is a narrow one: it counts civilian holdings, not the weapons the army issues to soldiers and reservists, and it predates October 2023. Israel's own longer record runs the other way from the American one until 2023. Individually licensed firearms fell from about 280,000 in 1998 (4.7 per cent of the population) to 147,000 in 2018 (1.6 per cent), according to a government report. [cite:us5_duke_reznik]

The October 2023 loosening

After the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir relaxed the licensing rules and pushed through issuance at an unprecedented pace. Geographic restrictions were eased, combat service of any kind qualified, and personal interviews were replaced by telephone interviews or none at all. About 250,000 applications arrived in the first 50 days, roughly as many as in the previous twenty years combined, and approvals averaged about 1,700 a day in November 2023. The stated aim was to triple the number of licence holders, and more than 800 new civilian emergency squads were set up in towns with minimal training. [cite:us5_duke_reznik] Dozens of communities were added to the list of eligible residence areas. The list was given to judges in a sealed envelope and has not been published. Rescue and fire volunteers and national-service members became eligible, and the three-year wait for new immigrants in eligible communities was cancelled. [cite:us5_jpost_gunreform]

By the reform's first anniversary about 188,000 licences had been issued from 365,000 applications. [cite:us5_jpost_gunreform] Against about 170,000 licences in force before 7 October 2023, that roughly doubled the number in a year, by this book's arithmetic. [cite:us5_duke_reznik] Much of the processing was done by temporary staff, mostly young women doing national service, who worked at the ministry from 8 October to 2 December 2023 without appropriate training. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara ordered their work halted. Police found that they had issued 23,000 temporary and 15,424 permanent licences, 1,146 of them suspected of breaching the criteria, and the Lahav 433 fraud unit opened an investigation in which people from Ben-Gvir's office were questioned. Ben-Gvir's associates called these cases negligible. [cite:us5_jpost_gunreform] The United States reportedly held back a shipment of rifles over concern that they could reach West Bank settlers. [cite:us5_duke_reznik] The UN counted 1,828 settler attacks causing casualties or damage in 2025. [cite:wb_ocha_snap2025] [scene:wb8_settlers|The West Bank, Documented: settlers]

The reform's effect is argued both ways. A former senior licensing official warned that "a weapon in inexperienced or unqualified hands could cause a disaster". The women's organisation WIZO argued that "the presence of a gun in the house is the issue". [cite:us5_jpost_gunreform] Ben-Gvir's office said that "no woman has been killed by a weapon provided under the reform", that murders of women "occurred with illegal weapons or kitchen knives", and that in recent attacks armed citizens were "the first to neutralize terrorists". [cite:us5_jpost_gunreform] [cite:us5a_jpost_gunreform] The Abraham Initiatives links the shootings in Arab communities to illegal firearms, and the government's response in July 2026 targeted smuggling and the illegal arms trade, not licensed guns. [cite:us5_toi_2023toll] [cite:us5_toi_shinbet] [scene:us5_arab|The killings in Israel's Arab communities]

Gun deaths: what the American figures show

The CDC recorded 44,447 gun deaths in the United States in 2024, the third annual fall in a row but still the fifth-highest total since 1968. Of these, 27,593 (62 per cent) were suicides and 15,364 (35 per cent) homicides. [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths] The overall gun death rate was 12.8 per 100,000, against a peak of 16.3 in 1974. The gun homicide rate was 4.7, down from 6.7 in 2021 and a peak of 7.2 in 1974. The gun suicide rate was 7.6, about equal to its record of 7.7 in 1977. [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths] By state, rates ranged from 3.7 per 100,000 in Hawaii to 28.0 in Mississippi. The largest part of America's gun toll is suicide, which comparisons limited to crime leave out. [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths]

No Israeli series combining firearm homicides, suicides and accidents was found for this book; the WHO mortality database could close that gap. The comparison made with confidence covers homicide alone. [scene:us5_homicide|Homicide over time]

Mass shootings and attacks

There is no agreed definition of a mass shooting. The Gun Violence Archive counts any incident in which four or more people are shot, not counting the shooter. By that measure the United States had 690 mass shootings in 2021, 645 in 2022, 660 in 2023 and 502 in 2024, with 510 deaths in 2024. [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths] The FBI's narrower "active shooter" count rose from 3 incidents in 2000 to 61 in 2021 and fell to 24 in 2024. [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths] In Israel, the shootings with the most victims have mostly been attacks classed as terrorism, which are counted separately from crime. On 8 September 2025, for example, two gunmen from the West Bank killed six people at Ramot Junction in Jerusalem before a security officer and a civilian shot them dead. [cite:us5_aje_ramot] Multi-victim shootings in Arab towns, most of them attributed to criminal groups and some to feuds in which several members of one family were killed, are counted in the Arab-community homicide figures rather than as mass shootings. [cite:us5_toi_2023toll] [cite:us5_maariv_2025]

The two systems have moved in opposite directions. The United States combines constitutionally protected, very high civilian gun ownership with a gun homicide rate falling from its 2021 peak and a gun suicide rate near its record. Israel's discretionary licensing shrank private gun ownership for two decades, then roughly doubled the number of licences in a year after October 2023, with investigators examining how some were issued as of late 2024, while the Arab-community killings, mostly with illegal guns, reached a record in 2025. [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths] [cite:us5_duke_reznik] [cite:us5_jpost_gunreform] [cite:us5_yahoo_herzog]

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: Citizenship and Immigration
chapters.intro: Part Six asks who may join each state and what happens to those who arrive without permission. It sets Israel's Law of Return and Nationality Law, which give every Jew and certain relatives of Jews an immediate right to citizenship and give citizenship at birth only to the children of citizens, beside the American rule of citizenship by birth on the soil, which the Supreme Court upheld in June 2026, and naturalisation after five years of permanent residence. It counts immigrants to Israel and naturalisations in the United States over four decades, and names who has no route in each country: Palestinian spouses barred since 2003, East Jerusalem's permanent residents and the people whose citizenship the state can now revoke, and America's unauthorised population. It then compares how the two governments treated asylum seekers, from Israel's Holot facility and its 2018 deportation plan to America's refugee ceilings, immigration courts, deportations and detention.
chapters.outro: Part Six established that the two states draw their membership lines on different principles. Israel grants immediate citizenship to Jews and their relatives under the Law of Return and gives citizenship at birth only to children of citizens; the United States grants it to almost everyone born on its soil, a rule the Supreme Court upheld on 30 June 2026, and naturalises permanent residents after five years. [cite:rs_ch01_lor_text] [cite:us6_refworld_nationality] [cite:us6_fd_barbara] Immigration to Israel came in waves, 199,516 arrivals in 1990 and 74,400 in 2022 but 22,522 in 2025, while American naturalisations rose from about 210,000 a year in the 1980s to 878,460 in 2023. [cite:us6_jvl_aliyah] [cite:us6_ohss_nat2023] Each system leaves people out: in Israel, Palestinian spouses of citizens under the 2003 law re-enacted in 2022, most of East Jerusalem's Palestinians, and those whose citizenship can be revoked under the 2023 law; in the United States, about 14 million unauthorised residents with no route to naturalise. [cite:rs_ch01_toi_citizenship2022] [cite:us6_aje_revocation] [cite:us6_pew_immig2025] Israel recognised fewer than 1 per cent of its African asylum seekers and held more than 13,000 in Holot before closing it in 2018, but about 25,000 remain; the United States cut refugee admissions to the lowest ceiling in its history, carried about 3.8 million cases in its immigration courts, and funded enforcement at several times its earlier level, while courts in both countries struck down parts of each government's programme. [cite:us6_mrg_african] [cite:us6_972_holot] [cite:us6_crs_refugees] [cite:us6_mpi_courts] [cite:us6_brennan_obbba] Part Seven turns to religion and the state. [scene:us7_israel|Part Seven: religion and state in Israel]

sections.h: Who Can Become a Citizen
sections.html:
The two states answer the question of who may join them by different rules. The United States grants citizenship to almost everyone born on its soil and lets lawful permanent residents apply after a waiting period, whatever their religion or origin. Israel grants citizenship by birth only to the children of citizens, gives every Jew, and certain relatives of Jews, an immediate right to immigrate and become a citizen, and offers everyone else a discretionary naturalisation route.

Israel: return, birth to a citizen, and discretion

The Knesset passed the Law of Return on 5 July 1950. Its first section reads: "Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh", an immigrant. The minister may refuse only a person acting against the Jewish people or likely to endanger public health or state security; a 1954 amendment added people with a criminal past likely to endanger public welfare. [cite:rs_ch01_lor_text] In 1970 the law was extended to the child and grandchild of a Jew and their spouses, and a Jew was defined as a person born of a Jewish mother or converted to Judaism who is not a member of another religion. [cite:rs_ch01_lor_text] The Nationality Law of 1952 then made every oleh a citizen "by return". [cite:rs_ch01_nationality_1952]

For everyone else the 1952 law gives two routes. A child born in Israel is a citizen at birth only if "his father or mother was an Israel national"; a child born abroad to an Israeli parent is also a citizen. There is no citizenship from birth on Israeli soil alone. An adult who is not covered by the Law of Return may be naturalised, at the Interior Minister's discretion, after a period of residence in the preceding five years, with a right to permanent residence, some Hebrew, an intention to settle, renunciation of any prior nationality and a declaration of loyalty. [cite:us6_refworld_nationality] Palestinian Arabs who stayed in Israel after 1948 became citizens "by residence" only if they had been registered as inhabitants on 1 March 1952 and had stayed continuously or entered legally. [cite:rs_ch01_nationality_1952]

Defenders of the Law of Return, such as the writer Alex Stein in a 2013 opinion essay, describe it as a refuge for Jews after centuries in which other states did not reliably protect them; critics note that Palestinian refugees and their descendants cannot return to the same land while any Jew may immigrate, and the Arab-Israeli legal centre Adalah lists the law in its database of discriminatory laws. [cite:rs_ch01_dailybeast_lor] [cite:rs_ch01_lor_text]

United States: soil and naturalisation

Under the Fourteenth Amendment, people born in the United States and "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" are citizens. On 20 January 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14160, which sought to deny citizenship to children of parents present unlawfully or temporarily. Lower courts blocked it, and on 30 June 2026, in Trump v. Barbara, the Supreme Court held in an opinion by Chief Justice John Roberts that such children are citizens at birth and rejected any test based on the parents' domicile or status; the order remains blocked. Three dissents argued that the clause requires domicile: one by Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch, one by Justice Samuel Alito and one by Justice Gorsuch; Justice Brett Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment and dissented in part. [cite:us6a_fd_barbara] [cite:us6_nlr_barbara]

An adult immigrant becomes a citizen by naturalisation. The applicant must be at least 18, have held lawful permanent residence (a green card) for five years, or three if married to an American citizen, speak and read basic English, pass a civics test and show good moral character. [cite:us6_mpi_nat] The conditions are the same whatever the applicant's religion or descent. The narrower gate is the green card itself, which an applicant must already hold; how green cards are allocated is outside the scope of this part.

The numbers over time

The two series measure different things. Israel's counts immigrants, almost all of whom arrive under the Law of Return and become citizens at once; America's counts naturalisations of people who are already permanent residents. Israel's arrivals came in waves. About 240,000 people arrived in 1949 alone. Arrivals fell to 20,428 in 1980 and 10,642 in 1985, then rose to 199,516 in 1990 and 176,100 in 1991 as emigration from the Soviet Union opened, before falling to 60,201 in 2000 and 16,635 in 2010. [cite:us6_jvl_aliyah] The war in Ukraine produced another wave: about 70,000 arrivals in 2022, the most in 23 years, led by 37,364 from Russia and 14,680 from Ukraine in the first eleven months. [cite:us6_ynet_aliyah2022] The final 2022 figure was 74,400; it fell to 46,033 in 2023, 32,161 in 2024 and 22,522 in 2025, though the share from Western countries rose from 21 to 38 per cent, including 3,781 from the United States. [cite:us6_jvl_aliyah] [cite:us6_ynet_aliyah2025] As the 1970 grandchild clause took effect, the share of immigrants who were not Jewish under religious law rose from nearly 20 per cent in 1990–94 to 53 per cent in 1998. [cite:rs_ch01_joppke_rosenhek]

American naturalisations rose over the same period. The Department of Homeland Security puts the annual average at about 210,000 in the 1980s, 500,000 in the 1990s, 680,000 in the 2000s and 730,100 in 2010–19. The pandemic cut the number to 628,250 in fiscal year 2020; it reached 969,380 in 2022 and 878,460 in 2023, the latest year in the department's report. Mexico was the leading country of birth, and the median new citizen had been a permanent resident for seven years. [cite:us6_ohss_nat2023] By 2023, 46 per cent of the country's immigrants were naturalised citizens. [cite:us6_pew_immig2025]

Scaled to population the two are closer than the raw numbers suggest. On this book's own rough arithmetic, 22,522 arrivals in 2025 against a population of about 10.3 million is about 2.2 per thousand, and 878,460 naturalisations in 2023 against about 342 million is about 2.6 per thousand; in 2022, Israel's figure was several times higher. [cite:us1_jpost_ilpop] [cite:us1_wa_uspop]

Who cannot become a citizen

In Israel the clearest exclusion is by marriage. The Citizenship and Entry into Israel Law, passed in 2003 during the Second Intifada as a one-year temporary measure, barred residence permits for Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza married to Israelis, and later for nationals of Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq. It was extended at least 17 times and upheld by the Supreme Court by one vote in 2006 and again in 2012. [cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] [cite:us6_adalah_cit2019] In 2020 Interior Ministry data showed 800–1,000 applications a year, and 45 people who had gained status through family unification were linked to terror offences between 2001 and 2020, none in 2018–2020. [cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] The law lapsed in July 2021 and was re-enacted on 10 March 2022 by 45 votes to 15, with a stated aim that includes protecting the Jewish majority. [cite:rs_ch01_toi_citizenship2022] In December 2022 the Supreme Court asked the state whether it would amend the new law; the Knesset extended it for a year on 5 March 2023 without amendments, with nine petitions pending and humanitarian permits capped at 58. [cite:us6_adalah_cit2023] This book did not find a primary record of each later renewal, so the law's exact status as of October 2026 is stated here as unverified. Part Eight takes up the effect on Arab citizens. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: equality among citizens]

A second exclusion concerns Palestinians in East Jerusalem, which Israel annexed in 1967. Most hold permanent residency, not citizenship. Reuters reported in 2015 that applications rose from 114 in 2003 to 800–1,000 a year and that in 2012–13, of 1,434 applications, 189 were approved and 169 rejected; a former Palestinian negotiator put the number naturalised since 1967 at about 24,000, about 10 per cent. [cite:us6_reuters_ej] Al Jazeera, citing Haaretz in 2022, gives 5 per cent; the two estimates differ in source and date. [cite:us6_aje_revocation] Palestinians in the rest of the West Bank and in Gaza have no route at all; Part Nine sets out their status. [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank]

Citizenship can also be taken away. The 1952 law already allowed the minister to revoke it for "a breach of allegiance". [cite:us6_refworld_nationality] A February 2023 law made revocation easier for people convicted of terrorism who receive payments from the Palestinian Authority, and in February 2026 Prime Minister Netanyahu signed the first orders under it, revoking the citizenship of two Palestinian citizens of Israel and ordering their deportation, subject to district court review within 30 days. Netanyahu said the two had carried out stabbing and shooting attacks on Israeli civilians and had been rewarded for them by the Palestinian Authority; Al Jazeera's report described the law as discriminatory. [cite:us6_aje_revocation]

In the United States the largest group without a route is the unauthorised population, which Pew estimated at a record 14 million in 2023. They cannot naturalise, because naturalisation requires lawful permanent residence first. [cite:us6_pew_immig2025] [cite:us6_mpi_nat] Their American-born children, however, are citizens, and the Supreme Court's June 2026 ruling kept it so. [cite:us6_nlr_barbara]

sections.h: Asylum, Detention and Deportation
sections.html:
Both states have made the people who arrive without permission a central political question, and both have built detention and removal systems to deal with them. The scale is very different. Israel's asylum population, mostly Eritreans and Sudanese who crossed from Egypt, never exceeded about 60,000 people; America's immigration courts alone had a backlog of about 3.8 million cases in 2025. This section sets out how each system has treated people seeking protection, and what each has spent and built to remove people.

Israel: from the Sinai border to Holot

Between 2006 and 2013 about 64,000 asylum seekers and migrants entered Israel across the land border with Egypt's Sinai Peninsula, among them about 50,000 Sudanese and Eritreans. [cite:us6_hrw_holot2014] The number in the country peaked at close to 60,000 in 2012. [cite:us6_972_holot] The government called them "work infiltrators" rather than refugees, and argued that not deporting them gave them adequate protection. [cite:us6a_hrw_govt] Its main legal tool was the Prevention of Infiltration Law of 1954, a statute that depends on the state of emergency in force since 1948, which Part Two describes. [cite:us2_adalah_emergency2003] [scene:us2_emergency|Part Two: emergency powers] Israel completed a fence along the Egyptian border, after which irregular entries, in Human Rights Watch's words, "fallen to near zero". [cite:us6_hrw_holot2014]

The Knesset and the Supreme Court then went back and forth over detention. A January 2012 amendment to the 1954 law allowed new arrivals to be held for long periods without trial; the court struck it down in September 2013. The Knesset passed a new amendment in December 2013 and opened Holot, an "open" facility in the Negev about 65 kilometres from Beersheba, surrounded by a four-metre fence, where residents had to report for roll call three times a day and be inside by 10 p.m. The government described it as an "open residency center"; Human Rights Watch called it "a detention center in all but name". On 22 September 2014 the court voided the Holot provisions by 7 to 2 and one-year detention of new arrivals by 6 to 3, giving the state 90 days. Interior Minister Gideon Sa'ar said he could not accept the ruling and warned that the borders would be overrun. [cite:us6_hrw_holot2014] [cite:us6a_hrw_govt] The government responded each time by changing the criteria and time limits, and Holot stayed open until 14 March 2018. More than 13,000 people were held there over its life. [cite:us6_972_holot]

Very few were recognised as refugees. Human Rights Watch reported in 2014 that Israel had rejected every Sudanese asylum claim and more than 99 per cent of Eritrean claims; Minority Rights Group put the recognition rate below 1 per cent in 2025. [cite:us6_hrw_holot2014] [cite:us6_mrg_african] Instead the state encouraged departure: 3,959 Eritreans and Sudanese left under a "voluntary return" programme from 2013 to 2017, and about 1,700 were transferred to Uganda from 2015 to 2018. [cite:us6_972_holot] [cite:us6_mrg_african] In January 2018 the government gave asylum seekers three months to leave or face indefinite imprisonment or deportation to Rwanda or Uganda; the Supreme Court issued an interim injunction on 15 March. [cite:us6_972_holot] On 2 April 2018 Israel and the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) agreed to resettle about half the population in Western states and give the rest temporary status; the government cancelled the agreement the next day under pressure from coalition partners. The court later ruled indefinite detention unlawful without formal agreements with receiving countries. [cite:us6_mrg_african]

About 38,000 asylum seekers remained in March 2018, and an estimated 25,000 in late 2025, most still without refugee status.
