[cite:us6_972_holot] [cite:us6_mrg_african] They are excluded from Israel's National Health Insurance, which covers citizens and permanent residents. [cite:us16_cwf_israel] [scene:us16_systems|Part Sixteen: health systems]

The United States: refugees, asylum and the border

The United States runs two protection systems. Refugees are selected abroad and resettled under an annual ceiling set by the president. The ceiling for fiscal year 1980, after the Vietnam War, was 231,700, and 207,116 refugees were admitted that year; before fiscal year 2018 the ceiling never fell below 67,000. On 20 January 2025 Executive Order 14163 suspended refugee entry except in individual cases, stating that further refugee entry "would be detrimental to the interests of the United States". [cite:us6a_crs_rationale] The ceiling for fiscal year 2025, set by President Biden, had been 125,000, and 38,102 were admitted, almost all before the suspension. For fiscal year 2026 the ceiling was set at 7,500, to be "primarily" allocated to Afrikaners from South Africa; it was raised in May 2026 to 17,500, still the lowest in the programme's history. By 30 June 2026, 7,730 had been admitted, nearly all South African. [cite:us6_crs_refugees]

Asylum, the second system, is claimed by people already in the country or at the border. Its courts are overwhelmed. The Migration Policy Institute counted a backlog of about 3.8 million cases in the immigration courts by mid-2025, more than double the 2021 level; the administration had fired more than 139 immigration judges, and about 68 per cent of people in removal proceedings had no lawyer. [cite:us6_mpi_courts] On his first day in office in 2025 the president also invoked his power to suspend entry to close the southern border to asylum claims. On 24 April 2026 the federal appeals court in Washington held, in RAICES v. Noem, that this power cannot be used to "override asylum laws established by Congress"; RAICES, one of the plaintiffs, expected an appeal to the Supreme Court. [cite:us6_raices_dccir] Status as of October 2026: this book did not find a Supreme Court ruling on the case.

Border crossings fell sharply in the same period. Customs and Border Protection recorded 3.3 million enforcement actions in 2023, 2.3 million in 2024 and 391,000 in 2025. [cite:us6_usafacts_enf]

Removals and detention over time

American removals, deportations under a formal order, have risen over four decades under presidents of both parties. The Department of Homeland Security counts 18,013 removals in fiscal year 1980, 30,039 in 1990, 188,467 in 2000 and 359,795 in 2008. They peaked under President Obama at 432,334 in 2013, a year in which, by Pew's count, 83 per cent of deportations were carried out without a hearing before a judge. Removals fell to 237,364 in 2020 and 85,783 in 2021, when many people at the border were expelled under a pandemic order and counted separately. [cite:us6_dhs_table39] [cite:us6_pew_2013] Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) carried out about 320,000 deportations in fiscal year 2025, 18 per cent more than the year before. [cite:us6_usafacts_enf] The DHS and ICE figures are different counts, the first covering all removals by every DHS agency and the second ICE alone, so the 2025 figure is not directly comparable with the earlier series.

Detention grew with it. ICE held a peak of 68,289 people in early February 2026, 73.6 per cent with no criminal conviction. [cite:us4_trac_ice] [scene:us4_detention|Part Four: detention] The budget act President Trump signed in July 2025 provided about $170 billion for immigration enforcement over four years, $75 billion of it for ICE, including about $45 billion for detention, and nearly $47 billion for the border wall; ICE's funding for fiscal year 2025, about $28.7 billion, was nearly three times its 2024 budget. [cite:us6_brennan_obbba] The data and surveillance tools that ICE uses, including software bought from Palantir, are described in The One-Way Mirror. [scene:ow9_ice|The One-Way Mirror: ICE]

What the two records show

In each country the courts set the outer limits. Israel's Supreme Court twice struck down detention without trial for asylum seekers and stopped the 2018 deportations; America's courts blocked the border asylum closure and the birthright order. [cite:us6_hrw_holot2014] [cite:us6_mrg_african] [cite:us6_raices_dccir] Inside those limits the two governments made different choices. Israel recognised almost no one and pressed people to leave, yet it never carried out a mass deportation and about 25,000 remain in a long-term legal limbo. [cite:us6_mrg_african] The United States has a large asylum and resettlement system on paper, but by 2026 it had set the lowest refugee ceiling in the programme's history, left millions of cases waiting in its courts, and funded immigration enforcement and detention at several times their earlier levels. [cite:us6_crs_refugees] [cite:us6_mpi_courts] [cite:us6_brennan_obbba]

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: Religion and State
chapters.intro: Part Seven compares how each state handles religion. In Israel there is no civil marriage: religious courts inherited from the Ottoman and British systems decide who may marry and divorce, the Chief Rabbinate decides who is Jewish for that purpose, and the state built exits abroad and online rather than a civil alternative at home. The part then follows the exemption from military service for men in full-time Torah study, from about 400 students in 1949 to tens of thousands today, the court rulings against it, and the budget money that sustains the institutions. On the American side it traces the First Amendment from the "wall of separation" of 1947 to the Supreme Court's turn toward religious exemptions and public money for religious schools, and ends with the two systems side by side, as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: Part Seven established that Israel leaves marriage and divorce to religious courts under arrangements dating from the Ottoman millet system, the 1947 status quo and the 1953 rabbinical-courts law, so that couples of mixed faith or the same sex, people the Rabbinate does not count as Jewish and wives refused a divorce have no full remedy inside the country; the state registers marriages made abroad, about 9,200 in 2022, rather than offering civil marriage. [cite:us7_wiki_marriage] [cite:us7_wiki_civmar] The exemption from military service for Torah students grew from about 400 in 1949 to about 63,000 in 2023, was ruled unlawful in 2012, 2017 and 2024, and was shielded in July 2026 by a new Basic Law and an arrest ban the High Court froze and, on 3 September 2026, struck down, while the 2026 budget gave NIS 2.2 billion in coalition funds to Haredi purposes. [cite:us7_globes_draft2024] [cite:us2_toi_torahlaw] [cite:us7_toi_arrestlaw2026] [cite:us19a_jpost_struck] [cite:us7_toi_coalfunds2026] The United States has civil marriage everywhere, but its Supreme Court has replaced the Lemon test, widened religious exemptions under RFRA and required that religious schools not be excluded from public tuition aid, while private school choice programmes grew from about 10,000 students in 1996 to more than 1.5 million in 2025. [cite:us7_wiki_kennedy] [cite:us7_wiki_hobbylobby] [cite:us7_wiki_carson] [cite:us7_edchoice_abcs2026] On Pew's index of government restrictions on religion both countries rose from 2007 to 2022, the United States from 1.6 to 2.7 and Israel from 3.9 to 6.7. [cite:us7_pew_gri2022] Part Eight turns to equality among citizens. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: equality among citizens]

sections.h: Israel: Religious Courts and Personal Status
sections.html:
Israel has no civil marriage. That fact, more than any other, defines how religion and the state meet in the country's law. Its roots are older than the state. Under Ottoman rule, marriage, divorce and other matters of personal status belonged to the courts of each recognised religious community, the millet system. The British Mandate kept a modified version, recognising eleven communities (Sunni Islam, Orthodox Judaism and nine Christian denominations) and setting up the Orthodox Chief Rabbinate; marriages outside those communities were not recognised. In 1947 David Ben-Gurion and the religious parties agreed that personal status would stay with the religious authorities, the arrangement known as the "status quo". In 1953 the new state gave the rabbinical courts, under the Chief Rabbinate, jurisdiction over the marriage and divorce of all Jews in Israel. Muslims marry and divorce in sharia courts, members of ten recognised churches in church courts, and Druze, recognised as a separate community in 1957, in their own courts since 1962. [cite:us7_wiki_marriage] The deadlock over religion's place was also one reason the first Knesset chose to legislate Basic Laws one by one rather than adopt a constitution, as Part Two describes. [scene:us2_founding|Part Two: how the state is built]

Who cannot marry in Israel

Because each community's court applies its own religious law, a couple can marry in Israel only if both partners belong to the same recognised community and that community's law permits the match. Religious authorities do not marry couples of different religions or couples of the same sex. Jewish law as the Rabbinate applies it also bars some Jewish couples: a man of priestly descent (a kohen) may not marry a convert, and children born of adultery or incest face limits on whom they may marry. People whose Jewish status the Rabbinate doubts, often immigrants from the former Soviet Union or Ethiopia, must undergo Orthodox conversion first, and the Rabbinate does not accept non-Orthodox conversions, or some Orthodox ones, for marriage. [cite:us7_wiki_marriage] The Law of Return draws the line differently: since its 1970 amendment it grants immigration rights to the child and grandchild of a Jew and their spouses, so the state admits as citizens many people its marriage law treats as not Jewish. [cite:rs_ch01_lor_text] [cite:rs_ch01_joppke_rosenhek]

How many people this affects is an estimate, not an official count. Hiddush, an Israeli organisation that campaigns for religious freedom, put the number of citizens registered as "without religion" and unable to marry in Israel at 300,000 in 2013. In January 2016 it told a Knesset conference that about 660,000 Jewish Israelis could not legally marry in the country, including 364,000 immigrants from the former Soviet Union, 284,000 gay and lesbian Israelis and 13,000 non-Orthodox converts, using polls and Central Bureau of Statistics data. [cite:us7_toi_hiddushmap] [cite:us7_jta_660k] On its own world map of marriage freedom, Hiddush placed Israel among the 45 of 194 countries with "severe restrictions", the only democracy in that group. [cite:us7_toi_hiddushmap]

The routes around the Rabbinate

The state built exits rather than an alternative. In 1962 the Supreme Court ordered the Interior Ministry to register civil marriages performed abroad, even between Israeli citizens, at first for statistical purposes; a 2006 ruling extended recognition to the marriage's validity, and the same year the court voted 6–1 to register same-sex marriages performed abroad. [cite:us7_wiki_civmar] Cyprus became the usual destination. About 9,000 couples registered overseas marriages with the Central Bureau of Statistics in 2011, and Hiddush reported in 2016 that one in five weddings registered in Israel had taken place abroad. [cite:us7_wiki_civmar] [cite:us7_jta_660k] Couples also married over video link before officiants in Utah. A court in Lod recognised those marriages in September 2022, and the Supreme Court upheld that ruling against the Interior Ministry on 7 March 2023; Hiddush estimated that more than 3,000 couples with an Israeli partner had married this way by 2024. The Central Bureau of Statistics identified 9,200 overseas weddings registered in 2022. [cite:us7_wiki_civmar] Same-sex couples registered 1,151 foreign weddings between 2006 and 2019. [cite:us7_wiki_civmar] Inside Israel the only civil option is the 2010 Civil Union Law, which applies only when both partners are registered as having no religion. [cite:us7_wiki_marriage]

Divorce stays with the same courts. A Jewish divorce requires the husband to give a writ of divorce, the get, and a wife whose husband refuses cannot remarry under religious law. Rules adopted in 2016 allow criminal prosecution for refusal, but only after a rabbinical court has issued an order of a kind it rarely issues. There were 11,145 Jewish divorces in 2018. [cite:us7_wiki_marriage]

Conversion and burial

Who counts as Jewish for the state's purposes has been fought out in the courts. On 1 March 2021 a nine-justice panel ruled 8–1 that conversions performed in Israel by the Reform and Conservative movements must be recognised for the Law of Return, after the court had waited about fifteen years for the Knesset to legislate; the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism condemned the ruling. [cite:us7_globes_conversion2021] The ruling concerned immigration and citizenship. It did not give those converts access to marriage through the Rabbinate. [cite:us7_wiki_marriage] Burial follows the same pattern of a religious default with a narrow exit. Local burial societies, 521 of them in 2016, operate under the Religious Services Ministry and bury Jewish Israelis at the National Insurance Institute's expense. A 1996 law gives every citizen the right to a secular burial on the same public funding, but by 2016 the state had established only a handful of civil cemeteries. [cite:us7_jn_burial]

One cross-country measure tracks the trend. The Pew Research Center's Government Restrictions Index scores each country from 0 to 10 on how far its government limits or controls religious activity, across many kinds of restriction, of which marriage law is only one. Israel scored 3.9 in the year to June 2007 and 6.7 in 2022, when a one-point rise moved it into Pew's "very high" band (6.6 and above). [cite:us7_pew_gri2022] [cite:us7_pew_gri2022rep] Part Six's account of the Law of Return shows the other side of the same definition of who is Jewish. [scene:us6_citizenship|Part Six: citizenship]

sections.h: Israel: The Haredi Exemption and Its Funding
sections.html:
The second pillar of the religious status quo, after personal status law, is the exemption from military service for men in full-time Torah study. It began in 1948–49 with about 400 yeshiva students. The cap rose to 800 a year after 1967 and was lifted entirely in 1977 under a coalition agreement between Likud and Agudat Yisrael. [cite:us7_globes_draft2024] [cite:us7_wiki_haredidraft] By the end of June 2023 the state counted about 63,000 exempt students. [cite:us7_globes_draft2024] Each attempt to regulate the exemption by law has fallen in court. The Tal Law of July 2002 let students defer service; in 2005 only 31 of the 41,450 students it covered later enlisted. The Supreme Court struck it down on 21 February 2012; a 2014 enlistment law was amended in 2015, and the court struck down those amendments on 12 September 2017. [cite:us7_wiki_haredidraft] On 25 June 2024 a nine-justice panel ruled unanimously that the government had no legal basis for a blanket exemption, that it must draft yeshiva students, and that it could not keep funding yeshivas and kollels (seminaries for married men) for students without a lawful exemption or deferral. The government had argued that the military had discretion over which groups to conscript; the ruling, written by Acting President Uzi Vogelman, rejected this as selective enforcement and found that the government had "severely harmed the rule of law and the principle that all individuals are equal before the law". [cite:us7_globes_draft2024] [cite:us7a_globes_govt]

Enforcement since then has been limited. Of 3,000 draft notices sent in July 2024, fewer than one in ten recipients reported; by November 2024 the army had approved 7,000 more orders and 1,126 arrest warrants. [cite:us7_wiki_haredidraft] The Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) counts 3,060 Haredi enlistments in the army or civilian service in 2025 against 3,022 in 2015, roughly flat in number while the Haredi population grew by about half (this book's arithmetic from the IDI population figures below), so about a third lower relative to population. [cite:us7_idi_haredi2025] The coalition answered the courts with legislation. On 13 July 2026 the Knesset passed Basic Law: Torah Study, 63 to 52, declaring Torah study a "foundational value"; the Movement for Quality Government petitioned against it the same day. [cite:us2_toi_torahlaw] A law passed the same month to bar arrests of Haredi draft evaders for about seven months was frozen by the High Court within a day; on 28 July 2026 a nine-justice panel extended the freeze, with the attorney general arguing that the law created unconstitutional discriminatory enforcement, the Knesset's legal adviser urging annulment on procedural grounds and the government boycotting the hearing. About 72,000 Haredi men aged 18 to 24 had ignored conscription orders. [cite:us7_toi_arrestlaw2026] [cite:us19a_toi_hearing] [cite:gi11_reuters_rzp2026] On 3 September 2026 the High Court unanimously struck down the arrest law, finding the legislative process fundamentally defective; eight of the nine justices also held it unconstitutional in substance, and the court said the law "never took effect". [cite:us19a_jpost_struck] No ruling on the petition against Basic Law: Torah Study had been reported in the sources this book found as of October 2026. Part Nineteen sets the exemption beside the US volunteer force. [scene:us19_service|Part Nineteen: who serves]

The money

The state funds the institutions. The 2026 budget, approved by the cabinet on 10 March 2026, carried more than NIS 5 billion ($1.6 billion) in discretionary coalition funds; by a Berl Katznelson Center count, NIS 2.2 billion of it, 53 per cent, went to Haredi purposes, including NIS 1.56 billion for Torah institutions such as yeshivas and kollels and NIS 107 million for Haredi schools outside the state system ("recognised but unofficial" and "exempt" schools, this book's sum). Hebrew media reported that the Finance Ministry opposed the allocation, and opposition leaders, among them Naftali Bennett, accused the government of transferring billions of shekels to draft evaders; the report carried no government justification, and the funds are allocated under coalition agreements between the parties. [cite:us7_toi_coalfunds2026] [cite:us7a_toi_funds] The population these policies govern is growing. The IDI counts about 750,000 Haredi Israelis in 2009 (10 per cent of the population), 948,000 in 2015 (11 per cent) and 1.45 million in 2025 (14.3 per cent). Yeshiva and kollel students numbered 169,366 in 2023, up 83 per cent in a decade, while employment among Haredi men rose from about a third around 2002 to 52 per cent in 2015 and about 54 per cent now, stalled since 2016. [cite:us7_idi_haredi2025] A third of Haredi families were below the poverty line, against 14 per cent of other Jewish families. [cite:us7_idi_haredi2025news] The schooling side of this record is in Part Seventeen. [scene:us17_schools|Part Seventeen: the school streams]

Who the arrangement serves and who it leaves out follows from its design. It gives each recognised religious establishment authority over its members' family life and gives the Haredi parties, as coalition partners from the 1977 agreement to the 2026 budget, a lever over the draft and over money. It leaves out citizens who belong to no recognised community, couples of mixed faith or the same sex, converts outside Orthodoxy and wives refused a divorce, and it places the burden of military service on those who are not exempt. Israel votes on 27 October 2026, and the draft law, the Torah Study law and the coalition funds are all live questions in that election. [cite:gi11_reuters_rzp2026] [cite:us2_toi_torahlaw]

sections.h: The United States: Separation, Exemptions and Public Money
sections.html:
The American arrangement starts from a text rather than an inherited system of religious courts. The First Amendment, ratified in December 1791, says that "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof". [cite:us7_wiki_estab] Marriage in the United States is a civil act licensed by the state; clergy may officiate, but no religious body decides who may marry. Since Obergefell v. Hodges, decided 5–4 on 26 June 2015, every state must license and recognise same-sex marriages, and the Respect for Marriage Act, signed on 13 December 2022, requires every state and the federal government to recognise same-sex and interracial marriages validly performed elsewhere. The Supreme Court later declined, without comment, a petition from the former Kentucky clerk Kim Davis asking it to overturn Obergefell. [cite:us7_wiki_obergefell] The live American questions are therefore not who may marry but two others: how far religious believers may be exempted from general laws, and how much public money may reach religious institutions. On the first, Congress and the Court have pulled in different directions since 1990; on the second, the Court has moved from permitting public money for religious schools to requiring that they not be excluded from it.

From the wall to history and tradition

The Establishment Clause was applied to the states in Everson v. Board of Education (1947), in which Justice Hugo Black invoked Thomas Jefferson's "wall of separation between church and State" while upholding New Jersey's payment of bus fares for pupils at parochial schools. In Lemon v. Kurtzman (1971) the Court struck down Pennsylvania laws paying for services and part of teachers' salaries at religious schools, and set a three-part test (secular purpose, primary effect, no excessive entanglement) that governed for decades. [cite:us7_wiki_estab] On 27 June 2022, in Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, the Court ruled 6–3 that a public-school football coach's personal prayer on the field was protected, and replaced the Lemon test with an approach based on history and tradition; in 2023 it described Lemon as "now abrogated". [cite:us7_wiki_kennedy]

Exemptions from general laws

The exemption question turned on a 1990 case. In Employment Division v. Smith the Court held that a neutral law that applies to everyone need not meet strict scrutiny merely because it burdens someone's religion. Congress responded with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 (RFRA), which requires the government to show a compelling interest pursued by the least restrictive means whenever a law substantially burdens religious exercise. [cite:us7_wiki_hobbylobby] On 30 June 2014, in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, the Court ruled 5–4 that RFRA protected closely held for-profit companies whose owners objected on religious grounds to the federal requirement that employee health plans cover contraception. [cite:us7_wiki_hobbylobby] The comparison with Israel's draft exemption is limited but real: in both countries a religious claim can lift an obligation that applies to everyone else. The difference lies in who decides. In the United States the courts weigh each claim against the government's interest case by case; in Israel the exemption from military service was a political arrangement that the courts have repeatedly found unlawful and that the government has enforced only in small part since the 2024 ruling. [cite:us7_globes_draft2024] [scene:us7_haredi|The Haredi exemption]

Public money for religious schools

The funding line has moved furthest. Zelman v. Simmons-Harris (2002) upheld vouchers that parents could spend at religious schools. [cite:us7_wiki_estab] The Court then turned from permitting such funding to requiring equal access to it: in Trinity Lutheran (2017) a state could not exclude a church school from a playground-resurfacing grant, in Espinoza (2020) a state scholarship programme could not exclude religious schools, and in Carson v. Makin, decided 6–3 on 21 June 2022, Maine could not limit its tuition payments to nonsectarian schools. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that Maine's rule "promotes stricter separation of church and state than the Federal Constitution requires". [cite:us7_wiki_carson] The line held once: on 22 May 2025 the Court split 4–4, with Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused, leaving in place an Oklahoma Supreme Court ruling that barred public money for St. Isidore, which would have been the first religious charter school; an even split sets no national precedent. [cite:us7_wiki_stisidore]

States and Congress have widened the channels. EdChoice, an organisation that promotes school choice, counts about 10,000 students in private school choice programmes in 1996, about 540,545 in 2019, more than a million in 2024 and more than 1.5 million in 75 programmes across 34 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico by December 2025; Arizona made its education savings accounts open to all students in 2022. [cite:us7_edchoice_1m] [cite:us7_edchoice_abcs2026] These counts include secular private schools, and no national series separates religious from secular recipients. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed on 4 July 2025, created the first federal programme of this kind, a tax credit for donations to scholarship organisations that takes effect on 1 January 2027; by 28 July 2026, 31 states had opted in or announced they would, and about 51.7 million of 56.4 million schoolchildren were expected to be eligible. [cite:us7_k12dive_taxcredit]

Churches also benefit from tax exemption, with a condition. Since 1954 the Johnson Amendment in section 501(c)(3) of the tax code has barred churches and other tax-exempt charities from endorsing or opposing candidates. [cite:us7_kpmg_johnson] On 7 July 2025, in a case brought by the National Religious Broadcasters in the Eastern District of Texas, the Internal Revenue Service joined the plaintiffs in asking the court to enter a consent judgment stating that a church's good-faith speech to its congregation on electoral matters during religious services is not campaign intervention. The settlement applies to the plaintiff churches and does not remove the Johnson Amendment from law; it required the judge's approval. [cite:us7_kpmg_johnson] [cite:us7_yahoo_johnson]

The two systems side by side

The religious make-up the two systems govern has changed too. The Pew Research Center's Religious Landscape Study found 78 per cent of American adults identifying as Christian in 2007, 71 per cent in 2014 and 62 per cent in 2023–24, while those with no religious affiliation rose from 16 to 23 to 29 per cent. [cite:us7_pew_rls2025] On Pew's Government Restrictions Index the United States scored 1.6 in 2007 and 2.7 in 2022, against Israel's 3.9 and 6.7. Both rose; Israel's started higher and rose further. [cite:us7_pew_gri2022]

The American gaps are of a different kind from Israel's. No American is barred from marrying by a religious court, but the line between public money and religious schooling that the Court drew in 1947 and 1971 has been redrawn, by the Court and by state legislatures, toward funding; and RFRA lets a religious objection lift a general legal duty, as it did for employers in the contraception case. [cite:us7_wiki_carson] [cite:us7_wiki_hobbylobby] The United States holds midterm elections on 3 November 2026; the federal tax credit, state voucher laws and the Johnson Amendment settlement are all in force or pending as described here, as of October 2026. [cite:us7_k12dive_taxcredit] [cite:us7_kpmg_johnson]

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: Equality Among Citizens
chapters.intro: Part Eight asks how each state treats its own citizens when they differ by origin, religion, sex, sexuality or disability. On the Israeli side it measures what the record shows for Arab citizens, Haredi Jews, Mizrahi Jews and Ethiopian Israelis: the law that frames their status, from the 1948 declaration to the 2018 Nation-State Law, the government plans meant to close the gaps, and poverty, employment, education and health over time. On the American side it follows the Black–white gaps in poverty, income, wealth and mobility from the 1960s civil-rights laws to the Supreme Court and executive decisions of 2013–2026 that narrowed them. A third section sets the two countries side by side on women's pay, LGBTQ rights and disability law. Palestinians under Israeli control who are not citizens are the subject of Part Nine.
chapters.outro: Part Eight established that both states promise equality to their citizens and fall short of it in measurable, documented ways. In Israel, Arab families' poverty fell from about 53 per cent in 2015 to 37.6 per cent in 2024 and Arab women's employment rose from a third to nearly half, after budgeted plans that were underspent and, since 2023, cut. Those gaps sit alongside a Nation-State Law that gives national self-determination to Jews alone. [cite:us8_nii_2015] [cite:us8_nii_2024] [cite:us8_globes_emp2023] [cite:us8_inss_922] [cite:us8_idi_550] [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] Official bodies have themselves documented unequal treatment of Arab and Ethiopian citizens, and the Mizrahi education gap narrowed only slowly. [cite:us8_wiki_orcomm] [cite:us8_wiki_ethiopian] [cite:us8_cle_mizrahi] In the United States, Black poverty fell from 41.8 per cent in 1966 to 17.3 per cent in 2025 but remained 2.2 times the white rate. The median white family held about nine times the wealth of the median Black family in 2025, after a 25 per cent fall in Black median wealth since 2022. Meanwhile the legal tools of the 1960s were narrowed from 2013 to 2026. [cite:us8_pf_1966] [cite:us8_jbhe_2025] [cite:us8_scf2025] [cite:us8_ncc_callais] On women's pay, LGBTQ rights and disability law, neither system leads on every measure: Israel's pay gap is wider and it performs no civil marriages, while the United States has narrowed transgender rights since 2025 and never ratified the UN disability convention. [cite:us8_jpost_shoresh] [cite:us8_cap_paygap] [cite:us8_wiki_lgbt_il] [cite:us8_wiki_lgbt_us] [cite:us8_wiki_crpd] Part Nine turns to the people under each state's control who are not its citizens, above all Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank]

sections.h: Israel: Equal Citizens on Paper, Unequal Outcomes in the Record
sections.html:
Israel's founding declaration of May 1948 promised "complete equality of social and political rights" to all inhabitants "irrespective of religion, race or sex". [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] No Basic Law since has restated that promise as a free-standing right; the nearest, the Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty of 1992, passed by 32 votes to 21, protects dignity and liberty without naming equality. [cite:us2_wiki_basiclaws] The Nation-State Law of 19 July 2018 then gave constitutional rank to a different principle: that "the right to exercise national self-determination" in the state "is unique to the Jewish people". [cite:gi5_toi_nslaw] An eleven-justice panel upheld it 10–1 on 8 July 2021, the majority holding that it did not license discrimination against non-Jewish citizens; Justice George Karra dissented. [cite:gi5_adalah_hcj] [cite:gi5_aje_hcj2021] The law and the ruling are set out in an earlier volume. [scene:gi5_nationstate|The Nation-State Law] This section measures what the record shows for four groups of citizens whose outcomes the state's own statistics track separately: Arab citizens, Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Jews, Mizrahi Jews and Ethiopian Israelis. The figures describe how laws, budgets and institutions have treated people. They say nothing about the character of any community.

Arab citizens: from military rule to five-year plans

Arab citizens are about a fifth of Israel's population. [cite:us5_cnn_killingaday] For the state's first eighteen years most of them lived under a military government, set up in October 1948 that, once the fighting ended, was "neither cancelled nor was it legally regularized". [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The Knesset voted to end it on 8 November 1966, and it was abolished on 1 December 1966. At that point it still covered about 150,000 Arab citizens, mainly along the Jordanian border and around Nazareth. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] [cite:rs_cw6_jta_jun1966] Earlier volumes trace that period and how it ended. [scene:rd6_military_government|Military government, 1948–1966] [scene:cw6_military_rule_end|The end of military rule]

The first official admission of unequal treatment came after October 2000, when police killed twelve Arab citizens and one Palestinian during demonstrations. The commission the government appointed to investigate, the Or Commission, reported on 1 September 2003. It found that Arab citizens faced discrimination and that the government had not given their needs fair and equal attention. Arab rights groups Adalah and Mossawa called this perhaps the first such official admission. [cite:us8_wiki_orcomm] The policy response came twelve years later. Government Resolution 922, adopted on 30 December 2015, was announced at NIS 15 billion over five years, NIS 5.8 billion of it for education. An evaluation for the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) found the real total, excluding education, was about NIS 10 billion. About NIS 9.6 billion was distributed and about NIS 6 billion, some 62 per cent, actually spent. [cite:us8_inss_922] Its successor, Resolution 550 of October 2021, budgeted about NIS 30 billion. After the war began in October 2023 it was cut by 15 per cent. In December 2025 the government proposed moving a further NIS 3 billion of it to the Ministry of National Security; the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) advised against the move. [cite:us8_idi_550] Part Five follows that money into policing, and the killings in Arab towns that it was meant to address. [scene:us5_arab|The killings in Israel's Arab communities]

The outcomes moved. Arab women's employment, about 26 per cent before Resolution 922, passed 40 per cent before the pandemic. Arab students rose from about a tenth of college and university students to 18 per cent of undergraduates in 2019–20. [cite:us8_inss_922] By Central Bureau of Statistics data, Arab women's employment rose from 33 per cent in 2014 to 45 per cent in mid-2023 and 46.1 per cent early in 2024. [cite:us8_globes_emp2023] [cite:us8_globes_emp2024] Poverty fell too, though it stayed far above the Jewish rate. The National Insurance Institute (NII) put the poverty rate of Arab families at 51.7 per cent in 2013 and 53.3 per cent in 2015, against 13.8 per cent for Jewish families. [cite:us8_nii_2015] For 2024 it reported 37.6 per cent, against 20.0 per cent for all families. Nearly half of Arab households (48.7 per cent) said they could not cover their monthly expenses, against 22.7 per cent of Jewish households. [cite:us8_nii_2024] The two reports come from the same annual series. This book has not established whether changes to the NII's survey method between them account for part of the fall. Health shows the same pattern. In 2022 infant mortality was 5.1 per 1,000 among Arab citizens and 2.1 among Jewish citizens, and the highest life expectancy in any Arab district (80.1) was four years below the highest Jewish one. [cite:us16_toi_moh_gaps] [scene:us16_outcomes|Health outcomes over time]

Haredi Jews: poverty tied to policy choices

Haredi families had a poverty rate of 52.4 per cent in 2014 and 48.6 per cent in 2015, by the NII's definition based on the last school a person attended, and 32.8 per cent in 2024. [cite:us8_nii_2015] [cite:us8_nii_2024] Employment among Haredi men stayed near half for a decade. It was 52 per cent in 2014 and 51 per cent in 2019, rose to a peak of 56.7 per cent at the end of 2023, and was 54.3 per cent early in 2024. Haredi women's employment was 74 per cent in 2019, against 82 per cent for other Jewish women. [cite:us8_taub_labor2019] [cite:us8_globes_emp2023] [cite:us8_globes_emp2024] The state's own arrangements shape these figures: the military exemption for yeshiva students, state funding for Torah study, and a school stream allowed to teach little of the core curriculum. Part Seven sets out that structure and its cost. [scene:us7_haredi|The Haredi exemption and its funding]

Mizrahi Jews: a gap that narrowed slowly

Israel's statistics do not track Jews of Middle Eastern and North African origin (Mizrahim) as a separate group after the second generation. The best long view therefore comes from survey research. Using the European Social Survey for Israel, the sociologists Yinon Cohen, Noah Lewin-Epstein and Amit Lazarus found that 63.9 per cent of second-generation Ashkenazim (Jews of European origin) held at least a bachelor's degree, against 30.5 per cent of second-generation Mizrahim. In the third generation the figures were 56.4 and 36.0 per cent. More than half of that narrowing came from falling attainment among Ashkenazim. [cite:us8_cle_mizrahi] The authors cite separate work showing the net income gap between Ashkenazi and Mizrahi households falling from about 40 per cent in the mid-1990s to 27 per cent in 2011. They suggest that schools in poorer and peripheral areas offered fewer advanced courses and steered more pupils into vocational tracks; their data did not allow them to test this. [cite:us8_cle_mizrahi] No official series continues the comparison to 2026.

Ethiopian Israelis: rescue, then unequal treatment

Israel brought about 6,500 Ethiopian Jews to the country in Operation Moses (November 1984 to January 1985) and 14,325 in 36 hours in Operation Solomon on 24–25 May 1991. [cite:us8_wiki_ethiopian] [cite:us8_wiki_solomon] The community numbered 168,800 in 2023. [cite:us8_mrg_ethiopian] State bodies then treated it differently in documented ways. In January 1996 the newspaper Ma'ariv revealed that the blood service, Magen David Adom, had been secretly discarding donations from Ethiopian immigrants. In January 2013 the Health Ministry's director-general ordered four organisations to stop giving Ethiopian women Depo-Provera contraceptive injections. A 2016 inquiry into the claims of 35 women found no evidence that injections had been forced. [cite:us8_wiki_ethiopian] On 30 June 2019 an off-duty policeman shot dead Solomon Tekah, an Ethiopian Israeli aged 19 (18 in some accounts), and protests followed across the country. At the time Ethiopian Israelis were about 1.7 per cent of the population but 20 per cent of young people in juvenile detention. [cite:us8_csm_tekah] [cite:us8_mrg_ethiopian]

The economic gap has narrowed. A Bank of Israel report found 54 per cent of Ethiopian-Israeli households in poverty in 2003 and 35 per cent in 2013, still nearly twice the national rate. [cite:us8_csm_tekah] In 2019 their average net household income was NIS 14,027 a month, against NIS 17,779 for all Jewish households and NIS 11,810 for Arab households. The gap in the share of pupils earning a matriculation certificate good enough for university fell from 27 percentage points in 2016 to 17 in 2022–23. [cite:us8_wiki_ethiopian]

The record shows two things together. Israel's official bodies have documented unequal treatment of Arab and Ethiopian citizens, from the Or Commission to the Health Ministry's 2013 order, and budgeted programmes to close the gaps. Those programmes moved employment and education measurably. The same record shows the money for Arab towns underspent in 2016–20 and cut after 2023, and the gaps still wide: Arab families' poverty nearly double the national family rate in 2024, Arab infant mortality more than twice the Jewish rate in 2022, and Arab homicide rates many times the Jewish rate since 2023. [cite:us8_inss_922] [cite:us8_idi_550] [cite:us8_nii_2024] [cite:us16_toi_moh_gaps] [cite:us5_taub_homicide]

sections.h: The United States: Civil-Rights Law and the Racial Gaps It Left
sections.html:
American equality law rests on a constitutional amendment and a cluster of statutes from the 1960s. The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) guarantees "the equal protection of the laws". The Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars discrimination in employment and in federally funded programmes. The Voting Rights Act followed in 1965. In September 1965 Executive Order 11246 required federal contractors not to discriminate by race, colour, religion, sex or national origin, and to "take affirmative action" in hiring. [cite:us8_wiki_eo11246] [cite:us8_wiki_sffa] [cite:us8_wiki_shelby] Unlike Israel, the United States has no law that defines the state as belonging to one group. Its gaps grew instead out of laws and practices that sorted people by race in housing, credit, schooling and voting, which the 1960s statutes outlawed. The record since then has two strands: how far the measured gaps closed, and how the legal tools built to close them have been narrowed since 2013.

Poverty and income: a long fall, then a plateau

The official poverty rate for Black Americans peaked at 41.8 per cent in 1966. It fell to 21.2 per cent in 2017, then a record low. The Census Bureau changed how it counted race after 2002, so the long series has a break. [cite:us8_pf_1966] The rate reached its lowest yet, 17.1 per cent, in 2022, rose to 18.4 per cent in 2024 and fell to 17.3 per cent in 2025. That was still 2.2 times the rate for non-Hispanic white Americans. On the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts taxes, benefits and living costs, the Black rate was 20.1 per cent in 2025 (11.3 per cent in 2021). Among children the 2025 official rates were 24.1 per cent for Black children and 8.5 per cent for non-Hispanic white children. [cite:us8_jbhe_2025] [cite:us8a_jbhe] For the whole population, official poverty was 10.2 per cent in 2025. The Hispanic rate, 13.9 per cent, and the child rate, 13.4 per cent, were the lowest on record. [cite:us8_census_2025] Median household income reached a record $87,460. The Black median rose 4.8 per cent to $59,980, about 69 per cent of the national median by this book's arithmetic. [cite:us8_census_2025] [cite:us8_be_income]

Wealth: the widest gap, and it widened again

The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), taken every three years since 1989, measures family net worth by race. Read by the Economic Policy Institute, it shows a median of $143,563 for white families and $8,552 for Black families in 1989, a ratio of about 17 to 1. By 2007 the figures were $211,726 and $25,923, about 8 to 1, and by 2019 $189,100 and $24,100, again about 8 to 1. [cite:us8_epi_wealth] The Fed's own note on the 2019 survey said the typical white family held "eight times the wealth of the typical Black family". [cite:us8_fed_2019note] The 2025 survey, published on 9 October 2026, shows the gap widening again. In 2025 dollars, median net worth for white non-Hispanic families rose 6 per cent between 2022 and 2025, to $332,100. For Black families it fell 25 per cent, to $36,800. Hispanic families' median rose 18 per cent, to $79,600. [cite:us8_scf2025] [cite:us8_fed_scf_pr] The white-to-Black ratio was therefore about 9 to 1 in 2025, by this book's arithmetic. The EPI series and the Fed's 2025 table use different price years, so ratios are compared here, not dollar amounts.

Home equity is the main store of wealth for most American families, and in 2019 the Fed found that 46 per cent of white families under 35 owned a home, against 17 per cent of young Black families. [cite:us8_fed_2019note] Israel has no survey that measures household wealth by population group in this way, so the wealth comparison runs on the American side only.

Mobility, health and policing

The economists Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, Maggie Jones and Sonya Porter found that, holding parental income constant, Black boys grew up to earn less than white boys in 99 per cent of census tracts; among women there was no such gap. Parents' marital status, education and wealth explained very little of the gap, and differences in ability did not explain it. The gaps were smallest in low-poverty neighbourhoods with less racial bias among white residents, but fewer than 5 per cent of Black children grew up in such places. [cite:us8_oi_race] [cite:us8a_oi] The same pattern runs through other systems this book measures. In 2023 the infant mortality rate was 10.93 per 1,000 for Black infants and 4.48 for white infants. [cite:us16_cdc_imr2023] By the count of Mapping Police Violence, a research project that tracks police killings, police killed Black Americans at 2.6 times the rate of white Americans in 2025. [cite:us4_mpv_2025] Black Americans' homicide victimisation rate averaged about eight times the white rate from 1976 to 2025. [cite:us5_ccj_trends] [scene:us4_policing|Part Four: policing] [scene:us16_outcomes|Part Sixteen: health outcomes]

The legal tools since 2013

Between 2013 and 2026 the Supreme Court and the executive narrowed the main legal tools of the 1960s. In Shelby County v. Holder (25 June 2013, 5–4) the Court struck down the formula that decided which states had to clear changes to voting rules with Washington in advance, ending that requirement unless Congress wrote a new formula. [cite:us8_wiki_shelby] In Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (29 June 2023, 6–2) it held race-conscious university admissions unconstitutional. [cite:us8_wiki_sffa] On 21 January 2025 President Trump's Executive Order 14173 revoked Johnson's 1965 order on federal contractors. The new order said that "Illegal DEI and DEIA policies" violate federal civil-rights law. [cite:us8_govinfo_eo14173] [cite:us8_wiki_eo11246] In Louisiana v. Callais, decided 6–3 at the end of April 2026, the Court struck down Louisiana's second majority-Black congressional district and held that the Voting Rights Act can justify drawing districts by race only in narrow cases. Justice Elena Kagan, dissenting, called it the "latest chapter in the majority's now-completed demolition of the Voting Rights Act". [cite:us8_ncc_callais] The executive order presents itself as enforcing the 1960s laws as written; the dissent in Callais read the same period as the dismantling of their remedies. The figures above are the measure either reading has to answer to. Part Three follows the voting cases into the 3 November 2026 midterms. [scene:us3_elections|Part Three: elections]

sections.h: Gender, LGBTQ and Disability Rights
sections.html:
Three further measures of equality among citizens apply to both countries in the same way: how the law and the labour market treat women, how the law treats lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, and what rights people with disabilities hold. On all three the two systems have moved in different directions at different times. Israel's courts and Knesset widened LGBTQ rights in steps while religious law still governs marriage. The United States legalised same-sex marriage nationwide in 2015 and has narrowed transgender rights since 2025. On the main gender index, Israel's score fell back after 2022 while the American score stayed above it.

Women: the index and the pay gap

The World Economic Forum's Global Gender Gap Index scores countries from 0 to 1 on economic participation, education, health and political empowerment. Israel scored 0.689 in 2006, 0.719 in 2016, 0.727 in 2022 and 0.709 in 2025, when it ranked 76th of 148 countries. The United States scored 0.704 in 2006, 0.722 in 2016, 0.769 in 2022 and 0.756 in 2025, ranking 42nd. [cite:us8_wiki_ggg] The two were close for the index's first decade. They separated after 2020, and Israel fell from 60th in 2022 to 83rd in 2023, when its political-empowerment rank dropped from 61st to 96th. [cite:us8_ynet_ggg2023] The index is a composite with its own weighting, and small changes in score move ranks a long way, so it is best read as a trend within each country, not as a verdict between them.

The pay gap is measured differently in each country, and the figures here are not strictly comparable. In Israel, the Shoresh Institution found that women's median monthly income was 76.9 per cent of men's in 2021–23. That gap was larger than in 35 of the 38 OECD countries, and larger than about fifteen years earlier. [cite:us8_jpost_shoresh] Monthly income includes the effect of shorter hours. The Taub Center, writing in March 2023, put the gap for non-Haredi Jewish women at 37 per cent in gross wages and 25 per cent per hour, and about 10 per cent once hours, industry and other factors were accounted for. Among Arab women, the gap rose from almost nothing in 2014 to 15 per cent by about 2018 as more of them entered paid work. [cite:us8a_taub_women] In the United States, women working full time all year earned 84 cents for every dollar men earned in 2025, three cents more than in 2024, by Census data. [cite:us8_cap_paygap] By the Bureau of Labor Statistics' weekly series the ratio was 82 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, down from a high of 85 per cent in 2023. [cite:us8_usafacts_paygap]

LGBTQ rights: two routes, different end points

Israel's route ran mainly through its courts and through laws on work and the army, not marriage. The Attorney General stopped enforcement of the sodomy law against consenting adults in 1953, and the Knesset repealed it in 1988. A 1992 law barred discrimination in employment by sexual orientation, and the army opened all roles to gay soldiers in 1993. In 2006 the Supreme Court ordered the population registry to record same-sex marriages performed abroad, while saying it was not creating same-sex marriage in Israel. Courts opened adoption in 2008, and surrogacy to same-sex couples from January 2022. [cite:us8_wiki_lgbt_il] Marriage inside Israel remains in the hands of religious authorities. There is no civil marriage for any couple, so same-sex couples, like mixed-faith couples, marry abroad. [cite:us8_wiki_lgbt_il] [scene:us7_israel|Part Seven: personal status law] In July 2015 an attacker stabbed six people at the Jerusalem Pride march; Shira Banki, 16, died of her wounds. [cite:us8_wiki_lgbt_il]

The American route ran through the Supreme Court, and in two directions. The Court struck down sodomy laws in Lawrence v. Texas (2003). It struck down the federal Defense of Marriage Act's definition of marriage in United States v. Windsor (2013), and required every state to license and recognise same-sex marriages in Obergefell v. Hodges (26 June 2015). In Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020) it held that federal job-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and gender identity. The military's "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" policy of 1993 ended in September 2011, and the Respect for Marriage Act of 2022 wrote same-sex marriage into federal statute. [cite:us8_wiki_lgbt_us] Since January 2025 the direction for transgender people has reversed. An executive order of 20 January 2025 defined sex as binary for federal purposes, and transgender people were barred from military service. In United States v. Skrmetti (June 2025) the Court upheld Tennessee's ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors. [cite:us8_wiki_lgbt_us]

Disability: rights laws, and the money behind them

The United States wrote disability rights into federal law first. President George H. W. Bush signed the Americans with Disabilities Act on 26 July 1990. It covers employment by firms of fifteen or more workers, state and local government services and transport, and privately run public places such as shops, hotels and restaurants. Congress widened its definition of disability in 2008. In Olmstead v. L.C. (1999) the Supreme Court held that keeping people in institutions without need is discrimination under the Act. [cite:us8_wiki_ada] Israel passed its Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities Law in 1998, a move from a welfare model to a rights model. In 2000 it created a Commission for Equal Rights of Persons with Disabilities in the Justice Ministry. [cite:us8_wiki_dis_il] Internationally the order is reversed. Israel signed the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities on 30 March 2007 and ratified it on 28 September 2012. The United States signed on 24 July 2009, but in December 2012 the Senate vote fell six short of the two-thirds needed to ratify. [cite:us8_wiki_dis_il] [cite:us8_wiki_crpd]

In Israel the conflict has been over the size of benefits. In 2017 the full disability pension was NIS 2,342 a month, when the minimum wage was NIS 5,000. [cite:us8_wiki_dis_il] A protest movement that began in March 2017, and blocked main roads repeatedly during that year, demanded benefits linked to the minimum wage. [cite:us8_toi_disability] [cite:us8a_toi_dis] On 13 February 2018 the Knesset voted 84–0 for increases of NIS 470 to NIS 770 a month from 1 March, taking the top benefit to nearly NIS 4,000, at a cost of NIS 4.3 billion over four years. Protesters said the rise was too small. The welfare minister, Haim Katz, called it "the first step to bringing it up to minimum wage". [cite:us8_toi_disability] [cite:us8a_toi_dis] American disability benefits, and how both countries' safety nets treat people who cannot work, are compared in Part Eighteen. [scene:us18_safetynet|Part Eighteen: the safety net]

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: People Under Control Without Citizenship
chapters.intro: Part Nine is about the people each state governs who cannot vote for its government. For Israel these are the Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza, who hold no Israeli status, and the Palestinians of East Jerusalem, who hold permanent residency but not citizenship. Together they number more than five million. The part sets out the two legal systems that run side by side in the West Bank, the residency regime in East Jerusalem and how residency has been revoked since 1967, and how Israel's control of Gaza changed after 2005 and again after 2023, with the status of each as of October 2026. It then asks what the American counterpart is: the residents of the five inhabited US territories, who are citizens or nationals but have no vote for president or a voting member of Congress; people held by the US military abroad, from occupied Iraq to Guantanamo; and non-citizens held in immigration detention. The comparison is unequal, and the part says so plainly: no part of the American system governs a population of comparable size, under military law, for this long. The West Bank, Documented and Gaza, Documented volumes hold the full record; this part links to them rather than repeating it.
chapters.outro: Part Nine established that roughly a third of the people living under Israeli control are not Israeli citizens: about 3.43 million Palestinians in the West Bank and 2.13 million in Gaza at the end of 2025. [cite:us9_pcbs_2025] In the West Bank they live under military orders and military courts beside about 530,000 settlers who carry Israeli law with them through emergency regulations renewed every five years, most recently to February 2028. [cite:wb_acri_twosys] [cite:us9_jp_regs2023] [cite:wb_wiki_popstats] East Jerusalem's Palestinians are permanent residents who may vote for the city council but not the Knesset; 14,808 lost that residency between 1967 and 2022, and few of those who applied for citizenship received it. [cite:us9_aje_ejvote] [cite:us9_hamoked_revoc] [cite:us9_reuters_ejcit] In Gaza, Israel's control changed form in 2005 and again after 2023, and as of October 2026 it held about 64 per cent of the strip, while the Palestinian elections set for November were postponed to September 2027. [cite:gz_hrw_anniv] [cite:us9_kt_postpone] The United States has its own people without a vote, the 3.6 million residents of its territories, and its own record of detention without trial in Iraq and at Guantanamo, but nothing of comparable size or duration under military law. [cite:us9_crs_territories] [cite:us9_ap_bucca] [cite:us4_amnesty_gtmo] Part Ten turns to how each state watches the people it governs. [scene:us10_israel|Part Ten: surveillance in Israel]

sections.h: The West Bank and East Jerusalem: Two Legal Systems, Three Statuses
sections.html:
Israel's own measures of how its system serves people cover its citizens. Most international indices do the same: Freedom House scored Israel 73 out of 100 in its 2026 report, and said the score did not reflect actions in the West Bank or Gaza, which it rated separately at 22 and 2, both "Not Free". [cite:us3_fh_il2026] This part is about the people those scores leave out. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated 3.43 million Palestinians in the West Bank and 2.13 million in Gaza at the end of 2025, about 5.56 million in all. [cite:us9_pcbs_2025] Israel's own population is about ten million, on World Bank figures for 2025. [cite:ir13_fred_ilpc] The two counts come from different statistical offices and may overlap in East Jerusalem, but on either reading roughly a third of the people in the territory Israel controls between the Jordan River and the sea are not its citizens. They fall into three statuses: Israeli citizens (including settlers), East Jerusalem residents, and West Bank and Gaza Palestinians with no Israeli status at all.

Two systems of law on one territory

Since 1967 the West Bank has been held under military rule. Palestinians there are governed by military orders issued since 1967 and by earlier Jordanian law, and are tried in military courts for offences ranging from traffic violations to theft. Israeli citizens living in the same territory are governed by Israeli law and tried in Israeli civilian courts. The Association for Civil Rights in Israel, which calls the arrangement "institutionalized discrimination", found in 2014 that an Israeli suspect had to be brought before a judge within 24 hours and a Palestinian within 96. [cite:wb_acri_twosys] An internal army document reported in 2011 showed that 99.74 per cent of military-court trials of Palestinians in 2010 ended in conviction. [cite:wb_972_conviction] Part Four and the West Bank volume set out the military courts, administrative detention and children in custody in detail. [scene:us4_detention|Part Four: detention and military courts] [scene:wb7_courts|The West Bank, Documented: the courts]

The legal device that carries Israeli law to Israeli citizens in the West Bank is a set of emergency regulations dating from after the 1967 war. They extend Israeli law to settlers personally, without annexing the land, and they are also the legal basis for holding Palestinian prisoners in jails inside Israel. They must be renewed by the Knesset every five years. [cite:us9_jta_regs2022] On 6 June 2022 the renewal failed, 58 to 52, when two left-wing members of Naftali Bennett's coalition voted against because they opposed the dual system, and Benjamin Netanyahu instructed Likud and his right-wing allies, most of whom backed the regulations, to vote against; JTA reported that his aim was to force a crisis in which he would replace Bennett. [cite:us9_jta_regs2022] [cite:us9a_jta] The next Knesset passed it on 24 January 2023, 39 to 12, for five more years, to 15 February 2028. [cite:us9_jp_regs2023] Justice Minister Yariv Levin, introducing the bill at its first reading on 10 January 2023, said, as quoted by Haaretz, "we have restored our belief that we have the right to the whole of the Land of Israel". [cite:us9_tna_regs2023]

The gap between the two systems widened after 2022. Under the coalition agreement of 1 December 2022, the Religious Zionism party received a minister in the Defence Ministry with authority over the Civil Administration, the body that rules on Palestinian building permits and movement, and in 2023 planning powers passed to that minister, Bezalel Smotrich. [cite:gi6_wiki_37gov] [cite:wb_pn_mirabilis] On 30 March 2026 the Knesset passed, 62 to 48, a law making hanging the default sentence for West Bank Palestinians convicted in military courts of nationalistic killings, while civilian courts trying Israelis may choose between death and life imprisonment. [cite:us4_ap_deathlaw] Petitions against it were pending before the High Court, and an army order applying it was signed on 17 May 2026; Part Four records its status as of October 2026. [cite:us4_wiki_deathlaw] [scene:us4_prisons|Part Four: prisons and the death penalty]

The settler population over time

The population living under the Israeli side of the dual system has grown in every decade. Peace Now's series, which excludes East Jerusalem, counts 1,500 settlers in 1972, 12,500 in 1980, 116,300 when the Oslo process began in 1993, 198,300 in 2000 and 311,100 in 2010. [cite:wb_peacenow_pop] In 2025 the figure was 529,704, with about 246,000 more in East Jerusalem. [cite:wb_wiki_popstats] Under the Oslo II agreement of 1995, Area C, where Israel keeps full civil and security control, was to shrink by stages; it still covered about 63 per cent of the West Bank in 2013, and from 2009 to 2018 only 98 of 4,422 Palestinian building-permit requests there were granted, about 2 per cent. [cite:wb_wiki_oslo2areas] [cite:wb_ocha_areac] [scene:wb5_areac|The West Bank, Documented: living in Area C]

East Jerusalem: residents, not citizens

East Jerusalem is the exception in law. Israel applied its law to the area in June 1967, and the Palestinians living there are permanent residents of Israel, not citizens. [cite:wb_wiki_ejannex] [cite:us9_wiki_jlm2024] [scene:wb3_jerusalem|The West Bank, Documented: Jerusalem] About 362,000 Palestinians lived in East Jerusalem in 2024. As residents they may vote in municipal elections but not for the Knesset. [cite:us9_aje_ejvote] Most have boycotted the municipal vote since 1967; in the February 2024 Jerusalem election no Palestinian ran for mayor, and the one list headed by an Arab candidate won 1.07 per cent and no seats. [cite:us9_aje_ejvote] [cite:us9_wiki_jlm2024] Residents are covered by Israel's National Health Insurance Law, which applies to citizens and permanent residents alike. [cite:us1_cmwf_israel]

Residency, unlike citizenship, can be revoked by the Interior Ministry. HaMoked, an Israeli rights group that calls the practice a "quiet deportation", compiled the ministry's own figures: 14,808 revocations from 1967 to 2022. The numbers were low for most of the first three decades, rose sharply after 1995, and peaked at 4,577 in 2008 alone; they then fell to double digits a year after 2016. [cite:us9_hamoked_revoc] Citizenship can be applied for, but few have received it. Reuters reported in March 2017 that about 15,000 East Jerusalem Palestinians had applied since 2003 and fewer than 6,000 had reportedly been approved; by figures first published by the Times of Israel, of more than 4,000 applications made from 2014 to September 2016, 84 had been approved, 161 rejected and the rest were pending, a slowdown the Interior Ministry attributed to its workload. Applying, Reuters wrote, still carried the stigma of implied acceptance of Israeli control. [cite:us9_reuters_ejcit] [cite:us9a_reuters] These counts cover a different period from the Reuters 2015 and Haaretz 2022 estimates given in Part Six. [scene:us6_citizenship|Part Six: citizenship]

Who votes, and for whom

The Knesset elected on 27 October 2026 will make law for the whole territory. Settlers vote in it as Israeli citizens; their Palestinian neighbours do not. An AP report from Mas'ha in 2019 described the arrangement in one place: the settlers of Elkana could vote, and the villagers of Mas'ha, on the other side of a wall and a gate, could not. [cite:us9_ap_masha] Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza vote, when votes are held, for the Palestinian Authority. The last legislative election was in 2006, the Legislative Council has not met since 2007, and President Mahmoud Abbas, whose term should have ended in 2009, rules by decree. [cite:us9_kt_postpone] Legislative elections had been set for 28 November 2026. On 10 October 2026 Abbas postponed them, together with the presidential vote, to 11 September 2027, citing "obstacles imposed by Israeli measures"; the Authority said Israel had refused its election officials access to East Jerusalem and Gaza. Israel's foreign minister, Gideon Saar, accused Abbas of "fooling the international community". [cite:us9_kt_postpone] [cite:us9_nat_elect] Both accounts are on the record: the Authority's own failure to hold elections for twenty years, and Israel's control of where Palestinian ballot boxes may go.

What the courts and Israel say

The International Court of Justice, in its advisory opinion of 19 July 2024, found Israel's continued presence in the occupied territory unlawful and found systemic discrimination in its legislation and measures there; eleven of fifteen judges agreed with all its findings. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu answered that "the Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land". [cite:wb_livelaw_icj2024] B'Tselem in 2021, Human Rights Watch in 2021 and Amnesty International in 2022 each concluded that the arrangement amounted to apartheid; Israel rejects the finding. [cite:wb_oj_apartheid] The Levy Report, commissioned by Netanyahu in 2012 but never formally adopted, argued that Israel's presence is not an occupation and that the settlements are legal. [cite:wb_wiki_levy] The West Bank volume sets these rulings and answers side by side. [scene:wb10_rulings|The West Bank, Documented: the rulings] [scene:wb7_watchers|The West Bank, Documented: the watchers]

sections.h: Gaza: Control Without Responsibility, and the Question of Who Governs
sections.html:
Gaza's two million people have never held Israeli status of any kind. What has changed over six decades is the form of Israel's control over them, and with it the argument over what Israel owes them in law. This section traces that form from direct military rule to the "Yellow Line" of October 2026, and sets out the legal positions on each side. The Gaza volume holds the full history, the war since 2023 and its toll; this section links to it rather than repeating it. [scene:gz3_withdrawal|Gaza, Documented: the withdrawal] [scene:gz7_toll|Gaza, Documented: the toll]

From military rule to "disengagement"

Israel captured Gaza from Egypt in 1967 and governed it directly, as it did the West Bank. The Oslo agreements of the 1990s created the Palestinian Authority: the Gaza–Jericho agreement of 4 May 1994 gave it civil powers in most of the strip, while Israeli troops stayed at the settlements and the Rafah crossing. [cite:gz_wiki_gazajericho] Oslo described the West Bank and Gaza as "a single territorial unit, whose integrity will be preserved". In practice movement between them narrowed in steps. Israel ended general exit permits in 1991; in 2000 it barred Gazans from studying in the West Bank and froze changes of address in the population registry. In September 2000 more than 500,000 exits through the Erez crossing were recorded in one month; by 2013 the figure was about 3,000 permits a month. Gisha, an Israeli group that tracks movement, said "It's not about security." [cite:hm_aj_separation]

In September 2005 Israel withdrew its settlers and soldiers from Gaza. It kept control of Gaza's airspace and territorial waters, of six of its seven land crossings, and of the population registry that decides who counts as a resident of Gaza; it kept the right to re-enter militarily; and the strip remained dependent on Israel for water, electricity and telecommunications. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] After Hamas won the Palestinian legislative election of January 2006 and took control of Gaza by force in June 2007, Israel imposed an indefinite blockade, citing weapons smuggling and rocket fire, and Egypt closed the Rafah crossing. [cite:hm_wiki_2006elect] [cite:gz_wiki_blockade] [scene:gz4_mechanics|Gaza, Documented: how the blockade worked] Approval of exit permits for medical treatment fell from 90 per cent in 2006 to 62 per cent in 2016. [cite:gz_un_gaza10]

The legal argument over occupation

Whether Gaza remained occupied after 2005 decides what Israel must provide there. Israel's Supreme Court, in the Al-Bassiouni case of 30 January 2008, held that "since September 2005 Israel no longer has effective control over what happens in the Gaza Strip" and therefore has no "general duty to ensure the welfare" of its residents; it found narrower obligations arising from the armed conflict, Israel's control of the crossings, and the residents' essential humanitarian needs, and upheld cuts to fuel and electricity on that basis. [cite:gz_ahmed_hcj] The United Nations, rights groups and most legal scholars took the opposite view, that Gaza remained occupied. [cite:gz_wiki_disengagement] The International Court of Justice, in July 2024, took a middle course: Israel's obligations under the law of occupation in Gaza after 2005 were "commensurate with the degree of its effective control". [cite:gz_lieber_icj] [cite:gz_oj_icj] In a further advisory opinion of 22 October 2025 the Court said that Israel, as occupying power, must "ensure the basic needs of the local population" and allow relief schemes by the United Nations, including UNRWA; the opinion is not binding, and Israel's foreign ministry said it "categorically rejects" it. [cite:gz_ji_ao2025] [scene:gz7_courts|Gaza, Documented: the courts]

The war and the people counted

The war that began with the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023 changed both the population and the territory. As of 12 October 2026 Gaza's health ministry counted 74,382 people killed since October 2023, 1,493 of them after the ceasefire of 10 October 2025; the ministry's count does not separate civilians from combatants. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] [cite:gz_yahoo_idf71k] Part Thirteen of the Greater Israel volume and the Gaza volume set out the counts and how each body arrives at them. [scene:gi14_gaza|Greater Israel: the ledger in Gaza] [scene:gz7_toll|Gaza, Documented: the toll] The Palestinian statistics bureau estimated Gaza's population at 2.13 million at the end of 2025, about 254,000 or 10.6 per cent below its pre-war estimate. [cite:us9_pcbs_2025] In 2012 the UN had projected 2.1 million by 2020. [cite:gz_un_gaza2020] UN figures for 2026 give the conditions of those who remain: 1.98 million people, 94 per cent, in need of shelter assistance, and 371,888 of 485,361 housing units destroyed or damaged. [cite:gi14_ocha_gazasnap]

Who governs Gaza, as of October 2026

A year after the ceasefire, Gaza had no government chosen by its residents and no single authority in charge. Human Rights Watch reported that reconstruction had not begun, and that the area behind the Yellow Line, which Israeli officials have called a "new border", covered about 64 per cent of the strip. [cite:gz_hrw_anniv] Al Jazeera put Israel's share at nearly two-thirds, against about half it was to keep under the ceasefire, and reported that no international stabilisation force had deployed. [cite:gz_aj_year2026] Hamas said on 6 July 2026 that it had dissolved the body that governed Gaza and was ready to hand power to a technocratic committee headed by Ali Shaath, which had stayed outside Gaza for months, reportedly because of Israeli objections. [cite:gz_aj_hamas_dissolve] Above both sits the Board of Peace, which the UN Security Council welcomed in Resolution 2803 of 17 November 2025 and which President Donald Trump announced on 15 January 2026 and chairs for life; critics say it gives Palestinians no say. [cite:gz_wiki_bop] [scene:gz11_board|Gaza, Documented: the Board of Peace] Movement out of the strip remains in Israeli hands: when the Rafah crossing reopened for people on 1 February 2026, returns were limited to those who had left during the war, "only after prior security clearance by Israel". [cite:gi15_almon_rafah]

The vote, too, stops at Israel's line. The Palestinian Authority's election commission said in October 2026 that Israel was blocking ballot boxes and voting ink from entering Gaza, and on 10 October Abbas postponed the legislative elections set for 28 November to September 2027. [cite:us9_nat_elect] [cite:us9_kt_postpone] Israeli officials say Hamas keeps violating the ceasefire, and Israel's foreign minister, Gideon Saar, accused Abbas of "fooling the international community" over the postponement. On disarmament, the accounts differ: the UN's envoy, Nickolay Mladenov, told the Security Council in August 2026 that Hamas had accepted an agreement covering every category of weapon, while a Hamas spokesman said it covered heavy weapons only, and Mladenov said Israeli strikes were delaying the process. [cite:gz_ih_mladenov] [cite:us9_kt_postpone] Whatever the cause, the record for 2026 is that the people of Gaza lived in a strip whose crossings, and about two-thirds of whose land, were under the military control of a state in which they cannot vote, beside an Authority that has not held an election in twenty years, under a board on which they have no seat.

sections.h: The American Counterpart, and Why the Comparison Is Unequal
sections.html:
The United States also governs people who cannot vote for its government. The cases are real and documented, and three stand out: the residents of the five inhabited territories, people held by the US military outside the country, and non-citizens held under immigration law. None of them matches what the two previous sections describe, and this section says where each comparison holds and where it fails.

The territories: citizens without a vote

Five inhabited territories belong to the United States without being part of it. At the 2020 census Puerto Rico had 3,285,874 residents, Guam 153,836, the US Virgin Islands 87,146, American Samoa 49,710 and the Northern Mariana Islands 47,329: together more than 3.6 million people, who are US citizens or US nationals. [cite:us9_crs_territories] [cite:us9_census_island] They cannot vote in presidential general elections, though they take part in party primaries. Each territory sends one member to the House of Representatives who may sit on committees but cannot vote on legislation, including bills the member introduced. [cite:us9_cb_territories] Congress holds broad authority over them under the Constitution, and the Supreme Court's Insular Cases, decided from 1901 after the Spanish-American War, distinguished "incorporated" territories on the way to statehood from "unincorporated" ones to which the Constitution applies only in part; all five are unincorporated. [cite:us9_crs_territories] [cite:us9_cb_territories]

The Insular Cases remain law. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote in 2022 that they "have no foundation in the Constitution" and rest on "racial stereotypes", and the Justice Department has criticised their "racist rhetoric and reasoning", but on 17 October 2022 the Supreme Court declined to reconsider them. [cite:us9_ap_samoa] [cite:us9_cb_territories] The same day it declined to hear a claim by people born in American Samoa that they are citizens by birth. They remain US nationals, not citizens: they cannot vote for president even when living in a state, and their only federal vote is for a non-voting House delegate. The appeals court left the question to Congress, and American Samoa's own government, like the Biden administration, opposed the suit, the territory's government saying citizenship by court ruling could disrupt the islands' cultural traditions. [cite:us9_ap_samoa]

This is the American case closest in kind to the Israeli one: people under the full authority of a government in which they have no vote. The differences are large. The territories' residents are, with the American Samoa exception, citizens, who gain the vote by moving to any state. They are governed by civil law and civilian courts, elect their own local governments, and are not under military rule, and American Samoa's own leaders defended the present arrangement in court. [cite:us9_ap_samoa] [cite:us9_cb_territories]

Military control abroad: Iraq and Guantanamo

The closest American parallel to military rule over a foreign population is the occupation of Iraq. On 22 May 2003 the UN Security Council, in Resolution 1483, recognised the United States and the United Kingdom as "occupying powers under unified command" and called on them to comply with the Geneva Conventions and the Hague Regulations. [cite:us9_icrc_1483] [cite:us9_wiki_1483] US forces detained Iraqis for years afterwards: detention peaked at 26,000 people in November 2007, 22,000 of them at Camp Bucca, some held for three years without charge. A security agreement that took effect in January 2009 required the United States to hand detainees to Iraqi courts or release them, and Camp Bucca closed that September. [cite:us9_ap_bucca]

Guantanamo, which Part Four sets out in detail, is the smaller and longer case. Nearly 800 men have been held there since 2002; by 1 July 2026, 15 remained, six of whom had never been charged. [cite:us4_amnesty_gtmo] [scene:us4_detention|Part Four: detention without trial] The legal principle, detention on the executive's security assessment without criminal trial, is the one critics of Israel's administrative detention object to; the scale is not comparable. In October 2026, by Israel Prison Service data compiled by HaMoked, Israel held 3,101 people classed as security inmates in administrative detention and 1,419 as "unlawful combatants". [cite:us4_hamoked_charts]

Immigration detention

Inside the United States, the largest group held without a criminal conviction is non-citizens in civil immigration detention. Immigration and Customs Enforcement held 68,289 people at the February 2026 peak, 73.6 per cent with no criminal conviction. [cite:us4_trac_ice] Their detention is civil, not criminal: they are held pending a decision on whether they may stay, not as punishment, and the group changes as cases are decided, unlike a population governed for decades. Part Six takes up the law, the asylum system and the politics. [scene:us6_asylum|Part Six: asylum and detention]

The comparison stated plainly

Both states govern people who have no vote in the government that governs them, and both have used detention without trial on security grounds. Both have courts that have accepted limits on the rights of those people: the Insular Cases in the United States, the Al-Bassiouni ruling and the dual legal system in Israel. [cite:us9_cb_territories] [cite:gz_ahmed_hcj] [cite:wb_acri_twosys] There the parallel ends. The United States governs no population of comparable size under military law today; its one recognised occupation of recent decades, in Iraq, ran under a UN resolution, and its mass detention there ended under an agreement with an Iraqi government. [cite:us9_icrc_1483] [cite:us9_ap_bucca] Israel has governed the West Bank under military law since 1967, roughly a third of the people under its rule hold no Israeli citizenship, and the people of the West Bank and Gaza have no route to it. [cite:us9_pcbs_2025] This difference governs every other comparison in this book. When Israel's figures for health, income or democracy are set beside America's, they describe Israel's citizens and residents, not the millions it controls without citizenship; the indices that rank Israel as a democracy say so in their own notes. [cite:us3_fh_il2026] [scene:us21_ledger|Part Twenty-One: the ledger]

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: Surveillance and Privacy
chapters.intro: Part Ten compares how each state watches the people under its authority and what limits its law sets. On the Israeli side it follows the Shin Bet's standing access to telephone data, the use of that access to track the population during the pandemic and the court rulings that narrowed it, the police Pegasus affair of 2022, the biometric database and the wartime powers to hack private cameras.
