On the American side it follows the line from the Church Committee and the 1978 surveillance act through the Snowden disclosures to Section 702, whose statute lapsed in June 2026 while collection continued, and then the newer questions: data the government buys rather than obtains by warrant, and tax and health records opened to immigration enforcement through software firms such as Palantir. Israel publishes no surveillance statistics comparable to America's, so the Israeli account rests on laws, rulings and official inquiries rather than a series.
chapters.outro: Part Ten established that both states write privacy into their highest law and require a judge for ordinary criminal wiretaps, and that both keep larger powers outside that rule. [cite:us10_coda_israel] [cite:us10_usc_wiretap2025] In Israel the Shin Bet may take any subscriber's communications data on the prime minister's authority alone; the government turned that access on the population in 2020 until the Supreme Court required a statute and then confined it, and an official inquiry found that the police, though they did not hack phones without warrants as first reported, collected more than their warrants allowed. [cite:us10_lawfare_isalaw] [cite:us10_adalah_hcj2020] [cite:us10_nif_hcj2021] [cite:us10_ih_marari] In the United States the targets of Section 702 rose from 89,138 in 2013 to 349,823 in 2025, its statute lapsed on 12 June 2026 with collection continuing under certifications valid to March 2027, and since 2025 immigration enforcement has drawn on tax and Medicaid records, with the courts divided. [cite:us10_db_2013targets] [cite:us10_odni_astr2026] [cite:us10_bcj_702] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:ow9_fortune_elite] Part Eleven turns from rights to money, beginning with how each economy has grown since 1980. [scene:us11_growth|Part Eleven: the economy]

sections.h: Israel: The Security Service at Home
sections.html:
Israel's law protects privacy at the highest level it has. Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty, passed in 1992, says in section 7 that "All persons have the right to privacy and to intimacy", which gives the right quasi-constitutional standing. Below it sit the Protection of Privacy Law of 1981 and the Wiretap Law of 1979, which requires a warrant from the president of a district court to tap a line, for up to three months at a time and renewable; it was extended in 1995 to mobile phones, computers and email. A 2007 criminal-procedure law lets the police obtain telephone metadata, meaning who called whom, when and from where, with a court order, and without one for up to 24 hours in some circumstances. [cite:us10_coda_israel] The civilian privacy regulator gained real teeth only recently: Amendment 13 to the 1981 law, in force from 14 August 2025, gave the Privacy Protection Authority powers to fine, to order processing stopped and to open criminal investigations, and added rules for data brokers. [cite:us10_iapp_amend13]

The Shin Bet's standing access

Beside that civilian structure stands a second one. The General Security Service Law of 2002, which governs the Shin Bet, the domestic security service, allows the prime minister in section 11 to require licensed telecommunications companies to hand the service "data, including communications data and excluding the contents of any conversation": in practice traffic, location, identification and web-use metadata. No judge approves this in advance. The Shin Bet's director authorises use of the data for up to six months, renewable without limit; the rules for its use and retention are set by the prime minister and are classified; and oversight runs after the fact, through quarterly reports to the attorney general and the prime minister and an annual report to a Knesset subcommittee [cite:us10a_lawfare]. A petition by the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) challenging section 11 was pending before the Supreme Court in March 2024, and in December 2023 the Justice Ministry published a draft bill that would add powers to acquire whole databases and to search computers remotely, while keeping authorisation within the executive. [cite:us10_lawfare_isalaw] The data system built under section 11 is known in Israel as "the Tool". According to Yedioth Ahronoth, the Shin Bet had used it for about two decades by 2021, mainly to find wanted Palestinians. [cite:us10_toi_tool] Because Israeli law sets no mandatory retention period for commercial telecoms, one legal summary describes the Tool as working in effect as a state-run retention system covering every telephone user. [cite:us10_coda_israel] [cite:us10a_coda]

The pandemic test

The Tool was turned on Israel's own population in March 2020. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government authorised the Shin Bet to track the phones of people with COVID-19, and those near them, by emergency regulation, without a Knesset vote. [cite:us10_newarab_hcj2020] Adalah petitioned on 18 March on behalf of the Joint List, joined by ACRI, the Journalists' Union and others. On 26 April 2020 the Supreme Court ruled that the Shin Bet Law did not allow the government to use the service for anything beyond national security, so that tracking citizens for public health required a statute; it was the first time the court had set a limit on the service's powers under that law. It let the tracking continue while the Knesset legislated and required separate permission before tracking journalists. [cite:us10_adalah_hcj2020] [cite:us10_newarab_hcj2020] The Knesset passed the law in July 2020. It allowed government orders of 21 days at a time, only while more than 200 new cases a day were recorded, each approved by a Knesset committee, with an appeal to the Health Ministry to be decided within 24 hours. The Privacy Protection Authority opposed it, saying the tool "egregiously violates" privacy. [cite:us10_pc_law2020]

The record on whether it worked is disputed. By the Health Ministry's figures, from July to the end of 2020 about 950,000 people were sent into quarantine on the Tool's say-so and 46,000 of them were found to be infected, against about 900,000 quarantined and 63,000 found infected through ordinary contact tracing. Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler of the Israel Democracy Institute estimated that at least 100,000 people had been quarantined wrongly, and the State Comptroller's interim report of October 2020 found ordinary tracing significantly more effective and the Shin Bet not always deleting data as the law required. [cite:us10_toi_tool] The law expired on 20 January 2021. In a ruling reported on 3 March 2021, a seven-justice panel presided over by Chief Justice Esther Hayut held that from 14 March the tracking could be used only for people who refused to cooperate with human contact tracers, and strongly recommended ending it altogether; Justice Anat Baron would have stopped it at once. [cite:us10_nif_hcj2021] In late November 2021 Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's government brought the tracking back for carriers of the Omicron variant, and four rights groups petitioned again. [cite:us10_ih_omicron]

The police and Pegasus

The second episode concerned the police, and its record shows how a strong allegation and a narrower official finding can both stand. On 18 January 2022 the business daily Calcalist reported that the police had used NSO Group's Pegasus spyware without warrants against mayors, former officials and leaders of the protests against Netanyahu. Public Security Minister Omer Barlev said there was "no practice" of police hacking devices without a judge's approval; the attorney general, the State Comptroller and the police opened inquiries. [cite:us10_jurist_calcalist] [cite:us10a_jurist] A team under Deputy Attorney General Amit Marari, including two former Shin Bet officials, reported on 21 February 2022 that it had found "no indication" that the police had infected the phone of anyone on Calcalist's published list without a court order. It also established that the police did hold a Pegasus licence, which a former police commissioner had denied, and a second, unnamed tool. Justice Minister Gideon Sa'ar called the newspaper's report "incorrect" and said no state commission of inquiry was needed; Calcalist said it would re-examine its findings. [cite:us10_toi_saar] [cite:us10a_toi_saar] The team's further findings, published in August 2022, again found no use without a judicial order, but found that when the technology was used the police collected information beyond what the warrants covered, which the team called a "violation of authority". ACRI said the findings showed "major failures" and asked for police use of such tools to be barred until specific legislation existed. [cite:us10_ih_marari] The firm and its exports are covered in The One-Way Mirror. [scene:ow10_nso|NSO and Pegasus]

Biometrics and the wartime powers

Two other laws widened what the state holds. The biometric database law of 2009 began as a voluntary pilot; in 2017 the Knesset made it permanent, with a facial image compulsory for every identity card and passport and fingerprints stored unless the applicant opts out, at the price of a document valid for five years rather than ten. The police were barred from the database until the Knesset issues regulations. [cite:us10_lawcoil_biometric] After 7 October 2023, emergency regulations of 14 and 17 October let the army and the Shin Bet hack the computers that run privately owned stationary cameras, without the owner's knowledge and without a court order, reporting monthly and confidentially to a Knesset committee and the attorney general, with no role for the courts or the Privacy Protection Authority. [cite:us10_ctech_cameras] The Knesset kept extending the power; on 25 June 2025 it voted 13–4 to extend it to 31 December 2025. [cite:us10_toi_cameras2025] In July 2026 the government also gave the Shin Bet a role against illegal weapons in Arab communities; Netanyahu said the state would not accept "violence, extortion and murder on the streets", while ACRI said the move exceeded the service's authority and noted that organised crime among Jewish citizens is handled by the police with ordinary tools. [cite:us5_toi_shinbet] [cite:us10a_toi_shinbet] [scene:us5_arab|Part Five: the Arab-community killings]

All of this concerns Israel's own citizens and residents. Palestinians in the West Bank live under a different regime: the army has run the Red Wolf facial-recognition system at Hebron checkpoints since 2022 on databases made up only of Palestinians' data, and Unit 8200 stored intercepted Palestinian calls on Microsoft's cloud until Microsoft cut off part of that service in September 2025. [cite:wb_toi_redwolf] [cite:ow4_tc_msft] [scene:wb7_watchers|The watchers] No series measures Israeli domestic surveillance over time the way the American transparency reports do; what exists is a record of laws, court rulings and official inquiries, and this section is built from those.

sections.h: The United States: Warrants, Loopholes and Immigration Data
sections.html:
The American framework was built after a scandal. In January 1975 the Senate voted 82–4 to create a select committee under Senator Frank Church to study the intelligence agencies. It documented the FBI's COINTELPRO programme against civil-rights and anti-war groups, including Martin Luther King Jr., and two NSA programmes, SHAMROCK and MINARET, that monitored communications into and out of the country. Its final report of 29 April 1976 found that "Intelligence agencies have undermined the constitutional rights of citizens." Congress responded with a permanent Senate Intelligence Committee in 1976 and the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of 1978, signed by President Jimmy Carter, which created a special court to approve national-security wiretaps. [cite:us10_senate_church] The ordinary criminal wiretap still needs a judge's order under the Fourth Amendment, and the courts publish a count every year. In 2025 federal and state judges authorised 1,735 wiretaps, 873 federal and 862 state, 24 per cent fewer than in 2024 and 58 per cent fewer than the 4,148 of 2015; narcotics cases accounted for 51 per cent of applications. [cite:us10_usc_wiretap2025]

From bulk collection to Section 702

After 2001 the national-security side grew past the criminal side. In June 2013 documents leaked by Edward Snowden showed that a FISA Court order required Verizon to hand over the call records of its customers in bulk. On 7 May 2015 the Second Circuit Court of Appeals held in ACLU v. Clapper that the programme "exceeds the scope of what Congress has authorized" under section 215 of the Patriot Act, and on 2 June 2015 Congress passed the USA FREEDOM Act, which restricted that kind of collection. [cite:us10_wiki_clapper] The same archive showed that since a 2009 agreement the NSA had sent Israel's Unit 8200 raw intercepts that could include Americans' communications; the NSA said such information was handled under procedures designed to protect privacy rights and that it could not use these relationships to circumvent US law. [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] [scene:ow4_memorandum|The NSA–8200 memorandum]

The larger authority is Section 702 of FISA. It lets agencies collect, without an individual warrant, the communications of foreigners reasonably believed to be abroad, from American providers; Americans' messages are collected when they are in contact with those targets, and the FBI may then search the stored data by an American's name or number, the so-called backdoor search. The number of targets has risen every year the government has reported it: 89,138 in 2013, more than 200,000 in 2021, 268,590 in 2023 and 349,823 in 2025, by the reports of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI). A target can be a group or a facility as well as a person. [cite:us10_db_2013targets] [cite:us10_jurist_fbi2021] [cite:us10_odni_astr2026] The FBI's searches for Americans moved the other way: nearly 3.4 million in 2021 (counting each query, some with thousands of terms), 57,094 in the year to November 2023, 5,518 in the year to November 2024 and 7,413 in the year to November 2025. [cite:us10_jurist_fbi2021] [cite:us10_odni_astr2026]

The 2026 lapse

Section 702 was due to expire on 20 April 2026. [cite:us10a_wamc] The dispute was the one that had run since 2013: lawmakers of both parties wanted a court's approval before agents could read Americans' data in the 702 databases, and the intelligence agencies said that would weaken the tool. The House failed to pass either a five-year renewal or the 18-month renewal President Donald Trump had asked for, and Congress passed a ten-day extension. [cite:us10_npr_702april] On 30 April the House voted 261–111 for a six-week extension to 12 June. [cite:us10_bgov_702] At midnight on 12 June the statute lapsed. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, which opposed renewal, tied the lapse to President Trump's naming of Bill Pulte, the federal housing-finance director, to replace Tulsi Gabbard as Director of National Intelligence after she announced her resignation: Senate Democrats, it reported, then refused to move their reauthorisation bill and the House refused a further short-term extension. [cite:us10_eff_702lapse] [cite:us10a_eff] Collection did not stop. The FISA Court had approved the year's certifications on 17 March 2026, and by the Brennan Center's reading of the statute they remain valid until 17 March 2027; as of 22 September 2026 the providers were still cooperating, and the government was reported to be pressing for renewal by November. [cite:us10_bcj_702] As of October 2026 no renewal had been enacted that this book could find; the question will fall to the Congress chosen on 3 November.

Buying what a warrant would require

The Supreme Court has narrowed the old rule that information handed to a company carries no privacy protection: Carpenter v. United States (2018) required a warrant for historical cell-site records, and Chatrie v. United States, decided 6–3 on 29 June 2026, held that obtaining two hours of Google location records is a search. Neither ruling addresses data the government buys. [cite:ow9_cornell_tpd] [cite:ow9_pw_chatrie] Agencies do buy it. The NSA's director confirmed in a letter published in January 2024 that it purchases commercially available internet netflow data that includes domestic communications, and Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have bought phone-location data from brokers. [cite:ow9_tc_nsanetflow] [cite:ow9_aclu_adid] The House passed the Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act, 219–199, on 17 April 2024, over the White House's opposition; it did not become law. [cite:ow9_cs_4thact]

Immigration enforcement and government data

Since 2025 the sharpest change has been the use of other agencies' records for immigration enforcement. In April 2025 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem signed an agreement for the Internal Revenue Service to check names for ICE. ICE asked about some 1.28 million people, and the IRS verified about 47,000. The administration said the agreement helped carry out the president's agenda to secure the borders. [cite:us10_abc_irs_feb] [cite:us10a_abc] Two lawsuits produced different results. In one, a District of Columbia Circuit panel declined on 24 February 2026 to block the sharing, finding the plaintiffs unlikely to win; Attorney General Pam Bondi called it a "crucial victory". In the other, Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly had stayed the agreement in November 2025 and in February 2026 found that the IRS broke the law "approximately 42,695 times" by disclosing confidential addresses; a unanimous panel of the same appeals court upheld her block on 8 September 2026. [cite:us10_abc_irs_feb] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] Medicaid data followed: 404 Media reported in January 2026 that an ICE tool called ELITE draws on Medicaid records under an agreement covering nearly 80 million patients. [cite:ow9_fortune_elite]

Much of this runs on private software, some of it Israeli. ICE paid Palantir $29.9 million in April 2025 for ImmigrationOS, a system to prioritise targets and track departures, on the ground that Palantir was "the only source", and in February 2026 the Department of Homeland Security signed a purchase agreement with Palantir worth up to $1 billion over five years. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:ow9_sa_dhsbpa] [scene:ow9_ice|Palantir and ICE] ICE's $2 million contract for Graphite, the spyware of the Israeli-founded firm Paragon, was paused under President Biden's 2023 order on commercial spyware and reactivated in 2025; in April 2026 the acting ICE director said it was used against drug-trafficking groups and certified no significant counterintelligence risk. [cite:ow10_poulson_ice] [cite:ow10_reg_paragon] [cite:ow10_tc_lyons] [scene:ow10_paragon|Paragon and ICE] The FBI had bought and tested Pegasus before deciding in July 2021 not to deploy it. [cite:ow10_globe_fbi]

Oversight

The independent watchdog for counterterrorism surveillance, the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board, was left without a quorum in 2025 after President Trump removed its Democratic members Travis LeBlanc and Edward Felten. Judge Reggie Walton ruled on 21 May 2025 that the removals were unlawful; the White House said it expected "ultimate victory". [cite:us10_rec_pclob] This book could not confirm the board's status as of October 2026.

The two systems fail in different places. Israel's courts have set limits case by case, but its security service holds standing access to every subscriber's metadata on the executive's authority alone, and the state publishes no counts. The United States publishes counts and requires a judge for criminal wiretaps, but its largest programme searches Americans' messages without a warrant, its agencies buy data a warrant would otherwise be needed for, and since 2025 records given to the tax and health systems have been opened to immigration enforcement, with the courts divided on whether that is lawful. [cite:us10_lawfare_isalaw] [cite:us10_odni_astr2026] [cite:ow9_aclu_adid] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep]

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: The Economy
chapters.intro: Part Eleven sets the two economies side by side from 1980 to 2026. It measures output per person in constant dollars and at purchasing-power parity, and growth decade by decade, and shows why total growth and growth per person tell different stories for a country whose population has more than doubled. It then sets Israel's 1985 stabilisation plan, which ended an inflation of several hundred per cent, beside the American turn of 1979 to 1986 under Paul Volcker's Federal Reserve and the tax laws of 1981 and 1986, and follows both central banks to their decisions of September 2026. It compares how much each state taxes, whom it taxes, and what each owes, and closes with concentration: Israel's business groups and the 2013 law that broke up their pyramids, set against the debate over corporate power in the United States, and the trade that runs between the two countries.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven established that, measured in constant dollars, Israel's output per person rose from 59.8 per cent of the American level in 1980 to 66.1 per cent in 2022 and fell back to 62.7 per cent in 2025 after two years of war, while its total output grew about six-fold against America's 3.3-fold because its population grew more than twice as fast. [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_const] [cite:us11_wb_pop] Israel's turn came on 1 July 1985, when a plan of budget cuts, devaluation, a wage pact with the Histadrut, a price freeze, a ban on printing money for the deficit and a $1.5 billion American grant ended inflation that had averaged 373 per cent in 1984; America's came through Volcker's Federal Reserve from October 1979 and the cut in the top tax rate from 70 to 28 per cent by 1988. [cite:us11_wb_cpi] [cite:us11_brookings_peres] [cite:us11_frh_volcker] [cite:us11_tpc_toprate] Israel taxes a larger share of its economy, leaning more on VAT and with about half of potential income-tax payers below the threshold, while in the United States the top 1 per cent's share of federal taxes and of income both doubled from 1979 to 2022. [cite:us11_oecd_rev_il] [cite:us11_globes_taxburden] [cite:us11_cbo_dist2022] Their debts moved in opposite directions: Israel's from about 163 per cent of GDP in the mid-1980s to 61.9 per cent in 2023 before the war pushed it to 68.5 per cent, America's from 26 per cent in 1980 to 99 per cent in 2025. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] [cite:us11_imf_debt] [cite:gi16_boi_2025] [cite:us11_omb_debt] [cite:us11_cbo_outlook2026] In September 2026 the Bank of Israel cut its rate to 3.25 per cent and the Federal Reserve raised its range to 3.75–4 per cent. [cite:us11_globes_boi_sep2026] [cite:us11_fed_sep2026] Israel broke up its business pyramids by statute in 2013, while the United States argues over how much its industries have concentrated and acts case by case, and trade under their 1985 agreement was $54.2 billion in 2025 despite the tariffs of that year. [cite:us11_toi_concentration] [cite:us11_gl_concentration] [cite:us11_itif_kennedy] [cite:us11_ustr_israel] Part Twelve turns to the industries behind these numbers, beginning with technology and venture capital. [scene:us12_tech|Part Twelve: tech and venture capital]

sections.h: Growth: Two Economies, 1980–2026
sections.html:
The comparison of the two economies starts with a measurement choice. Figures quoted in arguments about Israel and the United States often set a 2026 projection for one country against a past year for the other, or mix exchange-rate dollars with prices adjusted for what money buys. This section uses one source for both countries throughout: the World Bank's World Development Indicators, updated on 8 October 2026, which give gross domestic product per person in constant 2015 dollars (for real growth over time) and in purchasing-power-parity dollars (for living-standard levels across countries). The most recent full year is 2025. [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_const] [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_ppp]

Output per person over time

In constant 2015 dollars, Israel's GDP per person was $18,597 in 1980 and $42,596 in 2025; the American figure was $31,082 and $67,946. Over the forty-five years Israel's output per person grew by an average of 1.86 per cent a year and America's by 1.75 per cent. Israel's level as a share of America's, by this book's arithmetic from the same series, was 59.8 per cent in 1980, 57.1 per cent in 1990, 60.5 per cent in 2000, 63.1 per cent in 2010 and 64.4 per cent in 2019. It reached 66.1 per cent in 2022 and then fell back to 62.7 per cent in 2025. [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_const] Measured at market exchange rates in current dollars the gap narrowed further, from 37 per cent of the American level in 1985 to 67 per cent in 2025; the difference from the constant-dollar series reflects prices and exchange rates rather than output. [cite:us1_fred_uspc] [cite:ir13_fred_ilpc]

The decades differ. In the 1980s, which for Israel included the inflation crisis described in the next section, its output per person grew 1.88 per cent a year against America's 2.35 per cent. In the 1990s Israel grew faster (2.76 against 2.18), and again in the 2000s (1.25 against 0.83), a decade that held Israel's downturn of 2001–03, when unemployment reached about 10 per cent, and America's financial crisis of 2008–09. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] From 2010 to 2019 Israel still led (1.86 against 1.62). From 2019 to 2025, a span that holds the pandemic and, for Israel, the wars that began on 7 October 2023, the order reversed: 1.34 per cent a year in Israel and 1.80 in the United States. [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_const] Israel's GDP per person fell in both 2023 and 2024 and in 2025 stood 0.1 per cent above its 2022 level; American output per person rose in each of those years. [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_const] The Bank of Israel puts the gross budgetary cost of the war at about NIS 352 billion for 2023–2026, and defence spending at 8.4 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 7.8 per cent in 2025, against 4.2 per cent in 2022. [cite:gi16_boi_2025]

The level in purchasing power

Constant-dollar figures measure growth; they do not say how much a person's income buys in each country. For that the World Bank publishes GDP per person at purchasing-power parity, which adjusts for price levels. On that measure Israel stood at $15,712 against America's $23,889 in 1990 (65.8 per cent), $25,747 against $36,330 in 2000 (70.9 per cent), $29,418 against $48,643 in 2010 (60.5 per cent), and $59,717 against $90,027 in 2025 (66.3 per cent). [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_ppp] These are current international dollars, so the levels rise with prices; only the ratio is comparable across years. The PPP gap is about the same as the constant-dollar gap, at roughly two-thirds. One reason Israel's purchasing-power figure does not rise further is that its price level is high: the OECD ranked Israel fourth-highest among its members in comparable price levels in 2025, a finding Part Fourteen takes up. [cite:us14_oecd_survey2025] [scene:us14_basket|Part Fourteen: the basket]

Total growth and growth per person

Total output tells a different story because the populations grew at different speeds. Israel's population was 3.88 million in 1980, 6.29 million in 2000 and 10.12 million in 2025; America's was 227.2 million, 282.2 million and 341.8 million. [cite:us11_wb_pop] That is average growth of about 2.2 per cent a year for Israel and 0.9 per cent for the United States. Combining the two series, Israel's real GDP grew about six-fold over the period and America's about 3.3-fold, by this book's arithmetic. [cite:us11_wb_pop] [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_const] A claim that Israel's economy grew far faster than America's is therefore true of the total and not of output per person, where the two countries' long-run rates are close. Immigration law and family policy, the two drivers of that difference, are compared in Parts Six and Eighteen. [scene:us6_citizenship|Part Six: citizenship] [scene:us18_family|Part Eighteen: family policy]

Openness

The two economies also differ in how much they trade. Israel's exports and imports together equalled 80.0 per cent of its GDP in 1980, 60.9 per cent in 1990, 68.4 per cent in 2000 and 65.7 per cent in 2010, then fell to 51.1 per cent in 2020 and 53.0 per cent in 2025. The American figure was 20.1 per cent in 1980, 16.6 per cent in 1985, 25.1 per cent in 2000, 28.2 per cent in 2010 and 25.0 per cent in 2024. [cite:us11_wb_trade] A small economy trades more of what it makes, so the levels are not a verdict on either policy; the trends are the point. Israel's economy has become less dependent on trade as a share of output since 2000, while America's share has been roughly flat since then. The last section of this part sets out the trade between the two countries and the tariffs of 2025–26. [scene:us11_concentration|Concentration and trade]

What the averages do not show

GDP per person is an average. It does not say who receives the income, and on that the record for the United States is clear: the Congressional Budget Office finds that the top 1 per cent's share of household income before taxes and transfers doubled from 9 per cent in 1979 to 18 per cent in 2022, and after taxes and transfers rose from 7 to 14 per cent. [cite:us11_cbo_dist2022] Wages, the cost of living and poverty, the measures closer to what households experience, are compared in Parts Thirteen, Fourteen and Eighteen, with Israel's own distributional figures. [scene:us13_wages|Part Thirteen: wages] [scene:us14_wages|Part Fourteen: wages and prices] [scene:us18_poverty|Part Eighteen: poverty] Two further limits apply. Israel's figures do not include the Palestinian economies of the West Bank and Gaza, which Part Nine treats. [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank] And American aid, by Part One's arithmetic 12.7 per cent of Israel's GDP in 1985 and 0.6 per cent in 2025, weighed far more on Israel's economy at the start of this period than at the end. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] [scene:us1_aid|Part One: the aid]

sections.h: The Turn: Israel 1985, America 1979–86
sections.html:
Both economies changed direction in the first half of the 1980s, and both turns began with inflation. The American turn is often dated from the Federal Reserve's change of course in October 1979 through the tax laws of 1981 and 1986; the Israeli one from the Economic Stabilization Plan of July 1985. They were different in scale and in method. America brought inflation down from about 13.5 per cent a year; Israel brought it down from several hundred per cent. Setting them side by side shows what each state did with its central bank, its budget and its labour bargain, and how the institutions created or reshaped then still work in 2026.

Israel before the plan

By the World Bank's annual-average series, Israel's consumer prices rose 131 per cent in 1980, 120 per cent in 1982, 146 per cent in 1983 and 373 per cent in 1984. [cite:us11_wb_cpi] Measured from December to December, the Bank of Israel records a peak of 445 per cent in 1984, when prices rose about five and a half times in a year. [cite:us14_boi_hyper] The two figures measure different things and are both correct; this book gives the annual average when comparing with the United States. Brookings economist Dany Bahar describes annualised inflation of about 1,000 per cent in the second half of 1984 and a budget deficit of about 17 per cent of GDP, while capital flight drained the foreign reserves Israel needed to service its external debt. [cite:us11_brookings_peres] A crisis in the banking system in October 1983 had already brought the economy close to financial collapse. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] By the economists Rafi Melnick and Yosef Mealem's figures, public debt stood at about 163 per cent of GDP in the mid-1980s, public spending at about 60 per cent of GDP and defence spending at more than 20 per cent. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick]

The plan of 1 July 1985

The July 1984 election produced a national unity government of Labour and Likud under a rotation agreement that made Shimon Peres prime minister for its first two years. [cite:us11_brookings_peres] The plan, designed by a team of economists led by Michael Bruno (Wikipedia also credits Finance Minister Yitzhak Moda'i among its authors), took effect on 1 July 1985 after a night-long cabinet meeting. [cite:us11_wiki_esp] [cite:us11_brookings_peres] It had five parts. The budget deficit was cut by about 7.5 per cent of GDP, mainly by cutting food subsidies, with tax increases beside the spending cuts. The shekel was devalued by 20 per cent and then held at a fixed rate. Wages, prices and the exchange rate were frozen, with pre-set adjustments. Peres negotiated the wage freeze with the Histadrut, the labour federation, in a package with employers. And the Bank of Israel was barred from printing money to finance the government's deficit, the measure Melnick and Mealem call the "Non-Printing" law. [cite:us11_brookings_peres] [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] [cite:us11_wiki_esp] Interest rates were raised sharply. [cite:us11_brookings_peres]

The United States took part. An American advisory group of economists included Stanley Fischer, later governor of the Bank of Israel, and Washington provided an emergency grant of $1.5 billion over two years, about 3.5 per cent of Israel's GDP a year, tied to the reforms. [cite:us11_brookings_peres] [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] Part One sets that grant in the longer record of American aid. [scene:us1_aid|Part One: the aid] The results were quick. Monthly inflation fell from 11 per cent in the third quarter of 1985 to about 1 per cent a year later, and unemployment rose by only about two percentage points. [cite:us11_brookings_peres] Annual inflation fell to 47.6 per cent in 1986 and 19.1 per cent in 1987, stayed between about 10 and 20 per cent until the mid-1990s, and reached 1.0 per cent in 2000. [cite:us11_wb_cpi] The public sector, in deficit by about 14 per cent of GDP in 1984, ran surpluses in the following three years. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] Melnick and Mealem's verdict is that the plan "succeeded in achieving its two objectives". [cite:us11_jvl_melnick]

The plan was a fiscal and monetary rescue, but it also began a change in how Israel's economy was organised. The later reforms included "the privatization of many government-owned businesses", and public spending fell from about 60 per cent of GDP in the mid-1980s to about 43 per cent by the end of 2008. [cite:us11_wiki_esp] [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] The Histadrut, which had signed the 1985 wage pact as a central party, lost influence over the labour market from the early 1990s, in Melnick and Mealem's account. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] Part Thirteen follows the union side of that change and the American one. [scene:us13_unions|Part Thirteen: unions]

America, 1979–86

The American turn ran through the central bank first. On 6 October 1979 the Federal Reserve chair, Paul Volcker, announced after an unscheduled meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee that the Fed would target the volume of bank reserves rather than the daily interest rate, accepting that rates would "fluctuate over a wider range". The federal funds rate reached a record 20 per cent in late 1980; the economy went into a severe recession; unemployment peaked at 10.8 per cent in late 1982; and inflation fell to 3.7 per cent in 1983, by the Federal Reserve's own history. [cite:us11_frh_volcker] The World Bank's annual series shows consumer-price inflation of 13.5 per cent in 1980, 6.1 per cent in 1982 and 1.9 per cent in 1986. [cite:us11_wb_cpi]

Tax law changed next. The top federal income tax rate was 70 per cent in 1980. It fell to 50 per cent in 1982 after the 1981 tax act, to 38.5 per cent in 1987 and to 28 per cent in 1988 after the Tax Reform Act of 1986. It has since moved between 31 and 39.6 per cent and has been 37 per cent since 2018. [cite:us11_tpc_toprate] The Congressional Budget Office's long series shows the result for who pays: from 1979 to 2022 the average federal tax rate fell for every income group, and the share of income going to the top 1 per cent doubled. [cite:us11_cbo_dist2022] The next section takes up taxes and debt in both countries. [scene:us11_fiscal|Taxes, debt and the budget]

The two central banks now

The two central banks' legal mandates differ. The Federal Reserve works under a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices, with a 2 per cent inflation goal; its September 2026 statement referred to both. [cite:us11_fed_sep2026] The Bank of Israel Law of 2010 makes price stability the "primary goal". Supporting economic activity and financial stability are secondary aims, to be pursued only if the bank's Monetary Committee judges that price stability will not be harmed. The inflation target of 1 to 3 per cent was set by the government in 2000 and has applied since 2003; a review in November 2024 kept it. [cite:us11_boi_target] Israel's 2010 law also moved rate decisions from the governor alone to a committee. [cite:us11_boi_target]

In September 2026 the two banks moved in opposite directions. On 1 September the Bank of Israel cut its rate by a quarter point to 3.25 per cent, its fifth cut since November 2025, saying inflation had moderated. [cite:us11_globes_boi_sep2026] On 16 September the Federal Open Market Committee raised the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75–4 per cent, by 12 votes to none, stating that "Inflation remains elevated." [cite:us11_fed_sep2026] These are the latest decisions this book found as of October 2026.

The stabilisation plan holds lessons that each side of the American debate has claimed. It combined orthodox measures, deep spending cuts and tight money, with heterodox ones, a negotiated wage and price freeze in which the labour federation was a signatory, and Fischer himself credited the mix. [cite:us11_brookings_peres] The American turn relied on the central bank to break inflation, at the cost of what the Fed's own history calls a severe recession, and was followed by large cuts in the top income tax rate. [cite:us11_frh_volcker] [cite:us11_tpc_toprate] Which approach a reader prefers is a judgment. The record is that both ended high inflation; that Israel, starting from a far worse position, did so with unemployment rising by about two percentage points; and that American unemployment peaked at 10.8 per cent. [cite:us11_brookings_peres] [cite:us11_frh_volcker]

sections.h: Taxes, Debt and the Budget
sections.html:
How much a state takes in taxes, from whom, and how much it borrows are choices written into law, and the two countries have made different ones. This section compares total tax revenue as a share of the economy, the mix of taxes, who carries the burden, and the debt each government owes, over the longest periods the sources allow. The OECD totals used here count taxes at every level of government in both countries, which matters for the United States, where income, sales and property taxes are levied by states and localities as well as by Washington. The totals are therefore comparable; figures for the federal level alone, such as the Congressional Budget Office's, are not.

How much each state taxes

By the OECD's Revenue Statistics, all taxes in Israel, including social security contributions, came to 34.0 per cent of GDP in 2000, the highest level in the series since then, and 29.1 per cent in 2009, the lowest. They were 32.8 per cent in 2022 and 29.8 per cent in 2023, against an OECD average of 33.9 per cent. [cite:us11_oecd_rev_il] Israel's Finance Ministry chief economist reported in 2022 that the tax burden had fallen by 12 percentage points of GDP from its 1986 peak, the year after the stabilisation plan described in the previous section. [cite:us11_globes_taxburden] [scene:us11_turn|The turn] The American total, on the same OECD definition, was 23.6 per cent of GDP in 1965 and 27.7 per cent in 2022, the latest year in the published series, and has moved within a band of about 23 to 28 per cent throughout. [cite:us11_dbn_rev_us] Israel has therefore taxed a larger share of its economy than the United States, but by a narrowing margin: about 5 percentage points of GDP in 2022, against a 1986 Israeli peak of about 42 per cent implied by the ministry's figures, well above any American level in the series (this book's arithmetic). [cite:us11_globes_taxburden] [cite:us11_dbn_rev_us]

Which taxes

The mix differs more than the total. In 2022 Israel raised 23 per cent of its tax revenue from VAT and other taxes on goods and services, against an OECD average of 21 per cent, and 12 per cent from property taxes, against 5 per cent. Social security contributions brought in 15 per cent, against 25 per cent across the OECD, and personal income tax 22 per cent, against 24 per cent. [cite:us11_oecd_rev_il] Israel's standard VAT rate rose from 17 to 18 per cent on 1 January 2025, a measure presented as part of the effort to curb the wartime deficit; one estimate put the cost to a family at NIS 1,000–2,000 a year. [cite:us11_herzog_vat] [cite:us11_jns_vat] The United States has no national VAT; its consumption taxes are state and local sales taxes. Israel's top income tax rate in 2026 was 47 per cent above ILS 560,280 a year, with a 3 per cent surtax above ILS 721,560 bringing the maximum to 50 per cent, and from 2025 a further 2 per cent surtax on capital income above that threshold. [cite:us11_pwc_il_pit] The top American federal rate is 37 per cent, before state income taxes. [cite:us11_tpc_toprate]

Who pays

A heavy reliance on VAT matters for who pays, because a consumption tax takes a larger share of income from households that spend most of what they earn. Israel's income tax is narrow at the bottom: in 2021 about half of the people with income liable in principle to income tax earned below the threshold and paid none. In the Finance Ministry's figures the direct tax rate on gross income was about 40 per cent for the top tenth of earners, 30 per cent for the next-highest tenth and 10 per cent for the bottom tenth. [cite:us11_globes_taxburden] The United States runs part of its support for low earners through the income tax itself: the Congressional Budget Office finds that the average federal income tax rate in 2022 ran from about minus 10 per cent for the lowest fifth of households, meaning that credits paid out exceeded tax owed, to 17 per cent for the highest. Across all federal taxes the average rate for all households was 20.6 per cent, close to its 1979–2022 average of 20.9 per cent. The top fifth paid 70 per cent of federal taxes in 2022, against 55 per cent in 1979, and the top 1 per cent paid 27 per cent, against 14 per cent. That rise in the top's share of taxes came alongside a rise in its share of income: the top 1 per cent's share of pre-tax income doubled from 9 to 18 per cent over the same years. [cite:us11_cbo_dist2022] The CBO figures cover federal taxes only; state and local taxes are not included.

Debt over time

The two governments' debts have moved in opposite directions over forty years. Israel's public debt stood at about 163 per cent of GDP in the mid-1980s. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] The World Bank series for central government debt shows 132 per cent in 1990 and 88 per cent in 1999. [cite:us11_wb_cgdebt] On the IMF's measure of general government gross debt, Israel owed 77.5 per cent of GDP in 2000, 69.4 per cent in 2010, 63.2 per cent in 2015 and 61.9 per cent in 2023. [cite:us11_imf_debt] The war then reversed the trend. The Bank of Israel records gross public debt rising from 61.3 per cent of GDP in 2023 to 67.6 per cent in 2024 and 68.5 per cent in 2025, with deficits of 6.7 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 4.7 per cent in 2025. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] The IMF projected 68.8 per cent for 2026 and 71.9 per cent for 2030. [cite:us11_imf_debt]

American federal debt held by the public, the measure the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) uses, was 26.1 per cent of GDP in 1980, 42.0 per cent in 1990 and 49.2 per cent in 1995, fell to 33.0 per cent in 2001, and was 36.8 per cent in 2007. [cite:us11_omb_debt] It then rose to 99 per cent of GDP at the end of 2025; the World Bank's broader central-government series shows the steepest jumps in 2008–09 and in 2020, from 100 to 124.5 per cent of GDP in a single year. [cite:us11_wb_cgdebt] [cite:us11_cbo_outlook2026] CBO projected in February 2026 a deficit of $1.9 trillion, 5.8 per cent of GDP, for fiscal 2026, debt passing the 1946 record of 106 per cent of GDP in 2030 and reaching 120 per cent in 2036, and net interest costs of $1.0 trillion in 2026, 3.3 per cent of GDP. [cite:us11_cbo_outlook2026] The two countries' figures here use different definitions (general government gross debt for Israel, federal debt held by the public for the United States) and are shown for their trends, not to rank the levels.

What the budget pays for

The largest single change in Israel's budget over the period is defence. Melnick and Mealem put defence spending at more than 20 per cent of GDP in the mid-1980s and under 10 per cent by the time they wrote in 2009; the Bank of Israel records 4.2 per cent in 2022, before rising to 8.4 per cent in 2024 and 7.8 per cent in 2025. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] [cite:gi16_boi_2025] The fall in defence spending from the 1980s to 2022 coincided with Israel's falling tax burden and debt; the wars since 2023 have reversed part of it. The cost of the wars to each treasury is set out in detail elsewhere in the library, and defence budgets over time in Part Nineteen of this volume. [scene:gi16_costs|The bill: costs] [scene:us19_spending|Part Nineteen: defence spending] The American aid of $3.8 billion a year under the 2016 memorandum ($3.3 billion in military financing and $500 million for missile defence) is about half a per cent of Israel's GDP and, by CRS and INSS estimates, about 14–15 per cent of its defence budget; with offshore procurement ending in fiscal 2028, it goes almost entirely to procurement in the United States. [cite:gi16_inss_aid] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [scene:gi16_aid|The aid] For the United States the rising item is interest: CBO projects net interest of $1.0 trillion in 2026, 3.3 per cent of GDP, rising to $2.1 trillion, 4.6 per cent, in 2036. [cite:us11_cbo_outlook2026]

sections.h: Concentration and Trade
sections.html:
Both countries have argued over whether a few owners hold too much of their economies, and they answered the question in different ways. Israel passed a law in 2013 that took apart the pyramid structures through which a handful of business groups controlled banks, insurers, retailers and phone companies. The United States has no comparable statute; its debate runs through antitrust cases and through a live dispute among economists over whether American industries have become more concentrated at all. This section sets out both records, then the trade between the two countries, which began under America's first free trade agreement and was shaken by the tariffs of 2025–26.

Israel's business groups

The case for Israel's law rested on a Bank of Israel study of 2010. It found that 30 per cent of businesses in Israel belonged to pyramid structures, in which a family or individual controls a holding company that controls listed companies, which in turn control others, so that a small stake at the top commands a large share of the economy below. Ten business groups owned banks and holding companies that controlled 41 per cent of the market value of all public companies, and the study called Israel's the most concentrated economy in the Western world. [cite:us11_toi_concentration] Among the groups named in reporting at the time were Nochi Dankner's IDB Holdings, whose holdings included the mobile operator Cellcom and Supersol, the largest supermarket chain; Yitzhak Tshuva's Delek Group, which owned the Phoenix insurance company; and Shari Arison's large interest in Bank Hapoalim. [cite:us11_toi_concentration]

The government set up a committee on concentration and competitiveness on 24 October 2010. It published an interim report on 11 October 2011 and final recommendations in February 2012; it was separate from the Trajtenberg Committee, which reported on 26 September 2011 and which Part Fourteen covers. [cite:us11_wiki_concentration] [scene:us14_protests|Part Fourteen: the 2011 protests] The groups opposed it. In a filing of March 2011, IDB argued that there was no link between concentration and competitiveness and that Israel's concentration was average and declining. [cite:us11_wiki_concentration]

The 2013 law

The Knesset passed the Law for the Promotion of Competition and Reduction of Concentration in December 2013, by 72 votes to none with one abstention; 42 coalition and 30 opposition members voted for it. [cite:us11_toi_concentration] [cite:us11_wiki_concentration] It works in three ways. New pyramids may have no more than two layers of listed companies; existing ones had to come down to three layers within four years and to two within six. A controlling owner of a major non-financial company, one with turnover or credit above NIS 6 billion, may not also control a major financial company, one with assets above NIS 40 billion. And the state must weigh concentration when it hands out licences and rights. [cite:us11_wiki_concentration] The Finance Ministry's list of large non-financial entities covered by the law ran to 1,786 entities, 232 of them linked to IDB. [cite:us11_wiki_concentration] The chairman of the Knesset Finance Committee, Nissim Smoliansky, said: "From now on, we will see pyramids only when we go to Egypt." [cite:us11_toi_concentration]

The divestments that followed show the law biting. Delek Group sold 9.8 per cent of Phoenix in two deals in August and September 2018, for NIS 509 million, citing the concentration law and a shift to energy, and in 2019 sold its remaining controlling stake of 32.5 per cent to the private-equity firms Centerbridge Partners and Gallatin Point Capital for NIS 1.57 billion. [cite:us11_globes_delek2018] [cite:us11_lii_delek2019] IDB had made similar swap deals involving Discount Investment Corporation and Clal Insurance. [cite:us11_globes_delek2018] The law addressed control structures across groups rather than market shares within industries. Banking was handled separately: a 2016 committee recommended that Hapoalim and Leumi sell their credit-card companies. [cite:us11_wiki_concentration] Whether it lowered prices is a different question: the OECD in 2025 still ranked Israel's price level fourth-highest among its members and recommended lowering trade barriers to bring it down, which Part Fourteen examines. [cite:us14_oecd_survey2025] [scene:us14_basket|Part Fourteen: the basket]

Corporate power in the United States

The American debate is about measurement as much as remedy. In a widely cited 2019 study, the finance economists Gustavo Grullon, Yelena Larkin and Roni Michaely found that "Since the late 1990s, over 75% of US industries have experienced an increase in concentration levels", and that firms in the industries where concentration rose most earned higher profit margins and made more profitable acquisitions. [cite:us11_gl_concentration] Others dispute the scale. A 2020 report by Joe Kennedy for the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, a technology-policy think tank, found that in Census data for 2002–2012 the top four firms' share fell or held steady in 319 of 792 detailed industries, cited studies finding concentration in local markets steady or falling, and argued that the 2019 study's result depended on its 1997 starting point: measured from 1972, the median rise in concentration was about 25 per cent rather than over 70. [cite:us11_itif_kennedy] Both sides agree that national concentration measures are an imperfect guide to market power; they disagree on how much has changed.

The United States has handled the question case by case under its antitrust laws rather than by a structural statute like Israel's. The most important recent case concerns Google. Federal Judge Amit Mehta held that Google had illegally maintained a monopoly in general internet search, through multi-billion-dollar payments to Apple, Samsung, Mozilla and others to make its search engine the default. In his remedies ruling of September 2025 he did not ban those payments, allowing them to continue with minimal restrictions, citing the harm a ban could do to the partners who received them and to consumers. [cite:us11_hks_google] Eugene Kimmelman, writing for Harvard's Kennedy School in June 2026, noted that the court itself had found the search market "exceptionally resistant to change" and argued that the conduct behind its liability finding "can continue largely unchecked". [cite:us11_hks_google]

Trade between the two

The US–Israel Free Trade Agreement, America's first, entered into force on 1 September 1985, two months after Israel's stabilisation plan. [cite:us11_ustr_israel] [scene:us11_turn|The turn] In 2025 goods trade between the two countries was worth $34.4 billion: American exports of $13.7 billion and imports from Israel of $20.7 billion, leaving the United States with a goods deficit of $7.0 billion. Services trade added $19.7 billion, roughly in balance, for a total of $54.2 billion. Both goods exports and imports fell by about 7 per cent from 2024. [cite:us11_ustr_israel]

The tariffs of 2025 applied to Israel despite the agreement. On 2 April 2025 the Trump administration set a 17 per cent "reciprocal" tariff on Israeli goods; on 1 August it set a 15 per cent rate, when Israel had expected 10. Prime Minister Netanyahu had promised to cancel all of Israel's remaining tariffs on American imports, but the promise was not fully kept after pressure from Israeli farmers. [cite:us11_globes_tariff15] On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 in Learning Resources v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorise the president to impose tariffs, voiding the reciprocal tariffs. The administration announced a 10 per cent global tariff the same day under Section 122 of the Trade Act, which caps such surcharges at 15 per cent for 150 days, and ordered new investigations under Section 301. [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] This book did not establish what tariff applied to Israeli goods after that 150-day window; as of October 2026 the status should be checked against the latest proclamations. Part Twelve follows the industries behind these trade flows. [scene:us12_tech|Part Twelve: tech] [scene:us12_defence|Part Twelve: defence]

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: Industries
chapters.intro: Part Twelve turns from the economy as a whole to the industries inside it. It measures research spending in both countries since 1996, the weight of Israel's tech sector in its output, exports and jobs, and the boom and slump of venture money in each, before following American companies such as Intel and Nvidia into Israel and Israeli founders sold to American buyers. It then sets the two arms industries side by side: Israel's announced export records since 2022 and America's sales through government and commercial channels, measured also on SIPRI's common scale, and the co-production, aid and subsidiaries that join them. It ends with four industries that households pay into every day, natural gas, food, medicines and banking, where the comparison turns on how few firms supply each market and what each state has done about it. Figures are given with their source, year and definition, and the part says where only a snapshot exists. Status lines are as of October 2026, before Israel's election on 27 October and the American midterms on 3 November.
chapters.outro: Part Twelve established that Israel's research effort rose from about the American level in 1996, 2.59 against 2.45 per cent of GDP, to almost twice it, while its tech sector grew to about 17 per cent of output and 57 per cent of exports but stopped adding jobs after 2023. [cite:us12_im_rd_isr] [cite:us12_wiki_rd] [cite:us12_iia_2025] Venture money in both countries fell from its 2021 peak and recovered in 2025, in America on the back of a few very large AI deals. [cite:us12_jn_ivc2025] [cite:us12_nvca_q4_2025] American firms are among Israel's largest employers and exporters, and Israel's government paid Intel the largest grant it has given any company, $3.2 billion, while Intel's Israeli workforce fell from a 2021 peak of about 12,000 to about 9,350 in mid-2025. [cite:us12_globes_intel_grant] [cite:us12_calcalist_intel2025] Israel's announced defence exports rose to a record $19.2 billion in 2025, its share of world arms exports from 3.1 to 4.4 per cent, while America's share rose to 42 per cent; 68 per cent of Israel's arms imports came from the United States, much of it paid for with American grants spent with American firms. [cite:us12_mod_exports2025] [cite:us12_sipri_at2025] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] In gas, food and banking Israel's markets were dominated by a few firms, five banks holding 98 per cent of assets, and its regulators moved against them; America's are larger but consolidated, with four packers buying 85 per cent of fed cattle and the number of banks down 72 per cent since 1984. [cite:us12_toi_gasframework] [cite:us12_globes_banks] [cite:us12_ers_meatpacking] [cite:us12_farmdoc_banks] Part Thirteen turns to the people who work in these industries: wages, unions and the workers each system leaves outside. [scene:us13_wages|Part Thirteen: Labour]

sections.h: Tech and Venture Capital
sections.html:
No industry is cited more often in comparisons of the two countries than technology. American companies built the global platforms, and Israel, a country of about ten million people, became one of the places those companies buy from, invest in and recruit. [cite:us11_wb_pop] This section measures each country's research effort over time, sets the weight of the tech sector in each economy, follows venture money through its boom and slump, and then looks at the traffic between them: American firms in Israel and Israeli founders sold to American buyers. Its figures come from the World Bank, the OECD, Israel's Innovation Authority and the venture-data compilers in each country, whose definitions differ and are named as they appear.

Research spending over time

The clearest long series is research and development (R&D) spending as a share of GDP, which the World Bank publishes from UNESCO data. In 1996 the two countries spent almost the same share: 2.59 per cent in Israel and 2.45 per cent in the United States. Israel's share then pulled away, to 3.93 per cent in 2000, 3.94 per cent in 2010 and 4.94 per cent in 2018, while America's moved slowly from 2.63 per cent in 2000 to 2.74 per cent in 2010 and 2.83 per cent in 2018. [cite:us12_im_rd_isr] [cite:us12_im_rd_usa] The latest figures widen the gap. The World Bank puts Israel at 6.35 per cent of GDP in 2023 and the United States at 3.45 per cent; the OECD, measuring gross domestic spending on R&D, gives 6.76 and 3.45 per cent for 2024. [cite:us12_wiki_rd] The two sources use slightly different definitions, so the latest year should be read beside the World Bank series rather than spliced onto it. In money the comparison runs the other way: because the American economy is so much larger, 3.45 per cent of its GDP is many times Israel's total. The share measures how much of each economy is devoted to research, not who does more of it.

How much of the economy it is

Israel's Innovation Authority, a government agency, measures the sector each year. In its December 2025 report it put high-tech at about 17 per cent of Israel's GDP in 2024, about 57 per cent of exports in the first half of 2025 and about 403,000 employees, 11.5 per cent of the workforce. High-tech exports reached $78 billion in 2024. [cite:us12_iia_2025] The same report recorded a slowdown. Output was "virtually unchanged in 2024 for a second consecutive year"; employment, which had grown by more than 5 per cent a year for about a decade, grew by less than 2 per cent a year from 2023; and the number of R&D employees fell 6.5 per cent in the year to the first half of 2025. [cite:us12_iia_2025] No equivalent single figure for "high-tech" exists in American official statistics, so this book does not set one beside Israel's. What the Israeli numbers show is dependence: more than half of the country's exports come from a sector that employs about one worker in nine.

That dependence is also the sector's limit as a measure of how the system serves people. Nine in ten Israeli workers are outside it, and its slowdown since 2023 coincided with the war. The Innovation Authority's own figures show that three of every five shekels raised in 2025 went to cyber and organisational software, a narrow base for so large a share of exports. [cite:us12_iia_2025] Who works in high-tech, by gender, community and region, is examined in the parts on equality and labour rather than here. [scene:us8_israel|Equality among citizens] [scene:us13_wages|Wages]

Venture money: boom, slump and AI

Venture capital shows the cycle most sharply. By the count of the IVC research centre, Israeli tech companies raised a record $25.6 billion in 2021, $18.64 billion of it from foreign investors. [cite:us12_toi_ivc2021] Funding fell through 2022 and 2023; in the second quarter of 2023 it was about $1.78 billion, 65 per cent below the same quarter a year earlier. [cite:us12_toi_ivc2021] IVC and LeumiTech counted $11.1 billion in 418 rounds in 2025, up 15 per cent on 2024, which puts 2024 at roughly $9.7 billion by this book's arithmetic. [cite:us12_jn_ivc2025] The Innovation Authority summarised the recovery as a return to "2019-2020 levels". [cite:us12_iia_2025]

American venture investment, counted by PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association, followed the same curve at a far larger scale: $156.1 billion in 2019, $358.2 billion in 2021, $168.8 billion in 2023 and $339.4 billion in 2025. The recovery of 2025 was concentrated. Artificial intelligence and machine learning took 65.4 per cent of deal value, and half of all the money went to 0.05 per cent of completed deals; the largest round of the final quarter was Anthropic's $15 billion. [cite:us12_nvca_q4_2025] The two data sets are compiled differently, so the comparison is of direction and concentration, not of exact size. Both show money returning to the sector in 2025 while it narrowed to fewer companies and fewer fields.

The military pipeline

Part of Israel's tech sector grows out of its army. The founders of Check Point, set up in 1993, included two veterans of Unit 8200, the signals-intelligence unit; another 8200 alumnus who worked there, Nir Zuk, founded Palo Alto Networks; and the founders of CyberArk and Cybereason are described as 8200 alumni too. [cite:ow4_sw_alumni] The founders of Wiz met in the army's Talpiot programme; Google completed its $32 billion cash purchase of the company on 11 March 2026, the largest sale of an Israeli tech firm. [cite:ow4_sequoia_wiz] [cite:ow4_globes_wiz] The One-Way Mirror follows that unit and its ties to American agencies. [scene:ow4_gaza|Unit 8200] The United States has no equivalent conscript pipeline, but its own tech sector also drew on defence money: Palantir took early seed money from In-Q-Tel, the CIA's venture arm. [cite:ow9_ap_s1]

American firms in Israel

The largest American industrial presence in Israel is Intel, there since 1974. By the company's own figures it exported about $86 billion from Israel between 1974 and 2023, consistently 3.5 to 5.5 per cent of Israel's total exports, and invested about $27 billion in land, plant and equipment to 2021. [cite:us12_intel_israel] On 18 June 2023 Prime Minister Netanyahu announced a $25 billion expansion of its chip plant at Kiryat Gat, calling it "the largest investment by an international company ever in Israel". The state's grant was 12.8 per cent of the investment and the company's tax rate was set at 7.5 per cent. [cite:us12_reg_intel2023] Globes reported the grant as $3.2 billion, the largest the Israeli government had ever given a private company, paid against milestones. [cite:us12_globes_intel_grant] The record since then is of retrenchment. Intel's Israeli workforce fell from a peak of about 12,000 in 2021 to about 9,350 in mid-2025, and the future of the new fab was in doubt as the company cut costs worldwide. [cite:us12_calcalist_intel2025]

Nvidia was reported in February 2026 to be on course to become Israel's largest private tech employer. It bought the Israeli chip firm Mellanox in 2020 for a reported $6.9 billion and in February 2026 was planning a campus at Kiryat Tivon for up to 10,000 employees, its largest site outside the United States, with first occupancy planned for 2031. [cite:us12_jn_nvidia] These are the terms on which the two economies meet in tech: Israeli research and engineering, American ownership and markets, and Israeli state subsidy to keep the plants in Israel. The told-versus-record contrast is narrow but real. The 2023 announcement was presented as a vote of confidence in Israel's economy; the record two years later was of the same company's Israeli workforce down about 13 per cent from 2023 and more than a fifth from its 2021 peak (this book's arithmetic from Calcalist's figures). Both the grant and the jobs it was meant to buy are matters of public record, and the outcome depended on Intel's global fortunes more than on Israeli policy.

sections.h: Defence Industry and Arms Exports
sections.html:
Both countries are among the world's largest arms exporters, and their defence industries are joined by money, co-production and ownership. The United States is the largest exporter by a wide margin; Israel, with about a thirty-fourth of America's population, ranks seventh, and its Defence Ministry says it relies on exports to help pay for its own forces. [cite:us11_wb_pop] [cite:us12_sipri_at2025] This section measures each industry's exports over time, using two kinds of figure that must not be confused: the value of deals signed or authorised in a year, which each government announces, and the volume of major weapons actually delivered, which the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimates on a common scale. It then follows the ties between the two industries.

Israel: five years of records

Israel's Defence Ministry, through its export agency SIBAT, announces the value of export deals signed each year. It reported $12.5 billion in 2022 and a record $13.1 billion in 2023. [cite:us12_na_exports2023] The figure for 2024 was $14.8 billion, up 11.7 per cent, more than half of it to Europe and almost half of it air defence. [cite:hm_globes_exports] On 2 June 2026 the ministry announced $19.2 billion for 2025, up nearly 30 per cent and the fifth record in a row; it said exports had more than doubled in five years and quadrupled in a decade. Government-to-government deals made up about $10 billion. [cite:us12_mod_exports2025] The war did not reduce sales. Air-defence systems were 36 per cent of deals in 2023 and about 48 per cent in 2024, when a single sale of Arrow 3 to Germany of about $3.5 billion lifted Europe's share to 54 per cent; in 2025 air defence fell to 29 per cent, surveillance and optronics rose to 22 per cent, and states of the Abraham Accords took 15 per cent. [cite:us12_globes_exports2025]

The ministry's own statements tie exports to the defence budget. Its director-general, Amir Baram, said that "our force buildup budget relies heavily on these partnerships". [cite:us12_mod_exports2025] The head of SIBAT, Yair Kulas, observed that Israel was no longer the only country selling arms with a "combat-proven" label, since Ukraine now markets battlefield-tested products. [cite:us12_globes_exports2025] The phrase names a selling point that rests on use in war, and the ministry and its critics read it differently; this book records it as the industry's own description.

The United States: the largest seller

American arms sales are counted through two channels. Foreign Military Sales (FMS) are government-to-government sales managed by the Pentagon; Direct Commercial Sales (DCS) are licensed sales by companies. The State Department reported FMS of $51.9 billion in fiscal year 2022 and $80.9 billion in 2023, and DCS of $153.6 billion and $157.5 billion. [cite:us12_usni_fy2023] Its figures for fiscal 2025, as reported, were $331.18 billion in all, $104.4 billion of it FMS and $226.8 billion DCS, against $318.7 billion in fiscal 2024. [cite:us12_da_fy2025] These are authorisations and notified sales, many of which are delivered over years; they are not comparable with Israel's signed-deal figures, and both are far larger than what is shipped in any one year.

SIPRI's delivery-based measure gives the common scale. In 2021–25 the United States supplied 42 per cent of the world's major arms exports, up from 36 per cent in 2016–20, and its exports rose 27 per cent between the two periods; its largest customers were Saudi Arabia (12 per cent), Ukraine (9.4 per cent) and Japan (8.9 per cent). Israel was the seventh-largest exporter, with 4.4 per cent of the world total, up from 3.1 per cent, after its exports grew 56 per cent; India took 29 per cent of Israeli exports, Germany 21 per cent and the United States 7.8 per cent. [cite:us12_sipri_at2025] For 2019–23 SIPRI had ranked Israel ninth, with 2.4 per cent, and India's share of its exports at 37 per cent. [cite:pm_globes_exports] The five-year periods overlap, so they show a direction rather than separate points.

How the two industries are joined

The ties run in both directions. Israel is the fourteenth-largest arms importer, and 68 per cent of its major imports in 2021–25 came from the United States. [cite:us12_sipri_at2025] Much of that is paid for with American aid: the Foreign Military Financing grant of $3.3 billion a year must be spent on American equipment, and the share Israel may spend at home falls to zero in fiscal year 2028. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] The aid is therefore, in large part, a payment to American manufacturers for weapons Israel uses; its scale and what it frees up are measured in the volume's first part and in The Bill and America's Role. [scene:us1_aid|What the aid is] [scene:gi16_aid|The aid]

Missile defence is co-produced. From 2016 American production funding for David's Sling, built by Israel's Rafael with Raytheon, and Arrow 3, built by Israel Aerospace Industries with Boeing, was split half and half with the American partners. [cite:ow8_dn_coprod2016] On 9 October 2026 the Raytheon–Rafael joint venture delivered the first Tamir interceptors, the missile used by Iron Dome, built at Camden, Arkansas, its first plant outside Israel. [cite:ow8_rtx_camden] Israel's F-35s carry Israeli electronic-warfare equipment by Elbit and Israeli software. [cite:ow7_wiki_f35i] The One-Way Mirror follows this pipeline. [scene:ow8_coproduction|Co-production]

Israeli firms also sell inside the United States. Elbit's American subsidiary won a $145 million border-tower contract from Customs and Border Protection in 2014. [cite:ow10_globes_ift] Renamed Twenty-Six Defense on 8 September 2026, it is based in Fort Worth, employs about 3,300 people and held border contracts worth more than $370 million running to May 2029. [cite:ow10_dn_26] Israel's government says it has banned defence exports to Myanmar since 2017. [cite:ow10_aj_cognyte] Both governments license what their companies export, and in both the decision rests with the executive; how each answered challenges to sales during the Gaza war is set out in the volume's part on the courts and other states. [scene:gi17_courts|The courts]

Who these industries serve can be stated from the record. In Israel defence exports help pay for the army itself, as the ministry says, and the industry's growth since 2021 has coincided with the wars. In the United States the industry sells to many governments, Saudi Arabia above all, and Israel is one customer among many, though one whose purchases are financed by American grants. [cite:us12_mod_exports2025] [cite:us12_sipri_at2025] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] The costs of the wars these weapons are used in, for both treasuries, are set out in later parts. [scene:us19_spending|Defence spending] [scene:us20_flows|The money flow]

sections.h: Gas, Food, Medicines and Banks
sections.html:
Beyond tech and arms, four industries show how each state shapes markets that households pay into every day: energy, food, medicines and banking. In each the comparison runs on concentration, how few firms supply the market, and on what the state does about it. Israel's markets are small and were for decades dominated by a handful of business groups, a pattern its 2013 concentration law set out to break; America's are large but have consolidated in several of the same fields. [cite:us11_toi_concentration] [cite:us11_gl_concentration] The economy-wide picture is in the previous part. [scene:us11_concentration|Concentration] This section takes the industries one by one, with the series that exist and the snapshots where they do not.

Natural gas: two fields and an export trade

Israel's offshore gas fields came into production within a decade of each other. The Tamar field has produced gas since 2013, and the larger Leviathan field was to be developed by 2019 by the American company Noble Energy and Israel's Delek Group. [cite:us12_toi_gasframework] The two companies' hold on both fields became the central dispute. Israel's antitrust commissioner, David Gilo, resigned in May 2015 in opposition to their dominant position, and the government's gas framework of August 2015 required Delek to sell its holdings in Tamar and in the smaller Karish and Tanin fields within six years, and Noble to cut its share of Tamar to no more than 25 per cent, in return for regulated prices for six years and a ten-year commitment from the government. [cite:us12_toi_gasframework] Prime Minister Netanyahu said the deal would bring hundreds of billions of shekels to citizens; critics in the coalition, among them Finance Minister Moshe Kahlon, held out for stricter price controls. [cite:us12_toi_gasframework]

Production rose to 25.28 billion cubic metres (bcm) in 2023 and 27.38 bcm in 2024, by the Ministry of Energy's figures: 11.33 bcm from Leviathan, 10.09 bcm from Tamar and 5.96 bcm from Karish. Exports to Egypt and Jordan were 13.11 bcm in 2024, up from 11.56 bcm, so that about 48 per cent of output left the country. [cite:us12_enerdata_gas2024] In August 2025 the Leviathan partners signed a deal to sell Egypt about 130 bcm through 2040 for $35 billion, tripling previous export volumes; the largest partner, NewMed Energy, formerly Delek Drilling, held 45.3 per cent. [cite:us12_tml_leviathan] Netanyahu approved it on 17 December 2025 after ordering it held in September over Israeli allegations that Egyptian deployments in Sinai breached the peace treaty, which Egypt denies; Egypt's State Information Service called the deal "a purely commercial transaction". [cite:gi15_aje_gas] Who gains from the gas depends on how its rent is split between the state and the partners, and how much is kept for domestic power at regulated prices; both were contested in 2015 and this book has not measured the outcome.

The American system runs at another scale. The Energy Information Administration put dry gas production at 103.2 billion cubic feet a day in 2024 and forecast 107.1 for 2025, record levels driven by export demand. [cite:us12_boe_eia] That is about 1,070 bcm a year, roughly 39 times Israel's output, by this book's conversion. In both countries private firms drill under state licence; the difference is that Israel's market had two dominant producers at the start, which made the terms of the licence a national political question.

Food: few suppliers in both

Israel's food prices are among the highest in the developed world, and its State Comptroller has tied them partly to concentration. In a January 2024 audit the comptroller found that Israel's overall price level, on the OECD data it used, was 27 per cent above the OECD average in purchasing-power terms and that food prices were 37 per cent above the OECD's and 51 per cent above the European Union's. The ten largest food suppliers held more than half the market for food and consumer products, and the comptroller found "abnormal profit" among the largest food and pharmaceutical importers. When butter was taken off tight price supervision in November 2021, the average price of imported butter rose by about 60 per cent. [cite:us12_comptroller_food] OECD data reported in July 2024 put Israel's food and drink prices 52 per cent above the developed-country average, and the overall price level for 2022 38 per cent above it; the differences from the comptroller's figures reflect different data releases and reference groups. [cite:us14_toi_food52] The comptroller recommended more imports as the structural remedy and price supervision only as an interim one. The 2011 cottage-cheese boycott, when a container fell by about a quarter after a two-week consumer revolt, is told in the part on the cost of living. [cite:us14_ap_cottage] [scene:us14_protests|The 2011 protests]

The American food system is concentrated at a different link, between farmers and processors. The four largest beef packers bought 36 per cent of the country's fed cattle in 1980, 81 per cent in 1995 and about 85 per cent in the latest data, according to the Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service. Its review found that from 1980 to 2015 larger plants cut costs enough to offset packers' market power, but that after 2015 the gap between cattle and wholesale beef prices widened sharply. [cite:us12_ers_meatpacking] On these sources, concentration in Israel shows up mainly in what shoppers pay; in the American beef chain the ERS traces it at least as much in the spread between what ranchers are paid and wholesale prices.

Medicines: one company and one price system

Israel's pharmaceutical industry was for years dominated by one company, Teva, among the country's largest employers, with about 6,800 staff in Israel in 2017. Its purchase of Actavis Generics for about $40 billion left it with heavy debt, and on 14 December 2017 it announced about 14,000 job cuts, more than a quarter of its global workforce, with about 1,700 in Israel and the closure of its Jerusalem plant; about $10 billion of debt fell due within a year. The Histadrut labour federation called a nationwide general strike in response. [cite:us12_toi_teva2017] The episode showed how much of the Israeli economy can rest on a single firm. Medicines' prices are set very differently in the two countries. Israel's Ministry of Health fixes maximum prices from the three lowest of seven reference countries. [cite:us16_cwf_israel] In the United States, by RAND's 2022 comparison, drug prices were 278 per cent of those in 33 other high-income countries, though generics were cheaper in America than in most of them. [cite:us16_rand_drugs] The health part sets out what each system pays. [scene:us16_cost|What it costs]

Banks: five in Israel, thousands in America

Banking shows the starkest difference in structure. In Israel five banking groups, Leumi, Hapoalim, Discount, Mizrahi Tefahot and First International, held 98 per cent of the banking system's assets at the end of 2022, and the two largest 57 per cent.
