On 26 March 2024 the Competition Authority told them it planned to declare them a "concentration group" in retail banking, saying that barriers to entry and to switching banks "facilitate the stabilization of a coordinated equilibrium" among them. [cite:us12_globes_banks] The United States has thousands of banks, but far fewer than before: 14,483 federally insured commercial banks in 1984, 7,061 in 2008 and 4,027 in 2023, a fall of 72 per cent. [cite:us12_farmdoc_banks] One system is concentrated by size and history, the other is consolidating from a base of many small lenders.

Trade between them

The two economies have traded under a free trade agreement since 1 September 1985, the first the United States ever signed. In 2025 goods trade between them was $34.4 billion, with American exports of $13.7 billion and imports from Israel of $20.7 billion, and services trade added $19.7 billion, by the US Trade Representative's count. [cite:us11_ustr_israel] The flows traced in this part, Intel's exports from Kiryat Gat, Nvidia's and Google's purchases of Israeli firms, Noble's gas, Elbit's American subsidiary and Israel's purchases of American weapons, sit inside that trade. What each state does with the money its industries earn, and who pays the costs of its wars, is the subject of later parts. [scene:us20_flows|The money flow]

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: Labour
chapters.intro: Part Thirteen compares the two labour markets as each state has shaped them by law. It sets America's federal minimum wage, a fixed dollar sum that Congress last raised in 2009, beside Israel's, which since 1987 has been pegged to the average wage, and follows both from 1980 to 2026, with the state minimums that now set most American floors. It compares the hours worked in each country on the OECD's series, the paid leave each law guarantees, and the gap between men's and women's pay, stating where the two countries' measures differ. It then traces the fall of organised labour in both countries: the Histadrut, which in 1980 was employer, bank owner and health insurer as well as union, and America's firm-by-firm unions, whose membership halved from 1983. It ends with the workers neither system counts as its own: Palestinians on Israeli work permits, whose numbers collapsed after October 2023, the foreign workers recruited to replace them, and the millions of unauthorised workers in the United States.
chapters.outro: Part Thirteen established that the two systems set their wage floors on opposite principles: America's federal minimum has stood at $7.25 since 24 July 2009 and by 2023 had lost 42 per cent of its 1968 buying power, leaving thirty states to set higher floors, while Israel's, pegged by law to 47.5 per cent of the average wage, rose from NIS 2,348.88 a month in 1997 to NIS 6,443.85 in April 2026, though it was held at NIS 5,300 from 2017 to 2022. [cite:us13_dol_minwage] [cite:us13_epi_history] [cite:us13_bp_states2026] [cite:us13_nii_minwage] [cite:us13_kz_minwagelaw] Workers in Israel average more hours a year than in the United States, though the gap has narrowed since 2000; American law guarantees no paid vacation and Israel's only twelve days; and both countries' gender pay gaps are well above the OECD average, Israel's on a monthly measure that is not directly comparable. [cite:us13_wiki_hours] [cite:us13_dol_vacation] [cite:us13_toi_vacation] [cite:us13_oecd_lmf15] [cite:us13_jpost_shoresh] Organised labour shrank in both: the Histadrut lost most of its members when the 1995 health law cut the link with Clalit, while American membership fell from 20.1 per cent in 1983 to 10.0 per cent in 2025, 5.9 per cent in the private sector. [cite:us13_shalev_labor] [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] [cite:us13_bls_union2025] West Bank Palestinians working in Israel and the settlements fell from about 172,000 before October 2023 to about 51,000 at the end of 2025, as Israel turned to recruited foreign workers, while the United States relies on about 8.3 million unauthorised workers. [cite:us13_pcbs_workers2026] [cite:us13_tml_piba] [cite:us13_epi_unauth] These figures stand as of October 2026, before Israel's election on 27 October and America's midterms on 3 November. Part Fourteen asks what those wages buy. [scene:us14_wages|Part Fourteen: cost of living over time]

sections.h: Minimum Wage, Hours and Pay Gaps
sections.html:
An average wage says what a typical post pays; it says little about the bottom of the labour market, where a legal floor does most of the work. This section compares the two countries' floors over time, the hours people work, the leave the law guarantees them, and the gap between men's and women's pay. Each measure is taken from one series per country, and where the two countries' series are defined differently the difference is stated. Average pay against prices is the subject of Part Fourteen. [scene:us14_wages|Part Fourteen: wages against prices] [cite:us13_dol_minwage] [cite:us13_nii_minwage]

Two kinds of floor

The two minimum wages are built on opposite principles. America's federal minimum is a fixed dollar amount written into the Fair Labor Standards Act; it changes only when Congress passes, and the president signs, an amendment. The Labor Department's chart of the non-farm rate shows how irregular that has been: $1.60 from February 1968, $3.10 in January 1980, $3.35 in January 1981 and then no change for nine years, $3.80 in 1990, $4.25 in 1991, $4.75 in 1996 and $5.15 in September 1997, then another ten-year pause until three steps to $7.25 on 24 July 2009. [cite:us13_dol_minwage] As of October 2026 the federal rate is still $7.25: twenty states used it as their own minimum at the end of 2025, and by October 2026 it had gone more than seventeen years without an increase. [cite:us13_bp_states2026] [cite:us13_epi_history]

Israel's Minimum Wage Law, passed in 1987, ties the floor to pay in general. The monthly minimum is set at 47.5 per cent of the average wage and updated each 1 April; the hourly minimum is the monthly figure divided by 186. The law covers every employee aged 18 and over, part-timers in proportion to their hours, and, by its own terms, foreign and undocumented workers; minors receive a reduced rate, and an employer who fails to pay the minimum can face up to a year in prison or a fine. [cite:us13_kz_minwagelaw] Because the floor follows the average wage, it rises without a new vote. It has not always moved mechanically, however: the National Insurance Institute's table shows the monthly minimum at NIS 5,300 from December 2017 and unchanged at each April update from 2018 to 2022, before it resumed rising in April 2023. [cite:us13_nii_minwage]

A correction belongs here. A widely repeated figure gives Israel's minimum as NIS 6,247.67 "from 1 April 2026". The National Insurance Institute's own table shows that amount as the April 2025 rate; the rate from 1 April 2026 is NIS 6,443.85 a month, a rise of about 3.1 per cent. [cite:us13_nii_minwage]

What the floors are worth

A nominal rate frozen for seventeen years loses value every year that prices rise. The Economic Policy Institute calculated that the 1968 federal minimum of $1.60 was worth $12.50 in 2023 dollars and the 2009 rate of $7.25 only $10.33; by 2023 the federal minimum's buying power was at a 66-year low, 42 per cent below its 1968 peak. [cite:us13_epi_history] The federal figure is no longer the floor most American low earners face, because states have moved on their own. Thirty states and the District of Columbia set higher minimums; in 2026 twenty-two states and DC raised theirs, lifting the average state minimum from $11.18 to $11.51, with the District highest at $17.95. [cite:us13_bp_states2026] The result is a floor that depends on where a worker lives: $7.25 an hour in the twenty states that use the federal rate, more than twice that in the highest-paying jurisdictions.

Israel's floor is one national rate. Its height relative to typical pay has long been high by international standards. In 2010 the Taub Center put Israel's minimum at 58 per cent of the median wage, against an OECD average of 46 per cent and 34 per cent in the United States, while noting that Israel was "not a strict enforcer" of it. [cite:us13_taub_minwage2010] That ratio is a 2010 snapshot; the later direction for each country follows from the series above, since Israel's floor is pegged to the average wage and America's federal floor has not moved since 2009.

Hours and leave

The OECD's series of average annual hours actually worked per worker includes part-time workers and is published, in the OECD's own words, for comparing one country over time rather than levels between countries. [cite:us13_jil_hours] On that series Israel has worked more hours than the United States in every year shown, but the gap has narrowed: Israeli hours fell from 2,033 a year in 2000 to 1,957 in 2010 and 1,870 in 2025, while American hours moved from 1,832 to 1,772 and 1,800. The OECD average in 2025 was 1,736. [cite:us13_wiki_hours] A claim repeated in American commentary, that only Mexico, Costa Rica, Chile, South Korea and Israel work longer hours than the United States, does not hold for the 2025 table, in which eleven countries, among them Greece, Croatia and the Czech Republic, show more hours than the United States. [cite:us13_wiki_hours] The OECD revises the series: the edition reproduced by Japan's labour institute in August 2025 gave the United States 1,880 hours in 2000 and 1,796 in 2024, so figures from different editions should not be mixed. [cite:us13_jil_hours]

Leave law differs in kind. American federal law sets no paid vacation at all: the Labor Department states that the Fair Labor Standards Act "does not require payment for time not worked, such as vacations", which are left to agreement between employer and employee, with exceptions for some federal contracts. [cite:us13_dol_vacation] Israel's Annual Leave Law of 1951 does set a minimum, but a low one: 10 days a year until the first increase in the law's history, to 12 days from 1 January 2017 for employees with less than four years' seniority, rising each year after that. Most OECD countries guarantee 20 days or more. [cite:us13_toi_vacation] Paid parental leave, the larger difference between the two systems, is compared in Part Eighteen. [scene:us18_family|Part Eighteen: family policy]

The gap between men's and women's pay

The OECD measures the gender pay gap as the difference between men's and women's median earnings for full-time employees, as a share of men's. In the United States it narrowed steadily from the mid-1970s to the early 2010s and has changed little since 2014: 19.0 per cent in 2005, 18.8 per cent in 2010, 17.7 per cent in 2020 and 17.3 per cent in 2024. The OECD average in 2024 was 10.1 per cent, down 8.4 points since 2000. [cite:us13_jil_gendergap] [cite:us13_oecd_lmf15] Israel is one of the countries the OECD lists with gaps of 20 per cent or more. [cite:us13_oecd_lmf15] The Shoresh Institution found that Israeli women's median monthly income in 2021–2023 was 76.9 per cent of men's, a gap of 23.1 per cent that was wider than in 35 of the 38 OECD countries and wider than fifteen years earlier, and traced much of it to pay falling for women after children are born while men's rises. [cite:us13_jpost_shoresh]

The two figures are not on the same footing. The OECD notes that Israel's data are monthly earnings and America's weekly; a monthly figure counts differences in hours worked within full-time employment that an hourly measure would remove, so it tends to show a wider gap. [cite:us13_oecd_lmf15] What the record supports is narrower than a ranking: both countries' gaps are well above the OECD average; America's has been flat for a decade; and Israel's, on the Shoresh measure, has widened. How each system treats women and Arab citizens in employment more broadly is set out in Part Eight. [scene:us8_gender|Part Eight: gender]

sections.h: Unions: the Histadrut and American Labour
sections.html:
In 1980 the two countries' labour movements could hardly have been more different. Israel's Histadrut was not only a union federation but an employer, a bank owner and the gateway to most people's health care; America's unions were private associations bargaining firm by firm under federal law. Both lost most of their reach in the decades that followed, by different routes. This section traces the decline in each country with each country's own measure, and states where the two measures cannot be set side by side. [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] [cite:us13_bls_union2025]

Israel: from state-builder to union

The Histadrut, the General Federation of Labour, was founded in Haifa in December 1920 to represent Jewish workers in Mandatory Palestine; it began admitting Arab workers only in the 1950s. [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] Through its holding company, Hevrat HaOvdim, it owned industrial conglomerates, the shipping line ZIM, Bank Hapoalim until the state took over the banks after the 1983 bank-share crisis, and the Clalit sick fund, which covered about 70 per cent of Israelis in the mid-1980s. It still employed about 280,000 people in 1989. [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] Membership was close to universal because health care came with it: in 1983 the Histadrut counted about 85 per cent of wage earners, and the sociologist Michael Shalev found that until the early 1990s it negotiated for 85 per cent of all wage earners through framework agreements for the public and private sectors and spoke for about two-thirds of Israeli adults. [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] [cite:us13_shalev_labor]

That position was also a role in governing. In 1985 the Histadrut signed the wage freeze that, with spending cuts and a fixed exchange rate, ended the hyperinflation; it was a party to the plan, not merely consulted. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] [scene:us11_turn|Part Eleven: the 1985 plan] Within a decade the structure came apart. The Labour Party lost control of the Histadrut in its May 1994 elections, and the National Health Insurance Law, in force from 1995, ended the rule that tied Clalit care to membership. [cite:us13_shalev_labor] Membership fell from about 1.8 million, some 80 per cent of the workforce, to about 200,000 in 1994–95; the new leadership sold assets outside its union work. [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] The health law's side of this change is told in Part Sixteen. [scene:us16_systems|Part Sixteen: health systems]

The Histadrut rebuilt part of its base as an ordinary union: about 650,000 members in 2005 and 570,000 in 2017, with about 800,000 claimed more recently. [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] Measured as a share of employees, density was 27 per cent in 2016. The OECD's 2017 profile of Israeli bargaining put private-sector density at 10–20 per cent and collective-agreement coverage at 20–30 per cent of employees, with bargaining mostly at company or sector level and not coordinated. The labour ministry can extend a sector agreement to a whole industry, but the OECD described extensions as "uncommon". [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] [cite:us13_oecd_cb_israel]

The United States: half the density of 1983

American bargaining runs on the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, under which a union bargains for a workplace or firm once it wins recognition there, and represents everyone in that unit, members or not. There is no general mechanism to extend an agreement across an industry, so coverage stops at the edge of each organised firm; in a 2017 comparison of 21 OECD countries the United States ranked last in collective-bargaining coverage. [cite:us13_eg_bargaining] Section 14(b) of the Act allows states to ban union-security clauses, so that workers covered by a contract can decline to pay toward it; 26 states had such "right-to-work" laws after Michigan became the first state since Indiana in 1965 to repeal one, effective 13 February 2024. [cite:us13_littler_rtw] [cite:ad4_audit_bt_michigan]

The Bureau of Labor Statistics' consistent series begins in 1983, when 20.1 per cent of wage and salary workers, 17.7 million people, belonged to a union. By 2024 the rate was 9.9 per cent; in 2025 it was 10.0 per cent, or 14.7 million members. The split by sector is stark: 32.9 per cent of public-sector workers were members in 2025 against 5.9 per cent in the private sector. A further group is covered by contracts without joining, so 11.2 per cent of workers, 16.5 million, were represented by unions. Full-time union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404, against $1,174 for non-members, a raw comparison that does not adjust for occupation or industry. [cite:us13_bls_union2025] The 2025 figures omit October, when the federal shutdown stopped the survey. [cite:us13_bls_union2025] Before the BLS series, about one American worker in three was a union member in 1960. [cite:us13_eg_bargaining]

The two declines had different engines. Israel's density fell in a few years when the state cut the link between union membership and health care and the Histadrut ceased to be a conglomerate; it was a change of law. America's fell over four decades under a stable legal framework in which organising happens one workplace at a time, alongside the spread of right-to-work laws. [cite:us13_shalev_labor] [cite:us13_eg_bargaining] [cite:us13_littler_rtw] The result is a similar order of magnitude in both countries now, with Israel's coverage higher on the OECD's last estimate. The Israeli series has a gap: no official annual density series from 2016 to 2026 was found for this book, so Israel's current density is stated only as a range.

The political strike

The Histadrut has also used the national general strike, including over questions that were not about pay. It called one in February 2012 on behalf of subcontracted workers, settled four days later. [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] In late March 2023, after the prime minister announced the dismissal of the defence minister during the fight over the judicial overhaul, its chairman Arnon Bar-David called a general strike; it was called off the same day when Benjamin Netanyahu agreed to pause the legislation. [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] [scene:us2_courts|Part Two: the courts and the 2023 overhaul] On 2 September 2024, after the bodies of six hostages were recovered in Gaza, the Histadrut struck again to press the government on a ceasefire and hostage deal; Ben Gurion airport halted flights for several hours, and the Labour Court ordered the strike ended by 2.30 in the afternoon, which the Histadrut obeyed. Netanyahu, for his part, placed the blame on Hamas, saying that "whoever murders hostages does not want a deal". [cite:us13_npr_strike2024]

sections.h: Migrant and Palestinian Workers
sections.html:
Both labour markets depend on workers who are not citizens and do not have the rights citizens have. In Israel they are of two kinds: Palestinians from the West Bank and, until October 2023, Gaza, who entered on daily or seasonal permits issued by the military authorities; and foreign workers recruited abroad for set sectors. In the United States the largest group is unauthorised immigrants. The two cases differ in law and in scale, and each is stated on its own terms here; the status of Palestinians under Israeli control generally is the subject of Part Nine. [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank] [cite:us13_pcbs_workers2026] [cite:us13_epi_unauth]

Palestinian workers: permits, then the closure

After 1967 Israel integrated the territories' economy with its own, and from 1967 to 1990 between 35 and 40 per cent of employed Palestinians worked in Israel, mostly in low-paid jobs. In the early 1990s Israel introduced a closure regime under which every worker needed a permit subject to security clearance; the Oslo Accords did not end it. [cite:gz_carnegie_labor] [scene:gz2_economy|The economy after 1967] Permits are issued through the Civil Administration and COGAT, and a permit is tied to a named employer. [cite:wb_wiki_civadmin] [cite:us13_972_workers] Gaza's workers were barred from 2007 to 2014; about 18,500 Gazans held permits on the eve of the war, and all were revoked on 10 October 2023. [cite:gz_carnegie_labor]

The West Bank figures are the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics'. Before the war about 172,000 West Bank Palestinians worked in Israel and the settlements, about 127,000 of them with permits. In the last quarter of 2023 the number fell to about 25,000; by the last quarter of 2025 it had partly recovered to about 51,000, of whom only about 14,000 held permits. West Bank unemployment rose from about 13 per cent in the third quarter of 2023 to about 28 per cent at the end of 2025. In Gaza it rose from about 45 per cent to about 68 per cent by the end of 2024, the last figure the bureau gives. [cite:us13_pcbs_workers2026] Other counts of the pre-war workforce differ. +972 Magazine gives about 150,000 West Bank permit holders and about 50,000 working without permits, and reports that about 8,000 permits for work inside Israel were issued in 2025 and that more than 10,000 Palestinians still work in settlements. [cite:us13_972_workers] The difference turns on whether settlements and unpermitted work are counted; the PCBS survey is the only one of these that is a published statistical series.

Foreign workers: the replacement

Israel has recruited foreign workers since the closures of the 1990s; by 2000 there were about 240,000, documented and undocumented, roughly a tenth of the labour force. [cite:us13_972_workers] The state sets quotas by sector, about 30,000 each in agriculture and construction, with no cap in home care, and visas, typically for five years, are tied to the employer. [cite:us13_972_workers] After October 2023 the government turned to recruitment abroad to fill the jobs Palestinians had held. A government decision in May 2024 raised the quota for foreign workers to 3.3 per cent of the population; by The Media Line's account of figures from the Population and Immigration Authority, almost 61,000 new permits were issued in 2025, bringing the total to 227,044, and the authority still described a shortfall of about 100,000. [cite:us13_tml_piba] The workers' rights group Kav LaOved counts about 270,000 migrant workers in all; planned recruitment of about 65,000 workers from India, Sri Lanka and Uzbekistan was under discussion in 2026. [cite:us13_972_workers]

The law on paper covers them. Israel's Minimum Wage Law applies, by its own terms, to foreign and undocumented workers as to anyone else. [cite:us13_kz_minwagelaw] The record of compliance is weaker. Kav LaOved estimated in 2014 that migrant farm workers received on average about 70 per cent of the wages they were owed, and +972 reports withheld wages, unfit housing and pesticide exposure without protection. [cite:us13_972_workers] Foreign agricultural workers also bore part of the war's toll: Thai workers were among the people killed and taken hostage on 7 October 2023, and at least three migrant workers were killed by Iranian missiles in the 2026 war. [cite:us13_972_workers]

The United States: unauthorised workers

The American counterpart is larger in absolute terms and built on a different legal fact: most of these workers have no permit at all. The Pew Research Center estimated 8.3 million unauthorised immigrants in the American labour force in 2022, just under 5 per cent of all workers, up from 3.6 million in 1995 and level with its earlier peaks in 2008 and 2011. [cite:us13_epi_unauth] The Economic Policy Institute argues that without regular status, employers can use the fear of retaliation and deportation to pay them less, and that work authorisation raises wages and standards for the workers concerned. [cite:us13_epi_unauth] Enforcement against them, and the detention and deportation system, are covered in Parts Four and Six. [scene:us6_asylum|Part Six: asylum and the border] [scene:us4_detention|Part Four: detention]

The comparison is uneven in one respect that matters. The unauthorised American worker lives inside the country that sets the rules and can, in principle, be regularised by its legislature; the Palestinian permit worker lives under military rule in territory Israel controls and has no vote in Israel's elections, so the permit regime is set by a state in which the worker has no political voice. Both systems rely on workers whose status depends on someone else's decision; only one also governs where those workers live. [cite:us13_pcbs_workers2026] [cite:gz_carnegie_labor]

chapters.label: Part Fourteen
chapters.title: Cost of Living Over Time
chapters.intro: Part Fourteen asks what it costs to live in each country and how that has changed. It sets wages against prices from 1980, through Israel's hyperinflation and the long years of flat Israeli pay that followed, and America's long rise in household income with larger gains at the top. It then measures housing against income in each country's own terms, takes the household budget apart item by item (food, phones, childcare, college, health, fuel and debt), and builds the closest honest version of a family's monthly budget then and now from each country's expenditure survey. It ends with the summer of 2011, when a boycott of cottage cheese and a tent camp in Tel Aviv became, by many accounts, the largest social protest in Israel's history, and with what the government's Trajtenberg Committee changed and did not change. Each series is given with its source, year and definition, and the part says plainly where only a snapshot exists.
chapters.outro: Part Fourteen established that the two systems burden families in different places. Israeli real pay was flat for about fifteen years after 2000 and its OECD average wage fell from 76 to 66 per cent of America's between 2000 and 2024, while American median household income reached a record $87,460 in 2025, after gains since 1967 about twice as large at the ninetieth percentile as at the median. [cite:us14_globes_taubwages] [cite:us14_oecd_avwage] [cite:us14_census_story2025] Homes grew less affordable in both: 155 average monthly salaries for the average Israeli home in 2022, up from 129 in 2010, and an American price-to-income ratio of 5.0 in 2024, up from 3.2 in the 1990s, with half of American renters cost-burdened. [cite:us14_globes_salaries2023] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [cite:us14_nlihc_jchs2026] Israel's food and cars are among the OECD's dearest and its telecoms 30 per cent below the average, the result of a 2012 competition reform; its preschool is free from age three and its college tuition set nationally, while American families carry higher household debt and, for health, premiums of $26,993 a year for a family plan. [cite:us14_toi_food52] [cite:us14_globes_kahlon] [cite:us14_taub_preschool] [cite:us14_globes_mortgagegdp] [cite:us14_kff_ehbs2025] The 2011 protests won what a single decision could deliver, tax rises and free preschool, but not the market and housing changes that the OECD was still urging in 2025. [cite:us14_wiki_trajtenberg] [cite:us14_ecoscope] Part Fifteen turns to the land, planning and building systems behind the housing figures. [scene:us15_land|Part Fifteen: land]

sections.h: Wages Against Prices, 1980–2026
sections.html:
The plainest test of a cost of living is whether pay keeps up with prices. Both countries publish the series needed to answer it: Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) has measured consumer prices monthly since 1951 and average wages per employee post since the 1960s, and America's Bureau of Labor Statistics and Census Bureau have measured prices since 1913 and household income since 1967. This section reads each country's wages against its own prices first, in its own currency, and only then compares the two, using one source for both: the OECD's average annual wage in dollars of equal purchasing power. The two countries' figures are not converted at market exchange rates, which move with capital flows and say little about what a wage buys at home. [cite:us14_oecd_avwage] [cite:us14_census_story2025]

Israel: from hyperinflation to fifteen flat years

Any Israeli series that starts in 1980 runs through the worst inflation in the country's history. Prices rose 445 per cent in 1984, by the Bank of Israel's count, so that the average price level multiplied about five and a half times in a single year. The 1985 Economic Stabilization Plan froze the exchange rate, prices and wages for an extended period, drew on an American grant to cover part of the state's deficit, and was followed by a new shekel worth 1,000 old ones. Inflation then ran at about 20 per cent a year until the mid-1990s, when the central bank began setting annual targets; a long-term target of 1–3 per cent was fixed in the early 2000s. [cite:us14_boi_hyper] Nominal comparisons across 1980–1986 therefore mean little; the turn itself is set beside America's in Part Eleven. [scene:us11_turn|The 1985 plan and the American turn]

Once prices settled, the record shows pay barely moving. In a 2014 review, the Bank of Israel found that the gross real wage per employee post grew 0.8 per cent a year on average from 1996, fell 0.2 per cent a year from 2001 and grew 0.7 per cent a year from 2003, while output per employee grew about 1 per cent a year from 1990. The bank found no long-term gap between wages and productivity; the problem it identified was that productivity itself grew slowly, and in 2012 Israel's hourly wage was about 75 per cent of the OECD average in purchasing-power terms. [cite:us14_boi_wages2014] The Taub Center put it more bluntly in 2016: Israel's consumer prices rose 32 per cent from 2000 to 2014 and nominal wages rose by about as much, so there had been no rise in real wages for at least fifteen years. [cite:us14_globes_taubwages]

Pay has risen since, though unevenly. On the OECD's measure, in 2024 dollars of equal purchasing power, the Israeli average wage fell from $49,340 in 2000 to $46,050 in 2010, then rose to $51,659 in 2020 and $54,736 in 2024: a gain of about 11 per cent over the whole period, all of it after 2010. [cite:us14_oecd_avwage] In shekels, the CBS put the average monthly wage per employee post at NIS 14,672 in March 2025 and NIS 13,907 in April; April's pay was 3.6 per cent higher than a year earlier, the same as inflation, so the real gain was nil. In the technology sector, about a tenth of employee posts, the average was NIS 36,731. [cite:us14_globes_wage2025] An average is pulled up by high earners; the CBS does not publish a monthly median wage in the same release, which is one reason Part Thirteen measures low pay through the minimum wage. [scene:us13_wages|Part Thirteen: wages]

The United States: record household income, uneven gains

America's longest consistent income series is the Census Bureau's median household income, adjusted for inflation, from 1967. In 2025 it reached $87,460, up 2.6 per cent from $85,210 in 2024 and the highest on record; after taxes, the median was $76,060. Over the whole series the gains were not shared evenly: from 1967 to 2025, pre-tax household income rose about 56 per cent at the tenth and fiftieth percentiles and about 121 per cent at the ninetieth, and the ratio of the ninetieth to the tenth widened from 9.23 to 13.06. [cite:us14_census_story2025] [cite:us14_census_p60] A household measure counts every earner in the household; it is not the same as a wage.

On the OECD's wage measure, the American average rose from $64,928 in 2000 to $71,439 in 2010, $82,783 in 2020 and $82,933 in 2024, all in 2024 purchasing-power dollars: about 28 per cent over the period. [cite:us14_oecd_avwage] The Israeli average was 76 per cent of the American in 2000 and 66 per cent in 2024.

Prices now: two inflations in 2026

In 2026 the two countries' prices moved in different directions. Israel's annual inflation fell to 1.6 per cent in June, a five-year low and inside the Bank of Israel's 1–3 per cent target, and stood at 1.6 per cent in September, with the housing component at 3.8 per cent. [cite:us14_globes_cpi_june26] [cite:us14_te_cpi_sep26] American consumer prices rose 3.7 per cent in the year to September 2026. Most of the rise was energy: energy prices were up 20.4 per cent and petrol 34.2 per cent, in the year of the war with Iran, while food rose 2.5 per cent, shelter 3.2 per cent and prices excluding food and energy 2.6 per cent. [cite:us14_bls_cpi_sep26] What that war cost each treasury is set out elsewhere in the library. [scene:ir14_bill|The American bill, 1979–2026] [scene:gi16_costs|What the wars cost]

What the series show, and what they do not

Measured this way, the American average wage both started higher and grew faster after 2000, and American median household income set a record in 2025, while Israeli pay was flat in real terms for much of the 2000s and recovered only after 2010. [cite:us14_oecd_avwage] [cite:us14_globes_taubwages] Two cautions apply. First, these are averages and medians of pay; they say nothing yet about what that pay buys, because a purchasing-power wage already adjusts for each country's general price level but not for the particular things families must buy, such as housing, which the next section measures separately. Second, the American gains were concentrated at the top of the distribution, and the Israeli average is lifted by a technology sector paying more than twice the national figure. [cite:us14_census_story2025] [cite:us14_globes_wage2025] The Israeli series from 1980 to 1996 exists, but runs through hyperinflation and wage indexation; this book did not rebuild it year by year, and no figure here compares Israeli real wages before 1996.

sections.h: Housing Against Income
sections.html:
Housing is the largest single cost for most households in both countries and the item on which the two systems' records differ most. It is also the item on which their measures differ. Israeli statisticians usually count how many months of the average wage it takes to buy the average home; American researchers usually divide the median home price by median household income. Both are ratios of price to income, but one uses a single wage and the other a whole household's income, and a household often has more than one earner. The two sets of figures below are therefore set side by side over time within each country, not against each other as if they measured the same thing. [cite:us14_bls_ce2024] [cite:us14_reuters_cpiweights] [cite:us14_globes_salaries2023] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] Land, planning law and public housing, which drive these prices, are the subject of Part Fifteen. [scene:us15_housing|Part Fifteen: housing]

Israel: from 129 salaries to 155

Israel's housing measure rose across the 2010s. In 2010, by a survey published by the Housing and Construction Minister, an average-priced apartment cost 129 average monthly salaries. [cite:us14_wiki_j14] The Ministry of Construction and Housing put the figure at 146 salaries for 2014, and the CBS put it at 155 salaries, or 12.9 years of the average wage, for 2022, when the average home cost NIS 1.87 million and the average monthly salary was NIS 12,100. The spread between cities was wide: 26.9 years of the average wage in Jerusalem, 25.4 in Bnei Brak and 22.2 in Tel Aviv, against 10.1 in Haifa and 10 in Beersheba. [cite:us14_globes_salaries2023] The three estimates come from different bodies whose methods may not match exactly; they agree on the direction.

Behind the ratio is a long rise in prices. The CBS index of dwelling prices rose about 226 per cent in nominal terms from 2008 to 2025, and about 136 per cent after inflation, by Global Property Guide's compilation of the index. Real prices rose 15 per cent in 2009 alone and 10 per cent in 2021, and fell in only a few years, among them 2018, 2023 and 2025. [cite:us14_gpg_israel] By late 2025 the market had cooled: the annual rise had slowed to 0.5 per cent after peaking at 7.8 per cent earlier in the year, and in the third quarter the average apartment cost NIS 3.03 million in Tel Aviv and NIS 2.90 million in Jerusalem, against about NIS 1.57 million in the south and NIS 1.56 million in the north. [cite:us14_toi_housing_nov25] The Bank of Israel cut its policy rate to 4.25 per cent in November 2025, its first cut in almost two years, and by April–May 2026 home prices were about 2 per cent lower than a year earlier. [cite:us14_toi_housing_nov25] [cite:us14_globes_cpi_june26]

A fuller measure, Tel Aviv University's Alrov Institute Housing Affordability Index, combines the three things that decide whether a household can buy: home prices from Tax Authority transaction records, household income after tax from the CBS, and mortgage rates from the Bank of Israel, for a four-room flat in twelve cities, each quarter, most recently for the first quarter of 2026. [cite:us14_alrov_hai] Its values sit in quarterly reports that this book did not extract; they would allow an Israeli series with interest rates included, comparable in design to America's.

Rents rose with prices. They rose 34 per cent on average from 2005 to 2011, and 49 per cent in the Tel Aviv metropolitan area, by CBS figures; those increases were the immediate cause of the 2011 tent protest. [cite:us14_wiki_j14] The housing component of Israel's consumer price index was still rising faster than prices as a whole in 2026: it was up 3.8 per cent in the year to September against 1.6 per cent for all items. [cite:us14_te_cpi_sep26] The protest and the government's response are the subject of the last section of this part. [scene:us14_protests|The 2011 protests]

The United States: from three years of income to five

Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies (JCHS) tracks the national ratio of the median single-family home price to median household income. It averaged 3.2 in the 1990s, was 4.1 in 2019 and reached 5.0 in 2024, nearly matching the previous record. Between 2019 and 2024 median single-family prices rose 48 per cent while median household income rose 22 per cent. As in Israel, the spread between regions was wide: the ratio exceeded 12 in San Jose and was 7.3 in New York, but under 3 in McAllen, Akron and Toledo. [cite:us14_jchs_pti]

The same centre measures the share of households "cost-burdened", spending more than 30 per cent of income on housing. In 2024, 22.7 million renter households were cost-burdened, 49 per cent of all renters and a record number; the stock of units renting for under $1,000 a month fell from 8.3 million in 2014 to 5.8 million in 2024. [cite:us14_nlihc_jchs2026] Owners were burdened too: about 24 per cent of owner households, 20.7 million, spent 30 per cent or more of income on housing in 2024, four million more than in 2019. For buyers the change after the pandemic was steep: in March 2019, 49 per cent of homes listed for sale were affordable to a household earning $75,000 or less; in March 2026, 23 per cent were. [cite:us14_novoco_jchs2026]

Reading the two records together

A rough translation is possible, with its limits stated. Twelve point nine years of a single average wage, Israel's 2022 figure, is a heavier load than five years of a median household's income, America's 2024 figure, but an Israeli household often has more than one earner, and the Israeli figure uses the average home and the average wage rather than medians. [cite:us14_globes_salaries2023] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] The direction of travel is the firmer finding. In both countries homes became markedly less affordable relative to income: in Israel over the whole period from 2008, with real prices more than doubling, and in the United States most sharply after 2019. [cite:us14_gpg_israel] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] In both, the burden fell hardest on renters and on buyers in the largest cities.

sections.h: The Basket, Item by Item
sections.html:
A general price level hides the items that matter most to a given family. This section takes the household budget apart: food, cars and phones, where cross-country price levels exist; childcare, college and health, where each country's own system decides most of the cost; fuel and debt; and finally the closest honest version of a family's monthly budget then and now. Cross-country comparisons here use the OECD's purchasing-power price levels, which compare what the same basket costs in each country, not market exchange rates. [cite:us14_toi_food52]

Price levels: Israel among the dearest in the OECD

In 2022 Israel had the highest overall price level of any OECD member, 38 per cent above the member average, and its food and beverage prices were 52 per cent above the developed-country average in the data the OECD released in 2024, second only to South Korea. Dairy and eggs were 64 per cent above average, meat 64 per cent, bread and grains 49 per cent and cars 52 per cent, the highest in the OECD. One category ran the other way: telecommunications were 30 per cent below the average, while the United States was among the dearest for telecoms at 51 per cent above. [cite:us14_toi_food52] In its 2025 Economic Survey of Israel the OECD ranked Israel fourth for comparable price levels, gave a whole chapter to the cost of living, and warned that it "continues to reduce welfare and spur social tensions". [cite:us14_toi_oecd2025] [cite:us14_oecd_survey2025]

The OECD's explanation is mostly about the system that brings goods to market. It cites Israel's distance from its trading partners and tense relations with its neighbours, difficult border procedures, complex regulatory standards and agricultural tariffs, and recommends lowering tariffs on vegetables, fruit and dairy, cutting red tape at the border and negotiating new trade agreements. [cite:us14_ecoscope] [cite:us14_oecd_survey2025] Concentration compounds it: in a 2016 Brookings analysis, Dany Bahar found Israeli manufacturing, including food producers, about 70 per cent more concentrated than the OECD average and services about twice as concentrated, with low import competition to offset it. [cite:us14_brookings_bahar] Part Eleven sets out the 2013 law that tried to break up Israel's business groups. [scene:us11_concentration|Concentration]

Phones: the reform that worked

The one category in which Israel is cheap is the result of a deliberate policy. In 2011–12 the communications ministry under Moshe Kahlon pushed through a reform to bring competition into the mobile market. By the minister's own figures, presented to the cabinet in December 2012, the average price per minute fell from NIS 0.42 to NIS 0.10, average monthly spending per user fell from NIS 145 in 2010 to NIS 93, and the public saved NIS 5.7 billion in two years. [cite:us14_globes_kahlon] Bahar, writing independently, put the fall in average mobile bills at over 70 per cent. [cite:us14_brookings_bahar]

Childcare and college: where each system sets the price

Israel made preschool free for three- and four-year-olds after the 2011 protests. Following the Trajtenberg Committee, the Knesset extended the Compulsory Education Law to all children of those ages from the 2012–13 school year, and the Finance Committee added NIS 1.3 billion to the Education Ministry's budget to start building the classes. [cite:us14_taub_preschool] [cite:us14_jpost_saar] The saving to families was smaller than the law suggests: by the Taub Center's study, average parental payment for three- and four-year-olds fell 11.5 per cent, and household spending per child aged two to five only 3 per cent. [cite:us14_taub_preschool] The United States has no national free preschool; its childcare costs, subsidies and parental leave are compared in Part Eighteen, which uses the Labor Department's childcare price database. [scene:us18_family|Part Eighteen: family policy]

College is set nationally in Israel and by each state and institution in America. The Council for Higher Education links tuition to the consumer price index; for 2025–26 a bachelor's degree at the Hebrew University cost Israeli citizens NIS 12,017 a year. [cite:us14_huji_tuition] In the United States the average published tuition at a public four-year college for in-state students was $11,950 in 2025–26, and $45,000 at a private non-profit; in 2025 dollars the public figure had about doubled from $5,940 in 1995–96. Grants change the picture: after grant aid, the average in-state public student paid about $2,300 in net tuition in 2025–26, down from a peak of $4,450 in 2012–13. [cite:us14_cb_trends2025] [cite:us14_ncan_cb] Neither figure includes living costs; Part Seventeen compares the systems in full. [scene:us17_higher|Part Seventeen: universities]

Health: universal coverage, rising private payments

The two health systems put costs on families in different ways. Israel's 1995 law covers every resident through the health funds, but the private share of national health spending has grown: it was 39.9 per cent in 2012, when the public share was 60.1 per cent in Israel, 76.1 per cent across the OECD and 47.8 per cent in the United States. Real private health spending per Israeli rose 69.5 per cent from 1995 to 2011, against 20.8 per cent for public spending, and about 80 per cent of Israelis held supplementary insurance. Out-of-pocket payments alone were 2.05 per cent of GDP in Israel in 2011, more than in the United States (1.80 per cent) or the OECD average (1.47 per cent). [cite:us14_taub_health2014] American families pay mainly through premiums: the average employer family plan cost $26,993 in 2025, of which the worker paid $6,850, and premiums rose 26 per cent in five years against wage growth of 28.6 per cent; the average deductible for single coverage was $1,886. [cite:us14_kff_ehbs2025] [cite:us14_rise_kff] The Taub figures are a 2011–12 snapshot; Part Sixteen brings both systems' spending to 2024. [scene:us16_systems|Part Sixteen: health systems]

Fuel, energy and debt

Energy was the most volatile item in 2026. American energy prices rose 20.4 per cent and petrol 34.2 per cent in the year to September 2026, while Israeli fuel prices fell 3.1 per cent in June alone. [cite:us14_bls_cpi_sep26] [cite:us14_globes_cpi_june26] No comparable fuel-price series for the two countries is given here; snapshot figures from aggregators, converted at exchange rates, are not used.

Debt is where America's system carries more risk. American households owed $18.77 trillion in the second quarter of 2026: $13.12 trillion in mortgages, $1.26 trillion on credit cards, $1.71 trillion in car loans and $1.65 trillion in student loans, with 4.7 per cent of all debt in some stage of delinquency. [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026] Israeli households owed about NIS 890 billion at the end of the third quarter of 2025, NIS 644 billion of it for housing, which was growing about 8 per cent a year. [cite:us14_boi_debt_q3_2025] Set against each economy, by figures Globes compiled from two data services, household debt was 42.3 per cent of GDP in Israel and 69.2 per cent in the United States in 2024. [cite:us14_globes_mortgagegdp]

A family's budget, then and now

The only honest way to build a monthly budget over time is from each country's expenditure survey, and the two surveys differ: America's counts the average "consumer unit", Israel's the average household, and both report means, not medians. In the United States, the average consumer unit in 1984, of 2.6 people, had pre-tax income of $23,464 and spent $21,975, about $1,830 a month; housing took 30.4 per cent of spending, transport 19.6, food 15.0, insurance and pensions 8.6, health care 4.8 and education 1.4. [cite:us14_bls_ce1984] In 2024 it had pre-tax income of $104,207 and spent $78,535, about $6,545 a month; housing took 33.4 per cent, transport 17.0, food 12.9, insurance and pensions 12.5, health care 7.9 and education 2.0. [cite:us14_bls_ce2024] Housing, health and pensions grew as shares; food and transport shrank.

Israel's survey runs back to 1979–80, but this book could verify only recent points. In 2010 the average household spent NIS 13,496 a month on consumption, 35 per cent of it on housing and home maintenance; for the poorest fifth, housing and food together took half of spending, for the richest a third. [cite:us14_globes_hes2010] The 2023 consumer price index, whose weights the CBS takes from the survey, gave housing 26 per cent, food 18.3 per cent and transport and telecoms 17.5 per cent. [cite:us14_reuters_cpiweights] The categories are not the same as America's, and a price-index weight is not the same as a survey share, so the shares are read within each country, not across. Food's weight in Israel's index (18.3 per cent) is higher than its share of American spending (12.9 per cent), which fits the price levels above, but the difference in definitions means the gap should not be read as exact.

sections.h: Cottage Cheese, Tents and the Trajtenberg Committee
sections.html:
In the summer of 2011 the cost of living became, by many accounts, the largest social protest in Israel's history. It began with a dairy product and a Facebook page and grew, within weeks, into tent camps in city centres and marches of several hundred thousand people. The government answered with an expert committee whose recommendations were partly enacted. Because the episode tested what a state does when its citizens say they cannot afford to live, this section follows it from the price rise to the policy, and then sets the outcome beside what the OECD still found fourteen years later. [cite:us14_aje_timeline] [cite:us14_wiki_trajtenberg]

The cottage-cheese boycott

Israel lifted state price supervision of dairy products in 2006. By June 2011 the price of cottage cheese, a staple, had risen nearly 40 per cent in three years, to just over $2 for a standard tub; butter had risen 39.1 per cent and a small carton of cream 69 per cent. Tnuva was the main producer. [cite:us14_jta_cottage] In mid-June Yitzhak (Itzik) Alrov, a 25-year-old cantor, opened a Facebook page calling for a boycott until the price fell; it drew 90,000 members within a week and more than 105,000 in two weeks. Finance Minister Yuval Steinitz said he would "break the monopoly" in the dairy industry, and a Knesset committee called for price controls to be restored. [cite:us14_jta_cottage] [cite:us14_ap_cottage] On 30 June Tnuva cut the price of a 250-gram tub by about 25 per cent, from close to NIS 8 to NIS 5.90, and Strauss and Tara followed. [cite:us14_ap_cottage]

The tent protests

Two weeks later the anger moved to housing. On 14 July 2011 Daphni Leef, a 25-year-old video editor, pitched a tent in Habima Square in Tel Aviv and opened a Facebook page inviting others to join. [cite:us14_wiki_j14] Al Jazeera's timeline dates the encampment of hundreds of young people on Rothschild Boulevard, in protest at high rents, to 17 July. [cite:us14_aje_timeline] The context was rents up 34 per cent nationally and 49 per cent in the Tel Aviv area since 2005. [cite:us14_wiki_j14] Tens of thousands marched on 23 July; on 30 July more than 100,000 gathered in Tel Aviv, with hundreds of thousands protesting nationwide; about 300,000 demonstrated on 6 August. [cite:us14_aje_timeline]

The largest night came on 3 September, the "March of the Million". Israel Hayom counted at least 300,000 in Tel Aviv, 40,000 to 60,000 in Jerusalem and at least 35,000 in Haifa, more than 400,000 in all; Al Jazeera reported an estimated 400,000, and later accounts give about 460,000. The figures are estimates whose authors were not named. [cite:us14_ih_400k] [cite:us14_aje_timeline] [cite:us14_wiki_j14] The demands went beyond rent to the cost of raising children and, from southern dairy farmers, opposition to a government plan to import dairy products: the protest held consumers who wanted cheaper food and producers who feared cheaper imports. [cite:us14_ih_400k]

The government's answer

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded first with a housing package on 26 July, promising 50,000 homes and subsidised public transport for students, which the activists rejected as insufficient. [cite:us14_aje_timeline] On 8 August he appointed the Committee for Socioeconomic Change, chaired by Professor Manuel Trajtenberg, then head of the higher-education planning and budgeting committee. [cite:us14_wiki_trajtenberg] It reported on 26 September. Its main recommendations were 196,000 new flats over five years, a fifth of them affordable; free education from age three; corporate and capital-gains taxes raised to 25 per cent; lower prices for supervised products such as milk and eggs; express buses from the periphery; and a 50 per cent public-transport discount for students. Netanyahu called the report an important landmark. Leef said it contained no far-reaching change, and fellow organiser Regev Contes said the numbers "don't even come near what the public needs". [cite:us14_ynet_trajtenberg] The committee also recommended slower growth in defence spending and competition measures in cement, ports, fuel and dairy. [cite:us14_wiki_trajtenberg]

The cabinet chose to enact the package in stages rather than at once. The Knesset approved the tax changes on 5 December 2011; the competition measures passed the cabinet in December 2011 and the housing plan in March 2012; measures on Haredi employment were left out. [cite:us14_wiki_trajtenberg] Free preschool for three- and four-year-olds began in the 2012–13 school year, with NIS 1.3 billion added to the Education Ministry's budget. [cite:us14_jpost_saar] [cite:us14_taub_preschool] The mobile-phone reform, already under way, cut bills sharply over the same period. [cite:us14_globes_kahlon]

What changed and what did not

Measured against the protest's own grievances, the record is mixed. On this book's reading, the parts of the package that depended on a single decision were delivered: the tax rises, free preschool from three and, separately, mobile prices that by the OECD's 2024 data left telecoms 30 per cent below the member average. [cite:us14_wiki_trajtenberg] [cite:us14_taub_preschool] [cite:us14_toi_food52] The parts that depended on breaking market structure or building at scale were not. The cottage-cheese price cut held attention, but in 2014 a new protest compared the price of an Israeli chocolate pudding with a much cheaper German version, and in 2022 there were protests over pasta prices. [cite:us14_ecoscope] By the OECD's 2024 data, dairy and eggs in Israel cost 64 per cent more than the developed-country average, and the 2025 Economic Survey again recommended cutting the tariffs on dairy, fruit and vegetables. [cite:us14_toi_food52] [cite:us14_ecoscope] On housing, the number of average monthly salaries needed to buy the average home rose from 129 in 2010 to 155 in 2022. [cite:us14_wiki_j14] [cite:us14_globes_salaries2023]

The American record in the same years

The United States produced no comparable government commission on the cost of living in the sources used for this part, and its price pressures fell on different items. Its telecoms were among the OECD's dearest, at 51 per cent above the average, while Israel's were 30 per cent below it. [cite:us14_toi_food52] Its housing ratio rose from 4.1 in 2019 to 5.0 in 2024, and a record 22.7 million renter households paid more than 30 per cent of income for housing in 2024. [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [cite:us14_nlihc_jchs2026] Employer family health premiums rose 26 per cent in the five years to 2025. [cite:us14_kff_ehbs2025] The two countries hold national elections within a week of each other, Israel on 27 October and the United States on 3 November 2026; the figures in this part are as of October 2026.

chapters.label: Part Fifteen
chapters.title: Housing, Land and Infrastructure
chapters.intro: Part Fifteen turns from what housing costs to the systems underneath it: who owns the land, who may build on it, what each state does for those the housing market leaves out, and the public works on which daily life depends. In Israel the state manages almost all land and leases it to households, through an authority whose governing council includes the Jewish National Fund; the part follows the court rulings and laws on who may receive that land, and the planning and permit record of Arab towns and unrecognised Bedouin villages. In the United States most land is private and the decisive power is local zoning. The second section compares homeownership, public housing and homelessness, and the third compares water and Israel's turn to desalination, electricity and climate policy, public transport, and the response to disasters, including war damage in Israel. Status lines are as of October 2026, ahead of Israel's election on 27 October and America's on 3 November.
chapters.outro: Part Fifteen found two land systems built on opposite foundations that, on this book's reading, arrive at a similar result. Israel's state manages 93 per cent of the land and leases it; its courts barred allocation by religion or nationality in 2000 and the Attorney General opened JNF land to all bidders in 2005, but admissions committees may still screen applicants to small communities, and the Arab sector, whose 139 towns and villages sit on less than 3 per cent of the land, received 97 per cent of the administrative demolition orders issued in 2012–14. [cite:us15_wiki_ila] [cite:us15_ynet_mazuz2005] [cite:us15_aj_admissions2014] [cite:us15_acri_kaminitz] America's land is mostly private, and local zoning that reserves most residential land for detached houses sets the price of entry to a neighbourhood. [cite:us15_wiki_sfzoning] America counted 745,652 homeless people on one night in January 2025, against Israeli service counts in the low thousands, while Israel's public housing shrank from about 60,000 apartments to 53,000 in five years. [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] [cite:us15_comptroller_ph2020] In infrastructure, Israel's desalination now supplies most of its drinking water, but its electricity remains mostly gas-fired and its metro is a decade away; the United States has doubled its renewable share since 1990, left the Paris Agreement a second time on 27 January 2026, and is redesigning its disaster agency. [cite:us15_wiki_water] [cite:us15_calcalist_renew] [cite:us15_comptroller_metro] [cite:us15_eia_mix2025] [cite:us15_harvard_paris] [cite:us15_crs_fema] Part Sixteen turns to health. [scene:us16_systems|Part Sixteen: health systems]

sections.h: Who Owns the Land, and Who May Build on It
sections.html:
The two countries begin from opposite ends. In Israel almost all land is public and households lease it from the state; in the United States most land is private and the decisive public power is local zoning, which says what an owner may build. Each arrangement serves some people well and leaves others out, and in each the people left out are concentrated in identifiable places. This section sets out the law in each country, what the record shows about who gains access to land and building rights, and where the arrangement has been challenged in court or reformed. Land in the West Bank, which runs under a separate legal system, is treated in Part Nine and in the volume on the West Bank. [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank] [scene:wb4_land|The West Bank: land]

Israel: 93 per cent public, held on lease

The Israel Land Authority (ILA) manages 93 per cent of the land inside Israel, about 19.5 million dunams. That land belongs to three owners: the state, the Development Authority and the Jewish National Fund (JNF). The remaining 7 per cent is privately owned or held by religious bodies. An Israeli who "owns" a home usually holds a 49- or 98-year lease from the ILA; urban land is typically leased for 49 years with an option of a further 49. [cite:us15_wiki_ila] The system was set up in 1960 by four instruments: Basic Law: Israel Lands, the Israel Lands Law, the Israel Land Administration Law, and a covenant between the state and the World Zionist Organization for the JNF. The JNF's place in that covenant is visible in the governing body: the Israel Land Council has 22 members, 12 from government ministries and 10 from the JNF. [cite:us15_wiki_ila] A reform in 2009 replaced the old Israel Land Administration with the Israel Land Authority and converted long-term leases on some residential land into private ownership, with the stated aim of reducing bureaucracy for homeowners. [cite:us15_wiki_ila]

The JNF is older than the state. It was founded at the Fifth Zionist Congress in 1901, bought land to lease rather than sell, and held 936,000 dunams by the eve of statehood. [cite:dv2_wiki_jnf] Today it owns about 13 per cent of Israel's land and describes itself as the caretaker of the land on behalf of the Jewish people everywhere. [cite:us15_aj_jnf2007] That self-description is the source of the main legal question in the Israeli land system: whether land the state manages may be allocated by religion or nationality.

The courts and the JNF: Ka'adan, Mazuz and admissions committees

The courts have answered that question in principle. In the Ka'adan case of 2000, brought by an Arab family refused a home in the community town of Katzir, the High Court held that the state may not allocate land on the basis of religion or nationality, even through a third party such as the Jewish Agency. [cite:us15_wiki_ila] In 2004 the ILA barred non-Jews from a housing tender in Carmiel because the land was JNF land, and the rights group Adalah petitioned. On 26 January 2005 Attorney General Menachem Mazuz decided that all land the ILA manages, JNF land included, may be marketed to Jews and non-Jews without discrimination. A JNF spokesman objected that "it's only fitting our land would be solely for Jewish settlers" while Israel's security was not secured. [cite:us15_ynet_mazuz2005] The compromise was a swap: when a non-Jew wins JNF land, the ILA may compensate the JNF with other state land, so that the JNF's total holding is not reduced. Petitioners said in 2007 that the decision was still not being followed. [cite:us15_aj_jnf2007]

The Knesset then gave small communities a different tool. The Admissions Committees Law of 2011, an amendment to the Cooperative Societies Ordinance, lets admissions committees in small communities in the Negev and the Galilee reject applicants for incompatibility with the community's "social-cultural fabric". Adalah counted 434 localities covered. On 17 September 2014 the Supreme Court dismissed the petitions against the law by five votes to four. [cite:us15_aj_admissions2014] The majority did not hold the law valid in every use; it held the challenge was not yet ripe, because the law was not discriminatory on its face, included an anti-discrimination clause, and had produced no concrete case of discriminatory use before the court. [cite:us15_toi_fuchs_admissions] A 2009 sponsor, MK David Rotem, said it served communities "established by people who want to live with other Jews"; a council head said the committees had "nothing to do with Arab citizens". [cite:us15_aj_admissions2014]

Building in Arab towns: planning, permits and demolition

Most Arab citizens do not live in the small communities the admissions law covers. About 90 per cent live in 139 Arab towns and villages whose combined jurisdiction covers less than 3 per cent of the state's area, by the figures six Israeli civil-society groups compiled from official sources in 2017. Those jurisdictions had not grown with the population, and density within them had risen about elevenfold. [cite:us15_acri_kaminitz] Until 2000 the Arab localities had no up-to-date outline plans, the documents without which a building permit cannot be issued. The same paper, citing the Finance Ministry's 2015 "120-Day Team" report, put the Arab population's need at about 13,000 new homes a year against about 7,000 built, and found that from 2005 to 2009 about 20 per cent of planned units in Arab localities had been marketed, against 70 per cent in Jewish and mixed towns. [cite:us15_acri_kaminitz]

Building without a permit followed, and so did enforcement. By figures of the Knesset Research and Information Center, 97 per cent of administrative demolition orders issued from 2012 to 2014 were in the Arab sector, as were 97 per cent of the 1,348 judicial demolition orders in force in July 2015. [cite:us15_acri_kaminitz] On the night of 5 April 2017 the Knesset approved the Kaminitz Law, an amendment to the 1965 Planning and Building Law. Its stated aim was stronger enforcement against illegal building: it moved enforcement powers to a national body, widened administrative powers to demolish and evict while limiting court review, and sharply raised fines. Adalah called it discriminatory in effect against Arab citizens. [cite:us15_adalah_kaminitz] [cite:us15_acri_kaminitz] In the Negev, about 120,000 Bedouin citizens lived in 46 villages the state did not recognise in 2018; homes in the village of Umm el-Hiran were demolished in January 2017. [cite:us15_jpost_bedouin2018]

The government's answer on the planning side has been money and plans. Resolution 922 of 30 December 2015 funded outline plans for 20 Arab local authorities among much else, and Resolution 550 of 24 October 2021, worth NIS 30 billion over five years, set targets of marketing 5,000 homes on state land in Arab towns in 2022 and up to 9,000 by 2026. [cite:us15_inss_922] Part Eight covers the plans' wider results. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: equality among Israel's citizens] The money has been cut since the war: the Israel Democracy Institute recorded a 15 per cent cut after October 2023 and, in December 2025, a draft decision to move about NIS 3 billion from the plan to the Ministry of National Security, much of it from the housing and interior budgets. The institute advised against it. This book did not find the outcome of that proposal or of the plan's renewal due in 2026. [cite:us15_idi_550cut]

The United States: private land, federal West, local zoning

The federal government owns about 640 million acres, roughly 28 per cent of the country's 2.27 billion acres, but that land is concentrated in Alaska (61 per cent federal) and the eleven western states (46 per cent), against about 4 per cent in all other states. Four agencies hold almost all of it: the Bureau of Land Management (244 million acres), the Forest Service (193 million), the Fish and Wildlife Service (89 million) and the National Park Service (80 million). [cite:us15_crs_fedland] About 816 million acres of former public domain passed to private owners, nearly all before 1940; a 1976 law declared that the rest would generally stay federal. [cite:us15_crs_fedland]

Where Americans live, therefore, the land is mostly private, and the binding rules are local. In Village of Euclid v. Ambler (1926) the Supreme Court upheld a town's power to exclude apartment buildings from residential districts, with Justice Sutherland writing that "very often the apartment house is a mere parasite". By a 2019 New York Times analysis, about three-quarters of residential land in many American cities is zoned for detached single-family homes only, from 94 per cent in San Jose to 15 per cent in New York City. [cite:us15_wiki_sfzoning] Such rules name no group; their effect is to set a price of entry into a neighbourhood. Part Eight covers America's racial gaps and Part Fourteen the price of housing. [scene:us8_us|Part Eight: the United States] [scene:us14_housing|Part Fourteen: housing against income] Since 2018 a reform movement has loosened them: Minneapolis ended single-family-only zoning in December 2018, Oregon required duplexes and more in most cities from 2019, California's SB 9 allowed two to four homes on single-family lots from 2021, and Washington State followed in 2023. [cite:us15_wiki_sfzoning]

Israel's land figures are mostly snapshots, not series; the demolition data stop in 2015 and the unrecognised-village count in 2018, and this book did not find a current official count of either. The American zoning share is a city-level estimate from 2019, not a national series. What the record does show is that both systems have outlawed open allocation by group while keeping lawful screening devices, a community's "fabric" in one case and a lot size in the other, whose effects fall unevenly.

sections.h: Homes, Public Housing and Homelessness
sections.html:
Part Fourteen measured how far housing prices have run ahead of incomes in both countries. [scene:us14_housing|Part Fourteen: housing against income] This section looks at what each state does for the households the market does not house: how many own their homes, what public or subsidised housing exists, and how many people end up without a home at all. The two states measure these things differently, and in Israel some of them are measured only occasionally, so the figures below are set side by side within each country and compared across countries only where the definitions allow.

The United States: ownership at 65 per cent, unevenly shared

The Census Bureau's quarterly survey put the American homeownership rate at 65.0 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, unchanged from a year earlier. [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226] That is below the rate's peak of 69.2 per cent in 2004 and below its 25-year average of 66.3 per cent. [cite:us15_nahb_q226] Ownership is the main store of wealth for most American families, and its distribution is uneven. In the same quarter 74.5 per cent of non-Hispanic white households owned their homes, against 45.4 per cent of Black households and 58.6 per cent of Asian American and Pacific Islander households. Among householders under 35 the rate was 35.2 per cent, down from 36.4 per cent a year earlier. [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226] The racial gaps are the outcome of documented mechanisms, among them federal lending rules, zoning and wealth passed between generations, which Part Eight sets out; they are not a description of any group's choices. [scene:us8_us|Part Eight: the United States]

For households that cannot buy, the strain shows in the rental market Part Fourteen described: 22.7 million renter households, 49 per cent of all renters, spent more than 30 per cent of their income on housing in 2024. [cite:us14_nlihc_jchs2026]

American homelessness: a single night each January

The federal measure of homelessness is a count taken by local agencies on a single night each January, the point-in-time (PIT) count, of people in shelters and on the street. It is the longest consistent American series on the subject, running from 2007. It counted 647,258 people in 2007, fell to a low of 549,928 in 2016, and then rose, to 653,104 in 2023 and to a record 771,480 in January 2024, of whom 274,224 were unsheltered. [cite:us15_crs_homeless] The January 2025 count, published by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) on 29 May 2026, found 745,652 people, a fall of 3 per cent, with 266,320 unsheltered. [cite:us15_hud_pit2025]

The same release carried the administration's reading of those figures. HUD said homelessness had risen 27 per cent and chronic homelessness 81 per cent since 2013, the year it took as the start of the "Housing First" approach, which places people in housing before requiring treatment or work. Secretary Scott Turner's department said that approach "has failed to meaningfully reduce homelessness", and attributed the 2025 fall to decreases in what it called "Sanctuary Cities". [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] These are the department's stated positions. The count itself excludes people living in housing funded for the formerly homeless, which HUD put at a combined total of 1,456,923 people homeless or in such housing; so a policy that moves people off the street into subsidised housing lowers the PIT count by design. [cite:us15_hud_pit2025]

Israel: public housing that shrank by sale

Israel's public housing is small and shrinking. The State Comptroller found that the stock of public housing apartments fell from about 60,000 in 2014 to about 53,000 in 2019. The main reason was a policy choice: the law lets tenants buy their apartments at a discount, and about 10,000 were sold in those six years, with discounts worth NIS 3.2 billion, while the state bought only about 2,600 to replace them, at a cost of NIS 3.4 billion. [cite:us15_comptroller_ph2020] In 2019, 3,700 eligible people were waiting for a public apartment, and those who moved in that year had waited an average of 31 months. About 200 apartments were expected to be added in the following years, enough, by the comptroller's own reckoning, for only about 4.5 per cent of those waiting. [cite:us15_comptroller_ph2020] The waiting list counts only those eligible under the programme's rules; it is not a measure of the number of households who cannot afford housing.

Israel's main housing programme since 2015 has instead been aimed at buyers. Under Mehir Lamishtaken ("Buyer's Price"), from 2015, and its successor Mehir Matara ("Target Price"), the state markets land for new apartments that first-time buyers can win in a lottery at a discount of 20 per cent or up to NIS 300,000. The April 2022 lottery offered about 10,000 homes in 31 localities and drew 119,207 registered households, nearly twelve for every home. [cite:us15_toi_mehirmatara] Because the land is state land, the programme is a direct use of the land system described in the previous section: the state chooses where to release land and on what terms. [scene:us15_land|Who owns the land]

Israeli homelessness: small counts, thin data

Israel has no annual count like America's. A Knesset report published in 2022 used two sources. The Welfare Ministry's figures showed about 2,000 homeless people receiving aid in 2019 and 2,250 in 2020, 86 per cent of them men. Local authorities reported treating about 3,470 homeless people in 2020, and knew of about 800 more street dwellers not in treatment. Shelters had room for about a third of the street population. [cite:us15_ynet_homeless2022] These are counts of people known to services, not a street census, and they cover a period before the war; this book found no later national figure. Israel's housing emergency after October 2023 took a different form: the displacement of about 60,000 residents from the north, about half of whom had not returned by March 2025, which Part Fifteen's last section takes up with disaster response. [cite:hz7_afp_north_return] [scene:us15_infra|Water, power, transit and disasters]

What the two records show

Even allowing for different definitions and a far larger population, American homelessness is far higher: hundreds of thousands of people on one January night, against Israeli service counts in the low thousands. Per head, that is roughly 218 per 100,000 Americans in January 2025 against roughly 38 per 100,000 Israelis on the 2020 local-authority count (this book's arithmetic from World Bank population figures), on measures that are not strictly comparable. [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] [cite:us15_ynet_homeless2022] [cite:us11_wb_pop] The American count has a long, consistent series and is the subject of an open policy dispute over Housing First; the Israeli figures are irregular and pre-date the war. Israel's gap lies elsewhere: it sold more than three public apartments for every one it bought between 2014 and 2019 and steered its effort toward discounted ownership for first-time buyers, which helps those who can buy. In the United States, by HUD's own total, almost 1.5 million people were either homeless or living in housing funded for the formerly homeless. [cite:us15_comptroller_ph2020] [cite:us15_toi_mehirmatara] [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] In both, the households least served are those who can neither buy nor reach the head of a waiting list.

sections.h: Water, Power, Transit and Disasters
sections.html:
Infrastructure is where the difference in scale between the two countries matters most. Israel is a small, dry, densely settled state with a national water carrier and a state-owned electricity utility; the United States is a continent whose water, power and roads are run largely by state, local and private bodies. The comparison below therefore concerns how each system is organised and how it has performed over time, not which country has more. It covers water, electricity and climate policy, public transport, and the response to disasters, including war damage in Israel.

Water: Israel's turn to the sea

Israel's water is run nationally. Mekorot, the state-owned bulk supplier, operates the National Water Carrier and supplies about 70 per cent of all water and 80 per cent of drinking water; a Water Authority created by a 2006 amendment to the 1959 Water Law regulates the sector. [cite:us15_wiki_water] Over two decades the state changed where its drinking water comes from. Large seawater desalination plants opened at Ashkelon in 2005, Palmachim in 2007, Hadera in 2009, Soreq in 2013 and Ashdod in 2015, and a second Soreq plant of 200 million cubic metres a year in March 2025. Desalination supplied about 35 per cent of drinking water in 2014 and 86 per cent of drinkable water in 2022. Almost 90 per cent of treated sewage is reused, mainly on farms. [cite:us15_wiki_water] The result is a supply largely independent of rainfall, paid for through progressive household tariffs that rose by more than 30 per cent in the years before 2013. [cite:us15_wiki_water]

The national grid does not serve everyone under Israel's control on the same terms. Under the 1995 Interim Agreement Israel provided the Palestinians with 52 million cubic metres in 2011, and the agreement bars Palestinians from drilling new wells in the shared Mountain Aquifer. [cite:us15_wiki_water] Part Nine sets out the two legal systems in the West Bank under which that allocation runs. [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank] In the United States the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE), which grades the country's infrastructure every four years, gave drinking water a C-minus and wastewater a D-plus in 2025. [cite:us15_asce_2025]

Electricity and climate policy

Israel's power system was rebuilt around offshore gas. The Tamar field was discovered in 2009 and Leviathan began producing in late 2019; coal's share of generation fell from 52 per cent in 2013 to 17 per cent in 2023. [cite:us15_ita_israelenergy] By 2024 natural gas supplied 71 per cent of electricity, coal 14 per cent and solar and wind 14 per cent, up from 12 per cent in 2023. The government had set a 20 per cent renewable target for 2025, and an analyst at BDO estimated it would reach about 16 per cent; the coal phase-out date set in 2019 for 2025 had slipped to 2027 at the earliest. [cite:us15_calcalist_renew] A government decision of October 2020 targets 30 per cent renewable electricity by 2030. The state-owned Israel Electric Corporation still produced 56 per cent of electricity in 2023 and holds a monopoly of transmission and distribution, after a 2018 reform opened generation to private producers. [cite:us15_ita_israelenergy]

American utility-scale generation in 2025 came about 41 per cent from natural gas, 18 per cent from nuclear plants, 17 per cent from coal and 24 per cent from renewables, chiefly wind (11 per cent), solar (7 per cent) and hydropower (6 per cent). Renewables had supplied about 12 per cent in 1990. [cite:us15_eia_mix2025] Federal climate policy has reversed with each change of administration. The United States joined the Paris Agreement, left it on 4 November 2020 under President Trump, and, having rejoined, left again on 27 January 2026 under an order he signed on 20 January 2025; on 7 January 2026 the administration also announced withdrawal from the UN climate convention itself. The Inflation Reduction Act, signed on 16 August 2022, had been projected to help cut emissions to about 40 per cent below 2005 levels by 2030. [cite:us15_harvard_paris]
