Israel's climate policy has been slower to reach statute. The OECD's environmental review, released on 31 May 2023, found Israel not on track to meet its greenhouse-gas targets: emissions rose from 2014 to 2020 and fell afterwards, mainly because gas replaced coal, and renewables were 5 per cent of total energy supply against an OECD average of 12 per cent. It urged the Knesset to adopt "the government-approved draft Climate Law with its binding targets". [cite:us15_jpost_oecd_env] This book did not confirm whether that law had been enacted by October 2026. Over time, American fossil-fuel carbon dioxide emissions per person fell from about 21 tonnes in 2000 to about 13.6 tonnes in 2024, by the European Commission's EDGAR database. [cite:us15_wm_co2_us] The same database reports Israel together with the Palestinian territories, so its per-person figures are not Israel's own and are not used here. [cite:us15_wm_co2_il]

Transit and roads

Israel's crowded centre has paid for decades of delay in mass transit. The State Comptroller reported in December 2025 that congestion in the Tel Aviv area cost about NIS 10 billion in lost time in 2018 and would cost NIS 25 billion by 2040, that road service there was at the lowest grade, and that public transport's share of trips had fallen from 24 to 20 per cent against a target of 40 per cent. [cite:us15_comptroller_metro] Tel Aviv's first light-rail line, the Red Line, opened on 18 August 2023 after a private concession awarded in 2006 was revoked in 2010 and the project nationalised; it runs 24 kilometres and carries about 100,000 riders a day, with the Purple and Green lines due from 2027 to 2030. [cite:us15_wiki_tlvlr] A metro, authorised by a 2021 law at an approved cost of NIS 177 billion in 2025 prices, is scheduled to open its first phase in 2034; the Comptroller found its drilling surveys running behind. [cite:us15_comptroller_metro]

The United States has the opposite problem: an enormous road network in poor repair and thin transit outside a few cities. ASCE's 2025 report card gave the country an overall C, its highest grade since the report cards began in 1998 and up from C-minus in 2021, crediting the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021. It graded transit D, roads D-plus, bridges C and energy D-plus, and estimated a $3.7 trillion gap between planned and needed investment, up from $2.59 trillion four years earlier. [cite:us15_asce_2025]

Disasters and war damage

Federal disaster relief in the United States runs through the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), which pays states and households after a presidential disaster declaration. The administration has moved to redesign it. A FEMA Review Council created by executive order in January 2025 approved its final report on 7 May 2026. It recommended raising the damage thresholds for federal aid, replacing site-by-site reimbursement with up-front lump-sum grants to states, sliding-scale cost shares, and a single payment for survivors whose homes are uninhabitable. It backed away from a 50 per cent staff cut that drafts had proposed; the Government Accountability Office said earlier staff reductions had worsened FEMA's workforce problems. Many of the changes would need legislation. [cite:us15_crs_fema]

Israel's largest recent disasters have been wars. About 60,000 residents of the north were displaced after October 2023, and about half had not returned by March 2025. [cite:hz7_afp_north_return] Damage to homes and property from enemy fire is compensated by the state through the Property Tax Fund: the Bank of Israel put compensation for the June 2025 war with Iran at about NIS 4 billion, later about NIS 6 billion, financed by an addition to the budget. [cite:gi16_boi_2025b] The wider costs of the wars, and Israel's defence spending, are set out elsewhere. [scene:gi16_costs|The bill for the wars] [scene:us19_spending|Part Nineteen: defence spending]

Both records have gaps. Israel solved its water supply through national planning and desalination, but its electricity remains mostly fossil-fuelled, it missed its 2025 renewable target, its climate law had not been enacted as of the OECD's review, and its metro is a decade away. The United States has the larger renewable share and falling emissions per person, but its federal climate commitments have been reversed twice, its transit and roads are graded D and D-plus, and its disaster agency is being redesigned along lines that would raise the thresholds for federal aid and hand states lump-sum grants. [cite:us15_calcalist_renew] [cite:us15_jpost_oecd_env] [cite:us15_eia_mix2025] [cite:us15_asce_2025] [cite:us15_crs_fema]

chapters.label: Part Sixteen
chapters.title: Health
chapters.intro: Part Sixteen compares how the two states pay for and provide health care. It sets out Israel's National Health Insurance Law, in force since January 1995, which obliges every resident to join one of four nonprofit funds offering the same basket of services, beside the American mix of employer insurance, Medicare, Medicaid and Affordable Care Act plans, and it names the people each system leaves out. It then measures what each country spends, on one international definition from 2000 to 2023, what households pay out of pocket, the American burden of medical debt and the disputed figures about it, and how each government sets the price of medicines. Finally it follows the outcomes from 1980 to 2024, life expectancy, infant and maternal mortality and the gaps between groups of citizens inside each country, and the state of mental health care, which the war since October 2023 has put under particular strain in Israel. Figures are given as of October 2026, ahead of Israel's election on 27 October and the American midterms on 3 November.
chapters.outro: Part Sixteen established that Israel has covered every resident by law since 1995, through four funds financed by an earmarked health tax and the state budget, while the United States still has no universal coverage law: 26.7 million people, 7.9 per cent, were uninsured throughout 2025, and the Congressional Budget Office expects the 2025 reconciliation law to add about 10 million by 2034. [cite:us16_wiki_ilhealth] [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us16_kff_obbba] Israel's law has its own exclusions, asylum seekers, undocumented migrants and foreign workers among them, and a large private layer on top. [cite:us16_cwf_israel] On the World Health Organization's series the United States spent about 3.3 times as much per person as Israel in 2023, $13,473 against $4,033 in purchasing-power dollars, while households in Israel paid a larger share, but a smaller amount, out of pocket. [cite:us16_wb_chepc] [cite:us16_wb_oop] American drug prices stood at 278 per cent of those in 33 peer countries in 2022, and Medicare's first negotiated prices took effect only on 1 January 2026. [cite:us16_rand_drugs] [cite:us16_kff_negotiation] The two countries had the same life expectancy in 1980; by 2024 Israel's was about four years higher, and its infant mortality rate, once above America's, was half of it, though infant mortality among Arab citizens in Israel and among babies born to Black mothers in the United States was markedly above the national averages. [cite:us16_wb_le] [cite:us16_wb_imr] [cite:us16_toi_moh_gaps] [cite:us16_cdc_imr2023] In mental health, Israel's public system had waits of about six and a half months in 2024 as demand rose after 7 October 2023, and in the United States about half of adults with a mental illness received treatment. [cite:us16_boi_mental] [cite:us16_samhsa_tx] Part Seventeen turns to education. [scene:us17_schools|Part Seventeen: schools]

sections.h: Who Is Covered and Who Pays
sections.html:
The two systems start from different laws. Israel has a single statute that makes health insurance a condition of residence; the United States has several programmes, each with its own rules, and no law that covers everyone. This section sets out how each is built and who falls outside it; the next two set out what each spends and what each achieves. [scene:us16_cost|What it costs] [scene:us16_outcomes|Outcomes over time]

Israel: one law, four funds

Before 1995 health insurance in Israel was voluntary and ran through the sick funds. About 95 per cent of the population was insured by the early 1990s, but the largest fund, Clalit, required membership of the Histadrut labour federation or dependency on a member. [cite:us16_wiki_ilhealth] The Knesset passed the National Health Insurance Law in 1994 and it took effect on 1 January 1995. It made membership of one of the four funds compulsory and obliged every fund to accept any applicant. [cite:us16_wiki_ilhealth] A 2021 review in the Israel Journal of Health Policy Research summarised what changed: eligibility was cut loose from party or union membership, the funds lost the power to select healthier patients, a single government-funded basket of services was defined, and an earmarked health tax was created to pay for it. The state pays each fund by a capitation formula weighted for age, sex, area of residence and a small number of severe diseases. [cite:us16_ijhpr_nhil]

The four funds are Clalit, Maccabi, Meuhedet and Leumit. In 2024 Clalit held 50.96 per cent of members, Maccabi 27.48, Meuhedet 13.99 and Leumit 7.57. [cite:us16_wiki_ilhealth] The health tax is 3.2 per cent of monthly income up to 60 per cent of the average wage and 5.2 per cent above it; the government budget adds the rest, and public sources together paid 65 per cent of national health spending in 2024. [cite:us16_cwf_israel] The basket is the same in every fund and is widened each year on the recommendation of a public committee; in February 2025 it recommended adding 117 medicines and technologies. Cost-sharing is small and capped: NIS 22–35 (about $6–10) for the first specialist visit in a quarter, and 10 per cent of the maximum price for generic medicines and 15 per cent for branded ones, with a minimum of NIS 18. [cite:us16_cwf_israel] Coverage does not depend on a job: it follows residence, so losing work does not mean losing insurance. [cite:us16_ijhpr_nhil] [cite:us16_cwf_israel]

The record also shows the limits. The law excludes asylum seekers, undocumented migrants, foreign workers and holders of B1 work visas, who must rely on employer-bought or private policies; soldiers and prisoners, about 2 per cent of the population, are covered by separate systems. [cite:us16_cwf_israel] Asylum policy is treated in Part Six, and Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, who are not Israeli residents and are not covered by the law, in Part Nine. [scene:us6_asylum|Part Six: asylum] [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank] Inside the system, a large private layer has grown on top of the public one. Non-public sources paid about 36 per cent of national health spending by the time of the 2021 review; a Brookdale Institute study in 2016 found close to 85 per cent of households holding the funds' supplementary insurance and 57 per cent holding commercial insurance, and the Commonwealth Fund reports that 88 per cent of adults had both kinds in 2022. [cite:us16_ijhpr_nhil] [cite:us16_cwf_israel] Waiting is the most common complaint: in the first quarter of 2024 the national average wait to see an endocrinologist or a neurologist was 50 days. [cite:us16_cwf_israel]

The United States: several systems side by side

American coverage is a patchwork of employer insurance, the federal Medicare programme for people aged 65 and over, the joint federal-state Medicaid programme for people on low incomes, marketplace plans created by the Affordable Care Act of 2010, and military and veterans' care. A person can hold more than one kind in a year or none. In 2025, by the Census Bureau's count, 53.5 per cent of the population had employment-based coverage for some or all of the year, 35.8 per cent had public coverage, 17.1 per cent Medicaid and 20.1 per cent Medicare; 26.7 million people, 7.9 per cent, were uninsured for the whole year. [cite:us16_census_2025]

The uninsured count has moved with the law. More than 50 million Americans, nearly 17 per cent, were uninsured in 2009; about 42 million in 2013, the year before the Affordable Care Act's main coverage provisions began; and 28.1 million, a record low of 8.8 per cent, in 2016. [cite:us16_khn_uninsured] The Census Bureau changed its survey questions in this period, so early and late figures are not strictly comparable, but the direction is not in dispute. The rate was 8.0 per cent in 2024 and 7.9 per cent in 2025. [cite:us16_ib_subsidy] Two decisions point the other way from 2026. The enhanced marketplace premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025; by KFF's estimate the average premium paid by subsidised marketplace enrollees rose from $888 to $1,904 a year, and enrollment fell from about 24.2 million to about 23 million. [cite:us16_ib_subsidy] The budget reconciliation law signed on 4 July 2025 cuts Medicaid and marketplace spending; the Congressional Budget Office estimated that it will add about 10 million people to the uninsured by 2034, 7.5 million of them through the Medicaid changes, and about 14.2 million together with the expiry of the enhanced credits. [cite:us16_kff_obbba] These are projections, not outcomes, and the status of both is as of October 2026, ahead of the 3 November midterm elections.

For most working Americans coverage is tied to a job and paid partly from wages. In 2025 the average employer family premium was $26,993, of which the worker paid $6,850; family premiums rose 6 per cent that year against wage growth of 4 per cent and inflation of 2.7 per cent. The average deductible for single coverage was $1,886, and 34 per cent of covered workers faced a deductible of at least $2,000. [cite:us16_kff_ehbs2025] Part Fourteen sets these costs inside a family budget. [scene:us14_basket|Part Fourteen: the household basket]

The American military aid to Israel does not enter Israel's health budget: it is a grant for weapons, mostly bought from American firms, and has fallen to about half a per cent of Israel's GDP. [cite:gi16_inss_aid] [scene:gi16_aid|The aid] The comparison here is between two ways of organising coverage, each paid for by its own taxpayers.

sections.h: What It Costs
sections.html:
The coverage laws described in the previous section are paid for very differently, and the bills differ in size by a factor of more than three. This section sets the spending of the two countries side by side over time, then looks at two costs that fall on households: medical debt in the United States, and the price of medicines in both. All international comparisons use the World Health Organization's spending series as published by the World Bank, so that both countries are measured on one definition. [scene:us16_systems|Who is covered and who pays]

What each country spends

The United States spends far more than Israel by any measure. On the World Health Organization's series, published by the World Bank, current health spending was 12.5 per cent of GDP in the United States in 2000, 16.2 per cent in 2010, a peak of 18.5 per cent in the pandemic year 2020 and 16.7 per cent in 2023. Israel's was 6.6 per cent in 2000, 6.9 per cent in 2010, 7.7 per cent in 2020 and 7.1 per cent in 2023. [cite:us16_wb_chegdp] Per person, in dollars adjusted for purchasing power, the United States spent $4,549 in 2000, $7,836 in 2010 and $13,473 in 2023; Israel spent $1,750, $2,097 and $4,033. The American figure was about 3.3 times Israel's in 2023, not the "nearly four times" sometimes quoted from mismatched bases. [cite:us16_wb_chepc] The national accounts give the latest figures in each currency: $5.3 trillion in 2024, $15,474 per person and 18.0 per cent of GDP by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' definition, which is wider than the WHO's; NIS 146 billion and 7.3 per cent of GDP for Israel. [cite:us16_cms_nhe2024] [cite:us16_cwf_israel] The American series goes back further: $353 a person in 1970, or $2,208 in 2024 dollars. [cite:us16_pkff_spending]

One common claim does not hold in the form usually stated. Households in Israel pay a larger share of health costs out of pocket than households in the United States: 20.5 per cent of current health spending in 2023 against 10.9 per cent, down from 29.5 and 15.1 per cent in 2000. [cite:us16_wb_oop] Because total American spending is so much higher, the amounts run the other way. Out-of-pocket spending in the United States was $1,632 a person in 2024; Israel's 19.9 per cent share of $3,941 a person in 2024, at market exchange rates, works out at about $780. [cite:us16_pkff_spending] [cite:us16_cwf_israel] That last figure is derived here from the Commonwealth Fund's numbers, not published as such.

Medical debt: what is measured and what is disputed

The best-measured household cost in the American system is medical debt; this book found no comparable Israeli survey, so the figures here are American only. Using the Census Bureau's Survey of Income and Program Participation, the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker found that people in the United States owed at least $220 billion in medical debt at the end of 2021; about 20 million adults owed more than $250, 14 million more than $1,000 and 3 million more than $10,000. Eleven per cent of adults uninsured all year reported medical debt against 8 per cent of those insured all year, and 13 per cent of Black adults against 8 per cent of white adults. [cite:us16_pkff_debt] The often repeated claim that most American bankruptcies are medical is disputed. A 2018 study in the New England Journal of Medicine by Carlos Dobkin, Amy Finkelstein and colleagues found, using California hospital records, that hospitalisations caused about 4 per cent of bankruptcies among non-elderly adults, against a widely cited figure of about 60 per cent from surveys of people who had filed. [cite:us16_mit_bankruptcy] David Himmelstein, Steffie Woolhandler and Elizabeth Warren, authors of the earlier studies, replied that the method misses costs incurred outside hospital and illness in the family. [cite:us16_pnhp_reply] The book uses the measured debt, not either bankruptcy figure.

Medicines

The two governments set drug prices in different ways. Israel's Ministry of Health negotiates directly with manufacturers and fixes a maximum price for each prescription drug from the three lowest prices among seven reference countries; in 2024 it cut the maximum prices of 1,500 drugs by 3.6 per cent. Pharmaceuticals were 12.9 per cent of Israeli health spending in 2022, about $405 a person. [cite:us16_cwf_israel] In the United States Medicare paid no negotiated drug prices until 2026, as set out below. Prescription drugs were 8.8 per cent of national health spending in 2024; retail drug spending grew 7.8 per cent a year on average from 2020 to 2024. [cite:us16_pkff_spending] A RAND study of 2022 prices found American prices at 278 per cent of those in 33 other high-income countries across all drugs, and at 422 per cent for brand-name drugs before rebates and more than three times after estimated rebates. Unbranded generics were cheaper in the United States than in most of the comparison countries. [cite:us16_rand_drugs]

Medicare price negotiation began only recently. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 required the government to negotiate prices for some high-cost Medicare drugs. The first ten negotiated prices took effect on 1 January 2026; the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services estimated that they would have saved Medicare $6 billion, 22 per cent net, had they applied in 2023. Fifteen more, including Ozempic and Wegovy, take effect on 1 January 2027 with an estimated 44 per cent net saving, and a third round of 15 drugs was selected in January 2026 for 2028. The 2025 reconciliation law widened the exemption for drugs that treat rare diseases, which delayed the selection of Keytruda and Opdivo; the Congressional Budget Office put the cost at $8.8 billion over a decade. [cite:us16_kff_negotiation]

On spending, then, the gap is wide and long-standing, and it is not explained by households in Israel paying more out of their own pockets: they pay a larger share of a much smaller bill. [cite:us16_wb_chegdp] [cite:us16_wb_oop] What that spending buys in years of life, infant survival and access to care is the subject of the next section. [scene:us16_outcomes|Outcomes over time]

sections.h: Outcomes Over Time, Medicines and Mental Health
sections.html:
Spending is an input. This section turns to what the two systems produce, measured over four decades, to the gaps each leaves among its own citizens, and to mental health care, where both systems record long waits or low treatment rates. Health outcomes depend on far more than health care, including income, diet, violence, road deaths and drug overdoses, so the figures below describe the record of each country, not the effect of its insurance law alone. [scene:us16_systems|Who is covered and who pays] [scene:us16_cost|What it costs]

Life expectancy, 1980–2024

In 1980 the two countries stood level. On the World Bank's series, which uses the United Nations' model estimates for both, life expectancy at birth was 73.6 years in the United States and 73.9 in Israel. By 2000 it was 76.6 and 79.0; by 2010, 78.5 and 81.6; and in 2019, before the pandemic, 78.8 and 82.8. [cite:us16_wb_le] A Taub Center study found the same starting point: in 1980 life expectancy for Israeli Jews, for the United States and for the average of other OECD countries was about 74 years, while Israeli Arabs lived more than two years less; over the following three decades life expectancy rose by more than seven years for both Israeli Jews and Israeli Arabs, against about four years in the United States. [cite:us16_taub_healthy]

The pandemic widened the gap. American life expectancy fell to 76.3 years in 2021, while Israel's dipped only to 82.5. [cite:us16_wb_le] The American figure has since recovered: the National Center for Health Statistics put it at 79.0 years in 2024, up from 78.4 in 2023, with 76.5 for men and 81.4 for women. Deaths from unintentional injuries, the category that includes drug overdoses, fell by 14.4 per cent in age-adjusted terms that year. [cite:us16_cdc_db548] Israel's figure on the same World Bank series was 83.2 in 2024, so the gap stood at about four years, against about a quarter of a year in 1980. [cite:us16_wb_le] A reported fall in Israeli life expectancy after 7 October 2023 could not be confirmed from an official series and is not used here.

Infants and mothers

Infant mortality shows the clearest reversal. In 1980 Israel's rate, 15.5 deaths per 1,000 live births, was higher than America's 12.6. By 2000 Israel's was lower, 5.6 against 7.1, and by 2024 it was half the American rate, 2.7 against 5.5. [cite:us16_wb_imr] The American rate barely moved in 2024; the National Center for Health Statistics recorded 5.53 per 1,000 in 2024 and 5.60 in 2023, a change it judged not statistically significant. [cite:us16_cdc_db548] Maternal deaths, in the World Health Organization's modelled estimates, rose in the United States from 12 per 100,000 live births in 2000 to 22 in 2020 before falling to 17 in 2023; Israel's fell from 9 to 2. [cite:us16_wb_mmr] These are model estimates built to compare countries; national counts use different definitions and should not be mixed with them.

Gaps inside each country

Both systems leave measurable gaps between groups of their own citizens, and both governments publish them. Israel's Health Ministry, in a report on inequality in the health system based on 2022 data, put national life expectancy at 82.7 years, the same as the World Bank figure for that year. The highest regional figure for Jewish and other non-Arab citizens was 84.3 years, in greater Tel Aviv; the highest for Arab citizens was 80.1, in the north. Infant mortality was 5.1 per 1,000 among Arab citizens and 2.1 among Jewish citizens, a gap the ministry linked partly to differing attitudes toward prenatal genetic testing and to unequal access to women's and children's health services. The ministry also reported fewer doctors and specialists in the periphery, more emergency-room use in poorer areas because community services are weaker, and hospital beds cut over the decade mainly in the large cities while the north and south did not gain ground. [cite:us16_toi_moh_gaps] [cite:us16_wb_le] Part Eight sets these figures beside the other measures of equality among Israel's citizens. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: equality in Israel]

In the United States the national infant mortality rate in 2023 was 5.61 per 1,000; it was 10.93 for babies born to Black non-Hispanic mothers, 9.20 for American Indian and Alaska Native mothers, 5.03 for Hispanic mothers, 4.48 for white non-Hispanic mothers and 3.44 for Asian mothers. [cite:us16_cdc_imr2023] The rate for Black infants was more than twice the white rate, and above Israel's 2022 rate for Arab infants. Part Eight takes up the American gaps by group. [scene:us8_us|Part Eight: equality in the United States] Neither set of figures describes the people in a group; each measures how a system's services, income and geography reach them.

Mental health

Israel brought mental health into its insurance law late. Until July 2015 the state itself was responsible; a reform that month moved the insurance responsibility to the four funds, with NIS 2 billion added to their budgets in 2015–2016. From 2016 to 2024 the only dedicated addition was a one-off NIS 100 million during COVID-19, and the State Comptroller found an average wait of about 150 days for psychotherapy after diagnosis, on 2018 data. [cite:us16_boi_mental] The war that began on 7 October 2023 raised demand sharply. In the Central Bureau of Statistics' social survey, the share of adults reporting depression rose from 23–25 per cent before the war to 34 per cent in 2024; the share in treatment rose from 14 per cent in January 2024 to 18 per cent in October. In March and April 2024 the average public wait was about six and a half months, and 42 per cent of those who sought treatment went to private practitioners against 38 per cent to the funds. [cite:us16_boi_mental] The government answered with a National Mental Health Program in January 2024, about NIS 1.4 billion a year, partly paid for by a 2025 rise in the health tax worth about NIS 1 billion a year. Israel had about 0.17 psychiatrists per 1,000 people in 2023 against an OECD average of about 0.21, and very few therapists in the periphery and in Arab towns. [cite:us16_boi_mental] [cite:us16_cwf_israel]

In the United States mental health care is covered, if at all, through the same patchwork of plans. In 2024, 52.1 per cent of adults with any mental illness received mental health treatment in the previous year, by the National Survey on Drug Use and Health; a change in the questionnaire means this cannot be compared with earlier years. [cite:us16_samhsa_tx] Suicide was the tenth leading cause of death in 2024, with 48,824 deaths, an age-adjusted rate of 13.7 per 100,000. [cite:us16_cdc_db548]

The record therefore cuts both ways. Israel spends less than a third as much per person, covers every resident by law and has pulled ahead on life expectancy and infant mortality since 1980, but its residents wait long for specialists and for mental health care, pay a larger share out of pocket, and buy private cover in large numbers; and measured outcomes are worse for Arab citizens and in the periphery. The United States spends more than three times as much per person, covers about 92 per cent of its people, and records large gaps by group and drug prices far above those of its peers. [cite:us16_wb_chepc] [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us16_rand_drugs]

chapters.label: Part Seventeen
chapters.title: Education
chapters.intro: Part Seventeen compares how the two states educate their children and their students. It begins with the schools: Israel's single ministry and its separate streams, state, state-religious, Haredi and Arab, each funded and supervised on different terms, beside the American system of local districts paid for largely by states and property taxes. It sets out what each spends on one international definition, who is left behind inside each, and how 15-year-olds in both countries have scored on the OECD's PISA tests from the first rounds to the results published in September 2026, which recorded the steepest fall in Israel's history of the test. It then turns to universities: Israel's regulated public tuition and widening access for Arab and Haredi students, and the American mix of rising prices, grants and $1.65 trillion in student debt, with the federal loan changes that took effect in July 2026. Figures are given as of October 2026, ahead of Israel's election on 27 October and the American midterms on 3 November.
chapters.outro: Part Seventeen established that the two systems spend a similar share of national income on education, about 6 per cent of GDP, but that the United States spent almost twice as much per student, $19,973 against $10,279 in purchasing-power dollars, because Israel has far more children to teach. [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_usa] [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_isr] [cite:us17_toi_eag2024] Each system's gaps follow its structure: American spending per pupil ranged from $11,060 in Idaho to $31,918 in New York in 2024, while Israel funds Arab primary schools at about 12 per cent less per pupil than Hebrew state-religious ones and funds Haredi schools of which at least half, by an Israel Democracy Institute study's conservative estimate, do not teach the required core curriculum, with little enforcement; the ministry says it enforces the rules. [cite:us17_census_fy2024] [cite:us17_taub_primary2025] [cite:us17_toi_haredi_core] On PISA, Israel's scores rose to 2012 and then fell, sharply in 2025, to 436 in reading and 433 in mathematics, while American scores held near or above the OECD average with the widest gap between strong and weak readers of any country tested. [cite:us17_wiki_pisa] [cite:us17_ih_pisa2025] [cite:us17_edweek_pisa2025] Israel keeps university tuition low by regulation, NIS 12,017 a year at the Hebrew University in 2025–26, but spends less than half the OECD average per university student; the United States charges more and lends more, with $1.651 trillion in student debt and 9.3 million federal borrowers in default by mid-2026. [cite:us14_huji_tuition] [cite:us17_ynet_eag2026h] [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026] [cite:us17_ci_defaults] Part Eighteen turns to family policy and the safety net. [scene:us18_family|Part Eighteen: family policy]

sections.h: Schools: Streams, Money and Scores
sections.html:
Both countries promise free public schooling, but they organise it in very different ways. Israel runs one national ministry that funds several separate school streams, each with its own curriculum, language and religious character. The United States has no national school system at all: public schools are run by local districts under state law and paid for mostly by states and local property taxes. This section sets out how each is built, what each spends, who is left behind and how pupils have scored; the next turns to universities and debt. [scene:us17_higher|Universities, cost and debt]

Israel: one ministry, separate streams

Israel's Education Ministry funds four main streams: Hebrew-language state schools, state-religious schools, Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) schools, and Arabic-language schools for Arab citizens. The balance among them is shifting fast. In 2021–22 about 373,000 pupils were in Haredi education, 25.5 per cent of Hebrew-language pupils and 19.5 per cent of all pupils in the country. [cite:us17_idi_haredi2022] An analysis of Education Ministry data by Eli Morgenstern, a former senior Finance Ministry official, found that first-grade enrolment in secular Hebrew state schools fell by about 12 per cent between 2023 and 2026 while Haredi first-grade enrolment rose by about 11 per cent. In 2025 Arab schools had about 23 per cent of first graders and state-religious schools about 16 per cent; on his projection of current trends, Haredi schools will be the largest stream for first graders by 2030. [cite:us17_ynet_firstgrade]

The streams are funded differently, and the Haredi stream is funded on terms that no other stream receives. Only about 7 per cent of Haredi pupils attended the state's own Haredi schools in 2024–25. The rest attend schools that are privately run but state-funded in part or in full. "Exempt" schools receive about 55 per cent of the per-pupil funding of a state school in return for teaching 55 per cent of the core curriculum of language, mathematics, science and English; "recognised but unofficial" schools receive 75 per cent for teaching 75 per cent; and the two large networks tied to the Shas and United Torah Judaism parties are fully funded and expected to teach all of it. [cite:us17_toi_haredi_core] A study by Ariel Finkelstein for the Israel Democracy Institute, published in July 2025, found that the ministry did not enforce the curriculum in exempt and unrecognised schools; only 6 per cent of network schools had faced a budget cut, averaging NIS 225,000 in 2023–24; no school had ever been closed; and at least half of Haredi schools, by his conservative estimate, did not comply. In an earlier survey, 76 per cent of Haredi parents of boys said their sons learned no English at all. The Education Ministry replied that supervision of core studies "is carried out regularly and according to the procedures" and that "when violations are identified, clear enforcement measures are implemented." [cite:us17_toi_haredi_core] The rules have swung with coalitions. A 2013 law pressed by Yesh Atid made core subjects a condition of funding from 2018; on 24 July 2016, under a coalition deal with United Torah Judaism, ministers voted to repeal that clause and give the education minister discretion to fund schools that do not teach them. [cite:us17_toi_core2016] How this fits the wider bargain over Haredi exemptions is set out in Part Seven. [scene:us7_haredi|Part Seven: the Haredi exemptions]

The gap for Arab schools runs the other way: they teach the full curriculum but have long received less money per pupil. The Taub Center's study of official primary schools from 2014 to 2023 found that the per-pupil gap between Hebrew state-religious and Arab state schools narrowed from about 15 per cent to about 12 per cent, and concluded that "Arab State education continues to receive less funding than does Hebrew education." [cite:us17_taub_primary2025] The outcomes differ sharply by stream. In 2011, 48.1 per cent of Israeli pupils completed a matriculation certificate (the bagrut): 65 per cent of Jewish pupils outside the Haredi system, 38.2 per cent of non-Jewish pupils and 8.1 per cent of Haredi pupils. [cite:us17_toi_bagrut2011] In 2018–19, 14 per cent of Haredi pupils earned the certificate against 83 per cent in the state and state-religious streams; Haredi girls sitting at least one matriculation exam rose from 31 to 59 per cent between 2008–09 and 2019–20, while for Haredi boys the share stayed at about 15 per cent. [cite:us17_idi_haredi2022] These figures measure what each stream's schools are funded, required and permitted to teach, not the ability of the children in them.

The United States: fifty systems and the property tax

American public schools spent $17,619 per pupil in the 2024 fiscal year, up 6.6 per cent from $16,526 the year before, in figures the Census Bureau does not adjust for inflation. Of $994.9 billion in revenue, states provided 45.2 per cent, local governments 43.2 per cent and the federal government 11.6 per cent; property taxes made up 63.3 per cent of local revenue. [cite:us17_census_fy2024] Because so much money is raised locally, spending depends on where a child lives: it ranged from $31,918 per pupil in New York to $11,060 in Idaho. [cite:us17_census_fy2024] The federal role is small and shrinking. The Education Department had just over 4,100 employees when President Trump took office in January 2025; after the Supreme Court allowed mass layoffs to proceed in July 2025, the department was effectively cut in half, adult and career education were moved to the Labor Department, and, as reported in July 2025, moves of student aid to the Treasury and special education to Health and Human Services were proposed. Abolishing the department outright requires an act of Congress. [cite:us17_74_ed] The 2025 reconciliation law also created a federal Education Freedom Tax Credit, effective from 1 January 2027 in states that opt in; 31 states had done so or said they would by 28 July 2026. [cite:us7_k12dive_taxcredit] Part Seven sets out the church-and-state questions it raises. [scene:us7_us|Part Seven: religion and state in the United States]

What each spends, on one definition

The OECD's Education at a Glance puts both countries on one basis. In its 2023 edition Israel spent $10,279 per full-time student across all levels, in purchasing-power dollars, against $19,973 in the United States and an OECD average of $12,647. As a share of GDP the two were close: 6.4 per cent in Israel and 6 per cent in the United States, against about 5 per cent across the OECD. [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_isr] [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_usa] The two facts fit together because Israel has far more children: 43.1 per cent of its population was under 25 in 2022, against an OECD average of 29.7 per cent. [cite:us17_toi_eag2024] Israel's money is spread across more pupils in larger classes, 27 per primary class against an OECD average of 21 in the 2026 edition, and its teachers are paid less: a teacher with fifteen years' experience in upper-secondary school earned a statutory $39,321 in Israel in 2022, against $69,641 in the United States. [cite:us17_ynet_eag2026] [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_isr] [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_usa] No part of the American military aid to Israel goes into its education budget; the memorandum money is military financing. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [scene:gi16_aid|The aid]

Scores over time: PISA, 2000–2025

The OECD's PISA tests 15-year-olds every three years or so and is the only long series covering both countries on one scale. Israel sat the first round in 2002, two years late, and has taken part in every round since 2006. [cite:us17_oecd_pisa2018_isr] [cite:us17_wiki_pisa] In mathematics, Israel's average rose from 433 in that first round and 442 in 2006 to 466 in 2012, then slipped to 458 by 2022; the American average fell from 493 in 2000 to 465 in 2022. In reading, Israel rose from 439 in 2006 to 486 in 2012 and stood at 474 in 2022, while the United States stayed near 500 throughout, at 504 in 2022. In science the United States scored 499 in 2022 and Israel 465. [cite:us17_wiki_pisa] The OECD's own reading of the Israeli series was that most of the gains came before 2012 and that the gap between advantaged and disadvantaged pupils was wide and growing: 121 points in reading in 2018, against an OECD average of 89, up from 103 in 2009. [cite:us17_oecd_pisa2018_isr]

The 2025 round, sat in March and April 2025 and published on 8 September 2026, recorded a sharp fall in Israel. Reading dropped from 474 to 436, the lowest Israel has recorded, mathematics from 458 to 433, and science from 465 to 442; Israel ranked between 31st and 33rd of 38 OECD countries, against OECD averages of 461, 463 and 482. [cite:us17_ih_pisa2025] The test was taken eighteen months into the war that began in October 2023; the results do not by themselves show how much of the fall the war explains. The American reading score fell 14 points to 490, the same fall as the OECD average, while mathematics, at 463, and science were not significantly changed. [cite:us17_nw_pisa2025] [cite:us17_edweek_pisa2025] The United States ranked 13th in reading and science and 27th in mathematics, and had the widest gap between its highest- and lowest-scoring pupils in reading of any country tested. [cite:us17_gma_pisa2025] [cite:us17_edweek_pisa2025] America's national assessment shows the same pattern: in 2024 American twelfth-graders' average mathematics score was the lowest since 2005, their reading score the lowest on record, and the gap between high and low performers in mathematics the widest ever measured. [cite:us17_chalkbeat_naep]

Each system's weak point follows its structure. In the United States, spending gaps follow district lines drawn by local wealth, and its reading-score gap was the widest of any country tested in 2025. In Israel, the stream a child enters sets what the school is required and funded to teach, and the state has chosen, under successive coalitions, to fund schools that do not teach the full core curriculum; many Haredi boys' schools stop mathematics and English at sixth grade or earlier. [cite:us17_census_fy2024] [cite:us17_edweek_pisa2025] [cite:us17_toi_haredi_core] [cite:us17_toi_core2016] Part Eight sets these gaps beside the other measures of equality among each country's citizens. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: equality in Israel] [scene:us8_us|Part Eight: equality in the United States]

sections.h: Universities, Cost and Debt
sections.html:
Higher education is where the two systems differ most in who pays. Israel's universities and most of its colleges are funded through a national budget and charge a single regulated tuition fee. American higher education is a market of public, private non-profit and for-profit institutions whose prices are set by states and by the institutions themselves, financed largely by federal student loans. This section compares access, price and debt, and states where a comparable figure does not exist. [scene:us17_schools|Schools: streams, money and scores]

Israel: a regulated public system

Israel's Council for Higher Education accredits institutions and, through its planning and budgeting committee, allocates the state's money to them. It also sets tuition, which is linked to the consumer price index rather than left to each university: for 2025–26 a bachelor's degree at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem cost Israeli citizens NIS 12,017 a year. [cite:us14_huji_tuition] The system has grown and widened. The council counted 337,230 students in 2021–22, 256,170 of them on bachelor's degrees, and expected about 342,000 the following year; women were 60 per cent of students, and about a third of bachelor's students came from the four lowest of the ten socio-economic clusters. [cite:us17_che_2022]

The largest change has been among Arab citizens. Their share of bachelor's students rose from 10 per cent in 2009–10 to 18 per cent in 2020–21, and of master's students from 6.5 per cent in 2011–12 to 16 per cent; the number of Arab students more than doubled, from 25,951 to 57,552. Arab citizens remained under-represented at the doctoral level, at 8 per cent of PhD students. [cite:us17_che_arab] By 2022–23 Arab students numbered more than 60,000, 18 per cent of all students against 21 per cent of the population. [cite:us17_che_2022] Haredi students rose from 5,500 in 2010–11 to 16,575 in 2021–22, but were still 4.9 per cent of students against 13 per cent of the population, and only 8.5 per cent of them studied at universities rather than colleges, against 33.5 per cent of other Jewish students. [cite:us17_che_2022] [cite:us17_idi_haredi2022] The school figures in the previous section, where 14 per cent of Haredi pupils earned a matriculation certificate in 2018–19 against 83 per cent in the state streams, point to where that gap begins. [cite:us17_idi_haredi2022]

The weakness of the Israeli system is money per student. In the OECD's 2026 Education at a Glance, Israel spent $7,885 per university student in 2023, in purchasing-power dollars, against an OECD average of $16,405, fifth from the bottom of 33 countries; the government paid 38 per cent of higher-education spending against an average of 68 per cent. [cite:us17_ynet_eag2026h] Attainment is split by sex. Among 25- to 34-year-olds, 57 per cent of Israeli women held a tertiary degree in the 2023 edition, above the OECD average of 54 per cent, but only 36 per cent of men, below the average of 41 per cent; the men's figure had not moved since 2015 while the OECD average for men rose to 43 per cent. [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_isr] [cite:us17_ynet_eag2026h] Conscription, which for those who serve comes before university, is taken up in Part Nineteen; no source used here measures its effect on degree rates. [scene:us19_service|Part Nineteen: service]

The United States: price, grants and loans

The College Board's series shows how far American public tuition has risen. Average published tuition and fees at a public four-year college for in-state students were about $5,940 in 1995–96 in 2025 dollars; they rose to a peak of $13,150 in 2019–20 and 2020–21 and stood at $11,950 in 2025–26. Private non-profit four-year colleges averaged $45,000 and public two-year colleges $4,150. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] [cite:us14_cb_trends2025] Grants narrow the gap: after grant aid, the average in-state student at a public four-year college paid about $2,300 in net tuition in 2025–26, down from a peak of $4,450 in 2012–13. Neither figure includes living costs. [cite:us14_cb_trends2025] On the OECD's 2023 basis, 46 per cent of American men and 56 per cent of women aged 25 to 34 held a tertiary degree. [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_usa]

What families cannot pay up front, they borrow. Student loan balances almost tripled between 2004 and 2012, when the number of borrowers grew by about 70 per cent, and reached about $994 billion in the second quarter of 2013; student debt was the only kind of household debt that kept rising through the Great Recession. [cite:us17_nyfed_2013] By the second quarter of 2026 it stood at $1.651 trillion, by the New York Fed's count. [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026] The federal portfolio, by the government's own data to 30 June 2026, covered 42.3 million borrowers and more than $1.7 trillion. Of these, 9.3 million borrowers owing $234 billion were in default, about 400,000 more than three months earlier. Defaulted borrowers can have tax refunds and part of their Social Security benefits taken through the Treasury offset programme, and up to 15 per cent of disposable pay garnished. [cite:us17_ci_defaults]

The law changed in 2025. The reconciliation act signed on 4 July 2025, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, [cite:us16_kff_obbba] ends Grad PLUS loans for new graduate borrowers from 1 July 2026; caps unsubsidised graduate loans at $20,500 a year and $100,000 in all, and professional-school loans at $50,000 a year and $200,000; limits Parent PLUS loans to $20,000 a year and $65,000 per student; and replaces the repayment options for new loans with a single income-based Repayment Assistance Plan and fixed-term standard plans. [cite:us17_unmc_obbba] The new plan launched in July 2026; as of the government's update of 22 September 2026 it had not reported how many borrowers had joined it. [cite:us17_ci_defaults]

What the comparison shows

The two systems put the cost of a degree in different places. Israel holds tuition down by regulation and spends little per student by OECD standards; no national figure for Israeli student debt was found for this book, and none should be inferred from its absence. [cite:us17_ynet_eag2026h] [cite:us14_huji_tuition] The United States spends more and charges more, and has shifted much of the cost onto borrowers: about one in five borrowers in the federal portfolio was in default in mid-2026. [cite:us17_ci_defaults] Each system's access gap follows its school system. On the figures above, in Israel the stream a pupil attends is closely tied to whether they reach university; in the United States the published price and the grants a student qualifies for decide how much of a degree is borrowed against. [cite:us17_idi_haredi2022] [cite:us14_cb_trends2025] Israel's education minister, Yoav Kisch, was completing his four-year term as the election of 27 October 2026 approached, and the American loan changes were taking effect as Congress is chosen on 3 November; both records are stated as of October 2026. [cite:us17_ih_pisa2025] [cite:us1_wjla_midterms]

chapters.label: Part Eighteen
chapters.title: Family Policy and the Safety Net
chapters.intro: Part Eighteen compares what each state does for families and for people who cannot earn enough. It begins with leave after a birth, the price of childcare and the money each state gives parents: a universal monthly allowance in Israel, a tax credit in the United States. It then sets Israel's abortion committees, which approve almost every request, beside the United States after the Supreme Court's 2022 Dobbs ruling, and compares fertility treatment and birth rates. The third section turns to old-age and disability pensions, care in old age and unemployment benefit, including Israel's compulsory workplace pensions and the projected shortfall in America's Social Security trust funds. The last section sets the two countries' official poverty series side by side over time, explains why their headline rates are not measured the same way, and shows what transfers do to poverty in each.
chapters.outro: Part Eighteen established that Israel builds its family support into national insurance, as rights that follow residence and work: 15 weeks of paid maternity leave since 2017, a universal child allowance of NIS 173–219 a month per child in 2026, publicly funded IVF and, in practice, publicly funded abortion through committees that approved 99.6 per cent of requests in 2020. [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018] [cite:us18_nii_childrates] [cite:us18_toi_abortion2022] The United States guarantees unpaid leave, gives most child support through the tax code, spent 0.60 per cent of GDP on family benefits in 2023 against Israel's 1.89 per cent on the same OECD measure, and since June 2022 has let each state set abortion law, with 13 total bans in force in January 2026. [cite:us18_crs_leave] [cite:us18_socx_usa] [cite:us18_socx_isr] [cite:us18_kff_abortioncov] Each record has its own gaps: Israel's allowances were cut in 2002–04 and 2013, raising child poverty, and its child poverty rate was 28 per cent in 2024 on the national measure, and 23.4 per cent in 2023 on the OECD's comparable scale; America's Social Security trust funds are projected to be exhausted in 2034, and its child poverty rate more than doubled on the SPM when the expanded tax credit lapsed in 2022. [cite:us18_nii_survey2007] [cite:us18_nii_pov2024] [cite:us18_crs_ss2026] [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] The headline poverty rates, 10.2 per cent in the United States in 2025 and 20.7 per cent in Israel in 2024, use different definitions and cannot be set side by side as a measure of the gap. [cite:us18_census_p60290] [cite:us18_nii_pov2023] All figures are as of October 2026; Israel votes on 27 October and the United States on 3 November, and benefit levels and budgets should be rechecked after both elections. Part Nineteen turns to the military: conscription, defence spending and who pays for it. [scene:us19_service|Part Nineteen: military service]

sections.h: Leave, Childcare and Child Benefits
sections.html:
Family policy is where the two systems differ most in design. Israel built its family benefits into its national insurance system in the 1950s, as rights that follow residence and employment. The United States built most of its support for families into the tax code and the employer, with a federal floor that guarantees time off but not pay. This section compares the two on leave after a birth, the price of childcare and the money each state gives parents, with the years of each measure stated; the next section turns to abortion, fertility treatment and birth rates. [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018] [cite:us18_nii_children2018] [cite:us18_crs_leave] [scene:us18_reproduction|Abortion, IVF and birth rates]

Leave after a birth

Israel's maternity insurance came into effect on 1 April 1954, as one of the first five branches of the National Insurance Law. [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018] What it pays has lengthened in three steps. The paid allowance was 12 weeks (6 weeks for women with a shorter work record) until May 2007, 14 weeks (or 7) until the end of 2016, and 15 weeks (or 8) from January 2017. [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018] The allowance replaces earnings rather than paying a flat sum: the National Insurance Institute (NII) takes the higher of the mother's average daily income over the last three or six full months before leave, up to a ceiling of NIS 1,752.33 a day as of 1 January 2026. [cite:us18_nii_matrates] In 2018 the average allowance was NIS 285 a day, and the average recipient had earned 83.8 per cent of the national average wage. [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018] The labour law adds job protection around the paid weeks. Under the Employment of Women Law, as summarised by an Israeli law firm and by the immigrant-aid organisation Nefesh B'Nefesh, a woman with twelve months at her employer may take 26 weeks of leave (15 with shorter service), of which 15 are paid by the NII and the rest unpaid, and she may not be dismissed during the leave or for 60 days after it; dismissal during pregnancy needs a permit from the labour ministry. [cite:us18a_fbc_maternity] [cite:us18_nbn_women]

Fathers came later and remain few. Since 1998 a father may take part of the paid leave if the mother returns to work; in April 2017 the minimum the father must take was cut from 21 days to 7, and the number of fathers paid rose from 545 in 2016 to 1,266 in 2018, or 9.5 for every 1,000 women paid. [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018]

The United States has no national paid leave. The Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave for a birth or a family illness, but the leave is unpaid. [cite:us18_crs_leave] Pay depends on the employer or the state. In March 2023, 27 per cent of private-sector workers had paid family leave through their employer, about 17 percentage points more than in 2010; 13 per cent of workers in the lowest-paid quarter of jobs had it, against 44 per cent in the highest-paid quarter. [cite:us18_crs_leave] The Bureau of Labor Statistics found 90 per cent of civilian workers with access to unpaid family leave in 2023, and says it has no comparable paid-leave estimates for 2024 or 2025 because the survey's scope changed. [cite:us18_bls_leave] States have filled part of the gap. California started the first state programme on 1 July 2004; by March 2025 ten jurisdictions, including the District of Columbia, were paying benefits, and Delaware, Maine and Minnesota had enacted programmes due to start paying during 2026. [cite:us18_crs_leave] Maryland, which had planned to start in July 2026, delayed its programme by a law signed on 6 May 2025; benefits are now due to begin no later than 3 January 2028. [cite:us18a_bd_maryland] Federal civil servants gained paid parental leave in the defence authorisation act of December 2019. [cite:us18_crs_leave]

Childcare

Part Fourteen showed that Israel made preschool free for three- and four-year-olds from the 2012–13 school year, after the 2011 protests, and that the saving to families was smaller than the law implied. [scene:us14_basket|Part Fourteen: the basket] [cite:us14_taub_preschool] The United States has no national free preschool, and the Labor Department's National Database of Childcare Prices shows what families pay instead. In 2022, across 2,512 counties, full-day care for one child cost between $6,552 and $15,600 a year, between 8.9 and 16 per cent of the county's median family income. [cite:us18_dol_childcare] The database covers 2008 to 2022, so it describes the period before and during the pandemic rather than 2026 prices. [cite:us18_dol_childcare] This book found no Israeli series on the price of care for children under three that is defined the same way, so no side-by-side figure is given.

Money for children: an allowance and a tax credit

Israel pays a monthly child allowance through the NII to every family with children, whatever its income. The Children Insurance Law took effect in 1959, at first as a fixed payment to large families only. [cite:us18_nii_children2018] From 1 January 2026 the allowance is NIS 173 a month for the first child, NIS 219 for each of the second to fourth, and NIS 173 for the fifth and later. [cite:us18_nii_childrates] In 2018 about 1.19 million families with 2.88 million children received it. [cite:us18_nii_children2018]

The allowance has been cut and restored with changes of government, and the cuts fell hardest on large families, which is why its history matters for poverty. Allowances were cut in 2002–2004; children born from June 2003 were paid the same rate as the first two children, whatever their birth order, until June 2009. [cite:us18_nii_children2018] The NII found that the cutback starting in 2002 raised child poverty by 5 percentage points between 2002 and 2005 and deepened the poverty of those already poor. [cite:us18_nii_survey2007] What the NII calls the Streamlining Law cut allowances again in August 2013, to NIS 140 for new children; after a new government took office in May 2015 the allowances were raised, and from January 2017 the state also deposits NIS 50 a month into a long-term savings account for each child, to which parents may add NIS 50 from the allowance. [cite:us18_nii_children2018] The 2018 rate table shows the old tiering still in force for older children: NIS 336–354 a month for fourth and later children born before June 2003, against NIS 150–189 for the first three and for all children born since. [cite:us18_nii_children2018]

The United States gives most of its child support through the income-tax system rather than as a payment. Its largest test came in 2021, when Congress raised the Child Tax Credit from $2,000 to $3,000 per child, and $3,600 for children under six, for one year. When the credit returned to its usual level in 2022, child poverty on the Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts tax credits as income, rose from 5.2 per cent in 2021 to 12.4 per cent in 2022. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] Part of the change reflects the end of other pandemic measures in the same year; the measure itself does not separate them.

On the OECD's measure of public spending on families, the two countries sit far apart, but the measure needs care. The OECD's Social Expenditure Database (SOCX) counts cash benefits and services; on that basis the United States spent 0.77 per cent of GDP on families in 1980 and 0.60 per cent in 2023, and Israel 1.89 per cent in 2023, within a range of 1.74 to 2.49 per cent over the years the series covers. [cite:us18_socx_usa] [cite:us18_socx_isr] That series leaves out tax breaks, which is where most American support sits; the OECD's family database, which adds them, still put the United States below 1 per cent of GDP in 2021, against an OECD average of 2.35 per cent, with more than half of American spending going on services. [cite:us18_oecd_pf11] The OECD publishes Israel's figures from Israeli authorities' data. [cite:us18_oecd_pf11]

Who each design leaves out is different. Israel's allowance reaches every resident family with children, but its value has swung with coalition budgets, and the families that rely on it most, the largest and poorest, have taken the deepest cuts. [cite:us18_nii_survey2007] [cite:us18_nii_children2018] The American design pays most to families with enough earnings to use a tax credit, guarantees leave without pay, and leaves the price of care to the market; the 2021 experiment showed what a larger payment did to child poverty, and its expiry showed the reverse. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] [cite:us18_dol_childcare]

sections.h: Abortion, IVF and Birth Rates
sections.html:
On reproduction the usual picture of the two countries runs against expectation. Israel's law still requires a committee to approve each abortion, yet in practice the committees approve nearly every request and the state pays for most of them. The United States had a constitutional right to abortion from 1973 until the Supreme Court, by six votes to three, overruled Roe v. Wade in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization on 24 June 2022, and access now depends on the state. [cite:us18a_scotus_dobbs] [cite:us18_kff_abortioncov] Israel's health basket also pays for IVF on terms its own researchers describe as practically unlimited, and its fertility rate, 2.87 children per woman in 2024, was the highest in the OECD; the American rate fell to a record low in 2024. This section sets out each in turn; Part Eight treats gender equality more broadly. [cite:us18_toi_abortion2022] [cite:us18_ijhpr_ivf] [cite:us18a_oecd_sf21] [cite:us18_ap_tfr2024] [scene:us8_gender|Part Eight: gender and disability rights]

Israel: committees that almost always say yes

Israel's abortion law dates from 1977 and sits in the Penal Code. An abortion is lawful only with the approval of a termination committee of two physicians and a social worker, at least one of them a woman; there are 38 such committees in public and private hospitals. A committee may approve on fixed grounds: the woman is under 18 (later widened to under 20) or over 40; the pregnancy resulted from rape, incest or a relationship outside marriage; the fetus has a physical or mental defect; or the pregnancy endangers the woman's life or her physical or mental health. [cite:us18_wiki_abortion_il] There is no ground of simple choice, but the grounds are read widely; the encyclopaedia summary used here puts general approval at 98 per cent. [cite:us18_wiki_abortion_il] In 2020 the Central Bureau of Statistics recorded 16,492 requests to the committees, of which 99.6 per cent were approved; Health Ministry figures reported by Ynet put 2021 requests at 17,548. [cite:us18_toi_abortion2022] About 19,500 legal abortions were performed in 2003, and the rate per 1,000 women of childbearing age had fallen to 9 by 2016, below the American rate of 13.2 in the same comparison. [cite:us18_wiki_abortion_il]

The state pays for most of them. Before 2014 public funding covered approved abortions in certain cases for women aged 20 to 33; a change that year brought elective abortions into the state-funded health basket, though sources disagree on whether an upper age limit remained. Women who become pregnant during military service receive abortions free. [cite:us18_wiki_abortion_il] On 27 June 2022, three days after Dobbs, Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz announced new rules approved by a Knesset committee: applications could be made online without appearing before the committee, questions about contraception were removed from the form, the meeting with a social worker became optional, and drug abortions could be given at health-fund clinics rather than only in hospitals. "The rights to a woman's body are those of the woman alone," he said. Abolishing the committees would need a law, which the Times of Israel judged unlikely to pass. [cite:us18_toi_abortion2022]

The committee system has a documented gap of its own. A 2012 report found that about half of abortions took place in private clinics without committee approval; doctors who perform them risk a fine or up to five years in prison, but no prosecutions are known. [cite:us18_wiki_abortion_il]

The United States after Dobbs

Since 1977, under the Hyde Amendment as KFF summarises it, Congress has barred federal funds for abortion except where the woman's life is endangered or the pregnancy results from rape or incest, so Medicaid pays for abortion only where a state uses its own money; 13 states required such coverage as of mid-2026. [cite:us18_kff_abortioncov] After Dobbs returned the question to the states, 13 states had total bans in force as of 6 January 2026: Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas and West Virginia. [cite:us18_kff_abortioncov]

The bans changed where and how abortions happen more than how many. The Society of Family Planning's #WeCount study counted about 1.13 million abortions in the formal health system in 2025. Telehealth provision, mostly pills sent by mail, rose from 5 per cent of abortions in April 2022 to 25 per cent in December 2024 and 29 per cent in December 2025; in the total-ban states it made up 97 to 100 per cent of abortions in 2025. The study credits telehealth and providers operating under shield laws with keeping access open. [cite:us18_sfp_wecount]

Fertility treatment

Israel's national health basket pays for practically unlimited in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) for patients under 45 with no more than two children, single mothers included. The authors of a 2016 study of the Maccabi health fund's IVF registry state, citing earlier research, that Israel performs more IVF cycles relative to its population than any other country; they argue that many of these cycles have a low chance of success. [cite:us18_ijhpr_ivf] The same study cites 163,212 IVF cycles in the United States in 2013. [cite:us18_ijhpr_ivf] There is no federal entitlement to fertility treatment in the United States; cover depends on employer insurance and on state mandates. On 18 February 2025 President Trump signed an executive order asking for policy recommendations within 90 days on protecting access to IVF and lowering its cost, and AP reported in July 2025 that his administration was backing the idea of "baby bonuses" to encourage births. [cite:us18a_wh_ivf] [cite:us18_ap_tfr2024] What the order has changed in practice is not measured in any series this book found.

Birth rates over time

The two countries' fertility rates have moved apart. Israel's total fertility rate, the number of children a woman would have at current rates, averaged 2.93 in 1990–99, 2.92 in 2000–04, 3.04 in 2010–14 and 3.08 in 2015–19, and stood at 2.89 in 2022, by Central Bureau of Statistics data. [cite:us18_jvl_tfr] Within that steady total, the rates of different groups have converged: Muslim women's rate fell from 4.67 in the 1990s to 2.75 in 2024, while Jewish women's rose to 3.06. [cite:us18_jvl_tfr] The American rate was about 2.1 in 2007, then fell to 1.621 in 2023 and 1.599 in 2024, the lowest recorded. [cite:us18_ap_tfr2024] Provisional data for 2025 show 3,606,400 births and a general fertility rate of 53.1 per 1,000 women aged 15 to 44, down 23 per cent since 2007. [cite:us18_cdc_births2025]

None of this shows that policy alone sets birth rates. Israel's child allowances were cut in 2003 and 2013 without a lasting fall in the total rate, and its IVF and allowance policies sit alongside religious and family norms that the data do not separate. [cite:us18_nii_children2018] [cite:us18_jvl_tfr] What the record does show is a difference in what each state pays for: Israel funds fertility treatment, most abortions and a universal child allowance; the federal government in the United States funds none of the three as an entitlement, and since 2022 the law on abortion has depended on where a woman lives. [cite:us18_ijhpr_ivf] [cite:us18_kff_abortioncov]

sections.h: Pensions, Disability and Care in Old Age
sections.html:
Both countries run a social-insurance system founded in the twentieth century: the United States its Social Security programme, Israel its National Insurance Institute (NII). Both pay old-age, survivors' and disability pensions from payroll contributions; both sit beside a private layer of workplace pensions. They differ in how the private layer is built, in what the public pension is worth on its own and in how each state cares for older people who can no longer manage alone. This section compares them on each, with the limits of the record stated. The effect of all transfers together on poverty is the subject of the next section. [scene:us18_poverty|Poverty over time] [cite:us18_crs_ss2026] [cite:us18_nii_pov2023]

Old-age pensions: the public floor

Social Security is the largest anti-poverty programme in the United States by the Census Bureau's measure: in 2025 it lifted 28.8 million people above the Supplemental Poverty Measure's line. [cite:us18_census_p60290] It paid more than 71 million beneficiaries in 2025, at a total cost of $1,609.5 billion, 99.2 per cent of it in benefits. [cite:us18_crs_ss2026] Its finances are the main American pension question as of October 2026. The trustees' 2026 report projects that the old-age and survivors' trust fund will be exhausted in the fourth quarter of 2032 and the combined old-age and disability funds in the third quarter of 2034; after that, incoming payroll taxes would cover about 83 per cent of scheduled benefits, falling to 65 per cent by 2100, unless Congress acts. The 75-year shortfall grew from 3.82 per cent of taxable payroll in the 2025 report to 4.42 per cent in 2026. [cite:us18_crs_ss2026]

Israel's public pension is smaller relative to wages. The NII pays a flat old-age allowance, with increments, and a means-tested income supplement for older people with little else; a Taub Center brief of January 2014 estimated that the public pension alone would replace about 22 per cent of the wage of an average-wage man then entering the labour market (about 78 per cent with his workplace pension added), and found that only 24 per cent of the elderly received the supplement, most of them older immigrants, because strict means tests limited access for others. [cite:us18_taub_elderly] The same brief recorded official retirement ages of 67 for men and 62 for women, and a Knesset decision to postpone a planned rise in the women's age. [cite:us18_taub_elderly]

Workplace pensions: compulsory in Israel, voluntary in America

The larger difference lies in the second layer. Israel rebuilt its occupational pensions in stages: in 1995 it closed the old defined-benefit funds to new members; it moved new savers to defined-contribution funds; and in 2008 it made workplace pensions compulsory. [cite:us18_cup_pension] Under the 2008 order every salaried employee must be enrolled, and from January 2014 contributions reached at least 17.5 per cent of salary up to the average wage, about two-thirds of it paid by the employer. [cite:us18_taub_elderly] By the account of two Israeli economists, these reforms made long-term pension saving the main component of Israeli household saving. [cite:us18_cup_pension]

The United States has no equivalent federal requirement. The Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) regulates workplace plans that employers choose to set up, but, in the Labor Department's words, it "does not require any employer to establish a retirement plan." [cite:us18a_dol_erisa] Whether a worker has a workplace pension therefore depends on whether the employer offers a plan and whether the worker joins it. In March 2025, 72 per cent of private-sector workers had access to a retirement plan and 53 per cent took part; access ranged from 38 per cent in the lowest-paid tenth of jobs to 93 per cent in the highest-paid tenth. [cite:us18a_bls_ret2025] This book has not rebuilt an earlier American coverage series or an Israeli participation figure on the same basis, so the table below compares the two designs; Social Security is the one pension federal law provides to all who qualify by their earnings record. [cite:us18_crs_ss2026]

Disability

In both countries disability pensions come from the same social-insurance system as old-age pensions. In the United States the disability insurance trust fund is one half of the combined fund whose exhaustion the trustees now date to 2034. [cite:us18_crs_ss2026] In Israel the adequacy of the NII's general disability pension became a political fight. Disabled activists blocked roads and the Knesset entrance through 2017 and early 2018, demanding that the pension be raised to the level of the minimum wage; a bill to do so was rejected in committee for the third time in March 2017. On 13 February 2018 the Knesset passed, 84 to 0, a four-year plan costing NIS 4.3 billion ($1.23 billion) that raised monthly benefits by NIS 470 to 770, depending on the degree of disability, bringing the maximum to nearly NIS 4,000. The welfare minister, Haim Katz, called it "the first step to bringing it up to minimum wage"; protesters called it too small. [cite:us18_toi_disability] The NII's own figures credit disability pensions with reducing family poverty by 13.3 per cent in 2023, up from 12.3 per cent in 2022. [cite:us18_nii_pov2023]

Care in old age

Israel pays a long-term care benefit through the NII to older people who need help with daily living. A reform in force from November 2018 raised the number of benefit levels from three to six, let recipients choose cash, care hours or a mix and change the mix as their condition changes, and widened eligibility. In the four years after the reform the number of recipients grew by about 131,400; the NII now counts 309,435 older people receiving the benefit, about 55,000 of them in a serious nursing condition. About 14.5 per cent take cash, 57 per cent a hybrid and 28.5 per cent services in kind. [cite:us18_nii_ltc] The NII itself notes a weakness: because old-age pensions have not risen much in recent years, it believes some families use the cash care benefit to meet basic needs rather than for care. [cite:us18_nii_ltc] This part has not sourced a comparable American series on long-term care; Part Sixteen sets out how Medicare and Medicaid cover older and poorer Americans. [scene:us16_systems|Part Sixteen: who is covered] [cite:us16_census_2025]

Unemployment

Israel pays unemployment benefit nationally through the NII. The benefit is progressive: lower earners get a higher share of their last wage, from 33 to 80 per cent, capped at the average wage for the first five months and two-thirds of it after that; in 2015 the average benefit was 49.2 per cent of the average wage. [cite:us18a_nii_ui2015] It lasts 50 to 175 days, depending on age and the number of dependants: 50 days for a claimant under 25 with up to two dependants, 175 for one aged 45 or over. [cite:us18a_nii_uiperiod] The cuts of 2002–03 lengthened the qualifying period from six months' work in the previous year to twelve of the previous eighteen and halved the maximum for those under 25 from 100 days to 50; in 2015 about 35 per cent of the unemployed, some 70,000 of 202,000, received benefit. [cite:us18a_nii_ui2015] In the United States unemployment insurance is a federal-state system in which each state sets its own rules. Most states pay for up to 26 weeks; as of September 2026, 16 paid for fewer, and Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina and Tennessee for as few as 12. [cite:us18a_cbpp_uiweeks] The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning research group, calculated that the average benefit replaced 46.6 per cent of prior earnings in 2013, from 33.9 per cent in Alaska to 54.3 per cent in Hawaii, and that outside recessions fewer than half of unemployed workers have received benefits since the late 1950s: about 40 per cent at the end of 2013 and under 30 per cent in early 2014. [cite:us18a_cbpp_uiintro] These are snapshots from different years and on different definitions (Israel's figure is the average benefit against the national average wage; the American one is against each recipient's own prior earnings), so they show the designs rather than a measured gap. Both systems pay a minority of the unemployed.

The cost to Israel's budget of the wars since 2023, which competes with social spending, is set out elsewhere in the library. [scene:gi16_costs|The bill for the wars] [cite:gi16_boi_2025]

sections.h: Poverty Over Time: Two Official Measures
sections.html:
The most quoted comparison of the two safety nets sets an American poverty rate of about 10 per cent beside an Israeli rate of about 21 per cent. Both numbers are official and both are current. They do not measure the same thing. The United States counts people below a fixed income threshold; Israel counts people below half the typical income in their own country. This section sets out each country's own series over time, then the one comparison made on a shared definition, and then what each series shows about who is poor. [cite:us18_crs_pov2025] [cite:us18_nii_pov2018]

Two definitions

Israel's National Insurance Institute (NII) uses a relative line: a person is poor if the household's disposable income, after taxes and transfers and adjusted for household size, is below 50 per cent of the median. [cite:us18_nii_pov2018] In 2024 that line was NIS 3,547 a month per standard person, NIS 7,095 for a couple and NIS 13,303 for a couple with three children. [cite:us18_nii_pov2024] Because the line rises with median income, the rate falls only when the incomes of the poor rise faster than the middle.

The United States has two official measures. The official poverty measure compares cash income with fixed thresholds updated for prices: in 2025, $16,749 for a single person under 65 and $32,649 for two adults with two children. The Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) also counts refundable tax credits and non-cash benefits such as food assistance (SNAP). [cite:us18_crs_pov2025] Neither is a relative measure, so neither is directly comparable with the NII's.

The United States, 1959–2025

On the official measure, 22.4 per cent of Americans were poor in 1959. The rate fell to 11.1 per cent by 1973, then rose and fell with the business cycle: 13.0 per cent in 1980, 15.2 per cent in 1983, 13.5 per cent in 1990, 15.1 per cent in 1993, 11.3 per cent in 2000, 15.1 per cent again in 2010 after the financial crisis, and 10.5 per cent in 2019. [cite:us18_epi_povtrend] In 2025 it fell to 10.2 per cent, 34.5 million people, which Stateline reported as the lowest on record; the Census Bureau called child poverty, at 13.4 per cent, a historic low. [cite:us18_census_p60290] [cite:us18_njm_poverty] The 2024 figure appears as 10.6 per cent in the historical table and as 10.7 per cent in the Census Bureau's 2025 report (a fall of 0.5 points to 10.2) and the Congressional Research Service's comparison; the difference is unexplained in the sources this book used. [cite:us18_epi_povtrend] [cite:us18_census_p60290] [cite:us18_crs_pov2025]

The SPM, which counts what government programmes add, stood at 13.1 per cent in 2025, not statistically different from 2024. [cite:us18_census_p60290] It shows what transfers do: Social Security alone lifted 28.8 million people above the SPM line in 2025. [cite:us18_census_p60290] It also showed the effect of the 2021 expanded Child Tax Credit, when child poverty on the SPM fell to 5.2 per cent before rising to 12.4 per cent in 2022 after the credit lapsed. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] The 2025 figures predate most of the cuts to Medicaid and food assistance in the tax and spending law Congress passed in 2025. Experts cited, without names, by Stateline expected "grimmer statistics" in next year's report, and the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, which Stateline describes as left-leaning, counted 1.2 million fewer children receiving SNAP in July 2026 than a year earlier. [cite:us18_njm_poverty]

Israel, 2004–2024

The NII's own reports break Israel's series in 2011–12, when the survey changed from an income survey to an expenditure survey, so figures before and after are not strictly comparable. [cite:us18_nii_pov2018] On the earlier basis, 23.6 per cent of people and 33.2 per cent of children were poor in 2004, and 24.5 per cent of people and 35.8 per cent of children in 2006, after the cuts to child allowances and income support of 2002–2004.
