[cite:us18_nii_survey2007] On the later basis the person rate was about 21.9 per cent in 2010 and 22.3 per cent in 2015, 21.2 per cent in 2018, 20.1 per cent in 2020 (when emergency pandemic grants cut poverty sharply), 20.8 per cent in 2022 and 20.7 per cent in 2024. [cite:us18_nii_pov2023] [cite:us18_nii_pov2018] [cite:us18_nii_pov2024] Child poverty was 28 per cent in 2024, about 880,000 children. [cite:us18_nii_pov2024]

The one shared yardstick

The NII publishes its own figures recalculated on the OECD's equivalence scale, which allows a comparison with other countries on one relative definition. For 2023 it put Israel's person poverty rate at 19.5 per cent against an OECD average of 11.6 per cent, and its child poverty rate at 23.4 per cent against 12.4 per cent; on both measures Israel ranked second-highest, after Costa Rica. For people aged 66 and over the gap is smaller: 17.8 per cent against 15.1 per cent. [cite:us18_nii_pov2023] The American figure on the same OECD basis appears in the NII report only in a chart this book could not read, so it is not given here. What the shared yardstick does establish is that the common pairing of an American 10 per cent with an Israeli 21 per cent sets a fixed-threshold measure beside a relative one, and so does not measure the gap between the two countries.

What transfers do, and who is poor

Each country's transfers do much of the work. Without NII benefits, 31.5 per cent of Israelis and 34.5 per cent of families would have been poor in 2024, against 20.7 and 20.0 per cent after them. [cite:us18_nii_pov2024] Taxes and transfers together cut person poverty by 36.0 per cent in 2010, 30.1 per cent in 2019, 41.1 per cent in 2020 during the pandemic grants and 33.5 per cent in 2023. [cite:us18_nii_pov2023] Old-age and survivors' pensions do most of it, reducing family poverty by 24.2 per cent in 2023; income support, the NII's last-resort benefit, reduced it by only 1.3 per cent. [cite:us18_nii_pov2023] The erosion of that last-resort layer shows in the NII's own numbers: income support plus child allowances for a couple with two children fell from about 71 per cent of the poverty line in 2002 to 48.9 per cent in 2006. [cite:us18_nii_survey2007]

Older people show the clearest change in Israel. In the mid-2000s about one in five elderly Israelis was poor on disposable income, higher than in any of 21 OECD countries examined. [cite:us18_taub_elderly] The NII's figure for the elderly was 25.1 per cent in 2004 and 18.8 per cent in 2018; its current reports give 12.8 per cent for 2022 and 2023, though the revisions to the series between those reports mean the fall is partly one of method. [cite:us18_nii_survey2007] [cite:us18_nii_pov2018] [cite:us18_nii_pov2023] The NII still counted 158,700 poor older people in 2024 and put their rate above the OECD average. [cite:us18_nii_pov2024]

Poverty in Israel is concentrated in identifiable places and groups, and the units of measure need care. In 2024, 37.6 per cent of Arab families and 32.8 per cent of Haredi families were poor; these are family rates, to be set beside the national family rate of 20.0 per cent, not the person rate of 20.7 per cent. Jerusalem district had a family poverty rate of 36.5 per cent. [cite:us18_nii_pov2024] Part Eight sets out the mechanisms behind these gaps: labour-market access, schooling streams, planning law and the exemptions and stipends tied to Haredi study. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: Israel's equality record] In the United States the official rate among full-time, year-round workers was 1.6 per cent in 2025, against 10.2 per cent overall; Part Eight sets out the racial gaps. [cite:us18_crs_pov2025] [scene:us8_us|Part Eight: the US record] Food insecurity, a different measure, touched 28.1 per cent of Israelis in 2024, about a million of them children. [cite:us18_nii_pov2024]

chapters.label: Part Nineteen
chapters.title: Military and Security
chapters.intro: Part Nineteen compares how the two states raise, pay for and look after their armed forces. It sets Israel's conscript army and large reserve beside America's volunteer force, follows the yeshiva-student exemption to the High Court's ruling of June 2024 and the fight over enforcing it ahead of Israel's election, and measures the burden that the wars since 2023 have placed on reservists and their families. It compares the care each state gives its veterans, the American Department of Veterans Affairs and the Israeli Defence Ministry's rehabilitation system. It then traces defence spending as a share of each economy from the 1980s to 2025, and closes by asking precisely who has paid for Iron Dome and Israel's other missile defences.
chapters.outro: Part Nineteen established that the two states raise their armies by opposite laws: Israel conscripts most Jewish citizens under the 1949 Defense Service Law and leans on a reserve whose average member had served 233 days of the war by mid-2026, while the United States has relied on volunteers since 1973, with an active force that fell from 2.1 million in 1989 to about 1.28 million. [cite:us19_wiki_conscription] [cite:us19_taub_miluim] [cite:us19_crs_size2006] [cite:us19_crs_endstrength] Israel's High Court ruled on 25 June 2024 that yeshiva students had no legal exemption, yet about 80,000 eligible Haredi men had not enlisted by January 2026, and a July 2026 law to stop arrests was frozen by the court and struck down on 3 September 2026, ahead of the 27 October election. [cite:us19_globes_ruling2024] [cite:us19_toi_evaders2026] [cite:us19_globes_arrestlaw] [cite:us19a_jpost_struck] Veterans' care costs the United States $445.5 billion in 2026, while Israel's rehabilitation system was treating more than 82,000 people by December 2025, 22,000 of them since October 2023. [cite:us19_crs_va2026] [cite:us19_jns_rehab] Israel's defence burden fell from more than a fifth of GDP in the mid-1980s to 4.2 per cent in 2022 before the wars lifted it to 7.8 per cent in 2025; America's fell from 6.2 per cent in 1986 to 3.1 per cent. [cite:us1_jvl_melnick] [cite:gi16_boi_2025] [cite:us19_crs_budget2001] [cite:us19_sipri_fs2025] The United States has paid $6.08 billion for Iron Dome since 2011 and $14.8 billion for Israel's missile-defence programmes since 2006, for a system Israel developed alone, with a growing share built in American plants. [cite:us19_crs_md] [cite:ow8_rtx_camden] Part Twenty follows the rest of the money in both directions. [scene:us20_aid|Part Twenty: foreign policy and the money flow]

sections.h: Who Serves: Conscription, the Volunteer Force and the Veterans
sections.html:
Israel and the United States raise their armies by opposite methods. Israel conscripts most Jewish citizens at eighteen and calls them back as reservists for two decades; the United States has filled its ranks with volunteers since 1973. The method decides who carries the weight of a war, who is excused, and what the state owes afterwards. This section compares the two systems over time: the laws, the size of each force against its population, the exemptions, the burden on reservists, and the care each state gives to those wounded in its service. The money is counted in the next section. [scene:us19_spending|Defence spending and who pays]

Israel: a conscript army with a reserve behind it

The Knesset passed the Defense Service Law in 1949, giving the army authority to enlist citizens over eighteen. The law set service at 30 months for men and 18 for women; a temporary order in 1968 raised it to 36 and 24 months; men have served 32 months since 2015, and discharged soldiers remain liable for reserve duty to about age 40. Druze and Circassian men are conscripted, the Druze since 1956; other Arab citizens are not conscripted, though they may volunteer; religious Jewish women are exempt and many do civilian national service instead. In 2019, 69 per cent of Jewish men and 59 per cent of Jewish women were drafted; in 2013 the army exempted 26 per cent of potential conscripts, 13.5 per cent on religious grounds. [cite:us19_wiki_conscription] The International Institute for Strategic Studies counted 169,500 active troops and 465,000 reservists in 2025. [cite:hm_almon_idf] Against Israel's population of about 10.3 million, that standing force is about 1.6 per cent of residents, by this book's arithmetic. [cite:us1_jpost_ilpop]

The reserve is the army's mass. In the days after 7 October 2023 Israel mobilised about 360,000 reservists, some 300,000 of them in 48 hours, about 4 per cent of the population. [cite:hm_adn_360k] The Taub Center's July 2026 status report found that the average reservist had served 233 cumulative days since the war began, and that more than 100,000 fathers had served between 290 and 320 days. Its conservative estimate of their long-term wage loss was at least 4.7 per cent for the average reservist and 5.8 to 6.4 per cent for those fathers; on the average of the research literature the loss would be 19 to 21 per cent. Thirty per cent of reservists' salaried wives saw their wages cut and 3 per cent were dismissed, and about 70,000 students served in the 2024/25 academic year. The National Insurance Institute pays reservists' benefits; the report gives no total cost. [cite:us19_taub_miluim]

The Haredi exemption and the 2024 ruling

The largest exemption is the deferral for full-time yeshiva students, which Part Seven traces in full. [scene:us7_haredi|Part Seven: the Haredi exemption] About 400 students were exempted in 1949; by the end of June 2023 the state counted about 63,000. On 25 June 2024 a panel of nine High Court justices ruled unanimously that no law distinguished yeshiva students from anyone else liable to serve, that the government had "instructed the military authorities to apply illegitimate selective enforcement," and that state funding for yeshiva and kollel students without a lawful exemption or deferral must stop. [cite:us19_globes_ruling2024] The earlier statutory route, the Tal Law of 2002, had been struck down on 21 February 2012, and the 2014 enlistment amendments were struck down on 12 September 2017. [cite:us7_wiki_haredidraft]

Enforcement since the ruling has been slow. On 20 January 2026 an army officer told the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee that about 30,000 people were designated draft evaders, half of them Haredi, that about 80,000 Haredi men aged 18 to 24 were eligible but had not enlisted, and that the army urgently needed 12,000 more recruits. The chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, asked to restore men's service to 36 months. The government's bill, drafted by committee chairman Boaz Bismuth, would restore broad exemptions and half the lost yeshiva funding; critics including the army's leadership and the attorney general objected that it would not raise Haredi enlistment, by The Times of Israel's account. [cite:us19_toi_evaders2026] On 13 July 2026 the Knesset passed Basic Law: Torah Study, which declares Torah study a "foundational value" and which petitioners called "a draft exemption law through the back door." [cite:us2_toi_torahlaw] On 14 July it passed, by 58 votes to 54, a temporary amendment to the Security Service Law cancelling arrests of Haredi draft evaders; the next day Justice Ofer Grosskopf suspended it pending a hearing before an expanded panel. [cite:us19_globes_arrestlaw] A nine-justice panel kept the freeze after a hearing on 28 July that the government boycotted; the attorney general's representative argued that "a law that creates discrimination in criminal enforcement cannot stand, even if it is temporary." [cite:us19a_toi_hearing] In early August the public broadcaster KAN reported that Netanyahu had told officials he would not advance the law after the election, an account neither his office nor Likud confirmed. [cite:us19_jpost_netanyahu] On 3 September 2026 the court unanimously struck the law down for a defective legislative process, eight of the nine justices also finding it unconstitutional in substance; the ruling did not direct the army to make particular arrests. [cite:us19a_jpost_struck] As of October 2026 no replacement conscription law had been reported in the sources this book found, and Israel votes on 27 October 2026 with the draft one of the questions before voters. The coalition's stated position, written into the Basic Law, is that Torah study is a "foundational value"; on the record above, the arrangement it defends leaves the burden of service with those who are called up repeatedly. That is a description of how the law allocates duty, not of any community.

The United States: a volunteer force since 1973

The United States ended conscription in 1973 after the Gates Commission recommended an all-volunteer force. [cite:us19_cfr_avf] No draft has been activated since then. Men aged 18 to 25 must still register with the Selective Service System, and the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act made that registration automatic, from as early as December 2026. [cite:us19_kmph_sss]

The force has shrunk over time. Active-duty strength never fell below 2.0 million during the Cold War and peaked above 3.5 million during the Korean and Vietnam wars; it was 2.1 million in 1989 and fell to about 1.4 million by 1999. [cite:us19_crs_size2006] Congress authorised 1,284,500 for 2024 and 1,276,700 for 2025. [cite:us19_crs_endstrength] Against a population of 341.8 million in 2025, that is about 0.4 per cent of residents, by this book's arithmetic. [cite:us1_wa_uspop] Veterans made up about 18 per cent of American adults in 1980 and 6 per cent in 2022, by Census figures compiled by the Pew Research Center. [cite:us19_pew_veterans] A volunteer force must compete for recruits in the labour market: the Army missed its 2022 recruiting goal by 15,000. [cite:us19_cfr_avf] Military service in the United States is therefore concentrated in a small share of the population, chosen by enlistment rather than by law, and the burden of the 2026 war with Iran fell on that force: the Pentagon counted 21 service members killed in it by October 2026. [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026]

What each state owes afterwards

The United States cares for its veterans through a cabinet department. Congress enacted $445.49 billion for Veterans Affairs for fiscal year 2026, of which $312.30 billion was mandatory spending, mostly benefits; the total was up 21 per cent from $367.71 billion in 2025. VA appropriations were $37.47 billion in 1995; in 2025 dollars they rose from $72.20 billion to $391.03 billion between 1995 and 2025. Of about 17.6 million veterans, about 9.2 million are enrolled in VA health care, and VA expected to pay disability compensation to about 6.46 million in 2026; recipients rose from 3.3 million in 2011 to 5.8 million in 2024. The 2022 PACT Act's fund for illnesses linked to toxic exposures had received $108.90 billion by 2026. [cite:us19_crs_va2026]

Israel's care for wounded soldiers sits in the Defence Ministry's Rehabilitation Division. By December 2025 it was treating more than 82,000 people, 22,000 of whom had joined since 7 October 2023. [cite:us19_jns_rehab] In July 2025 the ministry said more than 10,000 were in treatment for war-related mental trauma, 3,769 had been recognised with post-traumatic stress, and it expected about 100,000 wounded and disabled veterans by 2028. [cite:us19_ynet_rehab] No published total budget for the division was found for this book; that gap is stated rather than estimated. The two systems differ in scale and in form, a separate department beside a ministry division, and both are growing: the American disability rolls since 2011, the Israeli rehabilitation caseload since 2023.

sections.h: Defence Spending Over Time, and Who Pays for Iron Dome
sections.html:
Both states spend more on their militaries than most of their peers, but the weight of that spending has moved in opposite directions over four decades. This section sets out the burden of defence on each economy from the 1980s to 2025, using each country's own series and SIPRI's common measure, and then asks a narrower question that is often asked loosely: who pays for Israel's missile defences, Iron Dome above all. The aid itself is set out in Part One and, in more detail, in an earlier volume. [scene:us1_aid|Part One: what the aid is] [scene:gi16_aid|The aid in detail]

Israel: from a fifth of GDP to a twentieth, and back up

In the mid-1980s Israel spent more than 20 per cent of its GDP on defence, with inflation above 400 per cent a year before the 1985 stabilisation plan, which an American grant of $1.5 billion over two years helped carry. [cite:us1_jvl_melnick] The burden then fell steadily. On the total-cost measure used by Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics, which adds costs outside the defence budget, it was 10 per cent of GDP in 1993, 8.2 per cent in 2000, 7.8 per cent in 2005 and 7.0 per cent in 2009. [cite:us1_inss_even2010] By the Bank of Israel's count, defence spending averaged 5.3 per cent of GDP in 2015–2019 and was 4.2 per cent in 2022, its lowest point; then the wars reversed the trend, to 5.2 per cent in 2023, 8.4 per cent in 2024 and 7.8 per cent in 2025. The central bank assumes about 5.5 per cent a year for 2026–2030. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] SIPRI, measuring on its own common definition, put Israel's military spending at $48.3 billion in 2025, 7.8 per cent of GDP and 120 per cent above 2016 in real terms. [cite:us19_sipri_fs2025] The Knesset's 2026 budget gave defence about $44.8 billion. [cite:gi16_bd_budget2026] These series do not use the same definition, and the points are shown separately rather than joined into one line.

The United States: Cold War peaks, a long decline

American defence outlays, on the Office of Management and Budget's measure, were 9.4 per cent of GDP in 1968, at the height of the Vietnam War, 4.9 per cent in 1980, 6.2 per cent in 1986 at the peak of the Reagan build-up, 5.2 per cent in 1990, 3.7 per cent in 1995 and 3.0 per cent in 2000. Defence took 27.6 per cent of federal outlays in 1986 and 16.3 per cent in 2000. [cite:us19_crs_budget2001] On SIPRI's measure the burden was 3.4 per cent of GDP in 2016 and 3.1 per cent in 2025, when American military spending reached $954 billion, a third of the world's total and 11 per cent above 2016 in real terms. [cite:us19_sipri_fs2025] The 2026 war with Iran came on top: Central Command put its cost at $43.6 billion as of 3 September 2026. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] That sum, for one American war over about six months, is close to Israel's entire defence budget for 2026, though the two figures count different things. [cite:gi16_bd_budget2026]

Two points follow. The first is that Israel's burden, even at its post-2023 level, is well below what it carried in the mid-1980s, while America's is close to its post-Cold War low of about 3 per cent; the ratio between the two burdens has narrowed from more than three to one in the mid-1980s to about two and a half to one in 2025. The second is the aid's weight within Israel's effort. The regular American grant, about $3 billion a year in 2011 and $3.8 billion under the 2016 agreement, was about a quarter of Israel's security outlays in 2011 by the Israeli economist Gazit's estimate; by 2025–26 the CRS put the military financing at "approximately 14%" of the defence budget and INSS at "roughly 15%". It was "about half a percent" of GDP by INSS's estimate, about 0.6 per cent in 2025 by this book's arithmetic. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] Israel's own taxpayers and borrowing carry the rest; the Bank of Israel counts the war's gross budget cost at about NIS 352 billion for 2023–2026. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] [scene:gi16_costs|What the wars cost]

Iron Dome: the told version and the record

A common claim in American debate holds that the United States pays for Iron Dome. The record is more specific. Israel developed Iron Dome on its own and initially retained the proprietary rights, and it was first fielded in 2011. [cite:us19_crs_md] [cite:ow1_csis_imd] American funding began in fiscal year 2011 with $205 million. By the Congressional Research Service's tables, Congress appropriated $6.08 billion for Iron Dome from 2011 to 2025, $3.83 billion for David's Sling, $3.71 billion for the two Arrow systems since 2006 and $1.2 billion for the Iron Beam laser, $14.8 billion in all for 2006–2025; the Arrow programme alone has received $4.75 billion since 1990. [cite:us19_crs_md] The Missile Defense Agency's obligations, a different measure that runs from earlier years, total $16.1 billion through 2025, of which $5.7 billion came in 2024 alone: the regular $500 million plus the April 2024 supplemental's $4 billion for Iron Dome and David's Sling and $1.2 billion for Iron Beam. [cite:us19_crs_md] [cite:hz12b_hac_onepager]

The 2016 agreement fixes the regular sum at $500 million a year from 2019 to 2028, divided roughly into $300 million for research and development, which Israel matches, and $200 million for procurement and co-production, at least half of which must be spent in the United States. [cite:us19_crs_md] The American share of Iron Dome production was 30 per cent by 2023 testimony, and on 9 October 2026 a Raytheon–Rafael joint venture delivered the first Tamir interceptors built in Camden, Arkansas. [cite:us19_crs_md] [cite:ow8_rtx_camden] The flow also ran the other way: the US Army bought two Iron Dome batteries in 2019, and in October 2023 the administration transferred them back to Israel under an arrangement a defence official described as a lease through a foreign military sale. [cite:ow7_twz_irondome] [cite:us19_crs_md] Congress has backed the programme by wide margins; in July 2025 the House rejected, by 422 votes to 6, an amendment to strip the $500 million. [cite:us1_ji_greene] The industrial side of this partnership is told in Part Twelve. [scene:us12_defence|Part Twelve: defence industry]

The record therefore supports a narrower statement than the common one. The United States has paid for a large share of Iron Dome's batteries and interceptors since 2011, and for just under half of Arrow's development costs, while Israel designed Iron Dome, initially held its technology rights, matches the research money and pays for the rest of its defence. A growing part of the American money is spent in American factories. [cite:us19_crs_md] When the threat came from Iran rather than from rockets, the United States also defended Israel with its own systems and paid for that from its own budget: an estimated 100 to 150 THAAD interceptors in June 2025, which Costs of War priced at $1.8 to 1.95 billion. [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025] [cite:hz12_cow_2025] [scene:ow7_iran|Defending Israel, fighting Iran] Both governments face their elections with these sums live: Israel votes on 27 October 2026, the United States on 3 November, and talks on the agreement that follows 2028 are covered in Part Twenty. [scene:us20_aid|Part Twenty: the aid and the next agreement]

chapters.label: Part Twenty
chapters.title: Foreign Policy and the Money Flow
chapters.intro: Part Twenty follows the money between the two countries in both directions and puts every sum in today's dollars. It first lists the American government's channels to Israel: the 2016 memorandum of understanding and its Foreign Military Financing, fixed in nominal dollars and shrinking in real value; the phase-out of the share Israel may spend at home; the missile-defence money that also buys Israeli systems for the US Army; the loan guarantees of 1992 and 2003, which moved credit rather than cash and were cut for settlement spending; and intelligence sharing, the one channel with no published price. It then sets beside them the private and commercial flows: tax-deductible American gifts to Israeli organisations, including settlements; Israel Bonds bought by American states and cities; investment and trade; and the weapons and defence work that move from Israel to the United States. The detail of the aid itself is in Part One and in the Greater Israel volume, and is linked rather than repeated.
chapters.outro: Part Twenty established that the American government's grant to Israel is fixed in nominal dollars: the $3.8 billion a year signed in 2016 buys about what $2.7 billion bought then, and about a third of what American aid bought in 1985, which was worth about $11.5 billion in today's money. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us20_bls_cpi_annual] The share Israel may spend at home falls to zero in fiscal 2028, missile-defence money of $14.8 billion since 2006 has paid for co-production in both countries, and the loan guarantees of 1992 and 2003 moved credit rather than cash and were cut by the amount Israel spent on settlements. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:us20_jvl_loans] Intelligence sharing, from the 1950s liaison to the raw signals data agreed in 2009 and the drone feeds of 2023, has no public price and unpublished terms. [cite:ow3_tablet] [cite:us20_aje_nsa] [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] Beside the grant run larger private and commercial flows: tax-deductible American giving of about $2.65 billion in 2021, with $224 million routed to settlements in 2009–2013 alone; Israel Bonds; $59.7 billion of American direct investment in Israel against $22.2 billion of Israeli investment in the United States; and a goods trade in which America buys more than it sells. [cite:us20_ejp_giving2021] [cite:us20_toi_settlements] [cite:us20_selectusa_israel] [cite:us11_ustr_israel] The successor to the 2028 agreement was still under negotiation as of October 2026, ahead of Israel's election on 27 October and America's on 3 November. [cite:ow1_mod_mou2026] Part Twenty-One brings the measures of the whole volume together and asks what the comparison shows. [scene:us21_ledger|Part Twenty-One: the ledger]

sections.h: The Government Channels: Grants, Guarantees, Missile Defence and Intelligence
sections.html:
The memorandum of understanding (MOU) is the channel everyone knows, and it is set out in full elsewhere: Part One of this volume weighs it against Israel's economy, and Part Fifteen of the Greater Israel volume follows the emergency money that came after October 2023. [scene:us1_aid|Part One: the aid] [scene:gi16_aid|The aid in detail] This section lists every channel through which the American government moves money, guarantees or information to Israel, states what each is worth in today's dollars, and marks which ones run the other way. "Today's dollars" in this part means the September 2026 consumer price index for all urban consumers (CPI-U), 336.940, set against the annual average for the year a sum was committed. [cite:us20_bls_cpi_sep26] [cite:us20_bls_cpi_annual] The conversions are this book's arithmetic and measure purchasing power in the United States, not the value of the goods to Israel.

The grant: fixed in dollars, shrinking in value

The 2016 MOU promised $38 billion for the fiscal years 2019 to 2028: $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing (FMF) and $5 billion for missile defence, or $3.8 billion a year. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] The sum is fixed in nominal dollars. Prices rose by about 40 per cent between the 2016 annual average and September 2026, so the $3.8 billion paid in 2026 buys what about $2.7 billion bought when the agreement was signed, by this book's arithmetic. [cite:us20_bls_cpi_annual] [cite:us20_bls_cpi_sep26] The long view shows the same erosion. American aid in 1985, $3.68 billion including an emergency economic grant, equals about $11.5 billion in September 2026 dollars; the Congressional Research Service (CRS) estimate of all aid since 1946, about $298 billion in 2024 dollars, equals about $320 billion today. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] Measured in what it buys, the regular grant is now about a third of its 1985 size, though the wartime supplemental of 2024 lifted that single year to about $12.5 billion. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable]

Where the grant may be spent

Under the 2007 MOU Israel could spend up to 26.3 per cent of its FMF inside Israel, a practice called offshore procurement; in 2016 that was $815 million. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_ni_osp] The 2016 MOU phases it out, slowly until fiscal 2024 and then sharply, "ending entirely in FY2028"; the fiscal 2025 appropriation allowed $450.3 million. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The White House said in 2016 that ending offshore procurement and the use of FMF for fuel would move up to $1.2 billion a year more into American-made goods. [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] Two details in the CRS account matter for the flow. Israel's Defence Ministry reportedly spends about one third of its FMF on direct commercial contracts with American firms rather than through government-to-government sales, and under a "Special Billing Arrangement" Israel may draw on its own cash reserves for sales costs beyond the MOU's amounts or term. If no successor agreement is reached and Congress stops appropriating FMF, Israel would have to pay for existing contracts with national funds, find other financing or cancel them. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] Interest earned on the early lump-sum payment cannot be used for purchases inside Israel. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025]

Missile defence: the channel that runs both ways

Missile defence is the one large channel in which money and goods move in both directions. CRS counts $14.8 billion in American missile-defence funding for Israel from fiscal 2006 to 2025, including about $6.1 billion for Iron Dome batteries, interceptors, co-production and maintenance and $1.2 billion for the Iron Beam laser, all of the latter in the 2024 supplemental. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] From 2016 production money for David's Sling and Arrow 3 was split about evenly between the Israeli makers and their American partners, Raytheon and Boeing; a 2014 agreement let Iron Dome parts be made in the United States and gave the Missile Defense Agency full access to the technology. [cite:ow8_dn_coprod2016] [cite:ow8_crs_irondome2014] The United States has also bought the product. On 6 February 2019 the two defence ministries confirmed that the US Army would buy two Iron Dome batteries, with 240 interceptors, for $373 million as an interim defence against cruise missiles. [cite:us20_toi_armyirondome] On 24 October 2023 Washington transferred two American-owned Iron Dome batteries to Israel. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] The One-Way Mirror volume sets out the co-production pipeline in detail. [scene:ow8_coproduction|Co-production]

Loan guarantees: credit, not cash

Loan guarantees move no American money unless the borrower defaults. Congress authorised $10 billion in 1992, in five annual tranches of $2 billion, for loans tied to Israel's effort "to resettle and absorb immigrants" arriving from the former Soviet Union; that is about $24 billion in today's dollars. [cite:us20_jvl_loans] [cite:us20_bls_cpi_annual] The law allowed the guarantees to be cut by an amount equal to Israel's spending on settlements in the occupied territories. Washington cut them by $1,358.8 million in 1994–97, restored $585 million for security reasons, and left $9,226.2 million available. [cite:us20_jvl_loans] A second programme of $9 billion followed in 2003, about $16.5 billion in today's dollars, and was cut by $289.5 million in 2003 and $795.8 million in 2005 on the same settlement test. [cite:us20_jvl_loans] [cite:gi16_jvl_loans] By 2025 Israel had issued $4.1 billion in American-guaranteed bonds under it, and the remaining authority, up to $3.814 billion, runs to the end of fiscal 2030 under the 2025 appropriations law. [cite:us20_jvl_loans] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] By the account of the CRS data compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, Israel has never defaulted and paid annual fees for the guarantees, so the direct cost to the American government has been nil; the benefit to Israel lay in borrowing on American credit. [cite:us20_jvl_loans] The settlement deductions are the only case this book found in which the American government priced a specific Israeli policy and subtracted it from assistance. [scene:gi16_aid|Testing the fungibility argument]

A smaller channel sits beside these. The United States also keeps a stockpile of its own munitions in Israel, War Reserve Stocks for Allies–Israel; additions are capped at $500 million a year through fiscal 2027. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] Israel has held the status of major non-NATO ally since February 1987. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

Intelligence: the channel with no price

Intelligence sharing has no dollar value in any public record, and its terms are not published; the American Civil Liberties Union lists data-sharing agreements with Israel among those whose texts it has sought. [cite:ow4_aclu] What is documented is its history. The liaison began in the early 1950s, and James Angleton, who became head of the CIA's new Counterintelligence Staff in 1954, took control of the Israel account. [cite:ow3_robarge] [cite:ow3_tablet] A strategic cooperation agreement signed in November 1981 was temporarily suspended by the Reagan administration weeks later, after the Knesset extended Israeli law to the Golan Heights without consulting Washington. [cite:gi8_wiki_golanlaw] In September 2013 The Guardian, drawing on documents leaked by Edward Snowden, reported that the National Security Agency had agreed in principle in March 2009 to share raw signals intelligence with Israel, including unfiltered communications of American citizens, under a memorandum that did not require such data to be removed first; the NSA said American data were handled under procedures "designed to protect privacy rights". [cite:us20_aje_nsa] According to reporting by David Sanger of The New York Times in 2012, the two governments built the Stuxnet cyber-weapon against Iran's enrichment plant together from 2006; neither government has officially confirmed it. [cite:ow3_sw_sanger] After 7 October 2023 a White House memorandum expanded sharing to include live drone feeds over Gaza, The Wall Street Journal reported in April 2024; Reuters reported in December 2025 that in the second half of 2024 the United States briefly cut one feed and restricted some uses over concern about civilian deaths, while the Israeli military said "the strategic intelligence cooperation continued throughout the war." [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] [cite:ow3_reu_withheld] The relationship also carries counterintelligence concerns: in June 2026 NBC News, citing unnamed officials, reported that the Defense Intelligence Agency had raised its counterintelligence threat rating for Israel to "critical". [cite:ow13_nbc_dia] The One-Way Mirror volume follows this channel in full. [scene:ow3_channel|The intelligence channel]

Status as of October 2026

Israel's Defence Ministry announced on 5 June 2026 that talks had opened on a framework to replace the MOU, aiming to "gradually transition from aid to a completely reciprocal partnership", and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that month that he wanted the grant to begin falling toward zero. [cite:ow1_mod_mou2026] [cite:gi16_ji_netanyahu] As of October 2026 no new agreement had been reported in the sources this book found. Israel votes on 27 October 2026 and the United States on 3 November 2026, and both governments that negotiate the successor may change. [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve] [cite:us1_wjla_midterms] For each country the record shows a gap. On the American side, the government's largest channels are set by an executive agreement and annual appropriations, and the one documented price signal, the settlement deduction, was last applied in 2005 on the record this book found. [cite:us20_jvl_loans] On the Israeli side, a defence ministry that has relied on the grant for decades would carry the full cost of contracts signed against it if the money stops without a successor. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025]

sections.h: Money in Both Directions: Donations, Bonds, Investment and Arms
sections.html:
The government grant is one stream among several, and it is not the only one that runs in Israel's favour, nor is every stream one-way. This section sets the private and commercial flows beside the public ones: tax-deductible gifts from Americans to Israeli organisations, including settlements; Israeli government bonds bought by American states and cities; investment and trade; and the weapons and defence work that move from Israel to the United States. Sums are converted to September 2026 dollars with the consumer price index as in the previous section; the conversions are this book's arithmetic. [cite:us20_bls_cpi_annual] [cite:us20_bls_cpi_sep26]

Tax-deductible giving: how the law routes it

American tax law lets a donor deduct a gift to a foreign charity only if it passes through an American organisation. Since 1938 such gifts have been deductible when they go to a not-for-profit incorporated in the United States with a mostly American board, when the foreign recipient is the equivalent of an American tax-exempt body, and when the American organisation oversees its foreign grants. The usual vehicle is an "American Friends" organisation, set up to raise money in the United States for one Israeli institution. [cite:us20_brandeis_philanthropy] The deduction is a public cost as well as a private gift, because the Treasury collects less tax on every dollar deducted; this book found no official estimate of the revenue forgone on gifts to Israeli causes.

The giving has a long series. A Brandeis University study by Eric Fleisch and Theodore Sasson, built from Internal Revenue Service filings, counted $283 million in 1975, $461 million in 1985 and $774 million in 1994, in the dollars of each year, rising to $2.06 billion raised in 2007, of which $1.65 billion was donated after fundraising costs and endowment activity. [cite:us20_brandeis_philanthropy] The number of American Friends organisations grew from 265 at the end of the 1980s to 436 in 2000 and 667 in 2010. [cite:us20_brandeis_philanthropy] A later study by researchers at New York University and Tel Aviv University found more than $2.65 billion given by American donors to Israel's non-profit sector in 2021, from about 1,200 American organisations, of which 161 gave more than 80 per cent; Friends organisations gave $824 million in 2015 and more than $1.2 billion in 2021. [cite:us20_ejp_giving2021] The two studies measure slightly different things, so the series is approximate. In September 2026 dollars, by this book's arithmetic, the giving was about $1.4 billion in 1985, $1.8 billion in 1994, $3.3 billion in 2007 (amount raised) and $3.3 billion in 2021. [cite:us20_bls_cpi_annual] During the war the Jewish Federations' Israel Emergency Campaign alone raised $683 million in 2024, according to federation figures. [cite:us20_bjf_iec2024] In 2021 private American giving, $2.65 billion, equalled about 70 per cent of that year's $3.8 billion military grant, by this book's arithmetic, though the two pay for entirely different things. [cite:us20_ejp_giving2021] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025]

Giving to settlements

Most of that money goes to universities, hospitals, welfare and religious institutions inside Israel. A part goes to settlements in the occupied West Bank. Fleisch and Sasson counted about $40 million raised for settlements in 2007, against $167 million for religious education and $46 million for progressive causes. [cite:us20_brandeis_philanthropy] A Haaretz investigation by Uri Blau, published in December 2015, found that some 50 American organisations raised $281 million in tax-deductible donations in 2009–2013 and transferred $224 million of it to settlements through Israeli non-profits, about $320 million in today's dollars at 2013 prices. It named the Central Fund of Israel, the Hebron Fund and Honenu, which in 2013 gave a grant to the family of Ami Popper, convicted of murdering seven Palestinian labourers in 1990. A White House official told Haaretz that the administration "never defended or supported any activity associated with the settlements". [cite:us20_toi_settlements] The contrast is between two arms of the same government: in 1994–2005 Washington cut loan guarantees by the amount Israel spent on settlements, while the tax code continued to subsidise private gifts to them. [cite:us20_jvl_loans] [cite:us20_toi_settlements]

Israel's law treats foreign money by its source. A 2016 law requires non-governmental organisations funded mainly by foreign governments to say so publicly, a rule that, by Freedom House's account, falls mainly on left-leaning groups, while private foreign donations, including the American gifts to settlement bodies, are not covered by it. [cite:us3_fh_il2025] A 2025 bill to tax foreign-government donations to non-profits at 80 per cent won government backing in February 2025. [cite:us3_toi_ngotax] Part Three sets out those laws. [scene:us3_speech|Part Three: speech and NGO laws]

Bonds, investment and trade

Israel Bonds are loans, not gifts: the Development Corporation for Israel, registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, sells Israeli government debt in the United States and has raised $52 billion since 1951; Israel Bonds says Israel has never missed a payment. American states and municipalities bought more than $1.7 billion of it between October 2023 and July 2024, about $1.8 billion in today's dollars; Palm Beach County in Florida held about $700 million of a $4.67 billion portfolio by April 2024. [cite:pm_icij_bonds] The Follow the Money volume examines the sales methods and the legal challenges. [scene:pm8_bonds|Israel Bonds]

Investment runs in both directions and is larger than the grant. The Commerce Department's SelectUSA office put the stock of American direct investment in Israel at $59.7 billion in 2025, with $16.6 billion flowing in that year, and Israeli direct investment in the United States, measured by ultimate beneficial owner, at $22.2 billion, down from $24.5 billion in 2021. [cite:us20_selectusa_israel] Single companies account for much of the American side. Intel says it invested about $27 billion in Israel from 1974 to 2021, and Google completed its $32 billion purchase of the Israeli cloud-security firm Wiz on 11 March 2026. [cite:us12_intel_israel] [cite:ow4_globes_wiz] Goods trade, under the first American free trade agreement, in force since 1985, came to $34.4 billion in 2025: American exports of $13.7 billion and imports of $20.7 billion, a deficit for the United States of $7 billion. [cite:us11_ustr_israel] Part Twelve covers the industries behind those numbers. [scene:us12_tech|Part Twelve: technology]

Arms and defence work, Israel to the United States

The defence flow runs both ways too. Nearly all of the FMF grant is now spent with American contractors, which makes it at once a transfer to Israel's defence budget and a purchase from American industry. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] Part of that money returns to Israel through industrial cooperation: when Israel bought the F-35, paid for with aid, Lockheed Martin pledged about $4 billion in purchases from Israeli firms, and Israel Aerospace Industries makes F-35 wings. [cite:ow7_wiki_f35i] Israel also sells to the American government. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute found that the United States took 7.8 per cent of Israel's arms exports in 2021–2025, while the United States supplied 68 per cent of Israel's imports. [cite:us12_sipri_at2025] Israel's Defence Ministry reported a record $19.2 billion in export deals in 2025, 13 per cent of them with North America, about $2.5 billion by this book's arithmetic, a figure that includes Canada. [cite:us12_mod_exports2025] Elbit Systems' American subsidiary, renamed Twenty-Six Defense in September 2026, employs about 3,300 people in the United States and holds Customs and Border Protection contracts worth more than $370 million. [cite:ow10_dn_26] The US Army's $373 million Iron Dome purchase of 2019 belongs in the same column. [cite:us20_toi_armyirondome]

What the two-way ledger shows

The common claim is that the money runs one way, from American taxpayers to Israel. The record supports a narrower statement. The government grant does run one way, and Israel does not raise that money itself; it is military money spent mainly in the United States, and it is now worth about a third, in real terms, of what American aid was worth in 1985. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] The larger flows are commercial and private, and several of them run toward the United States: Israel sells more goods to America than it buys, and Israeli firms invest and sell weapons there. [cite:us11_ustr_israel] [cite:us20_selectusa_israel] Each system has a gap the ledger exposes. In the United States a tax deduction subsidises private gifts to settlements whose expansion the government penalised through the loan-guarantee deductions, with no published estimate of the deduction's cost. [cite:us20_jvl_loans] [cite:us20_toi_settlements] In Israel the law scrutinises foreign-government money for advocacy groups while private foreign money for settlement bodies falls outside that rule. [cite:us3_fh_il2025]

chapters.label: Part Twenty-One
chapters.title: What About America?
chapters.intro: The last part brings the volume's twenty parts together and answers the question it began with. It first sets out a ledger: for each area the book measured, from courts, elections and prisons to wages, housing, health, schools, family benefits and defence, the named measure, the latest value for each country, its direction since about 1980 or 2000, and the part where the source and definition are given, followed by a short reading of each group of measures and the gaps each system leaves. It then sets the American aid against that ledger: what it is, what it frees, where it is spent and what it weighs in Israel's economy and America's budget, then and now. It brings together the common claims the parts tested, says plainly what a comparison of this kind can and cannot show, and lists what is still open as of October 2026, from the two elections of 27 October and 3 November to the court cases pending in both countries and the talks on the agreement that replaces the aid memorandum in 2028. Any judgment it gives is given measure by measure; the total, with every measure and weight shown, follows in Part Twenty-Two.
chapters.outro: This volume set two states side by side over four decades and found that neither serves the people under its authority better on every measure. Israel covers every citizen and resident's health care by a 1995 law, guarantees fifteen weeks of paid leave after a birth, ties its wage floor to the average wage, and has moved from level life expectancy with the United States in 1980 to about four years ahead, with half America's infant mortality. [cite:us16_wiki_ilhealth] [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018] [cite:us13_kz_minwagelaw] [cite:us16_wb_le] [cite:us16_wb_imr] The United States pays higher average wages, scored well above Israel in the 2025 PISA round, performs civil marriages in every state and ranks far higher for press freedom, while leaving 26.7 million people uninsured, holding its federal minimum wage at $7.25 since 2009, imprisoning 542 people per 100,000 and counting 745,652 homeless on one night. [cite:us14_oecd_avwage] [cite:us17_ih_pisa2025] [cite:us7_wiki_obergefell] [cite:us3_wboc_rsf] [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us13_dol_minwage] [cite:us4_wpb_us] [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] Israel's averages leave out the 5.56 million Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza, roughly a third of the people under its control, governed without Israeli citizenship; inside its citizenry, the killings in Arab communities reached a record 252 in 2025 and the Haredi exemption, ruled unlawful in 2012, 2017 and 2024, still left about 80,000 eligible men unenlisted in January 2026. [cite:us9_pcbs_2025] [cite:us5_yahoo_herzog] [cite:us7_globes_draft2024] [cite:us19_toi_evaders2026] None of those differences is paid for by the American aid: $3.8 billion a year of military money, spent mostly in the United States, which has fallen from 12.7 per cent of Israel's GDP in 1985 to 0.6 per cent and is about 0.05 per cent of American federal outlays. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] [cite:us1_crfb_fy2025] Both countries vote within a week of each other, Israel on 27 October and the United States on 3 November 2026, and the governments they choose will negotiate what follows the aid agreement of 2016; every status in this book is stated as of October 2026 and should be read again after both votes. [cite:gi6_aje_dissolve] [cite:us1_wjla_midterms] [cite:ow1_mod_mou2026] The American side of the relationship is followed further in the library's other closing verdicts: the aid and the wars it supplies in the Greater Israel volume [scene:gi13_record|Greater Israel: settled, contested and open], the American religious constituency for Israel in The Theology Shield [scene:ts14_record|The Theology Shield: what the record settles], and the 2026 war and its American cost in The Iran Architecture. [scene:ir15_record|The Iran Architecture: what the record settles]

sections.h: The Ledger: Twenty Parts, Measure by Measure
sections.html:
This section gathers what Parts One to Twenty measured into one ledger. Nothing new is introduced: every figure below is the one a part gave, with the source and the definition that part used, and each row links back to it. The rules are the ones Part One laid down. The ledger compares systems, laws and governments, never peoples; it puts the same source beside both countries wherever one exists; it gives a direction over time wherever a series exists and says so where only a snapshot does; and it states whom each figure covers. Israel's national figures describe its citizens and residents, about 10.3 million people in September 2026, not the Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza, whom Part Nine counts separately. [cite:us1_jpost_ilpop] [cite:us1_fh_israel2026] [scene:us1_compare|Part One: how this book compares] Where a judgment is given below, it is given for one measure at a time and says which way that measure points. No row is weighted against another here, because the measures are not in the same units and a reader who values them differently would weigh them differently; Part Twenty-Two adds a total in the open, with every goalpost and weight printed so that a reader can recompute it. [scene:us22_method|Part Twenty-Two: the scorecard]

State and rights

On the measures of how each state is governed, both records moved down in this decade, by different routes. Transparency International's index fell nine points for the United States between 2012 and 2025 and rose two for Israel, so on that measure Israel's trend is the better of the two; V-Dem moved both out of its top category, Israel in 2023 and the United States in 2025; and both fell in the 2026 press-freedom index. [cite:us2_wiki_cpi] [cite:us3_vdem2026] [cite:us3_rsf_il] [cite:us3_wboc_rsf] The forms differ. Israel restricts by statute, from a single state of emergency in force since 1948 to a military censor and a boycott tort; the American restrictions of 2025–26 came mainly by executive action, against a constitution that courts used to stop some of it, most visibly in the tariff ruling of 20 February 2026. [cite:us2_acri_emergency2012] [cite:us3_versa_avneri] [cite:us2_wiki_learning] On criminal justice the United States imprisons about two and a half times as many people per head, 542 against 217 per 100,000 in 2023, and executed 47 people in 2025; on those measures its record is the harsher. [cite:us4_wpb_us] [cite:us4_wpb_il] [cite:us4_dpic_2025] On detention without charge the order reverses: Israel held about 4,500 people in security detention in October 2026, almost all Palestinians from the territories, against 15 at Guantanamo, while America's own large category is civil immigration detention. [cite:us4_hamoked_charts] [cite:us4_amnesty_gtmo] [cite:us4_trac_ice] On homicide, the American rate fell to a record low of 4.1 in 2025 while Israel's national rate doubled in 2023; the rate in Israel's Arab communities, about 12 per 100,000 in 2025 on this book's arithmetic, was above any American national rate in the series, and its police solved about one Arab-community killing in ten. [cite:us5_fox_fbi2025] [cite:us5_taub_homicide] [cite:us5_toi_shinbet] On guns, the American toll of 44,447 deaths in 2024, most of them suicides, has no Israeli counterpart series. [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths]

Money and work

Output per person grew at almost the same rate in both countries over forty-five years, 1.86 and 1.75 per cent a year, and Israel's level stood at 62.7 per cent of America's in 2025 in constant dollars, after two years of war took it back from 66.1 per cent. [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_const] The fiscal records run in opposite directions: Israel's public debt fell from about 163 per cent of GDP in the mid-1980s to 61.9 per cent in 2023, America's rose from 26 per cent in 1980 to 99 per cent in 2025, on different definitions. [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] [cite:us11_imf_debt] [cite:us11_omb_debt] [cite:us11_cbo_outlook2026] For workers, Israel's legal floor follows the average wage and rose 174 per cent in shekels from 1997 to 2026, while the federal American floor has stood at $7.25 since 2009; on the measure of a national wage floor, Israel's law protects low earners more. [cite:us13_nii_minwage] [cite:us13_dol_minwage] On average pay the order reverses: the OECD's average American wage grew 27.7 per cent in real terms from 2000 to 2024 against Israel's 10.9 per cent. [cite:us14_oecd_avwage] Union membership fell steeply in both, and American law guarantees no paid vacation while Israel's guarantees twelve days. [cite:us13_bls_union2025] [cite:us13_wiki_histadrut] [cite:us13_dol_vacation] [cite:us13_toi_vacation]

Cost of living and housing

The two systems burden households in different places. Israel's prices for food, dairy and cars are among the dearest in the OECD, its telecoms 30 per cent below the average after a deliberate competition reform; American telecoms are 51 per cent above it. [cite:us14_toi_food52] [cite:us14_globes_kahlon] Housing grew less affordable in both, on measures that cannot be set against each other: from 129 to 155 average monthly salaries per average Israeli home between 2010 and 2022, and from 3.2 to 5.0 years of median household income per American home between the 1990s and 2024. [cite:us14_wiki_j14] [cite:us14_globes_salaries2023] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] American households carry more debt, 69.2 per cent of GDP against 42.3 per cent in 2024. [cite:us14_globes_mortgagegdp] On homelessness the American record is far worse on the figures available: 745,652 people on one January night in 2025, about 218 per 100,000 on Part Fifteen's arithmetic, against Israeli service counts in the low thousands; Israel's gap here is public housing, sold three apartments for every one bought between 2014 and 2019. [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] [cite:us15_ynet_homeless2022] [cite:us15_comptroller_ph2020]

Health, education and family

The clearest single difference in law is health coverage. Israel has covered every citizen and permanent resident since 1995; the United States left 26.7 million people uninsured all year in 2025, and the Congressional Budget Office expects its 2025 law to add about 10 million by 2034. [cite:us16_wiki_ilhealth] [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us16_kff_obbba] Spending less than a third as much per person, Israel moved from level life expectancy with the United States in 1980 to about four years ahead in 2024, and from a higher infant mortality rate to half the American rate; on those outcomes its record is the better, though Arab citizens and the periphery fare worse inside it, as Black Americans do inside the American one. [cite:us16_wb_chepc] [cite:us16_wb_le] [cite:us16_wb_imr] [cite:us16_toi_moh_gaps] [cite:us16_cdc_imr2023] In schools the order changes. The United States spends almost twice as much per student and its PISA reading score of 490 in 2025 stood well above Israel's 436, the lowest Israel has recorded. [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_usa] [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_isr] [cite:us17_edweek_pisa2025] [cite:us17_ih_pisa2025] Israel holds university tuition down by regulation; America carries $1.651 trillion in student debt. [cite:us14_huji_tuition] [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026] For families, Israel guarantees 15 weeks of paid leave by law and spends about three times America's share of GDP on family benefits on the OECD's cash-and-services measure; the United States guarantees none and its share fell from 0.77 to 0.60 per cent of GDP from 1980 to 2023. [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018] [cite:us18_crs_leave] [cite:us18_socx_usa] [cite:us18_socx_isr] On poverty, Israel's rate is higher on the one shared yardstick, 19.5 per cent against an OECD average of 11.6 per cent in 2023, with child poverty second-highest in the OECD on that basis; the common pairing of an American 10 per cent with an Israeli 21 per cent sets two different definitions side by side. [cite:us18_nii_pov2023] [cite:us18_census_p60290]

Security and the aid

Israel conscripts most Jewish citizens and leaned on reservists who averaged 233 days of service by mid-2026; the United States has relied on volunteers since 1973, and veterans fell from 18 to 6 per cent of its adults between 1980 and 2022. [cite:us19_wiki_conscription] [cite:us19_taub_miluim] [cite:us19_pew_veterans] Israel's defence burden, 7.8 per cent of GDP in 2025, is lower than in the mid-1980s and about two and a half times America's 3.1 per cent. [cite:gi16_boi_2025] [cite:us19_sipri_fs2025] The aid, set beside these figures, weighs about 0.6 per cent of Israel's GDP and 0.05 per cent of American federal outlays. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] [cite:us1_crfb_fy2025] The next section takes it up in full. [scene:us21_verdict|The aid, the claims and what is open]

The gaps each system leaves

Every part named both countries' gaps, and the ledger would mislead without them. Israel's largest is the one its own figures leave out: about 5.56 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, roughly a third of the people under its control, who hold no Israeli citizenship and, in the West Bank, are tried in military courts that convicted in 99.74 per cent of trials in 2010. [cite:us9_pcbs_2025] [cite:wb_972_conviction] [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine] Inside its citizenry, the record killings in Arab communities, 252 dead in 2025, met a police force that solved about one in ten and a development plan cut since 2023. [cite:us5_yahoo_herzog] [cite:us5_toi_shinbet] [cite:us8_idi_550] Housing rose to 155 average monthly salaries per home by 2022. [cite:us14_globes_salaries2023] And the Haredi exemption grew from about 400 yeshiva students in 1949 to about 63,000 in 2023, ruled unlawful in 2024 yet with about 80,000 eligible men not enlisted in January 2026, while Haredi schools are funded without an enforced core curriculum. [cite:us7_globes_draft2024] [cite:us19_toi_evaders2026] [cite:us17_toi_haredi_core] America's largest gaps are health coverage and cost, with 26.7 million uninsured and drug prices 278 per cent of its peers'; guns, with 44,447 deaths in 2024; incarceration, at 542 per 100,000; and the cost of living for those at the bottom, with a federal wage floor frozen since 2009, half of renters cost-burdened and 745,652 people homeless on one night. [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us16_rand_drugs] [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths] [cite:us4_wpb_us] [cite:us13_dol_minwage] [cite:us14_nlihc_jchs2026] [cite:us15_hud_pit2025]

sections.h: The Aid in That Light, the Claims Tested and What Is Open
sections.html:
The question this volume set out to answer is usually asked in one sentence: why does the United States send money to Israel when Americans lack things Israelis have? The ledger in the previous section shows what each system provides and fails to provide, measure by measure. [scene:us21_ledger|The ledger] This section sets the aid against that record, tests the claims most often made about it and about the two systems, states what the comparison can and cannot show, and lists what remains open as of October 2026, days before Israel votes on 27 October and the United States on 3 November.

What the aid is

Under the memorandum of understanding signed on 14 September 2016, the United States committed $38 billion over its fiscal years 2019 to 2028: $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing (FMF) and $5 billion for missile defence, or $3.3 billion and $500 million a year, running to 30 September 2028. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] It is military money. The economic grants Israel once received, about $1.2 billion a year through the 1990s, fell to $44 million in 2008, and none are listed from 2020. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] It is paid as a lump sum in the first month of the fiscal year into an interest-bearing account at the Federal Reserve. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] And it is spent mostly in the United States: the share Israel may spend on equipment made in Israel, 26.3 per cent under the 2007 agreement, was $450.3 million in fiscal 2025 and ends entirely in fiscal 2028, and Israeli researchers at INSS concluded in February 2026 that the aid now goes almost entirely to procurement in America. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] The White House said at signing that ending offshore procurement and fuel purchases would move up to $1.2 billion a year more into American-made goods. [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] The aid is therefore at once a transfer to Israel's defence budget and a purchase from American industry. [scene:us1_aid|Part One: the aid] [scene:gi16_aid|The aid in detail]

What it frees, and what it weighs then and now

What the aid frees in Israel's budget is the weapons it buys, which Israel would otherwise have had to pay for with its own shekels, delay or do without; to the extent Israel would have bought them anyway, an equal sum of its own money is left free for other uses, military or civilian. The money freed is at most the grant itself, and nothing in the record ties it to any particular Israeli programme. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] Israel's Finance Ministry books the grant as income: about ₪22 billion of the 2026 defence budget of about $44.8 billion is "expenditure contingent on income, including the U.S. aid grant". [cite:gi16_bd_budget2026] The buy-American rule has a cost of its own, which the Israeli analyst Gazit put at about $600 million a year in 2011, a view the American government has not endorsed. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] Washington acted on the fungibility argument once, cutting loan guarantees by an amount equal to Israel's settlement spending: by a net $773.8 million in 1994–97, $289.5 million in 2003 and $795.8 million in 2005. [cite:gi16_jvl_loans]

The aid's weight has fallen more than its dollar amount. On Part One's arithmetic from CRS and World Bank data, it equalled 12.7 per cent of Israel's GDP in 1985, when it was partly civilian and helped carry the stabilisation plan, 2.9 per cent in 2000, 1.3 per cent in 2010 and 0.6 per cent in 2025. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] [cite:us11_brookings_peres] Against Israel's defence spending it fell from about 24 per cent of security outlays in 2011, by Gazit's estimate, to "approximately 14%" by the CRS's account and "roughly 15%" by INSS's. [cite:gi16_cato_bandow] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid] Fixed in nominal dollars, the $3.8 billion paid in 2026 buys what about $2.7 billion bought in 2016, and about a third of what the aid of 1985 bought, by Part Twenty's conversion. [cite:us20_bls_cpi_annual] [cite:us20_bls_cpi_sep26] In the American budget it is small: about 0.05 per cent of the $7.0 trillion in federal outlays in fiscal 2025, or about $11 for each American resident. [cite:us1_crfb_fy2025] [cite:us1_cbo_fy2025] [cite:us1_wa_uspop] The parts give no figure for its share of the American budget in 1985, and none is estimated here. The wartime money is larger, at least $21.7 billion in military aid in two years by Brown University's Costs of War count, and America's own operations cost more again: Central Command put the 2026 war with Iran at $43.6 billion by 3 September 2026. [cite:gz_cow_aid] [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [scene:gi16_costs|What the wars cost]

Set beside the ledger, the arithmetic decides the opening question. Every advantage the ledger records for Israel over America, universal health coverage, paid maternity leave, a wage floor tied to the average wage, rests on Israeli laws paid for by Israeli taxes: a dedicated health tax of 3.2 and 5.2 per cent, national insurance contributions, a tax take of 29.8 per cent of GDP. [cite:us1_cmwf_israel] [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018] [cite:us11_oecd_rev_il] Every gap the ledger records for America, from 26.7 million uninsured to a federal wage floor frozen since 2009, is the product of American laws and budgets, and the aid, at 0.05 per cent of federal outlays, is not large enough to explain any of them. [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us13_dol_minwage] [cite:us1_crfb_fy2025] Whether the aid is good policy is a separate question of foreign policy and values, which this volume does not answer.

The claims tested

Parts One to Twenty each tested a common claim against the record where one existed. The table brings them together; each finding applies to that claim alone.

The volume also corrected a circulating figure. A widely repeated figure for Israel's minimum wage from 1 April 2026 was the 2025 rate; the 2026 rate is NIS 6,443.85. [cite:us13_nii_minwage] Two findings ran against expectation: households in Israel pay a larger share of health costs out of pocket than Americans, 20.5 against 10.9 per cent in 2023, but a smaller amount, because the American bill is so much larger; and Israel's abortion committees, whose existence suggests restriction, approved 99.6 per cent of requests in 2020. [cite:us16_wb_oop] [cite:us18_toi_abortion2022]

What the comparison shows, and what it does not

It compares systems, not peoples. Every gap between groups reported in this volume, Black and white Americans, Arab and Jewish Israelis, Haredi and other pupils, is a measure of how laws, budgets and institutions treat people, with the mechanism named where the record names it, and none describes the people in a group. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: Israel] [scene:us8_us|Part Eight: the United States]

It covers different populations unless it says otherwise. Israel's national figures, and Freedom House's score of 73, describe its citizens and residents; the 5.56 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, roughly a third of the people under Israel's control, appear in their own part and in the ledger's last row of gaps, not in Israel's averages. [cite:us1_fh_israel2026] [cite:us9_pcbs_2025] [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine] The American figures cover a federal country of 341.8 million in which most schooling, policing and much of health and welfare policy are set by fifty states, so national averages hide wide ranges, from $11,060 per pupil in Idaho to $31,918 in New York. [cite:us1_wa_uspop] [cite:us17_census_fy2024]

It depends on definitions. GDP per person stood at 67 per cent of the American level at market exchange rates in 2025 and 62.7 per cent in constant dollars; the poverty rates, the pay gaps (monthly against weekly), union density, the housing ratios and the debt figures are each defined differently in the two countries, and the ledger marks where they cannot be set against each other. [cite:us1_fred_uspc] [cite:ir13_fred_ilpc] [cite:us11_wb_gdppc_const] [cite:us13_oecd_lmf15]

It mixes series and snapshots. Where long series exist for both countries, life expectancy, infant mortality, GDP, incarceration, defence spending, the comparison over time is firm. Where they exist for only one, the American side is often the better documented: this book found no published Israeli series on people killed by police, homicide before 2009, household wealth by group, homeownership, student debt or surveillance counts, and it did not compare unemployment benefits at all. [cite:us4_mpv_2025] [cite:us5_taub_homicide] [cite:us8_epi_wealth] [cite:us10_odni_astr2026] Several Israeli series break, the prison count in 2006 and the poverty survey in 2011–12, and are read on each side of the break. [cite:us4_wpb_il] [cite:us18_nii_pov2018] A missing series is a gap in the record, not evidence that nothing is there.

It describes; it does not by itself explain. Outcomes such as life expectancy depend on far more than a single law, and the volume does not claim that Israel's health law alone explains its longer lives, or that American zoning alone explains its homelessness. It also gives no overall verdict. The total in Part Twenty-Two publishes every measure, goalpost and weight, because the measures are not in common units and their weights are a reader's judgment. [scene:us22_method|Part Twenty-Two: the scorecard] [scene:us1_compare|Part One: the rules]

What is open as of October 2026

In Israel, the election of 27 October will seat the Knesset under which the Judicial Selection Law of March 2025 takes effect. [cite:us2_toi_selection2025] Petitions against Basic Law: Torah Study and against the March 2026 death-penalty law were pending with no ruling reported, and no replacement conscription law had been reported after the High Court struck down the arrest-ban law on 3 September 2026. [cite:us2_toi_torahlaw] [cite:us4_wiki_deathlaw] [cite:us19a_jpost_struck] Prime Minister Netanyahu's trial had produced no verdict, plea agreement or pardon in the sources checked. [cite:us2_ynet_trial] [cite:us2_almonitor_pardon] The fate of the bill to tax foreign-government donations to NGOs, of the 2003 family-unification law's latest renewal and of the Arab-community development plan due for renewal in 2026 could not be confirmed. [cite:us3_jpost_ngotax] [cite:us6_adalah_cit2023] [cite:us15_idi_550cut] Palestinian elections were postponed to 11 September 2027, and Israel held about 64 per cent of Gaza behind the Yellow Line. [cite:us9_kt_postpone] [cite:gz_hrw_anniv]

In the United States, the midterms of 3 November choose all 435 members of the House and 35 senators. [cite:us1_wjla_midterms] Section 702 lapsed on 12 June 2026 with collection continuing under certifications valid to 17 March 2027; the border asylum case awaited a possible Supreme Court appeal; the tariff regime after the 150-day window had not been established; the expired marketplace credits and the 2025 law were projected to raise the uninsured count; and the Social Security trust funds were projected to be exhausted in 2034. [cite:us10_bcj_702] [cite:us6_raices_dccir] [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] [cite:us16_kff_obbba] [cite:us18_crs_ss2026] The two central banks were moving in opposite directions, the Bank of Israel cutting to 3.25 per cent on 1 September and the Federal Reserve raising its range to 3.75–4 per cent on 16 September. [cite:us11_globes_boi_sep2026] [cite:us11_fed_sep2026]

Between the two, talks on a framework to replace the 2016 agreement opened on 5 June 2026, with Israel's Defence Ministry aiming to "gradually transition from aid to a completely reciprocal partnership" and Netanyahu saying he wanted the grant to fall toward zero; no agreement had been reported. [cite:ow1_mod_mou2026] [cite:gi16_ji_netanyahu] If none is reached and Congress stops appropriating FMF, Israel would have to pay for existing contracts from its own funds, find other financing or cancel them. [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] Both governments that will negotiate it may change within a week of each other.

The answer, measure by measure

Asked "what about America?", the record gives an answer by measure rather than a single verdict. On health coverage, infant survival, life expectancy, paid leave after a birth, public spending on families, a national wage floor, household debt and homelessness, Israel's laws serve its citizens and residents better on the figures this volume found. [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us16_wb_imr] [cite:us16_wb_le] [cite:us18_crs_leave] [cite:us18_socx_usa] [cite:us13_dol_minwage] [cite:us14_globes_mortgagegdp] [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] On average pay, school results, spending per pupil, civil marriage and government restrictions on religion, press freedom rank, the burden of compulsory military service, and the share of the people it governs who have no citizenship or national vote, about 1 per cent against roughly a third, the American record is the better one. [cite:us14_oecd_avwage] [cite:us17_ih_pisa2025] [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_usa] [cite:us7_wiki_marriage] [cite:us7_pew_gri2022] [cite:us3_wboc_rsf] [cite:us19_taub_miluim] [cite:us9_pcbs_2025] On prices the record splits: Israel's food and cars are among the OECD's dearest and its telecoms far cheaper than America's. [cite:us14_toi_food52] Israel's poverty rate is high on the OECD's relative scale, but the parts found no American figure on that scale to set beside it. [cite:us18_nii_pov2023] On incarceration, executions, national homicide and guns, America's record is the harsher, while Israel holds far more people in detention without charge and its homicide rate for Arab citizens is above any American national rate on record. [cite:us4_wpb_us] [cite:us4_dpic_2025] [cite:us5_pew_gundeaths] [cite:us4_hamoked_charts] [cite:us5_taub_homicide] On democracy ratings both declined in this decade; on the corruption index America fell and Israel held roughly steady. [cite:us3_vdem2026] [cite:us2_wiki_cpi] None of these differences is paid for by the aid, which is military money, mostly spent in America, now about 0.6 per cent of Israel's economy and 0.05 per cent of America's budget. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_crfb_fy2025] [cite:gi16_inss_aid]

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Two
chapters.title: The Scorecard
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-One set every measure side by side and added no total. This part adds one, in the open. It first sets out how the scorecard grades, then follows three families, lower-income, middle and upper-middle, through each country's household survey, and grades both systems on 43 measures in twelve areas, from health and housing to a family-budget area, liberty, the economy and the gaps inside each society, against goalposts printed beside every row, and scores Israel twice: for its citizens, and for everyone it governs. Its last section adds the scores up, tests the totals under other choices, sets the household score beside what people who have lived in both countries describe, answers the questions readers ask most often, from who carries more debt and who works longer to which state is the more oppressive, and gives the volume's final assessment.
chapters.outro: On rules published in full, and on this scorecard's measures, Israel's system scores about 6.1 of 10 for its citizens and America's about 4.7, and that order survives every weighting tested, narrowly in one. On the household score alone, what a family feels in health, debt, housing, family support, safety, wellbeing and its budget, the gap is wider: about 6.4 against 4.6. Israel leads clearly on health, household debt, housing, family support, safety from homicide, wellbeing and the family budget; the United States leads clearly on schools, and narrowly on pay, output and the gaps between groups. On liberty the two tie for citizens, and the United States leads once the Palestinians Israel governs without citizenship are counted. The scorecard does not show that American aid pays for any of Israel's advantages: it is military money, spent mostly in the United States. [scene:us22_final|The final score] [scene:us21_verdict|The aid, the claims and what is open] Every score is stated as of October 2026 and should be checked again after Israel votes on 27 October and the United States on 3 November.

sections.h: How This Scorecard Grades the Two Systems
sections.html:
Part Twenty-One set every measure in one ledger and added no total. The question it left open is the one readers put first: taken together, which system serves the people under it better, and by how much? This part answers with a number, and grades both systems across everything this volume measured, publishing every score and every weight so that a reader who disagrees with a choice can change it and recompute. [scene:us21_ledger|Part Twenty-One: the ledger]

Any such number has to meet some plain tests. Each score must be checkable from a named figure, not from an unstated judgment. A score must not run against the figures beside it. A contested estimate must not carry a score on its own. Two figures that measure different things, such as a gun-homicide rate and a gun-death rate that also counts suicides and accidents, must not be set against each other. And a comparison of how two states treat the people under them must include rights and coercion, not only services, and must say whether it counts everyone a state governs or only its citizens.

The rules of the scorecard

The scorecard keeps separate totals for separate questions and can be checked line by line. It follows seven rules.

  • Every score is a measure. Each of the 43 rows in the next section is one named figure from one named source, taken from the part of this volume that measured it, or from the sources added for this part. No row is a judgment. Where the two countries define a figure differently, the row uses one definition for both, or is left out; firearm deaths, for example, are counted from all causes in both countries. Where only one country has a figure, the row is shown and left out of every total.
  • Every measure is scored against printed goalposts. Each measure has a floor worth 0 and a goal worth 10, round numbers chosen around the range of rich democracies; a country's score is its position between the two, capped at 0 and 10. This is the method the United Nations uses for its Human Development Index. The goalposts are a choice, so they are printed beside every row, so that a reader can see, for example, that the homelessness row runs from 300 per 100,000 (0) to none (10), and the final section tests how much they matter.
  • Results are scored, spending is reported. A system is graded on what its money delivers, so spending on health, schools and research is reported beside the results but not scored. The one exception is public family benefits, because there the spending is itself the benefit households receive.
  • Areas, not rows, are weighted equally. The rows fall into twelve areas: eight citizen services, a ninth on the family budget, which asks of both countries how much a family has left once it has paid what the system leaves it to pay, then liberty and coercion, the economy and public finances, and equity inside each system. Each area's score is the plain average of its rows, so an area with many rows does not outweigh an area with one.
  • Three totals answer three questions. A household score averages the nine household areas; a liberty score is the liberty-and-coercion area; an economy score is the economy area. The overall score averages all twelve areas. No total is offered as more than what it is: this book's disclosed synthesis of published measures, which a reader who weighs the areas differently will weigh differently.
  • Israel is scored twice where it matters. Its citizens view uses its national figures, which cover its citizens and residents.
