Its everyone-governed view adds the Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza wherever a measure concerns how the state treats the people under its control: the Freedom House score weighted by population, detention without charge, and the share of people governed who cannot vote for the government that rules them. The service areas are scored for citizens in both views, because under the Oslo accords the Palestinian Authority, not Israel, runs health, schools and welfare for most of the West Bank; a reader who holds Israel responsible for those services as the occupying power would score its services lower still.
  • Every total is tested. The final section recomputes the result under other choices: every row weighted equally, liberty counted twice, three broad pillars only, every goalpost range widened by a quarter, no goalposts at all, and each area or row left out in turn. A conclusion that holds under all of them is reported as a finding; one that flips is reported as depending on the choice that flips it.

Some systems are discussed in this volume but not scored here, because the volume found no figure measured the same way in both countries: emergency services, transport, construction, energy and water, where Part Fifteen compares how each is organised rather than how well it performs; the price of a home against income, where the two countries' affordability measures cannot be set against each other; police killings, for which Israel publishes no series; and student debt, medical debt and the top one per cent's share of income, which Israel does not compile in a comparable form. [scene:us15_infra|Part Fifteen: water, power, transit and disasters] [scene:us14_housing|Part Fourteen: housing prices] [scene:us4_policing|Part Four: policing] Leaving them out is a choice with a cost, and the next section names it row by row.

sections.h: The Scores, Area by Area
sections.html:
This section sets out every row of the scorecard. Each table gives the measure, its goalposts, each country's value and the score that value earns, from 0 at the floor to 10 at the goal; the area score below each table is the plain average of the rows scored for both countries. Green marks the higher score where the two differ by at least a quarter of a point. Rows a country cannot be scored on are shown and left out. The arithmetic can be checked by hand: a value halfway between floor and goal scores 5. [scene:us22_method|How this scorecard grades]

Health

Health is the area with the widest gap and the firmest data, and it is where Israel's lead is clearest. Israel's law covers every citizen and permanent resident; America left 7.9 per cent of its residents uninsured all year in 2025. Israel records longer lives, 83.2 years against 78.9, and half America's infant mortality, and its people live more of those years in good health: the World Health Organization's healthy life expectancy was 70.9 years in Israel and 63.2 in the United States in 2021. [cite:us22_who_hale21] Israel scores 8.4 and the United States 4.0. Spending is reported, not scored, under this scorecard's rules, but it sharpens the result: America spent about 3.3 times as much per person in 2023, $13,473 against $4,033, and 16.7 per cent of GDP against 7.1. The one exclusion matters at the edges: Israel's universal coverage leaves out asylum seekers, undocumented migrants and foreign workers, who are not counted in its uninsured rate. [scene:us16_systems|Part Sixteen: two health systems] [cite:us16_wb_chepc] [cite:us16_wb_chegdp]

Work and wages

This is one of the areas the United States wins, 4.5 to 3.9, though narrowly: the lead rests on the average-wage row, and without it Israel would lead, 3.6 to 3.3. American average pay is far higher in purchasing-power terms and grew faster after 2000, and Americans work about 70 fewer hours a year. Israel's law guarantees twelve days of paid vacation, which American federal law does not, and a larger share of its employees are covered by collective agreements; Israel's coverage figure is the midpoint of an OECD range of 20 to 30 per cent from about 2015, set against an American figure for 2025. A row Part Thirteen describes, Israel's wage floor tied by law to the average wage against a federal floor frozen since 2009, is not scored, because this part could not confirm the two countries' minimum-to-median ratios on one OECD basis before publication; it would narrow the American lead further. [scene:us13_wages|Part Thirteen: minimum wage, hours and pay gaps] [scene:us14_wages|Part Fourteen: wages against prices]

Household debt and prices

American households carry more debt, 69.2 per cent of GDP against 42.3 per cent; American inflation in the year to September 2026 ran further from the 2 per cent both central banks aim for; and an American public university's published tuition is more than three times an Israeli one's. Israel scores 8.1 and the United States 4.3. Two cautions belong here. Israel's prices for food, dairy and cars are among the OECD's highest, which the wage row captures only in part, because purchasing-power figures already adjust for prices. And on net price after grants, about $2,300 at an American public four-year college, the tuition row would reverse in America's favour; no comparable Israeli net figure exists, so published prices are compared. [scene:us14_basket|Part Fourteen: the basket] [scene:us17_higher|Part Seventeen: universities]

A widely repeated claim holds that 66.5 per cent of American bankruptcies are medically driven. That figure comes from a 2019 survey in which filers named medical bills or illness-related lost income as a contributing cause. [cite:us22_himmelstein2019] A 2018 study in the New England Journal of Medicine, which followed hospitalised adults through their credit and bankruptcy records, estimated that hospitalisation causes about 4 per cent of bankruptcies among non-elderly adults. [cite:us22_dobkin2018] The two answer different questions, contribution and cause, and neither has an Israeli counterpart, so neither is scored. The household-debt row carries the comparison instead.

Housing

The only housing measure both countries publish in a form that can be scored is homelessness, and on it the American record is far worse: about 218 people per 100,000 on one January night in 2025, against an Israeli figure of about 46 per 100,000 in 2020, counting the 3,470 people local authorities treated and the roughly 800 street dwellers they reported outside treatment. The two are counted differently, so Israel is scored on the highest count available. Israel scores 8.5 and the United States 2.7. House prices grew less affordable in both countries, but on measures this volume found cannot be set side by side, so they are not scored. Israel's own gap is public housing, sold faster than it was bought between 2014 and 2019. [scene:us15_housing|Part Fifteen: homelessness and public housing] [scene:us14_housing|Part Fourteen: housing prices]

Education

Education is the United States' clearest win, 6.0 to 2.4. American fifteen-year-olds scored 490 in reading in the 2025 PISA round, Israel's 436, the lowest Israel has recorded. Both systems leave a wide gap between advantaged and weaker pupils: Israel's was 121 points in reading in 2018 against an OECD average of 89, and in 2025 the United States had the widest gap between its highest- and lowest-scoring readers of any country tested. America also spends almost twice as much per student across all levels, $19,973 against $10,279; that figure is reported, not scored, because this scorecard grades what spending delivers. [scene:us17_schools|Part Seventeen: schools]

Family and safety net

Israel guarantees fifteen weeks of paid leave after a birth by national law; American federal law guarantees none. Israel spends 1.89 per cent of GDP on family benefits, more than three times America's 0.60 per cent; this is the one spending row scored, because the benefit is itself the money families receive, and the OECD measure leaves out tax breaks, among them the American Child Tax Credit, so it understates American support. A worker who loses a job on two-thirds of the average wage gets back about 65 per cent of previous net income in the first months in Israel and 55 per cent in the United States, on the OECD's 2025 calculation; for a worker on the average wage the figures are 59 and 38 per cent. Benefits last up to 26 weeks in most American states and from 50 to 175 days in Israel, depending on age and dependants. [cite:us22_oecd_nrr_isr67] [cite:us22_oecd_nrr_usa67] [cite:us22_oecd_nrr_isr100] [cite:us22_oecd_nrr_usa100] [cite:us22_cbpp_uiweeks] [cite:us22_nii_uiperiod] In old age, 22.9 per cent of Americans aged 66 and over were poor on the OECD's measure in 2023, against 15.3 per cent of Israelis in 2022. [cite:us22_oecd_idd_usa66] [cite:us22_oecd_idd_isr66] On poverty across all ages the order reverses, narrowly: on the OECD's common basis of half the median income, 18 per cent of Americans and 19.5 per cent of Israelis were poor in the latest year available. [cite:us22_statista_oecdpov] [cite:us18_nii_pov2023] Israel scores 5.3 on the area and the United States 2.8; like every area score, these average only the rows scored for both countries. Child poverty on the same basis is shown but not scored: Israel's rate, 23.4 per cent, is second-highest in the OECD, but this part could not confirm the American rate on that basis before publication. The final section shows that scoring it at any American value moves the area towards the United States without changing either total's order. [scene:us18_poverty|Part Eighteen: poverty] [scene:us18_family|Part Eighteen: family benefits]

Public safety

Israel's national homicide rate was 3.04 per 100,000 in 2023, the American 4.1 in 2025, America's lowest on record; Israel scores 7.3 and the United States 6.2. The national figure hides Israel's sharpest internal gap: Arab citizens were killed at 11.11 per 100,000 in 2023, about thirteen times the rate among Jewish citizens and above any American national rate in the series. Firearm deaths, 12.8 per 100,000 Americans in 2024, most of them suicides, are shown but not scored, because Israel publishes no comparable series. Imprisonment, a measure of the state's coercion as much as of safety, is scored in the next area. [scene:us5_homicide|Part Five: homicide] [scene:us5_guns|Part Five: guns]

Wellbeing

The World Happiness Report asks people to rate their lives from 0 to 10. Averaged over 2023 to 2025, Israelis rated theirs 7.187, eighth in the world, and Americans 6.816, twenty-third. [cite:us22_whr26_hli] [cite:us22_fox5_whr26] Israel scores 8.0 and the United States 7.0. Israel's rank held through two years of war, at eighth in both the 2025 and 2026 reports; the survey samples Israel's citizens and residents, not the Palestinians it governs. [cite:us22_jvl_whr]

Family budget and security: the American Dream test

This area asks a question usually asked of the United States alone: once a family has paid what the system leaves it to pay, how much is left, and how secure is it? American households have come to carry costs that other rich countries carry in common, from health care and childcare to college, retirement and the car needed to reach work. Here both countries are measured on the same rows. The area's seven scored rows split four to three, and Israel scores 6.0 against America's 3.4, because the rows it wins it wins by the width of a law.

Israeli families pay less out of pocket for health care, about $827 a person in 2023 against $1,469 in America; Israelis pay a larger share of their health costs directly, about a fifth against a ninth, but of a bill less than a third the size. [cite:us16_wb_oop] [cite:us16_wb_chepc] Israeli law guarantees paid sick leave, accruing at a day and a half a month, and requires employers and employees together to pay 18.5 per cent of wages into a pension and severance fund; American federal law requires neither, although 81 per cent of private-sector workers get paid sick days from their employers and 52 per cent take part in an employer retirement plan. [cite:us22_kolzchut_sick] [cite:us22_dol_sick] [cite:us22_bls_ebs26_sick] [cite:us22_boi_dp202508] [cite:us22_bls_ebs26] And a low-wage worker keeps more of each paycheck in Israel: on the OECD's 2025 figures, income tax and social contributions took 19.4 per cent of the labour cost of a single worker on two-thirds of the average wage in Israel and 27.5 per cent in the United States. That measure leaves out taxes on spending, which fall harder on Israelis: Israel's value added tax rose to 18 per cent in January 2025, while American state and local sales taxes averaged 7.53 per cent in 2026 and five states levy none. [cite:us22_oecd_tw26_ch3] [cite:us22_pwc_il_vat] [cite:us22_tf_sales26]

The other three rows go to the United States. Food took 17.9 per cent of Israeli household spending in 2023 against 12.9 per cent in America in 2024, and housing 21.1 against 16.5 per cent on the OECD's common measure; among low-income renters, 54.1 per cent in Israel and 48.3 per cent in America spent more than 40 per cent of their income on rent, though the American figure is measured against gross income. [cite:us22_cbs_hes23_food] [cite:us22_bls_ce24_food] [cite:us22_oecd_hpt_usa] [cite:us22_oecd_hpt_isr] Part of the food gap is arithmetic, since poorer households spend more of their budgets on food, and part is price: Israel's food and drink cost about 52 per cent more than the OECD average. [scene:us14_basket|Part Fourteen: the basket]

Several of the costs most often named in accounts of the American family budget could not be scored, because only one country publishes them. When a parent stops paying court-ordered child support, Israel's National Insurance Institute pays the award itself, under a law of 1972, and collects from the parent: about 11,564 women a month received such payments in 2023, averaging NIS 2,204. In the United States the state enforces but does not pay: 65 per cent of current support due was collected in 2024, and in 2017 fewer than half of custodial parents, 45.9 per cent, received the full amount. [cite:us22_nii_mezonot23] [cite:us22_ocss_fy24] [cite:us22_census_p60269] American student borrowers owed an average of $40,467 each in 2026, 42.6 million of them; Israel has no national student-loan programme or debt series, and tuition at the Hebrew University is NIS 12,017 a year. [cite:us22_edi_sld] [cite:us22_fsa_q2fy26] [cite:us22_huji_tuition] An American couple with two young children, both on the average wage, spent about a fifth of their disposable income on childcare in 2022, a single parent 37 per cent; Israel subsidises daycare for working parents of children up to three by income, but no OECD figure for its net cost was found. [cite:us22_statista_ncc] [cite:us22_idi_daycare] Americans owed at least $220 billion in medical debt in 2021. [cite:us16_pkff_debt] No recent OECD household saving rate for Israel was found to set beside America's 4.9 per cent, and the transport share of spending cannot be compared, because Israel's survey combines transport with communications.

Two cautions keep this area honest. It measures what the laws and national averages provide, and averages hide who is inside them: an Israeli family in the centre of the country with two salaries lives a different budget from a Haredi or Arab family, just as an American family with employer coverage lives a different one from a family without it. And many of Israel's guarantees, from the pension to the daycare subsidy, are tied to employment, so they reach families in work more fully than those outside it.

Liberty and coercion

This is the area where whom you count decides the result. For its own citizens, Israel scores 6.2 and the United States 5.8. Israel imprisons about two-fifths as many people per head, though its figure includes Palestinians held as security prisoners, and has executed no one since Eichmann in 1962, against 47 American executions in 2025; America scores higher on Freedom House's measure of political rights and civil liberties, on press freedom and on religious freedom, where Israel has no civil marriage. That lead is too narrow to call. Drop the prison row and the United States leads, 6.7 to 6.0; drop the executions row and it leads 5.8 to 5.4; and the executions row's floor of 3 per 10 million is a choice: set it at 10 and the United States leads the area. [scene:us4_prisons|Part Four: prisons]

For everyone each state governs, the United States scores 6.3 and Israel 5.5. Weighted by population, the Freedom House score of the people under Israel's control falls from 73 to about 53, because the West Bank scores 22 and Gaza 2; about 36 per cent of the people Israel governs cannot vote for its government, against about 1 per cent under American rule; and Israel holds about 29 people per 100,000 governed without criminal charge, against 20 in America's immigration detention at its 2026 peak. Measured over everyone it governs, Israel's prison rate falls to about 127 per 100,000, which scores in its favour. The order holds whichever single row is dropped except the vote row, the largest single difference, without which the two are level. Three choices in this view should be stated. Freedom House's West Bank and Gaza scores also reflect the Palestinian Authority's and Hamas's own rule; counting Gaza as governed by Israel is itself contested, though Part Nine sets out the control Israel exercises there; and the vote row counts Palestinians under Israeli control but not the foreign nationals living in the United States, who can vote in their own countries. The governed population used here is about 15.5 million: Israel's 10.3 million, plus 5.56 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, less about 362,000 East Jerusalem Palestinians counted in both. [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank] [scene:us4_detention|Part Four: detention without trial] [cite:us9_aje_ejvote] [cite:us4_wpb_il]

Economy and public finances

The United States scores 6.0 and Israel 5.6. America produces far more per person, $67,946 in constant 2015 dollars against $42,596; Israel's output per person grew slightly faster over the period, 1.86 per cent a year against 1.75 since 1980, and it carries less public debt, about 68 per cent of GDP against 99 per cent. The two debt figures are defined differently, and the American one, federal debt held by the public, is the narrower; counting all American government debt on Israel's basis would score the United States lower still. The American lead rests on output per person: without that row Israel would lead. Israel's research spending, 6.35 per cent of GDP in 2023 against America's 3.45 per cent, is reported, not scored. [scene:us11_fiscal|Part Eleven: taxes and debt] [scene:us11_growth|Part Eleven: growth] [scene:us12_tech|Part Twelve: technology] [cite:us12_wiki_rd]

Equity inside each system

Each system's internal gaps are of a similar order. Black American infants die at 2.44 times the rate of white infants, Arab Israeli infants at 2.43 times the rate of Jewish ones. The World Economic Forum ranks America 42nd and Israel 76th on its gender-gap index. The United States scores 4.0 and Israel 3.2, a lead that rests on the gender row; without it the two are level. Equity is the area with the fewest shared measures, and the poverty and homicide gaps in the areas above belong here too: Israel's Arab–Jewish homicide ratio of about thirteen to one in 2023 is wider than the American ratio between Black and white victims, about eight to one before the pandemic, while the American wealth gap between white and Black households, about nine to one in 2025, has no Israeli counterpart series. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: equality in Israel] [scene:us8_us|Part Eight: equality in America] [cite:us5_taub_homicide] [cite:us8_scf2025]

sections.h: What the Gap Means in a Life
sections.html:
A score of 6.4 against 4.6 is easy to state and hard to feel. This section turns the gap into the terms a household lives in: how far each system takes a family towards the goals the scorecard sets, where the distance between them is greatest, what it adds up to over a lifetime, and what it does not mean. Every figure is one already scored or reported in this part; the lifetime totals are this book's arithmetic from annual figures held at today's values, and they illustrate scale rather than forecast anyone's life. [scene:us22_scores|The scores, area by area]

Reading the distance

Each score measures how far a system gets from a floor, worth 0, to a goal, worth 10. On the nine areas a household feels, Israel's system takes its citizens about 64 per cent of the way and America's about 46 per cent. The gap of about 1.9 points means that, against the same goalposts, Israel's system carries a household about 1.4 times as far.

The gap is not spread evenly, and that is the most useful thing it says about the two systems. It is widest in housing, health, household debt, the family budget, and family support and the safety net, the areas where Israeli law guarantees what Americans are left to arrange and pay for themselves: coverage, paid leave, sick pay, a pension, an unemployment benefit that replaces more of a lost paycheck, and child support the state pays when a parent does not. It runs the other way in schools, where American fifteen-year-olds read better, and in work and wages, where Americans earn about half as much again on average and work fewer hours. In short, the American system pays its people more and asks them to buy their own security; the Israeli system pays less, charges more for food and housing, and builds more security into law.

Over a lifetime

Annual differences add up over the length of a life. The panel below sets out what the gap amounts to for one person or one family, from birth to old age, if each year looked like the latest one.

Some of these totals favour Israel and one does not. An Israeli lives about 4.3 years longer and about 7.7 more years in good health, is guaranteed about 480 days of paid vacation across a forty-year working life where American federal law guarantees none, and, on 2023 figures, pays about $642 a year less out of pocket for health care, which for a family of four over forty years comes to about $100,000. An Israeli also works about 2,800 more hours over the same forty years, and pays more for food and housing every year of it. [cite:us16_wb_le] [cite:us22_who_hale21] [cite:us13_toi_vacation] [cite:us13_wiki_hours] [cite:us16_wb_oop] [cite:us16_wb_chepc]

When things go wrong

The gap is largest at the moments a family does not choose: a birth, an illness, a layoff, a parent who stops paying, old age. Those are the moments the household score weighs most heavily, and the moments people who have lived in both countries most often describe.

Take a worker on two-thirds of the average wage who is laid off. In Israel the first months' benefit replaces about 65 per cent of what he took home; in the United States about 55 per cent, and for an average earner 59 against 38 per cent. If his child falls ill, Israeli law gives him paid sick days that build up at a day and a half a month; American federal law gives none, though 81 per cent of private-sector workers get them from their employers. If the child's other parent stops paying support, Israel's National Insurance Institute pays the award and pursues the parent; an American parent waits on enforcement that collected 65 per cent of current support due in 2024. And at 66 and over, 22.9 per cent of Americans were poor on the OECD's measure against 15.3 per cent of Israelis: about one in four and a half against one in six and a half. [cite:us22_oecd_nrr_isr67] [cite:us22_oecd_nrr_usa67] [cite:us22_kolzchut_sick] [cite:us22_bls_ebs26_sick] [cite:us22_nii_mezonot23] [cite:us22_ocss_fy24] [cite:us22_oecd_idd_usa66] [cite:us22_oecd_idd_isr66]

What the gap does not mean

Four limits keep the number honest. First, a system score is not a verdict on every life inside it. An American on a high salary with good employer coverage buys much of what Israeli law guarantees, and the American average wage, about half as much again as Israel's in purchasing-power terms, pays for a great deal; the systems differ most for households without that cover, which is where the household score weighs. Second, Israel's average hides the Arab and Haredi households whose poverty runs well above it, and leaves out the Palestinians it governs without citizenship, for whom the guarantees in this section largely do not exist. Third, some of Israel's guarantees, the pension and the daycare subsidy among them, follow employment, so they reach working families more fully than others. Fourth, the gap is not paid for by the United States: one of the final section's tests takes the full value of American aid out of Israel's family benefits, and the household score moves only from 6.43 to 6.39. The figure below shows how the overall lead holds under the other tests. [scene:us22_final|The final score, tested] [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank]

The full dashboard, with the area-by-area scores, the three areas outside the household score and every test, opens from any of the figures above.

sections.h: Three Families
sections.html:
A national score describes a system; a family lives a budget. This section follows three households in each country, a lower-income family, a middle family and an upper-middle family, and asks what each takes in, what the state takes, what the essentials cost and what is left over, using each country's own survey of real household budgets rather than invented examples. It then asks what would change for each American family under Israel's rules. [scene:us22_delta|What the gap means in a life]

Where the figures come from

The American families are the lowest, middle and fourth fifths of households in the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Expenditure Survey for 2024, ranked by income before taxes. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] The Israeli families are the same fifths in the Central Bureau of Statistics' Household Expenditure Survey for 2021, the latest year for which the bureau's full table of income, taxes and spending by income group could be obtained for this book; each fifth is the average of two of the table's tenths, which each hold a tenth of households. [cite:us22_cbs_hes21_t2] The bureau published headline results for 2024 in October 2026; on those figures the middle Israeli fifth kept about 23 per cent of its net income after spending, almost exactly the 2021 share, and this section will be updated when the full 2024 tables are released. [cite:us22_davar_hes24]

Four differences in how the surveys count are adjusted for or stated. The American survey reports income tax only up to 2023, so the 2024 American income tax is estimated by applying each fifth's 2023 ratio of tax to income, and American payroll taxes are computed at the legal 7.65 per cent of wages and 15.3 per cent of self-employment income; Israel's survey reports all compulsory payments, including income tax, National Insurance and the health tax. [cite:us22_bls_cesan24_nr] Pension and insurance contributions are left out of spending in both countries and counted as part of what is left over. Israel reports mortgage payments separately, as a form of saving, while the American survey counts mortgage interest as housing spending; to avoid flattering Israel, its mortgage payments, principal and interest, are subtracted in full. And the American fifths are ranked by household income, the Israeli ones by income per person, so the American middle family is a little smaller, 2.5 people against 3.2. Amounts are converted at the World Bank's purchasing-power rate for household consumption, 4.28 shekels to the dollar in 2020, the latest found, which already allows for Israel's higher prices. [cite:us22_wb_prvtpp]

The middle and upper-middle families

The middle families show the gap most clearly. The American family takes home about twice as much per person, in dollars that buy the same goods, and spends almost all of it: about 81 cents of every dollar of income goes on everyday spending and about 13 cents in taxes, leaving about 6 cents. The Israeli family takes home less, pays slightly less in tax and compulsory contributions even with its health tax included, spends about 69 cents of each shekel, puts about 5 into its mortgage, and has about 16 left. Even in dollars per person, after converting for prices, the Israeli middle family has more left over at the end of the year, about $2,290 against $1,760, though the years differ. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:us22_cbs_hes21_t2]

The upper-middle families divide differently. Both keep a meaningful share, about 18 per cent of income in America and 22 per cent in Israel, but the American family's larger income leaves it more in absolute terms, about $7,690 a person against $4,690. At this level the American system's higher pay outweighs its costs in dollars, while the Israeli family still keeps the larger share and holds more guarantees. Where the money goes also differs: the American families spend more on health care and transport, the Israeli families more on food and education, the last reflecting private lessons, after-school programmes and fees on top of free schooling.

The lower-income families

The bottom fifth cannot be compared the same way. In both surveys these households spend more than the income they report, about twice their income in the American survey and about 1.4 times in the Israeli one, because they draw down savings, receive help in kind, borrow or under-report income, and because the two groups are different people: the American bottom fifth averages 1.6 people with half an earner and a head of household aged 57, many of them retirees living alone; the Israeli bottom fifth averages 3.5 people, and in its poorest tenth 43 per cent of households are Arab. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:us22_cbs_hes21_t2] What can be compared for a low-income family is what the law guarantees, and there the systems differ most.

Holding it together: second jobs, hours, debt and the doctor

People who have lived in both countries often describe the difference less as income than as strain: one job being enough in Israel, a second job needed in America, and a visit to the doctor that is a decision in one country and not in the other. Some of that can be measured; some of it, on the figures this book could find, cannot yet be set side by side.

Three findings stand out, and they do not all point the same way. The first is that Israelis work longer, not shorter: a full-time Israeli employee usually works about 43 hours a week against 41 for an American, and more Israelis work 50 hours or more. The difference between the countries is not in how long the main job runs but in what one job pays for. An American family that needs a second income often finds it in a second job, and 5.4 per cent of employed Americans, about 8.8 million people, held more than one in 2025; Israel's labour force survey asks the question but this book found no published rate to set beside it. [cite:us22_bls_cpsaat36_25] [cite:us22_oecd_avgusl]

The second is debt. American households spent 11.1 per cent of their disposable income servicing debt in mid-2026, more than five cents of every dollar on credit cards, car loans and student loans alone, and on top of that paid about $160 billion in credit card interest and $31 billion in card fees in 2024, roughly $560 for every American. That money comes out of the thin margin the middle family's budget leaves. Israel publishes no overall equivalent, though its newest mortgages have grown heavier: about 42 per cent of new borrowers in late 2024 paid more than 30 per cent of their income. [cite:us22_fred_tdsp] [cite:us22_fred_cdsp] [cite:us22_cfpb_ccmr25] [cite:us22_boi_fsr24h2]

The third is the doctor. In 2026, 28 per cent of American adults said they had skipped or postponed care they needed because of the cost, and 27 per cent had not filled a prescription. In Israel's national survey of 2024, 12 per cent said they had given up treatment, a consultation or medicine because of the copayment. The questions differ, so the two figures are not an exact match, but both point the same way as the coverage figures: in Israel, cost is a smaller barrier to seeing a doctor. [cite:us22_kff_costs26] [cite:us22_brookdale_hs24]

If each American family lived under Israel's rules

No survey can move a family across the ocean, and wages, prices and jobs would not travel with it. What can be said is which of each family's costs the Israeli system would carry and which it would add. The lower-income family would gain the most: health cover without a premium, more of a lost paycheck replaced, a child allowance, state-paid child support and lower tax on its wages, against dearer food, rent and cars. The middle family would stop paying the $3,842 a year in health insurance premiums its American counterpart pays, face university fees of about NIS 12,000 a year rather than American tuition and debt, and gain paid leave, sick pay and a compulsory pension; on the surveys above, families at that rung in Israel keep a larger share of their income. The upper-middle family would lose most: Israel's income tax rises to 50 per cent at the top, its unemployment benefit is capped, and its cars and homes cost more, so American pay at that level buys more, though the family would keep the same guarantees as everyone else. [cite:us22_pwc_il_pit] [cite:us22_nii_uiamount] [cite:us14_huji_tuition]

Are they happier?

Each country measures this, but not in a way that can be laid side by side by income. In January 2025, 38 per cent of Americans in households earning under $40,000 said they were very satisfied with their personal lives, against 55 per cent of those earning over $100,000, a gap of 17 points that Gallup has found for years. [cite:us22_gallup_pl25] Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics found 92.2 per cent of adults satisfied with their lives in 2026, Arab citizens 90.6 per cent, but this book found no breakdown by income. [cite:us22_ynet_cbs5787] The World Happiness Report, which asks both populations the same question, ranks Israel eighth and the United States twenty-third. What the American figures show is that satisfaction there rises steeply with income; whether Israel's rises less steeply, as a system that guarantees more at the bottom might suggest, is not established by the data found.

What the record shows and does not. It shows real household budgets at three rungs of each country's income ladder, from each national survey, with every adjustment stated. It does not show a matched year: the Israeli table is from 2021 and will be replaced when the 2024 tables appear. It does not fully capture prices that differ item by item, quality, or the value of guarantees a family never draws on. And it cannot say how any particular family would fare if it moved.

sections.h: The Final Score, Tested
sections.html:
This section adds up the scores, tests the totals against the choices that produced them, answers directly the questions readers most often ask about the two systems, and gives this volume's final assessment. Every total below is this book's synthesis of the published measures in the previous section, made by the rules stated in the first; none is a fact in the way a census count is, and a reader who weighs the areas differently can recompute from the same rows. [scene:us22_scores|The scores, area by area] [scene:us22_method|How this scorecard grades]

The totals

On what households feel, Israel's system scores 6.4 and America's 4.6, on a method that publishes every row, scores results rather than spending and leaves the contested bankruptcy estimate unscored. Israel wins seven of the twelve areas clearly: health, household debt and prices, housing, family and the safety net, public safety, wellbeing, and the family budget. The United States wins education clearly, and work and wages, the economy and equity narrowly, each lead resting on a single row: average pay, output per person and the gender-gap index. Liberty and coercion goes to whichever side the reader counts.

The tests

The overall order holds in every test: under every weighting, every goalpost setting, every single area removed and with no goalposts at all, Israel's system scores higher, by between about 0.2 and 1.8 points of 10. The narrowest margin, 5.83 against 5.63, comes when only three broad pillars are averaged in the everyone-governed view, because liberty then carries a third of the weight; on that weighting the two systems are close to level. The household result holds the same way: Israel is ahead on 20 of the 28 household rows scored for both countries, and the household score holds whichever single area is removed. The liberty result does not hold. Counting citizens only, Israel's narrow lead depends on the prisons and executions rows and on where the executions floor is set; that is reported here as a tie. Counting everyone each state governs, the United States leads by 6.3 to 5.5, and the order survives the removal of any single row except the vote row, the largest single difference between the two states, without which they are level.

The household score and the lived difference

Readers who know Israelis who have lived in both countries often hear a sharper contrast than an overall score of 6.1 against 4.7 suggests: no hesitation before seeing a doctor, children without financial dread, money left for a holiday. The scorecard bears that out where it measures what a household feels. On the nine household areas Israel scores 6.4 and the United States 4.6, and the gap is widest exactly where those accounts put it: health, 8.4 against 4.0; housing, measured by homelessness; household debt; and family support, where Israeli law guarantees paid leave after a birth, a child allowance, paid sick days, a pension and, when a parent stops paying, child support paid by the state itself. [scene:us22_scores|The scores, area by area]

The overall score is closer because it also weighs things a family budget does not register: output per person and public debt, where America leads; PISA results, where America leads; and liberty, where counting the Palestinians Israel governs puts America ahead. Two further limits explain the rest. Some of what Israelis pay more for is real: food took 17.9 per cent of Israeli household spending against 12.9 per cent of American, and housing a larger share too, which is why hundreds of thousands of Israelis marched over the cost of living in 2011. [scene:us14_protests|Part Fourteen: the 2011 protests] And a national average includes everyone: the experience of a two-salary family in central Israel is not the experience of the Arab and Haredi households whose poverty rates in 2024, 37.6 and 32.8 per cent of families, ran well above the national 20.0 per cent [cite:us8_nii_2024], just as an American family with good employer coverage lives a different budget from one without it. [scene:us8_israel|Part Eight: equality in Israel] What no national survey here can score is the quality of food or the felt ease of daily life; those belong to testimony, and the book records what the measures can support.

One life in each system

The household score can also be read the way a person lives it, stage by stage. The table follows one life through both systems on the figures scored or reported above; green marks the system that comes out ahead at that stage where the figures point one way, and stages where they split are left unmarked.

Read stage by stage, the American system pays better and schools better, and asks its people to buy for themselves, through employers or out of pocket, much of what Israel's laws guarantee: care when sick, income when sick or laid off, leave after a birth, support when a parent stops paying, and saving for old age. Israel's system charges more for food and housing and pays less, and returns more of it as guarantees. The second is the life that people who have lived in both most often describe as less anxious, and the scorecard's household measures point the same way; for the Arab and Haredi citizens whose poverty rates are far above the average, and for the Palestinians Israel governs without citizenship, the table describes a life they do not fully share.

The questions readers ask

Which country carries more public debt? The United States, and its debt has risen for four decades while Israel's fell from the 1980s before rising again with the war. American federal debt held by the public was 99 per cent of GDP in 2025, up from 26 per cent in 1980, and the Congressional Budget Office projects 120 per cent by 2036. Israel's general government debt was about 68 per cent of GDP in 2025, up from 61.9 per cent in 2023 but far below the roughly 163 per cent of the mid-1980s. [cite:us11_omb_debt] [cite:us11_cbo_outlook2026] [cite:us11_imf_debt] [cite:us11_jvl_melnick] [scene:us11_fiscal|Part Eleven: taxes and debt]

Whose households carry more debt? American households: 69.2 per cent of GDP in 2024 against 42.3 per cent in Israel. On top of that, Americans owed $1.651 trillion in student loans in 2026, with 9.3 million borrowers in default; Israel keeps university tuition low by regulation and publishes no comparable national student-debt series. [cite:us14_globes_mortgagegdp] [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026] [cite:us17_ci_defaults] [cite:us14_huji_tuition]

Who spends more? It depends on who is spending, and on what. America spends far more per person on health, $13,473 in 2023 against $4,033, and almost twice as much per student across all levels of education, $19,973 against $10,279; on health it gets shorter lives for the money, on schools higher scores. Israel's governments take more in tax, 29.8 per cent of GDP in 2023 against America's 27.7 per cent in 2022, and spend about two and a half times America's share of GDP on defence, 7.8 per cent against 3.1 per cent in 2025. American aid equals about 0.6 per cent of Israel's GDP, and the Congressional Research Service put it at about 14 per cent of Israel's defence budget. [cite:us16_wb_chepc] [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_usa] [cite:us17_oecd_eag2023_isr] [cite:us11_oecd_rev_il] [cite:us11_dbn_rev_us] [cite:gi16_boi_2025] [cite:us19_sipri_fs2025] [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us1_fred_ilgdp] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025]

Who works more? Israelis, by about 70 hours a year: 1,870 against 1,800 in 2025, down from 2,033 against 1,832 in 2000, so the gap has narrowed from about 200 hours. Israeli law guarantees 12 days of paid vacation and 15 weeks of paid leave after a birth; American federal law guarantees neither. Israelis also serve: most Jewish citizens are conscripted, and reservists had averaged 233 days of service since October 2023 by mid-2026. [cite:us13_wiki_hours] [cite:us13_toi_vacation] [cite:us13_dol_vacation] [cite:us18_nii_maternity2018] [cite:us19_taub_miluim]

Who is taxed more? It depends on where a person sits. A low-wage worker loses less of each paycheck to income tax and social contributions in Israel, 19.4 per cent of labour costs against 27.5 per cent on the OECD's 2025 figures, but pays an 18 per cent value added tax on most of what he buys, against American sales taxes averaging 7.53 per cent. [cite:us22_oecd_tw26_ch3] [cite:us22_pwc_il_vat] [cite:us22_tf_sales26] At the top, Israel's highest personal rate is 50 per cent including its surtax, with a further 2 per cent on capital income since 2025, against an American federal top rate of 37 per cent plus any state tax. [cite:us22_pwc_il_pit] [cite:us22_irs_ty26] Both systems tax their largest companies below the headline rate. The combined American corporate rate averages 25.57 per cent with state taxes, and a study by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, an advocacy group, found that 342 large profitable companies paid an effective 14.1 per cent from 2018 to 2022; Israel's rate is 23 per cent, but its "preferred enterprise" regime taxes qualifying firms at 7.5 or 16 per cent, Intel's plant at 7.5 per cent after a $3.2 billion grant, and the State Comptroller counted NIS 67 billion of tax breaks in 2019. [cite:us22_tf_cit25] [cite:us22_itep_corp24] [cite:us22_pwc_il_cit] [cite:us22_pwc_il_incent] [cite:us22_ctech_intel] [cite:us22_mevaker_taxexp] On the whole economy, Israel's governments take a larger share in tax, 29.8 against 27.7 per cent of GDP. [cite:us11_oecd_rev_il] [cite:us11_dbn_rev_us]

Does Israel receive aid from other countries as well? Not on any scale this book found. The United States is the only state that gives Israel regular military aid. Germany has paid part of the cost of Israel's navy: it donated the first two Dolphin submarines, paid about half of the third and a third of the fourth and fifth, up to €135 million of the sixth, €115 million of the Sa'ar 6 corvettes, which cost about €430 million, and €540 million of a roughly €3 billion order for three new submarines agreed in 2022. [cite:us22_ynet_dolphin11] [cite:us22_solar_dolphin6] [cite:us22_gulf_saar6] [cite:us22_almon_dakar] No other government grant of comparable size was found. The larger outside flow is private: Israeli non-profits received $4.4 billion in 2015, $2.8 billion of it from abroad and $1.8 billion from American funders. [cite:us22_chron_giving] [scene:us20_flows|Part Twenty: the money flow both ways] The United States receives no foreign aid of this kind; it gives it, $73.5 billion in fiscal 2024 in 2025 dollars, about a quarter of it military and security aid. Japan's payments toward the American forces stationed there, ¥1,055 billion over five years, are cost-sharing for American bases, not aid. [cite:us22_pew_aid26] [cite:us22_ap_japanhns]

Could the aid explain the gap? The scorecard tests it directly. If Israel had to replace every dollar of American aid itself, about 0.6 per cent of its GDP, and took all of it from family benefits, cutting them from 1.89 to 1.29 per cent of GDP, its household score would fall from 6.43 to 6.39 and its overall score from 6.08 to 6.05; America's would stay at 4.57 and 4.74. The gap in how households live is paid for by how each country taxes and spends its own money, not by the aid. [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable] [cite:us18_socx_isr]

Who is happier? Israelis, on the one survey that asks both populations the same question: 7.187 against 6.816 out of 10, eighth against twenty-third in the 2026 World Happiness Report. [cite:us22_whr26_hli]

Which state is more oppressive? Measured by how each treats its own citizens, neither clearly: the scores tie. The United States imprisons people at two and a half times Israel's rate and still executes them; Israel restricts religion by law, has had a state of emergency in force since 1948, censors its press through a military censor and ranks 116th of 180 for press freedom, against America's 64th. Measured by how each treats everyone it governs, Israel is the more coercive state on most of the rows this volume could score, the vote, Freedom House's rating, press freedom, detention without charge, religion and corruption, though not on imprisonment or executions: about a third of the people under its control cannot vote for its government and, in the West Bank, are tried in military courts, and it holds about 4,500 people without charge. [scene:us4_prisons|Part Four: prisons] [scene:us2_emergency|Part Two: emergency powers] [scene:us3_speech|Part Three: speech and the press] [scene:us9_westbank|Part Nine: the West Bank] [cite:us4_hamoked_charts]

The final assessment

On this scorecard's published measures, Israel's system delivers more of what households need to the people it treats as citizens than America's does: in coverage, life expectancy, infant survival, household debt, homelessness, family support, safety from homicide and how people rate their lives, Israel scores higher, while spending less than a third as much per head on health. The United States delivers higher pay, higher output per person, better schools on the 2025 results and somewhat smaller gaps between groups on the measures this volume could compare. Taken together, on rules published in full and tested under every weighting above, Israel's system scores about 6.1 of 10 on this scorecard and America's about 4.7; on the household score alone, about 6.4 against 4.6.

That is a statement about systems, laws and governments, not peoples, and it has two limits a reader should keep in view. The first is coverage: Israel's citizens' figures leave out the 5.56 million Palestinians it governs without citizenship, and on liberty, the one area in which the people counted change the answer, counting them breaks the tie in America's favour. The second is cause. The scorecard measures what each system delivers; it does not show that American aid pays for any of Israel's advantages. The aid is military money, spent mostly in the United States, and weighs about 0.6 per cent of Israel's GDP; Israel's health law, wage floor and family benefits are paid for by Israeli taxes, though money is fungible, and aid that covers part of Israel's defence budget leaves an equal sum of Israel's own money free for other uses. [scene:us21_verdict|Part Twenty-One: the aid, the claims and what is open] [cite:gi16_crs_aid2025] [cite:us1_jvl_aidtable]

What the record does and does not show. It shows each system's score on 39 to 41 shared measures, each from a named source, scored against published goalposts, and shows that the overall ranking survives every weighting tested, narrowly in one. It does not show the result on measures neither country publishes comparably, among them police killings, firearm deaths, medical debt and house prices against income, nor on the spending this scorecard reports but does not score; one row, the American child-poverty rate on the OECD basis, awaits confirmation and is bounded above. Scores are as of October 2026, days before Israel votes on 27 October and the United States on 3 November, and several rows, from health coverage under America's 2025 budget law to Israel's wartime spending, are moving. The figures should be checked again after both votes. [scene:us16_systems|Part Sixteen: coverage] [scene:us19_spending|Part Nineteen: defence spending]

books.title: The American Dream Architecture
books.subtitle: The Promise as Taught and the System as Built
books.intro:
This volume is about a promise most Americans were taught before they could vote: that anyone who works hard and plays by the rules can own a home, hold a secure job, see a doctor when sick, retire without fear and give their children a better life than their own. It sets that promise, as schools, presidents of both parties and popular culture have taught it, beside the system that was actually built to deliver it, one mechanism at a time: wages and the minimum wage, unions and the shareholder turn, housing and zoning, schools and student loans, health insurance and medical debt, credit and fees, pensions and 401(k)s, taxes and benefit cliffs, wealth and inheritance, the courts and the poverty line, the lobbying that writes the rules, and the belief that keeps the promise alive. For each it asks who designed the mechanism and when, how it works step by step, who gains, who pays, and what the documented outcome is.

The book tests a thesis set out on the Sophia platform: that the Dream now works as an illusion, a story told to keep people working inside a system that extracts from them. It tests that thesis fairly. Where a mechanism really does move money from those who have less to those who have more, the book shows it with the numbers, as a money trail from input to who pays. Where the taught version holds, it says so, and early: Part Two sets out what has genuinely improved, and every part carries a passage on where the mechanism works as promised. Where the record is disputed, it shows both sides with their sources. Interpretations, including the illusion thesis itself, appear only in passages labelled as interpretation, each followed by the strongest readings against it.

The record it assembles is mixed, and specific. About nine in ten Americans born in 1940 went on to earn more than their parents; about half of those born in the early 1980s did. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] [cite:ad2_chetty_trends] The chance of climbing from the bottom fifth to the top has held near 8 or 9 in 100, and is about a quarter as high for Black children as for white. [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] Where federal law was built to keep the promise, it largely did: poverty among Americans over 65 fell from 35.2 per cent in 1959 to 9.9 per cent, and the share without health insurance is less than half what it was in 2009. [cite:ad10_census_a3] [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us16_khn_uninsured] Where costs outran incomes, the promise narrowed: a typical home now costs about 5.0 years of median household income against 3.2 in the late 1980s, and the largest federal college grant covers a little over a quarter of the cost of a year at a public university, against roughly three-quarters in the late 1970s. [cite:ad6_jchs_2018] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [cite:ad7_nasfaa_pell]

The book ends with a verdict in the open. Seven promises are scored on a scorecard whose every rule and weight is printed beside it, so that a reader who weighs things differently can recompute the result; the total is the book's editorial synthesis, not a discovered fact. The final part then sets out the levers with documented effects, from the 2021 child tax credit to automatic retirement enrolment and Medicaid expansion, with the evidence for and against each, and answers the volume's question in three registers: what the record documents, what it makes probable, and what it does not support. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] [cite:ad18_ucd_wherry] [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26]

Each part stands on its own and links to the parts that explain the figures it uses. Readers who want the numbers first can start with Part Two, which defines the measures used throughout (absolute and relative mobility, income and wealth, median and mean, real and nominal dollars), or with Part Seventeen, which follows three ordinary households through the whole machine in a single year.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Dream as Taught
chapters.intro: This part sets out the American Dream as Americans first meet it, before any of it is tested. It begins with the phrase itself: what the historian James Truslow Adams meant when he named it in 1931, which was more than cars and high wages, and the older ideas he drew on, from the Declaration of Independence to Lincoln's ladder of free labour and Horatio Alger's lucky clerk. It then shows how the Dream is taught today, quoting the national economics standards, a state's required course, a widely used textbook, the history curriculum, the citizenship test and the songs of Saturday-morning television, and how far Americans still believe it. Its last section turns to the sellers, presidents and candidates of both parties, builders and lenders, follows one national campaign to sell the Dream as a house from the podium to the outcome, and states the question the rest of the book sets out to answer.
chapters.outro: The Dream began as a claim about what a free society lets its people become; James Truslow Adams, who named it in 1931, said it was "not a dream of motor cars and high wages merely." [cite:ad1_taylor_adams] Its economic logic is older, Lincoln's ladder from wages to savings to ownership, and so is the companion claim that a person who stays on the bottom rung has only himself to blame. [cite:ad1_lincoln_1859] Schools teach the ladder in careful language, that pay "primarily" reflects the value of what workers produce and that skills raise living standards, while the citizenship test names the system in two words, capitalism and free market economy. [cite:ad1_cee2010] [cite:ad1_uscis2025] Presidents of both parties sell the same few outcomes, a decent wage, a home, savings and children who do better, and builders and lenders sell the same promise with a product attached; the one national campaign followed here lifted home ownership to 69.4 per cent in 2004 before it fell back to 63.1 per cent in 2016 (second-quarter, seasonally adjusted rates), amid a dispute over how much the campaign caused the crash between those two points. [cite:ad1_bush_2002] [cite:ad1_fred_hor] [cite:ad1_fcic_angelides] [cite:ad1_hw_wallison] Today about a third of adults say the Dream still holds, with sharp splits by party, age and race. [cite:ad1_apnorc26] Before testing where the promise fails, the book sets out where it holds and how to measure it. [scene:ad2_what_holds|Part Two: What Holds]

sections.h: The Phrase: What James Truslow Adams Meant
sections.html:
The American Dream has a birth year. In 1931, in one of the worst years of the Great Depression, the historian James Truslow Adams published a one-volume history of the United States called The Epic of America, and made "the American dream" its theme. He had wanted to call the book The American Dream; his publishers would not let him. The book became a bestseller anyway, and the phrase outlived it. [cite:ad1_brandt_ah] Adams was not a romantic outsider. He had been a partner in a Wall Street firm from 1907 to 1913 before retiring from business in his mid-thirties to write history, and his The Founding of New England won the Pulitzer Prize for History in 1922. [cite:ad1_audit_adams_ebsco] The man who named the Dream knew both the counting-house and the archive.

What he meant by it matters, because most of this book measures the Dream in dollars, and Adams warned against exactly that. He described "that dream of a land in which life should be better and richer and fuller for every man," and then, in the next breath, said what it was not: "It is not a dream of motor cars and high wages merely." It was, he wrote, a dream of a social order in which each person could reach the fullest stature they were capable of, and be recognised for what they are "regardless of the fortuitous circumstances of birth or position." [cite:ad1_taylor_adams] Elsewhere he called it "the dominant motif in the American epic" and "a moving force as truly as wheat or gold," and wrote of "a better, richer, and happier life for all our citizens of every rank." [cite:ad1_taylor_adams] [cite:ad1_brandt_ah]

Two features of that definition carry through the rest of this book. First, the original Dream was about a social order, not a shopping list: what a country lets its people become, not what each of them owns. Second, Adams did not say material security was irrelevant. "Merely" is the hinge word. Cars and wages were part of the Dream, but not the whole of it, and the later shorthand that equates the Dream with a house, a pension and a rising paycheck is a narrowing of what he wrote, not a betrayal of it.

Older than the phrase

Adams named something he believed was already there, and the record bears him out. The Declaration of Independence of 1776 lists "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness" among the unalienable rights governments exist to secure. [cite:ad1_decl] It promises the pursuit, not the happiness, and it says nothing about income. But it set the frame every later version works inside: the government's job is to keep the path open, and what each person finds at the end of it is their own.

Abraham Lincoln gave the economic version its first clear form. Speaking to the Wisconsin State Agricultural Society in Milwaukee on 30 September 1859, he described what he called the free-labour system: "The prudent, penniless beginner in the world, labors for wages awhile," saves a surplus to buy tools or land, works on his own account for a while, and at length hires another beginner to help him. Then he added the sentence that turns a description into a promise: "If any continue through life in the condition of the hired laborer, it is not the fault of the system," but of a dependent nature, improvidence, folly or singular misfortune. [cite:ad1_lincoln_1859] Two years later, in his message to Congress of 4 July 1861, he defined the purpose of the government the Union was fighting for: "to afford all an unfettered start and a fair chance in the race of life." [cite:ad1_lincoln_1861]

Those two Lincoln passages contain, in compressed form, both halves of what this book tests. The first is a claim about how the system works: wages lead to savings, savings to ownership, ownership to independence. The second is a claim about fault: when the ladder does not lead anywhere, the cause lies in the person, not the structure. The book's later parts take each mechanism in turn and ask which of the two halves the documented record supports, for whom, and when.

The popular fiction of the decade after the Civil War gave the promise a face. Horatio Alger wrote more than a hundred books for boys, which sold over 20 million copies; Ragged Dick, serialised in 1867 and published as a book in 1868, set the pattern of an honest, hardworking poor boy who is rewarded, though usually through luck. [cite:ad1_brit_alger] The story is remembered as "rags to riches," but that is not what happens in it. Dick saves, studies and refuses to steal; his break comes when he rescues a drowning child, and the grateful father gives him a job in his firm. He ends the book as a respectable clerk, not a rich man, which is why the critics Carl Bode and Gary Scharnhorst describe Alger's real theme as "rags to respectability." [cite:ad1_wiki_ragged] The best-known parable of American self-making turns, on the page, on a stroke of luck and a wealthy patron.

Adams was also not the first to use the words. The historian Sarah Churchwell has traced "the American dream" back to the 1910s and 1920s, when it stood for a broad vision of democratic and economic equality and was argued over in the same years as the slogan "America First." [cite:ad1_churchwell] The phrase was contested before it was popular, and it has stayed contested.

From a social order to a house

A dream about human development became, in common speech, a dream about a house with a yard, and part of the reason is that the house was sold, deliberately and early. Toward the end of the First World War, the National Association of Real Estate Boards launched an "Own Your Own Home" campaign, and the Department of Labor took it up in 1917–18, making it the first federal programme aimed explicitly at encouraging home ownership; it was purely promotional, with no money for buyers or builders. [cite:ad1_cannato] [cite:ad1_retsinas] In the early 1920s the Commerce Secretary, Herbert Hoover, led the Better Homes in America movement, backed by Presidents Harding and Coolidge. [cite:ad1_retsinas] Hoover wrote in 1925 that "Maintaining a high percentage of individual home owners is one of the searching tests" facing the nation. [cite:ad1_cannato]

Promotion alone did not move the numbers. The share of households owning their homes was 45.6 per cent in 1920, 47.8 per cent in 1930 and 43.6 per cent in 1940, after the Depression foreclosures. [cite:ad1_cannato] What changed it was finance. Before the New Deal, a typical mortgage ran five to ten years and covered about half the price of the house; the Federal Housing Administration's mortgage insurance made the fully amortised 20- to 30-year loan covering 80 per cent of the price the national norm. ("Fully amortised" means each monthly payment covers both interest and part of the principal, so the loan is paid off by the end rather than falling due in one large lump.) After the Second World War, the Veterans Administration guaranteed mortgages for returning veterans. [cite:ad1_cannato] [cite:ad1_retsinas]

Where it worked as promised

The postwar record is the strongest evidence that the promise, in its material form, could be kept on a national scale. Between 1940 and 1960 the home ownership rate rose from 43.6 to 61.9 per cent, an increase of 18.3 percentage points in twenty years, after three censuses (1920, 1930 and 1940) in which it had stayed between 43.6 and 47.8 per cent. [cite:ad1_cannato] For the generation that bought those homes, the chain Lincoln described (wages, savings, ownership) worked very close to the way it was later taught. The rate has never fallen back to its prewar level; in the second quarter of 2026 it stood at 65.2 per cent on the Census Bureau's seasonally adjusted measure, 65.0 per cent before adjustment. [cite:ad1_fred_hor] [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226]

The same record also shows who was left out. The developments that defined the new suburbs were sold with federal backing and private restrictions: Levittown on Long Island, advertised at $7,990 a house as "the housing buy of the century," used a 1947 rental contract that limited occupancy to "members of the Caucasian race," and in 1949 a salesman told a Black veteran that the builders "have not at this time decided to sell to Negroes." [cite:ad1_ah_levitt] How federal underwriting rules and private covenants shaped who could buy, and what that did to family wealth across generations, is the subject of [scene:ad6_redlining_to_suburbs|Part Six] and [scene:ad12_wealth_gap|Part Twelve]. For now the point is narrower: the Dream as a house became real for tens of millions of families at the same moment and by the same means that it was closed to others.

That is the inheritance the modern phrase carries. It began as a claim about what a free society lets people become, borrowed its economic logic from Lincoln's ladder, took its popular image from Alger's lucky clerk, and acquired its most concrete form, the owned home, through real estate promotion and federal mortgage finance. The next section looks at how that inheritance is taught today. [scene:ad1_as_taught|The Dream as taught]

sections.h: As Taught: The Promise in Standards, Textbooks and Tests
sections.html:
Most Americans never read The Epic of America. They met the Dream in school, in a form nobody would call a dream: as a set of plain statements about how the economy works. Taken together, those statements make a chain. Work and education raise what a person can earn; earnings, saved and borrowed against, buy a home; the home and the savings carry a family through illness and old age; and each generation, starting a little higher, does better than the last. No single document states the whole chain. Each link is taught somewhere, and this section sets out where, in the documents' own words.

The economics standards

The best-known national statement of what American schoolchildren should learn about the economy is the Council for Economic Education's Voluntary National Content Standards in Economics, whose second edition appeared in 2010. Its Standard 13, on income, reads: "Income for most people is determined by the market value of the productive resources they sell. What workers earn primarily depends on the market value of what they produce." [cite:ad1_cee2010] In plain terms, your pay reflects what your work is worth to buyers. Standard 15 adds the second link: investment in machinery and technology, "and in the health, education, and training of people," stimulates economic growth "and can raise future standards of living." [cite:ad1_cee2010] Economists call skills and education "human capital," because, like a machine, they cost something to acquire and raise what a person can produce afterwards.

The standards are voluntary, but the same ideas appear in the framework published in 2013 to guide states writing their own standards, the National Council for the Social Studies' College, Career, and Civic Life (C3) Framework. Its high-school economics indicator D2.Eco.13 asks students to explain why "investments in capital goods and human capital increase economic growth and standards of living." [cite:ad1_c3] A widely used college textbook, N. Gregory Mankiw's Principles of Economics, opens with ten principles, the eighth of which is that a country's standard of living depends on its production: the more goods and services a country produces, the higher its standard of living. [cite:ad1_mankiw]

Read carefully, these statements are narrower than the promise built from them. Standard 13 says "most people" and "primarily," not everyone and always. Mankiw's principle is about a country's average, not about any particular family. None of these documents says that productivity gains will be shared evenly, that a given worker's pay will rise with the economy's output, or that hard work guarantees a home. Those are the inferences a student, or a politician, draws from them. That distinction runs through the whole book: where a mechanism behaves as these standards describe, the taught version holds; where the record departs from them, the question is whether the standards were wrong or whether they were stretched to claim more than they said.

One state's version: Texas

State standards make the same points with more emphasis. In Texas, the required high-school economics course is titled "Economics with Emphasis on the Free Enterprise System and Its Benefits." Under the standards adopted in 2010, students must understand "the basic characteristics and benefits of a free enterprise system" and explain "the benefits of the U.S. free enterprise system, including individual freedom of consumers and producers." [cite:ad1_tx_teks] The title was not invented by the State Board of Education: it dates from 1997 and comes from wording the legislature wrote into the Texas Education Code. When the board approved the revised economics standards in May 2010, the vote was 14 to 0, the only part of that year's contested social studies revision to win support from both parties. [cite:ad1_edweek_tx] The same Texas course asks students to "analyze the costs and benefits of personal financial decisions," a strand that has grown nationally. [cite:ad1_tx_teks]

That growth is one of the clearest recent changes in how the Dream is taught. As of 22 October 2026, 30 states guarantee that every student takes a personal finance course before graduating from high school, 11 with the requirement fully in force and 19 still phasing it in; in 2022 the figure was 17. [cite:ad1_ngpf] Budgeting, saving and avoiding high-interest debt are useful skills, and later parts show how much an individual decision about a loan or a credit card can cost. But the shift also moves the lesson from how the system works to how an individual should navigate it, which is the emphasis of Lincoln's 1859 sentence about fault. [scene:ad1_the_phrase|Lincoln's ladder]

History class: the postwar boom as the model

Students who take Advanced Placement United States History meet the material version of the Dream at its peak. The College Board's course framework, in its unit on 1945 to 1980, asks students to "Explain the causes of economic growth in the years after World War II," and gives the answer as a key concept: "A burgeoning private sector, federal spending, the baby boom, and technological developments helped spur economic growth." A companion concept states that increasing social mobility encouraged the migration of the middle class to the suburbs. [cite:ad1_apush_ced] That is an accurate summary of what happened, and it matters for how the Dream is understood. The generation born around 1940 is the one for whom the taught chain worked most completely, and their experience became the benchmark against which later generations measure their own. [scene:ad2_what_holds|Where the Dream holds]

The civics test and Saturday-morning civics

The most compact official statement of the American economic creed is the one immigrants learn. The United States Citizenship and Immigration Services civics test, in its 2025 version of 128 questions, asks: "What is the economic system of the United States?" The accepted answers are "Capitalism" and "Free market economy." Another question asks in which founding document the words "Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness" appear, and a third asks why the colonists came to America, with "Economic opportunity" among the accepted answers. [cite:ad1_uscis2025] The phrase "American Dream" itself does not appear in the test; its parts do.

For several generations of children, civics also came set to music. Schoolhouse Rock! began running between ABC's Saturday-morning cartoons in January 1973; its America Rock series of 1975–76 produced "I'm Just a Bill," and a Money Rock series on personal finance was added when the programme was revived in 1993. The songs were added to the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry in 2018. [cite:ad1_loc_shr] Whatever else they taught, they taught that the system was knowable, orderly and fair to those who learned its rules.

What Americans now believe

The taught version is no longer the believed version for most adults. In a Wall Street Journal and NORC poll of 1,527 adults taken from 10 to 23 July 2025, 31 per cent said the American Dream still holds true, 46 per cent said it once did but no longer does, and 23 per cent said it never did. Only 25 per cent said they had a good chance of improving their standard of living, the lowest in that question's history since 1987, and 78 per cent were not confident their children's generation would be better off than their own. [cite:ad1_wsjnorc25] An AP-NORC poll of 2,596 adults taken from 16 to 20 April 2026, defining the Dream as the belief that if you work hard you will get ahead, found almost the same: a third said it still holds, half that it once did, and 15 per cent that it never had. [cite:ad1_apnorc26]

The same poll shows how much belief depends on who is asked. Republicans were more than three times as likely as Democrats to say the Dream still holds (57 per cent against 17), adults over 60 twice as likely as adults under 30 (46 against 22), and white adults about twice as likely as Black adults (40 against 19), with Black adults more likely to say it had never been true. Americans born abroad were about as likely as those born in the United States to say it still holds. [cite:ad1_apnorc26] The partisan split was already visible a year earlier: in July 2025, about 55 per cent of Republicans and 90 per cent of Democrats gave a negative outlook for themselves and their children. Gaps of this kind can move with which party holds the White House. [cite:ad1_wsjnorc25] Why belief moves with party, age and race, and why it survives at all where the data are discouraging, is the subject of [scene:ad16_belief_vs_data|Part Sixteen].

The taught version against the record, in brief

Each link of the taught chain is a claim that can be checked, and the parts that follow check them one at a time. The table below previews the main lines of evidence, so the reader can see from the start where the book is heading and where the record is disputed. "Real" means adjusted for inflation, so that a dollar in one year buys the same as a dollar in another; a "median" is the middle value, with half above and half below.

The taught version, in short, is not a caricature. It rests on real documents that say defensible things, and on a postwar generation for whom it was close to literal fact. What the documents do not say is who will be selling the promise to each new generation, in what words, and with what product attached. That is the subject of the next section. [scene:ad1_who_sells_it|Who sells it]

sections.h: Who Sells It
sections.html:
A school teaches the Dream once. It is sold continuously: by presidents and candidates of both parties, by the industries whose products are its parts, and by lenders who finance the gap between what the Dream costs and what a family earns. This section looks at the sellers and their words, and then follows one sales campaign, the national push for home ownership between 1995 and 2007, from the podium to the outcome. The purpose is not to accuse anyone of insincerity. A president who promises a better life may mean it, and a builder who advertises a house is selling a real house. The purpose is to show how the promise is phrased, what is attached to it, and what the record shows happened next.

The presidents

Bill Clinton, accepting the Democratic nomination on 16 July 1992, said he "was raised to believe the American Dream was built on rewarding hard work," and spoke for those who "play by the rules." [cite:ad1_clinton_1992] As president, on 17 February 1993, he made the promise specific: "if you work 40 hours a week and you've got a child in the house, you will no longer be in poverty," a pledge he tied to expanding the Earned Income Tax Credit, a refundable tax credit paid to low-wage working families. [cite:ad1_clinton_1993] On 5 June 1995 he announced a National Homeownership Strategy to "boost home ownership to 67.5 percent by the year 2000," calling home ownership "the new way home for the American middle class." [cite:ad1_clinton_nhs]

George W. Bush put the house at the centre. At St. Paul AME Church in Atlanta on 17 June 2002 he said, "if you own your own home, you're realizing the American Dream," and set a goal of 5.5 million more minority homeowners by 2010. [cite:ad1_bush_2002] Signing the American Dream Downpayment Act on 16 December 2003, which authorised $200 million a year to help at least 40,000 low-income families a year with down payments, he said "The dream of homeownership should be attainable for every hard-working American" and promised to "promote an ownership society in America." [cite:ad1_bush_addi]

Barack Obama gave the fullest list of the Dream's material parts. At Osawatomie, Kansas, on 6 December 2011, he called the moment "a make-or-break moment for the middle class" and described the goal as a country where working people "can earn enough to raise a family, build a modest savings, own a home, secure their retirement." [cite:ad1_obama_2011] In his State of the Union address of 28 January 2014 he said "Upward mobility has stalled" and proposed to "build new ladders of opportunity into the middle class," adding: "Opportunity is who we are." [cite:ad1_obama_2014]

Donald Trump began his first campaign on 16 June 2015 by declaring the opposite of the creed: "Sadly, the American dream is dead," and promising to bring it back "bigger and better and stronger than ever before." [cite:ad1_trump_2015] At his second inauguration, on 20 January 2025, he announced that "The golden age of America begins right now" and that "The American Dream will soon be back and thriving like never before." [cite:ad1_trump_2025] Kamala Harris, campaigning in Pittsburgh on 25 September 2024, called her programme an "opportunity economy" and proposed $25,000 in down-payment help for first-time buyers and three million new homes and rentals; the proposal ended with her defeat in November 2024 and was never enacted. [cite:ad1_harris_2024]

Read side by side, the speeches share a structure. The challenger says the Dream is endangered or dead; the incumbent says it is being restored; both locate its proof in the same few things: a job that pays enough, a home, savings and children who do better. The parties differ on the remedies, but not on the promise. That shared promise is what makes it testable. Each speaker named outcomes that can be measured, and the parts that follow measure them.

The industries

The house has had commercial sellers for as long as it has had political ones. The "Own Your Own Home" campaign that the Labor Department adopted in 1917 was launched by the National Association of Real Estate Boards.
