[cite:ad1_cannato] Builders advertised the postwar suburbs as the Dream made affordable: Levitt and Sons sold its Long Island houses at a fixed $7,990 and called them "the housing buy of the century," a claim one historian of the development judged probably true, on loan packages guaranteed by the Federal Housing Administration and the Veterans Administration. [cite:ad1_ah_levitt]

In the 1990s and 2000s the mortgage-finance industry adopted the phrase directly. By 2001 Fannie Mae, the government-sponsored company that buys mortgages from lenders so they can lend again, had pledged an "American Dream Commitment" of $2 trillion in housing finance for 18 million underserved families over ten years. [cite:ad1_fnma_zigas] In 2002 Bush announced that Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks would commit more than $440 billion to minority markets, and named the National Association of Home Builders and the Realtors among the private partners in his homeownership challenge. [cite:ad1_bush_2002] Among private lenders, Ameriquest Mortgage billed itself as the "sponsor of the American dream" and made at least $80.6 billion in high-interest loans between 2005 and 2007. [cite:ad1_cpi_ameriquest]

One campaign followed through

The homeownership push is the clearest case in the record of the Dream being sold as a national policy, with targets, money and industry partners, and then measured. The table follows it in five steps. The steps are documented; whether the push caused the crash that followed is disputed, and both sides of that dispute are given below.

The Ameriquest settlement of 23 January 2006 shows what selling the Dream could look like at its worst. The states alleged that the company misstated interest rates and prepayment penalties, inflated borrowers' incomes, including by inventing "sewing" or "lawn" businesses, and pressured appraisers to inflate home values. The company paid $325 million and agreed to an independent monitor; the settlement described the practices as allegations. [cite:ad1_ct_ameriquest] Ameriquest stopped lending in August 2007. [cite:ad1_cpi_ameriquest]

How much the public push contributed to the 2008 crisis is a genuine dispute. The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission concluded in 2011 that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac "contributed to the crisis but were not a primary cause," and that "government housing policies were not a significant factor." [cite:ad1_fcic_angelides] A dissenting commissioner, Peter Wallison, argued the reverse: that government housing policy was "the sine qua non of the financial crisis," having produced some 27 million subprime and other risky loans. [cite:ad1_hw_wallison] The foreclosures that followed, and who lost the most in them, are the subject of [scene:ad12_2008_foreclosures|Part Twelve].

Where it works as promised

Selling the Dream has not always meant selling it falsely. Clinton tied his 1993 pledge to an expansion of the Earned Income Tax Credit, and whether that credit keeps working families out of poverty is a measurable question, weighed in [scene:ad18_what_would_change_it|Part Eighteen]. The postwar sales campaign, for all its exclusions, was followed by a rapid expansion of home ownership: from 43.6 per cent of households in 1940 to 61.9 per cent in 1960. [cite:ad1_cannato] Even after the 2008 crisis, ownership never fell below about 63 per cent, and in 2026 about 65 per cent of households own their homes. [cite:ad1_fred_hor] A promise that is advertised can also be kept; the question in each case is for whom, at what price, and with what risk passed to whom.

Interpretation, not finding: the Dream as a sales story

The Sophia platform reads the Dream as a whole as an illusion: a story told to keep people working, borrowing and buying inside a system whose rules extract more from them than the story admits. In this reading, the shared presidential vocabulary, the industry slogans and the school standards are parts of one narrative whose function is to make each household's shortfall look like a personal failure, as Lincoln's 1859 sentence about fault already did, rather than a feature of how wages, housing, credit, health care and retirement are built.

The strongest counter-readings are substantial. A promise repeated by both parties for decades, and by people who enacted real benefits under its name, is more naturally read as an aspiration than as a cover story. The industries that use the phrase sell real products that many buyers value, and a slogan is evidence of marketing, not of deception. Belief in the Dream has fallen to about a third of adults, which suggests that the story does not, in fact, control what Americans think when their experience contradicts it. And a reading that explains every outcome as part of one design cannot be tested against any of them. This book therefore treats the illusion thesis as a question to be answered mechanism by mechanism, not as a premise.

The question this book asks

The book's central question follows from the promise as it is taught and sold. It asks whether work in the United States today reliably leads to a secure income, a home, health care, a debt-free retirement and children who do better, and, where it does not, whether the cause is a measurable feature of how the system is built or a matter of individual choices and luck. The answer is unlikely to be a single word. Some parts of the promise hold for most people; some hold for some people and not others; some show measured shortfalls; and on some the evidence is contested. The book sorts them.

The parts follow the promise clause by clause. Part Two sets out where the Dream holds and how to measure it, and Part Three the record on mobility between generations. Part Four examines the turn in the 1970s and 1980s when pay and productivity began to separate, and Part Five work itself: wages, hours, and the floors under them. Parts Six to Ten take the Dream's purchases in turn: housing, education, health care, the debt that finances them, and retirement. Part Eleven looks at the taxes, fees and fines a household pays, and Part Twelve at the difference between income and wealth. Part Thirteen asks who gets the Dream, Part Fourteen what happens at the bottom, and Part Fifteen who writes the rules. Part Sixteen asks why the belief survives, Part Seventeen follows families through the whole system in numbers, and Part Eighteen gives the verdict, row by row, on whether the Dream is an illusion, a mechanism or a promise. [scene:ad2_what_holds|Part Two: What Holds]

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: What Holds
chapters.intro: Before testing where the American Dream fails, this part sets out where it holds. Its first section gathers the documented record on the promise's side: household incomes at a record and among the highest in the rich world, low poverty among people who work full time, a century of upward mobility for immigrants' children, strong mobility for Hispanic Americans and recent gains for Black children, the places where children from the bottom still reach the top at high rates, the generation born around 1940 for whom the taught version was close to literal fact, and the falling cost of food and many goods. Its second section explains the measures needed to read the rest of the book: absolute and relative mobility, income and wealth, median and mean, real and nominal dollars, the choice of price index, households and individuals, and income before and after taxes and benefits.
chapters.outro: The promise holds in documented and specific ways. Real median household income reached $87,460 in 2025, the highest on record, and the American median disposable income ranked second in the OECD in 2021; official poverty among full-time, year-round workers was 1.6 per cent. [cite:us14_census_story2025] [cite:ad2_oecd_median] [cite:us18_crs_pov2025] Children of immigrants have out-climbed children of American-born parents for more than a century, Hispanic Americans move up strongly, and the earnings gap between white and Black children from low-income families narrowed by 30 per cent between the 1978 and 1992 birth cohorts. [cite:ad2_abramitzky_aer] [cite:ad2_oi_race_hisp] [cite:ad2_changing_opp] For children born around 1940, nine in ten out-earned their parents. [cite:ad2_chetty_fading] The same record sets the limits: the top gained about twice as much as the middle since 1967, the GI Bill widened the racial gap in the South, and the share of children out-earning their parents fell to about half for those born in the 1980s (60 to 68 per cent on alternative measures), while the odds of climbing from the bottom fifth to the top stayed near 8 or 9 per cent. [cite:us14_census_p60] [cite:ad2_turner_bound] [cite:ad2_reeves_winship] [cite:ad2_chetty_trends] Which of those figures a reader trusts depends on the measure, and the measures are now defined. Part Three takes up the mobility record in full: how far absolute mobility fell, why relative mobility held, how much place decides, and how the United States compares abroad. [scene:ad3_absolute_mobility|The Mobility Record]

sections.h: Where the Promise Holds
sections.html:
A book that tests a promise has to say first where the promise is kept. The American Dream as taught says that a person who works hard can earn a decent living, that the country's ordinary families live well by the standards of the world, that newcomers can rise, and that children can do better than their parents. Each of those claims has a documented side on which it holds. This section sets them out plainly, with the numbers, before the rest of the book examines the mechanisms where the record parts from the story. Nothing later in the book cancels what is established here; where a later part finds the promise failing, it fails in a named place, for a named group, through a named mechanism, beside the record set out below.

Incomes that are high by the world's standards

The typical American household is richer today than at any time since the government began measuring it. The Census Bureau's real median household income, meaning the income of the household exactly in the middle once all households are lined up from poorest to richest, adjusted for rising prices, was $87,460 in 2025, up 2.6 per cent in a year and the highest since the series began in 1967. After federal and state taxes and the value of tax credits, the median was $76,060. [cite:us14_census_story2025] Over the long run the gain is real but uneven: from 1967 to 2025 household income before taxes rose about 56 per cent at the median and at the 10th percentile, and about 121 per cent at the 90th. [cite:us14_census_p60] The household in the middle is better off than its counterpart of a generation ago; the household near the top gained about twice as much.

Compared abroad, the American middle is near the top. On the OECD's measure of median disposable household income, adjusted for household size and converted at purchasing-power rates so that a dollar buys the same basket in each country, the United States stood second among member countries in 2021 at about $46,600, behind only Luxembourg and ahead of Norway, Switzerland and Canada. [cite:ad2_oecd_median] The same organisation reports that the top fifth of Americans earn about eight times as much as the bottom fifth, a wider spread than in most rich countries; a high middle and a wide spread are both true at once. [cite:ad2_oecd_bli]

Work that keeps a family out of poverty

The taught version says that full-time work is a way out of poverty, and for the poverty line as officially defined it is. In 2025 the official poverty rate was 10.2 per cent, 34.5 million people; among people who worked full time all year it was 1.6 per cent. [cite:us18_crs_pov2025] The child poverty rate, 13.4 per cent, and the rate for Hispanic Americans, 13.9 per cent, were both the lowest ever recorded. [cite:us8_census_2025] On the Census Bureau's broader Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts taxes, benefits and costs such as medical bills, poverty was 13.1 per cent, and Social Security alone kept 28.8 million people above that line. [cite:us18_census_p60290] Public policy can move these numbers quickly: when the child tax credit was enlarged for 2021, supplemental child poverty fell to 5.2 per cent, and it rose to 12.4 per cent in 2022 after the larger credit expired. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] The federal tax system also leans toward lower earners: the Congressional Budget Office finds that average federal tax rates fell for every income group between 1979 and 2022, most of all for the lowest fifth, whose individual income tax rate was about minus 10 per cent once refundable credits are counted. [cite:us11_cbo_dist2022] Part Fourteen tests how well the official poverty line itself measures need. [scene:ad14_poverty_line|How the poverty line is drawn]

Children of immigrants rise

The immigrant chapter of the story holds over more than a century of data. Linking millions of fathers and sons from the 1880s to the present, Ran Abramitzky, Leah Boustan, Elisa Jácome and Santiago Pérez found that children of immigrants from nearly every sending country have higher upward mobility than children of parents born in the United States, both in the age of Ellis Island and today, even though the countries of origin and the immigration laws have changed completely. [cite:ad2_abramitzky_aer] The size of the advantage is steady: sons of immigrant fathers at the 25th percentile of income ended up 3 to 4 percentile points higher than comparable sons of American-born fathers in the 1880–1910 cohorts, and about 5 points higher in modern data. Part of the advantage comes from immigrant families settling in places with better prospects for children. The exceptions are few and named: in modern data, children of immigrants from Haiti and Jamaica do not show the advantage. [cite:ad2_abramitzky_nber] Part Thirteen follows these groups in detail. [scene:ad13_immigrants_latinos|Immigrants and Latino Americans]

The record for Hispanic Americans as a whole points the same way. Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, Maggie Jones and Sonya Porter, working from linked tax and Census records, conclude that Hispanic Americans "are moving up significantly in the income distribution across generations" because their rates of upward mobility are relatively high, in contrast with Black Americans, whose rates are substantially lower than white Americans'. [cite:ad2_oi_race_hisp]

Gains for Black children, and places where the ladder works

The racial gap in mobility is one of the largest failures this book documents, but it is narrowing for recent cohorts. Comparing children born in 1978 with those born in 1992, Chetty, Will Dobbie, Benjamin Goldman, Sonya Porter and Crystal Yang found that Black children's adult earnings rose at every level of parental income, and that the earnings gap between white and Black children from low-income families shrank by 30 per cent. The same study found the gap between rich and poor white children widening by 30 per cent, and similar patterns in schooling, test scores and mortality. [cite:ad2_changing_opp] Part Thirteen sets these gains beside the wealth record, which moved the other way. [scene:ad13_black_americans|Black Americans and the Dream]

Where a child grows up matters as much as the national average. In the commuting zone around San Jose, a child born into the bottom fifth of incomes had about a 12.9 per cent chance of reaching the top fifth; around Charlotte, about 4.4 per cent. The places with higher mobility had less residential segregation, less income inequality, better primary schools, more social capital and more stable families. [cite:ad2_land_opp] In those places the promise of rising from the bottom is kept at roughly three times the rate of the places where it is not. [scene:ad3_relative_and_place|Relative mobility and place]

The generation the promise described

For Americans born around 1940, the taught version was close to a literal description of life. About 90 per cent of children born that year grew up to earn more than their parents at the same age, after adjusting for inflation; for sons compared with fathers, 95 per cent. [cite:ad2_chetty_fading] [cite:ad2_oi_fading] That generation came of age as the Servicemen's Readjustment Act, the GI Bill, signed on 22 June 1944, paid for veterans' schooling and backed their mortgages. In 1947 veterans made up 49 per cent of college admissions; by the time the original programme ended in July 1956, 7.8 million of the 16 million veterans of the Second World War had used its education or training benefits, and between 1944 and 1952 the Veterans Administration backed nearly 2.4 million home loans. [cite:ad2_va_gibill]

The same record carries its own limit. The benefits were federal, but colleges, lenders and much of their administration were local, and in the segregated South they were not equally open. Sarah Turner and John Bound found that the war and the GI Bill together raised college attainment by about 0.4 years for Black men born outside the South, comparable to white men's gain, but brought few gains to Black men born in the South, where about a hundred colleges were open to them and few counsellors served them; for Southern men the bill "exacerbated rather than narrowed" the racial gap. [cite:ad2_turner_bound] Part Six follows the housing side of that story. [scene:ad6_redlining_to_suburbs|From redlining to the suburbs]

More for less in goods

Everyday goods take a smaller bite than they once did. In 1960 Americans spent about 17 per cent of their disposable income, the income left after taxes, on food; in 2025 they spent 9.7 per cent, including meals out. [cite:ad2_ers_food1960] [cite:ad2_ers_food] Air-conditioning was installed in 49 per cent of new single-family homes completed in 1973 and in 89 per cent by 2008. [cite:ad2_census_chars] The average hides the bottom: in 2024 the poorest fifth of households spent 33 per cent of their pre-tax income on food, the richest fifth 6.4 per cent. [cite:ad2_ers_food] The goods that grew cheaper are mostly manufactured and farmed; the costs this book follows in later parts, housing, college, health care and child care, are mostly services, and several of them moved the other way. Even there the record is mixed: the average net tuition paid at a public four-year college by in-state students, after grants, fell from a peak of about $4,450 in 2012–13 to about $2,300 in 2025–26, measured in 2025 dollars. [cite:us14_cb_trends2025] [scene:ad7_college_cost_pell|What college costs]

What this record does and does not show

The record above is not a verdict on the whole promise; it marks where the promise is kept. Three limits run through it. First, the averages are high partly because the top is very high: the same Census series that shows record median income shows the gap between the 90th and 10th percentiles widening from 9.2 times in 1967 to 13.1 times in 2025. [cite:us14_census_story2025] Second, the mobility record is two records. The chance of out-earning one's parents fell from about 90 per cent to about 50 per cent, but the chance of climbing from the bottom fifth to the top fifth stayed roughly where it was, about 8 or 9 per cent, for children born between 1971 and 1986. [cite:ad2_chetty_fading] [cite:ad2_chetty_trends] The ladder did not get steeper; the steps moved apart, and the economy's growth was shared less evenly. Third, gains for one group do not settle the record for another. Part Three measures the mobility record in full, and the next section explains the measures needed to read it. [scene:ad3_absolute_mobility|The fall in absolute mobility] [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|How to measure the Dream]

sections.h: How to Measure the Dream
sections.html:
Most arguments about the American Dream are arguments about measurement. Two honest people can look at the same economy and report that the typical family has never been richer and that half of all children now fall short of their parents, and both can be right, because they are measuring different things. This section sets out the six choices that decide what a number about the Dream means. The rest of the book names its choice each time it gives a figure, and states the trade-off once, here.

Absolute and relative mobility

Mobility means movement between the circumstances a person is born into and the circumstances they reach as an adult. It is measured in two different ways. Absolute mobility asks whether a child ends up with a higher income than their parents had at the same age, after adjusting for inflation. It answers the most common form of the promise, "my children will do better than I did." Relative mobility asks whether a child ends up higher or lower in the national ranking than their parents were. A family at the 20th percentile, the point below which a fifth of families fall, whose child reaches the 60th percentile has moved up in relative terms, whatever happened to incomes overall.

The two measures moved differently over the past eighty years. Absolute mobility fell from about 90 per cent of children born in 1940 to about 50 per cent of those born in the 1980s. [cite:ad2_chetty_fading] Relative mobility barely moved: the chance that a child from the bottom fifth would reach the top fifth was 8.4 per cent for children born in 1971 and 9.0 per cent for those born in 1986, and the authors call the rank-based measures "extremely stable" for the 1971 to 1993 cohorts. [cite:ad2_chetty_trends] The economists who produced both findings, Raj Chetty and his colleagues, explain the difference with a ladder. The chance of climbing from one rung to another has not changed, but "the rungs of the ladder have grown further apart," so the rung a child is born on matters more than it did. [cite:ad2_chetty_trends] Absolute mobility fell mainly because growth reached the bottom and middle less than it once did: the same researchers estimate that today's economy, if its growth were shared as it was for the 1940 cohort, would restore absolute mobility to about 80 per cent, while faster growth with today's sharing would reach only about 62 per cent. [cite:ad2_oi_fading]

Income and wealth

Income is what comes in over a period, usually a year: wages, salaries, business profits, interest, rent, pensions and government cash benefits. Wealth, also called net worth, is what a family owns at a moment, its house, savings, retirement accounts, business stakes and other assets, minus what it owes. A family can have a good income and little wealth, as many young professionals with student loans do, or modest income and great wealth, as many retirees with paid-off homes do. Wealth matters to the Dream because it is what pays for a down payment, survives a lost job and passes to the next generation.

The gaps between groups are much wider in wealth than in income. In the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances for 2025, the median white non-Hispanic family had an income of $95,300 and the median Black family $49,400, a ratio of about 1.9 to 1 ($95,300 ÷ $49,400 = 1.93). The median white family's net worth was $332,100 and the median Black family's $36,800, a ratio of about 9 to 1 ($332,100 ÷ $36,800 = 9.0). [cite:ad2_scf_t1] Part Twelve examines how that difference built up. [scene:ad12_wealth_gap|The wealth gap] The Federal Reserve publishes wealth figures from two sources built in different ways, the survey, taken every three years, and its quarterly Distributional Financial Accounts; this book does not join figures from the two.

Median and mean

The mean is the ordinary average: add up everyone's income and divide by the number of people. The median is the middle value: half of families have more, half have less. When a few people have very large amounts, the mean is pulled far above what a typical family has, and the median is the better guide to the typical case. In the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, mean family income was $145,200 and median income $82,200, so the mean was about 1.8 times the median. For net worth the gap is far wider: a mean of $1,241,500 against a median of $215,900, nearly 5.8 times ($1,241,500 ÷ $215,900 = 5.75). [cite:ad2_scf_t1] A claim that "the average family" has a million dollars is true of the mean and false of the typical family. This book reports medians for typical outcomes and names the mean wherever it uses one.

Real and nominal dollars

A nominal figure is the number of dollars as they were counted at the time. A real figure adjusts for changes in prices, so that a dollar in one year buys the same amount as a dollar in another. Comparisons across years are meaningful only in real terms. The Census Bureau reported that median household income in 2023 was $80,610 in the dollars of that year, which it restated as $82,690 in 2024 dollars after prices rose 2.6 per cent. [cite:ad2_census_ccpiu] In 2025 dollars, the median rose from $61,910 in 1984 to $87,460 in 2025, a real gain of about 41 per cent ($87,460 ÷ $61,910 = 1.41). The series is not a smooth climb: it fell after each recession, and in 2025 dollars the 2012 median, $69,070, was below the 1999 median, $73,760. [cite:ad2_fred_mhi]

Which price index

Turning nominal into real dollars requires a price index, a measure of how much a fixed basket of purchases costs from one year to the next, and the choice of index changes the answer. The best-known index, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), fixes the weights of its spending categories for a year at a time and assumes that households do not switch between categories when prices change. The chained CPI-U (C-CPI-U), published since 2002, updates its weights every month to allow for that switching; from 2001 to 2023 it rose on average about 0.2 percentage points a year more slowly than the CPI-U, though not in every year. [cite:ad2_bls_ccpiu] The Commerce Department's Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index uses another formula and a wider scope: it covers spending "by and on behalf of" households, where the CPI covers their out-of-pocket spending. [cite:ad2_bea_cpipce] Small yearly differences compound over decades. An index that rises more slowly makes past dollars worth less in today's money, and so shows more real growth.

The choice matters most for the mobility record. Chetty and his colleagues used the CPI-U-RS, a research version of the CPI-U, and report that their decline holds under other deflators. [cite:ad2_chetty_fading] The economist Scott Winship, re-estimating the figure for children born in the early 1980s, found that adjusting for smaller family sizes raised the share who out-earned their parents from 50 to 60 per cent, that switching to the PCE index and survey data raised it to 67 per cent, and that counting government benefits raised it to 68 per cent. [cite:ad2_reeves_winship] Both sides find a fall from about 90 per cent; they disagree on how far.

This book's rule is simple. Where a source already publishes real figures, they are reported in that source's own dollars and index, and labelled. Where the book converts dollars itself, it follows the Census Bureau's practice for household income: the chained CPI-U from 2000 onward and the CPI-U-RS before 2000. [cite:ad2_census_ccpiu] Where the choice of index would change a conclusion, as in the wage and productivity record of Part Four, both readings are shown. [scene:ad4_wage_split|The wage split]

Households and individuals

A household is everyone living in one home; a family is a household of related people; an individual is one person. Household income can rise because each earner earns more, or because more members work, and it can fall because households have grown smaller even when each person is better off. American households have shrunk: one-person households were 20 per cent of all households in 1975 and 29 per cent, 39.7 million, in 2025. [cite:ad2_census_hh2025] A household median therefore understates what the same income means per person today compared with fifty years ago, and a per-person or size-adjusted measure, which divides income by a factor that grows with household size, corrects for it. Wages, by contrast, are measured per worker or per hour, and say nothing about how many earners a family needs. Part Five takes up that question. [scene:ad5_hours_two_jobs|Hours and second jobs]

Before and after taxes and benefits

A last choice cuts across all the others: whether income is counted before or after taxes and government benefits. Market income, from work and investment alone, shows what the economy pays; income after taxes and transfers shows what families can spend. The Congressional Budget Office finds that the top 1 per cent's share of income before taxes and transfers doubled from 9 per cent in 1979 to 18 per cent in 2022, and after taxes and transfers rose from 7 to 14 per cent. [cite:us11_cbo_dist2022] Both figures are accurate, and they answer different questions. The book states which one each figure uses.

These choices are not tricks for reaching a desired answer; each measures something real. Absolute mobility tracks whether living standards rise across generations, relative mobility whether the starting line decides the finish, wealth whether families can weather shocks and pass on security, and the median what a typical household experiences. The book uses each where it answers the question at hand and names it there, beginning with the full mobility record in Part Three. [scene:ad3_absolute_mobility|The fall in absolute mobility] [scene:us22_method|How the US vs Israel scorecard measured]

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: The Mobility Record
chapters.intro: Part Three tests the promise at its most concrete: that children who work will end up better off than their parents, and that where they start will not decide where they finish. It follows the share of Americans who out-earn their parents from the generation born in 1940 to the one born in the 1980s, explains what that measure can and cannot show and what its critics dispute, sets it beside the steadier record of relative mobility, maps how sharply the odds of climbing vary from one city and neighbourhood to another and why, and compares the American ladder with those of Canada, Denmark and other rich democracies. [scene:ad3_absolute_mobility|The share who out-earn their parents]
chapters.outro: The mobility record confirms the promise for one generation and qualifies it for every generation since. Ninety-two per cent of children born in 1940 out-earned their parents; half of those born in 1980 and 1984 did, a fall that reached every state and hit children of middle-income parents hardest, and that the economists who measured it trace mainly to how growth was divided rather than how fast it came. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] [cite:ad3_fading_science] Critics using household-size adjustments, other price indexes and multi-year incomes put today's share at two-thirds to three-quarters, but accept the decline. [cite:ad3_brookings_winship] [cite:ad3_winship_archbridge] Relative mobility held steady, with a bottom-fifth child's odds of reaching the top fifth near 8 or 9 per cent for cohorts born from 1971 to 1986, while the widening gaps between rungs made the birth lottery matter more. [cite:ad3_trends_aerpp] [cite:ad3_nber_digest_trends] Place matters causally: the odds ranged from 4.4 per cent in Charlotte to 12.9 per cent in San Jose, children gain about 4 per cent of the difference for each year they grow up in a better area, and moves before age 13 raised earnings by 31 per cent. [cite:ad3_land_opp_pub] [cite:ad3_exposure_qje] [cite:ad3_mto_aer] Abroad, absolute mobility fell everywhere it has been measured, but most in the United States, where economic growth matched Norway's and less of it reached households. [cite:ad3_berman] [cite:ad3_manduca_iza] Part Four follows that division of growth into the wage record, starting with the years from 1973 when pay and productivity parted. [scene:ad4_wage_split|The wage split]

sections.h: The Share Who Out-Earn Their Parents
sections.html:
The simplest promise in the American Dream to check is the one most families use: that a child who works will end up better off than the parents who raised them. Economists call the measure that tests it absolute mobility. It asks one question of each person: is your household income, adjusted for inflation, higher than your parents' household income was at the same age? Absolute mobility is different from relative mobility, which asks whether a child climbs or falls in the national ranking, and which the next section takes up. [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|How to measure the Dream] Absolute mobility is the measure closest to the promise as families tell it, and the best record of it shows a fall from almost everyone to about half. [cite:ad3_oi_fading]

How the number was built

The standard estimate comes from a 2017 paper in the journal Science by Raj Chetty, David Grusky, Maximilian Hell, Nathaniel Hendren, Robert Manduca and Jimmy Narang, whose research group is now Opportunity Insights. [cite:ad3_oi_fading] They compared children's family income at about age 30 with their parents' family income at about the same age. Family income here means the pre-tax income of a person and any spouse added together, before taxes are taken out and before government benefits such as food assistance are added. All amounts were converted into 2014 dollars using the CPI-U-RS, a research version of the consumer price index that the Bureau of Labor Statistics recalculated backwards with today's methods; for years before 1977 the ordinary consumer price index was linked to it. [cite:ad3_fading_paper]

No single survey follows American families from 1940 to today, so the authors combined three: children's incomes from the Current Population Survey, the government's household survey, for 1970 to 2014; parents' incomes from the decennial census; and, for the link between a child's rank and the parent's rank, tax records for children born from 1980 to 1982, assumed to hold for earlier generations too. Whatever that link, the 1940 figure lies between 84 and 98 per cent, and assuming no link at all still gives 50 per cent for the 1980 cohort. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] A cohort is everyone born in the same year.

The record: ninety-two to fifty

For children born in 1940, 92 per cent grew up to have a higher family income at 30 than their parents had at 30. For children born in 1980, the figure was 50 per cent, and it was still 50 per cent for those born in 1984, the last group old enough to measure when the paper was written. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] [cite:ad3_fading_slides] A child born just before the Second World War was almost certain to out-earn the household that raised them; one born in the early 1980s had the odds of a coin toss. The fall was not steady. It was steepest between the 1940 and 1964 cohorts, paused for children born in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and then resumed. [cite:ad3_fading_paper]

Comparing individuals rather than households makes the fall sharper for men. Sons whose own earnings exceeded their fathers' earnings fell from 95 per cent for the 1940 cohort to 41 per cent for the 1984 cohort. Daughters compared with fathers start far lower, at 43 per cent in 1940, because few women of the mothers' generation worked for pay; the figure fell to 22 per cent for the 1960 cohort and recovered to 26 per cent by 1984 as women's earnings rose. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] The decline reached every state. It was largest in the industrial Midwest: about 48 percentage points in Michigan and about 45 in Indiana, Illinois and Ohio, against about 35 in Massachusetts, New York and Montana. [cite:ad3_fading_science]

Where on the ladder it fell

The odds always depend on where the parents started: a child of very poor parents needs only a modest income to beat them, a child of very rich parents faces a high bar. For the 1940 cohort, the share who out-earned their parents was 94 per cent for children of parents at the 10th percentile of income (poorer than nine in ten families), 93 per cent at the median and 88 per cent at the 90th percentile. For the 1980 cohort, those figures were 70, 45 and 33 per cent. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] The researchers Richard Reeves and Katherine Guyot of the Brookings Institution, working from the same published data, found that the largest single drop came between the 1940 and 1950 cohorts and was concentrated at the top, but that since 1950 the losses have fallen most heavily on the broad middle. [cite:ad3_brookings_middle] The promise stopped describing the typical outcome most clearly not for the poorest but for children of middle-income households.

Why it fell: how growth was shared

Two forces decide how many children out-earn their parents: how fast the economy grows, and how that growth is divided among households. The authors tested each by asking what absolute mobility for the 1980 cohort would have been under different conditions. If the economy had grown as fast as it did when the 1940 cohort was young, about 2.5 per cent a year in real output per family against about 1.5 per cent, but its gains had been divided as they actually were in the 1980s and after, absolute mobility would have risen only from 50 to 62 per cent. If the economy had grown at its actual later pace but its gains had been divided across income groups as they were for the 1940 cohort, absolute mobility would have reached 80 per cent, closing 71 per cent of the gap. Under the actual division, getting back to 1940 levels would have needed real growth above 6 per cent a year. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] [cite:ad3_fading_slides]

This is a counterfactual about how the gains of growth were spread across all income groups. It does not attribute a share of the decline to any named group, and a widely repeated summary that rising wealth at the very top "explains 70 per cent" of the decline misreads it: the 71 per cent is the share of the gap that would close if the whole distribution of growth looked as it did for the 1940 cohort. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] Census income data show the same pattern from another angle. Between 1967 and 2025, real household income at the 10th and 50th percentiles rose about 56 per cent, while income at the 90th percentile rose about 121 per cent. [cite:us14_census_p60]

The critics, and what survives them

The 50 per cent figure has been challenged on its measures, chiefly by Scott Winship of the Archbridge Institute and Michael Strain of the American Enterprise Institute. Households have shrunk; adjusting for household size raises the share of 1980s-born adults better off than their parents from 50 to 60 per cent. Using a different survey, the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, which follows the same families over decades, and a different price index, the PCE deflator, which shows lower inflation than the CPI-U-RS, raises it to 67 per cent. Counting government cash benefits brings it to 68 per cent. [cite:ad3_brookings_winship] Winship's own summary, averaging incomes over many years, is that roughly three in four adults, and the overwhelming majority of children raised poor, live better off than their parents. [cite:ad3_winship_archbridge] Strain, in The American Dream Is Not Dead (2020), puts the share at nearly three-quarters on a household-size-adjusted measure; his reviewer in National Review, Robert VerBruggen, questioned that adjustment on the ground that it would count having fewer children as upward mobility. [cite:ad3_nr_strain]

The Chetty team reported its own tests of most of these choices. Adjusting for household size gives a fall from 93 to 60 per cent; assuming inflation was 0.8 points a year lower than measured gives 93 to 59; assuming it was 2 points lower still leaves a 26-point decline; counting taxes and benefits raises every cohort by about 3 points without changing the trend; and measuring at age 40 instead of 30 gives 86 per cent for the 1940 cohort and 56 per cent for the 1970 cohort. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] Winship accepts that the share fell. [cite:ad3_brookings_winship] The dispute is over the level today, roughly half on one set of measures and two-thirds to three-quarters on another, not over the direction.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

For children raised near the bottom, the promise in its plainest form still largely holds. Seven in ten children of parents at the 10th percentile in the 1980 cohort had higher family incomes than their parents at the same age, and a child born at the 5th percentile in 1980 needed only to reach about the 12th percentile of their own generation to do so. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] [cite:ad3_brookings_middle] On the critics' measures, most adults of every recent generation live better than their parents did. [cite:ad3_winship_archbridge]

What is not yet known

The series stops with children born in 1984, who were 30 in 2014. No estimate on the same method for later cohorts had been published as of October 2026, so whether the share recovered for children born in the late 1980s and 1990s, who entered work during or after the 2008 recession, cannot be stated from this record. [cite:ad3_oi_fading]

Interpretation, not finding: the promise kept alive by its best generation

The Sophia platform reads this record as the core of its "illusion" thesis: the Dream, in this reading, was a true description of one generation's experience, roughly those born in the 1940s, that went on being taught as a general law after the conditions that produced it had changed, so that later generations measured their lives against a standard the economy no longer delivered to half of them. The strongest counter-readings are three. The first is the critics': on household-size-adjusted, multi-year or post-transfer measures, most Americans still out-earn their parents, so "illusion" overstates a fall from near-universal to a clear majority. The second is that the 1940 cohort's parents were measured at the end of the Depression and their children grew up in fast postwar growth, so 92 per cent may be the outlier, not the norm. The third is that the Chetty team's counterfactual locates the cause in a measurable pattern, the division of growth, which policy can change. The record establishes the fall; whether to call it an illusion is a judgment it leaves to the reader.

sections.h: The Ladder and the Map
sections.html:
Absolute mobility asks whether children out-earn their parents. Relative mobility asks a different question: whether the rung a child starts on decides the rung where the child ends up. A society can have low absolute mobility and steady relative mobility at once, if the whole ladder stops rising while the chances of moving up it stay the same; that is close to what the American record shows. The same research also found that the chances of climbing differ greatly from one city, and one neighbourhood, to the next, and that part of that difference is caused by the places themselves. This section sets out both findings and the evidence for each. [scene:ad3_absolute_mobility|The share who out-earn their parents]

A ladder whose rungs stayed the same distance apart

The usual measure of relative mobility ranks every parent from 1 to 100 by income, ranks every child the same way as an adult, and asks how closely the two ranks move together. The result is called the rank-rank slope. A slope of 0 would mean a child's rank had nothing to do with the parent's; a slope of 1 would mean every child landed exactly on the parent's rank. In a 2014 study using the tax records of children born from 1971 to 1993, Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, Patrick Kline, Emmanuel Saez and Nicholas Turner found the slope at about 0.30 across the cohorts they could measure: 0.299 for children born in 1971–74, 0.291 for 1975–78 and 0.313 for 1979–82, with no meaningful trend. [cite:ad3_trends_aerpp] [cite:ad3_uchicago_e350] In plain terms, ten percentile points of advantage for the parents went with about three points for the child, and that relationship did not change.

The chance that a child born to parents in the bottom fifth of incomes would reach the top fifth was 8.4 per cent for the 1971 cohort and 9.0 per cent for the 1986 cohort. For children too young to have settled incomes, the authors used college attendance instead: the gap between the highest- and lowest-income families was 74.5 percentage points for children born in 1984 and 69.2 points for those born in 1993. [cite:ad3_nber_digest_trends] The authors' conclusion was that children entering the labour market at the time of the study had the same chances of moving up, relative to their parents, as children born in the 1970s. [cite:ad3_trends_aerpp]

The same authors drew the necessary qualification. Because the rungs of the income ladder had moved further apart over those decades, the same rank-to-rank pattern now meant larger differences in actual living standards. In their words, "the consequences of the 'birth lottery'" were "larger today than in the past." [cite:ad3_trends_aerpp] The odds of climbing held steady; the distance between the bottom and the top grew.

The map: where a child grows up

The national average hides very large differences between places. In a companion 2014 study of more than 40 million children born from 1980 to 1982, Chetty, Hendren, Kline and Saez measured mobility for every commuting zone, an area defined by where people live and work, roughly a metropolitan region. Nationally, a child raised in the bottom fifth had a 7.5 per cent chance of reaching the top fifth. In Charlotte the chance was 4.4 per cent; in Salt Lake City, 10.8 per cent; in San Jose, 12.9 per cent. [cite:ad3_land_opp_pub] Areas with higher upward mobility shared five traits: less residential segregation, less income inequality, better primary schools, more social capital, meaning the strength of community ties and civic life, and more stable families. The authors stated that these were correlations and did not by themselves identify causes. [cite:ad3_land_opp]

Correlation raised the obvious objection: families who choose or can afford better places may differ in ways that would help their children anywhere. Three later bodies of evidence address it. First, Chetty and Hendren followed more than seven million families who moved between areas and found that children's adult outcomes shifted toward those of children already living in the destination by about 4 per cent for each year of childhood spent there. Because the gain accrues year by year, the earlier in childhood a family moves, the larger it is. [cite:ad3_exposure_qje] Second, the federal Moving to Opportunity experiment offered housing vouchers, by random assignment, to families living in high-poverty neighbourhoods, for use in lower-poverty ones, and measured the children's outcomes nearly two decades later. Children whose families moved before they turned 13 earned 31 per cent more a year in their mid-twenties, $3,477 on a control-group average of $11,270, and were more likely to attend college; for children who moved as teenagers, the effects were, if anything, negative, which the authors attribute partly to the disruption of moving. [cite:ad3_mto_aer] [cite:ad3_jpal_mto] A widely repeated version of the finding gives the 31 per cent gain without its age condition; it applies only to moves made before 13.

Third, the Opportunity Atlas, released by the Census Bureau with Chetty, Hendren and John Friedman on 1 October 2018, mapped adult outcomes for more than 20 million Americans born from 1978 to 1983 down to the census tract, a neighbourhood of a few thousand people. [cite:ad3_nlihc_atlas] For children of parents at the 25th percentile, average household income at 35 varied by about $5,000 (one standard deviation) between tracts within the same county, and a tract's own characteristics mattered far more than those of tracts a mile away. Upward mobility was only weakly related to conventional signs of local prosperity such as job growth, and the map's estimates matched the causal effects measured in the experiment. The study was published in the American Economic Review in 2026; data for children born from 1984 to 1989 were added in 2024. [cite:ad3_atlas] The Atlas also identified "opportunity bargains", neighbourhoods with good outcomes and median two-bedroom rents under $1,500 a month. [cite:ad3_nlihc_atlas]

What in a place makes the difference

The strongest single predictor found so far is social. A 2022 study in Nature, using 21 billion friendships among 72.2 million Facebook users aged 25 to 44, measured "economic connectedness", the share of friends from higher-income backgrounds among people from lower-income backgrounds. It was among the strongest predictors of upward mobility ever identified. The authors estimated that if lower-income children grew up in counties where they had as many higher-income friends as higher-income children do, their adult incomes would be about 20 per cent higher; that estimate rests on assumptions about causation that the study tests but cannot fully prove. [cite:ad3_nature_ec] A 2024 study of children born from 1978 to 1992 pointed in the same direction: children's outcomes rose or fell with the share of parents in work in their own community, and the effects ran through the people children grew up among. [cite:ad3_changing_opp]

Some of the friction in this map is designed and some is the residue of documented departures from equal treatment. School funding tied to local property taxes is a designed feature of American public finance, and its effect on places is examined in [scene:ad7_k12_property_tax|Part Seven]. Residential segregation, one of the five correlates, is traced in [scene:ad6_redlining_to_suburbs|Part Six] in part to federal mortgage policy and lending practices that excluded Black neighbourhoods, a documented departure from equal treatment. The mobility research measures the result; it does not by itself assign the cause to either.

The same map, by race

Holding parents' income constant, Black boys grew up to earn less than white boys in 99 per cent of census tracts; among women, there was no comparable gap. The gap was smallest in low-poverty neighbourhoods with low measured racial bias among white residents and many Black fathers present, but fewer than 5 per cent of Black children grew up in such places. [cite:us8_oi_race] The researchers found that parents' marital status, education and wealth explained very little of the gap at equal incomes, and that differences in ability did not explain it either. [cite:us8a_oi] The trend, however, is toward convergence. Among children born from 1978 to 1992, Black children's adult earnings rose at every level of parental income, and the earnings gap between white and Black children from low-income families narrowed by 30 per cent; over the same years, the gap between white children from high- and low-income families widened by 30 per cent. [cite:ad3_changing_opp] Part Thirteen takes up these gaps and their documented causes. [scene:ad13_black_americans|Who gets the Dream]

Where it works as promised

In parts of the country the ladder works much as taught. A child from the bottom fifth raised in San Jose or Salt Lake City had close to the odds that the Dream implies, about one in eight or one in nine of reaching the top fifth, and the Atlas found affordable neighbourhoods with strong outcomes in many metropolitan areas. [cite:ad3_land_opp_pub] [cite:ad3_nlihc_atlas] The relative odds nationally did not worsen over two decades of cohorts, and for Black children they improved. [cite:ad3_trends_aerpp] [cite:ad3_changing_opp] The causal evidence also shows that the effect of place can be changed: when low-income families with young children moved to lower-poverty areas, those children's incomes rose. [cite:ad3_mto_aer] The record therefore does not show a ladder that is fixed everywhere; it shows one whose rungs are spaced very differently depending on where a child is raised.

sections.h: The Ladder Abroad
sections.html:
The American Dream has long been taught as American in a particular sense: that the United States, more than other countries, lets children rise above the station of their parents. That is a comparative claim, and it can be checked against comparable data from other rich democracies. This section uses the comparison for one purpose only, to show which parts of the American mobility record are shared with peer countries and which are particular to the United States, and so to locate the American mechanism more exactly. The main evidence is the economist Miles Corak's international comparisons, the OECD's 2018 report A Broken Social Elevator? and newer estimates of absolute mobility in eight countries, set beside the strongest critics of the comparison.

The measure and the curve

Most international comparisons use the intergenerational earnings elasticity, usually shortened to IGE. It asks, for fathers and sons, how much a given percentage difference in fathers' earnings carries over into sons' earnings. An IGE of 0.5 means that if one father earned twice as much as another, the first father's son would on average earn about half again as much as the second's: roughly half of the father's advantage or disadvantage is passed on. An IGE near zero means sons' earnings have little to do with fathers'. [cite:ad3_corak_iza] Unlike the rank-rank slope in the previous section, the IGE is sensitive to how unequal incomes are, and to which years of income are used; estimates for the same country can differ by a wide margin. [cite:ad3_winship_archbridge]

In a widely cited 2013 paper in the Journal of Economic Perspectives, Corak plotted the IGE for sons born in the early to mid-1960s against each country's income inequality around 1985, measured by the Gini coefficient, a standard 0-to-1 index of how unequally income is spread. The more unequal countries had the higher elasticities. Alan Krueger, chairman of President Obama's Council of Economic Advisers, named the pattern the "Great Gatsby Curve" in a speech on 12 January 2012. [cite:ad3_corak_iza] On Corak's estimates, the United States, with an IGE of 0.47, sits beside the United Kingdom and Italy at about 0.5, against 0.19 for Canada and 0.15 to 0.18 for Denmark, Norway and Finland. [cite:ad3_epi_corak] Corak wrote that the curve "is not a causal relationship", while arguing it was "too glib to dismiss" as mere correlation. [cite:ad3_corak_iza]

Canada: a neighbour with a similar middle

Canada is the closest comparison: a similar economy, similar immigration and a shared continent. Corak found that the two countries differ mainly at the two ends of the ladder. About half of American sons of fathers in the bottom tenth of earnings rose no further than the third tenth, while a much larger share of Canadian sons from the bottom tenth reached the upper half. At the top, more than half of American sons of top-tenth fathers fell no further than the eighth tenth, a stickiness Canada showed less of. In the middle of the distribution, the two countries were similar. [cite:ad3_corak_iza] The American difference, in other words, is concentrated at the floor and the ceiling.

The OECD's generations

The OECD, the Paris-based organisation of mostly rich democracies, published A Broken Social Elevator? How to Promote Social Mobility on 15 June 2018. Its most quoted figure translates earnings persistence into time: with the average elasticity across member countries of about 0.38, and with the bottom tenth earning about a third of the mean, a child born into the bottom tenth of families would need four to five generations for the family to reach the average income. The report described mobility as weakest at the extremes, with "sticky floors" at the bottom and "sticky ceilings" at the top, and noted that in the United States and Germany almost half of the sons of high-earning fathers were themselves in the top quarter of earners. [cite:ad3_oecd_elevator] [cite:ad3_oecd_elevator_pdf] As reported from the same study, the estimate was five generations for the United States and two for Denmark, the shortest of any member. [cite:ad3_piie_denmark] [cite:ad3_statista_oecd] The report is not internally consistent on the Nordic figure: its executive summary gives about two generations, while its overview chapter says the Nordic countries would need at least four. [cite:ad3_oecd_elevator_pdf] The figure is a projection that assumes today's persistence holds unchanged for a century or more; it illustrates the size of the elasticity rather than forecasting any family's future.

Absolute mobility abroad: the decline is shared, the cause is not

A newer line of work compares the measure closest to the Dream, the share of children who out-earn their parents. Robert Manduca, one of the authors of the American study, and thirteen co-authors estimated it for children born from 1960 to 1987 in eight countries. For recent cohorts, the United States and Canada were both near 50 per cent, while Norway held steady at about 75 per cent and Finland above 70. [cite:ad3_manduca_iza] Denmark complicates the picture: its share was about 50 per cent for children born in 1982 when measured, as in the American study, on income before taxes, but above 65 per cent on income after taxes and benefits. [cite:ad3_manduca_iza] In Canada, measured on disposable income, the share was 57.5 per cent for the 1977 cohort and 57.1 per cent for 1984. [cite:ad3_manduca_iza]

The study's explanation for the American position is specific. American and Norwegian economies grew at almost the same rate per person over the period, 1.80 against 1.86 per cent a year, so slow growth does not explain the gap. What differed was how much of that growth reached households in the study's samples: American incomes rose only 71 per cent as fast as GDP, against 95 per cent in Norway. Replacing the American pattern of relative mobility with Norway's barely changed the American result. [cite:ad3_manduca_iza] A separate estimate by the economist Yonatan Berman found that absolute mobility fell in every country he studied, but that the United States had the largest decline since 1940, 39.2 percentage points, and that rising inequality accounted for 24.6 of those points against 14.5 for slower growth; in most other countries, slower growth was the larger factor. [cite:ad3_berman]

The critics of the comparison

The strongest critique of the Nordic comparison comes from Rasmus Landersø and James Heckman, a Nobel laureate, in a 2017 paper titled "The Scandinavian Fantasy". They found that Denmark is more mobile than the United States when mobility is measured by income but not when it is measured by education, and attributed Denmark's income advantage largely to taxes, transfers and a compressed wage scale rather than to greater equality of opportunity in childhood. Danish programmes for disadvantaged children raised test scores without improving educational attainment, which the authors linked in part to weaker financial rewards for more schooling in a highly redistributive system. [cite:ad3_landerso_heckman] Jacob Funk Kirkegaard of the Peterson Institute made a related point: Denmark's mobility rests on taxes and public spending well above American levels, and "there is no free lunch". [cite:ad3_piie_denmark] The measurement objections run in both directions. Scott Winship argues that, with better long-run data, American IGEs for family income are about 0.65 to 0.75, which would make the United States look less mobile than in Corak's figures, not more, while he also argues that absolute mobility is higher than the headline estimates. [cite:ad3_winship_archbridge]

Where it works as promised

In the middle of the earnings distribution, American sons moved about as freely relative to their fathers as Canadian sons did; the gap between the two countries lies at the extremes. [cite:ad3_corak_iza] The fall in absolute mobility is not an American peculiarity: it happened in every country Berman studied. [cite:ad3_berman] And before taxes and benefits, Denmark's most recent measured cohort out-earned its parents at about the American rate. [cite:ad3_manduca_iza] What does set the United States apart is narrower and measurable: higher persistence at the bottom and top of the ladder, and a smaller share of growth reaching the households whose children are being compared with their parents. Part Four follows that second mechanism into the wage record from 1973. [scene:ad4_wage_split|The wage split]

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: The Turn, 1973–1986
chapters.intro: For a generation after 1948, the American promise that more productive work brings higher pay held closely for the typical worker. This part dates the turn. It measures the split between productivity and the typical worker's pay that opened in the 1970s, sets the Economic Policy Institute's chart beside the economists who argue much of the gap is a matter of measurement, and shows what survives that dispute. It then follows two changes that can be dated to the years between 1973 and 1986: the fall of private-sector union power, from the air traffic controllers' strike of 1981 to the labour board of 2026, and the shareholder turn, from Milton Friedman's 1970 essay and the SEC's 1982 buyback rule to record buybacks, chief executives' pay and the tax and interest-rate decisions of the Reagan and Volcker years.
chapters.outro: The turn is documented, and its size depends on how it is measured. On the Economic Policy Institute's September 2026 edition, net productivity rose 93.7 per cent from late 1979 to mid-2026 while the typical worker's hourly compensation rose 32.7 per cent [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026]; critics who match price indexes and count all workers find average compensation kept far closer pace [cite:ad4_nber_feldstein] [cite:ad4_heritage_sherk], and the Bureau of Labor Statistics found that in the median industry about half the gap reflects price indexes and half a real fall in labour's share [cite:ad4_bls_btn2017]. Private-sector union membership fell from 16.8 per cent in 1983 to 5.9 per cent in 2025 [cite:ad4_bls_spotlight2016] [cite:us13_bls_union2025], large strikes became rare after 1981 [cite:ad4_bls_stoppages], and a labour law without fines was enforced by a board whose independence was in doubt by 2026 [cite:ad4_epi_unlawful] [cite:ad4_proskauer_slaughter]. Meanwhile the SEC's 1982 safe harbor eased buybacks that passed $1 trillion a year in 2025 [cite:ad4_sec_10b18_2003] [cite:ad4_spdji_q3_2025], and chief executives' pay rose from about 31 to about 325 times a typical worker's [cite:ad4_epi_ceo2025]. Part Five turns from the hinge to the present: the wages, hours and frozen wage floors that working Americans live with now. [scene:ad5_wages_floors|Part Five: Work]

sections.h: The Split: Productivity and Pay after 1973
sections.html:
The promise of hard work rests on an economic claim that most Americans never hear stated in so many words: when workers produce more in an hour, they will be paid more for that hour. Economists call output per hour of work "productivity". The claim is not a slogan; it is the standard account of how wages are set in a competitive market, and the economist Michael Strain of the American Enterprise Institute has defended it against those who say the link between pay and productivity has been "effectively severed". [cite:ad4_aspen_strain] For a generation after the Second World War, the record and the promise moved together. Some time in the 1970s they began to separate. This section sets out how far they separated, by which measure, and why careful economists on different sides still disagree about the size of the gap while largely agreeing on part of its cause.

Why the part begins in 1973

Three dates recur in this story, and each has its own reason. The first is 1973. By the Pew Research Center's count, the purchasing power of the average hourly wage peaked in January 1973, when the average was $4.03 an hour, worth $23.68 in 2018 dollars. [cite:ad4_pew_wages2018] The second is 1979, the starting point the Economic Policy Institute (EPI), a labour-aligned research group, uses for its widely quoted productivity–pay chart. The third is 1986, when the second of two large tax laws set the top income tax rate on a path down to 28 per cent. [cite:us11_tpc_toprate] The period between the first and last of these dates is the hinge of this book: the point at which the promise as taught and the system as built started to diverge in several mechanisms at once. The wage split comes first because every later part depends on it.

The EPI series

The EPI's chart is the version most readers have seen. Its September 2026 edition, with data to the second quarter of 2026, measures productivity as "net" output per hour for the whole economy, meaning output after subtracting the wear and tear on equipment and buildings, called depreciation. It measures pay as the average hourly compensation, wages plus benefits, of production and nonsupervisory workers in the private sector, a group that is roughly four in five private employees and leaves out managers. Both are converted into constant dollars with the same consumer price index. [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026] Constant or "real" dollars are dollars adjusted for inflation, so that a 1979 hour of pay and a 2026 hour of pay buy comparable baskets of goods.

On that basis the two lines ran close together for a generation. Setting both equal to 100 in early 1948, the EPI's index reaches 214.8 for productivity and 193.8 for pay by early 1973: productivity had risen by 114.8 per cent and pay by 93.8 per cent. [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026] The lines were not identical, but most of each gain in output was matched by a gain in the typical worker's hourly pay. From the fourth quarter of 1979 to the second quarter of 2026, the record is different. The productivity index rose from 216.8 to 419.9, an increase of 93.7 per cent; the pay index rose from 190.7 to 253.0, an increase of 32.7 per cent. [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026] Spread across those 46 and a half years, that is roughly 1.4 per cent a year for productivity and 0.6 per cent a year for pay (the compound rate that turns 1 into 1.937 and 1.327 respectively over the period). The EPI's own summary is that productivity "has grown 2.9x as much as pay". [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026]

The critics: how much of the gap is measurement

The EPI chart has been challenged for more than fifteen years, and the challenges are serious. They turn on three choices, each defensible, each of which widens the gap. The first is which workers are counted. The EPI's line covers production and nonsupervisory workers; managers and professionals, whose pay rose fastest, are left out, while productivity covers everyone's output. The second is whether pay means wages or total compensation. Health insurance and retirement contributions grew faster than wages for decades, so a wage-only line looks worse than a compensation line. The EPI uses compensation; many popular charts do not. The third, and the largest, is the price index used to turn dollars into real dollars, called the deflator. Productivity is usually measured with the prices of what the economy produces. Pay is usually deflated with the consumer price index, the prices of what households buy. When consumer prices rise faster than output prices, using the consumer index for pay and the output index for productivity opens a gap even if workers' share of income never changed. [cite:ad4_heritage_sherk] [cite:ad4_aspen_strain]

The economist Martin Feldstein made the case most directly in a 2008 National Bureau of Economic Research paper. Measuring total compensation and deflating it with the same nonfarm business price index used for productivity, he found that from 1970 to 2006 productivity grew 1.9 per cent a year and real compensation per hour 1.7 per cent a year. Employee compensation was 66 per cent of national income in 1970 and 64 per cent in 2006. [cite:ad4_nber_feldstein] James Sherk of the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, reached a similar conclusion in 2013: from 1973 to 2012, measured consistently, productivity rose 100 per cent and hourly compensation 77 per cent. He attributed 35 per cent of the apparent gap to counting only some workers and only wages, 44 per cent to the different price indexes and 21 per cent to other factors such as depreciation and import prices, and called most of the gap "a statistical illusion". [cite:ad4_heritage_sherk]

Strain's 2019 review for the Aspen Institute's Economic Strategy Group, summarising the economist Robert Lawrence, reported that switching to net output for the whole economy cut the gap by 20 per cent, using compensation instead of wages cut it by 8.2 per cent, including managers and professionals explained 30 per cent, and deflating wages with an output price index explained 35 per cent. [cite:ad4_aspen_strain] He also reported the work of Anna Stansbury and Lawrence Summers, who found that from 1975 to 2015 a one-point rise in productivity growth was associated with a 0.73-point rise in compensation growth for the median worker and 0.74 points for average compensation, but only 0.53 points for production and nonsupervisory workers. [cite:ad4_aspen_strain] Productivity, in other words, still pushes pay up; something else has been pushing the typical worker's pay down at the same time.

What survives the dispute

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the federal agency that produces both the productivity and the price data, tested the argument industry by industry. Its 2017 study of 183 industries from 1987 to 2015 found that productivity outpaced compensation in 83 per cent of them. In the median industry the output price index rose about 0.6 percentage points a year more slowly than consumer prices, and labour's share of income fell by about 0.6 per cent a year. The study's conclusion was that "the median effect of the change in labor share was the same as that of the difference in deflators." [cite:ad4_bls_btn2017] In plain terms, about half of the gap in a typical industry was a matter of which prices one uses, and about half was a real fall in the share of each industry's income that went to the people who worked in it.

That finding is close to what the careful critics themselves concede. Sherk acknowledged that median pay grew more slowly than average productivity, which he attributed to technology rewarding higher skills. [cite:ad4_heritage_sherk] Strain wrote that real wage growth of about half a per cent a year for production workers is not strong and that gains have been unequally shared. [cite:ad4_aspen_strain] Pew found that since 2000 real weekly wages rose 3 per cent for the lowest tenth of earners and 15.7 per cent for the top tenth. [cite:ad4_pew_wages2018] The dispute, then, is about size and cause, not about direction. Average compensation, counted fully, roughly kept up with average productivity, especially before 2000. The typical worker's pay did not; the difference went to higher earners and, in the BLS industry data, to capital.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

The taught version holds in two specific respects. For the generation from 1948 to 1973 the EPI's own index shows typical pay rising almost in step with output, the period many Americans remember as the Dream's high point. [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026] And across the whole economy, total compensation per hour has kept growing with productivity on Feldstein's matched measure, so that a worker's average hour bought more in 2006 than in 1970. [cite:ad4_nber_feldstein] Where the promise fails is narrower and more precise: for the worker in the middle, an extra unit of output after 1979 has translated into well under one unit of extra pay, by every measure reviewed here.

The EPI's explanation and its limits

The EPI's own account of why the split happened is policy-based. It lists "policy choices": tolerance of excess unemployment, minimum-wage increases that were "smaller and rarer", labour law that "failed to keep pace", lower top tax rates, deregulation and weaker antitrust enforcement. [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026] Those are causal claims, and each needs its own evidence. The next two sections take up two of them that can be dated precisely in the hinge years: the collapse of private-sector union power, and the shift in how corporations were told to measure success. The minimum wage and employer power over local labour markets are the subject of Part Five. [scene:ad5_wages_floors|Part Five: wages and the frozen floors] How this book chooses a single price index is set out in Part Two. [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two: how to measure]

sections.h: Labour Power: Unions, PATCO and the Law That Stayed Still
sections.html:
A union is the mechanism the American system built in 1935 to let workers bargain as a group rather than one by one. Under the National Labor Relations Act, workers at a workplace vote on whether to be represented; if they win, the employer must bargain with the union for everyone in that unit. There is no general way to extend an agreement across a whole industry, so bargaining power stops at the edge of each organised firm, and in a 2017 comparison of 21 rich countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) the United States ranked last for the share of workers covered by collective agreements. [cite:us13_eg_bargaining] This section follows what happened to that mechanism in and after the hinge years: how many workers it still reaches, the strike that changed its use, and how the law that governs it is enforced in 2026.

Density: two measures, one direction

"Union density" is the share of workers who belong to a union. The consistent federal series begins in 1983, and it must not be spliced onto older estimates built from different surveys. In 1983, 20.1 per cent of wage and salary workers were union members. The private-sector rate was 16.8 per cent and the public-sector rate 36.7 per cent. [cite:ad4_bls_spotlight2016] By 2025, overall membership was 10.0 per cent, or 14.7 million people; the public sector stood at 32.9 per cent and the private sector at 5.9 per cent. [cite:us13_bls_union2025] The private-sector rate therefore fell by about two-thirds (5.9 divided by 16.8 is 0.35) while the public-sector rate barely moved. In numbers, private-sector members fell from 11.9 million in 1983 to 7.6 million in 2015, during years in which wage and salary employment grew from 88.3 million to 133.7 million. [cite:ad4_bls_spotlight2016] Before the federal series began, about one American worker in three was a union member in 1960, on a different survey basis. [cite:us13_eg_bargaining]

The contrast between sectors matters for interpreting the decline. If shrinking union membership were simply a change in what workers wanted, it would be odd for public employees, who bargain under separate state and federal laws, to keep their rate close to a third for four decades while private employees' rate collapsed. The record points instead to the conditions under which private workers organise and bargain. Economists still dispute how much weight to give to each of those conditions: the shift of jobs from factories to services, competition from imports, employer opposition and the law itself. What the record does settle is that the decline was concentrated where the National Labor Relations Act applies. [cite:ad4_bls_spotlight2016]

Why density matters to the Dream

The economists Henry Farber, Daniel Herbst, Ilyana Kuziemko and Suresh Naidu assembled survey data on union membership back to 1936. They found that American income inequality "has varied inversely with union density over the past 100 years", that the household union pay premium held between 10 and 20 log points (roughly 10 to 20 per cent) throughout, and, using the 1935 legalisation of unions and the wartime labour board as natural experiments, that "unions reduce inequality". [cite:ad4_qje_farber] At the mid-century peak, union households were less educated and more often nonwhite than others: the union contract was one of the main routes into the middle class for workers without college degrees. [cite:ad4_qje_farber] The raw pay difference persists today; full-time union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404 in 2025, against $1,174 for non-members, a comparison that does not adjust for occupation or industry. [cite:us13_bls_union2025]

PATCO, August 1981

The Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (PATCO) represented the federal employees who direct the country's air traffic. In June 1981 its negotiators reached a tentative agreement raising pay by as much as 11 per cent, which the members rejected; the union wanted higher pay, shorter hours and earlier retirement. PATCO had endorsed Ronald Reagan over Jimmy Carter in 1980. [cite:ad4_aba_patco] About 13,000 controllers walked out at 7 a.m. on Monday, 3 August 1981. Federal law prohibited strikes by federal employees. Shortly before 11 a.m., Reagan announced from the Rose Garden that strikers had 48 hours to return or be fired. [cite:ad4_reagan_patco] On 5 August he dismissed the 11,345 who stayed out, and the union was decertified, stripped of its legal right to represent the controllers, on 22 October 1981. [cite:ad4_aba_patco] Reagan's stated reason was that government services must not be interrupted: "Government cannot close down the assembly line." [cite:ad4_aba_patco]

PATCO's strike was illegal and the firings were lawful; that was the administration's position, and the law supported it. The significance for private-sector workers lies elsewhere. Since the Supreme Court's decision in NLRB v. Mackay Radio of 16 May 1938, a private employer facing an economic strike "is not bound to discharge those hired to fill the places of strikers": it may hire permanent replacements, so that strikers keep their legal status but may have no job to return to. [cite:ad4_mackay_1938] That rule was designed friction, part of the 1938 settlement, not a product of the 1980s. What changed after 1981 was how often large strikes happened. The BLS counts major work stoppages, those involving 1,000 or more workers. There were 424 in 1974, 235 in 1979, 187 in 1980 and 145 in 1981; there were 54 in 1985, 44 in 1990, 39 in 2000 and five in 2009, the lowest on record. [cite:ad4_bls_stoppages] The firings alone did not cause that fall, and the count had already been sliding before August 1981, but the strike stands at the turning point of the series.

Right-to-work

Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act lets states ban "union-security" clauses, the contract terms that require every worker covered by a union contract to pay toward the cost of bargaining. In a right-to-work state, a worker covered by the contract can decline to pay while still receiving its wages and protections. Michigan became the first state since Indiana in 1965 to repeal such a law; the repeal took effect on 13 February 2024, earlier than the 30 March date first expected, because the legislature adjourned early. [cite:ad4_audit_bt_michigan] As of October 2026, 26 states have right-to-work laws; a New Hampshire bill to become the 27th stalled again in 2025.
