[cite:us13_littler_rtw] [cite:ad4_audit_nrtw_states] Supporters present these laws as protecting individual choice; unions argue that they let workers benefit without paying and so drain the resources needed to organise. Both are stated positions. The law's documented effect on density is disputed among economists, and this book does not resolve it.

Enforcement: a law without fines

Labour law is only as strong as its enforcement. An employer that fires a worker for organising breaks the law, but the National Labor Relations Act contains no civil penalties or punitive damages. A worker fired illegally is generally owed back pay, minus whatever the worker earned elsewhere in the meantime, and the usual remedies are orders to stop and notices posted at the workplace. [cite:ad4_epi_unlawful] In a 2019 study of elections supervised by the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) in 2016 and 2017, the EPI found that employers were charged with an unfair labour practice in 41.5 per cent of them, and with illegal firing in 19.9 to 29.6 per cent, depending on the definition. In units of more than 60 workers, the figure was 54.4 per cent. A charge is an allegation, not a finding of violation, as the authors note. They also estimated that employers spend nearly $340 million a year on consultants hired to defeat organising drives. [cite:ad4_epi_unlawful] The EPI is aligned with organised labour; the numbers come from NLRB case filings and Labor Department disclosures.

The Board in 2026

The agency that enforces the law was itself in question in 2025 and 2026. After the President removed member Gwynne Wilcox early in 2025, the Board's quorum was restored only on 7 January 2026, when James Murphy and Scott Mayer were sworn in; Crystal Carey became General Counsel the same day. [cite:ad4_butlersnow_nlrb] [cite:ad4_proskauer_slaughter] On 29 June 2026, in Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court held by six votes to three that for-cause removal protection for Federal Trade Commission members was unconstitutional, overruling Humphrey's Executor of 1935. The law firm Proskauer judged it "highly likely" that the equivalent protection for NLRB members would fall as well, and that Wilcox's challenge to her removal was in effect resolved. [cite:ad4_proskauer_slaughter] On 7 August 2026 the Senate confirmed James Macy, a Republican, and David Prouty, a Democrat renominated for a second term, giving the Board four members and a three-to-one Republican majority, with one seat vacant, as of October 2026. [cite:ad4_ogletree_nlrb] A Board whose members can be removed at the President's will is a change in design, not only in personnel: it applies to whichever party holds the White House.

The charts below plot the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; each caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

The bargain the 1935 law offered still works where it reaches. Union members earn more on the raw comparison, the household union premium has held at 10 to 20 per cent for nearly a century, and public-sector density has stayed near a third. [cite:us13_bls_union2025] [cite:ad4_qje_farber] [cite:ad4_bls_spotlight2016] Strikes have also returned from their low: there were 33 major stoppages in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 30 in 2025, several times the 2009 figure though far below the 1970s. [cite:ad4_bls_stoppages] The mechanism did not disappear. It shrank to a fraction of the private workforce, and the next section turns to what grew in the space it left: the claim of shareholders on what firms earn. Part Thirteen of the US System vs Israel System volume sets American unions beside Israel's Histadrut. [scene:us13_unions|US vs Israel: unions]

sections.h: The Shareholder Turn: Profits, Buybacks, Pay and Tax, 1970–1986
sections.html:
While union power shrank, the hinge years gave a new answer to an old question, whom a corporation is run for: the shareholder. It arrived in three forms that can each be dated: an argument in 1970 and 1976, a securities rule in 1982, and tax and monetary decisions between 1979 and 1986. None alone explains the wage split, but together they changed what managers were paid to do and what they could do with their firms' cash.

The argument: Friedman and agency theory

On 13 September 1970 the New York Times Magazine published an essay by the economist Milton Friedman titled "The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits". [cite:ad4_hoover_friedman] Friedman wrote that "a corporate executive is an employee of the owners of the business", and that there is "one and only one social responsibility of business": to use its resources to increase profits, "so long as it stays within the rules of the game". [cite:ad4_friedman1970] The qualifier is often dropped when the essay is quoted. Managers who spend shareholders' money on social goals of their own choosing, he argued, are in effect taxing the owners without a mandate.

Six years later, the economists Michael Jensen and William Meckling gave the idea a formal structure in the Journal of Financial Economics. Their paper defined "agency costs": the losses that arise when the people who run a firm (the agents) are not the people who own it (the principals), and so may run it for their own comfort rather than for the owners' return. [cite:ad4_jensen_meckling] The practical conclusion drawn in the following decades was to align managers with shareholders by paying them in stock and options. That conclusion links the 1970s argument to the CEO pay figures below. The doctrine has since been publicly qualified: on 19 August 2019, 181 chief executives in the Business Roundtable signed a statement committing to lead their companies "for the benefit of all stakeholders", a departure from the group's earlier shareholder-first principles. [cite:ad4_audit_brt2019]

The rule: SEC Rule 10b-18, November 1982

A company can return cash to shareholders as a dividend, a cash payment per share, or by buying back its own shares on the stock market, leaving each remaining shareholder a larger slice of the firm. Buybacks raise a legal problem: a company buying its own stock can push up its price, which securities law treats as possible manipulation. On 17 November 1982 the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) adopted Rule 10b-18, published in the Federal Register on 26 November, which created a "safe harbor". [cite:ad4_sec_10b18_2003] A company that buys back its shares within four conditions is not deemed to have manipulated the market "solely" because of how, when, at what price or in what volume it bought. The conditions are that it uses one broker a day; avoids buying at the opening trade and near the close; pays no more than the highest independent bid or last independent sale; and generally buys no more in a day than 25 per cent of the stock's average daily trading volume. [cite:ad4_sec_10b18_2003]

The rule's design matters for how it is described. Compliance is voluntary, and the SEC states that there is no presumption that purchases outside the harbor are manipulative; the harbor also does not protect repurchases that are fraudulent or manipulative when the facts are considered as a whole. [cite:ad4_sec_10b18_2003] Rule 10b-18 did not legalise buybacks as such; it gave firms a clear, low-risk path to do them at scale. Later attempts to tighten disclosure have not lasted. The SEC's 2023 rule requiring firms to report daily repurchase data and explain their buyback objectives was vacated by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals on 19 December 2023. [cite:ad4_debevoise_sec2023] Since 2023 a 1 per cent federal excise tax has applied to net buybacks; it was still being collected at that rate in late 2025. [cite:ad4_spdji_q3_2025]

The scale of buybacks

By the count of S&P Dow Jones Indices, companies in the S&P 500, the 500 large firms that make up the main stock-market index, spent $806.41 billion on buybacks in 2018, $519.76 billion in the pandemic year 2020, $922.68 billion in 2022 and a record $942.55 billion in 2024. In the twelve months to September 2025 the total passed $1 trillion for the first time, at $1.020 trillion. [cite:ad4_spdji_q3_2025] Buybacks are concentrated: the 20 largest buyers accounted for 49.5 per cent of the third-quarter 2025 total, against a historical average of 47.8 per cent. [cite:ad4_spdji_q3_2025] The index's senior analyst, Howard Silverblatt, called the 1 per cent excise tax "a manageable expense" that "has not impacted overall buybacks". [cite:ad4_spdji_q3_2025]

The totals establish size: in 2024, S&P 500 companies spent about $1.50 on buybacks for every $1 of dividends ($942.55 billion divided by $629.62 billion). [cite:ad4_spdji_q3_2025] What they mean is disputed. William Lazonick, the best-known critic, found that 449 companies in the index spent 54 per cent of their 2003–2012 earnings, $2.4 trillion, on buybacks and another 37 per cent on dividends, and argued that stock-based pay gave executives a reason to prefer this to higher wages or investment. [cite:ad4_audit_lazonick] Jesse Fried and Charles Wang replied that gross figures overstate the drain: net of the new shares firms issue, and counting research spending as investment, payouts were about 41 per cent of the income available for investment, and investment was near record levels. [cite:ad4_audit_friedwang] Buybacks also rise and fall with profits, as the 2020 dip shows, which defenders read as firms returning cash they cannot use well. Neither side's totals settle the question of motive.

Pay at the top

The EPI tracks the pay of chief executives at the 350 largest American companies by sales and compares it with the pay of production and nonsupervisory workers. Using "realised" pay, which counts stock options when they are cashed and stock awards when they vest, the average CEO earned 20.6 times as much as a typical worker in 1965 and 30.7 times as much in 1978. The ratio reached 379.6 in 2000, stood at 290.2 in 2024 and, on a projection from data through August 2025, 324.7 in 2025. From 1978 to 2025 realised CEO pay rose 1,316 per cent, adjusted for inflation, while typical workers' pay rose 28 per cent. [cite:ad4_epi_ceo2025] The ratio is an average of firm-by-firm ratios. Earlier editions of the series gave different values for the same years, so figures from different editions should not be mixed. Steven Kaplan and Joshua Rauh argue that top pay rose across many occupations, not only among executives, a pattern they find fits the growing scale of firms and technology better than managers setting their own pay. [cite:ad4_audit_kaplanrauh]

Tax and money: 1979 to 1986

Two other decisions shaped who kept what. The first was monetary. On 6 October 1979 the Federal Reserve chair, Paul Volcker, announced that the Fed would target the quantity of bank reserves rather than the daily interest rate. The federal funds rate reached a record 20 per cent in late 1980, the economy fell into a severe recession, unemployment peaked at 10.8 per cent in late 1982, and inflation fell to 3.7 per cent in 1983. [cite:us11_frh_volcker] Ending double-digit inflation was the stated goal, and it was achieved. The EPI counts the "tolerated excess unemployment" of later decades among the policy choices behind the wage split; that is the EPI's causal reading, not a settled finding. [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026]

The second was fiscal. The top federal income tax rate was 70 per cent in 1980. After the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 it was 50 per cent from 1982; after the Tax Reform Act of 1986 it was 38.5 per cent in 1987 and 28 per cent in 1988, the low point of the path since 1980. It rose to 31 per cent in 1991 and 39.6 per cent in 1993, fell to 35 per cent in 2003, returned to 39.6 per cent in 2013 and has been 37 per cent since 2018. [cite:us11_tpc_toprate] The common shorthand "70 per cent to 37 per cent" hides both the 28 per cent trough and the later increases enacted under presidents of both parties. The Congressional Budget Office's long series shows that from 1979 to 2022 average federal tax rates fell for every income group, most for the lowest fifth, while the share of pre-tax income going to the top 1 per cent doubled, from 9 to 18 per cent. [cite:us11_cbo_dist2022] Who pays taxes now is the subject of Part Eleven. [scene:ad11_who_pays|Part Eleven: who pays]

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

The shareholder model has support in the record. Jensen and Meckling's problem is real: owners who cannot watch managers bear costs, and stock-based pay answered it directly. [cite:ad4_jensen_meckling] Friedman's essay placed profit-seeking inside "the rules of the game", which leaves the rules, including labour and tax law, to democratic choice. [cite:ad4_friedman1970] The pay ratio is not on a one-way path: it fell from 379.6 in 2000 to 290.2 in 2024. [cite:ad4_epi_ceo2025] And the money returned to shareholders does not vanish; it goes to whoever holds the shares, including retirement accounts, a point Part Ten takes up. [scene:ad10_pension_shift|Part Ten: from pension to 401(k)] Ownership is concentrated, however: in mid-2026 the wealthiest tenth of households held about 88 per cent of corporate equities and mutual fund shares by value (50.9 per cent for the top 1 per cent plus 37.2 for the next 9), up from about 82 per cent in 1989, while the bottom half held 0.6 per cent. [cite:ad4_audit_dfa_top1eq] [cite:ad4_audit_dfa_90to99eq] [cite:ad4_audit_dfa_bot50eq]

Interpretation, not finding: extraction by design

The Sophia platform reads the hinge years as the moment the Dream became an extraction system: a set of rules written so that the gains from rising productivity flow upward to shareholders and executives while the story of shared prosperity keeps workers working. In this reading, Rule 10b-18, stock-based pay and the decline of private-sector bargaining are not separate events but parts of one machine. The "design" it names is an inference about purpose; no document in this part shows a common plan. The strongest counter-readings are three. First, each change had its own stated rationale, from controlling inflation to curbing managerial waste, and its own supporters across both parties. Second, the measurement critics show that average compensation kept far closer pace with productivity than the popular chart suggests. Third, the same decades saw technological change and global competition that would have pressed on less-skilled wages under almost any rules.

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: Work: Wages, Hours and the Frozen Floors
chapters.intro: Part Five turns to the first promise of the Dream: that work pays. It begins with the floors the law sets under work, the federal minimum wage, the cash wage for tipped workers and the salary line for overtime, each written as a fixed number of dollars, and follows what happened to their value when Congress stopped changing them, along with other dollar limits in federal law that have stood still for decades and one that was finally indexed. It then asks how much Americans work, how many hold a second job, what the law guarantees in time off, and why most families with children now depend on two earners, weighing the best-known account of that change against its critics and setting out what childcare costs. It ends with the forces that weaken a worker's ability to walk away for better pay: employer concentration, noncompete contracts, occupational licensing, health insurance tied to the job, and employers who do not pay what the law requires, with the disputes over how large each one is.
chapters.outro: Part Five established that the federal wage floors are fixed dollar sums that lose value whenever Congress does not act: the minimum wage has been $7.25 since 24 July 2009 and in 2025 bought about 40 per cent less than in 1968 and 31 per cent less than when last raised, a full year of full-time work at that rate falls below the 2026 poverty guideline for one person, the tipped cash wage has been $2.13 since 1991, and the overtime salary line stands at $684 a week after the 2024 increase was set aside in court. [cite:ad5_epi_real2025] [cite:us13_dol_minwage] [cite:ad5_de_pov2026] [cite:ad5_ogletree_tip] [cite:ad5_hunton_ot2024] It also showed where the floor works: thirty states and the District of Columbia set higher minimums, and only 1.0 per cent of hourly workers were paid at or below $7.25 in 2024. [cite:us13_bp_states2026] [cite:ad5_bls_mw2024] Second jobs are less common than in the mid-1990s and weekly hours have not lengthened, but paid leave is thin and unequal, both parents now work in two-thirds of married families with children, the claim that two incomes leave families no better off remains contested, and the federal cap on subsidised childcare copayments was repealed in 2026. [cite:ad5_mlr_mj2015] [cite:us22_fred_mjrate] [cite:us18_crs_leave] [cite:ad5_bls_famee2025] [cite:ad5_ppp_bruenig] [cite:ad5_acf_ccdf2026] Employer wage-setting power is documented but its size is disputed, from about 1 to 17 per cent by method; the federal noncompete ban was vacated and abandoned; licensing and health-linked job lock limit movement; and wage theft, illegal but rarely recovered, takes billions a year by the leading estimates. [cite:ad5_nber_azar] [cite:ad5_rinz2022] [cite:ad5_ftc_accede] [cite:ad5_wh_licensing] [cite:ad5_gallup_joblock] [cite:ad5_epi_theft2017] [cite:ad5_epi_theft2024] These figures stand as of October 2026. What those wages buy in the largest purchase of an American life is the subject of Part Six. [scene:ad6_redlining_to_suburbs|Part Six: Housing]

sections.h: The Frozen Floors
sections.html:
The promise that work pays has a legal form in the United States. On 24 May 1937 Franklin Roosevelt asked Congress for "a fair day's pay for a fair day's work," and on 25 June 1938 he signed the Fair Labor Standards Act, which took effect that October with a minimum wage of 25 cents an hour and a maximum workweek of 44 hours before overtime, covering industries that employed about a fifth of the labour force. [cite:ad5_dol_flsa1938] Every floor in this section descends from that act or sits beside it: the federal minimum wage, the lower cash wage for workers who earn tips, the salary line above which an employer need not pay overtime, and a handful of other dollar amounts written into federal law. What they share is that each is a fixed number of dollars. Congress, or the Labor Department acting under the law, has to change it by a deliberate act. When it does not, prices keep rising and the floor sinks without any vote being taken.

Two terms carry the argument. A nominal amount is the number printed in the law: $7.25. A real amount is what that number buys, restated in the prices of a single year so that different years can be compared; this section uses the Economic Policy Institute's series in 2025 dollars, which adjusts for consumer prices. [cite:ad5_epi_real2025] A floor that stays the same in nominal terms while prices rise is falling in real terms.

The federal minimum wage

Congress has raised the federal minimum many times, always by passing a new law with new dollar amounts. It went from $1.40 to $1.60 in February 1968, to $3.10 in 1980 and $3.35 in 1981, then waited nine years for $3.80 in 1990 and $4.25 in 1991. Two steps followed in 1996 and 1997, to $5.15. After another ten-year gap, a 2007 law raised it in three annual steps on 24 July of 2007, 2008 and 2009, to $7.25. It has not changed since. [cite:us13_dol_minwage] As of October 2026 the federal minimum has stood at $7.25 for more than seventeen years, the longest stretch without an increase since the law began; the previous longest, from 1997 to 2007, lasted ten. [cite:us13_dol_minwage]

In 2025 dollars, the minimum was worth $12.11 an hour in 1968, its highest point. It was worth $10.45 in 2009, the year it reached $7.25, and by 2025 the same $7.25 was worth exactly $7.25 in that year's prices. [cite:ad5_epi_real2025] The arithmetic: $7.25 divided by $12.11 is 0.60, so the floor buys about 40 per cent less than it did in 1968; $7.25 divided by $10.45 is 0.69, so it buys about 31 per cent less than when it was last raised. An earlier EPI calculation, in mid-2022 prices, found that $7.25 then bought less than the minimum had at any time since February 1956. [cite:ad5_epi_lowest2022] Different editions of EPI's series use different price adjustments and so give slightly different percentages for the same idea: an August 2023 EPI article put the 2023 loss at 42 per cent below 1968, while the 2025-dollar series used here puts 2023 at 37 per cent below and 2025 at 40. [cite:us13_epi_history] [cite:ad5_epi_real2025] The direction and rough size agree; the exact figure depends on the edition, and this book uses the 2025-dollar series throughout Part Five. Inflation in 2026 has continued to erode it: consumer prices rose 3.7 per cent in the twelve months to September 2026. [cite:us14_bls_cpi_sep26]

The national number now matters less than it once did, because states have moved. In 2026, 30 states and the District of Columbia set minimums above $7.25 and 20 states use the federal figure; the average state minimum rose from $11.18 in 2025 to $11.51 in 2026, and the District's reached $17.95 in July 2025. [cite:us13_bp_states2026] The Bureau of Labor Statistics counted about 843,000 hourly paid workers at or below $7.25 in 2024, 1.0 per cent of the 80.3 million paid by the hour, against 13.4 per cent in 1979. Only 82,000 were paid exactly $7.25; the other 760,000 earned less, which the law allows for some groups, chiefly tipped workers. About two-thirds worked in leisure and hospitality, mostly restaurants; 43 per cent were under 25 and 56 per cent worked part time. [cite:ad5_bls_mw2024]

The federal floor still marks what full-time work at the bottom is legally worth in the 20 states that use it. A worker paid $7.25 for 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year, earns $15,080. The federal poverty guideline for 2026 is $15,960 for one person and $21,640 for two, so a full year of full-time work at the federal minimum leaves a single adult $880 below the line and a parent with one child $6,560 below it. [cite:ad5_de_pov2026] [cite:ad5_usac_pov2026]

The tipped cash wage

Since the 1966 amendments, employers of workers who earn tips have been allowed to pay a lower cash wage and count tips toward the minimum. The cash wage was originally half the minimum, and in 1991 that half came to $2.13. In 1996 Congress changed the formula so that the cash wage stayed at $2.13 while the regular minimum went up, and it has stayed there since. [cite:ad5_ogletree_tip] If tips and cash wage together fall short of $7.25, the employer must make up the difference. The $2.13 is now 29 per cent of the federal minimum rather than 50. Measured with the same EPI price ratio used for the minimum, which turns 1991's $4.25 into $9.18 in 2025 dollars, the $2.13 of 1991 was worth about $4.60 in today's prices; it has lost a little over half its value. [cite:ad5_epi_real2025] This is a dollar figure that has not changed for thirty-five years, and it governs the industry where most sub-minimum pay is found. [cite:ad5_bls_mw2024]

The overtime line

The 1938 act requires time-and-a-half after the standard week, but it exempts executive, administrative and professional employees, and the Labor Department has always used a salary test to keep the exemption from swallowing low-paid workers. The test was $30 a week in 1938 and was raised every few years to 1975, when it reached $155 for executives and $170 for professionals. [cite:ad5_crs_ot2007] It then stayed put for 29 years, until a 2004 rule set $455 a week. The next attempt, a 2016 rule at $913, was blocked by a Texas federal court before it took effect. A 2019 rule raised the line to $684 a week, $35,568 a year, from 1 January 2020. [cite:ad5_kutak_ot2019] [cite:ad5_ogletree_ot2019] A 2024 rule raised it to $844 on 1 July 2024 and scheduled $1,128 for January 2025, with updates every three years; on 15 November 2024 Judge Sean Jordan of the Eastern District of Texas set the rule aside nationwide, finding that it let salary predominate over job duties, and the line returned to $684. [cite:ad5_hunton_ot2024] In April 2025 the government asked the appeals court to pause its appeals while the Labor Department reconsidered, and in May 2026 a further appeal was dropped and dismissed. [cite:ad5_k12dive_ot] [cite:ad5_law360_ot2026] Status as of October 2026: the line is $684 a week.

Using EPI's price ratios again, $455 in 2004 was worth about $735 in 2025 dollars and the $155 of 1975 about $790, so the current $684 buys less than either. [cite:ad5_epi_real2025] A salaried manager paid $36,000 a year can lawfully work fifty or sixty hours a week without overtime if the job meets the duties test; a raise in the line is the only federal mechanism that moves such workers back into overtime coverage.

The record on this floor runs across both parties in the same way. A Republican administration raised the line in 2004 and again in 2019; Democratic administrations wrote the 2016 and 2024 rules; courts struck down the two larger increases on the ground that the Labor Department had exceeded the authority Congress gave it. [cite:ad5_kutak_ot2019] [cite:ad5_hunton_ot2024] The Labor Department itself took the position in 2004 that automatic indexing was beyond its power, and the automatic updates in the 2016 and 2024 rules fell with them in court. [cite:ad5_dwt_ot2024]

Other numbers the law forgot, and one it remembered

The same pattern appears outside wage law. Supplemental Security Income, the federal cash benefit for poor older and disabled people, disqualifies anyone with more than $2,000 in countable savings, or $3,000 for a married couple. Those limits were reached by gradual steps between 1985 and 1989, the only increase since the programme was enacted with limits of $1,500 and $2,250 in 1972. Had they been indexed from 1972 they would have been $9,929 and $14,893 in 2023. The income rules are older still: benefits fall by $1 for every $2 earned above $65 a month and by a dollar for each dollar of other income above $20, amounts Congress has never raised since it created the programme in 1972. More than two-thirds of recipients have no savings at all. [cite:ad5_cbpp_ssi] [cite:ad5_audit_cbpp_ssiincome] A bill to raise the limits to $10,000 and $20,000 has sponsors from both parties in both chambers; as of June 2026 it had not passed. [cite:ad5_ffyf_ssi2026] [scene:ad11_benefits_cliff|Part Eleven] returns to how such limits interact with earnings.

The counterexample is the $600 threshold above which a business must file a Form 1099 reporting payments to a contractor. Set in 1954 and never indexed, its 1954 value equals about $5,900 in 2025 dollars, using EPI's price ratio for that year of about 9.8. [cite:ad5_onpay_1099] [cite:ad5_epi_real2025] The 2025 reconciliation law raised it to $2,000 for payments made after 31 December 2025 and indexed it to inflation from 2027. [cite:ad5_natp_1099] Congress can index a dollar figure when it chooses to; this one, a paperwork threshold for businesses, it did.

The money trail of a frozen floor

A frozen floor moves money without a transaction anyone sees. The figure below follows it in the five steps used throughout this book. Its last two cells are the contested ones: economists agree that a real decline in the minimum lowers pay at the bottom, but they disagree about how much of the saving stays with employers and how much reaches customers as lower prices, and about how many jobs a higher floor would cost.

Where the floor works as promised

The record also shows the floor doing what it was built to do. The share of hourly workers paid at or below the federal minimum fell from 13.4 per cent in 1979 to 1.0 per cent in 2024, and most of the remainder are teenagers, part-timers and tipped workers whose total pay may exceed the minimum once tips are counted. [cite:ad5_bls_mw2024] The federal system was designed to let states go higher, and they have: 30 states and the District of Columbia now set floors above the federal one. [cite:us13_bp_states2026] The strongest critics of a higher federal floor point to the Congressional Budget Office's 2019 analysis, which found that a $15 minimum would raise pay for at least 17 million people but could cost as many as 3.7 million jobs; the same report's central estimate and its low end of roughly zero are what supporters cite. [cite:ad5_wjct_cbo2019] Both readings rest on the same document. The disagreement is about trade-offs, not about whether the floor has fallen.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Interpretation, not finding: the frozen floor as a tax on time

The Sophia platform reads the frozen floors together as one mechanism: a set of fixed dollar figures that were never indexed and therefore work as a slow tax on the passage of time, levied on the people with the least room to absorb it. In this reading, the absence of an index is itself the design, because inaction requires no vote and leaves no record of who chose it.

The strongest counter-readings are these. First, the dollar form of the floors is old and was written into the 1938 act long before inflation became persistent; legislators of both parties have raised the minimum many times, and the Labor Department's view that it lacks power to index the overtime line was stated in 2004 and later matched by court rulings striking down automatic updates. [cite:ad5_dwt_ot2024] [cite:ad5_hunton_ot2024] Second, the federal floor now binds for very few workers because states have replaced it, which is how the federal design was meant to work. [cite:ad5_bls_mw2024] [cite:us13_bp_states2026] Third, Congress indexed the 1099 threshold in 2025, which shows that indexing is a choice made case by case rather than a rule against it. [cite:ad5_natp_1099] What the record establishes is narrower than either reading: each frozen figure named here lost much of its real value, the losses fell on low-paid workers, disabled people and older people with little savings, and in every case the remedy required an act that was not taken.

sections.h: Hours, Second Jobs and the Two-Income Household
sections.html:
The promise as taught says that one full-time job supports a household. Two claims now circulate against it. The first holds that Americans increasingly need a second job to get by. The second holds that a family which once lived on one income now needs two to reach the same place, and is more fragile for it. Both are partly right and partly wrong, and the record lets them be separated. This section looks at how many people hold more than one job and why, how long Americans work, what the law guarantees in time off, and what happened when the second parent went to work, including the cost of the childcare that made it possible.

Second jobs: high in number, not in share

A multiple jobholder, in the Bureau of Labor Statistics' monthly household survey, is anyone employed who held two or more jobs in the reference week. In 2025 there were about 8.8 million, 5.4 per cent of everyone employed; the 2025 figures are averages of eleven months because no survey was taken in October during the federal shutdown. [cite:us22_bls_cpsaat36_25] In September 2026 the seasonally adjusted count was 8.99 million, or 5.5 per cent. [cite:us22_fred_mjrate] The raw count is near the top of its history because the workforce is larger. The share is not. A Monthly Labor Review study of workers aged 16 to 64 found that the rate peaked at about 6.8 per cent in the summer of 1995, then fell steadily to about 5.0 per cent by the end of 2013, with the decline showing up in every education group. [cite:ad5_mlr_mj2015] The age bases differ slightly between the two series, but the direction is clear: holding two jobs is somewhat less common now than in the mid-1990s.

Who holds them also runs against the circulating picture. The rate rises with education: in January 1994 about 7.8 per cent of workers with a college degree held more than one job against about 3 per cent of those without a high-school diploma, and in 2013 the figures were 6.0 and 2.6 per cent. When the survey last asked why, in May 2004, 38.1 per cent said they wanted extra money, 25.6 per cent said they needed it to meet regular expenses or pay off debt, and 17.6 per cent said they enjoyed the second job. [cite:ad5_mlr_mj2015] A quarter working a second job to cover bills is a real finding about strain at the margin. It is not evidence that a second job has become the norm.

Hours: long, but shorter than they were

A widely repeated comparison holds that Americans work hundreds of hours a year more than Germans or the French. The source of such comparisons, the OECD's series on average annual hours, carries a warning that the figures "are intended for comparisons of trends over time" and are "unsuitable for comparisons of the level" across countries, because each country's data come from different sources. [cite:us22_oecd_annhrs_note] On the trend, which the series is built to show, average annual hours per American worker fell from about 1,880 in 2000 to about 1,800 in 2020 and 1,796 in 2024. [cite:us13_jil_hours] The comparable cross-country measure is usual weekly hours on the main job: in 2025 American employees usually worked 38.2 hours a week, 41.0 if full time, and 8.9 per cent usually worked 50 hours or more, down from 9.5 per cent in 2023. [cite:us22_oecd_avgusl] [cite:us22_oecd_lnghrs] Involuntary part-time work is harder to pin down because definitions differ. The OECD's narrow cross-country measure put it at 0.81 per cent of American employment in 2025. [cite:us22_oecd_invpt] The Bureau of Labor Statistics' own broader count of people working part time for economic reasons, because their hours were cut or they could not find full-time work, was 4.5 million in September 2026, a little under 3 per cent of the employed. [cite:ad5_audit_bls_empsit_sep26]

What sets the United States apart is less the length of the week than what the law guarantees around it. The Fair Labor Standards Act "does not require payment for time not worked, such as vacations"; paid vacation is a matter between employer and employee. [cite:us13_dol_vacation] In March 2026, 81 per cent of private-sector workers had access to paid sick leave, 88 per cent of full-time and 59 per cent of part-time workers. [cite:us22_bls_ebs26_sick] Federal law guarantees up to twelve weeks of unpaid, job-protected family leave to eligible workers under the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993; paid family leave reached 27 per cent of private workers in March 2023, but 13 per cent in the lowest-paid quarter against 44 per cent in the highest, and ten jurisdictions, including the District of Columbia, were running public paid-leave programmes in March 2025. [cite:us18_crs_leave] [cite:us18_bls_leave] Delaware and Minnesota were scheduled to begin paying benefits in January 2026 and Maine in May 2026, while Maryland's programme was postponed to 2028. [cite:ad5_audit_ebg_leave] Time off, in other words, is distributed by wage level, which places the least of it where hours are least secure.

The second earner

The larger change in American work since the 1970s is not the second job but the second worker. In March 1975, 47 per cent of mothers with children under 18 were in the labour force. By March 2000 the figure was 73 per cent, and it has stayed near that level since. [cite:ad5_ted_mothers] In 2025 it was 73.9 per cent, and 68.0 per cent for mothers of children under six; in 66.3 per cent of married-couple families with children, both parents were employed. [cite:ad5_bls_famee2025] Across all married couples, including retired ones, both spouses worked in 49.1 per cent. [cite:ad5_bls_famee2025]

Why the second earner went to work is the contested question. Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi argued in The Two-Income Trap that rising fixed costs, above all housing in districts with good schools, along with childcare and health insurance, absorbed the second income, so that a two-earner family in the early 2000s, earning about 75 per cent more after inflation than a one-earner family a generation earlier, had less discretionary money left and no reserve earner to fall back on if a paycheque was lost. They also found families with children nearly three times as likely as others to go bankrupt. [cite:ad5_audit_wharton_twoincome] [cite:ad5_ppp_bruenig]

The critique is strongest on the numbers. Matt Bruenig of the left-leaning People's Policy Project argued in 2019 that the book's key comparison used the wrong price index, the standard CPI-U rather than the research series CPI-U-RS, which by his calculation overstated the 1970s family's income by about 13 per cent; that it deflated every cost category by overall inflation rather than by each category's own; that the later family's higher mortgage bought a house about a third larger; and that $9,600 of the later family's extra fixed costs was childcare, which ends when children reach school age. He also cited research by Jonathan Gruber and Julie Berry Cullen finding little evidence that wives entered work to replace a husband's lost earnings, which undercuts the idea that the stay-at-home spouse had served as household insurance. [cite:ad5_ppp_bruenig] The record therefore supports the first half of the story, that the second earner became normal and that housing, childcare and health costs rose, and leaves the second half, that two-earner families are no better off, contested. Where costs rose for each mechanism, housing in [scene:ad6_price_and_rent|Part Six] and health in [scene:ad8_costs_and_coverage|Part Eight], is taken up there.

Childcare: the price of the second paycheque

Childcare is the cost that most directly sets the value of a second job. The Labor Department's National Database of Childcare Prices, covering 2,512 counties in 2022, found that full-day care for one child cost between $6,552 and $15,600 a year depending on the county and the type of care, equal to 8.9 to 16 per cent of the county's median family income for a single child. [cite:us18_dol_childcare] On the OECD's standard family, a couple with children aged two and three, both working full time at the average wage, an American family paid about 20 per cent of its disposable income for full-time centre care in 2022, and a single parent on the average wage 37 per cent; these figures are after any subsidies and tax relief. [cite:us22_statista_ncc] [cite:us22_oecd_pf34]

Federal policy on the price has reversed twice in two years. A rule issued in March 2024 required states using the Child Care and Development Fund to cap subsidised families' copayments at 7 per cent of family income. [cite:ad5_acf_ccdf2024] A new final rule published on 12 May 2026 and effective on 13 July 2026 repealed that federal cap, leaving states to set copayments subject only to the older standard that they must not block access to assistance. [cite:ad5_acf_ccdf2026] Status as of October 2026: no federal cap applies.

Where it works as promised

On time, the long record is better than the story. Usual weekly hours for full-time American employees sit close to forty a week, the share working fifty hours or more has fallen in recent years, and annual hours per worker have drifted down since 2000. [cite:us22_oecd_avgusl] [cite:us22_oecd_lnghrs] [cite:us13_jil_hours] Involuntary part-time work is low by either measure: under 1 per cent of employment on the OECD's narrow definition and under 3 per cent on the BLS's broader one. [cite:us22_oecd_invpt] [cite:ad5_audit_bls_empsit_sep26] Second jobs are held most often by the best-educated and are less common than a generation ago. [cite:ad5_mlr_mj2015] What the record does show is that the guarantees around work, paid leave and affordable childcare, are thin and unequally spread, and that the federal government has twice in two years changed its answer on what childcare should cost a subsidised family. [cite:us18_crs_leave] [cite:ad5_acf_ccdf2026] Earlier treatments of the same measures, set beside another country's, are in [scene:us13_wages|US System vs Israel System, Part Thirteen] and [scene:us22_families|its family budgets].

sections.h: Who Sets the Wage: Monopsony, Lock-in and Wage Theft
sections.html:
The taught version of the labour market is the one in the economics textbook: many employers compete for workers, a worker who is underpaid quits for a better offer, and so wages settle at roughly what each worker's labour is worth. That model is not wrong; it describes much of the economy much of the time. This section examines four documented ways in which real labour markets depart from it. Some employers face little competition for workers. Some workers sign contracts that stop them taking a rival's offer. Some occupations require a licence before anyone may enter them. And some employers simply do not pay what the law requires. Each departure has its own evidence and its own critics, and they are kept separate here.

Monopsony: when the employer sets the wage

A monopoly is a market with one seller; a monopsony is a market with one buyer. In a labour market the buyer is the employer, and economists now use the word for any situation in which an employer can pay less than a worker's output is worth without losing all its staff, because workers cannot easily find or move to another job. The gap between what a worker produces and what the worker is paid is called the markdown. Alan Manning's 2021 review of the field concluded that the evidence that employers hold "considerable monopsony power" had been mounting. [cite:ad5_manning2021] A survey published in August 2026 by Sydnee Caldwell, Arindrajit Dube and Suresh Naidu traces that power to three sources: the time and effort it takes to search for a job, workers' differing attachments to particular employers, and plain concentration, a few employers dominating a local market. They caution that the size of the markdown cannot be read straight off any one measure. [cite:ad5_nber_cdn2026]

How large the effect is remains disputed, and the estimates depend on the data and method. José Azar, Ioana Marinescu and Marshall Steinbaum measured concentration in more than 8,000 local occupational markets using job postings on CareerBuilder.com, found that the average market was highly concentrated by the standard used for company mergers, and estimated that moving from a market at the 25th percentile of concentration to one at the 75th was associated with posted wages 17 per cent lower. [cite:ad5_nber_azar] Efraim Benmelech, Nittai Bergman and Hyunseob Kim, using Census plant data from 1977 to 2009, found that local employer concentration had risen, that it was associated with lower wages, more so where unions were weak, and that wages tracked productivity more closely where markets were less concentrated. [cite:ad5_bbk2018] Kevin Rinz, a Census Bureau economist using tax records, found the opposite trend: local concentration generally fell between 1976 and 2015, to about three-quarters of its 1976 level, even as national concentration rose. His estimate of the wage effect was also smaller in practice: moving from the median to the 75th percentile of concentration would cut earnings by nearly 10 per cent, but a typical change within a market moved earnings by about 1 per cent. [cite:ad5_rinz2022] The range, then, runs from about one per cent for a typical change within a market to seventeen per cent for the widest comparison across markets, and the direction of the trend over time is itself contested.

Noncompetes: a contract that closes the exit

A noncompete clause is a term in an employment contract that bars the worker, after leaving, from working for a competitor or starting a competing business for a set time and area. In a survey of 11,505 workers, Evan Starr, J.J. Prescott and Norman Bishara found that about 18 per cent were bound by one and 38 per cent had signed one at some point. The clauses were most common in skilled, well-paid jobs but appeared often in low-wage jobs and even in states where courts will not enforce them; only 10 per cent of workers negotiated them, and about a third received the clause only after accepting the offer. Wages were lower where noncompetes were easier to enforce, and workers who were told of the clause before accepting fared better than those who received it afterwards. [cite:ad5_spb2021]

On 23 April 2024 the Federal Trade Commission voted to ban most noncompetes. It estimated that about 30 million workers, roughly one in five, were bound by them and that the ban would raise earnings by $400 to $488 billion over ten years, about $524 a year for the average worker; existing clauses for senior executives earning over $151,164 in policy-making roles were left in place. [cite:ad5_ftc_factsheet] The rule never took effect. On 20 August 2024 Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas, in Ryan LLC v. FTC, held that the Commission had exceeded its authority and that the rule was arbitrary and capricious, and set it aside nationwide. [cite:ad5_faegre_ryan] On 5 September 2025 the Commission, by three votes to one, dropped its appeals in two circuits and accepted the vacatur, turning instead to examining noncompetes case by case. [cite:ad5_ftc_accede] [cite:ad5_tsl_ftc] Status as of October 2026: there is no federal rule; enforceability is set by each state's law.

Licensing: a gate built for safety

An occupational licence is a government permission to work in a trade, granted after required training, examinations or fees. A 2015 report by the Treasury, the Council of Economic Advisers and the Labor Department found that fewer than 5 per cent of workers needed a state licence in the early 1950s and about a quarter did by the 2010s, and that two-thirds of the rise came from more occupations being licensed rather than from workers moving into already licensed ones. Licensed workers earned 10 to 15 per cent more after accounting for education and experience; workers in the most licensed occupations moved between states about 14 per cent less often; and most studies the report reviewed found higher prices for consumers. [cite:ad5_wh_licensing] Morris Kleiner and Alan Krueger, from a national survey, put the share fully licensed at 29 per cent and the wage gain at about 14 per cent. [cite:ad5_nber_kk] In 2025, 21.6 per cent of employed Americans held a licence and 24.0 per cent held a licence or certification. [cite:ad5_bls_cps49] Licensing is designed friction: it exists to protect the public from incompetent practitioners, and its defenders point to that purpose. The documented costs, fewer moves and higher prices, are the price of the protection, and how much protection each licence buys is the question the 2015 report put to state legislatures.

Job lock: insurance as a tether

For the many Americans insured through an employer, leaving a job can mean losing coverage. Economists call the result job lock. Brigitte Madrian's 1994 study estimated that it reduced the voluntary job-leaving rate of insured workers by about a quarter, from 16 to 12 per cent a year. [cite:ad5_nber_madrian] A West Health and Gallup survey fielded in late 2025 found that 24 per cent of workers covered through their employer, about 23 million people, were staying in a job they wanted to leave because they feared losing health insurance, eight points more than in 2021. The share was 44 per cent among those with medical debt they could not repay within a year, against 21 per cent among those without. [cite:ad5_gallup_joblock] The insurance system behind this is the subject of [scene:ad8_insurance_machine|Part Eight].

Wage theft: the departure that is simply illegal

Wage theft is the term used for an employer's failure to pay wages the law requires: pay below the minimum, unpaid overtime, work off the clock, tips taken, illegal deductions. Unlike the mechanisms above, it is not a matter of market structure or legal design. It is a breach of law, and the dispute is over its size. The 2009 study Broken Laws, Unprotected Workers surveyed 4,387 low-wage workers in Chicago, Los Angeles and New York in 2008, using methods designed to reach undocumented and cash-paid workers, and found that 26 per cent had been paid less than the minimum wage in the previous week, 76 per cent of those who worked over forty hours had not been paid overtime, and 68 per cent had suffered at least one pay violation. [cite:ad5_prospect_broken] The Economic Policy Institute, a labour-aligned research group, estimated in 2017 from the government's household survey that minimum-wage violations alone cost 2.4 million workers in the ten most populous states about $8 billion a year, an average of about $3,300 for a year-round worker, and extrapolated to more than $15 billion nationally. EPI itself notes that the figures rest on self-reported pay and hours, cover only minimum-wage violations, and treat the national total as an extrapolation rather than a measurement. [cite:ad5_epi_theft2017]

A study commissioned by the Labor Department from Eastern Research Group, using the same household survey and a second one for California and New York in 2011, found lower rates: 3.5 to 6.8 per cent of covered jobs, and 11 to 12 per cent of low-wage jobs, paid below the minimum, with losses of $20 to $29 million a week across the two states. Its estimates varied with the survey used. [cite:ad5_dol_erg2014] The difference between a quarter of workers in three cities' low-wage industries and about a tenth of low-wage jobs in two states is mostly a difference in who was surveyed and how, and both studies measure something real. Enforcement recovers a small part of any of these totals. EPI counted more than $1.5 billion recovered in 2021 to 2023 by the Labor Department ($659.8 million for 510,534 workers), state agencies and attorneys general, and the largest class-action settlements; it reported that by 2022 each federal investigator was responsible for almost three times as many workers as in 1973. [cite:ad5_epi_theft2024] Workers without legal status, about 8.3 million in the labour force in 2022, are the easiest to underpay, because a complaint can bring the threat of deportation. [cite:us13_epi_unauth]

Where the market works as taught

The textbook picture holds in more places than these mechanisms might suggest. On Rinz's evidence most local labour markets became less concentrated over four decades, and his estimate of what a typical change in concentration does to pay is about one per cent. [cite:ad5_rinz2022] Workers do quit and move: even under job lock as Madrian measured it, insured workers left their jobs at 12 per cent a year. [cite:ad5_nber_madrian] Most workers are not bound by noncompetes, and most low-wage jobs in the Labor Department's own study were paid at least the minimum. [cite:ad5_spb2021] [cite:ad5_dol_erg2014] Licences exist to protect the public, the purpose their defenders cite, and the 2015 report did not dispute that purpose. [cite:ad5_wh_licensing] The record does not show a labour market without competition. It shows specific, measured places where the worker's ability to walk away, which the taught version relies on, is weaker than the textbook assumes: a concentrated local market, a contract clause, a licence, a health plan, or a complaint that would cost more than the wage. How those weaknesses grew alongside the decline of unions is the subject of [scene:ad4_labor_power|Part Four], and how the rules governing them are written is examined in [scene:ad15_pricing_power|Part Fifteen].

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: Housing: The Asset That Built the Dream
chapters.intro: Part Six follows the asset at the centre of the American Dream: the home. It begins with the federal design that made ownership reachable on a wage, the long fixed-rate mortgage of the New Deal, and with the rules written into the same programmes that kept many families out of it: the HOLC maps and the FHA's underwriting manual, the local administration of the GI Bill, the covenants of Levittown and the zoning that still governs what can be built. It then measures what a home costs today in years of income, in monthly payments and in the age at which buyers first manage it, sets out what renters pay, and tests the claim that Wall Street is buying up the houses. It ends with the mechanisms through which housing takes from those who cannot own: eviction filings and the records they leave, tenant screening, the contract for deed and shared pricing software, and the count of those who end up with no home at all.
chapters.outro: Part Six established that the housing Dream was a federal design that partly worked. The long, fixed-rate, amortising mortgage built by HOLC and the FHA helped lift homeownership from 43.6 per cent of households in 1940 to 64 per cent by 1980, and it remains the standard loan. [cite:ad6_greenwachter] The same agencies wrote racial exclusion into their underwriting, and the Black–white ownership gap, 27 points in 1960, was 29.1 points in mid-2026. [cite:ad6_fha_manual] [cite:ad6_stateline_gap] [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226] A typical home now costs about 5.0 years of median household income against 3.2 in the 1990s, the 30-year mortgage rate stood at 7.40 per cent in October 2026, first-time buyers in the realtors' survey had a record median age of 40, and 49 per cent of renters spent more than 30 per cent of their income on housing. [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [cite:ad6_pmms] [cite:ad6_nar_2025] [cite:ad6_nlihc_son26] Large investors own a small share of single-family rentals nationally but a large one in some Sunbelt metros, and a federal ban on further purchases by the largest takes effect in January 2027. [cite:ad6_crs_inst] [cite:ad6_mayer_road] Where housing extracts, the record is specific: about 3.6 million eviction filings a year before the pandemic, records of which about a fifth are ambiguous or wrong, contract sales that cost Chicago's Black buyers an estimated $3.2–4.0 billion, and a pricing-software case settled without admission of wrongdoing. [cite:ad6_nlihc_pnas] [cite:ad6_porton] [cite:ad6_duke_plunder] [cite:ad6_wsoc_realpage] Part Seven turns to the other asset families were told to buy on credit: the education that was meant to pay for itself. [scene:ad7_k12_property_tax|Part Seven: Education]

sections.h: From Redlining to the Suburbs: How the Federal Government Built the Owner's Dream
sections.html:
The home is the part of the American Dream that the federal government built most directly. Before the 1930s, owning a house was something a household did largely on its own terms and with private lenders, and fewer than half of American households managed it. Within a generation the share had risen past three in five, and the change was not an accident of prosperity: it followed a set of federal laws, agencies and lending rules written between 1933 and 1956. The same rules decided who could use them. This section follows both halves of that record, the design that worked and the exclusions written into it, because the taught version of the postwar suburb usually tells only the first.

What a mortgage looked like before the New Deal

A mortgage is a loan secured on a home: if the borrower stops paying, the lender can take the house. Before the Great Depression, American home loans usually ran for five to ten years, carried interest rates that could change, and were rarely larger than half the value of the house. Most did not amortise, meaning the monthly payments covered interest but not the principal; the whole balance fell due at the end, and the borrower had to pay it off or find a lender willing to roll it over. Homeowners typically renegotiated every year. [cite:ad6_greenwachter] When the banking system seized up after 1929, lenders stopped rolling loans over. Foreclosures ran at about 250,000 a year from 1931 to 1935, and at the worst point of the Depression nearly one home in ten was in foreclosure. [cite:ad6_greenwachter]

Congress answered with two agencies. The Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC), created in 1933, bought defaulted mortgages from lenders and rewrote about one million of them as fixed-rate, 20-year loans that paid themselves off in equal monthly instalments. The Federal Housing Administration (FHA), created by the National Housing Act of 1934, did not lend at all; it insured private lenders against loss on loans that met its standards, at first up to 20 years and 80 per cent of the home's value. [cite:ad6_greenwachter] [cite:ad6_prrac_timeline] The limits were then stretched in steps. In 1948 the maximum FHA term rose to 30 years, and in 1956 the maximum loan rose to 95 per cent of value for new homes and 90 per cent for existing ones. [cite:ad6_greenwachter] The Housing Act of 1954 had already cut FHA down payments, which had been at least 20 per cent from 1947, to between 5 and 16 per cent depending on the size of the loan. [cite:ad6_fed_frydman]

This is the part of the record where the promise as taught holds. The long, fixed-rate, self-amortising loan turned a house from something bought with savings into something bought with income, paid down over a working life. Homeownership rose from 43.6 per cent of households in 1940 to 64 per cent by 1980. [cite:ad6_greenwachter] Among non-farm households the rate went from 41 per cent in 1940 to 61 per cent in 1960, with about 60 per cent of that rise completed by 1947; veterans' loans, available from 1944, are estimated to have raised the national rate by about 7 per cent on their own. [cite:ad6_fed_frydman] The 30-year mortgage was a deliberate public design, it was meant to spread ownership, and it did. It remains the standard American home loan today.

Who the design left out

The same agencies that built the new mortgage also decided where it could go. Between 1935 and 1940 HOLC surveyors drew "residential security" maps of American cities, grading neighbourhoods from A, coloured green, to D, coloured red. [cite:ad6_mapping_ineq] These maps are the most reproduced image of "redlining". The FHA wrote the rules down in its own manual. Its 1938 Underwriting Manual, the guide its appraisers used to decide which loans to insure, listed among the protections it recommended for a neighbourhood the "prohibition of the occupancy of properties except by the race for which they are intended", and said local schools "should not be attended in large numbers by inharmonious racial groups". [cite:ad6_fha_manual] A racially restrictive covenant is a clause in a deed or lease barring sale or occupancy to people of a named race; the FHA treated such covenants as a feature that made a loan safer.

The economic literature now disputes which agency did the most damage. A team led by economists Daniel Aaronson, Daniel Hartley and Bhashkar Mazumder at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago compared blocks on either side of HOLC grade boundaries and found that the lower-graded side had lower homeownership, house values and rents in later decades, and became more heavily Black; the gaps grew until about 1970 or 1980 and then narrowed, and along the boundary between C and D areas the homeownership gap fell after 1990. [cite:ad6_ahm_holc] A second team, Price Fishback, Jonathan Rose, Kenneth Snowden and Thomas Storrs, points out that HOLC had made 90 per cent of its loans before its map project began in 1935, judges it "very unlikely" that the maps guided lending, and concludes that the red lines drawn by the FHA "were likely far more impactful". The FHA, they find, redlined core urban neighbourhoods "from day one"; in Baltimore from 1935 to 1940 it insured loans for only about 25 Black households, while HOLC had lent to hundreds. [cite:ad6_chifed_rose] Both findings describe exclusion by federal agencies; they differ on which agency's lines did the work. The difference matters for anyone using the HOLC maps as a stand-in for the whole system, because the maps may not have been its main instrument.

The GI Bill and Levittown

The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, the GI Bill, offered returning veterans guaranteed loans for homes, farms and businesses, and paid for college or training. Its text did not mention race. Its administration was local: banks made the loans, and state and local offices handled much of the rest. The political scientist Ira Katznelson argues that Southern members of Congress, who chaired key committees, shaped the law so that local control could preserve the racial order of the region. His best-known figure comes from a 1947 survey by Ebony magazine of thirteen Mississippi cities: of 3,229 home, business and farm loans guaranteed under the GI Bill there that year, two went to Black veterans. [cite:ad6_katznelson] [cite:ad6_snopes_gi] The education record is more mixed, and the strongest study of it supports Katznelson for the South only. Economists Sarah Turner and John Bound found that the GI Bill raised college attainment for Black men born outside the South by about 0.4 years, comparable to the gain of about 0.3 years for white veterans, but produced few gains for Black men from the South, where the bill widened the gap with white veterans. [cite:ad6_turnerbound]

Levittown, on Long Island, is the postwar suburb the textbooks use as the picture of the Dream, and its record shows both halves of the design at once. Levitt & Sons began building in the spring of 1947 and had built 17,447 houses there by November 1951; they sold for under $8,000, with 5 per cent down, and veterans could buy with nothing down. [cite:ad6_audit_lipress_levitt] The standard lease, clause 25, required that no home "be used or occupied by any person other than members of the Caucasian race". [cite:ad6_nmaahc_levitt] [cite:ad6_audit_lipress_levitt] In 1948 the Supreme Court ruled in Shelley v. Kraemer that courts could not enforce such covenants, but the ruling did not stop private sellers and agents from refusing to sell, and the area remained almost entirely white for decades: the census counted 57 Black residents among 65,276 in 1960 and 387 among 53,067 in 2000. [cite:ad6_prrac_timeline] [cite:ad6_audit_sundown_levitt]

Federal design also shaped who gained within white America. Economists at the Federal Reserve Board, looking at home equity in the mid-century, found that white homeownership in the bottom third of the income distribution was flat from 1947 to 1960 while it rose substantially in the upper two thirds, and that FHA loans were held by 13.4 per cent of bottom-third homeowners against 20.5 per cent of the top third. [cite:ad6_fed_frydman] The programmes reached the middle class and above most easily; lower-income families often could not raise even the reduced down payment.

The gap the design left behind

The Fair Housing Act of 1968 made discrimination in sale and rental illegal, and the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 gave it an enforcement mechanism. [cite:ad6_prrac_timeline] The ownership gap those laws were meant to close has not closed. In 1960, 65 per cent of white households and 38 per cent of Black households owned their homes, a gap of 27 percentage points; in 2022 the figures were 74.6 and 45.3 per cent, a gap of about 29. [cite:ad6_stateline_gap] In the second quarter of 2026 the Census Bureau put non-Hispanic white homeownership at 74.5 per cent and Black homeownership at 45.4 per cent: 74.5 minus 45.4 is a gap of 29.1 points. [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226] Both rates rose over the six decades; the distance between them did not shrink. Part Thirteen sets out the documented causes of the gap and the disputes over their relative weight. [scene:ad13_black_americans|Part Thirteen: Black Americans and the Dream]

Zoning: the friction that stayed

Zoning is the local rule that says what may be built where. Its legal foundation is Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty (1926), in which the Supreme Court held that a town could use its police power to keep apartment buildings out of neighbourhoods of houses; Justice George Sutherland's opinion said that in such neighbourhoods "very often the apartment house is a mere parasite". [cite:ad6_audit_euclid] Zoning that permits only one detached house per lot is not racial on its face. Its effect on supply is the subject of a large literature. Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko argue that where house prices sit well above the cost of building, the gap works as a "regulatory tax" imposed by local rules, and that in many areas the tax appears larger than any reasonable estimate of the harm new building would cause neighbours. [cite:ad6_glaeser_gyourko] A 2019 New York Times analysis found that in many American cities it is illegal to build anything other than a detached single-family house on about three quarters of residential land. [cite:ad6_audit_uf_nyt2019] States and cities have started to change it: Minneapolis ended single-family-only zoning in late 2018, Oregon's legislature passed House Bill 2001 in 2019, California's SB 9 took effect in January 2022, and Washington's governor signed HB 1110 on 8 May 2023. [cite:ad6_audit_reason_zoning] [cite:ad6_audit_wgcu_or] [cite:ad6_audit_fox13_wa] The early results were small: Minneapolis gained 104 duplex and triplex units in the first two years, and a survey of 13 California cities found little or no building under SB 9, which suggests that zoning is one constraint among several, alongside land, construction and financing costs. [cite:ad6_audit_reason_zoning] Part Fifteen of the US System vs Israel System volume compares these land rules with Israel's. [scene:us15_land|US System vs Israel System: land and planning]

Two kinds of friction therefore sit in the housing record from the start. The long amortising mortgage, federal insurance and the later fair-housing laws are designed friction that did roughly what they were built to do: they made ownership reachable on a wage. The racial underwriting rules, the covenants and the local administration of a nominally race-blind veterans' law were designed too, and documented in the agencies' own manuals; they were later outlawed, and the gap they helped open has persisted. The next section turns to what it costs to buy or rent a home now.

sections.h: Price and Rent: What a Home Costs a Working Household Now
sections.html:
The promise attached to the postwar mortgage was simple enough to put in a statute. The Housing Act of 1949 set the national goal of "a decent home and a suitable living environment for every American family". [cite:ad6_prrac_timeline] The working version that followed was that a household with steady earnings could buy a house in early adulthood, pay it down over a career and own it outright by retirement, while renting was a stage on the way. This section measures that version against the current record with four numbers: how many years of income a home costs, how much of the household it takes to carry the loan, how old buyers are when they first manage it, and what renters pay meanwhile. A fifth question, whether large investors are buying up the houses, is answered at the end, because it is the most widely repeated explanation and the record on it is narrower than the claim.

Years of income: the price-to-income ratio

The simplest test of affordability divides the median price of a home by the median household income. A median is the middle value: half of homes cost more, half less, and the same for incomes. Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies (JCHS) computes this ratio each year for existing single-family homes. Across 1980 to 1999 it stayed between 3.1 and 3.4; it was 3.2 in 1988. It climbed to 4.7 in 2005 during the housing bubble, fell to 3.3 in 2011 after the crash, and stood at 4.2 in 2017. [cite:ad6_jchs_2018] It was 4.1 in 2019 and 5.0 in 2024. [cite:us14_jchs_pti] Dividing 5.0 by 3.2 gives 1.56: a typical home now costs a little over one and a half times as many years of the typical household's income as it did in the 1990s. Between 2019 and 2024 alone, median single-family prices rose 48 per cent while median income rose 22 per cent. [cite:us14_jchs_pti]

Two cautions keep that number honest. First, the ratio did not "double", as a widely repeated figure holds; it rose by roughly half. Second, JCHS has revised its own series between editions: a January 2024 release put the 2022 ratio at a record 5.6, while the October 2025 release describes 2024's 5.0 as nearly matching or returning to the record. [cite:ad6_jchs_2024] [cite:ad6_jchs_2025] The editions agree on the shape, a long plateau near 3 followed by a climb to about 5, and differ on the exact peak. National averages also hide a wide spread: in 2024 the ratio was over 12 in San Jose, 10.8 in Los Angeles and 7.3 in New York, but 2.9 in Akron and 2.8 in Toledo. [cite:us14_jchs_pti] In much of the country a house still costs about what it cost relative to income a generation ago; in the large coastal metros where many of the best-paid jobs are, it does not.

Carrying the loan: the interest rate

A buyer does not pay the price; a buyer pays the mortgage. The monthly cost of a 30-year fixed loan depends on the price and on the interest rate. On 15 October 2026 the average 30-year rate in Freddie Mac's weekly survey was 7.40 per cent, against 6.27 per cent a year earlier. [cite:ad6_pmms] By the standard amortisation formula, each $100,000 borrowed for 30 years costs about $617 a month in principal and interest at 6.27 per cent and about $692 at 7.40 per cent; at 3 per cent it would cost about $422. The same house therefore costs a new buyer about 64 per cent more each month at today's rate than at 3 per cent ($692 divided by $422 is 1.64), before taxes and insurance. Insurance itself has risen sharply: JCHS reports that average monthly home insurance premiums rose 72 per cent from 2019 to 2025. [cite:ad6_nlihc_son26] Among existing owners, about 24 per cent, or 20.7 million households, spent more than 30 per cent of income on housing in 2024, up 4 million since 2019, and in March 2026 only 23 per cent of homes listed for sale were affordable to a household earning $75,000 or less, against 49 per cent in March 2019. [cite:us14_novoco_jchs2026]

Who gets in, and when

The share of American households that own their home was 65.0 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, the same as a year earlier and below its peak of 69.2 per cent in 2004 and the 25-year average of 66.3 per cent. [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226] [cite:us15_nahb_q226] Over the longer run the rate has moved within a narrow band: about 63 to 66 per cent from 1965 through the mid-1990s, a rise to 69 in the mid-2000s, a fall to about 63 in 2016 and a recovery to 65. [cite:ad6_fred_hor] Among households headed by someone under 35 the rate was 35.2 per cent, down from 36.4 per cent a year earlier. [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226]

The figure most quoted about young buyers comes from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), the realtors' trade association. Its 2025 survey of recent buyers found that first-time buyers made up 21 per cent of purchases between July 2024 and June 2025, the lowest on record, and that their median age was 40, the highest; repeat buyers' median age was 62. [cite:ad6_nar_2025] The survey's method limits what the number can show. NAR mailed questionnaires to 173,250 recent buyers and received 6,103 usable answers, an adjusted response rate of 3.5 per cent. [cite:ad6_nar_2025] It counts only people who actually bought in that year, so its median age describes buyers, not the typical age at which Americans first own; in a year when many younger households are priced out, the buyers who remain are older partly because of who dropped out. The Census under-35 rate, drawn from a large household survey, points the same direction with a smaller move. It does not follow, and should not be said, that a typical buyer now finishes paying a 30-year loan at 70: many owners sell, refinance or repay early, and NAR's buyers are not a sample of the population.

Renting: the burden in the middle

A household is "cost-burdened", in the standard definition used by housing researchers, when it spends more than 30 per cent of its income on housing. In 2024 a record 22.7 million renter households, 49 per cent of all renters, were cost-burdened. [cite:ad6_nlihc_son26] The low-rent stock shrank at the same time: units renting for under $1,000 a month fell 30 per cent, from 8.3 million in 2014 to 5.8 million in 2024, while units at $1,000 or more rose 46 per cent and those over $2,000 doubled. [cite:ad6_nlihc_son26] Rent is the cost that most directly blocks the path to ownership, because every month of high rent is a month of savings not made toward a down payment.

Here the record also shows the market working as the textbook says it should. After a wave of apartment construction, national rents fell 0.5 per cent in the year to the first quarter of 2026, and they fell in most Southern and Western markets, where most of the new building went up, while they rose in most Midwestern and Northeastern markets. [cite:ad6_nlihc_son26] Asking rents for professionally managed apartments were still 29 per cent above their 2020 level. [cite:ad6_nlihc_son26] Where cities allowed supply to expand, prices responded; that is consistent with the argument, set out in the previous section, that local building rules act as a tax on housing in the places where prices sit far above the cost of construction. [cite:ad6_glaeser_gyourko]

The investor question

A widely repeated claim holds that Wall Street firms are buying up America's houses and pricing families out. The record supports a narrower version. Large investors in single-family rental homes are a creation of the 2008 crash: in late 2011 no investor owned 1,000 or more such homes, while by 2015 institutional investors held an estimated 170,000 to 300,000. [cite:ad6_gao_sfr] By 2022, 32 institutional investors owned about 450,000 homes, the five largest nearly 300,000. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) put that at about 2 per cent of the nation's single-family rental stock, but about 25 per cent in the Atlanta metro. [cite:ad6_nlihc_gao] The Congressional Research Service, surveying estimates in June 2026, puts institutional owners at roughly 3 to 5 per cent of single-family rental homes nationally, and a smaller share of all single-family homes; by the Census Bureau's 2024 rental-housing survey, about three quarters of the 15.7 million one-unit rentals belonged to owners with ten or fewer properties, and under 2 per cent to owners with more than 100. [cite:ad6_crs_inst]

Two things explain why the claim feels larger than the stock figures. Investors of all sizes, most of them small, bought about 30 per cent of single-family homes sold in December 2025 by one data firm's count, against about 18 per cent in 2018, while large and very large investors accounted for about 3 per cent each; and the large firms' holdings are concentrated in Sunbelt cities, where GAO found they make up a large portion of the single-family rental market. [cite:ad6_crs_inst] [cite:ad6_gao_sfr] The research on effects is mixed. GAO's review found that institutional investors may have contributed to rising prices and rents, and may also have helped stabilise neighbourhoods after the crash; a 2026 GAO study found that population growth and other market fundamentals drove rent increases in six metros; other studies link investor activity to higher prices and reduced access for first-time buyers. [cite:ad6_gao_sfr] [cite:ad6_crs_inst]

The federal government has now acted on the claim. President Trump's Executive Order 14376 of 20 January 2026 directed federal housing agencies to stop financing or facilitating purchases by large institutional investors and asked Treasury to define the term; it did not itself ban purchases. [cite:ad6_dechert_eo] Congress then passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, signed on 11 July 2026, which bars any investor controlling 350 or more single-family homes from buying more, with exemptions for build-to-rent, new and renovated homes, foreclosures and over-55 communities, and civil penalties of $1 million or three times the purchase price, whichever is greater. [cite:ad6_mayer_road] [cite:ad6_crs_inst] As of October 2026 the ban had not yet taken effect: it begins 180 days after enactment, on about 7 January 2027, and expires after 15 years. Since build-to-rent homes are exempt and made up 11 per cent of new single-family homes in 2025, the law caps one channel of investor growth rather than investor ownership as such. [cite:ad6_nlihc_son26]

The cost record, in sum, shows the designed core of the housing Dream intact and its price stretched. The 30-year loan still works; ownership rates sit near their long-run band; and where supply grew, rents fell. But a home costs about half again as many years of income as in the 1990s, the monthly cost of borrowing has risen, buyers are older, and half of renters pay more than the federal benchmark. Part Fourteen of the US System vs Israel System volume compares these measures with Israel's. [scene:us14_housing|US System vs Israel System: housing against income] The next section turns to the people for whom renting is not a stage but a trap.

The charts below plot the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; each caption names the source and definition.

sections.h: Eviction and the Traps: When Housing Extracts
sections.html:
For most owners, the house is the asset the Dream promised: a store of savings that grows while the family lives in it. For a large minority of households, housing works the other way. Rent takes a growing share of income, a court filing follows the tenant from one application to the next, and some buyers who cannot get a mortgage sign contracts under which they can pay for years and own nothing. This section sets out four of these mechanisms in turn: the eviction filing and the record it leaves, tenant screening, the contract for deed, and shared pricing software. Each is scoped to what the documents show, and each is set beside the evidence that cuts against the strongest reading of it.

The scale of eviction

An eviction filing is a landlord's lawsuit asking a court to remove a tenant; it is not the same as an eviction, because many cases are settled, dismissed or end with the tenant paying. A study of court records by Ashley Gromis and colleagues, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2022, estimated that landlords filed about 3.6 million eviction cases a year on average between 2000 and 2018, against about 2.7 million households; the difference reflects landlords filing repeatedly against the same tenants. The share of renter households threatened with eviction peaked at about 7.5 per cent in 2005 to 2008 and fell to about 6 per cent in recent years. [cite:ad6_nlihc_pnas] The lab's tracking system, which covers 48 cities and states holding about a third of renter households but is not a national sample, counted 1.23 million filings in 2025, down from 1.26 million in 2024 and 3.2 per cent below the 2023–24 average. The filing rate across those sites was 8.0 per cent, about one filing for every 13 renter households. [cite:ad6_el_2025]

The sociologist Matthew Desmond made eviction a national subject with Evicted: Poverty and Profit in the American City (2016), which followed eight families in Milwaukee's poorest neighbourhoods.
