[cite:ad6_audit_prh_evicted] It won the 2017 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction; the board's citation called evictions "less a consequence than a cause of poverty". [cite:ad6_pulitzer] That causal claim is the contested part. Economists John Eric Humphries, Nicholas Mader, Daniel Tannenbaum and Winnie van Dijk linked nearly two decades of Cook County court records to credit-bureau data and used the random assignment of cases to more and less lenient judges to separate cause from circumstance. They found that eviction does reduce tenants' access to credit and their spending on durable goods for several years, but that these effects are small next to the financial strain that rises sharply before a case is filed, for tenants who are evicted and for those who are not. [cite:ad6_audit_nber_humphries] On that evidence, eviction deepens hardship more than it creates it. On the count itself, a group of housing researchers and organisers argued in Shelterforce in 2018 that Princeton's Eviction Lab undercounts evictions, a gap they tied to its not working with local housing-justice organisations. [cite:ad6_shelterforce] The size of the count and the direction of cause are both disputed; the existence of millions of filings a year is not.

The record that follows the tenant

A filing does not end when the case does. Court records are bought in bulk by tenant-screening companies, which sell landlords reports on applicants. Adam Porton, Ashley Gromis and Matthew Desmond examined more than 3.6 million eviction records from 12 states and found that, on average, about 22 per cent contained ambiguous information on how the case was resolved or misstated the tenant's history. [cite:ad6_porton] A figure often attributed to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), that it found "22 per cent of eviction records are false", misstates the source: the CFPB's November 2022 report on the screening market cites that 22 per cent from the Porton study, and itself says there is "no definitive analysis of the frequency of matching errors" in the industry. [cite:ad6_cfpb_tbc]

What the CFPB report does document is how errors arise. Some screeners search court records using only partial names, a practice it calls "wildcard" matching; some include sealed records; a single case moved between courthouses can appear as two evictions. Automated pulls of court records rarely cost the screener more than $1, against about $7 for a manual check, and only five of the 17 firms the bureau examined advertised manual verification. [cite:ad6_cfpb_tbc] The report also notes that serial filings exceed 20 per cent of cases in at least four states and cites a Federal Reserve study finding that corporate landlords file at "substantially higher" rates. [cite:ad6_cfpb_tbc] In October 2023 the Federal Trade Commission and the CFPB charged TransUnion's rental-screening unit with reporting single cases as several evictions, omitting dismissals and labelling landlords' claims as court judgments; the companies agreed to pay $15 million, $11 million of it to consumers, the largest tenant-screening recovery in the FTC's history. [cite:ad6_ftc_turss]

The contract for deed: paying without owning

A contract for deed, also called a land contract, is an arrangement in which the seller keeps legal title to the house while the buyer makes a down payment and monthly instalments; the buyer receives the deed only after the last payment, pays the taxes, insurance and repairs meanwhile, and builds no equity along the way. One missed payment can mean eviction and the loss of everything paid. [cite:ad6_duke_plunder] It flourished where mortgages were refused. A 2019 study by Duke University's Samuel DuBois Cook Center on Social Equity and Chicago partners, built on the case files of the Contract Buyers League, a group of West Side homeowners who sued in the late 1960s, estimated that 75 to 95 per cent of homes sold to Black families in Chicago in the 1950s and 1960s were sold on contract. Sellers marked the homes up 84 per cent over what they had paid, and buyers paid about $587 a month more, in 2019 dollars, than they would have under a fairly priced FHA or conventional loan. [cite:ad6_duke_plunder] [cite:ad6_wbez_plunder]

The device returned after the 2008 crash. Harbour Portfolio Advisors bought foreclosed homes in bulk, mostly from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and between 2012 and 2016 resold them on contracts for deed to buyers unable to obtain conventional financing; it held hundreds of homes in Atlanta and thousands nationwide. [cite:ad6_cfpb_harbour] [cite:ad6_atlegal_harbour] In Atlanta, homes bought for as little as $10,000 were resold for $40,000 to $50,000 at about 10 per cent interest over 30 years, and Atlanta Legal Aid found the sales concentrated in census tracts that were 86 per cent African American; its suit on behalf of 17 buyers was settled with restructured loans and damages. [cite:ad6_atlegal_harbour] The CFPB's 2020 settlement with Harbour concerned credit-reporting practices, not the contracts themselves, and carried penalties of $25,000 and $10,000. [cite:ad6_cfpb_harbour] A Pew Charitable Trusts survey published in 2022 estimated that about 36 million Americans had used some form of alternative home financing, including land contracts, and about 7 million were in such arrangements at the time; most such deals are not recorded with any public office and are not regulated as mortgages are. [cite:ad6_npr_pew] This is the clearest case in the housing record of captured friction: an arrangement that exists to serve buyers outside the mortgage system and, where it is unregulated, transfers their payments to the seller.

Pricing by software: the RealPage case

Rents can also be raised by coordination. On 23 August 2024 the Justice Department and eight states sued RealPage, a Texas company whose software recommends rents to landlords. The complaint alleged that competing landlords fed the software nonpublic data on their own rents, that RealPage's "auto accept" feature and pricing advisers encouraged them to follow its recommendations, and that the software tended to push rents up and discourage concessions; it alleged RealPage held about 80 per cent of the market for such software for apartment buildings. [cite:ad6_doj_realpage24] These were allegations, and the company's later settlement with the government contains no admission of wrongdoing. [cite:ad6_wsoc_realpage]

Under the proposed terms filed on 24 November 2025, RealPage agreed to stop using competitors' nonpublic data in its live pricing, to train its models only on such data at least 12 months old, to stop modelling at any level narrower than a state, to remove features that limited rent cuts, and to accept a court-appointed monitor. [cite:ad6_doj_realpage25] A federal judge in North Carolina approved the judgment in May 2026. [cite:ad6_wsoc_realpage] Separately, in the private class action brought by renters in Tennessee, 41 landlords agreed to pay $359,925,000, and the court gave final approval in October 2026; no court has ruled on how much the software raised rents. [cite:ad6_mlex_class] New York's state ban on algorithmic rent-setting was blocked by a federal preliminary injunction in late September 2026 while RealPage's free-speech challenge proceeds. [cite:ad6_dive_ny]

The end of the line

Homelessness is the point at which these mechanisms end for some households. HUD's count on a single night in January 2025 found 745,652 people homeless, 266,320 of them unsheltered, down 3 per cent from the record 771,480 of 2024; chronically homeless individuals reached a record 155,750, while homeless veterans fell to 32,495, the lowest since 2009. [cite:ad6_crs_homeless26] [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] The count is a one-night snapshot and excludes people at imminent risk of losing their housing. HUD's current leadership attributed the 2025 decline to falls in "Sanctuary Cities" and said the "housing first" approach had failed; that is the department's stated position, and Part Fourteen weighs the evidence on it. [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] [scene:ad14_homelessness|Part Fourteen: homelessness]

Interpretation, not finding: the eviction machine

The Sophia platform reads these mechanisms together as an "eviction machine": a system in which rent extracts income, filings and screening records lock tenants out of better housing, and the loss falls on the same households that federal policy once excluded from ownership. Read through this lens, the contract for deed and algorithmic pricing are two forms of the same transfer, from people without access to credit to those who hold property. The strongest counter-readings are these: the mechanisms have different owners and different legal status, and no document shows them operating as one design; eviction filings fell in 2025 and rents fell where supply grew; and each mechanism above has drawn a legal answer, from the Fair Housing Act to the TransUnion and RealPage settlements, which is the system correcting itself, if slowly. The record supports the narrower claim that each mechanism, where unregulated, moves money from tenants and excluded buyers to landlords, sellers and data firms.

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: Education: The Credential and the Debt
chapters.intro: Part Seven follows the asset Americans are told to buy before any other: education. It begins with how public schools are paid for, largely by a tax on the value of local property, and with the 1973 Supreme Court decision that left that design in place, then sets the main measures of the resulting funding gaps beside the evidence that state aid narrows them and that money spent on schools shows up in children's adult earnings. It then measures what a year of college costs in real dollars, before and after grants, how far the federal Pell Grant has fallen behind those costs, what happened to borrowers at for-profit colleges, and how degree requirements spread to jobs that did not need them, and it weighs all of this against the college wage premium. It ends with the debt: how large it is, how the law made student loans almost impossible to discharge in bankruptcy, step by step from 1976 to 2005, how defaulted loans are collected, and where that stands as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: Part Seven established that the education promise is real on average and fragile at specific points. Public schools are free to attend, but about 27 cents of every school dollar comes from local property tax, the Supreme Court held in 1973 that unequal funding raises no federal constitutional issue, and the main studies find that districts serving the poorest pupils and most students of color receive less state and local money than their needs require, even though state aid on average more than offsets the local gap for poor pupils. [cite:us17_census_fy2024] [cite:ad7_edweek_rodriguez] [cite:ad7_edtrust_2018] [cite:ad7_chingos_ednext] Real published tuition at public four-year colleges doubled from 1995–96 to 2025–26 while net tuition has fallen by almost half since 2012–13, and the maximum Pell Grant, which covered about three-quarters of a public college year in the late 1970s, covers 28.6 per cent today. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] [cite:ad7_ace_pell] A bachelor's degree still brings about 75 per cent higher lifetime earnings, but defaults are concentrated among borrowers who did not finish or attended for-profit and two-year colleges, and degree requirements filter workers out of jobs that do not need a degree. [cite:ad7_cew_payoff] [cite:ad7_ly_press] [cite:ad7_hbs_skills] Since 1976 a sequence of laws, ending with the private-loan change of 2005, has made student debt almost impossible to discharge in bankruptcy; 9.3 million borrowers owing $234 billion were in default in June 2026, and as of October 2026 collections remained paused with no restart date, while a 2022 hardship process has produced discharges in nearly every case decided. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] [cite:us17_ci_defaults] [cite:ad7_ci_garnish] [cite:ad7_doj_2024] Part Eight turns to health care, the system inside the system, where the cost of staying well is set by insurers, hospitals and law. [scene:ad8_costs_and_coverage|Part Eight: Health]

sections.h: Schools Paid for by the House Next Door
sections.html:
The education promise begins long before college. Civics and economics standards teach that investment in "human capital", the skills and knowledge a person carries, raises productivity and living standards, and that a public school system open to every child is how a society makes that investment fairly. [cite:ad1_c3] [cite:ad1_cee2010] [scene:ad1_as_taught|The Dream as taught] What the standards do not usually explain is how the money for a given school is raised. In most of the United States a large part of it comes from a tax on the value of the land and buildings in the school district, so the price of the houses around a school sets much of what that school can spend. This section shows how that mechanism works, how the Supreme Court came to leave it in place in 1973, what the gaps it produces look like by the main published measures, and where the record shows that state money has narrowed them.

How the money is raised

In the 2024 fiscal year American public schools took in $994.9 billion. States provided 45.2 per cent, local sources 43.2 per cent and the federal government 11.6 per cent, and property taxes made up 63.3 per cent of local revenue. [cite:us17_census_fy2024] The arithmetic shows the weight of the property tax in the whole system: 43.2 per cent of $994.9 billion is about $429.8 billion of local money, and 63.3 per cent of that is about $272 billion, or roughly 27 cents of every dollar spent on public schools. Average current spending was $17,619 per pupil, but the average hides a range that runs from $31,918 in New York to $11,060 in Idaho. [cite:us17_census_fy2024] A school's local money depends on two things: the tax rate voters or officials set, and the taxable value of the property in its district. A district with expensive homes, offices or industry can raise a great deal at a modest rate; a district of low-value homes can tax heavily and still raise little. State aid formulas exist to offset this, and the federal government adds a smaller share, but the local base comes first and shapes everything that follows.

This is designed friction, not a hidden one. Local funding of schools by local property was a deliberate feature of American public education, defended as local control: the people who pay for a school decide how much to spend on it. The problem is that the base each community can tax is not equal, and that the value of housing was itself shaped by federal and local rules about who could live where. The federal underwriting manual of 1938 told appraisers that schools attended in large numbers by "inharmonious" groups lowered the value of a neighbourhood, tying school composition to property value in the government's own lending rules. [cite:ad6_fha_manual] [scene:ad6_redlining_to_suburbs|Part Six: redlining and the suburbs]

San Antonio v. Rodriguez, 1973

The constitutional test came from San Antonio. Parents in the Edgewood district, a poor district of about 22,000 pupils, sued over the Texas system. Edgewood taxed its property at the highest rate in the area and raised about $26 per pupil from it; Alamo Heights, a wealthier district of about 5,000 pupils, raised $333 per pupil at a lower rate. With state and federal money added, Edgewood spent $356 per pupil and Alamo Heights $594, a gap of $238, or 67 per cent more for each Alamo Heights child. [cite:ad7_edweek_rodriguez] [cite:ad7_aba_funding] A federal district court found the system unconstitutional. On 21 March 1973 the Supreme Court reversed it, five votes to four. [cite:ad7_wiki_rodriguez]

Justice Lewis Powell, writing for the majority, held that education "is not among the rights afforded explicit protection" by the federal Constitution, that the Texas scheme did not single out a definable class of poor people for disadvantage, and that the state's system therefore needed only a rational relationship to a legitimate purpose, which local control supplied. He left one door open: a system that produced an "absolute denial of educational opportunities" might be different. [cite:ad7_edweek_rodriguez] [cite:ad7_wiki_rodriguez] Justice Thurgood Marshall's dissent called the decision "a retreat from our historic commitment to equality of educational opportunity", and noted that state constitutions remained open to challenge. [cite:ad7_edweek_rodriguez]

That note set the course of the next half-century. Because the federal route was closed, school-finance fights moved to state courts under state constitutions, and most states have faced such suits. [cite:ad7_aba_funding] In Texas itself the state Supreme Court ruled in 1989, in a case led by Edgewood, that children in poor and rich districts must have "a substantially equal opportunity" to school funds; Texas courts found the system unconstitutional again in 1991, 1992 and 2005 and upheld it in 1995 and 2016. [cite:ad7_edweek_rodriguez] [cite:ad7_aba_funding] A 2020 federal appeals panel suggested a federal right to basic literacy might exist, but the full court vacated the ruling after Michigan settled. [cite:ad7_edweek_rodriguez] As of October 2026, Rodriguez remains the federal law: there is no federal constitutional right to equal school funding.

How large are the gaps?

Measuring the gap depends on what is compared, and the main studies compare different things. The Education Trust, an advocacy organisation for low-income students and students of color, compared state and local money only, leaving out federal funds, and found in 2018 that the highest-poverty districts received about $1,000, or 7 per cent, less per pupil than the lowest-poverty ones; after adjusting for the extra cost of educating children in poverty, the gap was about $2,000, or 16 per cent. Districts serving the most students of color received about $1,800, or 13 per cent, less. [cite:ad7_edtrust_2018] EdBuild, a school-finance research group, compared districts by racial composition after adjusting for local costs and reported in 2019 that predominantly white districts received $23 billion more than districts serving mostly students of color, about $2,226 less per pupil in the average nonwhite district. It found that high-poverty districts serving mostly students of color were about $1,600 per pupil below the national average, against about $130 for high-poverty, mostly white districts, and it tied part of the pattern to district size: mostly white districts averaged just over 1,500 pupils, mostly nonwhite ones more than 10,000, so small affluent districts could keep their tax base to themselves. [cite:ad7_npr_edbuild]

The Urban Institute measured the same question a third way, asking what the average poor pupil's district spends compared with the average non-poor pupil's, counting all sources. On 2013–14 data, the districts poor pupils attended received $12,961 per pupil against $12,640 for non-poor pupils, about 2.5 per cent more. The local money alone was about 15 per cent lower for poor pupils, a gap that had narrowed from 18 per cent in 1994–95, and state money about ten percentage points higher, more than closing it. [cite:ad7_chingos_ednext] The authors also found that many states with progressive formulas on paper did not achieve them in practice. [cite:ad7_urban_2017] Their method was later revised to correct how charter-school money was counted, which turned Pennsylvania from a state where poor pupils received 4 per cent more to one where they received 3 per cent less. [cite:ad7_chalkbeat_urban]

These findings are not contradictory. Read together they say that the local property-tax base is strongly unequal, that state aid, and to a lesser degree federal aid, offsets most or all of it on average, and that the offset is weaker in some states and for districts serving mostly Black and Hispanic pupils, where segregation by district line keeps poor children concentrated together. They also say that "equal dollars" is not "equal opportunity": children in poverty cost more to educate to the same standard, which is why a district can receive slightly more money and still be underfunded relative to need. The Education Law Center reported in 2021 that 14 states spent more per pupil in low-poverty districts than in high-poverty ones; in Nevada the figures were $12,798 against $8,731. [cite:ad7_aba_funding]

Does the money matter?

A long-running argument in school finance held that spending had little relation to results. The strongest recent evidence comes from court-ordered reforms that changed spending for reasons unrelated to a district's own choices, which allows a cleaner test. C. Kirabo Jackson, Rucker Johnson and Claudia Persico followed children who grew up through such reforms and found that a 10 per cent increase in per-pupil spending in every one of a child's twelve school years led to about 0.27 more years of completed education, 7.25 per cent higher adult wages and a 3.67 percentage-point lower chance of being poor in a given adult year, with much larger effects for children from low-income families. [cite:ad7_jjp_nber] That result is why the funding gap is a mechanism of the Dream and not only a budget question: money spent on a child's school shows up in that child's adult earnings.

The results the system produces have weakened recently across the board. On the 2024 national assessment, twelfth-grade mathematics scores were the lowest since 2005 and the gap between high and low performers the widest on record, and on the international PISA test of 2025 the United States had the largest gap between its strongest and weakest readers of any participating country. [cite:us17_chalkbeat_naep] [cite:us17_edweek_pisa2025] Both patterns fit a system in which where a child lives shapes what is spent on the child, though neither test result by itself shows how much of the spread comes from funding rather than from family income, the pandemic or other causes. [scene:us17_schools|US vs Israel: schools, money and scores]

Where it works as promised

The taught version holds in important respects. Public schooling remains free at the point of use for every child, and on the Urban Institute's all-sources measure the average poor pupil attends a district with slightly more money, not less, because state formulas push money towards weaker tax bases. [cite:ad7_chingos_ednext] The local-revenue gap between poor and non-poor pupils narrowed between 1994–95 and 2013–14, and in 35 states the formula adds money for low-income pupils. [cite:ad7_chingos_ednext] State courts, after Rodriguez, forced repeated reforms in Texas and elsewhere, and the evidence from those reforms is that added money reached children and changed their adult lives. [cite:ad7_aba_funding] [cite:ad7_jjp_nber] The mechanism is unequal by design, but the correction built on top of it is real and measurable; the record shows where it falls short, district by district and state by state, rather than a system in which the correction never happens.

sections.h: The Price of the Credential
sections.html:
The second half of the education promise is college. The national standards teach that investment in human capital raises living standards, and the civic version that follows from it is simple: a young person who works hard in school can go to college, the public colleges and federal grants will keep it within reach, and the degree will pay for itself. [cite:ad1_c3] [cite:ad1_cee2010] This section sets that version beside the price record, the record of the federal grant meant to keep college open to low-income students, the record of the for-profit colleges that grew on federal aid, and the spread of degree requirements to jobs that did not need them. It ends with the strongest evidence that the promise still holds: what a degree is worth.

What college costs, in real dollars

Prices in this section are in "real" or inflation-adjusted dollars: each year's price is restated in 2025 dollars so that a change shows how much more or less a year of college costs after general inflation is removed. Two prices matter. The published price, or "sticker price", is the tuition and fees a college lists. The net price is what students pay after grants and scholarships, which do not have to be repaid. By the College Board's annual survey, average published tuition and fees for in-state students at a public four-year college were $5,940 in 1995–96 and $9,050 in 2005–06, rose to a peak of $13,150 in 2019–20 and 2020–21, and then fell to $11,950 in 2025–26, all in 2025 dollars. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] The 30-year rise is a doubling: $11,950 divided by $5,940 is 2.01. Since the peak the real price has fallen about 9 per cent, as increases in current dollars stayed below inflation. Private non-profit four-year colleges averaged $45,000 in 2025–26 and public two-year colleges $4,150. [cite:us14_cb_trends2025]

A widely repeated figure holds that college tuition has risen more than 1,200 per cent since 1980, faster than any other cost. Figures of that kind compare tuition in current dollars, without removing the general rise in prices over the same decades, against an inflation index; in real terms the published in-state price at public four-year colleges roughly doubled over the 30 years the College Board's current series covers. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] The doubling is real and large. The larger figure is not a measure of it.

Net tuition tells a different story from 2012 onwards. For first-time, full-time in-state students at public four-year colleges, average net tuition and fees peaked at $4,450 in 2012–13 and fell to an estimated $2,300 in 2025–26, a fall of 48 per cent, as federal, state and institutional grants grew. At public two-year colleges, the average grant now exceeds tuition and fees, leaving a net figure of minus $1,190 that students can put towards other costs. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] Tuition is not the whole bill. Adding housing and food, the average budget for an in-state student living on campus at a public four-year college was $25,850 in 2025–26, and for most students living costs, not tuition, are now the larger share of what must be found or borrowed. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25]

Part of the rise in sticker prices traces to states. Public colleges are financed mainly by state appropriations and by tuition, so the two tend to move against each other. By the State Higher Education Executive Officers' count, education appropriations reached $12,082 per full-time student in 2025, 9.2 per cent above their 2008 level after inflation; the 2025 figure was down 1.0 per cent on 2024, the first per-student fall since 2012. Students' own tuition provided 38.4 per cent of public colleges' education revenue. [cite:ad7_shef_fy25] The College Board, using a broader measure of state and local funding, found it up 34 per cent per student after inflation between 2013–14 and 2023–24, to $11,680. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] The record shows per-student state support falling after 2008 and recovering after 2012, which matches the timing of the net-price decline above.

The Pell Grant, then and now

The federal Pell Grant is the main federal grant for low-income undergraduates. Its maximum award is set by Congress. In the late 1970s the maximum covered roughly three-quarters of the full cost of a year at a public four-year college, counting tuition, fees, room and board: 72 per cent in fiscal 1976 and 77 per cent in fiscal 1979. [cite:ad7_ace_pell] [cite:ad7_nasfaa_pell] The share fell below half in the late 1980s, reached 32 per cent in fiscal 2006, and stood at 34 per cent in 2010. [cite:ad7_ace_pell] The maximum has been $7,395 since 2023–24. Against the College Board's 2025–26 budget of tuition, fees, housing and food at a public four-year college, $25,850, it covers 28.6 per cent ($7,395 divided by $25,850). [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] The National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators, using federal cost-of-attendance data that also count books and other expenses, put the 2024–25 share at 27.2 per cent of $27,182. [cite:ad7_nasfaa_pell]

The grant did not shrink; costs outgrew it. The NASFAA brief converts the 1978 maximum of $1,400 into about $7,095 in 2026 dollars, so today's $7,395 buys about as much in general goods as the maximum did half a century ago, 4 per cent more. [cite:ad7_nasfaa_pell] What changed is the price of a year at college, which rose much faster than general prices. The gap between what the grant covers and what college costs is the space that loans came to fill. The 2025 reconciliation act, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, also made students ineligible for Pell if their family's calculated ability to pay, the Student Aid Index, is at least twice the maximum award. [cite:us17_unmc_obbba]

The for-profit colleges

The sharpest test of the promise came at for-profit colleges, companies that run schools for profit and draw much of their revenue from students' federal grants and loans. Average for-profit tuition was $16,030 in 2024–25, well above public four-year tuition. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] Adam Looney and Constantine Yannelis, in a paper for the Brookings Institution, traced the rise in student-loan defaults after 2000 to a change in who borrowed and where. For-profit borrowers were 18 per cent of borrowers starting repayment in 2000 and 31 per cent in 2011, about 930,000 people; with community-college borrowers they made up almost half of those starting repayment in 2011 and accounted for 70 per cent of the defaults among them. Within five years, 47 per cent of for-profit borrowers in the 2009 repayment group had defaulted, against 29 per cent in 1999. [cite:ad7_ly_press] [cite:ad7_ly_draft] The authors attributed the defaults to large borrowing at institutions with low completion rates, followed by weak earnings. [cite:ad7_ly_press] The finding cuts both ways for the taught version. It shows that the "student debt crisis" is concentrated: within two years of entering repayment, about 2 per cent of graduate borrowers and 8 per cent of traditional undergraduate borrowers had defaulted, against about 21 per cent of borrowers from for-profit and two-year colleges. [cite:ad7_ly_draft] It also shows that the federal aid system paid for a large expansion of programmes whose students often left with debt and without the earnings the promise assumed.

The credential requirement

The degree's value depends partly on employers demanding it. A 2017 study by Harvard Business School researchers led by Joseph Fuller, Dismissed by Degrees, estimated that 6.2 million jobs were at risk of "degree inflation", a rise in degree requirements beyond what the work needed. In job postings for production supervisors, 67 per cent asked for a college degree, while only 16 per cent of people already doing the job held one. Employers surveyed said they used the degree as a stand-in for hard skills (70 per cent) and soft skills (60 per cent). [cite:ad7_nysscpa_degrees] When many large employers and some states announced that they would drop degree requirements, a 2024 follow-up by Fuller's group and the Burning Glass Institute found that the change reached "not even 1 in 700 hires"; about 45 per cent of the firms changed in name only, and nearly all real change came from a minority of firms. Where firms did hire workers without degrees into such roles, those workers earned about 25 per cent more than before and, at the leading firms, stayed longer than degree holders. [cite:ad7_hbs_skills] The requirement works as a filter that keeps a degree necessary for jobs that do not need its content, which adds to what non-graduates lose without adding to what graduates know.

The charts below plot the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; each caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised: the college wage premium

The strongest counter-evidence to the illusion reading is the earnings record. Georgetown University's Center on Education and the Workforce, using Census survey data for 2009–2019, estimated median lifetime earnings for full-time, full-year workers aged 25 to 64 at $1.6 million with a high-school diploma, $2.0 million with an associate degree and $2.8 million with a bachelor's degree, and found that bachelor's holders earn 75 per cent more over a career than they would with a diploma alone ($2.8 million divided by $1.6 million is 1.75). [cite:ad7_cew_payoff] The same study warns against reading the medians as a guarantee: at least a quarter of high-school graduates earn more than the typical associate-degree holder, and field of study and occupation matter as much as level. [cite:ad7_cew_payoff] Debt among graduates has also fallen. Of students who earned bachelor's degrees in 2023–24, 47 per cent had borrowed, owing $29,560 on average, against 56 per cent and $35,310 in inflation-adjusted dollars for the 2018–19 graduates. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25]

Read together, the record says the education promise is true on average for those who finish a four-year degree, and that the net price at public colleges has fallen for a decade. Where it fails, it fails at identifiable points: a grant that no longer covers most of a year's costs, programmes with low completion and weak earnings, and a credential demanded for work that does not use it. The next section follows what happens to the debt when the promise fails, and why that debt, unlike almost any other, is so hard to shed. [scene:ad7_student_debt_law|Student debt and the law] [scene:us17_higher|US vs Israel: universities, cost and debt]

sections.h: The Debt That Stays
sections.html:
When the promise of a degree fails, through a programme not finished, a field that did not pay or a life that went wrong, what remains is the loan. Student loans differ from almost every other debt an American family carries in one respect: since 1976 the law has made them hard to wipe out in bankruptcy, the legal process that lets a person who cannot pay start again. This section sets out how large the debt is, how the bankruptcy rule was built step by step, who documented it and who lobbied on it, how collection works without a court, and where the record stands as of October 2026.

How much is owed

Student loan balances almost tripled between 2004 and 2012, when the number of borrowers grew by about 70 per cent, and reached about $994 billion in mid-2013. [cite:us17_nyfed_2013] They passed $1.26 trillion in the second quarter of 2016, $1.48 trillion in 2019 and $1.59 trillion in 2022, and then grew more slowly. [cite:ad7_audit_nyfed2016] [cite:ad7_audit_nyfed2019] [cite:ad7_audit_cr2022] By the New York Federal Reserve's count, drawn from credit reports, they stood at $1.65 trillion in the second quarter of 2026, down $7 billion in the quarter and up $13 billion on the year. [cite:ad7_nyfed_pr] The federal government's own portfolio data, to 30 June 2026, covered 42.3 million borrowers and more than $1.7 trillion. Of these, more than 9.3 million borrowers owing $234 billion were in default, the status a federal loan reaches after a long run of missed payments: about 14 per cent of the $1.64 trillion the government manages directly. Defaults rose by about 1.6 million borrowers and $54 billion in the first half of 2026 alone, and about 1.5 million more borrowers were in late-stage delinquency. [cite:us17_ci_defaults] [cite:ad7_ci_defaults2]

The law, step by step

Before 1976 an educational loan could be discharged in bankruptcy like any other unsecured debt. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] The change began not with a lender but with a public body. Congress created the Commission on the Bankruptcy Laws of the United States in 1970, and in its 1973 report the commission recommended that government educational loans not be dischargeable until five years after repayment began, unless repaying would cause "undue hardship". [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] The federal education department of the time, Health, Education and Welfare, had urged a restriction after reports of graduates escaping their loans. [cite:ad7_iowa_lr] Congress adopted the five-year rule in the Education Amendments of 1976, as a new Section 439A of the Higher Education Act, and delayed its start by nearly a year, partly to await a study by the General Accounting Office. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699]

Two years later Congress wrote a new Bankruptcy Code. The House Judiciary Committee's bill would have made student loans dischargeable again, and its report stated that "less than 1% of all federally insured and guaranteed educational loans were discharged in bankruptcy". That figure is often attributed to the General Accounting Office; the Congressional Research Service traces it to the House report. Representative Allen Ertel, opposing the committee's change, warned that discharge would be "almost specifically designed to encourage fraud", and a floor amendment adopted by voice vote restored the bar, which became Section 523(a)(8) of the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1978. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] [cite:ad7_iowa_lr] The rule was written against a stated fear, of graduates filing as soon as they left school, that the numbers Congress had did not show to be common.

Each later change widened the rule or removed a way out. A 1979 amendment extended it from loans owed to a government unit to any loan "made, insured, or guaranteed by a governmental unit" or made under a programme it funded. [cite:ad7_pl96_56] In 1984 Congress removed the words "of higher education", so that loans from any non-profit institution were covered. In 1990 the five-year period became seven, and student loans were taken out of the broader discharge that Chapter 13 repayment plans had allowed. In 1991 the six-year time limit on collecting defaulted federal loans was abolished, so a defaulted federal loan can be pursued for life. [cite:ad7_clla_2022] [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] In 1997 the National Bankruptcy Review Commission recommended repealing the student-loan exception altogether; Congress went the other way, and the Higher Education Amendments of 1998, signed by President Bill Clinton, removed the time route entirely, leaving undue hardship as the only way to discharge a federal loan. The Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005, signed by President George W. Bush, extended the same protection to private student loans made by banks and other lenders. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699]

"Undue hardship" is not defined in the statute, so the courts defined it. Most follow the test set out by a federal appeals court in Brunner v. New York State Higher Education Services Corp. (1987): a borrower must show that repaying would leave them unable to keep a minimal standard of living, that this is likely to last for much of the repayment period, and that they have made good-faith efforts to repay. All three must be met. [cite:ad7_iowa_lr] [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] Applied strictly, the test asks borrowers to prove that their hardship will last, not only that it exists.

Who documented it, who lobbied, and what the record does not show

The documented origin of the rule is public: a congressional commission in 1973 and a floor vote in 1978. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] The industry's lobbying record belongs to a later period. Stephen Burd of the New America Foundation, who covered the issue for the Chronicle of Higher Education, reported that Sallie Mae, then the largest student lender, spent $9 million lobbying Congress between 1999 and 2005, the years the 2005 bankruptcy bill was under consideration, and that its political action committee gave more than $130,000 to members of the House and Senate judiciary committees; he also reported that no hearings were held on the private-loan provision. [cite:ad7_npr_burd] A New America analysis in 2007 went further on what is not known: nothing in the Congressional Record explains the change, and on who pushed for it, "No one seems to know". It noted that Sallie Mae's internal strategy document listed preserving the provision's benefits as its second priority, because the rule lets lenders "go to the front of the line" in bankruptcy. [cite:ad7_newamerica_2007] The lobbying spending is a documented fact; that it caused the 2005 change is an inference the public record does not establish, since the spending covered many issues and the provision's sponsors left no explanation.

Collection without a court, and the 2026 status

Most creditors must sue and win a judgment before they can take part of a debtor's wages. For defaulted federal student loans the government can order an employer to withhold up to 15 per cent of disposable pay without a court order, and the Treasury Offset Program can take tax refunds and part of Social Security benefits. [cite:us17_ci_defaults] [cite:ad7_ci_garnish] After warning notices went out in early January 2026, the Education Department paused these involuntary collections on 16 January, saying it needed time to put in place the repayment changes of the 2025 reconciliation act. [cite:ad7_natp_pause] [cite:ad7_collegeave_pause] [cite:ad7_invest_pause] The same act ended Grad PLUS loans for new graduate borrowers from 1 July 2026, capped graduate and parent borrowing, and replaced income-driven plans for new loans with a single Repayment Assistance Plan, which launched in July 2026. [cite:us17_unmc_obbba] The Biden administration's SAVE repayment plan, blocked in court, was ended by a settlement with Missouri and other states announced on 9 December 2025, moving about 7 million enrolled borrowers to other plans. [cite:ad7_npr_save] [cite:ad7_ci_save] Status as of October 2026: the department and the Treasury have said they plan to resume wage garnishment this autumn but have announced no date, and the government has not yet reported how many borrowers have joined the new plan. [cite:ad7_ci_garnish] [cite:ad7_ci_defaults2]

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

The bankruptcy door, nearly shut by statute, was opened somewhat by practice. On 17 November 2022 the Justice and Education departments adopted a standard process: a borrower fills in an attestation form on income, expenses and repayment efforts, the government checks it against its own records, and the Justice Department decides whether to recommend discharge to the judge, who decides. [cite:ad7_doj_2022] By the department's July 2024 count, 1,220 cases had been filed under it to March 2024; 96 per cent of borrowers used the form, and 98 per cent of the cases courts had decided ended in full or partial discharge. [cite:ad7_doj_2024] The department revised the form in May 2025 and the process remains in use as of October 2026, under an administration of the other party. [cite:ad7_ap_form] The numbers are small beside 9.3 million defaulted borrowers, but they show that when the government chose to read "undue hardship" more generously, the courts agreed. The debt is also concentrated: graduates of four-year programmes default at low rates, and fewer bachelor's graduates borrowed, and borrowed less, in 2023–24 than five years earlier. [cite:ad7_ly_draft] [cite:ad7_cb_trends25]

Interpretation, not finding: the toll on the ladder

The Sophia platform reads the student-loan rules as the point where the Dream turns into an extraction mechanism: education is sold as the ladder to a better life, the ladder is financed by debt, and the law then makes that debt a lifelong claim on wages that survives even the failure of the promise that justified it. In this reading the sequence from 1976 to 2005, each step widening the rule while removing exits, looks less like a series of separate decisions than a design. That reading is an interpretation, not a documented finding.

The strongest counter-readings are on the record. The rule began with a public commission and a congressional floor debate, not with a lender, and its stated purpose was to stop borrowers who had gained an asset, their education, from shedding the debt before they could repay, which its supporters on the floor described as protection against fraud. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] [cite:ad7_iowa_lr] The documented lobbying belongs to the 1999–2005 period, and the record does not show that it caused the 2005 change. [cite:ad7_npr_burd] [cite:ad7_newamerica_2007] Congress and administrations of both parties built the rule, and an administration of each party has kept the 2022 process that loosened it. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] [cite:ad7_ap_form] And the defaults concentrate where the promise itself failed, among borrowers who did not finish or attended programmes with weak earnings, which points to the price and quality of the education as much as to the law that holds the debt in place. [cite:ad7_ly_press] Part Eight turns to the second great cost that sits inside the Dream: health care. [scene:ad8_costs_and_coverage|Part Eight: Health]

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: Health: The System Inside the System
chapters.intro: The taught Dream promises that a steady job brings health insurance and that insurance keeps a family safe from ruinous bills. This part tests that promise in three steps. The first section traces how health coverage came to be tied to the job, through wartime wage controls and a tax exclusion written into law in 1954, and sets national spending beside health outcomes, the price a family pays for coverage at work, the uninsured and the underinsured, and the changes made by the 2025 budget law. The second follows a claim and a prescription through the businesses that stand between patient and doctor: insurers that deny claims and require prior authorization, pharmacy benefit managers, and hospital prices. The third measures medical debt, explains why its published totals differ, follows a denied claim to a debt on a credit report, and sets out the disputed link to bankruptcy and the state of the credit-reporting rules as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: Health coverage in the United States is tied to the job by design: wage controls from 1942 exempted benefits, and a 1943 ruling and the 1954 tax code made employer coverage untaxed, a break worth $299 billion in 2022. [cite:ad8_thomasson2017] [cite:ad8_tpc_esi] The country spent $15,474 a person in 2024, nearly twice the OECD average share of its economy, yet its life expectancy was two years below the OECD average. [cite:us16_cms_nhe2024] [cite:ad8_cmwf_global26] A family plan at work cost $28,303 in 2026, and 23 per cent of working-age adults were insured all year but underinsured; the uninsured rate, 7.9 per cent in 2025, was less than half its 2009 level, but the 2025 law is expected by the CBO to add about 10 million uninsured by 2034, with Medicaid work requirements from 1 January 2027. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] [cite:ad8_cmwf_underins24] [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us16_kff_obbba] Marketplace insurers denied 19 per cent of in-network claims in 2024 and fewer than 1 per cent were appealed; two of the three largest PBMs settled the FTC's insulin case in 2026 and the third reached a proposed settlement, all denying the allegations, and a 2026 law rewrote how they are paid. [cite:ad8_kff_denials24] [cite:ad8_ftc_insulin] [cite:ad8_bp_optum] [cite:ad8_ajmc_caa26] Medical debt is measured three ways, from $88 billion in collections to at least $220 billion owed to 41 per cent of adults with some health care debt; its role in bankruptcy remains disputed; and the federal rule to keep it off credit reports was vacated in July 2025, leaving fifteen states and the District of Columbia with their own limits. [cite:ad8_cfpb_88bn] [cite:us16_pkff_debt] [cite:ad8_kff_debtsurvey] [cite:us22_dobkin2018] [cite:ad8_nclc_states] Part Nine follows debt more widely: how credit scores, fees and new lenders finance the parts of the Dream that wages do not cover. [scene:ad9_credit_and_scores|Debt: Financing the Dream]

sections.h: What Americans Pay, and What the Coverage Buys
sections.html:
The American Dream as taught includes a promise about health: a steady job comes with insurance, insurance protects a family from ruinous bills, and the country that spends the most on medicine gets the best care. Each part of that promise has a history and a record. This section starts with the history, because the link between a job and health insurance was not a law of nature or a free-market outcome. It was built, step by step, by wartime regulation and tax law. It then sets out what the country spends, what a family pays for coverage at work, who is left uninsured or thinly insured, and what the 2025 budget law changes. The promise as taught is set out in Part One. [scene:ad1_as_taught|How the Dream is taught]

Designed friction: how a job came to carry health insurance

Before the Second World War, few Americans had any health insurance; by 1940 roughly 9 per cent had coverage for hospital costs. During the war the National War Labor Board capped wage increases from 1942 to hold down inflation, but health insurance and other fringe benefits were exempted from the cap. Firms competing for scarce workers could not offer more pay, so they offered benefits. In 1943 an administrative tax ruling first excluded employer-paid premiums from workers' taxable income, in a narrow form, and the 1954 Internal Revenue Code wrote the exclusion into law. By 1950 about half the population had hospital coverage. [cite:ad8_thomasson2017] The economist Melissa Thomasson, studying the 1954 change, found that the tax subsidy increased the growth of group insurance, especially among union members and employed people. [cite:ad8_thomasson_aer]

This is friction by design in the plain sense: Congress chose to make health coverage bought through an employer cheaper, in after-tax terms, than coverage bought any other way. The choice is still large. The Tax Policy Center put the cost of the exclusion at $299 billion in lost income and payroll taxes in 2022, the single largest tax break in the federal code, and it is worth more to people in higher tax brackets: on a $1,000 premium, the saving is $254 for a worker in the 12 per cent bracket and $347 for one in the 22 per cent bracket. [cite:ad8_tpc_esi] The structure has a second consequence that the taught version rarely mentions: coverage is tied to the job, so losing or leaving the job can mean losing the insurance.

Public programmes were later built around the employer system rather than in place of it. President Lyndon Johnson signed Medicare, for people 65 and older, and Medicaid, for people with low incomes, on 30 July 1965. Medicare was extended to many disabled people and to people with kidney failure in 1972; the Children's Health Insurance Program followed in 1997, a prescription drug benefit (Medicare Part D) was enacted in 2003 and began in 2006, and the Affordable Care Act of 2010 created subsidised insurance marketplaces for people without job-based or public coverage. [cite:ad8_cms_history] Laws signed by presidents of both parties built this layered system; none replaced its employer core.

What the country spends, and what it gets

National health spending, as counted by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, reached $5.3 trillion in 2024, or $15,474 per person and 18.0 per cent of the economy. [cite:us16_cms_nhe2024] In 1970 the figure was $353 per person, which is $2,208 in 2024 dollars; spending per person has therefore risen about sevenfold after inflation ($15,474 ÷ $2,208 ≈ 7.0). [cite:us16_pkff_spending] On the World Health Organization's narrower international definition, measured in dollars adjusted for purchasing power so that a dollar buys the same basket in each country (purchasing power parity, or PPP), American spending per person rose from $4,549 in 2000 to $13,473 in 2023. [cite:ad8_wb_chepc]

The Commonwealth Fund's 2026 comparison of rich countries, using 2024 data, found the United States spending nearly twice the OECD average as a share of its economy and about one and a half times as much per person as Switzerland, the next-highest spender. Outcomes did not follow. American life expectancy, at 79 years, was two years below the OECD average; the country had the second-highest rate of avoidable deaths among the countries studied, after Mexico; maternal deaths were nearly 19 per 100,000 live births in 2023, against fewer than 5 in eleven of eighteen countries. The United States and Mexico were the only countries in the comparison without universal coverage. [cite:ad8_cmwf_global26] On the WHO's measure of healthy life expectancy, the years a newborn can expect to live in good health, the American figure for 2021 was 63.2 years. [cite:us22_who_hale21] Spending buys a great deal of care, and American life expectancy reached a record 79.0 years in 2024, but it does not buy outcomes in proportion. [cite:us16_cdc_db548] Why it costs so much is a question of prices as much as of use, and the next section follows the prices. [scene:ad8_insurance_machine|The insurance machine]

What a family pays for coverage at work

Three terms carry most of the cost of insurance. The premium is the price of the policy itself, paid every month whether or not anyone is sick. The deductible is the amount a patient pays for care each year before the insurer starts paying most of the bill. The out-of-pocket maximum is the ceiling on what a patient pays in a year, apart from premiums. KFF's annual Employer Health Benefits Survey, released on 22 October 2026, found that the average premium for family coverage through an employer was $28,303 in 2026, up about 5 per cent in a year. Workers paid $7,471 of it directly through payroll deductions, about 27 per cent; the employer paid the remaining $20,832 ($28,303 − $7,471). Among workers in plans with a general deductible, the average for single coverage was $1,955, and 38 per cent of covered workers faced a single deductible of $2,000 or more, up from 34 per cent a year earlier. Workers at firms with many lower-wage employees paid a larger share of the family premium, 31 per cent against 27 per cent. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026]

Over the last five years family premiums rose 28 per cent, against 26.9 per cent for wages and 24.4 per cent for prices generally, so the recent gap is narrow. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] Over longer periods it was wide. From 2001 to 2011 family premiums rose 113 per cent while workers' wages rose 34 per cent and inflation 27 per cent. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2011] From $15,073 in 2011 the family premium reached $28,303 in 2026, an 88 per cent rise. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2011] [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] Because the tax code treats the employer's share as untaxed pay, a dollar of premium growth is, for the worker, a dollar of compensation that arrives as insurance rather than wages. [cite:ad8_tpc_esi] Part Five follows wages themselves. [scene:ad5_wages_floors|Wages and floors]

The uninsured and the underinsured

The share of Americans with no insurance at all has fallen by half since the Affordable Care Act. More than 50 million people, nearly 17 per cent, were uninsured in 2009; the rate reached a then-record low of 8.8 per cent in 2016. [cite:us16_khn_uninsured] In 2025, 26.7 million people, 7.9 per cent, went without coverage all year; 53.5 per cent of people had coverage through employment and 35.8 per cent had public coverage. [cite:us16_census_2025]

Having a card is not the same as being protected. The Commonwealth Fund defines adults as underinsured when, despite being insured all year, their out-of-pocket costs other than premiums reach 10 per cent of household income (5 per cent for people below twice the poverty line), or their deductible reaches 5 per cent of income. In its 2024 survey of working-age adults, 56 per cent were adequately insured all year; 23 per cent were insured all year but underinsured, 12 per cent had a gap in coverage and 9 per cent were uninsured. Two thirds of the underinsured had coverage through an employer, and 44 per cent of the underinsured reported medical or dental debt. [cite:ad8_cmwf_underins24] Cost shapes behaviour: in May 2026, 28 per cent of adults told KFF they had skipped or postponed needed care in the past year because of cost. [cite:us22_kff_costs26]

The 2025 law and the end of enhanced subsidies, status as of October 2026

Two changes are now reshaping coverage. The first is the expiry of the enhanced marketplace subsidies enacted in 2021. They lapsed at the end of 2025; the House passed a three-year extension by 230 to 196 on 8 January 2026, but the Senate did not pass one. [cite:ad8_astho_ptc] KFF estimated that subsidised enrollees who kept the same plan would see their premium payments rise about 114 per cent on average, from $888 to $1,904 a year. [cite:ad8_kff_enroll26] [cite:us16_ib_subsidy] Plan selections for 2026 fell to 23.1 million, 4.9 per cent below the 2025 record of 24.3 million, before counting people who later dropped out for non-payment. [cite:ad8_hfma_enroll26] As of October 2026 Congress had not passed an extension for 2027, so the original, smaller credits apply again in the coming plan year. [cite:ad8_audit_hci2027]

The second is the budget reconciliation law signed on 4 July 2025. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the enacted law will leave about 10 million more people uninsured in 2034, 7.5 million of them through its Medicaid provisions and 2.1 million through marketplace changes; with the subsidy expiry, the total rises to about 14.2 million. [cite:us16_kff_obbba] The largest single provision is a work requirement. From 1 January 2027, adults aged 19 to 64 covered under the Medicaid expansion must show 80 hours a month of work, community service, a work programme or at least half-time education, or monthly income of at least $580. Parents of children aged 13 or younger, medically frail people, pregnant and postpartum women and several other groups are exempt. The law lets states seek good-faith extensions to the end of 2028, but the federal interim final rule of June 2026 limits the first extension to six months. [cite:ad8_ccf_ifr] The CBO estimated that the work requirement alone cuts federal Medicaid spending by $326 billion over ten years and adds 5.3 million uninsured in 2034; renewals every six months for expansion adults, starting with renewals due from 31 December 2026, add another 700,000. [cite:ad8_kff_obbba_prov] As of October 2026 the 1 January 2027 start date stood; five governors had asked the Department of Health and Human Services to delay enforcement until states could show they were ready, and no decision had been reported. [cite:ad8_audit_hfn_gov] Because compliance must be shown and renewed, the requirement adds a reporting step to coverage itself; Part Eleven follows how such rules interact with earnings and benefits. [scene:ad11_benefits_cliff|The benefits cliff]

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

Parts of the promise hold. Coverage is far wider than it was: the uninsured rate in 2025 was less than half its 2009 level, and of the 79 per cent of working-age adults insured all year in 2024, about seven in ten (56 ÷ 79) had coverage that met the Commonwealth Fund's adequacy test. [cite:us16_khn_uninsured] [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:ad8_cmwf_underins24] Americans pay a smaller share of the national bill out of their own pockets than they used to: 10.9 per cent of current health spending in 2023, down from 15.1 per cent in 2000. [cite:us16_wb_oop] Medicare, signed in 1965, made coverage close to universal at 65, and life expectancy in 2024 was the highest on record. [cite:ad8_cms_history] [cite:us16_cdc_db548] Over the most recent five years, premiums grew at almost the same pace as wages. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] The failures are specific: a high price level, a deductible-based design that leaves a quarter of insured working-age adults exposed, and coverage that depends on a job or, from 2027, on monthly proof of hours.

sections.h: The Insurance Machine: Prices, Denials and Middlemen
sections.html:
Between a patient and a doctor's bill stand several businesses that the taught version of the Dream never names. An insurer collects premiums and decides which claims to pay. A pharmacy benefit manager, or PBM, runs the drug side of most plans: it builds the list of covered drugs, negotiates with manufacturers and pays pharmacies. A hospital or physician group sets its prices in negotiation with insurers. This section follows a dollar through each of them, using the regulators' and researchers' own data, and sets each finding beside the industry's stated position. It separates two kinds of friction: designed friction, meaning checks built into the system on purpose, such as reviewing whether a treatment is needed; and captured friction, meaning documented practices that move money in ways the design did not intend or that regulators have challenged.

How a claim is paid or denied

A claim is the bill a doctor or hospital sends to the insurer after care. Before some services, the insurer requires prior authorization: the doctor must ask permission in advance, and the insurer decides whether it will pay. The best public data on denials come from plans sold on HealthCare.gov, the federal marketplace, which must report them to the government. KFF's analysis of 2024 data, published on 24 March 2026, found that insurers denied 19 per cent of in-network claims, about 85 million of 451 million, and 37 per cent of out-of-network claims. Rates varied widely between insurers, from 3 per cent to 36 per cent of in-network claims. Most denials were not explained in clinical terms: 36 per cent of denial reasons were listed as "other", 25 per cent were administrative, 13 per cent were for excluded services, 9 per cent for missing prior authorization or referral and only 5 per cent for lack of medical necessity. [cite:ad8_kff_denials24]

Patients rarely contest. Consumers filed at least 262,982 internal appeals, fewer than 1 per cent of denied claims, and insurers upheld 66 per cent of them; at least 5,881 went on to an independent external review. KFF cautions that the data cannot show which services were denied, that some denied claims are later paid after resubmission, and that denials made before care, through prior authorization, are not included. [cite:ad8_kff_denials24] A denial in these figures is therefore not always a final refusal; it is often a bill sent back for correction. What the data establish is the scale of the paperwork and how little of it patients challenge.

Medicare Advantage, the private-plan option within Medicare, gives the clearest picture of prior authorization. In 2024 its insurers made 52.8 million prior authorization decisions and denied 4.1 million requests in full or in part, 7.7 per cent, up from 6.4 per cent in 2023. Only 11.5 per cent of denials were appealed, but 80.7 per cent of appeals were fully or partly overturned. [cite:ad8_kff_ma_pa24] In rough numbers, 4.1 million × 11.5 per cent is about 470,000 appeals, of which about 380,000 succeeded, while about 3.6 million denials were never contested. Traditional Medicare uses prior authorization far less: 628,243 reviews in fiscal 2024, though with a higher denial rate of 22.9 per cent, and from 1 January 2026 a pilot called WISeR added prior authorization for selected services in six states. [cite:ad8_kff_ma_pa24]

The industry's stated position is that prior authorization exists to "ensure patients receive care that is safe, evidence-based and as affordable as possible", in the words of the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association. [cite:ad8_bcbsa_pa] On 23 June 2025 the Health and Human Services Secretary and the head of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced a voluntary pledge by insurers covering 257 million people: to show reductions in the services that need prior authorization by 1 January 2026, to honour existing approvals for 90 days when patients switch plans, to answer 80 per cent of complete electronic requests in real time by 2027, and to adopt a common electronic standard by 1 January 2027. [cite:ad8_healio_pa] A federal rule already requires Medicare Advantage and other public-programme plans to decide standard requests within seven days from January 2026 and to publish their approval statistics. [cite:ad8_kff_ma_pa24] Status as of October 2026: the insurers' associations say the first commitments took effect on 1 January 2026; in KFF's 2026 employer survey, 7 per cent of large firms said the number of services needing authorization had risen in the past year. [cite:ad8_bcbsa_pa] [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026]

The drug middlemen

Three PBMs dominate the drug side of American insurance. The Federal Trade Commission's interim staff report of 9 July 2024 found that the three largest, CVS Caremark, Express Scripts and Optum Rx, processed nearly 80 per cent of the roughly 6.6 billion prescriptions filled in 2023, and the six largest more than 90 per cent. Each is owned by a company that also owns a large health insurer and pharmacies, and the pharmacies affiliated with the big three took nearly 70 per cent of specialty drug revenue. The Commission voted 4 to 1 to publish; Commissioner Melissa Holyoak dissented, calling the report incomplete, and Commissioner Andrew Ferguson cautioned that much of it rested on public comments. [cite:ad8_ftc_pbm1]

The second interim report, of 14 January 2025, followed specialty generic drugs used for cancer, HIV and other serious conditions. It found that the big three's affiliated pharmacies earned $7.3 billion above the estimated cost of acquiring these drugs between 2017 and 2022, plus $1.4 billion from spread pricing, which is the practice of charging the employer or plan more than the PBM pays the pharmacy. [cite:ad8_ftc_pbm2] Of specialty generics dispensed by those pharmacies in 2020–2022, 63 per cent were marked up by 100 per cent or more over the national average acquisition cost, and 22 per cent by 1,000 per cent or more. The PBMs' trade association, the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, questioned the purpose of a second interim report and said PBMs are "the only entities in the supply chain dedicated to lowering the cost of prescription drugs". [cite:ad8_pcma_resp]

A rebate is a payment from a drug manufacturer to a PBM in return for placing its drug on the plan's list. The Commission's separate case over insulin, filed in the autumn of 2024, alleged that the three PBMs' rebating practices artificially inflated insulin list prices, steering patients toward higher-cost drugs that paid larger rebates. [cite:ad8_ftc_insulin] [cite:ad8_bp_optum] Status as of October 2026: Express Scripts settled on 4 February 2026, and the Commission estimates the agreement will lower patients' costs for drugs such as insulin by up to $7 billion over ten years; Caremark settled on 14 July 2026; Optum Rx reached a proposed settlement, announced on 12 June 2026, whose terms had still not been published in late July. [cite:ad8_audit_truveris] All three denied the allegations. [cite:ad8_ftc_insulin] [cite:ad8_ftc_caremark] [cite:ad8_bp_optum] Congress also acted: the Consolidated Appropriations Act signed on 3 February 2026 separates PBM pay in Medicare Part D from drug list prices, replacing it with flat fees, generally from 1 January 2028, and requires PBMs serving larger employer plans to pass through all rebates and disclose their pay, from about 2028. [cite:ad8_ajmc_caa26] [cite:ad8_bipc_caa26]

Prices, not visits

The largest driver of the American bill is the price of each service. RAND's employer-led study of hospital prices found that private insurers and employers paid hospitals on average 254 per cent of what Medicare would have paid for the same services in 2022, up from 224 per cent in 2020. Prices exceeded 300 per cent of Medicare in seven states, including California, Florida and New York, and stayed below 200 per cent in five, including Massachusetts and Michigan. The American Hospital Association called the study "skewed and incomplete", noting that it covers under 2 per cent of hospital spending and arguing that Medicare rates are not a fair benchmark. [cite:ad8_rand_hosp] For drugs, RAND found American prices averaged 2.78 times those in 33 other high-income countries in 2022, and brand-name drugs 4.22 times before rebates, while unbranded generics were cheaper in the United States than in most comparison countries. [cite:us16_rand_drugs] Under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, Medicare's first ten negotiated drug prices took effect on 1 January 2026; the 2025 budget law widened an exemption for drugs treating rare diseases, at a cost the CBO put at $8.8 billion. [cite:us16_kff_negotiation] Part Fifteen follows the lobbying behind such rules. [scene:ad15_lobbying_by_industry|Who writes the rules]

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

Most claims are paid, and most prior authorization requests are approved: in Medicare Advantage more than nine in ten requests went through in 2024, and in the marketplace about four in five in-network claims were paid on first submission. [cite:ad8_kff_ma_pa24] [cite:ad8_kff_denials24] Generic drugs, which make up most prescriptions, are cheaper in the United States than in most rich countries. [cite:us16_rand_drugs] And the system has shown that it can correct itself through ordinary law: a Biden-era statute let Medicare negotiate drug prices, a regulatory study and lawsuit under both administrations produced settlements, one still proposed, with all three large PBMs, and a funding law signed in 2026 rewrote how PBMs are paid. [cite:us16_kff_negotiation] [cite:ad8_ftc_insulin] [cite:ad8_ajmc_caa26] The documented problem is not that the machine never pays. It is that its prices are high, its denials are hard to read and seldom contested, and its middlemen were, on the regulators' findings, paid in ways tied to higher prices. When a denial or a deductible leaves a bill unpaid, the next stage is debt. [scene:ad8_medical_debt|Medical debt]

sections.h: Medical Debt: When the Bill Outlasts the Illness
sections.html:
The taught Dream treats debt as something a family chooses: a mortgage for a house, a loan for a degree. Medical debt is different. Nobody shops for a heart attack, and a bill can arrive after a denial, a deductible or an out-of-network charge that the patient did not know about in advance. This section measures how much medical debt Americans carry, explains why the published totals differ so widely, follows a denied claim to a debt on a credit report, sets out the disputed link between medical bills and bankruptcy, and gives the state of the credit-reporting rules as of October 2026.

Three numbers that measure different things

Three figures circulate, and they are often confused. The first comes from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the federal agency that supervises credit reporting. In March 2022 it estimated that $88 billion in medical bills sat on Americans' credit reports as debts in collections, meaning bills that a hospital or doctor had passed to a collection agency. As of mid-2021, 58 per cent of all collection debts on credit records were medical, and medical collections appeared on 43 million credit reports. [cite:ad8_cfpb_88bn] This number counts only debts that reached a collector and were reported to a credit bureau.

The second figure is larger. Researchers at Peterson-KFF, using the Census Bureau's Survey of Income and Program Participation, a household survey, found that Americans owed at least $220 billion in medical debt in December 2021. About 20 million adults owed more than $250, about 14 million more than $1,000 and about 3 million more than $10,000. [cite:us16_pkff_debt] This counts what households report owing for medical care, whether or not it has gone to collections, so it includes bills on payment plans that will never appear on a credit report.

The third figure is a share of people rather than a sum of dollars. KFF's Health Care Debt Survey of February and March 2022 found that 41 per cent of adults currently owed money for medical or dental care, using the broadest definition of the three: past-due bills, payment plans with providers, loans, credit card balances run up on medical bills and money borrowed from family or friends. [cite:ad8_kff_debtsurvey] The widely repeated statement that more than 100 million Americans carry health care debt comes from KFF Health News's reporting built on this kind of survey evidence, not from the CFPB. [cite:ad8_kffhn_100m] The three figures should never be added together or swapped for one another. They rise in size because each counts more: debt in collections, all medical debt owed, and any health care debt, including debt that has been moved onto a credit card.

Who carries it, and what it does

Medical debt is unevenly spread. In the Census-based data, 13 per cent of Black adults reported medical debt, against 8 per cent of white adults and 3 per cent of Asian adults; 11 per cent of people uninsured all year had it, against 8 per cent of those insured all year. [cite:us16_pkff_debt] The CFPB found past-due medical debt among 28 per cent of Black and 22 per cent of Hispanic people, against 17 per cent of white and 10 per cent of Asian people, and found it more common in the Southeast and Southwest, partly because states there did not expand Medicaid. [cite:ad8_cfpb_88bn] These gaps follow documented differences in insurance coverage, income and the state where a person lives; they are not traits of any group, and Part Thirteen follows the wider record. [scene:ad13_black_americans|Black Americans and the Dream] Insurance does not remove the risk. Among the underinsured, 44 per cent reported medical or dental debt, and people in employer and marketplace plans reported significantly higher rates of medical debt than people covered by Medicaid. [cite:ad8_cmwf_underins24]

The consequences reach past the bill. Of adults with health care debt in KFF's survey, 63 per cent had cut back on food, clothing or other basic household items in the past five years because of it, and 18 per cent said they did not expect ever to pay it off. [cite:ad8_kff_debtsurvey] Some patients move the bill onto a medical credit card. These often carry deferred interest: no interest during a promotional period, but interest charged back to the first day if the balance is not cleared in time. The CFPB estimated that Americans paid about $1 billion in deferred interest on medical credit cards and similar financing from 2018 to 2020, at rates up to 27 per cent; in 2013 it had ordered CareCredit, a medical credit card issued by Synchrony Bank, to set up a $34.1 million fund to repay patients. [cite:ad8_kffhn_medcards]

The disputed link to bankruptcy

A widely repeated claim holds that medical bills are the leading cause of personal bankruptcy in the United States. The record is contested, and the two best-known studies measure different things. David Himmelstein and colleagues surveyed 910 people who filed for bankruptcy between 2013 and 2016 and reported, in the American Journal of Public Health in 2019, that 66.5 per cent cited medical issues, either bills or income lost to illness, as contributing to their bankruptcy. That figure counts contribution as filers reported it, not cause. [cite:us22_himmelstein2019] Their work appears in peer-reviewed journals and is also published by Physicians for a National Health Program, an organisation that campaigns for a single-payer system; that link is part of the record when the number is weighed. [cite:us16_pnhp_reply]

Carlos Dobkin, Amy Finkelstein, Raymond Kluender and Matthew Notowidigdo took a different route. Linking California hospital records from 2003 to 2007 to credit and bankruptcy records for adults, they estimated in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 that hospitalisations cause about 4 per cent of bankruptcies among non-elderly adults, and argued that survey shares overstate causation because many filers have medical bills that would not by themselves have led to bankruptcy. [cite:us22_dobkin2018] [cite:us16_mit_bankruptcy] Himmelstein, Woolhandler and Senator Elizabeth Warren replied that the method undercounts medical bankruptcy, and the dispute remains unresolved. [cite:us16_pnhp_reply] Both findings can be true at once: medical costs can be present in most bankruptcies while a hospital stay is the decisive cause in a small share. Neither number belongs in a headline alone.

Credit reports: voluntary changes, a vacated rule and state laws, status as of October 2026

The CFPB's own research found that medical debt on a credit report predicts future repayment less well than debts such as loans and credit cards. [cite:ad8_cfpb_88bn] In March 2022 the three national credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, announced that paid medical collections would be removed from reports from 1 July 2022, that unpaid medical debts would wait a year rather than six months before appearing, and that medical collections under $500 would be dropped in the first half of 2023. Together, they said, these steps would remove nearly 70 per cent of medical collection entries. [cite:ad8_cra_2022]

In January 2025 the CFPB went further, with a rule that would have barred most medical debt from credit reports used by lenders; it estimated the rule would remove $49 billion of debt from the reports of 15 million people and raise their credit scores by about 20 points on average. On 11 July 2025 Judge Sean Jordan of the federal court for the Eastern District of Texas vacated the rule, holding that the Fair Credit Reporting Act does not give the CFPB that power, in a case brought by industry groups including the Consumer Data Industry Association. [cite:ad8_ap_vacatur] [cite:ad8_nclc_states] On 28 October 2025 the CFPB issued an interpretation stating that federal law pre-empts state laws on what credit reports may contain, while noting that the interpretation is not binding and that courts decide the question. As of September 2026, fifteen states and the District of Columbia had laws restricting medical debt on credit reports: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Washington. [cite:ad8_nclc_states] Part Nine follows how credit reports and scores shape the rest of a family's finances. [scene:ad9_credit_and_scores|Credit and scores]

Where it works as promised

Some protections did arrive. The bureaus' 2022–2023 changes removed most medical collection entries from credit reports, and a growing number of states have added their own limits. [cite:ad8_cra_2022] [cite:ad8_nclc_states] Most insured Americans do not carry medical debt, and the best causal study finds that hospital stays drive only a small share of bankruptcies among working-age adults. [cite:us16_pkff_debt] [cite:us22_dobkin2018] The insured are less exposed than the uninsured, 8 per cent against 11 per cent in the Census-based data, so wider coverage reduces the risk. [cite:us16_pkff_debt]

Interpretation, not finding: the system inside the system
