The Sophia platform reads American health care as the clearest case of its broader thesis: a system inside the Dream's system that converts illness into a revenue stream at each step, from the premium deducted from pay to the deductible, the denial, the financing charge and the collection entry, so that the cost of being sick is carried by the household while the institutions in between are paid in every case. In this reading, medical debt is not a failure of the machine but one of its outputs, and the employer link built in 1943 and 1954 keeps workers dependent on the job that carries their coverage.

The strongest counter-readings are documented. Most claims and most authorization requests are paid, and the share of national health spending paid directly out of pocket has fallen. [cite:ad8_kff_denials24] [cite:us16_wb_oop] The causal research of Dobkin and colleagues finds that hospital bills alone cause a small share of bankruptcies. [cite:us22_dobkin2018] The industry's stated purposes, checking that costly care is needed and using buying power to win discounts, are real functions, and its trade bodies dispute both the hospital-price benchmark and the regulators' account of PBMs. [cite:ad8_bcbsa_pa] [cite:ad8_rand_hosp] [cite:ad8_pcma_resp] And the record shows the system being changed through ordinary politics: coverage expanded in 2010, credit-reporting practice changed in 2022, PBM pay was rewritten in 2026. Equally, the 2025 law will reduce coverage, and the federal rule on medical debt was struck down. The documented finding is narrower than the interpretation: specific mechanisms, named above with their numbers, move the cost of illness onto households, and each can be measured and changed.

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: Debt: Financing the Dream
chapters.intro: Part Nine follows the money that Americans borrow to reach the Dream and to bridge the months when pay falls short. It begins with what households owe, about $18.8 trillion in mid-2026, and with the credit card: how two Supreme Court decisions in 1978 and 1996 let card issuers set rates and fees under the law of the state they chose, what a minimum payment costs over time at today's rates, and how a three-digit credit score built by a private company came to decide who borrows and at what price, with its errors and the millions it cannot see. It then turns to the fees charged for holding, or not holding, a bank account: overdraft and late fees, the two federal rules written in 2024 to limit them and how both were removed in 2025, and the price of cashing a paycheck outside a bank. It ends with the lenders that have grown up in the gap between bills and paydays, from storefront payday loans to buy-now-pay-later plans, wage-advance apps and credit cards offered in the dentist's office, setting out how each charges, what regulators and courts have found, the industry's case, and the status of each as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: Part Nine established that American households owed $18.771 trillion in June 2026, $1.263 trillion of it on credit cards, and that required debt payments took 11.1 per cent of after-tax income, well below the 2007 peak, while card balances moved into serious delinquency at about 7 per cent a year. [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026] [cite:ad9_fred_tdsp] Card rates have averaged about 21 per cent since 2023 under a framework the Supreme Court built in 1978 and 1996, which lets issuers export their home state's rates and fees; at those rates a $5,000 balance paid at the minimum takes more than nineteen years to clear. [cite:ad9_fred_ccall] [cite:ad9_marquette] [cite:ad9_smiley] Credit scoring made lending faster and more consistent, but one consumer in twenty had a report error likely to raise their costs and about 7 million adults had no credit file in 2020. [cite:ad9_fed_scoring2007] [cite:ad9_ftc_2013] [cite:ad9_cfpb_invis2025] Overdraft revenue at large banks halved between 2019 and 2023 through the banks' own changes, but the federal overdraft and late-fee limits written in 2024 were repealed by Congress and vacated in court in 2025, so fee levels are again set by each bank; 4.2 per cent of households remained unbanked. [cite:us22_cfpb_od23] [cite:ad9_plaw_119_10] [cite:ad9_hk_late] [cite:ad9_fdic2023] Payday loans cost about 391 per cent a year and are mostly renewed, wage-advance apps work out at similar rates on California's data, buy-now-pay-later loans go mostly to subprime borrowers, and medical cards charged patients about $1 billion in deferred interest in three years; as of October 2026 most federal limits proposed for these products have been withdrawn, while twenty-one states and the District of Columbia have enacted payday rate caps, Rhode Island's taking effect in January 2027. [cite:ad9_cfpb_apr] [cite:ad9_cfpb_rollover] [cite:ad9_nclc_ewa] [cite:ad9_cfpb_bnpl2025] [cite:ad9_cfpb_medcc] [cite:ad9_crl_ri] Debt finances the present; Part Ten turns to how Americans are expected to finance old age, and the shift from the pension to the 401(k). [scene:ad10_pension_shift|Part Ten: Retirement]

sections.h: Credit, Interest and the Score That Follows You
sections.html:
The promise as taught treats debt as a ladder. A mortgage buys the house, a car loan gets the worker to the job, a student loan buys the credential, and a credit card smooths the months when pay and bills fall out of step. Pay on time, the lesson goes, and a good credit record opens the next door at a lower price. Much of that is accurate, and this section says where. It also follows three things the lesson leaves out: how large household debt has become and what it is made of, how the price of revolving credit was freed from state limits by two Supreme Court decisions, and how a three-digit number built by private companies came to decide who borrows and at what cost.

What American households owe

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York counts household debt from a large sample of anonymised credit records. At the end of June 2026 American households owed $18.771 trillion. Mortgages made up $13.117 trillion of it, auto loans $1.713 trillion, student loans $1.651 trillion, credit cards $1.263 trillion, home-equity lines $0.459 trillion and other debts $0.568 trillion. Of the total, 4.7 per cent was in some stage of delinquency, meaning at least 30 days late. [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026] The figures are nominal, that is, in the dollars of each year without adjustment for prices; Part Two explains the difference between nominal and real amounts. [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two]

The total has grown in most years since the bank began the series. It peaked at $12.68 trillion in the third quarter of 2008, fell to $11.28 trillion by the third quarter of 2013 as families paid down and defaulted on mortgages, climbed back to $12.58 trillion by the end of 2016, just under the old peak, and reached $14.15 trillion at the end of 2019. [cite:ad9_nyfed_q3_2013] [cite:ad9_nyfed_q4_2016] [cite:ad9_nyfed_q4_2019] It rose to $16.90 trillion at the end of 2022 and $18.776 trillion at the end of 2025, then edged down by $13 billion in the second quarter of 2026. [cite:ad9_nyfed_q4_2022] [cite:ad9_nyfed_q4_2025] [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026] Credit-card balances followed their own path: $672 billion in the third quarter of 2013, $0.93 trillion at the end of 2019, a fall to $856 billion at the end of 2021 as pandemic aid let families pay cards down, and then a climb to $986 billion in 2022, about $1.13 trillion in 2023, $1.277 trillion at the end of 2025 and $1.263 trillion in June 2026. [cite:ad9_nyfed_q3_2013] [cite:ad9_nyfed_q4_2019] [cite:ad9_nyfed_q4_2022] [cite:ad9_aba_q4_2023] [cite:ad9_nyfed_q4_2025] [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026]

A rising total is not by itself a sign of strain, because incomes and the population also grow. The Federal Reserve's debt service ratio measures the burden directly: required payments of principal and interest on mortgages and consumer loans as a share of income after taxes. It stood at 11.11 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, well below its peak of 15.85 per cent at the end of 2007 and above its low of 9.05 per cent in early 2021. [cite:ad9_fred_tdsp] The burden is not evenly spread, however. The share of card balances moving into serious delinquency, 90 days or more late, was 6.97 per cent a year in the second quarter of 2026, against 5.32 per cent at the end of 2019. [cite:us14_nyfed_q2_2026] [cite:ad9_nyfed_q4_2019]

How the price of a card was set free

For most of the twentieth century each state set a usury ceiling, a legal maximum interest rate on consumer loans. In 1978 a Minnesota bank sued to stop the First National Bank of Omaha from charging Minnesota cardholders the rate Nebraska allowed, 18 per cent a year on the first $999.99 of a balance, when Minnesota's own cap was 12 per cent. On 18 December 1978 a unanimous Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice William Brennan, held in Marquette National Bank v. First of Omaha that the National Bank Act of 1864 let a national bank charge the rate permitted in the state where it was located, wherever the borrower lived. The Court added that any concern for protecting state usury laws was "better addressed to the wisdom of Congress than to the judgment of this Court." [cite:ad9_marquette]

The decision made a bank's home state worth choosing. South Dakota, already lifting its own ceilings, passed a law in a single day with an emergency clause declaring a shortage of financial capital; its governor, Bill Janklow, later said Citibank helped draft it and moved its card operation to Sioux Falls in 1981, promising 400 jobs, and that the operation grew to about 3,000 employees. Asked in 2004 whether he had helped foster the consumer-credit boom that followed, he answered, "The answer is yes, I do." [cite:ad9_janklow] In 1996 the Court extended the logic from interest to fees. In Smiley v. Citibank, decided on 3 June 1996, it accepted a regulation that the Comptroller of the Currency had adopted that February defining "interest" to include late fees, insufficient-funds fees, over-limit fees, annual fees and cash-advance fees, so that these too could be charged under the home state's law. [cite:ad9_smiley]

The fight over this design is still live. Colorado used a 1980 federal opt-out in 2023 to require out-of-state, state-chartered banks to obey its own rate limits when lending to Colorado residents. Bank trade associations sued; a district court blocked the law, a divided appeals panel upheld it on 10 November 2025, and on 2 April 2026 the full Tenth Circuit agreed to rehear the case, vacating the panel decision. The court's order left the injunction against the Colorado law in place while the rehearing was briefed, and no ruling from the full court had been reported by October 2026. [cite:ad9_cfm_colorado] The exportation rule is designed friction in the protocol's sense: it is the National Bank Act as the Supreme Court read it, open to change by Congress at any time.

The rate, the margin and the minimum payment

An annual percentage rate, or APR, is the yearly cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage of the amount owed, including interest and certain fees. The Federal Reserve's survey of commercial banks puts the average card APR across all accounts at 11.85 per cent in November 2013 and 14.87 per cent in November 2019. It jumped to 19.07 per cent in November 2022 and has stayed near 21 per cent since: 21.47 per cent in November 2024 and 21.19 per cent in August 2026. On the accounts that actually paid interest, the rate was 22.36 per cent in August 2026. [cite:ad9_fred_ccall] [cite:ad9_fred_ccint] Part of the rise followed the Federal Reserve's own rate increases. Part did not: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) reported in February 2024 that the average margin of card APRs over the prime rate had reached an all-time high of about 14 percentage points in 2023 and attributed it to issuers widening margins. [cite:ad9_orrick_margins] The Consumer Bankers Association answered that the bureau's comparisons mixed in credit unions, which are capped at 18 per cent by law, and that large issuers lend more to riskier customers and fund rewards programmes. [cite:ad9_cba_math] Card holders paid $160 billion in interest and $31.3 billion in fees in 2024 on the bureau's figures. [cite:us22_cfpb_ccmr25]

The minimum payment is where the rate compounds. Take a $5,000 balance at 22.36 per cent and assume a minimum payment equal to the month's interest plus 1 per cent of the balance, with a $25 floor, a common form of the formula. The monthly rate is 22.36 ÷ 12 = 1.86 per cent, so the first month's interest is about $93 and the first minimum about $143. Paying only the minimum and charging nothing new, the balance takes 231 months, more than 19 years, to clear, and the borrower pays about $13,240 in all, of which about $8,240 is interest. Paying a fixed $192 a month clears it in 36 months for about $1,910 in interest. At the 2013 rate of about 12.9 per cent, the same minimum-payment path costs about $4,570 in interest. (Book arithmetic, monthly compounding, no new purchases or fees.) Since 22 February 2010 the CARD Act has required every statement to show how long paying only the minimum would take, what it would cost, and the fixed payment that would clear the balance in three years. [cite:ad9_crl_card] [cite:ad9_fred_ccint]

The score

Fair, Isaac and Company, which built its first scoring system in 1958, released the first general-purpose credit score in 1989, a single number meant to work across all kinds of lending, and all three national credit bureaus were selling FICO scores by 1991. [cite:ad9_kgw_fico] FICO says its score weighs payment history at 35 per cent, amounts owed at 30 per cent, length of credit history at 15 per cent, new credit at 10 per cent and the mix of credit types at 10 per cent, and does not consider race, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, income or employment. [cite:ad9_myfico] Because it measures borrowing behaviour rather than ability to pay, a person who has never borrowed has no score at all, and a person who earns well but missed payments during an illness scores low.

The underlying files contain errors. In a study for Congress published in December 2012, the Federal Trade Commission had 1,001 consumers review nearly 3,000 of their own credit reports. Twenty-six per cent found at least one potentially material error; 13 per cent had an error that changed their score; and 5 per cent had errors that lowered their score enough to make credit likely to cost more. [cite:ad9_ftc_2013] A widely repeated claim holds that one American in four has an error that hurts their score; the study's figure for errors serious enough to raise borrowing costs is one in twenty.

Some people have no file at all. In 2015 the CFPB estimated that 11 per cent of adults, about 26 million people, were "credit invisible". In June 2025 it corrected that estimate after finding that its data had excluded records containing only collections, closed accounts or deferred student loans: the 2010 figure fell to 5.8 per cent, about 13.5 million, and the 2020 figure was 2.7 per cent, about 7 million adults. Another 9.8 per cent of adults in 2020 had a file too thin or stale to score. [cite:ad9_cfpb_invis2025] Mortgage scoring is changing as well. After years of review, the Federal Housing Finance Agency announced in April 2026 that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac would accept VantageScore 4.0, a rival model built by the three bureaus, and on 9 September 2026 Fannie Mae opened it to all its approved lenders, alongside the classic FICO score. [cite:ad9_bhfs_fhfa] [cite:ad9_fnma_ll2026] A CFPB rule to remove medical debt from credit reports was vacated by a federal court in Texas in July 2025, leaving in place the bureaus' voluntary 2023 decision to drop paid medical debts and those under $500. [cite:ad9_checkbook_med] Part Eight covers medical debt in full. [scene:ad8_medical_debt|Part Eight]

The charts below plot the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; each caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

Scoring did what its designers said it would in several measurable ways. The Federal Reserve's 2007 report to Congress found that automated scoring cut mortgage decision times "from several weeks to a matter of a few minutes", lowered some lenders' origination costs by as much as half, and brought "objectivity and consistency" that could reduce room for discrimination by individual loan officers. The same report found "very little evidence" that the spread of scoring had especially helped groups that historically borrowed little, and called that conclusion tentative. [cite:ad9_fed_scoring2007] The burden of debt payments, measured against income, is lower now than before the 2008 crisis. [cite:ad9_fred_tdsp] And cardholders who pay in full each month borrow free for weeks and often collect rewards; the interest in the money trail above is paid by those who carry a balance.

sections.h: Fees, the Unbanked and the Rules That Did Not Survive
sections.html:
The first practical lesson of the Dream as taught is to open a bank account. A paycheck goes in, bills come out, savings grow, and the account becomes the base for every later step, from a credit card to a mortgage. For most Americans it works that way. This section looks at the people for whom it costs more: account holders who pay overdraft and late fees, and households who stay outside the banking system and pay to cash their own wages. It also follows two federal rules written in 2024 to cut those fees, and what happened to each of them in 2025.

Overdraft: a loan that was not called one

An overdraft happens when a bank pays a card swipe, check or withdrawal that the account does not have the money to cover, and charges a fee for doing so. A non-sufficient-funds (NSF) fee is charged when the bank refuses the payment instead. When Congress passed the Truth in Lending Act in 1968 to make lenders disclose the cost of credit, the Federal Reserve Board in 1969 exempted overdrafts, then treated as an occasional courtesy for a check that had not yet cleared. [cite:ad9_cfpb_od_final] The exemption meant an overdraft fee was not disclosed as a finance charge or an APR, even though, treated as a loan, a $35 fee on a $50 overdraft repaid within a week works out to an APR of about 3,650 per cent (35 ÷ 50 × 365 ÷ 7; book arithmetic).

The fees were large and concentrated. Banks with more than $1 billion in assets collected $11.96 billion in overdraft and NSF fees in 2019. Earlier CFPB research found that nearly 80 per cent of those fees were paid by fewer than 9 per cent of account holders, those who overdrew more than ten times a year. [cite:us22_cfpb_od23] Then the largest banks changed their own policies, and the CFPB reported that the vast majority of NSF fees had been eliminated. Revenue at the same group of banks fell to $7.61 billion in 2022 and $5.83 billion in 2023, a drop of 51 per cent from 2019. The CFPB put the saving at about $6.1 billion a year, or about $185 for the average household that overdraws. [cite:us22_cfpb_od23] That figure covers only banks above $1 billion. The National Consumer Law Center, an advocacy group, estimated that all banks and credit unions together collected about $12.4 billion in overdraft and NSF fees in 2025, extrapolated from the largest banks' reports; the two numbers measure different sets of institutions and cannot be joined into one trend. [cite:us22_nclc_od26] The same brief reported that the top 20 banks' overdraft revenue rose 6.2 per cent between 2023 and 2025, and that BMO Bank raised its fee from $15 to $20 in 2026. [cite:us22_nclc_od26]

The overdraft rule, 2024–2025

In December 2024 the CFPB issued a rule ending the 1969 exemption for banks and credit unions with more than $10 billion in assets. Each could choose to charge no more than $5 per overdraft, to charge a fee no higher than its own costs and losses, or to treat overdraft as ordinary credit, with the disclosures and protections of a credit card. The bureau estimated savings of up to $5 billion a year and set an effective date of 1 October 2025. [cite:ad9_cfpb_od_final] The American Bankers Association called the rule "flawed and unlawful from the start", said most Americans value overdraft coverage, and argued that government price limits would make it harder for banks to offer it. [cite:ad9_aba_od]

The rule never took effect. Congress used the Congressional Review Act, which lets it overturn a recent agency rule by simple majority. The Senate passed the resolution 52 to 48 on 27 March 2025 and the House 217 to 211 on 9 April, largely along party lines, and President Trump signed it on 9 May 2025. [cite:ad9_ballotpedia_cra] [cite:ad9_plaw_119_10] As of October 2026 there is no federal limit on the size of an overdraft fee. The agency that wrote the rule is itself in dispute: in September 2026 a federal court in Oregon ruled that its acting director had unlawfully requested no funding from the Federal Reserve for the 2026 fiscal year, related cases were on appeal, and a House committee had advanced a bill to move the bureau's funding to annual appropriations. [cite:ad9_goodwin_cfpb]

The late-fee rule, 2024–2025

The CARD Act of 2009 requires credit-card penalty fees to be "reasonable and proportional" to the violation. The rules that carry it out include a safe harbor, a fee level an issuer may charge without proving its costs. In March 2024 the CFPB cut the safe harbor for the largest issuers from about $32 to $8, letting issuers charge more only if they showed their costs justified it; the National Consumer Law Center estimated that the change would save cardholders about $10 billion a year. [cite:ad9_hk_late] [cite:ad9_nclc_late] Bank and business groups sued in Texas before it took effect, and it never did. On 14 April 2025 the CFPB, under new leadership, joined the plaintiffs in asking the court to vacate it, agreeing that it violated the CARD Act, and on 15 April Judge Mark Pittman of the Northern District of Texas did so. [cite:ad9_hk_late] As of October 2026 the earlier safe harbor applies again. Cardholders paid $31.3 billion in card fees of all kinds in 2024. [cite:us22_cfpb_ccmr25]

Outside the bank

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation surveys about 30,000 households every two years. In June 2023, 4.2 per cent of American households, about 5.6 million, had no bank account, down from 8.2 per cent in 2011; another 14.2 per cent, about 19 million, had an account but also used non-bank services such as check cashers or money orders. The most common main reason given for having no account was not having enough money to meet minimum-balance requirements (23.3 per cent), followed by distrust of banks (15.7 per cent); reasons tied to fees or minimum balances together accounted for a third. [cite:ad9_fdic2023] The Federal Reserve's own 2025 survey of adults found 94 per cent had an account, but only 77 per cent of those with incomes under $25,000. [cite:ad9_shed2025]

The rates differ sharply by circumstance. Households with lower or more volatile incomes, less education or a single parent are more often unbanked; so are working-age households with a disability, at 11.2 per cent against 3.7 per cent for those without. Black (10.6 per cent), Hispanic (9.5 per cent) and American Indian or Alaska Native (12.2 per cent) households had rates several times that of white households, and the FDIC found the gaps persisted at every income level, which means income alone does not explain them; the survey reports the gaps without assigning a single cause. The FDIC attributed about two-thirds of the decline since 2011 to rising incomes and education rather than to changes in banking. [cite:ad9_fdic2023] Only 10 per cent of unbanked households held a credit card and 78.4 per cent had no mainstream credit of any kind, which ties this section back to the credit-invisible population in the last. [cite:ad9_fdic2023] [cite:ad9_cfpb_invis2025]

Life outside a bank has its own prices. A check casher charges a percentage of each check; New York, one of the states that caps the fee, allows the greater of $1 or 2.2 per cent for a paycheck and 1.5 per cent for a government benefit check. [cite:ad9_nydfs_cc] A worker in New York cashing a $1,000 paycheck every two weeks at the cap pays $22 a check, or $572 a year (2.2 per cent × $1,000 × 26; book arithmetic); states without caps allow more. About one unbanked household in five used a prepaid card in 2023, and two in three were cash only. [cite:ad9_fdic2023] Prepaid cards carry their own monthly, reload and ATM fees; since 1 April 2019 a federal rule has required a short fee chart on the package and fraud and error protection once the card is registered. [cite:ad9_nclc_prepaid]

Where it works as promised

The record here contains real progress that owed nothing to the two rules. Overdraft and NSF revenue at large banks halved between 2019 and 2023 through the banks' own policy changes, NSF fees largely disappeared at the biggest institutions, and the share of unbanked households halved between 2011 and 2023. [cite:us22_cfpb_od23] [cite:ad9_fdic2023] The banking industry's position is that customers value overdraft coverage and that price limits would make it harder to offer; the bureau's figures show that most of the cost fell on the small group who overdraw often, so the dispute was over price and over that group rather than over the service itself. [cite:ad9_aba_od] [cite:us22_cfpb_od23] What the record establishes is narrower than either side's slogan: the cost of an ordinary account falls mostly on a small group with thin balances, the two federal limits on that cost were removed in 2025 by a court and by Congress, and as of October 2026 the price of overdraft is set by each bank.

sections.h: The New Lenders: Payday, Buy Now Pay Later, Wage Apps and Medical Cards
sections.html:
For a household with no savings cushion, the gap between a bill and the next paycheck has to be bridged somehow. The Federal Reserve's 2025 survey found that 63 per cent of adults would cover an unexpected $400 expense with cash or its equivalent, down from 68 per cent in 2021; the rest would borrow, sell something or could not pay. [cite:ad9_shed2025] A set of lenders has grown up to serve that gap: storefront payday lenders, buy-now-pay-later plans at the online checkout, apps that advance part of a paycheck, and credit cards offered in the dentist's or doctor's office. Each presents itself as a cheaper, simpler or kinder alternative to the bank. This section sets out how each one charges, what the regulators and courts have found, the industry's case, and where each stood in October 2026.

Payday loans: the arithmetic of a two-week loan

A payday loan is a small loan, usually a few hundred dollars, due in full on the borrower's next payday, typically secured by a post-dated check or permission to debit the borrower's bank account. Its price is quoted as a fee, commonly $15 for each $100 borrowed. The CFPB shows how that becomes an annual rate: $15 over 14 days is about $1.07 a day, and $1.07 × 365 is about $391, so the APR is about 391 per cent. [cite:ad9_cfpb_apr] The quoted fee looks small because the loan is meant to last two weeks. The CFPB's 2014 study of millions of loans found that it usually did not: more than 80 per cent of payday loans were rolled over or followed by another loan within 14 days, about half of all loans were made in sequences of ten or more, and one borrower in five paid monthly stayed in debt for the whole year. [cite:ad9_cfpb_rollover]

The Pew Charitable Trusts' 2012 survey gave the borrower's side. About 12 million Americans a year took payday loans, spending more than $7 billion. The average borrower took eight loans of about $375 a year, paid about $520 in interest and was in debt about five months of the year. Sixty-nine per cent of first-time borrowers said they used the money for recurring bills such as rent, utilities or food, and 16 per cent for an unexpected emergency. [cite:ad9_pew2012] That is the core of the dispute: a product sold as an emergency bridge is used mostly to cover a shortfall that recurs, and each recurrence costs another fee.

Payday lending is regulated mainly by the states, and the states disagree. By the Center for Responsible Lending's count, Rhode Island in July 2025 became the 21st state, alongside the District of Columbia, to cap payday rates at about 36 per cent, a level that in practice ends the two-week product; its law takes effect on 1 January 2027. [cite:ad9_crl_ri] Pew found that 2.9 per cent of adults used payday loans in the most restrictive states against 6.6 per cent in the least, and that in states without storefronts only 5 in 100 would-be borrowers turned to online lenders instead. [cite:ad9_pew2012] Congress set a national cap for one group only: the Military Lending Act of 2006 limits the cost of most consumer credit to active-duty service members and their families to a 36 per cent military APR, and a 2015 Defense Department rule extended it to credit cards and most other loans. [cite:ad9_fdic_mla] The CFPB's 2017 payday rule would have required lenders to check that borrowers could repay; the bureau rescinded that requirement on 7 July 2020, before it took effect, and kept only the payment provisions, which bar a lender from trying again to debit an account after two failed attempts and require advance notices. [cite:ad9_crs_payday2020] Those took effect on 30 March 2025, but two days earlier, on 28 March, the bureau said it would not prioritise enforcing them, and its regulatory agenda of July 2026 announced a proposal to reconsider them; status as of October 2026: in force on paper, not a supervisory priority, under reconsideration. [cite:ad9_sheppard_payday]

The industry's case was put by Dennis Shaul of the Community Financial Services Association, the payday trade group, to Congress in 2016: demand for the loans reflects unstable incomes; for many customers a payday fee is cheaper than a bounced check, a late fee or a cut-off utility; states already license the business; and the CFPB's underwriting rule would "effectively end payday lending as it currently exists". [cite:ad9_cfsa_2016] There is evidence that access can help in a crisis. Adair Morse found that after natural disasters in California, foreclosures rose by about 4.5 per 1,000 homes and that the presence of payday lenders offset about 1.0 to 1.3 of them, with no such effect where homeowners' insurance covered the disaster. [cite:ad9_morse2011] Both findings can hold at once: a payday loan can be the least bad option for a one-time shock and an expensive trap for a recurring shortfall, and the CFPB data show the second use is the more common.

Buy now, pay later

Buy now, pay later (BNPL) plans split a purchase, usually into four payments over six weeks with a quarter paid at checkout, and generally charge the shopper no interest. The CFPB's January 2025 study of six large lenders counted about 277 million such loans worth $34 billion in 2022; daily applications had risen from just over 100,000 in 2019 to well over a million. More than 60 per cent of loans in 2021–2022 went to borrowers with subprime or deep-subprime scores, about 63 per cent of borrowers held more than one loan at the same time, and BNPL users carried card utilisation of 60 to 66 per cent of their limits against 34 per cent for non-users; the bureau said this showed association, not that BNPL caused the other debt. [cite:ad9_cfpb_bnpl2025] In 2025, 16 per cent of adults used BNPL, and 11 per cent of users said a BNPL payment had triggered an overdraft or NSF fee at their bank. [cite:ad9_shed2025] In May 2024 the CFPB issued an interpretive rule classing BNPL providers as credit-card issuers under the Truth in Lending Act; on 6 May 2025 it said it would not prioritise enforcing it, and on 12 May 2025 it withdrew it. [cite:ad9_orrick_bnpl] [cite:ad9_cfpb_bnpl_page] As of October 2026 no federal rule specific to BNPL applies.

Wage advances and cash-advance apps

Earned-wage access (EWA) products let a worker draw part of the pay already earned before payday, repaid automatically from the next paycheck. Some are offered through employers; others are phone apps that advance cash against expected pay and are repaid by debiting the user's bank account. Most do not charge interest. They charge fees for instant delivery, monthly memberships, or ask for "tips". California's financial regulator collected data from these companies for 2021; on the National Consumer Law Center's summary of it, users took about 36 advances a year, mostly between $40 and $100 for about ten days, and the average cost worked out to an APR of 334 per cent at tip-based companies and 331 per cent at those charging fees. Tips were paid 73 per cent of the time, and 97 per cent of advances were repaid. [cite:ad9_nclc_ewa] On 23 December 2025 the CFPB issued an advisory opinion that EWA repaid by payroll deduction, limited to wages already earned, with no recourse against the worker and no credit check, is not credit under the Truth in Lending Act, and that its delivery fees and tips are not finance charges; it rescinded a 2024 interpretation that had treated such products as loans. States are taking their own course, with California regulating EWA under its own consumer-finance law. [cite:ad9_mofo_ewa]

Federal enforcement has focused on how the apps were marketed. In November 2023 the Federal Trade Commission obtained $18 million in refunds from Brigit, which had advertised "instant" advances of up to $250 that few users received, charged a 99-cent fee for transfers it called free, and made its $9.99 monthly membership hard to cancel. [cite:ad9_ftc_brigit] The FTC sued Dave, Inc. in November 2024, alleging misleading advance amounts, undisclosed fees and tips taken without consent; the Justice Department added the chief executive as a defendant in December. [cite:ad9_ftc_dave] Dave called the suit "government overreach" and replaced tips and express fees with a new fee structure for new members from December 2024. [cite:ad9_pd_dave] A federal judge denied its motion to dismiss on 12 September 2025, and by the company's March 2026 annual report the city of Baltimore had filed its own suit. [cite:ad9_dave_10k] As of the company's report for the second quarter of 2026, published in August, the federal case was still pending, with no trial date, settlement or ruling reported. [cite:ad9_audit_dave_q2] None of these allegations has been decided at trial.

Medical and dental credit cards

Medical credit cards are offered at the point of care, often by staff in doctors' and dentists' offices, typically with a deferred-interest promotion: no interest if the balance is paid in full within, say, six to eighteen months. If any balance remains on the last day, all the interest that accrued from the purchase date is charged at once. The CFPB's May 2023 report found that the typical rate on these cards was 26.99 per cent, against about 16 per cent on general cards at the time; that about one promotion in five was not paid off in time; and that patients paid about $1 billion in deferred interest between 2018 and 2020. [cite:ad9_cfpb_medcc] [cite:ad9_cfpb_carecredit] Take a $2,400 procedure on a six-month promotion. A patient who pays nothing until the final month and then cannot clear the balance is charged six months' interest on the full $2,400 at once, about $324 at 26.99 per cent (2,400 × 0.2699 × 6 ÷ 12; book arithmetic, simple interest); one who paid most of it down is charged less, but still back to the purchase date. In 2013 the bureau ordered GE Capital Retail Bank and its CareCredit unit to refund up to $34.1 million to patients who had been enrolled in providers' offices believing the cards were interest-free. [cite:ad9_cfpb_carecredit] Part Eight follows what happens when such balances go unpaid. [scene:ad8_medical_debt|Part Eight]

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Interpretation, not finding: the poverty premium as a business model

The Sophia platform reads the products in this part as one system: the less money a household has, the more it pays to use money, through overdraft fees, check-cashing charges, payday rollovers and deferred interest, and the revenue from that premium gives the businesses that collect it a stake in the shortfall continuing. In this reading, the Dream's promise that credit is a ladder works in reverse for people at the bottom, for whom credit is the cost of being short.

The strongest counter-readings are these. First, small, short, unsecured loans to people with weak credit are costly to make, and losses and fixed costs explain part of the price; the industry argues that caps remove the product rather than lowering its price, and the Morse study shows access can prevent worse outcomes such as foreclosure. [cite:ad9_cfsa_2016] [cite:ad9_morse2011] Second, the record shows the market and the law moving in both directions: large banks cut overdraft revenue in half on their own, the unbanked share halved, twenty-one states and the District of Columbia enacted payday rate caps, and Congress protected service members. [cite:us22_cfpb_od23] [cite:ad9_fdic2023] [cite:ad9_crl_ri] [cite:ad9_fdic_mla] Third, the most clearly deceptive conduct has drawn enforcement: the CareCredit order (2013), the Brigit refunds (2023) and the Dave suit, filed in 2024 and still being litigated by the Justice Department under the following administration. [cite:ad9_ftc_brigit] [cite:ad9_ftc_dave] [cite:ad9_cfpb_carecredit] What the record establishes is narrower than either reading: each product here charges the most to borrowers who use it repeatedly, those borrowers are disproportionately people with the least cushion, and as of October 2026 most of the federal limits proposed in 2024 have been withdrawn, vacated or repealed.

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: Retirement: From Pension to 401(k)
chapters.intro: Part Ten follows the promise that a working life ends in a secure retirement. It begins with the private pension: the 1963 Studebaker collapse that led to federal pension insurance in 1974, the tax clause of 1978 that became the 401(k), and the four decades in which individual accounts replaced guaranteed pensions for most private-sector workers, with what that change did to who is covered, how much they hold, what fees take, and where the risk of running short now sits. It then turns to Social Security, the part of the retirement system that has most nearly done what it promised, setting out how it is built and financed, how far it reduced poverty in old age, how its rules were changed in 1983, why the cap on taxed wages now reaches less of the nation's pay, and what the 2034 trust-fund date does and does not mean. It ends with old age as it is lived now, measured by two official poverty rates, an index of what basic living actually costs older people, the savings older households hold, and the growing number of Americans still working past 65.
chapters.outro: Part Ten established that the private pension did not end by law but by choice: the active members of private defined-benefit plans fell from 71 per cent of the total in 1975 to about 10 per cent in 2023, so that by March 2026 only 14 per cent of private workers had a pension available while 70 per cent had a 401(k)-type account, which carries investment and longevity risk on the worker. [cite:ad10_dol_hist] [cite:ad10_bls_ebs26] Those accounts reach the low-paid least, hold a median of $44,115 against an average of $167,970, and leave 45 per cent of families with no retirement account at all, though automatic enrolment and falling fees show the model can be repaired. [cite:us22_bls_ebs25] [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] [cite:ad10_scf26] [cite:ad10_ici_fees25] Social Security is the part of the promise that has held: old-age poverty fell from 35.2 per cent in 1959 to 9.9 per cent in 2024, and the programme moved 28.8 million people out of poverty in 2025; its combined reserves are projected to run out in 2034, after which about 83 per cent of scheduled benefits would still be paid unless Congress acts, while the cap now leaves about a fifth of covered wages untaxed. [cite:ad10_census_a3] [cite:us18_census_p60290] [cite:ad10_crs_tr26] [cite:ad10_crs_base] Measured against what old age costs, the record is thinner: 15.4 per cent of older Americans were poor on the supplemental measure in 2025, half of older people living alone fell below the Elder Index in 2019, and nearly one in five people over 65 is still working. [cite:ad10_aarp_spm65] [cite:ad10_umb_2019] [cite:ad10_pew_older] These figures stand as of October 2026. Who pays for all of this, through taxes, fees and fines, is the subject of Part Eleven. [scene:ad11_who_pays|Part Eleven: Taxes, Fees and Fines]

sections.h: From Pension to 401(k)
sections.html:
The retirement half of the Dream was taught as a reward that arrived on its own: work for a good employer long enough and a monthly cheque follows you into old age. For a large share of private-sector workers in the 1970s that was a description of their plan. It no longer describes most plans. No law abolished pensions; what changed, slowly, was which plan employers chose to offer and who carries the risk that the money runs short.

Two terms carry the argument. A defined-benefit plan, the traditional pension, promises a defined amount, usually a monthly payment for life set by a formula of salary and years of service. The employer funds it, invests the money and makes up any shortfall, so the employer bears two risks: that investments do badly and that retirees live longer than expected. A defined-contribution plan, of which the 401(k) is the best-known kind, defines only what goes in. The worker, and often the employer, pays into an individual account; what the worker has at retirement depends on how much was paid in, what the investments earned, what fees were taken, and whether the money was withdrawn early. The worker must then make it last an unknown lifespan: the plan promises an account, not an income.

Studebaker, ERISA and the guarantee

The old pension had a weakness that one bankruptcy made national news. In 1963 the carmaker Studebaker closed its South Bend, Indiana, plant and terminated its pension plan. About 3,600 workers who had already retired received their full benefits. About 4,000 active employees received roughly 15 per cent of what they had been promised, and thousands under 40 received nothing; in all, more than 8,500 workers lost some or all of their pensions. [cite:ad10_pbgc_studebaker] [cite:ad10_pbgc_history] The pension had been a promise backed only by the company that made it.

Congress answered eleven years later. On 2 September 1974 President Gerald Ford signed the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, known as ERISA, which set rules for funding, vesting and the conduct of the people who run plans, and created the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, a federal insurer for private pensions funded by premiums from the plans it covers. PBGC paid its first benefit, $140.75, on 28 February 1975. It now pays about 926,000 retirees from more than 5,000 failed plans, owes benefits to another 428,000 who have not yet retired, and insures about 30 million people in private defined-benefit plans. [cite:ad10_pbgc_history] ERISA protected promises once made. It did not require anyone to make them: in the Labor Department's words, "ERISA does not require any employer to establish a retirement plan." [cite:us18a_dol_erisa]

A tax clause becomes the system

The 401(k) began as a paragraph in a tax bill. The Revenue Act of 1978, signed by President Jimmy Carter on 6 November 1978, was mainly a package of tax cuts; among its provisions was a new section 401(k) of the Internal Revenue Code, promoted by Representative Barber Conable, which confirmed that employees could have part of their pay put into a plan before income tax, effective from 1 January 1980. [cite:ad10_napa_1978] Arrangements of this "cash or deferred" kind had existed since the 1950s, approved by an IRS ruling in 1956. [cite:ad10_ici_retro] What turned the clause into a mass product was the IRS's proposed regulation of 10 November 1981, which made clear that ordinary salary reductions qualified; benefits writers date the modern 401(k) from that day. [cite:ad10_ici_retro] [cite:ad10_napa_1978] A long-time retirement-industry editor summarises the record plainly: the 401(k) was "never intended (nor designed) to replace defined benefit pensions." [cite:ad10_napa_1978]

How fast the shift came

The Labor Department's historical tables, built from the annual reports every plan files, show the change year by year. In 1975 private defined-benefit plans had 27.2 million active participants, meaning people still working and earning credit, against 11.2 million in defined-contribution plans. In 1984 the lines crossed, 30.5 million to 30.1 million. By 2000 it was 50.9 million against 22.2 million, and in 2023, the latest year, 96.4 million against 11.1 million. The number of defined-benefit plans peaked at about 170,000 in 1985 and stood at 46,233 in 2023, against 790,610 defined-contribution plans. [cite:ad10_dol_hist] These are counts of plan memberships, not of people: a worker in both kinds of plan is counted twice, and the Department changed its definition in 2004, so the series is best read as two segments. On either segment the direction is the same. The defined-benefit share of active participants, by this book's arithmetic, fell from 71 per cent in 1975 to 28 per cent in 2004 on the old definition, and from 25 per cent in 2004 to 10 per cent in 2023 on the new one. [cite:ad10_dol_hist]

Why it happened is disputed in a way the numbers alone cannot settle. The Investment Company Institute, the mutual fund industry's trade association, argued in its 25-year review that few employers replaced a pension with a 401(k) outright; most of the shift, in its account, came from the decline of the unionised manufacturing industries where pensions were common, from pension sponsors adding a 401(k) on top, and from new firms choosing the newer plan. [cite:ad10_ici_retro] The participant counts, which fall slowly rather than collapse, fit that account; it does not change where the risk now sits. In March 2026, 70 per cent of private-industry workers had access to a defined-contribution plan and 14 per cent to a defined-benefit plan, while 86 per cent of state and local government workers still had a pension available. [cite:ad10_bls_ebs26]

Who is in, and how much they have

Access to any workplace plan has been steady at about seven private workers in ten: 72 per cent in March 2026, with 52 per cent actually participating. [cite:ad10_bls_ebs26] The gap falls by pay. Among the lowest-paid tenth of private workers in March 2025, 38 per cent had access and 15 per cent participated; among part-time workers, 47 and 23 per cent. [cite:us22_bls_ebs25] Inside plans the pattern repeats: in Vanguard's 2025 records, covering about 1,300 plans and 4.6 million accounts, 43 per cent of eligible workers earning under $15,000 participated, against 74 per cent of those earning $30,000 to $50,000 and 95 per cent of those earning over $150,000. [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26]

Balances show why the difference between an average and a median matters (both are defined in [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two]). The average Vanguard account at the end of 2025 held $167,970; the median, the account in the middle, held $44,115. [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] A few large accounts pull the average up to almost four times the typical one. The Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which covers all families rather than one recordkeeper's clients, found that 54.9 per cent of families held any retirement account; among those that did, the median balance was $106,000. [cite:ad10_scf26] Widely shared figures putting the median 401(k) in a worker's fifties above $250,000 do not match either source.

Fees, and the money trail of the risk transfer

An account has costs a pension member never sees directly. Fees are charged as a percentage of assets each year, through each fund's expense ratio and the plan's administration charges, so small differences compound. The Labor Department's long-standing illustration takes a $25,000 balance growing for 35 years at 7 per cent a year: with fees of 0.5 per cent it ends at $227,000, with 1.5 per cent at $163,000, 28 per cent less. [cite:ad10_politifact_fees] A widely repeated version of that example claims Wall Street takes a third of workers' savings; fact-checkers rated it mostly false, because 1.5 per cent was well above the median all-in fee of 0.72 per cent found in a 2009 industry survey. [cite:ad10_politifact_fees] Fees have since fallen sharply. The asset-weighted expense ratio of equity mutual funds held in 401(k)s fell from 0.76 per cent in 2000 to 0.26 per cent in 2024, and target-date funds from 0.67 to 0.29 per cent between 2008 and 2024. [cite:ad10_ici_fees25] The sums remain large: mutual funds held $6.2 trillion of 401(k) assets in mid-2026, and 0.26 per cent of $6.2 trillion is about $16 billion a year, a rough order of magnitude since bond and hybrid funds charge different rates. [cite:ad10_ici_q2_26] [cite:ad10_ici_fees25]

The charts below plot the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; each caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

One design change has done much of what reformers hoped. When a plan enrols workers automatically and lets them opt out, rather than waiting for them to opt in, participation in Vanguard's plans was 94 per cent in 2025, against 64 per cent in plans without it; 61 per cent of its plans now enrol automatically. [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] The SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 requires most 401(k) and 403(b) plans set up after 29 December 2022 to enrol new workers at 3 to 10 per cent of pay, rising a point a year to at least 10 per cent, from plan years beginning in 2025; small and new employers are exempt, and the Treasury sent final rules for review on 23 June 2026. [cite:ad10_asppa_auto] Seventeen states have passed laws creating automatic payroll IRAs for workers whose employers offer no plan. [cite:ad10_aarp_autoira] Fees, as shown above, have fallen by roughly two-thirds since 2000. Running the other way, on 30 March 2026 the Labor Department proposed a safe harbour for plan managers who add private equity, real estate and crypto-assets to 401(k) menus, carrying out an August 2025 executive order; managers would have to weigh each option's fees, liquidity, valuation and complexity. [cite:ad10_block_alts] Status as of October 2026: proposed.

Interpretation, not finding: the account as a transfer of risk

The Sophia platform reads the move from pension to 401(k) as the clearest case of the Dream's design: the promise of a secure old age was kept in words while the risk of failing to reach it was handed, one account at a time, to the people least able to carry it, and a fee-earning industry grew in the space between. In this reading the 401(k) is not a failed pension but a successful transfer.

The strongest counter-readings are documented. The 401(k) was not designed to replace pensions, and the leading industry account attributes most of the shift to industrial change rather than substitution. [cite:ad10_napa_1978] [cite:ad10_ici_retro] Studebaker showed that an employer's pension promise could itself vanish. [cite:ad10_pbgc_studebaker] Automatic enrolment and falling fees show the account model can be repaired by ordinary legislation. What remains is the risk itself, which no reading disputes has moved.

sections.h: Social Security: The Floor That Held
sections.html:
If the 401(k) is the part of retirement where the taught promise and the record have drifted furthest apart, Social Security is the part where they sit closest together. It is the one income most Americans can count on in old age that does not depend on an employer's choice, on stock prices or on how long they live, and its record against poverty is the strongest of any programme examined in this book. Its difficulties are real, but they are financing problems with known sizes and dates, not the disappearance that is often predicted.

How it was built

President Franklin Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act on 14 August 1935. The first payments, in 1937, were one-time lump sums; the first monthly benefit, a cheque for $22.54, went to Ida M. Fuller on 31 January 1940. Amendments in 1939 added benefits for dependants and survivors, and in 1956 for workers with disabilities. [cite:ad10_audit_ssa_hist] In 1961 the earliest age at which anyone could claim a reduced retirement benefit was set at 62. In 1972 Congress made benefits rise automatically each year with consumer prices, starting in 1975, and created Supplemental Security Income for older, blind and disabled people with very low incomes. [cite:ad10_aarp_sstl]

The programme is financed mainly as it goes. Workers and employers each pay a payroll tax on wages up to a yearly ceiling; that money pays current retirees, and any surplus is lent to the Treasury and held in two trust funds, one for old-age and survivors insurance and one for disability. In 2025, 91.3 per cent of the programme's income came from payroll taxes, 4.0 per cent from income tax that higher-income retirees pay on their benefits, and 4.8 per cent from interest on the trust funds. [cite:ad10_crs_tr26] A worker's benefit is based on his or her own earnings record, and the yearly cost-of-living adjustment keeps it from losing value to inflation, the protection the federal minimum wage lacks. [cite:ad10_aarp_sstl] On 14 October 2026 the Social Security Administration announced a 3.6 per cent increase for 2027, raising the average monthly benefit from about $2,088 to about $2,163; more than 76 million people receive Social Security or SSI. [cite:ad10_napa_cola27]

The record against old-age poverty

In 1959, the first year the Census Bureau's official poverty series covers, 35.2 per cent of Americans aged 65 and over were poor. The rate was 28.5 per cent in 1966, 24.6 per cent in 1970 and 15.3 per cent in 1975, after the large benefit increases of the early 1970s and the start of automatic adjustments. It fell to about 10 per cent by the mid-1990s and has stayed near there since: 9.9 per cent in 2024. [cite:ad10_census_a3] On the official measure the rate fell by more than two-thirds, from 35.2 to 9.9 per cent.

The poverty table alone cannot say how much of that fall Social Security caused; Medicare from 1965, SSI from 1972, and the pensions of the post-war generation all arrived in the same years. The Census Bureau's supplemental poverty measure, which counts benefits and taxes as income, gives the programme's present weight directly: in 2025 Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of poverty, more than any other programme. [cite:us18_census_p60290] This is the plainest case in the volume of a mechanism that does what it was taught to do.

The rules that were changed: retirement age and the 1983 rescue

The programme's last major overhaul came when its reserves were running low. On 20 April 1983 President Ronald Reagan signed amendments based on the recommendations of the National Commission on Social Security Reform. They raised the age for a full, unreduced benefit, then 65, in two stages to 67, beginning with people born in 1938 and completed for those born in 1960 or later, who reach 67 in 2027; claiming at 62 remained possible with a larger reduction. They made up to half of benefits taxable for retirees whose income exceeded $25,000 (single) or $32,000 (married), delayed one cost-of-living increase by six months, brought forward scheduled payroll-tax increases, and brought new federal employees, members of Congress and the President into the system from 1984. [cite:ad10_ssa_1983] [cite:ad10_aarp_sstl]

The higher retirement age is a benefit cut by another name: claiming at any given age now pays less than it would have under the old rules. It was enacted openly, phased in over decades, and fell on every worker born after 1937, which is what distinguishes it from the hidden erosion of a frozen dollar threshold. It is a case of designed change, not captured friction.

The cap on taxable wages

The payroll tax stops at a ceiling. In 2026 no Social Security tax is due on wages above $184,500; in 2027 the ceiling will be $192,300. [cite:ad10_napa_cola27] Because benefits are also calculated only on wages up to the ceiling, the cap is a designed feature of an earned-benefit programme, not a loophole. What has changed is its reach. The 1977 amendments raised the cap faster than the automatic formula so that about 90 per cent of all wages in covered jobs would be taxed, and in 1982 that was the share. By 2021 it had fallen to 81 per cent, because earnings above the cap grew faster than earnings below it, even though only about 6 per cent of workers earn more than the ceiling. [cite:ad10_crs_base] In plain terms, the growing share of the nation's pay going to its highest earners has moved a growing share of pay outside the programme's tax base. A worker earning $60,000 pays the tax on every dollar; one earning $1 million pays it on less than a fifth, since $184,500 divided by $1,000,000 is 0.18.

The trust-fund date

The programme's trustees report each year on its finances. Their 2026 report, released on 9 June 2026, projects that the old-age and survivors fund will run out of reserves in the fourth quarter of 2032, and the combined old-age, survivors and disability funds in the third quarter of 2034; after that, continuing tax income would pay about 83 per cent of scheduled benefits, falling to 65 per cent by 2100. The disability fund alone is not projected to run out. [cite:ad10_aarp_sstl] [cite:ad10_crs_tr26]

The long-term shortfall widened from 3.82 per cent of taxable payroll in the 2025 report to 4.42 per cent. The trustees gave three main reasons: a lower assumed birth rate (1.75 children per woman rather than 1.90), lower projected immigration, which means fewer future workers paying in, and P.L. 119-21, the 2025 budget law signed by President Donald Trump, which reduces the programme's income from the tax on benefits. [cite:ad10_crs_tr26] The 4.42 per cent figure is the size of the problem in the trustees' own units: closing it over 75 years would take the equivalent of a payroll-tax increase of that many points, an equivalent cut in benefits, or a mix, including changes to the cap. [cite:ad10_crs_tr26] [cite:ad10_crs_base]

A widely repeated claim holds that Social Security "will not be there" for younger workers. The trustees' projections say otherwise: without any change in law, the programme would still pay roughly four-fifths of promised benefits after 2034 and about two-thirds at the end of the century, because payroll taxes do not stop when the reserves do. [cite:ad10_crs_tr26] The real risk is an automatic, across-the-board cut of about 17 per cent in 2034 if Congress does not act, which for the average benefit announced for 2027 would mean about $370 a month (17 per cent of $2,163). [cite:ad10_napa_cola27] The remedies on offer are the ones the 1983 law used: more revenue, such as raising or removing the cap, or lower benefits, such as a later retirement age or slower growth for higher earners. [cite:ad10_crs_base] No such package had been enacted when the trustees reported in June 2026. [cite:ad10_crs_tr26]

Social Security also cannot carry a retirement alone, and was not designed to. The average benefit of about $2,088 a month in 2026 comes to about $25,000 a year (12 × $2,088). [cite:ad10_napa_cola27] What that buys against the actual cost of living in old age is the subject of the next section. [scene:ad10_old_age|Old age, as lived]

sections.h: Old Age, as Lived
sections.html:
The taught version of retirement ends in a picture: a paid-off house, a pension, a Social Security cheque and savings, enough to stop working and live without fear of running out. The two previous sections took the parts of that picture one at a time. This section asks what they add up to for the people now old, using the government's two poverty measures, an independent measure of what old age actually costs, and the record of older Americans who are still at work.

Two poverty rates for the same people

The official poverty measure, set in the 1960s, compares a family's cash income before taxes with a threshold based on the cost of food, updated only for inflation. On it, 9.9 per cent of Americans aged 65 and over were poor in 2024, close to the level of the past quarter-century and far below the 35.2 per cent of 1959. [cite:ad10_census_a3] The Census Bureau's supplemental poverty measure counts things the official one leaves out: taxes, benefits paid in kind, and necessary spending such as housing and out-of-pocket medical care. On that measure 15.4 per cent of people 65 and over were poor in 2025, more than 10 million people, up from 12.7 per cent in 2019 and a low of 9.4 per cent in 2020; the rate was 13.7 per cent for older men and 16.8 per cent for older women. [cite:ad10_aarp_spm65] [cite:ad10_leadingage] The difference between 9.9 and 15.4 per cent is not a contradiction. It reflects what the supplemental measure subtracts before treating income as available to live on, including housing costs and out-of-pocket medical spending. [scene:ad8_costs_and_coverage|Part Eight: health costs]

A third measure compares countries. The OECD counts a person as poor in relative terms if household income, after taxes and benefits and adjusted for household size, falls below half the national median. By that measure 22.9 per cent of Americans aged 66 and over were poor in 2023, a higher rate than for Americans as a whole. [cite:us22_oecd_idd_usa66] The figure describes distance from the middle, not hardship as such: an older person can be above every American poverty threshold and still below half the median income of a high-income country.

The Elder Index: what old age costs

Poverty lines measure deprivation, not security. Researchers at the University of Massachusetts Boston built the Elder Index to measure the second: the income an older person needs, county by county, to pay for housing, food, transport, health care and other necessities without help. In 2019 the national average was $25,416 a year for a single older adult who rented and $36,204 for an older couple. By that standard half of older Americans living alone, 50 per cent, and 23 per cent of older couples had incomes too low to cover their basic costs. Among single older adults, 18.2 per cent were below the federal poverty line, and another 32.1 per cent were above it but below the Elder Index, a group the researchers describe as living "in the gap." [cite:ad10_umb_2019] More recent state reports find the same pattern where housing is dear: in Massachusetts in 2025, 60 per cent of older adults living alone had incomes below the index, the second-highest share of any state. [cite:ad10_umb_ma25]

The arithmetic against Social Security is direct. The average benefit in 2026 is about $2,088 a month, or about $25,000 a year (12 × $2,088). [cite:ad10_napa_cola27] That is already below the 2019 national Elder Index for a single renter, $25,416, before allowing for seven years of rising prices. [cite:ad10_umb_2019] For an older person living alone and renting, with no other income, the average benefit does not cover the basic budget the index describes. A pension, savings or work has to fill the gap.

The savings that are supposed to fill it

For many households they do. In 2025, among families whose head was 55 to 64 and who held an IRA or 401(k)-type account, the mean balance was $670,200; across all families, about one in four held a defined-benefit pension. [cite:ad10_scf26] But that mean is pulled up by large accounts, the same effect that puts Vanguard's average balance at almost four times its median of $44,115. [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] And 45.1 per cent of all families held no retirement account at all (100 minus the 54.9 per cent who did). [cite:ad10_scf26] For those families, old age rests on Social Security, home equity if they own a home, and whatever work they can still do. How wealth in general divides by age, income and race is set out in [scene:ad12_wealth_gap|Part Twelve].

Working longer

More older Americans are working. Pew Research Center, using federal survey data, found 19 per cent of adults aged 65 and over in work in 2023, against 11 per cent in 1987, and 9 per cent of those 75 and over, against 4 per cent; the older workforce, about 11 million people, has nearly quadrupled since the mid-1980s. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects the participation rate of people 65 and over will rise from 19 to 21 per cent by 2032. [cite:ad10_pew_older] The rise is partly a return: about 18 per cent of people 65 and over worked in the early 1960s, before the large increases in Social Security, so the 1980s low is as much the exception as today's level. [cite:ad10_pew_older]

Whether older Americans work because they want to or because they must is not settled by these figures. Pew points to several causes: more education and better health, both linked to working longer; jobs that have become less physically demanding; the shift from pensions, which encouraged retiring at a set age, to 401(k)-type accounts, which do not; and the later full retirement age set in 1983, which rewards staying on. In a Federal Reserve survey cited by Pew, 45 per cent of employed older adults described themselves as retired, which suggests that much later-life work is part-time work alongside a pension or benefit rather than a career that never ended. [cite:ad10_pew_older] [cite:ad10_ssa_1983] Others work because the arithmetic above leaves them no choice. Neither reading accounts for all of the change, and no national survey found here divides older workers cleanly between the two.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

The largest change in this part of the record is good news, and it should be stated without qualification. An American who reached 65 in 1959 had about a one-in-three chance of being poor on the official measure; one who reached 65 in 2024 had about a one-in-ten chance. [cite:ad10_census_a3] The principal reason in the current data is a public programme that pays an inflation-protected benefit earned by work, and that in 2025 kept 28.8 million people of all ages above the supplemental poverty line. [cite:us18_census_p60290] Where the record falls short of the promise, it falls short in specific places: older people who live alone, who rent in high-cost areas, who carry heavy medical costs, or who reached retirement without a pension or an account. Those are the households the supplemental measure and the Elder Index pick out, and they are where the shift from pension to 401(k) and the gap between the average benefit and the cost of living meet. [cite:ad10_aarp_spm65] [cite:ad10_umb_2019]

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: Taxes, Fees and the Benefits Cliff
chapters.intro: Part Eleven follows the money that leaves a household through the public side of the ledger: taxes, fees and the benefits a family loses as it earns more. It begins with who pays what share of all taxes, federal, state and local together, setting the progressive federal system beside the regressive state and local one, the cap on the payroll tax, the gap between taxes on wages and on investment gains, the disputed claim that the richest pay lower rates than working families, and the distribution of the 2025 budget law. It then turns to fees: prices hidden until checkout and the federal rule that now requires them to be shown, utility shutoffs counted nationally for the first time, and towns that fund themselves from the fines their courts impose. It ends with the benefits cliff, the point at which a raise can leave a low-income family worse off, with worked examples, the measured size of the problem and the evidence that the safety net still pays most people to work.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven established that the federal tax system is progressive, taking 1.4 per cent of the lowest fifth's income and 31.5 per cent of the top 1 per cent's in 2022, and that every income group pays a lower federal rate than in 1979, while state and local taxes run the other way, 11.3 per cent of income for the lowest fifth against 7.2 per cent for the top 1 per cent, leaving all taxes together only slightly progressive. [cite:ad11_tf_cbo2022] [cite:ad11_tpc_cbo7907] [cite:ad11_itep_wp7] [cite:ad11_itep_wp2024] The payroll tax stops at $184,500 of earnings, long-term gains are taxed at no more than 23.8 per cent, the claim that the richest 400 pay less than workers remains contested, and CBO found that the 2025 budget law lowers resources for the poorest tenth by about $1,200 a year while raising the top tenth's by about $13,600. [cite:ad11_ssa_2026] [cite:ad11_bti_cg2025] [cite:ad11_tpc_sz2019] [cite:ad11_cato_forbes400] [cite:ad11_tr_pl11921] Hidden ticket and lodging fees must now be shown up front and the rule has been enforced; utilities carried out 15.1 million shutoffs in 2024; Ferguson budgeted 23 per cent of its general revenue from fines and fees, though most local governments draw under 5 per cent; and at least 25 states and the District of Columbia have curbed licence suspensions for unpaid court debt. [cite:ad11_ftc_fees2025] [cite:ad11_hc_stubhub] [cite:ad11_iej_shutoffs] [cite:ad11_doj_ferguson] [cite:ad11_governing_fines] [cite:ad11_ncsl_dl] Benefits cliffs are real at specific lines, with median effective rates of 73 per cent on a $5,000 raise for subsidised childcare families just above poverty and a marketplace cliff at 400 per cent of poverty that returned in 2026, but the average effective rate for low- and moderate-income workers is about 31 per cent and the tax credit still adds 40 cents to each dollar earned at the bottom. [cite:ad11_aspe_ccdf] [cite:ad11_hi_cliff] [cite:ad11_cbo_emtr] [cite:ad11_cftd_rp2532] These figures stand as of October 2026. Taxes and fees take from income; the larger gap in American life lies in what households own, the subject of Part Twelve. [scene:ad12_wealth_gap|Part Twelve: Income vs Wealth]

sections.h: Who Pays
sections.html:
The civic version of American taxation is short: the more you earn, the larger the share of your income you hand over, so that those who gain most from the system carry most of its cost. That description fits the federal system. It fits much less well once the payroll tax, the sales tax and the property tax built into every rent are added in. This section measures the whole bill. An average (or effective) tax rate is the total tax a household pays divided by its income; it is the number that tells you how heavy the bill is. A marginal rate is the tax on the next dollar earned; it matters for the benefits cliff at the end of this part. Households are grouped into quintiles, five equal fifths ranked by income, with the top 1 per cent often shown on its own. For the difference between income and wealth, and between median and mean, see [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two].

The federal system: progressive, and taxing the bottom less than in 1979

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's nonpartisan scorekeeper, publishes the standard measure. Its latest report, released on 24 September 2026 and covering 2023, found that average federal tax rates fell for every income group between 1979 and 2023, and fell most for the lowest fifth. The individual income tax alone ranged from minus 11 per cent of income for the lowest fifth to 16 per cent for the highest; the minus sign means that refundable credits, chiefly the Earned Income Tax Credit and the Child Tax Credit, paid out more to low-income working families than they owed. The top fifth paid 70 per cent of all federal taxes in 2023, against 55 per cent in 1979, and the top 1 per cent paid 26 per cent, against 14 per cent. [cite:ad11_cbo_dist2023]

For 2022, the year before, the Tax Foundation, a research group that generally favours lower taxes, drew the quintile figures out of CBO's data: all federal taxes took 1.4 per cent of the lowest fifth's income, 23.2 per cent of the highest fifth's, and 31.5 per cent of the top 1 per cent's. The lowest fifth's rate had been minus 16.5 per cent in 2020 and minus 22.5 per cent in 2021, when pandemic relief paid out through the tax system, and it rose when that relief ended. [cite:ad11_tf_cbo2022] [cite:us11_cbo_dist2022] The same data carry a second point that the shares alone hide: the top fifth pays more of the taxes partly because it takes more of the income. The bottom 80 per cent paid 44.8 per cent of federal taxes in 1979 and 29.6 per cent in 2022, but its share of income also fell, from 54.6 to 45.1 per cent; the top 1 per cent's share of income before taxes roughly doubled over the same years. [cite:ad11_tf_cbo2022] [cite:us11_cbo_dist2022]

The long view runs the same way. On CBO's older method (not directly comparable with the 2026 reports), the lowest fifth's average federal rate was 8.0 per cent in 1979 and 4.0 per cent in 2007; the middle fifth's fell from 18.6 to 14.3 per cent; the top fifth's from 27.5 to 25.1 per cent; and the top 1 per cent's from 37.0 to 29.5 per cent, with a low of 25.5 per cent in 1986 and a rebound to 36.0 per cent in 1996 after the 1993 rate increase. [cite:ad11_tpc_cbo7907] On this measure too, the federal side of the taught version holds.

State and local taxes: the other half of the bill

Federal figures leave out roughly a third of what Americans pay: in ITEP's estimate below, state and local taxes were 10.3 of the 29.2 per cent of income that all taxes took in 2024. [cite:ad11_itep_wp2024] The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP), a research group that generally favours more progressive taxation, publishes the main estimate of state and local burdens, Who Pays?, now in its seventh edition, which applies 2024 state and local tax law to 2023 incomes. Averaged across the country, state and local taxes took 11.3 per cent of family income for the lowest fifth, 10.5 per cent for the middle fifth, 9.5 per cent for the next 15 per cent, 8.3 per cent for the next 4 per cent and 7.2 per cent for the top 1 per cent. The pattern runs the opposite way from the federal one: the lower the income, the higher the rate. [cite:ad11_itep_wp7]

The reason is what each group buys and owns. The lowest fifth spends most of what it earns, so sales and excise taxes alone took 7 per cent of its income, and property taxes, paid directly by owners and passed through in rent by landlords, took another 4.4 per cent; state income taxes, net of credits, were slightly negative. For the top 1 per cent, sales and excise taxes took 1 per cent, property taxes 1.9 per cent and income taxes 4.1 per cent. [cite:ad11_itep_wp7] The combined state and local sales tax rate averaged 7.53 per cent nationally in mid-2026, above 9.5 per cent in Louisiana, Tennessee and Washington. [cite:us22_tf_sales26]

Adding all levels together changes the picture of the whole. ITEP's 2024 estimate of every federal, state and local tax found total rates of 17.1 per cent for the lowest fifth, 26.4 per cent for the middle fifth, 28.8 per cent for the next 15 per cent and 34.8 per cent for the top 1 per cent. The top 1 per cent received 20.1 per cent of all income and paid 23.9 per cent of all taxes; the lowest fifth received 2.6 per cent of income and paid 1.5 per cent of taxes. ITEP's own summary is that the system is "just barely progressive." [cite:ad11_itep_wp2024] ITEP's combined study puts the lowest fifth's state and local rate at 13.5 per cent, above the 11.3 per cent in its Who Pays? edition, because the two use different years and methods. [cite:ad11_itep_wp2024] [cite:ad11_itep_wp7]

The payroll tax and its cap

For most working families the largest federal tax is not the income tax. Employees pay 6.2 per cent of wages for Social Security and 1.45 per cent for Medicare, 7.65 per cent in all, and employers pay the same again; the self-employed pay both halves, 15.3 per cent. The Medicare part applies to every dollar. The Social Security part stops at a ceiling, $184,500 of earnings in 2026, up from $176,100 in 2025. [cite:ad11_ssa_2026] The arithmetic of the cap is simple. A worker earning $50,000 pays $3,100 in employee Social Security tax, 6.2 per cent of pay. A worker earning ten times the cap, $1,845,000, pays the same tax as someone at the cap: 6.2 per cent of $184,500, or $11,439, which is 0.62 per cent of $1,845,000. That is why CBO's data show payroll taxes taking 9.5 per cent of the lowest fifth's income and 6.1 per cent of the highest fifth's. [cite:ad11_tf_cbo2022]

The cap is designed friction, not a loophole. Benefits are also calculated only on earnings up to the cap, and the benefit formula returns a higher share of past earnings to lower earners, so the program redistributes downward even though its tax does not. Whether the cap should rise is taken up in [scene:ad10_social_security|Part Ten]. [cite:ad11_ssa_2026]

A dollar earned two ways

The tax code treats income from work and income from owning assets differently. In 2026 the top federal rate on ordinary income, which includes wages, is 37 per cent on taxable income above $640,600 for a single filer. [cite:us22_irs_ty26] Gains on assets held longer than a year are taxed at 0, 15 or 20 per cent; in 2025 the 20 per cent rate began at $533,400 for a single filer, and a 3.8 per cent net investment income tax brings the top rate on such gains to 23.8 per cent. [cite:ad11_bti_cg2025] A wage dollar also carries Medicare tax; an asset sale does not. The gap matters because the very top of the income scale earns mostly from assets: the last published IRS data on the 400 highest-income returns, for 2014, reported about $77 billion from asset sales and $14 billion in dividends against under $6 billion in salaries and wages, and effective income tax rates flattening at the top for that reason. [cite:ad11_kenan_davids] [cite:ad11_tpc_sz2019]

The top 400: a disputed headline

A widely repeated claim holds that America's richest families pay a lower tax rate than its working class. Its source is the economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman, who estimated in October 2019 that the 400 richest families paid 23 per cent of their income in all taxes in 2018, against 24.2 per cent for the bottom half of households. The Tax Policy Center's Howard Gleckman questioned the comparison: it treated refundable credits as government spending rather than as negative taxes, which raises the measured rate at the bottom; it extrapolated 2018 from older data; and it rested on a group of 400 out of about 150 million taxpayers, where small errors compound. The Tax Policy Center's own estimate put the federal rate at 2.9 per cent for the lowest fifth and 30.6 per cent for the top 0.1 per cent. [cite:ad11_tpc_sz2019]

The dispute did not end there. A 2025 study by Saez, Zucman and two co-authors using IRS data estimated that roughly the 400 wealthiest paid about 24 per cent of their economic income in tax in 2018–2020, against about 30 per cent for the population as a whole.
