The economist David Splinter, who with Gerald Auten has tested how far such estimates depend on design choices, contends that correcting for double-counted unrealised gains, dynastic wealth spread across related returns and under-reported state taxes raises the top group's rate to about 38 per cent, and that counting transfers as income lowers the population's to about 25 per cent. The Cato Institute's Adam Michel, citing these adjustments and adding charitable giving, puts the range at 38 to 73 per cent. [cite:ad11_cato_forbes400] The finding that survives on both sides is narrower than the headline: the very richest, whose income is mostly unrealised gains on assets, pay a far smaller share of their economic gains each year than their statutory rates suggest, because gains are taxed only when sold. Whether that leaves them below working families depends on the definitions, and the claim is contested, not settled.

The 2025 law

On 4 July 2025 the President signed the budget reconciliation law, Public Law 119-21, which made permanent most of the 2017 individual tax cuts and cut projected spending on Medicaid and food assistance. In its analysis of 11 August 2025, CBO found that over 2026–2034 resources would fall for households toward the bottom of the income scale and rise for the middle and top. [cite:ad11_cbo_pl11921] As reported from CBO's tables, the lowest tenth of households would lose about $1,200 a year on average, 3.1 per cent of income, the fifth and sixth tenths would gain $800 to $1,200, and the top tenth would gain about $13,600 a year. [cite:ad11_tr_pl11921] CBO's totals show where the losses come from: federal and state in-kind transfers fall by about $900 billion over the period, mainly through lower spending on Medicaid and food assistance, which go chiefly to lower-income households. [cite:ad11_cbo_pl11921] As of October 2026 the law is in force; its Medicaid work requirements begin on 1 January 2027. [cite:ad8_ccf_ifr] Laws under both parties have moved these numbers before: the 1993 increase raised the top 1 per cent's rate, the 2001–03 cuts lowered rates across the scale, and pandemic relief pushed the bottom fifth's below zero. [cite:ad11_tpc_cbo7907] [cite:ad11_tf_cbo2022]

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

The federal tax system does what the civics description says. Every fifth pays a lower federal rate than in 1979, the lowest fifth pays almost nothing on net, and the income tax returns money to low-income working families through refundable credits. CBO finds that federal taxes and transfers together reduce income inequality in every year it measures, and reduced it by more in 2023 than in most years since 1979. [cite:ad11_cbo_dist2023] The regressive part of the bill sits in state and local taxes and in the payroll tax. The next section turns to charges that are not called taxes at all.

sections.h: Fees Everywhere
sections.html:
A tax is set by a legislature, applies to everyone in the same position and appears in a published schedule. A fee is a charge for a particular service or event: a booking, a missed payment, a reconnection, a court appearance. Fees are not unusual or improper in themselves; a toll for a bridge or a fee for a passport charges the user of a service rather than every taxpayer, which is often the fairest arrangement. This section looks at three places where fees behave differently from that model: where they are hidden until the end of a purchase, where they are the enforcement end of a household falling behind on a bill, and where a local government uses them to fund itself. Fees charged by banks and card issuers, overdraft and late fees above all, are covered in [scene:ad9_fees_and_unbanked|Part Nine] and are not counted again here.

The price you are shown and the price you pay

The practice called drip pricing works by advertising a lower number than the one the buyer will finally pay. Mandatory service, resort, cleaning or processing charges are added screen by screen, so that the full price appears only at checkout, after the buyer has compared offers on the advertised figure and invested time in the purchase. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the federal consumer-protection agency, voted 4–1 on 17 December 2024 to adopt a rule against it for two industries, live-event tickets and short-term lodging, with Commissioner Andrew Ferguson casting the dissenting vote. The FTC projected that the rule would save consumers up to 53 million hours a year of searching for true prices, a saving it valued at more than $11 billion over ten years. [cite:ad11_upi_fees] That figure values consumers' time; it is not a count of the fees themselves.

The rule took effect on 12 May 2025. It requires a business that advertises a price in those industries to show the total price up front, including mandatory fees, at every stage of the purchase, including the resale market for tickets. It does not ban any type of fee or cap its amount. [cite:ad11_ftc_fees2025] Government taxes, shipping and optional extras may be shown separately, but must be disclosed before payment, and each violation can draw a civil penalty of up to $51,744. [cite:ad11_btlaw_fees] The rule has been enforced: on 9 April 2026 the FTC announced a $10 million settlement with the largest ticket-resale platform in the country, whose filings name StubHub, over allegations that it did not show all-in prices at every stage and deliberately delayed compliance to gain an edge in sales of high-demand tickets. The company neither admitted nor denied the allegations. [cite:ad11_hc_stubhub] As of October 2026 the rule remains in force for those two industries only; hidden fees elsewhere, from apartment rentals to restaurant surcharges, fall under the FTC's general power against deceptive practices and under state law.

Falling behind on the lights

For a household that cannot pay a utility bill, the cost of falling behind is not only a late charge but the loss of the service. Until recently no one counted how often that happened nationwide. In April 2026 the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) published its first survey of residential disconnections, covering utilities that serve 93.5 per cent of electricity customers and 96.1 per cent of gas customers. In 2024 utilities sent 122 million final disconnection notices and carried out 15.1 million shutoffs, 13.4 million of electricity and 1.7 million of gas, and recorded 12.6 million reconnections. [cite:ad11_iej_shutoffs] The figures count events, not households, so one family disconnected twice appears twice; they are reported here as summarised by the Initiative for Energy Justice, an advocacy group. They show a large enforcement system operating on household arrears, most of it followed by reconnection within the year. Late-payment and reconnection charges, deposits and protections against shutoffs in extreme heat or cold are set state by state by utility regulators.

Fines and fees as a source of revenue

Courts fine people for traffic, parking and municipal-code violations and, in many places, add fees to cover the cost of the court, the prosecutor, probation or collections. The clearest documented case of a government relying on these charges to fund itself is Ferguson, Missouri. After the police shooting of Michael Brown in August 2014, the US Department of Justice investigated the city's police department and municipal court and published its findings on 4 March 2015. [cite:ad11_doj_ferguson]

The report traced the money. Fines and fees brought in $1.38 million of the city's $11.07 million in general-fund revenue in fiscal 2010, about 12 per cent. The court collected $2.46 million in fiscal 2013, more than the $2.11 million budgeted, and the city budgeted $3.09 million of $13.26 million for fiscal 2015, about 23 per cent. City officials pressed the police for more: in March 2010 the finance director warned of a shortfall "unless ticket writing ramps up significantly," and in March 2013 asked whether the department "could deliver 10% increase." The court issued over 9,000 warrants in 2013, mostly for minor offences such as parking, traffic and housing-code violations, and added charges each time a defendant missed a court date or a payment. The Department's finding was that "Ferguson's law enforcement practices are shaped by the City's focus on revenue rather than by public safety needs." [cite:ad11_doj_ferguson] The arithmetic of the shares: $1.38 million divided by $11.07 million is 12.5 per cent; $3.09 million divided by $13.26 million is 23.3 per cent.

Ferguson was not unique, but neither was it typical. A national review of local audits by the magazine Governing in 2019 found nearly 600 jurisdictions drawing more than 10 per cent of their general-fund revenue from fines and forfeitures, and at least 284 drawing more than 20 per cent; in Georgetown, Louisiana, the share was 92 per cent in 2018. The same review found that for most local governments fines are under 5 per cent of general revenue, and that the median among the 50 largest cities was 2 per cent. The heavy reliance is concentrated in small places, and the review called its counts low estimates because many governments do not report fines separately. [cite:ad11_governing_fines]

Unpaid court debt reaches beyond the courtroom through the driving licence. A driver whose licence is suspended for an unpaid fine must choose between not driving to work and driving illegally, which can add a new offence. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL), nearly 11 million people have faced debt-based suspensions; a New Jersey study found that nearly 45 per cent of suspended drivers lost their jobs; and a 2019 Brennan Center report found jurisdictions spending more than 42 cents on hearings and jail for every dollar they collected through these suspensions. [cite:ad11_ncsl_dl] The penalties that follow from unpaid court debt, including jail, bail and charges in prison, are the subject of [scene:ad14_justice_costs|Part Fourteen].

Where it works as promised

Each of these mechanisms has drawn a correction, and the corrections have come from both parties. The FTC's fee rule was adopted under one administration and took effect and was enforced under the next, against a major company. [cite:ad11_ftc_fees2025] [cite:ad11_hc_stubhub] Since 2017, at least 25 states and the District of Columbia have passed laws, largely bipartisan, to curb or end licence suspensions for unpaid debt; California, Colorado, Idaho, New Mexico and Virginia no longer suspend for these reasons, and California's on-time collection rate rose 8.9 per cent in the year after it stopped, a sign that ending suspensions did not reduce payment there. [cite:ad11_ncsl_dl] Ferguson's court itself eliminated the added charges for missed appearances while the federal investigation was under way. [cite:ad11_doj_ferguson] What remains is narrower than a system of extraction by fee: a federal price-disclosure rule that covers two industries, utility shutoffs counted nationally for the first time, and a minority of local governments that still fund a large share of their budgets from the people their courts fine.

sections.h: The Benefits Cliff
sections.html:
The modern safety net was rebuilt around one promise: that work should always pay. On 17 February 1993, asking Congress to expand the Earned Income Tax Credit, President Bill Clinton put it plainly: "if you work 40 hours a week and you've got a child in the house, you will no longer be in poverty." [cite:ad1_clinton_1993] For a family with low earnings, the promise largely holds; the tax credit adds money to every dollar earned. The trouble comes a little higher up, where a family that has climbed out of the poorest bracket starts to lose help from several programs at once. This section explains how that happens, measures how often it bites, and sets out the evidence on the other side.

The central measure is the effective marginal tax rate: the share of an extra dollar of earnings that a family loses, counting both the taxes it pays on that dollar and the benefits it gives up because its income rose. A rate of 30 per cent means the family keeps 70 cents of the dollar. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, which builds the most widely used tools for modelling this, distinguishes two cases. On a benefits plateau, lost benefits erase most of a raise. On a benefits cliff, a raise or promotion leaves the family financially worse off, because benefits fall by more than earnings rise: the effective rate on that step is above 100 per cent. [cite:ad11_atl_what] [cite:ad11_atl_bridge]

How the phase-outs stack

Each benefit program was written by a different Congress, for a different purpose, with its own income test. Some taper smoothly; some stop at a line. Take a single parent with two children, earning enough to be on the downward slope of the Earned Income Tax Credit in 2026. That credit pays 40 cents for each dollar earned up to $18,290, reaching a maximum of $7,316, then shrinks once income passes $23,890 until it disappears at $58,629. [cite:ad11_cftd_rp2532] The arithmetic of the shrinking part: $7,316 spread over the $34,739 between $23,890 and $58,629 is a loss of 21.06 cents of credit for each extra dollar. The payroll tax takes another 7.65 cents. [cite:ad11_ssa_2026] So before any other program is counted, this parent keeps about 71 cents of each extra dollar.

Food assistance comes next. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) assumes that a household can spend 30 per cent of its net income, income after the program's deductions, on food, and reduces the benefit by that amount; most households must also have gross income below 130 per cent of the federal poverty line to qualify at all. [cite:ad11_irp_snap] For a household of three in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia, that line is $2,960 a month for the year that began on 1 October 2026, and the maximum benefit is $808 a month. [cite:ad11_fns_fy27] If every extra dollar counted fully toward net income, SNAP would take up to 30 cents more, bringing the combined rate to as much as 58.7 cents in the dollar before any state income tax; deductions make the SNAP share somewhat smaller in practice. These are smooth slopes. The cliffs come from programs that end at a line.

The lines

Childcare subsidies are the steepest. Under the federal Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF), eligibility ends at no more than 85 per cent of a state's median income (states may set the line lower), and in many states that point is a sheer drop: the family goes from a subsidised copayment to the full price of care. [cite:ad11_atl_bridge] The Department of Health and Human Services' policy office (ASPE) measured what that means. Using 2014 data and a standard simulation model, it found that families receiving childcare subsidies with incomes between 100 and 149 per cent of the poverty line faced a median effective rate of 67 per cent on a $2,000 raise, 73 per cent on a $5,000 raise and 79 per cent on a $10,000 raise. On the $5,000 raise, the median family kept $1,350. Among subsidised families between 100 and 199 per cent of poverty, a $10,000 raise cost 37 per cent of them their entire subsidy, a median loss of $4,400 a year. [cite:ad11_aspe_ccdf] A 2024 federal rule had capped family copayments at 7 per cent of income; a new rule published on 12 May 2026 and effective 13 July 2026 repealed the cap. [cite:ad5_acf_ccdf2026]

Health coverage has its own lines. Adults in states that expanded Medicaid qualify up to 138 per cent of the poverty line. [cite:ad8_kff_obbba_prov] Above that, marketplace coverage under the Affordable Care Act is subsidised, and the enhanced premium credits in place from 2021 removed the old upper limit. Those enhanced credits expired at the end of 2025; the House passed a three-year extension on 8 January 2026, 230 to 196, but as of October 2026 no extension has become law. [cite:ad8_astho_ptc] [cite:us16_ib_subsidy] The cliff at 400 per cent of the poverty line therefore returned in 2026: $84,600 for a household of two. For a 63-year-old couple in Charleston, West Virginia, earning $84,500, the benchmark silver plan costs a little over $700 a month after the subsidy. At $85,000 they receive nothing, and the cheapest bronze plan costs $3,648 a month. The arithmetic: $500 more income moves the cost of the cheapest coverage to $43,776 a year, against about $8,400 a year for a better plan just below the line. [cite:ad11_hi_cliff]

Other limits work on savings rather than income. Supplemental Security Income, the federal benefit for poor disabled and older people, is denied to anyone with more than $2,000 in countable assets, or $3,000 for a couple, limits unchanged since 1989, and it reduces the benefit by a dollar for every two dollars earned above $65 a month. [cite:ad5_cbpp_ssi] A bill sponsored by senators and representatives of both parties, the SSI Savings Penalty Elimination Act, would raise the asset limits to $10,000 and $20,000; as of October 2026 it has not passed. [cite:ad5_ffyf_ssi2026]

A worked example

The Atlanta Fed's Career Ladder Identifier and Financial Forecaster (CLIFF) follows hypothetical families through real program rules. In one published case, a single mother of two in Clarke County, Georgia, works near the minimum wage as a concessions worker and trains toward nursing. Moving from concession work to certified nursing assistant leaves her more than $11,000 worse off in net resources over the first three years; moving from nursing assistant to licensed practical nurse costs more than $35,000 over the first three years, because hours fall while she studies and benefits fall away as pay rises. Over a lifetime, the Atlanta Fed finds that both steps pay off. [cite:ad11_atl_what] Families respond to these sums: in a 2021 survey of Florida businesses cited by the Atlanta Fed, about one in three reported employees or candidates turning down jobs, hours or promotions for fear of losing benefits. [cite:ad11_atl_action]

Where it works as promised

Cliffs are real, but they are not the typical experience of a low-wage worker. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that workers below 450 per cent of the poverty guidelines faced an average effective marginal rate of 31 per cent in 2016, counting income and payroll taxes, the SNAP phase-out and health-insurance subsidies, with wide variation at the lowest earnings. [cite:ad11_cbo_emtr] Even among families receiving childcare subsidies, ASPE found that a $2,000 raise pushed 10 per cent over a cliff, while 15 per cent faced a negative rate, gaining more than the raise because a credit was still phasing in. [cite:ad11_aspe_ccdf] At the bottom of the scale, the Earned Income Tax Credit works exactly as Clinton described: on the way up it adds 40 cents to each dollar earned. [cite:ad11_cftd_rp2532] Whether it draws more people into work is disputed. A long-standing consensus held that it raised employment among single mothers substantially; a 2024 reappraisal by Henrik Kleven found that apart from the 1993 expansion, later expansions show no clear, robust effect on employment, with about 500 estimates centred on zero. [cite:ad11_kleven_eitc] States have begun to file down the edges, through calculators that show families their options, income disregards in Indiana and Maine, the removal of welfare asset limits in Colorado and Massachusetts, gradual childcare phase-outs in Florida, Maine and Vermont, and transition payments in Ohio and Tennessee. [cite:ad11_atl_bridge]

What changed in 2025–2026

The 2025 reconciliation law, signed on 4 July 2025, extended SNAP's work requirement to adults aged 18 to 64 and narrowed the exemption for parents to those with children under 14; from 1 October 2026 states pay 75 per cent of SNAP's administrative costs, and from fiscal 2028 they pay up to 15 per cent of benefits depending on their error rates. As of October 2026 the work-requirement changes are in force and the administrative cost shift has just begun. [cite:ad11_mn_snap] [cite:ad11_ncsl_snap] From 1 January 2027, adults covered through the Medicaid expansion must show 80 hours a month of work, community service, training or half-time study, or income of at least $580 a month, which is 80 hours at the federal minimum wage of $7.25. [cite:ad8_ccf_ifr] Those rules add a cliff at the bottom as well as the top: a worker whose hours fall below the threshold can lose coverage, just as a worker whose pay rises above 138 per cent of the poverty line already loses Medicaid and must move to marketplace coverage with a premium.

Interpretation, not finding: the cliff as a ceiling

The Sophia platform reads the benefits cliff as the clearest case of the Dream's promise working in reverse: a set of rules that holds families near the bottom of the wage scale by charging the highest marginal rates in the country on the act of climbing, while the people at the top face lower rates on income from assets. Read this way, the cliff is part of the same structure as the regressive state and local taxes and the fines described earlier in this part.

The strongest counter-readings are these. First, the cliffs come from a trade-off rather than a plan: aid aimed at the lowest incomes must stop somewhere, and a slower taper reaches families further up the income scale and costs more, so every design chooses between steep rates, high cost and narrower help. Second, the programs were written separately, by Congresses of both parties over six decades, and no document shows them designed to interact; the stacking is what happens when they are not coordinated. Third, average rates are around 31 per cent, not above 100, and the long-run returns to advancement are positive even in the Atlanta Fed's hardest cases. [cite:ad11_cbo_emtr] [cite:ad11_atl_what] The record supports the narrower claim: at specific income lines, chiefly childcare, Medicaid and marketplace eligibility, a family that earns more can end the year with less, and the 2025–2026 changes added new lines without removing old ones.

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: Income vs Wealth
chapters.intro: Part Twelve separates the two measures the Dream tends to blur: income, what a household earns in a year, and wealth, what it owns minus what it owes. It sets the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances beside its quarterly Distributional Financial Accounts to show how far apart the two gaps are, by race, age and education and between the top 1 per cent and the bottom half, and it follows the arithmetic by which owned assets compound while wages do not. It then turns to what families inherit, how much inheritance explains, and the tax rules that decide how much of a large fortune passes on untaxed: the estate tax, now $15 million per person, the step-up in basis and the strategy known as "buy, borrow, die". It ends with the housing crash of 2008, when the middle class's main asset was lost on a scale the record can measure, and asks who was charged more for their loans, who lost their homes and who was rescued.
chapters.outro: Part Twelve established that the Dream's income story hides a wider wealth story. In 2025 the median white family earned about 1.9 times the median Black family but held about 9.0 times its net worth, and the Black median fell 25 per cent between 2022 and 2025, a change the Federal Reserve did not test for significance. [cite:ad2_scf_t1] [cite:us8_scf2025] [cite:ad12_scf25_t2] In the second quarter of 2026 the top 1 per cent held a record 32.5 per cent of household net worth and 36.5 per cent of financial assets; the bottom half held 2.3 per cent of net worth. [cite:ad12_audit_fred_t1nw] [cite:ad12_fred_t1fin] [cite:ad12_audit_fred_b50nw] White Americans born 1949–72 were more than twice as likely as Black Americans to have received an inheritance, though earnings and pensions, not bequests, explain most of the gap; the estate tax reaches fewer than one death in a thousand, and the step-up in basis lets lifetime gains pass untaxed. [cite:ad12_richmond_inherit] [cite:ad12_bostonfed_inherit] [cite:ad12_crs_estate] In 2008 the record is specific: Black and Hispanic buyers with equal credit were far more likely to get high-cost loans, two of the largest lenders settled federal discrimination cases, and median Hispanic and Black wealth fell 66 and 53 per cent between 2005 and 2009, while the government's investments in banks and other financial institutions, apart from AIG, were repaid with a net gain. [cite:ad12_bfr2018] [cite:ad12_doj_countrywide] [cite:ad12_doj_wells] [cite:ad12_pew2011] [cite:ad12_cbo_tarp] Part Thirteen asks how these mechanisms have played out for each of the groups the Dream has promised to include, beginning with Black Americans. [scene:ad13_black_americans|Part Thirteen: Who Gets the Dream]

sections.h: Income Is a Flow, Wealth Is a Stock: The Gap the Paycheck Does Not Show
sections.html:
The American Dream is usually taught as a story about income: work hard, earn more, and the rest follows. The record of the last three decades shows that the rest does not follow automatically, because the things the Dream promises most concretely, a paid-off home, a secure retirement and a head start for one's children, are bought with wealth, not with a single year's pay. Income is a flow: what a household takes in over a year from wages, interest, rents or government benefits. Wealth, or net worth, is a stock: what a household owns at a moment in time (a house, savings, retirement accounts, shares, a business) minus what it owes (mortgage, student loans, credit cards). Part Two sets out the two measures and why the median, the household in the exact middle, tells more than the average when a few households hold very large amounts. [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two: How to measure] This section follows the stock.

Two gaps of different size

The clearest way to see why the distinction matters is to set the two measures side by side for the same families in the same survey. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), a detailed interview of several thousand households conducted every three years, found that the median American family had an income of $82,200 in 2024 and a net worth of $215,900 in 2025, both in 2025 dollars. [cite:ad2_scf_t1] [cite:us8_fed_scf_pr] Split by race, median income for white non-Hispanic families was $95,300 and for Black non-Hispanic families $49,400: a ratio of a little under two to one ($95,300 ÷ $49,400 = 1.9). Median net worth was $332,100 and $36,800: a ratio of about nine to one ($332,100 ÷ $36,800 = 9.0). [cite:ad2_scf_t1] [cite:us8_scf2025] The income gap is real and large; the wealth gap is almost five times wider. A family can close much of an income gap in one career. A wealth gap of that size builds over decades and generations, through earnings histories, home buying, inheritance and the timing of when each family could first buy assets, and it compounds forward.

What the 2025 survey found, and how sure it is

The 2025 survey, released on 9 October 2026, reversed a story that had become common after 2022. Between 2022 and 2025, in 2025 dollars, the median net worth of white non-Hispanic families rose from $311,900 to $332,100 (up 6 per cent), Hispanic families from $67,400 to $79,600 (up 18 per cent), Asian families from $586,600 to $677,600, and Black families fell from $49,100 to $36,800 (down 25 per cent). [cite:us8_scf2025] A widely repeated figure from the 2022 survey held that the white–Black ratio had narrowed to about 6.3 to 1; on the same survey's 2022 figures the ratio was 6.4 ($311,900 ÷ $49,100), and in 2025 it was back to 9.0. [cite:us8_scf2025]

The Black decline needs a caution before it is treated as a trend. The Board's report says that statistical significance "generally is not addressed" in its summary tables, and it does not print standard errors for groups by race. [cite:ad12_scf25_t2] The nearest guide is the Board's 2019 analysis, which gave the Black median as $24,100 with a range of about $19,800 to $28,400, roughly 18 per cent either side ($4,300 ÷ $24,100). [cite:ad12_fed_2019race] A fall of 25 per cent between two waves, each estimated with that kind of imprecision, is larger than either wave's own margin but not by a wide distance. What the survey does establish firmly is the level: in no wave since 1989 has the Black median been more than about a sixth of the white median. [cite:ad12_epi_race]

Age and education matter as much as race. Median net worth for families headed by someone under 35 fell from $42,700 to $33,000 between 2022 and 2025, while families headed by someone 75 or older rose from $367,300 to $504,900. Families headed by a college graduate had a median of $505,400, against $106,700 for a high-school graduate and $18,600 for a head without a diploma. [cite:ad12_scf25_t2] Taken across all families, the Board concluded there was "little change in wealth inequality between surveys." [cite:ad12_scf25_t2]

The view from the top: the Distributional Financial Accounts

The SCF is precise about the middle but samples the very richest households only lightly. To see concentration at the top, the Federal Reserve also publishes the Distributional Financial Accounts (DFA), which spread the national balance sheet across wealth groups every quarter from the third quarter of 1989: the top 0.1 per cent, the rest of the top 1 per cent, the next 9 per cent, the next 40 per cent and the bottom half. [cite:ad12_dfa_overview] In the release of 18 September 2026, the top 1 per cent held a record 32.5 per cent of all household net worth in the second quarter of 2026, up from a low of 22.4 per cent in 1990; the bottom half of households held 2.3 per cent, against 3.5 per cent in 1989. [cite:ad12_audit_fred_t1nw] [cite:ad12_audit_fred_b50nw] [cite:ad12_ttt_top1] [cite:ad12_ad_bottom50] Put another way, the top 1 per cent of households held about 14 times as much wealth as the bottom 50 per cent combined (32.5 ÷ 2.3). The Fed revises the whole history at each release, so these shares describe that vintage. [cite:ad12_ttt_top1]

Financial assets, the part of wealth that pays dividends and interest, are more concentrated still and have been concentrating steadily. The top 1 per cent's share of all household financial assets (bank deposits, bonds, shares, funds, pension entitlements) rose from 25.8 per cent in 1989 to 31.2 per cent in 2007 and 36.5 per cent in the second quarter of 2026. Over the same years the bottom half's share of all assets, including homes and cars, fell from 7.2 per cent to 5.0 per cent. [cite:ad12_fred_t1fin] [cite:ad12_fred_b50assets]

How wealth compounds

The mechanism that turns a gap in stock into a widening gap is ordinary compounding, and it works the same way for every family that owns assets. A return is earned as a percentage of what is already owned. At a 5 per cent annual return, a family with $10,000 of savings gains $500 in a year; a family with $1 million gains $50,000, without either working an extra hour. Left to grow for 30 years at 7 per cent, $100,000 becomes about $761,000 ($100,000 × 1.0730). A wage, by contrast, is earned one hour at a time and stops when work stops. This is arithmetic, not a finding about anyone's conduct, but it explains why the shares above move in one direction during long periods of rising asset prices: families who already own more of the assets that rise collect more of the rise.

Which assets a family holds decides which rise it catches. Shares are concentrated at the top: the 2025 SCF found that 56 per cent of families owned stock directly or indirectly, mostly through retirement accounts, down from 58 per cent in 2022, with the decline among families outside the top tenth of income; only 19 per cent owned shares directly. [cite:ad12_scf25_t2] Reporting on the Fed's distributional data in April 2026 put the top tenth's share of corporate equities and mutual-fund shares above 87 per cent. [cite:ad12_thestreet_eq] For the middle, the main asset is the house. In 2005, home equity (the value of the home minus the mortgage) made up 44 per cent of the net worth of white households, 59 per cent for Black households and nearly two-thirds for Hispanic households. [cite:ad12_pew2011] A household whose wealth is mostly one house is exposed to one local market and carries a large debt against it; a household whose wealth is mostly a diversified share portfolio is not. That difference is what made 2008 so unequal, as the third section of this part shows. [scene:ad12_2008_foreclosures|The 2008 foreclosures]

The charts below plot the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; each caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

The record is not one of uniform loss. The bottom half's combined net worth collapsed after 2007 but then recovered strongly: from $331 billion in the third quarter of 2010 to $1.81 trillion in 2019 and $4.28 trillion in the second quarter of 2026, in current dollars. [cite:ad12_fred_b50nw] Between 2016 and 2019 the median net worth of Black families rose 32.6 per cent and of Hispanic families 64.9 per cent, faster than white families' 3.5 per cent, and Hispanic families gained again between 2022 and 2025. [cite:ad12_fed_2019race] [cite:us8_scf2025] Homeownership, the middle-class route into wealth, still reached 65.6 per cent of families in 2025. [cite:ad12_scf25_t2] The Boston Fed's analysis of the white–Black gap found that lifetime earnings, pensions and education explain about 80 per cent of it, which means that work, and the pensions tied to it, remain the main road to wealth for most families. [cite:ad12_bostonfed_inherit] The ownership route the Dream describes is open; what the record shows is that it starts from very different places and that its returns compound for those already on it.

Interpretation, not finding: the Dream as a story that keeps people on the wage side

The Sophia platform reads the income–wealth split as the centre of its "illusion" thesis: in this reading, the Dream is taught as an income story so that households keep working for wages while the returns that actually build security flow to those who own capital, and the gap between the two is the extraction. Read through this lens, the steady rise of the top 1 per cent's share of financial assets is the system doing what it is built to do. The strongest counter-readings are documented. The Federal Reserve's own conclusion for 2022–2025 was "little change" in overall inequality, not a sharp rise. [cite:ad12_scf25_t2] Much of the concentration of shares reflects age and life-cycle saving as well as class: the 75-and-over median is fifteen times the under-35 median ($504,900 ÷ $33,000). [cite:ad12_scf25_t2] And compounding is a property of all saving, including the retirement accounts held by a majority of families; no document shows that the civic teaching of the Dream was designed to keep anyone off the ownership side. The lens is an interpretation of the pattern, not a finding about intent.

sections.h: What Is Passed Down: Inheritance, the Estate Tax and "Buy, Borrow, Die"
sections.html:
The Dream promises that each generation can do better than the last by its own effort. It says less about what each generation is handed. Inheritance is the transfer of wealth at death; gifts are transfers made while the giver is alive; together economists call them intergenerational transfers. This section sets out who receives them, how much they explain of the gaps described in the previous section, and the tax rules that decide how much of a large fortune passes on untaxed: the estate tax, the "step-up in basis" and the borrowing strategy that combines them. [scene:ad12_wealth_gap|The wealth gap]

Who inherits

The Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond used the 2019 Survey of Consumer Finances, which asks families about every inheritance or large gift they have received, to compare Americans born between 1949 and 1972. Among white respondents, 34.8 per cent had received a transfer; among Black respondents, 13.2 per cent. When a transfer was received, the average white amount was $303,100 and the average Black amount $154,260, in 2019 dollars; the medians were closer, $100,830 and $74,460, because the white average is pulled up by a small number of very large transfers. Almost 5 per cent of white recipients reported $1 million or more; virtually no Black recipients did. Nearly one-third of white recipients had received more than one transfer, against 7 per cent of Black recipients. [cite:ad12_richmond_inherit] Most transfers arrive late: at least half of recipients get their first after age 40, which means inheritance more often pays off a mortgage or funds a retirement than buys a first home. [cite:ad12_richmond_inherit]

The Richmond authors also found that receiving a transfer rose steadily with parental education for white families, from 29.8 per cent where parents had not finished high school to 41.2 per cent where a parent held a bachelor's degree, while for Black families it varied only between 8.3 and 15.5 per cent with no steady rise. They call the reason unclear and suggest that parental education is a weak stand-in for accumulated family wealth among Black families. [cite:ad12_richmond_inherit] The history of how that wealth was built and lost, from the exclusions written into federal mortgage insurance to the loss of land and homes, is set out in Part Six and Part Thirteen. [scene:ad6_redlining_to_suburbs|Part Six: from redlining to the suburbs] [scene:ad13_black_americans|Part Thirteen: Black Americans]

How much inheritance explains, and the dispute

How much of the wealth gap these transfers account for is disputed among economists, and the range is wide. Earlier studies summarised by the Richmond Fed put inheritances at 10 to 20 per cent of the white–Black gap (a 1997 paper) and intergenerational transfers at 26 per cent (a 2020 simulation). [cite:ad12_richmond_inherit] A 2023 study by Jeffrey Thompson of the Boston Fed and John Sabelhaus of the Brookings Institution found that transfers explain 14 per cent of the gap without other controls, and that lifetime earnings, pension assets and education together explain about 80 per cent. About a third of white families and about one in ten Black families had received any inheritance, and more than half of all inheritances and gifts were under $50,000. [cite:ad12_bostonfed_inherit]

This is the part of the record where the taught version largely holds for the typical family: most family wealth in the middle is built from earnings and the pensions and homes those earnings buy, not from bequests. The two findings are compatible. Transfers matter a great deal at the top of the distribution, where the multi-million-dollar bequests are, and they matter in the timing and security they give, but for the median family the larger drivers are what a working life pays and whether it comes with a pension. [cite:ad12_bostonfed_inherit] [cite:ad12_richmond_inherit] Those drivers are the subject of Parts Five and Ten. [scene:ad5_wages_floors|Part Five: wages] [scene:ad10_pension_shift|Part Ten: from pension to 401(k)]

The estate tax: from 2 per cent of deaths to fewer than 1 in 1,000

The estate tax is a federal tax on the value of what a person leaves at death above an exempt amount, paid by the estate before heirs receive it. Gifts during life count against the same exemption, and anything left to a spouse or to charity is deducted. In 2001 the exemption was $675,000 and the top rate 55 per cent; by 2009 the exemption had risen to $3.5 million and the rate fallen to 45 per cent; in 2010 the tax lapsed for a year. Congress then set a $5 million exemption and a 35 per cent rate, made the tax permanent in the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 at a 40 per cent rate with the exemption indexed to inflation, doubled the exemption for 2018–2025 in the 2017 tax law, and in the 2025 reconciliation law (Public Law 119-21) set it at $15 million per person from 2026, indexed and without an end date. [cite:ad12_crs_estate] As of October 2026 that $15 million figure is the law in force.

The effect on who pays has been large. In 2001 about 2.1 per cent of people who died left a taxable estate; in 2016 it was 5,467 estates, 0.21 per cent of deaths; after the 2017 doubling it was 2,129 estates in 2019, 0.07 per cent, about one death in 1,400. The tax raised $32 billion in fiscal 2023, 0.7 per cent of federal revenue. Of what it collects, 90 per cent is paid by estates of people in the top tenth of the income distribution and 65 per cent by the top 1 per cent. [cite:ad12_crs_estate] It is one of the most progressive taxes in the federal system, and it now reaches almost no one.

The case against the tax is made on the record too. Opponents describe it as a second tax on money already taxed as income, argue that it harms family farms and businesses, and say it discourages saving. The Congressional Research Service notes that the double-taxation point does not apply to gains never taxed during life, that only about 300 estates made up mostly of farm or business assets were expected to pay, and that the evidence mostly finds small effects on the saving of those who leave estates. [cite:ad12_crs_estate]

The step-up in basis: gains that are never taxed

The larger rule for most inherited wealth is not the estate tax but the treatment of capital gains. A capital gain is the rise in an asset's value; it is taxed as income only when the asset is sold, and the tax is on the difference between the sale price and the "basis," usually what the owner paid. When an owner dies, the heir's basis is "stepped up" to the asset's value at the date of death. The Congressional Research Service gives the arithmetic: shares bought for $100,000 and worth $200,000 at death, later sold by the heir for $250,000, produce a taxable gain of $50,000; the $100,000 gain that built up during the original owner's life is never taxed by anyone. Under "carryover basis," the rule that applies to gifts made during life, the heir would be taxed on $150,000. [cite:ad12_crs_estate] The step-up is a long-standing provision of the income tax code; it is designed friction, a deliberate rule, not a loophole that appeared by accident. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that replacing it with carryover basis would raise $7.2 billion in fiscal 2024, rising to $26.6 billion by 2032. [cite:ad12_crs_estate]

"Buy, borrow, die"

The phrase "buy, borrow, die," attributed to the University of Southern California law professor Edward McCaffery, describes how the step-up combines with borrowing. [cite:ad12_propublica] An owner buys assets that rise in value and does not sell them, so no gain is taxed. To pay for living costs, the owner borrows against the assets; a loan is not income, because it must be repaid, so the cash arrives untaxed. At death, the heirs inherit with a stepped-up basis, sell enough to repay the loans, and the gain accumulated over a lifetime escapes income tax entirely. The Budget Lab at Yale calls it "a tax planning technique which allows wealthy Americans to pay low tax rates on consumed income." [cite:ad12_yale_bbd]

How much this matters is contested, and the strongest evidence cuts in two directions. ProPublica, using IRS records obtained from an undisclosed source, reported in June 2021 that the 25 richest Americans' wealth rose by $401 billion between 2014 and 2018, by Forbes's estimates, while they paid $13.6 billion in federal income tax, a "true tax rate" of 3.4 per cent; the typical household paid about 14 per cent of its income. [cite:ad12_propublica] That rate is ProPublica's own measure, comparing taxes with wealth growth rather than with income as the law defines it. The National Taxpayers Union Foundation answered that the comparison "knowingly compares apples to oranges" because the US taxes income, not paper wealth, while conceding that borrowing against assets is "a tax avoidance strategy that some wealthy individuals use." [cite:ad12_ntu_bbd] The Yale Budget Lab, using the SCF and Forbes data, found that borrowing is a "relatively minor source of cash income" for wealthy Americans in aggregate, about 1 per cent of the income of the top 0.1 per cent by net worth in one study it cites, and estimated that reform options would raise $102 billion to $147 billion over ten years. [cite:ad12_yale_bbd] The documented finding is the rule, the step-up, which lets lifetime gains pass untaxed whether or not the owner borrows; the borrowing strategy is real but narrower than its fame suggests.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

sections.h: 2008: How the Housing Crash Took the Middle's Main Asset
sections.html:
For most American families the home is the Dream's largest single asset, and in the first decade of this century it was also the asset most families borrowed most heavily against. When house prices fell nationally after 2006 and millions of mortgages failed, the loss fell hardest on the households whose wealth was mostly one house, and hardest of all on Black and Hispanic families who had been sold more expensive loans than similar white borrowers. This section follows that sequence with the record: how the loans were priced, what the Justice Department alleged and settled, how many homes were lost, how much wealth went with them, and who was rescued afterwards. [scene:ad12_wealth_gap|The wealth gap] Why the bubble formed at all is disputed, and Part One sets out the official inquiry's view and the main dissent. [scene:ad1_who_sells_it|Part One: who sells the Dream]

Pricing: when equal credit got unequal loans

A subprime loan is a mortgage made to a borrower judged a higher risk, usually at a higher interest rate and with higher fees; regulators track "high-cost" loans as those priced well above the rate on safe government bonds. Charging more to a borrower who is genuinely riskier is a designed feature of lending, known as risk-based pricing. Charging more to a borrower of the same risk because of race or national origin is a departure from that design and is illegal under federal fair-lending law. [cite:ad12_doj_countrywide] The record shows the second happened at scale. Patrick Bayer, Fernando Ferreira and Stephen Ross studied home-purchase loans in seven metropolitan areas from 2004 to 2007 using credit-bureau data. After controlling for credit scores and other risk factors, Black buyers were 105 per cent more likely and Hispanic buyers 78 per cent more likely than white buyers to have a high-cost mortgage. About 60 to 65 per cent of that difference came from which lenders borrowers ended up with, since Black and Hispanic buyers were more often served by high-risk lenders, and 35 to 40 per cent from those lenders treating equally qualified borrowers differently. [cite:ad12_bfr2018]

Two of the largest lenders settled federal cases over exactly these practices. On 21 December 2011 the Justice Department announced a $335 million settlement with Countrywide Financial, by then a subsidiary of Bank of America, its largest residential fair-lending settlement to that date. The government alleged that more than 200,000 African-American and Hispanic borrowers had paid higher fees and interest rates than non-Hispanic white borrowers between 2004 and 2008 because of their race or national origin rather than their creditworthiness, and that thousands had been placed in subprime loans when white borrowers with similar credit received prime ones. Attorney General Eric Holder said lenders should judge applicants on "creditworthiness, not on the color of their skin." [cite:ad12_doj_countrywide] On 12 July 2012 the department announced a settlement with Wells Fargo of more than $175 million, including $50 million in down-payment assistance, resolving allegations that about 4,000 African-American and Hispanic borrowers who came through mortgage brokers were steered into subprime loans between 2004 and 2008 and about 30,000 were charged higher fees and rates between 2004 and 2009. [cite:ad12_doj_wells] Both settlements resolved the government's allegations; neither release records an admission of liability. [cite:ad12_doj_countrywide] [cite:ad12_doj_wells]

The foreclosures

A foreclosure is the legal process by which a lender takes a home after the borrower stops paying. The Center for Responsible Lending, a non-profit lending-reform group, tracked loans made from 2004 to 2008 and reported in November 2011 that 2.7 million of those households had already lost their homes, with 3.6 million more at serious risk. About one in four Black and Hispanic borrowers had either been foreclosed on or was seriously behind on payments, against about 12 per cent of white borrowers. The gap did not close with income: among higher-income borrowers, 10 per cent of Black and 15 per cent of Hispanic borrowers had lost their homes, against 4.6 per cent of white borrowers. [cite:ad12_crl_lostground] Because loan pricing itself differed by race at equal credit, higher foreclosure rates among Black and Hispanic borrowers cannot be read as a simple measure of their risk; part of the risk was in the loans they were given. [cite:ad12_bfr2018]

Geography added to the loss. The Pew Research Center found that Hispanic families were hit hardest partly because many lived in California, Florida, Nevada and Arizona, where house prices fell furthest. [cite:ad12_pew2011] What happened to the foreclosed homes afterwards, including bulk sales to investors and resales on contracts for deed in mostly Black neighbourhoods, is covered in Part Six. [scene:ad6_eviction_and_traps|Part Six: eviction and housing traps]

The wealth that went with them

Because home equity was a larger share of Black and Hispanic wealth, the same fall in house prices took a larger share of it. On the Census Bureau's Survey of Income and Program Participation, Pew found that median household net worth between 2005 and 2009, in 2009 dollars, fell 16 per cent for white households (from $134,992 to $113,149), 53 per cent for Black households (from $12,124 to $5,677) and 66 per cent for Hispanic households (from $18,359 to $6,325). The share of households with zero or negative net worth rose to 35 per cent for Black and 31 per cent for Hispanic households, against 15 per cent for white households. [cite:ad12_pew2011] On the Federal Reserve's survey, median wealth fell by about the same proportion for each group between 2007 and 2010, roughly 27 per cent, but the recovery split: from 2010 to 2013, the white median rose 1.4 per cent while the Black median fell a further 23 per cent and the Hispanic median 21 per cent. [cite:ad12_fed_2019race]

The Distributional Financial Accounts show the scale for the bottom half of all households, whatever their race. Their combined net worth was $1.45 trillion in the third quarter of 2005 and $331 billion in the third quarter of 2010, in current dollars, a fall of 77 per cent ($331 billion ÷ $1,453 billion = 0.23). [cite:ad12_fred_b50nw] Their share of all household net worth fell to 0.4 per cent at the end of 2010 and stayed there into 2012. [cite:ad12_audit_fred_b50nw] For half the country, a decade of home equity had been almost entirely borrowed against or lost.

Who was rescued, and what it cost

The federal response to the crisis is often summarised as a rescue of banks and not of homeowners. The record supports part of that claim and corrects another part. The Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), enacted in October 2008 and run under two administrations of different parties, was authorised at $700 billion and disbursed $444 billion, about $410 billion of it by March 2011. In its final report, issued in April 2024, the Congressional Budget Office estimated the program's total cost at $31 billion. Transactions with financial institutions other than AIG yielded a net gain to the government through dividends, interest and capital gains; the cost came largely from aid to AIG, aid to the car industry, and foreclosure-prevention programs, which were grants to help homeowners rather than investments to be repaid. The last remaining investment was repaid in September 2023. [cite:ad12_cbo_tarp]

The asymmetry the record does show is one of timing and form. Financial institutions received capital quickly and repaid it once markets recovered, so the public was made whole on that part of the rescue. Homeowners received grants and modification programs that came later and reached fewer families than were losing homes, and a family that lost its house in 2009 did not get its equity back when prices recovered. [cite:ad12_cbo_tarp] [cite:ad12_crl_lostground] Comparisons that set the peak value of all emergency lending commitments against the money spent on homeowners mix different measures and overstate the gap; the documented contrast is between capital that was returned with interest and household equity that was not.

Where it works as promised, and the dispute over cause

The recovery did come for many. The bottom half's combined net worth rose from $331 billion in 2010 to $1.81 trillion in 2019 and $4.28 trillion in the second quarter of 2026. [cite:ad12_fred_b50nw] Between 2016 and 2019 the Black median rose 32.6 per cent and the Hispanic median 64.9 per cent. [cite:ad12_fed_2019race] The rescue of the financial system, judged on its own terms of repayment, worked. [cite:ad12_cbo_tarp] How the bubble was caused remains contested. The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission's majority concluded that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac "contributed to the crisis but were not a primary cause" and that government housing policies "were not a significant factor." [cite:ad1_fcic_angelides] A dissenting commissioner, Peter Wallison of the American Enterprise Institute, argued that government housing policy was "the sine qua non of the financial crisis." [cite:ad1_hw_wallison] The pricing findings above stand under either account: whatever drove the volume of lending, the documented settlements and studies concern how the loans were priced for borrowers of equal credit. [cite:ad12_bfr2018] [cite:ad12_doj_countrywide]

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: Who Gets the Dream
chapters.intro: Part Thirteen asks for whom the promise has been kept. It sets the documented record of four groups side by side on mobility, income, wealth, homeownership, education and health, and follows each gap to the policies and conditions the evidence ties it to, together with the disputes among scholars over how much each cause explains. It begins with Black Americans, where the federal record of the 1930s and 1940s is most fully documented and most argued over; turns to immigrants and Latino Americans, whose children's climb is some of the strongest evidence for the taught version, and to the taxes undocumented workers pay into programmes they cannot use; and ends with Asian Americans, whose high average conceals the widest spread of any group, and Native Americans, whose record runs through allotment, trust land and the Cobell settlement. [scene:ad13_black_americans|Black Americans]
chapters.outro: The promise has not been kept evenly, and the record shows where and through which mechanisms. Black Americans' poverty fell from 41.8 per cent in 1966 to 17.3 per cent in 2025, but the median white family held about nine times the wealth of the median Black family in 2025, and a Black child born to the bottom fifth had a 2.5 per cent chance of reaching the top fifth against 10.6 per cent for a white child. [cite:us8_pf_1966] [cite:us8_jbhe_2025] [cite:us8_scf2025] [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] The 1935 Social Security exclusions reached about 65 per cent of employed Black workers, a documented effect whose racial intent remains disputed, and economists divide over how much of the wealth gap today's earnings explain and how much a history that began under slavery. [cite:ad13_dewitt] [cite:ad13_barsky] [cite:ad13_dkks] The children of immigrants have out-climbed the children of US-born parents for more than a century, and Latino Americans reached record-low poverty in 2025, while undocumented workers paid an estimated $33.9 billion a year in payroll taxes for programmes they cannot use. [cite:ad2_abramitzky_aer] [cite:us8_census_2025] [cite:ad13_itep_sub] Asian Americans' high average sits on the widest income spread of any group, and American Indians, who lost about 90 million acres between 1887 and 1934, have the highest poverty and a life expectancy of 71.1 years. [cite:ad13_pew_ineq] [cite:ad13_gp_dawes] [cite:ad13_usafacts_pov] [cite:ad13_nchs_lt2024] Part Fourteen follows the families at the bottom of these distributions into the poverty line itself, the costs of the criminal-legal system and the count of those without a home. [scene:ad14_poverty_line|The poverty line]

sections.h: Black Americans: The Promise Measured Against the Policies That Shaped It
sections.html:
The taught version of the American Dream makes no exception by race: the same work brings the same home, the same security and the same better life for the next generation. For Black Americans the record can be tested more fully than for almost any other group, because the federal government both measured the outcomes and wrote down many of the rules that shaped them. This section sets out where Black households stand on income, poverty, wealth, homeownership, education and health in 2025 and 2026; what the largest study of mobility by race found; which federal policies are documented as having excluded Black workers and families, and where the intent behind them is disputed; and what economists argue about why the wealth gap is so much wider than the income gap. The gaps described here are outcomes with documented causes, not characteristics of the people who live them. Terms such as median, wealth and relative mobility are defined in [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two].

Where the record stands

The Census Bureau's 2025 figures, released in September 2026, put the official poverty rate for Black Americans at 17.3 per cent, 2.2 times the rate for non-Hispanic white Americans; under the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts benefits and necessary expenses, it was 20.1 per cent. Black child poverty was 24.1 per cent against 8.5 per cent for non-Hispanic white children. [cite:us8_jbhe_2025] The long-run direction is downward: Black poverty stood at 41.8 per cent in 1966, and reached a record low of 17.1 per cent in 2022. [cite:us8_pf_1966] [cite:us8_jbhe_2025] Median Black household income was $59,980 in 2025, up 4.8 per cent on the year, though the Census Bureau found the difference between Black and white income growth not statistically significant. [cite:us8_be_income] [cite:us8_census_2025]

Wealth tells a different story. The Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances put the median net worth of Black families at $36,800 and of white non-Hispanic families at $332,100, a ratio of about 9 to 1 (332,100 ÷ 36,800 = 9.0). The same survey put median family income at $95,300 for white non-Hispanic and $49,400 for Black families, a ratio of about 1.9 to 1 (the survey's family income differs from the Census household figure above). [cite:us8_scf2025] [cite:ad2_scf_t1] [scene:ad12_wealth_gap|Part Twelve] explains how much confidence a single survey round deserves for a group of this size. Homeownership, the asset most families hold, was 45.4 per cent for Black households and 74.5 per cent for non-Hispanic white households in the second quarter of 2026, a gap of 29.1 points; in 1960 it was 27 points (38 against 65 per cent). [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226] [cite:ad6_stateline_gap] In 2024, 29.6 per cent of Black adults aged 25 and over held a bachelor's degree, against 38.6 per cent of white adults. [cite:ad13_jbhe_ba] Life expectancy at birth in 2024 was 74.8 years for non-Hispanic Black Americans and 78.9 for non-Hispanic white Americans, and in 2023 the infant mortality rate was 10.93 deaths per 1,000 births for non-Hispanic Black infants against 4.48 for non-Hispanic white infants. [cite:ad13_nchs_lt2024] [cite:us16_cdc_imr2023]

What the mobility data show

The most detailed study of mobility by race, by Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, Maggie Jones and Sonya Porter, linked the tax and census records of 20 million children to their parents. It found that Black and American Indian children have substantially lower rates of upward mobility than other groups. A Black child whose parents were in the bottom fifth of the income distribution had a 2.5 per cent chance of reaching the top fifth, against 10.6 per cent for a white child from the same starting point. Black children raised in top-fifth families were almost as likely to fall to the bottom fifth as to stay at the top, while white children from the top fifth were nearly five times as likely to stay as to fall. [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum]

The gap is a gap among men. Black women earned slightly more than white women raised at the same parental income; Black men earned substantially less than white men, and Black boys had lower outcomes than white boys in 99 per cent of the census tracts studied. Twenty-one per cent of Black men born to the lowest-income families were incarcerated on any given day. [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] The authors tested the explanations most often offered and found that parents' marital status, education and wealth, and differences in ability, explained very little of the gap between children whose parents earned the same; the gaps persisted for children raised in the same tract and even on the same block. What did predict smaller gaps were neighbourhood conditions: low poverty, low measured racial bias among white residents, and a high share of Black fathers present in the area. Fewer than 5 per cent of Black children grew up in areas with poverty below 10 per cent and more than half of Black fathers at home, while 63 per cent of white children grew up in the comparable conditions for white families, and Black boys who moved to them earlier in childhood earned more and were less likely to be incarcerated. [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] [cite:us8_oi_race]

The policies behind the gap, and the dispute over intent

Three federal programmes of the 1930s and 1940s did more than any others to build the middle-class security the Dream describes: Social Security, federal mortgage insurance and the GI Bill. Each is documented as reaching Black Americans far less than white Americans. The extent and the intent are argued over separately, and this section keeps them apart.

The Social Security Act of 1935 excluded agricultural and domestic workers from old-age insurance. The exclusion was proposed by Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau in testimony to the House Ways and Means Committee on 5 February 1935, on the grounds that the Bureau of Internal Revenue doubted it could collect payroll taxes from farms and households. [cite:ad13_dewitt] Its effect by race is documented in the 1930 Census: about 65 per cent of employed Black workers (3,564,044 of 5,503,535) worked in those two sectors, against 27 per cent of white workers. Because there were many more white workers overall, 74 per cent of the people excluded were white and 23 per cent Black. Coverage was extended to farm and domestic workers with a regular employer in 1950 and to the rest in 1954. [cite:ad13_dewitt]

Whether the exclusion was racially motivated is contested. Scholars including the political scientist Robert Lieberman, who wrote that old-age insurance was "founded on racial exclusion", and the historian Linda Gordon, who called the exclusions "deliberate and mainly racially motivated", argued that race drove the choice of which workers to leave out. Larry DeWitt, a historian at the Social Security Administration, examined the legislative record in 2010 and concluded that the racial-bias allegations "do not hold up under detailed scrutiny": the exclusion came from Treasury and the planning staff on administrative grounds, and was accepted by both committees with little debate. [cite:ad13_dewitt] The historian David Kaiser cited DeWitt's account in 2023 against the claim that Southern chairmen forced the exclusion, and the writer Adam Hochschild, who had repeated that claim, replied that he found DeWitt convincing. [cite:ad13_nyrb_kaiser] On the record, the disproportionate effect is confirmed; the racial motive is contested and rests on inference.

Housing and the GI Bill are covered in full in [scene:ad6_redlining_to_suburbs|Part Six]. In brief: the Federal Housing Administration's 1938 Underwriting Manual recommended deed restrictions prohibiting occupancy "except by the race for which they are intended". [cite:ad6_fha_manual] Economists dispute how much the better-known HOLC "redlining" maps themselves mattered, since the HOLC had made 90 per cent of its loans before the maps were drawn, but the same researchers judge the FHA's own lending lines "likely far more impactful". [cite:ad6_chifed_rose] [cite:ad6_ahm_holc] The GI Bill was administered locally: of 3,229 VA-guaranteed home, business and farm loans made in Mississippi in 1947, two went to Black veterans. [cite:ad6_katznelson] For education, Sarah Turner and John Bound found that the bill raised college attainment for Black men born outside the South but widened the Black–white gap among Southern-born men. [cite:ad6_turnerbound]

Why the wealth gap is wider than the income gap

Economists agree that the wealth gap is far larger than the income gap; they disagree about how much of it comes from present-day earnings and how much from history. Robert Barsky, John Bound, Kerwin Charles and Joseph Lupton found in 2002 that differences in earnings account for roughly two-thirds of the Black–white wealth gap, once the comparison is made without assuming a fixed statistical relationship between income and wealth. [cite:ad13_barsky] On that reading the wealth gap runs largely through the income gap, which itself has the documented causes set out above. William Darity, Darrick Hamilton and their co-authors argued in 2018 that the usual individual remedies do not close it: Black households headed by a college graduate held less wealth than white households headed by someone without a high-school diploma, and white households with an employed head held more than ten times the wealth of comparable Black households. [cite:ad13_fortune_darity] Ellora Derenoncourt, Chi Hyun Kim, Moritz Kuhn and Moritz Schularick traced the gap from 1860 to 2020 and found that, because of the starting point under slavery, convergence would be distant even under equal conditions since Emancipation; actual convergence stalled after 1950, and since the 1980s the gap has widened again as capital gains have gone mainly to white households, who hold more of the assets that rose. [cite:ad13_dkks] The three findings are not exclusive: earnings explain much of the gap among families today, while the long-run studies explain why equal earnings now would not close a gap built over generations. Inheritance, one channel between the two, is measured in [scene:ad12_inheritance|Part Twelve].

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

Parts of the record move in the direction the taught version predicts. Black poverty fell by more than half between 1966 and 2025. [cite:us8_pf_1966] [cite:us8_jbhe_2025] A 2024 study by Chetty and co-authors of children born between 1978 and 1992 found that Black children's adult earnings rose at every level of parental income, and that the earnings gap between white and Black children from low-income families fell by 30 per cent; over the same cohorts the gap between white children from rich and poor families widened by 30 per cent. The authors trace both changes to shifts in parents' employment within communities, carried through social ties. [cite:ad2_changing_opp] [cite:ad3_changing_opp] Black women raised at a given income earn as much as or slightly more than white women. [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] These findings show that the gaps respond to changes in the conditions around children, which is what one would expect of outcomes with documented causes and would not expect of fixed differences between groups.

Interpretation, not finding: exclusion as design

The Sophia platform reads the record above as evidence that the Dream was built with a boundary: that the programmes which turned wages into homes, pensions and degrees were drawn, by design, around most Black workers, and that the gap of 2026 is that boundary's compound interest. In this reading the 1935 exclusions, the 1938 manual and the local administration of the GI Bill are one architecture rather than three accidents.

The strongest counter-readings are documentary. DeWitt's account of the Social Security exclusion attributes it to tax-collection limits that also excluded millions of white workers, and the coverage was extended within two decades. [cite:ad13_dewitt] Fishback and his co-authors show that the most famous redlining maps came after most HOLC lending. [cite:ad6_chifed_rose] The narrowing of the low-income gap for children born since 1978 shows the boundary moving. [cite:ad2_changing_opp] What the documents establish is disproportionate exclusion in specific programmes, with racial terms written explicitly into the FHA's manual; a single design across all of them is an interpretation the record does not settle.

sections.h: Immigrants and Latino Americans: The Second Generation and the Tax Ledger
sections.html:
For immigrants the American Dream is not a civic lesson but a decision: a family moves because it expects its children to do better than they would have at home. The record on that expectation is one of the strongest in this book for the taught version. It is also a record with a hard edge, because millions of the workers who make the move have no legal status, pay taxes into programmes they cannot draw on, and since 2025 have faced new limits on benefits and new uses of their tax records. This section takes the long mobility record first, then Latino Americans as the largest group with immigrant roots, then the tax ledger of undocumented workers and the laws that changed in 2025 and 2026.

The scale is large. The Pew Research Center counted 51.9 million immigrants in the United States in June 2025, 15.4 per cent of the population, down from a record 53.3 million in January 2025; the unauthorised population reached a record 14 million in 2023, and in 2023, 46 per cent of immigrants were naturalised citizens. [cite:us6_pew_immig2025] About 8.3 million unauthorised immigrants were in the labour force in 2022, just under 5 per cent of all workers. [cite:us13_epi_unauth]

The long record: children of immigrants climb

Ran Abramitzky, Leah Boustan, Elisa Jácome and Santiago Pérez linked millions of fathers and sons across more than a century of census and tax records. They found that the children of immigrants from nearly every sending country have higher upward mobility than the children of US-born parents who started at the same income, both a century ago and today. [cite:ad2_abramitzky_aer] Sons of immigrant fathers at the 25th percentile of the income distribution reached ranks about 3 to 4 percentiles higher than sons of US-born fathers between 1880 and 1910, and about 5 percentiles higher in modern data. The exceptions in the modern data include children of immigrants from Haiti and Jamaica, majority-Black countries whose children face the gaps described in [scene:ad13_black_americans|the previous section]. [cite:ad2_abramitzky_nber] Part of the advantage comes from where immigrant families settle: they tend to move to places with better opportunities, which the place research in [scene:ad3_relative_and_place|Part Three] shows matters causally. [cite:ad2_abramitzky_aer]

A percentile rank here means position in the national income distribution, from 1 at the bottom to 100 at the top; an edge of 5 ranks means that a son of immigrants raised at the 25th percentile ends up, on average, five places higher in that ranking than a son of US-born parents raised at the same income. The finding is a comparison of relative mobility (defined in [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two]) and holds for families starting at the same income, so it is not explained by immigrants being richer or poorer to begin with.

Latino Americans: convergence measured

Hispanic or Latino Americans (the Census Bureau's term covers people of any race with roots in Spanish-speaking countries) are both the largest group with recent immigrant roots and a group whose mobility can be measured over generations. The Chetty, Hendren, Jones and Porter study found that Hispanic children's upward mobility was slightly below that of white children and that Hispanic Americans are "moving up significantly in the income distribution across generations". [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] [cite:ad2_oi_race_hisp]

The current figures fit that path. The official poverty rate for Hispanic Americans was 13.9 per cent in 2025, the lowest on record, against 10.2 per cent for the whole population. [cite:us8_census_2025] Median Hispanic family net worth rose 18 per cent in real terms between 2022 and 2025, from $67,400 to $79,600 in 2025 dollars, still about a quarter of the white median ($79,600 ÷ $332,100 = 0.24). [cite:us8_scf2025] Hispanic homeownership rose from 41.2 per cent in 1994 to 49.5 per cent in 2005 in the Census Bureau's housing survey, and stood at 48.1 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, against 74.5 per cent for non-Hispanic white households. [cite:ad13_census_hvs05] [cite:ad13_epi_hvs_race] [cite:ad13_audit_hvs_q226] The share of Latino adults with a bachelor's degree rose from 14.0 per cent in 2013 to 20.8 per cent in 2023, against a national 36.2 per cent. [cite:ad13_pnpi_latino] Life expectancy at birth for Hispanic Americans was 81.8 years in 2024, nearly three years above non-Hispanic white Americans (78.9), despite lower incomes. [cite:ad13_nchs_lt2024]

The tax ledger of undocumented workers

Undocumented immigrants are, for most of the Dream's safety net, contributors without claims. The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP), a research group whose work generally favours progressive taxation, estimated that they paid $96.7 billion in federal, state and local taxes in 2022: $59.4 billion federal and $37.3 billion state and local. [cite:ad13_itep_state] [cite:ad13_itep_sub] Of the federal total, $25.7 billion was Social Security tax, $6.4 billion Medicare tax and $1.8 billion unemployment-insurance tax, funding programmes these workers are barred from using; ITEP found that in 40 states they pay a higher share of income in state and local taxes than the top 1 per cent of households there, and that they often cannot claim the Child Tax Credit or the Earned Income Tax Credit. [cite:ad13_itep_sub] [cite:ad13_itep_pr] Adding the payroll figures shows the size of the one-way flow: 25.7 + 6.4 + 1.8 = $33.9 billion a year, about 35 per cent of the total paid ($33.9bn ÷ $96.7bn).

The ledger has another side. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine reviewed the evidence in 2016 and found that first-generation immigrants cost governments more than the native-born, mainly at the state and local level; it found the second generation to be among the strongest fiscal contributors of any group, contributing the most of any generation to state budgets. Where it found negative wage effects, they fell on native-born workers without a high-school diploma and on earlier immigrants. [cite:ad13_nasem] The two findings measure different things: ITEP counts taxes paid by one group in one year, and the National Academies count taxes against the cost of services across generations. Both are needed to describe the ledger fairly.

What changed in 2025 and 2026 (status as of October 2026)

The budget reconciliation law signed on 4 July 2025 (Public Law 119-21, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) changed several of these terms. From 1 January 2026 it imposed a 1 per cent tax on international money transfers made in cash, by money order or by cashier's cheque, while transfers from bank accounts and cards were exempt. It required the adult filing for the Child Tax Credit, or one spouse on a joint return, to have a Social Security number, where before only the child needed one. It ended food-assistance (SNAP) eligibility for refugees, asylees and several other lawfully present groups; it limited Medicaid and CHIP to green-card holders, Cuban and Haitian entrants and migrants from the Pacific Compact states from 1 October 2026; and it limits ACA premium credits in the same way from 1 January 2027. [cite:ad13_usccb_obbba] Most of these changes fall on lawfully present immigrants, since undocumented immigrants were already excluded from the benefit programmes; the Child Tax Credit rule also reaches families in which a child has a Social Security number but the parents file with a taxpayer identification number instead.

Tax records also took on a new use. The Treasury and the Department of Homeland Security signed a data-sharing agreement in April 2025 under which Immigration and Customs Enforcement asked the IRS for the addresses of about 1.28 million people, and the IRS disclosed about 47,000 before courts intervened. [cite:us10_abc_irs_feb] [cite:ad13_audit_irs_dcir] The cases have gone different ways. On 24 February 2026 one federal appeals panel in Washington declined to block the sharing in a suit brought by workers' groups. [cite:us10_abc_irs_feb] In a second suit, brought by the Center for Taxpayer Rights and Main Street Alliance, District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly stayed the agreement in November 2025 and in February 2026 found about 42,695 unlawful disclosures; on 8 September 2026 another panel of the same appeals court unanimously upheld her block, finding that the IRS procedure did not ensure that ICE supplied the name and address the tax-privacy law requires. In Massachusetts, Judge Indira Talwani separately barred DHS and ICE in February 2026 from using taxpayer data obtained under the agreement, and an appeal there is pending. [cite:ad13_audit_irs_dcir] [cite:ad13_audit_irs_hoodline] Status as of October 2026: further disclosures remain blocked by court order while the appeals continue.

Where it works as promised

The second-generation record is the clearest evidence in this volume that the Dream as taught describes something real. For more than a century and in modern data, the children of immigrants who start poor climb further than the children of US-born parents who start at the same place, and Latino Americans, many of them children and grandchildren of immigrants, are closing gaps in poverty, wealth, homeownership and degrees. [cite:ad2_abramitzky_aer] [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] [cite:us8_census_2025] [cite:ad13_pnpi_latino] [scene:ad2_what_holds|Part Two] places this finding among the parts of the promise that hold. The exceptions are documented too: the children of Black immigrants, and the parents themselves when they lack legal status, who pay into the safety net without the right to use it.

sections.h: Asian and Native Americans: The Highest Average and the Longest Dispossession
sections.html:
The two groups in this section sit at opposite ends of most of the measures in this book.
