Asian Americans as a whole have the highest median income, wealth and life expectancy of any major group, a fact often cited as proof that the Dream is open to anyone. American Indians and Alaska Natives have among the lowest mobility, the highest poverty and the shortest lives, and their relationship with the federal government runs through land, trust and treaty rather than through the labour market alone. In both cases the single number hides the mechanism. For Asian Americans the average conceals the widest spread of income of any group; for Native Americans the outcomes trace to documented federal land policy and to the rules that still govern land held in trust.

The average behind the "model minority"

The phrase "model minority" entered American writing in the 1960s. One of the articles that introduced the idea, William Petersen's "Success Story, Japanese-American Style" in the New York Times Magazine of 9 January 1966, credited Japanese Americans' success despite severe discrimination to their cultural values and set them against Black Americans; scholars have since argued that the concept was used to cast doubt on social programmes for other groups. [cite:ad13_densho_petersen] The averages it rests on are real. The Federal Reserve's 2025 survey put the median net worth of Asian families at $677,600, about twice the white median of $332,100. [cite:us8_scf2025] Asian American life expectancy at birth was 85.8 years in 2024, the highest of any group and nearly seven years above the national 79.0, and the Asian infant mortality rate of 3.44 per 1,000 births in 2023 was the lowest. [cite:ad13_nchs_lt2024] [cite:us16_cdc_imr2023] Homeownership among Asian, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander households was 58.6 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, below the non-Hispanic white rate of 74.5 per cent. [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226]

Mobility data show where the high average comes from. The Chetty, Hendren, Jones and Porter study found that the children of Asian immigrants have much higher upward mobility than any other group, while Asian children of US-born parents have mobility similar to white children. [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] The advantage belongs mainly to the first step from immigrant parent to American child, the same pattern found for immigrants generally in [scene:ad13_immigrants_latinos|the previous section].

The widest spread of any group

The Pew Research Center measured income inequality within each group as the ratio between the income of a person at the 90th percentile (richer than nine in ten of the group) and one at the 10th percentile. In 2016 the ratio was 10.7 for Asian Americans, against 9.8 for Black, 7.8 for white and 7.8 for Hispanic Americans, and it had risen 77 per cent since 1970, from about 6.0. At the top, Asian Americans earned 13 per cent more than white Americans at the same percentile; at the bottom they earned 17 per cent less, where in 1970 they had earned 8 per cent more. [cite:ad13_pew_ineq]

Pew traced the spread mainly to immigration. Immigrants accounted for 81 per cent of the growth of the Asian adult population from 1970 to 2016, after the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, and they arrived with very different levels of education and income. Bachelor's degree attainment ranged from 9 per cent among Bhutanese Americans to 72 per cent among Indian Americans, and median household income from $36,000 for Burmese to $100,000 for Indian Americans; Pew also named discrimination, past and present, as a factor. [cite:ad13_pew_ineq] A 2024 Pew analysis of 2022 Census data found about one Asian American in ten in poverty: 19 per cent of Burmese, about 17 per cent of Hmong and about 16 per cent of Mongolian Americans, against about 6 per cent of Indian Americans. [cite:ad13_npr_pew_pov] For comparison, the official poverty rate for all Americans in 2025 was 10.2 per cent. [cite:us8_census_2025]

Native Americans: the land record

The federal government recognised 574 tribes and 325 reservations in 2025, and 7.7 million people identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, alone or with another race, in 2024. [cite:ad13_census_aian25] Their economic record cannot be separated from land. The General Allotment Act of 1887, known as the Dawes Act, divided reservation land held in common into individual parcels: 160 acres for a head of family and up to 80 acres for other individuals, with title held in trust by the federal government for 25 years. Land left over after allotment was declared "surplus" and could be sold to non-Indians. Indian-held land fell from 138 million acres to 48 million acres by 1934, when allotment stopped, and almost half of what remained was desert or semi-desert. [cite:ad13_gp_dawes] The arithmetic: 138 − 48 = 90 million acres, about 65 per cent of the 1887 total.

Land still held in trust was divided again with each generation of heirs. By 2012 more than 2.9 million fractional interests in trust land were owned by about 220,000 people. The federal government also managed the income from that land, and a class action brought on behalf of nearly 500,000 account holders, known as the Cobell case, alleged that it had failed to account for the money. Congress approved a $3.4 billion settlement in the Claims Resolution Act, signed on 8 December 2010, and it became final on 24 November 2012: $1.5 billion for the account and mismanagement claims and $1.9 billion for a land consolidation programme that buys fractional interests from individual owners who choose to sell. [cite:ad13_doi_cobell]

Why a reservation home is hard to finance

The asset that built the middle-class Dream, the mortgaged home described in [scene:ad6_redlining_to_suburbs|Part Six], works differently on trust land. Because trust land cannot be sold or pledged as collateral, a lender cannot take the land if the borrower defaults; the borrower usually holds a lease rather than ownership, and the Bureau of Indian Affairs must review the loan. In 2015 there were 22.3 home loans per 1,000 residents across the United States and 1.9 per 1,000 on reservations, and 46 per cent of Native applicants on reservations were denied, against 29 per cent off them. A federal guarantee programme, HUD's Section 184 created in 1992, made more than 90 per cent of its loans off reservations and fewer than 200 a year on them between 2005 and 2016. [cite:ad13_hac_trust] Many reservation families buy manufactured homes instead, financed as personal-property loans that cost about 1.5 percentage points more than mortgages; researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis found denial rates of about 75 per cent for such loans to American Indian applicants in mostly reservation tracts in 2015 and 2016, and judged that trust status may explain part of the pattern without reaching a firm conclusion. [cite:ad13_mplsfed_mh]

Outcomes

The poverty rate for American Indians and Alaska Natives was 19.3 per cent in 2024, the highest of the groups reported, against 7.5 per cent for Asian Americans. [cite:ad13_usafacts_pov] On reservation land it was 29.2 per cent in the mid-2010s, against 15.5 per cent nationally. [cite:ad13_hac_trust] Life expectancy at birth was 71.1 years in 2024 for non-Hispanic American Indians and Alaska Natives, eight years below the national 79.0 and nearly fifteen below Asian Americans; the infant mortality rate was 9.20 per 1,000 births in 2023, about twice the white rate of 4.48. [cite:ad13_nchs_lt2024] [cite:us16_cdc_imr2023] The Chetty study found that American Indian children, like Black children, have substantially lower rates of upward mobility than other groups, and that without a change in those rates neither group's position in the national income distribution is likely to change. [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum]

Where it works as promised

For Asian immigrants and their children, the record matches the promise at least as well as for any group in this book: the second generation climbs further than any other, and the group's life expectancy is the highest in the country. [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] [cite:ad13_nchs_lt2024] For Native Americans, the federal government has acknowledged part of the land record in law: allotment ended in 1934, and the Cobell settlement paid account holders and funded the purchase of fractional interests to consolidate divided land. [cite:ad13_gp_dawes] [cite:ad13_doi_cobell] What the record does not show is any of these measures closing the gaps in poverty, mobility or life expectancy, which for American Indians and Alaska Natives remain the widest in this part.

chapters.label: Part Fourteen
chapters.title: The Poverty Trap and the Criminal-Legal Bill
chapters.intro: Part Fourteen follows the people for whom the Dream's floor is thinnest. It begins with the official poverty line, built in 1963 from three times the cost of an emergency diet and raised only by inflation since, and sets it beside the Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure, the United Way's ALICE count of working households that cannot meet local costs, and the economists who argue that the official line overstates poverty. It then adds up the financial bill that the criminal-legal system sends alongside a sentence: bail premiums, fines and fees, the price of a phone call and a bar of soap inside, wages of cents an hour, child support that grows while a parent is locked up, and a record that cuts earnings for life, with the state of each rule as of October 2026. It ends with homelessness: the latest national count, why some regions have far more of it than others, the 2024 Supreme Court ruling on camping bans, and the 2025 turn of federal policy away from Housing First, weighed against the trial evidence on both sides.
chapters.outro: Part Fourteen established that the official poverty line still rests on three times the cost of a 1963 emergency diet, raised only by inflation since 1969, and that the measures built to replace or test it disagree in both directions: 10.2 per cent were officially poor in 2025 and 13.1 per cent on the Supplemental Poverty Measure, 41 per cent of households fell below the ALICE cost-of-living threshold, and an absolute full-income measure put poverty at 1.6 per cent in 2019. [cite:ad14_aspe_history] [cite:ad14_census_p60290pdf] [cite:ad14_alice_national] [cite:ad14_nber_fpm] A full-time job at the federal minimum wage pays $15,080, below the 2026 guideline for one person. [cite:ad14_hhs_guide2026] The criminal-legal system holds 3.6 times as many people as in 1980, a quarter of them unconvicted, and charges them and their families for bail, fees, calls and commissary goods while paying 15 to 52 cents an hour for prison work; the FCC's 2024 phone caps were raised in October 2025 and took effect in April 2026, and a record cuts lifetime earnings by hundreds of thousands of dollars. [cite:ad14_wpb_trend] [cite:ad14_ppi_bail] [cite:ad14_aclu_labor] [cite:ad14_ppi_fcc2025] [cite:ad14_brennan_earnings] Homelessness fell 3 per cent to 745,652 in January 2025 after a record in 2024; regional rates track rents more than addiction, Housing First keeps people housed but has not been shown to improve health, and federal policy turned away from it in 2025 while the courts decide the funding rules. [cite:ad14_hud_pit2025] [cite:ad14_ucp_colburn] [cite:ad14_jpal_hf] [cite:ad14_nasem_psh] [cite:ad14_crs_coc2026] Part Fifteen asks who writes these rules, industry by industry. [scene:ad15_lobbying_by_industry|Part Fifteen: Who Writes the Rules]

sections.h: The Poverty Line: A 1963 Grocery Bill, Still Counting
sections.html:
The taught Dream draws a line between the poor and everyone else and promises that work carries a family across it. Where that line sits decides who counts as poor, who qualifies for help and whether the promise looks kept. This section traces the official line back to the grocery budget it was built on in 1963, sets it beside the Census Bureau's newer Supplemental Poverty Measure, adds the private ALICE measure that tries to price what a household actually needs, and gives the strongest case that the official line overstates poverty rather than understates it. Part Two set out how poverty is measured and where the taught version holds; this section tests the measuring stick itself. [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two: How to Measure]

How the line was drawn

The official poverty thresholds were worked out in 1963 and 1964 by Mollie Orshansky, an economist at the Social Security Administration, and published in the Social Security Bulletin in January 1965. She started from the Agriculture Department's "economy food plan", the cheapest of its model diets, which the department itself described as "designed for temporary or emergency use when funds are low". She then multiplied its cost by three for families of three or more, and by 3.7 for couples, because the 1955 Household Food Consumption Survey showed that families of three or more spent about one-third of their after-tax income on food. [cite:ad14_aspe_history] The logic was simple: if a family's whole income was less than three times the cost of an emergency diet, it could not afford that diet and everything else as well.

The Office of Economic Opportunity, which ran President Johnson's War on Poverty, adopted the thresholds as its working definition in May 1965. In August 1969 the Bureau of the Budget made them the federal government's official statistical definition of poverty and changed the yearly update from the cost of the food plan to the Consumer Price Index, the government's main measure of inflation. In 1981 the separate thresholds for farm families and for families headed by women were dropped, shrinking the table from 124 thresholds to 48. [cite:ad14_aspe_history] Since then the line has been raised each year by inflation and nothing else. The Census Bureau's own description of the measure in its report on 2025 still reads "three times the cost of a minimum food diet in 1963", and the bureau says the measure has "remained mostly unchanged since it was introduced in the mid-1960s". [cite:ad14_census_p60290pdf] [cite:ad14_census_compare]

That is the sense in which the line was never re-based. Indexing to inflation keeps the 1963 diet's purchasing power constant, but it never asks again what share of a budget food takes, or what a household now needs that it did not need in 1963: child care so that both parents can work, a car to reach a job, a phone and internet to apply for one, health insurance premiums. The official measure also counts only cash income before taxes, so it ignores food stamps, housing aid and tax credits on one side and medical bills, work costs and taxes on the other, and it uses one line for the whole country whether rent is cheap or expensive. [cite:ad14_census_compare] This is designed friction rather than a hidden flaw: the method is published, and its limits have been known since a National Academy of Sciences panel proposed a new approach in May 1995. [cite:ad14_aspe_history]

Two lines, two answers

In 2025 the official threshold was $16,749 for a single person under 65 and $32,649 for two adults with two children. [cite:us18_crs_pov2025] The Department of Health and Human Services turns the thresholds into simpler "poverty guidelines" used to decide eligibility for programmes; for 2026 they are $15,960 for one person and $33,000 for a family of four in the 48 contiguous states. [cite:ad14_hhs_guide2026] A full-time worker at the federal minimum wage of $7.25 earns $7.25 × 40 hours × 52 weeks = $15,080 a year before tax, which is $880 below the 2026 guideline for one person and $1,669 below the 2025 Census threshold. Work at the legal floor does not, on its own, lift even a single adult over the line. [scene:ad5_wages_floors|Part Five: the frozen floors]

The Supplemental Poverty Measure, or SPM, was built from the 1995 panel's proposals after an interagency working group asked the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics to develop it in 2010. Its threshold is based on what families actually spend on food, clothing, shelter, utilities, telephone and internet, set at 82 per cent of the median spending on that bundle, averaged over five years, and adjusted for local housing costs and for whether a family rents, pays a mortgage or owns outright. Its resources add benefits such as food stamps, housing aid and tax credits, and subtract taxes, work expenses, medical spending and child support paid to another household. [cite:ad14_census_compare] [cite:ad14_census_p60290pdf]

The two measures give different answers. In 2025 official poverty was 10.2 per cent, 34.5 million people, while the SPM rate was 13.1 per cent, 2.9 points higher. [cite:ad14_census_p60290pdf] Since 34.5 million is 10.2 per cent of the population the measure covers, that population is about 338 million, and 13.1 per cent of it is about 44 million people. The SPM also shows which programmes and costs move people across the line. Social Security lifted 28.8 million people out of SPM poverty in 2025, cutting the rate by 8.5 points; refundable tax credits lifted 6.1 million, including 3.3 million children. Medical expenses, including insurance premiums, pushed 7.7 million people into poverty and added 2.3 points to the rate. [cite:ad14_census_p60290pdf] The SPM has its own weakness: in July 2026 the Bureau of Labor Statistics found errors in how in-kind benefits were imputed in its 2019–2024 thresholds, and the corrected rates for 2019–2023 came out 0.1 to 0.3 points lower than first published, without changing the trend. [cite:ad14_census_spmrevise] [cite:ad14_census_compare]

ALICE: the gap above the line

United Way's United For ALICE project measures a group that both official lines miss. ALICE stands for Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed: households that earn more than the federal poverty level but less than the cost of a bare-bones budget for housing, child care, food, transportation, health care and technology in their county. Using 2024 data, it counted 131.9 million households, of which 16.5 million (13 per cent) were below the poverty level and 38.0 million (29 per cent) were ALICE, so that 54.5 million households, 41 per cent, fell below what the project calls the ALICE Threshold. [cite:ad14_alice_national] The ALICE budget is a threshold chosen by an advocacy organisation, not an official statistic; its value is that it is priced county by county from current costs, which is exactly what the official line, frozen to a 1963 diet, does not do. It also counts households rather than people, which is why its poverty share differs from the Census rate.

Living below or just above any of these lines carries its own price list, from overdraft and late fees to check cashing and rent-to-own contracts. Those charges, and what happened to the federal rules on them in 2024 and 2025, are set out in Part Nine; the fines, fees and benefit cliffs that bear hardest on low incomes are in Part Eleven. [scene:ad9_fees_and_unbanked|Part Nine: Fees and the unbanked] [scene:ad11_fees_everywhere|Part Eleven: Fees everywhere] [scene:ad11_benefits_cliff|Part Eleven: the benefits cliff]

The case that the line overstates poverty

The strongest critics of the official line argue the opposite way: that it overstates poverty because it leaves out most of what government now provides. The economists Richard Burkhauser, Kevin Corinth, James Elwell and Jeff Larrimore built a "full-income" poverty measure that counts taxes, tax credits, food and housing aid and the value of health insurance, set its line so that it matched the official rate of 19.5 per cent in 1963, and then raised it only by inflation, as the War on Poverty's planners intended. On that absolute standard poverty fell to 1.6 per cent by 2019, while the official rate stood at 10.5 per cent; real median income more than doubled over the period and transfers did much of the rest. On a relative version of their measure, which moves with typical incomes, poverty fell only from 19.5 to 16.0 per cent. [cite:ad14_nber_fpm] The study was published in the Journal of Political Economy in 2024. [cite:ad14_nber_fpm]

Both critiques can be true at once, because they answer different questions. Measured against what a very poor family could buy in 1963, almost no American is now that poor, which is a real achievement of growth and of the programmes launched in the 1960s. Measured against what it costs to live in a given county in 2025, with rent, child care and health insurance priced in, tens of millions of working households fall short. The official line sits between these two answers and is accurate to neither.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

On its own terms the taught version holds for most full-time workers. Official poverty among people who worked full time all year was 1.6 per cent in 2025, and child poverty on the official measure was 13.4 per cent, a historic low. [cite:us18_crs_pov2025] [cite:us18_census_p60290] The official rate has fallen from 22.4 per cent in 1959 to 10.2 per cent in 2025, and the SPM shows that public programmes do much of that work: Social Security and refundable tax credits together lifted almost 35 million people (28.8 + 6.1) above the supplemental line in 2025. [cite:us18_epi_povtrend] [cite:ad14_census_p60290pdf] The safety net, in other words, works where it is funded. The open question for 2026 is whether it stays funded: the number of children receiving food stamps fell by 1.2 million between July 2025 and July 2026, according to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning research group, and analysts expect the 2025 budget law's cuts to Medicaid and food aid to show up in later poverty figures. [cite:us18_njm_poverty]

sections.h: The Criminal-Legal Bill: Bail, Fees, Phones and a Record That Follows You
sections.html:
The taught version of American justice says that a person accused is presumed innocent, that a person convicted pays a debt to society, and that once the sentence is served the debt is settled. The record shows a second, financial bill that runs alongside the sentence: money to get out of jail before trial, fees for the court and for supervision, prices for phone calls and soap inside, wages of cents an hour for work, child support that keeps growing while a parent is locked up, and lower earnings for the rest of a working life. This section sets out each charge, who collects it and what has changed as of October 2026. Part Four of the US System volume compares the prison systems themselves. [scene:us4_prisons|US vs Israel: prisons]

The scale

In 1980 there were 503,586 people in American prisons and jails, 220 per 100,000 residents. The number peaked at 2,307,504 in 2008, 755 per 100,000, and stood at 1,833,700 in 2023, 542 per 100,000: 664,200 in local jails, 1,013,500 in state prisons and 156,000 in federal prisons. [cite:ad14_wpb_trend] That 2023 total is 3.6 times the 1980 number (1,833,700 ÷ 503,586) and about 21 per cent below the 2008 peak; measured as a rate, which allows for population growth, incarceration is 2.5 times its 1980 level (542 ÷ 220). A widely repeated line says incarceration has risen "fourfold since the 1980s"; that was true at the peak and is no longer. About a quarter of those held, 467,600 people, had not been convicted and were awaiting trial. [cite:ad14_wpb_trend] Most convictions never reach a trial: in federal courts in 2022, 89.5 per cent of defendants pleaded guilty and fewer than 1 per cent were acquitted. [cite:us4_pew_plea2023]

Money bail

Bail was designed as a guarantee that a defendant will return to court: pay a sum, get it back on appearance. That design is intended friction. The commercial version adds a second party. A defendant who cannot pay the full amount pays a bail bond agent a non-refundable premium, usually about 10 per cent of the bond, often with collateral such as a car title; the agent posts no cash, only a promise to pay if the defendant disappears. Defendants and families pay about $2 billion a year in premiums. Insurance companies stand behind the agents and, in one review of 32 surety companies, paid out less than 1 per cent in bail losses; many forfeitures go uncollected, at least $35 million in Dallas County alone. Only two countries, the United States and the Philippines, allow commercial bail. [cite:ad14_ppi_bail] The figures come from the Prison Policy Initiative, a group that campaigns against mass incarceration, drawing on court audits and press reviews.

Illinois ended cash bail on 18 September 2023, under its Pretrial Fairness Act, leaving judges to decide release or detention on risk. In the first year, according to a review by Loyola University Chicago's Center for Criminal Justice, jail populations fell by about 14 per cent in Cook and the surrounding counties and 25 per cent in rural counties, the share of defendants missing court fell from 25.1 to 22.8 per cent across 21 counties, though it rose from 28.1 to 31 per cent for felonies that can no longer lead to detention, and reported crime fell 11 per cent in the first half of 2024, although the authors noted that crime was falling everywhere and called the court-appearance changes minimal. [cite:ad14_loyola_il] [cite:ad14_audit_dh_fta]

Fines, fees and the inability to pay

In Bearden v. Georgia, decided on 24 May 1983, the Supreme Court held that a court may not jail someone on probation for failing to pay a fine without first asking why; if the person tried and could not pay, the court must consider alternatives such as more time, a smaller fine or community service, because "it is fundamentally unfair to revoke probation automatically". [cite:ad14_bearden] The rule protects only those who can show they tried, and courts have kept adding fees for public defenders, probation and collections. Part Eleven traces how Ferguson, Missouri, budgeted court revenue and how unpaid court debt suspends driving licences. [scene:ad11_fees_everywhere|Part Eleven: fines and fees] A widely repeated claim says California banned all criminal fees in 2018; the law that went furthest, AB 1869, repealed 23 administrative fees charged to adults from 1 July 2021 and gave counties $65 million to replace the lost revenue. Fines and restitution were not part of it. [cite:ad14_ffjc_ab1869]

Phones and the commissary

Calls from prisons and jails are sold by a few private providers under contracts with corrections agencies, which for years took a share of the revenue as "site commissions". Congress passed the Martha Wright-Reed Just and Reasonable Communications Act to let the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) regulate all such calls, and in July 2024 the FCC cut the per-minute caps, capped video calls for the first time and banned site commissions. [cite:ad14_filter_fcc] On 30 June 2025 the FCC's Wireline Competition Bureau waived the compliance deadline from 1 April 2026 to 1 April 2027. [cite:ad14_filter_fcc] Then on 28 October 2025 the FCC adopted revised interim caps that raised the 2024 limits, for example from 6 to 11 cents a minute for prisons, and allowed providers to include the cost of call monitoring and other "safety and security" functions; the ban on site commissions stayed. [cite:ad14_ppi_fcc2025] Status as of October 2026: the revised caps took effect on 6 April 2026, with one provider, Securus, given until 6 July 2026 to convert its video pricing. [cite:ad14_fcc_da26319]

The commissary, the prison shop, sells food, hygiene products and stamps at prices set by contract. A study of Illinois, Massachusetts and Washington found that people spent on average $947 a year there, mostly on food, while typical prison jobs paid $180 to $660 a year; in Massachusetts, at 14 cents an hour, a $1.87 pack of dental floss cost more than 13 hours of work. [cite:ad14_ppi_commissary] The gap is filled by families outside.

Work inside

The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865, abolished slavery and involuntary servitude "except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted", and about 20 states have similar clauses in their own constitutions. A 2022 report by the American Civil Liberties Union and the University of Chicago's Global Human Rights Clinic estimated that about 800,000 incarcerated people work, producing at least $2 billion of goods and $9 billion of prison maintenance services a year. Average pay in ordinary prison jobs ran from 15 to 52 cents an hour; Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas paid nothing for most jobs; and up to 80 per cent of a paycheck could be withheld for room and board, taxes and court costs. [cite:ad14_aclu_labor]

The record after release

In a field experiment in Milwaukee, the sociologist Devah Pager sent matched pairs of applicants, identical except for race and a criminal record, to apply for jobs. White applicants without a record were called back 34 per cent of the time and those with a record 17 per cent; Black applicants without a record 14 per cent and with one 5 per cent. [cite:ad14_epi_pager] "Ban the box" laws, which bar asking about records on job applications, were meant to help. A study by Amanda Agan and Sonja Starr, sending about 15,000 online applications in New York City and New Jersey, found that applicants without a record got 63 per cent more callbacks, and that after the laws took effect white applicants' callback advantage over otherwise similar Black applicants at affected employers grew from about 7 per cent to about 45 per cent, which the authors attributed to employers guessing at records by race. [cite:ad14_umich_agan] A 2020 Brennan Center study estimated that imprisonment cuts annual earnings by up to 51.7 per cent and that people imprisoned as young adults lose $267,000 (white), $358,900 (Black) or $511,500 (Latino) over their lifetimes; across everyone with a conviction or prison history it put lost earnings at $372.3 billion a year. [cite:ad14_brennan_earnings] The racial gaps in these estimates describe how the labour market treats people, as the two callback studies document; they are not traits of any group.

Debt also grows inside. About one in five people in prison or jail has a child support order, and the average parent enters prison owing about $10,000 and leaves owing about $20,000, because orders keep running while earnings stop. As of July 2019 at least nine states and territories still treated incarceration as "voluntary unemployment" that barred a reduction, despite a 2016 federal rule prohibiting that treatment. [cite:ad14_aspe_childsupport]

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Interpretation, not finding: the poverty penalty as a closed loop

The Sophia platform reads these charges as one loop: poverty raises the odds of being held before trial, detention and fees deepen poverty, and the record then keeps earnings low enough to start the cycle again, with private contractors collecting at each step. Read through this lens, the Dream's promise of a fresh start after a debt is paid is withdrawn by design. The strongest counter-readings are these: each charge has a different owner and a different legal basis, and no document shows them coordinated; prices inside partly reflect real security costs, which the FCC now counts openly; and the direction since 2008 is toward fewer people in custody and lower charges, which is the opposite of a system built to maximise them. The record supports the narrower claim that each charge, unchecked, moves money from poor defendants and their families to contractors and local budgets.

Where it works as promised

Parts of the system have moved toward the taught version. The number of people in custody fell by about a fifth from its 2008 peak. [cite:ad14_wpb_trend] Illinois ended cash bail and in its first year saw fewer missed court dates overall and less reported crime, though both trends had other causes too. [cite:ad14_loyola_il] California stopped charging adults 23 administrative fees. [cite:ad14_ffjc_ab1869] Even after the 2025 revision, the FCC's caps and its ban on site commissions remain the first nationwide limits on what a call home from prison can cost. [cite:ad14_ppi_fcc2025] And the Supreme Court's 1983 rule still forbids jailing a person only because they are too poor to pay. [cite:ad14_bearden]

sections.h: Homelessness: The Count, the Court and the Fight Over Housing First
sections.html:
A home is the first asset of the taught Dream and the floor beneath every other part of it: an address to put on a job application, a place for children to sleep before school, somewhere to keep medicine and papers. Homelessness is the point at which that floor gives way. This section gives the latest national count and what changed in it, the evidence on why homelessness is higher in some places than others, the 2024 Supreme Court ruling that allowed cities to punish sleeping outside, the 2025 executive order and funding changes that turned federal policy away from "Housing First", and what the research shows about that approach and its critics, with the status of each as of October 2026.

The count and what changed in 2025

The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) measures homelessness with a point-in-time count: on one night in January, local agencies count people in shelters and transitional housing and people sleeping outside or in places not meant for living. The count was 647,258 in 2007, fell to 549,928 in 2016, rose to 653,104 in 2023 and jumped to a record 771,480 in 2024, of whom 274,224 were unsheltered. [cite:us15_crs_homeless] The January 2025 count, published on 29 May 2026, was 745,652, a fall of 3 per cent, with 266,320 unsheltered. HUD noted that the total was still 27 per cent above 2013, unsheltered homelessness 36 per cent higher, and chronic (long-term) homelessness 81 per cent higher. [cite:ad14_hud_pit2025] [cite:us15_hud_pit2025] A widely repeated claim says homelessness keeps setting records above 770,000 a year; on the latest count it fell.

The 2025 release also changed how the numbers were framed. HUD attributed the decline to "decreases in Sanctuary Cities", its term for cities that limit cooperation with immigration enforcement, and added a broader figure, 1,456,923, that combines the homeless count with people living in housing paid for by homelessness programmes. That second figure is not a count of homeless people; formerly homeless people in permanent housing are by definition housed, and the point-in-time count has always excluded them. [cite:ad14_hud_pit2025] Both framings are HUD's own and support its stated case, set out below, that spending on permanent housing has not paid off.

Why some places have more

Public debate often explains homelessness through addiction and mental illness. Those conditions are common among people living on the street, but they are also common in places with little homelessness. Gregg Colburn, a housing researcher at the University of Washington, and Clayton Page Aldern, a data scientist, tested the usual explanations against the wide differences between American cities in their 2022 book Homelessness Is a Housing Problem. Mental illness, drug use, poverty, weather and the generosity of local benefits did not explain why some regions have far higher rates; the cost and availability of rental housing did. [cite:ad14_ucp_colburn] That points back to the rent and supply record in Part Six. [scene:ad6_price_and_rent|Part Six: price and rent] [scene:ad6_eviction_and_traps|Part Six: eviction]

A widely shared comparison sets the roughly 15 million vacant homes in the country against the number of homeless people and concludes that there is no shortage, only a refusal to house people. The vacancy count includes homes listed for rent or for sale, homes between tenants and seasonal homes; some vacancy is what allows people to move at all, and the rental vacancy rate was 7.3 per cent in the second quarter of 2026. [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226] The comparison does not show that housing is withheld by design, and the record does not support that claim.

The court: punishing sleeping outside

Grants Pass, a small city in Oregon, enforced its ban on camping on public property with civil fines, then with bans from public spaces and short jail terms for repeat violators. Lower courts, relying on an earlier Ninth Circuit decision, Martin v. Boise, held that punishing homeless people in this way was cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment. On 28 June 2024 the Supreme Court reversed, 6–3, in City of Grants Pass v. Johnson. Writing for the majority, Justice Neil Gorsuch held that the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel and unusual punishment does not apply to general laws against camping on public property, leaving the policy to elected officials: "Homelessness is complex. Its causes are many." Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for the three dissenters, called the enforcement "unconscionable and unconstitutional". [cite:ad14_ncc_grantspass] The ruling did not require any city to ban camping; it removed a constitutional barrier for those that chose to.

The 2025 policy turn

Housing First is the approach of placing homeless people into permanent housing without first requiring sobriety or treatment, and offering services once they are housed. On 24 July 2025 President Trump signed an executive order, "Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets", that ended federal support for Housing First, directed HUD to make treatment a condition of its programmes, promoted civil commitment, the court-ordered treatment of people with severe mental illness, barred federal addiction grants from funding harm-reduction programmes such as syringe distribution, and told agencies to favour places that enforce bans on camping, loitering and open drug use. [cite:ad14_hma_eo] HUD Secretary Scott Turner stated that "the status quo of 'housing first' has failed to meaningfully reduce homelessness", pointing to a 151 per cent rise in federally funded beds and a 111 per cent rise in Continuum of Care spending since 2013. [cite:ad14_hud_pit2025]

The money flows mostly through HUD's Continuum of Care programme, about $4 billion a year in grants to local networks of providers. In November 2025 HUD capped permanent supportive housing, which made up about 87 per cent of the programme's spending, at 30 per cent of funds, and limited the share of existing grants protected for renewal to 30 per cent, down from about 90 per cent. Twenty-one state attorneys general and a group of counties and nonprofits sued; HUD withdrew the notice on 8 December 2025, and Congress, in the appropriations law of 3 February 2026, ordered expiring grants renewed in the meantime. [cite:ad14_naco_coc] HUD's next notice, issued on 1 June 2026, protected 60 per cent of renewals, set aside $1.3 billion of $4.04 billion for new transitional housing and services-only projects, and awarded points for requiring participation in treatment. A federal district court vacated it on 7 August 2026 under the Administrative Procedure Act; on 16 September 2026 the First Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that ruling pending appeal, and HUD reinstated the notice with a 30 September deadline. [cite:ad14_crs_coc2026] [cite:ad14_naco_vacate] Status as of October 2026: in the latest reports, from late September, the competition was proceeding under the stay and the appeal was pending.

What the evidence shows

Housing First has been tested in randomised trials, in which people are assigned by lottery to the programme or to the usual services. In Canada's At Home/Chez Soi trial in five cities, participants were stably housed for 73 per cent of a two-year period, against 32 per cent for the comparison group. In the HUD-VASH programme for veterans, Housing First participants were housed in 35 days rather than 223. Effects on health were unclear, substance use was about the same as under treatment-first programmes, and most of the cost was offset by savings on shelters, jails and hospitals, although that evidence is limited. [cite:ad14_jpal_hf] The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine reached a similar verdict in 2018: permanent supportive housing "increases an individual's ability to remain housed", but the committee "found no substantial evidence" that it improves health outcomes, except limited data for people with HIV/AIDS. [cite:ad14_nasem_psh]

The critics' strongest point is HUD's: national homelessness rose while spending on permanent housing grew. The strongest reply is that a programme can house the people it serves without lowering a regional count driven by rents, which is what the trials and the Colburn–Aldern findings together suggest. [cite:ad14_jpal_hf] [cite:ad14_ucp_colburn] The record supports neither the claim that Housing First has failed at what it measures, keeping people housed, nor the claim that it can end homelessness by itself while housing costs rise.

Where it works as promised

The safety net has caught people before. The national count fell by about 15 per cent between 2007 and 2016, from 647,258 to 549,928, and fell again in 2025. [cite:us15_crs_homeless] [cite:ad14_hud_pit2025] For the individuals it reaches, Housing First keeps people in a home more than twice as much of the time as the alternatives tested against it, and veterans in HUD's targeted programme were housed in about a month instead of more than seven. [cite:ad14_jpal_hf] What the record does not show is a national policy that has kept the floor of the Dream in place while rents climbed; that question returns in Part Fifteen, which asks who writes the rules. [scene:ad15_lobbying_by_industry|Part Fifteen: Who writes the rules]

chapters.label: Part Fifteen
chapters.title: Who Writes the Rules
chapters.intro: Every mechanism in this book runs on rules: tax provisions, bankruptcy law, lending regulations, court doctrines on contracts. The taught version says those rules are written by representatives answering to voters in open markets. This part asks who else takes part in writing them and what the record shows about the effect. The first section measures federal lobbying by industry, campaign spending after the Citizens United decision of 2010 and the revolving door between office and lobbying, sets the leading study of whose preferences shape policy beside its critics, and follows one documented trail from lobbying to a rule change to revenue. The second measures the share of corporate profits earned by finance and traces how arbitration clauses moved consumer and workplace disputes out of the courts. The third tests the promise of competitive prices: market concentration and markups, shared rent-pricing software, prices tailored to individual shoppers, hidden fees, and the laws that now give owners a right to repair what they buy.
chapters.outro: Who writes the rules is partly a matter of record. Reported federal lobbying rose from $3.30 billion in 2008 to about $5 billion in 2025, led by the health sector, and since Citizens United a handful of donors can supply a large share of a campaign's outside money on either side. [cite:ad15_247_lobby] [cite:us3_os_lobby2025] [cite:ad15_nbc_2023] [cite:ad15_brennan_cu15] Affluent and business preferences predict policy better than those of middle-income Americans, though critics show the two usually agree; lobbyists who once worked for a senator generate about a quarter less revenue once that senator leaves office; and the Direct File case shows documented lobbying, a rule change and industry revenue in one chain without proof that one caused the other. [cite:ad15_jr_gilens] [cite:ad15_enns] [cite:ad15_aer_revolving] [cite:ad15_ap_directfile] Finance earned about a fifth to a quarter of domestic corporate profits in the 2020s; mandatory arbitration clauses bind about 60 million non-union private-sector workers, about 25 million of whom have also waived class actions, and the one federal limit on them in consumer finance was repealed in 2017 by a 51–50 Senate vote. [cite:ad15_fred_finprof] [cite:ad15_epi_colvin] [cite:ad15_troutman_cra] Whether markups have risen across the economy is disputed, but shared pricing software, individualised prices and repair restrictions have each been checked by courts, regulators or new state laws. [cite:ad15_qje_markups] [cite:ad15_basu] [cite:ad6_wsoc_realpage] [cite:ad15_wiley_r2r] Part Sixteen asks why, against this record, belief in the Dream has proved so durable. [scene:ad16_belief_vs_data|Part Sixteen: Why the Belief Survives]

sections.h: Who Pays to Be Heard: Lobbying, Campaign Money and the Revolving Door
sections.html:
The civics version of how rules are made is short. Citizens elect representatives, representatives write and pass laws, and agencies carry them out. Generations of schoolchildren learned it from classroom units and from the Schoolhouse Rock cartoons that began airing on Saturday mornings in 1973, and the naturalisation test still asks new citizens to name the country's economic system as "capitalism" or a "free market economy". [cite:ad1_loc_shr] [cite:ad1_uscis2025] [scene:ad1_as_taught|The Dream as taught] Every rule this book has examined so far, from the tax treatment of a health plan to the bankruptcy treatment of a student loan, passed through that process. This section asks who else takes part in it, with what money, and what the evidence shows about whether that money changes the result. It keeps two questions apart throughout: what is disclosed, which is a matter of record, and what the disclosed money caused, which needs its own evidence.

The disclosed total

Lobbying, in the legal sense, is paid contact with members of Congress, their staff or senior executive officials on behalf of a client, on legislation, rules or policy. Under the Lobbying Disclosure Act, lobbyists and the organisations that employ them file reports with the Clerk of the House and the Secretary of the Senate, and since the Honest Leadership and Open Government Act, signed by President George W. Bush on 14 September 2007 after votes of 96 to 2 in the Senate and 411 to 8 in the House, those reports have been due every quarter rather than twice a year. [cite:ad15_wiki_hloga] OpenSecrets, a non-profit that compiles the filings, counted $3.30 billion in reported federal lobbying in 2008, by 14,125 registered lobbyists. Spending then held between about $3.2 billion and $3.5 billion a year for a decade, dipping to $3.16 billion in 2016, before rising to $3.73 billion in 2021. [cite:ad15_247_lobby] It reached $4.27 billion in 2023 and $4.44 billion in 2024. [cite:ad15_statista_lobby] OpenSecrets put 2025 at a record of about $5 billion, up 14 per cent on 2024 and the largest one-year rise since 2008; LegiStorm, which counts the same filings differently, put it at $5.24 billion. [cite:us3_os_lobby2025] [cite:ad15_legistorm_2025] These are nominal dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so part of the rise since 2008 is price growth rather than more activity.

Which industries spend

The money is not spread evenly. In 2023 the health sector, which in OpenSecrets' classification covers drug makers, insurers, hospitals and professional bodies, reported more than $739 million, the most of any sector. The two largest single spenders were the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, a business federation, at $69 million, and the National Association of Realtors, the trade body of real-estate agents, at $52 million; a year earlier the order was reversed, with the Realtors at $82 million and the Chamber at $81 million. [cite:ad15_nbc_2023] Within health, pharmaceuticals and health products reported $226.8 million in the first half of 2025 alone, and that industry has outspent every other industry in all but one quarter since 2010. Real estate reported $34.1 million in the second quarter of 2025, and the insurers' trade body, America's Health Insurance Plans, $4.1 million. [cite:ad15_os_q2_2025] The single most lobbied bill of 2025 was the budget reconciliation law, on which 2,145 clients reported lobbying. [cite:ad15_os_q2_2025]

These are the industries whose rules decide much of what earlier parts measured: the price of drugs and insurance ([scene:ad8_insurance_machine|Part Eight]), the terms on which homes are bought and sold ([scene:ad6_price_and_rent|Part Six]) and the treatment of private student loans in bankruptcy, changed in 2005. In the years that change was under consideration, Sallie Mae, the largest student lender, spent $9 million lobbying Congress (1999–2005) and its political action committee gave more than $130,000 to members of the judiciary committees ([scene:ad7_student_debt_law|Part Seven]). [cite:ad7_npr_burd] The spending and the change are both on the record; that the one produced the other is not documented; the provision was one section of a broad bankruptcy law. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] Lobbying is not one-sided in the filings: consumer groups, unions and advocacy groups also register and report. But the sums are of a different order: two single organisations, the Chamber and the Realtors, together reported $121 million in 2023. [cite:ad15_nbc_2023]

Campaign money after 2010

Lobbying pays for access and argument; campaign spending helps decide who holds the seat in the first place. On 21 January 2010, in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, the Supreme Court held by five votes to four that federal limits on independent political spending by corporations were unconstitutional, overruling its 1990 decision in Austin and part of its 2003 decision in McConnell. The majority held that independent expenditures "do not give rise to corruption or the appearance of corruption", while upholding the rules that require such spending to be disclosed and labelled. [cite:ad15_lii_cu] [cite:ad15_brennan_cu15] Two months later a federal appeals court applied the same reasoning to groups that only spend independently, and the result was the super PAC: a committee that may raise unlimited sums from individuals, companies or unions, provided it does not coordinate with candidates or give to them directly. [cite:pm_wiki_superpac]

The Brennan Center for Justice, a law and policy institute that supports campaign-finance limits, counted more than $1 billion from sources that did not disclose their donors flowing to committees supporting candidates of both parties in 2024. Roughly 44 per cent of the money raised to support Donald Trump, $481 million, came from ten individual donors; the ten largest donors backing Kamala Harris accounted for nearly 8 per cent, $126 million. [cite:ad15_brennan_cu15] Concentration at the top is a feature of both coalitions; what the numbers show is that a small number of donors can now supply a large share of a campaign's outside support.

Does the money change the outcome

Disclosure shows who paid; it does not show what the payment bought. The most cited attempt to measure influence is a 2014 study by the political scientists Martin Gilens and Benjamin Page. They compared the stated preferences of middle-income Americans, of affluent Americans and of organised interest groups on 1,779 policy questions asked in surveys between 1981 and 2002 with whether the policy was later adopted. Policies with low support among the affluent passed about 18 per cent of the time and those with high support about 45 per cent, and business-oriented groups had roughly twice the influence of mass-membership groups. They concluded that "mass-based interest groups and average citizens have little or no independent influence". [cite:ad15_jr_gilens]

Two critiques followed in 2015. Omar Bashir showed that the preferences of middle-income and affluent Americans were so closely correlated that the statistical model could not reliably separate their effects, and that the model explained less than a tenth of the variation in outcomes. In the study's own data, when 80 per cent or more of middle-income Americans favoured a change it happened 47 per cent of the time, against 52 per cent when the affluent were that keen; in the 185 cases where the two groups disagreed, the middle-income side got its way 47 per cent of the time. [cite:ad15_bashir] Peter Enns found that the two groups ranked policies so similarly (a correlation of 0.94 across 1,836 questions) that policy usually lands where the middle would want it even if only the affluent were heard, a result he called "coincidental representation"; he found much larger gaps between strong partisans than between income groups. [cite:ad15_enns] The honest summary is that the affluent and organised business are better placed to shape policy, and that the size of the advantage on ordinary questions is disputed.

The revolving door

Lobbying's value also comes from who the lobbyist knows. The 2007 law lengthened the period in which a former senator may not lobby Congress from one year to two, barred senior Senate staff from lobbying the whole Senate for a year, and barred senior House staff from lobbying their former office or committee for a year. [cite:ad15_wiki_hloga] A study in the American Economic Review measured what such connections are worth. Lobbyists who had worked for a senator saw the revenue they generated fall by 24 per cent when that senator left office, and the fall was larger the more senior and powerful the senator had been. The authors read this as evidence that lobbyists are paid for access to particular officials, not only for expertise. [cite:ad15_aer_revolving]

One trail: the free government tax filer

One recent case shows the full chain from disclosed lobbying to a rule change to revenue, and also why the chain is not proof of cause. Direct File was a free Internal Revenue Service program, built under the Biden administration, that let taxpayers with simple returns file online directly with the government. It accepted 140,803 returns in 2024 and 296,531 in 2025. [cite:ad15_ap_directfile] Commercial tax-preparation firms lobbied against it. Intuit, which makes TurboTax, reported about $3 million in federal lobbying in the first three quarters of 2025; H&R Block reported $2.4 million and warned in its filings that Direct File could hurt its revenue; and the American Coalition for Taxpayer Rights, which represents both, reported $270,000. Groups including Oxfam America lobbied in support. [cite:ad15_bt_directfile] The July 2025 budget law gave the IRS $15 million to study a public-private alternative; a provision to end Direct File outright was removed from the bill. On 5 November 2025 the Associated Press reported an IRS email stating that "IRS Direct File will not be available in Filing Season 2026". [cite:ad15_bt_directfile] [cite:ad15_ap_directfile] As of October 2026 no relaunch had been announced.

The stated reasons belong beside the money. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who also served as IRS commissioner, said the program "wasn't used very much" and that there were "better alternatives", and Republican lawmakers called it a waste of public money; Intuit said it "regularly engages with policymakers" on tax simplification. [cite:ad15_ap_directfile] [cite:ad15_bt_directfile] The use figures are real: 296,531 returns is a small share of all individual returns. The lobbying, the policy change and the revenue are each documented. That the lobbying caused the change is an inference, and on the record it remains contested.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

Several parts of the taught version hold. The spending is visible: quarterly lobbying reports and campaign-finance filings make it possible to write every figure in this section, which is not true in many democracies. Middle-income and affluent Americans agree on most policy questions, so on most votes the outcome matches what the middle wants, whoever is heard. [cite:ad15_enns] Congress also narrows practices that large employers had relied on, with votes from both parties: in 2022 a bill sponsored by a Democratic and a Republican senator, passed by voice vote in the Senate, ended forced arbitration of sexual-harassment claims, the subject of the next section. [cite:ad15_npr_efaa] And Direct File itself was built inside the same system that later closed it, which shows that the outcome is a matter of who holds office, not a fixed result.

Interpretation, not finding: the rules as the extraction layer

The Sophia platform reads lobbying, campaign finance and the revolving door as the layer that keeps the rest of the Dream's machinery in place: industries that profit from a mechanism pay to keep it, so the taught story of representative government covers a system in which those who gain from the rules help write them. Read through this lens, the Direct File case is one visible instance of a common pattern. The documents in this section support a narrower statement: industries spend heavily, connected lobbyists' revenue tracks their former employer's time in office, and the affluent's preferences predict outcomes better. The strongest counter-readings are that the measured influence gap on ordinary questions may be small because preferences overlap; that industries often lobby against one another, so spending does not add up to one interest; that much lobbying is defensive or informational; and that both parties have enacted rules opposed by the largest spenders. No document examined here shows a common plan.

sections.h: Finance's Share and the Private Courtroom: Financialization and Forced Arbitration
sections.html:
Two changes in how the economy is organised sit underneath many of the household costs measured in earlier parts. The first is the growing weight of finance: the share of the country's business profits earned by lending, trading, insuring and managing money rather than by making goods or providing other services. The second is a change in where disputes between companies and the people they serve are settled. Over the past fifteen years, the Supreme Court has allowed a clause in a credit-card agreement, a phone contract or a job offer to move a customer's or worker's complaint out of the public courts and into private arbitration, one person at a time. This section measures the first, traces the second through its court rulings and the one federal attempt to limit it, and sets the evidence for and against each side by side.

What financialization means and how big it is

The sociologist Greta Krippner defined financialization as "a pattern of accumulation in which profits accrue primarily through financial channels" rather than through trade and the production of goods. [cite:ad15_krippner] Using national accounts, she found that the ratio of financial to non-financial profits at the start of the 2000s was roughly three to five times its level in the 1950s and 1960s, depending on the measure, and that ordinary non-financial companies had also come to earn far more of their income from financial assets: their portfolio income, relative to their cash flow, peaked in the late 1980s at about five times its earlier level. [cite:ad15_krippner]

The Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes the current figures. Its measure of domestic corporate profits, adjusted so that inventory gains and depreciation are valued at current cost, was $3,551 billion in 2025, of which financial companies earned $840 billion. [cite:ad15_fred_domprof] [cite:ad15_fred_finprof] Dividing one by the other gives a finance share of 23.7 per cent. On the same industry classification, which begins in 1998, the share was 28.8 per cent in 2000 and reached 38.1 per cent in 2002 ($294.9 billion of $773.6 billion), the highest year in the series. [cite:ad15_audit_fred_early] It collapsed to 11.5 per cent in the crisis year 2008, recovered to 29.2 per cent in 2010, and stood at 18.1 per cent in 2023 and 19.9 per cent in 2024. [cite:ad15_fred_finprof] [cite:ad15_fred_domprof_data] [cite:ad15_fred_domprof] The series is volatile, because financial profits swing with asset prices and loan losses, and it measures where profits are booked, not who ends up owning them. What it shows is that roughly one dollar in four or five of domestic corporate profit in the 2020s was earned by finance.

For a household, finance's profit is in part the other side of its own payments: the interest on card balances and car loans, the fees on accounts, the margins on mortgages. Those were measured in Part Nine, and the shift of corporate cash toward share buybacks in Part Four. [scene:ad9_credit_and_scores|Part Nine] [scene:ad4_shareholder_turn|Part Four] Finance also provides services households value, from mortgages that make homes affordable to retirement accounts that hold their savings, so a high finance share is not by itself evidence of extraction. The question is how disputes over those services are resolved when something goes wrong.

Arbitration: from business disputes to consumer contracts

Arbitration is a private process in which a dispute is decided by an arbitrator chosen under the contract rather than by a judge or jury, usually in private and with limited appeal. The Federal Arbitration Act of 1925 requires courts to enforce agreements to arbitrate. [cite:ad15_lii_concepcion] What changed in recent decades was its use in contracts that customers and workers sign without negotiation, and the addition of a second clause: a waiver of the right to join with others in a class action, the lawsuit in which one or a few people sue on behalf of everyone harmed in the same way.

The decisive case concerned a mobile phone contract. The Concepcions, a California couple, were charged sales tax on phones that AT&T advertised as free, and their claim was joined to a class action. California's courts had held that class-action waivers in such consumer contracts were unconscionable, that is, too one-sided to enforce. On 27 April 2011, in AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion, the Supreme Court held by five votes to four that the Federal Arbitration Act overrides that California rule. [cite:ad15_lii_concepcion] Justice Stephen Breyer, dissenting, asked what "rational lawyer would have signed on to represent the Concepcions" in a case over a $30.22 claim. [cite:ad15_audit_concepcion_dissent] On 20 June 2013, in American Express v. Italian Colors Restaurant, the Court, by five votes to three, enforced a waiver even though expert proof of the restaurant's antitrust claim was estimated to cost several hundred thousand dollars or more, against a maximum individual recovery of $38,549 after trebling; Justice Elena Kagan's dissent summarised the majority's answer as "Too darn bad". [cite:ad15_audit_italiancolors] On 21 May 2018, in Epic Systems v. Lewis, the Court held, again by five to four, that employers may require workers to bring wage and other claims one by one, holding that "arbitration agreements providing for individualized proceedings must be enforced" and that federal labour law does not override them. [cite:ad15_lii_epic]

By then the clauses were common at work. A 2017 survey of private employers with 50 or more staff, run by Cornell University for the Economic Policy Institute, a labour-aligned research group, found that 56.2 per cent of non-union private-sector employees, about 60.1 million people, were bound by mandatory arbitration, against about 2 per cent of companies using it in 1992. About a quarter of all non-union private-sector workers, 24.7 million, had also waived class actions. The clauses were most common at establishments with an average wage under $13 an hour (64.5 per cent). [cite:ad15_epi_colvin]

What the regulator found, and what Congress did

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the federal consumer-finance regulator created in 2010, studied arbitration in consumer finance. Its 2015 study found that card issuers holding more than half of all credit-card debt, and banks holding 44 per cent of insured deposits, used arbitration clauses; that three in four consumers surveyed did not know whether their card agreement had one; and that only about 2 per cent would consult a lawyer or consider legal action over a small-dollar dispute. In roughly a thousand arbitration cases over two years, arbitrators awarded a total of about $360,000 to 78 consumers. Over five years, group lawsuits paid about $1 billion to more than 34 million consumers. [cite:ad15_cfpb_arb2017] On 10 July 2017 the Bureau issued a rule that would have let companies keep arbitration clauses but barred them from using them to block class actions. [cite:ad15_cfpb_arb2017]

The rule never took effect. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and others sued on 29 September 2017. The House voted 231 to 190 to overturn it under the Congressional Review Act, which lets Congress cancel a new rule by simple majority in both chambers, and on 24 October 2017 the Senate voted 51 to 50, with Vice President Mike Pence breaking the tie. [cite:ad15_troutman_cra] President Trump signed the resolution on 1 November 2017 and the Bureau removed the rule on 22 November. [cite:ad15_cfpb_arb2017] The same law may bar the Bureau from issuing a substantially similar rule. [cite:ad15_troutman_cra] As of October 2026 no general federal rule limits class-action waivers in consumer finance outside the statutory bars described below, and the Bureau's own funding was in litigation. [cite:ad9_goodwin_cfpb]

The case for arbitration

The defenders' case is substantial. In October 2017 the Treasury Department argued that the Bureau's own projections showed four in five class actions yielding nothing for class members, that only about 4 per cent of class members typically claim their share, that the typical settlement offered $32.35 a person, and that the rule would have sent about $330 million more to plaintiffs' lawyers over five years. [cite:ad15_treasury_arb] The two sides measure different things: the Bureau counted total relief reaching consumers, the Treasury the small sums each person receives and the share that goes to lawyers. Both sets of numbers are accurate on their own terms. The design question is whether a small, widely shared harm should be recoverable at all. The documented pattern is that, once group claims are waived, very few individual claims are brought.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Where it works as promised

Congress has drawn limits where it chose to. Arbitration clauses in residential mortgages are barred by statute, and the Military Lending Act bars them in many forms of credit to servicemembers. [cite:ad15_audit_cfpb_bars] In 2022 a bill sponsored by Senators Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat, and Lindsey Graham, a Republican, passed the Senate by voice vote and was signed on 3 March, letting anyone alleging sexual assault or harassment at work choose court over arbitration, including in pending cases. [cite:ad15_npr_efaa] [cite:ad15_wh_hr4445] The Federal Arbitration Act itself is designed friction: a deliberate choice, made a century ago, to make private agreements to arbitrate binding. Its extension to standard-form consumer and job contracts with class waivers came through court rulings and a congressional repeal, each with recorded votes and named parties on both sides. That is a record a voter can read and a legislature can change.

sections.h: Pricing Power: Concentration, Markups, Algorithms and the Right to Repair
sections.html:
The taught version of a market economy rests on competition. Many sellers compete for customers, so no one firm can set prices far above its costs for long, and what people pay, like what they earn, reflects market value. Economics standards written for American high schools put it in those terms, and the naturalisation test describes the country's system as a "free market economy". [cite:ad1_cee2010] [cite:ad1_uscis2025] This section tests the price side of that promise. It sets out what is known about whether markets have become less competitive and whether firms now charge more above cost, then follows three newer ways of setting prices: shared algorithms, prices tailored to the individual buyer, and fees added at the end of a purchase. It closes with the record on products built to be replaced, and the laws that have pushed back.

Concentration and markups: the evidence and its critics

Concentration measures how much of a market the largest firms hold. A 2019 study by Gustavo Grullon, Yelena Larkin and Roni Michaely found that "since the late 1990s, over 75% of US industries have experienced an increase in concentration levels", and that firms in the industries where concentration rose most earned higher profit margins. [cite:us11_gl_concentration] The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, a Washington technology-policy think tank, disputed the scale: in Census data for 2002 to 2012 the four largest firms' share fell or held steady in 319 of 792 detailed industries (40 per cent), and measured from 1972 instead of 1997 the rise in the typical industry is much smaller. [cite:us11_itif_kennedy] Local markets, where shoppers actually buy, have in several studies become less concentrated even as national ones became more so; one Census-based study found local employer concentration fell to about three-quarters of its 1976 level by 2015. [cite:ad5_rinz2022] [scene:ad5_monopsony_lockin|Part Five]

A markup is the ratio of a product's price to the cost of producing one more unit of it; a markup of 50 per cent means the price is one and a half times that cost. In the most cited estimate, published in 2020 by Jan De Loecker, Jan Eeckhout and Gabriel Unger, the average markup of US public companies rose from 21 per cent above marginal cost in 1980 to 61 per cent in their latest data, and the average profit rate from 1 per cent to 8 per cent. The rise came mainly from the firms with the highest markups; the median firm's markup did not change. [cite:ad15_qje_markups] The economist Susanto Basu, reviewing this and competing estimates in 2019, concluded that "existing methods cannot determine whether markups have been stable or whether they have risen modestly", because each method depends on assumptions about firms' costs that are hard to check. He added that even a modest rise could matter for workers' share of income. [cite:ad15_basu] The record therefore supports a narrower claim than the popular one: the most profitable firms have pulled away from the rest, and whether prices across the economy have risen relative to costs is disputed.

Algorithmic pricing: the rental software case

Part Six followed one documented case of shared pricing software in housing. [scene:ad6_eviction_and_traps|Part Six] On 23 August 2024 the Justice Department and eight states sued RealPage, whose revenue-management software recommends rents to landlords, alleging that competing landlords fed it their private rent data, that its features pushed them to accept its recommendations, and that it held about 80 per cent of the market for such software in commercial multifamily housing. [cite:ad6_doj_realpage24] RealPage did not admit wrongdoing. Under a settlement announced on 24 November 2025 and approved by the court in May 2026, it may no longer use competitors' non-public data in real-time pricing, must train its models only on non-public data at least a year old, may not build models narrower than a state, must remove features that discourage rent cuts, and will work under a court-appointed monitor. [cite:ad6_doj_realpage25] [cite:ad6_wsoc_realpage] As of October 2026 North Carolina's separate case continued, and a federal court had granted RealPage a preliminary injunction against New York's 2025 ban on algorithmic rent-setting, on free-speech grounds. [cite:ad6_wsoc_realpage] [cite:ad6_dive_ny]

Surveillance pricing

A newer practice sets prices for one buyer at a time. In July 2024 the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), by unanimous vote, ordered eight firms that sell pricing and data services to explain how they work. On 17 January 2025 its staff released initial findings: these intermediaries can draw on a shopper's demographics, location, browsing history and inferred behaviour, such as leaving an item in a basket, and the same tools used to target advertisements can be used to set an individual's price. [cite:ad15_bclp_surv] [cite:ad15_ftc_surv] The staff called the practice surveillance pricing. Commissioners Andrew Ferguson, who became chair three days later, and Melissa Holyoak dissented from releasing preliminary findings, while agreeing that more work was needed and that a final, fact-based report should follow. [cite:ad15_bclp_surv]

One case reached the public in December 2025. An investigation by Consumer Reports with two advocacy groups found that Instacart's software let grocery retailers show different shoppers different prices for the same item at the same store at the same time. On 22 December Instacart said it would end those price tests immediately, while maintaining that its software did not meaningfully raise grocery prices; the FTC said it was "disturbed" by the reports, and the attorneys general of New York and California opened inquiries. [cite:ad15_cr_instacart] New York became the first state to require disclosure: since 8 July 2025 a business that sets a price by algorithm using a shopper's personal data must say so, in capitals, next to the price, with fines of up to $1,000 a violation. A federal judge dismissed the retail industry's challenge to the law in October 2025. [cite:ad15_rin_nylaw]

Junk fees

Some pricing power works through how a price is shown rather than its level: a low headline price followed by mandatory fees at checkout. The FTC's rule on unfair or deceptive fees, finalised in December 2024 and in force since 12 May 2025, requires sellers of live-event tickets and short-term lodging, including resale and booking platforms, to show the total price up front. [cite:ad15_tc_junkfee] Fees on bank accounts, cards and other services are measured in Part Eleven. [scene:ad11_fees_everywhere|Part Eleven]

Built to be replaced, and the right to repair

Planned obsolescence, the practice of designing products to wear out or become unusable sooner than they need to, is often alleged and rarely documented. The best-known documented case involved Apple. A January 2017 software update slowed iPhones with ageing batteries, which Apple did not disclose until December 2017. In 2020 Apple agreed to pay up to $500 million, at least $25 for each affected iPhone 6, 6s, 7 and SE, to settle the resulting class action, without admitting wrongdoing and, by its account, to avoid the cost of litigation. [cite:ad15_9to5_apple] Repair restrictions are more common than proven obsolescence: manufacturers that limit access to parts, tools and manuals can steer repairs to their own service or toward replacement. In May 2021 the FTC, in a unanimous report requested by Congress, found "scant evidence to support manufacturers' justifications for repair restrictions", including claims about safety and data security. [cite:ad15_ftc_nixing]

Where it works as promised

On repair, the counter-evidence is legislation. New York's law took effect on 28 December 2023, California's and Minnesota's on 1 July 2024 and Colorado's on 1 January 2026, and Oregon has enacted its own. Each requires makers of consumer electronics to offer parts, tools and documentation to owners and independent shops on fair and reasonable terms; California requires parts at the same price and terms offered to authorised repairers, and Oregon and Colorado restrict "parts pairing", the use of software to reject replacement parts not approved by the maker. [cite:ad15_wiley_r2r] The broader record is mixed in the same way. Antitrust enforcement produced the RealPage settlement; New York's disclosure law survived its first court test; Instacart ended its price tests within days of publication; and on markups, the leading estimate finds the rise concentrated in a minority of firms while the median firm's markup did not change. [cite:ad6_wsoc_realpage] [cite:ad15_rin_nylaw] [cite:ad15_cr_instacart] [cite:ad15_qje_markups] [cite:us11_itif_kennedy] What the record does not support is the assumption that competition alone keeps every price close to cost: in each of these recent cases, the check came from a regulator, a court, a state legislature or a published investigation.

chapters.label: Part Sixteen
chapters.title: Why the Belief Survives
chapters.intro: Part Sixteen asks why the promise keeps its hold. It begins with what Americans now say about the Dream, using polls that have asked the same questions over years, and sets their beliefs about mobility beside the measured rates, with the studies that find people overestimate how often the poor rise and the one that finds the opposite. It then examines the habits of mind that lead people to read the outcome of a structure as a verdict on character, from belief in a just world to meritocracy and the survivorship bias of success stories, with the evidence against each. The second section sets the phrases both parties have used for the Dream, from "bootstraps" and "job creators" to "ownership society," "you didn't build that" and "make America great again," beside what each administration's enacted laws did to the mechanisms traced in earlier parts. The last section turns to the record in the body: the rise in deaths from drugs, alcohol and suicide among Americans without a degree, the dispute over its cause, the fall in overdose deaths since 2023, and the gap in life expectancy between rich and poor.
chapters.outro: Part Sixteen established that belief in the Dream has fallen but not collapsed. About a third of Americans told pollsters in 2025 and 2026 that the Dream still holds, against 53 per cent in 2012 on a different wording, and satisfaction with the chance to get ahead by working hard fell from 77 per cent in 2002 to 52 per cent in 2026, with a record partisan gap; yet two-thirds still say they have achieved the Dream or are on their way. [cite:ad1_wsjnorc25] [cite:ad16_colpol_apnorc] [cite:ad16_gallup_opp24] [cite:ad16_brookings_opp26] [cite:ad16_pew_top24] Americans overestimate how often a child from the bottom fifth reaches the top, 11.7 in 100 against 7.8, though one study found underestimation; meritocratic explanations grow with inequality, while the claim that the disadvantaged defend the system most did not survive a large-scale test. [cite:ad16_ast_aer] [cite:ad16_jr_chambers] [cite:ad16_mijs] [cite:ad16_forrt_brandt] Both parties have sold the same Dream in different phrases, and each has enacted laws that narrowed some of its mechanisms and widened others: cash aid reached 21 of every 100 poor families in 2023 against 68 in 1996, the uninsured rate halved after 2010, and the 2025 law lowers resources at the bottom and raises them at the top. [cite:ad16_cbpp_tanf] [cite:us16_khn_uninsured] [cite:ad11_cbo_pl11921] In the body, the richest men outlive the poorest by 14.6 years, midlife deaths without a degree rose from 1999, and overdose deaths, after a peak of 107,941 in 2022, fell to about 70,000 in 2025 on provisional counts, a decline that weighs against reading them as a simple gauge of the Dream. [cite:ad16_jama_chetty] [cite:ad16_princeton_cd] [cite:ad16_db522] [cite:ad16_nchs_2025] These figures stand as of October 2026. Part Seventeen follows the mechanisms of the whole book through the budgets of particular families. [scene:ad17_three_families|Part Seventeen: Families Through the Machine]
