sections.h: What Americans Believe, and What the Data Show
sections.html:
Fifteen parts of this book have set the promise beside the record, mechanism by mechanism. This part asks a different question: why the promise keeps its hold on people whose own lives, in many of the ways measured so far, do not match it. The answer has three parts. Belief in the Dream has in fact fallen, and fallen far, in the polls. What remains of it leans on beliefs about mobility that the data do not support, or support only for some groups. And there is a well-studied set of habits of mind that lead people to read the outcome of a structure as a verdict on someone's character.

How much belief is left

The question "does the American Dream still hold true?" has been asked often enough to show a direction, though not by one pollster with one wording. In 2012 the Public Religion Research Institute found 53 per cent of Americans saying the Dream still held; by 2014 it found 42 per cent. [cite:ad16_colpol_apnorc] The Wall Street Journal and NORC, the research centre at the University of Chicago, asked whether the Dream "still holds true," "once held true but not anymore" or "never held true." In 2023, 36 per cent chose the first answer, 45 per cent the second and 18 per cent the third. [cite:ad16_axios_wsj23] In July 2025 the same poll found 31 per cent, 46 per cent and 23 per cent; only a quarter said they had a good chance of improving their own standard of living, the lowest since the question was first asked in 1987, and 78 per cent were not confident that their children's generation would be better off. [cite:ad1_wsjnorc25] In April 2026 the AP-NORC poll, with a margin of error of 2.6 points, found 34 per cent saying the Dream (defined as "if you work hard, you'll get ahead") still holds and half saying it once did. [cite:ad1_apnorc26] [cite:ad16_colpol_apnorc] The wording differs across these polls, so the drop from 53 to about a third is a direction, not a precise measure. The direction is the same in every series.

A longer series with a single wording comes from Gallup, which every January asks whether Americans are satisfied with "the opportunity for a person in this nation to get ahead by working hard." Satisfaction stood at 76 per cent in 2001 and 77 per cent in 2002, fell to 53 per cent in 2012 after the financial crisis, recovered to 72 per cent in January 2020, and dropped to 56 per cent in 2024. [cite:ad16_gallup_opp24] In 2026 it was 52 per cent, with Republicans at 85 per cent and Democrats at 24 per cent, a 61-point gap, the widest Gallup has recorded on the question. [cite:ad16_brookings_opp26] A partisan gap that wide shows the answer measures mood about the country as much as any household's own experience.

When people are asked about their own lives the picture is less bleak. Pew Research Center asked the same question in December 2022 and April 2024: had respondents "achieved the American Dream," were they "on your way," or was it "out of reach for you"? The answers barely moved: 30, 37 and 31 per cent in 2022; 31, 36 and 30 per cent in 2024. [cite:ad16_pew_top24] Two-thirds, in other words, still placed themselves inside the Dream or on the road to it. In the 2024 survey, 64 per cent of upper-income adults said the Dream was still possible against 39 per cent of lower-income adults, a 25-point gap. Fifteen per cent of Black adults and 19 per cent of Hispanic adults said they had already achieved it, against 39 per cent of white adults, but 48 and 47 per cent said they were on their way. [cite:ad16_pew_2024] Those gaps follow the gaps in income and wealth documented in [scene:ad12_wealth_gap|Part Twelve] and [scene:ad13_black_americans|Part Thirteen]; they are not traits of any group.

What people believe about mobility

The Dream as taught is a claim about mobility: that a child born poor can, with effort, rise. [scene:ad3_absolute_mobility|Part Three] measured it. Economists distinguish absolute mobility, whether children earn more than their parents did at the same age, from relative mobility, whether children move up the ranking. The relative measure is usually stated with quintiles: the population is split into five equal groups by income, and the question is how often a child born in the bottom fifth reaches the top fifth.

The economists Alberto Alesina, Stefanie Stantcheva and Edoardo Teso asked about 4,700 Americans, and about 7,900 people in Britain, France, Italy and Sweden, to estimate exactly that. Americans guessed that 11.7 in 100 children from the bottom fifth would reach the top fifth; the benchmark the authors used was 7.8. That is an overestimate by half (11.7 ÷ 7.8 = 1.5). Their guess of how many stay at the bottom, 32.2, was close to the actual 33.1. Europeans erred the other way, underestimating the chance of rising and overestimating the chance of being stuck. [cite:ad16_ast_aer] When the researchers showed respondents pessimistic information about mobility, both left- and right-leaning Americans became more pessimistic, but only those on the left became more supportive of policies aimed at equal opportunity; those on the right changed none of their policy views. [cite:ad16_richmond_ast]

Psychologists have found the same overestimate with other methods. Michael Kraus and Jacinth Tan reported in 2015 that Americans substantially overestimated both education and income mobility; a pre-registered replication by Kraus with 763 adults found the effect again, larger when people judged mobility for "people like me," and larger among those who saw themselves as higher in social class and among conservatives. [cite:ad16_kraus_frontiers] Shai Davidai and Thomas Gilovich, surveying more than 3,000 adults, found that Americans overestimate upward mobility and underestimate downward mobility, and that poorer respondents and conservatives believed in more mobility than richer ones and liberals. [cite:ad16_cornell_dg]

The finding is not unanimous, and the dissent matters. Alexander Chambers, Lawton Swan and Martin Heesacker asked 410 adults to estimate movement between quintiles and found that they underestimated mobility; 56 per cent said it had declined over forty years, when relative mobility had in fact stayed roughly stable, and only 15 per cent answered correctly. Liberals underestimated most. [cite:ad16_jr_chambers] The difference lies partly in what is asked. Relative mobility has held steady for decades; absolute mobility, the share of children out-earning their parents, fell from about nine in ten for children born in 1940 to about half for children born in the 1980s. [cite:ad2_chetty_trends] [cite:ad2_chetty_fading] A respondent who says mobility has fallen is wrong about ranks and right about living standards. What the studies agree on is that most people's picture of mobility is inaccurate, and that the direction of the error follows politics.

Why structure gets read as character

Several lines of research try to explain why people, including people the system has not served well, keep a picture of it as fair. The oldest is the "just-world" idea, from the social psychologist Melvin Lerner: people want to believe that others get what they deserve, because the alternative, a world in which effort and outcome come apart, is frightening. The economists Roland Bénabou and Jean Tirole built that idea into a formal model in 2006. People, they argued, are motivated to believe that effort is rewarded, partly because the belief itself keeps them working; societies can settle into an "American" pattern, with widespread just-world belief and modest redistribution, or a "European" one, with more pessimism about effort and a larger welfare state. [cite:ad16_bt_nber] In their account the belief is not simply false consciousness: it changes how hard people work, and therefore what they earn.

System-justification theory, developed by John Jost and colleagues from 1994, goes further. It holds that people are motivated to defend the social arrangements they live under, and its strongest form predicted that the disadvantaged would sometimes defend those arrangements more than the advantaged, because "those who suffer the most also have the most to explain, justify, and rationalize." In one 2003 study, lower-income respondents were more likely than higher-income ones to say large income differences were needed to make people work hard. [cite:ad16_caricati] That strong form has not held up. Mark Brandt's 2013 test, using large surveys in the United States and many other countries, found no support for it: people of higher status defended the system as much as, or more than, people of lower status. [cite:ad16_forrt_brandt] [cite:ad16_caricati] The weaker claim, that people in general lean toward seeing their system as legitimate, survives; the claim that the poor are its most loyal defenders does not.

A third line concerns meritocracy, the belief that rewards follow talent and effort. The sociologist Jonathan Mijs, using about 25 years of International Social Survey Programme data, found that "the more unequal a society, the more likely its citizens are to explain success in meritocratic terms," and that they give less weight to family wealth and connections. [cite:ad16_mijs] The philosopher Michael Sandel argued in The Tyranny of Merit (2020) that politicians of both parties promised that a college degree would secure success, and that the creed "leads to hubris among the winners and humiliation for those who lose out." He pointed to selective colleges, where about 70 per cent of students come from wealthy families and about 3 per cent from the bottom fifth. [cite:ad16_duke_sandel] [scene:ad7_college_cost_pell|Part Seven] showed how college became the main ladder and its price; Sandel's point is about what happens to the people for whom it was not.

The last mechanism is the simplest. Success stories are told by those who succeeded. Of every 100 private business establishments opened in March 2013, about 80 were still operating a year later, about 51 after five years and about 35 after ten; 65 had closed. [cite:ad16_bls_survival] The founders who are interviewed, profiled and quoted come from the 35, and the lesson drawn from their stories (persistence pays) is drawn from a sample with the failures removed. This is survivorship bias: a conclusion that looks like a law because the counter-examples are no longer visible.

Where the belief is right

None of this means the belief is simply an error. Effort does change outcomes: [scene:ad2_what_holds|Part Two] documented that a full-time, year-round worker had an official poverty rate of 1.6 per cent, that the children of immigrants have climbed faster than the children of the American-born for more than a century, and that Hispanic Americans move up strongly across generations. [cite:us18_crs_pov2025] [cite:ad2_abramitzky_aer] [cite:ad2_oi_race_hisp] The 35 businesses that survived ten years are real, and their owners mostly did work hard. Bénabou and Tirole's model, and the evidence behind it, suggest that belief in reward for effort is partly self-fulfilling: people who hold it work more. [cite:ad16_bt_nber] The case against the belief is narrower than "the Dream is a lie." It is that the belief overstates how often effort alone moves a person from the bottom to the top, and that this overstatement makes the structures documented in earlier parts harder to see.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

Interpretation, not finding: the belief as the system's working part

The Sophia platform reads the persistence of the belief as the central mechanism of the Dream itself: a story told so that people keep working inside a system that takes more from them than it returns, and blame themselves rather than the design when it does not pay. In this reading the overestimate of mobility, the meritocratic explanation of inequality and survivorship bias are not separate quirks but one function. The strongest counter-readings are three. First, Brandt's finding that the disadvantaged do not defend the system more than others cuts against the idea that belief is installed in those it harms; belief is highest among those it has served. Second, belief has fallen sharply over two decades, after the financial crisis and again since 2020, which suggests people revise it in light of experience rather than hold it fixed. Third, a belief that raises effort can raise incomes, as Bénabou and Tirole argue, so its effects are not only extractive. [cite:ad16_forrt_brandt] [cite:ad16_gallup_opp24] [cite:ad16_bt_nber]

sections.h: Both Parties' Dream: The Words and the Laws
sections.html:
[scene:ad1_who_sells_it|Part One] showed that presidents of both parties promise the same Dream: a job that pays enough, a home, savings, a secure old age and children who do better. This section looks at the phrases each party has used to carry that promise, sets them side by side in the same register, and then asks what each party's enacted laws did to the mechanisms traced in Parts Four to Fifteen. The aim is not to score the parties against each other. It is to show that the rhetoric is shared, that the record of each party includes changes that strengthened some mechanisms of the Dream and weakened others, and that the gap between word and law is not the property of one side.

A phrase that began as a joke

The most durable figure of self-made success began as its opposite. The earliest uses of lifting oneself "by the straps of his boots," found in an 1834 Chicago newspaper and in print through the 1860s, mocked people who claimed to do the impossible, such as a man selling a perpetual-motion machine. The newer sense, of rising by one's own effort, is first recorded by the Oxford English Dictionary in James Joyce's Ulysses (1922), and became standard in the twentieth century. [cite:ad16_curzan_boot] The shift matters for this book's subject: a phrase that once named a physical impossibility now names the core of the taught Dream.

The phrases, both parties

Ronald Reagan accepted the Republican nomination in Detroit on 17 July 1980 by inviting voters into "a great national crusade to make America great again." [cite:ad16_reagan_1980] Donald Trump used the same words to close his announcement on 16 June 2015, after declaring "Sadly, the American dream is dead." [cite:ad16_trump_maga] [cite:ad1_trump_2015] George W. Bush, accepting renomination in New York on 2 September 2004, promised to "build an ownership society, because ownership brings security, and dignity, and independence," in which "more people will own their health care plans" and own "a piece of their retirement." [cite:ad16_bush_2004] Speaker John Boehner, arguing against tax increases in September 2011, said "Job creators in America are essentially on strike." [cite:ad16_abc_boehner]

On the Democratic side, Bill Clinton signed the welfare law on 22 August 1996 saying "Today we are ending welfare as we know it," so that welfare would be "a second chance, not a way of life." [cite:ad16_clinton_1996] Barack Obama, campaigning in Roanoke, Virginia, on 13 July 2012, told business owners "If you were successful, somebody along the line gave you some help," and continued: "Somebody invested in roads and bridges. If you've got a business, you didn't build that. Somebody else made that happen." [cite:ad16_obama_roanoke] Opponents quoted "you didn't build that" on its own, and the fuller passage is given here so that readers can judge what "that" refers to, as each phrase in this section is given with its occasion. Obama's 2014 State of the Union proposed to "build new ladders of opportunity into the middle class." [cite:ad1_obama_2014]

The DREAM Act took the Dream's name for a bill offering legal status to people brought to the United States as children who completed college or military service. The House passed it 216 to 198 in December 2010; on 18 December 2010 the Senate fell five votes short of the 60 needed to end debate, 55 to 41, with 36 Republicans and five Democrats voting no. [cite:ad16_mpi_dream] The Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals policy (DACA), created later by executive action, covered many of the same people with temporary protection and work permits. In January 2025 the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals held DACA unlawful but limited the effect to Texas, leaving the programme "largely intact" for about half a million recipients. [cite:ad16_abc17_daca] As of late April 2026, renewals were accepted nationwide, new applications were accepted but not processed, and recipients in Texas kept protection from deportation while awaiting a district court order on when their work permits end. [cite:ad16_fwd_daca] Status as of October 2026: Judge Andrew Hanen of the federal district court in Texas had still not issued that order (none had been issued as of 1 July 2026, and none was reported by early October), so Texas recipients' work permits remained valid; the Justice Department had proposed in September 2025 that they end; new applications were still accepted but not processed, and renewals were processed slowly, with about 125,000 pending, a record. No law has replaced the DREAM Act. [cite:ad16_audit_daca_forum]

Read together, the phrases divide the Dream's work between the individual and the public. "Bootstraps," "job creators" and "ownership society" place the engine in the person or the firm; "you didn't build that" and "ladders of opportunity" place part of it in shared investment. Both sets of phrases promise the same outcome, and each states a theory of how to reach it. The record shows how each theory fared when enacted.

What the laws did

The test of a promise is the law that follows it. Taking each administration since 1978 in turn, in the same register, the record of the mechanisms covered earlier in this book is mixed for both parties.

Under Jimmy Carter, a Democrat, the Revenue Act of 1978 added section 401(k) to the tax code; it was "never intended (nor designed)" to replace pensions, but private workers moved from guaranteed pensions to individual accounts over the following four decades, shifting investment and longevity risk onto the worker. [cite:ad10_napa_1978] [cite:ad10_dol_hist] Under Ronald Reagan, a Republican, the firing of more than 11,000 striking air-traffic controllers in August 1981, under a 1978 law barring federal strikes, marked the start of a long fall in large strikes; private-sector union membership fell from 16.8 per cent in 1983 to 5.9 per cent in 2025. [cite:ad4_reagan_patco] [cite:ad4_bls_spotlight2016] [cite:us13_bls_union2025]

Under Bill Clinton, the 1996 welfare law replaced open-ended cash aid with Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), a fixed block grant to states with time limits and work requirements. Its defenders point to the results: adult recipients fell from 4.38 million in 1995 to 570,000 in 2024, and work among the most disadvantaged mothers rose by almost 40 per cent in the four years from 1996, in a strong economy and alongside an expanded Earned Income Tax Credit. [cite:ad16_aei_welfare] Its critics point to reach: for every 100 families in poverty, 68 received cash aid in 1996 and 21 in 2023. [cite:ad16_cbpp_tanf] Both figures are accurate; they measure different things, and which matters more is a judgement the record cannot make. The Higher Education Amendments of 1998, also signed by Clinton, removed the last time-based route for discharging federal student loans in bankruptcy. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699]

Under George W. Bush, during the homeownership push documented in [scene:ad1_who_sells_it|Part One], the ownership rate reached its peak of 69.4 per cent (second quarter of 2004, seasonally adjusted); it fell back to 63.1 per cent by 2016, below its 1994 level. [cite:ad1_fred_hor] The record shows the timing, not how much of the rise the push itself produced. The 2005 bankruptcy law extended the bar on discharge to private student loans. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] The last increase in the federal minimum wage took effect in three steps from July 2007 to July 2009, reaching $7.25, where it has stayed through Congresses controlled by each party in turn. [cite:us13_dol_minwage]

Under Barack Obama, the Affordable Care Act of 2010 helped take the uninsured rate from nearly 17 per cent in 2009 to 8.8 per cent in 2016. [cite:us16_khn_uninsured] The DREAM Act failed in the Senate, as above. Under Joe Biden, the 2021 American Rescue Plan temporarily enlarged the child tax credit, from $2,000 to $3,000 per child ($3,600 under age six); child poverty on the Census Bureau's supplemental measure was 5.2 per cent in 2021 and rose to 12.4 per cent in 2022 after the expansion expired without renewal. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] Several rules aimed at other mechanisms in this book were set aside before they took full effect: the 2024 overtime salary threshold was vacated by a federal court in November 2024, the federal rule keeping medical debt off credit reports was vacated in July 2025, and the SAVE student-loan repayment plan was ended through a settlement announced in December 2025. [cite:ad5_hunton_ot2024] [cite:ad8_ap_vacatur] [cite:ad7_npr_save]

Under Donald Trump, the 2017 tax law doubled the maximum child tax credit, to $2,000, and the 2025 law raised it permanently to $2,200 per child, indexed to inflation, though families with very low earnings receive only part of it or none. [cite:ad16_audit_crs_ctc] The 2017 law also doubled the estate-tax exemption, and the 2025 reconciliation law set it at $15 million from 2026, indexed to inflation. [cite:ad12_crs_estate] The Congressional Budget Office found that the 2025 law lowers resources for households toward the bottom of the income distribution and raises them for the middle and top, with in-kind benefits, mainly Medicaid and food aid, cut by about $900 billion over 2026 to 2034, and that it will add about 10 million people to the uninsured by 2034. [cite:ad11_cbo_pl11921] [cite:us16_kff_obbba] In September 2025 the Federal Trade Commission dropped its appeals in defence of the nationwide ban on non-compete clauses. [cite:ad5_ftc_accede]

Where the words and the laws agreed

The record is not only one of gaps. Clinton's 1993 promise that a full-time worker with a child would not be poor was backed by an expansion of the Earned Income Tax Credit, and by 2025 the official poverty rate among full-time, year-round workers was 1.6 per cent. [cite:ad1_clinton_1993] [cite:us18_crs_pov2025] The Affordable Care Act did what its sponsors said it would do to the uninsured rate. Social Security, expanded under presidents of both parties, moved 28.8 million people out of poverty in 2025, and old-age poverty fell from 35.2 per cent in 1959 to 9.9 per cent in 2024. [cite:us18_census_p60290] [cite:ad10_census_a3] These are cases in which a promise was matched by a mechanism built to keep it, which is the standard the rest of the record can be held to.

What the side-by-side reading shows is that the rhetoric of the Dream is bipartisan and the enacted record is bipartisan too. Each party has passed laws that narrowed a mechanism of the Dream (pensions, bargaining power, bankruptcy relief, the reach of cash aid, health coverage) and laws that widened one. Neither party has raised the federal minimum wage since 2009. A reader who concludes that one party alone keeps or breaks the promise will find counter-examples in the record of each. Motive is a separate question: the record shows what each law did, not why each legislator voted for it, and the reasons stated at the time are given above in the speakers' own words.

sections.h: Despair: When the Promise Fails in the Body
sections.html:
A promise that fails can be measured in wages, debts and homes, as the earlier parts of this book have done. It can also be measured in deaths. In 2015 the economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton reported that death rates among middle-aged white Americans, which had been falling for decades, had turned upward, driven by drug and alcohol poisonings, suicide and liver disease. They later called these "deaths of despair" and tied them to the collapse of a way of life for Americans without a four-year degree. Their account became one of the most cited explanations of why the Dream's failure matters. It is also contested, and the overdose record since 2023 has moved in a direction their account did not predict. This section sets out the finding, the dispute and the latest data, and then turns to a related measure that is not disputed: how long Americans live depends strongly on how much they earn.

The original finding

Case and Deaton's paper, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in November 2015, studied white non-Hispanic Americans aged 45 to 54. Their death rate had fallen by about 2 per cent a year from 1978 to 1998. After 1998 it rose by about half a per cent a year, through 2013. Had the 1998 rate simply held, about 96,000 deaths would have been avoided between 1998 and 2013; had the earlier decline continued, about 488,500 would have been avoided between 1999 and 2013, a toll the authors compared to the AIDS epidemic. [cite:ad16_princeton_cd] The rise was concentrated among those with a high-school education or less, whose all-cause death rate rose 22 per cent; deaths from drug and alcohol poisoning in that group roughly quadrupled and suicides rose 81 per cent. For college graduates, death rates fell. Over the same years midlife death rates kept falling in France, Germany, Britain and Sweden, and among Black and Hispanic Americans in the United States. [cite:ad16_princeton_cd] The paper itself said the data could not establish a cause, and named the spread of opioids and economic insecurity as candidates.

The age-adjusted rate used here and below is a death rate per 100,000 people recalculated as if each year's population had the same age structure, so that years can be compared without an ageing population distorting the trend.

In their 2020 book, Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism, Case and Deaton widened the claim. They estimated that about 600,000 midlife deaths would have been avoided had the pre-1999 decline continued, and pointed to causes inside the system this book has traced: a job market that no longer offered a secure career to workers without a degree, the cost of employer health insurance pressing on wages, and the pricing power of drug makers. [cite:ad16_cato_cd2020] They reported that in 2017, 84 per cent of Americans aged 25 to 64 with a bachelor's degree were employed against 68 per cent of those with only a high-school diploma, and that wages for white men without a degree fell 13 per cent from 1979 to 2017. [cite:ad16_cato_cd2020] [scene:ad4_wage_split|Part Four] and [scene:ad8_costs_and_coverage|Part Eight] document those two mechanisms in detail.

The critics

The strongest challenge came from the economist Christopher Ruhm. Using county data from 1999 to 2015, he found that counties with worse economic decline did see faster growth in drug deaths, but that the link was weak and mostly explained by other factors; in his preferred estimates, changes in economic conditions explain "less than one-tenth of the rise in drug and opioid-involved mortality rates." [cite:ad16_ruhm] He concluded that the epidemic was better described as a drug problem, driven by the availability and price of opioids, than as a despair problem, and that improving the economy, though worthwhile for other reasons, was unlikely to cut overdose deaths much.

A second criticism concerns the wage evidence. The economist David Henderson, reviewing the 2020 book for the Cato Institute's Regulation, argued that measuring with a price index that rises more slowly (the personal consumption expenditures index rather than the consumer price index) turns the 13 per cent fall in non-college white men's wages into a 4.5 per cent rise from 1979 to 2017. [cite:ad16_cato_cd2020] That is the same measurement dispute set out in [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two] and [scene:ad4_wage_split|Part Four]: the choice of price index changes the direction of the wage record for some groups, though not the gap between those with and without a degree.

The overdose record, including the decline

Drug overdoses are the largest of the three causes, and the national count is the clearest series. Deaths from overdose rose from 25,785 in 2003 to 70,237 in 2017, jumped during the pandemic to 91,799 in 2020 and 106,699 in 2021, and peaked at 107,941 in 2022, an age-adjusted rate of 32.6 per 100,000, against 8.9 in 2003. In 2023 they fell slightly, to 105,007. [cite:ad16_db522] Provisional counts, which the National Center for Health Statistics revises as death records are completed, show the fall accelerating: an estimated 81,313 deaths in 2024 and 69,973 in 2025, a drop of almost 14 per cent in a year and the third annual decline in a row; deaths involving opioids fell from 55,296 to 44,564. [cite:ad16_nchs_2025] On these provisional figures, 2025 deaths were about 35 per cent below the 2022 peak (69,973 ÷ 107,941 = 0.65), though still more than two and a half times the 2003 count.

The decline is counter-evidence to any reading in which overdose deaths simply track the state of the Dream. Between 2022 and 2025 the federal minimum wage did not change, house prices relative to income stayed near their highs, and belief in the Dream fell further. [cite:us13_dol_minwage] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [cite:ad1_wsjnorc25] Overdose deaths still fell by a third. That pattern fits Ruhm's emphasis on the drug supply better than an account in which economic despair is the main driver. It does not refute Case and Deaton's finding about the education gap in midlife mortality, which concerns a longer period and more causes than overdoses alone. Suicide, the second cause, has not fallen in the same way: there were 48,824 suicides in 2024, an age-adjusted rate of 13.7 per 100,000, the tenth leading cause of death. [cite:us16_cdc_db548]

Income and the length of a life

Whatever the cause of deaths of despair, the link between income and longevity is not in dispute. Raj Chetty and colleagues matched tax records to death records for 2001 to 2014 and found that at age 40 the richest 1 per cent of men could expect to live 14.6 years longer than the poorest 1 per cent; for women the gap was 10.1 years. [cite:ad16_jama_chetty] The gap widened over the period: life expectancy rose by 2.34 years for men and 2.91 years for women in the top 5 per cent of incomes, and by 0.32 and 0.04 years in the bottom 5 per cent. [cite:ad16_jama_chetty] Place mattered: among the poorest quarter, life expectancy differed by about 4.5 years between the best and worst areas, and in some areas rose by more than four years while in others it fell by more than two.

What explained those differences between places is itself a finding that cuts against easy readings. Life expectancy for low-income people tracked health behaviours, smoking above all, and was higher in places with more immigrants, more college graduates and more local government spending. It was not significantly correlated with access to medical care, income inequality or local labour-market conditions. [cite:ad16_jama_chetty] The poor live shorter lives everywhere, but how much shorter depends on where they live and how people there live, more than on the local level of inequality.

The same gradient appears in how people feel. In January 2025, 38 per cent of adults in households earning under $40,000 said they were very satisfied with their personal lives, against 55 per cent of those earning $100,000 or more. [cite:us22_gallup_pl25] National life expectancy, 79.0 years in 2024, was the highest on record, up from 78.4 in 2023, which shows that the overall trend has recovered even as the gaps by income remain. [cite:us16_cdc_db548]

What this adds to the account

The despair record supports a narrower conclusion than either its advocates or its critics sometimes draw. It is documented that for Americans without a degree, middle age became more deadly from 1999 and that the gap with graduates widened; it is documented that the poorest live ten to fifteen years less than the richest and that the gap grew. What is contested is how much of the rise in deaths came from the failing economic promise rather than from a flood of cheap, potent opioids, and the decline in overdoses since 2023, with the economy's mechanisms unchanged, weighs on the side of the drug supply. The finding that bears most directly on this book is the education divide: the credential that [scene:ad7_college_cost_pell|Part Seven] showed to be the main ladder of the Dream also marks, in the vital statistics, the line between a lengthening life and a stalled one. Part Seventeen follows the mechanisms of the whole book through the budgets of particular kinds of family. [scene:ad17_three_families|Part Seventeen]

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

chapters.label: Part Seventeen
chapters.title: Families Through the Machine
chapters.intro: Part Seventeen brings the mechanisms of the whole book down to the scale of a household. Its first section runs the published budgets of the average household in four fifths of the American income ladder, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Expenditure Survey for 2024, through taxes, housing, transport, health care and debt, shows with the arithmetic what is left over at each level, and tests what one medical bill, job loss or rent increase would do to that margin. Its second section follows the taught life script from childcare to Social Security, giving the documented typical figure at each stage, from school funding and college debt to the first paycheck, the first rent or mortgage, the 401(k) and the retirement benefit, and pointing to the part of the book that explains the mechanism behind each number. No invented families appear in either section; every figure comes from a named survey or administrative source.
chapters.outro: Part Seventeen established that the machine described in the earlier parts leaves very different margins at different rungs. The middle fifth's average household took in $74,474 in 2024 and, after an estimated $9,412 in income and payroll taxes and $60,652 in spending, kept about $4,410, roughly 5.9 cents per dollar, of which about $2,900 was free for loan principal and emergencies; the fourth fifth kept about $22,288, or 18.3 per cent, and the two lower fifths reported spending more than their income in every year from 2020 to 2024. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:us22_fred_incafttxlb0104m] [cite:ad17_fred_q1exp] [cite:ad17_fred_q2exp] One average deductible of $1,955 takes 44 per cent of the middle margin and a Marketplace out-of-pocket maximum of $10,600 equals 2.4 years of it, at a time when 63 per cent of adults would cover a $400 emergency with cash. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] [cite:ad17_hcgov_oop] [cite:ad9_shed2025] Along the life script, childcare costs $6,552 to $15,600 a year, school budgets range from $11,060 to $31,918 per pupil by state, a median new home at October 2026 rates takes 35.1 per cent of median household income in principal and interest, and only 35.2 per cent of householders under 35 own; Social Security, the degree premium and the record median income of $87,460 in 2025 are the stages where the script holds. [cite:us18_dol_childcare] [cite:us17_census_fy2024] [cite:ad17_fred_mspus] [cite:ad6_pmms] [cite:ad17_census_hvs_q226] [cite:ad10_census_a3] [cite:ad7_cew_payoff] [cite:us14_census_p60] These figures stand as of October 2026. Part Eighteen gathers every mechanism into one ledger and delivers the verdict. [scene:ad18_told_vs_record|Part Eighteen: The Verdict]

sections.h: Three Families: What Comes In, What Goes Out
sections.html:
Every earlier part of this book followed one mechanism at a time: the wage, the mortgage, the premium, the loan, the tax. A household meets all of them at once, in one budget. This section runs real budgets through those mechanisms. They are not invented people. They are the average households in four fifths of the income ladder, as recorded by the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Expenditure Survey for 2024, the government's own survey of what American households earn and spend, grouped here as three families: the middle fifth, the fourth fifth (the upper-middle) and, below them, the two lower fifths taken together. For each it asks what comes in, what taxes and essentials take, what is left, and what one ordinary shock would do to what is left. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:ad17_bls_cesan24] The same budgets appeared once before in this library, set beside Israel's; here they stay on the American side and go further into each line. [scene:us22_families|Three Families (US System vs Israel System)]

Where the figures come from

The survey counts "consumer units": a family, a person living alone and paying their own way, or people sharing major expenses. It sorts them by income before taxes and splits them into five equal groups of about 27 million units each; in 2024 the middle fifth ran from $57,452 to $94,511 and the fourth fifth from $94,512 to $155,925. [cite:ad17_bls_cesan24] [cite:ad17_bls_gloss] The figures are averages (means) within each fifth, not medians, so a few large incomes pull them up; [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two] explains the difference. Income before taxes includes wages, self-employment income, Social Security and pensions, interest, rent, unemployment benefits and public assistance. [cite:ad17_bls_cesan24]

Three definitions matter for reading what follows. First, spending includes the sales and excise taxes paid at the till, and a homeowner's housing cost includes mortgage interest, property tax and insurance, but not repayments of the mortgage itself: the survey's glossary says principal "is not included in homeowner costs but is repayment of a loan". Repayments on goods already bought on credit are excluded in the same way. [cite:ad17_bls_gloss] So whatever a family has "left over" in this survey must still cover the principal on its mortgage and its other loans. Second, a line called "personal insurance and pensions" holds the worker's Social Security deductions and contributions to retirement plans; this section counts the Social Security part as a tax and the rest as part of what is left over, because it is saving. [cite:ad17_bls_cesan24] Third, the Bureau did not publish income taxes for 2024, because the outside tax model it uses was not updated. [cite:ad17_bls_cesan24] The income tax below is therefore estimated by applying each fifth's 2023 ratio of income tax to income (6.3 per cent for the middle fifth, 10.4 per cent for the fourth), and the payroll tax is computed at the legal 7.65 per cent of wages and 15.3 per cent of self-employment income. [cite:us22_fred_incafttxlb0104m] [cite:us22_fred_incafttxlb0105m]

The middle family

The middle fifth's average household has 2.5 people and 1.4 earners, and took in $74,474 before tax in 2024, $55,348 of it in wages and $3,349 from self-employment. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] The arithmetic of its year runs as follows. Income tax at about 6.3 per cent (6.26 per cent before rounding) is about $4,665; payroll tax is about $4,234 on the wages and $512 on the self-employment income, together $4,747. Taxes and compulsory contributions therefore take about $9,412, or 12.6 per cent. Spending, leaving out the insurance-and-pension line, comes to $60,652, or 81.4 per cent of income. What remains is $74,474 minus $9,412 minus $60,652: about $4,410, or 5.9 cents of every dollar. About $1,500 of that is already committed to private pensions and life insurance, so the money free for mortgage principal, debt repayment, emergencies and anything else is closer to $2,900 a year, about $240 a month. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:us22_fred_incafttxlb0104m]

Where the middle family's money goes follows the mechanisms of earlier parts. Housing takes 32.4 cents of each dollar, shelter alone ($15,257) 20.5 cents, in a period when home prices had risen from about 3.2 times median household income in the 1990s to 5.0 times in 2024. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:us22_fred_shelterlb0104m] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [scene:ad6_price_and_rent|Part Six] Transport takes 15.7 cents, health care 7.6 cents. The health figure counts only what the household pays; behind it sits the employer's share of the premium, $20,832 of an average $28,303 family policy in 2026, paid out of compensation the worker never sees as wages. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] [scene:ad8_costs_and_coverage|Part Eight]

The taxes the table does not show

The 12.6 per cent above counts only income and payroll taxes. Sales taxes are already inside the spending figures and property taxes inside housing. The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a research group that favours progressive taxation, estimated that in 2024 the middle fifth paid 26.4 per cent of its income in all federal, state and local taxes together, the fourth fifth 27.2 per cent and the lowest fifth 17.1 per cent; counting state and local taxes alone, the lowest fifth paid 11.3 per cent and the top 1 per cent 7.2 per cent, because sales and property taxes take a larger share of small incomes. [cite:ad11_itep_wp2024] [cite:ad11_itep_wp7] The federal side runs the other way. The Congressional Budget Office found that average federal tax rates fell for every income group between 1979 and 2023, most of all for the lowest fifth, whose individual income tax rate was minus 11 per cent in 2023 because refundable credits paid it more than it owed. [cite:ad11_cbo_dist2023] [scene:ad11_who_pays|Part Eleven]

The upper-middle family: where the promise works

The fourth fifth's average household, 2.9 people with 1.8 earners, took in $121,548. Income tax at 10.4 per cent is about $12,661 and payroll tax about $8,561, so taxes take $21,222, or 17.5 per cent; spending outside the insurance-and-pension line is $78,038; about $22,288, or 18.3 per cent, is left, of which about $3,400 goes to private pensions and life insurance. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:us22_fred_incafttxlb0105m] For this family the taught version largely holds. It saves real money every year, and families in the matching income band had a median net worth of $362,500 in 2025, up from $336,100 in 2022 after inflation; 78 per cent of the Federal Reserve's upper-middle income group owned their home. [cite:ad17_scf25_inc] Several mechanisms also tilt its way: the tax exclusion for employer health insurance saves $347 per $1,000 of premium in the 22 per cent bracket against $254 in the 12 per cent bracket, and 90 per cent of workers earning $100,000 to $150,000 take part in their employer's 401(k) where one is offered, against 74 per cent of those earning $30,000 to $50,000. [cite:ad8_tpc_esi] [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] The record therefore does not show a machine that leaves every family with nothing; it shows one in which the margin widens sharply as income rises.

The lower fifths

Below the middle, the survey's budgets cannot be balanced at all. The lowest fifth reported $16,658 of income and $35,046 of spending, 2.1 times as much; the second fifth reported $42,925 and spent $50,054, 1.17 times as much. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:ad17_fred_q2inc] [cite:ad17_fred_q2exp] These are not typical working families: the lowest fifth averages 1.6 people and half an earner, so many of its households have no one in work, and the second fifth's head of household averaged 56 years old; both fifths therefore include many retirees, people living alone and people out of work, whose spending can run on savings or on income the survey does not count. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:ad17_fred_q2age] Spending above income can mean savings being drawn down, help from relatives, borrowing, income in kind or income not fully reported; the survey does not say which, so this book does not compute a "left over" for them. What the figures do show is the weight of essentials: the lowest fifth's housing costs, $14,563, equal 87 per cent of its reported income and its health spending 21 per cent, and the second fifth spends 11.2 per cent of income on health and 19.6 per cent on transport. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:us22_fred_housinglb0102m] [cite:ad17_fred_q2health] [cite:ad17_fred_q2trans] The families in the matching income bands held a median net worth of $14,400 and $77,100 in 2025. [cite:ad17_scf25_inc]

For a lower-income family that works, the federal system adds as well as takes. In 2026 the earned income tax credit pays up to $7,316 to a family with two children, and the child tax credit is $2,200 a child, $1,700 of it refundable; from October 2026 a family of three can receive up to $808 a month in food assistance. [cite:ad11_cftd_rp2532] [cite:ad11_fns_fy27] These supports fall away as earnings rise, which is how a raise can leave a family worse off, the benefits cliff described in [scene:ad11_benefits_cliff|Part Eleven]. [cite:ad11_atl_what]

One shock

A margin of $4,410 a year is the middle family's whole defence against the unexpected. Nationally, 63 per cent of adults said in 2025 that they would cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent, down from 68 per cent in 2021, and 8.6 per cent of families were paying more than 40 per cent of their income in debt payments. [cite:ad9_shed2025] [cite:ad17_scf25_inc] Three ordinary shocks show what the margin can and cannot absorb; each uses a documented national figure and states its assumption.

The same shocks land differently up and down the ladder. The upper-middle family's $22,288 margin absorbs the $10,600 maximum with half the year's savings left. The lower fifths have no margin to absorb anything, which is where the medical debt carried by 41 per cent of adults in 2022, on the broadest definition, and the denials and collections of [scene:ad8_medical_debt|Part Eight] begin. [cite:ad8_kff_debtsurvey] A job loss also costs the family its employer health cover; since the enhanced Marketplace subsidies expired at the end of 2025, a couple just above $84,600 a year can again face the full premium. [cite:ad8_astho_ptc] [cite:ad11_hi_cliff] Unemployment insurance is weakest where it is needed: the OECD's modelled replacement for a worker on the average wage, 38 per cent of net income, is near the bottom of the range of 33 to 60 per cent that the series has shown for the United States since 2001. [cite:us22_oecd_nrr_usa100]

Over five years

The middle family's margin has also moved with prices. Measured simply as income before tax minus the survey's total spending, which already includes Social Security deductions but not income tax, the middle fifth kept 13.2 per cent of income in 2020, when pandemic spending fell, 5.6 per cent in 2022, when prices rose fastest, and 10.2 per cent in 2024. The fourth fifth kept between 24.6 and 26.0 per cent in every year. The second and lowest fifths spent more than their reported income in every year. [cite:ad17_fred_q1inc] [cite:ad17_fred_q1exp] [cite:ad17_fred_q2inc] [cite:ad17_fred_q2exp] [cite:ad17_fred_q3inc] [cite:ad17_fred_q3exp] [cite:ad17_fred_q4inc] [cite:ad17_fred_q4exp]

What the record shows and does not. It shows the budgets of the average household in four fifths of the income ladder, from the government's own survey, with every adjustment stated, and the arithmetic of three documented shocks. It does not show any single family: averages blend owners and renters, the young and the retired, and where spending exceeds income at the bottom, the survey does not separate the possible explanations. The 2024 income taxes are estimates, the net-worth bands match the survey fifths only approximately, and the shocks are illustrations built on national figures, not measurements of what happened to a household. The following section takes the same discipline from a budget to a lifetime. [scene:ad17_a_life_in_numbers|A Life in Numbers]

sections.h: A Life in Numbers: From Childcare to Social Security
sections.html:
The taught version of the Dream is a life script: a good school, college, a steady job with benefits, a first home, a retirement account and Social Security at the end. This section walks that script stage by stage using the documented typical figure at each step, most often the median, the middle value with half above and half below. It follows no real person and invents none. Each stage names the mechanism behind its number and points to the part of this book that explains it. Dollar figures are in the dollars of the year stated unless a source publishes them already adjusted for inflation, in which case its year is given.

Before school: childcare

The first large bill of a working family's life arrives before the child can walk. The Labor Department's National Database of Childcare Prices found that full-day care for one child cost between $6,552 and $15,600 a year across 2,512 counties in 2022, 8.9 to 16 per cent of the county's median family income. [cite:us18_dol_childcare] Set against the middle family of the previous section, the low end of that range is 8.8 per cent of its $74,474 income and the high end 20.9 per cent; five years of care before kindergarten would cost $32,760 to $78,000 in 2022 prices. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] Two incomes have become the norm that pays for it: both parents worked in 66.3 per cent of married-couple families with children in 2025. [cite:ad5_bls_famee2025] Federal childcare subsidies cap what a family pays only by rule, and the rule has moved: a 2024 rule limited subsidised families' copayments to 7 per cent of income, and a rule effective 13 July 2026 removed that federal cap, as of October 2026. [cite:ad5_acf_ccdf2024] [cite:ad5_acf_ccdf2026] [scene:ad5_hours_two_jobs|Part Five]

School: the address decides the budget

Public schools spent an average of $17,619 per pupil in fiscal 2024, but the average hides the spread: $31,918 in New York against $11,060 in Idaho. Local sources supplied 43.2 per cent of school revenue, and property taxes made up 63.3 per cent of that local money, so the value of the homes around a school helps set its budget. [cite:us17_census_fy2024] The Supreme Court declined to treat this as a constitutional problem in San Antonio v. Rodriguez on 21 March 1973, holding by five votes to four that education is not a fundamental right under the federal Constitution. [cite:ad7_edweek_rodriguez] The Education Trust found in 2018 that the highest-poverty districts received about $1,000 less per pupil in state and local money than the lowest-poverty ones, $2,000 less after allowing for the extra cost of teaching poorer children. [cite:ad7_edtrust_2018] The counter-evidence is real: counting federal money, the Urban Institute found that districts attended by poor students received about 2.5 per cent more per pupil than those attended by others in 2013–14, because states and Washington fill part of the local gap. [cite:ad7_chingos_ednext] The money matters either way: a 10 per cent rise in per-pupil spending throughout school was linked to 7.25 per cent higher adult wages, with larger effects for children from low-income families. [cite:ad7_jjp_nber] [scene:ad7_k12_property_tax|Part Seven]

College and the loan

A year at a public four-year college, counting in-state tuition, fees, housing and food, cost $25,850 in 2025–26. Published in-state tuition alone, in 2025 dollars, roughly doubled from $5,940 in 1995–96 to $11,950, but after grants the average net tuition fell to an estimated $2,300, below its 2012–13 peak of $4,450. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] The maximum Pell grant of $7,395 covered 27.2 per cent of the average cost of attendance in 2024–25; in 1975–76 it covered more than three-quarters. [cite:ad7_nasfaa_pell] Of 2023–24 bachelor's graduates, 47 per cent borrowed, with an average debt of $29,560, down from 56 per cent and $35,310 (in 2024 dollars) five years earlier. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] The degree still pays: median lifetime earnings were about $2.8 million for bachelor's holders against $1.6 million for high school graduates. [cite:ad7_cew_payoff] The risk sits with borrowers who do not finish or do not gain. Student debt totalled $1.65 trillion in mid-2026, about 7.7 million borrowers were in default at the start of the year, and the government planned to resume taking up to 15 per cent of a defaulted borrower's disposable pay without a court order in the autumn of 2026, with no start date announced as of October 2026. [cite:ad7_nyfed_pr] [cite:ad7_ci_garnish] [scene:ad7_college_cost_pell|Part Seven] [scene:ad7_student_debt_law|student debt law]

The first job

In the third quarter of 2026 the median full-time wage and salary worker aged 20 to 24 earned $802 a week, about $41,700 a year, and one aged 25 to 34 earned $1,173, about $61,000. Pay peaks in the next decade, at $1,414 a week for ages 35 to 44. [cite:ad17_bls_wkyeng_q3] From the first paycheck the machinery starts. Social Security and Medicare take 7.65 per cent, about $4,670 a year at $61,000; that money buys a future benefit. [cite:ad11_ssa_2026] If the employer offers health cover, as 67 per cent of firms with ten or more workers do, the average single policy cost $9,804 in 2026, of which the worker paid about 18 per cent, roughly $1,760, before an average deductible of $1,955. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] Whether a retirement account starts depends heavily on design: participation was 94 per cent in plans that enrol workers automatically against 64 per cent where workers must sign up, and 72 per cent of private workers had access to any retirement plan in 2026, 52 per cent took part. [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] [cite:ad10_bls_ebs26] [scene:ad5_wages_floors|Part Five]

Rent or own

The median asking rent for a vacant rental unit was $1,531 a month in the second quarter of 2026; to keep it at 30 per cent of gross income, the usual affordability line, a renter needs $61,240 a year, almost exactly the 25-to-34 median. Nearly half of all renter households, 22.7 million, paid more than 30 per cent in 2024, a record, although national rents fell 0.5 per cent in the year to early 2026. [cite:ad17_census_hvs_q226] [cite:ad6_nlihc_son26] Buying became harder over the same years. The national price of a home rose from about 3.2 times median household income in the 1990s to 5.0 times in 2024; the median new home sold for $410,700 in mid-2026, against $165,300 in early 2000. [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [cite:ad17_fred_mspus] At the 30-year mortgage rate of 7.40 per cent recorded in Freddie Mac's weekly survey on 15 October 2026, unchanged from the week before and up from 6.27 per cent a year earlier, a buyer putting 10 per cent down on that median new home would borrow $369,630 and pay about $2,559 a month in principal and interest, $30,711 a year, before property tax and insurance: 35.1 per cent of the 2025 median household income of $87,460. On the median asking price of homes listed for sale, $343,800, the same terms give about $2,142 a month. [cite:ad6_pmms] [cite:ad17_audit_pmms] [cite:ad17_census_hvs_q226] [cite:us14_census_p60] Homeownership among householders under 35 was 35.2 per cent in mid-2026, the only age group whose rate fell significantly from a year earlier; the realtors' trade association, from a survey with a 3.5 per cent response rate, puts the median first-time buyer's age at a record 40. [cite:ad17_census_hvs_q226] [cite:ad6_nar_2025] [scene:ad6_price_and_rent|Part Six]

Health cover through working life

Most working Americans are insured through a job: 53.5 per cent of residents had employment-based cover in 2025 and 7.9 per cent, 26.7 million, were uninsured all year. [cite:us16_census_2025] The average family premium reached $28,303 in 2026, of which workers paid $7,471, and over five years premiums rose 28 per cent against wages up 26.9 per cent. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] Insurance does not end the bills: in 2024, 23 per cent of working-age adults were insured all year but underinsured, meaning out-of-pocket costs high relative to income. [cite:ad8_cmwf_underins24] Those who buy their own cover lost the enhanced federal subsidies at the end of 2025, after the House passed an extension that stalled in the Senate. [cite:ad8_astho_ptc] [scene:ad8_costs_and_coverage|Part Eight]

Mid-life: debt and wealth

Debt runs through the middle decades. Three in four families, 77.0 per cent, held some debt in 2025, and the median family with debt spent 15.4 per cent of its income on payments. [cite:ad17_scf25_inc] Wealth climbs with age, though slowly at first: median net worth was $33,000 for families headed by someone under 35, $155,600 at 35 to 44, $253,700 at 45 to 54 and $411,900 at 55 to 64, in 2025 dollars; for the under-35s it fell from $42,700 in 2022. [cite:ad12_scf25_t2] Much of that wealth is home equity, which is why the housing stage above shapes the retirement stage below. [scene:ad12_wealth_gap|Part Twelve] [scene:ad9_credit_and_scores|Part Nine]

The 401(k) and Social Security

The private pension that paid a set income for life has largely given way to the 401(k), an account whose value depends on what a worker puts in and how markets perform. Just over half of families, 54.9 per cent, held a retirement account in 2025, with a median balance among holders of $106,000; in Vanguard's plans, the median balance was $44,115 against an average of $167,970, because a minority of large accounts pull the average up. [cite:ad10_scf26] [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] [scene:ad10_pension_shift|Part Ten] Social Security is the part of the script that holds for almost everyone. The full retirement age reaches 67 for people born in 1960 and later; the average monthly benefit was about $2,088 in 2026, about $25,000 a year, and rises 3.6 per cent to about $2,163 in January 2027. [cite:ad10_ssa_1983] [cite:ad10_napa_cola27] The combined trust funds are projected to run out in the third quarter of 2034, after which incoming taxes would pay about 83 per cent of scheduled benefits unless Congress acts. [cite:ad10_crs_tr26] Old-age poverty on the official measure fell from 35.2 per cent in 1959 to 9.9 per cent in 2024, but on the supplemental measure, which subtracts medical and other necessary costs, 15.4 per cent of people 65 and over were poor in 2025. [cite:ad10_census_a3] [cite:ad10_aarp_spm65] [scene:ad10_social_security|Part Ten]

Where the script works as promised

Several stages hold. Real median household income reached $87,460 in 2025, the highest since the series began in 1967. [cite:us14_census_p60] A bachelor's degree still raises lifetime earnings by more than a million dollars on average, and fewer graduates borrow than five years ago. [cite:ad7_cew_payoff] [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] Social Security turned old age from the poorest stage of American life in 1959 into one with an official poverty rate below 10 per cent. [cite:ad10_census_a3] And for the fourth fifth of the income ladder, as the previous section showed, the script largely runs as taught. What has weakened is the guarantee that following it at the median brings each stage on time: about half of children born in the 1980s earn more than their parents did at the same age, against about 90 per cent of those born in 1940. [cite:ad2_chetty_fading] [scene:ad3_absolute_mobility|Part Three]

Interpretation, not finding: the life course as a series of tollgates

The Sophia platform reads this sequence as a series of tollgates: at each stage of the script a payment comes due, for care, credentials, shelter, cover and a retirement stake, to an industry that sets its terms, so that a life spent following the script is, in this reading, a life spent paying for the right to continue it. Read through this lens, the Dream functions less as a destination than as the instruction that keeps the payments flowing.

The strongest counter-readings answer that most of these payments buy something real: payroll taxes return as Social Security, which moved 28.8 million people out of poverty in 2025 [cite:us18_census_p60290]; tuition buys a documented earnings gain; a mortgage builds equity that rent does not. Prices at several stages are set in competitive or publicly regulated markets rather than by any single gatekeeper, and some, such as net tuition at public universities, have fallen. The tollgate reading also cannot by itself distinguish a cost that rose by design from one that rose with demand, land scarcity or medical technology; those distinctions are made mechanism by mechanism in the parts linked above, not by the metaphor.

What the record shows and does not. It shows a documented figure at each stage of the taught life script, from national surveys and administrative data, with the arithmetic shown where this book combined them. It does not show one person's life: the median at one stage is not the same person as the median at the next, and the figures come from different years, between 2022 and 2026. The mortgage example leaves out property tax, insurance and closing costs, and the rent line uses asking rents for vacant units, which can differ from what sitting tenants pay.

chapters.label: Part Eighteen
chapters.title: The Verdict: Illusion, Mechanism or Promise?
chapters.intro: Part Eighteen brings the volume to its verdict. Seventeen parts have set the promise as taught beside the system as built, one mechanism at a time; this part sets them all in one place. The first section is a single ledger of fifteen mechanisms, from mobility and wages to the rules themselves and the belief that outlasts them, each with the version taught, the record and its key figure, whether the friction was designed or captured, who gains, who pays, and how firmly the record supports the finding. The second grades seven promises of the Dream, a better life than one's parents, a home, a secure job, health care, college as a ladder, a secure retirement and fair rules, on a scorecard whose every sub-score, weight and sum is printed so that a reader can recompute it. The third sets out the levers with documented effects, with the evidence for and against each, then gives the Sophia platform's reading of the Dream as an illusion, labelled as interpretation and answered by the strongest counter-readings, and closes by answering the volume's question in three registers: what is documented, what is probable, and what the record does not support.
chapters.outro: Part Eighteen set the whole volume in one ledger and found that the American Dream is a promise kept broadly for the generation born around 1940 and unevenly since: about half of children born in the early 1980s out-earned their parents, against nine in ten born in 1940, while the odds of climbing from the bottom fifth held near 8 or 9 in 100 and were about a quarter as high for Black children as for white. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] [cite:ad2_chetty_trends] [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] It found the promise kept where federal law was built to keep it, with old-age poverty cut from 35.2 to 9.9 per cent and the uninsured rate less than half its 2009 level, and narrowed where costs outran incomes, with a home at 5.0 years of median income against 3.2 in the 1990s and the largest college grant covering a little over a quarter of the full cost of a public college year against about three-quarters in the late 1970s. [cite:ad10_census_a3] [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us16_khn_uninsured] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [cite:ad7_ace_pell] [cite:ad7_nasfaa_pell] On a scorecard whose every rule and weight is printed, the seven promises averaged 4.7 out of 10, between 4.5 and 5.7 under every test: health care and a home hold with modification, a secure job and a secure retirement hold for some, and fair rules, college as a ladder and a better life than one's parents fall short on these measures, a result that is this book's editorial synthesis, not a discovered fact. The levers with documented effects, from the 2021 child credit, after whose expiry child poverty on the supplemental measure rose from 5.2 to 12.4 per cent, to automatic enrolment and Medicaid expansion, carry documented critics and have been pulled and reversed by both parties. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] [cite:ad18_nber_corinth] [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] [cite:ad18_ucd_wherry] [cite:ad18_ohp_nejm] The Sophia platform's reading of the Dream as a story that keeps an extraction system running remains an interpretation, answered by a record in which belief fell as outcomes fell and in which the same laws that narrowed some promises kept others. [cite:ad16_gallup_opp24] [cite:ad16_forrt_brandt] The Dream, on this record, is neither an illusion nor a guarantee but a promise carried by machinery that can be read, measured and changed. This closes the volume; the companion volume's verdict sets the same American mechanisms beside another country's. [scene:us21_verdict|US System vs Israel System: the verdict]

sections.h: The Master Ledger: Fifteen Mechanisms, Told and Recorded
sections.html:
The Dream as taught is a chain of promises, each resting on a mechanism. Work earns a fair share of what it produces; a home builds wealth; a degree lifts its holder; a job brings health coverage; savings and Social Security carry a family through old age; and the rules apply to everyone alike. Each earlier part of this book tested one link. This section sets every link in one ledger, so that a reader can see at a glance which promises the record keeps, which it keeps for some, and where it measures a shortfall. The terms are those set out in Part Two: absolute mobility is the share of children who out-earn their parents, relative mobility the odds of moving between rungs; a median is the household in the exact middle; real dollars are adjusted for inflation. [scene:ad2_how_to_measure|Part Two: How to measure]

Each row has six entries. "As taught" gives the promise in the words of a curriculum, a citizenship test or a president, sourced in Part One and the part named. "The record" gives the key figure. "Friction" says whether the gap is designed, a feature someone wrote into law or practice on purpose, or captured, a documented departure from the design such as a settled case of discriminatory pricing; many rows are mixed. "Who gains, who pays" names industries, institutions and positions in the distribution, never groups as such. "Register" says how firmly the record holds: documented, where primary data agree; disputed, where named researchers with credible methods disagree about size or cause; not supported, where a circulating claim fails against the record.

Work and income

The first five rows are the core of the taught Dream: that effort is rewarded and that each generation does better than the last. The mobility record confirms the promise for the generation born around 1940, when about nine in ten children out-earned their parents, and qualifies it for every cohort since; for children born in the early 1980s the share was about half. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] Critics who adjust for household size and use a different price index put the share at 60 to 68 per cent, but accept the decline. [cite:ad2_reeves_winship] The pay record shows the same pattern: productivity and typical pay rose together until the 1970s and then parted, by an amount that depends on the price index used. [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026] [cite:ad4_bls_btn2017]

The cost of the Dream's assets

The next five rows concern the things the Dream promises a working family can buy: a home, a degree, health care, credit on fair terms and a secure old age. Here the record is most mixed, because each of these markets was shaped by federal law and each has both a documented success and a documented failure. The long, fixed-rate mortgage built by federal agencies in the 1930s is still the standard loan, and 65.2 per cent of households owned their homes in the second quarter of 2026, against 65.6 per cent in 1980 (seasonally adjusted second-quarter rates, the convention of Part One). [cite:ad1_fred_hor] Yet the price of a typical home has risen from about 3.2 to 5.0 years of median household income since the 1990s. [cite:us14_jchs_pti] The degree still pays: bachelor's holders earn about 75 per cent more over a working life than high-school graduates. [cite:ad7_cew_payoff] But the largest federal grant, which covered about three-quarters of the full cost of a public college year in the late 1970s, now covers a little over a quarter: 27.2 per cent of the federal cost-of-attendance figure in 2024–25, or 28.6 per cent of the College Board's narrower 2025–26 budget. [cite:ad7_ace_pell] [cite:ad7_nasfaa_pell] [cite:ad7_cb_trends25]

Distribution and the rules

The last five rows ask who ends up with what and who writes the rules that decide it. Here the taught version holds most plainly on one point: the federal tax system is progressive, taking 1.4 per cent of the lowest fifth's income and 31.5 per cent of the top 1 per cent's in 2022. [cite:ad11_tf_cbo2022] It holds least on the gap between what families earn and what they own: in 2025 the median white family earned about 1.9 times the median Black family's income and held about 9.0 times its wealth. [cite:ad2_scf_t1] [cite:us8_scf2025]

What the ledger shows, read across

Three patterns run across the fifteen rows. The first is that almost every gap has a date and a designer. The pay floor was written as a fixed dollar sum in 1938 and has not moved since 2009; the tie between job and health coverage was written into the tax code in 1954; the bankruptcy treatment of student loans was set in a sequence of laws from 1976 to 2005; the 401(k) entered the tax code in 1978 and employers then chose it over the pension. [cite:ad5_epi_real2025] [cite:ad8_tpc_esi] [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] [cite:ad10_napa_1978] These are designed frictions in the protocol's sense: intended features, debated in public and enacted by Congresses and presidents of both parties. Captured frictions, documented departures from the design, are fewer and more specific: pricing that, the Justice Department alleged, charged Black and Hispanic borrowers more than white borrowers with similar credit, in cases two of the largest lenders settled; contract sales in Chicago; Ferguson's courts run for revenue. [cite:ad12_doj_countrywide] [cite:ad6_duke_plunder] [cite:ad11_doj_ferguson]

The second pattern is that the record turns on the difference between a level and a share. On levels, the taught version often holds: real median household income reached $87,460 in 2025, the highest on record, and the typical worker's pay rose by about a third since 1979. [cite:us14_census_story2025] [cite:ad4_epi_gap2026] On shares, it often does not: the proportion of children who out-earn their parents halved, the share of the economy's gains reaching typical pay narrowed, and the bottom half of households holds 2.3 per cent of the country's net worth. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] [cite:ad12_ad_bottom50] A reader who asks whether life got better and a reader who asks whether it got fairer will both find their answer in the same tables.

The third pattern is that the gaps fall on positions, not on character. The burden of each mechanism lands where the ledger says it lands: on renters and young buyers, borrowers who did not finish college, the underinsured, revolving borrowers, low-paid workers without a retirement plan, and the lowest fifth through state and local taxes. Where a gap follows race or origin, the record ties it to named programmes and practices, from FHA underwriting to the 1935 exclusions, and economists dispute how much of today's gap those histories explain. [cite:ad6_fha_manual] [cite:ad13_dewitt] [cite:ad13_barsky] [cite:ad13_dkks] Part Seventeen followed them into household budgets: the middle fifth's average household took in $74,474 in 2024 and kept about $4,410 after taxes and spending, roughly 5.9 cents per dollar, while the two lower fifths reported spending more than their income in every year from 2020 to 2024. [cite:us22_bls_ce24_q] [cite:ad17_fred_q1exp] [cite:ad17_fred_q2exp] [scene:ad17_three_families|Part Seventeen: Families Through the Machine]

Where the promise works as taught

The ledger also records where the promise is kept. Social Security cut old-age poverty from 35.2 per cent in 1959 to 9.9 per cent in 2024, and moved 28.8 million people above the supplemental poverty line in 2025. [cite:ad10_census_a3] [cite:us18_census_p60290] Children of immigrants have out-climbed the children of American-born parents for more than a century. [cite:ad2_abramitzky_aer] The uninsured rate in 2025 was less than half its 2009 level. [cite:us16_census_2025] [cite:us16_khn_uninsured] The degree still pays. Overdraft revenue at large banks halved between 2019 and 2023, largely through the banks' own changes, and overdose deaths fell for a third straight year in 2025. [cite:us22_cfpb_od23] [cite:ad16_nchs_2025] These are not footnotes to the ledger; they are rows of it, and any reading of the whole has to account for them.

Claims that did not survive the record

Several widely repeated claims failed when tested against primary data, and they belong in the ledger as findings in their own right. A widely repeated figure holds that house prices have doubled against incomes; the Harvard housing centre's series shows a rise of roughly half since the 1990s. [cite:us14_jchs_pti] Another holds that tuition has risen far faster than every other cost; real published tuition at public four-year colleges roughly doubled from 1995–96 to 2025–26, and net tuition after grants has fallen since 2012–13. [cite:ad7_cb_trends25] A third holds that medical debt is the leading cause of bankruptcy; the two main studies answer different questions, contribution against cause, and the dispute is open. [cite:us22_dobkin2018] [cite:us22_himmelstein2019] A fourth, that homelessness is maintained on purpose, rests on motive with no document behind it; regional rates track the cost and availability of rental housing rather than addiction, poverty or weather. [cite:ad14_ucp_colburn] A fifth, that the poor defend the system most, did not survive a large-scale test. [cite:ad16_forrt_brandt]

Read as a whole, the ledger does not describe a promise that was never kept, nor one kept for everyone. It describes a set of mechanisms, each built at a known time by known hands, that delivered the promise broadly to the generation born before 1950, kept parts of it for most families since, and moved others out of reach for families at specific positions in the distribution. The next section turns that ledger into grades. [scene:ad18_scorecard|The scorecard]

sections.h: The Scorecard: Seven Promises, Graded in the Open
sections.html:
A ledger records; a grade judges. The difference matters, and this section keeps it visible. A grade on a promise is not a fact found in a dataset in the way a poverty rate is. It is a judgment built from facts, and it is only as sound as the rules used to build it. So the scorecard below follows one discipline throughout: every sub-score is tied to a named figure from a named source; every rule that turns a figure into a score is printed; every weight is disclosed; and the arithmetic is shown, so that a reader who weighs things differently can recompute the result from the same numbers. The aggregate grade at the end is this book's editorial synthesis, not a discovery. The method follows the one the companion volume used to grade two national systems, adapted to grade one system against its own promises. [scene:us22_method|US System vs Israel System: how the scorecard grades]

The seven promises

The promises graded are the ones the Dream has been sold on, in the words of curricula and presidents of both parties traced in Part One: that a child will have a better life than his or her parents; that a working family can own a home; that steady work brings a secure job and a decent living; that a job brings health care; that college is a ladder; that a working life ends in a secure retirement; and that the rules are fair. [scene:ad1_as_taught|Part One: the Dream as taught] [cite:ad1_obama_2011] [cite:ad1_clinton_1992] [cite:ad1_bush_2002] Each is graded on four sub-scores, and the grade asks only whether the promise was kept on its own terms. It does not ask whether a given policy was good for the country, a question that depends on values no score can settle.

The four sub-scores and their rules

Fulfilment asks whether the promise is kept for those it was made to, and uses five status labels: delivered (4 points), meaning it holds on its own terms for about three in four or more; delivered with modification (3), meaning it holds for most but at a materially higher cost or in a narrower form; partial (2), meaning it holds for roughly half to two-thirds; attempted but blocked (1); and not delivered (0). Breadth asks whether the promise holds across groups: it divides the rate of the worst-off documented group by that of the best-off on the same measure, and scores 4 at 0.90 or above, 3 from 0.75, 2 from 0.60, 1 from 0.40 and 0 below. Reach asks whether the share for whom the promise is within reach has grown or shrunk since the earliest comparable point: 4 if it improved by 5 per cent or more, 3 if it changed by less than 5 per cent either way, 2 if it fell by 5 to 15 per cent, 1 if by 15 to 30 per cent, and 0 if by more than 30 per cent. Durability asks how the promise is backed: 4 if by a federal statute funded for the long term, 3 if by statute with a dated funding gap or enacted cuts, 2 if partly by statute and partly by employer or market choice, 1 if mainly by market or employer choice or if key protections were repealed or vacated in the last two years, and 0 if by nothing.

The weights, 40, 30, 20 and 10 per cent, put most weight on whether the promise is kept for the people it was made to and least on legal form. They are a choice. A reader who thinks breadth should count as much as fulfilment, or that durability matters more in an era of rules repealed within a year, can change them; the tests at the end show how much the result moves when they do.

The grades

The arithmetic for the first row shows how every row works. The promise of a better life than one's parents is partial: about half of children born in the early 1980s out-earned their parents, which scores 2. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] On breadth, a Black child born to the bottom fifth reaches the top fifth 2.5 per cent of the time against 10.6 per cent for a white child; 2.5 divided by 10.6 is 0.24, below 0.40, which scores 0. [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] On reach, the share fell from about 92 to about 50 per cent between the 1940 and 1984 birth cohorts, a fall of 46 per cent (42 divided by 92), which scores 0. On durability, the outcome is set by the market and backed by no statute, which scores 1. The weighted sum is 0.4 × 2 + 0.3 × 0 + 0.2 × 0 + 0.1 × 1 = 0.9; multiplied by 2.5, it gives 2.3 out of 10 (2.25 rounded).

Three rows need a word on the figures chosen. For a secure job, the fulfilment figure is a household's ability to meet a small emergency, the measure the Federal Reserve's annual survey uses for financial security, set beside the ALICE count of households below a local cost-of-living budget, a measure built by a United Way research group and higher than the official poverty count. [cite:ad9_shed2025] [cite:ad14_alice_national] Against those, official poverty among full-time, year-round workers was 1.6 per cent in 2025, which would grade the promise delivered on the narrowest reading.
