[cite:us18_crs_pov2025] For health, the reach figure joins a Census estimate for 2009 with the 2025 release, and survey methods changed in between, so the size of the gain is approximate; the uninsured share fell from nearly 17 per cent to 7.9 per cent, and any gain of 5 per cent or more in the insured share scores 4, about half the gain measured here. [cite:us16_khn_uninsured] [cite:us16_census_2025] For fair rules, the reach figure is a single mechanism, the spread of mandatory arbitration, measured by a survey of employers run by Cornell University for the Economic Policy Institute, a labour-aligned research group; it is the clearest long-run measure of access to court the volume found, and it is narrower than the promise it stands for. [cite:ad15_epi_colvin]

Costs and distribution, reported but not scored

Under this scorecard's rules, the cost of a promise and who gains or loses from it are reported beside the grade rather than folded into it, because how much a reader should mind a higher price depends on what it buys. They are the strongest reasons to read the two highest grades with care. The home that 65 per cent of households own costs about 5.0 years of median income against 3.2 in the 1990s, and ownership among householders under 35 was 35.2 per cent in mid-2026. [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [cite:us15_census_hvs_q226] The health coverage that all but 7.9 per cent had for at least part of 2025 costs $15,474 a person a year and $28,303 for a family plan at work. [cite:us16_cms_nhe2024] [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] On distribution, the 2025 budget law, scored by the Congressional Budget Office, lowers resources for the poorest tenth of households by about $1,200 a year and raises them for the top tenth by about $13,600, and the Social Security trust funds that carry the retirement grade are projected to pay about 83 per cent of scheduled benefits from 2034 unless Congress acts. [cite:ad11_tr_pl11921] [cite:ad10_crs_tr26]

Testing the result

A grade that flips under a reasonable change of rules is a grade about the rules. This one was recomputed four ways, then under every shift of ten points of weight. Fulfilment alone, the sub-score closest to a plain fact and the single most defensible number, sums to 16 of a possible 28 points (2 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 2), or 5.7 out of 10. With the four sub-scores weighted equally, the seven promises total 51 of a possible 112 points, or 4.6. If the secure-job promise is graded on full-time workers' poverty, fulfilment rises to 4, that promise's grade to 7.0, and the aggregate to 5.0 (35.0 divided by 7). If the mobility promise is graded on the most favourable alternative estimate, 68 per cent out-earning their parents, reach becomes a 26 per cent fall and scores 1, that grade rises to 2.8 and the aggregate to 4.8; the test is generous, because the same adjustments would also raise the 1940 baseline, and a reader who counts 68 per cent as most rather than about two-thirds, scoring fulfilment 3, gets 3.8 for that promise and 4.9 overall. Moving ten points of weight from any one sub-score to any other moves the aggregate between 4.5 (breadth 40, fulfilment 30) and 5.0 (fulfilment 50, breadth 20).

Every test keeps the aggregate between 4.5 and 5.7 out of 10, and none lifts it to 6.5, the band this scorecard treats as a promise kept. That is the finding of the scorecard, and it is a finding about a synthesis: by this book's disclosed rules, the American Dream as a bundle of promises is about half kept.

Which promises hold, for whom, and which fall short

Read by band, the seven grades fall into three groups. Two promises hold, with modification, at 6.5 or above: health care, at 6.8, and a home, at 6.5. Both reach most households, and both are carried by federal law built for the purpose; both cost far more than they did, and the home promise is harder to reach for the young and for Black households. Two promises hold for some, between 4.0 and 6.4: a secure retirement, at 5.3, where Social Security keeps its part and the private account leaves the low-paid behind, and a secure job, at 5.0, where real incomes have risen while more than a third of adults could not cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent. Three fall short on these measures, below 4.0: fair rules, at 3.8; college as a ladder, at 3.5, where the degree still pays its holders but the ladder's lowest rungs are harder to reach for children from poor families; and a better life than one's parents, at 2.3, the promise on which the Dream was first defined and on which the record has moved most. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] [cite:ad7_cew_payoff] [cite:ad10_census_a3]

The grades also show where the promise works as taught. Every promise scores at least 2 on fulfilment: none is a promise that was never kept. Three score the top mark on reach, a secure living, health care and retirement, where the share for whom the promise is within reach is larger today than at the earliest comparable point. The low grades come not from absence but from narrowing: the promises still hold for many, and less often for those who started lower. In a single household's budget the bands are concrete: one average deductible of $1,955 takes 44 per cent of the middle fifth's yearly margin, while Social Security, the degree premium and a record median income are the stages where the life script holds. [cite:ad8_kff_ehbs2026] [cite:ad10_census_a3] [cite:ad7_cew_payoff] [scene:ad17_a_life_in_numbers|Part Seventeen: a life in numbers] The last section asks what the record shows would move these grades.

The chart below plots the series this section relies on, from the volume's data dashboard; its caption names the source and definition.

sections.h: What Would Change It: The Levers, the Reading and the Verdict
sections.html:
If the gaps in the ledger have dates and designers, they can in principle be redesigned. This section sets out levers that have been tried in the United States and measured by named researchers, each with the strongest evidence for and against it and its status as of October 2026. None is offered as a programme: the choice depends on what a reader values and will pay, which no ledger settles. The section then gives the Sophia platform's reading of the Dream as a whole, with the readings that answer it, and the volume's answer to its own question.

Cash for children: the 2021 credit and its expiry

In 2021 Congress raised the child tax credit from $2,000 to $3,000 per child, $3,600 under age six, and paid much of it in monthly payments from July. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] [cite:ad18_nber_ananat] Child poverty on the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts tax credits, fell to 5.2 per cent in 2021; when the credit returned to its old form, it rose to 12.4 per cent in 2022. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] The dispute is over work. Elizabeth Ananat and colleagues, using Census survey data from April to September 2021, found "very small, inconsistently signed, and statistically insignificant" effects on parents' employment. [cite:ad18_nber_ananat] Kevin Corinth, Bruce Meyer and colleagues projected that a permanent version would lead about 1.5 million working parents, 2.6 per cent, to leave work, and that child poverty would then fall by at most 22 per cent rather than the 34 per cent a static count suggests. [cite:ad18_nber_corinth] The first measured six months; the second projects from estimated responses to work incentives, and its central employment assumption was called "really not credible" by the Stanford tax economist Jacob Goldin. [cite:ad18_cbs_ctc] As of October 2026 the credit is $2,200 per child, $1,700 of it refundable, and since the 2025 budget law it requires a Social Security number for the filer or a spouse. [cite:ad11_cftd_rp2532] [cite:ad13_usccb_obbba]

Saving by default

One retirement lever is not much disputed. In plans that enrol workers automatically, 94 per cent participated in 2025, against 64 per cent in plans where workers must sign up. [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] The 2022 retirement law, SECURE 2.0, requires most new 401(k) and 403(b) plans set up after 29 December 2022 to enrol workers automatically from 2025, with exemptions for the smallest and newest employers; as of October 2026 the requirement applies, and its final regulations had gone to the White House budget office for review in June. [cite:ad10_asppa_auto] The limits are in the same data: a default works only where a plan exists, and 70 per cent of private workers have a 401(k)-type plan available; participation among workers earning under $15,000 was 43 per cent; and the median balance was $44,115. [cite:ad10_bls_ebs26] [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26]

The wage floor

The Congressional Budget Office estimated in February 2021 that raising the federal minimum to $15 by 2025 would lift 900,000 people out of poverty and raise affected workers' pay by a net $333 billion, while about 1.4 million fewer workers would be employed. [cite:ad18_bt_cbo2021] A study of 138 state increases from 1979 to 2016 by Doruk Cengiz, Arindrajit Dube and colleagues found that the number of low-wage jobs was essentially unchanged five years after each increase. [cite:ad18_nber_cengiz] A review by David Neumark and Peter Shirley found that 79.2 per cent of the preferred estimates in the American literature were negative, with the evidence strongest for teenagers, young adults and less-educated workers. [cite:ad18_nber_neumark] Thirty states and the District of Columbia already set a higher floor. [cite:us13_bp_states2026]

Medicaid expansion

Under the 2010 health law states may extend Medicaid to low-income adults. In 2025, 9.0 per cent of working-age adults in expansion states were uninsured against 18.1 per cent in the others. [cite:ad18_nchs_unins25] Sarah Miller, Laura Wherry and colleagues, linking Census survey data to death records, found that expansion cut annual mortality among low-income adults aged 55 to 64 by about 9.4 per cent, and estimated that about 15,600 deaths would have been avoided had every state expanded. [cite:ad18_ucd_wherry] The one randomised trial points the other way on health. In Oregon's 2008 Medicaid lottery, coverage produced no measurable change in blood pressure, cholesterol or blood sugar after about two years; it cut depression by 30 per cent, nearly eliminated catastrophic out-of-pocket spending and cut the share borrowing money or skipping other bills to pay for care by 14.2 percentage points. [cite:ad18_ohp_nejm] A critic of the mortality study argues that its channel is unclear, since the effect barely differs between the previously uninsured and the whole sample. [cite:ad18_ohp_bjoerkheim] As of October 2026 the 2025 budget law adds work requirements for expansion adults from 1 January 2027, and the Congressional Budget Office expects about 10 million more uninsured by 2034. [cite:ad8_ccf_ifr] [cite:us16_kff_obbba]

Building more homes

Minneapolis ended citywide parking minimums, allowed taller apartment buildings along transit and commercial corridors, and allowed two- and three-unit buildings on every residential lot. Between 2017 and 2022 its housing stock grew 12 per cent against 4 per cent in the rest of Minnesota, and its rents rose 1 per cent against 14 per cent; most new units were in large apartment buildings, and the duplex change had a modest effect. [cite:ad18_pew_mpls] Researchers cited in 2026 attributed part of it to weaker demand after the unrest of 2020 and to low interest rates that fed construction, and reported that the period of slow rent growth had ended. [cite:ad18_axios_mpls]

Debt relief and the bankruptcy door

Student debt was made harder to discharge in bankruptcy in steps from 1976 to 2005. [cite:ad7_crs_rs22699] Under a process the Justice and Education Departments introduced in November 2022, borrowers won full or partial discharge in 98 per cent of the cases courts had decided by March 2024. [cite:ad7_doj_2024] Its limit is scale: 1,220 cases were filed in sixteen months, against 9.3 million borrowers in default in June 2026. [cite:ad7_doj_2024] [cite:us17_ci_defaults] For medical debt, the federal rule to keep it off credit reports was vacated in July 2025; fifteen states and the District of Columbia have their own limits, which the consumer bureau said in October 2025 federal law preempts, leaving the question to the courts. [cite:ad8_nclc_states]

An account at birth

Connecticut's baby bonds programme invests $3,200 for each child born on or after 1 July 2023 whose birth was covered by the state's Medicaid programme. It can be claimed at 18 to 30 for a home, a business, education or retirement in the state, and is projected to grow to $11,000 to $24,000. [cite:ad18_ct_babybonds] The case for the idea rests on simulation: one study found a universal national programme would cut the ratio of young white to young Black median wealth from about 15 to 1 to about 1.6 to 1. [cite:ad18_zewde] The case against its larger claims is arithmetic: the gap in average wealth, driven by the top, runs to trillions, beyond reach of a programme of about $80 billion a year. [cite:ad18_ppp_bruenig] No child can claim before 2041, so there is no evidence of effect yet. The 2025 budget law created a federal cousin of the idea: "Trump Accounts", with a $1,000 federal deposit for each US-citizen child with a Social Security number born from 2025 to 2028, open to contributions from 4 July 2026; by March 2026 more than 4 million children had been signed up. [cite:ad18_audit_irs_trumpacct] It is universal within those birth years rather than targeted at low-income births, and it too has no record of effect yet.

The levers with the firmest evidence act on a specific number: a participation rate, catastrophic bills, a poverty rate. The record of both parties runs through them in both directions. A Democratic Congress expanded the child credit in 2021 and let it lapse; a Republican Congress and president raised the permanent credit in 2025 and tied it to a Social Security number. The 2010 health law expanded coverage and the 2025 budget law is projected to reduce it; federal fee limits were written in 2024 and undone in 2025. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] [cite:ad11_cftd_rp2532] [cite:us16_kff_obbba] [cite:ad9_plaw_119_10] Even well-studied levers can surprise: a 2024 review of some 500 estimates found that, apart from the 1993 reform, expansions of the earned income tax credit show no clear employment effect, against a long-held consensus. [cite:ad11_kleven_eitc]

Interpretation, not finding: the Dream as the story that keeps an extraction system running

The Sophia platform reads the evidence of this volume as a single design. In this reading, the American Dream works as an illusion: a story taught in schools and repeated by presidents of both parties that keeps people working inside a system that extracts from them. The story is told as income and effort, so that a household blames itself when its paycheck falls short, while the returns that build security flow through channels the story does not name: shares bought back with profits, homes priced beyond a year's wage, credit priced at a fifth of the balance a year, a degree financed by a debt that bankruptcy cannot reach, health coverage that ties a worker to a job. Read through this lens, each designed friction in the ledger is a turnstile, each fee a toll, and the belief that hard work suffices is the mechanism that keeps people walking through. The fall in absolute mobility, the parting of pay and productivity, and the record share of wealth at the top are, in this reading, the system working as built.

The strongest counter-readings are documented in the same ledger. First, a design implies a designer, and the record shows many, at different dates, with opposed aims: the Congress that created Social Security and the one that wrote the 401(k); a Congress that expanded the child credit for a year and did not renew it; consumer limits written under one party and undone under the other. A system that cut old-age poverty from 35.2 to 9.9 per cent and halved the uninsured rate is hard to read as built only to extract. [cite:ad10_census_a3] [cite:us16_census_2025] Second, belief has tracked the record rather than masking it: satisfaction with the chance to get ahead fell from 77 to 52 per cent, only about a third say the Dream still holds, and the claim that the disadvantaged defend the system most did not survive a large test. [cite:ad16_gallup_opp24] [cite:ad16_brookings_opp26] [cite:ad1_apnorc26] [cite:ad16_forrt_brandt] Third, the levels moved up: real median household income was the highest on record in 2025, and relative mobility, the odds of climbing, held steady while the rungs moved apart. [cite:us14_census_story2025] [cite:ad2_chetty_trends] Fourth, absolute mobility fell in every rich country where it has been measured, though most in the United States. [cite:ad3_berman] Fifth, some extraction channels shrank without a new law, as overdraft revenue halved through banks' own changes. [cite:us22_cfpb_od23] The reading and its answers rest on the same documents; what divides them is whether the pattern is read as intended.

The answer in three registers

The volume asked whether the American Dream is an illusion, a mechanism or a promise. Documented: the Dream is a promise that was kept broadly for the generation born around 1940 and has been kept unevenly since. About half of children born in the early 1980s out-earned their parents; the odds of climbing from the bottom stayed near 8 or 9 in 100 and were a quarter as high for Black children as for white; real incomes and coverage rose while a home came to cost 5.0 years of income against 3.2 and the largest college grant shrank from about three-quarters of the full cost of a public college year to a little over a quarter; Social Security kept its promise and the private pension did not survive as the norm. [cite:ad3_fading_paper] [cite:ad2_chetty_trends] [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] [cite:us14_jchs_pti] [cite:ad7_ace_pell] [cite:ad7_nasfaa_pell] [cite:ad10_census_a3] [cite:ad10_bls_ebs26] Each gap runs through a mechanism with a date and a designer, most enacted in public by Congresses of both parties, a few captured departures documented in federal settlements and investigations. On this book's disclosed scorecard the promises are about half kept, 4.7 out of 10, an editorial synthesis rather than a measured fact.

Probable: the measured gaps owe something to measurement and something to policy. The pay–productivity gap is partly a matter of price indexes and partly a real fall in labour's share; the decline in union power, a wage floor left unchanged since 2009 and the rules on arbitration and bankruptcy probably shifted bargaining toward employers and lenders, though by how much is disputed. [cite:ad4_bls_btn2017] [cite:ad4_qje_farber] [cite:ad15_epi_colvin] The best-evidenced levers would probably move the specific numbers they were measured to move if restored or extended, at costs a reader must weigh. [cite:us18_scripps_ctc] [cite:ad10_vanguard_has26] [cite:ad18_ohp_nejm]

Not supported: that the Dream was never real; that the whole system was designed as one plan to extract from those who believe in it; that homelessness is maintained on purpose; that medical bills are settled as the leading cause of bankruptcy; and, at the other pole, that staying at the bottom reflects the person and not the system, a view Lincoln stated in 1859, allowing only for "singular misfortune", and one the record of who climbs and who does not cannot sustain. [cite:ad14_ucp_colburn] [cite:us22_dobkin2018] [cite:ad1_lincoln_1859] [cite:ad13_oi_race_sum] The Dream is neither an illusion nor a guarantee. It is a promise carried by machinery, and the machinery, unlike the promise, can be read, measured and changed.

books.title: The One-Way Mirror
books.subtitle: Israel Inside the American State: The Laws, Agencies and Contracts, from the CIA to the Pentagon
books.intro:
Most of what ties the American state to Israel is not secret. It sits in public laws, signed memoranda, contract notices, appropriations tables and court records, laid down one administration at a time since 1948. Because it was built slowly and in pieces, it is rarely seen whole. This volume puts the pieces together: the laws and the votes that created them; the Central Intelligence Agency's liaison with the Mossad; the National Security Agency's sharing of raw intercepts, including Americans' communications, with Israel's Unit 8200; the FBI's spy cases; Homeland Security, ICE and the police exchanges; the Pentagon and each of the armed services; the pipeline that moves American weapons; Palantir and the data contractors; the Israeli-founded spyware and security firms selling to American agencies; the legal shields in American law; what is and is not documented about Jeffrey Epstein; and, at the end, what the record shows about the asymmetry the title names. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow_aj_nsamou]

The title comes from a question: the United States hands Israel raw intelligence on its own citizens, so why can it not see what Israel does with American weapons and data in Gaza and the West Bank? The volume tests that question rather than assuming the answer. It records what the United States gets back, from missile-defence technology to intelligence on its adversaries, and gives the stated purpose of both governments beside each critical finding. Every connection in it is a documented relationship, a law, a contract, a memorandum, an appointment or a court finding, never an inference from anyone's identity. Where the record is contested, both sides are shown; where it is silent, the volume says so. It is a companion to Follow the Money, which maps the lobby and the campaign money behind the votes. [scene:ow1_founding|Part One: the legal spine]

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Legal Spine
chapters.intro: Part One sets out the legal spine of the relationship between the United States and Israel: every major law, memorandum and executive action from recognition in 1948 to the negotiations of 2026 over what replaces the current aid pledge, with the administration that made it and, where Congress voted, the margin. It follows how arms sales became an emergency statute in 1973, how the Reagan years built standing machinery, how the aid came to be paid and spent, how the partnership acts and the record pledge of 2016 were passed, and what the United States says it receives in return through the cooperative programmes. Each later part takes one strand of this spine into a single agency.
chapters.outro: Part One has established the paper on which everything else rests. The arms relationship began with the Hawk on credit in 1962 and became statutory with the Emergency Security Assistance Act of 1973, passed 66 to 9 after the Senate set aside a condition tied to Resolution 242. [cite:ow1_kramer_hawk] [cite:ow1_vv_rs587] [cite:ow1_vv_rs583] Between 1981 and 2008 the Reagan and later administrations built a strategic memorandum, a stockpile, a free trade agreement, major non-NATO ally status, early disbursement into a Federal Reserve account and a statutory qualitative military edge. [cite:ow1_wiki_1981isr] [cite:ow1_jinsa_wrsa] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] After 2009 Congress declared Israel a major strategic partner by margins such as 410 to 1, the 2016 memorandum pledged $38 billion, and the war after October 2023 brought the largest transfers since 1973, partly by emergency declaration. [cite:ow_jvl_2014act] [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] [cite:ow1_state_rubio2025] The cooperative programmes show real American returns in technology and industry, and the asymmetry lies in money, terms and law rather than in the joint programmes themselves. [cite:ow1_crs_irondome] [cite:ow1_crs_aid2025] Part Two turns to the people who voted these measures in, and to the organized money and advocacy around those votes.

sections.h: From Recognition to the Airlift, 1948–1975
sections.html:
The relationship this volume examines is built of paper: statutes, appropriations, memoranda, executive orders and letters exchanged between governments. Before the agencies are taken one by one in the parts that follow, this part sets out that paper in the order it was written, administration by administration. The timeline below is the spine of the whole volume; each later part returns to one of its points and follows it inside a single agency. This first section covers the years in which the United States moved from recognizing Israel to arming it, and in which Congress wrote the first law devoted to Israel's emergency military needs.

Recognition, 1948. On 14 May 1948 the Truman administration announced that "the United States recognizes the provisional government as the de facto authority of the new State of Israel." Full, de jure recognition followed on 31 January 1949. [cite:ow1_nara_recog] Recognition created a diplomatic relationship; it did not create a military one. Through the 1950s American aid to Israel was economic, and the United States declined to be its principal arms supplier, as earlier volumes of this library describe.

The Hawk, 1962. The first break came under President Kennedy. On 7 August 1962 Secretary of State Dean Rusk recommended offering Israel the Hawk anti-aircraft missile if no arms-limitation arrangement with Egypt looked likely within two months. Later that month the President's deputy special counsel, Myer Feldman, carried the decision to David Ben-Gurion and Golda Meir, and on 7 September a State Department circular instructed American posts to describe the Hawk as purely defensive. The sale was made on American credit, and the first batteries arrived by early 1965. [cite:ow1_kramer_hawk] Even inside the administration the decision was framed cautiously: Rusk told the British on 18 August that Feldman was "in no sense attempting to close a Hawk deal" and that a sale was open in principle "subject to the possibility of arms control arrangements in the area." [cite:ow1_frus_hood1962] The full story is told in [scene:cw4_hawk|the Hawk decision], and the first direct tank sale of 1965 in [scene:cw6_tanks|from Bonn to Washington].

The Phantoms, 1968. The Hawk was defensive; the next major sale was not. In July 1968 the Senate adopted a sense-of-Congress resolution calling on President Johnson to sell Israel supersonic aircraft, and the House later agreed. On 9 October 1968, signing the Foreign Assistance Act of 1968, Johnson said he had "taken note of the section concerning the sale of planes to Israel" and asked the Secretary of State to open negotiations. The sale of 50 F-4 Phantoms for $285 million was announced on 27 December 1968; 16 aircraft arrived in late 1969 and 34 in 1970. [cite:ow1_jvl_phantom] The negotiation carried a nuclear condition. In a letter of 22 November 1968, Ambassador Yitzhak Rabin reaffirmed that Israel "will not be the first power in the Middle East to introduce nuclear weapons" and agreed not to use American aircraft as nuclear carriers; the American reply reserved the right to cancel in "unusual and compelling circumstances." [cite:ow1_jvl_phantomconds] Part Eleven returns to how that formula became settled policy.

The airlift and the emergency law, 1973. The October 1973 war produced the first American law written specifically for Israel's military needs. From 14 October to 14 November 1973 the Air Force flew Operation Nickel Grass, delivering about 22,300 tons of equipment in 32 days. [cite:ow1_afhist_nickel] On 19 October President Nixon asked Congress for $2.2 billion in emergency security assistance for Israel. His stated reason was strategic: the United States was replacing Israeli losses to maintain "a balance of military capabilities" against "a large-scale resupply of Syria and Egypt by the Soviet Union." [cite:ow1_nixon_msg1973]

Congress passed the Emergency Security Assistance Act, Public Law 93-199, and it was signed on 26 December 1973. It authorized up to $2.2 billion for Israel as grants, credits, or both, as the President determined; amounts above $1.5 billion required a presidential finding of national interest and twenty days' notice to Congress, a condition waived if fighting resumed. Section 4 allowed the President to release Israel from paying for arms bought between 6 October 1973 and 30 June 1974. [cite:ow1_pl93_199] In practice the $2.2 billion was allocated as $1.5 billion in grants and $700 million in loans. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

The Senate vote of 20 December 1973 shows both the margin and the dissent. The bill passed 66 to 9. Before passage, Senator J. William Fulbright of Arkansas, chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, offered an amendment that would have made aid above $1.2 billion contingent on steps toward compliance with Security Council Resolution 242; the Senate tabled it 62 to 12. [cite:ow1_vv_rs587] [cite:ow1_vv_rs583] It was an early instance of a pattern Part Two follows: a proposal to attach a condition to aid for Israel, raised on the floor and set aside by a large majority.

The 1975 memorandum. The first written American commitments to Israel beyond arms sales came with the second Sinai disengagement agreement in September 1975. An accompanying US–Israel memorandum promised that, for five years, the United States would help Israel obtain oil if normal supply failed; that Washington would "view Israel's requests sympathetically, including its request for advanced and sophisticated weapons"; and that the United States would not recognize or negotiate with the Palestine Liberation Organization "so long as" it did not recognize Israel's right to exist and accept Resolutions 242 and 338. [cite:ow1_jvl_moa1975] These were executive commitments, not statutes, but the last of them bound American diplomacy for thirteen years.

By 1975, then, three features of the later relationship were in place. Arms flowed under presidential authority with congressional encouragement; Congress had written an Israel-specific emergency law that let the President forgive payment; and the executive had begun to make written political commitments to Israel outside the treaty process. [cite:ow1_pl93_199] [cite:ow1_jvl_moa1975] What did not yet exist was a standing structure. The next section follows how the Reagan years built one.

sections.h: Building the Machinery, 1981–2008
sections.html:
Between 1981 and 2008 the relationship acquired its permanent machinery: a strategic memorandum, a stockpile of American munitions on Israeli soil, a free trade agreement, a legal status shared with only a handful of countries, a special way of paying out aid, three ten-year aid pledges and a statute that made Israel's military edge a matter of American law. Each was created by a named act of a named administration, and most can still be read. This section follows them in order, then shows in one diagram how an aid dollar moves from Congress to a contractor.

The Strategic Cooperation memorandum, 1981. On 30 November 1981 Defense Secretary Caspar Weinberger and Defense Minister Ariel Sharon signed a Memorandum of Understanding on Strategic Cooperation. [cite:ow1_wiki_1981isr] It provided for a joint committee to plan exercises, for the Sixth Fleet's use of Israeli ports and for the pre-positioning of American supplies in Israel; as an executive memorandum it did not go to the Senate for ratification. [cite:ow_wiki_sca1981] It lasted eighteen days. On 14 December the Knesset passed the Golan Heights Law, applying Israeli law to the Golan, and on 18 December the Reagan administration suspended the memorandum. [cite:ow1_wiki_1981isr] Prime Minister Menachem Begin said Israel understood the suspension to mean cancellation. [cite:ow1_csm_1981] Strategic cooperation was not revived until late 1983, when Reagan and Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir agreed on 29 November to form a Joint Political-Military Group. [cite:ow1_reagan_1983] [cite:ow1_wiki_1981isr] The episode is the clearest early case of an American administration using the strategic relationship itself as leverage, and it was short.

The stockpile, 1984–1989. An April 1984 bilateral memorandum began the pre-positioning of American weapons in Israel. After a decision of September 1989, the stockpile became War Reserve Stocks for Allies–Israel, known as WRSA-I; in 1989 the United States agreed to place $100 million of equipment there. [cite:ow1_jinsa_wrsa] The 1989 agreement, signed on the Israeli side by Yitzhak Rabin and on the American side by Dick Cheney, also allowed Israel to lease American equipment. [cite:ow1_cie_sdi] The stockpile belongs to the United States. Israel may draw on it only with American approval, as it did with permission from the Bush administration in 2006 and the Obama administration in 2014, when the Pentagon said it was "vital to U.S. national interests to assist Israel." [cite:ow1_jinsa_wrsa] [cite:ow1_npr_wrsa2014] Congress sets how much may be added each year: since FY2025 the cap is $500 million a year through FY2027. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] Part Seven follows the stockpile inside the Pentagon.

Trade, missile defence and a new status, 1985–1988. In 1985 the United States–Israel Free Trade Agreement entered into force; the Office of the US Trade Representative describes it as "the United States' first FTA." In 2024 American goods exports to Israel were $14.8 billion and imports $22.2 billion. [cite:ow1_ustr_fta] On 6 May 1986 the two governments signed a secret agreement for Israeli participation in research under the Strategic Defense Initiative, the framework under which the Arrow missile-defence system was developed. [cite:ow1_cie_sdi] Section 1105 of the National Defense Authorization Act for FY1987 (Public Law 99-661, 4 November 1986) created the category of "major non-NATO ally," and Israel was designated in February 1987. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] On 21 April 1988 Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir and President Reagan signed a Memorandum of Agreement that recorded that designation and created standing bodies: a Joint Political-Military Group for combined planning, exercises and logistics, a Joint Security Assistance Planning Group to review Israel's aid requests each year, and a Joint Economic Development Group. It ran for five years and renews automatically. [cite:ow1_jvl_moa1988]

Early disbursement, 1991. The most unusual feature of the aid is how it is paid. Public Law 101-513, the appropriations act for FY1991, required that Israel's military aid be disbursed as a lump sum early in the fiscal year and held in an interest-bearing account at the Federal Reserve. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] Current appropriations require disbursement within 30 days of enactment. Israel used the interest for years to pay down its debts to the United States and, as of September 2024, had no outstanding sovereign debt to the US government; it may not use the interest for procurement inside Israel. [cite:ow1_crs_aid2025] A related authority under Section 23 of the Arms Export Control Act, known as cash-flow financing, lets Israel place multiyear orders and pay for them over time. [cite:ow1_crs_aid2025]

The diagram shows why the aid is often described as both a gift to Israel and a subsidy to American industry. The money is a grant to a foreign government, but almost all of it is spent in the United States, and the share Israel could spend at home has been cut to zero by the 2016 agreement. [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] What the arrangement gives Israel that other recipients do not is timing: the full year's money at once, earning interest, and the ability to commit future years' money to large orders.

The ten-year pledges, 1999 and 2007. From 1999 the aid was set by ten-year memoranda negotiated between the two executives and then funded year by year by Congress. The 1999 memorandum, covering FY1999–2008, totalled $26.7 billion, of which $21.3 billion was military; the 2007 memorandum, covering FY2009–2018, totalled $30 billion and allowed up to 26.3 per cent of it to be spent on Israeli-made equipment. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] (Some accounts attach the $30 billion figure to the 1999 memorandum; on the Congressional Research Service's figures it belongs to the 2007 one.) A memorandum is not a law. Congress is not bound by it, but it has appropriated the pledged amounts in every year since.

The edge becomes law, 2008. In 2008 the Naval Vessel Transfer Act, Public Law 110-429, wrote Israel's "qualitative military edge," or QME, over its neighbours into statute. It defined QME, required the executive to assess it every four years, and amended the Arms Export Control Act so that a proposed arms sale to another country in the Middle East must be accompanied by a determination that it will not adversely affect Israel's edge. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The law constrains what the United States sells to Israel's neighbours; it does not fix how much aid Israel receives, which is set by the memoranda and appropriations. Claims that the QME law makes it legally impossible to cut aid overstate it.

By the end of 2008 every element of the later relationship existed: political and military consultative bodies, a stockpile, a trade agreement, a privileged legal status, a unique payment method, a ten-year funding cycle and a statutory edge. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The next section shows how the years after 2009 turned this machinery into a declared "strategic partnership."

sections.h: The Partnership Era, 2009–2026
sections.html:
After 2009 the relationship was described in American law not as aid to a friendly state but as a partnership. Two statutes said so in their titles, a ten-year pledge set a record, the Pentagon moved Israel into the command that runs American forces in the Middle East, and the Department of Homeland Security opened America's borders to Israeli visitors without visas. After 7 October 2023 the scale of transfers changed again. This section follows the statutes and executive actions in order and closes with the negotiations, still open in October 2026, over what replaces the current pledge.

Two partnership acts, 2012 and 2014. The United States–Israel Enhanced Security Cooperation Act of 2012, H.R. 4133 in the House and backed in the Senate by Barbara Boxer of California with 71 co-sponsors, passed the Senate by unanimous voice vote on 29 June 2012 and was signed by President Obama on 27 July. It declared it American policy to help preserve Israel's qualitative military edge, extended the authority for the WRSA-I stockpile and for loan guarantees, called for support for Iron Dome and required a QME report within 180 days. [cite:ow_jvl_2012act] Two years later the United States–Israel Strategic Partnership Act of 2014, sponsored by Boxer and Roy Blunt of Missouri, passed the Senate unanimously on 18 September and the House by voice vote on 3 December. It declared Israel a "major strategic partner," again extended the stockpile authority, set out the visa-waiver goal, authorized joint homeland security research on border, maritime and aviation security, and asked for a report on cyber cooperation. [cite:ow_jvl_2014act] In the House both passed by overwhelming roll calls: the 2012 act 411 to 2 on 9 May 2012, and the 2014 act's House version 410 to 1 in March 2014, before the final Senate bill cleared by voice vote. [cite:ow2_stl_2012house] [cite:ow2_alg_2014house]

The record pledge, 2016. On 14 September 2016 the Obama administration concluded the third ten-year memorandum, for FY2019–2028: $38 billion, made up of $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing and $5 billion for missile defence, or $3.3 billion and $500 million a year. The White House called it "the largest single pledge of military assistance in U.S. history." The memorandum also ended Israel's right to spend part of its aid on Israeli-made equipment and on fuel, so that up to $1.2 billion more a year would go to American-produced capabilities. [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] Congress later wrote the FMF level into law: Section 1273 of the FY2021 National Defense Authorization Act authorizes not less than $3.3 billion a year through 2028. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

CENTCOM, 2021. On 15 January 2021, days before the Trump administration left office, the Pentagon moved Israel from the area of European Command to that of Central Command, which runs American operations from Egypt to Central Asia. The Wall Street Journal reported that President Trump ordered the change; the Pentagon said "the Abraham Accords paved the way." Israeli liaison officers now sit at CENTCOM's headquarters in Tampa. [cite:ow_inss_centcom] The change placed Israel inside the same American command structure as the Arab states it had long been kept apart from, and Part Seven follows its consequences.

Iron Dome and the visa waiver, 2021–2023. After the May 2021 Gaza war, House Democratic leaders removed $1 billion to replenish Iron Dome from a stopgap spending bill when some members objected, then passed it as a separate bill on 23 September 2021 by 420 votes to 9. [cite:ow1_pbs_irondome2021] On 27 September 2023 the Secretaries of Homeland Security and State designated Israel for the Visa Waiver Program, with Israeli travellers able to use the electronic system from 30 November, after Israel committed on 19 July 2023 to reciprocal treatment of all American citizens, including Palestinian Americans. [cite:ow_dhs_vwp] Part Six examines how that reciprocity commitment has been applied.

After 7 October 2023. The war that began with Hamas's attack on 7 October 2023 brought the largest transfers since 1973. Iron Dome batteries were supplied from US Army stocks. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] On 20 April 2024 the House passed the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 366 to 58, with 21 Republicans and 37 Democrats voting against; the Senate passed the combined package 79 to 18 on 23 April, and the President signed it as Public Law 118-50 on 24 April. [cite:ow1_clerk_roll152] [cite:ow1_lobby_hr815] It provided $3.5 billion in FMF, $4 billion for missile defence and $1.2 billion for the Iron Beam laser system. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] In August 2024 the State Department notified more than $20 billion in sales, including F-15IA aircraft. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] By April 2025 Israel had 751 active Foreign Military Sales cases worth $39.2 billion, and Israel's Ministry of Defense reported that 800 aircraft and 140 ships had delivered more than 90,000 tons of materiel by May 2025. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

Emergency authority, 2025. The Arms Export Control Act lets Congress review major arms sales before they proceed, but Section 36(b) allows the executive to waive that review by declaring an emergency. On 28 February 2025 Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed such a declaration covering about $4 billion in sales to Israel. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The State Department's statement of 1 March said nearly $12 billion in major sales had been approved since the inauguration, and that the declaration reversed what it called the previous administration's "partial arms embargo" and its "baseless and politicized conditions" on aid; Rubio said Israel has "no greater ally in the White House than President Trump." [cite:ow1_state_rubio2025] The critics' case, which Part Eight takes up, is that emergency declarations remove the one point at which Congress can examine a sale; the government's case is that a partner at war needs weapons faster than the review period allows. A Senate resolution introduced in December 2023 that would have required a human-rights report on Israel's use of American weapons under Section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act was defeated 72 to 11 in January 2024. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

What replaces the pledge, 2026. The 2016 memorandum expires at the end of FY2028. In January 2026 Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was reported to seek an end to American military aid within ten years, and on 1 June 2026 he wrote to Representative Marlin Stutzman that "the time has now arrived for us to move from aid recipient to partner." [cite:ow1_wiki_nextmou] On 5 June 2026 Israel's Ministry of Defense announced that formal talks had opened on a framework to "gradually transition from aid to a completely reciprocal partnership," based on joint research, development and co-production; the Israeli team is led by the ministry's director-general, Amir Baram, with Ambassador Yechiel Leiter, and the American team by State Department Counselor Daniel Holler and Ambassador Mike Huckabee. [cite:ow1_mod_mou2026] Reporting in July 2026 said Israel was pressing to accelerate the talks before the midterm elections. As of October 2026 the public record consulted does not show a concluded agreement. [cite:ow1_wiki_nextmou] Israel's government describes the shift as a move to reciprocity. Critics argue that it would hide the money rather than end it: Hadar Susskind of New Jewish Narrative, writing in The Nation on 22 June 2026, argued that folding support into Pentagon procurement and co-production would leave "no annual appropriation to debate" and "no line item to block." [cite:ow1_nation_susskind] Both are arguments about a framework whose terms are not yet public.

The partnership era thus did two things at once. It enlarged the transfers and embedded Israel more deeply in American command and border systems, and it began, at Israel's own suggestion, the move away from grants. [cite:ow1_mod_mou2026] What the United States receives through the cooperative programmes is the subject of the next section.

sections.h: What Washington Says It Gets: The Cooperative Programmes
sections.html:
This volume's title describes a one-way mirror: a relationship in which, critics argue, the United States gives far more than it can see or receive. That claim has to be tested against what the United States itself says it gains. The government's case is set out in the same documents as the aid: missile-defence systems developed jointly and partly built in America, access to Israeli technology, research foundations funded by both governments, and an aid package spent almost entirely on American products. This section sets out those programmes and their legal basis, then compares what each side receives on the documented record.

Missile defence. The largest cooperative programme began with the 1986 agreement on Israeli participation in the Strategic Defense Initiative, under which the Arrow anti-ballistic missile was developed. [cite:ow1_cie_sdi] Arrow 2 was first deployed in 2000 and Arrow 3 in 2017; development of David's Sling, against medium-range rockets, began in 2006 and it was fielded in 2017; Iron Dome, against short-range rockets, was first fielded in 2011. [cite:ow1_csis_imd] Iron Dome was built by Israel's Rafael, and American funding for it began in FY2011: $205 million in FY2011, $70 million in FY2012, $194 million in FY2013 and $460.3 million in FY2014 including an emergency supplemental, $929.3 million in its first four years. [cite:ow1_crs_irondome] In March 2014 the two governments signed a co-production agreement allowing Iron Dome components to be manufactured in the United States and giving the US Missile Defense Agency full access to Iron Dome technology, which had been proprietary; Raytheon became Rafael's American partner and received a $149 million contract for interceptor parts on 30 September 2014. [cite:ow1_crs_irondome] The 2016 memorandum fixed missile-defence support at $500 million a year and required that at least half of annual procurement and co-production funds be spent in the United States. [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] [cite:ow1_crs_aid2025]

Tunnels, drones and new technology. Congress has since added smaller programmes, each authorized in a defence bill. Section 1279 of the FY2016 National Defense Authorization Act created a US–Israel anti-tunnel cooperation programme, and Section 1278 of the FY2020 act a counter-drone programme. [cite:ow1_s554] For FY2025 they were funded at $47.5 million and $55 million, alongside $20 million for emerging technology, and the FY2025 defence act added joint subterranean exercises and a partnership with the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] A bill introduced in February 2025 by Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska and others would raise the caps and authorize $50 million a year for joint work on artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, robotics and quantum technology; its stated condition is a cost-sharing agreement before any money is spent. [cite:ow1_s554] Its status should be checked against the FY2026 defence act, which this section has not verified.

The research foundations. Older and less visible are the binational foundations. The Binational Industrial Research and Development (BIRD) Foundation was established by the two governments in 1977, with an endowment of $60 million raised to $110 million in 1984, contributed equally; it has approved more than 900 joint projects between American and Israeli companies. [cite:ow1_wiki_bird] Homeland security research runs through the same channel. Under a 2009 agreement on science and technology cooperation in homeland security, the Department of Homeland Security's Science and Technology Directorate and Israel's Ministry of Public Security set up a joint pilot in 2016, run by BIRD and renamed BIRD HLS in 2019; by 2021 the two ministries had put in $9.65 million and selected ten projects, which private partners matched with at least $20 million. [cite:ow1_dhs_birdhls] The 2014 Strategic Partnership Act authorized further joint research on border, maritime and aviation security. [cite:ow_jvl_2014act] Part Six follows this channel inside DHS.

The stated return. Read together, the official documents give four reasons the United States says the arrangement serves American interests. Strategically, they describe Israel as a partner that shares American goals in the region and whose qualitative edge, maintained with American weapons, is the best guarantee of stability; the White House called American capabilities "the best way" for Israel to keep that edge. [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] [cite:ow1_crs_aid2025] Technologically, co-production gave the Missile Defense Agency access to a combat-tested Israeli system. [cite:ow1_crs_irondome] Industrially, the end of offshore procurement means up to $1.2 billion more a year spent on American-made equipment. [cite:ow1_wh_mou2016] And logistically, the WRSA-I stockpile is American property on Israeli soil. [cite:ow1_npr_wrsa2014] Intelligence sharing, which the government also cites, is examined in Parts Three and Four.

Where the asymmetry lies. On this record the "one-way" description is too simple for the programmes themselves. The research foundations are funded equally; the missile-defence money buys systems the United States can now build and study; and most of the aid is recycled into American factories. The asymmetry the documents do show is of a different kind. It is in money: Israel received about 40 per cent of the worldwide Foreign Military Financing budget at the previous memorandum's closing level, according to former ambassador Daniel Shapiro. [cite:ow1_crs_aid2025] It is in terms: early disbursement, interest and cash-flow financing are privileges other recipients lack. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] And it is in law: the United States is bound by its own statute to protect Israel's edge, and the documents examined here contain no reciprocal commitment by Israel. Whether the United States can see what its money and weapons do once they arrive is the question the rest of this volume follows, agency by agency.

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: Who Voted It In
chapters.intro: Part Two follows how Congress built the legal spine described in Part One: the law that governs advocacy and the foreign-agent question first raised in 1962, the shift in 2021 when AIPAC began spending directly in elections, and the recorded votes on aid, missile defence, arms sales and related measures from 1973 to 2025. It links to the fuller accounts in the Follow the Money volume, and it keeps to what the filings and roll calls show: who spent what, and who voted how, without attributing motives the record does not contain.
chapters.outro: Part Two has established that AIPAC lobbies as a registered domestic organization, that the foreign-agent order of 1962 was directed at the American Zionist Council rather than AIPAC, and that FARA has been weakly enforced in general. [cite:ow2_doj_faq] [cite:ow2_barda_2026] [cite:ow2_pogo_oig2016] Since December 2021 AIPAC's PAC and super PAC have become among the largest spenders in congressional primaries, at $44 million in 2022, $95.1 million in 2024 and more than $104 million by August 2026, though analyses differ on whether the money changes outcomes beyond backing incumbents who already agree. [cite:pm_israelite_2024] [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:pm_guardian_2024] [cite:ow2_bahar_forward] The votes show large bipartisan majorities for aid and missile defence from 1973 to 2025, every attempt to condition or block aid defeated, and a Senate minority on arms sales that rose from 15 in April 2025 to 40 in April 2026. [cite:ow2_mt_apr2026] [cite:ow1_vv_rs583] [cite:pm_ji_mtg_amendment] [cite:ow2_jta_sanders2025] [cite:ow2_duckworth_jul2025] Part Three leaves Congress for the first of the agencies: the Central Intelligence Agency and its relationship with the Mossad.

sections.h: The Lobby and the Law: Lobbying, Foreign Agents and the 1963 Question
sections.html:
Part One listed the laws. This part turns to how they passed: the organized advocacy around Congress, the money that entered elections, and the votes themselves. It begins with the law that governs advocacy, because the central argument about the best-known pro-Israel organization, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, is a legal one. American law treats a citizen lobbying for a foreign-policy cause very differently from an agent acting for a foreign government, and the question of which side of that line AIPAC stands on has been argued since 1962. The Follow the Money volume of this library tells AIPAC's institutional history in [scene:pm2_origins|from a one-man office to the largest foreign-policy lobby]; this section sets out only the legal frame and the documented record of how it has been applied.

Two disclosure regimes. The Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938 requires registration by anyone who acts "at the order, request, or under the direction or control" of a foreign principal and engages in political activity for it. Lobbyists registered under the Lobbying Disclosure Act are exempt from FARA, but the exemption does not apply where a foreign government or foreign political party is the principal beneficiary. [cite:ow2_doj_faq] The difference matters. A FARA registrant must disclose its foreign principal, its activities and its payments in detail and label its informational materials; a domestic lobby discloses only its quarterly lobbying spending and the issues it lobbied on.

The 1962 order and the 1963 inquiry. AIPAC's founder, Isaiah L. Kenen, formed his committee in 1953 as a body separate from the American Zionist Council, partly because of concern about foreign-agent registration; it took the AIPAC name in 1959 by most accounts. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] The concern was tested in the early 1960s. On 21 November 1962 the Justice Department ordered the American Zionist Council, not AIPAC, to register as a foreign agent, alleging that it had received more than $5 million from the Jewish Agency, a body already registered under FARA; the Senate record carries a figure of $5,100,001.02 for 1955–1962. [cite:jta_fulbright_jewish_agency_hearing] The Senate Foreign Relations Committee under J. William Fulbright examined the payments in 1963, as part of a wider inquiry into the agents of foreign principals. Kobby Barda's 2026 study of the hearing record dates the funding inquiry to 2 August 1963 and reports testimony that the Agency paid $38,000 for subscriptions to Kenen's Near East Report through the Council; Kenen stated in an affidavit that the Council's purchases never exceeded 23 per cent of the newsletter's copies. Barda gives the Council's total receipts from the Agency as $1.5 million and concludes that the separation between the Agency and Kenen was "absolute," which is his interpretation. [cite:ow2_barda_2026] The two totals, $5.1 million and $1.5 million, have not been reconciled in any source consulted. The full account of the order and the hearing is in [scene:s11a|the order of 21 November 1962] and [scene:cw5_jewish_agency_hearing|the Jewish Agency before the Senate].

The position since. AIPAC has never registered under FARA. Its position is that it is an American organization, registered as a lobby and funded by private donations, that receives no financial assistance from Israel or any other foreign group. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] Fulbright in the 1970s and the former CIA officer Victor Marchetti in the 1980s argued that it should register anyway. [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] On the documents consulted, no public record shows the Justice Department ordering AIPAC itself to register, and no court has found it to be acting at the direction or control of the Israeli government. The argument for registration rests on structure and coordination; the argument against rests on the statutory test of direction or control, which requires more than shared aims.

The weakness of FARA enforcement in general is documented and should be kept in view. A Justice Department Inspector General audit published on 7 September 2016 found that 62 per cent of new registrants had filed late and half of the six-monthly supplemental statements were late, called the compliance rates "unacceptable," and stressed the need for "a comprehensive Department enforcement strategy on FARA." [cite:ow2_pogo_oig2016] Non-registration by an American advocacy group is therefore not, on its own, evidence of special treatment; the Act was weakly enforced across the board.

What AIPAC is, and spends. AIPAC is a 501(c)(4) social-welfare organization; donations to it are not tax-deductible, and its Forms 990 report revenue of $156.4 million in FY2024 and $122.5 million in FY2025. [cite:pm_pp_aipac990] Its lobbying disclosures are modest by comparison: about $3.5 million in 2018, roughly 147th among lobbying organizations that year, and about $3.3 million in 2024 and almost $3.8 million in 2025. [cite:pm_tablet_lobbying] [cite:pm_cjn_lobby2025] The gap between a small lobbying line and a large budget is examined in [scene:pm2_lobbying|the lobbying]: lobbying disclosures record what an organization pays lobbyists, not the time its members spend meeting their own representatives, and they do not record electoral money at all. AIPAC states its aim as persuading "the U.S. government to enact specific policies" that support the relationship, and it counted among its achievements of 2023–24 an emergency package of $14.3 billion and what it called the largest funding package in Israel's history. [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024]

The legal frame, then, is clear even where its application is argued. AIPAC lobbies as a domestic organization; the foreign-agent question was raised in 1962 against a different body and has not been resolved against AIPAC in any proceeding consulted. [cite:ow2_barda_2026] [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] The next section follows the change of 2021, when AIPAC moved from lobbying alone into direct electoral spending.

sections.h: From Lobby to Electoral Spender, 2021–2026
sections.html:
For most of its history AIPAC gave no money to candidates. Pro-Israel campaign money existed, but it flowed through separate political action committees and individual donors, and AIPAC itself lobbied. That changed in December 2021, and the change is the single largest shift in how the votes described in this part are contested. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] This section sets out the documented spending by cycle, with the date and source of each figure, and then the strongest evidence on both sides of the question of what the money achieves. The detailed accounts are in the Follow the Money volume: [scene:pm3_after_2021|the money after 2021] and the race-by-race record in [scene:pm5_2022|2022], [scene:pm5_2024|2024] and [scene:pm5_2026|2026].

The two committees. AIPAC announced in December 2021 that it would form a political action committee and a super PAC. AIPAC PAC was created on 15 December 2021 and the United Democracy Project, the super PAC, on 3 January 2022. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] The two do different legal work. The PAC collects contributions from AIPAC's members and passes them, almost all earmarked, to endorsed candidates within federal contribution limits. The super PAC may raise unlimited sums and spend them on advertising for or against candidates, provided it does not coordinate with campaigns. [cite:pm_sludge_pac2026] [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] UDP's spokesman said its aim was "to build the broadest bipartisan pro-Israel coalition in Congress possible." [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022]

The figures differ because they count different things: whether transfers to other committees and running costs are included, and when the filings were read. [cite:pm_sludge_final2024] [cite:pm_israelite_2024] None of the 2026 numbers is final; the general election of November 2026 and the reports that follow it will change them.

Where the money went. In the 2022 cycle every dollar of UDP's independent spending went into Democratic primaries; its largest donors were AIPAC itself ($8.5 million), Jan Koum ($2 million) and four donors at $1 million each. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2022] In 2024 the super PAC spent about $14.5 million against Representative Jamaal Bowman of New York and, by later counts including support for his opponent, about $8.6 million in the race that unseated Representative Cori Bush of Missouri. [cite:factcheck_udp_2024] [cite:rollcall_bush_primary_2024] AIPAC's own account of 2024 says its PAC endorsed 361 candidates, of whom 326 won their general elections, 120 Democrats and 206 Republicans, and that its endorsements covered 75 per cent of House members and 84 per cent of senators. [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024] In 2026 the super PAC began routing more than 40 per cent of its primary spending through committees with names unconnected to Israel, according to Politico as reported by FactCheck.org, spent more than $30.6 million in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, and lost it. [cite:pm_factcheck_udp_2026] [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] It spent about $4.1 million against Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, one of six members who voted in July 2025 to strip $500 million in missile-defence funding for Israel from the defence bill; [cite:pm_ji_mtg_amendment] Massie lost his primary on 19 May 2026, in a race in which a super PAC aligned with President Trump also spent heavily against him. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] That race is told in [scene:pm5_massie|the Massie primary].

Travel. A further channel bears directly on how members of Congress learn about Israel. AIPAC's affiliated charity, the American Israel Education Foundation, sponsored about 75 per cent of the privately funded trips by House members and staff to Israel since 2012, according to the Howard Center for Investigative Journalism's analysis of House disclosures; more than a quarter of all privately sponsored foreign trips by House members and staff went to Israel. [cite:cnsmd_trips_study] The trips are permitted under the congressional rules on privately sponsored travel, [cite:pm_citizen_travel] and are examined in [scene:pm7_congress|the trips].

What the money achieves: the evidence on both sides. That pro-Israel committees spend heavily, and that most members of Congress who vote for aid to Israel have received pro-Israel money, is documented. Whether the money causes the votes is a different claim, and the strongest evidence cuts both ways. A Guardian analysis found that pro-Israel donors had given more than $58 million to sitting members in their most recent elections, and that members who received more were more likely to back military support for Israel; members supportive of Israel after 7 October 2023 had received about $125,000 on average, against about $18,000 for members who spoke for Palestinians. The same analysis found that party, not money, best predicted members' statements on civilian casualties, and that the data could not show that money had changed anyone's position. [cite:pm_guardian_2024] An analysis by Dany Bahar, published as an opinion piece in The Forward in June 2026, examined 788 candidates backed by AIPAC's PAC in 2022 and 2024 and found that about 86 per cent were incumbents, who win about 95 per cent of the time whoever funds them; in tight primaries AIPAC's candidates won about 79 per cent, against 84 per cent for the NRA, 83 per cent for Planned Parenthood and 88 per cent for the Sierra Club. He concluded that AIPAC's results "do not outperform those of any other major single-issue lobby." [cite:ow2_bahar_forward] Against that, the defeats of Bowman, Bush and Massie are documented cases in which the super PAC was the largest outside spender against a sitting member who had opposed Israel policy, and each lost. [cite:rollcall_bush_primary_2024] [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding]

The record therefore supports two findings and not a third. It shows that the money is large and aimed, and that in a small number of primaries it was the largest single outside force. It shows that most of the money goes to incumbents who already vote with it. [cite:ow2_bahar_forward] [cite:pm_aipac_memo_2024] It does not show, for any named member, that a donation changed a vote; no member's own statement consulted says so, and this volume does not attribute motives that the record does not contain. The votes themselves are the subject of the next section.

sections.h: The Votes, 1973–2025
sections.html:
Every law in Part One passed through Congress, and the margins are part of the record. This section sets the main recorded votes side by side, from the emergency aid of 1973 to the arms-sale resolutions of 2025. Read in sequence, they show three things: near-unanimity in the House on aid and missile defence that has held for half a century; a small number of moments when the lobby lost or the executive overrode it; and, since 2024, a growing minority in the Senate willing to vote to block specific arms sales. The votes record what members did. They do not record why, and this section attributes reasons only where members gave them on the record.

The settled majority. The emergency aid of 1973 passed the Senate 66 to 9, and an amendment by Senator Fulbright tying part of it to compliance with Resolution 242 was tabled 62 to 12. [cite:ow1_vv_rs587] [cite:ow1_vv_rs583] Nearly four decades later the two partnership acts passed almost unopposed: the 2012 act 411 to 2 in the House and by unanimous voice vote in the Senate, and the 2014 act 410 to 1 in its House version and unanimously in the Senate. [cite:ow2_stl_2012house] [cite:ow2_alg_2014house] [cite:ow_jvl_2012act] [cite:ow_jvl_2014act] On missile defence the margin has stayed close to unanimous. The House approved $1 billion to replenish Iron Dome 420 to 9 on 23 September 2021, after Democratic leaders had first removed the money from a stopgap bill because some members objected; Majority Leader Steny Hoyer said "the overwhelming majority of this Congress — not in a partisan way but in an American way" supported it, while Representative Rashida Tlaib, the only member to speak against it, called the increase "absurd and unjustifiable." [cite:ow1_pbs_irondome2021] In July 2025 the House rejected, 422 to 6, an amendment by Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene to remove $500 million a year in cooperative missile-defence funding; the six in favour were Greene, Thomas Massie, Ilhan Omar, Al Green, Summer Lee and Tlaib. [cite:pm_ji_mtg_amendment]

When the lobby lost. The clearest documented defeat came in 1981. The Reagan administration proposed selling AWACS surveillance aircraft and F-15 enhancements to Saudi Arabia, and AIPAC campaigned against it. The House voted 301 to 111 on 14 October 1981 to disapprove the sale, but on 28 October the Senate rejected disapproval 48 to 52, and the sale went ahead. [cite:ow2_vv_awacs_house] [cite:ow2_vv_awacs_senate] [cite:pm_wiki_aipac] The episode is a reminder that a disapproval of an arms sale needs both chambers and, in practice, enough votes to survive a veto, which is why so few succeed in either direction.

After 7 October 2023. On 25 October 2023 the House adopted H.Res. 771, standing with Israel and condemning Hamas and Iran, 412 to 10. [cite:ow2_jns_hres771] The supplemental of April 2024 drew more opposition: on 20 April the House passed the Israel bill 366 to 58, with 37 Democrats and 21 Republicans against, and the Senate passed the combined package 79 to 18. [cite:ow1_clerk_roll152] [cite:ow1_lobby_hr815] On 1 May 2024 the House passed the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which would apply the IHRA definition of antisemitism in civil-rights enforcement, 320 to 91. [cite:ow2_wiki_aaa] Its Senate version stalled in committee in April 2025, and Part Eleven follows it.

The Senate minority grows. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont has repeatedly forced floor votes on resolutions to block or examine arms transfers to Israel. A January 2024 measure of his seeking a report on Israel's human-rights conduct under the Foreign Assistance Act failed 72 to 11; [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] in November 2024 three resolutions to block sales drew 19 senators; on 3 April 2025 a resolution covering about $8.8 billion in sales failed 82 to 15, with every vote in favour coming from the Democratic caucus and the Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, voting against. [cite:ow2_jta_sanders2025] On 30 July 2025 a resolution to block 20,000 automatic rifles for Israel's national police drew 27 votes and one to block $675 million in bombs drew 24, all from the Democratic caucus; senators who had voted no in April, among them Jeanne Shaheen, Jack Reed and Patty Murray, voted yes. [cite:ow2_duckworth_jul2025] [cite:ow2_bg_jul2025] On 15 April 2026 resolutions to block a $295 million sale of armoured bulldozers and a $151.8 million sale of 12,000 1,000-pound bombs failed 59 to 40 and 63 to 36, the largest minorities yet. [cite:ow2_mt_apr2026] Sanders argued that the sales would "clearly violate" the legal requirements for arms transfers because of civilian deaths in Gaza; the chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, Jim Risch of Idaho, called the resolutions "misguided" and said adopting them would abandon America's closest ally in the region. [cite:ow2_duckworth_jul2025]

What the votes show. On this record, measures that fund Israel's defence have passed by large and bipartisan margins for fifty years, while measures to condition or block aid have failed, also for fifty years, from Fulbright in 1973 to Sanders in 2025. The money described in the previous section flows to the members who cast those majorities, but so do party loyalty, constituency opinion and long-standing policy, and the record reached here cannot separate them for any individual vote. What it does show is a change at the margin: in the Senate, the number willing to vote to stop specific weapons sales roughly doubled between April and July 2025. [cite:ow2_jta_sanders2025] [cite:ow2_duckworth_jul2025] The parts that follow move from Congress to the agencies that carry out what it voted.

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: The CIA and the Mossad
chapters.intro: Part Three follows the Central Intelligence Agency's relationship with Israel's services from its beginning in the early 1950s to the summer of 2026. It shows how one officer, James Angleton, came to hold the Israel account inside the CIA's counterintelligence staff, and what passed through that channel, from Khrushchev's secret speech to captured Soviet equipment. It then sets out the CIA's own record of concern: the uranium missing from NUMEC, a 1979 report on Israel's intelligence services, and the damage assessment after the Pollard arrest. Finally it follows the partnership into Wye River, the cyberattack on Iran's Natanz plant, and the hostage negotiations after 7 October 2023, and asks what the CIA can and cannot see of what Israel does with what it receives.
chapters.outro: Part Three has shown that the CIA–Israel relationship rests on no published agreement and no act of Congress, but on a channel that began with a meeting of directors in 1951 and was held for two decades by one officer whose control of it the CIA's own historian called "an administrative anomaly." [cite:ow3_tablet] [cite:ow3_robarge] It produced documented returns for the United States, from Khrushchev's speech to Soviet radar and missile equipment, a shared attack on Natanz, and a working channel for the hostage negotiations of 2023–24. [cite:ow3_meq_siskind] [cite:ow3_npr_sanger] [cite:ow3_axios2023] It also produced the CIA's own record of concern, in NUMEC, the 1979 report and the Pollard assessment, none of which interrupted the liaison, and the NUMEC question remains officially unresolved. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] [cite:ow3_jta1982] [cite:ow3_nsa_pollard] What the record does not show is any American means of inspecting how Israel's services use what they receive: after October 2023 that rested on Israeli assurances, sometimes oral, and on the blunt option of cutting a feed. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] [cite:ow3_reu_withheld] Part Four turns to the signals relationship between the National Security Agency and Unit 8200, where the flow of raw data, including Americans' communications, is documented in the agencies' own papers.

sections.h: One Officer, One Account: The Liaison to 1967
sections.html:
The oldest of the agency ties described in this book was never written into a statute, and no vote of Congress created it. It began as an arrangement between two intelligence services, managed for its first two decades by one American officer, and it has been publicly acknowledged by both sides since the 1970s. How it began is told in detail, with the disagreements between the sources, in [scene:cw1_cia_liaison|the first ties with American intelligence] and [scene:cw2_angleton|the Angleton channel]. This section draws the outline needed for the rest of the volume: who held the account, what passed through it, and what each side received from it up to the war of June 1967.

According to the journalists Yossi Melman and Dan Raviv, the turn came in 1951, when David Ben-Gurion, on a visit to the United States, met Walter Bedell Smith, Truman's Director of Central Intelligence, and "convinced U.S. intelligence to give Israel a try." [cite:ow3_tablet] After that meeting, they write, James Jesus Angleton "was put in charge of the U.S. side", with Amos Manor and Teddy Kollek as his Israeli counterparts. [cite:ow3_tablet] No written agreement from that year has been published, and the sources disagree about when the arrangement became formal. Jeff McConnell, writing in 1986, said Angleton had exercised formal authority over the CIA's liaison with Israel from the early 1950s, how early being in dispute. [cite:ow3_merip]

The clearest description of the arrangement comes from inside the agency. David Robarge, the CIA's Chief Historian, wrote in the agency's journal in 2009 that Angleton became head of the new Counterintelligence Staff in 1954, and that his "control of that country's account at CIA, an administrative anomaly, was one of the foundations of his influence." [cite:ow3_robarge] Robarge added that Angleton "ardently supported Israel" and "saw Israel as a bastion against the Soviet Union." [cite:ow3_robarge] McConnell gave the structural detail: the Israel desk sat under Angleton's counterintelligence staff rather than in the section that handled the rest of the Middle East. [cite:ow3_merip] The consequence is the first asymmetry in this book, and it is an American one. The officer responsible for assessing whether a foreign service was working against the United States was the same officer who managed that service as a partner.

What came through the channel. The relationship's most famous product was the text of Nikita Khrushchev's secret speech of February 1956. Shammai Siskind, writing in the Middle East Quarterly in 2020, describes the route: a Polish journalist, Victor Grayevski, borrowed a copy in Warsaw; a Shin Bet agent, Yaakov Barmor, photographed it; Ben-Gurion sent it by diplomatic courier to Israel's intelligence liaison in Washington, Izzy Dorot; and only Angleton was to see it. [cite:ow3_meq_siskind] The text reached Allen Dulles by mid-April 1956, and the CIA gave it to the New York Times in early June. [cite:ow3_meq_siskind] Melman and Raviv call it "the great turning point" of the relationship. [cite:ow3_tablet]

The speech was not the only return. Israel's immigrants from the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, Melman and Raviv write, made it "an indispensable source" on Cold War questions. [cite:ow3_tablet] Siskind lists hardware and data that followed: a MiG-21 flown to Israel by a defecting Iraqi pilot in August 1966 and lent to the United States in 1968 (Siskind dates the defection to 1963; the defection itself is documented as 1966); a Soviet P-12 radar removed from Egypt in a 1969 raid and handed to Washington; an Egyptian SA-6 missile battery captured in October 1973 and shared with the United States; and, in the early 1970s, detailed information on the structure and deployment of much of the Soviet strategic missile force. [cite:ow3_meq_siskind] These are claims made by a writer sympathetic to the relationship, but they describe specific transfers, and they are the strongest documented answer to the question of what the United States received.

What Israel received. The sources for the 1950s and 1960s say less about the American side of the ledger. The critical account that dates the liaison to 1951 describes an exchange of American intelligence on the Arab states for high-value Israeli material, and that account is discussed with its weaknesses in [scene:cw1_cia_liaison|the section on the liaison's origins]. Later NSA documents, covered in Part Four, describe the American side of the signals relationship in much more concrete terms. [cite:ow_int_cash2014] For the CIA channel in its first two decades, the public record does not contain an inventory of what was given.

The war of 1967. The channel's most consequential use in this period was a conversation, not a document. On 1 June 1967, four days before the war began, Meir Amit, head of the Mossad, met Defense Secretary Robert McNamara in Washington, with the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence, Admiral Rufus Taylor, taking notes. [cite:ow3_frus_amit] Amit said the Egyptian blockade of the Straits of Tiran was "window dressing" for a larger threat, that "time is very much against Israel", and that Israel could expect about 4,000 casualties in Sinai if it held air superiority. He stressed that his remarks were "entirely informal, off the record," and McNamara said he would convey them to the President. [cite:ow3_frus_amit] What was decided afterwards, and how the American response was read in Jerusalem, is told in [scene:cw6_tiran_june4|the last days before the war]. The memorandum establishes the mechanism: Israel's foreign intelligence chief could put a case directly to the Secretary of Defense, in the presence of the CIA's second-ranking officer, without passing through the State Department.

The other side of the ledger. The same years produced the first American suspicions.
