In 1965 an audit found highly enriched uranium missing from the NUMEC plant at Apollo, Pennsylvania, a case told in [scene:fis_s07a|the NUMEC shortage] and taken up in the next section. And McConnell records that, in the mid-1950s, Angleton is generally credited with the effort to end covert operations by each service against the other. [cite:ow3_merip] Whether such an understanding existed, and whether it held, is disputed; the next section shows that the CIA's own analysts later reported Israeli collection inside the United States.

What the record does not settle. No written liaison agreement for these years has been published. The date of the no-spying understanding is uncertain, and so is whether it held. The public record does not list what American intelligence was given to Israel in return for the speech and the Soviet hardware. And the account of Angleton's alleged disclosures to Israel of CIA sources in Arab countries, which circulates in later writing, rests on no document cited in this book and is not repeated here as fact.

sections.h: What the CIA Itself Recorded, 1968–1987
sections.html:
The partnership described in the previous section was never the whole of the CIA's view of Israel. In the same decades the agency's analysts and directors produced a separate record: a request to investigate a uranium loss, a report on Israel's intelligence services that named the United States as a target, and a damage assessment after an Israeli-run spy was caught inside the US Navy. None of these documents ended the liaison. Together they show what the agency knew, when it knew it, and what it did with the knowledge.

NUMEC, 1968–1978. The shortage of highly enriched uranium at the NUMEC plant in Apollo, Pennsylvania, was found in 1965, and the first years of the case are told in [scene:fis_s07a|the NUMEC shortage]. The CIA's part began in 1968. On 2 April that year the Director of Central Intelligence, Richard Helms, asked Attorney General Ramsey Clark to "initiate a discreet intelligence investigation of an all source nature" of the company's president, Zalman Shapiro; J. Edgar Hoover approved a new FBI inquiry on 6 May. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] On 10 September 1968 four Israelis visited the plant, among them Rafi Eitan, who was later exposed as head of the scientific-intelligence bureau that ran Jonathan Pollard. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] On 3 September 1969 Hoover told Helms that the FBI was discontinuing its active investigation. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec]

The CIA's own judgment was firmer than the FBI's. A CIA memorandum of March 1972 called diversion "a distinct possibility", and in 1976 Carl Duckett, the agency's former deputy director for science and technology, briefed the Nuclear Regulatory Commission on the CIA's late-1960s conclusion that Israel's first weapons "owed in some measure to uranium from the NUMEC plant." [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] On the other side stand the Atomic Energy Commission, which told Congress in February 1966 that it had "found no evidence of theft"; President Carter's national security adviser, Zbigniew Brzezinski, who wrote in 1977 that there was "no evidence—despite an intensive search for some—to prove that one did" occur; and the General Accounting Office, which concluded in December 1978 that "a diversion could not be ruled out." [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] The editors of the fullest documentary collection judge the evidence "strong but not incontrovertible," and note that "the CIA has released none of its internal operational documents" behind its conclusions. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] No official body has found that a diversion occurred, and no one was charged. The question is officially unresolved, and this book treats it so.

The 1979 report. The second document reached the public by accident. When Iranian militants occupied the US embassy in Tehran in 1979, they seized classified papers and later published them. In February 1982 the Washington Post, in a story by Scott Armstrong, summarized one of them: a 47-page CIA report on Israel's intelligence services. [cite:ow3_jta1982] According to the summary, the report said Israel's collection of secret American policy information ranked "only second and third in priority" after the Arab states, and that its collection was "especially concentrated in the Soviet Union and the United States as well as the United Nations." [cite:ow3_jta1982] The Christian Science Monitor reported that the Post and the Boston Globe described papers saying Israeli services had "used blackmail, bugs, wiretaps, and bribe offers to US government employees"; the CIA had no comment. [cite:ow3_csm1982]

Israel's government rejected the report. Prime Minister Menachem Begin's spokesman, Uri Porat, called it a "cheap invention not worthy of comment"; an unnamed official in Jerusalem said the source, Iran, "cannot be described as a reliable source by any stretch of the imagination"; and a former Israeli intelligence officer said it was "highly unlikely" the CIA would have kept such a document in Tehran. [cite:ow3_jta1982] Both positions belong in the record. The document's authenticity has not been confirmed by the CIA, and the Monitor reported four years later that a classified 1979 CIA report "reportedly" named secret American policy information and scientific intelligence as Israel's top priorities in the United States. [cite:ow3_csm1986] The report's existence is therefore attested by repeated press summaries rather than by an official release.

A Justice Department veteran gave the same picture from the American side. John Davitt, who led the department's internal-security section and resigned in 1980, told the New York Times that "the Israeli intelligence service, when I was in the Justice Department, was the second most active" in the United States, after the Soviet Union's. [cite:ow3_merip] Stansfield Turner, CIA director under Carter, said after the Pollard arrest: "Of course it goes on." [cite:ow3_csm1986] Davitt's ranking and the later National Intelligence Estimate that placed Israel third, discussed in Part Four, come from different eras and different sources; they are not in conflict, and neither is a public finding.

Pollard, 1987. The third document is the most complete. After the FBI arrested Jonathan Pollard, a civilian analyst for the Navy, in November 1985, the CIA's Foreign Denial and Deception Analysis Committee wrote a damage assessment dated 30 October 1987. [cite:ow3_nsa_pollard] The CIA withheld most of it in 2006; the Interagency Security Classification Appeals Panel ordered much of it released in 2012. [cite:ow3_nsa_pollard] It found that Pollard had passed about 800 documents, many top secret or codeword, plus some 1,500 intelligence summary messages; that the bureau running him was LAKAM, then headed by Rafi Eitan; and that his Israeli taskings concerned Arab states, Pakistan and the Soviet Union. [cite:ow3_nsa_pollard] It also recorded what Israel did not ask for: the Israelis "never expressed interest in US military activities, plans, capabilities, or equipment." [cite:ow3_nsa_pollard] The prosecution, the sentence and the later release are told in Part Five.

What the documents show about the mechanism. In each case the CIA's knowledge travelled no further than an assessment or a referral. The agency could ask the FBI to investigate, as Helms did in 1968, and it could assess damage after an arrest, as in 1987. It had no authority of its own to act inside the United States, and the decisions that followed, whether to prosecute, to press Israel or to continue the partnership, were taken elsewhere. McConnell cited a 1978 Senate Intelligence Committee study finding that the FBI investigated "friendly" services only in response to specific complaints, that what it learned rarely reached prosecutors, and that the CIA and the State Department discouraged penalties against friendly services. [cite:ow3_merip] Melman and Raviv, writing from inside the relationship, acknowledge that American law enforcement "busted several conspiracies run by Israelis to procure defense and high-tech secrets," mostly run by military officers and LAKAM rather than the Mossad. [cite:ow3_tablet] Throughout these years the liaison itself continued.

What the record does not settle. Whether NUMEC uranium reached Israel remains unproven in either direction, and the CIA's operational files remain closed. The 1979 report has never been officially acknowledged, and its text is known only through press summaries of a document published by a hostile government. And no public document records any decision, in any administration, to limit the CIA–Israel liaison because of what these three files contained.

sections.h: Natanz, Wye River and the Hostage Channel, 1998–2026
sections.html:
After the Cold War the CIA–Israel relationship moved from the Soviet target to three others: the Israeli–Palestinian security arrangements of the 1990s, Iran's nuclear programme, and, after 7 October 2023, the hostages held in Gaza. Each is documented in public sources, and each shows the liaison working at the level of agency directors. This section sets out what is on the record, how the liaison exchange works as far as the sources describe it, and the one thing the record does not show: any American mechanism for overseeing what Israel's services do with what they receive.

Wye River, 1998. The agency's most public role came in the peace process. The Wye River Memorandum, signed on 23 October 1998, created American–Palestinian and American–Palestinian–Israeli security committees, the three-party one meeting at least every two weeks. [cite:ow3_crs_wye] The Congressional Research Service reported that its many references to the United States were "understood to create an unusually visible role for the CIA," that CIA Director George Tenet had been among the negotiators, and that some Members of Congress were concerned enough for the Senate Intelligence Committee to plan hearings. [cite:ow3_crs_wye] Melman and Raviv record that Tenet, as deputy director, had been tasked in 1996 with building Yasser Arafat's security forces into a professional body, and took charge of the mission again in 2001 after the second intifada began. [cite:ow3_tablet] The CIA's on-the-ground role in this period was therefore directed chiefly at the Palestinian side's security commitments; CRS describes a committee that reviewed Palestinian steps against armed groups. [cite:ow3_crs_wye]

Olympic Games, 2006–2010. The deepest operational partnership on record is the cyberattack on Iran's enrichment plant at Natanz. According to David Sanger of the New York Times, the programme, code-named Olympic Games, began under President George W. Bush around 2006, and Israel's Unit 8200 supplied technical expertise and intelligence on Natanz that was critical to its success. [cite:ow3_sw_sanger] Sanger said a "beacon" mapped the plant's systems and "phoned home, back to the National Security Agency and the Unit 8200." [cite:ow3_npr_sanger] He also gave the American reason for bringing Israel in: Bush "didn't want to see the Israelis bomb the Iran facilities," and "the Israelis needed to be convinced that there was an alternative to a military attack." [cite:ow3_npr_sanger] The worm escaped through a programming error and was discovered in July 2010; President Obama, briefed with Vice President Biden and CIA Director Leon Panetta, decided to continue, and the last attack took out nearly 1,000 of the 5,000 centrifuges then spinning. [cite:ow3_sw_sanger] The official internal estimate was a delay of 18 months to two years. [cite:ow3_npr_sanger] Neither government has officially acknowledged the operation; Sanger's account rests on unnamed participants. The partnership on Iran continued: in July 2026 Roman Gofman, who became head of the Mossad on 2 June 2026, made his first Washington visit to meet CIA Director John Ratcliffe and White House officials about Iran; the CIA and the Mossad declined to comment. [cite:ow3_fmt_gofman] [cite:ow3_axios_gofman]

The hostage channel, 2023–2024. After the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, the CIA director became one of the principal negotiators. On 9 November 2023 William Burns met the Mossad chief, David Barnea, and Qatar's prime minister in Doha; during the releases that followed, Burns and his staff were in constant contact with a joint Israeli–Qatari "situation room" at Mossad headquarters, and the first deal exchanged 50 hostages for 150 Palestinian prisoners and a four-day pause. [cite:ow3_axios2023] The three met again on 28 November, with Egypt's intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, also present. [cite:ow3_axios2023] On 28 January 2024 Burns, Barnea, the Qatari prime minister, Kamel and Israel's Shin Bet chief, Ronen Bar, met in Paris to discuss a framework for a two-month pause and phased releases. [cite:ow3_bs_paris] Neither Israel nor the United States negotiated directly with Hamas; Qatar mediated. [cite:ow3_axios2023] The last twenty living hostages were released on 13 October 2025. [cite:gz_kt_hostages]

What flowed the other way. The war also changed the American side of the exchange. The Wall Street Journal reported in April 2024 that a secret White House memorandum, issued shortly after 7 October and amended days later, expanded intelligence sharing with Israel to include raw material such as live drone video over Gaza. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] The same report said the United States had expanded its own collection on Gaza, having previously relied largely on Israel for it. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] The stated purpose was limited: an administration official said sharing "is focused on hostage-recovery efforts and preventing future incursions into Israel," and, according to people familiar with it, the United States did not share intelligence intended specifically for ground or air strikes. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] Israel's military spokesman, Rear Admiral Daniel Hagari, said: "We are experiencing unprecedented levels of intelligence coordination." [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing]

What the CIA does not do. The public record contains no mechanism by which the CIA, or any other American body, inspects how Israel's services use the intelligence they receive, or audits their operations in Gaza and the West Bank. The Journal reported that Israel certifies its own compliance with American conditions, "sometimes orally," and that officials found it hard to know how American intelligence was used once it was combined with Israel's own data. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] Representative Jason Crow wrote to the Director of National Intelligence in December 2023 asking for details, citing "some pretty big inconsistencies" between Israeli and American accounts of civilian harm. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing]

The levers that do exist are blunt. Reuters reported in December 2025 that, in the second half of 2024, the United States cut off a live drone feed over Gaza for at least a few days and restricted how Israel could use certain intelligence on high-value targets, because of concern over civilian deaths and over the Shin Bet's treatment of prisoners; sharing resumed after Israel gave assurances, and President Biden declined a more formal cutoff in his last weeks in office. [cite:ow3_reu_withheld] The Israeli military's response was: "The strategic intelligence cooperation continued throughout the war." [cite:ow3_reu_withheld] Reuters also reported that American intelligence gathered in 2024 indicated Israeli military lawyers had warned of evidence that could support war-crimes charges, and that government lawyers concluded it remained legal to keep supplying weapons and intelligence because the United States had not gathered its own evidence of violations. [cite:ow3_reu_lawyers] Israel strongly denies war crimes, and the State Department said: "We do not comment on intelligence matters." [cite:ow3_reu_lawyers]

The mechanism is therefore the reverse of the one Part Four documents for signals intelligence. There, American raw data goes to Israel under rules the United States wrote and Israel applies. Here, American visibility into what Israel does with the product depends on Israeli assurances, and the legal threshold for stopping the flow depends on evidence the United States has not, on the record, set out to collect itself. Both governments describe the relationship as one of mutual benefit, and the documented returns, from the Khrushchev speech to Natanz to the hostage negotiations, are real. [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] [cite:ow3_meq_siskind]

What the record does not settle. The text of the post-7 October memorandum has not been published. Whether the restrictions reported by Reuters remain in place, as of October 2026, is not publicly known. Sanger's account of Olympic Games has not been officially confirmed. And the public record does not show any congressional hearing devoted to the CIA–Israel liaison as such.

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: The NSA and Unit 8200
chapters.intro: Part Four turns to signals intelligence, the one strand of the relationship whose working rules are known from the agencies' own papers. It sets out the 2009 memorandum under which the National Security Agency sends Israel's Unit 8200 raw intercepts, Americans' communications included, and the few, unenforceable limits it places on their use. It then reads the NSA's own documents for what each side gets, how the NSA judged the balance, and how the same agency ranked Israel as an intelligence threat, alongside the American monitoring of Israel's prime minister. Finally it tests the volume's central claim: that American data flows to Israel while the United States has no comparable view of Israel's surveillance of Gaza and the West Bank, much of it reported to have been stored on an American company's cloud.
chapters.outro: Part Four has shown that the NSA "routinely" sends Unit 8200 raw collection, "minimised and unminimised," under a 2009 memorandum that lets Israel keep Americans' identities for a year, requires the destruction only of American officials' communications, rests Americans' other protections on non-binding Israeli undertakings, and creates no "legally enforceable rights." [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] The NSA's own history judged the exchange "arguably tilted heavily in favor of Israeli security concerns," while its threat assessments said "Israel also targets us," a charge Israel denies; the United States, for its part, kept monitoring Israel's prime minister. [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] [cite:ow_td_spying2015] [cite:ow4_aj_wsj2015] Joint operations such as the attack on Natanz show a real American return. [cite:ow3_npr_sanger] But on Gaza and the West Bank the American government's own words describe incomplete information and Israeli assurances, and the one documented review of Unit 8200's use of American cloud infrastructure was made by Microsoft, not by any oversight body. [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20] [cite:ow4_eweek_msft] Part Five turns to the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the agency charged with catching foreign spies on American soil, and to the cases in which Israel's services were the subject.

sections.h: The 2009 Memorandum: Raw Intercepts, Americans Included
sections.html:
The signals-intelligence relationship between the United States and Israel is the one tie in this book whose working rules are known from the agencies' own documents. Israel's signals unit, called the Israeli SIGINT National Unit (ISNU) in American papers and Unit 8200 in Israel, is reported to have been founded in 1952 under military intelligence, as told in [scene:cw1_cia_liaison|the first ties with American intelligence]. [cite:unit8200_wiki] Its partnership with the National Security Agency grew over the following decades, but its terms became public only in 2013, when The Guardian published a memorandum provided by the former NSA contractor Edward Snowden. This section sets out what that memorandum says, how the data moves, and what limits it places on each side.

What the memorandum says. The memorandum between the NSA and ISNU, agreed in principle in March 2009, begins with the practice it regulates: "NSA routinely sends ISNU minimised and unminimised raw collection." [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] [cite:ow_aj_nsamou] "Raw" is defined to include "unevaluated and unminimized transcripts," and the material is described in The Guardian's account as intercepts of telephone and internet traffic that had not been screened to remove information about American citizens. [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] "Minimization" is the American legal process for masking or deleting information about US persons before intelligence is shared or used; the memorandum covers material sent before that step. [cite:ow4_techdirt]

The obligations on Israel are few, and none is legally binding. Israel agreed not to deliberately target Americans identified in the data, to handle it according to US law and to respect Americans' constitutional privacy rights. [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] Israel may retain "any files containing the identities of US persons" for up to a year, and is to consult an NSA liaison when such files are found. [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] It must "destroy upon recognition" any communication to or from an official of the United States government, a category The Guardian described as covering the executive branch, Congress and the federal courts. [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] Access is limited to Israeli personnel with a "strict need to know." [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] Israel may pass material to "outside parties" with the NSA's written permission, after stripping out identifying details. [cite:ow4_techdirt] On the American side, the NSA undertakes to "regularly review a sample of files transferred to ISNU to validate the absence of US persons' identities." [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian]

The memorandum then removes its own force: "This agreement is not intended to create any legally enforceable rights," and it disclaims being an international agreement or a legally binding instrument. [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] Techdirt's summary of the document put the result plainly: the agreement "places no legally binding limits on the use of the data by the Israelis." [cite:ow4_techdirt]

The stated purpose. The NSA did not deny that Americans' communications were included. It said that any US-person information it acquires "is handled under procedures that are designed to protect privacy rights," that "whenever we share intelligence information, we comply with all applicable rules," and that "NSA cannot, however, use these relationships to circumvent US legal restrictions." [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] It declined to say whether the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court had approved the arrangement. [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] The rationale for sending raw rather than finished intelligence is not stated in the memorandum itself; the NSA's general position is that partnerships with foreign services strengthen the security of both nations. [cite:ow_int_cash2014]

The minimization asymmetry. Inside the United States, Americans' communications collected by the NSA pass through minimization before they are used or shared. The memorandum moves a part of that material to a foreign service before that step, and puts in its place non-binding Israeli undertakings (not to target Americans deliberately, one-year retention, destruction of officials' communications, need-to-know access) and one American sampling check. The protection is uneven even on its own terms: the communications of members of Congress, judges and executive officials are to be destroyed when recognized, while those of other Americans may be kept for a year. [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] And none of it is enforceable. [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] The published accounts of the memorandum describe no reciprocal clause obliging ISNU to send its own raw collection, or Israelis' communications, to the NSA under comparable terms. [cite:ow4_techdirt] [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian]

The limits the NSA did hold. The relationship has not been without American refusals. In an internal account of the 2006 war in Lebanon, published by The Intercept in 2019, the NSA's liaison officer in Tel Aviv described ISNU's heavy reliance on the agency for time-sensitive tasking, warning and geolocation on Hezbollah. [cite:ow4_int2019] The geolocation requests were "particularly problematic," because the NSA was prohibited from providing information usable in targeted killings; ISNU's commander sought an exemption, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence brokered a framework whose terms the documents do not give. [cite:ow4_int2019] A 2007 NSA presentation put ISNU's size at about 5,500 conscripts and 1,200 career officers. [cite:ow4_int2019]

Is it still in force? The memorandum of 2009 is the last version of the rules to have been published. The public record does not show whether it remains in force, has been renewed or has been replaced, as of October 2026, and neither government has said. The general terms of American intelligence-sharing agreements with foreign governments are not published; the American Civil Liberties Union, seeking them through freedom-of-information requests, listed Israel among the countries with which the United States has unilateral data-sharing arrangements, and noted that even the FBI's rules for sharing data collected under Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act are entirely redacted in the court-approved guidelines. [cite:ow4_aclu]

What the record does not settle. How much American data has been sent under the memorandum, how often the NSA's sample review has found US-person identities, and whether any file has been destroyed or retained under its terms are not public. Whether the arrangement was ever presented to the surveillance court is not known. And whether its terms still govern the flow in 2026 is, on the public record, an open question.

sections.h: What Each Side Gets, and Who Watches Whom
sections.html:
The 2009 memorandum governs one flow. The NSA's own papers, published from the Snowden archive in 2013, 2014 and 2015, describe the whole relationship: what Israel receives, what the United States receives, how the NSA itself judged the balance, and how the same agency classed Israel as a counterintelligence threat. They also show the United States collecting on Israel. Read together, they test the claim that the signals relationship runs one way.

The NSA's own description. An NSA document of 13 April 2013, titled "NSA Intelligence Relationship with Israel" and published by The Intercept in August 2014, says: "NSA maintains a far-reaching technical and analytic relationship with the Israeli SIGINT National Unit," "sharing information on access, intercept, targeting, language, analysis and reporting." [cite:ow_int_cash2014] [cite:ow_york_nsadoc] It describes "a dedicated communications line between NSA and ISNU [that] supports the exchange of raw material." [cite:ow_int_cash2014] On Israel's side of the ledger, it says Israel gains "expanded geographic access to world-class NSA cryptanalytic and SIGINT engineering expertise" and "controlled access to advanced U.S. technology and equipment via accommodation buys and foreign military sales." [cite:ow_int_cash2014] The geographic targets named include North Africa, the Middle East and the Persian Gulf, and Israel's priorities include what the NSA calls "Palestinian terrorism." [cite:ow_int_cash2014] Documents from 2003–04 negotiations over a proposed agreement code-named Gladiator include receipts for cash payments of $500,000 to Israeli officials for unspecified purposes; the agreement appears never to have been finalized. [cite:ow_int_cash2014] The NSA's public statement was that such cooperation "mutually strengthens the security of both nations." [cite:ow_int_cash2014]

The NSA's judgment of the balance. An internal NSA history of 2007, "History of the US – Israel Sigint Relationship, Post-1992," published by The Guardian, put the agency's view in two sentences: "Balancing the Sigint exchange equally between US and Israeli needs has been a constant challenge," and "In the last decade, it arguably tilted heavily in favor of Israeli security concerns." [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] This is the strongest documentary support for the one-way thesis, and it comes from the NSA itself. It is a judgment of balance, not a statement that nothing flowed to the United States.

What the United States received. The clearest documented American return is operational. Olympic Games, the attack on Iran's enrichment plant at Natanz, depended on intelligence and expertise from Unit 8200: David Sanger reported that the beacon which mapped the plant "phoned home, back to the National Security Agency and the Unit 8200," and that the American aim was to give Israel an alternative to bombing Iran. [cite:ow3_npr_sanger] [cite:ow3_sw_sanger] The CIA channel described in Part Three supplied Cold War intelligence and captured Soviet equipment. [cite:ow3_meq_siskind] The 2013 document names geographic access as something Israel gains, which implies that the regions in question were ones where Israeli collection was valued; it does not list Israeli products supplied to the NSA. [cite:ow_int_cash2014]

"Israel also targets us." The same archive records the NSA's view of Israel as an intelligence threat. A 2008 NSA document, an interview headed "Which Foreign Intelligence Service Is the Biggest Threat to the US?", said: "Israel also targets us," and noted that "a NIE [National Intelligence Estimate] ranked [Israel] as the third most aggressive intelligence service against the US." [cite:ow_td_spying2015] A senior NSA official quoted in a 2008 document said: "One of NSA's biggest threats is actually from friendly intelligence services, like Israel." [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] The intelligence community's 2013 budget request listed Israel, in The Intercept's description, among the most threatening cyber-adversaries, and as a "hostile" foreign intelligence service. [cite:ow_td_spying2015] After the Wall Street Journal reported in March 2015 that Israel had spied on the American negotiations with Iran and passed material to members of Congress, Prime Minister Netanyahu's office replied: "The state of Israel does not conduct espionage against the United States or Israel's other allies." [cite:ow4_statewatch2015] [cite:ow_td_spying2015] The denial and the documents stand side by side; the documents are the NSA's assessments, not findings tested in any court.

The mirror reflects back. The United States also collects on Israel. The Wall Street Journal reported in December 2015 that the NSA kept intercepting Netanyahu's communications after President Obama announced, in January 2014, curbs on monitoring the leaders of allied countries; Netanyahu was kept off the protected list because monitoring him served a "compelling national security purpose." [cite:ow4_aj_wsj2015] The intercepts gave the administration an inside view of Israel's campaign to turn Congress against the Iran agreement, and, according to the report, swept up communications with members of Congress; a 2011 NSA directive requires such communications to be destroyed unless the NSA director waives the rule for "significant foreign intelligence." [cite:ow4_aj_wsj2015] The National Security Council said the United States does not conduct foreign surveillance "unless there is a specific and validated national security purpose"; the Israeli embassy declined to comment. [cite:ow4_aj_wsj2015] Melman and Raviv describe American surveillance of Israel as routine. [cite:ow3_tablet] The documented asymmetry is not that only one side watches. It is in what is handed over by agreement.

What the record does not settle. No document published so far lists what ISNU sends to the NSA, in volume or in kind, so the balance can be judged only from the NSA's own words. The purpose of the Gladiator cash payments is not explained in the documents. The National Intelligence Estimate that ranked Israel third has not been published. And neither government has officially confirmed Sanger's account of Olympic Games.

sections.h: Unit 8200, Gaza and the Limits of American Sight
sections.html:
The question at the centre of this volume can be put precisely for signals intelligence. Americans' communications flow to Israel under the 2009 memorandum. Does any comparable flow, or any American oversight, reach the other way, into Israel's surveillance of Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank? This section tests the claim against what the documents show: what Unit 8200 does in the occupied territories, on whose infrastructure, what the United States says it receives about Gaza, and what American oversight bodies can see.

What Unit 8200 does at home. The NSA's 2013 description of the partnership lists Israel's priorities, among them what it calls "Palestinian terrorism." [cite:ow_int_cash2014] The clearest account of the unit's work on Palestinians came from its own reservists. In September 2014, 43 veterans and reservists of Unit 8200, ten of them officers, wrote to Prime Minister Netanyahu, the chief of staff and the head of military intelligence that "the intelligence gathered harms innocents and is used for political persecution," and that "our conscience no longer permits us to serve this system." [cite:ow4_jta_letter] One signatory said in a radio interview that the unit's task was "not defense but ruling another people." [cite:ow4_jta_letter] The signatories were 43 people from a unit the NSA counted in 2007 at about 5,500 conscripts and 1,200 career officers, and their account is their own; one signatory declined to give examples, citing field security. [cite:ow4_jta_letter] [cite:ow4_int2019]

On American infrastructure. In August 2025 a joint investigation by The Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call reported that Unit 8200 had stored millions of intercepted Palestinian phone calls from Gaza and the West Bank on Microsoft's Azure cloud, in data centres in the Netherlands and Ireland, under a system insiders described as handling "a million calls an hour"; at least 11,500 terabytes had been uploaded by July 2025. [cite:ow4_newarab_azure] Sources told the reporters the archive was used to identify airstrike targets in Gaza and to justify arrests in the West Bank. [cite:ow4_newarab_azure] The Israeli military said its cooperation with Microsoft rested on "legally supervised agreements" and complied with international law. [cite:ow4_newarab_azure]

Microsoft's response was the most concrete act of review in the record, and it came from a company, not a government. On 25 September 2025 its president, Brad Smith, said an internal review had found "evidence that supports elements of The Guardian's reporting," including the Israel Ministry of Defense's use of Azure storage in the Netherlands and of AI services, and that Microsoft would "cease and disable specified IMOD subscriptions and their services." [cite:ow4_eweek_msft] "We do not provide technology to facilitate mass surveillance of civilians," he wrote. [cite:ow4_tc_msft] Microsoft reviewed its own business records and did not access the customer's data. [cite:ow4_eweek_msft] An Israeli security official told the Associated Press the move would cause "no damage to the operational capabilities" of the military, and Israel Hayom reported a shift to another provider, reportedly Amazon Web Services. [cite:ow4_cbc_msft] [cite:ow4_ih_msft] The public record does not show any review of the matter by an American government body.

The people. Unit 8200's alumni hold documented roles in American technology. Check Point's founders Gil Shwed and Shlomo Kramer served in the unit; Nir Zuk, another alumnus, founded Palo Alto Networks; CyberArk's chief executive Udi Mokady is described as an alumnus. [cite:ow4_sw_alumni] Assaf Rappaport, a co-founder of Wiz, served in Unit 8200; he and his co-founders led Microsoft's Cloud Security Group after Microsoft bought their earlier company in 2015, and Google completed its $32 billion purchase of Wiz on 11 March 2026. [cite:ow4_sequoia_wiz] [cite:ow4_globes_wiz] These are records of military service and commercial careers. No document cited in this book shows any of these companies passing data to Israeli intelligence, and none is implied.

What the United States receives about Gaza. Before October 2023, according to the Wall Street Journal, the United States relied largely on Israel for intelligence on Gaza; after the Hamas attack it expanded its own collection. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] On 3 November 2023 the Pentagon announced: "In support of hostage recovery efforts, the U.S. is conducting unarmed [unmanned aerial vehicle] flights over Gaza." [cite:ow4_d1_drones] That is the documented American eye over Gaza, and its stated purpose is the hostages. On the conduct of the war, the government's own report to Congress of 10 May 2024, required by National Security Memorandum 20, said that "Israel has not shared complete information to verify whether U.S. defense articles were specifically used" in incidents of concern, and that the lack of American personnel on the ground made it "difficult to assess or reach conclusive findings on individual incidents." [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20] The same report found it "reasonable to assess" that American weapons had been used in instances inconsistent with Israel's obligations under international humanitarian law. [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20] It also recorded that Israel had shared some information on targeting decisions and battle-damage assessments. [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20]

What American oversight bodies can see. The memorandum creates no enforceable rights and its approval by the surveillance court has not been disclosed. [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] The terms of American intelligence-sharing agreements with foreign governments are not published at all: the most recent public text of the core Five Eyes agreement dates from 1955, and freedom-of-information requests for current terms had not produced records. [cite:ow4_js_ukusa] Members of Congress asking about the post-7 October sharing were writing letters to the Director of National Intelligence for details. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] And the use of shared intelligence inside Israeli operations rests, as Part Three showed, on Israeli assurances. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing]

The test, stated. On the documented record the claim holds in a precise form. Raw American intercepts, including Americans' communications, go to Israel by written arrangement; the published accounts describe no reciprocal arrangement; and the American government's own statements about Gaza describe incomplete information and reliance on Israeli assurances rather than independent sight. [cite:ow4_dawn_guardian] [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20] [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] The claim needs three qualifications. The United States watches Israel too, including its prime minister. [cite:ow4_aj_wsj2015] Since November 2023 it has flown its own drones over Gaza, for a stated and limited purpose. [cite:ow4_d1_drones] And the NSA treated some Israeli requests, such as targeting data for killings in 2006, as "particularly problematic"; the documents do not record the outcome. [cite:ow4_int2019] What is not documented is any American access to Unit 8200's own surveillance of Gaza and the West Bank comparable to Israel's access to American raw collection. The public record does not show that such access exists; it also does not prove that it does not.

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: The FBI
chapters.intro: Part Five follows the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the agency charged with catching foreign spies and unregistered foreign agents in the United States, through eighty years of cases involving Israel. It begins with what the Bureau knew of the arms network of 1945–48 and the early counterintelligence cases, and its part in the long and unresolved NUMEC inquiry. It then sets out the three cases that reached court, Jonathan Pollard, Ben-Ami Kadish and the AIPAC case, and one that is often miscounted. Finally it places the counterintelligence warnings of 1996 to 2026, each beside Israel's denial, alongside the other track of the relationship: the FBI's office in Israel, its training ties and its own description of a partnership that runs both ways.
chapters.outro: Part Five has shown that the FBI watched the arms network of 1945–48 while it ran, that its prosecutions were few and were later pardoned, and that its NUMEC inquiry ended in 1980 without a charge or a finding. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] [cite:nbc_bush_pardons_winters] [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] Of the three Israel-related cases that reached court, Pollard's ended in a life sentence, an Israeli apology and, in 2020, a prime minister's welcome; Kadish's in a fine; and the AIPAC case in dropped charges against the two staffers, while a fourth case, Nozette's, was an FBI sting. [cite:ow5_nsa_pollard] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] [cite:pm_wiki_franklin] [cite:justice_nozette] Counterintelligence warnings from 1996 to the Defense Intelligence Agency's reported "critical" rating in June 2026 have each been met with Israeli denial and no prosecution, while the Bureau's own office in Israel describes a partnership of real counterterrorism value. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] [cite:fbi_israel_story] Part Six turns from the intelligence and investigative agencies to the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the police.

sections.h: The Bureau Watching, 1945–1980
sections.html:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation is the American agency charged with catching foreign spies and unregistered foreign agents on American soil. Its record with Israel begins before the state existed and runs, in this part, to the summer of 2026. Unlike the CIA and the NSA, the FBI's tie to Israel is not mainly a partnership; for most of its history it is a file of investigations, a few of which ended in court. This section covers the first thirty-five years: the arms network of 1945–48, the early counterintelligence cases, and the Bureau's part in the NUMEC inquiry.

The arms network, 1945–1948. The story of how a network founded at Rudolf Sonneborn's New York apartment in July 1945 bought weapons, aircraft and machinery in the United States and moved them to the Haganah through neutral countries is told in full in [scene:s07d|the Sonneborn meeting] and [scene:s07e|the arms network in operation]. What matters here is what the Bureau knew. Federal agencies, the FBI and the Customs Service among them, documented parts of the operation while it was running, after President Truman's embargo on arms for Palestine of December 1947. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The prosecutions that followed, under the Neutrality Act, were few. Charles Winters was convicted and served 18 months; Hank Greenspun and Al Schwimmer were convicted and served no prison time; all three were later pardoned, Greenspun by Kennedy in 1961, Schwimmer by Clinton in 2000 and Winters posthumously by George W. Bush in 2008. [cite:nbc_bush_pardons_winters] A reference account of Israeli espionage in the United States summarizes the outcome: the FBI's investigations produced a few convictions, but most offenders avoided prison. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp]

The Bureau was watching on other grounds too, and the two should not be merged. FBI records obtained under the Freedom of Information Act show that between 1947 and 1948 it wiretapped activists linked to the International Workers Order, and kept the Zionist Organization of America under scrutiny, because it suspected Communist influence, not because of the arms network. [cite:cato_fbi_wiretap] The earlier wartime surveillance of the Bergson group, begun at the State Department's instigation, is told in [scene:fa_s01|who Washington watched]. And in 1952 the FBI's file on the donor Abraham Feinberg records an order to register as a foreign agent for a publication he ran, which he closed rather than register, as told in [scene:s07f2|one donor, one decision]. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file]

The first counterintelligence cases. Once the state existed, the Bureau's concern shifted from smuggling to espionage. The reference account records a 1948 complaint by Secretary of State George Marshall that Israeli delegates at the United Nations knew Truman's instructions "almost as soon" as they were sent, and an FBI finding in 1954 that Israeli intelligence had cultivated sources inside the American government. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] Stephen Green, writing in the Christian Science Monitor in 1989 from his research on Israeli intelligence in America, described a 1956 case in which an Israeli official offered payment to Earl Jensen, an American embassy employee, for classified material; Jensen cooperated with the FBI and the Justice Department and passed selected documents to two Israeli contacts, who were apparently not arrested or prosecuted. [cite:ow5_csm1989] Green described another between 1976 and 1979, when an assistant Israeli army attaché, Colonel Yosef Langotsky, repeatedly entered secure areas of the Pentagon and tried to recruit employees; the Defense Department cut off his access and Israel recalled him in early 1979. [cite:ow5_csm1989] Both are one researcher's accounts; neither led to a prosecution.

NUMEC. The Bureau's longest Israel-related file concerned the uranium missing from the NUMEC plant in Apollo, Pennsylvania, found in 1965. Its first contact, in June 1966, was an interview with the company's president, Zalman Shapiro, about whether he should register as a foreign agent; he was not asked about the missing material. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] The Atomic Energy Commission had told Congress that February that "an inquiry by the FBI is not now warranted." [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] The Bureau reopened the case at the CIA's request in April–May 1968, and on 3 September 1969 Hoover told the CIA that the FBI was discontinuing its active investigation. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] Green reported that in 1969, following FBI recommendations, NUMEC lost its uranium-processing contracts and its president's security clearances were lifted. [cite:ow5_csm1989] In April 1976 Attorney General Edward Levi told President Ford that the Justice Department could not rule out a criminal charge, and the FBI interviewed Shapiro again in 1977 and conducted further interviews into 1980. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] No one was charged. The CIA's view and the case's documentary record are set out in Part Three; the question of whether a diversion occurred remains officially unresolved. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec]

How the Bureau worked on friendly services. A Senate Intelligence Committee study of 1978, as summarized by Jeff McConnell in 1986, found that the FBI investigated "friendly" foreign services only in response to specific complaints, that what it developed rarely reached prosecutors, and that the CIA and the State Department discouraged penalties against friendly services. [cite:ow5_merip] John Davitt, the head of the Justice Department's internal-security section until 1980, told the New York Times that Israel's intelligence service had been "the second most active" in the United States in his time, after the Soviet Union's. [cite:ow5_merip] The two statements describe the same structure from two angles: a high level of activity, and a posture of response rather than pursuit.

What the record does not settle. The FBI's own files for most of these cases have not been released in full. The 1954 finding and the Jensen case are known from secondary accounts rather than published FBI documents. Whether NUMEC uranium reached Israel is unproven either way. And the 1978 Senate study is cited here through a 1986 article, not from its own text.

sections.h: Pollard, Kadish and the AIPAC Case, 1985–2020
sections.html:
Three FBI cases that reached American courts after 1980 form the core of the public record of Israeli intelligence collection inside the United States, and each ended differently: a life sentence, a fine, and dropped charges. A fourth, often counted with them, was not an Israeli operation at all. This section sets out each case as the court record and the agencies' own documents describe it, beside the explanation the Israeli government or the defendants gave.

Pollard. Jonathan Pollard, a civilian analyst working for the US Navy, first offered to supply classified documents at a meeting with an Israeli Air Force officer, Aviem Sella, in late May 1984, and spied for Israel through 1984 and 1985. [cite:ow5_nsa_pollard] FBI agents arrested him on 21 November 1985 outside the Israeli embassy in Washington, where he had tried to seek asylum, and he was arraigned six days later on espionage charges as a paid agent of Israel. [cite:ow5_merip] The operation was run not by the Mossad but by LAKAM, a scientific-liaison bureau of the Israeli defence establishment then headed by Rafi Eitan. [cite:ow5_merip] [cite:ow5_nsa_pollard] Pollard pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1987. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp]

Israel's first explanation was that the operation had been unauthorized, run by a small group of officials without the government's knowledge; some officials in the Reagan administration doubted this, citing court documents that showed an organized, well-financed ring involving Israeli officers and embassy staff. [cite:ow5_csm1986] On 1 December 1985 Prime Minister Shimon Peres formally apologized, saying such spying "was wrong" and "in total contradiction to our policy," and pledged to dismantle any unit involved; Israeli leaders apologized publicly again in March 1987. [cite:ow13_csm_1985] [cite:ow13_upi_1987] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] The CIA's damage assessment of October 1987 found that Pollard had passed about 800 documents and some 1,500 intelligence summaries, and that his Israeli taskings concerned Arab states, Pakistan and the Soviet Union; the Israelis "never expressed interest in US military activities, plans, capabilities, or equipment." [cite:ow5_nsa_pollard] It also recorded that his handler told him to ignore a request from a superior for "dirt" on senior Israeli officials. [cite:ow5_jp_pollard] The American objection, in the assessment and among officials, was to the act itself: an ally running a human penetration of the US government. [cite:ow5_jp_pollard]

Pollard was paroled in 2015, under conditions that included a ban on travel abroad, and was released from parole in November 2020. [cite:ow5_nsa_pollard] He then moved to Israel, where Prime Minister Netanyahu met him on the tarmac on 30 December 2020 and told him, "Now you are at home." [cite:ow5_nbc_pollard2020] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] The arc, from an "unauthorized" operation and a formal apology in 1985 to a prime minister's welcome in 2020, is the clearest documented case in which Israel's public position on an espionage case changed over time.

Kadish. The second case concerned the same years but surfaced two decades later. Ben-Ami Kadish, an engineer at the Army's Picatinny Arsenal in New Jersey, admitted passing classified material to an Israeli agent from about 1980 through 1985; he pleaded guilty on 30 December 2008 to one count of conspiring to act as an unregistered agent of Israel and was fined $50,000 on 29 May 2009. [cite:ow5_doj_kadish] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] In 2009, at the age of 85, he was fined under a plea agreement and given no prison sentence. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] Two points about the case are commonly misstated. The disclosures took place in the 1980s, before Pollard's arrest, not in the years after Israel's 1987 pledge. And the two men were not convicted of the same offence: Pollard pleaded guilty to espionage, while Kadish's case ended in a plea agreement whose result was a fine. The public record gives the outcomes, not the prosecutors' reasons for the difference.

The AIPAC case. The third case reached the most prominent pro-Israel organization in Washington. In 2004 the FBI's investigation of Lawrence Franklin, an analyst in the Defense Department, became public. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] Franklin pleaded guilty in 2005 to passing classified information, some of it to two senior staff of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, Steven Rosen and Keith Weissman, and was sentenced to about 12 years, later reduced. [cite:pm_wiki_franklin] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] AIPAC dismissed Rosen and Weissman in April 2005; they were indicted under the Espionage Act for receiving and passing on national defence information. [cite:pm_wiki_franklin] In 2009 the government dropped all charges against them, citing court rulings that made conviction unlikely and its unwillingness to expose classified information at trial. [cite:pm_wiki_franklin] Rosen and Weissman were never convicted of anything, and the case is not evidence of an espionage network; the questions it raised about AIPAC's legal status are taken up in [scene:ow2_lobby_law|the lobby and the law].

The case that was not Israeli. The arrest in October 2009 of Stewart Nozette, a former government scientist who gave classified information to a man he believed was an Israeli intelligence officer, is sometimes listed among Israeli cases. The man was an undercover FBI agent, and the Justice Department's charging documents state that they do not allege that the government of Israel or anyone acting on its behalf violated American law. [cite:csmonitor_nozette] [cite:justice_nozette] Nozette pleaded guilty to attempted espionage and was sentenced to 13 years. [cite:justice_nozette] The case documents the FBI's counterintelligence methods, not an Israeli operation.

What the cases show about the mechanism. In each case that reached court, the FBI's tools were the ordinary ones of criminal law: surveillance, arrest and prosecution of an American citizen. None of them reached an Israeli official. The scientific-liaison bureau that ran Pollard was a foreign government body, and the American courts had no jurisdiction over its officers; the remedy lay in diplomacy, which produced the apologies of 1985 and 1987. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] Where the person receiving information was not a government employee, as in the AIPAC case, the Espionage Act proved hard to apply. [cite:pm_wiki_franklin]

What the record does not settle. Who in the Israeli government authorized the Pollard operation has not been established in any public American or Israeli document. Kadish's handler, and how long the contact continued, are described in reporting that this book has not been able to recheck. And the full FBI files on all three cases remain unpublished.

sections.h: Warnings, Denials and the Bureau in Israel, 1995–2026
sections.html:
After Pollard the FBI's relationship with Israel ran on two tracks at once. On one, American counterintelligence reports kept naming Israel as an active collector against the United States, and Israel kept denying it. On the other, the Bureau opened an office in Israel, expanded cooperation on terrorism and crime, and described the relationship as one that runs both ways. This section sets the two tracks side by side, and marks which findings rest on documents and which on unnamed officials.

The 1990s warnings. A General Accounting Office report of 28 February 1996 said that an unnamed "Country A" "conducts the most aggressive espionage operation against the United States of any US ally"; press accounts identified Country A as Israel. Its concern was classified military information and sensitive military technology. [cite:ow5_gao_1996] [cite:ow5_wsws_gao] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] In the same period a memorandum from a field office of the Defense Investigative Service, first reported by Moment magazine in February 1996, called Israel a "non-traditional adversary" and suggested it used ties to American Jews; Assistant Secretary of Defense Emmett Paige called singling out an ethnic group "particularly repugnant" and cancelled it. [cite:ow5_jw_1996memo] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] The two documents should be kept apart. The GAO finding concerns the conduct of a foreign government's services. The memorandum's suggestion that Americans were suspect because of their religion or ancestry is the kind of identity-based inference this book does not accept, and the Pentagon itself withdrew it.

The 2014 briefings. In May 2014 Newsweek reported that American officials had told congressional staff in classified briefings that Israel was "crossing red lines" through espionage aimed at American firms, including energy and medical-technology companies, and that joint trade missions and front companies were used. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] The officials were unnamed, and Israel denied the claims. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] The report rests on anonymous sources and is labelled here as contested.

The devices near the White House, 2019. On 12 September 2019 Politico reported, citing three former senior officials, that cellphone surveillance devices known as IMSI catchers had been found near the White House and other sensitive sites in Washington, that the FBI and other agencies had linked them to Israeli agents, and that they appeared intended to monitor President Trump and his aides. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] No public rebuke followed. The Department of Homeland Security later told Senator Ron Wyden it could not determine who had placed the devices, and Israel's embassy called the report a "blatant lie" and "absolute nonsense." [cite:ow5_cbs_2019] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] Israel called the report a "blatant lie" and restated that it does not spy in the United States; President Trump said he found it hard to believe. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] The FBI made no public statement. The original report is known here through a reference summary of it and of the Guardian and Times of Israel coverage; it is a single-outlet claim from unnamed officials, denied by Israel, and is presented as contested.

June 2026. The most recent report concerns the Pentagon's own intelligence agency. In June 2026, according to reporting by NBC News, the Times of Israel and the New York Times as summarized in a reference account, the Defense Intelligence Agency raised its counterintelligence threat assessment for Israel to "critical," its highest level, out of concern that Israel was surveilling senior American officials to learn the administration's internal decision-making on the Middle East, including the war with Iran; a seven-page assessment was said to list the incidents behind the change, and a separate report described Israeli efforts to eavesdrop on named officials. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] NBC News reported a seven-page DIA assessment; it has not been published. Israel's embassy called the report "completely false," saying "Israel does not gather intelligence on American entities, let alone US government officials," and a White House official said "this entire story is false"; the Pentagon declined to comment. [cite:ow5_nbc_dia] It is included because it is recent and directly on point, and it should be read as reported, not confirmed. Its status, as of October 2026, may have changed.

The other track: the Bureau in Israel. In the same decades the FBI built a standing presence in Israel. Under Director Louis Freeh, who took office in 1993, the Bureau roughly doubled its network of legal attaché offices abroad, and Tel Aviv was among the new locations. [cite:fbi_legat_history] An assistant legal attaché post in Jerusalem was later added, by the FBI's own account, to build a relationship with the Palestinian Authority as well. [cite:fbi_israel_story] The Bureau states that its legal attachés "do not conduct foreign intelligence gathering or counterintelligence investigations"; they are liaison officers working through the host country's police and security services. [cite:fbi_intl_ops] An FBI official in Israel, Cary Gleicher, interviewed by the Bureau's own public-affairs office in 2017, described the relationship in reciprocal terms: "The FBI provides a great deal of support to the government of Israel through training opportunities, exchange of intelligence. And the Israelis do an unbelievable amount in the realm of counterterrorism for us." [cite:fbi_israel_story]

The training ties also run outside the Bureau. The best-known programme taking American police leaders to Israel, run by the Jewish Institute for National Security of America since 2002, was created by a former FBI assistant director, Steven Pomerantz; it and the other exchanges are examined in [scene:ow6_exchanges|the police exchanges]. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] And the FBI was itself a customer of Israeli surveillance technology: it bought NSO Group's Pegasus, tested it for about two years, and on 22 July 2021 decided to "cease all efforts" to deploy it, saying there had been no operational use, a story told in Part Ten. [cite:ow10_globe_fbi]

The pattern, and its limits. Across thirty years the findings share a shape: they appear in internal assessments, leaked documents or reporting from unnamed officials; Israel denies them; and no prosecution follows, because the conduct alleged is that of foreign officials whom American courts cannot reach, or because no case is brought. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] [cite:ow_td_spying2015] The partnership track meanwhile continued and widened. The FBI's own framing is that the relationship is valuable to the United States in counterterrorism, and the public record supports that claim at the level of statements rather than published cases. [cite:fbi_israel_story] What it does not show is any instance after 1987 in which a finding on the counterintelligence track changed the terms of the partnership track.

What the record does not settle. The 1996 GAO report is cited here through quotations rather than its own text. The 2014, 2019 and 2026 reports rest on unnamed officials, and the original articles could not be retrieved. The FBI's joint cases with Israeli police on cybercrime, and its work on the cases of Americans taken hostage on 7 October 2023, lie outside this section, and nothing is said about them here.

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: Homeland Security, ICE and the Police
chapters.intro: Part Six turns from the intelligence agencies to the agencies that police the American homeland. It follows four kinds of tie between the Department of Homeland Security and Israel: a 2007 memorandum between the two governments' security ministries; research programmes written into US law in 2014 and widened in 2016 and 2021; joint grants to companies; and the purchase by Immigration and Customs Enforcement of Israeli-made tools for opening phones. It then turns to the police: the private exchange programmes that have taken American police chiefs to Israel since 1992, who pays for them, what their sponsors say they teach, what their critics say, and what the evidence shows; and the New York Police Department's office inside an Israeli police headquarters. Each tie is set beside the reason its sponsors gave for it, and beside what the United States receives in return.
chapters.outro: Part Six found the homeland-security ties to be real but thin in law. The founding DHS–Israel memorandum, signed by Michael Chertoff and Avi Dichter in February 2007, is expressly non-binding and authorizes no classified sharing of its own; Congress added a research authority in 2014, widened it in 2016, and in December 2021 authorized at least $6 million a year in joint cybersecurity grants through fiscal 2026. [cite:ow6_jvl_dhsmou] [cite:ow6_lii_8606] The police exchanges are private programmes run by GILEE, JINSA and the ADL, partly paid for with DHS grant money; their critics' strongest claims about tactics are unsupported, while their influence on surveillance is reported but not documented, and Durham, Vermont's state police and Northampton stepped away. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] [cite:ow6_aj_durham] [cite:ow6_toi_newengland] The NYPD has kept an officer in Israel since 2007, inside an Israeli police headquarters since 2012, with private funding, and ICE has bought Israeli-made phone tools whose uses it has not disclosed. [cite:ow6_cs_nypd2026] [cite:ow6_ipt_cellebrite] [cite:ow6_guardian_paragon] Part Seven turns to the far larger relationship between Israel and the armed forces of the United States.

sections.h: The Department and the Ministry
sections.html:
The Department of Homeland Security, of which Immigration and Customs Enforcement is a component, was set up in 2002–03 after the attacks of 11 September 2001. Its ties to Israel were built afterwards, in four layers: a memorandum between ministers, a research authority written into a 2014 law, a grant programme run with a binational foundation, and a cybersecurity grant programme added by Congress in 2021. Each is small by the standards of the Pentagon programmes described in Part Seven, and each is documented in a public text. [cite:ow6_jvl_dhsmou] [cite:ow6_lii_8606]

The 2007 memorandum. The founding instrument is often dated to 2008; the text and the contemporary reporting date it to February 2007. That month the Secretary of Homeland Security, Michael Chertoff, and Israel's Minister of Public Security, Avi Dichter, signed a memorandum of understanding in Washington "setting the terms for security cooperation between the two nations". [cite:ow6_da_dhspact] Its subjects were counterterrorism and related serious crime; aviation security, including passenger and cargo screening; the training and exchange of analytical personnel; research and testing of explosives-detection technology; and the sharing of emergency planning and response information. Information was to pass on request or on either side's initiative, chiefly through the two embassies. [cite:ow6_jvl_dhsmou]

The memorandum is also notable for what it does not do. It states that it "does not independently authorize disclosure of classified information", which continued to move only under existing security agreements, and that it "does not impose any legal commitments on the Participants". Either side must obtain the other's consent before passing information it received to a third country. [cite:ow6_jvl_dhsmou] In other words, the 2007 text is a framework for cooperation, not a treaty: it creates no rights that a court could enforce and no obligation that Congress voted on. The public record does not show that it has been amended or replaced.

The 2014 research authority. Congress gave the department a statutory mandate seven years later. Section 7 of the United States–Israel Strategic Partnership Act of 2014 (Public Law 113-296, signed on 19 December 2014) authorized the Secretary of Homeland Security, acting through the department's advanced research agency and with the Secretary of State's agreement, to set up "pilot" cooperative research programmes with Israel. Their stated aim was to enhance Israel's capabilities in border, maritime and aviation security, explosives detection and emergency services. [cite:ow6_lii_8606] The Act passed the Senate unanimously on 18 September 2014 and the House by voice vote on 3 December 2014. [cite:ow_jvl_2014act] A 2016 law (Public Law 114-304) dropped the word "pilot", making the programmes permanent, and added cybersecurity as a fourth field; a 2021 law authorized $2 million for fiscal year 2021. [cite:ow6_lii_8606]

BIRD HLS. The money for joint projects has largely run through an older binational body, the Israel–United States Binational Industrial Research and Development (BIRD) Foundation. Since 2016 the department's Science and Technology Directorate and Israel's Ministry of Public Security have selected, with the Israel Innovation Authority, pairs of American and Israeli companies for "BIRD HLS" grants of up to $1 million each, covering up to half of a project's budget. In the 2020 round, BIRD committed $1.5 million to two pairings, with total project value of about $3 million once private money was counted. Israel's chief scientist for public security described the programme as one that "enables us to enhance public safety in Israel and in the United States". [cite:ow6_bird_hls2021]

The 2021 cybersecurity grants. The most recent layer came from the annual defence bill. In April 2021 Senators Susan Collins, Jacky Rosen, Sheldon Whitehouse and Todd Young introduced the US–Israel Cybersecurity Cooperation Enhancement Act, proposing a homeland-security grant programme of $6 million a year for five years. [cite:ow6_collins_cyber] Representative Andrew Garbarino offered the same measure as an amendment to the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal 2022, and the House adopted it on 23 September 2021. [cite:ow6_garbarino_ndaa] As enacted (section 1551 of Public Law 117-81, 27 December 2021), the programme funds joint ventures between American and Israeli businesses, universities, laboratories or governments; requires at least half of research costs to come from non-federal money; is limited to projects both countries deem unclassified; excludes applicants the Director of National Intelligence finds to be a counterintelligence threat; and authorizes "not less than $6,000,000" a year for fiscal years 2022 to 2026. [cite:ow6_lii_8606] An authorization is not an appropriation, and this book did not find a public accounting of how much has actually been awarded under it; as of October 2026 the authorization runs out with fiscal year 2026.

What each side gets. The texts present the relationship as mutual, and in its research layer it is. BIRD HLS and the 2021 grants fund only joint ventures, so an American company is a party to every project; Israel's ministry describes the gains as public safety in both countries. [cite:ow6_bird_hls2021] [cite:ow6_lii_8606] The 2014 statute is more one-sided in its wording: it states its purpose as enhancing Israel's capabilities, not those of the United States. [cite:ow6_lii_8606] The 2007 memorandum binds neither government to share anything, and its third-party consent clause means that information Israel gives the department cannot travel onwards without Israel's permission, and the reverse. [cite:ow6_jvl_dhsmou] What the public record does not contain is any audit of how much information or technology has flowed in each direction under these instruments. Unlike the arms programmes in Parts Seven and Eight, the homeland-security cooperation has no annual reporting requirement that would let Congress, or a reader, measure it.

sections.h: The Police Exchanges
sections.html:
American police do not train in Israel under any US–Israeli government agreement. The trips that have taken police chiefs, sheriffs and senior officers to Israel since the 1990s were organized by three private bodies: a programme based at Georgia State University, a Washington defence think tank, and a Jewish civil-rights organization. Public money has paid for some of the travel, but the programmes themselves are private, and that shapes what can be known about them. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] [cite:ow6_jpost_adl]

GILEE. The oldest is the Georgia International Law Enforcement Exchange, founded in 1992 at Georgia State University by the criminologist Robert Friedmann as Atlanta prepared for the 1996 Olympic Games. It has run exchanges with several countries, including China before the 2008 Beijing Olympics and, at the State Department's request, post-Soviet states such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan; Israel is its best-known partner. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] Counts of its participants differ because they measure different things. GILEE's own website, as reported in 2022, said over 1,100 officials had completed 290 training programmes; a 2023 count put participants in its exchanges at about 1,250 executives and attendees at its workshops and conferences in the United States at about 43,000. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] [cite:ow6_wiki_gilee] The foundation of the Home Depot co-founder Bernard Marcus gave GILEE at least $1.25 million from 2005, and the Atlanta police department spent at least $25,500 a year on it from 2017 to 2021; the department says it uses no federal money for Israel training. [cite:ow6_reason_cops]

JINSA. The Jewish Institute for National Security of America began bringing American police to Israel in the summer of 2002, in a programme created by a former assistant director of the FBI, Steven Pomerantz. JINSA pays participants' costs; the Marcus foundation gave it at least $2.38 million from 2011. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] The Justice Department's community-policing office described the programme in 2013 as teaching intelligence gathering and sharing, early detection of plots, post-attack forensic investigation and the ideologies of terrorist groups, on the premise that "if properly trained, U.S. law enforcement can better prevent and respond to terrorist threats". [cite:ow6_cops_leep] In 2026 JINSA said its trips focus on management and policy, not physical tactics. [cite:ow6_cs_nypd2026]

The ADL. The Anti-Defamation League set up an Advanced Training School in 2002 and began its Israel seminars in 2004. A leaked internal memo put the cost at about $115,000 a trip, plus some $200,000 a year in staff time; departments paid about $5,000 an officer. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] [cite:ow6_jpost_adl] The 2016 seminar included meetings with Israeli police, a tour of Jerusalem, visits to Gilboa prison and Hebron, and a meeting with Palestinian police in Bethlehem. [cite:ow6_reason_cops]

Public money. The trips are private, but not wholly privately funded. Reason found that Homeland Security grants had paid $480,466 for police travel abroad since 2015, more than 80 per cent of it for training in Israel. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] Records are hard to obtain: when Georgia State students sought GILEE's records in 2011, the request was treated as a security matter, and Georgia later passed a law allowing such records to be sealed. [cite:ow6_reason_cops]

What the sponsors say. The organizers describe the programmes as counterterrorism and leadership education drawn from a country with long experience of attacks. Friedmann has said Israel was "more than willing to share its lessons learned", and that Israeli use-of-force rules are "much more restrictive" than American ones; Pomerantz wrote that Israel's lessons "remain pertinent" to American policing. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] The ADL says it does not conduct practical field training. [cite:ow6_reason_cops]

What the critics say. In August 2016, after the Justice Department's report on the Baltimore police, Amnesty International USA noted that Baltimore officials had received training from Israel's police, military and intelligence services, and that since 2002 the ADL, the American Jewish Committee's Project Interchange and JINSA had taken police chiefs from more than a dozen states to Israel. It argued that the trips exposed American officers to forces with documented records of excessive force and weak accountability, and concluded that for de-escalation and the policing of protest, "Israel is not such a partner". [cite:ow6_amnesty_2016] Jewish Voice for Peace, an advocacy group opposed to Israeli policy, launched its "Deadly Exchange" campaign in 2017 and argued in a 2018 report that "these programs facilitate an exchange of methods in state violence and control". [cite:ow6_reason_cops] That is the campaign's characterization, not a finding.

What the evidence shows. The strongest specific claims do not hold up. Reason's 2022 investigation found less evidence that the training causes American excessive force than its critics allege, and no evidence for the claim that American officers learn chokeholds in Israel; Israel's national police, JINSA and the ADL all deny it. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] Where the record is clearer is surveillance and secrecy: the investigation found that the trips helped police justify more surveillance, and the architect of the New York police's Demographics Unit, which mapped Muslim communities, described it as modelled on Israeli intelligence work in the West Bank. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] That account is reported, not documented in a policy paper; the next section sets out what is documented about New York.

The responses. The campaign changed some decisions. On 16 April 2018 the Durham, North Carolina, city council unanimously adopted a statement that it "opposes international exchanges with any country in which Durham officers receive military-style training"; the police chief said Durham had not joined any Israel exchange under her leadership. [cite:ow6_aj_durham] In December 2018 the Vermont State Police and the police chief of Northampton, Massachusetts, withdrew from the ADL's New England seminar in Israel after local objections. [cite:ow6_toi_newengland] The ADL paused its trips in 2019. A June 2020 draft memo by two of its vice-presidents recommended ending them, warning however that doing so "could imply culpability when ADL does not believe we did anything wrong"; the ADL decided instead to continue with a revised curriculum, but as of 2022 no trip had resumed. [cite:ow6_jpost_adl] [cite:ow6_reason_cops] This book found no later report of a resumption.

sections.h: New York's Precinct in Israel, and ICE's Tools
sections.html:
Two further ties go beyond the occasional training trip. One is permanent: the New York Police Department keeps an officer inside an Israeli police headquarters. The other is commercial: Immigration and Customs Enforcement has bought Israeli-made technology for getting into telephones. Neither rests on an act of Congress, and both are documented mainly through procurement records and reporting.

The Kfar Saba office. The NYPD began stationing an officer in Israel in 2007 under its International Liaison Program, which places senior intelligence-bureau officers in cities abroad. [cite:ow6_cs_nypd2026] In September 2012 Israeli and American outlets reported that the department had opened a branch at the Israel Police's headquarters in Kfar Saba, the Sharon District command, chosen over the US embassy in Tel Aviv; its purpose, as reported, was daily cooperation with the Israel Police. [cite:ow6_toi_nypd2012] The officer chosen to open it was Detective Charlie Ben-Naim (also spelled Benaim), an NYPD veteran of Israeli origin and a former officer in the Israel Defense Forces, who in 2026 was still described as the department's officer in Israel, one of more than a dozen in the liaison programme. [cite:ow6_toi_nypd2012] [cite:ow6_cs_nypd2026] Accounts differ on whether he has held the post continuously since 2007 or since 2012; the public record does not settle it.

The office is not paid for entirely by the city. City & State reported in August 2026 that the liaison programme is partly funded by the New York City Police Foundation, a charity supported by private donors, among them the Tisch family; two trustees of the foundation, Andrew and Alexander Tisch, are the uncle and cousin of the police commissioner, Jessica Tisch. [cite:ow6_cs_nypd2026] Private funding means that the office's budget does not pass through the City Council. The same report found that the NYPD contracts with Terrogence Global, an Israeli-founded web-intelligence firm, and that department officials travelled to Israel for counterterrorism and antisemitism training as recently as September 2025. [cite:ow6_cs_nypd2026]

The 2026 position. As of August 2026, according to an NYPD spokesperson quoted by City & State, Mayor Zohran Mamdani had not directed the department to stop cooperating with the Israeli police or to stop attending related conferences; the NYPD said no trips to Israel were planned that year, and City Hall said no official had travelled to Israel on city business under Mamdani, while no rule barred travel to any country.
