[cite:ow6_cs_nypd2026] At an unrelated press conference, Mamdani said of the commissioner generally: "I would not have someone serving our city if I was not confident in what they were doing." [cite:ow6_cs_nypd2026] The department's stated rationale for the office, as for its other overseas posts, is counterterrorism: learning quickly from attacks abroad. The public record does not include any report of what information the office has sent to New York, or received from it, and no oversight body has published one.

ICE and Israeli phone tools. ICE's link to Israel runs through purchases, not exchanges. In March 2017 it bought phone-extraction technology from Cellebrite, an Israeli-founded company, for $2.2 million, and on 24 June 2019 it gave notice of its intent to award Cellebrite a contract worth up to $30–35 million for "universal forensic extraction devices", licences and training; the contracting officer declined to say how ICE would use them. [cite:ow6_ipt_cellebrite] In September 2024, under the Biden administration, ICE signed a $2 million contract with Paragon Solutions, an Israeli-founded company whose "Graphite" spyware can reach encrypted messaging applications. The contract was paused for review under Executive Order 14093, which limits the government's use of commercial spyware; in September 2025 the Guardian reported that procurement records showed the pause lifted, with ICE as the contracting agency. By then Paragon was owned by an American firm. [cite:ow6_wiki_paragon] [cite:ow6_guardian_paragon] John Scott-Railton of the Citizen Lab said such tools "were designed for dictatorships, not democracies"; neither ICE nor Paragon commented. [cite:ow6_guardian_paragon] Part Ten follows these companies, and others, in detail.

The direction of travel. This part's question is whether these ties run one way. Here the answer depends on the tie. The DHS research programmes fund joint ventures in which American companies take part. [cite:ow6_lii_8606] [cite:ow6_bird_hls2021] The police exchanges carry American officers to Israel to learn, by their sponsors' own account, Israeli methods; Israeli police are not described in the sources as coming to learn American ones. [cite:ow6_reason_cops] [cite:ow6_cops_leep] The NYPD's office sits inside an Israeli headquarters; this book found no report of an Israeli police office inside an American one. [cite:ow6_cs_nypd2026] And ICE's purchases send American public money to companies founded in Israel. [cite:ow6_ipt_cellebrite] [cite:ow6_wiki_paragon] None of this is concealed, but very little of it is reported to an elected body: the memorandum is non-binding, the trips are private, the New York office is partly privately funded, and the uses of the phone tools are undisclosed.

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: The Pentagon and the Services
chapters.intro: Part Seven follows the relationship between Israel and the US armed forces, from the strategic-cooperation agreements of the 1980s to the war with Iran in 2026. It begins with the framework: the joint planning groups set up in 1983, Israel's designation as a major non-NATO ally, the American weapons stockpile stored on Israeli soil, the American radar on a Negev hilltop, and the 2021 move of Israel into US Central Command. It then takes the services one by one, the Army, the Navy, the Air Force and the Marine Corps, and the exercises that join them to Israel's forces. It ends with the years in which American forces fought in Israel's defence: shooting down Iranian drones and missiles in 2024 and 2025, and striking Iran alongside Israel in 2026. For each, it sets out the official American rationale and what the United States has gained, as well as what it has spent.
chapters.outro: Part Seven traced a military relationship built without a defence treaty. Executive agreements in 1981, 1983 and 1988 created joint planning bodies and port access; a classified agreement governs an American-owned stockpile in Israel, which was drawn on for Israel in 2006 and 2014 and for Ukraine in 2023; an American radar has stood in the Negev since 2008; and Israel moved into Central Command in 2021. [cite:ow_wiki_sca1981] [cite:ow7_jvl_strategic] [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] [cite:ow7_sat_xband] [cite:ow_inss_centcom] Each service has its own tie, from the Army's THAAD battery and leased-back Iron Dome batteries to the Air Force's F-35, flown by Israel with Israeli systems, and the Marines' Iron Dome-based interceptor. [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024] [cite:ow7_twz_irondome] [cite:ow7_wiki_f35i] [cite:ow8_dn_mric] From 2024 American forces fought in Israel's defence, spent a quarter of their THAAD interceptors in June 2025, and joined Israel in a war on Iran in 2026 that had cost $43.6 billion by September 2026 and 21 American deaths, hostile and non-hostile, by October. [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025] [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] Part Eight follows the weapons themselves: how they are bought, approved and shipped, and what rules are meant to govern their use.

sections.h: The Framework: Planning Groups, a Stockpile and a Radar
sections.html:
The military relationship between the United States and Israel was not created by a single treaty. There is no mutual-defence pact between the two countries. What exists instead is a stack of executive agreements, statutes and command arrangements, laid down over four decades, most of them signed by defence officials rather than ratified by the Senate. Part One sets out the laws; this section follows how the Pentagon built on them.

The 1980s agreements. On 30 November 1981 the Secretary of Defense, Caspar Weinberger, and Israel's defence minister, Ariel Sharon, signed a memorandum on strategic cooperation that provided for joint exercises, the use of Israeli ports by the US Sixth Fleet and the pre-positioning of American supplies in Israel. As an executive memorandum it was not submitted to the Senate. [cite:ow_wiki_sca1981] On 29 November 1983 a further agreement created two standing bodies: the Joint Political-Military Group, first aimed at Soviet involvement in the region and later at chemical weapons and ballistic-missile proliferation, and the Joint Security Assistance Planning Group, which meets each year in Washington to review Israel's procurement needs and plan how its Foreign Military Financing will be spent. [cite:ow7_jvl_strategic] Under a category Congress created in 1986, the executive designated Israel a major non-NATO ally in early 1987, a status that opened some US defence contracts to Israeli firms on equal terms with NATO members, and in April 1988 a memorandum of agreement folded the earlier arrangements together. [cite:ow7_jvl_strategic] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

From Europe to the Middle East command. For most of this period Israel sat inside US European Command, an arrangement that kept it administratively apart from the Arab states covered by Central Command. On 15 January 2021, in the last week of the first Trump administration, the Pentagon moved Israel into Central Command's area in the Unified Command Plan. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump ordered the change; the Pentagon said that "the Abraham Accords paved the way". Israeli liaison officers now sit at CENTCOM's headquarters in Tampa. [cite:ow_inss_centcom] Oversight of the American stockpile in Israel moved with it, from European to Central Command, in September 2021. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa]

WRSA-I: the stockpile. The War Reserve Stockpile Allies–Israel began in the 1980s, when Israel invited the United States to store munitions on its territory for American use in war; a memorandum between the two governments, still classified, governs it. Congress later amended the stockpiling law so that such stocks could be held in major non-NATO allies, not only NATO states. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] The United States owns the stock until it is transferred; Israel pays for storage and upkeep; additions were capped at $200 million a year, and the Congressional Research Service has estimated the stock's value at up to $4.4 billion. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] The 2012 and 2014 Acts extended the authority, and a 2025 law set the cap on additions at $500 million a year through fiscal 2027. [cite:ow_jvl_2012act] [cite:ow_jvl_2014act] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

The stockpile has been drawn on in several directions. During the 2006 Lebanon war the Pentagon transferred precision-guided munitions from it to Israel. During the Gaza war of 2014 it sold Israel 120mm tank rounds and 40mm illumination rounds from it in a $3 million sale paid for with US grant aid; the Pentagon called the transfer "routine", and the White House was reportedly not told in advance. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] In 2023 the flow ran the other way: the United States moved about 300,000 155mm artillery shells out of the Israeli stockpile to supply Ukraine, promising to replenish it, and by January 2023 about half had reportedly reached Ukraine. Reporting at the time indicated that, although the shells were American property, the final approval rested with Israel's prime minister. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] [cite:ow7_fdd_ukraine] After 7 October 2023 the Biden administration asked Congress to lift the cap on additions and to allow any item in the stockpile to be transferred to Israel at terms set by the Secretary of Defense; Congress did not pass that version. A separate provision of the 2021 defence act already allowed precision-guided munitions to be transferred outside the cap, and it was extended to 2027. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa]

The radar on Har Keren. The one permanent American military presence in Israel is a radar. In late 2008, at the end of the George W. Bush administration, the United States deployed an X-band radar to the Negev with about 120 American personnel, to detect long-range missiles such as Iran's Shahab-3 and link Israeli and American missile-defence systems. [cite:ow7_sat_xband] The site, on Mount Har Keren some 20 miles from Gaza and known as Site 512, is focused on Iran rather than on Gaza. A Pentagon contract announcement of 2 August 2023 described $35.8 million for a "life support facility", barracks for personnel, as part of a "classified worldwide" project. [cite:ow7_int_site512] Secondary accounts say the radar gives Israel several extra minutes of warning of a launch from Iran and feeds data to American missile-defence centres. [cite:ow7_jvl_site512]

What each side gains. The framework is not purely a channel of benefit to Israel. The stockpile is American property held for American use, and in 2023 it supplied Ukraine; the radar watches Iran for the United States as well as for Israel; the CENTCOM move placed Israel in the same command as its Arab neighbours, a step the Pentagon tied to the Abraham Accords. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] [cite:ow7_int_site512] [cite:ow_inss_centcom] The asymmetries are of a different kind: the WRSA-I agreement is classified, the Har Keren project is described only obliquely in public contracts, and the 1981 and 1988 instruments were never put to a vote. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] [cite:ow7_int_site512] [cite:ow_wiki_sca1981] The rule that keeps other regional arms sales from eroding Israel's "qualitative military edge", by contrast, was written into statute in 2008. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

sections.h: Service by Service
sections.html:
Each branch of the US armed forces has its own tie to Israel, and they differ in kind: the Army runs radars and air-defence batteries, the Navy sails to Haifa and has shot down missiles aimed at Israel, the Air Force shares its newest fighter, and the Marine Corps is buying an air-defence system built on Israeli technology. They are joined by exercises run first under European Command and now under Central Command. This section takes them in turn.

The Army. The Army's presence is the most permanent. The X-band radar deployed to the Negev in 2008 came with about 120 American personnel, and the Har Keren site has since been expanded with barracks. [cite:ow7_sat_xband] [cite:ow7_int_site512] In 2019 the Army sent a THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) battery to Israel for training. [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024] On 13 October 2024, after Iran's missile attacks of 13 April and 1 October, Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin, "at the direction of the President", authorized a THAAD battery and its crew to deploy to Israel to augment its air defences; a battery of this kind generally needs about 95 soldiers. The Pentagon said the move "underscores the United States' ironclad commitment to the defense of Israel". [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024] [cite:ow7_ap_thaad2024]

The Army also became, for a time, an Iron Dome customer. It announced in August 2018 that it would buy the Israeli system as an interim defence against cruise missiles, bought two batteries in 2019 (delivered in late 2020 and early 2021), and sent one temporarily to Guam. It declined to buy more, partly because it could not easily network them with its other air-defence systems. In October 2023, after the Hamas attack, officials told Congress the Pentagon would lease both batteries back to Israel, and the Pentagon said the Tamir interceptors it was delivering came from Army stocks. [cite:ow7_twz_irondome] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

The Navy. The 1981 memorandum gave the Sixth Fleet use of Israeli ports, and Haifa now hosts around forty US Navy ships a year; the amphibious ship USS Iwo Jima docked there in March 2018 after a joint exercise. [cite:ow_wiki_sca1981] [cite:ow7_jvl_strategic] On 8 October 2023, the day after the Hamas attack, Austin ordered the USS Gerald R. Ford carrier strike group, with a cruiser and five destroyers, to the eastern Mediterranean and reinforced F-35, F-15, F-16 and A-10 squadrons in the region, saying the aim was to deter a wider war. [cite:ow7_ap_ford2023] Navy destroyers have since fired in Israel's defence, as the next section describes. [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] [cite:ow7_usni_oct2024]

The Air Force and the F-35. On 7 October 2010 Israel signed to buy twenty F-35s for about $3 billion, paid for with American military aid, and by November 2016 it had ordered fifty. [cite:ow7_wiki_f35i] Israel's version is designated F-35I "Adir" because, in the words of a 2010 report, "there will be unique Israeli features installed in them": Elbit electronic-warfare equipment installed under a 2012 contract, an Israel Aerospace Industries command-and-control software layer running on the jet's central computer, Israeli weapons and Israeli-made helmet displays. The United States at first refused to let Israel integrate its own electronic warfare; Israel's answer was a "plug-and-play" architecture for add-on Israeli electronics. [cite:ow7_wiki_f35i] On 22 May 2018 Israel's air force commander said Israel had become "the first country in the world to use the F-35 in combat". [cite:ow7_wiki_f35i] The industrial flow ran partly back to Israel: Lockheed Martin undertook to buy about $4 billion of parts and systems from Israeli firms, and Israel Aerospace Industries makes F-35 wings. [cite:ow7_wiki_f35i] In August 2024 the United States approved more than $20 billion in sales including new F-15IA fighters. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

The Marine Corps. This book found no standing Marine Corps programme with Israel before the 2020s. Since then the Marines have been developing a Medium-Range Intercept Capability that pairs Iron Dome's launcher and Tamir interceptor (called SkyHunter in American service) with Marine radars and command systems; it hit every target in a live-fire test at White Sands, New Mexico, on 30 June 2022. [cite:ow8_dn_mric] In October 2026 the Raytheon–Rafael joint venture delivered the first Tamir interceptors built at a new plant in Camden, Arkansas, the first outside Israel, and said it would build the Marine variant there. [cite:ow8_rtx_camden]

The exercises. The services meet Israel's forces in large joint exercises. Juniper Cobra, a ballistic-missile-defence exercise held every two years, reached its ninth edition in March 2018 with more than 2,500 American and about 2,000 Israeli personnel; European Command said it was not tied to any real-world event. [cite:ow7_eucom_jc2018] Juniper Oak 23.2, which ended on 26 January 2023 under Central Command, was the largest US–Israeli exercise to date: about 6,400 American and more than 1,500 Israeli troops, more than 140 aircraft including B-52 bombers, and the USS George H.W. Bush carrier strike group. CENTCOM's commander said it showed that "the partnership between CENTCOM and the IDF is stronger and continues to grow". [cite:ow7_navy_jo23] Congress has since written joint exercises, including underground warfare, into the 2025 defence act. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

Why the United States says it does this. The official rationales are consistent across administrations: deterrence and regional stability (the purpose Austin gave for the 2023 carrier deployment and CENTCOM gave for Juniper Oak), interoperability between allied forces, and a statutory commitment, written into law in 2008, to preserve Israel's "qualitative military edge" over its neighbours. [cite:ow7_ap_ford2023] [cite:ow7_navy_jo23] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The American gains are documented too: the Army and Marines acquired a combat-proven short-range interceptor, and in 2014 the Missile Defense Agency gained full access to Iron Dome's technology under a co-production agreement described in Part Eight. [cite:ow7_twz_irondome] [cite:ow8_dn_mric] [cite:ow8_crs_irondome2014] What is one-sided is the money: the Israeli F-35s, like most of Israel's American weapons, were bought with American grant aid, and part of that spending returned to Israeli companies through offsets. [cite:ow7_wiki_f35i]

sections.h: Defending Israel, Fighting Iran: 2024–2026
sections.html:
For forty years the military relationship was one of supply, planning and exercises. In April 2024 it became one of combat: American ships and aircraft shot down weapons fired at Israel, and in 2026 American forces went to war with Iran alongside Israel. This section sets out, from Pentagon statements and named reporting, what US forces did, what it cost, and what the United States said it was for. Because the 2026 war was still not formally ended when this was written, its figures are given as of October 2026.

13–14 April 2024. Iran and its allies launched more than 300 drones and missiles at Israel from Iran, Iraq, Syria and Yemen. The Pentagon said that about 99 per cent were brought down. American forces, including the destroyers USS Arleigh Burke and USS Carney and Air Force and Navy fighters, destroyed more than 80 one-way attack drones and at least six ballistic missiles aimed at Israel, among them a missile shot down near Erbil in Iraq. Austin, the Pentagon said, was "grateful for the professionalism and skill of the brave U.S. troops" who had defended Israel, and the United States would "continue to take all necessary action to defend Israel and U.S. personnel". [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024]

1 October 2024. When Iran fired about 200 ballistic missiles at Israel, the destroyers USS Bulkeley and USS Cole fired about a dozen interceptors; the Pentagon said no American ground-based interceptors were used. [cite:ow7_usni_oct2024] Twelve days later the THAAD battery described in the previous section was ordered to Israel, with its American crew. [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024]

June 2025. In the twelve-day war between Israel and Iran in June 2025, the THAAD batteries carried a large share of the defence. Two sources told CNN that the United States fired more than 100, and possibly as many as 150, THAAD interceptors, about a quarter of its supply, using two of its seven THAAD systems. An analysis by the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) estimated that THAAD accounted for almost half of all interceptions of Iranian missiles, and that replacing the stock would take three to eight years at current production rates. [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025]

The 2026 war. On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iran, named "Epic Fury" by the Pentagon and "Roaring Lion" by Israel; the American military described "full synchronization and coordination" between the two forces. Iranian state media confirmed that the Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, had been killed. President Trump said the aim was to defend Americans by removing imminent threats from the Iranian government; Prime Minister Netanyahu called it the removal of an existential threat. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] Iran answered with missile and drone attacks on Israel, on American bases and on American-allied states, and closed the Strait of Hormuz. A two-week ceasefire mediated by Pakistan began on 7–8 April, was extended, and was followed by the Islamabad Memorandum, signed by both presidents on 17 June; it collapsed on 8 July, and intermittent fighting between American and Iranian forces continued afterwards. [cite:ow7_wiki_ceasefire2026]

The cost, as of October 2026. A Central Command estimate given to Congress in September 2026 put the American cost of the war at $43.6 billion as of 3 September, more than half of it munitions, with defensive interceptors for the Patriot and THAAD systems the most sought-after; the Congressional Budget Office had put it at $38 billion through 1 August, rising by about $3 billion a month. The figure excludes damage to American bases, which a Pentagon inspector general found had been damaged or destroyed in eight countries. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] By 9 October 2026 the Pentagon's casualty database listed 21 American deaths, hostile and non-hostile, in operations against Iran, and 865 wounded; The Washington Post reported four more deaths than the official figure, which the Defense Secretary disputed. [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026]

What the United States said it was for. Each step came with a stated American purpose: deterring a wider regional war (October 2023), protecting Israel and American personnel from Iranian attack (2024), and, in 2026, removing what the President called imminent threats to Americans. [cite:ow7_ap_ford2023] [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024] [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] Trump's further claim that Iran was rebuilding its nuclear programme was disputed at the time by the International Atomic Energy Agency, which said it had no evidence that Iran had resumed enrichment. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury]

The balance. The 2024–26 record tests the "one-way" thesis directly. Israel's forces also defended themselves, and Israel's Arrow interceptors took part alongside THAAD in 2025. [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025] The American radar on Har Keren, the American THAAD batteries and the American destroyers protected American bases and personnel as well as Israeli cities. [cite:ow7_int_site512] [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024] But the costs fell unevenly. A quarter of the American THAAD stock was spent defending Israel in twelve days in 2025, and by September 2026 American and NATO officials were describing the shortage of interceptors in Europe as "beyond critical"; and in the war of 2026, which the United States joined alongside Israel, American service members died and the Treasury carried a bill of tens of billions of dollars. [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025] [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] Whether that was a price paid for Israel or for American aims against Iran is a political judgement, and the two governments' stated aims overlapped; what the record shows is who paid it.

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: The Weapons Pipeline
chapters.intro: Part Eight follows the weapons. The aid figures in Part One are, in practice, a flow of American-made bombs, shells, aircraft and interceptors, and this part shows how that flow works: the two legal routes by which arms leave the United States, the money that pays for them, the shorter congressional review that Israel shares with NATO and a handful of close allies, and the emergency powers that let an administration skip that review altogether. It measures the pace of deliveries since October 2023 and the one occasion on which an American president held a shipment back. It then turns to the weapons the two countries build together, the missile-defence systems funded by Congress and made partly in American factories, and ends with the rules that are meant to govern how the weapons are used: the Leahy laws, a special vetting forum used only for Israel, and a 2024 presidential memorandum that lasted a year.
chapters.outro: Part Eight followed the weapons. Israel's $3.3 billion a year in Foreign Military Financing is paid as a lump sum and spent through the Foreign Military Sales system, under a congressional review shorter than most countries face: 15 days, with higher thresholds, shared with NATO and a few close allies. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow8_crs_review2021] Since October 2023 that review has been skipped by emergency declaration in December 2023 and again in February and March 2025; by April 2025 there were 751 active cases worth $39.2 billion, and more than 90,000 tons had been delivered. The one hold, on 2,000-pound bombs in May 2024, was lifted in January 2025. [cite:ow8_ap_tank2023] [cite:ow8_at_155] [cite:ow8_toi_rubio2025] [cite:ow8_axios_pause] [cite:ow8_ap_unpause] Missile defence is the most two-way part of the pipeline: co-production with Raytheon and Boeing, US access to Iron Dome's technology, and US-built Tamir interceptors from 2026. [cite:ow8_crs_irondome2014] [cite:ow8_dn_coprod2016] [cite:ow8_rtx_camden] The rules on use are the least: no Israeli unit had been found ineligible under the Leahy laws by mid-2024, the May 2024 report could not verify specific uses, and NSM-20 was revoked in February 2025. [cite:ow8_js_blaha_ilvf] [cite:ow8_js_nsm20report] [cite:ow8_aca_rescind] Part Nine turns from weapons to data, and to the American contractors that work with both governments.

sections.h: Two Routes Out: Foreign Military Sales and Commercial Sales
sections.html:
American weapons reach a foreign army by one of two legal routes, both governed by the Arms Export Control Act. In a Foreign Military Sale, the buyer is a government and so is the seller: the foreign state buys from the US government, which in turn buys from the manufacturer or takes the item from Pentagon stocks. In a Direct Commercial Sale, the foreign government buys straight from an American company, which needs an export licence from the State Department. [cite:ow8_crs_fms2026] Most of what the United States pays for on Israel's behalf moves by the first route, because Israel's Foreign Military Financing grant is spent through the Foreign Military Sales system. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa]

The money. The 2016 memorandum of understanding commits the United States to $3.8 billion a year for fiscal years 2019 to 2028: $3.3 billion in Foreign Military Financing and $500 million for missile defence. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] Israel's financing is treated differently from other recipients' in one important respect. Since a 1990 appropriations law, it has been paid out as a lump sum in the first month of the fiscal year and held in an interest-bearing account at the Federal Reserve, rather than drawn down as bills come due. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] In fiscal 2025, Foreign Military Financing funded $17.9 billion of the $104.4 billion that passed through the whole Foreign Military Sales system worldwide; most sales are paid for by the buyers themselves. [cite:ow8_crs_fms2026]

The process. A sale begins with consultations and a formal Letter of Request from the buyer to the Pentagon agency that manages the item. That agency prices it and drafts a Letter of Offer and Acceptance; the Defense Security Cooperation Agency reviews it, and the State Department, which sets arms-transfer policy, approves the case. If the sale is large enough, Congress must be notified, and the offer cannot be issued until the review period has run. Once the buyer signs and pays a deposit into the Foreign Military Sales Trust Fund, the Pentagon receives authority to spend it, places contracts with manufacturers or takes the items from its own stocks, and delivers them; the sale is then subject to the Pentagon's "Golden Sentry" end-use monitoring. [cite:ow8_crs_fms2026]

Israel's shorter review. Congress is told of a sale formally only above certain values, and the thresholds and waiting periods depend on the buyer. For most countries, notification is required for major defence equipment worth $14 million or more, or other articles and services worth $50 million, and Congress has 30 days to act. For NATO, its members, Japan, Australia, South Korea, Israel and New Zealand, the thresholds are higher ($25 million and $100 million) and the period is 15 days. Before formal notification, the State Department informally consults the two foreign-affairs committees, under a "tiered review" of 20 to 40 days. [cite:ow8_crs_review2021] Congress can block a sale only by passing a joint resolution of disapproval in both chambers, which the President can veto; overriding a veto takes two-thirds of each chamber, and Congress has never blocked a sale this way. [cite:ow8_crs_review2021]

The emergency door. The Act also allows the review to be skipped. If the President states in the notification that "an emergency exists" requiring the immediate sale in the national security interests of the United States, with a detailed justification, the sale may go ahead at once. [cite:ow8_crs_review2021] This power, rarely used, has been used for Israel repeatedly since December 2023; the next section sets out when.

From a factory to Gaza. Put together, the steps can be followed for a single munition. The figure below traces a 2,000-pound bomb of the kind the United States sent Israel after October 2023, each step sourced to the law, the procedure or the record of what happened. It shows that the system has several points at which the United States can, in principle, stop or condition a transfer: the State Department's approval, Congress's review, the decision to ship, and end-use monitoring. It also shows how many of those points were bypassed or found unenforceable in practice.

What the routes mean. The official purpose of the system, in both governments' account, is to keep Israel able to defend itself against better-armed neighbours: the 2008 law that defines Israel's "qualitative military edge" requires every other arms sale to the region to be checked against it. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The American side of the bargain is also built in: because Israel's aid is spent through Foreign Military Sales, the money is paid to American manufacturers, and from fiscal 2028 the share Israel may spend in Israel falls to zero, as the section on co-production explains. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The asymmetry lies in the last step. Every stage up to delivery runs through American hands and American records; the use of the weapon does not, and the United States has said, in its own report, that it could not verify how its weapons were used. [cite:ow8_js_nsm20report]

sections.h: The Pace Since October 2023
sections.html:
Before the war in Gaza, the pipeline described in the previous section ran at the steady rhythm set by the 2016 memorandum. After 7 October 2023 it ran much faster, and the emergency power that lets an administration skip congressional review became a routine part of it. This section sets out the record under two administrations, Biden's and Trump's, which differed sharply in what they said and less in what they shipped.

The first emergencies, December 2023. On 8 December 2023 the State Department notified Congress that Secretary of State Antony Blinken had determined that "an emergency exists that requires the immediate sale" of 13,981 120mm tank cartridges to Israel, worth $106.5 million, bypassing the review period. The department said that "the United States is committed to the security of Israel". Such determinations were rare, though at least four administrations had used the power since 1979. [cite:ow8_ap_tank2023] On 29 December 2023 a second emergency sale followed, worth $147.5 million: 4,792 M107 155mm artillery rounds, 52,229 M795 rounds and 30,000 propelling charges, drawn from US Army stock. [cite:ow8_at_155] Of the 85 Foreign Military Sales cases notified to Congress worldwide in 2023, these two were the only ones to use the emergency exception. [cite:ow8_js_wrsa85] [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] A Senate resolution introduced that month (S.Res. 504), which would have required a human-rights report on Israel's use of American aid under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, later failed. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

Congress adds money, April 2024. In April 2024 Congress passed the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, which added $3.5 billion in Foreign Military Financing, $4 billion for missile defence and $1.2 billion for the Iron Beam laser. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] Brown University's Costs of War project calculated that the United States spent $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel between October 2023 and September 2025, not counting committed arms sales. [cite:gz_cow_aid]

The pause, May 2024. The only American hold on a shipment came in May 2024, when the administration paused a consignment of 1,800 2,000-pound bombs and 1,700 500-pound bombs to signal concern about a ground assault on Rafah, where more than a million displaced Palestinians were sheltering. [cite:ow8_axios_pause] President Biden explained: "Civilians have been killed in Gaza as a consequence of those bombs." The 500-pound bombs were released weeks later; the 2,000-pound bombs stayed held for eight months. [cite:ow8_ap_unpause] In August 2024 the administration approved more than $20 billion in new sales, including F-15IA fighters. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

The release and the second wave, 2025. Five days after taking office, on 25 January 2025, President Trump released the 2,000-pound bombs, writing that "a lot of things that were ordered and paid for by Israel, but have not been sent by Biden, are now on their way!" [cite:ow8_ap_unpause] In February 2025 the administration notified $8.4 billion in sales, by the Congressional Research Service's count. At the end of the month, by the Times of Israel's account, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived congressional review to fast-track about $3 billion of them, including heavy bombs and armoured bulldozers that the Biden administration had withheld, and on 1 March he announced that he had signed a declaration to expedite "approximately $4 billion in military assistance". These reported sums overlap and are not additive. He described Biden's policy as a "partial arms embargo" and said the administration had approved nearly $12 billion in major sales to Israel since 20 January. [cite:ow8_toi_rubio2025] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] Biden had denied withholding anything except the single batch of 2,000-pound bombs. [cite:ow8_toi_rubio2025]

The scale. By April 2025, according to the Congressional Research Service, the United States had 751 active Foreign Military Sales cases with Israel, worth $39.2 billion. By May 2025 Israel's Ministry of Defense said that some 800 aircraft and 140 ships had delivered more than 90,000 tons of American arms and equipment since the war began. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] In fiscal 2025, the Congressional Research Service noted, Israel was among the countries with the highest-value proposed sales in the whole programme. [cite:ow8_crs_fms2026]

The two administrations' accounts. The Biden administration justified the December 2023 emergencies by the United States' commitment to Israel's security and its right to self-defence, and the May 2024 pause by the harm the heaviest bombs did to civilians. [cite:ow8_ap_tank2023] [cite:ow8_ap_unpause] The Trump administration presented its emergencies as ending a "partial arms embargo" and the conditions that Biden had imposed through a national security memorandum, discussed in the last section of this part. [cite:ow8_toi_rubio2025] The record shows that the two differed in one decision, the hold on the 2,000-pound bombs; that both used the emergency power to bypass Congress; and that Congress, which has never blocked an arms sale by a resolution of disapproval, did not block any of these. [cite:ow8_crs_review2021] [cite:ow8_ap_tank2023] [cite:ow8_toi_rubio2025] Part Two sets out how Congress voted.

sections.h: Built Together: Iron Dome, David's Sling and Arrow
sections.html:
Not everything in the pipeline flows one way. Israel's three layers of missile defence, Iron Dome against short-range rockets, David's Sling against medium-range missiles and Arrow against ballistic missiles, were designed by Israeli state companies and paid for in large part by the United States, and they are increasingly built in American factories by American partners. This is the part of the relationship where the claim that the United States gets something back is easiest to test.

Iron Dome's funding. Iron Dome was developed by Israel's Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and first funded by the United States in fiscal 2011, with $205 million. Congress added $70 million in 2012, $194 million in 2013 and $235.3 million in 2014, plus a $225 million emergency appropriation during the Gaza war in the summer of 2014: $929.3 million in four years. [cite:ow8_crs_irondome2014] Since 2019 missile-defence funding has been part of the memorandum of understanding, at $500 million a year, and in wartime Congress has added more. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] On 23 September 2021, after Democratic leaders removed $1 billion to replenish Iron Dome from a stopgap spending bill in the face of objections from some members, the House passed it as a separate bill by 420 votes to 9; the appropriations chair, Rosa DeLauro, called it money "limited to a system that is entirely defensive". [cite:ow8_ap_irondome2021] The April 2024 supplemental added $4 billion for missile defence and $1.2 billion for Iron Beam, a laser system. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The House later rejected, by 422 votes to 6, an amendment by Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene to strip $500 million in annual cooperative missile-defence funding from the defence bill for fiscal 2026. [cite:pm_ji_mtg_amendment] [scene:pm6_greene|Part Six of Follow the Money]

The 2014 co-production deal. In March 2014 the two governments signed an agreement that allowed components of Iron Dome to be made in the United States and gave the US Missile Defense Agency full access to Iron Dome technology, which until then had been Israel's property. Raytheon became Rafael's American partner and received a $149 million contract for Tamir interceptor parts in September 2014; American officials expected modest cost savings. [cite:ow8_crs_irondome2014] The same model was applied to the upper layers. By 2016 American production funding for David's Sling, built by Rafael with Raytheon, and for Arrow 3, built by Israel Aerospace Industries with Boeing, was split equally between the Israeli prime contractor and its American partner; an Israeli missile-defence official described "true joint production" with about half the work done in the United States. [cite:ow8_dn_coprod2016]

A plant in Arkansas. The arrangement has since moved from components to whole interceptors. On 9 October 2026 Raytheon–Rafael Protection Systems, a joint venture, announced that it had delivered the first Tamir interceptors built at its plant in Camden, Arkansas, opened in late 2025 and the first facility outside Israel to make them. Its chief executive said: "For the first time, we can produce these interceptors in the United States." The plant is also to build the US variant for the Marine Corps' new air-defence system. [cite:ow8_rtx_camden] [cite:ow8_dn_mric]

The end of offshore procurement. The other half of the "buy American" story is in the aid memoranda. Israel had been permitted to spend part of its American military grant inside Israel, on its own defence industry, a practice called offshore procurement; under the 2007 memorandum that share could reach 26.3 per cent. The 2016 memorandum, signed on 14 September 2016, phases it out, so that by the end of the memorandum in fiscal 2028 the grant is to be spent in the United States; in fiscal 2025 the offshore share was $450.3 million. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:hm_dn_mou] As the share falls, more of each year's $3.3 billion is paid to American manufacturers, and less to Israeli ones. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

Who benefits. The record supports both readings of this relationship. The United States has paid for a large share of Israel's missile defences; and it has obtained, in return, access to the technology, a combat-tested interceptor for its own Marine Corps, an interceptor production line in Arkansas, and a guarantee that Israel's grant money will be spent with American firms. [cite:ow8_crs_irondome2014] [cite:ow8_dn_mric] [cite:ow8_rtx_camden] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The beneficiaries on the American side are named companies, Raytheon and Boeing above all, as well as the government. [cite:ow8_dn_coprod2016] The asymmetry is that the money is American public money, appropriated year after year with near-unanimous votes, while the systems' first purpose is the defence of Israel. [cite:ow8_ap_irondome2021] [cite:pm_ji_mtg_amendment] And, as Part Seven showed, when Israel's Arrow stocks ran low in 2025, American THAAD interceptors were fired alongside them. [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025]

sections.h: The Rules on Use: Leahy, the Forum and NSM-20
sections.html:
American law does not leave the use of American weapons entirely to the buyer. Two statutes named after former Senator Patrick Leahy bar aid to foreign security units that have committed gross violations of human rights, and in February 2024 a presidential memorandum required recipients to promise in writing to follow international law. This section sets out how those rules were applied to Israel: through a vetting process found, by the official who ran the standard one, to be unlike that used for any other country; through one unit's case; and through a memorandum that lasted just over a year.

The Leahy laws. The State Department's version (22 U.S.C. 2378d) prohibits assistance to any foreign security-force unit when the Secretary of State has credible information that it committed a gross violation of human rights; the Defense Department's version (10 U.S.C. 362) bars Pentagon-funded training, equipment or other assistance on the same basis. Vetting looks above all for torture, extrajudicial killing, enforced disappearance and rape under colour of law. "Credible information" is a deliberately low bar: in the 2024 appropriations act, information that "supports a reasonable belief that a violation has occurred". Both laws allow aid to resume if the government concerned takes effective steps to bring those responsible to justice. [cite:ow8_crs_leahy2025] The laws apply to Israel as they do to every recipient; the Congressional Research Service noted reports from former officials that the process for Israel differs. [cite:ow8_crs_leahy2025]

The Israel Leahy Vetting Forum. The most detailed account of the difference comes from Charles O. ("Cob") Blaha, who directed the State Department office responsible for Leahy vetting for seven and a half years before retiring in 2023, and who has since become a senior adviser to DAWN (Democracy for the Arab World Now), an advocacy group. [cite:ow8_js_blaha_ilvf] According to Blaha, the department set up a special "Israel Leahy Vetting Forum", which first met in 2020 under unpublished procedures. For Israel alone, he wrote, a decision that a unit is ineligible rests with the Deputy Secretary of State, which is "true for no other country in the world"; before a case reaches that level the department must send a formal written request for information to the Israeli government, which can take up to three months to reply. His conclusion, as of June 2024, was that "there are no ineligible Israeli units". [cite:ow8_js_blaha_ilvf] The State Department has not published the forum's procedures, and its own account of the process is not on the public record; Blaha's is that of a named former official with first-hand knowledge, now working with an advocacy group.

Netzah Yehuda. The forum's one public outcome concerned five Israeli units. On 29 April 2024 the State Department announced that Secretary Blinken had found that four had committed gross violations but had taken sufficient corrective steps, and that a fifth, the Netzah Yehuda battalion, had committed a gross violation and would remain eligible while the department worked with Israel on remediation. [cite:ow8_js_blaha_ilvf] On 9 August 2024 the State Department announced that Israel had "effectively remediated" the battalion's violations, making it fully eligible. Blaha, by his own account, replied that the only known measures were administrative, the discharge of two soldiers and a reprimand for a commander, that no member of the battalion had been punished or charged over the 2022 death of Omar Assad, and that the decision was "directly contrary to the Leahy law". The State Department's own description differs: it said two soldiers were removed from combat duty, vetting was changed and human-rights training required, as Part Eleven sets out. [scene:ow11_exceptions|Part Eleven: the Leahy Law] [cite:ow8_js_blaha_nz]

NSM-20. A broader rule came from the White House. On 8 February 2024 President Biden issued National Security Memorandum 20, which grew out of an amendment proposed by Senator Chris Van Hollen in December 2023 and backed by eighteen Democratic senators. It required countries receiving American weapons to give "credible and reliable written assurances" that they would use them in line with international law and would "facilitate and not arbitrarily deny, restrict, or otherwise impede" American-supported humanitarian aid; countries at war had 45 days, and the administration had to report to Congress within 90 days. [cite:ow8_aca_nsm20] Israel's defence minister gave the assurances on 14 March 2024, and Blinken accepted them on 25 March. [cite:ow8_js_nsm20report]

The May 2024 report. The report, released on 10 May 2024, said it was "reasonable to assess" that American weapons had been used by Israeli forces "in instances inconsistent with its IHL obligations". It made no finding about any specific incident, explaining that Israel "has not shared complete information" to verify whether American weapons were used in alleged violations. It judged Israel's assurances "credible and reliable", allowing deliveries to continue, and found no breach of the law that bars military aid to a government restricting American humanitarian aid, while describing aid reaching Gaza as "insufficient". [cite:ow8_js_nsm20report] The same week, the administration had paused the 2,000-pound bombs over Rafah. [cite:ow8_axios_pause]

Revocation. On 21 February 2025 President Trump revoked NSM-20, and on 14 March the White House rescinded the Biden administration's wider conventional arms transfer policy, which had aimed to prevent transfers risking "facilitating or otherwise contributing to violations of human rights"; it offered no explanation and issued no replacement. [cite:ow8_aca_rescind] Secretary Rubio described the memorandum as having imposed "baseless and politicized conditions on military assistance to Israel". [cite:ow8_toi_rubio2025] The Leahy laws, being statutes, remain in force as of October 2026; the memorandum's assurance-and-report system does not.

The asymmetry, stated plainly. The two governments' positions are on the record. The Biden administration's was that Israel's assurances were credible and that the law was being applied; the Trump administration's was that the conditions were themselves illegitimate. [cite:ow8_js_nsm20report] [cite:ow8_toi_rubio2025] What both positions share is the limit the May 2024 report admitted: the United States tracks its weapons up to the point of delivery, but depends on Israel for information about how they are used, and Israel did not supply it in full. [cite:ow8_js_nsm20report] That is the "one-way mirror" in its narrowest and best-documented form, and Part Thirteen returns to it.

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: Palantir and the Data Contractors
chapters.intro: Part Nine follows the American data company most often named in accounts of Israel inside the American state: Palantir Technologies. It begins with the company's origins in the CIA's venture fund and its growth into a contractor for the Army, the Pentagon's Maven programme and the Department of Homeland Security. It then follows Palantir's longest civilian relationship, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, through the contracts, the data those platforms run on and the legal doctrine that lets agencies buy data they could not seize. It ends with Palantir's January 2024 partnership with Israel's Ministry of Defense: what is documented, what Israeli reporting says, what the company denies, and how investors responded.
chapters.outro: Part Nine found Palantir to be, on the documents, an American contractor whose money and largest customers are American: seeded by the CIA's In-Q-Tel, holding a Maven contract with a ceiling near $1.3 billion and an Army enterprise agreement worth up to $10 billion, and embedded at ICE since 2014 through a series of contracts, including sole-source awards in 2025. [cite:ow9_ap_s1] [cite:ow9_ds_maven] [cite:ow9_bd_army] [cite:ow9_reg_immos] The data in those platforms comes from the agencies themselves, from other agencies and, increasingly, from brokers, under a third-party doctrine that the Supreme Court narrowed in 2018 and 2026 for compelled data but that Congress has not closed for purchased data. [cite:ow9_cornell_tpd] [cite:ow9_pw_chatrie] [cite:ow9_cs_4thact] Palantir's Israeli contract, signed in January 2024, is documented in outline only; Israeli reporting says Unit 8200 and the Shin Bet declined the company's services, Palantir denies any role in the Lavender and Gospel targeting systems, and the one documented case of Israeli intelligence data held on an American cloud concerns Microsoft. [cite:ow9_globes_palantir] [cite:ow9_pal_unletter] [cite:ow9_nbc_msft] No source shows American agency data passing to Israel through Palantir. Part Ten turns to the reverse direction: Israeli-founded firms selling surveillance and security tools to American agencies.

sections.h: From the CIA's Venture Fund to the Army's Ten-Year Deal
sections.html:
Palantir Technologies is an American company, and the first thing to establish about it is whose customer it is. It was founded in 2003 by a group of investors that included Peter Thiel, and it took early seed money for its government counterintelligence work from In-Q-Tel, the venture-capital arm of the Central Intelligence Agency. [cite:ow9_ap_s1] BuzzFeed News, reporting from inside the company, put In-Q-Tel's investment at about $2 million and said the money helped the start-up shape its data-analysis software to the CIA's work. [cite:ow9_bf_karp2015] The sources used here do not agree on the year the In-Q-Tel money arrived; they agree that it came early and that it was small beside what followed.

What followed was a business built mainly on the American state. When Palantir filed to list its shares in August 2020, the Associated Press reported from the filing that nearly half of its 2019 revenue of $746 million came from government agencies, that it had lost $580 million that year, and that the US Army alone had paid it $135 million since a court ruling in September 2018. [cite:ow9_ap_s1]

The intelligence agencies. Palantir's early work with American and allied intelligence is documented mainly through the Snowden archive. In February 2017 The Intercept published documents showing that Palantir had built a tool called "XKEYSCORE Helper," which let analysts move data from the National Security Agency's XKEYSCORE system into Palantir to sort and visualise it; by about 2010, the documents indicated, at least three of the Five Eyes countries were using Palantir to process intelligence. [cite:ow9_int_xks] After the 2013 disclosures Palantir denied any link to the NSA's PRISM programme; it did not answer The Intercept's questions about XKEYSCORE. [cite:ow9_int_xks] The NSA relationship did not last. BuzzFeed reported that by the summer of 2015 it had ended, that pilot work had never become a full contract, and that the chief executive, Alex Karp, told staff the two sides had "walked away" from each other. The same report described the company's software as deeply embedded at the CIA, which had considered cancelling its contract after a 2013 magazine profile and decided Palantir would be too hard to replace. [cite:ow9_bf_karp2015]

The Pentagon. The scale of Palantir's military business grew sharply after 2024. In May 2024 the Defense Department awarded it a five-year, $480 million contract for the Maven Smart System, the Pentagon's main platform for fusing sensor and intelligence data into a picture commanders can act on; in May 2025 the ceiling was raised by $795 million, to nearly $1.3 billion through 2029. The director of the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency said then that Maven had more than 20,000 active users across the services and combatant commands. [cite:ow9_ds_maven] In August 2025 the Army went further, folding 75 separate contracts, 15 with Palantir as prime contractor and 60 as subcontractor, into a single enterprise agreement worth up to $10 billion over ten years; the Army is bound only to a minimum, which was not disclosed. [cite:ow9_bd_army] In February 2026 the Department of Homeland Security signed a five-year blanket purchase agreement worth up to $1 billion, which, the next section shows, put Palantir's platforms within reach of every major DHS component. [cite:ow9_sa_dhsbpa]

What this means for the question of this book. The record above describes a company whose money, origins and largest customers are American. That matters because a common account of Palantir, repeated in material reviewed, treats it as a conduit through which American intelligence passes to Israel, often by pointing to the company's hiring of former Israeli intelligence soldiers or to Thiel's politics. Shared employers and shared opinions are not a documented channel; the NSA's actual channel to Israel, a 2009 memorandum, is described in [scene:ow4_memorandum|Part Four]. The documents used in this part show Palantir selling to US agencies and, from January 2024, to Israel's Ministry of Defense; they do not show data belonging to an American agency being passed by Palantir to Israel. Karp himself has described the Israeli business as small: "Israel has historically bought our product, it's not a commercially relevant part of our business," he said in March 2024. [cite:ow9_fortune_karp] The Israeli contract is examined in the third section, with what is documented, what is reported and what the company denies.

The company's stated purpose for its government work is consistent across these years: that its software lets agencies analyse data they already hold lawfully, faster and in one place. In its May 2025 letter to the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, it put the point plainly: "we do not conduct surveillance," the customer does, using data it has lawful access to. [cite:ow9_pal_unletter] That description is accurate as far as it goes, and it is also the reason the next section begins with the data rather than the software. Where the data comes from, and what law allows an agency to hold it, decides what a platform like Palantir's can be used to do.

sections.h: ICE, the Sole-Source Contracts and the Data They Run On
sections.html:
Palantir's longest civilian relationship is with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and it is the clearest case of how the company's platforms meet the data of the American state. It has three parts: the contracts, which are public in outline; the data the platforms draw on, which is partly public; and the law that lets an agency acquire much of that data without a judge, which is the part least understood.

The contracts. In 2014 ICE began using an Investigative Case Management system built by Palantir for its criminal-investigations arm, Homeland Security Investigations; Mother Jones reported in 2019 that the first contract was worth $41 million. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] A second Palantir tool, FALCON, a version of its Gotham software customised for HSI, lets agents pull data from other DHS offices, the FBI and other sources. The Intercept, reviewing ICE documents in March 2017, reported that the system "permits ICE agents to access information from the Central Intelligence Agency," and quoted a 2013 funding document saying Palantir "enables ICE/HSI to secure information sharing with other law enforcement agencies in real-time." [cite:ow9_int_falcon] The 2019 renewal of the case-management contract was worth about $49 million over three years, a figure revealed only because ICE's redactions could be undone by copying the text. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] In September 2022 ICE awarded Palantir a five-year contract reported at $95.9 million for installing and sustaining the system. [cite:ow9_eb_icm2022] [cite:ow9_vv_icm2022]

In April 2025, under the second Trump administration, ICE moved to pay Palantir $29.9 million to build "ImmigrationOS," a platform meant to select and prioritise people for arrest, to track people who leave the country on their own, and to follow each case from identification to removal. ICE's justification letter said "Palantir is the only source that can provide the required capabilities." [cite:ow9_reg_immos] By June 2025 ICE was preparing a further limited-sources justification for replacing the case-management system itself, again concluding that only Palantir could meet its needs, with a deadline of September 2026. [cite:ow9_bu_immos] In January 2026, 404 Media reported a further Palantir tool used by ICE, ELITE, which compiles dossiers and "leads" on people ICE believes may be deportable and gives each person's current address a "confidence score." Fortune, reporting on it, noted that ICE and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services had signed a data-sharing agreement covering nearly 80 million Medicaid patients; neither Palantir nor DHS answered questions about how ELITE was used. [cite:ow9_fortune_elite] In February 2026 DHS signed its five-year blanket purchase agreement with Palantir, worth up to $1 billion, under which CBP, ICE, FEMA and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency can all buy its platforms without separate competitions. [cite:ow9_sa_dhsbpa]

Totals for Palantir's ICE business vary widely in circulation, from under $250 million to more than $400 million, because they count different things: obligations or ceilings, ICE alone or all of DHS, and different end dates. This section gives the awards one by one with their dates rather than adding them into a single figure.

The data. Palantir's software holds nothing until an agency puts data into it. Some of that data is the agency's own: case files, border-crossing records, fingerprints. Some comes from other agencies under sharing agreements, as the Medicaid agreement shows. A growing share is bought. Documents the American Civil Liberties Union obtained through a lawsuit, published in January 2026, show that CBP paid Venntel more than $2 million in 2019 and 2020 for location data drawn from phone apps, that CBP and the Secret Service bought from Babel Street, and that ICE was returning to such purchases in 2026 through a contract with Penlink. [cite:ow9_aclu_adid] Other agencies do the same: in January 2024 the NSA's director, General Paul Nakasone, confirmed to Senator Ron Wyden that the agency buys commercially available "netflow" records, data on the flow of internet traffic, including wholly domestic traffic. [cite:ow9_tc_nsanetflow]

The law. Agencies can buy what they could not seize because of the third-party doctrine. In United States v. Miller (1976) the Supreme Court held that a customer had no Fourth Amendment protection for bank records held by the bank; in Smith v. Maryland (1979) it held that recording the numbers dialled from a home phone was not a search, because the caller had "voluntarily conveyed" them to the phone company. [cite:ow9_cornell_tpd] In Carpenter v. United States (2018) the Court refused to extend that rule to historical cell-site location records, which require a warrant, but it did not overturn Miller or Smith. [cite:ow9_cornell_tpd] On 29 June 2026, in Chatrie v. United States, a 6–3 majority held that obtaining even two hours of a person's location history from Google was a search. [cite:ow9_pw_chatrie] Both decisions concern data the government compels a company to hand over. The analyses checked do not say that either reaches data the government buys on the open market, and an ICE draft legal memorandum obtained by the ACLU argues that location data tied to advertising identifiers, rather than names, falls outside Carpenter; the ACLU calls this "a distinction without a difference." [cite:ow9_pw_chatrie] [cite:ow9_aclu_adid] Congress has considered closing the gap. The Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act, which would require a court order before law-enforcement and intelligence agencies buy Americans' data, passed the House on 17 April 2024 by 219 to 199, over the opposition of the Biden White House, a senior official of which called it "unworkable"; it did not become law in that Congress. [cite:ow9_aclu_adid] [cite:ow9_cs_4thact]

None of this chain runs through Israel. The point is worth stating because Palantir's ICE work and its Israeli work are often described together, as if one fed the other. The sources used here document no such link: ICE buys the platforms and owns the data in them, and the Israeli Ministry of Defense is a separate customer with separate data. [cite:ow9_calcalist_partner] [cite:ow9_pal_unletter] The Israeli phone-hacking and spyware tools that ICE has bought directly from Israeli-founded companies are a different matter, treated in [scene:ow6_nypd_ice|Part Six] and in Part Ten.

The governments' stated purposes are on the record. ICE describes these systems as tools for investigating crime and for enforcing immigration law efficiently, and its April 2025 justification framed speed as the reason for skipping competition. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] DHS, which announced in 2024 that it was ending bulk location-data contracts, has not explained its return to them. [cite:ow9_aclu_adid] Palantir's position is that it does not surveil anyone and that its customers work only with data they may lawfully hold. [cite:ow9_pal_unletter] The test of that position is the law on lawful holding, and on purchased data that law, as of October 2026, remains largely unwritten.

sections.h: Palantir and Israel: The Partnership, the Denials and the Investors
sections.html:
Palantir's tie to Israel is a contract between an American company and a foreign ministry of defence. It is documented in outline, its contents are not public, and the most serious claims made about it are denied by the company and contradicted by Israeli reporting. Each of those layers needs to be kept separate.

The partnership, January 2024. Three months into the Gaza war, Palantir held the first board meeting of 2024 in Tel Aviv, with Peter Thiel and Alex Karp among the executives who travelled, and announced a strategic partnership with Israel's Ministry of Defense to "supply Palantir technology to help the country's war effort." [cite:ow9_calcalist_partner] Globes, the Israeli business daily, reported on 29 January 2024 that after speaking at Tel Aviv University, Karp went to the military headquarters in Tel Aviv and signed an upgraded agreement with the ministry, and was photographed with Danny Gold, head of its Directorate of Defense Research and Development. Bloomberg reported that Israel was set to buy Palantir's AI platform, with revenue expected in the tens of millions of dollars. "None of the parties would elaborate" on what Palantir actually does. [cite:ow9_globes_palantir]

What Israeli reporting says it does, and does not do. The same Globes report gave the most specific account in the public record. Palantir, it said, was understood to work on some logistics and manpower management for the Israel Defense Forces but "does not work with military intelligence"; Unit 8200, the army's signals-intelligence unit, and the Shin Bet security service had examined its system and "decided not to hire its services." [cite:ow9_globes_palantir] This report rests on unnamed sources, and Globes did not say how it knew; it is nonetheless the only account in the sources used here that describes the work unit by unit, and it runs against the widespread claim that Palantir supplies Israel's targeting systems.

What Palantir says. The company has answered that claim in writing. In a letter of 22 May 2025 to the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, it said it "did not provide the technology for, nor is it involved with, Gospel or Lavender," two AI targeting systems named in reporting on the Gaza war; that its work for the Ministry of Defense "only began in the wake of the attacks of 7 October 2023," its earlier Israeli customers having been civilian agencies; that it "does not and has not supported predictive policing workflows in Israel"; and that its defence work is done "in accordance with domestic, international, and humanitarian law." [cite:ow9_pal_unletter] Karp has defended the work publicly and on political grounds. Asked in March 2024 about staff who left over it, he said: "We've lost employees, I'm sure we'll lose employees. If you have a position that does not cost you to ever lose an employee, it's not a position." [cite:ow9_fortune_karp]

A separate company: Microsoft and Unit 8200. The one documented case of an American technology company's infrastructure holding Israeli intelligence data on Palestinians does not involve Palantir. On 6 August 2025 The Guardian reported, citing eleven sources, that Unit 8200 had stored recordings of Palestinians' phone calls in a segregated area of Microsoft's Azure cloud. Microsoft ordered a review, and on 25 September 2025 its president, Brad Smith, said the review had found evidence that "supports elements of the Guardian's reporting," including the use of Azure storage in the Netherlands and of AI services, and that Microsoft had disabled the unit's use of those services. "We do not provide technology to facilitate mass surveillance of civilians," he said. Israel's Defense Ministry declined to comment. [cite:ow9_nbc_msft] The case is examined with Unit 8200 in [scene:ow4_gaza|Part Four]. Accounts that attach this story to Palantir conflate two companies; the material reviewed contains no source that does so.

Investors. Palantir's Israeli business has had a cost in its share register. In October 2024 Storebrand Asset Management, a large Norwegian investment firm, sold a holding worth about $24 million, saying it had excluded Palantir because of "sales of products and services to Israel" for use in the occupied Palestinian territories, which it believed included "AI-based predictive policing systems." [cite:ow9_globes_storebrand] [cite:ow9_silicon_storebrand] Palantir's later letter to the UN denies supporting predictive policing in Israel. [cite:ow9_pal_unletter] Neither report records a response from Palantir to Storebrand itself. Storebrand's holding was small beside the company's market value, then about $96 billion. [cite:ow9_globes_storebrand]

Testing the one-way claim. On the documents, the flow in this relationship runs from an American company to an Israeli customer, for payment, in a market Karp says is commercially minor. [cite:ow9_fortune_karp] What the United States receives is what any seller receives; no source used here records a reciprocal arrangement, Israeli access to American data through Palantir, or American access to what Israel does with Palantir's software. That last gap is the real asymmetry. The contract's terms are not public, the Israeli Ministry of Defense will not describe the work, and the only detailed account, from Globes, comes from unnamed Israeli sources. [cite:ow9_globes_palantir] The Pentagon's contracts with the same company are public in outline and its spending passes through Congress; the Israeli use of the company's tools passes through no process that Americans can see. That pattern, a documented American export and an undocumented use, recurs through the next part, which turns to the Israeli firms that sell their surveillance tools to American agencies.

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: Israeli Spyware and Security Firms in America
chapters.intro: Part Ten turns from an American contractor selling to Israel to Israeli-founded companies selling to, or operating in, the United States. It follows NSO Group, whose Pegasus spyware was licensed by Israel's Defense Ministry, used against American diplomats, blacklisted by the Commerce Department and tested by the FBI; Paragon Solutions, whose Graphite spyware ICE bought, paused and revived after the company passed into American ownership; and five other firms, Cellebrite, Elbit Systems' American subsidiary, Cognyte, Black Cube and Carbyne. For each it sets out the owners, the American customers and contract values, the role of Israeli export control, the controversies and the company's answer.
chapters.outro: Part Ten found that Israeli-founded surveillance firms reach the American state along two different roads. Firms whose ownership or operations moved substantially outside Israel sell to American agencies under contracts that are public in outline: Cellebrite to ICE, CBP and the military police; Elbit's subsidiary, renamed Twenty-Six Defense in September 2026, to CBP on the Mexican border; Paragon to ICE under a contract signed before, and revived after, its purchase by AE Industrial Partners; Carbyne to local 911 centres before and after its sale to Axon. [cite:ow10_reason_cb] [cite:ow10_dn_26] [cite:ow10_npr_lyons] [cite:ow10_p2_axon] Firms that stayed Israeli-controlled produced the cases in which Americans were the targets: NSO's Pegasus, exported country by country under Israeli Defense Ministry licence, was used against State Department employees, and Black Cube was hired against former American officials. [cite:ow10_ctech_37] [cite:ow10_reu_state] [cite:ow10_cnbc_bc] Washington's answer was to blacklist the company and to bar risky spyware from federal use, an order later applied so as to let ICE's Paragon contract proceed. [cite:ow10_doc_entity] [cite:ow10_eo14093] [cite:ow10_tc_lyons] Part Eleven turns to the legal shields that protect Israel and its supporters in American law.

sections.h: NSO Group: Licensed by Israel, Blacklisted by Washington, Tested by the FBI
sections.html:
NSO Group, maker of the Pegasus phone-hacking software, is the Israeli surveillance company whose relationship with the American state is the most contradictory. The United States blacklisted it in 2021 for selling tools used against American officials. In the same years the FBI bought its software, tested it and came close to using it. The company's Israeli licence, its American legal defeats and its 2025 change of ownership all bear on the same question: who decides where such a tool goes, and who answers for it. [cite:ow10_doc_entity] [cite:ow10_globe_fbi]

The Israeli licence. NSO cannot sell abroad without the Israeli state. Israel's Ministry of Defense decides to which countries Israeli companies may sell offensive cyber tools; it says it approves exports only to government bodies, for lawful use in preventing and investigating crime and fighting terrorism, under commitments from the buyer. NSO has said repeatedly that it sold only to countries the ministry approved. In November 2021, as scrutiny grew, the ministry cut the list of countries eligible to buy such tools from 102 to 37, dropping, among others, Morocco, Mexico, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates; it said the state was "constantly reassessing its policy." [cite:ow10_ctech_37] The licensing gives Israel's government a decisive role in where Pegasus went. It does not, on the public record, give it a role in how each customer used it, and NSO has argued throughout that it is not responsible for how its customers use the tool. [cite:ow10_axios_jury]

Pegasus and American officials. In December 2021 Reuters reported that the iPhones of at least nine State Department employees, based in Uganda or working on matters concerning it, had been hacked with NSO's tools; Reuters could not say who launched the attacks. NSO said it had no indication its tools were used but had cut off the relevant customers' access. The Israeli embassy in Washington said that if the claims were accurate, "it is a severe violation" of the terms on which the spyware is licensed for export, which permit use only against terrorism and serious crime. [cite:ow10_reu_state] A month earlier, on 3 November 2021, the Commerce Department had added NSO and another Israeli firm, Candiru, to its Entity List, which bars American companies from selling them technology without a licence, citing evidence that they "developed and supplied spyware to foreign governments" that used it to "maliciously target government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics, and embassy workers." [cite:ow10_doc_entity] In March 2023 President Biden's Executive Order 14093 barred federal agencies from operational use of commercial spyware that posed counterintelligence risks to the United States or risks of misuse by foreign governments, allowing waivers of up to a year. [cite:ow10_eo14093]

The FBI's own Pegasus. The New York Times reported in January 2022 that the FBI had secretly bought Pegasus, which it dated to 2019, and that NSO had shown the Bureau Phantom, a version able to hack American phone numbers; after about two years of deliberation the FBI decided in the summer of 2021 against using it. [cite:ow10_ai_nytmag] Documents the Times later obtained through a freedom-of-information lawsuit placed the first purchase in 2018, put the Bureau's payments to NSO at about $5 million, and showed that FBI officials pressed from late 2020 to mid-2021 to use the tool in criminal cases before the Bureau decided on 22 July 2021 to "cease all efforts regarding the potential use of the NSO product." The FBI says there was "no operational use of the NSO product to support any FBI investigation," and that the Pegasus licence was held for testing and evaluation. [cite:ow10_globe_fbi] A separate episode came to light in 2023: an American contractor, Riva Networks, had used NSO's location-tracking tool, Landmark, on Mexican phone numbers on the FBI's behalf after the 2021 ban. The FBI says it was misled into thinking Riva was using its own tool; Director Christopher Wray terminated the contract, and the White House said it had not known of the arrangement. [cite:ow10_9to5_riva] The reporting used here does not show that the FBI's Pegasus licence was bought through Riva; the two purchases should not be merged.

In American courts. WhatsApp, owned by Meta, sued NSO in 2019 over the hacking of about 1,400 of its users' devices. A federal judge in California found NSO liable in December 2024, and on 6 May 2025 a jury awarded Meta $444,719 in compensatory damages and $167.25 million in punitive damages. [cite:ow10_axios_jury] [cite:ow10_sw_contempt] NSO argued that it was not responsible for how its government customers used Pegasus, a tool it said was "deployed responsibly by authorized government agencies." [cite:ow10_axios_jury] In October 2025 Judge Phyllis Hamilton cut the punitive award to $4 million and issued a permanent injunction barring NSO from targeting WhatsApp or its users; NSO's spokesman called the reduction a step in the right direction. [cite:ow10_cs_inj] NSO appealed to the Ninth Circuit, and in June 2026 WhatsApp said it had detected a new NSO-linked phishing campaign against its users and was seeking a contempt order; neither the appeal nor the contempt motion had been decided in the reporting found. [cite:ow10_sw_contempt] Apple, which had sued NSO in 2021, asked to drop its case in September 2024, arguing that it might never obtain NSO's most important files and that disclosure could expose its own threat intelligence. Its filing cited a Guardian report that Israeli officials had taken files from NSO's offices and asked an Israeli court to keep the step secret; Israeli officials denied interfering in the American litigation. [cite:ow10_stripes_apple]

New owners, 2025. In late 2025 NSO said its three founders no longer held any stake; it was reported to be controlled by investors led by the Hollywood producer Robert Simonds, and in November it named David Friedman, President Trump's first-term ambassador to Israel, as executive chairman. Friedman said he expected the administration to be "receptive to considering any opportunity that might keep Americans safer," and called the WhatsApp ruling a "meaningful setback." [cite:ow10_rec_friedman] [cite:ow10_ts_owner] The record checked does not show NSO's removal from the Entity List as of October 2026.

The asymmetry here is specific. By NSO's own account, Israel's Defense Ministry approved every country it sold to, and when the tool was used against American diplomats, the Israeli government's answer was that the customer had broken the licence. [cite:ow10_reu_state] [cite:ow10_ctech_37] In the public record the hacking surfaced through Apple's alerts to the victims and Reuters' reporting; the record does not show Israel informing Washington. The United States sanctioned the company, not the licensing state. What the United States received in return is also on the record: an evaluation copy of the most capable phone-hacking tool on the market, which the FBI chose not to use. [cite:ow10_globe_fbi]

sections.h: Paragon: The Israeli Spyware ICE Bought, Paused and Revived
sections.html:
Where NSO was shut out of the American market, Paragon Solutions was let in. Its tool, Graphite, can take over a phone without the user clicking anything and read messages in encrypted apps. Between September 2024 and April 2026 Immigration and Customs Enforcement signed a contract for it, suspended the contract under a presidential order, saw the company pass into American ownership and then reactivated the deal. Each step is documented, and together they show how an Israeli offensive cyber tool becomes an American one. [cite:ow10_npr_lyons]

The company. Paragon is an Israeli company, operating under the close supervision of Israel's Ministry of Defense, which regulates offensive cyber firms. Its founders, as Globes listed them in December 2024, were Ehud Schneorson, then its chairman, Idan Nurick, its chief executive, Igor Bogudlov, Liad Avraham and Liran Elkayam; its investors included Battery Ventures and Red Dot. Ehud Barak, the former prime minister and defence minister, was reported to hold several percent of the company, worth an estimated $10–15 million before tax, and his involvement was said to have worried buyers that Israel's political leadership might oppose a sale. [cite:ow10_globes_ae]

The ICE contract. On 27 September 2024, according to the federal procurement record reported by the journalist Jack Poulson, ICE signed a $2 million contract with Paragon, number 70CTD024P00000012.
