In October 2024 a hold was placed on it for review under Executive Order 14093, Biden's 2023 order barring federal use of commercial spyware that poses counterintelligence risks or has been misused by foreign governments against journalists, activists or dissidents. [cite:ow10_poulson_ice] [cite:ow10_eo14093] The order contains no blanket exemption for American-owned vendors. It asks, among other things, whether the vendor is under the control of a foreign government engaged in intelligence against the United States, whether its tools have been used to target activists or journalists, and whether it has taken steps to stop such use, and it allows a one-year waiver in extraordinary circumstances. [cite:ow10_eo14093]

The sale to an American owner. In December 2024 Globes reported that AE Industrial Partners, an American private-equity firm, was buying Paragon for an estimated $900 million, half in cash and half in future milestone payments, and would merge it into REDLattice, a defence contractor it already owned in Virginia; the deal was reported to permit exporting Paragon's technology to the United States, while Paragon itself would remain an Israeli company. [cite:ow10_globes_ae] [cite:ow10_reg_paragon] On the question of Israeli approval, the reporting conflicts. Globes first reported, from unnamed sources, that senior ministry officials had approved the sale weeks earlier; three days later the ministry said the sale had "not yet received the required approval," that no formal report had been filed, that any transfer of technology to foreign hands required a special licence, and that its decision would be "purely professional." [cite:ow10_globes_ae] [cite:ow10_globes_mod] Globes reported on 30 January 2025 that the sale had closed in December 2024, with about $500 million in cash paid, before the Defense Ministry's formal approval; by April 2026 Paragon was described as owned by AE Industrial Partners and merged with REDLattice. [cite:ow10_globes_closed] [cite:ow10_npr_lyons]

Reactivation and use. On Saturday 30 August 2025, under the Trump administration, ICE modified the contract to lift the hold; Poulson reported the change from the procurement record on Monday 1 September, and other outlets confirmed that the deal had been allowed to proceed. [cite:ow10_poulson_ice] [cite:ow10_reg_paragon] In an April 2026 letter to three House Oversight Democrats, answering their questions of October 2025, the acting ICE director, Todd Lyons, acknowledged for the first time that Homeland Security Investigations was using the tool against foreign terrorist organisations, "particularly those involved in the trafficking of fentanyl." He wrote that its use would "comply with constitutional requirements," and certified under the 2023 order that it posed no significant counterintelligence risk and no significant risk of improper use by a foreign government. [cite:ow10_npr_lyons] [cite:ow10_tc_lyons] Representative Summer Lee, one of the letter's recipients, said ICE had given no substantive answer on who could be targeted or under what legal authority inside the United States; an unnamed DHS official said the agency uses such technology to support investigations while respecting civil liberties. [cite:ow10_npr_lyons]

Italy. How a government customer used the tool was tested in Europe. In early 2025 WhatsApp said about 90 journalists and members of civil society had been targeted with Graphite. [cite:ow10_npr_lyons] In June 2025 the Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto confirmed with high confidence that Graphite had been installed on the iPhones of two European journalists, one of them the Italian reporter Ciro Pellegrino; the Italian parliamentary intelligence committee, COPASIR, confirmed that the government had used Graphite against two activists, Luca Casarini and Giuseppe Caccia. Paragon offered to help investigate the targeting of the editor Francesco Cancellato; Italy declined. Paragon suggested it had ended its Italian contracts; Italy's security intelligence department disputed that account. [cite:ow10_is_italy] By April 2026, American reporting described Paragon as having cut off Italy's agencies. [cite:ow10_tc_lyons]

What the case shows. Paragon's path differs from NSO's in one decisive respect: ownership. A tool designed in Israel by Israeli engineers, under Israeli export control, entered American service after an American firm agreed to buy its maker, and after a change of administration in Washington. [cite:ow10_globes_ae] [cite:ow10_reg_paragon] What the United States gains is a capability its agencies say they need against cartels; what is not public is the list of targets, the legal process used for each, and, because Paragon was to remain an Israeli company after the sale, what if anything Israel's licensing authority retains over the tool. The sources used here do not answer that last question. For the ICE side of this story in the context of other Israeli-made tools the agency buys, see [scene:ow6_nypd_ice|Part Six].

sections.h: Cellebrite, Elbit, Cognyte, Black Cube and Carbyne
sections.html:
NSO and Paragon are the spyware firms. Five other Israeli-founded companies reach into American government or American life in different ways: one opens seized phones for federal agents, one builds surveillance towers on the Mexican border, one sells interception systems abroad, one is a private intelligence agency hired by American clients, and one routes 911 calls. They differ in ownership, in how much the Israeli state supervises their exports and in whether any American agency is their customer at all. This section takes them one at a time and then sets them side by side.

Cellebrite. Cellebrite was founded in 1999 in Petah Tikva, Israel, where it is still headquartered. Its largest shareholder is the Japanese company Sun Corporation, with about 44 percent, and it has traded on Nasdaq since August 2021, when it merged with a blank-check company. [cite:ow10_wiki_cellebrite] Its devices extract the contents of locked phones that police already hold, which makes it a forensic tool rather than remote spyware. ICE has bought it repeatedly: contracts worth about $2.2 million in 2017 and $30–35 million in 2019 are recorded, and in September 2025 ICE announced an $11 million contract while redacting the whole of its justification. [cite:ow10_wiki_cellebrite] [cite:ow10_reason_cb] Procurement papers for ICE's cyber crimes centre said there were "no other mobile forensic product suites that offer equivalent capabilities." [cite:ow10_fs_cb] Customs and Border Protection, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Marine Corps' criminal investigators also use it. [cite:ow10_reason_cb] Cellebrite stopped selling to Russian and Belarusian state bodies in March 2021, after its tools were linked to the persecution of activists there. [cite:ow10_gv_cb] In January 2026 the Citizen Lab reported that Jordan had used Cellebrite's extraction device on the phones of activists and journalists detained at protests against the war in Gaza; the company said it does "not comment on specifics" and that the rule of law and privacy are fundamental to it. [cite:ow10_occrp_jordan] The sources used here do not say whether Cellebrite's exports require Israeli Defense Ministry licences.

Elbit Systems of America, now Twenty-Six Defense. The American subsidiary of the Israeli arms maker Elbit Systems is the most deeply embedded of these firms in federal security. In February 2014 the subsidiary won a $145 million contract from DHS for Integrated Fixed Towers, sensor towers with command centres to detect and track movement along the border with Mexico in Arizona. [cite:ow10_globes_ift] In July 2026 it announced further Customs and Border Protection contracts worth more than $370 million, running to May 2029. On 8 September 2026 the subsidiary, headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas, with about 3,300 American employees, renamed itself Twenty-Six Defense; its chief executive, Luke Savoie, said the name "underscores our growth in the American market." Defense News noted that the change came as American opinion divided over the Gaza war; the company did not give that as a reason. It remains the American arm of Elbit Systems. [cite:ow10_dn_26] Its border work is the clearest case in this part of Israeli-owned technology used inside the United States by a federal agency, under a federal contract.

Cognyte. Cognyte, an Israeli company, was spun off from the interception company Verint Systems in February 2021 and is listed on Nasdaq. Reuters reported in January 2023 that it had won a tender to sell interception software to Myanmar's state-backed telecoms company about a month before the February 2021 coup; Reuters could not confirm the sale was completed or whether an Israeli export licence was issued. Israel has said it stopped defence exports to Myanmar after a 2017 Supreme Court ruling; the Defense Ministry declined to comment, and Cognyte did not respond. In 2021 Meta banned Cognyte from Facebook, saying its customers in Kenya, Mexico and Indonesia had targeted journalists and politicians with fake accounts. [cite:ow10_aj_cognyte] The sources used here document no American federal contract with Cognyte.

Black Cube. Black Cube is a private intelligence firm that describes itself as "a select group of veterans from the Israeli elite intelligence units." [cite:ow10_cnbc_bc] It has no documented contract with any American agency; its American work has been for private clients. From late 2016 Harvey Weinstein engaged Black Cube, and in July 2017 the law firm of his lawyer David Boies signed a contract with it, to stop publication of stories about Weinstein's abuse of women, and, as Ronan Farrow reported in The New Yorker in November 2017, two of its operatives, posing as wealth advisers, approached the actress Rose McGowan, one recording her secretly. [cite:ow10_npr_bc] [cite:ow10_cnbc_bc] In May 2018 The Observer and The New Yorker reported that Black Cube had been hired, by people the Observer described as Trump aides, in May 2017 to find damaging information on Ben Rhodes and Colin Kahl, two Obama officials who had worked on the Iran nuclear agreement, and that their wives received approaches from people using false identities. Black Cube said it "has no relation whatsoever to the Trump administration" or to the Iran deal; a source said the client was a private party with commercial interests in Iran sanctions. [cite:ow10_cnbc_bc]

Carbyne. Carbyne, founded in Israel in 2015 as Reporty, sells software that lets emergency dispatchers receive location, video and text from callers; it moved its headquarters to New York in 2019 and has been used by emergency services in 23 states. [cite:ow10_wiki_carbyne] Its early money is documented. Ehud Barak invested $1 million in 2015 and became chairman, holding his stake through a partnership he formed, Sum (E.B.) 2015; Israel's public broadcaster Kan reported that Jeffrey Epstein put $1 million into that partnership in 2016 through a British Virgin Islands company, Southern Trust. Peter Thiel's Founders Fund was among Carbyne's backers. [cite:ow10_ctech_barak] When the Epstein link was reported in July 2019, Barak said "a firm linked to Epstein has been a passive investor" and that he had told his lawyers to explore removing it. [cite:ow10_toi_barak] Barak left the board in 2020. In November 2025 the American company Axon agreed to buy Carbyne for $625 million, and the deal closed on 18 February 2026, making Carbyne wholly American-owned. [cite:ow10_p2_axon] [cite:ow10_wiki_carbyne] The Epstein investment is treated in full in [scene:ow12_ties|Part Twelve].

Reading the table. Two patterns stand out. The firms with the most American government business are those whose ownership or operations sit substantially outside Israel: Cellebrite, listed on Nasdaq with a Japanese largest shareholder; Elbit's American subsidiary, with its workforce in the United States; and Paragon and Carbyne after their purchase by American companies. Their tools are used under American contracts that are public in outline. [cite:ow10_wiki_cellebrite] [cite:ow10_dn_26] [cite:ow10_globes_ae] [cite:ow10_p2_axon] The firms whose tools were turned against Americans, NSO against diplomats and Black Cube against former officials and a woman who had accused Weinstein, were Israeli-controlled, and in NSO's case licensed by Israel's Defense Ministry. [cite:ow10_reu_state] [cite:ow10_cnbc_bc] In every case the American customer can see the contract; what it cannot see, for the firms still based in Israel, is what the Israeli licensing authority knows about the tool and its other buyers.

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: The Legal Shields
chapters.intro: Part Eleven examines the legal protections that surround Israel, or those who deal with it, in American law and policy: the federal anti-boycott law of 1977 and the state anti-BDS laws that followed it decades later; the IHRA definition of antisemitism in civil-rights enforcement, from Executive Order 13899 to the stalled Antisemitism Awareness Act; the sanctions imposed on the International Criminal Court's officials; and three general laws or powers applied to Israel in a particular way: the Leahy Law, the Security Council veto and the non-proliferation amendments. The foreign-agent question is treated in [scene:ow2_lobby_law|Part Two]. For each shield the part gives the government's stated reason beside the critics' case.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven has shown that the legal shields are of different kinds and different strengths. The federal anti-boycott law of 1977, renewed in 2018, protects American companies from a foreign government's boycott and was written with business support; the state laws of 2015 onward penalize Americans' own boycott choices and remain contested, though the Arkansas law stands. [cite:ow11_carter_1977] [cite:ow11_bis_oac] [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip] Executive orders since 2019 place the IHRA definition, with its examples about Israel, inside civil-rights enforcement, while the bill to make it statute has stalled and its own drafter has warned against its use. [cite:ow11_eo13899] [cite:ow11_eo14188] [cite:ow2_jlink_aaa] [cite:ow11_npr_stern] Since February 2025 the United States has sanctioned the prosecutor, judges and deputy prosecutors of the International Criminal Court, citing rulings on Israel, and those sanctions are being tested in American courts as of October 2026. [cite:ow11_eo14203] [cite:ow11_state_aug2025] [cite:ow11_jurist_judges2026] The Leahy Law applies to Israel but through a unique forum that has barred no unit; the veto has been cast on Israel-related drafts dozens of times since 1972; and the non-proliferation laws stay unused because the United States does not acknowledge an Israeli arsenal. [cite:ow11_js_blaha] [cite:ow11_afp_veto2025] [cite:ow11_aca_opacity] Part Twelve turns to the Epstein case, and to what the court records do and do not show.

sections.h: The Boycott Laws, 1977–2026
sections.html:
Parts One to Ten describe how the United States arms, funds and works with Israel. This part turns to a different kind of law: measures that protect Israel, or those who deal with it, from pressure. Some are old and uncontroversial in their original purpose; some are recent and contested in the courts. Each is set out here with the reason the government gave for it and the strongest case made against it. This first section covers the oldest: the federal law against complying with foreign boycotts, written in 1977 against the Arab League's boycott of Israel, and the state laws of the 2010s that are often confused with it.

The federal law of 1977. The Arab League's boycott of Israel did not only bar Arab states from trading with Israel. Its secondary and tertiary forms asked foreign companies to refuse business with Israel, or with firms on a blacklist, as a condition of trading in Arab markets, and to supply information about their dealings and about the religion or national origin of the people involved, which is what the American law that followed prohibits. [cite:ow11_bis_oac] [cite:ow11_carter_1977] Congress answered in two steps. The Ribicoff Amendment to the Tax Reform Act of 1976 added separate boycott-related prohibitions and reporting duties to the tax law. [cite:ow11_bis_oac] On 22 June 1977 President Jimmy Carter signed H.R. 5840, the Export Administration Amendments of 1977, Public Law 95-52, which barred American persons from complying with unsanctioned foreign boycotts. [cite:ow11_carter_1977] [cite:ow11_bis_oac]

Carter's stated reasons are on the record. He called the boycotts a "profound moral issue from which we should not shrink," tied the law to the special relationship with Israel and to the principle of free trade, and set out its limit: it did not "question the sovereign right of any nation to regulate its own commerce" and was aimed at no particular country. He credited Senators Adlai Stevenson and William Proxmire, Representatives Clement Zablocki, Benjamin Rosenthal, Lee Hamilton, Jonathan Bingham, Stephen Solarz and Charles Whalen, and outside groups including the Business Roundtable, the Anti-Defamation League, the American Jewish Committee and the American Jewish Congress, describing a joint effort of business, Jewish organizations, Congress and the executive. [cite:ow11_carter_1977]

The law today. The 1977 provisions became Section 8 of the Export Administration Act of 1979 and Part 760 of the Export Administration Regulations. On 13 August 2018 the Anti-Boycott Act of 2018, enacted as Part II of the Export Control Reform Act within the FY2019 defence authorization, became their statutory basis. [cite:ow11_bis_oac] The Commerce Department's Office of Antiboycott Compliance enforces it. American persons may not refuse to do business with a boycotted country or blacklisted firm for boycott reasons, discriminate on the basis of race, religion, sex or national origin, or furnish information about their business relationships or about anyone's religion or national origin; they must report boycott requests every quarter. The department states that the Arab League boycott of Israel "is the principal unsanctioned foreign boycott of concern today," though the rules apply to all such boycotts. Administrative penalties reach $374,474 per violation as of January 2025, and criminal penalties $1 million and twenty years in prison. [cite:ow11_bis_oac]

The state laws. The second wave is different in kind. Beginning in 2015, with South Carolina and Illinois, about 38 states passed laws or issued executive orders discouraging boycotts of Israel by the people and companies the state does business with: contractors must certify that they are not boycotting Israel, or state funds must divest from companies that do. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] Their target is not a foreign government's boycott but the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, a campaign by private actors. That difference is the root of the constitutional challenges they have faced. Federal courts enjoined laws in Kansas and Arizona in 2018, both later narrowed, a federal court preliminarily enjoined the Texas law in April 2019, an injunction vacated as moot in 2020 after the legislature narrowed the law; [cite:ow11_ca5_amawi] the full Eighth Circuit upheld Arkansas's law in June 2022, reasoning that purchasing decisions in a boycott are not expressive enough to be protected speech, and the Supreme Court declined to hear the case on 21 February 2023. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip] The laws' origins, text and litigation are told in full in [scene:pm8_laws|thirty-eight states].

The arguments on each side are well defined. Supporters argue that a state, like any purchaser, may choose whom it does business with, and that a commercial boycott is conduct, not speech; the Eighth Circuit accepted that the Arkansas law served commercial purposes. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds] Opponents, among them the American Civil Liberties Union, argue that the laws penalize one side of a political debate and that the right to boycott, recognized for civil-rights boycotts, should not depend on the target. [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip] Congress has declined to settle the question nationally: the Israel Anti-Boycott Act of 2017 died, and the Combating BDS Act passed the Senate on 5 February 2019, 77 to 23, as part of S.1, but [cite:ow11_sfrc_s1] was not taken up by the House. [cite:pm_wiki_antibds]

The two layers together form the oldest of the legal shields. The federal law of 1977 protects American companies from being drafted into a foreign government's boycott, and was written as a trade and anti-discrimination measure with business support. The state laws of 2015 onward penalize Americans' own boycott decisions, and remain contested. [cite:pm_aclu_waldrip] The next section follows a newer shield, built not in commercial law but in civil-rights enforcement.

sections.h: A Definition in Civil-Rights Law, 2016–2026
sections.html:
The second shield is a definition. The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance adopted a "working definition" of antisemitism on 26 May 2016, accompanied by contemporary examples, several of which concern Israel. [cite:ow11_eo13899] Since 2019 American executive orders have directed federal agencies to use it when enforcing the civil-rights law that governs schools and universities, and a bill to write it into statute passed the House in 2024. The dispute over it is not about whether antisemitism should be fought. It is about whether a definition that includes examples about Israel will be used to treat criticism of Israel as discrimination. This section sets out the instruments in order, with the governments' stated purpose and the critics' case side by side.

The definition and its caveat. The definition is non-binding. The Anti-Defamation League, which supports its use, describes it as a guide for education and assessment, not a "charging authority," and says it does not support using it to create new categories of prohibited speech. Its text states that "criticism of Israel similar to that leveled against any other country cannot be regarded as antisemitic." [cite:ow11_adl_ihra] According to the American Jewish Committee, the State Department has used a version of it in its international monitoring since 2006, and as of August 2024, 35 states and the District of Columbia had adopted or recognized it by proclamation, executive order or law. [cite:ow11_ajc_states]

Executive Order 13899, 2019. On 11 December 2019 President Trump signed Executive Order 13899, "Combating Anti-Semitism." It directs agencies enforcing Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bars discrimination on the basis of race, colour or national origin in federally funded programmes, to "consider" the IHRA definition and its contemporary examples when assessing evidence of discriminatory intent. Title VI does not cover religion, and the order explains that Jews may be protected when discrimination against them is based on race, colour or national origin. It contains its own limit: agencies "shall not diminish or infringe upon" any right protected by the First Amendment, and each case requires a detailed analysis of the allegations. [cite:ow11_eo13899] The order's stated purpose is to enforce Title VI against antisemitic discrimination as vigorously as against other forms. [cite:ow11_eo13899] The critics' concern, set out by the American Civil Liberties Union, is that a definition with examples about Israel would lead universities, which risk federal funds, to suppress speech critical of Israel. [cite:ow2_wiki_aaa]

Executive Order 14188, 2025. On 29 January 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14188, "Additional Measures To Combat Anti-Semitism." It reaffirms the 2019 order, which it says the previous administration had "effectively nullified," and responds to campus protests after 7 October 2023. It requires agencies to report within 60 days on their authorities and on pending complaints, encourages the Attorney General to use federal civil-rights criminal law, and directs the Secretaries of State, Education and Homeland Security to recommend how universities can be familiarized with the immigration law's grounds of inadmissibility so that they can monitor and report foreign students and staff, which could lead to investigation and removal. [cite:ow11_eo14188] The last provision moved the issue from civil-rights enforcement into immigration law, and Part Six returns to it.

The Antisemitism Awareness Act. Congress has twice considered putting the definition into statute. On 1 May 2024 the House passed the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which would require the Education Department to take the IHRA definition into account in Title VI enforcement, by 320 votes to 91. The ADL and the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations supported it; the ACLU called the definition "overbroad" and warned it "could result in colleges and universities suppressing a wide variety of speech critical of Israel"; and opposition also came from some Republicans, among them Marjorie Taylor Greene and Matt Gaetz, who argued it could be used against teachings drawn from the New Testament. [cite:ow2_wiki_aaa] The House bill stalled in the Senate. [cite:ow2_jlink_aaa] Its successor, S.558, came before the Senate committee on health, education, labor and pensions on 29–30 April 2025. Senators offered amendments, including one by Bernie Sanders stating that people may "criticize the government of Israel for their policies without being antisemitic"; the committee's chairman, Bill Cassidy, said "supporting these amendments is an effort to kill this bill," and Rand Paul said "every one of the 11 examples is about speech." No vote was taken, and the bill remained in committee. [cite:ow2_jlink_aaa] The latest report consulted is from July 2025; as of October 2026 this volume has not found a record of a Senate vote, and the status should be checked before it is relied on.

The drafter's objection. The strongest criticism comes from the definition's lead drafter. Kenneth Stern, who drafted it in 2004–05 and directs the Center for the Study of Hate at Bard College, told NPR in March 2025 that the administration was "absolutely weaponizing antisemitism," that the approach amounted to "McCarthyism," and that it made students "less safe," while acknowledging that antisemitism exists on campuses. The White House replied that "the only people weaponizing antisemitism are the liberal activists." [cite:ow11_npr_stern] The ADL's position sits between the two: it supports the definition as a reference but not as a basis for new speech restrictions. [cite:ow11_adl_ihra]

The definition is therefore a shield of a particular kind. It does not protect Israel's government from criticism in law; its own text says such criticism, like that of any country, is not antisemitic. [cite:ow11_adl_ihra] [cite:ow11_eo14188] What the executive orders do is place examples concerning Israel inside the machinery of federal civil-rights enforcement, where the sanction is the loss of federal funds and, since 2025, where immigration status can be at stake. Whether that machinery protects Jewish students from discrimination or chills speech about Israel is the question the courts and Congress have not yet settled. The next section turns from domestic law to an international court.

sections.h: Sanctioning a Court, 2020–2026
sections.html:
The third shield faces outward. The International Criminal Court in The Hague, created by the Rome Statute, prosecutes individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. Neither the United States nor Israel is a party to the statute. [cite:ow11_eo14203] When the court opened investigations that reached American personnel in Afghanistan and Israeli officials in the Palestinian territories, two American administrations responded with economic sanctions against the court's own officials, and the second extended them to judges, prosecutors, a United Nations rapporteur and Palestinian human rights organizations. [cite:ow11_js_revoke2021] [cite:ow11_wiki_eo14203] This section follows the orders, the designations and the lawsuits in sequence, to the latest point reached in October 2026.

The first round, 2020–2021. In June 2020 President Trump signed Executive Order 13928, authorizing sanctions on persons associated with the court, and in September 2020 the Treasury designated the prosecutor, Fatou Bensouda, and a senior official of her office, Phakiso Mochochoko. [cite:ow11_bm_2021] [cite:ow11_js_revoke2021] The Biden administration revoked the order on 1–2 April 2021. Its revocation did not mean agreement with the court: Secretary of State Antony Blinken said "we continue to disagree strongly with the ICC's actions relating to the Afghanistan and Palestinian situations," and the United States maintained its objection to the court asserting jurisdiction over nationals of non-parties such as the United States and Israel. [cite:ow11_js_revoke2021]

Executive Order 14203, 2025. After the court issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the former defence minister Yoav Gallant, on 6 February 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14203, "Imposing Sanctions on the International Criminal Court." Its stated rationale names Israel directly: the court had taken "illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel," including what the order called baseless warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant, although neither country is a party to the Rome Statute. It invokes the American Servicemembers' Protection Act of 2002, declares a national emergency, and authorizes the blocking of property of designated persons and the suspension of their entry, and that of their families, into the United States. [cite:ow11_eo14203] The court responded the next day that it "condemns the issuance by the US of an Executive Order seeking to impose sanctions on its officials" and "stands firmly by its personnel." [cite:ow11_icc_stmt2025]

The designations. The prosecutor, Karim Khan, was listed under the order in February 2025. On 5 June 2025 the State Department designated four judges, Beti Hohler, Reine Alapini-Gansou, Luz del Carmen Ibáñez Carranza and Solomy Bossa; on 9 July 2025 it designated Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, over statements that included recommending that the court prosecute Israeli officials; [cite:ow11_jurist_albanese2026] in September 2025 it added three Palestinian human rights organizations, Al Haq, Al Mezan and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights; and on 18 December 2025 two further judges. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the court as "a national security threat that has been an instrument for lawfare" against the United States and Israel. [cite:ow11_wiki_eo14203] The State Department's own fact sheet of 20 August 2025 shows how each designation was tied to a ruling: Judge Kimberly Prost for the decision authorizing the Afghanistan investigation, Judge Nicolas Guillou for the decision authorizing the Netanyahu and Gallant warrants, and the two deputy prosecutors, Nazhat Shameem Khan and Mame Mandiaye Niang, for "continuing to support illegitimate ICC actions against Israel." [cite:ow11_state_aug2025] [cite:ow11_wiki_eo14203]

The courts, 2026. The sanctions have been challenged in American courts on constitutional grounds. Albanese's husband and daughter sued in February 2026; on 13 May 2026 Judge Richard J. Leon of the federal district court in Washington preliminarily blocked her designation, finding it was imposed solely because she had encouraged the court to investigate Israeli officials and was likely to violate free-speech rights. [cite:ow11_jurist_albanese2026] [cite:ow11_jns_albanese_dc] On 22 May the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit stayed that order pending the government's appeal, and on 27 May the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control returned her to its list. [cite:ow11_jns_albanese_dc] [cite:ow11_jurist_albanese2026] Rubio said she had engaged in "biased and malicious activities"; she has said the sanctions made her a "non-person." [cite:ow11_jurist_albanese2026] In June 2026 three sitting ICC judges, Kimberly Prost, Solomy Bossa and Reine Alapini-Gansou, sued the President in the Southern District of New York, arguing that the order exceeds the emergency-powers statutes and violates due process; it was the sixth suit against the order and the first by a sitting judge. [cite:ow11_jurist_judges2026] In October 2026 a federal court in Maine refused the government's motion to dismiss a First Amendment challenge brought by two human rights advocates. [cite:ow11_gs_maine2026] As of October 2026 none of these cases had produced a final judgment in the sources reached here, and their status should be checked before it is relied on.

The two cases. The government's case is stated in the order itself: the United States and Israel never accepted the court's jurisdiction, the warrants against Israel's leaders are illegitimate, and the 2002 statute already expresses American opposition to the prosecution of its personnel by the court. [cite:ow11_eo14203] The critics' case is stated by the court and the plaintiffs: that sanctioning judges for their rulings attacks judicial independence, that it punishes speech and advocacy protected by the American Constitution, and that it uses emergency economic powers against an institution with 125 member states. [cite:ow11_icc_stmt2025] [cite:ow11_jurist_judges2026] What is documented beyond dispute is that an American sanctions programme under emergency economic powers was applied to the officials of an international court and a UN rapporteur, and that the State Department's own designations cite rulings and advocacy concerning Israel as the reason. [cite:ow11_state_aug2025]

sections.h: Laws Applied Differently: Leahy, the Veto and the Bomb
sections.html:
The last three shields are not laws written for Israel. They are general American laws and powers whose application to Israel has differed from their application elsewhere: a human-rights law applied through a special procedure, a veto used more often on Israel-related drafts than on any other subject, and nuclear non-proliferation laws that have never been invoked because the United States does not officially acknowledge what Israel is widely assessed to possess. For each, this section separates what the law says, how it has been applied, and what the government says in its defence.

The Leahy Law. Two statutes named after Senator Patrick Leahy bar American assistance to any unit of a foreign security force where there is credible information that it has committed a gross violation of human rights: Section 620M of the Foreign Assistance Act for State Department programmes and 10 U.S.C. 362 for the Pentagon. In practice vetting focuses on torture, extrajudicial killing, enforced disappearance and rape under colour of law. The State Department may resume aid if it determines that the government is "taking effective steps to bring the responsible members of the security forces unit to justice." [cite:ow11_crs_leahy] The law applies to Israel as to every recipient. The question is how it has been applied.

For Israel, the State Department created a separate procedure, the Israel Leahy Vetting Forum. Charles Blaha, a retired State Department official, wrote in June 2024 that under it a finding that an Israeli unit is ineligible rests with the Deputy Secretary of State, which he said was "true for no other country in the world"; that cases advance only after formal written requests to Israel, which may take "as long as three months" to answer; and that in over four years the forum had not identified a single ineligible Israeli unit. [cite:ow11_js_blaha] On 29 April 2024 the department announced its first such finding: five Israeli units had committed gross violations, all before October 2023 and outside Gaza. Four, it said, had "effectively remediated" them; the fifth, reported to be the Netzah Yehuda battalion, remained under review. An Israeli official said Israel "categorically rejects any attempts to harm the IDF." [cite:ow11_toi_leahy2024] On 9 August 2024 Secretary Blinken concluded that Netzah Yehuda's violations had also been remediated, after Israel removed two soldiers from combat duty, changed the unit's vetting and required human-rights training, and announced that it "can continue receiving security assistance." [cite:ow11_axios_ny2024] In October 2025 the Washington Post reported that a classified report by the State Department's Inspector General described "many hundreds" of potential violations by Israeli units in Gaza awaiting review, a backlog it said would take "multiple years" to clear; the department did not comment. [cite:ow11_wapo_oig]

The government's position is that the law has been applied: units were found responsible, Israel took corrective steps, and the statute's remediation clause allows aid to continue in those circumstances. [cite:ow11_crs_leahy] [cite:ow11_axios_ny2024] The critics' position, Blaha's among them, is that a procedure found nowhere else, with decisions reserved to the political level, has produced no barred unit at all. [cite:ow11_js_blaha] Both describe the same documents. A claim sometimes made, that Israel is exempt from the Leahy Law, is wrong: it is subject to the law, and the finding is how the law has been applied.

The veto. The United States first used its Security Council veto on an Israel-related draft on Sunday 10 September 1972, against a Somali resolution on Israeli air strikes in Syria and Lebanon after the killing of Israeli athletes at Munich; the vote was 13 to 1, with one abstention. Ambassador George H. W. Bush said the Middle East violence was "inextricably interwoven with the disaster in Munich" and criticized a "double standard" that ignored terrorism. [cite:ow11_djn_veto1972] [cite:ow11_un_s10790] Counts of the vetoes since then differ by method. Al Jazeera, using UN data, counted at least 53 American vetoes of drafts critical of Israel by May 2021; Agence France-Presse counted 46 Security Council vetoes, by all members, on the Palestinian territories since 1970, as of 18 September 2025. [cite:ow11_aj_vetoes2021] [cite:ow11_afp_veto2025] On that day the United States cast its sixth veto of a Gaza ceasefire demand since the war began, against the other fourteen members; its envoy, Morgan Ortagus, said the draft "fails to condemn Hamas or recognise Israel's right to defend itself." [cite:ow11_aj_veto2025] Successive American ambassadors have given the same kind of reason across decades: that the drafts were one-sided, or that the Council should not settle questions reserved for negotiation. In 2011 Susan Rice vetoed a draft on the illegality of settlements while saying Washington did not dispute its view of settlements but considered it "unwise" for the Council to try to resolve core issues. Earlier, John Negroponte said a 2001 draft aimed to "isolate politically one of the parties," and in 2018 Nikki Haley called a Gaza draft "a grossly one-sided view" of events. [cite:ow11_aj_vetoes2021]

The bomb that is not acknowledged. Israel has never signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. [cite:ow11_aca_opacity] Two American laws of the 1970s address proliferation by cutting off aid, and both are often misdescribed. The Symington Amendment of 1976, now Section 101 of the Arms Export Control Act, bars most assistance to a country that trafficks in uranium-enrichment equipment or technology outside international safeguards. The Glenn Amendment of 1977, now Section 102, bars assistance to a non-nuclear-weapon state that, among other things, detonates a nuclear explosive device; it was applied to India and Pakistan after their tests in 1998. [cite:ow11_aca_glenn] Neither law cuts off aid to a country simply because it is outside the NPT or is believed to hold nuclear weapons; statements that Symington "requires cutting off aid to non-signatories" are wrong. Neither has been applied to Israel. Glenn's trigger is a test, and Israel is not publicly known to have conducted one; Symington requires an executive determination about enrichment transfers that, as one 2026 analysis noted, no administration has made. [cite:ow11_mil_symington]

The reason no determination is made lies in a policy, not a statute. At a White House meeting on 26 September 1969, according to the scholarship of Avner Cohen as reviewed in Arms Control Today, President Nixon and Prime Minister Golda Meir reached an understanding: the United States would end its inspections of the Dimona reactor and stop pressing Israel to sign the NPT, so long as Israel did not declare, publicize or test its arsenal. The written record of that understanding has not been released. [cite:ow11_aca_opacity] Israel's formula, that it will not be the first to introduce nuclear weapons into the region, dates to the 1960s and appears in Rabin's letter on the Phantom sale described in [scene:ow1_founding|Part One]. [cite:ow1_jvl_phantomconds] The American side of the bargain is silence: by not acknowledging an Israeli arsenal, successive administrations avoid the question of whether the non-proliferation laws apply. Cohen describes the arrangement as giving "enough credible evidence to deter enemies but sufficient ambiguity" to avoid the consequences of declaration, and argues it has become "anachronistic and awkward because Israel's nuclear status is no longer ambiguous." [cite:ow11_aca_opacity] Whatever view is taken of it, the documented fact is that a policy of non-acknowledgement, not any statutory exemption, keeps the question closed.

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: Epstein: What Is Documented
chapters.intro: Part Twelve examines Jeffrey Epstein using only court records, official releases and named reporting on them. It first sets out what the courts and the Justice Department established, from the 2008 Florida agreement to the July 2025 memorandum, the Maxwell interview and the files released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. It then takes the claim that Epstein worked for an intelligence service apart into its pieces: the documented fact of Robert Maxwell's funeral in Jerusalem, the single-source report of Alexander Acosta's remark, and the theories with no document behind them. Finally it sets out Epstein's documented business with Ehud Barak, including the money that reached the 911 company Carbyne, and with Peter Thiel's Valar funds, and draws the line between documented association and an intelligence operation, which is not established.
chapters.outro: Part Twelve found that the official record on Epstein is a record of prosecutorial failure and of a conviction, not of espionage: a 2008 agreement that the Justice Department's own review called poor judgment, Maxwell's conviction and 20-year sentence, and a July 2025 memorandum that found no client list and "no credible evidence" of blackmail. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] [cite:ow12_wiki_gmaxwell] [cite:ow12_abc_memo] The claim that Epstein served an intelligence service rests on an anonymous, denied report of a remark by Alexander Acosta and on theories without documents. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] What is documented is business: dozens of meetings with Ehud Barak, Epstein money routed through Barak's partnership into Carbyne, joint promotion of Israeli surveillance packages abroad, and $40 million in Valar funds. [cite:ow12_wiki_barak] [cite:ow10_ctech_barak] [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] Those are associations with named men, not proof of a state's hand, and millions of pages remain under review. [cite:ow12_wiki_efta] Part Thirteen turns from Epstein to the question at the centre of this book: what Israel has done inside the American system, and what the United States cannot see.

sections.h: What the Courts and the Justice Department Established
sections.html:
Jeffrey Epstein appears in this book for one reason: a widely repeated claim that he worked for, or on behalf of, Israeli intelligence. Before that claim can be weighed, the ground has to be cleared of everything else, and the firmest ground is the record that courts and the Department of Justice have made. This section sets it out, in order, without the allegations against particular people that fill much of what is written about Epstein. Only findings of courts, official documents and named reporting on them are used.

The money and the first complaint. In July 1991 the retailer Leslie Wexner gave Epstein full power of attorney over his affairs, the documented foundation of Epstein's wealth and access. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] In 1996 the artist Maria Farmer reported to the FBI that Epstein had stolen and sold nude and semi-nude photographs of her sisters, aged 12 and 16, and had threatened her. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] The record used here shows no federal case arising from it.

The Florida deal, 2008. When federal prosecutors in southern Florida, under the United States Attorney Alexander Acosta, did investigate, they negotiated a non-prosecution agreement. It granted immunity from federal charges to Epstein, to four named co-conspirators and to unnamed "potential co-conspirators." On 30 June 2008 Epstein pleaded guilty in a Palm Beach County court to two state charges of soliciting prostitution, one involving a minor under 18; he was sentenced to 18 months, served 13 and was released on 22 July 2009. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] In 2019 Judge Kenneth Marra of the federal court in southern Florida ruled that the agreement had violated the Crime Victims' Rights Act, because the victims were not told of it; in 2020 the Eleventh Circuit reversed him. A 2020 report by the Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility found that Acosta had shown "poor judgment" in granting the agreement but had acted within the "scope of his authority." [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein]

New York, 2019. Epstein was arrested on 6 July 2019 at Teterboro Airport, New Jersey, and charged two days later by federal prosecutors in Manhattan with sex trafficking and conspiracy; bail was refused. He died in his cell on 10 August 2019, and his death was ruled a suicide by hanging. The charges were dismissed on 29 August. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] His associate Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted on 29 December 2021 on five of six counts, including sex trafficking of a minor, and sentenced on 28 June 2022 to 20 years. The Second Circuit upheld the conviction in September 2024, and in October 2025 the Supreme Court declined to hear her appeal. [cite:ow12_wiki_gmaxwell]

The Justice Department's memorandum, July 2025. On 7 July 2025 the Justice Department and the FBI released an unsigned two-page memorandum describing what they called a systematic review of their investigative holdings. "This systematic review revealed no incriminating 'client list,'" it said; there was "no credible evidence found that Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals as part of his actions"; and the department "did not uncover evidence that could predicate an investigation against uncharged third parties." It reaffirmed that Epstein had killed himself. [cite:ow12_abc_memo] It said further disclosure would not be "appropriate or warranted," citing child sexual abuse material and victims' privacy. [cite:ow12_npr_memo] This is the government's own position on the record, and it is the position against which any claim of a blackmail or intelligence operation must be set.

The Maxwell interview, July 2025. On 24 and 25 July 2025, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche questioned Maxwell for about nine hours in Tallahassee, Florida, with an FBI agent present; the department released the full transcript and audio on 22 August 2025. Blanche told her he was "not promising to do anything" in return, and warned that false statements could be prosecuted. Asked about a client list, Maxwell said: "There was never a list." [cite:ow12_gaz_maxwell] [cite:ow12_npr_maxwell] Her account has to be weighed with her record: prosecutors had earlier charged her with perjury over sworn statements in civil suits, counts dropped after her 2021 conviction. [cite:ow12_gaz_maxwell] Days after the interview she was moved from a Florida prison to a minimum-security camp at Bryan, Texas; the Bureau of Prisons confirmed the move on 1 August 2025, and the White House called it routine. On 9 February 2026, deposed by the House Oversight Committee, she invoked her Fifth Amendment right and declined to answer. [cite:ow12_wiki_gmaxwell]

The files, 2025–2026. The memorandum's refusal to release more did not hold. A discharge petition forced a House vote, and on 18 November 2025 the House passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act by 427 to 1; the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, and President Trump signed it on 19 November. It required release within 30 days and set no penalty for failing. The department released a first partial batch on 19 December 2025, about 3.5 million pages on 30 January 2026, which it said completed its obligations, and 16 further pages in March after saying they had been wrongly coded as duplicates; Representative Ro Khanna noted that the department itself had identified more than 6 million potentially responsive pages. Members of Congress began reading unredacted files in a department reading room in February 2026, the department's inspector general opened a compliance review in April, and in July Representative Thomas Massie introduced a second transparency bill. [cite:ow12_wiki_efta]

What this record establishes is a long failure by American prosecutors to stop a sex offender, a federal agreement that the Justice Department's own review called poor judgment, a conviction of his chief associate, and a government that has, on the record, found no client list and no evidence of blackmail. What it does not contain is any court finding or released official document stating that Epstein worked for any intelligence service, Israeli or other. The next section takes up the claims that he did, one by one. [cite:ow12_abc_memo]

sections.h: The Intelligence Question
sections.html:
The claim that Epstein was an intelligence asset, and specifically an asset of Israel's, is not one claim but several, resting on different kinds of evidence. Some are documented facts that are true but do not prove what they are used to prove. Some are reports from a single anonymous source. Some are theories with no document behind them. This section separates them, and sets each beside what the American government has said. The rule followed throughout is the one this book applies everywhere: an association between people, however close, is not evidence that a state directed either of them, and no claim here is extended from named individuals to any people collectively.

A documented fact: Robert Maxwell's funeral. Ghislaine Maxwell's father, the British publisher Robert Maxwell, was found dead in the sea off the Canary Islands in November 1991; a verdict of drowning was recorded. He was buried in Jerusalem. President Chaim Herzog delivered the eulogy and Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir attended, according to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency's report at the time; later accounts add that figures from Israeli intelligence were present. [cite:ow12_jta_maxwell1991] [cite:ow12_wiki_gmaxwell] A state funeral is a documented honour. It is not, by itself, evidence that Robert Maxwell worked for Israeli intelligence, and it is not evidence of anything about Jeffrey Epstein, whose own record is set out in the previous section. Claims that Robert Maxwell was an Israeli agent appear in books and articles; the sources reviewed contain no court finding and no released government document establishing it.

A single-source report: "belonged to intelligence." The most cited piece of evidence is a sentence attributed to Alexander Acosta. On 9 July 2019 The Daily Beast reported, from one anonymous former White House official, that Acosta, in interviews with President Trump's first transition team in 2017, had said he "was told Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and to 'leave it alone'," and that Epstein was "above his pay grade." [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] The report named no agency and no country. Acosta denied saying it in a transcribed interview with the House Oversight Committee on 19 September 2025: "I never made that assertion." [cite:ow12_oversight_acosta] [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] The Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility, which examined the 2008 agreement in depth, faulted Acosta's judgment but found he had acted within his authority. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] The remark therefore stands as an anonymous, second-hand report, denied by the person to whom it is attributed. It may be true; nothing in the released record confirms it.

Theories. The Acosta report "has generated many theories about the connections between Epstein and intelligence organizations," promoted by writers such as Whitney Webb. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] The strongest version, that Epstein ran a blackmail operation for Israel's Mossad, rests on secondary accounts; the sources reviewed contain no court record, sworn testimony or released government document that supports it. Against it stands the government's own finding of July 2025 that there was "no credible evidence" that Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals, and a 2025 email from a federal prosecutor to FBI officials, reported by the Associated Press from released Justice Department records, stating that the seized materials contained no evidence implicating "anyone other than Epstein and Maxwell." [cite:ow12_abc_memo] [cite:ow12_ap_comey] Those official findings are themselves contested: the department withheld millions of pages until Congress forced their release, and critics in both parties have said its compliance was incomplete. [cite:ow12_wiki_efta] A withheld page is not evidence of what it contains, in either direction.

The documented Israeli connections. What is documented is narrower and, for this book's question, more useful. Epstein had a business relationship with Ehud Barak, the former Israeli prime minister and defence minister, that included a joint investment in an Israeli emergency-call company and dozens of meetings; and emails released by the House Oversight Committee, together with emails from Barak's account published by a hacker group calling itself Handala, which Canada's government has linked to Iranian intelligence, and partly corroborated by The Sunday Times, show the two discussing Israeli surveillance and security packages for Ivory Coast between 2012 and 2014, for which Barak commissioned plans from former Israeli intelligence officers. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] [cite:ow12_wiki_barak] These are records of two private men brokering business, one of them a former head of Israel's government and defence establishment. They show Epstein inside the commercial world of Israeli security technology. They do not show the State of Israel or any Israeli agency directing him, and an archive obtained by hacking is a source to be weighed with care, whatever its authenticity.

The line. The difference between those two kinds of claim is the finding of this part. A documented association, with a former official, in a business, through a partnership, is a fact and can be stated. An intelligence operation, meaning an agency recruiting, tasking or protecting Epstein, is a claim about a state, and on the public record as of October 2026 it is not established for Israel or for any other country. Where the American government has spoken, it has said there is no credible evidence of blackmail, and where it has been accused of hiding the answer, Congress has forced the files out and the review continues. [cite:ow12_abc_memo] [cite:ow12_wiki_efta]

sections.h: Barak, Carbyne and Valar: The Documented Business
sections.html:
Two of Epstein's documented business ties lead toward the subjects of this book: one to Ehud Barak, a former Israeli prime minister and defence minister, and through him to an Israeli emergency-response company that now handles 911 calls in American cities; the other to Peter Thiel, Palantir's co-founder, through Thiel's venture firm. Both are documented by records, by the participants' own statements and by named reporting. Neither, as the previous section showed, is evidence of an intelligence operation. This section sets out what each contained.

Barak and Epstein. Barak has said the two first met in 2003, and no earlier meeting has been published. [cite:ow12_wiki_barak] Reporting based on Epstein's records found that they exchanged private emails and met about 36 times between 2013 and 2017, by The Wall Street Journal's count from Epstein's calendars, [cite:ow12_ynet_wsj] well after Epstein's 2008 conviction; Barak stayed at Epstein's New York apartments several times, and he has said he flew on Epstein's private planes twice, with his wife and security guards present. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] [cite:ow12_wiki_barak] Barak has denied any wrongdoing. [cite:ow12_wiki_barak] Defending the relationship on Israel's Channel 12 in July 2019, he said Epstein "had served his sentence." [cite:ow10_toi_barak]

The Carbyne investment. In 2015 Barak formed an Israeli limited partnership, Sum (E.B.) 2015, to invest in Reporty Homeland Security, a start-up that renamed itself Carbyne in 2018. Barak's partnership invested in the company's 2015 seed round, $1.5 million by the Times of Israel's account, and he became its chairman; [cite:ow12_toi_carbyne] the partnership held all of its series A preferred stock. [cite:ow10_ctech_barak] Haaretz reported in July 2019 that "a large part of the investment money was supplied by Epstein"; Israel's public broadcaster, Kan, reported that Epstein had put $1 million into the partnership in 2016 through Southern Trust, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands. [cite:ow10_toi_barak] [cite:ow10_ctech_barak] Barak's response, on Facebook, was that "a firm linked to Epstein has been a passive investor" in the partnership and that he had told his lawyers to explore removing it. [cite:ow10_toi_barak] Peter Thiel's Founders Fund was also among Carbyne's backers, joining in 2018; the reporting does not connect Founders Fund to the Barak partnership or to Epstein's money. [cite:ow10_ctech_barak] [cite:ow10_wiki_carbyne] Barak left Carbyne's board in 2020. The company moved its headquarters to New York in 2019, came to serve emergency centres in 23 states, and on 18 February 2026 became wholly owned by the American company Axon. [cite:ow10_wiki_carbyne] Its place among Israeli-founded firms in America is set out in [scene:ow10_firms|Part Ten].

Ivory Coast. The fullest picture of the Barak–Epstein business comes from emails released by the House Oversight Committee and from Barak's own correspondence, published by a hacker group calling itself Handala, which Canada's government has linked to Iranian intelligence, and partly corroborated [cite:ow12_aj_handala] by The Sunday Times. They show Epstein helping Barak promote an Israeli state-surveillance package to Ivory Coast between 2012 and 2014, for which Barak commissioned technical plans from former Israeli intelligence officers for monitoring the country's telephone and internet traffic, and Epstein promoting Israeli surveillance technology to the government of Mongolia. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] Barak was then a private businessman. The emails document a commercial venture that drew on Israeli security expertise; they do not document direction by the Israeli government, and the part of them that came from Barak's account was obtained by hacking, which is reason to weigh it with care and to rely on what official releases corroborate.

Thiel and Valar. Epstein invested $40 million in funds managed by Valar Ventures, a firm co-founded by Peter Thiel, in 2015 and 2016. Thiel had about six scheduled meetings with Epstein at his townhouse between 2014 and 2016; there is no record of Thiel visiting Epstein's homes or flying on his jet. Valar declined Epstein's 2016 pitch to invest in Reporty. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] The record does not show any connection between this investment and Palantir's government work.

Why the business ties matter, and why they do not prove more. These records are the documented intersection between Epstein and the Israeli security world. Through Barak, Epstein's money entered a company built by Israeli founders that came to process emergency calls for American cities, and through Barak's correspondence he appears as a facilitator of Israeli surveillance sales abroad. [cite:ow10_ctech_barak] [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] Through Valar, his money sat in funds run by Palantir's co-founder. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] Each tie is with a named person or firm, by a named instrument, on a known date. None is a finding that a state used Epstein, and none supports any claim about people beyond those named. The questions that remain open, what the withheld or still-redacted federal files contain and whether Epstein had any relationship with any intelligence service, are questions about documents not yet seen, and they are listed as open in Part Fourteen.

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: The One-Way Mirror
chapters.intro: Part Thirteen tests the claim in this volume's title. It first sets out the documented record of Israeli intelligence activity directed at the United States, from the Pollard case and the unresolved NUMEC question to the NSA's own assessments and the reported operations of 2015, 2019 and 2026, together with Israel's denials and the record of American collection on Israel. It then follows one item of American intelligence or one American weapon from the moment it leaves American hands, and shows where Washington's ability to verify its use ends: in Israeli systems, in a special vetting forum, and in a territory closed to independent reporters. It ends with why so little of this is followed up in the press, and with a single table of what flows each way and what the United States can see.
chapters.outro: Part Thirteen found that the one-way claim holds in a precise form, not the popular one. Israel has spied on the United States, proved in court once, in the Pollard case, and reported or assessed in others it denies; the United States has also collected on Israel's leaders. [cite:ow13_wiki_pollard] [cite:ow_td_spying2015] [cite:ow4_aj_wsj2015] What runs one way is verification: raw NSA intelligence shared under a memorandum that creates no enforceable rights, drone feeds whose use Israel certifies itself, weapons whose use in individual incidents the government's own review could not assess, a Leahy forum that found no Israeli unit ineligible in four years, and a Gaza closed to independent foreign reporters since October 2023. [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20] [cite:ow11_js_blaha] [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] The scarcity of follow-up reporting tracks classification, anonymous sourcing, denial and closed ground. [cite:ow3_nsa_pollard] [cite:ow4_aclu] Part Fourteen sets out, claim by claim, what this volume has found settled, what remains contested and what is still open.

sections.h: What Israel Has Done Inside the American System
sections.html:
The title of this volume describes an asymmetry: a relationship in which, as the critics put it, Israel can see into the American state and the American state cannot see into Israel's. That claim has two halves, and this section takes the first: the documented record of Israeli intelligence activity directed at the United States. It is limited to cases established by a court, by released American government documents, or by named reporting with the government's response beside it. It sets apart what is unresolved, and it records the cases in which the United States did the same to Israel, because a mirror that reflects both ways is not one-way.

Pollard, 1985. The one case proved in court is that of Jonathan Pollard, a civilian analyst for US Navy intelligence. FBI agents arrested him on 21 November 1985 as he left the grounds of the Israeli embassy in Washington; he pleaded guilty on 4 June 1986 to conspiracy to deliver national defence information to a foreign government and was sentenced to life on 4 March 1987. [cite:ow13_wiki_pollard] The CIA's damage assessment of October 1987, declassified in 2012, found that he had passed about 800 documents and some 1,500 messages; his Israeli handlers, of a Defense Ministry science-liaison bureau known as LAKAM, tasked him chiefly on Arab states, Pakistan and the Soviet Union, and "never expressed interest in US military activities, plans, capabilities, or equipment." [cite:ow3_nsa_pollard] Israel apologised in December 1985 and again publicly in March 1987, [cite:ow13_csm_1985] [cite:ow13_upi_1987] but described the operation as unauthorised until May 1998, when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu acknowledged that Pollard had been an Israeli agent. Released in 2015, Pollard arrived in Israel on 30 December 2020, after his parole ended, and Netanyahu met him at the airport. [cite:ow13_wiki_pollard] The FBI's side of the case is told in [scene:ow5_spies|Part Five], and the CIA's in [scene:ow3_alarm|Part Three].

NUMEC, 1965: unresolved. The most serious allegation, that highly enriched uranium missing from a nuclear-fuel plant in Apollo, Pennsylvania, reached Israel's weapons programme, has never been resolved. The editors of the National Security Archive's 2016 collection of the documents find "strong but not incontrovertible evidence that a diversion did occur"; the Atomic Energy Commission said it found no evidence of theft; the CIA has released none of its internal operational documents; no one was charged. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] The case is told in full in [scene:fis_s07a|the Cold War volume]. It belongs here only as what it is: an open question, not a finding.

What the NSA's own documents say. Documents taken by Edward Snowden and published by The Intercept in 2015 show how American signals intelligence regarded its Israeli partner. A 2008 NSA document said that Israel "also targets us," and that a National Intelligence Estimate had ranked Israel the third most aggressive intelligence service against the United States; a 2013 budget document listed Israel among hostile services and cyber threats. Netanyahu's office answered: "The state of Israel does not conduct espionage against the United States or Israel's other allies." [cite:ow_td_spying2015] A 2007 NSA history of the relationship, published by The Guardian in 2013, said that "balancing the Sigint exchange equally between US and Israeli needs has been a constant challenge" and that in the previous decade "it arguably tilted heavily in favor of Israeli security concerns." [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] [scene:ow4_memorandum|Part Four] sets out the 2009 memorandum under which the NSA shares raw intelligence with Israel's Unit 8200, and [scene:ow4_both_ways|who watches whom].

The Iran talks, 2015. In March 2015 The Wall Street Journal reported that Israel had spied on the American negotiations with Iran over its nuclear programme and passed what it learned to members of Congress in an effort to defeat the agreement; Netanyahu's office denied it, Israeli officials said the details had come from French officials, and American officials said their objection was to the sharing with Congress rather than to the spying itself. [cite:ow13_npr_wsj2015] In December 2015 the same newspaper reported the other side of the glass: the NSA had kept intercepting Netanyahu's communications after President Obama limited the monitoring of allied leaders in January 2014, keeping him off the protected list for a "compelling national security purpose," and the intercepts showed Israel's campaign in Congress against the deal. The National Security Council said there was no surveillance "unless there is a specific and validated national security purpose." [cite:ow4_aj_wsj2015]

Devices near the White House, 2019. In September 2019 Politico reported, from three former senior officials, that cell-phone surveillance devices found near the White House and other sensitive sites in Washington had been linked by FBI and DHS forensic analysis to Israeli agents, and that the administration issued no public rebuke. Israel called the report a "blatant lie"; President Trump said he found it hard to believe. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] The report rests on unnamed officials and has not been confirmed by any released document; the FBI's handling of such warnings is followed in [scene:ow5_counterintel|Part Five].

Pegasus and American diplomats, 2021. In 2021 NSO's spyware, sold under Israeli Defense Ministry licence, was used against at least nine State Department employees working on Uganda. The Israeli embassy said such use would be "a severe violation" of the export licence, and NSO cut off the customers involved; Reuters could not determine who launched the attacks, and NSO's tools are operated by the governments that buy them. [cite:ow10_reu_state] Part Ten tells the story.

2026. In June 2026 NBC News, citing unnamed officials, reported that the Defense Intelligence Agency had raised its counterintelligence threat assessment for Israel to "critical," out of concern that Israel was monitoring senior American officials involved in Middle East decisions. The report rests on unnamed officials, and the assessment is not public. Israel's embassy called it "completely false," and a White House official said the story was false. [cite:ow13_nbc_dia] [cite:ow5_nbc_dia]

What the record shows, and what the United States gets. The documented cases are few, spread over sixty years, and of different kinds: one court-proven espionage case, one unresolved nuclear question, intelligence assessments that rank Israel among the services targeting the United States, and several reported operations that Israel denies. The record also shows the United States collecting on Israel's leaders. [cite:ow4_aj_wsj2015] Set against these cases is what Washington says it receives: intelligence from Israeli sources, joint cyber operations against Iran's nuclear programme, and missile-defence systems developed together, set out in [scene:ow1_returns|Part One] and [scene:ow8_coproduction|Part Eight]. [cite:ow3_sw_sanger] The relationship is not one-way in what each side tries to learn about the other. Where it is one-way, the next section shows, is in what each side can verify about how the other uses what it is given.

sections.h: What Washington Cannot See
sections.html:
The second half of the one-way claim is about visibility. The phrase that prompted this volume put it plainly: Israel can see into American systems, but the United States cannot see what Israel does in Gaza or the West Bank. The record supports a version of that claim, but a narrower and more specific one than the slogan. What the United States cannot see is mostly not the territory as such, over which American drones have flown since 2023. [cite:ow4_d1_drones] It is how Israel uses what the United States gives it, and whether American law on that use is being kept.

Raw intelligence, without verification. Under the memorandum agreed in principle in March 2009, as published by The Guardian in 2013, the NSA sends Israel's Unit 8200 raw collection, including unevaluated and unminimised transcripts that may contain the communications of Americans. Israel undertakes to destroy communications of American officials "upon recognition," and the NSA undertakes to review a sample of what it sends; the memorandum states that it "is not intended to create any legally enforceable rights." [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] The NSA said in 2013 that it "cannot... use these relationships to circumvent US legal restrictions." [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] The terms of this and other American intelligence-sharing agreements have never been officially released; what is known comes from leaked documents, and freedom-of-information requests for the current terms of even the oldest such arrangement, with Britain, have produced nothing newer than a 1955 text. [cite:ow4_aclu] [cite:ow4_js_ukusa] The record does not document a reciprocal raw feed from Israel to the NSA on comparable terms; the memorandum is examined in [scene:ow4_memorandum|Part Four].

Gaza: sharing more, seeing less of the use. Before October 2023 the United States relied largely on Israel for intelligence about Gaza. After the Hamas attack, a White House memorandum expanded sharing to include raw intelligence such as live drone feeds, and the United States widened its own collection; the Pentagon said in November 2023 that it was flying unarmed drones over Gaza to support efforts to recover hostages. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] [cite:ow4_d1_drones] American officials told The Wall Street Journal in April 2024 that the United States does not share intelligence intended specifically for ground or air strikes, that Israel certifies its own compliance with the rules on use, sometimes orally, and that once American intelligence is combined with Israel's it is hard to know how it is used. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] Reuters reported in December 2025 that in the second half of 2024 the United States briefly cut off a live drone feed and restricted Israel's use of some intelligence on high-value targets, over civilian deaths and the treatment of prisoners, and resumed after assurances; the Israeli army said, "The strategic intelligence cooperation continued throughout the war." [cite:ow3_reu_withheld] The intelligence side of this is set out in [scene:ow4_gaza|Part Four].

Weapons, without a check on use. When President Biden required recipients of American weapons to give written assurances that they would use them lawfully, the resulting report of 10 May 2024 said that "Israel has not shared complete information to verify whether U.S. defense articles were specifically used" in incidents of concern, and that the lack of American personnel on the ground made it "difficult to assess or reach conclusive findings on individual incidents," though it was "reasonable to assess" that American weapons had been used in instances inconsistent with international humanitarian law. [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20] The Leahy laws bar American aid to foreign security units credibly implicated in gross violations of human rights, but for Israel alone, according to Charles Blaha, a former State Department official who worked on them, decisions on ineligibility are made at the level of the Deputy Secretary of State, through a special forum, the Israel Leahy Vetting Forum; Israel may take up to three months to answer American queries, and in more than four years the forum did not identify a single ineligible Israeli unit. [cite:ow11_js_blaha] A classified State Department inspector general's report, described by The Washington Post in October 2025, found a backlog of "many hundreds" of potential violations by Israeli units in Gaza that would take "multiple years" to review; the department did not comment. [cite:ow11_wapo_oig] The full mechanism is set out in [scene:ow8_leahy|Part Eight] and [scene:ow11_exceptions|Part Eleven].

No independent eyes. The public's view is narrower still. Since October 2023 Israel, which controls entry, has not allowed foreign journalists into Gaza except on visits escorted by its army. The Foreign Press Association petitioned Israel's Supreme Court; on 8 January 2024 the court rejected the petition on the state's security grounds, and the association called the ban "unprecedented." [cite:pr_mm_fpa2024] As of mid-October 2026, three years into the war and with a ceasefire in place, the ban remained. [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] Its course through the courts is told in [scene:pr8_gate|The Gate] and [scene:gz12_access|the Gaza volume]. The stated Israeli reason is the danger to reporters and to troops. The effect, for American oversight, is that the government's own finding on its weapons was limited by the absence of American personnel on the ground, and the press could not fill the gap independently. [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20]

The governments' positions. The American government's position, stated in each of these documents, is that sharing serves American interests in counterterrorism and in the release of hostages, that it does not supply intelligence for strikes, and that Israel's assurances are credible. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20] Israel's army has said that its intelligence cooperation with the United States "continued throughout the war," and its government has told its own courts that independent press access would endanger journalists and soldiers. [cite:ow3_reu_withheld] [cite:pr_mm_fpa2024] The asymmetry this section documents does not depend on deciding who is right. It is structural: at each step after an item leaves American hands, verification passes to the recipient.

sections.h: Why It Is Rarely Reported, and the Whole Mirror
sections.html:
Each of the cases in this part was reported, and most by major American outlets: Pollard's case widely, the NSA documents by The Guardian and The Intercept, the Iran-talks operation by The Wall Street Journal, the Washington devices by Politico, the Pegasus hacks by Reuters. [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] [cite:ow4_statewatch2015] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] [cite:ow10_reu_state] The common complaint that the news "doesn't report it" is, on the record, inexact. What is rare is the second story: official confirmation, a public consequence, or a follow-up that settles what happened. The reasons are documented, and they are mostly structural rather than editorial.

The documents are classified, and released late or never. The CIA's damage assessment in the Pollard case was written in 1987 and released only in 2012, after an appeal to the Interagency Security Classification Appeals Panel. [cite:ow3_nsa_pollard] The CIA has never released its internal operational documents on NUMEC, more than half a century after the uranium went missing. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec] The terms of American intelligence-sharing agreements are not published at all; what the public knows of the 2009 NSA memorandum comes from a leak. [cite:ow4_aclu] [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] A reporter can publish what a leaked document says; without the government's confirmation, the story stops there.

The sources are anonymous, and the answers are denials. The reports of Israeli operations after Pollard rest on unnamed officials: three former officials in Politico's 2019 report, and unnamed officials again in the 2026 reports on the Defense Intelligence Agency. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] The Israeli government's response has been categorical denial, "a blatant lie" in 2019, "does not conduct espionage against the United States" in 2015, and the American government's response has usually been silence: in 2019, according to Politico's sources, there was no public rebuke. [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] [cite:ow_td_spying2015] When the government that was targeted will not confirm, the reporting stays at the level of allegation, and the record in this book has to mark it so.

The courts open some doors and close others. One of the few public records of an Israeli spyware company's conduct was made in an American courtroom, in WhatsApp's suit against NSO, where a jury found against the company and awarded damages.
