[cite:ow10_axios_jury] The same litigation shows the limit: Apple abandoned its parallel suit in 2024, saying it might never obtain NSO's most important files, and citing a report that Israeli officials had taken files from NSO's offices and sought secrecy for the step, which Israeli officials denied was interference. [cite:ow10_stripes_apple]

The ground is closed. In Gaza the obstacle is physical. Since October 2023 foreign reporters have entered Gaza only on visits escorted by the Israeli army. [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] These conditions, and the debate over how American newsrooms covered the war, are documented in [scene:pr8_gate|The Gate], [scene:gz12_access|Who Could Report], [scene:gz12_coverage|Inside American Newsrooms] and [scene:pr11_america|How the Dead Were Reported]. Studies of that coverage reached opposite conclusions, and both belong in the record.

An interpretation, labelled as such. This volume's reading of the evidence is that the scarcity of follow-up reflects the four conditions above more than any decision by editors: a subject made of classified documents, anonymous sources, denials, and territory closed to independent reporters will produce first reports and few second ones. The record used here does not document an instruction to any American newsroom to avoid the subject, and this book does not assert one.

The finding. Read across the table, the one-way claim survives in a precise form. The relationship is not one-way in what moves: intelligence, technology and money flow in both directions, and the United States watches its partner as its partner watches it. [cite:ow4_aj_wsj2015] [cite:ow_td_spying2015] It is one-way in verification. For every major category of what the United States sends, the record shows American officials unable to see, or not permitted to check, how it is used once it arrives, and relying instead on Israeli assurances. [cite:ow3_wsj_sharing] [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20] [cite:ow11_js_blaha] That is the mirror the title names: the United States can see clearly what it gives, and the glass darkens at the point of use.

chapters.label: Part Fourteen
chapters.title: Settled, Contested and Open
chapters.intro: The last part gathers the volume's findings into three groups: what the record settles, what it leaves contested between documented positions, and what is still open as of October 2026. It ends with the whole architecture in one diagram.
chapters.outro: This volume set out the documented architecture that ties the American state to Israel: laws passed by large majorities since 1973, about $174 billion in aid, an intelligence liaison with no published agreement, raw intercepts including Americans' communications shared under a memorandum with no enforceable rights, a military relationship that became combat in Israel's defence, and contractors on both sides. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow3_robarge] [cite:ow_aj_nsamou] The United States gets real returns from it. What runs one way is the ability to verify: the means that exist, Leahy vetting, the 2024 review and Israeli assurances, have not let the United States independently verify how its intelligence and weapons are used in individual incidents in Gaza and the West Bank. [cite:ow4_axios_nsm20] [cite:ow11_js_blaha]

sections.h: What the Record Settles
sections.html:
The law. The relationship was built by statute and executive agreement over five decades: the Emergency Security Assistance Act of 1973, the strategic memorandum of 1981, major non-NATO ally status in 1987, early disbursement into an interest-bearing account at the Federal Reserve from 1991, the qualitative military edge written into law in 2008, the 2012 and 2014 cooperation acts, and three ten-year memoranda culminating in the $38 billion agreement of 2016. By the Congressional Research Service's count, American aid to Israel from 1946 to 2025 came to about $174 billion in current dollars. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow_wiki_sca1981] [cite:ow_jvl_2014act] It passed with large bipartisan majorities in both chambers, and every congressional attempt to condition it failed. [scene:ow2_votes|Part Two: the votes]

The intelligence agencies. The CIA's liaison with the Mossad dates from 1951 and rests on no published agreement. [cite:ow3_robarge] Under a 2009 memorandum, the NSA passes Unit 8200 raw intercepts, including Americans' communications, and the memorandum creates no legally enforceable rights; the NSA's own documents also describe Israel as a counterintelligence threat that "also targets us", which Israel denies. [cite:ow_aj_nsamou] [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] [cite:ow_td_spying2015] One Israeli spy, Jonathan Pollard, was convicted in an American court. [cite:ow13_wiki_pollard]

The military and the weapons. Without a defence treaty, the United States keeps a war-reserve stockpile in Israel, a radar in the Negev and, since 2024, a THAAD battery; Israel moved into Central Command in 2021; since April 2024 American forces have fought in Israel's defence; and in 2026 the United States joined Israel in a war on Iran. [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] [cite:ow7_sat_xband] [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024] [cite:ow_inss_centcom] Arms sales to Israel face a shorter congressional review than most countries', and since 2023 that review has been skipped more than once by emergency declaration. [cite:ow8_crs_review2021] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

The contractors. Palantir, seeded by the CIA's venture arm, holds ICE contracts justified as sole-source and a strategic partnership with Israel's Defense Ministry; Israeli-founded firms such as Cellebrite, Paragon and Elbit's American subsidiary sell to ICE and Customs and Border Protection, while NSO Group was blacklisted by the Commerce Department after its spyware was used against State Department employees. [cite:ow9_ap_s1] [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:ow10_reason_cb] [cite:ow10_doc_entity] [cite:ow10_reu_state]

sections.h: What Is Contested
sections.html:
Whether the money buys the votes. AIPAC's PAC and super PAC have become among the largest spenders in congressional primaries, but analysts disagree on whether the money changes outcomes or backs members who already agree. [cite:pm_sludge_100m_2026] [cite:ow2_bahar_forward]

NUMEC. The CIA concluded that uranium missing from the Pennsylvania plant went into Israel's weapons; the Atomic Energy Commission found no evidence of theft, and the government's later investigators said only that a diversion could not be ruled out. Officially, it is unresolved. [cite:ow3_nsa_numec]

Israeli espionage after Pollard. NSA documents, a reported Defense Intelligence Agency rating and press reports describe continuing Israeli intelligence activity against the United States; Israel denies spying on the United States, and no Israeli agent has been convicted of espionage since Pollard: Kadish's plea ended in a fine, and Franklin pleaded guilty to disclosing classified information, some of it to AIPAC staff. [cite:ow_td_spying2015] [cite:ow13_nbc_dia] [cite:ow5_wiki_esp] [cite:pm_wiki_franklin]

Palantir in Israel's wars. The company has a partnership with Israel's Defense Ministry; it denies any role in the Lavender and Gospel targeting systems, and Israeli reporting says Unit 8200 and the Shin Bet declined its services. [cite:ow9_globes_palantir] [cite:ow9_pal_unletter]

Epstein and intelligence. His business ties to Ehud Barak and Israeli security technology are documented; the claim that he worked for an intelligence service rests on a denied, anonymous report and on theories without documents. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] [cite:ow12_wiki_barak]

What Is Still Open

As of October 2026, it is not publicly documented whether the 2009 NSA–Israel memorandum is still in force or has been revised. [cite:ow4_alternet_guardian] Formal talks on the memorandum that will follow the 2016 aid agreement after 2028 opened on 5 June 2026, with no published text. [cite:ow1_wiki_nextmou] The sanctions on the International Criminal Court were being tested in American courts. [cite:ow11_jurist_judges2026] The rules that once required assurances on the use of American weapons, NSM-20, had been revoked in February 2025, and no Israeli unit had been publicly found ineligible under the Leahy laws. [cite:ow8_aca_rescind] [cite:ow11_js_blaha] And Gaza remained closed to independent foreign reporters, so the American public's view of how American weapons are used there still depends largely on Palestinian journalists and on Israel's own statements. [cite:pr_wlrn_ban_full] [scene:pr8_gate|PRESS: the gate]

books.title: The Dark Enlightenment Architecture
books.subtitle: Philosophy, Money, Technology and the Executive Without a Veto
books.intro:
This volume is about a set of ideas that began on the margins of the internet and now has readers in the highest offices of the American government. Between 2007 and 2014 a software engineer writing as Mencius Moldbug and a British philosopher named Nick Land set out an argument against democracy itself. In their account, elected government had become a façade over a permanent establishment of universities, newspapers and civil servants, which Moldbug called "the Cathedral". The cure they proposed was a state run like a company, with a chief executive answerable to its owners rather than to voters, and with "exit", the freedom to leave, taking the place of the vote. Land gave the body of writing its name, the Dark Enlightenment. [cite:de1_land_gwern] [cite:de1_tablet] [cite:de1_finley_tc] [cite:de2_land_ebook]

The book follows those ideas in three directions. It reads the texts closely, including their hardest passages, and asks whether the diagnosis is right and whether the cure would work. It follows the money and the people: Peter Thiel, who funded the company Moldbug founded; Elon Musk; J.D. Vance, who cited Moldbug, under his own name Curtis Yarvin, before he became vice president; and the network of investors who met at PayPal. And it follows the machinery of the state in 2025 and 2026: the Department of Government Efficiency created by executive order on the first day of the second Trump administration, the data systems that immigration enforcement now runs on, among them a Palantir platform called ImmigrationOS, and the rulings and orders that have widened the President's control over the executive branch. [cite:de1_wiki_urbit] [cite:de1_vox_vance] [cite:de0_eo14158] [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:de0_slaughter]

The reading this book tests

The book takes a hypothesis set out on the Sophia platform and states it plainly so that it can be tested. In its strongest form it holds that immigration enforcement and the campaign against government waste are the occasions, and that a sovereign executive without a veto, the end state the Dark Enlightenment texts describe, is the destination: that the tools built to find, track and remove immigrants, and the powers taken to cut and purge the civil service, add up to the machinery that state would need, and could be turned on anyone who criticises those in charge. This is the worst-case reading. It is not a finding, and nothing in this book assumes it is true. It is a lens held to every mechanism so that the record can answer it.

Every part therefore closes with a passage headed "The worst-case reading, tested", which sorts the part's material into three registers. Documented means a primary record or independent reporting establishes it. Probable means the record makes it likely without proving it, and the passage says what would settle it. Not supported means the record does not show it, or runs against it, and the passage says which. The book's central discipline follows from the same test: it shows convergence, not coordination. The money and the people are documented; no document shows a plan, and where a later policy resembles something Moldbug proposed, resemblance is reported as resemblance, not as authorship.

How the book is built

Book One reads the ideas: what they are, where they came from, the lives of their two authors, the strongest honest case for their diagnosis, and where their argument breaks. Book Two follows the men and the money, with full biographies of Thiel, Musk and Vance, each closing with a ledger of political money and a ledger of public claims set against the documented record. Book Three examines the Department of Government Efficiency: how it was set up, who ran it, what it reached inside federal systems, what it cut, who paid, and what it saved by the government's own auditors' count. Book Four turns to "exit": the charter cities and the digital network built on Moldbug's design. Book Five maps the surveillance toolkit, from commercial data, the records the state already holds and phones to travel and the border, faces, drones, money rails and Palantir, and the times American governments have turned such tools on their own citizens. Book Six asks how protections are removed and who would enforce a state without them, from immigration agents and local police to the military and the private companies that run detention. Book Seven is the test itself: what is built, what is missing, what a person would lose, who picks the chief executive, how the ideas are read abroad, the documented ties to Israel and only those, what does not fit, the labelled interpretations, and the verdict. [cite:us6_brennan_obbba]

The claims ledgers use four grades, applied in the same way to every person and every party. Red marks a public claim contradicted by the person's own documents or sworn statements. Orange marks a promise not delivered, or a claim the official auditor could not verify. Yellow marks a reversal, or a fact kept out of view while the opposite was said, shown with the person's own explanation. Grey marks a dispute in which credible accounts conflict, with both shown. The word "lie" appears only where the record shows a person knew a claim was untrue when making it.

Three rules hold throughout. The ideas are a body of texts, not an organisation, so the book maps who wrote, cited, published, funded and hired, never who "believes"; a named person's views come from that person's own words. A relative's record is not a person's own. And the ideas are kept distinct from their neighbours, from conservatism and the Republican Party to Christian nationalism and the violent groups that use the word "accelerationism" for terror, because confusing them would make the record harder, not easier, to read. Interpretations, including the readings of symbol and myth that the Sophia platform brings to this subject, appear only in passages labelled as interpretation, each followed by the strongest reading against it.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: The Question
chapters.intro: Part One sets out what this book is about before it says anything about who is involved. It describes the Dark Enlightenment, also called neoreaction, as what it is on the record: a body of writing by two authors, Curtis Yarvin and Nick Land, published mostly between 2007 and 2014, with four core claims about democracy, "the Cathedral," exit and the state run as a company. It then separates the documented spine of texts, citations, money and public statements from the overlay of resemblance and association that surrounds the subject, and shows how the label has spread to people who have never claimed it. It ends by stating the working hypothesis the book tests, and the grades it uses to test it.
chapters.outro: Part One established that the Dark Enlightenment is a shelf of texts, not an organisation: Yarvin supplied its political vocabulary, including "the Cathedral" and neocameralism, the idea that "a state is a business which owns a country," and Land named it and credited those terms to him. [cite:de1_land_gwern] [cite:de1_land_ebook] It showed that only the two authors claim the label in their own words; that Yarvin's self-descriptions run from "restorationist" in 2008 to "Monarch is good" in 2025, alongside qualified denials; that Thiel's best-known sentence, "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible," came with a programme of exit, not seizure; and that Vance's one documented link is a 2021 citation of Yarvin by name. [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] [cite:de1_nyt_interview] [cite:de1_cato_thiel] [cite:de1_vox_vance] It found that much of the label's later spread rests on adjacency and resemblance, and stated the book's working hypothesis and its grades. Part Two goes back to the beginning: the blog posts of 2007 and 2008, Land's serial of 2012, and the first readers who wrote about them.

sections.h: A Body of Texts, Not an Organisation
sections.html:
The Dark Enlightenment has no headquarters, no membership list, no charter and no budget. It is a shelf of writing. Most of it was published online between 2007 and 2014 by two authors: Curtis Yarvin, an American software engineer who wrote under the pen name Mencius Moldbug on a blog called Unqualified Reservations, and Nick Land, a British philosopher, who in 2012 wrote a long serial essay called "The Dark Enlightenment" that summarised, extended and named Yarvin's ideas. [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] [cite:de1_land_gwern] The same body of writing travels under a second name, "neoreaction", often shortened to NRx. Yarvin used the word "neoreactionary" for his own project from 2008; Land's serial opened under the title "Neo-reactionaries head for the exit." [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] [cite:de1_land_ebook] This book uses the two names for the same shelf, and treats it the way one treats any shelf: by asking who wrote what, when, who cited it, who paid for what was built around it, and who, in their own words, has said they agree.

That last point governs everything that follows. Because there is no organisation, there is nobody to join. A person is connected to these ideas in this book only by something documented: a text they wrote, a text they cited by name, money they gave to a named project, a job they held, or their own public statement. Being on the same stage, funding the same university or sounding similar does not count. The rest of this section sets out what the texts actually claim, in plain terms, before any question of influence arises.

Claim one: democracy has failed

The starting point is a verdict on democracy. Land put it in its strongest form in the first instalment of his serial, on 2 March 2012: "For the hardcore neo-reactionaries, democracy is not merely doomed, it is doom itself." [cite:de1_land_gwern] The argument behind the line runs like this. Democracy is not a stable arrangement but a direction of travel. Because elections are won by promising voters other people's money, and because schools and newspapers can be bought as easily as votes, a democratic state grows, borrows and spends until something breaks; politicians who try to economise lose. Land called this democracy as "a vector", and said that its reversal "lies beyond the bounds of democratic possibility." [cite:de1_land_ebook]

Yarvin's version, in his own later words, is milder in tone and the same in substance. In a January 2025 interview with The New York Times he said: "It's not even that democracy is bad, it's just that it's very weak." In the same conversation he said, "I don't believe in actually voting at all," and that he does not vote. [cite:de1_nyt_interview] [cite:de1_audit_nyt_voting] The claim, in both writers, is not that a particular government is bad. It is that the form itself, rule by elected representatives answerable to voters, cannot be fixed from inside.

Claim two: "the Cathedral"

The second claim explains why, in the authors' view, the failure is not obvious to most people. Yarvin coined the term "the Cathedral" for the institutions that, as he described them, shape what educated people believe: the leading universities, the prestige press and, in some versions, the permanent civil service. His central point is that these institutions behave "as if they were a single organizational structure," although no one directs them. [cite:de1_tablet] The journalist Klint Finley, in one of the first mainstream accounts of the subject in November 2013, summarised the idea as "a meta-institution" centred on Harvard and the other Ivy League schools, which enforces the limits of acceptable opinion. [cite:de1_finley_tc] The phrase "as if" matters. The Cathedral, as Yarvin describes it, is a pattern of agreement produced by shared training, status and incentives, not a committee that meets. That makes it a weaker claim than a conspiracy theory, and also a harder one to test, a problem taken up in [scene:de8_tests_it_fails|Part Eight].

The term is Yarvin's, not Land's. Land is explicit about this: after describing a ruling network of lobbyists, officials, journalists and academics, he writes, "Moldbug calls it the Cathedral." [cite:de1_land_gwern] Land also quotes Yarvin's account of the belief system the Cathedral transmits, which Yarvin called "Universalism", describing it as "a nontheistic Christian sect" descended from English Puritanism and "best described as a mystery cult of power." [cite:de1_land_ebook]

Claim three: exit over voice

The third claim is about what ordinary people should be able to do when government fails them. The vocabulary comes from the economist Albert O. Hirschman, whose 1970 book Exit, Voice, and Loyalty described two ways members respond when a firm, an organisation or a state declines: they can leave ("exit") or they can complain and try to change it from inside ("voice"). [cite:de1_hirschman] Democracy, in these terms, is a system built on voice. The Dark Enlightenment texts propose to give up voice and keep exit. Land quoted the seasteading advocate Patri Friedman: "we think that free exit is so important that we've called it the only Universal Human Right." [cite:de1_land_gwern] Finley quoted Yarvin's own compressed version: "The design is all 'exit,' no 'voice.'" [cite:de1_finley_tc] The idea is that a government with no voters would still be disciplined, because residents who disliked it could move to a better-run one, the way customers leave a bad shop.

Claim four: neocameralism, the state as a company

The fourth claim is the positive programme. Yarvin called it "neocameralism", after cameralism, the administrative science of eighteenth-century German states, and particularly Prussia under Frederick the Great. [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] Land quoted his definition at length: "To a neocameralist, a state is a business which owns a country." Ownership would be divided into shares, each share would carry one vote, the shareholders would elect a board, and the board would hire and fire the managers. Residents would be customers. "Misgovernment equals mismanagement." [cite:de1_land_gwern] Land added his own gloss: once the real holders of power were bought out and turned into shareholders, the board would appoint a chief executive, residents would have no reason to take any interest in politics, and unhappy customers could "take their custom elsewhere." His summary was four words: "No voice, free exit." [cite:de1_land_ebook]

Before neocameralism comes a simpler idea that Yarvin called formalism: the proposal to write down who actually holds power, as plainly as a property deed, so that the gap between the official account of power and the real one closes. Part Two follows how that idea opened his blog in 2007. Neocameralism is formalism carried to its end: if the real owners of a state can be identified, make them its legal owners, and let them run it for profit.

The texts concede that this has never existed. Land reproduces, without naming its source, a passage summarising the neocameralist position: "the full neocameralist approach has never been tried," and its closest historical equivalents are Frederick the Great's enlightened absolutism and three modern city-states, Hong Kong, Singapore and Dubai, described as "weak only in political freedom." [cite:de1_land_ebook] Whether those examples hold up is tested in [scene:de8_tests_it_fails|Part Eight].

What the shelf is not

Three things follow from treating this as a body of texts. First, the two authors are not interchangeable. Yarvin supplied most of the political vocabulary: the Cathedral, Universalism, formalism and neocameralism, all of which Land credits to him. Land supplied the name and a darker philosophical frame, rooted in his earlier work on technology and capitalism, which [scene:de4_the_2012_text|Part Four] reads in full. Second, the texts are not a manifesto for a party or a plan for a particular government. They describe an end state, a sovereign run like a company and answerable to no voters, and argue for it, but the 2007–2014 writing does not lay out who would carry it out in the United States, or when. Third, the shelf contains passages about race, surplus people and violence that are among the hardest in this book. Those passages are quoted accurately and in context in [scene:de4_the_hard_passages|Part Four] and [scene:de6_the_hard_posts|Part Six], with what the authors said they meant.

Those four claims, and the vocabulary in the figure, are what a reader needs to follow the rest of the book. The next section separates what is documented about the people and money around these texts from what is only inferred.

sections.h: The Spine and the Overlay
sections.html:
Most writing about the Dark Enlightenment mixes two kinds of statement without saying so. The first kind can be checked against a document: a blog post with a date on it, a donation in a public filing, a job title, a sentence a person said on the record. The second kind is a reading laid over those documents: a resemblance between an old blog post and a new policy, a shared dinner, a similar turn of phrase, a sense that certain people must think alike because they move in the same circles. This book calls the first kind the spine and the second kind the overlay. The spine carries weight. The overlay can be interesting, and some of it may turn out to be right, but it is never allowed to stand in for the spine.

What the spine is made of

The spine has four strands. The first is texts: who wrote what, and when. The authorship and dates of the core writing are firm. Yarvin's blog posts carry their own dates, and Land's serial was posted in ten dated instalments between 2 March and 20 July 2012 and gathered into an e-book compilation in 2014. [cite:de1_land_ebook] [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] The second strand is citation: who quoted whom by name. Land's serial, for example, names Moldbug more than thirty times [cite:de1_land_ebook] and quotes him at length, and it also quotes Peter Thiel's 2009 sentence "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible." [cite:de1_land_gwern]

The third strand is money. Some of it is small and documented: Yarvin founded a company, Tlon, to build a computer platform called Urbit, and its early investors included Thiel; his venture firm, Founders Fund, together with Andreessen Horowitz, put in $1.1 million. [cite:de1_wiki_urbit] Much larger sums appear later in this book, in campaign finance, in contracts and in the projects built around the idea of exit, and [scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen] maps them. The fourth strand is people and posts: who worked for whom, who sat on which board, who held which office, and what they said in public under their own names.

Each strand answers a narrow question. A citation shows that one writer read another, not that he agreed. An investment shows that money moved, not why. A job shows that two people worked together, not that they share a philosophy. The spine is strong precisely because each item claims so little.

What the overlay is made of

The overlay has three common forms. The first is rhyme: a later event looks like something in the texts. In 2012 Yarvin gave a talk proposing that a new American leader retire all government employees, a programme he called RAGE, for "Retire All Government Employees". [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin] In 2021 J.D. Vance said on a podcast that a president should "fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state." [cite:de1_nextgov_vance] In 2025 the new administration cut the federal workforce, a story told in Book Three. The resemblance between those three things is real. It does not by itself show that the third came from the first. A rhyme becomes provenance only when a document shows the chain: someone citing the idea, being given it, or carrying it into an office. In the case of Vance there is one such link, which the next section and [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|Part Twelve] examine: he named Yarvin on that podcast. Whether anything in the 2025 cuts traces back to Yarvin, rather than resembling him, is a separate question, tested in [scene:de17_money_to_office|Part Seventeen] and [scene:de33_two_tests|Part Thirty-Five].

The second form is adjacency. Two people speak at the same conference, attend the same party, invest in the same fund or are photographed together. Adjacency is a fact about where people were, and it can be recorded as such. It is not evidence of what either of them believes. The third form is resemblance of style: a speech that sounds like a blog post, an executive who talks about running a country like a company. Many people have said that governments should be run more like businesses without having read a word of Yarvin, and the idea long predates him, as [scene:de3_lineage|Part Three] shows.

A fourth temptation sits between the spine and the overlay: the inference that because several documented things point the same way, someone must have arranged them. This book calls that the difference between convergence and coordination. Convergence is documented throughout: wealthy technologists, a small number of writers and some politicians arrived at overlapping views and backed overlapping projects. Coordination would need a document showing a plan, an agreement or a chain of instruction. No such document appears anywhere in the record this book covers, and where the absence matters, the text says so.

A worked example: Thiel's 2009 sentence

The single most quoted line in this whole field shows how the two layers come apart. On 13 April 2009 Peter Thiel published an essay on the Cato Institute's online forum, Cato Unbound, titled "The Education of a Libertarian." In it he wrote: "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible." He argued that since 1920 the growth of welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the vote to women, "two constituencies that are notoriously tough for libertarians," had made "capitalist democracy" an oxymoron. [cite:de1_cato_thiel] Those are his words, and they are spine.

What he proposed in the same essay was not a seizure of government. He proposed escape: new spaces beyond the reach of existing states, in cyberspace, in outer space and on the oceans through seastead platforms. In a follow-up published on 1 May 2009, "Your Suffrage Isn't in Danger. Your Other Rights Are.", which Cato Unbound appended to the essay, he added: "While I don't think any class of people should be disenfranchised, I have little hope that voting will make things better." [cite:de1_cato_thiel] [cite:de1_audit_cato_followup] Three years later Land opened his serial by quoting the 2009 sentence as a milestone in the turn from voice to exit. [cite:de1_land_gwern] The citation is spine: it shows that Land read Thiel and found him useful. The inference that Thiel therefore subscribes to Land's or Yarvin's programme is overlay. Thiel's own words on Yarvin, given to The Atlantic in 2023 and reported by CNN, run the other way in part: he called Yarvin an "interesting and powerful" historian whose ideas, he said, would not "work." [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] What Thiel has actually funded and said is set out in [scene:de9_formation|Part Nine] and [scene:de10_girard_and_the_katechon|Part Ten], on the same terms.

A ladder of support

Because the overlay is so easy to produce, the book uses a fixed ladder to describe how any named person stands in relation to these texts. Each rung needs a different kind of evidence, and a person sits on the highest rung their own record supports, no higher.

Two features of the ladder deserve emphasis. A patron is not thereby a believer: someone can fund a company for the software and dislike its founder's politics, and the book records the money without guessing at the motive unless the person has explained it. And the rungs do not add up. Ten pieces of inference do not make one piece of on-record agreement. The ladder is applied the same way to every person in the book, whatever their party or reputation, and the next section uses it to sort who has said they hold these ideas, who has denied them, and who has simply had the label applied to them by others.

sections.h: How the Label Inflates
sections.html:
When Klint Finley introduced neoreaction to the readers of TechCrunch on 22 November 2013, he described it as "a community of bloggers" who wanted to turn the dial back to "the days before the French Revolution." He named Yarvin as its starting point and Land as the man who coined "dark enlightenment," and he mentioned Peter Thiel, carefully, as a PayPal founder who "has voiced similar ideas," quoting the 2009 sentence about freedom and democracy. [cite:de1_finley_tc] Thirteen years later the same label is attached, in newspapers, academic journals and online commentary, to billionaires, a vice president, an administration and much of Silicon Valley. Some of that spread follows documented ties. Much of it does not. This section shows how the label grows, sorts who has actually claimed it and who has denied it, and then sets out the working hypothesis the book tests.

Two worked examples from 2025

The clearest way to see inflation is to read claims against their own footnotes. In August 2025 the peer-reviewed journal Politics and Governance published an article by Danica Fink-Hafner of the University of Ljubljana comparing how liberal democracy, illiberal democracy and the Dark Enlightenment treat elections. It said the Dark Enlightenment had been "significantly empowered" by the world's richest individuals, "particularly Elon Musk," who "have adopted Dark Enlightenment ideas." Its source for that was a 2025 magazine article, not a statement by Musk. It said that Steve Bannon "also supports the Dark Enlightenment," citing a 2017 Politico list of books Bannon recommended. And it said that the ideology's "followers damage free and fair elections." [cite:de1_fh_2025] Each step moves from a text, a reading list or a news story to a belief held by a named person, and then to a group of "followers" who are never named at all.

A second 2025 paper, by Bahram Sarmast in the journal Interdisciplinary Studies in Society, Law, and Politics, went further. It said that J.D. Vance "has explicitly praised Yarvin's work," that the Trump administration's cuts to the civil service showed neoreactionary critiques "operationalized," and that a proposal to turn Gaza into a "Riviera of the Middle East" embodied "Yarvin's concept of neocameralist management." [cite:de1_sarmast_2025] The documented version of the Vance claim is narrower. In 2021, on a conservative podcast, Vance said "there's this guy, Curtis Yarvin, who has written about some of these things," and called for a president to fire "every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state." [cite:de1_vox_vance] [cite:de1_nextgov_vance] That is a citation by name, the third rung on the ladder in the previous section. It is not praise of Yarvin's work as a whole, and it says nothing about neocameralism. The Gaza example has no document linking it to Yarvin at all; it is resemblance offered as provenance.

Not all commentary inflates. A 2022 explainer in The Conversation on neoreaction in Republican politics laid out Yarvin's ideas from his own writing, recorded Vance's podcast remark and Thiel's funding of candidates, and then noted that neither Vance nor Blake Masters had explicitly called for dismantling American democracy. [cite:de1_conv_2022] That is the standard this book holds: what was said, by whom, and what was not said.

Who has said they hold it, and who has denied it

Only two people stand on the top rung, and both are authors. Land named the current in 2012 and wrote of it from the inside, calling Yarvin the "supreme Sith Lord of the neoreactionaries." [cite:de1_land_gwern] Yarvin has used several labels for himself. In 2008, in his "Open Letter to Open-Minded Progressives," he wrote that if he had to choose one word he would pick "restorationist," and that if he had to concede one pejorative that fair writers could apply, he would accept "reactionary." The same year he first used "neoreactionary" for his project. [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] In January 2025, when his interviewer at The New York Times used the word monarch for what he proposes, Yarvin interjected, "Monarch is good," adding, "It's a neutral term." [cite:de1_nyt_interview]

Yarvin's denials are as much part of his record as his claims, and they are often qualified in the same breath. In a 2007 post titled "Why I am not a white nationalist" he wrote that although he was not one, "I am not exactly allergic to the stuff." In a published response quoted by the Boulder Daily Camera, he wrote that he was not "an outspoken advocate for slavery, a racist, a sexist or a fascist." [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] When reports circulated in 2017 that he was advising Steve Bannon, he denied them. [cite:de1_tablet] Asked in 2025 about his friendship with Vance, he said it was "definitely overstated," and said his ideas spread "mostly through the staffers and the younger people." An adviser to Vance has said the two met "like once." [cite:de1_nyt_interview] [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] Asked about a 2016 email in which he described Thiel as "fully enlightened," Yarvin said that for him the phrase means "fully disenchanted." [cite:de2_pein2017] [cite:de1_nyt_interview] These statements are recorded here as what he said, not as settled facts; [scene:de6_claims_vs_record|Part Six] sets them against the documents.

No one else in this book has, in their own words, claimed the label. Thiel's own comment on Yarvin, as reported from a 2023 interview with The Atlantic, was that his ideas would not "work." [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] Marc Andreessen's 2023 "Techno-Optimist Manifesto" listed Land among its "patron saints," which is a citation of Land, documented, and not an adoption of neocameralism. [cite:de1_a16z_wiki] Vance's documented citation of Yarvin by name is the 2021 podcast remark. Everyone else to whom the label is applied sits on the lower rungs, and the book says which.

Neighbours, not the same thing

The label also inflates sideways, absorbing other currents that share a stage or a funder. The Dark Enlightenment is distinct from conservatism in general, which defends inherited institutions that these texts propose to replace; from the Republican Party, a mass electoral organisation; from Christian nationalism and Catholic integralism, which are religious and, in the first case, majoritarian, where these texts are secular and elitist; from pronatalism, a single policy aim; from the rationalist community, one of whose best-known writers, Scott Alexander, published a long rebuttal of neoreaction in 2013; and from "effective accelerationism," a technology-optimist current. It is, above all, distinct from the violent "accelerationism" of neo-Nazi terror groups, a doctrine of attacks meant to hasten collapse, which shares a word with Land's philosophy and must not be confused with it. [cite:de2_ssc_faq] [cite:de1_a16z_wiki] [scene:de16_neighbours_not_the_same|Part Sixteen] maps each neighbour and its documented touchpoints, on equal terms.

The working hypothesis, and how it is graded

The Sophia platform proposes a reading of the period that this book adopts as its working hypothesis, not as a finding. Stated in its worst case: that immigration enforcement and government cuts in 2025 and 2026 were the occasion, and that a sovereign executive without a veto, the end state the Dark Enlightenment texts describe, is the destination. The book reads every mechanism it examines in that worst case, and then tests the reading against the record.

Every part ends with a passage headed "The worst-case reading, tested," which grades what that part's material shows in three registers. Documented means a primary record or independent named reporting shows it. Probable means several documented facts point the same way and no documented fact points against, but the link itself is not on paper. Not supported means the record does not show it, or shows the opposite; where the record runs against the hypothesis, the passage says so plainly. The biography parts add a second scale for public claims set against the record: red where a claim is contradicted by the person's own documents or sworn record, orange where a promise is undelivered or unverifiable by the official auditor, yellow for a reversal or concealment shown with the person's own explanation, and grey where credible accounts conflict. The word "lie" is used only where the record shows a person knew a claim was untrue when making it. The same scales apply to every person, whatever their party. [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three] gathers every grade in one place.

The worst-case reading, tested

This part bears on the hypothesis in three ways. First, the destination is documented as a stated aim of the texts. Land's serial and the Yarvin passages it quotes describe a state owned and run like a company by a chief executive, with residents who have "no voice," and Yarvin said in 2025 that he does not believe in voting at all. [cite:de1_land_ebook] [cite:de1_nyt_interview] A sovereign executive without a veto is not an inference about these authors; it is what they wrote. Second, the claim that people in power hold this aim is, on this part's material, not supported beyond one documented link: Vance's 2021 citation of Yarvin by name. The other attributions examined here rest on adjacency or resemblance, and some are contradicted by the people concerned. Third, coordination is not supported: no document in this part shows a plan connecting the texts to the occasions the hypothesis names. The record also runs against the hypothesis in one respect worth noting at the start. The early texts, and Thiel's 2009 essay, framed the goal as exit, leaving existing states, rather than seizing one. Whether and when that changed is the question [scene:de2_core_texts|Part Two] and the parts after it take up.

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: The Name and the Texts
chapters.intro: Part Two goes back to the beginning of the shelf. It follows how the current acquired its names, from Curtis Yarvin's "formalism" in 2007 through "neoreactionary" in 2008 to Nick Land's "Dark Enlightenment" in 2012, and settles who coined which term. It then reads the core texts in order: the "formalist manifesto" that opened Yarvin's blog, the "Open Letter" he addressed to progressive readers, the "Patchwork" series that set out his design for states run as corporations, the 2012 talk that turned it toward the American government, and Land's ten-part serial. It ends with the first journalists and critics who read them.
chapters.outro: Part Two established the order of the record. Yarvin opened Unqualified Reservations with "A formalist manifesto," dated 23 April 2007, accepted "reactionary" and first used "neoreactionary" in 2008, and in November 2008 set out Patchwork: small states "each governed by its own joint-stock corporation without regard to the residents' opinions," with surplus residents' slums to be sold "out from under them" and a stated goal of "a humane alternative to genocide." [cite:de2_le] [cite:de2_tnr] [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin] Land named the whole current "the Dark Enlightenment" in a serial of ten instalments between 2 March and 20 July 2012, crediting the Cathedral and neocameralism to Moldbug. [cite:de1_land_gwern] [cite:de2_land_ebook] The first readers, from Scott Alexander and Klint Finley in 2013 to Corey Pein and Elizabeth Sandifer, described a small body of online writing, not an organisation. [cite:de2_ssc_faq] [cite:de1_finley_tc] [cite:de2_pein2017] [cite:de2_sandifer_gr] Part Three turns to the older writers these texts drew on, and to the earlier American dream of government by engineers.

sections.h: The Name: From "Formalism" to "the Dark Enlightenment"
sections.html:
The current this book follows has had at least four names, and the order in which they appeared explains a good deal of the confusion around it. It began, in 2007, as a blog with no label at all. Its author tried out "formalism" and "neocameralism," accepted "reactionary" and then "neoreactionary," and in 2012 a second writer gave the whole body of work the name by which it is now best known. Tracing the names one by one also settles two attributions that are widely repeated the wrong way round.

2007: a blog and a manifesto

In 2007 Curtis Yarvin, a software engineer, began a blog called Unqualified Reservations under the pen name Mencius Moldbug. Its inaugural post was titled "A formalist manifesto." [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin] The essay, dated 23 April 2007 and later issued as a short 14-page booklet, is now held by Princeton University Library. [cite:de2_princeton_fm] [cite:de2_le] Its word was "formalism," and in that first year Yarvin used it as the name for his position: the proposal that the real distribution of power in a society should be written down and made official, the way property is. The next section reads the manifesto's argument. Here what matters is that the first name for this body of thought was a method, not a mood.

Alongside it a second term appeared. Yarvin argued that a state could be run as a company owned by shareholders, and called the idea "neocameralism," after cameralism, the administrative science of eighteenth-century German states and particularly of Prussia under Frederick the Great. [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] As the sociologists Smith and Burrows put it in a 2021 study of the texts, his position was "originally called 'neocameralism'" before it "soon became known as 'neoreactionary' philosophy." [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin]

2008: "reactionary," then "neoreactionary"

In April 2008 Yarvin began a long serial addressed to progressive readers, "An Open Letter to Open-Minded Progressives," whose first chapter opened by asking whether the reader was one, and noting that the reader probably had friends who were. [cite:de2_upcarta] In it he addressed the question of labels directly. If he had to choose one word and stick with it, he wrote, he would pick "restorationist"; if he had to concede one pejorative that fair writers could fairly apply, he would accept "reactionary." [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] The word is chosen with care. A reactionary, in the historical sense, is someone who wants to undo a revolution and restore what came before it; for Yarvin the revolution in question was, broadly, the rise of popular sovereignty since the eighteenth century. The same year, he first used "neoreactionary" to describe his project. [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin] The prefix marks a difference from the older reactionaries of the nineteenth century: this was a reaction argued in the language of software, corporate governance and economics.

2012: Land names it

Four years later Nick Land, a British philosopher with a long prior career writing about technology and capitalism, began a serial essay that took Yarvin's work as its main subject. The first instalment, published on 2 March 2012, was titled "Neo-reactionaries head for the exit." Its opening paragraph introduced the phrase that became the second name. Land argued that "enlightenment," as a historical event, is self-confirming: once a society believes certain truths are self-evident, there can be no turning back, so "a retrograde, or reactionary, 'dark enlightenment' amounts almost to intrinsic contradiction." [cite:de1_land_gwern] A few paragraphs later he used the phrase for the thing he was describing: a current of thought, "recognizably Hobbesian, a coherent dark enlightenment," which treated democracy as an engine of decline and asked, "From Thomas Hobbes to Hans-Hermann Hoppe and beyond," how a sovereign could be stopped from "devouring society." [cite:de1_land_gwern] [cite:de2_land_ebook]

The name was a deliberate paradox. The Enlightenment, in the standard account, is the eighteenth-century movement of reason, rights and representative government; a "dark" enlightenment keeps the claim to clear-eyed reason and turns it against the political conclusions the original drew. Land titled the whole serial "The Dark Enlightenment," posted it in ten instalments between 2 March and 20 July 2012, and the parts were later compiled into a single e-book, dated 2014. [cite:de2_land_ebook] By the time Klint Finley wrote about the subject for TechCrunch in November 2013, the two names were interchangeable: "neoreaction," he wrote, was "also called 'dark enlightenment.'" [cite:de1_finley_tc]

Who coined what

Two attributions circulate the wrong way round. A widely repeated line credits Yarvin with coining "the Dark Enlightenment." He did not; Land did, in 2012, as the serial itself shows. [cite:de1_land_gwern] The reverse error is just as common: commentary, including some published as recently as 2025, credits Land with "the Cathedral." That term is Yarvin's, and Land says so in plain words. After describing a ruling network of officials, journalists and academics, Land wrote: "Moldbug calls it the Cathedral." He also credits Yarvin with neocameralism, which he introduces as "an approach he calls 'neo-cameralism,'" and with "Universalism," Yarvin's name for progressive belief understood as a secular religion. [cite:de1_land_gwern] [cite:de2_land_ebook]

The division of labour matters for how the rest of this book reads both men. Land's serial is, for long stretches, a reading of Yarvin, with a great deal of quotation. It calls him the "supreme Sith Lord of the neoreactionaries," a joke borrowed from Star Wars that is also a statement of rank, and quotes him asking whether one can "imagine a 21st-century post-demotist society," one "that saw itself as recovering from democracy, much as Eastern Europe sees itself as recovering from Communism." [cite:de2_land_ebook] But Land also added things Yarvin had not written: a philosophical frame built on his own earlier work on technology and capital, a lineage running back through Hobbes and the libertarian economist Hans-Hermann Hoppe, and extended treatment of race that [scene:de4_the_hard_passages|Part Four] quotes and examines. Yarvin's vocabulary and Land's frame travel together under one name, but they are two authors' work, and the book keeps them apart.

A label chosen by its own authors is useful evidence in one direction only. It shows what Yarvin and Land called their work. It does not show who else holds the ideas, a question Part One answered on the record, and it does not make the label a membership card for anyone who later uses a word from the vocabulary. The next section turns from the names to the texts that carry them.

sections.h: The Core Texts, 2007–2014, and Their First Readers
sections.html:
Unqualified Reservations was not an ordinary blog. Its posts were essays, often thousands of words long, frequently published as numbered series over weeks, written in a dense, allusive and deliberately provocative style that mixed history, software metaphors and jokes. Yarvin posted regularly from 2007, largely stopped in 2013 when he turned to building his computer platform Urbit, and in April 2016 announced that the blog had "completed its mission." [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin] Out of hundreds of posts, a handful carry most of the ideas that later writers quote. This section reads four of them, then Land's serial of 2012, and then the first critics and journalists who read both. The hardest passages in these texts are quoted here briefly and in context; [scene:de6_the_hard_posts|Part Six] and [scene:de4_the_hard_passages|Part Four] treat them in full.

"A formalist manifesto" (23 April 2007)

The blog's opening essay set out a theory of peace. Its definition of the problem was legal rather than moral: "Violence, then, is anything that breaks the rule, or replaces it with a different rule." Conflict, on this account, comes from disputes over who owns what, including who holds political power, and the cure is to settle those disputes by recognising the present distribution exactly as it is. "Formalism says: let's figure out exactly who has what, now, and give them a little fancy certificate." [cite:de2_le] The argument's appeal and its difficulty are both visible here. It promises an end to struggle by ending argument about justice: whoever holds power now gets a deed to it. It does not ask how the present holders came by what they hold, or what happens to people who hold nothing. Princeton University Library keeps the essay as a 14-page booklet prepared with the author's permission. [cite:de2_princeton_fm]

"An Open Letter to Open-Minded Progressives" (from 17 April 2008)

The second core text was a serial in many chapters, addressed to the kind of reader its author expected to disagree with him. Its first chapter, "A Horizon Made of Canvas," opened with the question "Are you an open-minded progressive?" and the observation that the reader probably had friends who were. [cite:de2_upcarta] The form matters as much as the content: rather than preaching to readers who already agreed, the Open Letter addressed the ones most likely to object. It is also where Yarvin, as Part One showed, accepted "reactionary" as a fair description of himself, while preferring "restorationist." [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin]

"Patchwork" (from 13 November 2008)

In November 2008 Yarvin turned from diagnosis to design. The series called "Patchwork: A Positive Vision" proposed replacing large states with a patchwork of small ones, "each governed by its own joint-stock corporation without regard to the residents' opinions." Residents would have one remedy: "If residents don't like their government, they can and should move." [cite:de2_le] This is the exit-over-voice idea of Part One in its most concrete form, and it is the model Land later summarised as "No voice, free exit." [cite:de1_land_ebook]

The series also asked what a profit-seeking sovereign corporation should do with residents who cost more than they pay. In the first instalment, writing of a hypothetical company-run San Francisco and its surplus residents, Yarvin's answer began: "Sell their slums out from under them, obviously," and went on to demolition and "possibly a little aerial bombing." [cite:de2_le] [cite:de2_audit_patchwork1] In the second instalment, on 20 November 2008, he raised converting such people "into biodiesel, which can help power the Muni buses," said he was "just kidding," and then stated: "Our goal, in short, is a humane alternative to genocide." The alternative he went on to describe was permanent confinement connected to virtual reality. [cite:de2_tnr] Yarvin has described the biodiesel line as a joke, and the text itself says so; the passage that follows it, stating the goal, is not framed as a joke. These are his words, and they belong in any honest account of what Patchwork proposed. [scene:de6_the_hard_posts|Part Six] gives the surrounding text and his later explanations.

The 2012 talk and the end of the blog

In 2012 Yarvin carried the ideas from the page to a stage. At a technology conference called BIL he gave a talk proposing that a new American leader "Retire All Government Employees," abbreviated RAGE. [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin] The proposal marks a turn worth noting. Patchwork had imagined new small sovereigns that people could choose between; RAGE imagined taking over the existing American government and emptying it. [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six] reads the talk, and the question of how far later events resemble it, without being derived from it, runs through Book Three. In 2013 Yarvin largely stopped posting to concentrate on Urbit, and the blog fell quiet. [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin]

Land's serial (2 March–20 July 2012)

Land's "The Dark Enlightenment" was published in ten instalments over five months. Read as a whole, it does three things. It restates Yarvin's diagnosis and design, with long quotations, crediting him with the Cathedral, neocameralism and Universalism. It places them in a longer line of thought running "From Thomas Hobbes to Hans-Hermann Hoppe," and in the contemporary turn of some libertarians, Peter Thiel and the seasteading advocate Patri Friedman among those quoted, from voting toward exit. And from the fourth instalment onward it turns, at length, to race, which the serial treats under headings such as "A multi-part sub-digression into racial terror." [cite:de2_land_ebook] Those passages, including Land's rejection of the slide from white identity politics into antisemitism, which he calls a "trap," are examined in [scene:de4_the_hard_passages|Part Four]. The serial ends with speculation about human genetic self-engineering and the line "It's time to move on." [cite:de2_land_ebook]

The first readers

For six years these texts circulated mainly among blog readers. One of the first accounts written for a broad technology audience was Klint Finley's "Geeks for Monarchy: The Rise of the Neoreactionaries," published by TechCrunch on 22 November 2013. Finley described the writers' preference for monarchy and hierarchy, defined the Cathedral, quoted Yarvin's "all 'exit,' no 'voice,'" and quoted the investor Balaji Srinivasan saying that a much-discussed speech of his was "more about emigration and exit." [cite:de1_finley_tc] A month earlier the blogger Scott Alexander, writing on Slate Star Codex, had published "The Anti-Reactionary FAQ" on 20 October 2013, a long point-by-point rebuttal that defined neoreaction as "a political ideology supporting a return to traditional ideas of government and society." [cite:de2_ssc_faq] That rebuttal came from inside the online rationalist community where many of Yarvin's early readers were found, which is one reason the two are often confused and one reason they should not be.

The critical reception hardened over the following years. The journalist Corey Pein wrote about the current for The Baffler on 19 May 2014 under the title "Mouthbreathing Machiavellis Dream of a Silicon Reich," and returned to it on 9 October 2017, writing that Yarvin's "Dark Enlightenment dogma is steeped in pseudoscientific racism" and calling neoreaction "a subset of what is now euphemistically termed the alt-right." [cite:de2_pein2017] His 2018 book, Live Work Work Work Die, is a frequently cited source for Yarvin's 2012 talk. [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin] The writer Elizabeth Sandifer crowdfunded a book-length essay, Neoreaction a Basilisk, first published on 24 June 2016, which read Yarvin and Land alongside the rationalist writer Eliezer Yudkowsky. [cite:de2_sandifer_gr] [cite:de2_sandifer_ep] Each of these readers is a named critic with a stated view, and each is quoted as such; their characterisations are theirs, set beside the texts they describe.

The worst-case reading, tested

The texts in this part bear on the hypothesis in two ways. The destination is documented in them: Patchwork's sovereign corporations govern "without regard to the residents' opinions," and Land's summary of the model is "No voice, free exit." [cite:de2_le] [cite:de1_land_ebook] So is a harsh answer to the question of people a profit-run sovereign does not want, stated in Yarvin's own words in November 2008, with one line marked as a joke and the stated goal not. [cite:de2_tnr] The shift from exit to takeover is also documented, in the move from Patchwork's new small states in 2008 to RAGE's emptying of the existing American government in 2012. [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin] That shift matters for the hypothesis, because a programme of leaving existing states poses little danger to them, while a programme of capturing one does.

What the texts of 2007–2014 do not show is any connection to the occasions the hypothesis names. They contain no plan for immigration enforcement and no link to any later government; the readers who first wrote about them, from Finley to Sandifer, described a small online body of writing, not an operation. That a later policy resembles RAGE is, on this part's material, not supported as provenance: rhyme is not descent, and the test of whether anything passed from these texts into office begins in [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|Part Twelve] and [scene:de17_money_to_office|Part Seventeen]. Part Three goes back further, to the older writers these texts drew on.

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: The Inheritance
chapters.intro: Part Three asks where the Dark Enlightenment's ideas came from. It begins with the ancestors the texts name for themselves, in Moldbug's and Land's own words: Hobbes, the Austrian economists Yarvin later renounced, Hans-Hermann Hoppe's case for monarchy over democracy, Thomas Carlyle, James Burnham and Frederick the Great. It then takes a lineage the texts never name but which is often drawn for them, from the 1930s Technocracy movement through Elon Musk's grandfather, Joshua N. Haldeman, and separates what is documented from what is only inferred. It ends with the libertarian idea of exit, the Austrian institutions, the cybernetic strand that Nick Land brought with him, and the places where scholars and the ancestors themselves dispute the family tree.
chapters.outro: Part Three found that the Dark Enlightenment texts document their own descent: from Hobbes's undivided sovereign, through an Austrian libertarianism that Yarvin himself declared abandoned in "From Mises to Carlyle," to Hoppe's argument that an owner preserves what a democratic caretaker consumes, and on to Carlyle's defence of hierarchy. [cite:de3_land_de] [cite:de3_princeton_carlyle] [cite:de3_wiki_dtgtf] Hoppe accepts that he was cited and rejects the corporate state built on the citation. [cite:de3_hoppe_reply] The Technocracy lineage rests on a family tie: Joshua N. Haldeman's record, including his defence of the Protocols and his praise of apartheid, is his own, and Musk's documented words about his grandfather concern adventure, not politics. [cite:de3_cbc_leo] [cite:de3_dcpd_musk] The strongest inherited idea is exit, which Thiel's 2009 essay framed as an escape from politics and backed with money for seasteading, and which points away from capturing a state rather than toward it. [cite:de3_cato_thiel] [cite:de3_wiki_tsi] Part Four turns to the writer who named the whole current, Nick Land, and to the engine of acceleration he built before he ever read Moldbug.

sections.h: The Ancestors the Texts Name
sections.html:
Every body of political writing tells a story about where it came from, and the story is itself an argument. A writer who says he descends from Thomas Hobbes is claiming the authority of the founder of modern political science; a writer who says he descends from a slaveholding Victorian sage is making a different claim, and a more dangerous one. This section takes the ancestors the Dark Enlightenment texts name for themselves, in their own words, and sets them beside what those ancestors actually wrote and what scholars of the texts have found. It keeps two questions apart throughout. The first is who Curtis Yarvin, writing as Mencius Moldbug, and Nick Land say they inherited from. The second is who other people say they inherited from. Only the first is evidence of what the authors were reading; the second is interpretation, sometimes good and sometimes careless, and it is treated in the last section of this part.

The body of texts is small and its authorship is clear. Yarvin wrote the blog Unqualified Reservations under the Moldbug pen name from 2007, largely stopping in 2013, and Land wrote a ten-part web serial titled "The Dark Enlightenment" between 2 March and 20 July 2012, which was gathered into an e-book in 2014. [cite:de3_wiki_yarvin] [cite:de3_land_de] Both are described in [scene:de2_core_texts|Part Two]. Land's serial is useful here for a particular reason: it is a reader's guide to Moldbug, written by an admirer who quotes him at length and says plainly which ideas are Moldbug's and which ancestors Moldbug claimed. Where Land's account of Moldbug can be set beside Yarvin's own catalogued writing, the two agree.

Hobbes and the problem of the sovereign

The first ancestor Land names is Hobbes. In the opening instalment he calls the current he is describing "recognizably Hobbesian, a coherent dark enlightenment," and sets out its question in a single line: "From Thomas Hobbes to Hans-Hermann Hoppe and beyond, it asks: How can the sovereign power be prevented – or at least dissuaded — from devouring society?" [cite:de3_land_de] The Hobbesian inheritance, as Land states it, is the belief that sovereignty cannot be abolished or divided, only located. He credits Moldbug with the same starting point: Moldbug's turn to reaction, he writes, came with "the (Hobbesian) recognition that sovereignty cannot be eliminated, caged, or controlled," so that constitutions "have exactly as much real authority as a sovereign interpretative power allows them to have." [cite:de3_land_de]

This is a genuine borrowing and an honest one. Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) argued that people escape a war of all against all by handing an undivided power to a sovereign, and the Dark Enlightenment texts share his low opinion of human appetites. They part from him in one respect that matters for the rest of this book. Hobbes grounded the sovereign's authority in the consent of those who authorise it; Land's version keeps the undivided sovereign and drops the consent, treating the democratic masses as "a howling irrational mob." [cite:de3_land_de]

The Austrian school, and the journey away from it

The second inheritance is libertarian economics of the Austrian school, the tradition of Ludwig von Mises and his American student Murray Rothbard, which holds that markets coordinate knowledge better than planners and that the state is at best a necessary evil. Here the texts are unusually frank, because the inheritance is described as something abandoned. Land writes that "Moldbug's formative influences are Austro-libertarian, but that's all over," and quotes Moldbug's reason: libertarians "cannot present a realistic picture of a world in which their battle gets won and stays won." [cite:de3_land_de]

Yarvin's own titles say the same. Princeton University Library holds an 82-page compilation, "Moldbug on Carlyle" (2010), which gathers three of his blog essays; the one he placed first, as the introduction, was published in February 2010 under the title "From Mises to Carlyle: My Sick Journey to the Dark Side of the Force." [cite:de3_princeton_carlyle] The historian Joshua Tait, who wrote the chapter on Moldbug in Oxford University Press's Key Thinkers of the Radical Right (2019), reports that the law professor and blogger Glenn Reynolds introduced Yarvin to Mises and Rothbard, and that the Austrian school's preference for deduction from first principles over empirical testing shaped his habits of argument. [cite:de3_tait] [cite:de3_wiki_yarvin]

Hans-Hermann Hoppe: the bridge

The figure who connects the two inheritances is Hans-Hermann Hoppe, a German-born economist who taught at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas from 1986 to 2008 and called Rothbard his "principal teacher." [cite:de3_wiki_hoppe] His collection Democracy: The God That Failed (2001) argued that monarchy, which he called "privately-owned government," is preferable to democracy, "publicly-owned government," while holding that both are worse than a stateless "natural order" or private law society. [cite:de3_wiki_dtgtf] Land quotes Hoppe's central passage at length: a hereditary king treats the country as his property and so has reason to preserve its value, while a democratic politician is a "temporary and interchangeable caretaker" who owns only its current use, "usufruct," and so consumes its capital. [cite:de3_land_de]

This argument is the hinge of the whole body of texts, because it turns a libertarian case against the state into a case for a particular kind of ruler. Moldbug's answer to Hoppe's problem was to make the owner a corporation rather than a family. The journalist Ava Kofman, writing in The New Yorker in 2025, credited Hoppe's book with pushing Yarvin from libertarianism toward monarchism, and quoted the scholar of authoritarianism Julian Waller calling it "such a direct influence that it's kind of obscene." [cite:de3_wiki_dtgtf] Hoppe's own response to that attribution, which complicates it, is examined in the third section of this part.

Thomas Carlyle

The most consequential ancestor Yarvin claimed is the Scottish writer Thomas Carlyle (1795–1881), who held that history is made by great men, that societies need strong rulers rather than parliaments, and who defended slavery in the West Indies. Yarvin did not cite him in passing. He devoted three essays to him: "Why Carlyle Matters" and "Carlyle in the 20th Century: Fascism and Socialism," posted in consecutive weeks in July 2009, and the February 2010 introduction already quoted, compiled together as Moldbug on Carlyle. [cite:de3_princeton_carlyle] Tait names Carlyle, with James Burnham and Hoppe, as the writers whose arguments that democracy had failed prompted Yarvin's endorsement of authoritarian rule. [cite:de3_tait] [cite:de3_wiki_yarvin]

The Carlyle essays also contain one of the hardest passages in Yarvin's writing. A 2009 post, quoted by Media Matters in 2021, said that "the innate character and intelligence of some is more suited to mastery than slavery. For others, it is more suited to slavery," and that the pattern was "most parsimoniously explained by genetic differences." [cite:de3_mm] [cite:de3_audit_mm] The line is in Yarvin's own voice. The paragraph that precedes it in the original post is not quoted in the reports that carry the line, and the passage is examined, with that limit stated, in [scene:de6_the_hard_posts|Part Six]. A widely repeated line attributing to him the words "some races are better suited for slavery than others" is a paraphrase circulated as a quotation; it is not his wording.

James Burnham and Frederick the Great

Two further names come from the texts' account of how power really works. James Burnham, an American former Trotskyist, argued in The Managerial Revolution (1941) that a class of managers, neither capitalists nor workers, was becoming the new ruling class, and followed it with The Machiavellians (1943) on how organised elites govern behind democratic forms. [cite:de3_wiki_burnham] Tait lists Burnham among Yarvin's sources. [cite:de3_tait] The debt shows in the idea that the official map of power diverges from the real one, which Moldbug called formalism: the proposal to make the real distribution of power official, so that whoever actually rules owns the rule openly. Land summarises the step: "Unless ownership of the state is formally transferred into the hands of its actual rulers, the neo-cameral transition will simply not take place." [cite:de3_land_de]

The last named ancestor is a ruler rather than a writer. Neocameralism, Moldbug's word for his proposed state, takes its name from cameralism, the administrative science of eighteenth-century German states, and his model monarch was Frederick the Great of Prussia (reigned 1740–1786). [cite:de3_wiki_yarvin] A passage Land reproduces, without naming its source, as a summary of the neocameralist position says the "full neocameralist approach has never been tried," but its closest equivalents are "enlightened absolutism as represented by Frederick the Great," and Hong Kong, Singapore and Dubai, states "weak only in political freedom." [cite:de3_land_de] That claim is a testable one, and [scene:de8_tests_it_fails|Part Eight] tests it.

What the lineage claims, against what the ancestors held

A claimed ancestry is not the same as a faithful one, and three of these borrowings change the ancestor in transit. Hoppe's preference for monarchy was a preference for the lesser of two evils; his stated ideal remained a world without a coercive state. [cite:de3_wiki_dtgtf] The texts' own admission that neocameralism "has never been tried" means the Frederick and Singapore comparisons are analogies, not precedents. [cite:de3_land_de] And Hobbes's sovereign rested on the consent of those who created it, the very thing the later texts discard. The comparison below sets each claim beside the record.

What this lineage establishes is a reading list and a direction of travel: from free-market libertarianism, through Hoppe's argument for ownership over stewardship, to an open defence of hierarchy and concentrated rule. Each step is documented in the authors' own titles and quotations. [cite:de3_princeton_carlyle] [cite:de3_land_de] The next section turns to a lineage the texts never name at all, but which is often drawn for them.

sections.h: Technocracy Inc. and the Grandfather
sections.html:
One inheritance is regularly drawn for the Dark Enlightenment that its own texts never mention. It runs from a Depression-era American movement called Technocracy, through a Canadian chiropractor who led it in his province, to that man's grandson, Elon Musk, and from Musk to the government cuts of 2025. The line has the appeal of a family saga and a real documentary core. This section separates the core from the saga. It sets out what Technocracy was, what is documented about Joshua N. Haldeman, what Musk himself has said, and where the line from the 1930s to 2025 is documented and where it is only drawn.

A rule governs the whole section. A grandfather's views are not his grandson's. Haldeman died in 1974, when Musk was two years old. [cite:de3_cbc_leo] What Haldeman wrote and did is his record; what Musk has said and done is Musk's. The two meet in this book only where Musk's own words make the connection.

What Technocracy was

Technocracy grew out of the work of Howard Scott, an engineer who, with the geologist M. King Hubbert, founded Technocracy Incorporated in 1933 after an earlier collaboration with Columbia University collapsed. [cite:de3_wiki_scott] Its central proposal was to abolish the "price system." Money, wages and markets would be replaced by energy accounting, and engineers and scientists would manage production and distribution. [cite:de3_wiki_scott] The historian Kevin Baker, writing in American Heritage, described the plan's currency: certificates equal to the energy the country used in a year, issued equally to every citizen, which had to be spent within the year or became worthless, so that no one could accumulate capital. [cite:de3_ah_baker]

The territory to be run this way was continental. Technocracy proposed merging Canada, Greenland, Mexico, the United States and parts of Central America into a single unit governed by technical principles, which it called the Technate. [cite:de3_townley] The movement's moment was brief. Baker reports that membership may have reached a quarter of a million Americans in early 1933, and that within days of a disastrous speech by Scott at New York's Hotel Pierre on 13 January 1933 Columbia distanced itself and Congress was mocking the movement; it survived into the Second World War but never regained momentum. [cite:de3_ah_baker] Scott himself, it emerged, had overstated his credentials. [cite:de3_wiki_scott]

Two features matter for comparison with the texts in this book. Technocracy was hostile to markets and private capital; it wanted to abolish money. And by Scott's own account, as the historian Jill Lepore quoted him in 2025, the movement "has no theory for the assumption of power." [cite:de3_lepore]

Joshua N. Haldeman

Haldeman was born in 1902 in Minnesota and raised in Saskatchewan, trained as a chiropractor, and lost his farm in the Depression. [cite:de3_cbc_leo] [cite:de3_audit_cbc] He was active in Technocracy Inc. from 1936 to 1941; Lepore describes him as its leader in Canada, technocrat No. 10450-1. [cite:de3_wiki_haldeman] [cite:de3_lepore] After Canada banned the organisation under its wartime regulations in 1940, he was arrested on 8 October 1940 and charged with membership in an illegal organisation; a Regina court fined him $200 later that month over a document titled "Statement of Patriotism by Those Who Were Technocrats." [cite:de3_wiki_haldeman] He left the movement in 1941, citing what he saw as its turn toward collaboration with the Soviet Union. [cite:de3_cbc_leo]

His later politics are documented in detail by CBC News, which reported in March 2025 from newspapers and his own pamphlets. He led the Social Credit party in Saskatchewan from 1945 and chaired its national council from 1946. When the party's Quebec wing published the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a forged text purporting to reveal a Jewish plot to rule the world, Haldeman defended the publication; whether the document was fraudulent, he said, "is not the point." [cite:de3_cbc_leo] In 1950 he moved his family to Pretoria. In 1951 he wrote in the Regina Leader-Post that South Africa's government "knows how to handle the native question," and later pamphlets described an "Invisible Government" serving an international conspiracy. [cite:de3_cbc_leo] He died in a plane crash on 13 January 1974. [cite:de3_cbc_leo] These are the documented views of Haldeman: support for apartheid, and the defence of an antisemitic forgery. His life is told more fully in [scene:de11_pretoria_and_haldeman|Part Eleven].

What Musk has said

Musk's documented references to his grandfather, as collected by CBC, concern adventure rather than politics: "My grandfather had this desire for adventure, exploration — doing crazy things," he told his biographer Ashlee Vance. [cite:de3_cbc_leo] His one documented use of the movement's name came in a post in June 2019: "Accelerating Starship development to build the Martian Technocracy." He gave no explanation of what he meant. [cite:de3_phys_tweet]

His own stated views on government point in more than one direction. Asked at the Code Conference on 2 June 2016 how Mars would be governed, he said it would "most likely" be "a direct democracy, not representative," with people "voting directly on issues." [cite:de3_inc_code] In the Oval Office on 11 February 2025, defending the cuts led by the Department of Government Efficiency, he framed his project as a defence of elected government against officials: "We don't live in a democracy. We live in a bureaucracy," and if the bureaucracy is in charge, "what meaning does democracy actually have?" [cite:de3_dcpd_musk] That is close to the opposite of Technocracy's programme, which wanted elected politicians replaced by unelected experts. Whether the stated reason is the true one is a separate question; the stated reason is documented, and it is not the technocrats' reason.

The line that is drawn, and the line that is documented

The case for a living inheritance has been made most forcefully by Lepore, in a New York Times guest essay of 4 April 2025. Her judgement, offered as opinion, was that "little of what Mr. Musk proposes is new" and that many of his ideas "resemble those championed by" his grandfather.
