[cite:de3_lepore] Dafydd Townley of the University of Portsmouth, writing in The Conversation in March 2025, found resonances, in the distrust of elected politicians and the drive for efficiency, and also differences: Musk's commerce is rooted in market competition, and the administration he served does not seek to abolish money or wages. [cite:de3_townley] Neither writer claims a document showing transmission of a political programme from grandfather to grandson.

A stronger version circulates widely online: that a continuous plan runs from the 1930s technocrats through later elite bodies to the present administration, and that the 2025 interest in Greenland, which the Technate map included, is that plan being executed. No document supports the claim. The individual facts in it are real; the continuity and the intention are supplied by the teller. A resemblance between a 1930s map and a 2025 policy is rhyme, not provenance.

The comparison with the Dark Enlightenment texts sharpens the point. Land's serial never mentions Technocracy, and the economic wish-list it offers, framed as "strictly hypothetical", runs the other way: hard money, "abolition of central banking," and the dismantling of "state monetary and fiscal discretion" so that the market can run without managers. [cite:de3_land_de] Technocracy wanted to abolish markets and money and put engineers in charge; Moldbug wanted a state owned by shareholders and run by a chief executive for profit. [cite:de3_land_de] [cite:de3_wiki_scott] They share a contempt for elected politicians and a faith in competence. They do not share a theory of property, of money, or of who should rule.

The documented line, then, is short. A man who led a technocratic movement in Canada and later defended an antisemitic forgery and apartheid was Elon Musk's maternal grandfather; Musk once used the word "Technocracy" in a single, unexplained post about Mars; and serious writers have argued that the family resemblance runs deeper. [cite:de3_cbc_leo] [cite:de3_phys_tweet] [cite:de3_lepore] What is not documented is any statement by Musk taking up his grandfather's programme, or any path by which Technocracy entered the Dark Enlightenment texts, which neither cite nor resemble it in their economics. [cite:de3_land_de] The family tie belongs in Musk's biography; it does not belong in his ideology unless he puts it there.

sections.h: Exit, the Austrians, the Machine, and the Disputes
sections.html:
Three other currents run into the Dark Enlightenment texts, and each is claimed by the texts in their own words. The first is the libertarian idea of exit: that freedom is secured less by voting than by the ability to leave. The second is the Austrian school's long quarrel with democracy, carried by Hans-Hermann Hoppe and the institutions around him. The third, quite different in temper, is the cybernetic and accelerationist strand that Nick Land brought with him from 1990s academic philosophy. This section takes each in turn, then sets out where scholars and the ancestors themselves dispute the lineage, and closes by testing the book's worst-case reading against what this part has found.

Exit: from an economist's vocabulary to a political programme

The words "exit" and "voice" come from the economist Albert Hirschman's 1970 book Exit, Voice, and Loyalty, which described the two ways people respond to a failing organisation: they complain, or they leave. The critic Shuja Haider observed that Land read Peter Thiel's call to escape politics through exactly these terms. [cite:de3_haider] In Land's 2012 serial, "Voice-vs-Exit" becomes the defining choice of the age, and libertarians "are opting for voiceless flight." [cite:de3_land_de] His summary of Moldbug's ideal state is three words: "No voice, free exit." [cite:de3_land_de]

The documented source of the exit current is a 2009 essay by Thiel. On 13 April 2009, in the online forum Cato Unbound, he wrote: "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible." [cite:de3_cato_thiel] He linked the decline of what he called capitalist democracy to the growth of welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the vote to women in 1920, and proposed three escape routes from politics: cyberspace, outer space and the ocean, where he backed the building of floating communities called seasteads; the libertarian's task, he wrote, was an "escape from politics in all its forms." [cite:de3_cato_thiel] On 1 May 2009 he posted a follow-up, "Your Suffrage Isn't in Danger. Your Other Rights Are," writing that "Voting is not under siege in America, but many other rights are." [cite:de3_cato_thiel] Land opened his 2012 serial with the 2009 discussion and Thiel's sentence; that quotation is the only appearance Thiel makes in the text. [cite:de3_land_de] Thiel's own later thinking is treated in [scene:de10_girard_and_the_katechon|Part Ten].

The seasteads had an institution behind them. The Seasteading Institute was founded on 15 April 2008 by the software engineer Wayne Gramlich and Patri Friedman, and Thiel gave $500,000 in seed money, as Wired reported on 18 May 2008. [cite:de3_wiki_tsi] Friedman supplied the line Land quotes as the creed of the current: "we think that free exit is so important that we've called it the only Universal Human Right." [cite:de3_land_de] Two figures circulate for Thiel's total giving. A 2011 report gave $1.25 million, with the institute insisting that its most generous funder "doesn't dictate" its plans; Business Insider in 2018 gave $1.7 million, reported that Thiel had left the board in 2011, and quoted him calling seasteads "not quite feasible." [cite:de3_yahoo_tsi] [cite:de3_bi_tsi] The two totals come from different dates and neither is itemised in a public filing. The institute's most concrete step, a memorandum signed with a French Polynesian minister on 13 January 2017, was declared by that government to have lapsed at the end of 2017. [cite:de3_wiki_tsi]

The Austrian institutions and the "odd marriage"

The Austrian current reached the texts through people and institutions as well as books. Hoppe was a fellow of the Mises Institute, founded in 1982 by Lew Rockwell, Burton Blumert and Rothbard, and in 2006 he founded the Property and Freedom Society, which holds annual conferences in Bodrum, Turkey. [cite:de3_wiki_hoppe] His book contains a passage that has followed him since, on how a libertarian covenant community should treat its opponents: "There can be no tolerance toward democrats and communists in a libertarian social order," continuing that they must be physically separated and expelled. [cite:de3_wiki_hoppe] That is an explicit call to exclude political opponents from a community, in the author's own words.

Land devoted a whole instalment of his serial, "Odd Marriages" (15 June 2012), to the alliance between this libertarian current and the nostalgic politics of the American South. He listed his evidence as "semi-random stripped-down data-points": the Mises Institute's founding in Auburn, Alabama; Ron Paul newsletters of the 1980s containing remarks "of a decidedly Derbyshirean hue", after the columnist John Derbyshire, whose 2012 race column is discussed in Part Four; Rothbard's writing in defence of "HBD", short for human biodiversity, a label for hereditarian claims about racial difference; and the libertarian Tom Palmer's charge that Rockwell and Hoppe had "Opened the Gates of Hell" to racists and cranks. [cite:de3_land_de] Land did not condemn the marriage. He concluded that "liberty has no future in the Anglophone world outside the prospect of secession." [cite:de3_land_de] The race material in that instalment is examined in [scene:de4_the_hard_passages|Part Four].

The cybernetic strand

The third current has nothing to do with Austrian economics. Land arrived at the Dark Enlightenment from continental philosophy, cybernetics and cyberpunk fiction, by way of a research group at the University of Warwick in the 1990s, and from a theory of capitalism as a self-accelerating machine that escapes human control. [cite:de3_haider] That strand, accelerationism, and its split into left and right versions are the subject of [scene:de4_ccru_acceleration|the next part]. It matters here for one reason: it means the Dark Enlightenment has two parents who do not agree. Moldbug's line runs from libertarianism to monarchy and asks who should own the state. Land's runs from a philosophy of runaway technological change, and in his serial treats Moldbug's corporate state as one vehicle among several for escaping democracy. [cite:de3_land_de]

Where the lineage is disputed

The most direct dispute comes from the most important ancestor. Asked in 2025 by Ava Kofman of The New Yorker about the claim that his book had midwifed Yarvin's politics, Hoppe replied: "I do not follow Yarvin's writings closely – too much rambling for my taste." [cite:de3_hoppe_reply] He said he had met Yarvin once, at a gathering to which Thiel had invited him, and that Yarvin had cited him on his blog. He set out his own ideal as "thousands upon thousands of Liechtensteins," small territories under a monarch or "member of the natural elite" from which subunits may secede, and he separated it from what he called the "Silicon valley crowd" model of running government like a business, arguing that states are founded on violence and should be dismantled rather than made efficient. [cite:de3_hoppe_reply] Kofman's sources called the influence direct and heavy; Hoppe accepts that he was cited and rejects the programme built on the citation. [cite:de3_wiki_dtgtf] [cite:de3_hoppe_reply] Both can be true: a book can open a door without approving of the house built beyond it.

The libertarian inheritance is disputed from the other side too. Moldbug himself declared it over, and Land's own case that libertarianism and the Confederate-nostalgic right had married was offered as a provocation that libertarian critics such as Palmer had already denounced. [cite:de3_land_de] The accelerationist inheritance is contested by its own founders, as the next part shows: Land's former colleague Ray Brassier said Land had gone from "Politics is dead" to "completely old-fashioned, standard reactionary stuff." [cite:de4_wiki_land] And the claim of a Technocracy lineage, set out in the previous section, rests on a family tie and a resemblance, not on any text. [cite:de3_cbc_leo]

The worst-case reading, tested

The book's working hypothesis, stated in the preface as the Sophia platform's and never as a finding, is that immigration enforcement and government cuts serve as the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. This part asked whether the inheritance of the texts supports it.

Documented: the texts descend, by their own account, from writers who preferred concentrated, owned rule to democratic rule, and Moldbug's line travelled openly from libertarianism to monarchy. [cite:de3_princeton_carlyle] [cite:de3_land_de] Documented too is a sharper strand of exclusion in the ancestry: Hoppe's "no tolerance" passage and Carlyle's defence of hierarchy, which Yarvin extended to a line on slavery in his own voice. [cite:de3_wiki_hoppe] [cite:de3_mm] Documented, finally, is Thiel's 2009 statement that freedom and democracy are incompatible, and his money behind the seasteading project. [cite:de3_cato_thiel] [cite:de3_wiki_tsi]

Probable: that the Hoppe-to-Moldbug step supplied the ownership argument on which the later case for a chief-executive state rests; Yarvin's own titles and Land's quotations make this the best reading, though Hoppe disowns the result. [cite:de3_hoppe_reply]

Not supported: that any of these lineages carries a plan for the American executive of 2025. The dominant inherited idea in this part is exit, which points away from capturing a national state, toward leaving it; Thiel's 2009 programme was an "escape from politics," and Hoppe's ideal is a scatter of small principalities from which subunits may secede. [cite:de3_cato_thiel] [cite:de3_hoppe_reply] The Technocracy line, often drawn to Musk and from Musk to the cuts of 2025, is a family tie and a resemblance; Musk's own stated case in February 2025 was for elected control over officials, and no document connects Technocracy to the Dark Enlightenment texts. [cite:de3_dcpd_musk] [cite:de3_land_de] On this part's material the record runs against the destination half of the hypothesis: the ancestors were mostly trying to get out of the state, not to seize it. Whether later readers turned an exit doctrine into a capture doctrine is a question for the parts on the men and the machinery, graded in [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|the final scorecard].

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: Nick Land: the Engine
chapters.intro: Part Four is about Nick Land, the English philosopher who coined the phrase "the Dark Enlightenment" in 2012. It follows him from the University of Warwick and the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit of the 1990s, through the idea of accelerationism and its split into left and right versions, to Shanghai, where he has lived and written since the 2000s. It then summarises his ten-part serial instalment by instalment, separating what he credits to Moldbug from what he added, and ends with the serial's hardest passages, on race and heredity, quoted exactly and in context, together with his 2014 "Hyper-Racism" post and the critics who answered him.
chapters.outro: Part Four found Nick Land to be a philosopher of runaway technological change who left Warwick in 1998, became the best-known theorist of a right-wing accelerationism that left accelerationists contested from 2013, and wrote "The Dark Enlightenment" from Shanghai between March and July 2012. [cite:de4_wiki_land] [cite:de4_accel_manifesto] [cite:de4_land_de] The serial credits the Cathedral and neocameralism to Moldbug, quotes Thiel once, prescribes exit, secession, hard money and an end to central banking, and expects nothing short of cataclysm to bring them about. [cite:de4_land_de] Its race passages make hereditarian claims in Land's own voice while rejecting white nationalism, the turn to antisemitism and Nazism as politics; in his examples, exit becomes sorting, from white flight to secession to genetic "speciation," and in a separate 2014 post to space colonisation as a "genetic filter." [cite:de4_land_de] [cite:de4_haider] Nothing in the text plans the capture of an American state. Part Five turns to the man whose program Land borrowed: Curtis Yarvin, from his childhood to the founding of Unqualified Reservations.

sections.h: Warwick, the CCRU and the Idea of Acceleration
sections.html:
Nick Land is the writer who gave the Dark Enlightenment its name, and he arrived at it from a direction no one would predict from the name alone. He was not a libertarian economist or a blogger in Silicon Valley. He was an English academic philosopher who spent the 1990s at the University of Warwick writing about Kant, Nietzsche and the French philosopher Georges Bataille, and who built, with a circle of students, a body of experimental writing about technology, capital and the future that still has admirers on the far left. This section follows that path: the Warwick years, the research group known as the CCRU, the idea that came to be called accelerationism, the split of that idea into left and right versions, and Land's move to Shanghai, where he has written ever since.

Warwick and the CCRU

Land, born in 1962, took his doctorate at the University of Essex and taught philosophy at Warwick from 1987 until he resigned in 1998. [cite:de4_wiki_land] The journalist Park MacDougald, writing in 2015, described his reputation there for unorthodox teaching and odd personal habits, and the mythology that gathered around him; the critic Mark Fisher later wrote that "Land was our Nietzsche." [cite:de4_awl] [cite:de4_wiki_land]

The Cybernetic Culture Research Unit, the CCRU, was founded at Warwick in 1995 by the cultural theorist Sadie Plant; after she resigned in 1997, Land took it over. [cite:de4_haider] It was less a department than a collective of graduate students and fellow travellers who mixed philosophy, cybernetics, cyberpunk fiction and the dance music of the period into what they called "theory-fiction." Robin Mackay, one of Land's students, recalled him living in his office and rarely sleeping. Land later claimed to be inhabited by named "entities" and, looking back on that writing, told Mackay, "I don't even remember writing half of those things." [cite:de4_haider] The group continued to meet under Land after he left Warwick, and dissolved in the early 2000s. [cite:de4_wiki_land] [cite:de4_wiki_accel] Its texts were later collected as CCRU Writings 1997–2003 (2015), and the small press Urbanomic published Land's collected essays, Fanged Noumena, in 2011; in 2014 Mackay and Armen Avanessian placed Land in the "Cyberculture" section of their anthology #Accelerate, beside Plant and Iain Hamilton Grant. [cite:de4_wiki_land] [cite:de4_frieze]

What accelerationism meant

Accelerationism, in its original philosophical sense, is the idea that the way beyond capitalism runs through it, by speeding up the processes it sets loose rather than resisting them. Its usual starting point is a passage in Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari's Anti-Oedipus (1972) calling, after Nietzsche, to "accelerate the process." [cite:de4_wiki_accel] The word itself came later. The British philosopher Benjamin Noys named the tendency in his 2010 book The Persistence of the Negative, as a description of a line of thinkers he criticised. [cite:de4_haider] [cite:de4_wiki_accel]

Land's version was the most radical. In his writing of the 1990s, capital and technology form a loop that feeds itself, gathering speed until it no longer needs, or tolerates, human direction; he wrote of "an invasion from the future by an artificial intelligent space." [cite:de4_haider] The reader of this book should hold on to one feature of that vision, because it separates Land from Yarvin. Land's engine does not want a king. It wants a process that escapes control, and the human institutions that try to steer it, democratic or otherwise, appear as brakes.

Left and right: the 2013 split

In May 2013 two young British theorists, Alex Williams and Nick Srnicek, published "#Accelerate: Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics" on the website Critical Legal Thinking. [cite:de4_clt_date] It claimed the idea for the left. The manifesto credited Land with capturing the dynamic "most acutely," with "a myopic yet hypnotising belief" that "capitalist speed alone could generate a global transition towards unparalleled technological singularity." [cite:de4_accel_manifesto] Their own programme was the reverse of Land's: "the material platform of neoliberalism does not need to be destroyed. It needs to be repurposed towards common ends." [cite:de4_accel_manifesto] Where Land saw a machine that would carry humanity past politics, they saw machinery that a democratic left could seize and steer.

Land rejected the left version. Haider records his verdict, "Neoreaction is Accelerationism with a flat tire," and his casting of the left as a "decelerator." [cite:de4_haider] Williams, for his part, described Land's late work as a "sick perversity." [cite:de4_haider] The philosopher Ray Brassier, whose own work draws on Land's, said in 2017 that Land had gone from arguing "Politics is dead" twenty years earlier to "completely old-fashioned, standard reactionary stuff." [cite:de4_wiki_land] From 2013, then, there were two accelerationisms, each claiming the same ancestry and each treating the other as a betrayal of it.

Three things that share the name and are not the same

Two later uses of the word must be kept apart from Land's. The first is "effective accelerationism," or e/acc, a slogan that spread among technology investors in the 2020s for pursuing artificial intelligence and other technologies with as few restraints as possible. [cite:de4_wiki_accel] It borrows the word and some of the mood. It is a distinct current, and this book treats it in [scene:de16_neighbours_not_the_same|Part Sixteen].

The second is a terror usage. Neo-fascist and white-supremacist networks use "accelerationism" to mean hastening racial conflict and social collapse through violence, assassination and sabotage, in the hope of building a white ethnostate on the ruins. [cite:de4_wiki_accel] The writer Zack Beauchamp has suggested that the label reached those networks through the overlap between Land's later politics and the online far right, while noting that Land's technocapitalist ideas are otherwise unrelated to that programme. [cite:de4_wiki_accel] No text by Land discussed in this book calls for violence of that kind, and the terror usage is never meant in this book when the word appears without qualification.

Shanghai

After leaving Warwick, Land dropped from view. He resurfaced in the 2000s as a journalist in Shanghai, writing opinion pieces and travel guides, and has lived there since. [cite:de4_haider] [cite:de4_spectator] From Shanghai he wrote his best-known political text, the serial "The Dark Enlightenment," published in ten instalments between 2 March and 20 July 2012 and gathered on its own website. [cite:de4_land_de] [cite:de4_awl] Its argument is summarised in the next section.

His writing from 2013 to 2017 was later collected as Xenosystems and published by Passage Press. [cite:de4_spectator] In October 2025 The Spectator described him as in his sixties, still in Shanghai, and noted that the investor Marc Andreessen lists him as a "patron saint" of his thinking. [cite:de4_spectator] In that interview Land called China's combination of communism and capitalism "the greatest political engine of social and economic development the world has ever known." [cite:de4_spectator] The citation by Andreessen is a documented tie of reading, not of policy; it shows that an investor counts Land among his influences, which is Andreessen's own statement, and it shows nothing about what Land has done, which on the record is to write.

The path matters for what follows. Land came to the Dark Enlightenment as a philosopher of runaway change who had already broken with the academic left, and he adopted Yarvin's corporate state as a political form for an engine he had been describing for twenty years. [cite:de4_awl] [cite:de4_land_de] His version of the ideas is darker in its metaphysics and harder in its writing about race than the program he borrowed, and it is less interested in who sits at the top.

sections.h: The Dark Enlightenment, Part by Part
sections.html:
"The Dark Enlightenment" is a serial of ten instalments, about 27,000 words, that Nick Land published between 2 March and 20 July 2012. [cite:de4_land_de] [cite:de4_awl] It was gathered into an e-book in 2014 with its text unchanged, and page numbers below refer to that compilation. It is the most widely read statement of the ideas this book maps, and it is often described rather than read. This section summarises what it actually says, instalment by instalment; notes what Land credits to Moldbug and what he adds himself; and records what the text does not contain. Its hardest passages, on race, are set out separately in the next section, because they need more room and more care than a summary allows.

Part 1: "Neo-reactionaries head for the exit" (2 March 2012)

Land opens with a problem of words. "Enlightenment," he writes, is a story of progress that cannot be reversed, so a "reactionary" enlightenment sounds like a contradiction. He then names a milestone: "the April 2009 discussion hosted at Cato Unbound among libertarian thinkers (including Patri Friedman and Peter Thiel)," and quotes Thiel's line, "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible." [cite:de4_land_de] That quotation, on page 2, is the only place Thiel appears in the serial.

The instalment sets out the thesis. Democracy, Land argues, is not a neutral system but a direction of travel, always toward a bigger state, because "winning elections is overwhelmingly a matter of vote buying." [cite:de4_land_de] Libertarians who once argued inside democracy are giving up on "voice," meaning participation and protest, and looking instead for "exit," the ability to leave. The current he describes is "recognizably Hobbesian, a coherent dark enlightenment," and it is the first appearance of the phrase that names this book. [cite:de4_land_de] He quotes Hans-Hermann Hoppe's argument that a king who owns a country preserves it while a democratic politician, a temporary "caretaker," consumes it, and draws the conclusion that democracy is "as close to a precise negation of civilization as anything could be." [cite:de4_land_de]

Then he introduces Moldbug, "supreme Sith Lord of the neoreactionaries," and quotes his proposal at length. Neocameralism, Moldbug's name for it, treats the state as a company: "To a neocameralist, a state is a business which owns a country," with shares, a board and managers, and residents as customers. [cite:de4_land_de] Land summarises: "No voice, free exit." The real ruling power of democratic society, the network of universities, media and officials whose favour is bought and sold, is to be mapped and converted into shares; "Moldbug calls it the Cathedral." [cite:de4_land_de] A quoted passage follows, reproduced without a named source, conceding that the approach "has never been tried," with Frederick the Great, Hong Kong, Singapore and Dubai offered as the nearest examples. [cite:de4_land_de] [cite:de1_audit_land_unattrib] Land closes with a set of anti-democratic quotations attributed to the American founders, and adds a note five days later conceding that the one attributed to Benjamin Franklin was probably invented in 1992. [cite:de4_land_de]

Parts 2 and 3: parasites and providence (9 and 19 March)

Part 2 argues that democracy does not produce prosperity but feeds on it: democracy "consumes progress," and the proper study of it is "general parasitology." [cite:de4_land_de] Welfare and shared risk, in this account, cut the "feedback loops" that let people feel the consequences of their own choices; Greece's borrowing inside the euro is his worked example. He then follows Moldbug's series "How Dawkins got pwned," which traces modern progressive belief to the radical Protestant sects of seventeenth-century England, and first touches on race. [cite:de4_land_de]

Part 3 develops the religious diagnosis. Progressive faith in history's direction is the Puritan doctrine of Providence in secular dress, and "hate" is "an offense against the Cathedral itself." [cite:de4_land_de] The instalment states what Land calls the "one iron law" of incentives: "Whatever is subsidized is promoted," from which he concludes that "No democracy could accept this, which means that every democracy will fail." [cite:de4_land_de] It quotes Moldbug's definition of the dominant creed, which he calls Universalism, as "a mystery cult of power," and ends with a table of four regimes. Communist tyranny scores low on voice and exit; "authoritarian capitalism" scores low on voice and high on exit, and life under it is "hard but productive"; social democracy is "soft and unsustainable"; the fourth regime is "zombie apocalypse." [cite:de4_land_de]

Parts 4 to 4d: the race digression (April to June)

From Part 4, "Re-running the race to ruin" (1 April), the serial turns into what Land himself calls a long digression on race in America, running through six instalments: white nationalism and its slide into antisemitism (Part 4); "white flight" and the 2012 dismissal of the columnist John Derbyshire by National Review (Part 4a); the Trayvon Martin case, equality and intelligence (Part 4b, "Obnoxious observations"); the civil-rights era and the "Cracker Factory" (Part 4c); and the alliance of libertarians with the nostalgic politics of the American South (Part 4d, "Odd Marriages"). [cite:de4_land_de] These instalments carry the material that most needs exact quotation, and they are treated in [scene:de4_the_hard_passages|the next section]. Here it is enough to record the political thread that runs through them: Land reads every historic escape, from the Exodus to American independence to the Underground Railroad, as "exit," and concludes in Part 4d that "liberty has no future in the Anglophone world outside the prospect of secession." [cite:de4_land_de]

Parts 4e and 4f: futures (3 and 20 July)

Part 4e, "Cross-coded history," sketches three futures for a declining modern world. The first, "Modernity 2.0," is a revival of growth from "a new ethno-geographical core," which Land calls "by far the most encouraging and plausible scenario" and expects to be realised "if China remains even approximately on its current track." [cite:de4_land_de] The others are a new dark age and a "Western Renaissance" after collapse. He then lists, "within a strictly hypothetical mode," what the West would have to do: replace "representational democracy" with "constitutional republicanism (or still more extreme anti-political governmental mechanisms)," downsize government, restore hard money and abolish central banking, and dismantle "state monetary and fiscal discretion." He adds at once that none of this "is going to happen short of an existential civilizational cataclysm." [cite:de4_land_de]

Part 4f, "Approaching the Bionic Horizon," closes the serial with biotechnology. The Cathedral is named again as "the Media-Academic complex" that "Mencius Moldbug names the Cathedral," and its central dogma is the "blank slate," the belief that human differences are cultural. [cite:de4_land_de] Land argues that genetic engineering will dissolve the old argument between nature and nurture, and ends with the biologist John H. Campbell's vision of elite groups engineering themselves into a new species. Secession, approaching this horizon, "takes on an altogether wilder and more monstrous bearing – towards speciation." The last line is "It's time to move on." [cite:de4_land_de]

What Land credits to Moldbug

The serial is scrupulous about attribution. The Cathedral, neocameralism, the "gov-corp" run by a chief executive, Universalism as a "nontheistic Christian sect," and the maxim that "progressivism has no enemies to the left" are all credited by name to Moldbug. [cite:de4_land_de] Later commentary that credits Land with coining "the Cathedral" has it backwards: the term is Moldbug's, and Land says so on page 6. The journalist Park MacDougald summarised the division of labour in 2015: Land's prescriptions of corporate rule were adopted from Moldbug. [cite:de4_awl] What Land adds is the frame, the name, the theology of the Cathedral as a religion, the cybernetic language of feedback and parasitism, the China-centred future, and the biotechnological ending.

What the text does not contain

A reader who comes to the serial from accounts of it may expect things it does not hold. It names no American politician as a vehicle for its ideas, proposes no plan for taking power in the United States, and says the changes it wants will not come "short of an existential civilizational cataclysm." [cite:de4_land_de] It does not mention Palantir, Urbit, Israel, Technocracy, or Yarvin by his legal name, and it does not contain the term "hyper-racism," which comes from a separate 2014 post discussed in the next section. [cite:de4_land_de] [cite:de4_wiki_land] Its single reference to Thiel is the 2009 quotation. The serial is a manifesto for leaving democracy, not a blueprint for capturing one.

sections.h: The Hard Passages: Race, Heredity and Exit as Sorting
sections.html:
About half of "The Dark Enlightenment" is about race. Race enters in the second instalment, and from April to June 2012 it is the main subject, as Land writes about white nationalism, crime, intelligence, the civil-rights era and the American South; the serial ends with a vision of human beings engineering themselves into separate species. [cite:de4_land_de] This section quotes those passages exactly and in context, says what Land said they meant where he said it, and names what they are.

Heredity and the charge of heresy

Race first enters in Part 2, through Moldbug. Land quotes Moldbug quoting the Victorian biologist Thomas Huxley on "our dusky cousins," and then Moldbug's question to Richard Dawkins: "In all seriousness, what is the evidence for fraternism?" [cite:de4_land_de] Land marks the moment himself: "This sure ain't vanilla-libertarian reaction anymore — it's getting seriously dark, and scary." [cite:de4_land_de] His own argument is that the belief in equal human potential is held as religion, not science: "it is surely beyond contention that the latter assumption, alone, is tolerated," and to question anti-racism is to commit what "we now call political incorrectness, and once knew as heresy." [cite:de4_land_de]

The claims become his own in Part 4a. Describing the safety of East Asian cities, Land attributes their order to populations who, "due to biological heredity, deep cultural traditions, or some inextricable entanglement of the two," find peaceful life easy, and sets them against Western inner cities where, in his words, "civilization has fundamentally collapsed." [cite:de4_land_de] In Part 4b he calls the belief in substantial human equality "sheer Gnostic delirium," names intelligence as "by far the most troublesome dimension of human bio-diversity," and in Part 4d writes that "stereotypes generally have high statistical truth-value." [cite:de4_land_de] "Human bio-diversity," or HBD, is the label the online right uses for hereditarian claims about differences between races. Haider calls it a euphemism for scientific racism, and cites the anthropologist Jonathan Marks: "the heredity of race is not genetic, but social." [cite:de4_haider]

Said plainly: the serial presents the view that differences in behaviour and ability between racial groups are probably in part inherited, and that stereotypes are statistically sound. That is a racist claim in the ordinary meaning of the word, and the text makes it in Land's own voice. [cite:de4_land_de]

The sentence about genocide

One line from Part 4b is often quoted alone: "Violence on a genocidal scale is required to even approximate to a practical egalitarian program." [cite:de4_land_de] In context it ends a paragraph arguing that "People are not equal, they do not develop equally," and it continues: "if anything less ambitious is attempted, people get around it." [cite:de4_land_de] The sentence is a claim about what forcing equality of outcome would require, offered as an argument against egalitarianism, not a call for violence; it rests on the hereditarian premise above.

What Land rejects

The same instalments reject several things, and the record must carry those too. Part 4 treats white nationalism as a dead end: for those who take it up, the path "demands rapid acceleration to a state of extreme alarm, or racial panic," and its grievance is "the werewolf curse that means it can only ever be a monster." [cite:de4_land_de] He describes the turn from white identity politics to blaming Jews, quoting a blogger who wrote "you do have to violate PC to say: Jews," and calls it "the labyrinth, the trap, with its pitifully constricted, stereotypical circuit." [cite:de4_land_de] In Part 4d he argues that Nazism is self-defeating: "Identity politics is for losers," and "racial Übermenschen make no real sense." [cite:de4_land_de]

His treatment of John Derbyshire, the columnist dismissed by National Review in April 2012 for a column advising his children to avoid black people, is partly critical. Land finds the column's wording "subtly, yet distinctly, menacing," and concedes the central objection made by William Saletan and Noah Millman: "Stereotypes, however rigorously confirmed, are essentially inferior to specific knowledge in any concrete social situation, because nobody ever encounters a population." [cite:de4_land_de] He quotes Millman's verdict in full: "Is Derbyshire's piece racist? Of course it's racist." [cite:de4_land_de] What he does not reject is the premise. Millman's point, which Land reproduces without dissent, was that Derbyshire's conclusions do not follow from his premises; the premises, about group differences, are left standing.

Hitler as the Cathedral's anti-Messiah

The passage most likely to be misread is in Part 4. Land quotes, and praises as reaching "the brink of genius," a Moldbug essay that compares the moral standing of Hitler and Stalin and asks why socialism does not arouse the horror that white nationalism does. [cite:de4_land_de] Land then argues that modern societies treat Hitler as a religious absolute: "it might be more helpful to compare Hitler to the Antichrist, which is to say: to a mirror Messiah, of reversed moral polarity." He calls this "less a pro-Nazi ideology than a universal faith," and mocks it as "the Church of Sacred Hitlerite Abomination." [cite:de4_land_de] The passage does not praise Hitler, whom Land describes as personifying "demonic monstrosity" in the common view he is describing. Its target is the treatment of Hitler as a metaphysical absolute of evil, which it reframes as a sacrament of the Cathedral's faith.

Exit as sorting

The thread that matters most for this book is the one that joins Land's race material to his politics. In Part 4a he takes the American term "white flight," the movement of white residents out of cities, and makes it the model of his idea: "all exit and no voice," the "spontaneous impulse of dark enlightenment." [cite:de4_land_de] He reads Derbyshire's advice to his children as having "converted white flight from a much-lamented but seemingly inexorable fact into an explicit imperative, even a cause. Don't argue, flee." [cite:de4_land_de] In Part 4c the progressive order becomes a "Cracker Factory," and he writes: "Like Hell, or Auschwitz, the Cracker Factory has a simple slogan inscribed upon its gate: Escape is racist." [cite:de4_land_de] By Part 4f secession leads "towards speciation," with elite groups using genetic engineering to leave the human species behind; "For racial nationalists, concerned that their grandchildren should look like them, Campbell is the abyss." [cite:de4_land_de]

Land took the step further two years later. On 4 October 2014 he published a post titled "Hyper-Racism" on the Alternative Right blog; the word does not appear in the 2012 serial. [cite:de4_wiki_land] [cite:de4_land_de] Haider, who quoted the post, reports that Land treated socioeconomic status as "a strong proxy for IQ," wrote of a "genetically self-filtering elite," and argued that "space colonization will inevitably function as a highly-selective genetic filter." [cite:de4_haider] On those quotations the term names not a hatred of other races but a future in which successful groups separate themselves physically and then genetically from everyone else.

The critics

Land's critics come mostly from the left that once read him closely. Haider's 2017 essay in Viewpoint Magazine argues that Land's race theory is not an aberration but mainstream meritocracy taken to its end: Land "simply carried the mainstream ideology to its inexorable result," and, unlike liberals who believe in that ideal, "admits its implications." [cite:de4_haider] Elizabeth Sandifer, whose Neoreaction a Basilisk (first published in 2016) is a book-length critical reading of these writers, said she gave the work "as much intellectual respect as I could before I took it out back and shot it," and that "Their ideas make no sense if you look at them under any scrutiny whatsoever." [cite:de4_ca_sandifer] [cite:de2_sandifer_ep]

The worst-case reading, tested

The working hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and not a finding, reads immigration enforcement and government cuts as the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. This part asked what Land's writing adds to it.

Documented: Land's serial rejects democracy as such and adopts, with credit, Moldbug's model of a state owned like a company and run by a chief executive, with "No voice, free exit" as its principle. [cite:de4_land_de] Documented too are hereditarian claims about race in his own voice, and a line of argument in which exit becomes sorting, first by neighbourhood and then by genome. [cite:de4_land_de] [cite:de4_haider] And documented is a tie of reading: the investor Marc Andreessen counts Land among his "patron saints." [cite:de4_spectator]

Probable: that Land's vocabulary of exit and acceleration reaches readers in technology investing, on the strength of Andreessen's citation; no document shows that any reader took the race passages from him, or which of his ideas anyone took. [cite:de4_spectator] On one point the record runs against the worst case directly: the sorting in Land's examples is the departure of those who can leave, by flight, secession or engineering, not the removal of others by a state. [cite:de4_land_de] Enforcement that removes people resembles a different text, Hoppe's call to expel political opponents from a covenant community, discussed in [scene:de3_other_lineages|Part Three], more than it resembles Land's. [cite:de3_wiki_hoppe]

Not supported: that Land supplies the destination. His text prescribes no American executive, expects no change "short of an existential civilizational cataclysm," places his hopes for growth in China, and imagines liberty only through secession and, in the end, speciation. [cite:de4_land_de] [cite:de4_spectator] That is a programme for leaving states, not for capturing one, and on this part's material the record runs against the idea that Land's engine was built to power a sovereign American executive. The hand-off from writing to government, if there was one, runs through Yarvin and the people around him, the subject of [scene:de5_programmer_to_moldbug|the next parts], and it is graded in [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|the final scorecard].

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: Curtis Yarvin: the Life
chapters.intro: This part tells the life of Curtis Yarvin, the software engineer who, as Mencius Moldbug, wrote the texts at the centre of this book. It separates what rests on his own account from what independent reporting carries: a childhood in a foreign-service family and three grades skipped, Brown at eighteen and a doctorate abandoned at Berkeley; a programming job at the dawn of the mobile web and a payout that bought years of reading; the blog he began in 2007 and ended in 2016; and Tlon, the company he founded in 2013 with money from Peter Thiel's and Marc Andreessen's venture firms, left in 2019 and took back as a "wartime C.E.O." in 2024. The last section follows his public years under his own name, from the newsletter he launched in 2020 to the debates, interviews and inaugural parties of 2025, names each documented contact with the type of connection it was, and tests the claim that the theorist is connected to the people who now hold power.
chapters.outro: The life sets limits on the legend. Yarvin was a precocious child of two federal civil servants, a Brown graduate at eighteen and a programmer who left a Berkeley doctorate for the mobile web, and his politics came later, from his own reading of Hoppe, Carlyle and Burnham. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] [cite:de3_tait] His one documented financial tie to Peter Thiel is a venture investment in his company, reported at $1.1 million alongside Andreessen Horowitz in 2013; no document shows anyone paying for his political writing. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] He left the company in 2019 and returned in 2024 as an informal "wartime C.E.O.," after which senior staff resigned; in October 2025 the galaxy owners replaced the Urbit Foundation's board and a new director succeeded him as he left to found a company. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_kumin_mars] [cite:de23_epoch_2025] J.D. Vance named him once, in 2021, while calling for the civil service to be fired; in 2025 Yarvin was a guest of honour at an inaugural gala and lunched with a State Department official, yet held no office, said his influence ran through young staffers, and by October was writing about leaving the country if the administration fell. [cite:de5_wbur_vance] [cite:de5_politico_ward] [cite:de5_sfstandard] What he actually proposes, and the hardest things he has written, are the subject of [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six].

sections.h: A Diplomat's Son, Three Grades Ahead
sections.html:
Curtis Guy Yarvin was born in 1973 into what his biographers describe as a liberal, secular family. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] The place and exact date of his birth are not in the published record, and much of what is known about his childhood comes from two kinds of source that need to be kept apart: his own accounts, given in interviews and on his blogs, and the reporting of journalists who spoke to him and, in some cases, to his relatives. Where the two agree the account below says so; where a detail rests on his word alone, it says that too.

His parents were both, in his own description to the New York Times in January 2025, career federal civil servants. [cite:de5_lgc_nyt] His father, Herbert Yarvin, worked for the United States government abroad. In an interview with the writer Max Raskin, Yarvin described him as a diplomat in Nicosia, the capital of Cyprus. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] Jacob Siegel, in a long profile for Tablet in 2022, reported that the family was posted to Portugal, Cyprus and the Dominican Republic, after earlier years in Fairfax County, Virginia. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] Ava Kofman, whose profile for The New Yorker appeared in June 2025 after months of access, reported that Herbert Yarvin held a doctorate in philosophy before he became a diplomat, and that the family lived in the Dominican Republic and Cyprus. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] The broad outline, a foreign-service family that moved between overseas postings, is therefore carried by two independent profiles as well as by Yarvin himself; the full list of his father's postings is not documented beyond those reports. The father's career is his own record and is not examined here.

His mother was a Protestant from Westchester County, New York, who later also joined the civil service; according to Siegel, his parents had met at Brown University in the mid-1960s. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] On his father's side, his grandparents were Jewish American communists, a detail Siegel reported and Yarvin has discussed in his own writing. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] It is a family fact, stated here once and plainly, and nothing in this book draws an inference from it.

A child moved ahead

The most consistent theme in every account of his early life is speed. Kofman reported that he was partly schooled at home by his mother, skipped three grades, and started high school at twelve after the family settled in Columbia, Maryland, a planned town between Baltimore and Washington. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] Siegel's figures are close: he was eleven in ninth grade, a twelve-year-old sophomore at a public high school in Columbia, after an admissions test moved him up two further grades. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] The school is identified as Wilde Lake High School, from which he graduated in 1988; the source for the school's name is one of his own later blog posts, not a school record. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin]

The Study of Mathematically Precocious Youth, a programme run from Johns Hopkins University since the 1970s, identified children who scored exceptionally well on college entrance tests at a young age and offered them accelerated courses. Accounts of Yarvin's place in it differ in date. Some biographical summaries say he entered it in 1985, at about twelve, a line that carries no cited source in the reference works that repeat it. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] Siegel reported that at fifteen he went to Johns Hopkins through the programme and, a year later, transferred to Brown University as a legacy admission, his parents having met there. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] The two accounts may describe two stages of the same relationship with the programme, a test at twelve and enrolment at fifteen; the published record does not settle it, and nothing turns on the difference beyond the plain fact, agreed by all sources, that he reached university years ahead of his age.

He graduated from Brown in 1992, at eighteen according to Kofman. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] He then began a doctorate in computer science at the University of California, Berkeley, and left after about a year and a half to take a job in the technology industry; the historian Joshua Tait, in a 2019 chapter on Yarvin, and Siegel both give that duration. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] He never completed the degree.

What the early record does and does not show

Three points from this part of the record matter for the rest of the book.

The first is that the man who would later argue that the American civil service should be retired wholesale was himself the child of two federal civil servants, and of a stepfather who, Siegel reported, also joined the civil service. [cite:de5_audit_tablet] [cite:de5_lgc_nyt] Yarvin raised the point himself in his 2025 New York Times interview, when he was asked how his proposal to empty the federal workforce would treat the people in it; his answer, that it should be handled "like a company that goes out of business," is examined in [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]. [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] The biography does not explain the ideas, and the book does not treat it as if it did: the record contains no statement by Yarvin tracing his politics to his parents' work, beyond his mention of it in answer to that question.

The second is that his formation was mathematical and technical, not historical or legal. Nothing in the documented record of his schooling involves political theory, history or law; he came to those, by his own account and by every biographer's, later and on his own, as an adult reading in San Francisco. The next section follows that turn. When later critics, from the political theorist Danielle Allen to the economist Garett Jones, debated him in 2025 on questions of government, they were debating a self-taught writer, and Yarvin has never presented himself otherwise. [cite:de5_crimson] [cite:de5_ylsfed]

The third is a matter of method. A good deal of what circulates about Yarvin's youth in online summaries, from the size of the family's moves to his supposed early reading, cannot be traced to a document or to a profile in which he or his relatives were interviewed. Those details are not repeated here. What can be said with confidence is short: a precocious child of a foreign-service family, moved through school years early, a graduate of Brown at eighteen and a Berkeley doctoral student who left to write software. The rest of his life is far better documented, much of it by himself.

sections.h: From Programmer to Mencius Moldbug
sections.html:
Yarvin left Berkeley in the early 1990s for the technology industry, and the company he joined is the first employer in his record that can be named. Siegel reported in Tablet that he worked at a mobile software company founded in 1996 as Libris, renamed Unwired Planet and then Phone.com, one of the firms that built the first systems for reading the web on mobile phones. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] Kofman reported in The New Yorker that he helped design an early mobile browser there. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] Programming remained his trade and his preferred self-description: Siegel noted that he calls himself a computer engineer or programmer because he thinks of himself as a builder. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel]

The two profiles give different figures for what the job paid him, and both are reported here. Yarvin, quoted by Siegel, said that after the dot-com crash a buyout left him with "a few hundred thousand dollars," which he described as considerably less than enough never to work again. [cite:de5_audit_tablet] Kofman wrote that the company's stock-market listing brought him roughly a million dollars. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] The accounts may describe different payments, a share of the listing and a later buyout, or the same money remembered differently; no public filing settles it. Both agree on what the money did. It gave a man in his late twenties several years in San Francisco without an employer, and he spent them reading. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] The crash, in his own words, also left him with "a newly acquired girlfriend (who would become my wife)," Jennifer Kollmer. [cite:de5_audit_tablet] [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin]

The reading

His own account of the reading has been consistent across interviews. He began, he told Siegel, with the Austrian school of economics, Ludwig von Mises and Murray Rothbard, and then moved to Hans-Hermann Hoppe, a German-born libertarian economist whose 2001 book Democracy: The God That Failed argued that a hereditary monarch, as the owner of his realm, has stronger reasons to preserve it than an elected caretaker who holds power for a term. "Hoppe opened a kind of door to the pre-revolutionary world for me," Yarvin said. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] The historian Joshua Tait, in the first scholarly account of Yarvin's thought, reported that the lawyer and blogger Glenn Reynolds had introduced him to Mises and Rothbard, and that Thomas Carlyle, James Burnham and Hoppe together prompted his turn to authoritarianism. [cite:de3_wiki_yarvin] [cite:de3_tait] Kofman, too, credits Hoppe's book with pushing him towards monarchy. [cite:de3_wiki_dtgtf]

The influence ran one way. Hoppe, asked in 2025, said he did not follow Yarvin's writing closely, "too much rambling for my taste," that he had met him once at a gathering to which Peter Thiel had invited them both, and that his own ideal of many small private-law territories was not the same thing as a state run like a business. [cite:de3_hoppe_reply] A reader's debt to an author is not the author's endorsement of the reader, and [scene:de3_lineage|Part Three] traces the inheritance in full.

He was also a long-standing participant in early online argument. Siegel described a formative period in late adolescence on Usenet, the pre-web discussion network, including a group called talk.bizarre. [cite:de5_audit_tablet] The habits of that culture, long posts, irony, provocation and an appetite for argument with strangers, are visible in everything he later wrote; his admirer Nick Land would write in 2012 that "irony is Moldbug's method, as well as his milieu." [cite:de4_land_de]

Two projects: a computer and a blog

In 2002, by the usual account, he began designing Urbit, a personal computing system built from scratch, with its own programming languages and its own network of permanent digital identities. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] It stayed a private project for years; its first public code release came in January 2010, announced in a post titled "Urbit: functional programming from scratch." [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] Urbit would become his company and the subject of the next section.

The other project made him known. In 2007, under the pen name Mencius Moldbug, he started a blog called Unqualified Reservations. Its first post, "A formalist manifesto," dated 23 April 2007, set out the idea he called formalism: that the way to end political conflict is to recognise, and then formalise as property, whatever distribution of power actually exists. "We need a rule that tells us whose wallet is whose," he wrote. [cite:de6_le_contra] Over the next two years came the texts on which his reputation rests: the posts defining neocameralism in 2007, a book-length "Open Letter to Open-Minded Progressives" from April 2008, which Kofman estimates at about 120,000 words and which proposed a "CEO-monarch," the "Patchwork" series of November 2008, a "Gentle Introduction" series in 2009, and three essays on Carlyle in 2009 and 2010. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de3_princeton_carlyle] [scene:de2_core_texts|Part Two] reads the canon in order; [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six] sets out the program and the hardest passages.

The blog's reach in its first years was small and specialised, a conversation among libertarian and contrarian bloggers. It widened in 2012, when Nick Land's long serial essay "The Dark Enlightenment" presented Moldbug as the central figure of a "neo-reactionary" current, credited him with the Cathedral and neocameralism, and called him, half in jest, the "supreme Sith Lord of the neoreactionaries." [cite:de2_land_ebook] It widened again in November 2013, when the technology site TechCrunch ran a piece on the "neoreactionaries" and connected the pen name to Yarvin, a San Francisco software entrepreneur. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] [cite:de1_finley_tc]

The end of Moldbug

By the time he was identified, the blog was winding down. In 2012 he gave his best-known public talk, at a technology "unconference" called BIL, proposing that a new national leader "retire all government employees"; the program it set out is read in [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]. [cite:de6_pein_2014] He largely stopped posting in 2013 to concentrate on Urbit, went quiet in 2014 after seven years, and in April 2016 announced that Unqualified Reservations had "completed its mission." [cite:de2_wiki_yarvin] [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] The pen name did not disappear; it became a label others used about him, and he returned to political writing four years later under his own name, as the last section of this part describes.

Two things about this period bear on the questions this book asks. The first is that the writing and the engineering were separate enterprises in public: Urbit was presented to investors and programmers as a technical project, and the political blog was pseudonymous until a journalist connected the two. When the connection became public, it followed him into his company: the Strange Loop programming conference withdrew an invitation to speak about Urbit in 2015, and speakers and sponsors left LambdaConf in 2016 when its organisers kept him on the programme. [cite:de5_dailydot] The second is that the money behind both enterprises in these years was his own. The documented outside money, from Peter Thiel's Founders Fund and others, arrived with the company in 2013, and the next section follows it. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit]

sections.h: Tlon: Founding, Exit and Return
sections.html:
In 2013 Yarvin turned Urbit from a private project into a company. He founded Tlon Corporation in San Francisco to build it, naming the firm after a Jorge Luis Borges story, "Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius," about an invented world whose internal logic slowly displaces the real one. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] Urbit, as Tlon described it, was a new personal computer reimagined from the ground up: its own programming languages, a peer-to-peer network, and a permanent cryptographic identity for each user, later recorded on the Ethereum blockchain in a registry called Azimuth. Its identity space was divided, like a feudal map, into 256 "galaxies," 65,280 "stars" and about four billion "planets." [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] How that address space was distributed and sold, and who holds it, is the subject of [scene:de23_address_space|Part Twenty-Three]. This section follows Yarvin's own place in the company: the money he raised, his departure in 2019 and his return in 2024.

The money

The outside money is the documented link between Yarvin and Peter Thiel, and its size has been reported in more than one way. Corey Pein, in his 2018 book Live Work Work Work Die, reported that Thiel's venture firm Founders Fund and Andreessen Horowitz, the firm led by Marc Andreessen, together invested $1.1 million in Tlon; whether that was each firm's stake or the combined round is not clear from the citation. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] Pein had reported Thiel's investment as early as May 2014, adding that Yarvin held the title "benevolent dictator for life" at the company, a term borrowed from open-source software culture for a project's founder who keeps the final say. [cite:de6_pein_2014] Kofman, writing in 2025, put the total investment in Urbit at about $30 million, without a breakdown. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] The two figures are not reconciled by any public filing; the first is a single seed-era round, the second a lifetime total that would include later investors and sales of address space. Both are reported, and neither is summed with the other.

Thiel's money reached Yarvin's circle by a second, earlier route. In May 2011 John Burnham, who went on to co-found Tlon, was named one of the first twenty Thiel Fellows, each of whom was to receive $100,000 from the Thiel Foundation over two years; Pein and the historian Joshua Tait both note the grant. [cite:de5_audit_tc2011] [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] It was a fellowship awarded to a young founder, not a payment to Yarvin. The connection types are worth stating exactly, because they are often blurred. Founders Fund's investment in Tlon is a direct financial tie between a Thiel vehicle and Yarvin's company. It is not a payment to Yarvin for his political writing, and no published document shows Thiel paying for the writing. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso]

The product, for most of its life, reached few people. In September 2022 the magazine The Point estimated its active users at "a few thousand," and described its main software at the time as a bare-bones text message board. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] Its executives also spent effort keeping the project apart from its founder's politics: Josh Lehman, executive director of the Urbit Foundation, the non-profit that came to steer the network's core development, told the magazine Astra in 2022 that the hardest part of his work had been distancing Urbit from Yarvin. [cite:de5_audit_wiki_urbit]

The exit, 2019

In January 2019 Yarvin left Tlon. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_kumin_mars] He explained his departure in a post titled "A Founder's Farewell." [cite:de5_kumin_mars] "From the very start," he wrote, "I knew Urbit could not succeed until it ceased to be mine and became the world's." He resigned as Tlon's chief technology officer, board member and voting shareholder, reassigned his galaxies to urbit.org, and kept a nonvoting minority stake and some time-locked stars, which he said gave him no power. [cite:de23_farewell_2019] The departure was presented, by him and by the company, as a founder stepping back so that a technical project could outgrow its author. [cite:de5_kumin_mars] The following year he returned to political writing under his own name.

The return, 2024–2025

The project ran short of money in 2024. A newsletter writer close to the community reported that the Urbit Foundation's board fired its executive director in about mid-2024, a step he tied to the Foundation running out of money, and that most of its staff quit in protest. [cite:de5_audit_rettig] A second account described 2024's funding problems as serious enough to prompt Yarvin's return. [cite:de5_audit_marbl] In August 2024 Yarvin announced, at an impromptu public meeting with investors and developers, that he was coming back "in a big way," in the words of Noah Kumin, a writer who had worked at Tlon. [cite:de5_kumin_mars] ARTnews and, later, Kofman reported that he returned without an official title as an informal "wartime C.E.O.," and that several of the project's senior employees resigned in protest. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] The phrase describes a familiar idea in Silicon Valley management writing: a founder who takes back personal control in a crisis and suspends ordinary consultation until the crisis passes.

The return did not end the turmoil. An account published in July 2025 described four executive directors at the Foundation in about a year, and a board fight in which the latest, Ryan Kneer, who had joined forces with Yarvin in November 2024, fired Yarvin from the board while Yarvin was lobbying the board's other two members to fire Kneer. Kneer then called a no-confidence vote and appealed to the holders of Urbit's 256 galaxies, the network's top-level owners, to replace the board. [cite:de5_marbl] [cite:de5_audit_marbl] A second newsletter writer, who holds some Urbit address space himself, reported in late July 2025 that Yarvin was acting as executive director "by fiat," quoted him calling the period "real Roman times," and reported, without knowing the terms, that Yarvin had secured a $4 million investment from Andreessen Horowitz earlier that year in exchange for more address space. [cite:de5_rettig] Kofman, who had been travelling with Yarvin, reported that his newest plan was to market Urbit as something like an exclusive private club. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso]

These later accounts come from community newsletters, not from filings or major outlets, and they are reported here with that standing. [cite:de5_marbl] [cite:de5_rettig] The outcome came from the Foundation itself. On 9 October 2025 it announced that "the Galactic Senate has elected to replace the board of the Urbit Foundation" after "multiple votes," installed a new three-seat board, and named a new executive director, ~sicdev-pilnup, in succession to ~sorreg-namtyv, Yarvin's Urbit identity, "who is leaving to found a new application development company." [cite:de23_epoch_2025] [cite:de23_farewell_2019] The announcement gave no vote counts and did not name his new company or its backers. As of October 2026 no named outlet had reported a return by him to a role at the Foundation; [scene:de23_wartime_ceo|Part Twenty-Three] tells the episode in full.

What the company record shows

The Tlon story establishes three things for this book. It documents the one financial tie between Peter Thiel and Yarvin: venture investment in a software company, beginning in 2013, alongside Andreessen Horowitz. That is a real connection of a specific type, and it is the strongest one in the record; [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|Part Twelve] and [scene:de14_network_map|the network map] place it among Thiel's other ties. It also shows that Yarvin's political writing and his company were kept apart in public, by him and by the company's later managers, and that the separation was imperfect: the Foundation's own director described distancing the project from him as the hardest part of his job, and conference organisers in 2015 and 2016 treated it as one. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_dailydot]

Finally, the company's governance gave a small, real-world view of how its founder behaves when he holds power and it is challenged. In 2019 he stepped back; in 2024, in a funding crisis, he returned and took control without a title, and senior staff left; in 2025 the board and the founder tried to remove each other, and in October the galaxy owners replaced the board and he left to found a new company. [cite:de23_epoch_2025] It would overstate the case to call this a test of his political theory. A start-up's board fight is not a state, Urbit's members could leave at any time, and nothing in the record shows violence or coercion of any kind. But it is his own record, in his own organisation, and the pattern of a founder reclaiming personal authority in an emergency is one his political writing recommends for countries. [scene:de23_wartime_ceo|Part Twenty-Three] tells the full story, and [scene:de33_two_tests|Part Thirty-Five] asks what it shows beside the federal government's experience in 2025. [cite:de5_kumin_mars] [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_marbl]

sections.h: The Public Years, 2016–2026
sections.html:
For most of the 2010s Yarvin's political influence, such as it was, ran through a pen name and a small readership. The decade that followed made him a public figure under his own name. This section follows that change, keeping documented contacts, each with its connection type, apart from the influence others attribute to him, as [scene:de1_spine_and_overlay|Part One] requires.

Thiel, Bannon and a leaked email, 2016–2017

In 2017 BuzzFeed News published emails between the far-right writer Milo Yiannopoulos and others, among them messages from Yarvin, written some time after May 2016, in which he said he had been "coaching Thiel," described Thiel as "fully enlightened, just plays it very carefully," and said he had "watched the election at his house." [cite:de5_pein_baffler] Corey Pein, reporting the emails for The Baffler, judged the coaching claim probably boastful. [cite:de5_pein_baffler] It is Yarvin's account of a relationship, not Thiel's, and Yarvin later said that for him "fully enlightened" meant "fully disenchanted." [cite:de1_nyt_interview] Thiel's own recorded view, reported from a 2023 interview with The Atlantic, was that he did not think Yarvin's ideas would "work," though he found him an "interesting and powerful" historian. [cite:de6_cnn_2025] What the record documents between the two men is a venture investment in Yarvin's company and personal acquaintance: Thiel attended a podcast recording Yarvin gave in Los Angeles in February 2020, according to Tablet. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] [cite:de5_wiki_urbit]

In early 2017, after Donald Trump's first inauguration, reports circulated that Yarvin was advising the President's strategist Steve Bannon. Yarvin denied them, "sometimes playfully and at other times strenuously," as Siegel put it. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] No document of any contact between the two has been published, and the claim stands as reported and denied.

Gray Mirror and a private loss, 2020–2022

In 2020 Yarvin returned to political writing, this time under his own name, on a paid Substack newsletter called Gray Mirror. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] Its own page describes it as "A portal to the next regime," says it has "tens of thousands of subscribers," and presents it as the working draft of a book, Gray Mirror of the Nihilist Prince, offering an "ex nihilo vision of governance." [cite:de5_gm_about] The money behind it is its readers' subscriptions; no institutional backer is documented. His books are published by Passage Publishing, which sells Gray Mirror: Fascicle I, Disturbance (2022) and two volumes of Unqualified Reservations. [cite:de5_passage]

In April 2021 his wife, Jennifer Kollmer, died; he announced her death on his newsletter. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] The record of his private life is otherwise left aside here, beyond the published fact that he married again in 2024. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin]

2021: the year his name entered politics

Three recorded conversations in 2021 carried his ideas into conservative politics. In May he recorded a conversation with the conservative writer Michael Anton for the Claremont Institute's podcast The American Mind, ostensibly about Anton's 2020 book The Stakes. [cite:de5_powerline] The Guardian later reported that Yarvin used it to discuss a president declaring a state of emergency in his inaugural address, while calling the idea of becoming "a Caesar" absurd; Anton's defenders replied that the newspaper's account did not match the recording. [cite:de5_brewminate] [cite:de5_powerline] The two accounts conflict, and both are given.

In September he appeared on Fox Nation's Tucker Carlson Today. [cite:de6_mm_2021] That same month J.D. Vance, then a candidate for the Senate in Ohio, named him on a podcast, Jack Murphy Live. "There's this guy, Curtis Yarvin," Vance said, "who's written about some of these things," and he went on: "I'm sympathetic to that project. But another option is that we should just seize the administrative state for our own purposes." [cite:de5_wbur_vance] [cite:de5_vox_2022] In the same appearance he said a future President Trump should "fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state" and "replace them with our people." [cite:de5_nextgov_vance] The remark dates to 2021; it was widely recirculated in 2024, after Vance became Trump's running mate. Kofman reported that the two men had first met in 2015, through Thiel. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] It is the one documented occasion on which Vance cited Yarvin by name in public, and [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|Part Twelve] places it in Vance's own career.

2025: the guest of honour who said he was outside

Trump's second inauguration brought Yarvin a burst of attention. On 18 January 2025 the New York Times published a long interview with him by David Marchese, in which he argued that presidents such as Washington, Lincoln and Franklin Roosevelt had been "basically national CEOs," and that "it's not even that democracy is bad, it's just that it's very weak." [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] The same week he attended the "Coronation Ball," an inaugural gala hosted by Passage Press, where Politico described him as "an informal guest of honor." [cite:de5_politico_ward] To the same reporter he described a lunch with Michael Anton, by then a senior State Department official, "at a coffee shop across the street from the State Department," and an encounter with the new Vice President at a party, where, he said, Vance greeted him as "Yarvin, you reactionary fascist." "I've interacted with Vance once since the election," he added. [cite:de5_politico_ward] Asked how he measured his influence, he answered: "how I measure my influence is that I try not to." [cite:de5_politico_ward] An adviser to Vance later told CNN the two had met "like once." [cite:de6_cnn_2025]

The rest of the year was a run of public appearances. On 5 May he debated the Harvard political theorist Danielle Allen at Harvard's Faculty Club, before about eighty people, in an event organised by his publisher and an undergraduate society and not sanctioned by the university; he called Harvard "an essentially oligarchic institution," and Allen framed the question as "regime change to unaccountable CEO monarchs." [cite:de5_crimson] In June The New Yorker published Kofman's profile. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] In September, at the HowTheLightGetsIn festival in London, he told the interviewer Alastair Campbell that the rule of law was a "polite fiction" for the rule of men. [cite:de5_spectator_au] On 7 and 8 October he debated twice at Yale, against the law professor Jed Rubenfeld on a motion to "end the democratic experiment" and, for the Yale Federalist Society, against the economist Garett Jones on "for-profit governance." [cite:de5_ravitch_ydn] [cite:de5_ylsfed] In late November he was a guest of honour at the founding convention of Brazil's newly registered Partido Missão in São Paulo, where in a six-minute speech he argued against racial quotas; he held no role in the party. [cite:de5_icl] The same month the historian Rutger Bregman, in the BBC's Reith Lectures, called him a "neofascist," a critic's label and recorded as such. [cite:de5_wiki_yarvin] Coverage continued into 2026, among it a segment on German-language public television in January. [cite:de5_zdf]

A critic of the government he is said to inspire

The most striking feature of Yarvin's record in 2025 is how often he criticised the administration he is said to have shaped. CNN reported in May his view that it was "barely scratching the surface" of the change needed, and that his influence ran "more through the kids in the administration." [cite:de6_cnn_2025] Kofman reported him complaining that the Department of Government Efficiency had too much libertarian DNA, and dismissing his own influence as worthless until the change he wanted actually came. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] In an essay earlier in the year he had written that the administration would "wither and eventually dissipate" unless it grew more extreme, and in a Gray Mirror post in early October 2025 he wrote that he had to "start thinking realistically about how to flee the country" if the Democrats returned, later editing the line to a "plan B for 2029." [cite:de5_sfstandard] He told the Berliner Zeitung the same month that he wished Trump were far more energetic. [cite:de5_bz] [scene:de6_claims_vs_record|Part Six] sets these statements against his other claims about his influence.

The worst-case reading, tested

This part's material bears on the hypothesis in one place: the claim, often made, that the theorist of a sovereign executive without a veto is connected to the people who hold executive power. Graded against the record, it divides as follows.

Documented: a Thiel fund and Andreessen Horowitz invested in Yarvin's company; Vance, before he held office, named Yarvin on a podcast and in the same breath called for firing the civil service; and Yarvin had social access to people in the new administration in 2025, a gala, a lunch with Anton and a greeting from the Vice President, on his own account. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_wbur_vance] [cite:de5_politico_ward] Probable, but not proven: that some younger staff in the administration had read him. He says so, and an anonymous adviser to the Department of Government Efficiency told the Washington Post that everyone designing policy had read him; one unnamed source and the subject's own claim are not a document. [cite:de5_politico_ward] [cite:de5_kofman_nuso]

Not supported: that Yarvin directs, advises or programs the administration. He holds no office and no contract; no political donations by him have been reported; no meeting with the President is on record; and a Vance adviser says the two met about once. [cite:de6_cnn_2025] On this point the record runs against the worst-case reading rather than merely failing to support it. The theorist's own statements in 2025 are those of an outsider dissatisfied with a government that has not done what he wants, and in October 2025 he was planning for the possibility that elections would remove it. [cite:de5_sfstandard] A destination that its best-known advocate fears is slipping away has not been reached; whether the machinery for it was built anyway, by others and for their own reasons, is the question of Books Three and Five. The next part turns from the man to the program itself. [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: Curtis Yarvin: the Program and the Hard Posts
chapters.intro: This part sets out what Curtis Yarvin actually proposes and the passages for which he is most often condemned. It begins with the program in his own words: formalism, the idea that real power should be made official property; the Cathedral, his name for the universities, press and civil service he believes really govern; neocameralism, a state run as a company that owns its country, under a chief executive answerable to a board; Patchwork, a world of small sovereign corporations that residents may only leave; and RAGE, his 2012 proposal to "Retire All Government Employees." It then reads five hard posts, on white nationalism, on the surplus residents of a company-run city, on biodiesel and virtual-reality confinement, on slavery and on the Breivik massacre, each dated, quoted briefly and set beside his own later account. The last section grades ten of his public claims about himself against his texts and the record, using the four flags the book applies to everyone.
chapters.outro: Yarvin's program is consistent across eighteen years: make real power into property, end the vote, place a chief executive answerable to a board over a state run as a company, and retire the civil service; residents who object may leave.
