[cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de6_land_ebook] [cite:de6_pein_2014] [cite:de6_cnn_2025] His hardest posts are real and are in his own voice: a rejection of white nationalism as ineffective and distorting rather than wrong, a sovereign corporation's slums cleared with "possibly a little aerial bombing," "a humane alternative to genocide" by permanent virtual confinement, a hereditary fitness for "mastery than slavery," and a Breivik post that condemned the massacre as ineffective. [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de6_tnr_duran] [cite:de6_mm_2021] Against his own public claims, the record yields no RED or ORANGE flags but two YELLOW and seven GREY: denials narrower than they sound and a vocabulary softened from "dictator" to "monarch" and "national CEO" around an unchanged design. [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] The texts name the destination the worst-case reading fears; they contain no immigration program and no call to violence, and the 2025 cuts resemble RAGE without descending from it on any document. Whether the diagnosis behind the program has merit is the question of [scene:de7_what_it_gets_right|Part Seven].

sections.h: The Program: From Formalism to RAGE
sections.html:
Yarvin's political writing is long, digressive and ironic, and it is easy to quote in pieces that make it sound either harmless or monstrous. Read in order, it has a clear structure: a diagnosis of who really rules, a design for a different kind of state, and a route from one to the other. This section sets out each, defines its terms in his own words where possible, and notes where the vocabulary changed between the pseudonymous blog of 2007–2014 and the interviews he gave under his own name in 2025. The hardest passages, which arise where the design meets people it has no use for, are the subject of [scene:de6_the_hard_posts|the next section].

The diagnosis: formalism and the Cathedral

The first post of Unqualified Reservations, "A formalist manifesto" of 23 April 2007, began from property. Political conflict, Yarvin argued, comes from disagreement about who owns what, and violence is "anything that breaks the rule, or replaces it with a different rule." His remedy was to stop arguing about who ought to hold power and to record who actually does: "We need a rule that tells us whose wallet is whose." "Formalism says: let's figure out exactly who has what, now, and give them a little fancy certificate." [cite:de2_le] [cite:de6_le_contra] Formalism, in short, is the proposal that real power should be made official, so that it can be owned, priced and held to account as property rather than hidden behind elections.

Applied to the United States, the formalist question was where real power sat, and his answer was the term for which he is best known. "The Cathedral," in Yarvin's usage, is the set of prestigious institutions, chiefly the universities and the established press, together with the permanent civil service that takes its cues from them, which he argued set the bounds of respectable opinion and policy without being elected. [cite:de6_pein_2014] [cite:de1_tablet] He has insisted that it is not a conspiracy: the institutions behave, as Siegel summarised it, "as if they were a single organizational structure" because of shared incentives, not coordination. [cite:de1_tablet] In a later interview he defined it in one line: "The cathedral is essentially the reification of the legitimate sources of information." [cite:de6_wbur] Nick Land, who popularised the term in 2012, credited it to him: "Moldbug calls it the Cathedral." [cite:de6_audit_land] Its creed, in Yarvin's account, is "Universalism," a secular descendant of New England Protestantism. [scene:de7_what_it_gets_right|Part Seven] weighs how much of the diagnosis survives scrutiny; [scene:de8_tests_it_fails|Part Eight] shows why critics find it unfalsifiable.

The design: neocameralism, the CEO-monarch and Patchwork

If power cannot be abolished, Yarvin's next step went, it should be owned. He called his model "neocameralism," after the cameralism of eighteenth-century Prussia, in which the state's finances were managed as a royal estate. Land's summary of Moldbug's definition is the clearest: "To a neocameralist, a state is a business which owns a country." Ownership is divided into shares, "each share has one vote, and the shareholders elect a board, which hires and fires managers," and the residents are customers. [cite:de6_land_ebook] [cite:de6_audit_land] Yarvin made the point with a fictional country: "Fnargland is a business. Like any business, it has no reason at all to alienate its customers." [cite:de6_le_contra] A passage Land reproduces without naming its source says that neocameralism "has never been tried" and that its nearest equivalents were Frederick the Great's Prussia and "Hong Kong, Singapore and Dubai." [cite:de6_land_ebook] [cite:de1_audit_land_unattrib]

At the head of such a state sits a chief executive with full authority, the figure Yarvin's "Open Letter to Open-Minded Progressives" of 2008, by Kofman's count about 120,000 words, called a "CEO-monarch." [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] He has not changed the model's core. In May 2025 he told CNN that the monarch "should operate like a startup CEO," answerable to a board rather than to voters. [cite:de6_cnn_2025] [cite:de8_cnn_yarvin] Kofman reported the safeguard he proposes against a bad ruler: a board, kept secret, that can select and recall the chief executive and holds cryptographic keys able to disable the government's weapons. [cite:de8_kofman_ny] The weakness of that safeguard is examined in [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight].

Patchwork, the series that began on 13 November 2008, scaled the design down and multiplied it. Large states would give way to a patchwork of small ones, "each governed by its own joint-stock corporation without regard to the residents' opinions," competing for residents who would have a single remedy: "If residents don't like their government, they can and should move." [cite:de2_le] This is the idea of exit in its purest form. The economist Albert Hirschman had distinguished "exit," leaving an organisation one dislikes, from "voice," trying to change it from within; Yarvin's design abolishes voice and relies on exit alone, the formula Land compressed to "No voice, free exit." [cite:de6_audit_land] Kofman reported that he still describes the end state as statelets "like Singapore or Dubai." [cite:de6_kofman_nuso]

The route: RAGE

Patchwork imagined new states; the route Yarvin proposed for the existing one was a takeover. In 2012, at a technology "unconference" called BIL, he gave a talk on how to reboot the American government. Corey Pein, writing in 2014, recorded its central lines: "If Americans want to change their government, they're going to have to get over their dictator phobia"; what the country needed was "a national CEO" or "what's called a dictator"; "There's really no other solution." Yarvin even proposed two, one for Republican states and one for Democratic ones. [cite:de6_pein_2014] The first step of the takeover was to "Retire All Government Employees," which he abbreviated RAGE. [cite:de6_tnr_duran] The acronym has only ever meant that; a version that expands it as "Random Acts of Government Efficiency" circulates online and is wrong. The idea travelled quickly: an online petition to the White House drafted later by the programmer Justine Tunney took its first demand, to retire all government employees, verbatim from the talk. [cite:de6_pein_2014]

How a leader would take that power was left vague in the early texts, and the vagueness matters. In his 2009 "Gentle Introduction" series Yarvin described the reaction's task as persuasion: "All the Reaction must do is convince reasonable, educated men and women of good will." Power, once won, would be held by a party "only as long as it takes to hire a qualified administrator." [cite:de6_le_contra] In his 2025 interviews the route ran through an election. A president, he told the New York Times, would take the kind of power he believed Franklin Roosevelt had demanded in 1933, which he paraphrased as "give me absolute power or I'll take it anyway." [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] The civil service would be wound down "like a company that goes out of business, but sort of more so," its former officials treated as ordinary people who had served a bad regime. A new regime "can't be" about bayoneting professors, he said; "Winning means these are your people now." [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] CNN reported a harder note from 2022: the image of loyal "ninjas" who would "seize all points of power, without respect for paper protections." [cite:de6_cnn_2025]

What changed, and what did not

Between 2012 and 2025 the words softened and the design did not. The 2012 talk asked Americans to get over their "dictator phobia"; the 2025 interviews spoke of national chief executives, "monarch" as a "neutral term," and a democracy that is not bad but "very weak." [cite:de6_pein_2014] [cite:de1_nyt_interview] The single executive with full authority, accountable to a board rather than to voters, and the retirement of the civil service, appear in both. Whether that change of vocabulary is a reversal or a repackaging is a judgement [scene:de6_claims_vs_record|the last section of this part] sets out with his own explanation beside it.

One more distinction belongs here because it is so often lost. In 2025 the federal government cut its workforce sharply and claimed broad new powers over the civil service, and many commentators described this as RAGE carried out. The resemblance is real; provenance is another matter. No published document shows a line of descent from the 2012 talk to any order or plan of 2025; the only reported link is an anonymous adviser's remark that the people designing the cuts had read him. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] Rhyme is not provenance. [scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|Part Thirty-Two] sets RAGE beside Schedule F and its successors clause by clause, and [scene:de33_two_tests|Part Thirty-Five] asks what the cuts actually achieved.

sections.h: The Hard Posts
sections.html:
Five passages from Unqualified Reservations account for most of what is said about Yarvin's character, by critics and defenders alike. Each is set out here in the same way: the date and title of the post, a short quotation in his own words, the context in which he wrote it as far as it can be established, his own later account where he has given one, and what his critics say. The quotations are kept short and exact. They are neither softened nor sharpened, and where a widely repeated version of a passage is not what he wrote, the section says so.

"Why I am not a white nationalist," 22 November 2007

The title is a denial, and the denial is real. "I am not a white nationalist," Yarvin wrote, "because I don't find white nationalism useful or effective." [cite:de6_le_contra] The grounds he gave were practical and epistemic rather than moral: he did not find it effective, and he wrote that it "distorts reality." [cite:de6_audit_le] In the same essay he wrote: "It should be obvious that, although I am not a white nationalist, I am not exactly allergic to the stuff," and described it as "the most marginalized and socially excluded belief system in the history of the world." [cite:de6_land_ebook] He listed white-nationalist blogs for readers, described sites such as VDARE as "thoughtful, well-written commentary" and wrote of feeling "the urge to defend" the ideology, while declining to link to what he called "out-and-out racist blogs" with their "racial epithets, anti-Semitism." [cite:de6_audit_mm] [cite:de6_audit_land] Nick Land, an admirer, read the essay as rejecting white nationalism "on grounds that owe nothing to conventional reflexes." [cite:de6_audit_land]

In January 2025 David Marchese of the New York Times read him a line from his own writing, "It is strategically barren," and answered that the trouble with white nationalism is that it is racist; Yarvin did not take up the point. [cite:de6_audit_nyt] Critics take the essay as the clearest statement of his sympathy: Media Matters titled its account of his 2021 Fox Nation appearance with the phrase "self-described defender of white nationalism," and the journalist Corey Pein wrote that his doctrine was "steeped in pseudoscientific racism." [cite:de6_mm_2021] [cite:de2_pein2017] The text supports a plain description: he rejected the label and white nationalism as a political project as ineffective and as distorting, not as wrong, and wrote with open sympathy for its arguments about race. Both halves belong in any honest summary, and this book prints them together.

"Patchwork: A Positive Vision (Part 1)," 13 November 2008

The passage that circulates online as the "Fris Corp" quotation is real. In the first instalment of Patchwork, discussing what a profit-seeking sovereign corporation running a city such as San Francisco would do with its surplus residents, those who cost more than they pay, Yarvin wrote: "Sell their slums out from under them, obviously;" then "demo everything, spray for roaches, rodents, and pit bulls," "smooth the rubble out with a bulldozer or two, and possibly a little aerial bombing," and "erect new residential districts suitable for Russian oligarchs." These people, he added, "can of course emigrate to any other realm in the Patchwork," and then conceded the catch himself: "This presumes, however, that said realm is willing to accept them." [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de6_audit_le] The scholar Vincent Lê, who quotes the passage with its source, reads it as leaving such residents with no realm willing to take them. [cite:de6_audit_le]

The passage is written in a mocking register, and it describes a hypothetical, not a plan for any real city. It is nevertheless a description, by its author, of how his preferred kind of sovereign would treat poor residents: dispossession and demolition, with bombing offered in passing. No later account by Yarvin explaining or withdrawing it is on record. [cite:de6_le_contra]

"Patchwork 2: Profit strategies for our new corporate overlords," 20 November 2008

A week later he returned to the same residents. He raised converting them "into biodiesel, which can help power the Muni buses," San Francisco's public buses, and then said he was "just kidding." [cite:de6_tnr_duran] The post did not stop there. "Our goal, in short, is a humane alternative to genocide," he wrote, and the best humane alternative he offered was to "virtualize" such people: to hold them in "permanent solitary confinement," connected to an "immersive virtual-reality interface." [cite:de6_tnr_duran] [cite:de2_tnr] Ava Kofman, in The New Yorker, reports that the post itself framed the aim as reaching the same result as mass murder without its moral stigma. [cite:de6_audit_kofman]

The disclaimer is inside the post itself, and it attaches to the biodiesel line. The stated goal and the confinement proposal that follow it are not marked as jokes. The text supports saying, in plain words, that Yarvin proposed the indefinite solitary confinement of people a sovereign corporation found unproductive, and presented it as preferable to killing them. Defenders call the post satire; the reading remains disputed, and [scene:de6_claims_vs_record|the last section] grades it as such. [cite:de6_tnr_duran] Whether that confinement amounts to anything that exists today is examined, rung by rung, in [scene:de35_the_consequence_ladder|Part Thirty-Seven].

"Why Carlyle Matters," July 2009

In July 2009 Yarvin published two essays on the Victorian writer Thomas Carlyle, whose case for strong rule he credited with his turn away from democracy; they were later collected, with a third, as Moldbug on Carlyle, a 2010 compilation now held by Princeton University Library. [cite:de3_princeton_carlyle] [cite:de6_princeton] [cite:de3_tait] In "Why Carlyle Matters" he wrote: "Not all humans are born the same, of course," and "the innate character and intelligence of some is more suited to mastery than slavery. For others, it is more suited to slavery." "A person makes a good slave if he is loyal, patient, and not exceptionally bright or stubborn." He attributed what he called "this broad pattern of observation" to heredity: it was "most parsimoniously explained by genetic differences." [cite:de6_mm_2021] [cite:de3_audit_mm]

These lines are in Yarvin's own voice, quoted in a block from the post, not lines of Carlyle's that he was reporting. The paragraph that precedes them in the original, which would show how he introduced the passage and what "pattern" he meant, could not be verified, and the reading here goes no further than the quoted words. What those words say is plain enough: that fitness to be a master or a slave is, for some people, innate and hereditary. That is a defence of natural hierarchy in its oldest form. In 2016, during the dispute over his invitation to the LambdaConf programming conference, he wrote that he was not an "outspoken advocate for slavery," a racist, a sexist or a fascist, putting the first phrase in quotation marks as his accusers' words. [cite:de6_audit_wiki] In 2025, pressed by Marchese on his writing that the Civil War had not made "anyone's life more pleasant, including that of freed slaves," he said that abolition "was a necessary step to get through that period." When Marchese called his own position on slavery "very morally clear," Yarvin replied that the interviewer was responding "in this kind of cartoonish way." [cite:de6_audit_nyt]

A sentence often attributed to him, that "some races are better suited for slavery than others," does not appear in the post. It is a paraphrase that has circulated as a quotation, and it is wrong as a quotation: the verified text speaks of individuals and of heredity, not of races by name. The correction does not make the passage milder; it makes the record accurate. [cite:de6_mm_2021] [cite:de3_mm]

"Right-wing terrorism as folk activism," 23 July 2011

On 22 July 2011 Anders Behring Breivik killed seventy-seven people in Norway, with a bomb in Oslo and a shooting at a political youth summer camp. [cite:de6_mm_2021] The next day Yarvin published a post about the attack. He called Breivik a terrorist, "ABB is a terrorist. Nelson Mandela is a terrorist," and argued that no one who condoned "Che, Stalin, Mao, or any other leftist murderer" had standing to demand that the right disown "a rightist who didn't even make triple digits"; he made the point with a vulgar line aimed at such critics. [cite:de6_mm_2021] [cite:de6_audit_mm] He also wrote: "At least he shot communists, not Muslims. He gored the matador and not the cape." [cite:de5_pein_baffler] [cite:de6_mm_2021] The journalist James Pogue, in Vanity Fair in 2022, summarised the post's objection: the killings were condemned "not on the grounds that terrorism is wrong but because the killings wouldn't do anything effective to overthrow" the Norwegian government. [cite:de6_audit_wiki]

A widely repeated claim says that Yarvin endorsed Breivik. The post does not; it calls him a terrorist. Its offence is different and is on the page: it judged a massacre at a youth camp by its usefulness, and used it to argue that Mandela deserved the same verdict. In 2025, asked about the post, Yarvin held the same equivalence and put it more soberly: "I prefer to condemn them both," since both, he said, killed innocent people. [cite:de6_nyt_transcript]

Read together, the five posts show a consistent habit: a provocation stated flatly, a qualification or a joke, and an argument that continues after the joke. They show contempt for democratic equality, sympathy for race science, and a willingness to describe the coercion of unwanted people, sometimes in comic dress, as administration. They do not show a call to violence by his readers, and in 2009 he described the reaction's task as persuasion. [cite:de6_le_contra] How his public statements about these texts compare with the texts themselves is the subject of the last section.

sections.h: His Claims Against His Record
sections.html:
Yarvin has spent nearly two decades explaining himself: that he is not a white nationalist, that a notorious passage was a joke, that his revolution needs no violence, that his influence is small, that his words about Peter Thiel meant something gentler than they sounded. This section tests those public claims against his own texts and against the documented record, using the same four grades the book applies to every person it examines. RED marks a claim contradicted by the person's own documents or sworn record. ORANGE marks a promise or claim not delivered, or not verifiable by the official auditor. YELLOW marks a reversal or concealment, shown with the person's own explanation. GREY marks a dispute in which credible accounts conflict, with both shown. The word "lie" is used only where the record shows the person knew a claim was false when making it; nothing below meets that bar, and the flags name contradictions for the reader to judge.

Flags on what he advocates

"Not a white nationalist" (22 November 2007): GREY. The claim is his own and stands: "I am not a white nationalist because I don't find white nationalism useful or effective." [cite:de6_le_contra] The record is the same essay, in which he was "not exactly allergic to the stuff," listed white-nationalist blogs for readers and wrote of "the urge to defend" it. [cite:de6_land_ebook] [cite:de6_audit_mm] Both are true at once. The denial is real, its grounds are tactical and epistemic (he wrote that white nationalism "distorts reality") rather than moral, and either half quoted alone misleads; [cite:de6_audit_le] Land, an admirer, and Media Matters, a critic, read the same pages in opposite directions. [cite:de6_land_ebook] [cite:de6_mm_2021]

"Just kidding" (20 November 2008): GREY. The joke marker is his own, written into the post after the line about converting surplus residents "into biodiesel." [cite:de6_tnr_duran] The record is that the post continues, unmarked, to its stated goal, "a humane alternative to genocide," and to a proposal of "permanent solitary confinement" in virtual reality. [cite:de6_tnr_duran] Defenders read the whole as satire; critics, including Kofman, read the confinement proposal as meant. [cite:de6_kofman_nuso] The disclaimer covers less of the passage than its defenders claim, and the dispute is real.

Slavery: "not an outspoken advocate" (2016) and "a necessary step" (2025): GREY. In 2016 he wrote that he was not an "outspoken advocate for slavery," a racist, a sexist or a fascist; in 2025 he called abolition "a necessary step to get through that period." [cite:de6_audit_wiki] [cite:de6_audit_nyt] The record is his 2009 sentence, in his own voice, that some people are by nature "more suited to mastery than slavery," with the pattern "most parsimoniously explained by genetic differences." [cite:de6_mm_2021] The 2016 wording is narrow enough to be literally consistent with the 2009 text, which describes a hierarchy rather than calling for slavery's return; whether it is a fair account of that text is disputed, and the paragraph introducing the 2009 passage could not be verified.

A revolution without violence: GREY. Siegel summarised the regime change Yarvin proposes as one "achieved without any violence or even activism," and in 2009 Yarvin wrote that the reaction need only "convince reasonable, educated men and women of good will." [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] [cite:de6_le_contra] In 2025 he said a new regime "can't be" about bayoneting professors: "Winning means these are your people now." [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] The record also contains the 2012 call for a "national CEO" or "what's called a dictator," the 2008 passages on "a little aerial bombing" of slums and the confinement of the unproductive, and, as CNN reported, a 2022 image of loyalists who "seize all points of power, without respect for paper protections." [cite:de6_pein_2014] [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de6_cnn_2025] The two can be reconciled only partly. His stated method of taking power is persuasion and election, not insurrection; the order he would build rests on power exercised without legal limit and on coercion of residents who do not fit. Credible readings differ on which is the real program, and both are recorded.

"Dictator" (2012) to "democracy is very weak" (2025): GREY. In 2012 he told Americans they would "have to get over their dictator phobia." [cite:de6_pein_2014] In 2025 he said "it's not even that democracy is bad, it's just that it's very weak," called "monarch" a neutral term and described past presidents as "basically national CEOs." [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] [cite:de1_nyt_interview] The tone is softer; the design is the same. The 2012 talk already used "a national CEO" as another name for "what's called a dictator"; in 2025 he kept the first phrase and left the second unspoken, and when Marchese called "CEO" his "friendlier term for a dictator," he answered that "monarch" is "a neutral term" (the published transcript does not label speakers, and the attribution follows the run of the exchange). [cite:de6_pein_2014] [cite:de6_audit_nyt] A single executive with full authority, answerable to a board rather than to voters, appears in both, as does the retirement of the civil service. [cite:de6_cnn_2025] Because he has not abandoned the earlier design, this is not a reversal; critics read the new wording as a rebranding of the old program, and he presents it as a neutral description of it. His own explanation is that a monarch must be "the president of all Americans" and that it is "not exactly time for that yet." [cite:de6_nyt_transcript]

Flags on his influence and his ties

His influence: GREY. In January 2025 he said "how I measure my influence is that I try not to," called himself an outsider, and said his friendship with Vance was "definitely overstated." [cite:de5_politico_ward] [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] [cite:de1_nyt_interview] In the same weeks he said people who read him young "are getting jobs more easily," and in May that his influence ran "more through the kids in the administration." [cite:de5_politico_ward] [cite:de6_cnn_2025] These statements are more consistent than they are often made to sound: he claims indirect influence through staff, not influence over principals. The record fits the narrower claim. He holds no office, a Vance adviser says the two met "like once," and the claim about staff rests on his word and on one anonymous adviser quoted by the Washington Post. [cite:de6_cnn_2025] [cite:de5_kofman_nuso]

"Coaching Thiel" (2016) to "fully disenchanted" (2025): YELLOW. In private emails published in 2017, he wrote that he had been "coaching Thiel" and that Thiel was "fully enlightened, just plays it very carefully." [cite:de5_pein_baffler] In 2025 he said that for him "fully enlightened" means "fully disenchanted." [cite:de1_nyt_interview] The later gloss reinterprets his own earlier words, and it is shown here with them. Thiel's side of the record runs against the 2016 boast: he is reported as saying in 2023 that Yarvin's ideas would not "work." [cite:de6_cnn_2025]

Steve Bannon (2017): GREY. Reports in 2017 said Yarvin was advising Bannon; Yarvin denied them. [cite:de5_tablet_siegel] No document of contact has been published, and neither account can be preferred on the record.

Urbit: a founder's farewell (2019) to "wartime C.E.O." (2024): YELLOW. In January 2019 he left Tlon in a post titled "A Founder's Farewell," presenting his departure as the founder stepping back. [cite:de5_kumin_mars] In August 2024 he returned to take control without a title, and senior staff resigned. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] The accounts tie the return to a crisis, the Foundation having run out of money, and his own description of the period was "real Roman times." [cite:de5_audit_rettig] [cite:de5_audit_marbl] The episode ended on 9 October 2025, when the galaxy owners replaced the Urbit Foundation's board and a new director succeeded him as he left to found a company; [scene:de23_wartime_ceo|Part Twenty-Three] tells it in full. [cite:de23_epoch_2025]

Breivik: no flag. In 2011 he wrote "ABB is a terrorist. Nelson Mandela is a terrorist"; in 2025 he said "I prefer to condemn them both." [cite:de6_mm_2021] [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] His position has been consistent. The record against him on this post is what he wrote in 2011, not a change of story.

The absence of RED and ORANGE flags is a finding, not a gap. Yarvin has never held an office that required sworn statements, filed accounts with an auditor, or made public promises that an official body could check; most of what he says about himself can be tested only against what he has written. Tested that way, the pattern is not one of outright contradiction. It is a pattern of denials that are narrower than they sound, and of a vocabulary that has dropped "dictator" for "monarch" and "national CEO" while the design underneath stayed where it was.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis this book tests holds that a sovereign executive without a veto is the destination. On that point this part's material is direct. Documented: the destination is in the texts, in Yarvin's own words, from the CEO-monarch of 2008 and the "national CEO" or "dictator" of 2012 to the startup-CEO monarch of 2025, answerable to a board and not to voters, with the civil service retired. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] [cite:de6_pein_2014] [cite:de6_cnn_2025] [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] Also documented: that the same texts describe, for a hypothetical sovereign corporation, the dispossession of poor residents and the permanent confinement of people judged unproductive, and that no withdrawal of those passages by the author is on record. [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de6_tnr_duran] Whether his softer vocabulary since 2020 reflects a change of view or a change of audience is a question about motive that the record does not settle; his own explanation is recorded above, and the book does not grade it as probable either way.

Not supported, on this part's material: that the texts contain a program for immigration enforcement or for surveillance of critics. The surplus residents of Patchwork are a company-city's poor, not migrants, and reading those passages as an immigration plan goes beyond what they say. [cite:de2_le] [cite:de6_le_contra] Not supported either: that Yarvin called on readers to use violence, which his texts do not do, or that the federal cuts of 2025 descend from RAGE, which remains a resemblance without a documented line of transmission. [scene:de8_tests_it_fails|Part Eight] tests whether the design would work; [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three] carries these grades into the book's final account. First, [scene:de7_what_it_gets_right|Part Seven] gives the diagnosis its strongest form.

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: The Diagnosis, Steelmanned
chapters.intro: Part Seven gives the Dark Enlightenment its strongest hearing. It separates the texts' diagnosis, that American democracy no longer does what it claims, from their cure, and tests the diagnosis against the record: the collapse of public trust since the 1960s, the government's own audits of failed delivery, the growth of rules written by agencies, the long dispute over whether policy follows voters or the affluent, and Franklin Roosevelt's 1933 inaugural, the precedent Curtis Yarvin cites for an executive who takes power from Congress. It then reads the same symptoms the other way, as capture by concentrated money and by platforms that charge rent, and asks what each reading implies for a cure that would concentrate power further.
chapters.outro: Part Seven established that the diagnosis holds in its weaker form. Trust in the federal government fell from 77 per cent in 1964 to 17 per cent in 2025; the government's auditors document failures of delivery; federal rules grew from 22,877 pages in 1960 to 188,346 in 2021 while the civilian workforce stayed the size it was in the mid-1960s; and when the affluent and everyone else disagree, the affluent have an edge, though how large an edge is disputed. [cite:de7_pew_trust2025] [cite:de7_gao_highrisk2025] [cite:de7_cei_cfr] [cite:de7_kamarck_size] [cite:ad15_jr_gilens] [cite:de7_branham_ifs] Roosevelt's 1933 request, the texts' favourite precedent, was conditional, answered by specific statutes and checked by the courts and the Senate. [cite:de7_fdr_1933] [cite:de7_brit_schechter] [cite:de7_ncc_courtpack] The same evidence fits a second diagnosis, capture by concentrated money, which the texts themselves describe as "vote buying" and propose to convert into shares in the state. [cite:de7_land_de] [cite:us3_os_lobby2025] If that reading is even partly right, the cure would complete the concentration rather than reverse it. Part Eight tests the cure. [scene:de8_tests_it_fails|Part Eight: the tests it fails]

sections.h: What the Diagnosis Gets Right
sections.html:
An argument is only tested fairly in its strongest form. The Dark Enlightenment texts make two separate claims, and they stand or fall separately. The first is a diagnosis: that American democracy no longer does what it says it does, that the people who formally govern are not the people who actually decide, and that the machinery has grown too large and too diffuse for anyone to answer for it. The second is a cure: a state run like a company, under a chief executive answerable to its owners rather than to voters. This part takes the diagnosis on its own terms and asks how much of it the record supports. The next part tests the cure.

Curtis Yarvin, writing as Mencius Moldbug, put the diagnosis in two words. "The Cathedral" was his name for the universities, the press and the permanent civil service, which in his account govern together as an unelected establishment through shared assumptions rather than a chain of command. "Formalism" was his name for the remedy's first step: making the official map of power match the real one, so that whoever actually rules does so openly and can be held to account. Nick Land, summarising the neoreactionary case in 2012, wrote that "winning elections is overwhelmingly a matter of vote buying" and that democracy drives the state ever larger. [cite:de7_land_de] [cite:de7_audit_land] In an interview with the New York Times in January 2025, Yarvin offered a milder version: "it's not even that democracy is bad, it's just that it's very weak." [cite:de7_yarvin_nyt2025] That second sentence is the strongest form of the diagnosis, and it is the one tested here.

Trust has collapsed

The first piece of evidence is that most Americans agree with the symptom, whatever they think of the cause. When the American National Election Studies first asked in 1958 how often people trusted the federal government to do what is right, 73 per cent said always or most of the time; in 1964 the figure reached 77 per cent, the highest in the series. In the Pew Research Center's survey completed on 28 September 2025 it was 17 per cent: 2 per cent "just about always" and 15 per cent "most of the time." Among Republicans it was 26 per cent; among Democrats, 9 per cent. [cite:de7_pew_trust2025]

Confidence in particular institutions has followed the same path. Gallup's average across nine institutions it has tracked since 1979 stood at 48 per cent in that first year and 28 per cent in its July 2025 reading, with Democrats' confidence at a record low of 26 per cent. [cite:de7_gallup_conf2025] In September 2026, 54 per cent of Americans told Gallup they had not very much or no trust in the judicial branch; trust in the courts first fell below half in September 2022, never before in a series that began in 1972. [cite:us2_axios_gallup2026]

The state struggles to deliver

The second piece of evidence is that the federal government often fails at things it sets out to do, and its own auditors say so. When the Government Accountability Office, the investigative arm of Congress, examined the launch of HealthCare.gov in October 2013, it found that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services had built the site and its supporting systems "without effective planning or oversight practices." Obligations for the core marketplace system rose from $56 million in September 2011 to more than $209 million by February 2014, and a replacement contract awarded for $91 million in January 2014 had passed $175 million by June. [cite:de7_gao_hcgov] In February 2025 the GAO listed 38 areas of government operations with serious vulnerabilities to waste, fraud or mismanagement, and reported that federal agencies had recorded an estimated $2.8 trillion in improper payments since 2003. [cite:de7_gao_highrisk2025]

What the GAO describes is not a government that has grown in people. Elaine Kamarck of the Brookings Institution reported in January 2025 that federal civilian employment "has stayed the same since the mid-1960s," falling from 1.1 per cent of the population in 1967 to 0.6 per cent in 2018, while the population grew by about two-thirds. The work moved to contractors, who by one estimate outnumber federal employees by more than two to one; federal contract spending was $694.2 billion in fiscal 2022. At the Social Security Administration, staff fell from nearly 67,000 in 2010 to 56,645 in 2024. [cite:de7_kamarck_size] This complicates the diagnosis in an important way. The texts describe a bloated bureaucracy; the record describes a thin one, carrying more work through contractors it struggles to oversee.

The rules grew; the people writing them did not

What did grow was the volume of rules. The Code of Federal Regulations, the compilation of standing federal rules, ran to 22,877 pages in 1960, 71,224 in 1975, 157,972 in 2008 and 188,346 at the end of 2021, by the count of the Competitive Enterprise Institute, a free-market group, from Office of the Federal Register data. [cite:de7_cei_cfr] Page counts measure length, not burden, and many pages replace older rules rather than adding new ones. But the direction is not in dispute, and it supports a real part of the diagnosis: much of what governs daily life is written by agencies rather than voted on by Congress.

The Dark Enlightenment texts did not discover the accountability problem that follows from this. In 1980 the political theorist Dennis Thompson named it "the problem of many hands" in the American Political Science Review: when outcomes are produced by many officials each doing a small part, it becomes hard to say who is responsible for any of them. [cite:de7_thompson_hands] The idea is a staple of mainstream public administration. Moldbug's version adds a claim Thompson did not make, that the diffusion is the purpose of the design rather than a cost of it; that further claim is his, and the record does not show it.

Who government listens to

The most cited evidence for the diagnosis is a 2014 study by the political scientists Martin Gilens and Benjamin Page. They matched 1,779 policy questions asked in surveys between 1981 and 2002 against what the government later did. They found that average citizens had little or no independent influence on outcomes once the preferences of the affluent and of organised interests were taken into account: a change opposed by economic elites passed about 18 per cent of the time, one they strongly favoured about 45 per cent, and business groups had roughly twice the influence of mass-membership groups. [cite:ad15_jr_gilens]

The finding has been seriously disputed, and the dispute matters for what it can carry. Peter Enns showed that the preferences of middle-income and affluent Americans were correlated at 0.94 across 1,836 survey questions, so the middle usually gets what it wants because the affluent want the same thing; he called this "coincidental representation." [cite:ad15_enns] Omar Bashir found that the model explained only about 7 per cent of the variation in outcomes, and that when median-income Americans strongly favoured a change it happened 47 per cent of the time, against 52 per cent for the affluent. [cite:ad15_bashir] J. Alexander Branham, Stuart Soroka and Christopher Wlezien found that the two groups agreed about 90 per cent of the time and that when they disagreed the rich won 53 per cent of the time, "only a little more often than the middle." [cite:de7_branham_ifs] Gilens and Page replied that none of these critiques, "individually or collectively," undermined their central claims. [cite:de7_gp_reply] What survives the exchange is narrower than the headline: when the affluent and everyone else disagree, the affluent have an edge. The stronger reading, that ordinary voters count for nothing, is contested.

The precedent: Roosevelt in 1933

The diagnosis comes with a precedent, and Yarvin returns to it often. On 4 March 1933, with the banking system collapsing, Franklin Roosevelt said in his first inaugural address that he hoped "the normal balance of executive and legislative authority" would be enough. If Congress failed to act on his measures and the emergency remained critical, he said, he would ask Congress for "broad Executive power to wage a war against the emergency, as great as the power that would be given to me if we were in fact invaded by a foreign foe." [cite:de7_fdr_1933] Yarvin told the New York Times that he reads this passage aloud in talks, and summarised it as Roosevelt saying, "hey, Congress, give me absolute power or I'll take it anyway." Asked whether Roosevelt took it, he said, "Yeah, he did." [cite:de7_yarvin_nyt2025] [cite:de7_audit_nyt]

The precedent is real, and it is the honest core of the case for an executive-centred fix: in a genuine emergency, Americans accepted a president who acted fast and asked Congress to follow. But the record is narrower than the paraphrase. Roosevelt's request was conditional and addressed to Congress, and it was never made in that form, because Congress acted. The Emergency Banking Act was introduced and passed on 9 March 1933, five days after the speech; it expanded the president's powers over banking and approved the bank holiday after the fact. [cite:de7_frb_eba] The powers that followed came statute by statute, and they stayed subject to the other branches. On 27 May 1935 the Supreme Court unanimously struck down the codes of the National Industrial Recovery Act as an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power. [cite:de7_brit_schechter] When Roosevelt answered with a plan announced on 5 February 1937 to add up to six justices, the Senate Judiciary Committee called it "an invasion of judicial power such as has never before been attempted in this country," and the Senate shelved it that July. [cite:de7_ncc_courtpack] After he won a third and a fourth term, the country amended the Constitution so that no president could be elected more than twice. [cite:de8_annenberg_22]

Taken together, the diagnosis holds in its weaker form. Americans have lost faith in their government; the government's own auditors document failures of delivery; rule-making has outgrown direct democratic control; responsibility is genuinely diffuse; and on the best evidence the affluent are heard more than everyone else when they disagree. What the record does not show is the further step the texts take: that the cause is democracy itself, rather than a particular way in which American democracy has come to be run. The next section reads the same symptoms the other way. [scene:de7_the_other_diagnosis|The other diagnosis]

sections.h: The Other Diagnosis: Capture, Not Too Much Democracy
sections.html:
The symptoms set out in the previous section can be read in two ways. The Dark Enlightenment texts read them as proof that democracy itself is the disease: power hidden behind elections, and a state that grows because voters can be bought. A second reading, held by critics on both the left and the right, takes the same facts and draws the opposite conclusion. On this account the trouble is not that the public has too much say but that it has too little, because influence has been concentrated in the hands of those who can pay for it. If that reading is right, a cure that concentrates power further would make the disease worse. This section sets out the second diagnosis, the evidence for it and its weaknesses, and then asks what the two readings mean for the texts' proposed cure.

Money as the mechanism

Gilens and Page did not conclude that voters were powerless because democracy is weak by nature. Their finding was that economic elites and organised groups representing business carried the weight, and that mass-membership groups carried much less. [cite:ad15_jr_gilens] Replying to their critics in 2016, they restated the finding as one about who holds influence: "Economic elites and interest groups can shape U.S. government policy," while "Americans who are less well off have essentially no influence." That is a claim about how influence is distributed, not about whether voting can work. [cite:de7_gp_reply] The record of money in American politics since their study gives that reading something to stand on. On 21 January 2010, in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, the Supreme Court struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations, holding that such expenditures do not give rise to corruption or its appearance. [cite:ad15_lii_cu] Federal lobbying reached a record of about $5 billion in 2025, up 14 per cent on the year before, according to OpenSecrets' analysis of disclosure reports. [cite:us3_os_lobby2025]

Spending is also concentrated in a small number of hands, on both sides. In the 2024 election cycle, OpenSecrets recorded more than $291 million in political giving from Elon Musk to Republican candidates, committees and outside groups. Timothy Mellon, Miriam Adelson, Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, Kenneth Griffin and Jeffrey and Janine Yass each gave $100 million or more, all on the Republican side. On the Democratic side, Michael Bloomberg gave $64 million and Dustin Moskovitz $51 million. [cite:de7_os_donors2024] A disclosure record of this kind shows who gave; it does not show what any donor received in return, and that distinction runs through the rest of this book. But it does establish the structure the second diagnosis describes: a political system in which a few people can spend more than most candidates raise.

What is striking is that the Dark Enlightenment texts agree about the mechanism. Land's 2012 serial does not deny that money buys government; it says so more bluntly than any reformer. Winning elections, it states, "is overwhelmingly a matter of vote buying." [cite:de7_land_de] Neocameralism, Moldbug's word for a state run as a joint-stock company, does not propose to stop the buying. In Land's summary, one of its first steps is that "the entire social landscape of political bribery ('lobbying') is exactly mapped," and the privileges those bribes purchase are "converted into fungible shares" in the state. The sovereign's revenue is called by its name: taxes become "sovereign rent." [cite:de7_land_de] Both diagnoses, in other words, name the same mechanism. They part company over the remedy. One proposes to limit what money can buy; the other proposes to give those who already buy influence formal title to the state.

Techno-feudalism and enshittification

A second strand of the counter-diagnosis looks beyond elections to the economy that now surrounds them. The Greek economist Yanis Varoufakis argues in Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism (2023) that capitalism "has not been overthrown but has instead become something else." In his account the owners of digital platforms no longer compete in markets; they own the markets, and draw rent, through what he calls "cloud capital," from everyone who must pass through them, while users, whose clicks and data produce the value, become "cloud serfs." Not every reader accepts the label. Reviewing the book for the Washington Post, the scholar Leif Weatherby wrote that he was "not convinced" capitalism had died, while crediting Varoufakis with posing a real problem. [cite:de7_varoufakis_wapo]

The writer Cory Doctorow described the same dynamic from the user's side and gave it a name that the American Dialect Society chose as its word of the year for 2023: "enshittification." In Doctorow's account, platforms first serve their users well, then turn on those users to serve their business customers, then turn on the business customers to take the value for themselves, and finally decline. [cite:de7_ads_enshit] The pattern depends on one condition: that leaving is costly. Users stay because their contacts, their data or their livelihoods are locked in.

Both writers are making economic arguments, and neither is about the Dark Enlightenment texts. Their relevance here is structural. The texts' model state is a platform in the same sense: residents are "customers," the state's income is "rent," and the only remedy for bad service is to "take their custom elsewhere." [cite:de7_land_de] The techno-feudal critique is, in effect, a description of what happens to customers of a sovereign provider when exit is expensive. It reads the private platforms of the 2020s as a warning about the public one the texts propose.

Two diagnoses, one cure tested

The two readings can be laid side by side. Both start from the same symptom, a government that answers to some citizens far more than others. The Dark Enlightenment traces it to democracy and proposes to replace voting with ownership. The counter-diagnosis traces it to concentrated money and proposes to reduce what money can buy, through campaign-finance rules, disclosure, lobbying limits and, for platforms, competition law. Both cannot be right about the cause, and the evidence of the previous section does not settle which is. It is consistent with either.

The counter-diagnosis has its own weak points, and they should be stated as plainly as the texts'. The studies set out in the previous section found that middle-income and affluent Americans agree most of the time, which limits how much of the gap money can explain. [cite:ad15_enns] [cite:de7_branham_ifs] A record of large donations is not proof that donations bought outcomes; disclosure shows timing and amounts, not motive. And the most direct reform the counter-diagnosis proposes, limiting independent spending, runs into the constitutional ruling in Citizens United, which only the Supreme Court or a constitutional amendment could undo. [cite:ad15_lii_cu]

Even with those limits, the comparison exposes the central weakness of the cure the texts propose. Yarvin has been candid about what it requires. Asked by CNN in May 2025 how his system would prevent a ruler from becoming a tyrant, he said that power must be concentrated "in a single individual" and that one must "then just hope somehow that this is the right individual, or close to the right individual." [cite:de8_cnn_yarvin] [cite:de7_audit_cnn] A cure that depends on hope is the opposite of formalism's own promise, which was to make power visible and accountable. If the counter-diagnosis is even partly right, and influence in America is already concentrated by money, then a state owned by its largest stakeholders and run by one executive would not reverse the concentration. It would complete it. Whether that state could at least be kept honest by its owners is the question of the next part.

The worst-case reading, tested

This part bears on the hypothesis in one direction only: what the texts' destination is and why it might appeal. Documented: the texts describe a real crisis of trust, and their own diagnosis names money and bribery as the mechanism of democratic politics; their stated remedy is to convert that influence into ownership of the state and to remove the vote. [cite:de7_land_de] [cite:de7_pew_trust2025] Documented: Yarvin in 2025 described the remedy as concentrating power in one person and hoping that person is the right one, and used Roosevelt's 1933 inaugural as his precedent for an executive taking power from a reluctant Congress. [cite:de8_cnn_yarvin] [cite:de7_yarvin_nyt2025] Where the record runs against the texts, it does so plainly: Roosevelt asked Congress conditionally, received specific statutes, and was checked by the courts and the Senate. [cite:de7_fdr_1933] [cite:de7_brit_schechter] [cite:de7_ncc_courtpack] Not supported in this part: any link between the diagnosis and the decisions of any government official. The fact that low trust and diffuse accountability are real makes an executive-centred cure easier to sell; it does not show that anyone is selling it. That question belongs to Books Two and Three, beginning with the money in [scene:de14_network_map|the network map] and the creation of the Department of Government Efficiency in [scene:de17_money_to_office|Part Seventeen].

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: Where the Argument Breaks
chapters.intro: Part Eight tests the Dark Enlightenment's cure, a state run as a company under a chief executive answerable to its owners. It checks the states the texts name as models, Singapore and Dubai, against how they are actually governed; sets the design against comparative research on one-person rule, corruption and succession; asks what happened when real companies failed and when companies actually ruled countries; and then turns to the question every form of government must answer, who removes a ruler who goes wrong. It closes with the worst-case reading tested for Book One as a whole.
chapters.outro: Part Eight established that the cure fails the tests the record can set. The texts' models are a party state rated Partly Free and hereditary monarchies rated Not Free, not sovereign companies; on the comparative evidence, rule by one person performs worst on growth and corruption; and failed companies, from Enron to FTX, and the company-states of the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries were corrected by a sovereign power outside them, which the design removes. [cite:de8_fh_sg2026] [cite:de8_fh_uae2026] [cite:de8_nber_w34093] [cite:de8_kn_corruption] [cite:de8_axios_ray] [cite:de8_brit_regact] The texts' only mechanism for removing a bad ruler, a secret board holding keys to disarm the state's weapons, has never been built or tried, and their substitute for the vote, exit, is the response Hirschman found least available to most people. [cite:de8_kofman_ny] [cite:de8_land_de] [cite:de8_hirschman] Book One closes with the end state documented in the texts' own words and nothing yet shown about its adoption. Book Two turns to the people who read and funded these ideas, beginning with Peter Thiel. [scene:de9_formation|Part Nine: Peter Thiel]

sections.h: The Tests It Fails
sections.html:
A diagnosis can be right and a cure still wrong. The Dark Enlightenment's cure is neocameralism, Moldbug's name for a state organised as a joint-stock company. In the passage Land quotes in his 2012 serial, "a state is a business which owns a country." Its ownership is divided into shares, each with one vote; the shareholders elect a board, the board hires and fires the managers, and the residents are the company's customers. [cite:de8_land_de] Because the texts make claims about how such a state would perform, those claims can be checked against states that exist, against the record of one-person rule, against companies that failed, and against the companies that once actually ruled countries. This section runs those four tests.

The models the texts name: Singapore and Dubai

The texts point to living examples. The neocameralist passage Land quotes says that the full approach "has never been tried," and that its closest equivalents are the enlightened absolutism of Frederick the Great and "lost fragments of the British Empire such as Hong Kong, Singapore and Dubai." Those states, it continues, are "weak only in political freedom, and political freedom is unimportant by definition when government is stable and effective." [cite:de8_land_de] Later in the serial Land uses Singapore, Hong Kong, Taipei and Shanghai as his measure of cities where it is safe to walk at night. [cite:de8_land_de] Yarvin has described the end state in the same terms: in Ava Kofman's 2025 account in the New Yorker, he proposes breaking nations into a "patchwork" of statelets, "like Singapore or Dubai," each with its own sovereign ruler. [cite:de8_kofman_ny]

Neither example is what the texts say it is. Singapore is not a company with a chief executive answerable to shareholders. It is a party state. Freedom House rates it Partly Free, 48 out of 100 in its 2026 report, and describes a system "dominated by the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) and the powerful Lee family since 1959," which "allows for some political pluralism" but constrains opposition parties and limits freedoms of expression, assembly and association. [cite:de8_fh_sg2026] Its leaders change by party procedure: on 15 May 2024 Lawrence Wong, chosen as party leader with the unanimous backing of the PAP's members of parliament, became the country's fourth prime minister since 1965, succeeding Lee Hsien Loong. [cite:de8_cnbc_wong] The political scientist Netina Tan describes Singapore as a hegemonic party autocracy whose resilience rests on what one of its own prime ministers called "a planned and orderly system of political succession." [cite:de8_tan_pap] In the standard typology of authoritarian rule developed by Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright and Erica Frantz, which sorts regimes into dominant-party, military, personalist, monarchical and other types, a ruling party with rules for choosing its leaders is a different kind of regime from rule by one person. [cite:de8_wiki_geddes]

Dubai is one of seven emirates in the United Arab Emirates, which Freedom House rates Not Free, 18 out of 100, with political parties banned and "all executive, legislative, and judicial authority" resting ultimately with the seven hereditary rulers. [cite:de8_fh_uae2026] That is a hereditary monarchy, not a joint-stock sovereign; there are no shareholders who can vote a ruler out. The texts' own models, in other words, are a party state and a set of hereditary monarchies. Each achieved order by means the texts reject or never describe: an institutionalised party in one case, dynastic succession in the other.

The evidence on one-person rule

The distinction between a party state and one-person rule matters because the comparative evidence turns on it. In a paper first issued by the National Bureau of Economic Research in August 2025, Christopher Blattman, Scott Gehlbach and Zeyang Yu compared the economic growth of democracies, institutionalised autocracies and personalist autocracies, those in which power sits with one individual or a small clique, across 179 countries from 1960 to 2010. They found that whenever an "autocratic penalty" on growth appears, it is concentrated in personalist regimes; institutionalised dictatorships grew at rates statistically similar to democracies. They traced the penalty to low private investment, weak provision of public goods and conflict. [cite:de8_nber_w34093] [cite:de8_harris_w34093] A 2025 study of 32 countries in Eastern Europe and Latin America by Tatiana Kostadinova and Milena Neshkova found that governments led by personalist leaders were associated with higher grand and petty corruption, and that "the time a regime stays in power intensifies its impact on malfeasance." [cite:de8_kn_corruption]

The record also contains a finding that favours part of the texts' argument, and it belongs here. Studying European monarchies from 1000 to 1800, Andrej Kokkonen and Anders Sundell found that the risk of a monarch being deposed was "several times higher" where the crown did not pass by primogeniture, inheritance by the eldest son, and that the spread of primogeniture largely explains why depositions became rarer. [cite:de8_ks_primogeniture] A settled rule of succession made monarchy more stable. But that is a finding about a rule binding the ruler, not about the ruler's freedom from rules, and neocameralism replaces inheritance with a board that hires and fires. Yarvin, asked by CNN in 2025 how his system would avoid a tyrant, argued that monarchies "don't generally see a Holocaust" and then conceded that it requires concentrating power "in a single individual" and hoping "that this is the right individual." [cite:de8_cnn_yarvin] On the comparative evidence, the design most like the one he proposes is the one that performs worst.

Companies fail too, and something outside them catches the failure

The texts' central analogy is the well-run company, and the analogy has a record of its own. Enron, the seventh-largest company in the United States, collapsed in December 2001 in what was then the largest bankruptcy in American history; on 25 May 2006 a jury in Houston convicted its former chiefs Kenneth Lay, on all six counts against him, and Jeffrey Skilling, on 19 of 28. [cite:de8_aj_enron] When the crypto exchange FTX filed for bankruptcy in November 2022, its new chief executive, John J. Ray III, who had worked on the Enron clean-up, told the court he had never seen "such a complete failure of corporate controls," with control concentrated in "a very small group." [cite:de8_axios_ray] Its founder Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted on seven counts, including fraud, in 2023 and sentenced on 28 March 2024 to 25 years in prison; at least $8 billion in customer funds had been taken. [cite:de8_npr_sbf]

Both companies had boards, shareholders and auditors, and in both the internal controls failed. What ended the damage came from outside the company: prosecutors, juries, bankruptcy courts and regulators, all part of a sovereign state that stood above the firm. A sovereign corporation has nothing above it. Its board would be the highest authority, and the courts, the police and the regulator would be its own departments. The corporate record does not show that boards reliably restrain chief executives; it shows that when they fail, the state catches what they miss.

When companies were sovereigns

The world has run the experiment the texts describe, though not under that name. The Dutch East India Company, the VOC, chartered on 20 March 1602 as one of the first joint-stock companies, held powers to wage war, imprison and execute, make treaties, mint coins and found colonies. Between 1609 and 1621 it conquered the Banda Islands to enforce its monopoly on nutmeg; of an estimated 15,000 inhabitants, about 1,000 remained. Its board was dismissed in 1796 and its charter expired on 31 December 1799, when its possessions and debts passed to the Dutch state. [cite:de8_wiki_voc] The English East India Company, chartered on 31 December 1600, came to govern and tax Bengal. [cite:dv2_wiki_eic] [cite:de8_hh_eic] A famine in 1769–70, made worse by the company's grain monopoly and taxation, killed a number commonly estimated at up to ten million people. [cite:de8_hh_eic]

What followed is the most direct test the texts could ask for. The company's shareholders did not correct its government of Bengal; Parliament did. The Regulating Act of 1773, prompted by "the company's misgovernment of its Bengal lands, brought to a crisis by the threat of bankruptcy" and its request for a government loan, placed the company under parliamentary supervision, created a governor-general and a supreme court, and reformed the shareholders' own voting, raising the qualification to vote from £500 to £1,000 to make it harder for factions to buy control. [cite:de8_brit_regact] After the rebellion of 1857, the Government of India Act of 1858 transferred the company's powers to the Crown, and an Act of Parliament of 1873 wound the company up; it was dissolved on 1 June 1874. [cite:de8_brit_goi] [cite:de8_hh_eic] [cite:dv2_wiki_eic] Each correction came from a sovereign outside the company. A neocameral state, by design, would have none.

Four tests, one pattern. The states the texts hold up as models are a party state and hereditary monarchies, not sovereign companies; the comparative evidence finds that rule by one person performs worst on growth and corruption; companies with boards and shareholders fail, and are caught by a power outside them; and the companies that once ruled territory were corrected, every time, by a state above them. None of this shows that the texts' authors want the failures. It shows that the design they propose removes the outside power that has caught such failures before. The next section asks what, in that design, would take its place. [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Who removes a bad sovereign]

sections.h: Who Removes a Bad Sovereign
sections.html:
Every system of government has to answer one question before any other: what happens when the person at the top goes wrong. A company answers it with a board, shareholders and, behind them, the courts of the state in which the company is registered. A constitutional republic answers it with elections, impeachment, courts, a legislature that controls money, and term limits; the American Constitution provides that a president "shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors." [cite:de8_lii_art2s4] The Dark Enlightenment's state is designed to remove most of those answers, so it must supply its own. This section examines the one it gives, its alternative to the vote, and the answer it rejects.

The problem the texts set themselves

The difficulty begins inside the texts. The neocameral state, as Land's 2012 serial summarises it, rests on what Land calls a "Hobbesian" recognition: that "sovereignty cannot be eliminated, caged, or controlled," that "divided powers flow back together," and that constitutions have "exactly as much real authority as a sovereign interpretative power allows them to have." [cite:de8_land_de] That premise is the texts' case against checks and balances: a written limit on power, they argue, binds only as long as whoever holds power chooses to honour it.

The same premise cuts against the texts' own design. A neocameral state's chief executive is supposed to answer to a board, and the board to shareholders. [cite:de8_land_de] But a charter that says the board may dismiss the executive is itself a written limit on power. If constitutions bind only as far as the sovereign allows, so does a corporate charter, and an executive who controls the police and the army has no more reason to obey a board than a president has to obey a court. The texts therefore need a mechanism that does not depend on anyone's willingness to comply.

Yarvin's answer: the keys

Yarvin's answer is technical. According to Ava Kofman's 2025 account in the New Yorker, legitimacy, accountability and succession in each sovereign corporation would rest with "a secret board with the power to select and recall the otherwise all-powerful C.E.O." To stop a chief executive staging a military coup, "the board members would have access to cryptographic keys that would allow them to disarm all government weapons." [cite:de8_kofman_ny] A summary of his Patchwork writings by a sympathetic reviewer describes the same feature: shareholders holding encryption keys that give access to the national arsenal, and a design said to be stable only with modern cryptography. [cite:de8_kossina_patchwork] CNN, reporting on his views in 2025, summarised the design as a monarch "held accountable by some sort of corporate board, but not by the average citizen." [cite:de8_cnn_yarvin]

The record on this mechanism is short: it has never been built or tested anywhere. The passage Land reproduces without naming its source concedes that the full neocameral approach "has never been tried." [cite:de8_land_de] No state has locked its weapons to keys held by a board, and no evidence exists of how such a system would behave in a crisis. What can be assessed is its logic, and here the following points are reasoning about the design, not findings from a record.

First, the keys do not remove the problem of an unchecked sovereign; they move it. Whoever holds the keys to every weapon in the state is, on the texts' own Hobbesian premise, the real sovereign. If the board can disarm the executive, nothing disarms the board. Second, the board would be secret, by Kofman's account, which is the opposite of the formalism the texts promise: the public would not know who held final power. [cite:de8_kofman_ny] Third, shares in such a state would be transferable, so control could be bought. A critique published in Compact in November 2025 observed that under ordinary corporate law a dominant shareholder can install loyal directors and rewrite a company's constitution, and that the result would be oligarchy, "managerial democracy in corporate drag." [cite:de8_compact_ceo] Fourth, weapons are carried by people. A lock on a device governs the device, not the loyalty of the soldiers and police who carry out orders, and the texts do not explain why those people would obey a remote board rather than the executive in front of them.

Yarvin's one built system of cryptographic ownership and identity is Urbit, a computer network whose first code he released in 2010 and which Tlon, the company he founded in 2013, developed with seed money from investors including Peter Thiel's Founders Fund and Andreessen Horowitz; he left Tlon in 2019. [cite:de8_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] It is the nearest thing to a test his ideas have had. What it shows, and what it does not, is the subject of [scene:de23_address_space|Part Twenty-Three] and [scene:de33_two_tests|Part Thirty-Five]; it governs computers, not people, and it does not test the keys to an arsenal.

Exit instead of voice

The texts' other answer to bad government is not removal but departure. In 1970 the economist Albert Hirschman distinguished two ways people respond when a firm or organisation declines. "Exit" is leaving: customers stop buying, members quit. "Voice" is speaking up: members "express their dissatisfaction directly to management." [cite:de8_hirschman] Land's serial adopts the distinction and chooses one side. Democracy is voice; the neocameral state offers its residents the other. If the state does not deliver value for its "sovereign rent," residents may complain to its customer service and, "if necessary take their custom elsewhere." Land's summary is four words: "No voice, free exit." [cite:de8_land_de]

Hirschman's own book argues against relying on exit alone. "The presence of the exit alternative," he wrote, "can therefore tend to atrophy the development of the art of voice." Those who care most about quality are the most likely to leave first, so the organisation loses its sharpest critics just when it most needs them; and where exit is unavailable, voice becomes the only way members can react. [cite:de8_hirschman] Leaving a country is not like changing brands. It requires another country willing to take you, money to move, and the abandonment of work, family and language, and the texts offer no guarantee that any other sovereign corporation would admit those who leave. The Compact critique made the same point: no one guarantees the right to exit, and a rival's immigration rules could make it meaningless. [cite:de8_compact_ceo] The platforms described in the previous part show what happens to customers who cannot easily leave. [cite:de7_ads_enshit] A state that removes voice and offers only exit removes the response Hirschman found most useful, and leaves the one least available to most people.

The designed answer: checks and balances

The answer the texts reject is the one the American founders wrote down. The Federalist No. 51, published in the New York Packet on 8 February 1788, started from the same distrust of rulers that the Dark Enlightenment claims as its own: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary." Its conclusion was the opposite. A government must first "control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself." The people were "the primary control," and the second was structural: "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition." [cite:de8_fed51] The design does not rely on a single good ruler or a single board. It divides power so that each holder has a motive to resist the others.

It is fair to say that the design has been tested and sometimes strained. The Supreme Court struck down part of Roosevelt's programme in 1935, the Senate shelved his plan to enlarge the Court in 1937, and the states limited presidents to two elected terms in 1951. [cite:de7_brit_schechter] [cite:de7_ncc_courtpack] [cite:de8_annenberg_22] In June 2026 the Supreme Court moved the balance the other way, overruling a 1935 precedent and holding that the President may remove commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission at will. [cite:de0_slaughter] Public trust in the courts that police the system is at a low. [cite:us2_axios_gallup2026] Checks and balances are not self-enforcing either; they depend, as Land's premise says, on people who choose to honour them. The difference is that the constitutional design spreads that choice across many hands, elected and appointed at different times by different people, so that no single defection settles the matter. The neocameral design concentrates it in one board.

The worst-case reading, tested: Book One

Book One asked what the texts say and whether their argument holds. On the worst-case reading, a sovereign executive without a veto is the destination; this book can grade only the first half of that claim, the destination as the texts describe it. Documented: the texts state that end state in their own words. Land's serial, partly in passages it quotes from Moldbug, describes a state owned as a business, run by a chief executive appointed by its owners, in which residents have "no voice" and political freedom is "unimportant by definition." [cite:de8_land_de] Asked in 2025 whether he votes, Yarvin said he did not "believe in actually voting at all," and he told CNN that power should be concentrated "in a single individual." [cite:de8_audit_nyt] [cite:de8_cnn_yarvin] Documented: the texts deny that constitutions can bind a sovereign, and the only removal mechanism they offer, a secret board with keys to the arsenal, has never been built or tried. [cite:de8_land_de] [cite:de8_kofman_ny] Documented: the diagnosis behind the end state is partly real, and the models the texts point to are not what they claim. The hardest passages, on surplus residents and on slavery, are set out in Yarvin's own words in [scene:de6_the_hard_posts|Part Six].

Not supported in Book One: anything about adoption. Nothing in the texts or in this part shows that any official has taken up the program, that the 2025 executive order creating the Department of Government Efficiency or the 2026 ruling on removal power owes anything to these writings, or that any plan connects them. [cite:de0_eo14158] [cite:de0_slaughter] Resemblance between a later policy and a proposal in the texts is rhyme, not provenance. Probable or not is a question this book cannot yet grade, because it depends on documents about people and money that Book One does not examine. Where the record runs against the worst-case reading, Book One says so: Roosevelt's precedent was conditional and checked, the checks held, and the texts' own design for removing a ruler is untested. Book Two turns from the texts to the people who read and funded them, beginning with [scene:de9_formation|Peter Thiel], and Book Three to the machinery built in 2025 and 2026; the verdict is gathered in [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|the worst-case scorecard].

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: Peter Thiel: the Life
chapters.intro: This part tells the life of Peter Thiel, the investor whose money, companies and protégés run through the rest of this book. It begins with a childhood that moved from Frankfurt to Cleveland to the mining towns of apartheid-era southern Africa and on to a California suburb, and follows him through Stanford, where he founded a student paper and met the philosopher René Girard, into law and finance. It then traces the fortune: PayPal, Palantir, the first outside stake in Facebook, and the funds that hold positions in SpaceX, Anduril and Curtis Yarvin's company, keeping each vehicle's money apart from his own. It sets out three episodes the public learned of late, the secret financing of the lawsuit that ended Gawker, a New Zealand citizenship granted after twelve days in the country, and a retirement account grown to about $5 billion, and then his politics from the 2009 essay that doubted democracy to the Senate campaigns of 2022 and his move to Buenos Aires in 2026. The last two sections are a ledger of his documented political money and influence, and a test of his own public claims against the record.
chapters.outro: The life sets the scale and the limits of the man at the centre of the network. Thiel built his fortune from PayPal, which eBay bought for $1.5 billion in 2002, from a $500,000 stake in Facebook that returned more than $1 billion, and from Palantir, which he incorporated in 2003 and still chairs; most of the companies attached to his name in the news are held by funds with outside investors, not by him. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de9_wiki_ff] He paid in secret, and lawfully, for the lawsuit that bankrupted Gawker, became a New Zealand citizen after twelve days in the country, and grew a retirement account from about $1,700 to about $5 billion, which tax specialists dispute but no authority has found unlawful. [cite:de9_tc_gawker] [cite:de9_nbr_12days] [cite:de9_pp_roth] He wrote in 2009 that freedom and democracy were no longer compatible, then spent about $32 million in 2022 behind two former employees' Senate campaigns, one of which made J.D. Vance a senator and, later, Vice President; and in 2026, after meetings with Javier Milei, he moved to Buenos Aires. [cite:de3_cato_thiel] [cite:de9_cnbc_2022] [cite:de9_fortune_ba] Tested against the record, his own claims yield no RED or ORANGE flags, two YELLOW and four GREY: a record of silences and disputed motives rather than of statements disproved. What he believes, and how Girard, the katechon and the Antichrist shape it, is the subject of [scene:de10_education_of_a_libertarian|Part Ten].

sections.h: Frankfurt, Swakopmund, Stanford: The Making of an Investor
sections.html:
Peter Andreas Thiel was born on 11 October 1967 in Frankfurt am Main, in what was then West Germany. His father, Klaus Friedrich Thiel, was a chemical engineer who went on to work for mining companies; his mother was Susanne Thiel. The family moved to the United States when he was about one year old and lived first in Cleveland, Ohio. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] Most of what is known about the next decade comes from biographies and from his own later remarks, and the two need to be kept apart. Where a detail rests on his own account, this section says so; where a detail belongs to his parents rather than to him, it says that too, because a father's employer is part of a child's setting, not part of the child's record.

Southern Africa, 1971–1977

In 1971 the family moved to South West Africa, the territory that became Namibia, then governed by South Africa, and it also lived for a time in South Africa itself. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] Klaus Thiel worked as a project manager on a uranium mine near the coastal town of Swakopmund. The boy attended Pridwin, a whites-only preparatory school in Johannesburg, and then spent two years at the German-language school in Swakopmund. [cite:de9_dm_davis] He changed elementary schools seven times in all.
