He later linked the Swakopmund school, with its strict discipline, to his dislike of regimentation, a remark that rests on his own account and is usually cited as an early root of his libertarian views. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] Max Chafkin, whose 2021 biography The Contrarian is the fullest independent account of these years, wrote that Thiel "often spoke fondly of his childhood in South Africa." [cite:de9_dm_davis] Nothing in the published record documents what a child between four and ten thought about the apartheid system around him, and nothing here suggests otherwise.

The family settled in Foster City, a planned suburb south of San Francisco, in 1977. At Bowditch Middle School he placed first in a statewide mathematics competition, and in 1985 he graduated as valedictorian of San Mateo High School. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel]

Stanford and the Review, 1985–1992

Thiel studied philosophy at Stanford University and graduated in 1989. There he encountered the French literary theorist René Girard, whose "mimetic" theory, that human desire is learned by imitation and that imitation breeds rivalry and violence, strongly influenced him as an undergraduate and has remained central to his thinking. [cite:de9_fortune_antichrist] [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] Girard's place in his thinking, up to the lectures on the Antichrist he gave in 2025, is the subject of [scene:de10_girard_and_the_katechon|Part Ten].

In 1987 he co-founded The Stanford Review, a conservative and libertarian student paper, and served as its first editor-in-chief until he graduated. The paper was launched in the middle of a campus argument over Stanford's decision to replace its required course on Western culture with a broader programme. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] It became a durable node in his later network: David Sacks, who would co-write a book with him and in 2025 became the White House's adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency, wrote for it. [cite:de9_fortune_net24] Who else passed through it, and where they sit now, is mapped in [scene:de13_who_they_are|Part Thirteen].

The apartheid remarks: an allegation and a denial

Two accounts from Stanford concern apartheid, and both are disputed. In November 2016, as Thiel's support for Donald Trump drew attention, Julie Lythcott-Haims, a former Stanford dean who lived in his freshman dormitory in 1985–86, said he had told her that "moral issues were irrelevant" to the apartheid government's economy. A second classmate, Megan Maxwell, said he had told her "you shouldn't judge a government based on whether it fits your view of morality." [cite:de9_wnyc_apartheid] His spokesperson replied: "Peter has never supported apartheid, but he can easily see how a conversation might be misremembered 30 years later." [cite:de9_wnyc_apartheid] Chafkin's biography later reported that two former peers recalled Thiel saying of apartheid "It works," and that South Africa's denial of civil rights to Black people "was economically sound"; Thiel's spokesperson denied that those encounters took place. [cite:de9_dm_davis]

These are recollections of private conversations three decades old, given on the record by named people, and denied by the man they concern. They are not documents, and no statement in Thiel's own hand or voice expressing support for apartheid is on the record. Both accounts are recorded here, and the dispute is graded in [scene:de9_claims_vs_record|the claims against the record].

The Diversity Myth, 1995

After Stanford, Thiel and Sacks turned the Review's preoccupations into a book, The Diversity Myth: Multiculturalism and Political Intolerance on Campus, published by the Independent Institute, a libertarian research organisation in Oakland. [cite:de9_indep_dm] Its argument, in the publisher's summary, was that Stanford's turn to multiculturalism in the 1980s and 1990s had produced less learning, not more: a curriculum stripped of its Western civilisation requirement, speech codes, lowered standards and a conformist culture that viewed minority identity mainly through the lens of oppression, amounting to an anti-Western bias rather than real openness. [cite:de9_indep_dm]

The book also contained passages on sexual assault that were widely quoted when he entered politics, among them the suggestion that a woman might "realize" that she had been "raped" the next day or even days later. [cite:de9_cnn_apology] On 25 October 2016 Thiel told CNNMoney: "More than two decades ago, I co-wrote a book with several insensitive, crudely argued statements," and "I regret writing passages that have been taken to suggest otherwise." [cite:de9_cnn_apology] The apology is his own explanation and is recorded beside the original text, not in place of it. The book's broader case against campus multiculturalism he has not withdrawn.

Law and finance, 1989–1998

Thiel took a law degree at Stanford Law School in 1992. He clerked for Judge James Larry Edmondson of the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit in 1992–93, then joined the New York firm Sullivan & Cromwell as a securities lawyer and left in less than a year. In 1993 he became a derivatives trader in currency options at Credit Suisse, and in the same years worked as a speechwriter for William Bennett, the former education secretary. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] He then went home to California and raised about $1 million from friends and family to start an investment firm, Thiel Capital Management; reference works date its founding to 1996. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] In 1998 he put $100,000 into a start-up called Fieldlink, the company that would become PayPal. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel]

What the formation shows

The documented formation is that of a gifted, mobile child of an engineering family, a philosophy student shaped by Girard, a campus polemicist and a lawyer who chose finance over the law within a year. Three features of it recur through the rest of this book. The first is the network: the Review and the book with Sacks were the start of a circle of collaborators that would follow him into PayPal and, decades later, into government. [cite:de9_fortune_net24] The second is the habit of contrarian argument in print, from the Review to The Diversity Myth to the 2009 essay in which he wrote that he no longer believed "freedom and democracy are compatible," discussed in [scene:de3_other_lineages|Part Three] and [scene:de10_education_of_a_libertarian|Part Ten]. [cite:de3_cato_thiel] The third is that the most damaging items in the early record, the apartheid remarks, are disputed recollections, while the most quoted written passages, in the 1995 book, are ones he has said he regrets. The rest of his life is a matter of companies, money and filings, and is far better documented, beginning in [scene:de9_paypal_palantir_facebook|the next section].

sections.h: PayPal, Palantir, Facebook and the Funds
sections.html:
Between 1998 and 2012 Thiel made the fortune and built the institutions that the rest of this book follows. The fortune came from three bets: a payments company he co-founded, a social network in which he was the first outside investor, and a data-analysis company he incorporated and chaired. The institutions were a set of investment vehicles, each with its own partners and money, which are often run together in public discussion as if they were one man's wallet. This section keeps them apart. A position held by Founders Fund is the fund's, owned with its outside investors; a contract won by Palantir is Palantir's; neither is a personal holding of Thiel's unless a filing says so.

PayPal, 1998–2002

In 1998 Thiel put the first $100,000 into Fieldlink, a start-up founded with the programmer Max Levchin, which became Confinity and in 1999 launched a service for sending money by email called PayPal. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] In January 1999, while Confinity was being formed, he bought 1.7 million of its founders' shares at a tenth of a cent each, about $1,700 in all, through a Roth individual retirement account, a tax-free savings vehicle designed for middle-income earners; what that account became is told in [scene:de9_gawker_citizenship_and_tax|the next section]. [cite:de9_pp_roth]

In March 2000 Confinity merged with X.com, the online bank founded by Elon Musk, and the combined company kept the X.com name with Musk as chief executive. In September 2000, as Musk left on a fundraising trip that was also to be his honeymoon, executives loyal to Levchin and Thiel delivered letters of no confidence to the board, which replaced Musk with Thiel. [cite:de9_snopes_paypal] The company took the PayPal name, went public on 15 February 2002, and was bought by eBay for $1.5 billion in October 2002. Thiel, chief executive until the sale, held about 3.7 percent, worth some $55 million. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de9_snopes_paypal] Musk's side of the episode is in [scene:de11_zip2_xcom_paypal|Part Eleven]. The early employees who left PayPal with money and with one another's phone numbers became the group that Fortune in 2007 called the "PayPal Mafia," mapped in [scene:de13_who_they_are|Part Thirteen]. [cite:de13_fortune_2007]

Clarium, 2002–2011

With $10 million of his PayPal proceeds Thiel started Clarium Capital, a "global macro" hedge fund that bets on large movements in currencies, interest rates and commodities. It returned 57.1 percent in 2005, lost 7.8 percent in 2006 and gained 40.3 percent in 2007, and by the first quarter of 2008 managed more than $7 billion. Then it turned sharply: by 2011 its assets had fallen to about $350 million, roughly two-thirds of it Thiel's own money. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] Clarium matters here mainly as a corrective to the image of an investor who never misjudges the world; his largest macro bets on the economy went badly wrong, and the money that endured came from start-ups.

Palantir, 2003

Palantir Technologies was incorporated in May 2003. Its initial funding of about $30 million came largely from Thiel and his fund, and he became, and remains, its chairman. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] In-Q-Tel, the venture-capital arm set up by the Central Intelligence Agency, made an early investment of about $2 million, dated to 2004 or 2005 by different accounts, and Palantir's software became deeply embedded at the agency. [cite:ow9_bf_karp2015] [cite:ow9_ap_s1] Fortune called In-Q-Tel the company's "first outside investor", a description that sets aside Thiel's own money, which came first; [cite:de10_fortune_palantir] Founders Fund, Thiel's own fund, is described as its first institutional investor. [cite:de9_wiki_ff] How the company was founded and who controls it is the subject of [scene:de27_origins_and_control|Part Twenty-Nine]; its federal contracts, including those with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, are in [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty]. The relationship of type here is exact: Thiel is a founder, the chairman and a large shareholder; Palantir's contracts are the company's.

Facebook, 2004–2022

In August 2004 Thiel paid $500,000 for 10.2 percent of Facebook, then a start-up run by Harvard students, valuing it at $4.9 million. It was the company's first outside investment, and he later took a seat on its board. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] He sold 16.8 million shares for $638 million at Facebook's public offering in May 2012 and nearly all the rest in August 2012 for about $395.8 million, taking his proceeds above $1 billion. He stayed on the board of Facebook, later Meta Platforms, for seventeen years, and announced on 7 February 2022 that he would leave it to support candidates in that year's elections. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel]

The funds, 2005–2013

In 2005 he founded the venture firm Founders Fund with two PayPal colleagues, Ken Howery and Luke Nosek, starting with $50 million; by 2025 it managed about $17 billion. [cite:de9_wiki_ff] It was the first institutional investor in Elon Musk's SpaceX, from 2008, in a deal led by Nosek, and in 2025 put $1 billion into the defence company Anduril, its largest single investment. [cite:de9_wiki_ff] Those are positions of the fund, held for its investors; a widely repeated line that Thiel personally owns a tenth of SpaceX confuses the fund with the man.

Three more vehicles complete the set. Valar Ventures was co-founded in 2010; Jeffrey Epstein became a limited partner in it from 2015, a passive investor with no management role, and Thiel's spokesman has denied a claim by the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak that Epstein co-owned it. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de9_byline_valar] The documents and what they do and do not show are examined in [scene:de14_epstein_valar|Part Fourteen]. Mithril Capital, launched in June 2012 with a $402 million fund, later employed J.D. Vance, the start of the working relationship told in [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|Part Twelve]. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de9_fortune_net24] And the Thiel Foundation, his charity, ran the Thiel Fellowship, which from 2011 paid young founders $100,000 each over two years; one of the first twenty fellows, John Burnham, went on to co-found Tlon, Curtis Yarvin's company, in which Founders Fund also invested in 2013. [cite:de5_audit_tc2011] [cite:de5_wiki_urbit]

By the end of 2012 Thiel had sold most of his Facebook stock, wound Clarium down to a vehicle mostly for his own money, and held his wealth chiefly through Palantir, still private, and through the funds. The pattern matters for every later chapter of this book. When his name is attached to a company in the news, the first question is which vehicle holds it and with whom; the answer is usually a fund with outside partners, and the connection to him is real but one step removed. Where the connection is direct, as with Palantir's chair or the Facebook board, the record says so, and so does this book.

sections.h: Gawker, Citizenship and the Roth
sections.html:
Three episodes in Thiel's life became public only because someone else revealed them: a media company destroyed in court by a lawsuit he had secretly paid for, a New Zealand citizenship he had held for six years before a newspaper reported it, and a retirement account worth billions that came to light through leaked tax records. Each is lawful on the record as it stands. Each also shows how a private fortune can be used against a publisher, for a second passport or inside the tax code, in ways the public learns of late. This section sets out what the documents show, his own explanations where he gave them, and what remains disputed.

Gawker, 2007–2016

In 2007 Valleywag, the Silicon Valley gossip site of the New York media company Gawker Media, published a post headlined "Peter Thiel is totally gay, people." [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de9_snopes_close] Thiel had not discussed his sexuality publicly. In May 2009, asked about the site, he said: "Valleywag is the Silicon Valley equivalent of Al Qaeda," and "I think they should be described as terrorists, not as writers or reporters." [cite:de9_sfist_aq]

By his own account he decided "several years ago" to act, and his first step was to hire lawyers to look for people with claims against Gawker whose cases he could finance. [cite:de9_tc_gawker] One was Terry Bollea, the wrestler known as Hulk Hogan, who sued after Gawker published parts of a video of him having sex. In March 2016 a Florida jury found Gawker liable for $130 million and its founder Nick Denton personally for $10 million, a total of $140 million. [cite:de9_aba_settle] Gawker Media filed for bankruptcy in June 2016; the Spanish-language broadcaster Univision bid $135 million for its other sites, and Gawker.com itself announced on 18 August 2016 that it would close within a week. [cite:de9_snopes_close]

Thiel's role became public in May 2016, two months after the verdict. He confirmed to Andrew Ross Sorkin of the New York Times that he had paid about $10 million towards Bollea's suit and others. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de9_fora_gawker] "It's less about revenge and more about specific deterrence," he said, and he accused Gawker of a "unique and incredibly damaging way of getting attention by bullying people even when there was no connection with the public interest." [cite:de9_tc_gawker] He called the funding one of the "greater philanthropic things that I've done," and, asked whether there were other cases, said: "It's safe to say this is not the only one." [cite:de9_fora_gawker] [cite:de9_tc_gawker] In a New York Times opinion article on 15 August 2016 he framed the campaign as a defence of privacy: "It is ridiculous to claim that journalism requires indiscriminate access to private people's sex lives." [cite:de9_cnn_oped] On 2 November 2016 Gawker's bankruptcy estate settled with Bollea for at least $31 million and agreed to remove the Hogan story and two others at issue in suits brought by the lawyer Thiel had backed. [cite:de9_aba_settle]

Everything in this sequence was lawful. Paying for another person's lawsuit is permitted in the United States, the verdict was a jury's, and the bankruptcy followed from the size of the judgment. What the episode documents is a capability: a single wealthy person, acting in secret through a third party's case, removed a publisher he had called a terrorist organisation. Forbes wrote that it "could serve as a blueprint for any billionaire who wants to lay siege against a media outlet." [cite:de9_snopes_close] His stated motive, deterrence of a publisher that harmed private people, and the critics' reading, revenge against the site that had outed him, are both on the record; the dispute is graded in [scene:de9_claims_vs_record|the claims against the record].

Citizenship: New Zealand, Germany, Malta

In January 2017 the New Zealand Herald reported that Thiel had become a New Zealand citizen six years earlier. The government then released his file. [cite:de9_ap_nz] It showed that he had been granted citizenship in 2011 under the "exceptional circumstances" clause, which lets a minister waive the residence rules, and had taken the oath at a private ceremony at the New Zealand consulate in Santa Monica, California. [cite:de9_ap_nz] The Department of Internal Affairs later confirmed he had spent "a total of 12 days" in the country, over four trips, before the grant, against a general rule of 1,350 days over five years. [cite:de9_nbr_12days] The minister who approved it, Nathan Guy, cited his investments in New Zealand start-ups through a local venture fund, including the accounting company Xero, and a "million-dollar donation" to relief after the Christchurch earthquake; Guy said afterwards that "exceptional circumstances are there for a reason." [cite:de9_ap_nz] [cite:de9_nbr_12days] The opposition MP Iain Lees-Galloway called the decision "entirely about money." [cite:de9_ap_nz] No document shows a bargain between the donation and the grant; the file shows only that officials weighed both.

In his application Thiel wrote that he had found "no other country that aligns more with my view of the future than New Zealand," and that it would give him "great pride to let it be known that I am a New Zealand citizen." He also said he would need to go on living in the United States to run his companies. [cite:de9_ap_nz] He did not make the citizenship known; it became public through the newspaper. Asked about it in 2017, he declined to comment. [cite:de9_nbr_12days] The 2011 documents also showed that he remained a citizen of Germany, his country of birth; whether he still holds German citizenship is not on the public record since. [cite:de9_ap_nz]

In October 2022 the New York Times reported that Thiel was "in the process of acquiring at least his third passport," from Malta, under its programme selling citizenship to investors, and that the residence he had listed there was a flat advertised as a holiday rental. He declined to comment. [cite:de9_mt_malta] No grant of Maltese citizenship has been documented. Reports in 2026 that Argentina was considering residence or citizenship for him, which Javier Milei's spokesperson denied, are covered in [scene:de9_politics_and_argentina|the next section]. [cite:de9_nn_nyt]

The Roth, 1999–2019

On 24 June 2021 ProPublica, drawing on confidential Internal Revenue Service records, reported how Thiel's retirement account had grown. A Roth IRA lets savers put in money that has already been taxed and then pays no tax on gains; contributions were capped at $2,000 a year when Thiel opened his, and the account is limited to people below an income threshold. [cite:de9_pp_roth] In January 1999, when he earned $73,263, under the $110,000 limit, he bought 1.7 million PayPal founders' shares at $0.001 each through the account. Its custodian reported it at $1,664 at the end of 1999. By the end of 2019 it held about $5 billion across 96 sub-accounts, built from PayPal, Palantir, Facebook and other holdings. [cite:de9_pp_roth] In 2018 he moved it to Rivendell, a family trust company in Las Vegas named after the elves' refuge in Tolkien. [cite:de9_pp_roth]

The legal question is the price. Assets may not be bought into an IRA below their true value, and PayPal's own securities filing said founders' shares had been sold to employees "below fair value." [cite:de9_pp_roth] The tax-law professor Victor Fleischer told ProPublica: "That's a huge scandal." A tax lawyer said the valuation could not be supported as reasonable, while the founder of the account's custodian called the purchase "very legitimate." [cite:de9_pp_roth] The IRS opened an audit of Thiel in 2011; the records do not show whether it covered the Roth, and it closed years later with no additional tax owed. [cite:de9_pp_roth] The account had been part of his case to New Zealand: a letter in his 2005 residency application stated that he had bought his PayPal shares "through his Roth IRA." [cite:de9_pp_roth] His spokesman accepted ProPublica's questions and did not answer them. [cite:de9_pp_roth]

The finding, then, is narrow and should be stated narrowly. No court or tax authority has found the account unlawful, and the one audit on record closed without additional tax. Tax specialists quoted by name dispute whether the founding share price could be defended, and the account turned a savings vehicle meant for middle earners into one of the largest tax-free fortunes on record. Both statements are documented; neither cancels the other.

sections.h: From Escape to Kingmaker, and on to Buenos Aires
sections.html:
Thiel's public politics run on two tracks that are often treated as contradictory. One is exit: leaving the state behind, by sea, by second passport or by moving country. The other is voice at full volume: speaking at a party convention, sitting on a presidential transition, and spending tens of millions of dollars to put his former employees into the Senate. This section follows both, from 2009 to October 2026. What he thinks, and how his reading of René Girard and the Christian idea of the katechon bears on it, is the subject of [scene:de10_education_of_a_libertarian|Part Ten]; here the record is what he said in public, what he paid for and where he went.

Exit, 2008–2011

On 13 April 2009, in an essay for the Cato Institute's online forum Cato Unbound, Thiel wrote: "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible." He linked the decline of what he called capitalist democracy to the growth of welfare beneficiaries and to the extension of the vote to women, and named three frontiers for "escape from politics in all its forms": cyberspace, outer space and the open sea. [cite:de3_cato_thiel] On 1 May 2009 he added a follow-up on the suffrage passage: "While I don't think any class of people should be disenfranchised, I have little hope that voting will make things better." [cite:de1_audit_cato_followup] The essay, and how Nick Land used it to open The Dark Enlightenment, are discussed in [scene:de3_other_lineages|Part Three].

The sea was the frontier he paid for. He gave $500,000 in seed money to the Seasteading Institute, founded in April 2008 to develop floating, self-governing communities. [cite:de3_wiki_tsi] His total giving was reported as $1.25 million in 2011, when the institute said he did not "dictate" its plans, and as $1.7 million by Business Insider in 2018, which also reported that he had left its board in 2011 and later called seasteads "not quite feasible." [cite:de3_yahoo_tsi] [cite:de3_bi_tsi] Both figures are reported; they are cumulative totals at different dates and are not added together. The same year, 2011, he became a New Zealand citizen, as told in [scene:de9_gawker_citizenship_and_tax|the previous section]. Where the exit projects went next is in [scene:de22_seas_and_zones|Part Twenty-Two].

Voice, 2016

On 21 July 2016 Thiel addressed the Republican National Convention in Cleveland. "I am proud to be gay. I am proud to be a Republican. But most of all I am proud to be an American," he said, and he dismissed the argument over transgender bathroom access as one of the "fake culture wars" that "distract us from our economic decline." [cite:de9_fortune_rnc] In October, in the campaign's final weeks, he pledged $1.25 million to help elect Donald Trump. On 11 November, after the election, Trump named him to the executive committee of the presidential transition, a body of more than a dozen members chaired by the vice-president-elect, Mike Pence. [cite:de9_cnn_transition] Defending his choice, he said: "Most Americans don't live by the [Washington] Beltway or San Francisco Bay." [cite:de9_cnn_transition] Curtis Yarvin claimed in private emails that year that he had watched the election at Thiel's house and had been "coaching" him; that is Yarvin's account, discussed in [scene:de5_the_public_years|Part Five], and Thiel has not confirmed it. [cite:de5_pein_baffler]

The Senate bets, 2021–2022

Thiel stayed out of the 2020 presidential race while giving to congressional Republicans, including more than $2 million to a committee backing Kris Kobach's Senate primary in Kansas. [cite:de9_bp_thiel] [cite:de9_mj_2025] In 2021 he introduced J.D. Vance, who had worked at his fund Mithril Capital, to Trump. [cite:de9_fortune_net24] On 7 February 2022 he announced that he would leave the board of Meta, after seventeen years, to support candidates in that year's elections. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel]

He backed two of his own former employees for the Senate. Blake Masters had been president of the Thiel Foundation from 2015 and chief operating officer of Thiel Capital from 2018, and had co-written Thiel's 2014 book on start-ups, Zero to One. [cite:de9_12news_masters] According to FEC records reported by CNBC, Thiel gave $15 million to the super PAC supporting Vance in Ohio's Republican primary, and $15 million to the one supporting Masters in Arizona's primary, plus $2.5 million in October, about $32 million across the midterms. [cite:de9_cnbc_2022] Other tallies differ: Ballotpedia, citing Forbes, gives $10 million to Protect Ohio Values, at least $20 million to Saving Arizona PAC and $35 million across sixteen federal races. [cite:de9_bp_thiel] [cite:de9_audit_bp_2022] Vance won his seat; Masters lost to Senator Mark Kelly. [cite:de9_cnbc_2022] The two campaigns, run on the same model, are compared in [scene:de15_vance_and_masters|Part Fifteen].

Stepping back, 2023–2024

In April 2023 Reuters, citing two people close to him, reported that Thiel did not plan to give to candidates in 2024, unhappy with the Republican Party's focus on cultural issues, though he might still support former employees. [cite:de9_reuters_2023] In November 2023 Barton Gellman of The Atlantic reported that Thiel wanted it published that he "wouldn't be giving money to any politician, including Donald Trump, in the next presidential campaign"; the words are Gellman's paraphrase. [cite:de9_pw_atlantic] He told Gellman that voting for Trump in 2016 "was like a not very articulate scream for help," and said he had turned down a $10 million request from Trump's campaign. [cite:de9_forbesau_vance] At the Aspen Ideas Festival in June 2024 he said: "If you hold a gun to my head, I'll vote for Trump," and "I'm not going to give any money to his super PAC." [cite:de9_nbc_aspen] After Trump chose Vance as his running mate in July 2024, Vance urged him, in an interview with the Financial Times, to "get off the sidelines." [cite:de9_forbesau_vance] A single magazine report that Thiel lobbied for Vance's selection is examined, as contested, in [scene:de12_senate_and_the_ticket|Part Twelve].

No gift from Thiel to Trump's 2024 campaign or its super PACs is on the record. Ballotpedia, citing FEC records, nonetheless puts his giving in the 2024 cycle at "over $1.7 million to candidates for federal office and political parties," without itemising it, while Bloomberg and Mother Jones describe him as having sat that cycle out. [cite:de9_bp_thiel] [cite:de9_bgov_cfg] [cite:de9_mj_2025] Because the cycle began in January 2023, before either statement, the figures cannot be tested against his words without dated line items; the conflict is recorded in [scene:de9_claims_vs_record|the claims against the record].

Re-engagement and departure, 2025–2026

In February 2025 Thiel gave $852,200 to Grow the Majority, the fundraising committee of the House speaker, Mike Johnson, and in February 2026 $1.5 million to Club for Growth Action, a conservative political action committee; Bloomberg described him as "ramping up his engagement with federal politics again." [cite:de9_mj_2025] [cite:de9_bgov_cfg] On 29 December 2025 he gave $3 million to the California Business Roundtable to fight a proposed one-time 5 percent tax on the wealth of California's billionaires. [cite:de9_fortune_cbrt] He had moved his voter registration to Florida in March 2024, and two days after that donation his investment firm opened an office in Miami. [cite:de9_bl_miami]

Argentina, 2024–2026

Thiel first visited Argentina's presidential palace, the Casa Rosada, in May 2024, accompanied by the businessman Alec Oxenford, later Argentina's ambassador in Washington. On 23 April 2026 President Javier Milei received him there with the foreign minister, Pablo Quirno, and two associates from Thiel Capital and Founders Fund. Milei called it "a wonderful meeting," described Thiel as "an anarcho-capitalist, just as I am philosophically," said both men regard "taxes as theft," and said no specific investments were discussed. [cite:de9_bat_milei] Several outlets reported that Thiel had bought a mansion in the Palermo Chico district of Buenos Aires for about $12 million. [cite:de9_bat_milei]

On 28 May 2026 the New York Times reported that the government was considering offering him permanent residence or citizenship; a spokesperson for Milei denied it. [cite:de9_nn_nyt] In July Fortune reported that he had moved to Buenos Aires with his family earlier that summer, and that Argentina's planned citizenship-by-investment scheme was not yet in operation. [cite:de9_fortune_ba] In late August a committee hearing in the Chamber of Deputies examined his presence and his ties to the government; he was invited and did not appear. Testimony noted that Palantir had registered with Argentina's industrial-property office in 2022 and had shown interest in digitising the archives of the 1994 AMIA bombing, but no Palantir contract with Argentina was reported. [cite:de9_bat_congress] As of October 2026 no grant of Argentine residence or citizenship to Thiel is documented. Milei's own programme and the exit zones around it are in [scene:de22_argentina_and_freedom_cities|Part Twenty-Two].

In September and October 2025, between these visits, Thiel gave four private, off-the-record lectures on the Antichrist at the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco, organised by the Acts 17 Collective and drawing on Girard. [cite:de9_fortune_antichrist] Their content, reported from recordings, belongs to [scene:de10_girard_and_the_katechon|Part Ten].

Read together, the two tracks are less contradictory than they look. In 2009 Thiel wrote that the libertarian's task was to escape politics; from 2016 he was inside it, as a speaker, a transition official and the largest backer of two Senate candidates. In 2026 he was again moving his life beyond the reach of a government that proposed to tax him, this time to a country whose president shares his description of taxation. The record shows one man using both levers, exit and voice, as circumstances changed. It does not show a plan to combine them, and his own explanations, where he has given them, are recorded beside each step.

sections.h: Money and Political Influence
sections.html:
This section is a ledger. It lists the political money from Thiel that is documented in federal filings or in reporting based on them, cycle by cycle, with the recipient, the amount and the standing of the source; then the documented influence, meaning appointments, hires and the people from his firms who came to hold office; then the government contracts of companies he is tied to, with the type of tie. It applies one rule throughout. A donation that comes before an outcome is a sequence, not a cause: that money was given and that a candidate later won, or a former employee was later appointed, are each documented facts, but no filing documents that the first produced the second, and where a causal claim circulates it is named as a claim.

The political money

By the accounts available, Thiel's federal giving was modest and conventional until 2016, then concentrated and very large in 2022, then small again. In the 2015–16 cycle he gave $2 million to a super PAC supporting Carly Fiorina's presidential campaign and, in the general election, $1.25 million to help elect Donald Trump. [cite:de9_bp_thiel] [cite:de9_cnn_transition] In 2018 he gave $1 million to Club for Growth Action and $100,000 to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House Republicans' super PAC; in 2020 more than $2 million to Free Forever PAC, which backed Kris Kobach in the Kansas Senate primary, and $100,000 to the Senate Leadership Fund. [cite:de9_bp_thiel] The 2022 cycle is the outlier: about $32 million, by CNBC's count of FEC records, almost all of it to two super PACs supporting Vance and Masters. [cite:de9_cnbc_2022] Super PACs are committees that may raise and spend unlimited sums on a candidate's behalf provided they do not coordinate with the campaign, which is why money that could not legally go to a candidate directly could go to them in eight-figure amounts.

Three cautions apply to the table. First, the figures for 2022 differ by source: CNBC's count from FEC records gives $15 million for Vance and $17.5 million for Masters, while Ballotpedia, relying on Forbes, gives $10 million and at least $20 million; the FEC-based figures are preferred here, and neither set is summed with the other. [cite:de9_cnbc_2022] [cite:de9_bp_thiel] [cite:de9_audit_bp_2022] Second, in October 2022 Thiel offered the Senate Leadership Fund a matched deal for Arizona of at least $10 million in all, half from him, if it found the other half; no record shows the match completed. [cite:de9_axios_masters] Third, the 2024-cycle figure is the least clear line in the ledger: an FEC-based total from Ballotpedia, without dates or recipients, against two outlets' descriptions of a cycle sat out. [cite:de9_bp_thiel] [cite:de9_mj_2025] Thiel's charitable vehicles, whose grants are reported on tax returns rather than to the FEC, are a separate and more opaque channel, examined in [scene:de14_foundations_and_opacity|Part Fourteen].

The documented influence

Influence is harder to measure than money, and the only kind this ledger records is the kind with a document behind it: a position held, a job given, an introduction made and reported. Thiel himself has held one official role, on the executive committee of Trump's 2016 transition. [cite:de9_cnn_transition] The larger pattern is that people who worked for him or alongside him came to hold office in 2025. The table names the type of each tie, and its degree: direct (worked for or with him), or one step removed (tied to a firm or fund rather than to him personally).

The table is a map of documented ties, not of control. Each person on it has a career and views of his own, and several held positions or relationships with Trump independent of Thiel. Fortune's reporting in December 2024 and May 2025 described the pattern as Thiel's network reaching into the administration; what it documents is employment and partnership histories, not instructions. [cite:de9_fortune_net24] [cite:de9_fortune_net25] The people themselves, and where each sits as of October 2026, are covered in [scene:de13_where_they_sit_now|Part Thirteen]; Musk's role is in [scene:de11_money_and_influence|Part Eleven] and Vance's in [scene:de12_money_and_influence|Part Twelve].

Contracts

Thiel holds no federal contract in his own name. Palantir, which he chairs and in which he is a large shareholder, does. By early May 2025 it had more than $113 million in new and existing federal contracts under the second Trump administration, by the New York Times's count, and a Defense Department contract for artificial-intelligence software worth $795 million, which could rise to $1.3 billion. [cite:de9_mj_2025] In August 2025 the Army consolidated dozens of Palantir agreements into one enterprise contract worth up to $10 billion over ten years. [cite:ow9_bd_army] These are the company's contracts, won by the company, and the tie to Thiel is that of chairman and shareholder: real, direct and financial, but not the same as a personal award. Companies held by Founders Fund, such as SpaceX and Anduril, have their own government contracts; the tie there is one step further removed, through a fund with outside investors. [cite:de9_wiki_ff] The contracts and their history are in [scene:de27_money_and_war|Part Twenty-Nine] and [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty].

What is not documented

Three things often said about this ledger are not in it. No document shows Thiel paying Curtis Yarvin for his writing; the documented ties are Founders Fund's investment in Yarvin's company and a Thiel Fellowship to a future co-founder of it. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_audit_tc2011] No document shows that Thiel's 2022 money bought Vance's selection as Trump's running mate in 2024; the claim that Thiel lobbied for it rests on a single report and is treated as contested in [scene:de12_senate_and_the_ticket|Part Twelve]. And no document shows that any contract to Palantir followed from his political giving; the sequence of donations, appointments and awards is documented, and so is the absence of any record connecting them as cause and effect. Where the money runs in loops, from donor to office-holder to contract and back, the candidate loops and their evidence are set out in [scene:de14_loops|Part Fourteen].

sections.h: His Claims Against His Record
sections.html:
Thiel says less in public than most men of his influence, and much of what is said about him comes from others: biographers, former classmates, a former Israeli prime minister in a private email, a theorist boasting to a friend. This section tests only what he or his authorised spokesperson has said, against the documents, using the four grades this book applies to every person it examines. RED marks a claim contradicted by the person's own documents or sworn record. ORANGE marks a promise or claim not delivered, or not verifiable by the official auditor. YELLOW marks a reversal or concealment, shown with the person's own explanation. GREY marks a dispute in which credible accounts conflict, with both shown. The word "lie" is used only where the record shows the person knew a claim was false when making it; nothing below meets that bar, and each flag names a contradiction for the reader to judge.

Flags on what he believed and wrote

Apartheid (1985–86, denied in 2016): GREY. His spokesperson said in 2016: "Peter has never supported apartheid, but he can easily see how a conversation might be misremembered 30 years later." [cite:de9_wnyc_apartheid] The record against it is the recollection of two named Stanford contemporaries in 2016, that he called moral issues "irrelevant" to apartheid's economy and said governments should not be judged by morality, and of two former peers interviewed for Chafkin's 2021 biography (the published summaries do not say whether they are the same two people), that he said "It works" and called the denial of civil rights "economically sound"; the spokesperson denied those encounters. [cite:de9_wnyc_apartheid] [cite:de9_dm_davis] The accounts are consistent with one another and given on the record; they are still recollections of private talk, against a denial, with no document in his hand. The dispute is real and stays open.

The Diversity Myth (1995) to "I regret" (2016): YELLOW. The 1995 book, written with David Sacks, suggested a woman might "realize" she had been "raped" the next day or later. [cite:de9_cnn_apology] In October 2016 he called the book's statements "insensitive" and "crudely argued" and said: "I regret writing passages that have been taken to suggest otherwise." [cite:de9_cnn_apology] This is a reversal, and his explanation is on the record with it. It came more than two decades after publication and three months after his convention speech, and it is limited to the passages on rape; the book's wider argument against campus multiculturalism he has not withdrawn. [cite:de9_indep_dm]

Suffrage (13 April and 1 May 2009): GREY. His 2009 essay named "the extension of the franchise to women" among the developments that had made "capitalist democracy" an oxymoron. [cite:de1_cato_thiel] Two and a half weeks later he wrote: "While I don't think any class of people should be disenfranchised, I have little hope that voting will make things better." [cite:de1_audit_cato_followup] The clarification is consistent with the original sentence read literally, which described a cause of decline rather than proposing a remedy, and he has not advocated taking the vote from anyone. Critics read the original as an argument against women's suffrage; he presents it as an observation. Both readings are on the record.

Flags on what he did

Gawker: "less about revenge and more about specific deterrence" (May 2016): GREY. His stated motive was to deter a publisher that, in his words, bullied people "even when there was no connection with the public interest," and he called the funding philanthropy. [cite:de9_tc_gawker] [cite:de9_fora_gawker] The record also contains his 2009 description of Valleywag as "the Silicon Valley equivalent of Al Qaeda," the 2007 post that outed him, his decision "several years" before 2016 to find cases to fund, and the secrecy of the funding until after the verdict. [cite:de9_sfist_aq] [cite:de9_tc_gawker] [cite:de9_aba_settle] Deterrence and revenge are not exclusive, the funding was lawful, and the outlet's own conduct was found unlawful by a jury. The question is his motive, which only his words can supply; they say deterrence, his earlier words show grievance, and the reader has both.

New Zealand: "great pride to let it be known" (2011): YELLOW. His citizenship application said it would give him "great pride to let it be known that I am a New Zealand citizen." [cite:de9_ap_nz] He did not let it be known: the grant was made at a private ceremony in California in 2011 and became public only when a newspaper reported it in January 2017, after he had spent twelve days in the country. [cite:de9_ap_nz] [cite:de9_nbr_12days] Keeping a citizenship private is lawful. The flag is the gap between the stated wish and the six years of silence that followed. He has offered no explanation; asked in 2017, he declined to comment. [cite:de9_nbr_12days]

The 2024 cycle: no money "to any politician, including Donald Trump" (November 2023): GREY. The pledge reached the public as a paraphrase by The Atlantic's Barton Gellman, after Reuters reported, citing people close to him, that he might still help former employees; in June 2024 he said in his own words: "I'm not going to give any money to his super PAC." [cite:de9_pw_atlantic] [cite:de9_reuters_2023] [cite:de9_nbc_aspen] No Thiel money to Trump or his super PACs is on record, so that part of the pledge was kept. Ballotpedia, citing FEC records, puts his 2024-cycle giving at "over $1.7 million to candidates for federal office and political parties," while Bloomberg and Mother Jones say he sat the cycle out. [cite:de9_bp_thiel] [cite:de9_bgov_cfg] [cite:de9_mj_2025] The cycle began in January 2023, before the pledge, and the total is not itemised; without dated line items the record cannot show whether any of it broke his word. This flag would move to YELLOW only if itemised records show gifts to candidates after November 2023.

Three tests that raise no flag

Valar and Epstein: "a limited partner," not a co-owner (2026): no flag. His spokesman confirmed that Jeffrey Epstein was a limited partner in Valar Ventures and denied that Epstein co-owned the fund. [cite:de9_byline_valar] Against the denial stands one sentence in a private email by Ehud Barak in February 2016 describing "a new Investment Fund owned by Peter Thiel and JE." [cite:de9_byline_valar] Barak's phrase is a third party's characterisation, not a fund document. The records of the investment itself, the fund statements sent to Epstein, the New York Times's account of a $40 million limited partnership and Valar's own spokesperson, all describe an investor, not an owner, and no ownership record published so far shows Epstein as an owner or manager. [cite:de14_nyt_valar] The record supports the spokesman's statement rather than contradicting it, so no flag is raised; the co-ownership claim itself is graded not supported in [scene:de14_epstein_valar|Part Fourteen], which also examines what the documents released in 2026 do and do not show about the two men's contacts.

Yarvin: ideas that would not "work" (2023): no flag. Thiel told The Atlantic he did not think Yarvin's ideas would "work," while calling him an "interesting and powerful" historian. [cite:de6_cnn_2025] The record is a 2013 venture investment by Founders Fund in Yarvin's company, and Yarvin's own 2016 boast of "coaching" him, which Thiel has not confirmed. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_pein_baffler] Investing in a company is not adopting its founder's politics, and Yarvin's claim is Yarvin's. Nothing in the record contradicts Thiel's statement.

The Roth: no public claim (2021): no flag. Thiel has made no public statement about the account; his spokesman took ProPublica's questions and did not answer them. [cite:de9_pp_roth] There is nothing of his to test. The record of the account itself is in [scene:de9_gawker_citizenship_and_tax|the third section].

The pattern is not one of statements broken by documents. Thiel has never held an office requiring sworn statements, and he speaks rarely; the gaps in his record are mostly silences, a citizenship not mentioned, a lawsuit funded quietly, questions about a tax account left unanswered, rather than claims proved false. The two YELLOW flags are a reversal he explained and a concealment he did not.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis this book tests holds that immigration enforcement and government cuts are the occasion, and a sovereign executive without a veto the destination. Thiel's life bears on it in four ways. Documented: that he wrote in 2009 that he no longer believed freedom and democracy compatible, and called for an escape from politics. [cite:de3_cato_thiel] Documented: that he put $15 million into a super PAC backing the 2022 Senate campaign of J.D. Vance, who became Vice President, and that people who had worked for him held or were named to federal posts in 2025. [cite:de9_cnbc_2022] [cite:de9_fortune_net24] Documented: that he used litigation funding, lawfully and in secret, to end a publication he had called a terrorist group, which shows that one private fortune can remove one check, a hostile press outlet, without any act of state. [cite:de9_tc_gawker] [cite:de9_snopes_close] And documented: that the company he chairs holds large and growing federal contracts, including with immigration enforcement. [cite:de9_mj_2025] [cite:ow9_bd_army]

Probable, on this part's material, is nothing beyond those facts. Not supported: that Thiel directs a plan to install an executive without limits. His own words point the other way as often as toward it: he has said Yarvin's ideas would not work, spent most of 2023–24 out of the presidential race, and in 2025–26 moved much of his life beyond the reach of a government his allies help run. [cite:de6_cnn_2025] [cite:de9_nbc_aspen] [cite:de9_fortune_ba] Not supported either: that his donations caused the appointments or the contracts that followed them; the sequence is documented and the causation is not. The record shows a man using both exit and voice, buying influence by lawful means at a scale few can match, and preparing more than one country to live in. Whether those choices serve the destination the hypothesis names is a question about intent that only his own words could settle, and his words, read as he wrote them, are tested in [scene:de10_philosophy_vs_practice|Part Ten]. [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three] carries these grades into the book's final account.

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: Peter Thiel: the Mind
chapters.intro: This part follows Peter Thiel's thinking rather than his life, which [scene:de9_formation|Part Nine] tells. It reads his main texts whole and in order: "The Straussian Moment," a long essay on Leo Strauss, Carl Schmitt and René Girard first delivered at a 2004 conference he funded; the 2009 Cato Unbound essay that declared freedom and democracy incompatible; the 2014 case for monopoly in Zero to One; and what he has said and signed about democracy since 2016. It then explains Girard's theory of imitation and the scapegoat, and the old Christian idea of the katechon, the force that holds back the end of the world, which Thiel carried from his 2004 essay to an on-the-record New York Times interview in June 2025 and to private lectures on the Antichrist in San Francisco, Paris, Cambridge and Rome. The last section sets his arguments beside what his companies and his money have done, with his own explanations, and tests the book's worst-case reading against the result.
chapters.outro: Thiel's written thought is consistent in its distrust of mass democracy and of deliberation, from the 2004 essay that preferred the Echelon intelligence network to the United Nations, to the 2009 sentence on freedom and democracy, to the 2014 praise of monopoly. [cite:de10_straussian_es] [cite:de10_cato] [cite:de10_netzpolitik] It is not a design for a sovereign American executive: in 2022 he signed a statement accepting "the Constitution of 1787" and a limited state, and the danger his 2025 Antichrist lectures name is a global authority that would stop science in the name of "peace and safety," with the United States as the candidate restrainer. [cite:de16_natcon_signers] [cite:de16_tac_natcon] [cite:de10_douthat_tx] [cite:de10_reason] The tensions between his arguments and his practice are documented and, on his own account, explained: Palantir won its way into Army work by suing to compete and now earns $1.855 billion a year from the federal government; he spent about $32 million on the 2022 Senate races while calling populism "still by far the best option we have"; and he answers the charge that he funds the tools of surveillance with the claim that targeted analysis can "end indiscriminate surveillance." [cite:de10_defnews] [cite:de10_pltr_fy25] [cite:de10_cnbc_2022] [cite:de10_fortune_palantir] The next part turns to the second founder of the PayPal story, beginning with [scene:de11_pretoria_and_haldeman|Elon Musk's childhood in Pretoria].

sections.h: The Education of a Libertarian
sections.html:
Peter Thiel has published relatively little under his own name, and what he has published tends to be quoted one sentence at a time. Read whole and in order, four texts carry most of his argument: a long essay on Leo Strauss, Carl Schmitt and René Girard, first delivered at a conference he paid for in 2004; the 2009 essay for the Cato Institute that contains the most quoted sentence in this book; a 2014 book on start-ups that made the case for monopoly; and a run of speeches, interviews and signatures since 2016 in which he has said what he thinks of democracy now. His life, from Frankfurt to Stanford to Buenos Aires, is told in [scene:de9_formation|Part Nine]; this section takes the texts on their own terms, in their own words, and asks what kind of argument they make.

"The Straussian Moment," 2004

The earliest of the four is the least read. Thiel first delivered "The Straussian Moment" at a 2004 conference called "Politics and the Apocalypse," which he funded, and it was published in 2007 in a volume of the same name edited by the Stanford theologian Robert Hamerton-Kelly, where it runs from page 189 to page 218. [cite:de10_larb] [cite:de10_straussian_es] It is a dense essay in political philosophy, and its subject is what the attacks of 11 September 2001, with which it opens, revealed about the modern West. [cite:de10_straussian_es]

Its argument runs roughly as follows. The Enlightenment compromise associated with John Locke set aside the old questions about human nature and the good life, putting in their place, as Thiel put it, an unknown "X," and "the new science of economics and the practice of capitalism filled the vacuum." [cite:de10_straussian_es] [cite:de10_larb] The attacks showed that this compromise could not answer people who were willing to die for a fundamental truth. Thiel then set three thinkers against one another. From Carl Schmitt, the German jurist who joined the Nazi Party in 1933 and helped give its seizure of power a legal form, he took the idea that politics is the field on which people are forced to choose between friend and enemy. [cite:de10_brit_schmitt] From Leo Strauss he took the idea that philosophers write on two levels, for the many and for "trustworthy and intelligent readers only," and he quoted Strauss's remark that "the most just society cannot survive without 'intelligence,' i.e., espionage." From Girard he took the theory, explained in the next section, that human societies were founded on a hidden act of collective violence, and that once the mechanism is revealed it cannot be hidden again. [cite:de10_straussian_es] [cite:de10_larb]

Two passages matter for this book. In one, Thiel proposed that instead of a United Nations of endless parliamentary debate one should consider Echelon, the secret signals-intelligence network shared by the United States and its allies, as a truly decisive path toward a Pax Americana. In the other he wrote that the Straussian project sets out to preserve the "katechon," the restraining force of Saint Paul's letter to the Thessalonians, a term he would return to two decades later. [cite:de10_straussian_es] The essay ends not with a call to arms but with advice that the Christian statesman would be wise, in every case, to side with peace. [cite:de10_straussian_es] It is a meditation on the limits of liberal politics after 2001, with a frank endorsement of secret intelligence over open deliberation. It is not a program, and it proposes no change to American elections.

Cato Unbound, 2009

The 2009 essay, and the follow-up on the suffrage passage that Thiel posted on 1 May, are set out in [scene:de1_spine_and_overlay|Part One], [scene:de3_other_lineages|Part Three] and [scene:de9_politics_and_argentina|Part Nine], and are not repeated here. Read whole, the essay contains several sentences that are quoted less often and say more about its shape. It locates the decline in time: "The 1920s were the last decade in American history during which one could be genuinely optimistic about politics." [cite:de10_cato] It places the remedy outside politics, in technology: the essay closes on the claim that "the fate of our world may depend on the effort of a single person who builds or propagates the machinery of freedom." [cite:de10_cato] The single person it has in mind is an inventor or founder, not a ruler; the "machinery" is cyberspace, seasteads and rockets.

The follow-up explains what he meant by politics. "Politics is about interfering with other people's lives without their consent," he wrote, and "I believe that politics is way too intense. That's why I'm a libertarian." [cite:de10_cato] He listed the rights he thought were actually in danger: people "imprisoned for using even very mild drugs, tortured by our own government, and forced to bail out reckless financial companies." [cite:de10_cato] And he described his own course as "focusing energy elsewhere, onto peaceful projects that some consider utopian." [cite:de10_cato] In 2009, then, the incompatibility of freedom and democracy was an argument for leaving politics, not for winning it. That is the reading Nick Land took from it three years later, when he opened his serial with the sentence as a sign that libertarians were choosing exit over voice. [cite:de1_land_gwern]

Zero to One, 2014

Five years later the argument moved from politics to markets. In September 2014 the Wall Street Journal ran an essay by Thiel adapted from his book Zero to One, written with Blake Masters, under the title "Competition Is for Losers." [cite:de10_lambert] The book argues that what Americans call competition destroys profit, that the "competitive ecosystem pushes people toward ruthlessness or death," and that what it called the "ideology of competition" distorts how people think. [cite:de10_netzpolitik] Its alternative is the "creative monopoly," a company so far ahead that it has no real rival, which Thiel distinguished from monopolies that are "illegal bullies or government favourites" and so do not deserve their rents. [cite:de10_netzpolitik] He added that "monopolists lie to protect themselves," pointing to Google, which he said presented itself as "just another tech company" to escape attention; in a debate with Google's Eric Schmidt he said a dominant position like Google's in search was "quite legal" so long as it was not abused. [cite:de10_netzpolitik]

The book's case is about business strategy, and it is in this book that Thiel's reading of Girard is easiest to see. Rivalry, in Girard's account, comes from imitation; in Thiel's business advice, a founder who copies rivals ends up fighting over the same prize. "If you're copying these guys, you have nothing new to offer," he said of the point. [cite:de10_worldcrunch] What the case for monopoly means when the company is a government contractor is taken up in [scene:de10_philosophy_vs_practice|the last section of this part].

Democracy, in his own words, 2016–2026

Since 2016 Thiel has not published a second essay on democracy, and his later statements have to be assembled from speeches, interviews and one signature. The signature is the most precise. In June 2022 he was among the signers, listed as "Peter Thiel / Founders Fund," of "National Conservatism: A Statement of Principles," issued by the Edmund Burke Foundation. [cite:de16_natcon_signers] The statement calls for "accepting and living in accordance with the Constitution of 1787" and for "a strong but limited state, subject to constitutional restraints and a division of powers," and it opposes transferring "the authority of elected governments" to supranational bodies. [cite:de16_tac_natcon] Whatever else it is, that is not a text about abolishing elections or retiring the Constitution, which is what Curtis Yarvin's program proposes ([scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]). The signature is the documented tie between Thiel and national conservatism, together with his 2019 speech; no Thiel money to the National Conservatism conferences or to the Edmund Burke Foundation that organises them is documented ([scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen]).

His speeches point in the same direction. Opening the first National Conservatism conference in Washington in July 2019, he called Google's conduct toward China "seemingly treasonous" and said "these questions need to be asked by the FBI and the CIA," which is a call for the existing state's agencies to act, not to be replaced. [cite:de16_bloomberg_natcon] In June 2025 Ross Douthat of the New York Times asked him about the populist turn he had backed since 2016; he said it was "still by far the best option we have." [cite:de10_douthat_tx] In November 2023 he had asked The Atlantic's Barton Gellman to publish his promise to give no money to any politician in the 2024 presidential race, in Gellman's paraphrase, and in the same series of interviews, as CNN later reported, he called Yarvin's ideas unworkable. [cite:de10_politicalwire] [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin] How that promise compares with his giving is tested in [scene:de9_claims_vs_record|Part Nine].

Read in sequence, the texts describe a man who has doubted mass democracy in writing for twenty years and has never published a design to replace it. The 2004 essay prefers intelligence services to parliaments in foreign affairs; the 2009 essay prefers exit to voting; the 2014 book prefers monopoly to competition; the 2022 signature accepts the Constitution. The common thread is a distrust of crowds and of deliberation, and a confidence in the exceptional individual, the founder or the statesman, that runs through all four. That distrust is documented in his own words. A plan to end elections is not, and on the record of these texts he sits on a different rung of the ladder from Yarvin: an on-record critic of democracy, not an author of the sovereign-executive design. [cite:de10_straussian_es] [cite:de10_cato] [cite:de10_netzpolitik] [cite:de16_tac_natcon] The thinker who shaped the deepest layer of this argument is the subject of the next section.

sections.h: Girard and the Katechon
sections.html:
Of all the influences on Thiel, the one he has named most often is a French literary scholar who taught at Stanford. René Girard was a professor of French and Italian whose theory of imitation and violence Thiel encountered as an undergraduate in the late 1980s, and whose work he has funded since 2007. [cite:de10_gsb] [cite:de10_worldcrunch] By 2025 the same intellectual line had brought Thiel to an older and stranger idea, the "katechon," the force in Saint Paul's letters that holds back the end of the world, and to a series of lectures on the Antichrist delivered in four cities over six months. This section sets out what Girard taught, how Thiel has used it, what Thiel has said about the Antichrist and the katechon, and how much of that is known from his own words rather than from secondhand accounts of private talks.

What Girard taught

Girard's theory has two parts. The first is "mimetic desire": people do not want things on their own account but learn what to want by imitating others, so that characters in novels from Don Quixote to Madame Bovary shape their desires on a model. Because imitators come to want the same things, imitation breeds rivalry, and rivalry, unchecked, spreads through a community. [cite:de10_worldcrunch] The second part is the "scapegoat mechanism." Archaic societies, Girard argued, ended these spreading crises by turning together on a single victim, whose killing restored peace and was then remembered as sacred; religion and political order grew from that hidden founding act. For Girard the Gospels were unique because they told the story from the side of the innocent victim, exposing the mechanism, so that scapegoating could no longer work as well once people saw it for what it was. [cite:de10_worldcrunch] [cite:de10_straussian_es]

What Thiel took from him

Thiel has described meeting Girard "when I was a student at Stanford in the late 1980s," and said that reading Girard's Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World "felt like you understood the meaning of history." [cite:de10_worldcrunch] He turned that interest into money for the field. In 2007 he co-founded Imitatio, with Hamerton-Kelly, to support research on mimetic theory, and it became one of the Thiel Foundation's three programmes, according to a Stanford Graduate School of Business case study; some later accounts date the fund to 2008. [cite:de10_gsb] [cite:de10_worldcrunch]

He used Girard in two directions. In his 2004 essay he set Girard against Strauss: Girard held that the revelation of founding violence was irreversible and might make the myths that hold societies together unsustainable, opening the way to apocalyptic violence, whereas Strauss would have kept such knowledge within a small circle. [cite:de10_straussian_es] In business he used the first half of the theory, imitation leading to rivalry, as an argument against copying competitors and for building something without rivals, as the previous section showed. [cite:de10_worldcrunch] He also passed the theory on. J.D. Vance has written that a talk Thiel gave at Yale "remains the most significant moment of my time at Yale Law School," and that Girard's account of mimetic rivalry "spoke directly to some of the pressures I experienced at Yale"; that story belongs to [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|Part Twelve]. [cite:de10_worldcrunch] A 2026 essay in the Los Angeles Review of Books argued that Vance's Girard is Thiel's Girard, taken from the 2004 essay; that is one critic's reading of the texts, not a finding about Vance's sources beyond what he has said himself. [cite:de10_larb]

The katechon

"Katechon" is a Greek word from the Second Letter to the Thessalonians, where Paul tells his readers that the "man of lawlessness" will not be revealed until something, or someone, that now "restrains" him is taken out of the way. Paul never says what the restrainer is. [cite:de10_rns_christensen] Catholic tradition linked it to the Roman Empire and its emperor; other readings have proposed the Church or the Holy Spirit; and in the twentieth century Carl Schmitt, in The Nomos of the Earth, made it the idea through which a Rome-centred Christianity held off the Antichrist and the end of the age. [cite:de10_wiki_katechon] Thiel's 2004 essay already described the Straussian project as an effort to preserve the katechon. [cite:de10_straussian_es] In 2025 he made the idea the centre of his public thinking.

The Douthat interview, June 2025

The clearest record of what Thiel thinks about the Antichrist is an on-the-record interview, published on 26 June 2025 in Ross Douthat's New York Times series "Interesting Times." Thiel argued that the danger of the age is not runaway technology but its suppression, and that a would-be world ruler would come to power by exploiting the fear of catastrophe. "The slogan of the Antichrist is 'peace and safety,'" he said, citing Paul; the political form he feared was "the one world totalitarian state." [cite:de10_douthat_tx] [cite:de10_nr_douthat] Asked who might play that role today, he said: "In our world, it's far more likely to be Greta Thunberg." [cite:de10_nr_douthat]

Two exchanges in the interview travelled furthest. When Douthat said he assumed Thiel would prefer the human race to endure, Thiel hesitated. "This is a long hesitation," Douthat said; asked directly, "Should the human race survive?", Thiel answered, "Yes," and added that he also wanted humanity to "radically solve these problems," in an exchange about transhumanism and the limits of the body. [cite:de10_douthat_tx] [cite:de10_nr_douthat] The second exchange went to his own business. Douthat observed that Thiel was "deeply invested in Palantir, in military technology" and in surveillance, and suggested that an Antichrist might use the very tools he was building. Thiel replied: "I obviously don't think that that's what I'm doing." [cite:de10_douthat_tx] Both exchanges are his own words, on the record; the second is examined in [scene:de10_philosophy_vs_practice|the next section].

The lectures, September 2025 to March 2026

Between September and October 2025 Thiel gave four lectures, of about two hours each, titled "The Antichrist: A Four-Part Lecture Series," at the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco. They were organised by the Acts 17 Collective, a non-profit that seeks to build a Christian community in the technology industry, and announced as drawing on Girard, Francis Bacon and Schmitt. [cite:de10_fortune_series] [cite:de10_sfstandard] The first was on 15 September 2025; protesters outside carried signs about Palantir and immigration enforcement. [cite:de10_sfstandard] Attendees were told the talks were off the record. On 10 October the Washington Post reported that it had reviewed audio of all four, and that a digital-forensics expert at Berkeley, Hany Farid, judged a sample probably authentic; the Guardian also reported from recordings. [cite:de10_wapo] [cite:de10_varsity]

Because the lectures were private, their content is known only from these leaked recordings and the reporting on them. On that basis, Thiel called the American empire "the natural candidate for Katechon," and also "ground zero of the one-world state"; warned of a "caesaropapist one-world state"; listed tax treaties, financial surveillance and the sanctions system as features of the global order he feared; said that "in the 21st century, the Antichrist is a Luddite who wants to stop all science"; and named the AI-risk writers Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nick Bostrom, with Thunberg, as "legionnaires of the Antichrist." [cite:de10_reason] [cite:de10_wapo] He described himself in the same lectures as "a humble classical liberal." [cite:de10_reason]

He then took the series abroad. On 26 January 2026 he spoke at the Académie des sciences morales et politiques in Paris, to a working group on the future of democracy, saying "je m'inquiète de l'Antéchrist" ("I worry about the Antichrist"); protesters gathered outside. [cite:de10_lgc_paris] [cite:de10_varsity] In late January or early February 2026 he gave closed "Antichrist Lectures" at St Catharine's College, Cambridge, by invitation of the divinity scholar James Orr, an adviser to the Reform UK party. [cite:de10_varsity] From 15 March 2026 he gave a closed, invitation-only series in Rome; Catholic universities denied hosting it, and the Pope's adviser on artificial intelligence, Father Paolo Benanti, called Thiel a "political theologian." [cite:de10_reuters_rome]

What the argument says, and what it does not

Taken from his own words, the argument is a theological case against global regulation of technology. The danger Thiel names is a single world authority that uses fear of catastrophe, nuclear, climatic or from artificial intelligence, to halt science; the restraining force he hopes for is, at least as a candidate, the United States. [cite:de10_reason] [cite:de10_douthat_tx] It is not an argument for a monarch or for ending elections, and in it the dangerous concentration of power is a global one, not the American executive. It does identify named critics of technology, by name, as servants of the Antichrist. That is a rhetorical attack on people, made in religious language, and it should be described as such; it is not a call for any action against them. [cite:de10_wapo] [cite:de10_reason]

Interpretation, not finding: the stones and the restrainer

The Sophia platform reads this material through two lenses. In the first, Palantir, named after the seeing stones of Tolkien's fiction, which show distant things to whoever holds them and can deceive a holder who thinks he is the one looking, is read as an instrument that could itself become the restrainer's opposite: the man worried about a world state of "peace and safety" owns a share in the software that makes total visibility possible. In the second, Thiel is read as having learned Girard's scapegoat mechanism and inverted it, building tools used on a population that can be blamed. These are readings, attributed to the platform, and they are developed in [scene:de39_seeing_stones|Part Forty-Two]. The strongest counter-reading comes from the record itself. Thiel has said in public that he does not think he is building the Antichrist's tools; his named fear is a global authority, not a national one; Girard's theory, as Thiel summarised it in 2004, treats the revelation of scapegoating as irreversible rather than as a technique to be used; and no document shows Thiel directing how Palantir's customers use its software. [cite:de10_douthat_tx] [cite:de10_straussian_es] Whether the readings illuminate anything is for the reader to judge; they are not evidence.

sections.h: Philosophy Against Practice
sections.html:
Thiel's critics often say that what he argues and what he does point in opposite directions: the champion of monopoly who sells to the state, the man who wrote that freedom and democracy are incompatible and then spent more than $30 million on elections, the defender of privacy whose best-known company is a data-analysis contractor to intelligence and immigration agencies. [cite:de10_cato] [cite:de10_cnbc_2022] [cite:de10_cnn_privacy] Some of these tensions are real and documented. Some dissolve when the texts are read whole. This section sets each argument beside the record of his companies and his money, gives his own explanation where he has offered one, and says which kind of tension each is. These are not claims contradicted by documents, which [scene:de9_claims_vs_record|Part Nine] grades on the book's red-to-grey scale, but gaps between a philosophy and a practice, and they are judged here on their own terms.

Monopoly, and a company that sells to the government

Zero to One argued that the best companies escape competition and become "creative monopolies," and drew a line between these and monopolies that are "illegal bullies or government favourites." [cite:de10_netzpolitik] Palantir, which Thiel co-founded in 2003 and whose early history is in [scene:de9_paypal_palantir_facebook|Part Nine], built much of its business on government contracts. In 2025 its revenue was $4.475 billion, of which $1.855 billion came from the United States government, a figure that grew 55 percent in a year. [cite:de10_pltr_fy25] Its contracts with immigration enforcement are set out in [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty].

The record here is more interesting than the slogan suggests. Palantir did not get its foothold in the Army by being a favourite. In 2016 it sued the Army in the Court of Federal Claims, arguing that the service had broken the Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act of 1994 by designing a new intelligence system in-house without checking whether a commercial product could do the job. In October 2016 the court agreed and ordered the Army to consider commercial options; in March 2019 Palantir won a contract for the system worth up to $876 million over ten years. [cite:de10_defnews] The company that a monopoly theorist co-founded forced its way into a market by suing for the right to compete. Once inside, a supplier of software that becomes woven into an agency's work can become hard to replace, a question of lock-in that [scene:de27_capability_not_intent|Part Twenty-Nine] examines. Whether that is a "creative monopoly" or a "government favourite" in the book's own terms is a judgment the record does not settle; what it shows is that the government is the largest single customer of a company whose co-founder distrusts the government.

Against democracy, and $32 million on elections

The second tension is the one most often cited. In 2009 Thiel wrote that he no longer believed freedom and democracy were compatible and recommended "focusing energy elsewhere, onto peaceful projects that some consider utopian." [cite:de10_cato] In 2016 he spoke at the Republican convention and pledged $1.25 million to help elect Donald Trump. [cite:de9_fortune_rnc] [cite:de9_cnn_transition] In 2022, according to FEC records reported by CNBC, he put $15 million behind J.D. Vance's Senate primary in Ohio and $17.5 million behind Blake Masters's in Arizona, about $32 million across the midterms. [cite:de10_cnbc_2022] [scene:de9_money_and_influence|Part Nine] gives the full ledger.

The tension is real, but it is not a contradiction of the 2009 text. That essay never said elections did not matter; it said they were not where freedom would be won, and the follow-up already conceded that "voting is not under siege in America." [cite:de10_cato] What changed is his judgment about where to put his energy. He has given his own reasons in pieces. In June 2025 he described the 2016 turn as a choice for a candidate who was not offering what he called the old Republican formula, and said populism was "still by far the best option we have." [cite:de10_douthat_tx] In late 2024 he told Fortune that he had stayed out of that year's presidential race because the campaign was not about "ending our decades-long technological and economic stagnation." [cite:de16_fortune_thielnet] On his own account, then, electoral spending is a tool for a goal, technological progress, that he does not expect democracy to deliver by itself. That is consistent with the 2009 essay's distrust of mass politics, and it is a reversal of its advice to stay out.

Privacy, and surveillance

On 15 August 2016, after the jury verdict against Gawker that his money had funded, Thiel wrote in the New York Times that "it is ridiculous to claim that journalism requires indiscriminate access to private people's sex lives," and that "protecting individual dignity online is a long-term project." [cite:de10_cnn_privacy] The Gawker case itself is in [scene:de9_gawker_citizenship_and_tax|Part Nine]. In the Antichrist lectures of 2025 he listed financial surveillance, tax treaties and the sanctions system among the marks of the world order he feared. [cite:de10_reason] Meanwhile Palantir sells data-integration software to the Army and other federal agencies, including immigration enforcement ([scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty]), [cite:de10_defnews] [cite:de10_pltr_fy25] and Thiel and the investor Naval Ravikant together put more than $200,000 into the facial-recognition company Clearview AI, money later converted into equity. [cite:de10_wiki_clearview]

Thiel has addressed the tension twice in his own words. In 2016 he told Fortune that the government had been collecting more data than it could analyse, and that "if we could help them make sense of data, they could end indiscriminate surveillance." [cite:de10_fortune_palantir] In 2025, when Ross Douthat put it to him that an Antichrist might use the surveillance tools he had invested in, he answered: "I obviously don't think that that's what I'm doing." [cite:de10_douthat_tx] His argument, then, is that targeted analysis replaces mass collection rather than adding to it. That is a claim about effects, and it can be tested: [scene:de27_capability_not_intent|Part Twenty-Nine] and [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty] set out what the software has been used for. The 2016 op-ed concerned the press publishing intimate details of private lives, which is a different thing from state use of data, so the two positions are not formally inconsistent. They do rest on different views of who should be trusted with information about a person.

Exit, and the turn to the nation

The last tension is the largest and the least discussed. Thiel's 2009 programme was exit: seasteads, cyberspace and space, and he backed the Seasteading Institute with money reported at $1.25 million or $1.7 million before calling the idea "not quite feasible."
