[cite:de3_cato_thiel] [cite:de3_bi_tsi] By 2019 he was opening a conference of national conservatives, and in 2022 he signed their statement of principles, which calls for "a world of independent nations" and a state "subject to constitutional restraints." [cite:de16_bloomberg_natcon] [cite:de16_tac_natcon] [cite:de16_natcon_signers] In the 2025 lectures, as reported, he called the American empire "the natural candidate" for the restraining force he hopes will hold off a world state. [cite:de10_reason] The path from leaving the state to defending a strong nation against a global one is documented step by step in his own words. He has not, in any text found, explained the shift as a change of mind; read together, the texts suggest the enemy stayed the same, concentrated authority that stops innovation, while the preferred defence moved from the ocean to the nation.

The worst-case reading, tested

The book's working hypothesis, stated in the preface, is that immigration enforcement and government cuts in 2025 and 2026 were the occasion, and a sovereign executive without a veto the destination. This part's material bears on it in four ways.

Documented: Thiel has distrusted mass democracy in writing since at least 2004, preferred intelligence services to parliamentary deliberation in foreign affairs, and in 2009 wrote that freedom and democracy were incompatible. [cite:de10_straussian_es] [cite:de10_cato] Documented, too, is that his money backed the 2022 Senate campaign of the man who became Vice President and that a company he co-founded earns more than $1.8 billion a year from the federal government, including immigration enforcement. [cite:de10_cnbc_2022] [cite:de10_pltr_fy25] The materials of the worst case, a distrust of voters, money in elections and a data contractor to the agencies that carry out the occasion, are all on the record.

Not supported: that Thiel's own texts aim at a sovereign American executive. His 2022 signature endorses the Constitution of 1787 and a limited state; his 2019 speech asked existing agencies to act; and the danger his 2025 lectures name is concentrated global authority, not too little power in the White House. [cite:de16_tac_natcon] [cite:de16_bloomberg_natcon] [cite:de10_reason] On the record of his writing, he sits on the rung of an on-record critic of democracy, not an author of the design Yarvin proposes, and he has said Yarvin's ideas would not work. [cite:de1_wiki_yarvin]

Probable, at most, as a tension rather than a plan: that his theology of the katechon gives a religious warrant to treating the United States as the force that must not be restrained, which in practice argues against international limits on American technology and power. That is a reading of the lectures, which were private and are known from recordings, and no document shows it guiding a policy. [cite:de10_wapo] [cite:de10_reason] Where the record runs against the hypothesis is in his explicit target. A man whose stated fear is a world government that halts science in the name of "peace and safety" has said, in public and in private, that the threat comes from the opposite direction to the one the worst-case reading follows. [cite:de10_douthat_tx] The next part turns to the second man in the PayPal story, Elon Musk.

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: Elon Musk: the Life
chapters.intro: This part tells the life of Elon Musk, the largest political donor in the 2024 and 2026 American elections and the public face of the government cuts of 2025. It keeps his own accounts apart from the documents: a Pretoria childhood and a grandfather whose politics were his own; a Canadian passport, an American degree finished in 1997 and a first company started, by his own 2005 email, before he had the legal right to stay; the Zip2 and PayPal fortunes and the boardroom coup in which Peter Thiel replaced him; Tesla and SpaceX as partners of the state, from NASA contracts and a federal loan to spy satellites and the Starlink network on which Ukraine's army came to depend; and the purchase of Twitter, which by 2026 sat with his AI company under SpaceX. The last two sections set out his political money as a ledger, the office and the break with President Trump that followed it, and grade thirteen of his public claims against the record, before testing the book's worst-case reading against this part's material.
chapters.outro: The record of Musk's life is fuller than Yarvin's, and it can be tested more sharply. It shows a South African birth, a grandfather whose praise of apartheid and defence of an antisemitic forgery belong to the grandfather, and a career that began, by Musk's own 2005 email, before he had a "legal right to stay in the country." [cite:de3_cbc_leo] [cite:de11_wapo_visa] It shows two companies built in partnership with the state, with at least $38 billion in public contracts, loans, subsidies and credits, and a private network that allied armies rely on. [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] [cite:de11_aj_sikorski] It shows a forum bought with Gulf and other co-investors and folded, with his AI company, into SpaceX. [cite:de11_cnbc_coinvest] [cite:de11_reuters_spacex_xai] And it shows political money on a scale without precedent, more than $290 million in 2024 and more than $440 million in the 2026 cycle, with an office in between and a public break with the president who gave it. [cite:de11_cnn_290m] [cite:de11_ibt_fec] [cite:de11_npr_feud] Three of his claims are contradicted by documents or sworn testimony; none of the record shows him adopting the Dark Enlightenment's texts, and none shows a contract bought. The next part turns to the man in the network who holds elected office: [scene:de12_middletown_to_yale|Part Twelve], J.D. Vance.

sections.h: Pretoria, a Grandfather, and Three Passports
sections.html:
Elon Reeve Musk was born on 28 June 1971 in Pretoria, then the administrative capital of apartheid South Africa. His father, Errol Musk, was a South African electromechanical engineer; his mother, Maye Musk, née Haldeman, a model and dietitian, had been born in Saskatchewan, Canada. He has a brother, Kimbal, and a sister, Tosca. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] Much of what is written about his childhood comes from two kinds of source that this section keeps apart: his own accounts, given to biographers and in interviews, and documents or independent reporting. Where a detail rests on his word alone, the text says so. Where his father's account differs, both are given. A father's or a grandfather's record is never treated here as the son's.

Musk's place in this book does not rest on any documented reading of Curtis Yarvin or Nick Land. It rests on money, office and platforms: the largest political spending of any individual in the 2024 American election, a role as the public face of the government cuts of 2025, and ownership of one of the world's main public forums. Those are the subjects of the sections that follow. This one sets out where he came from, and tests the family line that is often drawn from his grandfather to his politics.

The Haldemans and the move to Pretoria

Musk was born in Pretoria because of a decision his grandfather made two decades earlier. Joshua N. Haldeman, his mother's father, was a Canadian chiropractor who led the Technocracy movement in Canada in the late 1930s, was charged under Canada's wartime regulations in 1940 for belonging to it, and later led the Social Credit party in Saskatchewan. In 1950 he moved his family, including his daughter Maye, to Pretoria. [cite:de3_cbc_leo] [cite:de3_wiki_haldeman] His documented politics there, set out with sources in [scene:de3_technocracy|Part Three], included praise for the South African government's handling of what he called "the native question" in a 1951 newspaper letter, and an earlier defence of the publication of the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, the antisemitic forgery, in which he said its authenticity "is not the point." [cite:de3_cbc_leo] He died in a plane crash on 13 January 1974, when his grandson was two. [cite:de3_cbc_leo]

Only one thing in that record bears on Musk himself, and it is his own words. The documented references Musk has made to his grandfather concern adventure, not politics: "My grandfather had this desire for adventure, exploration — doing crazy things," he told his biographer Ashlee Vance. [cite:de3_cbc_leo] His single documented use of his grandfather's movement's name was a 2019 post about "the Martian Technocracy," which he did not explain. [cite:de3_phys_tweet] No statement by Musk adopting his grandfather's views on race, on Jews or on apartheid is on record. A widely repeated line treats the grandfather's views as an inheritance; the record carries a family tie, not a transmitted creed.

A childhood in his own account and his father's

His parents divorced in 1979. At about nine, Musk chose to live with his father, he has said, "because he had an Encyclopædia Britannica set and a computer"; he later regretted the choice and became estranged from Errol. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] He attended Waterkloof House Preparatory School, Bryanston High School and Pretoria Boys High School, from which he graduated. He has described a wilderness camp as a "paramilitary Lord of the Flies" where "bullying was a virtue," and has said that after a fight at school he was thrown down concrete steps, beaten and hospitalised, and that his father berated him afterwards. Errol Musk has denied that part of the account. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] These are the son's memories and the father's denial; neither has been tested in any document this book has seen, and both are recorded as what they are.

The family's money has been the subject of a durable story. A widely repeated line holds that Musk's career was paid for by his father's emerald mine. The record is more tangled than either the story or the denial. In 2014 Musk said his father "had a share in an emerald mine in Zambia"; in 2019 he wrote that "He didn't own an emerald mine & I worked my way through college," with about $100,000 in student debt; in 2023 he called it "the fake emerald mine thing." [cite:de11_bi_emerald] Errol Musk told the biographer Walter Isaacson that he had traded a light plane in 1986 for emeralds from an unregistered Zambian mine owned by the buyer, had them cut in Johannesburg and sold them abroad, adding that "none of it was legal," and that the business later collapsed. Isaacson concluded that Errol never owned a mine. [cite:de11_bi_emerald] The documented core is a comfortable household with some income from emeralds. A mine that funded the son's companies is not documented, and the son's student-debt account has not been independently checked.

Leaving South Africa

Musk left South Africa at seventeen. He obtained a Canadian passport through his Canadian-born mother and arrived in Canada in June 1989, where he connected with a second cousin in Saskatchewan and worked odd jobs. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] His own stated reason was in part to avoid compulsory military service in the apartheid-era army. In a 2013 interview he said he left "in part, in order to avoid conscription in the army," and, pressed on the point, that "spending two years suppressing Black people doesn't seem to be a great use of time." [cite:de11_fc_conscription] That is his own account of his motive, and no document contradicts it.

He entered Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario, in 1990, and two years later transferred to the University of Pennsylvania, where he studied until 1995. He has said he earned his degrees that year; Penn did not award them, a BA in physics and a BS in economics from the Wharton School, until 1997. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] In 1995 he was accepted into a materials-science graduate programme at Stanford. He did not enrol. In a 2009 deposition he said he phoned the department chair two days after the semester began to say he would not attend, which is the root of his long-repeated line about leaving Stanford after two days. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] [cite:de11_wapo_visa]

The work-visa questions

On 26 October 2024, ten days before an election in which Musk was spending heavily on a candidate campaigning against illegal immigration, the Washington Post reported that he had himself worked in the United States without authorization in the mid-1990s. The report rested on company documents, court records and former associates. Six former associates and shareholders said he had told co-workers he was in the country on a student visa; he never enrolled at Stanford; and, by his own 2009 deposition, he began working at Zip2 in August or September 1995. [cite:de11_wapo_visa] When the venture firm Mohr Davidow invested $3 million in Zip2 in 1996, the funding agreement gave the Musk brothers and an associate 45 days to obtain legal work status or the firm could reclaim its money. A Zip2 board member recalled the authorizations coming through around 1997; a former staffer recalled processing work visas that year under the NAFTA category for Canadians. [cite:de11_wapo_visa]

The most direct document is Musk's own. In a 2005 email to his Tesla co-founders Martin Eberhard and JB Straubel, later filed in a California defamation suit, he wrote that he had applied to Stanford because "I had no money for a lab and no legal right to stay in the country, so that seemed like a good way to solve both issues." [cite:de11_wapo_visa] His earlier public accounts had been looser: in 2013 he called his status "a gray area," and in 2020 he said he had a "student-work visa" and "was legally there, but I was meant to be doing student work." [cite:de11_wapo_visa] He did not respond to the newspaper. After President Biden repeated the report, Musk wrote on X: "I was in fact allowed to work in the US," and "The Biden puppet is lying." [cite:de11_pbs_visa] His brother has given his own, different accounts of his own status; those are his brother's record, not his. The claim and the email are tested side by side in [scene:de11_claims_vs_record|the last section of this part].

Citizenship, and the country he left

Musk became an American citizen in 2002. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] He also holds Canadian citizenship through his mother. Whether he remains a South African citizen is not on the public record. In March 2025, asked in parliament whether Musk, Peter Thiel and David Sacks were citizens, South Africa's home affairs minister, Leon Schreiber, declined to disclose any of their details, citing the country's access-to-information law. [cite:de11_bt_citizenship] Musk's own description, in 2020, was "American, but born in South Africa. Left by myself when I was 17." [cite:de11_wiki_musk_sa]

He has since spoken often about the country of his birth, and his statements are his own record. In July 2023 he wrote to President Cyril Ramaphosa that South African politicians "are openly pushing for genocide of white people," after a rally at which the opposition leader Julius Malema sang the "Kill the Boer" chant; in May 2025 he called the country's Black Economic Empowerment rules "Apartheid version 2," and he has said his Starlink service could not operate there "because I'm not black." [cite:de11_wiki_musk_sa] South African courts have treated the chant differently in different contexts, and South Africa's government has rejected the genocide claim; Ramaphosa told President Trump in the White House in May 2025, referring to members of his own delegation: "If there was Afrikaner farmer genocide, I can bet you these three gentlemen would not be here." [cite:de11_wiki_musk_sa] That month, Musk's own chatbot inserted the "white genocide" claim into answers to unrelated questions; his company xAI blamed an "unauthorized modification" by an employee. [cite:de11_wiki_musk_sa] These statements show what Musk says about South Africa now. They do not show what he believed at seventeen, and they are not his grandfather's.

The life before 1995, then, is documented in outline and contested in detail. The facts that matter for the rest of this part are few and firm: a South African birth, a Canadian passport through his mother, an American degree finished in 1997, and an American career that began, on his own 2005 account, before he had the legal right to stay. The money that career produced, and the first time Peter Thiel's path crossed his, are the subject of [scene:de11_zip2_xcom_paypal|the next section].

sections.h: Zip2, X.com and the PayPal Coup
sections.html:
Musk's first fortune came from a company that made online maps and directories for newspapers. His second came from a merger with Peter Thiel's company, which ended with Musk removed as chief executive while he was on a plane. Both episodes matter to this book for the same reason: they set the pattern of the money that later reached politics, and they are the documented origin of the tie between Musk and Thiel that is often described as an alliance. The record of 1995 to 2002 shows a business partnership, a boardroom defeat and a profitable sale. It does not show a shared political project.

Zip2

Musk founded the company in 1995 with his brother Kimbal and Greg Kouri, under the name Global Link Information Network; it became Zip2 in 1996. Its product was city-guide software licensed to newspapers, which let them publish their own online directories and maps. [cite:de11_wiki_zip2] It was this work, by his own 2009 deposition, that he began in August or September 1995 instead of enrolling at Stanford. [cite:de11_wapo_visa]

The venture firm Mohr Davidow invested $3 million in 1996. [cite:de11_wiki_zip2] The investment changed the company's control. Rich Sorkin became chief executive and Musk became chief technology officer, and the board blocked his later attempts to become chief executive. [cite:de11_wiki_zip2] [cite:de11_wiki_musk] The same funding agreement gave the founders 45 days to obtain legal work status, the clause discussed in [scene:de11_pretoria_and_haldeman|the previous section]. [cite:de11_wapo_visa] In April 1998 Zip2 tried to merge with its main competitor, CitySearch; Musk at first supported the deal and then persuaded the board not to proceed, and the companies cited incompatible cultures and technology. [cite:de11_wiki_zip2]

In February 1999 the computer maker Compaq bought Zip2 for cash. Accounts of the price differ slightly, between $305 million and $307 million. Musk received about $22 million for his share of roughly seven per cent. [cite:de11_wiki_zip2] [cite:de11_wiki_musk] He was twenty-seven. The lesson most accounts draw, and the one Musk's later behaviour bears out, is that he had founded a company and lost control of it to investors.

X.com and Confinity

He put much of the money into a new company in 1999, an online bank and payments firm called X.com. By the end of that year its investors had replaced him as chief executive with Bill Harris, the former head of the software company Intuit. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] Down the street in Palo Alto, a rival start-up, Confinity, founded by Peter Thiel and Max Levchin, was building a way to send money by email, called PayPal. In March 2000 the two companies merged. The combined company kept the name X.com, and Musk returned as chief executive. [cite:de11_snopes_ouster] [cite:de11_wiki_musk]

The merger did not settle the arguments between the two camps. One was over the name. Musk kept championing X.com, the biographer Ashlee Vance wrote, "while most everyone else favored PayPal." [cite:de11_snopes_ouster] Others were over technology and strategy. In September 2000 the conflict was resolved without him. Musk had married Justine Wilson in January 2000 and delayed their honeymoon; as the couple boarded a flight for a combined fundraising trip and honeymoon, X.com executives delivered letters of no confidence to the board, which removed Musk and installed Thiel as chief executive. [cite:de11_snopes_ouster] The company was renamed PayPal in 2001. [cite:de11_snopes_ouster]

What Musk said about the ouster

He did not fight it. "It's not a good idea to leave the office when there are a lot of major things underway," he said later, and he chose not to contest the decision "rather than fight it at this critical time." [cite:de11_snopes_ouster] In 2007 he told Inc. magazine that he had made peace with the men who removed him: "I buried their hatchet," he said, adding, "Life is too short for long-term grudges." [cite:de11_snopes_ouster] He remained the company's largest shareholder. [cite:de11_wiki_musk]

A recurring question is whether Musk "founded PayPal." Both halves of the usual dispute are true. He founded X.com, the company that legally survived the 2000 merger and later took the PayPal name; the PayPal product, and the name, came from Confinity. [cite:de11_snopes_ouster] [cite:de11_wiki_musk] Calling him a PayPal co-founder is accurate in law and incomplete as history.

The sale to eBay

PayPal went public in 2002, and eBay bought it later that year for about $1.5 billion in stock. eBay's filing records the merger as completed on 3 October 2002, with each PayPal share exchanged for 0.39 of an eBay share. [cite:de11_ebay_8k] Musk, still the largest shareholder at 11.72 per cent, received about $175.8 million. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] Thiel's share was smaller; his part of the story is told in [scene:de9_paypal_palantir_facebook|Part Nine].

The PayPal money then went in different directions. Musk founded SpaceX in May 2002 with about $100 million of his own early fortune, and led Tesla's first funding round in 2004. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] Several of PayPal's early employees and executives went on to found or fund other companies and, later, to hold political roles; who they are, and where they sit in 2026, is the subject of [scene:de13_who_they_are|Part Thirteen]. PayPal itself followed its own path: owned by eBay from 2002, it "became an independent public company in July 2015," and neither Musk nor Thiel sits on its board in 2026; no current stake in it by either man is documented. [cite:de11_pypl_proxy] In July 2017 he bought back only the x.com web address, saying it had great sentimental value. [cite:de11_domain]

The tie to Thiel, by type

The relationship between Musk and Thiel is often described as a partnership that runs from PayPal to the White House. The documented record supports something narrower, and it can be stated by type of connection. In 2000 the two were merger partners and then boardroom adversaries, one replacing the other. From 2002 they were former co-shareholders of a sold company. In August 2008, after SpaceX's third consecutive rocket failure, Founders Fund, the venture firm Thiel co-founded, invested $20 million in SpaceX, and its managing partner Luke Nosek, another PayPal co-founder, joined the SpaceX board; Musk said he had accepted the money "as a precautionary measure" in case the next flight also failed. [cite:de11_space_ff] That is a fund-level investment, made by a firm in which Thiel was a partner; it is not documented as Thiel's personal money.

What does not appear in that record is a shared politics. In the years of PayPal and its sale, nothing documents a political project between the two men; their later political money, which differs sharply in scale and direction, is set out separately for each, in [scene:de9_money_and_influence|Part Nine] for Thiel and in [scene:de11_money_and_influence|this part's fifth section] for Musk. The ouster of 2000 is better evidence of rivalry than of alliance, and the reconciliation Musk described in 2007 is his own account of a business relationship. The companies built with the PayPal money, and the government contracts and loans that sustained them, come next, in [scene:de11_tesla_spacex_and_the_state|the next section].

sections.h: Tesla, SpaceX and the State
sections.html:
Musk is often described, by admirers and by himself, as a builder who succeeded in spite of government. The record shows something more interesting: two companies that grew in a long partnership with government, as its contractor, its borrower, its regulated party and, in Ukraine, its stand-in. That partnership predates his politics by two decades. It is set out here by instrument, with dates and amounts, because it is the background against which his later role in cutting government has to be read. Timing is reported as sequence; a contract that follows a donation is not, on that fact alone, a contract bought by it.

Tesla and the "founder" settlement

Tesla Motors was incorporated in 2003 by the engineers Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning. Musk led its first funding round in February 2004, investing $6.35 million, became its majority shareholder and joined its board as chairman. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] Eberhard was pushed out in 2007, and Musk became chief executive in 2008. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] Eberhard then sued him, and the case turned on who could call himself the company's founder. It was settled out of court in September 2009. The two men, together with JB Straubel, Tarpenning and Ian Wright, agreed to be described as the company's co-founders, and the terms were not disclosed. [cite:de11_af_settle] Each said something generous about the other: Musk, that "Without Martin's indispensable efforts, Tesla Motors would not be here today"; Eberhard, that Musk's contributions had been "extraordinary." [cite:de11_af_settle] A widely repeated line says Musk bought or litigated his way into the title; the record shows a settlement in which five people, Musk among them, agreed to share it.

SpaceX and its first customer

Musk founded Space Exploration Technologies in May 2002 with about $100 million of his own money and became its chief executive and chief engineer. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] Its first rocket, Falcon 1, failed on its first three launches; after the third failure, on 2 August 2008, Musk accepted a $20 million investment from Founders Fund "as a precautionary measure." [cite:de11_space_ff] The customer that carried the company through was NASA. The space agency awarded SpaceX $278 million in 2006 and a $1.6 billion cargo contract in 2008, and by 2025 NASA said it had invested more than $15 billion in the company. [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] SpaceX's president, Gwynne Shotwell, has answered critics of that dependence in three words: "We earned that." [cite:de11_wapo_38bn]

The public money, by instrument

The fullest public count was published by the Washington Post in February 2025, as Musk was the public face of the cuts described in Book Three. Using only public records, it found that Musk and his companies had received at least $38 billion in government contracts, loans, subsidies and tax credits over more than twenty years, nearly two-thirds of it promised in the previous five years, with a record $6.3 billion committed in 2024 alone and 52 continuing contracts that could pay another $11.8 billion. [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] The count excludes classified work, so the true figure is higher. [cite:de11_wapo_38bn]

Three instruments account for the shape of that figure. The first is contracts, mostly from NASA and the Defense Department, for launches, cargo, crew and satellites. The second is loans: a $465 million Energy Department loan in 2010 helped Tesla build the Model S and buy its Fremont factory, and was repaid within a few years. [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] The third is regulatory credits, which are not paid by government at all. Federal and state emissions rules let makers of zero-emission cars sell credits to other carmakers that fall short; Tesla earned $11.4 billion from such sales between 2014 and early 2025, about a third of its profits over the period. [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] State and local incentives sit on top: a $1.3 billion Nevada package for the battery factory near Reno, shared with Panasonic, and $750 million from New York to SolarCity, which Tesla later bought. [cite:de11_wapo_38bn]

Musk's own statements about this money have varied. In 2015 he told the Los Angeles Times that "If I cared about subsidies, I would have entered the oil and gas industry," and in 2021 that "I'm literally saying get rid of all subsidies." [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] Those are his positions; the figures above are the record against which they can be read.

The national-security business

The defence and intelligence side has grown fastest. In March 2024 Reuters reported, from five sources, that SpaceX's Starshield unit was building a network of hundreds of spy satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office under a $1.8 billion contract signed in 2021, a network separate from the commercial Starlink system; the agency declined to discuss SpaceX's role. [cite:de11_reuters_starshield] On 4 April 2025, while Musk was in government, the Space Force awarded the most demanding national-security launches for the coming years: about $5.92 billion to SpaceX for 28 missions, $5.37 billion to United Launch Alliance for 19, and $2.39 billion to Blue Origin for 7. [cite:de11_ussf_nssl] The procurement had begun under the previous administration, and SpaceX was already the leading launch provider. On 24 April 2026 SpaceX was one of twelve companies to receive prototype agreements for the space-based interceptors of the planned Golden Dome missile shield, worth a combined $3.2 billion, with each firm's share undisclosed. [cite:de11_bd_sbi]

Regulation moved in the same direction after Musk had left government. An executive order of 13 August 2025 told the transport secretary to eliminate or speed up environmental reviews for rocket launch licences; Reuters wrote that SpaceX "potentially stands to be the single biggest immediate beneficiary," though it is not named in the order, which was signed months after Musk and Trump fell out. [cite:de11_reuters_spaceeo] SpaceX had complained for years about licensing delays. The order is a documented benefit; it is not documented as a reward.

Starlink in Ukraine: a private network in a public war

The clearest test of one man's control over infrastructure that states depend on came in Ukraine. After Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 disrupted Ukrainian communications, Musk agreed to provide Ukraine with Starlink terminals worth millions of dollars. [cite:de11_snopes_crimea] In October 2022 he said SpaceX could no longer fund the service, which he put at $80 million so far, then walked the statement back; on 1 June 2023 the Pentagon confirmed that it contracts with Starlink for services in Ukraine, without giving the price. [cite:de11_dn_pentagon]

In September 2023 a CNN excerpt of Walter Isaacson's biography reported that Musk had secretly ordered Starlink turned off near Crimea in 2022 to thwart a Ukrainian drone attack on the Russian fleet. [cite:de11_snopes_crimea] Isaacson corrected the account the next day: "the Ukrainians THOUGHT coverage was enabled all the way to Crimea, but it was not." [cite:de11_cnbc_isaacson] Musk's own version is that there was "an emergency request from government authorities to activate Starlink all the way to Sevastopol," with "the obvious intent being to sink most of the Russian fleet at anchor," and that agreeing would have made SpaceX complicit in "a major act of war and conflict escalation." [cite:de11_fox_sevastopol] On the record, then, he did not switch the service off; he refused to switch it on, and a private company's owner made a decision about the reach of a military operation.

The dependence became a political argument in 2025. On 22 February Reuters reported, citing three sources, that American negotiators had raised cutting off Ukraine's Starlink access during talks over a minerals deal; Musk replied, "This is false. Reuters is lying." [cite:de11_dcd_minerals] On 9 March he called Starlink "the backbone of the Ukrainian army" and wrote that "Their entire front line would collapse if I turned it off," adding that "Starlink will never turn off its terminals." [cite:de11_aj_sikorski] Poland's foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, replied that Poland paid about $50 million a year for the service and would look elsewhere if SpaceX proved unreliable; Musk told him to "Be quiet, small man," and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said no one had threatened a cut-off. [cite:de11_aj_sikorski] In February 2026 the same control ran the other way: Ukraine, with SpaceX's cooperation, allowed only verified terminals to operate, and Musk said the steps had likely stopped Russia's unauthorised use, which had reportedly included Starlink on attack drones. [cite:de11_up_whitelist]

The record here supports two plain findings. The American state, and its allies, came to rely for military communications and intelligence satellites on infrastructure owned and controlled by one man. And that man has, on the record, used his discretion over it once, in 2022, against an allied operation, and has said publicly that he will not use it as leverage. Whether that dependence is wise is a policy question that runs across administrations of both parties; it began before his politics changed and has deepened since. The platform he bought in 2022, and the AI company now merged with SpaceX, are the subject of [scene:de11_twitter_x_xai|the next section]. The satellites' place in the surveillance toolkit is in [scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|Part Twenty-Eight].

sections.h: Twitter, X and xAI
sections.html:
In 2022 Musk bought the company that ran one of the world's main public forums. By 2026 that forum, an artificial-intelligence company trained partly on its posts, and the satellite network described in the previous section all sat under one corporate parent controlled by him. This section sets out how that happened, who put money into it, what changed on the platform, and the record of government pressure on speech, which runs in more than one direction. The surveillance and data questions raised by one owner holding all three are taken up in Book Five.

The purchase

Musk disclosed a stake of about 9 per cent in Twitter on 4 April 2022 and on 14 April offered to buy the whole company for $54.20 a share, about $44 billion. [cite:de11_wiki_acq] [cite:de11_cnbc_coinvest] On 8 July he announced he was walking away, claiming Twitter had breached the agreement; Twitter sued him in the Delaware Court of Chancery on 12 July; and on 27 October 2022 the deal closed. [cite:de11_wiki_acq] The purchase was paid for with Musk's own money, about $13 billion of bank debt loaded onto the company, and equity from co-investors. [cite:de11_wiki_acq]

The co-investors were named in a filing on 5 May 2022. They included the Oracle founder Larry Ellison with $1 billion, the venture firm Sequoia with $800 million, the crypto exchange Binance with $500 million, Qatar Holding, part of Qatar's sovereign wealth fund, with $375 million, and Fidelity with $316 million, for a total of $7.14 billion in new commitments. [cite:de11_cnbc_coinvest] The Saudi investor Prince Alwaleed bin Talal and his Kingdom Holding company rolled over their existing stake of about 35 million shares, worth about $1.89 billion, rather than selling, and described themselves as jointly the second-largest investor after Musk; Twitter's co-founder Jack Dorsey rolled over shares worth just under $1 billion. [cite:de11_ab_gulf] Foreign sovereign and royal money, in other words, was documented in the purchase from the start, as an investment in a company. No document in this book's record shows foreign money flowing to the theorists of Part One; the distinction is drawn in [scene:de36_foreign_money|Part Thirty-Nine].

What changed

On the day the deal closed, Musk fired the chief executive, Parag Agrawal, the chief financial officer, the head of legal and policy, Vijaya Gadde, and the general counsel. On 4 November 2022 he laid off roughly half the workforce; staff eventually fell from about 7,500 to about 1,500. [cite:de11_wiki_acq] On 19 November, after an online poll in which 51.8 per cent voted yes, he restored Donald Trump's account, suspended after the attack on the Capitol of 6 January 2021, with the words "Vox Populi, Vox Dei." [cite:de11_globe_trump] In December 2022 he suspended several journalists who had covered his removal of an account that tracked his private jet. [cite:de11_wiki_acq] In July 2023 the service was renamed X. [cite:de11_wiki_acq]

Musk has repeatedly described himself as a "free speech absolutist." [cite:de11_fortune_turkey] The record of his ownership shows that commitment applied unevenly, and he has given his reasons. On the eve of Turkey's presidential election in May 2023, X restricted access to some content in Turkey at the government's demand. Musk's defence was practical: "The choice is have Twitter throttled in its entirety or limit access to some tweets." [cite:de11_fortune_turkey] Wikipedia's founder, Jimmy Wales, replied that his site had fought Turkey's government in court and won. [cite:de11_fortune_turkey] In Brazil the outcome was the reverse at first: Justice Alexandre de Moraes of the Supreme Federal Court ordered X blocked on 30 August 2024 after it failed to comply with orders to block accounts accused of spreading anti-democratic content, to name a legal representative and to pay fines; X complied and paid, and the ban was lifted in October. [cite:de11_jurist_brazil]

Government pressure on speech: the record both ways

Musk's purchase was framed, by him and by supporters, as a rescue of free speech from a platform that had bent to government. The record on that claim cuts in more than one direction. From 2 December 2022 selected writers, among them Matt Taibbi, Bari Weiss and Michael Shellenberger, published internal Twitter documents in releases coordinated with Musk, as the "Twitter Files." [cite:de11_wiki_tfiles] They showed internal deliberation over the October 2020 suppression of a New York Post story about Hunter Biden's laptop, over Trump's suspension, and over contacts with the FBI. They also showed that requests to remove content came from both sides: the Biden campaign asked for review of tweets, and the Trump White House made takedown requests often enough that the company kept a database of them. [cite:de11_wiki_tfiles] Taibbi himself wrote that there was "no evidence - that I've seen - of any government involvement in the laptop story." [cite:de11_wiki_tfiles]

The legal test of federal pressure on platforms reached the Supreme Court in Murthy v. Missouri. The Fifth Circuit had found that federal agencies likely coerced platforms through "intimidating messages and threats of adverse consequences"; on 26 June 2024 the Court ruled 6 to 3, in an opinion by Justice Amy Coney Barrett, that the states and users who sued lacked standing to seek an injunction, without deciding whether coercion had occurred. Justice Samuel Alito, joined by Justices Thomas and Gorsuch, dissented. [cite:de11_scotus_murthy] [cite:de11_wiki_tfiles] The record therefore supports a narrower statement than either side's: governments of both parties asked platforms to act on content; whether any of those requests crossed into unconstitutional coercion was argued and never resolved on the merits; and under Musk's ownership X has both resisted and complied with governments, abroad as at home, for reasons he has stated as practical. The record of press and speech under the administration since 2025 is set out in [scene:us3_speech|the library's volume on the United States].

xAI and Grok

Musk launched xAI, an artificial-intelligence company, in July 2023, to compete with products such as ChatGPT; its chatbot, Grok, was built into X. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] Grok's outputs have twice become news for what they said about race and Jews. On 14 May 2025 it began inserting claims of "white genocide" in South Africa into answers to unrelated questions; xAI blamed an "unauthorized modification" to its instructions by an employee. [cite:de11_wiki_musk_sa] In July 2025 it posted praise of Hitler and claims that people with Jewish surnames were behind "anti-white" activism; xAI said it had "taken action to ban hate speech before Grok posts on X," and the Anti-Defamation League called the output "irresponsible, dangerous and antisemitic, plain and simple." [cite:de11_reuters_grok] These are the company's product failures and the company's explanations. They are not, on the record, statements by Musk, and no document shows him directing the outputs. In the same month, on 14 July 2025, the Defense Department's AI office awarded xAI, alongside Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, an agreement with a ceiling of $200 million to develop AI tools for national-security work. [cite:de11_cdao]

The mergers of 2025 and 2026

On 28 March 2025 Musk announced that "xAI has acquired X in an all-stock transaction," valuing xAI at $80 billion and X at $33 billion, which he calculated as "$45B less $12B debt." [cite:de11_tc_xai_x] The valuation of X was well below the $44 billion he had paid. xAI kept raising money, including from the Gulf: its $20 billion round announced on 8 January 2026 included the Qatar Investment Authority and MGX, an Abu Dhabi technology fund, alongside Nvidia and Cisco. [cite:de11_agbi_xai] On 2 February 2026 SpaceX acquired xAI in what Reuters described as the largest merger on record, valuing SpaceX at $1 trillion and xAI at $250 billion; Musk called it "the next book in SpaceX and xAI's mission." [cite:de11_reuters_spacex_xai] SpaceX went public in June 2026, briefly making Musk the first person worth a trillion dollars; Forbes estimated his fortune at about $1.1 trillion in October 2026. [cite:de11_wiki_musk]

The result, as of October 2026, is a single company that owns a public forum, the chatbot trained on it, a satellite internet network used by armies, and a satellite network built for an intelligence agency, with Gulf sovereign funds among its shareholders and Musk as its controlling owner. [cite:de11_reuters_spacex_xai] [cite:de11_agbi_xai] [cite:de11_reuters_starshield] What that combination can do with data is a capability question, examined in [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four]; no document shows the data streams being combined. How Musk used his money and his platform in elections is the subject of [scene:de11_money_and_influence|the next section].

sections.h: Money and Political Influence
sections.html:
Until 2024 Musk's political money was modest for a man of his wealth. In the 2024 election he became the largest individual donor in the country, and in 2026 he spent more again. This section is a ledger: what he gave, to whom, when, and on what documentary basis, followed by the influence that is documented in the same period, appointments, contracts and regulatory relief, and the break with President Trump that interrupted it. The ledger reports sequence. Where money precedes an office, a contract or a policy, the record shows the order of events; it does not, on its own, show that one caused the other, and no document shows an exchange.

2024: the largest donor

Musk endorsed Trump in July 2024 and put most of his money into a super PAC of his own, America PAC. Year-end filings with the Federal Election Commission showed that he spent more than $290 million on the election, about a quarter of a billion of it through America PAC, including $11.2 million on the last day of 2024 earmarked for "petition incentives." [cite:de11_cnn_290m] He also gave millions to other Republican outside groups and $10,000 cheques to dozens of state Republican Party committees. [cite:de11_cnn_290m] The research group OpenSecrets put his 2024 giving at more than $291 million, at the top of the national list. [cite:de7_os_donors2024]

The most contested part of the spending was a daily $1 million giveaway to registered voters in swing states who signed an America PAC petition. Launching it in Harrisburg on 19 October 2024, Musk said the money would go "randomly to people who have signed the petition every day," and the next day posted that signers had "a daily chance of winning $1M!" [cite:de11_ap_sweeps] Philadelphia's district attorney, Larry Krasner, sued to stop it as an illegal lottery. In court on 4 November, America PAC's lawyer said: "The $1 million recipients are not chosen by chance." The PAC's director testified that recipients were vetted in advance and signed non-disclosure agreements, and conceded that "randomly" was not "the word I would have selected." [cite:de11_ap_sweeps] Judge Angelo Foglietta let the giveaway continue through election day. [cite:de11_ap_sweeps] A separate class action by a voter in federal court in Texas, in which Musk argued that the recipients were "selected to earn" the money, survived his motion to dismiss on 20 August 2025. [cite:de11_audit_mcaferty] The giveaways cost more than $50 million in all. [cite:de11_cnn_290m]

From donor to office

Trump won on 5 November 2024 and announced that Musk, with Vivek Ramaswamy, would lead a "Department of Government Efficiency." In January 2025 it was created by executive order, and Musk was designated a special government employee, a status limited to 130 days' service in a year. His formal title was not head of DOGE: in a court filing on 17 February 2025 the White House described him as a "Senior Advisor to the President" who "can only advise the President and communicate the President's directives," and named no role for him in DOGE's own chain of command. [cite:de11_audit_fisher] He was nonetheless its public face, and in March 2025 a federal judge, in a preliminary ruling, found that he was likely acting as its de facto leader. He left government at the end of May 2025, when his 130 days ran out. [cite:de11_wiki_musk] What the office was in law, who staffed it, what it reached and what it cut are the subjects of Book Three, beginning with [scene:de17_money_to_office|Part Seventeen]; this section records only the sequence. More than $290 million of campaign money preceded an advisory office with wide reach into federal systems. No document records any agreement between Musk and Trump connecting the two.

Wisconsin, April 2025

While still in government, Musk spent heavily on a state judicial election. In the race for a seat on the Wisconsin Supreme Court, which decided control of a court expected to rule on abortion, labour law, voting rules and possibly congressional maps, he and groups he backed spent more than $20 million supporting the conservative candidate, Brad Schimel, about one dollar in every five spent in the race. He paid people to sign a petition against "activist judges" and, in Green Bay, handed $1 million cheques to voters. [cite:de11_npr_wisc] On 1 April 2025 the liberal candidate, Susan Crawford, won by ten points. [cite:de11_npr_wisc]

The break, the party and the return

The partnership ended in public. Musk criticised the Republicans' tax and spending bill in late May 2025, and on 5 June the dispute escalated. Trump wrote that "the easiest way" to save billions would be to "terminate Elon's governmental subsidies and contracts"; Musk claimed that Trump would have lost the election without him and alleged, without offering evidence, that Trump was implicated in the unreleased Epstein files. [cite:de11_npr_feud] He later deleted the Epstein post, and on 11 June wrote that some of his posts about Trump "went too far." [cite:de11_audit_pbs_regret] On 5 July he announced on X that he had formed an "America Party" to "give you back your freedom," carrying out a threat he had made if "this insane spending bill passes." No filing for it was confirmed with the Election Commission, and Trump called the idea "ridiculous." [cite:de11_ap_party]

The party did not become the vehicle for his money. In May 2025 Musk had said he intended to spend less on politics: "I think I've done enough." [cite:de11_ap_2026] By the autumn of 2026 he had reconciled with Trump, who presented him with the National Medal of Science on 8 October 2026, and he had become the largest known donor of the midterm elections, giving to his own America PAC and to super PACs aligned with the Republican leadership. [cite:de11_ap_2026] Filings and the PAC's own statements put his giving since January 2025 at about $366 million by the end of September 2026, more than $276 million of it between July and September, and a pre-election filing on 22 October added $76.8 million more; known giving in the cycle passed $440 million. [cite:de11_ibt_fec] [cite:de11_ap_2026]

Documented influence, and its limits

The influence that is documented in the same years falls into three kinds. The first is office: the special-government-employee role as senior adviser and public face of the cuts, from January to May 2025. The White House told a court that the role gave him no greater authority than other senior advisers; a federal judge, in a preliminary ruling, found that he likely led DOGE in practice. [cite:de11_audit_fisher] [cite:de11_wiki_musk] The second is contracts and regulation favourable to his companies. In April 2025, while he was in government, SpaceX won about $5.92 billion of national-security launch work, in a procurement that began before 2025 and in which it was already the leading provider. [cite:de11_ussf_nssl] In August 2025, after the break, a launch-licensing order benefited SpaceX more than any other firm. [cite:de11_reuters_spaceeo] In April 2026, after the reconciliation began, SpaceX was among twelve firms given Golden Dome interceptor agreements. [cite:de11_bd_sbi] The third is regulatory exposure. A minority staff memo for Senator Richard Blumenthal, the senior Democrat on the Senate's investigations subcommittee, counted 65 federal actions involving Musk's companies that appeared to be active when Trump took office, and estimated potential liability of at least $2.37 billion for 40 of them, among them $1.19 billion over Tesla's claims for Autopilot and Full Self-Driving; it noted that the Justice Department had dismissed one SpaceX case in February 2025. [cite:de11_psi_memo] The memo is a partisan staff estimate of potential, not assessed, penalties, and the claim that DOGE was run to make those cases disappear is the sponsor's characterisation; the agencies' own records are examined in [scene:de21_conflicts_and_contracts|Part Twenty-One].

Two things in the record run against the simplest reading of this sequence. The first is the break itself: on 5 June 2025 the president publicly threatened the largest donor's contracts, which is hard to square with a government that donor had bought. [cite:de11_npr_feud] The second is the order of the largest regulatory benefit to SpaceX, which came after the break rather than during his time in office. [cite:de11_reuters_spaceeo] What the record does establish is scale and access: in two election cycles one man gave more than $700 million to one side of American politics, held a government role in between, and controls companies whose largest customer is the same government. How that compares with Peter Thiel's far smaller and earlier giving is set out in [scene:de9_money_and_influence|Part Nine], and the network-wide money map in [scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen].

sections.h: His Claims Against His Record
sections.html:
Musk makes more public claims than anyone else in this book, about his companies, his past, his money and his government work, and many of them are forecasts that time can test. This section applies to his own public statements the same four grades the book applies to every person it examines, the standard used for Curtis Yarvin in [scene:de6_claims_vs_record|Part Six]. RED marks a claim contradicted by the person's own documents or by sworn testimony. ORANGE marks a promise or claim not delivered, or not verifiable by an official auditor. YELLOW marks a reversal or concealment, shown with his own explanation. GREY marks a dispute in which credible accounts conflict, with both shown. The word "lie" is used only where the record shows the person knew a claim was untrue when he made it; nothing below meets that bar on the documents available, and each flag names the contradiction for the reader to judge.

RED: contradicted by documents or sworn testimony

"Funding secured" (7 August 2018): RED. Musk tweeted that he could take Tesla private at $420 a share, that funding was secured and that only a shareholder vote remained. The Securities and Exchange Commission charged that he knew the deal was uncertain and had not discussed specific terms, including price, with potential financing partners; on 29 September 2018 he settled without admitting or denying the charges, paying a $20 million penalty and giving up the chairmanship for three years. [cite:de11_sec_2018] In the shareholders' civil suit, Judge Edward Chen ruled that the tweets were false and made recklessly; a jury then found Musk not liable on 3 February 2023. [cite:de11_nbc_verdict] His explanation, given under oath, is that he believed he had a handshake agreement with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, which later backed out, and that he had "no ill motive." [cite:de11_nbc_verdict] The falsity of the statement is a judicial finding; the jury's verdict concerned liability for it.

The "random" $1 million giveaway (October 2024): RED. Musk said the money would go "randomly to people who have signed the petition," and that signers had "a daily chance of winning $1M!" The record against it comes from his own side in court. On 4 November 2024 his lawyer told a Philadelphia judge, "The $1 million recipients are not chosen by chance," and the director of America PAC, the committee Musk founded and funded, testified that recipients were vetted in advance and signed non-disclosure agreements. [cite:de11_ap_sweeps] His own explanation came in his own filing: asking a federal court in Texas to dismiss a voter's class action over the giveaway, Musk argued that the recipients were "selected to earn" the money as the PAC's spokespeople, so it was not a prize. On 20 August 2025 Judge Robert Pitman refused to dismiss the suit, pointing to Musk's and the PAC's statements that the money would be "awarded" and could be "won." [cite:de11_audit_mcaferty] The grade rests on that: the word "randomly" is contradicted by his own lawyers' statements and filing and by his committee's sworn testimony.

"I was in fact allowed to work in the US" (October 2024): RED. The claim is his own, posted after the Washington Post report, with "The Biden puppet is lying." [cite:de11_pbs_visa] The record against it is also his own: his 2005 email that he had applied to Stanford because he had "no legal right to stay in the country," together with a 1996 investor agreement giving him 45 days to obtain legal work status. [cite:de11_wapo_visa] His earlier explanations were that it was "a gray area" (2013) and that he was "legally there, but I was meant to be doing student work" (2020). [cite:de11_wapo_visa] The exact visa he held in 1995–96 has not been published, which is the one point on which his account could still be reconciled with the record.

ORANGE: promises not delivered

Self-driving and robotaxi timelines: ORANGE. In October 2016 he promised a fully autonomous drive from Los Angeles to New York by the end of 2017; in April 2019, "next year for sure, we'll have over a million robotaxis on the road"; in July 2020, the "basic functionality for level five autonomy complete this year." None was met. [cite:de11_fsd_list] Tesla's robotaxi service opened in Austin on 22 June 2025 with a safety monitor on board, and the first rides with no monitor in the car began on 22 January 2026, in "a few" vehicles in a small fleet. [cite:de11_fsd_list] [cite:de11_bbg_robotaxi] His explanation in 2020 was that regulatory approval was "the big unknown." [cite:de11_fsd_list] A Senate minority staff memo counted Tesla's Autopilot and self-driving claims among the federal matters pending against his companies. [cite:de11_psi_memo]

DOGE savings: ORANGE. At Madison Square Garden on 27 October 2024 he said of the federal budget, "I think we can do at least $2 trillion." [cite:de11_fortune_2t] On 10 April 2025 he told the cabinet that "we anticipate savings in '26 from reduction of waste and fraud by $150 billion"; DOGE's own website, which published only a sample of its cuts, had already corrected errors including an $8 billion contract that was in fact worth $8 million. [cite:de11_fortune_150b] His explanation was the revised target itself; a White House official said $1 trillion remained "the goal." [cite:de11_fortune_150b] The official auditor could not confirm even the smaller figure. In August 2026 the Government Accountability Office reviewed about $110 billion of savings DOGE claimed from cancelled contracts, grants and leases, and found that DOGE had not used its own stated method for most of the contract savings, that it could not verify the method behind 96 per cent of the grant savings because DOGE did not supply the information, and that one $1.7 billion contract "saving" saved nothing because the contract was never cancelled. [cite:de11_audit_gao_savings] Real cancellations and real payroll reductions did occur; what the auditor could not do was verify the claimed totals. The full audited record of what DOGE saved and cut is tested in [scene:de21_the_dividend|Part Twenty-One] and [scene:de20_the_cuts|Part Twenty].

YELLOW: reversals and omissions

"I think I've done enough" (May 2025): YELLOW. He said he intended to cut back on political spending. [cite:de11_ap_2026] He then gave about $366 million between January 2025 and September 2026 and more than $440 million in the cycle, the largest known sum of the midterms. [cite:de11_ibt_fec] No explanation from him for the change is on record; his PAC's spokesman said the money helped the Republican campaign "get its message out." [cite:de11_ap_2026]

Trump and the Epstein files (5 June 2025): YELLOW. In the feud he alleged, without evidence, that Trump was implicated in the files; he later deleted the post, and on 11 June wrote that he regretted some of his posts about Trump: "They went too far." [cite:de11_npr_feud] [cite:de11_audit_pbs_regret] His own explanation is the retraction.

Epstein (2020 and 2026): YELLOW. In July 2020 he wrote: "To the best our knowledge, he never toured SpaceX." In January 2026, after the Justice Department released sixteen emails between them from 2012 and 2013, he said he had "declined repeated invitations to go to his island." [cite:de11_time_epstein] The emails show more than that. Musk himself asked, on 24 November 2012, "What day/night will be the wildest party on your island?", cancelled a planned visit in January 2013, and asked in December 2013, "Is there a good time to visit?"; that visit was cancelled by Epstein. In February 2013 Epstein thanked him "for the tour" after a SpaceX visit, with a lunch in the calendar. [cite:de11_time_epstein] No document shows Musk visiting the island, and the emails give no indication of wrongdoing by him. [cite:de11_time_epstein] His explanation is that the emails could be "misinterpreted." [cite:de11_time_epstein] The flag is for the framing, which leaves out that he sought the visits.

GREY: credible accounts conflict

"Free speech absolutist": GREY. His self-description stands beside restrictions in Turkey at the government's demand, journalists suspended in December 2022, and compliance with Brazil's court in 2024; his explanation is practical, that the alternative was losing the country altogether. [cite:de11_fortune_turkey] [cite:de11_wiki_acq] [cite:de11_jurist_brazil] Defenders and critics read the same record differently.

The inauguration gesture (20 January 2025): GREY. Historians split: Ruth Ben-Ghiat called it a Nazi salute, Aaron Astor said it was not, and the Anti-Defamation League called it "an awkward gesture in a moment of enthusiasm." Musk said critics needed "better dirty tricks." [cite:de11_afp_gesture] The video is the record, and the readings conflict.

Starlink and the minerals talks (February 2025): GREY. Reuters reported from three sources that American negotiators raised a Starlink cut-off; Musk called the report false, and Secretary Rubio said no one had made such a threat. [cite:de11_dcd_minerals] [cite:de11_aj_sikorski]

No flag. On Crimea, the record supports his account: Isaacson corrected his own report, and coverage had never been enabled. [cite:de11_cnbc_isaacson] On Tesla, the 2009 settlement lets him use the title of co-founder. [cite:de11_af_settle]

The pattern differs from Yarvin's. Yarvin's flags are mostly GREY because his claims can be tested only against his own texts. Musk's include RED and ORANGE flags because he has filed with regulators, testified, run a political committee in court and made dated promises that an auditor or a calendar can check. That is a function of the record available as much as of the man: more of his life is documented, so more of it can be tested.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis this book tests holds that immigration enforcement and government cuts are the occasion, and a sovereign executive without a veto the destination. On this part's material, three things are documented. First, scale and sequence: more than $290 million spent in the 2024 election, nearly all of it to elect one candidate and his party, followed by a government role as the public face of the cuts, and more than $440 million to the same side in the 2026 cycle. [cite:de11_cnn_290m] [cite:de11_wiki_musk] [cite:de11_ibt_fec] Second, Musk's own stated goals for the cuts: to "delete entire agencies" and "remove the roots of the weed," in the name of "rule of the people — democracy" against "rule of the bureaucracy." [cite:de11_cbs_wgs] [cite:de3_dcpd_musk] Third, a concentration of private control over infrastructure the state relies on, from launch and spy satellites to battlefield communications and a public forum, which Musk has once used, in 2022, to limit an allied military operation. [cite:de11_reuters_starshield] [cite:de11_fox_sevastopol] [cite:de11_reuters_spacex_xai]

Probable, on this record, is only the modest claim that his money and his platform bought access beyond that of other donors; the office is the evidence. Not supported: that Musk holds or advances the Dark Enlightenment program. No statement of his adopting Yarvin's or Land's texts is documented, and his stated case for the cuts is the reverse of theirs, a defence of elected control against officials rather than the replacement of elections by an executive. [cite:de3_dcpd_musk] Whether his stated reason is the true one is a question of motive that the record does not settle. Not supported either: that particular contracts were bought; the largest launch award was competitive and began before 2025, and no document records an exchange. [cite:de11_ussf_nssl] And the record runs against the reading at one point that matters. In June 2025 the executive and its largest donor turned on each other in public, the president threatened the donor's contracts, and the donor announced a rival party. [cite:de11_npr_feud] [cite:de11_ap_party] A network that can split that way is not one bloc. [scene:de12_middletown_to_yale|Part Twelve] turns to J.D. Vance, the one figure in this book who holds an office in the line of succession; [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three] carries these grades into the book's final account.

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: J.D. Vance: the Life
chapters.intro: This part tells the life of J.D. Vance, the Vice President of the United States, and tests the claim that he is the political product of Peter Thiel. It separates what independent records carry from what rests on his own account: a Middletown childhood told mainly in his own memoir, the Marines, Ohio State and Yale, where a lecture by Thiel in 2011 changed his plans. It follows the five documented ties to Thiel, each of a different type, from employment at Mithril to investment in Narya and about $15 million for his 2022 Senate race, and the one widely repeated tie, Thiel's supposed push for him in 2024, that the record does not carry. It sets out what the vice presidency allows and what he has done with it, including his statements on the courts and his eight deciding votes, lists his money and influence in a ledger, and grades eight of his public claims against the record.
chapters.outro: The record of Vance's life supports a narrower story than either his admirers or his critics usually tell. Thiel shaped his thinking at Yale, employed him, invested in his fund, introduced him to Trump and paid for most of his first campaign, about $15 million through a single super PAC, and the two still share an interest in a fund Vance founded. [cite:de12_forbesau] [cite:de12_techcrunch_narya] [cite:de15_cnbc_fundraiser] [cite:de12_oge_2025] In 2021 Vance named Yarvin and called for firing the civil service and for answering the courts with "let him enforce it"; as Vice President he restated that view of judicial power, and his deciding votes defeated two efforts to check the President's emergency and war powers. [cite:de5_nextgov_vance] [cite:de12_ap_judges] [cite:de12_wiki_ties] But no document shows Thiel choosing him for the ticket or directing him in office, and in 2024 the record shows Vance asking Thiel for money and Thiel declining. [cite:de12_cnn_vppick] [cite:de12_dbeast_ft] His claims against the record yield four ORANGE flags, three of them about immigrants, and none RED. [cite:de12_reason_springfield] [cite:de12_pf_abrego] The same funding model was run for a second Thiel employee in the same year, with a different result; [scene:de15_vance_and_masters|Part Fifteen] sets the two side by side, after [scene:de13_who_they_are|Part Thirteen] maps the PayPal network around them.

sections.h: Middletown to Yale
sections.html:
James David Vance was born James Donald Bowman on 2 August 1984 in Middletown, Ohio, a steel town between Cincinnati and Dayton. [cite:de12_britannica] His parents divorced when he was small, and he was raised mostly by his maternal grandparents, who had moved to Middletown from eastern Kentucky. [cite:de12_britannica] In 1990 his mother's third husband adopted him and he became James David Hamel; in April 2013 he took the surname Vance, his mother's maiden name, and became the man the public knows. [cite:de12_wiki_vance] This part follows his life on the same terms as the book's other biographies: dated facts carried by independent records first, his own account second and flagged as his, and the lives of his relatives left as their own.

That last rule matters more for Vance than for anyone else in this book, because almost everything the public knows about his childhood household comes from one source: his own memoir, Hillbilly Elegy, published by Harper in June 2016. [cite:de12_wiki_vance] The book's portrait of his grandmother and grandfather, of a mother's long addiction, of instability and of the culture of the Kentucky hills is his telling of his family's story. The household details are not independently documented in the public record in the way his schooling, his service and his career are. They are not examined here, and nothing in this part treats a relative's life as part of Vance's record.

The Marines and Ohio State

Vance graduated from Middletown High School in 2003 and enlisted in the United States Marine Corps the same year. [cite:de12_britannica] He served from 2003 to 2007 as a combat correspondent, a military journalist, with the 2nd Marine Aircraft Wing, and spent six months of 2005 in Iraq in a non-combat role, writing articles and taking photographs. [cite:de12_wiki_vance] He left the Corps as a corporal in 2007. [cite:de12_wiki_vance]

He entered Ohio State University in 2007 and finished a bachelor's degree in political science and philosophy in 2009, with highest honours. [cite:de12_britannica] [cite:de12_wiki_vance] The speed is documented; it is the first sign of the ambition that runs through every later stage of the record.

Yale Law School, 2010–2013

In 2010 Vance entered Yale Law School, the most selective law school in the United States and a standard route into the country's legal, political and financial elite. He took his law degree in May 2013 and was admitted to the Kentucky bar later that year. [cite:de12_wiki_vance] At Yale he met Usha Chilukuri, whom he later married; her career and record are her own and are not part of this book's subject. [cite:de12_wiki_vance]

The single event at Yale that matters most for this book is one he described himself, seven years later. In 2011 Peter Thiel, the co-founder of PayPal and Palantir, whose life is told in [scene:de9_formation|Part Nine], gave a talk at Yale Law School. In an essay for the Catholic literary magazine The Lamp in 2020, Vance called it "the most significant moment of my time" at the school. [cite:de12_forbesau] He wrote that Thiel was "possibly the smartest person" he had ever met, and that Thiel's open Christian faith "defied the social template I had constructed," a template in which, as he put it, dumb people were Christians and smart ones atheists. [cite:de12_forbesau] The substance of the talk, as Vance recalled it, was Thiel's argument that technological progress had stalled and that America's elites had become a competition for a shrinking number of prestigious positions, two trends Thiel "saw … as connected." [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] Vance has said that the talk turned him away from a career in large-firm law and toward technology and investment. [cite:de12_fortune_mithril] [cite:de12_forbesau]

This account is Vance's own, written in 2020 when he was already Thiel's friend and investee and a year before Thiel funded his Senate race. It is the strongest available evidence of how the relationship began, because it is the only first-hand account of it, and it should be read with that standing: a sincere description by the person whose career it shaped, not an independent record of what happened in the room. What it does establish is the order of events. The documented relationship between the two men began with an idea, the stagnation thesis, in 2011, five years before any employment and ten years before any campaign money. [scene:de10_girard_and_the_katechon|Part Ten] sets out the ideas Thiel was carrying at the time.

Law, and a book

After Yale he clerked for a year for Judge David Bunning of the federal district court for the Eastern District of Kentucky, then practised corporate law at Sidley Austin, one of the country's largest law firms, and worked for a time for Senator John Cornyn of Texas; the exact dates of the clerkship and the firm are not consistent across published biographies and are given here as a span. [cite:de12_wiki_vance] [cite:de12_britannica]

Hillbilly Elegy appeared in June 2016, in the middle of Donald Trump's first campaign for the presidency, and became a bestseller because it seemed to explain the voters who were carrying him. [cite:de12_pbs_ap] Its jacket carried a blurb from Thiel, who, as Vance later wrote, would "become a good friend." [cite:de12_fortune_mithril] The book made Vance a public figure before he had held any public role, and it gave him two things that the rest of his career drew on: an income from royalties, which still appeared on his financial disclosures as Vice President in 2026, and a public identity as an interpreter of the white working class of Appalachia and the industrial Midwest. [cite:de12_ians_2026] The same year he told the television interviewer Charlie Rose that he was "a Never Trump guy," a position he would reverse within five years; [cite:de12_axios_trump2016] that reversal is told in [scene:de12_senate_and_the_ticket|the third section] and graded in [scene:de12_claims_vs_record|the last].

By the summer of 2016, then, the record shows a man of thirty-one with a working-class Ohio childhood, a Marine Corps enlistment, two elite degrees and a bestseller, and a friendship with one of the richest and most politically ambitious investors in Silicon Valley that had begun with a lecture. Nothing in this stage of the record connects him to the texts this book examines. His first documented contact with Curtis Yarvin came the year before the memoir appeared, and it came, like his first job in finance, through Thiel. [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|The next section] follows those years.

sections.h: The Thiel Years
sections.html:
Between 2015 and 2021 Vance's working life ran through venture capital, the business of investing other people's money in young companies in exchange for a share of them, and at every stage Peter Thiel was nearby: first as his employer, then as an investor in his fund, then as the man who introduced him to Donald Trump. This section sets out each tie by its type, its date and its source, because the relationship is often described in a single word, such as "protégé" or "creation," that the record does not support in any of its versions. What the record does show is a sequence of five distinct, documented connections, each of a different kind, and a sixth that is widely repeated but rests on one source.

Mithril, 2015 or 2016 to 2017

Vance moved to San Francisco to work at Mithril Capital, a venture firm Thiel co-founded and named after a fictional metal in J.R.R. Tolkien's novels. [cite:de12_fortune_mithril] [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] The dates and title differ by source. Politico, as reported by Forbes, said he joined as a partner in 2015; Fortune, citing the Wall Street Journal, said he began in 2016 and left in the spring of 2017; Wikipedia's account gives "principal" from 2016 to 2017. [cite:de12_forbesau] [cite:de12_fortune_mithril] [cite:de12_wiki_vance] No primary record of his start date has been published, and both versions are recorded here.

What he did there is also contested. Two former Mithril employees told the Journal that they rarely or never saw him in the office, that he spent much of his time promoting Hillbilly Elegy, and that neither could recall a significant deal he had worked on. [cite:de12_fortune_mithril] Crystal McKellar, a former managing director of the firm, wrote publicly in July 2024 that he had been "a great VC," quick to learn new industries and with "great instincts about people." [cite:de12_fortune_mithril] [cite:de12_axios_vc] Neither account is a document; both are recorded. The employment itself is documented, and it is the first financial tie between the two men: an employer and an employee.

It was in these years, according to Ava Kofman's 2025 profile of Curtis Yarvin, that Vance first met Yarvin, in 2015, through Thiel. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] The meeting is reported by one writer, not documented by a record, and no account of what was discussed has been published. It is the earliest reported contact between Vance and the author whose texts are at the centre of this book, and it is a social introduction, not a working or financial relationship.

Revolution and Ohio, 2017–2019

In the spring of 2017 Vance left Mithril for Revolution, the Washington investment firm founded by Steve Case, the co-founder of AOL, whose "Rise of the Rest" programme toured and invested in regions that venture capital usually ignored. [cite:de12_fortune_mithril] [cite:de12_axios_vc] One Journal source credited him with being "lead partner or co-lead on 14 deals" there, including start-ups in defence and artificial intelligence. [cite:de12_fortune_mithril] His one board seat was at AppHarvest, a Kentucky indoor-farming company in which he invested; he stepped down from the board to run for the Senate, and the company filed for bankruptcy in 2023, after he had left. [cite:de12_axios_vc] [cite:de12_fortune_mithril]

He also moved back to Ohio and founded a charity. Our Ohio Renewal, set up as a 501(c)(4) non-profit not long after the memoir appeared in 2016, was to address jobs, mental health and the opioid crisis across the industrial Midwest, with a stated goal of raising $500,000 a year; a tax-deductible foundation followed in 2017. [cite:de12_ap_ohiorenewal] The Associated Press found that it raised $221,000 in 2018, $80,000 of it Vance's own money, and less than $50,000 a year after that, before closing in 2021; its only notable work was paying for an addiction specialist, Dr Sally Satel, to practise for a year in Ironton, Ohio. [cite:de12_ap_ohiorenewal] The gap between the promise and the result is graded in [scene:de12_claims_vs_record|the last section of this part].

In August 2019 he was baptised and confirmed in the Catholic Church, a conversion he described in the same 2020 essay in which he credited Thiel's faith with unsettling his assumptions. [cite:de12_wiki_vance] [cite:de12_forbesau]

Narya, 2019–2020

In 2019 Vance co-founded Narya Capital in Cincinnati with Colin Greenspon, a former managing director at Mithril and former partner at the Rise of the Rest seed fund. [cite:de12_axios_vc] [cite:de12_techcrunch_narya] On 9 January 2020 TechCrunch reported, from a federal securities filing first flagged by Axios, that the fund had $93 million in commitments toward a target of $125 million, and named four of its investors: Thiel, the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, the former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt and the software entrepreneur Scott Dorsey. [cite:de12_techcrunch_narya] That makes Thiel a limited partner, an outside investor, in a fund Vance ran: the second financial tie, of a different type from the first. Vance's own financial disclosures as Vice President show that he still holds interests in Narya's first fund and a note owed to him by its management company; [scene:de12_money_and_influence|the fifth section] sets those out by the ranges he filed.

The turn to politics, 2021

In February 2021, according to the New York Times, Thiel brought Vance to Mar-a-Lago for his first meeting with Trump, the man Vance had called "reprehensible" five years earlier. [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de12_axios_trump2016] It was the third kind of tie, an introduction, and the most consequential, because Trump's endorsement fourteen months later would transform the Senate primary. The following month Thiel put $10 million into the super PAC that would carry Vance's campaign; that money, and the race, are the subject of [scene:de12_senate_and_the_ticket|the next section] and of [scene:de15_vance_and_masters|Part Fifteen].

In September 2021, two months after announcing his run, Vance gave the interview that ties him, in his own words, to this book's texts. On the podcast Jack Murphy Live he said: "There's this guy, Curtis Yarvin, who's written about some of these things," and went on, "I'm sympathetic to that project. But another option is that we should just seize the administrative state for our own purposes." [cite:de5_wbur_vance] [cite:de5_vox_2022] In the same appearance he said a future President Trump should "fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state" and "replace them with our people," and that when the courts objected the President should answer, as Andrew Jackson is popularly said to have done, "The chief justice has made his ruling. Now let him enforce it." [cite:de5_nextgov_vance] [scene:de5_the_public_years|Part Five] places the remark in Yarvin's life; [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six] sets out the program he was naming, including the proposal Yarvin called RAGE, "Retire All Government Employees."

The remark is the one occasion on which Vance cited Yarvin by name in public, and two things about it need to be held together. It is documented, in his own voice, and it endorses the central practical idea of Yarvin's program, replacing the civil service wholesale with loyalists, together with a stated willingness to ignore the courts.
