It is also a candidate's remark on a podcast, made in 2021, before he held any office; it is not a policy document, and it expressly offers the "seize the administrative state" route as an alternative to the project he was "sympathetic to," not as that project. Yarvin, for his part, later described their acquaintance as slight: he said he had interacted with Vance once after the 2024 election, at a party, and a Vance adviser told CNN in 2025 that the two had met "like once." [cite:de5_politico_ward] [cite:de6_cnn_2025] What happened to these words when their speaker reached office is the subject of [scene:de12_one_heartbeat_away|the fourth section].

Read as a whole, these six years support a narrow conclusion and rule out two broad ones. The narrow conclusion is that Thiel repeatedly backed, employed, invested alongside and introduced a man whose outlook he had already helped to shape, and that each tie was of a different, documented type. The broad readings it rules out, on the present record, are that Thiel "created" Vance, since the first tie was an idea Vance encountered as a student and the memoir that made him famous was his own, and that Thiel controlled him, since no document shows Thiel directing anything Vance said or did. [scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen] places these ties on the map of Thiel's wider network.

sections.h: The Senate and the Ticket
sections.html:
Vance went from private investor to Vice President of the United States in under four years, and he did it through two endorsements by Donald Trump: one for the Senate in April 2022 and one for the vice presidency in July 2024. Between and around those endorsements sits the money that made his first race possible, nearly all of it from one man, and a reversal of opinion about Trump that he has explained in his own words. This section sets out the race, the money and the reversal by date, and then examines the most widely repeated claim about his selection in 2024, which the record does not carry.

The money arrives first

On 15 March 2021, more than three months before Vance declared, Fox News reported that Thiel had put $10 million of his own money into a new super PAC, Protect Ohio Values, set up in anticipation of a Vance campaign, and that the family of the hedge-fund investor Robert Mercer had also made what the PAC called a "significant" donation. [cite:de12_foxbiz_pov] A super PAC is a committee that may raise and spend unlimited sums on a candidate's behalf, provided it does not coordinate with the candidate's own campaign; the form exists because of the Supreme Court's 2010 Citizens United decision and the appeals-court ruling that followed it. Vance announced his candidacy for the seat being vacated by Senator Rob Portman on 1 July 2021. [cite:de12_wiki_vance] [cite:de12_pbs_ap]

Thiel's money did more than buy advertising. Politico, as summarised by Forbes, reported that most of Vance's paid advertising was in effect outsourced to the super PAC, and that Thiel recruited about ten other major donors, among them his PayPal colleague David Sacks, who gave $1 million. [cite:de12_forbesau] [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] CBS News, citing the Kansas City Star and OpenSecrets, added that Thiel steered at least $200,000 more through Per Aspera Policy, a non-profit he controlled that did not have to disclose its donors. [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] Under federal law a super PAC must operate independently of the campaign it supports. In June 2022 the Campaign Legal Center, a non-partisan watchdog, complained to the Federal Election Commission that Protect Ohio Values had given the campaign polling and voter-targeting data worth more than $1 million through a website hidden from the public; in May 2024 the Commission dismissed the complaint "in light of the public nature of the communications at issue." [cite:de15_clc_complaint] [cite:de15_fec_mur8009] The allegation was made and was dismissed; no finding of illegal coordination exists.

The reversal

The obstacle to the endorsement Vance needed was his own record. In 2016 he had told Charlie Rose he was "a Never Trump guy" who "never liked him"; he wrote in The Atlantic that "Trump is cultural heroin"; in a private message to his former college roommate Josh McLaurin, later made public by McLaurin, he said he went back and forth between thinking Trump a cynic like Nixon and "America's Hitler"; and he posted that Trump was "reprehensible" and that he would vote for the independent Evan McMullin. [cite:de12_axios_trump2016] The Associated Press also recorded that he had called Trump "dangerous" and "unfit." [cite:de12_pbs_ap] Before Trump endorsed him, Vance apologised repeatedly and deleted the critical posts. [cite:de12_axios_trump2016] His explanation, given most fully after he joined the ticket, was that he had been "certainly skeptical" in 2016 but that Trump "was a great president, and he changed my mind," and that he had "bought into the media's lies and distortions." [cite:de12_mediaite_hannity] "When you see somebody, you were wrong about them," he said, "you ought to admit the mistake." [cite:de12_axios_trump2016] The change of position and the timing are both on the record; why he changed is a question about motive that his own account answers one way and his critics another, and [scene:de12_claims_vs_record|the last section] grades it on that basis.

The primary and the general election

Trump endorsed Vance on 15 April 2022, in a crowded primary field. [cite:de12_wiki_oh2022] The following week Thiel gave Protect Ohio Values another $3.5 million. [cite:de12_pw_pov] In May Vance won the Republican nomination with 32.2 per cent of the vote, ahead of Josh Mandel (23.9) and Matt Dolan (23.3). [cite:de12_wiki_oh2022] By the time of his last gift, in April, Thiel had given the PAC about $15 million, according to CNBC and to CBS citing OpenSecrets; NBC, from Federal Election Commission records in July, put it at "over $14 million," and Ballotpedia, citing Forbes, gives $10 million. [cite:de15_cnbc_fundraiser] [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de15_nbc_mtp] [cite:de12_ballotpedia_thiel] The figures reflect different counting dates and sources; the larger is the one most widely reported from the filings, and Politico called it the most ever given to a single Senate candidate. [cite:de12_fortune_mithril]

Thiel gave nothing more for the general election. CNBC reported in October that he had signalled he was done spending for Vance, whom he believed was on course to win. [cite:de15_axios_double] [cite:de15_cnbc_results] The money in the general came from elsewhere. In the third quarter Vance's own campaign raised more than $6.9 million against $17.2 million for his Democratic opponent, Tim Ryan, and the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with the Republican Senate leader Mitch McConnell, booked $28 million of advertising in Ohio; outside groups of all kinds spent about $94.8 million on the race. [cite:de12_vindy_q3] [cite:de12_propublica_oh] On 8 November 2022 Vance won by 53.0 per cent to 46.9. [cite:de12_wiki_oh2022] He was sworn in as a senator on 3 January 2023. [cite:de12_britannica]

The ticket, 2024

Trump announced Vance as his running mate on Truth Social on 15 July 2024, the first day of the Republican National Convention. [cite:de12_cnn_vppick] [cite:de12_britannica] CNN's reconstruction of the decision, published the next day, named the people who had pushed for him: Elon Musk, who took a call from Trump at the end; Donald Trump Jr., who told his father at a late dinner, "Listen, I think I've seen him on TV"; the broadcaster Tucker Carlson; Steve Bannon; David Sacks and the property developer Steve Witkoff; and Senators Tommy Tuberville and Jim Banks. [cite:de12_cnn_vppick] Others pushed against him: Rupert Murdoch lobbied for Doug Burgum, the Fox host Sean Hannity for Marco Rubio, and some donors for Glenn Youngkin. [cite:de12_cnn_vppick]

A line widely repeated since then says that Thiel "led the charge to convince Trump to pick Vance." It appeared in The New Republic on 22 July 2024, sourced by a link to a Rolling Stone article. [cite:de12_tnr] CNN's account does not mention Thiel at all, and Thiel's own public statements that summer were about money, not the choice of running mate: at the Aspen Ideas Festival in June he said, "If you hold a gun to my head, I'll vote for Trump," but that he would not give to the campaign. [cite:de12_cnn_vppick] [cite:de9_nbc_aspen] On the record as it stands, the claim is single-sourced and contested, and this book does not use it as a finding.

The record of the campaign itself runs, if anything, the other way. In April 2024 Trump asked Thiel for $10 million, and Thiel refused. [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] In November 2023 The Atlantic reported, in its writer's paraphrase, that Thiel wanted it known he "wouldn't be giving money to any politician, including Donald Trump, in the next presidential campaign." [cite:de9_pw_atlantic] In August 2024 Vance himself told the Financial Times that he was "talking to Peter and persuading him" to contribute. [cite:de12_dbeast_ft] No resulting gift to the Trump campaign or its super PACs has been reported; Federal Election Commission records summarised by Ballotpedia show Thiel giving just over $1.7 million to federal candidates and parties in the 2024 cycle as a whole, a total that is not itemised by date and is tested against his pledge in [scene:de9_claims_vs_record|Part Nine]. [cite:de12_ballotpedia_thiel] A running mate publicly lobbying his old employer for money, without visible result, does not fit a picture in which the employer was directing the ticket. Vance and Trump won on 5 November 2024; Vance resigned his Senate seat at midnight on 10 January 2025 and was sworn in as the fiftieth Vice President on 20 January. [cite:de12_wiki_vance]

The race and the ticket establish the core facts on which every later argument about Vance and Thiel rests. Thiel's money was the largest single source of funds behind Vance's primary campaign, and it arrived before the candidacy did. Trump's endorsement, which Vance sought after a public reversal, came next, and Thiel's money followed it again. In the general election the party's money replaced Thiel's, and in 2024 the record shows Vance asking Thiel for money rather than Thiel choosing Vance. [scene:de15_vance_and_masters|Part Fifteen] sets the 2022 race beside the one Thiel financed in Arizona the same year.

sections.h: One Heartbeat Away
sections.html:
The phrase that gives this section its title is old American shorthand for the vice presidency: an office with little power of its own whose holder is one death, resignation or removal from the presidency. For this book the phrase carries a specific weight. The man who stands there has named Curtis Yarvin approvingly in public, once urged a president to fire the civil service and defy the Supreme Court, and had his first campaign financed more heavily by Peter Thiel than by any other individual. This section sets out what the office actually allows, what Vance has done with it from January 2025 to October 2026, what he has said about the courts since taking it, and how succession works in law.

What the office allows

The Constitution gives the Vice President two functions. The first is in Article I: "The Vice President of the United States shall be President of the Senate, but shall have no Vote, unless they be equally divided." [cite:de12_cornell_art1] The second is succession. The Twenty-Fifth Amendment provides that if the President is removed from office, dies or resigns, "the Vice President shall become President." [cite:de12_crs_25th] Its third section lets a President hand power temporarily to the Vice President, who becomes Acting President; its fourth lets the Vice President, together with a majority of the heads of the executive departments, declare the President unable to serve. If the President disputes that declaration, Congress decides, and the Vice President continues to act only if two-thirds of both Houses agree within twenty-one days. [cite:de12_crs_25th] Everything else a Vice President does, from chairing councils to travelling abroad to raising money, is delegated by the President and can be withdrawn by him.

Three plain consequences follow. Vance is first in the line of succession, ahead of the Speaker of the House, the President pro tempore of the Senate and then the Cabinet in a fixed statutory order beginning with the Secretary of State. [cite:de12_cornell_3usc19] He cannot remove a President on his own: the incapacity procedure requires a majority of the Cabinet and, if contested, a two-thirds vote of Congress. [cite:de12_crs_25th] And no donor, adviser or private party has any role in succession at any point. The worst-case reading of this book attaches to the first consequence; the second and third set its limits.

The deciding votes

Because the Republicans hold a majority in the Senate, Vance's tie-breaking vote has mattered only when enough Republicans have joined the Democrats to produce a tie. By the count kept from the Senate's roll calls, he had cast eight such votes as of October 2026, the most recent on 14 January 2026. [cite:de12_wiki_ties] The first, on 24 January 2025, confirmed Pete Hegseth as Secretary of Defense, 51 to 50. On 30 April 2025 he voted to table a resolution that would have ended the national emergency on which the President's global tariffs rested. On 1 July 2025 he cast three votes on the reconciliation bill known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, two on amendments and the last on final passage. On 15 July 2025 he cast two procedural votes that moved the Rescissions Act of 2025, a bill cancelling previously approved spending, toward passage. [cite:de12_wiki_ties]

The eighth came on 14 January 2026, on a resolution under the War Powers Act to bar further military action against Venezuela without congressional approval. Three Republicans, Rand Paul, Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins, voted with the Democrats; two others who had signalled support changed their votes after receiving assurances from the White House and from Secretary of State Marco Rubio; and at 50 to 50 Vance announced "the point of order is sustained," ending the measure. [cite:de12_dw_venezuela] [cite:de12_wiki_ties] For comparison, Kamala Harris cast thirty-three tie-breaking votes as Vice President, the most in history. [cite:de12_wiki_ties]

The list is a matter of record, and one pattern in it is plain without interpretation: two of the eight votes defeated attempts by the Senate to limit the President's emergency and war powers. That is what a tie-breaking Vice President of the President's party is expected to do. It is also, in this book's terms, a documented instance of the office being used to keep a check on the executive from operating.

What he has said about the courts

In September 2021, as a candidate, Vance said a President who fired the civil service and was stopped by the courts should "stand before the country" like Andrew Jackson and say, "The chief justice has made his ruling. Now let him enforce it." [cite:de5_nextgov_vance] As Vice President he returned to the subject within three weeks of taking office. On 9 February 2025, the day after a federal judge in New York, Paul Engelmayer, temporarily barred the Department of Government Efficiency's staff from the Treasury's payment systems, he posted: "If a judge tried to tell a general how to conduct a military operation, that would be illegal. If a judge tried to command the attorney general in how to use her discretion as a prosecutor, that's also illegal. Judges aren't allowed to control the executive's legitimate power." [cite:de12_ap_judges] The post did not say the administration would disobey the order, and it did not say it would comply; the qualifier "legitimate" left the question of who decides what is legitimate unstated. [cite:de12_ap_judges]

The two statements are consistent with each other. Neither is an act: no document shows Vance, as Vice President, directing any official to disregard a court order, and the office gives him no power to do so. What they establish is his stated view of where executive power ends, in his own words, at two dates four years apart. The legal fights over that boundary in 2025 and 2026 are the subject of [scene:de19_the_courts|Part Nineteen].

The rest of the record in office

Three other episodes from the first months show how he has used the platform. On 7 February 2025, after a staff member of the Department of Government Efficiency, Marko Elez, resigned over racist posts the Wall Street Journal linked to him, Vance argued that he should be rehired: "I don't think stupid social media activity should ruin a kid's life." Trump answered, "I'm with the vice president." [cite:de12_ap_elez] On 11 February, at the AI Action Summit in Paris, he said he was "not here this morning to talk about AI safety," but "AI opportunity," and that "excessive regulation of the AI sector could kill a transformative industry." [cite:de12_wex_paris] On 14 February, at the Munich Security Conference, he told European leaders that "what I worry about is the threat from within" and that "in Britain and across Europe, free speech, I fear, is in retreat." [cite:de12_cnbc_munich] On 18 March the Republican National Committee named him its finance chairman, the first sitting Vice President to hold the post. [cite:de12_rnc_finance]

As of October 2026 he was campaigning for Republican candidates in the November midterm elections, dividing the map with the President, and had said he would decide about running for President in 2028 only after the midterms; Rubio had said publicly that he would support him if he ran. [cite:de12_cnn_2028] In August 2026 the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, called him "Peter Thiel's boy"; Vance replied that "the guy's crazy" and did not address Thiel. [cite:de12_wear_elsayed] No meeting or transaction between Vance and Thiel since January 2025 has been reported.

The position, then, is this. A man who in 2021 named Yarvin and endorsed replacing the civil service and ignoring the Supreme Court is first in line to the presidency, holds that view of judicial power in substantially the same words in 2025, and has used the one vote the Constitution gives him to defeat two attempts to check the executive. Nothing in the record shows him acting outside the office's limits, directing anyone to defy a court, or taking instructions from Thiel or anyone else; and the path from his office to the presidency runs, in law, only through the President's death, resignation or removal, or through a procedure that needs the Cabinet and, if contested, two-thirds of Congress. [cite:de12_crs_25th] [cite:de12_cornell_3usc19]

sections.h: Money and Political Influence
sections.html:
This section is a ledger. It lists the documented political money that has flowed to Vance as a candidate, the documented financial interests he holds as Vice President, and the documented acts of influence he has exercised in office, each with its date, amount or range, and source. It applies one rule throughout: timing is not causation. Where a donation precedes an outcome, the ledger records the sequence and says no more than the sequence shows; where a connection between Vance's office and a donor's interest is suggested but not documented, it says so.

Money in: the candidate

Almost all the documented money behind Vance's political rise came in one cycle, 2021–22, and most of it through one vehicle. Protect Ohio Values received $10 million from Thiel in March 2021, before Vance had declared, and $3.5 million more in the week after Trump's endorsement in April 2022, reaching about $15 million in all by April 2022 according to reporting from Federal Election Commission filings. [cite:de12_foxbiz_pov] [cite:de12_pw_pov] [cite:de15_cnbc_fundraiser] [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] Ballotpedia, citing Forbes, gives $10 million, and NBC, from the filings in July 2022, "over $14 million"; the differences reflect the counting date and are recorded rather than reconciled. [cite:de12_ballotpedia_thiel] [cite:de15_nbc_mtp] At least $200,000 more came through Per Aspera Policy, a non-profit Thiel controlled; the Mercer, Uihlein and Lindner families gave to the same PAC; and David Sacks, recruited by Thiel, gave $1 million to a pro-Vance super PAC. [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de12_forbesau] In the general election Thiel gave nothing, and the Senate Leadership Fund booked $28 million in Ohio advertising. [cite:de15_cnbc_results] [cite:de12_vindy_q3]

No comparable flow is documented in 2024. Vance said in August 2024 that he was "talking to Peter and persuading him" to give to the Trump campaign; Thiel had refused Trump's own request for $10 million that April, and no gift to the campaign or its super PACs has been reported. [cite:de12_dbeast_ft] [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de12_ballotpedia_thiel] Vance's own political giving as a private citizen before 2021 has not been publicly reported, and it is recorded here as unknown rather than as nothing.

Money held: the Vice President's disclosures

As Vice President, Vance files an annual public financial disclosure with the Office of Government Ethics on Form 278e, which reports assets, income and debts in statutory value ranges rather than exact sums. The ranges cannot be added into a single figure, and are given here as filed. His report covering 2024, filed in 2025, lists an interest in Narya Capital Fund I worth $500,001 to $1 million; a small interest in Narya Fund II; a share of Fund I's carried interest, the portion of profits paid to the fund's managers, at 56.4 per cent of the first $7 million; a receivable of $500,001 to $1 million; and a promissory note from Narya Capital Management valued at $1,000,001 to $5 million, which the form says had earlier been mischaracterised as equity, paying interest of $100,001 to $1 million. [cite:de12_oge_2025] It also lists an interest of $100,001 to $250,000 in the Rise of the Rest seed fund from his Revolution years, royalties from Hillbilly Elegy of $50,001 to $100,000, and a Charles Schwab line of credit of $1,000,001 to $5 million as a liability. [cite:de12_oge_2025]

His next annual report, made public on 1 July 2026 after a 45-day extension, again listed his Narya fund interests, carried interest and fee rights, now reporting the Narya note at $500,001 to $1 million with interest of $100,001 to $1 million; it showed book royalties of $1,000,001 to $5 million, holdings of $1 million to $5 million each in three exchange-traded funds that track broad stock indexes, and the same line of credit. [cite:de12_ians_2026] The two filings describe the note in different ranges; the second is the more recent and is the one in force as of October 2026.

These disclosures establish the one continuing financial link between Vance and Thiel that the public record shows. Thiel was named in January 2020 as an investor in Narya's debut fund; Vance still holds an interest in that fund, a share of its profits and a note owed to him by its management company. [cite:de12_techcrunch_narya] [cite:de12_oge_2025] Whether Thiel remains an investor in the fund is not shown in any public filing. The connection, then, is a shared financial interest at the level of a fund, documented as of 2020 on Thiel's side and as of 2026 on Vance's. It is not a transaction between the two men, and no transaction between them since January 2025 has been reported.

Influence exercised: the office

The documented acts of influence in Vance's record are those of the office. He has cast eight tie-breaking votes, among them the confirmation of the Secretary of Defense, the passage of the 2025 reconciliation bill and the defeat of resolutions on the tariff emergency and on war with Venezuela. [cite:de12_wiki_ties] He urged the rehiring of a Department of Government Efficiency staffer after racist posts, and the President agreed. [cite:de12_ap_elez] He set out a deregulatory position on artificial intelligence in Paris in February 2025, and since March 2025 he has chaired the Republican National Committee's finance operation, which makes him the party's chief fundraiser as well as a recipient of past fundraising. [cite:de12_wex_paris] [cite:de12_rnc_finance]

The deregulatory position on artificial intelligence overlaps with the commercial interests of Thiel's companies, as it overlaps with those of almost the entire American technology industry; the overlap is real, it is not specific to Thiel, and no document shows Thiel or any of his companies asking Vance to take it. One indirect exposure is documented. The news site Sludge reported in July 2025 that the Rise of the Rest seed fund, in which Vance holds an interest of up to $250,000 and a small share of the managers' profits, lists among its portfolio companies the defence firm Anduril, which had received more than $220 million in federal contract actions since January 2025; Vance holds no direct stake, and vice presidents are exempt from the rules that require many senior officials to sell such holdings. [cite:de12_sludge_rotr] [cite:de12_oge_2025] That is a fund-level exposure through Steve Case's firm, not a Thiel vehicle. Contracts awarded to Palantir and Anduril since 2025 were made by agencies under the President, not by the Vice President; they are listed in [scene:de27_money_and_war|Part Twenty-Nine] and [scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen], and none has been documented as involving Vance.

Appointments are a second channel of influence, and here too the record is the administration's rather than Vance's. People connected to Thiel and the PayPal network took posts in 2025, and their positions are set out in [scene:de13_where_they_sit_now|Part Thirteen]; no public document shows Vance recommending or securing any of those appointments, and none is attributed to him here.

The ledger supports three findings and no more. First, the money that launched Vance's political career came overwhelmingly from Thiel and arrived before the candidacy. Second, Vance and Thiel still share a documented financial interest at the level of a fund Vance founded, through disclosures that are public, filed in ranges and current to 2026. Third, nothing in the record connects any act of Vance's office to the interest of Thiel or any Thiel company. The sequence from donation to office is documented; the return path from office to donor is not. [scene:de14_loops|Part Fourteen] examines that path among the network's other candidate loops, and [scene:de17_money_to_office|Part Seventeen] the parallel case of Elon Musk.

sections.h: His Claims Against His Record
sections.html:
Vance is the first person in this book to have held elected office, so his statements can be tested against official findings, court records and his own disclosures. This section tests eight public claims that shaped how people saw him or the people he spoke about, using the four grades the book applies to everyone. RED marks a claim contradicted by the person's own documents or sworn record. ORANGE marks a claim not delivered, or not supported by the official record. YELLOW marks a reversal or concealment, shown with the person's own explanation. GREY marks a dispute in which credible accounts conflict, with both shown. The word "lie" is used only where the record shows that the person knew a claim was false when making it; one flag below comes close to that bar, and the section explains why it is not used.

Flags on what he said about others

Pets in Springfield (9–10 September 2024): ORANGE. On the morning of 9 September 2024, as a candidate for Vice President, Vance posted that "reports now show that people have had their pets abducted and eaten by people who shouldn't be in this country," referring to Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio. [cite:de12_reason_springfield] The same morning a member of his staff called the Springfield city manager, Bryan Heck, to ask whether the rumours were true. Heck told the Wall Street Journal: "I told him no. There was no verifiable evidence or reports to show this was true," and that he had said the claims were "baseless." [cite:de12_reason_springfield] The reporting does not establish whether the call came before or after the post. The next day Vance wrote that "it's possible, of course, that all of these rumors will turn out to be false," and told readers of his post to "keep the cat memes flowing." [cite:de12_reason_springfield] Ohio's Republican governor, Mike DeWine, called the story "a piece of garbage that was simply not true." [cite:de12_reason_springfield] The one police report Vance's staff supplied to support it concerned a resident's cat that was later found safe in her own basement. [cite:de12_reason_springfield] He said the claims came from "firsthand accounts from my constituents," ten of them "verifiable and confirmable"; no official body has confirmed any. [cite:de12_mediaite_bash]

This is the flag in Vance's record that comes closest to the book's bar for the word "lie": his office had the city's denial on the day he first spread the claim, he acknowledged the next day that it might be false, and he kept repeating it. It does not meet the bar, because the record does not show that he believed the claim false; he has said he relied on his constituents, and what he believed is a question of motive that only he can answer. The grade is ORANGE: a claim not supported, and directly contradicted, by the official record.

"Create stories" (15 September 2024): GREY. On CNN's State of the Union, asked about the pets claim, he said: "If I have to create stories so that the American media actually pays attention to the suffering of the American people, then that's what I'm going to do." [cite:de12_mediaite_bash] Critics read it as an admission of invention; in the same answer he gave his own meaning: "I say that we're creating a story, meaning we're creating the American media focusing on it." [cite:de12_mediaite_bash] Both readings are available from the words, and the book does not choose between them.

Springfield's Haitians as "illegal aliens" (September 2024): ORANGE. Vance repeatedly called Springfield's Haitian residents illegal immigrants, and said, "I'm still going to call them illegal aliens." [cite:de12_pf_haitians] City and state officials said most were in the country under humanitarian parole or temporary protected status, both lawful forms of temporary permission to live and work in the United States, and PolitiFact rated his description false. [cite:de12_pf_haitians] His argument, stated in his own words, was not that the permissions did not exist but that they were an illegitimate use of executive power, a "wand" waved to make unlawful entrants lawful. [cite:de12_pf_haitians] That is a real legal argument, and the administration he joined later moved to end both programmes. [cite:de12_ap_tps2025] As a description of his neighbours' legal status in 2024, however, the official record does not support the word he chose.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia "a convicted MS-13 gang member" (1 April 2025): ORANGE. As Vice President, Vance posted that Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran man the administration had deported to El Salvador weeks earlier, "was a convicted MS-13 gang member with no legal right to be here." [cite:de12_pf_abrego] He had never been convicted of any crime. A 2019 immigration bond denial rested on an informant's allegation of gang membership, which he denied, in a proceeding that was not a criminal trial; the same year a judge barred his removal to El Salvador, and government lawyers later called his deportation an "administrative error." [cite:de12_pf_abrego] Vance's office did not respond to PolitiFact, and no correction of the word "convicted" is on record. [cite:de12_pf_abrego] After his return to the United States he was charged with human smuggling in Tennessee; on 22 May 2026 Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed those charges on finding a presumption of vindictive prosecution, and the Justice Department said it would appeal. [cite:de12_npr_abrego] As of October 2026 he has no criminal conviction. The gang allegation itself remains contested; the word "convicted" is contradicted by the record.

Flags on his own record

Trump, 2016 against 2021 onward: YELLOW. In 2016 he called himself "a Never Trump guy," called Trump "cultural heroin" and "reprehensible," privately weighed whether he was "America's Hitler," and said he would vote for Evan McMullin. [cite:de12_axios_trump2016] From 2021 he sought and won Trump's endorsement, and in 2024 joined his ticket. [cite:de12_wiki_oh2022] [cite:de12_cnn_vppick] His explanation is that Trump's record as President "changed my mind," that he had "bought into the media's lies and distortions," and that "you ought to admit the mistake." [cite:de12_mediaite_hannity] [cite:de12_axios_trump2016] The reversal, the explanation and the timing, which coincided with his need for the endorsement, are all documented; the motive stays contested.

Our Ohio Renewal (2016–2021): ORANGE. Vance said his charity would raise $500,000 a year to fight addiction and unemployment across the industrial Midwest. It raised $221,000 in its best year, 2018, of which $80,000 was his own money, then less than $50,000 a year until it closed in 2021, and its one notable project was a year-long residency for an addiction specialist. [cite:de12_ap_ohiorenewal] Vance has acknowledged that the groups "fell far short of his aspirations," and his campaign pointed to a key organiser's cancer diagnosis. [cite:de12_ap_ohiorenewal] The promise was not delivered, by his own account as well as the record.

The courts (2021 and 2025): no flag. His 2021 call to answer the courts with "let him enforce it" and his 2025 post that "judges aren't allowed to control the executive's legitimate power" are consistent with each other. [cite:de5_nextgov_vance] [cite:de12_ap_judges] There is no contradiction to grade. The record against him on this point is what he said, and it is set out in [scene:de12_one_heartbeat_away|the fourth section].

His acquaintance with Yarvin: no flag. Vance named Yarvin once in public, in 2021; Kofman reported that they met in 2015 through Thiel; Yarvin described one encounter at a party in January 2025; and a Vance adviser said in 2025 that they had met "like once." [cite:de5_wbur_vance] [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] [cite:de5_politico_ward] [cite:de6_cnn_2025] Citing an author is not meeting him, and the accounts of contact are loose but not contradictory.

Accounts of his venture career conflict, from colleagues who recalled no significant deal at Mithril to a former managing director who called him "a great VC"; with no dated claim of his own for them to contradict, it is not graded. [cite:de12_fortune_mithril]

Yarvin's flags in [scene:de6_claims_vs_record|Part Six] were mostly GREY. Vance's are mostly ORANGE, and three of the four concern immigrants, in claims official records contradicted and he did not correct. None reaches RED: none is contradicted by his own documents or sworn testimony.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis this book tests holds that immigration enforcement and government cuts are the occasion, and a sovereign executive without a veto the destination. Vance's life bears on it more directly than any other in Book II, because he is the only person in the network who could become the executive. Documented: that a man whose first campaign was financed mainly by Thiel, who worked for and was invested in by Thiel, and who still shares a fund-level financial interest with him, is first in the line of succession. [cite:de12_foxbiz_pov] [cite:de12_techcrunch_narya] [cite:de12_oge_2025] [cite:de12_cornell_3usc19] Documented: that in 2021 he named Yarvin, endorsed firing the civil service and replacing it "with our people," and endorsed answering the Supreme Court with "let him enforce it"; that as Vice President he restated the core of that view of judicial power; and that he used his deciding vote to defeat two attempts to limit the President's emergency and war powers. [cite:de5_nextgov_vance] [cite:de12_ap_judges] [cite:de12_wiki_ties] Documented as well: that three of his four ORANGE flags concern false or unsupported claims about immigrants, the occasion the hypothesis names.

Probable: that the 2021 statements still describe how he understands the limits of executive power, since he has restated their core and has not withdrawn them. What he would do with that understanding as President is not documented, and the book does not grade it.

Not supported: that Thiel directs Vance, that Thiel chose him for the ticket in 2024, or that any act of Vance's office has benefited Thiel or a Thiel company. The record runs against the first two: in 2024 it shows Vance asking Thiel for money and Thiel declining to give it to the campaign, and the fullest reconstruction of the choice does not mention Thiel. [cite:de12_dbeast_ft] [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de12_cnn_vppick] Not supported either: that Yarvin's program is Vance's policy. The 2021 remark is rhyme and citation, not a line of command; Vance holds no power to retire the civil service, and the 2025 cuts were run by others, as [scene:de17_money_to_office|Book Three] shows. And not supported: that succession is being planned. In law the presidency passes to him only by death, resignation, removal or a contested procedure that needs the Cabinet and two-thirds of Congress. [cite:de12_crs_25th] [scene:de15_vance_and_masters|Part Fifteen] sets his first race beside the one Thiel financed for Blake Masters, and [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three] carries these grades into the book's final account.

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: The PayPal Network
chapters.intro: This part is about the people Peter Thiel and Elon Musk worked with at PayPal between 1998 and 2002, the group Fortune photographed in 2007 as "The PayPal Mafia." It names everyone in that photograph and the companies each went on to build, from YouTube and LinkedIn to Yelp, Yammer, Affirm and Founders Fund, and states the connection each has to Thiel today: business partner, former employee, investor, or simply former colleague. It shows that the group does not share one politics, since one of its best-known members is among the largest Democratic donors in the country. It then records which members of the network, and which former employees of Thiel's own firms, took federal posts in 2025 and 2026, how each post was filled, and where each person stood in October 2026.
chapters.outro: The PayPal network is a web of former colleagues bound by early wealth, shared investments and personal trust, with Thiel, in Fortune's 2007 phrase, "at the center of it all"; it is not an organisation and not a political bloc. [cite:de13_fortune_2007] Its members' politics run from Reid Hoffman's millions for Democrats to David Sacks's $12 million Trump fundraiser and Musk's more than $290 million in 2024. [cite:de13_badger_hoffman] [cite:de13_wiki_sacks] [cite:de14_cnn_musk290] In 2025 people tied to Thiel or PayPal held the vice presidency, the White House science office, the AI and crypto brief, DOGE and the embassy in Denmark; as of October 2026 Musk and Sacks had left their main posts, O'Neill had left HHS for an unconfirmed nomination, and Howery and Kratsios remained in office. [cite:de13_abc_musk_exit] [cite:de13_tc_sacks_exit] [cite:de13_wiki_oneill] [cite:de13_arctic_howery] [cite:de13_wiki_kratsios] The appointments are documented; a plan behind them is not. What the money around these people bought, and where it disappears from view, is the subject of [scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen].

sections.h: Who They Are
sections.html:
In October 2007 the business magazine Fortune gathered thirteen former employees of PayPal in Tosca, a bar in San Francisco, dressed them in tracksuits and gold chains in a nod to The Sopranos, and photographed them for a story it titled "The PayPal Mafia." [cite:de13_fortune_2007] [cite:de13_fortune_2024] The name stuck. It is a journalist's joke, not a description of any organisation: there is no charter, no membership roll, no common fund and no shared programme. What there is, and what the photograph records, is a group of people who worked together at one payments company between 1998 and 2002 and who, in the magazine's words, "call upon one another when they need money or advice." [cite:de13_fortune_2007] This section sets out who they are, what each went on to build, and how far their politics diverge, because the rest of the book traces money and appointments that run through some of them, and the reader needs to know from the start that the network is not one bloc.

The company they shared

PayPal began as two companies. Confinity was founded in December 1998 by Peter Thiel and Max Levchin, with Luke Nosek and Ken Howery among the co-founders; X.com was Elon Musk's online-banking start-up. The two merged in March 2000, and in September 2000 the board replaced Musk with Thiel as chief executive. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de13_wiki_howery] [cite:de9_snopes_paypal] The company went public on 15 February 2002 and eBay bought it for $1.5 billion that October. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de13_fortune_2007] Most of its senior people left eBay soon after, "but they stayed in touch." [cite:de13_fortune_2007] The founders' own story of PayPal, and Thiel's and Musk's parts in it, are told in [scene:de9_paypal_palantir_facebook|Thiel's life] and [scene:de11_zip2_xcom_paypal|Musk's life]; they are not repeated here.

One point about the present needs stating plainly, because it is often blurred. PayPal today is not a company of the people in the photograph. eBay owned it from 2002 until July 2015, when it was spun off as an independent company listed on the Nasdaq exchange under its own management. [cite:de13_rtp_spin] No reported stake by Thiel, Musk or any other alumnus in PayPal Holdings is on record since then; they are its founders and early staff, not its owners. The "PayPal network" in this book means the people, not the company.

The photograph, person by person

The caption Fortune printed in 2007 named each person and his job at the time. In the back row stood Jawed Karim, a co-founder of YouTube; Jeremy Stoppelman, chief executive of the review site Yelp; Andrew McCormack, then running a restaurant called Laiola; and Premal Shah, president of the micro-lending charity Kiva. In front of them were Luke Nosek and Ken Howery, managing partners of the venture firm Founders Fund; David Sacks, chief executive of the genealogy site Geni; Peter Thiel, of Clarium Capital and Founders Fund; Keith Rabois, then at the start-up Slide and an early YouTube investor; Reid Hoffman, the founder of LinkedIn; Max Levchin, chief executive of Slide; Roelof Botha, a partner at the venture firm Sequoia Capital; and Russel Simmons, Yelp's co-founder and technology chief. [cite:de13_fortune_2007] Musk was not in the picture: the magazine said he was in Chicago receiving an award. YouTube's other founders, Chad Hurley and Steve Chen, did not attend either. [cite:de13_fortune_2007]

The companies that came out of this group are large by any measure. Hurley, Chen and Karim founded YouTube in 2005 and sold it to Google on 9 October 2006 for $1.65 billion. [cite:de13_wiki_hurley] Hoffman built LinkedIn and later became a founding investor in OpenAI. [cite:de13_fortune_2024] Levchin sold Slide to Google in August 2010 for $182 million and in 2012 co-founded Affirm, a consumer-lending company. [cite:de13_wiki_levchin] Sacks founded the workplace network Yammer, which Microsoft bought in July 2012 for $1.2 billion, and in late 2017 co-founded the venture firm Craft Ventures. [cite:de13_wiki_sacks] Rabois was an executive at LinkedIn and later chief operating officer of the payments company Square, co-founded the home-selling company Opendoor in 2014, and has moved between the venture firms Khosla Ventures and Founders Fund. [cite:de13_wiki_rabois] Thiel co-founded Palantir in 2003 and Founders Fund in 2005, the latter with Howery and Nosek. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de9_wiki_ff] Musk went on to Tesla and SpaceX, and in August 2008 Founders Fund invested $20 million in SpaceX, with Nosek joining its board; Musk said the firm had "a track record of investing in companies with the potential to revolutionize industries." [cite:de13_space_ff] Andrew McCormack, the restaurateur in the back row, later came to lead, with James Fitzgerald, the financial-technology fund Valar Ventures, which Thiel co-founded; that fund returns in [scene:de14_epstein_valar|Part Fourteen]. [cite:de14_nyt_valar]

The degree of each tie matters for everything that follows. Nosek and Howery were Thiel's business partners for two decades, a direct tie by employment and ownership. Rabois worked inside Founders Fund for five years, a direct tie by employment that ended in January 2024. [cite:de13_wiki_rabois] Sacks co-wrote The Diversity Myth with Thiel in 1995 and shared PayPal with him, a direct tie by authorship and former employment; his later companies are his own. [cite:de13_wiki_sacks] Hoffman, Levchin, Botha, Stoppelman and the YouTube founders share the PayPal years and little documented since, which makes them, for this book's purposes, one step removed: former colleagues, not partners.

Not one bloc: the political spread

The most common error about the PayPal network is to treat it as a single political actor. The record does not allow that. Reid Hoffman, the second-best-known person in the 2007 photograph, is one of the largest Democratic donors in the country: since 2020 he has given nearly $9 million to the Wisconsin Democratic Party alone, and he gave at least $7 million to Kamala Harris's presidential campaign in 2024. [cite:de13_badger_hoffman] Fortune described him in 2024 as "a supporter of Democrats and various progressive causes" who had clashed with Thiel and Sacks over their support for Donald Trump. [cite:de13_fortune_2024] Levchin was appointed in 2015, under the Obama administration, to the advisory board of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, an agency many conservatives sought to abolish, and he and Rabois are both listed among the contributors to FWD.us, an immigration-reform lobbying group co-founded by Mark Zuckerberg. [cite:de13_wiki_levchin] [cite:de13_wiki_rabois]

Even the alumni who backed Trump arrived by different routes and at different times. Sacks gave $50,000 to Mitt Romney in 2012 and nearly $70,000 to Hillary Clinton's campaign in 2016; in 2022 he co-hosted a fundraiser with Rabois for the Senate candidates J.D. Vance and Blake Masters and gave more than $1 million to Senate candidates; in June 2024 he hosted a fundraiser for Trump at his home that raised about $12 million, and he spoke at the Republican convention that July. [cite:de13_wiki_sacks] [cite:de13_cbs_klaidman] Rabois said in January 2020 that he would rather vote for Trump than for Bernie Sanders, and in September 2024 hosted Vance at a fundraiser for Trump's campaign. [cite:de13_wiki_rabois] Thiel spoke for Trump at the 2016 convention and gave $1.25 million to help elect him, but in 2024 he turned down a $10 million request from the Trump campaign and said he would not give to Trump's super PAC. [cite:de9_cnn_transition] [cite:de13_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de9_nbc_aspen] Musk spent more than $290 million in support of Trump and other Republicans in 2024; his record is in [scene:de11_money_and_influence|Musk's money ledger]. [cite:de14_cnn_musk290]

Nor do the Trump-backing alumni agree with one another or with the texts this book examines. None of the people named in this section has, in any statement found, described himself as a follower of Curtis Yarvin's or Nick Land's program; Thiel, the one most often linked to Yarvin, said in 2023 that he did not think Yarvin's ideas would "work." [cite:de6_cnn_2025] Whatever links the network to the Dark Enlightenment's texts runs through specific, documented acts by specific people, which the following parts trace one by one, and not through shared membership in a group.

What the 2007 photograph does show is a real mechanism, one Fortune named at the time: a small set of people with early wealth from the same sale who fund one another's companies, hire one another, and, "when they need both" money and advice, "go to Thiel, who seems to be at the center of it all." [cite:de13_fortune_2007] That is a network of capital and trust. Its political expression, from 2022 onwards, has been partial: some of its members put money and time behind Vance, Masters and Trump, others put more money behind their opponents. The [scene:de13_where_they_sit_now|next section] records which of them took public office in 2025 and 2026, and on what terms.

sections.h: Where They Sit Now
sections.html:
A network of former colleagues becomes a political question only when its members hold public power. This section records which people from the PayPal network, and from Peter Thiel's own firms, took government posts in Donald Trump's second administration, what each post was, how each was filled, and where each stood as of October 2026. It keeps two groups apart. The first is PayPal alumni in the strict sense: people who worked at the company. The second is people who never worked at PayPal but worked for Thiel at Clarium Capital, Thiel Capital, the Thiel Foundation or Mithril Capital. Reporters often fold both into "the Thiel network," and Fortune did so in December 2024 and May 2025. [cite:de9_fortune_net24] [cite:de9_fortune_net25] The connection types differ, so the record is kept separate here.

David Sacks: from "czar" to adviser

Trump named David Sacks, PayPal's former chief operating officer, as White House "AI and crypto czar" on 5 December 2024, a post created for the occasion. [cite:de13_wiki_sacks] He served as Special Advisor for AI and Crypto from 20 January 2025 as a special government employee, a status that limits service to 130 days in a year, does not require Senate confirmation and carries lighter public financial disclosure than a confirmed post. [cite:de13_wiki_sacks] Executive Order 14177 of 23 January 2025, which re-established the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST), wrote him into a second role by title: "The APST and the Special Advisor for AI & Crypto shall serve as Co-Chairs of the PCAST," the APST being the president's science adviser, Michael Kratsios. [cite:de13_eo14177]

The terms of his service drew the most scrutiny of any network appointment. Sacks received two White House ethics waivers that allowed him to keep certain stakes while shaping federal policy on artificial intelligence and crypto. [cite:de13_tc_sacks_exit] On 30 November 2025 the New York Times reported that his disclosures listed 708 technology investments, 449 of them in AI companies, and that his filings did not show the remaining value of the holdings he had said he would sell, or when he sold them. [cite:de13_tc_nyt_sacks] Sacks called the story a "nothing burger"; the White House called him "an invaluable asset." [cite:de13_tc_nyt_sacks] These are documented facts about disclosure and waivers. Whether any specific policy he worked on benefited a specific holding is a separate claim that the published record does not settle; it is set out as a candidate loop in [scene:de14_loops|Part Fourteen].

On 26 March 2026 his non-consecutive 130 days ran out and his czar role ended. [cite:de13_tc_sacks_exit] He stayed on as PCAST co-chair, a body that studies and recommends but does not make policy, and said the post let him "make recommendations on not just AI but an expanded range of technology topics." He remained a partner at Craft Ventures. [cite:de13_tc_sacks_exit] Status as of October 2026: PCAST co-chair; no longer a special government employee in the czar role.

Ken Howery: Denmark and Greenland

Ken Howery, PayPal's first chief financial officer and a co-founder of Founders Fund, had already served Trump once, as ambassador to Sweden from 2019 to January 2021. [cite:de13_wiki_howery] On 22 December 2024 Trump announced him as ambassador to Denmark, writing in the same announcement that "ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity." [cite:de13_abc_greenland] [cite:de13_wiki_howery] The Senate confirmed him 51 to 47 in an en-bloc vote on 7 October 2025, and he took up the post on 5 November 2025. [cite:de13_arctic_howery] [cite:de13_wiki_howery] In December 2025 he travelled to Nuuk for the annual joint committee of the United States, Greenland and Denmark, and in January 2026 he hosted the embassy's New Year reception in Copenhagen. [cite:de13_hnn_nuuk] [cite:de13_amcham_2026] Status as of October 2026: ambassador, with no departure reported. His appointment places a Thiel business partner of twenty years in the diplomatic post that handles the president's stated Greenland ambition; it is documented as an appointment by the president, and no document shows Thiel or anyone else in the network seeking it for him. Thiel's own spokesperson has said that "Peter isn't involved in any plans or discussions regarding Greenland." [cite:de13_newsweek_greenland]

Elon Musk: DOGE, 130 days

Musk, PayPal's first chief executive, served as a special government employee leading the Department of Government Efficiency from January 2025. On 28 May 2025 he posted, "As my scheduled time as a Special Government Employee comes to an end," and the White House began off-boarding him; his 130-day limit fell as early as 30 May. [cite:de13_abc_musk_exit] What DOGE was in law, who staffed it and what it did are the subject of Book III, beginning with [scene:de17_money_to_office|the deal from campaign money to an office]; his later dealings with the administration are in [scene:de11_twitter_x_xai|Musk's life].

The Thiel firms, not PayPal

Two senior appointees came from Thiel's own companies rather than from PayPal. Michael Kratsios was chief financial officer at Clarium from 2010 and later a principal at Thiel Capital and Thiel's chief of staff; he served as United States chief technology officer from 2019 to 2021, was nominated to direct the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy on 22 December 2024 and was confirmed 74 to 25 on 25 March 2025. [cite:de13_wiki_kratsios] Status as of October 2026: OSTP director and PCAST co-chair. [cite:de13_wiki_kratsios] [cite:de13_eo14177] The vote, with a large bipartisan majority, is part of the record: his confirmation was not a party-line event.

Jim O'Neill was chief executive of the Thiel Foundation from 2009 to 2012 and a managing director at Clarium, Thiel Capital and Mithril. [cite:de13_wiki_oneill] He was confirmed as deputy secretary of Health and Human Services in June 2025 by 52 to 43, served as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 28 August 2025, and left both posts on 13 February 2026 in a reshuffle at the department. [cite:de13_wiki_oneill] [cite:de13_cnn_oneill] Trump nominated him to direct the National Science Foundation on 2 March 2026; in May 2026 the scientific society AAAS wrote to the Senate committee asking it to schedule his still-unheld confirmation hearing. [cite:de13_wiki_oneill] [cite:de13_aaas_nsf] Status as of October 2026: nominee, not confirmed.

Who holds no office

The absences are part of the finding. Keith Rabois, Luke Nosek, Max Levchin, Roelof Botha and Jeremy Stoppelman hold no federal appointment, and none is on record for 2025 or 2026. [cite:de13_wiki_rabois] [cite:de13_wiki_levchin] Reid Hoffman, the network's largest Democratic donor, is on the other side of the administration. [cite:de13_badger_hoffman] Peter Thiel himself holds no office: he served on Trump's transition executive committee in 2016 and has held no government post since. [cite:de9_cnn_transition] Vance's path from Thiel's employ to the vice presidency is told in [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|his life], and is not repeated here.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis this book tests reads the 2025 cuts and immigration enforcement as the occasion for building an executive without a veto. On the narrow question of this part, whether people from one network were placed in positions of public power, the answer is documented: six people with ties to Thiel or to PayPal, direct or one step removed, held federal posts in 2025, among them the vice president, the president's science adviser, the official writing AI and crypto policy and the head of DOGE. [cite:de13_wiki_sacks] [cite:de13_wiki_kratsios] [cite:de13_abc_musk_exit] Also documented: that the most prominent of these, Sacks, served under a status that avoided Senate confirmation and with ethics waivers whose full effect the public filings do not show. [cite:de13_tc_nyt_sacks]

Probable, on the record: that shared history made these appointments easier, since the people were known to the president's circle through Vance, Musk and Thiel. The record does not show the mechanism, and the grade stays at probable. Not supported: that the network acted as one bloc, or that the appointments followed any plan. The posts went through ordinary channels, including confirmation votes with Democratic support for Kratsios; [cite:de13_wiki_kratsios] several of the people in the 2007 photograph hold no office, and one of them funds the opposition. [cite:de13_badger_hoffman] Running against the hypothesis, too, is the short tenure of the two most powerful posts: Musk left after 130 days, and Sacks's czar role ended after fourteen months. [cite:de13_abc_musk_exit] [cite:de13_tc_sacks_exit] What the money behind these people bought, and where it is visible and where it is not, is the subject of [scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen]; the final grades go to [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three].

chapters.label: Part Fourteen
chapters.title: The Money
chapters.intro: This part follows the money around the people of Book II. It begins with a map on which every line is a documented transfer, job, investment, board seat, contract or appointment, with the amount, the date, the type of connection and how direct it is, from Peter Thiel's $32 million for two Senate candidates in 2022 to Elon Musk's $290 million in 2024 and the federal contracts held by Palantir and SpaceX. It then tests the loops often drawn on such maps, the chains in which money is said to return to where it began, and separates the one that closes on documents from the candidates that do not. It looks at the vehicles through which money becomes hard or impossible to trace: the Thiel Foundation, the donor-advised fund DonorsTrust, a nonprofit with no donor list and a donor network with no public face. It ends with Jeffrey Epstein's $40 million investment in Valar Ventures, a fund Thiel co-founded, and Thiel's documented contacts with Epstein: what the released files show, what they do not, and where the release of those files stood in October 2026.
chapters.outro: The documented money around the network is large and mostly visible: about $32 million from Thiel to the super PACs backing two of his former employees in 2022, more than $290 million from Musk in 2024, and long-running federal contracts for Palantir and SpaceX that began before any of the political spending. [cite:de14_cnbc_2022] [cite:de14_cnn_musk290] [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] No political loop closes on documents; each candidate loop lacks the arrow from public office to private gain. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:de13_tc_nyt_sacks] Some of the money cannot be traced at all, through DonorsTrust, Per Aspera Policy and the Rockbridge Network, and claims about where it went, in either direction, go beyond the record. [cite:de14_dg_donorstrust] [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge] Epstein's $40 million in Valar and years of meetings with Thiel after his conviction are documented; co-ownership, an island visit and any wrongdoing by Thiel are not. [cite:de14_nyt_valar] [cite:de14_sd_files] [cite:ow12_abc_memo] How the 2022 money worked in practice, in two races run on the same method, is the subject of [scene:de15_vance_and_masters|Part Fifteen].

sections.h: The Network Map
sections.html:
Books and articles about the Dark Enlightenment often contain a diagram: Peter Thiel at the centre, lines radiating out to Curtis Yarvin, J.D. Vance, Elon Musk, Blake Masters, David Sacks and the companies around them. Most such diagrams draw every line the same way. This part draws them differently. Each line below is a documented transfer of money, a job, an investment, a board seat or an appointment, with the amount where one is known, the date, the type of connection and its degree: direct (one party paid, hired or appointed the other), one step removed (the tie runs through a fund, company or committee), or shared interest only (no transfer at all). A line with no document behind it is not drawn. The biographies that supply most of these facts are in [scene:de9_money_and_influence|Thiel's money ledger], [scene:de11_money_and_influence|Musk's] and [scene:de12_money_and_influence|Vance's]; this section brings them onto one page and adds the ties that run between them.

The political money

The largest documented flows run from Thiel to two Senate campaigns in 2022. He gave $15 million to Protect Ohio Values, the super PAC that backed Vance in the Ohio primary. [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de14_forbesau] He gave $15 million to Saving Arizona PAC, which backed his former employee Blake Masters in the Arizona primary, and $2.5 million more in October, for $17.5 million in Arizona and about $32 million across the two races. [cite:de14_axios_masters] [cite:de14_cnbc_2022] [cite:de9_cnbc_2022] A super PAC is a committee that may raise and spend unlimited sums so long as it does not coordinate with the candidate; that is why a single donor could give it eight-figure sums. Vance won his seat; Masters lost to Mark Kelly. [cite:de14_cnbc_2022]

Smaller documented flows ran alongside. Per Aspera Policy, a nonprofit Thiel controlled that does not disclose its donors, sent at least $200,000 to Protect Ohio Values. [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] David Sacks gave $1 million of his own money to the pro-Vance super PAC, and, with Keith Rabois, co-hosted a spring 2022 fundraiser for Vance and Masters together; Thiel, according to Politico, helped recruit about ten major donors for Vance. [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de13_wiki_sacks] [cite:de14_forbesau] The Mercer, Uihlein and Lindner families, none of them from the PayPal network, gave hundreds of thousands to the same super PAC. [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] Vance's own story, and the parallel between his race and Masters's, is in [scene:de15_vance_and_masters|Part Fifteen].

Musk's money is larger than all of this together and runs on a separate line. He spent more than $290 million in the 2024 election, about a quarter of a billion of it through America PAC, his own super PAC, including more than $50 million on million-dollar giveaways to people who signed a petition. [cite:de14_cnn_musk290] No document shows Thiel money in America PAC or Musk money in the 2022 Vance and Masters super PACs; the two men's political spending meets only in the candidates they both came to support. Thiel's own spending since 2022 has been smaller and more conventional: $852,200 to Speaker Mike Johnson's committee in February 2025, $3 million against California's proposed billionaire tax in December 2025, and $1.5 million to Club for Growth Action in February 2026. [cite:de9_mj_2025] [cite:de9_fortune_cbrt] [cite:de9_bgov_cfg]

Jobs, investments and seats

Money is only one kind of line. Vance worked for Thiel at Mithril Capital before 2017, and when he founded his own venture firm, Narya Capital, in Ohio in 2019, it was reported to be backed by Thiel, Marc Andreessen and Eric Schmidt; the amounts have not been published. [cite:de14_forbesau] [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] In February 2021 Thiel brought Vance to Mar-a-Lago to meet Trump. [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] Masters co-wrote Thiel's book Zero to One (2014) and was chief operating officer of Thiel Capital and president of the Thiel Foundation until he resigned both posts in March 2022 to run. [cite:de14_wiki_masters] Founders Fund invested $20 million in SpaceX in August 2008, and its partner Luke Nosek joined SpaceX's board. [cite:de13_space_ff] Founders Fund, with the firm Andreessen Horowitz, invested $1.1 million in Tlon, the company Yarvin founded to build Urbit, and in May 2011 the Thiel Foundation named John Burnham, who went on to co-found Tlon, as one of its first Thiel Fellows, with $100,000 over two years. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_audit_tc2011] No other payment from Thiel to Yarvin is documented; nor is any Thiel money to the National Conservatism conferences or to the Edmund Burke Foundation that organises them; the documented tie there is his 2019 speech and his signature on the 2022 statement ([scene:de10_education_of_a_libertarian|Part Ten]).

The third kind of line is government money to companies the network owns. Thiel co-founded Palantir in 2003 and is its chairman. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] Immigration and Customs Enforcement has paid Palantir since 2014, a contract worth $41 million before the 2019 renewal; in April 2025 it agreed to pay $29.9 million for "ImmigrationOS" on the grounds that "Palantir is the only source that can provide the required capabilities," and in February 2026 the Department of Homeland Security signed a blanket purchase agreement with Palantir worth up to $1 billion over five years. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:ow9_sa_dhsbpa] SpaceX's government business, counted by the Washington Post at at least $38 billion over twenty years, long predates 2025. [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] These contracts are documented. That any of them followed from the political money above is not, and the [scene:de14_loops|next section] treats that question.

What the map shows, and what it leaves out

Drawn this way, the map has one centre for political money, Thiel, in one period, 2021 to 2022, aimed at two candidates who had worked for him; a second, much larger centre, Musk, in 2024, aimed at a presidential ticket that by then included one of the two. It also has a long-running commercial layer, Palantir and SpaceX, whose government contracts began years before any of the political spending. The people at its centre are a handful of named individuals, not a movement; and the lines between them are of different kinds, which is why the table names each.

The map also has edges it cannot draw. The donors behind Per Aspera Policy are not public. [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] The Rockbridge Network, a donor group that grew out of a 2019 summit Thiel and Vance convened in Ohio, has no website or public entity; only its affiliated super PAC, Turnout for America, files with the Federal Election Commission, reporting $34.5 million spent in the 2024 cycle. [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge] The Thiel Foundation's grants to the donor-advised fund DonorsTrust leave the foundation's books under DonorsTrust's name, and where they go after that is not disclosed. These gaps, and what can honestly be said about them, are the subject of [scene:de14_foundations_and_opacity|the third section]. Foreign money into the network's companies, such as Gulf investment in Musk's ventures, belongs to the companies and not to the theorists, and is treated in [scene:de36_foreign_money|Part Thirty-Nine].

sections.h: Loops: Documented and Candidate
sections.html:
A loop, in a money map, is a chain of documented transfers that returns to where it started: A pays B, B does something for C, C pays A. Loops matter because they are where influence becomes return, and they are the strongest kind of finding a network map can produce. They are also the easiest kind to invent. Any two people who know each other and any two transfers in the same year can be joined by an arrow, and the eye completes the circle. This section therefore holds each possible loop to one rule: a loop is documented only if every arrow in it is documented. If even one arrow is inferred from timing, from motive or from the logic of the situation, the loop is a candidate, and it is written with the inferred arrow marked. Timing is not causation: a donation that comes before a benefit is a sequence, not a proof that one caused the other.

Five chains are tested below. One closes on documents, and it is a commercial loop, not a political one. The other four are candidates, each with a single missing arrow, and for each the missing arrow is named.

The one closed loop: Valar and Epstein

The only chain in this book's material that closes on documents runs through Valar Ventures, a financial-technology fund co-founded by Thiel and led by Andrew McCormack and James Fitzgerald. In 2015 and 2016 Jeffrey Epstein put $40 million into two Valar funds; by 2025 the stake was worth nearly $170 million and was the largest asset left in his estate, and Valar said it hoped the eventual distribution could help his victims. [cite:de14_nyt_valar] The money went in, the fund invested it, and the gains are owed back to the estate: an ordinary limited partnership, with every arrow in the record. It is a loop of investment and return, not of political influence, and it shows nothing about government. What it does show, and does not show, about Thiel and Epstein is the subject of [scene:de14_epstein_valar|the last section].

Candidate loop 1: candidate, office, contract, portfolio

The loop most often drawn runs from Thiel to Vance to the government to Palantir and back to Thiel. Its documented arrows are strong. Thiel employed Vance, reportedly backed his venture firm, and gave $15 million to the super PAC that backed his 2022 campaign. [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de14_forbesau] Vance became Vice President in January 2025. In April 2025 ICE agreed to pay Palantir $29.9 million for "ImmigrationOS," and in February 2026 DHS signed a purchase agreement with Palantir worth up to $1 billion over five years; Thiel is Palantir's co-founder and chairman. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:ow9_sa_dhsbpa] [cite:de9_wiki_thiel]

The missing arrow is the one in the middle: from Vance's office to Palantir's contracts. No document shows the Vice President, or anyone acting for him, involved in any Palantir award. The contracts ran through ICE's and DHS's own procurement, and ICE justified the 2025 award on the grounds that "Palantir is the only source that can provide the required capabilities." [cite:ow9_reg_immos] Palantir's ICE business also began in 2014, under the Obama administration, and was renewed in 2019, years before Vance held office. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] The loop is a candidate: three arrows documented, one inferred. The inference is not unreasonable, since an administration whose vice president was once employed and politically funded by Palantir's chairman is not obviously a neutral buyer of Palantir's software; but a reasonable inference is still an inference, and the record has a simpler explanation for the contracts, which is that ICE had used Palantir for a decade.

Candidate loop 2: the czar's portfolio

The second runs through David Sacks. Its documented arrows: Sacks's financial disclosures listed 708 technology investments, 449 of them in AI companies, according to the New York Times; he served from January 2025 to March 2026 as the White House's adviser on AI and crypto, with two ethics waivers that let him keep certain stakes while shaping policy in both fields; and his public filings did not show the remaining value of the assets he said he would sell, or when he sold them. [cite:de13_tc_nyt_sacks] [cite:de13_tc_sacks_exit] The missing arrow: a specific policy he shaped that raised the value of a specific holding he kept. The Times report argued that his position could benefit his portfolio; Sacks called it a "nothing burger," and no document published so far ties a named decision to a named gain. [cite:de13_tc_nyt_sacks] The waivers are a documented conflict of interest in the legal sense, a situation in which private interest and public duty overlap, which the government itself acknowledged by issuing them; a loop of benefit is a candidate.

Candidate loop 3: the campaign, DOGE and the contractor

The third runs through Musk. Documented: more than $290 million spent to elect Trump and other Republicans in 2024; a post as a special government employee leading DOGE from January to May 2025; and companies, chiefly SpaceX, that the Washington Post counted as having received at least $38 billion in federal contracts, loans, subsidies and tax credits over twenty years. [cite:de14_cnn_musk290] [cite:de13_abc_musk_exit] [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] The missing arrow is from DOGE's work to a new benefit for Musk's companies. Most of SpaceX's government business predates 2025. Whether DOGE's access to agencies that regulate or contract with his companies produced any specific gain is examined in [scene:de21_conflicts_and_contracts|Part Twenty-One]; on this part's material the loop is a candidate.

Candidate loop 4: the donor network and the ticket

The fourth runs through the Rockbridge Network. Documented: Thiel and Vance convened the 2019 Ohio summit from which it grew; Sacks and Andreessen are described as members; its affiliated super PAC, Turnout for America, spent $34.5 million in the 2024 cycle; and many of its members, the Washington Post reported, hope Vance will be the 2028 nominee. [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge] The missing arrow is any documented return to the members: a contract, a regulation or an appointment traced to membership. The Post describes access, conferences with Cabinet-level speakers and a separate $500,000-a-head private club, Executive Branch, that Rockbridge's leader helped launch, but not a specific benefit. [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge] Candidate.

Candidate loop 5: the shared intermediary

The fifth is not a loop at all, though it is often drawn as one. The Thiel Foundation has made grants to DonorsTrust, a donor-advised fund, and DonorsTrust also funds a long list of conservative and libertarian groups, from the Federalist Society to Heritage and Cato. [cite:de14_kindora_thiel] [cite:de14_dg_donorstrust] Because DonorsTrust's grants appear under its own name and not the donor's, a shared intermediary does not show a flow from any particular donor to any particular recipient. The pipe is shared; what passes through it from Thiel is unknown. No arrow from Thiel's grants to any specific end recipient is documented, so no loop can be drawn, and the [scene:de14_foundations_and_opacity|next section] treats it as an opacity point, not a finding.

The pattern across the five is consistent. The arrows that carry money into politics are well documented, because federal law requires super PACs to report their donors; the arrows that would carry policy back to private gain are not, because no law requires anyone to document them, and because none has surfaced in litigation, audit or leak. A reader can take that absence two ways: as a sign that the returns do not exist, or as a sign that they are not the kind of thing that gets written down. The record does not decide between those readings, and this book does not pretend that it does. It grades each loop on what is written down, and on that standard none of the four political loops closes.

sections.h: Foundations and Opacity
sections.html:
Not all of the network's money moves through channels that name the giver and the receiver. Some passes through a private foundation, which must publish its grants but not its reasons; some through a donor-advised fund, which publishes its own grants but not whose money they were; some through a nonprofit that need not publish its donors at all; and some through a private group that has no public existence. This section sets out what each of these vehicles shows and what it hides, for the vehicles that touch Thiel and his circle. Its rule is the same as the rest of the book's: where the record stops, the account stops too, and the gap is named as a gap rather than filled.

The Thiel Foundation: what it publishes

The Thiel Foundation is a private foundation registered in Miami, and like every private foundation it files an annual Form 990-PF with the Internal Revenue Service, a return that lists its assets and its grants. [cite:de14_audit_pp_miami] Its filings show assets of about $45.2 million at the end of 2024 and charitable disbursements of about $3.4 million that year; disbursements were about $4.9 million in 2023, $5.1 million in 2022 and $11.0 million in 2021, the largest year on record. [cite:de14_pp_thielfdn] Its best-known programme is the Thiel Fellowship, which from 2011 gave each fellow $100,000 over two years; one of the first twenty fellows, John Burnham, went on to co-found Tlon with Curtis Yarvin. [cite:de5_audit_tc2011] Through a programme called Imitatio, the foundation funds scholarship on the work of the French thinker René Girard, with grants in 2024 and 2025 to the theologian James Alison, the Girard scholar Benoît Chantre, the Lumen Christi Institute in Chicago and the Colloquium on Violence and Religion, among others; Girard's place in Thiel's thought is in [scene:de10_girard_and_the_katechon|Part Ten]. [cite:de14_kindora_thiel] In 2024 it gave $100,000 to the Leo Strauss Foundation. [cite:de14_kindora_thiel]

Two of the foundation's former leaders later held public roles. Jim O'Neill was its chief executive from 2009 to 2012 before becoming deputy secretary of Health and Human Services in 2025; Blake Masters was its president until he resigned in March 2022 to run for the Senate with $17.5 million of Thiel's money behind him. [cite:de13_wiki_oneill] [cite:de14_wiki_masters] [cite:de14_cnbc_2022] These are documented ties of employment, not grants; the foundation's filings show no political spending, which private foundations are barred from making.

One of Thiel's older commitments shows how even a well-documented gift can carry two figures. Thiel pledged $500,000 to the Seasteading Institute, which promotes self-governing settlements on the open sea, at its launch in April 2008. [cite:de3_wiki_tsi] A 2011 account put his total giving at $1.25 million, and quoted the institute's co-founder, Patri Friedman: "Thiel is our most generous funder, but this doesn't mean that he dictates our plans." [cite:de14_yahoo_seastead] A 2018 account said that "Thiel invested $1.7 million" and that he left the institute's board in 2011. [cite:de14_bi_seastead] The two are best read as totals at different dates; the 2018 figure gives no source of its own, and the institute's public returns do not name its donors, so the difference cannot be closed. Both are reported here. The exit projects themselves are in [scene:de22_seas_and_zones|Part Twenty-Two].

DonorsTrust: where the trail goes dark

DonorsTrust, based in Alexandria, Virginia, and founded in 1999, runs donor-advised funds: accounts in which a donor places money, takes the tax deduction at once, and later recommends grants to charities. When DonorsTrust makes a grant, the recipient's records and DonorsTrust's own filings show the money as coming from DonorsTrust, not from the donor who advised it. [cite:de14_dg_donorstrust] It is large and openly conservative and libertarian in purpose: it granted $351 million in 2023, to recipients including the State Policy Network, the Federalist Society, Cato, Reason, Heritage and America First Legal, and its chief executive has said its aim is "to preserve donor intent for certain types of givers." [cite:de14_dg_donorstrust] [cite:de14_audit_dg_bader]
