The Thiel Foundation has made grants to DonorsTrust. Listings compiled from the foundation's filings show $1.4 million in 2022, $1,276,111 in 2024 and $426,775 in 2025; an earlier tally put the total for 2021 to 2024 at about $7.3 million, but the listings available do not cover every year, and that total could not be confirmed against them in full. [cite:de14_granted_thiel] [cite:de14_kindora_thiel] What can be said with confidence is that at least about $3.1 million has passed from Thiel's foundation into DonorsTrust since 2022. What cannot be said is where any of it went next. Because the grants leave the foundation's books under DonorsTrust's name, no public record links a dollar from Thiel to any end recipient. This is the single largest opacity point in the network's documented money.

The opacity cuts both ways, and the book applies it both ways. It means that no one can show the money went to a cause the Dark Enlightenment's critics would object to; it also means no one can show that it did not. A frequently drawn line runs from Thiel through DonorsTrust to the National Conservatism conferences, because DonorsTrust funds many groups in that world. That line is not documented. A shared intermediary is not a flow, and no grant from the Thiel Foundation to the Edmund Burke Foundation, which organises those conferences, appears in the published grant listings. [cite:de14_kindora_thiel] The honest description is the one already given in [scene:de14_loops|the loops section]: same pipe, unknown water.

The nonprofit with no donor list

Per Aspera Policy is a nonprofit that Thiel controlled and that does not disclose its donors. It sent at least $200,000 to Protect Ohio Values, the pro-Vance super PAC, in the 2022 race. [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman] The super PAC had to report Per Aspera's contribution; Per Aspera did not have to report where its own money came from. The amount is small beside Thiel's $15 million in direct, disclosed giving to the same committee, and it is not evidence of hidden donors so much as a demonstration of the mechanism: a political committee may be funded in part by an entity whose own funders are not public. [cite:de14_cbs_klaidman]

The group with no public face

The Rockbridge Network goes further. It grew out of a weekend summit Thiel and Vance convened in 2019 near Rockbridge, Ohio, attended by, among others, Rebekah Mercer, Tucker Carlson and the economist Oren Cass; it is now led by the publisher Chris Buskirk, whose magazine American Greatness Thiel had earlier funded. [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge] [cite:de14_audit_wapo_rockbridge] The Washington Post reported in November 2025 that the group "has no website or public-facing entity"; that David Sacks and Marc Andreessen are members; that it runs pollsters, data analysts and a documentary arm; and that its affiliated super PAC, Turnout for America, spent $34.5 million in 2024. [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge] The super PAC's spending is public because federal law requires it; the network's own membership, dues and budget are not, and the Post's account rests on its own reporting rather than on any filing. Thiel declined to comment. [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge]

None of these vehicles is unusual. Private foundations, donor-advised funds, undisclosed nonprofits and private donor networks are used across American politics, by donors of every persuasion. What the network's use of them establishes is narrower: that some of the money around Thiel and Vance cannot be traced to its end, and that claims about where it went, in either direction, go beyond the record.

sections.h: Epstein and Valar
sections.html:
Jeffrey Epstein pleaded guilty in Florida on 30 June 2008 to two state solicitation charges and served thirteen months of an eighteen-month sentence; he was arrested on federal sex-trafficking charges in July 2019 and died in a Manhattan jail cell on 10 August 2019, a death ruled a suicide. [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] Every contact described in this section took place after the 2008 conviction. This section sets out what the released records show about Epstein's money in Valar Ventures and his contacts with Peter Thiel, what they do not show, and the state of the Epstein files as of October 2026. It applies the strictest standard in the book. Thiel has not been charged with any crime connected to Epstein, and the presumption of innocence holds. A claim that any living person took part in Epstein's crimes would need court records or sworn testimony behind it; no such claim about Thiel exists in the record, and none is made here. The wider Epstein record, including the claims about intelligence services, is in [scene:ow12_ties|The One-Way Mirror].

The investment

Valar Ventures is a New York venture fund specialising in financial technology, co-founded by Thiel and led by Andrew McCormack, who stood in the back row of Fortune's 2007 PayPal photograph, and James Fitzgerald. [cite:de14_nyt_valar] [cite:de13_fortune_2007] According to the New York Times, Epstein put $40 million into two Valar funds in 2015 and 2016, and by 2025 the stake was worth nearly $170 million, the largest asset still held by his estate; the fund's spokesperson said a Valar representative had met Epstein in 2014, when he was seen as a "well-known adviser to world leaders, top universities and philanthropic organizations," and that the firm hoped the eventual distribution could help his victims. Thiel's spokesperson declined to comment. [cite:de14_nyt_valar]

Documents released by the Justice Department in early 2026 fill in the sequence, as reported by Byline Times, an independent British outlet, which did not give document numbers: an email of 15 November 2014 seeking $10 million to $20 million for Valar; a commitment of $15 million by June 2015 through Epstein's Southern Trust Company, as a limited partner, growing to about $40 million; fund statements sent to Epstein and his accountant; a June 2017 message offering him "super confidential" investment opportunities; and a further request for capital in November 2018. [cite:de14_byline_valar] The Stanford Daily, citing a specific file number, confirms the $40 million investment. [cite:de14_sd_files] A limited partner, in a venture fund, supplies money and receives a share of the returns but has no say in running the fund; that is the role Thiel's side says Epstein had.

The contacts

The released files show a relationship over several years. Emails from 2014 into early 2019 show the two men arranging meetings several times a year, at Epstein's New York house and at Thiel's office and home in San Francisco; earlier reporting counted about six scheduled meetings between 2014 and 2016. [cite:de14_sd_files] [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] In June 2014 Epstein offered advice on Thiel's taxes, and in another file he considered buying Palantir shares; no record shows that he did. [cite:de14_sd_files] Epstein called Thiel a "great friend" in messages to others; the phrase is Epstein's. [cite:de14_sd_files] He tried, on at least six occasions, to bring Thiel together with Ehud Barak, the former Israeli prime minister. [cite:de14_jacobin] Epstein repeatedly invited Thiel to his island; to one invitation Thiel answered, "When are you there?" [cite:de14_sd_files] When Epstein proposed in February 2016 to meet in Europe, on the island or in Saudi Arabia, Thiel replied: "Certainly not in Saudi — just think I will avoid the Middle East for the next decade or so." [cite:de14_jacobin] Thiel's spokesperson told the New York Times that Thiel "never went to Epstein's Island," and no document shows a visit to the island or a flight on Epstein's aircraft. [cite:de14_sd_files] [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein]

The contested claim: "owned by Peter Thiel and JE"

One document has done more than any other to shape public accounts. In February 2016 Barak wrote to Epstein and an associate describing two people as "seniors in a new Investment Fund owned by Peter Thiel and JE." [cite:de14_byline_valar] Thiel's spokesman denied that Epstein was a co-owner and confirmed that he was a limited partner. [cite:de14_byline_valar] The fund's own statements, the Times's account of a $40 million limited partnership and Valar's spokesperson all describe an investor, not an owner. [cite:de14_nyt_valar] Barak's phrase is a third party's description in a private email, not a record of ownership, and the documents that record the investment do not bear it out. The book grades the co-ownership claim as not supported; the headline that rests on it, "Jeffrey Epstein and Peter Thiel co-owned venture fund," states as fact what the underlying documents do not show. [cite:de14_byline_valar]

A second, lesser chain runs through Carbyne, an Israeli emergency-call technology company first called Reporty. Barak chaired it, and his investment partnership put money into it in 2015; Epstein put $1 million into that partnership in 2016. [cite:ow12_toi_carbyne] [cite:ow10_ctech_barak] Epstein and Barak planned to pitch the company to Valar, and Valar declined it in 2016. [cite:de14_byline_valar] [cite:ow12_wiki_epstein] Founders Fund, Thiel's separate firm, is also among Carbyne's backers. [cite:ow10_ctech_barak] Two investors in the same company are co-investors, not partners; the record shows no joint venture between Thiel and Epstein in Carbyne, and Barak's own record is his, not Thiel's.

Appearing in the files is not evidence of wrongdoing, and the same rule applies to everyone named in them. The files record, for example, an August 2015 dinner in Palo Alto that brought Epstein together with Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Reid Hoffman, among others. [cite:de14_sd_files] Attendance at a dinner is not a relationship, and each person's documented dealings with Epstein are their own; Musk's emails with Epstein are treated in [scene:de11_money_and_influence|his life], and nothing in one person's record transfers to another. The Justice Department's review, released in July 2025, said it "did not uncover evidence that could predicate an investigation against uncharged third parties." [cite:ow12_abc_memo]

Status of the Epstein files as of October 2026

Congress passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act in November 2025, and the president signed it on 19 November, setting a deadline of 19 December for release. [cite:de14_gma_engelmayer] The deadline was missed; in January 2026 a federal judge in New York, Paul Engelmayer, declined to appoint a special master to supervise the release, acknowledging "legitimate concerns" but finding he lacked jurisdiction. [cite:de14_gma_engelmayer] At the end of January the department released more than 3 million pages, 2,000 videos and 180,000 images, about 3.5 million pages in all under the law, and the deputy attorney general, Todd Blanche, called the review "very comprehensive." [cite:de14_sn_3m] [cite:de14_audit_sn_blanche] On 27 August 2026 the department published in the Federal Register its report under the Act, covering what was released and withheld, the legal basis for redactions, and the officials and politically exposed persons named in the material. [cite:de14_fr_report] Members of Congress from both parties have disputed whether the release is complete. [cite:de14_gma_engelmayer] The Thiel and Valar material described above comes from these releases; further documents may yet change the account, and this section reflects the record as of October 2026.

The worst-case reading, tested

This part's material bears on the hypothesis in one way: whether the money behind the people who hold power in 2025 and 2026 was organised to build an executive without a veto. Documented: that Thiel's money, about $32 million in 2022, backed the Senate campaigns of two of his former employees, one of whom became Vice President; that Musk spent more than $290 million in 2024 and then ran DOGE; that people from the network took posts that shape AI, crypto, science and Arctic policy; and that parts of the money around them, through DonorsTrust, Per Aspera and the Rockbridge Network, cannot be traced. [cite:de14_cnbc_2022] [cite:de14_cnn_musk290] [cite:de13_wiki_sacks] [cite:de14_dg_donorstrust] [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge] Probable: that this money bought access as well as campaign support, since the Post's account of Rockbridge describes exactly that; the record shows the access, not what was done with it. [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge]

Not supported: that any of this money flowed to the theorists beyond Tlon and one fellowship, or to a programme for dismantling checks and balances; that any political loop closes on documents; or that the opaque channels carried money anywhere in particular, a claim the opacity itself makes impossible to prove either way. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_audit_tc2011] Running against the hypothesis: the network split in 2024, Thiel declining to fund Trump while Hoffman funded his opponent, and the contracts most often cited as returns began under earlier administrations. [cite:de13_cbs_klaidman] [cite:de13_badger_hoffman] [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] On Epstein, the documented record is a $40 million limited partnership and years of meetings after his conviction, a matter of judgment the reader may weigh; it is not evidence of crime, and it does not bear on the hypothesis at all. [cite:de14_nyt_valar] [cite:ow12_abc_memo] [scene:de15_vance_and_masters|Part Fifteen] follows the 2022 races in detail; the grades go to [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three].

chapters.label: Part Fifteen
chapters.title: The Same Playbook, Twice
chapters.intro: This part sets two Senate races of 2022 side by side. In Ohio and in Arizona Peter Thiel backed a former employee, J.D. Vance and Blake Masters, by giving $10 million to a super PAC formed for one candidate before that candidate had declared, adding more around Donald Trump's endorsement, and stepping back after the primary. Both men won their primaries; one became Vice President, the other lost to Mark Kelly. The part gives the amounts, the dates, the endorsements and the outcomes, names the other donors who gave to both, records the complaints that were made and dismissed, and separates the method the record documents from the machine it is often said to show.
chapters.outro: The two races show one donor using one legal vehicle twice in one year: about $15 million for Vance through Protect Ohio Values and $17.5 million for Masters through Saving Arizona, each begun with $10 million before the candidate declared and each topped up around Trump's endorsement. [cite:de15_cnbc_fundraiser] [cite:de15_cnbc_results] [cite:de15_federalist_2021] [cite:de12_foxbiz_pov] Both men won their primaries; in the general election the party's money decided where support went, flowing to Vance in Ohio and away from Masters in Arizona, and Thiel at first declined to pay for the race he was losing. [cite:de12_vindy_q3] [cite:de15_axios_slf] [cite:de15_axios_double] The one coordination complaint was dismissed, and no return flow of money or contracts to Thiel is on record. [cite:de15_fec_mur8009] It is a documented method, not a machine: it put one man one heartbeat from the presidency and failed with the other. [scene:de16_the_valley|Part Sixteen] turns from the money to the people in the technology industry and the elite pipeline who took up these ideas, and to the neighbouring movements that are not the same thing.

sections.h: Two Employees, Two Super PACs
sections.html:
In the 2022 election cycle Peter Thiel financed most of the outside money behind two of his own former employees' campaigns for the United States Senate, in two states, at the same time, by the same method. In Ohio the candidate was J.D. Vance, who had worked at Thiel's venture firm Mithril and whose fund Thiel had backed. In Arizona it was Blake Masters, who had worked directly for Thiel for years. In each state Thiel gave the first $10 million to a super PAC formed to support one man before that man had declared, added more around Donald Trump's endorsement of his candidate, stopped giving after the primary, and saw his candidate win the Republican primary. Then the two races diverged: Vance won and became Vice President; Masters lost, and lost again two years later. This part sets the two cases side by side and separates what the record documents from what it is often taken to show.

Masters: from a Stanford classroom to Thiel Capital

Blake Masters was born on 5 August 1986 and studied at Stanford, taking a bachelor's degree in political science in 2008 and a law degree in 2012. [cite:de15_wiki_masters] In the spring of 2012 Thiel taught a class at Stanford on start-ups, and Masters's detailed notes of it, posted online, became popular in the technology industry; they grew into Zero to One, published in September 2014 under both men's names. [cite:de15_wiki_masters] [cite:de15_ap_endorse] He went to work for Thiel, rising to chief operating officer of Thiel Capital, the investment firm that manages Thiel's money, and president of the Thiel Foundation, his charity. [cite:de15_ap_endorse] He resigned both posts in March 2022 to run for the Senate. [cite:de15_wiki_masters] Where Vance's ties to Thiel were several and of different kinds, Masters's was simpler and closer: he was, until his campaign, one of Thiel's most senior employees.

Saving Arizona

Saving Arizona PAC was formed in April 2021 with the stated aim of unseating the Democratic senator Mark Kelly, and on 26 April 2021 The Federalist reported that Thiel had given it $10 million while Masters, still at Thiel Capital and the foundation, was expected to run. [cite:de15_federalist_2021] The timing is the same as in Ohio, where Thiel's $10 million to Protect Ohio Values was reported on 15 March 2021, more than three months before Vance declared. [cite:de12_foxbiz_pov] In both states the money came first and the candidate second.

Thiel added $3.5 million in May 2022, and Trump endorsed Masters on 2 June 2022, calling him a "great modern-day thinker." [cite:de15_wiki_masters] [cite:de15_ap_endorse] By late July NBC, from Federal Election Commission filings, reported that the PAC had "received over $13 million from Thiel alone"; CNBC later put his primary-season total at $15 million, the last of it given in July. [cite:de15_nbc_mtp] [cite:de15_cnbc_fundraiser] An Arizona television station, from the same filings, calculated that Thiel's $15 million made up 92 per cent of the PAC's money. [cite:de15_12news] On 2 August 2022 Masters won the primary with 40.2 per cent, against 28.1 for the businessman Jim Lamon and 17.7 for the state attorney general, Mark Brnovich. [cite:de15_wiki_az2022] During the race Masters said, "I think Trump won in 2020," a claim the investigations of that election did not support. [cite:de15_ap_endorse] [cite:de12_pbs_ap]

The general election: the money steps back

In both states Thiel stopped giving after the primary, and the two campaigns' fortunes then depended on whether other money stepped in. In Ohio it did: the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with the Republican Senate leader Mitch McConnell, booked $28 million of advertising for Vance. [cite:de12_vindy_q3] In Arizona it did not. On 20 September 2022 the Fund cancelled $9.6 million of television time it had reserved for Arizona, and Axios reported that Thiel had not personally given to Saving Arizona since the primary. [cite:de15_axios_slf] According to reporting in the Washington Post, summarised by Axios, McConnell and the Fund's president had asked Thiel to re-engage, and he had refused an earlier proposal to split the cost of the general election, citing his early investment and his concern that the spending would become a Democratic talking point. [cite:de15_axios_double] On 12 October Axios reported that he had offered a matching arrangement instead, at least $10 million between them, Thiel paying half. [cite:de15_axios_double] Whether it was agreed was not reported; CNBC reported after the election that Thiel gave $2.5 million more in October, bringing his total for the cycle to $17.5 million. [cite:de15_cnbc_results]

The candidate's own money could not fill the gap. Through the end of September Kelly had raised more than $52 million and Masters just under $5 million. [cite:de15_cnbc_q3] On 8 November 2022 Kelly won by 51.4 per cent to 46.5. [cite:de15_wiki_az2022] In September, at the National Conservatism conference, Thiel had already judged the year: "My scoring on the '22 cycle is we are doing even less well than '94." [cite:de15_cnbc_fundraiser] In 2024 Masters ran for an open House seat in Arizona's 8th district and lost the Republican primary to Abe Hamadeh, after Trump had first backed Hamadeh and then endorsed both men. [cite:de15_wiki_masters]

The other donors, and the complaints

Thiel was not alone, and the overlap among the other donors is itself a documented connection. Richard Uihlein gave $3 million to Saving Arizona, and the Uihlein family also gave to Protect Ohio Values; the Mercer family gave to the Ohio PAC; David Sacks, Thiel's PayPal colleague, gave $1 million to a pro-Vance super PAC; and Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss gave $1 million to the Arizona one. [cite:de15_cnbc_q3] [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] Over the whole cycle Saving Arizona reported receipts of about $21.6 million and independent spending of about $25.5 million. [cite:de15_propublica_sa] Thiel's total federal giving in the 2022 elections was reported at $32 million by CNBC and $35 million across sixteen races by Forbes; the two Senate PACs took most of it. [cite:de15_cnbc_results] [cite:de12_ballotpedia_thiel]

Both PACs drew regulatory attention, and neither produced a finding against them. The Federal Election Commission wrote to Saving Arizona in its first year about the timing of its reports of independent spending, a letter that a lawyer at the Campaign Legal Center called "a standard notification" rather than a sign of enforcement. [cite:de15_azmirror_fec] In June 2022 the Center complained that Protect Ohio Values had given the Vance campaign more than $1 million of polling and targeting data through a hidden website; in May 2024 the Commission dismissed the complaint "in light of the public nature of the communications at issue." [cite:de15_clc_complaint] [cite:de15_fec_mur8009]

What is documented and what is inferred

Documented: the employment ties, the amounts, the dates of the gifts, the fact that each first gift preceded the candidacy, the further gifts after Trump's endorsements, the withdrawal of Thiel's money before each general election, and the outcomes. These are the spine of the case, and they show a repeated method. Inferred, and not documented: that Thiel recruited either man to run, since no document records him asking either to; that his money, rather than Trump's endorsement, won the primaries, since the two arrived together and the record cannot separate them; that the PACs were coordinated with the campaigns, since the one complaint was dismissed; and what Thiel wanted from either senator, since he declined to comment to CBS News on his giving and has not publicly stated a purpose for it. [cite:de12_cbs_klaidman] Rhyme is not provenance here either. The two races look alike because the same donor used the same legal vehicle in the same year; that is a pattern in his behaviour, not evidence of a plan beyond it.

The worst-case reading, tested

The book's hypothesis treats the network around Thiel as a means of placing allies in power on the way to an executive without a veto. On this part's material, documented: that Thiel twice financed a former employee's Senate race through a single-candidate super PAC, giving most of each PAC's money, and that one of the two is now first in line to the presidency. [cite:de15_12news] [cite:de15_cnbc_results] [cite:de12_cornell_3usc19] Probable: that Thiel's money made both men competitive in their primaries, since in Ohio the PAC carried most of Vance's advertising and in Arizona the PAC spent about $25.5 million over the cycle while Masters's campaign raised about $12 million. [cite:de12_forbesau] [cite:de15_propublica_sa] [cite:de15_wiki_az2022] The share of credit that belongs to Trump's endorsements cannot be separated from the record.

Not supported: that the method is a machine that delivers office. It worked in Ohio and failed in Arizona, and the decisive general-election money in both states came from, or was withheld by, the party, not Thiel. [cite:de15_axios_slf] [cite:de12_vindy_q3] Not supported either: that Thiel directed either candidate, or that either race was illegally coordinated; the one formal complaint was dismissed. [cite:de15_fec_mur8009] And the record runs against the most extreme version of the reading in one respect: in the autumn of 2022 Thiel declined, at first, to keep paying for the candidate who was losing, citing his own investment and the political cost. [cite:de15_axios_double] [scene:de16_the_valley|Part Sixteen] turns from the money to the wider adoption of these ideas in the technology industry, and [scene:de14_loops|Part Fourteen] has already tested the network's candidate loops.

chapters.label: Part Sixteen
chapters.title: The Adoption Layer
chapters.intro: This part asks how a small body of texts could be adopted by people with money and power, and answers it from the documented record of what those people wrote, said and were appointed to. It follows the turn of part of Silicon Valley to the right in the 2020s through two men's public words: Marc Andreessen, whose 2023 "Techno-Optimist Manifesto" named Nick Land among its patron saints and who, with his firm's co-founder, endorsed Donald Trump in 2024, and Balaji Srinivasan, whose theory of the "network state" turned the idea of exit into a design. It then traces the pipeline of people from venture firms, Thiel's companies and conservative institutions such as the Claremont Institute and Hillsdale College into public office in 2025 and 2026, and separates those who have cited Curtis Yarvin from those who merely know him or worked near him. The last section defines the currents most often confused with the Dark Enlightenment, each from its own texts, from Catholic integralism and national conservatism to effective accelerationism, and keeps the violent "accelerationism" of terrorist groups strictly apart.
chapters.outro: The adoption of these ideas, where it is documented, is an adoption of people more than of a program. Part of the technology industry turned right in public and for stated reasons, and one of its texts named Land a patron saint; its firms and Thiel's supplied the administration with officials, from the director of the Office of Personnel Management to the head of White House science policy. [cite:de16_techcrunch] [cite:de1_a16z_wiki] [cite:de16_cnbc_picks] [cite:de16_fedsmith_kupor] Only one person in office, J.D. Vance, has cited Yarvin by name, in 2021; Michael Anton, Andreessen and Srinivasan have documented contacts with him but no statement of agreement; and the other appointees have said nothing about the texts. [cite:de5_wbur_vance] [cite:de5_powerline] [cite:de5_sfstandard] [cite:de16_bi_balaji] The neighbouring currents with the most political weight are, in their own founding documents, committed to the Constitution or to a strong administrative state, and the one such document Thiel signed commits its signers to "the Constitution of 1787"; no documented organisational, funding or personal link connects any of these men to the terror usage of "accelerationism." [cite:de16_tac_natcon] [cite:de16_vermeule] [cite:de16_isd] Book Three turns from the people to the machinery, beginning with [scene:de17_money_to_office|the deal that turned campaign money into an office].

sections.h: The Valley Turns
sections.html:
For most of the 2010s the technology industry's founders and investors were, in public, either apolitical or Democratic. By 2024 a visible part of it had moved right. Marc Andreessen, co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, known as a16z, endorsed Donald Trump; [cite:de16_techcrunch] Elon Musk, whose turn is told in [scene:de11_twitter_x_xai|Part Eleven], spent heavily for him; and a group of investors and engineers supplied the new administration with officials, recruiters and ideas. This section looks at the part of that turn that touches the texts at the centre of this book. It follows two men, Andreessen and the engineer and investor Balaji Srinivasan, through what they wrote and said in public, and places each on the ladder of support from [scene:de1_spine_and_overlay|Part One], from author down to inference only, using only their own documented words and transactions.

Andreessen: from Democrat to "techno-optimist"

Andreessen co-founded a16z with Ben Horowitz and is one of Silicon Valley's best-known investors. By his own account he was a Democrat for most of his life: he said in July 2024 that he had endorsed or voted for Bill Clinton, Al Gore, John Kerry, Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton. [cite:de16_techcrunch] His break came in two public steps.

The first was a text. On 16 October 2023 he posted "The Techno-Optimist Manifesto" on the a16z website, about 5,200 words in short numbered declarations. [cite:de16_wiki_tom] [cite:de16_scanalyst] Its core claim is that technology and markets are the source of human progress and that slowing either costs lives. "We believe in accelerationism," it says, "the conscious and deliberate propulsion of technological development," to ensure "the techno-capital upward spiral continues forever." [cite:de16_lyons_p2p] [cite:de16_grosser] On artificial intelligence it goes further: "We believe any deceleration of AI will cost lives. Deaths that were preventable by the AI that was prevented from existing is a form of murder." [cite:de16_lyons_p2p] Its section on enemies names "stagnation," "statism, authoritarianism, collectivism, central planning, socialism," "bureaucracy, vetocracy, gerontocracy," and "corruption, regulatory capture, monopolies, cartels," along with "existential risk" and "tech ethics" as ideas. [cite:de16_scanalyst] [cite:de16_sfstandard] It closes with a list of 56 "patron saints of techno-optimism," beginning with three pseudonymous online accounts credited with founding "effective accelerationism" and including Friedrich Nietzsche, Milton Friedman and Nick Land. [cite:de16_sfstandard] [cite:de1_a16z_wiki]

Three things about the manifesto matter here. It names Land, the philosopher who coined "dark enlightenment," among its saints; that is a citation, documented, and it puts Andreessen on the rung of on-record engagement with Land. [cite:de1_a16z_wiki] Its "accelerationism" is not Land's. Land's, explained in [scene:de4_ccru_acceleration|Part Four], describes capital as an inhuman process that uses people and will outrun them; Andreessen's is a humanist promise of abundance, and one critic, Thomas Murphy, called the current it draws on "Nick Land diluted." [cite:de16_wiki_eacc] And its enemies list runs against its neighbours in this book: it names "authoritarianism" and "monopolies" as enemies, where Yarvin proposes a single executive and Thiel praised the creative monopoly. [cite:de16_scanalyst] [scene:de10_education_of_a_libertarian|Part Ten] The manifesto contains no proposal about how the American state should be governed.

The second step was an endorsement. On 16 July 2024, on their podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz explained why they would back Trump. Horowitz said "the future of our business, the future of technology, and the future of America is at stake"; Andreessen called President Biden's proposed tax on unrealised capital gains "the final straw," and praised Trump's plans for cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence. [cite:de16_techcrunch] Their stated reasons were policy toward their industry, and they gave them in public.

After the election Andreessen moved from donor to recruiter. In December 2024 the Washington Post and the Financial Times reported that, without any formal title, he was identifying and interviewing candidates for the Department of Government Efficiency, including people from his own circle. [cite:de16_fortune_doge] That work is part of the story of DOGE's staffing in [scene:de18_the_team|Part Eighteen]; the officials his firm supplied to the administration are in [scene:de16_elite_pipeline|the next section]. The Washington Post has reported that he is a member of the Rockbridge Network, a private donor group discussed in [scene:de14_foundations_and_opacity|Part Fourteen]. [cite:de14_wapo_rockbridge]

His ties to Yarvin are of two kinds. His firm invested in Yarvin's company, Tlon, alongside Thiel's Founders Fund, and was again sought as an investor in 2025, as [scene:de5_tlon_exit_and_return|Part Five] records; that is the patron rung, a venture investment with no documented link to Yarvin's political writing. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] And Andreessen has called Yarvin a "good friend," which is a statement of friendship, not of agreement. [cite:de5_sfstandard] No published text by Andreessen endorses Yarvin's program of a sovereign executive.

Srinivasan: exit, then the network state

Balaji Srinivasan is an engineer and investor who became a general partner at a16z in December 2013 and was chief technology officer of the cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase from 2018 to 2019; the first Trump administration considered him for commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration in 2017. [cite:de16_wiki_balaji] His political writing is about exit, the same word Land and Thiel used, which comes from the economist Albert Hirschman's distinction between leaving an organisation and complaining within it. In 2013, at the start-up school run by the accelerator Y Combinator, he gave a talk titled "Silicon Valley's Ultimate Exit," urging the industry to leave the United States, digitally and physically, rather than reform it. [cite:de16_wiki_balaji]

His 2022 book The Network State turned the idea into a design. A network state, he wrote, is "a social network with a moral innovation, a sense of national consciousness, a recognised founder," along with in-person communities, a built-in cryptocurrency and a social contract written in software, which would crowdfund territory and eventually seek diplomatic recognition. [cite:de16_maverick] [cite:de16_wiki_balaji] It is a theory of founding new polities by consent and purchase, not of taking over existing ones. In September 2024 he opened a "Network School" on an island development in Forest City, Malaysia; in July 2026 Malaysian authorities ordered it to shut for alleged administrative violations, and it moved to Kazakhstan under a five-year memorandum of understanding with the government. [cite:de16_wiki_balaji] Where these projects sit among the exit zones is in [scene:de22_seas_and_zones|Part Twenty-Two].

Srinivasan has one documented contact with Yarvin. In February 2021 the New York Times reported a 2013 email in which Srinivasan wrote to Yarvin that, if things got heated, it might be interesting to "sic the Dark Enlightenment audience on a single vulnerable hostile reporter to dox them," that is, to publish the reporter's private details; he did not respond to a request for comment on the report. [cite:de16_bi_balaji] That email is his own written words, and it shows both acquaintance and a willingness, in private, to think of Yarvin's readers as an audience that could be aimed at a journalist. It is not a statement of agreement with Yarvin's program, and his published theory differs from it: the network state is founded by people who choose to join, while Yarvin's sovereign corporation rules people who happen to live in its territory.

The turn is documented, and it was made in public, for stated reasons that were mostly about taxes, cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence. Its texts share a vocabulary with the Dark Enlightenment, exit and acceleration above all, and one of them names Land as a saint. What they do not share is the destination. Neither Andreessen's manifesto nor Srinivasan's book proposes a sovereign executive over an existing country; the first names authoritarianism as an enemy, and the second asks people to leave and found something new. The shared words are real, and so is the difference in what they are used to argue for. [cite:de16_scanalyst] [cite:de16_maverick] [cite:de16_techcrunch]

sections.h: The Pipeline: From Firms and Think Tanks to Office
sections.html:
Ideas reach government through people, and people reach government through appointments that are announced, confirmed and recorded. This section follows the people from the network mapped in this book who took public posts in 2025 and 2026, and the conservative institutions that trained or published some of them. It then asks the question that matters most for the book's hypothesis: which of these officials has cited Curtis Yarvin or Nick Land, which has said he agrees with them, and which has neither. The appointees who came from PayPal and from Thiel's own firms are told in full in [scene:de13_where_they_sit_now|Part Thirteen]; they are summarised here only so that the whole pipeline can be seen at once.

The venture firms

On 22 December 2024 the president-elect announced a set of technology appointments in a single day. Two came from Andreessen Horowitz. Scott Kupor, the firm's managing partner and first employee, was nominated to direct the Office of Personnel Management, the agency that runs the federal civil service; Sriram Krishnan, a general partner, was named senior policy adviser for artificial intelligence in the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. [cite:de16_cnbc_picks] The Senate confirmed Kupor on 9 July 2025, and he was sworn in on 15 July. At his hearing he had said that "protecting data privacy is incredibly important" and that restructuring should be "surgical." [cite:de16_fedsmith_kupor] By December 2025, as director, he reported that about 317,000 federal employees had left government in 2025, including about 144,000 deferred resignations and about 24,000 involuntary separations. [cite:us2_bloomberg_317k] What that meant for the civil service is told in [scene:us2_integrity|the US vs Israel volume] and in [scene:de20_the_cuts|Part Twenty].

The same announcement named Ken Howery, co-founder of PayPal and Founders Fund, as ambassador to Denmark, and Michael Kratsios, a former chief of staff at Thiel Capital, as director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy; David Sacks, PayPal's former chief operating officer, had been named the White House "AI and crypto czar" earlier that month. [cite:de16_cnbc_picks] [cite:de16_fortune_thielnet] Jim O'Neill, a former chief executive of the Thiel Foundation and managing director at Mithril Capital, was confirmed as deputy secretary of Health and Human Services on 5 June 2025, also served as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 28 August 2025, left both posts on 13 February 2026, and was nominated to direct the National Science Foundation on 2 March 2026; no confirmation is recorded as of October 2026. [cite:de16_wiki_oneill] Sacks stepped down from the czar role on 26 March 2026, when his days as a special government employee ran out, and stayed on as co-chair of the president's science and technology council. [cite:de16_reuters_sacks] The vice president himself had worked for Thiel at Mithril, as [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|Part Twelve] records. [cite:de16_fortune_thielnet] Marc Andreessen took no post but helped recruit for the Department of Government Efficiency. [cite:de16_fortune_doge]

Claremont, Hillsdale and the national conservatives

The second channel ran through conservative institutions rather than venture firms, and its clearest case is Michael Anton. In September 2016, writing under the pseudonym Publius Decius Mus in the online edition of the Claremont Review of Books, published by the Claremont Institute, he wrote "The Flight 93 Election," which compared a Clinton victory to passengers failing to rush the cockpit of the hijacked plane. [cite:de16_wiki_anton] He served on the National Security Council staff from February 2017 to April 2018, then taught at Hillsdale College's Kirby Center in Washington and became a senior fellow of the Claremont Institute. [cite:de16_wiki_anton] His 2020 book, The Stakes, discussed a "red caesarism," one-man rule on the right, as a possibility for American politics. [cite:de16_wiki_anton] He served as the State Department's Director of Policy Planning from 20 January to 15 September 2025, and took part in that year's negotiations with Iran. [cite:de16_wiki_anton]

Anton's documented contacts with Yarvin are two. In May 2021 the two recorded a conversation for the Claremont Institute's podcast, The American Mind, ostensibly about Anton's book; the Guardian later reported that Yarvin used it to discuss a president declaring a state of emergency in his inaugural address, and Anton's defenders replied that the newspaper's account did not match the recording. [cite:de5_powerline] [cite:de5_brewminate] And in January 2025 Yarvin said he had recently had lunch with Anton "at a coffee shop across the street from the State Department." [cite:de5_politico_ward] Both are contacts, the first by recording and the second on Yarvin's word. Neither is a statement by Anton that he holds Yarvin's views, and none has been found.

The institutions also met in a document. In June 2022 the Edmund Burke Foundation, which organises the National Conservatism conferences, published a statement of principles; its signers included "Peter Thiel / Founders Fund," "Michael Anton / Hillsdale College Kirby Center" and the foundation's chairman, Yoram Hazony. [cite:de16_natcon_signers] The statement commits its signers to "the Constitution of 1787" and a state "subject to constitutional restraints and a division of powers," which is the opposite of the end state in Yarvin's texts. [cite:de16_tac_natcon] Neither Yarvin nor Land signed it. [cite:de16_natcon_signers] No Thiel money to the conferences is documented, as [scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen] records.

Citing Yarvin, and following him

A pipeline of people is not a pipeline of ideas, and the book's ladder of support exists to keep the two apart. Placed on it by their own words, the people in this section fall into three groups. One person in office has cited Yarvin by name: J.D. Vance, in 2021, before he held any office, when he said "There's this guy, Curtis Yarvin, who's written about some of these things" and called for firing the civil service. [cite:de5_wbur_vance] That is on-record engagement, not on-record agreement, and he has not repeated it. A second group has documented contact with Yarvin or his circle without any statement of agreement: Anton by conversation and lunch, Andreessen as investor and self-described friend, and Srinivasan by a 2013 email. [cite:de5_powerline] [cite:de5_politico_ward] [cite:de5_sfstandard] [cite:de16_bi_balaji] The third group, which includes Kupor, Krishnan, Kratsios, O'Neill, Howery and Sacks, has no documented statement about Yarvin or Land at all. To connect them to the texts requires adjacency, the rung the book calls inference only.

The last row is the one most often used to close the gap. Yarvin said in 2025 that his influence ran "more through the kids in the administration," and an anonymous adviser to the Department of Government Efficiency told the Washington Post that it was an open secret that everyone designing policy had read him. [cite:de6_cnn_2025] [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] That is a claim of influence from its beneficiary and from one unnamed source, and the book grades it as reported, not documented ([scene:de5_the_public_years|Part Five]). Having read Yarvin is also not the same as following him: the record of DOGE, set out in Book Three, will be tested on what was done, not on what its staff may have read.

The pipeline, then, is documented as a pipeline of people from a small number of firms and institutions into offices that matter for this book's worst case: the civil service's personnel office, the science office, health and the State Department's planning staff. [cite:de16_cnbc_picks] [cite:de16_wiki_anton] What is not documented is that these officials carried Yarvin's or Land's program with them. The one public citation is Vance's in 2021; everything else is contact, friendship, investment or employment, which the ladder records for what it is.

sections.h: Neighbours, Not the Same Thing
sections.html:
The Dark Enlightenment shares stages, funders and sometimes people with several other currents on the American right and in the technology industry, and commentary often folds them together. They are not the same, and several of them contradict it on the point that matters most to this book: who should rule and by what right. This section defines each neighbour from its own texts, records the documented overlaps in people, money and venues, and records the documented disagreements. A shared stage is recorded as a meeting, not as a shared belief. The last of these neighbours, the violent "accelerationism" of terrorist groups, is kept strictly apart, because it shares a word with Nick Land's philosophy and nothing else that the record shows.

Post-liberal Catholic integralism

Integralism is a Catholic political theory holding that temporal government should be ordered to the spiritual good; its members are a subset of a wider "post-liberal" circle of Catholic intellectuals who want, in the Associated Press's summary, a strong government that they control and who seek to take over institutions such as universities from within. [cite:de16_ap_postliberal] Its best-known legal text is the Harvard law professor Adrian Vermeule's essay "Beyond Originalism," published in The Atlantic on 31 March 2020, which argued that "strong rule in the interest of attaining the common good is entirely legitimate" and that the constitutional order's "main aim is certainly not to maximize individual autonomy." [cite:de16_vermeule] Patrick Deneen's 2023 book Regime Change called for "the peaceful but vigorous overthrow of a corrupt and corrupting liberal ruling class." [cite:de16_ap_postliberal]

The overlap with the Dark Enlightenment is a shared hostility to liberal elites. The disagreement is sharp. Vermeule described the bureaucracy "not as an enemy, but as the strong hand of legitimate rule," where Yarvin proposes to retire it entirely ([scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]); integralism grounds authority in natural law and the Church, where Yarvin's sovereign is a secular owner answerable to shareholders. [cite:de16_vermeule] The documented touchpoint is J.D. Vance, who has called himself "postliberal," praised Regime Change at a 2023 panel with Deneen, and said at Franciscan University of Steubenville in 2022, "You need to have a functional state that accomplishes some of the things that we care about." [cite:de16_ap_postliberal] No Thiel funding of integralist venues has been found.

Christian nationalism

Christian nationalism, as measured by the polling organisation PRRI, is a set of beliefs about American identity rather than a body of texts by named authors: that "the U.S. government should declare America a Christian nation," that "U.S. laws should be based on Christian values," and that "God has called Christians to exercise dominion over all areas of American society," among five statements. In PRRI's 2024 survey, PRRI classed 10 percent of Americans as "adherents" and 20 percent as "sympathizers"; 38 percent of those it classed as adherents agreed that "true American patriots may need to resort to violence in order to save our country," against 17 percent of all Americans. [cite:de16_prri] It is a mass, majoritarian identity, and it works through elections. The Dark Enlightenment is elitist, secular in its texts and contemptuous of elections. No documented tie links Yarvin or Land to Christian-nationalist organisations, and none of the officials in this book is documented using the label of himself.

National conservatism

National conservatism has a founding document. "National Conservatism: A Statement of Principles," published by the Edmund Burke Foundation on 15 June 2022, calls for "a world of independent nations," "much more restrictive" immigration, a public life "rooted in Christianity" where a Christian majority exists, and "accepting and living in accordance with the Constitution of 1787," with "a strong but limited state, subject to constitutional restraints and a division of powers." [cite:de16_tac_natcon] That last commitment is the disagreement: the national conservatives keep the constitutional state that Yarvin proposes to replace.

The overlaps are documented and specific. Peter Thiel gave the opening speech at the first National Conservatism conference in Washington in July 2019, and signed the 2022 statement; Michael Anton signed it too. [cite:de16_bloomberg_natcon] [cite:de16_natcon_signers] No Thiel money to the conferences or to the foundation is documented ([scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen]), and neither Yarvin nor Land signed. [cite:de16_natcon_signers]

Pronatalism

Pronatalism is a single policy aim, raising the birth rate, pursued by Catholic, secular and technology-industry advocates and, at its fringe, by people who openly link it to eugenics. Its main gathering, the Natal Conference, was first held in Austin in 2024; its 2025 edition met at a conference centre rented from the University of Texas, and its organiser, Kevin Dolan, has said that "pro-natalist and the eugenic positions are ... very much aligned." [cite:de16_kut] The aim also has a mainstream form: Vance told the March for Life on 24 January 2025, "I want more babies in the United States of America." [cite:de16_rns_vance] Pronatalism has no theory of sovereignty, and it is compatible with any form of government. No documented attendance by Vance or by Thiel at the Natal Conference has been found.

Rationalists and effective altruists

The rationalist community grew around the blogs Overcoming Bias, from November 2006, and LessWrong, launched on 1 February 2009 by Eliezer Yudkowsky, and its central concern became the risk that advanced artificial intelligence could destroy humanity; it is closely tied to effective altruism, a movement that tries to direct charity by evidence and, in its "longtermist" branch, toward the far future. [cite:de16_wiki_lw] Neoreaction circulated among a small share of its readers, which is why the two are often linked. The record shows the community rejecting it: Yudkowsky "has strongly rejected neoreaction"; only 0.92 percent of respondents to the forum's 2016 survey called themselves neoreactionary; and Scott Alexander, its best-known essayist, published a long rebuttal, "The Anti-Reactionary FAQ," on 20 October 2013. [cite:de16_wiki_lw] [cite:de2_ssc_faq]

Thiel's relation to this current changed. The Thiel Foundation gave Yudkowsky's institute, then the Singularity Institute and now the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, more than $1.6 million from 2006 onward. [cite:de16_wiki_thielfdn] In his 2025 lectures, as reported from recordings, Thiel named Yudkowsky among the "legionnaires of the Antichrist" for arguing for world government to stop dangerous technology. [cite:de10_reason] The documented relation, then, is a funder who became an adversary.

Effective accelerationism

"Effective accelerationism," shortened to e/acc, is an online current that first appeared in May 2022 in a newsletter by four pseudonymous accounts; in December 2023 Forbes identified the best known of them, "Beff Jezos," as Guillaume Verdon, a former Google quantum-computing engineer. It holds that unrestricted technological progress, artificial intelligence above all, is a moral good, and it opposes the AI-safety priorities of the effective altruists, whose name it parodies. [cite:de16_wiki_eacc] Its closest public expression is Andreessen's 2023 manifesto ([scene:de16_the_valley|the first section of this part]). Land has voiced support for it, which is a documented overlap; but its theory differs from his, which treats capital as an inhuman process indifferent to human ends, and a critic called it "Nick Land diluted." [cite:de16_wiki_eacc] It proposes no form of government.

Violent "accelerationism": a different thing

The word "accelerationism" is also used, in a completely different sense, by neo-Nazi terror networks. In that usage, as the Institute for Strategic Dialogue defines it, accelerationism is "an ideology focussed on the need for societal collapse to preserve the white race," to be brought about by violence; its groups include Atomwaffen Division and The Base, its key text is James Mason's neo-Nazi collection SIEGE, and the perpetrators of the Christchurch mosque massacre and the Poway synagogue shooting in 2019 cited it. [cite:de16_isd] On 13 January 2025 the State Department designated the Terrorgram Collective and three of its leaders as Specially Designated Global Terrorists, saying the group "promotes violent white supremacism, solicits attacks on perceived adversaries"; it has been linked to a 2022 shooting outside an LGBTQ bar in Slovakia. [cite:de16_state_terrorgram] [cite:de16_aj_terrorgram]

No documented organisational, funding, membership or personal link exists between these groups and Yarvin, Land, Thiel or Vance. One research group, the ISD, lists neoreaction, which it calls "a doctrine developed by Nick Land and Curtis Yarvin," as one of three ideological strands that fed into this usage, while noting that neoreactionaries blame democracy where white supremacists blame Jewish people and other minorities. [cite:de16_isd] That is one think tank's interpretive claim about the history of ideas, and it is recorded here as such, not as evidence of a tie. Land's own accelerationism, the subject of [scene:de4_ccru_acceleration|Part Four], is a philosophy of technology and capital, and the journalist Zack Beauchamp, among others, has described it as otherwise unrelated to the terror usage. [cite:de4_wiki_accel]

The worst-case reading, tested

This part asked how ideas from a small body of texts could be adopted by people with money and power. Documented: a visible part of the technology industry moved to the right in 2023 and 2024, for reasons its leaders stated in public, mostly about taxes, cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence; one of its texts names Land as a saint; and its firms supplied the administration with officials, including the director of the civil service's personnel office. [cite:de16_techcrunch] [cite:de1_a16z_wiki] [cite:de16_cnbc_picks] [cite:de16_fedsmith_kupor] Documented, too, are contacts between Yarvin and people near power: Vance's 2021 citation, Anton's recorded conversation and lunch, Andreessen's friendship and Srinivasan's 2013 email. [cite:de5_wbur_vance] [cite:de5_powerline] [cite:de5_sfstandard] [cite:de16_bi_balaji]

Probable, at most: that some staff in the administration had read Yarvin; it rests on his word and one anonymous source. [cite:de6_cnn_2025] [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] Not supported: that the officials who came through this pipeline carried the sovereign-executive program with them; none has said so, and most have said nothing about the texts at all. The record also runs against the hypothesis in a way this section makes plain. The neighbours with the most real political weight, national conservatism and Catholic post-liberalism, are documented in their own founding texts as committed to the Constitution or to a strong administrative state, and the one such document Thiel and Anton signed commits its signers to "the Constitution of 1787." [cite:de16_tac_natcon] [cite:de16_vermeule] The coalition around the administration is many currents, several of which contradict the Dark Enlightenment's end state in writing. Whether its practice followed its texts or the worst case is the question of Book Three, which begins with [scene:de17_money_to_office|the deal that turned campaign money into an office].

chapters.label: Part Seventeen
chapters.title: The Deal: Campaign Money to an Office
chapters.intro: This part opens Book Three, on the Department of Government Efficiency, by asking how a campaign donor came to hold an office and what that office was. It follows the sequence from Elon Musk's endorsement of Donald Trump in July 2024, through a proposal made in public during the campaign, more than $290 million in election spending and the announcement of a "Department of Government Efficiency" a week after the vote, to the executive order of 20 January 2025 that built something different from what had been announced: not an outside commission but a renamed White House office with a temporary unit, a fixed end date and teams inside every agency. It then sets out that office's legal form, who was in charge on paper and in practice, the special-government-employee status of its staff, the advisory-committee and freedom-of-information disputes, and what remained of it as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: The record of the deal is a sequence, not a contract. More than $290 million of Musk's money in 2024 was followed by an office he had been promised in public during the campaign, and no document connects the two as an exchange. [cite:de11_cnn_290m] [cite:de17_reuters_econclub] [cite:de17_aj_announce] The office itself was a renamed White House unit created by executive order, with a temporary organization that ended on 4 July 2026 and an access clause reaching every unclassified agency system. [cite:de17_eo_text] Its legal form, an adviser with "no actual or formal authority," diverged from its public form, a department "headed by Elon Musk"; one judge found that likely unconstitutional and an appeals court majority found it likely lawful. [cite:de11_audit_fisher] [cite:de17_abc_address] [cite:de17_upi_chuang] [cite:de17_hill_ca4] The Supreme Court narrowed discovery in 2025 without deciding whether DOGE is subject to FOIA and agreed in October 2026 to hear that question; the U.S. DOGE Service itself still exists. [cite:de17_scotus_order] [cite:de17_ncc_cert] [cite:de17_nextgov_108403] [scene:de18_the_team|Part Eighteen] names the people who staffed it.

sections.h: Campaign Money to an Office
sections.html:
Book Three turns from the men and their money to the office that one of them held. The Department of Government Efficiency, always called DOGE, was the most visible instrument of the 2025 government cuts, and in the book's worst-case reading it is the place where cuts become "the occasion": a reason, sold as thrift, to take hold of the machinery of the state. This section sets out how the office came to exist, step by step, from Elon Musk's endorsement of Donald Trump in July 2024 to the executive order of 20 January 2025. It reports a sequence. Money came first and an office followed; the record shows the order of those events and, as Part Eleven has already said, no document records an agreement between the two men linking one to the other. [scene:de11_money_and_influence|Part Eleven] gives Musk's political money in full; here it is the first link in a chain.

The endorsement and the idea

Musk endorsed Trump on the evening of 13 July 2024, within hours of the attempt on Trump's life at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania: "I fully endorse President Trump and hope for his rapid recovery." [cite:de17_reuters_endorse] Through the summer the two men discussed a role for him. On a podcast on 19 August Musk said he had spoken with Trump about it and would be interested in serving. On 5 September, at the Economic Club of New York, Trump announced the idea in public for the first time: a government efficiency commission "tasked with conducting a complete financial and performance audit of the entire federal government" and "making recommendations for drastic reforms," with a plan to eliminate "fraud and improper payments" within six months. He said Musk had agreed to lead it. Musk wrote on X the same day: "I look forward to serving America if the opportunity arises." [cite:de17_reuters_econclub]

The money came alongside the idea, and most of it after. Musk's year-end filings with the Federal Election Commission showed more than $290 million spent on the 2024 election, about a quarter of a billion of it through America PAC, the super PAC he founded and funded, and more than $50 million on giveaways to petition signers, among them the $1 million daily payments, in the last weeks of the campaign. [cite:de11_cnn_290m] At the rally in Madison Square Garden on 27 October he said that the federal budget could be cut by "at least $2 trillion," against total spending of about $6.75 trillion in the 2024 fiscal year. [cite:de11_fortune_2t] The promise and its fate are graded in [scene:de11_claims_vs_record|Part Eleven's claims ledger] and audited in [scene:de21_the_ending|Part Twenty-One].

The announcement

Trump won on 5 November. A week later, on 12 November, he announced that Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy, the entrepreneur who had run against him in the Republican primaries, would lead a "Department of Government Efficiency." The two men, he wrote, "will pave the way for my Administration to dismantle Government Bureaucracy, slash excess regulations, cut wasteful expenditures, and restructure Federal Agencies." He compared the project to "The Manhattan Project" and set its work to end by 4 July 2026, the 250th anniversary of independence. The body, as described that day, would give advice and guidance from outside government. Musk added: "This will send shockwaves through the system, and anyone involved in Government waste, which is a lot of people!" [cite:de17_aj_announce]

On 20 November Musk and Ramaswamy set out their plan in the Wall Street Journal. "We will serve as outside volunteers, not federal officials or employees," they wrote. They did not intend to wait for Congress: "Instead of new laws, existing legislation will lead DOGE to make the changes," and the president "can, by executive action, immediately pause the enforcement of those regulations." They named two recent Supreme Court decisions as their legal tools: Loper Bright v. Raimondo (2024), which ended the rule that courts defer to agencies' reading of ambiguous statutes, and West Virginia v. EPA (2022), which bars agencies from deciding "major questions" without clear authority from Congress. DOGE would identify "thousands" of regulations made by "unelected bureaucrats," find "the minimum number of employees required at an agency," and challenge "$500 billion plus in annual federal expenditures that are unauthorized by Congress." [cite:de17_li_oped] [cite:de17_jurist_oped] Over the following weeks Marc Andreessen, without any formal title, interviewed candidates for the new body, a story told in [scene:de16_the_valley|Part Sixteen]. [cite:de16_fortune_doge]

From commission to order

What was announced and what was built were different things. On the day of the inauguration, 20 January 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14158. It did not create an outside commission. It renamed an existing White House office, the United States Digital Service, as the United States DOGE Service, placed it in the Executive Office of the President, and set up inside it a temporary organization to end on 4 July 2026. [cite:de17_eo_text] [cite:de17_fnn_structure] Ramaswamy left the same day. A spokeswoman said he had "played a critical role in helping us create DOGE," that he intended "to run for elected office soon," and that "the structure that we announced today" required him to stay outside it; he was running for governor of Ohio. [cite:de17_wt_ramaswamy] Two weeks later the White House confirmed that Musk was not an outside volunteer but a special government employee, unpaid, with a government email account and an office in the White House complex. [cite:de17_ap_sge] What that structure was in law, and why it mattered, is the subject of [scene:de17_what_doge_was_legally|the next section].

What the sequence shows, and what it does not

The sequence is documented: the largest donor of the election was given, within three months of election day, a government role with a mandate across the whole executive branch. [cite:de11_cnn_290m] [cite:de7_os_donors2024] [cite:de17_eo_text] That is the core of the "bought office" reading, and it is a fair description of the order of events.

Three things in the record complicate it. First, the office was not a secret: the candidate proposed it from a public stage on 5 September 2024, two months before the vote, and named the man who would lead it, so voters were told before they voted. [cite:de17_reuters_econclub] Second, there is no statement from either man that ties the money to the role. The nearest thing on the record is Musk's own claim, during the public quarrel of 5 June 2025, that Trump would have lost the election without him; that is a boast about influence, not evidence of a bargain, and it came after he had left government. [cite:de11_npr_feud] Third, the money did not secure the relationship. Within a week of leaving office Musk was threatened by the president with the loss of his companies' contracts, as [scene:de11_money_and_influence|Part Eleven] records. [cite:de11_npr_feud]

Two other readings need a plain answer. The first is that DOGE was Curtis Yarvin's 2012 proposal, "Retire All Government Employees," put into practice. The resemblance between RAGE and a programme of mass federal job cuts is real, and [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six] sets out what Yarvin proposed. But no document shows a line from his talk to EO 14158, and the published plan for DOGE cited Supreme Court decisions and existing legislation, not Yarvin. [cite:de17_li_oped] Rhyme is not provenance, as [scene:de1_spine_and_overlay|Part One] explains. The second is that DOGE was a joint project of Musk and Peter Thiel. No published record shows Thiel in its creation, its chain of command or its staffing decisions; the ties that do exist between DOGE's staff and Thiel's companies and foundation are set out, by type and date, in [scene:de18_the_team|Part Eighteen].

sections.h: What DOGE Was in Law
sections.html:
For most of 2025 the public called DOGE a department and its leader Elon Musk. In law it was neither. It was a renamed White House office, a temporary organization inside it with a fixed end date, and small teams placed in agencies, all created by one executive order without an act of Congress. This section sets out that form, who was in charge on paper and in practice, how the courts dealt with the questions it raised, and what remained as of October 2026.

The order

Executive Order 14158, signed on 20 January 2025, "establishes the Department of Government Efficiency to implement the President's DOGE Agenda." First, it renamed the United States Digital Service, a technology unit the Obama administration had created after the troubled launch of HealthCare.gov, as the United States DOGE Service (USDS), "established in the Executive Office of the President," with an administrator "who shall report to the White House Chief of Staff." [cite:de17_eo_text] [cite:de17_fnn_structure] Second, it set up inside USDS a "U.S. DOGE Service Temporary Organization," "dedicated to advancing the President's 18-month DOGE agenda," which "shall terminate on July 4, 2026." Third, it told every agency head to create a "DOGE Team of at least four employees" within thirty days, typically "one DOGE Team Lead, one engineer, one human resources specialist, and one attorney," who could include special government employees. [cite:de17_eo_text]

The temporary organization was built on section 3161 of title 5 of the U.S. Code, which lets a president or Congress create a body "for a specific period not in excess of three years" and lets its head hire staff outside the normal competitive rules for terms of up to three years. [cite:de17_vlex_3161] Its stated programme was a "Software Modernization Initiative." Its most consequential sentence told agency heads, "to the maximum extent consistent with law," to give USDS "full and prompt access to all unclassified agency records, software systems, and IT systems." In return, "USDS shall adhere to rigorous data protection standards"; the order did not say what those standards were. [cite:de17_eo_text] How that clause was used is the subject of [scene:de19_the_access|Part Nineteen].

Special government employees

A special government employee is a temporary federal worker, normally limited to 130 days of service in a year, who is subject to lighter ethics and disclosure rules than a full-time official. On 3 February 2025 the White House confirmed that Musk held this status: unpaid, with a government email address and White House office space, and, a White House official said, unlikely to have to file a public financial disclosure report. [cite:de17_ap_sge] Others at DOGE used the same status to keep their private jobs, as [scene:de18_the_team|Part Eighteen] records. In August 2026 the Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's auditor, counted at least 206 DOGE personnel in Executive Office posts between 20 January 2025 and 31 January 2026; at least 27 of them, Musk among them, were special government employees, and at least 128 had left by the end of that period. [cite:de17_gao_108403] [cite:de17_nextgov_108403] The Executive Office of the President did not give GAO its records of ethics training or financial disclosures for these staff, and ten agencies did not answer at all. The Office of Government Ethics had no plans to review USDS's ethics programme. [cite:de17_gao_108403]

Who was in charge

Who ran DOGE was answered differently in court and in public. On 17 February 2025, in a suit brought by fourteen states, the director of the White House Office of Administration, Joshua Fisher, declared that Musk was a "Senior Advisor to the President," not an employee of USDS or its temporary organization, and that "Mr. Musk has no actual or formal authority to make government decisions himself. Mr. Musk can only advise the President and communicate the President's directives." [cite:de11_audit_fisher] [cite:de17_audit_fisher] For weeks the administration did not say who the administrator was; on 24 February a government lawyer told a judge he did not know. The next afternoon the White House named Amy Gleason, who had worked at the Digital Service from 2018 to 2021 on the federal coronavirus response and returned in January, as acting administrator. [cite:de17_ap_gleason] In a sworn declaration in March she stated: "Elon Musk does not work at USDS," and "I do not report to him, and he does not report to me." She reported to the chief of staff, Susie Wiles. [cite:de17_bi_gleason]

The president described it otherwise. In his address to Congress on 4 March 2025 Trump said he had "created the brand new Department of Government Efficiency, DOGE," "which is headed by Elon Musk, who is in the gallery tonight"; lawyers suing DOGE cited the line in court the next day. [cite:de17_abc_address] Judges split on whether the difference mattered. On 18 March Judge Theodore Chuang of Maryland found that Musk's role in closing USAID likely violated the Constitution's Appointments Clause, which requires officers who wield significant authority to be appointed through the proper process: to deny the claim because Musk had no formal title "would open the door to an end-run around the Appointments Clause." [cite:de17_upi_chuang] Ten days later the Fourth Circuit stayed his order. Judge Marvin Quattlebaum, joined by Judge Paul Niemeyer, wrote that "unconventional does not necessarily equal unconstitutional" and that the evidence showed "a strong likelihood that he functioned as an advisor to the President." Judge Roger Gregory agreed to the stay only because, in his view, the plaintiffs had sued the wrong defendants. [cite:de17_hill_ca4]

Advisory committee or agency

The legal form also decided which transparency laws applied. On inauguration day three suits argued that DOGE was an "advisory committee" under the Federal Advisory Committee Act of 1972 (FACA), which requires such bodies to have a fairly balanced membership, hold open meetings and keep public records. [cite:de17_lawfare_faca] [cite:de17_fnn_structure] The executive order signed that evening placed DOGE inside the government instead, which, the New York Sun noted two days later, "may nullify those legal challenges." [cite:de17_nysun_faca] Two sets of plaintiffs withdrew in March and May 2025; in the remaining case the government argued that Musk, as a presidential adviser, fell within FACA's exclusion for bodies made up wholly of federal employees, and its motion to dismiss was still undecided in 2026. [cite:de17_ch_pubcit]

The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) reaches agencies, not bodies that only advise the president. [cite:de17_ncc_cert] On 10 March 2025 Judge Christopher Cooper found that DOGE was likely an agency subject to FOIA, citing its "unusual secrecy" and "substantial authority over vast swathes of the federal government," in a suit by the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW). [cite:de17_reason_cooper] On 6 June 2025 the Supreme Court stayed his discovery orders, holding that parts requiring disclosure of USDS's internal recommendations were "not appropriately tailored" and that "separation of powers concerns counsel judicial deference and restraint." It did not decide whether DOGE is covered by FOIA; it said only that the question "cannot turn on the entity's ability to persuade." Three justices dissented. [cite:de17_scotus_order] The order is often described as exempting DOGE from FOIA; it did not. On 15 October 2026 the Court agreed to hear the dispute in full, as U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (No. 25-1103), with argument expected early in 2027; the question is whether USDS "wields independent authority or is merely a board that exists to advise the president." [cite:de17_ncc_cert] The wider litigation is in [scene:de19_the_courts|Part Nineteen].

The end, on paper

DOGE wound down before its deadline. In November 2025 the director of the Office of Personnel Management, Scott Kupor, told Reuters that DOGE "doesn't exist" as a "centralized entity," with many of its functions absorbed by his office and some staff moved to a new National Design Studio. [cite:de17_reuters_noexist] The temporary organization ended on 4 July 2026. USDS did not: the order had renamed it permanently, and GAO noted that "the EO does not call for the termination of the broader USDS entity." [cite:de17_nextgov_108403] The 2027 budget request sought $35 million for the U.S. DOGE Service, House appropriators asked "the Administrator of DOGE" for quarterly staffing reports, and Gleason was still listed as acting administrator while leading a health-technology office at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. [cite:de17_ee_end] As of October 2026, then, the office survives under its new name, the FOIA question is before the Supreme Court, and the advisory-committee case is undecided. [scene:de21_the_ending|Part Twenty-One] tells the ending in full.

The worst-case reading, tested

On this part's material, documented: that the largest donor of the 2024 election was given an office with a mandate across the executive branch within three months of the vote; that the office was built by executive order alone, around a clause granting access to all unclassified agency systems; that its legal form, an adviser without authority, differed from its public form, a department "headed by Elon Musk"; and that the Executive Office of the President did not give Congress's auditor the ethics records of its staff. [cite:de11_cnn_290m] [cite:de7_os_donors2024] [cite:de17_eo_text] [cite:de11_audit_fisher] [cite:de17_abc_address] [cite:de17_gao_108403] Probable: that the advisory structure reduced the reach of FACA, FOIA and public disclosure while the work went on; that was its effect in 2025, and no official has stated it as an intent. Not supported: that the office was bought, since no document records an exchange; that DOGE descended from Yarvin's RAGE; or that Thiel had any role in creating it.

Parts of the record run against the reading. The office was proposed in public during the campaign, not arranged in private. [cite:de17_reuters_econclub] It had an end date written into it, and the temporary organization did end. [cite:de17_eo_text] [cite:de17_ee_end] Courts heard the challenges to it, and two of three Fourth Circuit judges found Musk's role likely to be an adviser's. [cite:de17_hill_ca4] Congress's auditor counted its staff and published both what it found and what it was refused. [cite:de17_gao_108403] Who those staff were is the subject of [scene:de18_the_team|Part Eighteen].

chapters.label: Part Eighteen
chapters.title: The Operators
chapters.intro: This part names the people who ran and staffed DOGE, as far as major outlets named them: the Boring Company executive who managed it day to day, the acting administrator who led it on paper, the executives from Musk's companies and investors placed at the Treasury, the Office of Personnel Management, the Social Security Administration and the General Services Administration, and the engineers aged 19 to 24 whose presence in federal systems drew the most attention. It types each person's documented tie to Musk's or Thiel's companies, examines three individual records in detail with the answers given to each, sets out how staff were recruited and what Congress's auditor could and could not confirm about their vetting, and records where they went when the office wound down.
chapters.outro: DOGE's best-known operators came mostly from Musk's own companies and circle: a Boring Company executive ran it day to day, SpaceX and Tesla veterans took posts at the Office of Personnel Management and the General Services Administration, and a former Tesla director went to Social Security. [cite:de18_wiki_davis] [cite:de18_reuters_opm] [cite:de18_wiki_shedd] [cite:de18_bbg_ssa] Thiel's ties were thinner and indirect: a Thiel Foundation fellow among the engineers, Palantir alumni among the staff and recruiters. [cite:de18_hyper_farritor] [cite:de18_fox_wired] [cite:de18_indep_jancso] The records of three young staffers, a rehiring after racist posts on an account linked to him and a breach of Treasury data rules, a disputed internship and a reported customer link, and a disputed conflict of interest, are documented with the answers given to each. [cite:de18_bbg_elez] [cite:de18_mediaite_coristine] [cite:de18_pp_kliger] Congress's auditor could not confirm that most DOGE teams had been vetted; no record shows any operator acting for Musk's companies. [cite:de18_gao_108192] [scene:de19_the_access|Part Nineteen] follows them into the systems they reached.

sections.h: The Team
sections.html:
DOGE was staffed by a few hundred people, most of whom never became public figures. Congress's auditor counted at least 206 in posts in the Executive Office of the President by January 2026, 27 of them special government employees. [cite:de17_gao_108403] This section names only those whom major outlets named, gives their ages and backgrounds only as those outlets published them, and types each person's tie to Elon Musk's or Peter Thiel's companies by kind and date. Where no wrongdoing is documented, none is implied. Where a record is disputed, the person's or the government's answer is given beside it.

The leaders

Steve Davis ran DOGE day to day. He joined SpaceX in 2003 as roughly its fourteenth hire, led the Boring Company from 2018 and ran cost-cutting at X after Musk bought it in 2022.
