[cite:de18_wiki_davis] At DOGE he directed operations, including hiring and firing, as a special government employee who kept his job as head of the Boring Company; the New York Times described him as "effectively the leader of DOGE." [cite:de18_aol_davis] [cite:de18_wiki_davis] His departure was announced at the end of May 2025, the day after Musk's. [cite:de18_aol_davis] The legal head, the acting administrator Amy Gleason, was a health-technology executive who had served in the same office from 2018 to 2021; her role is set out in [scene:de17_what_doge_was_legally|Part Seventeen]. [cite:de17_ap_gleason]

Others came from Musk's companies or his investors. Tom Krause, chief executive of Cloud Software Group, took over the duties of the Treasury's fiscal assistant secretary, the official responsible for federal payments, after the senior career official, David Lebryk, retired following a clash with Musk's allies over access to the payment systems; Krause kept his company post as a special government employee. [cite:de18_reuters_krause] At the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), Reuters reported in January 2025, the chief of staff was Amanda Scales, a former Musk employee, and the senior advisers included Brian Bjelde, at SpaceX since 2003 and its vice-president for human resources, and Riccardo Biasini, a former Tesla engineer and Boring Company director; career managers there lost access to personnel databases holding Social Security numbers and home addresses. [cite:de18_reuters_opm] Antonio Gracias of Valor Equity Partners, a former Tesla director and early SpaceX investor, was sent to the Social Security Administration in March 2025 with two other finance executives. [cite:de18_bbg_ssa] Thomas Shedd, a Tesla engineer for about eight years, became director of the General Services Administration's Technology Transformation Services in January 2025, told staff the unit would be "AI-first," and later served as chief information officer at the Labor Department. [cite:de18_wiki_shedd]

The engineers

On 2 February 2025 Wired named six engineers aged 19 to 24 working with DOGE at OPM and the General Services Administration: Akash Bobba, a Berkeley graduate with internships at Bridgewater, Meta and Palantir; Edward Coristine, a recent high-school graduate who had studied at Northeastern and worked briefly at Neuralink; Luke Farritor, a former SpaceX intern; Gautier Cole Killian, formerly of the trading firm Jump Trading; Gavin Kliger, formerly of the AI company Databricks; and Ethan Shaotran, a Harvard student who had founded an AI start-up. [cite:de18_fox_wired] Farritor, 23, had shared a $700,000 prize in 2024 for using AI to read a carbonised scroll from Herculaneum, and was a fellow of the Thiel Foundation. [cite:de18_hyper_farritor] Musk wrote that reports that DOGE had "some of world's best software engineers" were "in fact true"; Trump said: "They're very smart, though, Peter. They're like you." A White House spokesman said the work was being done "in full compliance with federal law." [cite:de18_fox_wired]

Three records examined

Marko Elez, 25, worked on the Treasury's payment systems. On 6 February 2025 he resigned after the Wall Street Journal linked him to an account, which said its owner had worked at SpaceX and Starlink, that had posted "Just for the record, I was racist before it was cool" and "Normalize Indian hate." Vice President J.D. Vance urged that he be rehired ("So I say bring him back"), Musk agreed ("To err is human, to forgive divine"), and Trump said: "I'm with the vice president." [cite:de18_nbc_elez] [cite:de12_ap_elez] He was rehired, at the Social Security Administration. Treasury later told a court that he had briefly held read-write access to a payment system although the court had been told it was read-only, that its forensic review found no changes to the data, and that the same review, carried out after he resigned, found that while at Treasury he had emailed an unencrypted spreadsheet of names and payment amounts to two officials at another agency in breach of its rules; Treasury's privacy officer called the names "low-risk." [cite:de18_bbg_elez] [cite:de18_audit_elez_timing] In April 2026 Congress's auditor confirmed the inadvertent write access and the undetected transfer, and found that the bureau had not ensured the employee signed its security rules before getting a laptop. [cite:de18_gao_108131]

Edward Coristine was 19. Bloomberg reported that a data-security firm, Path Network, ended his internship in June 2022 "for leaking internal information to the competitors"; he wrote at the time that he had done "nothing contractually wrong." [cite:de18_mediaite_coristine] Reuters reported in March 2025 that a group an FBI agent said had been investigated in connection with "swatting" had publicly thanked a web-protection company Coristine ran for its services in 2023; Coristine did not reply. He was listed as a senior adviser at the State Department and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. [cite:de18_fortune_coristine] These reports concern an internship and a company's customer; no court or agency finding against him is part of this record. On 3 August 2025 he was the victim of an attempted carjacking in Washington, and Trump cited the attack in threatening federal control of the city. [cite:de18_ap_assault] By 2026 he worked at the National Design Studio. [cite:de17_ee_end]

Gavin Kliger, 25, was at OPM, then at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the IRS. ProPublica reported that his public disclosure listed Tesla shares worth $100,000 to $250,000, Apple shares and cryptocurrency, holdings barred for bureau staff, while a sworn declaration said he "managed" the firing of about 90 per cent of its employees. The White House called that account "an outright lie," said he "did not even manage" the layoffs, and pointed to a divestment deadline. [cite:de18_pp_kliger] In April 2025 he and Sam Corcos, chief executive of the health start-up Levels, planned an IRS hackathon to build "one new API to rule them all" over taxpayer data, with Palantir "consistently" named as a candidate vendor. [cite:de18_tc_irs] What happened inside those systems is the subject of [scene:de19_the_access|Part Nineteen].

Recruiting and vetting

Recruitment ran partly through Musk's and Thiel's networks. Marc Andreessen interviewed candidates in late 2024, as [scene:de16_the_valley|Part Sixteen] records. [cite:de16_fortune_doge] Anthony Jancso, a former Palantir employee brought on by Davis, wrote in a chat group of Palantir alumni: "I'm helping Elon's team find tech talent for the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in the new admin." [cite:de18_indep_jancso] These are ties of employment and recruitment, not evidence that Thiel or Palantir directed anyone. Some staff arrived with no government experience at all: two who reviewed humanities grants, Justin Fox and Nate Cavanaugh, used ChatGPT to flag "DEI" grants worth more than $100 million for cancellation, and in 2026 Cavanaugh, asked under oath whether they had reduced the deficit, answered: "No, we didn't." [cite:de18_abc_depos] When Congress's auditor sought proof that DOGE team members had passed background investigations, only the Securities and Exchange Commission documented any, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Education Department supplied none. [cite:de18_gao_108192] No documented waiver of a security clearance for a named operator has been published.

Where they went

The team dispersed before the office ended. Davis left with Musk at the end of May 2025, and DOGE's spokeswoman, Katie Miller, reportedly went to work for Musk. [cite:de18_aol_davis] By November 2025, Reuters reported, the Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, who had worked with DOGE, led a new National Design Studio; Zachary Terrell had become chief technology officer at Health and Human Services; Rachel Riley led the Office of Naval Research; and Jeremy Lewin oversaw foreign assistance at the State Department. Gleason had become an adviser to the health secretary. [cite:de17_reuters_noexist] These are ordinary appointments, documented as such; whether DOGE's methods went with them is examined in [scene:de21_the_ending|Part Twenty-One].

The worst-case reading, tested

The worst-case version of this part is that unvetted loyalists with ties to Musk's companies were given the keys to federal systems. Documented: the ages and inexperience of several named staff; direct ties of employment, investment or board service to Musk's companies for most of those named; a Thiel Foundation fellowship and Palantir backgrounds for some; a staffer rehired after racist posts on an account linked to him, who breached Treasury's rules in handling payment data; and agencies unable to show Congress's auditor that DOGE staff had been vetted. [cite:de18_nbc_elez] [cite:de18_gao_108131] [cite:de18_gao_108192] Probable: that vetting fell below normal federal standards. Not supported: that any named operator acted for Musk's companies, that Thiel chose or directed staff, or that any operator acted from a reading of Yarvin or Land; no operator's own words to that effect are on record. Against the reading: Treasury's review found no payment data altered, the White House disputed the conflict account, and the legal head, Gleason, was a veteran of the same office. [cite:de18_bbg_elez] [cite:de18_pp_kliger] [cite:de17_ap_gleason] Who paid for the cuts these staff carried out is the subject of [scene:de20_the_cuts|Part Twenty].

chapters.label: Part Nineteen
chapters.title: Inside the Systems
chapters.intro: This part goes inside the federal computer systems DOGE was ordered to reach, and then into the courtrooms where that access was fought over. The first section takes each system in turn, the Treasury's payment systems, the personnel files at the Office of Personnel Management, Social Security's master file of numbers, the tax agency, the labour board and six more agencies, and keeps three kinds of record apart: what auditors, inspectors general and courts found; what whistleblowers alleged under their own names; and what was reported from unnamed sources. The second section follows the main lawsuits and is exact about what each court did and did not decide, including the Supreme Court's emergency orders of June 2025 and the records case it agreed to hear in full, before testing the book's worst-case reading against this part's material.
chapters.outro: The record of DOGE inside the systems is now largely written by auditors and judges rather than by its critics or its defenders. It shows a standing order of access to every agency's unclassified systems; one Treasury employee with copy access to three payment systems, briefly write access to one, and unencrypted payment data sent out of the bureau; Social Security data placed on an unapproved commercial service, with contents the agency cannot determine; personnel files disclosed in violation of the Privacy Act; and six agencies whose DOGE access the auditors could not even measure. [cite:de19_eo14158] [cite:de19_gao_treasury] [cite:de19_abc_hatch] [cite:de19_bgov_afge] [cite:de19_gao_sixagency] It shows, too, how the courts mostly ruled on whether harm was irreparable rather than on whether access was lawful; that the Supreme Court's June 2025 orders stayed an injunction and narrowed discovery without exempting DOGE from the records law; and that the full Court will decide that question in 2027. [cite:de19_crs_lsb11370] [cite:de19_scotus_crew] [cite:de19_ncc_cert] Allegations of data taken abroad or to private hands remain allegations. [cite:de19_krebs_nlrb] [cite:de19_npr_ssaoig] [scene:de20_the_cuts|Part Twenty] turns to the cuts themselves, the workforce figures, and who paid.

sections.h: The Access: What Was Reached, and What the Record Shows
sections.html:
The executive order that created DOGE on 20 January 2025 gave it a technical mission, "modernizing Federal technology and software," required a DOGE team of at least four employees in every agency, and told agency heads to "ensure USDS has full and prompt access to all unclassified agency records, software systems, and IT systems." [cite:de19_eo14158] The legal shape of that office is the subject of [scene:de17_what_doge_was_legally|Part Seventeen]; this section follows what its teams actually reached. Two months later, on 20 March 2025, a second order, "Stopping Waste, Fraud, and Abuse by Eliminating Information Silos" (Executive Order 14243), told agency heads to ensure that designated federal officials "have full and prompt access to all unclassified agency records, data, software systems, and information technology systems." [cite:de19_eo14243] That order does not mention DOGE by name. [cite:de19_eo14243] What follows separates three kinds of record: what auditors and courts found, what whistleblowers alleged under their own names, and what was reported from anonymous sources. They carry different weight, and the section says which is which at each step.

The first public conflict over access came within two weeks, and over classified material, which the order did not cover. On 1 February 2025, according to a former official who spoke to the Associated Press, DOGE members gained access to classified information at the Agency for International Development (USAID); the agency's two senior security officers, John Vorhees and Brian McGill, who had refused to hand over material in restricted areas because the team lacked the necessary clearances, were placed on leave. Musk responded on X: "USAID is a criminal organization. Time for it to die." [cite:de19_pbs_usaid] What became of USAID is the subject of [scene:de20_the_cuts|Part Twenty].

Treasury: the payment systems

The Bureau of the Fiscal Service in the Treasury runs the systems through which most federal payments flow. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's audit agency, reviewed the DOGE team's access there from 20 January to 11 April 2025 and published its findings on 28 April 2026. One DOGE employee had access to three payment systems from January to February 2025 and could view, copy and print their data. He was also "inadvertently granted temporary access to create, modify, and delete data" in one of them; GAO found no evidence that any data was changed. [cite:de19_gao_treasury] He sent payment information to another agency's DOGE team without encryption or approval, and the bureau's security tools did not stop it. [cite:de19_gao_treasury] A letter from Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden on 21 July 2026, summarising the GAO report, said the payments concerned foreign aid and could have exposed the personal details of more than 350 people, and that a second DOGE employee had "over the shoulder access" to bureau data that the bureau could not later list. [cite:de19_ww_letter]

GAO found that the bureau had fully implemented only five of fourteen selected controls. It had not made sure the employee agreed to its security rules before he received a laptop, and it had not set its tools to catch unencrypted payment data leaving the bureau. GAO made six recommendations; the bureau agreed with three. [cite:de19_gao_treasury] The Treasury's own inspector general reached a milder overall verdict in report OIG-26-032, dated 8 June 2026: the payment systems' controls were "generally adequate," with weaknesses, and nine significant recommendations, including signed rules of behaviour before access and better controls on personal data sent outside the department. [cite:de19_oig_treasury] [cite:de19_ww_letter] The employee is named, with his resignation and rehiring, in [scene:de18_the_team|Part Eighteen].

The Office of Personnel Management: the personnel files

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) holds the records of the federal workforce. On 20 October 2026 Judge Denise Cote of the federal court in Manhattan ruled in AFGE v. OPM that OPM had violated the Privacy Act, the 1974 law that limits how agencies disclose records about individuals, by giving its DOGE team access to sensitive personal information, and that the unions had won their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act. She wrote that the government "barely defend[s] its legality." [cite:de19_bgov_afge] She also recorded that DOGE had been dissolved, that one of its agents remained at OPM, and that no DOGE agent had accessed sensitive OPM data since September 2025, which left the remedy undecided. [cite:de19_bgov_afge] This is the clearest merits finding of unlawful access in the record as of October 2026.

Social Security: the master file of numbers

The Social Security Administration (SSA) keeps the Numerical Identification System, NUMIDENT, the master record of every Social Security number issued, with names, birthplaces and parents' names. Charles Borges, the agency's chief data officer, filed a whistleblower complaint in August 2025 alleging that DOGE staff had in June copied NUMIDENT, covering more than 300 million people, to a cloud environment that only DOGE could reach, "without any independent security or oversight mechanisms in place." [cite:de19_nbc_borges] His complaint quoted a memo of 15 July 2025 in which the agency's chief information officer, Aram Moghaddassi, wrote that "the business need is higher than the security risk," and an internal assessment that warned of a "catastrophic impact" if the copy were breached. The agency answered that the data was "walled off from the internet" and that it was "not aware of any compromise." [cite:de19_nbc_borges]

The government's own filing then moved part of the story from allegation to admission. In a Notice of Corrections filed on 16 January 2026 in the union suit over SSA data, the Justice Department disclosed that DOGE team members had used Cloudflare, a commercial service, to share agency data; that "Cloudflare is not approved for storing SSA data"; and that the agency "has not been able to determine exactly what data were shared." [cite:de19_abc_hatch] [cite:de19_ch_afscme] It disclosed that an unnamed political advocacy group had contacted two DOGE team members in March 2025, seeking "to find evidence of voter fraud and to overturn election results in certain States," and that one of them signed an agreement that may have involved using Social Security data to match state voter rolls. The filing does not say any data was shared. The agency referred the two employees to the Office of Special Counsel for possible violations of the Hatch Act, which limits political activity by federal staff, and the filing corrected earlier sworn statements the government had made in court. [cite:de19_abc_hatch]

A further allegation remains open. On 6 March 2026 the agency's inspector general told Congress it was reviewing an anonymous complaint about "potential misuse of SSA data by a former DOGE employee"; press reports described alleged copies of NUMIDENT and the Death Master File and a thumb drive. The agency said the claims had been "strongly refuted by all named parties," and no findings have been issued. [cite:de19_npr_ssaoig]

The Internal Revenue Service, and the labour board

At the Internal Revenue Service, Wired reported in April 2025 that two DOGE staffers, Gavin Kliger and Sam Corcos, were organising a hackathon to build "one new API to rule them all," a single interface over taxpayer names, addresses, Social Security numbers and returns, with Palantir "consistently" named as a candidate vendor. [cite:de19_tc_irsapi] No final contract for that system has been documented. The separate agreement under which the IRS gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement the addresses of about 47,000 people was signed by the Treasury and Homeland Security, not by DOGE, and a federal judge later found about 42,695 of the disclosures unlawful; [scene:ad13_immigrants_latinos|The American Dream] sets out that record. [cite:us10_abc_irs_feb] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep]

At the National Labor Relations Board, Daniel Berulis, a security architect, wrote to the Senate Intelligence Committee on 14 April 2025 that DOGE staff had been given powerful administrator accounts exempt from logging from 3 March, that about 10 gigabytes left the case-management system early on 4 March, and that more than twenty login attempts from a Russian address using valid DOGE credentials were blocked. [cite:de19_krebs_nlrb] The board said DOGE "neither requested nor received access" and that "no breach of agency systems occurred." [cite:de19_krebs_nlrb] GAO later found no evidence that two DOGE detailees used the board's systems between 16 April and 25 July 2025, but it deliberately did not examine March, which is with the board's inspector general, whose investigation remains open. [cite:de19_gao_nlrb] The March allegation is therefore neither confirmed nor refuted.

Six more agencies, and the AI tools

On 29 September 2026 GAO reported on six more agencies. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Education, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Securities and Exchange Commission said their DOGE teams had access to more than 23 systems, but the extent "could not be determined." The Small Business Administration and Veterans Affairs did not list the systems at all. Only the SEC documented background investigations; none of the agencies let GAO observe their activity logs; and NOAA and the SEC questioned GAO's authority. GAO concluded that "Congress and the public lack assurance" that the systems and data were protected. The consumer bureau disputed the report. [cite:de19_gao_sixagency]

Reuters reported on 23 May 2025, from three unnamed sources, that DOGE was expanding the use of a customised version of Grok, the chatbot of Musk's company xAI, to analyse federal data, and two of them said DOGE staff had told Homeland Security officials to use it though it was not approved there. Reuters could not establish what data went in. The department denied that DOGE had pushed any tool. [cite:de19_reuters_grok] An ethics lawyer, Richard Painter, said that if Musk was directly involved in the decision it could breach the criminal conflict-of-interest law. [cite:de19_reuters_grok] That is a conditional; no finding of Musk's involvement exists. The documented use of an AI tool by DOGE staff is another one, at the National Endowment for the Humanities, where sworn testimony shows ChatGPT used to sort grants for cancellation; [scene:de20_the_cuts|Part Twenty] gives it.

The "master database"

A widely repeated claim holds that DOGE built, or had Palantir build, a single database joining tax, Social Security and immigration records. Reporting in 2025 described plans and Palantir's expanding federal work; Palantir answered that it "is not a vendor on any master database project to unify databases across federal agencies" and "has no contracts with DOGE." [cite:de19_palantir_record] What is documented is narrower and, in its way, more concrete: specific transfers between specific agencies under specific agreements, from tax addresses to ICE to Social Security data run through the citizenship-check system described in [scene:de19_the_courts|the next section]. Whether these add up to one integrated system is not established; the company's contracts are mapped in [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty].

sections.h: The Courts: What Was Decided, and What Was Not
sections.html:
DOGE was sued from its first weeks, by unions, retirees' groups, states, former USAID staff and a government-ethics group. There is no authoritative count of the suits. An early tally by NewsNation, on 20 March 2025, put "nearly a fifth" of the 132 cases then filed against the administration as related to Musk and DOGE. [cite:de19_nn_count] The Congressional Research Service, the research arm of Congress, counted ten pending suits under the Privacy Act alone on 17 September 2025, covering the Treasury, Labor, the consumer bureau, Education, OPM, the IRS and Social Security. [cite:de19_crs_lsb11370] Those ten are the only count from an official source; suits over appointments, records, layoffs and grants come on top. This section follows the cases that decided the most, and is exact about what each court decided, because the most common error in public accounts of these cases is to read an emergency order as a verdict.

The data suits and the gate of "irreparable harm"

To stop an action before trial, a plaintiff must show a likely win on the merits and also "irreparable harm," an injury that money or a later order could not repair. Most of the DOGE data suits turned on that second test. In Alliance for Retired Americans v. Bessent (the Treasury payment systems), AFL-CIO v. Department of Labor and EPIC v. OPM, judges refused preliminary injunctions because irreparable harm was not shown; in AFGE v. OPM the Manhattan court granted one; in a suit by teachers over Education and Treasury data, the appeals court for the Fourth Circuit vacated an injunction on 12 August 2025. [cite:de19_crs_lsb11370] A public account sometimes calls the Treasury case "AFL-CIO v. Treasury"; the labour federation's case was against the Labor Department, and the Treasury case was brought by a retirees' group.

The fullest arc is AFSCME v. SSA, brought on 21 February 2025 by two unions and the Alliance for Retired Americans. Judge Ellen Lipton Hollander in Maryland barred DOGE's access to Social Security systems holding personal data on 20 March and on 17 April issued a preliminary injunction ordering DOGE to delete non-anonymised personal data it held. [cite:de19_ch_afscme] On 6 June 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that injunction while the appeal went on. The stay decided nothing about whether the access was lawful; Justice Kagan noted her disagreement, and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, joined by Justice Sonia Sotomayor, dissented on the ground that the government had shown no irreparable harm to itself. [cite:de19_ch_afscme] [cite:de19_crs_lsb11370]

On 10 April 2026 the full Fourth Circuit, writing through Judge Toby Heytens, held by nine votes that the plaintiffs were likely to have standing, because handing their personal data to DOGE resembled the old wrong of intrusion upon seclusion, and then, in a part joined by only two other judges, vacated the injunction because irreparable harm had not been shown on the record the district judge had. [cite:de19_ca4_afscme] That part described "the even more recent—and even more alarming—allegations" the plaintiffs had raised in March, while ruling that they were not before the appeals court. [cite:de19_ca4_afscme] Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson, concurring, added that "the whistleblower report has not yet been substantiated." [cite:de19_ca4_afscme] Six judges, led by Judge Robert King, dissented, arguing that what the government's own corrections had disclosed was much worse than what the district court had seen. [cite:de19_ca4_afscme] Back in Maryland, on 26 June 2026 Judge Hollander allowed discovery into DOGE's handling of the data, citing the government's misstatements and its noncompliance with earlier orders; the case was in discovery as of the latest docket summary. [cite:de19_ch_afscme]

The one merits ruling on unlawful access came on 20 October 2026, when Judge Denise Cote held that OPM violated the Privacy Act by giving its DOGE team personnel data. [cite:de19_bgov_afge] The other direction is also on the record. In New York v. Trump, brought by nineteen states over the Treasury payment systems, Judge Jeannette Vargas had limited DOGE's access in February 2025 and later allowed vetted staff in; on 23 September 2026 she dismissed the access claims as moot because Treasury's DOGE team no longer existed, and dismissed the claims over an automated payment-review system because the states had not shown that any payment owed to them was frozen. [cite:de19_or_nyvtrump] [cite:de19_fox_vargas]

Records: what the Supreme Court did, and did not, decide

A widely repeated line says the Supreme Court exempted DOGE from the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), the law that opens agency records to the public. It did not. Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) asked for DOGE's records days after the January order and sued when refused; Judge Christopher Cooper found the U.S. DOGE Service "likely an agency subject to FOIA" and allowed CREW limited discovery to test that. [cite:de19_ncc_cert] On 6 June 2025 the Supreme Court stayed the discovery orders and sent the case back, holding that the parts requiring disclosure of the content of DOGE's recommendations inside the executive "are not appropriately tailored," and that "separation of powers concerns counsel judicial deference and restraint." [cite:de19_scotus_crew] On whether FOIA applies, the order said only that the test "cannot turn on the entity's ability to persuade"; Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson would have refused the government's application. [cite:de19_scotus_crew] In October 2026 the Court agreed to hear the case in full (No. 25-1103), on whether the office "wields independent authority or is merely a board that exists to advise the president," with argument expected early in 2027. [cite:de19_ncc_cert] The question is open as of October 2026.

Appointments: who was in charge

The Constitution's Appointments Clause requires officers who wield significant federal authority to be appointed by the president with the Senate's consent or under a law Congress passes. In Does 1–26 v. Musk, former USAID staff argued that Musk exercised such authority without either. The White House had told another court that Musk was a senior adviser with no authority of his own. [cite:de11_audit_fisher] On 18 March 2025 Judge Theodore Chuang wrote that if an adviser were "actually exercising significant authority on governmental matters," treating the clause as satisfied would reduce it to "a technical formality," and that the decision to shut USAID had "usurped the authority of the public's elected representatives in Congress." [cite:de19_upi_chuang] He ordered systems access restored. The Fourth Circuit stayed his order on 28 March 2025; the case went on, a class was certified in August 2025, and on 4 March 2026 the appeals court blocked the depositions of senior officials, Musk among them. The case was in discovery as of September 2026. [cite:de19_ch_does]

Where the data went next: tax addresses and citizenship checks

Two later fights concern uses of the data rather than DOGE's access to it. The IRS's disclosure of taxpayer addresses to ICE was stayed in November 2025 and the stay upheld on appeal on 8 September 2026. [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:ad13_audit_irs_dcir] The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) programme, which Homeland Security, its immigration service and DOGE announced they were overhauling on 22 April 2025, was linked for the first time to Social Security records and opened to bulk checks of whole voter rolls. [cite:de19_dhs_save] [cite:de19_npr_save] The government says it checked more than 65 million voters in 26 states and flagged 28,635; in Texas about a fifth of those flagged were later found to be citizens. [cite:de19_npr_save] In June 2026 Judge Sparkle Sooknanan held that the system broke the Social Security Act and the Privacy Act; on 25 September 2026 the Supreme Court stayed her order, relying on a 1996 immigration statute, over a dissent by the three liberal justices. [cite:de19_npr_save]

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis this book tests holds that government cuts were the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto the destination. On this part's material, the following is documented. DOGE teams were given a standing order of access to unclassified systems across the government; at Treasury, OPM, Social Security and six other agencies auditors and courts found controls bypassed, vetting unverifiable or access unlawful; Social Security data left the agency's approved systems for a commercial service, with the contents still unknown; and data held for benefits and taxes was put to immigration and voter-roll checks. [cite:de19_eo14158] [cite:de19_gao_treasury] [cite:de19_gao_sixagency] [cite:de19_abc_hatch] [cite:de19_bgov_afge] [cite:de19_npr_save] Documented, too, is the government's correction of its own sworn statements in court. [cite:de19_ch_afscme]

Probable, on this record, is that the speed of the access outran the safeguards the law requires, which is what the auditors' language says in plainer words. Not supported: that data was taken out to foreign hands or to Musk's companies, a claim that rests on allegations the agencies deny and inquiries still open; that a single "master database" was built; and that anyone used the voter-roll agreement to move data. [cite:de19_krebs_nlrb] [cite:de19_palantir_record] [cite:de19_abc_hatch] The record also runs against the reading in two ways. The courts did not give the executive a free hand: judges found access unlawful, ordered discovery after misstatements, and the Supreme Court took the records question for full review rather than closing it. [cite:de19_bgov_afge] [cite:de19_ch_afscme] [cite:de19_ncc_cert] And no document links this access to the Dark Enlightenment texts; the resemblance to Yarvin's program in [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six] is rhyme, not provenance, as [scene:de1_spine_and_overlay|Part One] defines the terms. [scene:de20_the_cuts|Part Twenty] turns from the systems to the cuts, and to who paid for them.

chapters.label: Part Twenty
chapters.title: The Cuts and Who Paid
chapters.intro: This part sets out what DOGE and the agencies cut in 2025 and 2026, and who bore the cost. The first section goes agency by agency, from the closing of USAID and the probationary firings to the layoffs at Education, Health and Human Services and the consumer bureau, the plans that were reversed at Veterans Affairs and the Weather Service, and grants sorted for cancellation with a chatbot; it follows the court rulings that let most of the cuts proceed, and reads the three common workforce figures each on its own definition, never added together. The second section weighs the cost: the death estimates for aid cut abroad, each with its method and its critics; service at home as the agencies and their auditors measured it; the workers and contractors who lost jobs; and what the cuts saved, ending with a money trail and a test of the book's worst-case reading.
chapters.outro: The cuts were real and large: USAID's programmes cut by 83 per cent and the agency closed as an implementer of aid; about 25,000 probationary employees dismissed by a direction a judge later held unlawful; layoffs allowed by Supreme Court stays that left their legality undecided; and a federal workforce about 256,000 smaller on GAO's net measure, or about 317,000 departures on OPM's gross count. [cite:de20_ewn_rubio83] [cite:de20_reuters_alsup] [cite:de20_npr_trumpvafge] [cite:de19_gao_workforce] [cite:us2_bloomberg_317k] Their cost abroad is projected by models whose estimates run from about half a million deaths in a year to more than 14 million by 2030 and are disputed on method; their cost at home is measured in waits and lost staff that the agencies and their auditors count differently. [cite:de20_cgd_update] [cite:de20_ucla_lancet] [cite:de20_reason_brown] [cite:de20_fnn_ssa] What they saved is in doubt: most claimed savings could not be verified, and a DOGE staffer testified that the deficit was not reduced. [cite:de20_gao_receipts] [cite:de20_abc_depos] Several cuts were reversed, and the courts kept one agency's layoffs on hold. [cite:de20_bl_va] [cite:de20_ab_cfpb] [scene:de21_the_dividend|Part Twenty-One] turns to the promises made for the cuts, the conflicts of interest around them, and how the office ended.

sections.h: The Cuts: Agencies, Firings and the Size of the Workforce
sections.html:
Musk stated the aim in public before the office existed and repeated it after. At Madison Square Garden on 27 October 2024 he said, "I think we can do at least $2 trillion" in cuts; on 13 February 2025 he told the World Governments Summit, "I think we do need to delete entire agencies," because "if we don't remove the roots of the weed, then it's easy for the weed to grow back." [cite:de11_fortune_2t] [cite:de11_cbs_wgs] This section sets out what was actually cut, agency by agency, how the courts handled the main firing programmes, and what the workforce figures show when each is read on its own definition. Who bore the cost is the subject of [scene:de20_who_paid|the next section]; whether the savings were real is graded in [scene:de11_claims_vs_record|Part Eleven] and [scene:de21_the_ending|Part Twenty-One].

USAID: an agency closed

The Agency for International Development (USAID), which ran most American foreign aid, was the first and largest target. Musk called it "a criminal organization" on 2 February 2025, as two of its security chiefs were put on leave for refusing his team classified material. [cite:de19_pbs_usaid] On 10 March Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote, "After a 6 week review we are officially cancelling 83% of the programs at USAID": about 5,200 contracts ended, and the remaining 1,000 or so programmes were to be run by the State Department. He thanked DOGE. [cite:de20_ewn_rubio83] He then announced that "as of July 1st, USAID will officially cease to implement foreign assistance." [cite:de20_ap_usaidjuly] A federal judge found in March 2025 that the shutdown had likely "usurped the authority" of Congress, which created and funded the agency, but his order was stayed within ten days; [scene:de19_the_courts|Part Nineteen] follows that case. [cite:de19_upi_chuang] [cite:de19_ch_does] USAID did not supply data for the government auditors' workforce count, so its staff losses are not in the official totals below. [cite:de19_gao_workforce]

Probationary firings

Probationary employees, usually those in their first year in a job, have fewer protections against dismissal. On 14 February 2025 OPM emailed agency personnel chiefs asking them to separate probationary staff not identified as mission-critical. [cite:de20_crs_probation] About 25,000 people were targeted. [cite:de20_reuters_alsup] Judge William Alsup in San Francisco found on 13 March 2025 that OPM's direction was beyond its legal authority and ordered reinstatements at six agencies; a Maryland judge separately ordered reinstatements at eighteen agencies for nineteen states and Washington, D.C. [cite:de20_crs_probation] Both orders were stayed within days. On 8 April 2025 the Supreme Court stayed Alsup's order because the nonprofit plaintiffs it rested on had not shown standing, without deciding whether the firings were lawful, over the dissents of Justices Sotomayor and Jackson; the next day the Fourth Circuit stayed the Maryland order. [cite:de20_crs_probation] On 12 September 2025 Alsup ruled on the merits that OPM had unlawfully ordered the firings, but he did not order reinstatement, citing the Supreme Court's emergency rulings and the fact that many of those fired had found other work; he ordered nineteen agencies to correct their personnel files instead. [cite:de20_reuters_alsup] The firings were found unlawful and stood.

Reductions in force, and the agencies that reversed

A reduction in force (RIF) is the formal procedure for laying off permanent federal staff. A February 2025 executive order told agencies to prepare "large-scale" RIFs. Judge Susan Illston blocked the plans; on 8 July 2025 the Supreme Court lifted her order, adding that "we express no view on the legality of any" particular plan. Justice Jackson dissented, calling the decision "hubristic and senseless." [cite:de20_npr_trumpvafge] On 14 July the Court likewise allowed the layoff of more than 1,000 Education Department staff; Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, wrote that it "hands the Executive the power to repeal statutes by firing all those necessary to carry them out," and Secretary Linda McMahon called the president "the ultimate authority to make decisions about staffing levels." [cite:de20_rollcall_mcmahon] By January 2026 Education's workforce had fallen by more than 45 per cent, the steepest decline of any large agency. [cite:de19_gao_workforce]

The Health and Human Services department eliminated about 10,000 posts, including 3,500 at the Food and Drug Administration, 2,400 at the Centers for Disease Control and 1,200 at the National Institutes of Health, with total departures of up to 20,000 by its own figures; Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. later said upwards of 2,000 people had been "cut by mistake," and hundreds were rehired. [cite:de20_biospace_hhs] Veterans Affairs announced in 2025 a cut of more than 80,000 and then, on 7 July 2025, dropped it: "A department-wide RIF is off the table," Secretary Doug Collins said, and about 30,000 positions were to go through attrition and voluntary departures instead. [cite:de20_bl_va] The National Weather Service lost more than 550 staff, mostly through probationary firings and early retirements, and in August 2025 was given permission to hire 450 meteorologists, hydrologists and technicians back. [cite:de20_cnn_nws]

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the regulator for lenders and payment firms, is the case that did not resolve. Its acting leadership planned to cut staff from about 1,175 to 556; a court injunction obtained by the employees' union blocked the layoffs, and on 19 June 2026 the full appeals court in Washington refused to lift it and sent the revised plan back to the trial judge. [cite:de20_orrick_cfpb] [cite:de20_ab_cfpb] In July 2026 the parties agreed, and Judge Amy Berman Jackson ordered, that nothing would move until 60 days after a new director, Brian Johnson, is confirmed, or until 3 January 2027. [cite:de20_ab_cfpb] The Senate Banking Committee advanced his nomination 13 to 11 on 17 September 2026, with no floor vote scheduled when last reported. [cite:de20_cfm_johnson] Status as of October 2026: the injunction stands, and the bureau's 2026 budget was capped at $446.8 million, against $785.4 million in 2024. [cite:de20_ab_cfpb]

Grants sorted by a chatbot

At the National Endowment for the Humanities, two DOGE staffers with no prior government experience, Justin Fox and Nate Cavanaugh, used ChatGPT to flag more than $100 million in grants as related to diversity, equity and inclusion; the grants were then cancelled. Their prompt, quoted in court filings, began: "From the perspective of someone looking to identify DEI grants, does this involve DEI?" [cite:de20_abc_depos] Asked under oath why a documentary about Holocaust survivors had been flagged, Fox answered, "It's a gender-based story that's inherently discriminatory to focus on this specific group." [cite:de20_abc_depos] The deposition is sworn testimony in a pending civil suit; it shows how the list was made, not a court finding about the cancellations.

The size of the workforce: three measures

Three figures for the shrinking federal workforce are widely quoted, and they measure different things. GAO, using data from 22 major agencies, counted about 378,000 separations during 2025 and about 127,000 hires, including temporary staff, for a net decline of nearly 256,000, more than 11 per cent, between December 2024 and January 2026; losses ranged from about 1 per cent at Homeland Security to more than 45 per cent at Education. [cite:de19_gao_workforce] OPM's director, Scott Kupor, counted about 317,000 employees who left during 2025, a gross figure of departures: some 144,000 deferred resignations, about 17,000 layoffs, about 7,000 probationary dismissals, about 21,000 early retirements and buyouts, and about 129,000 ordinary attrition. [cite:us2_bloomberg_317k] Reuters, measuring from September 2024 to January 2026, reported a 12 per cent fall. [cite:us2_reuters_workforce] A figure of about 386,800 also circulates, sometimes attributed to GAO; it is the headcount behind Reuters' 12 per cent fall over September 2024 to January 2026, a net measure over a longer period, and not GAO's count of separations, which is about 378,000. [cite:de20_audit_reuters_386k] [cite:de19_gao_workforce] One press account of the GAO report added that 83 per cent of those who left did so voluntarily and that about 129,000 left through the deferred-resignation offer known as the "Fork in the Road"; GAO's own summary does not state those figures, and the 129,000 is not the same count as OPM's 144,000 deferred resignations. [cite:de20_cs_256k] [cite:us2_bloomberg_317k]

None of these figures can be added to another. The net figure is the honest answer to how much smaller the government became; the gross figures describe how people left. The cuts were also uneven by design or by result: Education lost almost half its staff while Homeland Security, where immigration enforcement sits, was nearly flat. [cite:de19_gao_workforce] That contrast matters to the worst-case reading this book tests, and [scene:de20_who_paid|the next section] takes it up with the question of who bore the cost.

sections.h: Who Paid: Lives Abroad, Services at Home, and the Ledger
sections.html:
The cost of the cuts fell on three groups: people abroad who had relied on American aid, people at home who use the agencies that shrank, and the workers and contractors who lost their jobs. The evidence is of very different kinds for each. Deaths abroad are, so far, the output of models, not counts. Service at home is measured by agency statistics that the agencies themselves and their critics read differently. Lost jobs are counted, though on more than one definition, as [scene:de20_the_cuts|the previous section] explained. This section keeps each kind of evidence in its own register and does not infer harm from a cut alone.

The USAID estimates: what each study did

The most quoted figure comes from a study in The Lancet, published on 1 July 2025 by Daniella Cavalcanti, Davide Rasella, James Macinko and colleagues from Brazil, Spain, the United States and Mozambique. They compared mortality in 133 low- and middle-income countries from 2001 to 2021 with the amount of USAID support each received, controlling for income, education, population and health systems, and found the aid associated with about 91 million deaths averted, a 15 per cent lower all-cause death rate and a 32 per cent lower death rate among children under five. Then they ran a simulation to 2030: if the 83 per cent cut held, they projected more than 14 million additional deaths, including more than 4.5 million children under five. [cite:de20_ucla_lancet] Those are projected deaths from a statistical model, not deaths observed or counted.

Three other estimates use different methods. The Center for Global Development's Charles Kenny and Justin Sandefur multiplied average costs per life saved, about $3,457 for health aid and $17,837 for humanitarian and food aid, by the dollars actually cut, and arrived at roughly 500,000 to 1 million lives lost on 2025 spending, or 670,000 to 1.6 million on commitments; they wrote that without direct monitoring data "any estimates of lives lost remain guesswork," and that their figures might be pessimistic because some lifesaving aid was protected. [cite:de20_cgd_update] A second Lancet paper, published on 3 February 2026 by a team including Rasella, modelled cuts by all donors, not only the United States, and projected 9.4 million additional deaths by 2030 in its baseline and 22.6 million in a severe scenario. [cite:de20_st_lancet26] A live model run at Boston University by Brooke Nichols showed 781,343 projected deaths for one year as of 30 July 2026. [cite:de20_reason_brown]

The studies are disputed on method. Aaron Brown, a statistician at New York University, called the 14 million figure "patently absurd," arguing that a design comparing trends over time would credit almost anything that grew while death rates fell. [cite:de20_fix_brown] Writing in Reason in August 2026, he set the first study's 91 million averted deaths against his own estimate of about 79 million for the entire global decline in deaths over the period, noted that the two Lancet papers cannot both be right about the size of USAID's effect, and cited one early check against observed data: in Egypt in May 2025 the United Nations recorded 46,365 deaths, against about 58,000 implied by the model, a single data point that he said proved little either way. [cite:de20_reason_brown] Nichols, defending the first paper, called its look backward "quite robust" while agreeing that its projections "carry greater uncertainty." [cite:de20_fix_brown] The State Department's response was through an unnamed official, who said the studies rested on "incorrect assumptions," and later through a statement that "some recent 'studies' are rooted in outdated thinking." [cite:de20_ap_usaidjuly] [cite:de20_st_lancet26] Full mortality data for the poorest countries will take years to arrive. [cite:de20_reason_brown]

Services at home

Social Security is the clearest case of a service measured two ways. In July 2025 the Washington Post reported that monthly calls to the agency had risen from about 6.6 million to 8.6 million, that average hold times had grown from 75 to 93 minutes, that the agency had stopped publishing its wait-time figures, and that it was moving about 1,000 field-office staff to the phones; some forty of its roughly 1,200 field offices had lost at least a quarter of their staff, and the agency was cutting 7,000 jobs to reach 50,000. [cite:de20_wapo_ssa] In June 2026 Commissioner Frank Bisignano told Congress that phone hold times had fallen 89 per cent, from 42 minutes to under five, and field-office waits by 30 per cent, with more than 2,000 staff reassigned to the phones. [cite:de20_fnn_ssa] The agency's inspector general had found that in fiscal 2025 callers who took a call-back waited more than 100 minutes on average to reach an agent, and about 15 minutes excluding call-backs; the methods behind the commissioner's figures and the inspector general's are not the same and cannot be compared directly. [cite:de20_fnn_ssa] Staff and union witnesses said the phone gains came at the expense of claims work and training. [cite:de20_fnn_ssa]

At the IRS the Treasury's tax inspector general counted 25,386 separations and 294 layoff notices by May 2025, about a quarter of the workforce, including about 26 per cent of revenue agents, the staff who audit returns; the National Taxpayer Advocate warned that a filing season needs "a sufficient number of trained employees." [cite:de20_tigta_irs] The National Weather Service, down more than 550 staff, was operating with fewer weather-balloon launches, and vacancies at Texas forecast offices drew scrutiny after the July 2025 floods; it was then allowed to rehire 450. [cite:de20_cnn_nws] Scrutiny is not a finding, and no official review cited here attributes any forecast failure to the vacancies. At Veterans Affairs the planned 80,000 layoffs were dropped. [cite:de20_bl_va] At the consumer bureau, an injunction has kept most staff in place while its budget was cut nearly in half. [cite:de20_ab_cfpb]

Workers and contractors

The workers who paid are counted in the previous section: about 25,000 probationary employees whose dismissal a judge later found unlawful but did not reverse, and a net federal workforce about 256,000 smaller. [cite:de20_reuters_alsup] [cite:de19_gao_workforce] Contractors paid too, though the record is thinner. Booz Allen Hamilton, one of the largest government consultancies, announced on 23 May 2025 that it would cut about 2,500 jobs, 7 per cent of its staff, mostly in its civilian business, citing the push to cut civilian contract spending and slower procurement. [cite:de20_ng_booz] At the same time, many claimed cancellations were not what they seemed. GAO found that only 43.2 per cent of DOGE's claimed contract savings were tied to contracts actually terminated in whole or part, that 2,503 contracts listed as cut, worth $27.4 billion in claimed savings, showed no termination at all, and that the method behind about 96 per cent of claimed grant savings could not be verified. [cite:de20_gao_receipts] One early entry, a $1 billion Social Security contract with the firm Leidos, turned out to be a single $560,000 task order to redesign a form. [cite:de20_ge_contracting]

What the cuts bought

Asked under oath whether DOGE had reduced the deficit, Nate Cavanaugh answered, "No, we didn't." [cite:de20_abc_depos] Chris Edwards of the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank that favours smaller government, estimated that the workforce reductions save about $41 billion a year, just over 2 per cent of the deficit, and said, "They reduced the workforce, but that really hardly affected the deficit." [cite:de20_cs_256k] DOGE's own website claimed about $110 billion in contract, grant and lease savings by July 2026, a figure GAO could not verify for most of its parts; the office did not respond to the auditors. [cite:de20_gao_receipts] The full claims ledger is in [scene:de21_the_ending|Part Twenty-One].

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis this book tests treats government cuts as the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. On this part's material, the following is documented. An agency created and funded by Congress was dismantled by executive action, and a judge found it likely that this usurped Congress's authority, though the finding was stayed. [cite:de20_ewn_rubio83] [cite:de19_upi_chuang] Firings a court later held unlawful were allowed to stand, and layoffs went ahead under Supreme Court stays that expressly left their legality undecided, in what one justice called the power "to repeal statutes by firing all those necessary to carry them out." [cite:de20_reuters_alsup] [cite:de20_npr_trumpvafge] [cite:de20_rollcall_mcmahon] The cuts were uneven, with Education nearly halved and Homeland Security nearly untouched, and, on a DOGE staffer's own sworn answer and a libertarian economist's estimate, their stated fiscal purpose of cutting the deficit was not met. [cite:de19_gao_workforce] [cite:de20_abc_depos] [cite:de20_cs_256k]

Probable is that the cuts moved capacity away from regulatory, aid and service agencies and left enforcement intact; that is a pattern in the numbers, not a stated plan. The intent behind it is contested: Musk's own words are on record for USAID ("Time for it to die") and for the need to "delete entire agencies," while the administration's stated aim was efficiency. [cite:de11_cbs_wgs] [cite:de19_pbs_usaid] Not supported: that the deaths projected abroad are counted deaths, or that any study's single figure is settled; and that the cuts were aimed at a sovereign executive as the Dark Enlightenment texts describe one, for which no document exists. The record also runs against the reading. Several cuts were reversed, at Veterans Affairs, the Weather Service and Health and Human Services, often after public pressure; the consumer bureau's layoffs remained blocked by the courts as of October 2026; and the auditors, inspectors general and judges who documented all this kept working. [cite:de20_bl_va] [cite:de20_cnn_nws] [cite:de20_biospace_hhs] [cite:de20_ab_cfpb] The resemblance to Yarvin's RAGE, "Retire All Government Employees," described in [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six], is rhyme, not provenance. [cite:de6_tnr_duran] [scene:de21_the_dividend|Part Twenty-One] turns to the promises made for the cuts, the conflicts around them, and how the office ended.

chapters.label: Part Twenty-One
chapters.title: Promises, Conflicts and the Ending
chapters.intro: This part closes Book Three. It follows three things that the cuts left behind. The first is a promise: the "DOGE dividend," a cheque of about $5,000 per household that an investor proposed, Elon Musk passed to the president and the president said he loved, and what became of it once the savings it depended on were audited. The second is the conflict at the centre of the office: a man whose companies the government regulated, investigated and paid, serving inside that government, and what happened, matter by matter, to the cases and contracts involving those companies during his service and after it. The third is the ending: Musk's departure and his break with Trump, the fading of DOGE's central office, its legal termination on 4 July 2026, what persisted inside the state, and a ledger of DOGE's public claims against the record. The last section tests the book's worst-case reading against Book Three as a whole.
chapters.outro: The record of DOGE's last chapter is a record of claims that did not survive checking and of a structure that outlived its name. The dividend was endorsed by the president and never legislated or paid, and the savings it rested on were, on the auditor's account, mostly unverifiable: GAO could confirm DOGE's own method for barely a quarter of its contract savings and could not check 96 per cent of its grant savings. [cite:de21_reuters_dividend] [cite:de21_gao_full] Musk's companies saw a suit dropped, a securities case settled for a fraction of what was first sought and labour cases halted by a court, while a safety regulator opened a larger Tesla investigation after he left and no document shows him steering a contract or a case. [cite:de21_axios_doj] [cite:de21_bberg_sec] [cite:de21_franczek_nlrb] [cite:de21_ap_nhtsa] The temporary organization ended on 4 July 2026 without a closing report; its service, its alumni, a smaller workforce and a new civil-service schedule remain. [cite:de21_fnn_vought] [cite:de21_ee_end] [cite:de21_gao_workforce] [cite:us2_opm_schedpc] On Book Three as a whole, the occasion in the worst-case reading is documented and the destination is not. Book Four turns from the state to the attempts to leave it, beginning with charter cities and sea colonies in [scene:de22_seas_and_zones|Part Twenty-Two].

sections.h: The Dividend That Was Never Paid
sections.html:
For a few weeks in February 2025 the government cuts came with an offer attached. If the Department of Government Efficiency found the savings it promised, part of the money would come back to taxpayers as a cheque. The idea, called the "DOGE dividend," was proposed by an investor, endorsed by Elon Musk within a day and by President Trump within two, and polled well. It was never legislated and never paid. This section sets out where the idea came from, the arithmetic it rested on, what happened to it, and what its fate does and does not show. It is a small episode, but it is the clearest case in Book Three of a public promise that can be checked against a calendar and a ledger.

The proposal

The proposal came from James Fishback, chief executive of an investment firm, Azoria Partners. On 18 February 2025 he posted a four-page memo on X proposing that 20 per cent of whatever DOGE saved be returned to taxpayers. Taking the $2 trillion figure Musk had used during the campaign, he put that share at $400 billion, enough for a cheque of about $5,000 to every tax-paying household, to be sent after DOGE's scheduled end in July 2026; the rest of the savings would go to paying down the national debt. [cite:de21_reuters_dividend] [cite:de21_usat_dividend] The household count he used was about 78 million. [cite:de21_usat_dividend] Musk replied the same day: "Will check with the President." [cite:de21_reuters_dividend]

The next day, 19 February, Trump spoke in Miami at an investment conference hosted by Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund. He said a "new concept" was "under consideration," under which 20 per cent of DOGE savings would go to American citizens and 20 per cent to paying down the debt. [cite:de21_reuters_dividend] Asked about it aboard Air Force One, he said: "I love it." [cite:de21_ap_dividend] He also presented the cheque as a reason for citizens to report waste themselves: "They participate in the process of saving us money." [cite:de21_ap_dividend] Reuters reported that Fishback was in contact with the administration about the plan. [cite:de21_reuters_dividend]

The idea was popular. A poll of 1,001 registered voters taken on 24 and 25 February 2025 found two-thirds in favour of $5,000 cheques, 46 per cent strongly. [cite:de21_usat_dividend] The people whose votes would have been needed were cooler. A cheque from the Treasury requires an appropriation, which only Congress can pass. Speaker Mike Johnson said he would be "happy" to consider it "once we balance the budget." [cite:de21_bi_dividend] At the Conservative Political Action Conference he put the objection plainly: "Politically, that would be great for us, you know, because everybody gets a check," but "I think we need to pay down the credit card." [cite:de21_usat_dividend] Senator Thom Tillis preferred to reduce the debt, Senator Josh Hawley wanted the money for a child tax credit, and Republican House members Celeste Maloy and Riley Moore said savings should go to the deficit. [cite:de21_bi_dividend] [cite:de21_usat_dividend] Musk, for his part, said the decision was "entirely up to" the president. [cite:de21_bi_dividend]

The arithmetic it rested on

Everything in the proposal followed from the size of the savings, and the savings never approached the figure the cheque was built on. When Fishback wrote, Musk was already describing $2 trillion as a best case and $1 trillion as the goal, and a Reuters analysis of the partial data DOGE had published found that its contract cancellations to that point had saved $8.5 billion. [cite:de21_reuters_dividend] By April 2025 Musk told the cabinet that he anticipated $150 billion in savings in the following fiscal year, and at his farewell on 30 May the DOGE website estimated $175 billion. [cite:de11_fortune_150b] [cite:de21_wt_farewell] When the website stopped being updated, on 1 January 2026, it claimed $215 billion, or $1,335.40 per taxpayer. [cite:de21_ee_end]

Even on DOGE's own final claim the dividend would have been a fraction of what was floated. Twenty per cent of $215 billion is $43 billion; spread over 78 million households, it comes to about $550 each, roughly a ninth of the $5,000 figure. And the $215 billion was itself a claim the official auditor could not confirm. In August 2026 the Government Accountability Office examined the $110.34 billion of it that DOGE attributed to cancelled contracts, grants and leases. It found that DOGE had followed its own stated method for only 27.5 per cent of the contract savings; that 2,503 contracts, carrying $27.4 billion of claimed savings, showed no termination action at all in the federal procurement database; that it could not verify how 96 per cent of the $49.21 billion in grant savings had been calculated, because DOGE "did not provide sufficient information"; and that a $1.7 billion saving on a military health contract was no saving, since "no action was taken to terminate the contract, or to reduce scope, value, or funding." [cite:de21_gao_full] GAO also noted that money released from cancelled awards "could reduce federal spending or be spent on higher priority agency needs"; a cancellation is not the same as a dollar returned. [cite:de21_gao_full] A dividend paid out of such figures would have been paid out of savings that, on the auditor's account, could not be shown to exist in the amounts claimed.

What became of it

The dividend did not fail by vote. It stopped being discussed. No bill to create it was enacted and no cheque was issued. DOGE's temporary organization reached its legal end on 4 July 2026, the date on which Fishback had proposed the cheques should go out, without a final account of its savings: the director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russell Vought, told a House subcommittee on 30 June 2026 that the administration had "no plans to do kind of a closing DOGE report." [cite:de21_ee_end] [cite:de21_fnn_vought] In the language of a promise ledger, its status is "not attempted": endorsed by the president in public, never sent to Congress in a form Congress could pass.

Two features of the episode should be kept in view. The first is that the dividend was never a formal promise. Trump called it a concept "under consideration" and said he loved it; he did not sign anything, and Musk handed the decision to him. [cite:de21_reuters_dividend] [cite:de21_bi_dividend] The second is that the obstacle that stopped it was ordinary and visible: the leaders of the president's own party in Congress said they would rather reduce the debt, and the power of the purse sat with them. [cite:de21_usat_dividend] That is the constitutional design working as it was taught, in the case of a popular idea that a president endorsed.

Against the record

On the book's red-flag scale, the dividend is ORANGE: a public claim that was not delivered, resting on a savings figure the official auditor could not verify. [cite:de21_gao_full] The grade attaches to the endorsement and the arithmetic behind it, not to any finding about intent. The explanation on the record from those who floated it is the conditional built into the proposal itself: the cheques were to come out of savings, and the savings were not found. No statement by Trump or Musk shows that either knew, when endorsing it, that the money would not appear; the word "lie" is therefore not used.

For the hypothesis this book tests, which treats the cuts as an occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination, the dividend bears in a limited way. Documented: a cash payment was publicly endorsed while the cuts were most contested, and was never paid. [cite:de21_ap_dividend] [cite:de21_ee_end] Not supported: that it was offered as bait in bad faith; the proposal came from an outside investor, the endorsement was conditional, and no document shows a decision to use it to sell the cuts. The record runs against the worst case on one point. The dividend stalled on objections from the president's own party in Congress, which holds the power of the purse; an executive acting without a check would not have needed them. The question of what the cuts actually saved, and who bore their cost, is taken up in [scene:de20_the_cuts|Part Twenty] and [scene:de20_who_paid|its second section]; Musk's own savings figures are graded in [scene:de11_claims_vs_record|Part Eleven]. The next section turns from what the public was offered to what Musk's companies faced, and received, while he held office.

sections.h: Conflicts and Contracts
sections.html:
Musk came into government owning companies that depended on it. SpaceX launched the Pentagon's satellites and NASA's astronauts; Tesla answered to federal safety and securities regulators; Starlink sold to the armed forces and to civilian agencies; and xAI, the artificial-intelligence company that came to own X, was a new federal vendor. [cite:de11_wapo_38bn] While Musk served as a special government employee, from January to May 2025, the same government regulated, investigated and bought from those companies. This section sets out, matter by matter, what is documented about those regulators and contracts during his time in office and after it. It asks one question of each: what happened, and when. Sequence is not causation here either. A case dropped or a contract won while Musk was in government does not show that he caused it, and the section says where the record runs the other way.

The safeguards on paper

Questions about conflicts were raised at once. On 5 February 2025 the White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said that if Musk found a conflict with contracts or funding DOGE oversaw, "Elon will excuse himself from those contracts." [cite:de21_ap_recuse] That was a promise of self-policing, and its fulfilment cannot be checked. When the Government Accountability Office later audited DOGE's personnel, it identified 206 people who had held positions in the Executive Office of the President, 27 of them special government employees, the category Musk belonged to; the Executive Office "did not respond to GAO's requests for access to training records and financial disclosures for DOGE personnel." [cite:de21_gao_personnel] No public record shows Musk recusing himself from any matter, and none shows him declining to. The White House's position in court, that he was a senior adviser with no formal authority over DOGE, is examined in [scene:de17_what_doge_was_legally|Part Seventeen]. [cite:de11_audit_fisher]

The most complete inventory of what was at stake for his companies came from the opposition. On 28 April 2025 Democratic staff of the Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, working for its ranking member, Senator Richard Blumenthal, counted 65 actual or potential enforcement actions involving Musk's companies across 11 federal agencies, and estimated potential liability of $2.37 billion for the 40 they could quantify, calling the figure "a credible, conservative estimate." Their examples included the Federal Aviation Administration's case over SpaceX launch requirements, safety investigations of Tesla's self-driving software, animal-welfare allegations against Neuralink, labour cases at SpaceX and Tesla, and a dropped discrimination suit. They said the companies had given "abjectly inadequate cooperation." [cite:de21_reg_psi] [cite:de11_psi_memo] The memo is a partisan staff estimate of potential penalties, not assessed ones, and its conclusion that Musk's DOGE decisions were marked by "self-enrichment" is the authors' characterisation. [cite:de21_reg_psi] It is useful as a list. What follows tests the items on it that later records resolved.

Regulators: what happened to the cases

The Justice Department's SpaceX suit. In 2023 the department sued SpaceX for discouraging refugees and asylees from applying for jobs; SpaceX denied wrongdoing, and the case had been paused since November 2023 by the company's challenge to the department's authority. On 20 February 2025, a month into Musk's service, the department asked the court to let it dismiss the case with prejudice, so that it could not be brought again. It gave no reason. [cite:de21_axios_doj] This is the clearest instance of an enforcement action against a Musk company ending while he was in government. No document shows that he asked for it.

The Federal Aviation Administration. In September 2024 the FAA proposed $633,009 in civil penalties against SpaceX for using an unapproved launch control room and an unapproved propellant farm in 2023. [cite:de21_faa_penalty] Musk called it "more lawfare" and said SpaceX would sue the agency; on 25 September 2024 he wrote of the FAA's administrator, Mike Whitaker, "He needs to resign." [cite:de21_axios_faa] [cite:de21_snopes_whitaker] Whitaker announced his resignation on 12 December 2024 and left on inauguration day, about fifteen months into a five-year term. A widely repeated line holds that Musk forced him out; a fact-check found that agency heads often leave as administrations change and found no evidence that Musk arranged it. [cite:de21_snopes_whitaker] No resolution of the proposed penalties had been made public as of October 2026.

The National Labor Relations Board. SpaceX did not wait for the executive branch to change. It sued the board, arguing that the job protections of its members and judges were unconstitutional, and on 19 August 2025 the Fifth Circuit agreed that its structure was likely unconstitutional and upheld injunctions barring the board from pursuing unfair-labour-practice cases against SpaceX and two other employers. [cite:de21_franczek_nlrb] [cite:de21_cwc_nlrb] That relief came from a court, on an argument other employers also made, and the Supreme Court's decision in Trump v. Slaughter on 29 June 2026, which overruled the 1935 precedent protecting independent commissioners from removal, was decided in a case about the Federal Trade Commission. [cite:de0_slaughter] Both rulings helped SpaceX; neither was a decision of DOGE.

The Securities and Exchange Commission. In January 2025 the commission sued Musk for disclosing his Twitter stake late in 2022, alleging that the delay cost other shareholders more than $150 million; in December 2024 its lawyers had asked him to pay more than $200 million. The case settled for $1.5 million, which the agency called a record for a late disclosure and Musk's lawyer called a "small fine." Approving the settlement in July 2026, Judge Sparkle Sooknanan said she did so "despite its significant misgivings," having said in May that it raised "red flags," including whether Musk had received "special treatment"; she held that the court "may not step in the shoes of the SEC." [cite:de21_bberg_sec] The judge's question is on the record. The answer to it is not.

Vehicle safety. One regulator kept going. On 7 October 2025 the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation covering 2,882,566 Teslas equipped with Full Self-Driving, after 58 reports of the cars breaking traffic laws, including running red lights; it had opened a separate inquiry into late crash reporting by Tesla that August, and earlier probes continued. [cite:de21_ap_nhtsa] An agency that had been listed among those Musk's position might neutralise opened its largest Tesla investigation after he left office.

Payments. On 28 January 2025 X announced a payments service, X Money, with Visa. [cite:de21_engadget_xmoney] On 9 May 2025 Trump signed a resolution of Congress, S.J.Res. 28, repealing a rule of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau that would have placed large digital-payment apps under federal supervision. [cite:de21_hk_cra] The repeal was passed by both houses of Congress under the Congressional Review Act and applied to the whole industry. That it benefited X is an inference from structure; no lobbying record tying the repeal to X has been published.

Contracts: what was won

The FAA episode is the one in which Musk's companies and his government role met most directly. In February 2025 the agency began testing Starlink terminals at sites in Alaska, Oklahoma City and Atlantic City, under an existing contract held by L3Harris; SpaceX said the kits were leased "free-of-charge," and three SpaceX engineers received ethics waivers to serve at the FAA as special government employees while remaining at the company. Musk wrote that the Verizon system for air-traffic communications was "breaking down very rapidly," then corrected himself to say that the failing system was L3Harris's and Verizon's was "not yet operational." SpaceX said there was "no effort or intent for Starlink to 'take over'" Verizon's $2.4 billion contract, and the Transportation Secretary, Sean Duffy, called Starlink "part of a solution." [cite:de21_ap_starlink] The contract that mattered went elsewhere: in December 2025 the department named Peraton as prime integrator for the air-traffic-control overhaul, with $12.5 billion appropriated by Congress. [cite:de21_ain_peraton]

The larger awards are already set out in [scene:de11_money_and_influence|Part Eleven] and are only summarised here. SpaceX won about $5.92 billion of national-security launches on 4 April 2025, in a competitive procurement begun before 2025 in which it shared the work with two rivals; an executive order of 13 August 2025, after the break with Trump, eased launch licensing in a way Reuters said would benefit SpaceX most; and in April 2026 SpaceX was one of twelve firms given Golden Dome interceptor agreements. [cite:de11_ussf_nssl] [cite:de11_reuters_spaceeo] [cite:de11_bd_sbi] On 25 September 2025 the General Services Administration made xAI's Grok models available to every federal agency for $0.42 per agency for eighteen months, describing it as the last frontier model added to a government-wide programme that already offered others. [cite:de21_gsa_xai] Palantir, the company Peter Thiel co-founded, won a $29.9 million ImmigrationOS contract from Immigration and Customs Enforcement in April 2025 and an Army enterprise agreement worth up to $10 billion over ten years that August. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:ow9_bd_army] These are sequence: they fell in the same months as DOGE, and no document links any of them to a DOGE decision. Palantir's government business is the subject of [scene:de27_origins_and_control|Part Twenty-Nine].

What the record shows, and what it does not

Documented: the overlap itself. Musk held a government role while companies he controlled faced dozens of federal matters, his promised recusal cannot be checked because the financial disclosures were not produced to the auditor, and several matters ended in his companies' favour during or after his service: a suit dropped without explanation, a settlement a federal judge approved with open misgivings, and labour cases halted by a court. [cite:de21_gao_personnel] [cite:de21_axios_doj] [cite:de21_bberg_sec] [cite:de21_franczek_nlrb] Open, and not graded probable: that the presence of the 2024 election's largest donor inside the government made enforcers more cautious toward his companies. Timing allows the inference, no document supports it, and the regulator with the most open cases against Tesla cuts against it. Not supported: that Musk directed any contract to his companies or ordered any case closed. The largest award was competitive, the air-traffic contract went to another firm, the most consequential relief came from courts, and the regulator with the most open cases against Tesla opened a bigger one after he left. [cite:de11_ussf_nssl] [cite:de21_ain_peraton] [cite:de21_ap_nhtsa] The next section follows Musk out of government and DOGE to its end.

sections.h: The Ending: What DOGE Left Behind
sections.html:
DOGE was built to end. The executive order that created it gave its temporary organization a termination date, 4 July 2026, the 250th anniversary of independence. [cite:de0_eo14158] [cite:de21_ee_end] Its public leader left thirteen months before that, quarrelled with the president, and returned to his side as a donor. Its central office faded through the autumn of 2025, and by the time the date arrived there was no final report and no final count. This section follows that ending: Musk's departure and the break, the wind-down, what persisted inside the government, and the ledger of DOGE's public claims against the record. It closes with the test of the book's worst-case reading against Book Three as a whole.

Musk leaves

On 28 May 2025 Musk posted that his "scheduled time as a Special Government Employee" was coming to an end; the 130-day limit on that status could be reached on 30 May. [cite:de13_abc_musk_exit] At a farewell in the Oval Office that day, Trump gave him a golden key and Musk said: "This is not the end of DOGE. It's really just the beginning." The DOGE website then claimed $175 billion in savings, and Musk said he still expected a trillion over time. [cite:de21_wt_farewell] Six days later the two men were at war in public over the Republicans' tax and spending bill. Trump threatened Musk's government contracts; Musk said Trump would have lost the election without him and posted, without evidence, that Trump was in the Epstein files, a post he deleted. [cite:de11_npr_feud] On 11 June he wrote that some of his posts "went too far," and on 5 July he announced an "America Party." [cite:de11_audit_pbs_regret] [cite:de11_ap_party] The party went no further. On 21 September 2025, at the memorial for Charlie Kirk, Musk sat beside Trump and posted a photograph captioned "For Charlie"; Trump said, "I thought it was nice that he came over." [cite:de21_cnn_kirk] In December 2025 Musk said that DOGE had been "a little bit successful" and that he would not do it again.
