[cite:de21_ee_end] By October 2026 he was the largest known donor of the midterm elections, and on 8 October Trump presented him with the National Medal of Science. [cite:de11_ap_2026]

The office fades

Without Musk, DOGE lost the centre it had in public view. In November 2025 the director of the Office of Personnel Management, Scott Kupor, told Reuters that DOGE "doesn't exist," then wrote that it "may not have centralized leadership" but that "the principles of DOGE remain alive and well." [cite:de21_ee_end] The administration disputed reports that DOGE had disbanded as a central entity. [cite:de21_fnn_vought] Its savings page was not updated after 1 January 2026, and the website later went offline. [cite:de21_ee_end] [cite:de21_fnn_vought] On 30 June 2026 the budget director, Russell Vought, told House appropriators that there would be no closing report and that "the fruits of their labor are sprinkled all across the government." [cite:de21_fnn_vought] The temporary organization terminated on 4 July. The U.S. DOGE Service itself, the renamed U.S. Digital Service, did not: the president's budget sought $35 million for it, a House appropriations report asked "the Administrator of DOGE" for quarterly reports on hires and transfers, and its acting administrator, Amy Gleason, said it was "largely continuing that same mission" as the digital office it replaced. [cite:de21_ee_end]

The people went into permanent posts. GAO counted 206 DOGE personnel in the Executive Office of the President between January 2025 and January 2026, of whom at least 128 had left those positions; ten agencies did not answer its questions about the rest. [cite:de21_gao_personnel] Gleason moved to lead a health-technology office at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services; Joe Gebbia, a co-founder of Airbnb, became chief design officer of a new National Design Studio reporting to the White House chief of staff, where Edward Coristine and Zachary Terrell also went. [cite:de21_ee_end] Who these operators were is set out in [scene:de18_the_team|Part Eighteen].

What persisted

Three things outlasted the office. The first is the smaller workforce: across 22 agencies the civilian workforce fell by nearly 256,000, more than 11 per cent, between December 2024 and January 2026, on GAO's count, though some agencies had begun rehiring by mid-2026. [cite:de21_gao_workforce] [cite:de21_fnn_vought] (OPM's own figure uses a different definition; both are set out in [scene:de20_the_cuts|Part Twenty].) The second is a change to the terms of the civil service that DOGE did not make but that followed the same direction: OPM's "Schedule Policy/Career" rule, in effect from 8 March 2026, which removes standard removal protections from career positions judged to influence policy, with up to 50,000 employees estimated to be covered; OPM says it forbids loyalty tests and patronage, and its critics say it can be used to remove experts. [cite:us2_opm_schedpc] [cite:us2_govexec_schedf] The third is the legal fight over what DOGE was. The Supreme Court agreed in October 2026 to decide whether the DOGE Service is subject to the Freedom of Information Act, with argument expected early in 2027; the administration's case is that it "does not exercise independent authority." [cite:de21_ncc_cert] That and the other suits are the subject of [scene:de19_the_courts|Part Nineteen], and the line from Yarvin's 2012 proposal to the 2026 rule is examined in [scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|Part Thirty-Two].

The claims ledger

DOGE's public case rested on claims that can now be checked. The headline figure is the clearest. Musk promised "at least $2 trillion" in October 2024, a claim graded in [scene:de11_claims_vs_record|Part Eleven]; DOGE's final figure was $215 billion; and GAO, examining the $110 billion of it attributed to contracts, grants and leases, could not verify most of it. [cite:de11_fortune_2t] [cite:de21_ee_end] [cite:de21_gao_full] Itemised entries failed earlier. In February 2025 the "Wall of Receipts" listed an $8 billion ICE contract worth $8 million and counted one USAID cut three times; DOGE said it had "always used the correct $8M in its calculations." [cite:de21_nyt_receipts] In the same month Musk said the Social Security rolls included people "150 years old." The records were real; a 2023 inspector general's report had found millions of entries with no date of death, and the acting commissioner said such people "are not necessarily receiving benefits." [cite:de21_abc_ssa150] [cite:de21_aa_dudek] Musk's general answer to errors, given that month about another claim, was: "Nobody's going to bat a thousand." [cite:de21_abc_ssa150]

On openness, Musk wrote in November 2024 that "there should be no need for FOIA requests," and said in February 2025 that "all of our actions are maximally transparent." Two weeks later the government told a court that "USDS is not subject to FOIA." [cite:de21_reason_foia] Its explanation is a legal one, that the office only advises the president, and the Supreme Court will rule on it. [cite:de21_ncc_cert]

Five of the seven are ORANGE: claims the official auditor or the agency's own records could not bear out. One is YELLOW, a stated position on openness abandoned in court, with the government's legal explanation; one is GREY, because the administration's own officials describe DOGE's survival differently. None is RED, because no sworn statement or document of the speaker's own contradicts the claim, and the word "lie" is not used: the record shows claims that were wrong or unverifiable, not that the speakers knew them to be false.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis is the Sophia platform's, not a finding: government cuts as the occasion, a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. Across Book Three, what the reading calls the occasion, cuts carried out through an office with reach into the machinery of the state, is documented; that the cuts were used as a pretext for something further is not. An executive order alone created the office; its public face was the largest donor of the 2024 election, though in law he did not lead it; its legal form, an adviser's office rather than an agency, is the basis of the government's argument that it owes the public no records under the Freedom of Information Act, and the White House told a court that its public leader was not in charge of it ([scene:de17_money_to_office|Part Seventeen], [scene:de17_what_doge_was_legally|its second section]). [cite:de11_cnn_290m] [cite:de7_os_donors2024] [cite:de21_ncc_cert] [cite:de11_audit_fisher] Its teams reached systems whose extent the auditor could not determine, at agencies that refused to cooperate with the audit ([scene:de19_the_access|Part Nineteen]). [cite:de21_gao_systems] The workforce shrank by a quarter of a million, and the aid cuts carry modelled projections of millions of deaths whose methods are disputed ([scene:de20_who_paid|Part Twenty]). [cite:de21_gao_workforce] [cite:de21_ucla_lancet] Its savings claims and its promises did not survive audit. [cite:de21_gao_full]

Probable: that the opacity was a matter of policy rather than accident, since refusals to the auditor came from the Executive Office and from several agencies over many months, some disputing GAO's authority itself. That rests on pattern and timing, not on a document. Whether the presence of the 2024 election's largest donor made enforcement against his companies more cautious stays open: timing allows the inference, no document supports it, and the vehicle-safety regulator's larger investigation of Tesla cuts against it. [cite:de21_gao_personnel] [cite:de21_gao_systems] [cite:de21_bberg_sec]

Not supported: that DOGE was the Dark Enlightenment's program in operation. Yarvin's 2012 proposal to retire all government employees, RAGE, rhymes with DOGE [cite:de6_tnr_duran], but no document shows it as DOGE's source, and rhyme is not provenance ([scene:de6_the_program|Part Six], [scene:de1_spine_and_overlay|Part One]). Musk's own stated case was the reverse of the sovereign-executive design, "rule of the people — democracy" against "rule of the bureaucracy." [cite:de3_dcpd_musk] And the record runs against the destination at several points. The dividend stalled on the objections of the president's own party in Congress, which holds the purse. Courts blocked parts of the programme ([scene:de19_the_courts|Part Nineteen]), and the Supreme Court will rule on its secrecy. [cite:de21_usat_dividend] [cite:de21_ncc_cert] The donor and the president split in public. DOGE ended on the date its own order set, and agencies began rehiring. [cite:de11_npr_feud] [cite:de21_fnn_vought] What moved durably toward the presidency, the Schedule Policy/Career rule and the removal power the Supreme Court confirmed in Trump v. Slaughter, moved through rule-making and a court ruling, channels that stayed open to challenge; that is a real shift of power toward the presidency, documented as such, but not an executive without a veto. [cite:us2_opm_schedpc] [cite:de0_slaughter] The occasion happened; the destination is not shown. How DOGE compares with the theorists' own test of their ideas is taken up in [scene:de33_two_tests|Part Thirty-Five], and these grades are carried into [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three]. Book Four turns from the state to the attempts to leave it, beginning with [scene:de22_seas_and_zones|Part Twenty-Two].

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Two
chapters.title: Exit Zones
chapters.intro: This part opens Book Four, on exit: the idea, central to the Dark Enlightenment texts, that people should be free to leave a state and choose another rather than vote to change their own. It follows what happened when investors and writers in the circle around those texts tried to build places to go. The first section traces the projects from the Seasteading Institute's floating platforms to Paul Romer's charter cities, Honduras's special zones, the venture fund Pronomos Capital, the network-state company Praxis and Balaji Srinivasan's Network School, naming who paid for each. The second follows Próspera, the zone on the Honduran island of Roatán that became a working place, through its charter, its neighbours' complaints, the repeal of its law, a court ruling that voided it and an arbitration claim against Honduras first priced at more than $10 billion. The third asks what Javier Milei's Argentina and Donald Trump's promise of "freedom cities" actually produced, and tests the book's worst-case reading against the part as a whole.
chapters.outro: Exit, as it was built, turned out to depend on the states it set out to leave. The seasteading platform ended when French Polynesia let its memorandum lapse at the end of 2017, Praxis's Greenland plan ran into Danish law, and the Network School left Malaysia for Kazakhstan after a licensing notice in July 2026. [cite:de22_rnz_fp] [cite:de22_giz_praxis] [cite:de22_newswav_ns] Thiel's money reached the zones one step removed, through Pronomos Capital, which he anchored in 2019. [cite:de22_bbg_pronomos] Próspera, the one zone that became a working place, gives its company a blocking vote under its own charter; after Honduras's Congress repealed the ZEDE law and its Supreme Court voided it from inception on 20 September 2024, the company pressed its case through a treaty tribunal, with a claim first put at up to $10.775 billion that its memorial of 15 October 2025 restated as restitution or, in the alternative, $1.63 billion in damages; the case was pending on the merits as of October 2026. [cite:de22_charter] [cite:de22_cc_ruling] [cite:de22_po6] [cite:de22_eyn_2025] Argentina under Milei created no exit zone, and Trump's 2023 pledge of ten freedom cities was rated "Stalled," with no bill or order, because Congress holds the land. [cite:de22_unlp_delrio] [cite:de22_pf_fc] [cite:de22_bblaw_fc] On this part's evidence, exit produced enclaves governed by investors, not a route to a sovereign executive. [scene:de23_address_space|Part Twenty-Three] turns to the digital version of exit: Urbit, the network Yarvin designed as a landed hierarchy of addresses.

sections.h: Seas, Zones and Network States
sections.html:
Book Three followed an attempt to change a state from the inside. Book Four follows the older and, in the texts, more central idea: leaving. Exit, the word the economist Albert Hirschman used for walking away from a failing organisation rather than complaining inside it, runs through every core text of the Dark Enlightenment. In Curtis Yarvin's Patchwork series of 2008, small states owned by corporations would compete for residents, whose one remedy was this: "If residents don't like their government, they can and should move." [cite:de2_le] The lineage of that idea, and Peter Thiel's 2009 case for an "escape from politics" through cyberspace, outer space and the sea, are set out in [scene:de3_other_lineages|Part Three] and [scene:de2_core_texts|Part Two]. This section follows what happened when people tried to build it: first on the ocean, then in a Central American country's special zones, then through venture funds and online communities that buy or borrow land. It names who paid for each project, from the documents that show it, and what became of each.

The sea: a memorandum that lapsed

The Seasteading Institute was founded on 15 April 2008 by Patri Friedman, a former Google engineer and grandson of the economist Milton Friedman, and the software engineer Wayne Gramlich, with $500,000 in seed money from Thiel. [cite:de3_wiki_tsi] [cite:de22_bbg_pronomos] [cite:de22_chequeado] Thiel's total giving was put at $1.25 million in a 2011 report and at $1.7 million in a 2018 one; the first is an itemised total as of 2011, the second gives no source of its own, and the institute's public returns do not name donors, so the two cannot be reconciled from filings. [cite:de3_yahoo_tsi] [cite:de3_bi_tsi] [cite:de14_bi_seastead] Thiel left the board in 2011 and later called seasteads "not quite feasible." [cite:de3_bi_tsi]

The institute's one concrete step toward a floating community came a decade after its founding. On 13 January 2017 it signed a memorandum of understanding with a minister of French Polynesia for a platform in a sheltered lagoon. [cite:de3_wiki_tsi] It did not survive local politics. An opposition politician, Valentina Cross, asked the government to withdraw, and residents objected; in February 2018 the governing party, Tapura Huiraatira, said that "nothing had been signed," that the agreement "was not a legal document," and that it had expired at the end of 2017. [cite:de22_rnz_fp] The Floating Island Project ended there. No seastead of the kind the institute was founded to build has been built. [cite:de3_bi_tsi]

Land: Romer's charter cities and Honduras's zones

The move from sea to land had a separate intellectual source, older than the projects that later borrowed from it and unconnected to the Dark Enlightenment texts. In 2009 the economist Paul Romer began presenting the idea of "charter cities": new cities on empty land, governed under a charter written with outside help, which poor countries could use to import good rules quickly. [cite:de22_od_romer] Honduras took up a version of it. In January 2011 its Congress voted 124 to 1 for a constitutional amendment allowing "special development regions," known by their Spanish initials as REDs. [cite:de22_fee_bell] Romer agreed to chair a transparency commission that would oversee them, but in September 2012 the government signed the first RED contract with foreign investors without telling him; he learned of it from a newspaper and resigned. [cite:de22_od_romer] On 18 October 2012 the Supreme Court declared the REDs unconstitutional as a violation of national sovereignty and territory. [cite:de22_fee_bell]

Congress tried again. Its president, Juan Orlando Hernández, announced a new framework, the Zones for Employment and Economic Development, or ZEDEs; the law passed on 12 June 2013 by 102 votes to 26. [cite:de22_od_romer] [cite:de22_cc_ruling] The main difference from the REDs was the land. A RED would have been granted by the state; a ZEDE would be built on land bought from its owners, although the law still allowed expropriation. [cite:de22_od_romer] Three ZEDEs were eventually established; the best known, Próspera on the island of Roatán, is the subject of [scene:de22_prospera_v_honduras|the next section]. Romer had left the Honduran effort the year before. [cite:de22_od_romer]

The fund: Pronomos Capital

The money that linked the seasteading circle to the Honduran zones went through a venture fund. In August 2019 Patri Friedman incorporated Pronomos Capital to invest in semi-autonomous cities on land in developing countries. Bloomberg Businessweek reported in December 2019 that Thiel was its anchor investor, supplying more than half of about $9 million raised, and named Marc Andreessen, the bitcoin investor Roger Ver and Balaji Srinivasan as other seed backers; Erick Brimen, who would run Próspera, was then working informally with Friedman. [cite:de22_bbg_pronomos] [cite:de22_mr_pronomos] Friedman himself has dated the fund a year earlier: speaking on a podcast, he said that in 2018, when Próspera was about to be approved, he created Pronomos "with financing from Peter Thiel." [cite:de22_chequeado] By December 2023 the fund had raised at least $13.3 million, with Thiel and Andreessen among its named investors, and its projects included a planned city in the Mediterranean, a zone on an island in Honduras and an online business hub in Nigeria. [cite:de22_db_pronomos] Michael Gibson, formerly vice-president of grants at the Thiel Foundation, advises it. [cite:de22_giz_praxis] Pronomos's limited partners and stakes have not been published in full, and the named list should be read as what reporters were told.

The online community: Praxis

Praxis began as an online community of would-be founders that, in 2022, described its future city as a "crypto-state"; by 2026 it claimed some 150,000 members. [cite:de22_perfil_bastitta] Pronomos is among its backers, alongside the crypto investment firm Paradigm and the trading firms Alameda Research and Three Arrows Capital. [cite:de22_giz_praxis] [cite:de22_block_praxis] On 15 October 2024 it announced $525 million, which it described as "primarily consisting of a drawdown facility" from lenders including Arch Lending and GEM Digital: a commitment that can be drawn on, by its own account, not cash in hand. [cite:de22_block_praxis]

The search for land became public in Greenland. In November 2024 Praxis's chief executive, Dryden Brown, posted: "I went to Greenland to try to buy it." When President-elect Trump wrote of acquiring the island, the Praxis account reposted him with the words "According to plan." [cite:de22_giz_praxis] Reuters later reported, from unnamed sources, a push for a "freedom city" in Greenland that two of them said Thiel and Andreessen supported; Thiel's spokesperson said that "Peter isn't involved in any plans or discussions regarding Greenland." [cite:de13_newsweek_greenland] The obstacle was law: Greenland's independence requires the approval of its own parliament, a referendum and the Danish parliament, and a Danish MP, Rasmus Jarlov, said there was "no way" Denmark would approve independence so that Greenland could be bought. [cite:de22_giz_praxis] [cite:de22_xataka_praxis] In 2026 Praxis turned to Uruguay, signing a memorandum with +Colonia, a property development near Colonia del Sacramento, which both sides described as mostly non-binding. [cite:de22_xataka_praxis] [cite:de22_perfil_bastitta] Perfil reported that former team members allege an "authoritarian" vision of governance and racist opinions inside the project; these are allegations by unnamed former staff, not findings. [cite:de22_perfil_bastitta]

The network state

Srinivasan's 2022 book The Network State, discussed in [scene:de16_the_valley|Part Sixteen], gave this cluster a theory: an online community with a shared purpose and a founder that crowdfunds territory and eventually seeks recognition. [cite:de16_maverick] His own pilot was a school. Announced in August 2024, the Network School opened on 23 September 2024 at Forest City, a development in the Malaysian state of Johor, with about 128 participants, and launched a permanent programme in May 2025. [cite:de22_newswav_ns] In July 2026, after unverified social-media claims about who had enrolled, the Johor government ordered an inquiry and on 17 July issued a cessation-of-business notice, citing premises operating without a valid local licence and office space used as classrooms without approval. Srinivasan said more than RM100 million had been invested "without government funding" and put a planned RM500 million expansion on hold. [cite:de22_newswav_ns] On 22 July he announced a memorandum of understanding with Kazakhstan, signed for the government by Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, for a new campus he called "a haven for the global community optimistic about technology." [cite:de22_vibes_ns] Who funds the school, beyond his own statement, is not documented.

What the record shows

Three things follow from these projects taken together. First, the money is real and traceable along a short line: Thiel funded the seasteading institute directly and anchored the fund that invested in both Próspera and Praxis, so his money reaches the zones one step removed; no document shows him investing in either directly, and he denies involvement in the Greenland plans. [cite:de22_bbg_pronomos] [cite:de13_newsweek_greenland] Second, most projects stalled or moved when a government said no: French Polynesia let its memorandum lapse, Denmark's law closed Greenland, Johor shut the school's premises. [cite:de22_rnz_fp] [cite:de22_giz_praxis] [cite:de22_newswav_ns] Third, the idea that went furthest on land came from Romer, an economist outside this circle, and was turned into law by Honduran politicians; it was then taken up by the fund the circle financed. That is borrowing, not authorship. The texts' Patchwork imagined sovereign corporations; what was built was a zone inside a country's legal order, and the following section shows what happened when that country changed its mind.

sections.h: Próspera against Honduras
sections.html:
Próspera is the one exit project in this book that became a functioning place with residents, businesses and its own rules, and it is also the one that collided most directly with the state around it. It sits on the island of Roatán, off Honduras's Caribbean coast, under the ZEDE law of 2013 described in [scene:de22_seas_and_zones|the previous section]. This section sets out how it is governed, on the evidence of its own charter; what its nearest neighbours said about it; how Honduras repealed the law it was built on and then had its highest court declare that law void; and how the company answered with an investment arbitration claim first priced at more than $10 billion. Each side's stated position is given beside the other's, and the status of every proceeding is given as of October 2026.

The company and the charter

Erick Brimen, an entrepreneur who became its chief executive, formally applied for a charter city in Honduras in 2017; construction of the first buildings began in 2021, and by 2024 Próspera was reported to have about 2,000 residents. [cite:de22_wiki_prospera] Its organiser is Honduras Próspera, a company incorporated in Delaware and funded by venture investors, which reported raising more than $120 million by 2024, including from funds backed by Thiel, Andreessen and Sam Altman. [cite:de22_charter] [cite:de22_chequeado] Among those funds is Pronomos Capital, whose founder says he created it in 2018 "with financing from Peter Thiel"; that places Thiel's money one step removed from Próspera, and no document shows a direct investment by him. [cite:de22_chequeado] On 21 January 2025 Próspera announced a "strategic investment" by Coinbase Ventures, the venture arm of the cryptocurrency exchange, with North Island Ventures and BoostVC; no amount was disclosed. [cite:de22_coinbase]

The zone's founding charter is dated 23 August 2018, and an amended text was published in 2026. [cite:de22_charter] It sets up a nine-member Próspera Council. Residents choose four trustees and the company, as "Promoter and Organizer," chooses four; a technical secretary chairs it. Two of the resident seats are reserved for landowners until the zone reaches urban population density. Ordinary business passes by a majority, but resolutions, prior approval of statutes and regulations, and amendments to the charter itself need two-thirds of the whole council: six votes of nine. [cite:de22_charter] The company's four trustees can therefore block any of those measures on their own. Earlier reporting described the same arrangement as giving the company an effective veto. [cite:de22_wiki_prospera] Residents aged 18 and over vote, one each; "e-residents," who register remotely, do not; and residents gain the power to repeal rules by referendum only once the population passes 10,000. [cite:de22_charter] Amendments also go to the Committee for the Adoption of Best Practices, a body appointed under the Honduran ZEDE law, which approves them unless it objects within 45 days. [cite:de22_charter] [cite:de22_wiki_prospera] Services can be contracted to a "general service provider" for up to 50 years, though not policing or courts, and disputes go to the zone's own court subject to binding private arbitration. [cite:de22_charter] Honduran criminal law continues to apply. [cite:de22_wiki_prospera]

The neighbours: Crawfish Rock

The first part of Próspera was built beside Crawfish Rock, a small community on Roatán. On the evening of 18 September 2020 a meeting between company executives and residents ended in a confrontation with municipal police. The next day Próspera "strongly" rejected accusations of any intent or authority to expropriate land, published a unanimous resolution of its council that the project would "in no case" benefit from expropriation, said all land purchases were voluntary, and said its first 58-acre development lay "far" from Crawfish Rock. [cite:de22_heraldo_2020]

Residents told a different story to reporters. In 2022 Luisa Connor, president of the community association, told The Guardian: "We didn't even know what a Zede was," and "They deceived us big time." The fear was expropriation: drawings of later phases on Próspera's website appeared to include the centre of the village, and the ZEDE law contained a clause allowing land to be taken. Próspera's representatives said they had informed the community in June 2019, citing a resolution signed by 49 residents that described the project as "a real estate and community development project," and promised not to expropriate. [cite:de22_guardian_cr] In 2023 Connor told CorpWatch that "the city will grow like a tumor," and another community leader, Venessa Cárdenas, said residents had a right to be consulted and were not. [cite:de22_corpwatch] Próspera's charter now requires compensation of twice the greater of market value or loss for any taking, and its chief executive backed a national ban on expropriation in July 2023; disputes over groundwater, sewage and shared roads continued to be reported in 2025. [cite:de22_charter] [cite:de22_wiki_prospera] Both accounts are on the record: the company's written commitments, and residents' statements that they agreed to something they did not understand.

The repeal and the ruling

President Xiomara Castro called for the zones to be abolished. [cite:de22_stab_ruling] On 21 April 2022 Congress repealed the ZEDE law unanimously. [cite:de22_cc_repeal] The repeal of the matching constitutional articles needed ratification by a later session, which never came, so the existing zones went on operating legally for more than two years. [cite:de22_cc_ruling] On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court, in a ruling signed by its fifteen magistrates, declared the whole ZEDE framework unconstitutional from its inception: the 2013 constitutional reforms, the ZEDE law, its investor guarantees and a 2021 resolution on special jurisdiction. [cite:de22_cc_ruling] Castro called the ruling "patriotic, historic, fair, and legal," and wrote that it meant not "selling off our territory piecemeal or privatizing our sovereignty." [cite:de22_cc_ruling] [cite:de22_stab_ruling] The court said it would rule separately on zones already operating. [cite:de22_stab_ruling]

Próspera had warned the day before that a retroactive ruling would "have no legitimacy," and that "there is nothing to gain from such a ruling": it would unsettle investors and workers, harm Honduran banks with loans to the zones and damage relations with the United States. [cite:de22_prospera_stmt] Another zone's secretary called the ruling "abusive." The government's commissioner on the ZEDEs, Fernando García, said it would work with investors who "act in good faith." [cite:de22_cc_ruling] Próspera kept operating; its technical secretary, Jorge Colindres, said in 2026 that the ruling had cost 1,500 jobs and that the zone counted 974 jobs in March 2026. [cite:de22_heraldo_2026]

The dispute was also fought in Washington. The State Department raised concerns in July 2022 that the repeal could breach the Central America free-trade agreement, CAFTA-DR, and a House committee report of 14 June 2024 urged Honduras to let the zones continue. [cite:de22_wiki_prospera] In January 2023 Próspera welcomed a bill from Representative Paul Gosar to widen sanctions for expropriation, with Brimen saying there should be "more serious consequences for expropriation and threats of expropriation." [cite:de22_prospera_gosar] On 12 January 2024 Representative Steven Horsford, a Nevada Democrat, urged in the Congressional Record that visas be denied to Honduran officials who advocated expropriating American investments, citing Próspera and its "50-year legal stability guarantee." [cite:de22_crec_horsford] Bloomberg reported that Brimen had given $5,000 to Horsford's campaign in 2023; that is a sequence on the record, not evidence that the donation caused the statement. [cite:de22_wiki_prospera] On the other side, 32 members of Congress wrote to President Biden that corporations had "weaponized" investor-state dispute settlement. [cite:de22_corpwatch]

The arbitration

Próspera's main answer was a claim against Honduras at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), the World Bank body that hears investor-state cases. The request was filed on 19 December 2022 by Honduras Próspera Inc., St. John's Bay Development Company and Próspera Arbitration Center under CAFTA-DR, and registered as case ARB/23/2. [cite:de22_po6] [cite:de22_italaw] The claim was for up to $10.775 billion if the investment were lost entirely, on the basis of a 50-year legal stability guarantee. [cite:de22_eyn_2022] Reporters put that at about a third of Honduras's economic output; the economy minister, Pedro Barquero, said the country could not pay it without diverting money from development, and Brimen said Honduras had been unwilling to settle. [cite:de22_ct_econ] [cite:de22_eyn_2022] [cite:de22_eyn_2023]

Honduras fought on two fronts. It notified the World Bank on 24 February 2024 that it was leaving the ICSID Convention, with effect from 25 August 2024; a letter from 85 economists praised the withdrawal as a "critical defense of Honduran democracy." [cite:de22_icsid_den] [cite:de22_ct_econ] The withdrawal did not stop the case, which had been filed while Honduras was a member. Inside the case, Honduras challenged the tribunal and lost; on 26 February 2025 the tribunal rejected its preliminary objection, and on 19 March 2026 it refused to split off six further objections, including an essential-security defence and a claim that there was no protected investment, ruling that they would be heard with the merits. [cite:de22_po6] In their memorial of 15 October 2025 the claimants asked for restitution of their assets or, in the alternative, $1.63 billion in damages; the alternative claim is about 85 per cent below the $10.775 billion first claimed. [cite:de22_po6] [cite:de22_eyn_2025] [cite:de23_riotimes_icsid] Honduras's Attorney General's Office attributed the reduction to the state's defence and called the claim "unjust and inadmissible," built on "speculations without legal basis." [cite:de22_eyn_2025]

Castro's successor, President Nasry Asfura, re-signed the ICSID Convention on 6 March 2026; Honduras deposited its ratification on 17 July and rejoined on 16 August 2026, presented as a signal of legal security for investors. [cite:de22_heraldo_2026] [cite:de22_icsid_rat] Honduras then faced fourteen pending ICSID cases. Colindres said Próspera hoped the case could reach "a conciliation." [cite:de22_heraldo_2026] Status as of October 2026: the arbitration is pending on the merits, no hearing date or award has been published, and Próspera continues to operate.

What the case shows

Three points are documented. A private company holds, under its own charter, a blocking vote over the rules of the place where some 2,000 people live, and residents' fuller powers are deferred until the population reaches a size it has not approached. [cite:de22_charter] [cite:de22_wiki_prospera] When an elected government and a unanimous court revoked the law beneath it, the zone did not leave; it relied on rules made by states, a trade treaty and a World Bank tribunal, and on pressure from members of the United States Congress. [cite:de22_po6] [cite:de22_crec_horsford] And the money it asks of Honduras, once the claim was set out in full, became restitution or, in the alternative, $1.63 billion in damages, against the $10.775 billion first claimed; the case was pending on the merits as of October 2026. [cite:de22_po6] [cite:de22_eyn_2025] The texts imagined exit as leaving the state behind. The one working example depends on the oldest instruments of state power, treaties and tribunals, to hold its ground, which is the problem [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight] found in the theory: a charter binds only as far as someone outside it will enforce it.

sections.h: Argentina, and the Freedom Cities
sections.html:
Two governments in the Americas have been named in connection with exit zones since 2023. One is Javier Milei's Argentina, whose president calls himself an anarcho-capitalist and to which Peter Thiel moved in 2026. The other is the United States, where Donald Trump promised in his 2023 campaign to charter up to ten new "freedom cities" on federal land. This section sets out what each government has actually done, keeping campaign words, advocates' plans and enacted policy apart, and then tests the book's worst-case reading against the whole of Part Twenty-Two.

Argentina: a president's philosophy and a neighbour's development

Milei's own label for his philosophy is anarcho-capitalism, a strand of libertarianism that would replace the state's services with private ones. After receiving Thiel at the Casa Rosada on 23 April 2026, he called him "an anarcho-capitalist, just as I am philosophically," said both men regard "taxes as theft," and said no specific investments were discussed. [cite:de9_bat_milei] Thiel's meetings with Milei, his move to Buenos Aires and the reports of a citizenship offer, which Milei's spokesperson denied, are set out in [scene:de9_politics_and_argentina|Part Nine]. [cite:de9_nn_nyt] [cite:de9_fortune_ba]

On exit zones specifically, the record in Argentina is thin. Milei's government has deregulated rents, property transactions and mortgages by decree, which an academic review of its urban policy describes as a "libertarian city" in an analytical sense; the same review cites no charter city, free city or special governance zone created by the government. [cite:de22_unlp_delrio] An essay on the Mises Institute's Spanish-language site argued in 2024 that Argentina needed "free cities," semi-autonomous zones with their own economic rules; it attributed no such proposal to Milei's government. [cite:de22_mises_ar] What the government did create, by Decree 524/2025 published on 31 July 2025, was a programme of citizenship by investment run by an agency of the economy ministry; as of January 2026 its rules were still unwritten and it was not operating, and Fortune reported in July 2026 that it was still not live. [cite:de22_cronista_cbi] [cite:de9_fortune_ba] Citizenship for sale is a route for individuals to join a state, not a zone exempt from one.

The nearest documented link between Milei and an exit-style project lies across the River Plate in Uruguay. On 30 August 2023, after the primaries and before he was elected, Milei made a short trip to Colonia del Sacramento, met the businessman Eduardo Bastitta and toured +Colonia, a 500-hectare development Bastitta was planning as a technology hub. [cite:de22_lanacion_colonia] [cite:de22_perfil_bastitta] Bastitta, a self-described libertarian, later served on Milei's council of advisers. [cite:de22_perfil_bastitta] In 2026 Praxis, the network-state project described in [scene:de22_seas_and_zones|the first section], signed a mostly non-binding memorandum with +Colonia. Bastitta has said the development will not have a separate legal order and compared it to Nordelta, a private gated development outside Buenos Aires; residents would choose between Uruguayan and Argentine tax and legal arrangements. [cite:de22_perfil_bastitta] [cite:de22_xataka_praxis] The tie is between a former adviser's private development and Praxis. It is not a tie between Milei's government and Praxis, and no document shows the Argentine state taking part. Nor does any document link Milei to Yarvin's or Land's texts.

The pledge: ten cities on federal land

On 3 March 2023 Trump's campaign released a video, part of its "Agenda47" series, promising "a quantum leap in the American standard of living." Among its proposals, with flying cars and "baby bonuses," was a plan to set aside a small share of federal land and charter up to ten new cities through a national contest: "These freedom cities will reopen the American frontier." [cite:de22_hill_fc] The video did not describe how the cities would be governed. After 2023, according to PolitiFact's check of the transcript archive FactBase, Trump did not mention them again; neither did the White House in his second term. [cite:de22_pf_fc]

Others filled the space. In March 2025 Wired reported that a new lobbying group, the Freedom Cities Coalition, was drafting legislation for zones where anti-ageing trials, nuclear start-ups and construction could proceed without prior approval from the Food and Drug Administration, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission or the Environmental Protection Agency. The coalition is a project of NeWay Capital, a firm involved in developing Próspera, and Próspera's chief of staff, Trey Goff, said its representatives had met the administration, which was "very receptive." [cite:de22_giz_fc] A model Freedom Cities Act drafted by Tom W. Bell, a law professor at Chapman University, would let a federal board waive large parts of the tax code, environmental and labour law; Bell called the cities "small safely-contained experiments in governance." [cite:de22_bblaw_fc] Published summaries of the draft record that it would also bar residents from voting in state elections. [cite:de22_wiki_fc] In April 2025 the American Enterprise Institute's housing centre proposed selling 850 square miles of land managed by the Bureau of Land Management, 600 of them for about twenty new cities, and Paul Dans, who had directed the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025, described freedom cities to NBC News as part of a "construction phase" after the "demolition" of the administrative state. [cite:de22_wiki_fc] By February 2026 the Frontier Foundation, another advocate, told PolitiFact that "Drafts are circulating. This promise will be fulfilled," and in June advocates were pressing for the first sites to be unveiled on 4 July 2026, the 250th anniversary of independence. [cite:de22_pf_fc] [cite:de22_inq_fc]

What happened, and the legal limits

Nothing was enacted. PolitiFact rated the promise "Stalled" on 10 February 2026: no bill in Congress mentioned freedom cities, no executive order had been issued, and the White House did not answer a request for comment. [cite:de22_pf_fc] The nearest legislative step went the other way. Senator Mike Lee put a provision in the Senate's 2025 budget bill requiring the sale of between 0.25 and 0.5 per cent of Bureau of Land Management land in eleven Western states for housing; he withdrew it on 28 June 2025 after the Senate parliamentarian ruled against it and House Republicans threatened to oppose the bill. [cite:de22_kpcw_lee] The Interior secretary, Doug Burgum, proposed selling up to 625 square miles near existing cities for housing, a different plan from new chartered cities; the Bureau's acting director said it had seen no specific freedom-city proposal. [cite:de22_bblaw_fc] As of late July 2026, the German daily taz reported, no law mentioned freedom cities; no unveiling on 4 July was reported. [cite:de22_taz_fc] Status as of October 2026: a campaign pledge, not a policy.

The limits are structural, and they sit with Congress. The Constitution's Property Clause gives Congress, not the president, the power to dispose of federal land and make rules for it; large transfers of Bureau of Land Management land need an act of Congress, and the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 ended homesteading and narrowed sales. [cite:de22_bblaw_fc] [cite:de22_inq_fc] Exempting a zone from the tax code, the Clean Water Act or federal labour law would likewise take a statute, which is why the advocates drafted bills rather than orders. Andrew Mergen of Harvard Law School told Bloomberg Law that Congress has broad authority over federal land, but "this would be at a whole other scale"; states, Bell said, would have little power over such enclaves, much as over military bases. [cite:de22_bblaw_fc] An executive acting alone could not create such a city; at most it could propose one.

On the book's red-flag scale, the freedom-city pledge is ORANGE: a public promise not delivered. The grade attaches to the outcome, not to intent. Trump has given no explanation on the record for dropping it, and the obstacle that stands in the way, Congress's control of federal land, is visible and ordinary.

The worst-case reading, tested

The book's working hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and never a finding, reads immigration enforcement and government cuts as the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. Exit zones bear on it in a particular way. On one reading they are an escape: people who dislike a state leave it and build elsewhere, which is what Patchwork and Thiel's 2009 essay proposed. On the other they are an enclave for the few: territory carved out of a country where a company sets the rules, residents have a weaker vote, and the surrounding state's law stops at the gate.

Documented: Próspera's charter gives its company a blocking vote over the zone's rules, defers residents' fuller powers until a population it has not approached, and gives remote "e-residents" no vote at all. [cite:de22_charter] Documented too: when Honduras's elected Congress and its Supreme Court revoked the law beneath the zone, the company sought restitution or damages through a treaty tribunal and drew support from members of the United States Congress. [cite:de22_po6] [cite:de22_crec_horsford] [cite:de22_cc_ruling] Documented: Thiel's money reaches Próspera and Praxis one step removed, through Pronomos, and people working for Próspera lobbied the Trump administration for freedom cities in the United States. [cite:de22_bbg_pronomos] [cite:de22_giz_fc] And documented: advocates' drafts would remove federal law within the zones and bar residents from state elections. [cite:de22_wiki_fc]

Probable: that "enclave for the few" describes Próspera better than "escape for the many." The zone's own rules give investors more power than residents, and its neighbours' account is that they were not told what was being built; this is a reading of documented facts, and Próspera's stated position, that it is a voluntary, job-creating community that has renounced expropriation, is also on the record. [cite:de22_guardian_cr] [cite:de22_heraldo_2020]

Not supported: that the exit projects are a path to a sovereign executive over the United States. The record runs against it. Every zone described in this part depends on a host state's law: French Polynesia let a memorandum lapse, Danish and Greenlandic law closed off Greenland, Johor shut the Network School's premises, and Honduras repealed and voided the ZEDE law, leaving Próspera operating while it pursues a pending treaty claim that now asks for restitution or, in the alternative, $1.63 billion, against the $10.775 billion first claimed. [cite:de22_rnz_fp] [cite:de22_giz_praxis] [cite:de22_newswav_ns] [cite:de22_cc_ruling] [cite:de22_po6] [cite:de22_eyn_2025] In the United States the only government step toward freedom cities was a campaign video; Congress holds the land and did not act, and the one legislative provision to sell some of it was withdrawn. [cite:de22_pf_fc] [cite:de22_kpcw_lee] In Argentina no exit zone exists. Exit, as built, has meant leaving or carving out small places, not capturing a large one. Whether the digital version of exit fared differently is the subject of [scene:de23_address_space|Part Twenty-Three].

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Three
chapters.title: Urbit: the Digital Exit
chapters.intro: This part closes Book Four with the one exit project its central theorist built himself. Urbit is a computer network that Curtis Yarvin began writing in 2002, and its names are cut into a fixed hierarchy of 256 "galaxies," 65,280 "stars" and about four billion "planets," owned, traded and, at the top, given a vote. The first section reads the design and its author's own descriptions of it, from "digital feudalism" in 2010 to "Urbit is land" in 2016, and sets them against who actually came to own the map and how many people use it. The second follows Yarvin's return in August 2024 as a self-described "wartime CEO," the board fight of 2025 and the vote by which the galaxy owners settled it, and then tests the book's worst-case reading against Book Four as a whole: exit as an escape for anyone, or an enclave for the few.
chapters.outro: Urbit's map was drawn as property and described as such by its author, who named the design "digital feudalism" in 2010, called the result land owned "by the homestead principle," and let only the owners of the 256 galaxies vote; in 2019 an independent count put 185 of them with the company, its staff and its foundation. [cite:de23_moronlab_2010] [cite:de23_objections_2016] [cite:de23_compact_2025] Its use stayed small, a few thousand active users by one 2022 estimate, and it is neither anonymous nor linked by any document to crime. [cite:de23_point_2022] [cite:de23_tlon_faq] In August 2024, with the Foundation's money nearly gone, Yarvin returned without a title as a "wartime CEO"; in 2025 the board and the founder tried to remove each other, and on 9 October 2025 the galaxy owners replaced the board and a new director succeeded him as he left to found a company. [cite:de23_coindesk_2024] [cite:de23_marbl] [cite:de23_epoch_2025] On Book Four as a whole, rule by owners is documented by design, the enclave is probable only at the top, and a sovereign without a veto is not supported: owners, legislatures and courts used the vetoes the worst case says would vanish, though in Urbit the check came from the galaxy owners, not the ordinary users. [cite:de23_epoch_2025] [cite:de23_riotimes_icsid] [cite:de23_politifact_fc] Book Five turns from leaving the state to the tools that watch the people who stay, beginning with data and its fusion in [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four].

sections.h: The Address Space: a Map Drawn as Property
sections.html:
Urbit is a piece of software, and most of what it does is ordinary for a computer network: it runs a personal server, stores a user's data and sends encrypted messages to other users. What makes it matter to this book is the way its author divided the network's names. Every Urbit identity is a number, and the numbers were cut into a fixed hierarchy before anyone used them. At the top are 256 "galaxies," an 8-bit space. Each galaxy can issue 255 "stars," giving 65,280 in all, a 16-bit space. Each star can issue 65,535 "planets," about 4.29 billion, a 32-bit space, which is where ordinary users live; planets in turn issue "moons" for devices, and below them sits a practically unlimited tier of free "comets." [cite:de23_smith_burrows] [cite:de23_addrspace_2016] Since 2019 the register of who owns which identity has been kept on the Ethereum blockchain, in a set of contracts called Azimuth, and Tlon, the company that makes the main Urbit app, describes each identity as a cryptographic proof on Ethereum that a user holds much as one holds a digital token. [cite:de23_tlon_faq] [cite:de23_bloglist] [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] The company behind it is the subject of [scene:de5_tlon_exit_and_return|Part Five]; this section is about the map: who drew it, how he described it, and who came to own it.

What he called it

On 13 January 2010, writing as Mencius Moldbug on a short-lived technical blog, he introduced Urbit as "a programming environment specified as a single stateless, frozen function." He wrote that the hardest problem it faced was allocating the namespace, which runs into a known trade-off in computer science called Zooko's triangle: a naming system cannot easily be at once secure, decentralised and readable by people. His answer was a compromise, and he gave it a name. "This quasi-solution is a design I call digital feudalism," he wrote, "of which more later." [cite:de23_moronlab_2010] The magazine The Point, reviewing Urbit in 2022, reported that the project's 2010 whitepaper gave its section on address allocation the same title. [cite:de23_point_2022] Earlier versions of the hierarchy, according to a 2017 report in The Verge summarised by the sociologists Harrison Smith and Roger Burrows, named the tiers "Lords," "Dukes" and "Earls," and Yarvin derived the scheme from the libertarian theory of homesteading, John Locke's idea that a person comes to own unclaimed land by being the first to work it. [cite:de23_smith_burrows] Two later accounts, in Compact and The New Yorker, report that in his original design Yarvin gave himself the position of "prince." [cite:de23_compact_2025] [cite:de23_kofman]

The feudal vocabulary gave way to a property vocabulary when the project went public. In June 2016 Yarvin and his co-founder Galen Wolfe-Pauly published "The Urbit Address Space," which put the idea in one line: "If Bitcoin is money, Urbit is land," and Urbit was "digital land, not digital money." [cite:de23_addrspace_2016] A post the same summer, "Common Objections to Urbit," which the Urbit blog lists under Yarvin's identity, took the land comparison further: "Curtis invented Urbit. So by the homestead principle, he started out owning all of it." It likened the result to land ownership in a real city, "complex and asymmetrical," and described the government plainly: "Urbit is designed to govern itself collectively by address space ownership," which it called "effectively, 'proof of stake.'" [cite:de23_objections_2016] Four years later Urbit's blog still used the image, describing an Urbit identity as "a self-authenticating property title," and gave the practical reason for scarcity: "Urbit IDs are scarce in order to discourage spam and abuse." [cite:de23_value_2020] Compact reported that Yarvin has called Urbit "a transparent plutocracy," a phrase that means rule by owners in proportion to what they own, openly declared. [cite:de23_compact_2025]

The same texts stated an ideal that pulled the other way. The 2016 post said ownership had been deliberately scattered "across a diverse set of entities" so that the system would be "unlikely to collapse back into a single landlord," and it set out conventions to keep it that way: address blocks should split and never merge, galaxies and stars should have different owners, and galaxies should belong to individuals rather than corporations. It also admitted that Urbit "does not live up to these ideals at present." [cite:de23_addrspace_2016] "Common Objections" answered the charge that Urbit was not really decentralised with an argument that will be familiar to any reader of [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]: "When it's impossible to eliminate centralized power, it becomes necessary to tame, stabilize, and limit it." [cite:de23_objections_2016] Josh Lehman, who ran the Urbit Foundation from 2021, rejected the feudal label outright when a journalist put it to him in 2022: "No. Facebook is digital feudalism. When you don't have explicit hierarchies, it's way worse." [cite:de23_astra_2022]

Who owned the map

The first published distribution shows how concentrated the top tier was at the start. As of 1 June 2016, Tlon held 95 of the 256 galaxies; 50 were reserved for urbit.org, the future community foundation; 40 went to Tlon's employees and their families, 24 of them to Yarvin personally; 34 went to Tlon's outside investors, who are not named in the post; and 37 went to 33 other people, for donating, contributing code or winning contests. [cite:de23_addrspace_2016] No published document shows which investors received galaxies, or that Peter Thiel or his Founders Fund holds one; the investment by Founders Fund in Tlon itself is documented, and is set out in [scene:de5_tlon_exit_and_return|Part Five]. In 2020 the company explained the origin of its own holding in the same homesteading terms: all of the address space had once belonged to Yarvin, and "Tlon bought half the address space from Curtis." [cite:de23_value_2020]

An independent count three years later found the concentration largely intact. The researcher Francis Tseng calculated that as of 2019, 185 of the 256 galaxies were owned by Tlon, its employees and the employees of the Urbit Foundation, along with almost 38,000 of the network's roughly 65,000 stars, a calculation reported in Compact in 2025 under the verdict that "address space ownership is highly concentrated." [cite:de23_compact_2025] Smith and Burrows, using Tseng's shares, put Tlon at about 37 per cent, urbit.org at 19, Tlon employees at 15, outside investors at 13 and donors and contributors at 14. [cite:de23_smith_burrows] The founder's own share changed hands in January 2019. In "A Founder's Farewell," he wrote that he had reassigned his personal galaxies to urbit.org, which remained in Tlon's custody, and kept "a few thousand stars" in long time-locked contracts and a nonvoting minority stake in Tlon, which he said gave him no power over either. [cite:de23_farewell_2019] Urbit's own posts give him 24 galaxies in one place and 20 in another; the difference is not explained, and both describe the period before 2019. [cite:de23_addrspace_2016] [cite:de23_objections_2016]

Ownership of a galaxy carries a vote. The 2016 "Interim Constitution" set up a four-part structure on a Roman model, a consulate, a galactic senate of galaxy holders, a congress of stars and an assembly of planets, but stated that "for the interim, full authority is held by the (Roman style) consulate," which it described as effectively Tlon, and that the document "may be updated arbitrarily." It promised that Tlon would eventually "surrender governance of Urbit to its users." [cite:de23_constitution_2016] Once the register moved to Ethereum, the Galactic Senate became a working body written into the contracts: voting is "a power available to galaxies," on two kinds of proposal, upgrades to the contracts and documents recording decisions, with a quorum of 64 galaxies and an absolute majority at 129, and each vote closing at thirty days. [cite:de23_voting_docs] [cite:de23_governance_page] The Senate took its first concrete action, an upgrade to the contracts, in June 2021. [cite:de23_bloglist] Planets and stars have no vote. That is the plutocracy the founder described: the rulers are visible, and they are those who own the scarcest addresses.

What Urbit does, and for how many

In 2022 a star traded for about $6,000 on the open market and galaxies changed hands privately at values reported to exceed one million dollars. [cite:de23_point_2022] [cite:de23_astra_2022] By August 2024 the price of a star had fallen, on market data cited by CoinDesk, from a peak of about $27,000 in late 2021 to a little over $1,000. [cite:de23_coindesk_2024] An ordinary planet is no barrier to entry: Tlon's app generates one for each new user and keeps the keys on the user's behalf. "We custody the wallet for you, but it is yours," the company says, and a user can take full control and run the server alone. [cite:de23_tlon_faq]

The number of people using it has stayed small, and no audited count has been published. The Point in September 2022 described the system as "a bare-bones messaging server, with, at most, a few thousand active users." [cite:de23_point_2022] CoinDesk reported in May 2023 that the number of running Urbit servers had roughly doubled that year and that about 90 developers worked on it in a given month. [cite:de23_coindesk_2023] The New Yorker, after an estimated $30 million of investment over the project's life, found it closer to the Usenet discussion forums of the 1990s than to a feudal society. [cite:de23_kofman] The Foundation's blog in 2025–26 shows technical work continuing, including a new runtime and tools for running language models on a personal server, but gives no user figures. [cite:de23_bloglist] The main consumer product is Tlon Messenger, a chat app. [cite:de23_tlon_faq]

Two common claims about Urbit fail. It is not an anonymity tool: ownership and keys sit on a public blockchain, and each identity is a permanent, named account rather than a disguise. [cite:de23_tlon_faq] [cite:de23_smith_burrows] And no published report ties Urbit to crime or illicit use. What the design does is plainer. It makes identity scarce, ownable and saleable, and it gives the owners of the scarcest identities the vote.

Interpretation, not finding: the Patchwork in miniature

Smith and Burrows read Urbit as a working model of Yarvin's politics. Its constitution, in their reading, contains no democratic voice; it is "necessarily governed by a technocratic elite of stars and galaxies," and "the only liberty is exit," which makes it a digital companion to the sea colonies of [scene:de22_seas_and_zones|Part Twenty-Two] and to the Patchwork of sovereign corporations set out in [scene:de2_core_texts|Part Two]. [cite:de23_smith_burrows] The Sophia platform holds a similar reading: the address space as a charter written in code, with the owners as shareholders and the founder, at first, as the prince. The strongest counter-reading comes from the record. The scarcity has an engineering reason, spam, that has nothing to do with politics. [cite:de23_value_2020] Any user can leave at no cost, an exit no state offers so cheaply. The founder gave away his galaxies in 2019, and in 2025 a vote of the galaxy owners, not the founder, chose the Foundation's board. [cite:de23_epoch_2025] And the Foundation's own director called the explicit hierarchy fairer than the hidden one of a large platform, while its fullest outside portrait found a chat forum rather than a fief. [cite:de23_farewell_2019] [cite:de23_astra_2022] [cite:de23_kofman] On that reading the feudal names matched his politics, but what was built is a small, open, owner-governed network.

sections.h: The Wartime CEO: the Return, the Board Fight and the Owners' Vote
sections.html:
When Yarvin left in January 2019, he made more than one promise. "A Founder's Farewell" announced that he had resigned as chief technology officer, board member and voting shareholder of Tlon, that he had handed his galaxies to urbit.org, and that he would no longer contribute code to Urbit or write or speak about it in public. It also set out what the network had to be once he was gone: "The soil in which these flowers grow must be level and neutral." [cite:de23_farewell_2019] Two years later the project was split in two. Tlon, the company, kept building products, chiefly a chat app now called Tlon Messenger, and in 2021 it created the Urbit Foundation, a non-profit, to look after the open-source core of the system. [cite:de23_tlon_faq] [cite:de23_coindesk_2023] Josh Lehman became the Foundation's executive director the same year. [cite:de23_coindesk_2024] This section follows what happened when the money ran short, the founder came back, and the owners of the address space described in [scene:de23_address_space|the previous section] were asked to settle who was in charge.

The return, August 2024

By the summer of 2024 the Foundation was, in CoinDesk's words, "running out of money, with a runway measurable in months." In the week before 21 August its board dismissed Lehman and named Christopher Colby, the founder of a prediction-market start-up, as interim executive director; the Foundation's chief technology officer, Ted Blackman, and a senior engineer, Liam Fitzgerald, left. The board scrapped Lehman's plan to raise money by building a new blockchain layer on top of Ethereum, and the new strategy under discussion was a "utility token," possibly on Base, the network run by the exchange Coinbase. A board member said half the staff would be kept. [cite:de23_coindesk_2024] Another account says the Foundation "admitted that it had run out of capital" and that developers were being paid in address space. [cite:de23_compact_2025]

Yarvin explained his part in his own words. "Josh is an excellent peacetime CEO," he told CoinDesk, but the moment needed someone else: "For that, you need a wartime CEO." He held "no formal position at the foundation" but would lead its strategy, and he summed up the task as "We're here to fix this." [cite:de23_coindesk_2024] Noah Kumin, writing in the Mars Review of Books, reported that the return was announced at an impromptu public meeting and would be "in a big way." [cite:de5_kumin_mars] ARTnews and The New Yorker reported that several senior employees resigned in protest. [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] [cite:de23_kofman] Yarvin later described the state he found the project in as "controlled flight into terrain," a pilot's term for a working aircraft flown into the ground. [cite:de23_compact_2025]

The phrase he chose has a source. In April 2011 Ben Horowitz, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz, one of Tlon's original investors, published a much-read essay distinguishing two kinds of chief executive. "Peacetime CEO knows that proper protocol leads to winning. Wartime CEO violates protocol in order to win," he wrote; the wartime chief "neither indulges consensus-building nor tolerates disagreements." [cite:de23_horowitz_2011] [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] In start-up writing the idea is a management doctrine, not a political one. It is also close to the argument Yarvin has made for countries since 2008, that a state should be run by a single chief executive who need not win consent, which [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six] sets out from his texts. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] No document shows him linking the two, and the parallel is noted here as a parallel.

Two organisations and a senate

The return took place at the Foundation, not at Tlon, and the difference matters for what followed. Tlon is a company with shareholders. The Foundation is a non-profit whose board, under the network's rules, answers to the Galactic Senate, the 256 galaxies, which the Foundation later described as having a "duty to select the board of directors." [cite:de23_epoch_2025] One account notes that the relationship between the two bodies "was unclear to the casual user." [cite:de23_compact_2025] A founder without a title, a board of three and a senate of owners made an unusual chain of command, and 2025 tested every link.

The fight, 2025

Money remained the first problem. In February 2025 Yarvin sought new funding from Andreessen Horowitz, The New Yorker reported. [cite:de23_kofman] A newsletter writer reported in July that he had persuaded the firm to invest $4 million "in exchange for more address space," adding that he did not know the terms; no filing or named outlet has confirmed the amount. [cite:de23_rettig] The New Yorker also reported, from an unpublished draft of his, that his newest plan was to promote Urbit as an elite private club whose members would be the stars of a new public sphere. [cite:de23_kofman]

The leadership fight is documented only in community newsletters, and both writers declared an interest. On 6 July 2025 a writer publishing as Cordelia, who said she had known the Foundation's executive director Ryan Kneer for more than a decade and urged a vote in his favour, reported that the Foundation had had four executive directors in a year. Kneer, in charge for eight months, had "joined forces" with Yarvin the previous November. In late June or early July, she wrote, Kneer removed Yarvin from the board while Yarvin was lobbying the board's other two members to dismiss Kneer, and Kneer then called a vote of no confidence and asked the galaxy holders to replace the board; at the time of writing 19 galaxies had voted, 18 for and one against. [cite:de23_marbl] On 27 July a second writer, Lane Rettig, who said he owns some Urbit address space, described Yarvin as "Executive Director-by-fiat," quoted him calling the period "real Roman times," and called the Foundation "default dead," start-up slang for an organisation that will run out of money without new funding. [cite:de23_rettig] Yarvin's own account of the dispute has not been published, and neither newsletter quotes him on it.

The owners decide, October 2025

The outcome came from the Foundation itself. On 9 October 2025 it announced that "the Galactic Senate has elected to replace the board of the Urbit Foundation," after "multiple votes," with a three-seat board identified, as is the custom, only by Urbit names. The new board appointed a new executive director, ~sicdev-pilnup, in succession to ~sorreg-namtyv, Yarvin's Urbit identity, "who is leaving to found a new application development company" to build on the Urbit stack. [cite:de23_epoch_2025] [cite:de23_farewell_2019] The announcement admitted that the Foundation "struggled during periods of uncertainty around both funding and leadership," and said its outside capital had come from venture capitalists and Bitcoin philanthropists. [cite:de23_epoch_2025] It did not give the vote counts, say whether Kneer's July proposal was the one that passed, or name Yarvin's new company or its backers, and no named outlet has reported them.

Status as of October 2026: the Foundation has operated under that board and director for a year, publishing technical work through at least May 2026. [cite:de23_bloglist] Its accounts are not public, and the a16z investment reported in 2025 is the last reported financing. Tlon continues to run its messenger and hosting service. [cite:de23_tlon_faq] No named outlet has reported Yarvin's return to a role at the Foundation, or further changes to its governance, since the October 2025 announcement.

What the episode shows

[scene:de6_claims_vs_record|Part Six] graded the move from "A Founder's Farewell" to "wartime CEO" YELLOW, a reversal shown with his own explanation, and the fuller record leaves that grade where it was. He had promised to stay silent about Urbit and to leave it level and neutral; he came back to run its strategy without a title, explaining that the crisis needed a different kind of leader. The record also adds the end of the story: the owners' senate, not the founder, chose who would run the Foundation, and the founder left to start something else. [cite:de23_farewell_2019] [cite:de23_coindesk_2024] [cite:de23_epoch_2025] No account documents coercion, misuse of money or any wrongdoing by anyone in the dispute.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis is the Sophia platform's, not a finding. For Book Four it reads exit in its worst case: not an escape open to anyone who wants to leave a state, but an enclave for the few, in which owners rule without a veto from the people who live there, a rehearsal for the sovereign executive the theorists describe. Both kinds of exit in this book, the physical zones of [scene:de22_seas_and_zones|Part Twenty-Two] and the digital one in this part, can be tested against it.

Documented: the design of Urbit rule by ownership, in its author's own words. He called its naming scheme "digital feudalism," its government "proof of stake" and, by one account, "a transparent plutocracy"; only galaxies vote; and the top tier was concentrated in the hands of the company, its staff and its foundation, 185 of 256 galaxies in 2019. [cite:de23_moronlab_2010] [cite:de23_objections_2016] [cite:de23_compact_2025] Documented, too, is the founder returning in a crisis to lead the Foundation's strategy without a title, under a phrase whose source text says the wartime leader does not tolerate disagreement; one newsletter writer called him executive director "by fiat." [cite:de23_coindesk_2024] [cite:de23_horowitz_2011] [cite:de23_rettig] Among the physical zones, Próspera's company-run charter on a Honduran island, set out in [scene:de22_prospera_v_honduras|Part Twenty-Two], led to an arbitration claim against Honduras first put at up to $10.775 billion; in their memorial of 15 October 2025 the claimants sought restitution or, in the alternative, $1.63 billion in damages, and the case was pending on the merits as of October 2026. [cite:de22_po6] [cite:de23_riotimes_icsid]

Probable: that Urbit's design carried its author's politics. The vocabulary is his and documented, from "digital feudalism" in 2010 to "accountable monarchies" in a 2024 podcast, but he also insisted the network be neutral, and no document states that Urbit was built to demonstrate his political program. [cite:de23_moronlab_2010] [cite:de23_blockworks] [cite:de23_farewell_2019] Probable, too, that exit was costly at the top and cheap at the bottom: a galaxy was reported at over a million dollars in 2022, while an ordinary user's identity is issued free by the main app. [cite:de23_astra_2022] [cite:de23_tlon_faq] The enclave, on this record, is the governing tier, not the network.

Not supported: that any exit project has worked as a sovereign without a veto. The record runs against it at every level. In Urbit the founder was checked: the galaxy owners used their vote, replaced the board, and a new director succeeded him as he left. [cite:de23_epoch_2025] The check came from the same narrow tier the design empowers, not from the users; holders of planets still have no vote, and their remedy remains to leave, which they can do at no cost. [cite:de23_voting_docs] [cite:de23_tlon_faq] The network is small, and no published report links it to crime or to the machinery of the state. [cite:de23_point_2022] In Honduras, the host state's Congress repealed the law on private zones in April 2022 and its Supreme Court ruled the zones unconstitutional on 20 September 2024. [cite:de23_riotimes_icsid] In the United States, the 2023 pledge of ten "Freedom Cities" on federal land had produced no bill, executive order or land action by 2026, and was rated stalled ([scene:de22_argentina_and_freedom_cities|Part Twenty-Two]). [cite:de23_politifact_fc] What exit has needed, in each case, is a host's law and an investor's money, and the hosts' legislatures, courts and owners have used the vetoes the worst case says would vanish. Who enforces a charter against the person holding power, the question [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight] asks of Yarvin's state, was answered in his own network by a vote of the owners; [scene:de33_two_tests|Part Thirty-Five] sets that answer beside the federal government's experience, and these grades are carried into [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three].

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Four
chapters.title: The Toolkit I: Data
chapters.intro: Book Five turns from leaving the state to the tools that watch the people who stay, and it begins with data. The first section maps the records that already exist about most American adults and can be bought or borrowed: data brokers and the two investigative databases immigration enforcement licenses, fusion centres, licence-plate cameras, and the government's own files opened to new uses since 2025. The second reads what the apps on a phone, the artificial-intelligence assistants and the shops say they keep, and judges the court cases against them by what actually changed. The third tests the promise on which the commercial trade rests, that data stripped of a name stays anonymous, and describes, as a mechanism rather than a documented practice, how an integration platform could turn an unnamed trail into a person. Each section ends by asking what these systems could do if they were joined, graded from documented to not supported, and the part closes by testing the book's worst-case reading.
chapters.outro: The data layer is documented: records on most adults are sold or shared, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has licensed LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters databases since 2021, and in August 2026 required the LexisNexis feed to connect to "the Palantir platform." [cite:de24_bu_lexis] [cite:de24_lawnext_tr] The government's own files were opened to enforcement from 2025, and the courts pushed back in part, finding 42,695 unlawful IRS disclosures and pausing Medicaid sharing after a January 2026 dataset reached Palantir over a Teams chat. [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de24_npr_medicaid_pal] Anonymity is the weakest link: three facts single out 63 to 87 percent of Americans, and four location points 95 percent. [cite:de24_golle_2006] [cite:de24_sweeney_2000] [cite:de24_demontjoye_2013] No record shows these tools used against critics for their speech or derived from the Dark Enlightenment texts; they were built under both parties from 2003 on. [cite:de24_psi_fusion] [cite:de24_upi_vigilant] The next part turns to the records the state already holds on benefits, schooling, work and credit, beginning with [scene:de24b_benefits|benefits].

sections.h: The Data Layer: Brokers, Cameras and the Government's Own Files
sections.html:
Book Five puts the same five questions to every tool it examines: what the tool collects or does, who uses it and under what contract, where it has been misused or got things wrong, what the law and the courts allow, and what its worst use would look like. The last belongs to the book's working hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and never a finding. Throughout, capability is not intent: what a tool can do is a documented fact, and its use against a critic needs a document of its own. This section begins with the layer every other tool draws on, the records about people that already exist and can be bought, borrowed or joined. Palantir's platforms and the rule that lets an agency buy what it could not seize without a warrant are in [scene:ow9_ice|ICE, the sole-source contracts and the data they run on] and [scene:us10_us|the United States section of US vs Israel].

What a data broker holds

California, which keeps a public register, defines a data broker as "a business that gathers and sells consumer information that a consumer didn't give them directly." More than 500 were registered there by the end of 2025. [cite:de24_ca_drop] Their raw material is ordinary paperwork: property and court records, vehicle registrations, marketing lists, and "credit header" data, the identifying top lines of credit files (name, addresses, birth date, Social Security number). Brokers match records on shared keys and sell searchable access. The intelligence agencies buy too. A report for the Director of National Intelligence, declassified on 12 June 2023, found that the intelligence community acquires a "significant amount" of commercially available information and that such data "can reveal sensitive and intimate information about individuals." [cite:de24_lawfare_odni]

One episode shows how far an ordinary record can travel. The National Consumer Telecom and Utilities Exchange, a group of utility and telephone companies, licensed the names, home addresses, Social Security numbers and other details of more than 170 million people to the credit bureau Equifax, which sold them on as "utility header data" into investigative databases including Thomson Reuters' CLEAR. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) paid tens of millions of dollars for access to it through CLEAR. After The Washington Post reported it in February 2021 and Senator Ron Wyden pressed the exchange, it told Equifax to stop selling new data in October 2021, and Equifax stopped supplying it to law enforcement on 23 October 2021; data sold before then remained in use. [cite:de24_globe_utility]

The two investigative databases

Two companies, better known for legal research, supply most of the commercial records ICE searches. LexisNexis Risk Solutions holds a contract signed in February 2021, under President Biden, worth about $24.5 million, that gives ICE its Accurint and LexID people-search tools; a 2021 change added jail-booking data. ICE users ran more than 1.2 million Accurint person searches between March and September 2021. The contract was due to end on 31 August 2026, and on 10 August 2026 ICE gave notice of a $6.7 million sole-source bridge whose work statement says the system "must connect through application programming interfaces" to ICE applications including "the Palantir platform". [cite:de24_bu_lexis] An application programming interface, or API, is a standard doorway through which one program asks another for data automatically, without a person typing each search.

Thomson Reuters' CLEAR was renewed for the Department of Homeland Security without competition from 31 March 2026, on the justification that "only CLEAR provides the range of law enforcement data the agency requires"; the data types listed include utility data, credit reporting bureaus and licence-plate records. The company told the legal-technology writer Bob Ambrogi that it does "not comment on specific customer contracts" and that "Palantir is not a customer of CLEAR." [cite:de24_lawnext_tr] Which ICE contracts these are, set beside the Palantir awards, is listed in [scene:de28_ice_contracts|the ICE contracts section].

Fusion centres

A fusion centre is a state or city intelligence office where police, federal agents and analysts share reports and records so that, in principle, a clue held by one agency reaches another. The model spread after the attacks of 11 September 2001 with federal money. A bipartisan Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations inquiry, led by Senators Tom Coburn, a Republican, and Carl Levin, a Democrat, reported on 2 October 2012. It counted more than 70 centres and found that the Department of Homeland Security could estimate its spending on them since 2003 only as somewhere between $289 million and $1.4 billion. The intelligence its officers produced there was of "uneven quality – oftentimes shoddy, rarely timely," the subcommittee found,. [cite:de24_psi_fusion] The report also said the reporting was "sometimes endangering citizens' civil liberties and Privacy Act protections." [cite:de24_govexec_fusion]

Licence-plate readers
