An automated licence-plate reader (ALPR) is a camera that photographs every passing number plate, reads it by software and stores it with a time and a place. Millions of readings, searched together, show where a car has been. In February 2014 Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson cancelled an ICE request for a nationwide plate-tracking database, saying ICE's leaders had not known of it. [cite:de24_physorg_2014] In January 2018 ICE gained that access through a contract with West Publishing, part of Thomson Reuters, working with Vigilant Solutions; ICE called it "one tool in support of its investigations." [cite:de24_upi_vigilant]

The largest network today belongs to Flock Safety, whose cameras were in more than 4,000 communities by August 2025. On 25 August 2025 Flock paused pilot programmes with Customs and Border Protection and its investigative arm after Illinois' Secretary of State, Alexi Giannoulias, said an audit had found CBP searching Illinois plate data in breach of state law. "We clearly communicated poorly," said Flock's chief executive, Garrett Langley; federal searches would be labelled as such and limited to one police agency at a time. [cite:de24_ap_flock] In Woodburn, Oregon, a city audit found that the Department of Homeland Security and the Border Patrol ran 6,089 searches through a Flock trial between January and November 2025, although the police department's own policy barred immigration use; the city ended its contract at the end of April 2026. [cite:de24_katu_woodburn] The cameras also misread. In August 2020 police in Aurora, Colorado, held Brittney Gilliam's family at gunpoint after a misread, and the city paid $1.9 million. [cite:de24_eff_alpr]

The government's own files, reused

The newest change since 2025 is not a purchase but a reuse: records people gave the government for one purpose opened to another. The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system, long used to check benefit applicants' immigration status, was linked to Social Security data in May 2025 and from 15 August 2025 could check voters in bulk with only the last four digits of a Social Security number; election officials had run more than 33 million voters through it by September 2025. The state agreements let DHS use the data "for any purpose permitted by law," and no accuracy testing had been published. [cite:de24_npr_save] In April 2025 the Internal Revenue Service agreed to check names and addresses for ICE; a federal judge later found the IRS had broken the law "approximately 42,695 times," and an appeals panel upheld her block on 8 September 2026, while another panel had declined to block the sharing in February. [cite:us10_abc_irs_feb] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] For Medicaid, Judge Vince Chhabria ruled on 29 December 2025 that, for the twenty states that sued, health officials could pass ICE only five fields about people not lawfully present (status, address, phone, date of birth and Medicaid number), and no health records. [cite:de24_wt_medicaid] How each of these walls was built and breached is the subject of [scene:de30_silos_and_subpoenas|the section on the data walls], and the wider set of records the state already holds, on benefits, schooling, work and credit, is mapped in [scene:de24b_benefits|the benefits section], [scene:de24b_schools|the section on schools], [scene:de24b_work_and_vetting|on work and vetting] and [scene:de24b_credit_and_money|on credit and money]; the ICE tool reported to draw on Medicaid data is described in [scene:ow9_ice|the One-Way Mirror]. [cite:ow9_fortune_elite]

The Homeland Advanced Recognition Technology system (HART), meant to replace a 1990s database of faces, fingerprints and irises, was contracted to Northrop Grumman for $95 million in February 2018, under President Trump's first term. [cite:de24_wt_hart2018] In September 2023 the Government Accountability Office found it years late, $354 million over its earlier estimate and meeting 5 of 12 federal privacy requirements; the old system held over 290 million identities. [cite:de24_gao_hart] In August 2026 Kyle Schutt, who had worked with the Department of Government Efficiency, took over the biometrics office, with HART due to reach initial operation "no later than September 2026." [cite:de24_bu_schutt] Whether that deadline was met could not be confirmed as of October 2026.

If it were connected

The book's working lens for Book Five is that these mechanisms need not be joined today to matter: they exist, and in the worst case they could be joined. Each toolkit section therefore ends by naming the joins, what each would let a government do to a person, what step it would take, and what stands in the way, graded documented (it exists, with a source), probable (a contract, interface or legal authority already points to it), possible (technically feasible, with no document) or not supported (the record runs against it). "Possible" is used for joins between systems only, never for facts about people.

Commercial databases to the integration platform: documented as a requirement, probable as a working flow. The LexisNexis bridge's work statement requires interfaces to "the Palantir platform," which would put a person's addresses, vehicles and jail bookings into an ICE case file automatically; the contract is the step. [cite:de24_bu_lexis] Older ICE records, from 2014 to 2022, show the opposite arrangement for CLEAR, which agents were told to search separately because it was "not connected to Palantir tools." [cite:de24_guardian_icm] Medicaid records to the same platform: documented, once, beyond the court's limit. A dataset sent to ICE on 7 January 2026 went on to Palantir, which runs ICE's address tool, over a Microsoft Teams chat, according to a declaration filed by California; Palantir said it was purged "pursuant to government instruction," copies were later found with six users, and Judge Chhabria paused the sharing in late May 2026; after a hearing on 3 September 2026 no further ruling had been located as of October 2026. [cite:de24_npr_medicaid_pal] [cite:de24b_chn_medicaid] Plate readers to federal agencies: documented in pilots and now narrowed; a standing feed from a city network such as Flock into a federal platform is possible, with no document, and would need a new contract or a reversal of Flock's August 2025 limits and of state laws like Illinois'. [cite:de24_ap_flock] [cite:de24_katu_woodburn] Voter checks to enforcement: probable, because the state agreements already let DHS use uploaded data "for any purpose permitted by law"; no use beyond citizenship checks has been reported. [cite:de24_npr_save] How all six layers fit together is drawn in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|the ecosystem map].

What this layer documents is supply: records on most adults, sold or shared, with doorways built to let one system ask another. It does not document a single master file on every American, or the use of these sources to find a critic for speech. What the joining platform does is argued in [scene:de27_capability_not_intent|the Palantir part].

sections.h: What the Apps and the AI Companies Keep
sections.html:
The records in [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|the previous section] were mostly collected about people. This section turns to what people hand over themselves, through the apps on their phones, the artificial-intelligence assistants they type into, and the shops they buy from. The companies' own documents come first.

Inside the phone

An app can see what its permissions allow: precise or approximate location, camera, microphone, contacts, photos. Even without permissions it receives the phone's network address, model and settings. Many apps also carry a software development kit, or SDK, a ready-made block of code supplied by another company, often to count users, report crashes or serve advertisements; an "analytics SDK" reports how people use the app back to its supplier, and it inherits every permission the host app holds. That is how location data from a prayer app reached the military. Motherboard reported, in an investigation it followed up in January 2021, that Muslim Pro, downloaded more than 96 million times, had sent users' precise locations to the broker X-Mode, which sold location data to defence contractors, and that US Special Operations Command had bought access to products built on commercial phone-location data. Apple and Google banned X-Mode's code from their stores in December 2020. [cite:de24_vice_xmode] The market that grew from such code, and the federal agencies that bought from it, are followed in [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|the section on phone location].

Apps have also grown heavy. The analytics firm Sensor Tower found that the ten most-downloaded iPhone apps in the United States averaged about 2.2 gigabytes in May 2021, against about 550 megabytes at the start of 2016; TikTok and Instagram grew about sixfold. [cite:de24_imore_size] Part of the weight is machine learning: a trained "model", a large file of numbers that lets a program recognise images, sounds or language, can now run on the phone itself. Meta's engineers described in July 2025 models inside Instagram that cut a person out of a photo, inside WhatsApp that estimate network speed for calls, and inside Messenger that detect a message's language so that translation works while messages stay end-to-end encrypted, meaning only the sender and recipient hold the keys to read them. Meta presented this as privacy, "keeping data on users' devices." [cite:de24_meta_executorch] The size of an app is not in itself evidence of spying; most of it is code, models and stored media. What matters is what the code sends, and to whom.

The AI assistants

A chatbot receives every question and uploaded file, with the account and network address; the companies differ in how long they keep it, whether people read it, whether it trains models or feeds advertising, and who else can obtain it. OpenAI trains on the chats of its free and individual paid ChatGPT users by default, unless they switch off a setting called "Improve the model for everyone"; business and developer accounts are excluded, and even "temporary" chats may be kept for up to 30 days. [cite:de24_kaspersky_openai] Anthropic told users of its consumer Claude plans in August 2025 that they had until 28 September 2025 to choose whether their chats would train its models; chats from those who agreed would be kept for five years instead of 30 days, and business and education plans were excluded. [cite:de24_macrumors_anth] Google says a sample of Gemini conversations is read by human reviewers and that those are kept for up to three years even if the user deletes his or her history; with history switched off, chats are still held for 72 hours, and a general location is always collected. [cite:de24_gemini_hub] Meta announced on 1 October 2025 that from 16 December 2025 people's conversations with Meta AI would be used to personalise advertisements and content, with no opt-out except not using the assistant, and with conversations on religion, politics, health, sexual orientation and similar subjects excluded from ad use. [cite:de24_9to5_metaai]

Perplexity, an AI search company, says in its privacy policy of 31 October 2025 that it collects prompts, device identifiers, approximate location and network address, may use them to improve its models unless a user opts out, and receives data from "consumer marketing databases or other data enrichment companies" to tailor its own advertising; it states that it does not "sell" or "share" personal information as California law defines those words. [cite:de24_pplx_policy] Its chief executive, Aravind Srinivas, said on a podcast in April 2025 that the company's new browser was meant "to get data even outside the app to better understand you," adding, "we plan to use all the context to build a better user profile." [cite:de24_mb_srinivas]

All of it can be reached by legal process. OpenAI's policy requires a subpoena or court order for account details and a search warrant for content, and promises users notice unless the law forbids it. [cite:de24_openai_lep] In the second half of 2025 it received 75 requests for content and produced data in 62, and 224 requests for other records, producing data in 146. [cite:de24_openai_tr] Anthropic, much smaller, reported two content requests in the same period, both answered, and twenty for other records, seven answered. [cite:de24_anthropic_tr] A private litigant can reach further than either. In the New York Times' copyright suit, a magistrate judge ordered OpenAI on 13 May 2025 to preserve "all output log data that would otherwise be deleted"; the broad order ended in September 2025, but the company was required to produce a de-identified sample of 20 million consumer chat logs. [cite:de24_itg_nyt] The AI companies' contracts with the government, a separate matter, are in [scene:de26_ai_layer|the section on the AI layer].

The PayPal offer

On 3 September 2025 PayPal offered its and Venmo's users in the United States and some other markets "a free 12-month trial of Perplexity Pro valued at $200" with early access to the Comet browser, for first-time users, until 31 December 2025. The announcement says nothing about sharing data between the two companies. [cite:de24_paypal_pplx] Perplexity's policy covers the category in general terms: partners that give free access may send it information, and it shares information with them when a user signs up through their offer, without listing which fields. [cite:de24_pplx_policy] That is the whole documented link. No document shows PayPal payment data going to Perplexity, or Perplexity's prompts going to PayPal. Nor does the offer connect the network this book follows to either company today. Peter Thiel and Elon Musk were among PayPal's founders, as [scene:de9_paypal_palantir_facebook|Part Nine] and [scene:de11_zip2_xcom_paypal|Part Eleven] describe, but eBay bought PayPal on 3 October 2002 and spun it off as an independent public company in July 2015, and neither man appears among the directors nominated in PayPal's 2026 proxy statement. [cite:de11_ebay_8k] [cite:de13_rtp_spin] [cite:de11_pypl_proxy]

What the court cases changed

Fines and settlements make headlines; the test used here is whether practice changed. In Brown v. Google, settled on 1 April 2024, Google agreed to delete old private-browsing records, rewrite its disclosures and limit collection for five years, with no money for the class. [cite:de24_winston_brown] In Rodriguez v. Google, a jury awarded about $425 million in September 2025 for collecting app activity from users who had switched tracking off, but the judge refused a permanent injunction, finding no "prospective, irreparable harm," so nothing had to change. [cite:de24_mlm_rodriguez] Texas obtained $1.375 billion from Google in May 2025, with no admission; Google said the claims concerned "product policies we have long since changed." [cite:de24_hunton_txgoogle] Texas's $1.4 billion from Meta in July 2024 concerned a face-tagging feature that had already ended in November 2021, after an Illinois settlement. [cite:de24_bbl_txmeta] TikTok changed owners rather than practices: a joint venture led by Oracle, Silver Lake and the Abu Dhabi fund MGX took over its American business on 22 January 2026, retraining a licensed algorithm on American data, with ByteDance keeping nearly 20 percent. [cite:de24_axios_tiktok] The Justice Department's children's-privacy case against TikTok ended on 21 August 2026 in a $400 million settlement with no injunction, no finding of a violation, and the 2019 order against the company to be vacated. [cite:de24_hunton_tiktok]

The shopping basket

Retailers know a great deal. Kroger's data-science arm, 84.51°, builds shoppers' loyalty-card profiles and enriches them with broker data that can include estimated race and ethnicity, finances and employment, and sells insights drawn from them to the brands on its shelves; its policy says what it shares is "anonymized and aggregated." [cite:de24_npr_kroger] Target's statistician Andrew Pole described a model for predicting customers' pregnancies in 2010, later made famous by The New York Times; a much-repeated story of a father learning of his daughter's pregnancy from Target's coupons has never been substantiated. [cite:de24_kdn_target] On 17 January 2025 the Federal Trade Commission's staff reported that eight firms, among them Mastercard, JPMorgan Chase, Accenture and McKinsey, helped about 250 retailers vary prices using shoppers' location, timing and behaviour; the incoming chairman, Andrew Ferguson, who had dissented, closed the public inquiry days later. [cite:de24_rb_ftcpricing] No record shows a federal agency buying shopping baskets or loyalty-card histories. The documented commercial pipe into immigration enforcement carries identity, address, utility and plate records. [cite:de24_globe_utility] [cite:de24_lawnext_tr] Payment controls, which can stop a purchase rather than record it, are in [scene:de26_money_rails|the section on money rails] and [scene:de35_the_consequence_ladder|the consequence ladder].

If it were connected

Graded on the same scale as [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|the previous section]. AI chat records to an agency: documented, by legal process, one account at a time; OpenAI produced content under 62 of 75 warrants in late 2025. [cite:de24_openai_tr] A standing feed from a chat company to an agency would let investigators search what people ask machines about health, money or politics without a warrant per person; it would need a contract or a new law, and none is documented, so it is possible only. Marketing data into an AI company: documented, since Perplexity says it buys from consumer marketing databases for its advertising. [cite:de24_pplx_policy] The reverse, AI-company profiles sold to brokers: not supported, since the companies cited say they do not sell such data and no record shows it. Payment data from PayPal to Perplexity: possible, because Perplexity's policy permits unspecified exchanges with partners, but no document shows any. [cite:de24_pplx_policy] [cite:de24_paypal_pplx] Loyalty and basket data to immigration enforcement: possible, with a documented precedent in the utility records that reached ICE through Equifax and Thomson Reuters' CLEAR until 2021, and no record of any purchase. [cite:de24_globe_utility] One frequently misread join can be set aside. Palantir's software lists ready-made "connectors" to Facebook, Instagram, Twitter Ads, Slack and Microsoft Teams, for "connectivity between Foundry and your systems"; a connector reaches the customer's own accounts, not a platform's users, so a connector is not access. [cite:de24_pal_connectors] The documented case is humbler and more telling: the January 2026 Medicaid file reached Palantir through an ordinary Teams chat. [cite:de24_npr_medicaid_pal] Benefits, school and employment records, which hold more than any app, are in [scene:de24b_benefits|the part on records the state already holds].

The common thread is retention. Each of these companies keeps records it could, under subpoena or warrant, be made to hand over, and several keep more than before. That is a capability. The documented attempts to unmask government critics through technology companies, by administrative subpoena, are set out in [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|the section on brokers and doctrine]; whether any of these records stays anonymous once handed over is the next section's question.

sections.h: The Myth of Anonymous Data
sections.html:
Almost every company in [scene:de24_apps_and_ai_companies|the previous section] says that the data it shares is anonymous, aggregated, de-identified or hashed. The words mean different things. Data is anonymous only if it can never be linked back to a person. It is pseudonymous if the name has been swapped for a code, such as an advertising number or a customer ID, which still follows the same person from record to record. It is de-identified if obvious identifiers have been removed, which says nothing about whether the rest can be matched. A hash is the output of a one-way mathematical function that turns, say, an email address into a fixed string of characters; the same address always produces the same string. The Federal Trade Commission's technologists put the consequence plainly in July 2024: "hashes aren't 'anonymous' and can still be used to identify users," because a hash "still creates a unique signature that can track a person or device over time." [cite:de24_ftc_hashing]

Three facts about a person

The modern study of the problem began with Latanya Sweeney, a computer scientist, who in 1997 linked the Governor of Massachusetts, William Weld, to his own medical records using publicly available records. [cite:de24_wiki_sweeney] In a working paper of 2000 she estimated, from 1990 Census data, that 87 percent of Americans, 216 million of 248 million, were probably unique on just three facts: five-digit ZIP code, sex and date of birth; she noted that the voter list for Cambridge, Massachusetts, which carries those facts with names, could be bought for $20. [cite:de24_sweeney_2000] A recomputation by Philippe Golle on the 2000 Census put the share at 63 percent, lower but in his words in general agreement. [cite:de24_golle_2006] Both are estimates of likely uniqueness, not counts of people identified. In July 2019 a team led by Luc Rocher and Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye built a statistical model that estimated 99.98 percent of Americans would be correctly re-identified in any dataset with 15 demographic attributes, the kind of detail a marketing file routinely holds. [cite:de24_rocher_2019]

Four points in time and space

Movement and spending are more identifying still. In March 2013 Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye and colleagues studied fifteen months of phone-location data for one and a half million people and found that four points, each a place and an hour, were enough to single out 95 percent of them; making the data coarser helped little, because uniqueness fell only very slowly as the resolution dropped. [cite:de24_demontjoye_2013] In January 2015 the same lead author, with others, studied three months of credit-card records for 1.1 million people, stripped of names, and found that four purchases, each a shop and a day, identified 90 percent; knowing the price of a purchase raised the risk by 22 percent on average, and women were easier to identify than men. [cite:de24_demontjoye_2015] Tastes work the same way. When Netflix released "anonymous" film ratings for about 500,000 subscribers for a public prize contest, Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov showed that eight ratings with dates, two of them allowed to be wrong, picked out 99 percent of the records, and two ratings with dates sufficed for 68 percent; matching a few users to their public reviews on another site revealed what appeared to be their political preferences. [cite:de24_netflix_2006]

From the laboratory to the newsroom

Journalists then did with commercial data what the researchers had predicted. In December 2018 The New York Times reported that at least 75 companies received precise, supposedly anonymous location data from phone apps, that several claimed to track up to 200 million American devices, and that one database logged a phone's position as often as every two seconds. The companies said the data was tied "not to someone's name" but to a unique code; the reporters followed one such code to a mathematics teacher in upstate New York, Lisa Magrin, from her home to a weight-loss meeting and a dermatologist's office. [cite:de24_nyt_2018] A year later the paper's opinion desk obtained a single file of more than 50 billion location points from over 12 million phones in 2016 and 2017, traced the movements of a senior Defense Department official, and concluded that "it's child's play to connect real names to the dots"; the law professor Paul Ohm told it that precise location over time is "absolutely impossible to anonymize." [cite:de24_nyt_2019] In July 2021 a Catholic newsletter, The Pillar, bought commercially available app location data from an unnamed vendor, matched a device to the general secretary of the US bishops' conference, Monsignor Jeffrey Burrill, and reported his use of a dating app; he resigned before publication, and the app's maker, Grindr, called the report a "witch hunt" and said it did not believe it was the source. [cite:de24_ap_pillar] It showed that anyone with money, not only a state, could do it.

The industry has also linked codes to names on purpose. Researchers at IMDEA Networks in Madrid, Radboud University and KU Leuven reported on 3 June 2025 that from September 2024 Meta's Facebook and Instagram apps on Android listened on hidden local channels inside the phone, so that a Meta tracking code on an ordinary website could pass the browser's anonymous cookie to the app, which sent it to Meta with the logged-in account. It worked in private browsing and after cookies were cleared. Meta "paused" the feature the same day, citing "a potential miscommunication" with Google over its app-store rules. [cite:de24_reg_localhost] The FTC's hashing warning drew on similar cases, among them a counselling service, BetterHelp, which the commission said shared hashed email addresses with Facebook knowing they would be matched back to people. [cite:de24_ftc_hashing]

How a fusion platform would join it

What remains is to describe, as a mechanism and not as a documented use, how a data-integration platform of the kind Palantir sells could turn a stripped trail into a named person. Each step below rests on a documented capability; the chain as a whole has not been documented in any specific case. A location trail tied to an advertising number, of the kind brokers sell (see [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|the section on phone location]), rests most nights at one address. An address is a key in the investigative databases ICE already licenses: LexisNexis's Accurint lets users search by name, address, Social Security number and licence plate, and its 2026 work statement requires a direct API connection to "the Palantir platform." [cite:de24_bu_lexis] An ICE legal memorandum obtained by the American Civil Liberties Union argued that location data tied to advertising numbers rather than names falls outside the Supreme Court's warrant rule for phone records, which is the legal premise for buying it. [cite:ow9_aclu_adid] And an ICE tool reported in January 2026 already gives each target's address a "confidence score." [cite:ow9_fortune_elite]

The platform does not collect; it joins what its customer loads, and Palantir describes itself as a "data processor" whose customers control their own data. [cite:de24_guardian_icm] [cite:de24_npr_medicaid_pal] Whether that is a limit or only a description is argued in [scene:de27_capability_not_intent|the Palantir part]. The anonymity the commercial trade relies on does not survive a well-stocked identity database, and agencies hold such databases already.

If it were connected

The joins this section turns on, graded as in [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|the first section]. Phone-location trails to ICE: documented. ICE bought licences through Penlink for Tangles and Webloc, tools that can watch a city block for phones and follow a device home, and its own legal analysis says the data "can be queried without a warrant." [cite:de24_404_webloc] Those trails to the identity databases: probable, since the LexisNexis work statement names Penlink as one of the systems its data must reach. Those trails to the Palantir platform: possible; the same statement lists Penlink and "the Palantir platform" as separate destinations, and no document shows a Penlink-to-Palantir feed. [cite:de24_bu_lexis] Seized-phone contents, student-visa records and airline passenger data to ICE's Palantir case system: documented in Homeland Security Investigations records from 2014 to 2022, which describe agents importing Cellebrite phone extractions and searching the student-visa database SEVIS and the airline-manifest system APIS. [cite:de24_guardian_icm] What travel records hold, and who can stop a person travelling, is in [scene:de25b_who_knows_you_travel|the section on travel records]. Together, these joins would let an agency start from an unnamed dot on a map and end with a name, a home, a car and a file, which is what the flow above describes. The steps in the way are a warrant rule for bought data, which does not exist, and the court orders and contract terms that limit particular sources, which do. The whole system, layer by layer, is drawn in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|the ecosystem map].

The worst-case reading, tested

Documented: that records on most American adults can be bought or borrowed, and that immigration enforcement buys them. ICE paid for Accurint from 2021 and ran more than 1.2 million searches in seven months; it bought CLEAR, which carried utility records on more than 170 million people until October 2021 and was renewed without competition in 2026; and in 2026 it required its LexisNexis bridge to connect directly to "the Palantir platform." [cite:de24_bu_lexis] [cite:de24_globe_utility] [cite:de24_lawnext_tr] Documented, too, that the government's own files were opened to enforcement from 2025: Social Security data inside SAVE, tax addresses and Medicaid contact data. [cite:de24_npr_save] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de24_wt_medicaid] And documented that "anonymous" commercial data can be named by anyone with money and a second database. [cite:de24_nyt_2019] [cite:de24_ap_pillar]

Probable: that the pieces described in the flow above can be joined for an individual target, since each is in place and the software is built to join. What would settle it is a record of one case run that way. None has been published. [cite:ow9_fortune_elite] Probable, also, that reuse of civil records will continue to widen while the courts are divided: one appeals panel declined to stop the IRS sharing in February 2026 and another upheld a block in September. [cite:us10_abc_irs_feb] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep]

Not supported: that the data layer has been used to find critics for their speech; the documented attempts to unmask critics ran through administrative subpoenas to platforms, set out in [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|the section on brokers and doctrine]. Not supported: that agencies buy shopping baskets or loyalty-card histories. Not supported: that any of these tools was designed from, or ordered because of, the Dark Enlightenment texts. Federal money for fusion centres dates from 2003, ICE's plate-data access from 2018, the LexisNexis contract from 2021; they were built and bought under presidents of both parties, and a later policy that rhymes with a theorist's wish is not thereby his (see [scene:de1_spine_and_overlay|Part One]). [cite:de24_psi_fusion] [cite:de24_upi_vigilant] [cite:de24_bu_lexis]

The record also runs against the worst case in specific places. A Democratic administration cancelled ICE's first plate-database request in 2014; utility data stopped flowing in 2021 after press reports and a senator's pressure; a court found 42,695 unlawful IRS disclosures and limited Medicaid sharing to five fields; Flock paused its federal pilots after a state audit, and an Oregon city tore its cameras down; California now lets residents send one deletion request to every registered broker. [cite:de24_physorg_2014] [cite:de24_globe_utility] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de24_wt_medicaid] [cite:de24_ap_flock] [cite:de24_katu_woodburn] [cite:de24_ca_drop] What none of them touches is the purchase itself: the House passed a bill to require warrants for bought data in April 2024, and it did not become law. [cite:ow9_cs_4thact]

These grades are carried into [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|the closing scorecard].

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Five
chapters.title: The Records the State Already Holds
chapters.intro: The tools in [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|the toolkit part on data] were bought or built; the records in this part were already in the state's hands, or one request away, because people handed them over to get help, go to school, take a job or borrow money. The first section follows benefit files: how eligibility is checked against dozens of other records, and how Medicaid, food-aid and cash-aid data moved toward immigration enforcement in 2025 and 2026. The second turns to schools, where a federal privacy law protects education records but not the cameras of a school's police unit, and to the student-visa database built for enforcement. The third follows the gates to work, from E-Verify and payroll databases to the continuous vetting of millions of federal workers and the revocation of security clearances. The fourth traces credit files, the Treasury's payment and debt machinery and a cash-reporting order aimed at the southern border, and closes with the part's test of the worst-case reading. Each section ends by grading which joins between these records are documented, probable, possible or not supported.
chapters.outro: This part found that the state's own records moved toward enforcement in 2025 and 2026 along routes that were mostly legal and mostly visible. Food-aid records from at least 27 states were run through the DHS system SAVE, a Medicaid file covering millions reached Palantir's enforcement software by mistake and was ordered purged, and a notice opening cash-aid records to DHS took effect after a court declined to block it. [cite:de24b_npr_snap27] [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] School records stayed protected while cameras run by school police did not, answering 620 immigration searches on one district's network in a month. [cite:de24b_ed_leu] [cite:de28_74_flock] Work and money gates were largely built before 2025 and under both parties, from E-Verify to continuous vetting and the offset program, but the regulator's guidance on worker scores was withdrawn, Do Not Pay was opened to wider data sharing, and clearances were revoked from officials accused of politicising intelligence. [cite:de24b_ev_manual] [cite:de24b_bu_cv] [cite:de24b_cs_withdraw] [cite:de24b_eo14249] [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] The brakes that held were specific statutes and courts. No record shows a single file joining all of these for any person. [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|The next part] turns from records people hand over to the location their phones give away.

sections.h: Benefits: The Records of Need
sections.html:
A person who asks the government for help with food, health care or rent hands over more about themselves than almost anyone else does: income, employer, household members, address, Social Security number and, for non-citizens, immigration status. This section describes how those records are matched and what crossed from them to immigration enforcement in 2025 and 2026, picking up where [scene:de30_silos_and_subpoenas|the section on silos and subpoenas], on the legal walls around tax, Social Security and the first round of Medicaid sharing, leaves off. As throughout this book, a capability is a fact; its use against a given person needs a document of its own.

How eligibility is checked

"Data matching" means running one list of people against another, usually by Social Security number, name and date of birth, and flagging where the two disagree. In February 2021 the Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's auditor, reviewed six programmes: housing vouchers, Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, formerly food stamps), the Earned Income Tax Credit, home-energy aid and Supplemental Security Income. It found 34 electronic sources in use to verify income or assets: 13 federal, 14 state and 7 commercial. All six programmes drew on state unemployment records. The cost, GAO noted, falls on applicants, who face delays and extra burden when records disagree. [cite:de24b_gao_21183]

The largest commercial source is a single company's database. The Work Number, run by Equifax Workforce Solutions, holds pay and employment data "collected from employers and payroll processors," and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau lists government agencies among its users, for public-assistance eligibility and child-support enforcement. [cite:de24b_cfpb_twn] On 2 February 2026 Senators Elizabeth Warren, Ron Wyden and Bernie Sanders wrote to Equifax's chief executive that about half the states use it, that per-query prices had risen by 126 per cent in Colorado and 120 per cent in Kansas over four years, and that the company had called the 2025 budget law's new work requirements "a big positive" for its business. [cite:de24b_warren_equifax] [cite:de24b_warren_letter] The law signed on 4 July 2025 requires adults in the Medicaid expansion group aged 19 to 64 to show 80 hours a month of work, community service, a work programme or half-time education, starting 1 January 2027; as of 5 October 2026 the start date had not been delayed. [cite:ad8_ccf_ifr] [cite:ad8_audit_hfn_gov] It also extended SNAP's work rule to adults aged 18 to 64. [cite:ad11_mn_snap] Proving hours is a data-matching job. The senators' letter recalled that when Arkansas imposed a Medicaid work requirement in 2018, about 18,000 people lost coverage in under a year. [cite:de24b_warren_letter]

Food aid: the SNAP demand

SNAP is run by the states with federal money, so the federal Department of Agriculture (USDA) did not hold recipients' files. In May 2025 it told states to send them: names, dates of birth, home addresses, Social Security numbers and benefit amounts going back to 2020. By October 2025 at least 27 states, with about 15.7 million enrollees, had complied or were in the process; A USDA official's court filings said the department was running the data through SAVE, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) system built to check immigrants' eligibility for benefits and since linked to Social Security records. USDA's June 2025 notice allowed disclosure, where a record "indicates a violation or potential violation of law," to the appropriate federal, state, local, tribal or foreign agency. USDA said it needed the data to find waste, fraud and abuse. [cite:de24b_npr_snap27]

Twenty-one states and the District of Columbia sued. Judge Maxine Chesney of the federal court in San Francisco found the planned uses "well beyond those permitted" by the SNAP law, issued a temporary order in September 2025 and, on 15 October 2025, barred USDA from withholding administrative funds from the plaintiff states. [cite:de24b_npr_snap27] When USDA renewed its demand in December and threatened again to stop paying states' administrative costs, she said in February 2026 that the government still could not force the states to comply, and on 26 February expanded her order, finding a cut-off likely "contrary to the SNAP Act." [cite:de24b_wcax_snap] [cite:de24b_bl_snapfeb] No later ruling lifting the order had been reported as of October 2026. The map is divided: records in complying states went to USDA and through SAVE; records in the suing states did not.

Medicaid after the December ruling

On 29 December 2025 Judge Vince Chhabria let the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) give Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) five fields about people not lawfully present in the suing states: status, address, phone, date of birth and Medicaid number, and no medical records. [cite:de30_bl_medicaid] The data sent went beyond that. Federal officials admitted that a dataset sent on 7 January 2026 covered millions of people, including people in the country lawfully. On 30 April Chhabria warned: "If the federal government cannot be sufficiently careful then it can't use the information." In late May he paused CMS-to-ICE sharing for enforcement. Court filings in July then showed that ICE had passed the January dataset to Palantir, which runs ELITE, the app ICE agents use to see the addresses of possible deportation targets. The government said the file had been shared in a Microsoft Teams chat and deleted from it. Palantir said: "the dataset in question was purged pursuant to government instruction." CMS then re-sent the same file by mistake, and a wider search found half a dozen users still holding copies. [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] At a hearing on 3 September 2026 the judge said valid visa holders' data should not be shared and that the question had to be settled "category by category"; no formal ruling had been located as of October 2026. [cite:de24b_chn_medicaid]

Cash assistance: TANF

Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), the federal cash-aid programme, went the other way in court. The Department of Health and Human Services published a notice allowing recipients' information to be disclosed to other federal, state or private entities, including DHS, to check that states follow programme rules, among them immigration-status rules. Two dozen states and the District of Columbia asked for an injunction. On 28 September 2026 Chief Judge James Boasberg refused it: the states had offered "vague, unsubstantiated predictions" about immigrant communities' fears, and DHS had not said it would use the data for enforcement. The notice took effect on 30 September 2026. [cite:de24b_bl_tanf]

If it were connected

Each join is graded: documented (it exists, with a source), probable (a contract, notice or authority already points to it), possible (feasible, no document) or not supported (the record runs against it). Medicaid records into Palantir's enforcement software: documented, once, by mistake, in court filings, and stopped by a judge. [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] SNAP records into SAVE: documented, from USDA's own filings, for the complying states. [cite:de24b_npr_snap27] SNAP records onward to ICE: probable rather than documented, because the June 2025 notice already permits disclosure to any agency where a record suggests a possible violation, and no transfer has been reported. TANF records to DHS: documented as an open route since the disclosure notice took effect on 30 September 2026; the court noted that DHS has not said it will use them for enforcement. TANF records onward to Palantir's systems: possible, with no document. [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] Payroll data from The Work Number to ICE: possible. No document shows it, but an Equifax-held dataset has reached ICE before: utility records on more than 170 million people flowed through Equifax into a people-search service ICE used, until 2021. [cite:de24_globe_utility]

The joins that matter most for people who are not immigrants run through work requirements. From 2027 the same matching that checks income will check hours, and a mismatch will end coverage unless the person answers in time. That is documented as design; how many eligible people lose cover through errors is not yet known. What stands in the way of the wider joins is specific: the SNAP law's data-security terms, Medicaid confidentiality and Judge Chhabria's categories, and the Privacy Act's rule that a new use be published first. The TANF case shows that last brake is procedural: a published notice can open a route, and a court may decline to stop it before harm is shown. The records people hand over to schools are the next section's subject.

sections.h: Schools: The Longest File
sections.html:
A school record is often the first file the state keeps on a person and among the longest kept: attendance, grades, discipline, special-education plans, counselling notes, and now the alerts produced by software that reads what students type on school laptops. Colleges add financial-aid forms that carry parents' incomes and Social Security numbers, and for foreign students a federal immigration database tracks enrolment itself. This section sets out who holds these records, which law protects them and where it stops, and what reached enforcement in 2025 and 2026. As elsewhere in this book, a tool's capability is documented as a fact; its use against a given person or group needs its own document.

FERPA and the camera outside its reach

The main federal shield is the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974 (FERPA), which limits what schools may release from a student's "education records" without consent, subject to listed exceptions such as a health or safety emergency. The definition matters more than the rule. Records that a school's own law-enforcement unit, such as a district police department, creates and maintains for law-enforcement purposes are not education records at all, so FERPA's protections do not apply; their release is governed by school policy and state law, and the Education Department advises schools to keep them separate. [cite:de24b_ed_leu] The same applies to cameras. Surveillance video that a law-enforcement unit creates and keeps for a law-enforcement purpose is not an education record; a copy handed to the principal for a disciplinary case may become one. [cite:de24b_ed_video]

That gap became concrete when school districts bought licence-plate cameras from Flock Safety, the company whose network of automatic plate readers is described in [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|the toolkit part on data]. Flock lets customers share their camera data with other agencies across its network. An investigation by The 74, published with The Guardian on 10 February 2026, examined logs from six Texas districts. On the eight cameras of one district, Alvin, more than 3,100 agencies ran more than 733,000 searches in a single month from December 2025 to January 2026, and 620 of those searches, from 30 agencies, cited immigration reasons. The districts themselves showed no immigration searches, and Flock said customers control their sharing settings. [cite:de28_74_flock] The camera sat at a school, but its data was not a school record.

Software that reads students' writing

Thousands of American schools now use software that scans students' school accounts and devices around the clock for signs of self-harm, violence or bullying and alerts staff. Gaggle is used in about 1,500 districts; GoGuardian and Securly sell similar products. In March 2025 the Associated Press and The Seattle Times reported that a public-records request to Vancouver Public Schools in Washington had returned nearly 3,500 unredacted student documents behind links with no password, that at least six students had potentially been outed to school officials after writing about their sexuality or gender, and that a 2023 RAND study had found "scant evidence" of either benefit or harm. Gaggle said it had since restricted the links to logged-in users after 72 hours. [cite:de24b_ap_gaggle] In Lawrence, Kansas, an AP analysis of public records found more than 1,200 alerts in ten months, nearly two-thirds judged non-issues by school officials and more than 200 set off by homework; nine current and former students sued the district in federal court in August 2025, alleging violations of free speech and unlawful searches. The district declined to comment on the pending case. [cite:de24b_ljw_lawrence] No record links these monitoring products to immigration enforcement.

The files that follow a student

Two larger stores sit above the school. Since November 2005 the federal Institute of Education Sciences has given grants of up to $20 million each to build Statewide Longitudinal Data Systems, which link individual student records from early learning through college and into the workforce, a span the programme calls "P-20W." [cite:de24b_nces_slds] They exist to measure what schooling does for earnings; they are also, by design, a join between education and employment records held by a state.

At the federal level, the Education Department holds the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA), whose accounts hold applicants' and parents' identifying and financial details, and the loan records of more than 42 million borrowers. [cite:us17_ci_defaults] In 2025 financial-aid advisers warned families with an undocumented parent that filing carried some risk; as of May 2025 no sharing of FAFSA data with DHS had been documented, and none is documented since. [cite:de24b_nasfaa_fafsa] What is documented is access from inside: GAO reported on 29 September 2026 that teams from the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) had access to more than 23 systems across four agencies including Education, and that Education gave GAO no record of their background investigations. [cite:de19_gao_sixagency] How defaulted loans reach wages and tax refunds is the subject of [scene:de24b_credit_and_money|the last section of this part].

SEVIS: the one school file built for enforcement

Foreign students are different, because their school record is an immigration record. The Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), run by ICE, records each student's enrolment, and a terminated record can end a student's lawful status. Freedom-of-information records from 2014 to 2022 show ICE's investigations branch training agents in March 2020 to search SEVIS's 4.9 million records through its Palantir case system. [cite:de24_guardian_icm] In the spring of 2025 more than 1,800 international students had their SEVIS records terminated or their visas revoked, many after checks against the FBI's criminal database; at a court hearing on 25 April 2025 the Justice Department said records would be reactivated while ICE wrote a new policy. The association of international educators, NAFSA, said the reasons given had "ranged from wholly absent, to conflicting, to downright baseless." [cite:de24b_pie_sevis] The use of visa status against student speech, and the court ruling on it, are in [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|the section on brokers and doctrine].

If it were connected

Graded as in [scene:de24b_benefits|the previous section]. School-adjacent cameras into immigration searches: documented, through Flock's sharing network, with the district not the searcher. [cite:de28_74_flock] SEVIS into Palantir's case system: documented for 2014–22 records. [cite:de24_guardian_icm] FAFSA into immigration enforcement: possible. The data would let an officer find a parent's address through a child's aid form; it would need a new disclosure notice or agreement, and none is documented. [cite:de24b_nasfaa_fafsa] Monitoring alerts into police or immigration files: possible, and the FERPA line explains how: an alert passed to a school police unit and kept there would leave FERPA's protection. [cite:de24b_ed_leu] No case of it is documented. State longitudinal systems into enforcement: possible in principle, not supported by any record; they are state-held, and the plainest brake is state law. The strongest protection for a child's file is its dispersal across thousands of districts and fifty states. The weakest point is definitional: a record moved into the hands of a school's police unit, or a camera feed shared across a vendor's network, is no longer an education record. Work and vetting records come next.

sections.h: Work and Vetting: The Gates to a Job
sections.html:
Most adults meet the state's records not at a border but at a job. Before a first day of work an employer may check a new hire's right to work against federal databases, verify past pay through a commercial service, and buy a background report; anyone who works for the federal government or holds a security clearance is now checked not once but continuously. Each of these gates draws on records described elsewhere in this book, and each can close. This section sets out how they work, who decides, what notice and appeal exist, and what changed in 2025 and 2026. A gate's existence is documented; its use against a particular person for a political reason needs a document of its own.

The right to work: E-Verify

E-Verify is an online system run by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). An employer enters the details from a new hire's Form I-9, the federal employment-eligibility form, and the system checks them against Social Security Administration and DHS records. Congress created it in 1996, in the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, as a pilot. It is voluntary for most employers but required for those holding covered federal contracts and, in some states, by state law. [cite:de24b_ev_manual] When records disagree the result is a "mismatch," which, the system's own guidance says, "does not necessarily mean" the worker is unauthorised; the worker has ten federal working days to say whether they will contest it, and if they do not respond the employer may close the case. [cite:de24b_ev_tnc] Because it reads Social Security records, any change to those records travels with it. In April 2025, about 6,300 immigrants DHS had identified as people on a terrorist watch list or with FBI criminal records were entered into Social Security's list of the dead; AP reported that the people affected were in the country legally and that without a working number they could not legally work. [cite:de30_ap_ssadead] The broader repurposing of Social Security data for checking voters is in [scene:de30_silos_and_subpoenas|the section on silos and subpoenas].

Past pay and background reports

The second gate is commercial. The Work Number, the Equifax payroll database described in [scene:de24b_benefits|the section on benefits], also sells employment and salary verification to employers and lenders, along with, according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), criminal-record, driving-record and drug-test information. [cite:de24b_cfpb_twn] Background-screening firms assemble similar reports from court records and data brokers. The Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), the law that governs credit reports, also governs these when they are used for employment: the employer needs the worker's permission, must give a copy of the report before taking adverse action, and the screening company must follow reasonable procedures for accuracy and investigate disputes. [cite:de24b_cfpb_circ]

On 24 October 2024 the CFPB issued a circular saying that the newer products of workplace monitoring, among them dossiers that include collective-bargaining activity and algorithmic scores built from keystrokes, browsing and time off-task, some of them predicting union activity, are often consumer reports under the same law, carrying the same duties. On 12 May 2025 the bureau withdrew it, among 67 guidance documents, saying such guidance does not create rights and some had read the statute too broadly. [cite:de24b_cfpb_circ] [cite:de24b_cs_withdraw] The law itself did not change; what was withdrawn was the regulator's statement that it reaches worker scores.

Continuous vetting

Government work adds a deeper gate. Under a reform called Trusted Workforce 2.0, the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which vets about 95 per cent of the federal government, enrolled every national-security clearance holder in "continuous vetting" by October 2021: automated, ongoing checks of criminal, terrorism and financial databases and public records, including credit data. In September 2024 DCSA said more than 3.8 million people were enrolled and began extending continuous checks of arrest records to the much larger "public trust" workforce in non-security posts; social media was not then checked. [cite:de24b_bu_cv] The software behind it, the National Background Investigation Services system (NBIS), has been in development since 2016. GAO testified on 24 February 2026 that $2.4 billion had been spent through 2024 on it and the older systems, with $2.2 billion more projected to 2031, that the reform's completion had slipped to the end of 2028, and that continuous-vetting alerts needing human review had risen from about 30,000 a quarter in 2023 to more than 100,000 in mid-2025. [cite:de24b_gao_nbis]

The military's own personnel records are held in other systems. On 16 March 2026 the Army ordered $3.68 million of work from Palantir to support its Personnel Data Environment, a personnel-data system, through 15 November 2026, under the Army's enterprise agreement with the company; the order sustains a system that already existed. [cite:de24b_govly_pde] What data it holds beyond personnel records, and any link to the Army's retention decisions, is not documented. The rules that let the civil service reclassify and dismiss policy staff are in [scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|the section on RAGE and the new schedules].

Clearances as a political gate

A clearance is also a decision, and in 2025 it became a visible one. On 19 August 2025 the Director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, revoked the clearances of at least 37 current and former national-security officials, among them people involved in the 2016 assessment of Russian election interference and members of President Biden's National Security Council. The memo accused them of "politicization or weaponization of intelligence"; according to a source who saw it, it cited no specific evidence. Gabbard wrote that a clearance "is a privilege, not a right." [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] In 2025 executive orders against four law firms, Perkins Coie, Susman Godfrey, WilmerHale and Jenner & Block, had restricted their lawyers' clearances and access to federal buildings over the firms' past clients and hires. Four district judges found the orders unconstitutional; the Justice Department moved to withdraw its appeal in March 2026, reversed itself within a day, and argued it before the D.C. Circuit on 14 May 2026, and no ruling had been reported as of October 2026. At least nine other firms settled, pledging pro bono work. [cite:de24b_gma_lawfirms]

If it were connected

Graded as in [scene:de24b_benefits|the first section of this part]. Social Security records into E-Verify: documented, by design; the April 2025 death-file entries show that a change made for an immigration purpose reaches a person's ability to work. [cite:de30_ap_ssadead] [cite:de24b_ev_manual] Financial and criminal databases into continuous vetting: documented, for more than 3.8 million clearance holders. [cite:de24b_bu_cv] Social media into continuous vetting: possible, and DCSA has said public profiles may be added; it was not checked as of 2024. [cite:de24b_bu_cv] Non-immigration flags pushed into E-Verify, so that a job check turns on something other than work eligibility: not supported by any record, and it would need a change in law. Workplace monitoring scores sold to the government: possible, with no document; the withdrawn circular shows that such scores exist and that the regulator has stepped back from them. [cite:de24b_cfpb_circ] Palantir's Army personnel work joined to its immigration systems at ICE: not supported; they are separate orders for separate customers, and nothing shows data moving between them. [cite:de24b_govly_pde]

The clearance revocations are the one place in this part where a gate already closed on people the government described as political opponents. They did not depend on joined data; they depended on discretion. The law-firm orders show the other side: where a clearance sanction reached private lawyers for their clients, four courts said no. How credit and payment records complete the set is the last section's subject.

sections.h: Credit and Money: The Ledger Behind a Name
sections.html:
The last set of records the state can reach is financial: the credit files that private bureaus keep on almost every adult, the payments the federal government makes and the debts it says it is owed, and the reports banks and money transmitters must file about their customers. Some of these the government holds itself; others it can buy or compel. This section explains how each works, what changed in 2025 and 2026, and what joins are documented. Bank surveillance reports and account closures in both political directions are treated in [scene:de26_money_rails|the section on money rails]; this section adds the credit file, the Treasury's payment and debt machinery, and a reporting order aimed at the southern border.

The credit file

Three private bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, hold files on most American adults: accounts, balances, payment history, past addresses and employers. The Fair Credit Reporting Act limits who may obtain a full report to those with a "permissible purpose," such as a lender or, with consent, an employer. One section carves out the government: notwithstanding those limits, a bureau "may furnish identifying information respecting any consumer" to a government agency, meaning name, current and former addresses, and current and former places of employment. [cite:de24b_justia_1681f] That top block of a credit file, often called "credit header" data, is also sold onward. Thomson Reuters' people-search service CLEAR, renewed without competition for DHS from 31 March 2026, lists credit-bureau data among its sources, along with utility records and licence-plate reads. [cite:de24_lawnext_tr] The precedent for a bureau's data reaching immigration enforcement is documented: utility account records on more than 170 million people, held by an industry exchange and licensed to Equifax, flowed into CLEAR and were used by ICE until Equifax stopped supplying law enforcement in October 2021 under pressure from Senator Ron Wyden. [cite:de24_globe_utility]

The Treasury as the government's payment hub

Almost every federal payment, from tax refunds to Social Security to contractor invoices, is disbursed by the Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service, which is why access to its systems was among the first disputes over the Department of Government Efficiency in early 2025 ([scene:de19_the_access|Part Nineteen]). On 25 March 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14249, "Protecting America's Bank Account Against Fraud, Waste, and Abuse." It requires payments to pass Treasury "pre-certification verification" before they go out, including checks that payees are not dead, through the Treasury's Do Not Pay system, and tells Treasury to "minimize administrative barriers to accessing and using data," including by waiving the Privacy Act's computer-matching requirements where it can. Agencies had 90 days to change their published records notices to allow disclosure to Treasury. The order excludes data "such as health records." [cite:de24b_eo14249] In August 2025 the budget office told agencies to add those disclosures and offered a four-year waiver of formal matching agreements, while keeping safeguards: a written agreement, a public notice with 30 days for comment, independent checking of any match, and notice to people found, with the right to contest. It also called Do Not Pay "poorly managed over the last four years." [cite:de24b_omb_m2532] On 22 September 2025 Treasury announced that Palantir would build a "common API layer" within the modernisation of the Internal Revenue Service; an API, or application programming interface, is a standard doorway through which one program asks another for data. No value or data scope was published. [cite:de27_treasury_api]

Debts collected from payments

The Treasury Offset Program (TOP) works in the other direction: it takes money owed to the government out of money the government pays. An agency owed a federal debt more than 120 days overdue must refer it; before referral it must send the debtor a letter at least 60 days in advance offering a chance to pay, agree a plan or dispute the debt. When a federal payment is about to go out, the payee's name and taxpayer number are compared with the debtor list, and the payment is cut. [cite:de24b_fs_top] A tax refund can be taken in full; Social Security retirement benefits and federal salaries up to 15 per cent, though disability and Supplemental Security Income payments are excluded. Unpaid child support and some state debts are collected the same way. In the year to September 2020 TOP and the IRS's parallel levy programme collected $10.4 billion. [cite:de24b_crs_top] The largest group exposed in 2026 was student borrowers: 9.3 million were in default on federal loans by 30 June 2026, owing $234 billion. [cite:us17_ci_defaults] The Education Department paused offsets and wage garnishment on 16 January 2026, and as of 19 October 2026 planned to resume garnishment that autumn, with no date set. [cite:ad7_natp_pause] [cite:ad7_ci_garnish] The debts at issue were real and the process had notice; what the machinery shows is how one flag in one database reaches every federal payment to a person.

A border-zone reporting order

Banks and money transmitters must already file a currency transaction report with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), a Treasury bureau, for cash dealings over $10,000. [cite:de26_aba_fincen] A "geographic targeting order" lowers that threshold in named places for a limited time. On 11 March 2025 FinCEN ordered money transmitters, currency exchanges and check cashers in 30 ZIP codes in Texas and California to report cash transactions from $200. Plaintiffs told the courts they lost 50 to 60 per cent of their customers in the one week it applied. On 13 July 2026 the Ninth Circuit upheld an injunction in southern California, holding that the order was likely a rule that needed public notice and comment and that FinCEN had not weighed its costs. [cite:de24b_orrick_gto] FinCEN reissued narrower versions; the order of 2 September 2026 sets a $1,000 threshold in ZIP codes of five Texas and three New Mexico counties, drops Arizona and California, requires identity checks, and runs to 1 March 2027. A Texas court's injunction covers only members of the trade association that sued. [cite:de24b_mofo_gto]

If it were connected

Graded as in [scene:de24b_benefits|the first section of this part]. Credit-bureau identifying data to immigration enforcement: documented, through the statute's government carve-out and through resellers whose products ICE buys. [cite:de24b_justia_1681f] [cite:de24_lawnext_tr] Agency records into Treasury's payment checks: documented as policy, through the order and the August 2025 memo. [cite:de24b_eo14249] [cite:de24b_omb_m2532] Palantir's Treasury API layer joined to its immigration systems at ICE: possible, with no document; the Treasury work's data scope is unpublished, and nothing shows a link. [cite:de27_treasury_api] Debt flags used to stop payments for non-financial reasons, such as a fine for protest conduct: not supported; the offset rules require a legally enforceable debt and prior notice. [cite:de24b_fs_top] Border cash reports into immigration investigations: probable, since DHS personnel already run hundreds of thousands of searches of FinCEN reports a year and the order targeted the border, but no use against a named person is documented. [cite:de26_aba_fincen] What stands in the way is mostly procedural law: the Privacy Act notices the memo still requires, the notice-and-comment rule that sank the first border order, and the offset statute's debt and notice requirements.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis for this part is that records collected to give people help, schooling, work and credit can be turned into a single instrument of enforcement. Documented: civil records crossed to immigration enforcement in 2025 and 2026, from SNAP files run through SAVE in at least 27 states to a Medicaid file that reached Palantir's software by mistake; school-adjacent cameras answered 620 immigration searches in a month; continuous vetting checks the criminal and financial records of more than 3.8 million people; and clearances were revoked from officials the government accused of politicising intelligence. [cite:de24b_npr_snap27] [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] [cite:de28_74_flock] [cite:de24b_bu_cv] [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] Probable: SNAP records moving on to ICE under a notice already in force, and border cash reports feeding investigations; the TANF route to DHS has been open since 30 September 2026, and no enforcement use of it is yet shown. Not supported: a single score or file joining benefits, schooling, work and credit for any person, or any of these records used against a critic outside the clearance cases. [cite:de24b_bl_tanf]

The record also runs against the hypothesis in plain ways. Courts blocked the SNAP demand for 22 jurisdictions, paused Medicaid sharing after the overshare, struck down the law-firm orders and enjoined the first border order. [cite:de24b_bl_snapfeb] [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] [cite:de24b_gma_lawfirms] [cite:de24b_orrick_gto] Most of the machinery predates 2025 and was built under both parties: E-Verify in 1996, continuous vetting by 2021, the offset program and eligibility matching well before 2025. [cite:de24b_ev_manual] [cite:de24b_bu_cv] [cite:de24b_gao_21183] What changed is direction: data collected to verify eligibility began to move toward enforcement, and the brakes that held were statutory and specific. Where a person is, and what their phone reports, is the subject of [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|the next part].

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Six
chapters.title: The Toolkit II: Where You Are
chapters.intro: This part follows the tools that can tell where a person is and what is on the devices they carry. The first section explains the three ways a phone reports its location, how app and advertising data became a product that federal agencies buy without a warrant, how the telephone companies sold location and searched call records for police, and what the courts decided in 2018 and 2026. The second section separates three kinds of phone tools that are often confused, remote spyware, forensic extraction and fake phone towers, and traces Pegasus, Paragon's Graphite, Cellebrite, GrayKey and cell-site simulators through American contracts, foreign abuses and the rules that apply. The third turns to cars, wearables and the connected home, distinguishing what such devices could collect from what their makers say they collect and from what the state has documentably obtained, and closes with the book's test of its worst-case reading against the part as a whole.
chapters.outro: The documented record in this part is one of capability bought under both parties and limits set mostly by courts and regulators. Federal agencies have bought app-derived location since at least 2020, broke their own privacy rules in doing so, and in 2026 the FBI said it still buys such data and ICE was shown to hold a tool that watches neighbourhoods for phones. [cite:de25_vice_venntel] [cite:de25_oig_ctd] [cite:de25_tc_patel] [cite:de25_404_webloc] The Supreme Court made geofence access a search and upheld nearly $200 million in fines on carriers that sold location, but no court has ruled on purchased data. [cite:de25_crs_chatrie] [cite:de25_rec_fcc] ICE revived a paused spyware contract in August 2025 and confirmed its use in April 2026, though the department later said it had "no relationship" with the maker; it also holds extraction tools for phones and cars and cell-site simulators bought under Biden and Trump alike; the documented spyware abuse in this part was abroad, in Italy and Serbia. [cite:ow10_tc_lyons] [cite:de25_npr_paragon] [cite:de25_tc_tosv] [cite:de25_cl_cancellato] [cite:de25_ci_serbia] Cars, televisions and doorbells collect more than most owners know, yet the state reaches them case by case, and no government purchase of such data is on the record. Of the joins between these tools and the platforms that link records, two are documented, broker identity data required to reach ICE's Palantir platform and phone extractions imported into Palantir tools in 2014–22; the rest are possible, not documented. [cite:de25_bu_lexis] [cite:de25_gdn_palantir] [cite:de25_wm_letter] [cite:de25_mb_samsung] [cite:de25_cnn_ring] [scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|Part Twenty-Eight] turns to the tools that identify faces and watch from above, the code and cloud beneath them, and the money rails.

sections.h: Where the Phone Says You Are
sections.html:
Book Five asks the same five questions of every surveillance tool: what it collects or does, who uses it and under what contract, where it has been misused or got things wrong, what the law and the courts allow, and what its worst use would look like. The last question is the book's working hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and never a finding, in which immigration enforcement is the occasion for building a machine that could later be pointed at anyone. A tool's ability is a documented fact; its use against critics needs a document of its own. [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four] described the data brokers, licence-plate cameras and fusion platforms that join records into a picture of a person, and [scene:de24_the_myth_of_anonymous_data|the section on anonymous data] showed why a trail stripped of a name rarely stays nameless. This section follows the most revealing single kind of record those systems hold: where a phone, and so its owner, has been.

Three ways a phone reports its location

A mobile phone gives away its position by three separate routes, each held by a different company and each reached by the state in a different way. The first is the carrier. To deliver calls and data, a phone keeps connecting to nearby cell towers, and the carrier logs which tower and which side of it the phone used. This is called cell-site location information. In a city, where towers are close together, it can place a phone within a block or two; in the countryside, within a few kilometres. A "tower dump" is a request for every phone that connected to one tower in a stretch of time, which in practice means thousands of people who had nothing to do with the matter under investigation. The second route is the phone's own operating system. Phones fix their position from satellites (GPS) and nearby Wi-Fi networks, often to within a few metres, and companies such as Google kept that history on their servers; a "geofence" request asks such a company for every account that was inside a drawn area at a given time. [cite:de25_crs_chatrie] [cite:de25_wlox_tower]

The third route runs through the apps on the phone, and it is the one that grew fastest. Many free apps carry pieces of code supplied by other companies, called software development kits or SDKs, which can report the phone's position back to the supplier. Others show advertisements. Every phone has an advertising identifier, a string of letters and numbers (on Apple devices the IDFA, on Android the AAID) that advertisers use to recognise the same device across apps without knowing its owner's name. When an app with an empty advertising slot opens, an auction is held in the milliseconds before the advertisement appears. The Federal Trade Commission's technologists described it in December 2024: the app's publisher offers the slot on an exchange, advertisers bid, and to help them decide, the exchange often sends details "like location or personal characteristics" to dozens of bidders at once, of whom only one wins. [cite:de25_ftc_rtb] That stream of auction data is called the bidstream. A company that takes part in enough auctions can collect location points from millions of phones without ever showing an advertisement. The FTC's staff put its view in five words: "location data is sensitive data, full stop." [cite:de25_ftc_rtb]

The sellers and what regulators found

The FTC's cases against location brokers, brought in 2024 and 2025, set out how the trade worked. In January 2024 it reached its first settlement with a location broker, X-Mode Social, later renamed Outlogic. The commission said X-Mode sold precise locations tied to advertising IDs that were not anonymised and could be matched to individuals' visits; until May 2023 it had no way of removing visits to clinics, places of worship or shelters; and its hundreds of clients included "private government contractors." [cite:de25_ftc_xmode] In December 2024 the FTC alleged that Mobilewalla had kept data from advertising auctions it lost, against the exchanges' rules. [cite:de25_wh_mobilewalla] [cite:de25_ftc_rtb] On 14 January 2025, by five votes to none, it finalised an order against Gravy Analytics and its subsidiary Venntel, which it said had collected location data without consent "for commercial and government uses." The order bars them from selling or using sensitive location data, with an exception for "limited circumstances involving national security or law enforcement." [cite:de25_ftc_gravy] Each of these orders regulates how a seller treats consumers. None stops a government agency from buying.

The buyers, under both parties

Federal purchases began in Donald Trump's first term and continued under Joe Biden and in Trump's second. The Wall Street Journal reported in February 2020 that Venntel sold phone-movement data to government agencies, which had used it to find border crossings and make arrests. On 5 August 2020 Customs and Border Protection paid just under $476,000 for "Venntel Software"; a CBP spokesperson said the agency had "acquired limited access to commercial telemetry data," the government's term for app-derived location. Senator Ron Wyden's office found that the criminal investigators of the Internal Revenue Service had used Venntel data under a year-long contract and failed to locate any targets with it. [cite:de25_vice_venntel] Local police bought the same kind of data more cheaply. An investigation by the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the Associated Press, published on 1 September 2022, found that Fog Data Science sold access, for under $10,000 a year, to what it described as billions of location points from more than 250 million devices, with at least 18 local, state and federal clients, often searched without a warrant. [cite:de25_eff_fog]

In September 2023 the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security reported that CBP, ICE and the Secret Service had bought and used commercial telemetry data without following the department's privacy policies or completing the privacy impact assessments the E-Government Act of 2002 requires before such data is acquired. Auditors found shared accounts and passwords, ad hoc records and no supervisory review, and one CBP employee had used the data to track coworkers; the inspector general recommended that ICE stop using it until the assessments were approved. [cite:de25_oig_ctd] [cite:de25_hst_ctd] In 2025 ICE returned to the market through Penlink, a Nebraska company controlled since 2022 by the private-equity firm Spire Capital, which in 2023 bought the Israeli-founded Cobwebs Technologies and with it two products: Tangles, which gathers open-web and social-media material, and Webloc, which searches phone movements by place and time. In the autumn of 2025 ICE agreed to pay Penlink $2.3 million for licences to both; it bought the software, not the company. Penlink says its tools "exclusively use publicly or commercially available data." [cite:de25_ffp_penlink] [cite:de25_db_webloc] In January 2026 404 Media described its Webloc product as able to watch a neighbourhood for phones and follow them over time, using data from "hundreds of millions of phones"; an internal ICE legal analysis said it could be searched without a warrant. [cite:de25_db_webloc] [cite:de25_404_webloc] On 3 March 2026 seventy members of Congress asked the department's inspector general to investigate the no-bid Penlink contract. [cite:de25_keyt_letter] The full roster of ICE's data contracts is in [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty].

The FBI's position changed twice. Its director Christopher Wray told senators in 2023 that the bureau had bought location data in the past but was not doing so.
