On 18 March 2026 his successor Kash Patel, asked by Wyden to commit to not buying Americans' location data, said: "We do purchase commercially available information that is consistent with the Constitution and the laws." He named no broker and gave no number. [cite:de25_tc_patel]

The carriers

The telephone companies sold location too. The Federal Communications Commission found that AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile and Sprint had shared access to their customers' locations with "aggregators," which resold it to other brokers, without customers' consent and without "reasonable measures" to protect it. In April 2024 it fined AT&T about $57 million, Verizon about $47 million, T-Mobile $80 million and Sprint about $12 million, nearly $200 million in all. [cite:de25_rec_fcc] [cite:de25_wcc_fcc] The companies paid and sued, arguing that a penalty imposed without a jury trial was unconstitutional; the Fifth Circuit agreed with AT&T and the Second Circuit sided with the FCC against Verizon. [cite:de25_aa_fcc] On 4 June 2026 the Supreme Court upheld the fines by eight votes to one, in an opinion by Chief Justice John Roberts with Justice Clarence Thomas dissenting. [cite:de25_rec_fcc]

A second carrier arrangement served the police directly. In early September 2013 the New York Times revealed Hemisphere, a programme launched in 2007 in which AT&T employees worked alongside drug agents searching the company's call records; one slide told officials to "never refer to Hemisphere in any official document." [cite:de25_reg_hemisphere] The White House drug-policy office paid for it. Wyden's letter to Attorney General Merrick Garland of 20 November 2023 set out what had followed. Renamed Data Analytical Services, the programme searched records going back to 1987, to which about four billion were added each day, "trillions" in all; any federal, state, local or tribal officer could send a request to an AT&T analyst, often with an administrative subpoena rather than a warrant, and the searches did not have to concern drugs. Federal funding was paused in 2013 under Barack Obama, resumed in 2017 under Trump, paused in 2021 under Biden and restarted in 2022 with $270,000. [cite:de25_wyden_hemisphere] Its status after 2023 has not been reported.

What the courts have said

The Supreme Court has narrowed the old rule that information handed to a company loses its privacy. In Carpenter v. United States (2018) it required a warrant for a carrier's historical cell-site records. [cite:ow9_cornell_tpd] On 29 June 2026, in Chatrie v. United States, the Court ruled 6–3: Justice Elena Kagan, writing for five justices, with Justice Neil Gorsuch concurring in the judgment, held that obtaining Google Location History through a geofence warrant is a search under the Fourth Amendment; the case concerned a bank robbery, a 150-metre circle and an hour around the crime. The Court did not declare geofence warrants unconstitutional; it sent the case back to decide whether this warrant was adequate at each stage. Google had already said in 2023 that it would keep Location History on users' devices. [cite:de25_crs_chatrie] In August 2026 Judge Carlton Reeves of the Southern District of Mississippi went further for tower dumps, upholding a magistrate's refusal of requests covering towers near nine crime scenes and holding such warrants unconstitutional in every case: "The government cannot have access to an entire haystack because it may contain a needle." The ruling binds only that district. [cite:de25_wlox_tower]

Neither Carpenter nor Chatrie concerned data the government buys, and the FTC's orders bind sellers, not buyers; the doctrine that has grown in that gap, and the bills to close it, are the subject of [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty]. The errors are documented alongside the purchases: a year of IRS searches that found no one, a CBP employee tracking colleagues, and, in the Fog records, a babysitter in a Missouri murder case tracked although she was never a suspect. [cite:de25_vice_venntel] [cite:de25_oig_ctd] [cite:de25_eff_fog]

The worst-case extension follows from the table, not from any document of intent. Location bought from brokers needs no judge, already reaches hundreds of millions of phones, and can be searched by place: a protest, a clinic, a mosque or a meeting hall can be drawn on a map and the devices present listed. That is a capability the record establishes. That any agency has used it to list people at a protest or to find a critic is not documented in the record as of October 2026.

If it were connected

A location trail on its own names a device, not a person. Its power depends on what it is joined to, and the joins are graded here as documented (it exists, with a source), probable (a contract, interface or authority already points to it), possible (technically feasible, no document) or not supported (the record runs against it). The full map of these systems is drawn in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty].

Joined to identity records: documented. LexisNexis's Accurint service, which ICE uses, includes device-geolocation analysis alongside names, addresses, Social Security numbers and plates, and an ICE notice of 10 August 2026 required LexisNexis to connect by programming interfaces, the standard plugs by which one system queries another, to ICE applications "such as but not limited to" the Palantir platform and PenLink. [cite:de25_bu_lexis] Joined to the case-management and targeting systems that Palantir runs for ICE: possible for Penlink's location data. The same notice names PenLink and the Palantir platform as separate destinations for LexisNexis's identity data, which is not a feed from one to the other, and no document shows Webloc's output flowing into Palantir. [cite:de25_bu_lexis] [cite:de25_404_webloc] Joined to the government's own records of benefits, schooling and work, set out in [scene:de24b_benefits|Part Twenty-Five], so that a phone seen at a protest resolves to a name, an address and an eligibility file: possible; each piece exists, and the join would need only a query across systems an agency already licenses, but no record shows it. Joined to travel and border records ([scene:de25b_who_knows_you_travel|Part Twenty-Seven]), so that a location trail ends at a flagged boarding pass: possible, with no document. What stands in the way is thin: the FTC's orders bind sellers, the courts have not ruled on purchase, and the brake that remains is the agencies' own privacy rules, which their inspector general found they did not follow. [cite:de25_ftc_gravy] [cite:de25_oig_ctd] In April 2026 thirty-three members of Congress asked the Homeland Security department which commercial datasets sit inside its Palantir-built systems; no reply had been reported as of October 2026. [cite:de25_goldman_letter]

sections.h: Inside the Phone: Spyware, Extraction and Fake Towers
sections.html:
The location trail described in [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|the previous section] shows where a phone has been. A second family of tools goes after what is on it: messages, photographs, contacts, notes, passwords. They come in three kinds, governed by different law. Remote spyware is installed from a distance, without the owner touching anything. Forensic extraction tools copy a phone that investigators already hold, after an arrest, seizure or border inspection. Cell-site simulators are portable fake phone towers that make nearby phones reveal themselves. The Israeli origins of several of these firms, and Israel's own export controls, are set out in [scene:ow10_nso|the library's account of NSO] and [scene:ow10_paragon|of Paragon]; this section concentrates on their use in the United States.

One term needs defining first. End-to-end encryption, used by Signal, WhatsApp and Apple's iMessage, scrambles a message on the sender's phone and unscrambles it only on the recipient's, so a warrant served on the company carrying it yields at most who talked to whom and when, which is called metadata. It does not protect the phone at either end: a tool that runs on the phone itself reads the message after it has been unscrambled for display. That is why spyware and extraction tools matter more as encryption spreads. [cite:ow6_guardian_paragon] [cite:de25_fs_forecast]

How a zero-click attack works

The most closely documented example is FORCEDENTRY, an exploit used by the Israeli company NSO Group to install its Pegasus spyware on iPhones in 2021. Google's Project Zero researchers Ian Beer and Samuel Groß dissected it on 15 December 2021. The attacker needed only the target's phone number or Apple ID and sent a message through iMessage; the owner did not have to open it. A file named as a GIF image was in fact a PDF document containing a compressed image format called JBIG2. A counting error in the phone's JBIG2 decoder let the attacker write beyond the memory set aside for the image, and from there the attacker used more than 70,000 of the format's simple logical operations to assemble a small working computer inside the image decoder, which then ran the next stage of the attack. The researchers called it "one of the most technically sophisticated exploits we've ever seen." Apple fixed the flaw on 13 September 2021, after the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab found a sample. [cite:de25_pz_forcedentry] Each such exploit stops working once its flaw is found and patched.

Pegasus: blacklisted, tested and not deployed

The American record on Pegasus is one of purchase and refusal. The FBI bought it, paying NSO about $5 million, tested it for about two years at a facility in New Jersey, including a version called Phantom designed to work on American phone numbers, and on 22 July 2021 decided to "cease all efforts" to use it; the bureau says it never used it operationally. [cite:ow10_ai_nytmag] [cite:ow10_globe_fbi] On 3 November 2021 the Commerce Department put NSO on its Entity List, which bars American firms from supplying it without a licence, for providing spyware used to "maliciously target" officials, journalists and activists. [cite:ow10_doc_entity] In 2023 the New York Times reported that a contractor, Riva Networks, had used another NSO tool, the geolocation product Landmark, on the FBI's behalf after the ban; the bureau said it had been misled and ended the contract. [cite:ow10_9to5_riva] A California jury on 6 May 2025 ordered NSO to pay WhatsApp $167.25 million in punitive damages for hacking about 1,400 users; the judge cut that to $4 million in October 2025 and barred NSO from targeting WhatsApp, and in June 2026 WhatsApp sought a contempt finding for breach of that order. [cite:ow10_axios_jury] [cite:ow10_cs_inj] [cite:ow10_sw_contempt]

NSO has since changed owners and set out to win American business. It was reported in late 2025 to be controlled by investors led by the film producer Robert Simonds, with David Friedman, ambassador to Israel in Trump's first term, as executive chairman. [cite:ow10_rec_friedman] It issued a "transparency report" in January 2026, and its 2025 attempt to leave the Entity List was reported to have been refused. [cite:de25_wpn_nso] No removal from the list and no American government contract for Pegasus had been reported as of October 2026.

Graphite: bought, paused and revived at ICE

Paragon Solutions' Graphite, which can take over a phone without a click and read encrypted messaging apps, took the opposite path. ICE signed a $2 million contract for it on 27 September 2024. In October 2024 the Biden administration put the contract on hold for review under Executive Order 14093, Biden's March 2023 bar on federal use of commercial spyware that poses counter-intelligence risks or has been misused abroad. [cite:ow10_poulson_ice] [cite:ow10_eo14093] An American private-equity firm, AE Industrial Partners, agreed in December 2024 to buy Paragon. On 30 August 2025 ICE lifted the hold, and on 1 April 2026 its acting director, Todd Lyons, told members of Congress that Homeland Security Investigations was using the tool against foreign terrorist organisations, "particularly those involved in the trafficking of fentanyl," and had certified under the same executive order that it posed no significant counter-intelligence risk. [cite:ow10_reg_paragon] [cite:ow10_tc_lyons] The record after that is less clear than either side's statements. A procurement notice shows the contract closed out on 20 January 2026, before Lyons said he had approved the tool's use, and on 22 May 2026 the department told NPR that "ICE has no relationship with Paragon Solutions, Inc. or with the company that acquired them" and had signed no new contract, while declining to "confirm or deny" whether ICE still had the capability. The two accounts are consistent if ICE kept using what it had already bought; whether it does is not answered. [cite:de25_npr_paragon]

How a government customer used the same tool was tested in Italy. Early in 2025 WhatsApp told about 90 journalists and members of civil society that they had been targeted with Graphite; Citizen Lab confirmed infections among them, including two journalists at the news site Fanpage and activists of Mediterranea Saving Humans, a group that rescues migrants at sea. [cite:ow10_is_italy] In June 2025 the parliamentary committee overseeing Italy's intelligence services found that the targeting of the activists had been lawful and found no evidence that the Fanpage editor Francesco Cancellato had been targeted. In March 2026 prosecutors in Rome and Naples confirmed by forensic analysis that Cancellato's phone had been hacked; they could not reach the same conclusion for his colleague Ciro Pellegrino. Paragon had cancelled its contracts with Italy's two intelligence agencies and, as of April 2026, had not answered the prosecutors' request for information; Giorgia Meloni's government denies hacking journalists. [cite:de25_cl_cancellato] [cite:de25_tc_italy]

The law that governs Graphite's use inside the United States has not been set out in public. Criminal wiretaps of communications need a judge's order, and American judges authorised 1,735 of them in 2025. [cite:us10_usc_wiretap2025] Representative Summer Lee, one of the members who received ICE's April 2026 letter, said the agency had given no substantive answer on who could be targeted or under what legal authority inside the United States; an unnamed homeland security official said the technology supports investigations while respecting civil liberties. [cite:ow10_npr_lyons] The executive order remains the operative federal limit on commercial spyware, and it is a presidential order that a president can amend or revoke. [cite:ow10_eo14093]

Extraction: Cellebrite and GrayKey

Forensic extraction is far more common than spyware. A device made by Cellebrite, an Israeli company with about 7,000 customers, or GrayKey, made by the American firm Magnet Forensics, is connected to a phone that agents hold, exploits flaws in the phone's software to get past the lock screen, and copies its contents. [cite:de25_fs_forecast] [cite:de25_tc_graykey] ICE has bought Cellebrite since at least March 2017, when it spent $2.2 million, and in June 2019 it announced plans for a contract of up to $30–35 million. [cite:ow6_ipt_cellebrite] In 2025 its cyber-crime unit said no other product offered "equivalent capabilities" for "logical, file system, physical, and password data extraction." [cite:ow10_fs_cb] A Homeland Security forecast published in May 2026 planned a five-year contract with Cellebrite worth up to $100 million for ICE and HSI, covering phones and, after Cellebrite's purchase of a drone-forensics firm, drones; it called Cellebrite's tool "the most widely utilized and deployed computer forensic tool" in HSI. [cite:de25_fs_forecast] HSI signed a $3 million licence contract with Magnet Forensics in September 2025, which TechCrunch judged was most likely for GrayKey, after a $5 million GrayKey contract in 2024; ICE declined to say whether it uses the devices on the phones of arrested migrants. [cite:de25_tc_graykey]

The documented misuse came from a foreign customer. Amnesty International's Security Lab found that Serbian authorities had used a chain of previously unknown flaws, linked to Cellebrite's equipment, to unlock a student activist's Android phone while he was held by police in Belgrade on 25 December 2024, before an attempt to install spyware on it. On 25 February 2025 Cellebrite said it had "suspended product usage by certain Serbian customers." [cite:de25_ci_serbia] American critics point to reach rather than documented abuse: the Electronic Frontier Foundation objected to a Cellebrite feature that defeats the automatic restarts relocking seized phones, and Cellebrite answered that its tools require "valid legal authorization." [cite:de25_fs_forecast]

At the border, which [scene:de25b_who_knows_you_travel|Part Twenty-Seven] covers in full, the warrant rule that protects a phone elsewhere does not apply in the same way. Customs and Border Protection searched a record 55,318 electronic devices in the year to September 2025, about 17 per cent more than the year before; 50,922 of them were "basic" searches, a manual look through the phone that CBP may carry out without any suspicion, and 13,590 belonged to American citizens. [cite:de25_dn_cbp] [cite:de25_iptp_cbp]

Fake towers: cell-site simulators

A cell-site simulator, often called by the brand name Stingray, is a box, usually mounted in a vehicle, that imitates a phone tower so that phones nearby connect to it and give up their identifiers and location; some models can also intercept calls and texts. [cite:de25_tc_tosv] On 3 September 2015 the Justice Department required its agents to obtain a warrant on probable cause before using one, with exceptions for "exigent" and "exceptional" circumstances, barred their use to collect the content of communications in criminal cases, and ordered data deleted "as soon as that device is located, and no less than once daily." [cite:de25_doj_css] A 2023 audit by the Homeland Security inspector general found that the Secret Service and ICE "did not always adhere to statute and policies," and recommended controls to separate genuine emergencies from policy exceptions and to record data deletion accurately. [cite:de25_oig_css] ICE used simulators at least 1,885 times between 2013 and 2017 and at least 466 times between 2017 and 2019, and it bought simulator vehicles from TechOps Specialty Vehicles for $818,000 in September 2024, under Biden, and $825,000 in May 2025, under Trump. [cite:de25_tc_tosv]

Put together, the record shows an immigration agency that now holds every class of phone tool: remote spyware, extraction for seized phones, and fake towers for finding a phone in a crowd or a building. Most purchases predate 2025; the decisive change of 2025 was the revival of a spyware contract the previous administration had paused. The worst-case extension is plain from the capabilities. Graphite reads encrypted messages on the phone itself, and a simulator can sweep every phone near a gathering. ICE's stated use of commercial spyware is against drug-trafficking groups, and no document as of October 2026 shows any of these tools used in the United States against a journalist, an activist or a political critic. The Italian case shows that a government customer can turn such a tool on journalists and that discovery depended on a messaging company, an academic laboratory and prosecutors, not on the vendor. [cite:ow10_tc_lyons] [cite:de25_tc_italy] Which of these safeguards would operate in the United States, and which have actually stopped a tool, is examined in [scene:de26_counterweights|Part Twenty-Eight].

If it were connected

A phone tool yields contents: contacts, messages, photographs, the names and numbers of everyone a person deals with. Joined to a platform that links records, those contents become a map of a person's associates. Joined to extraction: documented. Internal ICE documents from 2014 to 2022, obtained by Just Futures Law and reported by the Guardian, show that agents could import phone extractions made with Cellebrite into Palantir's investigative tools and search the names and numbers found on them against the student-visa database SEVIS and airline passenger data. [cite:de25_gdn_palantir] Joined to spyware: possible, with no document showing a feed from Paragon's tool to Palantir's systems; members of Congress asked in April 2026 which datasets sit in DHS's Palantir-built systems and named Paragon and cell-site simulators among the tools of concern, and the department gave no public answer. [cite:de25_goldman_letter] [cite:de25_npr_paragon] Joined to the location purchases of [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|the previous section], so that a device seen in a neighbourhood is tracked, located with a simulator and then searched: possible, since ICE holds all three kinds of tool, but no document shows them used in sequence against one person. Joined to the government's records on work and security vetting in [scene:de24b_work_and_vetting|Part Twenty-Five], so that a seized phone's contents feed a clearance or employment decision: possible, with no document. What stands in the way of a wider join is mostly procedure: a warrant or border authority for each search, the spyware order's certifications, and the inspector general's findings that ICE did not always follow the simulator rules it already had. [cite:de25_doj_css] [cite:ow10_eo14093] [cite:de25_oig_css] The full set of joins is mapped in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty].

sections.h: The Car, the Wrist and the Living Room
sections.html:
The phone is not the only object that reports on its owner. A connected car, a watch, a television, a speaker and a doorbell each send some of what they sense to their maker. The distinction that matters here is between what a device could collect, a matter of its sensors, and what its maker says it collects, keeps and hands over, a matter of policy that can change with an update. The state can reach that data by three routes: a legal demand on the company, seizure of the device, or purchase in the market. This section takes the car, the body and the home in turn, and closes the part with the book's test of its worst-case reading.

Cars: the driving record and who gets it

Telematics is the term for the data a connected car sends home: location, speed, braking, acceleration, mileage. In March 2024 the New York Times reporter Kashmir Hill showed that General Motors' OnStar Smart Driver feature had passed drivers' trip records, including hard braking and rapid acceleration, to risk-profiling companies such as LexisNexis, which supplied insurers; some drivers' reports ran to hundreds of pages, and a salesman told her he always clicked "yes" on the enrolment screen himself. GM stopped sharing the data with brokers and ended Smart Driver. [cite:de25_mkt_gm] Texas sued GM in August 2024 on behalf of more than 1.5 million drivers whose data, it alleged, fed insurers' "Driving Scores." [cite:de25_tx_gm] In January 2026 the Federal Trade Commission, by two votes to none, finalised a 20-year order that bars GM for five years from sharing geolocation and driving-behaviour data with consumer reporting agencies, requires express consent for collecting or sharing connected-car data, and lets owners delete it and switch off precise location. [cite:de25_rdn_gm] [cite:de25_tc_gm] The case was about insurers, not police; no government purchase of car telematics has been reported.

Police reach car data by asking the manufacturer. Answers published by Senators Ron Wyden and Edward Markey on 30 April 2024 showed five automakers requiring a warrant for location and seven handing it over on a subpoena, which a prosecutor or agency can issue without a judge; Hyundai kept location for up to 15 years, and only Tesla told customers when the government asked. [cite:de25_wm_letter]

The second route is the car itself. Berla's iVe kit, plugged into a vehicle's infotainment system, recovers texts, call logs and contacts synced from a driver's phone, GPS tracks, and the times doors opened and the ignition turned on, across 20,752 vehicle types by March 2022. Customs and Border Protection paid more than $450,000 for five kits, and courts in at least six states have allowed police to download such data without a warrant. A Homeland Security spokesperson said in 2023 that the department "no longer partners" with Berla. [cite:de25_rec_berla] In practice its investigative arm, Homeland Security Investigations, placed a roughly $130,000 order with Berla in 2025, posted a notice on 28 August 2026 to renew it without competition, and in September 2025 paid $311,250 for 325 covert GPS trackers made by Ensurity. [cite:de25_bu_berla]

Tesla: what the notice says and what has happened

Tesla's cameras, satellite positioning and permanent cellular link could in principle record a continuous history of where a car went and what was around it. What Tesla says it does is narrower. It told the senators in 2024 that it receives a car's location only for "a critical safety event (such as a collision, an airbag deployment, or automatic emergency braking event)." [cite:de25_wm_letter] Its customer privacy notice says that camera recordings shared for development "remain anonymous and are not linked to you or your vehicle." [cite:de25_reu_tesla] Its law-enforcement guidelines require a valid legal basis or the customer's consent, allow emergency disclosure only on a good-faith belief of "danger of death or serious physical injury," and promise "reasonable efforts" to tell customers unless a court order forbids it. [cite:de25_tesla_ler]

Three episodes test those words. In April 2023 Reuters reported, from nine former employees, that groups of Tesla staff had shared customer camera recordings in internal chats between 2019 and 2022, among them a crash in which a car hit a child on a bicycle; seven said the labelling tool could show where a recording was made. Tesla did not respond. [cite:de25_reu_tesla] In 2024 Oakland police obtained court orders in at least three cases to tow Teslas and copy the Sentry Mode footage that parked cars record onto a drive inside the vehicle; footage of a shooting on 13 July helped charge two people with murder. [cite:de25_p1_oakland] After a Cybertruck exploded in Las Vegas on 1 January 2025, the county sheriff said Elon Musk had sent footage from Tesla charging stations across the country "directly to us" and explained how the vehicle had locked, and Musk posted that "all vehicle telemetry was positive" at the time. No legal process was mentioned. [cite:de25_bi_vegas] Whether that was an emergency disclosure under Tesla's own rules is not documented.

Musk's government role in 2025 ([scene:de11_tesla_spacex_and_the_state|Part Eleven], [scene:de19_the_access|Part Nineteen]) raised a further question. On 5 February 2025 Senator Richard Blumenthal asked Tesla and five other Musk companies whether they had received "any nonpublic data" from the Department of Government Efficiency. [cite:de25_blum_letters] The letters are questions. No transfer of federal data to Tesla, and no bulk transfer of Tesla customer data to the government, had been documented as of October 2026.

Wearables and health apps

HIPAA, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, binds doctors, hospitals and insurers, not the makers of fitness bands, watches, rings or apps sold to consumers, whose data is governed by their own terms of service. [cite:de25_ahcj_rfk] The gap grew in importance when Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told Congress on 24 June 2025 that wearables are "a way people can take control of their own health" and announced a campaign to promote them. [cite:de25_ahcj_rfk]

The record shows wearable data used in criminal cases and health data leaking into advertising. Connie Dabate's Fitbit recorded her moving for about an hour after the time her husband said an intruder had shot her in Connecticut on 23 December 2015; he was sentenced on 18 August 2022 to 65 years. [cite:de25_ct_dabate] On 5 August 2025 a California jury found that Meta had violated the state's Invasion of Privacy Act by collecting Flo app users' menstrual data; Google and Flo had settled, and Meta said it would explore "all legal options." [cite:de25_tc_flo] No case of police obtaining a period-tracking app's records had been reported as of October 2026. Design matters: Apple says Health data on a current, protected device is end-to-end encrypted and "not readable by anyone — even Apple," though it remains on the phone, within reach of the extraction tools in [scene:de25_spyware_and_phones|the previous section]. [cite:de25_apple_health] Washington State's My Health My Data Act, in force since March 2024, covers health data including location that suggests a person sought care, and lets individuals sue; the first suit was filed against Amazon on 10 February 2025. [cite:de25_wh_mhmda]

The living room and the front door

Many smart televisions use automatic content recognition, or ACR: at intervals the set takes a sample of the picture or sound, reduces it to a digital fingerprint and matches it against a database of programmes and advertisements, so the maker knows what is being watched and when. [cite:de25_mb_samsung] In 2017 Vizio paid $2.2 million to the FTC and New Jersey for capturing "second-by-second" viewing on 11 million televisions and selling it without consent. [cite:de25_ftc_vizio] In December 2025 Texas sued Sony, Samsung, LG, Hisense and TCL, alleging screen captures "as often as every half second"; Samsung settled by March 2026, agreeing not to collect such data from Texans without explicit, informed consent. [cite:de25_pg_acr] [cite:de25_mb_samsung] As with cars, the documented buyers are advertisers; no government purchase of television viewing data has been reported.

Voice assistants listen for a wake word and send what follows to the company. On 28 March 2025 Amazon ended an option that let some Echo devices process requests locally, so that all recordings would go to its cloud for the new Alexa+. [cite:de25_tc_alexa] In an Arkansas murder case of 2015, Amazon refused to release a suspect's Echo recordings without "a valid and binding legal demand," then released them when he consented; prosecutors also used his smart water meter's readings, and dropped the charges in November 2017. [cite:de25_npr_bates] In 2023 the FTC obtained $25 million from Amazon over children's Alexa recordings and $5.8 million in refunds from Ring, one of whose employees had watched thousands of female customers' private videos, including in bathrooms and bedrooms. [cite:de25_thn_ring]

Ring, Amazon's doorbell company, built the most direct channel to police. In 2022 Amazon told Senator Markey that 2,161 agencies used its Neighbors service and that Ring had given police footage without the owner's consent 11 times that year, each on its own finding of "imminent danger." [cite:de25_ax_ring] Local police can ask owners for video through Axon's evidence platform, and owners may decline; in February 2026 Ring dropped a planned link with the licence-plate camera firm Flock and said it "has no partnership with ICE." [cite:de25_cnn_ring] In February 2026 FBI Director Kash Patel said video from a missing woman's Nest doorbell in Arizona had been "recovered from residual data located in backend systems," although the sheriff said she had no subscription that saved video; Google did not explain its retention. [cite:de25_nbc_nest]

The devices in an ordinary home could, between them, record where a family drives, how it sleeps, what it watches and who comes to the door. What the record shows the state doing with them is narrower and older in form: case-by-case demands, warrants, a forensic kit for cars, and voluntary or emergency disclosures.

If it were connected

The devices in this section matter most for what they could add to the systems in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|the ecosystem map]. Car data to brokers: documented; GM's trip records reached LexisNexis until 2024. [cite:de25_mkt_gm] Broker identity data to ICE's Palantir platform: documented as a requirement, in the August 2026 LexisNexis notice, and probable as a working flow. [cite:de25_bu_lexis] Car driving records from that broker to ICE: possible; LexisNexis's insurance and investigative products are separate lines of business, and no document shows driving data in what ICE buys. A car's forensic download imported into a case platform: possible by analogy with phone extractions, which ICE agents could import into Palantir tools, but no document shows it for vehicles. [cite:de25_gdn_palantir] [cite:de25_bu_berla] Doorbell video to local police: documented, by request and owner consent; to ICE: not supported, on Ring's own statement. [cite:de25_cnn_ring] Wearable, health-app or television data to any agency: not supported; the documented flows run to advertisers and insurers. [cite:de25_tc_flo] [cite:de25_mb_samsung] Tesla's fleet data to the government in bulk, or federal data to Musk's companies: not supported. [cite:de25_blum_letters] The step any of these joins would need is a purchase, a contract clause or a rule change, not new technology, which is why the brakes that matter are the FTC's orders, state laws such as Washington's, and the companies' own policies, each of which can change. [cite:de25_rdn_gm] [cite:de25_wh_mhmda] How the government's own records of benefits, schooling and work could join the same picture is set out in [scene:de24b_benefits|Part Twenty-Five] and [scene:de24b_schools|its section on schools].

The worst-case reading, tested

The book's working hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and never a finding, reads immigration enforcement as the occasion for building a surveillance machine that could serve a sovereign executive without a veto. Documented: federal agencies buy phone location data drawn from apps and advertising auctions without a warrant, and in 2026 both the FBI and ICE said or showed that they do; the products can list every device seen at a place. [cite:de25_tc_patel] [cite:de25_404_webloc] Documented: ICE bought and used remote spyware that reads encrypted messages (whether it still has it, the department will neither confirm nor deny), and holds forensic tools for seized phones and cars, covert trackers and cell-site simulators. [cite:ow10_tc_lyons] [cite:de25_npr_paragon] [cite:de25_fs_forecast] [cite:de25_bu_berla] [cite:de25_tc_tosv] Documented: these purchases ran under both parties. Location buying began in 2019 and 2020 under Trump's first administration and continued under Biden; ICE bought simulators and signed the Paragon contract under Biden; the one sharp political reversal was the revival in August 2025 of a spyware contract the previous administration had paused. [cite:de25_vice_venntel] [cite:de25_oig_ctd] [cite:ow10_poulson_ice] Documented too: the agencies broke their own privacy rules in using bought location data. [cite:de25_oig_ctd]

Probable: that bought data is now the route of least resistance. The courts have narrowed the compelled routes, through Carpenter, Chatrie and, in one district, the end of tower dumps, while no court has ruled on purchase and the FTC's orders bind sellers only. [cite:de25_crs_chatrie] [cite:de25_wlox_tower] [cite:de25_ftc_gravy] This is a structural reading of documented law, not a documented policy decision by any agency. Probable as well: that ICE's location tools serve removals, since CBP's purchases were reported to have led to border arrests; Webloc's specific uses are unpublished. [cite:de25_vice_venntel] [cite:de25_404_webloc]

Not supported: that any of these tools has been used in the United States against a journalist, an activist or a political opponent; the documented spyware abuse in this part took place in Italy and Serbia. [cite:de25_tc_italy] [cite:de25_ci_serbia] Not supported: that the state buys car, television or wearable data, or that Musk's companies received government data through DOGE or handed customer data over in bulk. [cite:de25_blum_letters] Not supported: a single system joining a person's phone, car, home and body into one live picture; the joins graded above are documented for brokers' identity data and past phone extractions, and possible, not documented, for the rest. Where the record runs against the hypothesis it does so concretely: the FBI tested Pegasus and refused to deploy it; the Supreme Court upheld nearly $200 million in fines on carriers that sold location; Ring says federal agencies cannot use its request channel, and Tesla tells its customers when police ask. [cite:ow10_ai_nytmag] [cite:de25_rec_fcc] [cite:de25_cnn_ring] [cite:de25_wm_letter] Capability, on this part's evidence, is well ahead of documented intent. Faces, drones, satellites, cloud and money follow in [scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|Part Twenty-Eight]; the platform that joins layers, in [scene:de27_capability_not_intent|Part Twenty-Nine]; the running tally, in [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|the final part].

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Seven
chapters.title: Moving: Travel, the Border and the Exit
chapters.intro: Part Twenty-Seven follows the traveller. Its first section sets out what the state learns when a person flies: the name and birth date checked by TSA's Secure Flight, the passport details and booking records sent to Customs and Border Protection and kept for fifteen years, the faces photographed at checkpoints and borders, the identity rules of REAL ID, and the private biometric lane run by CLEAR; it ends with the first documented join, the passenger lists TSA has passed to ICE since 2025. The second section asks who can already stop a person flying or leaving: the no-fly list and the court cases that opened it, passport denial for tax and child-support debt, the 2025 proposal to revoke passports for "material support" that was withdrawn, and trusted-traveller revocations used as leverage. It compares the American rule, under which a passport is the only exit permit, with the Soviet exit visa, China's exit bans and Russia's draft-linked bans, grades which travel systems could be joined to the rest of the book's map, and tests the worst-case reading.
chapters.outro: Travel is the one place where a person must identify themselves to the state on demand. Secure Flight checks every passenger against the watch lists, booking and manifest records enter a targeting system that keeps them for fifteen years, non-citizens have been photographed at entry and exit since 26 December 2025, and since 2025 TSA has passed passenger lists to ICE, which counted more than 800 arrests by February 2026. [cite:de25b_fr_secureflight] [cite:de25b_pia_ats] [cite:de25b_mit_entryexit] [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice] The United States has no exit permit, but its passport serves as one: it can already be denied for tax debt over $66,000, child-support arrears over $2,500 and certain drug convictions, while the courts have barred denial for belief since 1958 and a 2025 attempt to add "material support" determinations was struck within days. [cite:de25b_irs_passport] [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] [cite:de25b_kent] [cite:de25b_int_mast] Trusted-traveller status has twice been used as leverage, against New York in 2020 on what DHS admitted were inaccurate statements, and, on allegations not yet tried, against observers of immigration agents in 2026. [cite:de25b_abc_ny] [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] Measured against the Soviet exit visa, China's exit bans and Russia's draft bans, the American exit remains open; the worst-case reading finds the records documented, their drift into enforcement probable, and an exit permit not supported. [cite:de25b_aj_china] [cite:de25b_ng_russia] Book Five turns next to the cameras, drones and satellites that see people without asking them, in [scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|Part Twenty-Eight].

sections.h: Who Knows You Travel
sections.html:
Book Five asks the same questions of every tool: what it collects, who uses it, where it has gone wrong, what the law allows, and what its worst use would look like. The last is the book's working hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and never a finding, in which immigration enforcement is the occasion for building a machine that could later be pointed at anyone; a tool's ability is a documented fact, and its use against critics needs a document of its own. The earlier parts followed data a person gives away without noticing, through phones, cars and brokers ([scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four], [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|Part Twenty-Six]). Travel is different. To board a plane a person must hand over a name, a birth date and a face, and must do it to the state. This section sets out what each system takes, how long it keeps it, and where in 2025 and 2026 the first of these records began to flow to immigration enforcement.

The booking: Secure Flight

Every domestic and international flight on a US airline, and every foreign airline's flight to or from the United States, passes through a Transportation Security Administration (TSA) programme called Secure Flight. Its final rule, published on 28 October 2008 and in force from 29 December 2008, moved the job of checking passengers against government watch lists from the airlines to TSA itself. Airlines must ask for a passenger's full name, date of birth and gender, and for a redress number or Known Traveler Number if the passenger has one; TSA compares them with two subsets of the government's terrorist screening database, the No Fly list (barred from boarding) and the Selectee list (extra screening), and may check larger lists "when security conditions warrant". [cite:de25b_fr_secureflight] The privacy assessment published before launch set the retention clock: a passenger who matched nothing is kept for seven days after the trip, a possible match for seven years, and a confirmed match for 99 years. The same document promised that Secure Flight "does not use algorithms to assign risk scores to individuals" and used no commercial data. [cite:de25b_pia_secureflight]

A second TSA programme did score travellers. Quiet Skies used an algorithm to review travel patterns, foreign connections and other government data, and sent federal air marshals to watch people who were on no FBI watch list and were suspected of nothing. On 5 June 2025 Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem ended it, calling it "a political rolodex of the Biden Administration"; the trigger was the case of Tulsi Gabbard, later Director of National Intelligence, who said she had been listed after criticising Vice President Kamala Harris. CNN reported that the reason for her listing was never made clear, and the Washington Times put the programme's cost at about $200 million a year. [cite:de25b_cnn_quietskies] [cite:de25b_wt_quietskies] The episode belongs in the record for both parties at once: a rules-based watch on unaccused citizens was in use under a Democratic administration, and a Republican one shut it down while accusing its predecessor of political targeting.

The international trip: manifests, booking records and a fifteen-year archive

For international flights two more streams reach the government before the plane moves. The Advance Passenger Information System (APIS) is the passenger manifest: since 19 February 2008 airlines have had to send US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) the details from each passenger's passport page, at the latest 30 minutes before the doors close, or passenger by passenger up to the moment they close, for flights leaving the United States as well as those arriving. A passenger who comes back "not-cleared" cannot be given a boarding pass. [cite:de25b_fr_apis] The second stream is the Passenger Name Record (PNR), the airline's own booking file. It is richer than the passport page. Under the 2012 agreement that governs transfers from European airlines, a PNR can include travel dates and itinerary, ticket details, addresses and telephone numbers, the payment method and card number, the travel agent, the seat and the baggage. The agreement lets the Department of Homeland Security keep it for up to five years in an active database, with names masked after six months, and then for up to ten more years in a "dormant" one. [cite:de25b_ep_pnr] Europe's data-protection supervisor called a fifteen-year maximum "clearly disproportionate" while the deal was being negotiated. [cite:de25b_pm_pnr]

The streams meet in CBP's Automated Targeting System (ATS), which compares travellers with law-enforcement and intelligence records using "risk-based rules". Its published privacy assessment lists what it takes in: the APIS manifest, visa-waiver (ESTA) and visa applications, arrival records, the student-visa system SEVIS, booking records and, for some flights, TSA's Secure Flight data. It states that "ATS is retaining ingested information consistent with its own 15-year retention period", even where the source system would have deleted it sooner. [cite:de25b_pia_ats] Records of this family have travelled further. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) documents from 2014 to 2022, released under the Freedom of Information Act and reported by the Guardian, show investigators planning in 2020 to search APIS and border-crossing data through Palantir's case system, and training on searching SEVIS. [cite:de24_guardian_icm]

The face

Congress first ordered a biometric record of foreign visitors' entries and exits after 2001. A final rule published on 27 October 2025 and in force from 26 December 2025 completed it: CBP may photograph every non-citizen on entry and exit at airports, land crossings and seaports. US citizens are outside the rule and take part only voluntarily. [cite:de25b_mit_entryexit] [cite:de26_bu_entryexit] The camera at the departure gate is covered in [scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|the section on faces]. At the security checkpoint, TSA compares a live photograph with the photo on the traveller's ID. It had the cameras at 84 airports in May 2025 and planned for about 400. TSA says a traveller may decline "without recourse" and keep their place in line, and that images are deleted once identity is confirmed, except for members of its PreCheck Touchless ID service (24 hours after departure) and photos kept to test accuracy. [cite:de25b_siw_tsaface] A survey by the Algorithmic Justice League found 74 per cent of respondents had not been told facial recognition was in use. A bipartisan group led by Senator Jeff Merkley reintroduced the Traveler Privacy Protection Act, which would make the opt-out a matter of law rather than policy, in May 2025; as of October 2026 it has not been enacted. [cite:de25b_reg_tsaface]

The identity document changed too. REAL ID enforcement, required by a 2005 Act that followed a recommendation of the 9/11 Commission, began on 7 May 2025: only licences meeting the federal standard, or a passport, now get a traveller through security. [cite:de25b_tsa_realid] From 1 February 2026 a traveller without one can pay $45 for a TSA check called ConfirmID, which asks questions only the real person should be able to answer and lasts ten days. [cite:de25b_az_confirmid]

The private lane: CLEAR

One name needs separating first. Thomson Reuters CLEAR, the investigative database ICE pays for and which is described in [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four], is a different company from CLEAR the airport service. The airport CLEAR is Clear Secure, Inc. It began in 2003 as Verified Identity Pass, shut down after bankruptcy in 2009, was bought in 2010 by the investor Caryn Seidman Becker and her partner Ken Cornick, relaunched in 2012 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021 under the ticker YOU. [cite:de25b_wiki_clear] Its annual report states plainly that "we are controlled by the Founder Post-IPO Members", the founders' holding entities. [cite:de25b_10k_2025] At the end of 2025 it counted 38.0 million members, of whom 7.6 million were active paying members of its airport lane, CLEAR+, at 60 airports, on revenue of $900.8 million. [cite:de25b_pr_clearfy25]

Its privacy notice, last updated on 26 June 2026, lists what it takes: "faceprints, fingerprints, iris scans", a selfie and a photo of the traveller's ID. For CLEAR+ it shares data "with the Transportation Security Administration"; it discloses to government "if required by law or legal process"; it may share data with third parties for advertising and marketing; and it says it "does not sell your biometrics or sensitive Personal Data". [cite:de25b_clear_privacy] Its ties to the state are commercial and regulatory: it works under TSA's Registered Traveler programme, holds a Homeland Security certification under the SAFETY Act, was picked by TSA in January 2020 to enrol people in PreCheck and did so at 340 shops by the end of 2025, and on 9 December 2025 announced a contract with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to verify identities for Medicare.gov accounts from early 2026. [cite:de25b_10k_2023] [cite:de25b_pr_clearfy25] [cite:de25b_clear_cms] Its record has one documented failure: in July 2022 a passenger travelling under a false identity and carrying ammunition got through its lane before TSA stopped him; CLEAR called it "a single human error", and TSA responded by requiring its own officers to check CLEAR members' IDs. [cite:de25b_cbs_clear] No document shows CLEAR giving member biometrics to ICE.

The first join: Secure Flight to ICE

One of these systems has been joined to immigration enforcement, and the join is documented. The New York Times reported on 12 December 2025 that TSA sends ICE lists of air travellers' names several times a week, which ICE matches against people with final removal orders. A memorandum of agreement signed in May 2025, released in a records lawsuit brought by the group American Oversight, cites the Secure Flight rule as TSA's legal basis and says ICE will keep what it receives in its own repository; the list of shared data fields is almost entirely redacted. The acting TSA administrator had told Congress that TSA does not "send the information to ICE". [cite:de25b_ipt_tsaice] [cite:de25b_ao_moa] Reuters, reviewing internal ICE data, counted records on more than 31,000 travellers passed from January 2025 to February 2026 and more than 800 arrests; it noted that the regulation creating Secure Flight said it was not meant to track immigration offenders. [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice]

If it were connected

Graded on the scale used across Book Five, for joins only. Secure Flight names to ICE: documented, by the May 2025 agreement and the Reuters count; onward into Palantir's systems: possible, since no record shows that path. [cite:de25b_ao_moa] [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice] Student-visa and airline-manifest records searched through ICE's Palantir case system: documented in Homeland Security Investigations records from 2014 to 2022. [cite:de24_guardian_icm] The faces gathered at checkpoints and gates joined to DHS's next biometric system, HART, which is designed to be shared across agencies and foreign partners: possible, since HART was not yet operational in August 2024. [cite:de28_hart_pia] The airport company CLEAR's irises and faces to immigration enforcement: possible only through the legal process its notice allows, with no document showing it; it is a different company from Thomson Reuters' CLEAR people-search database, which ICE does buy. [cite:de25b_clear_privacy] Together these would let an agency know, from a name, when and where a person has flown; what stands in the way is mostly the purpose language of each system's rule, and the 2025 agreement put Secure Flight to a use its own rule said it was not meant for. The full set of joins is drawn in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|the ecosystem map].

Knowing that someone travels is one power; stopping them is another. [scene:de25b_who_can_stop_you|The next section] sets out who in the United States can already keep a person on the ground or inside the country, how other states have done it, and what would have to change for these records to be used that way.

sections.h: Who Can Stop You
sections.html:
This section asks who in the United States can already stop a person from boarding a plane or leaving the country, on what trigger, with what notice, and before which judge. "Exit", the Dark Enlightenment's word for the resident's one remedy against a bad government, assumes the resident can leave ([scene:de2_core_texts|Part Two], [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight]). Whether that holds depends less on airport cameras than on the passport.

The passport is the exit permit

The United States has no exit visa. It has something close to one in law: federal statute makes it unlawful "for any citizen of the United States to depart from or enter" the country "unless he bears a valid United States passport". [cite:de25b_usc_1185] Whoever controls the passport controls departure, and that control has been used for politics before. In the early Cold War the State Department refused passports to people it suspected of Communist ties. In Kent v. Dulles, decided on 16 June 1958, the Supreme Court held that the Secretary of State had no authority to deny passports for beliefs and associations, and declared that "the right to travel is a part of the 'liberty'" the Fifth Amendment protects. [cite:de25b_kent] In 1964, in Aptheker v. Secretary of State, it struck down a statute barring Communist Party members from holding passports. [cite:de25b_aptheker] The limit cuts both ways. In Haig v. Agee (1981), the Court upheld, 7 to 2, the revocation of the passport of Philip Agee, a former Central Intelligence Agency officer who was publicly exposing agents, and told courts to defer to the executive on national security. [cite:de25b_mtsu_agee] Belief alone cannot cost a citizen a passport; conduct the executive calls dangerous can.

The no-fly list

The government's terrorist screening database held about two million identities at the end of 2023, up from 1.16 million in 2017; most are not US citizens or permanent residents, though "thousands of Americans" are included. The No Fly list is one part of it, and its size is not public. [cite:de25b_cbs_watchlist] For years a listed person could not learn whether they were on it or why. In June 2014, in Latif v. Holder, a federal judge in Oregon found the redress process "wholly ineffective", recognised "a constitutionally protected, private interest in international travel by air", and ordered the government to tell plaintiffs their status and its reasons. [cite:de25b_lf_latif] The government revised the procedure in 2015. In Kashem v. Barr, on 21 October 2019, the Ninth Circuit upheld the revised process and the list's criteria as applied to the men before it, and confirmed that the final order comes from the TSA administrator and can be challenged only in a federal appeals court. [cite:de25b_kashem] On 19 March 2024 the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in FBI v. Fikre that the government could not end an Oregon man's challenge simply by taking him off the list with a pledge not to relist him "based on the currently available information"; Yonas Fikre had learned of his listing while in Sudan in 2010. The Court did not decide whether the listing was lawful. [cite:de25b_scb_fikre]

Passports and debt

Two statutes already let one agency's certificate stop a citizen leaving. Under section 7345 of the Internal Revenue Code, the Internal Revenue Service certifies "seriously delinquent tax debt" to the State Department, which then refuses a new passport and may revoke a current one. The threshold for 2026 is $66,000, indexed each year. The debt must carry a filed tax lien with appeals exhausted, or a levy; it does not count if the taxpayer is on a payment plan, has asked for a collection hearing, is bankrupt or cannot pay because of hardship. The taxpayer gets a notice and the right to sue in the Tax Court or a district court over a wrong certification. [cite:de25b_irs_passport] The second is child support. Since 1996 states have certified parents with arrears to the federal Office of Child Support Enforcement, which passes them to the State Department's lookout system; the threshold, first $5,000, has been $2,500 since the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005. It has collected nearly $621 million since its start. Existing passports can be revoked only when the State Department physically holds them, for a renewal or a name change. On 27 April 2026 the House passed by voice vote a bill, H.R. 6903, that would make revocation mandatory; the Senate referred it to its Finance Committee the next day. [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] [cite:de25b_fd_hr6903] Criminal law adds a narrow third bar: a person convicted of a felony drug offence that involved crossing a border gets no passport while in prison or on parole. [cite:de25b_usc_2714]

A broader power was proposed and withdrawn. In September 2025 the House Foreign Affairs Committee's State Department bill included a provision letting the Secretary of State deny or revoke the passports of citizens he deemed to have "materially supported terrorists". An American Civil Liberties Union lawyer called it "a huge risk of abuse, of politicized enforcement", and activists said it could be aimed at critics of Israel. The committee's chairman, Brian Mast, filed an amendment striking it within days. [cite:de25b_int_mast] [cite:de25b_gu_mast]

The convenience tier as leverage

Global Entry and TSA PreCheck are memberships that buy a faster line; their loss keeps no one at home. They are also the one travel benefit the government has demonstrably withdrawn as leverage. In February 2020 the Department of Homeland Security barred every New York resident from its trusted-traveller programmes because the state's Green Light Law limited federal access to driving-licence records. It lifted the bar on 23 July 2020, after the government admitted in court that statements DHS had made to justify it were "inaccurate and misleading"; New York's attorney general called the policy "political retribution, plain and simple". [cite:de25b_abc_ny]

In 2026 the question came back in individual form. Nicole Cleland, a Minnesota resident, said in a sworn court declaration that on 10 January 2026, while she was watching vehicles she believed carried immigration agents, a Border Patrol agent called her by name, told her he had facial recognition and accused her of impeding agents; three days later her Global Entry and PreCheck were revoked without explanation. [cite:de25b_kstp_cleland] In late July 2026 she and two other citizens, represented by the Electronic Privacy Information Center, sued in federal court in San Diego under the Administrative Procedure Act, the Privacy Act and the First Amendment. A South Carolina woman says her Global Entry was revoked ten days after she observed an enforcement operation in Charlotte and later reinstated without explanation; a San Diego woman says hers was restored after a reporter asked about it. CBP denies revoking memberships in retaliation for protected speech and says they can be withdrawn for crimes, warrants, customs or immigration violations or failure to remain "low-risk". The allegations have not been tested in court. [cite:de25b_bu_cleland]

Where leaving needs permission

Other states have made leaving itself require permission. Soviet citizens needed an exit visa. Those refused, the "refuseniks", were often turned down for "months, years, and even decades" and lost their jobs; Mikhail Gorbachev let most of them go from 1987. [cite:de25b_enc_refuseniks] From August 1972 Moscow also charged emigrants "education reimbursement fees" that could reach tens of thousands of dollars; the US answer, the Jackson–Vanik amendment to the Trade Act of 1974, tied trade benefits to the freedom to emigrate and to the absence of "a more than nominal tax on emigration". [cite:de25b_crs_jv] China's exit bans today run on at least 15 laws; the rights group Safeguard Defenders counted court-record mentions rising from under 5,000 in 2016 to 39,000 in 2020, estimated bans "in the millions" counting those imposed by ethnicity, and documented their use against critics' families, journalists and foreign businessmen. [cite:de25b_aj_china] Russia's law of 14 April 2023 made a draft summons count as delivered seven days after it is posted to the state services portal, and barred its recipient from leaving the country; after 20 days without reporting, he loses access to loans and property registration. Since July 2025 border guards have had direct access to the draft register. [cite:de25b_ng_russia] [cite:de25b_mt_russia]

If it were connected

The travel systems could be joined to the rest of the book's map, the six layers set out in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|the ecosystem map]. Secure Flight to ICE's removal records is documented: an agreement signed in May 2025 and more than 800 arrests. [cite:de25b_ao_moa] [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice] A face identification in the street followed by a trusted-traveller revocation is alleged in a pending suit and denied by CBP; as a join between systems it is possible, and as cause it is unproven. [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] Booking and manifest records to Palantir's case system is documented for 2014–2022 investigative use, though not shown as a standing feed. [cite:de24_guardian_icm] The debt certificate extended to other government "debts", such as fines, is possible: it needs only an Act of Congress, and Congress moved in 2026 to tighten the child-support route, not to widen the categories. [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] The airport company CLEAR's biometrics to immigration enforcement are possible only through legal process, which its notice allows; no document shows it. [cite:de25b_clear_privacy] A passport bar for speech or politics is not supported: the 2025 attempt was struck, and Kent and Aptheker stand in its way. [cite:de25b_int_mast] [cite:de25b_aptheker] The same pattern across credit, work and benefits is in [scene:de35_the_consequence_ladder|the consequence ladder].

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and never a finding, reads immigration enforcement as the occasion for building a machine that a sovereign executive without a veto could turn on anyone. Documented: the state already holds a fifteen-year archive of international travel, routinely photographs non-citizens at the border and many travellers at checkpoints, and since 2025 has passed domestic passenger lists to ICE under an agreement made public only through a records lawsuit; a counter-terrorism system was put to an immigration use its own rule disclaimed. [cite:de25b_pia_ats] [cite:de25b_ao_moa] [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice] Documented: the government has twice used trusted-traveller status as leverage, against a whole state in 2020 by an admitted false justification, and, on sworn allegations not yet tried, against observers in 2026. [cite:de25b_abc_ny] [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] Probable: that travel records, being complete and archived, will keep finding enforcement uses beyond their founding purpose; that is a reading of the documented drift, not of any stated plan. Not supported: any US exit permit, or any power to deny a passport for speech. The record runs against the worst case here more than in most parts: the courts closed political passport denial in 1958 and 1964, forced the no-fly process open in 2014 and kept Fikre's suit alive in 2024; a House chairman dropped the "material support" clause within days; DHS reversed its New York ban; and a Republican administration ended a programme it said a Democratic one had abused. [cite:de25b_kent] [cite:de25b_lf_latif] [cite:de25b_scb_fikre] [cite:de25b_gu_mast] [cite:de25b_cnn_quietskies] The same standard applies in both directions: the watch on unaccused travellers and the no-fly secrecy grew under both parties, and so did the brakes. The exit still opens, for those whose passport is good and whose debts are below the line. The next part turns to the faces, drones and satellites in [scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|Part Twenty-Eight]; the running tally is kept in [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|the final part].

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Eight
chapters.title: The Toolkit III: Seeing, Paying, Building
chapters.intro: This part closes the survey of the toolkit with three kinds of power that do not depend on reading anyone's files. The first is sight: face recognition at the border and on an officer's phone, drones and sensor towers, and a classified constellation of spy satellites built by one company. The second is the infrastructure underneath everything else: the few firms whose clouds host the state's data, the code platforms and app stores that decide what software exists and who can get it, and the AI models now installed inside federal agencies, including the one dispute in which a vendor's limits on use were tested in court. The third is money: the reports banks file on their customers, the closing of accounts in both political directions, and the freeze-and-burn switch that federal law now requires in every regulated stablecoin. A last section asks what has actually stopped any of these tools, and closes with the book's worst-case reading tested against the part as a whole.
chapters.outro: The seeing tools are documented and in federal hands: ICE's Mobile Fortify app scans faces against about 200 million images with no way to refuse and keeps citizens' photographs for 15 years, CBP photographs every non-citizen at the border and flew drones for ICE at least 50 times, and Clearview's scraped gallery is under ICE contract while its class settlement was vacated on 13 July 2026. [cite:de26_reason_fortify] [cite:de26_bu_entryexit] [cite:de26_404_drones] [cite:de26_duane_clearview] A few firms host the state's computing, and the lever they hold has been pulled both ways, by Microsoft against a foreign defence ministry and by officials against an app, pressure a judge found likely coercive. [cite:de26_ng_jwcc] [cite:ow4_tc_msft] [cite:de26_reason_rosado] Frontier AI models sit inside agencies at a dollar or less, and the one vendor that held out for written limits on domestic surveillance was excluded, a decision one court set aside and another upheld. [cite:de26_fs_onegov] [cite:de26_taft_dccir] The GENIUS Act requires every regulated stablecoin to carry a switch to "seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer" of tokens on a lawful order, while the same administration barred a central-bank digital currency. [cite:de26_crec_genius] [cite:de26_fr_14178] Courts, state laws, encryption and company decisions have narrowed particular uses, but none reaches the federal purchase of commercial data or the integration of what is bought. That integration is the business of one company, and [scene:de27_origins_and_control|Part Twenty-Nine] turns to Palantir.

sections.h: Faces, Drones and Satellites: Seeing at a Distance
sections.html:
The tools in the parts before this one work through records; the tools here work through sight. A camera on a phone, a tower on the border, a drone over a protest and a satellite in low orbit all collect images, and software turns images into identities and tracks. Face recognition is the technology that does the turning, so it comes first. A face-recognition system converts a photograph into a "template," a list of numbers that describes the geometry of the face, and compares templates. There are two kinds of comparison. One-to-one "verification" asks whether a face matches one stored photograph, as at a passport gate. One-to-many "identification" asks who, in a whole collection of stored photographs called the gallery, this face most resembles, and it always returns a ranked list of candidates; a threshold set by the operator decides which candidate counts as a "match." [cite:de26_nist_frvt] [cite:de26_duane_clearview]

Clearview and the scraped gallery

Clearview AI is distinguished less by its software than by its gallery. The company describes itself as a search engine for faces: it collects photographs of people from public websites and builds a facial vector for each, so a single photograph returns other pictures of the same person and links to where they appeared. [cite:de26_duane_clearview] Its early investors included Peter Thiel, who with Naval Ravikant put in more than $200,000 that later converted into equity, a tie set out in [scene:de10_philosophy_vs_practice|Part Ten]. [cite:de10_wiki_clearview] On 5 September 2025 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) finalised a sole-source contract with Clearview with a total value of $9.225 million over a base year and three option years, and $3.75 million obligated at signing, citing the company's "unique proprietary capabilities"; its stated purposes were child-exploitation cases and investigations of assaults on officers. [cite:de26_bu_clearviewice] [cite:de28_audit_clearview_piid] Private suits over the gallery have not ended. A class settlement under Illinois's biometric privacy law, which would have paid class members a 23 per cent equity stake in the company, was vacated by the Seventh Circuit on 13 July 2026, because the nationwide class had no representative of its own when the stake was divided; the case went back to the district court, and as of October 2026 there is no completed settlement. [cite:de26_duane_clearview] An earlier settlement with the American Civil Liberties Union, which does bind the company, is in [scene:de26_counterweights|the last section of this part].

Mobile Fortify: the face check in the street

ICE's own face-recognition tool is a phone app. Mobile Fortify, first reported by 404 Media on 17 July 2025, lets an officer point a phone at a person's face and compare it against about 200 million images drawn from Homeland Security, State Department, Customs and Border Protection (CBP), FBI and state records; it returns a name, date of birth, nationality, an "alien number" and whether an immigration judge has ordered the person removed. [cite:de26_404_fortify] A Homeland Security privacy assessment dated February 2025, obtained by 404 Media under the Freedom of Information Act and reported in November, said plainly that "ICE does not provide the opportunity for individuals to decline or consent" to the scan. Photographs taken are kept for 15 years, including those of United States citizens, since an officer cannot know a person's status before running the check. Representative Bennie Thompson said ICE officials had indicated they would treat a Mobile Fortify hit as outweighing documentary proof of citizenship such as a birth certificate, and called the practice "frightening, repugnant, and unconstitutional." [cite:de26_reason_fortify]

The border as a camera

At ports of entry the face check has become a rule rather than an option for non-citizens. A CBP final rule published in November 2025 and effective on 26 December 2025 lets the agency photograph all non-citizens on entry and exit, by air, land and sea, removing earlier exemptions for diplomats and most Canadian visitors. Under the governing records notice, non-citizens' photographs may be kept for up to 75 years; citizens may opt out by asking for manual inspection, and their verification photographs are deleted within 12 hours. CBP's operations chief called the rule "a major milestone" toward the biometric entry-exit system Congress first required after 2001. [cite:de26_bu_entryexit]

What goes wrong

The documented failures are of two kinds. The first is in the algorithms. In December 2019 the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the federal standards laboratory, tested 189 algorithms from 99 developers and found that "the majority" showed demographic differentials: in one-to-one matching, false positives for Asian and African American faces were often 10 to 100 times higher than for white faces, depending on the algorithm, though the most equitable algorithms were also among the most accurate. [cite:de26_nist_frvt] The second is in the people using them. A Washington Post investigation in January 2025 found at least eight Americans wrongfully arrested after face-recognition searches, seven of them Black, across 15 police departments in 12 states; in six of the eight cases police did not check the person's alibi. [cite:de26_fortune_wapo] No comparable public count exists for Mobile Fortify.

Drones and towers

Overhead, the border agency's aircraft have been lent to the interior. Flight logs obtained by 404 Media show that CBP flew drones at least 50 times in support of ICE between March 2024 and March 2025, a period spanning two administrations, possibly including its MQ-9 Predators; in June 2025 CBP flew Predators over protests against ICE in Los Angeles, which it described as "officer safety surveillance." [cite:de26_404_drones] On the ground, the border is being lined with sensor towers. In June 2026 Anduril, the defence company whose federal contracts and investor ties are listed in [scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen], announced a $363 million CBP award for more than 200 Extended Range Sentry Towers, which detect and track objects more than five miles away and feed Anduril's Lattice software, the program that fuses sensor feeds into one picture for an operator. [cite:de26_eb_anduril]

Satellites and one provider

In March 2024 Reuters reported, from five sources, that SpaceX's Starshield unit was building a network of hundreds of imaging and relay satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office under a $1.8 billion contract signed in 2021, designed to give near-continuous imagery of most of the Earth; the network is separate from Starlink, SpaceX's commercial internet constellation, and the agency declined to describe SpaceX's role. [cite:de26_toi_starshield] SpaceX and Anduril were also among 12 companies given prototype agreements, with a combined ceiling of $3.2 billion, for space-based interceptors in the Golden Dome missile-defence plan; Palantir was not among them. [cite:de26_st_sbi] The dependence this creates is not hypothetical. In Ukraine, a single company's decisions on where Starlink would work shaped a war, as [scene:de11_tesla_spacex_and_the_state|Part Eleven] sets out; the Pentagon confirmed in June 2023 that it was paying for the service. [cite:de11_dn_pentagon] [cite:de11_cnbc_isaacson] At home, the Federal Aviation Administration tested Starlink terminals in 2025 while the company's founder held a government role ([scene:de21_conflicts_and_contracts|Part Twenty-One]). [cite:de21_ap_starlink] Even the Pentagon's AI chat platform now reaches Grok through "Starshield AI." [cite:de26_ds_genaimil]

Capability is not intent

Each layer here is documented and in federal hands. Persistent overhead imaging combined with plate readers and face recognition could reconstruct a person's movements without a phone. That combination is a capability, stated as such. What the record does not show is the layers joined into one domestic tracking system, or any of them pointed at a named critic for speech; that would need its own document, and none has surfaced. The fusion of data the layers produce is the subject of [scene:de27_capability_not_intent|Part Twenty-Nine]; the stack ICE buys is in [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty]. [cite:de26_404_fortify] [cite:de26_404_drones]

If it were connected

The seeing tools already touch one other layer each. Documented: Mobile Fortify joins a face seen in the street to the government's own records, matching it against DHS, State Department, CBP and FBI images and returning a name and immigration history; and CBP's drones have flown for ICE. [cite:de26_404_fortify] [cite:de26_404_drones] One case shows a face match reaching the travel layer: a Minnesota woman was addressed by name by a Border Patrol agent who said he had used face recognition, and her Global Entry was revoked three days later; the link between the two is alleged in a pending suit, set out in [scene:de25b_who_can_stop_you|Part Twenty-Seven]. [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] Possible, with no document: Mobile Fortify's matches, Clearview's results or drone video feeding ICE's Palantir systems, where a name can be resolved to an address with a "confidence score," and HART, DHS's planned biometric system designed to be shared across agencies but not operational when last assessed; the ecosystem map in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty] grades each of these links possible, because the tools share a customer but no record shows a feed. [cite:ow9_fortune_elite] [cite:de28_hart_pia] Such a join would need an interface and a work order inside the agency, not a new law; what stands in the way is agency policy, the privacy assessments DHS's inspector general found skipped in 2023, and the courts. [cite:de28_oig_23_61] Not supported: a standing link from the NRO's satellite imagery to domestic enforcement; no contract, interface or authority in the record points to one.

sections.h: Code and Cloud: Who Holds the Servers
sections.html:
Almost none of the tools in this book run on computers their users own. They run in "the cloud," which means rented space in data centres operated by a handful of companies; a government agency that uses a cloud service is renting someone else's machines, storage and network. Three layers sit on top of one another, and keeping them apart prevents a common error. The cloud host owns the buildings and machines. A software platform, such as Palantir's, runs on those machines and organises the customer's data. The customer, an agency, decides what goes in and who may look at it. Hosting is not access: a company that rents out the machines does not thereby read what is stored on them, any more than a landlord reads his tenants' letters, and the contracts and law that govern each layer are different. [cite:de26_reg_oracle] [cite:de26_ng_jwcc] A fourth layer sits beside them: the code platforms and app stores where software itself is written, stored and distributed. This section takes each in turn.

The government cloud: a few firms

Most American defence and intelligence computing now runs on four or five companies. In November 2020 the Central Intelligence Agency awarded its Commercial Cloud Enterprise contract, reported as "worth tens of billions of dollars" over about fifteen years, to Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, Google, Oracle and IBM, for the CIA and sixteen other intelligence agencies; Amazon had been the agency's cloud since 2013. [cite:de26_dcd_c2e] On 7 December 2022 the Pentagon awarded its Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability contract, with a $9 billion ceiling, to Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle, for services "across all security domains and classification levels." It replaced JEDI, a single-vendor plan worth up to $10 billion that had been tied up in litigation and was cancelled in 2021. [cite:de26_ng_jwcc] The first award was made under the first Trump administration and the second under Biden; the move from one vendor to several was a deliberate choice to avoid dependence on a single company.

Before an agency may use a commercial cloud service it needs an authorisation under FedRAMP, the federal security-review programme run by the General Services Administration. In March 2025 GSA announced "FedRAMP 20x," which replaces annual paper assessments with automated, near-real-time security indicators; in its first phase, services were authorised without an agency sponsor, and as of October 2026 the programme is in its third phase, with a pilot for the highest-sensitivity tier planned for 2027.
