[cite:de26_fedramp_20x] Faster authorisation is the stated purpose; whether automated checks catch what manual reviews did is not yet shown either way.

The concentration cuts both ways. In September 2025 Microsoft announced that it would "cease and disable specified" subscriptions of Israel's Ministry of Defence after reporting that intercepted Palestinian phone calls were stored on its Azure cloud, stating that it does not provide technology to facilitate mass surveillance of civilians; the episode is set out in [scene:ow9_israel|The One-Way Mirror]. [cite:ow4_tc_msft] One provider's decision changed what a government's intelligence service could do. The same lever, held by a different company or pressed by a different government, could work the other way.

Oracle and Palantir: hosting, not access

In April 2024 Oracle and Palantir announced a partnership under which Palantir would move workloads for its Foundry platform to Oracle's cloud and make its Gotham and AI platforms deployable across Oracle's infrastructure, including "air-gapped regions for defense and intelligence customers," meaning data centres physically cut off from the public internet. Even so, the reporting noted, it was "up to the customer which cloud to deploy on," and some Palantir systems, such as its contract with England's health service, run on Amazon and Microsoft. [cite:de26_reg_oracle] The partnership puts Palantir's software on Oracle's machines. It does not give Oracle the data its government customers load into Palantir, and no document shows that it does; Palantir's own architecture and its claim that customers control their data are tested in [scene:de27_capability_not_intent|Part Twenty-Nine].

The code platforms

GitHub, owned by Microsoft, is where most of the world's open-source software and much private code is stored. In 2019 its employees learned that ICE held a licence for GitHub's product, worth about $200,000, which was up for renewal. The chief executive, Nat Friedman, wrote to staff that GitHub and Microsoft opposed policies such as family separation but that the company "can't be held responsible" for how customers use its products; it renewed the licence and donated $500,000 to immigration nonprofits, and at least five employees quit. [cite:de26_bhr_github] What became of the licence after 2019 is not on the public record. GitHub also publishes the requests governments send it to remove content. It reported 98 such requests for all of 2025 and 708 for the first half of 2026, and said the rise was "largely" a change in how it counts, now including duplicates and every type of request, "not a corresponding increase in content removals." [cite:de26_gh_transparency]

The app store as a gate

For software meant to reach ordinary people, the gate is the phone's app store. ICEBlock was an iPhone app that let users report, anonymously, where they had seen immigration agents. On 2 October 2025 Apple removed it and similar apps after the Justice Department asked; Attorney General Pam Bondi said, "ICEBlock is designed to put ICE agents at risk just for doing their jobs," and Apple said it acted on information from law enforcement about safety risks. [cite:de26_audacy_iceblock] The app's developer, Joshua Aaron, who said it had more than a million users, sued Bondi, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and other officials in December 2025, alleging that pressuring Apple and threatening him violated the First Amendment. [cite:de26_abc_iceblock_suit] In a parallel case brought for the creators of a Chicago Facebook group and an app called Eyes Up, Judge Jorge Alonso of the Northern District of Illinois found in April 2026 that their injuries were "likely traceable to government-coerced enforcement," calling the officials' statements "intimations of a threat," and preliminarily barred the Justice and Homeland Security departments from pressing Apple and Facebook to keep the plaintiffs off. [cite:de26_reason_rosado] The government's position is that the apps endanger officers; the plaintiffs' is that reporting what agents do in public is protected speech. The pressure on a private platform from officials, known as "jawboning," is the same legal question raised about the previous administration's dealings with social-media companies, which reached the Supreme Court in Murthy v. Missouri in 2024 without a ruling on the merits ([scene:de11_twitter_x_xai|Part Eleven]). [cite:de11_scotus_murthy]

What this layer means for the worst case

The record shows a small number of companies holding the machines on which the state's data and software run, and a small number holding the gates through which software reaches the public. It shows one provider cutting off a foreign defence ministry, and one government persuading a platform to remove an app aimed at its own agents, a removal a federal judge has since found likely coerced. Concentration makes these firms points of leverage for whoever holds power, and the documented examples run in both directions. What the record does not show is any cloud host reading an agency's data, or a code platform handing over users' code to immigration enforcement; the worst-case extension, a few firms refusing service to the government's critics at its request, has one documented instance at the app-store layer, and it is in court. [cite:ow4_tc_msft] [cite:de26_reason_rosado]

If it were connected

The cloud is the floor every other layer stands on, so the join that matters here is access to what is stored. Not supported: a cloud host reading or passing on its government customers' data; the record shows hosting contracts, Oracle's partnership with Palantir leaves the data to the customer, and Microsoft said its own review of Israel's use did not access the customer's content. [cite:de26_reg_oracle] [cite:ow4_tc_msft] Documented, once: ordinary office software carrying a government dataset to a vendor, when ICE passed a Medicaid file to Palantir over a Microsoft Teams chat in January 2026, outside a court's limits; the channel was a chat window, not a designed interface. [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] Documented as well: officials asking an app store to remove software aimed at their agents, and the store complying. [cite:de26_audacy_iceblock] Possible, with no document: the same lever used to deny a named critic a service, or a code platform's records on a user reaching ICE through the kind of administrative subpoena DHS has served on Google and Meta ([scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty]). The first would need only a request and a willing company, the second only a subpoena; what stands in the way is a company's refusal, notice to the user, and, since April 2026 in Chicago, an injunction against government pressure on platforms. [cite:de28_eff_letter] [cite:de26_reason_rosado]

sections.h: The AI Layer: Models Inside the State
sections.html:
A large language model is a program trained on vast amounts of text to predict and produce language; it can summarise documents, translate, write code and sort messages by topic or tone at a speed no team of analysts can match. "Agentic" systems go a step further and let a model take actions, such as searching databases or filling in forms, in a chain of steps. For a government, the attraction is scale: a model can read every document in a case file, every post in an applicant's history, or every intercepted message in a language its analysts do not speak. The risk is the same scale applied to error, since models produce confident wrong answers on sarcasm, quotation and slang. Government use is graded by security level: the Pentagon's "Impact Level" ratings run from public data to IL5, for sensitive unclassified information, and IL6, for data classified up to Secret. [cite:de26_ds_genaimil] [cite:de26_reg_claudepal] This section follows the policy that governs these models, the contracts that put them inside the government, and the one dispute in which a vendor's limits on use were tested.

The policy turn

On 30 October 2023 President Biden signed Executive Order 14110 on the "safe, secure, and trustworthy" development and use of AI, the federal government's main rulebook for the technology at the time. On 20 January 2025, his first day back in office, President Trump revoked it in Executive Order 14148, a list of rescissions that also revoked the 2021 order on private prisons. [cite:de26_ucsb_14148] On 23 July 2025 he signed three further orders alongside an "AI Action Plan": one to remove regulations the administration called onerous, one to promote exports of American AI, and one titled "Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government," which directs agencies to buy only models that are "truth-seeking" and ideologically neutral and that do not skew answers toward positions such as diversity programmes. [cite:de26_nbc_woke] The orders loosen rules on how models are built and add a content condition on what the government buys.

The contracts

The models entered the state under both administrations. In November 2024, under Biden, Anthropic, Palantir and Amazon Web Services announced that Anthropic's Claude models would run inside Palantir's AI platform on Amazon's cloud at IL6; Anthropic said it granted exceptions to its usage rules that were "carefully calibrated" for "carefully selected government agencies," including foreign intelligence analysis, while keeping bans on uses such as disinformation and weapons. [cite:de26_reg_claudepal] On 14 July 2025 the Pentagon's Chief Digital and AI Office announced awards of up to $200 million each to Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI to build "agentic AI workflows across a variety of mission areas." [cite:de26_cdao] The same day xAI launched "Grok for Government," days after apologising for its chatbot's antisemitic posts on X. [cite:de26_eng_grokgov] [cite:de11_reuters_grok] Through GSA's "OneGov" programme, OpenAI and Anthropic offered their government models for $1 per agency per year, and on 25 September 2025 xAI offered Grok 4 for 42 cents; an earlier xAI deal had reportedly fallen through after the antisemitic output, more than thirty advocacy groups objected, and GSA said Grok 4 met its guidelines. [cite:de26_fs_onegov] The Pentagon's internal chat platform, GenAI.mil, opened with Google's Gemini for Government and was planned for more than three million personnel; ChatGPT and Grok were added at IL5 on 31 August 2026. [cite:de26_ds_genaimil] Inside DOGE, Reuters reported in May 2025 that staff were expanding use of a customised Grok to analyse federal data, which [scene:de19_the_access|Part Nineteen] examines. [cite:de19_reuters_grok]

The supply-chain-risk case

The one documented test of whether a vendor could limit how the government uses its model began in February 2026. The Pentagon sought to replace two prohibitions in its contract with Anthropic, on mass domestic surveillance and on fully autonomous weapons, with permission for "all lawful use," and on 24 February set a deadline of 27 February. [cite:de26_d1_anthropic] On 26 February Anthropic's chief executive, Dario Amodei, said that in a "narrow set of cases" AI "can undermine, rather than defend, democratic values," named those two uses, and said the company "cannot in good conscience accede." The Pentagon's spokesman, Sean Parnell, said the department had no interest in mass surveillance of Americans, which he called illegal, or in autonomous weapons without human involvement, and asked only to use the model "for all lawful purposes," adding: "We will not let ANY company dictate the terms regarding how we make operational decisions." [cite:de26_wt_anthropic]

On 27 February Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that Anthropic would be designated a supply-chain risk, a status normally used to keep products from untrusted suppliers out of military systems, and the President ordered all agencies to stop using Anthropic's services; the designation was formalised on 3 March. Under Secretary Emil Michael wrote that no private company would "insert their opinions in the chain of command." [cite:de26_d1_anthropic] [cite:de26_eng_openai] As the designation was announced, on 27–28 February, OpenAI also announced an agreement to deploy its models on a classified Pentagon network, cloud-only; its chief executive, Sam Altman, said the agreement included "prohibitions on domestic mass surveillance" and "human responsibility for the use of force," and that OpenAI had asked for the same terms to be offered to every AI company. [cite:de26_eng_openai] The contract text has not been published, so how its terms compare with those Anthropic refused cannot be checked from the record.

The two court rulings rest on different statutes and, by the reading of commercial lawyers, do not conflict. The California court found that the narrower statute, aimed at adversaries, did not reach a company's good-faith negotiation of usage limits; reporting described the judge as calling the Pentagon's actions "troubling and retaliatory." The appeals court held that the broader procurement statute reaches "any person," and that the department could reasonably conclude a supplier able to change its model's behaviour through training posed a risk to its use. [cite:de26_taft_dccir] [cite:de26_ds_enbanc] Anthropic said it "respectfully disagree[s]" and noted that another court had held the parallel designation unlawful; the Pentagon did not comment on the rehearing petition. [cite:de26_d1_anthropic] [cite:de26_ds_enbanc]

What the record shows, and does not

Documented: the federal rules on how AI is built were withdrawn and replaced with a procurement test on content; frontier models from four companies sit inside defence and civilian agencies at prices of a dollar or less; and the one vendor that held out for written limits on domestic surveillance was excluded, an exclusion one court has set aside and another has upheld. Reported, from officials speaking to Axios in March 2025 and not confirmed by a published document: a State Department effort called "Catch and Revoke" that would use AI-assisted reviews of tens of thousands of student-visa holders' social-media accounts; the department did not comment directly. [cite:de26_audit_axios_catchrevoke] [cite:de26_audit_catchrevoke] The published social-media vetting rules are in [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty], and ICE's address-scoring tool in [scene:de28_ice_contracts|its first section]. Not documented: any of these models being used for mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon has said it does not seek that and that it is illegal; the record cannot show a negative, and the contract terms that would settle the question are not public. The capability a frontier model adds, reading everything at once, is real; its use against domestic critics would need its own document, and none has surfaced. [cite:de26_wt_anthropic] [cite:de26_eng_openai]

If it were connected

A model placed inside an integration platform is the clearest join in this layer. Documented: since November 2024 Anthropic's models have been offered inside Palantir's AI platform at the Secret level, so a language model can sit on top of whatever data a Palantir customer has loaded; and frontier models from four companies are installed across defence and civilian agencies. [cite:de26_reg_claudepal] [cite:de26_ds_genaimil] Reported: AI-assisted reading of visa holders' posts. [cite:de26_audit_axios_catchrevoke] Possible, with no document: a model running over ICE's joined records, the people-search profiles, Medicaid addresses and phone extractions that [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|the ecosystem map] shows reaching its platforms, to rank people for arrest or to read everything a flagged person has posted. That would need only a deployment inside the agency's own system, not a new law or a new contract type; what stands in the way is contract terms that are not public and, for the one vendor that wrote limits down, an exclusion still in court. Not supported: any model in use for mass surveillance of Americans; the Pentagon says it seeks no such use, and no record shows one. [cite:de26_wt_anthropic]

sections.h: Money Rails: Watching Payments, Stopping Them
sections.html:
Every electronic payment runs on "rails," the networks of banks, card companies and settlement systems that move money from one account to another, and every rail keeps records. Two powers sit on those records. The first is to watch: banks must report certain transactions to the government. The second is to stop: an account can be closed, a payment refused, a balance frozen. Both powers are old, both have been used by administrations of both parties, and both are now being rebuilt for digital money. This section sets out what the law requires, what has been documented in practice, and how far the worst case would have to stretch it. The denial of commerce to particular people, from sanctions lists to emergency freezes, is the "denied" rung of the ladder in [scene:de35_the_consequence_ladder|Part Thirty-Seven] and is only pointed to here.

The watching power

The Bank Secrecy Act of 1970 requires banks and other financial institutions to file a Currency Transaction Report for cash dealings over $10,000 and a Suspicious Activity Report, or SAR, whenever they suspect a transaction may involve crime; the reports go to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, FinCEN, a bureau of the Treasury. Since United States v. Miller in 1976, the Supreme Court has treated bank records as information the customer handed to a third party, so agencies may search the reports without a warrant. The volume is large. In fiscal year 2024 institutions filed 4.7 million SARs, about 12,870 a day, and 20.5 million currency reports, and personnel of the Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent, ran about 290,000 searches of the reporting in the same period. [cite:de26_aba_fincen] The customer is not told a SAR has been filed. The rule that protects location data after Carpenter ([scene:de26_counterweights|the last section of this part]) has not been extended to bank records.

The stopping power, both directions

Banks may close accounts largely at their own discretion, and governments of both parties have leaned on that discretion. In 2013, under President Obama, the Justice Department began "Operation Choke Point," aimed at keeping fraudsters out of the payment system; guidance from the bank regulator FDIC listed "high-risk" merchants that included payday lenders and sellers of firearms and ammunition. Critics said lawful industries were being cut off; the list was withdrawn in 2015, and on 16 August 2017 the Justice Department wrote that the initiative was "no longer in effect, and it will not be undertaken again." [cite:de26_cfslm_chokepoint] In December 2025 the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency reported preliminary findings that the nine largest national banks, between 2020 and 2023, had restricted service to whole sectors, among them firearms, coal, Arctic oil and gas, private prisons, payday lending, tobacco, adult entertainment, digital assets, and political action committees and political parties, often for reasons of reputation rather than financial risk. It was still reviewing nearly 100,000 complaints and had made no finding of political or religious debanking. [cite:de26_occ_debank]

On 7 August 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14331, "Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans." It defines "politicized or unlawful debanking" as restricting service because of a customer's political or religious beliefs or lawful business the provider disfavours for political reasons, and orders regulators to strip "reputation risk" from their guidance within 180 days and to review banks' past policies. Only religion-based debanking may be referred to the Attorney General. [cite:de26_fr_14331] The record therefore runs in both directions at once: pressure on lawful sectors under one administration, bank policies that restricted political committees and private prisons under the next, and an order against those policies under the third.

Programmable money

Digital money adds a third power: to stop a payment by code. A "stablecoin" is a cryptocurrency token designed to hold a fixed value, usually one dollar, backed by reserves the issuing company holds. It moves on a public blockchain, a shared ledger on which every transfer between addresses is visible to anyone, permanently. The issuer controls the token's software and can mark an address so that its tokens cannot move, a "freeze," or destroy them, a "burn." A central bank digital currency, or CBDC, would instead be money issued directly by the central bank in digital form. [cite:de26_fr_14178] [cite:de26_crec_genius]

The United States has rejected the second and written the first into law. Executive Order 14178 of 23 January 2025 states that agencies "are hereby prohibited from undertaking any action to establish, issue, or promote CBDCs," unless required by law. [cite:de26_fr_14178] The GENIUS Act, signed on 18 July 2025 as Public Law 119-27, did the opposite for private issuers. [cite:de26_crs_genius] Its text provides that a permitted stablecoin issuer "shall be treated as a financial institution for purposes of the Bank Secrecy Act," which brings SAR filing to stablecoins; that it must keep "technical capabilities, policies, and procedures to block, freeze, and reject specific or impermissible transactions"; and that it must have "the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order." It defines a lawful order to include one requiring an issuer to "seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins." [cite:de26_crec_genius] Implementing rules were still being written in 2026. [cite:de26_crs_genius]

The power is already used at scale by issuers acting on their own terms. Tether, which issues the USDT stablecoin, said in February 2026 that it had frozen about $4.2 billion linked to illicit activity and had worked with more than 310 agencies in 64 countries, including the Justice Department and the Secret Service; the figures are the company's own. [cite:de26_forklog_tether] On 23 April 2026 it froze more than $344 million in two addresses, working with the Treasury's sanctions office and American law enforcement; its chief executive, Paolo Ardoino, said, "USDT is not a safe haven for illicit activity." [cite:de26_decrypt_tether] Documented uses so far concern sanctions, fraud and crime. No freeze aimed at a person for political speech has been documented.

The theorists and the rails

The texts this book maps do not ask for this machinery. Nick Land's wish-list in The Dark Enlightenment calls for "Restoration of hard money (precious metal coins and bullion deposit notes) and abolition of central banking," and the "Dismantling of state monetary and fiscal discretion," a programme that points away from a state able to freeze accounts by code. [cite:de4_land_de] Curtis Yarvin's own answer to who controls a sovereign corporation is a board holding cryptographic keys to the state's weapons ([scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight]); a freeze switch built into money rhymes with that design, but rhyme is not provenance, and no document links the GENIUS Act, a banking statute passed by Congress, to either writer. [cite:de8_kofman_ny] [cite:de26_crs_genius]

Capability is not intent

The capability is documented: a reporting system that files thousands of reports a day and is searchable without a warrant, a history of sector-wide account closures under both parties, and a federal statute that requires every regulated stablecoin to carry a freeze-and-burn switch for lawful orders. The worst-case extension is plain to state: if payroll and retail moved onto stablecoins, a lawful order could stop a named person's money at once, with any hearing afterward. What the record does not show is that switch, or any other rail, used against a critic for speech. The same administration that legislated the switch also barred a central-bank digital currency and ordered regulators to stop reputation-based debanking, which cuts against the reading that the rails are being prepared as a political weapon. [cite:de26_fr_14178] [cite:de26_fr_14331] [cite:de26_crec_genius]

If it were connected

The money layer is already joined to enforcement at one point. Documented: DHS searches the banks' reports to FinCEN, about 290,000 times in fiscal year 2024, and the September 2025 domestic-terrorism memorandum tells the Treasury to guide banks on suspicious-activity reports about the funders of political violence ([scene:de30_nspm7_and_detachment|Part Thirty-Two]). [cite:de26_aba_fincen] [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] Possible, with no document: those reports, or the Treasury's own records through the "common API layer" Palantir has been building for IRS modernisation since September 2025, loaded into ICE's integration platforms beside its location and people-search data; and a stablecoin freeze order aimed at the addresses of a person on an enforcement list. The first would need an agreement between agencies, and the IRS records are behind the tax-privacy wall the courts enforced in 2025–26; the second would need a "lawful order" under the GENIUS Act and an exchange's records linking an address to a name. [cite:de27_treasury_api] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de26_crec_genius] Not supported: any rail, report or freeze used against a person for political speech; the documented freezes concern sanctions and crime. [cite:de26_decrypt_tether]

sections.h: Counterweights: What Has Actually Stopped the Tools
sections.html:
The toolkit parts describe what exists. This section takes a narrower subject: what has actually stopped, narrowed or turned back one of these tools. Six kinds appear: encryption, courts, state laws, companies and their employees, journalists, and juries; each has a documented win and a documented limit. A counterweight counts here only where a document shows it changed what a tool did.

Encryption

End-to-end encryption means a message is scrambled on the sender's phone and unscrambled only on the recipient's, so the company carrying it holds no readable copy. The practical effect shows in what such a company can hand over. When a federal grand jury in the Central District of California subpoenaed Signal, the encrypted messaging service, for a user's identity, contacts, activity and correspondence, Signal produced two timestamps: when the account was created and when it last connected. "Signal still knows nothing about you," the company said. [cite:de26_sw_signal] Governments have pushed back on the design itself. Britain's government ordered Apple, under its Investigatory Powers Act, to provide access to its encrypted iCloud backups; Apple stopped offering its Advanced Data Protection to new users in the United Kingdom rather than build a back door, and on 19 August 2025 the US Director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, said Britain had agreed to drop the demand. [cite:de26_ai_appleuk] Encryption's limit is the device. Spyware reads messages after they are unscrambled, and a seized phone can be copied, as [scene:de25_spyware_and_phones|Part Twenty-Six] sets out.

Courts

Two Supreme Court rulings have carried the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement into location data. In Carpenter v. United States (22 June 2018), decided 5–4 in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts, the Court held that police generally need a warrant to obtain historical records of a phone's location from a carrier: "We decline to grant the state unrestricted access to a wireless carrier's database of physical location information." [cite:de26_jurist_carpenter] In Chatrie v. United States (29 June 2026), decided six to three, Justice Kagan, writing for five, held that obtaining a person's Google Location History is a search, rejecting the argument that sharing data with a company forfeits privacy in it; Justice Gorsuch concurred in the judgment and Justices Alito, Thomas and Barrett dissented. The Court did not declare such "geofence" warrants unconstitutional and sent the case back to decide whether the warrant was valid. [cite:de26_crs_chatrie] Both rulings govern data the government compels from a company. Neither reaches data the government buys, the gap examined in [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty].

Lower courts have checked particular uses. A federal judge in Chicago found in April 2026 that the Justice and Homeland Security departments had likely coerced Apple and Facebook into removing tools that tracked immigration agents, and enjoined further pressure ([scene:de26_code_and_cloud|the second section of this part]). [cite:de26_reason_rosado] A federal court in San Francisco set aside one of two designations excluding an AI company that had refused domestic-surveillance uses, while an appeals court upheld the other ([scene:de26_ai_layer|the third section]). [cite:de26_taft_dccir] Rulings on government datasets shared with ICE are in [scene:de30_silos_and_subpoenas|Part Thirty-Two].

State laws

Where Congress has not legislated, a few states have. Illinois's Biometric Information Privacy Act of 2008 forbids a private entity to collect a person's face or fingerprint template without a written release, and lets the person sue for $1,000 per negligent violation and $5,000 per intentional or reckless one. [cite:de26_justia_bipa] After the Illinois Supreme Court's 2019 Rosenbach ruling set off a wave of class actions, Facebook settled a class action over its photo-tagging feature for $650 million. [cite:de26_br_bipa] Under a consent order of 11 May 2022 in a suit brought by the ACLU, Clearview AI is permanently barred from making its faceprint database available to most private companies nationwide, and for five years could not sell to any Illinois entity, including police. [cite:de26_aclu_clearview] The law's limit is written into it: "A private entity does not include a State or local government agency," and it does not apply to contractors of a state agency; federal agencies are outside it entirely. [cite:de26_justia_bipa]

Other states have followed different paths. Washington's My Health My Data Act, in force since March 2024, covers health data that falls outside federal medical privacy law and lets individuals sue; the first suit, filed on 10 February 2025, accused Amazon of collecting location and advertising identifiers through code embedded in other companies' apps. [cite:de26_wh_mhmda] California's Delete Request and Opt-out Platform let residents send one deletion request to more than 500 registered data brokers from 1 January 2026, with brokers required to process requests every 45 days from 1 August 2026. [cite:de26_cppa_drop] Montana in May 2025 became the first state to forbid its own agencies to buy communications, precise location or other sensitive data without a warrant or investigative subpoena. [cite:de26_reason_mt282] And Illinois's licence-plate law stopped a federal use directly: after the Secretary of State's audit found that CBP had accessed Illinois plate data in "a clear violation of the state law," the camera company Flock paused its pilots with CBP and Homeland Security Investigations on 25 August 2025. [cite:de26_ap_flock]

Companies and their employees

In June 2018, after thousands of Google employees petitioned and dozens quit, Google said it would not renew its contract for Project Maven, the Pentagon's drone-imagery AI programme. [cite:de26_eng_maven] The programme continued with other contractors; Palantir's Maven Smart System contract was raised to nearly $1.3 billion in May 2025. [cite:ow9_ds_maven] In June 2020 Amazon put a one-year moratorium on police use of its face-recognition product, and IBM left the business. [cite:de26_idt_rekognition] Microsoft's September 2025 decision to disable specified Israeli defence subscriptions followed press reporting on how the service was used. [cite:ow4_tc_msft] GitHub's employees, by contrast, did not stop the company renewing its ICE licence in 2019. [cite:de26_bhr_github]

Journalists and juries

Much of this part became public through reporting and records requests, not agency disclosure: Mobile Fortify's no-consent rule through a privacy assessment obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, CBP's drone flights through flight logs, Starshield through Reuters' sources, and the wrongful arrests through the Washington Post's count. [cite:de26_reason_fortify] [cite:de26_404_drones] [cite:de26_toi_starshield] [cite:de26_fortune_wapo] Juries have acted on the spyware trade, as in WhatsApp's verdict against NSO Group, set out in [scene:de25_spyware_and_phones|Part Twenty-Six].

If it were connected

Every join on [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|the ecosystem map] has to pass one of these counterweights or go around it. Documented: counterweights have stopped particular joins between layers. Illinois's audit cut a federal agency off from the state's plate data; a judge first limited Medicaid sharing with ICE to five fields and later paused it; and the courts blocked the IRS address exchange after 42,695 unlawful disclosures. [cite:de26_ap_flock] [cite:de30_bl_medicaid] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] Not supported: that any counterweight here reaches a join made inside an agency between records it already holds or has bought; none of the six acts at that step, which is governed by internal policy, privacy assessments and, afterwards, inspectors general and congressional letters, so the joins graded possible on the map would meet no court, state law or encryption on the way in. What would act at the join itself is a court ruling on purchased data, or a state law that limits what local agencies pass to federal ones; no such ruling exists, and Montana's law limits only what the state's own agencies buy. [cite:de26_reason_mt282]

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis is the Sophia platform's, not a finding: immigration enforcement as the occasion, a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. On this part's material, the occasion is documented. ICE holds a face-recognition app that gives the person scanned no way to refuse and keeps citizens' photographs for 15 years; CBP photographs every non-citizen at the border and lent its drones to ICE at least 50 times; Clearview's scraped gallery is under ICE contract; and the money rails now carry a statutory freeze-and-burn switch for stablecoins and a warrantless reporting system DHS searched about 290,000 times in a year. [cite:de26_reason_fortify] [cite:de26_bu_entryexit] [cite:de26_404_drones] [cite:de26_bu_clearviewice] [cite:de26_crec_genius] [cite:de26_aba_fincen] It is also documented that the one AI vendor that demanded written limits on domestic surveillance was excluded from federal work, and that officials pressed Apple to remove an app that tracked immigration agents, pressure a federal judge found likely coercive. [cite:de26_d1_anthropic] [cite:de26_reason_rosado]

Probable: that concentration makes the few firms that host the state's data and distribute the public's software into points of leverage, since the record shows that lever pulled in both directions, by a company against a foreign ministry and by a government against an app. That rests on two cases, not on a documented policy. [cite:ow4_tc_msft] [cite:de26_audacy_iceblock]

Not supported: that these tools have been joined into one domestic tracking system, that any of them has been turned on a named critic for speech, or that the theorists' texts call for this machinery; Land's programme calls for hard money and the end of central banking, the reverse of a freeze switch. [cite:de4_land_de] And the record runs against the worst case at several points. The administration that wrote the stablecoin switch also barred a central-bank digital currency and ordered an end to reputation-based debanking; most of the tools here began or grew under both parties; and courts, a state audit and company decisions narrowed particular uses. [cite:de26_fr_14178] [cite:de26_fr_14331] [cite:de26_ap_flock] [cite:de26_crs_chatrie] The counterweights have one shared gap: none of them reaches the federal purchase of commercial data, which is the subject of [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty], or the integration that Palantir's software performs, which is the subject of [scene:de27_origins_and_control|Part Twenty-Nine]. The book's overall grading of the hypothesis is in [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three].

chapters.label: Part Twenty-Nine
chapters.title: Palantir
chapters.intro: This part turns from the tools to the company that joins them. Palantir Technologies, co-founded in 2003 by Peter Thiel and run since 2004 by Alex Karp, sells software that lets governments and companies bring separate records together, match those that belong to the same person and search the result. Its early history with American intelligence is told in the library's earlier volume; this part asks who controls the company, what its software does and does not do, what its makers say it is for, how much money it now takes from the American state and from wars, and why several European governments and one constitutional court have refused it or set conditions on it. Throughout, it holds to one rule: what the software can do is documented by how it is built and used, and what anyone intends to do with it only by their own words or acts.
chapters.outro: Palantir is a software company that does not collect data and whose purpose is to make collected data more powerful by joining it. Three founders, Cohen, Karp and Thiel, hold up to 49.999999 percent of its votes through a voting trust. [cite:de27_10q_q2_2026] Its chief executive describes its work as national defence and says plainly that it is used "on occasion" to kill. [cite:de27_inverse_karp2020] Its United States government revenue reached $809 million in the second quarter of 2026, up 90 percent, with new awards at the Army, the Treasury and ICE. [cite:de27_8k_q2_2026] [cite:de27_hg_ero] The one documented case of data reaching it outside the law's limits was a Medicaid dataset that ICE passed to it over a Teams chat in January 2026, beyond a court's limits; Palantir says it was purged on the government's instruction, and copies were later found at ICE. [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] European buyers refused it or set terms for stated reasons of sovereignty and constitutional threshold, not for documented misuse. [cite:de27_site36_swiss] [cite:de27_bverfg_2023] What matters most is the data the platform is fed and the law that governs it, which is where [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty] turns, to ICE's whole data stack.

sections.h: Founders, the CIA's Fund and a Block of Votes That Cannot Be Outvoted
sections.html:
Palantir Technologies sits at the point where the people of Book Two meet the machinery of Book Five. Peter Thiel co-founded it and chairs it; the Army, the Pentagon's intelligence programmes and Immigration and Customs Enforcement run on its software; and its chief executive has written a book arguing that Silicon Valley owes the nation its engineering. The library has already told the company's early history with American intelligence, from the CIA's venture fund through the NSA's XKEYSCORE to the Army's ten-year deal, in [scene:ow9_origins|The One-Way Mirror], and Thiel's part in founding it in [scene:de9_paypal_palantir_facebook|Part Nine]. This section does not repeat those accounts. It asks two narrower questions: who controls the company, and what, in plain terms, it sells.

The founding, and a year that will not settle

Palantir was founded in 2003 by Thiel with four others: Stephen Cohen, Joe Lonsdale, Alex Karp and Nathan Gettings. Karp, a former Stanford Law School colleague of Thiel's, was hired as chief executive in 2004 and has held the post ever since. [cite:de27_wiki_pltr] It was incorporated in May 2003 with about $30 million in initial funding, most of it from Thiel and his fund. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] The name comes from the seeing stones of Tolkien's fiction, which show distant things to whoever holds them; what that name has been made to mean by critics and by the company's admirers is a matter of interpretation, set out under that label in [scene:de39_seeing_stones|Part Forty-Two].

Karp's own background is often misdescribed. He holds a doctorate in social theory from Goethe University in Frankfurt, which is routinely reported as having been written under the philosopher Jürgen Habermas. His supervisor, the sociologist Karola Brede, said in March 2026 that Karp was not Habermas's doctoral student: Habermas had asked her to meet the young American, the two men talked, and Karp drew on Habermas's idea of the "lifeworld," but the thesis, on aggression as a force that holds social groups together, was written "under my supervision." [cite:de27_lgc_brede] The correction matters only because the Habermas line is used, by admirers and critics alike, to make Karp a product of the Frankfurt School; the record shows a doctorate in Frankfurt and conversations with its most famous living thinker, not discipleship.

The CIA connection is real and small. In-Q-Tel, the agency's venture-capital arm, invested about $2 million. Fortune, in a 2016 profile, called it Palantir's "first outside investor." [cite:de10_fortune_palantir] [cite:ow9_bf_karp2015] The year is less certain than it is usually made to sound. One widely used account puts the investment at the company's launch in 2004; other accounts give 2005; the library's [scene:ow9_origins|earlier volume] gives no year, and the date is best stated as 2004 or 2005. [cite:de27_wiki_pltr] What the sources do agree on is the order of events: the CIA's fund came first, its money was modest, and until 2010, by Fortune's account, Palantir's "only customers were in intelligence, law enforcement, and defense." [cite:de10_fortune_palantir] The question of whether the agency shaped the product is answered in the library's earlier account: it helped fund and test software for its own analysts' work, and the relationship with the NSA ended in 2015 without a full contract. [cite:ow9_bf_karp2015]

From private start-up to S&P 500

For seventeen years the company stayed private. It moved its headquarters to Denver, Colorado, in August 2020 and listed its shares on the New York Stock Exchange by direct public offering on 30 September 2020, without the usual underwritten sale of new stock. S&P Global announced on 6 September 2024 that it would join the S&P 500 index; in November 2024 it moved its listing to Nasdaq, effective 26 November; and in February 2026 it announced plans to move its headquarters again, to Miami. [cite:de27_wiki_pltr] The filing for the 2020 listing showed a company that had lost $580 million the previous year and drew nearly half its revenue from governments. [cite:ow9_ap_s1] By 2026 it was profitable and large, as [scene:de27_money_and_war|the third section] shows.

Who controls it: three classes of share and a voting trust

The most important fact about Palantir's governance is in its own filings, and it is not hidden. The company has three classes of common stock. Class A shares, the ones bought and sold on Nasdaq, carry one vote each; there were about 2.3 billion of them at 30 June 2026. Class B shares, which are not listed, carry ten votes each; there were about 101 million. And there is a small third class, Class F, about one million shares, which are not counted by number at all. [cite:de27_10q_q2_2026] In the company's words, "All shares of Class F common stock are held in a voting trust established by Stephen Cohen, Alexander Karp, and Peter Thiel." [cite:de27_10q_q2_2026]

A voting trust is a legal arrangement in which shareholders hand the voting rights of their shares to a trustee who votes them as the founders direct. The Class F shares are designed to carry whatever number of votes is needed to top up the founders' total. The quarterly report states that the arrangement "generally gives the Founders the ability to control up to 49.999999% of the total voting power" of the company's stock, so long as the three men and their affiliates together hold at least 100 million of the company's equity securities, the threshold that applied at 30 June 2026. [cite:de27_10q_q2_2026]

In plain arithmetic, a block of just under half of all votes cannot be outvoted unless almost every other vote is cast against it, and in practice many shareholders do not vote. The structure gives three men a durable say over the election of directors and over any change to the company's charter, however much of the company's economic value the public comes to own. Dual-class structures of this kind are common among founder-led technology companies, and they are lawful; investors who buy Class A shares are told of the arrangement in the filings. Palantir's version is unusual in one respect: the founders' share of votes is set by formula, up to a fixed ceiling, rather than simply by the number of shares they hold, so long as they stay above the ownership threshold. [cite:de27_10q_q2_2026]

Two points of precision follow. First, Stephen Cohen is the least discussed of the three people who control the company, though his legal position in the trust is the same as Thiel's and Karp's; public argument about Palantir tends to run through Thiel's politics and Karp's speeches, and leaves him out. Second, control of the company is not control of its customers. The voting trust decides who sits on Palantir's board; it does not decide what the Army or ICE does with the software they license, which is set by those agencies' own law, as the next section examines. Thiel's position, stated exactly, is co-founder, chairman, a large shareholder and one of the three founders who established the voting trust; Palantir's contracts are the company's, not his. [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] [cite:de27_10q_q2_2026]

What it sells, in plain terms

Palantir sells software, not data. Its products are platforms: programs that let an organisation pull records from many separate systems into one place, match the records that refer to the same person, place or object, and then search, map and analyse the result. [cite:de27_pal_notdata] There are four that matter here. Gotham, released in 2008, is the platform built for defence, intelligence and police customers. [cite:de27_wiki_pltr] Foundry is its counterpart for companies and civilian agencies. Apollo is the company's system for delivering and continuously updating its software inside customers' own computer systems. And AIP, the Artificial Intelligence Platform launched in April 2023, lets customers put large language models, the kind of AI behind chatbots, to work on the data already inside Gotham or Foundry. [cite:de27_wiki_pltr]

The company's own description of its role is consistent: it says it does not collect, store or sell personal data, and that it acts for its customers as a "data processor, not a data controller," which in European data law means the party that handles data on another's instructions rather than the party that decides why it is held. [cite:de27_pal_notdata] Whether that description is the whole story, and what follows from software whose value lies in joining records, is the subject of [scene:de27_capability_not_intent|the next section].

sections.h: Capability Is Not Intent: What the Software Does and What Its Makers Say
sections.html:
Every argument about Palantir turns on one distinction, which this book holds to throughout: what a tool can do is documented by how it is built and used; what anyone intends to do with it is documented only by their own words or acts. This section sets out both, then the strongest case on each side of the question that matters here, whether Palantir is neutral plumbing or something more.

Integration, not collection

Palantir's software does not go out into the world and gather information. It has no cameras, phone taps or web crawlers of its own. It works on records the customer already holds or chooses to load: case files, border-crossing logs, police reports, purchased commercial data, sensor feeds. Its job is integration, in three steps. It connects to many separate databases, often through an API, an application programming interface, the standard doorway by which one program asks another for data. It performs what engineers call entity resolution: deciding that the "J. Smith" in one file, the "John Smith" at the same address in another and the owner of a particular phone in a third are one person, and linking those records. And it lets analysts search, map and chart the linked result, and set alerts when something new appears. [cite:de27_pal_notdata]

The company's own account is precise. "We do not collect, store, or sell personal data," it says; its customers "define what can and cannot be done with their data," and "We do not and cannot reuse or transfer our clients' data for our own purposes." [cite:de27_pal_notdata] It builds in fine-grained permissions, so that an analyst sees only what his role allows, and a default configuration that records every user's actions, an audit log. It adds a caution that bears on everything that follows: "technical controls alone cannot avert negative societal outcomes." [cite:de27_pal_pcl]

One common misreading should be cleared here. Palantir's documentation lists ready-made "connectors" to a long roster of systems: databases, cloud storage, business software such as SAP and Salesforce, messaging tools such as Slack and Microsoft Teams, and social and advertising platforms including Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn, for "connectivity between Foundry and your systems." [cite:de27_pal_connectors] A connector is a plug, not a key. It lets a customer pull in data from an account it already controls, such as its own advertising account, with its own credentials; it does not open Facebook's or Microsoft's users to Palantir or anyone else. A list of connectors documents what a customer could wire in, not what any customer has: connector is not access.

What the men who run it say it is for

The people who run Palantir have said a great deal about what they built it to do, and their words are the right evidence for their own purposes. Karp's are unusually direct. In an Axios interview broadcast on HBO in May 2020 he said the product was used "on occasion" to target and kill, describing the hunt for a terrorist: "you're probably doing the operation that actually takes out the person with another product we built." Asked whether he regretted the ICE work, he said, "No, no, no." [cite:de27_inverse_karp2020] On a call with investors in early February 2025 he said Palantir was there, when necessary, "to scare enemies and on occasion kill them." [cite:de27_giz_karp2025] His book with Nicholas Zamiska, Palantir's head of corporate affairs, The Technological Republic (18 February 2025), indicts "Silicon Valley's failure to come to the defense of the nation that made its rise possible"; a 22-point summary the company posted on 18 April 2026 added that "National service should be a universal duty." [cite:de27_prh_techrep] [cite:de27_reason_manifesto]

Read on their own terms, these statements describe a company that sees itself as an arm of national defence and law enforcement, proud of lethal work against foreign enemies and of its immigration contracts. They are not statements of intent to watch domestic political opponents, and none by Karp, Thiel or Cohen found here says so. The words are hard and should be quoted as hard, not converted into something they do not say. Thiel's own 2016 account of the founding purpose was that helping the government make sense of its data could "end indiscriminate surveillance"; how that claim fares against his later politics is examined in [scene:de10_philosophy_vs_practice|Part Ten]. [cite:de10_fortune_palantir]

The strongest case that it is only a tool

The case that Palantir is a sophisticated database program and nothing more rests on documented points. The data belongs to the customer, which decides what goes in and who may see it. [cite:de27_pal_notdata] Audit logs make misuse more traceable than in the scattered systems the software replaces. [cite:de27_pal_pcl] The company's government work has limits it did not set: the NSA relationship ended in 2015 without a contract, and in 2025 Palantir said it "is not a vendor on any master database project to unify databases across federal agencies." [cite:ow9_bf_karp2015] [cite:de19_palantir_record] And what a customer may do is bounded by the customer's law, not by Palantir's code. On this view the right target for anyone worried about surveillance is the law of data acquisition, where [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty] turns.

The strongest case that it is more

The case that it is more also rests on documented points. Integration is itself the power: records harmless apart can be revealing together, which is why stripping names protects less than it seems ([scene:de24_the_myth_of_anonymous_data|Part Twenty-Four]). Joined data has reached people with no direct link to wrongdoing: the sociologist Sarah Brayne's 2017 study of the Los Angeles police, based on interviews with 75 officers and staff, found that its Palantir system held people who had never had direct contact with the police, linked to a "person of interest" by something as slight as a car accident with a gang member, and that a points system for "risk" sent officers to stop the same people again, adding more points; Palantir and the department declined to comment. [cite:de27_cnn_brayne] [cite:de27_asa_brayne] The company's engineers work inside customers, reviewing their data sources and adding new ones, so "the customer decides" is thinner than in an ordinary licence. [cite:de10_fortune_palantir] Lock-in makes the platform a hub: ICE has called Palantir "the only source that can provide the required capabilities," and a data broker's 2026 work statement requires connections to "the Palantir platform." [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:de28_bu_lexis] And the outputs are judgements: ICE's ELITE tool gives each person's address a "confidence score." [cite:ow9_fortune_elite]

One documented incident shows both cases at once. In the suit by more than twenty states over Medicaid data sharing, government filings disclosed in July 2026 that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services had sent ICE, on 7 January 2026, a dataset covering millions of people, including lawful residents, beyond what the court allowed. ICE shared it with Palantir, which runs ELITE, "over a Microsoft Teams chat," then deleted it; Palantir said "the dataset in question was purged pursuant to government instruction." CMS later re-sent the dataset by mistake, and about six ICE users were found still holding copies. Judge Vince Chhabria, who had allowed a narrow five-field exchange in December 2025, paused the sharing in late May 2026; at a hearing on 3 September he said valid visa holders' data should not be shared and that the court would go "category by category," but no formal ruling had been located as of October 2026. [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de24b_chn_medicaid] The data was the government's and the vendor acted on instruction, as Palantir's account says; and once it was in a chat window, the safeguards depended on people finding every copy.

If it were connected

A platform built to be joined invites the question of which joins exist. Documented: Medicaid records reached Palantir through ICE, once, outside a court's limits. [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] Probable: a standing feed from LexisNexis's people-search data into ICE's Palantir systems, because the August 2026 work statement requires the API. [cite:de28_bu_lexis] Possible, with no document: a join to the "common API layer" Palantir has been building for the Treasury's IRS modernisation since September 2025, which would let a government check a taxpayer's records against an enforcement list on one screen; it would need an agreement between agencies and a connection built by the customer, and tax-confidentiality law and the courts stand in the way, as [scene:de30_silos_and_subpoenas|Part Thirty-Two] shows for the tax-address agreement. [cite:de27_treasury_api] Not supported: a join between ICE's systems and the Army's Personnel Data Environment, which Palantir maintains under a separate $3.68 million order to 15 November 2026 for a separate customer, with nothing showing data moving between them; nor that Palantir itself holds a cross-government dataset, which the company denies and no record shows. [cite:de27_govly_pde] [cite:de19_palantir_record] The capability to turn scattered records into a list of people and likely addresses exists at ICE today; whether it reaches beyond the people the law already targets is a question of law, policy and courts, taken up in the next part, after the money.

sections.h: The Money and the Wars: Revenue, Contracts and Ukraine
sections.html:
Palantir's argument about itself is that it serves the West; its accounts show how much of its money comes from the American state, and how fast that has grown. This section gives the figures, then the contracts behind them, listed one by one rather than added together, because ceilings, obligations and payments are different things and different awards run over different years. Figures are as of the latest reported quarter at 28 October 2026, the second quarter of 2026; third-quarter results were due in early November.

The revenue

When Palantir filed to list its shares in 2020, it reported 2019 revenue of $746 million, nearly half from government agencies, and a loss of $580 million. [cite:ow9_ap_s1] For 2025 it reported revenue of $4.475 billion, of which United States government revenue was $1.855 billion, up 55 percent on the year. [cite:de10_pltr_fy25] In the second quarter of 2026, reported on 3 August 2026, revenue was $1.935 billion, up 93 percent on a year earlier. United States government revenue was $809 million, up 90 percent, and United States commercial revenue $764 million, up 149 percent; net income attributable to shareholders was about $1.06 billion for the quarter. The company raised its forecast for the year to between $8.150 and $8.158 billion. [cite:de27_8k_q2_2026] No single customer accounted for more than a tenth of revenue. [cite:de27_10q_q2_2026]

Two things follow. The American government is Palantir's largest source of money, at about 42 percent of revenue in the latest quarter, and its spending with the company nearly doubled in a year. And the commercial business, selling the same platforms and the AI layer to companies, has grown even faster, so that the company is less dependent on government as a share of its income even as government pays it more. [cite:de27_8k_q2_2026] The Brennan Center, counting the Department of Homeland Security's commitments alone, found them rising from $20.4 million in 2024 to $162.2 million in 2026 by late July. [cite:de27_brennan_tools]

The defence contracts

Palantir did not enter the Army as a favourite. In 2016 it sued the Army for refusing to consider commercial software for its intelligence-analysis system, won, and in 2019 won a contract worth up to $876 million; that story is told in [scene:de10_philosophy_vs_practice|Part Ten]. [cite:de10_defnews] The scale changed after 2024. The Pentagon's Maven Smart System, which fuses sensor and intelligence data into a picture commanders can act on, was awarded at $480 million in May 2024 and raised to nearly $1.3 billion through 2029 in May 2025. [cite:ow9_ds_maven] NATO completed its own purchase of the system on 25 March 2025, at an undisclosed price, for intelligence fusion, targeting and planning. [cite:de27_dp_nato] In August 2025 the Army folded 75 contracts into a single enterprise agreement worth up to $10 billion over ten years. [cite:ow9_bd_army] Under that agreement, on 16 March 2026, the Army ordered $3.68 million of work to "maintain and sustain" its Personnel Data Environment, a system holding soldiers' personnel data, through 15 November 2026; the order sustains a system that already existed. [cite:de27_govly_pde] In August 2026 Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg pledged up to $243.9 million for Palantir software through March 2027 and told departments to identify options for more through December 2028; the analytics firm GovTribe counted $3.2 billion of obligations to Palantir since 2024, about half without competition, and the department said it had issued similar memos for other companies. [cite:de27_wt_feinberg]

A widely repeated claim puts Palantir in the Golden Dome missile-defence programme. When the Space Force announced prototype agreements for its space-based interceptors on 24 April 2026, the twelve companies named included SpaceX and Anduril; Palantir was not among them. [cite:de27_bd_sbi]

The civilian and enforcement contracts

The company's civilian federal work has widened in the same period. On 22 September 2025 the Treasury announced that Palantir would build a "common API layer," a shared set of connections for developer platforms, workflow automation and analytics, as part of modernising the Internal Revenue Service; no value was stated. [cite:de27_treasury_api] At Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the work that began in 2014 under the Obama administration grew into the $29.9 million ImmigrationOS award of April 2025 and a Department of Homeland Security purchase agreement worth up to $1 billion in February 2026. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:ow9_sa_dhsbpa] Under that agreement, on 5 May 2026, ICE ordered $86.3 million of work, fully obligated, for the "modernization of enforcement removal operations and operational capability" through May 2027; its statement of work is not public, so the data it covers is not known. [cite:de27_hg_ero] The ELITE tool, reported in January 2026, is Palantir's. [cite:ow9_fortune_elite] [cite:de27_brennan_tools] The full ICE list, with the other vendors, is in [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty]. Abroad, England's National Health Service awarded Palantir a £330 million, seven-year data-platform contract in 2023, now under review, as [scene:de27_europe_says_no|the next section] describes. [cite:de27_reuters_nhs]

Ukraine

Palantir's largest documented war use outside American command is in Ukraine. On 1 June 2022 Karp crossed into Ukraine with five colleagues and met President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv the next day, offering to open an office and deploy the company's software. By early 2024, TIME reported, more than half a dozen Ukrainian agencies used it: the military to analyse satellite imagery, drone footage, open-source data and ground reports, and the prosecutor general to link alleged war crimes to evidence such as satellite images and social-media posts, while the economy ministry used its models to decide where clearing landmines would return the most farmland to use. Karp said the software was "responsible for most of the targeting in Ukraine." Palantir provided the tools free of charge; partner countries contributed tens of millions of dollars to offset the cost. [cite:de27_time_ukraine] Palantir's work for Israel's Ministry of Defense since January 2024 is set out in [scene:ow9_israel|The One-Way Mirror] and in [scene:de37_palantir_and_israel|Part Forty]; the documented record there is a contract whose contents are not public, and the company denies building Israel's AI targeting systems.

What the figures do not show is a causal line from politics to contracts. Thiel chairs the company, J.D. Vance once worked for and was funded by Thiel, and Palantir's federal business has grown fast since 2025; those facts form a sequence, examined as a candidate loop in [scene:de14_loops|Part Fourteen] and [scene:de21_conflicts_and_contracts|Part Twenty-One]. No document shows the Vice President or any political appointee directing an award to Palantir, and the ICE business, the Army lawsuit and the Maven award all began before the 2025 administration. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:de10_defnews] [cite:ow9_ds_maven] The more ordinary explanation, a decade of incumbency, sole-source justifications and a habit of buying without competition that the Pentagon says it applies to other companies too, is itself documented. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:de27_wt_feinberg]

sections.h: Where Governments Said No: Switzerland, Germany, Britain and Denmark
sections.html:
Palantir's platforms run in American agencies with little public argument about whether to buy them; the arguments are about how they are used. In Europe the argument has often come earlier, at the point of purchase, and several governments and one constitutional court have said no, or not yet, or only on conditions. Their reasons are worth reading closely, because they are the clearest statements on record of what a careful buyer thinks the risks of such a platform are. Israel's contract with the company is treated separately, in [scene:de37_palantir_and_israel|Part Forty] and in the library's [scene:ow9_israel|One-Way Mirror].

Switzerland: seven years of refusals

In December 2025 the Swiss online magazine Republik and the investigative collective WAV published the results of 59 freedom-of-information requests to 41 federal offices. They documented at least nine approaches by Palantir to Swiss authorities over seven years, all unsuccessful, and an internal assessment of about twenty pages by the Swiss army, prompted by a meeting between Palantir's European head, Louis Mosley, and the army's chief, which advised against working with the company. Its central concern was the risk that data could flow to United States government agencies; it also weighed dependence on a single foreign supplier and named open-source alternatives, though its authors had not tested them in depth. [cite:de27_site36_swiss] [cite:de27_np_republik] Palantir's answer was that it is "not a surveillance company," that no data is passed to American authorities and that it would resist any order to do so, and that its systems are self-contained, with customers keeping control. [cite:de27_site36_swiss]

Palantir then went to court, demanding that Republik publish a counter-statement on 23 points it said were inaccurate. The Zurich Commercial Court ruled on 4 June 2026 for the magazine on 22 of the 23, ordering one minor correction about the development history of a Palantir product. [cite:de27_np_republik] On 29 June Palantir said it accepted the ruling and would not appeal. [cite:de27_srf_accepts] The Swiss record is therefore a well-documented refusal for stated reasons of data sovereignty, not a finding that Palantir had misused anything.

Germany: a constitutional threshold, and a split between states and army

Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled on 16 February 2023 that the police laws of Hesse and Hamburg allowing "automated data analysis" were unconstitutional. The court described what such analysis does, establishing "relationships or connections between persons, groups of persons, institutions, organisations, objects or matters," including through data mining and self-learning systems, and held that for so intrusive a power the law must require a "sufficiently identifiable danger," a threshold the two laws fell "far short" of. Hamburg's provision was void at once; Hesse's could run, with restrictions, until 30 September 2023. [cite:de27_bverfg_2023] The court named Hesse's platform, hessenDATA, but not its supplier; Hesse had used Palantir's software since 2017, and a Palantir executive responded that the company "merely provides the software for processing data, not the data itself." [cite:de27_reuters_bverfg] [cite:de27_wiki_pltr]

The ruling did not end German police use; it set conditions for it. Bavaria, North Rhine-Westphalia and Hesse use Palantir's software, and in November 2025 Baden-Württemberg's parliament voted 113 to 22 to let its police use Gotham from the second quarter of 2026, while passing a resolution calling for a "European Palantir alternative by 2030 at the latest"; the civil-liberties group GFF has suits pending against two states' laws. [cite:de27_posteo_bw] The armed forces went the other way. In April 2026 Germany ruled out Palantir's Maven Smart System for the Bundeswehr, and in September the head of its cyber command said it was evaluating 30 AI tools, most of them German, with a prototype due in 2027. [cite:de27_tnw_bundeswehr]

Britain: a health contract under review

In 2023 NHS England awarded Palantir a £330 million, seven-year contract to build a Federated Data Platform linking health-service data. [cite:de27_reuters_nhs] [cite:de27_wiki_pltr] In June 2026 the technology secretary, Liz Kendall, said the government was "reviewing every single aspect" of the deal, citing patient confidentiality, public trust and reliance on an American supplier; the initial term ends in early 2027, when it must decide whether to continue. [cite:de27_reuters_nhs] The government's infrastructure authority had meanwhile raised the platform's whole-life cost to £1.1 billion and cut its forecast benefits to £808 million, while still rating the project green; two parliamentary committees urged ministers to consider the break clause, and NHS England apologised in August for a privacy assessment that wrongly said only NHS staff could see identifiable data. [cite:de27_computing_nista] Palantir's British head, Louis Mosley, called a review clause "good and normal practice" and warned against "ideologically motivated campaigners." [cite:de27_guardian_mosley] In May 2026 London's mayor blocked a £50 million police contract with the company. [cite:de27_reuters_nhs] As of October 2026 no decision on the health contract had been announced.

Denmark: a system in use, a supplier unnamed

Denmark's national police have run a system called POL-INTEL since 2017, and it is widely reported to be built on Palantir's Gotham. [cite:de27_wiki_pltr] The government's own answers to parliament describe it as integrating internal and external data sources to strengthen "intelligence-led" policing, but do not name a supplier. [cite:de27_ftdk_polintel] The Danish case is documented as a system and reported as Palantir's.

Read together, Europe has not said no to Palantir; it has said no in some places and set terms in others. The refusals rest on two documented arguments. One is legal: a constitution can require a concrete danger before police may run joined data through an analytic engine, which American law does not require for data an agency already holds or buys. The other is sovereignty: a buyer outside the United States worries that an American company could be compelled by American law to hand over what it holds, which Palantir denies would happen. Neither argument is a finding that the company has misused data, and the record in this part contains none outside the Medicaid incident, where the data was the American government's own. [cite:de27_bverfg_2023] [cite:de27_site36_swiss] [cite:de27_npr_medicaid]

The worst-case reading, tested

The book's working hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and never a finding, reads immigration enforcement as the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. Palantir bears on it as the joining layer: the tool that would turn the state's scattered records into one view of a person.

Documented: Palantir's platforms sit at the centre of the Pentagon's targeting and planning, the Army's data, and ICE's enforcement, with US government revenue of $809 million in a single quarter, up 90 percent. [cite:de27_8k_q2_2026] Three men control just under half of all shareholder votes through a voting trust. [cite:de27_10q_q2_2026] Its chief executive speaks openly of lethal use against enemies abroad. [cite:de27_giz_karp2025] And in January 2026 Medicaid data reached the company through ICE outside a court's limits, with copies later found. [cite:de27_npr_medicaid]

Probable: that Palantir is becoming the hub through which ICE's other data passes, because contracts and work statements require it, and that this lock-in would carry any future change of policy through the same platform. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:de27_hg_ero]

Not supported: that Palantir has used, or been directed to use, its software against political critics in the United States, or that its federal growth was arranged by its chairman's political allies; no document shows either. The record runs against two parts of the worst case. The ICE work began in 2014 under the Obama administration, so the tool predates the occasion. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] And the strongest checks on platforms of this kind, a constitutional court's threshold, a buyer's refusal on sovereignty grounds, a judge's pause on Medicaid sharing, are documented as working, in Europe and in one American courtroom. [cite:de27_bverfg_2023] [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] Whether the American law around the platform supplies such checks is the subject of [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty].

chapters.label: Part Thirty
chapters.title: ICE and the Data Stack
chapters.intro: This part follows the data. Immigration and Customs Enforcement does not run one surveillance system; it buys many, from a software platform that joins records to people-search databases, phone-location trails, social-media monitors, face recognition, phone-cracking devices and, for a time, spyware. The first section lists those contracts one by one, with dates, values and the administration that signed each, because the stack was built across both parties. The second sets out the law that lets an agency buy data it could not seize without a warrant, what Congress has tried and failed to do about it, and how DHS has used subpoenas and visa vetting to identify critics. The third draws the whole ecosystem on one map, six layers and the joins between them, and grades each join as documented, probable, reported, possible or not supported.
chapters.outro: ICE's data stack is built from commercial parts bought over four administrations: Palantir since 2014, Babel Street and ShadowDragon under Trump's first term, LexisNexis and Paragon under Biden, Penlink, Zignal and Clearview since 2025. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] [cite:de28_epic_babel] [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:de28_ffp_penlink] The law lets agencies buy what a warrant would otherwise gate; the House passed a fix in 2024 that never became law, and the inspector general found in 2023 that the purchases skipped required privacy reviews. [cite:de28_pogo_4th] [cite:de28_oig_23_61] DHS used administrative subpoenas to try to unmask critics, and a federal court found a policy of targeting non-citizen academics for their speech unconstitutional; the appeal was pending as of October 2026. [cite:de28_eff_letter] [cite:de28_ch_aaup] On the map of six layers every adjacent link has a documented instance, LexisNexis is wired to Palantir by design and Medicaid data reached it once, but no single system carries a person from camera to cell outside immigration enforcement. [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de28_brennan_consol] Whether such tools have been turned on Americans before is a question with a documented answer, given in [scene:de29_the_precedent|Part Thirty-One].

sections.h: ICE's Data Contracts, Vendor by Vendor
sections.html:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement does not run one surveillance system. It buys many services from many companies, each sold for a stated purpose, and the question for this book is what they add up to. This section lists the documented contracts by what they supply, with the date, the administration that signed it and the value as reported. The figures are not added together: some are ceilings, some obligations, some the cost of a single licence, and they run over different years. The agency's overall budget growth, $75 billion for ICE in the budget act signed in July 2025, is set out in [scene:us6_asylum|US vs Israel]; Palantir's part is in the previous part and in the library's [scene:ow9_ice|One-Way Mirror].

The platform: Palantir

Palantir has worked for ICE since 2014, when the agency's criminal investigators, Homeland Security Investigations, began using its Investigative Case Management system under a contract first reported at $41 million; renewals followed in 2019 and 2022. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] [cite:ow9_eb_icm2022] In April 2025 ICE paid $29.9 million for ImmigrationOS, a platform to prioritise people for arrest and track departures; in February 2026 the Department of Homeland Security signed a five-year purchase agreement worth up to $1 billion; and on 5 May 2026 ICE ordered $86.3 million of work under it to modernise its Enforcement and Removal Operations systems. [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:ow9_sa_dhsbpa] [cite:de27_hg_ero] Its ELITE tool gives each target's address a "confidence score." [cite:ow9_fortune_elite] Records from 2014 to 2022 released under freedom-of-information law showed agents being trained to search the student-visa database SEVIS through the case system, planning searches of airline passenger and border-crossing data, and able to import phone extractions; the same records said the people-search service CLEAR "is not connected to Palantir tools." [cite:de28_guardian_icm]

People data: LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters

The second layer is the commercial people-search business, which compiles names, addresses, phone numbers, vehicles, property and court records into searchable profiles. LexisNexis Risk Solutions has supplied its Accurint service under a contract signed in February 2021, under the Biden administration, with about $24.5 million obligated, which ran to 31 August 2026; ICE users ran more than 1.2 million person searches in seven months of 2021. On 10 August 2026 ICE gave notice of a sole-source bridge contract of about $6.7 million, whose work statement requires connections to ICE systems "such as but not limited to" the Palantir platform, PenLink and ICE's own analytics. [cite:de28_bu_lexis] Thomson Reuters supplies CLEAR, a people-search service unrelated to the airport-security company of the same name, which draws on licences, vehicle registrations, credit data, property and court records and, per a DHS justification, utility data; its DHS contract was renewed without competition from 31 March 2026. Separately it supplied licence-plate-reader data under a $22.8 million contract from May 2021 to May 2026. Thomson Reuters says CLEAR excludes immigration status, call logs and bank data, and that Palantir is not a CLEAR customer. [cite:de28_lawsites_tr]

Phone location: Babel Street and Penlink

The third layer is location data from phone apps, sold through advertising networks and resold to government. ICE bought Babel Street software, whose location product is called Locate X, through a reseller in September 2018 for $1.1 million and directly in September 2019 for $1.5 million, under the first Trump administration. [cite:de28_epic_babel] In September 2023 DHS's inspector general found that ICE, Customs and Border Protection and the Secret Service had bought and used such "commercial telemetry data" without completing the privacy assessments the law requires, and recommended that ICE stop until they were done. [cite:de28_oig_23_61] In autumn 2025 ICE returned to the market with a $2.3 million contract with Penlink, a Nebraska company, covering Tangles, a tool for searching the open web and social media, and Webloc, a database of phone movements. Both products came from Cobwebs Technologies, an Israeli firm Penlink bought in 2023; ICE bought licences, not the company. Penlink says its tools "exclusively use publicly or commercially available data."
