[cite:de28_ffp_penlink] What Webloc can do, and the ICE legal analysis saying it can be searched without a warrant, are described in [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|Part Twenty-Six]. [cite:de25_404_webloc]

Social media: ShadowDragon and Zignal

ICE bought ShadowDragon's SocialNet, which compiles information about people from social media and other sites, through resellers: $289,500 from July 2020, under the first Trump administration, and $602,056 from August 2021, under Biden. [cite:de28_epic_shadowdragon] In September 2025 it became public that HSI had bought $5.7 million of licences over five years for Zignal Labs, through the reseller Carahsoft, for "real-time data analysis for criminal investigations"; Zignal says it analyses more than eight billion posts a day, and a 2025 company pamphlet claimed it gave "tactical intelligence" to operators in Gaza. Zignal did not respond to questions. [cite:de28_lever_zignal]

Phones, faces and spyware

The remaining tools act on a person directly. Cellebrite's phone-extraction devices have been bought by ICE since at least March 2017, and a May 2026 DHS forecast planned a five-year contract worth up to $100 million covering phones and drones. [cite:ow6_ipt_cellebrite] [cite:de28_fs_cellebrite] Clearview AI's face-recognition service was bought by HSI on 5 September 2025, $3.75 million at award and $9.225 million in total with three option years, for child-exploitation cases and assaults on officers. [cite:de28_bu_clearview] [cite:de28_audit_clearview_piid] Paragon's Graphite spyware was bought for $2 million in September 2024, under Biden, paused for review, and reactivated in August 2025; the contract was closed out on 20 January 2026, ICE's acting director told lawmakers on 1 April 2026 that he had approved HSI's use of a commercial spyware tool, and on 22 May DHS said ICE had "no relationship" with Paragon while declining to confirm or deny whether it still had the capability. [cite:ow10_poulson_ice] [cite:de28_npr_paragon] [cite:de25_npr_paragon] These are examined in [scene:de25_spyware_and_phones|Part Twenty-Six] and [scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|Part Twenty-Eight].

Two corrections to common accounts follow from the list. A widely repeated line says ICE bought the Israeli company Cobwebs; it did not. Penlink bought Cobwebs, and ICE bought licences from Penlink. [cite:de28_ffp_penlink] And the stack is not the creation of one administration. Babel Street and ShadowDragon were first bought under Trump's first term, LexisNexis, the plate-reader data, a second ShadowDragon order and Paragon under Biden, and Palantir under Obama; what changed after 2025 was the volume, the new tools and the money. [cite:de28_epic_babel] [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019]

If it were connected

Each vendor sells one thing; the worst case is what they do joined. Documented: Palantir's case system has drawn on SEVIS, passenger and border-crossing data and phone extractions (2014–22 records), and Medicaid records reached Palantir in January 2026. [cite:de28_guardian_icm] [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] Probable: LexisNexis people-search data flowing into the Palantir platform, because the 2026 work statement requires the connection. [cite:de28_bu_lexis] Possible, with no document: Penlink's phone-location trails, Zignal's social-media alerts and Clearview's face matches feeding Palantir, so that a face in a protest photograph could be matched to a name, the name to an address with a confidence score and the address to a phone's movements on one screen; the join would need only an API and a work order, since all are ICE's own licences, and what stands in the way is agency policy, the privacy assessments the inspector general found missing in 2023, and the courts. [cite:de28_oig_23_61] Not supported: CLEAR feeding Palantir, which both 2014–22 records and Thomson Reuters say does not happen. [cite:de28_guardian_icm] [cite:de28_lawsites_tr] The law that governs these purchases is the subject of [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|the next section].

sections.h: Buy It, Don't Warrant It: The Law Around the Stack
sections.html:
The vendors in the previous section sell to ICE because the law lets ICE buy. This section sets out the legal doctrine that makes the purchases possible, what the intelligence community's own advisers said about it, what Congress has and has not done, and then the other half of the system, the tools by which agencies identify people who have not been charged with anything: administrative subpoenas, social-media vetting and the policy a federal court found unconstitutional in 2025.

The doctrine: commercially available information

The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and generally requires a warrant, a judge's order based on probable cause, before the government searches a person's private things. Under the third-party doctrine, set by the Supreme Court in the 1970s, records a person hands to a business, such as bank records or the numbers dialled from a phone, lose that protection. In Carpenter v. United States (2018) the Court refused to extend the doctrine to historical phone-location records, and on 29 June 2026, in Chatrie v. United States, it held by six votes to three (five justices joining Justice Kagan's opinion and Justice Gorsuch concurring in the judgment) that obtaining even two hours of a person's location history from Google was a search. Both rulings concern data the government compels a company to hand over; neither addresses data the government simply buys. [cite:ow9_cornell_tpd] [cite:ow9_pw_chatrie] [cite:de26_crs_chatrie] The library's account of these cases is in [scene:ow9_ice|The One-Way Mirror] and [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|Part Twenty-Six].

Into that gap falls "commercially available information," the government's term for data anyone can buy: location trails from apps, people-search profiles, licence-plate reads, social-media archives. Agencies have taken the view that buying it is not a search. An internal ICE legal analysis concluded that Webloc's phone-location data "can be queried without a warrant," and in March 2026 the FBI director told the Senate: "We do purchase commercially available information that is consistent with the Constitution and the laws." [cite:de25_404_webloc] [cite:de25_tc_patel] That position has not been tested in the Supreme Court.

What the intelligence community's own advisers said

The clearest official description of the stakes came from inside government. A senior advisory group to the Director of National Intelligence reported in January 2022, in a document declassified on 12 June 2023, that intelligence agencies were acquiring "a significant amount" of commercially available information, and that such data "can reveal sensitive and intimate information about individuals." [cite:de28_lawfare_cai] It could be used, the report said, to "cause harm to an individual's reputation, emotional well-being, or physical safety," and it now covered nearly everyone, supplying details that once would have required a targeted investigation to obtain. [cite:de28_fortune_cai] It recommended cataloguing what agencies bought and writing standards for its use; it did not recommend a warrant requirement. [cite:de28_lawfare_cai]

DHS's own inspector general found in September 2023 that ICE, Customs and Border Protection and the Secret Service had bought and used phone-location data without completing the privacy impact assessments that the E-Government Act of 2002 requires, and recommended that ICE stop using it until they were approved. [cite:de28_oig_23_61] ICE's return to the market through Penlink in 2025 drew a letter from seventy members of Congress in March 2026 asking the inspector general to investigate; ICE said it "does not purchase illegal information." [cite:de28_reg_wyden70]

What Congress did

The House of Representatives passed the Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act on 17 April 2024, by 219 votes to 199, with members of both parties in the majority and over the Biden White House's opposition. It would have required a court order before law-enforcement and intelligence agencies buy Americans' data. The Senate did not take it up and it died with that Congress. [cite:de28_pogo_4th] [cite:ow9_cs_4thact] On 14 April 2026 Representative Warren Davidson, an Ohio Republican, offered an amendment to the bill reauthorising Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act that would "prohibit the federal government from purchasing Americans' private information and data from third-party brokers." [cite:de28_davidson_2026] No reauthorisation was enacted; Section 702 lapsed on 12 June 2026, while collection continued under existing court certifications, as [scene:us10_us|US vs Israel] describes. [cite:us10_eff_702lapse] As of October 2026 no federal statute requires a warrant before an agency buys data it could not compel without one. Montana became the first state to pass such a rule, for its own agencies, in May 2025; it does not bind federal ones ([scene:de26_counterweights|Part Twenty-Eight]). [cite:de28_reason_montana]

Unmasking critics: the administrative subpoena

An administrative subpoena is a demand for records that an agency can issue on its own authority, without a judge. It cannot reach the content of messages, but it can reach a user's name, address, IP address and session times. [cite:de28_eff_letter] Three documented cases show how DHS used it in 2025. On 31 March 2025 Homeland Security Investigations subpoenaed Google for the account of Amandla Thomas-Johnson, a Cornell doctoral student on a visa, citing a provision on documents relating to a person's right to enter or reside in the country; Google complied without first telling him and produced basic subscriber information. [cite:de28_int_thomasjohnson] In early September 2025 DHS asked Meta for the "names, email addresses, and phone numbers" behind six Instagram accounts that had named a Border Patrol agent during raids in Los Angeles; a magistrate judge ordered Meta not to comply, and DHS withdrew the demands before any ruling. [cite:de28_int_meta] [cite:de28_eff_letter] And a Philadelphia-area man who emailed a DHS lawyer urging "common sense and decency" in an Afghan asylum case was the subject of a subpoena to Google issued four hours later; two DHS agents and a local police officer came to his home to question him, before Google had produced anything. The ACLU moved to quash it in February 2026 and announced on 10 February that DHS had withdrawn it. [cite:de28_aclu_doe]

The scale is unknown. Google reported 28,622 subpoenas of all kinds in the first half of 2025 and Meta 14,520, but neither breaks them out by agency. On 10 February 2026 the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the ACLU of Northern California asked ten companies to require a court order before complying with DHS subpoenas, to notify users early and to resist gag orders. [cite:de28_eff_letter]

Speech as a ground: vetting and AAUP v. Rubio

For non-citizens, speech has become a formal factor in decisions. On 9 April 2025 US Citizenship and Immigration Services said it would screen applicants' social media for antisemitic activity and support for named terrorist groups as grounds to deny green cards and student benefits; the Council on American-Islamic Relations and J Street, a group that calls itself pro-Israel and pro-peace, both said it threatened free speech. [cite:de28_npr_uscis] A State Department cable of 18 June 2025 told consular officers to require student-visa applicants to make their social media public and to look for "hostile attitudes toward our citizens, culture, government, institutions, or founding principles." [cite:de28_reuters_visa]

The test case for where this leads was AAUP v. Rubio. At the trial in July 2025, Peter Hatch of DHS's intelligence office testified that a "Tiger Team" of analysts had produced more than a hundred reports on foreign students and academics, drawing names from a list of about 5,000 compiled by Canary Mission, a privately run website that profiles campus activists; he said he had never before been asked for reports on foreign students. [cite:de28_crimson_hatch] On 30 September 2025 Judge William Young found the government's policy unconstitutional and said it had "chilled the speech of non-citizen academics"; in January 2026 he vacated it, presumed retaliation in any immigration action against the plaintiff groups' members, and stayed their removal. The government appealed to the First Circuit, which had not ruled as of October 2026. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] The domestic-terrorism directive that names ideas as indicators is in [scene:de30_nspm7_and_detachment|Part Thirty-Two].

If it were connected

Documented: each link from a post to a doorstep exists separately; in the Philadelphia case a critical email led within hours to a subpoena and within weeks to agents at the door, though no record shows that the address came from a broker or a platform. [cite:de28_aclu_doe] Possible, with no document: that subpoena returns and vetting flags are loaded into the same case systems as broker data, and beyond that a standing rule that runs every flagged post through people-search and location data automatically; either would need only an internal procedure, not a new law. What stands in the way is narrow: a judge who blocked one subpoena, withdrawals of others once challenged, a vacated policy under appeal, and no statute. Not supported: that such an automatic pipeline exists; none of the documented cases shows one. The full map follows.

sections.h: The Ecosystem Map: Six Layers and the Joins Between Them
sections.html:
This section puts the tools on one map, because the worst-case reading is about what they could do joined: the Sophia platform's framing is that the mechanisms may not be connected now, but they exist. The map does two things. It shows what exists, in six layers, and it grades every link between them on one scale, the same one used at the end of each toolkit section: documented (it exists today, with a source), probable (a contract, interface or legal authority already points to it), reported (named reporting, not yet confirmed by a primary record), possible (technically feasible, with no document showing it) and not supported (the record runs against it). "Possible" is a grade for a join between systems only, never for a fact about a person.

The six layers

The first layer is the records the government already holds because people must give them: tax returns, Medicaid enrolment, Social Security numbers, welfare files, visa and student records, travel manifests and the fingerprints, faces and irises in DHS's biometric systems. How the walls between them came down in 2025–26 is told in [scene:de30_silos_and_subpoenas|Part Thirty-Two]. Documented joins to enforcement now include the April 2025 agreement under which ICE submits names to the IRS for address checks, the linking of Social Security data to the SAVE citizenship-check system in May 2025, and Medicaid data sent to ICE under a court order that limits it to five fields for people not lawfully present. [cite:de30_ap_krause] [cite:de24_npr_save] [cite:de30_hipaa_chhabria] On 28 September 2026 a federal judge declined to block HHS from sharing welfare (TANF) recipient data with DHS, calling the states' fears "vague, unsubstantiated predictions"; the disclosure notice took effect on 30 September. [cite:de28_bl_tanf] DHS's next-generation biometric system, HART, is designed to be shared across DHS, the Justice and Defense Departments, the intelligence community, state and local police and foreign partners, but was not yet operational in August 2024. [cite:de28_hart_pia]

The second layer is surveillance the government runs: face matching in the field through ICE's Mobile Fortify app, phone extraction with Cellebrite devices, Paragon's spyware, whose contract was closed out in January 2026 although DHS will neither confirm nor deny that ICE still has the capability, and drones, on which Customs and Border Protection has committed more than $675 million to one manufacturer. [cite:de26_404_fortify] [cite:de28_fs_cellebrite] [cite:de28_npr_paragon] [cite:de28_brennan_tools]

The third layer is state and local systems that federal agents can reach. The clearest example is licence-plate cameras. In one month at a Texas school district's eight Flock cameras, more than 3,100 agencies ran more than 733,000 searches, and 620 of them cited immigration reasons, from 30 agencies; the district itself showed no immigration use, and Flock says its customers control sharing. [cite:de28_74_flock] DHS has also queried driver and vehicle records nationwide through information-sharing contracts. [cite:de28_brennan_tools] What school cameras and records mean for students is examined in [scene:de24b_schools|Part Twenty-Five].

The fourth layer is commercial surveillance vendors selling to ICE directly: Clearview's faces, Penlink's Tangles and Webloc, Zignal's and ShadowDragon's social-media tools, Babel Street's location software, all listed in [scene:de28_ice_contracts|the first section]. The fifth is data brokers whose products are people: LexisNexis's Accurint, Thomson Reuters's CLEAR and plate reads, Venntel's app-location data, and the employment and utility files held by credit bureaus. An Equifax-held utility file once reached ICE through CLEAR, until the utilities' exchange told Equifax to stop in 2021; Equifax's Work Number, built from employers' payroll data, supplies government agencies for welfare eligibility and child-support enforcement, and no record shows it reaching ICE. [cite:de24_globe_utility] [cite:de28_cfpb_twn]

The sixth layer is integration: the platforms that join the rest. At ICE that means Palantir's case-management system, ImmigrationOS, ELITE and the May 2026 enforcement-operations order, and a parallel system, RAVEn, which the Brennan Center describes as letting investigators "search and combine information from multiple databases to create detailed profiles," built with Booz Allen Hamilton, Acuity and Alethix, each paid tens of millions of dollars. [cite:de27_hg_ero] [cite:de28_brennan_tools] A 2020 solicitation described "FALCON/Raven Palantir systems," so RAVEn and Palantir may have been intertwined in an earlier period; the record does not settle it, and RAVEn should not be called a Palantir system without that caveat. [cite:de28_bu_lexis] The Brennan Center counted at least $2.9 billion committed by DHS to surveillance, data-collection and analytics tools since January 2021, a minimum. [cite:de28_brennan_tools]

Walking the map

From a person's point of view, the map is a chain. A face is matched in the street or a plate is read by a school camera; a name resolves to records in the people-search databases; those records, and the government's own, are joined on an integration platform; the platform produces a lead, an address and a confidence score; and an officer acts. The Brennan Center's July 2026 report described Palantir's case system as one that "structures and links data collected from these vendors and other commercial entities" and is being made Homeland Security Investigations' "authoritative data source," and ImmigrationOS as assembling "ICE's data streams into a central hub." [cite:de28_brennan_consol] Every adjacent pair in the chain has at least one documented instance. What the record does not show is one system carrying a person from the first link to the last in a single flow outside immigration enforcement, and the commercial vendors' data, apart from LexisNexis by design, has not been shown entering the integration layer at all. The same chain reaches beyond immigration only at its edges: TSA passed records on more than 31,000 travellers to ICE between January 2025 and February 2026, and a Minnesota citizen who had been watching agents lost her Global Entry three days after a Border Patrol agent named her, saying he had used face recognition, a link alleged in her pending suit and denied by CBP. [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice] [cite:de25b_bu_cleland]

Who has asked, and who has answered

Congress has asked about the joins repeatedly; the answers are mostly missing. Senators Mark Warner and Tim Kaine wrote to DHS's inspector general on 29 January 2026 about ICE's and CBP's growing use of biometric and surveillance data, and the inspector general opened an audit of the department's security of biometric data and personal information in February; no report had been located by late October 2026. [cite:de28_warner_audit] [cite:de28_bu_warner] Seventy members asked in March 2026 for an investigation of ICE's location-data purchases. [cite:de28_reg_wyden70] On 14 April 2026 thirty-three members, led by Representatives Dan Goldman and Nydia Velázquez and Senator Ron Wyden, asked DHS for every contract with Palantir since 2020, the datasets in Palantir-built systems, any citizens' data in them, face-recognition errors and any use against observers and protesters; no reply had been found by October. [cite:de28_goldman_letter] DHS says its methods comply with the Constitution, including the Fourth Amendment. [cite:de28_reg_wyden70]

The worst-case reading, tested

The book's working hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and never a finding, reads immigration enforcement as the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. This part bears on the occasion directly: ICE's data stack is the most complete set of surveillance tools any American civilian agency holds.

Documented: every layer of the map exists and ICE can reach each one, by contract, by agreement or through other agencies. The government buys data a warrant would otherwise gate, and no federal law stops it. [cite:de28_oig_23_61] [cite:de28_pogo_4th] DHS used administrative subpoenas, without a judge, to try to unmask people who criticised or tracked ICE, and in one case agents came to a critic's home. [cite:de28_aclu_doe] [cite:de28_int_meta] A federal court found that a policy of targeting non-citizen academics for their speech was unconstitutional. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] And Medicaid data reached Palantir outside a court's limits. [cite:de27_npr_medicaid]

Probable: that the integration layer will absorb more of the map, because work statements already require connections to it and DHS spending on Palantir rose roughly eightfold from 2024 to 2026. [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:de28_brennan_tools]

Possible, as joins only: the commercial vendors' location, face and social-media data feeding the same platform; HART's biometrics and the newly opened welfare records joined to it. Each would need an API, an agreement or a rule change, not a new law.

Not supported: one standing system that carries a person from a camera to a cell outside immigration enforcement, or the stack's systematic use against citizens for political speech. The record runs against the worst case in three places. The stack was built across four administrations of both parties. [cite:de28_epic_babel] [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] Its brakes have worked in part: a magistrate judge stopped one unmasking, DHS withdrew others when challenged, a court vacated the speech-targeting policy and another paused Medicaid sharing. [cite:de28_int_meta] [cite:de28_aclu_doe] [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] And they have also failed in part: a welfare-data suit lost, the subpoena scale is unknown, and the oversight letters of 2026 are unanswered. [cite:de28_bl_tanf] [cite:de28_eff_letter] [cite:de28_goldman_letter] The gap between "every link exists" and "one machine runs them" is now mostly data-sharing agreements and internal rules, the layer being loosened. How the same capabilities were used against Americans in an earlier era is the subject of [scene:de29_the_precedent|Part Thirty-One].

chapters.label: Part Thirty-One
chapters.title: When It Was Used at Home
chapters.intro: This part takes up the oldest question behind Book Five: whether the American state has ever turned its surveillance on its own lawful political life, and what stopped it when it did. The first section reads the record of the decades before the 1975 reforms, programme by programme, from the National Security Agency's copying of international telegrams and its watch list of Americans to the FBI's COINTELPRO, the CIA's Operation CHAOS, the Army's files on protesters and the tax agency's lists of activist groups, and it follows the pattern into the twenty-first century. The second lists what was exposed between 2013 and 2017, from bulk phone records and Section 702 to the CIA's hacking tools, and gives each programme's status as of October 2026, including what lapsed, what continues and what has been replaced by buying data. The third sets those who disclosed the programmes beside the officials who misdescribed them, gives both sides of the argument over the messengers, and closes by testing the book's worst-case reading against this part's record.
chapters.outro: The American state has turned its surveillance on its own lawful political life before, under presidents of both parties: the NSA copied international telegrams for three decades and kept a watch list of some 1,650 Americans that included two senators of opposite parties, the FBI's COINTELPRO ran from 1956 to April 1971, and the CIA's Operation CHAOS indexed about 300,000 names before a presidential commission found that it "unlawfully exceeded" the agency's authority. [cite:de29_schneier_shamrock] [cite:de29_nbc_minaret] [cite:de29_wiki_cointelpro] [cite:de29_rock_chaos] Most of these programmes were ended or brought to account through exposure from outside, a burglary, the press or a congressional inquiry, and the record of the abuse is the government's own. [cite:de29_csm_media] Of the programmes exposed after 2013, bulk phone-record collection was ruled unlawful and ended, and section 215 expired in 2020; Section 702 collection continues under certifications to March 2027 although its statute lapsed in June 2026; collection under the president's own order and the purchase of commercial data, which the FBI confirmed in March 2026, grew. [cite:de29_eff_215] [cite:us10_bcj_702] [cite:de29_ap_ciabulk] [cite:de29_tc_patel] Those who disclosed the programmes were imprisoned or exiled, while the official who told the Senate "Not wittingly" was never charged; the asymmetry is documented, a deliberate double standard is not. [cite:de29_cbs_winner] [cite:de29_doj_snowden] [cite:de29_wex_clapper] The precedent is proven; its present repetition against political opponents is not documented. The next part turns from the tools to the law that now governs them, beginning with the path from Yarvin's RAGE to the Schedule Policy/Career rule in [scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|Part Thirty-Two].

sections.h: The Precedent: When the Tools Were Turned Inward
sections.html:
The worst-case reading of Book Five asks whether surveillance built for foreign enemies and for immigration enforcement could be turned on Americans who oppose the government. That question is not hypothetical. It happened, in the United States, under presidents of both parties, between the end of the Second World War and the middle of the 1970s, and the record that proves it is the government's own: a Senate committee, a presidential commission, the National Security Agency's (NSA's) official history and the files of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). The Senate's inquiry under Frank Church, the vote that created it and its finding that "Intelligence agencies have undermined the constitutional rights of citizens" are set out in [scene:us10_us|the library's account of the American framework] and are not repeated here. [cite:us10_senate_church] This section looks at the programmes themselves, one by one, at who was watched, and at what actually stopped each of them, because that last question bears most directly on the present.

Six programmes

The oldest was the NSA's SHAMROCK. After the Second World War three telegraph companies, Western Union, RCA and ITT, gave the agency and its predecessor copies of the international telegrams that passed through their offices. At its height NSA analysts reviewed about 150,000 messages a month, and in 1966 the NSA and the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) set up a front office in lower Manhattan to handle the traffic. No warrant, no statute and no court was involved at any stage. Church called it "probably the largest government interception program affecting Americans ever undertaken." The NSA's director, Lew Allen, ended it in May 1975, as the Senate investigators closed in. [cite:de29_schneier_shamrock]

The second was MINARET, the NSA's watch list. Other agencies, chiefly the FBI, sent the NSA names, and the NSA searched its intercepts of overseas calls and cables for them. About 1,650 American citizens were on the list. When the National Security Archive at George Washington University forced the release of the relevant pages of the NSA's own Cold War history in September 2013, after some eight years of requests and appeals, the names included Martin Luther King Jr., the civil-rights leader Whitney Young, the boxer Muhammad Ali, the New York Times columnist Tom Wicker, the humorist Art Buchwald, and two sitting senators: Frank Church, a Democrat from Idaho, and Howard Baker, a Republican from Tennessee. [cite:de29_nbc_minaret] [cite:de29_gwt_minaret] The agency's own historian, Thomas Johnson, wrote that officials understood at the time that the programme was "disreputable if not outright illegal" (one account renders the last words "downright illegal"). Accounts differ on its start, from 1961 to the late 1960s; all put its end in 1973. [cite:de29_nbc_minaret] [cite:de29_gwt_minaret]

The third, and the best known, was the FBI's COINTELPRO, short for counterintelligence programme. It began in 1956 against the Communist Party and widened to the Socialist Workers Party in 1961, the Ku Klux Klan and other "white hate groups" in 1964, Black nationalist organisations in 1967 and the New Left in 1968. Its methods went past watching into disruption, through anonymous letters and informants placed inside the groups. On 21 November 1964 the FBI mailed King an anonymous package of recordings with a letter that he read as urging him to kill himself. The Church Committee called the whole effort a "sophisticated vigilante operation." [cite:de29_wiki_cointelpro] The programme was officially terminated in April 1971. [cite:de29_wiki_cointelpro]

The fourth was the CIA's Operation CHAOS, set up in August 1967. Two presidents, Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon, wanted proof that the anti-war and Black political movements were directed from abroad; in the words of the presidential commission that later examined it, "Two Presidents and their staffs made continuing and insistent requests." The CIA built a computer index of about 300,000 names of people and organisations, most of them American, and opened about 7,200 personal files and nearly 1,000 files on organisations. Its own analysts found no evidence of foreign control of the movements, in 1969 and again in 1970. The commission chaired by Vice-President Nelson Rockefeller concluded in June 1975 that "Some domestic activities of Operation CHAOS unlawfully exceeded the CIA's statutory authority", though it held that the stated mission, looking abroad for foreign influence, had been proper. CHAOS was terminated on 15 March 1974. [cite:de29_rock_chaos]

The fifth was the Army's. From the late 1960s plainclothes military intelligence agents attended protests and civil-rights meetings and kept files on civilians. When people named in those files sued, the Supreme Court refused to hear the merits. In Laird v. Tatum, decided 5–4 on 26 June 1972, Chief Justice Warren Burger described the Army's system as "the collection of information about public activities" and held that a claimed chilling effect, without more, was not "an adequate substitute for a claim of specific present objective harm." [cite:de29_laird] The ruling set a pattern that still matters: people who cannot prove they were watched usually cannot get into court to challenge the watching.

The sixth was the Internal Revenue Service's Special Service Staff. By 1969, under pressure from the White House and Congress, the tax agency had a unit that examined about 8,000 individuals and 3,000 groups for their political activity rather than for evidence of tax violations, working from lists of activists supplied by the FBI and the Justice Department. Among the organisations listed were the Ford Foundation and the Urban League. A new commissioner, Donald Alexander, dissolved it in mid-1973. [cite:de29_hnn_irs]

What stopped them

The most important fact about these programmes is how they ended. None was ended by the agency's own compliance system at the point the abuse began. COINTELPRO came to light because of a crime. On the night of 8 March 1971 a group calling itself the Citizens' Commission to Investigate the FBI broke into the bureau's field office in Media, Pennsylvania, took its files and mailed them to journalists. Betty Medsger of the Washington Post published first. Among the papers was a routing slip carrying the word COINTELPRO, which no reporter yet understood. [cite:de29_csm_media] The programme was shut within weeks. [cite:de29_wiki_cointelpro] The burglars, among them John and Bonnie Raines and Keith Forsyth, named themselves only in 2014; the FBI had closed its case on 11 March 1976, three days after the limitation period ran out, and none was ever charged. [cite:de29_csm_media] SHAMROCK and MINARET ended under the approach of the congressional inquiry; CHAOS was wound down within the agency in 1974 and then examined by the Rockefeller Commission; the IRS unit ended because a new commissioner found it. [cite:de29_schneier_shamrock] [cite:de29_nbc_minaret] [cite:de29_rock_chaos] [cite:de29_hnn_irs] The Army's programme survived its day in the Supreme Court. [cite:de29_laird]

The sequence that recurs is exposure from outside, then oversight. Internal stops did happen, but under pressure or the threat of exposure. The reforms that followed, a permanent intelligence committee in each house and the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of 1978, which put national-security wiretaps under a special court, were real. [cite:us10_senate_church]

The pattern after the reforms

The reforms did not end the pattern; they changed its form. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 President George W. Bush authorised the NSA, in secret and outside FISA, to collect the content of some Americans' international calls and emails and bulk records of their communications. The programme, code-named Stellar Wind, was examined by five inspectors general in 2009 in a report the New York Times obtained in full through a lawsuit in April 2015. A 2004 FBI review it cited found that only 1.2 per cent of the leads the programme produced between 2001 and 2004 made a "significant contribution" to identifying a terrorist or developing an informant, and none from the content collection between August 2004 and January 2006 proved useful. Its limits were set not by the agency but by the Justice Department's own lawyers, who in March 2004 confronted the White House over its legality. [cite:de29_ap_stellarwind]

The most recent documented misuse is smaller and better recorded. A ruling of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, released in redacted form on 19 May 2023, found that FBI staff had improperly searched data collected under Section 702 of FISA (described in [scene:us10_us|the library's account]) for more than 100 people arrested at the racial-justice protests of June 2020, for suspects in the attack on the Capitol of 6 January 2021, and in one batch for some 19,000 donors to a congressional campaign, of whom the Justice Department found only eight had a sufficient tie to foreign influence. The FBI blamed confusion over the rules, required written justifications for each search and reported compliance rising from 82 to 96 per cent. [cite:de29_ap_fisc2023] The people searched sat on the left and on the right. That is the honest shape of the modern record: misuse of an existing database by its routine users, caught by the court that oversees it, rather than a programme aimed at political opponents.

sections.h: The Catalogue: What Was Exposed, and What Still Runs
sections.html:
Between June 2013 and 2017 the public learned more about American and British signals intelligence than in the forty years before. Most of it came from the archive that Edward Snowden, a contractor working for the National Security Agency (NSA), took and gave to journalists; some came from other sources, which matters for accuracy. This section lists the main programmes, says in plain words what each did, and gives its status as of October 2026. Three terms recur. Metadata is the record of a communication rather than its content: who called whom, when, for how long, from where. Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) is the 2008 law that lets agencies collect, without an individual warrant, the communications of foreigners abroad from American companies; Americans in contact with them are collected too. Executive Order 12333, signed by President Ronald Reagan in 1981, is the president's own rulebook for intelligence collected abroad; it was never passed by Congress, and Congress does not vote to renew it. How 702 works, its target counts and its 2026 lapse are set out in [scene:us10_us|the library's account] and are only summarised here.

The phone records: exposed, ruled unlawful, ended

The first disclosure, in June 2013, was an order of the surveillance court requiring Verizon to hand over its customers' call records in bulk under section 215 of the Patriot Act. In May 2015 the Second Circuit held that the programme exceeded what Congress had authorised, and in June 2015 the USA FREEDOM Act ended bulk collection, leaving the records with the phone companies for the NSA to query number by number. [cite:us10_wiki_clapper] The successor system failed on its own terms. In June 2018 the NSA announced it was deleting more than 685 million call records collected since 2015 because of "technical irregularities" in data from the carriers, which had sent it records it was not authorised to receive. [cite:de29_voa_685m] Section 215 itself expired on 15 March 2020, with an exception for investigations already open; no renewal had been reported as of October 2026. [cite:de29_eff_215] Of everything exposed in 2013, this is the one programme that was clearly stopped, and it was stopped by a leak, then a court, then Congress.

Section 702: PRISM and Upstream

On 6 June 2013 the Washington Post and the Guardian described PRISM, the part of 702 collection that draws on the large internet companies. The Post's account suggested nearly direct access to company servers; the companies named, among them Google, Apple, Facebook, Microsoft and Yahoo, denied it. Facebook said it did not provide "any government organization with direct access" to its servers, and Apple said it had never heard of PRISM. [cite:de29_tc_prism] The accurate description is the legal one: the companies hand over the accounts of designated foreign targets when the government serves them with directives under 702. The second part, Upstream, copies traffic as it crosses the internet's main cables inside the United States, with the help of the carriers that run them. Until 2017 Upstream also collected messages that merely mentioned a target, called "about" collection. The NSA ended it on 28 April 2017 after an internal review found compliance lapses that it had reported to Congress and the court, and it deleted most of the Upstream data it held. [cite:de29_nsa_about]

The statute behind both lapsed at midnight on 12 June 2026. Collection did not stop: the certifications approved by the surveillance court in March 2026 run, on the Brennan Center's reading, to 17 March 2027. [cite:us10_eff_702lapse] [cite:us10_bcj_702] No renewal had been reported as enacted as of October 2026. The structural effect of the lapse runs against intuition: until those certifications expire, there is no deadline at which Congress can attach conditions.

Collection abroad under the president's own order

Two of the most consequential programmes ran under Executive Order 12333 rather than FISA, outside the surveillance court. XKEYSCORE is software the NSA's analysts use to search the agency's stored collection, including bulk collection abroad; the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board (PCLOB) finished a study of it in December 2020 and released it, heavily redacted, on 12 February 2024, with a dissent from one member, Travis LeBlanc. [cite:de29_savage_xks] MUSCULAR, reported by the Washington Post on 30 October 2013, was a joint NSA and British GCHQ operation that copied whole data flows on the private links between Google's and Yahoo's data centres. In one 30-day period it sent back more than 180 million records. Google said it was "not aware of this activity", and Yahoo said it had given no agency access to its data centres. [cite:de29_ap_muscular] The companies encrypted the traffic between their own buildings; the authority itself was untouched.

Britain's equivalent of bulk cable tapping, run by GCHQ under a programme the Guardian named Tempora in June 2013, reached a court. In Big Brother Watch v. United Kingdom, on 25 May 2021, the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights held that bulk interception is not in itself unlawful but that the British regime lacked the safeguards required, from independent authorisation to later review, and so violated the rights to privacy and to free expression, the second because journalists' material was unprotected. [cite:de29_asil_bbw]

The CIA has its own bulk holdings under the same order. On 10 February 2022 Senators Ron Wyden and Martin Heinrich, both Democrats, made public a letter of April 2021 saying a CIA programme operated "outside the statutory framework that Congress and the public believe govern this collection." Released papers showed that analysts searching it for Americans were not required to record why, and that a programme collecting financial data on the Islamic State had swept in Americans' records. The CIA said it "may incidentally acquire information about Americans" and protects it under procedures approved by the attorney general. [cite:de29_ap_ciabulk] What the programme holds, and whether it continues, has not been disclosed.

The hacking tools, and a catalogue that was not Snowden's

The agencies also break into devices. An exploit is a piece of code that uses a flaw in software to take control of a phone, computer or television without the owner knowing. On 29 December 2013 Der Spiegel published an NSA catalogue of hardware and software implants for phones, computers and network equipment, known as the ANT catalogue. It is often credited to Snowden; it was never attributed to him, and both Bruce Schneier and Glenn Greenwald, who worked on the Snowden archive, said it came from a second, unidentified source. [cite:de29_es_ant]

The CIA's equivalent came out through WikiLeaks as "Vault 7", beginning on 7 March 2017 with 8,761 documents. One tool, Weeping Angel, put certain Samsung televisions into a false "off" mode and recorded through their microphones; others read Signal and WhatsApp messages on iPhones and Android phones by taking over the handset rather than breaking the encryption. [cite:de29_sg_vault7] The source was Joshua Schulte, a CIA software engineer, who copied the archives in 2016; he was convicted of espionage in 2022 and, in a separate trial, of possessing child sexual abuse material, and was sentenced to 40 years. [cite:de29_ng_schulte] The CIA's own task force, in an October 2017 report released by Wyden in June 2020, found security in the unit that built the tools "woefully lax" and wrote that had the tools been stolen and not published, "we might still be unaware of the loss." [cite:de29_aje_lax] The leaked tools themselves were burned; the capability to build new ones was not.

From collecting to buying

The largest change since 2013 is not in the leaked programmes but beside them. Data that once required a court order can now be bought from brokers, the companies that gather location and browsing data from apps and advertising (explained in [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four] and [scene:de25_location_and_mobile|Part Twenty-Six]). A report written for the Director of National Intelligence and declassified in June 2023 said such information "historically could have been obtained, if at all, only through targeted (and predicated) collection." [cite:de29_fortune_cai] On 18 March 2026 the FBI's director, Kash Patel, told Wyden: "We do purchase commercially available information that is consistent with the Constitution and the laws," declined to commit to stop, and the bureau maintains that no warrant is needed, a position no court has yet tested. [cite:de29_tc_patel] The legal doctrine of buying rather than asking a judge is examined in [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty].

If it were connected

The catalogue and the immigration ecosystem of [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty] run under different laws; the question is where they meet. Documented: in the market. The FBI buys commercially available information, and ICE buys people-search profiles and phone-location trails from the same kind of broker. [cite:de29_tc_patel] [cite:de28_bu_lexis] Documented too: intelligence holdings searched for domestic ends, when FBI agents ran improper 702 queries on people arrested at the 2020 racial-justice protests and on suspects of 6 January. [cite:de29_ap_fisc2023] Possible, with no document: 702 or Executive Order 12333 material reaching ICE's integration platforms beside a broker's address and a Medicaid record; that would need the agencies' sharing rules to allow it and a request through the FBI or DHS's intelligence office. Not supported: a standing feed from NSA or CIA collection into immigration enforcement; the record shows the two systems meeting in the market, not in a pipe.

sections.h: The Messengers: Who Was Punished, and Who Was Not
sections.html:
Almost everything in the previous section is known because someone broke the law or a promise to make it known. That is the paradox this section sets out. The people who revealed the programmes were prosecuted, imprisoned or driven into exile; the officials who misdescribed the programmes to Congress, or ran them past their legal limits, were not charged. Both halves are documented. What they mean is argued, in good faith, on both sides, and both arguments are given here.

The disclosers

Edward Snowden was charged in June 2013, in a sealed complaint in the Eastern District of Virginia, with theft of government property, unauthorised communication of national defence information and wilful communication of classified communications intelligence, the last two under the Espionage Act; each count carries up to ten years. [cite:de29_jurist_snowden] He flew to Moscow, received asylum, and on 26 September 2022 was made a Russian citizen by President Vladimir Putin's decree. [cite:de29_npr_citizen] The government also sued him. In a civil case, not a criminal one, a federal court found in December 2019 that he had broken the agreements he signed with the CIA and the NSA by publishing his memoir, Permanent Record, and giving 56 speeches without submitting them for review, and on 29 September 2020 it entered a judgment of more than $5.2 million and placed his future earnings from them in trust for the United States; the suit did not try to stop the book. [cite:de29_doj_snowden] President Donald Trump said on 15 August 2020 of a pardon, "I'm going to start looking at it." [cite:de29_aawsat_trump2020] A viral claim in July 2026 that he would be pardoned on 4 July had no basis, and no pardon could be found as of October 2026. [cite:de29_meaww_pardon] At her confirmation hearing as Director of National Intelligence on 30 January 2025, Tulsi Gabbard said he "broke the law" but had exposed "illegal and unconstitutional programs", and declined senators' requests to call him a traitor. [cite:de29_rec_gabbard]

Chelsea Manning, an Army intelligence analyst, gave WikiLeaks hundreds of thousands of military and diplomatic records in 2010, including video of a 2007 helicopter attack in Baghdad, the Afghan and Iraq war logs, published in July and October 2010, and 251,287 State Department cables, published from 28 November 2010. [cite:de29_wiki_cables] [cite:de29_npr_manning] A court-martial acquitted her of aiding the enemy in July 2013 and she was sentenced to 35 years; President Barack Obama commuted the sentence in January 2017, and she left prison on 17 May 2017 after about seven years. [cite:de29_npr_manning] The publisher, Julian Assange, was indicted in 2019 on 18 counts, fought extradition from a British prison for five years, and on 26 June 2024 pleaded guilty in the Northern Mariana Islands to one count of conspiracy to obtain and disclose national defence information, receiving a sentence of time served. [cite:de29_cbs_assange]

Two later cases drew the longest sentences. Reality Winner, an NSA contractor, mailed a classified report on Russian attempts to penetrate an American voting-software supplier to a news outlet; on 23 August 2018 she was sentenced to 63 months, which prosecutors called "the longest sentence served by a federal defendant for an unauthorized disclosure to the media." [cite:de29_cbs_winner] Daniel Hale, a former Air Force analyst, gave The Intercept documents on the drone programme, including one showing that in a five-month operation in Afghanistan nearly 90 per cent of those killed were not the intended targets; on 27 July 2021 he was sentenced to 45 months. Judge Liam O'Grady told him, "You are not being prosecuted for speaking out about the drone program killing innocent people," but for taking the documents. [cite:de29_globe_hale] Joshua Schulte, the source of the CIA's Vault 7 tools, received 40 years in 2024, part of it for a separate child-abuse-material conviction ([scene:de29_the_catalogue|the previous section]). [cite:de29_ng_schulte] The prosecutions ran under three presidents of both parties: Manning and the Snowden charges under Obama, Winner and the Assange indictment under Trump, Hale's sentence and Assange's plea under Joe Biden. [cite:de29_npr_manning] [cite:de29_cbs_winner] [cite:de29_globe_hale] [cite:de29_cbs_assange]

The officials

On 12 March 2013, three months before the first Snowden story, Senator Ron Wyden asked the Director of National Intelligence, James Clapper, at an open hearing whether the NSA collected "any type of data at all on millions, or hundreds of millions of Americans." Clapper answered, "No, sir," and then, "Not wittingly." After the phone-records order was published he told NBC he had given the "least most untruthful" answer available in an open setting, and on 21 June 2013 he wrote to the committee's chair that "My response was clearly erroneous," explaining that he had been thinking of a different programme. [cite:de29_pf_clapper] The five-year limitation periods for charging false statements to Congress ran out on 12 March 2018 with no charge brought. [cite:de29_wex_clapper] No public Justice Department document explains why.

In 2014 CIA officers searched computers used by the Senate Intelligence Committee's staff, who were writing the committee's report on the agency's detention and interrogation programme. The CIA's inspector general found the access improper and the director, John Brennan, apologised to the committee. An internal accountability board chaired by the former senator Evan Bayh called the search "clearly inappropriate" but found no bad faith, and no one was disciplined; the agency had meanwhile referred the committee's own staff to the Justice Department. [cite:de29_npr_ciassci] The surveillance court's repeated findings that the government had misdescribed its own programmes, and the 2023 rebuke over FBI searches described in [scene:de29_the_precedent|the first section], likewise led to rule changes rather than charges. [cite:de29_ap_fisc2023]

The paradox, argued both ways

The case for prosecution is that secrecy agreements are the condition of access, that a disclosure cannot be limited to the parts that serve the public, and that harm need not be visible to be real. The House Intelligence Committee, summarising a 36-page classified report on 15 September 2016, said Snowden's disclosures "caused tremendous damage," that most of what he took concerned military and intelligence matters of interest to adversaries rather than privacy, and that he was "not a whistleblower." [cite:de29_cnbc_hpsci] In Manning's material, the unredacted release of all the cables in September 2011, after a password published in a Guardian journalist's book let others decrypt a copy, exposed the names of people who had spoken to American diplomats in confidence; the newspapers that had worked with WikiLeaks condemned it. [cite:de29_wiki_cables] Prosecutors made the same point when Assange pleaded guilty. [cite:de29_cbs_assange]

The case for the disclosers is that the record vindicated much of what they exposed. Courts found the bulk phone-records programme unlawful and Congress ended it ([scene:de29_the_catalogue|the previous section]). Eric Holder, who as attorney general oversaw the charges against Snowden, said in 2016 that he had "actually performed a public service by raising the debate," while adding that "He harmed American interests" and "there has to be a consequence." [cite:de29_npr_holder] No death has been publicly tied to Manning's leaks: at her sentencing a brigadier general's testimony about one Afghan killed was struck because the man's name was not in the files, and Defense Secretary Robert Gates had called the consequences "fairly modest." [cite:de29_pf_mccain] At Assange's plea the judge noted that no actual physical harm had been shown. [cite:de29_db_manglona] The fair reading is narrow: no documented death, but harm unproven in public rather than disproven, since the damage assessments remain classified.

The asymmetry in outcomes is a documented fact. A deliberate double standard is not: no Justice Department document gives a reason for declining to charge Clapper or the CIA officers, and the leak prosecutions followed statutes that apply to anyone who discloses classified material, whatever their motive. The structural point stands without a motive. The law as written punishes disclosure of a programme more surely than it punishes the programme's excesses, and most of the Church-era abuses in [scene:de29_the_precedent|the first section] were ended, or first brought to account, through a disclosure of one kind or another.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis is the Sophia platform's, not a finding: immigration enforcement as the occasion, a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination, and in this part the question of whether surveillance would be turned on Americans who object. Documented: it has been done before. Between the Second World War and 1975 five arms of the federal government watched or disrupted lawful domestic political activity under presidents of both parties, from Martin Luther King Jr. and two senators of opposite parties to the Klan and the IRS's lists of activist groups, and the proof is in the government's own reports. [cite:de29_rock_chaos] [cite:de29_nbc_minaret] [cite:de29_wiki_cointelpro] [cite:de29_hnn_irs] Documented, too: much of what was exposed in 2013 still exists in some form, and the authorities least subject to Congress, the president's own Executive Order 12333 and the purchase of commercial data, are the ones that grew. [cite:de29_ap_ciabulk] [cite:de29_tc_patel] And documented: those who disclosed the programmes were punished more surely than those who misdescribed them. [cite:de29_wex_clapper] [cite:de29_cbs_winner]

Probable, as a structural inference rather than a finding of abuse: capability now outruns statute in the same places where the Church-era abuses ran, executive-only authority and purchased data, and a 702 certification that runs to March 2027 with the statute lapsed leaves Congress with less leverage, not more, until it expires. [cite:us10_bcj_702] [cite:de29_tc_patel] Capability is not intent; this says what could be done, not what is being done.

Not supported, as of October 2026: any documented current use of the catalogued NSA or CIA programmes against domestic political opponents. The most recent documented misuse, the FBI's searches of 702 data in 2020 and 2021, touched people on the left and the right, was caught by the surveillance court and was answered with rule changes. [cite:de29_ap_fisc2023] The record also runs against the destination at several points. Courts ruled the bulk phone programme unlawful; Congress ended it and let section 215 expire; Congress let 702 lapse in June 2026 rather than renew it on the executive's terms; and the surveillance court put its rebuke of the FBI on the record. [cite:us10_wiki_clapper] [cite:de29_eff_215] [cite:us10_eff_702lapse] [cite:de29_ap_fisc2023] The precedent is proven; its present repetition is not. What the law now permits, and how the walls between government datasets came down, is the subject of [scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|Part Thirty-Two] and [scene:de30_silos_and_subpoenas|its second section]; the consequences that would follow if the tools were turned are graded in [scene:de35_the_consequence_ladder|Part Thirty-Seven], and these grades carry into [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three].

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Two
chapters.title: The Legal Architecture
chapters.intro: The tools of the previous parts operate inside a body of law, and this part examines the law itself as it changed in 2025 and 2026. The first section follows a single idea, making career civil servants easier to remove, from Curtis Yarvin's 2012 proposal to retire them all, through the Schedule F order of 2020 and J.D. Vance's remark of 2021, to the rule and order of 2026 that moved about 8,000 senior officials into a new category, and sets each against the others clause by clause. The second traces the legal walls built in the 1970s between the government's separate stores of personal data, and how each was breached for immigration enforcement and tested in court. The third reads the September 2025 directive on domestic terrorism and its implementing memorandum, and the Army's commissioning of technology executives, and closes Book Five by testing the book's worst-case reading against everything the toolkit parts have documented.
chapters.outro: The legal architecture moved in one direction in 2025 and 2026, and the courts did not stop all of it. About 8,000 senior career officials lost their removal protections by an order of 3 June 2026, under a rule that forbids loyalty tests and is still in court; its documented defenders argue from accountability, and no document traces it to Yarvin's RAGE, which it resembles only in part. [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] [cite:de30_npr_8000] [cite:de30_govexec_sherk] The walls built after Watergate between tax, health, benefit and child-welfare records and enforcement were breached; judges held 42,695 tax disclosures unlawful, narrowed Medicaid sharing to five fields and paused it after a file went beyond them to Palantir, and rejected the Justice Department's demands for state voter rolls, while the Supreme Court let the voter-checking system resume. [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de30_bl_medicaid] [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] [cite:de19_npr_save] A presidential memorandum names ideas as indicators of domestic terrorism and points investigators at funders, with prosecutions so far for violence and no revocation of any nonprofit's status on record; four technology executives took Army commissions under ethics terms the Army tightened a year later. [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] [cite:de30_kera_prairieland] [cite:de30_wyden_letter] [cite:de30_ds_det201] On Book Five as a whole, the parts are documented and several joins between them are on the record; the targeting of critics is documented for non-citizens and in specific cases for citizens, not as a programme; and the executive without a veto is not shown. [cite:de30_audit_aaup] Book Six turns from what has been built to the brakes that remain, beginning with [scene:de31_five_patterns|Part Thirty-Three].

sections.h: From RAGE to Schedule Policy/Career
sections.html:
In 2012 Curtis Yarvin proposed that a new American leader begin by retiring every government employee. In 2020 a president created a new category of federal job whose holders could be removed with fewer protections. In 2021 J.D. Vance said a future president should fire every mid-level civil servant. In 2026 the government finished the rule that brought the 2020 category back and moved its first 8,000 senior officials into it. Commentators have often run these four things together as one plan carried out in stages. This section sets them side by side, clause by clause, separates what each actually says from what it is said to say, and asks which links in the chain are documented. It also places the change beside the Supreme Court's ruling of June 2026 on the president's power to remove officials, which moved the same way at the top of the government. Status is as of October 2026.

Three proposals

Yarvin's version came first and went furthest. At a technology "unconference" called BIL in 2012 he told the audience that Americans would have to "get over their dictator phobia" and that the first step of a takeover was to "Retire All Government Employees," which he abbreviated RAGE. [cite:de6_tnr_duran] [cite:de6_pein_2014] He returned to the idea in an interview with the New York Times in January 2025, saying the government should be treated "like a company that goes out of business, but sort of more so," and that its former officials should be treated as ordinary people who had served a bad regime. [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] RAGE is a proposal to remove everyone, not to sort anyone by loyalty, and the program it belongs to, a single executive answerable to no electorate, is set out in [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six].

The second version was an executive order. In October 2020 President Trump signed Executive Order 13957, which created "Schedule F" for career positions of a "confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character" that are "not normally subject to change as a result of a Presidential transition." [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] A schedule, in the federal civil service, is a category of job with its own rules for hiring and removal; most career staff are in the "competitive service," where removal for poor performance or misconduct follows set procedures and can be appealed to the Merit Systems Protection Board, an independent tribunal. Schedule F took those procedures away from the jobs placed in it. President Biden revoked the order in January 2021, before it had been fully put into effect, and in April 2024 the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) adopted a rule guaranteeing that employees moved into such a category kept their right of appeal. [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] [cite:de30_fedsmith_order]

The third version was spoken. In September 2021, then a Senate candidate, Vance told the podcast Jack Murphy Live that a future President Trump should "fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state" and "replace them with our people." [cite:de5_nextgov_vance] In the same interview he named Yarvin: "There's this guy, Curtis Yarvin, who's written about some of these things," adding, "I'm sympathetic to that project. But another option is that we should just seize the administrative state for our own purposes." [cite:de5_wbur_vance] The second sentence matters. Vance described Yarvin's project and then offered a different one: not retiring the state, as RAGE proposed, but taking control of it and staffing it with allies. The place of the remark in his life is set out in [scene:de12_the_thiel_years|Part Twelve].

The rule and the order

On his first day back in office, 20 January 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14171, "Restoring Accountability to Policy-Influencing Positions Within the Federal Workforce." It reinstated the 2020 order with amendments, renamed Schedule F "Schedule Policy/Career," and revoked Biden's revocation. [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] OPM published its final rule on 6 February 2026, and it took effect on 8 March. [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] [cite:us2_govexec_schedf] Under it, positions judged to influence policy lose the statutory procedures for removing employees for poor performance and misconduct, and the 2024 appeal-rights rule is rescinded; the president, not OPM, decides which positions move. Holders keep competitive hiring, trial periods and veterans' preference, and the rule forbids patronage and loyalty tests. [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] [cite:us2_opm_schedpc] Officials estimated that up to 50,000 employees could eventually be covered. [cite:us2_govexec_schedf]

The first move came on 3 June 2026. Executive Order 14410, "Implementing Schedule Policy/Career in the Excepted Service," placed the positions listed in its appendix into the new schedule, declared them "exempted from the adverse action procedures," let agencies remove their holders for unacceptable performance or misconduct by written notice, and stated that they "will be filled based on merit and not political affiliation." Its stated purpose is that the president "relies on subordinates in the executive branch to help him faithfully execute the laws." [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] About 8,000 employees were moved, nearly all at GS-15, the top grade of the general civil service: heads of policy offices and their chiefs of staff, regional directors, programme managers and senior communications staff. For comparison, the government has about 4,000 political appointees. [cite:de30_npr_8000]

Each side stated its case in plain terms. OPM's director, Scott Kupor, said: "This is very much about accountability," and called it "a restoration, in our mind, of the democratic process"; he said no loyalty tests would be used and whistleblower protections remained, though enforcing the ban on political tests falls to the agencies themselves. [cite:de30_npr_8000] He also said the employees moved could be "removed effectively at will." [cite:de30_fedsmith_order] Donald Moynihan, a public-policy scholar at the University of Michigan, warned that "It creates bubbles around policymakers," and the president of the largest federal union called the order, if it stands, "one of the largest acts of political corruption in American history." [cite:de30_npr_8000] [cite:de30_fedsmith_order]

What the comparison shows, and what it does not

Read clause by clause, the three are not one plan. RAGE removes the whole state; the 2026 rule removes procedures from about 0.4 per cent of the civil service and keeps merit hiring. Vance's 2021 remark sits between them: it shares RAGE's mass firing and Schedule Policy/Career's aim of a staff responsive to the elected president, but on the documented record it was a podcast answer, not a policy he has since put in writing. The resemblance is real and runs in one direction, toward a civil service more easily directed by the president. [cite:de30_npr_8000] [cite:de5_nextgov_vance]

The line of descent is another matter. Schedule F has documented defenders, and none of them cites Yarvin. James Sherk, a former special assistant to President Trump who later worked at the America First Policy Institute, argued for it in 2023 on grounds of accountability: "Every federal employee should serve at the pleasure of the president." [cite:de30_govexec_sherk] That claim is broader than the rule that followed, and it is Sherk's, not Yarvin's. The only reported link between Yarvin and the people who designed the 2025 personnel changes is an anonymous adviser's remark to the Washington Post that everyone designing policy had read him. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] Yarvin himself said in 2025 that the administration was "barely scratching the surface" and that his influence ran "more through the kids in the administration." [cite:de6_cnn_2025] Neither remark is a document showing that the order or the rule came from his writing. The book's rule holds here: rhyme is not provenance ([scene:de1_spine_and_overlay|Part One]).

The removal power at the top

The civil-service rule changed who can be removed below the political level. A ruling of the Supreme Court changed it above. On 29 June 2026, in Trump v. Slaughter, the Court overruled its 1935 decision in Humphrey's Executor by six votes to three and held that the president may remove members of the Federal Trade Commission at will; it left open offices traditionally outside the executive branch and named the Federal Reserve, and the same day it declined, in Trump v. Cook, to let the president remove a Fed governor pending her case. [cite:de0_slaughter] Taken together, the ruling and the rule extend the president's control over the people who carry out the law, at the commissions and in the career service. Both moved through channels that remain open to challenge, a court's judgment and a rule under existing statute, which is why [scene:de21_the_ending|Part Twenty-One] describes them as a real shift of power toward the presidency, documented as such, rather than an executive without a veto. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412]

The checks still in play

The rule has been in court since the day the 2025 order was signed. The National Treasury Employees Union sued in Washington on 20 January 2025, and in March 2026 the judge allowed it to amend its complaint once positions were actually moved; a separate suit by Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility and other unions, joined by the American Federation of Government Employees, challenges the order, the rule and the reclassification in federal court in Maryland. [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] [cite:de30_afge_lit] No court had blocked the conversions as of October 2026, and the June order is in effect. [cite:de30_afge_lit] Congress has a bill before it, the Saving the Civil Service Act, which would limit the president's power to reclassify positions; it had not passed. [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] Whether the 8,000 are removed for performance, as the order's text provides, or for their views, as its critics fear, is a question of practice that the record does not yet answer; [scene:us2_integrity|the library's account of the civil service] sets the same rule against the wider cuts, and [scene:de21_the_ending|Part Twenty-One] places it among what DOGE left behind.

sections.h: Silos and Subpoenas: How the Walls Between Datasets Came Down
sections.html:
The federal government holds more personal information than any company: tax returns, Social Security records, Medicaid claims, the files of children who arrived alone at the border and the adults who took them in. For half a century each store was collected for one purpose and walled off by law from the others. Officials call such separate stores "silos." The walls were not accidents. They were built in the 1970s, after investigations showed what a president could do when the files were joined. This section sets out those walls, how each was breached in 2025–26 for immigration enforcement, and what the courts said. The tools that join data once it moves, from brokers to fusion platforms, are the subject of [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four]; here the subject is the law.

Why the walls were built

The Privacy Act of 1974 was Congress's answer to two worries. The Justice Department's own account of the law names them: "curbing the illegal surveillance and investigation of individuals by federal agencies" exposed during Watergate, and "the government's increasing use of computers to store and retrieve personal data." The Act restricts what an agency may disclose about a person from its records. [cite:de30_doj_privacy] Tax records got a stronger wall two years later. Lawrence Gibbs, a former IRS commissioner who helped draft the 1976 rewrite of section 6103 of the tax code, has written that President Nixon "attempted to cause the IRS to provide him with confidential taxpayer information" to audit his enemies, a charge in the articles of impeachment of 1974; the rewrite made every return confidential unless the law expressly allowed disclosure. [cite:de30_bl_gibbs] Section 6103 still lets the IRS give another agency a person's address for a criminal investigation, but only on a written request that supplies the person's name and address and meets the statute's conditions. [cite:ad13_audit_irs_dcir] The domestic surveillance that produced these laws is described in [scene:de29_the_precedent|Part Thirty-One].

On 20 March 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14243, "Stopping Waste, Fraud, and Abuse by Eliminating Information Silos," directing agency heads to give designated federal officials "full and prompt access to all unclassified agency records, data, software systems, and information technology systems." [cite:de19_eo14243] The order did not repeal the statutes; it could not. What followed was a series of agreements between agencies, each tested in court against the old walls.

Tax records

The Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, and the Homeland Security Secretary, Kristi Noem, signed an agreement on 7 April 2025 under which Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) would send the IRS names and addresses of people it said were in the country unlawfully, to be checked against tax records. The Treasury said it rested on "longstanding authorities granted by Congress"; ICE's acting director said it was "strictly for the major criminal cases." The acting IRS commissioner, Melanie Krause, was reported by two people familiar with her decision to be resigning over it. [cite:de30_ap_krause] ICE then asked for the addresses of about 1.28 million people, and the IRS turned over about 47,000 before the courts intervened. [cite:us10_abc_irs_feb] [cite:ad13_audit_irs_dcir] In a suit by the Center for Taxpayer Rights, Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly stayed the arrangement in November 2025 and in February 2026 found that the IRS had broken the law "approximately 42,695 times"; on 8 September 2026 a unanimous appeals panel upheld her block, holding that the procedure failed to ensure ICE's requests met the statute's name-and-address requirement. [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:ad13_audit_irs_dcir] Another panel of the same court had declined in February to stop the sharing in a separate suit, and a federal judge in Massachusetts barred ICE from using the data already received. [cite:us10_abc_irs_feb] [cite:ad13_audit_irs_hoodline] Status as of October 2026: further disclosures are blocked while appeals continue. The effect on immigrant taxpayers is set out in [scene:ad13_immigrants_latinos|the library's volume on the American Dream].

Social Security

Social Security's records were used in two ways. In April 2025, according to an administration official speaking anonymously, about 6,300 immigrants whom DHS identified as paroled people on a terrorist watch list or with FBI criminal records were entered into the agency's Death Master File, the list of people reported dead, which the White House renamed the "Ineligible Master File." The White House said removing the "monetary incentive" would "encourage them to self-deport." AP reported that the people affected were in the country legally; without a working number they could not legally work or use many financial services. [cite:de30_ap_ssadead] The second use was larger. In April and May 2025 DHS, its immigration service and DOGE overhauled SAVE, the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system built to check immigrants' eligibility for benefits, linked it for the first time to Social Security records, and opened it to bulk checks of whole state voter rolls. [cite:de19_dhs_save] [cite:de24_npr_save] The government says it ran more than 65 million voters in 26 states and flagged 28,635; in Texas about a fifth of those flagged were later found to be citizens. Judge Sparkle Sooknanan held in June 2026 that the system broke the Social Security Act and the Privacy Act; on 25 September the Supreme Court stayed her order over three dissents. [cite:de19_npr_save] A tool built to check immigrants was, by this route, used on citizens.

Medicaid and children's sponsors

Health records crossed in June 2025, when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, on the direction of the Health Secretary and over objections from its own staff, began sharing Medicaid enrollees' personal data with ICE; a July agreement gave DHS access to names, addresses, birth dates, ethnicity and Social Security numbers. ICE had followed a policy since 2013 of not using Medicaid data for enforcement. Twenty states sued, and in August Judge Vince Chhabria blocked the sharing for their residents, writing that "The record in this case strongly suggests that no such process occurred," meaning the reasoned decision the law requires. [cite:de30_hipaa_chhabria] On 29 December 2025 he let a narrower exchange proceed: for people not lawfully present, five fields only, citizenship or immigration status, address, phone number, date of birth and Medicaid ID, which he found "clearly authorized by law"; medical information was not cleared. [cite:de30_bl_medicaid] The limits did not hold in practice. On 7 January 2026 CMS sent ICE a dataset covering millions of people, including lawful residents, beyond what the court allowed; ICE passed it to Palantir over a Microsoft Teams chat; Palantir says it was purged on the government's instruction, but CMS later re-sent the file by mistake and about six ICE users were found still holding copies. The judge paused the sharing in late May 2026, and at a hearing on 3 September signalled that valid visa holders' data should not be shared; no formal ruling had been located as of October 2026. [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de24b_chn_medicaid]

The files of unaccompanied children show the wall moving in both directions under different presidents. In April 2018 the first Trump administration signed an agreement requiring the refugee office that places these children to share information on their sponsors with immigration enforcement. A Biden rule effective 30 April 2024 barred that sharing. An interim rule of 25 March 2025 removed the bar; in June 2025 a judge blocked new documentation demands on sponsors but left the rule itself in force. [cite:de30_tracker_orr]

Voter rolls

The largest demand was for state voter registration lists, which states hold, not the federal government. The Justice Department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for unredacted rolls including Social Security and driver's-licence numbers, arguing that the National Voter Registration Act, the Help America Vote Act and the Civil Rights Act of 1960 require states to hand them over for list maintenance. [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] [cite:de30_wex_ninth] By 13 July 2026 it had lost every one of the 13 trial-court decisions on the merits and one appeal. Judge Thomas Johnston in West Virginia found no adequate stated basis or purpose and wrote that "one is left to wonder what the real purpose was," while noting that question was not before him.
