[cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] The Ninth Circuit heard the California and Oregon appeals on 19 May 2026 and "sharply questioned" the department; the appeals were pending as of October 2026. [cite:de30_wex_ninth] [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls]

Side doors and subpoenas

A wall in law is only as good as the doors around it. Washington State bars its agencies from sharing data for civil immigration enforcement, yet by 13 October 2026 researchers at the University of Washington had confirmed 356 cases in which federal agents looked up the state's driver's-licence records before an immigration arrest, through a national police data network called Nlets, data brokers or local police; closing one route, they found, pushes agencies to another. [cite:de30_uwchr_dmv] Brokers are a door of their own: utility records on more than 170 million people reached ICE through a commercial database until the supplier stopped in 2021. [cite:de24_globe_utility] The government also has its own key, the administrative subpoena, a demand for records an agency can issue without a judge; DHS's use of it to unmask anonymous critics of ICE online is set out in [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty], and its reported use for the financial records of unions and nonprofits in the next section.

Two things in this record cut against a simple story. The walls were not all built by one party or breached by one: the children's-sponsor arc runs from a Republican agreement to a Democratic bar to a Republican repeal. And the walls mostly held where they were statutory and specific: the tax-privacy section and the federal election laws stopped the largest transfers in court, while SAVE, defended under a 1996 immigration statute, survived the Supreme Court's stay. [cite:de30_tracker_orr] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] [cite:de19_npr_save] What is new in 2025–26 is not any single tool but the joining of civil records, collected to tax, insure and protect, to enforcement.

sections.h: NSPM-7 and Detachment 201
sections.html:
Two documents of 2025 complete the legal architecture this book has followed: a presidential memorandum of September on domestic political violence, which names the ideas it calls warning signs, and the swearing-in of four technology executives as Army officers in June. Neither is a surveillance tool. One sets who the tools are pointed at; the other places the builders of the tools inside the force that buys them. This section sets out each, then tests the book's worst-case reading against Book Five as a whole.

What NSPM-7 says

A National Security Presidential Memorandum (NSPM) is a directive from the president to the agencies, published but not passed by Congress. NSPM-7, "Countering Domestic Terrorism and Organized Political Violence," was signed on 25 September 2025. It cites the assassination of Charlie Kirk that month, alongside the killing of a health-insurance executive in 2024, the 2022 attempt on Justice Kavanaugh and attacks on ICE officers. Section 1 names the "common threads animating this violent conduct": "anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity," "support for the overthrow of the United States Government," and "extremism on migration, race, and gender." [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] Section 2 directs the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Forces to investigate "institutional and individual funders, and officers and employees of organizations"; the Treasury to "identify and disrupt financial networks" and guide banks on filing Suspicious Activity Reports, the confidential reports banks send to the Treasury; and the IRS to ensure that no tax-exempt body is "directly or indirectly financing political violence or domestic terrorism." Section 3 lets the Attorney General recommend groups for designation as a "domestic terrorist organization," citing the definition of domestic terrorism in federal criminal law, 18 U.S.C. 2331(5). The memorandum does not mention the First Amendment; it says it "shall be implemented consistent with applicable law." [cite:de30_wh_nspm7]

No federal statute provides for designating a domestic group as terrorist. [cite:de30_dla_nspm7] The criminal code defines domestic terrorism but, unlike the State Department's foreign list, attaches no list or penalties to it. A law firm's analysis for its clients concluded that NSPM-7 "creates no new legal authority" and that a domestic label carries reputational and practical, not formal legal, consequences. [cite:de30_dla_nspm7] Three days before the memorandum, on 22 September, the president had signed an order stating, "I hereby designate Antifa as a 'domestic terrorist organization,'" calling it "a militarist, anarchist enterprise" and directing agencies to "investigate, disrupt, and dismantle" its operations and their funders; the order cites no statute. [cite:de30_govinfo_antifa] On 13 November the State Department used the foreign-list power it does have against four European groups. [cite:de30_state_fto]

The Attorney General's implementing memorandum of 4 December 2025, addressed to all federal prosecutors, made the program operational. It ordered the FBI to "compile a list of groups or entities engaged in acts that may constitute domestic terrorism," updated every 30 days, set up cash rewards for informants, reached back five years and told prosecutors to consider tax crimes. Its list of indicators includes "opposition to law and immigration enforcement," "radical gender ideology," and "anti-Christianity." A footnote states: "No investigation may be opened based solely on activities protected by the First Amendment." [cite:de30_bondi_memo]

What has been done under it

The documented prosecutions concern violence. On 4 July 2025 a police officer was shot, and survived, outside the Prairieland ICE detention centre in Alvarado, Texas. By April 2026 a federal jury in Fort Worth had convicted eight of nine defendants, whom prosecutors called the "North Texas Antifa Cell," of providing material support to terrorists, built on attempted murder of a federal officer; the prosecutor told jurors they were on trial for their conduct, not their beliefs. [cite:de30_kera_prairieland]

The use against organisations is reported, not adjudicated. On 2 September 2026 Senators Ron Wyden and Raphael Warnock wrote to the Treasury citing press reports that officials were reviewing the tax-exempt status of the Open Society Foundations, the Southern Poverty Law Center and the Council on American-Islamic Relations under a "blueprint," and that IRS criminal investigators were working with the FBI on nonprofits; the letter asked whether any group had been recommended for examination or revocation and reports none completed. [cite:de30_wyden_letter] An amicus brief filed on 25 August 2026 for FIRE, the Society for the Rule of Law and the libertarian Cato Institute argues that DHS has used NSPM-7 to infiltrate meetings, monitor encrypted chats and seize years of financial records from unions and nonprofits, and that the memorandum "treats left-leaning political viewpoints as indicia of domestic terrorism." These are allegations; no court has ruled on them. [cite:de30_pd_amicus] Ideological deportation cases and the unmasking subpoenas are in [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty]; the best-known earlier federal programme aimed at domestic political groups, the FBI's COINTELPRO, which ended in April 1971, is in [scene:de29_the_precedent|Part Thirty-One]. [cite:de29_wiki_cointelpro]

Detachment 201

On 13 June 2025 the Army swore in four executives as lieutenant colonels in the Army Reserve: Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir; Andrew Bosworth, chief technology officer of Meta; Kevin Weil, chief product officer of OpenAI; and Bob McGrew, an adviser at Thinking Machines Lab and formerly OpenAI's chief research officer. As "Detachment 201" they serve part-time as senior advisers on technology for the Army's reorganisation. [cite:de30_army_det201] An Army spokesman said in June 2025 that "They're not making acquisition decisions" and that the conflict rules were those for any reservist. [cite:de30_d1_det201] When three more executives were commissioned on 10 June 2026, the Army described stricter terms: "mandatory" recusal under the Joint Ethics Regulation, confidential financial disclosure, legal review of each task and a bar from vendor selection. [cite:de30_ds_det201]

Sankar's company has been an Army software contractor since 2019 ([scene:de27_money_and_war|Part Twenty-Nine]). [cite:de10_defnews] That is a documented conflict of position, which the 2026 rules exist to manage; no document shows any member steering a contract.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis is the Sophia platform's, not a finding: immigration enforcement as the occasion, a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. Book Five has read the toolkit through one lens, that the mechanisms may not be connected now but exist, so the test asks three things: whether the parts exist, which joins are on the record, and what has been done to critics.

The parts exist; that is documented in all nine parts. Brokers sell location trails and profiles, and "anonymous" data can be traced to the person ([scene:de24_the_myth_of_anonymous_data|Part Twenty-Four]); the state holds benefit, school, vetting and credit records ([scene:de24b_benefits|Part Twenty-Five]); phones can be followed through data an internal ICE analysis said needs no warrant ([scene:de25_location_and_mobile|Part Twenty-Six]); TSA and CBP record who travels ([scene:de25b_who_knows_you_travel|Part Twenty-Seven]); ICE matches faces in the street, and every regulated stablecoin must carry a freeze switch ([scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|Part Twenty-Eight]). Palantir sells the platform that joins records ([scene:de27_capability_not_intent|Part Twenty-Nine]), and ICE buys from every layer ([scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty]). The precedent of such tools turned on lawful political life is proven ([scene:de29_the_precedent|Part Thirty-One]), and a federal directive now names ideas, including opposition to immigration enforcement, as indicators of domestic terrorism. [cite:de25_404_webloc] [cite:de26_404_fortify] [cite:de26_crec_genius] [cite:ow9_reg_immos] [cite:de30_bondi_memo]

Documented joins: a Medicaid dataset went from CMS to ICE and on to Palantir over a Teams chat in January 2026, beyond a court's limits [cite:de27_npr_medicaid]; TSA passed records on more than 31,000 travellers to ICE between January 2025 and February 2026, with more than 800 arrests by ICE's own count [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice]; records from 2014 to 2022 show student-visa and air-passenger data searched, and phone extractions imported, through ICE's Palantir case system [cite:de28_guardian_icm]; and Social Security data was linked to SAVE and run against citizens' voter rolls. [cite:de19_npr_save] Probable: LexisNexis's people-search data flowing into "the Palantir platform," which its 2026 work statement requires. [cite:de28_bu_lexis] Possible, with no document: the commercial vendors' location, face and social-media data, the newly opened welfare files and DHS's planned biometric system joined to the same platform; each would need an interface or an agreement, not a new law. Not supported: Thomson Reuters's CLEAR feeding Palantir, or one standing system that carries a person from a camera to a cell outside immigration enforcement. [cite:de28_lawsites_tr]

The targeting of critics has to be graded by group. For non-citizens it is documented: after testimony that a DHS team had written more than a hundred reports drawing on a private list of campus activists, a federal court found on 30 September 2025 that a policy of targeting non-citizen academics for their speech violated the First Amendment, and on 22 January 2026 it vacated the policy; the government's appeal was pending as of October 2026. [cite:de28_crimson_hatch] [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de30_audit_aaup] For citizens the record holds specific cases, not a programme. DHS used administrative subpoenas, without a judge, to try to unmask people who criticised or tracked its agents, and in one case agents came to a critic's home; it withdrew the demands when challenged. [cite:de28_aclu_doe] [cite:de28_int_meta] A Minnesota citizen who had been watching agents lost her Global Entry three days after an agent named her using face recognition, a link alleged in her pending suit and denied by CBP. [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] The Director of National Intelligence revoked the clearances of at least 37 current and former officials, in a memo reported to cite no specific evidence. [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] Use of the surveillance stack as a programme against citizens for their speech is not documented: no court has found it, no nonprofit has lost its status, and the terrorism convictions on record follow a shooting.

Probable: that the indicator lists steer investigative attention toward critics of immigration policy and the left, because the texts name them and the reported reviews of nonprofits follow them; this rests on text and reports, not on a finding about any person. [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] [cite:de30_wyden_letter] Not supported: that any of it came from the Dark Enlightenment's texts; the line from RAGE to the new civil-service schedule is rhyme, not provenance ([scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|the first section]).

Against the destination, the vetoes worked in many places: courts held 42,695 tax disclosures unlawful, limited Medicaid sharing to five fields and paused it after the January breach, vacated the speech-targeting policy and handed the Justice Department thirteen straight losses on voter rolls; a camera company paused federal searches after a state audit; and much of the toolkit was built or bought under presidents of both parties ([scene:de26_counterweights|Part Twenty-Eight]). [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de30_bl_medicaid] [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] [cite:de24_ap_flock] [cite:de30_tracker_orr] They lost others: the Supreme Court stayed the SAVE ruling, no court has blocked the new civil-service schedule, and Trump v. Slaughter widened the removal power. [cite:de19_npr_save] [cite:de30_afge_lit] [cite:de0_slaughter] The parts exist, several joins are documented and more are designed; the executive without a veto is not shown. Book Six asks what removing the remaining brakes would take, beginning with [scene:de31_five_patterns|Part Thirty-Three], and the grades go to [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three].

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Three
chapters.title: The Pathway: Removing the Brakes
chapters.intro: Book Six turns from the tools of the state to the limits on it. A brake, here, is a veto point: a commissioner who cannot be fired for disagreeing, an inspector general who reports to Congress, a sum Congress has ordered spent, a court that can halt an order, a law that keeps tax or health records apart. This part traces five patterns in the orders, rulings and notices of 2025 and 2026 that weakened those brakes, sets each beside the times earlier presidents of both parties used the same powers, follows who gained and who paid, and records which brakes held when the courts, Congress and the states pressed on them, as of October 2026.
chapters.outro: The brakes came off in five patterns at once: the Supreme Court let a president remove Federal Trade Commission members at will and an order moved about 8,000 career officials to removal by notice; 17 inspectors general were removed in one night, unlawfully in process and without reinstatement; GAO found seven unlawful withholdings in 2025 and about $4 billion in foreign aid lapsed by pocket rescission; emergency powers were used for tariffs; and tax, Medicaid and welfare records were opened to immigration enforcement. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de30_npr_8000] [cite:de31_wt_storch] [cite:de31_sac_fema] [cite:de31_rc_scotus_aid] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] Presidents of both parties had used each power before, and the documented gainer is the office, not a donor; no document links the patterns to the Dark Enlightenment's texts or its funders. [cite:de31_govexec_saul] [cite:de31_gao_ukraine] [cite:de31_ag_nebraska] Many brakes held: the Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs and kept the Fed apart, both houses voted against a tariff emergency, and courts blocked tax sharing and narrowed Medicaid sharing; but the tariffs returned under other statutes. [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] [cite:de31_ap_house] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de31_cg_301] Orders still need people to carry them out, and [scene:de32_ice_as_template|Part Thirty-Four] asks who would.

sections.h: Five Patterns: How the Brakes Came Off
sections.html:
A brake, in this part, means a veto point: a person or rule other than the president that can say no and make it stick. A commissioner who cannot be fired for disagreeing is one. So is an inspector general, the internal auditor Congress placed inside each large agency to look for waste and wrongdoing and report to Congress as well as to the agency head. So is a career official with a right of appeal, a sum of money Congress has ordered spent, a court with power to halt an order, and a law that keeps tax or health records away from police. Between 2017 and 2026 orders, rulings and notices weakened each of these, and they fall into five patterns. This section sets out each one with one test for every president: where an earlier administration of either party used or widened the same power, it says so. The five are not one plan. No document shows them designed together, and the book's rule holds: convergence is not coordination ([scene:de1_spine_and_overlay|Part One]). Status is as of October 2026.

Pattern one: who the president can remove

Since 1935 the Supreme Court's decision in Humphrey's Executor had let Congress protect the members of multi-member commissions, such as the Federal Trade Commission, from removal except for cause. On 29 June 2026, in Trump v. Slaughter, the Court overruled it by six votes to three and held that the president may remove FTC commissioners at will. It left open offices traditionally outside the executive branch, naming the Federal Reserve, and the same day, in Trump v. Cook, it refused the government's request to remove a Fed governor while her case continued. [cite:de0_slaughter] The ruling gave constitutional footing to an order already in force. Executive Order 14215 of 18 February 2025 sent the significant rules of independent agencies, including the Federal Election Commission, to the White House's regulatory review office before publication, let the budget office adjust how much of their money they may spend, and declared that the president's and the attorney general's legal opinions "are controlling on all employees." Only the Fed's monetary policy was excepted. [cite:de31_fr_14215]

The same pattern ran through the career service. The rule of 6 February 2026 and Executive Order 14410 of 3 June 2026 moved about 8,000 senior officials into Schedule Policy/Career, where they can be removed by written notice without the usual procedures; [scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|Part Thirty-Two] sets that change clause by clause against Curtis Yarvin's 2012 proposal and finds rhyme, not provenance. [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] [cite:de30_npr_8000]

The removal power did not grow under one party alone. On 9 July 2021 President Biden removed the Commissioner of Social Security, Andrew Saul, although the statute allowed his removal only for cause. A Justice Department opinion issued the same day, relying on two Supreme Court decisions of 2020 and 2021, concluded that "the statutory restriction on removing the commissioner is unconstitutional." Saul replied, "I consider myself the term-protected Commissioner of Social Security." [cite:de31_govexec_saul] What is new in 2025 and 2026 is the reach: from one officer to the commissions as a class and to thousands of career posts.

Pattern two: the watchdogs

On the night of Friday 24 January 2025 17 inspectors general were dismissed by short emails, effective immediately. The law requires the president to give Congress 30 days' notice and reasons before an inspector general is removed, and Congress received neither. Senator Chuck Grassley, a Republican who had defended an inspector general against President Obama in 2009, wrote that "There may be good reason the IGs were fired. We need to know that if so." Senator Elizabeth Warren called it "a purge of independent watchdogs in the middle of the night." [cite:de31_npr_igs] Eight of those removed sued. At a hearing in March 2025 a Justice Department lawyer told the court, "we don't dispute that the president did not comply with the sentence in the statute," while arguing that the notice rule did not bind him. [cite:de31_gma_storch] On 24 September 2025 Judge Ana Reyes ruled: "President Trump violated the IGA. That much is obvious." She still declined to reinstate them, because they had not shown irreparable harm and the president could simply fire them again after giving notice. [cite:de31_wt_storch]

Removing inspectors general is not new, and both parties have done it. President Obama removed the AmeriCorps inspector general, Gerald Walpin, in June 2009, saying he had lost confidence in him; Grassley questioned then too whether the notice rule had been met. [cite:de31_govexec_walpin] In 2020 President Trump replaced several, including those at Defense and in the intelligence community. [cite:de31_npr_igs] In December 2022 Congress tightened the law to require "a substantive rationale, including detailed and case-specific reasons," and the first tests came from President Biden, who gave notice in 2024 that he was removing the Railroad Retirement Board's inspector general after an integrity inquiry. [cite:de31_crs_in12363] The 2025 removals differ in scale and in form: seventeen at once, with no stated reasons and no notice.

Pattern three: the purse

The Constitution gives Congress the power to spend, and the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, passed after President Nixon refused to spend money Congress had voted, sets the rules for withholding it. An impoundment is a withholding; a rescission is a cancellation, which Congress must approve within 45 days. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's own auditor, rules on whether a withholding is lawful. By 29 September 2025 it had found seven violations in that year alone, covering electric-vehicle charging, museums and libraries, Head Start, school energy upgrades, medical research at the National Institutes of Health and two sets of disaster funds. "The burden to justify withholdings rests with FEMA," it wrote of the last. [cite:de31_sac_fema]

On 28 August 2025 the White House sent Congress a "pocket rescission": a request to cancel nearly $5 billion in foreign aid, sent so late that the money would expire before the 45 days ran out, whatever Congress did. The budget office argued that the statute allowed it; GAO held that the provision "may not lawfully be used to effect a pocket recission." [cite:de31_crs_pocket] On 26 September 2025 the Supreme Court, in a short unsigned order, let about $4 billion of it lapse, saying the Act likely barred the aid groups' suit. Justice Kagan, for the three dissenters, wrote that the majority had "effectively altered the balance of power between Congress and the president over the power of the purse." [cite:de31_rc_scotus_aid]

GAO found on 16 January 2020 that the first Trump administration's hold on military aid to Ukraine broke the same law: "OMB violated the ICA when it withheld USAI funds for a policy reason." [cite:de31_gao_ukraine] On 15 June 2021 it found that President Biden's pause of more than $1 billion in border-wall money was a lawful "programmatic delay," and two Republican senators answered that this showed "two sets of rules." [cite:de31_rc_wall] Presidents of both parties have held back money they asked Congress to cancel. [cite:de31_crs_pocket] The new step was the pocket rescission upheld, for now, in a ruling the Court said was not final.

Pattern four: emergencies

The National Emergencies Act of 1976 lets a president declare a national emergency, which unlocks powers in other laws. The most used is the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), which lets a president block transactions with foreign threats. By May 2022 presidents had declared 75 emergencies under the Act, 68 of them mainly to impose IEEPA sanctions, and 41 were still running; the oldest dated from 1979. [cite:us2_brennan_2022] In 2025 the emergencies were used for a new purpose: tariffs on most of the world's goods, declared over drug trafficking, migration and trade deficits. [cite:us2_cato_nea50] On 20 February 2026, in Learning Resources v. Trump, the Supreme Court held by six votes to three that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs. [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] The administration moved the policy to other statutes, as [scene:de31_what_was_blocked|the third section] traces. The library's comparison of emergency rule in two countries is in [scene:us2_emergency|its section on emergency powers].

The emergency as a route around Congress had been tried by the other party. In 2022 President Biden relied on the COVID-19 national emergency and a 2003 law, the HEROES Act, to cancel student debt covering more than $430 billion in principal. On 30 June 2023 the Court struck it down by six to three, saying the Secretary of Education could not "rewrite the statute from the ground up." [cite:de31_ag_nebraska]

Pattern five: the walls between datasets

The fifth pattern loosened the rules that keep records given for one purpose from being used for another. Tax records went to immigration enforcement under an agreement of April 2025; Medicaid records followed under a July 2025 agreement; a federal notice effective 30 September 2026 allows the records of families on cash welfare (Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF) to be disclosed to other agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security, to check immigration status. [cite:de30_ap_krause] [cite:de30_hipaa_chhabria] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] On the consumer side, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau withdrew guidance that treated background dossiers on workers as regulated credit reports, and on 15 May 2025 withdrew a proposed rule on data brokers, citing "its changed policy objectives." [cite:de24b_cs_withdraw] [cite:de31_fr_broker] The fullest account of these walls and the courts' answers is in [scene:de30_silos_and_subpoenas|Part Thirty-Two] and [scene:de24b_benefits|Part Twenty-Five].

This pattern also predates 2025. The first Trump administration agreed in 2018 to share data on the sponsors of migrant children with immigration enforcement; the Biden administration barred that use by a rule effective 30 April 2024; the bar was rescinded on 25 March 2025. [cite:de30_tracker_orr]

If it were connected

Each pattern removes a brake on its own; joined, they would remove the brakes on one another. Each join is graded documented, probable, possible or not supported. Removal and data: the acting head of the tax agency reportedly stepped down over the tax-sharing agreement in April 2025, and under the new schedule an official in her chain who objected to a data transfer could be removed by written notice. That join is possible; no removal for refusing a transfer is on record. [cite:de30_ap_krause] [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] Watchdogs and data: inspectors general are the offices that audit how agencies use personal records, and the Homeland Security inspector general opened such an audit in February 2026. Removing the auditor of a data join is possible; it has not happened at that office. [cite:de28_warner_audit] The purse and the watchdogs: an oversight office whose funds are withheld stops working without anyone being fired; possible, with no document. Removal and the commissions: after Slaughter a president can remove the members of a commission that enforces privacy or election law; that is documented as a power and not yet as a use against a sitting regulator of data. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de31_fr_14215] What stands in the way of every join is the same short list: the notice and reasons rules Congress wrote, courts that will still rule on them, and the Fed's carve-out. [scene:de31_who_benefits|The next section] asks who gains from each pattern and who pays.

sections.h: Who Gains, Who Pays
sections.html:
Every brake that comes off moves power from one place to another, and money often moves with it. This section follows each of the five patterns of [scene:de31_five_patterns|the previous section] along one chain: the input (the order, ruling or notice), the mechanism (what it changes in practice), who gains, and who pays. Two rules govern it. A donor, lobby or company appears only where a document shows its role, and where none does the section says so. And timing is not causation: an interest that gained after a change did not thereby cause it. The chain shows one thing plainly. For most of these patterns the documented winner is not a company or a donor but an office, the presidency, and that office passes to whoever wins the next election.

Removal: the office gains

The input is Trump v. Slaughter, Executive Order 14215 and the new civil-service schedule. The mechanism is removal at will: a commissioner of the Federal Trade Commission, or one of about 8,000 senior career officials, now holds the post at the president's pleasure, and every independent agency's major rules pass through the White House first. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de31_fr_14215] [cite:de30_npr_8000] The gain goes to the sitting president, of either party; the removal theory that won in 2026 is the one a Biden Justice Department opinion used in 2021 to remove the Social Security commissioner. [cite:de31_govexec_saul] The cost falls on the officials who lost their protection and on the design Congress chose for such commissions, whose members could be removed only for cause. The office's own director stated the purpose as accountability, "a restoration, in our mind, of the democratic process"; a scholar warned that it "creates bubbles around policymakers." [cite:de30_npr_8000] No donor or company is documented as seeking these changes; the case that ended Humphrey's Executor began with the removal of a single commissioner. [cite:de0_slaughter]

Watchdogs: the audited gain room

The input is the removal of 17 inspectors general on 24 January 2025. The mechanism is that the offices lost their confirmed heads overnight, without the notice and reasons the law requires. [cite:de31_npr_igs] [cite:de31_crs_in12363] The gain is structural: the agencies they audited lost, for a time, the auditor Congress had placed inside them. The cost is measurable in what the offices had been returning. Across government, inspectors general reported about $71 billion in monetary impact in fiscal 2024 against budgets of about $3.9 billion, a return of about 18 to 1; a report by the senior Democrat on the Senate's oversight committee counted $175 billion in potential savings on open recommendations from the offices of the 19 inspectors general removed in 2025. [cite:de31_lawfare_igs] Those are claims about potential, not money recovered, and the report's comparison with DOGE's savings depended on which DOGE figure was used. No specific audit is on record as stopped because of the removals, and no company or donor is documented as having sought them.

The purse: Congress pays

The input is the withholding of appropriated money and the pocket rescission. The mechanism is time: money held until its legal life ends is cancelled without a vote. [cite:de31_crs_pocket] The gain goes to the executive's spending priorities over Congress's; the budget director called the Supreme Court's order "a major victory." [cite:de31_rc_scotus_aid] The cost is concrete and named in the auditor's own findings: Head Start programmes, medical research at the National Institutes of Health, museums and libraries, school energy upgrades, and FEMA's emergency food and shelter and disaster-warning grants. [cite:de31_sac_fema] About $4 billion in foreign aid lapsed in September 2025, foreign aid Congress had voted and the president had asked it to cancel. [cite:de31_rc_scotus_aid] The deepest cost is to Congress's power of the purse itself, in Justice Kagan's words the "balance of power between Congress and the president." [cite:de31_rc_scotus_aid] No private beneficiary is documented; the money was not redirected to a contractor but left unspent.

Emergencies: importers paid, then were repaid

The input is a set of emergency declarations under IEEPA. The mechanism was a tax set by the president alone: tariffs, which by law are paid by the importer of record when goods cross the border. The government collected about $166 billion in these duties before the Supreme Court struck them down on 20 February 2026, from more than 330,000 importers. [cite:de31_gt_s122] [cite:us2_wiki_learning] The gain went to the Treasury while the duties lasted; the cost fell first on importers, among them the educational-toy company whose name the case bears. After the ruling the money began to flow back through a customs refund system opened in late April 2026, which only the importer of record can use; whether customers who paid higher prices see any of it is a question the refunds do not reach. [cite:de31_gt_s122] No donor is documented as having sought the emergency tariffs. The replacements came under other laws, and those are traced in [scene:de31_what_was_blocked|the next section].

Data walls: enforcement gains, the record-holders pay

The input is the tax and Medicaid agreements, the TANF notice and the withdrawn consumer-data rules. The mechanism is reuse: records people gave to get health cover, cash help or a tax refund are matched against immigration files. [cite:de30_ap_krause] [cite:de30_hipaa_chhabria] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] The documented gain is to immigration enforcement, which receives addresses it did not have. A private company also appears in the documented record. In January 2026 a Medicaid dataset covering millions of people went from the health agency to ICE and was shared with Palantir, the data-integration company Peter Thiel co-founded and chairs, over a Teams chat, according to a sworn declaration in the California case; Palantir said the data was "purged pursuant to government instruction." [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] [cite:de9_wiki_thiel] That is a documented use of Palantir's platform by the government, not a document showing that Palantir sought the data rules; none does. On the consumer side, the data-broker industry welcomed the withdrawal of the proposed rule: the head of its trade association thanked the bureau's acting director for "recognizing the concerns we flagged." [cite:de31_cdia] The cost falls on the people in the records, not all of them the intended targets: one dataset sent in error included a Minnesota file of refugees that contained citizens, and a judge found the tax agency had disclosed information unlawfully about 42,695 times. [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [scene:de24b_benefits|Part Twenty-Five] follows what those records hold.

One brake removed by Congress itself

Not every brake was taken off by the executive. On 9 May 2025 the president signed a resolution of Congress, passed under the Congressional Review Act, cancelling a consumer bureau rule that would have capped overdraft fees at large banks at $5 or at cost; the bureau had estimated savings of up to $5 billion a year, about $225 for each household that paid overdraft fees. [cite:de21_hk_cra] [cite:ad9_cfpb_od_final] A consumer group later counted about $4 billion in overdraft revenue at the twenty largest banks in 2025, up 6.2 per cent on 2023. [cite:us22_nclc_od26] The beneficiaries are documented as a class, banks with more than $10 billion in assets; the payers are the households charged the fees. This was Congress using its own check by majority vote, the opposite of the patterns above, and it belongs in the ledger for that reason.

What the chains show, and what they do not

The chains show a transfer of discretion toward the presidency, documented in each pattern, and costs that fall on named programmes, officials and record-holders. They show one company from the network the book maps, Palantir, inside a documented data transfer, and one industry, the data brokers, welcoming a rule's withdrawal in its own words. They do not show Peter Thiel, Elon Musk or any other figure of the earlier parts drafting or lobbying for any of the five patterns; the money ledgers of [scene:de14_network_map|Part Fourteen] and [scene:de17_money_to_office|Part Seventeen] record campaign money and contracts, not authorship of these orders. The gainer that recurs is the office, and the office has been used the same way by presidents of both parties, as Biden's removal of a protected commissioner shows. [cite:de31_govexec_saul] Whether the brakes held is the next section's subject.

sections.h: What Was Blocked, and What Was Not
sections.html:
A brake is tested only when someone presses on it. Between January 2025 and October 2026 the courts, Congress and the states pressed on each of the five patterns of [scene:de31_five_patterns|the first section]. Some held, some gave way, and some held in law while the policy found another road. This section sets out the record by institution, dated, with status as of October 2026, and closes the part by testing the worst-case reading against it.

The courts: where they held

The largest single check came from the Supreme Court. On 20 February 2026, in Learning Resources v. Trump, it held by six votes to three that the emergency-powers law does not authorise tariffs, ending duties that had raised about $166 billion. [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] [cite:de31_gt_s122] When the administration replaced them with a 10 per cent global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, a law that allows a temporary surcharge for balance-of-payments problems, the Court of International Trade held on 7 May 2026, by two to one, that the proclamation exceeded that authority. It gave relief only to the plaintiffs, two importers and the State of Washington, and the Federal Circuit paused even that while the government appealed. [cite:de31_gt_s122] In the removal cases the Court that overruled Humphrey's Executor drew a line at the Federal Reserve, and Governor Lisa Cook stayed in office while her case went on. [cite:de0_slaughter]

Lower courts held the walls between datasets in several places. A federal judge found that the tax agency had disclosed taxpayer information to immigration enforcement unlawfully about 42,695 times, and the appeals court in Washington upheld the block on 8 September 2026. [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] Judge Vince Chhabria in San Francisco first blocked Medicaid sharing in August 2025, then on 29 December 2025 allowed only basic identifying and contact fields, then paused the transfers after the January 2026 overshare. [cite:de30_hipaa_chhabria] [cite:de30_bl_medicaid] [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] The Justice Department's demands for states' full voter rolls had lost all thirteen trial-level decisions by 13 July 2026. [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] An injunction against mass layoffs at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau remained in force after the full appeals court refused to modify it on 19 June 2026. [cite:de20_orrick_cfpb]

The courts: where they did not

The courts also declined to stop much. The inspectors general won the argument and lost the remedy: Judge Reyes found the removals unlawful and reinstated no one, and the case was stayed until Slaughter; by late October 2026 it had reached the summary-judgment stage with no ruling on the merits. [cite:de31_wt_storch] [cite:de31_ch_storch] The pocket rescission stood on the Supreme Court's stay of 26 September 2025. [cite:de31_rc_scotus_aid] Slaughter itself ran against the challengers. [cite:de0_slaughter] No court had blocked the civil-service schedule; suits in Washington and Maryland were pending. [cite:de30_afge_lit] On 28 September 2026 Chief Judge Boasberg refused to halt the TANF notice, calling the states' fears "vague, unsubstantiated predictions," and three days earlier the Supreme Court had let the citizenship-checking system linked to Social Security records resume. [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] [cite:de19_npr_save]

The courts also narrowed their own brake. On 27 June 2025, in Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court held that universal injunctions, orders that protect everyone and not only the parties, "likely exceed the equitable authority that Congress has granted to federal courts." Before the ruling, district courts had issued 34 such injunctions against the administration in five months. The ruling left class actions open, and on 10 July 2025 a New Hampshire court used one to block the birthright-citizenship order for a whole class of children. [cite:de31_crs_casa] The brake was narrowed, not removed, and the narrowing had been urged by Justice Department officials of the first Trump administration in 2019 and 2020. [cite:de31_crs_casa]

Congress

Congress voted against the emergency tariffs more than once. On 29 October 2025 the Senate voted 50 to 46 to end the emergency behind the Canada tariffs, with Republicans Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins, Mitch McConnell and Rand Paul joining every Democrat; it had passed a similar resolution on Brazil the day before. [cite:de31_bnn_senate] House leaders adopted rules that let them keep such resolutions off the floor, but on 11 February 2026 the House voted 219 to 211, with six Republicans, to end the Canada emergency. Representative Don Bacon, a Republican, said, "We should defend our authorities"; the president's economic adviser answered that "The president will make sure they don't repeal his tariffs." [cite:de31_ap_house] Nine days later the Supreme Court settled the legal question. On 1 July 2025 the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a ten-year bar on state laws regulating artificial intelligence from the budget bill, on an amendment led by two Democrats and a Republican, keeping the states' power to legislate. [cite:de31_markey_ai]

Elsewhere Congress did not act. The Saving the Civil Service Act, which would limit the president's power to reclassify posts, had not passed. [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] No law reversed the pocket rescission or the removal of the inspectors general. And Congress removed one consumer brake itself, by majority vote under the Congressional Review Act, when it cancelled the overdraft rule in May 2025. [cite:de21_hk_cra]

The states

States were the plaintiffs in most of the data cases. Twenty sued over Medicaid sharing and won limits; about two dozen and the District of Columbia sued over the TANF notice and lost the first round; state election officials beat the voter-roll demands; and Washington State won relief from the Section 122 tariff for its own imports. [cite:de30_hipaa_chhabria] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] [cite:de31_gt_s122] Their reach is also their limit: a state can protect the records it holds and sue over federal ones, but cannot reinstate a federal officer or release federal funds.

The road around the brake

The tariffs show a pattern that the scorecard has to record. When the Supreme Court closed the emergency-powers route, the policy moved to a second statute, and when the second expired on 24 July 2026 after its 150-day limit, it moved to a third: the same day the administration imposed "Forced Labor Tariffs" of 10 to 12.5 per cent on goods from 60 economies under Section 301 of the Trade Act, said to reach 99 per cent of imports with exemptions. [cite:de31_cg_301] The brake held in law and the policy continued by another route, under statutes Congress had written. The inspectors general case showed the same shape: the court held the process unlawful and said the president could reach the same result by giving notice first. [cite:de31_wt_storch]

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis is the Sophia platform's, not a finding: immigration enforcement and government cuts as the occasion, a sovereign executive without a veto, the end state Curtis Yarvin's program describes ([scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]), as the destination. This part asked whether the brakes on such an executive are coming off.

Documented: in 2025 and 2026 orders, rulings and notices weakened veto points in all five patterns at once. A president may now remove members of the Federal Trade Commission at will, under a ruling that overruled the precedent protecting such commissions, and about 8,000 senior career officials by written notice; 17 inspectors general were removed in one night without the notice the law requires; about $4 billion that Congress had voted lapsed unspent; and tax, health and welfare records were opened to immigration enforcement. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de30_npr_8000] [cite:de31_npr_igs] [cite:de31_rc_scotus_aid] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] Also documented, and running against a one-party reading: presidents of both parties used the same powers before, from Obama's removal of an inspector general to Biden's removal of a protected commissioner and his use of an emergency to cancel student debt. [cite:de31_govexec_walpin] [cite:de31_govexec_saul] [cite:de31_ag_nebraska] What is new is that the five moved together and at scale.

Probable: that many of the remaining brakes are procedural and can be met rather than overcome. The record points that way in two places: a judge said the president could remove the same inspectors general again after giving notice, and the tariffs moved from one statute to a second and then a third when courts and time closed each. [cite:de31_wt_storch] [cite:de31_cg_301] That rests on these two documented cases, not on any statement of intent.

Not supported: that the five patterns were drawn from the Dark Enlightenment's texts, or designed by Peter Thiel, Elon Musk or anyone else the book maps. No document links any of the orders, rulings or notices to them; the documented defenders of these changes argue from accountability and presidential control, and the one company that appears, Palantir, appears as a recipient of data, not as an author of rules. [cite:de30_govexec_sherk] [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] The rule holds: rhyme is not provenance. Not supported either, on this record: an executive without a veto. The Supreme Court struck down the largest use of emergency power and kept the central bank out of the removal power; both houses of Congress voted against a tariff emergency, with Republicans among the majorities; states won limits on Medicaid sharing and every voter-roll case decided at trial; and a court found 42,695 tax disclosures unlawful. [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de31_bnn_senate] [cite:de31_ap_house] [cite:de30_bl_medicaid] [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep]

The brakes are thinner and fewer; they are not gone. Removing the remaining ones would take more than orders: it would take people willing to carry out the orders. [scene:de32_ice_as_template|Part Thirty-Four] turns to them, and the grades go to [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three].

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Four
chapters.title: The Force: Who Would Enforce It
chapters.intro: A sovereign executive without a veto, the end state the texts of Book One describe, would need people to carry out its orders, and the book's worst-case reading holds that it would repurpose the forces that already exist rather than build new ones. This part examines those forces as they stood in October 2026. The first section follows Immigration and Customs Enforcement through the hiring surge, the borrowed agents and the city operations of 2025 and 2026, and the deaths and court findings that came with them. The second turns to local police deputised under the 287(g) programme and the state laws that require or refuse it. The third sets out the law that keeps soldiers out of policing and the Guard deployments, threats and military detention sites that tested it. The fourth follows the money through the private detention companies, which also monitor the people they release. The fifth asks what has actually stopped any of it, and tests the worst-case reading against the record.
chapters.outro: The forces grew fast and were pointed at a single priority. ICE says it doubled its workforce to about 22,000 while cutting training to about eight weeks, and an ICE disclosure counted 28,390 federal law-enforcement personnel diverted to its work in August 2025. [cite:de32_kwtx_hiring] [cite:de32_aj_training] [cite:de32_cato_diverted] Local deputisation under 287(g) rose from 137 agreements to 1,372 in under a year, strongest where state law required it and absent in eight states. [cite:de32_ice_287g] [cite:de32_fwd_287g] [cite:de32_kocher_287g] The Guard was sent into cities without governors' consent until the courts closed that route, and the Supreme Court's Illinois order left the Insurrection Act as the remaining switch, which the president has threatened and not used as of 28 October 2026. [cite:de32_breyer_judgment] [cite:de32_lawdork_il] [cite:de32_hill_time] The private detention companies, which held about 90 percent of detainees under both parties, recorded their best year, and GEO now both holds people and tracks those it releases. [cite:de32_trac_private] [cite:de32_geo_fy25] [cite:de32_lt_isap] The brakes that held were courts, governors and the anti-commandeering rule; no refusal by soldiers has been documented, and no order that would test one is on the record. Book Six closes by setting two live trials of the chief-executive idea side by side in [scene:de33_two_tests|Part Thirty-Five].

sections.h: ICE as the Template
sections.html:
Every design for an executive without a veto runs into the same practical question: who carries out the orders. Curtis Yarvin's answer, set out in [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight], was a board holding cryptographic keys able to "disarm all government weapons." [cite:de8_kofman_ny] Weapons, though, are carried by people, and the book's worst-case reading, the Sophia platform's hypothesis and never a finding, holds that a sovereign executive would not need to build a new force. It would repurpose the ones that exist. This part examines those forces in turn, beginning with the one that grew fastest in 2025 and 2026. Capability is not intent: what follows documents what each force is, what it did and what limited it, and keeps separate any claim about what it might be used for.

What ICE is and where it came from

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) opened on 1 March 2003 as part of the new Department of Homeland Security, created by the Homeland Security Act that President George W. Bush signed on 25 November 2002 "in response to 9/11." It took over the enforcement work of two older agencies, the Immigration and Naturalization Service and the Customs Service, and in its own words holds "a unique combination of civil and criminal authorities." [cite:de32_ice_history] Its arrest-and-removal arm, Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO), handles civil immigration cases; its investigative arm, Homeland Security Investigations, handles crimes. [cite:de32_ice_history] The software ICE has run on since 2014, and the data that feeds it, are traced in [scene:ow9_ice|the library's account of ICE and its contracts] and [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty]. This section concerns the people.

The money and the hiring surge

The budget law signed on 4 July 2025, known as H.R. 1, gave about $170 billion to immigration and border enforcement over four years, roughly $75 billion of it to ICE. [cite:us6_brennan_obbba] Within that sum were $45 billion for detention, a $29.9 billion lump sum for enforcement and removal including hiring, and funding for 10,000 new ICE officers over five years, with money available until 30 September 2029. [cite:de32_aic_hr1] How the budget compares with earlier years is set out in [scene:us6_asylum|the library's chapter on asylum].

The hiring came faster than the law required. On 5 January 2026 the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said ICE had hired "more than 12,000 officers and agents," taking its workforce from about 10,000 to about 22,000 out of more than 220,000 applicants; its spokeswoman called it "a 120% increase." These are the agency's own figures and have not been independently audited. [cite:de32_kwtx_hiring] Training was shortened to match. ICE's own recruitment page had described almost five months of training for new officers: five weeks of language training and sixteen weeks of law enforcement. In January 2026 a senior DHS official said ERO officer training "is 8 weeks long." The Atlantic, citing unnamed officials, had reported 47 days; DHS called that "false," and a fact-check rated the 47-day claim mostly true because the confirmed schedule, six days a week for eight weeks, comes to about the same. [cite:de32_aj_training]

Agents borrowed from other agencies

ICE did not rely on its own hires alone. An ICE disclosure obtained by the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, counted 42,153 people diverted to help ERO between 5 and 28 August 2025, 28,390 of them from federal law-enforcement agencies. Cato's analyst David Bier estimated the shares by agency: about 2,840 from the FBI, 2,181 from the Drug Enforcement Administration (close to half its agents), 1,778 from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (more than two-thirds), 650 from the US Marshals and 6,198 from Homeland Security Investigations; a DHS memorandum had also deputised up to 600 State Department security agents. [cite:de32_cato_diverted] The chief of the IRS's criminal investigators said in December 2025 that 250 of his agents had been working on immigration since May. [cite:de32_ap_irsci] Moving agents between priorities is lawful. What the figures document is that a single executive priority could redirect a large share of federal law enforcement within months, without new legislation.

In the streets

The new force was used in surges into cities, often led by Border Patrol units under Commander Gregory Bovino. In Chicago, after the autumn 2025 operation called Midway Blitz, Judge Sara Ellis issued a 233-page opinion finding that "video disproves Defendants' contentions" about protesters, that Bovino admitted lying about a rock striking him before he used tear gas, and that one agent had used ChatGPT to write a use-of-force report. [cite:de32_cbs_ellis] The Seventh Circuit called her injunction "overbroad" and later vacated it after the plaintiffs dropped the suit. [cite:de32_yahoo_7th] In Los Angeles, a lower court had barred stops based on apparent race or ethnicity, accent, location or type of work; on 8 September 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that order 6–3, Justice Kavanaugh writing that such factors can "constitute at least reasonable suspicion" and Justice Sotomayor, dissenting, that people who "look a certain way" could now be stopped. [cite:de32_scotusblog_perdomo]

In Minneapolis, during the operation DHS called its largest, an ICE officer shot and killed Renee Good on 7 January 2026, and federal agents shot and killed Alex Pretti on 24 January; both were US citizens. Federal officials said there would be no federal investigation of Good's death, and evidence in both cases reached the county prosecutor only in July 2026, after a state lawsuit; as of that month no charging decision had been made. A separate ICE agent was charged by the state with assault and filing a false report over a January shooting that wounded a Venezuelan man; he has not been tried and is presumed innocent. [cite:de32_fox9_mn] ProPublica counted 506 US citizens held by immigration agents by October 2026, including at least 70 children; 36 were held for a day or more without contact with a lawyer or family, and about a dozen, mostly children, were deported. The government does not publish a count of its own. [cite:de32_dn_propublica]

Agents often worked masked. California banned face coverings for officers; on 10 February 2026 Judge Christina Snyder blocked the ban as applied to federal agents because it exempted state police, while upholding California's rule that agents display their agency and badge number, and noting that "federal officers can perform their federal functions without wearing masks." [cite:de32_ktvu_masks]

Deaths in custody

Twenty-nine people died in ICE custody in the fiscal year that began in October 2025 by mid-April 2026, passing the previous record of 28 in fiscal 2004. Senators Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock counted 49 deaths since January 2025. At Camp East Montana, the tent camp at Fort Bliss described in [scene:de32_the_military_at_home|the military section], the county medical examiner ruled the death of Geraldo Lunas Campos a homicide, by "asphyxia due to neck and torso compression," and the FBI opened an investigation. DHS said the rise reflected the number held and put the death rate at 0.009 percent of the detained population. [cite:de32_npr_deaths]

If it were connected

Each join is graded documented, probable, possible or not supported. ICE's arrest force joined to its data platforms: documented, through the case-management and targeting systems built by Palantir and the broker contracts mapped in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty's ecosystem map]. Other federal law-enforcement agencies joined to ICE's priorities: documented, by ICE's own disclosure of 28,390 diverted personnel. [cite:de32_cato_diverted] The same enlarged force joined to the domestic-terrorism framework of NSPM-7, which names "opposition to law and immigration enforcement" among its indicators: probable, because the memorandum and the Attorney General's implementing order already point federal task forces at that category, though those task forces are the FBI's and no document shows ERO officers assigned to political cases. [cite:de30_bondi_memo] ICE pointed at political opponents as such, beyond immigration: not supported. Its statutory mandate is immigration and customs; turning it elsewhere would need a new authority, a designation of the kind traced in [scene:de30_nspm7_and_detachment|Part Thirty-Two], or the Insurrection Act discussed later in this part. What stands in the way is set out in [scene:de32_what_stops_it|the final section].

sections.h: Local Police: The Multiplier
sections.html:
The United States has thousands of separate police and sheriff's agencies and no national police force. Any federal government that wants enforcement on a national scale has to borrow local officers, and the law already provides a way to do it. This section follows that route, the 287(g) programme, as it grew from about 135 agreements to well over a thousand in a single year; the state laws that pushed it forward in some places and blocked it in others; and the intelligence hubs, called fusion centres, that link local and federal information. The pattern that emerges is geographic: the borrowed force is large where state governments want it and small where they do not.

What 287(g) is

Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, added by the immigration law of 1996, lets ICE sign agreements that deputise state and local officers to perform some immigration functions. ICE runs three models. Under the jail enforcement model, officers in a local jail identify and process people held there who may be removable. Under the warrant service officer model, jail officers are trained to serve ICE's administrative warrants on people already in custody. Under the task force model, officers can question and arrest people for immigration violations in the course of ordinary policing, on the street. [cite:de32_ice_287g] [cite:de32_tpr_sb8] The task force model is the one that turns a local patrol officer into an immigration agent. The Obama administration ended it at the end of 2012, after documented abuses including racial profiling by the sheriff's office in Maricopa County, Arizona; in 2025 it became the programme's largest model. [cite:de32_fwd_287g]

From 135 to 1,372

ICE's own page counted 137 agreements on 15 February 2025: 60 jail, 75 warrant service and just 2 task force. [cite:de32_ice_287g] By 15 August 2025 an academic tally of ICE's published spreadsheets counted 896 agreements with about 690 agencies, 443 of them on the task force model. Florida alone had 318, more than a third of the national total, and Texas 137. Eight states had none: California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, New Jersey, Oregon and Washington. [cite:de32_kocher_287g] By 26 January 2026 the count stood at 1,372 agreements with 1,169 agencies, 764 of them task force agreements, according to FWD.us, an immigration-reform advocacy group whose counts follow ICE's data. ICE reported 8,501 local officers trained for the task force model by September 2025. [cite:de32_fwd_287g]

Money changed the terms. Until September 2025 ICE paid for training and computer links. From then, by FWD.us's reading of ICE's materials, ICE offered to pay trained officers' full salary and benefits, start-up costs, overtime and "performance" bonuses tied to immigration arrests. FWD.us estimates that this could transfer $1.4 billion to $2 billion to local police in 2026, against $665 million for the main federal community-policing grant programme in fiscal 2024; that is the group's projection, not a record of payments. Not every department accepted: Dallas's police chief and city council declined an offer reported at $25 million, conditioned on every officer being trained and making at least one immigration arrest. [cite:de32_fwd_287g]

States that require it, cities that refuse it

State legislatures decided much of the outcome. Texas's SB 8, in force from 1 January 2026, requires every sheriff who runs a jail to enter a 287(g) agreement by December 2026, lets the state attorney general sue those who refuse, and funds the cost for counties under a million people. Supporters described it as necessary funding for counties; opponents argued it would push victims and witnesses away from the police. [cite:de32_tpr_sb8] Florida accounted for the largest share of agreements nationally. [cite:de32_kocher_287g]

Other places used their own law to say no, and the courts have so far upheld their right to. The legal basis is a 1997 Supreme Court ruling, Printz v. United States, which held 5–4 that Congress could not order local sheriffs to run federal gun background checks; Justice Scalia wrote that "such commands are fundamentally incompatible with our constitutional system of dual sovereignty." [cite:de32_ncc_printz] The principle, known as anti-commandeering, means the federal government can invite local police into immigration work and pay them for it, but cannot compel them. In July 2025 the Justice Department sued New York City over laws limiting its cooperation with ICE; in October 2026 Judge Ramon Reyes dismissed the suit, holding that federal law does not require local governments to share release dates or custody information and that the federal government cannot force them to help enforce immigration law. [cite:de32_dr_nyc]

The fusion centres

Alongside officers, there is shared information. Fusion centres are state and local intelligence hubs, supported by DHS since 2003, where police, federal agencies and sometimes private partners pool reports. A bipartisan investigation by the Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, published on 2 October 2012, found their counter-terrorism reporting "oftentimes shoddy, rarely timely" and could find no case in which they had uniquely helped disrupt a terrorist plot; DHS's own spending estimates on them ranged from $289 million to $1.4 billion. [cite:de24_psi_fusion] They have also watched protest. In 2018 a DHS contractor, LookingGlass, compiled a spreadsheet of more than 600 planned "Family Separation Day" protests against the first Trump administration's border policy and circulated it to fusion centres; a DHS official called the list "unsolicited." The emails came out through a records request. [cite:de32_ow_lookingglass] No comparable record has been published for the protests of 2025 and 2026. The network was built under both parties, and its data links to licence-plate readers and brokers are described in [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four].

If it were connected

Local jail bookings joined to ICE: documented, by design, under the jail and warrant service models, and in mandate states by law. [cite:de32_ice_287g] [cite:de32_tpr_sb8] Local patrol officers joined to immigration arrests: documented under the task force model, with ICE offering pay linked to arrests. [cite:de32_fwd_287g] Local surveillance cameras joined to federal agencies: documented once and then cut back, when an Illinois audit found that Customs and Border Protection had searched Illinois licence-plate data in breach of state law and the camera company paused its federal pilots on 25 August 2025. [cite:de24_ap_flock] Fusion centres joined to monitoring of protest against immigration enforcement: documented in 2018, possible for 2025 and 2026, with no published record. Deputised local officers joined to political rather than immigration cases: not supported; their authority under 287(g) is limited to immigration functions, and widening it would need a new agreement or law. What stands in the way is mostly state law and the anti-commandeering rule, which means the multiplier is as strong as each state government allows. In Texas and Florida it is very strong; in the eight states with no agreements, it barely exists. The armed forces, which no state can veto in the same way, are the next section's subject.

sections.h: The Military at Home
sections.html:
The armed forces are the largest force any president commands, and American law has kept them out of ordinary policing for almost 150 years. In 2025 and 2026 that line was tested more often than at any time since the civil-rights era: National Guard troops were sent into several cities, Marines into one, military land was turned into a border zone and a detention camp, and the president twice said he might invoke the one law that lets troops enforce the law. This section sets out the legal routes, what was done along each, and what the courts said.

The rules

The Posse Comitatus Act, first passed on 18 June 1878 and now 18 U.S.C. 1385, makes it a crime to use any part of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force or Space Force "as a posse comitatus or otherwise to execute the laws," except where the Constitution or an Act of Congress expressly allows it. [cite:de32_govinfo_1385] A posse comitatus is the old common-law body of citizens a sheriff could summon; the Act stops the military being used as one. The main exception is the Insurrection Act of 1807, which lets a president deploy troops to enforce the law when unrest makes ordinary courts and police unable to; the Brennan Center counts 30 uses, the last in Los Angeles in 1992. [cite:de32_aj_insurrection] The National Guard sits between the two worlds. Under Title 32 of the US Code a governor commands it, with federal money, and Posse Comitatus does not apply; under Title 10 it is federalised and the Act does. A separate statute, 10 U.S.C. 12406, lets a president federalise the Guard to repel invasion or suppress rebellion, or when he is "unable with the regular forces" to execute the laws. As Joseph Nunn of the Brennan Center put it, the limit on Title 32 is that "there needs to be a cooperative governor." [cite:de32_csm_guard] [cite:de32_lawdork_il]

Four cities

In June 2025, without the consent of California's governor, who sued, about 4,000 California Guard members were federalised under section 12406 and 700 Marines deployed to Los Angeles during protests against immigration raids. [cite:de32_fox_breyer] The wider context is in [scene:us3_speech|the library's chapter on speech]. After a trial, Judge Charles Breyer entered judgment for California on its Posse Comitatus claims on 2 September 2025, warning against "creating a national police force with the President as its chief" and barring uses such as riot control, arrests and traffic stops in the state. [cite:de32_breyer_judgment] [cite:de32_fox_breyer] In Oregon, Judge Karin Immergut, appointed in the president's first term, permanently barred a Guard deployment to Portland, finding that "the President's determination was simply untethered to the facts." [cite:de32_nbc_immergut]

Illinois went to the Supreme Court. On 23 December 2025, ruling on an emergency stay application rather than the merits, the Court refused 6–3 to let the deployment proceed. Its unsigned order read "regular forces" in section 12406 as the regular military, so a president must first be unable to execute the laws with the military, and found the government had "failed to identify a source of authority" letting the military execute the laws in Illinois. Justice Alito, dissenting on other grounds, wrote that the country has "traditionally been wary of using soldiers as domestic police." [cite:de32_lawdork_il] The deployments in Los Angeles, Chicago and Portland ended on 31 December 2025. [cite:us3_audit_lawdork_il] The practical effect is that section 12406 now offers little against an objecting governor, leaving the Insurrection Act as the remaining federal route. [cite:de32_votebeat_polls]

Washington, DC, is different because it is not a state. Judge Jia Cobb ruled on 20 November 2025 that using the DC Guard for crime control and bringing in troops from other states was unlawful; on 17 December the D.C. Circuit stayed her order, citing the president's "unique power within the District." [cite:de32_nbcw_dc] In July 2026 the DC deployment was extended to 2029 with about 5,000 personnel. [cite:us3_audit_dc_guard]

Standing forces, the Insurrection Act and the words at Quantico

Memorandums from the National Guard Bureau in October 2025 told every state to form a quick reaction force, often 500 troops each and more than 23,000 in all, trained in crowd control with batons, shields, Tasers and pepper spray, a quarter of them deployable within eight hours, and operational by 1 January 2026. [cite:de32_mt_qrf] About 1,700 Guard members in 20 states led by Republican governors were authorised to do clerical, transport and processing work at ICE facilities; Vermont's Republican governor, Phil Scott, refused. [cite:de32_csm_guard]

On 15 January 2026, during the Minneapolis protests, the president wrote that unless state officials stopped "professional agitators and insurrectionists," "I will institute the INSURRECTION ACT." [cite:de32_aj_insurrection] About 1,500 soldiers of the 11th Airborne Division were put on orders to deploy if it was invoked; the president then said there was no reason to use it "right now," adding, "If I needed it, I'd use it." [cite:de32_ap_11th] Asked in an interview published on 1 October 2026 about the midterm elections, he said "I'm not committing to anything" and, of the Act, "I've never used it. I could use it." [cite:de32_hill_time] [cite:de32_meaww_time]

The language around the force changed too. On 21 February 2025 the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, the chief of naval operations, the Air Force vice chief and the top lawyers of the Army and Air Force were removed; the defence secretary said the lawyers were not "well-suited" to advise on lawful orders. [cite:de32_mt_jags] An executive order of 5 September 2025 authorised "Department of War" as a secondary title for the Department of Defense; its legal name is unchanged unless Congress acts. [cite:de32_fr_14347] On 30 September 2025, addressing hundreds of senior officers at Quantico, the president said "We should use some of these dangerous cities as training grounds for our military" and "We're under invasion from within," and called it "a war from within." [cite:de32_ap_quantico] [cite:de32_abc_quantico] Words are not orders, and no order to treat a city as a training ground is on the record.

The border and the bases

On 18 April 2025 a strip of about 180 miles along the New Mexico border became a "National Defense Area," military land where migrants could be charged with trespass. A magistrate judge dismissed charges against those arrested there because the complaints did not show they "knew he/she was entering" a military zone. [cite:de32_aj_nda] Military bases also became detention sites. Camp East Montana at Fort Bliss, Texas, holds up to 5,000 people in soft-sided structures, as many as 72 to a pod; Human Rights Watch and the ACLU, from interviews with 80 people, reported beatings and medical neglect in July 2026. [cite:de32_hrw_bliss] Guantánamo Bay received its first migrants on 4 February 2025 after a memorandum of 29 January; about 1,100 troops were moved there, and 832 people passed through in the year to May 2026, when fewer than 2 percent of about 400 beds were occupied. [cite:de32_wiki_gtmo]

History cuts both ways. In September 1957 President Eisenhower federalised the Arkansas Guard and sent 1,000 troops of the 101st Airborne to protect Black students entering Central High School in Little Rock, against a governor who had used the Guard to keep them out. [cite:de32_nara_10730] In June 2020, in the same president's first term, Defense Secretary Mark Esper said, "I do not support invoking the Insurrection Act." [cite:de32_mil_esper] Troops at home have enforced civil rights, and their own leaders have argued against using them.

If it were connected

The Guard's quick reaction forces joined to an Insurrection Act order: possible. The forces exist and are trained for crowd control, and the order would be a single presidential proclamation; nothing documents a plan to issue it, and courts would review it. [cite:de32_mt_qrf] Guard units joined to ICE's operations: documented, under Title 32 in consenting states, in support roles. [cite:de32_csm_guard] Military land joined to the detention system: documented at Fort Bliss and Guantánamo. [cite:de32_hrw_bliss] [cite:de32_wiki_gtmo] Troops joined to elections: not supported. Federal law bars troops or armed men at polling places, and the White House chief of staff called the idea "categorically false, will not happen." [cite:de32_votebeat_polls] What stands in the way of the wider joins is the Supreme Court's reading of section 12406, the Posse Comitatus Act as applied in California, and the refusal of governors; the Insurrection Act is the one switch that would bypass most of them, and it had not been used as of 28 October 2026.

sections.h: The Detention Business
sections.html:
When ICE arrests someone, the person is usually held in a building ICE does not run. About 90 percent of people in ICE detention in early 2025 were in facilities owned or operated by private contractors. [cite:de32_trac_private] That arrangement was not created in 2025; it held under both parties. What changed was the volume of money flowing through it, and the fact that the same company can now hold a person in a cell, track them on release and, in some cases, find them in the first place. This section follows the money from Congress to the two largest contractors, the GEO Group and CoreCivic, and to the people held.

The structure, under both parties

On 26 January 2021 President Biden signed Executive Order 14006, directing the Justice Department not to renew its contracts with private prisons. It covered the Bureau of Prisons and the US Marshals; it did not cover ICE, and neither the Obama nor the Biden administration directed the Department of Homeland Security to move away from private immigration detention. In 2023 ICE supplied 43 percent of GEO's revenue and 30 percent of CoreCivic's. [cite:de32_brennan_14006] On 20 January 2025 President Trump revoked the order in a single line, section 2(q) of Executive Order 14148, among dozens of rescissions. [cite:de26_ucsb_14148]

Contracts also guarantee payment for empty space. CoreCivic's annual report says some federal contracts "guarantee the federal partner access to a minimum bed capacity in exchange for a fixed monthly payment." [cite:de32_cxw_10k] The Government Accountability Office reported in February 2021 that such guaranteed-minimum contracts rose from 29 in fiscal 2017 to 43 in fiscal 2019, and that in May 2020 ICE was paying for an average of 12,027 empty beds a day, $20.5 million for the month. Those years span the first Trump administration and the start of the pandemic. [cite:de32_pln_gao]

New beds and new revenue

GEO's filings show the expansion. In February 2025 it announced a 15-year fixed-price ICE contract for Delaney Hall, a 1,000-bed site in Newark, worth more than $60 million a year and about $1 billion over the term. [cite:de32_geo_delaney] By the end of 2025 it had added about 6,000 ICE beds, taking its capacity from about 20,000 to about 26,000, and called 2025 "the most successful year for new business wins in our Company's history." It also won a two-year ICE contract for "skip tracing," the work of locating people. [cite:de32_geo_fy25] In July and August 2026 it opened two more sites under five-year contracts, Big Horn in Colorado (1,188 beds, about $85 million a year) and Rivers in North Carolina (1,320 beds, about $80 million a year), with ICE reimbursing start-up costs. [cite:de32_geo_q226]

CoreCivic reopened or acquired sites at Dilley and Farmville, California City, West Tennessee and Diamondback in Oklahoma. [cite:de32_cxw_fy25] Its ICE revenue rose from $564.8 million in 2024, 29 percent of the total, to $770.7 million in 2025, 35 percent; it lists 16 facilities where ICE is the main customer. [cite:de32_cxw_10k] Its net income rose 69 percent to $116.5 million, and it spent $218.4 million buying back its own shares. [cite:de32_cxw_fy25] GEO reported 2025 revenue of $2.63 billion and net income of $254.3 million, but that profit includes a $232.4 million gain from selling a prison to the state of Oklahoma, so it is not a measure of what detention earned. [cite:de32_geo_fy25] In the second quarter of 2026 GEO's revenue rose 15 percent to $732.1 million, and it raised its forecast for the year to $2.95–3.05 billion. [cite:de32_geo_q226]

On 6 November 2024, the day after the election, GEO's shares rose 42 percent and CoreCivic's 29 percent in a single session. [cite:de32_fortune_stocks] GEO's executive chairman, George Zoley, spoke of "an expected sea change" and said "The GEO Group was built for this unique moment." [cite:de32_fb_geo]

The political money

Each company gave $500,000 to the Trump-Vance inaugural committee; CoreCivic's gift is dated 19 December 2024 in its lobbying disclosure. CoreCivic's chief executive gave $300,000 to the Trump joint fundraising committee, and a GEO subsidiary gave $1 million to the main pro-Trump super PAC, MAGA Inc., in 2024. [cite:de32_sludge_gifts] [cite:de32_fb_geo] In the 2026 cycle another GEO subsidiary gave $4.4 million to MAGA Inc. and $1.3 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House Republican super PAC; the companies' political action committees gave the maximum to the Republican chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, and Scripps found the giving "overwhelmingly" Republican. CoreCivic said its political activity informs policymakers about its services. [cite:de32_scripps_pac] The Attorney General, Pam Bondi, had been a registered lobbyist for GEO before taking office; that is her record, not the company's conduct. [cite:de32_fb_geo]

The gifts came about a month before the revocation of the 2021 order, and the contracts followed.
