That is a documented sequence, not a documented cause: no record shows a contract or a policy given in exchange for a donation. CoreCivic states that it does "not, under longstanding policy, lobby for or against policies or legislation" that determine the basis or length of anyone's detention; giving to a party and bidding for contracts falls outside that statement rather than contradicting it. [cite:de32_cxw_10k]

The jailer runs the tracker

People released from detention are often placed in ICE's Intensive Supervision Appearance Program (ISAP), run by GEO's subsidiary BI Incorporated, which won a new two-year contract on 30 September 2025. [cite:de32_geo_fy25] On its August 2026 earnings call GEO reported about 184,000 people in the programme and nearly 54,000 on GPS ankle monitors, up from about 17,000 a year earlier, as use of its smartphone check-in app, SmartLINK, fell. An ankle monitor earns GEO more than $2 per person per day, against about $0.96 for the app. [cite:de32_lt_isap] Records obtained under the Freedom of Information Act show that BI collects facial images and voice prints, that ICE's contract gives the agency "unlimited rights to use, dispose of, or disclose" the data, and that location data shared by BI contributed to 40 arrests in Virginia in 2018. [cite:de32_cs_smartlink]

Work for a dollar a day

Detainees who join the "voluntary work program," cooking, cleaning and doing laundry, are paid "at least $1 per day," a rate set when Congress funded detainee pay under a 1950 law; in 1982 the immigration service asked for $4 and Congress did not act. [cite:de32_pogo_dollar] In 2021 a federal jury in Washington State found that GEO owed more than 10,000 people held at its Tacoma centre $17.3 million in back pay under the state minimum wage, and a judge added $5.9 million for unjust enrichment; the Ninth Circuit affirmed on 16 January 2025, calling GEO "a private for-profit employer." [cite:de32_wa_nwauzor] GEO petitioned the Supreme Court (No. 25-828); the Court asked for the government's views on 18 May 2026, and the Solicitor General filed on 15 September; according to the detainees' supplemental brief, the government urged review and argued the ruling "threatens to upend" ICE's reliance on private contractors. The petition was set for the Court's conference of 6 November 2026. [cite:de32_scotus_25828] [cite:de32_nwauzor_supp] In a separate Colorado case, where detainees allege they were made to clean without pay on pain of up to 72 hours in solitary confinement, the Supreme Court ruled against GEO on 25 February 2026 that it could not take an early appeal on a claim of contractor immunity, sending the case back toward trial. [cite:de32_lii_menocal]

The state-run camps and the inspectors

Florida opened a detention camp in the Everglades, called Alligator Alcatraz, on 1 July 2025, run by its emergency-management division through emergency-standby vendors; it cost $390.2 million by October 2025. [cite:de32_fp_alligator] Inspecting it in January 2026, the DHS Inspector General found less than half the required living space, cages of about 18 square feet used to hold people for up to two hours, once as punishment, and legal phones that did not work; staff did not know which standards applied, and ICE said Florida ran the site under a 287(g) agreement. [cite:de32_aic_oig2622] On 21 April 2026 the Eleventh Circuit lifted an order to wind it down, holding 2–1 that "until Homeland Security officials decide to fund the facility, no final agency action occurs." [cite:de32_wflx_11th] At GEO's Adelanto centre in California, four people died between August 2025 and August 2026, the most at any facility, while the share of ICE facilities given "superior" grades by ICE's own inspectors tripled. [cite:de32_laist_pogo]

If it were connected

Detention joined to monitoring in one company: documented, by GEO's own filings. Monitoring data joined to arrests: documented, in 2018. GEO joined to locating people for ICE: documented, by the skip-tracing contract. [cite:de32_geo_fy25] [cite:de32_cs_smartlink] BI's location data joined to the Palantir platforms ICE uses for targeting: possible; the contract's "unlimited rights" clause would allow it, and no document shows it. The question of compelled labour on a wider scale belongs to [scene:de35_the_consequence_ladder|Part Thirty-Seven]; on the record here, the dollar-a-day rate rests on a law and an appropriation that long predate 2025, not on any new order. [cite:de32_pogo_dollar]

sections.h: What Stops It
sections.html:
The previous sections described forces that grew: an immigration agency doubled in size, local police deputised by the thousand, Guard units trained for crowd control, a detention industry with record revenue. This section asks the opposite question, using only what happened: when the force was pointed somewhere, what actually stopped it, and what did not. The answer is a set of brakes that are real but uneven. Some held, some slipped on appeal, and one, the refusal of soldiers to obey, has not been tested at all.

Courts

Courts were the brake used most often, and they ruled both ways. Against the government: Judge Breyer found a Posse Comitatus violation in California; Judge Immergut permanently barred the Portland deployment; the Supreme Court refused the Illinois deployment, after which the federalised Guard left Los Angeles, Chicago and Portland on 31 December 2025. [cite:de32_breyer_judgment] [cite:de32_nbc_immergut] [cite:de32_lawdork_il] [cite:us3_audit_lawdork_il] Judge Reyes dismissed the Justice Department's suit against New York City's sanctuary laws, and the Supreme Court ruled against GEO's bid for an early appeal on contractor immunity in a forced-labour case. [cite:de32_dr_nyc] [cite:de32_lii_menocal] Judge Richard Leon blocked the defence secretary's attempt to punish Senator Mark Kelly for a video telling service members they could refuse illegal orders, finding that the secretary had "trampled on Senator Kelly's First Amendment freedoms." [cite:de32_npr_kelly]

For the government: the Supreme Court allowed immigration stops based on factors including apparent ethnicity in Los Angeles; the D.C. Circuit kept the Guard in Washington; the Seventh Circuit vacated Judge Ellis's limits on force in Chicago; the Eleventh Circuit let Florida's Everglades camp stay open; and Judge Snyder struck California's mask ban for federal agents while keeping its badge rule. [cite:de32_scotusblog_perdomo] [cite:de32_nbcw_dc] [cite:de32_yahoo_7th] [cite:de32_wflx_11th] [cite:de32_ktvu_masks] Several of the main questions are still open as of October 2026: the appeals on Posse Comitatus, the D.C. Circuit's ruling on the merits, and GEO's petition on detainee wages, which the Supreme Court was due to consider on 6 November 2026. [cite:de32_scotus_25828]

Governors and states

The Constitution divides the force between two levels of government, and in 2025–26 that division did real work. Because Title 32 deployments need a willing governor, Vermont's Republican governor could refuse to send his Guard to support ICE. [cite:de32_csm_guard] Because federalising the Guard against a governor's wishes now requires showing that the regular military could not execute the laws, the Supreme Court's Illinois order has, in one analysis, functionally limited Guard deployments to states whose governors consent. [cite:de32_votebeat_polls] The anti-commandeering rule means no state can be forced to lend its police, and eight states had signed no 287(g) agreement by August 2025. [cite:de32_ncc_printz] [cite:de32_kocher_287g] The same division also works the other way: Texas requires its sheriffs to cooperate, and Florida signed more agreements than any other state. [cite:de32_tpr_sb8] [cite:de32_kocher_287g]

Prosecutors and juries

A magistrate judge in New Mexico dismissed trespass charges against migrants arrested in a new military zone because the government could not show they knew they had entered it. [cite:de32_aj_nda] In Minnesota the Hennepin County Attorney charged an ICE agent with assault and with lying about a shooting, and the state sued to obtain federal evidence in the two Minneapolis killings; it received the evidence in July 2026 and had made no charging decision by then. [cite:de32_fox9_mn] Juries cut the other way as well: a federal jury in Fort Worth convicted eight people of providing material support to terrorists after a police officer was shot outside an ICE centre on 4 July 2025. [cite:de30_kera_prairieland]

Inside the forces

Every service member swears an oath to the Constitution. Military law presumes orders lawful, and only a "manifestly illegal" order, one a person "of ordinary sense and understanding" would recognise as a crime, may be refused; a debatable order must be obeyed, and the Manual for Courts-Martial warns that an order "is disobeyed at the peril of the subordinate." [cite:de32_stripes_orders] That bar is high by design. Individual refusals of conscience exist: Colonel Doug Krugman of the Marine Corps resigned after 24 years in September 2025, writing that service members "should be confident in questioning possibly immoral or illegal orders." [cite:de32_aol_krugman] At the top, the precedent is mixed. In June 2020 Defense Secretary Mark Esper publicly opposed invoking the Insurrection Act. [cite:de32_mil_esper] In February 2025 the Army's and Air Force's top lawyers were removed as not "well-suited" to advise on lawful orders. [cite:de32_mt_jags] No refusal of a domestic order by a unit or service member in 2025 or 2026 has been documented, which may mean that no clearly unlawful order was given, or that the brake was never pulled; the record does not say which.

Exposure and its effects

Several operations ended after the record about them became public. Border Patrol's units left Chicago soon after Judge Ellis's injunction of early November 2025, whose written opinion later found that video contradicted agents' accounts. [cite:de32_yahoo_7th] [cite:de32_cbs_ellis] After agents killed two US citizens in Minneapolis and protests followed, the Border Patrol commander, Gregory Bovino, was reassigned in January, and the border czar announced the end of the surge there on 12 February 2026. [cite:de32_yahoo_7th] [cite:de32_kaxe_surge] Independent counts filled gaps the government left: ProPublica's tally of 506 citizens held, human-rights investigators' report on Fort Bliss, the Inspector General's report on the Everglades camp. [cite:de32_dn_propublica] [cite:de32_hrw_bliss] [cite:de32_aic_oig2622] Elections have their own statutory brake: federal law bars troops at polling places, and the White House chief of staff said troops at the polls "will not happen." [cite:de32_votebeat_polls]

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and never a finding, is that immigration enforcement is the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto the destination, and that such an executive would repurpose existing forces rather than build new ones. Documented: the forces were enlarged and pointed at one priority with remarkable speed. ICE doubled its workforce on its own count and shortened training; 28,390 federal law-enforcement personnel were diverted to its work; local deputisation grew tenfold; Guard quick reaction forces of more than 23,000 were stood up; and the detention business recorded its best year, with the jailer also running the tracker. [cite:de32_kwtx_hiring] [cite:de32_cato_diverted] [cite:de32_fwd_287g] [cite:de32_mt_qrf] [cite:de32_geo_fy25] Documented too are the costs: record deaths in custody, two citizens killed in Minneapolis, more than 500 citizens held, and a court finding of false use-of-force reports. [cite:de32_npr_deaths] [cite:de32_fox9_mn] [cite:de32_dn_propublica] [cite:de32_cbs_ellis]

Probable: that the enlarged force, once built, will be available to whatever priority a future order sets, because its funding runs to 2029 and its legal mandates are broad; that is a reading of capacity, not of any stated plan. Not supported: that these forces have been turned on political opponents as such, that troops have been used at the polls, or that the Insurrection Act has been invoked; it had not been as of 28 October 2026, though the president said in October that he "could use it." [cite:de32_hill_time] [cite:de32_meaww_time] Not supported either: any document linking the build-up to the theorists of [scene:de2_core_texts|Part Two]; the resemblance to their design of an all-powerful chief executive whose check is control of the state's weapons is rhyme, not provenance. [cite:de8_kofman_ny] The record runs against the worst case in the courts' Illinois ruling, the governors' veto over the Guard, the anti-commandeering rule, the Guard withdrawals from Los Angeles, Chicago and Portland, and the end of the Minneapolis surge. The same standard applies to both parties: the private detention structure, the guaranteed bed payments and the fusion centres were built and kept under Democratic and Republican administrations alike. [cite:de32_brennan_14006] [cite:de32_pln_gao] Whether the brakes that held would hold against the Insurrection Act is the open question this part leaves. The next part sets two live tests of the chief-executive idea side by side in [scene:de33_two_tests|Part Thirty-Five].

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Five
chapters.title: Two Tests, One Result
chapters.intro: This part closes Book Six with the two occasions on which the idea at the centre of this book, a chief executive who fixes a failing institution by setting aside the usual consultation, was tried in public. The first was small and voluntary: Curtis Yarvin's return in August 2024 as the self-described "wartime CEO" of the foundation behind his own network, Urbit, and the owners' vote that ended it. The second was national: the Department of Government Efficiency of 2025 and 2026, which was not his program and which he criticised. The single section sets the two cases side by side, what each promised, what happened, who checked it and what lasted, states the strongest readings against treating either as a test, and then grades the book's worst-case reading against Book Six as a whole: the pathway, the force and these two tests together.
chapters.outro: Set side by side, the two tests show one result as far as the record carries it. In each, a leader took authority without a formal title in the name of a crisis: Yarvin at the Urbit Foundation in August 2024, and Musk at DOGE, whom the White House told a court had "no actual or formal authority." [cite:de23_coindesk_2024] [cite:de17_audit_fisher] In each, the claimed result could not be verified: no published accounts of the foundation's results were located, and GAO could not verify most of the $110 billion of DOGE savings it examined. [cite:de21_gao_full] In each, the leader left early and the body above had the last word: the galaxy owners replaced the Urbit board on 9 October 2025, and DOGE ended on 4 July 2026 without a closing report. [cite:de23_epoch_2025] [cite:de21_fnn_vought] What lasted came through ordinary procedure, including about 8,000 senior posts made at-will by order. [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] Neither case tested neocameralism as written, and DOGE was not Yarvin's. On Book Six as a whole, the pathway is documented and partly travelled: the removal power widened and enforcement capacity grew. The executive without a veto is not supported. The Supreme Court refused the Illinois Guard deployment at an interim stage, the deployments ended on 31 December 2025, and the tariff powers were struck down. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:us6_brennan_obbba] [cite:de33_rollcall_illinois] [cite:de33_pbs_guard] [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] Book Seven turns to the test itself, beginning with an audit of what has already been built in [scene:de34_what_is_built|Part Thirty-Six].

sections.h: Two Tests, One Result: Urbit and DOGE
sections.html:
The question this book keeps returning to was put most sharply in [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight]: if a country is run by a chief executive, who removes a bad one? Yarvin's own answer is a board. He has said a monarch should answer to a corporate board rather than to citizens, and in his design for a patchwork of small sovereign states a board selects and recalls the chief executive. [cite:de8_cnn_yarvin] [cite:de8_kofman_ny] Between August 2024 and July 2026 the idea of a chief executive who fixes a failing institution by setting aside the usual consultation was tried twice in public. Once it was tried in Yarvin's own network, Urbit, by Yarvin himself. The second time it was tried in the federal government, through the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which was not his. This section sets the two cases side by side: what each promised, what happened, who checked it and what lasted. It then closes Book Six by testing the book's worst-case reading against the pathway, the force and these two tests together.

Neither case was a test of Yarvin's theory as he wrote it, and the record does not allow either to be presented as one. Urbit is a small voluntary network whose users can leave at no cost. DOGE was an office created by executive order inside a constitutional government. Its savings goals, its public leader and its methods came from the president and Elon Musk, and no document traces it to Yarvin's 2012 proposal to retire all government employees, which it resembles; rhyme is not provenance ([scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|Part Thirty-Two]). [cite:de0_eo14158] [cite:de6_tnr_duran] Yarvin himself disowned it as a model. He complained that DOGE had too much libertarian DNA, and he said the administration was "barely scratching the surface" of the change he wanted. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] [cite:de6_cnn_2025] What the two cases share is narrower and can be documented: in each, someone took authority without a formal title, in the name of a crisis, over an institution with a body above it.

What each promised

The Urbit Foundation's money was nearly gone in August 2024, with a runway "measurable in months." Its board dismissed the executive director, and Yarvin returned to lead its strategy while holding "no formal position at the foundation." His words were: "For that, you need a wartime CEO," and "We're here to fix this." [cite:de23_coindesk_2024] The phrase comes from a 2011 essay by the investor Ben Horowitz, whose wartime chief executive "neither indulges consensus-building nor tolerates disagreements." [cite:de23_horowitz_2011]

DOGE's promises were larger. Musk said at a rally in October 2024 that he could cut "at least $2 trillion." [cite:de11_fortune_2t] In their November 2024 op-ed he and Vivek Ramaswamy wrote that they would serve "as outside volunteers, not federal officials or employees," and that existing law, not new legislation, would carry the changes. [cite:de17_li_oped] In February 2025 Musk set out the case in the Oval Office: "We don't live in a democracy. We live in a bureaucracy." [cite:de3_dcpd_musk] He called DOGE's actions "maximally transparent." [cite:de21_reason_foia] He too held no formal command. A White House declaration filed in court on 17 February 2025 said he had "no actual or formal authority to make government decisions himself" and could "only advise the President." [cite:de17_audit_fisher]

What happened

In Urbit, the return did not settle the crisis. Several senior staff resigned. In 2025 the Foundation's director removed Yarvin from the board while Yarvin was lobbying the other two members to remove the director. The director then asked the owners of the network's 256 "galaxies," its top-level addresses, to replace the board. [cite:de23_marbl] [cite:de5_wiki_urbit] On 9 October 2025 the Foundation announced that "the Galactic Senate has elected to replace the board" after "multiple votes." The new board named a new executive director to succeed Yarvin's Urbit identity, ~sorreg-namtyv, "who is leaving to found a new application development company." [cite:de23_epoch_2025] The full account is in [scene:de23_wartime_ceo|Part Twenty-Three].

In the federal government, Musk left in May 2025, saying "This is not the end of DOGE. It's really just the beginning." [cite:de21_wt_farewell] DOGE's final claim was $215 billion in savings. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's auditor, examined the $110 billion of that figure attributed to contracts, grants and leases. It found that DOGE's own stated method had been followed for 27.5 per cent of the contract savings, and that 96.2 per cent of the grant savings could not be checked. [cite:de21_gao_full] Asked under oath whether their grant cancellations had reduced the deficit, a DOGE staffer answered: "No, we didn't." [cite:de18_abc_depos] The civilian workforce of 22 agencies fell by nearly 256,000 between December 2024 and January 2026. [cite:de21_gao_workforce] The temporary organization ended on 4 July 2026, the date its own order set, and the budget director told appropriators there would be no closing report. [cite:de0_eo14158] [cite:de21_fnn_vought] [scene:de21_the_ending|Part Twenty-One] tells that ending in full.

Who checked it

In Urbit the check came from the body Yarvin's own design put on top. Only galaxies vote in the Galactic Senate; a vote needs a quorum of 64 galaxies and passes with an absolute majority of 129. [cite:de23_voting_docs] That body removed the board the founder had fought, and the founder left. In one sense the theory's own remedy worked: the owners recalled the executive. The check also came from a narrow tier. In 2019 an independent count put 185 of the 256 galaxies with the company, its staff and the Foundation, and the network's ordinary users, the holders of "planets," had no vote at all. [cite:de23_compact_2025] [cite:de23_voting_docs] Their remedy was to leave.

DOGE answered to more bodies, and they did not all pull the same way. The courts checked it in part. A federal judge found in October 2026 that the Office of Personnel Management had broken the Privacy Act by giving DOGE access to personnel records, and the Supreme Court agreed that month to decide whether the U.S. DOGE Service must answer requests under the Freedom of Information Act. [cite:de19_bgov_afge] [cite:de21_ncc_cert] The courts also let DOGE proceed: on 6 June 2025 the Supreme Court stayed an injunction that had barred DOGE from Social Security records. [cite:de19_ch_afscme] The auditor checked it after the fact. GAO also reported that agencies refused or limited cooperation and that the extent of DOGE's access to systems "could not be determined." [cite:de21_gao_systems] Congress checked it and ratified it in turn. It never legislated the proposed "DOGE dividend," but on 24 July 2025 a law cancelled about $9 billion in spending, mostly foreign aid and about $1.1 billion for public broadcasting, in programmes DOGE had targeted. [cite:de21_usat_dividend] [cite:de33_wdbj_rescission] The last check was the president, who held the office's legal authority throughout. When he and Musk fell out in June 2025, it was Musk who left. [cite:de11_npr_feud]

What lasted, and the one result

What outlasted each experiment came through ordinary channels. In Urbit, the Foundation went on under the board the owners chose and was still publishing technical work in 2026. [cite:de23_bloglist] In Washington, the lasting changes were a smaller workforce, former DOGE staff in permanent posts and the U.S. DOGE Service itself, which still has a budget request. [cite:de21_gao_workforce] [cite:de21_ee_end] To these came a change DOGE did not make: the Schedule Policy/Career rule of 2026, under which an order of 3 June moved about 8,000 senior career officials into at-will employment. [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] [cite:de30_npr_8000] That change came by rule-making and executive order. It is challenged in court and, as of October 2026, has not been blocked. [cite:de30_afge_lit]

The one result, stated as far as the record carries it, is this. In both cases a leader took exceptional authority without a formal title, in the name of a crisis, and promised a fix. In both, the claimed result could not be verified. In both, the leader left before the work was done. And in both, the body above the institution had the last word: the galaxy owners in Urbit, and in Washington the president, the auditor, the courts and Congress. What lasted was what had been written into ordinary procedure. Two cases make a pattern, not a law. They differ in scale and in kind, since one is voluntary and the other carried the force of a state, and their sequences are rhymes, not one plan.

The strongest counter-reading is Yarvin's own, and it should be stated in full. On his account neither case tested his idea. A start-up foundation is not a sovereign. DOGE was a libertarian cost-cutting office inside a system he holds to be unreformable, run by people who never claimed sovereign power and under a president he judged far too timid. [cite:de5_kofman_nuso] [cite:de6_cnn_2025] The record supports the premise of that reply: the CEO-state as he describes it, with a board holding the keys to the state's weapons, was not tried, and was not proposed by anyone in office. [cite:de8_kofman_ny] A second counter-reading runs the other way. The checks on DOGE were partial and late. Its teams reached systems whose extent the auditor could not establish, the highest court let it into Social Security records, and Congress turned part of its target list into law. [cite:de21_gao_systems] [cite:de19_ch_afscme] [cite:de33_wdbj_rescission] The bodies above both institutions held, and they did not hold everywhere.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis is the Sophia platform's, not a finding. Immigration enforcement and government cuts are the occasion, and a sovereign executive without a veto is the destination. Book Six asked what removing the remaining brakes would take ([scene:de31_five_patterns|Part Thirty-Three]), who would enforce the result ([scene:de32_ice_as_template|Part Thirty-Four]) and how the chief-executive idea fared when tried. The three can now be graded together.

Documented: real powers moved toward the presidency through rulings, rules and statutes. The Supreme Court's decision in Trump v. Slaughter on 29 June 2026 let the president remove members of independent commissions at will. About 8,000 senior officials became removable at will by an order of 3 June 2026. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] The force grew as well. The 2025 budget act gave ICE about $75 billion over four years, and Guard troops were federalised in Los Angeles without the governor's consent. The Washington, D.C., deployment was extended in July 2026 to 2029. [cite:us6_brennan_obbba] [cite:us3a_fh_us2026] [cite:us3_audit_dc_guard] In both tests, authority was taken without a title in the name of a crisis. Who gained from each step, and what was blocked, is set out in [scene:de31_who_benefits|Part Thirty-Three] and [scene:de31_what_was_blocked|its third section]. The detention contractors and the military at home are covered in [scene:de32_the_detention_business|Part Thirty-Four] and [scene:de32_the_military_at_home|its third section].

Probable: that changes accumulate through ordinary channels rather than in one break, and that each leaves machinery behind for the next occasion. DOGE's service, its alumni and its rule changes outlived its name. The president said in December 2025 that the Guard would return "perhaps in a much different and stronger form." [cite:de21_ee_end] [cite:de33_pbs_guard] Whether that happens is open; what persists is documented.

Not supported: an executive without a veto. The record runs against it at each point where it was tested. On 23 December 2025 the Supreme Court refused, at an interim stage and over three dissents, to let the administration deploy the Guard in Illinois. It found that the government had "failed to identify a source of authority that would allow the military to execute the laws." By 31 December 2025, eight days later, the deployments in Chicago, Los Angeles and Portland were ended. [cite:de33_rollcall_illinois] [cite:de33_stlpr_illinois] [cite:de33_pbs_guard] The Court held in February 2026 that the emergency-powers law the president had used for tariffs does not authorise them. [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] Congress refused the dividend and kept the purse. DOGE ended on the date its own order set, and in Urbit the owners removed the founder. [cite:de21_usat_dividend] [cite:de21_fnn_vought] [cite:de23_epoch_2025] None of this shows a plan, and the vetoes did not hold everywhere: the removal power widened, and no court has blocked the new civil-service schedule ([scene:de32_what_stops_it|Part Thirty-Four] weighs what has actually stopped the force). [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de30_afge_lit] Book Six ends where Book Five did: the pathway is documented and partly travelled, and the destination is not shown. Who chooses and removes a chief executive is the subject of Part Thirty-Eight. The grades go to [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three], and Book Seven begins with what has been built, in [scene:de34_what_is_built|Part Thirty-Six].

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Six
chapters.title: The Readiness Audit
chapters.intro: This part opens Book Seven, the test, with an audit. The first section lists, layer by layer, what had been built by October 2026: the records, sensors, brokers and integration platforms of Book Five, the gates that decide who may travel, work or bank, the legal changes of Book Six, and the enlarged force. Each item is tied to the part that documents it, along with when and under whom it was built. The second section asks whether tools built for immigration enforcement have been turned on critics, including critics of foreign governments. It sets the documented cases against the absence of any documented programme and names the legal step that repurposing would need. The third lays the whole worst-case pipeline end to end, from identification to compelled labour, and grades each link with the grades of the ecosystem map. The fourth names what the pipeline still lacks and the dated events that would move a grade, and closes with the part's test of the worst-case reading.
chapters.outro: The audit found the occasion fully built. For non-citizens every link from a face in the street to a detention bed exists, is funded to 2029 and is in daily use, and the joins between links are documented in specific cases, from a Medicaid dataset that reached Palantir to the travel records TSA passed to ICE. [cite:us6_brennan_obbba] [cite:de34_trac_66k] [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice] Immigration and foreign-affairs tools were turned on named non-citizen critics: a court found the policy against non-citizen academics unconstitutional, a student was detained over an op-ed before her case was dropped, and a UN rapporteur's sanctions stayed in force pending appeal. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de34_wt_ozturk] [cite:de34_jurist_albanese] For citizens the record holds specific cases, most of them withdrawn or enjoined, and no programme. [cite:de28_aclu_doe] [cite:de32_npr_kelly] Four pieces are still missing: an identity spine, a legal trigger for citizens, a lawful route to use force against them, and courts that would allow it. The NSPM-7 list exists but is secret, and no statute supplies a domestic designation. [cite:de34_int_list] [cite:de30_dla_nspm7] The next part, [scene:de35_three_layers|Part Thirty-Seven], asks what the state could do to a person if the pieces were joined and enforced, rung by rung and domain by domain.

sections.h: What Is Built: An Inventory, Layer by Layer
sections.html:
Book Seven tests the book's working hypothesis against everything the first six books documented. The hypothesis is the Sophia platform's, and it has never been a finding: immigration enforcement and government cuts as the occasion, and a sovereign executive without a veto, the end state Curtis Yarvin's program describes ([scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]), as the destination. A test needs an inventory first. This section lists what exists as of October 2026, layer by layer, with the part of the book that documents each item, when it was built and under which administration. It adds no new machinery. It sets out on one page what the earlier parts established one at a time, so that the next three sections can ask what the parts could do together and what they still lack.

The inventory follows one rule throughout the book: capability is not intent. That a tool exists is a documented fact. That it has been used, or will be used, against a particular kind of person needs a document of its own. The list below records capability. The repurposing test in the next section looks at use.

The end state, in writing

The destination exists as text. Between 2007 and 2014 Yarvin, writing as Mencius Moldbug, and the philosopher Nick Land set out a state run like a company, with a chief executive answerable to owners rather than voters, and an exit for anyone who objected ([scene:de2_core_texts|Part Two]). Yarvin's 2008 answer for residents his sovereign corporation found unproductive was confinement, which he called "a humane alternative to genocide." [cite:de6_tnr_duran] His check on a bad chief executive was a board able to recall him and holding keys to disable the state's weapons, a design [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight] found unanswered on who would check the board. [cite:de8_kofman_ny] These are the theorists' own words. The machinery below was not built from them; no document traces any of it to their texts.

Records, sensors, brokers and the integration layer

The first layer is the records the state holds because people must give them: tax returns, Medicaid and welfare files, Social Security numbers, visa and student records, travel manifests, and the fingerprints, faces and irises in DHS's biometric systems. Since 2025 several of these have been opened to immigration enforcement. The IRS agreed in April 2025 to check addresses for ICE. Social Security data was linked to DHS's citizenship-check system, SAVE, in May 2025. Food-aid records from at least 27 states were run through SAVE. A notice opening cash-aid (TANF) records to DHS took effect on 30 September 2026 after a federal judge declined to block it. [cite:de30_ap_krause] [cite:de24_npr_save] [cite:de24b_npr_snap27] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] The travel archive is older and deeper. CBP's targeting system keeps booking and manifest records for fifteen years, and TSA passed records on more than 31,000 travellers to ICE between January 2025 and February 2026 ([scene:de25b_who_knows_you_travel|Part Twenty-Seven]). [cite:de25b_pia_ats] [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice]

The second layer is surveillance the government runs itself. ICE's Mobile Fortify app matches faces in the street against about 200 million images; the person scanned cannot decline, and photographs of citizens are kept for fifteen years. CBP has photographed every non-citizen at entry and exit since 26 December 2025 ([scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|Part Twenty-Eight]). [cite:de26_404_fortify] [cite:de26_reason_fortify] [cite:de26_bu_entryexit] ICE also holds phone-extraction tools ([scene:de25_spyware_and_phones|Part Twenty-Six]). Its contract with the spyware maker Paragon was closed out in January 2026, and in May DHS would neither confirm nor deny that ICE still had the capability. [cite:de28_npr_paragon] The third layer is state and local systems that federal agents can search, chief among them licence-plate cameras. The fourth and fifth are the vendors and data brokers that sell to ICE directly: location trails, people-search profiles, face galleries and social-media monitoring ([scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four], [scene:de28_ice_contracts|Part Thirty]). By the Brennan Center's count, which it calls a minimum, DHS committed at least $2.9 billion to surveillance, data and analytics tools from January 2021 to July 2026. [cite:de28_brennan_tools]

The sixth layer joins the rest. Palantir does not collect data; it joins whatever data a customer is authorised to give it ([scene:de27_capability_not_intent|Part Twenty-Nine]). Its work for ICE dates from 2014. In 2025 and 2026 it added ImmigrationOS, the ELITE targeting tool that gives addresses a "confidence score," and an $86.3 million enforcement-operations order dated 5 May 2026. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] [cite:ow9_fortune_elite] [cite:de27_hg_ero] Outside ICE it holds an Army order to maintain the Personnel Data Environment, a system of Army personnel records, until 15 November 2026, and it is building a "common API layer" inside the IRS's modernisation. [cite:de24b_govly_pde] [cite:de27_treasury_api] Part Thirty's map grades each of these joins, and the end-to-end map in this part reuses those grades exactly.

Gates: who can be stopped, denied or cut off

A second set of tools does not watch people. It decides what they may do. Many of these gates long predate 2025. E-Verify, which checks a new hire's papers against SSA and DHS records, was created in 1996. Since October 2021 more than 3.8 million clearance holders have been under continuous vetting, with automated checks of criminal and financial records. [cite:de24b_ev_manual] [cite:de24b_bu_cv] A passport can be denied for tax debt over $66,000 in 2026 or for child-support arrears over $2,500. The government's terrorist screening dataset held about two million entries at the end of 2023, most of them people who are neither citizens nor permanent residents ([scene:de25b_who_can_stop_you|Part Twenty-Seven]). [cite:de25b_irs_passport] [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] [cite:de25b_cbs_watchlist] Banks file millions of confidential suspicious-activity reports a year; DHS ran about 290,000 queries of that reporting system in a year. Since 2025 the GENIUS Act has required every regulated stablecoin issuer to be able to "block, freeze, and reject" transactions on a lawful order ([scene:de26_money_rails|Part Twenty-Eight]). [cite:de26_aba_fincen] [cite:de26_crec_genius] Sanctions under the International Criminal Court order of February 2025 have frozen the assets of court officials and of a United Nations rapporteur. [cite:ow11_wiki_eo14203] [cite:de34_jurist_albanese]

Law, command and force

The legal layer moved in 2025 and 2026 ([scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|Part Thirty-Two], [scene:de31_five_patterns|Part Thirty-Three]). On 29 June 2026, in Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court held that a president may remove members of the Federal Trade Commission at will. An order of 3 June 2026 made about 8,000 senior career officials removable by notice. On 24 January 2025 17 inspectors general were removed in one night. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de30_npr_8000] [cite:de31_npr_igs] A presidential memorandum of September 2025, NSPM-7, names ideas as indicators of domestic terrorism, and the Attorney General acknowledged in February 2026 that a list of groups compiled under it exists but is not public ([scene:de30_nspm7_and_detachment|Part Thirty-Two]). [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] [cite:de34_int_list]

The force is larger than at any time in ICE's history ([scene:de32_ice_as_template|Part Thirty-Four]). The 2025 budget law gave ICE about $75 billion over four years, about $45 billion of it for detention, with funds available to 30 September 2029. [cite:us6_brennan_obbba] [cite:de32_aic_hr1] On DHS's own figures ICE grew from about 10,000 to about 22,000 officers and agents. Agreements deputising local officers rose to 1,372 by January 2026. ICE held nearly 66,000 people on 11 July 2026, after a record of 70,766 in late January; in early 2025 about nine in ten detainees were held in privately run facilities. [cite:de32_kwtx_hiring] [cite:de32_fwd_287g] [cite:de34_trac_66k] [cite:de32_trac_private] GEO's subsidiary monitored about 184,000 people in the alternatives-to-detention programme in August 2026, nearly 54,000 of them on ankle monitors. [cite:de32_lt_isap] National Guard quick reaction forces totalling more than 23,000 were stood up in every state. [cite:de32_mt_qrf]

What the inventory shows, and what it does not

Three things stand out. First, most of the machinery was not built for this purpose or by these people. The ICE–Palantir relationship began under Obama. E-Verify, continuous vetting, the travel archive, private detention and the fusion centres were built and kept by Democratic and Republican administrations alike. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] [cite:de32_brennan_14006] Second, what changed in 2025 and 2026 is mainly direction and scale, not invention: records collected to check eligibility began moving toward enforcement, and the force that acts on them doubled. Third, some pieces were switched off. DOGE's temporary organisation ended on 4 July 2026. Quiet Skies, a programme that sent air marshals to watch travellers who were not on any watch list, was ended in June 2025. The Guard deployments to Los Angeles, Chicago and Portland ended on 31 December 2025 after the Supreme Court refused, at an interim stage, to allow the Illinois one. [cite:de21_ee_end] [cite:de25b_cnn_quietskies] [cite:de33_pbs_guard]

What the inventory does not contain is as important as what it does. It contains no single identity file joining a person's records across all these layers, no statute letting the government designate a domestic group as terrorist, no exit permit and no court order upholding the use of any of these tools against citizens for their speech. [cite:de30_dla_nspm7] [cite:de25b_kent] [scene:de34_missing_pieces_and_triggers|The last section] returns to those gaps. First comes the question the inventory raises: whether tools built for one group could be pointed at another.

sections.h: The Repurposing Test
sections.html:
Book Five showed that most of the inventory was built or bought for immigration enforcement. The worst-case reading needs it to be turned to another use: against critics. This section tests that step. A critic here is defined by what a person said or did. That includes critics of the US government and critics of any foreign government, since several of the cases on record concern speech about Israel's war in Gaza. The section does not ask whether the tools could be aimed at people because of their religion or ethnicity. That is a different question under different law, and none of the cases below was argued or decided on that footing.

The test separates two things the record keeps separate. One is a documented case, a named person or group against whom a tool was used, with a dated outcome. The other is programme-level use, a standing practice of turning the tools on critics as a class. The first exists. The second, as of October 2026, does not appear in any document, ruling or admission.

Non-citizens: speech as a ground

For people who are not citizens, speech became a formal factor in 2025. The test case was AAUP v. Rubio. At trial in July 2025, Peter Hatch of DHS's intelligence office testified that a "Tiger Team" of analysts had written more than a hundred reports on foreign students and academics. The names came from a list of about 5,000 compiled by Canary Mission, a privately run website that profiles campus activists. [cite:de28_crimson_hatch] On 30 September 2025 Judge William Young found the policy unconstitutional. On 22 January 2026 he vacated it and presumed retaliation in any adverse immigration action against the plaintiff groups' members. The government's appeal to the First Circuit had not been decided as of October 2026. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de30_audit_aaup]

Two individual cases show the route in practice. Rumeysa Öztürk, a Turkish doctoral student at Tufts, was arrested on a street in Somerville, Massachusetts, in March 2025 after the State Department revoked her visa. The only basis that emerged was an opinion piece she had co-written in the student newspaper about her university's response to the war in Gaza. She spent 45 days in detention in Louisiana before a federal judge ordered her release, finding a substantial claim that she was being punished for her speech. On 29 January 2026 an immigration judge ended the removal case, finding that DHS had not proved her deportable. [cite:de34_an_ozturk] In April 2026 the government settled: it dropped the deportation effort and affirmed her lawful status, and she finished her doctorate and returned to Turkey. [cite:de34_wt_ozturk]

Mahmoud Khalil, a permanent resident and recent Columbia graduate active in the campus protests over Gaza, was arrested on 8 March 2025. On 11 April an immigration judge found him removable solely on the Secretary of State's determination that his presence "would have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences." A federal judge found that policy likely unconstitutional and released him in June 2025. In September an immigration judge ordered him deported on a separate ground, alleged omissions in his green-card application. [cite:de34_ccr_khalil] [cite:de34_tribune_khalil] On 15 January 2026 the Third Circuit, by two votes to one, held that the district court had lacked jurisdiction. Rehearing by the full court was denied on 22 May, and on 26 May the court stayed its mandate while Khalil asked the Supreme Court to hear the case. DHS said he should "self-deport now." [cite:de34_ccr_khalil] [cite:de34_tribune_khalil] [cite:de34_nfts_khalil]

Visa revocation is the quieter tool. By 18 August 2025 the State Department said it had revoked more than 6,000 student visas since January. About 4,000 were for violations of law such as assault or drunk driving, and an official put about 200 to 300 at "support for terrorism," without saying what conduct that covered beyond fundraising for Hamas. [cite:de34_ewn_6000] [cite:de34_fox_6000] On 14 October 2025 it revoked the visas of six foreigners over social-media comments on the assassination of Charlie Kirk, saying the country "has no obligation to host foreigners who wish death on Americans." [cite:de34_gn_kirkvisas] A consular cable of 18 June 2025 told officers to look for "hostile attitudes toward our citizens, culture, government, institutions, or founding principles" in student applicants' public posts. [cite:de28_reuters_visa]

Critics of a foreign government: sanctions

The sanctions tool reached furthest. Under the February 2025 order against the International Criminal Court, the government designated the court's prosecutor, judges and three Palestinian human-rights groups. On 9 July 2025 it designated Francesca Albanese, the UN's special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, citing her calls for ICC warrants against Israel's prime minister and former defence minister. [cite:ow11_wiki_eo14203] [cite:de34_jurist_albanese] A designation freezes the person's assets in the United States and bars Americans from dealing with them. Her husband and daughter sued. A district judge blocked the sanctions on 13 May 2026 as likely to violate free speech; the D.C. Circuit stayed that order on 22 May, OFAC relisted her on 27 May, and an appeals order in June kept the sanctions in force while the appeal continues. [cite:de34_audit_albanese_dn] [cite:de35_reuters_albanese] [cite:ow11_jurist_albanese2026] [cite:ow11_jns_albanese_dc] [cite:de34_jurist_albanese]

Citizens: specific cases, each with an outcome

For citizens the record holds cases, not a programme, and most were checked. DHS used administrative subpoenas, demands for records issued without a judge, to try to unmask the people behind six Instagram accounts that had named a Border Patrol agent. A magistrate judge ordered Meta not to comply, and DHS withdrew. [cite:de28_int_meta] A Philadelphia-area man who emailed a DHS lawyer urging "common sense and decency" in an asylum case was the subject of a subpoena issued four hours later. Agents came to his home, and DHS withdrew the subpoena when the ACLU moved to quash it in February 2026. [cite:de28_aclu_doe] Nicole Cleland, a Minnesota citizen who had been observing agents, lost her Global Entry and PreCheck three days after a Border Patrol agent addressed her by name and said he had used face recognition. Her suit, filed in July 2026, is pending, and CBP denies retaliation; the link from face recognition to the revocation is alleged and denied, possible as a join and not documented. [cite:de25b_bu_cleland]

The Director of National Intelligence revoked the security clearances of at least 37 current and former officials in August 2025, citing "politicization or weaponization of intelligence"; the memo reportedly cited no specific evidence. [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] Executive orders against four law firms restricted their clearances and building access. Four district judges found them unconstitutional, and the government's appeal was argued in the D.C. Circuit on 14 May 2026. [cite:de24b_gma_lawfirms] After six members of Congress told service members in a video that they could refuse illegal orders, the Pentagon moved to discipline one of them, Senator Mark Kelly. Judge Richard Leon enjoined it in February 2026, finding that the Defense Secretary had "trampled on Senator Kelly's First Amendment freedoms." [cite:de32_npr_kelly] Officials pressed Apple and Facebook to remove tools that tracked immigration agents, pressure a federal judge found likely coercive. [cite:de26_reason_rosado]

What repurposing would legally need

The cases show where the law draws its lines. For non-citizens, immigration law itself supplies a route. Visas can be revoked, and a removal ground can be invoked on the Secretary of State's word, so the tools built for immigration can reach a critic without any new authority, subject to the courts. For citizens there is no removal and no visa, and the State Department may not deny a passport for belief without authority from Congress, which the Supreme Court found lacking in Kent v. Dulles in 1958. [cite:de25b_kent] To turn the stack on a citizen as a critic, the state would need one of four things.

The first is a criminal charge, which brings a grand jury, a trial jury and a judge. The terrorism convictions on record since the directive followed a shooting at an ICE centre in July 2025; a grand jury reportedly declined to indict in the Kelly matter. [cite:de30_kera_prairieland] [cite:de32_npr_kelly] The second is a "terrorism" label. NSPM-7 lets the Attorney General recommend domestic groups for designation and names "anti-capitalism," "anti-Christianity" and opposition to immigration enforcement among its indicators. No statute provides for designating a domestic group, so the label carries investigative and reputational consequences, not the asset freezes and material-support liability that attach to foreign designations. [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] [cite:de30_bondi_memo] [cite:de30_dla_nspm7] The third is a new statute, and Congress has passed none of this kind. The fourth, and the cheapest, is a rule change: an internal procedure, a data-sharing notice or a vetting cable. Several of these were issued in 2025 and 2026, but for non-citizens or for eligibility checks, not for citizens' speech. [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] [cite:de28_reuters_visa]

If it were connected

The join this test points to is between the "terrorism" route and the integration layer. An entry on the Attorney General's list, which is not public, could be matched against the same people-search, travel and financial records ICE already reaches. Treasury and IRS investigators are already directed by NSPM-7 to trace funders. [cite:de34_int_list] [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] Grade: possible. The tools and the directive both exist, but no document shows list entries loaded into a case system, and an amicus brief's claims that DHS used the directive to monitor nonprofits are allegations no court has ruled on. [cite:de30_pd_amicus] Each documented case above went through a named official and a human decision, and most were reviewed by a judge.

The test therefore returns a split result. Turning immigration and foreign-affairs tools on non-citizen critics is documented: the policy existed, a court found it unconstitutional, and the visas and sanctions tools remain in use. Turning the stack on citizen critics is documented only case by case, and most of those cases were blocked, withdrawn or are still being litigated. A programme against critics as a class is not supported: no document shows one. [scene:de34_the_end_to_end_map|The next section] lays out the whole pipeline the worst case would need, link by link.

sections.h: The End-to-End Map
sections.html:
The worst-case reading describes a pipeline: a person is identified, their records are collected and joined, a system scores or flags them, an official decides, and the state denies them something, enforces against them, confines them and, at the far end, compels their labour. This section walks that pipeline one link at a time. For each link it names the systems that do the job today, citing the part of the book that documents them; grades the join to the next link; and says what stands in the way. The grades for joins between data systems are taken unchanged from the ecosystem map in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty]: documented (it exists today, with a source), probable (a contract, interface or authority already points to it), reported (named reporting, not yet confirmed by a primary record), possible (technically feasible, no document) and not supported (the record runs against it). "Possible" grades a join between systems, never a fact about a person.

Every link has to be read twice, because the pipeline runs differently for the two populations the law separates. For non-citizens in immigration enforcement, almost every link is documented and in daily use. For citizens, the links exist but are mostly unjoined, and where they have touched citizens the record shows error or a specific case, not design.

Identify, collect, join

Identification is the most fully built link. ICE's Mobile Fortify app returns a name, date of birth and removal status from a face in the street, and CBP photographs every non-citizen at the border ([scene:de26_faces_drones_satellites|Part Twenty-Eight]). Plate cameras on local networks answer federal searches: one Texas school district's eight cameras received 620 immigration-related searches in a single month. [cite:de26_404_fortify] [cite:de26_bu_entryexit] [cite:de28_74_flock] DHS's next-generation biometric system, HART, is built to be shared across DHS, the Justice and Defense Departments, the intelligence community, police and foreign partners. In August 2026 it was scheduled to reach initial operation by September. [cite:de28_hart_pia] [cite:de24_bu_schutt] Part Thirty grades the join from these sensors to the integration layer as possible: no record shows a feed from Fortify, drones or Paragon into Palantir. The join from plate cameras is reported for federal agents and possible for Palantir. [cite:de28_npr_paragon]

Collection draws on the state's own records and on the market ([scene:de24b_benefits|Part Twenty-Five], [scene:de24_data_and_fusion|Part Twenty-Four]). The joins graded documented in Part Thirty are specific. A Medicaid dataset reached Palantir once, over a Teams chat in January 2026, beyond a court's limits. Student-visa and air-passenger data was searched through Palantir systems, and phone extractions were imported into them, in records from 2014 to 2022. A 2026 work statement requires LexisNexis's people-search data to connect to "the Palantir platform," documented as a requirement and probable as a flow. [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de28_guardian_icm] [cite:de28_bu_lexis] The IRS, SSA and TSA links are documented as far as DHS or ICE; the onward path to Palantir is not shown. The new TANF disclosures are documented to DHS and possible to Palantir. Thomson Reuters's CLEAR feeding Palantir is not supported: a training record says it "is not connected to Palantir tools." [cite:de30_ap_krause] [cite:de24_npr_save] [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice] [cite:de28_bl_tanf] [cite:de28_lawsites_tr]

Score, decide, deny

Scoring exists in narrow forms. ELITE gives addresses a "confidence score," drawing on Medicaid and other data. [cite:ow9_fortune_elite] SAVE flags people whose citizenship it cannot confirm. Its record shows the cost of error: the government said it had checked more than 65 million voters in 26 states and flagged 28,635, and in Texas about a fifth of those flagged were later found to be citizens. [cite:de19_npr_save] Continuous vetting runs automated checks on the criminal and financial records of more than 3.8 million clearance holders. [cite:de24b_bu_cv] No document shows a general score that rates a person's loyalty or speech. The one programme that flagged unaccused travellers by algorithm, Quiet Skies, was ended in June 2025 by Secretary Kristi Noem, who called it "a political rolodex of the Biden Administration." [cite:de25b_cnn_quietskies]

Every decision on the record was made by a named official or office: an immigration judge in the Öztürk and Khalil cases, the Secretary of State in visa revocations, the Director of National Intelligence on clearances, OFAC on sanctions ([scene:de34_the_repurposing_test|the previous section]). [cite:de34_ccr_khalil] [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] That matters for the worst case, because a human decision can be challenged, appealed and found unlawful, and in this record several were. Denial then draws on gates built long before 2025: passport denial for tax debt over $66,000 or child-support arrears over $2,500, the no-fly list, E-Verify, benefit eligibility checks and trusted-traveller revocation ([scene:de25b_who_can_stop_you|Part Twenty-Seven], [scene:de24b_work_and_vetting|Part Twenty-Five]). [cite:de25b_irs_passport] [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] [cite:de24b_ev_manual] The join from "flagged" to "denied" is documented for non-citizens in visa and sanctions cases. For citizens it is documented only in specific contested cases, such as the clearance revocations; in the Global Entry case the step from a face-recognition match to the revocation is alleged and denied, and Part Thirty grades that join possible. [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] Which denials US law already allows, and for what, is the subject of [scene:de35_the_consequence_engine|the consequence engine] in the next part.

Enforce, confine, compel

Enforcement and confinement are built at a scale without precedent for ICE, and they are pointed at one population ([scene:de32_ice_as_template|Part Thirty-Four]). ICE doubled its workforce on its own count and was funded to 2029. Local deputisation grew roughly tenfold in a year, and detention stood near 66,000 in July 2026, in a system where about nine in ten detainees were already held in privately run facilities in early 2025. [cite:de32_kwtx_hiring] [cite:us6_brennan_obbba] [cite:de32_fwd_287g] [cite:de34_trac_66k] [cite:de32_trac_private] The link touches citizens by error, and the record documents the error. ProPublica counted 506 US citizens detained by immigration agents, at least 70 of them minors, and about a dozen deported, most of them children. [cite:de32_dn_propublica] Against citizens as such, enforcement would need different authority: the criminal process, or troops under the Insurrection Act, which had not been invoked as of 28 October 2026. The Supreme Court's Illinois order found the government had "failed to identify a source of authority" for the military to execute the laws there. [cite:de32_hill_time] [cite:de32_lawdork_il]

The last link is the weakest on the record. Detainees in the "voluntary work program" are paid at least $1 a day, a rate Congress funded in 1950. A Washington jury ordered GEO to pay about $23.2 million in back wages and unjust enrichment, and the Supreme Court is weighing whether to hear GEO's challenge. Claims that detainees were made to clean without pay under threat of solitary confinement are being litigated as forced labour, and in GEO v. Menocal in February 2026 the Supreme Court held that GEO's defence as a government contractor could not be appealed before trial, so the case continues. [cite:de32_pogo_dollar] [cite:de32_wa_nwauzor] [cite:de32_scotus_25828] [cite:de32_lii_menocal] Compelled labour as a policy of the state is not supported. Nor does any of the theorists' texts prescribe forced labour: Yarvin's documented answer for people he deemed surplus was confinement ([scene:de6_the_hard_posts|Part Six]). [cite:de6_tnr_duran] The ladder from watched to compelled is set out rung by rung in [scene:de35_the_consequence_ladder|Part Thirty-Seven].

Reading the map

Read end to end, the map has a clear shape. For non-citizens the pipeline is complete in practice: each link is documented, and several joins between links are documented too. That is the occasion the worst-case reading names, and it is on the record. For citizens the pipeline is a set of separate pieces. The first two links are built and reach everyone, since faces, plates, travel, tax and benefit records do not sort by citizenship. The middle links are joined for citizens only by accident, as in the Medicaid dataset and the citizens flagged by SAVE, or in specific contested cases. The last links have no legal route for citizens without a criminal charge or military authority that has not been used.

What separates the pieces is mostly not technology. Part Thirty found that every join between adjacent links needs an interface, an agreement or a rule change, not a new law. [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:de28_brennan_consol] The barriers that held were courts and statutes. Judges found 42,695 tax disclosures unlawful, limited Medicaid sharing to five fields and paused it after the January breach, vacated the speech-targeting policy, and refused the Illinois Guard deployment. [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de30_bl_medicaid] [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de32_lawdork_il] Some barriers gave way: the Supreme Court let SAVE checks resume, and a judge declined to block the TANF notice. [cite:de19_npr_save] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] [scene:de34_missing_pieces_and_triggers|The next section] asks what the pipeline still lacks to run as one machine, and which dated events would move its grades.

sections.h: Missing Pieces and Triggers
sections.html:
The end-to-end map showed a pipeline that is complete in practice for non-citizens and in pieces for citizens. This section names what the worst case still lacks to run as one machine against anyone, and lists the dated events that would move a grade. Four pieces are missing: a unified identity spine, a legal trigger that reaches citizens, enforcement capacity that can lawfully act on citizens at scale, and courts that would let all of it stand. Each is examined against the record as of October 2026, in the same grades used throughout the book.

A unified identity spine

A system that carries a person from camera to cell needs one key that links all their records. The United States has no national identity card and no single population register. REAL ID, enforced at airports since 7 May 2025, sets a standard for state driver's licences; it does not create a federal database of them ([scene:de25b_who_knows_you_travel|Part Twenty-Seven]). [cite:de25b_tsa_realid] What exists instead are partial spines. The Social Security number links tax, benefit, employment and credit files. The face links DHS's biometric records. Since May 2025 the SAVE system has linked Social Security records to DHS's immigration files, so that a state can check a person's citizenship by name, date of birth and the last four digits of a Social Security number. Queries are kept for ten years, and the agreements allow DHS to use them "for any purpose permitted by law." [cite:de24_npr_save] HART, built to hold faces, fingerprints and irises and to be shared across the federal government, police and foreign partners, was scheduled in August 2026 to reach initial operation by September. GAO had found its schedule slipping by years and only five of twelve privacy requirements met. [cite:de24_bu_schutt] [cite:de28_hart_pia] [cite:de24_gao_hart]

Grades. The components of a spine are documented. That SAVE becomes a standing citizenship check for more purposes is probable, because its agreements already authorise wider use and it has been run against more than 65 million voters since May 2025. [cite:de19_npr_save] A single file joining one person's records across all six layers of Part Thirty's map is possible as a join and not supported as a fact: no document shows one. [cite:de28_brennan_consol]

A legal trigger for citizens

For non-citizens, immigration law supplies the trigger, as [scene:de34_the_repurposing_test|the repurposing test] showed. For citizens there is none of comparable reach. A citizen cannot be removed. The State Department may not deny a passport for belief without authority from Congress, under Kent v. Dulles (1958). No statute lets the government designate a domestic group as terrorist. [cite:de25b_kent] [cite:de30_dla_nspm7] The nearest thing on the record is NSPM-7 and the Attorney General's December 2025 memorandum. Together they name ideas such as "anti-capitalism," "anti-Christianity" and "opposition to law and immigration enforcement" as indicators, direct the FBI to keep a list of groups, and send Treasury and IRS investigators after funders. [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] [cite:de30_bondi_memo] On 11 February 2026 the Attorney General told the House Judiciary Committee that the list exists, said antifa was on it and declined to share it. [cite:de34_int_list] The documented terrorism prosecutions since the directive concern violence. Senators reported in September 2026 a Treasury review of three named nonprofits' tax status, but no revocation is on record. [cite:de30_kera_prairieland] [cite:de30_wyden_letter]

Grades. A designation process aimed at domestic groups is documented as a directive and a secret list. Its use to deny citizens anything for their speech alone is not supported; the Attorney General's memo itself bars investigations "based solely" on protected activity. [cite:de30_bondi_memo] The trigger would become real with a statute, a public designation with legal consequences, or the first revocation of a nonprofit's status under the directive.

Enforcement capacity that can act on citizens

The capacity is built and funded to 2029, but its legal mandate is immigration ([scene:de32_ice_as_template|Part Thirty-Four]). [cite:de32_aic_hr1] Acting on citizens at scale would need one of two things. One is the criminal process, which runs through prosecutors, grand juries and trial juries, and the record shows a grand jury reportedly declining to indict in the case of the six lawmakers' video. [cite:de32_npr_kelly] The other is the military, which the Posse Comitatus Act bars from executing the laws unless Congress or the Constitution expressly allows it. [cite:de32_govinfo_1385] The Insurrection Act is that exception. It had not been invoked as of 28 October 2026, though the president said in October, "I could use it." [cite:de32_meaww_time] The Guard quick reaction forces of more than 23,000 exist. No order to use troops against citizens' political activity is on the record, and so no soldier's refusal of one has been tested ([scene:de32_what_stops_it|Part Thirty-Four]). [cite:de32_mt_qrf] [cite:de32_stripes_orders]

Courts that would let it stand

The fourth piece is the one the theorists themselves left unsolved ([scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight]). The record in 2025 and 2026 runs both ways. The government lost on the speech-targeting policy, on 42,695 tax disclosures, on every voter-roll demand decided at trial, on the Illinois Guard deployment, on the emergency tariffs and on the law-firm orders at the district level. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] [cite:de32_lawdork_il] [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] [cite:de24b_gma_lawfirms] It won on the removal power, on SAVE's resumption, on immigration stops in Los Angeles, on Khalil's case on jurisdiction and, for now, on Albanese's sanctions. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de19_npr_save] [cite:de32_scotusblog_perdomo] [cite:de34_ccr_khalil] [cite:de34_jurist_albanese] Many of the wins came on the Supreme Court's emergency docket, at interim stages. Courts that would uphold the use of the stack against citizens for speech are not supported on this record. Courts that defer to the executive on immigration and foreign affairs are documented.

The triggers, dated

A trigger here is an event, scheduled or possible, that would move one of the grades. The dated ones are set out below. The open-ended ones matter as much: the first invocation of the Insurrection Act, the publication of the Attorney General's list or a designation with legal effect, the first nonprofit to lose its tax status under the directive, the first enforcement use of welfare records that DHS has not yet said it plans, a confirmed flow of LexisNexis data into Palantir, and a reply to the members of Congress who asked DHS in April 2026 for every Palantir dataset and any use against observers and protesters. [cite:de32_hill_time] [cite:de30_wyden_letter] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:de28_goldman_letter] The full watch list is kept in [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|Part Forty-Three].

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis is the Sophia platform's, never a finding: immigration enforcement and government cuts as the occasion, a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. This part audited what is built, tested whether it can be turned on critics, mapped the whole pipeline and named what it lacks.

Documented: the occasion. Every link from identification to confinement exists and is in daily use for non-citizens, and the inventory was enlarged, funded and pointed at that population in 2025 and 2026. [cite:us6_brennan_obbba] [cite:de34_trac_66k] Documented too: the turning of immigration and foreign-affairs tools on non-citizen critics, including critics of a foreign government's war. A policy of targeting non-citizen academics for their speech was found unconstitutional and vacated, and visas and sanctions were used against named people for what they said. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de34_an_ozturk] [cite:de34_gn_kirkvisas] [cite:de34_jurist_albanese] For citizens, documented cases exist: unmasking subpoenas, a revoked Global Entry whose link to face recognition is alleged and denied, revoked clearances, orders against law firms, discipline of a senator. Most were withdrawn, enjoined or are still in court. [cite:de28_aclu_doe] [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] [cite:de32_npr_kelly]

Probable: that the identity components converge further, because SAVE's agreements already authorise wider use; that the integration layer absorbs more of the map, because work statements require it; and that the NSPM-7 indicators steer investigative attention toward critics of immigration policy, a reading of the directive's text and the reported reviews, not a finding about any person. [cite:de24_npr_save] [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:de30_wh_nspm7]

Possible, as joins only: a single file per person across all six layers; list entries under the directive matched against the integration layer; HART's biometrics shared into the same platform.

Not supported: a programme turning the stack on citizens for their speech; one standing system from camera to cell outside immigration enforcement; compelled labour as state policy; a lawful route to use troops or detention against citizens' political activity; and any document tracing this machinery to the Dark Enlightenment's texts, which it resembles in its centralised executive but with which it shares no documented paper trail. [cite:de28_brennan_consol] [cite:de32_lawdork_il] [cite:de8_kofman_ny]

The record runs against the worst case in the places the four missing pieces sit. No identity spine, no statutory trigger for citizens, no invoked military authority, and courts that, case by case, still say no often enough to matter. It also runs against it in authorship. Much of the machinery was built under presidents of both parties, and the one programme that flagged unaccused travellers by algorithm was ended by the current administration. [cite:ow9_mj_icm2019] [cite:de25b_cnn_quietskies] The gap between "every piece exists" and "one machine runs them" is now made of agreements, rules and judges. Those are the brakes the worst case needs removed, and the triggers above are where to watch. What the state could do to a person if it were enforced is the subject of [scene:de35_three_layers|Part Thirty-Seven].

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Seven
chapters.title: If It Were Enforced
chapters.intro: The Readiness Audit counted what has been built. This part asks what would happen to the people living under it if the end state the texts describe were actually enforced. It separates three layers: the end state in Yarvin's and Land's own words, the machinery American law already contains as of October 2026, and the gap between them. It then climbs a ladder of consequences, from being watched to compelled labour, rung by rung; goes domain by domain through what the state can already deny a person, from a bank account to a passport; sets thirteen constitutional rights beside what the texts say about each; and ends with the texts' harshest subject, people judged unproductive, before testing the worst-case reading against the whole record.
chapters.outro: The part found that the end state and the machinery meet at the level of consequences but not of design. The texts remove, in their own words, the vote, the removal of rulers, independent courts, the press and due process, and Yarvin's answer for unwanted residents is "permanent solitary confinement"; no text examined prescribes fines, purchase bans or forced labour. [cite:de35_land_ebook] [cite:de35_nyt_interview] [cite:de6_tnr_duran] American law already supplies every rung of the ladder for some group, almost always for a debt, a conviction, a status or a foreign designation: passport denial for debt, garnishment without a court order, sanctions that cut judges and a UN rapporteur off from banking, detention at record scale, and compelled labour through the Thirteenth Amendment's exception and the $1 detainee rate. [cite:de25b_irs_passport] [cite:ad7_ci_garnish] [cite:de35_ap_icc] [cite:de32_npr_deaths] [cite:de35_lii_13th] [cite:de32_pogo_dollar] What is missing is a shared trigger read by every gatekeeper and a lawful route to use it on citizens for their speech, and the courts have so far refused several of the attempts that came closest. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de35_hm_harvard] [cite:de35_jc_stay] The texts never say who would choose, or remove, the chief executive at the top of this ladder; [scene:de35b_what_the_texts_say|Part Thirty-Eight] takes up that missing election.

sections.h: Three Layers
sections.html:
The Readiness Audit in [scene:de34_what_is_built|Part Thirty-Six] counted what has been built. This part asks a narrower and harder question: if the end state the texts describe were actually enforced on the people living under it, what would happen to them, and how much of that already exists in American law. The answer has three layers, and they have to be kept apart, because the worst-case reading depends on running them together. The first is the end state itself, in the texts' own words. The second is the machinery that exists in the United States as of October 2026, almost all of it built by governments of both parties, and almost all of it for some other purpose. The third is the gap between the two: what a government would still need, in law, in capacity and in the consent of courts, to turn the second layer into the first. The sections that follow take the consequences rung by rung, then domain by domain, then right by right, and end with the question the texts treat most harshly, what becomes of people judged unproductive.

The first layer: the end state, in the texts' words

The clearest compact statement of the end state is not Curtis Yarvin's but Nick Land's summary of him, written in 2012. "To a neocameralist, a state is a business which owns a country," Land quotes Yarvin, writing as Mencius Moldbug; ownership is divided into shares, "each share has one vote, and the shareholders elect a board, which hires and fires managers," and "this business's customers are its residents." [cite:de35_land_ebook] Neocameralism, the name for this design, is defined in [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]. Land then draws the consequence for the residents in his own voice. Once power is turned into shares, the owners can begin "rational corporate governance, beginning with the appointment of a CEO," and "there is no longer any need for residents (clients) to take any interest in politics whatsoever. In fact, to do so would be to exhibit semi-criminal proclivities." Taxes become "sovereign rent." A resident who is badly served can "notify its customer service function" or leave. The slogan follows: "No voice, free exit." [cite:de35_land_ebook]

The passage Land quotes next sets out what the residents would keep and what they would lose. The model states, Yarvin wrote, have "minimal crime and high levels of personal and economic freedom"; they are "weak only in political freedom, and political freedom is unimportant by definition when government is stable and effective." [cite:de35_land_ebook] Yarvin has kept the substance since. In 2012 he told an audience of technology workers that Americans would have to "get over their dictator phobia" and accept "a national CEO [or] what's called a dictator." [cite:de6_pein_2014] In January 2025 he told the New York Times that "monarch is good, it's a neutral term." [cite:de6_audit_nyt] Asked in the same interview about rulers like Nero, he called it "the most important question of all" and gave no mechanism for removing one. [cite:de35_nyt_interview]

Two things about this layer matter for everything that follows. The first is what the texts say about the people who do not fit. Yarvin's answer for residents who cost a sovereign corporation more than they pay, in the 2008 Patchwork posts, was emigration if any other realm would take them and, failing that, "permanent solitary confinement" in virtual reality, which he called "a humane alternative to genocide." [cite:de6_audit_le] [cite:de6_tnr_duran] The second is what the texts do not contain. They specify no penal code, no list of punishments for dissent, no system of fines, blacklists or purchase controls, and no programme of compelled labour. Land's own economic program points the other way, toward "hard money" and the abolition of central banking. [cite:de35_land_ebook] The end state is a structure of authority, not an enforcement manual, and the enforcement manual has to be read from somewhere else.

The second layer: the machinery that exists

That somewhere else is the American state as it stood in October 2026. Its pieces were set out across Books Five and Six, and are only listed here. The state already holds records on most residents' benefits, schooling, employment and credit, and since 2025 several of those walls have been lowered: Medicaid data reached ICE and was shared with Palantir before a court paused it, and a federal judge in September 2026 let a notice allowing welfare data to go to DHS take effect ([scene:de24b_benefits|Part Twenty-Five]).
