[cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] It knows who travels, and it can stop some of them: passports are denied for tax debt over $66,000 and child-support arrears over $2,500, and a Minnesota woman's trusted-traveller status was revoked three days after a Border Patrol agent identified her by face while she watched an immigration operation ([scene:de25b_who_can_stop_you|Part Twenty-Seven]). [cite:de25b_irs_passport] [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] Its immigration agency runs an integration layer that joins brokers, government records and field data, graded link by link in [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty]. Its money rails can freeze a person out of banking without a court, as the sanctions on judges of the International Criminal Court showed ([scene:de26_money_rails|Part Twenty-Eight]). [cite:de35_ap_icc] Its legal levers were loosened in the same years: the president gained at-will removal of independent commissioners, about 8,000 senior civil servants were moved into a schedule exempt from adverse-action procedures, and a national security memorandum told investigators to pursue the funders of groups it described ([scene:de30_nspm7_and_detachment|Part Thirty-Two]). [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] [cite:de30_npr_8000] [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] And its enforcement arm doubled: ICE says it grew from about 10,000 to about 22,000 officers and agents, funded with $45 billion for detention to 2029 ([scene:de32_ice_as_template|Part Thirty-Four]). [cite:de32_kwtx_hiring] [cite:de32_aic_hr1]

None of these pieces was built from the texts. Most predate the 2025 administration; several were built or kept by its predecessors. The child-support passport rule dates from 1996, the terrorist watchlist from the years after 2001, and the private detention estate from administrations of both parties. [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] [cite:de25b_cbs_watchlist] [cite:de32_brennan_14006] What changed in 2025 and 2026 was scale, speed and the lowering of walls between systems that were built apart.

The third layer: the gap

The gap between the two layers is not a matter of tools. It is a matter of triggers, joins and consent. Almost every consequence in the machinery fires on something specific and contestable: a debt of a set size, a conviction, a lapsed visa, a designation by name. For non-citizens, immigration law supplies a trigger of wide reach, and the record shows it used on speech: a federal judge found in September 2025 that the government had pursued an ideological deportation policy against non-citizen academics, and vacated it in January 2026. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de30_audit_aaup] For citizens, no trigger of comparable reach exists. No statute lets the government designate a domestic group as terrorist, and the law firm DLA Piper's reading of the 2025 memorandum is that it creates no new legal authority. [cite:de30_dla_nspm7] [scene:de34_missing_pieces_and_triggers|Part Thirty-Six] lists the dated events that would change that.

The joins are the second part of the gap. Each system in the second layer keeps its own list. A tax debt reaches the passport office; a sanctions designation reaches every bank. No document shows one standing list, carried from system to system, that marks a person as an enemy and denies them everything at once; China's court blacklist of judgment debtors, which airlines and railways enforce, is the nearest working model, and its trigger is unpaid debt, not speech ([scene:de36_the_reference_model|Part Thirty-Nine]). [cite:de35_tr_china] The third part of the gap is consent. Courts struck down the law-firm orders, the Harvard funding freeze and the speech-based deportation policy, vacated food-restriction waivers in five states, and briefly lifted the sanctions on a United Nations rapporteur before an appeals court restored them. [cite:de24b_gma_lawfirms] [cite:de35_hm_harvard] [cite:de35_bd_aragon] [cite:de35_jc_stay] Those rulings were not final in every case, and others went the government's way.

Read together, the layers give the part its method. The worst case is not a new apparatus; it is the existing one with a common trigger and fewer brakes. The question for each rung of consequence is therefore the same: what the theorists prescribe, in their own words; what exists now, and against whom; and what extension would be needed to reach the end state. No document shows that anyone is building that extension, and the texts' authors did not ask for most of it. [cite:de30_dla_nspm7] [cite:de35_land_ebook] The next section climbs the ladder from being watched to compelled labour.

sections.h: The Consequence Ladder
sections.html:
A state can do seven broad things to a person it wants to control, each harsher than the last: watch them, deny them things, fine them, prosecute them, remove them, confine them, and make them work. This section climbs that ladder one rung at a time and asks three questions at each: what the theorists prescribe, in their own words; what exists in American law now, and for whom; and what the worst-case extension would be. Two findings run through every rung. No text by Yarvin or Land examined for this book prescribes forced labour, fines or purchase bans for dissenters. And Yarvin's one documented answer for people a sovereign corporation does not want is not labour but confinement. [cite:de35_land_ebook] [cite:de6_tnr_duran]

Watched and denied

The texts examined contain no programme of surveillance. The nearest thing is Land's statement that a resident who takes an interest in politics would "exhibit semi-criminal proclivities," which describes a disposition the sovereign would look on with suspicion without saying what it would do about it. [cite:de35_land_ebook] What exists now is extensive, and most of it was described in Book Five. ICE's Mobile Fortify application lets an officer photograph a face in the street and match it against about 200 million images; a DHS privacy document says people are given no chance to decline. [cite:de26_404_fortify] [cite:de26_reason_fortify] DHS has used administrative subpoenas, which no judge approves in advance, to seek the identities behind social-media accounts critical of immigration agents, and withdrew at least one when challenged. [cite:de28_int_meta] [cite:de28_eff_letter] The worst-case extension is watching as a sorting step, the "identify" and "flag" links of [scene:de34_the_end_to_end_map|the end-to-end map]. The second rung, denial, is the largest, and the next section takes it domain by domain. Its defining feature is that it rarely needs a court.

Fined and prosecuted

The texts treat taxes as "sovereign rent" and say nothing about fines as punishment. [cite:de35_land_ebook] The federal government already takes money without a lawsuit for debts it is owed: the Treasury Offset Program can take up to all of a tax refund and up to 15 per cent of a Social Security payment, after at least 60 days' notice, and defaulted student loans can be collected by garnishing up to 15 per cent of disposable pay without a court order. [cite:de24b_crs_top] [cite:ad7_ci_garnish] These are debt-collection tools, aimed at debts, with notice and a right to dispute. The worst-case extension would key them to something other than a debt, for example a civil penalty for protest conduct; no such use is on the record.

On prosecution, Yarvin's texts are more explicit. CNN reported that in 2022 he described "ninjas" who would "seize all points of power, without respect for paper protections." [cite:de6_cnn_2025] In 2025 he told the Times that a new regime "can't be" about bayoneting professors, and that former officials should be treated as ordinary people who had served a bad regime. [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] What exists is a directive, not a statute: National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 of 25 September 2025 tells joint terrorism task forces to investigate "institutional and individual funders" of groups it describes, and the Attorney General's memorandum of 4 December 2025 orders a running list of groups engaged in acts that "may constitute domestic terrorism." [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] [cite:de30_bondi_memo] The documented terrorism prosecutions since it was issued concern violence, not speech ([scene:de34_missing_pieces_and_triggers|Part Thirty-Six]).

Removed

Removal is the rung on which the texts and the record come closest. In the first Patchwork post of 13 November 2008, Yarvin's sovereign corporation would "sell their slums out from under them, obviously," and its surplus residents "can of course emigrate to any other realm in the Patchwork. This presumes, however, that said realm is willing to accept them." [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de6_audit_le] In the United States removal applies only to non-citizens. For them it has been used on speech: more than 1,800 international students had their records terminated or visas revoked by 25 April 2025, and a federal judge found in September 2025 that the government had run an ideological deportation policy against non-citizen academics, vacating it in January 2026; the appeal was pending in October 2026. [cite:de24b_pie_sevis] [cite:de28_ch_aaup] Citizens cannot lawfully be deported, but the record shows the line is not always held in practice: ProPublica counted 506 citizens detained by immigration agents, and about a dozen deported, most of them children. [cite:de32_dn_propublica]

Confined

Here the texts are plain. In "Patchwork 2" of 20 November 2008, after a line about biodiesel that he marked "just kidding," Yarvin set out "a humane alternative to genocide": holding unwanted residents in "permanent solitary confinement," connected to a virtual-reality interface. [cite:de6_tnr_duran] The New Yorker in 2025 summarised the regime he described as one that would "imprison 'decivilized populations.'" [cite:de35_ny_autocracy] What exists is immigration detention on a scale never seen before: $45 billion for detention to 2029, about 90 per cent of detainees held in privately run sites, and a record number of deaths in custody in fiscal 2026 ([scene:de32_the_detention_business|Part Thirty-Four]). [cite:de32_aic_hr1] [cite:de32_trac_private] [cite:de32_npr_deaths] The confined rung also holds the sharpest case abroad. In March and April 2025 the United States sent 252 Venezuelans to El Salvador's CECOT prison. Human Rights Watch and Cristosal documented near-daily beatings, sexual violence and four months of incommunicado detention amounting to enforced disappearance, until their release in a prisoner exchange on 18 July 2025. Their report does not describe forced labour; CECOT belongs on this rung, not the next. [cite:de35_hrw_cecot]

Compelled labour

No text by Yarvin or Land examined for this book calls for forced labour. The passage most often cited as if it did is from "Why Carlyle Matters" of July 2009, in which Yarvin wrote that the "innate character and intelligence of some is more suited to mastery than slavery," and that "a person makes a good slave if he is loyal, patient, and not exceptionally bright or stubborn." [cite:de6_mm_2021] It is a claim, in his own voice, that fitness for servitude is hereditary; it is not a proposal to compel anyone to work, and in 2025 he called abolition "a necessary step." [cite:de6_audit_nyt] The rung is supplied instead by American law. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude "except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted," words adapted from the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. [cite:de35_lii_13th] After the Civil War, every former Confederate state except Virginia leased convicts, most of them Black and many convicted on dubious charges, to mines and plantations; in Alabama their death rate ran about ten times that in states without leasing, and leasing brought in 73 per cent of the state's revenue in 1898. Alabama ended it last, on 1 July 1928. [cite:de35_eh_mancini] The Supreme Court did draw one limit: in Bailey v. Alabama (1911) it held that a state "may not compel one man to labor for another in payment of a debt." [cite:de35_lii_13th]

Today about 800,000 incarcerated people work. Seven states pay nothing for most jobs, others average 15 to 52 cents an hour for non-industry jobs, and 76 per cent of workers surveyed by the ACLU and the University of Chicago reported punishment, such as solitary confinement or lost visits, for refusing. [cite:de35_aclu_captive] Immigration detainees, who are held without criminal conviction, are paid "at least $1 per day" under a rate set by a 1950 law; Congress declined to raise it to $4 in 1982. [cite:de32_pogo_dollar] Courts have resisted that rate. A Washington jury awarded detainees $17.3 million in back pay, and the state $5.9 million more, against GEO Group, which the Ninth Circuit affirmed; GEO's petition, which the Solicitor General urged the Supreme Court to hear, was set for conference on 6 November 2026. [cite:de32_wa_nwauzor] [cite:de32_scotus_25828] [cite:de32_nwauzor_supp] In GEO Group v. Menocal the Court ruled 9–0 on 25 February 2026 that GEO could not appeal early on a contractor defence, sending a forced-labour claim over unpaid cleaning, enforced by solitary confinement, back toward trial. [cite:de32_lii_menocal]

Eight states have removed the exception from their own constitutions: Colorado in 2018, Nebraska and Utah in 2020, Alabama, Oregon, Tennessee and Vermont in 2022, and Nevada in 2024, whose text now reads that "neither Slavery nor involuntary servitude shall ever be tolerated." [cite:de35_ap_13th2022] [cite:de35_ni_q4] Louisiana's measure failed in 2022 after its own sponsors urged a "no" vote over ambiguous wording, and California voters rejected Proposition 6 in 2024 leaving mandatory prison work there at under 74 cents an hour. [cite:de35_ap_13th2022] [cite:de35_cm_prop6] The change in text has not always changed practice, and the federal exception stands. [cite:de35_ap_13th2022]

The ladder therefore has an uneven shape. The theorists are explicit about the top rungs that concern status, removal and confinement, and silent about the middle ones; the record supplies the middle rungs in full, for other purposes, and supplies the last rung through a constitutional exception that predates the theorists by a century and a half. The worst-case extension on that last rung would be compelled work attached to detention that follows no conviction. The $1 rate is the nearest existing thing, and the courts' answer to it was still pending in October 2026. [cite:de32_pogo_dollar] [cite:de32_scotus_25828]

sections.h: The Consequence Engine
sections.html:
The second rung of the ladder, being denied things, is where the worst case would do most of its work, because denial rarely needs a judge. This section goes domain by domain through what American law already lets public bodies, or private firms acting on public signals, withhold from a person: money and credit, purchases, education, work, travel, time off, housing, benefits and a presence online. For each it asks what triggers the denial today, who decides, what notice and appeal the person gets, how often it happens, and what the worst-case extension would be. The finding to keep in view is that each of these levers exists, and each was built for something else: a debt, a conviction, a lapsed status, a foreign designation. No theorist text examined here prescribes any of them; the denied rung is supplied entirely by existing law. [cite:de35_land_ebook]

Money: credit, banking and purchases

The federal government collects debts it is owed without suing. The Treasury Offset Program takes tax refunds, part of Social Security and federal salaries for overdue federal debts and child support, after at least 60 days' notice and a chance to dispute. [cite:de24b_crs_top] Defaulted student loans, owed by about 9.3 million borrowers in mid-2026, can be collected by garnishing up to 15 per cent of disposable pay without a court order; the Department of Education paused these collections in January 2026 and planned to resume them in the autumn. [cite:us17_ci_defaults] [cite:ad7_natp_pause] [cite:ad7_ci_garnish]

The sharpest money lever is a sanctions designation. Once a person is placed on the Treasury's list of blocked persons, American banks, card networks and technology firms may not deal with them, and foreign banks tend to follow for fear of sanctions of their own. The 2025 order against the International Criminal Court showed what that means for an individual. Nine court officials were designated; the prosecutor's bank accounts were closed and his visa revoked, and Judge Kimberly Prost lost her credit cards "immediately," while Amazon's Alexa stopped answering her. "Your whole world is restricted," she said. [cite:de35_ap_icc] The UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese, designated in July 2025, said that "no bank can open a current account for me" and that she could no longer rent a car without a credit card. [cite:de35_jc_albanese] A federal judge enjoined her designation on 13 May 2026 on free-speech grounds in a suit by her husband and daughter; an appeals court paused that ruling, Treasury re-listed her on 27 May, and on 15 June the appeals court let the sanctions stand while the appeal continued. [cite:de34_audit_albanese_dn] [cite:de35_reuters_albanese] [cite:de35_jc_stay] No American is known to have been designated for speech ([scene:de34_the_repurposing_test|Part Thirty-Six]).

Private debanking runs both ways. Under President Obama, a Justice Department initiative put pressure on banks over gun sellers and payday lenders until it was declared ended in 2017; between 2020 and 2023 the largest banks restricted lawful sectors including firearms, private prisons and political action committees, the Comptroller of the Currency found; and an August 2025 order told regulators to end "politicized" debanking. [cite:de26_cfslm_chokepoint] [cite:de26_occ_debank] [cite:de26_fr_14331] Purchases can also be restricted. Federal law bars gun sales to defined categories of people, and the FBI's check system issued 110,505 denials in 2024, of which 28.6 per cent of those appealed were overturned. [cite:de35_fbi_nics] Twenty-three states won federal waivers to bar food-stamp purchases of candy and sugary drinks, until a federal judge vacated five of them in June 2026, holding that the department "cannot act with the force of law" without Congress. [cite:de35_bd_aragon] Stablecoin issuers must by law be able to comply with lawful orders to "seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer" of their tokens, and Tether says it has frozen about $4.2 billion linked to illicit activity ([scene:de26_money_rails|Part Twenty-Eight]). [cite:de26_crec_genius] [cite:de26_forklog_tether] Outside the United States, Canada's government in 2022 used emergency powers to have banks freeze at least 257 accounts of protesters and donors without a court order; two Canadian courts later found the invocation unreasonable, and the Supreme Court of Canada agreed on 22 October 2026 to hear the government's appeal. [cite:de35_ps_rcmp] [cite:de35_cp24_scc]

Learning and working

Federal student aid once carried conduct conditions: men who had not registered for the draft and students with certain drug convictions were barred. Congress removed both in December 2020. [cite:de35_uc_fafsa] For international students the lever is status. More than 1,800 had records terminated or visas revoked by April 2025, many restored after a court hearing, and the speech-based deportation policy behind some of the revocations was later found unconstitutional. [cite:de24b_pie_sevis] [cite:de28_ch_aaup] Universities have been denied as institutions: the government halted more than $2 billion in Harvard's research grants in April 2025, and a federal judge held in September that the action violated the First Amendment and called its stated rationale "a smokescreen"; the government's appeal argued in April 2026 that grants are contracts it may end. [cite:de35_hm_harvard]

Work can be withheld in four ways. E-Verify checks a new hire against Social Security and DHS records, and a mismatch, which "does not necessarily mean" a person cannot work, must be contested within days. [cite:de24b_ev_manual] [cite:de24b_ev_tnc] Security clearances can be pulled with little review: the Director of National Intelligence revoked those of 37 current and former officials in August 2025, citing "politicization or weaponization of intelligence." [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] Orders against four law firms barred their lawyers from federal buildings and clearances until four district judges struck them down; the appeal was argued on 14 May 2026. [cite:de24b_gma_lawfirms] And licences can be suspended for debt: in 2018, by the count of the National Conference of State Legislatures, nineteen states could suspend a professional licence for student-loan default, though at least nine repealed or changed those laws in 2018 and 2019. [cite:de35_ncsl_licence]

Moving, resting and living

The United States has no exit permit, but a citizen may not leave without a valid passport, and passports are denied for tax debt over $66,000 in 2026, for child-support arrears over $2,500 and for certain drug-trafficking convictions. [cite:de25b_usc_1185] [cite:de25b_irs_passport] [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] [cite:de25b_usc_2714] The terrorist watchlist held about two million names at the end of 2023, mostly foreigners; trusted-traveller status can be revoked without a conviction, as in the Minnesota case of January 2026 described in [scene:de25b_who_can_stop_you|Part Twenty-Seven]. [cite:de25b_cbs_watchlist] [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] Russia's 2023 law bars a man from leaving the country once an electronic draft summons is deemed served, and China's courts block flights and trains for judgment debtors. [cite:de25b_ng_russia] [cite:de35_tr_china] Time off is not a public right at all: federal law requires no paid sick leave, and the Family and Medical Leave Act gives eligible workers up to twelve weeks of unpaid leave, so rest is largely the employer's to grant. [cite:us22_dol_sick] [cite:us18_crs_leave] In housing, federally assisted landlords must refuse any household with a member on a lifetime sex-offender registry, and private landlords rely on screening reports whose errors led to a $15 million federal settlement with one screening firm in 2023. [cite:de35_lii_13663] [cite:ad6_ftc_turss]

Benefits carry the newest conditions. From 1 January 2027 adults aged 19 to 64 covered by the Medicaid expansion must show 80 hours a month of work, study or service, and the 2025 law raised food-stamp work requirements to age 64. [cite:ad8_ccf_ifr] [cite:ad11_mn_snap] Arkansas's 2018 experiment with a Medicaid work rule cost about 18,000 people their coverage in under a year. [cite:de24b_warren_equifax] Online, the denial can come from a private platform under pressure: Apple removed the ICEBlock app in October 2025 at the Justice Department's request, and a federal judge in Illinois found in April 2026 that injuries to two other ICE-tracking platforms were "likely traceable to government-coerced enforcement." [cite:de26_audacy_iceblock] [cite:de26_reason_rosado]

If it were connected

Every row of the table runs on its own list, kept by its own office. The worst case is not a new lever; it is a shared trigger. If a single flag, "critic" for example, were written once and read by all of these gatekeepers, a person could lose their passport, their clearance, their benefits, their bank and their platform in the same week. The pattern for that already exists in two places. In the United States, the child-support and tax rules carry one certified debt from a state or the IRS to the State Department's passport system, a debt flag enforced by a different agency. [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] [cite:de25b_irs_passport] In China, a court list of judgment debtors is enforced by airlines and railways that blocked tickets 17.5 million and 5.5 million times in 2018. [cite:de35_tr_china] Graded as a join, the shared trigger is possible: the data paths partly exist, as [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|the ecosystem map] shows, but no document shows a common flag for speech. A sanctions designation is the one existing tool that already behaves like a shared trigger, because every bank and firm must obey it; its use against foreigners is documented, against Americans for speech it is not supported. What stands in the way is law: each lever's statute names its own trigger, and adding "critic" to any of them would take a new statute or rule, which courts have so far tested against the First Amendment, as in the Harvard and Albanese cases. [cite:de35_hm_harvard] [cite:de35_reuters_albanese]

sections.h: The Rights Ledger
sections.html:
A democratic republic is defined less by its elections than by the rights it guarantees against its own government. This section sets thirteen of those rights, as the American Constitution states them, beside what the Dark Enlightenment texts say about each, and reads from the texts' own words what would become of it under a sovereign run as a company. It does not infer intent beyond the words. Where the texts say nothing about a right, the ledger says so, because silence is a finding too: a design that does not mention a right offers it no protection, but it does not announce its abolition either. The texts used are Land's 2012 serial, which summarises Yarvin's design, Yarvin's own posts and interviews, and, for one right, Peter Thiel's 2009 essay.

The vote, the removal of rulers and the petition

The texts are clearest on the rights that concern power. In the design Land summarises, only shareholders vote, by share, and they elect a board that "hires and fires managers"; residents are customers, and for a customer to take an interest in politics would "exhibit semi-criminal proclivities." [cite:de35_land_ebook] Yarvin drew the distinction himself in January 2025: "free speech is a freedom. The right to vote is a form of power." He called voting "this almost pornographic stimulus," and said he does not vote. [cite:de35_nyt_interview] [cite:de8_audit_nyt] Thiel's 2009 essay declared, "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible," but his reply of 1 May 2009 added that he did not "think any class of people should be disenfranchised" and that "voting is not under siege in America, but many other rights are." [cite:de10_cato] The two men should not be merged: Thiel's text doubts the vote's usefulness; Yarvin's design removes it from residents.

On removing a bad ruler, the design gives the power to the board, and The New Yorker's account of Yarvin's plan has board members holding cryptographic keys able to disarm the state's weapons, to prevent a coup. [cite:de8_kofman_ny] The residents have no such power. Asked in 2025 about rulers like Nero, Yarvin called the question "the most important question of all" and offered no mechanism; his idea of selection was to take a Fortune 500 chief executive, "pick one at random and put him or her in charge of Washington." [cite:de35_nyt_interview] The Constitution, by contrast, lets Congress remove a president by impeachment and, since 1951, limits him to two elected terms. [cite:de8_lii_art2s4] [cite:de8_annenberg_22] The question of who would choose and remove the chief executive is the subject of [scene:de35b_what_the_texts_say|Part Thirty-Eight]. The right of petition survives in the design only as a consumer complaint: a dissatisfied resident may "notify its customer service function." [cite:de35_land_ebook]

Courts, due process and the jury

The Constitution gives federal judges office "during good Behaviour" and pay that "shall not be diminished," so that a president cannot remove or starve them. [cite:de35_ncc_art3] The texts treat any such independence as illusory. In Land's summary of Yarvin's reasoning, sovereignty "cannot be eliminated, caged, or controlled," and constitutions have "exactly as much real authority as a sovereign interpretative power allows them to have." [cite:de35_land_ebook] Yarvin in 2025 described rule by "people in the courts and lawyers and professors" as aristocracy rather than democracy. [cite:de35_nyt_interview] The design names no court above the sovereign corporation; its courts would be its own departments, as [scene:de8_tests_it_fails|Part Eight] showed.

Due process, the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments' bar on taking "life, liberty, or property, without due process of law," fares worse in the texts. [cite:de35_na_bor] [cite:de35_bp_14th] The 2008 Patchwork posts describe residents' slums sold "out from under them" and the unwanted held in "permanent solitary confinement," with no hearing mentioned. [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de6_tnr_duran] CNN reported that in 2022 Yarvin described agents who would act "without respect for paper protections." [cite:de6_cnn_2025] Against that stands his 2025 statement that a new regime "can't be" about bayoneting professors and should treat the old regime's officials as ordinary people. [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] The jury is the one right a text praises: Land quotes, with approval, the economist Steve Hanke's line that "the only thing that the citizens can demand from the State, under the Bill of Rights, is for a trial by a jury." [cite:de35_land_ebook] The praise belongs to Land's account of the old American republic, though; the neocameral design itself says nothing about juries.

Speech, press, assembly and religion

The First Amendment protects speech, the press, assembly, petition and religion in one sentence. [cite:de35_na_bor] The texts separate them. The design promises personal freedom without political freedom: the model states have "high levels of personal and economic freedom" and are "weak only in political freedom," which is "unimportant by definition when government is stable and effective." [cite:de35_land_ebook] Speech that is merely personal would on this reading be tolerated; speech that seeks power is exactly the "voice" the design abolishes. The press fares worse, because Yarvin counts it, with the universities and the civil service, as part of "the Cathedral," the unelected establishment he set out to dismantle ([scene:de6_the_program|Part Six]). [cite:de6_pein_2014] In 2025 he called the New York Times "a fifth generation hereditary absolute monarchy." [cite:de35_nyt_interview] The New Yorker summarised his regime as one that would "destroy universities, abolish the press"; the Harvard Crimson quoted a 2021 post in which he wrote that "regime change" would require "all accredited universities be both physically and economically liquidated," though at a Harvard debate in May 2025 he said the university should be remade, not destroyed. [cite:de35_ny_autocracy] [cite:de35_crimson_univ]

On assembly the texts examined say nothing directly; it falls under the general abolition of "voice." On religion they say nothing about freedom of worship. What they say concerns the established creed: Land writes that democracy is asserted "as a religious creed," and Yarvin, quoted by Land, calls the Cathedral's faith "Universalism," "a nontheistic Christian sect." [cite:de35_land_ebook] The design would disestablish that creed; whether it would protect anyone's worship is a question the texts leave open.

Privacy, equality and the right to leave

The Fourth Amendment protects "persons, houses, papers, and effects" against unreasonable searches. [cite:de35_na_bor] The texts examined say nothing about privacy. On equal protection they say something worse than nothing. The Fourteenth Amendment forbids a state to deny anyone "the equal protection of the laws." [cite:de35_bp_14th] Yarvin's 2009 essay on Carlyle holds that for some people character and intelligence are "more suited to mastery than slavery," and that this is "most parsimoniously explained by genetic differences." [cite:de6_mm_2021] That is a doctrine of natural inequality; the design builds no guarantee against it.

The right to leave is the texts' own answer to every other loss. "No voice, free exit," Land writes. [cite:de35_land_ebook] The American right to travel is recognised as part of the liberty the Fifth Amendment protects, since Kent v. Dulles in 1958. [cite:de25b_kent] But the exit the texts promise depends on someone else. Yarvin's surplus residents may emigrate, he wrote, only if another realm "is willing to accept them." [cite:de6_audit_le] Exit also needs money, a passport and a place to go, which [scene:de35b_what_citizens_become|the next part] and [scene:de25b_who_can_stop_you|Part Twenty-Seven] examine. [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport]

The strongest counter-reading

The texts' defenders would say the ledger counts the wrong things. Yarvin's point is that freedom and power are different, and that a stable sovereign could leave people freer in daily life than a democracy does, as the model cities show: "minimal crime and high levels of personal and economic freedom." [cite:de35_land_ebook] [cite:de35_nyt_interview] The record gives that claim a test, and it does not pass cleanly. Singapore, the model most often cited, scored 48 of 100 in Freedom House's 2026 report, and only 29 of 60 on civil liberties, the personal freedoms the design says it would keep. [cite:de8_fh_sg2026] The ledger's finding is narrower than the fear and firmer than the defence: the texts remove, in their own words, the rights by which people hold rulers to account, and promise nothing enforceable for the rest.

sections.h: "The Unproductive"
sections.html:
Every political order has to decide what it owes people who cannot or do not support themselves. Of all the questions the Dark Enlightenment texts take up, they answer this one most harshly. American law also sorts people by productivity, through work requirements for benefits and the "public charge" test for immigrants. This section sets the two side by side: what the texts say, in their own words; what policies do now; and where the line between them runs. It closes the part by testing the worst-case reading against everything the part has found.

What the texts say

Yarvin's answer is the sharpest, and it is set out in full in [scene:de6_the_hard_posts|Part Six]. In the first Patchwork post of 13 November 2008, a profit-seeking sovereign corporation running San Francisco meets residents who cost more than they pay. Its first step is to "sell their slums out from under them, obviously," with demolition, "possibly a little aerial bombing," and new districts "suitable for Russian oligarchs"; the residents may emigrate if another realm will take them. [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de6_audit_le] A week later he raised turning them "into biodiesel," called that "just kidding," and then set out his goal: "a humane alternative to genocide," which was to hold them in "permanent solitary confinement" connected to a virtual-reality interface. [cite:de6_tnr_duran] The joke marker covers the biodiesel line; the confinement proposal is stated as the goal. In plain words, Yarvin proposed the indefinite confinement of poor people a sovereign corporation found unprofitable, and presented it as better than killing them. Defenders call the post satire; no later retraction by him is on record. [cite:de6_le_contra]

Land's treatment is different in kind. He concedes that social disadvantage "in large part – perhaps overwhelmingly large part – … reflects sheer misfortune," and that "dim, impulsive, unhealthy, and unattractive people, reared chaotically in abusive families," have "every reason to curse the gods before themselves." Then he dismisses the point: "In regards to effective incentive structures, however, none of this is of the slightest importance," because "whatever is subsidized is promoted." [cite:de35_land_ebook] Elsewhere he writes that "the war on poverty creates a chronically dysfunctional underclass." [cite:de35_land_ebook] The passage is contemptuous in its description and absolute in its rule, but it is an argument against subsidy, not a call to confine or compel anyone. Yarvin's 2009 Carlyle essay adds a claim about nature, that some people are by heredity "more suited to mastery than slavery." [cite:de6_mm_2021] Thiel's 2009 essay belongs in the record for one sentence: he wrote that the growth of welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the vote to women had made "capitalist democracy" an oxymoron, and later said he did not think any class should be disenfranchised. [cite:de1_cato_thiel] None of the three texts proposes making the unproductive work.

How American law sorts by productivity now

American law has always attached conditions to help. The Immigration Act of 3 August 1882 barred any immigrant "unable to take care of himself or herself without becoming a public charge." Guidance in 1999 limited the test to cash assistance or long-term care at public expense; a 2019 rule widened it to food stamps, Medicaid and public housing used for more than twelve months in three years, and was repealed in March 2021. [cite:de35_wiki_publiccharge] In 2026 DHS rescinded the 2022 public-charge regulations, with effect from 18 September, so that officers may weigh a wider range of benefits and information. [cite:de35_ey_publiccharge] The public-charge test applies to non-citizens seeking admission or permanent residence, not to citizens.

For citizens, the sorting runs through benefits. The 1996 welfare law tied cash aid to work, and the adult caseload fell by about 85 per cent by 2024. [cite:ad16_aei_welfare] The 2025 budget law extended food-stamp work requirements to adults up to 64 and limited the exemption for parents to those with children under 14. [cite:ad11_mn_snap] From 1 January 2027, adults aged 19 to 64 covered by the Medicaid expansion must report 80 hours a month of work, community service, a work programme or half-time study, with exemptions for parents of young children, the medically frail, pregnant women and others. [cite:ad8_ccf_ifr] As of early October 2026 the start date had not moved, though five governors asked for time. [cite:ad8_audit_hfn_gov] The risk the record shows is not the rule but its administration: Arkansas's 2018 work requirement cost about 18,000 people their coverage in under a year, and the private verification service about half of states use, Equifax's The Work Number, called the new requirements "a big positive" for its business. [cite:de24b_warren_equifax]

The line between the two

Three distinctions separate today's policies from the texts' answer, and each can be checked. The first is what a person loses. A work requirement or a public-charge finding takes away a benefit or an immigration status; Yarvin's proposal takes away liberty. The second is process. The Medicaid rule lists exemptions and runs through state fair hearings; the passages in the texts describe no hearing at all. [cite:ad8_ccf_ifr] [cite:de6_tnr_duran] The third is who is sorted. Today's rules apply to defined claimants and applicants by age, ability and status; Yarvin's "surplus" are residents as such, judged by whether they pay their way. The line blurs in two places on the record: where data matching ends cover for people who qualify, as in Arkansas, and where immigration detention holds people without conviction and pays them $1 a day for work ([scene:de35_the_consequence_ladder|the consequence ladder]). [cite:de24b_warren_equifax] [cite:de32_pogo_dollar] The worst case would cross the line entirely by confining or removing citizens for being unproductive. No law, rule or official proposal to do that is on the record.

The worst-case reading, tested

The book's working hypothesis, the Sophia platform's and not a finding, is that immigration enforcement and government cuts are the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto the destination. This part asked what such a sovereign would do to the people under it. Documented: the texts' own words remove the rights by which people hold rulers to account, the vote, removal, independent courts, the press and due process, and propose confinement for the unwanted. [cite:de35_land_ebook] [cite:de35_nyt_interview] [cite:de6_tnr_duran] Documented too: every rung of the ladder below compelled labour without conviction exists in American law for some group, and for non-citizens the whole ladder has been climbed, from street face-matching to speech-based visa revocation to detention at record scale; sanctions have cut foreign judges and a UN rapporteur off from banking without a hearing. [cite:de26_404_fortify] [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de32_npr_deaths] [cite:de35_ap_icc] Compelled labour exists through the Thirteenth Amendment's exception and the $1 detainee rate, a century and a half older than the theorists. [cite:de35_lii_13th] [cite:de32_pogo_dollar]

Probable: that levers built for debts and statuses will be used wherever their triggers allow, as the widening of the public-charge test and the automated end of cover in Arkansas show; that is a reading of how such systems behave, not of anyone's stated plan. [cite:de35_ey_publiccharge] [cite:de24b_warren_equifax] Possible, as a join only: one "critic" flag read by every gatekeeper in [scene:de35_the_consequence_engine|the consequence engine]. Not supported: any theorist text prescribing forced labour, fines or purchase bans; any American designated under sanctions for speech; confinement of citizens for their status or productivity; forced labour at CECOT; and any document linking the texts to the machinery. [cite:de35_hrw_cecot] [cite:de30_dla_nspm7]

The record runs against the worst case in plain places. Courts vacated the speech-based deportation policy, the Harvard freeze, the law-firm orders and five food-restriction waivers, and the Supreme Court ruled 9–0 against GEO's shortcut in a detainee forced-labour case. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de35_hm_harvard] [cite:de24b_gma_lawfirms] [cite:de35_bd_aragon] [cite:de32_lii_menocal] Eight states struck the punishment exception from their constitutions, and Congress removed conduct conditions from student aid in 2020. [cite:de35_ap_13th2022] [cite:de35_uc_fafsa] The same administration that built much of the 2025 machinery also ordered an end to politicised debanking and barred work on a central bank digital currency, and Yarvin himself said in 2025 that a new regime "can't be" about bayoneting professors. [cite:de26_fr_14331] [cite:de26_fr_14178] [cite:de6_nyt_transcript] The same standard applies to both parties: the private detention estate, the prison-labour exception that California and Louisiana voters kept, the 2013 banking pressure on gun sellers and Canada's 2022 account freezes were the work of governments across the spectrum. [cite:de32_brennan_14006] [cite:de35_cm_prop6] [cite:de26_cfslm_chokepoint] [cite:de35_cp24_scc] What the part leaves open is the question the texts leave open: who would choose, and who could remove, the chief executive at the top of this ladder.

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Eight
chapters.title: The Missing Election: Who Picks the CEO
chapters.intro: Every system of government has to say who chooses the person at the top, who can remove that person, and what everyone else is allowed to do about it. A democratic republic answers with elections. The Dark Enlightenment's texts abolish that answer and offer another: shareholders who elect a board, a board that appoints a chief executive, and residents who may complain to customer service or leave. This part examines that substitute. The first section sets out what Moldbug, Land and Thiel actually wrote and said about choosing and removing a ruler, including what Curtis Yarvin did not answer when the question was put to him directly in January 2025. The second looks at how real systems have chosen and removed their rulers, from the East India Company and a Roman throne sold at auction to Gulf succession councils, China's party state and a modern corporate board, and at what went wrong in each. The third asks what citizens become under the design: customers rather than voters, with exit open mainly to those who hold passports and money. It closes by testing the book's worst-case reading against the material.
chapters.outro: Part Thirty-Eight found that the texts replace the election with ownership. In the passage Land quoted, shareholders elect a board that "hires and fires managers"; in Land's own gloss the shares go to existing holders of political influence, voters' portion is "estimated with appropriate derision," and residents' interest in politics would "exhibit semi-criminal proclivities." [cite:de35b_land_ebook] Moldbug's patchwork is governed "without regard to the residents' opinions" and is "all 'exit,' no 'voice.'" [cite:de35b_le] Asked in January 2025 how a bad ruler would be removed, Yarvin called it "the most important question of all" and gave no mechanism in the exchange. [cite:de35b_nyt] Real systems answered the question only where some independent power existed: Parliament curtailed and then abolished the East India Company's directors, the Danube legions ended a purchased reign, Kuwait's parliament removed an incapable emir, and OpenAI's staff reversed their board within five days, while China's congress removed the limit meant to bind its leader. [cite:de35b_banglapedia_cod] [cite:de35b_brit_julianus] [cite:de35b_mg_kuwait] [cite:de35b_gma_altman] [cite:de35b_npr_xi] Exit, the residents' only remedy, depends on passports and money, and is most available to those who already have both. [cite:de25b_usc_1185] [cite:de9_nbr_12days] The texts' end state is documented; its arrival in the United States is not supported. [scene:de36_who_reads_it_abroad|Part Thirty-Nine] turns to readers, publics and money beyond America.

sections.h: What the Texts Say About Choosing the Ruler
sections.html:
A democracy settles the question of succession on a calendar. On a fixed day, voters choose who governs, and on a later fixed day they may choose someone else. The texts examined in this book reject that arrangement, and they are explicit about it. What they put in its place, and what they leave out, can be read in their own words. [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight] examined the texts' answer to a ruler who goes wrong, the board's cryptographic keys, and Albert Hirschman's distinction between exit and voice. This section looks at the step before removal: who picks the ruler in the first place, who counts in that choice, and what the authors said when asked how a bad ruler would be replaced.

Moldbug's design: shares, a board and a manager

The clearest statement of the design is a passage from Moldbug that Nick Land reproduced in the first instalment of his 2012 serial. "To a neocameralist, a state is a business which owns a country," it begins. Ownership is divided into "negotiable shares," each paying a fraction of the state's profit, and "Each share has one vote, and the shareholders elect a board, which hires and fires managers." The business's customers, it continues, are its residents. [cite:de35b_land_ebook] Neocameralism, Moldbug's coinage, means exactly this: a state run as a joint-stock company, with the chief executive answering to owners rather than to voters. [scene:de6_the_program|Part Six] traces how the idea developed.

Moldbug presented the joint-stock form as a cure for monarchy's oldest weakness. Writing on 25 July 2007, he said it would eliminate "the hereditary principle which caused so many problems for so many monarchies." [cite:de35b_le] In "Patchwork: A Positive Vision", posted on 13 November 2008, he described a world broken into small states, "each governed by its own joint-stock corporation without regard to the residents' opinions." The remedy he offered the residents was departure: "If residents don't like their government, they can and should move." He summed up the design in one line: "The design is all 'exit,' no 'voice.'" [cite:de35b_le] Exit here means leaving; voice means speaking up, voting or protesting to change things from inside. The resident's opinion is not an input to the choice of ruler at any stage.

Land's gloss: who gets the shares

Land's own summary, which follows the quoted passage, is more specific about who the first shareholders would be, and it is the part of the design most often skipped. The first step, he wrote, is "to squash the democratic myth that a state 'belongs' to the citizenry." The point of neocameralism is "to buy out the real stakeholders in sovereign power." To find them, "the entire social landscape of political bribery ('lobbying')" must be "exactly mapped," and the administrative, legislative, judicial, media and academic privileges that such bribes buy must be "converted into fungible shares." Voters are not wholly excluded: "Insofar as voters are worth bribing," their portion of sovereignty "will be estimated with appropriate derision." [cite:de35b_land_ebook]

Once that conversion is done, Land continued, the owners "can initiate rational corporate governance, beginning with the appointment of a CEO," and the state's interest becomes "the maximization of long-term shareholder value." Residents, whom he calls "clients," no longer need to take "any interest in politics whatsoever. In fact, to do so would be to exhibit semi-criminal proclivities." If the state fails to deliver value for its taxes, which he calls "sovereign rent," residents "can notify its customer service function, and if necessary take their custom elsewhere." His summary is four words: "No voice, free exit." [cite:de35b_land_ebook] On the same page he quotes Patri Friedman, the seasteading advocate, saying that free exit is so important "that we've called it the only Universal Human Right." [cite:de35b_land_ebook]

Read plainly, the passage answers the question this part asks. The ruler is chosen by the owners of shares; the shares go to those who already hold political influence, measured by what it costs to buy; the ordinary voter's share, if any, is discounted; and the resident's only formal role after the transfer is as a customer who may complain or leave. Land wrote these sentences as a summary of Moldbug's position rather than as a manifesto of his own, but he wrote them without objection, and the serial as a whole endorses the turn from voice to exit. [cite:de35b_land_ebook]

The transition: one vote to end voting

The texts do allow one election, at the start. In the ninth part of his "Gentle Introduction" series, Moldbug described a party that wins power and holds it "only as long as it takes to hire a qualified administrator," whom he imagined as "an experienced corporate CEO, perhaps." [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de35b_le] In a talk to technology workers in 2012 he put the same idea more bluntly: "If Americans want to change their government, they're going to have to get over their dictator phobia," and the country needed "a national CEO [or] what's called a dictator." [cite:de6_pein_2014] The election in this sequence is a means of transferring authority to someone who is not then subject to election. The texts describe no second vote.

The question put directly, January 2025

In January 2025 the New York Times interviewer David Marchese put the removal question to Yarvin in its oldest form. He contrasted good monarchs with bad ones, Marcus Aurelius with Nero, and listed the dictators of the twentieth century. Yarvin replied: "Your question is the most important question of all." He went on to discuss the twentieth century, democracy's own "mixed bag" record and the Holocaust as a new kind of evil. In the exchange he did not describe any mechanism by which a bad ruler would be removed. [cite:de35b_nyt]

Two other remarks in the interview are often quoted out of context, and both should be read precisely. Asked why he trusted chief executives, Yarvin said the median Fortune 500 chief executive would outperform the present government, so one could "just pick one at random and put him or her in charge of Washington." [cite:de35b_nyt] That is an argument about the competence of corporate managers as a class, not a proposed selection rule. Asked whether he votes, he said no, that he does not believe "in actually voting at all," and that voting provides "this almost pornographic stimulus," a sense of status and relevance like supporting a sports team. [cite:de8_audit_nyt] [cite:de35b_nyt] He also said that any American monarch would have to "be the president of all Americans," reaching out to his opponents rather than demonising them. [cite:de35b_nyt] In a CNN interview in 2025 he described the monarchical bet as concentrating power "in a single individual and then just hope somehow that this is the right individual." [cite:de6_cnn_2025]

The one removal mechanism attributed to the design, a board holding cryptographic keys able to disarm the state's weapons, rests on two secondary accounts: Ava Kofman's New Yorker profile and a reviewer's summary of Patchwork. The primary wording of the 2008 posts on that point has not been located, and the mechanism should be read as a paraphrase until it is. [cite:de8_kofman_ny] [cite:de8_kossina_patchwork]

Thiel: escape rather than selection

Peter Thiel's writing does not propose a way of choosing a ruler at all. In "The Education of a Libertarian", published by Cato Unbound on 13 April 2009, he wrote: "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible," and proposed seeking "an escape from politics in all its forms" through cyberspace, outer space and seasteading. In a follow-up of 1 May 2009 he added: "While I don't think any class of people should be disenfranchised, I have little hope that voting will make things better." [cite:de10_cato] [scene:de10_education_of_a_libertarian|Part Ten] reads the essay in full. In practice Thiel has used elections rather than tried to escape them: according to Forbes, as summarised by Ballotpedia, he gave $35 million across 16 federal races in 2022. [cite:de9_audit_bp_2022] He has said he did not think Yarvin's ideas would "work." [cite:de6_cnn_2025]

Taken together, the texts answer two of the three questions and leave the third open. Owners choose; residents leave. Who removes a chief executive who refuses to go is the question Yarvin called the most important of all, and it is the one the texts do not settle. The next section turns from the texts to the record of systems that have actually had to answer it.

sections.h: How Real Systems Choose and Remove
sections.html:
The design described in the previous section has no working example; Land's quoted passage concedes that the full approach "has never been tried." [cite:de35b_land_ebook] Pieces of it have been tried, however. Companies have governed territories, thrones have been bought, families have chosen heirs by council, parties have chosen leaders behind closed doors, and corporate boards fire chief executives every year. Each of these systems had to answer the question the texts leave open: who removes a ruler, and with what power behind them. [scene:de8_tests_it_fails|Part Eight] tested the texts' named models, Singapore and Dubai, and the record of the company-states. This section looks only at the mechanics of choosing and removing, case by case, and at where each failed.

A company that ruled: the East India Company

The nearest historical match to "shareholders elect a board" is the English East India Company, which governed much of the Indian subcontinent. Its shareholders, the Court of Proprietors, elected a Court of Directors of 24 members, six of whom rotated out every April. [cite:de35b_banglapedia_cod] The arrangement did not hold on its own terms. After the Company's misgovernment of Bengal brought it to the edge of bankruptcy, Parliament intervened with the Regulating Act of 1773, which among other things doubled the stock needed to vote. [cite:de8_brit_regact] Pitt's India Act of 1784 went further: it created a parliamentary Board of Control whose consent was needed for revenue and political decisions, and after it the proprietors could discuss the directors' policies but no longer annul them. [cite:de35b_banglapedia_cod] The Court of Directors was abolished in 1858, when the Crown took over the Company's powers. [cite:de35b_banglapedia_cod] [cite:de8_brit_goi] In the one long test of shareholder sovereignty, the shareholders' vote was progressively narrowed and the final check came from outside the company, from a Parliament answerable to an electorate.

A throne for sale: Rome, 193

The texts propose that power should be openly owned and transferable. The Roman Empire once made its highest office transferable for cash, briefly. On 28 March 193, after the murder of the emperor Pertinax, the Praetorian Guard sold its support to the highest bidder. Didius Julianus outbid Sulpicianus, the dead emperor's father-in-law, by offering the largest payment to the soldiers, and was made emperor. He reigned about two months. The legions on the Danube marched on Italy under their commander Septimius Severus, and Julianus was killed in June 193. [cite:de35b_brit_julianus] The episode does not test neocameralism, which proposes shares rather than a one-off auction, but it shows the problem raised in Part Eight in its plainest form: when an office can be bought, the people with weapons decide whether the purchase stands.

Choosing by lot to defeat bribery: Venice, 1268

One long-lived republic designed its selection rule specifically against the buying of office. From 1268 the Venetian doge was chosen through ten rounds that alternated drawing names by lot with voting: colleges of 30, 40, 25 and 45 were drawn by lot, and colleges of 9, 12, 9, 11 and finally 41 were elected, the last needing 25 votes to name the doge. In a 2007 analysis, the computer scientists Miranda Mowbray and Dieter Gollmann noted that the lot made it hard for would-be bribers to predict who the final electors would be. [cite:de35b_mowbray_doge] Venice's electorate was an oligarchy of noble families, not a people. The contrast with the texts is still instructive. Yarvin's "pick one at random" was an argument about the competence of chief executives; Venice used chance for the opposite purpose, to keep any single faction or purse from capturing the choice. [cite:de35b_nyt] [cite:de35b_mowbray_doge]

Family councils and a parliament: Saudi Arabia and Kuwait

Hereditary monarchies in the Gulf, the region the texts point to, choose heirs by decree and family council. On 21 June 2017 King Salman of Saudi Arabia named his son Mohammed bin Salman, then 31, crown prince, removing his nephew Mohammed bin Nayef, 57, as heir and as interior minister. The Allegiance Council, made up of senior members of the ruling family, endorsed the change by 31 of its 34 members. [cite:de35b_aj_mbs] The council confirmed a decision; there is no record of it overturning one.

Kuwait offers a different case: a hereditary ruler removed by an elected body. On 24 January 2006 Kuwait's 65-member parliament voted unanimously, at the government's request, to remove Emir Sheikh Saad al-Abdullah al-Sabah, whom the government said had "lost his health capability" to exercise his constitutional powers; removal required a two-thirds majority. His letter of abdication arrived just after the vote, and the prime minister, Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah, succeeded him. [cite:de35b_mg_kuwait] [cite:de35b_jurist_kuwait] Even within a dynasty, the removal of an incapable ruler ran through a constitution and a vote.

The party state: China and Singapore

One-party systems choose leaders inside the party, and their stability depends on the party's own rules. In 1982 China capped the presidency at two consecutive terms, a limit associated with Deng Xiaoping and intended to prevent a return to the one-man rule of the Mao years. On 11 March 2018 the National People's Congress removed the limit by 2,958 votes to 2, with 3 abstentions; Xi Jinping had not named a successor at the end of his first term, breaking with recent practice. [cite:de35b_npr_xi] The rule that had governed succession was changed by the body it was meant to bind, which is the failure Land's quoted passage predicts for constitutions generally. [cite:de8_land_de]

Singapore, the texts' own favourite example, works differently. Its leaders change by party procedure: Lawrence Wong became prime minister on 15 May 2024, chosen as leader of the People's Action Party with the unanimous backing of its members of parliament, and the political scientist Netina Tan describes the system's resilience as resting on a planned succession. [cite:de8_cnbc_wong] [cite:de8_tan_pap] Singapore also holds general elections, though Freedom House describes politics there as dominated by the People's Action Party and the Lee family since 1959. [cite:de8_fh_sg2026] Its example shows a rule for succession, not a joint-stock sovereign.

Corporate boards: OpenAI and the founders' trust

The design borrows its vocabulary from the corporate board, so the board's own record is relevant. On 17 November 2023 the board of OpenAI dismissed its chief executive, Sam Altman, saying he had not been "consistently candid in his communications with the board." Nearly all of the company's roughly 800 employees signed a letter threatening to leave for Microsoft unless the board resigned and Altman returned. On 21 November the company announced that he would come back, with a largely new board. [cite:de35b_gma_altman] A board formally empowered to fire its chief executive did so, and was itself replaced within five days by the pressure of the people the executive led and the partner on whom the company depended.

Companies controlled by the network this book maps show the opposite design: founders shielding themselves from shareholders. Palantir's Class F shares are held in a voting trust established by Stephen Cohen, Alexander Karp and Peter Thiel, which gives the founders the ability to control up to 49.999999 per cent of the total voting power, subject to a minimum holding. [cite:de27_10q_q2_2026] [scene:de27_origins_and_control|Part Twenty-Nine] explains the structure. It is a lawful and disclosed arrangement in a company, not a state; it shows that those who build such companies often choose not to be removable by ordinary shareholders.

What the cases have in common

The following is a reading of the cases, not a finding from any one of them. In every case where a ruler was actually removed against his will or without his initiative, the removal came from someone with power of their own: a Parliament with authority over the company's charter, an army, an elected chamber operating under a constitution, or employees and a commercial partner whose departure would have emptied the company. Where no such independent power existed or chose to act, as in the Saudi council or China's congress in 2018, the body that was supposed to check the ruler confirmed the ruler's wishes. The texts name shareholders as the check, but they do not say where shareholders' power would come from if the chief executive commands the police and the army, which is the gap Part Eight identified. [scene:de8_who_enforces_the_charter|Part Eight] The record does not show that shareholders, as such, have ever removed a sovereign ruler.

sections.h: Customers, Not Voters
sections.html:
If the ruler is chosen by owners, everyone who is not an owner needs a new name. The texts supply one. In "Good Government as Good Customer Service", posted on 25 May 2007, Moldbug imagined a state called Fnargland and wrote: "Fnargland is a business. Like any business, it has no reason at all to alienate its customers." [cite:de35b_le] Land's 2012 summary calls residents "clients," gives them a "customer service function" to complain to, and leaves them the choice to "take their custom elsewhere." [cite:de35b_land_ebook] This section asks what that change of name means in practice: what a customer can and cannot do that a citizen can, who the owners would be, and who could actually use the one remedy the design offers, which is leaving.

What changes when a citizen becomes a customer

A citizen of a democratic republic has a share of the choice of government that does not depend on wealth: one vote, the right to stand for office, the right to petition and assemble, and access to courts that can rule against the state. [scene:de35_the_rights_ledger|Part Thirty-Seven] sets those rights against the texts one by one. A customer has a different relationship. The firm owes the customer the service it chooses to offer, and the customer's leverage is the threat to take business elsewhere. The texts accept this exchange openly. Land wrote that residents no longer need to take "any interest in politics whatsoever," and that to do so "would be to exhibit semi-criminal proclivities." [cite:de35b_land_ebook] Moldbug described the small states of his patchwork as governed "without regard to the residents' opinions." [cite:de35b_le]

The strongest case for the exchange, which the texts make and which [scene:de7_what_it_gets_right|Part Seven] examines, is that a ruler who profits from a well-run territory has a reason to run it well, and that competition between territories would discipline bad rulers better than elections do. The case depends on two conditions: that the owners' interest and the residents' interest coincide, and that residents can in fact leave. The texts assert the first and assume the second.

Who the owners would be

The design's first shareholders are the people who already hold influence. Moldbug's formalism, set out in "A formalist manifesto" on 23 April 2007, proposed "a rule that tells us whose wallet is whose": "let's figure out exactly who has what, now, and give them a little fancy certificate." [cite:de6_le_contra] Land's summary applies that rule to the state itself. The landscape of "political bribery" is mapped, and the privileges it buys in administration, legislation, the courts, the media and the universities become shares. [cite:de35b_land_ebook] The owners, in other words, are the existing holders of political favour, converted from informal to formal. The ordinary voter enters the calculation only "insofar as voters are worth bribing." [cite:de35b_land_ebook] The texts do not describe any later issue of shares to residents.

The two places where people associated with these ideas have actually written a constitution show how ownership and residence divide. Próspera, the private charter city on the Honduran island of Roatán, is governed by a nine-member council. Under its charter of 23 August 2018, residents select four trustees and the company that organised the zone selects four, and important decisions need a two-thirds majority, which gives the company an effective veto; about 2,000 people lived there in 2024. [cite:de22_charter] [cite:de22_wiki_prospera] Urbit, Yarvin's computer network, gives votes on its governance only to holders of its 256 "galaxies"; ordinary users, who hold "planets," have none. As of 2019, 185 of the 256 galaxies were held by the company Tlon, its employees and the employees of the Urbit Foundation. [cite:de23_compact_2025] [scene:de22_prospera_v_honduras|Part Twenty-Two] and [scene:de23_address_space|Part Twenty-Three] tell both stories. Neither is a state run by Yarvin or Land, and neither proves how a neocameral state would behave; both show owners holding the deciding vote.

Exit: who can actually leave

Leaving a country is not like changing shops. It needs a document, money, and another country willing to admit you. In the United States, federal law makes it unlawful for a citizen to leave or enter the country without a valid passport. [cite:de25b_usc_1185] In fiscal year 2025 there were 183.2 million valid American passports in circulation, a count of documents rather than people, since some people hold both a passport book and a card. [cite:de35b_usafacts_pass] The government can already deny a passport for certified tax debt above $66,000 in 2026 and for child-support arrears above $2,500. [cite:de25b_irs_passport] [cite:de25b_crs_childsupport] Renouncing citizenship carried a fee of $2,350 from 2015 until a final rule of 13 March 2026 cut it to $450; at least 8,755 Americans paid the higher fee after the cut was first promised in 2023. [cite:de35b_pbs_renounce]

The states that most restricted exit show what happens when a ruler controls the door. Soviet citizens needed exit visas, and the so-called refuseniks were denied them "for months, years, and even decades"; in 1972 the Soviet Union briefly charged emigrants "education reimbursement fees" of up to tens of thousands of dollars, which fell mainly on Jews seeking to leave for Israel or the United States, and the United States answered with the Jackson-Vanik amendment tying trade to freedom to emigrate. [cite:de25b_enc_refuseniks] [cite:de25b_crs_jv] China's use of exit bans has grown sharply, according to the rights group Safeguard Defenders. [cite:de25b_aj_china] The United States has no exit permit for citizens. [scene:de25b_who_can_stop_you|Part Twenty-Seven] sets out what the government can already do to stop a person travelling.

For those with means, exit is a different matter, and the record of this book's own subjects illustrates it lawfully. Peter Thiel obtained New Zealand citizenship in 2011 after spending a total of 12 days in the country, under an "exceptional circumstances" exemption; the New York Times reported in October 2022 that he was acquiring a Maltese passport through that country's investment scheme; and in the summer of 2026 he moved with his family to Buenos Aires. [cite:de9_nbr_12days] [cite:de9_mt_malta] [cite:de9_fortune_ba] None of this is alleged to be improper. It shows that the remedy the texts offer every resident is, in practice, most available to those who already have several passports and the money to move.

When exit replaces voice

Albert Hirschman, whose 1970 distinction between exit and voice the texts borrow, warned that the presence of exit "can therefore tend to atrophy the development of the art of voice," because those who care most about quality tend to leave first. [cite:de8_hirschman] A design that offers only exit therefore leaves behind the residents least able to go, without the one remedy, voice, that does not require money. The texts say little about those residents. Where Moldbug did address people a sovereign corporation would not want, in his 2008 "Patchwork" posts, his answer was to sell their housing out from under them and, after a line about biodiesel that he followed with "just kidding," to hold them in "permanent solitary confinement" connected to a virtual-reality interface; [scene:de6_the_hard_posts|Part Six] sets those passages out in context. [cite:de6_le_contra] [cite:de6_tnr_duran]

The worst-case reading, tested

The book's working hypothesis, which is the Sophia platform's and not a finding, is that immigration enforcement and government cuts are the occasion and a sovereign executive without a veto is the destination. This part bears on the destination. It is documented that the texts' stated end state has no election and no voice: owners choose the ruler, shares go to existing holders of influence, residents' interest in politics is described as "semi-criminal," and the only remedy left to non-owners is to leave. [cite:de35b_land_ebook] [cite:de35b_le] It is documented that Yarvin, asked in January 2025 how a bad ruler would be removed, called it "the most important question of all" and gave no mechanism in the exchange, and that the one mechanism attributed to the design, board-held keys over the state's weapons, is known only from secondary accounts. [cite:de35b_nyt] [cite:de8_kossina_patchwork]

The record of real systems runs against the design's central promise. In every case examined, rulers were removed only by someone with independent power, a Parliament, an army, an elected chamber or a workforce, and the one long experiment with shareholder sovereignty, the East India Company, ended with Parliament curtailing the shareholders and then abolishing the Court of Directors. [cite:de35b_banglapedia_cod] That a chief executive without an election would be removable by owners alone is not supported.

That the United States is moving toward the texts' end state is not supported by this part's material. No statute, order or bill examined in this book proposes abolishing federal elections, converting political influence into shares, or restricting citizens' exit by permit, and the United States has no exit permit for citizens. [cite:de25b_usc_1185] The rhyme that does exist is narrower and is documented elsewhere: the growth of what the executive can deny a person, from passports to benefits, without an election being involved at all, which [scene:de35_the_consequence_engine|Part Thirty-Seven] examines. Exit, the texts' remedy, already depends on documents the state can withhold, which is the point at which the design and the present machinery meet. The next part asks whether anyone outside the United States reads these texts, and whether publics elsewhere would want what they propose.

chapters.label: Part Thirty-Nine
chapters.title: Beyond America
chapters.intro: The Dark Enlightenment was written in English, mostly in San Francisco and Shanghai, and most of what this book has examined happened in the United States. This part looks outward. The first section maps who outside America has documented ties to the texts: where Nick Land lives and publishes, where Curtis Yarvin has been invited to speak and what he said there, and which governments the authors praise, keeping the rule that a writer praising a state is not that state adopting his ideas. The second asks whether publics elsewhere would want the kind of rule the texts propose, using the best cross-national polling on strong leaders and military rule. The third follows foreign and sovereign money, which is documented in the network's companies and not in its theorists. The fourth examines China's social credit system, the one existing system often described as the integrated machine this book's worst case imagines, separating what it is from what it is rumoured to be, and closes by testing the worst-case reading against the material.
chapters.outro: Part Thirty-Nine found that the Dark Enlightenment's footprint abroad is documented and small. Nick Land has written from Shanghai since the 2000s and treats China as the likely core of a "Modernity 2.0"; Curtis Yarvin's foreign platforms were a critical Paris review, in which he called Bukele proof the world is "ripe for monarchy," a privately hired Oxford lecture, and a Brazilian party convention and meeting with MBL members. [cite:de36_land_ebook] [cite:de36_lgc_bukele] [cite:de36_cherwell_oxford] [cite:de36_publica] No state claims the texts as a source, and no Yarvin or Land tie to Milei is documented. Publics mostly reject unchecked rule: a 26 per cent median across 24 countries called a strong leader without parliament or courts good, against 77 per cent for representative democracy, and openness is higher among poorer, right-leaning and, in the United States, younger respondents. [cite:de36_pew_systems] [cite:de36_pew_short] Foreign and sovereign money is documented in the network's companies, from Qatar and Saudi stakes in X, xAI and SpaceX to Norway's index holding in Palantir, and not in its theorists. [cite:de11_cnbc_coinvest] [cite:de36_bl_humain] [cite:de36_aicio_nbim] China's social credit system has no national score; its core is a court list of judgment defaulters enforced by many gatekeepers, a joint-punishment pattern the United States has only in single-purpose lists. [cite:de36_daum] [cite:de36_scmp_ndrc] The next part applies the same documented-ties standard to Israel, in [scene:de37_palantir_and_israel|Part Forty].

sections.h: Who Reads It Abroad
sections.html:
An idea's reach abroad is easy to overstate. Commentators have linked the Dark Enlightenment to governments from Budapest to Beijing on the strength of resemblance: a strong executive here, contempt for parliaments there. Resemblance is not influence. This section uses the same standard as the rest of the book, mapping only documented ties: who wrote where, who published whom, who invited whom to speak, and who cited the texts by name. It keeps two further distinctions. A theorist praising a foreign state is a fact about the theorist, not about the state. And the neighbouring ideas that circulate abroad, from Javier Milei's anarcho-capitalism to Nayib Bukele's security state, are different things with their own texts, as [scene:de16_neighbours_not_the_same|Part Sixteen] sets out for the American neighbours.

Shanghai: where Land writes

The Dark Enlightenment's second author has lived outside the West for most of the century. After leaving the University of Warwick in 1998, Nick Land resurfaced in the 2000s as a journalist in Shanghai, where he wrote the 2012 serial whose title named this body of writing and where he still lived in October 2025. [cite:de4_haider] [cite:de4_spectator] [scene:de4_ccru_acceleration|Part Four] tells that story. His published work in China includes two guidebooks issued in 2010 by China Intercontinental Press, The Shanghai World Expo Guide 2010 and Shanghai Basics. [cite:de36_wiki_land] That is commercial publishing, and no document shows Chinese state funding of his political writing.

Land's own words about China are admiring and specific. The serial names Hong Kong, Singapore and Dubai, in a passage he quotes, as the closest equivalents of the neocameral state, and later uses Singapore, Hong Kong, Taipei and Shanghai as its measure of cities safe to walk at night. [cite:de8_land_de] In its final instalments he sketched three futures for modernity and called "Modernity 2.0," modernisation "re-invigorated from a new ethno-geographical core," the "most encouraging and plausible scenario," adding that "if China remains even approximately on its current track it will be assuredly realized." [cite:de36_land_ebook] In a 2025 interview with The Spectator he called China's mix of communism and capitalism "the greatest political engine of social and economic development the world has ever known." [cite:de4_spectator] None of this shows the Chinese state reading or adopting his work. It shows a writer in China treating China as the model.

Land's books travel through small publishers in several countries: Urbanomic in Britain, which issued his academic writing in Fanged Noumena (2011) and Fission (2014); Imperium Press, which published The Dark Enlightenment in print in 2022; and Passage Publishing in the United States, which issued his Xenosystems writings in 2024. [cite:de36_wiki_land] [cite:de4_spectator] He met Yarvin in person for the first time in San Francisco in February 2026. [cite:de36_wiki_land]

Yarvin's platforms abroad

Yarvin's documented engagements outside the United States are few and recent. In April 2025 the Paris-based review Le Grand Continent, which publishes in French, Italian and Spanish, ran a three-part interview with him conducted by Gilles Gressani and Mathéo Malik. [cite:de36_lgc_bukele] In it he said that "Bukele es otra prueba de que el mundo está maduro para la monarquía," that Bukele, El Salvador's president, is further proof the world is ripe for monarchy. [cite:de36_lgc_bukele] In the same interview he criticised China's Communist Party, which he said would rather "censurar y ocultar con mentiras" (censor and hide with lies) an evident reality, while describing the students and workers of Tiananmen Square as "una operación del NED, es decir, de la CIA con otro nombre," an operation of the National Endowment for Democracy, which he called the CIA by another name.
