Tolkien's fiction: Palantir Technologies, after the seeing stones; Valar Ventures, registered in New Zealand in 2009, after the powers that shaped Middle-earth; Mithril Capital, founded in 2012, after the rare metal, which a partner said "protects" and is "transformative"; and Rivendell One LLC and Lembas LLC, vehicles named in a 2016 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission and used to sell Facebook shares. [cite:de39_qz_names] The reporting does not say who chose each name. Anduril, the defence company, is often added to the list, but it is Palmer Luckey's company and Luckey named it after the sword; Founders Fund was an investor. [cite:de39_cm_rings] [cite:de39_qz_names] Thiel has been reported as reading and rereading the books in his teens, and in 2023 told The Atlantic that he had read the series at least a dozen times. [cite:de39_cm_rings] [cite:de39_lithub_fan]

The Sophia platform reads the naming as a vocabulary chosen by a reader who knew the story well, so that the story's warnings travel with the names whether or not anyone intended them. The strongest counter-reading is that names from a beloved book are common in technology, that a name is a gesture of taste and not a programme, and that nothing shows the founders meant the darker parts of the story to apply. The platform accepts this as the plain reading; what follows reads the story, not anyone's mind.

Interpretation, not finding: who looks, and who is seen

In Tolkien's fiction the palantíri are seeing stones made by the Elves and used by Men. They show distant things to whoever holds them. Their danger lies in what happens when a stronger mind is on the other end: the stone in Orthanc beguiled Saruman, and Sauron, holding another stone, used it to deceive his enemies and to drive Denethor, the steward of Gondor, to despair by showing him true things chosen to make defeat seem certain. Denethor burned himself holding his stone. The same stone of Orthanc was later used by Gandalf and Aragorn against Sauron. [cite:de39_arda_stones]

The Sophia platform reads the stone as an image of a fused data view, a single screen on which records from many sources appear joined around one person. Earlier parts documented such views being built: Palantir's case-management system for ICE "structures and links data collected from these vendors and other commercial entities", and ImmigrationOS gathers the agency's data streams into a central hub. [cite:de28_brennan_consol] In the platform's reading the stone has two sides that never meet. The one who looks chooses what to search; the one who is seen does not know a search has happened. And the user can be corrupted by the stone without any villain behind it, as Saruman and Denethor were: a view that shows true fragments, selected and joined, can produce false certainty. The record holds an example of the mechanism, not of any person's corruption: when a federal citizenship-check system was run against 18 million Texas voter records, 2,724 people were flagged, and about a fifth of those were later found to be citizens. [cite:de19_npr_save] The record was true in each fragment and wrong in its conclusion.

The strongest counter-reading starts with the story itself. In Tolkien the stones are not evil; they were made for communication between allied kingdoms, and the rightful heir used one to good effect. The corruption came from a hostile mind on the other end, not from the stone. Palantir says it does not collect, store or sell personal data, that it acts as a processor for customers who decide what can be done with their data, and that its software records what each user does by default. [cite:de27_pal_notdata] [cite:de27_pal_pcl] Thiel's own stated purpose, in 2016, was the reverse of the platform's image: helping a government swamped with data to "make sense" of it so that it could "end indiscriminate surveillance". [cite:de10_fortune_palantir] [scene:de27_capability_not_intent|Part Twenty-Nine] sets out both cases at length.

Interpretation, not finding: the restrainer and the stone

This reading begins with Thiel's own. The katechon, "the one who withholds" in Paul's second letter to the Thessalonians, is the force that holds back the Antichrist; tradition has identified it with the Roman Empire, the Church and other powers, and Paul never explains it. [cite:de10_wiki_katechon] [cite:de10_rns_christensen] Thiel has said that the slogan of the Antichrist is "peace and safety" and that the danger is a "one world totalitarian state". [cite:de10_douthat_tx] In his 2025 lectures, as reported from leaked audio, he called the American empire "the natural candidate for Katechon" and also "ground zero of the one-world state", and named financial surveillance and the sanctions architecture among the tools of such a state. [cite:de10_reason] [scene:de10_girard_and_the_katechon|Part Ten] covers the argument in full.

The Sophia platform reads the two images together. On Thiel's own terms the restrainer and the danger can live in the same empire. The platform's reading is that they can also live in the same instrument: a system that sees enough to restrain catastrophe also sees enough to rule, and the stone that watches for the Antichrist watches everyone. The strongest counter-reading is Thiel's: his named fear is a global authority, not a national government doing its lawful work; he has argued against concentration at the world level, not for it at home; and no document shows him directing how any customer uses Palantir's software. [cite:de10_douthat_tx] [cite:de10_reason] The platform's reading turns his own warning back on his tools; it does not show that he made that turn.

Interpretation, not finding: the archons and the copy

The Apocryphon of John survives in three copies among the Nag Hammadi codices, found in Egypt in 1945 and probably made in the fourth century, and in a fourth copy in Berlin. In it the visible world is made by Ialdabaoth, "a lesser being, a ruler (archon)", who is "unaware of any power above him" and rules the cosmos "with subordinate powers who are his own imperfect offspring". The material world is "a copy of the perfect spiritual realm", and birth into it brings "a forgetting" of the divine origin. [cite:de39_brit_apjohn]

The Sophia platform reads the archons as offices, not persons: administrators of an order made of copies. A modern administrative state decides on the record of a person, not the person, and the record is a copy. The platform's reading is that the danger the text names is a ruler who does not know there is anything above him, and in institutional terms that is a process that acts on the copy and no longer checks it against the person or against the law above it. The Texas flags read above are the copy mistaken for the person. [cite:de19_npr_save] The platform adds a warning the lens requires. Images of hidden rulers have a long history of being turned against a people or a faith; this reading names no group and refuses that use entirely.

The strongest counter-reading is that the Gnostic texts concern the cosmos and salvation, not government, and that reading them as an account of records offices is anachronism. Records also protect rights: a court docket, a birth certificate and an audit log are copies too, and they let a citizen prove a mistake and hold an office to account. In the Texas case, it was a check of the copy against the person that found the error. [cite:de19_npr_save]

Interpretation, not finding: the second extraction

Robert Monroe (1915–1995), a radio executive who wrote three books on out-of-body experience, coined the word "loosh" in Far Journeys (1985) for a kind of energy produced by beings in intense fear, grief or despair, which in his account non-human beings harvest. His claims are not scientifically established. [cite:de39_wiki_monroe]

The Sophia platform uses the word only as a lens and only on measured outcomes. Its reading is of a double extraction: a surveillance system takes data from the people it watches, and the fear it creates does further work of its own, changing behaviour without any officer acting. The measured outcomes are these. In the KFF and New York Times survey of 1,805 immigrants, taken between 28 August and 20 October 2025, 41 per cent feared that they or a family member could be detained or deported, up from 26 per cent in 2023, with the rise largest among lawfully present immigrants and naturalised citizens; 30 per cent said they avoided travel, work, public places or medical care; and 40 per cent reported effects on their health such as stress, anxiety or sadness. [cite:de39_kff_2025]

The strongest counter-reading is plain. Monroe's harvesting beings have no evidence behind them, and an effect is not a design. Deterrence has been an openly stated aim of border enforcement since at least the Border Patrol's strategic plan of 1994, adopted under President Clinton and used since; an aim stated in public is not a hidden harvest. [cite:de39_wiki_ptd] The survey measures what people report, not what caused it. And no document shows anyone gaining from fear as such. The platform keeps the word for what it is, a writer's image applied to a measured cost.

Each reading is offered because it makes a documented structure easier to see, not because it shows anything the record does not. [scene:de39_the_runtime|The next section] turns from story to code.

sections.h: The Runtime: Reading Institutions as Code
sections.html:
The second family of images comes from software. Objective-C is the programming language in which Apple's Mac and iPhone software was written for decades, and its most unusual feature is the runtime, the layer that decides, at the moment a program is running, which piece of code answers a request. Apple's own guide puts it plainly: "messages aren't bound to method implementations until runtime." [cite:de39_apple_msg] A request carries a name; what the name does is looked up only when it is called, and it can be changed while the program runs. The Sophia platform reads institutions the same way: an office, a title or a rule keeps its name while what it does is swapped underneath. This section is interpretation throughout; each pattern is described from the documentation, translated, set beside a documented fact and answered by the strongest counter-reading.

Interpretation, not finding: swizzling, the same title with new behaviour

Method swizzling lets a programmer "swap the implementations of two methods" while the program runs, so that a call to a familiar name runs different code; a standard reference advises that it "should always be done in load()", before the rest of the program starts. [cite:de39_nsh_swizzle] In plain words: the label on the button stays the same, and the button does something else.

The Sophia platform reads the federal civil service through this pattern. On 20 January 2025 an executive order renamed Schedule F as Schedule Policy/Career, and on 3 June 2026 a further order moved listed positions into it and exempted them "from the adverse action procedures" that protect career staff. [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] The job titles and the work remain; the rule behind them, how a person in the job can be removed, was swapped. [scene:de30_rage_to_schedule|Part Thirty-Two] traces the change. The strongest counter-reading is that swizzling is hidden and this was not: the orders were published, the rule went through notice in the Federal Register, unions sued, and the same order states that the positions "will be filled based on merit and not political affiliation". [cite:de30_wh_eo14410] [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412] The swap is also reversible in public: Schedule F was created in October 2020, revoked in 2021 and restored in 2025, each time by a signed order. [cite:de30_crs_lsb11412]

Interpretation, not finding: the proxy, no answerable party

Apple describes NSProxy as a class for objects "that act as stand-ins for other objects or for objects that don't exist yet". When an object cannot answer a request itself, forwarding passes it to another, and the forwarding is "transparent to the message sender". Asked whether it can do the thing it just did, the stand-in can truthfully answer no. [cite:de39_apple_proxy] [cite:de39_apple_fwd] In plain words: the one you asked is not the one who acted, and neither has to say so.

The platform reads the commercial data market this way. ICE bought licences to Penlink's tools, including Webloc, which can watch an area for phones and follow devices over time, and an internal ICE legal analysis said the data "can be queried without a warrant"; it bought licences, not the company. [cite:de25_ffp_penlink] [cite:de25_404_webloc] A Medicaid dataset sent to ICE on 7 January 2026 reached Palantir over a Microsoft Teams chat, according to a declaration in a California court; Palantir says it acts "as a data processor, not a data controller". [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de27_pal_notdata] The broker says the agency decides; the processor says the customer decides; the agency says the data was bought, not seized. In the platform's reading, every link forwards and none answers. The strongest counter-reading is that the law already names who answers: the agency is the controller, and Palantir's own statement says so. Oversight has followed the chain: seventy members of Congress asked the DHS inspector general to examine the Penlink purchase, a court paused the Medicaid sharing, and Montana in 2025 became the first state to bar its agencies from buying such data without a warrant or investigative subpoena. [cite:de25_keyt_letter] [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid] [cite:de26_reason_mt282]

Interpretation, not finding: key-value observing, watched without knowing

Key-value observing lets one object be "notified of changes to specified properties of other objects". Apple's implementation notes are striking: when an observer registers, the runtime quietly changes the watched object's class to a generated one, while the object's own report of its class still returns the true one. [cite:de39_apple_kvo] [cite:de39_apple_kvoimpl] In plain words: the thing being watched is altered to make watching possible, and if asked, it says it is unchanged.

The platform reads data bought on the open market and administrative subpoenas this way. A government report declassified in June 2023 found that commercially available data "can reveal sensitive and intimate information" that once could have been obtained only by targeted collection. [cite:de28_lawfare_cai] [cite:de29_fortune_cai] In March 2025 Google answered an immigration subpoena for a student journalist's account without notifying him first. [cite:de28_int_thomasjohnson] The person's life goes on unchanged from the inside while it is observed from the outside. The strongest counter-reading is that observation of this kind is fenced, and the fences have held in court: the Supreme Court's Carpenter decision of 2018 requires a warrant for historical phone-location records, a magistrate ordered Meta not to unmask Instagram accounts in September 2025, and an encrypted messenger served with a subpoena could give only two timestamps. [cite:de26_jurist_carpenter] [cite:de28_int_meta] [cite:de26_sw_signal] [scene:de28_brokers_and_doctrine|Part Thirty] sets out the doctrine and its limits.

Interpretation, not finding: +load, the charter that runs first

The +load method is "invoked whenever a class or category is added to the Objective-C runtime", and it runs in a fixed order before much of the rest of the program has started. [cite:de39_apple_load] In plain words: some code runs before anything that might check it has been switched on.

The platform reads first-day instruments this way. On 20 January 2025 the order creating DOGE directed agencies to give it "full and prompt access to all unclassified agency records, software systems, and IT systems", and on 24 January 17 inspectors general, the internal watchdogs, were dismissed without the thirty days' notice to Congress the law requires. [cite:de19_eo14158] [cite:de31_npr_igs] Próspera's charter in Honduras rested on a fifty-year legal stability guarantee written before the country's Congress repealed the law that allowed it. [cite:de22_eyn_2022] The strongest counter-reading is that first-day orders are routine for every new administration, and that oversight loaded anyway: Senator Grassley objected in public at once, the DOGE temporary organisation ended on 4 July 2026 as its own order provided, and Honduras's Supreme Court ruled the zone decrees unconstitutional. [cite:de31_npr_igs] [cite:de21_ee_end] [cite:de23_riotimes_icsid]

Interpretation, not finding: objc_msgSend, one point of dispatch

Every request in an Objective-C program passes through one function, objc_msgSend, which looks it up in a dispatch table and caches the result. [cite:de39_apple_msg] In plain words: all traffic runs through one junction.

The platform reads integration platforms this way. Palantir's case system is being made the "authoritative data source" for ICE's investigations arm; a 2026 statement of work for LexisNexis data requires connections to "the Palantir platform"; and Treasury in September 2025 engaged Palantir to build a "common API layer", a shared set of connections, for IRS systems. [cite:de28_brennan_consol] [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:de27_treasury_api] [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty] grades each join. The strongest counter-reading is that one junction is also one place to watch: Palantir's software logs each user's actions by default, it says it is not a vendor on any project to unify databases across federal agencies, and a single dispatch point is easier to audit than a hundred private copies. [cite:de27_pal_pcl] [cite:de19_palantir_record]

Interpretation, not finding: as above, so below

The phrase "as above, so below" is a modern paraphrase, popularised by Helena Blavatsky, of a line in the Emerald Tablet, a Hermetic text whose oldest version is Arabic, from the late eighth or early ninth century; Newton translated the line as "That which is below is like that which is above". [cite:de39_wiki_emerald] The Sophia platform reads the runtime patterns through this correspondence: the same structure appears in a program, in an institution and in a person's inner life, and the contemplative traditions that taught self-knowledge as freedom can be captured and sold back as control. The strongest counter-reading is that correspondence finds a pattern anywhere it looks: every one of these code patterns was built by engineers for ordinary reasons, swizzling for testing and analytics among them, and the same lens could be laid over any government of any party. That is exactly why it is not evidence.

The worst-case reading, tested

Nothing in this part moves a grade. The readings point at structures earlier parts already documented, a fused view, chains of stand-ins, observation without notice, first-day orders and a single junction for data, and those structures keep the grades given them in [scene:de34_the_end_to_end_map|Part Thirty-Six] and [scene:de28_the_ecosystem_map|Part Thirty]. [cite:de28_brennan_consol] [cite:de25_404_webloc] Any inference from the images to intent or design is not supported: a name taken from a novel, a fear measured in a survey or a resemblance to a programming pattern shows nothing about what anyone planned, and no document shows a plan. [scene:de38_the_honest_nulls|Part Forty-One] What the readings do is point both ways. Each image of capture came with a documented counterweight, a published rule, an audit log, a warrant requirement, a court order or a state law, and the record runs against the worst case wherever those counterweights have held. [cite:de26_jurist_carpenter] [cite:de24b_npr_medicaid]

chapters.label: Part Forty-Three
chapters.title: The Verdict and What to Watch
chapters.intro: This part closes the book. The first section gathers every grade the earlier parts gave the worst-case reading into one scorecard, sub-claim by sub-claim, with the part that grounds each one and the places where the record runs against it, separate rows for non-citizens and citizens, and an aggregate that is labelled as the Sophia platform's editorial synthesis and whose method is stated so that a reader can recompute it. The second lists the dated and pending events, rechecked on 28 October 2026, that would move those grades in either direction: court dates, contract renewals, data-sharing notices, oversight requests, the midterm elections and the powers the president has said he could use. The third turns to what has held, and to what ordinary people can do that the record shows works, before the part and the book close with the worst-case reading, tested.
chapters.outro: The book set out to test a reading, not to prove it. The record shows that the destination is written down, in the texts' own words: a state owned like a company, run by a chief executive, with no vote for those who live in it. [cite:de8_land_de] [cite:de8_cnn_yarvin] It shows that the occasions happened, an office that cut the government by executive order and an enforcement force enlarged and funded to 2029, and that the machinery exists in every layer, with several of its joins on paper and its brakes thinner than they were. [cite:de17_eo_text] [cite:de32_aic_hr1] [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de0_slaughter] It shows that machinery turned on non-citizen critics for their speech, and on some citizens in specific cases, most of them since withdrawn, enjoined or still in court. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de28_aclu_doe] It does not show a plan, a line from the texts to any office, or an executive that no court, legislature or electorate can stop; the judges, states, juries, reporters, owners and voters who said no are part of the same record. [cite:de17_li_oped] [cite:de33_rollcall_illinois] [cite:de31_ap_house] The grades will move, and [scene:de40_watch_list|the watch list] says where to look. What the record finally shows is that the outcome is not yet written, and that the people who will write it include the ones reading this book.

sections.h: The Worst-Case Scorecard
sections.html:
The preface set out a hypothesis from the Sophia platform so that the record could answer it. In its strongest form it holds that immigration enforcement and the campaign against government waste were the occasions, and that a sovereign executive without a veto, the end state the Dark Enlightenment texts describe, is the destination: that the tools built to find, track and remove immigrants, and the powers taken to cut and purge the civil service, add up to the machinery such a state would need, and could be turned on anyone who criticises those in charge. Forty-two parts have tested pieces of that reading. This section gathers every grade in one place. It adds no new evidence; each row below rests on a part that sets out the record in full, and the reader can follow the link to check it.

The method, disclosed

A hypothesis this large cannot be true or false as a single sentence, so the scorecard breaks it into the sub-claims it needs, in the order the argument runs: the destination as written, the people and money that might carry it, the occasions, the machinery, the removal of brakes, the force, the turn of the machinery on critics, and the destination reached. Each sub-claim keeps the grade the grounding part gave it, in the book's four registers. Documented means a primary record or independent named reporting shows it. Probable means several documented facts point the same way and none points against, but the link itself is not on paper. Possible is allowed only for joins between systems, never for facts about people: technically feasible, with no document. Not supported means the record does not show it, or shows the opposite. A fourth column says where the record runs against the hypothesis even when a row is documented, because a fact can be true and still be checked.

Where the hypothesis turns on people who are not citizens and people who are, the scorecard gives them separate rows. The law treats them differently, the machinery has been used on them differently, and merging them would make the record look either stronger or weaker than it is.

What the rows show

The shape of the table matters more than any one line in it. The documented rows cluster at the two ends that need no plan: the texts' own words and the machinery of the state. The texts do describe an owned state run by a chief executive with "no voice" for residents, and Yarvin said in 2025 that power should be concentrated "in a single individual." [cite:de8_land_de] [cite:de8_cnn_yarvin] The state does hold, buy and join records at a scale no earlier civilian agency reached, with a Medicaid file sent on to Palantir's software over a chat channel in January 2026 and travel records passed from TSA to ICE more than 31,000 times. [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice] And the brakes did thin: the Supreme Court let presidents remove commissioners at will on 29 June 2026, and about 8,000 senior officials became removable by an order of 3 June. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de30_wh_eo14410]

The rows graded not supported cluster in the middle, where the hypothesis needs a connection: a plan, a hand-off from the texts to an office, money to the theorists, a programme against citizens. Those are the places the record would show such a thing if it existed, in filings, sworn statements, contracts and court findings, and it does not. [cite:de17_li_oped] [cite:de16_natcon_signers] [cite:de30_dla_nspm7] The probable rows sit between, and each names what would settle it.

Non-citizens and citizens

For people who are not citizens, almost the whole chain has been run. A face can be matched in the street, records joined, a visa revoked for speech, a person detained and a $1-a-day work programme offered, and a federal court found that a policy of targeting non-citizen academics for their speech violated the First Amendment before vacating it on 22 January 2026. [cite:de26_404_fortify] [cite:de30_audit_aaup] [cite:de32_pogo_dollar] For citizens the record holds cases, not a system: subpoenas to unmask critics that DHS withdrew when challenged, a Global Entry card revoked three days after an agent named an observer, a link alleged in her pending suit and denied by CBP, revoked clearances, and orders against law firms that four judges struck down. [cite:de28_aclu_doe] [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] [cite:de24b_kvia_gabbard] [cite:de24b_gma_lawfirms]

The aggregate, labelled as editorial synthesis

Any single verdict on a hypothesis this broad is a judgment, not a finding, and what follows is the Sophia platform's editorial synthesis, with its method stated so that a reader who weighs the rows differently can recompute it. The first method is a plain tally, every row counting once and no row weighted: of the 25 sub-claims, 10 are documented, 5 probable, 1 possible as a join and 9 not supported. The second method treats the hypothesis as the chain it is, occasion to machinery to the turn on critics to the destination, and grades the whole by its weakest necessary link. For non-citizens, the occasion, the machinery and the turn are documented and the destination, a ruler no court or legislature can stop, is not supported. For citizens, the turn as a programme and the destination are both not supported.

Read together, the two methods say one thing. The occasion and the means are documented; the plan and the destination are not. That is neither the comfort of "nothing is happening" nor the alarm of "it has already happened." It is a narrower and more useful finding: the parts of a machine exist, several are joined, its brakes are thinner than they were, and what has stood between the parts and the worst case, as of October 2026, has been agreements, rules, judges, legislators and voters. Each of those can change, which is why [scene:de40_watch_list|the next section] lists the dated events that would move these grades in either direction. [cite:de28_brennan_consol] [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] [cite:de21_usat_dividend]

sections.h: The Watch List
sections.html:
A grade in this book is a statement about the record on a date, 28 October 2026, not a forecast. The record keeps moving, and the scorecard in [scene:de40_worst_case_scorecard|the previous section] is only useful if a reader can see what would change it. This section lists the triggers: dated or pending events, each checkable in a public docket, a contract database, a federal register or an election result, with the row it would move and in which direction. Some would push a grade toward the worst case; as many would push it away. The list builds on the four missing pieces set out in [scene:de34_missing_pieces_and_triggers|Part Thirty-Six] and was rechecked for this section on 28 October 2026.

The courts

The nearest date is a conference. On 6 November 2026 the Supreme Court is due to consider whether to hear GEO Group's challenge to the Washington verdict that required it to pay the state's minimum wage to detainees who worked in its Tacoma centre, instead of the $1 a day the federal programme has set since 1950. The petition was filed on 9 January 2026; the Court asked for the government's views in May, and the United States filed its brief on 15 September. [cite:de40_scotus_25828] [cite:de32_wa_nwauzor] [cite:de32_pogo_dollar] A refusal to hear the case would leave the $23.2 million judgment standing and keep state wage law as a check on the "compel" rung of [scene:de35_the_consequence_ladder|the consequence ladder]; a grant followed by a reversal would weaken it. Neither would make compelled labour a policy.

Early in 2027 the Court is expected to hear argument in U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, No. 25-1103, which it agreed to decide in October 2026. The question is whether the service is an agency subject to the Freedom of Information Act or an adviser to the President outside it, and whether the watchdog CREW may take discovery, including the deposition of its administrator, Amy Gleason. [cite:de40_ncc_doge] [cite:de40_kmph_doge] A ruling that the service was outside the Act would settle in law the opacity that [scene:de21_the_ending|Part Twenty-One] graded probable as a matter of design; a ruling the other way would open DOGE's records to the public.

Mahmoud Khalil, a lawful permanent resident arrested in March 2025 and found removable on the Secretary of State's determination that his advocacy harmed American foreign policy, petitioned the Supreme Court in October 2026 after a divided appeals court held that he could not litigate his claims before a judge until his immigration case ended. Justice Alito had twice extended his time to file, the second time to 19 October. ABC News reported that the justices were likely to consider the petition in January; he was free pending it and has not been charged with any crime. [cite:de40_scotus_26a90] [cite:de40_abc_khalil] [cite:de34_ccr_khalil] The case decides how quickly a non-citizen critic can reach a federal judge, the remedy row in the scorecard's second table.

Four appeals bear on the turn against critics. In AAUP v. Rubio the government appealed the vacatur of its speech-based deportation policy to the First Circuit on 9 February 2026, and the plaintiffs cross-appealed; the district court refused to stay most of its judgment. [cite:de40_cl_aaup] The challenge by four law firms to the executive orders against them was argued in the D.C. Circuit on 14 May 2026, where the panel appeared inclined to keep the orders blocked; no decision had been published by 28 October. [cite:de40_chn_lawfirms] [cite:de40_bl_lawfirms] In the case of Francesca Albanese, the UN rapporteur sanctioned in July 2025, a district judge enjoined the sanctions on 13 May 2026, and the same appeals court stayed that injunction pending appeal on 15 June 2026 without ruling on whether the sanctions are lawful. [cite:de36_audit_albanese_pi] [cite:de40_jc_albanese] [cite:de34_jurist_albanese] And a Minnesota observer's suit over the loss of her Global Entry card remained pending in the Southern District of California. [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] An appellate ruling upholding any of these measures would move row 19 or row 20 toward the worst case; rulings against them would hold it where it is.

Two cases decide how far the state's own records travel. In California v. HHS, Judge Vince Chhabria's injunction of 29 December 2025 limits what Medicaid data HHS may give ICE to five fields on people not lawfully present; at a hearing in September 2026 he said holders of valid visas should be protected and told the parties to agree, category by category, on who else is. No further ruling had been found by 28 October. [cite:de40_bl_medicaid] [cite:de40_chn_medicaid] In the welfare case, Chief Judge James Boasberg refused on 28 September 2026 to block an HHS notice letting TANF recipients' information go to DHS, and the notice took effect on 30 September. [cite:de24b_bl_tanf] The first documented enforcement use of TANF records would move row 14 from possible toward documented. In PEER v. Trump, the challenge to the new civil-service schedule, motions to dismiss and to amend were pending, with no injunction sought. [cite:de40_cl_peer]

Contracts and systems

The integration layer runs on orders with end dates. The Army's order for Palantir to sustain its Personnel Data Environment, $3.68 million, runs to 15 November 2026. [cite:de24b_govly_pde] ICE's newest Palantir order, $86.3 million to modernise the case system of its removal operations, runs from 5 May 2026 to 4 May 2027. [cite:de27_hg_ero] ImmigrationOS itself was added in 2025 as a $29.9 million modification to an older order for ICE's investigative case system, which can be extended to 26 September 2027. [cite:de40_os_immos] [cite:de40_hg_icm] Renewals at larger scope, or a new order joining HART or welfare data, would move row 13 or 14; a lapse would not, because the data already joined stays joined. DHS's biometric system, HART, was scheduled to reach initial operation no later than September 2026; no public confirmation that it had was found by 28 October. [cite:de40_bu_hart] Its operation would supply the nearest thing to the identity spine [scene:de34_missing_pieces_and_triggers|Part Thirty-Six] found missing.

Oversight, directives and elections

Three questions put to the executive in 2026 were unanswered at the date of this book. The DHS inspector general opened an audit of biometric data security in February 2026 and had published no report. [cite:de28_warner_audit] Thirty-three members of Congress asked DHS on 14 April 2026 for every dataset in its Palantir systems and any use against observers and protesters, with no published reply. [cite:de28_goldman_letter] And the Attorney General confirmed on 11 February 2026 that a list of domestic terrorist organisations exists under her December 2025 memorandum, but declined to share it. [cite:de34_int_list] Senators reported in September 2026 a Treasury review of three named nonprofits; no revocation is on record. [cite:de30_wyden_letter] The publication of the list with legal effect, or a first revocation, would move row 21; a report finding no misuse would move row 22 down.

The midterm elections fall on 3 November 2026. Federal law makes it a crime to station troops or armed men at polling places. [cite:de32_votebeat_polls] Asked by TIME about an emergency before the vote, the president said he did not rule "anything out or in," and of the Insurrection Act, "I've never used it. I could use it." It had not been invoked as of 28 October 2026. [cite:de40_dbeast_time] [cite:de32_hill_time] An invocation, or troops near the polls, would be the largest single move on the scorecard, against rows 23 and 25. An election held and certified in the ordinary way would be the strongest evidence that row 25 stays where it is. The vice president, the one person in this book's network in the line of succession, has said he will decide on 2028 after the midterms. [cite:de12_cnn_2028]

Two kinds of trigger are missing from the dated list because they cannot be dated: a document and a refusal. A memo, a sworn account or a disclosed message showing that someone in power set out to build what the texts describe would move the not-supported rows faster than any ruling, and [scene:de38_the_honest_nulls|Part Forty-One] lists where such a document would be found if it existed. [cite:de17_li_oped] The other is the moment someone asked to carry out an unlawful order declines, which military law expects of an order that is "manifestly illegal"; no refusal of that kind is on the public record for 2025 or 2026. [cite:de32_stripes_orders] [scene:de40_the_garden|The last section] turns to those people.

sections.h: The Garden
sections.html:
This book has spent most of its length on machinery: the texts that describe a state run like a company, the money and people around them, and the systems a government now holds to find, join, flag and confine. The last section turns to the other half of the record, the part that kept the worst case from being a finding. The title borrows an image rather than an argument. A machine is built once and then runs; a garden has to be kept, by many hands, season after season, and it fails quietly when no one tends it. The checks that held in 2025 and 2026 behaved more like the second than the first. None of them worked by itself, and each depended on particular people doing particular work.

What held

The courts held more often than the worst case predicts, and less often than its opponents hoped. A federal judge found that a policy of targeting non-citizen academics for their speech violated the First Amendment and vacated it on 22 January 2026. [cite:de30_audit_aaup] Another found 42,695 disclosures of taxpayers' addresses to ICE unlawful. [cite:us10_cpa_irs_sep] The Supreme Court refused, at an interim stage, to let troops be deployed in Illinois, because the government had "failed to identify a source of authority that would allow the military to execute the laws," and on 31 December 2025 the president said he was withdrawing the Guard from Chicago, Los Angeles and Portland. [cite:de33_rollcall_illinois] [cite:de33_pbs_guard] It held that the emergency-powers law did not authorise the tariffs, and ruled 9–0 that GEO could not end a detainee forced-labour suit early by claiming a contractor's immunity. [cite:us11_ks_ieepa] [cite:de32_lii_menocal] By July 2026 the Justice Department had lost every one of the 13 trial-level rulings in its demands for states' unredacted voter rolls. [cite:de30_bgov_voterrolls] The same courts also widened the president's removal power and let the SAVE checks resume, and the book has set those beside the losses. [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de19_npr_save]

States held in their own way. Twenty states sued over Medicaid data going to ICE and won limits on it. [cite:de30_hipaa_chhabria] An Illinois audit found federal agents searching the state's licence-plate data against state law, and the camera company paused its federal pilots. [cite:de24_ap_flock] Woodburn, Oregon, learned from its own audit that federal agencies had run 6,089 searches through its cameras and took the cameras down. [cite:de24_katu_woodburn] Juries held: a Washington jury awarded detainees back pay at the state minimum wage, a verdict the Ninth Circuit affirmed, and a grand jury reportedly declined to indict over six lawmakers' video telling service members they could refuse illegal orders. [cite:de32_wa_nwauzor] [cite:de32_npr_kelly]

Others held without any office at all. Thousands of Google employees petitioned against a military AI contract in 2018 and the company did not renew it. [cite:de26_eng_maven] Microsoft, after The Guardian reported on an Israeli military unit's use of its cloud, found evidence supporting elements of the reporting and disabled the unit's subscriptions in September 2025. [cite:ow4_tc_msft] Journalists brought most of the record in this book into view: the location trails of more than 12 million phones, published in 2019, the TSA's passenger lists passed to ICE, the documents on ICE's Palantir system. [cite:de24_nyt_2019] [cite:de25b_reuters_tsaice] [cite:de28_guardian_icm] Utility records on more than 170 million people stopped flowing to ICE's data vendor in 2021 after press reports and a senator's letters. [cite:de24_globe_utility] In Urbit, the galaxy owners used their vote, replaced the board, and a new director succeeded the founder as he left; in Honduras an elected Congress repealed the law beneath the private zones and the Supreme Court declared them unconstitutional. [cite:de23_epoch_2025] [cite:de23_riotimes_icsid] Congress refused the DOGE dividend, and both houses voted against a tariff emergency with members of the president's party in the majority. [cite:de21_usat_dividend] [cite:de31_bnn_senate] [cite:de31_ap_house]

What ordinary people can do that the record shows works

The first thing is to know where the lines are. An administrative immigration warrant, signed by an officer rather than a judge, generally does not authorise forced entry into a home, and people may generally refuse entry on one; in January 2026 the Associated Press reported an internal ICE memo, disclosed by whistleblowers, asserting that officers could force entry on such a warrant for people with a final removal order, a position the department defended and legal scholars disputed. [cite:de40_ap_memo] Under a Supreme Court ruling of 1958, the State Department has no authority from Congress to deny a passport for a person's beliefs. [cite:de25b_kent] Messages sent through an end-to-end encrypted service, one in which only the sender and recipient hold the keys, leave little to hand over: when Signal received a grand jury subpoena, it could produce only the date an account was created and the last time it connected. [cite:de26_sw_signal]

The second is to use the data rights that exist, because most of the machinery in Book Five runs on commercial data before it runs on government files. Nineteen states had enacted consumer privacy laws by the International Association of Privacy Professionals' count in late 2024. [cite:de40_iapp_states] Since 1 January 2026 a California resident can send one deletion request to every registered data broker, more than 500 of them, and brokers must process it every 45 days from August 2026. [cite:de24_ca_drop] Washington's health-data law lets people sue over location and health data collected without consent, and Illinois's biometric law requires a written release before a company collects a face or fingerprint, though it does not bind the government. [cite:de25_wh_mhmda] [cite:de26_justia_bipa] Opting out of brokers and advertising identifiers shrinks the trail that can be bought.

The third is to ask. Under the Freedom of Information Act any person, citizen or not, may request federal records, and there is no fee to file. [cite:de40_foia_faq] Much of what this book could document arrived that way: the TSA's agreement with ICE was released in a records lawsuit, and the documents on ICE's Palantir system came from a records request. [cite:de25b_ao_moa] [cite:de28_guardian_icm] The fourth is local and electoral. A city council decided Woodburn's cameras, state attorneys general brought the Medicaid and voter-roll cases, and the midterm elections of 3 November 2026 choose the Congress that holds the purse and the oversight power. [cite:de24_katu_woodburn] [cite:de30_hipaa_chhabria] [cite:de32_votebeat_polls] The fifth is to support the people who do the checking: the plaintiffs, whether a professors' association, a free-speech group or a Minnesota observer, the reporters, the auditors and inspectors general, and the employees who say no inside their own companies. [cite:de28_ch_aaup] [cite:de26_reason_rosado] [cite:de25b_bu_cleland] The same standard applies whichever party holds office, because much of the machinery was built under both and will pass to whoever wins next.

The worst-case reading, tested

The hypothesis was the Sophia platform's and never a finding: immigration enforcement and government cuts as the occasion, a sovereign executive without a veto as the destination. This part gathered the grades. Documented: the destination as the texts describe it, in their authors' own words; the occasions, an office that cut the government by executive order and an enforcement force enlarged and funded to 2029; the machinery, every layer of which exists and several of whose joins are on paper; the thinning of the brakes; and the turning of the machinery on non-citizen critics for their speech. [cite:de8_land_de] [cite:de17_eo_text] [cite:de32_aic_hr1] [cite:de27_npr_medicaid] [cite:de0_slaughter] [cite:de28_ch_aaup] Probable: that the enlarged force and the integration layer will serve whatever priority comes next, and that the national-security directive of 2025 steers attention toward critics. [cite:de28_bu_lexis] [cite:de30_wh_nspm7] Not supported: a plan, a line from the texts to any office, a programme against citizens for their speech, and an executive without a veto. [cite:de17_li_oped] [cite:de16_natcon_signers] [cite:de33_rollcall_illinois]

The record runs against the destination in the places this section has listed, and it does so through people rather than through design. The theorists' own design never solved who removes a ruler; the American system has an answer, and in 2025 and 2026 it was used, unevenly, by judges, states, juries, reporters, owners, voters and legislators, some of them in the president's own party. [cite:de35b_nyt] [cite:de31_ap_house] The parts of the machine are real and the joins are growing. What stands between the parts and the worst case is ordinary work in institutions that still answer to the people who use them, and that work is open to anyone willing to do some of it.

books.title: The Hezbollah Architecture
books.subtitle: Lebanon, the Houthis, the Iraqi Militias and the Wars That Never End
books.intro:
This volume is about Hezbollah and the other armed groups that Israel and the United States have fought across the region: where they came from, what they have done, how much power they actually hold, and what the wars against them have produced. It was written to answer four direct questions: whether Hezbollah would exist if Israel had not invaded Lebanon in 1982 and occupied its south for eighteen years; what it is, beyond the label; what its strength is, and Lebanon's, against Israel's and the American aid behind it; and whether Hezbollah, the Houthis and the Iraqi militias are the standing reason for wars that do not end, for military aid that does not stop, and for an America drawn in again and again.

The record answers some of these questions and not others. It shows that Shia political mobilisation in Lebanon began before 1982, with Musa al-Sadr and Amal, and that Iran set out from 1979 to export its revolution. [cite:hz1_brit_sadr] [cite:hz1_iran_const] It shows that Israel invaded in 1982, armed and paid a Lebanese militia to hold a strip of the south, and that Hezbollah formed in the invasion's wake, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards in the Bekaa. [cite:hz2_idf_lw1] [cite:hz1_olj_sla] [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] It shows the bombings of 1983, among them the attack on the Marine barracks that killed 241 American service members, which US courts attributed to Hezbollah with Iranian support and which both deny, and Hezbollah's stated policy of answering Israeli shelling with rockets on northern Israel. [cite:hz12_cia_embassy] [cite:hz2_anderson] [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] It shows the 2006 war, the support front of 2023, the pagers, the ceasefire of November 2024 and what followed it, the war of 2026, and the Houthis' and Iraqi militias' campaigns, each with the counts of the dead and how they were made. [cite:hz7_toi_text] [cite:hz7_acled_year_pdf]

It tests the claim that these groups have become the excuse for everything, the way The Hamas Architecture tested it for Hamas, and it separates what is documented, including the armed groups Israel itself has paid or supplied, from what is argued about motive. [scene:hz11_pattern|Always the Axis?] [cite:hz11_toi_eisenkot] [cite:hz11_npr_clans] What would have happened otherwise cannot be documented, and the volume labels every such reading as an argument. It is a companion to The Hamas Architecture and The One-Way Mirror.

chapters.label: Part One
chapters.title: Before Hezbollah
chapters.intro: Hezbollah was founded in 1982, but the conditions it grew out of are forty years older. Part One follows them from Lebanon's independence in 1943 to the eve of Israel's 1982 invasion: a state built on a confessional bargain that left its Shia community on the margins; the cleric Musa al-Sadr, who organised that community and gave it a militia, Amal, before he vanished in Libya in 1978; the Palestinian refugees of 1948 and the PLO, which made southern Lebanon its base after 1970 under an agreement the Lebanese state signed in secret; the attacks and reprisals across the border and the civil war of 1975; Israel's invasion of 1978, the UN force it produced, and the Lebanese militia Israel armed and paid; and Iran's revolution of 1979, whose constitution committed it to carrying the revolution abroad.
chapters.outro: Part One set out what came before Hezbollah. Lebanon's 1943 settlement divided power by religious community on a 1932 census and left the Shia of the south and the Bekaa on the political and economic margins. [cite:hz1_wiki_pact] [cite:hz1_mrg_shia] Musa al-Sadr organised them in the Movement of the Deprived in 1974 and armed them in Amal in 1975, years before Iran's revolution and Israel's occupation; he disappeared in Libya on 31 August 1978, and no court has established what happened to him. [cite:hz1_brit_amal] [cite:hz1_olj_sadr] The Cairo Agreement of 1969 and the PLO's expulsion from Jordan made the south a base for attacks on Israel, including the killing of Israeli children at Kiryat Shmona and Ma'alot, and a target of Israeli reprisals that the Security Council condemned. [cite:hz1_cairo_text] [cite:hz1_wiki_1974] [cite:hz1_unscr262] Israel's 1978 invasion killed, by different estimates, between 1,100 and about 2,000 people in Lebanon; the Security Council ordered it out and created UNIFIL, and Israel handed its positions to Saad Haddad's militia, which it armed and paid. [cite:hz1_wiki_litani] [cite:hz1_unifil_bg] [cite:hz1_csm_haddad] In 1979 Iran's new constitution committed it to the continuation of its revolution abroad. [cite:hz1_iran_const] Part Two follows what happened when Israel invaded again, in June 1982. [scene:hz2_invasion|The 1982 invasion]

sections.h: A State Built on a Census
sections.html:
Lebanon became independent in 1943 on the strength of an agreement that was never written down. The National Pact, worked out that summer between President Bechara el-Khoury, a Maronite Christian, and Prime Minister Riad al-Solh, a Sunni Muslim, and made public on 7 October 1943, assigned the state's top offices by religious community: the presidency to a Maronite, the premiership to a Sunni, the speakership of parliament to a Shia, and the deputy posts to Greek Orthodox Christians. Seats in parliament were shared six to five in favour of Christians. [cite:hz1_wiki_pact] The ratio rested on the census of 1932, which counted Christians as a slim majority; no full census has been taken since. [cite:hz1_bpb_refugees]

The pact was also a bargain about borders and allegiance. Muslim leaders accepted the frontiers France had drawn in 1920 and gave up the goal of union with Syria; Christian leaders gave up seeking French protection and accepted that Lebanon had an "Arab face". [cite:hz1_loc_pact] The Library of Congress country study on Lebanon judges that the arrangement "merely perpetuated the power of the privileged", guaranteeing the position of each community's established leaders rather than of the communities themselves. [cite:hz1_loc_pact] The six-to-five ratio lasted until the Taif Agreement of 1989, which ended the civil war and moved parliament to an even split between Christians and Muslims while trimming the Maronite president's powers. [cite:hz1_wiki_pact]

The Shia Periphery

Of the large communities, the Shia gained least from this design. Most lived in two regions far from Beirut's banks and ports: the south, known historically as Jabal Amel, and the Bekaa valley in the east. Minority Rights Group International, in its profile of the community, writes that before the 1960s most Shia "remained on the political and economic periphery", represented in parliament by a few wealthy landowning families. [cite:hz1_mrg_shia] From the 1960s many moved to the capital in search of work. By 1975, by the same account, 40 per cent of the Shia of Jabal Amel had moved to Beirut, where the newcomers from the south and the Bekaa settled in the poor districts on the city's southern edge and became, in that profile's words, "acutely aware of their comparative poverty". [cite:hz1_mrg_shia] The same profile gives the community's present weight as almost a third of the population, up to 32 per cent, against 21 per cent of the seats in parliament; because no census has been taken, both the population share and the size of the gap are estimates. [cite:hz1_mrg_shia]

The south was also the region nearest Israel. That geography would matter more than any other fact in this book: from the late 1960s onward, the villages that were already the poorest in Lebanon became the ground on which Palestinian guerrillas, the Israeli army and, later, Hezbollah fought. The next section follows how that happened. [scene:hz1_plo|The PLO in Lebanon]

Musa al-Sadr and the Movement of the Deprived

The person who turned this community into a political force was a cleric born outside Lebanon. Musa al-Sadr was born in Qom, Iran, in 1928, the son of an ayatollah, and trained in Qom and in Najaf in Iraq, with a period studying law and economics at Tehran University. [cite:hz1_brit_sadr] He arrived in Tyre in late 1959 as an emissary of senior Shia clerics, and spent his first years in social work among a community that Encyclopaedia Britannica calls "largely disenfranchised". [cite:hz1_wiki_sadr] [cite:hz1_brit_sadr] In 1969 he became the first head of the Supreme Islamic Shia Council, and Britannica dates the formation of this higher council to 1968–69. [cite:hz1_wiki_sadr] [cite:hz1_brit_sadr]

In 1974 he founded, with Hussein el-Husseini, the Movement of the Deprived (Harakat al-Mahrumin), which pressed for better economic and social conditions for the Shia and built schools and clinics across the south. [cite:hz1_wiki_sadr] When the civil war broke out in 1975, the Shia were the only major community without a militia. Al-Sadr's answer was Amal, formed in 1975 as the movement's armed wing to defend the community. [cite:hz1_brit_amal] [cite:hz1_wiki_sadr] Amal was a Lebanese party with Lebanese aims: protection of the community and a larger share of the state. Its later relations with Syria were close, and Minority Rights Group describes it as a pragmatic party that cooperated with Damascus against a Palestinian armed revival in the 1980s. [cite:hz1_mrg_shia]

This matters for the question at the centre of Part Three: whether Hezbollah would exist without Israel's invasions. Lebanon's Shia had begun to organise politically, and to arm, years before 1982, through a movement that was not created by Iran's revolution (which came later) or by Israel. [cite:hz1_brit_amal] Part Two follows how Hezbollah's founding drew on, and split from, this existing movement. [scene:hz2_founding|The founding] That is a documented sequence of events; what weight to give it is an argument, taken up in Part Three. [scene:hz3_question|Would Hezbollah exist?]

The Disappearance

On 25 August 1978 al-Sadr flew to Libya at the invitation of its ruler, Muammar Gaddafi, with Sheikh Mohammad Yaacoub and the journalist Abbas Badreddine. The three were last seen on 31 August 1978 and were never heard from again. [cite:hz1_wiki_sadr] [cite:hz1_olj_sadr] Libya's government said they had left Tripoli that evening on an Alitalia flight to Rome. Passengers and crew told Italian investigators they had not seen anyone resembling al-Sadr, and Italian authorities concluded in July 2015 that he never set foot in Italy. [cite:hz1_olj_sadr] Lebanon's government indicted Gaddafi over the disappearance on 27 August 2008; Libya under Gaddafi consistently denied any responsibility. [cite:hz1_wiki_sadr]

The case is still open. Gaddafi's son Hannibal was seized by armed men in December 2015, taken to Lebanon and then held by the Lebanese authorities on a charge of withholding information about the disappearance. He was never tried, and was released on bail of $900,000 in November 2025. [cite:hz1_newarab_hannibal] What happened to al-Sadr has not been established by any court. The public record does not show who killed him, or whether he was killed in Libya, and the accounts of former Libyan officials remain the claims of those officials.

The disappearance removed Amal's founder in the same year that Israel's 1978 invasion of the south drove more than a hundred thousand people from their homes in the south, and less than six months before a revolution in Iran brought clerics into power in the country of his birth. Some of his followers would later find a different patron in Tehran. [cite:hz1_wiki_litani] [cite:hz1_aawsat_arafat] [scene:hz1_1978|1978 and 1979]

sections.h: Refugees, 1948
sections.html:
The war of 1948 brought Palestinian refugees into Lebanon. The camps set up for them held an estimated 100,000 people when they first arrived; by 1956 seventeen of them were official camps run by the UN agency for Palestine refugees, UNRWA. [cite:hz1_bpb_refugees] Lebanon did not give them citizenship. Their status has stayed precarious: Palestinians in Lebanon are barred from most professions and may not own property, and 452,669 were registered with UNRWA in January 2015, though the number actually living in the country is believed to be lower. [cite:hz1_bpb_refugees] For the war and the flight itself, see Gaza, Documented. [scene:gz1_refugees|The refugees of 1948]

Raids and Reprisals, 1968–1969

In the late 1960s Palestinian guerrilla groups, the fedayeen, began attacking Israel from southern Lebanon, and Israel answered with airstrikes and raids on Lebanese territory. [cite:hz1_olj_cairo] The best-known early reprisal hit the Lebanese state itself rather than the guerrillas. Overnight on 28 December 1968, 64 Israeli commandos led by Rafael Eitan, later Israel's chief of staff, landed at Beirut's international airport and destroyed twelve Middle East Airlines aircraft, by Al Majalla's count. Israel's stated reason was an attack on an Israeli airliner by the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, which was based in Beirut. [cite:hz1_majalla_airport] The UN Security Council, unanimously, condemned Israel "for its premeditated military action in violation of its obligations under the Charter" and said Lebanon was entitled to redress. [cite:hz1_unscr262]

The raids put the Lebanese government between two pressures. Arab governments pressed it to let the Palestinians fight; many Lebanese wanted the state to reassert control over its own territory, and through 1969 the Lebanese army clashed with the guerrillas. President Charles Helou turned to Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, to broker a settlement. [cite:hz1_olj_cairo]

The Cairo Agreement

The settlement was signed in Cairo on 3 November 1969 by the commander of the Lebanese army, General Emile Bustani, and the chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization, Yasser Arafat, with Egyptian ministers present. [cite:hz1_cairo_text] Its unofficial text, published by the Institute for Palestine Studies, recognised the right of Palestinians in Lebanon to join "the Palestinian Revolution through armed struggle", provided they respected Lebanese sovereignty; gave the guerrillas crossing points and observation posts along the frontier and a right of passage to the Arqub district in the south-east; and placed control of arms in the camps with Palestinian "Armed Struggle" posts. Clause 15 read: "This agreement shall remain top secret." [cite:hz1_cairo_text]

It did not stay secret. An unofficial version appeared in the Beirut daily An-Nahar on 20 April 1970. [cite:hz1_wiki_cairo] Its practical effect was to move sixteen UNRWA camps, home to about 300,000 refugees, out of the jurisdiction of the Lebanese army's intelligence bureau and under the PLO's Armed Struggle Command, and to let the guerrillas establish control over much of the border area. [cite:hz1_wiki_cairo] The Lebanese state had, in writing, licensed a foreign armed movement to wage war on a neighbour from its soil. Lebanon's parliament annulled the agreement on 21 May 1987, long after it had ceased to matter. [cite:hz1_wiki_cairo]

Black September and the Move to Lebanon

The PLO's centre of gravity was then not Lebanon but Jordan, where its groups had built a rival authority to King Hussein's. On 17 September 1970 the Jordanian army launched an offensive to retake the territory they held; a ceasefire was signed in Cairo on 27 September. [cite:hz1_afp_blacksept] The death toll is disputed. Jordan put it at about 3,000, fighters, soldiers and civilians together; the PLO spoke of tens of thousands, and Arafat of 25,000; other estimates of Palestinians killed run from about 2,000 to 3,400. [cite:hz1_afp_blacksept] [cite:hz1_wiki_blacksept] Fighting resumed in 1971, and in July 1971 the Jordanian government drove the remaining fighters out. They went to Lebanon. [cite:hz1_afp_blacksept] [cite:hz1_wiki_blacksept]

From then on the PLO's leadership, its fighters and its institutions were in Beirut and the south, under the terms of the Cairo Agreement. In effect, the PLO established a state within a state. [cite:hz1_wiki_cairo] The south, Lebanon's poorest region and the home of most of its Shia, became the front line.

Attacks Across the Border

Guerrilla groups based in Lebanon carried out some of the deadliest attacks on Israeli civilians of the decade. On 11 April 1974 three gunmen who had crossed from Lebanon killed 18 people, eight of them children, in an apartment building in Kiryat Shmona; the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine – General Command is named as responsible. Two days later Israeli forces raided villages in southern Lebanon. [cite:hz1_wiki_kiryat] On 15 May 1974 members of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine, also crossing from Lebanon, seized a school in Ma'alot; 25 hostages were killed, 22 of them children, when an Israeli unit stormed the building and the gunmen opened fire and threw grenades. [cite:hz1_wiki_1974]

The two governments explained these years differently. Israel's position, as its defence establishment put it in 1979, was that its operations in the south were meant to "deter the Palestinian terrorists from carrying out operations against Israeli targets". [cite:hz1_jta_cluster] The Cairo Agreement stated the PLO's position: armed struggle was a right of the Palestinians in Lebanon. [cite:hz1_cairo_text] Lebanon's government, which had signed that right away under pressure, also bore the reprisals, and in March 1978 it told the Security Council that it had no connection with the Palestinian operation that preceded Israel's invasion. [cite:hz1_unifil_bg]

Civil War, 1975

Lebanon's civil war began on 13 April 1975. That morning gunmen fired on a church in the Christian suburb of Ain el-Rummaneh, killing four people; hours later Phalangist militiamen killed about 30 Palestinians travelling through the suburb on a bus. [cite:hz1_wiki_civilwar] The fighting that followed set the Lebanese Front, mainly Maronite parties including the Phalange (Kataeb), against the Lebanese National Movement, an alliance of leftist and Muslim parties allied with the PLO. [cite:hz1_wiki_civilwar] The war's causes were Lebanese and Palestinian: the confessional settlement of 1943 and the armed Palestinian presence licensed in 1969. Foreign states then joined. On 1 June 1976 about 12,000 Syrian troops entered Lebanon and fought the Palestinian and leftist militias; Israel, from 1976, backed Christian militias against the PLO. [cite:hz1_wiki_civilwar] [cite:hz1_wiki_freeleb] By its end in 1990 the war had killed about 120,000 people and displaced nearly a million. [cite:hz1_wiki_civilwar]

sections.h: The Good Fence
sections.html:
Israel's first allies inside Lebanon were in the border villages. In 1976, as the civil war spread south, Israel opened its northern border to residents of Lebanese villages along the frontier under a policy it called the Good Fence, offering medical care and economic help; from 1977 southern Lebanese Christians were allowed to work in Israel and to export goods through Haifa, crossing at the Fatima Gate near Metula. [cite:hz1_wiki_freeleb] [cite:hz1_alhurra_fence] Alhurra, describing the policy in 2026, gives its aim as winning the villages' loyalty and turning the strip into a security belt against the Palestinian factions. [cite:hz1_alhurra_fence]

The policy had a military side from the start. In August 1977 Israel's foreign minister, Moshe Dayan, told the United States that Israel wanted to help the Christians of the south "in a military way", and the US embassy reported that Prime Minister Menachem Begin had admitted publicly, for the first time, that Israel had been supporting them with artillery fire from inside Israel. [cite:hz1_frus_1977] On 24 September 1977 President Jimmy Carter sent Begin a message stating that "current Israeli military actions in Lebanon are a violation of our agreements", which limited the use of American weapons to self-defence, and warning that Congress would be informed and further deliveries ended if they did not stop. [cite:hz1_frus_carter]

The local commander of this alliance was Saad Haddad, a Greek Catholic major in the Lebanese army who commanded a battalion of about 700 men at Marjayoun and broke with the army command in 1976. [cite:hz1_olj_sla] [cite:hz1_wiki_haddad]

Operation Litani

On 11 March 1978 a squad of Palestinian fighters that had sailed from Lebanon landed on the Israeli coast near Ma'agan Michael and killed 38 Israeli civilians, 13 of them children; the PLO claimed the attack. Counts of the dead and wounded differ slightly between sources. [cite:hz1_wiki_coastal] On the night of 14–15 March Israel invaded Lebanon, and within a few days it held the whole south except the city of Tyre and its surroundings. [cite:hz1_unifil_bg] [cite:hz1_wiki_litani] About 25,000 Israeli troops took part. [cite:hz1_wiki_litani] On 15 March Lebanon protested to the Security Council, stating that it had no connection with the Palestinian operation. [cite:hz1_unifil_bg]

Estimates of Lebanese and Palestinian dead run from about 1,100, the figure given by the American scholar Augustus Richard Norton, most of them Palestinian and Lebanese, to about 2,000 in other accounts; by Israeli military reporting, at least 550 of the dead were Palestinian fighters. The sources do not give a reliable split between fighters and civilians. Between 18 and 20 Israeli soldiers were killed. Estimates of the displaced run from 100,000 to 250,000. [cite:hz1a_wiki_litani] Israel used American cluster bombs in the operation. In August 1979 Secretary of State Cyrus Vance said Israel "may have violated its agreement" with the United States through its use of American weapons in the south; Israeli military sources acknowledged that the use of cluster bombs in the Litani operation had breached the agreement, while Israeli defence officials denied any other violation and said their operations were meant to deter attacks on Israeli targets. [cite:hz1_jta_cluster]

Resolution 425 and UNIFIL

On 19 March 1978 the Security Council adopted Resolutions 425 and 426. They called on Israel to cease its military action immediately and withdraw its forces from all Lebanese territory, called for strict respect for Lebanon's sovereignty within its internationally recognised boundaries, and set up the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) to confirm Israel's withdrawal, restore international peace and security, and help the Lebanese government restore its authority in the south. The first UNIFIL troops arrived on 23 March. [cite:hz1_unifil_bg] The force was meant to be interim. It stayed for decades, and its record, and the argument over its future, run through the later parts of this book. [scene:hz8_terms|The 2024 terms]

When Israel withdrew later in 1978, it did not hand its positions to UNIFIL or to the Lebanese army. It handed them to Haddad's militia. [cite:hz1_wiki_litani] The resolution asked Israel to leave all Lebanese territory; what it left behind was a strip along the border held by a Lebanese force that Israel supplied.

Free Lebanon

On 18 April 1979 Haddad, speaking from Metulla in Israel, proclaimed the area his men held to be "Free Lebanon". The next day the Lebanese government branded him a traitor and dismissed him from the army. [cite:hz1_olj_sla] [cite:hz1_wiki_freeleb] His force was mainly Christian, but it also recruited Shia and Druze men from the south; L'Orient-Le Jour reports that its salaries drew recruits in hard times and that Shia later became the majority of its ranks. [cite:hz1_olj_sla] In May 1980 the militia took the name South Lebanon Army. After Haddad died of cancer on 15 January 1984 a former Lebanese army general, Antoine Lahad, took command in April 1984. [cite:hz4_olj_sla] It collapsed when Israel withdrew in May 2000, and most of its members fled to Israel. [cite:hz1_olj_sla] Part Four covers its role in the occupied zone. [scene:hz4_zone|The security zone]

That Israel armed and financed this militia is documented, not inferred. In July 1982 Haddad himself told the Christian Science Monitor that Israel had contributed about $10 million toward his men's salaries since 1978, paying $100 a month per man, and had provided weapons and civilian services such as roads and hospitals. [cite:hz1_csm_haddad] In April 1981 senior Israeli military sources acknowledged for the first time that Israel was also supplying equipment to Christian forces in northern Lebanon, and the same report described Israel as giving full backing to Haddad's militia on the border. [cite:hz1_csm_1981] A 2026 Alhurra account puts Israel's support for Haddad's forces at about $35 million a year, without specifying the years; that figure is single-sourced, and Haddad's own figure for salaries is far lower. The Congressional Research Service gave the same $35 million a year as the estimated cost of the later South Lebanon Army, including maintenance and infrastructure, which may be the origin of Alhurra's figure. [cite:hz1_alhurra_fence] [cite:hz4_crs_sla]

The two governments described the arrangement in opposite terms. Begin spoke of a "moral commitment" to Lebanon's Christians, and Israeli officers argued that if Christian forces were destroyed the PLO and Syria would have free movement up to Israel's border. [cite:hz1_csm_1981] The Lebanese government, which never recognised Free Lebanon, treated its founder as a traitor. [cite:hz1_wiki_freeleb] For the question Part Eleven tests, whether armed groups in this region have served Israel as tools as well as threats, this is the first documented case: a Lebanese force that Israel paid, armed and used to hold ground it had been asked by the Security Council to leave. [scene:hz11_proxies|Groups Israel armed] Whether that served Israel's security or prolonged the conflict is an argument, taken up there.

Iran, 1979

Less than six months after Musa al-Sadr disappeared, a revolution in the country of his birth brought clerics to power. The new government broke with Israel at once. On 17 February 1979 Yasser Arafat became the first official visitor to the new Islamic Republic, and Iran handed the PLO the building that had housed Israel's mission in Tehran. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini urged Arafat to call the Palestinian revolution an Islamic one; Arafat replied that it was a national movement of Muslims and Christians. [cite:hz1_aawsat_arafat]

The new state declared that its revolution was not meant to stop at its borders. The constitution adopted in October 1979 says in its preamble that it "provides the necessary basis for ensuring the continuation of the Revolution at home and abroad", and gives the armed forces, including the Revolutionary Guards, "the ideological mission of jihad in God's way", described as extending the sovereignty of God's law throughout the world. [cite:hz1_iran_const] In his New Year message broadcast on 21 March 1980, Khomeini said: "We should try hard to export our revolution to the world." The same message named the enemy as the powers "led by America, Israel and Zionism" and pledged support for "beloved Palestine and beloved Lebanon". [cite:hz1_merip_khomeini]

By the spring of 1980, then, two of the forces that would produce Hezbollah were in place: a Lebanese Shia community that had organised and armed under al-Sadr, and a government in Tehran committed in its constitution to exporting its revolution. The third, an Israeli army occupying much of Lebanon, arrived in June 1982. [cite:hz1_iran_const] [cite:hz1_wiki_sadr] [scene:hz2_invasion|The 1982 invasion]

chapters.label: Part Two
chapters.title: The Founding
chapters.intro: Part Two covers the three years in which Hezbollah came into being. It begins with Israel's invasion of Lebanon in June 1982: the shooting in London that Israel cited, the aim it announced and the distance its army actually went, the siege of Beirut, the departure of the PLO and the massacre at Sabra and Shatila. It then follows Iran's Revolutionary Guards into the Bekaa Valley and the Lebanese clerics and breakaway militiamen who joined them, setting out Iran's role as Iranian officials, American courts and Hezbollah itself have described it. It records the 1983 bombings of the US embassy and of the American and French barracks in Beirut, who claimed them, what US judges later found and who denied what. It ends with the Open Letter of February 1985, in which the movement announced itself, and with what changed when Hezbollah rewrote its programme in 2009.
chapters.outro: Part Two established the sequence in which Hezbollah formed. Israel invaded Lebanon on 6 June 1982 after the shooting of its ambassador in London, with a stated aim of 40 kilometres, and its army reached Beirut within a week. The PLO left by sea, and Kataeb militiamen then killed hundreds, by some counts thousands, in Sabra and Shatila, camps that Israeli troops had surrounded. [cite:hz2_idf_lw1] [cite:hz2_wiki_1982il] In the same year Iran's Revolutionary Guards set up a base in the Bekaa. There they brought together Islamic Amal and Lebanese clerics, and a US court later found the resulting organization "formed under the auspices of the government of Iran", in a case Iran did not contest. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] [cite:hz2_anderson] The bombings of 1983 killed 63 at the US embassy, then 241 American and 58 French service members. They were claimed by the "Islamic Jihad Organization". US courts later attributed the barracks bombing to Hezbollah acting with Iranian direction, in cases Iran did not contest, while Hezbollah and Iran have denied any part. The Marines left Lebanon in February 1984. [cite:hz2_an_1983] [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] [cite:hz2_peterson07] [cite:hz2_aj_theft] In February 1985 the movement announced itself with a letter that named Israel and the United States as enemies and Khomeini as its authority. In 2009 it revised its programme for Lebanon but not its armed stance toward Israel, and in 1985 Israel itself pulled back to an occupied zone in the south. [cite:hz2_cep_letter] [cite:hz2_belfer_cohen] [cite:hz4_crs_sla] Part Three asks whether Hezbollah would have existed without the invasion and the occupation, and treats the answers as argument.

sections.h: Peace for Galilee
sections.html:
On 3 June 1982 a gunman from the Abu Nidal Organization shot Shlomo Argov, Israel's ambassador in London, outside the Dorchester Hotel. Argov survived with severe injuries and died of them in 2003. [cite:hz2_wiki_1982il] [cite:hz2_inn_argov] The next day Israeli jets bombed PLO ammunition depots and training bases in Lebanon, and PLO artillery answered against northern Israel. On 6 June the Israeli cabinet launched Operation Peace for Galilee. [cite:hz2_inn_argov] [cite:hz2_begin_pfg]

The stated aim. The Israel Defense Forces' own history says the operation followed "the attempted assassination of the Israeli Ambassador to the UK by a terrorist cell". It gives the objective as "pushing the latter 40 km to the north", meaning armed Palestinian groups, to keep their weapons out of range of northern Israeli towns. [cite:hz2_idf_lw1] The Menachem Begin Heritage Center, which keeps the record of the prime minister who ordered the war, describes the same aim differently: to "ensure that the forty miles surrounding the border would be terrorist-free". Forty miles is about 64 kilometres. [cite:hz2_begin_pfg] Neither account names the Abu Nidal Organization or explains why the PLO was the target. The Begin Center calls the London attackers only "Palestinian". [cite:hz2_idf_lw1] [cite:hz2_begin_pfg]

The advance. The army did not stop at either distance. On 9 June the Israeli Air Force attacked the Syrian air-defence network in the Bekaa Valley and destroyed 17 of its 19 missile batteries. On 13 June Israeli forces reached West Beirut. [cite:hz2_wiki_1982il] The Begin Center says the army "was forced to continue north all the way to Beirut". That is the official Israeli explanation for the gap between the announced aim and where the army ended up. [cite:hz2_begin_pfg] By the IDF's account the war lasted more than three months. The siege of Beirut tightened from late June, and Israeli forces took the high ground over the city between 20 and 25 June. [cite:hz2_idf_lw1] An account of the US Marine deployment says the invasion went ahead with tacit US approval. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks]

The evacuation. A multinational force of American, French and Italian troops landed in Beirut on 24 August 1982 to oversee the departure of PLO fighters. [cite:hz2_an_1983] The IDF says the evacuation by sea was completed on 31 August. The Begin Center says the fighting "forced the PLO leader Yasser Arafat to leave Lebanon". [cite:hz2_idf_lw1] [cite:hz2_begin_pfg] The US Marines left on 10 September, their stated task done. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] What grew in the space the PLO left is the subject of the rest of this part and of Part Three. [scene:hz3_question|Part Three: Would Hezbollah exist?]

Sabra and Shatila. Shortly before, President-elect Bachir Gemayel, leader of the Kataeb (Phalange) party, had been assassinated. Between 16 and 18 September, Kataeb militiamen entered the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps in West Beirut, which Israeli troops had surrounded, and killed civilians, mostly Palestinians and Lebanese Shia. The killings were presented as revenge for Gemayel. [cite:hz2_wiki_1982il] [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] Estimates of the dead run from about 700 to 3,500 or more, and they come from different counts made by different bodies with different access.
