[cite:hz2_wiki_1982il] The Lebanese government said in October 1982 that 762 bodies had been recovered from the camps and that some 1,200 more had been buried privately by relatives, putting the toll close to 2,000. The figures could not be independently checked because the Red Cross had left the search after less than a week. [cite:hz2b_csm_toll762] The Israeli commission of inquiry described below, citing Israeli military intelligence, put the number at 700 to 800 and called that the figure "most closely corresponding with reality". [cite:hz2b_jvl_kahan] The Israeli journalist Amnon Kapeliouk and other researchers put it closer to 3,500. [cite:hz2b_aj_battah] The Institute for Palestine Studies' encyclopedia says "more than 3,000" were killed and notes that bulldozed rubble and mass graves make an exact count impossible. [cite:hz2b_palquest_ss] This book does not choose among them. The Begin Center's timeline says "Christian Phalanges Massacred a Muslim refugee camp". [cite:hz2_begin_pfg] In Israel, 400,000 people marched on 25 September 1982 to demand that Begin resign. [cite:hz2_wiki_1982il] Four days later the US Marines returned to Beirut, joining 2,200 French and Italian troops already in place. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks]

The Kahan Commission. Israel's commission of inquiry had three members: Yitzhak Kahan, president of the Supreme Court, Justice Aharon Barak and Major General (res.) Yona Efrat. It reported on 8 February 1983. [cite:hz2b_jvl_kahan] It found that the killings were carried out by a Phalangist unit acting on its own, that no Israeli was directly responsible, and that Israel bore indirect responsibility because its forces controlled the area and allowed the militia in. [cite:hz2b_jvl_kahan] [cite:hz2b_csm_kahan] It found that Defence Minister Ariel Sharon bore "personal responsibility" for ignoring the danger of bloodshed and revenge when he approved the Phalangists' entry, and it recommended that he resign or, if he did not, that the prime minister remove him. It severely criticized the chief of staff, Rafael Eitan, and recommended that the director of military intelligence not continue in his post. [cite:hz2b_jvl_kahan] [cite:hz2b_csm_kahan] [cite:hz2b_wiki_kahan] Sharon at first refused to go. On 10 February 1983 a grenade was thrown into a Peace Now rally outside the prime minister's office in Jerusalem that was demanding the report be carried out. It killed Emil Grunzweig, a reserve officer, and wounded others. Yonah Avrushmi was convicted of the murder in 1985. [cite:hz2b_wiki_grunzweig] [cite:hz2b_csm_sharon] Sharon then gave up the defence ministry, which Begin took over, but stayed in the cabinet as a minister without portfolio. [cite:hz2b_csm_sharon] [cite:hz2b_wiki_kahan]

What the counts show. The war's death tolls need the same care as later ones in this book, because the published figures cover different periods. On the Israeli side, the army reported 330 soldiers killed by late August 1982 and 446 killed and 2,383 wounded between 4 June and 19 November 1982. [cite:hz2b_csm_nov82] [cite:hz2b_csm_dec82] The Ministry of Defense archive gives 353 soldiers killed "in the warfare" of 1982. [cite:hz2b_mod_1982] By June 1985, when the army pulled back to the border zone, its spokesman put the total at 654 killed, 3,195 wounded and four missing, close to the 656 killed often repeated elsewhere. [cite:hz2b_csm_jun85] [cite:hz2_njop_pfg] On the Lebanese side, the figures most often quoted come from the Lebanese police and were reported at the time. In November 1982 the Christian Science Monitor gave 17,825 killed and 30,103 wounded between 6 June and 25 August. In December it reported revised police figures of 19,085 killed and 30,302 wounded between 4 June and 31 August; the paper did not break the totals down by status, but its regional breakdowns show they included Palestinian, Syrian and Lebanese fighters as well as civilians. [cite:hz2b_csm_nov82] [cite:hz2b_csm_dec82] [cite:hz2a_csm_dec82] In Beirut, the police counted 6,775 dead, 84 per cent of them civilians; in the south about 20 per cent of the dead were civilians and the rest Palestinian, Syrian or Lebanese fighters. [cite:hz2b_csm_dec82] The paper did not explain how the police counted, and no later audit of these numbers was found. They are best read as a contemporary official estimate of about 18,000 to 19,000 dead in less than three months, not as a verified total.

sections.h: The Guards in the Bekaa
sections.html:
The men who formed Hezbollah came from a community that had already organized. Lebanon's Shia are today estimated at almost a third of the population but hold 21 percent of parliamentary seats, and by 1975 many had moved from the south to the edges of Beirut. [cite:hz1_mrg_shia] Amal had been formed in 1975 as the armed wing of Musa al-Sadr's Movement of the Deprived. Sadr himself disappeared in Libya in August 1978. [cite:hz1_brit_amal] [cite:hz1_olj_sadr] Part One sets out that background. [scene:hz1_lebanon|Part One: Lebanon's divided state] What was new in 1982 was a foreign state with a stated policy of exporting its revolution, and an Israeli invasion that gave it the opening. On 21 March 1980 Ayatollah Khomeini had told Iranians: "We should try hard to export our revolution to the world." Iran's 1979 constitution gives its armed forces "the ideological mission of jihad in God's way". [cite:hz1_merip_khomeini] [cite:hz1_iran_const]

The base. In 1982 Iran set up a base in the Bekaa Valley, which Syria controlled. From there, by the standard account, its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps founded, financed, trained and equipped Hezbollah. The Sheikh Abdullah barracks in Baalbek was believed to house the Guards training Lebanese recruits. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] A Belfer Center study published in July 2026 opens from the same premise: the party was "Founded in 1982 under Iranian Revolutionary Guard sponsorship". [cite:hz2_belfer_cohen] Published figures for the size of the Guards contingent differ. The most common is about 1,500: the Wilson Center's Islamists programme says Iran dispatched "some 1,500 IRGC trainers and advisers", and the US Institute of Peace's Iran Primer says 1,500 advisers arrived in the Bekaa within weeks of the invasion. [cite:hz2b_wilson_1500] [cite:hz2b_usip_timeline] A standard reference account traces the same figure to the Library of Congress country study of Lebanon published in 1989. [cite:hz2b_wiki_hzir] PBS's Frontline/World gives 1,000, sent at the end of the siege of Beirut. [cite:hz2b_pbs_1000] The magazine Al Majalla, drawing on the papers of the former Syrian vice-president Abdul Halim Khaddam, describes "a brigade and experts" of the Guards sent through Syria, most of them to the Sheikh Abdullah barracks in Baalbek, without a number. [cite:hz2b_majalla_hamidi] Lower figures of about 800 and higher ones of up to 5,000 also circulate. The 800 figure is attributed in that reference account to a 1993 article that, on checking, does not mention the Guards, and no source for the higher figures was verified. This book therefore gives the contingent as roughly 1,000 to 1,500, as reported, not as a counted number. [cite:hz2b_wiki_hzir]

Islamic Amal and the clerics. Hezbollah did not start as a single body. One of its building blocks was Islamic Amal, a faction that broke from Amal under Hussein Musawi. Accounts of the bombings below describe it as an autonomous part of the "embryonic" Hezbollah. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] Historians do not agree on whether Hezbollah existed as an organization by late 1983. The group announced itself only in 1985. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] The best-known cleric of the period, Sheikh Mohammed Hussein Fadlallah, later became a grand ayatollah and the top spiritual leader of Lebanon's Shia community. Lebanese and American intelligence officials named him as the man who blessed the 1983 suicide bombers. He denied any role until his death in 2010. [cite:hz2_wilson_fadlallah] American intelligence had a name for the network by 1984. A CIA note written after the September 1984 bombing of the US embassy annex referred to "Hizb Allah, operating with Iranian support under the cover name of Islamic Jihad". [cite:hz2_d1_levitt]

Iran's role in its own words. Iran's government has not formally acknowledged directing any of the attacks of this period. The fullest account from an Iranian official comes from Sayyed Issa Tabatabai, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei's representative in Lebanon, in an interview with Iran's state news agency, IRNA. He said Hezbollah's efforts "started in [Lebanon's] Baalbek area", where Revolutionary Guards arrived. He said that for two years "[Hezbollah's] military base was located in my home", and that he "quickly went to Lebanon and provided what was needed". [cite:hz2_fox_tabatabai] The interview is known in English through a translation by the Middle East Media Research Institute (MEMRI). MEMRI says IRNA removed the passage in which Tabatabai acknowledged receiving Khomeini's ruling ordering attacks. MEMRI notes that Iran "has always vehemently denied any role in the bombings". [cite:hz2_fox_tabatabai] It is a single interview, reported in English through one translator. It shows how an Iranian official close to the Supreme Leader described Iran's founding role, but it is not a government admission.

What US courts found. The most detailed findings on Iran's role come from American civil suits brought by families of the Marines killed in October 1983. In Peterson v. Islamic Republic of Iran (2003), Judge Royce Lamberth found that Hezbollah "was formed under the auspices of the government of Iran". He found that it "received massive material and technical support from the Iranian government". [cite:hz2_anderson] Expert witnesses included Patrick Clawson, who testified that "Hezbollah is largely under Iranian orders", and Reuven Paz, who said it was "totally controlled by Iran". [cite:hz2_anderson] [cite:hz2_fain] These findings carry weight, but two limits apply. Iran did not appear to contest them, so the cases were decided by default. And the legal test was evidence "satisfactory to the court", which the court said means it may not simply accept unsupported allegations. [cite:hz2_anderson] Iran has called the rulings "baseless" and "politically motivated". [cite:hz2_jurist_2007]

Hezbollah's own account. The movement's founding document, read in February 1985, describes the Israeli invasion and the Western forces in Beirut as its enemies. It also declares obedience to "one leader, wise and just", meaning Khomeini. [cite:hz2_wiki_ideology] Both parts of that self-description matter. Part Three examines the argument over which mattered more, and labels it as argument. [scene:hz3_question|Part Three: Would Hezbollah exist?]

sections.h: The Bombings of 1983
sections.html:
The multinational force that came back to Beirut in late September 1982 was meant to be neutral, and many Lebanese did not see it that way. Lebanese Muslims came to believe that the force, and the Americans in particular, were "unfairly siding with the Maronite Christians". The Amal leader Nabih Berri asked the United States and France to leave. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] In 1983 the American role moved from oversight to fighting. On 8 September 1983 US destroyers offshore fired in defence of the Marines during battles around Souk el-Gharb in the mountains above Beirut. The Defense Department's commission of inquiry later recorded a "prevalent view" among American commanders that this fire was linked to the attack that followed. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] That spring Lebanon and Israel had also signed an agreement, described below. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks]

The embassy, 18 April 1983. A suicide bomber drove into the US embassy in Ain al-Mraiseh, on the Beirut seafront. The blast killed 63 people, 17 of them Americans. [cite:hz2_an_1983] [cite:hz2_rf_pence] Arab News, reviewing the attacks in 2025, gives two different figures for the Lebanese dead, 35 in its text and 46 in a photo caption, without noting the difference. [cite:hz2a_an_1983]

The barracks, 23 October 1983. At about 06:22 a truck bomb destroyed the building near Beirut airport where the US Marines were quartered. Minutes later a second bomb hit the French paratroopers' building, known as the Drakkar. The attacks killed 241 American service members (220 Marines, 18 sailors and 3 soldiers), 58 French paratroopers and 6 civilians. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] [cite:hz2_an_1983] An FBI explosives expert later testified that the blast was equal to between 15,000 and 21,000 pounds of TNT. [cite:hz2_anderson]

Who claimed it, and who denied it. Two telephone callers claimed the bombing in the name of the Islamic Jihad Organization. [cite:hz2_d1_levitt] A statement sent to the Beirut daily As-Safir claimed it for an "Islamic Revolution Movement". Syria, Iran and Amal denied involvement, and the United States first blamed Amal and its offshoot, Islamic Amal. [cite:hz2_an_1983] Hezbollah, which had not yet announced itself, later officially denied involvement while praising the "two martyr mujahideen" who carried it out. Hezbollah, Iran and Syria have continued to deny any part in the bombings. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] The US government had warning it did not use. The National Security Agency intercepted a message of 26 September 1983 from Iran's intelligence ministry to its ambassador in Damascus. It was not passed to the Marines until 26 October, three days after the bombing. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks]

The 17 May agreement. A month after the embassy bombing, on 17 May 1983, Lebanon and Israel signed an agreement negotiated with the United States. Its text declared that the state of war between them "has been terminated and no longer exists" and that the border was inviolable. Israel was to withdraw all its forces within 8 to 12 weeks of the agreement entering into force. Lebanon was to enforce security arrangements in a "Security Region" in the south and to prevent "irregular forces, armed bands" from operating against Israel, and a joint liaison committee with American participation would oversee it. [cite:hz2b_jvl_may17] It set up liaison offices rather than embassies. [cite:hz2b_majalla_may17] Israel made its withdrawal conditional on Syria withdrawing too. [cite:hz2b_wiki_may17] Lebanon's parliament approved it in June 1983, with two votes against and three abstentions among 72 members present. Syria's president, Hafez al-Assad, rejected it, and with Syrian troops still in Lebanon it was never carried out. [cite:hz2b_majalla_may17] [cite:hz2b_wiki_may17] The two governments said in it that they recognised their "right and obligation to live in peace with each other"; many Lebanese Muslims and much of the Arab world opposed it as a surrender imposed on Lebanon. [cite:hz2b_majalla_may17] [cite:hz2b_wiki_may17]

What US courts found. On 30 May 2003 Judge Royce Lamberth of the federal court in Washington ruled for the families of the servicemen in Peterson v. Islamic Republic of Iran. [cite:hz2_wt_2003] His findings, later relied on in further suits, were these. Iran's Ministry of Information and Security told the Iranian ambassador to Syria to have his group attack the multinational force and to "take a spectacular action against the United States Marines". At a meeting in Baalbek, held at the ambassador's direction, Hezbollah and Revolutionary Guard members planned simultaneous attacks on the American and French barracks. The truck was "driven by an Iranian member of Hezbollah". [cite:hz2_anderson] [cite:hz2_fain]

Iran did not appear to contest the case. The court decided it by default, on evidence it found "satisfactory to the court". [cite:hz2_anderson] On 7 September 2007 Lamberth awarded the families about $2.66 billion. His opinion, setting out the families' case, described Hezbollah as "the terrorist organization that orchestrated and carried out the bombing". [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] [cite:hz2a_peterson07] Iran called that ruling "baseless" and "politically motivated", saying a court that heard only one side had no legal value. [cite:hz2_jurist_2007] In April 2016 the US Supreme Court, by six votes to two, upheld a 2012 law directing about $2 billion in frozen Iranian central bank assets to more than 1,300 relatives of victims of attacks linked to Iran. [cite:hz2_pbs_markazi] Iran's foreign ministry called the ruling "a theft", and Iran continued to deny any link to the bombing. [cite:hz2_aj_theft] Iran then took the United States to the International Court of Justice. On 30 March 2023 the court ruled it had no jurisdiction over the central bank funds, but found that other US measures against Iranian companies breached a 1955 treaty between the two countries. [cite:hz2_iranprimer_icj]

The American response. Vice-President George H. W. Bush, visiting Beirut the day after the barracks bombing, said: "We will not allow terrorism to dictate or change our foreign policy." [cite:hz2_an_1983] The Pentagon's commission of inquiry, under retired Admiral Robert Long, put the blame for the security failures on the military chain of command. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] The fighting went on. Israel pulled its forces out of the Aley and Shouf districts on 4 September 1983. The battleship USS New Jersey shelled Druze and Syrian positions on 14 December 1983, and again on 8 February 1984. France struck positions in the Bekaa that it said belonged to the Revolutionary Guards. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] On 7 February 1984 President Reagan ordered the Marines to begin leaving, largely because support in Congress was fading. The last Marines left Beirut airport on 26 February. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] Days later, on 5 March 1984, the Lebanese government formally repudiated the 17 May agreement; parliament revoked it in May 1987. [cite:hz2b_majalla_may17] [cite:hz2b_wiki_may17] Thirty-four years later, Vice-President Mike Pence called the bombing "the opening salvo in a war that we have waged ever since". [cite:hz2_rf_pence] Part Twelve follows that thread. [scene:hz12_wars|Part Twelve: the wars]

sections.h: The Open Letter
sections.html:
On 16 February 1985 Sheikh Ibrahim al-Amin, Hezbollah's spokesman, read a text aloud at the al-Ouzai mosque in west Beirut. It was published in the newspaper al-Safir as an open letter "to all the Oppressed in Lebanon and the World". [cite:hz2_wiki_ideology] A study for Harvard's Belfer Center gives 22 February 1985 as the date it appeared in print, and notes that it was written after the suicide bombings of American and French forces. [cite:hz2_belfer_cohen] With this letter the movement that had operated under other names, or under no name, announced itself. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks]

What it says about Israel and the United States. The English text most often reproduced, published by the Council on Foreign Relations in 1988, puts Israel at the centre. "We see in Israel the vanguard of the United States in our Islamic world," it says, and the struggle "will end only when this entity is obliterated". It continues: "We recognize no treaty with it, no cease fire, and no peace agreements, whether separate or consolidated." It warns of an Israel extended "from the Euphrates to the Nile". [cite:hz2_cep_letter] It calls the United States "that arrogant superpower". [cite:hz2_wiki_ideology] There is one caveat about the text. A note in a standard reference account says the line about obliteration appears in the Arabic original but is missing from one English translation and is not on Hezbollah's website. [cite:hz2_wiki_ideology] Israel has relied on the programme ever since. In a letter to the UN Secretary-General in February 2000, Israel's mission cited it as stating "the complete destruction of the State of Israel" as Hezbollah's goal. That letter dates the programme to 16 December 1985, which does not match the February reading. [cite:hz2_un_israel2000]

What it says it wants. The letter set out its aims as expelling "the Americans, the French and their allies definitely from Lebanon", and bringing the Phalangists to justice for crimes against Muslims and Christians. [cite:hz2_wiki_ideology] On government it said two things at once. It allowed that the Lebanese people should "choose in all the liberty the form of government" they wanted. It also said that "only an Islamic regime" could stop future imperialist infiltration. [cite:hz2_wiki_ideology] On authority it was plain: "We obey the orders of one leader, wise and just", meaning Khomeini. [cite:hz2_wiki_ideology] The Belfer study reads the document as rejecting Lebanon's confessional power-sharing outright and aiming at a borderless Islamic republic. It also notes that the letter made obedience to Khomeini a binding religious duty. [cite:hz2_belfer_cohen] The letter therefore pointed in two directions. It made Israel's invasion and the Western forces in Beirut the immediate enemy, and it placed the movement under a foreign cleric's authority. Part Three examines which of the two mattered more. [scene:hz3_question|Part Three: Would Hezbollah exist?]

Violence in Beirut in 1985. Three weeks after the reading, on 8 March 1985, a car bomb exploded in Beirut's Shia southern suburbs. It was aimed at Fadlallah, who escaped unhurt, and it killed 80 civilians and wounded more than 250. The CIA "vehemently denied any role", and a House Intelligence Committee report backed that denial. Bob Woodward later reported that the operation had been run off the books by CIA Director William Casey and Saudi Prince Bandar bin Sultan, with $3 million in Saudi money. Woodward's account remains disputed. [cite:hz2_wilson_fadlallah]

Israel pulls back. On 14 January 1985 Israel's cabinet decided to withdraw in three phases, ending along the border while keeping "a zone in southern Lebanon where local forces (SLA) will operate with IDF backing". [cite:hz2b_jvl_jan85] The army handed Sidon to the Lebanese army on 16 February, left the Bekaa on 24 April and Tyre on 29 April, and by 10 June 1985 most of its troops had left, with a smaller force staying to back the South Lebanon Army. [cite:hz2b_wiki_slc] [cite:hz2b_csm_apr85] [cite:hz2_begin_pfg] The zone was about nine miles deep and covered some 850 square kilometres, roughly a tenth of the country. It held about 150,000 people in 162 villages and towns. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] Israel held it with the South Lebanon Army. The Congressional Research Service describes the SLA as "an allied militia that it fully funded and equipped". [cite:hz4_crs_sla] Antoine Lahd had taken command of the militia in April 1984. [cite:hz4_olj_sla] The occupation the Open Letter named as its target lasted until May 2000, and Part Four follows it. [cite:hz4_merip_2000] [scene:hz4_zone|Part Four: the security zone]

The 2009 revision. In November 2009 Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah presented a new political document, 52 pages long by the Belfer study's count, at a press conference, approved by the party's General Congress. [cite:hz2_belfer_cohen] According to the Belfer study, it publicly dropped the immediate demand for an Islamic state in Lebanon and accepted Lebanon's power-sharing among religious communities. It grounded Hezbollah's weapons in a formula of "Army-People-Resistance", on the argument that the Lebanese army was too weak to defend the country alone. [cite:hz2_belfer_cohen] Nasrallah said the party would accept "consensus democracy" until sectarianism in politics was abolished. He also called for a defence strategy relying on "a popular resistance participating in defending the country" alongside the army. [cite:hz2_cp_lamb] Franklin Lamb, an American commentator sympathetic to the party, wrote that the document was drafted not to recant the 1985 letter but to address subjects it had not covered. [cite:hz2_cp_lamb] Reading the 2009 text, Nasrallah said: "Our problem with [the Israelis] is not that they are Jews, but that they are occupiers." [cite:hz2_wiki_ideology] By the sources' own descriptions, the revision changed Hezbollah's programme for Lebanon. It did not change the armed stance toward Israel, and CNN, in coverage Lamb criticised as skewed, reported Nasrallah as saying in a televised speech that "American terrorism is the source of every terrorism in the world". [cite:hz2a_cp_lamb] Israel's letter to the UN in 2000 had relied on the 1985 text. [cite:hz2_un_israel2000]

chapters.label: Part Three
chapters.title: Would Hezbollah Exist?
chapters.intro: Part Three asks the question that sits under every argument about Hezbollah: would it exist if Israel had not invaded Lebanon in 1982 and stayed in the south for eighteen years? No document can prove what would have happened in a history that did not occur, so everything in this part that answers the question is argument, and is labelled as such. What the record can do is set out who has made each argument, on what evidence, and which pieces of that evidence are documented facts. The first section gives the case that the invasion and the occupation made Hezbollah, much of it in the words of Israeli officials. The second gives the case that it would have formed anyway, in this or another shape, because of Lebanese Shia politics, clerical networks reaching back to Iraq, and Iran's stated aim of exporting its revolution, and ends with what can and cannot be settled.
chapters.outro: Part Three set out both sides of a counterfactual that no record can settle. The case that Israel made Hezbollah rests on documented facts: the organisation took shape during the 1982 invasion, named the occupation as its first enemy, and was called the occupation's product by Ehud Barak, in words reported since 2006 though their original source is unconfirmed, while Yitzhak Rabin warned in 1985 of the Shia resistance it was producing and the leading American scholar, Augustus Richard Norton, said it was "created by the Israeli occupation of Lebanon and by Iran". [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] [cite:hz3_statesman_barak] [cite:hz3_djn_rabin85] [cite:hz3_npr_norton] The case that it would have formed anyway rests on facts too: Musa al-Sadr's movement and Amal's armed wing predated 1982, Hezbollah's founders came from a clerical network trained in Najaf, and Iran's revolutionary state sent an ambassador and Revolutionary Guards to build it, which an Israeli researcher argues was decided in Tehran before the invasion and which Naim Qassem has said the invasion did not cause. [cite:hz3_wiki_amal] [cite:hz3_wiki_dawa] [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] The documented answer is that Hezbollah had more than one parent; which one was decisive is an argument, labelled here as such. Part Four follows the eighteen-year occupation and the war fought inside it, from the security zone to the withdrawal of May 2000. [scene:hz4_zone|Occupation and resistance]

sections.h: The Case That Israel Made Hezbollah
sections.html:
The argument that Israel's invasion and occupation created Hezbollah is an argument, not a finding: it is a claim about what would have happened in a Lebanon that Israel never entered, and no record can test that directly. What makes it more than a slogan is that it has been made, in plain words, by people who ran Israel's war in Lebanon, and by the leading American scholar of Lebanon's Shia politics. This section sets out that case and separates the facts it rests on from the inference it draws.

The facts it starts from. Israel invaded on 6 June 1982, as Part Two describes. [scene:hz2_invasion|The invasion] Two days later, on 8 June, a group of about fifty Shia fighters ambushed an Israeli armoured column at Khalde, south of Beirut; Hezbollah has since treated that ambush as the founding story of its military wing, an account recorded by the journalist Robert Fisk and by the Israeli general and historian Shimon Shapira. [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] In the weeks after the invasion, Iranian Revolutionary Guards, usually counted at 1,000 to 1,500, arrived in the Bekaa valley with Syrian permission and began training Lebanese fighters at a base there. [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] [scene:hz2_founding|The Guards in the Bekaa] When Hezbollah published its founding manifesto on 16 February 1985, read by Sheikh Ibrahim al-Amin, the first aim it named was a fight against American and Israeli power, including Israel's occupation of the south. [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] [scene:hz2_letter|The Open Letter] Those are documented events. They show that the organisation took shape during the invasion and named the occupation as its first enemy. They do not, by themselves, show that it would not have taken shape without it.

What Israeli officials said. The most quoted statement comes from Ehud Barak, the prime minister who ordered the withdrawal of May 2000. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] In 2006 he was quoted as saying: "When we entered Lebanon, there was no Hezbollah. We were accepted by perfumed rice and flowers by the Shi'a in the south." And: "It was our presence there that created Hezbollah." [cite:hz3_statesman_barak] [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] The original source is less certain than the words. Later accounts date the remark to 2006 without naming the outlet, and the Meir Amit Intelligence and Terrorism Information Center, an Israeli research centre, quotes a shorter version without a date. [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] The earliest attestation found is from July 2006, when the scholar Augustus Richard Norton told American radio that Barak had "noted that the Israeli presence in Lebanon basically created Hezbollah". [cite:hz3a_npr_norton] This book could not confirm the original interview and gives the quotation as reported. Barak's own recent words, which are confirmed, point the same way: in July 2026 he told the Associated Press that in 1985 he had warned "Our very presence will become the only goal", and that the occupation was "not serving Israeli security". [cite:hz3a_ap_barak] On that record, a senior Israeli commander and prime minister has described the occupation as a cause.

Yitzhak Rabin, defence minister when Israel pulled back to a strip of the south in 1985, said much the same in the language of warning. In February 1985, in an interview with Time magazine reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, he said that if Israel had merely swapped the threat of the Palestine Liberation Organization for a Shia one, "we have done the worst (thing) in our struggle against terrorism", and that the Shiites "have the potential for a kind of terrorism" Israel had not yet experienced. [cite:hz3_djn_rabin85] [cite:hz3a_djn_rabin85] A month later a Christian Science Monitor correspondent, reporting on attacks on Israeli troops in the south, wrote of Shiite fighters "sworn to drive the Israelis out of Lebanon", and reported that Rabin dreaded their animosity more than the Palestinian guerrilla attacks that preceded the 1982 invasion. [cite:hz3_csm_mar85] [cite:hz3a_csm_mar85] Rabin's policy was not to leave the south entirely. On the strip Israel kept, he said, "If there is a problem we will bomb them." [cite:hz3_djn_rabin85] [cite:hz3a_djn_rabin85] In September 1986 he said Israel would back the South Lebanon Army "with our firepower to permanently break any future offensive". [cite:hz3_ina_rabin86] That militia, according to the Congressional Research Service, was one Israel "fully funded and equipped"; by L'Orient-Le Jour's account its rank and file came to be mostly Shia, drawn in part by salaries, while the CRS cited estimates of about 30 per cent Shia, with some putting the share as high as half. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz4_olj_sla] [scene:hz4_zone|The security zone]

What the occupation did, in documented acts. The case does not rest on officials' remarks alone. When Israel pulled back in April 1985, it took more than 1,000 Shia detainees, most of them held at the Ansar camp, across the border into Israel; the International Committee of the Red Cross and the United States condemned the transfer as a breach of the Geneva Convention. [cite:hz3_csm_jun85] Israel's government said it had "always intended to return the Shiites to south Lebanon"; the sources consulted do not record its reason for moving them. [cite:hz3a_csm_jun85] Over the next fifteen years, Israel and its militia held a strip of the south, kept the Khiam prison, for whose abuses Human Rights Watch held Israel responsible in 1999, and fought Hezbollah there; [cite:hz4_hrw_khiam99] about 250 Israeli soldiers were killed there between 1985 and 2000, by a Reuters count cited by the Congressional Research Service. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [scene:hz4_zone|Part Four] The argument is that each of these acts gave the new organisation recruits, a cause the wider public in the south could share, and a battlefield on which to prove itself.

What the leading scholar argued. Augustus Richard Norton, a Boston University professor and the author of a widely used short history of Hezbollah, put it plainly on American radio in July 2006: "Hezbollah didn't exist in the early 1980s and was in effect created by the Israeli occupation of Lebanon and by Iran." [cite:hz3_npr_norton] He cited Barak's view that "the Israeli presence in Lebanon basically created Hezbollah", and said Iran "was attempting to extend its revolutionary goals to places like Lebanon". [cite:hz3_npr_norton] [cite:hz3a_npr_norton] In his book, as reviewers summarised it, Norton argued that the "profoundly destructive Israeli invasion of Lebanon in 1982" broke the PLO and helped create a "far more formidable" opponent, and he quoted both Barak and Rabin conceding that the occupation "provided the context in which Hezbollah was created". [cite:hz3_divine_norton] [cite:hz3_aljadid_norton] Norton's own formula names two causes, not one, a point the next section takes up.

Hezbollah's own account. Hezbollah tells its origin both ways, and that is itself part of the record. Its founding story centres on Khalde and the occupation, and its leaders have long described the fight against Israel as the reason the organisation exists; Naim Qassem, long its deputy leader, has called that struggle the central rationale of the party. [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] Yet the same 1985 manifesto pledged allegiance to Iran's supreme leader and to Ayatollah Khomeini's doctrine of rule by the senior jurist, and set the goal of making Lebanon part of the project of Iran's 1979 revolution. [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] And Qassem has also written, as quoted by the Israeli researcher Shapira, that "the Israeli invasion of Lebanon was not the reason Hezbollah was founded." [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] Hezbollah, in other words, presents itself as a resistance to occupation and as part of a revolutionary religious movement led from Tehran, and its own statements support both readings.

What the case shows and what it assumes. The documented part is strong: Hezbollah formed during the invasion, fought the occupation for eighteen years, and was described as its product by an Israeli prime minister, in words reported but not traced to their original source, and foreseen in the warnings of Israel's defence minister at the time. The inference, that without the invasion there would be no Hezbollah, assumes that the other forces at work in 1982 would not have produced an armed movement on their own. Even Barak's statement is a judgement made in hindsight, not evidence about the alternative. The record also shows that the organisation outlived the occupation, a fact the other side of the argument presses and the next section examines.

sections.h: The Case That It Would Have Formed Anyway
sections.html:
The opposite argument holds that Hezbollah, or something like it, would have formed without the invasion, because the forces that built it were already moving before June 1982. This too is an argument about a history that did not happen. It rests on three bodies of documented fact: Shia political mobilisation in the 1960s and 1970s, a network of Islamist clerics trained in Iraq, and revolutionary Iran's declared aim of exporting its revolution.

Mobilisation before 1982. Lebanon's Shia community did not enter politics in 1982. The cleric Musa al-Sadr moved from Najaf in Iraq to Tyre in late 1959, became the first head of the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in 1969, and in 1974 founded the Movement of the Deprived with Hussein el-Husseini. [cite:hz3_wiki_sadr] Its armed wing, formed in January 1975, became known as Amal. [cite:hz3_wiki_amal] Amal drew on a community that the historical record describes as the poorest in Lebanon and the most neglected by the state, and its support grew after three events: al-Sadr's disappearance on a visit to Libya at the end of August 1978, Israel's invasion of the south that year, and Iran's revolution in 1979. [cite:hz3_wiki_amal] [cite:hz3_wiki_sadr] [scene:hz1_1978|Operation Litani] An organised, armed Shia party therefore existed before 1982. But Amal was founded as a secular movement to reform the Lebanese system on behalf of the deprived, not a religious revolutionary one; [cite:hz3_wiki_amal] the Israeli researcher Shimon Shapira notes that it rejected Khomeini's doctrine of rule by the senior jurist and stayed loyal to the Lebanese government, which is why Tehran looked elsewhere. [cite:hz3_itic_shapira]

The clerical network. The men who led Hezbollah came largely out of a different tradition, formed in the seminaries of Najaf. Mohammad Hussein Fadlallah, often called Hezbollah's spiritual mentor, a title he and the group both denied, studied in Najaf for twenty-one years before settling in Beirut in 1966. [cite:hz3_wiki_fadlallah] The Islamic Dawa Party, an Iraqi Shia Islamist party founded around Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr between the late 1950s and late 1960s, had a Lebanese branch that, by Wikipedia's account, later became Hezbollah; among its members it lists the Hezbollah co-founders Abbas al-Musawi and Mohammad Yazbek. [cite:hz3_wiki_dawa] Norton, in his history, stresses Iraq rather than Iran as the place "where many of Hezbollah's leading intellectuals originated", and describes a directive from Iraq for these clerics to work inside Amal to give it a more Islamic character. [cite:hz3_aljadid_norton] Naim Qassem has said that Hezbollah began as factions of Islamic movements inspired by Fadlallah. [cite:hz3_wiki_fadlallah] In the summer of 1982, Amal's deputy leader Husayn al-Musawi broke away to form Islamic Amal, one of the groups later folded into Hezbollah. [cite:hz3_wiki_amal]

Iran's stated aim. The third force is the one this side of the argument treats as decisive. After 1979, Ayatollah Khomeini's government declared that it would export its revolution, and, according to Shapira, a network built under a cleric named Montazeri supported Shia Islamist movements in the Hijaz in Saudi Arabia, in Bahrain, in Kuwait and in Lebanon. [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] Shapira, a retired Israeli brigadier general writing for the Meir Amit Intelligence and Terrorism Information Center, an Israeli research centre, puts the thesis directly: "The decision to establish Hezbollah was made in Tehran three years before Israel invaded Lebanon." [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] He names Ali Akbar Mohtashami, Iran's ambassador in Damascus, as the organisation's architect, and dates his posting to August 1981, a date this book could not confirm independently. [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] For him the invasion was a catalyst that gave Iran's plan its opening, not the plan itself. Hezbollah's own manifesto of 1985, with its pledge to Iran's supreme leader, and Qassem's statement that "the Israeli invasion of Lebanon was not the reason Hezbollah was founded", are the strongest evidence this side has, because they come from the organisation itself. [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] Norton, on the other side, does not deny Iran's role; his own formula is that Hezbollah was "created by the Israeli occupation of Lebanon and by Iran". [cite:hz3_npr_norton]

Where Israel did not occupy. One way to test the argument is to look at what the same networks did in countries Israel never entered. On 12 December 1983, bombs struck the American and French embassies, the airport and the main oil refinery in Kuwait; seventeen suspects were arrested, most of them members of the Iraqi Dawa party, and the attacks were described as punishment for Kuwait's, America's and France's support of Iraq in its war with Iran. [cite:hz3_wiki_dawa] The network Shapira describes reached Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Kuwait as well. [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] These facts show that Iran's revolutionary network sought armed allies, and found some, where there was no Israeli occupation; their stated enemies were the governments that backed Iraq. They do not show that any of those allies would have become what Hezbollah became, a political party with its own army, and the sources gathered do not settle that question. The groups Iran later backed in Iraq and Yemen grew out of other wars, and Part Ten follows them. [scene:hz10_iraq|Iraq's militias] [scene:hz10_houthis|The Houthis]

The test of 2000. A second test is what happened when the occupation ended. If occupation alone explained Hezbollah, its end should have weakened the case for its arms. Instead Hezbollah kept its weapons after the Taif agreement required militias to disarm, on the ground, which the agreement's text does not state, that it was resisting Israel's occupation of the south, and kept them again after Israel's withdrawal in May 2000, citing the Shebaa Farms and Lebanese prisoners. [cite:hz4_lbc_arms] [cite:hz4a_olj_taif] [cite:hz4_merip_2000] One side reads that as evidence that resistance was the means and Iran's project the end; the other reads it as the ordinary persistence of an armed movement whose grievances were not all settled, since Lebanon still claims the farms and Israel still held Lebanese prisoners, some until an exchange in 2004 and others, among them Samir Kuntar, until July 2008; Israel says the farms are Syrian land, and the UN placed them on the Syrian side of its line. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] [cite:hz4_wiki_raid2000] [cite:hz5b_aj_swap] [scene:hz4_withdrawal|The withdrawal] Both readings are arguments about motive. The documented fact is the persistence.

Compared with Hamas. Part Three of the Hamas volume reached a two-part answer: the Islamist movement in Gaza predated Israel's occupation, but the armed organisation called Hamas was founded in the uprising against it. [cite:hm_pbs_baconi] [cite:hm_wsj_spawn] [scene:hm3_question|Would Hamas exist?] Hezbollah's case is similar in its first half and different in its second. Shia political mobilisation and the Najaf clerical network both predated 1982. But Hezbollah was born with a foreign state's Revolutionary Guards training it and a pledge of loyalty to that state's leader in its founding text, while Hamas grew out of a movement, the Muslim Brotherhood, rather than out of a state. [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] [cite:hm_pbs_baconi] The occupation explains more of Hamas's armed turn than of Hezbollah's; Iran explains more of Hezbollah's shape than of Hamas's.

What cannot be known. No source can say whether Iran's ambassador and the Revolutionary Guards would have found a Lebanese foothold without an Israeli army in the south, whether the Najaf-trained clerics would have taken Amal over or split from it anyway, or whether a small armed Islamist party would ever have grown into the force described in later parts of this book. What the record does support is narrower. Every one of the forces in the figure above is documented; the invasion brought them together in the same place and time; and among the people with most reason to play down the occupation's part, an Israeli prime minister said it created Hezbollah and an Israeli defence minister warned in 1985 of what it was producing, while the organisation itself has described its founding both as a response to the occupation and as something the occupation did not cause. This book's reading, offered as argument, is that Hezbollah had more than one parent, and that removing any one of them changes what would have been born.

chapters.label: Part Four
chapters.title: Occupation and Resistance
chapters.intro: Part Four covers the fifteen years between Israel's pullback to a strip of southern Lebanon in 1985 and its withdrawal in May 2000, the period in which Hezbollah grew from a cluster of armed cells into the force that pushed Israel out. It sets out how the "security zone" worked and who paid for it, including the Lebanese militia Israel funded and armed and the Khiam prison that militia ran; how Hezbollah fought its Shia rival Amal and came out of the civil war as the only militia allowed to keep its weapons; the two Israeli air and artillery campaigns of 1993 and 1996, the shelling of the UN compound at Qana and the written rules that followed; the withdrawal, the dispute over the Shebaa Farms that kept the conflict alive, and the attacks abroad, in Buenos Aires and later in Bulgaria, that courts attributed to Hezbollah and that Hezbollah denies.
chapters.outro: Part Four established that Israel held a strip of south Lebanon for fifteen years through a Lebanese militia it created, paid about $500 to $800 a man each month and equipped, and that this militia ran the Khiam prison, whose interrogators Israel's Shin Bet trained. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz4_hrw_khiam99] It showed how Hezbollah came out of the civil war as the one militia allowed to keep its arms, as "resistance" to that occupation, a status the agreement's text never names. [cite:hz4_wiki_taif] [cite:hz4_lbc_arms] [cite:hz4a_olj_taif] Two Israeli campaigns whose stated method was to move civilians north killed about 120 Lebanese civilians in 1993 and 154 in 1996, including about 100 at Qana, where the UN found error "unlikely" and Israel maintained it was a mistake; Hezbollah's rockets, fired as stated reprisals, killed and wounded Israeli civilians in the same years. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] [cite:hz4_hrw_grapes] [cite:hz4_un_qana] The withdrawal of May 2000 ended the occupation the UN certified, and the Shebaa Farms dispute gave Hezbollah a stated reason to keep its weapons. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] [cite:hz4_merip_2000] Argentine and Bulgarian courts attributed the Buenos Aires and Burgas bombings to Hezbollah, and in Argentina to Iran, in proceedings against absent defendants; both deny it. [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] [cite:hz4_aje_burgas] Part Five turns to the cross-border raid of July 2006 and the war that followed. [scene:hz5_war|Part Five: the 2006 war]

sections.h: The Security Zone
sections.html:
When Israel pulled most of its army back from central Lebanon in 1985, it did not go home. It kept a self-declared "security zone" along the border, about nine miles deep, which covered roughly a tenth of the country. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] Human Rights Watch put the zone at about 850 square kilometres, with some 150,000 residents in 162 villages and towns. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] The zone lay south of the Litani River, not along or north of it as some later accounts have it. It lasted fifteen years, from 1985 to May 2000; the phrase "eighteen-year occupation" counts from the 1982 invasion, and "twenty-two years" counts from the 1978 one. [cite:hz4_merip_2000]

Israel did not hold the zone mainly with its own soldiers. Human Rights Watch counted 1,000 to 1,200 Israeli troops in it, alongside 2,500 to 3,000 fighters of the South Lebanon Army (SLA), a Lebanese militia. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] That arrangement is the first documented fact this book sets against the thesis it is testing: that armed groups on Israel's borders serve as reasons for war rather than only as its targets. Whatever one makes of the thesis, the SLA is not an inference. It was a Lebanese armed force that Israel created, paid and supplied.

Who built the SLA. The militia began in the civil war, when Lebanon's army broke apart. Major Saad Haddad, a Greek Catholic officer with about 700 men at Marjayoun, joined other Christian officers and, coordinating with Israel, took control of areas near the border; in April 1979 he proclaimed a "State of Free Lebanon" from Metulla, inside Israel. [cite:hz4_olj_sla] Human Rights Watch reported that Israel helped establish this force in 1976 and later supplied it with advisers and equipment. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] Haddad renamed it the South Lebanon Army in May 1980; after he died of cancer in January 1984, a defected Lebanese army general, Antoine Lahad, took command in April 1984. [cite:hz4_olj_sla]

Who paid for it. The US Congressional Research Service described the SLA as "an allied militia that [Israel] fully funded and equipped." Israel paid its members about $500 to $800 a month, and the annual cost, with maintenance and infrastructure, was estimated at $35 million. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] A former Israeli general, Avraham Tamir, said "huge sums of money were invested in fortifying and equipping the SLA." [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] Its commanders were mostly Christian, but its ranks were not: CRS cited estimates of about 30 percent Shia, 13 percent Druze and 7 percent Sunni, with some observers putting the Shia share as high as half, and L'Orient-Le Jour reported that Shia recruits became the majority partly because the salaries drew men in hard times. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz4_olj_sla] Israel's stated position throughout was that the SLA was an ally defending its own area and that Israel's aim was to protect its northern towns. [cite:hz4_jvl_rabin93]

Khiam. At Khiam, a town in the zone, the SLA ran a detention centre from 1985 until 2000. Amnesty International reported in May 1992 that about 200 people were held there with no legal basis, that the International Committee of the Red Cross had never been allowed to visit, and that since 1988 detainees had had no contact with their families; it said the evidence "suggests that Israeli officials have been directly involved" in interrogation and torture, at least until 1988. [cite:hz4_ai_khiam92] Human Rights Watch, which documented torture of detainees held without charge through the 1980s and 1990s, held Israel ultimately responsible as the occupying power. [cite:hz4_hrw_khiam99]

Israel's own account came in a September 1999 affidavit to its High Court. The defence ministry said Khiam was "under the responsibility" of the SLA and that its interrogators and jailers were Lebanese. It also admitted that officers of the Shin Bet, Israel's internal security service, met SLA interrogators several times a year, that they "cooperate with members of the SLA, and even assist them by means of professional guidance and training," and that Israel and the SLA consulted on arrests and releases. [cite:hz4_hrw_khiam99] Shin Bet documents released years later, after a petition by the Israeli lawyer Eitay Mack, include a 1987 report saying the SLA ran the prison with staff trained by the army and the Shin Bet, and that detainees were held without charge or detention orders for indefinite periods. [cite:hz4_mee_khiam] Israel maintains that it did not run Khiam. The record shows it paid the force that did, trained its interrogators and had a say in who was held.

The war between the Shia parties. Inside the community Hezbollah drew on, its first major armed contest was not with Israel but with Amal, the older Shia movement. From April 1988 to November 1990 the two fought in the south, the Bekaa and Beirut's southern suburbs; Amal was backed by Syria and Hezbollah by Iran. In April and May 1988 Amal drove Hezbollah out of most of its southern positions. [cite:hz4_wiki_brothers] A Damascus Agreement signed on 30 January 1989, supervised by Syria's foreign minister Farouk al-Sharaa and Iran's Ali Akbar Velayati, gave Amal responsibility for security in the south and let Hezbollah resume political and social work there. [cite:hz4_wiki_brothers] Casualty estimates for the conflict vary widely and none is authoritative. Fighting continued until late 1990.

Taif: the militia that was not a militia. The Taif Agreement, signed in Saudi Arabia on 22 October 1989 and ratified by Lebanon's parliament on 5 November, ended the civil war. It split parliament equally between Christians and Muslims and required all Lebanese and non-Lebanese militias to be disbanded and their weapons handed to the state within six months; it also called for "all requisite measures to liberate all Lebanese land from Israeli occupation", and the word "resistance" does not appear in it. [cite:hz4a_olj_taif] Parliament ordered the militias dissolved by 30 April 1991. [cite:hz4_wiki_taif] [cite:hz4a_nd_taif] Amal handed its weapons to the Lebanese army and the Druze PSP gave its arms to the Syrian army. "Hezbollah, however, neither surrendered its weapons nor entered any discussions on disarmament." [cite:hz4_lbc_arms] It was allowed to remain active, treated in practice as a "resistance force" against Israel's occupation of the south rather than as a militia. [cite:hz4_wiki_taif] [cite:hz4a_nd_taif] No clause of the agreement grants that status. Hezbollah and its allies argue that the militia clause never applied to it and point to successive governments' ministerial statements endorsing the resistance; its critics call that reading retroactive and say such statements have no binding force. [cite:hz4a_olj_taif] The exemption tied Hezbollah's weapons to Israel's presence. That link is why the withdrawal of 2000, and the argument over what remained occupied afterwards, mattered so much. [scene:hz4_withdrawal|The withdrawal and the Shebaa Farms]

Musawi and Nasrallah. On 16 February 1992 Israeli helicopters fired missiles into the motorcade of Abbas al-Musawi, Hezbollah's secretary-general, killing him, his wife, his five-year-old son and others. [cite:hz4_wiki_musawi] Israel described the strike as retaliation for the capture of Israeli servicemen; later reporting by Ronen Bergman and Dieter Bednarz said the original plan had been to abduct him for a prisoner exchange, and some Israeli officers warned that a more radical successor would follow. [cite:hz4_wiki_musawi] The successor was Hassan Nasrallah, who would lead the organisation into the wars that the rest of this book describes. [cite:hz4_wiki_musawi] A month later, on 17 March 1992, the Israeli embassy in Buenos Aires was bombed, in an attack claimed as revenge for Musawi's killing. [cite:hz4a_infobae_1992] [scene:hz4_abroad|Attacks abroad]

In August 1992, in the first post-war election, Hezbollah entered Lebanon's parliament for the first time, winning what the Christian Science Monitor called a "landslide" in the east. [cite:hz4_csm_1992] From then on it was both an armed force exempted from disarmament and a party in the state, the dual form the rest of this book follows. [scene:hz6_state|Hezbollah as a party and a state within a state]

sections.h: Accountability, Grapes of Wrath and Qana
sections.html:
Through the 1990s the war in the south ran on a pattern that both sides described openly. Hezbollah attacked Israeli and SLA positions in the zone. When Israeli or SLA fire killed civilians in Lebanese villages, Hezbollah fired Katyusha rockets into northern Israel. When the rockets hit Israeli towns, Israel struck far beyond the zone. Twice, in 1993 and 1996, that cycle produced a week or more of bombardment, and each time it ended in an unwritten or written set of rules about civilians. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns]

Operation Accountability, July 1993. On 25 July 1993 Israel began a week of air and artillery strikes across southern Lebanon. Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin told the Knesset on 28 July that Hezbollah, backed by Iran, had fired Katyushas at the zone and at Kiryat Shmona and Nahariya, that Syria had "turned a blind eye," and that 92 Israeli soldiers and civilians had been killed since the zone was created. He named the operation's goal as restoring "security to the lives of residents in communities of the north." [cite:hz4_jvl_rabin93] He also stated its method: Lebanese civilians would be moved north, away from villages where Hezbollah operated, so that, he said, the army could fight Hezbollah without harming them, and the Lebanese and Syrian governments would be pressured to restrain it; residents could return only "if fire at the northern communities ceases." [cite:hz4_jvl_rabin93] The commander of Israel's artillery corps said the aim was "to destroy the villages and the houses of the activists and the locations from which the rockets are fired." [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns]

Israel's artillery fired about 25,000 rounds; Hezbollah fired about 150 rockets into northern Israel. [cite:hz4_wiki_accountability] Human Rights Watch counted about 120 Lebanese civilians killed, close to 500 injured and some 300,000 Lebanese villagers and Palestinian refugees displaced; Hezbollah's rockets killed two Israeli civilians and injured 24. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] The fighting stopped on 31 July under a US-brokered understanding that was never written down: Hezbollah would not fire rockets into northern Israel, and Israel and the SLA would not attack civilians in Lebanon. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns]

The rule both sides stated. The rules broke down repeatedly. In 1995, Human Rights Watch recorded, Katyusha attacks killed two civilians and injured 31 in Israel. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] Hezbollah's deputy leader, Naim Qassem, set out its policy in April 1995: "whenever the Israeli enemy shells and harms civilians in our villages, we will shell northern Palestine." [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] Human Rights Watch's report on these years, titled Civilian Pawns, treated both the rocket fire on Israeli towns and Israel's shelling of Lebanese villages as violations of the laws of war, whatever reprisal each side claimed. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns]

Grapes of Wrath, April 1996. On 11 April 1996, after weeks of escalating attacks, Israel launched Operation Grapes of Wrath. By 15 April, warnings to leave had gone to 86 Lebanese communities. [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] An unnamed Israeli official told the Wall Street Journal that the policy was to force civilians out to pressure the Lebanese government: "let's just say we hope Lebanon understands the message." [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] The UN estimated that at least 400,000 people, about one in eight Lebanese, were displaced. The Lebanese army counted 154 civilians killed and 351 injured over the sixteen days. [cite:hz4_hrw_grapes] Hezbollah kept firing rockets at northern Israel; on 9 April alone, five Israelis were wounded and 38 treated for shock. [cite:hz4_hrw_grapes]

Qana, 18 April 1996. On the afternoon of 18 April, Israeli artillery shelled the compound of the UN peacekeeping force's Fijian battalion at Qana, where hundreds of villagers had taken shelter. The UN's investigator recorded "an estimated 100 persons" killed; Human Rights Watch counted 102 by 24 April; the figure most often given since is 106. [cite:hz4_un_qana] [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] [cite:hz4_army_qana]

The UN Secretary-General sent his military adviser, Major-General Franklin van Kappen of the Netherlands, to investigate. His report of 1 May 1996 found that Hezbollah fighters had fired mortars from about 220 metres from the centre of the compound, about 15 minutes before the shelling, and had fired rockets from nearby earlier that day. [cite:hz4_un_qana] It found that an Israeli drone had been over the area, contrary to earlier Israeli denials, and that almost all the proximity-fused shells, which burst in the air above their target, fell on the compound. It concluded that "it is unlikely that the shelling of the United Nations compound was the result of gross technical and/or procedural errors," while adding that this "cannot be ruled out completely." [cite:hz4_un_qana] An addendum recorded Israel's correction that a drone had been operating but was sent to Qana after the shelling ended. [cite:hz4_un_qana]

Israel's position, given to the UN, was that the deaths resulted from "a sequence of operational mistakes and technical failures, compounded by chance," and that it was "not Israeli policy to target civilians or the United Nations." [cite:hz4_un_qana] Prime Minister Shimon Peres said, "We did not know that several hundred people were concentrated in that camp," and that Hezbollah had "used the U.N. as a shield." [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] A 2016 article on the US Army's website argued that the pattern of impacts fits fire-direction and map errors rather than intent. [cite:hz4_army_qana] Human Rights Watch did not find intent proven but called the barrage at minimum "a reckless and negligent attack," and disputed Israel's statement that it did not know civilians were sheltering there. It also noted that UNIFIL counted about 270 incidents of fire at or near UN positions in the operation, about 15 of them by Lebanese guerrillas and the rest by Israeli or SLA forces. [cite:hz4_hrw_grapes] Whether the shelling was deliberate is contested and the record does not settle it. That it was Israeli fire, that it followed Hezbollah fire from beside a crowded UN base, and that the UN found error "unlikely" are all documented. The UN General Assembly later requested that Israel pay for the damage, and draft resolutions put the sum at some $1.12 million; the UN Secretary-General reported that Israel had not responded. [cite:hz4_un_qanacost]

The April Understanding. The operation ended on 27 April 1996 with a written text brokered by the United States and France. Armed groups in Lebanon would not attack Israel with Katyushas or any other weapon; Israel "and those cooperating with it", meaning the SLA, would not fire at civilians or civilian targets in Lebanon; both sides committed that civilians would never be targeted and that populated areas would not be used as launching grounds; and nothing in it barred self-defence. [cite:hz4_jvl_april] A Monitoring Group of the United States, France, Syria, Lebanon and Israel would hear complaints filed within 24 hours. [cite:hz4_jvl_april] The text said nothing about attacks on soldiers. That silence left the fighting between Hezbollah and Israeli and SLA forces inside the zone outside its terms, and within that frame the fighting went on for four more years. [scene:hz4_withdrawal|The withdrawal]

sections.h: The Withdrawal and the Shebaa Farms
sections.html:
By the late 1990s the security zone had become a political cost inside Israel. In 1997, 73 soldiers were killed in a helicopter accident, and four mothers whose sons were serving there started a movement, Four Mothers, that demanded only one thing: withdrawal. It drew in bereaved parents, former soldiers and a former army commander in Lebanon, and made open criticism of the army's presence there acceptable. [cite:hz4_csm_mothers] Ehud Barak pledged in 1999 to withdraw and, as prime minister, promised to "bring the boys home" by July 2000. [cite:hz4_olj_sla] [cite:hz4_csm_mothers] [cite:hz4_merip_2000] After his pledge, desertions from the SLA became common. [cite:hz4_olj_sla]

The counts of what the zone cost Israel depend on the window. CRS, citing Reuters, gave roughly 250 Israeli soldiers killed between 1985 and April 2000; Israel Hayom, marking the twentieth anniversary, gave 414 for Israel's presence in south Lebanon without stating the start date. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz4_ih_20yrs] The SLA said it had lost 621 fighters and 200 civilians from its founding to March 2000. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] The public record does not show a comparable official count of Lebanese civilians and Hezbollah fighters killed in the zone over the fifteen years; Part Nine returns to the counting. [scene:hz9_ledger|The ledger]

Forty-eight hours in May. The withdrawal came weeks ahead of schedule and all at once. Word of the first pullbacks spread on 22 May 2000; Lebanese civilians and Hezbollah fighters moved into villages faster than the Israeli army and the SLA could leave them. [cite:hz4_merip_2000] Barak ordered the withdrawal on 23 May and it was complete the next day. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] What had been planned as a gradual, UN-supervised handover was, in MERIP's words, "crammed into a chaotic 48 hours." [cite:hz4_merip_2000] At Khiam, villagers broke open the cells. [cite:hz4_merip_2000]

The end of the SLA. The militia Israel had paid for fifteen years abandoned its posts and dissolved rather than fight alone. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] About 1,500 members crossed into Israel, with dependants making 6,000 to 7,000 people in all, mostly mid- and high-ranking Christian officers; Israel had expected only a few hundred. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] The Lebanese army held 1,488 who stayed. A Beirut military tribunal convicted 77 of them on 5 June with sentences of one month to five years, far lighter than the death and life sentences passed in absentia on senior officers. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] About 7,500 former members and their families still lived in Israel when L'Orient-Le Jour reviewed the militia's history; a 2011 Lebanese law meant to let them return never received its implementing decrees, largely because of Hezbollah's opposition. [cite:hz4_olj_sla]

Who won. In Lebanon, 25 May is marked as the day the south was liberated, and Hezbollah claimed the withdrawal as the resistance's achievement, while saying it was not yet complete. [cite:hz4_lbc_arms] [cite:hz4_merip_2000] Israel presented it as a unilateral decision taken by an elected government and certified by the UN as full compliance with Security Council Resolution 425 of 1978. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] Both accounts hold as far as they go: an Israeli government decided to leave, and the Israeli movement that pressed it to do so cited soldiers' deaths in the zone, including those caused by Hezbollah's attacks, as its reason.

The Blue Line. Because Lebanon and Israel had no agreed border, the UN drew a line of withdrawal. In a report of 22 May 2000 the Secretary-General used, for the eastern sector, the old boundary between the areas of UNIFIL, the peacekeepers in Lebanon, and UNDOF, the observers on the Golan. The Security Council endorsed the report on 23 May, and on 16 June 2000 the Secretary-General reported that Israel had withdrawn in compliance with Resolution 425. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] The line was drawn "without prejudice" to any future border agreement between Lebanon and Syria. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa]

The Shebaa Farms. That line left in Israeli hands a strip of about 25 square kilometres on the western slope of Mount Hermon, around fourteen farmsteads, known as the Shebaa Farms. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] Israel had taken it from Syria in 1967. The UN treated it as Syrian territory on the Golan, governed by Resolutions 242 and 338, not by 425. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] Lebanon claimed it, citing title deeds, a reported 1964 joint commission and a 1966 map; Syria's foreign minister told the Secretary-General on 16 May 2000 that Syria supported the claim, but the two governments never filed an agreed border to settle it. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] Israel's position was that the farms are part of the Syrian Golan and that the UN's determination bound it. The United States endorsed the UN's withdrawal requirements and took no position on who owns the farms. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa]

The dispute mattered because of Taif. Hezbollah's weapons had been tolerated as "resistance" to occupation, a status the agreement's text does not mention. [cite:hz4_wiki_taif] [cite:hz4a_olj_taif] If the occupation was over, so was the exemption. Nasrallah said in May 2000 that the withdrawal would not be complete until the Shebaa Farms were freed and the Lebanese detainees held in Israel were released. [cite:hz4_merip_2000] Some analysts argued that Syria kept the issue open to keep pressure on Israel over the Golan, which Syria denied. [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] Whether the farms were a real grievance, a pretext or both is an argument, and both sides of it are on the record. What the record shows is that a 25-square-kilometre strip gave an armed movement a stated reason to stay armed after the occupation that created it had ended.

7 October 2000. Less than five months after the withdrawal, Hezbollah ambushed an Israeli patrol on the border near the Shebaa Farms and took three soldiers: Adi Avitan, Benyamin Avraham and Omar Sawaid. [cite:hz4_wiki_raid2000] [cite:hz4_crs_shebaa] Israeli military intelligence later assessed that they were killed during the attack or immediately after it. Hezbollah also seized Elchanan Tenenbaum, an Israeli businessman and reserve colonel, after luring him abroad. On 29 January 2004 Israel released 435 prisoners, among them about 400 Palestinians and 30 Lebanese and other Arab prisoners, returned the remains of 59 Lebanese and handed over maps of its minefields in the south; it received Tenenbaum alive and the remains of the three soldiers. [cite:hz4_wiki_raid2000] The capture set the pattern for the next one: in July 2006 another cross-border raid to take soldiers for exchange started a war. [scene:hz5_war|The 2006 war]

sections.h: Attacks Abroad: Buenos Aires and Burgas
sections.html:
Hezbollah's war with Israel in these years was fought mostly in south Lebanon. Twice in the 1990s, and again in 2012, bombs went off far from it, against Israeli and Jewish targets in Argentina and against Israeli tourists in Bulgaria. Courts in both countries attributed the attacks to Hezbollah, and in Argentina to Iran as the state that ordered them. Hezbollah denies all three; Iran denies the Argentine charges and called the Burgas accusation baseless. This section sets out what the courts found, how they reached it and what remains unresolved.

The Israeli embassy, 17 March 1992. A van loaded with explosives was driven into Israel's embassy in Buenos Aires. The usual count is 29 dead and more than 200 injured; a 1999 act of Argentina's Supreme Court set its own count of the dead at 22. [cite:hz4_infobae_1992] Two days later a statement signed "Islamic Jihad Organization" was sent to the Beirut daily An-Nahar. It called the bombing retaliation for the killing a month earlier of Abbas al-Musawi, Hezbollah's secretary-general, by Israeli helicopters; one reference account says it named his five-year-old son Hussein, killed with him. [cite:hz4a_infobae_1992] [cite:hz4a_wiki_emb1992] [cite:hz4_wiki_musawi] [scene:hz4_zone|Musawi and Nasrallah] On 10 May 1999 Argentina's Supreme Court found that Islamic Jihad organised and carried out the attack; later rulings in the case named Imad Mughniyeh, a senior Hezbollah security commander, as responsible and an international warrant was issued for him. [cite:hz4_infobae_1992] Infobae's account treats "Islamic Jihad" as a cover name for Hezbollah and takes the group's release of video footage to Lebanese television as confirmation of authorship; Hezbollah, under its own name, denies involvement. [cite:hz4a_infobae_1992] [cite:hz4a_wiki_emb1992]

AMIA, 18 July 1994. A car bomb destroyed the building of the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association (AMIA), the main Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires, killing 85 people and injuring about 300. It remains the deadliest attack in Argentina's history. [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] The investigation became a scandal of its own. The first investigating judge, Juan José Galeano, was later convicted for paying a suspect to give false testimony against provincial police officers, and in 2024 his sentence was cut from six years to four on appeal. Former president Carlos Menem, accused of covering up a "Syrian connection," was acquitted. [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] Thirty-two years on, no one has been arrested for the bombing itself. [cite:hz4_bat_cassation]

In October 2006 Argentine prosecutors formally accused Iran of ordering the attack and Hezbollah of carrying it out, and asked for the arrest of former president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, six other senior Iranian officials and Imad Mughniyeh. Iran's foreign ministry called the charges "Zionist propaganda" and cited Galeano's corruption as proof they were baseless. [cite:hz4_aje_2006] Hezbollah rejected the claims too; when prosecutors named a Lebanese man as the suicide bomber, it said he had been killed fighting Israeli forces in south Lebanon. [cite:hz4_jpost_hzdeny] The lead prosecutor, Alberto Nisman, was found dead on 18 January 2015, hours before he was due to present evidence to Congress that President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner had covered up Iran's role through a deal with Tehran. In December 2017 a federal judge ruled that his death "could not have been a suicide." Kirchner called the accusation against her an "absurdity." [cite:hz4_toi_nisman] Who killed Nisman has not been established in court.

The 2024 cassation ruling. On 11 April 2024, ruling on appeals in the cover-up trial, Argentina's Federal Criminal Cassation Court (judges Carlos Mahiques, Ángela Ledesma and Diego Barroetaveña) found in a 711-page decision that Iran ordered both the 1992 embassy bombing and the 1994 AMIA bombing, and that Hezbollah carried them out under "the inspiration, organisation, planning and financing of state and parastatal bodies subordinate to the Ayatollahs' government." [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] It declared both attacks crimes against humanity, which places them beyond any statute of limitations, and called Iran "a terrorist state." [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] [cite:hz4_almon_cassation] It found the motive in Argentina's 1991–92 cancellation of three nuclear technology contracts with Iran. [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] Judge Mahiques said the attack was carried out "under the mandate of a government, of a State." [cite:hz4_almon_cassation] Iran has denied involvement throughout and refuses to hand over the accused. [cite:hz4_bat_absentia]

Status as of October 2026. Under a law that took effect in March 2025 allowing trials of defendants who evade justice, Federal Judge Daniel Rafecas ordered in June 2025 that ten Iranian and Lebanese suspects be tried in absentia, among them former intelligence minister Ali Fallahian, former foreign minister Ali Akbar Velayati, former Revolutionary Guard commander Mohsen Rezai, former Quds Force commander Ahmad Vahidi and three named Hezbollah members. [cite:hz4_bat_absentia] In a ruling reported on 24 September 2026, the Cassation Court rejected a constitutional challenge to the in-absentia law, clearing the way for an oral trial; as of October 2026 no trial date had been reported. [cite:hz4_dc_absentia] [cite:hz4a_dc_absentia] The court findings are the strongest attribution in this book's record for any attack abroad: a judgment of the country's highest criminal appeals court after three decades of investigation. They are also findings against defendants who have never appeared, in an investigation once corrupted by its own judge, and the denials of Iran and Hezbollah stand beside them.

Burgas, 18 July 2012. A bomb exploded on a bus carrying Israeli tourists at the airport in Burgas, on Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, killing five Israelis and the Bulgarian driver. The man carrying it, Mohamad Hassan El Husseini, a dual Lebanese-French citizen, also died. [cite:hz4_aje_burgas] Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu blamed Hezbollah and Iran within hours; Iran called the accusation "baseless." [cite:hz4_wiki_burgas] On 5 February 2013 Bulgaria's interior minister, Tsvetan Tsvetanov, said investigators had followed the suspects' financing and contacts in Australia and Canada and that "a reasonable assumption can be made that the two of them were members of the militant wing of Hezbollah." [cite:hz4_lwj_burgas13] After a change of government, the new foreign minister said in June 2013 that there was "no conclusive evidence"; in July the new interior minister said there were "clear signs" of Hezbollah's responsibility. [cite:hz4_wiki_burgas] In September 2020 Bulgaria's Specialised Criminal Court, trying them in absentia, sentenced Meliad Farah, an Australian of Lebanese origin, and Hassan El Hajj Hassan, a Canadian of Lebanese origin, to life without parole for giving the bomber logistical support. Hezbollah denies involvement. [cite:hz4_aje_burgas]

The EU listing. On 22 July 2013 EU foreign ministers agreed unanimously to put Hezbollah's "military wing" on the EU terrorism list, citing Burgas, a conviction of a Hezbollah member in Cyprus and its fighting in Syria. The EU's foreign policy chief, Catherine Ashton, said the step did not prevent "dialogue with all political parties in Lebanon." [cite:hz4_lwj_eu13] The split between wings was the EU's construction, not Hezbollah's: its deputy leader, Naim Qassem, had said in 2012, "We don't have a military wing and a political one." [cite:hz4_lwj_eu13] Israeli ministers welcomed the decision; one, Avigdor Lieberman, said the EU had gone only halfway. [cite:hz4_lwj_eu13]

These cases matter to this book's thesis in a specific way. When Israel or the United States names Hezbollah as a threat beyond Lebanon, part of the record behind the claim is court findings, not intelligence assessments alone: an Argentine appellate judgment and a Bulgarian conviction, each with its weaknesses stated above. The thesis that Hezbollah serves as a justification for war has to be weighed against that record, as Part Eleven does. [scene:hz11_pattern|The pattern tested]

chapters.label: Part Five
chapters.title: The 2006 War
chapters.intro: Part Five covers the war that began with Hezbollah's cross-border raid of 12 July 2006 and ended with a ceasefire 34 days later. It sets out what each side said it was doing and what it did: Israel's strikes on Lebanon's roads, bridges, airport and Beirut's southern suburbs, and Hezbollah's rockets on northern Israel. It gives the dead on both sides with the source and counting method of each figure, the Qana strike of 30 July, and the cluster munitions fired in the war's last three days, beside the findings of Human Rights Watch and the responses of the parties. It then turns to what came after: Security Council Resolution 1701 and the record of its terms, Israel's own Winograd inquiry, and the "Dahiya doctrine" that Israel's northern commander announced in 2008, which made the destruction of 2006 an explicit model for future wars.
chapters.outro: Part Five established that Hezbollah began the 2006 war with a raid that killed eight Israeli soldiers and captured two for a prisoner exchange, and that Israel answered with a campaign against Lebanon's infrastructure as well as Hezbollah, on the stated ground that the Lebanese state was responsible. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Human Rights Watch identified at least 1,109 Lebanese killed by Israeli attacks, the vast majority civilians, and found Israel's failure to distinguish civilians from fighters the main cause; Hezbollah's roughly 4,000 rockets killed 44 Israeli civilians, and 121 Israeli soldiers died. [cite:hz5_rw_why] [cite:hz5_hrw_why9] [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Israel fired up to four million cluster submunitions by the UN's estimate, and as many as 4.6 million on information from its own soldiers, about 90 percent of the strikes in the final 72 hours; its own commission found that use in breach of international law on protecting civilians. [cite:hz5b_hrw_flooding] [cite:hz5a_irin_winograd] Resolution 1701 required Hezbollah to stay out of the south and Israel to stop offensive operations and withdraw; by 2024 neither the disarmament nor the end of violations had happened. [cite:hz5_un_1701] [cite:hz5_wiki_1701] Israel's Winograd Commission called the war "a serious missed opportunity," and the commander of Israel's northern front promised, in 2008, that what happened to the Dahieh would happen "in every village from which Israel is fired on." [cite:hz5_jvl_winograd] [cite:hz5_jps_khalidi] Part Six turns to Hezbollah itself in the years after 2006: a party in government, an army in Syria and a financial network. [scene:hz6_state|Part Six: Hezbollah as its own actor]

sections.h: Thirty-Four Days
sections.html:
