On the morning of 12 July 2006 Hezbollah fighters crossed the border into Israel and attacked an army patrol. They killed three soldiers in the ambush and took two reservists, Ehud Goldwasser and Eldad Regev, back into Lebanon. An Israeli tank sent after them struck a large mine; five more soldiers died in the failed rescue attempt. Eight Israeli soldiers were killed that day and two were captured. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Accounts that give three dead count only the ambush; the figure of eight includes the pursuit. [cite:hz5_wiki_war]

The raid was not a new tactic. In October 2000 Hezbollah had captured three Israeli soldiers in the Shebaa Farms area and traded their bodies, with a captured Israeli businessman, for prisoners in 2004. [scene:hz4_withdrawal|The 2000 capture and the 2004 exchange] Hezbollah's stated aim in 2006 was the same: to hold soldiers and swap them for four Lebanese held in Israel. Its secretary-general, Hassan Nasrallah, said the only way to get them back was "indirect negotiations and a swap." [cite:hz5_wiki_war]

Israel's answer. The Israeli cabinet met the same day and said it would "respond aggressively and harshly to those who carried out, and are responsible for, today's action." Its communiqué held the "Lebanese Government responsible for the action that originated on its soil," while also saying that "Israel is not fighting Lebanon but the terrorist element there." Israel's case rested in part on UN Security Council Resolution 1559 of 2004, which called for militias in Lebanon to disarm; the Lebanese state, Israel argued, had failed to carry it out. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] The chief of staff, Lieutenant General Dan Halutz, was reported as saying that if the soldiers were not returned, "we will turn Lebanon's clock back 20 years." [cite:hz5_wiki_war] The state commission Israel later appointed found that Prime Minister Ehud Olmert's government chose an immediate, intensive strike without a detailed, approved military plan. [cite:hz5_mjl_winograd] [scene:hz5_doctrine|The Winograd findings]

The air and sea campaign. Within days Israel destroyed the runways of Beirut's international airport, imposed an air and naval blockade on Lebanon, and bombed bridges over the Litani and Zahrani rivers. A strike on the Jiyeh power station released fuel oil into the sea in what became the largest oil spill recorded in the Mediterranean. By the war's end, damage included about 640 kilometres of roads and 73 bridges, around 15,000 homes destroyed and about 130,000 damaged; Lebanon's Council for Development and Reconstruction put damage to civilian infrastructure at close to $2.5 billion. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] The Israeli Air Force flew 11,897 combat missions, more than in the 1973 war. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Human Rights Watch counted "some 7,000 bomb and missile strikes" on Lebanon, plus naval and artillery fire. [cite:hz5_rw_why] Beirut's southern suburbs, the Dahieh, where Hezbollah had its headquarters, were struck repeatedly and large parts of them were flattened. [cite:hz5_wiki_dahiya]

The rockets. Hezbollah fired between 3,970 and 4,228 rockets into Israel over the 34 days, more than 100 a day, most of them unguided short-range Katyushas. An estimated 23 percent landed in towns and built-up areas; the rest fell in open ground. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] They reached Haifa, Israel's third city. Nasrallah said Hezbollah had first aimed only at military sites and turned to Israeli cities in response to Israel's bombing of Lebanese civilian areas. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Human Rights Watch's Peter Bouckaert said Hezbollah was "directly targeting civilians," and the organisation found that civilian places appeared about four times as often as military ones in Hezbollah's own wartime communiqués. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Its 2007 report on the rockets concluded that Hezbollah fired "indiscriminately and at times deliberately" into civilian areas, including cluster rockets packed with steel spheres, and rejected Hezbollah's stated justification of retaliation as having no basis in the laws of war. [cite:hz5b_hrw_civassault] Between 300,000 and 500,000 Israelis left the north during the war; in Lebanon about one million people were displaced. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] [cite:hz5_rw_why] The next section sets out the deaths on both sides and how they were counted. [scene:hz5_toll|The toll]

The ground war. Israeli ground forces fought Hezbollah in the border villages from July, at first in limited operations. On 9 August the security cabinet approved a wider ground offensive, and it was launched in the last days before the ceasefire. [cite:hz5_jvl_winograd] More than 30 Israeli soldiers were killed in that final push. [cite:hz5_ap_winograd] The commission found that this offensive did not achieve its aim of limiting rocket fire. [cite:hz5_jvl_winograd] Before the ceasefire took effect at 08:00 on 14 August Israel was still seizing ground and bombing while Hezbollah kept up what it called "defensive operations." [cite:hz5_wiki_1701]

The United States. The record documents three American roles. The first was diplomatic. As Lebanon's government and many states called for an immediate ceasefire, the United States, with Britain, held out for a different sequence. On 21 July Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said the aim was a framework for lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire, which she called "a guarantee of future violence," while adding: "We do seek an end to the current violence, and we seek it urgently." [cite:hz5b_wf_rice] In the same round of remarks, reported on 22 July, she described what was happening as "the birth pangs of a new Middle East," and said a ceasefire "would be a false promise if it simply returns us to the status quo." By then, Al Jazeera reported, at least 305 Lebanese civilians had been killed. [cite:hz5b_npr_birthpangs] [cite:hz5b_aj_birthpangs] John Bolton, then US ambassador to the UN, told the BBC after leaving the post that the United States joined efforts to end the fighting only once Israel's campaign appeared to be failing, and told the Associated Press that "many" Arab governments had privately wanted Israel to destroy Hezbollah. [cite:hz5b_rferl_bolton] A Security Council resolution came only on 11 August, the 31st day. [cite:hz5_un_1701] The US position throughout was the one Rice stated: a truce that left Hezbollah armed on the border would only set up the next war. [cite:hz5b_wf_rice] The second role was material. On 22 July The New York Times reported that the Bush administration was rushing precision-guided bombs to Israel, at Israel's request, from a sale package approved in 2005 that included the GBU-28 "bunker-buster"; the decision, officials said, was taken with relatively little debate, and some officers called the request for expedited delivery unusual. [cite:hz5b_nyt_bombs] [cite:hz5b_otb_bombs] [cite:hz5b_aj_bombs] The first publicly reported transfer from the US war-reserve stockpile held in Israel, known as WRSA-I, also took place during this war. [cite:ow7_js_wrsa] The third was intelligence. An internal National Security Agency account, published by The Intercept in 2019, records that Israel's signals intelligence unit relied heavily on the NSA during the war and pressed it for geolocation data on Hezbollah figures; the NSA liaison called that request "particularly problematic" because US law barred the agency from supplying intelligence for targeted killing, and Israel's unit commander sought an exemption. [cite:ow4_int2019] [scene:ow4_memorandum|ONE-WAY MIRROR: the intelligence relationship] The text the Council finally adopted, negotiated between the United States and France, tied the end of the fighting to keeping armed Hezbollah personnel out of the area south of the Litani. [cite:hz5_un_1701] [cite:hz5_wiki_1701]

Two things about the start of the war are not in dispute in the sources used here. Hezbollah's cross-border raid, which killed eight soldiers and took two, began it. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] And Israel's response was aimed from the first day at the Lebanese state's infrastructure as well as at Hezbollah, on the stated ground that the state was responsible for what came from its territory. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Whether that response was proportionate is the question the rest of this part examines through the casualty record, the war's own inquiry, and the doctrine Israeli commanders drew from it.

sections.h: The Toll and How It Was Counted
sections.html:
The 2006 war has no single agreed death toll, and the differences come mostly from who counted and what they counted. The figures below give each source and its method. One misreading should be set aside first. Human Rights Watch's count is sometimes quoted as showing "400+" civilian deaths. It does not. Human Rights Watch identified at least 1,109 Lebanese killed by Israeli attacks, "the vast majority of whom were civilians." [cite:hz5_rw_why] [cite:hz5_hrw_why9]

Lebanese dead. Human Rights Watch spent five months in Lebanon and Israel. It investigated 561 deaths in depth through site visits and separate witness interviews, and gathered information on 548 more from graveyards and hospital records, for a total of 1,109 named deaths; it said the list was incomplete because some strikes went unreported. [cite:hz5_hrw_why10] To separate civilians from fighters it checked cemeteries, where Hezbollah buried its dead as "martyrs" with distinct markings, and the movement's own "martyr" posters. [cite:hz5_hrw_whymethod] In the 94 attacks it examined most closely, 510 civilians and 51 Hezbollah fighters were killed, and at least 300 of the 510 civilians were women or children. [cite:hz5_hrw_pr] [cite:hz5_rw_why] The Lebanese government put the national toll at 1,123 and its Higher Relief Council at 1,191; about 4,400 people were wounded. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] [cite:hz5_rw_why]

Hezbollah's dead. Here the sources are far apart and each has a stake in its number. Hezbollah said 250 of its fighters were killed. Israel's Foreign Ministry put the figure at "over 600." A UN official estimated about 500, not all of them front-line fighters. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] None of these is an independent count, and the range should be read as 250 to 600.

Israeli dead. Israel lost 121 soldiers. Hezbollah's rockets and mortars killed 44 Israeli civilians; different tallies give 43, 44 or 46. At least 19 of the civilians killed were Arab citizens of Israel. [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Human Rights Watch's own count was 43 Israeli civilians and 12 soldiers killed by rockets; its separate report on Hezbollah's rockets documented at least 39 civilian deaths from rocket fire and 101 people moderately or seriously injured. [cite:hz5_rw_why] [cite:hz5b_hrw_civassault] The total of about 165 Israeli dead follows from the official breakdown of 121 soldiers and 44 civilians; the totals of 158 and 159 that appear in some summaries do not match it.

On these figures, Lebanese deaths outnumbered Israeli deaths by roughly seven to one, and, taking Human Rights Watch's estimate of about 900 Lebanese civilian dead, civilian deaths by about twenty to one. [cite:hz5_hrw_pr] The ratio describes the outcome; why it came out that way is what the investigators argued about.

What the investigators found about Israel. Human Rights Watch concluded that the main cause of the civilian toll was Israel's targeting: Israel "often, even though not deliberately attacking civilians, did not distinguish between military objectives and civilians." It warned civilians to leave the south by leaflet, radio, phone message and loudspeaker, then acted as though everyone still there was a combatant, treating the area "effectively as a free-fire zone." Many who stayed were old, poor or unable to leave. [cite:hz5_hrw_why9] [cite:hz5_hrw_whymethod] Its overall judgement was that Israel "conducted the war with reckless indifference to the fate of Lebanese civilians," and that responsibility for the death toll "lies squarely with Israeli policies." [cite:hz5_rw_why] Israel's position was that civilian deaths were the result of Hezbollah fighting from among civilians and using them as "shields," and that it attacked only military targets. Human Rights Watch replied that this claim "rings hollow" because Israeli officials had publicly named Hezbollah's political, social and welfare institutions as targets. [cite:hz5_hrw_whymethod]

What the investigators found about Hezbollah. The same report found that Hezbollah broke the laws of war on some occasions: it fired rockets from populated areas, kept weapons in at least one apartment building in the Dahieh, and in at least one case sheltered armed fighters in a basement with civilians. But it found "a handful of instances but nothing to suggest a widespread practice" of using civilians as shields; most rockets and fighters were placed outside villages. [cite:hz5_hrw_why9] [cite:hz5_rw_why] Hezbollah's own rocket fire was a separate violation. Its rockets were unguided and most were fired at towns, and Human Rights Watch said it was "directly targeting civilians." [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Nasrallah's stated position was that Hezbollah struck Israeli cities in response to Israel's bombing of Lebanese civilians. [cite:hz5_wiki_war]

Qana, 30 July 2006. Ten years after the shelling of the UN compound there, Qana was hit again. [scene:hz4_qana|Qana, 1996] An Israeli strike brought down a house where 63 members of two extended families had taken shelter. First reports said at least 54 were dead. Human Rights Watch's later investigation confirmed 27, including 16 children, and traced the earlier figure to a misreading of the shelter's register rather than deliberate inflation. [cite:hz5_hrw_why10] Israel's explanations changed: one spokesperson said the bombs had missed a Hezbollah target about 300 metres away; another said the house had been used by Hezbollah; a senior air force officer said the building was struck on the assumption that it sheltered rocket crews and that "had we known there were that many civilians inside, we certainly would not have attacked." The army later produced no evidence of rocket launches from the house. [cite:hz5_hrw_why10] After the strike Israel announced a pause in its air attacks. [cite:hz5_wiki_war]

Cluster munitions. In the war's final days Israel fired cluster munitions across south Lebanon. The UN Mine Action Coordination Centre in south Lebanon estimated that Israel fired as many as four million submunitions in 962 separate strikes (a range of 2.6 to 4 million); information Israeli soldiers gave Human Rights Watch about resupplying rocket units put the figure as high as 4.6 million. By the UN's count about 90 percent of the strikes came in the last 72 hours, most of them after the Security Council had adopted Resolution 1701 and before the ceasefire took effect. [cite:hz5b_hrw_flooding] On 30 August 2006 the UN's humanitarian chief, Jan Egeland, said: "What's shocking and I would say completely immoral is that 90 per cent of the cluster bomb strikes" came in those final days; the UN had by then identified 359 strike sites. [cite:hz5b_aj_egeland] Human Rights Watch found the use "indiscriminate and disproportionate." [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Clearance experts put the average failure rate at about 25 percent, reaching 70 percent in places, and the UN estimated that the strikes left "hundreds of thousands and possibly up to one million unexploded submunitions" in fields, orchards and homes. [cite:hz5b_hrw_flooding] By 20 June 2007 they had killed 24 civilians and injured 183 after the ceasefire; by 15 January 2008 the UN centre counted at least 192 civilian casualties, 61 of them under 18, and 29 among deminers. [cite:hz5_hrw_whymethod] [cite:hz5b_hrw_flooding] Israel's position was that its use accorded with "the principles of armed conflict," that cluster munitions were chosen only after other options were found less effective against launch areas, and that most were "directed at open areas, keeping a safe distance from built up areas"; Human Rights Watch's field research found many strikes at or near towns with no evident military target. [cite:hz5b_hrw_flooding] [cite:hz5_hrw_whymethod] Israel's own Winograd Commission, in its final report, found that the use of cluster munitions had violated international law on the protection of civilians: firing them at built-up areas, it said, "does not comply with the rationale on which the restrictions" on their use are based, even where Hezbollah had used those areas, and it called for the army's rules to be reviewed. An Israeli defence official answered that deminers should "ask Hezbollah where their launch sites were." [cite:hz5a_irin_winograd] [cite:hz5_wiki_war]

Washington's finding. On 29 January 2007 the State Department sent Congress a preliminary report, prepared by the under secretary for arms control, Robert Joseph, concluding that Israel had likely violated its classified agreements with the United States on the use of American-supplied cluster munitions, which officials said were not supposed to be used in populated areas. The spokesman, Sean McCormack, called it "a set of preliminary findings" and would not say what action might follow; the Israeli embassy said the weapons had been used in self-defence against Hezbollah rocket fire on Israeli towns. [cite:hz5b_voa_cluster] The issue was not new for Washington: in 1979 the US secretary of state said Israel "may have violated" its agreement with the United States by using American cluster bombs in south Lebanon. [cite:hz1_jta_cluster] [scene:hz1_1978|The 1978 precedent]

sections.h: Resolution 1701, Winograd and the Dahiya Doctrine
sections.html:
The war ended on paper before it ended on the ground. On 11 August 2006 the Security Council adopted Resolution 1701 by 15 votes to none. [cite:hz5_un_1701] [cite:hz5_wiki_1701] Lebanon's cabinet accepted it unanimously the next day; Israel's cabinet approved it on 13 August by 24 votes to none with one abstention; the ceasefire took effect at 08:00 on 14 August. [cite:hz5_wiki_1701] What the resolution required of each side, what Israel's own inquiry concluded about the war, and the doctrine Israeli commanders drew from it shaped every round of fighting that followed.

What 1701 required. The resolution called for "the immediate cessation by Hizbollah of all attacks and the immediate cessation by Israel of all offensive military operations." Israel was to withdraw all its forces from south Lebanon "in parallel" with the deployment of the Lebanese army and the UN force. Between the Blue Line and the Litani river there was to be "an area free of any armed personnel" other than the Lebanese army and UNIFIL, whose ceiling was raised to 15,000 troops. The resolution called for full implementation of the Taif Agreement and of Resolutions 1559 and 1680, "that require the disarmament of all armed groups in Lebanon," and asked the Secretary-General to propose a delineation of Lebanon's borders, "including by dealing with the Shebaa farms area." Its preamble stressed "the unconditional release of the abducted Israeli soldiers" and encouraged efforts to settle "the issue of the Lebanese prisoners detained in Israel." [cite:hz5_un_1701]

Each side read it its own way. Nasrallah said on 12 August that Hezbollah would "not be an obstacle to any decision taken by the Lebanese government," and on 14 August that its fighters would not be forced to give up their weapons, citing a weak Lebanese army and continued Israeli occupation. Israel's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Mark Regev, said on 18 August that the resolution required a Hezbollah-free zone south of the Litani and that Israel would act if Hezbollah was not disarmed. [cite:hz5_wiki_1701] The record over the next eighteen years supports neither side's claim to have complied. Hezbollah kept fighters and weapons south of the Litani and rebuilt an arsenal estimated by 2024 at 120,000 to 200,000 rockets and missiles. Lebanon recorded more than 7,000 Israeli violations, most of them overflights, and a UN report of 2015 described near-daily Israeli drone and jet flights over Lebanon. [cite:hz5_wiki_1701] The same resolution was the base text for the ceasefire of November 2024. [scene:hz8_terms|The 2024 terms]

The prisoners. Two weeks after the ceasefire, on 27 August 2006, Nasrallah told Lebanon's New TV that Hezbollah had not thought, "even one per cent," that the capture would lead to a war of that size; asked whether he would have ordered the raid had he known, he said: "I say no, absolutely not." [cite:hz5b_aj_nasrallah] The question that Hezbollah said began the war was settled two years later. On 16 July 2008, in an exchange run by the Red Cross at the border, Israel released Samir Kuntar, convicted in 1979 of killing an Israeli man and his four-year-old daughter, with four other prisoners. [cite:hz5b_aj_swap] Hezbollah handed over the remains of Ehud Goldwasser and Eldad Regev, whose fate had been unknown, and Israel returned the bodies of Hezbollah and other fighters as part of the exchange. [cite:hz5_wiki_war]

Israel's inquiry. Under public pressure, Olmert appointed a commission of inquiry chaired by the retired judge Eliyahu Winograd. Its interim report of 30 April 2007 faulted Olmert, Defence Minister Amir Peretz and Halutz for choosing "an immediate and intensive military strike" without "a detailed, comprehensive, and authorized military plan." Peretz and Halutz both left their posts. [cite:hz5_mjl_winograd] The final report, released on 30 January 2008, called the war "a serious missed opportunity" from which Israel emerged without a military victory, found "serious failings and shortcomings in the decision-making processes and staff-work" in both the political and military echelons, and assigned the army the main responsibility for the military outcome. [cite:hz5_jvl_winograd] On the most criticised decision, the ground offensive of the last days, in which more than 30 soldiers died, it said "There was no failure in that decision in itself," judging it on what was known at the time, but found the offensive had not improved Israel's position or curbed rocket fire. [cite:hz5_jvl_winograd] [cite:hz5_ap_winograd] It made no personal recommendations; Winograd said Olmert had acted in what he believed was the interest of the state, and Olmert's office said it was "breathing a sigh of relief." [cite:hz5_jvl_winograd] [cite:hz5_ap_winograd] Olmert announced his resignation in July 2008, under corruption investigations as well as the war's verdict. [cite:hz5_mjl_winograd]

The Dahiya doctrine. The lesson some Israeli commanders drew was the opposite of restraint. In early October 2008 the head of Northern Command, Major General Gadi Eisenkot, told Yedioth Ahronoth: "What happened in the Dahiya quarter of Beirut in 2006 will happen in every village from which Israel is fired on. We will apply disproportionate force on it and cause great damage and destruction there. From our standpoint, these are not civilian villages, they are military bases." He added: "This is not a recommendation. This is a plan. And it has been approved." [cite:hz5_jps_khalidi] [cite:hz5_inss_shalom] He dismissed the alternative of chasing rocket crews: "This won't be another 'launcher hunt.'" [cite:hz5_inss_shalom] Writing that month for the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, Zaki Shalom called it "indeed a new policy of exercising force against Hizbollah." [cite:hz5_inss_shalom] An INSS researcher, Gabi Siboni, had argued the same year for a disproportionate response aimed at Hezbollah's assets and "the centers of civilian power" that support it, and Giora Eiland, writing for the same institute that November, proposed warning Lebanon's government that its army and civilian infrastructure would be destroyed if Hezbollah attacked. [cite:hz5_gs_dahiya] [cite:hz5_wiki_dahiya] Israel's stated rationale is in Eisenkot's own words: villages used to fire at Israel are military bases, and the cost of firing must be high enough to deter it. When Eisenkot became chief of staff, the army's 2015 strategy document did not name the doctrine but said that in a war in Lebanon "tens of thousands of targets" would be attacked. [cite:hz5_gs_dahiya]

How it was read. On 27 December 2008, less than three months after Eisenkot's interview, Israel launched Operation Cast Lead in Gaza. [cite:gz_wiki_castlead] [scene:gz5_castlead|GAZA: Cast Lead] The UN fact-finding mission led by Richard Goldstone, in its September 2009 report, traced Israel's tactics in Gaza to Lebanon in 2006, where "a concept known as the Dahiya doctrine emerged," involving disproportionate force and great damage to civilian property and infrastructure; it concluded that "what was prescribed as the best strategy appears to have been precisely what was put into practice," and described the Gaza operation as "a deliberately disproportionate attack designed to punish, humiliate and terrorize a civilian population." [cite:hz5a_un_goldstone] [cite:hz5a_csm_goldstone] Israel had not cooperated with the mission. In April 2011 Goldstone wrote that Israel had not intentionally targeted civilians as a matter of policy, citing Israel's own investigations; Netanyahu said the reversal "must lead to the shelving of this report once and for all," while Goldstone's three co-authors said they stood by it. [cite:gz_jvl_goldstone] [cite:gz_aj_goldstone_coauthors] Commentators have since described Israel's strikes on civilian infrastructure in Gaza after October 2023 as a possible extension of the doctrine. [cite:hz5_wiki_dahiya] The connection that can be documented is narrower and firmer: the commander who said the 2006 destruction of the Dahieh would be repeated in every village became the army's chief of staff, and his strategy promised tens of thousands of targets in the next Lebanon war. [cite:hz5_gs_dahiya] Whether that amounts to a policy of collective punishment, as its critics argue, or to lawful deterrence against an armed group fighting from towns, as its authors argue, is a legal and moral argument; the words themselves are on the record.

chapters.label: Part Six
chapters.title: Hezbollah as Its Own Actor
chapters.intro: Part Five ended with a war that Hezbollah began by a raid across the border and Israel fought by bombing Lebanon. Part Six turns from the wars with Israel to what Hezbollah did with its power at home and next door: how it sat in Lebanon's parliament and cabinet while keeping an army the state did not control, how it turned its guns on Beirut in May 2008, how a United Nations-backed court convicted its members of killing a former prime minister, how it fought for Bashar al-Assad in Syria, and who paid for all of it. Hezbollah is not only a product of Israel's invasions and Iran's ambitions; its own choices are set out here in the same plain register used for Israel's elsewhere in this library.
chapters.outro: Part Six set out Hezbollah's own record. It sat in parliament and cabinet from 1992 and 2005 while keeping the only army in Lebanon outside the state's control, and in May 2008 it turned that army on Beirut and came away with a veto over the cabinet. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] [cite:hz6_crs_2008] [cite:hz6_aje_2008tl] A UN-backed tribunal convicted three of its members of the 2005 bombing that killed Rafik Hariri and 21 others; Hezbollah denied any role and never handed them over. [cite:hz6_un_stl2020] [cite:hz6_almon_stl2022] Its supporters attacked protesters in 2019, and its leaders demanded the removal of the judge investigating the port explosion, an inquiry that, as of October 2026, had still produced no indictment. [cite:hz6_hrw_2019] [cite:hz6_aje_nasrallah_bitar] [cite:hz6_cm_port2026] [cite:hz6a_olj_nassar] It sent thousands of fighters to keep Bashar al-Assad in power and lost an estimated 1,000 to 2,000 of them, and by its own leader's account its budget and its weapons come from Iran, put by US officials at about $700 million a year. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] [cite:hz6_alarabiya_2016] [cite:hz6_icg_crt2018] Part Seven turns to the front it opened against Israel on 8 October 2023.

sections.h: A Party With an Army
sections.html:
Hezbollah entered Lebanon's parliament in the August 1992 elections, the first held after the civil war, and did best in the east of the country. [cite:hz4_csm_1992] It won eight of the 128 seats in its own name, with four more independents counted in its bloc; sources that give "12 seats" for 1992 are counting the bloc. Its own seat count has stayed in a narrow band since: seven in 1996, ten in 2000, fourteen in 2005, and thirteen in each of 2009, 2018 and 2022. It first took cabinet posts in 2005, after Syria's troops left Lebanon, holding the ministries of labour and of energy and water. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] [cite:hz6_conv_rebeiz] In May 2018 Hezbollah and its allies won 71 seats, a majority, and Hassan Nasrallah said: "Today I can say that our goals have been achieved." [cite:hz6_wilson_record] In May 2022 that coalition fell to 61 seats and lost its majority, though Hezbollah and its ally Amal kept all 27 seats reserved for Shia members under Lebanon's confessional system. [cite:hz6_nbc_2022]

The votes rested on services as well as on the claim to be resisting Israel. Hezbollah runs hospitals and clinics in the south, the Bekaa and Beirut's southern suburbs, licensed through an Islamic Health Authority tied to the party, with al-Rasool al-Azam hospital in Bourj al-Brajneh as the flagship. Those services were never wholly separate from the state. In 2020 the health ministry under Prime Minister Hassan Diab added fifteen Hezbollah-sponsored medical centres to the list the state pays for, and state funding to Hezbollah-run hospitals rose from about 16 billion to 30 billion Lebanese pounds. [cite:hz6_now_welfare] By the party's own count, set out by its deputy leader Naim Qassem, it repaired 17,212 homes damaged in Israeli raids between 1991 and 2000; one academic study put the number of people its health network served in 2000 at about 400,000. [cite:hz6_swj_gabrielsen] Support divides sharply by community. An Arab Barometer poll in early 2024 found that 30 per cent of Lebanese trusted Hezbollah and 55 per cent did not trust it at all; trust stood at 85 per cent among Shia respondents and below 10 per cent among Sunni, Druze and Christian respondents. [cite:hz6_conv_rebeiz]

The phrase "state within a state" describes the arrangement that made this possible. The 1989 Taif Agreement required every militia to disarm, and the others did; Hezbollah alone kept its weapons, accepted as a "resistance force" while Israel occupied the south. [cite:hz4_wiki_taif] [cite:hz4_lbc_arms] After Israel withdrew in 2000 the weapons stayed, and the rest of this part shows what happened when the state tried to touch them, or tried to hold anyone in the party to account.

The Hariri assassination and the tribunal

On 14 February 2005 a bomb in Beirut killed Rafik Hariri, the former prime minister, and 21 others, and injured 226. A United Nations-backed court, the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, sitting near The Hague, tried four men in their absence. On 18 August 2020 its trial chamber unanimously convicted Salim Ayyash, found "beyond a reasonable doubt" to have taken part in the conspiracy to carry out the bombing, and acquitted the other three. The judges said they had found no evidence implicating Hezbollah's leadership and "no direct evidence" of Syrian involvement, while noting that Syria and Hezbollah "may have had motives" to eliminate Hariri. A fifth accused, the Hezbollah commander Mustafa Badreddine, had been dropped from the case after he was killed in Syria in 2016. [cite:hz6_un_stl2020] Ayyash was sentenced to life imprisonment. In March 2022 the appeals chamber overturned two acquittals and convicted Hassan Habib Merhi and Hussein Oneissi, finding they had circulated a video in which a fictitious group claimed the bombing in order to shield the real perpetrators; on 16 June 2022 both were sentenced to life. [cite:hz6_almon_stl2022]

Hezbollah denied any role. [cite:hz6_un_stl2020] When the tribunal indicted four of its members in July 2011, Nasrallah said they would not be found or arrested "in 30 days or 60 days, or in a year, two years, 30 years or 300 years", and Hezbollah and its allies brought down the government that year in a dispute over the court. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] Nasrallah refused to recognise the tribunal and Hezbollah never handed over any of the three men convicted. The court, which cost an estimated $600 million to $1 billion and drew 49 per cent of its budget from Lebanon, ran short of money and wound down with no one in custody. [cite:hz6_almon_stl2022]

May 2008: the guns turned inward

On 6 May 2008 the cabinet of Prime Minister Fouad Siniora declared Hezbollah's private telephone network illegal and removed the head of security at Beirut airport, who was close to the opposition. On 8 May Nasrallah called the decisions "a declaration of war". [cite:hz6_crs_2008] Hezbollah said the network was part of its military apparatus and the decisions were aimed at the resistance against Israel. [cite:hz6_wiki_2008] Its fighters and those of Amal fought pro-government gunmen across the capital, took control of West Beirut on 9 May, forced the Future Movement's television station off the air and attacked an affiliated newspaper. [cite:hz6_voa_2008] [cite:hz6_aje_2008tl] Siniora called it an attempted coup. [cite:hz6_aje_2008tl] The government reversed both decisions on 14 May. Lebanese officials put the dead at 81 by 12 May; a United Nations report counted 69 dead and Human Rights Watch at least 71, and estimates run from about 70 to 110. [cite:hz6_crs_2008] [cite:hz6_wiki_2008]

The Doha Agreement of 21 May 2008 ended the crisis. Michel Suleiman was elected president on 25 May, and the new 30-member cabinet gave the opposition led by Hezbollah eleven seats, more than a third, which Al Jazeera described as an "effective veto" over executive decisions. The parties pledged not to use weapons or violence to settle political disputes; the question of Hezbollah's own arms was left to a later national dialogue. [cite:hz6_aje_2008tl] [cite:hz6_wiki_doha] [cite:hz6_wiki_2008] Hezbollah had turned its weapons on other Lebanese and come away with the blocking third it had long demanded.

The 2019 protests and the port explosion

In October 2019 protests spread across Lebanon against the cost of living and the confessional political class as a whole. Human Rights Watch documented a series of attacks on protesters. On 23 October in Nabatieh more than 400 men, whom protesters identified as Hezbollah supporters, beat demonstrators with sticks and metal objects. On 29 October in Beirut, hundreds of men chanting for Nabih Berri of Amal and for Nasrallah burned and looted the protest tents in Martyrs' Square. No attackers were arrested, and the organisation recorded at least six occasions on which security forces failed to protect protesters. [cite:hz6_hrw_2019] The pattern matched Hamas's response to Gaza's protests the same year (see [scene:hm6_rule|How Hamas Ruled Gaza]).

On 4 August 2020 about 3,000 tons of improperly stored ammonium nitrate at Beirut port exploded, killing more than 220 people. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] [cite:hz6_na_bitar2025] Nasrallah denied that Hezbollah bore any responsibility for the explosion. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] Judge Tarek Bitar, who took over the inquiry in 2021, sought to question former ministers, including Ali Hassan Khalil of Amal; he did not seek to question members of Hezbollah itself. [cite:hz6_obs_bitar] On 20 September 2021 Wafiq Safa, the head of Hezbollah's liaison unit, was reported by Lebanese media to have told senior judges that "should he drift off the course, we will remove him". Bitar reported the warning in a letter to the prosecutor and the justice minister; Safa did not respond to requests for comment, and the remark rests on those reports. [cite:hz6_an_safa] [cite:hz6_obs_bitar] On 11 October Nasrallah said Bitar was using "the blood of the victims to serve political interests" and called his choice of targets "clearly political targeting". [cite:hz6_aje_nasrallah_bitar]

Three days later, on 14 October 2021, Amal and Hezbollah supporters marched on the Palace of Justice against Bitar's warrant for Khalil. Gunfire in the Tayouneh district killed seven people, three Amal members, three Hezbollah members and a woman hit by a stray bullet. Amal and Hezbollah blamed gunmen of the Lebanese Forces party, which denied it; Nasrallah accused that party of seeking a new civil war. A year later no official finding on who fired first had been published. [cite:hz6_olj_tayouneh] What is documented is that Hezbollah publicly demanded the judge's removal and called the protest; who fired first remains unresolved.

The inquiry then stalled for more than three years under lawsuits from the officials it named and a block by the public prosecutor, until Bitar resumed work on 16 January 2025. [cite:hz6_na_bitar2025] He sent his report to the prosecutor in late March 2026, reportedly accusing 70 people; no indictment had been issued by August 2026, and on 30 September the justice minister, Adel Nassar, said one was expected "before the end of the year." [cite:hz6_cm_port2026] [cite:hz6a_olj_nassar] Elections due in May 2026 did not take place: on 9 March 2026, a week after Hezbollah opened fire on Israel in the wider war on Iran, parliament voted 76 to extend its own term by two years. [cite:hz6_rt_extend] Days earlier the cabinet had banned all military and security activity by Hezbollah (see [scene:hz8_disarm|the disarmament decision]). [cite:hz8_olj_ban]

sections.h: The War for Assad
sections.html:
Hezbollah's founding claim was that its weapons existed to fight Israel. Within the first years of Syria's war it used them in another country's civil war, on the side of the government. It first sent small groups across the border, presented as protection for villages of Lebanese Shia families on the Syrian side. By 2014 it had thousands of fighters in Syria, fighting alongside the Syrian army, Iranian advisers and Iraqi militias. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] Mireille Rebeiz of Dickinson College puts it plainly: Hezbollah sent thousands of fighters "to help the government suppress the uprising". [cite:hz6_conv_rebeiz]

For months Hezbollah did not say so. On 25 May 2013 Hassan Nasrallah confirmed for the first time that its fighters were in combat in Syria. He gave two reasons. The first was strategic: "Syria is the backbone of the resistance (in the region) and its main supporter." The second was defensive: if rebels took the areas along the border, he said, that would be "a great threat to Lebanon". [cite:hz6_wilson_record] Both are Hezbollah's own account. The first is the more revealing, because it names the alliance itself, not any threat to Lebanon, as the reason to fight.

Qusayr

The battle that made Hezbollah's role impossible to deny was fought for al-Qusayr, a town in Homs province about eight kilometres from the Lebanese border. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria, in its report of 16 August 2013, recorded that "pro-Government forces, including Hezbollah, launched a major offensive" on the Qusayr region, "supported by foreign combatants including thousands of Hezbollah fighters". By early May, it found, Hezbollah had taken the area's water stations and held the villages south-west of the town, and the government and Hezbollah besieged it from different sides. [cite:hz6b_coi2013] Government troops and Hezbollah fighters took the town on 5 June 2013 after about seventeen days of street fighting. [cite:hz6b_coi2013] [cite:hz6b_csm_qusayr] A Hezbollah veteran told the Christian Science Monitor that about 1,200 of its special forces led the assault; opposition sources put its dead at 70 to 110. Its deputy leader, Naim Qassem, called the victory "a sharp blow to the American-Israeli-Takfiri project". [cite:hz6b_csm_qusayr] Civilians were trapped for weeks without water or electricity. [cite:hz6b_aje_qusayr] On 29 May the UN Human Rights Council, by 36 votes to 1, condemned foreign combatants fighting for the government at Qusayr, without naming Hezbollah. [cite:hz6b_hrc23_1]

The war soon went far beyond the border villages. In December 2016 Hezbollah, with other militias backed by Iran, played a central part in the battle that returned Aleppo, Syria's largest city, wholly to government control; the government declared victory on 22 December. [cite:hz6_wiki_hziran] [cite:hz6_wilson_record] Aleppo lies far from the Lebanese border, and the fight there had nothing to do with Israel or Lebanese villages; it served the first of Nasrallah's two reasons, not the second. The UN Commission of Inquiry found that in eastern Aleppo pro-government ground forces, "composed mostly of Syrian and foreign militias", executed surrendered fighters and perceived opposition supporters, and that opposition groups shelled western Aleppo indiscriminately. Its published summary does not name Hezbollah among those militias, so the executions are not attributed to it here. [cite:hz6b_un_aleppo]

Sieges: Madaya and Zabadani

The UN commission's 2013 report had already found that government forces, backed by Hezbollah, tightened sieges in Homs province before ground offensives, and concluded that the government and Hezbollah had both carried out siege operations in breach of their obligations under international humanitarian law. [cite:hz6b_coi2013] The best-known case came later, near the Lebanese border west of Damascus. In July 2015 pro-government forces opened an offensive on the rebel-held town of Zabadani; a rebel alliance that included al-Qaeda's Syrian affiliate answered by besieging Foua and Kefraya, two towns in Idlib province with mainly Shia populations. [cite:hz6b_newarab_truce] Neighbouring Madaya, home to about 40,000 people, was besieged from July 2015 by the Syrian army and Hezbollah, according to residents interviewed by Human Rights Watch and to VOA. [cite:hz6b_hrw_madaya] [cite:hz6b_voa_madaya] Médecins Sans Frontières reported that 23 patients at a health centre it supported in Madaya had died of starvation after 1 December 2015, and on 29 January 2016 that 16 more had starved to death since the first aid convoy arrived that month; MSF's own statements attributed the siege to the "Syrian government-led coalition". [cite:hz6b_hrw_madaya] [cite:hz6b_msf_madaya] Paulo Pinheiro, chair of the UN commission, said such sieges "target the civilian population by subjecting them to starvation", and the commission condemned starvation as a weapon by both sides; armed groups including al-Nusra were then besieging about 12,500 people in Foua and Kefraya. [cite:hz6b_ap_coi_madaya] [cite:hz6b_hrw_madaya]

Hezbollah's response was to deny that the starvation was real or its doing. It said militants inside Madaya were "withholding food from the locals", and its television station, Al-Manar, called the photographs fabrications. [cite:hz6b_voa_madaya] A truce for the four towns, negotiated in September 2015 between the rebel group Ahrar al-Sham and Iran, with Hezbollah among the pro-government parties, ended in an exchange of populations in April 2017. [cite:hz6b_newarab_truce] On 15 April a car bomb struck the waiting Foua and Kefraya convoy at Rashidin, outside Aleppo, killing at least 126 people, at least 109 of them evacuees and 68 of them children; no group claimed it. [cite:hz6b_aje_fourtowns] The record supports a precise statement. The UN commission found in 2013 that the government and Hezbollah ran sieges in Homs province in breach of humanitarian law. At Madaya, residents, HRW and VOA name Hezbollah with the army as the besiegers and MSF documented starvation deaths, while MSF's and the UN's own statements name the government-led side rather than Hezbollah specifically. Opposition groups ran sieges of their own.

What it cost Hezbollah

The losses were heavy. The Wilson Center, drawing on published estimates, puts Hezbollah's dead at no fewer than 1,300 by 2015, and estimates for 2018 range from 1,000 to 2,000. The Associated Press in October 2018 reported an estimated 2,000 killed and thousands more wounded. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] [cite:hz6_ap_sanctions2018] Hezbollah publishes no total; these are estimates, not a count the public can check. Among the dead was Mustafa Badreddine, a senior Hezbollah commander, killed in Damascus in 2016. The Special Tribunal for Lebanon then dropped its Hariri case against him. [cite:hz6_un_stl2020] [cite:hz6_alarabiya_2016]

The war also strained its money. The AP reported that Hezbollah's budget had been under pressure since it entered Syria in 2013, because it kept paying stipends to the families of the dead and medical care for the wounded. By 2018, under new US sanctions on Iran, it was cutting the number of fighters it kept in Syria. Nasrallah conceded in August 2018 that the sanctions "will have an effect for sure", and was reported to have told cadres in a closed meeting, "We have to tighten belts a bit." [cite:hz6_ap_sanctions2018] Iran carried most of the cost of the wider war: the State Department said in 2018 that Iran had spent more than $16 billion since 2012 supporting Assad and its allied forces in Syria, Iraq and Yemen, and had given the Syrian government $4 billion in credit lines. [cite:hz6_ap_sanctions2018] These are US government figures, issued during Washington's pressure campaign on Iran.

In Lebanon the war reshaped how others saw the party. A movement that had built its standing on fighting Israel's occupation of the south was now fighting Syrians on behalf of a government whose troops had stayed in Lebanon itself for more than sixteen years after the 1989 Taif Agreement called for them to remain for two. [cite:hz6_conv_rebeiz] The Arab Barometer figures in the previous section, with trust in Hezbollah below 10 per cent among Sunni, Druze and Christian respondents in 2024, measure a divide the Syrian war did much to deepen (see [scene:hz6_state|A Party With an Army]). [cite:hz6_conv_rebeiz]

The fall of Assad

Eleven years of fighting did not save the government Hezbollah went to defend. On 6 December 2024 anti-Assad fighters took the Iraq–Syria border crossing, cutting the land route by which, under Assad, weapons and equipment had moved from Iran through Iraq and Syria into Lebanon; two days later, on 8 December, rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham entered Damascus and Assad's government fell. Before they arrived, Hezbollah sent officers to oversee the withdrawal of its own fighters from the city. [cite:hz6b_newarab_qassem] It came at the worst moment: less than two weeks earlier a US-brokered ceasefire with Israel had taken effect, ending fourteen months of war in which many of its top officials, Nasrallah among them, had been killed (see [scene:hz7_war|the 2024 war]). [cite:hz6b_ap_assadfall]

Naim Qassem, by then secretary-general, gave Hezbollah's account of the cost in a televised speech on 14 December 2024, without naming Assad. "Hezbollah has lost the military supply route through Syria at this stage," he said, calling the loss "a detail in the resistance's work"; a new government might reopen the route, he added, "and we could look for other ways." [cite:hz6b_newarab_qassem] Analysts judged it larger than a detail. Aron Lund of Century International told the AP that Iran could still "fly in some things and smuggle some things", but "not even close" to the previous scale; Firas Maksad of the Middle East Institute said Hezbollah faced "an entirely new reality". Hezbollah's MP Hassan Fadlallah said the change would "not weaken us". [cite:hz6b_ap_assadfall] Measured against Nasrallah's reason for going in 2013, to defend "the backbone of the resistance", the war ended in losing what it was fought to keep.

sections.h: Who Pays for Hezbollah
sections.html:
The plainest statement of where Hezbollah's money comes from was made by Hezbollah. In a televised speech on 24 June 2016, marking forty days since the death of its commander Mustafa Badreddine, Hassan Nasrallah said the group was open about the fact that its budget, income and expenses, "everything it eats and drinks, its weapons and rockets, come from the Islamic Republic of Iran." He added: "As long as Iran has money, we have money." [cite:hz6_alarabiya_2016] He was answering the Hezbollah International Financing Prevention Act, signed by President Obama on 18 December 2015, which threatened sanctions on banks knowingly handling significant transactions for the group. Nasrallah's reply was that the law could not touch Hezbollah because "we don't transfer our money through the Lebanese banking system" and kept no money in Lebanese banks. [cite:hz6_alarabiya_2016] Four years earlier, in February 2012, he had acknowledged Iran's "moral, and political and material support in all possible forms" since 1982, while insisting that Hezbollah took support, not orders, from Tehran. [cite:hz6_wilson_record]

Neither Hezbollah nor Iran has published a sum, so every figure is an outside estimate, almost all from the US government. In about 2010 US officials put Iran's support at $100 million to $200 million a year. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] [cite:hz6_wiki_hziran] In June 2018 Sigal Mandelker, the Treasury's under secretary for terrorism and financial intelligence, told a meeting of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies that "Iran provides upwards of $700 million a year to Hezbollah". [cite:hz6_jp_mandelker] The State Department's Country Reports on Terrorism for 2018 repeated "an estimated $700 million per year" and said this was "the overwhelming majority of the group's annual budget". [cite:hz6_icg_crt2018] On 13 November 2018 Nathan Sales, the State Department's counterterrorism coordinator, put Iran's spending on armed allies across the region at close to $1 billion a year, about $700 million of it for Hezbollah and $100 million for Palestinian groups. Iranian officials answered that US sanctions would not stop Iran supporting its allies in Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Iraq. [cite:hz6_rferl_sales]

The jump from about $200 million to $700 million should be read with care. The higher figure came in 2018, the year the United States left the nuclear agreement and began its "maximum pressure" sanctions, from officials running that campaign, and none of these statements gives a method. [cite:hz6_now_welfare] That does not make it wrong, but it is a government estimate, not an audited number. The origin of the money is not in dispute, because Hezbollah's leader stated it; the size is.

Sanctions and the crime accusation

The legal basis for most US measures is older than these estimates: on 8 October 1997 Secretary of State Madeleine Albright designated "Hizballah" a Foreign Terrorist Organization, and it was listed as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist in October 2001. [cite:hz6b_fr_fto1997] [cite:hz6b_dea_lcb2011] Beyond the 2015 banking law, the US kept widening its financial measures. In October 2018 President Trump signed a law widening who could be sanctioned for dealing with Hezbollah, at an event marking the 35th anniversary of the 1983 Marine barracks bombing (see [scene:hz2_1983|the 1983 bombings]), and on 15 October Attorney General Jeff Sessions named Hezbollah one of five top transnational organised crime threats to the United States. [cite:hz6_ap_sanctions2018] It reflected a long-running US accusation that Hezbollah raises money from laundering and drugs as well as from Iran. Nasrallah rejected the accusation in February 2012, saying Iran met the group's needs. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] Rebeiz describes the financial network around Hezbollah as involving money laundering and drug trafficking. [cite:hz6_conv_rebeiz] Because the accusation is the US government's and Hezbollah denies it, the cases behind it are best taken one at a time.

The strongest is the Lebanese Canadian Bank. On 10 February 2011 the Treasury named the bank, with 35 branches in Lebanon, a "primary money laundering concern" under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act. It said a network run by Ayman Joumaa, designated a drug kingpin that January, had used the bank to launder up to $200 million a month in proceeds of cocaine moved from South America through West Africa, and that "U.S. Government information indicates" Hezbollah drew financial support from the network. [cite:hz6b_dea_lcb2011] The bank was then sold, and in a civil case in Manhattan the US alleged that from 2007 to early 2011 at least $329 million had been wired to the United States to buy used cars for resale in West Africa, with the proceeds, mixed with drug money, returned to Lebanon through "Hizballah-controlled money laundering channels". On 25 June 2013, in a settlement entered by a federal judge, the bank agreed to forfeit $102 million of $150 million the US had seized in August 2012. [cite:hz6b_sdny_lcb2013] That was a settlement, not a verdict; the announcement does not say the bank admitted wrongdoing, and the Hezbollah link rests on US allegations never tested at trial.

The most disputed is Project Cassandra. In December 2017 Politico, in a report by Josh Meyer, described a Drug Enforcement Administration campaign launched in 2008 whose agents believed Hezbollah earned about $1 billion a year from drug and weapons trafficking, and alleged that the Obama administration let the group "off the hook" to secure the nuclear agreement with Iran. [cite:hz6b_snopes_cassandra] Former officials disputed it. Kevin Lewis, Obama's spokesman and a former Justice Department official, said there had been "a consistent pattern of actions taken against Hezbollah" before and after the deal; Derek Maltz, a former DEA special-operations chief, pointed instead to turf battles between law-enforcement and intelligence agencies. [cite:hz6b_snopes_cassandra] Daniel Byman, in Lawfare, found much of the Hezbollah material convincing but the sourcing one-sided and the evidence stronger for interagency rivalry than for White House pressure; Daniel Benjamin, the former State Department counterterrorism coordinator, called the report a "woefully one-sided recitation from DEA". [cite:hz6b_lawfare_byman] The claim is contested, and the $1 billion is the agents' belief, not a documented sum.

The newest is Captagon, an amphetamine pill made in Syria, much of it trafficked through Lebanon. Here the documented finding concerns the Assad government more than Hezbollah. The Treasury said on 28 March 2023 that Maher al-Assad, the president's brother, and the army's Fourth Division he commanded facilitated Captagon production and trafficking, and that the Assad family dominated the trade. [cite:hz6b_tr_captagon2023] OCCRP linked a 14-tonne seizure at Salerno in 2020 to the president's family network, and the New Lines Institute called the government "the main supplier and sponsor of the industry", with exports worth at least $5.7 billion in 2021. [cite:hz6b_occrp_salerno] [cite:hz6b_nl_endgame] [cite:hz6b_newarab_57bn] The Hezbollah-specific claims are narrower and weaker. The same action sanctioned two Lebanese men, saying one, Hassan Daqqou, ran operations with the Fourth Division "with cover reportedly provided by Hizballah" and the other had ties to "certain members of Hizballah". [cite:hz6b_tr_captagon2023] Daqqou told Lebanese investigators he worked with Hezbollah, but OCCRP found many Lebanese officials reluctant to tie Hezbollah directly to the trade. [cite:hz6b_occrp_drugwar] After Assad fell, US and Arab officials told the Wall Street Journal that Hezbollah "facilitated trafficking in areas under their control", while saying its profits were unknown. [cite:hz6b_wsj_captagon] Nasrallah called the reports "baseless lies" in May 2023 and said Captagon was "religiously prohibited". [cite:hz6b_voa_nasrallah2023] On the public record the Assad government's role is well documented; Hezbollah's is alleged by US and Arab officials and investigators, and denied by Hezbollah, with no court finding behind it.

The pressure campaign on Iran did reach Hezbollah's books. According to the AP in October 2018, the group was cutting costs while still paying stipends to families of its dead, care for its wounded and pensions, and could draw on tens of thousands of donation boxes in Shia neighbourhoods of Lebanon. Nasrallah admitted that the sanctions "will have an effect for sure", and Kataib Hezbollah, an Iraqi militia, offered to help it financially if needed (see [scene:hz10_iraq|the Iraqi militias]). [cite:hz6_ap_sanctions2018] NOW reported in 2022 that the sanctions had sharply cut the money reaching Hezbollah and forced austerity. [cite:hz6_now_welfare]

Its own bank, and the state's money

Nasrallah's statement that Hezbollah keeps its money outside Lebanese banks points to the parallel system it built instead. Al-Qard al-Hassan, a lending association, is described by the researcher Yara Asmar as Hezbollah's own alternative to the Lebanese banking system. [cite:hz6_now_welfare] [cite:hz6_alarabiya_2016] The US Treasury designated it on 24 July 2007, saying "Hizballah has used AQAH as a cover to manage its financial activity" and had moved part of that activity there after earlier designations in 2006. [cite:hz6b_tr_2007] On 11 May 2021 it designated seven more people: Ibrahim Ali Daher, named as head of Hezbollah's central finance unit, and six Al-Qard al-Hassan officials. Treasury said the association, licensed by the Interior Ministry as a non-profit, offered bank-like services without banking regulation, and that accounts held by five of its officials had moved more than $500 million through Lebanon's banks over a decade. [cite:hz6b_tr_2021] That sits uneasily with Nasrallah's statement that Hezbollah kept its money out of Lebanese banks; the Treasury's account is a sanctions finding, not a court ruling.

The state's money also reaches Hezbollah's institutions, legally. In 2020, under Prime Minister Hassan Diab, the health ministry, then run by Hezbollah according to NOW, added fifteen Hezbollah-sponsored medical centres to the list of providers the state pays, and state payments to Hezbollah-run hospitals nearly doubled, from about 16 billion to 30 billion Lebanese pounds. In 2020 the US refused to send aid to the health ministry while Hezbollah held it. [cite:hz6_now_welfare] The two streams, Iran's money for weapons and fighters and the Lebanese state's money for services, show how Hezbollah sits both outside and inside the state at once (see [scene:hz6_state|A Party With an Army]).

chapters.label: Part Seven
chapters.title: The Support Front
chapters.intro: Part Seven covers the fourteen months from 8 October 2023, when Hezbollah opened what it called a support front for Gaza, to the ceasefire of 27 November 2024. It sets out who fired how often, by the count of an independent monitor and by Israel's own count; the people displaced on both sides of the border; the deaths of a Reuters journalist in southern Lebanon and of twelve children on a football pitch in the Golan Heights, with each side's account; the pager and radio detonations of September 2024, how they were carried out and the legal argument they started; the air campaign, the killing of Hassan Nasrallah and the ground invasion that followed; the toll by source; and what the ceasefire text said, beside the American letter to Israel that was reported to go with it.
chapters.outro: Part Seven followed the support front from start to ceasefire. Hezbollah opened fire on 8 October 2023 "in solidarity" with Gaza and said it would stop when Gaza did; Israel struck Lebanon roughly four to five times as often as Hezbollah struck Israel, by ACLED's count of events, while the Israeli army pointed to thousands of projectiles fired at its north. [cite:hz7_aj_8oct] [cite:hz7_ml_qassem] [cite:hz7_aj_acled_year] [cite:hz7_c4_acled] Civilians were killed on both sides, among them a Reuters journalist hit by Israeli tank fire and twelve children in Majdal Shams, whose deaths Israel and the US attributed to a Hezbollah rocket and Hezbollah denied. [cite:hz7_npr_abdallah] [cite:hz7_wiki_majdal] The pager and radio detonations of 17 and 18 September 2024 killed 37 to 39 people and wounded about 3,000; UN experts called them violations of international law, and Netanyahu later acknowledged them. [cite:hz7_lbci_abiad] [cite:hz7_ohchr_experts] [cite:hz7_toi_netanyahu_pagers] The air campaign and ground invasion that followed killed Nasrallah and most of the Lebanese dead of the war: at least 4,047 by the health ministry's count, against 45 Israeli civilians and 83 soldiers by an Israeli institute's count. [cite:hz7_ap_nasrallah_site] [cite:hz7_olj_abiad_4047] [cite:hz7_alma_summary] The ceasefire of 27 November bound both sides to stop and Israel to withdraw within 60 days, while a reported US letter recognised Israel's right to keep acting against threats. [cite:hz7_toi_text] [cite:hz7_olj_sideletter] Part Eight follows what happened to those terms. [scene:hz8_terms|The broken ceasefire]

sections.h: The Support Front
sections.html:
8 October 2023. The morning after Hamas's attack on southern Israel, Hezbollah fired guided rockets and artillery at three Israeli army posts in the Shebaa Farms, the strip of land at the foot of Mount Hermon that Lebanon claims and Israel holds. Its statement called them "3 Zionist occupation sites" and said the attack was carried out "in solidarity with the victorious Palestinian resistance and the steadfast Palestinian people." The Israeli army answered with artillery at the launch area and a drone strike on a Hezbollah post, and said it was "prepared for all scenarios." [cite:hz7_aj_8oct] The public record reviewed does not show Hezbollah taking part in planning the 7 October attack; its own framing, from the first day, was that it was opening a second front to support Gaza. That is why the period that followed is called the "support front": Hezbollah's stated aim was to tie down Israeli forces in the north, not to win a war of its own. Part Six described the organisation that made this choice. [scene:hz6_state|Hezbollah as its own actor]

The stated condition. Hezbollah attached a condition to the front and repeated it for a year: it would stop when the war in Gaza stopped. Its deputy leader, Naim Qassem, told the Associated Press in July 2024: "If there is a cease-fire in Gaza, we will stop without any discussion." [cite:hz7_ml_qassem] Hassan Nasrallah said the same on 19 September 2024, after the pager detonations described in the next section: "the fighting on the Lebanese front will not stop before the war in Gaza ends." [cite:hz7_axios_nasrallah] The condition matters for how the war ended. By late October 2024, the Wall Street Journal reported, Hezbollah was moving away from its demand for a Gaza ceasefire first, and the agreement of 27 November 2024 contained no Gaza clause at all. [cite:hz7_toi_freedom] [cite:hz7_toi_text] Israel's stated position was the reverse of Hezbollah's: that a hostile armed group on its border, firing in support of the group that had carried out 7 October, could not be allowed to set the terms. On 18 September 2024 Defense Minister Yoav Gallant said "The center of gravity is moving northward," and he, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the army chief all named the return of displaced northern residents as the military's task. [cite:hz7_afp_gravity]

Who fired more. The exchange was not even. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (ACLED), which counts reported incidents of political violence, recorded 8,099 Israeli strike events on Lebanon against 1,623 Hezbollah strike events on Israel between 7 October 2023 and 20 September 2024, about five to one, with 798 deaths in Lebanon linked to Israeli attacks and 28 in Israel linked to Hezbollah's. [cite:hz7_c4_acled] Over the first full year, to 18 October 2024, ACLED counted 11,238 Israeli attacks (about 83 per cent of the total) and 2,370 by Hezbollah and allied groups. [cite:hz7_aj_acled_year] Two cautions apply. ACLED counts events, not munitions: a barrage of dozens of rockets fired at one place at one time is a single event, which narrows the gap in projectiles fired. And the Israeli army disputed the comparison. It called the analysis "baseless," said more than 9,000 Hezbollah projectiles had crossed into Israel by October 2024 and later put the figure at 12,400 for the year, and argued that a casualty comparison ignored how many attacks Israel's air defences stopped. [cite:hz7_c4_acled] [cite:hz7_acled_year_pdf] Both numbers can be true at once: Hezbollah fired thousands of rockets, drones and missiles, and Israel struck Lebanon far more often and killed far more people. ACLED recorded Israeli strikes in 449 Lebanese localities in that first year. [cite:hz7_acled_year_pdf]

Displacement on both sides. On 8 October Israel began emptying its border communities, and about 60,000 residents of northern Israel left their homes, according to official data reported by AFP. They were not cleared to return until 1 March 2025, and about half had still not gone back a week later. [cite:hz7_afp_north_return] On the Lebanese side the International Organization for Migration counted 76,018 people displaced by early January 2024, mostly from the south, and 110,099 by mid-August 2024. [cite:hz7_an_iom_jan24] [cite:hz7_olj_iom_aug24] The Lebanese figure was already nearly twice the Israeli one by the summer of 2024; after September it grew more than tenfold, as the next sections show.

The journalists at Alma al-Shaab. One of the first deaths on the Lebanese side was a journalist. On 13 October 2023 a group of clearly marked reporters filming near the village of Alma al-Shaab was hit by two Israeli tank rounds fired 37 seconds apart, according to a Reuters investigation published that December. The first killed Reuters videographer Issam Abdallah, 37, and badly wounded AFP photographer Christina Assi, who lost a leg; at least five others were wounded. AFP's own investigation, and separate reports by Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, reached conclusions consistent with Reuters': that Israeli forces knew or should have known the group were civilians. The Israeli army said it was looking into the incident, and its officials repeated that they do not target journalists. [cite:hz7_npr_abdallah] Two Al Mayadeen journalists were killed in a separate Israeli strike on 21 November 2023. [cite:hz7_npr_abdallah]

Majdal Shams. The deadliest single attack on the Israeli-held side came on 27 July 2024. A rocket struck a football pitch in Majdal Shams, a Druze town in the Golan Heights that Israel captured from Syria in 1967 and still holds. Twelve children and teenagers, aged about ten to sixteen, were killed and at least 42 people were wounded. According to the town's council, none of the twelve held Israeli citizenship; most residents of Majdal Shams identify as Syrian. [cite:hz7_wiki_majdal] Israel attributed the strike to Hezbollah. Its military spokesman, Daniel Hagari, said: "Our intelligence is clear. Hezbollah is responsible for the killing of innocent children," and identified the weapon as an Iranian-made Falaq-1 rocket. [cite:hz7_aj_majdal] Secretary of State Antony Blinken said "every indication" was that the rocket came from Hezbollah; Human Rights Watch said the damage was consistent with a Falaq-type rocket, possibly one that overshot an Israeli army position on Mount Hermon. [cite:hz7_wiki_majdal] Hezbollah denied it: "The Islamic Resistance has no connection to this incident." It had claimed several other rocket attacks that day, which it described as retaliation for Israeli strikes at Kfar Kila. [cite:hz7_aj_majdal] The weight of independent assessment points to a Hezbollah rocket; whether the town was the intended target is not established in the public record, and no independent international investigation, which the EU's foreign policy chief called for, has reported. [cite:hz7_wiki_majdal]

Fuad Shukr. Three days later, on the evening of 30 July 2024, an Israeli strike hit a building in Haret Hreik in Beirut's southern suburbs. Israel said it had killed Fuad Shukr, a senior Hezbollah military commander, and held him responsible for Majdal Shams. Lebanon's health ministry said three people, two of them children, were killed in the strike and 74 wounded. Hezbollah confirmed Shukr's death the next day. Hours after the Beirut strike, Hamas's political leader Ismail Haniyeh was killed in Tehran; the UN Secretary-General called the two strikes a "dangerous escalation." [cite:hz7_aj_shukr] The pattern of this period was set: each side's attacks killed civilians; each named the other's attack as the cause; and Israel answered with strikes on commanders in the capital.

sections.h: Pagers and Radios
sections.html:
17 September 2024. Thousands of pagers carried by Hezbollah members and others across Lebanon, and some in Syria, beeped and then exploded, in homes, shops, cars and streets. The next day Lebanon's health minister, Firas Abiad, put the toll at 12 dead, among them a girl and a boy and four health workers employed by private hospitals in Beirut's southern suburbs who carried the devices, and between 2,750 and 2,800 wounded, nearly 300 of them critically. About 1,850 of the wounded were in Beirut and its southern suburbs, about 750 in the south and about 150 in the Bekaa. [cite:hz7_na_pager_toll] On 18 September a second wave struck: handheld radios, also issued within Hezbollah, exploded. [cite:hz7_ohchr_experts] On 19 September Abiad gave per-day figures: 12 killed and 2,323 injured by the pagers, and 25 killed and 608 injured by the radios. [cite:hz7_lbci_abiad]

The toll and its limits. The counts differ by date and by what they include. Abiad's per-day figures add up to 37 dead and 2,931 injured; by November 2024 the Times of Israel was reporting 39 killed and more than 3,400 wounded across both days, and ACLED's September overview also gave at least 39 deaths. [cite:hz7_lbci_abiad] [cite:hz7_toi_netanyahu_pagers] [cite:hz7_acled_sep24] Some secondary accounts give 42 killed; this volume has not found a ministry figure to support that number and uses the range of 37 to 39. None of the official tolls separated civilians from Hezbollah members. A Hezbollah official told Reuters a week later that about 1,500 of its fighters had been put out of action by their injuries. Among the wounded was Iran's ambassador in Beirut, Mojtaba Amani. [cite:hz7_toi_netanyahu_pagers] The devices were given to people inside Hezbollah's networks, which is why most of the wounded were members; but they exploded wherever their holders happened to be, which is why children, medical staff and bystanders were among the dead and wounded.

How it was done. Reporting by the New York Times, summarised by L'Orient Today on 19 September, traced the pagers to BAC Consulting, a company registered in Budapest that held a licence to make pagers under the brand of Gold Apollo, a Taiwanese firm. The Times described BAC as a shell company set up as part of an Israeli plan to pose as an international pager producer, and reported that at least two other shell companies were created to hide who was really making the devices. The batteries, it reported, had been packed with the explosive PETN. Shipments to Lebanon began in small numbers in the summer of 2022 and grew after Nasrallah urged his followers not to use mobile phones; thousands more arrived in the summer of 2024. Gold Apollo said it had only authorised BAC to use its brand and that BAC alone was responsible for the design and manufacture; BAC's chief executive denied making the devices and told NBC: "I am just the middleman." [cite:hz7_olj_nyt_bac] In December 2024 two former Mossad officers, interviewed under pseudonyms by CBS's 60 Minutes, gave their account. They said the operation began about ten years earlier with radios fitted with explosives, of which Hezbollah eventually bought more than 16,000; that the pager phase began in 2022; that a Gold Apollo saleswoman Hezbollah was used to dealing with, hired by the Mossad, offered the first batch; and, in CBS's narration, that by September 2024 Hezbollah held about 5,000 of the pagers. One said the charge had been calibrated in tests with dummies so that "the only one that will get injured" was the holder. These are the officers' own claims, made under pseudonyms with faces masked, and the public record does not independently confirm them. [cite:hz7_cbs_60min]

Israel's position. Israel did not comment at first. On 20 September its ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, asked about the blasts, said Israel would "do everything we can to target those terrorists," and that Israel did not seek war with Hezbollah but could not accept the existing situation on its border. [cite:hz7_toi_turk] On 10 November 2024 Netanyahu told his cabinet that "The pager operation and the elimination of [Hassan] Nasrallah were carried out despite the opposition" of senior defence officials and political figures, a remark widely read as aimed at Gallant, whom he had just dismissed; his office confirmed Israel's responsibility the next day. [cite:hz7_toi_netanyahu_pagers] Netanyahu's statement is the formal acknowledgement. Reporting that particular Israeli units or private companies supplied software or technical help to the operation rests on single sources and is not used here.

Hezbollah's response. Nasrallah spoke on 19 September. He called the detonations "a declaration of war," "an unprecedented and historic blow" that "crossed all rules and red lines," and promised "a just punishment." [cite:hz7_axios_nasrallah] Eight days later he was dead.

The legal argument. The operation set off a debate in international law that remains unsettled. On 19 September a group of UN human rights experts called the detonations "terrifying" violations of international law. "Simultaneous attacks by thousands of devices would inevitably violate humanitarian law, by failing to verify each target," they said, since no one could know who held each device or who was near it at the moment of detonation; they said the attacks could amount to war crimes, including murder and indiscriminate attack, and that a modified civilian pager could be a prohibited booby-trap disguised as a harmless object. [cite:hz7_ohchr_experts] The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told the Security Council the next day that international humanitarian law "prohibits the use of booby-trap devices in the form of apparently harmless portable objects," called for an independent investigation and said: "This cannot be the new normal." [cite:hz7_toi_turk] Human Rights Watch pointed to Article 7(2) of Amended Protocol II to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which bans booby-traps in the form of apparently harmless portable objects and to which both Israel and Lebanon are party; its regional director, Lama Fakih, said an explosive device whose location "could not be reliably known would be unlawfully indiscriminate." [cite:hz7_npr_law]

The opposing argument was made by military lawyers and analysts. John Spencer of the Modern War Institute at West Point said the attack met the tests of necessity, proportionality and distinction and called it "a very precise sabotage of an enemy piece of equipment used for military purposes." William Boothby, a retired legal officer of the Royal Air Force, wrote that it was probably reasonable to assume pagers issued through a military network would be with their military users, and that the real question was whether enough weight was given to expected harm to others nearby. [cite:hz7_npr_law] No court has ruled on the operation. The record supports two statements at once: the devices were aimed at an armed group's communications and most of the casualties were its members; and the people who set them off could not see where each device was when it exploded, and children and health workers were killed.

sections.h: The Autumn War and the November Ceasefire
sections.html:
23 September 2024. Six days after the pagers, Israel turned the support front into a full war. On 23 September its air force carried out about 200 airstrike events across five Lebanese governorates in a single day, roughly three times the previous peak, according to ACLED. Lebanon's health ministry first reported 558 killed over two days and later gave 569 for 23 September alone, among them 50 children and 94 women; the UN Secretary-General called it the deadliest day for Lebanon in decades. [cite:hz7_acled_sep24] [cite:hz7_ap_558] Over September as a whole ACLED recorded more than 1,700 Israeli strikes in Lebanon, an increase of more than 125 per cent on August. [cite:hz7_acled_sep24]

The scale of the air campaign. Between 16 September and 25 October ACLED recorded more than 3,250 Israeli airstrike events in Lebanon, and found that the number of airstrike events in Lebanon in both September and October was higher than in any single month it had recorded anywhere in the region since 2017, including Syria in April 2017, and higher than any single month in Gaza in the preceding year. An ACLED "event" is one incident in one place on one day and can include several individual strikes. [cite:hz7_acled_qa] A figure of more than 5,700 airstrike events for mid-September to November circulates in secondary accounts and is attributed to ACLED; this volume could not find it in ACLED's published overviews and uses the 3,250 figure for the period ACLED itself reported. ACLED's November overview said the air campaign stayed at "heightened levels" that month, about a fifth lower than in October. [cite:hz7_acled_nov24]

Nasrallah. On the evening of 27 September Israeli aircraft struck a cluster of buildings in Haret Hreik, in Beirut's southern suburbs, where Israel said Hezbollah's leadership was meeting in an underground compound. Israel later released footage of at least eight F-15I jets that took part; experts consulted by the Associated Press said the damage was consistent with 2,000-pound-class bombs designed to penetrate before exploding. Hezbollah confirmed the next day that Hassan Nasrallah, its secretary-general for 32 years, had been killed. [cite:hz7_ap_nasrallah_site] In the last week of September at least seven senior Hezbollah figures were killed, according to ACLED, on top of at least 21 commanders killed between October 2023 and 22 September 2024. [cite:hz7_acled_sep24] His likely successor, Hashem Safieddine, a relative of Nasrallah who headed the group's executive council, was killed in a later Israeli strike; Hezbollah confirmed his death on 23 October. [cite:hz7_dh_safieddine] Netanyahu later said the strike on Nasrallah, like the pager operation, had gone ahead over the opposition of some senior officials. [cite:hz7_toi_netanyahu_pagers]

The ground invasion. On the night of 30 September Israeli paratroopers and commandos of the 98th Division crossed the border. The army described "limited, localized, and targeted ground raids" on villages it said posed "an immediate threat to Israeli communities in northern Israel." It was Israel's first ground invasion of Lebanon since 2006. [scene:hz5_war|The 2006 war] Naim Qassem, Hezbollah's deputy leader, said: "The Islamic resistance will continue to confront the Israeli enemy." President Joe Biden, asked about the operation, said he was "comfortable with them stopping" and that "We should have a ceasefire now"; the Pentagon announced a few thousand more troops for the region.
