[cite:hz7_cbc_ground] Hezbollah kept firing: ACLED recorded more than 50 armed clashes in the first four weeks of the ground operation, more than 60 other Hezbollah attacks on Israeli forces inside Lebanon, and rocket fire into Israel of hundreds a day. On 13 October a Hezbollah drone killed four soldiers of the Golani Brigade at a base near Binyamina, about 70 kilometres south of the border. [cite:hz7_acled_qa]

UNIFIL. The UN peacekeeping force in the south, UNIFIL, found its positions in the line of fire. On 10 October it said an Israeli tank had fired at an observation tower at its headquarters in Naqoura, injuring two Indonesian peacekeepers, after Israeli soldiers had the day before deliberately fired at and disabled cameras at another position. Israel acknowledged that its forces had fired in the area, said Hezbollah operated near UN posts, and said it had told peacekeepers to take shelter first. Italy's defence minister, Guido Crosetto, said the incidents could amount to war crimes; the White House said it was "deeply concerned." [cite:hz7_almon_unifil] Part Eight follows UNIFIL's records of the truce that followed. [scene:hz8_violations|Violations after the truce]

The toll. On 4 December 2024 Lebanon's health minister, Firas Abiad, said at least 4,047 people had been killed and 16,593 wounded in Lebanon by Israeli attacks since 8 October 2023, 3,402 of the dead after 15 September 2024; he counted 790 women and 316 children among the victims and said the real toll might be higher. The ministry did not separate civilians from fighters. [cite:hz7_olj_abiad_4047] On the day the ceasefire was agreed, Lebanese government figures put the dead at nearly 3,800 and the displaced at more than a million, about a quarter of the population. [cite:hz7_bg_ceasefire] On the Israeli side, the Alma Research and Education Center, an Israeli institute that tracks the northern front, counted 45 civilians and 83 soldiers killed in the northern arena between 8 October 2023 and the ceasefire, in figures updated to 16 December 2024; AP put Israel's dead at about 100. [cite:hz7_alma_summary] [cite:hz7_bg_ceasefire] Israel's army published claims of Hezbollah fighters killed (more than 800 in the first year, by its count); Hezbollah did not publish a full count, and the public record does not contain an independent figure, so none is given here. [cite:hz7_acled_year_pdf]

The ceasefire of 27 November 2024. The agreement, brokered by the United States and France, took effect at 04:00 on 27 November. Its published text has thirteen points. Lebanon's government would prevent Hezbollah and other armed groups from attacking Israel, and Israel would stop offensive operations against Lebanese targets by land, air or sea. Both affirmed UN Security Council Resolution 1701 of 2006, and both kept "their inherent right of self-defense, consistent with international law." South of the Litani river, only Lebanon's official forces could hold arms; the Lebanese state would control arms sales and production and "dismantle all existing unauthorized facilities involved in the production of arms and related materiel," starting in the south; the US and France would help bring the Lebanese army in the south to 10,000 soldiers. A monitoring "Mechanism," "hosted by UNIFIL, chaired by the US, and including France," would receive complaints from both sides. Israel would withdraw in phases south of the Blue Line as the Lebanese army deployed, over a period "which should not exceed 60 days." [cite:hz7_toi_text]

The side letter. Before the deal Israel asked Washington for a separate written commitment to its freedom of action if Hezbollah broke the truce; Hezbollah told mediators the 60-day arrangement left the door open to "Israeli aggression in Lebanon." [cite:hz7_toi_freedom] Hours after the ceasefire began, Israel's Channel 13 broadcast what it said was the American letter. In it, as reported, the United States "recognizes Israel's right to respond to threats from Lebanese territory, in accordance with international law"; outside southern Lebanon, Israel reserved the right to act against developing threats if Lebanon could not or would not stop them; Israeli flights over Lebanon would be limited to intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance; the two governments would share intelligence on violations; and the United States would work with Israel to stop Iranian weapons reaching Lebanon. [cite:hz7_olj_sideletter] Netanyahu presented the deal in those terms. Israel was "preserving full military freedom of action," he said, and "The length of the cease-fire will depend on what happens in Lebanon"; he gave three reasons for accepting it: to focus on Iran, to rest the army and restock its weapons, and to separate Hamas from its allies. Biden said the arrangement was "designed to be a permanent cessation of hostilities" and that "Israel did not launch this war." The security cabinet approved it 10 to 1; Itamar Ben-Gvir called it "a historic mistake." [cite:hz7_bg_ceasefire] The gap between the published text, which bound both sides, and the reported letter, which gave one side a further right to act, is where the next part begins. [scene:hz8_terms|The terms and what followed]

chapters.label: Part Eight
chapters.title: The Broken Ceasefire and the 2026 War
chapters.intro: Part Eight covers the two years after the ceasefire of 27 November 2024. It sets out what the agreement actually said and what each government said it meant; how Israel kept five hilltop positions after the withdrawal deadline; how many violations and deaths the UN, the Lebanese government and the Israeli army each counted while the truce was nominally in force; how Lebanon's new president and prime minister tried to bring Hezbollah's weapons under the state; and how the war that began on 2 March 2026, inside the wider American and Israeli war on Iran, overturned all of it. Because nearly all of this is recent, figures are given with the date and the body that produced them, and the status of anything still moving is marked as of the latest reporting this book could verify.
chapters.outro: Part Eight established four things. The November 2024 agreement bound Israel to stop offensive operations and leave within sixty days and bound Lebanon to disarm every group beginning in the south, while Israel said publicly that it kept "full freedom of military action." [cite:hz8_toi_text] [cite:hz8_jvl_netanyahu] Israel stayed on five hilltops after 18 February 2025 and struck Lebanon almost daily: UNIFIL recorded about 7,800 air violations in the first year, Lebanon's health ministry counted 331 dead by November 2025, and the UN verified at least 127 of them as civilians, while Hezbollah's documented fire amounted to two incidents, one of which it denied. [cite:hz8_national_five] [cite:hz8_un_unifil_year] [cite:hz8_aa_tabatabai] [cite:hz8_ohchr_nov25] [cite:hz8_toi_metula] Lebanon's new government took the state's monopoly on arms further than any before it, and its army reported control south of the Litani by January 2026, but Hezbollah refused to disarm further while Israel struck and occupied, and Israel refused to stop or leave while Hezbollah stayed armed. [cite:hz8_euronews_aug7] [cite:hz8_cnn_phase1] Then, inside the US–Israeli war on Iran, Hezbollah fired on 2 March 2026 in defiance of its own government, and Israel's response killed 2,294 people in Lebanon in six weeks, on the health ministry's provisional count, and displaced more than a million; by 11 October the ministry's count since 2 March stood at 4,387, while Israel put its own losses at 39 soldiers, a contractor and two civilians. [cite:hz8_olj_ban] [cite:hz8_olj_toll] [cite:hz8_aj_may2] [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] As of October 2026 the ceasefire of 19 June held only in that Hezbollah had stopped firing: Israel still struck the south and held a zone covering about 6 percent of Lebanon, and the June framework tying its withdrawal to Hezbollah's disarmament had stalled. [cite:hz8b_olj_qassem] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] Part Nine sets these wars against the balance of power behind them: what Hezbollah actually has, what Israel has, and who pays for each. [scene:hz9_ledger|The power ledger]

sections.h: What Was Agreed, and What Each Side Said It Meant
sections.html:
The war described in [scene:hz7_war|Part Seven] ended, formally, at four o'clock on the morning of 27 November 2024. The text that the United States and France announced the day before was titled "Announcement of a Cessation of Hostilities and Related Commitments on Enhanced Security Arrangements and Toward the Implementation of UNSCR 1701." It was short: thirteen numbered points, which the Times of Israel published in full the same afternoon. [cite:hz8_toi_text]

The core obligations ran in both directions. Lebanon's government was to prevent Hezbollah and every other armed group in Lebanon from carrying out operations against Israel. Israel was to carry out no offensive military operations against Lebanese targets, civilian or military, by land, air or sea. Both sides committed to steps toward the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 1701, the text that had ended the 2006 war. And point four preserved for both the "inherent right of self-defense, consistent with international law." [cite:hz8_toi_text]

The rest of the text dealt with who could carry weapons, and where. Only the official forces of the Lebanese state, which the text listed as the army, the Internal Security Forces, General Security, State Security, customs and municipal police, were to be armed in the "Southern Litani Area," the strip between the Israeli border and the Litani river. The Lebanese government was to control all sales, supply and production of arms in the country and to dismantle unauthorized facilities and confiscate unauthorized weapons, "starting in the Southern Litani Area." The United States and France would work to bring the Lebanese army's strength in the south to 10,000 soldiers. Israel was to withdraw its forces in phases to the south of the Blue Line while the army deployed, on a coordinated plan that "should not exceed 60 days." [cite:hz8_toi_text]

Enforcement was given to a body the text called the Mechanism: a reformulated version of an existing tripartite committee, hosted by UNIFIL, chaired by the United States and including France. Violations were to be reported to it and to UNIFIL, without prejudice to either government's right to go to the Security Council directly. [cite:hz8_toi_text]

The side letter

What the published text did not contain was the point Israel had pressed hardest. At the end of October 2024, Israel's Channel 12 reported that Israel was seeking a side letter in which Washington would commit to giving Israel "freedom of action to respond to any violation of the ceasefire deal by Hezbollah"; Axios reported the same demand as "active enforcement." [cite:hz8_toi_sideletter] When the deal was announced, Channel 12 reported that such a letter existed and affirmed Israel's right to act against threats from Lebanon and to keep flying reconnaissance over it. The Times of Israel said it had not seen the letter. [cite:hz8_toi_text] Hours after the truce began, Israel's Channel 13 broadcast what it said was the letter's content, set out in [scene:hz7_war|Part Seven]; neither government has published it. [cite:hz7_olj_sideletter] What is on the official record is how the two leaders described the arrangement.

On 26 November, Benjamin Netanyahu told Israelis: "With the United States' full understanding, we maintain full freedom of military action." If Hezbollah tried to rearm, rebuild near the border, launch a rocket, dig a tunnel or bring in "a truck carrying rockets," he said, "we will attack." He gave three reasons for agreeing to a ceasefire at all: "to focus on the Iranian threat," "to give our forces a breather and replenish stocks," and "to separate the fronts and isolate Hamas." [cite:hz8_jvl_netanyahu] President Joe Biden said the same evening that the arrangement was "designed to be a permanent cessation of hostilities," that Israel "retains the right to self-defense consistent with international law," and that Hezbollah's infrastructure in the south "will not be allowed to be rebuilt." [cite:hz8_biden_dcpd]

Hezbollah's new secretary-general, Naim Qassem, gave his account on 29 November. He called the outcome a "divine victory," larger than that of 2006, and said coordination between "the resistance" and the Lebanese army "will be at a high level" in carrying out the agreement. [cite:hz8_aj_qassem] The two readings were not compatible. Israel read the deal as permission to keep striking anything it judged a threat; Hezbollah read it as an obligation on Israel to stop and leave, with the south handed to the army.

The deadlines

The sixty days ran out on 26 January 2025, and Israel had not withdrawn. Residents of border villages tried to return that day; Lebanese health officials said Israeli fire killed at least 22 people, among them six women and a soldier, and wounded 124. The Israeli army said its troops had fired warning shots to "remove threats" from suspects approaching them, and blamed Hezbollah for organizing the marches. The same day the White House announced that the arrangement "will continue to be in effect until February 18, 2025." [cite:hz8_nbc_jan26]

On 17 February, the eve of the new deadline, the Israeli army said it would stay past it at five posts inside Lebanon, which The National listed as Jabal Blat, Labbouneh, and the hills of Al Azziyeh, Al Awidah and El Hamames. "We need to remain at those points at the moment to defend Israeli citizens," said the military spokesman, Lt Col Nadav Shoshani, describing the aim as eventually handing over to the Lebanese army. President Joseph Aoun rejected reports that Lebanon had agreed to any extension. Qassem said: "Israel must fully withdraw on February 18, it has no excuse." A Hezbollah-allied MP called the decision a "new violation of the ceasefire agreement." [cite:hz8_national_five]

The text itself said nothing about Israel keeping positions after the withdrawal, and Israel's stated reason was a security judgment rather than a clause. The text also said nothing that allowed Hezbollah to keep weapons anywhere in Lebanon, a point that would matter later: the obligation to bring all arms under the state ran, in the agreement's words, to the whole country, "starting" in the south. Each side's subsequent conduct, set out in the next section, followed its own reading.

sections.h: A Ceasefire Counted in Violations
sections.html:
Between 27 November 2024 and the end of February 2026 the ceasefire was in force on paper, and the fighting did not stop. What changed was its shape: instead of two armies exchanging fire, one side struck almost every day and the other almost never answered. The counts below come from four different bodies, each with its own method, and they should not be added together.

What the UN counted

UNIFIL, the UN force in the south, published its first-year figures for 27 November 2024 to 27 November 2025. It recorded almost 7,800 Israeli air violations, more than 2,500 Israeli military activities north of the Blue Line, more than 100 air attacks, and more than 1,000 trajectories of fire crossing the Blue Line, "almost all" from the Israeli side. In the same year its patrols found more than 360 caches of unauthorized weapons and ammunition, which it handed to the Lebanese army. It also recorded that Israel remained at five locations inside Lebanon and maintained two buffer zones that kept the Lebanese army from deploying fully. [cite:hz8_un_unifil_year] In its anniversary statement UNIFIL summed this as more than "10,000 Israeli air and ground violations" in twelve months. [cite:hz8_olj_unifil10k] UNIFIL counts what it observes and does not attribute the weapons caches it finds to a named owner.

The UN human rights office counted deaths. On 25 November 2025 it said it had verified that at least 127 civilians had been killed in Lebanon by Israeli forces since the ceasefire began, through 24 November. Its examples included a strike on the Ein el-Hilweh Palestinian refugee camp near Sidon that killed at least 13 civilians, 11 of them children, and a 16 November strike on a cement and asphalt plant in Ansar that, in its words, hindered reconstruction. About 64,000 people were still displaced. High Commissioner Volker Türk called on both parties to comply in good faith. [cite:hz8_ohchr_nov25]

What Lebanon counted

Lebanon's health ministry counts everyone killed by Israeli fire, civilians and fighters together, without separating them. By its count at least 331 people had been killed and 945 injured between the ceasefire and 24 November 2025. That count included the strike of 23 November on Beirut's southern suburbs that killed Haytham Ali Tabatabai, Hezbollah's senior military commander, with four other people; Netanyahu said he had ordered it because Tabatabai led Hezbollah's "buildup and armament." [cite:hz8_aa_tabatabai] L'Orient-Le Jour's own tally for roughly the same year, 27 November 2024 to 14 November 2025, was more than 12,000 Israeli violations and 343 deaths. [cite:hz8_olj_unifil10k] In January 2026 Lebanon's foreign ministry told the Security Council that it had documented 2,036 Israeli violations in the last three months of 2025 alone: 542 in October, 691 in November and 803 in December. [cite:hz8_aj_complaint]

That last figure is sometimes cited as the total for the whole truce "by January 2026," beside a death toll of fifteen. Both readings are wrong: 2,036 is one quarter's count, and the deaths during the truce, on Lebanon's figures, ran into the hundreds. [cite:hz8_aj_complaint] [cite:hz8_aa_tabatabai]

What Israel counted

Israel described its strikes as enforcement of the agreement, not breaches of it. On the first anniversary the Israeli army said that its forces and the air force had "eliminated more than 370 terrorists" from Hezbollah, Hamas and other armed groups in Lebanon during the year, and that a single division had carried out about 1,200 "targeted activities" and found dozens of weapons stores and launch sites. [cite:hz8_idf_year] That figure is the army's own and is not broken down by group or independently checked; it is larger than the health ministry's total of 331 for all deaths, so the two counts cannot both be complete on the same basis, and neither has been independently reconciled. What the UN did verify is that at least 127 of the dead were civilians.

What Hezbollah did

Hezbollah's documented fire during these fifteen months was slight. On 2 December 2024 it fired two projectiles at the Israeli-held Shebaa Farms, which it called a "defensive and warning response" to Israeli violations; they fell in open ground. [cite:hz8_pbs_dec2] On 22 March 2025 six rockets were fired at the Israeli town of Metula; three were intercepted and three fell inside Lebanon. Hezbollah denied firing them and said it remained committed to the ceasefire. Defence Minister Israel Katz ordered a response and said "the fate of Metula is the same as Beirut"; Israeli artillery and air strikes that day killed at least six people in Lebanon, among them a child, according to the health ministry. [cite:hz8_toi_metula] Security Council Report, summarizing UN reporting in late 2025, recorded March 2025 as the last reported rocket fire toward Israel. [cite:hz8_scr_nov25] Israel's case against Hezbollah during the truce therefore rested less on attacks than on rearmament: the weapons caches, the claimed rebuilding of infrastructure, and men like Tabatabai. Hezbollah has not published a count of its own losses during the truce.

How the Mechanism worked

The body meant to settle these disputes met rarely and did not publish findings. Its thirteenth meeting, at Ras al-Naqoura in November 2025, was about a month after its twelfth; Lebanese military sources described it as routine. The Lebanese army complained there that Israel was not notifying the committee in advance of sites it suspected of holding weapons, as the agreed procedure required; Israel had refused to do so. [cite:hz8_olj_mechanism] The Mechanism did not issue public rulings on which side had breached the agreement, and the reporting this book found does not show any Israeli strike being halted or reversed because of a complaint lodged with it. Lebanon took its counts to the Security Council instead, asking it to compel Israel to withdraw "beyond the internationally recognised borders." [cite:hz8_aj_complaint]

The committee changed shape in December 2025. On 3 December Lebanon sent a civilian, the former ambassador Simon Karam, to sit alongside its officers at the Naqoura meeting, and Israel sent civilian representatives too, with the US envoy Morgan Ortagus present. L'Orient Today called it the first direct talks between the two states in more than forty years. [cite:hz8_olj_karam] Whether this was a step toward a settlement or toward the political deal Israel and the United States wanted from Lebanon is the question the next section takes up.

sections.h: A State Monopoly on Arms, on Paper
sections.html:
The 2024 war changed Lebanon's politics as much as its border. The presidency had been vacant for more than two years. On 9 January 2025 parliament elected the army commander, Joseph Aoun, with 99 of 128 votes. In his acceptance speech he promised to "confirm the state's right to monopolise the carrying of weapons." [cite:hz8_na_aoun] Four days later Aoun asked Nawaf Salam, then president of the International Court of Justice, to form a government; Salam won the support of more than half of the members of parliament, and Hezbollah, which had backed the caretaker prime minister Najib Mikati, did not nominate him. [cite:hz8_aj_salam]

The August 2025 decisions

The pledge became a cabinet decision on 5 August 2025. The government tasked the army with drawing up a plan to restrict weapons to the army and other state forces "before the end of this year," with the plan itself due before the end of August. Two ministers, Health Minister Rakan Nassereddine of Hezbollah and Environment Minister Tamara al-Zein of Amal, walked out. Qassem's answer was that "any timetable presented for implementation under... Israeli aggression cannot be agreed to." [cite:hz8_nn_aug5]

Two days later the cabinet adopted the objectives of a paper submitted by the American envoy Tom Barrack. As reported by AP, its goals were a "gradual end of the armed presence of all non-state actors, including Hezbollah, in all Lebanese territory"; the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the south; a halt to Israeli air strikes; the release of Lebanese prisoners held in Israel; and eventual demarcation of the border. The Shia ministers walked out again. Hezbollah said it would "treat this decision as if it does not exist," and its officials said they would not discuss the rest of their arsenal until Israel left the five hills and stopped its near-daily strikes. [cite:hz8_euronews_aug7] The paper put obligations on both sides in one document; Hezbollah's objection was to the order, since it wanted the Israeli withdrawal and the end of strikes first.

On 5 September the army commander, Rodolphe Haykal, presented the plan. The cabinet "welcomed" it without formally adopting it, and without a timetable; the information minister said implementation depended on the army's logistical, material and personnel capacity and might need "additional time." Five Shia ministers left the room as Haykal came in. A Hezbollah-aligned minister argued that any decision taken without the Shia ministers was void under Lebanon's sectarian power-sharing rules, and Qassem had already warned in August of street protests and raised the prospect of civil war if the government confronted the group. [cite:hz8_aj_sep5] The plan's details were kept secret, but media reports summarized by Security Council Report described five phases: south of the Litani first, then the area between the Litani and the Awali, then Beirut and its surroundings, then the Bekaa, then the whole country. [cite:hz8_scr_nov25]

The first phase

By October 2025, according to a statement by US Central Command, the Lebanese army had removed about 10,000 rockets, 400 missiles and more than 205,000 pieces of unexploded ordnance. [cite:hz8_scr_nov25] On 8 January 2026 the army announced that its plan had "reached an advanced stage" and that it had operational control south of the Litani, except at the five Israeli positions. Netanyahu's office called this an "encouraging start" but "far from sufficient," saying "Hezbollah must be fully disarmed" and citing Hezbollah efforts to rearm with Iranian help, which CNN could not verify. Hezbollah had largely allowed the army to work south of the Litani and refused to give up its weapons north of it, citing the continuing occupation. The government said the army would bring a plan for the area north of the Litani in February. [cite:hz8_cnn_phase1]

On 16 February the cabinet "took note" of the army's second phase, the area between the Litani and the Awali, with four months allotted and room to extend; Qassem told the government to "stop all action to restrict weapons," and Israel called the army's progress insufficient. [cite:hz8b_aj_phase2] That plan was overtaken by events. In the same months that the army was clearing the south, the Israeli strikes counted in [scene:hz8_violations|the previous section] continued, including the killing of Tabatabai in Beirut, and Israel did not leave the five hills. Each side pointed to the other's failure as the reason for its own. Hezbollah said it could not disarm while Israel struck and occupied; Israel said it could not stop or leave while Hezbollah kept weapons anywhere in Lebanon.

Reconstruction as leverage

Money sat beside the arms question. The World Bank estimated in March 2025 that the war from 8 October 2023 to 20 December 2024 had cost Lebanon $14 billion, $6.8 billion in physical damage and $7.2 billion in economic losses, that recovery and reconstruction would need $11 billion, and that the economy had shrunk 7.1 percent in 2024, on top of a fall of nearly 40 percent since 2019. Housing was the worst-hit sector, at $4.6 billion. [cite:hz8_wb_rdna] The south, the Bekaa and Beirut's southern suburbs, where most of Hezbollah's constituents live, were, Al Jazeera reported in May 2025, Hezbollah's priority for rebuilding; the same report said that major donors, the United States among them, were pushing for Hezbollah's disarmament as a precondition for reconstruction aid. [cite:hz8_aj_donors] The UN rights office, for its part, said Israeli strikes on factories, roads and housing were themselves hindering reconstruction and return. [cite:hz8_ohchr_nov25] This book did not find a published US document setting disarmament as a formal condition; the linkage is reported, not documented in a text.

On the record compiled here, the Lebanese state did more of what it promised than either armed party. That record ended on 2 March 2026, when Hezbollah fired on Israel and the government that had been negotiating its disarmament banned its military activity outright. [cite:hz8_olj_ban]

The disarmament question returned after the war in a different form. The framework agreement Israel and Lebanon signed in Washington on 26 June 2026 tied Israel's withdrawal to Hezbollah's disarmament, through "pilot zones" handed one at a time to the army; Hezbollah rejected it as "a surrender of sovereignty," while saying in August that it would pull back south of the Litani but not disarm north of it. [cite:hz8b_aj_reject] [cite:hz8b_aj_rome] As of October 2026 the process had stalled, and the public record shows no completed phase north of the Litani; [scene:hz8_war2026|the next section] gives the status in full. [cite:hz8b_national_tampa]

sections.h: The 2026 War
sections.html:
The ceasefire did not collapse over Lebanon. It collapsed over Iran. On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel opened a joint air campaign against Iran; Israel described its strikes as pre-emptive, and President Donald Trump announced American combat operations. Within hours Trump wrote that Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran's supreme leader, was dead, and Iranian state television confirmed it early the next day. [cite:hz8_am_khamenei] Khamenei was killed in those opening strikes of 28 February, which were joint American and Israeli operations; his son Mojtaba was named his successor on 8 March. [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar] The wider war, its causes and its costs belong to [scene:ow7_iran|the account of American forces in that war] and to [scene:hz12_wars|Part Twelve]; this section follows the Lebanese front.

How it started

On 2 March Hezbollah launched missiles and drones at Israel, its first fire since the strikes on Iran began and its first acknowledged attack on Israel since December 2024. Its statement tied the attack to Khamenei's killing and to fifteen months of Israeli strikes in Lebanon, saying Israel's continued attacks and assassinations gave it "the right to defend ourselves and respond at the appropriate time and place." The Israeli army began striking targets across Lebanon, including Beirut's southern suburbs, and said it "will not enable the organization to constitute a threat to the State of Israel." On 28 February Lebanon's presidency had said the American ambassador assured it Israel would not escalate against Lebanon so long as there were no hostile acts from the Lebanese side. [cite:hz8_am_mar2]

The Lebanese government's response was without precedent. On the afternoon of 2 March the cabinet banned all "military and security actions" by Hezbollah and ordered the army to "immediately and firmly begin implementing" its disarmament plan north of the Litani, using "all necessary means." Salam announced the "absolute rejection, without ambiguity or possible interpretation, of any military or security action" from Lebanese territory outside state institutions. Hezbollah's two ministers objected to the text but did not resign; "We expressed our opposition to the text, and that's all," said one of them, Mohammad Haidar. [cite:hz8_olj_ban] Hezbollah thus went to war against Israel in defiance of a decision of the government it sat in, and Israel went to war against Hezbollah in a country whose government had just outlawed Hezbollah's military activity.

Israel's campaign

On 16 March troops of the Israeli army's 91st Division began what it called "limited and targeted ground operations against key Hezbollah strongholds in southern Lebanon." An army spokesman said Hezbollah was "firing hundreds of rockets a day" at Israel. Defence Minister Israel Katz said displaced Lebanese would not be allowed back "south of the Litani area until the safety of residents in the north (of Israel) is guaranteed." Lebanese authorities then counted about 850 dead and more than 830,000 people registered as displaced. [cite:hz8b_afp_ground] By 24 March, AFP reported, Israeli strikes had killed at least 1,039 people in Lebanon and displaced more than a million. [cite:hz8_am_mar24] On 8 April, the day a ceasefire between the United States and Iran took effect, Israel struck what it said were more than 100 Hezbollah command centres and military sites in Beirut, the Bekaa and the south, its heaviest strikes of the war. "The battle in Lebanon continues, and the ceasefire does not include Lebanon," the army said. Three Lebanese sources told Reuters that Hezbollah had stopped attacking Israeli targets that morning. [cite:hz8b_reu_apr8] Reuters reported dozens killed that day and hundreds wounded. [cite:hz8b_reu_apr8]

Israel's stated aim throughout was to remove Hezbollah's ability to threaten northern Israel. Hezbollah's stated aim was to answer the killing of Khamenei and the strikes of the truce years. By 31 May Netanyahu claimed that 3,000 Hezbollah fighters had been killed; Hezbollah did not publish figures of its own, and the claim is Israel's alone. [cite:hz8b_ap_beaufort] On Israel's side, the army reported 32 soldiers and four civilians killed by 19 June. [cite:hz8b_olj_jun19] By September Israel put its losses to Hezbollah attacks at 39 soldiers, one military contractor and two civilians, and UNIFIL said seven of its peacekeepers had been killed during the year. [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] The two Israeli counts do not match on civilians; each is given as reported.

The toll, by date

Lebanon's health ministry counts all deaths from Israeli attacks, without separating civilians from fighters, and calls its figures provisional until rubble is cleared and bodies identified. For 2 March to midnight on 16 April it reported 2,294 killed and 7,544 injured, including 100 health and rescue workers killed. [cite:hz8_olj_toll] The government's disaster-management unit raised the toll to 2,454 dead and 7,658 wounded on 21 April. [cite:hz8_aawsat_2454] By 2 May the ministry's count was 2,659 killed and 8,183 injured, with 41 dead in the previous 24 hours and more than one million people registered as displaced. [cite:hz8_aj_may2] It reached 3,350 by 31 May, 3,912 by 19 June when the fighting largely stopped, and 4,246 by 27 June. [cite:hz8b_ap_beaufort] [cite:hz8b_olj_jun19] [cite:hz8b_aj_reject] On 11 October 2026 the ministry's emergency operations centre gave 4,387 killed and 12,424 injured since 2 March. The ministry's larger headline figure, 8,954 killed and 30,660 injured, counts from 8 October 2023 and so includes the 2023–24 war and the truce months; it should not be quoted as the toll of the 2026 war. [cite:hz8b_qna_toll] Totals above 4,000 that are sometimes given for the period before the April truce do not match the ministry's own dated counts. The Lebanese government put the number displaced at more than 1.2 million. [cite:hz8b_npr_lines]

A truce with shooting

A ten-day truce, on terms released by the US State Department, took effect on the night of 16 April, after 46 days of bombardment and ground fighting. Israel kept its forces in place behind what its officers called a "Yellow Line," modelled on the one in Gaza, about 10 kilometres deep, and barred residents from returning to 55 Lebanese towns and villages inside it. Netanyahu said the army was staying in a "reinforced security buffer zone": "we are not leaving." Lebanon and Hezbollah called the zone an occupation; Hezbollah called the truce "an insult to our country" and the government's parallel talks with Israel a "humiliation." [cite:hz8b_aj_yellow] It did not stop the strikes. Lebanon's government counted 3,491 Israeli air strikes, 407 controlled demolitions and six operations that razed villages between 17 April and 7 June, while Hezbollah kept firing at northern Israel and Israel answered with strikes on Beirut's suburbs. Trump said that in the Middle East ceasefires involve "shooting in a more moderate manner." [cite:hz8_an_jun8]

Talks went on alongside the fighting: on 29 May Israeli and Lebanese military officers met at the Pentagon for the first time in decades. [cite:hz8b_nn_pentagon] On 31 May Israeli troops crossed the Litani and captured Beaufort castle near Nabatieh, which Israel had held from 1982 to 2000, the army's deepest push into Lebanon in more than 25 years. Netanyahu called it "a dramatic shift in the policies we are leading"; Katz said Israel would hold the castle while troops destroyed homes and other sites he said Hezbollah used. Israel declared the land between the Litani and the Zahrani a combat zone. [cite:hz8b_ap_beaufort]

The war on this front largely stopped on 19 June. A US official announced an Israel–Hezbollah ceasefire from 4 p.m. that day, brokered by American and Qatari negotiators with Iran's help, under an interim US–Iran deal that called for military operations to end on all fronts, Lebanon included. Israeli forces were to stay in the south, and Israel kept the right to act against emerging threats. An Israeli official said: "If Hezbollah does not attack us, then for us it is not a time of war." [cite:hz8b_olj_jun19] Hezbollah has not answered Israeli strikes since mid-June, though the strikes have continued. [cite:hz8b_olj_qassem]

On 26 June the Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors in Washington signed a US-brokered framework agreement at the State Department. As Reuters reported it, the agreement set out a process, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio described as clear, to restore Lebanese sovereignty and disarm Hezbollah, and would let Israel withdraw to its borders once the danger to its citizens ended; it also created a three-party Military Coordination Group for Lebanon, facilitated by the United States. [cite:hz8b_almon_framework] It set out a path toward ending the state of war and a full peace agreement, but, Al Jazeera's correspondent noted, "the word withdrawal is not in [the] text." Qassem called it "humiliating, shameful and a surrender of sovereignty" and rejected tying Israel's withdrawal to Hezbollah's disarmament; a Hezbollah MP, Hassan Fadlallah, warned that any attempt by the army to enforce it would lead to "civil war." Katz said he and Netanyahu had ordered forces to prepare for an "extended stay." [cite:hz8b_aj_reject]

The agreement's mechanism was a set of "pilot zones": small areas from which Israel would withdraw and which the Lebanese army would take over, with US Central Command coordinating. No timetable for wider withdrawal was set, and Israeli officials said their forces would stay in a 10-kilometre security zone for as long as Hezbollah stayed armed. [cite:hz8b_afp_pilot] Israel left the first village, Zawtar al-Gharbieh, at the end of July. [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] Aoun met Trump in Washington on 21 July; Rubio told him Lebanon would "never be fully at peace" until the Hezbollah question was settled. [cite:hz8b_ap_aoun] A seventh round of talks, in Rome on 4 and 5 August, ended split over disarmament: Hezbollah, which is not a party to the talks, said it would pull back south of the Litani but would not disarm north of it. [cite:hz8b_aj_rome]

sections.h: Where Things Stand, October 2026
sections.html:
As of 19 October 2026 the 19 June ceasefire was holding in the limited sense that Hezbollah had stopped firing; Israel had not stopped. Israeli strikes and demolitions in the south continued through the summer and autumn, including beyond Israel's declared security zone, and Hezbollah had not responded to them since mid-June. [cite:hz8b_olj_qassem] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] Israeli forces still held a strip behind the Yellow Line covering about 6 percent of Lebanon, in places about eight kilometres deep, with dozens of villages emptied or flattened and their residents barred; NPR reported Israeli tanks in Zawtar al-Gharbieh and fighting on Ali al-Taher hill near Nabatieh in September. [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] [cite:hz8b_olj_salam] Netanyahu said he did not trust Lebanon's government to disarm Hezbollah and that "we will remain in this zone." [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] The US–Iran memorandum of 17 June, under which the Lebanese ceasefire had been agreed, collapsed on 8 July, and intermittent fighting between American and Iranian forces followed; the public record reviewed here does not show Hezbollah resuming fire after that collapse. [cite:ow7_wiki_ceasefire2026] [cite:hz8b_olj_qassem]

Direct talks had become routine. After five rounds in Washington and two in Rome by early August, the two sides had agreed in September to separate a political track from a military one, and military delegations were due to meet again in Tampa, Florida, on 20 October, with the United States in the middle. Lebanon went in refusing US proposals for its army to coordinate directly with Israel's and demanding third-party verification and a full withdrawal; the pilot-zone process had stalled for months, and the verification mechanism had not been agreed. [cite:hz8b_aj_rome] [cite:hz8b_national_tampa] On disarmament, the army's phased plan had reached its second phase, the land between the Litani and the Awali, on 16 February, with four months allotted, two weeks before the war overtook it; Qassem had called the focus on disarmament "a grave sin." [cite:hz8b_aj_phase2] The public record does not show any further cabinet decision or completed phase since then. Hezbollah's position on 6 October was that it was "ready to cooperate" on the state's monopoly on arms on the basis of the constitution, but would accept no "American diktats," and that "Israel cannot remain in southern Lebanon indefinitely." [cite:hz8b_olj_qassem]

About 40 percent of the displaced had gone home by late June; Salam said in September that return "cannot wait until the crisis ends," while the first prefabricated houses reached Zawtar al-Gharbieh, and the finance minister put the war's cost at roughly $20 billion. [cite:hz8b_olj_salam] UNIFIL's mandate, extended "for a final time" by the Security Council in August 2025 under resolution 2790, ends on 31 December 2026, with the force to leave during 2027; NPR reported that US and Israeli opposition ruled out a renewal. Aoun has said he would prefer an extension and, failing that, another international force; none had been agreed by late September. [cite:hz8_scr_nov25] [cite:hz8b_dn_unifil] [cite:hz8b_olj_unifil] [cite:hz8b_olj_salam] [cite:hz8b_npr_lines] What the dated record settles is that the ceasefire of November 2024 did not survive into the spring of 2026: it ended in a war that killed more people in Lebanon in six weeks than the whole truce had in fifteen months, and that left Israeli troops holding ground deeper inside Lebanon than at any time since the withdrawal of 2000. [cite:hz8_olj_toll] [cite:hz8_aa_tabatabai] [cite:hz8b_ap_beaufort]

chapters.label: Part Nine
chapters.title: The Power Ledger
chapters.intro: Part Nine measures the two sides, as Part Eight of the Hamas volume did for Gaza. Hezbollah is often described as the strongest non-state armed group in the world, and Lebanon and Israel are formally two states at war; in resources neither pairing is close. This part first sets Hezbollah's fighters, rockets, missiles, drones and Iranian money, all of them estimates, beside Israel's army, air force, missile defences, budget and American aid, and records how Israel's own estimates of what it destroyed changed between 2024 and 2026. It then compares the two economies: Lebanon's, which lost most of its dollar value after 2019 and was damaged again by war, and Israel's, which grew through two years of fighting. It closes by putting the gap in everyday terms.
chapters.outro: Part Nine set the two sides side by side. Hezbollah's strength rests on estimates: 25,000 to 50,000 fighters by most counts against Nasrallah's claimed 100,000, and 75,000 to 200,000 rockets before 2024, mostly unguided, paid for in large part by Iran at an estimated $100 million to $1 billion a year. [cite:hz9_ap_100k] [cite:hz9_usip_arsenal] [cite:hz9_nyt_half] [cite:hz9_wiki_irfund] Israel's claims to have destroyed 70 to 90 percent of that arsenal were revised in April 2026, when its northern commander acknowledged that Hezbollah was still standing. [cite:hz9a_jpost_8590] [cite:hz9_toi_milo] Against it stood an army of 169,500 active troops and 465,000 reservists, 316 combat aircraft, layered missile defence, a military budget of $48.3 billion in 2025 and $3.8 billion a year in American aid. [cite:hm_almon_idf] [cite:hz9_sipri_2025] [cite:hm_dn_mou] Lebanon's whole economy, about $55 billion in 2018, had fallen to just over $20 billion by 2023, and the 2023–24 war cost it a further $14 billion. [cite:hz9_ifl_rdna] [cite:hz9_wb_rdna] Hezbollah is the largest of the armed groups Iran supports, but not the only one. Part Ten turns to the others: the Houthis in Yemen, the militias in Iraq, Syria and Palestinian Islamic Jihad. [scene:hz10_houthis|The Houthis]

sections.h: Arms, Fighters and Money
sections.html:
Hezbollah publishes no order of battle and no budget, so every figure for its side of the ledger in this section is an estimate, and the estimates differ by a factor of two or more. They are given here with their source and date. Israel's figures come from the International Institute for Strategic Studies, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute and the US Congressional Research Service, and are far more precise. That difference is itself part of the picture: one side is a state with published budgets and a professional army, the other an armed movement inside a weaker state.

Fighters. On 18 October 2021, in a speech after a gun battle in Beirut that killed seven people, Hassan Nasrallah said for the first time that Hezbollah had 100,000 trained fighters. [cite:hz9_iranintl_100k] This was his claim. The Associated Press reported that most estimates put the force at 25,000 to 50,000, including about 10,000 in the Radwan special forces, and that experts considered the 100,000 figure an exaggeration; Sarit Zehavi, a former Israeli military intelligence officer, said Nasrallah had greatly exaggerated the group's strength. [cite:hz9_ap_100k] If his figure were accurate, Hezbollah would be larger than Lebanon's own army, estimated at about 85,000. [cite:hz9_iranintl_100k] Israel's forces, by the IISS count, number 169,500 active personnel and 465,000 reservists. [cite:hm_almon_idf] On the common estimate, Israel's active army alone is three to seven times Hezbollah's whole force; with reservists, thirteen to twenty-five times.

Rockets and missiles before 2024. Israeli sources estimated Hezbollah's stockpile at about 15,000 rockets before the 2006 war, of which nearly 4,000 were fired at Israel. By 2018 the Center for Strategic and International Studies put it at about 130,000, mostly small unguided artillery rockets. [cite:hz9_csis_2018] By 2024 the estimates ran from 75,000, the figure of Israel's Alma Research and Education Center, to "up to 200,000" from other analysts; estimates from 2023 cited by the Times of Israel, without naming their author, put it at about 150,000; and American and Israeli officials quoted by the New York Times gave 120,000 to 200,000. [cite:hz9_usip_arsenal] [cite:hz9_toi_barrages] [cite:hz9_nyt_half] Observers agreed that most of the arsenal was unguided. [cite:hz9_usip_arsenal] The most dangerous part, by the Israeli military's account, was a smaller stock of precision-guided missiles, which it put at "hundreds" at the start of the 2023–24 fighting, and drones, which Alma estimated at about 2,500 larger models. [cite:hz9_jpost_depleted] [cite:hz9_alma_ceasefire]

Money. Hezbollah does not publish its accounts. In November 2018 Nathan Sales, the State Department's counterterrorism coordinator, said Iran gave Hezbollah "some $700 million a year", out of close to $1 billion a year that Iran spent on its allied armed groups. [cite:hz9_usip_sales] Earlier American estimates were lower, at $100 million to $200 million a year; the Wilson Center has cited $700 million to $1 billion. [cite:hz9_wiki_irfund] In February 2012 Nasrallah acknowledged that Hezbollah had received moral, political and material support from Iran since 1982, but gave no figure, and said the group took support, not orders. [cite:hz9_wiki_irfund] The other parts of Hezbollah's income, including its own businesses and the networks the United States has designated, are set out in Part Six. [scene:hz6_money|Hezbollah's money]

What was destroyed, by whose count. The figures for what Israel destroyed come almost entirely from Israel's military, and they changed over time. On 1 October 2024, senior Israeli and American officials told the New York Times that about half of Hezbollah's rockets and missiles had been destroyed, while tens of thousands remained. [cite:hz9_nyt_half] On 10 November 2024 the Jerusalem Post, citing the Israeli military, reported that 80 percent of rockets with a range up to 40 kilometres had been destroyed, short-range stocks had fallen from more than 44,000 to about 10,000, and precision missiles from hundreds to fewer than a hundred. [cite:hz9_jpost_depleted] By the ceasefire of 27 November 2024, Alma's estimate was that 70 to 80 percent of the arsenal had been destroyed and that 2,500 to 3,000 Hezbollah members had been killed. [cite:hz9_alma_ceasefire] Part Seven sets out the fighting itself. [scene:hz7_war|The 2024 war]

The 2026 war tested those claims. Before Hezbollah resumed fire on 2 March 2026, Alma estimated it had about 25,000 rockets and missiles left. [cite:hz9_toi_barrages] On 15 March 2026 the Israeli military said it had now destroyed 85 to 90 percent of the pre-2023 arsenal, that about 30,000 rockets had remained in 2025, and that about 1,000 long-range precision rockets were left; the Jerusalem Post inferred from the update that 10,000 to 23,000 rockets remained. [cite:hz9a_jpost_8590] On 5 April 2026 the head of Israel's Northern Command, Maj. Gen. Rafi Milo, acknowledged a "gap" between how the 2024 operation had been concluded and the fact that Hezbollah was still standing; Israel's Channel 12 reported that officials now believed Hezbollah had tens of thousands of rockets and hundreds of launchers, enough for about 200 launches a day for five more months. [cite:hz9_toi_milo] [cite:hz9_newarab_milo] The public record does not contain an independent count of Hezbollah's arsenal at any point; the honest range for what it held in 2026 runs from about 10,000 to "tens of thousands", depending on which Israeli estimate is used. Part Eight covers the 2026 war. [scene:hz8_war2026|The 2026 war]

Israel's side. Israel spent $46.5 billion on its military in 2024 by SIPRI's count, 8.8 percent of its economy, and $48.3 billion in 2025, 7.8 percent, the eleventh-largest military budget in the world. [cite:hm_globes_sipri] [cite:hz9_sipri_2025] Its air force has 316 combat aircraft, its navy five submarines, and SIPRI estimates that it holds about 90 nuclear warheads. [cite:hm_almon_idf] It has a layered missile defence of Iron Dome, David's Sling and the Arrow systems, built and paid for in part by the United States. [cite:ow1_csis_imd] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] Under the 2016 memorandum, the United States provides $3.8 billion a year, $500 million of it for missile defence; it gave at least $21.7 billion more in military aid between October 2023 and September 2025, and the April 2024 supplemental alone added $4 billion for missile defence and $1.2 billion for the Iron Beam laser. [cite:hm_dn_mou] [cite:hm_an_costsofwar] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

What the air gap means. The difference that decided the shape of both wars is in the air. Hezbollah had no aircraft and no air defence able to contest Israel's air force; Israel could strike anywhere in Lebanon, from the border villages to Beirut's southern suburbs and the Bekaa, and did so more than 8,000 times in the first year of fighting, by the US Institute of Peace's count. Hezbollah, in the same year, launched more than 8,800 rockets, missiles and drones at Israel. [cite:hz9_usip_arsenal] Hezbollah's power was the power to inflict damage and displacement on northern Israel, which Part Seven records [scene:hz7_front|The support front]; it was never the power to defend Lebanon's territory or airspace. Asymmetry of this kind does not make either side's attacks on civilians lawful, and it does not mean Hezbollah's arsenal was harmless: American officials warned in June 2024 that some Iron Dome batteries could be overwhelmed in a full-scale war. [cite:hz9_usip_arsenal] What it measures is the distance between the two forces that met in 2024 and again in 2026.

sections.h: Two Economies, and the Aid Behind Them
sections.html:
By the 2020s the economies of Lebanon and Israel were not in the same class. The gap widened in two steps: Lebanon's own financial collapse from 2019, which began four years before the war with Israel, and then the damage of the wars of 2023–24 and 2026. This section sets out both, then sets the armies' budgets and their foreign aid side by side.

Lebanon's collapse. Lebanon's economy was worth about $55 billion in 2018. In 2019 its banking system and currency collapsed, and by 2023 its output, measured in dollars, was just over $20 billion: it had lost almost two-thirds of its value in five years, before the war with Israel began. [cite:hz9_ifl_rdna] Measured in real terms, the World Bank estimated that the economy shrank by about 40 percent between 2019 and 2024. [cite:hz9_wb_rdna] The crisis reached the state's own army. By early 2022 the pay of a junior Lebanese soldier had fallen to about $100 a month, one-eighth of its pre-crisis value, and in 2020 the army stopped serving meat to its troops. [cite:hz9_fdd_laf] Part Six covers the crisis, the protests of 2019 and Hezbollah's place in the political system that presided over it. [scene:hz6_state|Hezbollah and the state]

What the 2023–24 war cost Lebanon. The World Bank's Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment, published on 7 March 2025 and covering 8 October 2023 to 20 December 2024, put the war's cost to Lebanon at $14 billion: $6.8 billion in physical damage and $7.2 billion in lost economic activity. Housing took the heaviest damage, $4.6 billion; commerce, industry and tourism lost $3.4 billion. Real output fell 7.1 percent in 2024, against 0.9 percent growth the Bank estimated without the war. It put recovery and reconstruction needs at $11 billion, of which $3 billion to $5 billion would have to come from public money. [cite:hz9_wb_rdna] The Lebanese finance ministry's institute, summarising the same assessment, found that the Nabatiyeh governorate in the south bore 47 percent of the damage, and that $8.4 billion of the needs were immediate, for 2025 to 2027. [cite:hz9_ifl_rdna] [cite:hz9_lol_rdna] The war's $14 billion cost equals about two-thirds of Lebanon's entire output in 2023. A comparable World Bank assessment for the March–April 2026 war had not been located as of October 2026; its human toll is set out in Part Eight. [scene:hz8_war2026|The 2026 war]

Israel's economy. Israel's economy, by World Bank figures, produced $513 billion in 2023, $542 billion in 2024 and $611 billion in 2025: it grew through two years of war on several fronts. [cite:hm_fred_ilgdp] In 2023 it was about 25 times the size of Lebanon's. Israel's arms industry alone exported a record $14.8 billion in 2024, nearly three-quarters of Lebanon's whole 2023 output; Part Eleven examines who gains from the wars. [cite:hm_globes_exports] [scene:hz11_gains|Who gains]

The aid to the two armies. The United States funds both armies, on very different scales. Israel receives $3.8 billion a year under the 2016 memorandum, at least $21.7 billion more in military aid in the two years after 7 October 2023, and a cumulative total since 1946 that the Congressional Research Service puts at about $174 billion in current dollars. [cite:hm_dn_mou] [cite:hm_an_costsofwar] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] The Lebanese Armed Forces have received, by the State Department's figure in May 2021, more than $2.5 billion in American security assistance since 2006, an average of roughly $200 million a year in military and economic aid together; in 2021 the United States added packages of $105 million, $15 million and $67 million as the army's pay collapsed, and the administration requested $160 million for 2022. [cite:hz9_fdd_laf] The figures this book could verify for Lebanese army aid stop in 2022; they are drawn from a 2022 study by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank that argued for reassessing the aid, which quotes the State Department's own totals. [cite:hz9_fdd_laf]

The two programmes rest on different legal footing. Since 2008, US law has defined Israel's "qualitative military edge", requires it to be assessed every four years, and bars arms sales to other states in the region that would adversely affect it. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] No comparable statutory guarantee applies to Lebanon; its aid is set year by year, and the FDD study argued that it should be reassessed altogether. [cite:hz9_fdd_laf] Part Eight sets out the Lebanese army's 2025 plan to disarm Hezbollah and how far it went. [scene:hz8_disarm|Disarmament]

The gap, in everyday terms. The figures are easier to hold when set against one another. The comparisons below are this book's own arithmetic from the sources cited; they compare annual flows with annual flows, and say so where they do not.

What the gap does not mean. Lebanon's poverty is not only a product of Israel's wars: by the World Bank's figures, most of the loss in its economy's dollar value came between 2019 and 2023, before the war began. [cite:hz9_ifl_rdna] Part Six covers the domestic causes. [scene:hz6_state|Hezbollah and the state] Nor does the gap settle the question of who threatens whom: a weaker force can still do great harm, as Part Seven records for northern Israel. [scene:hz7_front|The support front] Israel's and Hezbollah's stated reasons for their arsenals, and how those claims compare with outcomes, are tested in Part Eleven. [scene:hz11_pattern|The pattern] What the numbers do show is that the contest is between a state with one of the world's largest military budgets, supplied by the United States, and an armed movement inside a state whose whole economy is smaller than that budget.

chapters.label: Part Ten
chapters.title: The Rest of the Axis
chapters.intro: Part Ten leaves Lebanon for the other armed groups of what Iran and its allies call the "axis of resistance." It follows the Houthis from a Zaidi religious revival in northern Yemen through six wars with their own government, the capture of Sanaa and a Saudi-led war that the United States supported, then sets the documented Iranian arms trail beside the evidence that the movement makes its own decisions. It traces the Houthis' campaign against Red Sea shipping and Israel after October 2023, the American, British and Israeli strikes that answered it, the truce that took the United States out and the new war with Saudi Arabia in 2026. It then turns to the Iraqi militias, the groups that have most often fought American troops directly, from the chain of attacks that ended in the killing of Qasem Soleimani to the deaths of three soldiers at Tower 22. Throughout, it gives each government's and group's stated position beside the record, and says where the evidence does not settle who decides.
chapters.outro: Part Ten established that the Houthis began as a local Zaidi movement in 1992 and went to war with Yemen's own government in 2004, years before the earliest date, about 2009, that experts give for Iranian military support, and that Iran has since supplied the missiles and drones that made their campaign possible, while specialists still divide over whether Tehran directs it. [cite:hz10_nh_saada] [cite:hz10_cfr_iranhouthis] [cite:hz10_un_poe2024] [cite:hz10_npr_roule] Their attacks sank four ships and killed at least eight sailors; the American response cost more than $1 billion in seven weeks of 2025 alone and killed, by Airwars' count, at least 224 civilians, before an Omani-brokered truce took the United States out of the fight and left Israel in it. [cite:hz10_olj_factbox] [cite:hz10_nbc_rrcost] [cite:hz10_airwars_rr] [cite:hz10_aje_truce] The Houthis paused when Gaza's ceasefires held and fired again a month into the Iran war, a pattern that fits both their stated Gaza condition and their alignment with Tehran. [cite:hz10_usni_crs2026] [cite:hz10_na_houthis2026] In Iraq, a single rocket attack in December 2019 escalated within a week to the killing of Soleimani, and in January 2024 the militias' campaign killed three American soldiers at Tower 22, after which Kata'ib Hezbollah halted under pressure it attributed to Iran and Iraq. [cite:hz10_fox_pentagon2020] [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] [cite:hz10_at_farida] In Syria, Israel struck Iranian and Hezbollah targets hundreds of times, armed rebel groups on the Golan, and after Assad's fall held a buffer zone it had called temporary, still there as of October 2026. [cite:hz10s_jc_netanyahu] [cite:hz10s_toi_eisenkot] [cite:hz10s_eb_sufa] Part Eleven tests whether these groups, and the ones Israel itself armed, have served as the standing reason for war. [scene:hz11_pattern|Always the Axis?]

sections.h: Ansar Allah: From Saada to Sanaa
sections.html:
Of the armed groups that Israel and the United States describe as Iran's network, the Houthis are the one whose origins lie furthest from both Israel and Iran. The movement grew out of a religious revival in Saada, the mountainous governorate on Yemen's northern border with Saudi Arabia. A movement known as Believing Youth (al-Shabab al-Mumin) was founded there in 1992 to teach young people Zaidism, the branch of Shia Islam whose imams had ruled northern Yemen for centuries and whose revivalists, by the 1990s, saw it as pressed by the government of President Ali Abdullah Saleh and by Saudi-funded Salafi preaching in its own heartland. [cite:hz10_nh_saada] [cite:hz10_albab_houthi] Zaidis make up about a third of Yemen's roughly 34 million people. [cite:hz10_cfr_iranhouthis]

The movement's first leader, Hussein al-Houthi, was the son of a prominent Zaidi cleric, Badreddin al-Houthi, and sat in Yemen's parliament from 1993 to 1997 for the small al-Haqq party before breaking with it. [cite:hz10_wiki_hussein] [cite:hz10_albab_houthi] From January 2002 his followers adopted a slogan, first chanted at a school in Marran in Saada: "God is great, Death to America, Death to Israel, Curse on the Jews, Victory to Islam." [cite:hz10_wiki_sarkha] The slogan names the United States and Israel as enemies, and its fourth line is directed at Jews as such; it has been the movement's emblem ever since and appears on banners at its rallies. [cite:hz10_wiki_sarkha]

The state's war with the movement began on 18 June 2004. [cite:hz10_nh_saada] Hussein al-Houthi was killed on 10 September 2004 at Marran; Yemen's interior and defence ministries announced that he and 20 aides had died. His father briefly led the movement, and his brother Abdul-Malik al-Houthi then took command. [cite:hz10_wiki_hussein] [cite:hz10_nh_saada] Between 2004 and 2010 the government and the Houthis fought "a series of six intermittent wars" in Saada. [cite:hz10_albab_houthi] By mid-2008 a humanitarian news agency counted hundreds killed, thousands displaced and, according to local rights groups, about 3,000 arrests of supporters. [cite:hz10_nh_saada] The movement took the formal name Ansar Allah, "Supporters of God." [cite:hz10_albab_houthi] It was in these wars, the Council on Foreign Relations notes, that a political movement became an army. [cite:hz10_cfr_iranhouthis]

The Arab uprisings of 2011 forced Saleh from office, and the transition that followed gave the Houthis their opening. On 21 September 2014 Houthi fighters occupied the prime minister's compound, an army command centre and the state television complex in Sanaa after four days of clashes in which more than 100 people died; the prime minister resigned, and the parties, including the Houthis, signed a UN-brokered agreement at the presidential palace that same day. [cite:hz10_voa_sanaa2014] The agreement did not hold. By early 2015 the Houthis controlled the capital and much of the north, and as of April 2026, by the Council on Foreign Relations' account, they ruled about a third of Yemen's territory and about two-thirds of its people. [cite:hz10_crs_if12587] [cite:hz10_cfr_iranhouthis]

The Saudi-led war and the American role

In March 2015 Saudi Arabia formed a coalition and launched military operations in Yemen to restore the ousted government. On 25 March 2015 the United States announced that it would provide "logistical and intelligence support." According to the Congressional Research Service, that support grew to include in-flight refuelling of coalition aircraft, weapons transfers, intelligence and training, coordinated through a joint US–Saudi planning cell. [cite:hz10_crs_yemencongress] After a coalition airstrike on a funeral hall in Sanaa killed 140 people in October 2016, the Obama administration held back a sale of precision munitions and limited intelligence sharing, while keeping refuelling; the Trump administration went ahead with the deferred sales in May 2017. [cite:hz10_crs_yemencongress]

The refuelling ended on 9–10 November 2018, when the coalition announced it would refuel its own aircraft, a decision Defense Secretary Jim Mattis backed after having warned that US support was "not unconditional." [cite:hz10_aje_refuel2018] [cite:hz10_crs_yemencongress] In 2019 both chambers of Congress passed a War Powers resolution directing the removal of US forces from hostilities in Yemen, the Senate 54–46 in March and the House 247–175 on 4 April 2019. President Trump vetoed it on 16 April, and on 2 May the Senate failed to override, 53–45. In May 2019 the administration also declared an emergency to push through arms sales worth more than $8 billion; the Senate then passed 22 resolutions of disapproval, and the President vetoed the three that also cleared the House. [cite:hz10_crs_yemencongress]

The UN Development Programme projected that by the end of 2021 the war would have caused about 377,000 deaths, some 60 percent of them from indirect causes such as hunger and preventable disease rather than combat. [cite:hz10_aje_undp377k] That figure counts all parties' violence, including the Houthis' own, and the war's blockade and economic collapse; it is a projection by modelling, not a count of names. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 then froze the front lines for about four years. [cite:hz10_usni_crs2026] [cite:hz10_ahram_taiz]

Iran's role: supplier, partner or master

That Iran arms the Houthis is no longer seriously disputed. Some experts date Iranian military support to around 2009, and most agree Iran was supplying weapons by 2014; the Congressional Research Service says Iran "has increased its support" since 2014–2015, including ballistic and cruise missiles and drones. [cite:hz10_cfr_iranhouthis] [cite:hz10_crs_if12587] The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, which monitors the Security Council's arms embargo, has traced the trail in detail. Its January 2020 report described engines that were unlicensed copies of foreign designs Iran produces, and a disassembled Quds-1 cruise missile seized at sea that carried a Farsi label recording a test at an Iranian facility in February 2019. [cite:hz10_wi_poe2020] Its October 2024 report found that "without foreign support, the entity does not have the capacity to develop and produce complex weapon systems," listed 53 items with strong similarities to Iranian materiel, and reported that a Quds Force general held a predominant advisory role in the Houthi command. [cite:hz10_un_poe2024] In July 2025 Yemeni government forces seized 750 tonnes of weapons and components bound for the Houthis, the largest such shipment yet found. [cite:hz10_cfr_iranhouthis] Iran's officials, for their part, told the UN Panel that certain small arms with Iranian-like markings did not match their production. [cite:hz10_un_poe2024]

Supplying weapons is not the same as giving orders, and here specialists divide. The same UN report found that Hezbollah, not only Iran, is "one of the most important supporters of the Houthis," and recorded a senior Houthi official saying that although the axis coordinated with Iran, the decision to seize the Galaxy Leader in November 2023 "was made by the Houthi leaders." [cite:hz10_un_poe2024] Two researchers writing in January 2024 called the Houthis "strategic allies" rather than "mere proxies," with their own local base and politics. [cite:hz10_conv_proxies] Norman Roule, a former CIA manager for Iran, ranked Hezbollah closest to Tehran and the Houthis the most distant, and argued that Iran "seeks the product of militia actions, not the process of controlling them." [cite:hz10_npr_roule] Others put more weight on Tehran: many experts quoted by the Council on Foreign Relations describe an "informal partner" whose claims of responsibility can give Iran deniability for attacks it ordered or helped carry out. [cite:hz10_cfr_iranhouthis] The record supports the supply relationship; it does not settle who decides. [scene:hz11_proxies|Part Eleven tests the proxy frame across the network.]

sections.h: The Red Sea War, 2023–2026
sections.html:
After 7 October 2023 the Houthis did what no other member of Iran's network did: they took the Gaza war to a global shipping lane. From November 2023 they attacked commercial and naval vessels in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, which they said showed solidarity with the Palestinians, and they fired missiles at Israel, many of them intercepted by Israeli or US forces. [cite:hz10_crs_if12587] Their stated condition was consistent throughout: the attacks were support for Gaza and would stop when the war on Gaza stopped. [cite:hz10_aje_truce] [cite:hz10_aje_rahawi]

The first act set the pattern. On 19 November 2023 Houthi forces seized the car carrier Galaxy Leader and took its 25 crew; they were held for more than a year and freed in January 2025. [cite:hz10_un_poe2024] [cite:hz10_olj_factbox] The Houthis said they targeted ships linked to Israel. The UN Panel of Experts, counting at least 134 attacks between 15 November 2023 and 31 July 2024 on merchant ships and US and British warships, found instead that "the Houthis have been indiscriminately targeting vessels navigating in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden." [cite:hz10_un_poe2024] Many shipping companies diverted around Africa, taking longer and costlier routes. [cite:hz10_crs_if12587]

By the count Reuters compiled in July 2025, the Houthis had targeted more than 100 merchant ships, sunk four, seized one and killed at least eight sailors. The Rubymar, struck in February 2024, sank on 2 March 2024, the first ship lost; three seafarers were killed on the True Confidence that March; the Tutor sank in June 2024 with one crew member never found; and in July 2025, after months of quiet, the Houthis sank the Magic Seas on 6 July and the Eternity C on 9 July, killing four of the Eternity C's crew and leaving eleven missing. [cite:hz10_olj_factbox] Counts differ by window and by method, which is why other tallies run higher or lower.

The American and British response

On 18 December 2023 Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin announced Operation Prosperity Guardian, a multinational naval mission "to jointly address security challenges in the southern Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden," naming Britain, Bahrain, Canada, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, the Seychelles and Spain as partners, though some contributed only staff officers. [cite:hz10_dn_opg] On 11–12 January 2024 the United States and Britain began striking Houthi targets in Yemen; President Biden called the strikes a response to the attacks on shipping and said he "will not hesitate" to order more. [cite:hz10_mm_biden2024] [cite:hz10_crs_if12587] The strikes continued through 2024 without stopping the attacks, which ran until December 2024 and paused in early 2025. [scene:hm12_ceasefires|The Gaza ceasefires] [cite:hz10_usni_crs2026]

Israel and the Houthis also fought each other directly. On 19 July 2024 a Houthi drone killed one person in central Tel Aviv near the US embassy; the next day Israel struck the port of Hodeidah, which an Israeli official called the main entry point for Iranian weapons. The Houthi-run health ministry reported 80 wounded. Defense Minister Yoav Gallant said the Houthis had attacked Israel more than 200 times. [cite:hz10_nbc_hodeidah2024]

Rough Rider and the Oman truce

The second Trump administration escalated. Operation Rough Rider began on 15 March 2025. US officials told NBC News it cost more than $1 billion by early May and used roughly 2,000 bombs and missiles, including at least 75 Tomahawks; the Houthis shot down seven US drones, and two US fighter jets were lost at sea. [cite:hz10_nbc_rrcost] The US military said it struck more than 800 targets. [cite:hz10_cfr_iranhouthis]

By the count of the monitoring group Airwars, the civilian toll was the heaviest of any American campaign in Yemen. On 17 April 2025 US strikes on the Ras Isa fuel terminal killed at least 74 people and injured 171, according to the Houthi-run health ministry, which Reuters could not verify; Central Command said the aim was "to degrade the economic source of power of the Houthis." [cite:hz10_gc_rasisa] On 28 April a US strike hit a migrant detention centre in Saada. Houthi authorities told Amnesty International that 61 of 117 detained migrants were killed and 56 injured; Amnesty found no evidence the site was a military objective and called for the strike to be investigated as a war crime. Central Command replied that it was "assessing all reports of civilian harm." [cite:hz10_ai_saada] Airwars documented at least 224 civilians allegedly killed by US strikes in the roughly seven weeks of Rough Rider, against 258 in all US actions in Yemen from November 2002 to January 2025. [cite:hz10_airwars_rr]

On 6 May 2025 President Trump said the Houthis had "capitulated" and the bombing would stop. Oman's foreign minister announced that "neither side will target the other," and the State Department said the deal covered US shipping, not the conflict between the Houthis and Israel. [cite:hz10_aje_truce] Israeli officials said they had no advance notice; Prime Minister Netanyahu said Israel "will defend itself by itself." [cite:hz10_wiki_truce2025] Neither the Congressional Research Service in July 2026 nor later monitoring reported a resumption of direct US–Houthi hostilities. [cite:hz10_usni_crs2026] [cite:hz10_ctp_sep26]

Israel's war with the Houthis, and the pause test

The Houthis said the US truce did not apply to Israel, and the exchange continued. [cite:hz10_aje_truce] On 24 August 2025 Israeli strikes on Sanaa killed 10 people, according to health officials; Israel said it hit military sites and the presidential palace. On 28 August a strike on Sanaa killed the Houthi prime minister, Ahmed al-Rahawi, and several ministers. Israel's military called the target "a Houthi terrorist regime military target," and Defense Minister Israel Katz reportedly said he sought to target the Houthi leadership as Israel had other groups' leaders. [cite:hz10_aje_rahawi]

The record allows one test of the Houthis' stated condition. They paused shipping attacks in early 2025, during the first Gaza ceasefire, and they suspended attacks on Israel after the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire. [cite:hz10_usni_crs2026] When the United States and Israel went to war with Iran on 28 February 2026, the Houthis held back for a month, then fired ballistic missiles at southern Israel on 28 March, saying they targeted only "the Israeli and American enemy." [cite:hz10_na_houthis2026] None of the roughly ten launches recorded between 28 March and 9 June caused reported injuries in Israel, and the attacks paused after the April ceasefire in the Iran war before brief launches in June. [cite:hz10_wiki_houthi2026] The pattern fits both the Houthis' Gaza condition and their alignment with Iran; it does not on its own show which drove the decision.

Their next war was with Saudi Arabia. After strikes on Sanaa airport that they blamed on Riyadh, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia on 20 July 2026, attacked Saudi tankers and energy sites, and forced Aramco to suspend its Jazan refinery; Saudi Arabia formed a Red Sea coalition with 13 other states. [cite:hz10_usni_crs2026] [cite:hz10_lwj_saudi2026] As of early October 2026 the 2022 truce has collapsed: Houthi and Saudi-backed government forces are fighting around Taiz and near the Bab al-Mandab, with 80 combatants reported killed in a single day; the Houthis say Saudi aircraft have carried out 1,350 strikes and a market raid near Taiz that killed or wounded nearly 50, figures not independently verified. [cite:hz10_ahram_taiz] [cite:hz10_dawn_taiz] The World Food Programme says nearly three-quarters of Yemenis cannot meet basic food needs. [cite:hz10_ahram_taiz] [scene:hz12_costs|Part Twelve counts the American costs.]

sections.h: The Iraqi Militias and the American Bases
sections.html:
Iraq's armed groups are the part of Iran's network that has most often fought the United States directly. Their history is bound up with the American occupation of Iraq: armed militias began to emerge after the US invasion of 2003 and grew stronger when they organised to fight the Islamic State. In 2014 the Popular Mobilisation Forces (al-Hashd al-Shaabi) were established as an umbrella for mainly Shia paramilitary units, and became the main such force confronting the group; after its territorial defeat they turned increasingly to American targets. [cite:hz10_at_farida] The groups describe themselves as muqawama, "resistance," against the United States and its allies. [cite:hz10_at_farida] Washington has designated three of them, Kata'ib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, as Foreign Terrorist Organizations; the Revolutionary Guards and their Quds Force are under US terrorism sanctions. [cite:hz10_crs_if12587]

The man who held the network together was Qasem Soleimani, an IRGC major general who rose in the Iran–Iraq war and commanded the Quds Force, the Guards' external arm, from 1998. [cite:hz10_rudaw_soleimani] His Iraqi counterpart was Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, deputy head of the Popular Mobilisation Forces. [cite:hz10_rudaw_soleimani] [cite:hz10_airwars_soleimani] The way both men died shows how a single exchange between the militias and the United States can climb to the top of two governments in about a week.

From a contractor's death to Soleimani's, December 2019 – January 2020

In late December 2019 a rocket attack on an Iraqi military base killed an American contractor; Defense Secretary Mark Esper dated it to 27 December, and the United States blamed Kata'ib Hezbollah. [cite:hz10_fox_pentagon2020] US airstrikes on 29 December killed 25 of the militia's fighters. Militia members and supporters then stormed the US embassy compound in Baghdad, breaching the reception area and setting parts of it on fire in a siege that ended on 1 January 2020; President Trump ordered about 750 more soldiers to the region. [cite:hz10_fox_pentagon2020] [cite:hz10_rudaw_soleimani] Shortly after midnight on 3 January, a US drone strike on a convoy leaving Baghdad airport killed Soleimani, al-Muhandis and others; Airwars records 11 to 13 combatants and possibly one civilian killed. [cite:hz10_airwars_soleimani]

The Pentagon called the strike "decisive defensive action," said Soleimani "was actively developing plans to attack American diplomats and service members in Iraq and throughout the region," and said it "was aimed at deterring future Iranian attack plans." [cite:hz10_fox_pentagon2020] [cite:hz10_rudaw_soleimani] Iran's supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, warned of "harsh retaliation." The New York Times reported that the strike was carried out without congressional approval, and it was unclear whether Iraq's government had been consulted. [cite:hz10_rudaw_soleimani] The strike was a United States operation.

The Gaza war and Tower 22

After 7 October 2023 the Iraqi groups, operating under the banner of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella that includes Kata'ib Hezbollah, launched more than 160 attacks on US forces in Iraq and Syria in under four months, by the count cited in early February 2024. [cite:hz10_at_farida] On 28 January 2024 a drone struck Tower 22, a small US base in north-eastern Jordan near the Syrian border, and killed three American soldiers, Sergeant William Jerome Rivers and Specialists Kennedy Ladon Sanders and Breonna Alexsondria Moffett; many more were wounded. President Biden blamed Iran-backed militia groups.
