[cite:hz10_abc_tower22] The United States named Kata'ib Hezbollah, which announced within days that it was "halting" its military operations, under pressure, it said, from Iran and the Iraqi government. [cite:hz10_at_farida] In the following week the United States struck targets in Iraq, Syria and Yemen; the White House described the message to Iran as a demand that it rein in its proxies. [cite:hz10_npr_roule]

Iran's stated position is that it did not order the attacks and that each faction acts on its own to oppose "aggression and occupation"; the head of the Revolutionary Guards said Tehran was "not looking for war." [cite:hz10_at_farida] Analysts read the same events differently. Norman Roule, the former CIA manager for Iran, told NPR that Iran controls the militias' weapons, money and key political relationships and so has enough leverage to shape their behaviour, while preferring "the product of militia actions" to day-to-day command; he ranked the Iraqi groups' closeness to Tehran as variable. [cite:hz10_npr_roule] Kata'ib Hezbollah's quick halt after Tower 22, which the group itself attributed partly to Iranian pressure, is evidence of leverage; the attacks before it are consistent both with Iranian direction and with the groups' own long campaign against the American presence. [cite:hz10_at_farida]

The network also coordinated across borders. In June 2024 the Houthi leader confirmed that his movement was coordinating military activities with the "so-called Islamic Resistance in Iraq," and the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported joint operations rooms in Iraq and Lebanon with Houthi representation. [cite:hz10_un_poe2024]

Status as of October 2026

The Iraqi groups' role in the 2026 war has been harder to pin down than the Houthis'. On 27 July 2026 drones hit Saudi Arabia's Abqaiq energy facility; the Houthis claimed the attack, while Riyadh blamed Iran-backed Iraqi militias. [cite:hz10_lwj_saudi2026] By late September 2026 the Critical Threats Project's daily Iran update reported "nothing significant" in Iraq. [cite:hz10_ctp_sep26] [scene:hz12_wars|Part Twelve sets out the American deployments these attacks targeted.]

sections.h: Syria: The Corridor, the Campaign and the Buffer Zone
sections.html:
Syria was never an armed group in Iran's network. It was a state ally, and for four decades it was the route by which Iranian weapons and equipment reached Hezbollah. When the civil war began in 2011, Iran spent billions of dollars to keep Bashar al-Assad in power, deployed thousands of military advisers and troops, and mobilised tens of thousands of foreign fighters, many from Afghanistan and Pakistan. [cite:hz10s_usip_iran] Hezbollah sent thousands of its own fighters, a story told in Part Six ([scene:hz6_syria|The War for Assad]). Iran's stated position throughout was that it had entered Syria "at the official invitation of the Syrian government" and would keep its advisers there as long as Damascus wished; its foreign ministry repeated this on 2 December 2024, six days before Assad fell. [cite:hz10s_rferl_advisers]

The campaign between the wars

Israel answered that presence with a long air campaign that, for years, it would neither confirm nor deny. The scale became public in January 2019, when two officials described it in the same weekend. At a cabinet meeting on 13 January, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said "the IDF has attacked hundreds of times Iranian and Hezbollah targets." [cite:hz10s_jc_netanyahu] The outgoing chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot, told the Sunday Times that Israel had begun striking Iranian infrastructure in Syria in January 2017, that about 2,000 bombs had been dropped on Iranian targets in 2018 alone, and that "we carried out thousands of attacks without taking responsibility and without asking for credit." [cite:hz10s_jc_netanyahu] [cite:hz10s_toi_eisenkot]

The figures differ because they count different things. The Times of Israel noted that accounts of the number of raids in his interviews ranged from 200 to 400. [cite:hz10s_toi_eisenkot] "Hundreds of strikes" and "thousands of bombs" are both supported by Israeli officials' own statements; "thousands of strikes" depends on how a single attack is counted. Israel's stated aim was to stop Iran entrenching in Syria: Eisenkot said Israeli intelligence had identified an Iranian plan to build a force of about 100,000 Shia fighters there by the end of 2018. That figure is an Israeli intelligence claim, not independently confirmed. [cite:hz10s_jc_netanyahu] Iran's position was that its forces were in Syria as guests of its government. [cite:hz10s_rferl_advisers]

Israel's own Syrian partners, 2013–2018

In the same interview Eisenkot made a second admission. He said Israel had given light weapons to rebel groups along the Golan frontier, "for self-defense." It was the first official acknowledgement; until then Israel had said only that it gave humanitarian aid. [cite:hz10s_toi_eisenkot]

The humanitarian programme was real and was announced. The IDF said that more than 4,900 Syrians wounded in the war, 1,300 of them children, had been treated in Israel since 2013, and about 7,000 people at a border clinic. It named the work Operation Good Neighbor in 2016, calling it "reaching out to needy civilians on the borders of the country," and closed it in September 2018 after Assad's forces retook southern Syria. [cite:hz10s_jta_goodneighbor]

In June 2017 the Wall Street Journal, citing about half a dozen Syrian fighters, reported that Israel had for years given rebels on the Golan cash, food, fuel and medical supplies, that the money paid salaries and bought ammunition and weapons, and that Israel had set up a unit to oversee it. The main partner was named as Fursan al-Joulan, the "Knights of the Golan," whose spokesman said, "We wouldn't have survived without Israel's assistance." The IDF neither confirmed nor denied the report. [cite:hz10s_jn_wsj] In September 2018 Foreign Policy, drawing on interviews with more than two dozen commanders and fighters, reported that Israel had armed and funded at least 12 groups in southern Syria from 2013 until July 2018, supplying assault rifles, machine guns, mortars and vehicles, money to buy arms, and about $75 a month per fighter, through the aid crossings. The Israeli embassy in Washington declined to comment. [cite:hz10s_fp_rebels] When the government offensive came in summer 2018, Israel did not intervene; one Fursan al-Joulan fighter told the magazine, "This is a lesson we will not forget about Israel." [cite:hz10s_fp_rebels]

Both accounts give the same purpose: to keep Iran-backed fighters and Islamic State militants away from the Israeli frontier. [cite:hz10s_fp_rebels] [cite:hz10s_jn_wsj] That is a documented case of Israel arming non-state groups across a border, the pattern Part Eleven examines ([scene:hz11_proxies|the proxy frame]).

After Assad, December 2024 to October 2026

Assad fell on 8 December 2024. The same day Netanyahu declared that the 1974 disengagement agreement with Syria "has collapsed, the Syrian soldiers have abandoned their positions," and said he had ordered the army to seize the UN-patrolled buffer zone "and the commanding positions nearby." [cite:hz10s_newarab_collapse] Israeli forces took the Syrian side of Mount Hermon. Over the next two days, the military said, it carried out about 480 strikes across Syria, hitting most of the country's strategic weapons stockpiles, and its navy struck two naval facilities where 15 vessels were docked. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said the aim was to keep weapons from falling "into the hands of extremists." [cite:hz10s_cnn_480] Israel told the Security Council it had "deployed temporarily in few points." [cite:hz10s_cnn_480] UNDOF, the UN force on the line, said Israel was in "violation of the 1974 disengagement agreement," and Secretary-General António Guterres said he was "deeply concerned by the recent and extensive violations of Syria's sovereignty," insisted the agreement "remains in force," and called for withdrawal. [cite:hz10s_almon_katz] [cite:hz10s_un_guterres]

"Temporary" soon changed. On 28 January 2025 Defence Minister Israel Katz said on the summit of Hermon that the army would stay there and in the security zone "for an indefinite period," adding, "We will not return to the reality of October 7." [cite:hz10s_ih_hermon] On 16 July 2025, during fighting between government forces and Druze militias in Sweida that a UK-based monitor said had killed about 260 people, Israel bombed the defence ministry in Damascus and an area near the presidential palace. Netanyahu said Israel was "acting to save our Druze brothers" and was committed to keeping southwestern Syria demilitarised. Syria's foreign ministry condemned the strikes "in the harshest terms"; its defence ministry blamed Druze militias for breaking a ceasefire. [cite:hz10s_npr_sweida]

In Paris on 6 January 2026 the two sides agreed to a US-supervised communication cell for de-escalation and intelligence sharing; the US statement spoke of "lasting security and stability arrangements," but nothing committed Israel to stop striking. [cite:hz10s_almon_paris] By late June, Katz was quoted as saying, "we will not withdraw from the security zone in Syria." [cite:hz10s_jpost_slim] Syria's foreign minister met an Israeli delegation in Jordan on 23 August 2026; Damascus said the priority was an Israeli return to the lines of 8 December 2024 and that the Golan's final status was not yet on the table. [cite:hz10s_eb_amman] On 23 September Syria's president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, said the talks had reached "almost 90%" agreement before Israel pulled back or added conditions; this is his account, and the report carried no Israeli response. [cite:hz10s_jpost_sharaa90] On 4 October Israel resumed work on Sufa 53, a fortified line of military road, five-metre berms and trenches inside the buffer zone in Quneitra, begun in 2022. Israel says it is meant to stop attacks by Iran-backed groups; Syria called it a "flagrant breach" of the 1974 agreement, and Jordan and Qatar condemned it. [cite:hz10s_eb_sufa] [cite:hz10s_aa_sufa] As of October 2026 there is no signed agreement, Israeli forces remain in the zone and on Hermon, and the US-mediated channel remains open.

Assad's fall cut Iran's land route to Hezbollah. Iran's president said on 8 December that it was for "the Syrian people" to decide their future; Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei blamed "a joint American-Zionist plot." [cite:hz10s_usip_iran] Iran's ally was gone; Israel's strikes and its forces in the south remained. Part Eleven tests whether that is a response to a threat or a standing posture.

Palestinian Islamic Jihad

Palestinian Islamic Jihad was founded in Gaza in 1981 by Fathi Shaqaqi and Abd al-Aziz Awda, former members of the Muslim Brotherhood who thought it too moderate; it rejects negotiation and seeks Israel's destruction by force. [cite:hz10s_aph_pij] The US designated it a Foreign Terrorist Organization on 8 October 1997 and says it "receives financial assistance and training primarily from Iran"; its record includes suicide bombings against Israeli civilians and rocket fire on southern Israel. [cite:hz10s_state_pij] Its relationship with Iran and its fighters' share of the dead in Gaza are covered in the Hamas volume ([scene:hm6_allies|Patrons, Not Masters]; [scene:hm11_scale|The Two Forces]).

chapters.label: Part Eleven
chapters.title: Always the Axis?
chapters.intro: Part Eleven tests the thesis that runs beneath this volume: that Hezbollah, the Houthis and the other groups aligned with Iran have served as the standing reason for wars that never end, for military aid that never stops and for drawing the United States in. It sets the warnings about Iran's bomb beside what intelligence agencies, Israel's included, assessed at the time; follows the threat into the laws that fund Israel's military; and asks whether each war in Lebanon ended the threat it was fought against. It then sets out the armed groups Israel itself paid or armed, in south Lebanon, southern Syria and Gaza, and what those cases do and do not show. Last, it names who gains from continued conflict, in money and in politics, and gives the case against the thesis in full: the groups' own attacks, Iran's own aims, and the ceasefires Israel accepted and the restraint Washington applied. Facts, patterns and arguments about motive are kept apart throughout.
chapters.outro: Part Eleven found the thesis partly supported and partly not. The specific warning of an Iranian bomb within about a year, given in 2012, was not borne out, and US agencies still assessed in 2025 that Iran was not building one, while the same agencies recorded a stockpile larger than ever. [cite:hz11_rferl_spycables] [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard] Each campaign in Lebanon was followed by another, from the invasion that saw Hezbollah founded to the truce of 2024 that ended in the war of 2026. [cite:hz4_wiki_taif] [cite:hz8_am_mar2] Israel itself paid and armed the South Lebanon Army and, by its chief of staff's acknowledgment, supplied Syrian rebel groups with light arms; in Gaza, Netanyahu confirmed that it had "activated" clans opposed to Hamas, which ACLED assesses it has armed, and none of them brought lasting security. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz11_toi_eisenkot] [cite:hz11_ynet_clans] [cite:hz11_acled_gaza] Continued conflict has documented beneficiaries, from Israel's record military budget and exports to American co-producers of its interceptors, but the record examined here shows no decision on war taken to secure them. [cite:hm_globes_sipri] [cite:hm_globes_exports] [cite:ow8_dn_coprod2016] Against the thesis stand Hezbollah's and the Houthis' own attacks, Iran's own record, the 2024 truce Netanyahu signed over a coalition partner's objection, and a United States that paused bombs in 2024 and left the Houthi war in 2025. [cite:hz7_aj_8oct] [cite:hz10_olj_factbox] [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] [cite:hz7_bg_ceasefire] [cite:ow8_axios_pause] [cite:hz10_aje_truce] Part Twelve turns to the United States: its dead, its costs and the decisions that drew it into these wars. [scene:hz12_costs|Dragging America in]

sections.h: The Thesis and the Test
sections.html:
The thesis this part tests is that Hezbollah, the Houthis and the other armed groups aligned with Iran serve as a standing reason for continuing wars, for continuing military aid to Israel and for drawing the United States into the region's wars. The Hamas volume ran the same test on its own subject, setting the claims made in Hamas's name against what the record later showed. [scene:hm11_claims|The Hamas Architecture: claims made in Hamas's name] The method here is the same. Three kinds of statement are kept apart: documented facts, which rest on a document, an order, a law or an official's own words; patterns, which can be shown by setting what was claimed beside what followed; and inferences about motive, which are arguments, are labelled as arguments, and are given with the case against them.

The Bomb That Was About a Year Away

The largest threat named in this story is Iran itself, the state whose Revolutionary Guards trained Hezbollah's first fighters and which funds and arms most of the groups in this volume. [cite:hz3_wiki_hezbollah] [cite:hz6_icg_crt2018] [cite:hz10_un_poe2024] In September 2012 Benjamin Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly, as the reports on the leak summarised his speech, that Iran was about one year from being able to build a nuclear weapon. A Mossad assessment dated the following month, shared with South Africa's intelligence service and published in the leaked "Spy Cables" by The Guardian and Al Jazeera in February 2015, said Iran "is not performing the activity necessary to produce weapons" and "does not appear to be ready to enrich" its uranium to higher levels. [cite:hz11_rferl_spycables] [cite:hz11_wiki_spycables] The two documents can be read in more than one way. The Times of Israel argued at the time that they were "hardly contradictory": the full Mossad passage described an Iran still closing gaps toward a weapon, and Netanyahu's deadline concerned enough enriched uranium for a bomb, not a finished bomb, so the disagreement was over speed rather than direction. [cite:hz11_toi_spycables]

The 2012 deadline was the latest of several. In 1992, as a member of the Knesset, Netanyahu is reported to have said Iran was three to five years from being able to produce a nuclear weapon and that the threat had to be "uprooted by an international front headed by the U.S."; the retrospectives that repeat the remark trace it to a newspaper timeline, and this book did not find the Knesset record itself. [cite:hz11b_week_1992] [cite:hz11b_intercept_wolf] [cite:hz11b_aje_rhetoric] His 1995 book Fighting Terrorism gave a similar short estimate, though accounts of its wording differ: one quotes it as placing Iran "between three and five years away from possessing the prerequisites required," another as "five to seven years at most." [cite:hz11b_mw_book] [cite:hz11b_week_1992] On 10 July 1996, as prime minister, he told a joint session of Congress that Iran was "the most dangerous" of the region's regimes, that its acquiring nuclear weapons "could presage catastrophic consequences," and that the deadline for stopping it was "getting extremely close." [cite:hz11b_jvl_1996] On 12 September 2002, out of office, he told a House committee that Saddam Hussein "is seeking and is working and is advancing toward the development of nuclear weapons," that Iraq and Iran were vying to be first to the bomb, and that removing Saddam "will have enormous positive reverberations on the region"; asked about Iran, he said, "I don't know that Iran has nuclear weapons." [cite:hz11b_gpo_2002] The Iraq Survey Group reported in October 2004 that Saddam had ended Iraq's nuclear programme after the 1991 Gulf War and held no stockpiles of banned weapons when the invasion began. [cite:hz11b_cnn_duelfer] A US embassy cable of February 2009, later published by WikiLeaks, recorded Netanyahu telling visiting members of Congress that Iran was "probably one or two years away." [cite:hz11b_intercept_wolf] [cite:hz11b_week_1992] At the UN on 27 September 2012 he asked for a "clear red line" before Iran finished the second stage of enrichment, which, by the UN's own summary of the speech, he said it could do by the following summer at the latest. [cite:hz11b_un_2012] None of those dates brought an Iranian bomb. Israel's stated case rested on two things the record does support: Iran's enrichment, which kept growing, and its concealment. On 30 April 2018 Netanyahu presented what he said were about 55,000 pages and 183 discs from Iran's secret "Project Amad" weapons programme, taken by Israeli intelligence from a Tehran warehouse, and said they proved Iran had lied. The documents appeared to date from the early 2000s, and he showed no direct evidence that Iran had broken the 2015 nuclear agreement; Iran, which denies ever seeking nuclear weapons, called the presentation a propaganda show, and its foreign minister called Netanyahu "the boy who can't stop crying wolf." [cite:hz11b_cbs_archive]

American intelligence assessments over the same years ran on a separate track. The National Intelligence Estimate of December 2007 judged "with high confidence" that Iran had halted its covert nuclear weapons programme in the autumn of 2003, and with moderate confidence that it had not restarted it by mid-2007; the White House, releasing the finding, said the risk of Iran acquiring a weapon "remains a very serious problem." [cite:hz11_wh_nie2007] [cite:hz11_npr_nie2007] A report compiled in November 2024 said Iran "is not building a nuclear weapon" but had "undertaken activities that better position it to produce one, if it so chooses." On 26 March 2025 the Director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, told the House Intelligence Committee that the intelligence community "continues to assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon" and that Ali Khamenei "has not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003." In the same testimony she said Iran's enriched-uranium stockpile was at its highest level, "unprecedented for a state without nuclear weapons," and the head of US Central Command told Congress that Iran could produce enough material for ten weapons in three weeks. [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard] [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] [cite:hz11_pbs_gabbard]

In June 2025, as Israel and Iran fought what became the twelve-day war, President Trump was asked about Gabbard's assessment and said, "I don't care what she said," adding that Iran was "very close" to a bomb; Netanyahu had described a nuclear-armed Iran as an imminent threat. Iran maintained that its programme was peaceful. [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] [cite:hz11_pbs_gabbard] The United States fired between 100 and 150 of its THAAD interceptors defending Israel in that war, about a quarter of its supply. [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025] On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel struck Iran together, and Trump said the aim was to remove imminent threats. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury]

The pattern the record shows has two halves. The specific claim, a weapon within about a year, was not borne out on its own timeline: more than twelve years after the UN speech, America's intelligence agencies still assessed that Iran was not building one. The broader claim, that Iran was building the capacity to make a weapon quickly if it chose to, was supported by the same agencies' own findings about its stockpile. Which of the two halves drove the decisions to go to war in 2025 and 2026 is a question of motive, and Part Twelve takes it up. [scene:hz12_wars|Dragging America in]

The Threat in the Budget

The threat posed by Iran and its allies is also written into the laws that fund Israel's military. In April 2024 Congress passed the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, which totalled $26.38 billion and provided, among other items, $3.5 billion in Foreign Military Financing, $4 billion for the Iron Dome and David's Sling missile-defence systems and $1.2 billion for the Iron Beam laser system; [cite:hz12b_hac_onepager] the House approved it 366 to 58 on 20 April, the Senate 79 to 18 three days later, and it became law on 24 April. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [cite:ow1_clerk_roll152] [cite:ow1_lobby_hr815] Brown University's Costs of War project counted at least $21.7 billion in US military aid to Israel in the two years after 7 October 2023, plus $9.65 billion to $12.07 billion spent on American operations in the region, including against the Houthis. [cite:hm_an_costsofwar] In February 2025 the administration used an emergency declaration to approve about $4 billion in arms sales to Israel without the usual congressional review period. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025]

The fire those sums answered was real, and it ran both ways. Between 7 October 2023 and 18 October 2024 the monitoring group ACLED counted 13,608 cross-border attacks between Israel and Lebanon: 2,370 by Hezbollah and allied groups, which killed at least 41 people in Israel, and 11,238 by Israel, which killed at least 2,318 people in Lebanon. [cite:hz7_aj_acled_year] The threat that the missile-defence money was voted to meet existed; it was also, by this count, less than a fifth of the cross-border fire.

Whether the Wars Ended the Threat

Israel's stated aim in its Lebanese campaigns was security for the north: in 1993 Rabin told the Knesset the goal was to "restore security to the lives of residents in communities of the north," and in September 2024 Yoav Gallant made the return of the north's displaced residents the task. [cite:hz4_jvl_rabin93] [cite:hz7_afp_gravity] Each campaign was followed, sooner or later, by the next. Hezbollah itself was founded during the 1982 invasion and the occupation that followed it, which Yitzhak Rabin, as defence minister, warned in February 1985 risked replacing PLO attacks with Shiite ones. [scene:hz2_founding|The founding] [cite:hz3_djn_rabin85] When the Taif Agreement of 1989 required Lebanon's militias to disarm, Hezbollah was allowed to keep its weapons as a "resistance force" against Israel's occupation of the south. [cite:hz4_wiki_taif] The 2006 war, set out in Part Five, did not end its arsenal; on 8 October 2023 it was able to open a front against Israel "in solidarity" with Gaza. [scene:hz5_war|The 2006 war] [cite:hz7_aj_8oct] In September 2024 Israel removed much of its chain of command in about ten days. [cite:hm_ns_hezbollah] Announcing the ceasefire that followed, President Biden said Hezbollah's infrastructure "will not be allowed to be rebuilt"; by October 2025 US Central Command said the Lebanese army had removed some 10,000 rockets and 400 missiles, and the Israeli army said it had killed more than 370 members of armed groups in the truce's first year. [cite:hz8_biden_dcpd] [cite:hz8_scr_nov25] [cite:hz8_idf_year] In January 2026 Netanyahu's office called the Lebanese army's progress "far from sufficient" and said "Hezbollah must be fully disarmed." [cite:hz8_cnn_phase1] On 2 March 2026, two days after Khamenei was killed, Hezbollah fired missiles and drones at Israel again; in the six weeks that followed, Israeli strikes killed 2,294 people in Lebanon by the health ministry's provisional count. [cite:hz8_am_mar2] [cite:hz8_olj_toll] Part Eight sets out where that war stood as of October 2026. [scene:hz8_war2026|The 2026 war]

The pattern is not that the threats were invented. Hezbollah's rockets fell on Israeli towns and Iran's stockpile grew. It is that the threat was repeatedly described as nearer, larger or closer to removal than the record later bore out, while each campaign launched to remove it was followed by another.

sections.h: Armed by Israel
sections.html:
Hezbollah, the Houthis and the Iraqi militias are commonly described as Iran's proxies: armed groups that a state pays, arms and uses to fight where it does not want to fight itself. Part Ten examined how far that description fits each group. [scene:hz10_houthis|The rest of the axis] The record also documents a second set of cases, in which Israel itself chose armed non-state groups as instruments, paid or armed them, and in some cases acknowledged it. Three are set out here. A fourth, Israel's licensing of the Islamist charity network in Gaza from which Hamas later grew, is in the Hamas volume. [scene:hm1_tolerated|The Hamas Architecture: licensed and left alone]

The South Lebanon Army, 1976–2000

The force that became the South Lebanon Army began in 1976 as a breakaway Lebanese army unit under Major Saad Haddad, which Israel backed with money and arms while its "Good Fence" policy opened the border to southern villagers for medical care and work; in April 1979 Haddad proclaimed a "State of Free Lebanon" from the Israeli border town of Metula, and the Lebanese government dismissed him as a traitor. [cite:hz1_olj_sla] [cite:hz1_wiki_freeleb] [cite:hz1_alhurra_fence] Haddad said in 1982 that Israel had contributed about $10 million to his men's salaries since 1978, at about $100 a month each, and supplied weapons and services. [cite:hz1_csm_haddad] After Israel's partial withdrawal in 1985 it formalised the arrangement. In the words of the US Congressional Research Service, Israel established the SLA as "an allied militia that it fully funded and equipped": 2,500 to 3,000 fighters, paid $500 to $800 a month according to media reports, at an estimated cost of $35 million a year, with obsolete tanks and artillery. Most of its commanders were Christian, but by the reported figures about half its members were not; Human Rights Watch reported involuntary conscription, including of children. [cite:hz4_crs_sla]

The SLA ran the Khiam detention centre inside the occupied zone. In a September 1999 affidavit to Israel's High Court, the defence ministry said Khiam was "under the responsibility" of the SLA and its staff were Lebanese, while acknowledging that Shin Bet personnel met SLA interrogators several times a year and gave them "professional guidance and training." Human Rights Watch held Israel, as occupying power, ultimately responsible for abuses there, including torture and detention without charge. [cite:hz4_hrw_khiam99] When Prime Minister Ehud Barak ordered the withdrawal on 23 May 2000, the SLA abandoned its posts rather than fight Hezbollah alone; Hezbollah and other groups captured its heavy weapons, and about 1,500 members fled to Israel with their families, some 6,400 to 7,000 people. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] Part Four tells that story in full. [scene:hz4_zone|The security zone]

Syrian rebels on the Golan, 2013–2018

In September 2018 Foreign Policy reported, from interviews with more than two dozen rebel commanders and fighters, that Israel had secretly armed and funded at least twelve rebel groups in southern Syria from 2013 until July 2018. Fighters were paid about $75 a month, and the groups received money to buy weapons on the black market; Israel supplied assault rifles, machine guns, mortar launchers and vehicles through three gates on the occupied Golan Heights. The early weapons were mostly American M16s; later ones included arms from an Iranian shipment to Hezbollah that Israel had seized in 2009. The stated purpose, as the fighters understood it, was to keep Iran-backed forces and the Islamic State away from Israel's border. Israel's embassy in Washington declined to comment. [cite:hz11_fp_rebels] In January 2019 the outgoing chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot, told the Sunday Times that Israel had supplied the rebels with light arms "for self-defense"; until then Israel had acknowledged only humanitarian aid. [cite:hz11_toi_eisenkot]

The programme ended when the Syrian government, backed by Russia, retook the south in the summer of 2018 and Israel did not intervene. "This is a lesson we will not forget about Israel," one fighter told the magazine. [cite:hz11_fp_rebels]

Gaza's militias, 2024–2026

In October 2024 an internal UN memo, obtained by The Washington Post, said armed gangs looting aid convoys in Gaza "may be benefitting from a passive if not active benevolence" or "protection" from the Israeli army, and that one gang leader had set up a "military-like compound" in an area "restricted, controlled and patrolled by the IDF." [cite:hz11_aj_unmemo] On 5 June 2025 the opposition politician Avigdor Lieberman, a former defence minister, disclosed that the government was arming clans in Gaza and said it was giving weapons to "a group of criminals and felons identified with Islamic State"; NPR could not substantiate the Islamic State claim. Israeli media identified one recipient as the gang of Yasser Abu Shabab, whom other Palestinians accused of looting UN convoys. [cite:hz11_npr_clans] Netanyahu responded the same day in a video statement, confirming the policy without saying what the clans had been given: "Liberman leaked that on security officials' advice, we activated clans in Gaza who oppose Hamas. What's wrong with that? It's only good. It only saves IDF soldiers' lives." He called the disclosure "a criminal leak." [cite:hz11_ynet_clans]

Abu Shabab's group, the Popular Forces, operated in eastern Rafah under Israeli control. He was killed on 4 December 2025 in a clash with members of a local family, the Abu Suneimas, who claimed responsibility; accounts of the shooting conflict, the group said he died trying to settle a family dispute and denied that Hamas was responsible, Hamas called him a "collaborator with the occupation," and his deputy, Ghassan Duhine, declared himself leader. [cite:hz11_na_abushabab] [cite:hz11_wiki_abushabab] By April 2026 ACLED counted at least five anti-Hamas armed groups operating from Israeli-held areas east of the "Yellow Line," involved in more than 40 violent events and nearly 80 deaths since the October 2025 ceasefire, including the abduction and killing of civilians accused of working with Hamas. ACLED assessed that Israel supplied them with weapons, logistics, intelligence and training and had used drones in their clashes; Israel has not detailed its support beyond Netanyahu's statement. Hamas cited that support when it rejected a full-disarmament proposal. ACLED judged that the groups posed no existential threat to Hamas on their own. [cite:hz11_acled_gaza]

What These Cases Show, and What They Do Not

They show, first, that the practice Israel's leaders describe in Iran is one Israel has used itself. A state paying an armed group's salaries, supplying its weapons and relying on it to fight where its own soldiers would otherwise go is how Hezbollah's patron is documented to operate: Hassan Nasrallah said in 2016 that Hezbollah's budget, "its weapons and rockets, come from the Islamic Republic of Iran," and the US State Department estimated that support at about $700 million a year. [cite:hz6_alarabiya_2016] [cite:hz6_icg_crt2018] Israel did this in south Lebanon for a quarter of a century, as its own records and the CRS show; in southern Syria for five years, by its chief of staff's acknowledgment and Foreign Policy's reporting; and in Gaza from at least 2025, by Netanyahu's statement and ACLED's assessment. The difference in scale is large: Iran's support for Hezbollah alone was estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars a year, while Israel's payments to the SLA, its largest client, were estimated at about $35 million. The mechanism is the same one. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz11_toi_eisenkot] [cite:hz11_ynet_clans]

They show, second, a recurring outcome. None of the three created lasting security. The SLA collapsed as Israel withdrew and its heavy weapons passed to Hezbollah and other groups; the Syrian groups were left to the Syrian government and its allies when Israel did not intervene; the Gaza groups, by ACLED's assessment, could not displace Hamas. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz11_fp_rebels] [cite:hz11_acled_gaza] The occupation the SLA helped hold is at the centre of the argument over why Hezbollah exists, which Part Three sets out. [scene:hz3_question|Would Hezbollah exist?]

They do not show that Israel created, armed or funded Hezbollah, the Houthis or the Iraqi militias. The public record examined contains no such case. Nor do they show, on their own, that these programmes were designed to keep wars going. In each case the stated reason was immediate and military: to hold a border zone, to keep hostile forces back, to spare soldiers. That the instruments failed and the wars continued is a documented pattern; that the failure was the purpose would be an inference about motive, and the record does not supply it.

sections.h: Who Gains: the Money
sections.html:
Continued conflict with Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iran has been accompanied by record sums moving through documented channels. Israel's military spending rose 65 percent in 2024 to $46.5 billion, 8.8 percent of its economy, by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute's count. [cite:hm_globes_sipri] Its defence exports reached a record $14.795 billion the same year, up 11.7 percent; 54 percent went to Europe, and air-defence systems made up about 48 percent. [cite:hm_globes_exports] The European share, in the years of Russia's war in Ukraine, is a reminder that demand for Israeli weapons does not come only from Israel's own wars; how much of the record the fighting with Hezbollah and Iran produced is not something the export figures can settle.

On the American side, much of the money returns home. Under the 2016 memorandum of understanding, Israel's permission to spend part of its US military financing on Israeli industry is being phased out, so the aid is spent in the United States. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] Since 2016, US production funding for the David's Sling and Arrow 3 missile-defence systems has been split with American partners, Raytheon and Boeing respectively. [cite:ow8_dn_coprod2016] On 9 October 2026 a Raytheon–Rafael joint venture delivered the first Tamir interceptors, the missile Iron Dome fires, built at a plant in Camden, Arkansas. [cite:ow8_rtx_camden] By April 2025 Israel had 751 active US arms-sale cases worth $39.2 billion. [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] And the defence of Israel draws on American stocks directly: in the June 2025 war with Iran the United States fired 100 to 150 THAAD interceptors, about a quarter of its supply. [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025]

The money record establishes who receives. It does not establish that anyone prolonged a war in order to receive it. The public record examined contains no document, testimony or court finding showing a decision on war or ceasefire in Lebanon, Yemen or Iran taken to secure aid, contracts or exports. That beneficiaries exist is documented; that they caused the wars is a separate claim, and on the evidence here it is unsupported. Part Twelve sets out the American side of the ledger. [scene:hz12_costs|What it cost America]

Who Gains: the Politics

The political argument centres on Netanyahu. His documented incentives are set out in the Hamas volume: a corruption trial running since 2020, from which he asked President Isaac Herzog for a pardon in November 2025 and sought further delays in April 2026; no state commission of inquiry into 7 October three years on; and a New York Times investigation, based on more than 110 officials, reporting that he shelved a Gaza truce under coalition threat, which his office said "defames Israel." [cite:hm_npr_pardon] [cite:hm_toi_trialdelay] [cite:gz_ynet_inquiry2026] [cite:hm_toi_nyt_prolonged] [scene:hm11_incentives|The Hamas Architecture: why the war lasted] Whether the same incentives operated on the Lebanese front is a separate question.

On the Lebanese front, the record cuts both ways. In November 2024 Netanyahu accepted a ceasefire with Hezbollah that his own national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, called "a historic mistake"; the security cabinet approved it ten to one. Netanyahu gave three reasons: to focus on Iran, to give the army a rest and replenish its stocks, and to separate the fronts and isolate Hamas. [cite:hz7_bg_ceasefire] [cite:hz8_jvl_netanyahu] A leader keeping war going for its own sake would not obviously have signed that truce over a coalition partner's objection. A leader choosing which war to fight next, and when, might have. Both readings fit the document; neither is proved by it.

The Case Against the Thesis

The groups' own acts. Hezbollah opened the 2023 front itself, on 8 October, "in solidarity with the victorious Palestinian resistance," and tied its fire to Gaza: "If there is a cease-fire in Gaza, we will stop," Naim Qassem told AP. [cite:hz7_aj_8oct] [cite:hz7_ml_qassem] On 27 July 2024 a rocket killed twelve Druze children and teenagers on a football pitch in Majdal Shams; Israel and the United States attributed it to Hezbollah, Human Rights Watch found the damage consistent with a Hezbollah Falaq-type rocket, and Hezbollah denied any connection. [cite:hz7_wiki_majdal] [cite:hz7_aj_majdal] About 60,000 residents of northern Israel were displaced. [cite:hz7_afp_north_return] On 2 March 2026 Hezbollah again fired first, after Khamenei's killing. [cite:hz8_am_mar2] In 1995 Qassem had stated the rule plainly: "whenever the Israeli enemy shells and harms civilians in our villages, we will shell northern Palestine." [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] By a Reuters count of July 2025, the Houthis had targeted more than 100 merchant ships since November 2023, sunk four and killed at least eight sailors; a UN panel found them "indiscriminately targeting vessels." [cite:hz10_olj_factbox] [cite:hz10_un_poe2024]

Iran's own aims. Khomeini declared in March 1980, "We should try hard to export our revolution to the world," naming America and Israel. [cite:hz1_merip_khomeini] An Argentine appeals court ruled in April 2024 that Iran ordered the 1992 and 1994 bombings in Buenos Aires and that Hezbollah carried them out; Iran denies involvement. [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] Analysts who study the network describe a patron that "seeks the product of militia actions, not the process of controlling them," and allies such as the Houthis that are more than mere proxies. [cite:hz10_npr_roule] [cite:hz10_conv_proxies] These are aims and acts of the groups and their patron, not inventions of their enemies.

Restraint and ceasefires. Israel accepted the April Understanding of 1996, which committed both sides not to target civilians; withdrew from Lebanon in May 2000; and accepted the November 2024 truce. [cite:hz4_jvl_april] [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hz7_bg_ceasefire] The United States paused a shipment of 2,000-pound bombs in May 2024 over a planned assault on Rafah, a hold President Trump lifted in January 2025. [cite:ow8_axios_pause] And in May 2025 the United States agreed a truce with the Houthis that did not cover their conflict with Israel; Netanyahu said Israel "will defend itself by itself." [cite:hz10_aje_truce] [cite:hz10_wiki_truce2025] In that instance Washington stepped out of a war with an "axis" group while Israel's continued, which is the opposite of being drawn in.

Two Readings

The first reading: the axis is the standing justification. On this reading, the threat from Hezbollah and Iran was repeatedly described as nearer or more nearly removed than the record bore out, each campaign renewed the enemy it was meant to end, Israel itself armed proxies when it suited, and the result was record budgets, record exports, tens of billions in American aid and a prime minister whose trial waited while the wars went on. [cite:hz11_rferl_spycables] [cite:hz11_bg_gabbard] [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:hm_globes_sipri] [cite:hm_an_costsofwar] [cite:hm_toi_trialdelay]

The second reading: the axis is the reason. On this reading, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iran chose to attack, killed civilians, stated their aims openly and were funded by a state that ordered bombings abroad; Israel accepted truces, the United States restrained it and broke from it, and the money followed the threat rather than creating it. [cite:hz7_aj_8oct] [cite:hz7_wiki_majdal] [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] [cite:hz7_bg_ceasefire] [cite:ow8_axios_pause] [cite:hz10_aje_truce]

What survives the test is narrower than the thesis and harder to dismiss. The threats were real, and the groups chose their own wars. The record also shows threats described as closer than they proved, campaigns that renewed the enemy they targeted, an Israeli practice of arming proxies of its own, and documented beneficiaries of every round. Whether those beneficiaries steer the wars, rather than profit from them, is the part of the thesis the evidence does not reach.

chapters.label: Part Twelve
chapters.title: Dragging America In
chapters.intro: Part Twelve turns from the region to the United States. The thesis this volume tests holds that the groups in this book serve, among other things, as the reason the United States is drawn into Israel's wars. This part counts what that involvement has cost Americans, in lives and in money, from the bombing of the Marine barracks in Beirut in 1983 to the war with Iran that began on 28 February 2026, and separates the deaths these groups caused from the costs the United States took on by choosing to fight, deploy and defend. It then follows the two wars with Iran of 2025 and 2026: who argued for them, who decided, what the administration said they were for, what its critics said, how Congress voted, and what the public thought.
chapters.outro: Part Twelve established the American bill. Groups in this book killed Americans directly: 17 at the Beirut embassy in an attack claimed by Islamic Jihad, and 241 servicemen at the Marine barracks in 1983, which a US court found Hezbollah carried out with Iranian support and which Hezbollah and Iran deny; a CIA station chief and a Navy diver in 1984–85, in cases the United States ties to men linked to Hezbollah and which Hezbollah denies; and three soldiers at Tower 22 in 2024, an attack Washington blamed on Kata'ib Hezbollah. [cite:hz12_cia_embassy] [cite:hz12_dcd_anderson] [cite:hz12_wiki_barracks] [cite:hz12_wiki_buckley] [cite:hz12_nbc_twa847] [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] Most of the money, though, followed decisions taken in Washington: $9.65 billion to $12.07 billion for regional operations and $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel in the two years after October 2023, then $43.6 billion for a war with Iran that the United States launched with Israel on 28 February 2026 and that had cost 21 American lives by October. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] [cite:hm_cow_hartung] [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] Netanyahu argued for striking Iran for years and, by reporting this book could not independently confirm, lobbied for the 2026 strike; the order was Trump's, on grounds the IAEA's findings and most voters did not support, and Congress neither authorized the war nor stopped it: the war-powers resolution it passed in June was never sent to the President and the White House said it had no force of law, and the House rejected, by 104 to 314, an amendment to cut Israel's military financing. [cite:hz12_cato_hoffman] [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar] [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [cite:hz12_qu_mar2026] [cite:hz12_clerk_hcr86] [cite:hz12b_cnn_senate] [cite:hz12a_cbs_massie] Part Thirteen sets out what across this volume is settled, what is contested and what remains open. [scene:hz13_record|Settled, contested and open]

sections.h: The American Bill, 1983–2026
sections.html:
The United States has paid for the wars in this book in two different ways, and they need to be kept apart. Some Americans were killed by the groups themselves: by the bombers of Beirut in 1983, by hijackers and kidnappers in Lebanon in the 1980s, and by an Iraqi militia's drone in 2024. Other costs came from decisions taken in Washington: to send warships, to shoot down missiles aimed at Israel, to bomb Yemen, to pay for Israel's air defences. This section sets out both, with the stated reasons of each government and group beside them.

Beirut, 1983–1985

American troops were in Beirut because of the Israeli invasion of 1982. A Multinational Force of American, French and Italian troops arrived on 24 August 1982 to oversee the PLO's evacuation; the Marines left on 10 September and were sent back on 29 September, after the massacre at Sabra and Shatila. [cite:hz2_an_1983] [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] Part Two follows how the force came to be seen as a party to Lebanon's war. [scene:hz2_1983|The founding years]

On 18 April 1983 a suicide truck bomb destroyed the American embassy in West Beirut, killing 63 people, 17 of them Americans and 8 of those CIA officers. The Islamic Jihad Organization, which the CIA says later became part of Hezbollah, claimed it. [cite:hz12_cia_embassy] On 23 October 1983 a second truck bomb destroyed the Marine barracks at Beirut airport, killing 241 American servicemen; a near-simultaneous attack on the French contingent killed 58 French soldiers. [cite:hz12_wiki_barracks]

Responsibility was settled in American courts, not by any admission. In Peterson v. Islamic Republic of Iran (30 May 2003), Judge Royce Lamberth found that Hezbollah carried out the barracks attack, that it had been "formed under the auspices of the government of Iran", and that "it is beyond question that Hezbollah and its agents received massive material and technical support from the Iranian government." In a 2010 judgment in a related suit, the same court found that Iran and its intelligence ministry "played crucial and necessary roles in planning and ordering" the bombing. [cite:hz12_dcd_anderson] Iran was served but did not answer the families' suit, and the court entered damages of about $2.66 billion in 2007; in 2016 the Supreme Court allowed frozen Iranian central-bank assets to be used to pay. Hezbollah officially denied any involvement, and Hezbollah, Iran and Syria have continued to deny it. [cite:hz12_wiki_barracks] President Reagan ordered the Marines to begin withdrawing on 7 February 1984; the last left Beirut airport on 26 February. [cite:hz12_wiki_barracks]

The kidnappings followed. William Buckley, the CIA's Beirut station chief, was seized on 16 March 1984; Islamic Jihad announced on 4 October 1985 that it had executed him, while the National Security Council concluded he had probably died in captivity on 3 June 1985. His remains were found beside a road near Beirut airport in December 1991. [cite:hz12_wiki_buckley] On 14 June 1985 TWA Flight 847, flying from Athens to Rome, was hijacked; the next day the hijackers killed Robert Stethem, a 23-year-old US Navy diver, and threw his body onto the tarmac in Beirut. The United States indicted Imad Mughniyeh, Hassan Izz-al-Din and Ali Atwa, men it linked to Hezbollah, and offered $5 million for information on them; Hezbollah denied any link. [cite:hz12_nbc_twa847] The effort to free the hostages held in Lebanon fed directly into the Reagan administration's secret arms sales to Iran. [cite:hz12_wiki_buckley]

Iraq, Jordan and the Red Sea, 2023–2025

After 7 October 2023 the United States sent the USS Gerald R. Ford carrier strike group to the eastern Mediterranean, saying the aim was to deter a wider war. [cite:ow7_ap_ford2023] Iran-aligned militias in Iraq and Syria then attacked American bases repeatedly: Military Times, tracking incidents announced by Central Command, counted at least 217 involving US forces between October 2023 and the autumn of 2024. [cite:hz12_cow_2024] On 28 January 2024 a drone struck Tower 22, a small US outpost in north-eastern Jordan, killing Sergeant William Jerome Rivers, Specialist Kennedy Ladon Sanders and Specialist Breonna Alexsondria Moffett; President Biden blamed Iran-backed militia groups. [cite:hz10_abc_tower22] Washington named Kata'ib Hezbollah, part of the umbrella calling itself the Islamic Resistance in Iraq; Kata'ib Hezbollah said it was halting its operations, and Iran denied ordering the attacks and said the factions acted on their own. [cite:hz10_at_farida] Part Ten sets out the Iraqi militias' history. [scene:hz10_iraq|The Iraqi militias]

The same month two American service members were lost at sea during an operation that seized Iranian-made missiles from a vessel bound for Yemen. [cite:hz12_cow_2024] In the Red Sea, Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin announced Operation Prosperity Guardian on 18 December 2023, and American and British aircraft began striking Houthi targets on 12 January 2024; Biden said he would "not hesitate" to order further measures. [cite:hz10_dn_opg] [cite:hz10_mm_biden2024] By June 2024 the Navy had fired about $1 billion of munitions there. [cite:hz12_cow_2024] Operation Rough Rider, the Trump administration's campaign from 15 March 2025, cost more than $1 billion in its first weeks by NBC's reporting, used about 2,000 bombs and missiles and lost two fighter jets at sea; it ended on 6 May 2025 in an Omani-brokered deal under which the Houthis stopped attacking American ships, a deal the State Department said did not cover Israel. [cite:hz10_nbc_rrcost] [cite:hz10_aje_truce] The Houthis' stated position throughout was that their attacks supported Gaza. [cite:hz10_aje_truce] The campaign itself is told in Part Ten. [scene:hz10_redsea|The Red Sea war]

Defending Israel

From April 2024 the costs changed in kind. When Iran fired more than 300 drones and missiles at Israel on 13–14 April 2024, American ships and aircraft destroyed more than 80 drones and at least six ballistic missiles; on 1 October 2024 two American destroyers fired about a dozen interceptors; on 13 October the United States sent a THAAD battery, which needs about 95 soldiers, to Israel. [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] [cite:ow7_usni_oct2024] [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024] [cite:ow7_ap_thaad2024] In the twelve-day war of June 2025 American batteries fired between 100 and 150 THAAD interceptors, roughly a quarter of the stock; the Costs of War project, counting about 150, valued them at $1.8 billion to $1.95 billion. [cite:ow7_cnn_thaad2025] [cite:hz12_cow_2025] The One-Way Mirror sets these operations out in full. [scene:ow7_iran|Defending Israel, fighting Iran] The Pentagon's stated purpose each time was to protect Israel and American personnel from Iranian attack. [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] [cite:ow7_dod_thaad2024]

The money

Congress paid for much of this in the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act (H.R. 8034), which the House passed 366–58 on 20 April 2024 and the Senate 79–18 on 23 April; it became law on 24 April as Public Law 118-50. [cite:ow1_clerk_roll152] [cite:ow1_lobby_hr815] By the House Appropriations Committee's own summary the act totalled $26.38 billion, "to support Israel in its effort to defend itself against Iran and its proxies"; that sum also included more than $9 billion in humanitarian aid, much of it for Gaza. [cite:hz12b_hac_onepager] [cite:hz12b_fox_apr2024] The Costs of War project at Brown University counted $14.1 billion in it for Israel's military, including $4 billion for Iron Dome and David's Sling, $1.2 billion for the Iron Beam laser, $3.5 billion in Foreign Military Financing, $1 billion for artillery and other critical munitions and $4.4 billion to replenish American stocks sent to Israel, and a further $2.4 billion for American operations, force protection and deterrence in Central Command's region; the committee's summary gives the same figures. [cite:hz12_cow_2024] [cite:hz12b_hac_onepager] Its later accounting put the cost of American military operations in the wider Middle East from October 2023 to September 2025 at $9.65 billion to $12.07 billion, excluding aid to Israel, and at $31.35 billion to $33.77 billion including the $21.7 billion of military aid. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] [cite:hm_cow_hartung] In 2025 Central Command's region took 41 per cent of the Navy's carrier steaming days, against 8 per cent the year before. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] The war with Iran that began in 2026, described in the next section, cost a further $43.6 billion by 3 September 2026 on Central Command's estimate. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026]

What the record shows

The two kinds of cost point in different directions for the thesis. The deaths of 1983–85 and of Tower 22 were caused by the groups themselves, and the court findings and the record of claims and denials are as set out above; they are the strongest evidence that these groups have been a real danger to Americans, not only a pretext. But they also came where American forces had been placed inside a war: in Beirut after the 1982 invasion, and in Iraq, Syria and Jordan during the Gaza war, when the militias said they were acting over Gaza. [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks] [cite:hz10_at_farida] The larger costs, the interceptors, the carriers, the supplementals, were choices made in Washington for reasons Washington stated: deterrence, freedom of navigation, the defence of an ally and of American troops. [cite:ow7_ap_ford2023] [cite:hz10_mm_biden2024] [cite:ow7_dod_apr2024] Whether those reasons were sufficient, or whether the groups' existence was what made the choices easy to justify, is the argument Part Eleven set out; this book's finding is the bill itself: most of the American deaths before 2026 were caused by attack, but most of the money was spent by decision. [scene:hz11_gains|Who gains]

sections.h: Two Wars With Iran, 2025–2026
sections.html:
Twice in eight months the United States went from defending Israel against Iran to attacking Iran itself. This section separates three things the public argument often runs together: advocacy, meaning who argued for war and for how long; decision, meaning who ordered it and on what stated grounds; and consent, meaning what Congress and the public did. It gives the administration's stated reasons beside its critics' analysis and does not resolve the motive question, which the documents do not settle. The 2026 war was not formally over when this was written, so its figures are given as of October 2026.

The advocacy

The case for striking Iran had a long Israeli advocate. A Cato Institute analysis of April 2024 traced Benjamin Netanyahu's record: testimony to Congress in 2002 backing the overthrow of Saddam Hussein; a request, by his own account in his memoir, that President Obama strike Iran's nuclear sites in 2013, which Obama declined; and his 2015 address to Congress against the nuclear agreement. The author, Jon Hoffman, also noted Ehud Olmert's request in 2008 for American approval to bomb Iran, which President Bush refused, and argued that Netanyahu had domestic political reasons to widen the conflict. [cite:hz12_cato_hoffman] That record shows advocacy. It does not by itself show that Israel caused an American decision; each refusal in it was an American choice too.

American intelligence did not support the claim that a bomb was near, though it did record a growing stockpile. In March 2025 the Director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, told Congress the intelligence community "continues to assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon," while calling Iran's enriched-uranium stockpile "unprecedented for a state without nuclear weapons"; in June 2025 President Trump said "I don't care what she said" and that Iran was "very close" to a bomb. Iran says its programme is peaceful. [cite:hz11_ap_gabbard] [cite:hz11_pbs_gabbard] Part Eleven sets out this record of warnings against assessments. [scene:hz11_pattern|The pattern of threat claims]

June 2025

Israel began striking Iran on 13 June 2025 in what it called Operation Rising Lion. On 21 June, Washington time, the United States joined with Operation Midnight Hammer, striking the enrichment plants at Fordow and Natanz and the nuclear technology centre at Isfahan with B-2 bombers carrying 14 GBU-57 bunker-busting bombs and with 24 Tomahawk missiles. Iran answered by firing at the American base at Al Udeid in Qatar, after notifying the United States in advance; American Patriot batteries fired at least 14 interceptors and no Americans were reported killed. The Costs of War project put the American cost of the June war at $2.04 billion to $2.25 billion. [cite:hz12_cow_2025] Congress was not asked to authorize the strikes. On 27 June the Senate rejected, 47–53, a motion to bring up Senator Tim Kaine's resolution directing the removal of American forces from hostilities against Iran not authorized by Congress; the administration had told Congress the strikes were "limited in scope and purpose." [cite:hz12_sen_sjr59] [cite:hz12b_ap_jun2025]

The decision of February 2026

On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel opened a joint campaign against Iran, which killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in its first strikes. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar] Reuters reported on 24 March, citing three people briefed on the call who spoke anonymously, that Netanyahu telephoned Trump less than 48 hours before the strikes, after Israeli intelligence showed Khamenei and his senior aides would meet at his Tehran compound, and argued that there might never be a better chance to kill him. By then, Reuters said, Trump had already approved the idea of an operation but not its timing; its sources believed the call and the closing window of intelligence helped prompt his order of 27 February, though Reuters could not determine how much the argument weighed. The White House did not address the call, and Trump has said the decision was his alone. [cite:hz12b_reuters_call] Netanyahu, asked on 19 March about claims that Israel had dragged the United States into the war, called them "fake news" and said, "Does anyone really think that someone can tell President Trump what to do?" [cite:hz12b_mediaite_bibi] The order itself was Trump's, given on his own authority, while nuclear talks with Iran were still under way. [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar]

The stated reasons were these. Trump said the aim was to defend Americans by eliminating "imminent threats from the Iranian regime", claimed Iran was rebuilding its nuclear programme, and told Iranians, "When we are finished, take over your government." Netanyahu said the aim was to "remove the existential threat posed by the terrorist regime in Iran." [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] Trump's statement that day also cited Iran's support for Hamas and Hezbollah, its killing of protesters and its record of attacks on Americans back to the 1979 hostage crisis. [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar] The British government's research service summarized the American position as self-defence, with stated aims of regime change and the destruction of Iran's nuclear and missile programmes. [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026]

The critics' analysis rested on the record. The International Atomic Energy Agency had said it had no evidence that Iran had resumed enriching uranium, which undercut the claim of a rebuilt programme. [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] In the week after the strikes 55 per cent of registered voters told Quinnipiac that Iran had not posed an imminent military threat. [cite:hz12_qu_mar2026] Whether Netanyahu's advocacy was decisive, or whether a president who had called Iran "very close" to a bomb nine months earlier needed no persuading, is a question about motive; the documents show both men wanted the war, and that only one of them could order American forces into it.

The war, Hormuz and the cost

Iran answered with missiles and drones against Israel, American bases and Gulf states, and said it would shut the Strait of Hormuz. [cite:ow7_wiki_ceasefire2026] [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar] Shipping through the strait came almost to a standstill; by April "almost all shipping has ceased", the House of Commons Library reported, and the 32 members of the International Energy Agency released 400 million barrels from their reserves to hold prices down. On 13 April the United States imposed its own blockade on ships bound for Iranian ports. [cite:hz12_hcl_iran2026] American gasoline averaged just over $4 a gallon by late July, against about $3 before the war. [cite:hz12_almon_ipsos] A Pakistani-mediated ceasefire began on 7–8 April, was extended, and led to the Islamabad Memorandum signed on 17 June; it collapsed on 8 July. [cite:ow7_wiki_ceasefire2026] The war's effects in Lebanon are told in Part Eight. [scene:hz8_war2026|The 2026 war in Lebanon]

The American dead came early and kept coming. By AP's count in July, six soldiers were killed by an Iranian drone at a civilian port in Kuwait soon after 28 February, one died of wounds from an attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, six died when a KC-135 tanker crashed in Iraq in March, a Navy pilot died in a helicopter crash on 1 July, and two were killed in Jordan on 18 July defending against Iranian missiles and drones. [cite:hz12_ktar_deaths] Counts rose over time and differ by method. AP's report of mid-September cited 18 dead and more than 830 wounded; The Intercept, reading the official figures at the end of September, counted at least 19 dead, 11 of them killed by hostile fire. By 9 October, The Washington Post reported, the Pentagon's casualty database listed 21 deaths in operations against Iran and 865 wounded, or 22 dead in the region since 28 February counting a training accident recorded under another operation. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] [cite:hz12_intercept_cas] [cite:ow7_inq_deaths2026] The administration declared Operation Epic Fury concluded on 7 July, but by The Intercept's reading of the official figures 444 of the dead and wounded were added after that date, about 100 of them in September; it called the count an undercount, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called a Washington Post report of suppressed numbers "DISGUSTING and FAKE." [cite:hz12_intercept_cas] Central Command estimated the cost at $43.6 billion as of 3 September, and the Congressional Budget Office put it at $38 billion through 1 August, rising by about $3 billion a month. [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026]

Congress

Congress neither declared war nor authorized it. On 3 June 2026 the House adopted, 215–208, a concurrent resolution under the War Powers Resolution directing the President to remove American forces from hostilities with Iran, with four Republicans voting for it; the Senate agreed, 50–48, on 23 June. In the House the four Republicans were Brian Fitzpatrick, Tom Barrett, Warren Davidson and Thomas Massie, and Trump called it "a meaningless vote"; in the Senate Republicans Bill Cassidy, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul voted in favour, the Democrat John Fetterman against, and two Republicans who had opposed earlier measures, Mitch McConnell and Dave McCormick, did not vote. [cite:hz12_clerk_hcr86] [cite:hz12b_npr_house] [cite:hz12_sen_hcr86] [cite:hz12b_sen_daily] [cite:hz12b_cnn_senate] Because it was a concurrent resolution, it was never sent to the President, so there was nothing to sign or veto. A White House official said concurrent resolutions "have no force of law" and that there were no hostilities to end, since they had "terminated with the ceasefire on April 7th"; a House Democratic aide argued the measure was binding. Trump called the Senate vote "poorly timed and meaningless." [cite:hz12b_cnn_senate] Nothing followed in law. The fighting resumed after the ceasefire collapsed on 8 July, and on 24 September the Senate failed, 49–50, to adopt another Iran war-powers resolution; by ABC News's count it was the Senate's fourteenth vote on the matter that year, and June's was the only one to pass. [cite:ow7_wiki_ceasefire2026] [cite:hz12b_abc_sep]

On 15 July the House voted on an amendment by Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, to bar funding for Israel in the 2027 State Department and national security appropriations bill, which would have removed about $3.3 billion a year in military financing. It failed, 104 to 314, with 10 voting present: 103 Democrats and Massie, the only Republican, voted for it. Some reports gave the yes total as 103, leaving out Massie's own vote. [cite:hz12a_cbs_massie] [cite:hz12a_fmep_massie] The Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, called the amendment "overly broad"; Nancy Pelosi and Katherine Clark voted for it while saying they still supported the relationship with Israel. [cite:hz12_na_massie] Massie had already lost his Republican primary on 19 May to a Trump-endorsed challenger in the most expensive House primary on record, in which pro-Israel PACs spent about $8 million against him; AIPAC congratulated the winner on "defeating anti-Israel incumbent Thomas Massie", and Massie said a "foreign lobby has fully funded" the effort. AP judged Trump's endorsement the key factor. [cite:lpm_massie_gallrein_funding] [cite:mee_massie_aipac] [cite:pbs_massie_takeaways]

The public

The war began unpopular and stayed so. Quinnipiac's poll of 6–8 March found 53 per cent of registered voters opposed and 40 per cent in favour, with 85 per cent of Republicans in favour and 89 per cent of Democrats and 60 per cent of independents opposed; 74 per cent opposed sending ground troops. [cite:hz12_qu_mar2026] A Fox News poll at the same time found voters split evenly, and about six in ten said Iran posed a real national security threat. [cite:hz12_pbs_polls] By late July Reuters/Ipsos found about one in three Americans supporting the war, and 69 per cent, including four in ten Republicans, saying Trump had not clearly explained its goals. [cite:hz12_almon_ipsos] Pew Research Center, surveying 3,524 adults on 16–22 March, found 59 per cent saying the United States had made the wrong decision in using force against Iran and 38 per cent the right one, with 88 per cent of Democrats calling it wrong and 71 per cent of Republicans right. [cite:hz12b_pew_mar2026] Gallup's poll of 1–15 June put approval of the military action at about 34 to 35 per cent, lower than for most American military operations it had measured since the 1980s. [cite:hz12b_fox_gallup]

Where it stands, October 2026

As of October 2026 no agreement had formally ended the war. Fighting resumed when the ceasefire collapsed in July, American casualties were still being added in September, and the bill was rising by billions a month. [cite:ow7_wiki_ceasefire2026] [cite:hz12_intercept_cas] [cite:ow7_ap_cost2026] By mid-October the contest had moved largely to the sea: the United States was blockading Iran's ports, a blockade Central Command dated from 14 July, and Iran was attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz; Iran had offered a ceasefire in late September that Trump publicly rejected while talks continued through mediators, and Trump had announced that he would not launch new strikes on Iran until after the November midterm elections. [cite:hz12a_cbs_oct] On the other fronts, the Critical Threats Project and the Institute for the Study of War reported nothing significant from Iraq or Lebanon in late September, while the Houthis were fighting Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. [cite:hz10_ctp_sep26] In Lebanon, as Part Eight sets out, Hezbollah had not fired since mid-June while Israeli strikes in the south continued. [scene:hz8_now|Where things stand]

chapters.label: Part Thirteen
chapters.title: Settled, Contested and Open
chapters.intro: The last part takes the volume's findings in three groups, as the Hamas volume did: what the record settles about Hezbollah and the wars fought with it from 1978 to 2026, what it leaves in dispute between documented positions, with the basis of each side, and what is still open or cannot be known as of October 2026. It ends by setting the thesis this volume was written to test, that these armed groups serve as tools and excuses for continued war, military aid and American involvement, against the record, separating what the documents support, what they do not, and what remains argument.
chapters.outro: This volume followed Hezbollah from the confessional state and the PLO's war in the south, through the 1982 invasion in which it formed with Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the eighteen years of occupation, the wars of 2006, 2023–24 and 2026, and the other armed groups Iran supplies. [cite:hz1_wiki_pact] [cite:hz2_idf_lw1] [cite:hz2b_wilson_1500] [cite:hz5_wiki_war] [cite:hz7_aj_8oct] [cite:hz8_am_mar2] [cite:hz10_un_poe2024] Its record is of an armed movement with its own aims and its own crimes, fought by a state whose military budget alone is more than twice Lebanon's economy, in a cycle of attack, campaign and ceasefire that no round has ended. [cite:hz5b_hrw_civassault] [cite:hz6_almon_stl2022] [cite:hz9_sipri_2025] [cite:hz9_ifl_rdna] [cite:hz8_toi_text] The thesis that these groups serve as tools and excuses holds in its documented parts, Israel's own proxies and the threat written into aid law, and fails where it would need the threats to be invented or a war shown to be prolonged for money. [cite:hz4_crs_sla] [cite:ow_crs_aid2025] [scene:hz11_gains|Who gains] The same test run on Hamas reached a parallel answer in The Hamas Architecture [scene:hm10_settled|What the record settles] [scene:hm10_open|What is contested and open], and the American side of the relationship that pays for these wars is set out in The One-Way Mirror. [scene:ow14_settled|The One-Way Mirror: what the record settles] [scene:ow14_open|The One-Way Mirror: what is open]

sections.h: What the Record Settles
sections.html:
Before Hezbollah. Organised, armed Shia politics in Lebanon predates Israel's 1982 invasion and Iran's revolution: Musa al-Sadr founded the Movement of the Deprived in 1974 and its armed wing, Amal, in 1975. [cite:hz1_brit_amal] [cite:hz1_wiki_sadr] Iran's 1979 constitution committed the new state to "the continuation of the Revolution at home and abroad". [cite:hz1_iran_const] Israel paid and armed a Lebanese militia from the late 1970s: Saad Haddad said Israel had given about $10 million toward his men's salaries by 1982, and the Congressional Research Service later described the South Lebanon Army as a militia Israel "fully funded and equipped". [cite:hz1_csm_haddad] [cite:hz4_crs_sla] By the defence ministry's own 1999 affidavit, Shin Bet officers gave the militia's interrogators at Khiam "professional guidance and training". [cite:hz4_hrw_khiam99]

The founding. Israel invaded on 6 June 1982 with a stated aim of 40 kilometres and reached Beirut within a week; Lebanese police counted about 18,000 to 19,000 dead by the end of August, and Israel's Kahan Commission found Ariel Sharon personally responsible for ignoring the danger of the Sabra and Shatila killings. [cite:hz2_idf_lw1] [cite:hz2b_csm_dec82] [cite:hz2b_jvl_kahan] Iran's Revolutionary Guards, about 1,000 to 1,500 of them, set up in the Bekaa the same year. [cite:hz2b_wilson_1500] [cite:hz2b_pbs_1000] The Open Letter of February 1985 named Israel and the United States as enemies and Khomeini as the movement's authority. [cite:hz2_cep_letter] [cite:hz2_wiki_ideology] In 2016 Hassan Nasrallah said that everything Hezbollah "eats and drinks, its weapons and rockets, come from the Islamic Republic of Iran". [cite:hz6_alarabiya_2016]

The killing of civilians, by both sides. Hezbollah stated its rule in 1995: when Israel shelled its villages, "we will shell northern Palestine". [cite:hz4_hrw_pawns] Human Rights Watch found in 2006 that Hezbollah fired rockets "indiscriminately and at times deliberately" into Israeli towns, and that Israel treated south Lebanon "effectively as a free-fire zone"; at least 1,109 Lebanese were killed, the vast majority civilians, against 121 Israeli soldiers and 44 civilians. [cite:hz5b_hrw_civassault] [cite:hz5_hrw_why9] [cite:hz5_wiki_war] Israel fired up to four million cluster submunitions, about 90 percent of the strikes in the last 72 hours, and its own Winograd Commission found the use out of conformity with international law. [cite:hz5b_hrw_flooding] [cite:hz5_wiki_war] In 2008 the head of Northern Command said that what happened to the Dahieh would happen "in every village from which Israel is fired on". [cite:hz5_jps_khalidi]

Hezbollah's own conduct at home. It turned its guns on Beirut in May 2008 and came away with a cabinet veto; a UN-backed tribunal convicted three of its members over Rafik Hariri's killing, and Hezbollah never handed them over; it fought for Bashar al-Assad from 2013, in sieges the UN commission found unlawful. [cite:hz6_crs_2008] [cite:hz6_aje_2008tl] [cite:hz6_almon_stl2022] [cite:hz6b_coi2013]

The war of 2023–24 and after. Hezbollah opened fire on 8 October 2023 "in solidarity" with Gaza. [cite:hz7_aj_8oct] ACLED counted 11,238 Israeli attacks on Lebanon and 2,370 by Hezbollah and its allies in the first year. [cite:hz7_aj_acled_year] Lebanon's health ministry counted at least 4,047 dead by December 2024; an Israeli institute counted 45 Israeli civilians and 83 soldiers. [cite:hz7_olj_abiad_4047] [cite:hz7_alma_summary] Netanyahu acknowledged the pager operation. [cite:hz7_toi_netanyahu_pagers] The ceasefire text of 27 November 2024 bound both sides; Israel stayed on five hilltops after the deadline, and Hezbollah fired again on 2 March 2026, after which Israeli strikes killed 2,294 people in Lebanon in six weeks by the ministry's provisional count. [cite:hz8_toi_text] [cite:hz8_national_five] [cite:hz8_am_mar2] [cite:hz8_olj_toll]

The balance of power. Israel's 2025 military budget, $48.3 billion, was more than twice Lebanon's whole 2023 economy, and the United States provides $3.8 billion a year besides. [cite:hz9_sipri_2025] [cite:hz9_ifl_rdna] [cite:hm_dn_mou] Israel itself armed or backed groups across its borders, by its own officials' statements: rebels on the Golan, whom a former army chief acknowledged arming, and clans in Gaza, which Netanyahu said Israel had "activated". [cite:hz11_toi_eisenkot] [cite:hz11_ynet_clans]

What Is Contested

Whether Israel made Hezbollah. Ehud Barak's view that Israel's presence in Lebanon created Hezbollah is attested from July 2006, when the scholar Augustus Richard Norton paraphrased it on American radio; the widely quoted wording, "It was our presence there that created Hezbollah", could not be traced to its original interview, though in July 2026 Barak told the Associated Press that the occupation was "not serving Israeli security". [cite:hz3a_npr_norton] [cite:hz3a_ap_barak] [cite:hz3_statesman_barak] [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] Augustus Richard Norton named two causes, the occupation "and Iran". [cite:hz3_npr_norton] Shimon Shapira argues the decision was taken in Tehran before the invasion, and quotes Naim Qassem saying the invasion "was not the reason Hezbollah was founded". [cite:hz3_itic_shapira] Each side rests on documented facts; the conclusion each draws is a counterfactual and stays an argument.

Who bombed the barracks. A US judge found in 2003 that Hezbollah carried out the 1983 bombing on Iranian orders, and awarded about $2.66 billion in 2007. [cite:hz2_anderson] [cite:hz2_peterson07] Iran did not appear, so the judgments were entered by default; Iran called them "baseless" and "politically motivated", and Hezbollah, Iran and Syria deny any part. [cite:hz2_jurist_2007] [cite:hz2_wiki_barracks]

Buenos Aires. Argentina's Cassation Court ruled in April 2024 that Iran ordered the 1992 and 1994 bombings and Hezbollah carried them out. [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] The investigation's first judge was convicted of paying for false testimony, the accused have never appeared, and Iran's foreign ministry called the charges "Zionist propaganda". [cite:hz4_bat_cassation] [cite:hz4_aje_2006]

Qana, 1996. The UN's investigator found it "unlikely" that the shelling of the UN compound was the result of gross error; Israel said it was a chain of mistakes. [cite:hz4_un_qana]

Majdal Shams. Israel and the United States attributed the rocket that killed twelve children on 27 July 2024 to Hezbollah, and Human Rights Watch found the damage consistent with a Falaq-type rocket; Hezbollah said it had "no connection to this incident" and blamed an Israeli interceptor, and no independent international investigation has reported. [cite:hz7_wiki_majdal] [cite:hz7_aj_majdal]

The pagers. UN experts and Human Rights Watch called the detonations unlawful booby-traps; military lawyers called them precise sabotage of military equipment. No court has ruled. [cite:hz7_ohchr_experts] [cite:hz7_npr_law]

Hezbollah's strength. Pre-war estimates of its rockets ran from 75,000 to 200,000; Israel's claims to have destroyed 70 to 90 percent were followed in April 2026 by its northern commander's admission of a "gap". [cite:hz9_usip_arsenal] [cite:hz9a_jpost_8590] [cite:hz9_toi_milo] Estimates of Iran's money range from $100 million to $1 billion a year; the most cited, $700 million, came in 2018 from US officials running a pressure campaign. [cite:hz6_wilson_record] [cite:hz9_wiki_irfund] [cite:hz6_icg_crt2018]

The truce counts. UNIFIL recorded about 7,800 Israeli air violations in the first year; Lebanon counted 331 dead, the UN verified 127 civilians, and the Israeli army said it killed more than 370 members of armed groups, which it called enforcement, not breach. The counts cannot all be complete on the same basis. [cite:hz8_un_unifil_year] [cite:hz8_aa_tabatabai] [cite:hz8_ohchr_nov25] [cite:hz8_idf_year]

Who pushed the 2026 war. Netanyahu argued for striking Iran for years, and reporting this book could not independently confirm says he lobbied for the February 2026 strike; the order was Trump's, on the stated ground of "imminent threats", while the IAEA had no evidence enrichment had resumed and in the week after the strikes 55 percent of registered voters told Quinnipiac that Iran had not posed an imminent military threat. [cite:hz12_cato_hoffman] [cite:hz8_wiki_iranwar] [cite:ow7_npr_epicfury] [cite:hz12_qu_mar2026] Which man's will was decisive is argument.

sections.h: What Remains Open
sections.html:
The 2026 war.
